title: 1.01  What a Web API Is
body: Programs talking to programs - what an API is, how web APIs use HTTP, resources and endpoints in the REST style, the other styles you will meet (GraphQL, RPC, WebSockets), and what calling one from Python looks like with urllib and requests. Programs as users An API (application programming interface) is a way for one program to use another. You have used many already: the Python standard library is an API, and so is the Windows API. A web API is one you reach over the network, with HTTP: weather services, payment providers, chat platforms, your own server. The program offering it is the server ; yours is the client . What makes web APIs special is that the two sides share nothing but messages. They may be written in different languages, run on different continents, and be upgraded at different times. Everything you need to know must be in the request you send, the response you get, and the documentation . Resources and endpoints Most web APIs follow the REST style: the server exposes resources (users, orders, messages) at URLs , and you act on them with HTTP methods : Method Meaning Example --- --- --- GET read GET /books/42 gives book 42 POST create (or run an action) POST /books with a new book in the body PUT replace PUT /books/42 with the whole new book PATCH change some fields PATCH /books/42 with {"title": "..."} DELETE remove DELETE /books/42 A method and a path pattern together are an endpoint : GET /books/{id} . The documentation lists the endpoints, what each accepts and what it returns. The data travels as JSON almost everywhere (lesson 1.03). Other styles Style Idea You will notice --- --- --- REST resources at URLs, HTTP methods many endpoints, simple requests GraphQL one endpoint; the client sends a query naming exactly the fields it wants always POST /graphql , errors inside a 200 response RPC (JSON-RPC, gRPC) call named procedures POST /rpc with {"method": "getBook", "params": ...} ; gRPC uses binary messages WebSockets, server-sent events a connection that stays open for live updates messages arrive without a request Webhooks the server calls you when something happens milestone 4 The ideas in this course (requests, errors, authentication, paging, retries) apply to all of them. A first call From Python, the standard library can make requests with urllib.request ; most people install the friendlier requests package ( pip install requests ). The same call both ways: python-norun import json import urllib.request with urllib.request.urlopen("https://api.example.com/books/42", timeout=10) as response: book = json.load(response) print(book "title" ) python-norun import requests response = requests.get("https://api.example.com/books/42", timeout=10) response.raise_for_status() an exception for 4xx and 5xx statuses book = response.json() print(book "title" ) The practice in this course cannot reach the internet, so it uses small fake servers that behave like real ones, including all the ways real ones fail. That is also how professional code is tested: a client that takes its transport (the thing that actually sends requests) as a parameter can be tested without a network, and pointed at the real service in production. Check yourself quiz ? What is an endpoint? - Any URL on the API's host, whatever method you use - The base URL that every request starts with + A method and a path pattern together, such as GET /books/{id} - The JSON document the server sends back An endpoint pairs a method with a path pattern: GET /books/{id} and DELETE /books/{id} are two endpoints on the same path. ? Which method changes only some fields of a resource? + PATCH - PUT - POST - GET PATCH sends just the fields to change. PUT replaces the whole resource with what you send. ? In GraphQL, how do you usually learn that a request failed? - From a 4xx or 5xx status code, as with REST - From a Retry-After header on the response - The connection is closed without any response + From an errors list in the response body, often with status 200 GraphQL usually answers with 200 and reports problems in an errors list, so checking the status alone is not enough. ? Why pass the transport into a client instead of calling the network directly? - Because the standard library cannot make HTTP requests itself + So tests can swap in a fake transport and script every failure - So the client runs faster by skipping the network stack - So the client can switch between JSON and XML bodies A client that takes its transport as a parameter can be given a fake in tests, scripted to fail in every way a real server can, and the real one in production.

title: Matching endpoints
body: An API's reference lists its endpoints as a method and a path pattern (lesson 1.01). Write the matching a server does with them, which is also how you check you have understood an endpoint list: python class Router: def add(self, method, template, name): ... def match(self, method, path): ... returns (status, name, params) - add registers an endpoint such as add("GET", "/books/{id}", "get_book") . A template is made of segments separated by / ; a segment written {name} is a path parameter that matches any one non-empty segment. - match splits path the same way and finds the first registered template, in the order added, with the same number of segments where every fixed segment is equal and every parameter segment is non-empty: - if one is found for this method , return (200, name, params) , with params a dict of the parameter values unescaped with urllib.parse.unquote (so a%2Fb becomes a/b ); - if templates match the path but none for this method , return (405, None, {}) ; - if nothing matches the path, return (404, None, {}) . - Methods are compared ignoring case. A trailing / on the path is ignored ( /books/ is /books ), and so is any query string after ? .

title: 1.02  Requests and Responses
body: The parts of an HTTP request and response as an API client sees them - method, URL with path and query, headers such as Content-Type, Accept and Authorization, the body, status codes and their families, response headers worth reading, and timeouts. The request Every call you make is an HTTP request with four parts: text POST /v1/books?notify=true HTTP/1.1 Host: api.example.com Content-Type: application/json Accept: application/json Authorization: Bearer abc123 {"title": "Dune", "year": 1965} - The method and the URL : scheme and host ( https://api.example.com ), path ( /v1/books ) and query string ( ?notify=true ), name-value pairs after the ? , separated by & . - Headers : metadata. Content-Type says what the body is; Accept says what you want back; Authorization carries your credentials (milestone 2); User-Agent names your program; Idempotency-Key (milestone 3) makes a retry safe. - The body : the data you send, for POST , PUT and PATCH . For JSON APIs, a JSON document. The response text HTTP/1.1 201 Created Content-Type: application/json Location: /v1/books/77 X-Request-Id: 9f2c1e {"id": 77, "title": "Dune", "year": 1965} The status code is the first thing to check. Its first digit is its family: Family Meaning Common codes --- --- --- 2xx success 200 OK, 201 Created, 202 Accepted, 204 No Content 3xx go elsewhere 301 Moved Permanently, 304 Not Modified (lesson 3.05) 4xx your request is wrong 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict, 422 Unprocessable, 429 Too Many Requests 5xx the server failed 500 Internal Server Error, 502 Bad Gateway, 503 Service Unavailable, 504 Gateway Timeout The distinction between 4xx and 5xx drives your error handling: repeating a 4xx request unchanged gives the same error (fix the request), while a 5xx or a 429 may succeed if you retry later (milestone 3). Response headers worth reading: Content-Type (is it really JSON?), Location (where a created resource lives), Retry-After (how long to wait), ETag (lesson 3.05), rate-limit headers, and a request id such as X-Request-Id , which you should log: it is what the API's support team asks for. Error bodies Most APIs also put details of an error in the body, often in a documented shape: json {"error": {"code": "invalid_year", "message": "year must be between 0 and 2100", "field": "year"}} Your client should surface the status, the API's error code and message, and the request id, rather than a bare "request failed". Timeouts A request without a timeout can hang forever if the server or network stalls. Always pass one: urlopen(url, timeout=10) or requests.get(url, timeout=(3, 10)) (connect and read timeouts). Choose it from what your program can afford to wait, and treat a timeout like a 5xx: maybe retry, maybe give up. Check yourself quiz ? A request fails with 422. Should you retry it unchanged? - Yes, after a short wait it will probably succeed + No: a 4xx means the request itself is wrong, so fix it first - Yes, but only once, with a longer timeout - No, because 422 means the server is down Repeating a 4xx request unchanged gives the same error. A 5xx or a 429 is the kind that may succeed later. ? Which header tells the server what format your body is in? - Accept - Authorization + Content-Type - User-Agent Content-Type describes the body you send. Accept says what format you want back. ? What does 204 No Content mean for your code? - The request failed and should be retried - The resource was not found - The response body is JSON but empty, so json.loads returns None + Success with no body: do not try to parse JSON from it 204 is a success that carries no body. Parsing the empty text as JSON raises an error. ? Why log the response's request id? + The provider can find that exact request in their logs - It is needed to send the same request again - It proves the response was not tampered with - It tells you how long to wait before retrying A request id such as X-Request-Id is what the provider's support team asks for: it points them to that one request.

title: Understanding a response
body: Write the function every client needs first: one that looks at a raw response and says what happened (lesson 1.02). python def describe_response(status, headers, body): ... headers is a dict whose names may be in any case; body is text. Return a dict with: Key Value --- --- family "informational" (1xx), "success" (2xx), "redirect" (3xx), "client error" (4xx) or "server error" (5xx) retryable true for 408, 429, 500, 502, 503 and 504; false otherwise request_id the X-Request-Id header's value, found ignoring the case of the name; None if absent data the parsed JSON body, if the Content-Type header's media type is application/json (ignoring case and anything after ; , such as ; charset=utf-8 ) and the body is not empty; otherwise None message for 4xx and 5xx: the JSON body's error.message if it is a string; otherwise the text "HTTP <status " . For other statuses, None A JSON content type with a body that does not parse is an error in the response: raise ValueError .

title: 1.03  JSON in Python
body: The JSON format and how Python's json module maps it to dicts, lists, strings, numbers, True, False and None - parsing and producing text, what happens with errors, numbers and Unicode, and checking that a document from an API has the shape your code expects. The format JSON (JavaScript Object Notation, RFC 8259) is the language of web APIs. It has six kinds of value: JSON Example Python after json.loads --- --- --- object {"id": 7, "tags": } dict array 1, 2, 3 list string "Dune" str number 42 , -1.5 , 2e3 int (no fraction or exponent) or float true / false true True / False null null None Strings use double quotes only; object keys are always strings; there are no comments and no trailing commas. Reading and writing python import json text = '{"id": 7, "title": "Dune", "price": 9.5, "tags": "sf" , "sequel": null}' book = json.loads(text) text - Python objects print(book "title" , book "price" 2, book "sequel" is None) book "year" = 1965 print(json.dumps(book)) Python objects - text print(json.dumps({"b": 1, "a": True, None }, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"))) Dune 19.0 True {"id": 7, "title": "Dune", "price": 9.5, "tags": "sf" , "sequel": null, "year": 1965} {"a": true,null ,"b":1} - json.load(f) and json.dump(obj, f) work with files and responses directly. - indent=2 makes readable output; sort_keys=True and compact separators make output canonical , which matters when you sign it (lesson 2.04). - ensure_ascii=False keeps non-ASCII characters readable instead of é escapes. When parsing fails Invalid text raises json.JSONDecodeError (a ValueError ) with the position of the problem: python import json try: json.loads('{"id": 7,}') except json.JSONDecodeError as e: print("bad JSON at line", e.lineno, "column", e.colno, "-", e.msg) bad JSON at line 1 column 9 - Illegal trailing comma before end of object An API that is failing badly may return an HTML error page with status 502 instead of JSON. Check the status (and ideally the Content-Type ) before parsing, and catch the decode error, so that your message says "the server returned HTML with 502" rather than a confusing parse error. Numbers and other surprises - Python's json keeps integers exact however large; other languages (JavaScript) lose precision above 2⁵³, which is why some APIs send big ids as strings . Read the documentation. - Money is often sent as an integer number of the smallest unit (cents) or as a string, to avoid float rounding. - Dates are not a JSON type: they arrive as strings, usually ISO 8601 ( "2026-11-19T08:30:00Z" ), or as numbers of seconds since 1970 (lesson 5.02). - json.dumps refuses some Python values ( datetime , set , bytes ) with TypeError ; convert them yourself first. Checking the shape Code like book "author" "name" crashes with KeyError or TypeError the day the API returns something slightly different: an author that is null , a missing field, a number sent as a string. At the boundary where data enters your program, check it, and turn it into your own types: python-norun def parse_book(data): if not isinstance(data, dict): raise ValueError("book: expected an object") title = data.get("title") if not isinstance(title, str) or not title: raise ValueError("book.title: expected a non-empty string") year = data.get("year") if year is not None and (not isinstance(year, int) or isinstance(year, bool)): raise ValueError("book.year: expected an integer or null") return Book(title=title, year=year) ( isinstance(True, int) is true in Python, hence the extra bool check.) Libraries such as pydantic do this from a declared model; the idea is the same. Check yourself quiz ? What does json.loads(" 1, 2.0, null ") return? - 1, 2, None + 1, 2.0, None - 1.0, 2.0, None - 1, 2.0, "null" A number with a fraction becomes a float , one without becomes an int , and null becomes None . ? Why might an API send an id as "9007199254740993" instead of a number? - JSON numbers cannot have more than 15 digits - Strings are faster to parse than numbers + Some languages cannot hold such large integers exactly - Ids must always be strings in JSON JavaScript and others lose precision above 2⁵³. Python's json keeps big integers exact, but the API is written for every client. ? What should you check before parsing a response as JSON? - Only that the body is not empty - That the request id header is present - Nothing: catching the decode error is enough + The status code, and ideally that the Content-Type is JSON A failing server may send an HTML page with 502. Checking the status and type first gives a clear error instead of a confusing parse error. ? Why is isinstance(value, int) not enough to check for a JSON integer? - JSON integers become float in Python + True and False are also instances of int in Python - Large integers become strings in Python - None is also an instance of int in Python bool is a subclass of int , so a JSON true would pass. Check isinstance(value, bool) as well.

title: Checking a JSON document
body: Data from an API should be checked where it enters your program (lesson 1.03). Write the check for a book, and the canonical form you would send back. python def parse_book(text): ... def to_canonical_json(book): ... parse_book takes JSON text and returns a dict with exactly the keys id , title , year , tags and price . It raises ValueError with a message starting with the field's path when anything is wrong: Field Rule Message starts with --- --- --- the text valid JSON book: invalid JSON the document an object book: expected an object id required; an integer (not a boolean), at least 1 book.id title required; a string, not empty after stripping spaces; returned stripped book.title year optional; missing or null gives None ; else an integer (not a boolean) book.year tags optional; missing gives ; else a list of strings book.tags price optional; missing or null gives None ; else a number (integer or float, not a boolean), not negative book.price Other keys in the document are ignored. to_canonical_json returns the JSON text for a book dict with keys sorted, no spaces ( separators=(",", ":") ) and non-ASCII characters kept as they are, so that the same book always gives exactly the same text.

title: 1.04  Reading an API Reference
body: Getting everything you need from a web API's documentation - base URL and versions, the endpoint list, path and query parameters, request and response bodies, error codes, authentication and limits - and the OpenAPI description many APIs publish, which you can read and even generate clients from. What the reference must tell you Before writing code against a web API, collect these from its documentation (the Reading Documentation course is about doing this precisely): Question Where it usually is --- --- Base URL, and per region or sandbox? "Getting started", "Environments" How do I authenticate? "Authentication" (milestone 2) Which version, and how is it chosen? "Versioning": in the path ( /v2/ ), a header, or a date What endpoints exist? the reference, one page per endpoint What may I send, what will I get? each endpoint's parameters, request body and response schemas How do errors look? "Errors": status codes and the error body shape How much may I call? "Rate limits" (lesson 3.02) How do lists work? "Pagination" (lesson 3.01) What changed? "Changelog" A sandbox or test mode environment, if the API has one, is where you develop: same API, fake money, fake messages. One endpoint, read fully A typical endpoint page, summarised: Create a book - POST /v1/books Body (JSON): title string, required, 1 to 200 characters; year integer, optional; tags array of strings, optional, at most 10. Query : notify boolean, default false . Responses : 201 the created book, with a Location header; 400 invalid JSON; 409 a book with that ISBN exists; 422 a field fails validation, with error.field naming it. From that alone you know which fields to send, which to check, and four outcomes your code must handle differently. Kinds of parameter you will see: - Path parameters are part of the path: GET /books/{id} . They must be escaped (lesson 1.05): an id of a/b must not create a new path segment. - Query parameters filter or shape results: GET /books?author=Herbert&limit=20 . - Header parameters: authentication, versions, idempotency keys. - Body fields, described by a schema with types, required fields and limits. OpenAPI Many APIs publish their reference as an OpenAPI document (formerly Swagger): a YAML or JSON file describing every endpoint, parameter and schema. The pretty documentation pages are often generated from it. An excerpt: text paths: /books/{id}: get: parameters: - name: id in: path required: true schema: { type: integer } responses: "200": content: application/json: schema: { $ref: " /components/schemas/Book" } "404": description: no such book Because it is machine-readable, tools can generate client code, mock servers and request validators from it, and you can search it for facts the prose pages leave out. When the pretty page and the OpenAPI file disagree, check against the live sandbox (lesson 5.03 of Reading Documentation). Versions and deprecation APIs change while your code runs. Read how the provider versions it: a new path ( /v2/ ), a header ( Accept: application/vnd.example.v2+json ), or a dated version you choose per request ( Api-Version: 2026-10-01 ). Pin the version explicitly, read the changelog before moving, and watch for deprecation notices, sometimes sent as a Deprecation or Sunset response header. Check yourself quiz ? Where do you send a parameter documented as in: path ? - In the query string, after the ? - In a request header of the same name + Inside the URL path, in place of its {name} , escaped - As a field in the JSON body A path parameter replaces its {name} in the path, such as /books/{id} , and must be escaped so it stays one segment. ? An endpoint documents 409 and 422 responses. Why handle them differently? + 409 is a conflict with existing data, such as a duplicate; 422 is invalid data; the fixes differ - 409 is a server error to retry; 422 is a client error to fix - 409 means the rate limit was hit; 422 means the token expired - They mean the same thing, so one handler is enough Both are 4xx, but a conflict needs a different reaction (find the existing record) from a field that fails validation (fix the data). ? What is an OpenAPI document good for besides reading? - Making the API's requests faster at run time - Replacing authentication with a published schema - Encrypting the traffic between client and server + Generating clients, mock servers and validators Because it is machine-readable, tools can generate code and mock servers from it, and you can search it for facts the prose pages leave out. ? Why pin an API version explicitly? - Because unpinned requests are rejected with 400 + So a new default version cannot change your program's behaviour - Because pinned versions are billed at a lower price - So that the provider can never deprecate your version If you rely on the default, a provider upgrade can change responses under your running code. Pin it and move deliberately after reading the changelog.

title: A request from an endpoint description
match: A request from an endpoint description
body: API references are often generated from OpenAPI descriptions (lesson 1.04). Here an endpoint is described by a small dict in the same spirit: python spec = { "method": "GET", "path": "/libraries/{library}/books/{id}", "parameters": {"name": "library", "in": "path", "required": True}, {"name": "id", "in": "path", "required": True}, {"name": "fields", "in": "query", "required": False}, {"name": "include_deleted", "in": "query", "required": False}, {"name": "Api-Version", "in": "header", "required": True}, , } Write the function that turns such a description and some arguments into the request to send: python def build_request(spec, args): ... returns (method, target, headers) - method is the spec's method. target is the path with each {name} replaced by its argument converted to text and escaped with quote(value, safe="") , followed by the query string, if any. headers is a dict of the header parameters. - Query parameters appear in the order of the parameters list, only if given and not None , encoded with urlencode . A list value repeats the parameter ( fields=a&fields=b ); booleans become true and false ; other values are converted with str . - Header and path values are converted with str (booleans also become true and false ). - Raise ValueError if a required parameter is missing or None , or if args contains a name the spec does not describe.

title: 1.05  Building URLs and Clients Safely
body: Building requests that do not break on unusual input - escaping path segments and query values with urllib.parse, why string concatenation goes wrong, lists and booleans in query strings - and structuring a small API client around an injectable transport with one place for errors. Never paste values into URLs Building a URL with string formatting works until a value contains a special character: python-norun url = f"https://api.example.com/users/{name}/books?q={query}" name = "a/b" - /users/a/b/books: a different path query = "x&admin=1" - an extra parameter you did not mean to send query = "café 50%" - invalid characters in a URL That is a bug at best and a security hole at worst. urllib.parse escapes values correctly: python from urllib.parse import quote, urlencode name = "a/b c" query = {"q": "café & more", "limit": 20, "tags": "sf", "classic" } path = "/users/" + quote(name, safe="") + "/books" print(path) print(urlencode(query)) print(urlencode(query, doseq=True)) /users/a%2Fb%20c/books q=caf%C3%A9+%26+more&limit=20&tags=%5B%27sf%27%2C+%27classic%27%5D q=caf%C3%A9+%26+more&limit=20&tags=sf&tags=classic - quote(value, safe="") escapes everything that is not a letter, digit or one of _.-~ , including / . (Its default safe="/" keeps slashes, which is right for a whole path and wrong for one segment.) - urlencode builds a query string, encoding text as UTF-8. Spaces become + in queries, %20 in paths: both are correct in their place. - A list becomes its Python text unless you pass doseq=True , which repeats the key. Some APIs want tags=sf,classic instead: the documentation says which. - Booleans become True and False , which many APIs do not accept: convert to "true" and "false" yourself. - Leave out parameters whose value is None rather than sending None . A client with one door Small API clients stay manageable when every request goes through one method that knows the base URL, the headers, the timeout and how to turn errors into exceptions. Everything else calls it: python-norun class ApiError(Exception): def __init__(self, status, code, message, request_id): super().__init__(f"{status} {code}: {message} (request {request_id})") self.status, self.code, self.request_id = status, code, request_id class BooksClient: def __init__(self, transport, base_url, timeout=10): self.transport = transport anything with .send(method, url, headers, body, timeout) self.base_url = base_url.rstrip("/") self.timeout = timeout def request(self, method, path, query=None, body=None): url = self.base_url + path if query: url += "?" + urlencode({k: v for k, v in query.items() if v is not None}, doseq=True) headers = {"Accept": "application/json"} data = None if body is not None: headers "Content-Type" = "application/json" data = json.dumps(body).encode() status, resp_headers, raw = self.transport.send(method, url, headers, data, self.timeout) payload = json.loads(raw) if raw else None if status = 400: error = (payload or {}).get("error", {}) raise ApiError(status, error.get("code"), error.get("message"), resp_headers.get("X-Request-Id")) return payload def get_book(self, book_id): return self.request("GET", "/books/" + quote(str(book_id), safe="")) The transport is the only part that touches the network. In production it wraps urllib.request or a requests.Session (which also reuses connections); in tests it is a fake that records what was sent and returns scripted responses. The practice in this milestone builds exactly this, piece by piece. Check yourself quiz ? What does quote("a/b", safe="") return, and why use safe="" for a path segment? - a/b : slashes are always safe in URLs + a%2Fb : the slash must be escaped so the value stays one segment - a%2Fb : so the URL is shorter - a+b : so spaces and slashes are encoded the same way With the default safe="/" the slash would survive and split the value into two path segments. ? How should a None query value be handled? - Send it as q=None - Send it as q=null - Send it as an empty q= + Leave the parameter out urlencode would send the text None , which the API reads as a real value. Leave the parameter out instead. ? What does urlencode({"t": "a", "b" }, doseq=True) produce? - t=a,b + t=a&t=b - t=%5B%27a%27%2C+%27b%27%5D - t =a&t =b doseq=True repeats the key for each item. Without it the list is sent as its Python text, escaped. ? Why route every call through one request method? - Python allows only one network call per object - It makes each request use less bandwidth on the wire + Headers, timeouts and errors are handled in one place - It lets requests run in parallel automatically One door means one place to get escaping, headers, timeouts and errors right, and one place to plug in a fake transport.

title: Building URLs safely
body: Write the URL builder from lesson 1.05, so that no value can change the shape of the URL: python def build_url(base, segments, query=None): ... - base is the API's base URL, with or without a trailing / . - segments is a list of path segments; each is converted to text and escaped with quote(..., safe="") , then they are joined with / after the base. - query is an optional dict. Entries whose value is None are left out; True and False become true and false ; a list or tuple repeats the key; anything else is converted with str . The query string is built with urlencode in the dict's order, and added after ? only if something is left. python build_url("https://api.example.com/v1/", "users", "a/b", "books" , {"q": "café", "limit": None, "tags": "x", "y" }) "https://api.example.com/v1/users/a%2Fb/books?q=caf%C3%A9&tags=x&tags=y"

title: A safe URL builder
body: Build request URLs without breaking them with spaces or symbols. build("https://api.example.com", "/search", q="café & tea", page=2) - https://api.example.com/search?q=caf%C3%A9+%26+tea&page=2 build("https://api.example.com/", "users/ada lovelace") - https://api.example.com/users/ada%20lovelace

title: Reading a raw response
body: Take apart an HTTP response written as text. status 200 (OK) content-type: application/json 3 headers body: {'id': 7, 'name': 'Ada'}

title: What does that status mean?
body: Turn status codes into advice for a client. 200 OK success 201 Created success 304 Not Modified use your cached copy 400 Bad Request fix the request; do not retry 401 Unauthorized sign in again 404 Not Found stop: the thing is not there 429 Too Many Requests wait (Retry-After: 30 s), then retry 503 Service Unavailable retry later with backoff

title: A JSON explorer
body: Print every value in a nested JSON document with its path. user.name = "Ada" user.langs 0 = "Python" user.langs 1 = "C" user.address.city = "London" active = true

title: A small API client
body: Build a client for a books API, structured as lesson 1.05 suggests: one request method that every call goes through, and a transport passed in from outside. The tests pass a fake transport that records each request and returns scripted responses, including the failures a real service produces. The transport has one method: python-norun transport.send(method, url, headers, body, timeout) - (status, headers, body) body is bytes or None on the way out; the response's headers is a dict (names in any case) and its body is bytes . python-norun class ApiError(Exception): attributes: status, code, message, request_id class BooksClient: def __init__(self, transport, base_url, api_key, timeout=10): ... def request(self, method, path, query=None, body=None): ... def list_books(self, author=None, limit=None): ... def get_book(self, book_id): ... def create_book(self, title, year=None): ... def delete_book(self, book_id): ... request builds and sends one request and interprets the response: - The URL is the base URL (without a trailing / ) followed by path , and, if query has any entries that are not None , ? and the query encoded with urlencode (booleans as true / false ). - Headers: always Accept: application/json and Authorization: Bearer <api_key ; with a body, also Content-Type: application/json , and the body is the JSON text encoded as UTF-8. - The timeout given to the constructor is passed to the transport. - A 2xx response returns the parsed JSON body, or None when the body is empty. - Any other status raises ApiError with: status ; code and message from the JSON body's error object when the response's content type is JSON and they are present (otherwise code is None and message is "HTTP <status " ); and request_id from the X-Request-Id header (any case), or None . - A 2xx response whose JSON content cannot be parsed raises ApiError with that status, code "invalid_json" and message "the response was not valid JSON" . The endpoints: Method Request Returns --- --- --- list_books(author, limit) GET /books?author=...&limit=... (each only when not None ) the items list of the response get_book(book_id) GET /books/<id , the id escaped as one path segment the book, or None if the API answers 404 create_book(title, year) POST /books with {"title": ...} , plus "year" only when it is not None the created book delete_book(book_id) DELETE /books/<id True ; and False if the API answers 404

title: 2.01  API Keys and Where Secrets Belong
match: 2.01 API Keys and Where Secrets Belong
body: The simplest way APIs identify a caller - the API key - how to send it, why never in the URL, where secrets live (environment variables, untracked files, secret managers, never in code), keeping keys narrow in what they can do, and what to do the day one leaks. Who is calling? Almost every API needs to know who is calling: to bill them, to limit them, to decide what they may see. The simplest answer is an API key : a long random string the provider gives you, which you send with every request. python-norun headers = {"Authorization": "Bearer sk_live_51Hx...", "Accept": "application/json"} or, depending on the API: headers = {"X-Api-Key": "sk_live_51Hx..."} The documentation says which header. Some old APIs accept the key in the query string ( ?api_key=... ): avoid that whenever there is a choice. URLs end up in server logs, proxy logs, browser history and error reports; headers usually do not. A key is a password Anyone who has the key is you, as far as the API knows. So: - Never put it in code. Code is committed, shared, pasted into questions, and published. Keys pushed to a public repository are found by automated scanners within minutes. - Read it from the environment , or a configuration file that is not tracked by git (add it to .gitignore ), or a secret manager (Windows Credential Manager, macOS Keychain, cloud secret stores) in production. - Fail clearly when it is missing, without printing it when it is present. python-norun import os api_key = os.environ.get("BOOKS_API_KEY", "").strip() if not api_key: raise SystemExit("Set the BOOKS_API_KEY environment variable (see README).") On Windows, set it for the current terminal with set BOOKS_API_KEY=... (cmd) or $env:BOOKS_API_KEY="..." (PowerShell); .env files loaded by a library such as python-dotenv are a common convenience for development, and they too stay out of git. Narrow keys Most providers let you create several keys with different powers. Use that: - Test and live keys separately ( sk_test_... and sk_live_... are a common naming): development never touches real data. - Restricted keys with only the permissions the program needs: a reporting script gets read-only access. - One key per program or server , so one can be revoked without breaking the others, and logs show which one did what. When a key leaks It will happen eventually: a commit, a screenshot, a log file. The response is always the same: 1. Revoke (or "roll") the key at the provider immediately. Deleting the commit is not enough: it is already copied. 2. Create a new key and put it where your programs read it. 3. Check the provider's logs for use you did not make. 4. Find how it leaked and close that path (lesson 2.05). Check yourself quiz ? Why prefer a header to a query parameter for an API key? - Headers are encrypted and query strings are not - Query strings cannot hold long values + URLs are recorded in many logs and histories; headers usually are not - APIs reject keys sent in the query string Both travel over the same HTTPS connection; the difference is that URLs end up in server logs, proxy logs, browser history and error reports. ? Where should a development key live? + In an environment variable or an untracked local file, never in the code - In a constant at the top of the module, so it is easy to change - In a comment in the README, so teammates can find it - In the code, as long as the repository is private Code gets committed, shared and published. Read the key from the environment or a file listed in .gitignore . ? A key was committed and the commit was deleted an hour later. Is it safe? - Yes, deleting the commit removes it from the history - Yes, if the repository was private - Only if nobody cloned the repository in that hour + No: revoke it and make a new one; it may already have been copied Scanners find pushed keys within minutes, and a deleted commit may already be copied. Revoking is the only safe answer. ? Why create a separate restricted key for a reporting script? - Restricted keys never expire, so it needs no rotation - Restricted keys are not subject to rate limits + A leak can only read, and revoking it breaks nothing else - The provider requires one key per programming language A narrow key limits the damage of a leak, and one key per program means revoking it breaks nothing else.

title: Settings that keep their secret
where: 2.01 API Keys and Where Secrets Belong
body: Load an API client's settings from the environment, failing clearly without ever showing the key (lesson 2.01). python class Settings: def __init__(self, api_key, base_url, timeout): ... def __repr__(self): ... def mask(secret): ... def load_settings(env): ... env is a dict of environment variables (the real program passes os.environ ). - BOOKS_API_KEY is required. Spaces around it are removed; it must then be at least 8 characters with no whitespace inside. Otherwise raise ValueError("BOOKS_API_KEY is not set") when it is missing or empty, and ValueError("BOOKS_API_KEY is not valid") otherwise. No error message may contain the key's value. - BOOKS_BASE_URL defaults to https://api.example.com/v1 . It must start with https:// (otherwise ValueError("BOOKS_BASE_URL must use https") ); a trailing / is removed. - BOOKS_TIMEOUT defaults to 10. It must be a whole number from 1 to 120 written in digits (otherwise ValueError("BOOKS_TIMEOUT must be a whole number from 1 to 120") ). - mask returns followed by the last 4 characters, or just for a secret shorter than 8 characters. - repr of a Settings is Settings(base_url='<url ', timeout=<n , api_key='<masked key ') .

title: 2.02  Bearer Tokens and Expiry
body: Access tokens that expire - the Authorization Bearer header, expires_in and computing when to renew with a safety margin, refresh tokens, retrying once after a 401, caching a token across calls, and what a JWT is and why a client should not trust what it reads in one. Tokens instead of keys Many APIs do not want your long-lived secret on every request. Instead you exchange credentials for an access token that works for a short time, often an hour, and send that: text Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9... "Bearer" means whoever holds (bears) the token may use it, so it is still a secret, just a short-lived one. A token endpoint typically answers: json {"access_token": "eyJ...", "token_type": "Bearer", "expires_in": 3600, "refresh_token": "def50200..."} expires_in is in seconds from now . Record the time you received it, and renew a little before it runs out: clocks differ, and a request sent one second before expiry may arrive one second after. A margin of 30 to 60 seconds is usual: python-norun self.token = data "access_token" self.expires_at = clock() + data "expires_in" def valid(self, clock, margin=30): return self.token is not None and clock() < self.expires_at - margin Caching Getting a token costs a request (and some token endpoints are rate-limited strictly), so keep it and reuse it until it is due for renewal. One token per credentials, shared by every request the program makes. Practice 2.02 builds this cache with a fake clock, which is how you test time-dependent code without waiting. When the API says 401 Even a "valid" token can be rejected: revoked, the server's clock disagrees, the key was rotated. The standard reaction to 401 Unauthorized : 1. Throw away the cached token. 2. Get a new one. 3. Repeat the request once . 4. If it fails again, report the error: the credentials themselves are wrong, and looping would only hammer the server. A 403 Forbidden is different: you are authenticated but not allowed. A new token will not help. Refresh tokens With OAuth (next lesson), the token response may include a refresh token : a long-lived secret used only at the token endpoint to get new access tokens without asking the user to sign in again. Store it like a password. Some providers issue a new refresh token on each use and invalidate the old one ("rotation"): always save the one you got last. JWTs Access tokens often look like xxxxx.yyyyy.zzzzz : a JWT (JSON Web Token), three base64url parts: a header, a payload of claims ( sub who, exp expiry time, scope ), and a signature. You can decode the middle part and read it: python import base64, json token = "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJzdWIiOiJ1c2VyNDIiLCJleHAiOjE3OTM1MjM2MDB9.c2ln" payload = token.split(".") 1 payload += "=" (-len(payload) % 4) restore the padding base64url drops print(json.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(payload))) {'sub': 'user42', 'exp': 1793523600} Reading it is fine for debugging. But a client must not make decisions from claims it has not verified: verifying the signature needs the issuer's keys, and that is the server's job. Treat the access token as an opaque string, and use expires_in from the token response for timing. Check yourself quiz ? A token response says expires_in: 3600 and arrived at time 1000. With a 30-second margin, when should you renew? - At time 3570 - At time 4600 + At time 4570 - At time 4630 expires_in counts seconds from when it arrived: 1000 + 3600 = 4600 is the expiry, and the margin brings renewal 30 seconds earlier. ? What should a client do after a 401 with a cached token? - Retry the same request until it succeeds + Discard the token, get a new one, and retry the request once - Give up immediately: 401 always means the credentials are wrong - Wait for the token's exp time, then retry The cached token may have been revoked or rotated. One retry with a fresh token fixes that; failing again means the credentials themselves are wrong. ? Does a new token help after a 403? - Yes: 403 means the token has expired - Yes, if you also wait for Retry-After + No: 403 means you are known but not allowed - No: 403 means the server is down 401 is "who are you?"; 403 is "I know who you are, and you may not". A new token carries the same identity. ? Why should a client not trust the exp it decodes from a JWT? + It has not verified the token's signature - The exp claim is encrypted and cannot be decoded - exp is in milliseconds, not seconds - JWTs do not contain an expiry time Anyone can decode the payload, but only the issuer's keys can verify it. Treat the token as opaque and time it from expires_in .

title: A token cache
body: Cache an access token until shortly before it expires, and recover once from a 401 (lesson 2.02). Time comes from a clock function passed in, so the tests can move time forward without waiting. python class TokenCache: def __init__(self, fetch, clock, margin=30): ... def token(self): ... def invalidate(self): ... def call(self, send): ... - fetch() asks the token endpoint and returns a dict with access_token (a non-empty string) and expires_in (seconds, a positive integer). Anything else is a broken response: raise ValueError . - token() returns the cached token if clock() is still before expiry - margin , where expiry is the clock reading when the token was fetched plus its expires_in . Otherwise it fetches a new token, caches it and returns it. - invalidate() forgets the cached token. - call(send) calls send(token) , which returns a tuple whose first item is the HTTP status. If that status is 401, it invalidates the token and calls send once more with a fresh token. It returns the result of the last send .

title: 2.03  OAuth 2.0 and PKCE
body: Acting on behalf of a user without ever seeing their password - the OAuth 2.0 roles, the authorization code flow step by step with PKCE and the state parameter, scopes and redirect URIs, the client credentials flow for server-to-server calls, and why you use a well-tested library. The problem OAuth solves Your program wants to read a user's calendar at another service. The bad solution is to ask for their password. OAuth 2.0 lets the user sign in at the service itself and grant your program limited access, which it receives as tokens. The user's password never reaches you, and they can revoke your access at any time. The roles: the resource owner (the user), the client (your program), the authorization server (where the user signs in and tokens come from) and the resource server (the API). The authorization code flow with PKCE The flow used by apps, websites and command-line tools today: 1. Make a code verifier : a random secret string (43 to 128 characters of A-Z a-z 0-9 - . _ ~ ), and its code challenge : base64url(SHA-256(verifier)) without = padding. This is PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange, RFC 7636). 2. Make a state : another random string, remembered for this attempt. 3. Send the user's browser to the authorization URL: text https://auth.example.com/authorize?response_type=code&client_id=myapp &redirect_uri=http%3A%2F%2F127.0.0.1%3A8765%2Fcallback&scope=calendar.read &state=Xy7...&code_challenge=E9Mel...&code_challenge_method=S256 4. The user signs in there and approves the scopes you asked for. 5. The service redirects the browser to your redirect URI with ?code=...&state=... (or ?error=access_denied ). 6. Check the state equals the one you made; otherwise reject: it protects against a forged callback. 7. Exchange the code at the token endpoint: POST with grant_type=authorization_code , the code , the redirect_uri , your client_id and the code verifier . The server hashes the verifier and checks it matches the challenge from step 3. 8. You receive the access token (and usually a refresh token). Why PKCE? A code intercepted on its way to your redirect URI (by another app on the device, for example) is useless without the verifier, which never left your program. It replaces the older "client secret" for apps that cannot keep a secret, and is recommended for every client now. python import base64, hashlib verifier = "dBjftJeZ4CVP-mB92K27uhbUJU1p1r_wW1gFWFOEjXk" the example from RFC 7636 digest = hashlib.sha256(verifier.encode("ascii")).digest() print(base64.urlsafe_b64encode(digest).rstrip(b"=").decode()) E9Melhoa2OwvFrEMTJguCHaoeK1t8URWbuGJSstw-cM Scopes and redirect URIs - Scopes name what you may do: calendar.read , repo , offline_access (for a refresh token). Ask for the fewest you need; users are more likely to approve, and a leaked token can do less. - The redirect URI must be registered with the service in advance and match exactly. Desktop and command-line programs use a loopback address such as http://127.0.0.1:8765/callback , running a tiny local server for the moment of the callback. Client credentials: no user involved For server-to-server calls, where your program acts as itself, the client credentials flow is a single request: text POST /token Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded grant_type=client_credentials&client_id=myservice&client_secret=...&scope=reports.read The answer is an access token as in lesson 2.02. Note the body is form-encoded , not JSON: token endpoints follow the OAuth specification, not the API's usual style. Use a library The flows are simple to describe and easy to get subtly wrong (state checks, redirect matching, token storage). In real programs use a maintained library ( authlib , requests-oauthlib , or the provider's SDK) and read its documentation. Building the pieces once, as the practice does, is how you learn what the library is doing for you, and how to debug it when a sign-in fails. Check yourself quiz ? What is the code challenge for a verifier? - The verifier itself, sent a second time - The SHA-256 hash of the verifier, in hexadecimal + The base64url encoding, without padding, of the SHA-256 hash of the verifier - The verifier encoded as base64url, without hashing The challenge is base64url(SHA-256(verifier)) with the = padding removed; the verifier itself stays secret until the token exchange. ? Why check the state on the callback? - To find out which scopes the user approved + To reject a callback that did not come from the sign-in you started - To prove the code has not expired - Because the token endpoint needs the state instead of the verifier The state ties the callback to the attempt you began, so a forged or replayed callback is rejected. ? What makes an intercepted authorization code useless with PKCE? - The code expires before anyone else could use it - The code is encrypted with the user's password - The redirect URI is kept secret from other apps + Exchanging it needs the verifier, which stays in your program Only the challenge travelled through the browser. Without the verifier that hashes to it, the code cannot be exchanged for a token. ? Which flow does a nightly server job use to call an API as itself? - Authorization code with PKCE + Client credentials - A refresh token from a user's sign-in - The user's password, read from an environment variable With no user involved, the program authenticates as itself with its client id and secret in one request to the token endpoint.

title: The pieces of PKCE
body: Write the client side of the OAuth authorization code flow with PKCE from lesson 2.03 (RFC 7636 and RFC 6749, summarised). python def make_verifier(random_bytes): ... def challenge_for(verifier): ... def authorization_url(endpoint, client_id, redirect_uri, scopes, state, challenge): ... def read_callback(url, expected_state): ... - make_verifier encodes the given random bytes (a real program passes secrets.token_bytes(32) ) with URL-safe base64 without = padding. The result must be a valid verifier, so the number of bytes must be from 32 to 96; otherwise raise ValueError . - challenge_for returns the S256 challenge: URL-safe base64, without padding, of the SHA-256 hash of the verifier's ASCII bytes. It raises ValueError if the verifier is not 43 to 128 characters long or contains anything other than A - Z , a - z , 0 - 9 , - , . , _ and ~ . - authorization_url returns endpoint + ? + the query, built with urlencode from these pairs, in this order: response_type=code , client_id , redirect_uri , scope (the scopes joined with single spaces), state , code_challenge , code_challenge_method=S256 . - read_callback reads the redirect the browser was sent to and returns the authorization code. In this order: if the state parameter is missing or differs from expected_state (compare with hmac.compare_digest ), raise ValueError("state mismatch") ; if there is an error parameter, raise PermissionError with a message containing the error's value; if there is no non-empty code , raise ValueError("no code") .

title: 2.04  Signing Requests with HMAC
body:
Proving a request came from you and was not changed - HMAC with a shared secret, building a canonical string from the method, path, sorted query, timestamp and body hash, why every byte must be agreed, timestamps against replay, and comparing signatures in constant time. Why sign? A bearer token proves who you are only as long as nobody else has it, and says nothing about whether the request was changed on the way. Some APIs (cloud storage, payment and exchange APIs, and webhooks in milestone 4) instead have you sign each request with a secret that is never sent: - The server can check the request came from someone who knows the secret ( authenticity ). - Any change to the signed parts breaks the signature ( integrity ). - With a timestamp in the signed data, an old request cannot be replayed later. HMAC The tool is HMAC (hash-based message authentication code): a hash of the message mixed with a secret key. In Python: python import hashlib, hmac secret = b"s3cr3t-key" message = b"GET
/v1/books
limit=5
1793523600
" print(hmac.new(secret, message, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()) 48cc02d9fdfca3bf5e2b37130edce25564f2c28edb8ee0ad8cf87f2bb3171dfa Without the secret, nobody can compute it; change one byte of the message and the result is completely different. The canonical string The hard part is agreeing exactly which bytes are signed. Both sides must build the same message from the same request, so APIs define a canonical string . A typical definition: text METHOD upper case: POST PATH as sent, escaped: /v1/books QUERY sorted by name, then value, each name and value escaped, joined with &: a=1&tag=sf&tag=x TIMESTAMP seconds since 1970: 1793523600 BODY HASH SHA-256 of the body in hex (of no bytes when there is no body) each on its own line. Every detail matters: upper or lower case, the escaping rules, the order of repeated query keys, whether the body is hashed before or after compression, the final newline. A one-character difference makes every request fail with "invalid signature", so implement the provider's definition exactly , test it against the examples in their documentation, and log the canonical string (not the secret) when debugging. Replay protection The timestamp goes into the canonical string and a header ( X-Timestamp ). The server rejects requests whose timestamp is more than a few minutes away from its own clock, so a captured request stops working quickly. Some APIs add a random nonce that the server remembers for that window, so a request cannot be replayed even within it. Comparing signatures The server (and you, when verifying webhooks) must compare the received signature with the expected one using hmac.compare_digest , never == . An ordinary comparison stops at the first differing character, and the time it takes can leak how many leading characters were right, letting an attacker guess a valid signature one character at a time. compare_digest takes the same time however much matches. python-norun expected = hmac.new(secret, canonical.encode(), hashlib.sha256).hexdigest() if not hmac.compare_digest(expected, received): reject() Check yourself quiz ? What does HMAC give that a plain SHA-256 hash of the request does not? - It is shorter, so it fits in a header - It encrypts the request so nobody can read it + It needs the secret key, so only someone with the key can produce it - It can be reversed to recover the request Anyone can compute a plain hash of a request they changed. HMAC mixes in a secret, so a valid code proves the sender knew the key. ? Why include a timestamp in the signed data? + So the server can reject old, replayed requests - So the signature changes length every second - So the server can sort requests by time - Because HMAC needs a number as well as a key A captured request stops working once its timestamp is too far from the server's clock, and the timestamp cannot be changed without breaking the signature. ? Your signatures are always rejected. What is the most useful thing to log? - The secret key, to check it was read correctly - Only the final signature you computed + Your canonical string, to compare with the documentation - The full response body from the server Almost every "invalid signature" is a difference in the canonical string. Log it, never the secret. ? Why use hmac.compare_digest instead of == ? - == cannot compare hexadecimal strings - compare_digest also checks the timestamp - compare_digest is faster on long strings + Its timing does not reveal how much of the signature matched == stops at the first differing character, and that timing can leak how much of a guess was right.

title: Signing and verifying requests
body: Implement the signing scheme described in lesson 2.04, exactly as defined here, for both the client (signing) and the server (verifying). python def canonical_string(method, path, query, timestamp, body): ... def sign(secret, method, path, query, body, timestamp): ... def verify(secret, method, path, query, body, headers, now, tolerance=300): ... secret is bytes ; query is a list of (name, value) string pairs (names may repeat); body is bytes or None . The canonical string is five lines joined with \n , with no newline at the end: 1. the method in upper case; 2. the path as given; 3. the query pairs sorted by name and then by value, each written name=value with both escaped by quote(..., safe="-_.~") , joined with & (an empty line if there are none); 4. the timestamp as a decimal integer; 5. the SHA-256 of the body in lower-case hex ( None counts as no bytes). sign returns the headers to send: {"X-Timestamp": "<timestamp ", "X-Signature": "<hex HMAC-SHA256 of the canonical string, keyed with secret "} . verify is the server's check. It returns False if either header is missing (header names are matched ignoring case), if X-Timestamp is not a whole number, if it is more than tolerance seconds away from now in either direction, or if the signature does not match (compare with hmac.compare_digest ). Otherwise it returns True .

title: 2.05  Keeping Secrets Out of Logs
body: The many quiet ways secrets leak - URLs, headers and bodies in logs, error messages, tracebacks, object reprs and debugging output - and how to redact them systematically, from masking a key for display to scrubbing nested JSON, plus a test that proves no secret reaches the log. Logs are where keys leak Logging requests is essential for debugging an integration (lesson 5.05). It is also the most common way secrets escape: logs are kept for months, copied into tickets, shipped to monitoring services, and read by many people. The leaks are rarely deliberate: Leak How it happens --- --- URL a token or key in the query string, logged with the request line headers logging all request headers, including Authorization and Cookie bodies logging a token response, or a login form with a password exceptions a library's error message includes the URL or the body reprs print(settings) shows every field of a config object debugging a temporary print(headers) that is never removed Redact at one place The reliable fix is a redaction step that every log line passes through, rather than remembering at each call: - Headers : replace the values of Authorization , Proxy-Authorization , Cookie , Set-Cookie and any X-...-Key or X-...-Token header. For Authorization , keeping the scheme ( Bearer REDACTED ) still helps debugging. - URLs : parse the query string and replace the values of known secret parameters ( api_key , token , access_token , client_secret , signature ). - Bodies : walk the parsed JSON and replace values of keys such as password , secret , token , refresh_token , at any depth. - Display : when a human must recognise which key is configured, show only the last few characters: a1b2 . python from urllib.parse import parse_qsl, urlencode, urlsplit, urlunsplit SECRET_PARAMS = {"api_key", "token", "access_token", "client_secret", "signature"} def redact_url(url): parts = urlsplit(url) query = (k, "REDACTED" if k.lower() in SECRET_PARAMS else v) for k, v in parse_qsl(parts.query, keep_blank_values=True) return urlunsplit(parts._replace(query=urlencode(query))) print(redact_url("https://api.example.com/v1/books?limit=5&api_key=sk_live_abc")) https://api.example.com/v1/books?limit=5&api_key=REDACTED Objects that hide their secrets Give configuration and credential classes a __repr__ that masks the secret, so an accidental print , a debugger view or an exception message cannot show it: python-norun class Settings: def __repr__(self): return f"Settings(base_url={self.base_url!r}, api_key=' {self.api_key -4: }')" Test it Write a test that runs a request through your client with a known fake secret and asserts that the secret appears nowhere in the captured log. It costs a few lines and catches the regression the day someone adds log(headers) for debugging. Check yourself quiz ? Which request headers should always be redacted? - Only Authorization : the others never carry secrets - Cookie and Set-Cookie , but not Authorization - Authorization , User-Agent and X-Request-Id + Authorization , Cookie , Set-Cookie and any key or token header Every header that carries a credential must be masked, Proxy-Authorization included. X-Request-Id is the opposite: you want it in the log. ? Why redact in one shared function instead of at each log call? + So no call can forget it, and the rules are in one place - Because logging libraries allow only one function - Because it makes the log files smaller - So that secrets are encrypted rather than removed Remembering at every call fails the day someone adds a quick log(headers) . One step that every line passes through cannot be skipped. ? How can a config object leak its key without anyone logging it on purpose? - Through its __init__ method being called twice - By being listed in the project's .gitignore file + Through its default repr , shown by a print or a debugger - Only when the object is converted to JSON text The default repr shows every field. Giving the class a __repr__ that masks the secret closes that path. ? What does a "no secrets in the log" test do? - Checks that the log file is empty after each run - Deletes log files that are older than one day - Encrypts the log and checks it can be decrypted + Uses a known fake secret and checks the log never contains it A known fake value makes the check simple: search the captured log for it. It catches a debugging print before it ships.

title: A redaction toolkit
body: Write the redaction functions every log line in an API client should pass through (lesson 2.05). python def redact_headers(headers): ... def redact_url(url): ... def redact_json(value): ... redact_headers returns a new dict with the same names, in the same order. Names are compared ignoring case: - Authorization and Proxy-Authorization : if the value has a space, keep the scheme before it and replace the rest with REDACTED ( Bearer REDACTED ); otherwise the whole value becomes REDACTED . - Cookie , Set-Cookie , and any name starting with x- and ending with -key or -token (such as X-Api-Key ): the value becomes REDACTED . - Everything else is unchanged. redact_url replaces the values of the query parameters api_key , key , token , access_token , refresh_token , client_secret , signature and password (any case) with REDACTED , and a password in the URL itself ( https://user:pass@host/ ) with REDACTED . If a query parameter was replaced, the query is rebuilt with urlencode from the pairs in their original order (blank values kept); otherwise the query is kept exactly as given, and a URL with nothing to redact is returned unchanged. redact_json returns a copy of a parsed JSON value in which, at any depth, the value of every object key named password , secret , client_secret , token , access_token , refresh_token or api_key (any case) is replaced by REDACTED . The input is not changed.
