title: An authenticated session
body: Combine the pieces of this milestone into one object that a client can send every request through: it gets a token with the OAuth client credentials flow, caches it, signs each request, recovers once from a 401, and keeps a log in which no secret ever appears. python-norun class AuthError(Exception): attribute: status class AuthSession: def __init__(self, transport, token_url, client_id, client_secret, signing_secret, clock, margin=30): ... def send(self, method, url, body=None): ... - (status, headers, body) log a list of strings The transport is the one from the milestone 1 project: transport.send(method, url, headers, body, timeout) returns (status, headers, body) , always called here with a timeout of 10. Getting a token. POST token_url with headers Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded and Accept: application/json , and the body urlencode of grant_type=client_credentials , client_id , client_secret (in that order), encoded as UTF-8. The response must be status 200 with a JSON object holding a non-empty string access_token , a token_type equal to Bearer ignoring case, and a positive integer expires_in . Anything else raises AuthError with the response's status. A token is reused until clock() reaches its expiry minus margin (practice 2.02). Sending a request. send(method, url, body) (body is bytes or None ): 1. Get a token. 2. Sign the request as in practice 2.04, with signing_secret (bytes): the path of url ( / if empty), its query pairs in order ( parse_qsl with blank values kept), the body, and the timestamp int(clock()) . 3. Send it with headers Authorization: Bearer <token , X-Timestamp , X-Signature , and Content-Type: application/json when there is a body. 4. If the status is 401 , forget the token, get a new one, sign again with the current time, and send once more. 5. Return the last response. The log. After every call to the transport (token requests included), append "<METHOD <url - <status " , with the URL redacted as in practice 2.05 (it is enough to redact the query parameters listed there). The access token, the client secret and the signing secret must never appear in the log.

title: 3.01  Pagination
body: Getting long lists from an API one page at a time - offset and limit, page numbers, cursors and Link headers - how each behaves when data changes while you read, loop protection, and Python generators that make paging invisible to the rest of your code. Lists come in pages An endpoint that lists things ( GET /books ) never returns a million rows at once. It returns a page and a way to ask for the next one. The documentation's "Pagination" section says which style it uses. Style Request Response tells you --- --- --- offset and limit ?offset=40&limit=20 maybe a total page number ?page=3&per_page=20 maybe total_pages cursor ?cursor=eyJpZCI6MTAyfQ&limit=20 next_cursor (or has_more ) Link header follow the URL given Link: <https://api.example.com/books?cursor=abc ; rel="next" Why cursors win Offsets break when the list changes while you read it. Suppose you read page 1 (items 1 to 20), and someone deletes item 5 before you ask for offset=20 : everything shifts left by one, and you skip the item that moved from position 21 to 20. An insert at the front makes you see an item twice . A cursor is an opaque marker of "where I got to" (often the last id or sort key, encoded). The next page starts after that point regardless of inserts and deletes before it. Treat a cursor as an opaque string: do not decode or build it yourself, just pass back what you were given. With any style: - Keep the sort order fixed (the API's default, or an explicit sort=id ); paging over an unstable order is meaningless. - Ask for the largest page the API allows when you want everything: fewer requests, fewer rate-limit problems. - Deduplicate by id when the API only offers offsets. Link headers GitHub and many others put the next URL in a Link header (RFC 8288): text Link: <https://api.example.com/books?page=3 ; rel="next", <https://api.example.com/books?page=9 ; rel="last" Follow rel="next" exactly as given (it already contains every parameter), and stop when there is none. Parsing this header properly is practice 3.01. Generators hide the paging In Python, a generator turns "fetch page, process, fetch next page" into a plain loop for the rest of your code, and fetches lazily, only as far as the caller reads: python-norun def all_books(client): cursor = None seen = set() while True: page = client.request("GET", "/books", {"limit": 100, "cursor": cursor}) yield from page "items" cursor = page.get("next_cursor") if not cursor: return if cursor in seen: raise RuntimeError("the API returned the same cursor twice") seen.add(cursor) for book in all_books(client): pages are fetched as the loop needs them if book "year" < 1950: print(book "title" ) The seen check is loop protection : a server bug that returns the same cursor forever would otherwise make your program run, and spend your rate limit, forever. Check yourself quiz ? Why can offset paging skip items? - The server returns its pages in a random order - The limit is ignored on every page after the first + A delete before the offset shifts later items back by one - Offsets only work for the first 1,000 items Offsets count positions, and positions move when the list changes. A delete shifts items left and one is skipped; an insert shifts them right and one is seen twice. ? How should you treat a cursor value? + As opaque: pass back exactly what the API gave you - Decode it and add the page size to it - Build it yourself from the last id you saw - Increase it by one for each page A cursor's contents are the server's business and may change. Send back exactly the string you were given. ? When does a paging loop stop with a Link header? - When a page has fewer items than the limit - After the number of pages in rel="last" - When the response has no Link header for one request + When the response has no rel="next" link Follow rel="next" until there is none. A short page is not a reliable end signal, and the next URL already holds every parameter. ? What is loop protection in paging? - Limiting each page to at most 100 items - Sorting the results so no item appears twice + Stopping with an error if a cursor comes back a second time - Waiting a second between pages to spare the server A server bug that returns the same cursor forever would otherwise make the loop run, and spend your rate limit, forever.

title: Cursors and Link headers
body: Write the two pieces of paging from lesson 3.01. python def iterate_pages(fetch): ... def parse_link_header(value): ... iterate_pages is a generator that yields every item of a cursor-paginated list. fetch(cursor) returns a dict with items (a list) and next_cursor (a string, or None ). Call it first with None , then with each next_cursor , until next_cursor is None or empty. Fetch lazily: a page is fetched only when the caller asks for an item beyond those already fetched. If a cursor comes back that was already used, raise RuntimeError (loop protection). parse_link_header reads an HTTP Link header (RFC 8288, simplified) and returns a dict from each relation type to its URL: - The header is a list of links separated by commas. Each link is <url followed by parameters, each ; name=value , where the value may be in double quotes. - Commas inside <... or inside quotes do not separate links. - The rel parameter (name compared ignoring case) may hold several relation types separated by spaces: each maps to the link's URL. Relation types are compared and returned in lower case. - If the same relation appears twice, the first one wins. Links without rel are ignored. None or an empty header gives {} .

title: 3.02  Rate Limits
body: How APIs limit how fast you call them - per-second, per-minute and daily limits, the 429 status, Retry-After in seconds or as a date, rate-limit headers - and staying under the limit on your side with a token bucket instead of waiting to be told off. Why limits exist Every public API limits how many requests a client may make: "100 requests per minute per key", "10 per second", "5,000 per hour". The limits protect the service from overload and from one customer starving the others. Your integration will hit them, most often while backfilling data or paging through everything. Being told to slow down When you go over, the API answers 429 Too Many Requests (some old APIs use 403 or 503), usually with headers saying when to come back: text HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests Retry-After: 12 X-RateLimit-Limit: 100 X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0 X-RateLimit-Reset: 1793523612 - Retry-After is standard HTTP, and comes in two forms: a number of seconds ( 12 ) or an HTTP date ( Wed, 21 Oct 2026 07:28:00 GMT ). Handle both (practice 3.02); email.utils.parsedate_to_datetime reads the date form. - X-RateLimit- headers are a common convention, not a standard: limit, remaining in the window, and when the window resets (often seconds since 1970, sometimes seconds from now: read the documentation). A newer standard spells them RateLimit-Limit , RateLimit-Remaining and RateLimit-Reset . Waiting at least as long as Retry-After says, then retrying, is the minimum. Ignoring it and retrying at once gets keys blocked. Staying under the limit yourself Better than hitting the limit is not hitting it. A token bucket paces requests on the client: - The bucket holds up to capacity tokens and starts full. - It refills continuously at rate tokens per second. - Each request takes one token; with none available, wait until one has refilled. python-norun class TokenBucket: def __init__(self, rate, capacity, clock): self.rate, self.capacity, self.clock = rate, capacity, clock self.tokens, self.updated = capacity, clock() def _refill(self): now = self.clock() self.tokens = min(self.capacity, self.tokens + (now - self.updated) self.rate) self.updated = now def try_take(self): self._refill() if self.tokens = 1: self.tokens -= 1 return True return False The capacity allows short bursts, the rate keeps the average under the limit. Set the rate a little below the documented limit, since other programs using the same key share it. Other ways to need fewer requests - Use bulk endpoints when they exist (fetch 100 ids in one call). - Use the largest page size . - Cache what does not change (lesson 3.05). - Use webhooks (milestone 4) instead of polling for changes. Check yourself quiz ? What are the two forms of Retry-After ? - Seconds or milliseconds + A number of seconds, or an HTTP date - An HTTP date, or seconds since 1970 - A number of requests, or a number of seconds Retry-After is either a delay in seconds ( 12 ) or an HTTP date. Seconds since 1970 is what many X-RateLimit-Reset headers use, which is a different header. ? What does a token bucket's capacity control, and what does its rate control? - The capacity sets the average rate; the rate sets the longest wait - The capacity is the total requests per day; the rate is per hour + The capacity allows short bursts; the rate sets the average number of requests per second - Both control the same thing, in different units A full bucket lets several requests go at once; after that, requests can only go as fast as tokens refill. ? Why set your client's rate slightly below the documented limit? - Because documented limits are always rounded up + Other programs may share the key, and windows never line up - Because the server counts each request twice - So that the server never has to send Retry-After The limit is per key, not per program, and your idea of the window never matches the server's exactly. A margin keeps you clear of 429s. ? Which of these is a way to need fewer requests? - Retrying every failed request at once - Asking for the smallest page size - Polling for changes more often + Using a bulk endpoint that fetches many ids in one call Bulk endpoints, the largest page size, caching and webhooks instead of polling all cut the number of requests. Small pages and frequent polling do the opposite.

title: Retry-After and a token bucket
body: Read the server's "come back later", and pace your own requests so you rarely hear it (lesson 3.02). python def parse_retry_after(value, now): ... class TokenBucket: def __init__(self, rate, capacity, clock): ... def try_take(self): ... def wait_time(self): ... parse_retry_after returns how many whole seconds to wait, or None if the header is missing or invalid. now is a timezone-aware datetime . After stripping spaces: - digits only: that many seconds; - otherwise an HTTP date ( Wed, 21 Oct 2026 07:28:00 GMT , which email.utils.parsedate_to_datetime reads): the seconds from now until then, rounded up , and 0 if it is in the past; - anything else (including negative numbers, or a date without a time zone): None . TokenBucket starts full with capacity tokens and refills continuously at rate tokens per second, never above capacity . clock() gives the time in seconds. - try_take takes one token and returns True if at least one is available; otherwise returns False and takes nothing. - wait_time returns how many seconds until one token will be available (0 if one is available now), without taking anything.

title: 3.03  Retries with Backoff
body: Recovering from the failures that go away by themselves - which errors and statuses are worth retrying, why only idempotent requests are safe to repeat, exponential backoff with a cap, full jitter, honouring Retry-After, and limiting attempts and total time. Transient failures Networks drop connections, servers restart, load balancers time out, and rate limits fill up. These transient failures often succeed a moment later, so robust clients retry. But retrying the wrong thing, or retrying too eagerly, makes problems worse. What to retry Outcome Retry? --- --- connection refused or reset, DNS failure, timeout yes (the request may not have arrived) 408 Request Timeout, 429 Too Many Requests yes, after waiting 500, 502, 503, 504 yes 501 Not Implemented no (it will never be implemented by retrying) any other 4xx no: the request is wrong 2xx, 3xx no: done Only if it is safe to repeat A retry may happen after the first attempt did reach the server and did take effect: the response was lost, not the request. So only repeat requests that are idempotent , meaning doing them twice has the same effect as once: - GET , HEAD , OPTIONS : read only. - PUT : replaces with the same content. - DELETE : the second delete finds nothing to delete. - POST and PATCH are not idempotent in general: a repeated "create order" creates two orders. Retry them only with an idempotency key (lesson 3.04). Backoff and jitter Retrying immediately hits a struggling server when it is weakest. Wait longer after each failure, exponential backoff : text attempt 1 fails: wait up to 0.5 s attempt 2 fails: wait up to 1 s attempt 3 fails: wait up to 2 s ... base × 2^(n-1), capped (for example at 8 s) If a thousand clients failed at the same moment and all wait exactly 0.5 s, 1 s, 2 s, they all come back at the same moments, in synchronised waves. Jitter spreads them out. The simplest and very effective form, full jitter , waits a random time between 0 and the backoff value: python-norun delay = rng.uniform(0, min(cap, base 2 (attempt - 1))) When the response carries Retry-After , it overrides the computed delay: the server knows best. Knowing when to stop Always limit retries, by number of attempts (3 to 5 is common) and ideally by a total deadline ("this whole operation may take at most 30 s"). After the last attempt, report the last error with how many attempts were made. Endless retrying hides outages and burns your rate limit. Pass the clock, the sleep function and the random number generator into your retry code: production passes time.monotonic , time.sleep and random.Random() , tests pass fakes, and a test of "retries four times with these delays" runs in a millisecond. Practice 3.03 is built that way. Check yourself quiz ? Should a client retry a 422? - Yes, with exponential backoff and jitter - Yes, but only once, after a short wait + No: the request is invalid and will fail again - Only if the response has Retry-After A 4xx other than 408 and 429 says the request itself is wrong. Repeating it unchanged gives the same answer. ? Why is retrying a POST without precautions dangerous? + The first attempt may have succeeded; repeating it can create a duplicate - POST requests cannot be sent twice on one connection - The server will block the key after a second POST - A POST body is lost after the first attempt The response may have been lost, not the request. POST is not idempotent, so retry it only with an idempotency key. ? With base 0.5 s and cap 8 s, what is the maximum wait after the fifth failure? - 2.5 s - 16 s - 4 s + 8 s 0.5 × 2⁴ = 8 s, which is exactly the cap. Uncapped, the sixth failure would give 16 s; the cap keeps it at 8. ? What does jitter prevent? - Retrying a request that is not idempotent - Waiting longer than Retry-After says + Many clients retrying at the same moments - A retry loop that never stops Without randomness, every client that failed together comes back together. Limits on attempts and deadlines are what stop endless loops.

title: A retry loop
body: Write the retry loop from lesson 3.03. sleep and rng are passed in, so the tests can record the delays instead of waiting. python def call_with_retries(send, method, sleep, rng, max_attempts=4, base=0.5, cap=8.0, idempotency_key=None): ... send() performs one attempt. It returns (status, headers) or raises an exception. 1. An attempt is retryable if it raised ConnectionError or TimeoutError , or returned status 408, 429, 500, 502, 503 or 504. Any other exception is raised at once. 2. A request is safe to repeat if its method (ignoring case) is GET , HEAD , OPTIONS , PUT or DELETE , or if an idempotency_key is given. 3. After a retryable attempt of a safe request, if fewer than max_attempts attempts have been made, sleep and try again. The delay after attempt n (counting from 1) is: - the Retry-After header of the response (name in any case), if it is a whole number of seconds written in digits; - otherwise rng.uniform(0, min(cap, base 2 (n - 1))) . 4. Otherwise stop: return the last response, or raise the last exception.

title: 3.04  Idempotency Keys and Timeouts
body: Making non-idempotent requests safe to retry - the Idempotency-Key header, one key per logical operation, what the server stores and replays, conflicts when the same key comes with a different request - and timeouts, unknown outcomes and deadlines that span several calls. The unknown outcome You send POST /payments and the connection drops before the response arrives. Did the payment happen? You cannot know. Retrying might pay twice; not retrying might not pay at all. Timeouts create the same uncertainty: a timeout says you stopped waiting , not that the server did nothing. Idempotency keys Many APIs that create things (payments, orders, messages) solve this with an idempotency key : a unique value the client generates for each logical operation and sends as a header: text POST /v1/payments Idempotency-Key: 6f1c2b7e-4a5d-4c3e-9b8a-1d2e3f4a5b6c Content-Type: application/json {"amount": 1999, "currency": "EUR"} The server remembers the key with the response it gave. If the same key arrives again: - with the same request: it does not repeat the operation; it replays the stored response. Your retry is now safe. - with a different request (another amount): it refuses, typically with 409 or 422, because reusing a key for a different operation is a client bug. Rules for the client: - Generate the key once per operation ( uuid.uuid4() ), before the first attempt, and reuse it for every retry of that operation. - A new operation (the user clicks "pay" again for a second item) gets a new key. - Keys expire on the server after some time (often 24 hours); retries happen within seconds or minutes, so this does not matter for them. Practice 3.04 builds the server side of this, which is the best way to understand what the client relies on. Timeouts and deadlines Every request needs a timeout (lesson 1.02). When an operation makes several requests, with retries, also give it a deadline : a total time budget. Each attempt gets the smaller of its usual timeout and the time left, and the operation stops when the budget is spent: python-norun deadline = clock() + 30 for attempt in range(1, 5): remaining = deadline - clock() if remaining <= 0: raise TimeoutError("gave up after 30 s") response = send(timeout=min(10, remaining)) ... Deadlines keep a slow dependency from making your whole program slow: a web page that must answer in 2 s cannot spend 40 s retrying. Check yourself quiz ? When must a client generate a new idempotency key? - For every attempt, including retries + Before each new operation's first attempt; its retries reuse it - Only after the server rejects the old key with 409 - Once when the program starts, for all requests The key names the operation, not the attempt. A new key on a retry would let the server perform the operation twice. ? What does the server do with a repeated key and the same request? - Performs the operation again and returns the new result - Refuses it with 409 Conflict + Returns the stored response without performing the operation again - Ignores the request and returns 204 No Content Replaying the stored response is what makes the retry safe. A refusal is for the same key with a different request. ? A request timed out. Did the server do nothing? - Yes: a timeout means the request never arrived - Yes, because the server cancels work when the client stops waiting - No: a timeout always means the server succeeded + Not necessarily: the timeout only means you stopped waiting The outcome is unknown. The request may have taken effect, which is exactly why idempotency keys exist. ? Why give a multi-request operation a deadline? + So retries and slow calls cannot make the whole operation take longer than it can afford - So the server knows how long to keep the idempotency key - Because each request's timeout is ignored once retries start - So that every attempt gets the same timeout Per-request timeouts limit one attempt; a deadline limits the whole operation. Each attempt gets the smaller of its timeout and the time left.

title: Idempotency keys on the server side
match: Idempotency keys on the server side
body: To understand what clients rely on, build the part of a server that makes Idempotency-Key work (lesson 3.04), and the deadline helper a client uses around its retries. python class KeyConflict(Exception): ... def fingerprint(method, path, body): ... class IdempotencyStore: def __init__(self, clock, ttl=86400): ... def run(self, key, request_fingerprint, operation): ... - (result, replayed) class Deadline: def __init__(self, total, clock): ... def remaining(self): ... def timeout(self, longest): ... fingerprint identifies a request's content: the SHA-256, in hex, of the JSON text of the list METHOD in upper case, path, body written with sorted keys and separators=(",", ":") . Equal content in any key order gives the same fingerprint. IdempotencyStore.run : 1. First remove every stored key whose time is up: stored at t , it expires when clock() = t + ttl . 2. If key is None , run operation() and return (result, False) , storing nothing. 3. If key is stored with the same fingerprint, return (stored result, True) without running the operation. 4. If key is stored with a different fingerprint, raise KeyConflict . 5. Otherwise run operation() . If it raises, store nothing and let the exception through. If it returns, store the key with the fingerprint, the result and the time, and return (result, False) . Deadline starts its budget of total seconds when it is created. remaining() is the time left, never below 0. timeout(longest) returns the timeout for the next call, the smaller of longest and the time left, and raises TimeoutError if no time is left.

title: 3.05  Caching with ETags
body: Not asking for what you already have - HTTP caching headers as an API client uses them, Cache-Control max-age and no-store, ETags with If-None-Match and the 304 Not Modified answer, Last-Modified, and a small client-side cache that saves requests and rate limit. Why cache Much API data changes rarely: a user's profile, a product catalogue, configuration. Fetching it again and again wastes time and rate limit. HTTP has caching built in, and many APIs support it. Freshness: Cache-Control The response says how long it may be reused without asking again: text Cache-Control: max-age=300 For the next 300 seconds, use your stored copy without a request. Other directives: no-cache (you may store it but must check with the server before each use), no-store (do not keep it at all: often on personal or secret data), private (only the end client may cache it, not shared proxies). Validation: ETags After the copy goes stale, you can ask cheaply whether it changed. The original response carried an ETag , a version identifier for that content: text HTTP/1.1 200 OK ETag: "v42-a7f3" Cache-Control: max-age=60 Next time, send it back: text GET /v1/catalogue If-None-Match: "v42-a7f3" - If nothing changed, the server answers 304 Not Modified with no body: reuse your copy (and its new freshness headers, if any). Many APIs do not count 304s against your rate limit, or count them less. - If it changed, you get a normal 200 with the new body and a new ETag. Last-Modified and If-Modified-Since work the same way with dates; ETags are more precise. Send the ETag exactly as received, quotes and W/ prefix included. A small client cache python-norun entry = cache.get(url) if entry and clock() < entry.fresh_until: return entry.body no request at all headers = {"If-None-Match": entry.etag} if entry and entry.etag else {} status, resp_headers, body = transport.send("GET", url, headers) if status == 304 and entry: entry.fresh_until = clock() + max_age(resp_headers) return entry.body if status == 200 and "no-store" not in cache_control(resp_headers): cache url = Entry(body, resp_headers.get("ETag"), clock() + max_age(resp_headers)) return body Practice 3.05 builds this with every rule spelled out. A real program would also bound the cache's size and key it by anything that changes the response (query parameters, the Accept header, the user). Caching your own results Beyond HTTP caching, cache derived data in your program: the list of countries you fetched at startup, a lookup from user id to name. Give each cache entry a time to live, and invalidate it when you change the data yourself through the API. Check yourself quiz ? A response says Cache-Control: max-age=300 . What may you do for five minutes? - Keep it, but check with the server before each use + Reuse it without making a request - Send If-None-Match every time you use it - Nothing: you must not store it For 300 seconds the copy is fresh and needs no request at all. "Check before each use" describes no-cache . ? What does 304 Not Modified mean, and is there a body? - The resource has moved; the body holds the new URL - The resource changed; the body holds the new version - The request was invalid; the body holds the error + The cached copy is still current; there is no body 304 answers a conditional request: reuse your stored copy, along with any new freshness headers. ? What header carries the ETag back to the server? - ETag - If-Modified-Since + If-None-Match - Cache-Control The server sends ETag ; the client sends it back, exactly as received, in If-None-Match . If-Modified-Since carries a date instead. ? A response has Cache-Control: no-store . What should the cache do? - Keep it, but revalidate before each use - Keep it for the default time - Keep it only in memory, not on disk + Not keep it at all no-store means do not store the response anywhere. Revalidating before each use is what no-cache asks for.

title: A cache with ETags
body: Build the client-side cache sketched in lesson 3.05. python class CachingClient: def __init__(self, transport, clock): ... def get(self, url): ... - (status, body) transport.send(method, url, headers) returns (status, headers, body) ; header names may be in any case. The cache keeps, per URL, the body, the ETag (if any) and the time until which it is fresh. get(url) : 1. If the URL is cached and clock() is before its fresh-until time, return (200, cached body) without sending anything. 2. Otherwise send GET with the header Accept: application/json , plus If-None-Match: <etag if the URL is cached with an ETag. 3. 304 with a cached entry: the entry becomes fresh for the response's max-age from now; if the 304 carries an ETag , it replaces the stored one. Return (200, cached body) . (A 304 without a cached entry is returned as it is.) 4. 200 : if Cache-Control contains no-store , remove any entry for the URL. Otherwise store the body, the response's ETag (or none) and fresh-until = now + max-age. Return (200, body) . 5. Any other status is returned as it is, and the cache is left unchanged. max-age is read from the Cache-Control header: directives are separated by commas, names compared ignoring case; max-age=N with N in digits (optionally in double quotes) gives N seconds. If the header is missing, has no valid max-age, or contains no-cache , max-age is 0.

title: A polite harvester
where: Paging, Rate Limits and Retries projects
body: Write the component every integration eventually needs: something that reads every item of a paginated list from an API, however long it is and however badly the API behaves along the way. It follows Link headers, paces itself, retries what can be retried with backoff, honours Retry-After , removes duplicates, and refuses to loop forever. python class HarvestError(Exception): ... class Harvester: def __init__(self, transport, clock, sleep, rng, max_attempts=4, min_interval=0.2): ... def fetch_all(self, url): ... - list of items requests how many requests were sent retries how many of them were retries transport.send(method, url, headers) returns (status, headers, body) (header names in any case, body as bytes ) or raises ConnectionError or TimeoutError . sleep(seconds) waits; in the tests it moves the fake clock forward. Pages. fetch_all(url) requests url with GET and the header Accept: application/json . A successful page has status 200 and a JSON object body with an items list. The next page's URL is the rel="next" link of the Link header (practice 3.01); with none, the harvest is complete. If a next URL was already requested during this harvest, raise HarvestError (a pagination loop). Items. Return the items of all pages in order, without duplicates : an item is a duplicate if it has the same id as an earlier one; only the first is kept. Pacing. Before every request (retries included), if fewer than min_interval seconds have passed since the previous request was sent, sleep for the difference first. Retries , as in practice 3.03: an attempt that raised ConnectionError or TimeoutError , or returned 408, 429, 500, 502, 503 or 504, is retried until max_attempts attempts have been made for that page . Before a retry, sleep for the Retry-After header's seconds if it is a whole number in digits, otherwise rng.uniform(0, min(8, 0.5 2 (n - 1))) after attempt n . When the attempts run out, raise HarvestError . Other failures raise HarvestError at once: any other status, a body that is not valid JSON, or a JSON body that is not an object with an items list.

title: 4.01  Webhooks versus Polling
body: Two ways to learn that something changed at another service - asking repeatedly (polling) and being told (webhooks) - what each costs, polling done carefully with an updated-since cursor and adaptive intervals, and how webhook subscriptions, events and deliveries work. "Has anything changed?" Integrations constantly need to know when something happens elsewhere: a payment succeeded, an issue was closed, a file was uploaded. There are two ways to find out. Polling Ask, again and again: python-norun since = load_checkpoint() while True: changes = client.request("GET", "/orders", {"updated_since": since}) for order in changes "items" : handle(order) since = max(since, order "updated_at" ) save_checkpoint(since) sleep(interval) Polling is simple and works with any API, but: - Most polls find nothing, and each one costs a request and some of your rate limit. - Changes are noticed up to one interval late. Shorter intervals cost more requests. - "Updated since" has an edge case: several items updated in the same second as your checkpoint. Asking for updated_at since can miss some; asking for = since returns ones you have already seen. The usual fix is = plus remembering which ids you saw at exactly that timestamp (practice 4.01). An adaptive interval reduces the cost: poll more often while things are happening, back off when they are quiet (halve the interval after finding changes, double it after an empty poll, within limits). Webhooks With a webhook , the service calls you : when an event happens, it sends an HTTP POST to a URL you registered, with the event as JSON. text POST /webhooks/payments HTTP/1.1 Content-Type: application/json Webhook-Id: evt_01HX9F... Webhook-Signature: t=1793523600,v1=a3f19c...c09e {"id": "evt_01HX9F", "type": "payment.succeeded", "created": 1793523600, "data": {"object": {"id": "pay_42", "amount": 1999}}} - You subscribe in the service's dashboard or through its API: the URL, and which event types you want. - Each event has an id, a type and the data (sometimes the whole object, sometimes only its id, so you fetch the current state yourself). - Each attempt to send it is a delivery . If your endpoint does not answer with a 2xx in time, the service retries later, with backoff, for hours or days. Webhooks are near-instant and cost nothing when nothing happens. In exchange your program must run a public HTTP endpoint , check that requests really come from the service (lesson 4.02), and cope with deliveries that arrive late, twice or out of order (lesson 4.03). Use both Webhooks can be missed: your server was down for longer than the retry window, or the subscription was misconfigured. Robust integrations use webhooks for speed and a slow reconciliation poll (every hour or night) to catch anything missed. Check yourself quiz ? Why can updated_at since miss changes? - Because updated_at is in milliseconds and since is in seconds + Later changes in the same second as the checkpoint are skipped - Because the API returns items in random order - Because is not supported by most APIs Several items can share the checkpoint's timestamp. Use = and remember the ids already seen at exactly that time. ? What makes an adaptive polling interval cheaper? - It asks for smaller pages - It skips the checkpoint on quiet days + It polls less often when nothing is changing - It uses webhooks when the API is busy It backs off after empty polls and speeds up when changes appear, so quiet periods cost few requests. ? What does the service do if your webhook endpoint answers 500? - It drops the event for good - It sends the event to a different URL - It disables the subscription at once + It retries the delivery later, with backoff Any answer other than a 2xx in time counts as a failed delivery, and the service retries it for hours or days. ? Why keep a slow reconciliation poll alongside webhooks? + To catch events whose deliveries were missed - Because webhooks are slower than polling - Because webhooks only carry event ids - To verify the webhooks' signatures Webhooks can be lost when your server is down past the retry window or a subscription is wrong. An occasional poll catches what slipped through.

title: Polling done carefully
body: Before webhooks, write the poller lesson 4.01 describes, including its awkward edge case. python class Poller: def __init__(self, fetch, min_interval=5, max_interval=300): ... def poll(self): ... - list of new or changed items since the checkpoint interval seconds until the next poll fetch(since) returns every item whose updated_at is greater than or equal to since (all items when since is None ). Each item is a dict with an id and an integer updated_at . poll() calls fetch(self.since) and returns, in the order fetched, the items that are new or changed since the last poll: - An item whose updated_at is greater than the checkpoint is always returned. - An item whose updated_at equals the checkpoint is returned only if its id was not already seen at that timestamp. (With = , the API sends back items you already have.) - Afterwards the checkpoint since becomes the largest updated_at fetched, if that is larger, and the ids seen at the checkpoint timestamp are remembered (all of them: those from earlier polls at the same timestamp as well). interval starts at min_interval . After a poll that returned something, it halves, but not below min_interval ; after a poll that returned nothing, it doubles, but not above max_interval .

title: 4.02  Verifying Webhook Signatures
body: Making sure a webhook really came from the service - why a public endpoint must verify every request, the common signature scheme of timestamp plus HMAC of the raw body, signature headers with several values during secret rotation, tolerance windows, and the mistakes that break verification. Anyone can POST to your URL A webhook endpoint is a public URL. Anyone who finds it can send it a request that looks like a "payment succeeded" event. If your code believes it, someone gets goods for free. So every webhook must be verified before you act on it. Services sign their deliveries with a secret shared with you when you set up the subscription (the signing secret , often starting whsec_ ). The scheme most services use, in slightly different spellings: text Webhook-Signature: t=1793523600,v1=a3f19c...c09e - t is the time the service signed it. - v1 is the hex HMAC-SHA256, keyed with the signing secret, of the signed payload : the timestamp, a dot, and the raw request body : "1793523600." + body . To verify: 1. Parse the header into t and the list of v1 values. 2. Reject if t is too far from your clock (5 minutes is typical): this stops replays of old captured deliveries. 3. Compute the HMAC of f"{t}.".encode() + raw_body with your secret. 4. Accept if it equals any of the v1 values, compared with hmac.compare_digest . Use the raw body The signature covers the exact bytes that were sent. If you parse the JSON and dump it again, spaces, key order and escapes change, and the signature no longer matches. Verify before parsing, on the body exactly as received. Web frameworks that parse bodies for you usually have a way to get the raw bytes; use it. Several signatures: secret rotation When you (or the service) rotate the signing secret, there is a period when deliveries may be signed with the old or the new one. Services handle this by sending several v1 values, one per active secret, and your verifier may also hold several secrets. Accept the delivery if any of your secrets matches any of the signatures; this is why step 4 says "any". Other schemes - Some services sign only the body, with the result in a header such as X-Hub-Signature-256: sha256=<hex (GitHub). No timestamp, so no replay protection beyond event ids. - Some send the signature base64-encoded instead of hex. - The Standard Webhooks specification uses webhook-id , webhook-timestamp and webhook-signature headers and signs id.timestamp.body . Each provider's documentation states exactly which bytes are signed and how the result is encoded. Implement it exactly, and test it with the example payload and signature from their documentation. Check yourself quiz ? Why must the signature be checked on the raw body rather than re-serialised JSON? - Because JSON text cannot hold a signature field - Because parsing JSON is too slow for webhooks + Re-serialising changes the bytes, and the signature covers exact bytes - Because the raw body is encrypted and must be decrypted json.dumps(json.loads(body)) rarely gives back the same bytes, so the HMAC would not match. Verify first, then parse. ? What does checking t against your clock protect against? - A wrong signing secret + Replays of old, captured deliveries - Deliveries that arrive out of order - A body that was changed in transit An attacker could resend a captured delivery with its valid signature. Rejecting old timestamps makes such a capture useless after a few minutes. ? Why accept a match with any of several v1 values? - Because each v1 covers a different part of the body - Because the service signs each delivery twice for safety - Because one of the values is always a decoy + During secret rotation, deliveries may be signed with the old and the new secret While a secret is being rotated, both are active, and the service sends one signature per active secret. ? Why compare with hmac.compare_digest ? - Because it also checks the delivery's timestamp - It accepts hex and base64 signatures alike + So its timing cannot reveal how much of the signature matched - Because == cannot compare two bytes objects An ordinary comparison stops at the first difference, and its timing can leak how many leading characters were right.

title: Verifying webhook signatures
body: Implement the signature scheme of lesson 4.02, on both sides. python class SignatureError(Exception): ... def sign_webhook(secret, body, timestamp): ... def verify_webhook(header, body, secrets, now, tolerance=300): ... secret and each of secrets are bytes ; body is the raw request body, bytes . sign_webhook returns the header value t=<timestamp ,v1=<hex , where the hex is the HMAC-SHA256, keyed with secret , of f"{timestamp}." encoded as ASCII followed by the body bytes. verify_webhook returns the timestamp (an int ) if the delivery is genuine, and otherwise raises SignatureError with one of these messages: Message When --- --- missing signature the header is None or empty bad timestamp there is not exactly one t= item, or its value is not digits no v1 signature there is no v1= item timestamp out of range the timestamp is more than tolerance seconds from now signature mismatch no v1 value equals the expected signature for any of the secrets The header is a comma-separated list of name=value items; spaces around items are ignored, and items with other names (such as v0= ) are ignored. Compare signatures with hmac.compare_digest .

title: 4.03  Handling Deliveries
body: What a webhook endpoint must assume about deliveries - they are retried, so they arrive more than once; they arrive out of order; and they must be answered quickly - and the techniques that cope - acknowledge fast and queue, idempotent processing by event id with bounded memory, and versions or fetching current state for ordering. At least once, in any order Services promise at-least-once delivery: every event is delivered, possibly more than once. And they do not promise order: a retried order.created can arrive after the order.shipped that followed it. Your handler must be correct anyway. Answer quickly The service waits only a few seconds for your answer; after that it counts the delivery as failed and retries. So: 1. Verify the signature. 2. Store the event (in a database table or a queue). 3. Answer 2xx immediately. 4. Process it afterwards, in a background worker. A handler that does the real work (sending emails, calling three other APIs) before answering will time out under load, causing retries, causing more load. What to answer: Situation Answer Effect --- --- --- verified and stored (or already seen) 200 done signature invalid 400 or 401 the service may retry, but it will keep failing: that is fine event type you do not handle 200 otherwise it is retried for days your own temporary failure (database down) 500 or 503 the service retries later: exactly what you want Duplicates: idempotent processing Because of retries, the same event id will arrive again. Make processing idempotent : record the ids you have processed, and skip ones already recorded. - Record the id after processing succeeds, in the same database transaction as the effect if possible. Recording first and then failing would drop the event forever. - Memory is not infinite: keep ids for longer than the service's retry window (a few days), and drop older ones. In memory, a bounded structure that forgets the oldest ids is enough (practice 4.03). Order: versions or fresh state Two common ways to stop an old event from overwriting newer data: - Versions or timestamps. If events carry the object's version (or updated_at ), remember the latest version applied per object and ignore anything older. - Fetch the current state. Treat the event only as a notification ("order 42 changed") and fetch order 42 from the API before acting. Whatever order events arrive in, you always act on the current truth. This costs a request per event but is the simplest correct approach, and some services send "thin" events for exactly this reason. Check yourself quiz ? What does at-least-once delivery mean for your handler? + The same event may arrive more than once, so processing must be idempotent - Each event arrives exactly once, in the order it happened - Some events may never arrive, so you must poll for all of them - The service waits for your handler to finish before sending the next event Retries mean duplicates. Record processed event ids and skip ones already seen. ? Why answer 200 for an event type you do not handle? - So the service stops sending you any events + Otherwise the service treats it as failed and keeps retrying it - Because 4xx answers are not allowed for webhooks - So the event is passed on to another subscriber A non-2xx answer means "try again", and an event you will never handle would then be retried for days. ? Why record a processed event id after processing, not before? - Because the id is only known after processing - So that duplicates are processed a second time - Because recording first is slower under load + If processing then fails, the retry is skipped and the event lost Recording first and then failing marks the event as done when it is not. Ideally record it in the same transaction as the effect. ? An order.updated event with version 7 arrives after version 9 was applied. What should happen? - It is applied, because it arrived last - It is answered with 500 so the service sends it again later + It is ignored as stale - It replaces version 9 and version 9 is fetched again Remember the latest version applied per object and ignore anything older, or fetch the current state before acting.

title: Duplicates and late arrivals
body: Process webhook events at least once delivered and in any order, the way lesson 4.03 describes. python class EventProcessor: def __init__(self, apply, memory=1000): ... def handle(self, event): ... - "processed", "duplicate" or "stale" Each event is a dict with an id , an object_id and an integer version (the object's version after the change). apply(event) makes the change. handle(event) : 1. If the event's id is remembered, return "duplicate" . 2. If a version of the same object_id has already been applied and the event's version is not greater , remember the event's id and return "stale" . 3. Otherwise call apply(event) . If it raises, let the exception through and remember nothing (so a retry of the same event works). If it returns, remember the id and the object's new version, and return "processed" . Remembered ids are kept in the order they were remembered; when more than memory are kept, the oldest are forgotten. The versions of objects are always kept.

title: 4.04  A Webhook Receiver
body:
The HTTP side of a webhook endpoint - what a raw request looks like on the wire, parsing the request line, headers and body by Content-Length, choosing status codes for every failure, a minimal receiver with Python's http.server, and what production adds (a framework, HTTPS, a queue). The request on the wire A webhook delivery is an ordinary HTTP request. On the wire, before any framework has touched it: text POST /webhooks HTTP/1.1
 Host: hooks.example.org
 Content-Type: application/json
 Content-Length: 58
 Webhook-Signature: t=1793523600,v1=...
 
 {"id":"evt_1","type":"order.paid","data":{"order":"o_42"}} - The request line : method, path, version. - Headers , one per line, Name: value ; names are case-insensitive. - An empty line, then the body , exactly Content-Length bytes. Frameworks parse this for you, but knowing the shape helps when debugging (what exactly arrived?) and is the clearest way to see which bytes the signature covers. Practice 4.04 parses it by hand. Every way it can fail A receiver should answer each failure with a status that tells the sender the truth: Problem Status --- --- malformed request (bad request line, header without : , body shorter than Content-Length ) 400 wrong path 404 method other than POST 405 missing or invalid signature, timestamp out of range 401 (or 400) body is not valid JSON, or not an event 400 your own failure while storing 500 accepted (new or duplicate) 200 A minimal receiver Python's standard library can run a small HTTP server, enough for development and for understanding: python-norun import json from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer SECRETS = os.environ "WEBHOOK_SECRET" .encode() class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler): def do_POST(self): if self.path != "/webhooks": return self.reply(404) length = int(self.headers.get("Content-Length", "0")) raw = self.rfile.read(length) the raw bytes: verify these if not verify(self.headers.get("Webhook-Signature"), raw, SECRETS, now=time.time()): return self.reply(401) try: event = json.loads(raw) except ValueError: return self.reply(400) queue.put(event) process later self.reply(200) def reply(self, status): self.send_response(status) self.end_headers() HTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 8080), Handler).serve_forever() In production - Run it in a real web framework (Flask, FastAPI, Django) behind a production server, with HTTPS : services refuse to deliver to plain HTTP, and secrets travel in these requests. - Put events on a durable queue or table, and process them in a worker (lesson 4.03). - Log each delivery's event id, type, signature result and status (redacted, lesson 2.05). - Limit the body size: a receiver that reads any Content-Length can be made to allocate gigabytes. Check yourself quiz ? How does the receiver know where the body ends? - At the first newline after the headers - When the sender sends a second empty line + From Content-Length : that many bytes follow the empty line - When the JSON's closing brace is read The empty line ends the headers; Content-Length says how many bytes of body follow. A body shorter than that is malformed. ? Which status for a GET to the webhook URL? - 404 Not Found + 405 Method Not Allowed - 400 Bad Request - 401 Unauthorized The path exists, but only POST is allowed on it. 404 is for a wrong path. ? Why limit the body size a receiver will read? - Because HTTP bodies cannot exceed 64 KB - Because signatures only cover the first megabyte + Otherwise anyone can make it allocate huge amounts of memory - So that duplicate events are smaller The URL is public, and a request can claim any Content-Length . A limit stops it from making you allocate gigabytes. ? Why do services insist on HTTPS endpoints? - Plain HTTP cannot carry JSON bodies - HTTPS makes deliveries arrive in order - HTTPS replaces the need to verify signatures + Deliveries must not be readable or changeable on the way HTTPS protects the delivery in transit. You still verify the signature, which proves who sent it.

title: Parsing a raw HTTP request
body: Parse a webhook delivery as it arrives on the wire (lesson 4.04), so nothing a framework does is hidden from you. python def parse_request(raw, max_body=1_000_000): ... - (method, path, headers, body) raw is bytes . Raise ValueError for anything malformed. The rules: 1. The head ends at the first \r\n\r\n ; if there is none, the request is incomplete. Decode the head as latin-1 . 2. The first line is the request line : exactly three parts separated by single spaces, the method, the path and a version starting with HTTP/1. . 3. Each following line is a header Name: value . A line without : , or with an empty name or a name containing spaces, is malformed. Names are returned in lower case ; values have spaces around them removed. If a name appears more than once, the values are joined with ", " in order. 4. If there is a content-length header, it must be digits, and not more than max_body (otherwise ValueError ); the body is exactly that many bytes after the head, and if fewer bytes are there, the request is incomplete. Bytes after the body are ignored. Without content-length , the body is b"" .

title: 4.05  Testing Webhooks
Fixture deliveries
body: Write the test helpers from lesson 4.05: signed deliveries built in code, and the bad variants every receiver must reject. python def make_delivery(secret, event, timestamp, path="/webhooks", method="POST", sign_with=None, header=True): ... def variants(secret, event, timestamp): ... make_delivery returns the raw HTTP request as bytes : - The body is json.dumps(event, separators=(",", ":"), sort_keys=True) encoded as UTF-8. - The head is these lines, each ending \r\n , followed by an empty line ( \r\n ): <method <path HTTP/1.1 , Host: localhost , Content-Type: application/json , Content-Length: <body length in bytes , and, if header is true, Webhook-Signature: t=<timestamp ,v1=<hex . - The signature is the HMAC-SHA256 of f"{timestamp}." plus the body, keyed with sign_with if given, otherwise secret . variants returns a dict of named deliveries for the same event, all at timestamp unless stated: Name Delivery --- --- valid correctly signed wrong_secret signed with secret + b"-wrong" old correctly signed, but with the timestamp one hour (3600 s) earlier unsigned no signature header get correctly signed, but with method GET changed_body the valid delivery with the last byte of the body replaced by a space (the length stays the same)

title: Check a webhook signature
body: Accept a webhook only when its signature matches. valid delivery: accepted body changed: rejected (bad signature) no signature: rejected (missing header)

title: Deliveries that arrive twice
body: Handle the same webhook event only once, even when it is delivered again. evt_1 order.paid - handled evt_2 order.paid - handled evt_1 order.paid - already handled, skipped evt_3 refund - no handler, acknowledged

title: Old deliveries
body: Refuse webhook deliveries that are too old, to stop replays. timestamp 1767225600, now 1767225660: ok (60 s old) timestamp 1767225000, now 1767225660: refused (660 s old) timestamp in the future by 10 s: ok (clocks differ a little)

title: An event router
body: Send each webhook event to the right handler, with wildcards. order.paid - on_order_paid, log_everything order.refunded - on_any_order, log_everything user.created - log_everything

title: A webhook receiver
body: Build the whole receiving side of webhooks: from raw HTTP bytes to the right handler, answering every delivery with the status that tells the sender the truth. It combines everything in this milestone. python class WebhookReceiver: def __init__(self, secrets, clock, path="/webhooks", tolerance=300, memory=1000): ... def on(self, event_type, handler): ... def receive(self, raw): ... - HTTP status ignored ids of events nobody handles secrets is a list of signing secrets ( bytes , several during rotation); clock() gives the time in seconds. on registers the handler for an event type; a handler is called with the event dict. receive(raw) goes through these steps and returns the status of the first that decides: Step Status --- --- Parse the request as in practice 4.04 (bodies up to 1 000 000 bytes); malformed 400 The path (without any ?query ) is not the receiver's path 404 The method is not POST 405 Verify the Webhook-Signature header against the raw body as in practice 4.02, with every secret, clock() as now and the tolerance; any failure 401 The body is not JSON for an object with a string id , a string type , a string object_id and an integer version (not a boolean) 400 The event id is remembered (a duplicate) 200 The object already has a version applied and this event's version is not greater (stale): remember the id 200 No handler is registered for the type: add the id to ignored , remember the id 200 The handler raises any exception: remember nothing 500 The handler returns: remember the id and the object's version 200 Remembered event ids are bounded by memory as in practice 4.03 (the oldest are forgotten); object versions are always kept.

title: 5.01  Designing an Integration
body: The decisions to make before writing code that connects two services - which system owns which data, one-way or two-way, triggered by webhooks, schedules or users, how records in one system find their partners in the other, and writing it all down on one page. Two systems, one picture Most real API work is integration : making two services that were not designed for each other work together. An online shop and an accounting package; a form tool and a CRM; an issue tracker and a chat app. The code is rarely the hard part. The hard part is the decisions, and they are best made before the first request. The running example for this milestone: paid orders in a shop become invoices in an accounting system . Who owns what? For every kind of data, decide which system is the source of truth : Data Owner The other system --- --- --- orders, customers, prices shop receives copies invoice numbers, payment status in the books accounting never writes these back into the shop Copies are never edited by hand in the receiving system, or the next sync overwrites the edit (or worse, sometimes does and sometimes does not). If both systems must edit the same data, you need conflict rules (lesson 5.03), and it is worth trying hard to avoid that. Which direction, triggered how? - One-way (shop to accounting) is far simpler than two-way . Choose it whenever you can. - Triggers : a webhook from the shop (fast, lesson 4.01); a schedule (every 10 minutes, simple and robust); or a user action ("send to accounting" button). Many integrations combine a webhook for speed with a scheduled sync to catch anything missed. Finding partners: the id map The shop's order 1001 becomes the accounting system's invoice INV-2026-0042 . The integration must remember that pair, so that a later change to the order updates the invoice instead of creating a second one. Two ways: - Store the other system's id in a field of the record, if the API allows custom fields or an external reference ( "external_ref": "shop-1001" ), and look it up there. - Keep your own id map : a small table of (shop id, accounting id) pairs (practice 5.01). An external reference in the target system also makes your integration recoverable: if your id map is lost, it can be rebuilt by searching. Write it down Before coding, write one page: the systems and versions; what flows where and who owns it; the triggers; the field mapping (next lesson); what happens on deletes, on errors, and on the first run with existing data; and how someone will know it is working (lesson 5.05). It is the document the next person (often you, months later) needs, and writing it surfaces the questions the business must answer: "should refunds void the invoice or create a credit note?" Check yourself quiz ? Why should copies in the receiving system not be edited by hand? - The receiving system's API does not allow edits + The next sync may overwrite the edits - Hand edits are slower than API calls - Edited copies cannot be deleted later The source of truth owns that data. Edits to a copy are overwritten by the next sync, or worse, sometimes kept and sometimes not. ? Why is one-way sync preferred when possible? - It needs fewer API keys and scopes - It makes webhooks unnecessary - It copies data faster than two-way sync + It avoids conflicts and update loops With one direction there is a single owner per record, so there is nothing to reconcile and no echo to suppress. ? What is the id map for? - Translating field names between the two APIs + Pairing records across the systems, so changes update, not duplicate - Listing the endpoints that each system offers - Storing the API keys used for each system When order 1001 changes, the map says it is invoice INV-2026-0042, so the integration updates that invoice rather than creating a second one. ? Which two triggers do integrations often combine? - Two webhooks, one from each system - A user action and a manual export + A webhook for speed and a scheduled sync to catch anything missed - A scheduled sync every minute and another every hour The webhook brings changes in quickly; the slower schedule catches any delivery that was missed.

title: An id map
body: Keep track of which record in system A corresponds to which record in system B (lesson 5.01), one to one, and save it between runs. python class IdMap: def link(self, a, b): ... def b_for(self, a): ... def a_for(self, b): ... def unlink(self, a): ... def __len__(self): ... def to_json(self): ... @classmethod def from_json(cls, text): ... - link records that a and b belong together. Linking a pair that is already linked does nothing. If a is linked to a different b , or b to a different a , raise ValueError and change nothing. - b_for and a_for look up the partner, or return None . - unlink removes a and its partner; it returns whether there was anything to remove. - len is the number of pairs. - to_json returns a JSON array of a, b pairs sorted by a . from_json builds a map from such text; a pair that is not a list of two strings, or pairs that break the one-to-one rule, raise ValueError .

title: 5.02  Mapping Data Between APIs
body: Turning one API's records into another's - a field mapping table, money as integers or decimals rather than floats, enumerations mapped explicitly with a decision for unknown values, names and emails, missing versus null, and dates and times across time zones with ISO 8601, datetime and zoneinfo. The mapping table Write the mapping as a table first, with a row for every target field and where its value comes from: Invoice field From the order Rule --- --- --- external_ref id "shop-" + id date created_at the local date in the company's time zone customer_name customer.first_name , customer.last_name joined with a space, trimmed email customer.email lower case amount total_cents "19.99" : a decimal string state status paid to open , refunded to void ; anything else is an error Each row hides a decision; the rest of this lesson is about the common ones. Money Never use binary floating point for money: 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004 . APIs send money as an integer of the smallest unit ( 1999 cents) or a decimal string ( "19.99" ). Convert with integer arithmetic or decimal.Decimal : python from decimal import Decimal cents = 1999 print(f"{cents // 100}.{cents % 100:02d}") print(Decimal(cents) / 100, Decimal("19.99") 3) print(0.1 + 0.2) 19.99 19.99 59.97 0.30000000000000004 Also check the currency : not every currency has two decimal places (yen has none), so cents / 100 is only right for the ones that do. Enumerations Status fields are the most common source of silent bugs. Map them with an explicit table, and decide what happens to a value not in it: raise an error, skip the record, or use a documented default. Never let an unknown status fall through as some default by accident; the day the shop adds partially_refunded , you want to know. Missing, null and empty {"phone": null} , {"phone": ""} and {} may mean different things: "known to have none", "entered blank", "not sent in this partial update". In particular, a PATCH -style partial update must not turn "not sent" into "erase the value". Decide per field, and write it in the mapping table. Dates and times Timestamps travel as ISO 8601 strings ( 2026-11-19T23:30:00Z , where Z means UTC, or with an offset like +01:00 ) or as seconds since 1970. Rules that avoid nearly every time bug: - Keep everything in UTC internally, as timezone-aware datetime objects. - Convert to local time only at the edge where a human-facing date is needed, such as an invoice date. - An order paid at 23:30 UTC on 19 November is dated 20 November in Amsterdam (UTC+1). Using the UTC date puts it in the wrong day, and at month end in the wrong month and the wrong tax period. python-norun from datetime import datetime from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo on Windows: pip install tzdata created = datetime.fromisoformat("2026-11-19T23:30:00+00:00") local = created.astimezone(ZoneInfo("Europe/Amsterdam")) print(local.date().isoformat()) 2026-11-20 Prefer named time zones ( Europe/Amsterdam ) over fixed offsets in real code: they know about daylight saving time. (The practice uses fixed offsets so it runs anywhere.) Keep the mapping testable Write the mapping as a pure function , record in, record out, with no requests inside. It is then trivial to test with sample records, including the awkward ones: a missing last name, an unknown status, a timestamp just before midnight. Check yourself quiz ? Why not convert total_cents with total_cents / 100 and store a float? + Binary floats cannot hold most decimal amounts exactly - Division by 100 rounds the cents away - JSON cannot hold floating-point numbers - Floats are too large to store in an invoice 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004 . Integer cents or decimal.Decimal keep money exact. ? The shop adds a new order status. What should your mapping do? - Map it to the most common existing status - Skip the order without recording why + Fail loudly, or follow a documented rule for unknown values - Copy the new status text into the invoice unchanged An explicit table with a deliberate rule for unknown values means you find out the day partially_refunded appears. ? An order was created at 2026-11-30T23:30:00Z. What is its invoice date in Amsterdam (UTC+1)? - 30 November 2026 - 29 November 2026 - 1 November 2026 + 1 December 2026 23:30 UTC is 00:30 the next day in UTC+1, which is also the next month. Using the UTC date would put the invoice in the wrong month and tax period. ? Why write the mapping as a pure function? - Pure functions run faster than methods - It lets the mapping make its own API requests + It can be tested with sample records, without any API - Because the target API requires it Record in, record out, no requests: awkward cases like a missing last name or a timestamp just before midnight become one-line tests.

An order looks like this: python-norun {"id": "1001", "created_at": "2026-11-19T23:30:00Z", "currency": "EUR", "total_cents": 2497, "status": "paid", "customer": {"first_name": "Ada", "last_name": "Lovelace", "email": " Ada@Example.com "}, "lines": {"sku": "BK-1", "qty": 2, "unit_cents": 999}, {"sku": "PEN", "qty": 1, "unit_cents": 499} } Return a dict with these keys, in this order, or raise ValueError as described: Key Rule --- --- external_ref "shop-" followed by the order's id date created_at read with datetime.fromisoformat , converted to the company's time zone, a fixed UTC offset of offset_minutes ; its date as YYYY-MM-DD .
