title: 5.03  Incremental Sync
body: Copying only what changed since last time - checkpoints and updated-since queries, upserting by external id so that reruns are safe, deletes through tombstones or periodic reconciliation, the first run over existing data, and the extra problems of two-way sync - conflicts and echo loops. Not everything, every time Copying all records on every run works for ten records and fails at ten thousand. An incremental sync asks only for what changed since the last run: 1. Load the checkpoint : the largest updated_at processed last time. 2. Fetch changes updated_since the checkpoint (paging through them, lesson 3.01). 3. For each change, in order, upsert it into the target. 4. Save the new checkpoint after the changes are safely applied. If the program crashes between steps 3 and 4, the next run processes some changes again. That is fine, as long as step 3 is idempotent . Upsert by external id Upsert means "update if it exists, otherwise insert". With the id map (lesson 5.01), or an external reference in the target, reapplying the same change finds the existing record and updates it to the same values: nothing is duplicated. Never write a sync whose correctness depends on running each change exactly once. The boundary problem from lesson 4.01 appears here too: ask for updated_at = checkpoint and skip records already applied at exactly that timestamp, or a record updated in the same second as the checkpoint can be lost. Deletes A deleted record does not show up in "what changed" unless the source tells you: - Tombstones : the API returns deleted records in the change feed, marked "deleted": true (or has a separate deleted-records endpoint). Apply them as deletes, voids or archives. - Reconciliation : otherwise, periodically fetch the full list of ids from the source, compare with your id map, and handle the missing ones. Slower, but catches everything. Decide what a delete means in the target: in accounting, you never delete an invoice; you void it or issue a credit note. The first run On the first run there is no checkpoint, and the target may already contain records created by hand before the integration existed. Plan the backfill : fetch everything (respecting rate limits), match existing target records by a natural key (an order number, an email) before creating new ones, and set the checkpoint at the end. Two-way sync When both systems may change the same records, two new problems appear: - Conflicts : the record changed on both sides since the last sync. Common rules: last writer wins by updated_at (simple, can lose an edit), field ownership (the shop owns the address, the CRM owns the notes), or flagging the conflict for a person. - Echo loops : you write a change into B; B reports it as a change; you copy it back into A; A reports it... Prevent it by remembering what you wrote (and ignoring the echo), comparing values before writing (no change, no write), or marking records with the integration as their last editor. Check yourself quiz ? Why save the checkpoint only after the changes are applied? - So the checkpoint is never larger than the current time + If the run crashes, the changes are fetched again rather than lost - Because the API only accepts checkpoints at the end of a run - So every change is processed exactly once Saving first and then crashing would skip the unapplied changes forever. Saving after means a crash repeats some, which upserts make harmless. ? What makes reprocessing a change harmless? - Deleting the target record before each write - Processing each change exactly once - Sorting the changes by id before applying them + Upserting by external id, so it updates the same record An upsert finds the existing record and sets it to the same values, so nothing is duplicated however often it runs. ? How can a sync learn about deleted records? - They appear in the change feed with their old values - The checkpoint goes backwards when a record is deleted + Tombstones in the change feed, or reconciling against all ids - It cannot: deletes are never visible through an API A plain "changed since" feed does not show what is gone. Tombstones mark deletes; reconciliation finds ids that have disappeared. ? What is an echo loop in two-way sync? + Your own write to B comes back as a change and is copied to A - Two systems editing the same record at the same moment - A sync that fetches the same page twice - A webhook delivered twice by the same service Remember what you wrote, skip writes that change nothing, or mark the integration as last editor, so your own writes are not copied back.

title: One incremental sync run
body: Write one run of the incremental one-way sync from lesson 5.03. python def sync_once(source, target, state): ... - summary dict - source.changes(since) returns the changes whose updated_at is at least since (all of them when since is None ). Each is a dict with an id , an integer updated_at , a data dict, and optionally "deleted": True . - target.upsert(id, data) creates or updates; target.delete(id) deletes and returns whether there was something to delete. - state is a dict with since (an integer or None ) and seen (a list of the ids already applied at exactly since ). Update it in place. The run: 1. Fetch source.changes(state "since" ) . 2. Skip a change whose updated_at equals since and whose id is in seen (count it as skipped ). 3. If an id appears several times among the rest, apply only its last change in order of updated_at (for equal times, the later one in the list), and count the others as skipped . 4. Apply the remaining changes in order of updated_at : a deleted change calls delete (counted as deleted only if it returned true); any other calls upsert with its data (counted as upserted ). 5. Update the state: since becomes the largest updated_at fetched, if that is larger than before; seen becomes the ids of all fetched changes at exactly the new since (plus the previous seen , if since did not move), sorted. Return {"upserted": n, "deleted": n, "skipped": n} .

title: 5.04  Partial Failure and Dead Letters
body: What to do when some records fail and others succeed - never letting one bad record stop the rest, sorting failures into transient and permanent, retrying the transient ones, keeping the permanent ones in a dead-letter list with the reason, replaying them after a fix, and the outbox pattern for keeping a database and an API in step. One bad record A sync processes a thousand orders and order 417 has an email address the accounting API rejects. The worst possible behaviour is the most common one: an exception stops the run, the checkpoint is not saved, and the next run fails on order 417 again, forever. Nothing after it is ever synced. Transient or permanent? Sort every failure into one of two kinds: Kind Examples Action --- --- --- transient timeout, connection reset, 429, 5xx retry (lesson 3.03); usually works soon permanent 400 or 422 validation errors, an unmapped status, a missing required field retrying cannot help; set the record aside Make the distinction explicit in code, with your own exception classes, so the processing loop can act on it: python-norun class TransientError(Exception): ... class PermanentError(Exception): ... for record in records: try: with_retries(lambda: handle(record)) retries TransientError a few times except (TransientError, PermanentError) as e: dead_letters.append({"record": record, "reason": str(e)}) continue the rest still get processed Dead letters A dead-letter queue (or list, or table) holds the records that could not be processed, each with: - the record (or its id), - the reason , as specific as possible ("accounting rejected email: invalid format"), - how many attempts were made and when. The run continues past them and its checkpoint advances: the dead letters, not the checkpoint, remember what still needs doing. Someone (or an alert, lesson 5.05) looks at them, the cause is fixed (the mapping, the data in the shop, a bug), and the dead letters are replayed : processed again, and removed when they succeed. Practice 5.04 builds both halves. A dead-letter list that only grows is a sign nobody is looking. Count it, alert on it. Keeping a database and an API in step: the outbox A common shape: your program saves an order in its own database and must tell another API about it. Doing both directly fails awkwardly: save succeeds and the API call fails, and the API never hears; or the API call succeeds and the save fails, and you told it about something that does not exist. The outbox pattern fixes this: in the same database transaction as the order, insert a row "send order 42 to accounting" into an outbox table. A separate worker reads the outbox, makes the API call (with retries and an idempotency key, lesson 3.04), and marks the row done. The database transaction makes "order saved" and "message queued" happen together or not at all; the worker makes delivery eventually happen. Check yourself quiz ? Why must one failing record not stop a sync run? - Because exceptions cannot be caught inside a loop - Because the failing record will fix itself on the next run + Otherwise the checkpoint never advances and every later record is blocked behind it - Because the API counts failures against the rate limit The run would fail on the same record every time. Set it aside as a dead letter and carry on. ? Is a 422 from the target transient or permanent? + Permanent: the data is invalid and will fail again - Transient: retry it with backoff - Transient: wait for Retry-After , then retry - Permanent, but only after three attempts Validation errors do not go away by waiting. Timeouts, 429 and 5xx are the transient ones. ? What should a dead letter record? - Only the record's id, to keep it small - The full stack trace and nothing else + The record, a specific reason, and its attempts - The checkpoint at the time it failed A specific reason and the attempt history are what a person needs to fix the cause and replay it. ? What problem does the outbox pattern solve? - Retrying requests that hit a rate limit - Storing webhooks that arrive out of order - Removing duplicate records from a sync + Making a database change and its API call happen together The outbox row is written in the same transaction as the change, and a worker delivers it later with retries.

title: Dead letters and replay
body: Process a batch so that bad records are set aside instead of stopping everything, and replay them later (lesson 5.04). python class TransientError(Exception): ... class PermanentError(Exception): ... def process_batch(records, handler, dead_letters, max_attempts=3): ... def replay(dead_letters, handler, max_attempts=3): ... process_batch calls handler(record) for each record, in order, and returns {"ok": <records handled , "dead": <records added to dead_letters } . For each record: - If the handler returns, the record is done. - TransientError : try the same record again, up to max_attempts attempts in all. If the last attempt also fails, add a dead letter. - PermanentError : add a dead letter at once. - Any other exception: add a dead letter at once. A dead letter is a dict {"record": record, "reason": reason, "attempts": n} , appended to the dead_letters list, where n is the number of attempts made and reason is "transient: <message " , "permanent: <message " or "unexpected: <ExceptionType : <message " , using the last exception. Either way, the batch continues with the next record. replay processes each dead letter's record again with the same rules, in order. Records that now succeed are removed from the list; the others stay, in their original order, with their reason replaced by the new one and their attempts increased by the attempts just made. It returns how many succeeded. The list is changed in place.

title: 5.05  Keeping an Integration Observable
body: Knowing an integration works without watching it - structured log lines with correlation ids, a summary per run, the few numbers worth tracking (processed, failed, dead letters, lag), alerts that fire on the right things, health checks, and scheduling runs with cron or Windows Task Scheduler. Silent failure Integrations fail quietly. Nobody looks at a sync until the accountant asks why no invoices arrived for three weeks. Building in observability (being able to tell from the outside what it is doing) is part of the job, not an extra. Structured logs Log events , one JSON object per line, with fixed fields, rather than free text: text {"ts": "2026-11-19T10:00:03Z", "level": "info", "msg": "invoice created", "run": "r-0193", "order": "1001", "invoice": "INV-42"} {"ts": "2026-11-19T10:00:04Z", "level": "error", "msg": "dead letter", "run": "r-0193", "order": "1017", "reason": "422 invalid email"} - Machines can search and count them: "all errors for order 1017", "invoices created per day". - Every line of one run shares a run id ; lines about one record share its id; requests carry the API's request id (lesson 1.02). These correlation ids let you follow one record through the whole system. - Redact secrets before writing (lesson 2.05). A summary per run At the end of each run, write one summary line: when it started, how long it took, how many records were created, updated, skipped and dead-lettered, and the new checkpoint. Most questions ("is it running?", "did yesterday's run do anything?") are answered by the last few summaries. The numbers that matter Metric Tells you --- --- records processed per run it is doing work errors and dead letters something needs attention lag : now minus the checkpoint (or the oldest unprocessed change) how far behind it is time since the last successful run whether it is running at all API error rates and 429s the other side is struggling, or you are calling too fast Lag and time since the last success catch the failures that produce no errors at all: a scheduler that stopped, a webhook subscription that was deleted. Alerts Alert on things a person must act on, rarely enough that alerts are not ignored: - no successful run for N intervals; - lag above a threshold; - new dead letters (or the count above zero for a day); - the error rate far above normal. Scheduling and health A scheduled sync runs from cron on Linux and macOS, Task Scheduler on Windows, or a cloud scheduler. Make each run safe to run twice at once (or prevent it with a lock), since schedulers sometimes overlap runs. A webhook receiver should expose a health check URL that a monitor can call, returning 200 only if it can reach what it depends on. Check yourself quiz ? Why log JSON objects instead of free-text lines? - JSON lines are shorter than free text + Machines can search, filter and count them by field - JSON lines cannot contain secrets - Log files must be valid JSON documents Fixed fields make questions like "all errors for order 1017" a filter, not a guess. Secrets still need redacting. ? What is a correlation id? - The id of the API key that made a request - A number that counts the lines of a log + An id shared by every log line about one run or record - The checkpoint saved at the end of a run Run ids, record ids and the API's request ids let you follow one thing through every log line it touched. ? Which metric catches a sync that silently stopped running? - The number of errors per run - The API's error rate - The number of dead letters + Time since the last successful run (or lag) A sync that stopped produces no errors at all. Only "how long since it last worked" or "how far behind it is" notices. ? Why make a scheduled run safe to run twice at the same time? - Because each run must process every record twice + Schedulers can start a new run while the previous one is still going - Because cron always starts two copies - So the health check can call it Overlapping runs happen; make them harmless, or prevent them with a lock.

title: Orders to invoices
body: Build the integration this milestone has been describing: paid shop orders become invoices in an accounting system, incrementally, safely rerunnable, with failures set aside rather than blocking everything. It combines the id map, the mapping, the incremental run and the dead letters of practices 5.01 to 5.04. python class Transient(Exception): ... class OrderSync: def __init__(self, shop, books, offset_minutes, state=None): ... def run(self): ... - summary state a dict that survives json.dumps and json.loads The services. shop.changed_orders(since) returns the orders whose updated_at (an integer) is at least since (all orders when since is None ), sorted by updated_at . An order has the fields of practice 5.02, or is a tombstone {"id": ..., "updated_at": ..., "deleted": True} . The accounting system offers books.create_invoice(invoice) , which returns the new invoice's id, books.update_invoice(invoice_id, invoice) and books.void_invoice(invoice_id) . Each may raise Transient (try again) or ValueError (the data was rejected). The state starts as {"since": None, "seen": , "links": {}, "dead": } when none is given: the checkpoint, the ids already handled at exactly the checkpoint (as in practice 5.03), the links from order id to invoice id, and the dead letters. Only strings, numbers, lists, dicts and None go in it. A run: 1. Fetch shop.changed_orders(since) and skip the orders already handled at the checkpoint, as in practice 5.03. 2. Handle each remaining order in the order given: - A tombstone : if the order is linked, void its invoice (counted as voided ); otherwise nothing. - Any other order: map it with order_to_invoice(order, offset_minutes) from practice 5.02 (include that function in your code). If the order is linked, update its invoice ( updated ); otherwise create one, link the order to the new id ( created ). 3. A call to books that raises Transient is tried again, up to 3 attempts in all. 4. If mapping raises ValueError , or a books call raises ValueError or fails with Transient 3 times, the order becomes a dead letter {"order": id, "reason": reason} , with reason "mapping: <message " or "books: <message " , and the run continues. Each order has at most one dead letter: a new failure replaces its old entry, and a later success removes it. 5. Update the checkpoint from all fetched orders, as in practice 5.03. run() returns {"created": n, "updated": n, "voided": n, "dead": <dead letters added or replaced in this run , "since": <the new checkpoint } .

title: 6.01  Why Python Calls C
body: The other kind of API - a native library's functions - why C's calling convention is the common language every other language can speak, what you gain by calling into C from Python, the tools available (ctypes, cffi, extension modules), and the new kind of failure it brings - crashes instead of exceptions. A different kind of API Web APIs connect programs over a network. A native library (a .dll on Windows, .so on Linux, .dylib on macOS) offers its API as functions in the same process : no HTTP, no JSON, just a call with arguments in registers and memory. The Windows API, SQLite, zlib, OpenSSL, graphics drivers and countless vendor SDKs are all native libraries with C interfaces. C as the common language Almost every language can call functions that follow the C calling convention (the ABI : how arguments are passed, who cleans up the stack, how structures are laid out in memory), and most libraries offer a C interface even when written in C++ or Rust. So C is the lingua franca: a library with a C API can be used from Python, C , JavaScript, Go, Java and more. Reasons to call C from Python: - Use something only available natively : an operating system function, a hardware vendor's SDK, a library with no Python package. - Speed : a hot loop moved into C (NumPy, Pillow and most of the scientific stack do this). - Reuse : a company's existing C or C++ code, without rewriting it. The tools Tool How it works Good for --- --- --- ctypes (standard library) describe the C types in Python, load the library, call quick bindings, no compiler needed cffi (package) paste the C declarations; it works out the types larger APIs, written from the header C extension modules write C against Python's own C API, compile it maximum speed and control pybind11 , nanobind C++ templates generate the extension wrapping C++ classes Cython Python-like language compiled to C speeding up Python code, calling C This milestone uses ctypes , because it needs nothing installed and shows exactly what every binding tool must do underneath: describe each type, each function's arguments and result, and who owns which memory. A new kind of failure Inside Python, a mistake raises an exception you can catch and read. Across the boundary into C, Python cannot check anything: if you describe a function wrongly (an int where the library expects a pointer, a buffer that is too short, a structure laid out differently), the program crashes with an access violation, or worse, keeps running with corrupted memory. So binding code is written carefully, from the header file , with every type spelled out (lesson 6.02), and tested. Check yourself quiz ? Why do so many libraries offer a C interface? - C is the only language that can be compiled into a library - C functions run faster than functions in any other language + Nearly every language can call C functions, so a C API reaches every language - Operating systems refuse to load libraries written in other languages The C calling convention is the common ground. A library written in C++ or Rust usually exposes a C API for exactly this reason. ? Which of these is a good reason to call C from Python? + Using a vendor SDK that only exists as a native library - Making a web API respond faster - Getting Python exceptions with clearer messages - Avoiding the need to read a library's documentation Native-only features, speed in a hot loop, and reusing existing C code are the usual reasons. Errors across the boundary get harder, not clearer. ? What happens if a ctypes binding declares an argument with the wrong type? - ctypes raises a TypeError explaining the mismatch - The C compiler reports an error when the library loads + Usually a crash or memory corruption, not a Python exception - The value is converted to the right type automatically Python cannot check what C expects. A wrong declaration means C reads the wrong bytes, which crashes or silently corrupts memory. ? Where should the type information for a binding come from? - From calling each function and seeing what comes back - From the library's file name - From guessing, then fixing whatever crashes + From the library's header file (its C declarations) The header states each function's argument and result types exactly. Write the binding from it, type by type.

title: From C declarations to ctypes
body: Translating a header into ctypes is mechanical (lesson 6.02), so let a program do it. Write the two functions every binding generator starts with. python def ctypes_name(c_type): ... def parse_prototype(line): ... - (restype, name, argtypes ) ctypes_name returns the ctypes spelling of a C type, as text: - const is ignored, and spaces around do not matter. - Base types: void → None , char → c_char , signed char → c_byte , unsigned char → c_ubyte , short → c_short , unsigned short → c_ushort , int → c_int , unsigned int and unsigned → c_uint , long long → c_longlong , unsigned long long → c_ulonglong , float → c_float , double → c_double , bool → c_bool , size_t → c_size_t , wchar_t → c_wchar , and int8_t ... uint64_t → c_int8 ... c_uint64 . - struct NAME → NAME . - Pointers: the first on char , wchar_t and void gives c_char_p , c_wchar_p and c_void_p ; every other wraps what is there in POINTER(...) . So int → POINTER(c_int) , char → POINTER(c_char_p) , struct point → POINTER(point) . - long and unsigned long raise ValueError : their size differs between Windows and other systems. Any unknown type also raises ValueError . parse_prototype reads one function declaration such as int32_t compress(const uint8_t in, size_t n, uint8_t out ); (with or without the final ; ). It returns the ctypes names of the return type, the function's name, and the list of parameter types. The return type and the name may be written char name(...) or char name(...) . Each parameter's name is optional and is left out of the type; a parameter written name or name N is a pointer. A parameter list of void or nothing is empty. Anything that is not a declaration raises ValueError .

title: 6.02  ctypes Basics
body: Calling a C function from Python with ctypes - loading a library on Windows, Linux and macOS, the ctypes types that match C types, why argtypes and restype must always be set, how ints, bytes, str and None are passed, and translating a function's declaration from its header line by line. Loading a library python-norun import ctypes, ctypes.util, sys if sys.platform == "win32": kernel32 = ctypes.WinDLL("kernel32", use_last_error=True) Windows API functions libc = ctypes.CDLL("msvcrt") the old C runtime, for examples else: libc = ctypes.CDLL(ctypes.util.find_library("c")) libc.so.6 or libSystem mylib = ctypes.CDLL("./mylib.dll") your own library, by path CDLL uses the C calling convention; WinDLL uses stdcall , which the Windows API uses on 32-bit Windows (on 64-bit Windows both are the same, but WinDLL documents intent). Library functions are attributes: libc.strlen , kernel32.GetTickCount64 . Types C ctypes Python value --- --- --- int , unsigned int c_int , c_uint int long long , int64_t , uint8_t ... c_longlong , c_int64 , c_uint8 ... int size_t c_size_t int double , float c_double , c_float float bool c_bool bool char c_char one-byte bytes const char (text) c_char_p bytes (or None for NULL) const wchar_t c_wchar_p str void c_void_p int address or None T POINTER(T) (lesson 6.03) Beware long : it is 32 bits on Windows and 64 bits on Linux and macOS, so c_long changes size between systems. Prefer fixed-width types ( int32_t , c_int32 ) in your own C APIs. Always set argtypes and restype Without declarations, ctypes guesses : every return value is treated as a C int , and arguments are converted from whatever Python value you pass. The guess is wrong for anything returning a pointer, a double or a 64-bit value, and the error is silent: a 64-bit pointer is cut to 32 bits, and later use crashes. So, for every function, write both from its declaration: python-norun C: size_t strlen(const char s); libc.strlen.argtypes = ctypes.c_char_p libc.strlen.restype = ctypes.c_size_t print(libc.strlen(b"hello")) 5 C: double pow(double x, double y); libm.pow.argtypes = ctypes.c_double, ctypes.c_double libm.pow.restype = ctypes.c_double print(libm.pow(2.0, 10.0)) 1024.0 C: void free_thing(struct thing t); mylib.free_thing.argtypes = ctypes.c_void_p mylib.free_thing.restype = None void With argtypes set, ctypes also checks the arguments: passing a str where c_char_p is declared raises ArgumentError instead of handing C a pointer to the wrong thing. Text across the boundary C strings are bytes. A c_char_p argument takes bytes : encode your text first ( "café".encode("utf-8") ), and decode results you get back. Wide wchar_t strings, which the W functions of the Windows API use, map to str with c_wchar_p . A function returning c_char_p gives you a copy as bytes ; the original memory still belongs to the library (lesson 6.03 is about ownership). Reading a declaration Turning a header line into a binding is mechanical, which is why practice 6.01 makes a program do it: text int32_t compress_block(const uint8_t input, size_t length, uint8_t output, size_t capacity); │ │ │ │ │ │ restype the name POINTER(c_uint8) c_size_t POINTER(c_uint8) c_size_t c_int32 Check yourself quiz ? What does ctypes assume a function returns if restype is not set? - void + A C int - A pointer - A double Without restype , the result is read as an int . A 64-bit pointer is cut to 32 bits, and a double comes back as nonsense. ? Why is c_long risky in a binding meant for Windows and Linux? - c_long does not exist on Windows - c_long is always 64 bits, but C's long is 32 bits + long is 32 bits on Windows and 64 bits on Linux and macOS - c_long is unsigned on Linux The size of C's long depends on the platform, and c_long follows it. Fixed-width types like c_int32 mean the same everywhere. ? What Python value do you pass for a const char parameter? - A str , which ctypes encodes for you - An int holding the string's address - A list of one-character strings + bytes (encoded text), or None for NULL C strings are bytes: encode text first. With argtypes set, passing a str raises ArgumentError ; c_wchar_p is the type that takes a str . ? What does restype = None mean? - The result type is guessed from the value - The function returns NULL on failure + The function returns void - The function returns a Python None object as a pointer None as restype declares a void function, so ctypes does not try to read a result.

title: Structure layout by hand
body: Compute where a C compiler puts each field of a structure (lesson 6.03), and check yourself against ctypes, which follows the same rules. python def layout(fields, pack=None): ... - {"offsets": {...}, "size": n, "align": a} fields is a list of (name, type) pairs. A type is one of the names below, or an array written type n : Type Size and natural alignment --- --- char , bool , int8_t , uint8_t 1 short , int16_t , uint16_t 2 int , int32_t , uint32_t , float 4 long long , int64_t , uint64_t , double , pointer 8 The rules (for 64-bit Windows, Linux and macOS): 1. A field's alignment is its natural alignment, or pack if that is given and smaller. An array has the size of n elements and the alignment of one element. 2. Each field goes at the first offset after the previous field that is a multiple of its alignment. The bytes skipped are padding. 3. The structure's alignment is the largest field alignment (1 for an empty structure), and its size is the end of the last field rounded up to a multiple of that alignment. Unknown types, and arrays whose length is not a positive whole number, raise ValueError .

title: 6.03  Structures, Pointers and Buffers
body: Passing data rather than single values - ctypes Structure and the C rules for field alignment and padding, packed structures, arrays, passing by reference with byref and pointer, buffers created with create_string_buffer, and the question that decides crashes - who owns and frees each piece of memory. Structures A C struct becomes a ctypes.Structure subclass whose _fields_ list the members in the same order with the same types : python import ctypes class Point(ctypes.Structure): _fields_ = ("x", ctypes.c_int), ("y", ctypes.c_double) p = Point(3, 4.5) print(ctypes.sizeof(Point), Point.x.offset, Point.y.offset) print(p.x, p.y) 16 0 8 3 4.5 The size is 16, not 12: C aligns each field to a multiple of its own size (up to 8 on 64-bit systems), so 4 bytes of padding follow x to put y at offset 8; the whole structure's size is rounded up to a multiple of its largest alignment, so arrays of it stay aligned. ctypes follows the same rules as the C compiler, which is the point: the bytes must match exactly. Practice 6.02 computes these layouts by hand. Some structures are packed ( pragma pack(1) or __attribute__((packed)) in the header): no padding at all. Mirror that with _pack_ = 1 in the class, or every field after the first gap is read from the wrong place. Arrays and buffers python import ctypes numbers = (ctypes.c_int 4)(1, 2, 3, 4) int numbers 4 print(list(numbers), ctypes.sizeof(numbers)) buf = ctypes.create_string_buffer(b"hi", 8) char buf 8 , writable print(buf.raw, buf.value) 1, 2, 3, 4 16 b'hi\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00' b'hi' Use create_string_buffer(size) (or create_unicode_buffer for wchar_t ) whenever C writes into a buffer you provide, passing its size as the function's documentation says (the buffer-size patterns of the Reading Documentation course, milestone 3, apply unchanged). Pointers - ctypes.byref(obj) passes the address of obj : the light way to pass a structure or a number for C to fill in ( int out ). - ctypes.pointer(obj) makes a real pointer object you can store; POINTER(Point) is the type "pointer to Point", for argtypes , restype and structure fields. - A returned pointer is read with result.contents (one object) or indexing result i (an array). python-norun C: int get_position(struct point out); lib.get_position.argtypes = ctypes.POINTER(Point) lib.get_position.restype = ctypes.c_int pos = Point() if lib.get_position(ctypes.byref(pos)) == 0: print(pos.x, pos.y) Who owns the memory? Every pointer crossing the boundary raises one question, and the header or documentation must answer it: Situation Rule --- --- you pass a buffer or structure you created you own it; it must stay alive for as long as C uses it C returns a pointer to its own data C owns it; do not free it, and copy what you need before it changes C returns memory it allocated for you you must free it, with the function the library documents ( mylib_free(p) ), never Python's or another C runtime's free Python objects are freed when nothing references them. If C keeps a pointer to a buffer after the call returns (registering a buffer for later use), keep a Python reference to that buffer for as long as C might use it, or C writes into freed memory. Check yourself quiz ? Why is struct { int x; double y; } 16 bytes and not 12? - ctypes adds 4 bytes of bookkeeping to every structure - int is 8 bytes on 64-bit systems + y must be 8-byte aligned, so 4 bytes of padding follow x - double takes 12 bytes on most systems Each field is aligned to its own size, so y starts at offset 8, and the total is rounded up to a multiple of 8. ? What does _pack_ = 1 do? - Sorts the fields from largest to smallest + Removes padding, to match a packed C structure - Makes the structure read-only - Aligns every field to 1 KB It mirrors pragma pack(1) in the header. Without it, every field after the first gap is read from the wrong place. ? When do you use byref instead of pointer ? - byref is for numbers and pointer is for structures - byref copies the object; pointer passes the original - They are identical; byref is just an older name + For one call's address; pointer makes an object to keep byref is the light way to hand C an address during a call. pointer builds a real pointer object you can store or put in a structure. ? C returns a string it allocated for you. How must it be freed? - Python frees it automatically when the bytes copy is collected - With any C runtime's free + With the free function the library documents, not any other allocator's - It must not be freed: C always owns returned memory Memory must go back to the allocator that made it. Another runtime's free can corrupt the heap.

title: Packing records like C
body: Write and read the bytes of a C structure with Python's struct module, so that a C program (or a file it wrote) and Python agree byte for byte. Use the layout rules of practice 6.02. python def struct_format(fields, pack=None): ... def pack_record(fields, values, pack=None): ... def unpack_record(fields, data, pack=None): ... fields uses the types of practice 6.02. Each type has a struct code: Type Code Python value --- --- --- char c bytes of length 1 bool ? bool int8_t , uint8_t b , B int short , int16_t , uint16_t h , h , H int int , int32_t , uint32_t i , i , I int float , double f , d float long long , int64_t , uint64_t , pointer q , q , Q , Q int struct_format returns the format: < (little-endian, no automatic padding), then for each field the padding before it as Nx (only when N 0) followed by its code, then any padding at the end as Nx . An array char n is ns (one bytes value); any other array T n is n followed by T's code (a list of n values). pack_record takes a dict of values by field name and returns the bytes ( struct fills a short char n value with zero bytes). unpack_record returns the dict back; arrays (other than char n ) come back as lists. Data whose length is not the structure's size raises ValueError .

title: 6.04  Callbacks and Errors
body: When C calls back into Python - CFUNCTYPE and WINFUNCTYPE, keeping callbacks alive, exceptions inside callbacks - and how C reports errors - return codes, errno with use_errno, GetLastError with use_last_error and WinError, and errcheck to turn return codes into Python exceptions automatically. Functions as arguments Many C APIs take a function pointer : qsort takes a comparison function, Windows' EnumWindows calls you once per window, libraries call you with progress or log messages. In ctypes, describe the function type with CFUNCTYPE(restype, argtypes) ( WINFUNCTYPE for Windows API callbacks), and wrap a Python function with it: python import ctypes BINARY = ctypes.CFUNCTYPE(ctypes.c_int, ctypes.c_int, ctypes.c_int) def add(a, b): return a + b c_add = BINARY(add) a real C function pointer that runs the Python code print(c_add(2, 3)) 5 A classic use, sorting a C array with the C library's qsort : python-norun CMP = ctypes.CFUNCTYPE(ctypes.c_int, ctypes.POINTER(ctypes.c_int), ctypes.POINTER(ctypes.c_int)) def compare(a, b): return (a 0 b 0 ) - (a 0 < b 0 ) values = (ctypes.c_int 5)(5, 1, 4, 2, 3) libc.qsort.argtypes = ctypes.c_void_p, ctypes.c_size_t, ctypes.c_size_t, CMP libc.qsort.restype = None libc.qsort(values, len(values), ctypes.sizeof(ctypes.c_int), CMP(compare)) print(list(values)) 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 Keep the callback alive The C function pointer only exists while the Python wrapper object exists. If C stores the callback to call later (an event handler, a timer), and your code keeps no reference to the CFUNCTYPE object, Python frees it and C later jumps into freed memory: a crash, possibly minutes later. Store such callbacks somewhere long-lived (an attribute of the object that registered them) until you unregister them. Exceptions cannot cross An exception raised inside a callback cannot travel up through C frames. ctypes prints it, and C receives a meaningless result. So catch everything inside the callback, store the error, and check it after the C function returns: python-norun errors = def safe_compare(a, b): try: return compare(a, b) except Exception as e: errors.append(e) return 0 How C reports errors C has no exceptions. Libraries report failure in the ways the Reading Documentation course described: - a return code (0 for success, negative for errors) or a special value ( NULL , -1 ); - errno : load with CDLL(name, use_errno=True) and read ctypes.get_errno() right after the call; - on Windows, GetLastError : load with WinDLL(name, use_last_error=True) , read ctypes.get_last_error() , and ctypes.WinError(code) turns it into an OSError with the system's message. ctypes saves errno and the last error immediately after each call when asked to, which matters because Python itself may make system calls (and change them) before your next line runs. errcheck Checking every return value by hand is repetitive and easy to forget. A function's errcheck attribute runs after every call and may raise: python-norun def check_zero(result, func, args): if result != 0: raise OSError(result, f"{func.__name__} failed with {result}") return result lib.open_device.argtypes = ctypes.c_char_p, ctypes.POINTER(DeviceHandle) lib.open_device.restype = ctypes.c_int lib.open_device.errcheck = check_zero now a failure raises like normal Python Wrapping a C library this way, with types declared, errors turned into exceptions and resources freed in __del__ or context managers, gives the rest of the program an API that feels like ordinary Python. Check yourself quiz ? What does CFUNCTYPE(c_int, c_int, c_int) describe? - A C function taking three int s and returning nothing + A C function taking two int s and returning an int - A C function taking an int and returning two int s - An array of three int s The first argument is the result type, and the rest are the argument types. ? Why must you keep a reference to a callback that C stores? - So that C can raise exceptions through it - Because C copies the Python function's code when it stores it + Otherwise Python frees the wrapper, and C later calls freed memory - So the callback runs on the same thread as Python The C function pointer lives only as long as the CFUNCTYPE object. Without a reference, the crash can come minutes later. ? What happens to an exception raised inside a ctypes callback? - It travels up through C and can be caught after the C call - It stops the C function at once and returns -1 - It is turned into errno for the caller to read + It cannot cross into C: it is printed, and C receives a meaningless result Exceptions cannot pass through C frames. Catch everything inside the callback, store the error, and check it after the call. ? How do you read a Windows error code reliably after a call through ctypes? + Load the DLL with use_last_error=True and call ctypes.get_last_error() - Call kernel32.GetLastError() yourself on the next line - Read ctypes.get_errno() after the call - Catch the OSError that ctypes raises after every failure ctypes saves the error immediately after the call, before Python's own system calls can change it. Calling GetLastError later may read a different value.

title: Callbacks through C function pointers
body: Use real C function pointers made with ctypes.CFUNCTYPE (lesson 6.04): a comparison callback driven the way qsort drives it, and a registry that keeps callbacks alive and keeps exceptions from crossing into C. python CMP = ctypes.CFUNCTYPE(ctypes.c_int, ctypes.POINTER(ctypes.c_int), ctypes.POINTER(ctypes.c_int)) BINARY = ctypes.CFUNCTYPE(ctypes.c_int, ctypes.c_int, ctypes.c_int) def make_comparator(key=None, reverse=False): ... def c_style_sort(array, comparator): ... class CallbackRegistry: def register(self, name, func): ... - the callback's address (an int) def unregister(self, name): ... def call(self, address, a, b): ... errors exceptions caught inside callbacks - make_comparator returns a CMP function pointer. Called with two pointers to C int s, it returns -1, 0 or 1 as the first value is less than, equal to or greater than the second, comparing key(value) when key is given, and with the result negated when reverse is true. - c_style_sort sorts a ctypes c_int array in place with insertion sort, calling comparator with pointers to the two elements being compared, as qsort would. Make each pointer from the array's address: ctypes.cast(ctypes.addressof(array) + i ctypes.sizeof(ctypes.c_int), ctypes.POINTER(ctypes.c_int)) . - register wraps func (a Python function of two ints) in a BINARY callback and keeps it alive until it is unregistered; it returns its address, ctypes.cast(callback, ctypes.c_void_p).value . If func raises, the callback catches the exception, appends it to errors and returns 0. Registering a name again replaces the old callback. - unregister forgets the callback and returns whether there was one. - call calls the C function pointer at address with two ints: BINARY(address)(a, b) .

title: 6.05  Other Ways to Bind C
body: Beyond ctypes - cffi working from C declarations, extension modules and pybind11 for speed and C++, generating bindings from headers - and how other languages call the same C API - C P/Invoke, JavaScript through N-API and FFI packages, Rust's extern blocks and bindgen - and how to choose. cffi: from the declarations cffi ( pip install cffi ) reads C declarations directly, so you paste from the header instead of translating each type: python-norun from cffi import FFI ffi = FFI() ffi.cdef(""" typedef struct { int x; double y; } point; int get_position(point out); """) lib = ffi.dlopen("./mylib.dll") pos = ffi.new("point ") if lib.get_position(pos) == 0: print(pos.x, pos.y) It can also compile a small C module ahead of time ("API mode"), which is faster and checks the declarations against the real header. Extension modules, pybind11 and Cython When speed matters or the library is C++, bindings are compiled: - A C extension module uses Python's C API directly. Most control, most code. - pybind11 (and the newer nanobind ) wraps C++ functions and classes with a few lines of C++ templates, converting std::string , std::vector and exceptions automatically. - Cython writes Python-like code that compiles to C and can call C functions directly. These need a compiler for every platform you ship to, usually built into wheels by CI. Generating bindings Large APIs are rarely bound by hand. Tools read the header and generate the binding: ctypeslib and pyclibrary for ctypes, cffi itself, bindgen for Rust, SWIG for many languages at once. Even then, a person decides ownership rules and error handling, which no header states completely. The milestone project writes a small generator for a subset of C, which shows what such tools do. The same C API from other languages Language Mechanism Example --- --- --- C P/Invoke DllImport("mylib") static extern int get_position(out Point p); with StructLayout(LayoutKind.Sequential) JavaScript (Node) N-API addons in C/C++, or FFI packages an addon compiled with node-gyp , or a runtime FFI library describing types like ctypes Rust extern "C" blocks, bindgen to generate them unsafe { get_position(&mut p) } Go cgo import "C" with the header in a comment Java the Foreign Function and Memory API (Java 22+), JNI before it Linker.nativeLinker().downcallHandle(...) The questions are the same in every language: the exact types and layout, who owns which memory, how errors are reported, and which thread may call what. Answer them once, from the header and documentation, and the binding in any language follows. Choosing - A few functions, no compiler available: ctypes . - A larger C API, especially one under active development: cffi . - Performance-critical code or C++ classes: pybind11 or an extension module. - An existing popular library: look for a maintained Python package first; someone has probably done the work. Check yourself quiz ? What is cffi's main advantage over ctypes for a large API? - It needs no library file at run time - It is part of the standard library + It reads the C declarations from the header directly - It turns every C error into a Python exception automatically You paste the header's declarations into cdef , so a large API is not translated type by type. cffi is a package you install. ? When would you choose pybind11? - To call a few C functions without a compiler - To bind a large C API from its header at run time + To bind C++ code, especially classes, or when speed matters - To call web APIs from C++ pybind11 wraps C++ functions and classes with templates and needs a compiler. A few functions with no compiler is a job for ctypes. ? What does C 's StructLayout(LayoutKind.Sequential) correspond to in ctypes? - A Structure with _pack_ = 1 , so no padding is added - A Structure whose _fields_ are sorted by size - A POINTER(T) to memory laid out by C + A Structure with _fields_ in declaration order Both lay out the fields in declaration order with the C compiler's alignment rules. _pack_ = 1 would be the packed variant, and ctypes never reorders fields. ? Which questions does every binding have to answer, whatever the language? - Which web framework to use, and which JSON library + Exact types and layout, memory ownership, error reporting, and threading rules - How to compile the library, and which compiler version - How many functions the library exports, and their names The mechanism differs per language, but those four questions come from the C API itself, and the header and documentation answer them.

title: Generating ctypes bindings
body: Turn a list of C function declarations into the Python lines that bind them, the way binding generators do (lesson 6.05). Reuse your ctypes_name and parse_prototype from practice 6.01, included in your code. python def generate_bindings(header, lib="lib"): ... - Python source text header is text with one declaration per line. Blank lines, lines starting with // and lines starting with are skipped. For each declaration, in order, produce two lines: python-norun lib.compress_block.argtypes = ctypes.c_int32, ctypes.POINTER(ctypes.c_uint8), ctypes.c_size_t lib.compress_block.restype = ctypes.c_int32 - Every ctypes name gets the ctypes. prefix, including inside POINTER(...) : ctypes.POINTER(ctypes.c_uint8) . None stays None , and a structure name (from struct point ) stays as it is. - The argument list is written a, b, c with , between items, or . - Use the lib name given. Join the lines with \n (no newline at the end). A line that is not a valid declaration raises ValueError mentioning its line number (counting from 1).

title: A binding generator for a C header
match: A binding generator for a C header
body: Write a small version of what tools like ctypeslib and cffi do: read a C header, with structures and function declarations, and produce a Python module that binds the library with ctypes. The tests run the module you generate and check the structures' real sizes and offsets, and the functions' types, through ctypes itself. python def generate_module(header, lib="lib"): ... - Python source text What the header may contain: - Comments, / ... / (possibly over several lines) and // ... , and preprocessor lines starting with , which are ignored. - Structures , written struct TAG { fields }; , typedef struct TAG { fields } ALIAS; or typedef struct { fields } ALIAS; . The Python class is named ALIAS when there is one, otherwise TAG ; afterwards both struct TAG and ALIAS mean that class. - Fields , separated by ; , each TYPE NAME or TYPE NAME N (an array of N). The of a pointer may be written next to the type or the name. A field type may be any type of practice 6.01, or a structure defined earlier in the header. - Function declarations , each ending with ; , as in practice 6.01, whose types may also be earlier structures. Raise ValueError for anything else: an unknown type or a structure used before it is defined, a field declaring several names ( int a, b; ), a typedef struct without an alias, a struct with neither tag nor alias, or a malformed declaration. The module you return starts with import ctypes , then defines, in header order, one ctypes.Structure subclass per structure with its _fields_ (an array field is element_type N ), then sets argtypes and restype for each function on the object named by lib , in header order, exactly as in practice 6.05. It is run with that name already defined.

title: Glossary
body: ABI : the binary rules for calling functions and laying out data, which let languages call C. (6.01) Access token : a short-lived credential sent with requests, usually as Authorization: Bearer . (2.02) API key : a long secret string that identifies the calling program. (2.01) argtypes / restype : the ctypes attributes describing a C function's parameter and return types. (6.02) At-least-once delivery : every event is delivered, possibly more than once. (4.03) Backoff : waiting longer after each failed attempt. (3.03) Bearer token : a token that grants access to whoever holds it. (2.02) Canonical string : the exact text that is signed, defined so both sides build the same bytes. (2.04) Checkpoint : the point an incremental sync got to, often the largest updated_at processed. (5.03) Client credentials flow : the OAuth flow for a program acting as itself. (2.03) Correlation id : an id shared by log lines about one run, record or request. (5.05) Cursor : an opaque marker of the position in a paginated list. (3.01) Dead letter : a record that could not be processed, kept with the reason. (5.04) Endpoint : a method and a path pattern, such as GET /books/{id} . (1.01) ETag : a version identifier for a response, used with If-None-Match . (3.05) HMAC : a hash keyed with a secret, proving authenticity and integrity. (2.04) Idempotent : doing it twice has the same effect as once. (3.03) Idempotency key : a client-chosen id that lets the server recognise a retried operation. (3.04) Jitter : randomness added to retry delays so clients do not retry in waves. (3.03) JSON : the text format most web APIs use for data. (1.03) JWT : a JSON Web Token: header, claims and signature in base64url. (2.02) Lag : how far an integration is behind the source. (5.05) Link header : a response header naming related URLs, such as the next page. (3.01) Mapping : the rules that turn one system's records into another's. (5.02) OAuth 2.0 : the standard for granting a program limited access on a user's behalf. (2.03) OpenAPI : a machine-readable description of a REST API. (1.04) Outbox pattern : queuing an API call in the same database transaction as the change it reports. (5.04) PKCE : Proof Key for Code Exchange, protecting the OAuth authorization code with a verifier. (2.03) Polling : asking repeatedly whether something changed. (4.01) Rate limit : the maximum number of requests allowed in a period. (3.02) Reconciliation : comparing full lists to find what an incremental sync missed. (5.03) Redaction : replacing secrets with a placeholder before logging. (2.05) Refresh token : a long-lived secret used to get new access tokens. (2.02) REST : the style of resources at URLs acted on with HTTP methods. (1.01) Retry-After : a header saying how long to wait before trying again. (3.02) Scope : a named permission requested in OAuth. (2.03) Source of truth : the system that owns a piece of data. (5.01) Structure (ctypes) : a Python class mirroring a C struct. (6.03) Tombstone : a change-feed entry saying a record was deleted. (5.03) Token bucket : a pacing algorithm allowing bursts up to a capacity at an average rate. (3.02) Transport : the part of a client that actually sends requests; replaceable in tests. (1.05) Upsert : update if the record exists, otherwise insert. (5.03) Webhook : an HTTP request a service sends to your URL when an event happens. (4.01)

title: 1.01  What Assembly Is
body: A processor runs machine code - numbers that each mean one small instruction. Assembly gives every instruction a name, and an assembler turns the names back into the numbers. This course writes x86-64 assembly in Intel syntax with NASM, for Linux. A program has sections for data and code, labels that name addresses, and starts at _start. The processor's own language A processor does not understand C or Python. It runs machine code : bytes in memory, each group of them one small instruction such as "add these two registers" or "jump to that address". The bytes 48 01 d8 , for example, tell an x86-64 processor to add rbx to rax . Nobody wants to write bytes by hand, so each instruction has a short name, a mnemonic , and a program called an assembler translates the names into bytes: Assembly Machine code Means --- --- --- mov eax, 1 b8 01 00 00 00 put 1 in the register eax add rax, rbx 48 01 d8 rax = rax + rbx ret c3 return from a function One line of assembly is one instruction. There is no if , no for , no variables with types: only what the hardware does. Every language you have used is turned into these instructions in the end, by a compiler (C, Rust), or by an interpreter that is itself made of them (Python). Which assembly? Every processor family has its own instruction set, so there are many assembly languages: Family Found in --- --- x86-64 (also called x64, AMD64) most PCs, laptops and servers ARM64 (AArch64) phones, tablets, Apple-chip Macs, many servers RISC-V a newer open design, in microcontrollers and growing This course teaches x86-64 , written in Intel syntax ( mov eax, 1 : destination first), with the NASM assembler, for Linux . Lesson 6.05 compares ARM64. The ideas carry over to all of them. !note Why learn assembly? Few programs are written in assembly today, but reading it is a superpower: you see what your C, C++ or Rust really does, how fast it can be, why a crash happened, and how operating systems, debuggers, compilers and security exploits work. It also makes pointers, the stack and memory obvious forever. A whole program Here is a complete program. Press Run : nasm global _start section .data message: db "Hello from assembly!", 10 length equ $ - message section .text _start: mov eax, 1 ; system call 1: write mov edi, 1 ; to file 1: standard output lea rsi, rel message ; the address of the bytes mov edx, length ; how many bytes syscall ; ask Linux to do it mov eax, 60 ; system call 60: exit xor edi, edi ; with exit code 0 syscall Every part is explained in the next lessons, but you can read the shape already: - ; starts a comment , to the end of the line. - section .data holds data; section .text holds the instructions (the "text" of the program). - A name followed by a colon, like message: or _start: , is a label : a name for the address where the next byte goes. - db ("define bytes") puts bytes into the program: the letters of the message, then 10, the new line character. - _start is where the program begins, and global _start makes that name visible to the linker , which builds the final program file and needs to know where it starts. - The instructions are indented by convention; labels are not. No safety net A C program that reaches the end of main returns to the C library, which exits for you. An assembly program has no one to return to. If you leave out the exit system call at the end, the processor keeps running whatever bytes come next in memory, and the program crashes with a segmentation fault. Try it: delete the last three lines and run. How the website runs it The website sends your program to Compiler Explorer, which assembles it with NASM into an object file, links it with ld , and runs it on a 64-bit Linux machine, exactly like these commands: nasm -f elf64 hello.asm -o hello.o ld hello.o -o hello ./hello elf64 is the format Linux uses for programs: ELF, the Executable and Linkable Format. Check yourself quiz ? What does an assembler do? - Runs assembly one line at a time - Turns C into assembly + Turns assembly mnemonics into machine code bytes A compiler goes from C to assembly; the assembler goes from assembly to bytes. ? Which syntax does mov eax, 1 use, and what does it do? - AT&T syntax: it copies eax into 1 - Intel syntax: it copies eax into 1 + Intel syntax: it puts 1 into eax In Intel syntax the destination comes first. AT&T syntax, used by GNU tools by default, writes the same thing as movl $1, %eax . ? What is _start? - A system call - A C function + The label where the program begins global _start tells the linker about it. ? What happens if an assembly program has no exit system call at the end? - It exits normally with code 0 + The processor runs on into whatever follows - The assembler adds an exit for you There is nothing to return to, so the processor executes the bytes after the code and the program crashes.

title: 1.02  Registers
body: Registers are the processor's own tiny, fast storage - sixteen 64-bit general-purpose ones on x86-64, plus rip (the next instruction) and rflags. The low 32, 16 and 8 bits of each have their own names, such as eax, ax and al. Writing a 32-bit register clears the top half of the 64-bit one; writing 8 or 16 bits does not. Storage inside the processor Memory is big but, by the processor's standards, slow: reading it can take a hundred cycles. Registers are a handful of storage slots inside the processor itself, read and written in a fraction of a cycle. Almost every instruction works on registers, so programs constantly move values from memory into registers, work on them, and store the results back. x86-64 has 16 general-purpose registers , each 64 bits: Register Traditional use --- --- rax accumulator: results, return values, system call numbers rbx base: a general register that functions keep safe rcx counter: loop counts, shift counts, 4th argument rdx data: the high half in multiply and divide, 3rd argument rsi , rdi source and destination index: the 2nd and 1st arguments rbp base pointer: the stack frame (lesson 5.03) rsp stack pointer : the top of the stack. Leave it alone for now r8 to r15 eight more, added when x86 went 64-bit The "traditional uses" come from the 1970s Intel 8086. Today most instructions work on any register, but some conventions (which registers hold arguments, which ones functions must keep) matter a lot, as module 5 shows. Two special registers cannot be used directly: rip , the instruction pointer, holds the address of the next instruction, and rflags holds the flags that comparisons set (lesson 2.04). Smaller views of the same register Each register has names for its lower parts, a history of how x86 grew from 16 to 32 to 64 bits: 64 bits low 32 low 16 low 8 --- --- --- --- rax eax ax al rbx ebx bx bl rcx ecx cx cl rdx edx dx dl rsi esi si sil rdi edi di dil rbp ebp bp bpl rsp esp sp spl r8 r8d r8w r8b ... r15 r15d r15w r15b eax is not a separate register: it is the bottom 32 bits of rax . (There are also ah , bh , ch , dh for bits 8 to 15 of the first four, a leftover you will rarely need.) demo-asm title: One register, four names init: rax=0x1122334455667788 mov al, 0xAA mov ax, 0xBBBB mov eax, 0xCC mov rax, -1 ret Step through it and watch rax : 1. mov al, 0xAA changes only the lowest byte. 2. mov ax, 0xBBBB changes only the lowest 16 bits. 3. mov eax, 0xCC sets the low 32 bits and clears the upper 32 . 4. mov rax, -1 sets all 64 bits to 1. !tip The 32-bit rule Writing a 32-bit register ( eax , r9d ) always zeroes the top 32 bits of the 64-bit register. Writing an 8- or 16-bit one leaves the rest alone. That is why compilers so often write mov eax, 5 instead of mov rax, 5 : it does the same thing with a shorter instruction. Values have no types A register holds 64 bits, nothing more. Whether those bits are a number, a character, an address or a negative number is up to the instructions you use on them. -1 and 18446744073709551615 are the same 64 bits (all 1s, in two's complement, from the Fundamentals course): add does not care, but comparisons and divisions come in signed and unsigned versions (lesson 3.03). Check yourself quiz ? How many general-purpose registers does x86-64 have? - 8 + 16 - 64 rax to rsp, and r8 to r15. ? What is eax? - A separate 32-bit register + The low 32 bits of rax - An older name for rax that no longer works Changing eax changes rax. ? rax holds 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF. After mov eax, 1, what is rax? - 0xFFFFFFFF00000001 - 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF + 1 Writing a 32-bit register clears the upper half. ? Which register holds the address of the next instruction? - rsp + rip - rax rsp is the stack pointer.

title: Parts of a register
body: These tasks are checked by calling functions you write. A function here is a label, some instructions, and ret at the end. Its first argument arrives in rdi , the second in rsi , and it leaves its result in rax . (Module 5 explains why.) For example: nasm-norun same: ; same(x) gives back x mov rax, rdi ret Write these four, using only mov (and xor to clear a register), and the register names from the lesson: Function Result in rax --- --- keep32(x) the low 32 bits of x, the rest 0 keep16(x) the low 16 bits of x, the rest 0 keep8(x) the low 8 bits of x, the rest 0 with_low_byte(x, y) x, but with its lowest byte replaced by the lowest byte of y For example keep16(0x1122334455667788) is 0x7788 , and with_low_byte(0x1234, 0xAB) is 0x12AB .

title: 1.03  mov and Exit Codes
body: mov copies a value into a register - a constant, another register, or (later) memory. Both sides must be the same size. A program's exit code is the number it hands to the exit system call, and it is the simplest way to see a result. xor of a register with itself is the usual way to set it to 0. mov copies mov destination, source copies the source into the destination. The source is unchanged. nasm-norun mov eax, 42 ; a constant (an "immediate") into a register mov ebx, eax ; one register into another mov rcx, -7 ; negative numbers are fine mov edx, 0x2A ; hex: also 42 mov esi, 0b101010 ; binary: also 42 mov edi, 'A' ; a character: its code, 65 Rules: - The destination comes first: think eax = 42 . - Both sides must be the same size: mov eax, rbx is an error ("invalid combination of opcode and operands"). Use mov eax, ebx or mov rax, rbx . - A constant cannot be the destination ( mov 5, eax makes no sense). The exit code: your first result When a program ends, it hands a number to the operating system: its exit code . 0 means success; anything else usually means something went wrong. Exit is system call 60, and the code goes in rdi : nasm global _start section .text _start: mov ebx, 20 mov ecx, 22 mov edi, ebx ; the exit code will be 20... add edi, ecx ; ...plus 22 mov eax, 60 ; system call 60: exit syscall Run it: the website shows exit code 42 . Before you can print text, the exit code is a handy way to see a number. On Linux you would see it with echo $? after the program ends. Exit codes are a single byte: 0 to 255. Exit with 300 and you get 44 (300 − 256), the lowest 8 bits. Setting a register to zero You will see this everywhere: nasm-norun xor eax, eax ; eax = eax XOR eax, which is always 0 It means the same as mov eax, 0 , but the instruction is 2 bytes instead of 5, and processors recognise it and do it for free. Compilers always use it, and so does this course. Swapping and order Instructions run strictly in order, one after another. To swap two registers you need a third, or the special xchg instruction: nasm global _start section .text _start: mov eax, 3 mov ebx, 9 mov ecx, eax ; ecx = 3 mov eax, ebx ; eax = 9 mov ebx, ecx ; ebx = 3 xchg eax, ebx ; and swap them back with one instruction mov edi, eax ; exit code: 3 mov eax, 60 syscall Check yourself quiz ? What does mov ecx, eax do? - Copies ecx into eax + Copies eax into ecx - Swaps them The destination comes first. ? Why is mov eax, rbx an error? - rbx cannot be read - mov only takes constants + The two sides are different sizes Use mov rax, rbx or mov eax, ebx. ? Which register holds the exit code for system call 60? - rax + rdi - rsi rax holds the system call number. ? What does xor eax, eax do? - Flips the bits of eax - Nothing + Sets eax to 0 Anything XOR itself is 0.

title: 1.04  System Calls write and exit
body: A program cannot touch the screen, files or the keyboard itself - it asks the operating system with the syscall instruction. On Linux the call's number goes in rax and its arguments in rdi, rsi, rdx, r10, r8 and r9, and the result comes back in rax. write (1) prints bytes, read (0) reads them, exit (60) ends the program. Asking the operating system Programs run in user mode , where the processor refuses to touch hardware directly. Printing, reading the keyboard, opening files, and even ending the program are done by the operating system's kernel , and a program asks for them with a system call . The syscall instruction switches the processor into the kernel, which does the work and comes back. On 64-bit Linux: Register Holds --- --- rax the system call's number; afterwards, its result rdi , rsi , rdx , r10 , r8 , r9 its arguments, in that order syscall itself changes rcx and r11 (it uses them to remember where to come back to), so don't keep anything there across a system call. The three you need Number Name Arguments Returns --- --- --- --- 0 read file, buffer address, maximum bytes bytes read (0 at the end) 1 write file, bytes' address, how many bytes written 60 exit exit code does not return Files are numbered: 0 is standard input, 1 standard output, 2 standard error. These are the same streams as stdin , stdout and stderr in C, whose printf ends up making exactly this write call. Printing nasm global _start section .data greeting: db "Hello, ", 0 name: db "Ada", 10 name_length equ $ - name section .text _start: mov eax, 1 ; write mov edi, 1 ; standard output lea rsi, rel greeting mov edx, 7 ; "Hello, " is 7 bytes syscall mov eax, 1 ; write again (rax now holds the last result, so set it again) mov edi, 1 lea rsi, rel name mov edx, name_length syscall mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall - lea rsi, rel greeting puts the address of the label into rsi (lesson 4.01 explains lea and rel ). write needs to know where the bytes are, not what they are. - write prints exactly the number of bytes you ask for. Ask for 3 and you get Hel ; ask for too many and you print whatever follows in memory. - A system call puts its result in rax , so set eax again before the next call. Errors When a system call fails, it returns a negative number: minus an error code. write to file 9, which is not open, returns −9 ( -EBADF , "bad file descriptor"). C's library turns those into errno (from the C course). Here you can see it as an exit code: nasm global _start section .data text: db "lost", 10 section .text _start: mov eax, 1 mov edi, 9 ; a file that is not open lea rsi, rel text mov edx, 5 syscall ; rax = -9 neg rax ; make it positive mov rdi, rax ; exit code 9 mov eax, 60 syscall Standard error Write to file 2 instead of 1 and the text goes to standard error. On the website it still appears in the console, but it is a separate stream: running ./program out.txt in a terminal saves only standard output. !note Hundreds of system calls Linux has over 350 system calls: open (2), close (3), mmap (9) for memory, fork (57) and execve (59) for new programs, and more. Every program, in any language, does its work through them. The command strace ./program lists each one a program makes. Check yourself quiz ? Where does the system call number go? - rdi - rcx + rax The arguments go in rdi, rsi, rdx, r10, r8, r9. ? write(1, address, 5) prints... - The number 5 - The first line at the address + 5 bytes from the address, to standard output write knows nothing about lines or terminators. ? What does a failing system call return in rax? - 0 - It crashes the program + A negative error code For example -9 for a bad file number. ? Which registers does syscall itself overwrite? - rax only - None + rcx and r11 Plus rax, which gets the result.

title: 1.05  Data db, dw, dd, dq and equ
match: 1.05 Data db, dw, dd, dq and equ
body: db, dw, dd and dq put 1, 2, 4 and 8-byte values into the program, stored little-endian. A label is just the address of the next byte, $ is the current address, and equ names a constant such as a length. times repeats, .bss reserves zeroed space with resb and resq, and .rodata holds data that must not change. Defining bytes Directive Size Example --- --- --- db 1 byte db 65, "text", 10, 0 dw 2 bytes (a "word") dw 1000 dd 4 bytes (a "double word") dd 100000, -1 dq 8 bytes (a "quad word") dq 0x1122334455667788 These are not instructions: they tell the assembler to place bytes in the program file. In db , a string in quotes stands for its characters' codes, one byte each; there is no terminator unless you add 0 yourself. The names come from the 16-bit 8086, where a "word" was 16 bits; that is why a 32-bit value is a "double word". Instructions use the same names: byte , word , dword , qword . Little-endian x86 stores multi-byte values lowest byte first . dd 0x11223344 becomes the bytes 44 33 22 11 . The Fundamentals course has a demo of it. demo-bytes value: 287454020 order: little Labels are addresses A label means "the address where the next byte goes". It is not a variable and has no type or size: count: dd 5 only names the first of the four bytes. The instruction that uses it decides how many bytes to read. $ and equ $ is the address of the current position. $ - message , written right after the message, is "here minus where the message started": its length, worked out by the assembler. equ gives a name to a number. It takes no space in the program; it is like define in C: nasm global _start section .data banner: db " Xenon ", 10 banner_len equ $ - banner STDOUT equ 1 SYS_WRITE equ 1 SYS_EXIT equ 60 section .text _start: mov eax, SYS_WRITE mov edi, STDOUT lea rsi, rel banner mov edx, banner_len syscall mov eax, SYS_EXIT mov edi, banner_len ; exit code: the length, 14 syscall times times count thing repeats something: nasm global _start section .data line: times 20 db "=" db 10 line_len equ $ - line section .text _start: mov eax, 1 mov edi, 1 lea rsi, rel line mov edx, line_len syscall mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall The sections Section Holds Can change --- --- --- .text instructions no .data data with starting values yes .rodata read-only data: constant text and tables no (writing crashes) .bss space reserved and set to zero when the program starts yes .bss takes no room in the program file, only a note of how much to reserve. Reserve with resb (bytes), resw , resd , resq : nasm-norun section .bss buffer: resb 256 ; 256 bytes, all 0 counts: resq 10 ; ten 8-byte numbers, all 0 The operating system loads each section into memory with the right permissions: .text can run but not be written, .data can be written but not run. A program that writes to its own code crashes, which is a protection against attacks. Check yourself quiz ? How many bytes does dd 7 take? - 1 - 8 + 4 d for double word: 4 bytes. ? db "Hi" - is there a zero byte at the end? - Yes, always + No, only the two letters - Only in .data Add , 0 yourself for a zero-terminated string. ? msg: db "hello" then len equ $ - msg. What is len? - The address of msg - 6 + 5 $ is the address after the five bytes. ? What is special about .bss? - It cannot be written to + Its zeroed space is not stored in the file - It holds the program's instructions .bss reserves memory that starts as zeros, so the program file only records its size. resb and friends reserve it.

title: 1.06  Xenon's Print and Read Routines
body: Turning a number into printed digits takes a loop and a division, which come later in the course. Until then, Xenon adds ready-made routines to any program that calls them - print_str, print_int, print_hex, print_bin, print_newline, read_int, read_char and read_line. Put the argument in rdi (and rsi), call, and expect rax, rcx, rdx, rsi, rdi and r8 to r11 to change. Why routines? write prints bytes . To print the number 42 you need the bytes '4' and '2' , which means dividing by 10 and turning remainders into characters: a loop (module 3) with division (module 2). Lesson 2.05 builds it. Until then, the website gives you a small library. When your program calls one of these names and does not define it itself, the website adds the routine's code to the end of your program before assembling it. That is all: no magic in the processor. You can read their source in the Cheat Sheet - Routines reference page. The routines Routine Give it Does --- --- --- print_str rdi = address of a zero-terminated string prints it print_char dil (low byte of rdi ) = a character prints one character print_newline nothing prints a new line print_int rdi = a signed number prints it in decimal: -42 print_uint rdi = an unsigned number prints it in decimal print_hex rdi = a number prints 0x2a print_bin rdi = a number, rsi = how many bits prints 00101010 read_int nothing reads a whole number: rax = the number, rdx = 1, or 0 in both at the end of the input read_char nothing rax = the next character, or −1 at the end read_line rdi = a buffer, rsi = its size reads a line without its new line; rax = its length, or −1 at the end call call name jumps to a routine, which runs and then comes back to the instruction after the call (lesson 5.01 shows how). Arguments go in rdi , then rsi : the same registers C uses on Linux, so these routines are exactly like calling C functions. nasm global _start section .data label: db "The answer is ", 0 ; print_str needs the 0 at the end section .text _start: lea rdi, rel label call print_str mov edi, 42 call print_int call print_newline mov rdi, -1 call print_int ; -1 call print_newline mov rdi, -1 call print_uint ; the same bits, unsigned: 18446744073709551615 call print_newline mov edi, 255 call print_hex ; 0xff call print_newline mov edi, 5 mov esi, 8 call print_bin ; 00000101 call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall Registers that change A routine is allowed to use some registers for its own work, so after any call : May have changed Are kept as they were --- --- rax , rcx , rdx , rsi , rdi , r8 , r9 , r10 , r11 rbx , rbp , rsp , r12 , r13 , r14 , r15 So keep values you still need in rbx or r12 to r15 while calling routines. This rule is the calling convention that every function on Linux follows (lesson 5.02). Reading numbers nasm global _start section .data ask: db "Two numbers: ", 0 said: db "Their sum is ", 0 section .text _start: lea rdi, rel ask call print_str call read_int ; rax = the first number mov rbx, rax ; keep it safe in rbx call read_int ; rax = the second add rbx, rax lea rdi, rel said call print_str mov rdi, rbx call print_int call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall On the website an assembly program gets all of its input when it starts. When you run one that reads, the console asks for the input first: type each line, then press Enter on an empty line (or Ctrl+D) to start the program. In checked tasks the test's input is used. !warning Don't mix with your own read calls read_int , read_char and read_line read the input in big pieces and keep what they have not used yet. A program that also makes its own read system calls would miss those bytes. Use one or the other. Check yourself quiz ? Which register holds the number for print_int? - rax + rdi - rsi The first argument always goes in rdi. ? After call read_int, where is the number? - In rdi - On the stack + In rax, with rdx = 1 Results come back in rax. At the end of the input both rax and rdx are 0. ? You need a value to survive a call to print_int. Where should you keep it? - In rcx + In rbx or r12 to r15 - In rdi Routines keep rbx, rbp and r12 to r15 as they were. ? Does print_str need a zero byte at the end of the text? - No, it knows the length - Only for long strings + Yes, it prints up to the 0 Unlike write, which takes a length.
