title: 2.01  add, sub, inc, dec and neg
match: 2.01 add, sub, inc, dec and neg
body: add and sub combine two operands into the first, inc and dec add or take away one, and neg flips the sign. Results wrap around at the register's size, so 32-bit arithmetic wraps at 2 to the 32 and also clears the upper half. The same add instruction serves signed and unsigned numbers, because two's complement makes them the same bits. Two operands, one result x86 arithmetic overwrites its first operand: Instruction Does --- --- add rax, rbx rax = rax + rbx sub rax, 5 rax = rax − 5 inc rcx rcx = rcx + 1 dec rcx rcx = rcx − 1 neg rax rax = −rax There is no "c = a + b" in one instruction (except with lea , lesson 4.01): copy first, then add. nasm global _start section .text _start: mov rbx, 1000 mov rax, rbx add rax, 337 ; rax = 1337 sub rax, 1300 ; rax = 37 inc rax ; 38 dec rbx ; rbx = 999 neg rbx ; -999 add rax, rbx ; 38 - 999 = -961 mov rdi, rax call print_int call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall Wrapping around A register has a fixed number of bits, so results wrap around like a car's odometer. With 8 bits, 255 + 1 is 0; with 64 bits, the biggest unsigned number plus one is 0 too. demo-asm title: Wrapping at 8, 32 and 64 bits init: rax=0 mov al, 255 add al, 1 mov eax, 0xFFFFFFFF add eax, 1 mov rax, -1 add rax, 1 ret Watch the CF (carry) flag in the demo: it is set each time a result wrapped past the top. Lesson 2.04 is about the flags. !tip 32-bit arithmetic clears the top too Like mov , any instruction writing a 32-bit register zeroes the upper half. add eax, 1 with rax = 0x1_FFFFFFFF gives rax = 0 , not 0x2_00000000 . Use 64-bit registers when numbers can grow beyond about 4 billion. One add for signed and unsigned In two's complement (from the Fundamentals course), −1 is all 1 bits. Adding 1 to it gives all 0 bits: 0, which is right whether you read the bits as signed (−1 + 1) or unsigned (the largest value + 1, wrapping). That is the beauty of two's complement: the same add and sub work for both . Only comparisons, division and widening need to know which you mean. Instructions with memory Arithmetic can read or update memory directly (lesson 4.01 shows addressing): nasm-norun add rax, rel total ; rax += the 8 bytes at total add qword rel total , 5 ; the 8 bytes at total += 5 inc dword rel count ; the 4 bytes at count += 1 When neither operand is a register, NASM cannot tell the size, so you write it: byte , word , dword or qword . Only one operand may be in memory: add a , b does not exist. Check yourself quiz ? What does sub rax, rbx do? - rbx = rbx - rax - rax = rbx - rax + rax = rax - rbx The first operand is the destination. ? al is 250. After add al, 10, what is al? - 260 + 4 - 255 260 wraps around at 256. ? Why can the same add instruction handle signed and unsigned numbers? - add checks the sign first + In two's complement both give the same bits - It cannot: there is a separate signed add Comparisons and division are where the difference matters. ? What is wrong with inc rel count ? - inc cannot use a memory operand - Nothing: it assembles as it is + The size is unknown; write dword or another size With no register in the instruction, NASM cannot tell how many bytes to change, so write inc dword rel count .

title: Adding and subtracting

body: Write these functions (arguments in rdi , rsi , rdx ; result in rax ): Function Result --- --- add_sub(a, b, c) a + b − c negate(x) −x plus_two(x) x + 2, with two inc distance(a, b) b − a (it may be negative) add32(a, b) a + b done in 32-bit registers, so it wraps at 2³²: add32(0xFFFFFFFF, 1) is 0

title: 2.02  Multiplying and Dividing
body: imul multiplies with two or three operands and keeps the low bits of the answer. div and idiv divide the 128-bit number in rdx:rax by an operand, leaving the quotient in rax and the remainder in rdx - so rdx must be prepared first, with xor for unsigned and cqo for signed. Dividing by zero stops the program. imul Form Does --- --- imul rax, rbx rax = rax × rbx imul rax, rbx, 10 rax = rbx × 10 imul rcx, rel price rcx = rcx × the 8 bytes at price The answer of a 64 × 64-bit multiplication can need 128 bits; these forms keep the low 64 and drop the rest. For signed and unsigned numbers the low bits are the same, so imul serves both. nasm global _start section .text _start: mov rax, 12 imul rax, rax ; 144 imul rbx, rax, 3 ; rbx = 432 mov rdi, rbx call print_int call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall The old one-operand forms, mul rbx (unsigned) and imul rbx (signed), multiply rax by the operand and put the full 128-bit answer in rdx:rax : the high 64 bits in rdx , the low 64 in rax . You need them when the high half matters. Division: rdx:rax Division is the awkward one. div rbx divides the 128-bit number made of rdx (high half) and rax (low half) by rbx : - the quotient goes in rax , - the remainder in rdx . So before dividing, rdx must hold the right high half: Numbers Before Divide --- --- --- unsigned xor edx, edx (high half 0) div rbx signed cqo (copies rax's sign bit into all of rdx) idiv rbx nasm global _start section .text _start: mov rax, 17 xor edx, edx ; unsigned: rdx:rax = 17 mov ecx, 5 div rcx ; rax = 3, rdx = 2 mov rbx, rdx ; keep the remainder mov rdi, rax call print_int call print_newline mov rdi, rbx call print_int call print_newline mov rax, -17 cqo ; signed: rdx = all 1s, because -17 is negative mov ecx, 5 idiv rcx ; rax = -3, rdx = -2 (rounds towards zero, like C) mov rbx, rdx mov rdi, rax call print_int call print_newline mov rdi, rbx call print_int call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall !danger Forgetting rdx If rdx still holds something from earlier, div divides a huge 128-bit number, and when the quotient does not fit in 64 bits the processor raises a divide error : the program stops with exit code 136, "Floating point exception" (an old name: it is an integer problem). Always set rdx right before div , and remember that div also overwrites rdx . Dividing by zero does the same. The divisor cannot be a constant ( div 10 does not exist): put it in a register first. Dividing by constants without div div is slow (around 20 to 40 cycles, against 3 for imul ), so compilers avoid it: - Dividing an unsigned number by a power of two is a right shift: shr rax, 3 divides by 8 (lesson 2.03). - Dividing by other constants becomes a multiplication by a "magic" reciprocal, then a shift. You will see code like imul rax, rax, 1431655766 in compiler output and now know why (lesson 6.01). Check yourself quiz ? Where does div put the quotient and remainder? - Quotient in rdx, remainder in rax + Quotient in rax, remainder in rdx - Both in rax It divides rdx:rax by the operand. ? What must you do before idiv rcx? - xor edx, edx - Nothing + cqo, to fill rdx with the sign of rax xor edx, edx is for unsigned div. ? What does imul rax, rbx, 10 do? - rax = rax rbx 10 - rbx = rax 10 + rax = rbx 10 The three-operand form. ? A program stops with exit code 136 at a div. What are the likely causes? - A missing exit system call - Too many registers in use at once + Dividing by zero, or a quotient too big The processor raises a divide error (SIGFPE). A quotient too big usually means rdx was not prepared before the div.

title: Multiplying and dividing
body: Write these functions: Function Result --- --- square(x) x × x mul_add(a, b, c) a × b + c quotient(a, b) a ÷ b for signed numbers, rounded towards zero like C: quotient(-7, 2) is −3 remainder(a, b) the signed remainder: remainder(-7, 2) is −1 minutes(seconds) the whole minutes in an unsigned number of seconds: minutes(125) is 2 last_digit(n) the last decimal digit of an unsigned n The tests never divide by zero. Remember: div and idiv need rdx prepared, take their divisor in a register, and overwrite rdx . Note that the second argument arrives in rsi while rdx is about to be used for the division.

title: 2.03  Bit Instructions and Shifts
body: and, or, xor and not work on every bit at once and make masks for testing, setting and clearing bits. shl and shr shift bits left and right - multiplying and dividing unsigned numbers by powers of two - while sar keeps the sign for signed numbers. rol and ror rotate, a variable shift count goes in cl, and lea multiplies by 3, 5 and 9 in one step. and, or, xor, not Instruction Each result bit is 1 when Typical use --- --- --- and rax, rbx both bits are 1 keep some bits, clear the rest: and eax, 0xFF or rax, rbx either bit is 1 set bits: or eax, 0x20 xor rax, rbx the bits differ flip bits; xor eax, eax is 0 not rax the bit was 0 flip every bit test rax, rbx is an and that only sets the flags and throws the result away: the usual way to ask "is this bit set?" or "is this register zero?" ( test rax, rax ). nasm global _start section .text _start: mov ebx, 'a' ; 0110 0001 and ebx, 0xDF ; clear bit 5: 'A' (0100 0001) mov edi, ebx call print_char or ebx, 0x20 ; set bit 5 again: 'a' mov edi, ebx ; (print_char may change edi, so copy again) call print_char call print_newline mov edi, 0xF0 not edi ; ...FFFFFF0F and edi, 0xFF ; keep the low byte: 0x0F call print_hex call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall The Fundamentals course shows why one bit separates upper and lower case in ASCII. Shifts Instruction Does Same as --- --- --- shl rax, n bits move left n places, 0s come in × 2ⁿ shr rax, n bits move right, 0s come in unsigned ÷ 2ⁿ sar rax, n bits move right, copies of the sign bit come in signed ÷ 2ⁿ (rounding down) rol rax, n / ror rax, n rotate: bits leaving one end come back at the other The count is a constant, or the register cl for a count worked out at run time ( shl rax, cl ). Only 6 bits of the count are used, so shifting a 64-bit register by 64 shifts by 0. demo-asm title: shr and sar on a negative number init: rax=-16 mov rbx, rax shr rax, 2 sar rbx, 2 ret shr treats −16 as a huge unsigned number; sar keeps it negative and gives −4. Masks with shifts Combine a shift and and to pull a field out of a number, like the C course's bit lessons: nasm-norun mov eax, edi shr eax, 8 ; move bits 8..15 to the bottom and eax, 0xFF ; keep just them and build a one-bit mask from a run-time position: nasm-norun mov ecx, esi ; the bit number, which must be in cl mov eax, 1 shl rax, cl ; rax = 1 << n or rdi, rax ; set bit n of rdi x86 also has single instructions for one bit: bt (test), bts (set), btr (clear), btc (flip). Multiplying with lea and shifts lea computes an address expression without touching memory, and the expression can be base + index × 1, 2, 4 or 8 . That makes it a quick multiplier: nasm-norun lea rax, rdi + rdi 2 ; rax = rdi 3 lea rax, rdi + rdi 4 ; rax = rdi 5 lea rax, rdi 8 + rdi ; rax = rdi 9 lea rax, rax + rax 4 add rax, rax ; with the line above: 10 Compilers turn x 10 into exactly that pair. Check yourself quiz ? What does and eax, 0xFF do? - Sets the low 8 bits to 1 - Adds 255 + Keeps the low 8 bits of eax and clears the rest and with a mask keeps only the mask's bits. ? Which shift divides a negative number by 4 correctly? - shr rax, 2 + sar rax, 2 - shl rax, 2 sar copies the sign bit in. ? Where does a variable shift count go? - rdx + cl - Any register shl rax, cl. ? What does lea rax, rdi + rdi 4 compute? - The value in memory at rdi 5 + rdi 5 - rdi + 4 lea computes the address but never reads memory.

title: Bits and shifts
body: Write these functions, without imul , mul or div : Function Result --- --- is_odd(x) 1 if x is odd, else 0 ( and with 1) set_bit(x, n) x with bit n set; n from 0 to 63 (the count must be in cl ) times10(x) x × 10, with lea and/or shifts div8(x) a signed x ÷ 8 rounded down , with one shift: div8(-9) is −2 byte_of(x, k) byte k of x, k from 0 to 7: byte_of(0x1122334455667788, 1) is 0x77 swap_nibbles(x) the low byte of x with its two hex digits swapped: swap_nibbles(0xAB) is 0xBA

title: 2.04  The Flags
body: Arithmetic and logic instructions record facts about their result in rflags - ZF when it is zero, SF when it is negative, CF when an unsigned result wrapped, OF when a signed result overflowed. cmp and test set flags without keeping a result. adc and sbb use the carry to work on numbers bigger than a register. Notes about the last result Most arithmetic and logic instructions leave notes about their result in the rflags register. Four of the single-bit flags matter most: Flag Name Set when the result... --- --- --- ZF zero is 0 SF sign has its top bit set: negative, read as signed CF carry wrapped past the top or below 0, read as unsigned OF overflow is wrong, read as signed : two positives gave a negative, or two negatives a positive mov , lea , push and pop do not change the flags; add , sub , and , or , xor , neg , cmp , test and shifts do. ( inc and dec change all but CF.) demo-asm title: Watch the flags init: rax=0 mov eax, 5 sub eax, 5 sub eax, 1 mov eax, 0x7FFFFFFF add eax, 1 mov eax, 0xFFFFFFFF add eax, 1 ret Step through and read the flags after each line: 1. 5 - 5 is 0: ZF . 2. 0 - 1 is −1 (all 1s): SF , and CF , because as unsigned numbers 0 − 1 went below zero. 3. 0x7FFFFFFF + 1 : the biggest signed 32-bit number plus one becomes the most negative one: OF and SF. As unsigned it is fine (2,147,483,648), so no CF. 4. 0xFFFFFFFF + 1 wraps to 0: CF and ZF. As signed it is −1 + 1 = 0, perfectly fine, so no OF. The processor doesn't know whether you meant signed or unsigned, so it records both: CF for unsigned, OF for signed. cmp and test The next module's jumps read the flags. To set them without changing anything: - cmp a, b subtracts b from a, sets the flags, and throws the answer away. After cmp rax, rbx , ZF means they were equal, and CF means rax < rbx as unsigned numbers. - test a, b does an and , sets the flags and throws the answer away. test rax, rax sets ZF if rax is 0 and SF if it is negative. Bigger than 64 bits: adc and sbb The carry flag is the "carry the one" of long addition. adc (add with carry) adds the operand and CF, so you can add numbers of any size, 64 bits at a time: nasm-norun ; a 128-bit number in rdx:rax plus another in rcx:rbx add rax, rbx ; the low halves; CF = the carry out adc rdx, rcx ; the high halves, plus that carry sbb (subtract with borrow) does the same for subtraction. A neat trick: after cmp a, b , sbb eax, eax gives −1 if a < b as unsigned numbers and 0 otherwise, without any jump. Keeping a flag as a number adc with zero turns the carry into a number: nasm global _start section .text _start: mov rax, -1 ; the largest unsigned 64-bit number xor ebx, ebx add rax, 1 ; wraps: CF = 1 adc rbx, 0 ; rbx = 0 + 0 + CF = 1 mov rdi, rbx call print_int call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall Lesson 3.05 shows setc , setz and friends, which do this for any flag. Check yourself quiz ? Which flag says an unsigned result wrapped around? - OF, overflow + CF, carry - ZF, zero OF is the signed version. ? 0x7FFFFFFF + 1 in a 32-bit register sets which flag that 0xFFFFFFFF + 1 does not? - CF + OF - ZF As signed numbers, the first overflowed and the second did not. ? What does cmp rax, rbx change? - rax + Only the flags - rbx It subtracts and throws the result away. ? What is adc for? - Adding two characters together - Adding a value to an address + Adding with the carry from the last addition adc adds the carry flag too, which chains additions for numbers bigger than a register: long addition, 64 bits at a time.

title: Carries and borrows
body: Use the carry flag, through adc and sbb , with no jumps : Function Result --- --- carry_out(a, b) 1 if the unsigned 64-bit sum a + b wraps around, else 0 add128_high(a_low, a_high, b_low, b_high) the high 64 bits of the 128-bit sum (a_high:a_low) + (b_high:b_low) below(a, b) 1 if a < b as unsigned numbers, else 0 sum_with_carry(a, b) a + b, plus 1 more if a + b wrapped: sum_with_carry(-1, 1) is 1 The four arguments of add128_high arrive in rdi , rsi , rdx and rcx .

title: 2.05  Printing Digits Yourself
body: To print a number, split it into decimal digits with div - by 100 for the hundreds, by 10 for the tens, the remainder for the units - and turn each digit into a character by adding '0'. Store the characters in a buffer and write them. print_int does the same with a loop, building the digits from the right. Digits are remainders The number 427 is 4 hundreds, 2 tens and 7 units. Division pulls them apart: quotient remainder --- --- --- 427 ÷ 100 4 27 27 ÷ 10 2 7 Each digit 0 to 9 becomes its character by adding '0' (48): the characters '0' to '9' have the codes 48 to 57, in order. So 4 becomes '4' (52). A three-digit printer nasm global _start section .bss digits: resb 4 ; three digits and a new line section .text _start: mov eax, 427 ; the number, 0 to 999 xor edx, edx mov ecx, 100 div ecx ; eax = hundreds, edx = the rest add al, '0' mov rel digits , al mov eax, edx ; the rest, 0 to 99 xor edx, edx mov ecx, 10 div ecx ; eax = tens, edx = units add al, '0' mov rel digits + 1 , al add dl, '0' mov rel digits + 2 , dl mov byte rel digits + 3 , 10 mov eax, 1 ; write the 4 bytes mov edi, 1 lea rsi, rel digits mov edx, 4 syscall mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall - div ecx is the 32-bit form: it divides edx:eax by ecx . That is enough for small numbers and faster than the 64-bit form. - mov rel digits + 1 , al stores one byte at the address digits + 1 . Lesson 4.01 covers addresses. - This version always prints three digits: 7 comes out as 007 . Any number of digits A number can have up to 20 decimal digits (2⁶⁴ is about 1.8 × 10¹⁹). Instead of a fixed set of divisions, print_uint repeats one step: divide by 10, and the remainder is the last digit. Then the quotient's last digit is the one before, and so on, until the quotient is 0. Because the digits come out from right to left, it fills its buffer backwards: nasm-norun print_uint: sub rsp, 40 ; room on the stack for the digits (lesson 4.04) lea rsi, rsp + 32 ; start at the right-hand end mov rax, rdi mov ecx, 10 .digit: xor edx, edx div rcx ; rax = rax / 10, rdx = the last digit add dl, '0' dec rsi ; move one place left mov rsi , dl ; store the character test rax, rax jnz .digit ; more digits while the quotient is not 0 ... ; then write from rsi to the end jnz means "jump if not zero", back to .digit : a loop. That is the subject of module 3. After it, you will write your own version, and lesson 6.02 handles signed numbers and reading digits back in. Printing in other bases The same method works for any base: divide by 2 for binary, by 16 for hexadecimal (where digits 10 to 15 become 'a' to 'f' ). Since 2 and 16 are powers of two, shifts and masks replace the divisions: the last hex digit is n & 15 , and n 4 drops it. That is how print_hex works. Check yourself quiz ? What is the character for the digit 7? - 7 + 7 + '0', which is 55 - '0' - 7 The digit characters are in order from 48. ? 427 divided by 10 leaves remainder 7. What does that give? - The first digit - The number of digits + The last digit Division by 10 peels digits off the right. ? Why does print_uint fill its buffer from the end? - Because the stack grows down + Division by 10 produces the digits from right to left - To print the number backwards The last digit comes out first. ? Before div ecx, why xor edx, edx? - To clear the flags before dividing - To make the remainder come out as 0 + div ecx divides edx:eax, so edx must be 0 The 32-bit form uses edx as the high half of the number being divided. For a 32-bit number in eax, that half must be zero.

title: 3.01  Compare and Jump
body: jmp always jumps to a label. A conditional jump such as je, jne, jl or jg jumps only when the flags say so, which usually means right after cmp or test. An if statement becomes a compare, a jump over the code that should not run, and a label. Labels starting with a dot are local to the label above them. jmp jmp label makes the processor continue at the label instead of the next line: it just puts a new address in rip . nasm-norun jmp done ; skip everything up to done mov eax, 99 ; never runs done: Conditional jumps A conditional jump looks at the flags and jumps only if its condition holds; otherwise it carries on with the next line. After cmp a, b : Jump Jumps if Meaning --- --- --- je / jz ZF = 1 a == b (or: the result was zero) jne / jnz ZF = 0 a != b jl SF ≠ OF a < b, signed jle ZF = 1 or SF ≠ OF a <= b, signed jg ZF = 0 and SF = OF a b, signed jge SF = OF a = b, signed jb CF = 1 a < b, unsigned ("below") jbe CF = 1 or ZF = 1 a <= b, unsigned ja CF = 0 and ZF = 0 a b, unsigned ("above") jae CF = 0 a = b, unsigned js / jns SF = 1 / 0 negative / not negative You never need to remember the flag formulas: read cmp rax, rbx followed by jl as "jump if rax < rbx". Lesson 3.03 explains the signed and unsigned pairs. if C's c-norun if (temperature < 0) { puts("Freezing"); } puts("Done"); becomes a compare and a jump over the body, using the opposite condition: nasm global _start section .data freezing: db "Freezing", 10, 0 done_msg: db "Done", 10, 0 section .text _start: call read_int ; the temperature cmp rax, 0 jge .after ; NOT below zero: skip the body lea rdi, rel freezing call print_str .after: lea rdi, rel done_msg call print_str mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall Try it with -5 and with 12 as the input. if and else With an else , the "then" part must jump over the "else" part when it is done: nasm-norun cmp rax, rbx jle .else ; not (rax rbx) ; ... rax is bigger ... jmp .end .else: ; ... rbx is bigger or equal ... .end: demo-asm title: The larger of two numbers init: rdi=12, rsi=30 mov rax, rdi cmp rdi, rsi jge done mov rax, rsi done: ret This shorter pattern is common: put one answer in place, and jump past the line that would replace it. Local labels Every label in a file must be unique, which gets tedious: .after , .loop , .done would be needed many times. In NASM a label starting with a dot is local : it belongs to the most recent ordinary label above it, so each function can have its own .done . nasm-norun max: mov rax, rdi cmp rdi, rsi jge .done ; this is really max.done mov rax, rsi .done: ret min: mov rax, rdi cmp rdi, rsi jle .done ; min.done: no clash mov rax, rsi .done: ret Check yourself quiz ? After cmp rax, 10, which jump goes when rax is 10 or more (signed)? - jg + jge - jl jg would skip 10 itself. ? To skip the body of if (x == 0) { ... }, which jump do you use? - je + jne, the opposite condition - jmp Jump over the body when the condition does not hold. ? What does jmp do? - Jumps only if the last result was zero - Calls a function + Always continues at the label It sets rip to the label's address. ? What is special about a label like .done? - It marks the end of the program + It is local to the label above it - It cannot be the target of a jump NASM joins it to the previous ordinary label's name, so .done can be reused under every function.

title: 3.02  Loops
body: A loop is a jump backwards. Counting loops often count down to zero with dec and jnz, since dec sets the zero flag for free. A while loop tests at the top and a do-while at the bottom; compilers prefer the bottom test with one check in front. Reading until read_int reports the end of the input makes a loop over all the input. A jump backwards nasm global _start section .text _start: mov ebx, 1 ; i = 1 .loop: mov edi, ebx call print_int call print_newline inc ebx ; i++ cmp ebx, 5 jle .loop ; while i <= 5, go round again mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall The counter lives in rbx because print_int may change rcx , rdx , rsi and rdi . Counting down to zero dec sets ZF when it reaches zero, so a loop that counts down needs no cmp : demo-asm title: Add up 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 init: ecx=5 xor eax, eax top: add eax, ecx dec ecx jnz top ret That is the classic assembly loop. (x86 even has a loop instruction that decrements rcx and jumps, but on modern processors it is slower than dec + jnz , so compilers never use it.) while and do-while A do-while tests at the bottom, so the body always runs at least once: nasm-norun .body: ; ... cmp ... jcc .body A while loop must test first, in case it should run zero times. The straightforward version tests at the top and jumps back from the bottom: nasm-norun .test: cmp ... jcc .end ; the opposite condition: leave the loop ; ... body ... jmp .test .end: That is two jumps per round. Compilers turn it into a single test in front plus a do-while, called a rotated loop, which takes one jump per round: nasm-norun cmp ... jcc .end ; skip the loop entirely if it should not run .body: ; ... body ... cmp ... jcc .body ; one jump per round .end: Reading until the end of the input read_int returns rdx = 0 when there are no more numbers. Testing it after each call makes a loop over the whole input: nasm global _start section .data s_count: db " numbers, total ", 0 section .text _start: xor ebx, ebx ; total xor r12d, r12d ; count .next: call read_int test rdx, rdx jz .done ; no more numbers add rbx, rax inc r12 jmp .next .done: mov rdi, r12 call print_int lea rdi, rel s_count call print_str mov rdi, rbx call print_int call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall Try it with several numbers on several lines. Loops inside loops Keep each counter in its own register that survives the calls inside (here r12 and r13 ): nasm global _start section .text _start: mov r12d, 1 ; row .row: mov r13d, 1 ; column .col: mov edi, ' ' call print_char inc r13d cmp r13d, r12d jle .col ; columns 1..row call print_newline inc r12d cmp r12d, 4 jle .row mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall Check yourself quiz ? Why does dec ecx followed by jnz top work without a cmp? - jnz compares ecx with 0 itself - dec jumps automatically + dec sets the zero flag when ecx reaches 0 Arithmetic sets the flags as a side effect. ? Which loop always runs its body at least once? - One that tests at the top (while) - Neither + One that tests at the bottom (do-while) A while loop may run zero times. ? Why keep a loop counter in rbx or r12 to r15 when the loop calls print_int? - Only those registers can count - Those registers are faster than the others + Calls may change rcx, but not rbx or r12 to r15 By the calling convention, routines may change rcx, rdx, rsi and rdi, but must keep rbx and r12 to r15. ? How does a loop over all the input know when to stop? - read_int returns -1 in rax + read_int returns rdx = 0 at the end - The program crashes at the end Test rdx after each call; -1 is a number the input could really contain.

title: 3.03  Signed and Unsigned Conditions
body: The same bits compare differently as signed and unsigned numbers - all 1s is -1 or the largest number. cmp sets flags for both readings, and you choose with the jump - jl, jg for signed, jb, ja for unsigned. Using the wrong one is a classic bug, and one unsigned compare can check a whole range. Same bits, two orders Take rax = -1 and rbx = 1 . Which is bigger? - As signed numbers: −1 < 1. - As unsigned numbers: 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF (18,446,744,073,709,551,615) 1. The bits do not say which reading you mean, so cmp sets flags for both, and the jump decides : signed unsigned --- --- --- < jl (less) jb (below) <= jle jbe jg (greater) ja (above) = jge jae Equality ( je , jne ) is the same for both. nasm global _start section .data s_less: db "signed: -1 is less than 1", 10, 0 s_above: db "unsigned: -1 is above 1", 10, 0 section .text _start: mov rbx, -1 cmp rbx, 1 jge .unsigned lea rdi, rel s_less call print_str .unsigned: cmp rbx, 1 jbe .done lea rdi, rel s_above call print_str .done: mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall Both messages print: the same comparison, read two ways. How the flags tell them apart cmp a, b works out a − b: - For unsigned numbers, a < b exactly when the subtraction had to borrow: CF = 1 . So jb is jc (jump if carry). - For signed numbers the sign of the result would tell you, except that the subtraction may overflow and flip it. So the rule is "less when SF ≠ OF": the sign is wrong exactly when overflow happened. Which one to use The values are Use --- --- sizes, counts, addresses, array indexes unsigned: jb , ja , ... characters (bytes 0 to 255) unsigned values that can be negative signed: jl , jg , ... C compilers choose from the declared types: int gives jl , unsigned and size_t give jb . In assembly there are no types: you must remember which you meant. !warning The negative index bug Checking an index with cmp rax, rcx / jge .out_of_range (signed) lets a negative index through, because −5 is less than the length. jae (unsigned) rejects it, since −5 as unsigned is huge. One unsigned compare checks both ends. A range in one compare The same trick checks whether a value is between low and high : subtract low , then compare unsigned against high - low . Anything below low wraps to a huge number: nasm-norun ; is the character in al a digit, '0' to '9'? sub al, '0' cmp al, 9 jbe .is_digit ; 0..9 after the subtraction: a digit Compilers do this all the time for if (c = '0' && c <= '9') . Check yourself quiz ? rax = -1, rbx = 1. After cmp rax, rbx, does jb jump? - Yes, because -1 is less than 1 + No: as unsigned, -1 is the largest number - It depends on the instruction before the cmp jb compares unsigned, and -1 as unsigned is all ones, above rbx. jl would jump, because as signed numbers -1 < 1. ? Which jump treats the numbers as signed? - ja - jae + jg Greater and less are signed; above and below are unsigned. ? Why is jae better than jge for checking an index against a length? - jae is faster than jge - jge does not work with lengths + A negative index looks huge, so it is caught too As unsigned, a negative index is above any length, so one compare checks both ends. ? What does sub al, '0' followed by cmp al, 9 and jbe test? - Whether al is negative - Whether al is 9 + Whether al held a digit character Values below '0' wrap to large numbers.

title: 3.04  if, else and switch from C
match: 3.04 if, else and switch from C
body: Chains of if and else become a series of compares, each jumping to the next test. && jumps out at the first false part and at the first true part. A switch over close-together values becomes a jump table - an array of addresses indexed by the value - after one unsigned compare that sends everything out of range to default. else if chains c-norun if (score = 90) grade = 'A'; else if (score = 75) grade = 'B'; else if (score = 50) grade = 'C'; else grade = 'F'; Each test jumps to the next test when it fails, and each body jumps to the end: nasm-norun cmp rdi, 90 jl .not_a mov eax, 'A' jmp .end .not_a: cmp rdi, 75 jl .not_b mov eax, 'B' jmp .end .not_b: cmp rdi, 50 jl .not_c mov eax, 'C' jmp .end .not_c: mov eax, 'F' .end: && and C's && and stop as soon as the answer is known, and in assembly that is just where the jumps go: c-norun if (x = 1 && x <= 10) { ... } // both must hold if (c == ' ' c == '\n') { ... } // either is enough nasm-norun ; x = 1 && x <= 10: leave at the first part that fails cmp rdi, 1 jl .skip cmp rdi, 10 jg .skip ; ... body ... .skip: ; c == ' ' c == '\n': enter at the first part that holds cmp dil, ' ' je .body cmp dil, 10 jne .skip2 .body: ; ... body ... .skip2: switch and jump tables A switch over a few values could be a chain of compares. Over many close-together values, compilers build a jump table : an array of label addresses, and one indirect jump that picks an entry with the value as the index. nasm global _start section .data s_zero: db "zero", 10, 0 s_one: db "one", 10, 0 s_two: db "two", 10, 0 s_three: db "three", 10, 0 s_many: db "lots", 10, 0 section .rodata table: dq _start.case0, _start.case1, _start.case2, _start.case3 ; each case's address section .text _start: .next: call read_int test rdx, rdx jz .exit cmp rax, 3 ja .default ; unsigned: catches negative numbers too lea rcx, rel table jmp rcx + rax 8 ; jump to the address stored in table rax .case0: lea rdi, rel s_zero jmp .print .case1: lea rdi, rel s_one jmp .print .case2: lea rdi, rel s_two jmp .print .case3: lea rdi, rel s_three jmp .print .default: lea rdi, rel s_many .print: call print_str jmp .next .exit: mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall Run it with the input 2 0 7 -1 3 . - dq _start.case0, ... stores the 8-byte addresses of the labels. The cases are local labels inside _start , and their full names are _start.case0 and so on. The table must spell them out, because inside the table a plain .case0 would belong to the label table . - jmp rcx + rax 8 reads 8 bytes from the table and jumps there: an indirect jump . - The one ja check sends both too-big and negative values to the default, the unsigned trick from lesson 3.03. Without it, a bad value would jump to whatever address happened to be in memory past the table. The table costs the same however many cases there are: one compare and one jump. Interpreters for languages like Python dispatch their instructions this way. Check yourself quiz ? How does if (a && b) skip its body when a is false? - It tests both, then jumps - It cannot: && needs a special instruction + It jumps past the body right after testing a, without testing b Short-circuiting is just where the jumps go. ? What is in a jump table? - The case values + The addresses of the code for each case - A copy of each case's code jmp table + index 8 picks one. ? Why does the switch code check cmp rax, 3 / ja .default first? - To make the switch faster + So no value, negative or large, indexes past the table - Because jmp cannot take a register One unsigned compare refuses everything outside 0 to 3, negative values included. ? Each entry of the table is 8 bytes. Why? - Each case has 8 instructions + Each is a 64-bit address - The table is aligned So the index is multiplied by 8.

title: 3.05  Branch-Free Code cmov and setcc
body: Processors guess which way each jump will go and work ahead; a wrong guess wastes many cycles. cmovcc copies a value only if a condition holds, and setcc turns a condition into a 0 or 1 byte, so simple choices need no jump at all. Compilers use them for min, max, abs and boolean results. Why avoid jumps? A modern processor works on many instructions at once, in a long pipeline . When it meets a conditional jump it does not wait to find out the answer: it predicts which way the jump will go and carries on working down that path. If the guess was right, nothing is lost. If wrong, all that work is thrown away, which costs around 15 to 20 cycles. Predictors are very good at patterns (a loop that runs 1000 times is predicted right 999 times), but a jump that depends on random data is wrong about half the time. For small choices, it is better not to jump at all. cmov: copy only if cmovcc destination, source copies the source only when the condition holds. The conditions are the same letters as the jumps: cmove , cmovne , cmovl , cmovg , cmovb , cmova , ... demo-asm title: max(a, b) with no jump init: rdi=12, rsi=30 mov rax, rdi cmp rdi, rsi cmovl rax, rsi ret The processor always runs all three instructions; there is nothing to guess. Some useful ones: nasm-norun ; abs(x) mov rax, rdi neg rax ; rax = -x, and the flags say whether -x is negative cmovs rax, rdi ; if -x is negative, x was positive: use x ; clamp x to at most 100 mov rax, rdi mov ecx, 100 cmp rax, rcx cmovg rax, rcx cmov cannot take a constant as its source, so put the constant in a register first, as above. setcc: a condition as a number setcc writes 1 or 0 into a byte register depending on the condition: nasm-norun ; return (a == b) xor eax, eax ; clear all of rax first... cmp rdi, rsi sete al ; ...because sete only writes al ret Clear the register before the cmp : xor changes the flags, so doing it after would wreck the comparison. Then sete al writes 1 or 0 into the low byte, and the rest is already 0. (The other way is movzx eax, al after the setcc .) Tricks with no compare at all Some answers fall straight out of arithmetic: nasm-norun ; sign(x): -1, 0 or 1 mov rax, rdi sar rax, 63 ; -1 if negative, else 0 xor ecx, ecx test rdi, rdi setg cl ; 1 if positive, else 0 or rax, rcx ; -1, 0 or 1 ; abs(x) with a mask mov rax, rdi sar rax, 63 ; all 1s if negative, else 0 xor rdi, rax ; flip the bits if negative sub rdi, rax ; and add 1 if negative: two's complement negation mov rax, rdi When to use them A jump is still better when the choice skips a lot of work (computing both sides costs more than a misprediction), or when the pattern is predictable. For a quick choice between two ready values, cmov or setcc wins. Compilers decide this for you at -O2 , which is why you see cmov in their output so often. Check yourself quiz ? What does cmovl rax, rsi do after cmp rdi, rsi? - Always copies rsi into rax - Jumps if rdi < rsi + Copies rsi into rax only if rdi < rsi Conditional move: no jump. ? Why is a branch on random data slow? - Jumps are always slow + The processor guesses wrong about half the time - Random data is slow to read from memory Each wrong guess throws away the work done on the guessed path. Predictable branches are almost free. ? After sete al, what is in the rest of rax? - 0 + Whatever was there before - 1 setcc writes only one byte, so clear eax before the compare. ? Why must xor eax, eax come before cmp, not between cmp and sete? - xor is a slow instruction + xor changes the flags that cmp just set - sete only works when eax is already 0 xor sets the flags itself, which would destroy the comparison's result. Order matters with the flags.

title: 4.01  Addressing Modes
body: Square brackets mean memory. An address can be built from a base register, an index register times 1, 2, 4 or 8, and a constant, or relative to rip for labels. The size comes from the register or is written as byte, word, dword or qword. movzx and movsx widen small values, and lea computes an address without reading it. Brackets mean memory Without brackets an operand is a register or a number; with brackets it is the memory at that address : nasm-norun mov rax, rbx ; rax = rbx mov rax, rbx ; rax = the 8 bytes at the address in rbx mov rbx , rax ; store rax's 8 bytes at that address Only one operand of an instruction may be in memory: to copy memory to memory, go through a register. Building an address An x86 address can combine up to four parts: base + index scale + displacement Part Is --- --- base any register index any register except rsp scale 1, 2, 4 or 8 displacement a constant, or a label That covers almost everything a program needs in one instruction: C Assembly (rdi = the array, rsi = i) --- --- p- field at offset 16 rdi + 16 a i for 8-byte elements rdi + rsi 8 a i for 4-byte int s rdi + rsi 4 a i + 1 rdi + rsi 8 + 8 bytes i rdi + rsi Labels: rel A label is an address fixed when the program is built. Programs today are often loaded at a random address (a protection called ASLR), so code refers to its data relative to rip , the address of the current instruction: rel label . The assembler works out the distance. nasm-norun mov rax, rel total ; read the 8 bytes at total lea rsi, rel message ; the address of message itself ( default rel at the top of a file makes every label rip-relative, so you can leave out rel .) Sizes The register says how many bytes move: mov eax, rdi reads 4, mov al, rdi reads 1. When no register is involved, write the size: nasm-norun mov byte rdi , 'A' ; store one byte mov dword rdi + 4 , 100 ; store 4 bytes add qword rel count , 1 ; add to 8 bytes Widening: movzx and movsx To read a small value into a big register, say how to fill the rest: Instruction Fills the upper bits with For --- --- --- movzx eax, byte rdi 0s unsigned bytes, characters movsx rax, byte rdi copies of the sign bit signed bytes movsx rax, word rdi signed 16-bit numbers movsxd rax, dword rdi signed 32-bit numbers to 64 (32-bit unsigned needs nothing special: mov eax, rdi already clears the top half.) demo-asm title: The same byte, zero- and sign-extended init: rdi=0x2000, mem@0x2000=-3 movzx eax, byte rdi movsx rbx, byte rdi ret The byte is 0xFD : movzx gives 253, movsx gives −3. lea: the address, not the contents lea (load effective address) works out the address in brackets and puts the number in the register, without reading memory: nasm-norun lea rax, rdi + rsi 8 ; rax = the address of a i mov rax, rdi + rsi 8 ; rax = a i itself That is how C's &a i compiles, and it is also why lea doubles as an adder (lesson 2.03). nasm global _start section .data values: dq 10, 20, 30, 40 section .text _start: lea rbx, rel values ; the array's address mov rdi, rbx + 2 8 ; values 2 = 30 add rdi, rbx + 3 8 ; + values 3 = 70 call print_int call print_newline mov qword rbx , 99 ; values 0 = 99 mov rdi, rbx call print_int call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference between mov rax, rbx and mov rax, rbx ? - None: both copy rbx into rax - The second copies rax into rbx + The first copies rbx; the second reads memory Brackets mean memory: rbx is the value stored at the address in rbx. ? rdi points at an array of 4-byte ints and rsi is i. Which is a i ? - rdi + rsi + dword rdi + rsi 4 - rdi 4 + rsi The index is multiplied by the element size. ? Why write mov byte rdi , 5 rather than mov rdi , 5? - byte makes the store faster + NASM cannot tell how many bytes to store - rdi is not allowed on its own With no register in the instruction, the size is unknown. Write byte, word, dword or qword. ? What does lea rax, rdi + 8 do? - Reads the 8 bytes at rdi + 8 - Adds 8 to the memory at rdi + Puts rdi + 8 in rax Load effective address computes the address without touching memory.

title: 4.02  Arrays
body: An array in assembly is an address and a count - nothing marks its end or its type. Loop with an index and a scaled address, or move a pointer along by the element size until it reaches the end. Arrays come from the data section, .bss, or the caller, and the code must know whether each element is 1, 4 or 8 bytes. An address and a count In memory an array is just elements side by side. Nothing records how many there are or what they are, so functions take the address of the first element and the count , exactly like C functions taking (const long values, size_t count) . Looping with an index nasm global _start section .data scores: dq 72, 95, 61, 88, 100, 54 count equ ($ - scores) / 8 ; 6: the bytes divided by the element size section .text _start: lea rsi, rel scores xor ecx, ecx ; i = 0 xor eax, eax ; total = 0 .loop: add rax, rsi + rcx 8 ; total += scores i inc rcx cmp rcx, count jb .loop ; while i < count (unsigned: it is an index) mov rdi, rax call print_int ; 470 call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall Looping with a pointer Instead of an index, move a pointer along by the element size and stop at the end address, the begin/end style from the C course: nasm-norun ; rdi = the array, rsi = the count. Returns the largest element (count = 1). max_of: lea rdx, rdi + rsi 8 ; end = one past the last element mov rax, rdi ; best = the first add rdi, 8 .loop: cmp rdi, rdx jae .done mov rcx, rdi cmp rcx, rax cmovg rax, rcx add rdi, 8 ; the next element jmp .loop .done: ret Both styles are common in compiler output; the pointer style saves the multiplication in the address (which is free anyway on x86) and frees a register. Element sizes C type Size Read with --- --- --- char , unsigned char , int8_t 1 movzx eax, byte rdi + rcx / movsx short , int16_t 2 movsx eax, word rdi + rcx 2 int , int32_t 4 mov eax, rdi + rcx 4 ( movsxd to 64 bits) long , pointers, int64_t 8 mov rax, rdi + rcx 8 Get the size wrong and you read pieces of two elements at once, with no error. Assembly will not stop you. Changing an array Storing works the same way in reverse. This doubles every element in place: nasm global _start section .data values: dq 1, -2, 3, 40 section .text _start: lea rbx, rel values xor ecx, ecx .double: shl qword rbx + rcx 8 , 1 ; values i = 2, right in memory inc rcx cmp rcx, 4 jb .double xor r12d, r12d ; print them .print: mov rdi, rbx + r12 8 call print_int mov edi, ' ' call print_char inc r12 cmp r12, 4 jb .print call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall The print loop uses r12 , not rcx , because the routines may change rcx . !danger No bounds Reading values 10 of a 4-element array reads whatever follows it: other data, or memory that does not belong to the program (a segmentation fault). Every check is yours to write, usually one unsigned compare (lesson 3.03). Check yourself quiz ? What does a function need to work on an array? - Only its address - Only its name + Its address and how many elements it has Nothing in memory marks the end. ? count equ ($ - scores) / 8 gives... - The size in bytes - The address of the last element + The number of 8-byte elements in scores $ - scores is the size in bytes. ? An array of 4-byte ints is at rdi. Which reads element rcx? - mov rax, rdi + rcx 8 - mov eax, rdi + rcx + mov eax, rdi + rcx 4 Scale by the element size, and read 4 bytes. ? Why does the pointer-style loop stop at jae rather than jge? - jae is faster - jge does not work with registers + Addresses are unsigned numbers Compare addresses and indexes unsigned.

title: Array loops
body: Every function gets an array of signed 8-byte numbers in rdi and its count in rsi : Function Result --- --- sum(array, n) the total (0 for an empty array) max_of(array, n) the largest, n = 1 count_equal(array, n, v) how many elements equal v index_of(array, n, v) the first index holding v, or −1 reverse(array, n) reverses the array in place add_to_all(array, n, k) adds k to every element in place

title: 4.03  Strings
body: A string is bytes in memory, ending with a 0 byte by C's convention. Loops over strings read one byte at a time with movzx and stop at the 0. Length, copy, compare and case changes are all short loops. The string instructions rep movsb and rep stosb copy and fill whole blocks in one instruction. Bytes with a zero at the end Text is bytes: one per ASCII character (or several per character in UTF-8). Assembly has no string type, so programs follow a convention. The C convention, used by print_str and by every C library function, is a zero byte at the end. demo-text title: "Hi!" in memory text: Hi! Length nasm-norun ; rdi = a zero-terminated string. Returns its length. length: xor eax, eax .loop: cmp byte rdi + rax , 0 je .done inc rax jmp .loop .done: ret cmp byte rdi + rax , 0 compares one byte of memory with 0 directly: no register needed. Reading characters To work on a character, read it with movzx so the rest of the register is clean, then compare and change the low byte: nasm global _start section .data text: db "Hello, assembly world!", 0 section .text _start: lea rbx, rel text mov rsi, rbx .loop: movzx eax, byte rsi test al, al jz .done ; the 0 at the end cmp al, 'a' jb .next cmp al, 'z' ja .next sub al, 32 ; 'a' to 'z' become 'A' to 'Z' mov rsi , al ; write it back .next: inc rsi jmp .loop .done: mov rdi, rbx call print_str call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall This changes the string where it is, which works because it is in .data . Text in .rodata would crash when written. Copying and comparing nasm-norun ; rdi = destination, rsi = source. Copies the string with its 0. copy: .loop: movzx eax, byte rsi mov rdi , al inc rsi inc rdi test al, al jnz .loop ; the 0 was copied too: stop ret ; rdi, rsi = two strings. Returns 1 if they are equal. equal: .loop: movzx eax, byte rdi cmp al, rsi jne .no ; a difference test al, al jz .yes ; both ended together inc rdi inc rsi jmp .loop .yes: mov eax, 1 ret .no: xor eax, eax ret The destination must have room: copying a long string into a short buffer overwrites whatever follows, the buffer overflow of C, with no warning at all here. The string instructions x86 has instructions made for blocks of memory. With a rep prefix they repeat rcx times: Instruction Does, each time --- --- rep movsb copy the byte at rsi to rdi , then move both on rep stosb store al at rdi , then move it on repne scasb compare al with rdi , move on, stop at a match nasm-norun ; fill 64 bytes at buffer with '-' lea rdi, rel buffer mov al, '-' mov ecx, 64 rep stosb ; copy rcx bytes from rsi to rdi rep movsb They move forwards as long as the direction flag is clear, which the calling convention guarantees. Modern processors run rep movsb very fast for large blocks, and C's memcpy and memset often use it. Check yourself quiz ? How does a C-style string mark its end? - With its length stored first + With a zero byte - With a new line print_str and the C library both rely on it. ? Why read characters with movzx eax, byte rsi ? - It reads the whole string at once + It reads one byte and zeroes the rest - mov cannot read single bytes mov al, rsi would leave the old upper bits of eax in place. ? Which instruction copies rcx bytes from rsi to rdi ? - rep stosb + rep movsb - mov rdi , rsi Memory-to-memory mov does not exist. ? What happens when copy is given a destination that is too small? - It stops at the end of the buffer + It writes past the end, over whatever follows - It crashes at once, every time The function cannot know the buffer's size.

title: 4.04  The Stack push and pop
body: The stack is memory that grows downwards from a high address, and rsp always points at its top. push moves rsp down 8 bytes and stores a value; pop loads it and moves rsp back up. It saves registers that must be kept, holds temporary space reserved with sub rsp, and must end exactly where it started. A stack of plates The stack is a region of memory the operating system gives every program, a few megabytes in size. rsp points at the item on top. It grows downwards : pushing makes rsp smaller. Instruction Same as --- --- push rax sub rsp, 8 then mov rsp , rax pop rbx mov rbx, rsp then add rsp, 8 The last thing pushed is the first popped: a "last in, first out" stack. demo-asm title: push and pop init: rax=11, rbx=22, rcx=33 push rax push rbx push rcx pop rax pop rbx pop rcx ret Step through and watch rsp and the values on the stack. Popping in the same order as pushing reverses them: afterwards rax = 33 and rcx = 11. Saving registers The most common use: keeping a register's value safe while you need the register for something else. A function that wants to use rbx (which it must give back unchanged) saves it first: nasm-norun sum_squares: ; rdi = a, rsi = b; returns a a + b b push rbx ; save the caller's rbx mov rbx, rdi imul rbx, rdi ; rbx = a a mov rax, rsi imul rax, rsi ; rax = b b add rax, rbx pop rbx ; give rbx back ret Pops must match pushes, in reverse order : push rbx , push r12 ... pop r12 , pop rbx . Temporary space Subtracting from rsp reserves bytes on the stack; adding gives them back. This is how functions get local arrays and buffers without .bss : nasm global _start section .text _start: sub rsp, 16 ; 16 bytes of space at rsp to rsp + 15 mov byte rsp , 'O' mov byte rsp + 1 , 'K' mov byte rsp + 2 , '!' mov byte rsp + 3 , 10 mov eax, 1 mov edi, 1 mov rsi, rsp ; the address of the bytes on the stack mov edx, 4 syscall add rsp, 16 ; give the space back mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall Reversing with the stack Since the stack reverses order, it can turn a string around: push every character, then pop them back in: nasm global _start section .data text: db "stressed", 0 section .text _start: lea rsi, rel text xor ecx, ecx ; how many pushed .push: movzx eax, byte rsi + rcx test al, al jz .popping push rax inc rcx jmp .push .popping: xor edx, edx .pop: cmp rdx, rcx jae .done pop rax mov rsi + rdx , al inc rdx jmp .pop .done: lea rdi, rel text call print_str ; desserts call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall Rules !warning Leave the stack as you found it - Every push needs a pop (or an add rsp ) before the function returns, or ret will jump to a wrong address (lesson 5.01 shows why) and the program crashes. - Never read below rsp after the space is given back: the next push or system call overwrites it. - Before calling a function, rsp must be a multiple of 16 (lesson 5.02). The routines in this course do not mind, but C functions can crash otherwise. Check yourself quiz ? What does push rax do? - Stores rax at rsp and moves rsp up - Copies rax into rsp + Moves rsp down by 8 and stores rax at the new rsp The stack grows downwards. ? After push rax, push rbx, pop rax, pop rbx - what happened? - Nothing changed + rax and rbx were swapped - Both hold the old rbx Last in, first out. ? How does a function make room for 32 bytes of local space? - With push 32 + With sub rsp, 32, undone before ret - With mov rsp, 32 Subtracting from rsp reserves space on the stack; add rsp, 32 gives it back before returning. ? A function pushes rbx and r12 at the start. In which order should it pop them? - pop rbx, then pop r12 + pop r12, then pop rbx - Either Reverse order.

These functions must use rbx and r12 (or other callee-saved registers) for their work, so save them with push and restore them with pop : Function Result --- --- sum_of_squares(a, b, c) a² + b² + c², keeping a running total in rbx reverse_string(s) reverses the string in place by pushing every character and popping them back largest_gap(array, n) the largest difference between two neighbours, array i+1 - array i , for n = 2; keep the best so far in r12

title: 4.05  Buffers and Input
body: Input arrives as bytes in a buffer, from the read system call or the read_line routine. Turning typed digits into a number is the reverse of printing - multiply what you have by 10 and add the next digit. Always pass the buffer's size, check what came back, and handle the end of the input. The read system call read (system call 0) copies up to a given number of bytes from a file into a buffer and returns how many it got: fewer than asked if that is all there is, 0 at the end of the input, negative on an error. nasm global _start section .bss buffer: resb 64 section .text _start: xor eax, eax ; read xor edi, edi ; standard input lea rsi, rel buffer mov edx, 64 ; at most 64 bytes syscall test rax, rax jle .exit ; nothing read, or an error mov rdx, rax ; echo exactly the bytes that came in mov eax, 1 mov edi, 1 lea rsi, rel buffer syscall .exit: mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall A single read may return part of a line, or several lines at once: it returns whatever bytes are ready. Real programs loop until they have what they need. That bookkeeping is what read_line and read_int do for you. read_line read_line (from lesson 1.06) fills a buffer with exactly one line, without the new line, ends it with a 0, and returns its length, or −1 at the end of the input. The buffer and its size are yours: nasm global _start section .bss line: resb 100 section .data s_len: db " characters: ", 0 section .text _start: .next: lea rdi, rel line mov esi, 100 call read_line cmp rax, -1 je .exit mov rdi, rax call print_int lea rdi, rel s_len call print_str lea rdi, rel line call print_str call print_newline jmp .next .exit: mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall Digits into a number Typed text "427" is the bytes 52, 50, 55. Converting it is printing in reverse: start at 0, and for each digit multiply by 10 and add the digit's value: Character number × 10 + digit --- --- 0 '4' 0 × 10 + 4 = 4 '2' 4 × 10 + 2 = 42 '7' 42 × 10 + 7 = 427 nasm-norun ; rdi = a string of digits. Returns its value (stops at the first non-digit). parse: xor eax, eax .loop: movzx ecx, byte rdi sub ecx, '0' cmp ecx, 9 ja .done ; not a digit (the 0 at the end included) imul rax, rax, 10 add rax, rcx inc rdi jmp .loop .done: ret The one unsigned compare checks for a digit (lesson 3.03). read_int is this loop, plus skipping spaces and handling a minus sign. Lesson 6.02 writes the whole thing. Buffer rules - Pass the real size, and never write past it. read_line is told the size and cuts long lines short; your own loops must count too. - Remember what the buffer holds after a call: read does not add a 0, while read_line does. - Check the result before using the buffer: 0 bytes or −1 means there is nothing there. Check yourself quiz ? What does the read system call return at the end of the input? - -1 + 0 - The buffer's size A negative number means an error. ? Does one read call always return exactly one line? - Yes, on every system + No: it returns whatever bytes are ready - Only on Linux A read can return part of a line or several lines at once. That is why read_line exists. ? The text "35" is being parsed. After '3', the number is 3. What is it after '5'? - 8: 3 + 5 + 35: 3 10 + 5 - 53 Multiply by 10, then add the digit. ? Does the read system call put a 0 after the bytes it read? - Yes + No, it only returns how many it read - Only for text read_line adds one; read does not.

Convert the text to a number yourself (no read_int ): multiply by 10 and add each digit. For Hello world assembly is fun x print 1: 11 chars, 2 words, reversed: dlrow olleH 2: 19 chars, 3 words, reversed: nuf si ylbmessa 3: 1 chars, 1 words, reversed: x lines: 3 longest: " assembly is fun" vowels: 7 - A word is a run of characters that are not spaces (only the space character counts here). - reversed: is the whole line backwards, spaces included (the second line's reversed text ends with the two spaces that started it). - longest: is the longest line in quotes (the first one if tied); with no lines at all print lines: 0 and nothing else. - vowels: counts a, e, i, o, u in either case, in all the lines. - Lines are at most 200 characters.

title: 5.01  call and ret
body: call pushes the address of the next instruction onto the stack and jumps to the function; ret pops that address back into rip. That is all a function call is. Because the return address lives on the stack, a function must pop exactly what it pushed before ret, and functions can call other functions as deep as the stack allows. Two instructions You have used call print_int since module 1. Here is what it does: Instruction Same as --- --- call label push the address of the next instruction, then jmp label ret pop an address into rip : jump back to it The pushed address is the return address : where to carry on afterwards. Nothing else happens. There are no parameters, no local variables and no return values in the hardware: those are all conventions built from registers and the stack. demo-asm title: A call and a return init: rdi=7 call double add rax, 1 ret double: lea rax, rdi+rdi ret Step through and watch rsp and the stack: call pushes the return address (rsp goes down 8), ret pops it (rsp goes back up) and execution continues at add rax, 1 . (The last ret ends the demo.) Writing your own functions nasm global _start section .text ; square: rdi = x. Returns x x in rax. square: mov rax, rdi imul rax, rdi ret ; sum_of_squares: rdi = a, rsi = b. Returns a a + b b. sum_of_squares: push rbx push r12 mov r12, rsi ; keep b: square may change rsi call square ; a a (a is already in rdi) mov rbx, rax mov rdi, r12 call square ; b b add rax, rbx pop r12 pop rbx ret _start: mov edi, 3 mov esi, 4 call sum_of_squares ; 25 mov rdi, rax call print_int call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall - A function is a label, instructions, and ret . Write a comment saying what goes in and what comes out: nothing else will tell the reader. - Functions can be anywhere in .text ; the program still starts at _start . Make sure execution cannot "fall into" a function by accident. - sum_of_squares calls square , so it keeps what it needs in rbx and r12 , and saves the caller's values of those first. The return address must be on top When ret runs, whatever is on top of the stack is taken as the return address. If a function pushed something and forgot to pop it, ret jumps to that value instead, which is almost always a crash: nasm-norun broken: push rbx ; ... forgot pop rbx ... ret ; "returns" to the address that rbx held This is also how a classic stack buffer overflow attack works: a program writes past a local buffer on the stack, over the return address, and ret jumps wherever the attacker chose. Modern systems defend with stack canaries, non-executable stacks and address randomisation. Calls inside calls Each call pushes another return address, so calls nest naturally: _start calls sum_of_squares , which calls square , and each ret goes back exactly one level. The stack holds the chain of "where to go back to", which is what a debugger shows as the backtrace . Check yourself quiz ? What does call square push on the stack? - The address of square + The address of the instruction after the call - The arguments That is the return address. ? What does ret do? - Returns rax to the caller - Ends the program + Pops the top of the stack into rip The value in rax is only a convention. ? A function does push rbx and returns without popping. What happens at ret? - It returns normally + It jumps to the value of rbx - The assembler refuses it ret pops the top of the stack as the return address, which is now the saved rbx, so it probably crashes. ? Why does sum_of_squares keep b in r12 before calling square? - r12 is faster + square may change rsi, but must keep r12 - square reads its argument from r12 Callee-saved registers survive calls.

title: Functions calling functions
body: Write square first, then build the others on it with call (each must call square , not multiply on its own): Function Result --- --- square(x) x × x cube(x) x × square(x) sum_of_squares(a, b) square(a) + square(b) distance2(x1, y1, x2, y2) the squared distance (x2 − x1)² + (y2 − y1)² Remember: square may change any scratch register ( rax , rcx , rdx , rsi , rdi , r8 to r11 ), so keep what you need across a call in rbx or r12 to r15 , and save those with push and pop .

title: 5.02  The System V Calling Convention
body: Linux and macOS follow the System V AMD64 convention. Integer and pointer arguments go in rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8 and r9, the rest on the stack, and the result comes back in rax. rbx, rbp, rsp and r12 to r15 must survive a call; everything else may be changed. rsp must be a multiple of 16 at every call. Why a convention? The hardware does not say where arguments go. If every function chose for itself, no code could call code written by someone else. A calling convention is the agreement that lets C, Rust, Go and your assembly call each other. Linux, macOS and the BSDs use the System V AMD64 convention; Windows uses its own (lesson 5.05). Arguments and results Registers --- --- integer and pointer arguments, in order rdi , rsi , rdx , rcx , r8 , r9 more than six pushed on the stack, the 7th at the lowest address floating-point arguments xmm0 to xmm7 integer or pointer result rax (and rdx for a 128-bit result) floating-point result xmm0 So the C function long clamp(long x, long low, long high) gets x in rdi , low in rsi , high in rdx , and returns in rax . Smaller types use the low part: an int argument is in edi , an int result in eax , and the upper bits are not guaranteed to be anything in particular. Who saves what Kind Registers Rule --- --- --- callee-saved ("non-volatile") rbx , rbp , r12 , r13 , r14 , r15 (and rsp ) a function must give them back unchanged: save with push , restore with pop caller-saved ("volatile", "scratch") rax , rcx , rdx , rsi , rdi , r8 to r11 any call may change them: if you need one after a call, keep it somewhere safe Choose by how long a value must live: - Needed only until the next call? Use a scratch register: no saving needed. - Needed after a call? Put it in a callee-saved register (saving the caller's value first), or on the stack. The tests on this website check this rule after every call: change rbx without restoring it and the test reports it. Stack alignment At the moment of a call instruction, rsp must be a multiple of 16 . The call then pushes 8 bytes, so inside a function rsp is 8 more than a multiple of 16, until the function pushes or subtracts something. Why? Instructions that move 16 bytes at a time (SSE, used by C library functions like printf and memcpy ) can require 16-byte-aligned addresses, and compilers assume the rule holds. Break it and calls into C may crash on an instruction like movaps for no visible reason. nasm-norun my_function: ; on entry: rsp = 16n + 8 (the return address was pushed) push rbx ; rsp = 16n: aligned again call other ; fine pop rbx ret two_saves: push rbx ; 16n push r12 ; 16n - 8: not aligned! sub rsp, 8 ; 16n - 16: aligned call other add rsp, 8 pop r12 pop rbx ret At _start the stack is aligned, which is why _start can call functions directly. The red zone A function that calls nothing (a leaf function) may use the 128 bytes below rsp without moving rsp at all: the convention promises nothing else will touch them. Compilers use this "red zone" for small leaf functions. (The Linux kernel cannot rely on it, and Windows has no red zone.) Reading a C prototype C Arrives in Returns in --- --- --- size_t strlen(const char s) s in rdi rax void memset(void p, int c, size_t n) rdi , esi , rdx rax (p) int max3(int a, int b, int c) edi , esi , edx eax long sum8(long a, ..., long h) 6 registers, then g and h on the stack rax Check yourself quiz ? Where does the third integer argument go? - rcx - r8 + rdx rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9. ? Which registers must a function give back unchanged? - rax, rcx and rdx + rbx, rbp, rsp and r12 to r15 - All of them The rest may be changed by any call. ? What must be true of rsp when a call instruction runs? - It is a multiple of 8 - It is 0 + It is a multiple of 16 Inside the function it is then 16n + 8. ? A value is needed after a call. Where can it be kept? - In rcx - In rdi + In a saved r12, or on the stack Scratch registers may be changed by the call. A callee-saved register such as r12 works once you save its old value.

title: Following the convention
body: Function Result --- --- sum6(a, b, c, d, e, f) the total of all six arguments (they arrive in rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9) pick(n, a, b, c, d) a if n is 0, b if 1, c if 2, d if 3, otherwise 0 scale_all(array, count, factor) multiplies every element of an 8-byte array in place by factor, by calling multiply(x, factor) for each one multiply(x, y) x × y min_max(array, count) returns the smallest element in rax and the largest in rdx (count = 1), like a C function returning a struct of two longs The tests also check that rbx , rbp and r12 to r15 are the same after each call as before.

title: 5.03  Stack Frames and Locals
body: A function's stack frame holds its return address, saved registers and local variables. The classic prologue pushes rbp and copies rsp into it, so locals sit at fixed offsets like rbp - 8 however the stack moves; the epilogue undoes it with leave and ret. Optimised code often skips rbp and addresses locals from rsp. A frame per call Each call gets its own region of the stack, its frame : the return address call pushed, the callee-saved registers the function saved, and room for local variables that do not fit in registers (arrays, buffers, values kept across calls). demo-stack title: Frames for main calling area, which calls square call main The program starts. main's frame holds its own locals. local w = 6 local h = 7 call area width=6 height=7 call pushes a return address; area's prologue saves rbp and makes room for its locals. local result = 42 A local kept at a fixed offset from rbp. call square x=6 square gets a frame too. Its locals are separate from area's. return 36 square's epilogue removes its frame; ret pops the return address. return 42 area returns, and its frame disappears in turn. set total = 42 return 0 The prologue and epilogue The traditional frame uses rbp as a fixed anchor: nasm-norun my_function: push rbp ; save the caller's rbp mov rbp, rsp ; rbp = the frame's base, fixed from now on sub rsp, 32 ; room for 32 bytes of locals: rbp - 32 to rbp - 1 mov qword rbp - 8 , 0 ; a local variable lea rdi, rbp - 32 ; the address of a local buffer ; ... the body: pushes and calls can move rsp, rbp stays put ... leave ; mov rsp, rbp then pop rbp ret Offset from rbp Holds --- --- rbp + 16 , rbp + 24 ... the 7th, 8th... arguments, if any, pushed by the caller rbp + 8 the return address rbp the caller's saved rbp rbp - 8 and below this function's locals Each frame's saved rbp points at the frame before it, so the frames form a linked list up the stack. Debuggers and profilers follow that chain to print a backtrace. Keep sub rsp a multiple of 16 (after push rbp the stack is aligned again), and call stays aligned. A local buffer A function can build text in a buffer on its own stack, as print_uint does. This one writes a number's digits into the caller's buffer, building them backwards in a local one first: nasm global _start section .bss out: resb 32 section .text ; to_text: rdi = destination buffer, rsi = an unsigned number. Writes its digits and a 0; returns the length. to_text: push rbp mov rbp, rsp sub rsp, 32 ; a local buffer at rbp - 32 .. rbp - 1 lea r8, rbp - 1 ; write digits backwards from the end mov rax, rsi mov ecx, 10 .digit: xor edx, edx div rcx add dl, '0' mov r8 , dl dec r8 test rax, rax jnz .digit inc r8 ; the first digit lea rcx, rbp sub rcx, r8 ; how many digits mov rax, rcx ; the result: the length mov rsi, r8 rep movsb ; copy them to the destination mov byte rdi , 0 leave ret _start: lea rdi, rel out mov esi, 90210 call to_text mov rbx, rax lea rdi, rel out call print_str mov edi, ' ' call print_char mov rdi, rbx call print_int ; 5 digits call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall Without a frame pointer At -O2 , GCC and Clang usually leave rbp out ( -fomit-frame-pointer ), freeing it as a general register and addressing locals from rsp : rsp + 8 . It is faster, but the offsets change whenever rsp moves, so the code is harder to read. Debuggers then use separate unwind tables instead of the rbp chain. Small leaf functions often need no frame at all. Check yourself quiz ? What does the prologue push rbp / mov rbp, rsp set up? - Space for the arguments + A fixed anchor for this frame - The return address The caller's rbp is saved and rbp then points at this frame, so locals sit at fixed offsets from it. ? Where is the return address, relative to rbp, after the classic prologue? - rbp - 8 - rbp + rbp + 8 rbp holds the saved rbp. ? What does leave do? - Returns from the function - Frees the heap + mov rsp, rbp then pop rbp ret follows it. ? Why do optimised builds often skip rbp? - rbp is a slow register - The stack is not used at all + It frees one more register Locals are then addressed from rsp, and debuggers use unwind tables instead.

title: A frame with a buffer
body: Write to_decimal(buffer, n) : it writes the signed number n into the buffer as text with a 0 at the end (a minus sign for negative numbers), and returns the number of characters, not counting the 0. Use a classic stack frame: push rbp , mov rbp, rsp , sub rsp, 32 for a local buffer where you build the digits backwards, then copy them to the caller's buffer, and finish with leave and ret . The most negative number, −9223372036854775808, has no positive twin: negating it gives itself. Divide it as an unsigned number after negating and it works.

title: 5.04  Recursion
body: A recursive function calls itself, and each call has its own frame, so it works like any other call - as long as values needed after the inner call are saved first. Every level costs stack space, a base case stops the descent, and recursion too deep runs off the end of the stack and crashes. Nothing special To the processor, a function calling itself is just another call : a new return address on the stack, and the same code running again with new register values. The only thing to get right is the usual rule: anything needed after the call must survive it . nasm global _start section .text ; factorial: rdi = n (0 to 20). Returns n!. factorial: cmp rdi, 1 jg .recurse mov eax, 1 ; the base case: 0! = 1! = 1 ret .recurse: push rbx mov rbx, rdi ; keep n: the inner call changes rdi lea rdi, rdi - 1 call factorial ; rax = (n - 1)! imul rax, rbx ; n (n - 1)! pop rbx ret _start: mov edi, 10 call factorial mov rdi, rax call print_int ; 3628800 call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall Each level saves the caller's rbx , then uses rbx for its own n . When the inner call returns, that level's n is still in rbx , because the inner call saved and restored it. Ten levels deep, there are ten saved rbx values and ten return addresses on the stack. Two calls: Fibonacci nasm-norun ; fib: rdi = n. Returns the nth Fibonacci number: fib(0) = 0, fib(1) = 1. fib: cmp rdi, 1 jg .recurse mov rax, rdi ; fib(0) = 0, fib(1) = 1 ret .recurse: push rbx push r12 sub rsp, 8 ; keep rsp aligned for the calls mov rbx, rdi ; n lea rdi, rbx - 1 call fib ; fib(n - 1) mov r12, rax ; keep it across the second call lea rdi, rbx - 2 call fib ; fib(n - 2) add rax, r12 add rsp, 8 pop r12 pop rbx ret The first result must survive the second call, so it goes in r12 . This version makes about 2ⁿ calls; a loop does it in n steps, which is why recursion is not always the right tool. How deep can it go? The main stack on Linux is usually 8 MB. A frame of 32 bytes allows about 250,000 levels; past that, the next push writes below the stack's end, the processor faults, and the program dies with a segmentation fault : a stack overflow . Some languages turn tail calls (a call that is the last thing a function does) into jumps so they need no extra stack; C and assembly do so only when the optimiser chooses to, or when you write jmp yourself. Check yourself quiz ? Why does factorial save n in rbx before calling itself? - rbx is the only register imul can use + The inner call overwrites rdi, and rbx is kept by every call - To make the call faster The usual rule for values needed after a call. ? What stops the recursion? - The stack running out + The base case returns without calling again - ret Without a base case it would recurse until it crashed. ? In fib, why is fib(n - 1) moved to r12 before the second call? - r12 holds the result - To align the stack + The second call would overwrite rax And r12 was saved, so it is the function's to use. ? What happens when recursion goes far too deep? - It slows down but finishes + The stack runs out and it crashes - The assembler warns about it A stack overflow usually ends with a segmentation fault.

title: Recursion
body: Write each of these as a recursive function (it calls itself): Function Result --- --- fact(n) n! for n from 0 to 20 fib(n) the nth Fibonacci number: fib(0) = 0, fib(1) = 1, fib(n) = fib(n−1) + fib(n−2); n up to 25 power(b, e) b to the power e by squaring: if e is 0, 1; if e is even, power(b, e/2) squared; if odd, b × power(b, e−1) digit_sum(n) the sum of the decimal digits of n = 0: digit_sum(n / 10) + n mod 10, and 0 for 0

title: 5.05  Working with C
body: Assembly functions that follow the calling convention can be called from C, and C functions from assembly, using global and extern and a linker. int values live in the low 32 bits with undefined upper bits. Windows x64 uses rcx, rdx, r8 and r9 with 32 bytes of shadow space and different saved registers. GCC's inline asm puts single instructions inside C. Assembly called from C Because your functions follow the System V convention, a C program can call them. The assembly side makes the name visible to the linker with global ; the C side declares the prototype: nasm-norun ; mathlib.asm global add_scaled section .text ; long add_scaled(long a, long b, long scale): a + b scale add_scaled: mov rax, rsi imul rax, rdx add rax, rdi ret c-norun // main.c include <stdio.h long add_scaled(long a, long b, long scale); // written in assembly int main(void) { printf("%ld\n", add_scaled(1, 2, 10)); // 21 return 0; } nasm -f elf64 mathlib.asm -o mathlib.o gcc main.c mathlib.o -o app That is how the hot loops of codecs, crypto libraries and game engines are written: most of the program in C, a few functions in hand-tuned assembly. C called from assembly The other way round, extern declares a name that another file defines, and the program is linked with the C library (so it starts at C's main rather than _start ): nasm-norun extern printf global main section .data format: db "%d squared is %d", 10, 0 section .text main: push rbx ; also aligns the stack to 16 mov ebx, 12 lea rdi, rel format mov esi, ebx imul ebx, ebx mov edx, ebx xor eax, eax ; variadic functions: al = how many vector registers are used call printf xor eax, eax ; return 0 from main pop rbx ret Built with gcc program.o -o program . The website links assembly without the C library, which is why the course uses system calls and Xenon's routines instead. int is 32 bits C's int is 32 bits, so an int argument is in edi and an int result in eax . The convention says nothing about the upper 32 bits of the register: they may hold anything. So: - Read int arguments through the 32-bit names ( edi , esi ), never the full register, unless you extend them first: movsxd rax, edi for a signed int , mov eax, edi for an unsigned . - char and short arguments are in dil , di and so on. C compilers rely on this, which is why their output is full of movsxd and 32-bit instructions. You can see C do it This C function contains one assembly instruction, written with GCC's inline assembly . Run it (it is C, compiled with GCC): c include <stdio.h long times_three(long x) { long result; __asm__("lea (%1,%1,2), %0" : "=r"(result) : "r"(x)); // GCC's own (AT&T) syntax return result; } int main(void) { printf("%ld\n", times_three(14)); return 0; } Inline assembly uses GCC's AT&T syntax by default (source first, % before registers), and the : "=r"(result) : "r"(x) parts tell the compiler which registers to use. It is handy for a single special instruction; for anything longer, a separate .asm file is clearer. Windows does it differently The Microsoft x64 convention, used by Windows, differs in the details: System V (Linux, macOS) Microsoft x64 (Windows) --- --- --- integer arguments rdi , rsi , rdx , rcx , r8 , r9 rcx , rdx , r8 , r9 callee-saved rbx , rbp , r12 to r15 the same plus rdi , rsi and xmm6 to xmm15 before a call 32 bytes of shadow space reserved on the stack for the callee red zone 128 bytes none long 64 bits 32 bits Same instructions, different agreement: code written for one convention cannot simply be called with the other. (The website's C++ course compiles with MSVC by default, which follows the Windows convention.) Check yourself quiz ? What does global add_scaled do? - Makes the function run faster - Declares a function written in C + Makes the label visible to the linker Other files can then call it. extern is the opposite: a name defined elsewhere. ? A C function takes an int. Where is it, and what about the rest of the register? - In rdi, sign-extended to 64 bits + In edi; the upper half of rdi is garbage - On the stack, above the return address Only the low 32 bits are set. Extend it yourself with movsxd if you need 64 bits. ? Where does the first integer argument go on Windows x64? - rdi + rcx - rax Then rdx, r8, r9. ? What is shadow space? - Another name for the red zone + 32 bytes the caller reserves on Windows - Memory that the debugger uses In the Windows convention the caller reserves 32 bytes on the stack for the callee to store its register arguments. System V has no shadow space.

title: Like a C compiler
body: Implement these C functions the way a C compiler would on Linux. Remember: an int argument is only in the low 32 bits ( edi , esi ), and the upper half of the register may hold anything. The tests deliberately put garbage there. c int add_ints(int a, int b); / a + b, wrapping at 32 bits / long widen(int x); / x as a 64-bit number: widen(-1) is -1 / unsigned widen_unsigned(unsigned x); / the 32-bit pattern of x with the upper half 0 / int is_negative(int x); / 1 if x < 0 / long dot3(const int a, const int b); / a 0 b 0 + a 1 b 1 + a 2 b 2 , each product done in 64 bits / The tests compare all 64 bits of rax . A 32-bit result written to eax has its upper half cleared, so add_ints(-2, -3) shows as 0xFFFFFFFB (−5 in 32 bits), and that is what the test expects.
