title: A small maths library
body: Write a library of functions that call each other, all following the System V convention. The tests call every function and check that rbx , rbp and r12 to r15 come back unchanged. Function Result --- --- gcd(a, b) the greatest common divisor of two numbers = 0, recursively : gcd(a, 0) = a, otherwise gcd(b, a mod b) lcm(a, b) the least common multiple, a / gcd(a, b) × b, calling gcd ; lcm with a 0 is 0 is_prime(n) 1 if n is prime, else 0 (try divisors d while d × d <= n) nth_prime(k) the kth prime, k = 1: nth_prime(1) is 2; calls is_prime insertion_sort(array, n) sorts an array of signed 8-byte numbers in place, smallest first median(array, n) sorts the array (calling insertion_sort ) and returns the middle element, or for an even n the lower of the two middle ones binary_search(array, n, value) in a sorted array, the index of value, or −1; recursive on the half that can hold it, through a helper that takes the low and high bounds

title: 6.01  Reading Compiler Output
body: Compiler output follows recognisable patterns. Leaf functions have no frame, xor zeroes, lea does arithmetic, and test, setcc and cmov replace branches. Division by a constant becomes a multiplication by a magic reciprocal, loops are rotated with one test in front, and simple loops over arrays are vectorised to work on 16 bytes at a time. Where to look gcc -O2 -S -masm=intel file.c writes the assembly to file.s ; objdump -d -M intel program disassembles a finished program; Compiler Explorer (godbolt.org) shows both live, colour-coded line by line. Its Intel syntax is the GNU assembler's, slightly different from NASM's: QWORD PTR rdi where NASM writes qword rdi , and movabs for a mov of a 64-bit constant. Everything below is real GCC 15 output at -O2 . Small functions c-norun long times9(long x) { return x 9; } int is_even(int x) { return x % 2 == 0; } nasm-norun times9: lea rax, rdi+rdi 8 ; x + x 8: no multiply at all ret is_even: mov eax, edi not eax ; flip the bits: the lowest is now 1 for even x and eax, 1 ret No push rbp , no frame: a leaf function that keeps everything in registers needs none. Arguments arrive in rdi ( edi for an int ), the answer leaves in rax ( eax ). Division by a constant c-norun unsigned long div10(unsigned long x) { return x / 10; } nasm-norun div10: movabs rax, -3689348814741910323 ; 0xCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCD mul rdi ; rdx:rax = x that mov rax, rdx ; keep the high 64 bits shr rax, 3 ret No div anywhere. The constant is about 2⁶⁷ ÷ 10, so taking the high 64 bits of the product (that is, dividing by 2⁶⁴) and shifting right by 3 more divides by 2⁶⁷ × 10 ÷ 2⁶⁷: by 10. The constant is chosen so the result is exact for every 64-bit x. mul takes about 3 cycles; div takes 20 to 40. Signed division adds a correction for negative numbers: nasm-norun sdiv3: ; long sdiv3(long x) { return x / 3; } movabs rax, 6148914691236517206 ; 0x5555555555555556, about 2^64 / 3 imul rdi sar rdi, 63 ; -1 if x was negative, else 0 mov rax, rdx sub rax, rdi ; add 1 for negative x, to round towards zero ret When you see a huge strange constant followed by mul or imul and a shift, think "division". Loops c-norun long sum(const long v, long n) { long t = 0; for (long i = 0; i < n; i++) t += v i ; return t; } nasm-norun sum: test rsi, rsi jle .L9 ; n <= 0: skip the loop entirely lea rdx, rdi+rsi 8 ; end = v + n xor eax, eax .L8: add rax, QWORD PTR rdi ; t += v add rdi, 8 ; v++ cmp rdi, rdx jne .L8 ret .L9: xor eax, eax ret The index i has disappeared: GCC turned v i into a moving pointer and compares it with an end pointer. The loop is rotated (one test before it, one jump per round), exactly as lesson 3.02 described. Vectorised loops At -O3 a simple loop over arrays becomes SIMD code that handles four int s per instruction (lesson 6.04): c-norun void add(int restrict d, const int restrict a, const int restrict b) { for (int i = 0; i < 1024; i++) d i = a i + b i ; } nasm-norun add: xor eax, eax .L2: movdqu xmm0, XMMWORD PTR rdx+rax ; 16 bytes of b: four ints movdqu xmm1, XMMWORD PTR rsi+rax ; four ints of a paddd xmm0, xmm1 ; four additions at once movups XMMWORD PTR rdi+rax , xmm0 ; store four results add rax, 16 cmp rax, 4096 jne .L2 ret 256 rounds instead of 1024. ( restrict promises the arrays do not overlap; without it GCC would add a check.) A reading checklist 1. Find the arguments: rdi , rsi , rdx , rcx , r8 , r9 (32-bit names for int s). 2. Find the result: whatever ends up in rax before ret . 3. Find the loops: backward jumps to a label. 4. Name each register by what it holds (a pointer, a count, a total) and write it as a comment. 5. Look for the patterns: xor reg, reg is 0, lea is arithmetic, a magic constant is a division, cmov and set are small if s. Check yourself quiz ? A function multiplies by 0xCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCD, keeps rdx and shifts right by 3. What does it compute? - A multiplication by 10 + An unsigned division by 10 - A random number Magic reciprocal division. ? Why do optimised leaf functions often have no push rbp? - push rbp is not allowed at -O2 - The caller saves rbp for them + They keep everything in registers and need no frame Frames are only built when needed. ? In GCC's sum loop, what happened to the index i? - It is kept in rcx - It is kept on the stack + It became a pointer into the array The pointer moves through the array and is compared with an end pointer. Compilers do this "strength reduction" all the time. ? What does paddd xmm0, xmm1 do? - One 128-bit addition + Four 32-bit additions in one instruction - Adds two doubles Lesson 6.04 is about SIMD.

title: Dividing without div
body: Do what GCC does: divide unsigned numbers by constants with mul and a magic number, never div . mul rdi multiplies rax by rdi into rdx:rax ; the high half, rdx , is the product divided by 2⁶⁴. Function Result GCC's recipe --- --- --- udiv10(x) x ÷ 10 high half of x × 0xCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCD , then shr by 3 udiv3(x) x ÷ 3 high half of x × 0xAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAB , then shr by 1 urem10(x) x mod 10 x − 10 × udiv10(x), with lea for the × 10 digit_sum(x) the sum of x's decimal digits a loop using the udiv10 recipe All the numbers are unsigned 64-bit, including the largest, 18446744073709551615.

title: 6.02  Parsing and Printing Numbers
body: Now you can write the routines you have been borrowing. Parsing skips spaces, reads an optional sign, and multiplies and adds digit by digit, with any base and an overflow check. Printing divides by the base to produce digits from the right, handles the sign and the most negative number, and maps digits above 9 to letters. Parsing in any base The rule from lesson 4.05 works for every base: value = value × base + digit . Hex digits a to f (or A to F ) are worth 10 to 15. nasm-norun ; parse: rdi = a string, rsi = the base (2 to 16). ; Returns the value in rax, and in rdx a pointer to the first character it did not use. parse: xor eax, eax .next: movzx ecx, byte rdi lea edx, rcx - '0' cmp edx, 9 jbe .have ; '0'..'9' or ecx, 0x20 ; lower case lea edx, rcx - 'a' cmp edx, 5 ja .stop ; not 'a'..'f' either add edx, 10 .have: cmp rdx, rsi jae .stop ; a digit too big for this base imul rax, rsi add rax, rdx inc rdi jmp .next .stop: mov rdx, rdi ret Returning "where it stopped" lets the caller check that the whole text was a number (it should stop at the 0), just like C's strtol . Overflow imul and add silently wrap if the number is too big. A careful parser checks the overflow flag after each step: jo .too_big right after the imul , and again after the add . For unsigned numbers, check the carry flag ( jc ) after add , and use mul (which sets CF and OF when the high half is not zero). Printing in any base Printing divides by the base: each remainder is the next digit from the right. nasm global _start section .data digits: db "0123456789abcdef" section .bss out: resb 72 section .text ; print_base: rdi = an unsigned number, rsi = the base (2 to 16). Prints it. print_base: lea r8, rel out + 71 ; the end of the buffer lea r9, rel digits mov rax, rdi .digit: xor edx, edx div rsi ; rdx = the next digit, from the right movzx ecx, byte r9 + rdx ; its character, from the table mov r8 , cl dec r8 test rax, rax jnz .digit inc r8 ; the first digit lea rdx, rel out + 72 sub rdx, r8 ; the length mov rsi, r8 mov eax, 1 mov edi, 1 syscall ret _start: mov edi, 3054 mov esi, 10 call print_base call print_newline mov edi, 3054 mov esi, 16 call print_base ; bee call print_newline mov edi, 3054 mov esi, 2 call print_base call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall Looking digits up in a table, r9 + rdx , avoids an if for digits above 9. Signed numbers To print a signed number: if it is negative, print - and print its negation as unsigned. That even works for the most negative number, −2⁶³: neg leaves it unchanged (it has no positive twin), but read as unsigned it is 2⁶³, exactly the right digits. To parse one: remember whether there was a - , parse the digits, then neg at the end. Skipping and checking A friendly parser also skips leading spaces and tabs, and the caller decides what to do with leftovers: "12abc" stops at a , so it is not a clean number. That is all read_int does: skip spaces, check for - , parse digits, and put back the character that stopped it, for the next read. Check yourself quiz ? What is the value of "1f" in base 16? - 115 - 16 + 31 1 16 + 15. ? Why does parse return where it stopped? - So it can be called again for the next digit - It must, by the calling convention + So the caller can tell whether all the text was a number Like strtol's end pointer. ? How is the most negative number printed correctly? - It cannot be printed - Add 1 first + Negate it and print the result as unsigned neg leaves it unchanged, and as unsigned it is 2 to the 63. ? Which flag shows that imul overflowed? - ZF + OF (and CF) - SF only Check it with jo.

title: A base converter
body: Read lines with read_line . Each holds one unsigned number written in decimal ( 255 ), hexadecimal ( 0xff or 0XFF ) or binary ( 0b11111111 ). Parse it yourself and print it in all three bases: 255 = 0xff = 0b11111111 For the input 255 0x1F 0b101 0 banana 0x 12z print 255 = 0xff = 0b11111111 31 = 0x1f = 0b11111 5 = 0x5 = 0b101 0 = 0x0 = 0b0 not a number: banana not a number: 0x not a number: 12z The numbers fit in 64 bits. Write your own printing too: you may use print_str and print_char for text, but not read_int , print_int , print_uint , print_hex or print_bin . One function that prints in any base (dividing by the base, with a table of digit characters) does all three.

title: 6.03  Optimisation Basics
body: Speed depends less on how many instructions run than on what they wait for. Memory is far slower than registers and caches hide it only for data used together. Chains of dependent instructions cannot overlap, wrong branch guesses cost many cycles, and division is slow. Measure with rdtsc before and after every change. What is slow A modern x86 core can start several instructions per cycle, if they do not wait for each other. Rough costs: Operation Cycles (about) --- --- add , and , mov between registers under 1 (several per cycle) imul 3 reading memory that is in the L1 cache 4 to 5 a mispredicted branch 15 to 20 div (64-bit) 20 to 40 reading memory from the L3 cache about 40 reading memory from RAM 100 to 300 The Fundamentals course explains caches: memory moves in 64-byte lines , so reading one byte brings its neighbours too. Code that walks memory in order is fast; code that jumps around a big area waits for RAM over and over. Dependency chains nasm-norun ; one running total: every add waits for the one before .loop: add rax, rdi add rdi, 8 cmp rdi, rdx jne .loop Each add rax, ... needs the previous rax , so the additions happen one after another, however many the processor could do at once. Splitting the work into independent chains lets them overlap: nasm-norun ; four running totals, combined at the end .loop: add rax, rdi add rcx, rdi + 8 add r8, rdi + 16 add r9, rdi + 24 add rdi, 32 cmp rdi, rdx jne .loop add rax, rcx add r8, r9 add rax, r8 This is loop unrolling with several accumulators: fewer loop instructions per element, and four additions in flight at once. (The count must then be a multiple of four, or the leftovers handled separately.) Measuring: rdtsc Guessing about speed is usually wrong; measure. rdtsc reads the processor's time-stamp counter, which counts up at a steady rate, into edx:eax : nasm global _start section .bss array: resq 4096 section .data s_one: db "one total: ", 0 s_four: db "four totals: ", 0 section .text _start: lea rdi, rel array ; touch the array once first, so the timings mov ecx, 4096 ; do not include the operating system .warm: mov rdi , rcx ; handing out its memory on first use add rdi, 8 dec ecx jnz .warm lea rdi, rel s_one call print_str rdtsc shl rdx, 32 or rax, rdx mov rbx, rax ; the start time mov r12d, 1000 ; repeat to get a measurable time .rep1: lea rdi, rel array lea rdx, rdi + 4096 8 xor eax, eax .one: add rax, rdi add rdi, 8 cmp rdi, rdx jne .one dec r12d jnz .rep1 rdtsc shl rdx, 32 or rax, rdx sub rax, rbx mov rdi, rax call print_int call print_newline lea rdi, rel s_four call print_str rdtsc shl rdx, 32 or rax, rdx mov rbx, rax mov r12d, 1000 .rep4: lea rdi, rel array lea rdx, rdi + 4096 8 xor eax, eax xor ecx, ecx xor r8d, r8d xor r9d, r9d .four: add rax, rdi add rcx, rdi + 8 add r8, rdi + 16 add r9, rdi + 24 add rdi, 32 cmp rdi, rdx jne .four dec r12d jnz .rep4 rdtsc shl rdx, 32 or rax, rdx sub rax, rbx mov rdi, rax call print_int call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall The numbers are "ticks", and they change from run to run (the machine is shared, and its clock speed varies), but the second loop is usually clearly faster. Real measurements repeat many times and take the minimum. On Linux, perf stat counts cycles, cache misses and mispredicted branches for a whole program. Rules of thumb 1. Measure first. Find where the time goes before changing anything. 2. Better algorithms beat better instructions. An O(n log n) sort in C beats a hand-tuned O(n²) one in assembly. 3. Keep data together and in order. Arrays beat linked lists; walk memory forwards. 4. Avoid unpredictable branches in hot loops: cmov , setcc and arithmetic (lesson 3.05). 5. Avoid div when a shift, a mask or a multiplication will do. 6. Break dependency chains with several accumulators. 7. Use SIMD for doing the same thing to many values (next lesson). Compilers already do most of this. Hand-written assembly wins mostly where you know something the compiler cannot: that arrays never overlap, that a value is always in range, or that a special instruction exists for the job. Check yourself quiz ? Why can one running total limit a loop's speed? - Registers can only be added once per loop + Each addition must wait for the previous one - Additions are slow Independent accumulators can overlap. ? About how long does reading from RAM take, compared with a register add? - About the same - Twice as long + Hundreds of times longer Caches hide it only for data used together. ? What does rdtsc give? - The time of day + A time-stamp counter in edx:eax, for measuring time - The number of instructions run Subtract two readings. ? What is usually the biggest speed-up? - Replacing mov with xchg + A better algorithm or data layout - Writing everything in assembly Measure, then fix what matters.

title: Faster code

title: 6.04  SIMD Many Numbers at Once
body: SIMD instructions do the same operation on several values at once. Every x86-64 processor has sixteen 128-bit xmm registers that hold 16 bytes, 8 words, 4 dwords or 2 qwords, with instructions like paddb, paddd and paddq. movdqu loads and stores 16 bytes, and a horizontal sum combines the lanes at the end. AVX widens this to 256 and 512 bits. One instruction, many values SIMD means "single instruction, multiple data". An x86-64 processor has 16 registers xmm0 to xmm15 , each 128 bits wide, and instructions that treat them as several lanes : Lanes Add Example --- --- --- 16 × 8-bit bytes paddb pixels, text 8 × 16-bit words paddw audio samples 4 × 32-bit dwords paddd int arrays 2 × 64-bit qwords paddq long arrays 4 floats / 2 doubles addps / addpd graphics, physics Every x86-64 processor has SSE2, so these always work. Each lane is separate: a carry never crosses into the next lane. Moving data in and out Instruction Does --- --- movdqu xmm0, rsi load 16 bytes from any address ("u" for unaligned) movdqu rdi , xmm0 store 16 bytes movdqa the same, but the address must be a multiple of 16 movq xmm0, rax / movq rax, xmm0 move 64 bits between a general register and the low lane pxor xmm0, xmm0 zero a vector register Adding arrays nasm global _start section .data a: dq 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 b: dq 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60 section .bss c: resq 6 section .text _start: lea rsi, rel a lea rdx, rel b lea rdi, rel c xor ecx, ecx ; byte offset .loop: movdqu xmm0, rsi + rcx ; two numbers of a movdqu xmm1, rdx + rcx ; two numbers of b paddq xmm0, xmm1 ; two additions at once movdqu rdi + rcx , xmm0 add rcx, 16 cmp rcx, 6 8 jb .loop xor ebx, ebx ; print c .print: lea rax, rel c mov rdi, rax + rbx 8 call print_int mov edi, ' ' call print_char inc rbx cmp rbx, 6 jb .print call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall Horizontal sum Adding up all the elements of an array uses lanes as separate running totals (like the four accumulators of lesson 6.03), then combines them at the end, a horizontal step: nasm-norun pxor xmm0, xmm0 ; two totals: 0, 0 .loop: movdqu xmm1, rdi paddq xmm0, xmm1 ; add two elements, one into each total add rdi, 16 cmp rdi, rdx jb .loop pshufd xmm1, xmm0, 0x4E ; swap the two 64-bit halves paddq xmm0, xmm1 ; now both lanes hold the sum movq rax, xmm0 pshufd rearranges the four 32-bit pieces of a register; the constant 0x4E (binary 01 00 11 10 ) picks pieces 2, 3, 0, 1, which swaps the halves. Saturation and comparisons Some SIMD instructions have no ordinary equivalent: - paddusb adds bytes with saturation : 200 + 100 gives 255 instead of wrapping to 44. Perfect for brightening pixels. - pcmpeqb compares 16 bytes at once, giving 0xFF where they are equal and 0 elsewhere, and pmovmskb turns those 16 results into 16 bits of a general register. That is how fast strlen and memchr implementations scan 16 bytes per step. - pminub , pmaxub , pavgb : lane-wise minimum, maximum, average. Wider: AVX Newer processors add AVX2 (256-bit ymm registers: 8 ints at once) and AVX-512 (512-bit zmm : 16 ints). Code must check the processor supports them first (with the cpuid instruction), which is why compilers use only SSE2 unless told -mavx2 or -march=native . ARM's version is called NEON . Check yourself quiz ? How many 32-bit ints does one xmm register hold? - 2 - 8 + 4 128 bits / 32. ? What does paddq xmm0, xmm1 do? - One 128-bit addition - Four 32-bit additions + Two separate 64-bit additions, one per lane q for quad word. ? Why is movdqu used instead of movdqa for arrays from anywhere? - movdqu is faster + movdqa requires a 16-byte-aligned address - movdqa only loads u for unaligned. ? 200 + 100 with paddusb gives... - 44 + 255 - 300 Unsigned saturation stops at the maximum.

title: 6.05  Beyond x86 ARM64 and Debuggers
body: ARM64, in phones and Apple-chip Macs, is a load-store design with 31 registers and fixed 4-byte instructions, so arithmetic never touches memory directly. RISC-V is a small open design built on the same ideas. A debugger such as gdb steps through instructions and shows registers and memory, and objdump shows any program's machine code. The same ideas, another instruction set You now know how a processor works: registers, memory, flags, jumps, a stack, a calling convention. Every other instruction set is a variation on these themes. The big one is ARM64 (AArch64): almost every phone, Apple-chip Macs, and a growing share of servers. ARM64 at a glance x86-64 ARM64 --- --- --- registers 16 general 31 general ( x0 to x30 , 32-bit halves w0 to w30 ) plus a zero register instruction size 1 to 15 bytes always 4 bytes memory in arithmetic yes: add rax, rdi no: only ldr (load) and str (store) touch memory operands two: add rax, rbx overwrites rax three: add x0, x1, x2 return address pushed by call kept in register x30 by bl arguments rdi , rsi , rdx , rcx , r8 , r9 x0 to x7 result rax x0 The same C function, compiled by GCC for each: c-norun long sum(const long v, long n) { long t = 0; for (long i = 0; i < n; i++) t += v i ; return t; } nasm-norun ; x86-64 sum: test rsi, rsi jle .L9 lea rdx, rdi+rsi 8 xor eax, eax .L8: add rax, QWORD PTR rdi add rdi, 8 cmp rdi, rdx jne .L8 ret .L9: xor eax, eax ret // ARM64 (GCC 15, -O2) sum: cmp x1, 0 ble .L4 mov x2, x0 // the pointer add x1, x0, x1, lsl 3 // end = v + n 8 (lsl 3: shifted left by 3) mov x0, 0 // the total, in the result register .L3: ldr x3, x2 , 8 // load v, then v += 8 add x0, x0, x3 cmp x2, x1 bne .L3 ret .L4: mov x0, 0 ret The shape is identical: a test in front, a rotated loop, a moving pointer. ARM64 loads into a register first ( ldr with "post-increment", moving the pointer in the same instruction), then adds. Fixed-size instructions and load-store design make the processor's job of decoding easier, which is part of why ARM chips are so power-efficient. x86 chips do the same internally: they translate x86 instructions into simpler micro-operations. RISC-V is a newer open instruction set in the same style, free for anyone to build: 32 registers, lw / sw to load and store, add a0, a0, a1 . It appears in microcontrollers, storage drives and research chips, and anyone can design a RISC-V processor without a licence. Debuggers A debugger runs a program under control: stop at an instruction, step one at a time, look at registers and memory. On Linux, gdb : nasm -f elf64 -g -F dwarf program.asm -o program.o -g: debugging information ld program.o -o program gdb ./program (gdb) layout asm show the instructions (gdb) break _start stop at _start (gdb) run (gdb) stepi one instruction (nexti steps over calls) (gdb) info registers rax rbx rsp (gdb) x/16xb $rsp 16 bytes at rsp, in hex (gdb) x/s &message a string in memory (gdb) backtrace the chain of return addresses (gdb) continue The demos in this course do what stepi and info registers do. On Windows, Visual Studio and WinDbg have the same features; on macOS, lldb . Looking inside any program objdump -d -M intel /bin/ls less disassembles a real program: every instruction with its address and machine-code bytes. You can now read it. That is the starting point of reverse engineering, malware analysis and security research, and of understanding exactly what your own compiler produced. Where next - Read compiler output for code you write in C, C++ or Rust: Compiler Explorer with -O2 . - The Intel and AMD manuals (free) describe every instruction; Agner Fog's optimisation guides and instruction tables give real timings. - Write an operating system : the OSDev wiki starts from a boot sector in assembly. - Try ARM64 or RISC-V with QEMU, an emulator that runs other instruction sets on your computer. Check yourself quiz ? Which ARM64 instructions are the only ones that touch memory? - All of them can - add and sub + Loads and stores, such as ldr and str It is a load-store design: arithmetic works only on registers. ? Where does ARM64's bl keep the return address? - On the stack + In register x30 (the link register) - In x0 A function that calls others saves x30 itself. ? What does gdb's stepi do? - Runs to the end of the function + Runs exactly one machine instruction - Steps one line of C nexti steps over calls. ? What does objdump -d show? - The program's source code + The machine code, as instructions - The program's output It disassembles the program's bytes, so every program is readable at this level.

title: From ARM64 to x86-64
body: GCC compiled four C functions for ARM64 . Read them, work out what they do, and write the same functions for x86-64. ARM64 reminders: arguments arrive in x0 , x1 , x2 , and the result goes back in x0 . Instructions have three operands: sub x0, x0, x2 means x0 = x0 − x2. ldr x3, x2 , 8 loads the 8 bytes at x2 into x3, then adds 8 to x2. lsl 3 and lsr 63 shift an operand left by 3 or right by 63 on the way in. csel x0, x1, x0, ge picks x1 if the last comparison said "greater or equal", otherwise x0; csneg x0, x0, x0, ge picks x0 if "greater or equal", otherwise its negation. mystery1: mul x0, x0, x1 sub x0, x0, x2 ret mystery2: cmp x0, 0 csneg x0, x0, x0, ge ret mystery3: cmp x1, 0 ble .L8 mov x2, x0 add x1, x0, x1, lsl 3 mov x0, 0 .L7: ldr x3, x2 , 8 add x0, x0, x3, lsr 63 cmp x1, x2 bne .L7 ret .L8: mov x0, 0 ret mystery5: cmp x1, x0 csel x0, x1, x0, ge ret

title: An RPN calculator
body: Build a calculator for Reverse Polish Notation , where the operator comes after its numbers: 3 4 + is 7, and 3 4 + 2 is (3 + 4) × 2. No brackets are needed, and it is exactly how a stack works: numbers are pushed, and an operator pops two, works them out, and pushes the answer. Old HP calculators and the Forth and PostScript languages work this way, and so does the Java virtual machine. Read lines until the input ends. Each line is one calculation of tokens separated by spaces; print its result, or an error: 3 4 + 3 4 + 2 10 3 - -7 2 / -7 2 % 2 3 4 + 5 0 / 1 + 1 2 4 x prints 7 14 7 -3 -1 14 error: division by zero error: not enough numbers error: 2 numbers left error: unknown token x Token Does --- --- a whole number, perhaps with a - in front pushes it + - / pops b, then a, and pushes a + b, a − b, a × b, a ÷ b (rounded towards zero) % the remainder, with the sign of a, as in C dup pushes a copy of the top number swap swaps the top two - A line ends with exactly one number on the stack: print it. More than one: error: N numbers left . None (an empty line): print nothing. - An operator with fewer than two numbers (one for dup ): error: not enough numbers . Dividing by zero: error: division by zero . Anything else: error: unknown token and the token. After an error, skip the rest of the line. - A lone - is subtraction; - followed by digits is a negative number. - At most 100 numbers on the stack, and lines of at most 200 characters.

title: 7.01  Floating Point with SSE
body: Doubles and floats in x86-64 - the xmm registers, movsd and movss, addsd, subsd, mulsd, divsd and sqrtsd, converting with cvtsi2sd, cvttsd2si and cvtsd2si, comparing with comisd and the flags it sets, constants in .data, and the calling convention for floating-point arguments and results. A second set of registers Integers live in rax , rbx and friends. Floating-point numbers live in the sixteen 128-bit xmm registers , xmm0 to xmm15 , and use their own instructions. Lesson 6.04 used them to process four numbers at once; this lesson uses them for one number at a time, which is how compilers do ordinary double arithmetic. Instructions ending in sd work on one s calar d ouble (64 bits), those ending in ss on one s calar s ingle (a 32-bit float ). Instruction Meaning --- --- movsd xmm0, rel x / movsd rel x , xmm0 load or store a double movsd xmm1, xmm0 copy between xmm registers addsd , subsd , mulsd , divsd arithmetic: addsd xmm0, xmm1 is xmm0 += xmm1 sqrtsd xmm0, xmm1 xmm0 = sqrt(xmm1) minsd , maxsd smaller, larger cvtsi2sd xmm0, rax integer to double cvttsd2si rax, xmm0 double to integer, t runcating (dropping the fraction) cvtsd2si rax, xmm0 double to integer, rounding to the nearest (ties to even) comisd xmm0, xmm1 compare, setting the flags pxor xmm0, xmm0 make zero There is no "load an immediate" for floats: constants go in .data (or .rodata ) and are loaded from memory. A first calculation nasm global _start section .data radius: dq 2.5 pi: dq 3.141592653589793 hundred: dq 100.0 section .text _start: movsd xmm0, rel radius mulsd xmm0, xmm0 ; r r mulsd xmm0, rel pi ; pi r r = 19.6349... mulsd xmm0, rel hundred ; two decimals as a whole number cvtsd2si rdi, xmm0 ; 1963 (rounded) call print_int call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall dq 2.5 stores the 8-byte double for 2.5; NASM knows a number with a decimal point is floating point. Integers in, integers out Converting is the bridge between the two worlds. The average of integers, for example, is computed in doubles and converted back: nasm global _start section .data values: dq 4, 9, 10 section .text ; average_x10: rdi = an array of 8-byte integers, rsi = count ( = 1). ; Returns the average times 10, truncated: 4, 9, 10 gives 76 (7.666...). average_x10: pxor xmm0, xmm0 ; the sum xor ecx, ecx .loop: cmp rcx, rsi jae .done cvtsi2sd xmm1, qword rdi + rcx 8 addsd xmm0, xmm1 inc rcx jmp .loop .done: cvtsi2sd xmm1, rsi divsd xmm0, xmm1 ; the average mov eax, 10 cvtsi2sd xmm1, rax mulsd xmm0, xmm1 cvttsd2si rax, xmm0 ; drop the fraction ret _start: lea rdi, rel values mov esi, 3 call average_x10 mov rdi, rax call print_int ; 76 call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall Note cvtsi2sd xmm1, qword ... : the size has to be stated when the source is memory. Rounding: truncate or round? cvttsd2si always cuts towards zero: 7.9 becomes 7 and −7.9 becomes −7. cvtsd2si uses the current rounding mode, which is round to nearest, ties to even unless a program changes it: 7.5 becomes 8, 6.5 becomes 6, −3.5 becomes −4. Ties to even avoids the steady upward drift that "always round .5 up" causes over many operations. Comparing comisd xmm0, xmm1 compares two doubles and sets the flags like an unsigned comparison : use ja , jae , jb , jbe , je (not jg and jl ). If either value is NaN the result is "unordered", which sets the parity flag ( jp ). nasm-norun comisd xmm0, xmm1 jp .not_a_number ; NaN involved jb .smaller ; xmm0 < xmm1 maxsd and minsd often replace the comparison entirely. The calling convention In the System V convention (lesson 5.02), the first eight floating-point arguments arrive in xmm0 to xmm7 , separately from the integer registers, and a floating-point result is returned in xmm0 . double scale(long n, double factor) gets n in rdi and factor in xmm0 . All xmm registers are caller-saved: any call may change them. Check yourself quiz ? Why is there no mov xmm0, 2.5 ? - XMM registers can only be loaded from other XMM registers + SSE has no floating-point immediates - 2.5 would have to be written as 25 and divided Constants are stored in memory, for example two_half: dq 2.5 , and loaded with movsd xmm0, rel two_half . ? Which jumps follow comisd ? - The signed ones: jg , jl , jge , jle - Only je and jne + The unsigned ones, plus jp for NaN comisd sets ZF, PF and CF the way an unsigned compare would, so use ja , jb , jae , jbe and je . PF is set when either value is NaN. ? What does cvttsd2si give for -2.7? - -3 + -2 - 3 - 2 cvttsd2si truncates: it cuts the fraction off, towards zero.

title: 7.02  NASM Macros and Conditional Assembly
body: Writing less assembly by hand - single-line macros with %define, multi-line macros with %macro and their parameters, local labels with %%, repeating code with %rep and %assign, choosing code with %if and %ifdef, and macros that generate whole functions. The preprocessor Before NASM assembles anything, its preprocessor expands macros, much as C's preprocessor does (C course lesson 5.04). Macros remove repetition that functions cannot: saving the same registers in every function, unrolling a loop, defining a family of similar functions. %define: single-line macros nasm-norun %define SYS_WRITE 1 %define SYS_EXIT 60 %define STDOUT 1 %define ELEMENT(base, i) base + (i) 8 ; a macro with parameters mov eax, SYS_WRITE mov rax, ELEMENT(rdi, 3) ; becomes mov rax, rdi + (3) 8 %define is pure text replacement. equ (lesson 1.05) defines a number the assembler knows; %define can stand for any text, including registers and operands. %macro: multi-line macros A multi-line macro has a name and a number of parameters ; inside, %1 , %2 ... are the arguments: nasm global _start section .text %macro EXIT 1 mov eax, 60 mov edi, %1 syscall %endmacro %macro PRINT_NUMBER 1 mov rdi, %1 call print_int call print_newline %endmacro _start: mov rbx, 6 imul rbx, 7 PRINT_NUMBER rbx ; 42 PRINT_NUMBER 100 EXIT 0 A range like %macro SAVE 1-3 accepts one to three arguments; %0 is how many were given. Local labels: %% A label inside a macro would be defined twice if the macro is used twice. Prefixing it with %% makes NASM invent a fresh name at each use: nasm global _start section .text ; CLAMP reg, low, high: keeps reg between low and high (registers or numbers). %macro CLAMP 3 cmp %1, %2 jge %%not_low mov %1, %2 %%not_low: cmp %1, %3 jle %%done mov %1, %3 %%done: %endmacro _start: mov rax, -40 CLAMP rax, 0, 255 mov rdi, rax call print_int ; 0 call print_newline mov rax, 900 CLAMP rax, 0, 255 mov rdi, rax call print_int ; 255 call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall Repeating: %rep and %assign %rep n ... %endrep copies its body n times. %assign sets a number the preprocessor can compute with, so each copy can be different. Together they unroll a loop: nasm global _start section .data numbers: dq 3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6 section .text ; sum8: rdi = an array of exactly 8 qwords. No loop counter, no jumps. sum8: xor eax, eax %assign i 0 %rep 8 add rax, rdi + i 8 %assign i i + 1 %endrep ret _start: lea rdi, rel numbers call sum8 mov rdi, rax call print_int ; 31 call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall The listing of the assembled program shows eight add instructions with offsets 0, 8, 16 ... 56. Choosing code: %if and %ifdef nasm-norun %define DEBUG 1 %if DEBUG call dump_registers ; only assembled when DEBUG is non-zero %endif %ifdef WINDOWS ; the Windows calling convention %else ; System V %endif Pass definitions on the command line with nasm -dDEBUG=1 ... to build different versions from one source. Macros that write functions A macro can produce a whole function, with names glued together from its parameters: nasm global _start section .text %macro MAKE_SCALER 2 ; name, factor scale_%1: mov rax, rdi imul rax, %2 ret %endmacro MAKE_SCALER double, 2 MAKE_SCALER triple, 3 MAKE_SCALER dozen, 12 _start: mov edi, 5 call scale_dozen mov rdi, rax call print_int ; 60 call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall When to use them Macros are great for boilerplate that must be identical everywhere (prologues, system calls, error checks) and for unrolling. Overused, they hide what the code really does and make debugging harder, because the debugger shows the expanded instructions. A plain call to a function is often clearer and smaller. Check yourself quiz ? Why does a label in a macro need %% ? + Without it, using the macro twice would define the same label twice - %% makes the label global so other files can jump to it - Labels inside macros are not allowed without a prefix %%loop gets a new unique name every time the macro is expanded, so two uses do not clash. ? What is the difference between %rep and a loop? - %rep runs faster because it uses a hidden counter register + %rep copies the code when assembling - %rep repeats the code only in debug builds After %rep 4 the code appears four times in the output, with no counter or jump. A loop is assembled once and runs several times. ? Inside %macro ADD3 3, what is %2? - the macro's name + the second argument of the use - the number of arguments - a local label %1, %2 and %3 are the arguments; %0 is how many were given.

title: 7.03  Files with System Calls
body: Working with files without any library - open with its flags and permission mode, read and write loops that handle partial transfers, close, lseek to move and to find a size, unlink, and reading errors from the negative value the kernel returns. Files are numbers Lesson 1.04 wrote to the screen with system call 1, write , on file descriptor 1 (standard output). A file you open is just another descriptor: a small number the kernel hands out, which read , write and close then use. Call rax Arguments Returns --- --- --- --- read 0 rdi = fd, rsi = buffer, rdx = size bytes read, 0 at the end write 1 rdi = fd, rsi = buffer, rdx = count bytes written open 2 rdi = path (zero-terminated), rsi = flags, rdx = mode the new fd close 3 rdi = fd 0 lseek 8 rdi = fd, rsi = offset, rdx = whence the new position unlink 87 rdi = path 0 (Newer programs use openat , 257, which takes a directory fd first; open is the same with the current directory.) Errors are negative A system call that fails returns a negative error number in rax : −2 is ENOENT (no such file), −13 EACCES (permission denied), −9 EBADF (bad descriptor). C's errno is just that number made positive by the library. So every call is followed by a check: nasm-norun syscall test rax, rax js .failed ; negative: an error Opening The flags are bits ORed together: Flag Value Meaning --- --- --- O_RDONLY 0 read only O_WRONLY 1 write only O_RDWR 2 both O_CREAT 0x40 create it if it does not exist O_TRUNC 0x200 empty it if it does O_APPEND 0x400 every write goes to the end With O_CREAT , rdx is the permission mode of a new file, usually written in octal: 0o644 means the owner may read and write, everyone else may only read. Write, then read back nasm global _start section .data path: db "xenon_demo.txt", 0 text: db "written by assembly", 10 length equ $ - text section .bss buffer: resb 64 section .text _start: ; fd = open(path, O_WRONLY O_CREAT O_TRUNC, 0644) mov eax, 2 lea rdi, rel path mov esi, 0x241 mov edx, 0o644 syscall test rax, rax js .fail mov rbx, rax ; keep the fd mov eax, 1 ; write(fd, text, length) mov rdi, rbx lea rsi, rel text mov edx, length syscall mov eax, 3 ; close(fd) mov rdi, rbx syscall mov eax, 2 ; fd = open(path, O_RDONLY) lea rdi, rel path xor esi, esi syscall test rax, rax js .fail mov rbx, rax xor eax, eax ; n = read(fd, buffer, 64) mov rdi, rbx lea rsi, rel buffer mov edx, 64 syscall mov r12, rax mov eax, 3 mov rdi, rbx syscall mov eax, 1 ; show what came back mov edi, 1 lea rsi, rel buffer mov rdx, r12 syscall mov eax, 87 ; unlink(path): tidy up lea rdi, rel path syscall xor edi, edi jmp .exit .fail: mov rdi, rax call print_int ; the negative error number call print_newline mov edi, 1 .exit: mov eax, 60 syscall Partial reads and writes read may return fewer bytes than asked for, even before the end of the file (always with pipes and sockets), and write may write fewer than given. Robust code loops: nasm-norun ; write_all: rdi = fd, rsi = buffer, rdx = count. Returns 0, or the negative error. write_all: .again: test rdx, rdx jz .ok mov eax, 1 push rdi push rsi push rdx syscall pop rdx pop rsi pop rdi test rax, rax js .error add rsi, rax ; skip what was written sub rdx, rax jmp .again .ok: xor eax, eax .error: ret (The syscall instruction itself overwrites rcx and r11 ; the pushes here keep the arguments for the next round.) lseek lseek(fd, offset, whence) moves the read and write position: whence 0 ( SEEK_SET ) from the start, 1 ( SEEK_CUR ) from the current position, 2 ( SEEK_END ) from the end. lseek(fd, 0, SEEK_END) returns the file's size. Check yourself quiz ? How does a failed system call report its error? - It sets the carry flag and leaves the error code in rdx - It returns 0 in rax and sets a global errno + It returns a negative number in rax : minus the error code Raw Linux system calls return −errno directly, for example −2 for "no such file". The C library is what turns that into −1 and errno . ? Why loop around write ? - write only writes one byte per call + It may write fewer bytes than asked, so the loop continues with the rest - The loop retries until write stops returning an error write returns how many bytes it wrote, which can be less than requested (for pipes, sockets or signals). Advance the pointer, reduce the count and call again. ? Which flags create a file for writing and empty it if it already exists? - 0 - 0x40 + O_WRONLY O_CREAT O_TRUNC (0x241) - O_RDONLY O_APPEND Write-only (1), create (0x40) and truncate (0x200) together make 0x241.

title: 7.04  Structures and Data Layout
body: Records in assembly - NASM's struc and endstruc for field offsets, istruc and at for initialised records, reaching fields through a pointer, arrays of structures and the index arithmetic they need, matching a C struct's layout and padding, and structure of arrays versus array of structures. A struct is offsets To the processor, a C struct is just a block of bytes, and each field is a fixed offset from its start. p- hp is "load from the address in p plus the offset of hp". In assembly you could write the numbers yourself ( rdi + 8 ), but names are far easier to read and to change. struc and endstruc NASM's struc defines a list of field offsets and the total size, without reserving any memory: nasm-norun struc player .id: resq 1 ; offset 0, 8 bytes .hp: resq 1 ; offset 8 .score: resq 1 ; offset 16 .name: resb 16 ; offset 24, 16 bytes endstruc ; defines player_size = 40 Now player.hp is the number 8 and player_size is 40. Fields are reached through a pointer: nasm-norun mov rax, rdi + player.score ; rdi points at a player add qword rdi + player.hp , 10 ; heal by 10 istruc: a filled-in record istruc lays out an actual record in the data section, with at placing each value at its field: nasm global _start struc point .x: resq 1 .y: resq 1 endstruc section .data corner: istruc point at point.x, dq 3 at point.y, dq 4 iend section .text _start: lea rbx, rel corner mov rax, rbx + point.x imul rax, rax mov rcx, rbx + point.y imul rcx, rcx add rax, rcx ; x x + y y mov rdi, rax call print_int ; 25 call print_newline mov rdi, point_size call print_int ; 16 call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall Arrays of structures In an array of records, element i starts at base + i size . With a size of 1, 2, 4 or 8 the addressing mode can do the multiplication; other sizes need an imul (or a running pointer that adds the size each time): nasm global _start struc item .price: resq 1 .count: resq 1 .flags: resq 1 endstruc section .data stock: dq 250, 4, 0 ; three items of three qwords each dq 1000, 1, 1 dq 75, 12, 0 section .text ; stock_value: rdi = an array of items, rsi = how many. Returns the sum of price count. stock_value: xor eax, eax .loop: test rsi, rsi jz .done mov rcx, rdi + item.price imul rcx, rdi + item.count add rax, rcx add rdi, item_size ; on to the next record dec rsi jmp .loop .done: ret _start: lea rdi, rel stock mov esi, 3 call stock_value mov rdi, rax call print_int ; 250 4 + 1000 1 + 75 12 = 2900 call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall Matching C's layout To share a struct with C (lesson 5.05), your offsets must match the C compiler's, padding included (C course lesson 7.02). For struct { char tag; double value; int count; } on x86-64, C puts value at 8 (after 7 padding bytes) and count at 16, and the size is 24. Write the padding into your struc , or use alignb : nasm-norun struc reading .tag: resb 1 alignb 8 ; pad to the next multiple of 8 .value: resq 1 ; offset 8, like C .count: resd 1 ; offset 16 alignb 8 endstruc ; reading_size = 24 Array of structures or structure of arrays? An array of structures (AoS) keeps each record together: good when code uses all the fields of one record at a time. A structure of arrays (SoA) keeps each field in its own array: good when a loop uses one field of every record, because the values it needs are next to each other in memory (the cache works better) and SIMD can process several at once (lesson 6.04). Games often keep positions, velocities and health in separate arrays for exactly this reason. Check yourself quiz ? What does struc reserve in memory? + Nothing: it only defines names for the offsets and the size - One instance of the structure in the .bss section - One instance in .data, filled with zeros Inside struc , resq and friends just count bytes to give each field its offset. Reserve real memory with resb point_size or build one with istruc . ? How do you reach element i of an array of 24-byte records? - base + i 24 , since any scale works in an address + Compute i × 24 with imul , or step a pointer - base + i 8 three times in a row An address's scale factor must be 1, 2, 4 or 8, so base + i 24 does not assemble. Multiply first, or add item_size to a pointer each step. ? After struc s / .a: resq 1 / .b: resd 1 / endstruc, what is s.b? - 4 + 8 - 12 - 16 .a takes 8 bytes from offset 0, so .b starts at 8.

title: 7.05  Bit Scanning and Atomics
body: Instructions that work on single bits - popcnt, bsf, bsr, tzcnt and lzcnt, bt, bts, btr and btc - and the instructions behind every lock and atomic variable - the lock prefix, xadd, xchg and cmpxchg - with a compare-and-swap loop and a spinlock. Counting and finding bits Lesson 2.03 handled bits with and , or , shl and loops. Modern x86 has single instructions for the common questions: Instruction Result --- --- popcnt rax, rdi how many bits of rdi are 1 tzcnt rax, rdi how many 0 bits come before the lowest 1 (64 if rdi is 0) lzcnt rax, rdi how many 0 bits come before the highest 1 (64 if rdi is 0) bsf rax, rdi the position of the lowest 1 bit (undefined if rdi is 0: ZF is set) bsr rax, rdi the position of the highest 1 bit (undefined if rdi is 0) tzcnt and lzcnt are the newer, safer versions of bsf and bsr because they define the zero case. nasm global _start section .text _start: mov rbx, 0b1011000 ; 88 popcnt rdi, rbx call print_int ; 3 bits set call print_newline tzcnt rdi, rbx call print_int ; 3: the lowest 1 is bit 3 call print_newline bsr rdi, rbx call print_int ; 6: the highest 1 is bit 6 call print_newline lzcnt rdi, rbx call print_int ; 57 leading zeros call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall The position of the highest set bit is ⌊log₂ n⌋, which makes bsr a fast integer logarithm, and tzcnt finds the next free slot in a bitmap of used and free slots in one step. Testing and changing one bit Instruction Effect --- --- bt rax, n copies bit n into the carry flag bts rax, n the same, then sets the bit btr rax, n the same, then clears it btc rax, n the same, then flips it Follow them with jc or setc . With a memory operand and a register bit number, bt can reach any bit of a large bitmap: bt rel bitmap , rcx . Why "atomic" When two threads run add counter , 1 on different cores, each core reads the value, adds and writes it back; both can read the same old value and one increase is lost (the same race as in the C and C++ concurrency lessons). The lock prefix makes a read-modify-write instruction atomic : no other core can touch that memory in the middle of it. nasm-norun lock add qword rel counter , 1 ; safe from every thread lock inc qword rel hits lock or qword rel flags , 4 xadd, xchg and cmpxchg Three instructions give the building blocks of every lock and lock-free structure: Instruction Effect --- --- lock xadd mem , rax adds rax to memory and puts the old value in rax: fetch-and-add xchg mem , rax swaps them; with a memory operand it is always atomic, even without lock lock cmpxchg mem , rcx if memory equals rax, stores rcx there and sets ZF; otherwise loads memory into rax and clears ZF cmpxchg is compare-and-swap : "change it only if nobody else did in the meantime". Wrapped in a loop it performs any update atomically: nasm global _start section .data best: dq 40 section .text ; atomic_max: rdi = address of a qword, rsi = a candidate. Stores the candidate if it is larger. ; Returns the value that was there before. atomic_max: mov rax, rdi .retry: cmp rax, rsi jge .done ; already at least as large lock cmpxchg rdi , rsi ; still rax? then store rsi jne .retry ; someone changed it: rax now holds the new value, try again .done: ret _start: lea rdi, rel best mov esi, 75 call atomic_max mov rdi, rel best call print_int ; 75 call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall A spinlock The smallest lock: a qword that is 0 when free and 1 when taken. nasm-norun ; spin_lock: rdi = address of the lock spin_lock: mov eax, 1 .try: xchg rdi , rax ; take it, and see what it was test rax, rax jz .got ; it was free: we have it .wait: pause ; be kind to the other hyper-thread cmp qword rdi , 0 jne .wait ; spin on a plain read until it looks free mov eax, 1 jmp .try .got: ret spin_unlock: mov qword rdi , 0 ; a plain store releases on x86 ret Spinning on a plain read (instead of hammering xchg ) keeps the cache line from bouncing between cores. Spinlocks suit very short critical sections; anything longer should use the operating system's locks, which put waiting threads to sleep. Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference between bsf and tzcnt for an input of 0? - Both return 64 - bsf returns 0; tzcnt returns −1 + bsf 's result is undefined; tzcnt gives 64 With no set bit there is nothing for bsf to find, so it sets ZF and leaves its destination undefined. tzcnt defines the answer as the operand size. ? What does lock cmpxchg do when memory no longer equals rax ? - It writes the new value anyway and sets ZF + It loads the current memory value into rax and clears ZF - It waits until the memory equals rax again On a mismatch nothing is stored; rax gets the fresh value, so a retry loop can compute again and retry. ? Which instruction both adds to memory and returns the old value? - lock add + lock xadd - xchg - bts xadd exchanges and adds: memory gets the sum, the register gets the old value.

title: A bitmap allocator
body: Operating systems, file systems and game engines hand out fixed-size slots (pages, disk blocks, particles) from a bitmap : one bit per slot, 1 meaning used. Build one in assembly, using the bit instructions from lesson 7.05, a struc for its header (lesson 7.04) and a macro (lesson 7.02). The allocator lives in memory the caller provides, laid out as: nasm struc pool .count: resq 1 ; how many slots there are (at most 64 4 = 256) .used: resq 1 ; how many are in use .bits: resq 4 ; the bitmap: bit i of the whole 256-bit field is slot i endstruc Write these functions (the tests pass the pool as an array of six qwords): Function Effect Returns --- --- --- pool_init(pool, count) sets count, clears used and every bit count, or −1 if count is 0 or more than 256 (and then changes nothing) pool_alloc(pool) finds the lowest free slot, marks it used the slot number, or −1 if all are used pool_free(pool, slot) marks the slot free 1 if it was in use, 0 if it was already free or out of range pool_is_used(pool, slot) 1 or 0 (0 when out of range) pool_count_used(pool) counts the 1 bits with popcnt the number of used slots

title: 8.01  String Instructions
body: The x86 instructions built for blocks of memory - movsb, stosb, lodsb, scasb and cmpsb with rsi, rdi and rcx, the rep, repe and repne prefixes, the direction flag and cld, writing memcpy, memset, strlen and memcmp with them, and when a plain loop or SIMD is faster. Instructions for blocks of bytes Lesson 4.03 walked through strings one byte at a time with a loop. x86 also has string instructions that do one step of such a loop each, using fixed registers: instruction does then --- --- --- movsb copies the byte at rsi to rdi rsi++ , rdi++ stosb stores al at rdi rdi++ lodsb loads the byte at rsi into al rsi++ scasb compares al with the byte at rdi (sets flags) rdi++ cmpsb compares rsi with rdi (sets flags) rsi++ , rdi++ Each has w , d and q forms ( movsq copies 8 bytes and moves the pointers by 8). The pointers move forwards when the direction flag is clear, which the System V convention guarantees on entry to every function. cld clears it explicitly; std sets it to go backwards, and code that sets it must clear it again before calling anything. rep: repeat rcx times The rep prefix repeats the instruction rcx times, counting rcx down to 0. rep movsb is a whole memcpy , and rep stosb a whole memset : nasm global _start section .data src: db "assembly!", 0 src_len equ $ - src section .bss dst: resb 32 section .text _start: cld lea rdi, rel dst ; fill dst with ' ' first mov al, ' ' mov ecx, 20 rep stosb mov byte rdi , 0 ; rdi now points just past the 20 stars lea rdi, rel dst call print_str call print_newline lea rsi, rel src ; then copy the string over the start lea rdi, rel dst mov ecx, src_len rep movsb lea rdi, rel dst call print_str call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall Modern processors run rep movsb and rep stosb very fast for large blocks, so compilers often use them for memcpy and memset . repne and repe: repeat while repne ("repeat while not equal") repeats while rcx is not 0 and the comparison was not equal. With scasb , that searches for a byte, which gives a strlen : nasm global _start section .data text: db "hello, world", 0 section .text my_strlen: ; rdi = string, returns its length in rax xor eax, eax ; al = 0, the byte to find mov rcx, -1 ; as many steps as it takes mov rdx, rdi repne scasb ; stops after the zero byte sub rdi, rdx ; bytes scanned, including the zero lea rax, rdi - 1 ret _start: lea rdi, rel text call my_strlen mov rdi, rax call print_int ; 12 call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall repe ("repeat while equal") with cmpsb compares two blocks and stops at the first difference, a memcmp : nasm global _start section .data a: db "apple pie" b: db "apple tart" section .text my_memcmp: ; rdi, rsi, rdx = length; returns <0, 0 or 0 mov rcx, rdx xor eax, eax test rcx, rcx jz .done repe cmpsb ; flags from the last compared pair je .done ; all equal movzx eax, byte rsi - 1 ; the first different bytes movzx ecx, byte rdi - 1 sub rax, rcx ; 64-bit, so a negative difference stays negative .done: ret _start: lea rsi, rel a lea rdi, rel b mov edx, 9 call my_memcmp mov rdi, rax call print_int call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall cmpsb compares rsi with rdi , so here the first block is in rsi : "apple p" against "apple t" gives 'p' - 't' , a negative number, meaning a sorts first. lodsb: reading through a string lodsb pairs naturally with a loop that transforms each byte: nasm global _start section .data msg: db "Shout This", 0 section .bss out: resb 32 section .text _start: lea rsi, rel msg lea rdi, rel out .next: lodsb ; al = next byte, rsi++ cmp al, 'a' jb .keep cmp al, 'z' ja .keep sub al, 32 ; lower to upper case .keep: stosb ; store it, rdi++ test al, al jnz .next ; stop after copying the zero lea rdi, rel out call print_str call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall When to use them - rep movsb / rep stosb for copying and filling large blocks: short, and fast on current processors. - repne scasb and repe cmpsb are compact but slower than they look; compilers rarely use them, preferring loops or SIMD (lesson 6.04) that check 16 or 32 bytes at once. - Remember which registers they use: rsi , rdi and rcx change, so save anything you still need. Check yourself quiz ? After rep movsb with rcx = 10, what are rcx , rsi and rdi ? - rcx is 10, and rsi and rdi are unchanged - rcx is 0, and rsi and rdi are back where they started + rcx is 0, and rsi and rdi have each moved forward by 10 bytes Each step copies a byte, moves both pointers (forward when the direction flag is clear) and decrements rcx until it reaches 0. ? Why does my_strlen start with rcx = -1? + So the count runs out only at the zero byte - −1 tells scasb to search backwards - It marks the string as signed rcx = −1 is the largest unsigned count, so repne scasb stops at the zero byte first. The length is worked out from how far rcx counted down. ? Which instruction stores al at rdi and moves rdi on? - movsb + stosb - lodsb - scasb stosb stores; lodsb loads; movsb copies; scasb compares.

title: 8.02  Multiplying and Dividing by Constants
body: How compilers avoid slow instructions - multiplying by small constants with lea and shifts, dividing unsigned numbers by powers of two with shr, signed division by powers of two with a bias, replacing division by any constant with a multiply by a magic number and a shift, and computing remainders from the quotient. Why avoid div? imul takes about 3 cycles; div and idiv can take 10 to 40 or more. Division by a constant (by 10 to print a number, by 60 for minutes) is common, so compilers replace it with faster instructions. Recognising these patterns makes compiler output (lesson 6.01) readable, and lets you write them yourself. Multiplying with lea lea computes base + index × scale + displacement without touching memory, with a scale of 1, 2, 4 or 8. That makes small multiplications one instruction: nasm global _start section .text _start: mov rbx, 7 lea rdi, rbx + rbx 2 ; 3 x call print_int call print_newline lea rdi, rbx + rbx 4 ; 5 x call print_int call print_newline lea rdi, rbx 8 + rbx ; 9 x call print_int call print_newline lea rax, rbx + rbx 4 ; 5 x lea rdi, rax + rax ; then 2 x: 10 x call print_int call print_newline mov rdi, rbx shl rdi, 4 ; 16 x sub rdi, rbx ; 15 x call print_int call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall Powers of two are a shift; other constants become a short combination of lea , shl , add and sub . Dividing by powers of two For unsigned numbers, dividing by 2^k is shr k , and the remainder is and with 2^k − 1: nasm global _start section .text _start: mov rbx, 1000 mov rdi, rbx shr rdi, 3 ; 1000 / 8 = 125 call print_int call print_newline mov rdi, rbx and rdi, 7 ; 1000 % 8 = 0 call print_int call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall For signed numbers, sar rounds towards minus infinity (−7 1 is −4), but C's division rounds towards zero (−7 / 2 is −3). The fix is to add 2^k − 1 first when the number is negative: nasm global _start section .text div4: ; rdi / 4, rounding towards zero like C mov rax, rdi sar rax, 63 ; all 1s if negative, else 0 and rax, 3 ; 3 if negative, else 0 add rax, rdi sar rax, 2 ret _start: mov rdi, -7 call div4 mov rdi, rax call print_int ; -1, as -7 / 4 in C call print_newline mov rdi, 7 call div4 mov rdi, rax call print_int ; 1 call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall Dividing by any constant: the magic number To divide by 10, multiply by 2^67 / 10 (rounded up) and keep only the top bits: x / 10 = (x × 0xCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCD) 67 . The 64-bit mul leaves the high half of the 128-bit product in rdx , which is already a shift by 64; three more give 67: nasm global _start section .text div10: ; unsigned rdi / 10 mov rax, 0xCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCD mul rdi ; rdx:rax = rdi magic mov rax, rdx shr rax, 3 ret _start: mov rdi, 1234567 call div10 mov rdi, rax call print_int ; 123456 call print_newline mov rdi, -1 ; the largest unsigned number call div10 mov rdi, rax call print_uint ; 1844674407370955161 call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall The magic number and the shift are chosen so the result is exact for every 64-bit input. Compilers compute them for any divisor; you can see them by compiling x / 7 or x / 1000 on Compiler Explorer. Signed division uses a signed magic number and a correction for negative values. Remainders from the quotient Once you have q = x / 10 , the remainder is x − q × 10 , with no second division: nasm global _start section .text _start: mov rbx, 1234567 mov rax, 0xCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCD mul rbx shr rdx, 3 ; rdx = 123456 lea rcx, rdx + rdx 4 ; q 5 add rcx, rcx ; q 10 mov rdi, rbx sub rdi, rcx ; 1234567 - 1234560 = 7 call print_int call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall This pair is exactly what a fast "print a number" routine does for each digit (lesson 6.02's printer can use it). Is it worth it? Write division as div first; it is correct and clear. Change it to a multiply when it is in a hot loop and the divisor is fixed, and test the result against div for many values, including 0, 1, the largest value and numbers just around multiples of the divisor. Check yourself quiz ? How does lea rax, rdi + rdi 4 multiply by 5? - It reads the value at address rdi 5 - lea has a hidden multiply-by-5 mode + It computes the address rdi + rdi × 4 That is 5 × rdi . lea only does the address arithmetic and puts the result in rax ; nothing is read from memory. ? Why does signed division by 4 add 3 to negative numbers before sar ? - To turn the number positive before shifting + sar rounds down; adding 3 first makes it round towards zero, as idiv and C do - Because sar shifts by one place too few for negative numbers −7 sar 2 gives −2 (rounded down), but −7 / 4 in C is −1. Adding 3 (divisor − 1) first gives −4 sar 2 = −1. ? After mul rdi, where is the high half of the 128-bit product? - rax + rdx - rcx - in memory mul puts the low 64 bits in rax and the high 64 bits in rdx.

title: 8.03  Jump Tables and Function Pointers
body: Code addresses as data - a jump table that turns a switch into one bounds check and one indirect jump, tables of function addresses, calling through a register, passing a function to another function as a callback, and dispatching commands by number; with the bounds checks that keep indirect jumps safe. Addresses of code A label in the text section is just an address, like a label in the data section. You can store it, load it and jump to it. That gives two powerful tools: jump tables (a fast switch ) and function pointers (callbacks, plug-in functions, command tables). A jump table A switch with many cases on small numbers becomes a table of addresses. The code checks the range once, then jumps through the table: nasm global _start section .data names: db "zero", 0, "one", 0, "two", 0, "many", 0 section .text describe: ; rdi = n; prints a word for 0, 1, 2, else "many" cmp rdi, 2 ja .many ; unsigned: also catches negative numbers lea rax, rel .table jmp rax + rdi 8 .case0: lea rdi, rel names jmp .print .case1: lea rdi, rel names + 5 jmp .print .case2: lea rdi, rel names + 9 jmp .print .many: lea rdi, rel names + 13 .print: call print_str call print_newline ret section .data align 8 .table: dq describe.case0, describe.case1, describe.case2 section .text _start: xor ebx, ebx .loop: mov rdi, rbx call describe inc rbx cmp rbx, 4 jl .loop mov rdi, -1 call describe mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall The ja check is essential: without it, a large or negative number would read an address from past the end of the table and jump there. One unsigned comparison covers both directions, because a negative number viewed as unsigned is huge. The local labels .case0 belong to describe , so from the data section they are written as describe.case0 . Calling through a register call rax (or call rax ) calls whatever address the register holds. A table of function addresses lets a number choose the function: nasm global _start section .text add_op: lea rax, rdi + rsi ret sub_op: mov rax, rdi sub rax, rsi ret mul_op: mov rax, rdi imul rax, rsi ret section .data align 8 ops: dq add_op, sub_op, mul_op OPS equ ($ - ops) / 8 section .text apply_op: ; rdi = op number, rsi = a, rdx = b; -1 for a bad op mov rax, -1 cmp rdi, OPS jae .bad lea rcx, rel ops mov rcx, rcx + rdi 8 ; the function's address mov rdi, rsi mov rsi, rdx jmp rcx ; a tail call: its ret returns to our caller .bad: ret _start: xor ebx, ebx .next: mov rdi, rbx mov esi, 12 mov edx, 5 call apply_op mov rdi, rax call print_int call print_newline inc rbx cmp rbx, 4 jl .next mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall jmp rcx at the end is a tail call : instead of call rcx followed by ret , it jumps, and the called function's own ret goes straight back to apply_op 's caller. Callbacks A function can take another function as an argument, as C's qsort takes a comparison. Here map applies a function to each element of an array: nasm global _start section .data values: dq 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 COUNT equ ($ - values) / 8 section .text square: mov rax, rdi imul rax, rdi ret negate: mov rax, rdi neg rax ret map: ; rdi = array, rsi = count, rdx = function; changes the array in place push rbx push r12 push r13 mov rbx, rdi mov r12, rsi mov r13, rdx .loop: test r12, r12 jz .done mov rdi, rbx call r13 ; the callback, called with the element mov rbx , rax add rbx, 8 dec r12 jmp .loop .done: pop r13 pop r12 pop rbx ret print_all: push rbx push r12 lea rbx, rel values mov r12d, COUNT .p: mov rdi, rbx call print_int mov edi, ' ' call print_char add rbx, 8 dec r12 jnz .p call print_newline pop r12 pop rbx ret _start: lea rdi, rel values mov esi, COUNT lea rdx, rel square call map call print_all lea rdi, rel values mov esi, COUNT lea rdx, rel negate call map call print_all mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall map keeps the array pointer, the count and the callback in callee-saved registers, because the callback may change any scratch register. Three pushes plus the return address leave the stack 16-byte aligned at each call . Safety An indirect jump or call goes wherever the register says. Bugs (or attackers) that control that value control the program, which is why: - every table index is bounds-checked first, with an unsigned comparison; - tables of addresses live in read-only data where possible ( section .rodata ); - modern systems add protections such as Control-flow Enforcement Technology, which require indirect targets to start with an endbr64 instruction. Compilers add it for you; hand-written code that runs with those protections on needs it too. Check yourself quiz ? Why is the bounds check before a jump table an unsigned comparison? - Jump tables can only hold unsigned addresses + One ja then also refuses negative indexes - cmp cannot compare signed numbers A negative index looks like a huge unsigned number. A signed check would need two tests, below 0 and above the maximum. ? Why does map keep the callback in r13 rather than rdx ? - rdx cannot hold an address + The callback may change rdx , but not r13 - call needs its target in r13 rdx is caller-saved, so any call may change it. r13 must be preserved by the callee, so it survives every call ( map itself must save and restore it). ? What does jmp rcx at the end of a function do, compared with call rcx then ret? - The same thing, only slower + The same, but the callee returns to our caller - It jumps away and never returns - It returns to the instruction after jmp This is a tail call: jumping reuses our return address on the stack, so the callee's ret goes straight to our caller.

title: 8.04  Memory from the Kernel
body: Getting memory at run time without a C library - the mmap system call with anonymous private pages, its six arguments and the flags that matter, errors as negative return values, munmap to give memory back, page sizes and rounding, the older brk call, and a bump allocator built on one mmap. Where does malloc get memory? The .bss section gives a fixed amount of memory decided when the program is assembled. To get more while the program runs, a program asks the kernel. C's malloc does exactly that underneath, with the system calls this lesson uses directly. mmap mmap (system call 9 on Linux x86-64) maps memory into the program's address space. For plain memory, ask for anonymous (not backed by a file), private pages: register meaning value here --- --- --- rdi where (0 lets the kernel choose) 0 rsi how many bytes the size rdx protection PROT_READ PROT_WRITE = 3 r10 flags MAP_PRIVATE MAP_ANONYMOUS = 0x22 r8 file descriptor -1 (no file) r9 offset in the file 0 Note the fourth argument goes in r10 , not rcx : the syscall instruction itself overwrites rcx (and r11 ). nasm global _start SYS_MMAP equ 9 SYS_MUNMAP equ 11 PROT_RW equ 3 MAP_PRIV_ANON equ 0x22 section .text _start: mov eax, SYS_MMAP xor edi, edi mov esi, 4096 4 ; four pages mov edx, PROT_RW mov r10d, MAP_PRIV_ANON mov r8, -1 xor r9d, r9d syscall test rax, rax js .failed ; a negative result is -errno mov rbx, rax ; the new memory, zero-filled mov qword rbx , 42 ; use it like any other memory mov qword rbx + 16000 , 7 mov rdi, rbx add rdi, rbx + 16000 call print_int ; 49 call print_newline mov eax, SYS_MUNMAP mov rdi, rbx mov esi, 4096 4 syscall xor edi, edi jmp .exit .failed: neg rax mov rdi, rax call print_int ; the error number call print_newline mov edi, 1 .exit: mov eax, 60 syscall New anonymous memory is always zero-filled, so you never see another program's data. Errors are negative Raw system calls do not use errno . They return -errno in rax on failure (lesson 7.03): -12 is ENOMEM , -22 is EINVAL . Because no valid address is that close to the top of the range, js (jump if the sign bit is set) after test rax, rax is the usual check. Pages The kernel works in pages of 4096 bytes. mmap rounds the size up to whole pages, so asking for 10 bytes gives you a page. Round sizes yourself so you know what you got: nasm global _start section .text round_to_page: ; rdi = bytes, returns them rounded up to a multiple of 4096 lea rax, rdi + 4095 and rax, -4096 ; clear the low 12 bits ret _start: mov edi, 1 call round_to_page mov rdi, rax call print_int ; 4096 call print_newline mov edi, 8193 call round_to_page mov rdi, rax call print_int ; 12288 call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall -4096 in two's complement is all 1s except the low 12 bits, so and clears exactly those (lesson 2.03). brk, the old way brk (system call 12) moves the end of the program's data area. brk(0) returns the current end; brk(new_end) asks to grow it and returns the new end (or the old one if it failed). Early malloc s were built on it; modern ones use mmap for large blocks and both for small ones. mmap is simpler to use correctly, so prefer it. A bump allocator Allocating with one system call per object would be slow. Instead, map one large region and hand out pieces by moving a pointer, as lesson 6.02 of the pointers course and the arena idea describe: nasm global _start section .bss arena_next: resq 1 arena_end: resq 1 section .text arena_init: ; rdi = size; returns 0 or -errno mov rsi, rdi mov eax, 9 xor edi, edi mov edx, 3 mov r10d, 0x22 mov r8, -1 xor r9d, r9d push rsi syscall pop rsi test rax, rax js .done mov rel arena_next , rax add rsi, rax mov rel arena_end , rsi xor eax, eax .done: ret arena_alloc: ; rdi = bytes; returns an 8-byte-aligned pointer, or 0 when full add rdi, 7 and rdi, -8 ; round up to a multiple of 8 mov rax, rel arena_next lea rdx, rax + rdi cmp rdx, rel arena_end ja .full mov rel arena_next , rdx ret .full: xor eax, eax ret _start: mov edi, 64 call arena_init mov edi, 10 call arena_alloc mov rbx, rax mov edi, 20 call arena_alloc sub rax, rbx ; 16: 10 rounded up to 16 mov rdi, rax call print_int call print_newline mov edi, 100 call arena_alloc ; does not fit in 64 bytes mov rdi, rax call print_int ; 0 call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall A bump allocator cannot free single objects; everything is released together (with munmap , or by resetting arena_next ). For many programs, such as a compiler handling one file or a game handling one frame, that is exactly what is wanted, and it is far faster than a general allocator. Check yourself quiz ? Why does the fourth mmap argument go in r10 instead of rcx ? + syscall itself overwrites rcx - rcx is reserved for the length of the mapping - mmap takes its arguments in reverse order syscall saves the return address in rcx (and the flags in r11 ), so Linux takes the fourth argument from r10 . Ordinary functions still use rcx . ? How do you tell that mmap failed? - It returns 0 in rax - It sets the carry flag + It returns a negative number (−errno) Like other raw system calls it returns −errno on failure, which test rax, rax and js catch. A real mapping is never at a negative address. ? What does and rax, -4096 do to an address? - Adds 4096 to it + Rounds it down to a page boundary - Makes it negative - Divides it by 4096 -4096 is all 1s except the lowest 12 bits, so the AND clears those bits.

title: 8.05  Command-Line Arguments and the Environment
body: What a Linux program finds on its stack at _start - argc, the argv pointers and the zero that ends them, the environment strings after them, walking them in assembly, comparing a string prefix to find a variable such as HOME, turning arguments into numbers, and setting the exit code that scripts check. The stack at _start When Linux starts a program, the kernel puts information on the stack before the first instruction runs. At _start , rsp points at: address holds --- --- rsp argc , the number of arguments (including the program's name) rsp + 8 argv 0 , a pointer to the program's name rsp + 16 argv 1 , the first real argument ... ... rsp + 8 × (argc + 1) 0, the end of argv after that pointers to the environment strings "NAME=value" , then 0 Each pointer leads to a zero-terminated string. _start is not a function (nothing called it), so there is no return address; read these before pushing anything. Printing the arguments nasm global _start section .data count_msg: db "arguments: ", 0 section .text _start: mov r12, rsp ; argc lea r13, rsp + 8 ; &argv 0 lea rdi, rel count_msg call print_str mov rdi, r12 call print_int call print_newline xor ebx, ebx .next: cmp rbx, r12 jge .done mov rdi, rbx call print_int mov edi, ':' call print_char mov edi, ' ' call print_char mov rdi, r13 + rbx 8 ; argv i call print_str call print_newline inc rbx jmp .next .done: mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall On this site, the Run options let you give arguments; without any, argc is 1 and only the program's name is printed. In a terminal, ./program one "two words" gives argc = 3, and the quotes keep two words together as one argument. The environment The environment strings start right after the zero that ends argv . To find one variable, compare the start of each string with "NAME=" : nasm global _start section .data want: db "PATH=", 0 label: db "PATH is: ", 0 none: db "not set", 0 section .text starts_with: ; rdi = text, rsi = prefix; rax = 1 if text starts with prefix .loop: movzx eax, byte rsi test al, al jz .yes ; reached the end of the prefix cmp al, rdi jne .no inc rdi inc rsi jmp .loop .yes: mov eax, 1 ret .no: xor eax, eax ret _start: mov rax, rsp ; argc lea rbx, rsp + 8 + rax 8 + 8 ; skip argc, the argv pointers and their zero .scan: mov r12, rbx test r12, r12 jz .missing mov rdi, r12 lea rsi, rel want call starts_with test eax, eax jnz .found add rbx, 8 jmp .scan .found: lea rdi, rel label call print_str lea rdi, r12 + 5 ; the value, just after "PATH=" call print_str call print_newline jmp .exit .missing: lea rdi, rel none call print_str call print_newline .exit: mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall The runner on this site starts programs with an almost empty environment, so the value may be blank here; in a terminal you see your real PATH . The comparison stops at the end of the prefix, so PATH= does not match a variable called PATHEXT= by accident, because = must match too. Numbers from arguments Arguments are always text. Parse them with the same digit loop as lesson 6.02: nasm global _start section .data sample: db "-250", 0 section .text parse_int: ; rdi = string; rax = value, rdx = 1 if valid xor eax, eax xor ecx, ecx ; 1 if negative cmp byte rdi , '-' jne .digits mov ecx, 1 inc rdi .digits: movzx edx, byte rdi test dl, dl jz .end sub edx, '0' cmp edx, 9 ja .bad ; not a digit imul rax, rax, 10 add rax, rdx inc rdi jmp .digits .end: test ecx, ecx jz .ok neg rax .ok: mov edx, 1 ret .bad: xor eax, eax xor edx, edx ret _start: lea rdi, rel sample call parse_int mov rdi, rax call print_int ; -250 call print_newline mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall With real arguments, pass r13 + 8 ( argv 1 ) instead of sample , after checking that argc is at least 2. The exit code The number in rdi for the exit system call is what the shell sees in $? . Scripts depend on it: 0 for success, anything else for failure. A tool that was called wrongly usually prints a short usage message to standard error (file descriptor 2) and exits with 2. Run this one here without arguments and the result shows the message and exit code 2: nasm global _start section .data usage: db "usage: tool NUMBER", 10 usage_len equ $ - usage section .text _start: cmp qword rsp , 2 ; argc < 2: no NUMBER given jge .ok mov eax, 1 ; write(2, usage, usage_len) mov edi, 2 lea rsi, rel usage mov edx, usage_len syscall mov eax, 60 mov edi, 2 syscall .ok: mov eax, 60 xor edi, edi syscall Check yourself quiz ? Where is argv 1 at _start ? - At rsp + 8 + At rsp + 16 - In rsi , as in a C main At _start , rsp is argc , rsp + 8 is argv 0 and rsp + 16 is argv 1 . Registers like rdi and rsi hold arguments only when a C runtime calls main . ? How do you find the first environment pointer? - It is at rsp + 8 , right after argc + At rsp + 8 + argc × 8 + 8 - At rsp + argc × 8 , after the last argv pointer Skip argc , the argc pointers of argv and the zero that ends them; the environment pointers come next. ? A program is run as ./tool a b. What is argc? - 2 + 3 - 1 - 0 argv 0 is the program's name, so argc counts every word on the command line, the name included.
