title: 3.04  const and Pointers
body:
const marks something as read-only, and with pointers there are two things it can protect. const int p cannot change what it points at; int const p cannot point anywhere else. Taking const pointers in functions that only read documents the promise, lets callers pass read-only data, and turns accidental writes into compile errors. const variables c-norun const double pi = 3.14159265358979; pi = 3; // error: assignment of read-only variable 'pi' const asks the compiler to refuse any change. It is a promise checked at compile time; it costs nothing when the program runs. Two places for const Read pointer declarations from right to left : Declaration Reads as p = 5 p = &other --- --- --- --- int p p is a pointer to int ok ok const int p p is a pointer to an int that is const error ok int const p p is a const pointer to int ok error const int const p a const pointer to a const int error error int const p means the same as const int p : what matters is whether const is left or right of the . c include <stdio.h int main(void) { int a = 1, b = 2; const int reader = &a; // can look, cannot touch printf("%d
", reader); reader = &b; // fine: it may point elsewhere // reader = 5; // error: read-only location int const fixed = &a; // always points at a fixed = 10; // fine: a changes // fixed = &b; // error: read-only variable printf("%d %d
", a, reader); return 0; } The first kind, const T , is the one you will use all the time. const in function parameters A function that only reads through a pointer should say so: c-norun size_t strlen(const char s); // reads s char strcpy(char dest, const char src); // writes dest, reads src int sum(const int values, size_t count); The signature is documentation the compiler enforces: const char src guarantees strcpy will not change the source. It also lets callers pass things that are read-only, such as string literals: c include <stdio.h int count_spaces(const char s) { int count = 0; for (; s != '\0'; s++) { // moving s is fine: the pointer is not const if ( s == ' ') count++; } return count; } int main(void) { printf("%d
", count_spaces("a b c d")); // 3 return 0; } If count_spaces took a plain char , writing through it by mistake would compile, and on a literal it would crash. Converting between them - int to const int happens automatically: adding a promise is always safe. - const int to int needs a cast, and GCC warns without one ("discards const qualifier"). Casting const away and then writing is undefined if the object really was const. Do not do it. !note Why strchr returns char strchr(const char s, int c) returns a plain char into s : C has no overloading, so one function serves both writable and read-only strings. Keep the result const char when the string was const. Check yourself quiz ? With const int p, which is allowed? - p = 5; - Both + p = &other; - Neither The int is read-only; the pointer can move. ? With int const p, which is allowed? - p = &other; - Both + p = 5; - Neither The pointer is fixed; the int can change. ? Why should size_t length(const char s) take a const pointer? - It makes the function run faster + It promises not to write, so literals can be passed - Because every string in C is const The function only reads, and const is a promise the compiler checks. It can then be called with string literals and other read-only text. ? Is passing an int to a const int parameter allowed? - Only with a cast + Yes, automatically - No Adding const is always safe; removing it is not.

title: 3.05  Pointers to Pointers and argv
body:
A pointer is a variable too, so it has an address, and a pointer to a pointer (char ) lets a function move the caller's pointer. An array of strings is an array of char pointers, and main's argc and argv are exactly that - the words typed after the program's name. Sorting strings means swapping pointers, not text. A pointer to a pointer A pointer is a variable, so it lives at an address too: c include <stdio.h int main(void) { int value = 7; int p = &value; int pp = &p; // the address of the pointer printf("%d %d %d
", value, p, pp); // 7 7 7 pp = 8; // follow twice: changes value printf("%d
", value); // 8 return 0; } Why bother? For the same reason as lesson 3.03: to let a function change the caller's pointer , the function needs the pointer's address. c include <ctype.h include <stdio.h // Reads one word starting at cursor, copies it into out, and moves cursor past it. int next_word(const char cursor, char out, size_t size) { const char s = cursor; while (isspace((unsigned char) s)) s++; if ( s == '\0') return 0; size_t n = 0; while ( s != '\0' && !isspace((unsigned char) s)) { if (n + 1 < size) out n++ = s; s++; } out n = '\0'; cursor = s; // the caller's pointer moves on return 1; } int main(void) { const char text = " three little words "; char word 20 ; while (next_word(&text, word, sizeof word)) { printf(" %s 
", word); } return 0; } This is how strtol(text, &end, 10) hands back end : its parameter is a char . Arrays of strings An array of strings is usually an array of pointers , each pointing at its own text: c include <stdio.h int main(void) { const char planets = {"Mercury", "Venus", "Earth", "Mars"}; size_t count = sizeof planets / sizeof planets 0 ; for (size_t i = 0; i < count; i++) { printf("%zu: %s (starts with %c)
", i, planets i , planets i 0 ); } return 0; } planets holds 4 addresses (32 bytes), not the letters. planets i 0 follows pointer i and takes its first character. Passed to a function, it becomes const char . Compare a real two-dimensional array, char names 4 8 , which holds 4 × 8 = 32 characters in place, every row the same length. The pointer version lets every string have its own length. argc and argv main can take the words typed after the program's name in a terminal: c-norun int main(int argc, char argv ) Running ./greet Ada Grace gives argc = 3 and --- --- argv 0 "./greet" : the program's own name argv 1 "Ada" argv 2 "Grace" argv 3 NULL : the end marker c include <stdio.h int main(int argc, char argv ) { printf("%d argument(s)
", argc); for (int i = 0; i < argc; i++) { printf("argv %d = %s
", i, argv i ); } return 0; } On the website, type arguments under Program arguments in the editor's Input tab, then run. Command-line tools such as gcc -Wall hello.c are just programs reading their argv . Sorting strings: move the pointers To put an array of strings in order, swap the pointers, never the characters. Every swap moves 8 bytes, however long the text: c include <stdio.h include <string.h void sort_words(const char words , size_t count) { for (size_t i = 1; i < count; i++) { // insertion sort const char current = words i ; size_t j = i; while (j 0 && strcmp(words j - 1 , current) 0) { words j = words j - 1 ; j--; } words j = current; } } int main(void) { const char words = {"pear", "apple", "fig", "banana"}; sort_words(words, 4); for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) printf("%s
", words i ); return 0; } Check yourself quiz ? int pp = &p; where p points at x. What is pp? - p + x - The address of x Follow pp to p, then p to x. ? Why does a function take char cursor instead of char cursor? - So it can read two strings + So it can move the caller's pointer - To make the string longer The same reason swap takes int . ? With ./tool one two, what is argc? - 2 + 3 - 1 argv 0 is the program's name. ? const char names = {"a", "bb"}; - what does the array hold? - The characters a, b, b - Two arrays of 8 characters + Two pointers to text stored elsewhere An array of strings is an array of pointers.

title: 4.01  malloc and free
body:
Stack memory disappears when a function returns and must have a size known in advance. The heap gives memory of any size that lasts until you free it. malloc returns NULL when it fails, calloc clears the memory, and every malloc needs exactly one free - never zero, never two. Two places for memory The stack The heap --- --- --- holds local variables and parameters whatever you ask for size fixed when the code is written chosen while the program runs lasts until the function returns until you free it limit a few megabytes most of the computer's memory Locals are perfect until you need memory that outlives the function, or whose size you only learn while the program runs, like "as many numbers as the user types". Then you ask the heap. malloc malloc(bytes) (in stdlib.h ) finds a block of at least that many bytes and returns its address as a void , which converts to any pointer type: c include <stdio.h include <stdlib.h int main(void) { int count = 5; int squares = malloc(count sizeof squares); if (squares == NULL) { fprintf(stderr, "out of memory
"); return 1; } for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) { squares i = i i; } for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) { printf("%d ", squares i ); } printf("
"); free(squares); return 0; } - count sizeof squares is "count elements of whatever squares points at". Writing sizeof squares instead of sizeof(int) stays right if the type changes later. - Memory from malloc holds garbage until you write to it. - malloc returns NULL when it cannot find the memory. Check it. - A pointer to heap memory is used exactly like an array: squares i . calloc(count, size) does the same but sets every byte to 0, and checks that count size does not overflow: c-norun int counts = calloc(26, sizeof counts); // 26 ints, all 0 free free(pointer) hands the block back. After that the memory is not yours: !danger The three classic heap bugs - Memory leak : never calling free . The memory stays taken until the program ends. Leaking inside a loop in a long-running program (a server, a game) eventually uses up everything. - Use after free : reading or writing through a pointer after freeing it. The block may already belong to something else. - Double free : freeing the same block twice. It corrupts the heap's own bookkeeping and usually crashes, sometimes much later. Lesson 4.06 shows the tool that catches all three. A good habit: set the pointer to NULL after freeing it. free(NULL) is defined to do nothing, so a second free becomes harmless, and a use after free becomes an obvious NULL crash instead of silent corruption. Who frees? Every block needs exactly one owner responsible for freeing it. When a function returns heap memory, its documentation must say so: c include <stdio.h include <stdlib.h include <string.h // Returns a new copy of s on the heap. The caller must free it. char copy_text(const char s) { size_t size = strlen(s) + 1; // + 1 for the terminator char copy = malloc(size); if (copy == NULL) return NULL; memcpy(copy, s, size); return copy; } int main(void) { char name = copy_text("Dennis Ritchie"); if (name == NULL) return 1; name 0 = 'd'; printf("%s
", name); free(name); name = NULL; return 0; } Unlike a local's address (lesson 3.03), returning heap memory is fine: it lives until it is freed. (C23 adds this exact function as strdup .) What malloc really does The heap is a big region of the program's memory that the C library manages. malloc keeps lists of free blocks, carves out one big enough, and writes a little header just before it recording its size; that is how free knows how much to give back from the pointer alone. When the heap runs out, the library asks the operating system for more (on Linux with the brk and mmap system calls). Check yourself quiz ? When is heap memory released? - When the function that allocated it returns + When the program calls free on it (or the program ends) - Automatically, when it is no longer used C has no garbage collector. ? What does malloc return when it cannot allocate? - A pointer to 0 bytes + NULL - It stops the program Always check. ? Why is int p = malloc(n sizeof p) a good pattern? - sizeof p is faster than sizeof(int) - It sets the memory to 0 + The size follows the pointer's type automatically Change int to long and the allocation is still right. ? What is a memory leak? - Reading past the end of an array - Freeing a pointer twice + Allocated memory that is never freed The memory stays taken until the program exits.

title: 4.02  Growing Arrays with realloc
body: realloc resizes a heap block, moving it if it has to. Assign its result to a temporary so a failure does not lose the old block. A growing array keeps a length and a capacity and doubles the capacity when it is full, so adding stays fast on average - the same trick as Python lists and C++ vectors. realloc realloc(pointer, new_size) makes a heap block bigger or smaller and returns its (possibly new) address. If there is no room right after the block, it allocates a new one, copies the old contents across, and frees the old one. c-norun int bigger = realloc(numbers, 2 capacity sizeof numbers); if (bigger == NULL) { // numbers is still valid and still needs freeing } else { numbers = bigger; // the old address may now be invalid capacity = 2; } !warning Never write p = realloc(p, ...) If realloc fails it returns NULL and leaves the old block alone. p = realloc(p, size) would then overwrite your only pointer to that block: a leak. Use a temporary. Also, after a successful realloc , any other pointers into the old block are dangling: the data may have moved. Length and capacity A growing array keeps three things together: the pointer, how many elements are used ( length ) and how many fit ( capacity ). When length reaches capacity, grow: c include <stdio.h include <stdlib.h int main(void) { size_t length = 0; size_t capacity = 4; int numbers = malloc(capacity sizeof numbers); if (numbers == NULL) return 1; int value = 0; while (scanf("%d", &value) == 1) { if (length == capacity) { size_t new_capacity = capacity 2; int bigger = realloc(numbers, new_capacity sizeof numbers); if (bigger == NULL) { free(numbers); return 1; } numbers = bigger; capacity = new_capacity; printf("(grew to %zu)\n", capacity); } numbers length++ = value; } for (size_t i = length; i 0; i--) { printf("%d ", numbers i - 1 ); // backwards } printf("\n"); free(numbers); return 0; } Try it with ten or so numbers (press Ctrl+D to end the input in the console). Why double? Growing by one each time would copy every element on every addition: adding n elements would copy about n²/2 of them. Doubling means copies happen rarely: after adding n elements the total copying is less than 2n, so each addition costs a constant amount on average ("amortised O(1)"). Python's list , C++'s std::vector , Rust's Vec and Java's ArrayList all work exactly like this underneath. Wrapping it up in functions Passing three separate variables everywhere is clumsy. The next lesson's structures bundle them into one thing: c-norun struct int_list { int items; size_t length; size_t capacity; }; bool list_push(struct int_list list, int value); // grows when needed void list_free(struct int_list list); That is your first real data structure , and you will build it in the practice. Check yourself quiz ? What can realloc do when the block cannot grow where it is? - Fail every time - Overwrite the memory after the block + Allocate a new block, copy the data and free the old one That is why old pointers into the block become invalid. ? Why is p = realloc(p, n) a bug? - realloc cannot be given the same pointer - It frees p twice + If realloc fails, the only pointer to the old block is lost Use a temporary variable. ? Why does a growing array double its capacity instead of adding one? - Memory only comes in powers of two - Doubling uses less memory overall + So copying is rare and adding is fast on average Doubling gives amortised constant-time adds; growing by one would copy everything on every add. ? What do length and capacity mean? - Bytes used and elements used - Two names for the same number + Elements in use, and elements there is room for When length reaches capacity, grow.

title: 4.03  Structures
body:
A struct groups named fields of different types into one value. Fields are reached with a dot, or with an arrow through a pointer. Structs are copied when assigned or passed, so large ones go by pointer. The compiler adds padding between fields so each one sits at an address that suits it. Grouping data c include <stdio.h struct point { int x; int y; }; struct player { char name 20 ; int score; struct point position; // a struct inside a struct }; int main(void) { struct player p = {"Ada", 1200, {3, 4}}; p.score += 50; p.position.x = 10; printf("%s has %d points at (%d, %d)
", p.name, p.score, p.position.x, p.position.y); return 0; } - struct point { ... }; defines a new type called struct point . Note the semicolon at the end. - . reaches a field. - Initialise in order with { } , or by name with designated initialisers , which are clearer and leave the rest as 0: c-norun struct player q = {.name = "Grace", .score = 900}; // position is {0, 0} Structs are values Unlike arrays, structs can be assigned, passed and returned, and that copies every field: c include <stdio.h struct point { int x; int y; }; struct point moved(struct point p, int dx, int dy) { p.x += dx; // changes the copy p.y += dy; return p; } int main(void) { struct point a = {1, 2}; struct point b = moved(a, 10, 0); printf("a=(%d,%d) b=(%d,%d)
", a.x, a.y, b.x, b.y); // a unchanged return 0; } Even an array inside a struct is copied. But == does not work on structs: compare field by field. Pointers to structs: the arrow To change a caller's struct, or to avoid copying a big one, pass a pointer. p- field is short for ( p).field : c include <stdio.h struct account { char owner 32 ; long cents; }; void deposit(struct account a, long cents) { a- cents += cents; } void print_account(const struct account a) { printf("%s: %ld.%02ld
", a- owner, a- cents / 100, a- cents % 100); } int main(void) { struct account acc = {"Ken", 1050}; deposit(&acc, 299); print_account(&acc); // Ken: 13.49 return 0; } Structs on the heap work the same way: struct account a = malloc(sizeof a); then a- cents = 0; . Arrays of structs c include <stdio.h struct item { const char name; int quantity; double price; }; int main(void) { struct item cart = { {"tea", 2, 3.50}, {"bread", 1, 2.25}, {"jam", 3, 4.00}, }; double total = 0; for (size_t i = 0; i < sizeof cart / sizeof cart 0 ; i++) { total += cart i .quantity cart i .price; } printf("%.2f
", total); return 0; } Padding: structs in memory Fields are stored in the order you write them, but the compiler may add unused padding bytes so that each field is aligned : an int at an address divisible by 4, a double by 8. The processor reads aligned values faster, and some processors cannot read unaligned ones at all. c include <stdio.h include <stddef.h struct messy { char a; double b; char c; }; // 1 + 7 padding + 8 + 1 + 7 padding struct tidy { double b; char a; char c; }; // 8 + 1 + 1 + 6 padding int main(void) { printf("messy: %zu bytes, b at offset %zu
", sizeof(struct messy), offsetof(struct messy, b)); printf("tidy: %zu bytes
", sizeof(struct tidy)); return 0; } Putting the biggest fields first often makes a struct smaller. It matters when you have millions of them, or when the struct must match a file format byte for byte (lesson 5.02). Check yourself quiz ? What does p- score mean when p is a struct pointer? - p.score + ( p).score - The address of score The arrow follows the pointer and picks the field. ? What happens when one struct variable is assigned to another? - Both names now refer to the same struct + Every field is copied, arrays inside included - It does not compile Structs are values. ? Why can sizeof(struct) be bigger than the sum of its fields? - The struct stores its own name + Padding is added to keep fields aligned - sizeof counts the pointer too Reordering fields can reduce it. ? How do you compare two structs? - With == - With strcmp + Field by field C has no == for structs.

title: 4.04  typedef, enum and union
body:
typedef gives a type a new name, often used to drop the word struct. enum names a set of integer constants and makes switch statements readable. A union stores one of several types in the same memory, and a tagged union pairs it with an enum saying which one is there. typedef typedef makes a new name for an existing type: c include <stdio.h typedef struct { double x; double y; } Vec2; typedef unsigned char byte; Vec2 add(Vec2 a, Vec2 b) { return (Vec2){a.x + b.x, a.y + b.y}; // a compound literal: a struct value on the spot } int main(void) { Vec2 v = add((Vec2){1.5, 2}, (Vec2){0.5, 1}); byte flags = 255; printf("(%.1f, %.1f) %d
", v.x, v.y, flags); return 0; } Styles differ: the Linux kernel avoids typedefs for structs so you always see struct ; many other projects typedef everything. Both are fine; be consistent. A struct that points to its own type (the next lesson) needs its struct name too: c-norun typedef struct node { int value; struct node next; // the typedef name does not exist yet at this point } Node; enum An enum names a set of whole-number constants: c include <stdio.h enum direction { NORTH, EAST, SOUTH, WEST }; // 0, 1, 2, 3 enum direction turn_right(enum direction d) { return (enum direction)((d + 1) % 4); } const char direction_name(enum direction d) { switch (d) { case NORTH: return "north"; case EAST: return "east"; case SOUTH: return "south"; case WEST: return "west"; } return "?"; } int main(void) { enum direction facing = WEST; facing = turn_right(facing); printf("now facing %s (%d)
", direction_name(facing), facing); return 0; } - Values count up from 0 unless you set them: enum http { OK = 200, NOT_FOUND = 404 }; . - An enum is really an int ; C will not stop you storing 17 in one. But -Wall warns when a switch over an enum forgets a value, which catches bugs when you add a new one. - Use enums instead of "magic numbers" like if (state == 3) . union A union looks like a struct, but all its fields share the same memory : it holds one of them at a time, and its size is that of the biggest. c include <stdio.h union number { int i; float f; unsigned char bytes 4 ; }; int main(void) { union number n; n.f = 1.0f; printf("%zu bytes
", sizeof n); printf("1.0f is stored as %02x %02x %02x %02x
", n.bytes 3 , n.bytes 2 , n.bytes 1 , n.bytes 0 ); return 0; } Writing one field and reading another reinterprets the bytes. Here it shows that 1.0f is 3f 80 00 00 in IEEE 754 (the Fundamentals course explains the format). Tagged unions The useful pattern pairs a union with an enum saying which field is in use. It is how a value can be "one of several kinds", like a number or a piece of text: c include <stdio.h enum kind { NUMBER, TEXT }; struct value { enum kind kind; union { double number; const char text; }; // an anonymous union (C11): fields used directly }; void print_value(struct value v) { switch (v.kind) { case NUMBER: printf("number %g
", v.number); break; case TEXT: printf("text "%s"
", v.text); break; } } int main(void) { struct value list = { {.kind = NUMBER, .number = 3.5}, {.kind = TEXT, .text = "hello"}, }; for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) print_value(list i ); return 0; } This is exactly how interpreters for Python or JavaScript store their values, and what Rust's enum and C++'s std::variant do safely for you. Check yourself quiz ? What does typedef struct { int x; } Point; let you write? - A struct with a default value - A pointer type + Point p; instead of struct ... p; typedef only adds a name. ? enum color { RED, GREEN, BLUE }; - what is BLUE? - 3 + 2 - "BLUE" Counting starts at 0. ? How big is a union of an int, a double and a char 3 ? - The sum of all three + The size of the double: the biggest member - 1 byte All members share the same memory. ? What is the enum in a tagged union for? - Making the union bigger + Saying which member currently holds the value - Numbering the members Without it you cannot tell what is stored.

Write the functions in solution.c : c enum shape_kind { CIRCLE, RECTANGLE, TRIANGLE }; typedef struct { enum shape_kind kind; union { struct { double radius; } circle; struct { double width, height; } rectangle; struct { double a, b, c; } triangle; / the three side lengths / }; } Shape; const char kind_name(enum shape_kind kind); / "circle", "rectangle", "triangle" / double area(const Shape s); / a triangle's area by Heron's formula / double perimeter(const Shape s); Shape make_square(double side); / a RECTANGLE / Heron's formula: with p = (a + b + c) / 2 , the area is sqrt(p (p - a) (p - b) (p - c)) . M_PI is not part of standard C, so write pi out: 3.14159265358979323846 . Use a switch on the kind.

title: 4.05  Linked Lists
body: A linked list is a chain of nodes on the heap, each holding a value and a pointer to the next, ending in NULL. Adding at the front is instant and nothing ever has to move, but finding the nth element means walking the chain. Inserting and removing use a pointer to the link being changed, and freeing the list walks it once. Nodes that point to the next c-norun struct node { int value; struct node next; // NULL in the last node }; A list is just a pointer to the first node (the head ), and NULL for an empty list: Unlike an array, the nodes can be anywhere in memory. Each one only knows where the next one is. Pushing onto the front c include <stdio.h include <stdlib.h struct node { int value; struct node next; }; // Adds value at the front. Returns false if memory ran out. int push_front(struct node head, int value) { struct node n = malloc(sizeof n); if (n == NULL) return 0; n- value = value; n- next = head; // the new node points at the old first node head = n; // and becomes the first node return 1; } void print_list(const struct node head) { for (const struct node n = head; n != NULL; n = n- next) { printf("%d - ", n- value); } printf("NULL\n"); } void free_list(struct node head) { while (head != NULL) { struct node next = head- next; // save it before freeing free(head); head = next; } } int main(void) { struct node list = NULL; push_front(&list, 9); push_front(&list, 3); push_front(&list, 7); print_list(list); // 7 - 3 - 9 - NULL free_list(list); return 0; } - push_front changes the caller's head pointer, so it takes struct node (lesson 3.05). - The loop for (n = head; n != NULL; n = n- next) visits every node: memorise it. - free_list must read head- next before freeing head ; afterwards it would be a use after free. Removing: a pointer to the link Removing a node means making the link that points at it skip over it. The neat way keeps a pointer to that link (either head itself or some node's next ), so the first node needs no special case: c-norun // Removes the first node holding value. Returns 1 if one was removed. int remove_value(struct node head, int value) { for (struct node link = head; link != NULL; link = &( link)- next) { if (( link)- value == value) { struct node gone = link; link = gone- next; // the link now skips the node free(gone); return 1; } } return 0; } Linus Torvalds called this pointer-to-pointer version "good taste": the special case for the head has disappeared. Lists or arrays? Growing array Linked list --- --- --- get element i instant walk i nodes add at the end fast (on average) fast if you keep a tail pointer add at the front or middle move everything after it change two pointers memory one block, packed together one allocation per node, plus a pointer each Modern processors read memory that sits together much faster (thanks to caches, see the Fundamentals course), so arrays usually win in practice. Linked lists still shine where elements must never move, and inside operating systems, which link processes and buffers together this way all the time. Check yourself quiz ? How does the last node of a linked list mark the end? - Its value is 0 + Its next pointer is NULL - The list stores its length Loops stop when they reach NULL. ? Why does push_front take struct node head? - The list holds pointers to pointers - To return two values + It must change the caller's head pointer The same idea as swap(int , int ). ? In free_list, why save head- next before calling free(head)? - free changes head- next to NULL - To make it faster + After free, reading head- next is a use after free Freed memory is no longer yours. ? Which is faster on a linked list than on an array? - Reading the 500th element - Adding up every element + Inserting at the front Arrays win at access by index and at walking through memory.

title: 4.06  Memory Bugs
body: Overflows, use after free, double frees, leaks and uninitialised reads often run without any visible problem - until they don't. AddressSanitizer adds checks around every memory access and reports the exact line, and Valgrind does it without rebuilding. Warnings and simple habits prevent most of them in the first place. Silent bugs C trusts you. When a program writes past the end of an array, nothing stops it: the write lands on whatever is next. It might crash at once, crash minutes later somewhere unrelated, print wrong results, or work perfectly on your computer and fail on someone else's. These bugs are the reason most serious security holes in C programs exist. Bug Example --- --- buffer overflow int a 4 ; a 4 = 1; use after free free(p); p- x = 1; double free free(p); free(p); memory leak malloc with no free uninitialised read int x; if (x 0) ... returning a local's address return &local; AddressSanitizer AddressSanitizer (ASan) is built into GCC and Clang. Compiling with -fsanitize=address makes the compiler add a check before every memory access and keep a "shadow" map of which bytes may be touched. The moment a program steps out of bounds, it stops with a report showing the bad access, the line, and where the memory came from. On this website, turn it on with Memory checks (AddressSanitizer) in the editor's menu, then run this: c include <stdio.h include <stdlib.h int main(void) { int scores = malloc(4 sizeof scores); if (scores == NULL) return 1; for (int i = 0; i <= 4; i++) { // one too many scores i = i 10; } printf("%d\n", scores 0 ); free(scores); return 0; } Without memory checks, it probably prints 0 and looks fine. With them, it stops with heap-buffer-overflow and points at the line inside the loop: "0 bytes after 16-byte region", which is exactly the fifth int of a four- int block. The website's memory checks also switch on UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer ( -fsanitize=undefined ), which catches things like signed integer overflow and shifts by too much (lesson 6.02). !tip Use it all the time while developing Programs run about twice as slowly with ASan, which hardly matters while you are testing. Professional C projects run their whole test suite with sanitizers on. Valgrind On Linux, Valgrind runs an ordinary, unchanged program inside a simulated processor and checks every access. It is slower (20 to 50 times) but needs no recompiling, and its leak report at the end lists every block that was never freed: $ valgrind --leak-check=full ./program ==1234== 40 bytes in 1 blocks are definitely lost in loss record 1 of 1 ==1234== at 0x483B7F3: malloc ==1234== by 0x109162: main (program.c:6) ASan finds leaks too, when the program ends (on Linux). Habits that prevent them - Compile with -Wall -Wextra and fix every warning: uninitialised variables and returned local addresses are warnings. - Give every variable a value when it is declared, pointers included ( NULL if nothing else). - Keep the size next to the pointer, and use size_t and < for loops: for (size_t i = 0; i < count; i++) . - Use the length-taking functions: snprintf and fgets , never gets (removed from C) or sprintf into a small buffer. - Decide who owns every heap block, and free it in one place. Set the pointer to NULL afterwards. - For every malloc , check NULL . Why other languages exist Every one of these bugs is impossible in safe Rust, which checks ownership at compile time, and in garbage-collected languages like Python and Java, which free memory for you and check every index. C gives up those checks for speed and control. That trade-off is why the C you write today should be tested with sanitizers, and why parts of Linux, Windows and Android are now being written in Rust. Check yourself quiz ? Why are memory bugs in C dangerous even when the program seems to work? - They always crash the program at once + They silently touch other memory, with effects later - They only slow the program down The bad access reads or changes memory that belongs to something else, and the effects show up later or elsewhere. That is why tools are needed to find them. ? What does AddressSanitizer do? - Frees leaked memory automatically - Makes the program run faster + Checks memory accesses and reports bad ones It adds checks to every memory access and reports the first bad one with its line. Turn on Memory checks in the editor's menu. ? Which function should never be used to read a line? - fgets + gets - getline gets cannot know the buffer size. It was removed in C11. ? Which tool checks an unchanged program for leaks on Linux? - printf + Valgrind - The preprocessor ASan needs a rebuild; Valgrind does not.

title: A shop inventory
body: Keep a shop's stock in a growing array of structures, driven by commands, one per line: add apple 3 0.50 add pear 2 0.75 add apple 2 0.45 remove pear 1 remove kiwi 1 remove apple 9 list total sell prints Added 3 apple Added 2 pear Added 2 apple Removed 1 pear No kiwi Only 5 apple apple x5 @ 0.45 = 2.25 pear x1 @ 0.75 = 0.75 Total: 3.00 (2 items, 6 units) Could not read: sell Command Does --- --- add NAME QUANTITY PRICE adds stock. If the item exists, the quantity goes up and the price becomes the new one. Prints Added QUANTITY NAME remove NAME QUANTITY takes stock away: Removed QUANTITY NAME . An item whose quantity reaches 0 is deleted. Prints No NAME if there is no such item and Only N NAME if there is not enough (and changes nothing) list every item in alphabetical order , as "%-16s x%-4d @ %7.2f = %8.2f\n" (name, quantity, price, quantity × price), or (empty) total Total: VALUE (N items, M units) with the value to 2 decimals Names are a single word of at most 31 characters, quantities are whole numbers from 1 up, prices are not negative. Anything else - an unknown command, a missing or bad number, a name too long - prints Could not read: and the line. Empty lines are skipped.

title: 5.01  Bitwise Operators
body:
& ^ and ~ work on each bit separately, and << and slide bits left and right. With a mask you can test, set, clear and flip single bits, which is how flags, permissions and hardware registers are handled. Shift unsigned values, and keep shift counts below the width of the type. Working on bits C can work on the individual bits of an integer. Each operator treats the bits one position at a time: Operator Bit is 1 when Example (8 bits) --- --- --- a & b both bits are 1 (AND) 1100 & 1010 = 1000 a \ b either bit is 1 (OR) 1100 \ 1010 = 1110 a ^ b the bits differ (XOR) 1100 ^ 1010 = 0110 ~a the bit is 0 (NOT) ~00001111 = 11110000 a << n bits slide n places left, 0s come in on the right 00000011 << 2 = 00001100 a n bits slide n places right 00001100 2 = 00000011 demo-bits title: Try the bits of a byte bits: 8 value: 202 Shifting left by n multiplies by 2ⁿ; shifting right divides by 2ⁿ (rounding down). 1u << 10 is 1024. Don't confuse them with the logical operators: && and treat whole values as true or false; & and combine bit by bit. 6 && 1 is 1, but 6 & 1 is 0. Masks A mask is a number with 1s in the positions you care about. 1u << n is the mask for bit n: c include <stdio.h int main(void) { unsigned int flags = 0; flags = 1u << 3; // set bit 3 flags = 1u << 0; // set bit 0 printf("%u
", flags); // 9: binary 1001 flags &= ~(1u << 3); // clear bit 3 flags ^= 1u << 5; // flip bit 5 printf("%u
", flags); // 33: binary 100001 if (flags & (1u << 5)) { // test bit 5 printf("bit 5 is set
"); } return 0; } Do Write --- --- set bit n x \ = 1u << n clear bit n x &= ~(1u << n) flip bit n x ^= 1u << n test bit n (x n) & 1 or x & (1u << n) keep the low 4 bits x & 0xF Flags Bits make compact on/off settings, each named by a constant: c include <stdio.h enum { PERM_READ = 1 << 2, // 4 PERM_WRITE = 1 << 1, // 2 PERM_EXEC = 1 << 0, // 1 }; void show(unsigned perms) { printf("%c%c%c
", perms & PERM_READ ? 'r' : '-', perms & PERM_WRITE ? 'w' : '-', perms & PERM_EXEC ? 'x' : '-'); } int main(void) { unsigned owner = PERM_READ PERM_WRITE; show(owner); // rw- show(owner PERM_EXEC); // rwx show(05); // r-x: an octal number, like chmod 755 return 0; } This is exactly how Unix file permissions work: chmod 755 is three octal digits, each one 3 bits of read, write and execute. Pulling fields out of a number Shift down, then mask: an RGB colour packed as 0xRRGGBB : c include <stdio.h int main(void) { unsigned colour = 0x3A7BD5; unsigned red = (colour 16) & 0xFF; unsigned green = (colour 8) & 0xFF; unsigned blue = colour & 0xFF; printf("%u %u %u
", red, green, blue); // 58 123 213 unsigned back = (red << 16) (green << 8) blue; printf("%06X
", back); // 3A7BD5 return 0; } XOR tricks XOR is its own undo: x ^ k ^ k == x . That makes it the heart of simple ciphers and checksums, and x ^ x is always 0 (compilers zero registers with xor eax, eax , as the Assembly course shows). !warning Shifting safely - Shift unsigned values. Shifting a negative number left is undefined, and shifting one right may or may not copy the sign bit. - The shift count must be less than the type's width: 1u << 32 on a 32-bit unsigned is undefined. For bit 40 use 1ull << 40 . - 1 << 31 overflows a signed int : write 1u << 31 . Check yourself quiz ? What is 12 & 10? - 14 + 8 - 6 1100 & 1010 = 1000. ? How do you clear bit 2 of x? - x = 1u << 2; - x ^= 2; + x &= ~(1u << 2); AND with a mask that has a 0 in that position only. ? What is 1u << 4? - 4 + 16 - 5 Shifting left by n multiplies by 2 to the n. ? (0xABCD 8) & 0xFF gives... - 0xCD + 0xAB - 0xABCD Shift the byte you want to the bottom, then mask.

title: 5.02  Fixed-Width Integers and Binary Data
body:
The size of int and long depends on the system, so stdint.h gives types of exact sizes like uint8_t and int64_t, printed with the macros in inttypes.h. Writing a number's bytes in a fixed order with shifts makes data that every machine reads the same way, whatever its endianness. How big is an int? The C standard only promises minimums: int at least 16 bits, long at least 32. On 64-bit Linux and Mac long is 64 bits; on 64-bit Windows it is 32. When the exact size matters (file formats, network messages, hardware), use stdint.h : Type Size Range --- --- --- int8_t / uint8_t 8 bits −128 to 127 / 0 to 255 int16_t / uint16_t 16 bits −32,768 to 32,767 / 0 to 65,535 int32_t / uint32_t 32 bits about ±2.1 billion / 0 to 4.29 billion int64_t / uint64_t 64 bits about ±9.2 × 10¹⁸ / 0 to 1.8 × 10¹⁹ Also size_t for sizes, intptr_t for an integer big enough to hold a pointer, and limits such as INT32_MAX and UINT8_MAX . Printing them printf has no letter for uint32_t , because its real type differs between systems. inttypes.h provides the right format as a macro that joins onto the string: c include <inttypes.h include <stdio.h int main(void) { uint8_t small = 250; int64_t big = INT64_MAX; uint32_t hex = 0xDEADBEEF; small += 10; // wraps to 4 printf("%" PRIu8 " %" PRId64 " %" PRIX32 "
", small, big, hex); printf("sizes: %zu %zu %zu
", sizeof(uint8_t), sizeof(int64_t), sizeof(long)); return 0; } "%" PRIu8 becomes something like "%hhu" ; adjacent strings in C are glued together by the compiler. Bytes in memory: endianness A uint32_t is 4 bytes, but which comes first? x86 and ARM computers are little-endian : the lowest byte is stored first. demo-bytes value: 3735928559 order: little c include <stdint.h include <stdio.h int main(void) { uint32_t value = 0x11223344; const unsigned char bytes = (const unsigned char )&value; for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) { printf("%02x ", bytes i ); // 44 33 22 11 on a little-endian machine } printf("
"); return 0; } Looking at any object's bytes through an unsigned char is always allowed in C. Writing a fixed order with shifts If a program writes a number's raw bytes into a file, a big-endian machine would read them back wrongly. File formats and network protocols therefore fix the order. Shifts produce it on any machine: c include <stdint.h include <stdio.h void put_u32_be(unsigned char out, uint32_t v) // big-endian: most significant first { out 0 = (unsigned char)(v 24); out 1 = (unsigned char)(v 16); out 2 = (unsigned char)(v 8); out 3 = (unsigned char)v; } uint32_t get_u32_be(const unsigned char in) { return (uint32_t)in 0 << 24 (uint32_t)in 1 << 16 (uint32_t)in 2 << 8 in 3 ; } int main(void) { unsigned char buffer 4 ; put_u32_be(buffer, 0xCAFEBABE); printf("%02x %02x %02x %02x
", buffer 0 , buffer 1 , buffer 2 , buffer 3 ); printf("%08x
", get_u32_be(buffer)); return 0; } The shifts work on the value , not on memory, so this code gives the same bytes everywhere. Networks use big-endian ("network byte order"); most file formats today (PNG is an exception) use little-endian. !warning Cast before shifting up in 0 << 24 first turns in 0 into a signed int ; a byte of 0x80 or more then overflows into the sign bit. (uint32_t)in 0 << 24 is safe. A hex dump Programmers inspect binary data as hex: 16 bytes per line, with the printable characters at the side. Tools like xxd and hexdump do it, and you will write one: 00000000 48 65 6c 6c 6f 2c 20 43 21 0a 00 ff Hello, C!... Check yourself quiz ? Which type is exactly 16 bits and unsigned? - unsigned short (always) + uint16_t - int16_t short is usually 16 bits, but only uint16_t promises it. ? On a little-endian computer, which byte of 0x11223344 is stored first? - 0x11 + 0x44 - 0x22 The least significant byte comes first. ? Why build a file's bytes with shifts rather than writing a uint32_t's memory directly? - Shifts are faster + Shifts give the same byte order on every machine - fwrite cannot write integers The value, not the memory layout, decides the bytes. ? What does "%" PRIu64 do? - Prints the number in base 64 - Prints the number as a pointer + Gives the right printf format for uint64_t The macro expands to a string like "lu" or "llu", whichever this system needs.

title: 5.03  Files
body:
fopen opens a file and returns a FILE pointer, or NULL with errno saying why. The familiar fprintf, fgets and fscanf work on any FILE, and stdin, stdout and stderr are FILEs too. fwrite and fread move raw bytes, fseek and ftell move around in a file, and every opened file must be closed. Opening and closing c include <stdio.h int main(void) { FILE out = fopen("scores.txt", "w"); if (out == NULL) { perror("scores.txt"); // prints the reason, such as "Permission denied" return 1; } fprintf(out, "Ada 1200
Grace 950
Linus 1100
"); fclose(out); FILE in = fopen("scores.txt", "r"); if (in == NULL) { perror("scores.txt"); return 1; } char name 32 ; int score = 0; while (fscanf(in, "%31s %d", name, &score) == 2) { printf("%-8s %5d
", name, score); } fclose(in); return 0; } Programs on this website run in a small sandbox with a folder of their own, so they can create and read files; the files disappear when the run ends. Mode Opens for If the file exists If not --- --- --- --- "r" reading read from the start fails "w" writing emptied created "a" appending write at the end created "r+" reading and writing kept fails add b : "rb" , "wb" binary The b matters on Windows, where text mode turns 
 into 
 on the way out and back on the way in. On Linux and Mac there is no difference, but write it for binary files anyway. Errors: NULL and errno Opening fails for many reasons: no such file, no permission, a folder in the way. fopen returns NULL and sets errno (in errno.h ) to a code. perror("text") prints your text and the reason; strerror(errno) gives the reason as a string. c include <errno.h include <stdio.h include <string.h int main(void) { FILE f = fopen("does-not-exist.txt", "r"); if (f == NULL) { printf("could not open: %s
", strerror(errno)); return 1; } fclose(f); return 0; } stdin, stdout, stderr The three streams every program starts with are ordinary FILE s: - printf(...) is fprintf(stdout, ...) . - fgets(line, size, stdin) reads the keyboard or input. - fprintf(stderr, ...) writes errors. They go to a separate stream, so program out.txt saves the results while errors still show on screen. That means a function written as void report(FILE out) can print to the screen or into a file. Binary files: fwrite and fread fwrite(pointer, size, count, file) writes count items of size bytes, straight from memory. fread reads them back. Both return how many items they managed: c include <stdio.h int main(void) { double readings 4 = {20.5, 21.25, 19.75, 22.0}; FILE f = fopen("readings.bin", "wb"); if (f == NULL) return 1; size_t written = fwrite(readings, sizeof readings 0 , 4, f); fclose(f); printf("wrote %zu doubles
", written); double back 4 = {0}; f = fopen("readings.bin", "rb"); if (f == NULL) return 1; size_t got = fread(back, sizeof back 0 , 4, f); fclose(f); for (size_t i = 0; i < got; i++) printf("%.2f
", back i ); return 0; } Raw memory is quick to save, but the file then depends on the machine's endianness and type sizes. For files shared between machines, write each field's bytes in a fixed order (lesson 5.02). Moving around - ftell(f) returns the current position in bytes. - fseek(f, offset, SEEK_SET) jumps to a position from the start ( SEEK_CUR from here, SEEK_END from the end). - rewind(f) goes back to the start. c-norun fseek(f, 0, SEEK_END); long size = ftell(f); // the file's size in bytes rewind(f); Buffering, and why fclose matters FILE streams collect output in a buffer in memory and write it out in big pieces, because every system call to the operating system costs time. fclose (or fflush ) sends what is left. A program that crashes or forgets fclose can lose the end of its output. Every program has a limit on open files, too, so close each one you open. Check yourself quiz ? What does fopen("log.txt", "w") do to an existing log.txt? - Appends to it - Fails + Empties it Use "a" to add to the end instead. ? How do you find out why fopen failed? - fopen returns a negative error code + errno, through perror or strerror - It prints the reason itself fopen returns NULL and sets errno. ? fread(buffer, 4, 10, f) returns 7. What happened? - Exactly 7 bytes were read - There was an error in item 7 + Only 7 items of 4 bytes could be read The count is in items, not bytes. Fewer than asked usually means the end of the file (or an error, which ferror tells apart). ? Why write errors to stderr instead of stdout? - stderr is faster than stdout - stdout cannot print error text + They stay visible when output is redirected Results and messages go to different places, so prog out.txt still shows errors on the terminal.

body: Read lines of name score from the input, then work with a file: 1. Write every valid line into scores.txt as name,score (a comma, no spaces). title: 5.04  The Preprocessor
body:
Before compiling, the preprocessor runs the lines starting with . include pastes in a file, define replaces names with text, and if keeps or drops code. Macros are text replacement, not functions, so parenthesise everything and avoid arguments with side effects. assert checks your assumptions while you develop. Text before code The first stage of building (lesson 1.01) is the preprocessor . It knows nothing about C; it edits text, following the lines that start with , and hands the result to the compiler. Directive Does --- --- include <file pastes in a system header include "file" pastes in your own file (looks in the current folder first) define NAME text from here on, replaces NAME with text if , ifdef , else , endif keeps or removes lines undef NAME forgets a definition Constants c include <stdio.h define MAX_PLAYERS 8 define GAME_NAME "Xenon Quest" int main(void) { int scores MAX_PLAYERS = {0}; printf("%s has room for %d players (%zu bytes)
", GAME_NAME, MAX_PLAYERS, sizeof scores); return 0; } The compiler never sees MAX_PLAYERS , only 8 . By convention macro names are in capitals so they stand out. For typed constants inside functions, const variables and enum values are often better, because they follow C's rules for types and scope. Macros with parameters c include <stdio.h define SQUARE_BAD(x) x x define SQUARE(x) ((x) (x)) int main(void) { printf("%d
", SQUARE_BAD(1 + 2)); // 1 + 2 1 + 2 = 5 ! printf("%d
", SQUARE(1 + 2)); // ((1 + 2) (1 + 2)) = 9 return 0; } !danger Macros paste text - Put parentheses around every parameter and around the whole body. - An argument may be evaluated twice: SQUARE(i++) becomes ((i++) (i++)) , which is undefined. - For anything bigger than a line, write a function. A static inline function is just as fast and has real types. Two special operators: x turns an argument into a string, and a b glues two names together: c include <stdio.h define SHOW(expr) printf("%s = %d
", expr, (expr)) int main(void) { int width = 7, height = 3; SHOW(width height); // prints: width height = 21 return 0; } Built-in names __FILE__ , __LINE__ and __func__ give the current file, line and function, which is handy for messages: c include <stdio.h define LOG(msg) fprintf(stderr, "%s:%d in %s: %s
", __FILE__, __LINE__, __func__, msg) int main(void) { LOG("starting"); printf("done
"); return 0; } Conditional code c include <stdio.h define DEBUG 1 int main(void) { if DEBUG printf("debug build
"); endif ifdef _WIN32 printf("compiled for Windows
"); elif defined(__APPLE__) printf("compiled for macOS
"); elif defined(__linux__) printf("compiled for Linux
"); endif return 0; } Compilers predefine names for the system they build for, which is how one source file supports several systems. gcc -DDEBUG=0 defines a macro from the command line. Include guards If a header is included twice (directly and through another header), its definitions appear twice and the compiler complains. An include guard makes the second copy vanish: c-norun ifndef SHAPES_H define SHAPES_H struct point { double x, y; }; double distance(struct point a, struct point b); endif Most compilers also accept pragma once at the top, which does the same. assert assert(condition) from assert.h stops the program with a message naming the file, line and condition if the condition is false: c include <assert.h include <stdio.h double average(const int values, int count) { assert(values != NULL && count 0); long long sum = 0; for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) sum += values i ; return (double)sum / count; } int main(void) { int v = {2, 4, 9}; printf("%.2f
", average(v, 3)); printf("%.2f
", average(v, 0)); // stops here return 0; } Asserts check things that can only be false if the program has a bug. Release builds often define NDEBUG , which removes them, so never put work that must happen inside an assert . Check yourself quiz ? define DOUBLE(x) x + x. What is 3 DOUBLE(2)? - 12 + 8 - 6 It becomes 3 2 + 2. Parenthesise the body. ? What does an include guard prevent? - Including system headers - Macros being redefined in other files + A header's contents appearing twice when it is included twice ifndef NAME / define NAME / ... / endif. ? Why is MAX(i++, j) risky with define MAX(a, b) ((a) (b) ? (a) : (b))? - MAX cannot take expressions + i++ may run twice - It does not compile Macro arguments are pasted wherever the parameter appears. ? When does the preprocessor run? - While the program runs + Before the compiler, on the source text - After linking It only edits text.

title: 5.05  Programs in Several Files
body: Real programs split into modules - a header (.h) declaring what a module offers and a .c file defining it. Each .c file compiles on its own, and the linker joins them, matching declarations to definitions. extern shares a variable, static keeps things private, and make rebuilds only what changed. Splitting a program A program of any size is split into modules . Each one has: - a header ( stack.h ) that declares what other files may use: types, function prototypes, constants. It is the module's public face. - a source file ( stack.c ) with the definitions: the function bodies and any private helpers. c-norun // stack.h ifndef STACK_H define STACK_H include <stdbool.h include <stddef.h define STACK_MAX 100 struct stack { int items STACK_MAX ; size_t size; }; void stack_init(struct stack s); bool stack_push(struct stack s, int value); bool stack_pop(struct stack s, int out); endif c-norun // stack.c include "stack.h" void stack_init(struct stack s) { s- size = 0; } bool stack_push(struct stack s, int value) { if (s- size == STACK_MAX) return false; s- items s- size++ = value; return true; } bool stack_pop(struct stack s, int out) { if (s- size == 0) return false; out = s- items --s- size ; return true; } c-norun // main.c include <stdio.h include "stack.h" int main(void) { struct stack s; stack_init(&s); stack_push(&s, 1); stack_push(&s, 2); int top = 0; while (stack_pop(&s, &top)) printf("%d\n", top); return 0; } In the editor, add files with the New file button above the file list (or right-click the list). Every .c file in the project is compiled and linked into the program. Compile separately, link together Each .c file is compiled on its own into an object file ( .o ), knowing only what its headers declared. main.o contains a note: "I call stack_push , address unknown". The linker then joins the object files and the C library, filling in every such address. gcc -c stack.c stack.c - stack.o gcc -c main.c main.c - main.o gcc main.o stack.o -o app That explains two error messages that come from the linker, not the compiler: Message Means --- --- undefined reference to 'stack_push' declared (so it compiled), but no file defines it, or that file was not linked in multiple definition of 'counter' two files define the same thing, often a variable defined in a header Sharing variables: extern A header must only declare a shared variable, with extern ; exactly one .c file defines it: c-norun // settings.h extern int verbose; // a declaration: "it exists somewhere" // settings.c int verbose = 0; // the one definition Functions need no extern : a prototype is already a declaration. Keeping things private: static Anything at file level without static is visible to the linker and can clash with the same name in another file. Mark helpers and file-private variables static (lesson 2.03); only what is in the header should be public. Rebuilding with make Recompiling everything after each change wastes time in big projects. A Makefile lists what each file depends on, and make rebuilds only the files whose sources changed: CFLAGS = -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -g app: main.o stack.o $(CC) main.o stack.o -o app main.o: main.c stack.h stack.o: stack.c stack.h Bigger projects generate their build files with CMake or Meson , but the idea is the same. Check yourself quiz ? What belongs in a header file? - The function bodies, so every file gets them - The main function and the global variables + Declarations: types, prototypes, extern variables Definitions go in the .c file; a header that defines things causes duplicate definitions when two files include it. ? "undefined reference to foo" comes from... - The preprocessor + The linker: foo was never defined - A missing semicolon The code compiled fine because foo was declared, but nothing linked in defines it, so the pieces did not join up. ? How should a global variable be shared between files? - Define it in the header file + extern in the header, one definition in a .c file - Make it static in every file Defining it in the header gives a definition in every file that includes it; static would give each file its own variable. ? What does make do? - It writes the code for you + It rebuilds only what changed - It runs the tests make follows the dependencies listed in the Makefile and compares file times, rebuilding only targets older than their sources.

title: 6.01  Function Pointers and qsort
body:
A function has an address too, and a function pointer can be stored, passed and called. That lets code take behaviour as a parameter - qsort sorts anything given a comparison function, and tables of function pointers replace long switch statements. A void parameter lets callbacks carry data of any type. Functions have addresses A compiled function is a sequence of machine instructions somewhere in memory, so it has an address. A function pointer stores it: c include <stdio.h int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; } int multiply(int a, int b) { return a b; } int main(void) { int ( operation)(int, int) = add; // a pointer to a function taking (int, int), returning int printf("%d
", operation(6, 7)); // 13 operation = multiply; printf("%d
", operation(6, 7)); // 42 return 0; } The declaration reads from the name outwards: operation is a pointer ( operation) to a function taking (int, int) and returning int . The parentheses matter: int operation(int, int) would declare a function returning int . A typedef makes it readable: c-norun typedef int ( binary_op)(int, int); binary_op op = add; Passing behaviour as a parameter c include <stdio.h typedef int ( transform)(int); int twice(int x) { return 2 x; } int square(int x) { return x x; } void apply(int values, size_t count, transform f) { for (size_t i = 0; i < count; i++) { values i = f(values i ); } } int main(void) { int v = {1, 2, 3, 4}; apply(v, 4, square); apply(v, 4, twice); for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) printf("%d ", v i ); // 2 8 18 32 printf("
"); return 0; } The function passed in is called a callback . It is C's version of passing a lambda in other languages. qsort qsort in stdlib.h sorts an array of anything. It knows nothing about your elements, so you tell it their size and give it a comparison function: c-norun void qsort(void base, size_t count, size_t size, int ( compare)(const void , const void )); The comparison gets pointers to two elements and returns negative, zero or positive, like strcmp : c include <stdio.h include <stdlib.h include <string.h struct city { const char name; int population; }; int by_population(const void a, const void b) { const struct city x = a; const struct city y = b; if (x- population < y- population) return 1; // biggest first if (x- population y- population) return -1; return 0; } int by_name(const void a, const void b) { const struct city x = a; const struct city y = b; return strcmp(x- name, y- name); } int main(void) { struct city cities = {{"Oslo", 709000}, {"Lagos", 15400000}, {"Lima", 10900000}, {"Bern", 134000}}; size_t n = sizeof cities / sizeof cities 0 ; qsort(cities, n, sizeof cities 0 , by_population); for (size_t i = 0; i < n; i++) printf("%s %d
", cities i .name, cities i .population); qsort(cities, n, sizeof cities 0 , by_name); for (size_t i = 0; i < n; i++) printf("%s ", cities i .name); printf("
"); return 0; } !warning Don't compare by subtracting return x- population - y- population; is a popular shortcut that overflows for large or negative values and then sorts wrongly. Compare with < and . bsearch uses the same kind of function to find an element in a sorted array. Tables of functions An array of function pointers maps a choice to behaviour without a long switch : c include <stdio.h include <string.h static double add(double a, double b) { return a + b; } static double sub(double a, double b) { return a - b; } static double mul(double a, double b) { return a b; } struct command { const char name; double ( run)(double, double); }; static const struct command commands = { {"add", add}, {"sub", sub}, {"mul", mul}, }; int main(void) { const char wanted = "mul"; for (size_t i = 0; i < sizeof commands / sizeof commands 0 ; i++) { if (strcmp(commands i .name, wanted) == 0) { printf("%g
", commands i .run(6, 7)); } } return 0; } This is also how C does what other languages call methods or interfaces: a struct full of function pointers. The Linux kernel describes every kind of file this way, with a struct file_operations holding pointers to its read , write and open functions. Carrying data: void A callback often needs extra information. The C convention passes a void alongside, which the callback converts back to what it really is: c-norun void for_each(const int values, size_t count, void ( visit)(int value, void data), void data); void add_up(int value, void data) { long total = data; total += value; } long total = 0; for_each(values, n, add_up, &total); Check yourself quiz ? What is int ( f)(double)? - A function returning a pointer to int + A pointer to a function taking a double and returning an int - An array of functions The parentheses around f make it a pointer. ? What must a qsort comparison function return? - true or false + Negative, zero or positive - The smaller of the two elements The sign says the order of the two elements, like strcmp. ? Why does qsort take void pointers? - To make sorting faster - Because the array may be NULL + To sort arrays of any element type The element size is given separately, and the comparison function knows the real type. ? Why is return a - b; a risky comparison? - It is too slow - It returns the wrong sign + The subtraction can overflow for large values Compare with < and instead.

In the second, each element is a const char , so the comparison receives pointers to those pointers .

title: 6.02  Undefined Behaviour
body: For some mistakes the C standard sets no rules at all - signed overflow, out-of-bounds access, using freed memory, dividing by zero. The optimiser assumes they never happen and builds on that assumption, so their effects can be strange and far away. Learn the list, compile with warnings, and test with sanitizers. Three kinds of "it depends" Kind Means Example --- --- --- implementation-defined each compiler chooses and documents it the size of long , whether char is signed unspecified one of several outcomes, not documented which argument of f(a(), b()) is worked out first undefined the standard says nothing at all: anything may happen INT_MAX + 1 , a 10 in an int a 10 Undefined behaviour (UB) is not "a random value" or "a crash". The compiler is allowed to assume it never happens, and it optimises on that basis. The usual suspects - signed integer overflow: INT_MAX + 1 - reading or writing outside an object: arrays, strings without terminators - using a pointer after free , or to a local that has gone - dereferencing NULL - dividing by zero, or INT_MIN / -1 - shifting by a negative amount or by the width of the type or more - reading an uninitialised local - changing a variable twice without a sequence point: i = i++ + 1; - modifying a string literal - a non-void function falling off its end when the caller uses the result How the optimiser uses it c include <limits.h include <stdio.h int will_overflow(int x) { int bigger = x + 1; return bigger < x; // only true if x + 1 overflowed } int main(void) { printf("%d\n", will_overflow(INT_MAX)); return 0; } At -O0 (the website's normal build) this prints 1 : the addition wraps and the test sees it. Switch the build to Release (click Debug in the editor's status bar), which compiles with -O2 , and GCC prints 0 , because it reasons: "signed overflow cannot happen, so x + 1 is always bigger than x", and replaces the whole function with return 0 . (Written as one expression, return x + 1 < x; , GCC removes it even in a debug build.) Neither answer is a bug in GCC. The program had none to give. Real damage happens the same way. In 2009 a Linux kernel driver read a field through a pointer before checking the pointer for NULL . Since dereferencing NULL is UB, the compiler concluded the pointer could not be NULL and deleted the check, which created a security hole. !tip Check before the operation, not after To find out whether a + b would overflow, test first: if (b 0 && a INT_MAX - b) . Or use the builtins: __builtin_add_overflow(a, b, &result) returns true on overflow (C23 adds ckd_add in stdckdint.h ). Unsigned arithmetic is safe Unsigned types are defined to wrap around: UINT_MAX + 1u is 0 , always. That is why hash functions and checksums use uint32_t or uint64_t . Defending yourself - -Wall -Wextra catch many cases at compile time. - Memory checks in the editor's menu turn on AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer, which report each overflow, bad shift or bad memory access as it happens, with a message such as runtime error: signed integer overflow: 2147483647 + 1 cannot be represented in type 'int' . - Prefer size_t for sizes and indexes, and unsigned types for bit work. - Keep functions small enough to check every path by eye. Check yourself quiz ? What may a program with undefined behaviour do? - Always crash at the bad line + Anything, including appearing to work - Always print 0 The standard places no requirements on it, so the program may work today and fail with another compiler or flag. ? Why can x + 1 < x be replaced by 0? - The compiler has a bug + The compiler may assume signed overflow never happens - x + 1 is always computed as a double It optimises on that assumption. ? Which of these is defined behaviour? - INT_MAX + 1 - 1 << 40 on a 32-bit int + UINT_MAX + 1u, which is 0 Unsigned arithmetic wraps by definition. ? How do you safely test whether a + b would overflow for positive b? - if (a + b < a) after adding + if (a INT_MAX - b) before adding - if (a + b INT_MAX) The other two tests rely on the overflow having happened.

title: Arithmetic without undefined behaviour
body: Write checked arithmetic for int in solution.c . Each function returns false (and leaves result alone) when the true answer does not fit in an int , and otherwise stores it and returns true : c bool safe_add(int a, int b, int result); bool safe_subtract(int a, int b, int result); bool safe_multiply(int a, int b, int result); bool safe_abs(int a, int result); / INT_MIN has no positive int / The rules: test before doing the operation, using INT_MAX and INT_MIN from limits.h . No wider types ( long long ) and no compiler builtins: the point is to reason about the limits.

title: 6.03  How C Becomes Assembly
body: Each C construct turns into a few machine instructions. Locals live in registers or on the stack, arguments arrive in registers, if and loops become compares and jumps, and array indexing becomes an address calculation. Reading compiler output shows what your code costs and what the optimiser does with it. Looking at the output gcc -S -masm=intel program.c stops after compiling and writes the assembly to program.s . Compiler Explorer (godbolt.org), the service this website compiles with, shows the same side by side with the source. The Assembly course teaches the language properly; here is enough to read it. x86-64 has 16 general registers ( rax , rbx , rcx , rdx , rsi , rdi , rbp , rsp , r8 to r15 ). Their low halves have names too: eax is the low 32 bits of rax . On Linux and Mac, the first six integer or pointer arguments arrive in rdi , rsi , rdx , rcx , r8 , r9 , and the result goes back in rax ( eax for an int ). A simple function c-norun int add3(int a, int b, int c) { return a + b + c; } GCC with -O2 : nasm add3: add edi, esi ; a += b lea eax, rdi+rdx ; result = a + c (lea computes an address, here used as an adder) ret Three instructions, no memory touched at all. With -O0 the same function stores each argument on the stack and loads it back, which is easier to debug and much slower: nasm add3: push rbp mov rbp, rsp mov DWORD PTR rbp-4 , edi ; a mov DWORD PTR rbp-8 , esi ; b mov DWORD PTR rbp-12 , edx ; c mov edx, DWORD PTR rbp-4 mov eax, DWORD PTR rbp-8 add edx, eax mov eax, DWORD PTR rbp-12 add eax, edx pop rbp ret DWORD PTR rbp-4 is "the 4 bytes at address rbp - 4": a local variable in the stack frame (lesson 2.02's frames, for real). if becomes compare and jump c-norun int sign(int x) { if (x 0) return 1; if (x < 0) return -1; return 0; } GCC with -O0 : nasm sign: push rbp mov rbp, rsp mov DWORD PTR rbp-4 , edi cmp DWORD PTR rbp-4 , 0 ; compare x with 0, setting the flags jle .L2 ; jump if less or equal: skip the first return mov eax, 1 jmp .L3 .L2: cmp DWORD PTR rbp-4 , 0 jns .L4 ; jump if not negative (the sign flag is clear) mov eax, -1 jmp .L3 .L4: mov eax, 0 .L3: pop rbp ret The processor has no if . It has flags , set by comparisons, and conditional jumps that go to a label depending on them. With -O1 , GCC gets rid of the jumps altogether: nasm sign: mov eax, edi sar eax, 31 ; shift the sign bit all the way down: -1 if x < 0, else 0 test edi, edi mov edx, 1 cmovg eax, edx ; "move if greater": 1 if x 0 ret sar copies the sign bit as it shifts, so a negative number becomes all 1 bits, which is -1. cmovg is a conditional move : no jump, so the processor never has to guess which way the code will go. Loops and arrays c-norun int sum(const int values, int count) { int total = 0; for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) total += values i ; return total; } Indexing becomes an address calculation, values + i 4 , folded into one memory operand. Step through a loop like the one GCC writes, as the CPU runs it: demo-asm title: sum(values, 3) with values = {5, 7, 9} init: rdi=0x2000, esi=3, mem@0x2000=5 7 9 xor eax, eax test esi, esi jle done xor edx, edx top: add eax, dword ptr rdi+rdx 4 inc edx cmp edx, esi jl top done: ret rdi+rdx 4 is values i : base address plus index times the size of an int . That is pointer arithmetic (lesson 3.02), done in one instruction by the hardware. What the optimiser does At -O2 and -O3 GCC also: - keeps variables in registers instead of memory - inlines small functions, pasting their bodies in place of the call - replaces multiplications by shifts and adds ( x 9 becomes lea eax, rdi+rdi 8 ) - unrolls and vectorises loops, adding 4 or 8 values per instruction with SIMD registers - deletes code whose result is never used This is why -O2 C is so fast, and also why undefined behaviour (lesson 6.02) gets "optimised" in surprising ways. The other way round Assembly to machine code is a simple one-to-one translation, done by the assembler : add edi, esi is the two bytes 01 f7 . The Fundamentals course shows how those bytes drive the circuits; the Assembly course has you write the instructions yourself. Check yourself quiz ? Where does the first int argument arrive on x86-64 Linux? - On the stack + In edi (the low half of rdi) - In eax Then rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9. ? What does values i become for an int array? - A function call - A loop over the array + A memory access at values + i 4 rdi+rdx 4 in Intel syntax. ? How does an if statement appear in assembly? - An if instruction + A comparison that sets flags, then a conditional jump - A call to a library function The processor has jumps, not structured statements. ? What does inlining mean? - Putting all the code on one line + Copying a function's body in place of the call - Writing assembly inside C code Inlining removes the call, which saves its cost and opens more optimisations.

title: 6.04  The Standard Library Tour
body:
The C standard library is small but covers the basics - input and output, strings, memory, maths, time, random numbers, sorting, characters and errors. Knowing what is there saves rewriting it. Beyond it, POSIX adds the operating system's services, and C23 brings a few modern conveniences. The headers Header Gives --- --- stdio.h printf , scanf , fgets , files, snprintf , perror stdlib.h malloc , free , qsort , bsearch , strtol , strtod , rand , exit , abs , getenv string.h strlen , strcmp , strchr , strstr , memcpy , memmove , memset , memcmp , strerror ctype.h isalpha , isdigit , isspace , toupper , tolower math.h sqrt , pow , sin , cos , floor , ceil , round , fabs , hypot , NAN , INFINITY stdint.h , inttypes.h exact-width integers and their formats stdbool.h , stddef.h bool ; size_t , NULL , offsetof limits.h , float.h INT_MAX , LLONG_MIN , DBL_EPSILON time.h time , clock , localtime , strftime assert.h , errno.h assert ; errno and its codes stdarg.h functions like printf that take any number of arguments On Linux, GCC needs -lm to link the maths library; the website adds it for you. memmove, for overlapping memory memcpy must not be used when the source and destination overlap; memmove handles that correctly: c include <stdio.h include <string.h int main(void) { char text = "abcdef"; memmove(text + 2, text, 4); // shift right by 2, overlapping printf("%s
", text); // ababcd return 0; } Time c include <stdio.h include <time.h int main(void) { time_t now = time(NULL); // seconds since 1 January 1970 (UTC) struct tm utc = gmtime(&now); char text 64 ; strftime(text, sizeof text, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S UTC", utc); printf("%s
", text); clock_t start = clock(); // processor time used so far volatile double x = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 10000000; i++) x += i 0.5; printf("the loop took %.3f s of processor time
", (double)(clock() - start) / CLOCKS_PER_SEC); return 0; } volatile tells the compiler the variable may change in ways it cannot see, so the loop is not optimised away. Random numbers rand() returns a number from 0 to RAND_MAX ; srand(seed) chooses where the sequence starts. The same seed always gives the same sequence, which is useful for tests and replays: c include <stdio.h include <stdlib.h int roll(void) { return rand() % 6 + 1; // 1 to 6 (very slightly uneven, fine for games) } int main(void) { srand(42); // srand((unsigned)time(NULL)) for different runs for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) printf("%d ", roll()); printf("
"); return 0; } rand is fine for games and simulations, never for passwords or keys: use the operating system's secure generator ( getrandom on Linux, arc4random on BSD and Mac, BCryptGenRandom on Windows). Variable arguments printf takes any number of arguments through stdarg.h . Your own functions can too: c include <stdarg.h include <stdio.h int sum_ints(int count, ...) { va_list args; va_start(args, count); int total = 0; for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) total += va_arg(args, int); va_end(args); return total; } void log_message(const char level, const char format, ...) { va_list args; va_start(args, format); fprintf(stderr, " %s ", level); vfprintf(stderr, format, args); // the v versions take a va_list fprintf(stderr, "
"); va_end(args); } int main(void) { printf("%d
", sum_ints(4, 10, 20, 30, 40)); log_message("info", "loaded %d items in %.1f ms", 120, 3.5); return 0; } The function cannot know how many arguments it got or their types; the caller must say (here count , in printf the format string). Getting it wrong is undefined. Leaving the program return from main ends the program; so does exit(status) from anywhere, which still flushes and closes files. atexit(function) registers clean-up to run then. EXIT_SUCCESS and EXIT_FAILURE are the portable status codes. Beyond the standard - POSIX (Linux, Mac, BSD) adds the operating system's services: open , read , write , fork , exec , pthread_create for threads, sockets for networking, getline , strdup . - Windows has its own API ( CreateFile , CreateThread ) alongside the standard library. - C11 added threads.h and stdatomic.h ; C23 adds bool as a keyword, nullptr , typeof , constexpr , binary literals like 0b1010 , strdup and checked arithmetic. Check yourself quiz ? Which function copies memory correctly when the source and destination overlap? - memcpy + memmove - strcpy memcpy is allowed to assume they do not overlap. ? What does srand(42) followed by rand() calls give in every run? - A different sequence each time + The same sequence of numbers - Only the number 42 Seed with time(NULL) for different runs. ? Is rand() suitable for making passwords? - Yes, it is random enough - Only with a large seed + No: its sequence is predictable Use the operating system's secure random generator for anything secret. ? How does a variadic function know how many arguments it was given? - va_count returns the number + The caller tells it, such as with a count - It always gets exactly ten stdarg.h gives no way to ask; the caller passes a count, a sentinel or a format string.
