title: Common Errors
body: GCC's messages name the file, line and column: main.c:7:12: error: ... . Fix the first error first: later ones are often caused by it. Compiler errors Message Usual cause --- --- expected ';' before ... a missing semicolon at the end of the line before 'x' undeclared a misspelt name, a variable used outside its scope, or a missing include implicit declaration of function 'foo' no prototype before the call: include the header, or declare it higher up conflicting types for 'foo' the prototype and the definition disagree incompatible types when assigning assigning, say, a struct to an int, or an array to an array lvalue required as left operand of assignment assigning to something that is not a variable: 5 = x , a + b = c subscripted value is neither array nor pointer using on a plain number invalid type argument of unary ' ' dereferencing something that is not a pointer request for member 'x' in something not a structure . on a pointer (use - ), or a typo too few arguments to function the call does not match the declaration expected declaration or statement at end of input a missing closing } missing terminating " character a string not closed on the same line Warnings worth fixing Warning Means --- --- 'x' is used uninitialized reading a local before giving it a value: garbage format '%d' expects argument of type 'int', but argument 2 has type 'double' the printf letter does not match the value suggest parentheses around assignment used as truth value if (x = 5) : you meant == comparison of integer expressions of different signedness int compared with size_t ; negative numbers break it control reaches end of non-void function a path that returns no value function returns address of local variable a dangling pointer passing argument 1 of 'f' discards 'const' qualifier handing read-only data to a function that may change it unused variable 'x' leftover code, or a typo using another name this statement may fall through a case without break array subscript N is above array bounds an index past the end that the compiler could see Linker errors Message Means --- --- undefined reference to 'foo' declared but never defined, or the file defining it was not built in undefined reference to 'sqrt' the maths library is missing: add -lm multiple definition of 'x' a variable or function defined in a header included by two files: declare it extern there undefined reference to 'main' no main function, or it is misspelt When it runs What you see Usual cause --- --- Segmentation fault (exit code 139) following NULL or a garbage pointer, an index far out of range, or a stack overflow from endless recursion Floating point exception (exit code 136) integer division or remainder by zero Aborted (exit code 134) a failed assert , a double free, or heap corruption detected by free strange characters after a string a missing '\0' terminator a loop that never ends the condition never becomes false, or scanf keeps failing on the same bad input numbers suddenly negative or tiny integer overflow: use a bigger type or check first heap-buffer-overflow , heap-use-after-free (Memory checks on) exactly what they say; the report gives the line runtime error: signed integer overflow (Memory checks on) undefined behaviour caught by the sanitizer

title: Glossary
body: The terms from the course, in alphabetical order. The lesson that introduces each one is in brackets. Term Meaning --- --- _Generic Chooses an expression by the type of another, at compile time. (7.03) _Static_assert A condition checked by the compiler; false stops the build. (7.03) Address The number of a byte in memory. &x gives the address of x . (3.01) AddressSanitizer A compiler option ( -fsanitize=address ) that checks every memory access and reports the first bad one. On the website: Memory checks. (4.06) Alignment Placing a value at an address that is a multiple of its size, which the processor reads fastest. (4.03) Amortised Averaged over many operations: a growing array's push is constant time on average even though it sometimes copies. (4.02) Anonymous member A struct or union inside another with no name, whose fields are reached directly. (7.03) argc / argv The number of command-line words and the array of them, passed to main . (3.05) Array A fixed number of values of one type, side by side in memory. (2.04) assert A check that stops the program with a message if a condition is false. (5.04) Atomic A variable whose operations happen as one indivisible step, from <stdatomic.h . (7.05) Big-endian Storing the most significant byte of a number first. (5.02) Bit field A struct member with a width in bits: unsigned flag : 1; . (7.02) Bitwise operator & \ ^ ~ << : operators that work on each bit separately. (5.01) Bucket One slot of a hash table, holding the entries whose hash leads there. (6.05) Buffer overflow Writing past the end of an array into whatever memory follows. (2.04) C23 The 2023 C standard: bool and nullptr keywords, typeof , constexpr , embed and more. (7.03) Callback A function passed to another function to be called by it. (6.01) calloc Allocates heap memory set to zero. (4.01) Capacity How many elements a growing array has room for, as opposed to its length. (4.02) Cast Converting a value to another type explicitly: (double)n . (1.04) Collision Two keys landing in the same bucket of a hash table. (6.05) Comparison function A function returning negative, zero or positive, used by qsort and bsearch (8.02) Compiler The program that turns C source into machine code. (1.01) Compound literal An unnamed object written (type){ ... } where a value is needed. (7.03) Condition variable cnd_t : lets a thread sleep until another signals a change. (7.05) const Marks something read-only; const T p cannot change what it points at. (3.04) Dangling pointer A pointer to memory that has been freed or to a local that no longer exists. (3.03) Declaration Tells the compiler a name and its type: a prototype or an extern variable. (2.02) Default argument promotions Extra arguments are widened: char and short to int , float to double . (7.01) Definition Creates the thing itself: a function's body or a variable's storage. Exactly one per program. (5.05) Dereference Following a pointer to the value it points at: p . (3.01) Designated initializer An initializer that names its fields or positions: { .width = 10, 3 = 7 } . (7.03) Double free Freeing the same heap block twice. (4.01) Element size The number of bytes of one element, passed with a void pointer so generic code can step through an array (8.02) enum A type whose values are named integer constants. (4.04) EOF The value input functions return at the end of the input. (2.01) errno A variable library functions set to an error code when they fail. (5.03) Exit code The number main returns: 0 for success. (1.01) extern Declares a variable defined in another file. (5.05) FILE The type of an open stream: a file, or stdin , stdout , stderr . (5.03) Fisher-Yates shuffle The fair way to shuffle: from the end, swap each element with a random one at or before it (8.06) Flexible array member A last struct member written type name ; , sized when the struct is allocated. (7.02) Function pointer A variable holding the address of a function, which can be called through it. (6.01) goto cleanup The idiom of jumping to shared cleanup labels at the end of a function on failure. (7.04) Hash function Turns a key into a number used to pick a bucket. (6.05) Hash table A structure that finds values by key in about constant time. (6.05) Header file A .h file of declarations that other files include . (5.05) Heap Memory allocated with malloc that lasts until free . (4.01) Include guard ifndef / define / endif around a header so it only counts once. (5.04) Inlining The optimiser pasting a function's body where it is called. (6.03) Integer promotion Small integer types such as char and short becoming int before arithmetic (8.05) Linked list A chain of nodes, each pointing to the next. (4.05) Linker Joins object files and libraries into a program, matching calls to definitions. (1.01, 5.05) Little-endian Storing the least significant byte first, as x86 and ARM do. (5.02) Load factor Entries divided by buckets in a hash table. (6.05) Macro A define name the preprocessor replaces with text, possibly with parameters. (5.04) malloc / free Allocate and release heap memory. (4.01) Mask A number with 1 bits where you want to test, set or clear. (5.01) Memory leak Heap memory that is never freed. (4.01) mktime Turns a local struct tm into time_t and normalises out-of-range fields (8.03) Modulo bias The unfairness of rand() % n when the generator's range is not a multiple of n (8.06) Mutex mtx_t : lets one thread at a time into a critical section. (7.05) NULL The pointer that points at nothing. (3.01) Object file A .o file: one compiled source file, not yet linked. (5.05) Off-by-one A loop or index that goes one too far or stops one short. (2.01) offsetof A macro giving a field's distance in bytes from the start of its struct. (7.02) Optimiser The part of the compiler that makes code faster at -O2 . (6.03) Ownership Which part of a program must free a block of memory; a function that returns new memory gives it to the caller (8.01) Padding Unused bytes the compiler puts in a struct to keep fields aligned. (4.03) Pointer A variable holding an address. (3.01) Pointer arithmetic Adding to a pointer moves it by whole elements: p + 1 is the next one. (3.02) Preprocessor The first build stage, which handles lines starting with . (5.04) Prototype A function's first line ending in a semicolon, declaring it. (2.02) qsort The standard library's sort, given a comparison function. (6.01) realloc Resizes a heap block, moving it if needed. (4.02) Recursion A function calling itself. (2.02) Return code A function's return value used to report success or the kind of failure. (7.04) Scope Where in the code a name can be used. (2.03) Seed The starting value of a random number generator; the same seed gives the same sequence (8.06) Segmentation fault The crash when a program touches memory it does not own. (3.01) Sentinel A special last argument, such as NULL , that marks the end of a variadic list. (7.01) setjmp and longjmp Save a point of execution and jump back to it from deeper calls, skipping everything between. (7.04) Shadowing A local hiding an outer variable of the same name. (2.03) Short-circuit && and \ \ stopping as soon as the answer is known. (1.05) size_t The unsigned type for sizes and counts, printed with %zu . (2.04) sizeof Gives the size of a type or object in bytes. (1.02) Stack frame The memory a function call gets for its parameters and locals. (2.02) Standard error The output stream for messages and errors, kept apart from the results on standard output (8.04) static On a local: keeps its value between calls. On a global or function: private to its file. (2.03) stdint.h The header with exact-width types like uint8_t and int64_t . (5.02) strftime Formats a struct tm as text by a pattern such as %Y-%m-%d (8.03) String An array of char ending in '\0' . (2.05) String buffer A growable piece of text kept with its length and capacity, grown with realloc (8.01) struct A type grouping named fields. (4.03) struct tm A time broken into year, month, day, hour, minute and second; tm_year counts from 1900 and tm_mon from 0 (8.03) Tagged union A union with an enum saying which member is in use. (4.04) Terminator The zero byte '\0' that ends a string. (2.05) thrd_create Starts a C11 thread running a function int f(void ) . (7.05) ThreadSanitizer A compiler option ( -fsanitize=thread ) that reports data races while the program runs. (7.05) time_t A point in time as one number, usually seconds since 1970 UTC (8.03) typedef Gives a type another name. (4.04) Undefined behaviour Code the C standard sets no rules for, such as signed overflow; anything may happen. (6.02) union A type whose members share the same memory. (4.04) Use after free Using heap memory after it was freed. (4.01) Usual arithmetic conversions The rules that bring both operands to one type; with signed and unsigned of the same size, the signed one becomes unsigned (8.05) va_list The type that walks a variadic function's extra arguments with va_start , va_arg and va_end . (7.01) Valgrind A Linux tool that checks an unchanged program's memory use. (4.06) Variadic function A function whose parameter list ends in ... , taking any number of extra arguments. (7.01) void \ A pointer to anything, which must be converted before use. (3.01) vsnprintf The va_list form of snprintf; with a size of 0 it measures how long the output would be (8.01) Warning A compiler message about legal but suspicious code. Treat them as errors. (1.01)

title: 1.01  How C++ Works
body: You write text (source code). A compiler translates it into machine code . A linker joins the pieces into one program that your computer runs directly. The big picture A computer's processor (the CPU) understands only numbers. Nobody wants to write programs as long lists of numbers, so we write them in a language people can read, and a tool translates that into the numbers the processor needs. C++ is one of those languages. The translating happens before the program runs. Step What it does Think of it as --- --- --- You write Type instructions into a text file ending in .cpp Writing a recipe Compiler Checks the file follows the rules of C++ and translates it Translating the recipe into the cook's language Linker Joins your translated code with ready-made library code Binding the chapters into one book Run The finished program starts Cooking You will hear three words constantly. They are worth learning now: - Source code : the text you write. - Build (or compile ): turn source code into a program. This is both steps above, compiler then linker. - Run : start the program that was built. Why translate ahead of time? Some languages, such as Python, are translated a line at a time while the program runs. C++ does all of that work once, in advance. !info The trade You get speed. Nothing stands between your program and the processor. That is why games, web browsers, operating systems and trading systems are written in C++. You pay with strictness. The compiler refuses to build anything it cannot make sense of. That feels harsh in week one. Later you will be glad of it, because every mistake it catches is one that never reaches your running program. Three kinds of mistakes Every programmer makes all three, every day. Knowing which kind you are looking at tells you where to look. When it shows up Name Example Who notices --- --- --- --- While building Compile error You forgot a ; The compiler. Nothing is built. While building Linker error You promised a function existed but never wrote it The linker. Nothing is built. While running Logic error (a bug ) It builds and runs, but prints the wrong total Only you !tip Errors are not a judgement A compile error is the compiler saying "I got stuck here". It gives you the line number. Read it, fix it, build again. Professionals do this hundreds of times a day. Where C++ came from C++ gets a new version every three years, named after the year. This course teaches modern C++ (C++20, with the useful parts of C++23). You do not need to know the history yet; the full story is in 13.10 C++ Standards Timeline and Where to Go Next . Check yourself quiz ? What is the job of the compiler? - It runs your program one line at a time as you type it - It finds the logic mistakes in what your program does + It checks your source code follows the rules of C++ and translates it into machine code - It stores your source code so the computer can read it later The compiler checks the rules and translates source code into machine code; it cannot tell whether your program does what you meant. ? Your code builds fine but prints 5 when it should print 6. What kind of mistake is that? + A logic error - A compile error - A syntax error - A linker error The build succeeded, so the code is valid C++. The compiler cannot know what you meant , so a wrong result is a logic error . ? What is the difference between building and running? - Building runs the program once to test it; running runs it for real - They are two names for the same step - Running turns source code into a program; building starts it + Building turns your source code into a program; running starts that program Building produces the program from your source code and running starts it. If the build fails, there is nothing to run.

title: 1.02  Setup and Your First Program
body:
There is nothing to install. Type the program, press Run , read what comes back. Then break it on purpose to see what errors look like. You are already set up Xenon has an editor and a real C++ compiler built in. Anywhere you see code with a Run button, you can change it and run it. You want to Do this --- --- Run the code in the editor Run , or Ctrl + Enter Have your answer to a task checked Check Try something of your own Open the Playground in the sidebar See what the compiler complained about The Problems tab under the editor Hello, World! This is the traditional first program. It puts one line of text on the screen. Press Run . cpp include <iostream int main() { std::cout << "Hello, World!
"; return 0; } Output: Hello, World! Do not worry about what each line means yet. That is the next lesson. For now, notice two things: - The text between the double quotes is what appears on the screen. - The 
 at the end did not appear. It means "start a new line". The loop you will repeat for the rest of your life Nobody writes a program correctly in one go. Programming is this loop: write a little, run it, fix it, repeat. Small steps make it fast, because when something breaks you know it was the last thing you changed. Break it on purpose The quickest way to stop fearing error messages is to cause a few. In the program above: 1. Delete the ; at the end of the std::cout line and press Run . 2. Open the Problems tab. It names the line and explains the error in plain English. 3. Put the ; back and run again. Now try misspelling cout as cuot , and deleting the last } . !warning Always read the first error first One mistake can confuse the compiler so badly that it reports twenty errors below it. Fix the top one, build again, and most of the rest usually vanish. !tip Type the code, do not paste it Typing is slower, and that is the point. Your fingers learn where the brackets and semicolons go, and you make the small mistakes now, while they are cheap. Later: on your own computer Xenon is all you need for this course. When you start building bigger projects of your own, you will want a full development environment. On Windows the usual choice is Visual Studio Community (free) with the "Desktop development with C++" option. There is no hurry. Check yourself quiz ? You get 14 errors after changing one line. Where do you start? - With the last one, since it is the most recent + With the first one; later errors often follow from it - With whichever error is easiest to fix - With the line you changed, ignoring the messages Start with the first error. Later errors are often just the compiler being confused by the first one, and they can vanish once it is fixed. ? What does 
 do inside the quotes? - It prints a backslash followed by the letter n - It adds a space between two words + It ends the line, so the next output starts on a new line - It ends the program after the text is printed 
 is the newline character: whatever is printed next starts on a new line. It is not printed as the two characters \ and n . ? Why write and run in small steps? - Because the compiler can only build a few lines at a time - Because small programs run faster than big ones - Because each run must be shorter than the last + When something breaks, you know the cause is the small thing you just changed Small steps keep the search area tiny: if it worked a minute ago and fails now, the cause is the change you just made.

title: 1.03  Anatomy of a Program
body:
A program is a list of statements inside a function called main . They run from top to bottom. Each statement ends with ; . Comments are notes for humans. Hello World, line by line cpp include <iostream // 1. bring in the tools for printing int main() // 2. the program starts here { // 3. main's instructions begin std::cout << "Hi!
"; // 4. one instruction: print Hi! return 0; // 5. finish, and report "all went well" } // 6. main's instructions end Piece What it means --- --- include <iostream "I want to use the input/output tools." Without it, std::cout does not exist. int main() The starting point. Every program has exactly one main . { and } Braces mark where a group of instructions begins and ends. std::cout << "Hi!
"; Send the text Hi! to the screen. std:: "From the standard library", the toolbox that comes with C++. ; The end of an instruction, like a full stop ends a sentence. return 0; End main . 0 tells the operating system that nothing went wrong. Two words for what you just read: - A statement is one complete instruction. It ends with ; . - A function is a named group of statements. main is the one that runs first. Statements run top to bottom cpp include <iostream int main() { std::cout << "One
"; std::cout << "Two
"; std::cout << "Three
"; return 0; } One Two Three The computer does one statement, then the next, and never skips ahead. When a program does something unexpected, walking through it one line at a time, in order, is how you find out why. Comments A comment is a note for whoever reads the code. The compiler ignores it completely. cpp // Everything after two slashes, to the end of the line, is a comment. / A comment between these markers can run over several lines. / !tip Say why, not what Weak: lives = lives + 1; // add one to lives . The code already says that. Useful: lives = lives + 1; // bonus life every 10,000 points . That is something the code cannot tell you. Putting // in front of a line switches it off without deleting it. This is called commenting out , and it is handy when you are hunting for a problem. Spacing is for people The compiler does not care about extra spaces or blank lines. To the compiler, these are identical: cpp std::cout<<"Hi"; std::cout << "Hi" ; People care a great deal. Indent the statements inside braces by four spaces, as every example here does, and your code will show its own structure. Four mistakes everybody makes Mistake What the compiler says --- --- Forgetting a ; expected ';' (often reported on the next line) Writing Main or MAIN No starting point found. C++ is case-sensitive : capitals matter. Leaving out include <iostream 'cout' is not a member of 'std' A { without its } An error at the very end of the file Check yourself quiz ? Where does every C++ program start running? + At the first statement inside main - At the first line of the file - At the first include line - At the first std::cout in the file Every program starts at the first statement inside main , wherever main is in the file. Lines like include are handled before the program is even built. ? Is int Main() a valid starting point? - Yes, the compiler ignores capital letters in names - Yes, as long as there is only one function called that + No, C++ is case-sensitive, so Main and main are different names C++ is case-sensitive. Main is just another function; the program needs one called exactly main . ? What does std:: in front of cout mean? - That cout is a variable you have to create first + That cout comes from the standard library supplied with C++ - That cout prints to a file instead of the screen - That cout is a special keyword of the language std:: says the name comes from the standard library , the toolbox supplied with C++. cout is not a keyword. ? The compiler reports a missing ; on line 8, but line 8 looks fine. Where do you look? - At the last line of the program - At line 9, because the compiler counts from zero + At the end of line 7 - At the include lines at the top The compiler only notices the ; is missing when it reaches the next thing, so the real mistake is usually at the end of the line before.

title: 1.04  Variables and Initialization
body: A variable is a named box in memory that holds one value of one type . Always give it a starting value: int age{ 25 }; A variable is a labelled box Programs need to remember things: a score, a name, a price. A variable is a piece of the computer's memory with a name on it, so you can put a value in and look at it later. int age{ 25 }; double price{ 9.99 }; char grade{ 'A' }; ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ │ 25 │ │ 9.99 │ │ 'A' │ └──────────────┘ └──────────────┘ └──────────────┘ age price grade (an int) (a double) (a char) Creating one takes three parts: cpp int age{ 25 }; Part Here Meaning --- --- --- Type int What kind of value the box can hold Name age What you call it in the rest of the program Starting value { 25 } What is in the box to begin with Five types to start with Type Holds Examples --- --- --- int whole numbers 42 , -7 , 0 double numbers with a decimal point 3.14 , -0.5 char one single character, in single quotes 'x' , '7' bool a yes/no answer true , false std::string text, in double quotes (needs include <string ) "Hello" The type is fixed for the life of the variable. An int box can never hold text. Always give a starting value cpp int a{ 5 }; // a holds 5 int b{}; // empty braces: b holds 0 int c; // DANGER: c holds whatever happened to be in that memory !danger Never leave a variable uninitialized int c; reserves a box but puts nothing in it. The box contains leftover junk from whatever used that memory before. Your program might print 0, or 32767, or behave differently every time you run it. Always write the braces. You will see two other ways to give a starting value in other people's code. They work, but braces are safer: cpp int x = 4.7; // builds, and quietly throws away the .7 (x is 4) int y{ 4.7 }; // refuses to build: "narrowing conversion". The mistake is caught. Giving a variable its first value is called initialization . Changing the value later cpp include <iostream int main() { int score{ 10 }; // create the box, holding 10 score = 25; // replace the contents with 25 score = score + 5; // read 25, add 5, store 30 std::cout << score << '\n'; return 0; } Putting a new value into an existing variable is called assignment . The old value is gone. !note = does not mean "equals" In C++, = means "work out the right-hand side, then store it in the variable on the left" . That is why score = score + 5 makes sense: read the old score, add 5, store the result back. Choosing names Allowed Not allowed --- --- playerHealth , max_speed , count2 2count (starts with a digit) letters, digits and _ my-var , my var (hyphen, space) words C++ already uses: int , return , class A good name says what is in the box. secondsElapsed tells the reader something; s does not. This course uses camelCase : lower-case first word, a capital at the start of each later word. Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference between initialization and assignment? - They are two names for the same thing - Initialization replaces a value; assignment gives the first one + Initialization gives the first value when a variable is created; assignment replaces an existing value - Initialization only works with numbers; assignment works with any type Initialization happens at the moment a variable is created. Assignment later replaces the value of a variable that already exists. ? What does int n{}; contain? - Whatever garbage value was left in memory + 0 - 1 - Nothing; it is a compile error Empty braces mean "the zero value for this type", so n holds 0 . Leaving out the braces entirely ( int n; ) is what gives an unpredictable value. ? Why does this course write int x{ 5 }; instead of int x = 5; ? - Braces make the program run faster - = cannot be used to give a variable its first value - Braces let an int hold decimals as well as whole numbers + Braces refuse to silently lose information With braces, int x{ 4.7 }; is an error, while int x = 4.7; quietly stores 4. Both forms are valid for 5 . ? What does total = total + 1; do? - It is an error, because total cannot equal itself plus one - It checks whether total is equal to total + 1 + It reads total , adds 1, and stores the result back in total - It creates a second variable called total = is assignment, not a statement of equality: the right side is worked out first, then the result is stored in total .

title: 1.05  Input and Output
body:
std::cout << sends values out to the screen. std::cin brings values in from the keyboard. The arrows point the way the data moves. Follow the arrows A program that cannot show anything or ask anything is not much use. C++ gives you two tools for talking to the person at the keyboard. You write Read it as Data moves --- --- --- std::cout << x; "send x to the screen" from x to the screen std::cin x; "read from the keyboard into x" from the keyboard to x If you ever forget which arrows go with which, look at where they point. Printing with std::cout cpp include <iostream int main() { int apples{ 5 }; std::cout << "I have " << apples << " apples
"; std::cout << "Line 1
" << "Line 2
"; return 0; } I have 5 apples Line 1 Line 2 Three things to notice: - You can chain several << in one statement. Each piece is printed in order. - Text in quotes is printed exactly as written. A variable name without quotes prints the value inside the variable. - std::cout adds nothing for you. No spaces, no new lines. If you want a space between two things, put it inside the quotes. Special characters A backslash inside quotes starts a code for a character you cannot simply type. Code What it prints --- --- 
 the start of a new line 	 a tab (a jump to the next column) " a double quote \ one backslash !note You will also see std::endl std::cout << "Hi" << std::endl; also ends the line. It does a little extra work each time, so this course uses 
 , which is the normal choice. Reading with std::cin cpp include <iostream int main() { std::cout << "Enter your age: "; int age{}; std::cin age; std::cout << "In 10 years you will be " << age + 10 << '
'; return 0; } Enter your age: 21 In 10 years you will be 31 The steps are always the same: The program stops at std::cin and waits until the person types something and presses Enter. Reading two values cpp int width{}; int height{}; std::cin width height; The person can type 3 7 on one line, or 3 , Enter, 7 , Enter. std::cin skips spaces and new lines to find the next value. Reading a whole line of text std::cin stops at the first space. That is fine for a number, but wrong for a full name. cpp include <iostream include <string int main() { std::cout << "Your full name: "; std::string name{}; std::getline(std::cin std::ws, name); std::cout << "Hello, " << name << "!
"; return 0; } Typed std::cin name stores std::getline(std::cin std::ws, name) stores --- --- --- Ada Lovelace Ada Ada Lovelace For now, treat std::getline(std::cin std::ws, name) as the recipe for "read the rest of the line". The std::ws part skips any leftover Enter from an earlier answer. Two mistakes to expect Mistake What happens --- --- Arrows the wrong way: std::cin << x A long, confusing compile error. Check the arrows first. Typing letters when the program wants a number The read fails and the variable is left at 0. You will learn to handle this in 3.07 Input Validation and assert . Check yourself quiz ? Which way do the arrows point for input? - std::cin << variable; , towards the keyboard + std::cin variable; , from the keyboard into the variable - variable std::cin; , from the variable to the keyboard - Either way; the direction does not matter For input the data moves from std::cin into the variable, so the arrows point at the variable: std::cin variable; . ? The person types John Smith . What does std::cin name; store? - John Smith - Smith + John - Nothing, because the input contains a space Reading with stops at the first space, so name gets only John . Smith is left waiting for the next read. ? What is the difference between std::cout << "age"; and std::cout << age; ? - There is none; both print the value of age - The first prints the value; the second prints the word age + The first prints the word age ; the second prints the value stored in age Text in quotes is printed exactly as written. Without quotes, age is the name of a variable, so its value is printed. ? Why does std::cout << "Hello" << "World"; print HelloWorld ? - Each << removes the spaces from the text - std::cout can only print one word at a time - The second << overwrites the first word + std::cout adds no spaces of its own std::cout prints exactly what you give it and adds nothing between items. Put the space inside the quotes: "Hello " .

title: 1.06  Operators and Expressions Basics
body: An expression is anything that works out to a value, such as 2 + 3 or price count . Operators are the symbols that do the work. One surprise: with whole numbers, 7 / 2 is 3 . Doing arithmetic The symbols + , - , , / and % are called operators . Something that works out to a value, like 7 + 2 , is called an expression . Operator Meaning Example Result --- --- --- --- + add 7 + 2 9 - subtract 7 - 2 5 multiply 7 2 14 / divide 7 / 2 3 (see below) % remainder 7 % 2 1 You can use an expression anywhere a value is expected: cpp include <iostream int main() { int price{ 4 }; int count{ 3 }; int total{ price count }; // store the result std::cout << total << '\n'; // 12 std::cout << total + 10 << '\n'; // 22, worked out and printed directly return 0; } Dividing whole numbers throws away the decimals This is the one that catches everybody. 7 / 2 is 3.5 in maths but C++ gives 3 9 / 10 is 0.9 in maths but C++ gives 0 When both numbers are whole numbers ( int ), the answer is a whole number too. The part after the decimal point is cut off. It is not rounded. If at least one side is a decimal number, you get a decimal answer: Expression Result Why --- --- --- 7 / 2 3 both whole 7.0 / 2 3.5 one side is a decimal 7 / 2.0 3.5 one side is a decimal !warning An average that comes out wrong int total{ 7 }; int count{ 2 }; then total / count is 3 , not 3.5 . To get the real answer from two int variables you convert one first. That is covered in 2.05 Type Conversion and static_cast . The remainder operator % % gives what is left over after dividing. Share 7 biscuits between 2 people: 7 biscuits, 2 people each person gets 7 / 2 = 3 left on the plate 7 % 2 = 1 It looks minor, and it turns up everywhere: Question Expression --- --- Is n even? n % 2 is 0 What is the last digit of 1234? 1234 % 10 is 4 What is 1234 without its last digit? 1234 / 10 is 123 90 seconds is how many minutes and seconds? 90 / 60 is 1 , 90 % 60 is 30 Which part is worked out first? The same order as in school maths: , / and % first, then + and - . Operators of equal rank go left to right. Brackets change the order: (2 + 3) 4 is 20 . !tip If you have to stop and think, add brackets Brackets cost nothing, and the next reader (often you, next week) will not have to stop and think either. Shortcuts for changing a variable Changing a variable based on its own value is so common that there are shorter ways to write it. Long form Short form Meaning --- --- --- x = x + 5; x += 5; add 5 to x x = x - 5; x -= 5; take 5 from x x = x 5; x = 5; multiply x by 5 x = x / 5; x /= 5; divide x by 5 x = x + 1; ++x; add 1 to x x = x - 1; --x; take 1 from x You will also see x++ . For now it does the same job as ++x . The small difference is explained in 2.08 Operators Deep Dive . Check yourself quiz ? What is 17 % 5 ? - 3 + 2 - 3.4 - 12 % gives the remainder: five goes into 17 three times (15), and 2 is left over. 3 is the result of 17 / 5 , not the remainder. ? What is 9 / 10 when both are int ? - 0.9 - 1 + 0 - 9 Dividing two int s cuts off the part after the decimal point. The real answer 0.9 becomes 0 ; it is not rounded up to 1. ? What does 2 + 3 2 work out to? - 10 - 12 - 7 + 8 Multiplication happens before addition: 3 2 is 6, then 2 + 6 is 8. Working left to right would wrongly give 10. ? score holds 10. What does it hold after score += 5; and then ++score; ? + 16 - 15 - 11 - 6 score += 5 makes it 15, and ++score adds 1 more, giving 16.

title: 1.07  Functions Basics
body:
A function is a named set of instructions you can use again and again. You hand it values ( arguments ), it does its work, and it can hand one value back (the return value ). A function is a machine Put values in, get a result out. You have already written one function, main . Now you will write your own. cpp include <iostream int add(int x, int y) { return x + y; } int main() { int sum{ add(3, 4) }; std::cout << sum << '
'; // 7 return 0; } The parts of a function what it its what it needs hands back name to be given │ │ │ int add (int x, int y) { return x + y; the body: what it does } Word Meaning In the example --- --- --- Return type The type of value the function hands back int Parameter A variable that receives a value when the function is used x and y Call Using the function add(3, 4) Argument A value you give in the call 3 and 4 Return value What comes back 7 What happens when you call it 1. main pauses at the call. 2. The arguments are copied into the parameters. 3. The function's body runs. 4. return sends a value back, and main carries on where it stopped. !info The function gets copies Because the arguments are copied, changing x inside add changes nothing in main . The two functions have separate boxes. (When you do want a function to change the caller's variable, you use a reference: 4.03 References .) Functions that hand nothing back Some functions just do something. Their return type is void , which means "nothing". cpp include <iostream void printBanner() { std::cout << "==========
"; std::cout << " MY APP 
"; std::cout << "==========
"; } int main() { printBanner(); printBanner(); // written once, used twice return 0; } Empty brackets mean the function needs no values. You still have to write the brackets when you call it. The compiler reads from the top A function has to be known before the line that calls it. The simplest way is to write your functions above main . The other way is to announce the function first and write it later. The announcement is called a declaration : cpp include <iostream int add(int x, int y); // declaration: "this function exists" int main() { std::cout << add(3, 4) << '
'; return 0; } int add(int x, int y) // definition: the actual instructions { return x + y; } Variables inside a function stay inside cpp void countCoins() { int coins{ 5 }; // created here } // gone here int main() { countCoins(); // coins does not exist in main. Using it here is a compile error. return 0; } A variable created inside a function is called a local variable . It belongs to that function alone. Two functions can each have a variable called total without affecting each other. Why bother? Reason What it means --- --- Reuse Write the instructions once, call them as often as you like Readability calculateTax(price) says what is happening without showing how Easier fixing A mistake lives in one place, so you fix it in one place Smaller problems A big task becomes several small ones you can solve one at a time !tip One function, one job If you cannot give a function a short, clear name, it is probably doing two jobs. Split it. Three mistakes to expect Mistake What happens --- --- No return in a function that promised a value The compiler warns you, and the program misbehaves Calling without brackets: printBanner; Nothing happens. The brackets are what make it a call. Writing one function inside another Not allowed. Each function sits on its own, outside the others. Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference between a parameter and an argument? - They are two names for the same thing - A parameter is the value given in the call; an argument is the variable in the definition + A parameter is the variable named in the definition; an argument is the value given in the call - A parameter is the function's result; an argument is its input A parameter is the variable in the function's definition. An argument is the value you pass when you call it, which the parameter starts with. ? A function changes its parameter. Does the caller's variable change? + No, the parameter is a copy - Yes, the parameter and the caller's variable are the same box - Yes, but only if the function returns it - Only if both variables have the same name The parameter is a copy of the argument, so changing it inside the function leaves the caller's variable alone, even if they share a name. ? What does void mean as a return type? - The function always returns 0 when it finishes - The function can return any type + It hands nothing back; you call it for what it does - The function takes no parameters void means no return value. A function with no parameters is written with empty brackets, which is a different thing. ? What is a declaration for? - It runs the function once, automatically, when the program starts + It tells the compiler the function exists, so it can be called earlier - It creates a copy of the function for each call - It hides the function from the rest of the file The compiler reads from the top. A declaration (the first line followed by ; ) tells it the function exists, so calls above the definition compile.

title: 1.08  Multiple Files and Headers
body: Real programs are split across files. A header ( .h ) says what exists . A source file ( .cpp ) says how it works . include the header wherever you need those functions. Why split a program up? A program in one file is fine at fifty lines. At five thousand it is a nightmare to find anything in. So programmers group related functions into their own files. That raises a problem you met in the last lesson: a function must be known before it is called. If add lives in another file, how does main.cpp know about it? The answer is a header file . Menu and kitchen Think of a restaurant. The menu lists what you can order. The kitchen is where the food is made. You only need the menu to order. File Contains Example --- --- --- mathx.h Declarations : the name of each function, what it needs and what it returns int add(int x, int y); mathx.cpp Definitions : the actual instructions int add(int x, int y) { return x + y; } main.cpp Code that uses the functions add(2, 3) mathx.h cpp pragma once int add(int x, int y); int multiply(int x, int y); mathx.cpp cpp include "mathx.h" int add(int x, int y) { return x + y; } int multiply(int x, int y) { return x y; } main.cpp cpp include <iostream include "mathx.h" int main() { std::cout << add(2, 3) << ' ' << multiply(2, 3) << '\n'; return 0; } In Xenon, tasks with several files show each file as a tab above the editor, and all of them are built together when you press Run . What include really does Nothing clever. It pastes the contents of the named file in at that spot, before the compiler starts. main.cpp as you wrote it main.cpp as the compiler sees it ┌──────────────────────────┐ ┌────────────────────────────┐ │ include "mathx.h" │ ───▶ │ int add(int x, int y); │ │ │ │ int multiply(int x, int y);│ │ int main() { ... } │ │ int main() { ... } │ └──────────────────────────┘ └────────────────────────────┘ Written as Used for --- --- include <iostream Headers that come with C++ include "mathx.h" Headers you wrote yourself How the pieces are joined Remember the compiler and the linker from the first lesson? This is where the linker earns its place. Each .cpp file is compiled separately . While compiling main.cpp , the compiler only has the declaration of add . It trusts that the real thing exists somewhere. The linker then checks that it does. !warning "Unresolved external symbol" This is the linker saying: "something calls add , but no file provides it." Either you declared a function and never wrote it, or its definition does not match the declaration exactly (a different name or different parameters). pragma once Put this as the first line of every header you write. It stops the header being pasted twice into the same file, which can cause "already defined" errors as programs grow. One rule to remember How many times? Where it goes --- --- --- Declaration ( int add(int x, int y); ) As often as you like The header Definition (the version with a body) Exactly once in the whole program A .cpp file If you put a function's body in a header, every file that includes it gets its own copy, and the linker complains that it has too many. Check yourself quiz ? What goes in a header file? - The main function + Declarations: the functions that exist, without their bodies - The full definitions of every function - Only include lines A header is the "menu": declarations of what exists. The bodies go in a .cpp file, which is compiled once. ? What is the difference between <iostream and "mathx.h" in an include ? - Angle brackets are for .h files; quotes are for files without an extension - There is none; both forms mean exactly the same + Angle brackets are for headers that come with C++; quotes are for your own files - Quotes include the file once; angle brackets include it every time Use <... for the standard headers that come with C++ and "..." for headers you wrote, which are looked for next to your code first. ? You get "unresolved external symbol add". Is that the compiler or the linker? - The compiler: add was never declared + The linker: no file provides the definition of add - The compiler: add has a typo in its body - Neither; it is a crash while the program runs The compiler was happy because it saw a declaration. The linker then could not find any file that defines add . ? What does include actually do? - It links a finished library into the program - It lets the compiler look up names in another file only when needed + It pastes the contents of the named file in at that point before compiling include is a plain copy and paste, done before the compiler proper sees the code.

title: 1.09  Debugging Basics
body: A bug is a place where what the program does differs from what you expected . Debugging is finding that place. Do it with a method: read the message, look at the values, narrow it down. Bugs are normal Every programmer writes bugs all day. What separates a beginner from an expert is not how few bugs they write. It is how quickly they find them. That is a skill, and it has a method. The step people skip is the fourth. If you change things until it seems to work without knowing why, the bug is usually still there. First, which kind of problem is it? What you see Kind Where to look --- --- --- It will not build Compile or linker error The Problems tab. Start with the first message. It builds, then stops with an error Crash The message in the console, and the last thing printed before it It runs and gives the wrong answer Logic error The values of your variables, step by step Reading a compiler message main.cpp(8,5): error C2146: missing ';' before identifier 'std' │ │ │ └── what the compiler got stuck on │ │ └── column │ └── line └── file Go to that line. If it looks fine, look at the line above it. A missing ; is only noticed when the compiler reaches the next thing. Technique 1: print the values When the answer is wrong, some variable holds a value you did not expect. So look. cpp include <iostream int main() { int price{ 4 }; int quantity{ 3 }; int total{ price + quantity }; std::cerr << "DEBUG total=" << total << '\n'; std::cout << "You owe " << total << '\n'; return 0; } std::cerr works like std::cout . It is meant for messages to the programmer, not for the program's real output. The DEBUG label makes these lines easy to spot and delete when you have finished. Here the debug line shows total=7 . You expected 12, so the mistake is on the line that calculates total . Technique 2: be the computer Go through the program one line at a time and write down what every variable holds. This is called tracing , and it is the most reliable debugging tool there is. cpp int a{ 4 }; int b{ 5 }; int c{ 6 }; int average{ a + b + c / 3 }; After the line a b c average --- --- --- --- --- int a{ 4 }; 4 int b{ 5 }; 4 5 int c{ 6 }; 4 5 6 int average{ ... }; 4 5 6 4 + 5 + (6 / 3) = 11 The trace shows the problem. Division happens before addition, so only c is divided. The fix is brackets: (a + b + c) / 3 . !tip Do what the code says, not what you meant The difficult part of tracing is being honest. Your eyes see what you intended to write. Follow each symbol exactly as it is written. Technique 3: cut the problem in half When you have no idea where the mistake is, print a value in the middle of the program. Each check halves the search. Even in a thousand lines you find the spot in about ten checks. Technique 4: explain it out loud Describe your code line by line to someone else, or to an object on your desk. Programmers call this rubber duck debugging . You will often stop mid-sentence because you have just heard yourself say something that is not true. Writing fewer bugs Habit Why it helps --- --- Run after every few lines A new problem must be in the lines you just wrote Read every warning A warning usually means "this is legal, and probably not what you meant" Give every variable a starting value Removes a whole family of unpredictable behaviour Keep functions small A small piece is easy to check on its own Later: a debugger Professional tools such as Visual Studio include a debugger . It pauses a running program on any line you choose, shows every variable, and lets you move forward one line at a time. It automates the tracing you just did by hand. Once you know how to trace, a debugger takes minutes to learn. Check yourself quiz ? A program builds and runs but gives the wrong answer. What kind of error is it, and what do you do? - A compile error; read the first compiler message - A linker error; check that every function has a definition + A logic error; check the variables' values until you find the first one that is wrong - A logic error; rewrite the program from scratch It built and ran, so it is a logic error . Print the values or trace by hand until you find the first one that is not what you expected. ? The compiler reports an error on a line that looks correct. Where do you look next? + The line above it - The last line of the file - The first line of the file - The line below it A missing ; or bracket is reported where the compiler notices it, which is often one line after the real mistake. ? Why print a value in the middle of the program first? - Because printing slows the program down, which reveals the bug - Because the middle of a program is where bugs usually are + It tells you which half the mistake is in, so each check halves the search - Because the compiler only checks the middle of the program Checking the middle tells you whether the mistake is before or after that point. Each check cuts the search area in half. ? What is tracing? - Letting the compiler list every line it compiled + Going through the code line by line, noting what each variable holds after each line - Printing every variable once at the end of the program - Copying the program into a new file to see if it still fails Tracing is "being the computer": you follow each line in order and write down every variable's value as it changes.

title: 1.10  Compiler Settings, Build Configurations and Undefined Behavior
match: 1.10 Compiler Settings, Build Configurations and Undefined Behavior
body: Turn compiler warnings up and read them. Build in Debug while you work and Release when you finish. And meet the most important phrase in C++: undefined behaviour . The compiler has settings So far you have pressed Run and let the compiler get on with it. It has a few settings that matter, and Xenon has already chosen sensible ones. This lesson explains what they are, so they are not a mystery when you set up your own tools one day. Warnings: the compiler's advice An error means "I cannot build this". A warning means "I can build this, but it looks like a mistake". cpp include <iostream int main() { int total{ 10 }; int count{ 3 }; int unused{ 5 }; std::cout << total / count << '\n'; return 0; } This builds and runs. With warnings turned up, the compiler also tells you that unused is never used. Perhaps you meant to use it and forgot. Error Warning --- --- --- Does the program build? No Yes Should you fix it? You have to Yes, nearly always !tip Treat warnings as errors Xenon compiles at a high warning level and shows warnings in the Problems tab. Some tasks are marked strict : they only pass when there are no warnings at all. That is how professional teams work, and it is a good habit to start now. Debug and Release The same source code can be built in two ways. Debug Release --- --- --- Speed Slower Often many times faster Extra checks for mistakes Yes No Use it when You are still working You are finished, or measuring speed In an optimised build the compiler rearranges your code to run faster while producing the same results. Xenon uses Debug unless you change it, because the extra checks catch mistakes. You can switch in Settings . Which version of C++? C++ is revised every three years, and a compiler has to be told which version to follow. Xenon uses the newest. If you copy code from an old tutorial and it looks different from what you learn here, a different version is usually the reason. Undefined behaviour This is the single most important idea in the lesson. Most languages stop you when you do something senseless. C++ often does not. For certain mistakes, the rules of the language simply do not say what happens. That is called undefined behaviour , usually shortened to UB . You have already met one example: cpp int score; // never given a value std::cout << score << '\n'; // undefined behaviour This might print 0. It might print 32767. It might print something different on another computer or after an unrelated change. All of those are "allowed", because the rules promise nothing. !danger "It works on my machine" proves nothing Code with undefined behaviour can pass every test you run and still be wrong. The only safe approach is to know the rules and not break them. The Debug build's extra checks catch some cases for you, which is one more reason to use it. The ones you will meet in this course Mistake Covered in --- --- Reading a variable that was never given a value 1.04 Variables and Initialization A whole number growing too large for its type 2.02 Integers Dividing a whole number by zero 2.03 Floating Point Numbers Reading past the end of a list 5.01 std::vector Basics Following a pointer that points at nothing 4.04 Pointers Using something after it has been destroyed 7.02 new and delete — Dynamic Memory You do not need to understand these yet. Just notice the pattern: each is something a careful programmer checks for. The complete picture comes much later, in 13.01 Undefined Behavior and Object Lifetime . Words you cannot use as names C++ reserves about ninety words for itself, called keywords . You have used several already: int , double , return , void , true , false . You cannot name a variable or a function with one of them. The editor shows keywords in their own colour, so if a name you chose changes colour, pick another. Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference between an error and a warning? - A warning stops the build; an error only gives advice + An error stops the build; a warning flags a likely mistake - Errors are about spelling; warnings are about maths - There is none; both stop the build An error means the code is not valid C++ and the build stops. A warning lets the build finish but flags something that is probably a mistake. ? What does undefined behaviour mean? - The program will always crash straight away - The compiler refuses to build the program - The program prints a message saying what went wrong + The rules of C++ say nothing about what happens, so the result can be anything With undefined behaviour the program might work, give a wrong answer or crash, and it can change between runs or computers. The compiler often does not stop it. ? Why is "it printed the right answer" not proof that code is correct? - Because the screen might show the wrong output + Code with undefined behaviour can appear to work by luck - Because the compiler only checks the first run - Because Release builds always print different answers Undefined behaviour gives no guarantee. Code can look right today and fail on another run, computer or compiler setting. ? When would you use a Release build? - While writing and fixing the program, for its extra checks - Only when the Debug build will not compile + For the finished program, or when measuring how fast it runs - To get more warnings from the compiler Release is optimized for speed. While writing and fixing code, Debug is better because of its extra checks and easier debugging.

title: 2.01  Memory, Bits and Fundamental Types
body:
Memory is a long row of numbered bytes . A byte is 8 bits . A variable's type decides how many bytes it gets and what the bits in them mean. What the boxes are made of In Milestone 1 a variable was "a labelled box". Now look inside the box. Knowing what is in there explains why whole numbers have limits, why decimals are slightly inexact and why types matter at all. Bits and bytes A bit is a switch that is either 0 or 1 . Eight of them make a byte . Each bit is worth double the one to its right, and you add up the ones that are switched on: worth: 128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1 bits: 0 1 0 0 0 0 0 1 64 + 1 = 65 Every extra bit doubles how many different values you can store. Bits Different values --- --- 1 2 8 (one byte) 256 16 65,536 32 about 4.3 billion 64 about 18 billion billion Memory is a street of numbered houses Your computer's memory is a very long row of bytes. Each one has a number, called its address . address: 1000 1001 1002 1003 1004 1005 1006 1007 ┌──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┐ │ int score (4 bytes) │ char │ bool │ free ... │ └──────┴──────┴──────┴──────┴──────┴──────┴──────┴──────┘ A variable is a run of neighbouring bytes with a name on it. The type gives the bits a meaning Bits on their own mean nothing. The pattern 01000001 is the number 65 if you treat it as a whole number, and the letter A if you treat it as a character. That is the job of a type. It tells the compiler two things: how many bytes to reserve, and how to interpret what is in them. The fundamental types These are built into the language. Everything else in C++ is made from them. Kind Type Usual size Holds --- --- --- --- True or false bool 1 byte true , false Character char 1 byte one character Whole number short 2 bytes about ±32 thousand int 4 bytes about ±2.1 billion long long 8 bytes about ±9.2 billion billion Decimal number float 4 bytes about 7 significant digits double 8 bytes about 15 significant digits Nothing void none "no value" !tip Your defaults Use int for whole numbers and double for decimals unless you have a reason not to. The others exist for special cases, which the next lessons cover. Asking how big something is sizeof reports the size of a type, or of a variable, in bytes. cpp include <iostream int main() { std::cout << "bool: " << sizeof(bool) << " bytes
"; std::cout << "char: " << sizeof(char) << " bytes
"; std::cout << "int: " << sizeof(int) << " bytes
"; std::cout << "long long: " << sizeof(long long) << " bytes
"; std::cout << "double: " << sizeof(double) << " bytes
"; return 0; } !note Sizes are not identical everywhere The language only promises minimum sizes. An int is 4 bytes on every ordinary computer today, but long is 4 bytes on Windows and 8 on Linux and macOS. When the exact size matters, there are types with the size in their name, such as std::int32_t . They are in 2.02 Integers . Asking for the limits Fewer bytes means a smaller range. The header <limits tells you the exact ends of it. cpp include <iostream include <limits int main() { std::cout << std::numeric_limits<int ::max() << '
'; // 2147483647 std::cout << std::numeric_limits<int ::min() << '
'; // -2147483648 return 0; } Do not worry about the angle brackets yet. Read std::numeric_limits<int ::max() as "the largest int ". Check yourself quiz ? How many different values can one byte hold? - 8 - 255 + 256 - 16 A byte is eight bits, and each bit doubles the count: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 256. The largest unsigned value is 255, but 0 counts too. ? What two things does a type tell the compiler? + How many bytes to reserve, and how to interpret the bits stored in them - Which address to use, and how long the variable lives - The variable's name, and its starting value - Whether the value can change, and who may read it The same bits mean different things as an int , a char or a double . The type says how much memory to set aside and how to read it. ? Which types should you reach for by default? - long for whole numbers and float for decimals - short for whole numbers and float for decimals - unsigned int for whole numbers and double for decimals + int for whole numbers and double for decimals int and double are the everyday defaults. Pick another type only when you have a reason, such as needing a bigger range. ? Is sizeof(long) the same on every computer? - Yes, the standard fixes it at 4 bytes - Yes, the standard fixes it at 8 bytes + No: 4 bytes on Windows, 8 on most Linux and macOS The standard only sets minimum sizes, so long varies between platforms. Use the fixed-width types such as std::int64_t when the exact size matters.

title: 2.02  Integers
body: Integers hold whole numbers. Signed ones can be negative; unsigned ones cannot. Going past the limit is overflow : unsigned wraps round to the other end, and signed is undefined behaviour. Signed and unsigned An integer is a whole number. Every integer type comes in two versions. 8 bits, signed : -128 ────────── 0 ────────── 127 8 bits, unsigned : 0 ─────────────────────────── 255 Both have 256 values to spend. The signed version spends half of them below zero. The unsigned version starts at zero and reaches twice as high. cpp int temperature{ -5 }; // signed: this is the default unsigned int population{ 8000 }; // unsigned: never negative Overflow What happens when a number goes past the end of its range? Think of a car's mileage counter rolling from 99999 back to 00000. cpp include <iostream int main() { unsigned int u{ 0 }; u = u - 1; std::cout << u << '\n'; // 4294967295 return 0; } The two versions behave very differently here. What overflow does --- --- Unsigned Wraps round to the other end. Guaranteed, on every computer. Signed Undefined behaviour. Anything may happen. !danger Signed overflow is undefined behaviour int big{ 2147483647 }; ++big; has no defined result. In practice you often see a large negative number, but nothing promises that. If a value might pass two billion, use a bigger type. Why not use unsigned for anything that cannot be negative? It sounds sensible: a count is never negative, so make it unsigned. In practice this causes more bugs than it prevents. cpp include <iostream int main() { unsigned int items{ 3 }; int change{ -1 }; std::cout << (change < items) << '\n'; // prints 0, meaning false return 0; } When signed and unsigned meet, the signed value is converted to unsigned. So -1 becomes 4294967295, which is not less than 3. !tip The rule this course follows Use plain int for counts and arithmetic. Keep unsigned for working with individual bits ( 2.09 Bit Manipulation ). Integers with an exact size When you need a guaranteed size, include <cstdint gives you types with the number of bits in the name. Type Bits Range --- --- --- std::int8_t / std::uint8_t 8 -128 to 127 / 0 to 255 std::int16_t / std::uint16_t 16 about ±32 thousand / 0 to 65,535 std::int32_t / std::uint32_t 32 about ±2.1 billion / 0 to 4.2 billion std::int64_t / std::uint64_t 64 about ±9.2 billion billion One more turns up constantly: std::size_t . It is the unsigned type C++ uses for sizes, including the result of sizeof . !warning The 8-bit types print as characters std::cout << std::int8_t{ 65 }; prints A , not 65 . On most systems these types are really char underneath. Writing whole numbers in code A value written directly in your code is called a literal . There are several ways to write an integer literal. cpp int decimal{ 255 }; int hex{ 0xFF }; // base 16, also 255 int binary{ 0b1111'1111 }; // base 2, also 255 int million{ 1'000'000 }; // ' is only there to help you read it long long big{ 9'000'000'000LL }; // LL marks the literal as long long Prefix or suffix Meaning --- --- 0x hexadecimal (base 16) 0b binary (base 2) ' between digits a separator the compiler ignores LL at the end this literal is a long long u at the end this literal is unsigned !warning A leading zero means octal 017 is not seventeen. A literal starting with 0 is read in base 8, so it is 15. Never pad a number with zeros. Two reminders from Milestone 1 - Dividing integers cuts off the decimals: 7 / 2 is 3 . - With % , the sign of the result follows the left-hand side: -7 % 3 is -1 . Check yourself quiz ? What happens when an unsigned int goes below zero? - It stops at 0 - It becomes negative, like a signed int + It wraps round to a very large positive number - Undefined behaviour Unsigned arithmetic wraps round, and this is guaranteed behaviour: 0 minus 1 gives the largest value the type can hold. ? What happens when a signed int goes past its maximum? - It always wraps round to the most negative value + Undefined behaviour; the language makes no promise about the result - It stops at the maximum value - The program stops with an error message Signed overflow is undefined behaviour. It often wraps in practice, but the compiler is allowed to assume it never happens. ? Which type suits a value that may exceed two billion? - int - short + std::int64_t (or long long ) - unsigned short An int is usually 32 bits, which tops out at about 2.1 billion. std::int64_t or long long gives you 64 bits. ? Why does -1 < 3u come out false? - Because comparing a negative number is undefined behaviour - Because 3u means 3 thousand - Because < compares the number of digits + Mixing signed and unsigned converts -1 to unsigned, where it becomes about 4.29 billion When signed and unsigned values meet, the signed one is converted to unsigned. -1 becomes a huge positive number, which is not less than 3.

title: Number bases
body: The same number can be written in different bases. Define four int variables using the literal style named in each comment, then print them. Printed normally they all come out in decimal: 255 10 8 1000000

title: How far does light go?
body: Light travels about 299,792 kilometres every second. Read a number of days and print how many kilometres light covers in that time: In 1 days light travels 25902028800 km The answer overflows a 32-bit int straight away, so choose your types with care. Use named variables for the speed of light and the seconds in a day rather than bare numbers (in lesson 2.06 you will learn to lock them with const ).

title: 2.03  Floating Point Numbers
body:
float and double store decimals approximately . 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3 . Use double by default, never compare with == , and never use them where every cent must be exact. Decimals are approximate Write one third as a decimal and you get 0.3333... for ever. You have to stop somewhere, so what you write down is slightly off. Computers have the same problem in binary, with different numbers. In binary, 0.1 goes on for ever . The computer stores the closest value that fits. cpp include <iomanip include <iostream int main() { double x{ 0.1 + 0.2 }; std::cout << std::setprecision(17) << x << '
'; // 0.30000000000000004 std::cout << (x == 0.3) << '
'; // 0, meaning false return 0; } Types that work this way are called floating point types. How much precision do you get? A floating point number is stored like scientific notation: some significant digits, and a power that says where the point goes. 6.02 × 10^23 ──── ──── digits where the point goes ┌──────┬───────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ sign │ exponent │ the digits │ │ 1 bit│ 11 bits │ 52 bits │ └──────┴───────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────┘ a double: 64 bits in total Only so many digits fit. Anything beyond that is rounded away. Type Size Reliable significant digits --- --- --- float 4 bytes about 7 double 8 bytes about 15 float holding 123456789 prints 123456792 (ran out of digits) double holding 123456789 prints 123456789 !tip Use double The extra precision is nearly always worth four more bytes. float is for cases where you hold millions of values and memory is tight, such as graphics. Writing decimal literals cpp double d{ 3.14 }; // a literal with a point is a double float f{ 3.14f }; // the f suffix makes it a float double big{ 6.02e23 }; // 6.02 × 10^23 double tiny{ 1.5e-9 }; // 0.0000000015 Controlling how they print By default std::cout shows about six significant digits. The header <iomanip lets you choose. cpp include <iomanip include <iostream int main() { double pi{ 3.14159265 }; std::cout << pi << '
'; // 3.14159 std::cout << std::setprecision(3) << pi << '
'; // 3.14 (3 significant digits) std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(2) << pi << '
'; // 3.14 (2 digits after the point) return 0; } Setting Meaning --- --- std::setprecision(n) alone n significant digits in total std::fixed then std::setprecision(n) exactly n digits after the point Comparing safely Because of the tiny errors, asking "are these exactly equal?" is the wrong question. Ask "are these close enough?" cpp include <cmath bool approxEqual(double a, double b) { return std::abs(a - b) < 1e-9; } std::abs gives the size of the difference without its sign. If that is smaller than a tiny tolerance, treat the two as equal. Special values Floating point has three values that are not ordinary numbers. Expression Result Meaning --- --- --- 1.0 / 0.0 inf infinity -1.0 / 0.0 -inf negative infinity 0.0 / 0.0 nan "not a number" !danger Integers are different Dividing a floating point number by zero gives inf . Dividing an integer by zero ( 5 / 0 ) is undefined behaviour and usually crashes the program. Money Do not store money in a double . Errors of a fraction of a cent add up, and they anger accountants. Store the amount in the smallest unit as an integer: cpp std::int64_t priceInCents{ 1999 }; // 19.99 Check yourself quiz ? Why is 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 false? - Because == cannot be used with double + The values are stored inexactly in binary, so the sums differ slightly - Because the compiler rounds 0.3 down to 0 - Because addition of decimals is undefined behaviour 0.1 , 0.2 and 0.3 are all stored as the nearest binary value. The sum comes out a tiny bit different from the stored 0.3 . ? What type is the literal 2.5 ? - float + double - int - long double A decimal literal is a double unless you add a suffix. Write 2.5f for a float . ? How do you compare two floating point values? - With == , exactly as you would for integers - Convert both to int and compare those + Check that the size of their difference is below a tolerance - Print both and compare the printed text Rounding errors make == unreliable. Test something like std::abs(a - b) < 1e-9 instead. ? How should you store an amount of money? - As a float , because it is small and fast - As a double rounded to two decimals - As a std::string , such as "9.99" + As an integer count of the smallest unit, such as cents Integers are exact, so store 999 cents rather than 9.99. A double cannot hold most amounts exactly, and rounding errors add up.

title: 2.04  bool and char
body:
bool holds true or false , stored as 1 or 0. char holds one character, stored as a small number: 'A' is 65. bool : yes or no A bool holds the answer to a yes/no question. It is the type every decision in a program is built on. cpp include <iostream int main() { bool isAlive{ true }; bool hasKey{ false }; std::cout << isAlive << '
'; // 1 std::cout << std::boolalpha << isAlive << '
'; // true std::cout << !hasKey << '
'; // true return 0; } Two things to notice: - A bool prints as 1 or 0 unless you send std::boolalpha to std::cout first. - ! means not . It flips true to false and back. Where bools come from You rarely type true or false yourself. Usually a bool is the result of a comparison. Expression Value when age is 20 --- --- age = 18 true age == 21 false age % 2 == 0 true A function that returns bool reads like a question. Name it that way: isEven , hasKey , canJump . cpp bool isEven(int n) { return n % 2 == 0; } Numbers and bools convert to each other Converting Rule --- --- A number to bool 0 becomes false . Anything else becomes true . A bool to a number true becomes 1 , false becomes 0 . char : a number wearing a costume A char stores a small number. A standard table, called ASCII , says which character each number stands for. 'A' = 65 'B' = 66 ... 'Z' = 90 'a' = 97 'b' = 98 ... 'z' = 122 '0' = 48 '1' = 49 ... '9' = 57 ' ' = 32 '
' = 10 cpp include <iostream int main() { char c{ 'A' }; std::cout << c << '
'; // A std::cout << static_cast<int (c) << '
'; // 65 return 0; } static_cast<int (c) means "treat this value as an int ". It gets a full lesson next: 2.05 Type Conversion and static_cast . Why the table's order is useful The letters are in order and so are the digits. That makes some common jobs a single subtraction. Goal Expression Why it works --- --- --- Turn the character '7' into the number 7 '7' - '0' 55 − 48 = 7 Find a letter's position in the alphabet 'c' - 'a' 99 − 97 = 2 The next letter after c static_cast<char (c + 1) one further along the table !warning '7' is not 7 The character '7' is stored as 55. If you read a digit as a char and do arithmetic with it directly, the answers come out wrong by 48. For everyday checks, include <cctype has ready-made functions: Function Question or action --- --- std::isdigit(c) Is it a digit? std::isalpha(c) Is it a letter? std::isspace(c) Is it a space, tab or new line? std::toupper(c) / std::tolower(c) Convert the case Single quotes and double quotes Written Type What it is --- --- --- 'A' char exactly one character "A" text a string that happens to be one character long They are different types and cannot be swapped. char c{ "A" }; does not compile. Reading one character cpp char answer{}; std::cin answer; // skips spaces and new lines, then reads one character Check yourself quiz ? What does std::cout << true; print? + 1 - true - True - 0 A bool prints as 1 or 0 by default. Send std::boolalpha first to see the words true and false . ? What is 'c' - 'a' ? - 'b' + 2 - 1 - An error: you cannot subtract characters Characters are stored as numbers, and c is two places after a in the table, so the result is the int 2. ? What is the difference between 'x' and "x" ? - There is none; both are one character - 'x' is a string and "x" is a char + 'x' is a single char ; "x" is a string, a different type - "x" is a char that prints with quotes Single quotes make one char . Double quotes make a string literal, even when it holds only one character. ? Which numbers convert to true ? - Only 1 - Only positive numbers + Every number except 0 - Every number, including 0 0 converts to false and every other value, negative ones included, converts to true .

title: 2.05  Type Conversion and static_cast
body: C++ converts between types automatically when it has to. Some conversions lose information . When you want a conversion, say so with static_cast<Type (value) . Conversions happen without being asked Whenever a value of one type is used where another is expected, C++ converts it. This is called an implicit conversion : the compiler does it without you writing anything. cpp double d{ 5 }; // the int 5 becomes the double 5.0 int i = 3.9; // the double 3.9 becomes the int 3: the .9 is gone The first is harmless. The second lost information, and nothing warned you. Widening and narrowing Direction Safe? --- --- --- Widening To a type that can hold every value of the original Yes Narrowing To a type that cannot Only if you know the value fits This is why the course uses braces. Brace initialization refuses to narrow: cpp int a = 3.5; // compiles; a is 3 int b{ 3.5 }; // error: narrowing conversion Mixed arithmetic When an operator has two different types to work with, the compiler converts one side first so both match. Roughly, the "smaller" type is converted to the "larger" one. Expression Result type Note --- --- --- int + double double int + long long long long char + char int types smaller than int are widened to int first int + unsigned unsigned the trap from 2.02 Integers The important detail: the conversion happens one operator at a time , not for the statement as a whole. cpp include <iostream int main() { int total{ 7 }; int count{ 2 }; double wrong{ static_cast<double (total / count) }; // 3 double right{ static_cast<double (total) / count }; // 3.5 std::cout << wrong << ' ' << right << '\n'; return 0; } In the first line the division is finished, as integer division, before any double is involved. Converting on purpose static_cast is how you tell the compiler, and the next reader, "I mean this conversion". cpp static_cast<new type (value) cpp double price{ 9.99 }; int whole{ static_cast<int (price) }; // 9 char letter{ static_cast<char (72) }; // 'H' int code{ static_cast<int ('H') }; // 72 It also satisfies brace initialization, because you have stated your intent: cpp int b{ static_cast<int (3.5) }; // fine: 3 !tip Why not the shorter (int)price ? That older form comes from C and still compiles. It will attempt almost any conversion, including dangerous ones, and it is hard to search for. static_cast only performs sensible conversions and stands out in the code. Converting is not rounding static_cast<int cuts off the decimals. It does not round. For rounding, use <cmath . Call Result Rule --- --- --- static_cast<int (2.9) 2 cut off std::round(2.5) 3.0 to the nearest whole number std::floor(2.9) 2.0 always down std::ceil(2.1) 3.0 always up The <cmath functions return a double . To store a rounded value in an int , combine the two: cpp int rounded{ static_cast<int (std::round(2.7)) }; // 3 Other casts exist C++ has three more named casts for specialised jobs. You will not need them for a long time. The one you will meet is dynamic_cast , in 8.06 Object Slicing, Casting and Composition . Check yourself quiz ? What does double x{ 5 / 2 }; hold? - 2.5 + 2.0 - 3.0 - Nothing; it does not compile 5 / 2 is integer division, giving 2, and only then is it converted to double . Write 5.0 / 2 to get 2.5. ? What is the type of 'a' + 'b' ? - char - std::string + int - bool Types smaller than int are widened to int before arithmetic, so adding two char s gives an int , not a joined string. ? Does static_cast<int (3.99) round? + No, it cuts off the decimals and gives 3 - Yes, it gives 4 - Yes, it rounds to the nearest even number - No, it keeps 3.99 and only changes the label Converting a decimal to an integer type drops everything after the point. Use std::round first if you want rounding. ? What is a narrowing conversion? - A conversion that makes a value smaller, such as from 10 to 5 - Any conversion written with static_cast + A conversion to a type that cannot hold every value of the original, so information may be lost - A conversion from a wide character to a normal one Narrowing goes to a type with a smaller range or less precision, such as double to int . Brace initialization refuses it.
