title: 2.06  const and constexpr
body: const means "this value never changes after it is set". constexpr means "this value is known while compiling ". Use them wherever you can: they prevent mistakes and cost nothing. const : a locked box Most values in a program never need to change after they are set. Marking them const lets the compiler enforce that. cpp const double gravity{ 9.81 }; gravity = 10.0; // error: you cannot assign to a const variable ┌──────────────┐ │ 9.81 │ gravity (locked: read only) └──────────────┘ Two rules: - A const variable must be given its value when it is created. - That value may come from anywhere, including the keyboard. It simply cannot change afterwards. cpp int age{}; std::cin age; const int ageNextYear{ age + 1 }; // set once while running, then locked !tip Make things const by default When you read const on a variable, you know its value at every later line without checking. In a long function that is a real help. Leave const off only when the value has to change. constexpr : worked out by the compiler Some values are known before the program ever runs: the number of seconds in a day, the size of a chess board. constexpr asks the compiler to calculate them during the build. cpp constexpr double pi{ 3.14159265358979 }; constexpr int secondsPerDay{ 24 60 60 }; // the compiler stores 86400 int x{}; std::cin x; constexpr int bad{ x 2 }; // error: x is not known while compiling You will hear these two phases called compile time and run time . The distinction comes up again and again in C++. const constexpr --- --- --- Can change after it is set No No Value may come from input while running Yes No Calculated during the build Sometimes Always Use it for Any value you will not modify True constants: pi , maxPlayers , gridSize constexpr functions A function can be constexpr too. That means the compiler may run it during the build when its arguments are known. cpp include <iostream constexpr int square(int n) { return n n; } int main() { constexpr int a{ square(5) }; // worked out while compiling: 25 int side{}; std::cin side; int b{ square(side) }; // the same function, used while running std::cout << a << ' ' << b << '\n'; return 0; } One function serves both purposes. Replace magic numbers with names A magic number is a bare number in the code with no explanation. cpp total = price 1.08; // what is 1.08? cpp constexpr double salesTaxRate{ 0.08 }; total = price (1.0 + salesTaxRate); The second version explains itself. And when the rate changes, you change one line instead of hunting for every 1.08 . Sharing constants between files Constants that several files need go in a header, grouped under a name: cpp // constants.h pragma once namespace constants { inline constexpr double pi{ 3.14159265358979 }; inline constexpr int maxPlayers{ 4 }; } Any file that includes the header writes constants::pi . Take the namespace and inline parts on trust for now. Both are explained in Milestone 3: 3.05 Scope, Lifetime and Namespaces and 3.06 Global Variables, static and Linkage . const parameters A parameter can be const as well: the function promises not to change it. cpp void printPrice(const double price) For a simple value that is copied anyway, this is optional. It becomes important with references, where it means "I will look at your data but not alter it": 4.03 References . Check yourself quiz ? Can a const variable get its value from user input? - No, a const must be known while compiling + Yes, it is set once while running and cannot change afterwards - Yes, and it can be changed again later with another std::cin - Only if it is also constexpr const only means "cannot change after it is set". It is constexpr that needs a value known while compiling, so it cannot come from input. ? What is a magic number? - A number the compiler works out during the build - A number too large for an int + An unexplained number written directly in the code - A random number chosen at run time A magic number is a bare value like 86400 with no name. Replace it with a named constant such as secondsPerDay . ? What is the difference between compile time and run time? - They are the same; the program is built as it runs + Compile time is while the program is being built; run time is while it is running - Compile time is how long the build takes; run time is how long the program takes - Compile time happens after run time, when the program finishes Compile time is while the compiler builds the program. Run time is while the finished program runs, which is when user input arrives. ? Does a constexpr function always run during the build? - Yes, that is exactly what constexpr means - No, it never runs during the build - Yes, unless it has no parameters + No; only when its arguments are known while compiling A constexpr function can run while compiling. With values only known while running, it runs like any other function.

title: 2.07  Strings — std::string and std::string_view
body:
std::string owns its text and can change it. std::string_view is a cheap, read-only window onto text that lives somewhere else. Functions that only read text should take a std::string_view . A string is a row of characters std::string name{ "Hello" }; index: 0 1 2 3 4 ┌────┬────┬────┬────┬────┐ │ H │ e │ l │ l │ o │ name.length() is 5 └────┴────┴────┴────┴────┘ name 0 is 'H' name 4 is 'o' Each character has a position, called its index . Counting starts at 0 , so the last index is always the length minus one. !danger Stay inside the string name 5 on a five-character string reads past the end. That is undefined behaviour. The compiler will not stop you. Calling a string's own functions A std::string comes with functions attached. You call them with a dot after the variable: name.length() . Functions attached to a value like this are called member functions . cpp include <iostream include <string int main() { std::string first{ "Ada" }; std::string last{ "Lovelace" }; std::string full{ first + ' ' + last }; std::cout << full << " has " << full.length() << " characters
"; // 12 std::cout << "Initials: " << first 0 << last 0 << '
'; // AL std::cout << "Surname starts at index " << full.find(last) << '
'; // 4 return 0; } The toolbox Assume std::string s{ "Hi" }; for each row. To Write Result --- --- --- Get the length s.length() 2 Get one character s 0 'H' Join two strings s + " there" "Hi there" Add to the end s += "!"; s is now "Hi!" Compare s == "Hi" true Check for empty s.empty() false Find text s.find("i") 1 Take a piece s.substr(0, 1) "H" (start index, how many) Insert s.insert(0, " ") " Hi" Remove s.erase(0, 1) "i" (start index, how many) Replace a piece s.replace(0, 1, "Oh") "Ohi" Converting between text and numbers: To Write Result --- --- --- Number to text std::to_string(42) "42" Text to int std::stoi("42") 42 Text to double std::stod("3.5") 3.5 !note When find finds nothing It returns a special value, std::string::npos . Always compare the result against it before using it as an index: cpp if (s.find("x") == std::string::npos) { / not there / } !warning "Hello" + " World" does not compile Text in quotes is a string literal , which is a more primitive thing than a std::string . The + only joins when at least one side is a real std::string : write std::string{ "Hello" } + " World" . std::string_view : look, do not copy Passing a std::string to a function copies the whole text, as with any other argument. For long text that is wasted work when the function only wants to read it. A std::string_view holds no text of its own. It records where some existing text is and how long it is. cpp include <iostream include <string include <string_view void greet(std::string_view name) { std::cout << "Hello, " << name << '
'; } int main() { greet("Ada"); // works with a literal std::string s{ "Grace" }; greet(s); // works with a std::string, without copying it return 0; } std::string std::string_view --- --- --- Owns the text Yes No Can change the text Yes No Cost of passing it to a function Copies every character Tiny: a location and a length Use it for Text you store or modify Parameters that only read !danger A view must not outlive what it looks at cpp std::string_view broken() { std::string temp{ "oops" }; return temp; // temp is destroyed here; the view now points at nothing } A view is only valid while the text it refers to still exists. This idea, something referring to data that has gone, returns in Milestone 4 under the name dangling . Check yourself quiz ? What does std::string{ "banana" }.find("na") return? - 3 - 1 + 2 - true find returns the index where the first match begins. Counting from 0, b =0, a =1, n =2. ? When should a function take a std::string_view ? - When it needs to store the text for later - When it needs to change the caller's text + When it only needs to read the text, not store it or change it - Whenever the text is longer than 100 characters A std::string_view looks at existing text without copying it. It cannot change the text, and it must not outlive the string it views. ? What does find return when the text is not there? - -1 - 0 + std::string::npos - The length of the string minus one find returns the special value std::string::npos when there is no match. 0 would mean a match at the very start. ? What is the index of the last character of a string of length 8? + 7 - 8 - 9 - 0 Indexes start at 0, so a string of length 8 has indexes 0 to 7. Index 8 is one past the end.

title: 2.08  Operators Deep Dive
body: Comparisons ( == , < ...) produce a bool . Logical operators ( && , , ! ) combine bools and stop early when the answer is settled. ++x and x++ differ in the value they give back. ?: chooses between two values. Comparison operators Each of these compares two values and produces a bool . Operator Meaning 5 ? 3 --- --- --- == equal to false != not equal to true < less than false greater than true <= less than or equal to false = greater than or equal to true !danger = stores, == compares x = 5 puts 5 into x . x == 5 asks whether x is 5. Writing one where you meant the other is among the most common mistakes in C++, and it compiles. The compiler warns about it, which is one more reason to read warnings. Logical operators These combine yes/no answers. Operator Name True when --- --- --- a && b AND both are true a \ \ b OR at least one is true !a NOT a is false a b a && b a \ \ b !a --- --- --- --- --- true true true true false true false false true false false true false true true false false false false true cpp bool canVote{ age = 18 && isCitizen }; bool isWeekend{ day == 6 day == 7 }; bool isTeen{ age = 13 && age <= 19 }; !warning Ranges need two comparisons Maths lets you write 13 ≤ age ≤ 19. In C++, 13 <= age <= 19 compiles and is always true . It works out 13 <= age first, giving true or false , which is 1 or 0, and then compares that with 19. Short-circuit evaluation && and look at the left side first. If that already settles the answer, the right side is never run . This is a tool you can rely on, not just a speed-up: cpp if (count != 0 && total / count 10) When count is 0 the division never happens, so there is no divide-by-zero. Prefix and postfix ++ Both add one to the variable. They differ in the value the expression gives back. int x{ 5 }; int a{ ++x }; prefix: add first, then give the new value a is 6, x is 6 int b{ x++ }; postfix: give the old value, then add b is 6, x is 7 On a line of its own, ++x; and x++; do the same thing. !tip Two habits Use prefix ++x unless you specifically need the old value. And never change a variable with ++ and also use it elsewhere in the same expression: x++ + x++ has no dependable answer. The conditional operator ?: It chooses between two values according to a condition. cpp condition ? value if true : value if false cpp int larger{ (a b) ? a : b }; std::cout << (score = 50 ? "Pass" : "Fail") << '\n'; Use it to pick a value . To choose between actions , use if : 3.01 if and else . Precedence: what binds tightest Higher rows are worked out first. Level Operators --- --- 1 x++ x-- and function calls 2 ++x --x ! -x (negative) static_cast 3 / % 4 + - 5 << 6 < <= = 7 == != 8 && 9 \ \ 10 ?: = += and the other assignments You do not have to memorise this. Remember three facts: arithmetic comes before comparison, comparison before && , and && before . For anything else, add brackets. !warning Printing a comparison needs brackets std::cout << a < b; fails, because << is above < in the table. Write std::cout << (a < b); . Maths functions Call Result Header --- --- --- std::pow(2, 10) 1024 (as a double ) <cmath std::sqrt(16) 4 <cmath std::abs(-3) 3 <cmath std::max(a, b) , std::min(a, b) the larger, the smaller <algorithm Check yourself quiz ? In a && b , when is b not evaluated? - When a is true + When a is false - Never; both sides are always evaluated - When b is false If a is false, the whole && is already false, so b is skipped. This is called short-circuit evaluation. ? After int x{ 2 }; int y{ x++ }; , what are x and y ? - x is 3 and y is 3 - x is 2 and y is 3 + x is 3 and y is 2 - x is 2 and y is 2 Postfix x++ increases x but gives back the old value, so y gets 2. Prefix ++x would give back 3. ? Why is 10 < x < 20 wrong in C++? - It does not compile + 10 < x gives 0 or 1 first, and that is always below 20 - It checks x < 20 first and ignores 10 < x - It is fine; C++ reads it like maths The comparisons run one at a time, and true / false (1/0) is always below 20. Write x 10 && x < 20 . ? What does score = 50 ? "Pass" : "Fail" produce when score is 50? - "Fail" - true - 50 + "Pass" 50 = 50 is true, so the conditional operator picks the first value, "Pass" .

title: 2.09  Bit Manipulation
body:
Bitwise operators work on the individual bits of a number: & AND, OR, ^ XOR, ~ NOT, << and shift. They let you pack many on/off settings into one number and pull packed values apart. Why work with single bits? A bool takes a whole byte to store one yes/no answer. One byte has eight bits, so it could hold eight. When memory is tight, or a file format or a piece of hardware dictates the layout, programmers pack several small values into one number and operate on its bits directly. This lesson is the most technical in the milestone. It builds on 2.01 Memory, Bits and Fundamental Types and 2.02 Integers . Binary and hexadecimal position: 7 6 5 4 3 2 1 0 worth: 128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1 bits: 0 0 0 0 1 1 0 1 = 8 + 4 + 1 = 13 Bits are numbered from the right, starting at 0. Hexadecimal (base 16) is the usual shorthand, because one hex digit is exactly four bits: Hex Binary Hex Binary --- --- --- --- 0 0000 8 1000 1 0001 A 1010 4 0100 D 1101 7 0111 F 1111 So 0xFF is 1111 1111 , a full byte of ones. The six operators Each works on every bit position separately. a = 1100 a = 1100 a = 1100 b = 1010 b = 1010 b = 1010 a & b = 1000 a b = 1110 a ^ b = 0110 both are 1 either is 1 they differ ~a = 0011 every bit flipped a << 1 = 1000 moved left one place: the top bit falls off, a 0 comes in a 2 = 0011 moved right two places Operator Name A result bit is 1 when --- --- --- & AND both bits are 1 \ OR either bit is 1 ^ XOR the bits are different ~ NOT the bit was 0 << left shift (moves bits left; each place doubles the value) right shift (moves bits right; each place halves the value) !warning Do not confuse these with the logical operators && and combine two bool values into one. & and combine two numbers bit by bit. And here << shifts bits; it only means "print" when the left side is std::cout . Seeing the bits std::bitset prints a number in binary and has functions for individual bits. cpp include <bitset include <iostream int main() { std::bitset<8 bits{ 0b0000'1101 }; std::cout << bits << '
'; // 00001101 bits.set(7); // switch bit 7 on bits.flip(0); // toggle bit 0 std::cout << bits << '
'; // 10001100 std::cout << bits.test(2) << '
'; // 1: bit 2 is on std::cout << bits.count() << '
'; // 3 bits are on return 0; } Bit flags A flag is a single yes/no setting. Give each flag its own bit by shifting a 1 into place. A value with one chosen bit set, used to pick that bit out, is called a mask . cpp include <cstdint constexpr std::uint8_t flagRead{ 1 << 0 }; // 0000 0001 constexpr std::uint8_t flagWrite{ 1 << 1 }; // 0000 0010 constexpr std::uint8_t flagExecute{ 1 << 2 }; // 0000 0100 There are exactly four things you ever do with a flag: To Write Why it works --- --- --- Switch on flags \ = mask; OR with 1 forces the bit to 1 Switch off flags &= ~mask; AND with 0 forces the bit to 0; all other bits are ANDed with 1 and survive Toggle flags ^= mask; XOR with 1 flips the bit Test (flags & mask) != 0 AND leaves only that bit; non-zero means it was on cpp std::uint8_t perms{ 0 }; perms = flagRead; // 0000 0001 perms = flagWrite; // 0000 0011 perms &= ~flagWrite; // 0000 0001 perms ^= flagExecute; // 0000 0101 bool canRead{ (perms & flagRead) != 0 }; // true Packing and unpacking with masks A colour on screen is three values from 0 to 255: red, green and blue. They are commonly packed into one 32-bit number written 0xRRGGBB . color = 0000 0000 1111 1111 1000 1000 0000 0000 0xFF8800 color 8 = 0000 0000 1111 1111 1000 1000 green is now at the bottom & 0xFF = 1000 1000 keep only the lowest 8 bits The pattern for extracting a field is always shift it to the bottom, then mask off the rest : cpp std::uint32_t color{ 0xFF8800 }; std::uint32_t red{ (color 16) & 0xFF }; // 0xFF std::uint32_t green{ (color 8) & 0xFF }; // 0x88 std::uint32_t blue{ color & 0xFF }; // 0x00 Packing is the reverse, shift each part into position, then OR them together : cpp std::uint32_t packed{ (red << 16) (green << 8) blue }; !warning Use unsigned types for bit work Shifting a negative signed number gives results that depend on details you do not want to rely on. This is the main job unsigned types exist for. Check yourself quiz ? How do you switch off bit 3 of flags ? - flags = (1u << 3); + flags &= ~(1u << 3); - flags ^= (1u << 3); - flags &= (1u << 3); The mask has only bit 3 set, ~ inverts it, and AND clears just that bit. = would switch it on and ^= would flip it. ? What is 5 << 2 ? - 7 - 10 + 20 - 25 Shifting left one place doubles a number, so two places multiplies by 4: 5 × 4 = 20. ? What is 0b1010 ^ 0b0110 ? - 0b0010 , which is 2 - 0b1110 , which is 14 - 0b0000 , which is 0 + 0b1100 , which is 12 XOR gives 1 where the bits differ. 0b0010 would be AND and 0b1110 would be OR. ? What are the two steps for extracting a field from a packed number? + Shift the field down to the lowest bits, then AND with a mask - OR with a mask, then shift the field up - Invert all the bits, then shift left - AND with zero, then OR with the field Shift right so the field sits in the lowest bits, then AND with a mask (such as 0xFF ) to remove everything above it.

title: Power of two
body: A power of two (1, 2, 4, 8, 16 ...) has exactly one bit switched on. Subtracting 1 from it flips that bit off and every lower bit on, so the two numbers share no bits: 8 = 1000 8 - 1 = 0111 8 & 7 = 0000 Write bool isPowerOfTwo(unsigned int n) using that trick. Zero is not a power of two.

title: Four bit tricks
body: Flags pack several on/off switches into one number. Write the four standard operations. bit is the position, counting from 0 at the right-hand end. Function Does Recipe --- --- --- setBit(flags, bit) switches the bit on OR with the mask clearBit(flags, bit) switches it off AND with the inverted mask toggleBit(flags, bit) flips it XOR with the mask testBit(flags, bit) is it on? AND with the mask, compare with 0 The mask for a bit is 1u << bit . The first three return unsigned int ; testBit returns bool .

title: Pack a colour
body: Screens store a colour as three numbers from 0 to 255: red, green and blue. Graphics code often packs all three into one 32-bit number laid out as 0x00RRGGBB . Write four functions: - std::uint32_t pack(std::uint32_t r, std::uint32_t g, std::uint32_t b) builds the packed colour - std::uint32_t redOf(std::uint32_t colour) , greenOf(...) , blueOf(...) pull each part back out r = 0xFF, g = 0x88, b = 0x00 - 0x00FF8800 Shift a part into place with << , combine with . To read one back, shift right with and keep the low 8 bits with & 0xFF .

title: 3.01  if and else
body:
if (condition) { ... } runs a block only when the condition is true. else if adds further choices and else catches everything left. Only the first branch that matches runs. Programs that decide Until now every statement ran, top to bottom, every time. Control flow is how a program chooses which statements to run. if is the foundation of it. cpp include <iostream int main() { int score{ 73 }; if (score = 90) { std::cout << "A
"; } else if (score = 80) { std::cout << "B
"; } else if (score = 70) { std::cout << "C
"; } else { std::cout << "F
"; } return 0; } Part Meaning --- --- if (condition) Run the block when the condition is true else if (condition) Otherwise, try this condition else Otherwise, when nothing above matched Each path through the statement is called a branch . The conditions are tested in order, and only the first true branch runs . The rest are skipped, even if their conditions would also be true. !tip Order does the work for you Because of that rule, else if (score = 80) does not need to say && score < 90 . If execution reaches it, the first test has already failed. Always use braces Without braces, an if controls exactly one statement. cpp if (lives == 0) std::cout << "Game over
"; resetGame(); // NOT part of the if. This runs every time. The indentation suggests one thing and the compiler does another. Write the braces every time, even for one line. Combining conditions Two nested tests can usually be flattened with && : cpp if (hasTicket) { if (age = 18) { std::cout << "Enjoy the film
"; } } cpp if (hasTicket && age = 18) { std::cout << "Enjoy the film
"; } The second says the same thing with less to read. Early return Deeply nested code is hard to follow. A common remedy is to deal with the unusual cases first and leave. cpp double safeDivide(double a, double b) { if (b == 0.0) { std::cout << "Cannot divide by zero
"; return 0.0; } return a / b; } A check at the top that rejects bad input is called a guard clause . With the problem cases out of the way, the main logic sits at the outer level with no indentation. A variable that belongs to the if You can create a variable inside the if itself. It exists only for that statement. cpp if (int remainder{ n % 3 }; remainder == 0) { std::cout << "divisible by three
"; } // remainder no longer exists here The part before the ; creates the variable and the part after is the condition. This keeps a helper variable from lingering where it is not needed. Four classic traps Written Problem --- --- if (x = 5) Assigns 5 to x , then treats 5 as true . You meant == . if (x 0); The ; ends the if . The block after it always runs. if (0 < x < 10) Always true. Write x 0 && x < 10 . if (a == b) with two double values Rounding makes this unreliable: 2.03 Floating Point Numbers The compiler warns about the first two. Check yourself quiz ? In an if / else if chain, how many branches can run? - Every branch whose condition is true + At most one: the first whose condition is true - Exactly one, always - At most two: the first true one and the else The chain stops at the first true condition. If none is true and there is no else , no branch runs at all. ? What is wrong with if (x 5); ? - Nothing; the semicolon is optional - It does not compile + The ; ends the if , so the block always runs - The block that follows never runs ; is an empty statement, so the if controls nothing. The braces after it are just an ordinary block that always runs. ? What is a guard clause? - An else branch at the end of a chain that catches everything else - A comment that warns the reader about tricky code + A check at the start of a function that handles a bad case and returns immediately - A pair of braces around a single statement A guard clause deals with the bad or unusual case first and returns, so the rest of the function can assume the normal case. ? Why does else if (score = 80) not need to check score < 90 ? - Because else if checks both limits automatically - Because scores above 90 are not allowed - It does need it; leaving it out is a bug + It is only reached when the earlier test score = 90 was false An else if only runs when every earlier condition was false, so score < 90 is already known.

title: 3.02  switch
body:
switch compares one value against a list of fixed options and jumps to the matching case . End each case with break , or execution carries on into the next one. One value, many options A long if / else if chain that keeps testing the same variable against fixed values is clearer as a switch . cpp include <iostream int main() { int choice{}; std::cin choice; switch (choice) { case 1: std::cout << "Starting a new game
"; break; case 2: std::cout << "Loading
"; break; case 3: std::cout << "Goodbye
"; break; default: std::cout << "Not an option
"; break; } return 0; } Part Meaning --- --- switch (value) The value to examine case 1: Where to jump to when the value is 1 break; Leave the switch default: Where to jump to when no case matches Fall-through A case is only a label : a place to jump to. It is not a block with an end. Without break , execution simply continues into whatever comes next. switch (2) case 1: print "one" case 2: print "two" jumps in here case 3: print "three" no break above, so this runs too default: print "other" and so does this Output: two three other Forgetting a break is the classic switch bug. Fall-through is useful in one situation: several values that share the same code. cpp switch (letter) { case 'a': case 'e': case 'i': case 'o': case 'u': std::cout << "vowel
"; break; default: std::cout << "consonant
"; break; } !tip Marking it as deliberate If a case does some work and you want it to continue into the next, write fallthrough ; at that point. It tells the compiler and the reader that the missing break is intended. return also leaves Inside a function, a return ends the function, and therefore the switch . No break is needed after it. cpp std::string_view dayName(int day) { switch (day) { case 1: return "Monday"; case 2: return "Tuesday"; case 3: return "Wednesday"; default: return "unknown"; } } The rules Rule Detail --- --- The value must be integer-like int , char , bool or an enum. Not std::string , not double . Each case must be a constant A literal, or a constexpr value. Not an ordinary variable. No ranges There is no case 1 to 5 . Use if for ranges. Variables inside a case need braces case 1: { int x{ 5 }; ... break; } switch or if ? Use switch when Use if when --- --- Comparing one value against several fixed values Testing ranges, such as score = 90 Menus, commands, single characters, enums Text, decimals or conditions that combine several variables switch becomes much more valuable once you meet enums in 4.05 Enums , where the compiler can warn you if you forget one of the options. Check yourself quiz ? Can you switch on a std::string ? - Yes, like any other type + No, only integer-like types such as int , char , bool and enums - Yes, but only if every case is a string literal - Only for strings of one character switch needs an integer-like value. To choose on text, use an if / else if chain. ? What happens when a case has no break ? - The compiler reports an error - The switch ends anyway after that case + Execution continues into the next case's statements - The program jumps to default This is fall-through: without break (or return ), execution runs straight on into the next case. ? What is default for? + It is where execution goes when the value matches none of the cases - It is the case that always runs first - It sets the value being switched on when it is missing - It is required, or the switch will not compile default catches every value with no matching case . It is optional, but a good place to handle unexpected values. ? When is fall-through the right thing? - When every case should run all the cases below it - When you forgot which case should run + When several values should share the same code Stacking case 'a': case 'e': ... above one block makes them share code. Elsewhere, fall-through is usually a missing break .

title: 3.03  Loops — while, do-while, for
body: Loops repeat code. while repeats as long as a condition holds. do-while runs the body at least once. for is built for counting. break leaves a loop and continue skips to the next round. Three loops, one idea All three repeat a block while a condition is true. They differ in when the condition is tested and where the counting lives. One pass through the body is called an iteration . while cpp int count{ 1 }; while (count <= 5) { std::cout << count << ' '; ++count; } // 1 2 3 4 5 The condition is tested before each iteration. If it is false at the start, the body never runs. If nothing in the body ever makes it false, the loop never ends: an infinite loop . do-while cpp int choice{}; do { std::cout << "Enter 1 to 3: "; std::cin choice; } while (choice < 1 choice 3); The condition is tested after each iteration, so the body always runs at least once. That suits "ask, then check the answer". Note the ; after the closing bracket. for A counting loop needs three things: a starting value, a condition and a step. for puts all three on one line. cpp // start condition step for (int i{ 0 }; i < 5; ++i) { std::cout << i << ' '; } // 0 1 2 3 4 Trace it: i i < 5 ? Action --- --- --- 0 true print 0, then ++i 1 true print 1, then ++i ... 4 true print 4, then ++i 5 false the loop ends The patterns you will write most: To loop over Write --- --- 0 up to n − 1 (n iterations) for (int i{ 0 }; i < n; ++i) 1 up to n for (int i{ 1 }; i <= n; ++i) 10 down to 1 for (int i{ 10 }; i 0; --i) Every second value for (int i{ 0 }; i < 20; i += 2) !tip Start at 0, test with < Programmers count from zero because indexes start at zero. for (int i{ 0 }; i < n; ++i) runs exactly n times and visits exactly the valid indexes of something with n elements. Make it your default shape. Which loop? Situation Loop --- --- You know how many iterations, or you are counting for You repeat until something happens, and it may already have happened while The body must run once before you can test do-while break and continue cpp for (int i{ 1 }; i <= 10; ++i) { if (i == 3) { continue; // skip the rest of this iteration } if (i == 7) { break; // leave the loop altogether } std::cout << i << ' '; } // 1 2 4 5 6 Statement Effect --- --- break Ends the loop immediately continue Ends this iteration; in a for loop the step still runs A loop written as while (true) relies on a break inside it to end. That is a normal pattern when the exit test belongs in the middle of the body. Nested loops A loop inside a loop. The inner loop runs in full for every single iteration of the outer one. cpp for (int row{ 1 }; row <= 3; ++row) { for (int col{ 1 }; col <= 4; ++col) { std::cout << ' '; } std::cout << '\n'; } outer loop: 3 iterations inner loop: 4 iterations each time 12 stars in all The inner loop's limit can depend on the outer variable. Changing col <= 4 to col <= row gives a triangle: Building up a result A very common shape: create a variable before the loop and update it on each iteration. That variable is called an accumulator . cpp int sum{ 0 }; for (int i{ 1 }; i <= 100; ++i) { sum += i; } std::cout << sum << '\n'; // 5050 The same shape counts things, finds a maximum, builds a string, and much more. Three classic bugs Bug Cause Check --- --- --- Off by one <= where you needed < , or the wrong start Trace the first and the last iteration by hand Infinite loop Nothing in the body moves towards the exit Ask what changes on each iteration Unsigned countdown for (unsigned i{ 5 }; i = 0; --i) An unsigned value is always = 0 , so the test never fails Check yourself quiz ? How many times does for (int i{ 0 }; i < 10; i += 3) run? - Three times + Four times - Ten times - Five times i takes the values 0, 3, 6 and 9. The next step makes it 12, which fails i < 10 . ? When is do-while the right choice? - When the loop may need to run zero times - When you know exactly how many times to loop + When the body must run at least once, as in asking for input - When the loop must count down instead of up do-while checks its condition after the body, so the body always runs once. That suits "ask, then check". ? What does continue do? - It ends the loop completely - It restarts the loop from the very first iteration - It pauses the loop until the user presses a key + It skips the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next continue jumps to the next iteration; in a for loop the step still runs. break is the one that leaves the loop. ? An outer loop runs 5 times and its inner loop runs 6 times. How often does the inner body run? - 11 times + 30 times - 6 times - 5 times The inner loop runs completely for each outer iteration: 5 × 6 = 30.

title: 3.04  Random Numbers
body: Create one random engine, seed it once, and use a distribution to turn its output into numbers in the range you want. Never create a new engine each time you need a number. Computers cannot be random A computer follows instructions exactly, so it cannot roll a real die. What it can do is run a formula whose output looks random: each number is calculated from the one before. These are called pseudo-random numbers. Because every number depends on the previous one, the starting value decides the whole sequence. That starting value is the seed . Three parts Part Job Like --- --- --- Seed The starting point of the sequence Shuffling a deck Engine Produces a long stream of raw, random-looking numbers The shuffled deck Distribution Converts raw numbers into what you asked for, such as 1 to 6 The rules for reading a card The code cpp include <iostream include <random int main() { std::mt19937 rng{ std::random_device{}() }; // one engine, seeded once std::uniform_int_distribution die{ 1, 6 }; // 1 to 6, both included for (int i{ 0 }; i < 10; ++i) { std::cout << die(rng) << ' '; } std::cout << '\n'; return 0; } Piece What it is --- --- std::mt19937 A well-tested engine (the "Mersenne Twister") std::random_device{}() Asks the operating system for an unpredictable seed std::uniform_int_distribution{ 1, 6 } Whole numbers from 1 to 6, each equally likely die(rng) Draw one number: the distribution takes what it needs from the engine Other distributions Distribution Produces --- --- std::uniform_real_distribution{ 0.0, 1.0 } Decimals from 0 up to, but not including, 1 std::bernoulli_distribution{ 0.5 } true or false , here with a 50% chance std::normal_distribution{ 170.0, 10.0 } A bell curve centred on 170 The same seed gives the same sequence seed 42 gives 17, 3, 88, 41, ... seed 42 gives 17, 3, 88, 41, ... identical seed 99 gives 62, 9, 14, 77, ... This is a feature. A fixed seed makes a "random" program repeatable, which is exactly what you need when testing or chasing a bug. cpp std::mt19937 testRng{ 42 }; // same numbers on every run You want Seed with --- --- Different results on every run (a game) std::random_device{}() Identical results on every run (a test) a fixed number One engine for the whole program !danger Do not create an engine inside the function that uses it cpp int roll() { std::mt19937 rng{ std::random_device{}() }; // a new engine on every call return std::uniform_int_distribution{ 1, 6 }(rng); } This throws away the engine after one number. It is slow, and you lose the quality the engine is designed to give over a long sequence. The usual solution is a small header that every file shares: cpp // random.h pragma once include <random namespace Random { inline std::mt19937 rng{ std::random_device{}() }; inline int get(int min, int max) { return std::uniform_int_distribution{ min, max }(rng); } } cpp int roll{ Random::get(1, 6) }; The engine is created once, when the program starts, and every call to Random::get draws from it. The namespace and inline keywords are explained in the next two lessons. !warning You will see rand() in old code std::rand() % 6 + 1 is the method inherited from C. Its numbers are of poor quality and slightly favour some results. Recognise it; do not write it. Check yourself quiz ? Why seed only once? + One seed gives a long, good sequence; re-seeding restarts it - Seeding twice makes the program crash - The compiler only allows one seed per program - Seeding again would make the numbers less likely to repeat One engine seeded once gives the best sequence. Re-seeding (especially with the same seed) restarts it and can repeat numbers. ? What does std::uniform_int_distribution{ 1, 6 } produce? - Whole numbers from 1 to 5, each equally likely + Whole numbers from 1 to 6 inclusive, each equally likely - Decimal numbers between 1 and 6 - Numbers from 1 to 6, with the middle values more likely Both ends are included, and each value is equally likely, so it works like a fair die. ? Why would you ever want a fixed seed? - It makes the numbers more random - It is the only way to get numbers in a range + Every run then gives the same numbers, so bugs can be repeated - It makes the engine run faster A fixed seed gives a repeatable sequence, which is exactly what you want when testing or chasing a bug. ? What does "pseudo-random" mean? - The numbers are only random in Release builds - The numbers are taken from the computer's clock each time - The numbers are truly random but only within a range + The numbers come from a formula and are completely determined by the seed A pseudo-random engine uses a formula. The numbers look random, but the same seed always gives the same sequence.

title: Roll a die
body: Write int rollDie(std::mt19937& rng) that returns a random whole number from 1 to 6, each equally likely. The random engine is handed in (the & means the function uses the caller's engine rather than a copy, which you will learn about in milestone 4). Your job is the distribution: cpp std::uniform_int_distribution<int die{ 1, 6 }; return die(rng); The tests roll it thousands of times and check that every result is between 1 and 6 and that all six numbers turn up.

title: Random in a range
body: Write int randomBetween(std::mt19937& rng, int low, int high) returning a random whole number from low to high , both included.

title: Same seed, same game
body: A random engine started from the same seed always produces the same sequence. Games use this for replays, and tests use it to get repeatable results. Read a seed and a number of rolls. Seed a std::mt19937 with that seed, roll a six-sided die that many times, and print the rolls on one line separated by spaces, then how many sixes there were: Rolls: 1 5 2 6 4 Sixes: 1 (The exact numbers depend on the seed.) To match the expected output, create one engine, one std::uniform_int_distribution<int { 1, 6 } , and call it exactly once per roll.

title: 3.05  Scope, Lifetime and Namespaces
body:
Scope is where in the code a name can be used. Lifetime is when during the run the variable exists. Namespaces group names so that two things called the same do not clash. Two questions about every variable Question Called Decided --- --- --- On which lines may I use this name? Scope By where it is declared in the source For how long does the value exist in memory? Lifetime While the program runs For the local variables you have used so far the two coincide, which is why they are easy to mix up. They come apart in the next lesson. Every pair of braces is a scope A name declared inside a block can be used from its declaration to the block's closing brace. ┌─ main ───────────────────────────────────┐ │ int x{ 1 }; │ │ │ │ ┌─ if block ─────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ int y{ 2 }; │ │ │ │ can use: x, y │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ ┌─ for block ──────────────────┐ │ │ │ │ │ int z{ 3 }; │ │ │ │ │ │ can use: x, y, z │ │ │ │ │ └──────────────────────────────┘ │ │ │ │ z is out of scope │ │ │ └────────────────────────────────────┘ │ │ y and z are out of scope │ └──────────────────────────────────────────┘ Code can see outwards, never inwards. An inner block can use names from the blocks around it. An outer block cannot reach into an inner one. Lifetime of a local variable A local variable is created when execution reaches its definition and destroyed at the closing brace of its block. That is automatic, and it explains the name for this kind of lifetime: automatic storage duration . !tip Keep scopes small Declare each variable in the smallest block that needs it, as close to its first use as you can. Fewer lines can touch it, so fewer lines can break it. Shadowing An inner block may declare a name that already exists in an outer block. The inner one hides the outer one until its block ends. cpp include <iostream int main() { int apples{ 5 }; { int apples{ 10 }; // a second, separate variable std::cout << apples << '
'; // 10 } std::cout << apples << '
'; // 5 return 0; } This is legal and almost always a mistake. You think you are changing one variable and you are changing another. Give the inner variable a different name. Namespaces As programs grow, names collide. Two libraries may each have a function called add . A namespace is a named group that keeps them apart, in the way a surname separates two people called Sam. cpp include <iostream namespace Math { constexpr double pi{ 3.14159 }; int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; } } namespace Game::Utils { int clamp(int value, int low, int high) { return value < low ? low : (value high ? high : value); } } int main() { std::cout << Math::add(2, 3) << ' ' << Math::pi << '
'; std::cout << Game::Utils::clamp(15, 0, 10) << '
'; // 10 return 0; } :: is the scope resolution operator . Read Math::add as "the add that lives in Math ". You have used it since your first program: std::cout is "the cout in std ". A name declared outside every function and every namespace belongs to the global namespace . using : shorter names, with a cost Form Effect Verdict --- --- --- using std::cout; Lets you write cout for this one name Fine inside a function or a .cpp file using namespace std; Brings in every name from std Avoid namespace GU = Game::Utils; A short alias for a long namespace Fine !danger Why this course never writes using namespace std; std contains thousands of names, including common words such as count , max , distance and swap . Importing all of them invites clashes with your own names, and the errors that result are baffling. In a header it is worse still, because it leaks into every file that includes that header. Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference between scope and lifetime? - They mean the same thing + Scope is where a name can be used; lifetime is when the variable exists - Scope is about time; lifetime is about places in the file - Scope applies to functions; lifetime applies to variables Scope is a property of the source code (which lines can use the name). Lifetime is a property of the running program. ? Can code in an outer block use a variable declared in an inner block? - Yes, as long as the inner block has already run - Yes, if the outer code uses the same type + No; inner blocks can see out, but outer blocks cannot see in A name declared inside braces is only in scope until the closing brace. Code outside cannot use it. ? Why avoid using namespace std; ? - It makes every program noticeably slower to run + It pulls in thousands of names that can clash with yours - It stops std::cout from working in that file - It is not allowed in modern C++ It is legal, but it pulls every standard name into scope, which can clash with your names and cause confusing errors. ? What is shadowing? - Two functions with the same name in different files - A variable that is never used - Copying a variable into a function parameter + An inner variable hiding an outer one with the same name The inner variable hides the outer one inside its block. It is legal, but easy to misread, so compilers can warn about it.

title: The shadow
body: This program reads scores until it sees -1 , and should print the highest score. It always prints 0 . The bug is shadowing : a second variable with the same name hides the first one. Find it and fix it. (In the Problems tab the compiler even warns about it.) For the input 40 95 70 -1 the output should be: Highest: 95

title: 3.06  Global Variables, static and Linkage
body: Globals exist for the whole run of the program. Linkage decides whether other .cpp files can see a name. A static local keeps its value between calls. Avoid globals that can change. Global variables A variable defined outside every function is global . Any function below it in the file can use it. cpp include <iostream int g_score{ 0 }; void addPoints() { g_score += 10; } int main() { addPoints(); std::cout << g_score << '\n'; // 10 return 0; } Local variable Global variable --- --- --- Scope Its block The rest of the file Lifetime Until its block ends The whole run: created before main , destroyed after it If you give no value Unpredictable Zero Here scope and lifetime separate. This lifetime is called static storage duration . The g_ prefix is a common convention that marks a name as global. !danger Avoid globals that can change When any function anywhere can modify g_score , a wrong value makes every function a suspect. A function that only uses its parameters can be understood and tested on its own. Pass values in as arguments and hand results back with return . Global constants are fine. Nothing can change them, so nothing can break them. Linkage: can other files see it? Scope is about one file. In a program with several .cpp files there is a further question: can a name defined in one file be used from another? That property is linkage . Linkage Meaning --- --- External One shared thing that every file can refer to Internal Private to this file. Another file may use the same name for something else. What you write at file level decides which you get: Written outside any function Linkage Typical use --- --- --- void helper(); or a function definition external Functions other files call int counter{ 0 }; external (A changeable global: avoid) static void helper() internal A helper that only this file needs namespace { void helper() {} } internal The modern way to say the same constexpr int limit{ 5 }; internal A constant used in one file inline constexpr int limit{ 5 }; in a header external A constant shared by many files To use another file's external variable you declare it with extern : "this exists, and it is defined somewhere else". The usual place for such declarations is a header. inline : defined in a header, without breaking the rule You met the One Definition Rule in 1.08 Multiple Files and Headers : a definition may appear only once in the program. A header is pasted into every file that includes it, so anything defined in a header would break that rule. inline is the exception. It tells the linker: "this definition will turn up in several files; they are all the same one." cpp // constants.h pragma once namespace constants { inline constexpr double gravity{ 9.81 }; inline constexpr int maxPlayers{ 4 }; } This is the standard way to share constants. It is also why the Random helper in 3.04 Random Numbers used inline . static locals: a function with a memory Put static on a local variable and it gets the long lifetime of a global while keeping the small scope of a local. cpp include <iostream int nextId() { static int s_id{ 0 }; // initialized once, the first time through return ++s_id; } int main() { std::cout << nextId() << ' ' << nextId() << ' ' << nextId() << '\n'; // 1 2 3 return 0; } Call s_id before s_id after --- --- --- first 0 1 second 1 2 third 2 3 An ordinary local would be created afresh at 0 on every call. Only nextId can touch s_id , which makes this far safer than a global counter. One word, several meanings static is the most overloaded keyword in C++. Its meaning depends on where it appears. Where Meaning --- --- On a local variable Lives for the whole run and keeps its value between calls On a global variable or function Internal linkage: private to this file On a class member Shared by all objects of the class: 6.05 Static Members and Friends Check yourself quiz ? How does a static local differ from an ordinary local? - It can be used from any function + It is initialized once and keeps its value between calls - It cannot be changed after it is created - It is created again on every call, like a parameter A static local lives for the whole program, so it remembers its value between calls. Its scope is still just the function. ? How should a constant be shared across several files? - As a plain global variable in one .cpp file - As a static variable inside main + As an inline constexpr variable in a header, inside a namespace - Copied by hand into every file that needs it inline constexpr in a header gives every file the same constant without breaking the one-definition rule. ? What is the difference between internal and external linkage? - Internal linkage is for functions; external linkage is for variables - Internal names are faster to call than external ones + An external name is one thing shared by every file; an internal name is private to its own file - There is none; both are visible to every file External linkage means every file refers to the same entity. Internal linkage (for example static at file level) keeps a name private to one file. ? Why are changeable global variables a problem? - They use more memory than local variables - They cannot be initialized - The compiler copies them into every function + Any function can change them, so bugs are hard to trace Anything anywhere can change a non-const global, which makes bugs hard to track down. Constants are fine.

title: A function with a memory
body: Write int nextId() that returns 1 the first time it is called, 2 the second time, 3 the third, and so on. A normal local variable starts afresh on every call. A static local is created once and keeps its value between calls.

title: Get rid of the global
body: applyDiscount reads and changes a global variable. That makes it hard to test and easy to break: any other function could change g_price behind its back. Rewrite it as a function that takes what it needs as parameters and returns its answer: double applyDiscount(double price, double percent) For a price of 200 and 15 percent it returns 170. There must be no global variable left.

title: Running average
body: A sensor produces one reading at a time. Write double runningAverage(double reading) that returns the average of every reading it has been given so far . cpp runningAverage(10.0) // 10 (just the one) runningAverage(20.0) // 15 (10 and 20) runningAverage(30.0) // 20 (10, 20 and 30) The function needs to remember two things between calls. Use static local variables: this is exactly what they are for.

title: 3.07  Input Validation and assert
body:
People type things you did not expect. When std::cin number receives letters it enters a fail state : you must clear() it and discard the bad input. Use assert to catch mistakes in your own code while developing. Two kinds of things go wrong Kind Example Whose fault Response --- --- --- --- Bad input The user types abc for their age Nobody's. It will happen. Detect it and ask again. Never crash. A bug Your function is called with a count of 0 The programmer's Stop loudly so it gets fixed A robust program treats these differently. This lesson covers both. What std::cin does with bad input int age{}; std::cin age; the user types: abc then Enter waiting input: a b c 
 ▲ cannot make a number from 'a' 1. age is set to 0 2. std::cin enters a FAIL STATE: every later is silently skipped 3. "abc" is STILL waiting to be read Point 2 is the dangerous one. After a single bad entry, every later read in the program does nothing, and a loop that asks again will spin for ever. The repair: clear, then discard Step Code Why --- --- --- Detect if (!std::cin) A stream used as a condition is false when it has failed Reset std::cin.clear(); Leaves the fail state so reading works again Discard std::cin.ignore(...) Throws away the bad characters still waiting A reusable getInt cpp include <cstdlib include <iostream include <limits include <string_view void ignoreLine() { std::cin.ignore(std::numeric_limits<std::streamsize ::max(), '
'); } int getInt(std::string_view prompt, int min, int max) { while (true) { std::cout << prompt; int x{}; std::cin x; if (!std::cin) { if (std::cin.eof()) { std::exit(0); // the input was closed: nothing more can arrive } std::cin.clear(); ignoreLine(); std::cout << "That is not a number. Try again.
"; continue; } ignoreLine(); if (x < min x max) { std::cout << "It must be between " << min << " and " << max << ".
"; continue; } return x; } } int main() { int age{ getInt("Enter your age (0-120): ", 0, 120) }; std::cout << "You are " << age << '
'; return 0; } Enter your age (0-120): abc That is not a number. Try again. Enter your age (0-120): 500 It must be between 0 and 120. Enter your age (0-120): 25 You are 25 ignoreLine reads as "skip characters, however many there are, up to and including the next new line". The long expression is simply the largest count the function accepts. Notice the shape: while (true) with continue for every rejection and a single return for success. It is the standard pattern for "keep asking until the answer is acceptable". !tip Keep this function Put getInt and ignoreLine in a header of your own. Almost every interactive program you write from here on needs them. assert : catching your own mistakes An assertion states something that must be true at that point if the program is correct. If it is false, the program stops at once and reports the file and line. cpp include <cassert double average(int total, int count) { assert(count 0 && "count must be positive"); return static_cast<double (total) / count; } Assertion failed: count 0 && "count must be positive", file main.cpp, line 5 The && "text" is a trick for attaching a message: a string literal counts as true, so it does not change the test, and it appears in the report. Property Detail --- --- Checked when While the program runs, in Debug builds In Release builds Removed entirely: no check, no cost Use it for Conditions that can only be false if the code has a bug !danger Never validate input with assert Assertions vanish in Release builds, so the check would disappear from the finished program. And bad input is not a bug: it deserves a polite message, not a crash. static_assert : checked by the compiler cpp static_assert(sizeof(int) = 4, "this program needs an int of at least 32 bits"); The condition must be something the compiler can work out. If it is false, the program does not build. There is no cost at run time at all. Choosing the right tool Situation Tool --- --- The user typed something unusable Validate and ask again Something outside your control failed (a missing file) Report and recover, later with exceptions: 9.05 Exceptions "This cannot happen" in your own logic assert An assumption about types or the platform static_assert Check yourself quiz ? Which two steps recover std::cin after a failed read? - std::cin.ignore() then std::cin.clear() + std::cin.clear() , then std::cin.ignore(...) - std::cin.reset() then read again - Read into a std::string twice First clear() so std::cin works again, then ignore the bad characters still waiting. Ignoring first does nothing while the fail state is set. ? Should assert be used to check what the user typed? - Yes, it is the standard way to validate input - Yes, but only in Release builds, where it is kept + No; it is removed from Release builds and is for programmer mistakes assert catches bugs in your own code. Users typing nonsense is expected, so handle it with ordinary checks. ? What happens to later reads if you do not clear the fail state? - They work normally - The program crashes on the next read + They are all skipped silently, so a loop that asks again never stops - They read the bad input again and fail once more with an error message While std::cin is in the fail state, every read does nothing at once, which turns an "ask again" loop into an endless one. ? How does static_assert differ from assert ? + static_assert is checked by the compiler during the build; assert is checked while the program runs - static_assert only works inside static functions - static_assert is checked while running; assert is checked while compiling - They are the same; static_assert is just the older name static_assert tests a condition known while compiling and stops the build if it fails. assert tests while running.

title: Ask until it is a number
match: Ask until it is a number
body: Write int readInt() that reads a whole number from std::cin and returns it. If the user types something that is not a number, it must recover and try again, as many times as it takes. When std::cin value fails, two things are wrong and both need fixing: 1. std::cin is in a failed state: std::cin.clear(); 2. the bad text is still waiting in the input: throw the rest of the line away with std::cin.ignore(...) . The tests feed it lines such as abc , x9 and then 12 , and expect 12 back.

title: A number in range
body: Write int readIntInRange(int low, int high) . It keeps reading until it gets a whole number between low and high (both allowed). Text that is not a number, and numbers outside the range, are both rejected.

title: Add up what you can
body: A file of measurements has been damaged: some entries are numbers and some are junk. Read entries separated by spaces or new lines until the input ends. Add up the whole numbers, count the entries you had to skip, and print: Sum: 20 Skipped: 2 (for the input 4 x 10 abc 6 ). Reading stops when there is nothing left. A read can fail for two reasons, and you must tell them apart: - the input ran out: std::cin.eof() is true, so stop; - the next entry is not a number: clear the error, read the junk into a std::string to remove it, count it, carry on.

title: 3.08  Halts, goto, and Testing Your Code
match: 3.08 Halts, goto, and Testing Your Code
body:
std::exit ends the program from anywhere; std::abort ends it at once with no clean-up. goto exists and you almost never want it. Testing each function with known inputs as you write it is the cheapest way to catch bugs. Ways a program ends How Clean-up Use it when --- --- --- return from main Complete Always, if you can std::exit(code) Partial A fatal problem deep in the program with no sensible way back std::abort() None Something is so wrong that continuing would do harm cpp include <cstdlib include <iostream include <string_view void fatal(std::string_view message) { std::cerr << "Fatal: " << message << '
'; std::exit(EXIT_FAILURE); } The number handed to std::exit , like the one returned from main , is the program's exit code . EXIT_SUCCESS (0) means it worked. Anything else means it did not, and other programs can check that. "Clean-up" will mean more in Milestones 6 and 7, when objects start releasing files and memory as they are destroyed. That is why returning from main is preferred: it is the only route on which everything is released properly. goto goto jumps to a labelled statement elsewhere in the same function. cpp int attempts{ 0 }; retry: ++attempts; if (attempts < 3) { goto retry; } It works, and a loop says the same thing more clearly. Code that jumps around freely becomes impossible to follow, which programmers call spaghetti code . Loops, break , continue and functions cover everything goto did, with structure a reader can see. The one case people defend is leaving several nested loops at once. A function with return does that better: cpp bool containsPair(int limit, int target) { for (int a{ 1 }; a <= limit; ++a) { for (int b{ 1 }; b <= limit; ++b) { if (a b == target) { return true; // leaves both loops } } } return false; } Testing your code This is the part of the lesson that will change how you work. A test is code that calls your function with inputs whose correct answer you already know, and checks the result. Every Check button you have pressed in Xenon has run tests like that against your code. Testing each function as you finish it means a failure can only be in the few lines you just wrote. Testing a whole program at the end means it could be anywhere. A small test function cpp include <iostream bool isLeapYear(int year) { return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) year % 400 == 0; } int testIsLeapYear() { if (isLeapYear(2024) != true) { return 1; } if (isLeapYear(2023) != false) { return 2; } if (isLeapYear(1900) != false) { return 3; } // divisible by 100 if (isLeapYear(2000) != true) { return 4; } // divisible by 400 return 0; } int main() { const int failed{ testIsLeapYear() }; if (failed != 0) { std::cout << "Test case " << failed << " FAILED
"; } else { std::cout << "All tests passed
"; } return 0; } Tests stay useful after they pass. Run them again whenever you change the function, and they tell you immediately if you broke something that used to work. Choosing test cases Typical values are the least likely to reveal a bug. Bugs gather at the edges. For clamp(value, 0, 10) : Kind of case Examples Why --- --- --- Ordinary 5 gives 5 Does it work at all? On the boundary 0 gives 0 , 10 gives 10 Catches < written for <= Just outside -1 gives 0 , 11 gives 10 Catches off-by-one errors Extremes The largest and smallest int Catches overflow Odd input Low limit above high limit Did you decide what should happen? Coverage A test can only find a bug in code it actually runs. Coverage measures how much of your code the tests execute. Level Meaning --- --- Statement coverage Every line ran at least once Branch coverage Every if went both ways at least once If no test ever makes a condition false, the else branch is untested, however many tests you have. !info Real projects use a testing framework Libraries such as Catch2 and GoogleTest remove the repetitive parts and report failures clearly. The idea is exactly the one above. See 13.09 Testing, Sanitizers, Static Analysis and Tooling . The usual suspects When a test fails, check these first. They account for most logic errors in the first three milestones. Error Example --- --- Wrong comparison age 18 where = was meant Off by one i <= size Loop that never ends The step is missing Precedence a + b / 2 Integer division 1 / 2 x is always 0 Stray semicolon if (x); or for (...); = for == if (x = 0) Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference between std::exit and std::abort ? - There is none - std::abort cleans up first; std::exit stops at once + std::exit does some clean-up first; std::abort does none - std::exit only works inside main std::exit runs some clean-up (such as flushing output) before ending. std::abort stops the program at once. ? Why test boundary values? - Because they are the easiest values to type - Because the compiler only checks the middle of a range + Off-by-one errors and wrong comparisons show up at the edges - Because values in the middle never cause problems Mistakes like < instead of <= only show at the edge of a range, so test values just inside, on and just outside it. ? Why test each function as soon as it is written? - Because functions cannot be tested once main is written + A failure must then be in the few lines just written, which makes it quick to find - Because the compiler forgets functions that are not tested - So that the program needs fewer tests overall Testing straight away keeps the search small: if it fails, the bug is in what you just wrote. ? What is branch coverage? - The number of functions that have at least one test - The share of lines that have a comment - How many if statements a program contains + Whether every decision has been taken both ways by at least one test Branch coverage asks whether each if (and loop condition) has been tested both true and false.

Somebody else wrote a function clamp(value, low, high) that should force a value into a range: - below low it returns low , - above high it returns high , - otherwise it returns value unchanged. Write int testClamp(...) that calls the function with well-chosen inputs and returns 0 if every answer is right, or any other number if something is wrong. The first line of testClamp looks odd because it receives the function to test as a parameter (function pointers are a later lesson). Inside, just call clamp(5, 0, 10) like any function. Loop over the characters once (a for loop over the indexes, reading password i ), setting a bool flag for each thing you find. std::isdigit from <cctype (lesson 2.04) does the digit test, and its relatives std::isupper and std::islower test for upper- and lower-case letters in the same way.
