title: 4.01  Function Overloading and Default Arguments
body:
Overloading gives several functions the same name with different parameters, and the compiler picks the best match for each call. Default arguments supply a value when the caller leaves a parameter out. One name, several functions Two functions may share a name as long as their parameter lists differ. This is overloading . cpp include <iostream int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; } double add(double a, double b) { return a + b; } int add(int a, int b, int c) { return a + b + c; } int main() { std::cout << add(1, 2) << '
'; // the (int, int) version std::cout << add(1.5, 2.5) << '
'; // the (double, double) version std::cout << add(1, 2, 3) << '
'; // the three-parameter version return 0; } The caller writes add and the compiler chooses. That choice is called overload resolution , and it happens entirely at compile time. How the compiler ranks the candidates For each argument, the compiler prefers the candidate that needs the least conversion. Rank Kind of match Example --- --- --- 1 (best) Exact int to int 2 Promotion char or short to int ; float to double 3 Standard conversion int to double ; double to int 4 User-defined conversion Conversions you define on classes (Milestone 6) If two candidates are equally good, the call is ambiguous and does not compile: cpp void f(long value); void f(double value); f(5); // error: int to long and int to double are both rank 3 Fix it by making the argument's type exact ( f(5L) or f(5.0) ) or by adding an int overload. What makes two overloads different? The functions differ in Allowed? --- --- Number of parameters Yes Types of parameters Yes Only the return type No Only the parameter names No The return type is not considered, because a call such as add(1, 2); gives the compiler no way to tell which result you wanted. Default arguments A parameter can name a value to use when the caller supplies none. cpp include <iostream void printLine(int length = 20, char symbol = '-') { for (int i{ 0 }; i < length; ++i) { std::cout << symbol; } std::cout << '
'; } int main() { printLine(); // 20 dashes printLine(5); // 5 dashes printLine(5, ' '); // 5 stars return 0; } Rule Detail --- --- Defaults go on the right void f(int a, int b = 2) is fine. void f(int a = 1, int b) is not. Arguments fill from the left You cannot skip length and give only symbol . State the default once When a function has a declaration in a header, put the default there and not in the definition. !warning Overloads and defaults can collide void log(int level); together with void log(int level, int indent = 0); makes log(3) ambiguous. Use one mechanism or the other for a given name. Forbidding an overload = delete declares that a particular overload must not be called. It is a precise way to block an unwanted conversion. cpp void printInt(int x); void printInt(char) = delete; void printInt(bool) = delete; printInt(5); // fine printInt('a'); // error: this overload is deleted Without the deleted versions, 'a' would be promoted to int and print as 97. Check yourself quiz ? Can two functions differ only in their return type? - Yes, the compiler picks one from the type you store the result in + No, the compiler chooses an overload from the arguments alone - Yes, but only if one of them returns void - Only if they are in different files Overload resolution looks only at the arguments, so the return type cannot tell two functions apart. ? Is void f(int x = 1, int y); valid? - Yes, y simply has no default - Yes, and calling f() uses 1 for both + No, defaulted parameters must come after the others Defaults fill in from the right, so every parameter after one with a default must also have one. Write void f(int y, int x = 1); . ? What makes a call ambiguous? + Two or more overloads are equally good matches - No overload matches the arguments exactly - The function has default arguments - The overloads are declared in different orders If one overload is a better match the compiler picks it. Ambiguity means two are tied, and the call is a compile error. ? What does void print(bool) = delete; achieve? - It removes every overload of print - It makes print return nothing when given a bool + Calling print with a bool becomes a compile error - It deletes print at the end of the program A deleted overload still takes part in choosing, so a bool argument picks it and the call fails to compile, rather than quietly converting to print(int) .

title: Two kinds of area
body: Write two functions that share the name area : - double area(double radius) returns the area of a circle (use 3.14159 for pi), - double area(double width, double height) returns the area of a rectangle. The compiler picks the right one by counting the arguments.

title: A default argument
body: Write std::string repeat(std::string_view text, int times = 2) that returns text repeated times times. If the caller leaves times out, it repeats twice. cpp repeat("ab") // "abab" repeat("ab", 3) // "ababab"

title: One name, four types
body: Write four overloads of describe , each returning a std::string that names the type and shows the value: Call Returns --- --- describe(42) "int: 42" describe(2.5) "double: 2.500000" describe(true) "bool: true" describe(std::string_view{ "hi" }) "text: hi" std::to_string turns a number into text (for a double it always shows six decimals).

title: 4.02  Function Templates
body:
A template is a pattern for a function with a placeholder type T . The compiler generates a real function for each type you use it with. Write it once and it works for int , double , std::string and more. The problem: the same code for every type Overloading lets these share a name, but you still write each body: cpp int maxOf(int a, int b) { return a b ? a : b; } double maxOf(double a, double b) { return a b ? a : b; } // ...and again for every other type The bodies are identical. Only the type changes. A function template lets you write the body once and leave the type as a parameter. cpp include <iostream include <string template <typename T T maxOf(T a, T b) { return a b ? a : b; } int main() { std::cout << maxOf(3, 7) << '
'; // T is int std::cout << maxOf(2.5, 1.5) << '
'; // T is double std::cout << maxOf<char ('a', 'z') << '
'; // T given explicitly return 0; } template <typename T introduces T as a type parameter : a stand-in for a type that is filled in later. Instantiation A template is not a function. It is a recipe from which the compiler makes functions on demand. Generating a concrete function from a template is called instantiation . It happens at compile time, once per distinct type, and the result is exactly as fast as a function written by hand. Deducing T Usually you do not say what T is. The compiler works it out from the arguments, which is called template argument deduction . Call Result --- --- maxOf(3, 7) Both are int , so T is int maxOf(3, 7.5) Error: T cannot be both int and double maxOf<double (3, 7.5) You chose T ; the 3 is converted to 3.0 Deduction does not apply conversions. Each argument must agree on T exactly. More than one type parameter When the arguments may legitimately have different types, give each its own parameter: cpp template <typename T, typename U auto addMixed(T a, U b) { return a + b; } addMixed(3, 7.5); // T is int, U is double, the result is double auto as the return type asks the compiler to work it out from the return statement. The short form Since C++20, auto in a parameter list makes a function a template without the template line: cpp auto addMixed(auto a, auto b) { return a + b; } Each auto parameter is its own independent type parameter. The type has to support what the body does A template compiles for a given type only if every operation in its body is valid for that type. cpp struct Cat {}; maxOf(Cat{}, Cat{}); // error: Cat has no operator The error is reported at the point of instantiation, and for templates it can be long. C++20 concepts let a template state its requirements up front, which gives far clearer errors: 9.04 Concepts (C++20) . Templates live in headers To instantiate a template, the compiler must see its full body at the place where it is used. A declaration alone is not enough. Kind of function Declaration Definition --- --- --- Ordinary Header .cpp file Template Header Header as well Check yourself quiz ? When is a function actually generated from a template? - When the program starts running - When the template is first written in the header + At compile time, when the template is used with a specific type - Once per call, while the program runs Using the template with a type makes the compiler generate (instantiate) that version during the build. ? Why does maxOf(3, 4.5) fail? - Templates cannot work with double + T would have to be both int and double - maxOf needs at least three arguments - The compiler converts both to int and loses the .5 Deduction finds int from one argument and double from the other, so it fails. Write maxOf<double (3, 4.5) or use two type parameters. ? Why must a template's body be in the header? - Because templates cannot be declared without a body - Because the linker refuses to link .cpp files with templates - Because headers compile faster than .cpp files + The compiler needs the full body to generate code for each type To instantiate a template for a type, the compiler must see its full definition in that file, so it goes in the header. ? What happens if you use a template with a type that lacks a required operation? - The function silently does nothing for that type - The program crashes when that line runs + A compile error at the point of instantiation - The compiler converts the value to int first The generated function would contain invalid code, such as < on a type that has none, so the build fails.

title: maxOf for any type
body: Write one function template maxOf that returns the larger of two values of the same type. It should work for int , double , std::string and anything else that supports .

title: clampValue
body: Write a template clampValue(value, low, high) that forces value into the range from low to high : - below low , it returns low , - above high , it returns high , - otherwise value . All three parameters have the same type T .

title: A small generic toolkit
body: Write three templates: - largestOf(a, b, c) returns the largest of three values of the same type. - isBetween(value, low, high) returns true when low <= value <= high . - addMixed(a, b) adds two values that may have different types (for example an int and a double ) and returns the natural result type. This one needs two template parameters and an auto return type.

title: 4.03  References
body:
A reference is a second name for an existing variable. Pass by reference to let a function change the caller's variable. Pass by const reference to avoid copying something large. A second name for the same box cpp include <iostream int main() { int x{ 5 }; int& ref{ x }; // ref is another name for x ref = 10; std::cout << x << '
'; // 10 return 0; } x ─┐ ├──▶ ┌──────┐ ref ─┘ │ 10 │ one box, two names └──────┘ int& reads "reference to int". There is no second box. Anything done to ref is done to x . Rule Consequence --- --- A reference must be initialized int& r; does not compile It cannot be made to refer to something else ref = y; copies the value of y into x It always refers to something There is no "empty" reference Pass by value and pass by reference This is what references are for. cpp include <iostream void addOneByValue(int n) { ++n; // changes the copy } void addOneByReference(int& n) { ++n; // changes the caller's variable } int main() { int score{ 5 }; addOneByValue(score); std::cout << score << '
'; // 5 addOneByReference(score); std::cout << score << '
'; // 6 return 0; } Pass by const reference Copying an int costs nothing. Copying a std::string of a million characters copies a million characters. A const reference gives the function access to the original with a promise not to change it. cpp void printReport(const std::string& report) { std::cout << report << '
'; } No copy is made, and the compiler rejects any attempt to modify report inside the function. Choosing a parameter type This decision comes up for every function you will ever write. Learn the three outcomes. Returning more than one value A function has one return value. Reference parameters, often called out-parameters , are one way round that: cpp void minMax(int a, int b, int& outMin, int& outMax) { outMin = a < b ? a : b; outMax = a < b ? b : a; } int low{}; int high{}; minMax(8, 3, low, high); // low is 3, high is 8 It works, but nothing at the call site shows that low and high will be changed. Returning a struct is usually clearer: 4.06 Structs . Dangling references A reference is only valid while the thing it refers to exists. cpp int& broken() { int local{ 5 }; return local; // local is destroyed here } The caller receives a reference to a variable that no longer exists. Using it is undefined behaviour. A reference in this state is said to be dangling . !danger Never return a reference to a local variable Return by value instead. Returning a reference is only safe when the object outlives the function call, for example a parameter that was itself passed by reference. What a reference can bind to Declaration Allowed? Why --- --- --- int& r{ x }; Yes x is a variable int& r{ 5 }; No 5 is a temporary value with no lasting home const int& r{ 5 }; Yes A const reference may bind to a temporary and keeps it alive This is why const std::string& parameters accept string literals and results of expressions. Two terms you will meet often from here on: Term Roughly Examples --- --- --- lvalue Something with a name and a lasting location x , name , values 0 rvalue A temporary value 5 , x + 1 , the result of a function returning by value They matter a great deal in 7.05 Move Semantics . Check yourself quiz ? After int& r{ a }; r = b; , what has changed? + a now holds the value of b ; r still refers to a - r now refers to b , and a is unchanged - b now holds the value of a - Nothing; a reference cannot be assigned to A reference cannot be re-aimed. Assigning to r assigns to a , the variable it names. ? What is the best parameter type for a function that only reads a std::string ? - std::string , so the function gets its own copy - std::string& , so no copy is made + const std::string& , or std::string_view - std::string , so the caller can pass nullptr A const reference (or a std::string_view ) avoids the copy and guarantees the function cannot change the caller's string. ? Why is returning a reference to a local variable dangerous? - It makes a copy that is slow to create - The compiler cannot work out the return type + The local is destroyed when the function returns, so the reference dangles - The caller can change the local after the function ends Once the function returns, the local no longer exists, so using the reference is undefined behaviour. ? Why can const int& bind to 5 when int& cannot? - 5 is too small to need a non-const reference - int& can only bind to variables declared const - They both can; int& just gives a warning + A const reference may bind to a temporary; a non-const one may not A non-const reference promises it can change what it refers to, which makes no sense for a literal. A const reference can safely hold on to a temporary.

title: Swap, for real this time
body: Write void swapInts(int& a, int& b) that exchanges the two variables the caller passes in. Without the & the function would swap two private copies and the caller would see nothing. With it, a and b are other names for the caller's own variables.

title: Read without copying
body: Write int countSpaces(const std::string& text) that returns how many space characters are in the text. The parameter is a const reference : the function reads the caller's string directly (no copy, which matters when the text is long) and promises not to change it.

title: Two answers from one function
body: A function can only return one value, but it can hand back more through reference parameters. Write void minMax(int a, int b, int c, int& smallest, int& largest) . It stores the smallest of the three numbers in smallest and the largest in largest .

title: Shout
body: Write two functions that show the two reasons to use a reference: - void toUpperInPlace(std::string& text) changes the caller's string, turning every letter into upper case. - std::string shout(const std::string& text) leaves the caller's string alone and returns a new one: the upper-case version with "!" on the end. shout should reuse toUpperInPlace on a copy rather than repeating its loop. std::toupper from <cctype converts one character. It takes and returns an int , so convert back to char .

title: 4.04  Pointers
body:
A pointer is a variable that stores a memory address . &x gives the address of x . ptr follows the address to the value. Unlike a reference, a pointer can be nullptr and can be aimed at something else. A variable that holds an address Every variable lives at an address in memory ( 2.01 Memory, Bits and Fundamental Types ). A pointer stores one of those addresses. cpp int x{ 42 }; int ptr{ &x }; // ptr holds the address of x ptr x ┌────────────┐ ┌────────────┐ │ 0x7ff0 ──┼───────────▶ │ 42 │ └────────────┘ └────────────┘ lives at 0x7ff8 lives at 0x7ff0 Expression Meaning Value here --- --- --- x The value of x 42 &x The address of x 0x7ff0 ptr The address stored in ptr 0x7ff0 ptr The value at that address 42 &ptr The address of the pointer itself 0x7ff8 Following a pointer to the thing it points at is called dereferencing . cpp ptr = 100; // change x through the pointer std::cout << x << '
'; // 100 !info and & each have two meanings Symbol In a declaration In an expression --- --- --- int p : p is a pointer to int p : dereference p & int& r : r is a reference to int &x : the address of x Aiming a pointer somewhere else cpp include <iostream int main() { int a{ 1 }; int b{ 2 }; int p{ &a }; std::cout << p << '
'; // 1 p = &b; // p now points at b std::cout << p << '
'; // 2 return 0; } Assigning to p changes where it points . Assigning to p changes the thing it points at . Keep those two apart and pointers stop being confusing. nullptr : pointing at nothing A pointer can deliberately point at nothing. That value is nullptr . cpp int p{ nullptr }; if (p != nullptr) { std::cout << p << '
'; } else { std::cout << "no value
"; } A pointer converts to false when it is null, so if (p) means the same as if (p != nullptr) . !danger Dereferencing a null pointer is undefined behaviour In practice the program usually crashes with an access violation . Whenever a pointer might be null, test it before you dereference it. Passing an address to a function cpp void reset(int p) { if (p) { p = 0; } } int score{ 99 }; reset(&score); // the & at the call shows that score may be changed reset(nullptr); // allowed: "there is nothing to reset" A pointer parameter can express "there might be no object". A reference parameter cannot. Pointers and const const can apply to the thing pointed at, to the pointer itself, or to both. Read the declaration from right to left. Declaration Read as Change the value through it? Aim it elsewhere? --- --- --- --- const int p pointer to const int No Yes int const p const pointer to int Yes No const int const p const pointer to const int No No The first is by far the most common. It means "I will look, but not touch", exactly like a const reference. Pointers to structs: - To reach a member through a pointer, use - . cpp struct Point { int x{}; int y{}; }; Point pt{ 3, 4 }; Point pp{ &pt }; std::cout << ( pp).x << '
'; // 3: dereference, then take the member std::cout << pp- x << '
'; // 3: the same thing, written the usual way Pointer or reference? Reference T& Pointer T --- --- --- Can be null No Yes Can be aimed elsewhere No Yes Must be initialized Yes No, but always do it Used like The variable itself p and p- Use a reference unless you need one of the two things only a pointer can do. Pointers become essential with dynamic memory: 7.02 new and delete — Dynamic Memory . Dangling pointers Like a reference, a pointer can outlive its target. cpp int p{}; { int temp{ 5 }; p = &temp; } // temp is destroyed here p = 1; // undefined behaviour: p is dangling Nothing sets p to null for you. It still holds the old address, and that memory may now be used for something else. Check yourself quiz ? After int p{ &x }; p = 7; , what is x ? - Unchanged - The address 7 + 7 - Undefined, because p was never initialized p is the variable p points at, so assigning through it changes x to 7. ? What is the difference between const int p and int const p ? + The first cannot change the value it points at; the second cannot be aimed at a different address - The first cannot be aimed elsewhere; the second cannot change the value - There is none; the const can go on either side - The first points at a constant; the second is not allowed Read right to left: const int is a pointer to a const int; int const is a const pointer to an int. ? When would you choose a pointer over a reference? - Always, because pointers are faster - Whenever the function only reads the value it is given + When it may point at nothing, or at different objects over time - Whenever the value is an int A pointer can be nullptr and can be re-aimed. When neither is needed, a reference is simpler and safer. ? What is the difference between p = &b; and p = b; ? - There is none - The first copies b 's value; the second makes p point at b - Both make p point at b ; the second also copies its value + The first makes p point at b ; the second copies b 's value into whatever p points at Without you change the pointer itself. With you change the object it points at.

If p is null it does nothing. - int valueOr(const int p, int fallback) returns the pointed-to value, or fallback if p is null. p follows the pointer to the value it points at. Following a null pointer crashes the program, so always check first.

title: Swap through pointers

This is the C way of doing what swapInts(int&, int&) did in the last lesson. Notice the difference at the call site: the caller has to write &x to pass an address.

title: Which is larger?
body: Write const int largerOf(const int a, const int b) . - If either pointer is null, return nullptr . - Otherwise return whichever pointer points at the larger value ( a if they are equal). It returns a pointer , not a value: the caller can see which of their variables won.

title: Find the first negative
body: Write int findFirstNegative(int a, int b, int c) . It looks at the three pointed-to numbers in order and returns a pointer to the first one that is below zero. If none is negative it returns nullptr . Any of the three pointers may itself be null: skip those. Because it returns a pointer to the caller's own variable, the caller can change the number it found. The tests do exactly that.

title: 4.05  Enums
body: An enum is a type with a fixed list of named values, such as enum class Color { red, green, blue }; . Use enum class : its names stay inside the enum and it does not silently turn into a number. A type for "one of these" Many values come from a small fixed set: a direction, a day of the week, the state of a game. You could store them as numbers. cpp int direction{ 2 }; // 2 means... south? Nothing says so, and 57 is also accepted. An enumeration (an enum) gives the set a type and each member a name. cpp include <iostream enum class Direction { north, east, south, west, }; int main() { Direction d{ Direction::east }; if (d == Direction::east) { std::cout << "Heading east\n"; } return 0; } Each named value is an enumerator . Behind the scenes they are numbered from 0 in the order written: Direction::north is 0 Direction::east is 1 Direction::south is 2 Direction::west is 3 With an int With an enum --- --- The meaning of 2 lives in your head Direction::south says what it is Any number is accepted Only the listed values exist A direction can be passed where a colour is expected Different enums are different types Enums and switch This is the pairing promised in 3.02 switch . cpp std::string_view toString(Direction d) { switch (d) { case Direction::north: return "north"; case Direction::east: return "east"; case Direction::south: return "south"; case Direction::west: return "west"; } return "unknown"; } !tip Leave out default when switching on an enum With every enumerator listed and no default , the compiler warns you if you later add an enumerator and forget to handle it here. A default would hide that warning. Converting to and from numbers An enum class does not convert to an integer by itself. That strictness is deliberate: it stops enumerators being used in arithmetic by accident. cpp int n{ static_cast<int (Direction::south) }; // 2 Direction d{ static_cast<Direction (3) }; // Direction::west To print an enumerator's number, cast it. To print its name, write a function like toString above. The older, unscoped enum Without the word class you get the original C form. You will meet it in older code. cpp enum Color { red, green, blue }; enum Fruit { apple, banana, red }; // error: red is already defined Color c{ red }; int x{ c }; // converts silently enum enum class --- --- --- How you write a value red Color::red Names spill into the surrounding scope Yes No Converts to int silently Yes No Use it Rarely By default Because its names are contained, enum class is also called a scoped enumeration . Choosing the numbers and the size cpp enum class HttpStatus { ok = 200, notFound = 404, serverError = 500, }; enum class Tile : std::uint8_t { empty, wall, water, }; Feature Effect --- --- name = value Sets that enumerator's number. Later ones continue counting from it. : type after the name Sets the underlying type used for storage. The default is int . A Tile here occupies one byte, which matters when a map holds a million of them. using enum Inside a scope where the enum's name would be repeated many times, C++20 lets you import the enumerators: cpp switch (d) { using enum Direction; case north: return "north"; case east: return "east"; case south: return "south"; case west: return "west"; } Looping over an enum There is no built-in way to visit every enumerator. The common idiom adds a final count entry, whose number equals how many real entries there are. cpp enum class Suit { clubs, diamonds, hearts, spades, count }; for (int i{ 0 }; i < static_cast<int (Suit::count); ++i) { const Suit suit{ static_cast<Suit (i) }; // use suit } This works only when the enumerators have their default numbers, 0 upwards with no gaps. Check yourself quiz ? Why prefer enum class to a plain enum ? - It uses less memory - It can hold strings as well as numbers + Its names are scoped and it does not convert to an integer without a cast - It can be used in a switch and a plain enum cannot enum class names are written Color::red , so they cannot clash, and it will not silently turn into an int . ? How do you print an enum class value as a number? - std::cout << value; + std::cout << static_cast<int (value); - std::cout << int value; - std::cout << value.number(); An enum class does not convert to an integer by itself, so cast it with static_cast<int . ? Why omit default when a switch handles every enumerator? - default is not allowed in a switch on an enum - It makes the switch run faster + The compiler can then warn when a new enumerator is added and not handled - Without default every case falls through With a default , a new enumerator silently goes there. Without one, the compiler can point at every switch that misses it. ? What does enum class Tile : std::uint8_t change? - It limits the enum to 8 enumerators + The underlying type: each Tile is stored in one byte instead of an int - It makes Tile convert to std::uint8_t automatically - It numbers the enumerators in steps of 8 The type after : is the underlying type, so each value takes one byte. It still needs a cast to become a number.

Define enum class Light { green, yellow, red }; and write: Function Returns --- --- Light next(Light now) the light that follows: green, then yellow, then red, then green again int seconds(Light light) how long it stays on: green 30, yellow 5, red 25 std::string_view action(Light light) "go" , "slow down" or "stop" int secondsFor(Light start, int changes) total time spent, starting at start and showing changes lights in a row (including the first) secondsFor(Light::green, 3) is 30 + 5 + 25 = 60.

title: 4.06  Structs
body:
A struct bundles related variables into one new type, such as struct Player { std::string name; int hp; }; . Reach the members with . , or - through a pointer. Pass structs by const& . Data that belongs together A player has a name, hit points and a level. As loose variables, two players already need six names, and nothing ties hp1 to name1 . A struct defines a new type that holds them as one unit. cpp struct Player { std::string name{}; int hp{ 100 }; int level{ 1 }; }; Player hero ┌────────────────────────────┐ │ name : "Aria" │ │ hp : 100 │ │ level : 1 │ └────────────────────────────┘ The variables inside are members . The value after each one is its default member initializer : what the member holds unless you say otherwise. Give every member one, for the same reason every variable gets a starting value. Creating and using one cpp include <iostream include <string struct Player { std::string name{}; int hp{ 100 }; int level{ 1 }; }; int main() { Player a{}; // all defaults Player b{ "Aria", 80, 5 }; // values in member order Player c{ .name = "Bo", .level = 3 }; // by name; hp keeps its default b.hp -= 10; std::cout << b.name << " has " << b.hp << " HP
"; std::cout << c.name << " is level " << c.level << " with " << c.hp << " HP
"; return 0; } Form Name Notes --- --- --- Player a{}; Value initialization Every member takes its default Player b{ "Aria", 80, 5 }; Aggregate initialization Values are matched to members in declaration order Player c{ .name = "Bo", .level = 3 }; Designated initializers (C++20) Names must appear in declaration order; skipped members keep their default The dot in b.hp is the member access operator . Structs and functions Structs follow the parameter rules from 4.03 References . They are rarely cheap to copy, so: cpp void printPlayer(const Player& p) // only reads: const reference { std::cout << p.name << " (level " << p.level << ") HP: " << p.hp << '
'; } void heal(Player& p, int amount) // modifies: reference { p.hp += amount; } Player makePlayer(std::string_view name) // creates: return by value { return Player{ std::string{ name }, 100, 1 }; } Returning several values A struct is the clean answer to "a function can return only one thing". cpp struct MinMax { int min{}; int max{}; }; MinMax findMinMax(int a, int b) { return a < b ? MinMax{ a, b } : MinMax{ b, a }; } auto low, high { findMinMax(9, 4) }; // low is 4, high is 9 The last line uses structured bindings : it unpacks the members into separate named variables, in order. Structs inside structs A member can be another struct. cpp struct Vec2 { double x{}; double y{}; }; struct Entity { std::string name{}; Vec2 position{}; Vec2 velocity{}; }; Entity ball{ "Ball", { 0.0, 0.0 }, { 1.5, -2.0 } }; ball.position.x += ball.velocity.x; Building types out of smaller types like this is called composition . Most of a real program's design is done this way. Through a pointer cpp Player pp{ &a }; pp- hp = 50; // the same as ( pp).hp = 50 Size and padding A struct can be larger than the sum of its members. cpp struct S { char c{}; int i{}; }; // sizeof(S) is usually 8, not 5 c pad pad pad i i i i Processors read an int fastest when it starts at an address that is a multiple of 4, so the compiler inserts unused padding bytes to arrange that. Declaring members from largest to smallest usually minimises it. The full story is in 13.02 Memory Layout, Alignment, Unions and Bit Fields . What comes next A struct can also contain functions. By convention, struct is used for plain bundles of data with everything accessible, and class for types that protect their data behind functions. That is Milestone 6: 6.01 Classes and Objects . Check yourself quiz ? How do you access a member through a pointer? - With . , as in ptr.member - With , as in ptr member + With - , as in ptr- member - With & , as in &ptr.member ptr- member is shorthand for ( ptr).member . Plain . works on the struct itself, not on a pointer to it. ? Why pass a struct by const& ? - So the function can change the caller's struct + It avoids copying every member and the function cannot modify it - Because structs cannot be passed by value - So that the struct is destroyed when the function ends A const reference gives read-only access without a copy. Passing by value would copy every member. ? What does auto a, b { f() }; do? - It creates an array of two elements - It calls f twice, storing the results in a and b - It declares a lambda with two captures + It unpacks the members of the returned struct into a and b This is a structured binding: the members of the struct returned by f() are given the names a and b , in order. ? Why might sizeof a struct exceed the total size of its members? + The compiler adds padding so members are suitably aligned - The struct also stores the names of its members - Every struct holds a hidden pointer to itself - sizeof counts the struct's functions too Padding bytes keep members aligned. Ordering members from largest to smallest often reduces it.

title: 4.07  auto, Type Deduction and Type Aliases
match: 4.07 auto, Type Deduction and Type Aliases
body: auto asks the compiler to work out a variable's type from its initializer. using Name = Type; gives a type a second name. Both shorten code; use them where the type is obvious or noisy. auto : let the compiler name the type Every initializer already has a type. With auto , the variable simply takes it. cpp auto a{ 5 }; // int auto b{ 5.0 }; // double auto c{ 'x' }; // char auto d{ add(2, 3) }; // whatever add returns This is type deduction . The variable still has one fixed type, chosen at compile time. auto is not "any type". !warning Text in quotes is not a std::string auto s{ "hi" }; deduces const char , the primitive C form of a string, because that is what a string literal is. Write the type out when you want a std::string . auto drops const and references This is the rule that catches people. cpp const int ci{ 5 }; auto x{ ci }; // int: const is dropped const auto y{ ci }; // const int: you added it back int n{ 1 }; int& ref{ n }; auto z{ ref }; // int: a COPY of n, not a reference auto& z2{ ref }; // int&: a reference to n Plain auto always means "a fresh copy". Anything more, you ask for: You write You get --- --- auto A copy, not const const auto A const copy auto& A reference const auto& A const reference: no copy, no modification const auto& is the form you will write most, in loops over containers in Milestone 5. When to use it Good use Why --- --- The type is written on the same line auto p{ static_cast<double (x) }; repeats nothing The type is long and adds nothing Iterators and lambdas, coming in Milestone 5 Loop variables for (const auto& item : items) Poor use Why --- --- The type is not obvious from the line auto x{ getValue() }; hides whether x is an int or a double You want a conversion auto never converts; it takes exactly the initializer's type The test is whether a reader can tell the type without looking elsewhere. Deduced return types A function can use auto in place of its return type. cpp auto average(int total, int count) { return static_cast<double (total) / count; // deduced: double } Every return in the function must produce the same type. For functions other people call, writing the return type out is usually kinder to the reader. You will also see the trailing return type form, which means the same as the ordinary one: cpp auto add(int a, int b) - int { return a + b; } Type aliases using gives an existing type an additional name. cpp using Score = int; using Inventory = std::vector<std::string ; Score best{ 9001 }; Benefit Example --- --- States intent Score says more than int Shortens long types Inventory instead of std::vector<std::string One place to change Switching Score to long long later is a one-line edit The older spelling is typedef int Score; . It does the same thing and reads backwards. Prefer using . !note An alias is not a new type Score and int are the same type and mix freely. The compiler will not stop you passing a Score where an Age is expected. For a type that is truly distinct, use a struct or an enum class . decltype decltype(expression) is the type of an expression, without evaluating it. cpp int x{ 5 }; decltype(x) y{ 10 }; // y is int Unlike auto , it keeps const and references exactly as they are. It earns its place in templates, where you need to name a type you cannot write directly. Check yourself quiz ? After const int& r{ x }; auto y{ r }; , what is the type of y ? - const int& - const int + int - int& Plain auto drops both the const and the reference, so y is a separate, changeable copy. Write const auto& to keep them. ? Is using Age = int; a new, distinct type? + No, it is another name for int and the two are interchangeable - Yes, an Age cannot be assigned to an int - Yes, but only inside the namespace where it is declared - No, it creates a variable called Age with type int A type alias is just a second name. The compiler treats Age and int as exactly the same type. ? What does const auto& give you? - A copy that cannot be changed + A const reference: no copy, and no changes through it - A reference that can be re-aimed at other objects - A pointer to a constant const auto& deduces the type but keeps the reference and the const, so it avoids a copy and is read-only. ? When does auto make code worse? - Whenever the type is longer than five characters - Always; auto should be avoided - When used for loop variables + When it hides a type that matters, or blocks a wanted conversion auto is great when the type is obvious or long. It hurts when the type matters but is hidden, or when it stops a conversion you wanted.

title: 5.01  std::vector Basics
body: std::vector<T is a resizable list of elements stored side by side in memory. Reach elements with v i (fast, unchecked) or v.at(i) (checked). It is the container to reach for first. Many values of one type A program that handles a hundred scores does not want a hundred variables. A container holds a collection of values under one name, and std::vector is the standard general-purpose one. cpp include <vector std::vector<int scores{ 90, 72, 85, 64 }; index: 0 1 2 3 ┌──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┐ scores: │ 90 │ 72 │ 85 │ 64 │ scores.size() is 4 └──────┴──────┴──────┴──────┘ The type in angle brackets is the element type . std::vector is a template ( 4.02 Function Templates ), which is why one container works for any type. The elements sit next to each other in one block of memory. They are contiguous , and that is what makes a vector fast: the address of element i is a single calculation, and the processor reads neighbouring memory quickly. Creating a vector Code Result --- --- std::vector<int a{}; Empty std::vector<int b{ 1, 2, 3 }; Three elements: 1, 2, 3 std::vector<int c(5); Five elements, all 0 std::vector<int d(5, 7); Five elements, all 7 std::vector e{ 1.5, 2.5 }; Element type deduced: std::vector<double !warning Braces and parentheses mean different things here std::vector<int v{ 5 }; is one element with the value 5. std::vector<int v(5); is five elements, all zero. Braces list the contents. Parentheses give a count. This is the one place in the course where you must use parentheses on purpose. Reaching the elements Code Meaning If the index is out of range --- --- --- v i Element i Undefined behaviour: no check is made v.at(i) Element i Throws a std::out_of_range error v.front() The first element Undefined behaviour if empty v.back() The last element Undefined behaviour if empty v.size() The number of elements v.empty() Whether the size is 0 Valid indexes run from 0 to v.size() - 1 . !tip Xenon's Debug build checks v i for you In a Debug build the standard library verifies indexes and stops the program with a clear message. In Release that check is gone, so the habit of staying in range has to be yours. Adding and removing cpp include <iostream include <vector int main() { std::vector<int v{ 1, 2, 3 }; v.push_back(4); // 1 2 3 4 v.pop_back(); // 1 2 3 v.insert(v.begin(), 0); // 0 1 2 3 v.erase(v.begin() + 1); // 0 2 3 v.resize(5); // 0 2 3 0 0 std::cout << v.size() << '\n'; v.clear(); // empty return 0; } Operation Effect Cost --- --- --- push_back(x) Add at the end Fast pop_back() Remove the last Fast insert(position, x) Insert before a position Slow in the middle: every later element shifts along erase(position) Remove at a position Slow in the middle, for the same reason resize(n) Change the size to n Adds default values or drops the tail clear() Remove everything v.begin() is the position of the first element, so v.begin() + 1 is the position of index 1. Positions like these are iterators , covered in 5.06 Iterators and STL Algorithms . Vectors and functions A vector may hold millions of elements. Passing it by value copies all of them. cpp double average(const std::vector<int & v) // reads: const reference { if (v.empty()) { return 0.0; } int sum{ 0 }; for (int x : v) { sum += x; } return static_cast<double (sum) / static_cast<double (v.size()); } void addBonus(std::vector<int & v, int bonus) // modifies: reference { for (int& x : v) { x += bonus; } } std::vector<int makeRange(int n) // creates: return by value { std::vector<int result{}; for (int i{ 0 }; i < n; ++i) { result.push_back(i); } return result; } Returning a vector by value is cheap: the contents are handed over, not copied. The mechanism is explained in 7.05 Move Semantics . Vectors of structs The element type can be anything, including your own types. cpp struct Item { std::string name{}; double price{}; }; std::vector<Item cart{ { "Milk", 1.99 }, { "Bread", 2.49 } }; cart.push_back({ "Eggs", 3.10 }); std::cout << cart 2 .name << '\n'; // Eggs A vector of structs is the workhorse data structure of most programs. Check yourself quiz ? What does std::vector<int v(3, 9); contain? - Two elements, 3 and 9 + Three elements, each 9 - Nine elements, each 3 - Three elements: 0, 0 and 9 With round brackets the first number is the count and the second is the value. Braces, { 3, 9 } , would give the two elements 3 and 9. ? Why pass a vector by const& ? - So the function can add elements to the caller's vector - Because vectors cannot be passed by value + Passing by value copies every element, which is slow and usually pointless - So the vector is emptied when the function returns A const& gives read-only access to the caller's vector without copying it. Use a plain & only when the function must change it. ? What is the index of the last element of v ? - v.size() + v.size() - 1 - v.size() + 1 - -1 Indexes start at 0, so the last one is size() - 1 , provided the vector is not empty. v v.size() is one past the end. ? What is the difference between v i and v.at(i) ? - There is none - v i checks the index; v.at(i) does not - v.at(i) returns a copy; v i returns the element itself + v.at(i) checks the index and reports an error if it is out of range; v i does not check v i makes no check, so a bad index is undefined behaviour. v.at(i) checks and reports the error.
