title: 7.06  Smart Pointers
body:
Smart pointers are RAII wrappers that delete a heap object automatically. std::unique_ptr has one owner and is the default. std::shared_ptr shares ownership by counting references. std::weak_ptr observes without owning. Create them with std::make_unique and std::make_shared . Ownership, in the type 7.02 new and delete — Dynamic Memory ended on a problem: a raw pointer cannot say who is responsible for deleting. A smart pointer is a small class that owns a heap object and deletes it in its destructor. It is RAII for new . All three live in <memory . std::unique_ptr : one owner cpp include <iostream include <memory include <string struct Player { std::string name{}; int hp{ 100 }; }; int main() { auto hero{ std::make_unique<Player ("Aria", 100) }; hero- hp -= 10; std::cout << hero- name << ' ' << hero- hp << '
'; return 0; } // the Player is deleted here, automatically hero (unique_ptr) ──owns──▶ Player "Aria" hero goes out of scope: its destructor deletes the Player Property Detail --- --- Use Like a pointer: p , p- member , if (p) Cost The same size and speed as a raw pointer Copying Not allowed: two owners would both delete Moving Allowed: ownership is transferred cpp auto a{ std::make_unique<int (5) }; auto b{ std::move(a) }; // b now owns the int; a is null if (!a) { std::cout << "a is empty
"; } std::make_unique<T (arguments) allocates and constructs in one step and returns the unique_ptr . There is no new in your code and no delete anywhere. Passing smart pointers to functions This is where people go wrong. Most functions should not mention the smart pointer at all. The function wants to Parameter type Call --- --- --- Use the object Player& or const Player& heal( hero); Use it, and it may be absent Player inspect(hero.get()); Take over ownership std::unique_ptr<Player by value adopt(std::move(hero)); A function that only uses a Player has no business knowing how its caller stores it. Taking a reference keeps it usable with objects on the stack too. std::shared_ptr : shared ownership Sometimes an object has several owners and no way to know which will finish with it last. A shared_ptr keeps a reference count of its owners and deletes the object when the count reaches zero. cpp auto texture{ std::make_shared<Texture ("grass.png") }; // count is 1 { auto alias{ texture }; // count is 2 std::cout << texture.use_count() << '
'; // 2 } // count is 1 // when the last owner goes, the Texture is deleted sprite1 ─┐ sprite2 ─┼──▶ control block: count 3 ──▶ Texture sprite3 ─┘ each copy adds 1, each destruction subtracts 1, and at 0 the object is deleted It is not free: there is a separate control block holding the count, and updating the count must be safe across threads. Use it only when ownership really is shared. If one clear owner exists, use unique_ptr and give everyone else a reference. Cycles and std::weak_ptr Reference counting has one failure mode. cpp struct Person { std::string name{}; std::shared_ptr<Person partner{}; }; auto ann{ std::make_shared<Person ("Ann") }; auto bob{ std::make_shared<Person ("Bob") }; ann- partner = bob; bob- partner = ann; // ann and bob go out of scope: each count drops to 1, never to 0. Both leak. Each keeps the other alive for ever. The fix is for one direction not to own. A std::weak_ptr refers to an object managed by shared_ptr without adding to the count. cpp struct Person { std::string name{}; std::weak_ptr<Person partner{}; }; if (auto p{ ann- partner.lock() }) { std::cout << p- name << '
'; } A weak_ptr cannot be dereferenced directly, because the object might already be gone. lock() returns a shared_ptr that is either valid or empty, so the check and the access cannot be separated. The usual shape: a parent owns its children, and each child refers back to its parent with a weak_ptr or a plain pointer. Summary unique_ptr shared_ptr weak_ptr Raw T --- --- --- --- --- Owns the object Yes, alone Yes, jointly No No, by convention Can be copied No, only moved Yes Yes Yes Overhead None A control block and counting Small None Deletes automatically Yes When the count reaches 0 No !tip The modern rules - Do not write new or delete in ordinary code. Use std::make_unique and std::make_shared . - Raw pointers and references are fine, as non-owning observers. - Default to unique_ptr . Reach for shared_ptr only when you can explain why there are several owners. A unique_ptr can also manage things other than memory, by giving it a function to call in place of delete . That function is a custom deleter : cpp std::unique_ptr<std::FILE, int ( )(std::FILE ) file{ std::fopen("data.txt", "r"), &std::fclose }; Check yourself quiz ? Why can a unique_ptr not be copied? + A copy would create two owners of the same object, and both would delete it - Because it is stored on the heap - Because it has no copy constructor by accident - Because copying a pointer is undefined behaviour unique_ptr means one owner. Ownership can be handed over with std::move , but not duplicated. ? How does weak_ptr break a cycle? - It deletes one of the objects in the cycle + It does not add to the reference count, so the counts can still reach zero - It makes the shared_ptr s unique - It copies the objects so they no longer refer to each other Two shared_ptr s pointing at each other keep both counts above zero forever. A weak_ptr observes without owning. ? What should a function that only reads a Player take? - std::shared_ptr<Player - std::unique_ptr<Player + const Player& - Player it must delete A function that only uses an object should not care how it is owned. Pass smart pointers only when ownership is part of the job. ? When is shared_ptr the right choice? - Whenever you allocate on the heap - When you want the fastest smart pointer - When the object has one clear owner + When several owners share it and none is clearly last shared_ptr costs a reference count. Use unique_ptr by default and shared_ptr only for truly shared ownership.

title: 7.07  Object Relationships
body: Objects relate in a few standard ways. Composition : a part that is owned and dies with the whole. Aggregation : has it, but does not own it. Association : knows about it. Dependency : uses it briefly. Which one applies decides how you store the member. Five relationships Designing a program is largely deciding how its objects relate. Each relationship has a name, a meaning, and a natural way to write it in C++. Relationship Say it as Does A control B's lifetime? Typical code --- --- --- --- Composition A car has an engine, as a part Yes: the part dies with the whole A value member, or a std::unique_ptr Aggregation A department has teachers No: they exist independently A pointer, or a std::weak_ptr Association A doctor treats patients No Pointers or identifiers Dependency A printer uses a document No: only during a call A function parameter Inheritance A dog is an animal class Dog : public Animal (Milestone 8) The middle column is the one that matters for this milestone. It is the ownership question from 7.02 new and delete — Dynamic Memory , asked about members. Composition The part belongs to the whole and has no life outside it. cpp class Engine { public: void start() { std::cout << "vroom\n"; } }; class Car { public: void drive() { m_engine.start(); } private: Engine m_engine{}; std::vector<Wheel m_wheels{ 4 }; }; ┌─────── Car ────────┐ │ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ │ destroy the Car and the │ │Engine│ │Wheels│ │ Engine and Wheels go with it │ └──────┘ └──────┘ │ └────────────────────┘ A value member is the simplest, fastest and safest form. Use a std::unique_ptr member only when you need what a pointer offers: the part may be absent, may be replaced, or is of a type chosen while running. Aggregation The whole refers to parts that exist on their own and may outlive it. cpp class Department { public: void add(Teacher& teacher) { m_teachers.push_back(&teacher); } private: std::vector<Teacher m_teachers{}; // not owned }; Teacher bob{ "Bob" }; { Department maths{}; maths.add(bob); } // the Department is gone. Bob is unaffected. The raw pointers here are observers, which is a legitimate use. The obligation runs the other way: the teachers must outlive the department's use of them, or the pointers dangle. !note A vector cannot hold references std::vector<Teacher& does not compile, because a reference cannot be reassigned and a vector must be able to move its elements. Use pointers, or std::vector<std::reference_wrapper<Teacher . Association Two independent objects that know about each other. cpp class Patient; class Doctor { public: void addPatient(Patient& patient); private: std::vector<Patient m_patients{}; }; class Patient { private: std::vector<Doctor m_doctors{}; }; Links in both directions have to be kept consistent: adding a patient to a doctor must also add the doctor to the patient, and removal must undo both. Prefer a link in one direction, or store an identifier and look the object up when needed. Dependency The lightest relationship. One class uses another for the length of a function call and keeps nothing. cpp class Printer { public: void print(const Document& document); }; Choosing !tip Prefer the weakest relationship that works A dependency is easier to reason about than a stored link, and composition is easier than inheritance. The well-known advice "favour composition over inheritance" is explained in 8.06 Object Slicing, Casting and Composition . Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference between composition and aggregation? - Composition uses pointers; aggregation uses values + In composition the whole owns the part's lifetime; not so in aggregation - Aggregation is when two classes inherit from each other - There is none; they are two names for one idea A car's engine (composition) is created and destroyed with the car. A department's teachers (aggregation) exist on their own. ? Why can you not write std::vector<Teacher& ? - Because Teacher is a class - Because vectors can only hold built-in types + References cannot be reassigned, as elements must be - Because references are always const Elements must be assignable objects. Store pointers or std::reference_wrapper<Teacher instead. ? What is the simplest way to express composition? - A raw pointer member created with new - A std::shared_ptr member set in the constructor - A global variable + A plain value member of the class A plain member is part of the object, so its lifetime is tied to the whole automatically. ? Why are links in both directions hard to maintain? + Every change must be made on both sides, and a missed update leaves the objects disagreeing - Because C++ does not allow two classes to refer to each other - Because they always cause memory leaks - Because they make the program slower to compile A two-way link is two pieces of data that must stay consistent. Prefer one direction unless both are needed.

title: 7.08  Container Classes and std::initializer_list
body: A container class holds and manages a collection, like a small std::vector of your own. Building one brings together the whole milestone: heap memory, RAII, the Rule of Five and operators. std::initializer_list lets it accept { 1, 2, 3 } . Everything at once This lesson builds IntArray , a resizable array of int . You would use std::vector in real code. Writing one yourself is how you find out whether the last seven lessons have landed. ┌──────────────────────── IntArray ────────────────────────┐ │ data: int m_data std::size_t m_size │ ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ construct: IntArray() IntArray(n) IntArray{1, 2, 3} │ │ destroy: ~IntArray() │ │ copy: IntArray(const IntArray&) │ │ move: IntArray(IntArray&&) noexcept │ │ assign: operator=(IntArray) │ │ access: operator size() begin() end() │ │ modify: resize(n) push_back(x) │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ cpp include <algorithm include <cassert include <cstddef include <initializer_list include <iostream include <utility class IntArray { public: IntArray() = default; explicit IntArray(std::size_t size) : m_data{ size ? new int size {} : nullptr }, m_size{ size } { } IntArray(std::initializer_list<int values) : IntArray(values.size()) { std::copy(values.begin(), values.end(), m_data); } ~IntArray() { delete m_data; } IntArray(const IntArray& other) : IntArray(other.m_size) { std::copy(other.m_data, other.m_data + m_size, m_data); } IntArray(IntArray&& other) noexcept : m_data{ std::exchange(other.m_data, nullptr) }, m_size{ std::exchange(other.m_size, 0) } { } IntArray& operator=(IntArray other) noexcept { std::swap(m_data, other.m_data); std::swap(m_size, other.m_size); return this; } int& operator (std::size_t i) { assert(i < m_size); return m_data i ; } const int& operator (std::size_t i) const { assert(i < m_size); return m_data i ; } std::size_t size() const { return m_size; } void resize(std::size_t size) { IntArray replacement(size); std::copy(m_data, m_data + std::min(size, m_size), replacement.m_data); this = std::move(replacement); } void push_back(int value) { resize(m_size + 1); m_data m_size - 1 = value; } int begin() { return m_data; } int end() { return m_data + m_size; } const int begin() const { return m_data; } const int end() const { return m_data + m_size; } private: int m_data{ nullptr }; std::size_t m_size{ 0 }; }; int main() { IntArray a{ 1, 2, 3 }; a.push_back(4); for (int x : a) { std::cout << x << ' '; // 1 2 3 4 } std::cout << '\n'; return 0; } Where each idea appears Part of the class Lesson --- --- new int size {} and delete 7.02 new and delete — Dynamic Memory The destructor releases what the constructor acquired 7.04 RAII and the Rule of Three The copy constructor allocates and copies 7.03 Copy Semantics — Shallow vs Deep The move constructor takes the pointer and leaves nullptr 7.05 Move Semantics Constructors delegate to IntArray(size) 6.02 Constructors Two operator overloads, one const 6.08 Operator Overloading — Advanced assert on the index 3.07 Input Validation and assert Two details deserve a closer look. One assignment operator serves both copy and move. It takes its parameter by value . When the argument is an lvalue, the parameter is built by the copy constructor. When it is an rvalue, it is built by the move constructor. Either way, the function swaps contents with it and lets it carry the old data away. That is copy and swap again. begin() and end() make the range-based loop work. A range-based for needs nothing more than those two functions returning something that behaves like an iterator, and a plain pointer does. std::initializer_list IntArray a{ 1, 2, 3 }; └───┬───┘ the compiler builds a hidden constant array 1, 2, 3 and passes a small view of it: std::initializer_list<int with begin() end() size() A constructor taking a std::initializer_list<T is what lets a class be initialized from a braced list of any length. !warning Braces prefer the list constructor If a class has an initializer_list constructor, brace initialization chooses it whenever it can. That is the reason for the rule in 5.01 std::vector Basics : std::vector<int v{ 5 }; is one element with the value 5. std::vector<int v(5); is five elements. IntArray has the same behaviour, which is why resize writes IntArray replacement(size); with parentheses. What a real vector does better push_back here reallocates and copies every time , so adding n elements costs O(n²) in total. std::vector keeps a capacity larger than its size and grows it by a constant factor when full, making push_back amortized constant time ( 5.03 Vector as a Stack, and Capacity ). Adding that is the natural next step. Check yourself quiz ? Why can one operator=(IntArray other) handle both copy and move assignment? - Because the compiler converts all moves into copies + The parameter is copied or moved, depending on the argument - Because IntArray has no move constructor - Because assignment never needs to copy The caller's argument decides how other is built. The body is the same swap either way. ? What does a class need for a range-based for loop to work on it? - An operator and a size() function - To inherit from std::vector + begin() and end() functions that return iterators - A constructor taking an std::initializer_list The range-based for calls begin() and end() . For an array-backed class, pointers to the first and one-past-last elements will do. ? Why does IntArray replacement(size); use parentheses? - Because braces cannot be used with a variable - Because braces would make the array const - Because parentheses are faster + Braces would pick the initializer_list constructor Braces prefer an initializer_list constructor when there is one, so { size } means "the list containing size ". ? Why is this push_back slow compared with std::vector 's? - Because it checks every element first - Because it allocates on the stack + It reallocates and copies everything on every call - Because it uses delete instead of delete Growing by one each time makes n insertions cost O(n²). Doubling the capacity makes the average push_back constant time.

title: 8.01  Inheritance Basics
body:
Inheritance defines a new class (the derived class) from an existing one (the base class), reusing its members and adding more. It models is-a : a Dog is an Animal . The base part is constructed first and destroyed last. Modelling "is-a" Composition says one thing has another. Inheritance says one thing is a kind of another. A derived class contains everything its base class has, and can be used wherever the base is expected. Term Also called Meaning --- --- --- Base class Parent, superclass The class being inherited from Derived class Child, subclass The class that inherits Hierarchy The tree formed by the classes Syntax cpp include <iostream include <string class Animal { public: std::string name{}; int age{}; void eat() const { std::cout << name << " eats
"; } }; class Dog : public Animal { public: void fetch() const { std::cout << name << " fetches
"; } }; int main() { Dog rex{}; rex.name = "Rex"; rex.eat(); // inherited from Animal rex.fetch(); // Dog's own return 0; } : public Animal makes Dog a derived class of Animal . A Dog object physically contains an Animal , called its base subobject , followed by whatever Dog adds. a Dog object ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │ ┌── Animal subobject ─────┐ │ │ │ name age │ │ the base part comes first │ └─────────────────────────┘ │ │ Dog's own members │ └─────────────────────────────┘ Construction and destruction order A derived object is built from the inside out. cpp include <iostream include <string include <string_view class Animal { public: explicit Animal(std::string_view name) : m_name{ name } { std::cout << "Animal constructed
"; } ~Animal() { std::cout << "Animal destroyed
"; } protected: std::string m_name{}; }; class Dog : public Animal { public: Dog(std::string_view name, std::string_view breed) : Animal{ name }, m_breed{ breed } { std::cout << "Dog constructed
"; } ~Dog() { std::cout << "Dog destroyed
"; } private: std::string m_breed{}; }; int main() { Dog d{ "Rex", "Collie" }; return 0; } Animal constructed Dog constructed Dog destroyed Animal destroyed Step Order --- --- Construction Base class, then the derived class's members, then the derived constructor's body Destruction Exactly the reverse The reasoning is the one from 6.03 Destructors and Object Lifetime : the derived part may depend on the base part, so the base must exist first and outlast it. !note A derived class initializes its base through a base constructor Dog cannot write m_name{ name } in its own initializer list, because m_name is not Dog 's member to initialize. It names a base constructor instead: Animal{ name } . If none is named, the base's default constructor is used, and if there is none the code does not compile. Inheriting constructors Constructors are not inherited by default. When a derived class adds no data that needs initializing, it can adopt the base's constructors wholesale: cpp class Dog : public Animal { public: using Animal::Animal; }; The is-a test Inheritance is a strong commitment. Before using it, ask whether every derived object can stand in for a base object everywhere a base is used. This is the idea of substitutability . Proposed Verdict Why --- --- --- Circle is a Shape Yes Anything valid for a shape is valid for a circle Stack is a Vector No A vector allows insertion anywhere; a stack must not. Use composition. Square is a Rectangle Usually no Code that sets a rectangle's width and height independently breaks a square When the test fails, the relationship is "is implemented using", and that is composition: 7.07 Object Relationships . Check yourself quiz ? Which constructor runs first, the base's or the derived class's? + The base's; destructors then run in the reverse order, derived first - The derived class's; the base's runs at the end of it - Whichever is declared first in the file - They run at the same time The base part must exist before the derived part is built on top of it, and it is torn down last. ? How does a derived constructor initialize base members? - By assigning to them in the constructor body + By naming a base constructor in its member initializer list - By calling super() as the first statement - It cannot; base members are always default-initialized Write Derived(int x) : Base{ x } { } . Private base members can only be set through a base constructor. ? What is a base subobject? - A pointer from the derived object to a separate base object - A copy of the base class made when the derived class is copied + The part of a derived object that is a complete base object embedded in it - A static member shared by all derived classes Every derived object contains a full base object inside it, which is why it can be used wherever a base is expected. ? Why is "a stack is a vector" a poor use of inheritance? - Because a vector cannot be inherited from - Because a stack has no members - Because inheritance makes the stack slower + A stack must not allow all that a vector allows Public inheritance would expose insert , operator and the rest, breaking the stack's rules. Hold a vector as a member instead.

Vehicle (the base): - Vehicle(std::string name, int wheels) - const std::string& name() const , int wheels() const - std::string describe() const returns for example "Civic has 4 wheels" Car (derived from Vehicle ): - Car(std::string name, int doors) : always 4 wheels - int doors() const Motorbike (derived from Vehicle ): - explicit Motorbike(std::string name) : always 2 wheels - bool hasSidecar() const (false until attachSidecar() is called, which also makes wheels() report 3) For the sidecar, Vehicle needs a way for derived classes (but not outsiders) to change the wheel count: give it a protected void setWheels(int) .

title: 8.02  Inheritance and Access
body:
protected members are visible to derived classes but not to outside code. The kind of inheritance ( public , protected , private ) caps how inherited members appear. A derived class can add functions, hide base ones, extend them by calling the base version, or change their access . Three access levels A member that is Its own class Derived classes Outside code --- --- --- --- public Yes Yes Yes protected Yes Yes No private Yes No No cpp class Base { public: int pub{}; protected: int prot{}; private: int priv{}; }; class Derived : public Base { void f() { pub = 1; // fine prot = 2; // fine priv = 3; // error: private to Base } }; A derived object still contains the private members of its base. It simply cannot name them. !tip Prefer private data with protected functions Protected data lets every derived class depend on, and corrupt, the base's internals. The base can then no longer guarantee its own invariants or change its representation. Keep the data private and give derived classes a protected function that does what they need. The kind of inheritance The keyword after the colon sets an upper limit on the access of inherited members. Declared as Base public members become Base protected members become --- --- --- class D : public B public protected class D : protected B protected protected class D : private B private private Only public inheritance models is-a, because only then can outside code treat a D as a B . Private inheritance means "implemented in terms of", for which a member is nearly always the better tool. The default is private for a class and public for a struct . Write public explicitly every time. What a derived class can do with base functions cpp include <iostream include <string_view class Base { public: void greet() const { std::cout << "Hello from Base
"; } void hello(int) {} void hello(double) {} }; class Derived : public Base { public: void wave() const { std::cout << "waving
"; } // 1. add void greet() const // 2. hide Base::greet { Base::greet(); // 3. extend: call the base version std::cout << "and from Derived
"; } using Base::hello; // 4. keep the base overloads visible void hello(std::string_view) {} }; int main() { Derived d{}; d.greet(); d.hello(5); // Base::hello(int), reachable thanks to the using-declaration return 0; } Action How --- --- Add Declare a new function Hide Declare a function with the same name Extend Hide it, and call Base::function() inside Change access using Base::name; in the section with the access you want Remove void name() = delete; Name hiding Name lookup works outwards one scope at a time and stops at the first scope that contains the name . Overload resolution happens afterwards, among what was found there. So declaring one hello in Derived hides every hello in Base , whatever their parameters. !warning One overload hides them all using Base::hello; brings the base overloads into the derived scope so they take part in overload resolution alongside the new one. Changing access cpp class Derived : public Base { public: using Base::protectedFunction; // now public in Derived private: using Base::greet; // no longer callable on a Derived }; Restricting access this way is cosmetic: greet is still callable through a Base& . This is not polymorphism yet cpp Derived d{}; Base& b{ d }; b.greet(); // calls Base::greet The function is chosen from the type of the reference , at compile time. Derived::greet hides the base function; it does not replace it. Making b.greet() call the derived version requires virtual , the subject of 8.03 Virtual Functions and Polymorphism . Check yourself quiz ? Can a derived class access the private members of its base? - Yes, it inherits them, so it can use them + No, only the public and protected ones - Only through this - Only in its constructor Private members are part of the derived object but are only accessible to the base class's own code. ? How do you call the base version of a function the derived class has hidden? - this- functionName() - super.functionName() + Base::functionName() - base- functionName() Qualifying the name with the base class picks that version explicitly. ? Why does declaring one overload in a derived class hide all base overloads of that name? - Because overloads are never inherited - Because the compiler copies only the first overload - Because the derived class must re-declare every function + Name lookup stops at the first scope containing the name, before overloads are compared The compiler finds the name in the derived class and stops looking. Add using Base::functionName; to bring the others back. ? Which kind of inheritance models is-a? - Private inheritance - Protected inheritance + Public inheritance - Virtual inheritance Public inheritance keeps the base's interface public, so a derived object can be used as a base. The others hide it.

Account : - long long balance() const - bool deposit(long long cents) : refuses amounts that are not positive - a protected void adjust(long long cents) that changes the balance by any amount, no questions asked SavingsAccount (derived from Account ): - explicit SavingsAccount(double yearlyRatePercent) - void addMonthlyInterest() : adds one twelfth of the yearly rate, in whole cents rounded down, using adjust - bool withdraw(long long cents) : allowed at most 3 times in total; refuses amounts that are not positive or exceed the balance Outside code must not be able to call adjust .

title: 8.03  Virtual Functions and Polymorphism
body: A virtual function called through a base pointer or reference runs the version belonging to the object's actual class. That is polymorphism : one interface, many behaviours. Mark overrides with override , and give polymorphic base classes a virtual destructor. One call, many behaviours cpp include <iostream include <string_view class Animal { public: virtual ~Animal() = default; virtual std::string_view speak() const { return "..."; } }; class Dog : public Animal { public: std::string_view speak() const override { return "Woof"; } }; class Cat : public Animal { public: std::string_view speak() const override { return "Meow"; } }; void makeNoise(const Animal& animal) { std::cout << animal.speak() << '\n'; } int main() { const Dog dog{}; const Cat cat{}; makeNoise(dog); // Woof makeNoise(cat); // Meow return 0; } makeNoise is written once, against Animal . It works for every class derived from Animal , including ones written years later, without being recompiled. Static type and dynamic type Every expression has two types. Meaning Known --- --- --- Static type The type written in the code At compile time Dynamic type The type of the object actually referred to At run time In makeNoise(dog) , the parameter's static type is const Animal& and its dynamic type is Dog . Function Chosen by --- --- Non-virtual The static type virtual The dynamic type Choosing the function at run time is dynamic dispatch . A derived function that replaces a virtual one overrides it, which is different from the hiding described in 8.02 Inheritance and Access . Polymorphic collections cpp std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Animal zoo{}; zoo.push_back(std::make_unique<Dog ()); zoo.push_back(std::make_unique<Cat ()); for (const auto& animal : zoo) { std::cout << animal- speak() << '\n'; // Woof, Meow } !important Polymorphism requires a pointer or a reference A std::vector<Animal stores Animal objects by value. Putting a Dog in it copies only the Animal part and discards the rest. That is slicing : 8.06 Object Slicing, Casting and Composition . override and final cpp class Dog : public Animal { public: std::string_view speak() const override; // checked: a matching virtual must exist }; Without override , a small mismatch, such as a missing const or a different parameter type, silently declares a new, unrelated function. With it, the mismatch is a compile error. Specifier Effect --- --- override The compiler verifies that this overrides a base virtual function final on a function Derived classes may not override it further final on a class Nothing may derive from it !tip Always write override It costs one word and converts a silent bug into a diagnostic. Virtual destructors cpp Animal a{ new Dog{} }; delete a; If ~Animal is not virtual, the destructor is chosen by the static type. Only ~Animal runs, the Dog part is never destroyed, and the behaviour is undefined. The base class Destructor should be --- --- Will be deleted through a base pointer public and virtual Must never be deleted through a base pointer protected and non-virtual A working rule: a class with any virtual function gets a virtual destructor. Covariant return types An override must normally match the base signature exactly. One relaxation: where the base returns a pointer or reference to a class, the override may return a pointer or reference to a class derived from it. cpp class Shape { public: virtual ~Shape() = default; virtual Shape clone() const = 0; }; class Circle : public Shape { public: Circle clone() const override { return new Circle{ this }; } }; Printing polymorphic objects operator<< is a non-member, so it cannot be virtual. Have it forward to a virtual member function: cpp class Shape { public: virtual ~Shape() = default; friend std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& out, const Shape& shape) { return shape.print(out); } private: virtual std::ostream& print(std::ostream& out) const = 0; }; class Circle : public Shape { private: std::ostream& print(std::ostream& out) const override { return out << "Circle(r=" << m_radius << ')'; } double m_radius{ 1.0 }; }; One non-virtual public function delegating to a private virtual one is a common and useful shape, known as the non-virtual interface idiom. Three traps Trap What happens --- --- Calling a virtual function from a constructor or destructor The current class's version runs. The derived part does not exist yet, or no longer exists. Giving an override a different default argument Default arguments are taken from the static type, so the base's default is used with the derived function Calling Base::f() explicitly Dynamic dispatch is bypassed Check yourself quiz ? Which two things are required for dynamic dispatch? - A template and a pointer + A virtual function, and a call through a base pointer or reference - An abstract class and a dynamic_cast - A virtual destructor and a copy constructor Calling a virtual function on an object directly (not through a pointer or reference) uses its static type. ? Why always write override ? + The compiler checks that a matching base virtual exists - It makes the function virtual in the base class too - It makes the call faster - Without it, the function cannot be called A typo or a missing const silently creates a new function. override turns that into a compile error. ? What is the difference between static type and dynamic type? - Static type is for static variables; dynamic type for heap variables - They are always the same + Static is the type in the code; dynamic is the real object's type - The dynamic type is decided by auto For Animal p{ &dog }; the static type of p is Animal , but the dynamic type is Dog . ? Why does a polymorphic base class need a virtual destructor? - So the derived class can have a destructor at all - So the object is destroyed automatically - To make delete faster + So delete through a base pointer runs the derived destructor With a virtual destructor, delete basePtr runs the derived destructor first, then the base one.

title: 8.04  How Virtual Works — vtables
body: Ordinary calls are resolved at compile time (early binding). Virtual calls are resolved at run time (late binding) through a hidden pointer in each object, the vptr , to a per-class table of function addresses, the vtable . The cost is one pointer per object and one indirection per call. Early and late binding Binding Decided --- --- --- Non-virtual call Early (static) By the compiler Virtual call Late (dynamic) While the program runs The standard does not say how virtual dispatch must be implemented. Every mainstream compiler uses the mechanism below. The vtable cpp class Animal { public: virtual ~Animal() = default; virtual void speak() const; virtual void move() const; }; class Dog : public Animal { public: void speak() const override; // move is not overridden }; class Cat : public Animal { public: void speak() const override; void move() const override; }; OBJECTS VTABLES: one per CLASS, shared by all its objects ┌────────────┐ Dog's vtable │ rex (Dog) │ ┌──────────────┬──────────────────┐ │ vptr ──────┼──────────▶ │ slot 0 dtor │ ~Dog │ │ members │ │ slot 1 speak │ Dog::speak │ overridden └────────────┘ │ slot 2 move │ Animal::move │ inherited └──────────────┴──────────────────┘ ┌────────────┐ Cat's vtable │ tom (Cat) │ ┌──────────────┬──────────────────┐ │ vptr ──────┼──────────▶ │ slot 0 dtor │ ~Cat │ │ members │ │ slot 1 speak │ Cat::speak │ └────────────┘ │ slot 2 move │ Cat::move │ └──────────────┴──────────────────┘ Piece Where Holds --- --- --- vtable One per class with virtual functions The address of that class's version of each virtual function vptr One hidden member in every object of such a class The address of its class's vtable Every class in a hierarchy uses the same slot number for the same function. So animalRef.speak() compiles to three steps that work without knowing the dynamic type: 1. Read the object's vptr . 2. Read slot 1 of the table it points to. 3. Call the address found there. The cost Cost --- --- Memory per object One pointer, 8 bytes on a 64-bit system, plus any padding Memory per class One table Time per call Two extra memory reads and an indirect call Lost optimisation The compiler generally cannot inline a virtual call, which is often the larger effect cpp struct NoVirtual { int x; }; // sizeof is 4 struct HasVirtual { int x; virtual ~HasVirtual() = default; }; // sizeof is 16: an 8-byte vptr, the int, and 4 bytes of padding In most code this is immaterial. It becomes measurable when a tiny virtual function is called millions of times in a tight loop over small objects. Alternatives for those cases: Alternative Lesson --- --- Compile-time polymorphism with CRTP 11.05 CRTP, Mixins and Static Polymorphism A closed set of types in a std::variant 10.04 stdoptional, stdvariant, stdany and stdtuple Grouping objects by type and processing each group in bulk 13.04 Performance, Caches and Data-Oriented Design Devirtualization When the compiler can prove the dynamic type, it replaces the virtual call with a direct one, which can then be inlined. This is devirtualization . Situation Why the type is known --- --- A call on a local object by value Its type is exactly the declared one The class or the function is final Nothing can override further Whole-program optimisation shows a single implementation There is only one candidate Marking leaf classes final is therefore a small, free optimisation. Why virtual calls in constructors do not dispatch The vptr is set by each constructor in turn. constructing a Dog: Animal's constructor runs vptr points at Animal's vtable Dog's constructor runs vptr points at Dog's vtable While Animal 's constructor is running, the object is an Animal : the Dog members are not yet constructed. A virtual call at that moment reaches Animal 's version, which is the only safe choice. Destruction mirrors it: by the time ~Animal runs, the Dog part has already been destroyed and the vptr has been set back. Check yourself quiz ? How many vtables exist for a class that has 1,000 objects? - 1,000, one per object + One - One per virtual function - None until a virtual function is called The vtable is per class. Each object holds its own vptr, and all of them point at that single table. ? What is late binding? - Calling a function after the object is destroyed - Linking a library after the program has started + Choosing the function to call at run time, by dynamic type - Defining a function after it is first called Early binding fixes the function while compiling. Late binding looks it up through the vptr while running. ? Why does adding five more virtual functions not increase sizeof the class? - Because virtual functions are stored on the heap + They add vtable slots; each object still has one vptr - Because sizeof ignores functions and pointers - It does; each adds 8 bytes The extra function pointers live in the shared table, not in every object. ? Besides the indirection, what is the main performance cost of a virtual call? - It allocates memory on every call - It copies the object - It always causes a cache miss + The compiler usually cannot inline it Without knowing the target, the compiler cannot inline the call or optimise across it. Devirtualization recovers this when the type is known.

title: What a virtual function costs
body: An object with any virtual function carries one hidden pointer (the vptr ) to its class's table of virtual functions. See it for yourself. Write two structs with the same two double members, x and y : - PlainPoint : nothing else; - VirtualPoint : also has a virtual destructor ( virtual ~VirtualPoint() = default; ). Then write std::size_t vptrCost() returning how many bytes bigger the second one is. Compute it with sizeof ; do not type a number.

title: final
body: final closes a door: a final class cannot be inherited from, and a final virtual function cannot be overridden further down. It documents intent, and it lets the compiler turn some virtual calls back into direct ones. Given Shape , write: - class Polygon : public Shape that overrides sides() (returning the number it was constructed with) and overrides kind() as final , returning "polygon" ; - class Square final : public Polygon that always has 4 sides.

title: 8.05  Abstract Classes and Interfaces
body:
A pure virtual function, declared = 0 , has no implementation in the base: derived classes must supply one. A class with any pure virtual function is abstract and cannot be instantiated. A class made only of pure virtual functions is an interface : a contract. Pure virtual functions Animal::speak in the last lessons returned "..." because it had to return something. Often there is no sensible default: what is the area of "a shape"? A pure virtual function declares the operation without defining it. cpp include <iostream include <string_view class Shape { public: virtual ~Shape() = default; virtual double area() const = 0; virtual std::string_view name() const = 0; void describe() const { std::cout << name() << " with area " << area() << '
'; } }; class Circle : public Shape { public: explicit Circle(double radius) : m_radius{ radius } {} double area() const override { return 3.14159 m_radius m_radius; } std::string_view name() const override { return "Circle"; } private: double m_radius{}; }; int main() { // Shape s{}; error: Shape is abstract const Circle c{ 2.0 }; c.describe(); // Circle with area 12.5664 return 0; } Term Meaning --- --- Pure virtual function Declared with = 0 ; derived classes must override it Abstract class Has at least one pure virtual function; cannot be instantiated Concrete class Has none left unimplemented; can be instantiated A derived class that fails to override even one pure virtual function is itself abstract. The compiler enforces completeness for you. Notice describe : a non-virtual function in the base that calls the virtual ones. The base class fixes the overall behaviour and the derived classes supply the variable parts. Interfaces An interface is an abstract class with no data and only pure virtual functions (plus the virtual destructor). It states what a type can do and nothing about how. cpp class ILogger { public: virtual ~ILogger() = default; virtual void log(std::string_view message) = 0; }; class ConsoleLogger : public ILogger { public: void log(std::string_view message) override { std::cout << " console " << message << '
'; } }; class FileLogger : public ILogger { public: void log(std::string_view message) override { m_file << message << '
'; } private: std::ofstream m_file{ "app.log" }; }; class Game { public: explicit Game(ILogger& logger) : m_logger{ logger } {} void start() { m_logger.log("Game started"); } private: ILogger& m_logger; }; C++ has no interface keyword; this is a convention. The I prefix is one common way to mark it. Why depend on an interface? Game knows about ILogger and about no particular logger. Benefit Example --- --- Implementations can be swapped Log to a file in production and to the console while developing, with no change to Game Testing is easy Pass a FakeLogger that records messages, then check what was logged Compilation is decoupled Changing FileLogger does not recompile Game High-level code depending on an abstraction, with the details plugged in from outside, is the dependency inversion principle . Supplying the dependency through the constructor, as here, is dependency injection . A pure virtual function with a body A pure virtual function may still have a definition, written outside the class. Derived classes must override it, and can call the base version explicitly. cpp class Animal { public: virtual ~Animal() = default; virtual void speak() const = 0; }; void Animal::speak() const { std::cout << "(a generic sound)
"; } class Fish : public Animal { public: void speak() const override { Animal::speak(); } }; This offers a default while forcing each derived class to opt in deliberately. The non-virtual interface idiom A public non-virtual function fixes the sequence of steps. Private virtual functions are the points derived classes may customise. cpp class Report { public: void generate() { header(); body(); footer(); } private: virtual void header() { std::cout << "== REPORT ==
"; } virtual void body() = 0; virtual void footer() { std::cout << "== END ==
"; } }; Derived classes can override a private virtual function; they just cannot call it. So the base keeps control of when each step runs, and can add checks or logging around them in one place. In design-pattern terms this is the Template Method pattern: 13.08 C++ Idioms and Design Patterns . Check yourself quiz ? What makes a class abstract? - Having no member variables - Having a virtual destructor + At least one pure virtual function not yet overridden - Having only private constructors and no public ones An abstract class cannot be instantiated. A derived class becomes concrete once it overrides every pure virtual function. ? Why depend on an interface instead of a concrete class? + Implementations, even test fakes, can be swapped freely - Interfaces make calls faster - Concrete classes cannot be passed by reference - The compiler requires it for virtual functions Code written against Logger& works with a file logger, a console logger or a fake in a test. ? What is an interface in C++? - A keyword, like interface in Java - Any class with public members - A header file containing only declarations + An abstract class with no data, only pure virtual functions C++ has no interface keyword. An abstract class with only pure virtual functions plays that role. ? In the non-virtual interface idiom, why are the virtual functions private? - So derived classes cannot override them - Because virtual functions must be private + So only the base class decides when they are called - To stop them appearing in the vtable The public non-virtual function controls the order and checks, and calls the private virtual hook. Overriding does not need access.

Write ILogger with a virtual destructor and one pure virtual function, virtual void log(std::string_view message) = 0; 2. Write void runJob(ILogger& logger, int steps) , which logs "start" , then "step 1" , "step 2" ... up to steps , then "done" . runJob depends only on the interface, so it would work unchanged with a logger that writes to a file, the console or the network.

title: Notifiers that plug together
body: Small classes behind one interface can be combined like building blocks. The interface: INotifier with virtual void send(std::string_view message) = 0; and a virtual destructor. Write three implementations: Class Behaviour --- --- ListNotifier stores every message; const std::vector<std::string & sent() const PrefixNotifier constructed with (std::string prefix, INotifier& next) ; forwards each message to next with the prefix in front. It decorates another notifier. MultiNotifier void add(INotifier& target) ; forwards each message to every target, in the order added. It is a composite . Because PrefixNotifier and MultiNotifier are themselves notifiers, they can wrap each other to any depth.

title: 8.06  Object Slicing, Casting and Composition
body:
Copying a derived object into a base value discards the derived part: that is slicing . dynamic_cast converts down a hierarchy safely, but needing it often points to a design problem. And the standing advice: favour composition over inheritance . Object slicing cpp include <iostream include <string include <string_view class Animal { public: virtual ~Animal() = default; virtual std::string_view speak() const { return "..."; } }; class Dog : public Animal { public: std::string_view speak() const override { return "Woof"; } private: std::string m_trick{ "roll over" }; }; int main() { const Dog dog{}; const Animal animal{ dog }; // sliced std::cout << animal.speak() << '
'; // ... return 0; } Dog dog Animal animal{ dog } ┌──────────────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ │ Animal part │ ──────▶ │ Animal part │ an Animal, with Animal's vptr ├──────────────────────┤ └──────────────┘ │ m_trick │ not copied └──────────────────────┘ Animal animal{ dog } calls Animal 's copy constructor, which knows only about Animal 's members. The result is a complete, genuine Animal . It is not a Dog viewed as an Animal . The same happens wherever a base is held by value : Code Sliced? --- --- Animal a{ dog }; Yes void f(Animal a); called with a Dog Yes std::vector<Animal Yes, on every insertion Animal& a{ dog }; , Animal p{ &dog }; No std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Animal No Many codebases make polymorphic base classes non-copyable so that slicing cannot compile: cpp class Animal { public: Animal() = default; Animal(const Animal&) = delete; Animal& operator=(const Animal&) = delete; virtual ~Animal() = default; }; When copies of polymorphic objects are needed, provide a virtual clone() that returns a std::unique_ptr<Animal . Upcasting and downcasting Direction Safe? How --- --- --- Upcast , derived to base Always Implicit: Animal& a{ dog }; Downcast , base to derived Only if the object really is of that type dynamic_cast dynamic_cast cpp void interact(Animal& animal) { if (auto dog{ dynamic_cast<Dog (&animal) }) { dog- fetch(); } else { std::cout << "not a dog
"; } } Form On failure --- --- dynamic_cast<Dog (pointer) Returns nullptr dynamic_cast<Dog& (reference) Throws std::bad_cast It checks the object's dynamic type at run time, using run-time type information (RTTI) stored alongside the vtable. Consequently it requires a polymorphic base class and has a real cost. static_cast<Dog (&animal) also compiles and performs no check. If the object is not a Dog , the behaviour is undefined. Use it only when the type is guaranteed by other means. !tip A chain of dynamic_cast tests is a missing virtual function cpp if (dynamic_cast<Dog (a)) { ... } else if (dynamic_cast<Cat (a)) { ... } This re-implements dynamic dispatch by hand, and breaks whenever a new derived class appears. Add a virtual function and let each class provide its own behaviour. typeid cpp include <typeinfo std::cout << typeid(animal).name() << '
'; typeid gives the dynamic type of a polymorphic object. The text of name() is implementation-defined, so it is useful for diagnostics and not for logic. Composition or inheritance Inheritance Composition --- --- --- Coupling Tight: the derived class depends on the base's details Loose: only on the part's public interface Flexibility Fixed at compile time Parts can be replaced while running Scaling Deep hierarchies become fragile Stays flat Use it for A true is-a relationship that needs polymorphism Reusing behaviour Where inheritance breaks down Suppose enemies can walk, fly or swim, and attack by melee or by shooting. As a hierarchy: FlyingEnemy, SwimmingEnemy, FlyingShootingEnemy, SwimmingShootingEnemy, FlyingSwimmingEnemy, FlyingSwimmingShootingEnemy ... Every new ability multiplies the number of classes. With composition, an entity has behaviours: cpp class Entity { public: void update() { m_movement- move( this); m_attack- attack( this); } void setMovement(std::unique_ptr<IMovement movement) { m_movement = std::move(movement); } private: std::unique_ptr<IMovement m_movement{}; // Walk, Fly or Swim std::unique_ptr<IAttack m_attack{}; // Melee, Shoot or None }; Three movement classes and three attack classes give nine combinations, and an entity can change behaviour while the program runs. Inheritance is still used, but only for the small interfaces. This is the Strategy pattern, and the thinking behind entity-component systems in game engines. Check yourself quiz ? What is object slicing? - Splitting an object across two files + Copying a derived object into a base, losing the derived part - Deleting part of an object through a pointer - Casting a base pointer to a derived pointer The derived members and overrides are lost. Pass by reference or pointer to keep the whole object. ? What does dynamic_cast<Dog (animalPtr) return if the object is really a Cat ? - A pointer to the Cat , treated as a Dog - It throws an exception + nullptr - It does not compile A failed dynamic_cast to a pointer type gives nullptr . To a reference type it throws std::bad_cast . ? Why is a chain of dynamic_cast tests a design smell? - Because dynamic_cast is not allowed on pointers - Because it only works for two classes - Because it is undefined behaviour + It redoes a virtual function's job and needs editing for each new class Asking "are you a Dog? a Cat?" spreads type knowledge around. A virtual function puts the behaviour in each class. ? Why does composition scale better than inheritance for combinations of behaviours? - Because composition uses less memory - Because inheritance cannot model more than two behaviours + Each new behaviour is one new part, not a new set of subclasses - Because composed classes cannot have virtual functions With inheritance, every combination needs its own class. With composition, an object holds the parts it needs.

title: Stop the slicing
body: chorus is meant to return what every animal says. It takes a std::vector<Animal : a vector of base objects by value . Putting a Dog in there copies only its Animal part; the dog-ness is sliced off, and everything says "..." . Change chorus to take a const std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Animal & so that the real objects are kept. The body needs one small change to match. For two dogs and a cat it should return "Woof Woof Meow" .

title: dynamic_cast
body: Sometimes you hold a pointer to a base class and need to know whether the object is really a particular derived type. dynamic_cast<Dog (animal) checks at run time: it returns the pointer as a Dog , or nullptr if the object is not a dog. Write: - Dog asDog(Animal animal) : null in gives null out; - int totalTricks(const std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Animal & animals) : adds up tricks() for the dogs only (other animals have no such function).

title: Behaviour you can swap
body: Inheritance fixes behaviour when the object is created. Composition lets you change it while the program runs: the object has a behaviour and can be handed a different one. Write: - an interface IMovement with virtual std::string move() const = 0; - Walk (returns "walks" ), Fly (returns "flies" ), Swim (returns "swims" ) - a class Robot : - Robot(std::string name, std::unique_ptr<IMovement movement) - void setMovement(std::unique_ptr<IMovement movement) - std::string act() const : for example "R2 walks" . If the robot has no movement (a null pointer was given), it returns "R2 stands still" . Notice there is no FlyingRobot or SwimmingRobot class, and no need for one.

title: 8.07  Multiple Inheritance and Virtual Base Classes
match: 8.07 Multiple Inheritance and Virtual Base Classes
body:
A class may inherit from several bases. That works well for combining interfaces . When two bases share a common base, the result is the diamond problem , which virtual inheritance solves. Use it sparingly. Several base classes cpp include <iostream class IDrawable { public: virtual ~IDrawable() = default; virtual void draw() const = 0; }; class IClickable { public: virtual ~IClickable() = default; virtual void onClick() = 0; }; class Button : public IDrawable, public IClickable { public: void draw() const override { std::cout << " OK 
"; } void onClick() override { std::cout << "clicked
"; } }; void render(const IDrawable& item) { item.draw(); } void press(IClickable& item) { item.onClick(); } int main() { Button button{}; render(button); press(button); return 0; } A Button is substitutable for either interface. Implementing several interfaces is the common, uncontroversial use of multiple inheritance . Base subobjects are constructed in the order they are listed after the colon, and each has its own vptr . Name clashes Two bases may supply members with the same name. cpp class USBDevice { public: int id() const { return 1; } }; class NetworkDevice { public: int id() const { return 2; } }; class WirelessAdapter : public USBDevice, public NetworkDevice { }; WirelessAdapter adapter{}; adapter.id(); // error: ambiguous adapter.USBDevice::id(); // fine: qualified The diamond problem Scanner and Printer each contain a PoweredDevice . With ordinary inheritance, a Copier therefore contains two . Copier ┌──────────────────────────────┐ │ Scanner │ │ └─ PoweredDevice (first) │ │ Printer │ │ └─ PoweredDevice (second) │ two copies of the same base └──────────────────────────────┘ Any use of a PoweredDevice member through a Copier is ambiguous, and state stored in the base exists twice and can disagree. Virtual inheritance Declaring the inheritance virtual asks for one shared base subobject, however many paths lead to it. cpp include <iostream class PoweredDevice { public: explicit PoweredDevice(int watts) { std::cout << "PoweredDevice " << watts << "W
"; } }; class Scanner : virtual public PoweredDevice { public: Scanner(int, int watts) : PoweredDevice{ watts } {} }; class Printer : virtual public PoweredDevice { public: Printer(int, int watts) : PoweredDevice{ watts } {} }; class Copier : public Scanner, public Printer { public: Copier(int scanner, int printer, int watts) : PoweredDevice{ watts }, Scanner{ scanner, watts }, Printer{ printer, watts } { } }; int main() { Copier copier{ 1, 2, 300 }; // prints "PoweredDevice 300W" once return 0; } Copier ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Scanner ─┐ │ │ Printer ─┴──▶ PoweredDevice (one, shared)│ └──────────────────────────────────────────┘ Rule Detail --- --- Who constructs the virtual base The most-derived class, here Copier When Before every non-virtual base The intermediate classes' initializers Scanner 's and Printer 's calls to PoweredDevice{ watts } are ignored when they are subobjects of a Copier The price is extra indirection: because the shared base's position varies with the most-derived type, each object locates it through a stored offset. Access to virtual-base members is slightly slower, and objects are slightly larger. Guidelines Use Advice --- --- Inheriting several interfaces with no data Fine and common Inheriting several implementations with data Think hard, and prefer composition A diamond Avoid if you can. If you cannot, use virtual inheritance. Adding reusable behaviour to a class Consider template-based mixins: 11.05 CRTP, Mixins and Static Polymorphism !tip Design to avoid the question Most diamonds arise because a base class carries both an interface and state. Split it: keep the interface free of data, and put shared state in a component the classes hold. The diamond then disappears, or becomes a harmless diamond of pure interfaces. Check yourself quiz ? What does virtual inheritance guarantee? + That the object holds exactly one shared virtual base - That every function in the base is virtual - That the base class cannot be instantiated - That the derived classes are constructed in parallel Both paths in the diamond share one base subobject, so there is no duplicated state or ambiguity. ? Which class constructs a virtual base? - The first class that inherits from it - The class listed first in the base list + The most-derived class - Each intermediate class, once each Since the virtual base is shared, the most-derived class is responsible for constructing it, exactly once. ? Why is inheriting from several interfaces considered safe? - Because interfaces cannot have virtual functions - Because the compiler merges them into one class + Interfaces hold no data, so there is no duplicated state - Because interfaces are always inherited virtually The trouble with multiple inheritance comes from duplicated data. Pure interfaces have none. ? What goes wrong in a diamond without virtual inheritance? - The program never compiles, whatever you do - The base class is never constructed - Virtual functions stop working + The object holds two copies of the common base Each path brings its own base subobject, so obj.baseMember is ambiguous and the two copies can disagree.

title: 9.01  Class Templates
body: A class template is a pattern for classes, parameterized by type: Box<int , Box<std::string . It is how std::vector<T works. The compiler can often deduce the arguments ( CTAD ), and alias templates give long instantiations short names. One template, many classes 4.02 Function Templates parameterized a function by type. A class template does the same for a class. cpp include <iostream include <string include <utility template <typename T class Box { public: explicit Box(T value) : m_value{ std::move(value) } {} const T& get() const { return m_value; } void set(T value) { m_value = std::move(value); } private: T m_value{}; }; int main() { Box<int a{ 5 }; Box<std::string b{ "hello" }; std::cout << a.get() << ' ' << b.get() << '\n'; return 0; } Each distinct set of arguments instantiates a separate class. Box<int and Box<std::string are unrelated types: neither converts to the other, and each has its own static members. Member functions of a class template are instantiated only if used . A Box<T whose T lacks some operation is fine as long as no code calls the member that needs it. Several parameters cpp template <typename K, typename V struct Pair { K key{}; V value{}; }; Pair<std::string, int score{ "Ann", 90 }; Defining members outside the class cpp template <typename T class Stack { public: void push(const T& item); T pop(); bool empty() const { return m_items.empty(); } private: std::vector<T m_items{}; }; template <typename T void Stack<T ::push(const T& item) { m_items.push_back(item); } template <typename T T Stack<T ::pop() { T top{ std::move(m_items.back()) }; m_items.pop_back(); return top; } Each out-of-class definition repeats the template header and qualifies the name with Stack<T :: . Inside the class's own scope, the bare name Stack means Stack<T . !important The whole template belongs in the header As with function templates, the compiler needs the full definition at every point of use. Declarations and member definitions all go in the header. Class template argument deduction Since C++17 the compiler can deduce a class template's arguments from the constructor arguments. This is CTAD . cpp std::pair p{ 1, 2.5 }; // std::pair<int, double std::vector v{ 1, 2, 3 }; // std::vector<int Box b{ 3.14 }; // Box<double Deduction guides When the default deduction gives the wrong answer, a deduction guide states the mapping explicitly. cpp Box(const char ) - Box<std::string ; Box text{ "hello" }; // Box<std::string , not Box<const char A guide has the form constructor-like signature - resulting type . It affects only deduction; the object is then constructed by an ordinary constructor of the deduced class. Alias templates A using alias can itself take template parameters. cpp template <typename T using Grid = std::vector<std::vector<T ; Grid<char map(10, std::vector<char (10, '.')); template <typename V using StringMap = std::map<std::string, V ; An alias template is purely a shorthand. Grid<char is std::vector<std::vector<char , not a new type. Default template arguments cpp template <typename T, typename Container = std::vector<T class Stack2 { private: Container m_items{}; }; Stack2<int a{}; // stores in a std::vector<int Stack2<int, std::deque<int b{}; // stores in a std::deque<int This is how std::stack and std::queue are defined in the standard library: they are adaptors that provide an interface over a container you can choose. Templates and inheritance compared Both give "one piece of code, many types". They differ in when the type is fixed. Class template Virtual functions --- --- --- Type chosen At compile time At run time Cost per call None; calls can be inlined An indirect call Different types in one container No: Box<int and Box<double are unrelated Yes, through a base pointer Requirement on the type It must support the operations used It must derive from the base They are sometimes called static and dynamic polymorphism . Check yourself quiz ? Are Box<int and Box<long the same type? - Yes, both are Box - Yes, because int converts to long + No, each instantiation is a distinct, unrelated type - Only on systems where int and long are the same size Each set of template arguments produces its own class. A function taking Box<int will not take a Box<long . ? What is CTAD? + Deducing class template arguments from constructor arguments - A rule that templates must be defined in headers - A way to convert one template type to another - Compile-time assertion of deduction CTAD lets you write Box b{ 5 }; instead of Box<int b{ 5 }; . ? What does a deduction guide do? - It prints the deduced type as a compiler message - It checks the template arguments while the program runs + It tells CTAD which arguments to deduce for given constructor arguments - It forbids deduction for one constructor A guide such as Box(const char ) - Box<std::string ; steers CTAD where the obvious deduction would be wrong. ? Is an alias template a new type? - Yes, it is distinct from the type it names - Yes, but it converts automatically - Only if it has a default argument + No, it is another name for the type it expands to template <typename T using Vec = std::vector<T ; makes Vec<int exactly std::vector<int .

Member Behaviour --- --- void push(T value) adds to the top bool pop() removes the top; returns false if the stack was empty const T& top() const the top element (only called when not empty) bool empty() const , std::size_t size() const Define push outside the class body, to practise the syntax: template <typename T void Stack<T ::push(T value) { ... }

Member Behaviour --- --- Maybe() empty Maybe(T value) holds the value (not explicit , so a function returning Maybe<int can return 5; ) bool hasValue() const const T& value() const the value; throws std::logic_error if empty T valueOr(T fallback) const the value, or the fallback if empty void reset() becomes empty template <typename F auto map(F function) const if there is a value, returns a Maybe holding function(value) ; if empty, an empty Maybe of that result type Storing a T plus a bool flag is fine (so T must be default-constructible).

title: 9.02  Non-Type Parameters and Template Specialization
body:
Templates can take values as well as types, as in template <int N : that is how std::array<T, N knows its size. Specialization supplies a custom version for particular arguments: full ( Box<bool ) or partial ( Box<T ). Non-type template parameters A template parameter can be a compile-time value . cpp include <cstddef include <iostream template <typename T, std::size_t N class StaticArray { public: constexpr std::size_t size() const { return N; } T& operator (std::size_t i) { return m_data i ; } const T& operator (std::size_t i) const { return m_data i ; } private: T m_data N {}; }; int main() { StaticArray<int, 5 a{}; a 0 = 42; std::cout << a.size() << ' ' << a 0 << '
'; return 0; } N is part of the type. StaticArray<int, 5 and StaticArray<int, 6 are different classes, and the size costs nothing at run time because it is not stored anywhere. Allowed as a non-type parameter Since --- --- Integers, char , bool , enums Always Pointers and references to objects with static storage Always auto (the type is deduced from the argument) C++17 Floating-point types, and simple class types C++20 The argument must be a constant expression, since templates are resolved by the compiler. Full specialization A specialization replaces the general template for specific arguments. A full (or explicit ) specialization fixes all of them. cpp template <typename T class Storage { public: explicit Storage(T value) : m_value{ value } {} void print() const { std::cout << m_value << '
'; } private: T m_value{}; }; template < class Storage<double { public: explicit Storage(double value) : m_value{ value } {} void print() const { std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(2) << m_value << '
'; } private: double m_value{}; }; The original is called the primary template . A specialization is an entirely separate class: it shares nothing with the primary template except the name, and may have different members altogether. !warning std::vector<bool is a specialization The library specializes std::vector<bool to pack eight elements into each byte. Its elements are therefore not real bool objects: operator returns a small proxy object, and you cannot take a bool& or bool to an element. It is widely regarded as a mistake, and a good illustration of how a specialization can break the expectations set by the primary template. Specializing function templates Function templates can be fully specialized too: cpp template <typename T void printValue(const T& value) { std::cout << value << '
'; } template < void printValue<bool (const bool& value) { std::cout << (value ? "yes" : "no") << '
'; } !tip For functions, prefer overloading An ordinary overload, void printValue(bool value) , does the same job and takes part in overload resolution in the normal way. Function template specializations do not, which leads to surprising choices. Reserve specialization for class templates. Partial specialization A partial specialization covers a family of arguments. It is itself still a template. cpp include <array include <iostream include <string_view template <typename T struct TypeName { static constexpr std::string_view value{ "something else" }; }; template <typename T struct TypeName<T { static constexpr std::string_view value{ "a pointer" }; }; template <typename T, std::size_t N struct TypeName<std::array<T, N { static constexpr std::string_view value{ "a std::array" }; }; int main() { std::cout << TypeName<int ::value << '
'; // something else std::cout << TypeName<int ::value << '
'; // a pointer std::cout << TypeName<std::array<char, 3 ::value << '
'; // a std::array return 0; } The pattern in angle brackets after the name, such as T , is matched against the arguments. TypeName<int matches T with T being int . Only class templates and variable templates can be partially specialized. Function templates cannot; they overload instead. Which one is chosen? most specialized wins: full specialization the best-matching partial specialization the primary template If two partial specializations match and neither is more specialized than the other, the use is ambiguous and does not compile. Using partial specialization to ask questions about types at compile time, as TypeName does, is the foundation of 11.02 Type Traits . Computing with templates Non-type parameters and specialization together can compute values during compilation: recursion on N , with a specialization as the base case. cpp template <int N struct Factorial { static constexpr int value{ N Factorial<N - 1 ::value }; }; template < struct Factorial<0 { static constexpr int value{ 1 }; }; static_assert(Factorial<5 ::value == 120); This is the original form of template metaprogramming. A constexpr function says the same thing far more readably, and is what you should write today. The technique reappears in 11.07 Template Metaprogramming Techniques . Check yourself quiz ? Can a function template be partially specialized? - Yes, like a class template + No, only class and variable templates; functions overload - Yes, but only for pointer types - Only if it has no default arguments of any kind Functions get the same effect from overloading. Partial specialization is only for class and variable templates. ? Why is std::vector<bool unusual? - It cannot be resized - It stores each bool as an int + It stores one bit per element, not real bool objects - It is the only vector that cannot be sorted Packing bits saves space, but v 0 returns a proxy object, not a bool& , which breaks some generic code. ? What is the primary template? - The first specialization written + The general template, used when no specialization fits - The template with the most parameters - The template used by main Specializations refine the primary template for particular arguments; everything else uses the primary. ? Are StaticArray<int, 5 and StaticArray<int, 6 the same type? - Yes, the number is only a starting size - Yes, because both hold int + No, the non-type argument is part of the type Like std::array , the size is a template argument, so each size is a different type.

title: 9.03  Variadic Templates and Fold Expressions
body:
A variadic template accepts any number of arguments of any types, written template <typename... Args . The arguments form a parameter pack , which you expand with args... . Fold expressions apply an operator across a whole pack in one expression. Parameter packs cpp include <iostream template <typename... Args void count(const Args&... args) { std::cout << sizeof...(args) << " arguments:"; ((std::cout << ' ' << args), ...); // explained below std::cout << '
'; } int main() { count(); // 0 arguments: count(1, "hi", 3.5); // 3 arguments: 1 hi 3.5 return 0; } Syntax Name Holds --- --- --- typename... Args A template parameter pack Zero or more types const Args&... args A function parameter pack Zero or more values , one of each type sizeof...(args) The number of elements, as a compile-time constant args... A pack expansion The elements, separated by commas For count(1, "hi", 3.5) , Args is int, const char , double . A pack is not a container. You cannot index it or loop over it at run time. It can only be expanded , and the expansion happens entirely during compilation. This is the type-safe replacement for the C-style ... in 5.10 Function Pointers, Callbacks and Command-Line Arguments . Fold expressions A fold expression combines every element of a pack with a binary operator. cpp include <iostream template <typename... Ts auto sum(Ts... xs) { return (xs + ...); } template <typename... Ts void printAll(const Ts&... xs) { ((std::cout << xs << ' '), ...); std::cout << '
'; } int main() { std::cout << sum(1, 2, 3, 4) << '
'; // 10 printAll(1, "two", 3.0, 'x'); // 1 two 3 x return 0; } The parentheses around a fold are required. Form Name Expansion for a pack p1, p2, p3 --- --- --- (pack op ...) Unary right fold p1 op (p2 op p3) (... op pack) Unary left fold (p1 op p2) op p3 (pack op ... op init) Binary right fold p1 op (p2 op (p3 op init)) (init op ... op pack) Binary left fold ((init op p1) op p2) op p3 Left or right matters for operators that are not associative. With the pack 10, 3, 2 : (... - xs) is (10 - 3) - 2 = 5 (xs - ...) is 10 - (3 - 2) = 9 !warning Empty packs A unary fold over an empty pack is an error for most operators. (Only && , and the comma operator have defined results: true , false and nothing.) Use a binary fold with an initial value when the pack may be empty: (xs + ... + 0) . The comma fold printAll folds over the comma operator : ((std::cout << xs << ' '), ...) . The pattern inside the inner parentheses is repeated for each element, in order. This is the general way to "do something for every argument". Useful folds cpp template <typename... Ts bool allTrue(Ts... values) { return (values && ...); } template <typename... Ts bool anyTrue(Ts... values) { return (values ...); } template <typename T, typename... Ts bool isOneOf(const T& value, const Ts&... options) { return ((value == options) ...); } isOneOf(command, "quit", "exit", "q"); In isOneOf , the pattern (value == options) is expanded once per option, and short-circuits as usual. The older technique: recursion Before C++17, a pack was processed by peeling off one argument at a time. cpp void print() { std::cout << '
'; } template <typename T, typename... Rest void print(const T& first, const Rest&... rest) { std::cout << first << ' '; print(rest...); } Each step instantiates a new function with one fewer parameter, until the non-template overload with no parameters ends the chain. It is recursion in form only: every "call" is to a different function, and they are usually all inlined. if constexpr removes the need for a separate base case: cpp template <typename T, typename... Rest void print2(const T& first, const Rest&... rest) { std::cout << first << ' '; if constexpr (sizeof...(rest) 0) { print2(rest...); } } if constexpr is evaluated during compilation, and the branch not taken is discarded : it is not instantiated at all. Without that, print2() with no arguments would have to exist. Prefer a fold where one fits; use recursion when each step depends on the previous one. Forwarding a pack A wrapper that passes its arguments straight on to another function, as std::make_unique does, expands a pack through std::forward : cpp template <typename T, typename... Args std::unique_ptr<T makeIt(Args&&... args) { return std::unique_ptr<T (new T(std::forward<Args (args)...)); } The expansion std::forward<Args (args)... applies the pattern to each element in step, pairing each type with its value. What Args&& and std::forward achieve is the subject of 11.01 Value Categories and Perfect Forwarding . Variadic class templates Classes can be variadic too. std::tuple<int, std::string, double and std::variant<int, std::string are the two you will use most: 10.04 stdoptional, stdvariant, stdany and stdtuple . Check yourself quiz ? What does sizeof...(args) give? - The total size in bytes of all the arguments + The number of elements in the parameter pack, as a compile-time constant - The size of the largest argument - The number of template parameters, including non-packs sizeof... counts the elements of a pack. It has nothing to do with bytes. ? Expand (... - xs) for the pack 10, 3, 2. + (10 - 3) - 2 , which is 5 - 10 - (3 - 2) , which is 9 - 2 - 3 - 10 , which is -11 - -(10 + 3 + 2) , which is -15 With the ... on the left it is a left fold, grouping from the left. (xs - ...) would be the right fold giving 9. ? Why use (xs + ... + 0) instead of (xs + ...) ? - To make the result an int - Because (xs + ...) adds the elements twice + (xs + ...) does not compile for an empty pack - It is only a matter of style Only && , and , have a value for empty packs. The + 0 gives the fold a starting value. ? What does if constexpr do with the branch that is not taken? - It runs it anyway, then discards the result - It reports a compile error - It moves it to run time + It discards it at compile time, so that branch is never instantiated Inside a template, the discarded branch can contain code that would not compile for this type.
