Write: - int daysBetween(std::chrono::year_month_day from, std::chrono::year_month_day to) : how many days from one date to the other (negative if to is earlier). - bool isWeekend(std::chrono::year_month_day date) : build a std::chrono::weekday from the date's sys_days and compare it with std::chrono::Saturday and std::chrono::Sunday . - bool isRealDate(int year, int month, int day) : construct the date and ask it .ok() . A date is written std::chrono::year{ 2026 } / 11 / 12 .

title: 10.09  CMake, Libraries and Package Managers
body: Real projects have many files and use third-party libraries. CMake describes what to build portably and generates the build files for your tools. Libraries are static (copied into your executable) or dynamic (loaded while running). vcpkg and Conan download libraries for you. Beyond a single program Xenon compiles your files for you. A real project needs a description of what to build: which source files form which programs and libraries, with which settings, depending on which outside code. This lesson is about that machinery. It cannot be run inside Xenon, but you will need it for your first project outside. Static and dynamic libraries A library is compiled code packaged for reuse. Static Dynamic --- --- --- When it is joined to your program By the linker When the program starts Executable size Larger Smaller What you distribute One file The executable and the library file Update the library without rebuilding No Yes Shared in memory between programs No Yes Using a library takes three things What Who needs it Why --- --- --- The headers The compiler To know what the library declares The library file The linker To resolve the calls The dynamic library , if there is one The running program It must be found beside the executable or on the system path Missing headers give compile errors. A missing library file gives "unresolved external symbol". A missing DLL gives an error when the program starts. Knowing which stage failed tells you which of the three is wrong ( 1.08 Multiple Files and Headers ). CMake CMake does not compile anything. It reads a description of your project and generates build files for whatever tool you use: a Visual Studio solution, Makefiles or Ninja files. my_game/ ├── CMakeLists.txt ├── src/ │ ├── main.cpp │ └── game/ │ ├── Player.h │ └── Player.cpp └── tests/ └── test_player.cpp CMakeLists.txt cmake cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.25) project(MyGame VERSION 1.0 LANGUAGES CXX) set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20) set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON) set(CMAKE_CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF) A library holding the game logic add_library(game_core src/game/Player.cpp) target_include_directories(game_core PUBLIC src) if (MSVC) target_compile_options(game_core PRIVATE /W4 /permissive-) else() target_compile_options(game_core PRIVATE -Wall -Wextra -Wconversion -pedantic) endif() The program add_executable(my_game src/main.cpp) target_link_libraries(my_game PRIVATE game_core) Building bash cmake -S . -B build bash cmake --build build --config Release Everything generated goes into build/ , separate from your sources. Visual Studio, CLion and VS Code all open a CMake project directly. Targets Modern CMake is organised around targets : a library or an executable, together with what it needs. Command Does --- --- add_executable(name sources...) Defines a program add_library(name sources...) Defines a library target_include_directories(...) Says where a target's headers are target_compile_options(...) Adds compiler flags for a target target_link_libraries(a PRIVATE b) Makes a use b Each property carries a visibility keyword that says who it applies to. Keyword Applies to --- --- PRIVATE This target only PUBLIC This target and everything that links to it INTERFACE Only the things that link to it (as for a header-only library) game_core 's include directory is PUBLIC , so my_game receives it automatically by linking to game_core . Putting the logic in a library, with a thin executable on top, also lets a test program link the same library. Getting third-party libraries FetchContent Built into CMake: it downloads and builds a dependency as part of your project. cmake include(FetchContent) FetchContent_Declare(fmt GIT_REPOSITORY https://github.com/fmtlib/fmt.git GIT_TAG 11.0.2) FetchContent_MakeAvailable(fmt) target_link_libraries(my_game PRIVATE fmt::fmt) vcpkg A package manager downloads, builds and caches libraries, so each project only lists what it needs. vcpkg is Microsoft's; it works on every platform. bash vcpkg new --application bash vcpkg add port raylib nlohmann-json cmake find_package(raylib CONFIG REQUIRED) target_link_libraries(my_game PRIVATE raylib) Pass vcpkg's toolchain file when configuring, and find_package locates what it installed. Conan is a widely used alternative with the same purpose. Approach Good for --- --- FetchContent A few small dependencies; nothing extra to install vcpkg or Conan Many or large dependencies; builds are cached and shared across projects Libraries worth knowing Area Libraries --- --- Formatting and logging {fmt}, spdlog JSON nlohmann/json, simdjson Testing GoogleTest, Catch2, doctest 2D games and graphics raylib, SFML, SDL 3D graphics OpenGL with GLFW and glm; Vulkan User interfaces Dear ImGui, Qt Networking Asio, cpr Mathematics Eigen, glm Much else Boost Check yourself quiz ? What does target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE core) do? - It makes core part of app 's public interface for everything that links app + It links core into app and gives app the PUBLIC properties of core , without passing them on - It copies the source files of core into app - It builds core only in Debug builds PRIVATE means app uses core internally. Anything linking to app does not inherit core 's requirements. ? Which kind of library needs a file distributed with the executable? - A static library + A dynamic library - A header-only library - Every kind of library A static library is copied into the executable while linking. A dynamic library ( .dll , .so ) is loaded when the program starts. ? Does CMake compile your code? - Yes, it is a compiler + No, it generates build files for other tools - Only for C files, not for C++ - Only when using a package manager CMake describes the project and generates, for example, Ninja files or a Visual Studio solution. Those then run the compiler. ? The program builds but fails on start-up saying a DLL is missing. Which of the three requirements failed? - The compile-time one: the header was not found - The link-time one: the import library was not linked + The run-time one: the DLL is not where it can be found It built, so compiling and linking succeeded. Only the run-time search for the DLL failed.

title: Describe a project to CMake
body: This small project has a library ( shapes.h and shapes.cpp ) and a program that uses it ( main.cpp ). The code is finished. What is missing is the file that tells a build system how the pieces fit: CMakeLists.txt . Write it. It should: 1. start with cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20) (or newer) and a project(...) line naming the project Shapes with LANGUAGES CXX ; 2. ask for C++20: set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20) and set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON) ; 3. define a library target named shapes built from shapes.cpp : add_library(shapes shapes.cpp) ; 4. define an executable target named app built from main.cpp : add_executable(app main.cpp) ; 5. link the program against the library: target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE shapes) . The check compiles the C++ as usual (the program must still print 12 and 3.14159 ) and reads your CMakeLists.txt to see that the five pieces are there. On your own machine, with CMake installed, cmake -S . -B build followed by cmake --build build would then build it anywhere.

title: 11.01  Value Categories and Perfect Forwarding
body: Every expression has a type and a value category : lvalue, xvalue or prvalue. In a template, T&& is a forwarding reference : it binds to anything and records whether the argument was an lvalue or an rvalue. std::forward<T (x) passes it on with that category intact, which is perfect forwarding . Value categories, precisely 7.05 Move Semantics used a two-way split into lvalues and rvalues. The standard uses three primary categories, defined by two independent properties: does the expression have identity (does it refer to a particular object), and may its resources be moved from ? Category Identity Movable Examples --- --- --- --- lvalue Yes No x , p , v 0 , a string literal xvalue ("expiring") Yes Yes std::move(x) , static_cast<T&& (x) prvalue ("pure rvalue") No Yes 42 , x + 1 , T{} , make() A value category is a property of an expression , not of an object or a type. The same object can be named by an lvalue expression ( x ) and by an xvalue expression ( std::move(x) ). !important A named rvalue reference is an lvalue cpp void f(std::string&& s) { g(s); // s is a name, so this expression is an lvalue: g copies g(std::move(s)); // an xvalue: g may move } The type of s is std::string&& . The value category of the expression s is lvalue, because it has a name and could be used again. This is what makes forwarding necessary. Forwarding references T&& has a special meaning when, and only when, T is a template parameter deduced from that very parameter. cpp template <typename T void wrapper(T&& arg); // forwarding reference: binds to anything void f(std::string&& s); // rvalue reference: binds to rvalues only auto&& x{ expression }; // also a forwarding reference Declaration Kind --- --- template <typename T void f(T&&) Forwarding reference auto&& Forwarding reference void f(Widget&&) Rvalue reference: no deduction template <typename T void f(const T&&) Rvalue reference: const disqualifies it template <typename T void f(std::vector<T &&) Rvalue reference: not of the form T&& Reference collapsing Two rules produce the behaviour. A special deduction rule. When an lvalue of type A is passed to T&& , T is deduced as A& . When an rvalue is passed, T is deduced as A . Reference collapsing. A reference to a reference, which can only arise through templates and aliases, collapses: & & becomes & & && becomes & && & becomes & && && becomes && an lvalue reference anywhere wins Argument T deduced as T&& becomes --- --- --- An lvalue std::string std::string& std::string& && , which collapses to std::string& An rvalue std::string std::string std::string&& So T itself encodes the argument's original value category. std::forward Inside wrapper , arg is a name and therefore an lvalue, whatever was passed. std::forward<T (arg) restores the original category by reading it back out of T . cpp include <iostream include <string include <utility void process(const std::string&) { std::cout << "copy\n"; } void process(std::string&&) { std::cout << "move\n"; } template <typename T void relay(T&& arg) { process(std::forward<T (arg)); } int main() { std::string name{ "Ann" }; relay(name); // copy relay(std::string{ "Bo" }); // move relay(std::move(name)); // move return 0; } std::forward<T (arg) is static_cast<T&& (arg) . With T as std::string& it collapses to an lvalue reference; with T as std::string it is an rvalue reference. std::move(x) std::forward<T (x) --- --- --- Produces Always an rvalue An lvalue or an rvalue, as recorded in T Use with An rvalue reference or object you are finished with A forwarding reference Template argument Deduced Must be written explicitly The standard use: wrapping construction cpp template <typename T, typename... Args std::unique_ptr<T make(Args&&... args) { return std::unique_ptr<T { new T(std::forward<Args (args)...) }; } Each argument reaches T 's constructor exactly as the caller supplied it: lvalues are copied from, rvalues moved from, and nothing is copied in between. std::make_unique , emplace_back and the constructor of std::thread all work this way. decltype and decltype(auto) Expression Yields --- --- decltype(x) where x is a name The declared type of x decltype((x)) , or any other lvalue expression of type T T& decltype( an xvalue ) T&& decltype( a prvalue ) T cpp int x{}; decltype(x) a{}; // int decltype((x)) b{ x }; // int&: the parentheses make it an expression, not a name auto strips references and top-level const . decltype(auto) deduces with the decltype rules, preserving them. That is what a forwarding wrapper needs for its return type: cpp template <typename F, typename... Args decltype(auto) call(F&& f, Args&&... args) { return std::forward<F (f)(std::forward<Args (args)...); } If f returns a reference, so does call . std::invoke(f, args...) generalises the call itself to member function pointers and member data pointers. Pitfalls Pitfall Why --- --- Forwarding the same argument twice The first use may move from it Overloading on a forwarding reference template <typename T void f(T&&) is an exact match for almost anything and beats f(const Widget&) for a non-const lvalue. Constrain it with a concept. A forwarding constructor It can hijack copy construction from a non-const lvalue. Constrain it. return (x); under decltype(auto) The parentheses make it T& : a reference to a local Check yourself quiz ? When is T&& a forwarding reference? - Whenever it appears in a template - Whenever T is a class type + When T is deduced from that very parameter, or as auto&& - Only when it is passed to std::forward In template <typename T void f(T&& x) it is a forwarding reference. In a member of Box<T where T is already fixed, T&& is a plain rvalue reference. ? What is T deduced as when an lvalue int is passed to a T&& parameter? - int + int& - int&& - const int& For an lvalue, T becomes int& , and int& && collapses to int& . For an rvalue, T is plain int . ? Why is a named rvalue reference an lvalue? + A value category belongs to an expression, and a name refers to an object that can be used again - Because the compiler converts all references to lvalue references - It is not; it stays an rvalue everywhere - Because rvalue references cannot have names Inside the function, x can be used many times, so using its name is an lvalue expression. That is why you write std::move(x) or std::forward<T (x) . ? What is the difference between std::move and std::forward ? - std::move copies; std::forward moves the object - They are the same - std::forward always produces an lvalue reference + std::move always gives an rvalue; std::forward keeps the caller's std::forward restores the category the caller passed, which T recorded. std::move is unconditional.

title: Forward it untouched
body: receive has two overloads: one for objects that must be copied (lvalues) and one for temporaries that may be moved from (rvalues). Write template <typename T std::string relay(T&& widget) that passes its argument on to receive exactly as it arrived : an lvalue stays an lvalue, an rvalue stays an rvalue. Inside relay , widget has a name, so on its own it is always an lvalue. std::forward<T (widget) restores the original category.

title: A factory that wastes nothing
body: Write two helpers that construct objects in place, forwarding every argument perfectly so that nothing is copied on the way. - make<T (args...) : returns a std::unique_ptr<T built from the arguments. This is essentially std::make_unique . - emplaceBack(vector, args...) : constructs a new element at the end of a std::vector<T from the arguments and returns a reference to it. Both take a parameter pack of forwarding references ( Args&&... args ) and expand it with std::forward<Args (args)... . The tests use a type that counts how often it is copied. Passing a temporary through your helpers must cause zero copies.

title: 11.02  Type Traits
body: Type traits , in <type_traits , are compile-time questions about types and transformations of them: "is T an integer?", "T without its const". Each is a template yielding a value or a type . With if constexpr and static_assert , they let code adapt to the types it is given. Computing with types A type trait is a class template whose result is a member: a value for a question, or a type for a transformation. They are functions from types to values or to other types, evaluated entirely by the compiler. Using them to shape code is metaprogramming . Query traits cpp include <type_traits static_assert(std::is_integral_v<int ); static_assert(std::is_floating_point_v<float ); static_assert(std::is_pointer_v<int ); static_assert(std::is_same_v<int, signed int ); Trait Asks --- --- is_integral_v<T , is_floating_point_v<T , is_arithmetic_v<T What kind of number? is_pointer_v<T , is_reference_v<T , is_array_v<T , is_enum_v<T , is_class_v<T What category of type? is_const_v<T Is it const -qualified? is_same_v<T, U Are they exactly the same type? is_base_of_v<Base, Derived , is_convertible_v<From, To How are two types related? is_trivially_copyable_v<T Can it be copied as raw bytes? is_nothrow_move_constructible_v<T Is its move constructor noexcept ? is_invocable_v<F, Args... Can F be called with these arguments? trait_v<T is a variable template, short for trait<T ::value . Transformation traits Trait Result --- --- remove_const_t<const int int remove_reference_t<int& int remove_cvref_t<const int& int add_pointer_t<int int decay_t<const int 5 const int : what passing by value does make_unsigned_t<int unsigned int conditional_t<condition, A, B A if true, otherwise B common_type_t<int, double double underlying_type_t<Enum The enum's integer type trait_t<T is an alias template, short for typename trait<T ::type . std::remove_cvref_t is the one you will reach for most. Inside a template with a forwarding reference, T may be Widget& or const Widget& , and most questions should be asked about plain Widget . Using traits static_assert : state a requirement cpp template <typename T void writeBytes(std::ostream& out, const T& value) { static_assert(std::is_trivially_copyable_v<T , "writeBytes needs a trivially copyable type"); out.write(reinterpret_cast<const char (&value), sizeof(T)); } A violated requirement becomes a compile error with your message, in place of undefined behaviour at run time. if constexpr : one function, a branch per type cpp include <iostream include <string include <type_traits template <typename T std::string toString(const T& value) { if constexpr (std::is_same_v<T, std::string ) { return value; } else if constexpr (std::is_arithmetic_v<T ) { return std::to_string(value); } else if constexpr (std::is_pointer_v<T ) { return value ? toString( value) : "null"; } else { static_assert(false, "toString: unsupported type"); } } int main() { const int n{ 42 }; std::cout << toString(n) << ' ' << toString(std::string{ "hi" }) << ' ' << toString(&n) << '\n'; return 0; } The condition of if constexpr is evaluated at compile time, and the branches not taken are discarded : they are not instantiated for that T . That is the whole point. std::to_string(value) would not compile for a std::string , and here it is never asked to. How traits are built There is no compiler magic in most of them. A trait is a primary template giving the general answer and specializations giving the exceptions ( 9.02 Non-Type Parameters and Template Specialization ). cpp template <typename T struct IsPointer : std::false_type {}; // in general: no template <typename T struct IsPointer<T : std::true_type {}; // for anything of the form T : yes template <typename T inline constexpr bool isPointer_v{ IsPointer<T ::value }; static_assert(isPointer_v<int ); static_assert(!isPointer_v<int ); std::true_type and std::false_type are tiny classes with a static value of true or false . Inheriting from one is the conventional way to give a trait its result. A transformation works the same way, with a nested type as the result: cpp template <typename T struct RemoveConst { using type = T; }; template <typename T struct RemoveConst<const T { using type = T; }; template <typename T using RemoveConst_t = typename RemoveConst<T ::type; The typename keyword is required before RemoveConst<T ::type because it is a dependent name : until T is known, the compiler cannot tell whether ::type names a type or a value, and assumes a value unless told otherwise. A few traits cannot be written in the language at all and are supplied by the compiler: is_trivially_copyable , is_class , is_enum and underlying_type among them. Detecting capabilities Asking "does T have a size() member?" used to need the machinery of the next lesson. With C++20 it is one requires-expression ( 9.04 Concepts (C++20) ): cpp template <typename T inline constexpr bool hasSize{ requires(const T& t) { t.size(); } }; static_assert(hasSize<std::vector<int ); static_assert(!hasSize<int ); Traits or concepts? Type traits Concepts --- --- --- Produce A boolean or a type A named constraint Constrain a template Through enable_if : awkward Directly Take part in overload ordering No Yes, by subsumption Transform types Yes No Use concepts to constrain . Use traits to compute types, and inside if constexpr . Most standard concepts are defined in terms of traits. Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference between the _v and _t suffixes? - _v is for variables, _t is for templates + _v gives the trait's value ; _t gives its type - _t is for traits that run at run time - There is none std::is_pointer_v<T is std::is_pointer<T ::value , and std::remove_const_t<T is typename std::remove_const<T ::type . ? Why does if constexpr matter when using traits? - Because traits only work inside if constexpr - Because it runs the trait at run time + Branches not taken are not instantiated for this type - Because a normal if cannot test a bool With a plain if , both branches must compile for every T , even the one that never runs. ? How is a trait such as is_pointer implemented? - With a run-time check of the value - With a built-in compiler keyword only + A false_type primary template and a true_type one for T - With a virtual function in each type Pattern matching by specialization: T matches the specialization, everything else gets the primary template. ? Why is typename needed in typename RemoveConst<T ::type ? - Because type is a reserved word - Because the trait returns a value, not a type - It is only needed in C++11, not later + The name depends on T , so it must be marked as a type Until T is known, the compiler cannot tell whether ::type is a type or a value. typename says it is a type.

title: 11.03  SFINAE, enable_if and Tag Dispatch
body: SFINAE , "Substitution Failure Is Not An Error": if substituting a type into a template's declaration produces invalid code, that overload is silently removed instead of causing an error. Code before C++20 used it, through std::enable_if , void_t and tag dispatch, to constrain templates. Concepts do the job better now, but you must be able to read it. The rule When the compiler considers a function template for a call, it deduces the template arguments and substitutes them into the declaration. If that substitution produces an invalid type or expression, the template is dropped from the set of candidates. The program is not ill-formed. The rule exists so that an overload set may contain templates that are only meaningful for some types. Library authors turned it into a way of deliberately making a template vanish unless a condition holds. !warning Only the immediate context counts SFINAE applies to failures in the function's declaration : its return type, its parameter types and its template parameter list. An error inside the function body is a hard error. This is why a constraint has to be expressed in the signature. std::enable_if enable_if is a trait built to fail on purpose. cpp template <bool Condition, typename T = void struct enable_if {}; // no member named type template <typename T struct enable_if<true, T { using type = T; // present only when the condition is true }; std::enable_if_t<false names a member that does not exist. That is a substitution failure, so the overload disappears. cpp include <iostream include <type_traits template <typename T, std::enable_if_t<std::is_integral_v<T , int = 0 T half(T x) { return x / 2; } template <typename T, std::enable_if_t<std::is_floating_point_v<T , int = 0 T half(T x) { return x T{ 0.5 }; } int main() { std::cout << half(10) << ' ' << half(3.0) << '\n'; // 5 1.5 // half("x"); error: no matching function, both overloads were removed return 0; } Read std::enable_if_t<condition, int = 0 as "an unused template parameter of type int , defaulted to 0, which only exists when the condition is true". The same device appears in three places: Position Looks like --- --- A defaulted template parameter template <typename T, std::enable_if_t<C, int = 0 The return type std::enable_if_t<C, T half(T x); An extra function parameter T half(T x, std::enable_if_t<C = nullptr); The same thing with concepts cpp auto half(std::integral auto x) { return x / 2; } auto half(std::floating_point auto x) { return x 0.5; } The requirement is stated, not encoded. That is why 9.04 Concepts (C++20) exist. Detecting members Two more tools make it possible to ask whether an expression is valid. Tool Does --- --- std::declval<T () Yields a T&& without constructing anything. Usable only where nothing is evaluated, such as inside decltype . std::void_t<Ts... Is void if every Ts is a valid type; otherwise substitution fails cpp template <typename, typename = void struct HasSize : std::false_type {}; template <typename T struct HasSize<T, std::void_t<decltype(std::declval<T ().size()) : std::true_type {}; static_assert(HasSize<std::string ::value); static_assert(!HasSize<int ::value); How it works, for HasSize<X : 1. The primary template gives the second argument its default, void , so the lookup is for HasSize<X, void . 2. The partial specialization is tried. If X has .size() , the decltype is a valid type, void_t is void , and the specialization matches HasSize<X, void and is preferred. 3. If not, substitution fails, the specialization is discarded, and the primary template's false_type remains. This is called the detection idiom . A trailing return type achieves a similar effect for functions: cpp template <typename C auto printSize(const C& container) - decltype(container.size(), void()) { std::cout << container.size() << '\n'; } The comma expression requires container.size() to be valid and then yields void as the return type. Tag dispatch A different technique with the same purpose: choose an implementation by overloading on an empty tag type. cpp template <typename It void advanceImpl(It& it, int n, std::random_access_iterator_tag) { it += n; // O(1) } template <typename It void advanceImpl(It& it, int n, std::input_iterator_tag) { while (n-- 0) { ++it; // O(n) } } template <typename It void myAdvance(It& it, int n) { advanceImpl(it, n, typename std::iterator_traits<It ::iterator_category{}); } Each iterator type declares its category as a tag type. The tags form an inheritance hierarchy, so a random-access iterator's tag also converts to input_iterator_tag , and overload resolution picks the most specific implementation available. Nothing is removed; ordinary overloading does the selection. The modern form needs no helper functions: cpp template <typename It void myAdvance(It& it, int n) { if constexpr (std::random_access_iterator<It ) { it += n; } else { while (n-- 0) { ++it; } } } How the techniques evolved Standard Tools for constraining and selecting --- --- C++98 Tag dispatch, specialization of traits C++11 enable_if , decltype , declval , SFINAE on expressions C++17 void_t , if constexpr C++20 Concepts and requires Write concepts in new code. Read SFINAE in everything written before 2020, including most of the libraries you will use. Check yourself quiz ? Is an error in the body of a function template subject to SFINAE? - Yes, any error anywhere removes the overload + No, an error in the body is a hard error - Only in Debug builds - Only for class templates SFINAE applies to the immediate context: the signature, return type and template arguments. The body is too late. ? What does std::declval<T () do? - It constructs a default T for use in decltype - It declares a variable of type T + It gives a T&& without building one, for decltype only - It checks whether T is declared decltype(std::declval<T ().size()) asks about size() even when T has no default constructor. Calling it for real is an error. ? How does std::enable_if_t<false remove an overload? - It makes the function return void - It throws when the function is called - It marks the function as deleted + It names a missing member type, so substitution fails std::enable_if<false has no type member, so substituting fails and overload resolution ignores that template. ? How does tag dispatch differ from SFINAE? + It removes nothing; normal overloading picks on a tag argument - It works only at run time - It uses virtual functions to choose - It is the same technique under another name A public function forwards to impl(args, std::true_type{}) or impl(args, std::false_type{}) , and normal overloading picks.

title: 11.04  Compile-Time Programming — constexpr, consteval, constinit
body: Modern C++ can run real code inside the compiler : loops, std::vector , std::string , even new and delete , provided nothing allocated escapes to run time. constexpr may run at compile time, consteval must , and constinit guarantees a static variable is initialized at compile time while leaving it mutable. The keywords 2.06 const and constexpr introduced constexpr . Here is the full set. Keyword Applies to Meaning --- --- --- constexpr A variable Its value is a compile-time constant; implies const constexpr A function May be evaluated at compile time when its arguments are constant; otherwise runs normally consteval A function Must be evaluated at compile time. An immediate function . constinit A static or thread-local variable Initialized at compile time, but not const if constexpr A branch Selected at compile time; the other branch is discarded if consteval (C++23) A branch Taken when the function is being evaluated at compile time An evaluation done by the compiler is a constant evaluation . It is forced wherever the language needs a constant: the initializer of a constexpr variable, a template argument, an array bound, a case label, a static_assert . !note constexpr on a function is a permission, not a guarantee int x{ sq(5) }; with a non- constexpr x may or may not be folded by the optimiser. To be certain, initialize a constexpr variable, or make the function consteval . Real algorithms at compile time cpp include <array include <cstddef include <iostream constexpr bool isPrime(int n) { if (n < 2) { return false; } for (int i{ 2 }; i i <= n; ++i) { if (n % i == 0) { return false; } } return true; } template <std::size_t N constexpr std::array<int, N firstPrimes() { std::array<int, N result{}; std::size_t found{ 0 }; for (int n{ 2 }; found < N; ++n) { if (isPrime(n)) { result found++ = n; } } return result; } constexpr auto primes{ firstPrimes<10 () }; static_assert(primes 9 == 29); int main() { for (int p : primes) { std::cout << p << ' '; } std::cout << '\n'; return 0; } The loop runs in the compiler. The executable contains the finished table and no code to compute it. This is the modern way to build lookup tables. Containers at compile time Since C++20, dynamic allocation is permitted during constant evaluation, on one condition: everything allocated must be released before the evaluation ends. This is a transient allocation . cpp constexpr int sumOfSquares(int n) { std::vector<int values{}; for (int i{ 1 }; i <= n; ++i) { values.push_back(i i); } return std::accumulate(values.begin(), values.end(), 0); } // the vector is destroyed here, inside the evaluation static_assert(sumOfSquares(3) == 14); std::vector and std::string are usable inside a constexpr function. What you cannot do is make a constexpr variable of those types that holds heap memory, because that memory would have to survive into the running program. Return a std::array or a plain value instead. Hashing strings for a switch A switch needs integer constants ( 3.02 switch ). A constexpr hash function supplies them from strings and also runs normally on run-time input. cpp constexpr std::uint32_t hashName(std::string_view text) { std::uint32_t hash{ 2166136261u }; for (char c : text) { hash ^= static_cast<std::uint8_t (c); hash = 16777619u; } return hash; } switch (hashName(command)) // run time: hashes what the user typed { case hashName("jump"): jump(); break; // compile time: a case label must be a constant case hashName("run"): run(); break; } One function, used in both worlds. Two different strings can hash to the same value, so real code confirms the match afterwards. consteval cpp consteval int square(int n) { return n n; } constexpr int a{ square(8) }; // 64, computed by the compiler int x{ 3 }; int b{ square(x) }; // error: x is not a constant expression Use consteval when a run-time call would be a mistake. Its best-known use is validation : std::format checks its format string through a consteval constructor, which is how a wrong format string becomes a compile error ( 10.07 Formatting with stdformat and stdprint ). You can do the same: cpp consteval int checkedPercent(int value) { if (value < 0 value 100) { throw "percentage out of range"; // reaching a throw makes the evaluation fail } return value; } constexpr int volume{ checkedPercent(80) }; // fine // constexpr int bad{ checkedPercent(140) }; // compile error constinit A global with a dynamic initializer is initialized at program start, before main . Across different source files the order is unspecified, so one global's initializer may use another that has not been initialized yet. That is the static initialization order fiasco . cpp constinit int g_counter{ 0 }; // initialized at compile time; still modifiable constinit thread_local int t_calls{ 0 }; constinit makes the compiler verify that the initializer is a constant expression. A variable initialized at compile time exists before any code runs, so it cannot be caught in that ordering problem. Unlike constexpr , it does not make the variable const . Values with constexpr , types with templates The original way to compute at compile time was recursion through template instantiation ( 9.02 Non-Type Parameters and Template Specialization ): cpp template <unsigned N struct Factorial { static constexpr unsigned value{ N Factorial<N - 1 ::value }; }; template < struct Factorial<0 { static constexpr unsigned value{ 1 }; }; Today: cpp constexpr unsigned factorial(unsigned n) { return n <= 1 ? 1 : n factorial(n - 1); } !tip The division of labour Compute values with constexpr functions: they are ordinary code, testable at run time too. Use templates and traits to compute types : 11.07 Template Metaprogramming Techniques . What is not allowed Restriction Detail --- --- Undefined behaviour The compiler rejects it during constant evaluation Input and output No streams, no files reinterpret_cast Not permitted Non-transient allocation Memory must be released before the evaluation ends Unbounded work Compilers limit the number of steps and the recursion depth The first row is a benefit. An overflow, an out-of-bounds index or a read of an uninitialized variable inside a constant evaluation is a compile error. Testing a constexpr function with static_assert therefore proves those cases are free of undefined behaviour. Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference between a constexpr function and a consteval function? - There is none - A consteval function may run at run time; a constexpr one may not + Only a consteval function must run at compile time - A constexpr function cannot have loops consteval makes an "immediate function": every call must produce a constant, or the build fails. ? What does constinit add to a static variable? - It makes the variable const + Compile-time initialization, while staying modifiable - It makes the variable thread-local - It delays initialization until first use constinit avoids the static initialization order problem without making the variable read-only. ? Why can a constexpr function use a std::vector internally but not return one into a constexpr variable? - Because vectors cannot be used at compile time at all - Because constexpr variables must be integers + Compile-time allocations must be freed before evaluation ends - Because returning a vector always throws Compile-time allocation is allowed only if it is freed within the same evaluation, so the vector cannot survive into the program. ? What happens to undefined behaviour during constant evaluation? - It behaves the same as at run time - It is silently ignored + The compiler diagnoses it as an error - It is turned into a warning Constant evaluation must be well defined, so overflow or out-of-bounds access there stops the build. This makes constexpr tests useful.

title: 11.05  CRTP, Mixins and Static Polymorphism
body: The Curiously Recurring Template Pattern : class Derived : public Base<Derived . The base knows the derived type at compile time, so it can call derived functions without virtual . That is static polymorphism. It suits mixins and interfaces with no run-time overhead. C++23's deducing this simplifies it. The shape of the pattern A class derives from a template and passes itself as the argument. cpp include <iostream template <typename Derived class Shape { public: double area() const { return static_cast<const Derived& ( this).areaImpl(); } }; class Square : public Shape<Square { public: double areaImpl() const { return m_side m_side; } private: double m_side{ 2.0 }; }; template <typename T void printArea(const Shape<T & shape) { std::cout << shape.area() << '\n'; } int main() { const Square square{}; printArea(square); // 4 return 0; } This is the Curiously Recurring Template Pattern (CRTP). Inside Shape<Derived , the object is known to be a Derived , so the static_cast down to it is valid, and the call to areaImpl is an ordinary direct call that the compiler can inline. It is legal for Square to name itself as a template argument before it is complete, because the bodies of Shape<Square 's member functions are not instantiated until they are used, and by then Square is complete. Dynamic and static polymorphism virtual (dynamic) CRTP and templates (static) --- --- --- The call is resolved At run time, through the vtable At compile time Inlining Usually not possible Yes Per-object overhead A vptr None Different types in one container Yes: std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Shape No: Shape<Square and Shape<Circle are unrelated types New types without recompiling users Yes No Code size One function body One instantiation per type Use CRTP when the set of types is known at compile time and the call sits on a hot path. Use virtual when types must be chosen or mixed at run time. The mechanics of the virtual side are in 8.04 How Virtual Works — vtables . Mixins The more common use of CRTP is not polymorphism. It is to inject functionality into a class. A base class used this way is a mixin . An object counter per class cpp template <typename T class Counted { public: static int alive() { return s_alive; } protected: Counted() { ++s_alive; } Counted(const Counted&) { ++s_alive; } ~Counted() { --s_alive; } private: static inline int s_alive{ 0 }; }; class Enemy : public Counted<Enemy { }; class Bullet : public Counted<Bullet { }; Counted<Enemy and Counted<Bullet are different classes, so each has its own static counter. A non-template base would give one counter shared by everything. The protected destructor prevents deletion through a Counted<T , so no virtual destructor is needed. Generating operators cpp template <typename D struct EqualityComparable { friend bool operator!=(const D& a, const D& b) { return !(a == b); } }; struct Point : EqualityComparable<Point { int x{}; int y{}; friend bool operator==(const Point& a, const Point& b) { return a.x == b.x && a.y == b.y; } }; The derived class supplies one operation and the mixin derives the rest. C++20's defaulted comparisons ( 6.07 Operator Overloading Basics ) have made this particular example unnecessary, but the technique is everywhere in older libraries. Removing clone boilerplate cpp template <typename Base, typename Derived class Cloneable : public Base { public: std::unique_ptr<Base clone() const override { return std::make_unique<Derived (static_cast<const Derived& ( this)); } }; class Circle : public Cloneable<Shape, Circle { // clone() is supplied }; Here CRTP and virtual functions work together: the hierarchy is dynamic, and the repetitive override is generated statically. Deducing this C++23 lets a member function declare its object parameter explicitly, and deduce its type. cpp struct Shape { double area(this const auto& self) { return self.areaImpl(); } }; struct Square : Shape { double side{ 2.0 }; double areaImpl() const { return side side; } }; self is deduced as the actual type of the object the function is called on, so no template base and no cast are required. The feature is called an explicit object parameter . It also removes the duplication between const and non-const overloads ( 6.04 this, const Member Functions and Chaining ): cpp class Text { public: template <typename Self auto&& at(this Self&& self, std::size_t i) { return std::forward<Self (self).m_text i ; } private: std::string m_text{}; }; One function serves const objects, non-const objects and temporaries, with the right return type for each. Pitfalls Pitfall Consequence Defence --- --- --- Naming the wrong type: class Circle : public Shape<Square Compiles; the static_cast is undefined behaviour Make the base constructor private and declare friend Derived; so only the named class can construct it The derived class omits areaImpl A confusing error, or endless recursion if base and derived use the same name Use distinct names, or constrain with a concept Expecting a common base type Shape<A and Shape<B share nothing Add a non-template base if run-time polymorphism is also needed Check yourself quiz ? Why can CRTP shapes of different types not be stored in one vector? - Because CRTP classes cannot be copied - Because CRTP classes have no size - Because vectors cannot hold templates + Each has a different base, so there is no common base Static polymorphism gives every class its own base type. For a mixed collection you need virtual functions or a variant. ? What does CRTP use in place of the vtable? + A static_cast to the derived type, known when compiling - A dynamic_cast to the derived type - A function pointer stored in each object - A std::function member The base knows the derived type as its template argument, so static_cast<Derived& ( this) calls it directly and can be inlined. ? Why does Counted<T give each class its own counter? - Because the counter is not static - Because each object has its own counter + Each Counted<T is a distinct class with its own static - Because the counter is stored in the derived class Each instantiation of the template is a separate class, so each gets its own copy of the static member. ? What does C++23's deducing this provide? - A way to change this to point at another object - Automatic const on every member function - A virtual function without a vtable + An explicit object parameter deduced as the real type void draw(this const auto& self) sees the real derived type as self , which replaces many CRTP uses.
