The catalogue Category Examples --- --- Arithmetic Signed integer overflow; division by zero; shifting by a negative amount or by the width of the type or more; INT_MIN / -1 Memory Out-of-bounds access; dereferencing null; use after free; double delete; mismatched new and delete Lifetime Dangling references and pointers; returning a reference to a local; using an object after its destructor has run Initialization Reading an uninitialized variable Type punning Accessing an object through a pointer to an unrelated type; reading the inactive member of a union Concurrency Data races Library preconditions v v.size() ; front() on an empty container; a comparator for std::sort that is not a consistent ordering; modifying a key in a std::set Others Flowing off the end of a non- void function; modifying a const object; violating the One Definition Rule The standard distinguishes three weaker cousins: Term Meaning Example --- --- --- Implementation-defined The compiler chooses and documents it sizeof(int) Unspecified One of several allowed results, undocumented The order in which function arguments are evaluated Erroneous (C++26) Wrong, but with bounded, defined consequences Reading an uninitialized local, from C++26 Strict aliasing and type punning The strict aliasing rule : an object may be accessed only through an expression of its own type (with a few allowances for const , signedness and base classes). It lets the compiler assume that a float and an int never refer to the same memory, which enables important optimizations. cpp float f{ 1.0f }; std::uint32_t bad{ reinterpret_cast<std::uint32_t (&f) }; // undefined: aliasing violation std::uint32_t good{ std::bit_cast<std::uint32_t (f) }; // defined, and constexpr std::uint32_t older{}; std::memcpy(&older, &f, sizeof older); // the pre-C++20 way Reinterpreting the bits of one type as another is type punning . std::bit_cast and std::memcpy both copy the representation into a fresh object of the target type, and compilers turn either into a single move instruction. One exception is always allowed: any object's bytes may be examined through a pointer to char , unsigned char or std::byte . Object lifetime Memory existing is not the same as an object existing. storage obtained ─▶ lifetime: initialization complete ... destructor begins ─▶ storage released ▲ the object may be used only inside this window ▲ Event Lifetime --- --- Storage is obtained, and initialization finishes Begins The destructor starts, or the storage is released or reused Ends Using an object outside its lifetime is undefined, even when the bytes are still there and look intact. You can control the two halves separately: cpp alignas(Widget) std::byte buffer sizeof(Widget) ; Widget w{ std::construct_at(reinterpret_cast<Widget (buffer), arguments) }; // lifetime begins std::destroy_at(w); // lifetime ends Facility Purpose --- --- std::construct_at , std::destroy_at Begin and end a lifetime in existing storage: 13.03 Custom Memory Placement new, Allocators and PMR Implicit-lifetime types Simple types (scalars, trivial structs, arrays of them) come into existence in storage from malloc or after a memcpy without explicit construction std::start_lifetime_as<T (p) (C++23) Declares that bytes received from a file or the network are a T std::launder Obtains a usable pointer in rare cases where storage is reused for an object with const or reference members Temporaries A temporary lives until the end of the full expression that created it. One rule extends that: binding a temporary directly to a const reference (or an rvalue reference) keeps it alive as long as the reference. Code Result --- --- const std::string& r{ std::string{ "hi" } }; Fine: the lifetime is extended to that of r std::string_view sv{ std::string{ "temp" } }; Dangles at the end of the statement: a view is not a reference binding auto& first{ std::vector{ 1, 2, 3 } 0 }; Dangles: the reference binds to an element, not to the temporary const auto& n{ makePlayer().name() }; Dangles if name() returns a reference into the temporary Extension applies only to the temporary itself, not to things reached through it. Defences Tool Catches --- --- AddressSanitizer Out-of-bounds access, use after free, leaks UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer Overflow, invalid shifts, null dereference, misalignment ThreadSanitizer Data races Constant evaluation The compiler rejects undefined behaviour inside a constexpr evaluation: 11.04 Compile-Time Programming — constexpr, consteval, constinit A hardened standard library Bounds checks on operator , front() and iterators. Xenon's Debug build has these on. Warnings and static analysis Many patterns, before the program runs: 13.09 Testing, Sanitizers, Static Analysis and Tooling No tool finds everything. The durable defence is habit: prefer the constructs that cannot go wrong ( std::vector::at , ranges, smart pointers, std::bit_cast , RAII), so that the dangerous ones are rare and visible. Check yourself quiz ? Why can undefined behaviour affect code that runs before the faulty operation? - Because the program runs its lines in a random order - Because the processor predicts the error in advance + The optimizer assumes the undefined behaviour never happens - It cannot; only later code is affected The compiler reasons "this path would be UB, so it cannot happen" and may remove or rearrange earlier code on that basis. ? What is the safe way to reinterpret a float 's bits as an integer? - reinterpret_cast<std::uint32_t (&f) - static_cast<std::uint32_t (f) - Write the float into a union and read the integer member + std::bit_cast<std::uint32_t (f) , or std::memcpy before C++20 reinterpret_cast through a pointer breaks strict aliasing and the union trick is UB in C++. static_cast converts the value, not the bits. ? What does the strict aliasing rule allow the compiler to assume? + That pointers to unrelated types do not refer to the same object - That no two pointers ever hold the same address - That every pointer is non-null - That char pointers never alias anything A write through a float cannot change an int , so the compiler may keep the int in a register. ( char and std::byte are the exceptions that may alias anything.) ? When does a temporary's lifetime get extended? - Whenever it is assigned to a variable - When it is passed to a function by value + When it is bound directly to a const reference or an rvalue reference - Never; temporaries always die at the end of the statement It then lives as long as that reference. Binding through a function's returned reference does not extend it.

title: Three ways to step off the edge
match: Three ways to step off the edge
body: Each of these functions is correct for ordinary inputs and has undefined behaviour for an edge case its author never thought about. Find the edge case in each and fix the function so it does what the comment says. Undefined behaviour does not mean "returns the wrong value". It means the compiler may assume it never happens, so the damage can show up anywhere. Close each gap at its source.

title: Look at the bits, legally
body: Reading a float 's bytes through an int breaks the strict aliasing rule: the compiler is allowed to assume a float and an int never occupy the same memory, and to optimise on that basis. std::bit_cast (C++20, in <bit ) does the same job correctly: it produces a new object of another type with the same bits. Rewrite both functions with std::bit_cast : - std::uint32_t bitsOf(float value) - bool isNegative(float value) : true when the sign bit (the top bit) is set. This is true for -0.0f as well, which value < 0 would miss.

title: 13.02  Memory Layout, Alignment, Unions and Bit Fields
match: 13.02 Memory Layout, Alignment, Unions and Bit Fields
body: Every type has a size and an alignment : its address must be a multiple of the alignment. The compiler inserts padding to arrange that. Unions overlay members in the same memory. Bit fields pack members into bits. Endianness fixes the byte order. All of it matters for performance, file formats, networking and hardware. Alignment and padding A processor reads a value fastest, and on some architectures only, when it starts at an address that is a multiple of a particular number. That number is the type's alignment . cpp struct Loose { char a{}; double b{}; char c{}; }; // sizeof is 24 struct Tight { double b{}; char a{}; char c{}; }; // sizeof is 16 Loose: a · · · · · · · b b b b b b b b c · · · · · · · 24 bytes 1 7 padding 8 1 7 padding Tight: b b b b b b b b a c · · · · · · 16 bytes 8 1 1 6 padding Rule Consequence --- --- Each member is placed at the next offset that satisfies its alignment Padding appears between members A struct's alignment is that of its most strictly aligned member A struct's size is rounded up to a multiple of its alignment Padding appears at the end , so that arrays of the struct stay aligned Members are laid out in declaration order Reordering them changes the size Facility Does --- --- sizeof(T) The size in bytes alignof(T) The alignment offsetof(S, member) The byte offset of a member alignas(N) Requests a stricter alignment, for SIMD or to avoid false sharing ( 12.05 Atomics and the Memory Model ) no_unique_address Allows an empty member to occupy no space !tip Order members from the largest alignment to the smallest That minimises padding without thought. Where a size matters, pin it down: static_assert(sizeof(Tight) == 16); In a million-element array, the difference between 24 and 16 bytes is 8 MB, and more elements per cache line: 13.04 Performance, Caches and Data-Oriented Design . Endianness A multi-byte number has to be laid out in some byte order. For 0x12345678 : address: +0 +1 +2 +3 little-endian: 78 56 34 12 least significant byte first: x86, most ARM big-endian: 12 34 56 78 most significant byte first: "network byte order" cpp include <bit if constexpr (std::endian::native == std::endian::little) { // this machine is little-endian } const std::uint32_t swapped{ std::byteswap(x) }; // C++23 Within one program it never matters. It matters the moment bytes leave the process: a file format or a network protocol must state its byte order, and code must convert explicitly. Serializing with shifts and masks ( 2.09 Bit Manipulation ) gives the same bytes on every machine, because shifts are defined on values, not on memory. Unions A union gives all its members the same storage. Its size is that of its largest member. cpp union Value { int i; float f; char bytes 4 ; }; // sizeof is 4 ┌─────────────────┐ │ i / f / bytes │ one piece of storage; only the member last written is "active" └─────────────────┘ Rule Detail --- --- One active member at a time Writing a member makes it the active one Reading an inactive member is undefined in C++ It is permitted in C. Use std::bit_cast for punning: 13.01 Undefined Behavior and Object Lifetime Members with non-trivial constructors or destructors You must construct and destroy them yourself, with std::construct_at and std::destroy_at A union alone does not know which member is active. Pairing it with a discriminator gives a tagged union : cpp struct Token { enum class Kind { number, op } kind{}; union { double number; char op; }; }; That is precisely what std::variant is, with the bookkeeping and lifetime management done correctly for you ( 10.04 stdoptional, stdvariant, stdany and stdtuple ). Write a raw union only when you must match an externally defined layout. Bit fields A member can be given a width in bits . cpp struct Flags { std::uint8_t visible : 1; std::uint8_t solid : 1; std::uint8_t layer : 3; // 0 to 7 std::uint8_t unused : 3; }; // sizeof is 1 one byte: unused unused unused layer layer layer solid visible The compiler generates the shifts and masks. Assigning a value too large for the field truncates it. Limitation Detail --- --- No address You cannot take a pointer or reference to a bit field Layout is implementation-defined The order of the fields within the storage unit, and how they straddle units, vary between compilers Not atomic Adjacent bit fields share a memory location, so two threads writing different fields race !warning Not for portable formats Because the layout varies, a bit-field struct written to a file by one compiler may be misread by another. For anything that crosses a boundary, use explicit shifts and masks. Categories of type Several operations are valid only for types with simple layouts. Property Means Query --- --- --- Trivially copyable Can be copied with memcpy and written as raw bytes std::is_trivially_copyable_v<T Standard layout Its layout is compatible with C std::is_standard_layout_v<T Aggregate Can be brace-initialized member by member std::is_aggregate_v<T Implicit-lifetime Can come into existence in raw storage without a constructor call A type loses trivial copyability by having a user-provided copy operation or destructor, a virtual function, or a member that is not trivially copyable, such as a std::string . Talking to C cpp extern "C" void callback(int value); C++ encodes a function's parameter types into its linker symbol, a process called name mangling , which is what makes overloading work. extern "C" turns that off for a declaration, so C code, or an operating system or another language, can find the function by its plain name. Such functions cannot be overloaded. Check yourself quiz ? Why does a struct holding a char followed by a double occupy 16 bytes? - Because every member takes 8 bytes + The double needs 8-byte alignment, so 7 bytes of padding follow - Because the compiler stores the struct twice - Because the struct also stores its size 1 byte of char , 7 of padding, then 8 of double : 16 in total. ? In C++, may you read a union member other than the one last written? - Yes, that is what unions are for - Yes, if both members have the same size + No, it is undefined behaviour; use std::bit_cast - Only for int and float Only the last-written member is active. C allows type punning through unions; C++ does not. ? Why is there padding at the end of a struct? - To store a hidden pointer - To leave room for future members + So each element of an array of the struct stays aligned - Because the compiler always adds 8 bytes In an array, each element starts where the previous one ends, so the size must keep the next element aligned. ? Why are bit fields unsuitable for portable file formats? - Because they cannot be written to files - Because they are slower than whole integers - Because they are limited to 8 bits + Their order and packing differ between compilers Two compilers may lay the same bit fields out differently. Use shifts and masks on a fixed-width integer for file formats.

title: Squeeze out the padding
where: 13.02 Memory Layout, Alignment, Unions and Bit Fields
body: Every type has an alignment, and the compiler inserts invisible padding bytes so that each member starts at a suitable address. The order you declare members in decides how much. Wasteful holds 18 bytes of real data but takes up 32 . Write a struct Compact with the same six members (same names, same types) in a better order, so that it takes up only 24 . Rule of thumb: put the members with the largest alignment first.

title: Byte order
where: 13.02 Memory Layout, Alignment, Unions and Bit Fields
body: A four-byte number can be stored lowest byte first ( little-endian , as on your PC) or highest byte first ( big-endian , the order network protocols use). Programs that read files or talk over a network have to convert. Write, using only shifts and masks (no library byte-swap): - std::uint32_t swapBytes(std::uint32_t value) : reverses the order of the four bytes, so 0x12345678 becomes 0x78563412 . - std::array<std::uint8_t, 4 toBigEndian(std::uint32_t value) : the four bytes, most significant first, whatever machine the code runs on. - std::uint32_t fromBigEndian(const std::array<std::uint8_t, 4 & bytes) : the reverse. Because the last two are defined by arithmetic rather than by peeking at memory, they give the same answer on every computer.

title: 13.03  Custom Memory: Placement new, Allocators and PMR
match: 13.03 Custom Memory: Placement new, Allocators and PMR
body:
new does two things: it obtains raw memory and constructs an object in it. The two can be separated. Placement new , or std::construct_at , constructs in memory you already have. Custom allocators and PMR (polymorphic memory resources) let containers draw their memory from arenas, pools or the stack. new is two operations Separating allocation from construction is what makes most of the standard library possible. cpp include <cstddef include <iostream include <memory include <new struct Widget { Widget(int a, int b) : sum{ a + b } { std::cout << "constructed
"; } ~Widget() { std::cout << "destroyed
"; } int sum{}; }; int main() { alignas(Widget) std::byte storage sizeof(Widget) ; Widget w{ ::new (static_cast<void (storage)) Widget{ 1, 2 } }; // construct only std::cout << w- sum << '
'; w- ~Widget(); // destroy only Widget w2{ std::construct_at(reinterpret_cast<Widget (storage), 3, 4) }; std::cout << w2- sum << '
'; std::destroy_at(w2); return 0; } Form Does --- --- ::new (address) T{ args } Placement new : constructs a T at address ; allocates nothing std::construct_at(pointer, args...) The same, as a function usable in constexpr code p- ~T() , std::destroy_at(p) Runs the destructor; releases nothing The storage must be large enough and suitably aligned, hence alignas(Widget) . The destructor call is the one place where invoking a destructor explicitly is correct: nothing else will do it. Library type How it uses the separation --- --- std::vector reserve obtains capacity without constructing elements; push_back constructs into it std::optional Holds storage for a T inline and constructs it only when given a value std::variant One buffer, re-used for whichever alternative is active Replacing operator new A class can supply its own allocation functions, which new and delete then use for that class. cpp struct Particle { static void operator new(std::size_t size); static void operator delete(void p) noexcept; }; The global operator new can be replaced too, by defining it once in the program. That is how tools count or trace every allocation. Why replace the allocator at all? A general-purpose allocator must cope with any size, any lifetime and any thread. That generality costs time per call, and it scatters objects across memory. When you know more about the pattern of use, you can do far better. The arena arena: ■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■□□□□□□□□□□□□□□□□□□□□□□ ▲ next allocate(n): result = next; next += n; a pointer increment deallocate: nothing reset: next = start; everything released at once An arena (also called a bump or monotonic allocator) hands out consecutive pieces of one large block. Individual deallocation does nothing; the whole arena is released or reset in one step. It is the fastest allocation strategy there is, and suits anything with a shared lifetime: the objects for one frame, one request or one parse. Polymorphic memory resources Since C++17, the containers in namespace std::pmr take a memory resource chosen at run time. cpp include <array include <cstddef include <iostream include <memory_resource include <string include <vector int main() { std::array<std::byte, 64 1024 buffer{}; std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource arena{ buffer.data(), buffer.size() }; std::pmr::vector<int numbers{ &arena }; for (int i{ 0 }; i < 1000; ++i) { numbers.push_back(i); // no call to the heap } std::pmr::vector<std::pmr::string names{ &arena }; names.emplace_back("a string long enough to need an allocation of its own"); std::cout << numbers.size() << ' ' << names.size() << '
'; return 0; } // the arena is released in one step std::pmr::vector<T is an alias for std::vector<T, std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator<T . The allocator holds a pointer to a std::pmr::memory_resource , an abstract base class, and forwards to it. Because the resource is not part of the container's type , two pmr vectors using different resources are the same type and can be passed to the same functions. It is type erasure applied to allocation ( 11.06 Type Erasure ). Note std::pmr::vector<std::pmr::string : a pmr container passes its resource on to elements that are themselves pmr-aware, so the strings' characters come from the arena too. A plain std::string element would still use the heap. Resource Suits --- --- monotonic_buffer_resource Short bursts with one shared lifetime: parsing, per-frame scratch data unsynchronized_pool_resource Many small allocations and deallocations on one thread synchronized_pool_resource The same, across threads null_memory_resource() As the upstream of an arena: it throws, proving the buffer was never exceeded Resources chain. Each has an upstream resource to fall back on when it runs out, the default being the heap. Writing a resource cpp class CountingResource : public std::pmr::memory_resource { public: std::size_t allocations{ 0 }; private: void do_allocate(std::size_t bytes, std::size_t alignment) override { ++allocations; return m_upstream- allocate(bytes, alignment); } void do_deallocate(void p, std::size_t bytes, std::size_t alignment) override { m_upstream- deallocate(p, bytes, alignment); } bool do_is_equal(const std::pmr::memory_resource& other) const noexcept override { return this == &other; } std::pmr::memory_resource m_upstream{ std::pmr::get_default_resource() }; }; Three virtual functions define a resource. The public allocate and deallocate are non-virtual and call them: the non-virtual interface idiom from 8.05 Abstract Classes and Interfaces . Classic allocators The older mechanism makes the allocator a template parameter: std::vector<T, MyAllocator<T . Template allocator PMR --- --- --- The strategy is fixed At compile time, in the container's type At run time Containers with different strategies Are different types Are the same type Cost per allocation None beyond the allocation One virtual call Effort to write Considerable Three functions Prefer PMR unless the virtual call is shown to matter. !warning The resource must outlive the container A pmr container stores a raw pointer to its resource. Destroy the arena first and every later allocation or deallocation touches a dead object. Declare the resource before the containers that use it, so it is destroyed after them. Check yourself quiz ? What does placement new do? + It constructs an object in existing memory, allocating nothing - It allocates memory at a chosen address - It moves an object to a new place - It allocates on the stack instead of the heap new (buffer) T{ ... } only runs the constructor. You must later call the destructor yourself and release the memory separately. ? Why is a monotonic buffer so fast? - It allocates from the stack only - It reuses freed blocks immediately + Allocating bumps a pointer, and freeing does nothing - It runs allocations on a separate thread It never tracks individual frees, which is perfect for short-lived bursts of allocations. ? Why can two std::pmr::vector<int with different resources be passed to the same function? - Because the resource is copied into each element - Because pmr vectors convert to std::vector<int + The resource is a run-time pointer, not part of the type - Because both resources must be the same type Classic allocators are template arguments and change the type. A pmr container holds a std::pmr::memory_resource instead. ? Why must a memory resource outlive the containers that use it? - Because the resource stores the container's elements' types - Because resources cannot be destroyed - Because the containers copy the resource + The containers use it until they are destroyed themselves Destroying the resource first leaves the containers with a dangling pointer for their final deallocation.

title: Construct in memory you already have
match: Construct in memory you already have
where: 13.03 Custom Memory: Placement new, Allocators and PMR
body: new does two jobs: it gets memory, and it constructs an object there. They can be separated. This is how std::optional and std::vector hold space for an object that does not exist yet. Write template <typename T class Slot : storage for one T that may or may not currently hold an object. - The storage is a raw buffer inside the slot, correctly sized and aligned: alignas(T) std::byte m_storage sizeof(T) ; No heap allocation at all. - template <typename... Args T& emplace(Args&&... args) : if an object is already there, destroy it first; then construct a new T in the buffer with std::construct_at and return it. - void reset() : destroys the object if there is one ( std::destroy_at ). - bool hasValue() const , and T& get() (only called when there is a value). - The destructor calls reset() . - Not copyable.

title: An arena
where: 13.03 Custom Memory: Placement new, Allocators and PMR
body: General-purpose new has to find a suitable free block every time, and track it so it can be freed later. When many small things are allocated together and thrown away together (everything needed to draw one frame, or to answer one request), there is a far faster scheme: take one big block and hand out pieces by moving a pointer along it. Freeing is a single reset of that pointer. Write class Arena : - explicit Arena(std::size_t capacity) : owns one buffer of that many bytes (a std::unique_ptr<std::byte is fine). - void allocate(std::size_t bytes, std::size_t alignment) : returns the next free address that is a multiple of alignment , and moves past it. Returns nullptr if there is not enough room. alignment is a power of two. - template <typename T, typename... Args T create(Args&&... args) : allocates room for a T with the right alignment and constructs it there; returns nullptr if it does not fit. - std::size_t used() const , std::size_t capacity() const . - void reset() : everything is free again. (Objects are not destroyed, so an arena suits types with nothing to clean up.) To round a position up to a multiple of a power-of-two alignment: (position + alignment - 1) & ~(alignment - 1) . Align the real address , not just the offset.

title: 13.04  Performance, Caches and Data-Oriented Design
body: Modern processors are fast and memory is slow . Performance comes from keeping data in the cache : contiguous arrays, predictable access, small hot data. Measure first , optimize the hot spot, and measure again. Data-oriented design arranges data around how it is processed. The memory hierarchy A processor can execute several instructions in the time light travels a few centimetres. Fetching a value from main memory takes hundreds of times longer. Between the two sits a stack of caches : small, fast memories that hold recently used data. approximate time to read size register 0.3 ns bytes L1 cache 1 ns █ 32 to 64 KB per core L2 cache 4 ns ████ 256 KB to 2 MB per core L3 cache 15 ns ███████████████ 8 to 64 MB, shared main memory 80 ns ████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████ SSD 100,000 ns Fact Consequence --- --- Memory moves between levels in cache lines of 64 bytes Touching one byte brings its 63 neighbours with it at no extra cost A request the cache cannot satisfy is a cache miss It costs roughly a hundred instructions' worth of time The processor's prefetcher detects regular patterns Walking an array in order is fetched ahead of you; hopping around is not For most programs, how the data is laid out in memory matters more than how many instructions are executed. Access patterns cpp // Rows are contiguous in memory. for (int r{ 0 }; r < n; ++r) { for (int c{ 0 }; c < n; ++c) { sum += grid r c ; // sequential: every byte of each cache line is used } } for (int c{ 0 }; c < n; ++c) { for (int r{ 0 }; r < n; ++r) { sum += grid r c ; // jumps a whole row each step: a new cache line nearly every access } } row by row: ■■■■■■■■ ■■■■■■■■ ■■■■■■■■ every element fetched is used column by column: ■······· ■······· ■······· one element used per line fetched Same work, same Big-O, and the second can be five to ten times slower on a large grid. The same reasoning explains 10.01 Choosing STL Containers . A std::list or std::map puts each node in its own allocation, so every step of a traversal may be a miss. A std::vector is one contiguous run. Arrays of structs and structs of arrays cpp // Array of structs struct Particle { Vec3 position{}; Vec3 velocity{}; Color color{}; float age{}; bool alive{}; std::string name{}; }; std::vector<Particle particles{}; // Struct of arrays struct Particles { std::vector<Vec3 positions{}; std::vector<Vec3 velocities{}; std::vector<float ages{}; // colours and names live elsewhere: they are not needed every frame }; updating positions, array of structs: pos vel color age alive name pos vel color age alive name ... most of each line is not needed updating positions, struct of arrays: positions: p p p p p p p p ... velocities: v v v v v v v v ... every byte loaded is used Array of structs Struct of arrays --- --- --- Natural to write Yes Less so All fields of one object One line of cache One miss per field One field across many objects Wastes most of each line Ideal Automatic vectorization Harder Easy Data-oriented design starts from the question "what transformations happen to this data, and how often?" and lays the data out to suit the common ones. Data read together is stored together; data used every frame ( hot ) is separated from data used rarely ( cold ). The other large gains Technique Why --- --- A better algorithm O(n log n) beats any tuning of O(n²): 5.11 Sorting, Searching, Big-O and Timing Your Code reserve before filling a vector Avoids repeated reallocation and copying Pass by const& , std::string_view , std::span Avoids copies Move instead of copy Transfers buffers: 7.05 Move Semantics No allocation in a hot loop A heap allocation costs tens of nanoseconds or more. Reuse buffers or use an arena: 13.03 Custom Memory Placement new, Allocators and PMR Predictable branches A mispredicted branch costs 15 to 20 cycles No virtual calls in the innermost loop They block inlining: 8.04 How Virtual Works — vtables Smaller data More elements per cache line: 13.02 Memory Layout, Alignment, Unions and Bit Fields Branch prediction The processor guesses which way each branch will go and runs ahead. A wrong guess discards that work. cpp for (int x : data) { if (x = 128) { sum += x; } } On random data, this branch is a coin toss and mispredicts half the time. On the same data sorted , it is false for a long run and then true for a long run, and the loop becomes several times faster. Removing the branch has the same effect: cpp for (int x : data) { sum += (x = 128) x; // no branch to predict } likely and unlikely let you tell the compiler which path to lay out as the fast one. Measure, do not guess Intuition about performance is unreliable, including the intuition of experts. The method is empirical. Tool For --- --- A profiler (Visual Studio's, perf , VTune, Tracy) Finding where the time actually goes A micro-benchmark library (Google Benchmark) Timing one small piece with proper statistics Compiler Explorer (godbolt.org) Reading the machine code the compiler produced A profiler samples the running program and reports which functions the time was spent in. Typically a few percent of the code accounts for most of the run time. Optimizing anything else achieves nothing. Benchmarking has traps of its own. The optimizer deletes work whose result is unused, so benchmark libraries provide a way to mark a value as used. Run several times and distrust small differences. Always measure a Release build. cpp include <benchmark/benchmark.h static void BM_VectorPush(benchmark::State& state) { for (auto _ : state) { std::vector<int v{}; for (int i{ 0 }; i < state.range(0); ++i) { v.push_back(i); } benchmark::DoNotOptimize(v.data()); } } BENCHMARK(BM_VectorPush)- Range(8, 1 << 16); BENCHMARK_MAIN(); !warning Two opposite mistakes Premature optimization : contorting code for speed before knowing where the time goes. It costs clarity and usually gains nothing. Premature pessimization : needless copies, a std::list by default, an allocation per loop iteration. That is not simplicity; it is carelessness. Write code that is efficient by default and clear. Optimize deeply only where measurement points. Check yourself quiz ? What is a cache line, and why does it matter? - A queue of instructions waiting to run + The 64-byte unit memory moves in; in-order access uses all of it - A line of code that the compiler caches - The connection between two processor cores Memory arrives a cache line at a time. Walking through memory in order uses every byte fetched; jumping around wastes most of each line. ? When is a struct of arrays the better layout? - When each object is always used as a whole - When there are only a few objects + When loops use one or two fields of many objects - When the struct has only one member Keeping each field in its own array means a loop over positions reads only positions, with no other fields filling the cache. ? Why can sorting data make a loop with a condition faster? - Because sorted data takes less memory - Because the compiler removes the condition + The branch becomes predictable, so the processor stops mispredicting it - Because sorted data fits in fewer cache lines With sorted data, the condition is false for a long run and then true for a long run, which the branch predictor learns. ? What should you do before optimizing anything? - Rewrite the code in a lower-level style - Turn on every compiler warning - Switch to a Debug build to see more detail + Profile a Release build to find where the time is actually spent Guesses about performance are usually wrong. Measure optimized code, then fix the parts that really dominate.

title: Reserve before you fill
body: A vector that runs out of room allocates a bigger block, moves every element across and frees the old block. Filling a vector of a thousand strings one push_back at a time does that about eighteen times. When you know how many elements are coming, say so first with reserve . Then there is exactly one allocation. Fix labels so the vector it returns has room for exactly count elements and no more.

title: Swap and pop
body: erase in the middle of a vector slides every later element down by one. For a big vector that is a lot of copying, and often the order does not matter at all (a list of live particles, enemies, open connections). When order does not matter there is a constant-time way: overwrite the doomed element with the last one, then pop_back . Rewrite removeUnordered that way.

title: Structure of arrays
body: The obvious way to store particles is a vector of structs, each with a position and a velocity. But a loop that only reads positions then drags every velocity through the cache as well. Structure of arrays turns it inside out: one tightly packed array per field. A loop that needs only x touches only the x array, and the processor reads memory in the straight line it is fastest at. Write class Particles that stores four separate std::vector<float (x, y, velocity x, velocity y): - std::size_t add(float x, float y, float vx, float vy) : adds a particle and returns its index. - std::size_t size() const - void step(float dt) : moves every particle: x += vx dt , y += vy dt . - std::span<const float xs() const and ys() const : a view of each whole array. - float kineticEnergy() const : the sum of 0.5 (vx vx + vy vy) over all particles. - void remove(std::size_t index) : removes a particle with swap-and-pop on all four arrays, so they stay in step.

title: 13.05  Modules (C++20) and import std (C++23)
body: Modules replace header files: you export what is public and import it elsewhere. A module is compiled once , leaks no macros and has no include-order problems. C++23's import std; brings in the whole standard library in one line. What is wrong with headers include is textual substitution ( 1.08 Multiple Files and Headers ). That simple model has real costs. Headers Modules --- --- --- Processed Every time one is included Once Macros defined inside Leak into every file that includes it Stay inside The order of inclusion Can change the meaning Is irrelevant Include guards Required Not needed Private helpers Visible to everyone, by convention "do not touch" Invisible unless exported Build time Dominated by re-parsing Often much lower Writing a module math.cppm: the interface cpp module; // the global module fragment: old-style includes go here include <cmath export module math; // this file is the interface of module "math" export namespace math { constexpr double pi{ 3.14159265358979 }; double circleArea(double radius) { return pi radius radius; } template <typename T T square(T x) { return x x; } } double helper() { return 42.0; } // not exported: importers cannot see it main.cpp cpp import std; // C++23: the entire standard library import math; int main() { std::println("{}", math::circleArea(2.0)); // helper(); error: not visible outside the module return 0; } Line Meaning --- --- export module math; Declares a module interface unit : the file that defines what module math offers export on a declaration or a block Makes it visible to importers import math; Makes the exported names of math available module; followed by include s The global module fragment , for headers that must still be included textually Everything not exported has module linkage : it is usable throughout the module and invisible outside it. That is true encapsulation at the level of a library, which headers never offered. Templates may live in a module interface and be exported like anything else. Interface and implementation As with a header and a source file, a module can separate what it declares from how it is implemented. cpp // geometry.cppm: the interface export module geometry; export double area(double width, double height); cpp // geometry.cpp: an implementation unit module geometry; double area(double width, double height) { return width height; } A change to the implementation unit does not force importers to recompile. Partitions A large module can be divided into partitions , which are internal to it. cpp // physics.cppm export module game:physics; export double gravity(); cpp // game.cppm export module game; export import :physics; // re-export the partition Users write import game; . The partitions are an organisational detail they never see. import std; import std; makes the whole standard library available. Because the library is compiled once into a module, importing all of it is typically faster than including <iostream alone. import std.compat; additionally provides the C library names in the global namespace. Building Modules introduce an ordering requirement that headers did not have: a module's interface must be compiled before anything that imports it. The build system has to discover those dependencies by scanning the sources. cmake cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.30) project(ModuleDemo LANGUAGES CXX) set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 23) set(CMAKE_CXX_MODULE_STD ON) add_executable(app main.cpp) target_sources(app PUBLIC FILE_SET CXX_MODULES FILES math.cppm) CMake 3.28 and later handle the scanning, with the Ninja generator or Visual Studio. The interface file's extension is a convention: .cppm for Clang and GCC, .ixx for Visual Studio. Toolchain Status --- --- Microsoft's compiler The most mature support Clang 17 and later, GCC 14 and later Work well with CMake and Ninja Third-party libraries Most still ship headers only !note You need both Headers are not going away. Existing libraries use them, and a module can still include them in its global module fragment. Know both models: write new code as modules where your tools allow, and expect to consume headers for years. Xenon compiles each task as plain source files with headers, so the exercises in this course do not use modules. This lesson is preparation for your own projects. Check yourself quiz ? What does export do in a module? - It writes the module to a file + It makes a declaration visible to the module's importers - It makes the module's macros available to importers - It compiles the module into a library Only exported declarations are seen by importers. Unexported helpers are invisible outside the module. ? Do macros defined in a module affect its importers? - Yes, like a header - Only if they are exported + No, modules do not export macros - Only macros defined before export module Importing a module never brings in its macros, which is one of the ways modules are cleaner than headers. ? Why are modules faster to build than headers? - Because modules contain less code - Because modules are compiled in parallel - Because modules skip type checking + Its interface is compiled once, not re-parsed per file Each include pastes and re-parses the header text. An import loads an already compiled interface. ? What is the global module fragment for? + Including ordinary headers before the module declaration - Declaring global variables shared by all modules - Exporting every declaration at once - Listing which modules to import It starts with module; and holds include lines whose contents should not become part of the module.

title: 13.06  Preprocessor Deep Dive, Attributes and User-Defined Literals
match: 13.06 Preprocessor Deep Dive, Attributes and User-Defined Literals
body:
The preprocessor is a text-substitution engine that runs before compilation: powerful, and blind to types and scope. Know macros, conditional compilation, and , and X-macros, and when not to use them. Attributes give the compiler extra information. User-defined literals let you write 5_km . Macros The preprocessor works on tokens before the compiler proper sees anything. A macro is a rule for replacing one sequence of tokens with another. cpp define PI 3.14159 // object-like define SQUARE(x) ((x) (x)) // function-like It knows nothing about types, scopes or namespaces, which is the source of every problem with macros. Use Expands to Result --- --- --- SQUARE(1 + 2) ((1 + 2) (1 + 2)) 9. Without the inner parentheses it would be 1 + 2 1 + 2 , which is 5. SQUARE(i++) ((i++) (i++)) i is modified twice in one expression: undefined behaviour A function evaluates its argument once. A macro pastes it wherever the parameter appears. Operator Effect Example --- --- --- x Turns the argument into a string literal define STR(x) x makes STR(hello) into "hello" a b Joins two tokens into one define VAR(n) var n makes VAR(1) into var1 __VA_ARGS__ The arguments of a variadic macro define LOG(...) print(__VA_ARGS__) __VA_OPT__(x) Emits x only if there are variadic arguments (C++20) Predefined macros and std::source_location Macro Value --- --- __FILE__ , __LINE__ The current file name and line number __func__ The enclosing function's name (strictly a predefined variable) __cplusplus The language version, such as 202302L _WIN32 , __linux__ , __APPLE__ Defined on the corresponding platform _MSC_VER , __GNUC__ , __clang__ Defined by the corresponding compiler NDEBUG Defined in release builds; disables assert __FILE__ and __LINE__ used to require a macro so that they expanded at the call site. std::source_location does it with a default argument: cpp include <print include <source_location include <string_view void log(std::string_view message, std::source_location where = std::source_location::current()) { std::println("{}:{} {} {}", where.file_name(), where.line(), where.function_name(), message); } int main() { log("starting up"); // reports THIS line, in main return 0; } A default argument is evaluated where the call is written, so current() captures the caller's location. Conditional compilation cpp if defined(_WIN32) include <windows.h elif defined(__linux__) include <unistd.h endif ifndef NDEBUG define DEBUG_LOG(message) std::cerr << message << '
' else define DEBUG_LOG(message) ((void)0) endif if __has_include(<format ) include <format endif Code in a branch that is not selected is removed before compilation, so it need not even be valid for the current platform. That is the preprocessor's one irreplaceable job: choosing between pieces of code that cannot all compile in one place. Directive Purpose --- --- if , ifdef , ifndef , elif , else , endif Select code __has_include(<header ) Tests whether a header exists Feature-test macros, from <version Test for a language or library feature, such as __cpp_lib_print error "message" Stops compilation with a message pragma once , pragma warning(...) Compiler-specific instructions X-macros Some lists must appear in several forms that have to stay in step: an enum, its names as strings, a count. An X-macro defines the list once and expands it differently each time. cpp include <iostream include <string_view define COLOR_LIST(X) \ X(red) \ X(green) \ X(blue) enum class Color { define X(name) name, COLOR_LIST(X) undef X }; constexpr std::string_view toString(Color color) { switch (color) { define X(name) case Color::name: return name; COLOR_LIST(X) undef X } return "?"; } int main() { std::cout << toString(Color::green) << '
'; // green return 0; } COLOR_LIST takes the name of another macro and applies it to each entry. Define X one way to produce enumerators, another way to produce case lines. Add a colour to the list and both update. Until reflection arrives ( 11.07 Template Metaprogramming Techniques ), this is the standard way to do it. !warning Rules for macros - Name them in ALL_CAPS , so they cannot be mistaken for anything else. - Parenthesize every parameter and the whole replacement. - undef helper macros when finished. - Prefer constexpr variables and functions, templates, inline functions and std::source_location wherever they can do the job. Macros ignore namespaces and scope, so a macro in one header can silently rewrite code in another. The classic case is <windows.h defining min and max , which breaks std::min and std::max unless NOMINMAX is defined first. Attributes An attribute attaches information to a declaration or statement. It never changes the meaning of a correct program; it affects diagnostics and optimization. Attribute Meaning --- --- nodiscard , nodiscard("reason") Warn if the result is ignored maybe_unused Do not warn that this is unused deprecated("use g instead") Warn wherever this is used fallthrough Falling into the next case is deliberate noreturn The function never returns to its caller likely , unlikely Which branch to optimize for no_unique_address An empty member need not occupy storage assume(expression) (C++23) The optimizer may take the expression as true. If it is not, the behaviour is undefined. cpp nodiscard std::expected<Data, Error load(std::string_view path); load("x.dat"); // warning: the result is discarded if (x 0) likely { fastPath(); } nodiscard is the one to use freely: on any function whose result is the whole point of calling it, and especially on functions that report errors through their return value. User-defined literals A literal operator gives meaning to a suffix on a literal. cpp include <iostream struct Meters { double value{}; }; constexpr Meters operator""_m(long double v) { return Meters{ static_cast<double (v) }; } constexpr Meters operator""_m(unsigned long long v) { return Meters{ static_cast<double (v) }; } constexpr Meters operator""_km(long double v) { return Meters{ static_cast<double (v) 1000.0 }; } int main() { constexpr auto distance{ 3.5_km }; constexpr auto height{ 12_m }; std::cout << distance.value << ' ' << height.value << '
'; // 3500 12 return 0; } Literal The operator's parameter --- --- An integer, 12_m unsigned long long A floating-point number, 3.5_km long double A character, 'x'_c char A string, "text"_s (const char , std::size_t) Suffixes you define must begin with an underscore. Those without one are reserved for the standard library: s , ms , h , sv , i and so on. Literals make units part of the type at no run-time cost, as <chrono does ( 10.08 Time and stdchrono ). Made consteval , a literal operator can also validate its argument during compilation: cpp consteval std::uint32_t operator""_rgb(const char text, std::size_t length); const auto orange{ " FF8800"_rgb }; // a malformed colour would be a compile error Check yourself quiz ? Why does SQUARE(i++) misbehave? - Macros cannot take expressions as arguments - The macro squares i before increasing it + The text i++ appears twice, so i changes twice - i++ is evaluated once but its result is discarded A macro is text substitution: ((i++) (i++)) . A constexpr function would evaluate its argument once. ? What does nodiscard do? - It stops the function being called - It removes the function from Release builds + The compiler warns if the return value is ignored - It prevents the return value being copied Use it on functions whose result matters, such as error codes, so ignoring the result is flagged. ? How does std::source_location::current() as a default argument report the caller's location? - It reads the call stack while running + Default arguments are evaluated where the call is - The compiler inserts the caller's name by a macro - It only works inside main The default argument is evaluated where the call is written, which gives the caller's file and line. ? What job can only the preprocessor do? - Defining named constants for the program - Writing generic functions - Computing values at compile time + Choosing between code that cannot all compile together constexpr and templates replace most macros, but if is still needed to choose code that would not even compile on other platforms.

title: Your own literals
where: 13.06 Preprocessor Deep Dive, Attributes and User-Defined Literals
body: 10s and "text"s are literals with a suffix the standard library defined. You can define your own. A suffix of your own must start with an underscore. A literal operator for whole numbers takes unsigned long long ; one for decimals takes long double . Write: - struct Distance { double metres; }; - _m and _km literals that work for both whole numbers and decimals ( 250_m , 1.5_km ), giving a Distance . - operator+ for two distances. - _kb and _mb literals for whole numbers, giving a std::uint64_t count of bytes (1 KB = 1024 bytes, 1 MB = 1024 KB). Make everything constexpr , so 1.5_km + 250_m is worked out by the compiler.

title: One list, three uses
where: 13.06 Preprocessor Deep Dive, Attributes and User-Defined Literals
body: An enum, a function that turns each value into its name, and a count of the values: three things that must always agree. Written by hand, somebody eventually adds a value to one and forgets the others. The X-macro trick keeps one list and generates all three from it. COLOR_LIST(X) applies whatever macro X you give it to every entry. Define X one way to make enumerators, another way to make case lines, and undef it after each use. Inside a macro, name turns the argument into a string: "red" . From COLOR_LIST , generate: - enum class Color with one enumerator per entry, in order, - constexpr std::string_view toString(Color color) , - inline constexpr int colorCount . Do not type any colour name yourself. The tests add nothing to the list, but your code should keep working if someone did.

title: Tell the compiler what you meant
match: Tell the compiler what you meant
where: 13.06 Preprocessor Deep Dive, Attributes and User-Defined Literals
body: Attributes are notes to the compiler in double square brackets. Three are worth knowing by heart: Attribute Meaning --- --- nodiscard Warn if the caller ignores this function's result maybe_unused This is deliberately unused; do not warn about it fallthrough ; Running on into the next case is deliberate The code below works, but it leaves the compiler guessing. Fix that, without changing what the code does: - Ignoring the result of parsePort is always a mistake: mark it. - onEvent has to accept context to match a callback signature, but does not use it yet: say so, so the build has no warnings . - In priority , high deliberately runs on into medium : mark it.

title: 13.07  Name Lookup, ADL, Inline Namespaces and the ODR
match: 13.07 Name Lookup, ADL, Inline Namespaces and the ODR
body: How does the compiler decide what a name refers to? Unqualified lookup searches outwards through scopes. ADL also searches the namespaces of the arguments' types, which is why std::cout << x finds std::operator<< . Inline namespaces version an interface. The One Definition Rule keeps definitions consistent across the program. Lookup comes first Before a call is resolved, three things happen in a fixed order. A surprising amount of C++ behaviour follows from that order. A function that would be a perfect match is never considered if lookup does not find it, and a private function can win overload resolution and then be rejected. Unqualified lookup A name written without :: is searched for from the innermost scope outwards. namespace app { int x; searched third namespace ui { int x; searched second void f() { int x; searched first: found, so the search stops use(x); } } } The search stops at the first scope that contains the name . It does not go on to see whether an outer scope has a better candidate. That is the mechanism behind name hiding in derived classes ( 8.02 Inheritance and Access ), where one function in the derived class hides every base overload of the same name. A qualified name, such as app::x or ::x , is looked up only in the scope named. Argument-dependent lookup For an unqualified function call , there is a second search. cpp include <iostream namespace geo { struct Point { int x{}; int y{}; }; void print(const Point& p) { std::cout << p.x << ',' << p.y << '\n'; } } int main() { const geo::Point p{ 1, 2 }; print(p); // found without writing geo:: return 0; } Argument-dependent lookup (ADL) adds, for each argument, the namespace in which its type is defined. The functions found both ways are combined into one set of candidates. The motivation is operators. std::cout << text must find std::operator<<(std::ostream&, const std::string&) . Nobody wants to write std::operator<<(std::cout, text) . ADL makes a type's interface include the free functions in its namespace. The two-step swap Generic code that swaps should use a type's own swap if it provides one, and std::swap otherwise. cpp template <typename T void exchange(T& a, T& b) { using std::swap; // makes std::swap a candidate swap(a, b); // unqualified: ADL adds any swap in T's namespace } Written as Finds --- --- std::swap(a, b) Only std::swap . A type's optimized swap is ignored. swap(a, b) alone Only what ADL finds. Fails for int , which has no namespace. using std::swap; swap(a, b); Both, and overload resolution prefers the more specific std::ranges::swap performs this dance for you. !warning ADL works when you did not ask for it An unqualified call can select a function from an argument's namespace that you have never heard of. In generic code, qualify calls that you do not intend to be customisable: write std::move , std::forward and std::addressof in full. Hidden friends A friend function defined inside a class is not visible to ordinary lookup at all. It can be found only by ADL, when one of the arguments has that class type. cpp struct Vec2 { double x{}; double y{}; friend Vec2 operator+(Vec2 a, Vec2 b) { return { a.x + b.x, a.y + b.y }; } }; Benefit Why --- --- Smaller overload sets The operator is a candidate only when a Vec2 is involved Fewer accidental conversions It cannot be selected through an implicit conversion of some unrelated type Faster compilation, clearer errors The compiler has fewer candidates to consider and report This is the recommended way to write operators, and what the examples in 6.07 Operator Overloading Basics were quietly doing. Inline namespaces The members of an inline namespace are treated as members of the enclosing namespace too. cpp namespace lib { namespace v1 { void parse(); } inline namespace v2 { void parse(); } } lib::parse(); // v2, the current version lib::v1::parse(); // the old version, still reachable Libraries use this for versioning . Callers write lib::parse and get whichever version is marked inline ; the version name is still part of each symbol, so code built against different versions cannot be linked together by mistake. The standard library's literal suffixes live in inline namespaces, which is why using namespace std::chrono_literals; and using namespace std::literals; both work. Unnamed namespaces cpp namespace { int helper() { return 1; } } Everything in an unnamed namespace has internal linkage : it is private to its source file ( 3.06 Global Variables, static and Linkage ). Unlike static , it applies to types as well as to functions and variables, which matters for the next section. The One Definition Rule The One Definition Rule (ODR) has three parts. Scope Rule --- --- Within one translation unit An entity is defined at most once Across the whole program A non-inline function or variable that is used is defined exactly once Classes, templates, inline functions and inline variables May be defined in several translation units, but every definition must be identical , token for token and in meaning A translation unit is one source file after all its include s have been pasted in. The third rule is the dangerous one. a.cpp: struct Config { int width; int height; }; b.cpp: struct Config { int width; int height; int depth; }; Each file compiles. The program links. No error, no warning. Code in a.cpp and b.cpp now disagree about the size and layout of a Config. A violation of this kind is "ill-formed, no diagnostic required". The linker sees two things called Config and assumes they are the same. The result is memory corruption that appears far from its cause. How it happens Defence --- --- Two source files each define a helper class with the same name Put file-local types in an unnamed namespace Two libraries define the same name in the global namespace Give every library its own namespace A header is included with different macros defined beforehand Avoid macros that alter definitions Object files built with different settings that change layouts Build everything with the same options An inline function in a header that behaves differently per file Keep headers free of dependence on file-local context Modules ( 13.05 Modules (C++20) and import std (C++23) ) remove much of this class of problem: a module's entities are attached to that module, so same-named entities in different modules do not collide. Check yourself quiz ? Why does std::cout << "hi" work without writing std::operator<< ? + Argument-dependent lookup searches std , home of cout 's type - Because operator<< is a keyword - Because <iostream adds using namespace std; - Because operators are always global ADL looks in the namespaces of the arguments' types, so it finds the operator<< declared in std . ? What makes violations of the One Definition Rule so dangerous? - The compiler rejects them with confusing messages - They make the program slower + They are usually not diagnosed at all - They only happen in Release builds Two different definitions with the same name in different files can silently pick either one, with no error. ? Why write using std::swap; before an unqualified swap(a, b) ? - Because swap is not in std otherwise - To force std::swap to be called + std::swap becomes a fallback while ADL can find a better one - To stop ADL from looking anywhere This "two-step" lets a type's own efficient swap win when it exists, and uses std::swap when it does not. ? How can a hidden friend be found? - By ordinary unqualified lookup from anywhere - By qualifying it with the class name - By including the header twice + Only through argument-dependent lookup A friend defined inside the class is not visible to normal lookup. That keeps overload sets small and avoids surprises.

title: The two-step swap
where: 13.07 Name Lookup, ADL, Inline Namespaces and the ODR
body: When you call a function without a namespace in front, the compiler also searches the namespaces of the argument types . That is argument-dependent lookup (ADL), and it is why std::cout << x finds an operator<< that lives in std . It matters for swap . A type can supply its own, faster swap in its own namespace. Writing std::swap(a, b) skips it. Writing plain swap(a, b) finds it, but then fails for int , which has no namespace to search. The idiom that works for everything has two steps: cpp using std::swap; // the fallback swap(a, b); // unqualified: ADL picks a better one if the type has it Fix orderTwo to use it.

title: Two versions side by side
where: 13.07 Name Lookup, ADL, Inline Namespaces and the ODR
body: A library sometimes has to change what a function does while old code still needs the old behaviour. An inline namespace handles that: its contents are visible as if they were in the enclosing namespace, so it marks the current version. Right now geometry::area uses a rough value of pi. Reorganise it: - Move the existing function, unchanged, into namespace v1 inside geometry . - Add an inline namespace v2 inside geometry with an area that uses std::numbers::pi . Afterwards geometry::area(r) means the new one, and anyone who needs the old result can still ask for geometry::v1::area(r) .

title: One definition, please
where: 13.07 Name Lookup, ADL, Inline Namespaces and the ODR
body: This program is split across three .cpp files that all include ids.h . Each file compiles on its own without complaint. Then the linker refuses to join them: the header defines a variable and a function, so every .cpp that includes it gets its own copy, and the One Definition Rule allows only one. Fix ids.h so the program links and prints 1 2 3 . Change only the header. There are two quick fixes that look similar. One gives the whole program a single shared counter. The other quietly gives every .cpp file a private counter of its own, and the program prints 1 1 1 .

title: 13.08  C++ Idioms and Design Patterns
body: Idioms are solutions specific to C++: RAII, pImpl, copy and swap, the Rule of Zero, CRTP, type erasure. Design patterns are recipes that apply in any language: Strategy, Observer, Factory, Visitor. Knowing their names lets you design faster and talk to other programmers. A shared vocabulary Saying "use the Strategy pattern here" communicates a whole design in four words. That is the value of naming these things. This lesson collects the names, most of which you have already used. The idioms you already know Idiom In one line Lesson --- --- --- RAII A resource's lifetime is tied to an object's 7.04 RAII and the Rule of Three Rule of Zero / Three / Five Declare all the special members, or better, none 7.05 Move Semantics Copy and swap Assignment with the strong guarantee 7.03 Copy Semantics — Shallow vs Deep Non-virtual interface A public non-virtual function calling private virtual ones 8.05 Abstract Classes and Interfaces CRTP Static polymorphism and mixins 11.05 CRTP, Mixins and Static Polymorphism Type erasure Polymorphism with value semantics 11.06 Type Erasure Hidden friends Operators found only through ADL 13.07 Name Lookup, ADL, Inline Namespaces and the ODR Two-step swap using std::swap; swap(a, b); 13.07 Name Lookup, ADL, Inline Namespaces and the ODR pImpl "Pointer to implementation". A class's private members are part of its definition, so they sit in the header. Every file that includes the header must be recompiled when they change, and must also include whatever headers those members need. pImpl moves them out of sight. cpp // Widget.h: all that users of the class ever see pragma once include <memory class Widget { public: Widget(); ~Widget(); Widget(Widget&&) noexcept; Widget& operator=(Widget&&) noexcept; void draw() const; private: struct Impl; // declared, not defined std::unique_ptr<Impl m_impl; }; cpp // Widget.cpp include "Widget.h" include <string include <vector struct Widget::Impl { std::string name{}; std::vector<int data{}; }; Widget::Widget() : m_impl{ std::make_unique<Impl () } {} Widget::~Widget() = default; Widget::Widget(Widget&&) noexcept = default; Widget& Widget::operator=(Widget&&) noexcept = default; void Widget::draw() const { // uses m_impl- name and m_impl- data } Gain Cost --- --- Changing private members recompiles one file One heap allocation per object Heavy headers stay out of the public header One pointer indirection per access The object's size and layout never change: a stable binary interface Copying must be written by hand if wanted !warning The destructor must be defined in the source file std::unique_ptr<Impl can only delete an Impl where Impl is a complete type. If the destructor were left implicit, it would be generated in the header, where Impl is only declared, and the code would not compile. The same applies to the move operations. Declare them in the header and define them as = default in the .cpp file, after Impl . Design patterns in modern C++ The classic patterns were described in terms of class hierarchies. Lambdas, std::function and std::variant often express the same intent with far less code. Strategy: an interchangeable algorithm cpp class Compressor { public: using Algorithm = std::function<std::string(std::string_view) ; explicit Compressor(Algorithm algorithm) : m_algorithm{ std::move(algorithm) } {} std::string run(std::string_view input) const { return m_algorithm(input); } private: Algorithm m_algorithm{}; }; Compressor compressor{ runLengthEncode }; The classic form needs an abstract CompressionStrategy and a class per algorithm. A callable is enough. Observer: notify whoever is listening A subject keeps a list of callbacks and invokes them when something happens. The subject does not know who is listening. cpp template <typename... Args class Signal { public: void connect(std::function<void(Args...) listener) { m_listeners.push_back(std::move(listener)); } void emit(Args... args) const { for (const auto& listener : m_listeners) { listener(args...); } } private: std::vector<std::function<void(Args...) m_listeners{}; }; The hazard is lifetime: a listener that captures an object must be disconnected before that object dies. Return a connection object that disconnects in its destructor, or hold listeners through std::weak_ptr . Factory: create by name cpp using Creator = std::function<std::unique_ptr<Shape () ; const std::unordered_map<std::string, Creator registry{ { "circle", { return std::make_unique<Circle (); } }, { "square", { return std::make_unique<Square (); } }, }; auto shape{ registry.at("circle")() }; It decouples the code that needs an object from the knowledge of which concrete class to build, which is what loading objects from a file requires. Builder: readable construction cpp const auto request{ HttpRequest::Builder{} .url("https://example.com") .method("POST") .header("Accept", "json") .timeout(5s) .build() }; Each setter returns the builder ( 6.04 this, const Member Functions and Chaining ). It replaces a constructor with eight parameters whose order nobody remembers. Designated initializers on a plain options struct are a lighter alternative. Visitor and State Pattern Classic form Modern form --- --- --- Visitor : an operation over a closed set of types A Visitor interface with one visit overload per class, and an accept in each class std::variant with std::visit : 10.04 stdoptional, stdvariant, stdany and stdtuple State : behaviour that changes with state A class per state behind a common interface std::variant<Idle, Running, Jumping , with transitions written as visitors With a variant, a forgotten state or type is a compile error. Singleton, and why to avoid it cpp Logger& logger() { static Logger instance{}; return instance; } A function-local static is initialized once, on first use, safely across threads. That is the correct way to write a singleton. Whether to write one is another matter: Problem Why --- --- It is a global variable Any code can reach and change it: 3.06 Global Variables, static and Linkage It hides dependencies A function's signature no longer shows what it uses It resists testing A test cannot substitute a fake Prefer passing the dependency in ( 8.05 Abstract Classes and Interfaces ). The SOLID principles Five guidelines for object-oriented design, widely quoted by their initials. Principle In C++ terms --- --- S ingle responsibility A class or function has one reason to change: 6.09 Designing Good Classes O pen/closed Extend behaviour by adding types or strategies, not by editing working code L iskov substitution A derived class must honour everything the base class promises: 8.01 Inheritance Basics I nterface segregation Several small interfaces serve better than one large one D ependency inversion Depend on abstractions (interfaces, concepts) and inject the concrete parts !tip Patterns are a vocabulary, not a goal Reach for a pattern when you recognise the problem it solves. Code written to "use patterns" for their own sake acquires layers of indirection that no requirement asked for. Check yourself quiz ? Why must the destructor of a pImpl class be defined in the source file? - Because destructors cannot be defined in headers + Deleting Impl needs its full definition, found only there - To make the destructor virtual - Because the destructor must call delete manually Defining the destructor (even as = default ) in the .cpp , after Impl is defined, lets unique_ptr delete it. ? What is the modern C++ alternative to the classic Visitor pattern? - Virtual inheritance - Function pointers in a table + std::variant with std::visit - std::any with std::any_cast A variant of the node types plus std::visit handles each type, with the compiler checking every case is covered. ? What are the costs of pImpl? + A heap allocation per object and an extra indirection - The class can no longer be copied or moved - Every member function becomes virtual - The header must include every implementation header In exchange you get a stable header and faster rebuilds, since private changes no longer recompile users. ? Why is a singleton discouraged? - Because it cannot be thread-safe - Because it uses too much memory - Because C++ forbids static local variables + It is a global in disguise that hides dependencies Code that reaches for Logger::instance() hides that it needs a logger. Passing the dependency in makes it visible and replaceable.

title: Hide the implementation
body: Every private member in a header is visible to every file that includes it. Change one, and all of those files recompile. The pImpl idiom ("pointer to implementation") moves the private members into a struct that only the .cpp file can see. The header keeps a single pointer. Account.h is finished: it declares struct Impl; without defining it and holds a std::unique_ptr<Impl . Write Account.cpp : - Define struct Account::Impl with the owner's name, the balance in cents and a std::vector<long long history of deposits. - The constructor creates the Impl . - deposit adds to the balance and records the amount. Amounts of zero or less are ignored. - balance , owner and transactionCount report from the Impl . - The destructor and the two move operations are = default , but written here in the .cpp : Account::~Account() = default; That last point is the one everybody trips over. std::unique_ptr can only delete an Impl in a place where Impl is a complete type, and that place is this file, after the struct's definition.

title: Signals
body: The observer pattern lets one object announce that something happened without knowing who is listening. A button does not call the save code; it emits "clicked", and whoever connected to that gets called. In modern C++ the listeners are simply callables. Write template <typename... Args class Signal : - int connect(std::function<void(Args...) listener) : adds a listener and returns an id for it. Ids are never reused. - bool disconnect(int id) : removes that listener; returns whether it was found. - void emit(Args... args) const : calls every connected listener, in the order they connected. - std::size_t listenerCount() const One detail makes the difference between a toy and something usable: a listener may disconnect itself (or another listener) while emit is running . Looping directly over the container while it changes underneath you is undefined behaviour. The simplest safe approach is to loop over a copy.

title: 13.09  Testing, Sanitizers, Static Analysis and Tooling
match: 13.09 Testing, Sanitizers, Static Analysis and Tooling
body: Professional C++ is supported by tools. Unit tests check behaviour. Sanitizers catch undefined behaviour as the program runs. Static analysis finds defects without running it. Formatters , fuzzers and continuous integration apply all of it to every change. Layers of defence No single technique finds every defect. Each layer catches what the previous ones missed, and the earlier a problem is caught, the cheaper it is to fix. Layer Runs the code? Finds --- --- --- Warnings, static analysis No Suspicious patterns on every path, including ones no test exercises Unit tests Yes Wrong results, for the inputs you thought of Sanitizers Yes Undefined behaviour on the paths the tests exercise Fuzzing Yes Failures on inputs you did not think of Unit testing You have been on the receiving end of unit tests throughout this course: every Check in Xenon ran a set of them against your code. 3.08 Halts, goto, and Testing Your Code introduced the idea with a hand-written test function. A test framework supplies the infrastructure: registering tests, running them, reporting failures and summarizing. With Catch2: cpp include <catch2/catch_test_macros.hpp include "Fraction.h" TEST_CASE("Fractions reduce automatically", " fraction ") { const Fraction f{ 2, 4 }; REQUIRE(f.numerator() == 1); REQUIRE(f.denominator() == 2); } TEST_CASE("Adding fractions") { SECTION("the same denominator") { CHECK(Fraction{ 1, 4 } + Fraction{ 2, 4 } == Fraction{ 3, 4 }); } SECTION("a zero denominator throws") { REQUIRE_THROWS_AS(Fraction(1, 0), std::invalid_argument); } } Macro On failure --- --- REQUIRE(expression) Reports and stops the current test case CHECK(expression) Reports and continues REQUIRE_THROWS_AS(expression, type) Fails unless the expression throws that type GoogleTest is the other widely used framework: TEST(Fraction, Reduces) { EXPECT_EQ(f.numerator(), 1); } . The ideas are identical. Either is added to a CMake project with FetchContent ( 10.09 CMake, Libraries and Package Managers ): cmake include(FetchContent) FetchContent_Declare(Catch2 GIT_REPOSITORY https://github.com/catchorg/Catch2.git GIT_TAG v3.7.1) FetchContent_MakeAvailable(Catch2) add_executable(tests tests/test_fraction.cpp) target_link_libraries(tests PRIVATE fraction_lib Catch2::Catch2WithMain) include(CTest) include(Catch) catch_discover_tests(tests) What makes code testable Property Why --- --- Small, pure functions The same input always gives the same output, so a test is one line Dependencies passed in A test can supply a fake clock, file system or network: 8.05 Abstract Classes and Interfaces No hidden globals Tests do not interfere with each other: 13.08 C++ Idioms and Design Patterns Logic separated from input and output The logic can be tested without a console or a file Code that is hard to test is usually code with too many responsibilities or hidden dependencies. The difficulty is design feedback. How good are the tests? Measure Asks --- --- Coverage Which lines and branches did the tests execute? Uncovered code is untested. Covered code is not necessarily tested well . Mutation testing If a small bug is introduced deliberately, does any test fail? If not, the tests are not checking that behaviour. Test-driven development reverses the usual order: write a failing test, write the least code that passes it, then tidy up. It guarantees that every piece of behaviour has a test and that the test can fail. Sanitizers A sanitizer is a compiler option that adds checks to the generated program. The program runs slower and reports errors precisely as they happen. Sanitizer Flag (GCC, Clang) Microsoft Detects --- --- --- --- AddressSanitizer -fsanitize=address /fsanitize=address Out-of-bounds access, use after free, double free, leaks UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer -fsanitize=undefined Signed overflow, bad shifts, null dereference, misalignment ThreadSanitizer -fsanitize=thread Data races, inconsistent lock ordering MemorySanitizer (Clang) -fsanitize=memory Reads of uninitialized memory bash g++ -std=c++20 -g -O1 -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer main.cpp -o app ==12345==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free on address 0x602000000010 READ of size 4 at 0x602000000010 thread T0 0 0x4011a6 in main main.cpp:9 The report names the exact line, and where the memory was allocated and freed. A bug that might have surfaced weeks later as an unrelated crash is pinned down the first time it executes. Limit Detail --- --- Only executed code is checked A sanitizer is as good as the tests that drive it Cost Two to three times slower for ASan; more for TSan Combinations ASan and TSan cannot be used in the same build The standard practice is to run the whole test suite under ASan and UBSan, and again under TSan for concurrent code. The beaker button above Xenon's editor ("Memory checks") builds your code with AddressSanitizer. Static analysis Static analysis examines source code without executing it, so it can reason about every path, including error handling that tests rarely reach. Tool Notes --- --- Compiler warnings The first and cheapest analyzer. Turn them up and treat them as errors. clang-tidy Hundreds of checks in families: bugprone- , modernize- , performance- , cppcoreguidelines- . Many can fix the code automatically. Microsoft Code Analysis /analyze , with a C++ Core Guidelines checker cppcheck Free and standalone yaml .clang-tidy Checks: 'bugprone- ,modernize- ,performance- ,readability- ,-modernize-use-trailing-return-type' WarningsAsErrors: 'bugprone- ' Static analysis can report problems that are not real (false positives) and cannot find everything. It complements testing; it does not replace it. Formatting clang-format rewrites code to a style defined in a .clang-format file. Format on save, and arguments about brace placement end for good. Code reviews can then be about substance. The wand button above Xenon's editor (or Shift+Alt+F ) runs it. Fuzzing A fuzzer calls a function with enormous numbers of generated inputs, guided by which code paths each one reaches, looking for crashes. Combined with sanitizers it is extremely effective on anything that parses untrusted input. cpp extern "C" int LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput(const std::uint8_t data, std::size_t size) { parseConfig(std::string_view{ reinterpret_cast<const char (data), size }); return 0; } bash clang++ -fsanitize=fuzzer,address fuzz.cpp parser.cpp You write the single function above; the fuzzer does the rest. The debugger A debugger pauses a running program and lets you inspect it.
