title: A generic repository
body: Build an in-memory repository that any entity type can use, with validation rules, change events, transactions and paging. It brings together generics, delegates and events, exceptions, IDisposable and iterators. csharp public interface IEntity { int Id { get; } } public record Product(int Id, string Name, decimal Price) : IEntity; public record Change<T (string Kind, T? Before, T? After); // Kind is "added", "updated" or "removed" public class ValidationException(IReadOnlyList<string errors) : Exception { public IReadOnlyList<string Errors { get; } // Message is the errors joined with "; " } public class Repository<T where T : class, IEntity { public event EventHandler<Change<T ? Changed; public int Count { get; } public void AddRule(Func<T, string? rule) // returns an error message, or null when fine public void Add(T item) public void Update(T item) public bool Remove(int id) public T? Find(int id) public IEnumerable<T Where(Func<T, bool predicate) // lazy, in id order public IEnumerable<IReadOnlyList<T Pages(int size) // in id order public Transaction BeginTransaction() public sealed class Transaction : IDisposable { public void Commit(); public void Dispose(); } } The tests use public record Product(int Id, string Name, decimal Price) : IEntity; , which is already in the starter. Rules - Add throws InvalidOperationException("duplicate id <id ") when the id is taken. Update throws KeyNotFoundException("no item <id ") for an unknown id. Both first run every rule and throw a ValidationException with all the error messages (in the order the rules were added) if any rule fails; nothing changes then. - After a successful Add , Update or Remove , Changed is raised with the item before and after ( null where there is none). Remove of an unknown id returns false and raises nothing. - Where is lazy: it runs only when enumerated, and sees the items as they are then. - Pages(size) gives lists of up to size items; size below 1 throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException immediately . - Transactions : while a transaction is open, changes apply to the repository at once (so Find sees them), but Changed events are held back. Commit raises the held events in order. Disposing without committing undoes every change made since BeginTransaction and drops the held events. Only one transaction can be open at a time ( InvalidOperationException ); Commit after Commit or after Dispose throws InvalidOperationException ; Dispose can be called more than once.

title: 5.01  Tasks and async/await
body: Asynchronous code in C - why waiting should not block a thread, Task and Task<T , async methods and await, running work in sequence or at the same time with Task.WhenAll and WhenAny, exceptions in async code, async void and why to avoid it, ValueTask, async streams with IAsyncEnumerable, and never blocking with .Result. Waiting without blocking Much of a program's time is spent waiting : for a file, a database, a web server. A thread that sits waiting cannot do anything else. In a desktop app that freezes the window; in a server it wastes a thread that could serve another request. Asynchronous code starts the operation, gives the thread back while waiting, and continues when the result is ready. In C , an operation in progress is a Task : Task for one with no result, Task<T for one that produces a T . async and await csharp Console.WriteLine("ordering"); string coffee = await MakeCoffeeAsync(); Console.WriteLine(coffee); static async Task<string MakeCoffeeAsync() { Console.WriteLine(" grinding..."); await Task.Delay(200); // waits 200 ms without blocking a thread Console.WriteLine(" brewing..."); await Task.Delay(300); return "a flat white"; } - async on a method allows await inside it; the method returns Task or Task<T . - await task pauses this method until the task finishes, then gives its result. The thread is free in the meantime. - Top-level statements may use await directly, as here. - By convention, async method names end in Async . Sequence or at the same time Each await waits before the next line starts. When operations do not depend on each other, start them all first and await them together: csharp var sw = System.Diagnostics.Stopwatch.StartNew(); string a = await FetchAsync("a", 300); string b = await FetchAsync("b", 300); Console.WriteLine($"one after another: {a}{b} in ~{sw.ElapsedMilliseconds / 100 100} ms"); sw.Restart(); Task<string ta = FetchAsync("a", 300); // started Task<string tb = FetchAsync("b", 300); // started too string both = await Task.WhenAll(ta, tb); Console.WriteLine($"together: {string.Join("", both)} in ~{sw.ElapsedMilliseconds / 100 100} ms"); sw.Restart(); Task<string first = await Task.WhenAny(FetchAsync("slow", 500), FetchAsync("fast", 100)); Console.WriteLine($"first finished: {await first}"); static async Task<string FetchAsync(string name, int ms) { await Task.Delay(ms); return name; } Task.WhenAll finishes when all tasks have, with their results in the order given. Task.WhenAny finishes with the first task to complete. Exceptions An exception inside an async method is stored in its task and thrown again where the task is awaited , so ordinary try / catch works: csharp try { await LoadAsync(-1); } catch (ArgumentException e) { Console.WriteLine($"caught: {e.Message}"); } static async Task<int LoadAsync(int id) { await Task.Delay(10); if (id < 0) throw new ArgumentException("id must not be negative"); return id 2; } With Task.WhenAll , await throws the first exception; the task's Exception property holds all of them. Rules that save you trouble - Async all the way : a method that awaits must itself be async and return a Task , up to the top ( Main , an event handler, a web endpoint). - Never block on a task with .Result or .Wait() . In desktop apps it can deadlock; everywhere it wastes the thread that async was meant to free. await it instead. - Avoid async void . Nobody can await it, and an exception in it crashes the process. The only exception is event handlers, which must return void . - CPU work is different : await helps with waiting, not computing. To move heavy computation off the UI thread, use await Task.Run(() = Compute()) (lesson 5.02). - A method that usually completes at once (from a cache) can return ValueTask<T to avoid an allocation; use plain Task unless you have measured. Async streams IAsyncEnumerable<T is a sequence whose items arrive over time. Produce it with yield return in an async iterator and consume it with await foreach : csharp await foreach (var reading in ReadSensorAsync(3)) { Console.WriteLine($"reading {reading}"); } static async IAsyncEnumerable<int ReadSensorAsync(int count) { for (int i = 1; i <= count; i++) { await Task.Delay(50); // e.g. waiting for the next value from a device yield return i 10; } } Check yourself quiz ? What does await do to the thread while the awaited task is not finished? - It blocks the thread until the task is finished + It frees the thread; the method resumes when the task is done - It starts a new thread that waits for the task - It cancels the task if it takes too long await returns control to the caller instead of blocking, so the thread can do other work. The rest of the method runs after the task completes. ? Why should you not call .Result on a task? - It returns a value before the task has finished - It runs the task a second time from the start + It blocks the thread, and on a UI thread it can deadlock .Result waits by blocking, which wastes the thread. On a UI thread that can deadlock, because the task may need that very thread to finish; await instead. ? Two independent operations take 1 second each. How long does await Task.WhenAll(A(), B()) take? - About 2 seconds - No time at all - It depends on which is awaited first + About 1 second Both tasks are started before waiting, so they run at the same time.

title: async and await
body: Write three async helpers in a static class AsyncTools : csharp public static async Task<int LoadAllAsync(int ids, Func<int, Task<int load) public static async Task<string FirstSuccessfulAsync(params Func<Task<string sources) public static async Task<T WithTimeoutAsync<T (Task<T task, TimeSpan timeout) - LoadAllAsync starts every load at once and returns the results in the order of ids . - FirstSuccessfulAsync tries the sources one after another and returns the first result that does not throw. If all fail, it throws an AggregateException holding every exception, in order. With no sources it throws ArgumentException . - WithTimeoutAsync returns the task's result if it finishes within timeout , and otherwise throws a TimeoutException (the task may keep running in the background). An exception from the task itself comes through unchanged.

title: 5.02  Parallel Work and Cancellation
body: Using several cores and stopping work politely - Task.Run for CPU-bound work, Parallel.For and Parallel.ForEachAsync, limiting concurrency with SemaphoreSlim, thread safety with lock, Interlocked and concurrent collections, CancellationToken and CancellationTokenSource, timeouts, and progress reporting. CPU-bound work async / await is about waiting . Heavy computation needs threads: Task.Run runs a function on the thread pool, which keeps a UI responsive and lets several computations run on different cores: csharp var sw = System.Diagnostics.Stopwatch.StartNew(); Task<long jobs = Task.Run(() = SumOfPrimes(200_000)), Task.Run(() = SumOfPrimes(200_001)) ; long results = await Task.WhenAll(jobs); Console.WriteLine($"{results 0 } {results 0 == results 1 }"); static long SumOfPrimes(int limit) { long sum = 0; for (int n = 2; n < limit; n++) { bool prime = true; for (int d = 2; d d <= n; d++) if (n % d == 0) { prime = false; break; } if (prime) sum += n; } return sum; } For loops over data, Parallel.For and Parallel.ForEach split the work across cores: csharp double values = new double 1_000_000 ; Parallel.For(0, values.Length, i = values i = Math.Sqrt(i)); Console.WriteLine(values 999_999 .ToString("F2")); Parallelism only helps when each piece of work is independent and big enough to outweigh the cost of coordinating threads. Shared data needs care When several threads change the same data at the same time, updates get lost. count++ is read, add, write: two threads can read the same old value. csharp int unsafeCount = 0, safeCount = 0, lockedCount = 0; object gate = new(); Parallel.For(0, 100_000, _ = { unsafeCount++; // a race: some increments are lost Interlocked.Increment(ref safeCount); // an atomic increment lock (gate) { lockedCount++; } // only one thread at a time inside }); Console.WriteLine($"{unsafeCount <= 100_000} {safeCount} {lockedCount}"); var words = new System.Collections.Concurrent.ConcurrentDictionary<string, int (); Parallel.ForEach(new { "a", "b", "a", "c", "a" }, w = words.AddOrUpdate(w, 1, (_, n) = n + 1)); Console.WriteLine(words "a" ); Tool Use --- --- lock (obj) { ... } A block that only one thread runs at a time Interlocked Atomic increments, adds and swaps of single values ConcurrentDictionary , ConcurrentQueue , ConcurrentBag Collections that many threads may use at once SemaphoreSlim Allow at most N at a time (also for async code) The simplest thread safety is no shared mutable data : let each task compute its own result and combine the results at the end, as Task.WhenAll does above. Limiting concurrency Starting 1000 downloads at once overloads servers and your machine. Parallel.ForEachAsync runs async work with a limit: csharp int running = 0, peak = 0; await Parallel.ForEachAsync(Enumerable.Range(1, 12), new ParallelOptions { MaxDegreeOfParallelism = 3 }, async (n, ct) = { int now = Interlocked.Increment(ref running); InterlockedMax(ref peak, now); await Task.Delay(30, ct); Interlocked.Decrement(ref running); }); Console.WriteLine($"peak {peak}"); static void InterlockedMax(ref int target, int value) { int current; while ((current = Volatile.Read(ref target)) < value && Interlocked.CompareExchange(ref target, value, current) != current) { } } SemaphoreSlim does the same by hand: await sem.WaitAsync(); try { ... } finally { sem.Release(); } . Cancellation Long operations should be cancellable : the user closes the window, a request times out. .NET's pattern is a CancellationToken , passed down to every method that might take a while: csharp using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(250)); // cancels itself after 250 ms try { await CountSlowlyAsync(10, cts.Token); } catch (OperationCanceledException) { Console.WriteLine("cancelled"); } static async Task CountSlowlyAsync(int to, CancellationToken token) { for (int i = 1; i <= to; i++) { token.ThrowIfCancellationRequested(); // for loops doing CPU work await Task.Delay(100, token); // async methods take the token and stop early Console.WriteLine(i); } } - The caller owns a CancellationTokenSource and calls Cancel() (or gives it a timeout). - The worker receives a CancellationToken , passes it on, and checks it in loops. - Cancellation surfaces as an OperationCanceledException ; catch it where cancelling is expected. - Make CancellationToken cancellationToken = default the last parameter of your async methods. Progress IProgress<T reports progress back to the caller (in a UI app, on the UI thread): csharp var progress = new Progress<int (p = Console.WriteLine($"{p}%")); await ProcessAsync(progress); await Task.Delay(50); // let the last report print static async Task ProcessAsync(IProgress<int progress) { for (int i = 1; i <= 4; i++) { await Task.Delay(20); progress.Report(i 25); } } Check yourself quiz ? Why can count++ from several threads give a total that is too low? - Each thread works on its own copy of count, and only one copy is kept - Threads that start late miss the first increments + count++ reads, adds and writes in separate steps, so two threads can read the same old value If two threads both read 7 and both write 8, one increment is lost. Interlocked.Increment or a lock makes the step atomic. ? Who creates the CancellationTokenSource and who checks the token? + The caller creates and cancels the source; the worker receives the token and checks it - The worker creates the source; the caller checks the token - Each worker creates its own source and cancels itself on a timer - The caller creates it, and cancelling stops the worker's thread by itself Cancellation is cooperative: nothing stops the worker unless it checks the token (or passes it to methods that do). ? Which is the right tool to run a heavy calculation without freezing a desktop app's window? - await Task.Delay + await Task.Run(() = Calculate()) - calling Calculate() inside an async method - Thread.Sleep An async method still runs its CPU work on the calling thread; Task.Run moves it to the thread pool.

title: Limits and cancellation
body: Write a work queue that runs async jobs with a concurrency limit and supports cancellation: csharp public static class Worker { public static async Task<int ProcessAsync<T ( IEnumerable<T items, Func<T, CancellationToken, Task work, int maxConcurrency, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) public static long CountPrimes(int limit) // primes below limit, using all cores } - ProcessAsync runs work for every item with at most maxConcurrency at a time and returns how many finished successfully. maxConcurrency below 1 throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException at once. - When the token is cancelled, no new items start, running work receives the cancellation through its token, and ProcessAsync throws OperationCanceledException . - If a job throws (not because of cancellation), the remaining items are still processed; at the end ProcessAsync throws an AggregateException with every such exception. - CountPrimes must give the right answer while splitting the work across threads (use Parallel.For or tasks and combine the counts safely).

title: 5.03  Files and Streams
body:
Reading and writing files with File's one-line helpers and their async versions, paths with Path, directories, StreamReader and StreamWriter for large files line by line, encodings, the Stream abstraction, handling IOException, and reading CSV safely. The quick way For small files, the File class does everything in one call: csharp File.WriteAllText("hello.txt", "Hello
from C 
"); File.AppendAllText("hello.txt", "one more line
"); string text = File.ReadAllText("hello.txt"); string lines = File.ReadAllLines("hello.txt"); Console.WriteLine($"{text.Length} characters, {lines.Length} lines, last: {lines ^1 }"); File.WriteAllLines("numbers.txt", Enumerable.Range(1, 5).Select(n = n.ToString())); int sum = File.ReadLines("numbers.txt").Sum(int.Parse); Console.WriteLine(sum); Console.WriteLine(File.Exists("numbers.txt") + " " + File.Exists("missing.txt")); ReadAllLines loads the whole file into an array; ReadLines reads it lazily , one line at a time, which works for files larger than memory. Each has an ...Async version ( ReadAllTextAsync , WriteAllLinesAsync ) for use with await . Paths Never glue paths together with + and "\" : the separator differs between Windows and Linux. Path handles it: csharp string folder = Path.Combine("data", "2026", "march"); string file = Path.Combine(folder, "report.csv"); Console.WriteLine(file); Console.WriteLine($"{Path.GetFileName(file)} {Path.GetExtension(file)} {Path.GetFileNameWithoutExtension(file)}"); Console.WriteLine(Path.ChangeExtension(file, ".json")); Directory.CreateDirectory(folder); // creates every missing level, fine if it exists File.WriteAllText(file, "id,total
1,9.50
"); foreach (string f in Directory.EnumerateFiles("data", " .csv", SearchOption.AllDirectories)) Console.WriteLine($"found {f.Replace('\', '/')}"); Relative paths are relative to the current directory , which is not always the folder of your program. For files that ship with your app, use AppContext.BaseDirectory ; for user data, Environment.GetFolderPath(Environment.SpecialFolder.ApplicationData) . Streams All file, network and memory I/O in .NET goes through streams : a sequence of bytes you read from or write to. StreamReader and StreamWriter add text on top, with an encoding (UTF-8 by default): csharp using (var writer = new StreamWriter("log.txt")) { for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) writer.WriteLine($"entry {i}"); } // disposing flushes and closes the file using var reader = new StreamReader("log.txt"); string? line; int count = 0; while ((line = reader.ReadLine()) != null) { count++; Console.WriteLine($"{count}: {line}"); } Always wrap streams in using (lesson 4.04): a writer that is not disposed may never write its last data to disk. Other streams work the same way: FileStream for raw bytes, MemoryStream for bytes in memory, GZipStream to compress, the response stream of an HTTP request. Code written against Stream or TextReader works with all of them, which makes it easy to test with a StringReader : csharp Console.WriteLine(CountWords(new StringReader("one two
three"))); static int CountWords(TextReader reader) { int words = 0; string? line; while ((line = reader.ReadLine()) != null) words += line.Split(' ', StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries).Length; return words; } When things go wrong File operations fail for reasons outside your program: the file is missing, locked by another program, the disk is full, permission is denied. Catch the specific exceptions where you can do something useful: csharp try { string config = File.ReadAllText("settings.ini"); } catch (FileNotFoundException) { Console.WriteLine("no settings file: using defaults"); } catch (UnauthorizedAccessException) { Console.WriteLine("not allowed to read the settings"); } catch (IOException e) { Console.WriteLine($"could not read settings: {e.Message}"); } Checking File.Exists first does not remove the need for try : the file can disappear between the check and the read. CSV Comma-separated files look simple, but fields can contain commas inside quotes: "Smith, Ada",36 . Splitting on , breaks those. For real data use a library such as CsvHelper; for simple, known files, a small parser that understands quotes is enough (practice 5.03 builds one). When writing numbers and dates to files, use CultureInfo.InvariantCulture , so that 9.50 does not become 9,50 on a computer set to another language. Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference between File.ReadAllLines and File.ReadLines? - ReadLines returns the whole file as one string + ReadAllLines loads every line into an array at once; ReadLines reads lazily as you loop - ReadAllLines reads lazily; ReadLines loads the whole file first - ReadLines skips empty lines; ReadAllLines keeps them ReadLines returns a lazy sequence, so a huge file never has to fit in memory. The whole file as one string is ReadAllText . ? Why use Path.Combine instead of joining strings with a backslash? - Path.Combine also creates any folders that do not exist yet - Path.Combine checks that the file exists + The separator differs between operating systems, and Path.Combine uses the right one Windows uses \ and Linux and macOS use / . Path.Combine picks the right separator and avoids doubled slashes; it does not touch the disk. ? A StreamWriter is created without using and never disposed. What can happen? - Nothing: each line is written to the file at once + The last lines stay in its buffer and never reach the file - The program does not compile without using - The file is deleted when the program ends Writers buffer data, and disposing flushes the buffer and closes the file. Without it the end of the data can be lost and the file can stay locked.

title: Reading and writing files
body: Write a small CSV toolkit in a static class Csv : csharp public static List<string ParseLine(string line) public static string FormatLine(IEnumerable<string fields) public static Dictionary<string, decimal TotalsBy(TextReader reader, string keyColumn, string valueColumn) public static async Task<int CopyColumnsAsync(string inputPath, string outputPath, params string columns) - ParseLine splits on commas, except inside double quotes. Inside quotes, "" stands for one " . a,"b, c","say ""hi""" gives a , b, c , say "hi" . An empty line gives one empty field. - FormatLine does the reverse: fields containing a comma, a quote or a line break are quoted, with quotes doubled. - TotalsBy reads CSV with a header row from any TextReader , and sums valueColumn (an invariant-culture decimal) per value of keyColumn . A missing column throws ArgumentException . Blank lines are skipped. - CopyColumnsAsync reads a CSV file and writes a new one with only the named columns, in the order given (header included), and returns the number of data rows written. A missing input file lets the FileNotFoundException through.

title: 5.04  JSON with System.Text.Json
body: Converting objects to and from JSON with JsonSerializer - serialising records and collections, options for naming, indentation and enums, attributes like JsonPropertyName and JsonIgnore, deserialising safely with nullable results and validation, reading unknown JSON with JsonDocument and JsonNode, and saving settings files. Objects to JSON and back JSON is the standard text format for data: web APIs, configuration and save files. .NET includes System.Text.Json : csharp using System.Text.Json; var order = new Order(17, "Ada", new("tea", 2, 2.50m), new("cake", 1, 4.25m) , DateTime.Parse("2026-03-14T09:30:00")); string json = JsonSerializer.Serialize(order); Console.WriteLine(json); Order? back = JsonSerializer.Deserialize<Order (json); Console.WriteLine(back!.Lines 1 .Item + " " + back.Placed.Hour); record Order(int Id, string Customer, List<OrderLine Lines, DateTime Placed); record OrderLine(string Item, int Quantity, decimal Price); Serialize writes every public property; Deserialize<T builds a T from JSON, using its constructor for records. Lists become arrays, dictionaries become objects, and DateTime is written in ISO 8601 form. Options Web APIs usually use camelCase names, while C properties are PascalCase . Options control this and more: csharp using System.Text.Json; using System.Text.Json.Serialization; var options = new JsonSerializerOptions { PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase, WriteIndented = true, DefaultIgnoreCondition = JsonIgnoreCondition.WhenWritingNull, Converters = { new JsonStringEnumConverter() }, }; var task = new TaskItem("Write report", Priority.High, null, "work" ); string json = JsonSerializer.Serialize(task, options); Console.WriteLine(json); var back = JsonSerializer.Deserialize<TaskItem (json, options)!; Console.WriteLine(back.Priority); enum Priority { Low, Normal, High } record TaskItem(string Title, Priority Priority, string? Notes, List<string Tags); Create one options object and reuse it: building a new one each time is slow. JsonSerializerOptions.Web is a ready-made set for web conventions. Attributes Attributes change how one property is handled: csharp using System.Text.Json; using System.Text.Json.Serialization; var user = new User { Id = 7, Name = "Ada", PasswordHash = "secret-hash" }; Console.WriteLine(JsonSerializer.Serialize(user)); class User { JsonPropertyName("user_id") public int Id { get; set; } public string Name { get; set; } = ""; JsonIgnore public string PasswordHash { get; set; } = ""; // never written out } Reading JSON you do not control Deserialize can return null (for the JSON text null ) and throws JsonException for invalid JSON or wrong types. Data from outside should be checked like any input: csharp using System.Text.Json; foreach (string text in new { """{"Name":"Ada","Age":36}""", "{ broken", """{"Name":"Bo","Age":"old"}""", "null" }) { try { var p = JsonSerializer.Deserialize<Person (text); if (p is null string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(p.Name)) Console.WriteLine("missing data"); else Console.WriteLine($"ok: {p.Name} {p.Age}"); } catch (JsonException e) { Console.WriteLine($"bad JSON: {e.Message ..30 }..."); } } record Person(string Name, int Age); Missing properties get default values ( null , 0 ) rather than an error. Mark them required in a class, or check after deserialising. When the shape is unknown or you only need a few values, read the JSON as a tree with JsonNode (editable) or JsonDocument (read-only, fast): csharp using System.Text.Json.Nodes; var node = JsonNode.Parse("""{"city":"Oslo","current":{"temp":-3.5,"wind": 4,7 }}""")!; double temp = node "current" ! "temp" !.GetValue<double (); int gust = node "current" ! "wind" ! 1 !.GetValue<int (); Console.WriteLine($"{node "city" }: {temp} C, gusts {gust}"); node "checked" = true; Console.WriteLine(node.ToJsonString()); Saving settings A common use: keep an app's settings or data in a JSON file. csharp using System.Text.Json; var path = "settings.json"; var settings = Load(path); settings = settings with { LaunchCount = settings.LaunchCount + 1 }; File.WriteAllText(path, JsonSerializer.Serialize(settings, new JsonSerializerOptions { WriteIndented = true })); Console.WriteLine(File.ReadAllText(path)); static AppSettings Load(string path) { try { return JsonSerializer.Deserialize<AppSettings (File.ReadAllText(path)) ?? new AppSettings(); } catch (Exception e) when (e is FileNotFoundException or JsonException) { return new AppSettings(); // first run, or a damaged file } } record AppSettings(string Theme = "light", int FontSize = 14, int LaunchCount = 0); Check yourself quiz ? When can JsonSerializer.Deserialize<T return null? - When the JSON text is not valid JSON - When a property in T is missing from the JSON + When the JSON text is the literal null - Never: it always returns an object or throws Invalid JSON throws a JsonException, and missing properties are just left at their defaults. Only the JSON text null gives null. ? How do you make the JSON use camelCase names for PascalCase properties? - Set PropertyNameCaseInsensitive = true in JsonSerializerOptions + Set PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase in JsonSerializerOptions - Nothing: JsonSerializer always writes camelCase names The naming policy renames properties when writing (and reading). Case-insensitive only affects reading, and by default the names are written as declared. JsonPropertyName renames single properties. ? A JSON object lacks a property that the record has. What does Deserialize do by default? - Throws JsonException + Leaves that property at its default value (null, 0, false) - Returns null for the whole object - Uses the property's name as its value Missing properties are not an error unless you require them.

title: JSON in and out
body: A to-do app saves its tasks as JSON. Write: csharp public enum Priority { Low, Normal, High } public record TodoItem(int Id, string Title, Priority Priority, bool Done, DateOnly? Due); public static class TodoJson { public static string Save(IEnumerable<TodoItem items) public static List<TodoItem Load(string json) public static List<string OverdueTitles(string json, DateOnly today) } - Save writes camelCase property names, enums as strings ( "high" in camelCase too), leaves out due when it is null, and is not indented. - Load reads what Save writes. The JSON text null , an empty string or invalid JSON gives an empty list rather than an exception; so do items with a missing or blank title, which are skipped. - OverdueTitles reads the JSON as a tree with JsonNode (without deserialising to TodoItem ) and returns the titles of items that are not done and whose due date is before today , in file order. Example of saved JSON: {"id":1,"title":"Tea","priority":"high","done":false,"due":"2026-03-01"}

title: 5.05  HTTP with HttpClient
body: Calling web APIs - one shared HttpClient, GET and POST with JSON helpers, status codes and EnsureSuccessStatusCode, headers and authentication, query strings, timeouts and cancellation, retries for transient failures, typed API clients, and testing code that uses HTTP. HttpClient HttpClient sends HTTP requests. The practice sandbox has no internet access, so the examples in this lesson are for reading and for running on your own computer. csharp-norun using System.Net.Http.Json; using var http = new HttpClient { BaseAddress = new Uri("https://api.example.com/") }; Todo? todo = await http.GetFromJsonAsync<Todo ("todos/1"); Console.WriteLine(todo?.Title); HttpResponseMessage response = await http.PostAsJsonAsync("todos", new Todo(0, "Learn HttpClient", false)); response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode(); // throws HttpRequestException for 4xx and 5xx Todo? created = await response.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<Todo (); record Todo(int Id, string Title, bool Done); System.Net.Http.Json adds GetFromJsonAsync , PostAsJsonAsync and ReadFromJsonAsync , which use System.Text.Json (lesson 5.04) with web defaults (camelCase). One client, reused HttpClient is meant to be created once and reused . Creating one per request ( using var http = new HttpClient() inside a loop) can run out of network sockets under load. In a small program, keep one in a static readonly field; in larger apps, IHttpClientFactory (lesson 6.03) manages them for you. Status codes A response always has a status. Check it before reading the body: csharp-norun using var response = await http.GetAsync($"users/{id}"); if (response.StatusCode == HttpStatusCode.NotFound) return null; if (!response.IsSuccessStatusCode) { string body = await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync(); throw new ApiException($"GET users/{id} failed: {(int)response.StatusCode} {body}"); } return await response.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<User (); Status Meaning Retry? --- --- --- 200, 201, 204 Success - 400, 422 Your request was wrong No: fix it 401, 403 Not authenticated / not allowed No 404 Not found No 408, 429 Timeout / too many requests Yes, after a pause 500, 502, 503, 504 Server failure Yes, a few times Headers, queries and authentication csharp-norun http.DefaultRequestHeaders.Authorization = new AuthenticationHeaderValue("Bearer", token); http.DefaultRequestHeaders.UserAgent.ParseAdd("MyApp/1.0"); string query = $"search?q={Uri.EscapeDataString("tea & cake")}&page=2"; var results = await http.GetFromJsonAsync<List<Item (query); Always escape values put into URLs with Uri.EscapeDataString . Keep tokens and API keys out of source code: read them from configuration or environment variables (lesson 6.03). Timeouts and cancellation HttpClient.Timeout defaults to 100 seconds. Pass a CancellationToken (lesson 5.02) for finer control: csharp-norun using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5)); try { var data = await http.GetFromJsonAsync<Report ("reports/latest", cts.Token); } catch (OperationCanceledException) { Console.WriteLine("the server took too long"); } Retrying Networks fail briefly now and then. Retry only failures that may succeed later (timeouts, 429, 5xx), only a few times, and wait longer each time: csharp-norun static async Task<T RetryAsync<T (Func<Task<T action, int attempts = 3) { for (int i = 1; ; i++) { try { return await action(); } catch (HttpRequestException e) when (i < attempts && IsTransient(e.StatusCode)) { await Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(200 Math.Pow(2, i - 1))); } } } static bool IsTransient(HttpStatusCode? code) = code is null or HttpStatusCode.RequestTimeout or HttpStatusCode.TooManyRequests (int?)code = 500; Libraries such as Polly (and Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience ) provide retries, circuit breakers and timeouts ready-made. A typed client Wrap an API in a class with methods named after what they do. The rest of the program then knows nothing about URLs or JSON: csharp-norun public interface IWeatherApi { Task<Forecast? GetForecastAsync(string city, CancellationToken ct = default); } public sealed class WeatherApi(HttpClient http) : IWeatherApi { public Task<Forecast? GetForecastAsync(string city, CancellationToken ct = default) = http.GetFromJsonAsync<Forecast ($"forecast?city={Uri.EscapeDataString(city)}", ct); } Because the program depends on IWeatherApi , tests can pass a fake implementation that returns fixed data, with no network at all. This is how the practice task and project for this milestone are built: the HTTP part is an interface, and the logic around it is tested with fakes. Check yourself quiz ? Why should one HttpClient be reused instead of creating one per request? - An HttpClient can only send one request in its lifetime - A second HttpClient in the same program throws an exception + Each new client can hold sockets open after use, and many under load can run out of them A client can send many requests, even at once. Creating and disposing one per request leaves connections lingering, which can exhaust the machine's sockets. ? Which failures are worth retrying? - Any failure, since retrying never hurts + Transient ones: timeouts, 429 Too Many Requests and 5xx server errors - Only 404 Not Found, since the page may appear later - Only 400 Bad Request, since the server may accept it next time A 4xx error such as 400, 401, 403 or 404 says the request itself is wrong, so sending it again gives the same answer. Retrying everything also adds load to a failing server. ? What does response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode() do for a 404 response? - Returns false - Nothing + Throws an HttpRequestException - Retries the request It throws for any status outside 200-299.

body: A weather API is reached through an interface, so the logic around it can be tested without a network: csharp public record Forecast(string City, double TempC, string Summary); public interface IWeatherApi { Task<Forecast GetAsync(string city, CancellationToken ct = default); // throws HttpRequestException on failure } public class WeatherService(IWeatherApi api, Func<DateTime clock) { public async Task<string DescribeAsync(string city, CancellationToken ct = default) } DescribeAsync returns "<City : <TempC with 1 decimal C, <Summary " (invariant culture), and: - trims the city name and treats it case-insensitively; a blank name throws ArgumentException before any call; - caches results per city for 10 minutes, measured with clock() (so the tests can move time forward); - retries an HttpRequestException whose StatusCode is null, 429 or 500 and above, up to 3 attempts in total, waiting 10 ms then 20 ms; other errors (such as 404) are not retried; - when every attempt fails but a cached result exists (even an old one), returns that result with (cached) added; otherwise lets the last exception through.

title: A log analyzer
body: Servers write log files with lines like: 2026-03-14T09:30:05Z ERROR auth: login failed for user 17 2026-03-14T09:31:00Z INFO web: GET /home 200 Write a tool that reads several log files concurrently , summarises them, and saves the summary as JSON. csharp public record LogEntry(DateTime Time, string Level, string Source, string Message); public record Report( int Entries, int Malformed, SortedDictionary<string, int ByLevel, List<string TopErrorSources, DateTime? First, DateTime? Last, int? BusiestHour, List<string MissingFiles); public static class LogTools { public static LogEntry? ParseLine(string line) public static IAsyncEnumerable<LogEntry ReadAsync(string path, CancellationToken ct = default) public static Task<Report AnalyzeAsync(IEnumerable<string paths, CancellationToken ct = default) public static Task SaveAsync(Report report, string path) public static Task<Report? LoadAsync(string path) } Parsing : a line is a UTC time in the form yyyy-MM-ddTHH:mm:ssZ , a space, a level in brackets ( DEBUG , INFO , WARN or ERROR , any case, stored in upper case), a space, a source (letters, digits, . , - and _ ), a colon and a space, and the message (possibly empty). ParseLine returns null for anything else. The Time has DateTimeKind.Utc . ReadAsync yields the entries of one file in order, skipping lines that do not parse, reading the file line by line (not all at once) and stopping when the token is cancelled. AnalyzeAsync reads all files at the same time and returns: - Entries : entries parsed; Malformed : non-blank lines that did not parse; - ByLevel : the count per level (levels that occur only); - TopErrorSources : the sources with the most ERROR entries, at most 3, ties by name (ordinal); - First and Last : the earliest and latest time, or null with no entries; - BusiestHour : the hour of the day (0 to 23, UTC) with the most entries, the earliest on a tie, or null ; - MissingFiles : the paths that do not exist, sorted (ordinal). Missing files are not an error. SaveAsync writes the report as indented JSON with camelCase names; LoadAsync reads it back, returning null for a missing file or invalid JSON.

title: 6.01  Solutions, Projects and NuGet
body: How real .NET code is organised - the .csproj file and its key settings, solutions with several projects, class libraries and project references, NuGet packages and versions, the dotnet CLI for building, testing, running and publishing, build configurations, and a sensible folder layout. Projects A project is a folder with a .csproj file and the source files under it. It builds into one assembly (a .dll , or an executable). The project file is short XML: xml <Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk" <PropertyGroup <OutputType Exe</OutputType <TargetFramework net9.0</TargetFramework <Nullable enable</Nullable <ImplicitUsings enable</ImplicitUsings <TreatWarningsAsErrors true</TreatWarningsAsErrors </PropertyGroup <ItemGroup <PackageReference Include="Spectre.Console" Version="0.49.1" / <ProjectReference Include="..\Budget.Core\Budget.Core.csproj" / </ItemGroup </Project Setting Meaning --- --- OutputType Exe for a program; leave it out for a class library TargetFramework The .NET version to build for: net9.0 , net8.0 Nullable Turns on nullable reference warnings (lesson 2.05): always enable ImplicitUsings Adds global usings for System, LINQ, collections and more TreatWarningsAsErrors Makes every warning stop the build: a good habit Every .cs file under the folder is compiled automatically; you do not list them. Solutions and libraries A solution ( .sln or the newer .slnx ) groups related projects. A typical application splits its code: text Budget/ Budget.sln src/ Budget.Core/ class library: the domain and rules, no I/O Budget.Core.csproj Ledger.cs Transaction.cs Budget.Cli/ the console program: input, output, files Budget.Cli.csproj (references Budget.Core) Program.cs tests/ Budget.Core.Tests/ unit tests for the library (lesson 6.02) Budget.Core.Tests.csproj Keeping the logic in a class library with no console or file code means a test project, a desktop UI and a web API can all reuse it. A ProjectReference makes one project use another; public types of the library are visible to it, internal ones are not. The dotnet CLI bash dotnet new sln -n Budget dotnet new classlib -o src/Budget.Core dotnet new console -o src/Budget.Cli dotnet new xunit -o tests/Budget.Core.Tests dotnet sln add src/Budget.Core src/Budget.Cli tests/Budget.Core.Tests dotnet add src/Budget.Cli reference src/Budget.Core dotnet add tests/Budget.Core.Tests reference src/Budget.Core dotnet build compile everything dotnet test run all test projects dotnet run --project src/Budget.Cli -- report 2026-03 arguments after -- go to the program dotnet publish src/Budget.Cli -c Release -r win-x64 --self-contained a folder you can ship Builds come in configurations : Debug (the default, easy to debug) and Release (optimised, for shipping): dotnet build -c Release . NuGet packages NuGet is .NET's package manager. dotnet add package Name downloads a package and adds a PackageReference with its version: bash dotnet add src/Budget.Cli package Spectre.Console dotnet list package --outdated newer versions available dotnet list package --vulnerable known security problems Versions follow semantic versioning ( MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH ); a plain version like 0.49.1 means "this version or higher, preferring the lowest that works". Packages that every .NET developer meets: Package For --- --- Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting Dependency injection, configuration and logging (lesson 6.03) xunit , NUnit , MSTest Unit testing (lesson 6.02) Spectre.Console Rich console output: tables, colours, prompts CsvHelper Reading and writing CSV Dapper , Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore Databases Serilog Structured logging Every package is code from someone else that runs with your program's permissions. Prefer well-known packages, check how actively they are maintained, and keep them updated. Reading a project file in code Project files are XML, which System.Xml.Linq reads easily. Tools that report on many projects (which packages are used where, which projects target an old framework) do exactly this: csharp using System.Xml.Linq; var xml = XDocument.Parse(""" <Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk" <PropertyGroup <TargetFramework net9.0</TargetFramework </PropertyGroup <ItemGroup <PackageReference Include="Serilog" Version="4.0.1" / <PackageReference Include="CsvHelper" Version="33.0.1" / </ItemGroup </Project """); Console.WriteLine(xml.Descendants("TargetFramework").First().Value); foreach (var p in xml.Descendants("PackageReference")) Console.WriteLine($"{p.Attribute("Include")?.Value} {p.Attribute("Version")?.Value}"); Check yourself quiz ? Why put the domain logic in a class library instead of the console project? + So tests, a UI or a web API can reference and reuse it, free of input and output code - Console projects cannot contain classes - Code in a class library runs faster than code in a console project - A solution may only contain one console project A library can be referenced by any number of projects. Keeping Console calls out of it means each front end decides how to show results. ? What does dotnet run -- report 2026-03 pass to the program? - It runs a project named report with the setting 2026-03 - Nothing: dotnet reads both words as its own build options + The arguments after --: "report" and "2026-03" arrive in args - One string, "report 2026-03", in args 0 -- separates dotnet's own options from the program's arguments, and args are split at spaces, so args is "report", "2026-03" . ? Which project setting turns on warnings for possibly-null references? - TreatWarningsAsErrors - ImplicitUsings + Nullable - TargetFramework <Nullable enable</Nullable turns on nullable reference types.

title: Reading project files
body: Write a tool that reads .csproj files with System.Xml.Linq and reports on them: csharp public record Package(string Name, string Version); public record ProjectInfo(string? TargetFramework, bool IsExe, bool NullableEnabled, List<Package Packages, List<string References); public static class ProjectReader { public static ProjectInfo Read(string xml) public static List<string Outdated(IEnumerable<ProjectInfo projects, IReadOnlyDictionary<string, string latest) } - TargetFramework is the element's text, or null when missing. IsExe is true when OutputType is Exe (ignoring case). NullableEnabled is true when Nullable is enable . - Packages come from PackageReference elements ( Include and Version attributes; a missing version is "" ), sorted by name ignoring case. - References are the ProjectReference paths reduced to the project name: ..\Budget.Core\Budget.Core.csproj gives Budget.Core . Paths may use \ or / . - Outdated lists, for every package used in any project whose version is lower than the one in latest , a line "<name : <version - <latest " , once per name and version, sorted. Compare versions as numbers part by part ( System.Version ), so 9.0.0 is lower than 10.0.0 . Packages not in latest , or with a version that cannot be parsed, are skipped. - Invalid XML throws FormatException with the XmlException as its inner exception.

title: 6.02  Unit Testing
body: Writing automated tests with xUnit - test projects, Facts and Theories with InlineData, Arrange-Act-Assert, asserting values, collections and exceptions, testing async code, fakes for dependencies, what makes code testable, test naming, and how a test framework finds and runs tests with attributes and reflection. Why tests A unit test is code that runs a small part of your program with known inputs and checks the result. A good test suite lets you change code without fear: if you break something, a test fails within seconds. Every practice task in this course has been checked this way. xUnit xUnit is the most common test framework for .NET. A test project references the code under test and contains classes of test methods: csharp-norun using Xunit; public class LedgerTests { Fact public void Deposit_increases_the_balance() { // Arrange var ledger = new Ledger(100m); // Act ledger.Deposit(25m); // Assert Assert.Equal(125m, ledger.Balance); } Fact public void Withdrawing_too_much_throws() { var ledger = new Ledger(10m); var ex = Assert.Throws<InvalidOperationException (() = ledger.Withdraw(50m)); Assert.Contains("not enough", ex.Message); } Theory InlineData(2024, true) InlineData(1900, false) InlineData(2000, true) public void Leap_years(int year, bool expected) { Assert.Equal(expected, Dates.IsLeapYear(year)); } } - Fact marks a test with no parameters; Theory with InlineData(...) runs the same test for each set of data. - Arrange, Act, Assert : set up, do the one thing being tested, check the result. - Name tests after the behaviour they check, so a failing name explains the problem. - dotnet test builds and runs every test, and reports failures with the expected and actual values. Assertions Assertion Checks --- --- Assert.Equal(expected, actual) Values (records and collections compare by content) Assert.True(cond) , Assert.False(cond) Conditions Assert.Null(x) , Assert.NotNull(x) Null Assert.Contains(item, collection) , Assert.Empty(c) , Assert.Single(c) Collections Assert.Throws<T (() = ...) An exception of exactly type T await Assert.ThrowsAsync<T (() = ...) The same for async code Assert.InRange(x, low, high) Numbers in a range Async tests return Task : public async Task Loads_settings() { var s = await store.LoadAsync(); Assert.Equal(...); } . Testable code Code is easy to test when its dependencies come in from outside. Code that reads DateTime.Now , the file system or the network directly can only be tested by changing the computer's clock or files. Code that receives an IClock , a TextReader or an IWeatherApi (lessons 3.04, 5.03, 5.05) can be given fakes : csharp var clock = new FixedClock(new DateTime(2026, 3, 31)); var invoices = new InvoiceService(clock); var invoice = invoices.Create("Ada", 120m); Console.WriteLine($"{invoice.Due:yyyy-MM-dd} {invoice.Due == new DateTime(2026, 4, 30)}"); public interface IClock { DateTime Today { get; } } public sealed class FixedClock(DateTime today) : IClock { public DateTime Today = today; } public record Invoice(string Customer, decimal Amount, DateTime Due); public class InvoiceService(IClock clock) { public Invoice Create(string customer, decimal amount) = new(customer, amount, clock.Today.AddDays(30)); } Fakes can be hand-written classes like FixedClock , or made with a mocking library such as NSubstitute or Moq. Hand-written fakes are often clearer for small interfaces. What to test: the rules and calculations (the class library), the edge cases (empty lists, zero, the last day of a month, invalid input), and every bug you fix (a test that fails before the fix and passes after). How a test framework works There is no magic in Fact . An attribute is a class that attaches information to code. At run time, reflection lets a program inspect types and their methods, read their attributes, and call them. A test runner finds every public method with Fact , creates the class, invokes the method, and records whether it threw: csharp using System.Reflection; foreach (var (name, passed, error) in MiniRunner.Run(typeof(MathTests))) Console.WriteLine($"{(passed ? "PASS" : "FAIL")} {name}{(error is null ? "" : ": " + error)}"); AttributeUsage(AttributeTargets.Method) public sealed class FactAttribute : Attribute { } public class MathTests { Fact public void Adding() { if (2 + 2 != 4) throw new Exception("2 + 2 is not 4"); } Fact public void Dividing() { if (7 / 2 != 3.5) throw new Exception($"7 / 2 gave {7 / 2}"); } public void NotATest() { } } public static class MiniRunner { public static IEnumerable<(string Name, bool Passed, string? Error) Run(Type testClass) { foreach (MethodInfo method in testClass.GetMethods().Where(m = m.GetCustomAttribute<FactAttribute () != null).OrderBy(m = m.Name)) { object instance = Activator.CreateInstance(testClass)!; // a fresh object for every test string? error = null; try { method.Invoke(instance, null); } catch (TargetInvocationException e) { error = e.InnerException?.Message; } yield return (method.Name, error is null, error); } } } xUnit does the same with many more features: theories, async tests, parallel runs, fixtures for shared setup. Practice 6.02 builds a fuller runner. Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference between Fact and Theory ? - A Fact must pass, but a Theory may fail without failing the run - A Theory is a test that has not been written yet + A Fact is one test without parameters; a Theory runs once for each InlineData set - A Fact has one assert, but a Theory may have several A Theory is a parameterised test: each InlineData(...) line gives one set of arguments and one test run. ? Why does an InvoiceService that takes an IClock test more easily than one that reads DateTime.Now? + A test can give it a fixed clock, so the due date is the same on every run - Calling an interface is faster than reading DateTime.Now - xUnit does not allow DateTime.Now inside a test With DateTime.Now the expected due date changes every day. A fixed clock makes the result predictable. ? xUnit creates a new instance of the test class for each test. What does that guarantee? - The tests run faster than with one shared instance + Tests cannot affect each other through instance fields - The tests run in the order they are written - Static fields are reset between tests A fresh object per test keeps tests independent. Static state is still shared, which is one more reason to avoid it.

title: A test runner with reflection
body: Build a small test framework like xUnit. The attributes are given; write the runner: csharp public record TestResult(string Name, string Outcome, string? Message); // Outcome: "passed", "failed" or "skipped" public static class Runner { public static List<TestResult Run(Type testClass) } - Run every public instance method marked Fact or Theory , in order of method name (ordinal). Methods without either are ignored. - Each test runs on a new instance of the class. - A Fact is named after its method. A Theory runs once per InlineData attribute (in the order they are written), named Method(arg1, arg2) with the arguments as text (strings in double quotes, true / false for bools, numbers with invariant formatting). - A test passes when it returns normally. If it throws, it fails with the exception's message (the real exception, not reflection's TargetInvocationException wrapper). - A method returning Task is awaited (call .GetAwaiter().GetResult() on it); an exception from the task fails the test the same way. - Fact(Skip = "reason") is not run and gives skipped with the reason as the message. - A theory whose data has the wrong number of arguments fails with the message expected N arguments .

title: 6.03  Dependency Injection and Configuration
body: Building applications from small services - constructor injection, the composition root, Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection with singleton, scoped and transient lifetimes, the generic host, configuration from appsettings.json, environment variables and user secrets bound to options classes, logging with ILogger, and how a container resolves constructors. Constructor injection Dependency injection means a class receives the services it needs through its constructor instead of creating them itself: csharp // Wires everything together in one place: the "composition root". IClock clock = new SystemClock(); INotifier notifier = new ConsoleNotifier(); var reminders = new ReminderService(clock, notifier); reminders.Check(new { ("Pay rent", DateTime.Today.AddDays(-1)), ("Call Ada", DateTime.Today.AddDays(3)) }); public interface IClock { DateTime Now { get; } } public interface INotifier { void Notify(string message); } public sealed class SystemClock : IClock { public DateTime Now = DateTime.Now; } public sealed class ConsoleNotifier : INotifier { public void Notify(string message) = Console.WriteLine($" notice {message}"); } public class ReminderService(IClock clock, INotifier notifier) { public void Check(IEnumerable<(string Task, DateTime Due) items) { foreach (var (task, due) in items) if (due < clock.Now) notifier.Notify($"{task} is overdue"); } } ReminderService does not know whether it prints to a console, sends an email or writes to a test list. Each class has one job, depends on interfaces, and is testable with fakes (lesson 6.02). A container In a big application, building every object by hand gets long. A DI container does it: you register which implementation goes with each interface, and it resolves a class by creating its constructor's arguments, and theirs, recursively. csharp-norun using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection; var services = new ServiceCollection(); services.AddSingleton<IClock, SystemClock (); // one instance for the whole app services.AddTransient<INotifier, ConsoleNotifier (); // a new instance every time services.AddScoped<IUnitOfWork, UnitOfWork (); // one per scope (in a web app: per request) services.AddTransient<ReminderService (); using var provider = services.BuildServiceProvider(); var reminders = provider.GetRequiredService<ReminderService (); Lifetime One instance Use for --- --- --- Singleton For the whole application Stateless services, caches, HttpClient factories, configuration Scoped Per scope (a web request) Database contexts, per-request state Transient Per resolution Light services with no shared state Never inject a scoped or transient service into a singleton: the singleton would keep it forever. Practice 6.03 builds a small container with reflection to show how resolution works. The generic host Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting combines DI, configuration and logging, and is how ASP.NET Core, worker services and well-structured console apps start: csharp-norun using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection; using Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting; var builder = Host.CreateApplicationBuilder(args); builder.Services.Configure<ReminderOptions (builder.Configuration.GetSection("Reminders")); builder.Services.AddSingleton<IClock, SystemClock (); builder.Services.AddSingleton<INotifier, ConsoleNotifier (); builder.Services.AddHostedService<ReminderWorker (); // a background service that runs until stopped using IHost host = builder.Build(); await host.RunAsync(); Configuration Settings should not be hard-coded. Configuration is read from several providers , later ones overriding earlier ones: 1. appsettings.json 2. appsettings.{Environment}.json (for example appsettings.Development.json ) 3. user secrets during development (kept outside the project folder, never committed) 4. environment variables ( Reminders__CheckEveryMinutes=5 : a double underscore separates sections) 5. command-line arguments ( --Reminders:CheckEveryMinutes 5 ) json { "Reminders": { "CheckEveryMinutes": 15, "Channel": "email" }, "Logging": { "LogLevel": { "Default": "Information" } } } Bind a section to a class with the options pattern , and inject IOptions<T : csharp-norun public sealed class ReminderOptions { public int CheckEveryMinutes { get; set; } = 10; public string Channel { get; set; } = "console"; } public class ReminderWorker(IOptions<ReminderOptions options, ILogger<ReminderWorker logger) : BackgroundService { protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken) { var every = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(options.Value.CheckEveryMinutes); while (!stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested) { logger.LogInformation("Checking reminders via {Channel}", options.Value.Channel); await Task.Delay(every, stoppingToken); } } } Secrets (API keys, connection strings with passwords) belong in user secrets during development and in environment variables or a secret store in production, never in appsettings.json in source control. Logging ILogger<T is injected like any service. Use message templates with named placeholders rather than interpolated strings: logger.LogWarning("Order {OrderId} failed after {Attempts} attempts", id, n) . Structured logging tools then store OrderId and Attempts as searchable fields. Check yourself quiz ? What is a composition root? - The base class that every service inherits from - The folder that holds all the projects of a solution + The one place near the program's start where objects are created and connected - The first object the container creates, which owns all the others Only the composition root knows which concrete classes are used; the rest of the code just receives its dependencies through constructors. ? Why should a singleton not depend on a scoped service? - Singletons cannot have constructor parameters + The singleton lives for the whole app and would keep one scoped instance forever - The scoped service would then be created again on every call - It would make the singleton scoped too, created once per request A singleton is created once, so it captures the scoped instance it got first and shares it across all scopes. Being created on every request is what a transient service is. ? An environment variable Reminders__Channel=sms is set and appsettings.json says "email". Which value does configuration give? - email + sms - both, as an array - it throws Environment variables are added after appsettings.json, so they override it; __ separates sections.

title: A dependency injection container
body: Write a small DI container that builds objects through their constructors with reflection: csharp public class Container { public void AddSingleton<TService, TImpl () where TImpl : TService public void AddTransient<TService, TImpl () where TImpl : TService public void AddInstance<TService (TService instance) where TService : notnull public T Resolve<T () } - Resolve<T looks up the registration for T . A singleton is created on first use and then reused; a transient is created on every resolve; an instance is always that object. - To create an implementation, use its public constructor with the most parameters , and resolve each parameter's type from the container (recursively). - Registering the same service type again replaces the earlier registration. - Errors ( InvalidOperationException ): - no registration for <TypeName when a type (or one of the parameters needed on the way) is not registered; - circular dependency: A - B - A when building a type needs itself, listing the chain of type names. The sample services ( IClock , FixedClock , IGreeter , Greeter , Ping , Pong ...) are in the project already.

title: 6.04  Desktop UI and MVVM
body: Building desktop applications with C - the choices (WinForms, WPF, WinUI, Avalonia, .NET MAUI), event-driven UI and the UI thread, XAML and data binding, the MVVM pattern with INotifyPropertyChanged, ObservableCollection and ICommand, keeping the UI responsive with async, and testing view models without a window. The choices Framework Runs on Notes --- --- --- WinForms Windows The oldest; drag-and-drop designer, quick for simple tools WPF Windows XAML markup, data binding, rich styling; very widely used WinUI 3 Windows Microsoft's newest Windows UI Avalonia Windows, macOS, Linux WPF-like XAML that runs everywhere .NET MAUI Windows, macOS, Android, iOS One code base for desktop and mobile This lesson's ideas apply to all of them. The practice sandbox has no screen, so UI code here is for reading; the view model logic below runs anywhere and is what the practice tests. Event-driven code and the UI thread A UI program waits for events : a click, a key, a timer. Each handler runs on the UI thread , the one thread allowed to touch the window. While a handler runs, the window cannot redraw or respond. So handlers must be quick, and slow work must be awaited (lesson 5.01): csharp-norun // WinForms: a button's Click event private async void LoadButton_Click(object sender, EventArgs e) // async void is right for event handlers { loadButton.Enabled = false; statusLabel.Text = "Loading..."; try { var report = await _service.LoadReportAsync(); // the window stays responsive while waiting reportGrid.DataSource = report.Rows; // back on the UI thread after await } catch (HttpRequestException ex) { MessageBox.Show(this, ex.Message, "Could not load"); } finally { loadButton.Enabled = true; statusLabel.Text = ""; } } XAML and binding WPF, WinUI, Avalonia and MAUI describe windows in XAML and connect them to data with bindings : xml <StackPanel Margin="12" <TextBox Text="{Binding NewTitle, UpdateSourceTrigger=PropertyChanged}" / <Button Content="Add" Command="{Binding AddCommand}" / <ListBox ItemsSource="{Binding Items}" / <TextBlock Text="{Binding Summary}" / </StackPanel {Binding NewTitle} keeps the text box and the NewTitle property of the window's DataContext in sync, in both directions. The XAML contains no logic at all. MVVM Model-View-ViewModel separates a UI into three parts: - Model : the domain data and rules (your class library). - View : the XAML window: layout and looks only. - ViewModel : a plain class exposing what the view shows (properties) and does (commands). It knows nothing about controls. For bindings to notice changes, the view model implements INotifyPropertyChanged , lists use ObservableCollection<T , and actions are ICommand s: csharp using System.Collections.ObjectModel; using System.ComponentModel; using System.Runtime.CompilerServices; using System.Windows.Input; var vm = new TodoViewModel(); vm.PropertyChanged += (_, e) = Console.WriteLine($"changed: {e.PropertyName}"); Console.WriteLine(vm.AddCommand.CanExecute(null)); vm.NewTitle = "Buy tea"; Console.WriteLine(vm.AddCommand.CanExecute(null)); vm.AddCommand.Execute(null); Console.WriteLine($"{vm.Items.Count} item, title now '{vm.NewTitle}', {vm.Summary}"); public abstract class ViewModelBase : INotifyPropertyChanged { public event PropertyChangedEventHandler? PropertyChanged; protected bool Set<T (ref T field, T value, CallerMemberName string? name = null) { if (EqualityComparer<T .Default.Equals(field, value)) return false; field = value; PropertyChanged?.Invoke(this, new PropertyChangedEventArgs(name)); return true; } protected void Raise(string name) = PropertyChanged?.Invoke(this, new PropertyChangedEventArgs(name)); } public sealed class RelayCommand(Action execute, Func<bool canExecute) : ICommand { public event EventHandler? CanExecuteChanged; public bool CanExecute(object? parameter) = canExecute(); public void Execute(object? parameter) { if (CanExecute(parameter)) execute(); } public void NotifyCanExecuteChanged() = CanExecuteChanged?.Invoke(this, EventArgs.Empty); } public sealed class TodoViewModel : ViewModelBase { private string _newTitle = ""; public ObservableCollection<string Items { get; } = new(); public RelayCommand AddCommand { get; } public TodoViewModel() { AddCommand = new RelayCommand(Add, () = !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(NewTitle)); Items.CollectionChanged += (_, _) = Raise(nameof(Summary)); } public string NewTitle { get = _newTitle; set { if (Set(ref _newTitle, value)) AddCommand.NotifyCanExecuteChanged(); } } public string Summary = Items.Count == 1 ? "1 item" : $"{Items.Count} items"; private void Add() { Items.Add(NewTitle.Trim()); NewTitle = ""; } } CallerMemberName fills in the property's name automatically. The CommunityToolkit.Mvvm package generates this plumbing from attributes ( ObservableProperty , RelayCommand ), but it is worth knowing what it writes. Why MVVM pays off The whole behaviour of the screen (when Add is enabled, what the summary says, what happens after adding) is in TodoViewModel , an ordinary class. It is tested like any other code, without opening a window, which is exactly what practice 6.04 does. The view can be redesigned without touching the logic, and the same view model can serve a WPF and an Avalonia view. Check yourself quiz ? Why must a UI event handler not run a 5-second calculation directly? - Event handlers may not change controls, so the result could not be shown - Windows stops any handler that runs for longer than a second + It runs on the UI thread, so the window freezes until it finishes While the handler runs, the UI thread cannot draw or respond to clicks. Await the work instead (with Task.Run for CPU work). ? What does INotifyPropertyChanged do for data binding? + It raises PropertyChanged when a property changes, so bound controls read the new value - It stops properties from changing while the window is being drawn - It copies every property to its control on a timer - It checks that new property values are valid Binding reads a property once; the PropertyChanged event is how the view model tells the controls that a value has changed. ? In MVVM, where does the rule "the Add button is disabled while the title is empty" belong? - In the XAML - In the button's Click handler in the window's code-behind + In the view model, as the command's CanExecute - In the model's database code The view model holds the screen's behaviour; the view only binds to it.

title: A view model
body: Write the view model behind a tip calculator window. It never touches a window, so it can be tested like any class: csharp public abstract class ViewModelBase : INotifyPropertyChanged public sealed class RelayCommand(Action execute, Func<bool canExecute) : ICommand // with NotifyCanExecuteChanged() public sealed class TipViewModel : ViewModelBase { public string BillText { get; set; } // what the user typed, "" at the start public int TipPercent { get; set; } // 15 at the start, kept between 0 and 30 public int People { get; set; } // 1 at the start, kept at 1 or more public string Total { get; } // e.g. "57.50", or "" when the bill is not valid public string PerPerson { get; } // the total divided between people, or "" public string Error { get; } // "Enter the bill amount" when BillText is not a positive number, else "" public RelayCommand AddPersonCommand { get; } public RelayCommand RemovePersonCommand { get; } // can execute only while People 1 public RelayCommand ResetCommand { get; } // back to "", 15, 1 } - The bill is parsed with the invariant culture. Total = bill × (1 + tip / 100) and per person = total / people, both rounded to cents (halves away from zero) and shown with 2 decimals. - Setting a property to the value it already has raises nothing . Otherwise PropertyChanged is raised for the property itself and then for every computed property that depends on it ( Total , PerPerson , Error ), in that order. Values outside the allowed range are clamped first. - When People changes, RemovePersonCommand raises CanExecuteChanged .

title: 6.05  Project: A Complete Application
body: Designing and building a whole application from the course's parts - a budget tracker with a domain library, commands parsed from input, services behind interfaces, JSON persistence with versions, reports with LINQ, error handling at the edges, tests, and where to go next with C . The application The final project is a budget tracker : record income and expenses, set monthly budgets per category, see a monthly report, undo mistakes, and save everything to a file. It is small enough to finish and has every part a real application has. The layers Domain (a class library in a real solution): records and the rules, no input or output. csharp-norun public record Transaction(int Id, DateOnly Date, decimal Amount, string Category, string Description) { public bool IsExpense = Amount < 0; } public class Ledger { private readonly List<Transaction _transactions = new(); private readonly Dictionary<string, decimal _budgets = new(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase); private int _nextId = 1; public IReadOnlyList<Transaction Transactions = _transactions; public Transaction Add(DateOnly date, decimal amount, string category, string description) { ... } public Transaction? UndoLast() { ... } public void SetBudget(string category, decimal monthly) { ... } public decimal? BudgetFor(string category) = _budgets.TryGetValue(category, out var b) ? b : null; } Reports : pure functions from a ledger and a month to a report record, written with LINQ, easy to test: csharp-norun public record CategoryLine(string Category, decimal Spent, decimal? Budget) { public bool Over = Budget is decimal b && Spent b; } public static MonthReport ForMonth(Ledger ledger, int year, int month) { var inMonth = ledger.Transactions.Where(t = t.Date.Year == year && t.Date.Month == month).ToList(); var byCategory = inMonth.Where(t = t.IsExpense) .GroupBy(t = t.Category) .Select(g = new CategoryLine(g.Key, -g.Sum(t = t.Amount), ledger.BudgetFor(g.Key))) .OrderByDescending(l = l.Spent).ThenBy(l = l.Category, StringComparer.Ordinal) .ToList(); ... } Storage behind an interface, with a version number in the file so later versions of the app can still read old files (lesson 5.04): csharp-norun public interface ILedgerStore { Task SaveAsync(Ledger ledger, string path); Task<Ledger? LoadAsync(string path); } Commands : the input is parsed into a command and its arguments, and each command has a small handler that validates the arguments, calls the domain, and returns the text to show. Errors that the user can fix (a bad date, an unknown command) become messages; bugs still throw. Building it step by step 1. Write the domain records and Ledger with their rules. Test them. 2. Write the report function. Test it with a ledger built in the test. 3. Write the command loop with add , list and quit ; run it by hand. 4. Add budget , report and undo , one at a time, each with its error messages. 5. Add save and load with JSON. 6. Read through the code: are names clear, is each method short, is every rule in the domain rather than in the input code? This order keeps a working program at every step: each feature is small, finished and checked before the next one starts. Where to go next - Web : ASP.NET Core minimal APIs and Blazor use everything in this course (DI, configuration, async, records, JSON). dotnet new webapi is a good start. - Data : Entity Framework Core maps classes to database tables; Dapper runs SQL with less ceremony. - Desktop and mobile : WPF or Avalonia with MVVM (lesson 6.04), or .NET MAUI. - Games : Unity and Godot are scripted in C . - Deeper C : Span<T and performance, source generators, System.Threading.Channels , and the Roslyn compiler APIs. Check yourself quiz ? Why is the report a pure function of the ledger and the month? - Pure functions run faster because their results are cached + It can be tested with any ledger built in memory, with no side effects to set up or clean up - Pure functions cannot throw exceptions A pure function's result depends only on its arguments, so a test just builds a ledger and checks the report. No files or clock are involved. ? Why store a version number in the saved file? - So the file can only be opened by the version that wrote it - To check that no other program changed the file + So a later version of the app can recognise and convert files written by older versions When the format changes, the version number tells the loader which layout it is reading, so old files keep working. ? In this design, where should the rule "an amount of 0 is not allowed" be checked? - Only in the input parser, before a command is built + In the domain, in Ledger.Add - In the JSON storage, when the ledger is saved - In the report, when the month is summed Rules live in the domain so every way of adding a transaction obeys them; the command handler at the edge turns the error into a message.

title: Parsing commands
body: The final project reads commands like add 2026-03-01 -12.50 food "Lunch with Ada" --tag=work --split . Write the parser: csharp public record ParsedCommand( string Name, IReadOnlyList<string Args, IReadOnlyDictionary<string, string Options, IReadOnlySet<string Flags); public static class CommandParser { public static List<string Tokenize(string line) public static ParsedCommand? Parse(string line) } Tokenize splits on spaces (runs of spaces count as one). A token can be quoted with " ; inside quotes spaces are kept and \" is a quote and \\ a backslash. Quotes may start in the middle of a token: a"b c"d is one token ab cd . An unclosed quote throws FormatException("unclosed quote") . "" is an empty token. Parse tokenizes, then: - returns null for a blank line; - the first token, in lower case, is the Name ; - --key=value sets an option (keys in lower case; the value keeps its case and may be empty); a later one with the same key wins; - --flag (no = ) adds a flag in lower case; - a token -- on its own ends the options: every token after it is an argument, even if it starts with -- ; - everything else is an argument, in order. Only unquoted tokens can be options or flags: "--x" in quotes is an argument.
