title: A budget tracker
body: Build the application from lesson 6.05: a budget tracker that reads commands, one per line, until quit or the end of the input. Split it into files: Program.cs (the command loop), Ledger.cs (the domain), Reports.cs and Storage.cs . add 2026-03-01 2500 salary March pay add 2026-03-02 -100 rent Storage unit add 2026-03-03 -12.50 food Lunch with Ada add 2026-03-09 -199.90 food Groceries budget food 200 report 2026-03 quit prints Added 1: 2026-03-01 salary 2500.00 March pay Added 2: 2026-03-02 rent -100.00 Storage unit Added 3: 2026-03-03 food -12.50 Lunch with Ada Added 4: 2026-03-09 food -199.90 Groceries Budget for food: 200.00 Report for 2026-03 Income: 2500.00 Expenses: 312.40 Net: 2187.60 By category: food 212.40 of 200.00 OVER rent 100.00 Bye. Commands (the command word ignores case; blank lines are ignored; amounts use . and are printed with 2 decimals): Command Does Errors --- --- --- add <date <amount <category <description Adds a transaction; positive amounts are income, negative are expenses. The category is stored in lower case; the description is the rest of the line, words joined by single spaces. Prints Added <id : <date <category <amount <description . Ids count from 1. Fewer than 4 arguments: Usage: add <date <amount <category <description . A date not in yyyy-MM-dd form or not a real date: Bad date: <text . An amount that is not a number, is 0, or has more than 2 decimals: Bad amount: <text . budget <category <amount Sets a monthly budget: Budget for <category : <amount Not exactly 2 arguments: Usage: budget <category <amount . Amount not above 0: Bad amount: <text list or list <yyyy-MM Every transaction (or those in that month), by date then id, as <id <date <category padded to 10 <amount right-aligned in 9 <description ; or No transactions. Bad month: <text report <yyyy-MM Report for <month , then Income: , Expenses: and Net: lines (label left in 9 characters, amount right in 10; expenses shown positive), then, if there are expenses, By category: and a line per category: two spaces, the category in 10, the amount spent right in 8, then of <budget if it has one and OVER if the spending is above it. Categories by spending (most first), then name. A month with no transactions prints No transactions. after the title. Usage: report <month , Bad month: <text undo Removes the most recently added transaction still present: Removed <id , or Nothing to undo. save <file Writes everything as JSON: Saved <n transactions to <file Usage: save <file load <file Replaces everything with the file's contents: Loaded <n transactions from <file . New ids continue after the highest loaded id; undo starts empty. Usage: load <file ; a missing or invalid file: Could not load <file (nothing changes) quit Stops. Bye. is printed when the program ends, whether by quit or the end of the input. Anything else: Unknown command: <word

title: 7.01  Operators, Indexers and Conversions
body: Making your own types feel built in - overloading arithmetic and comparison operators, equality done right, indexers with this ... , Index and Range support, implicit and explicit conversion operators, and when not to overload. Operators on your own types A type for money, vectors or fractions reads best when a + b works on it. An operator is a public static method named operator plus the symbol: csharp var a = new Vec2(1, 2); var b = new Vec2(3, 4); Console.WriteLine(a + b); // Vec2 { X = 4, Y = 6 } Console.WriteLine(a 3); // Vec2 { X = 3, Y = 6 } Console.WriteLine(-a); // Vec2 { X = -1, Y = -2 } public readonly record struct Vec2(double X, double Y) { public static Vec2 operator +(Vec2 l, Vec2 r) = new(l.X + r.X, l.Y + r.Y); public static Vec2 operator -(Vec2 l, Vec2 r) = new(l.X - r.X, l.Y - r.Y); public static Vec2 operator (Vec2 v, double s) = new(v.X s, v.Y s); public static Vec2 operator (double s, Vec2 v) = v s; public static Vec2 operator -(Vec2 v) = new(-v.X, -v.Y); } Defining + also makes += work. Operators come in required pairs: == with != , < with , <= with = . Equality and comparison A record (lesson 3.02) already writes == , != , Equals and GetHashCode from its fields. For a class you write yourself, implement IEquatable<T and keep all four consistent: csharp var x = new Version2(1, 4); var y = new Version2(1, 10); Console.WriteLine($"{x < y} {x == new Version2(1, 4)} {x.CompareTo(y)}"); public sealed class Version2 : IEquatable<Version2 , IComparable<Version2 { public int Major { get; } public int Minor { get; } public Version2(int major, int minor) = (Major, Minor) = (major, minor); public int CompareTo(Version2? other) = other is null ? 1 : (Major, Minor).CompareTo((other.Major, other.Minor)); public bool Equals(Version2? other) = other is not null && Major == other.Major && Minor == other.Minor; public override bool Equals(object? obj) = Equals(obj as Version2); public override int GetHashCode() = HashCode.Combine(Major, Minor); public static bool operator ==(Version2? l, Version2? r) = l is null ? r is null : l.Equals(r); public static bool operator !=(Version2? l, Version2? r) = !(l == r); public static bool operator <(Version2 l, Version2 r) = l.CompareTo(r) < 0; public static bool operator (Version2 l, Version2 r) = l.CompareTo(r) 0; public static bool operator <=(Version2 l, Version2 r) = l.CompareTo(r) <= 0; public static bool operator =(Version2 l, Version2 r) = l.CompareTo(r) = 0; } Comparing tuples, (Major, Minor).CompareTo(...) , compares field by field, which saves writing the chain by hand. Equal objects must have equal hash codes, or dictionaries and sets lose them. Indexers An indexer lets an object be used with square brackets, like an array or dictionary. It is a property named this with parameters: csharp var grid = new Grid(3, 2); grid 1, 0 = 'X'; Console.WriteLine(grid 1, 0 ); Console.WriteLine(grid); public class Grid(int width, int height) { private readonly char _cells = Enumerable.Repeat('.', width height).ToArray(); public char this int x, int y { get = _cells Index(x, y) ; set = _cells Index(x, y) = value; } private int Index(int x, int y) = x < 0 x = width y < 0 y = height ? throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException($"({x}, {y}) is outside the grid") : y width + x; public override string ToString() = string.Join("\n", Enumerable.Range(0, height).Select(y = new string(_cells, y width, width))); } public class Grid(int width, int height) is a primary constructor (C 12): the parameters are available in the whole class body. Index and Range items ^1 (the last item) and items 1..3 (a slice) work on your type if it has an indexer taking int , a Count or Length , and (for ranges) a Slice(start, length) method. The compiler translates ^1 and 1..3 into those calls. Conversion operators implicit conversions happen automatically and must never lose information or throw. explicit ones need a cast and may do either: csharp Celsius c = 25.0; // implicit: double to Celsius double raw = c; // implicit back var f = (Fahrenheit)c; // explicit: a deliberate change of scale Console.WriteLine($"{raw} {f.Value}"); public readonly record struct Celsius(double Value) { public static implicit operator Celsius(double value) = new(value); public static implicit operator double(Celsius c) = c.Value; public static explicit operator Fahrenheit(Celsius c) = new(c.Value 9 / 5 + 32); } public readonly record struct Fahrenheit(double Value); When not to Overload an operator only when its meaning is obvious to every reader: + on vectors and money, < on versions and dates. If you have to explain what means for your type, a named method ( Scale , Merge ) is clearer. Check yourself quiz ? If you define operator == , what else must you write? - Nothing: the compiler generates != from == - Only GetHashCode , so the type works as a dictionary key - operator < and operator , so the values can be sorted + operator != , and overrides of Equals and GetHashCode that agree with it C requires == and != to be defined in pairs. Equals and GetHashCode should give the same answers too, or collections and == will disagree. ? Why should an implicit conversion never throw? + It happens with no visible code at the call site, so a failure would be a surprise nobody can see coming - The compiler does not allow throw inside a conversion operator - Implicit conversions run at compile time, so they cannot fail at run time Nothing at the call site shows that a conversion runs. If it can fail or lose information, make it explicit so the caller has to write a cast. ? What does public char this int x, int y declare? - a method named this + an indexer used as grid x, y - a constructor - a two-dimensional array field An indexer is a property with parameters, reached with square brackets.

title: 7.02  Collections in Depth
body: Choosing the right collection - Stack, Queue and PriorityQueue, LinkedList, SortedDictionary and SortedSet, read-only views, immutable and frozen collections, concurrent collections for threads, and what each operation costs. Beyond List and Dictionary List<T , Dictionary<K, V and HashSet<T (lessons 2.02 and 2.03) cover most needs. The others exist because some jobs are much faster or clearer with them. Stack and Queue A stack is last in, first out (undo history, matching brackets); a queue is first in, first out (work waiting its turn): csharp var undo = new Stack<string (); undo.Push("type a"); undo.Push("type b"); Console.WriteLine(undo.Pop()); // type b Console.WriteLine(undo.Peek()); // type a (still there) var waiting = new Queue<string (); waiting.Enqueue("first"); waiting.Enqueue("second"); Console.WriteLine(waiting.Dequeue()); // first Console.WriteLine(waiting.TryDequeue(out var next) ? next : "empty"); PriorityQueue PriorityQueue<TElement, TPriority always hands out the element with the smallest priority next. It is the heart of Dijkstra's algorithm, schedulers and "the top N" problems: csharp var tasks = new PriorityQueue<string, int (); tasks.Enqueue("write report", 2); tasks.Enqueue("fix outage", 0); tasks.Enqueue("lunch", 5); while (tasks.TryDequeue(out var task, out int priority)) Console.WriteLine($"{priority}: {task}"); Elements with equal priority come out in no guaranteed order. For "largest first", pass a comparer: new PriorityQueue<string, int (Comparer<int .Create((a, b) = b.CompareTo(a))) . LinkedList LinkedList<T is a doubly linked list: inserting or removing next to a node you already hold is instant, but finding the n-th item means walking. It suits "move this to the front" structures such as an LRU cache: csharp var recent = new LinkedList<string ( "a", "b", "c" ); var node = recent.Find("c")!; recent.Remove(node); recent.AddFirst(node); Console.WriteLine(string.Join(",", recent)); // c,a,b Sorted collections SortedDictionary<K, V and SortedSet<T keep their contents in key order at all times (they are balanced trees), so iterating them is always sorted, and SortedSet can answer range questions: csharp var scores = new SortedDictionary<string, int { "zoe" = 3, "ada" = 9, "max" = 5 }; Console.WriteLine(string.Join(" ", scores.Keys)); // ada max zoe var times = new SortedSet<int { 30, 5, 90, 45, 12 }; Console.WriteLine(string.Join(" ", times.GetViewBetween(10, 50))); // 12 30 45 Console.WriteLine($"{times.Min} {times.Max}"); What things cost Collection Add Find by key or value Remove Notes --- --- --- --- --- List<T O(1) at end O(n) O(n) index O(1) Dictionary , HashSet O(1) O(1) O(1) no order SortedDictionary , SortedSet O(log n) O(log n) O(log n) always sorted Stack , Queue O(1) — O(1) at the ends PriorityQueue O(log n) — O(log n) smallest LinkedList O(1) next to a node O(n) O(1) given the node Read-only, immutable and frozen - Read-only views ( list.AsReadOnly() , returning IReadOnlyList<T ) stop callers changing your collection through that reference, but you can still change it. - Immutable collections ( System.Collections.Immutable : ImmutableList , ImmutableDictionary ) never change; "adding" returns a new collection that shares most of the old one. Safe to share between threads without locks. - Frozen collections ( FrozenDictionary , FrozenSet , .NET 8) are built once and then optimised for very fast lookups: ideal for tables loaded at start-up. csharp using System.Collections.Frozen; using System.Collections.Immutable; var v1 = ImmutableList.Create(1, 2, 3); var v2 = v1.Add(4); Console.WriteLine($"{v1.Count} {v2.Count}"); // 3 4 var codes = new Dictionary<string, int { "en" = 1, "de" = 2 }.ToFrozenDictionary(); Console.WriteLine(codes "de" ); Collections for threads Ordinary collections are not safe when several threads change them at once. System.Collections.Concurrent has versions that are: ConcurrentDictionary (with AddOrUpdate and GetOrAdd ), ConcurrentQueue , ConcurrentBag , and BlockingCollection for producers and consumers (lesson 7.06 shows the modern Channel ). Check yourself quiz ? Which collection hands out the item with the smallest priority next? - SortedList<TKey, TValue - Queue<T + PriorityQueue<TElement, TPriority - Stack<T PriorityQueue dequeues the element with the lowest priority first. Queue is first in, first out, and Stack is last in, first out. ? What is the difference between a read-only view and an immutable collection? - None: neither can ever change + A read-only view only blocks changes through that reference; an immutable collection can never change - A read-only view can never change; an immutable one can still be changed by its owner A ReadOnlyCollection wraps a list that its owner can still change, and the view shows those changes. An immutable collection has no way to change at all. ? You need to iterate keys in sorted order while adding and removing often. Which fits? - List<T - Dictionary<K, V + SortedDictionary<K, V - Queue<T A SortedDictionary keeps its keys in order after every change, at O(log n) per operation.

title: An LRU cache
body: Write public class LruCache<TKey, TValue where TKey : notnull that keeps at most capacity entries and drops the least recently used one when full. Every operation is O(1): combine a Dictionary<TKey, LinkedListNode<(TKey Key, TValue Value) with a LinkedList<(TKey Key, TValue Value) whose front is the most recently used entry. - new LruCache<K, V (capacity) ; a capacity below 1 throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException . - bool TryGet(TKey key, out TValue value) : on a hit, the entry becomes the most recently used. - void Set(TKey key, TValue value) : adds or replaces, and makes the entry the most recently used; when a new key would pass the capacity, the least recently used entry is removed first. - int Count and IEnumerable<TKey KeysByRecency (most recent first).

title: 7.03  Reflection and Attributes
body: Programs that look at themselves - Type objects, reading properties and methods with reflection, creating objects and calling methods by name, attributes as labels on code, writing and reading your own attributes, and why source generators replace much of this today. Types are data too Every object knows its type, and a Type object describes it: name, properties, methods, attributes. Inspecting and using that at run time is reflection . Serializers, test frameworks, dependency injection and object mappers are built on it. csharp var book = new Book("Dune", 1965); Type type = book.GetType(); // or typeof(Book) when you have no object Console.WriteLine($"{type.Name} in {type.Namespace ?? "(no namespace)"}"); foreach (var p in type.GetProperties()) Console.WriteLine($" {p.Name}: {p.PropertyType.Name} = {p.GetValue(book)}"); public record Book(string Title, int Year); Members by name csharp using System.Reflection; var counter = new Counter(); Type t = typeof(Counter); MethodInfo add = t.GetMethod("Add")!; add.Invoke(counter, 5 ); // like counter.Add(5) PropertyInfo total = t.GetProperty("Total")!; Console.WriteLine(total.GetValue(counter)); // 5 FieldInfo secret = t.GetField("_calls", BindingFlags.NonPublic BindingFlags.Instance)!; Console.WriteLine(secret.GetValue(counter)); // 1: private members are reachable too object made = Activator.CreateInstance(t)!; // new Counter() without naming it Console.WriteLine(made.GetType().Name); public class Counter { private int _calls; public int Total { get; private set; } public void Add(int n) { Total += n; _calls++; } } Reflection is slow compared with normal calls and the compiler cannot check names written as strings, so a typo is only found when the code runs. Use nameof(Counter.Add) instead of "Add" where you can. Attributes An attribute is a label attached to code in square brackets. It does nothing by itself; code that reads it (the compiler, a framework, your own reflection) decides what it means. You have already met several: Attribute Read by Effect --- --- --- Obsolete("use X") the compiler a warning wherever it is used JsonPropertyName("id") System.Text.Json (lesson 5.04) the JSON name of a property Fact , Theory xUnit (lesson 6.02) marks a test Flags Enum.ToString prints combined flags as "Read, Write" Your own attribute An attribute is a class that derives from Attribute . AttributeUsage says what it can be put on: csharp using System.Reflection; foreach (var p in typeof(SignUp).GetProperties()) { var max = p.GetCustomAttribute<MaxLengthAttribute (); if (max is not null) Console.WriteLine($"{p.Name}: at most {max.Length} characters"); } AttributeUsage(AttributeTargets.Property) public sealed class MaxLengthAttribute(int length) : Attribute { public int Length { get; } = length; } public class SignUp { MaxLength(20) public string Name { get; set; } = ""; MaxLength(80) public string Email { get; set; } = ""; public int Age { get; set; } } The name MaxLengthAttribute can be written MaxLength(...) : the Attribute ending is optional where it is used. Generic code and reflection together A validator that works for any class, driven by attributes: csharp using System.Reflection; static List<string Validate(object obj) { var problems = new List<string (); foreach (var p in obj.GetType().GetProperties()) { if (p.GetCustomAttribute<RequiredAttribute () is not null && p.GetValue(obj) is null or "") problems.Add($"{p.Name} is required"); } return problems; } Console.WriteLine(string.Join("; ", Validate(new Contact { Name = "" }))); AttributeUsage(AttributeTargets.Property) public sealed class RequiredAttribute : Attribute; public class Contact { Required public string? Name { get; set; } Required public string? Phone { get; set; } } Source generators Reflection decides at run time; a source generator reads your code (and its attributes) at compile time and writes extra C for you. The result is as fast as hand-written code, works where reflection is restricted (trimmed and native AOT apps), and errors appear while compiling. System.Text.Json , logging ( LoggerMessage ) and regular expressions ( GeneratedRegex , lesson 7.05) all offer generated versions. When a library offers both, prefer the generated one. Check yourself quiz ? Does an attribute do anything on its own? - Yes: it changes how the method it is placed on runs - Yes: the runtime checks its values when the program starts + No: it is data that some code must read and act on An attribute is only metadata stored with the code. It has an effect only when the compiler, a framework or reflection code looks for it. ? Why prefer nameof(Counter.Add) to "Add" in reflection code? - nameof is faster at run time than a string literal + The compiler checks nameof , so a rename updates it or causes a compile error - Reflection methods do not accept string literals nameof becomes the same constant string at compile time, so it is not faster. The gain is that a typo or rename is caught by the compiler instead of failing at run time. ? Which call creates an object of a Type t without naming its class in code? - new t() - t.Create() - typeof(t) + Activator.CreateInstance(t) Activator.CreateInstance calls the type's parameterless constructor at run time.

title: 7.04  Span, Memory and Performance
body: Writing fast C without unsafe code - value types and the stack, Span<T and ReadOnlySpan<T as views over arrays and strings, slicing without copying, stackalloc, ArrayPool for reusing buffers, ref struct rules, and measuring before optimising. Where allocations come from Every new of a class, every string operation that produces a new string, every ToArray() and Substring() puts an object on the heap , and the garbage collector must later clean it up. In most code that cost is invisible. In code that runs millions of times (parsers, games, servers) it adds up. Modern C gives tools to do the same work without allocating. Span<T : a view, not a copy A Span<T is a window onto a run of elements that already exist: part of an array, a block on the stack, or memory owned by someone else. Slicing a span makes a new window, not a copy: csharp int numbers = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 ; Span<int middle = numbers.AsSpan(1, 4); // 2, 3, 4, 5: no new array middle 0 = 20; // writes into numbers Console.WriteLine(string.Join(",", numbers)); // 1,20,3,4,5,6 Console.WriteLine(middle ^1 ); // 5 Console.WriteLine(middle.Slice(1, 2).Length); // 2 ReadOnlySpan<T is the read-only version; a string gives one with AsSpan() . Parsing without Substring csharp static int SumFields(ReadOnlySpan<char line) { int total = 0; while (true) { int comma = line.IndexOf(','); ReadOnlySpan<char field = comma < 0 ? line : line ..comma ; total += int.Parse(field); // int.Parse accepts a span: no string made if (comma < 0) return total; line = line (comma + 1).. ; } } Console.WriteLine(SumFields("10,20,30,40")); // 100 Split(',') would allocate an array and four strings; this allocates nothing. int.Parse , double.TryParse , string.Concat , StringBuilder.Append , Stream.Read and many more have span overloads. stackalloc A small temporary buffer can live on the stack, freed automatically when the method returns: csharp static string Reverse(string text) { Span<char buffer = text.Length <= 256 ? stackalloc char text.Length : new char text.Length ; text.AsSpan().CopyTo(buffer); buffer.Reverse(); return new string(buffer); } Console.WriteLine(Reverse("stressed")); // desserts Keep stack buffers small (a few hundred bytes to a few KB): the stack is about 1 MB in total. The rules of ref struct Span<T is a ref struct : it may point into the stack, so the compiler makes sure it never outlives what it points at. It cannot be a field of a class, be boxed, be captured by a lambda, or cross an await . When you need a span-like thing that can be stored or used in async code, use Memory<T / ReadOnlyMemory<T and call .Span at the moment you work on it. Reusing buffers: ArrayPool For large buffers, rent from a pool instead of allocating a new array each time: csharp using System.Buffers; byte buffer = ArrayPool<byte .Shared.Rent(64 1024); // may be larger than asked try { Console.WriteLine(buffer.Length = 64 1024); // ... read a file or socket into buffer ... } finally { ArrayPool<byte .Shared.Return(buffer); } Structs and in parameters Small value types (a readonly record struct Vec2 ) live inline in arrays and locals with no allocation. Passing a large struct copies it; in passes it by reference without allowing changes: static double Length(in Matrix4 m) . Measure first Most code does not need any of this. Write it clearly, measure with a profiler or BenchmarkDotNet ( MemoryDiagnoser shows allocations per call), and only then optimise the hot spot you found. Stopwatch is fine for a first look: csharp using System.Diagnostics; var watch = Stopwatch.StartNew(); long sum = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 10_000_000; i++) sum += i; Console.WriteLine($"{sum} in {watch.ElapsedMilliseconds} ms"); Check yourself quiz ? Does numbers.AsSpan(1, 4) copy the elements? - Yes: it copies four elements into a new array - Only when you write to it, like copy-on-write + No: it is a view over the same array A span is a pointer and a length over existing memory. Nothing is copied, so span 0 = 9 changes numbers 1 . ? Why can a Span<T not be a field of a class? + It may point into a stack frame that the object outlives - It is too large to be stored as a field of a class - Fields of a class cannot have generic types Span<T is a ref struct , allowed only on the stack, so it can never dangle. Store a Memory<T in a field instead. ? Which avoids creating new strings while splitting "a,b,c"? - line.Split(',') - line.Substring(0, 1) + slicing line.AsSpan() at each comma - string.Join Spans view the original characters; Split and Substring create new strings.

A missing column throws FormatException .

title: 7.05  Regular Expressions and Text
body: Finding and transforming text - the Regex class, patterns, groups and named groups, Matches and Replace with a MatchEvaluator, options, timeouts, GeneratedRegex for speed, and culture-aware comparison, formatting and normalisation of strings. The Regex class A regular expression describes a shape of text (the pattern language is the same in most languages). System.Text.RegularExpressions.Regex checks, finds and replaces: csharp using System.Text.RegularExpressions; Console.WriteLine(Regex.IsMatch("due 2026-11-20", @"\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}")); // True Match m = Regex.Match("Order 4512 shipped", @" (\d+)\s+(\w+)"); Console.WriteLine($"{m.Success} {m.Groups 1 .Value} {m.Groups 2 .Value}"); // True 4512 shipped Write patterns as verbatim strings ( @"..." ) so backslashes need no doubling. Pattern reminder Pattern Matches --- --- \d \w \s digit, word character, whitespace a-z ^, a character in a range, not a comma + ? {2,5} repeats; add ? to make them lazy ^ $ \b start, end, word boundary (...) (?<name ...) (?:...) group, named group, group without capturing a\ b either Named groups and every match csharp using System.Text.RegularExpressions; var line = "x=1, y=22, z=333"; foreach (Match m in Regex.Matches(line, @"(?<key \w)=(?<value \d+)")) Console.WriteLine($"{m.Groups "key" .Value} - {int.Parse(m.Groups "value" .Value)} at {m.Index}"); Replacing Regex.Replace takes a replacement string (with $1 or ${name} ) or a MatchEvaluator , a function that builds each replacement: csharp using System.Text.RegularExpressions; Console.WriteLine(Regex.Replace("2026-11-20", @"(\d+)-(\d+)-(\d+)", "$3/$2/$1")); // 20/11/2026 Console.WriteLine(Regex.Replace("make it loud", @"\b\w", m = m.Value.ToUpper())); // Make It Loud Console.WriteLine(string.Join(" ", Regex.Split("a, b;c ,d", @"\s ,; \s "))); // a b c d Options and timeouts RegexOptions.IgnoreCase , Multiline ( ^ and $ per line), Singleline ( . matches new lines) and IgnorePatternWhitespace (spaces and comments in the pattern for readability). A badly written pattern on hostile input can take a very long time ( catastrophic backtracking ), so give patterns that run on user input a timeout: csharp using System.Text.RegularExpressions; var safe = new Regex(@"^(\w+\s?)+$", RegexOptions.None, TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(100)); try { Console.WriteLine(safe.IsMatch(new string('a', 30) + "!")); } catch (RegexMatchTimeoutException) { Console.WriteLine("gave up"); } RegexOptions.NonBacktracking (.NET 7) guarantees linear time for patterns that do not need backtracking features. GeneratedRegex A pattern used often should be built once: keep it in a static readonly Regex field, created with RegexOptions.Compiled for speed. In a normal .NET project the best way is a source-generated regex (lesson 7.03): the compiler writes the matching code at build time, so there is no start-up cost at all. (Xenon compiles without source generators, so this example is for your own projects.) csharp-norun using System.Text.RegularExpressions; Console.WriteLine(Patterns.Email().IsMatch("ada@example.com")); static partial class Patterns { GeneratedRegex(@"^ ^@\s +@ ^@\s +\. a-z {2,}$", RegexOptions.IgnoreCase) public static partial Regex Email(); } Comparing text correctly Text comparison has more traps than it looks: csharp using System.Globalization; using System.Text; Console.WriteLine(string.Equals("FILE", "file", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)); // True Console.WriteLine("straße".Equals("STRASSE", StringComparison.InvariantCultureIgnoreCase)); var turkish = new CultureInfo("tr-TR"); Console.WriteLine("title".ToUpper(turkish)); // TİTLE: dotted capital İ in Turkish Console.WriteLine("title".ToUpperInvariant()); // TITLE string composed = "é"; // one character string decomposed = "é"; // e + combining accent Console.WriteLine(composed == decomposed); // False Console.WriteLine(composed.Normalize() == decomposed.Normalize()); // True Rules of thumb: use StringComparison.Ordinal or OrdinalIgnoreCase for identifiers, file names, keys and protocols; use a culture-aware comparison only for text shown to people and sorted for them; Normalize() text from different sources before comparing it. Check yourself quiz ? Why write regex patterns as @"..." strings? - Regex only accepts verbatim strings as patterns + A backslash stays a backslash, so \d needs no doubling - The @ makes the pattern compile once and run faster - The @ turns on case-insensitive matching Regex patterns are full of backslashes. In a normal string \d would have to be written \\d ; @"..." keeps them as written. It changes nothing about how the regex runs. ? Why is ToUpper() without a culture risky for identifiers? - It only changes ASCII letters and leaves the rest + It uses the current culture, and some (Turkish, for example) change letters differently - It throws on computers whose language has no capital letters In Turkish, "i".ToUpper() gives "İ", so the same code gives different results on different computers. Use ToUpperInvariant() or an ordinal comparison. ? Which is right for comparing two file extensions ignoring case? - StringComparison.CurrentCulture - == - string.Compare with the Turkish culture + StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase Extensions are identifiers, not text for people: compare them ordinally, ignoring case.

title: 7.06  Async Streams and Channels
body: Data that arrives over time - IAsyncEnumerable with yield return and await foreach, cancellation with EnumeratorCancellation , System.Threading.Channels for producers and consumers, bounded channels and back-pressure, and pipelines of async stages. Results one at a time, asynchronously Task<List<T waits for all the results before returning any. When results arrive over time (pages of an API, lines of a big file, sensor readings), an async stream , IAsyncEnumerable<T , hands each one over as soon as it exists. You write it with async plus yield return , and consume it with await foreach : csharp await foreach (int reading in Readings(5)) Console.WriteLine($"reading {reading}"); static async IAsyncEnumerable<int Readings(int count) { for (int i = 1; i <= count; i++) { await Task.Delay(20); // stands in for waiting on a device or the network yield return i 10; } } The consumer starts working on the first item while later ones are still on their way. Cancellation An async stream takes a CancellationToken through a parameter marked EnumeratorCancellation , so WithCancellation(token) on the consumer side reaches it: csharp using System.Runtime.CompilerServices; using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(120)); try { await foreach (int n in Ticks().WithCancellation(cts.Token)) Console.WriteLine($"tick {n}"); } catch (OperationCanceledException) { Console.WriteLine("stopped"); } static async IAsyncEnumerable<int Ticks( EnumeratorCancellation CancellationToken token = default) { for (int i = 0; ; i++) { await Task.Delay(50, token); yield return i; } } LINQ for async streams ( Where , Select , ToListAsync ...) is in the System.Linq.Async package, and is built into .NET 10. Channels: a queue between async code System.Threading.Channels.Channel<T is a thread-safe queue made for async : producers await writing, consumers await reading, and nobody blocks a thread while waiting. It is the modern replacement for BlockingCollection . csharp using System.Threading.Channels; var channel = Channel.CreateUnbounded<string (); var producer = Task.Run(async () = { foreach (var job in new { "resize", "upload", "notify" }) { await channel.Writer.WriteAsync(job); await Task.Delay(10); } channel.Writer.Complete(); // no more items: readers finish }); await foreach (var job in channel.Reader.ReadAllAsync()) Console.WriteLine($"doing {job}"); await producer; ReadAllAsync() ends when the writer has called Complete() and the channel is empty. Bounded channels and back-pressure An unbounded channel grows without limit if producers are faster than consumers. A bounded channel holds at most N items; a producer writing to a full channel waits until there is room. That waiting is back-pressure : it slows the fast side down to the speed of the slow side instead of filling memory. csharp using System.Threading.Channels; var bounded = Channel.CreateBounded<int (new BoundedChannelOptions(2) { FullMode = BoundedChannelFullMode.Wait, // or DropOldest, DropNewest, DropWrite SingleReader = true, }); await bounded.Writer.WriteAsync(1); await bounded.Writer.WriteAsync(2); Console.WriteLine(bounded.Writer.TryWrite(3)); // False: full Console.WriteLine(await bounded.Reader.ReadAsync()); Console.WriteLine(bounded.Writer.TryWrite(3)); // True: there was room again Several consumers Several consumers can read from the same channel; each item goes to exactly one of them. Start them with Task.WhenAll : csharp using System.Threading.Channels; var work = Channel.CreateBounded<int (10); var results = new System.Collections.Concurrent.ConcurrentBag<int (); async Task Consumer() { await foreach (int n in work.Reader.ReadAllAsync()) results.Add(n n); } var consumers = Enumerable.Range(0, 3).Select(_ = Consumer()).ToArray(); for (int i = 1; i <= 10; i++) await work.Writer.WriteAsync(i); work.Writer.Complete(); await Task.WhenAll(consumers); Console.WriteLine(results.Sum()); // 385 Chaining channels gives a pipeline : stage 1 reads files into channel A, stage 2 parses from A into B, stage 3 saves from B, each stage running at its own pace. Check yourself quiz ? When is an IAsyncEnumerable<T better than a Task<List<T ? + When results arrive over time and can be handled one by one - When there are few results and you want them all together - When the results must be sorted before they are used - Never: it is an older way to write the same thing With await foreach , the consumer can start on the first item as soon as it arrives. A Task<List<T makes the caller wait until every item is ready. ? What does a bounded channel do when it is full and its mode is Wait ? - It drops the new item - It drops the oldest item to make room + The writer's WriteAsync waits until a reader makes room - WriteAsync throws an exception Waiting is back-pressure: a fast writer is slowed to the reader's pace. Dropping items is what the DropNewest , DropOldest and DropWrite modes do. ? How does a consumer's await foreach over channel.Reader.ReadAllAsync() know to stop? - After it has read a fixed number of items + When the writer calls Complete() and the channel is empty - As soon as the channel's buffer is full - It never stops, so the consumer must break out Complete() marks the end of the data; ReadAllAsync finishes once the remaining items are read.

body: Build the core of a small command console: methods marked with an attribute become commands, found by reflection, with their arguments parsed from text and help generated automatically. csharp public class Tools { Command("add", "Adds two whole numbers") public int Add(int a, int b) = a + b; Command("greet", "Says hello") public string Greet(string name, bool shout = false) = shout ? $"HELLO {name.ToUpper()}!" : $"hello {name}"; } var console = new CommandConsole(new Tools()); console.Run("add 2 40"); // "42" console.Run("greet Ada"); // "hello Ada" console.Run("greet Ada true"); // "HELLO ADA!" console.Run("help"); // add a b: Adds two whole numbers // greet name shout : Says hello Write: - AttributeUsage(AttributeTargets.Method) public sealed class CommandAttribute(string name, string description) : Attribute with Name and Description properties. - public class CommandConsole taking any object in its constructor. It finds the object's public instance methods that have Command . Two commands with the same name throw InvalidOperationException from the constructor. - string Run(string line) : - The line is split on whitespace; the first word is the command name. A blank line returns "" . - help lists every command sorted by name as "<name <params : <description " , joined with "\n" . Parameters with default values are shown in square brackets. - The remaining words are converted to the parameter types ( int , double , bool , string ) with Convert.ChangeType(word, type, CultureInfo.InvariantCulture) . Missing words use the parameter's default value. - The result is the method's return value as text ( "" for a void method). - Errors are returned as text, never thrown: "unknown command: <name " , "usage: <name <params " for too few or too many words, and "bad value for <param : <word " when a conversion fails.

title: 8.01  LINQ in Depth
body: The rest of LINQ - query syntax and how it maps to methods, joining two sequences with Join and GroupJoin, flattening with SelectMany, Aggregate, Zip, Chunk and the By methods, ToLookup, set operations, and the deferred execution rules that decide when a query actually runs. Beyond Where and Select Lesson 2.04 introduced LINQ's everyday methods. This lesson covers the ones that combine several sequences, summarise them in custom ways, and the rule that surprises everyone: when a query runs. The examples use these records: csharp-norun record Customer(int Id, string Name, string City); record Order(int Id, int CustomerId, decimal Total); Query syntax C has a second way to write queries that reads like SQL. The compiler turns it into the method calls you already know: csharp var customers = new List<Customer { new(1, "Ada", "London"), new(2, "Bob", "Paris"), new(3, "Cy", "London") }; var londoners = from c in customers where c.City == "London" orderby c.Name descending select c.Name; Console.WriteLine(string.Join(", ", londoners)); // Cy, Ada // the same as: customers.Where(c = c.City == "London").OrderByDescending(c = c.Name).Select(c = c.Name) record Customer(int Id, string Name, string City); Most C code uses the method form. Query syntax shines for joins and let , which names an intermediate value. Joining two sequences Join pairs items from two sequences whose keys match: csharp var customers = new List<Customer { new(1, "Ada", "London"), new(2, "Bob", "Paris"), new(3, "Cy", "London") }; var orders = new List<Order { new(10, 1, 25m), new(11, 2, 40m), new(12, 1, 15m) }; var lines = customers.Join(orders, c = c.Id, o = o.CustomerId, (c, o) = $"{c.Name}: order {o.Id} {o.Total}"); foreach (var line in lines) Console.WriteLine(line); // GroupJoin keeps every customer, with the list of their orders (possibly empty) var totals = customers.GroupJoin(orders, c = c.Id, o = o.CustomerId, (c, os) = new { c.Name, Count = os.Count(), Sum = os.Sum(o = o.Total) }); foreach (var t in totals) Console.WriteLine($"{t.Name}: {t.Count} orders, {t.Sum}"); record Customer(int Id, string Name, string City); record Order(int Id, int CustomerId, decimal Total); Join is an inner join: Cy, who has no orders, does not appear. GroupJoin is the left join: everyone appears, Cy with 0 orders. Flattening with SelectMany SelectMany turns each item into a sequence and joins all those sequences into one: csharp var teams = new Dictionary<string, string { "red" = "Ada", "Bob" , "blue" = "Cy" , }; var everyone = teams.SelectMany(t = t.Value, (t, player) = $"{player} ({t.Key})"); Console.WriteLine(string.Join(", ", everyone)); // Ada (red), Bob (red), Cy (blue) var pairs = from x in new { 1, 2 } from y in new { "a", "b" } select $"{x}{y}"; Console.WriteLine(string.Join(" ", pairs)); // 1a 1b 2a 2b Summaries of your own: Aggregate Sum , Max and friends cover common cases. Aggregate folds a sequence with any function, starting from a seed: csharp var words = new { "tea", "coffee", "milk" }; string longest = words.Aggregate((best, w) = w.Length best.Length ? w : best); string csv = words.Aggregate(new System.Text.StringBuilder(), (sb, w) = sb.Append(sb.Length 0 ? "," : "").Append(w)).ToString(); int product = Enumerable.Range(1, 5).Aggregate(1, (acc, n) = acc n); Console.WriteLine($"{longest} {csv} {product}"); // coffee tea,coffee,milk 120 Zip, Chunk and the By methods csharp var names = new { "Ada", "Bob", "Cy" }; var scores = new { 91, 48, 77 }; foreach (var (name, score) in names.Zip(scores)) Console.Write($"{name}={score} "); Console.WriteLine(); foreach (var chunk in Enumerable.Range(1, 7).Chunk(3)) Console.Write($" {string.Join(",", chunk)} "); Console.WriteLine(); var people = names.Zip(scores, (n, s) = (Name: n, Score: s)).ToList(); Console.WriteLine(people.MaxBy(p = p.Score).Name); // Ada Console.WriteLine(string.Join(",", people.DistinctBy(p = p.Score / 50).Select(p = p.Name))); // Ada,Bob MaxBy , MinBy , DistinctBy , UnionBy , IntersectBy and ExceptBy compare by a key but return whole items. Lookups and sets ToLookup is a GroupBy that runs at once and can be indexed; a missing key gives an empty sequence instead of an exception: csharp var words = new { "apple", "avocado", "banana", "cherry" }; var byLetter = words.ToLookup(w = w 0 ); Console.WriteLine(string.Join(",", byLetter 'a' )); // apple,avocado Console.WriteLine(byLetter 'z' .Count()); // 0 int a = 1, 2, 3, 4 , b = 3, 4, 5 ; Console.WriteLine($"{string.Join(",", a.Union(b))} {string.Join(",", a.Intersect(b))} {string.Join(",", a.Except(b))}"); When does a query run? Most LINQ methods are deferred : they build a description of the work, and nothing happens until something enumerates the result ( foreach , ToList , Count , First ...). Each enumeration runs the whole query again: csharp int evaluated = 0; var numbers = new List<int { 1, 2, 3 }; var doubled = numbers.Select(n = { evaluated++; return n 2; }); Console.WriteLine(evaluated); // 0: nothing has run yet numbers.Add(4); // the query sees this, because it has not run Console.WriteLine(doubled.Sum()); // 20 Console.WriteLine(doubled.Count()); // 4: it ran again Console.WriteLine(evaluated); // 8 var snapshot = doubled.ToList(); // run once and keep the results Console.WriteLine(evaluated); // 12 Rules of thumb: - Call ToList() or ToArray() when you will use the results more than once, or when the source may change. - Methods that return a single value ( Count , Sum , First , Any , ToList , ToDictionary ) run at once. - A query over a database (Entity Framework) is translated into SQL when it runs; deferred execution is what makes that possible. Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference between Join and GroupJoin ? - Join keeps items with no match; GroupJoin leaves them out - GroupJoin is just Join followed by OrderBy - Join works on lists and GroupJoin on dictionaries + Join drops items with no match; GroupJoin keeps them Join gives one result per matching pair, an inner join. GroupJoin gives one result per item of the first sequence with all its matches, possibly none. ? Why might a LINQ query run more slowly than expected inside a loop? + Deferred queries run again every time they are enumerated; ToList() runs them once - LINQ copies the whole source list on every call to Where - Lambdas are compiled again on every round of the loop A query is a recipe, not a result. Enumerating it inside a loop repeats all the work each time unless the results are stored. ? numbers.Where(n = n 2) is assigned to q, then 5 is added to numbers. What does q.Count() count? - only the numbers there before 5 was added + every number above 2, including the 5 - it throws because the list changed - nothing, because Where already ran The query is deferred, so it runs when Count is called and sees the current list.

title: 8.02  Pattern Matching in Depth
body: Every pattern C can match - type, constant and relational patterns, and, or and not, property patterns with nested and extended forms, positional patterns with Deconstruct, list patterns with slices, var patterns, switch expressions that the compiler checks for completeness, and how to keep complex matches readable. Patterns everywhere Lesson 2.05 used is and switch with simple patterns. Patterns are a small language of their own: they appear after is , in switch statements and in switch expressions, and they combine. Type, constant and relational patterns csharp static string Describe(object o) = o switch { null = "nothing", 0 = "zero", int n when n < 0 = "a negative int", int and 100 = "a big int", int = "an int", string { Length: 0 } = "an empty string", string s = $"text of length {s.Length}", _ = o.GetType().Name, }; foreach (var x in new object? { null, 0, -5, 500, 7, "", "hi", 2.5 }) Console.WriteLine(Describe(x!)); - A type pattern ( int , string s ) matches values of that type and can give the value a name. - A constant pattern ( 0 , null , "yes" ) matches one value. - A relational pattern ( 100 , <= 0 ) compares. - and , or and not combine patterns, and brackets group them: = 'a' and <= 'z' or = 'A' and <= 'Z' . - A when clause adds any extra condition. is not null is the clearest null check in modern C . Property patterns { Property: pattern, ... } looks inside an object, and patterns nest: csharp static string Category(Person p) = p switch { { Age: < 18 } = "child", { Home.Country: "UK", Age: = 65 } = "UK pensioner", { Home: { City: "Paris" or "Lyon" } } = "lives in a French city", _ = "other", }; Console.WriteLine(Category(new("Ada", 70, new("Leeds", "UK")))); Console.WriteLine(Category(new("Bob", 30, new("Lyon", "France")))); Console.WriteLine(Category(new("Cy", 12, new("Rome", "Italy")))); record Address(string City, string Country); record Person(string Name, int Age, Address Home); Home.Country: "UK" is the extended form of Home: { Country: "UK" } . Property patterns never match null , so they double as null checks. Positional patterns A type with a Deconstruct method (every positional record has one) can be matched by position: csharp static string Where(Point p) = p switch { (0, 0) = "origin", (0, _) = "on the y axis", (_, 0) = "on the x axis", (var x, var y) when x == y = "on the diagonal", ( 0, 0) = "top right", _ = "somewhere else", }; foreach (var p in new Point { new(0, 0), new(0, 5), new(3, 3), new(2, 7), new(-1, 4) }) Console.WriteLine(Where(p)); record Point(int X, int Y); Tuples work the same way, which makes matching on two values at once neat: csharp static string Rps(string a, string b) = (a, b) switch { var (x, y) when x == y = "draw", ("rock", "scissors") or ("scissors", "paper") or ("paper", "rock") = "first wins", _ = "second wins", }; Console.WriteLine(Rps("rock", "paper")); List patterns Lists and arrays can be matched by their elements, with .. for "any number of elements here": csharp static string Shape(int xs) = xs switch { = "empty", var only = $"one: {only}", var first, .., var last when first == last = "starts and ends the same", 1, 2, .. = "starts with 1, 2", .., < 0 = "ends with a negative", _, _, .. var rest = $"two and then {rest.Length} more", }; foreach (var a in new { new int 0 , 5 , 3, 9, 3 , 1, 2, 8 , 4, 6, -1 , 7, 8, 9, 10 }) Console.WriteLine(Shape(a)); .. var rest captures the middle part as a new array (or a slice for spans and strings). List patterns are perfect for command lines: csharp static string Run(string line) = line.Split(' ', StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries) switch { "help" = "commands: add, list", "add", var item = $"added {item}", "add", var item, var qty when int.TryParse(qty, out var n) = $"added {n} x {item}", "add", .. = "usage: add <item qty ", = "", var cmd, .. = $"unknown command {cmd}", }; foreach (var l in new { "help", "add tea", "add tea 3", "add", "fly away" }) Console.WriteLine(Run(l)); The compiler checks switch expressions A switch expression must cover every possible input. If it does not, the compiler warns, and at run time an unmatched value throws SwitchExpressionException . For enums and sealed hierarchies, listing every case without _ means adding a new case later gives a warning everywhere it is not handled yet. csharp static int Seconds(Light l) = l switch { Light.Red = 30, Light.Amber = 5, Light.Green = 25, _ = throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(l)), // enums can hold other numbers too }; Console.WriteLine(Seconds(Light.Amber)); enum Light { Red, Amber, Green } Keeping it readable - Order arms from most specific to most general; the compiler reports an arm that can never be reached. - When a pattern gets long, move part of it into a well-named property or method ( p.IsAdult ). - Prefer a switch expression that returns a value over if / else chains that assign a variable. Check yourself quiz ? What does _, .., 0 match? - A list of exactly three elements whose last is 0 + A list of at least two elements whose last element is 0 - A list of at least one element that contains a 0 somewhere - A list whose elements after the first are all 0 _ needs one element, .. matches zero or more, and 0 must be the last element. So the shortest match is two elements. ? Why is { } a useful pattern? - It matches only an object with no properties set - It matches any value at all, including null + It matches any value that is not null An empty property pattern has no conditions except that the value is not null, so if (x is { } value) checks for null and names the value. var is the pattern that also matches null. ? Which pattern matches a char that is a letter from a to z? - 'a'..'z' + = 'a' and <= 'z' - in 'a' to 'z' - between 'a' and 'z' Relational patterns combined with and express a range.

title: Shipping rules with patterns
body: Shipping cost depends on the parcel and where it goes. The records are defined for you. title: 8.03  Generic Math and Static Abstract Members
match: 8.03 Generic Math and Static Abstract Members
body: Writing one method that works for every number type - why generics could not do arithmetic before, the INumber<T family of interfaces, T.Zero, T.One and T.CreateChecked, static abstract and static virtual interface members, defining operators in your own generic interfaces, and when generic math is worth it. The old problem Before C 11, this did not compile: csharp-norun static T Sum<T (IEnumerable<T values) { T total = 0; // error: cannot convert 0 to T foreach (var v in values) total += v; // error: + is not defined for T return total; } Generics could call instance methods of an interface, but numbers are added with static operators, and interfaces had no way to require those. So libraries wrote the same method once for int , once for double , once for decimal ... INumber<T .NET 7 added interfaces for every ability numbers have, in System.Numerics . INumber<T gathers the common ones, and every built-in number type implements it: csharp using System.Numerics; static T Sum<T (IEnumerable<T values) where T : INumber<T { T total = T.Zero; foreach (var v in values) total += v; return total; } static T Average<T (IReadOnlyCollection<T values) where T : INumber<T = Sum(values) / T.CreateChecked(values.Count); Console.WriteLine(Sum(new { 1, 2, 3 })); Console.WriteLine(Sum(new { 1.5, 2.25 })); Console.WriteLine(Average(new { 1m, 2m, 4m })); Console.WriteLine(Average(new { 1, 2, 4 })); // 2: int division - T.Zero and T.One are the type's 0 and 1. - T.CreateChecked(x) converts any number to T , throwing OverflowException if it does not fit; CreateSaturating clamps and CreateTruncating wraps instead. - Operators such as + , / and < come from interfaces like IAdditionOperators that INumber<T includes. Smaller interfaces let you ask for exactly what you need: IAdditionOperators<T, T, T , IComparisonOperators<T, T, bool , IFloatingPoint<T (adds Floor , Round ), IBinaryInteger<T (adds bit operations and PopCount ). csharp using System.Numerics; static T Clamp<T (T value, T min, T max) where T : INumber<T = T.Max(min, T.Min(max, value)); static int Bits<T (T value) where T : IBinaryInteger<T = int.CreateChecked(T.PopCount(value)); Console.WriteLine($"{Clamp(15, 0, 10)} {Clamp(-0.5, 0.0, 1.0)} {Bits(255)} {Bits((byte)7)}"); How it works: static abstract members Interfaces can now declare static abstract members, which every implementing type must provide, and generic code calls them through the type parameter ( T.Zero ): csharp static string UnitArea<T () where T : IShape = $"unit {T.Kind}: {T.Unit().Area():F2}"; Console.WriteLine(UnitArea<Square ()); Console.WriteLine(UnitArea<Circle ()); interface IShape { static abstract string Kind { get; } static abstract IShape Unit(); double Area(); } record Square(double Side) : IShape { public static string Kind = "square"; public static IShape Unit() = new Square(1); public double Area() = Side Side; } record Circle(double R) : IShape { public static string Kind = "circle"; public static IShape Unit() = new Circle(1); public double Area() = Math.PI R R; } This is something instance interfaces cannot do: ask a type for something without having an object of it. Factory methods, parsing ( T.Parse , which IParsable<T provides) and constants all fit. static virtual members are the same but come with a default implementation that types may override. Your own operators in a generic interface A type can promise operators through an interface, so generic code can use them: csharp using System.Numerics; static T Total<T (IEnumerable<T items) where T : IAdditionOperators<T, T, T , IAdditiveIdentity<T, T { T sum = T.AdditiveIdentity; foreach (var x in items) sum += x; return sum; } Console.WriteLine(Total(new { new Money(1.5m), new Money(2m) })); Console.WriteLine(Total(new { 1, 2, 3 })); readonly record struct Money(decimal Amount) : IAdditionOperators<Money, Money, Money , IAdditiveIdentity<Money, Money { public static Money operator +(Money a, Money b) = new(a.Amount + b.Amount); public static Money AdditiveIdentity = new(0); } The same Total adds integers and your Money . Parsing generically csharp static List<T ParseAll<T (string csv) where T : IParsable<T = csv.Split(',').Select(s = T.Parse(s.Trim(), System.Globalization.CultureInfo.InvariantCulture)).ToList(); Console.WriteLine(string.Join(" ", ParseAll<int ("1, 2, 3"))); Console.WriteLine(string.Join(" ", ParseAll<double ("1.5, 2"))); Console.WriteLine(string.Join(" ", ParseAll<DateOnly ("2026-11-20"))); When to use it Generic math is worth it in libraries that really serve many number types: maths and statistics helpers, vectors and matrices, parsers. In application code that only ever uses decimal , plain code is simpler to read. Check yourself quiz ? Why could T total = 0; not work in a generic method before C 11? - Generic methods could not declare local variables of type T - Number literals were not allowed inside generic methods + T could not be required to have a zero or a + operator T might not be a number, and constraints could only require instance members. C 11's static abstract members let INumber<T require T.Zero and + . ? What is the difference between CreateChecked and CreateSaturating ? + CreateChecked throws on overflow; CreateSaturating clamps - CreateChecked clamps on overflow; CreateSaturating throws - CreateSaturating wraps around, like unchecked arithmetic byte.CreateChecked(300) throws an OverflowException and byte.CreateSaturating(300) gives 255, the maximum. Wrapping around is what CreateTruncating does. ? Which constraint allows a generic method to use T.Parse(text, provider)? - where T : struct - where T : INumber + where T : IParsable<T - where T : new() IParsable<T declares a static abstract Parse method that every implementing type provides.

title: 8.04  Dates, Times and Culture
body: Getting time and formatting right in .NET - DateTime and its Kind, DateTimeOffset for moments, DateOnly and TimeOnly for calendar values, TimeSpan and date arithmetic, time zones with TimeZoneInfo, TimeProvider for testable code, and CultureInfo for numbers and dates that look right in every country and parse the same everywhere. Which type? You mean Use --- --- an exact moment (a log entry, when an order was placed) DateTimeOffset (or DateTime in UTC) a calendar date with no time (a birthday, a due date) DateOnly a time of day (opening hours) TimeOnly an amount of time (3 hours 20 minutes) TimeSpan DateTime is the oldest type and the most confusing, because the same type can mean three things, shown by its Kind : Utc , Local (the computer's time zone) or Unspecified . csharp var utc = new DateTime(2026, 11, 20, 9, 30, 0, DateTimeKind.Utc); var unspecified = new DateTime(2026, 11, 20, 9, 30, 0); Console.WriteLine($"{utc:O} {utc.Kind}"); Console.WriteLine($"{unspecified:O} {unspecified.Kind}"); The O format ("round-trip") writes ISO 8601 and keeps everything needed to read the value back. DateTimeOffset: a moment with its offset csharp var placed = new DateTimeOffset(2026, 11, 20, 18, 0, 0, TimeSpan.FromHours(1)); // 18:00 in a UTC+1 country Console.WriteLine(placed); Console.WriteLine(placed.UtcDateTime.ToString("u")); Console.WriteLine(placed.ToOffset(TimeSpan.FromHours(-5)).ToString("yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm zzz")); Console.WriteLine(placed == placed.ToUniversalTime()); // true: the same moment Two DateTimeOffset values are equal when they are the same moment, whatever their offsets. Store and send moments as UTC (or with their offset), and convert to local time only to show them. Calendar values: DateOnly and TimeOnly csharp var due = new DateOnly(2026, 11, 30); var today = new DateOnly(2026, 11, 20); Console.WriteLine($"{due.DayNumber - today.DayNumber} days left, due on a {due.DayOfWeek}"); Console.WriteLine(due.AddMonths(3)); // the end of the month is kept sensible: 28/02/2027 in some cultures var opens = new TimeOnly(9, 0); var closes = new TimeOnly(17, 30); var now = new TimeOnly(18, 15); Console.WriteLine(now.IsBetween(opens, closes) ? "open" : "closed"); Console.WriteLine(closes - opens); // 08:30:00 Arithmetic csharp var start = new DateTime(2026, 1, 31, 0, 0, 0, DateTimeKind.Utc); Console.WriteLine(start.AddMonths(1).ToString("yyyy-MM-dd")); // 2026-02-28: no 31st, so the last day Console.WriteLine(start.AddDays(30).ToString("yyyy-MM-dd")); // 2026-03-02 TimeSpan t = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(200); Console.WriteLine($"{t.Hours}h {t.Minutes}m, {t.TotalHours:F2} hours in total"); Console.WriteLine(new DateTime(2026, 12, 25) - new DateTime(2026, 11, 20)); Hours is the hours part (3); TotalHours is the whole length in hours (3.33). Mixing them up is a common bug. Time zones A time zone is more than an offset: it has rules for daylight saving time that change over the year and over history. TimeZoneInfo knows them: csharp-norun var london = TimeZoneInfo.FindSystemTimeZoneById("Europe/London"); // IANA ids work on every system in .NET 6+ var moment = new DateTimeOffset(2026, 7, 1, 12, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero); var there = TimeZoneInfo.ConvertTime(moment, london); Console.WriteLine(there); // 01/07/2026 13:00:00 +01:00 (summer time) Store the zone's id ( "Europe/London" ) with a future appointment, not just an offset, because the offset of a future date can change if the rules change. Code that asks for the time DateTime.Now inside a method makes it impossible to test "what happens at midnight". .NET 8 added TimeProvider : pass one in, use TimeProvider.System in the program, and a fake in tests. csharp Console.WriteLine(new Greeter(new FixedClock(new DateTimeOffset(2026, 11, 20, 8, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero))).Greet()); Console.WriteLine(new Greeter(TimeProvider.System).Greet().Length 0); class Greeter(TimeProvider clock) { public string Greet() = clock.GetUtcNow().Hour < 12 ? "Good morning" : "Good afternoon"; } class FixedClock(DateTimeOffset now) : TimeProvider { public override DateTimeOffset GetUtcNow() = now; } Culture: how numbers and dates look 1234.5 is written 1,234.50 in the UK, 1.234,50 in Germany and 1 234,50 in France. Formatting and parsing use the current culture unless you say otherwise: csharp using System.Globalization; double price = 1234.5; var date = new DateTime(2026, 11, 20); foreach (var name in new { "en-GB", "de-DE", "fr-FR", "ja-JP" }) { var c = CultureInfo.GetCultureInfo(name); Console.WriteLine($"{name}: {price.ToString("N2", c)} {date.ToString("d", c)} {date.ToString("MMMM", c)}"); } The rule that prevents the most bugs: - Show values to people with their culture (the default). - Store and exchange values (files, JSON, logs, URLs) with CultureInfo.InvariantCulture , or fixed formats like ISO 8601. csharp using System.Globalization; string saved = 3.75.ToString(CultureInfo.InvariantCulture); // always "3.75" double back = double.Parse(saved, CultureInfo.InvariantCulture); Console.WriteLine($"{saved} {back}"); Console.WriteLine(double.TryParse("3,75", NumberStyles.Float, CultureInfo.InvariantCulture, out _)); // False A program that saves 3,75 on a German computer and reads it back on an English one gets 375 or an error: that is the bug invariant culture prevents. String comparisons have the same choice: StringComparison.Ordinal for identifiers and keys, culture-aware comparison for sorting names for people. Check yourself quiz ? Why store moments in UTC? - UTC values take less memory than local times - A DateTime cannot hold a local time correctly + UTC has no daylight saving jumps and is the same everywhere Local times repeat or skip an hour at daylight saving changes and differ between places, so UTC values compare and sort correctly. Convert to local time only to display. ? Which culture should a CSV file your program writes and reads use for numbers? + CultureInfo.InvariantCulture , so the file reads back the same on any computer - CultureInfo.CurrentCulture , so numbers look right to the user - The culture of the computer that wrote it, saved in the first line With the current culture a German computer writes 1,5, which breaks the commas of a CSV and reads back differently elsewhere. The invariant culture is fixed. ? A TimeSpan of 200 minutes: what are Hours and TotalHours? - 200 and 3.33 + 3 and 3.33 - 3.33 and 3 - 3 and 200 Hours is the whole hours part; TotalHours is the full length expressed in hours.

title: 8.05  Variance and Advanced Generics
body: The finer points of generics - why a List<Cat is not a List<Animal , covariance with out and contravariance with in, which built-in interfaces and delegates are variant, writing variant interfaces of your own, default(T), static data per closed generic type, generic caches, and constraints for enums, delegates and unmanaged types. A puzzle A Cat is an Animal . Is a List<Cat a List<Animal ? csharp-norun List<Cat cats = new Cat() ; List<Animal animals = cats; // error animals.Add(new Dog()); // ...because this would put a dog among the cats No: if it were allowed, code that thinks it has a list of animals could add a dog to the list of cats. Generic types are invariant by default: List<Cat and List<Animal are unrelated types. Covariance: out IEnumerable<T only ever gives T s out; you cannot add to it. So treating a sequence of cats as a sequence of animals is safe, and C allows it: csharp IEnumerable<Cat cats = new List<Cat { new("Tom"), new("Kit") }; IEnumerable<Animal animals = cats; // fine: covariance foreach (var a in animals) Console.WriteLine(a.Name); Func<Cat makeCat = () = new Cat("New"); Func<Animal makeAnimal = makeCat; // a function returning cats returns animals Console.WriteLine(makeAnimal().Name); record Animal(string Name); record Cat(string Name) : Animal(Name); This works because IEnumerable<T is declared IEnumerable<out T : the out promises T only appears in output positions (return values). Contravariance: in The opposite direction works for things that only take T s in. Something that can compare any two animals can certainly compare two cats: csharp IComparer<Animal byName = Comparer<Animal .Create((a, b) = string.Compare(a.Name, b.Name, StringComparison.Ordinal)); IComparer<Cat forCats = byName; // fine: contravariance var cats = new List<Cat { new("Tom"), new("Kit") }; cats.Sort(forCats); Console.WriteLine(string.Join(", ", cats.Select(c = c.Name))); Action<Animal feed = a = Console.WriteLine($"feeding {a.Name}"); Action<Cat feedCat = feed; // something that feeds any animal can feed a cat feedCat(new Cat("Tom")); record Animal(string Name); record Cat(string Name) : Animal(Name); IComparer<in T and Action<in T are marked in : T only appears as a parameter. Common variant types: covariant ( out ) contravariant ( in ) --- --- IEnumerable<T , IReadOnlyList<T , IReadOnlyCollection<T , IEnumerator<T IComparer<T , IEqualityComparer<T , IComparable<T Func<..., TResult (the result) Action<T , Func<T, ... (the arguments) Variance only works for reference types: IEnumerable<int is not an IEnumerable<object . Your own variant interfaces csharp IProducer<Animal source = new Shelter(); IConsumer<Cat catVet = new Vet(); catVet.Consume((Cat)source.Produce()); interface IProducer<out T { T Produce(); } interface IConsumer<in T { void Consume(T item); } class Shelter : IProducer<Cat { public Cat Produce() = new("Rescued"); } class Vet : IConsumer<Animal { public void Consume(Animal a) = Console.WriteLine($"checked {a.Name}"); } record Animal(string Name); record Cat(string Name) : Animal(Name); The compiler refuses out T on an interface that takes T as a parameter, and in T on one that returns it, so a variance mistake cannot slip through. default(T) default(T) (or just default where the type is known) gives null for reference types and zero for value types. Use it for "no value yet" in generic code, but prefer T? and TryGet patterns where you can, so callers can tell "missing" from "a real zero": csharp static bool TryFirst<T (IEnumerable<T items, Func<T, bool test, out T? found) { foreach (var x in items) if (test(x)) { found = x; return true; } found = default; return false; } Console.WriteLine(TryFirst(new { 0, 4, 5 }, n = n 3, out var n) ? n : -1); Console.WriteLine(TryFirst(new { 1, 2 }, x = x 3, out var m) ? m : -1); Static data per closed type Each "closed" generic type ( Cache<int , Cache<string ) has its own static fields. That makes a fast cache keyed by type, with no dictionary at all: csharp Console.WriteLine(TypeInfo<int .Name); Console.WriteLine(TypeInfo<int .Name); // the static constructor ran once for int Console.WriteLine(TypeInfo<string .Name); // and once for string static class TypeInfo<T { public static readonly string Name = typeof(T).Name; public static readonly int Calls; static TypeInfo() = Console.WriteLine($"computing info for {typeof(T).Name}"); } EqualityComparer<T .Default and Comparer<T .Default are built this way. More constraints csharp static string Names<T () where T : struct, Enum = string.Join(",", Enum.GetNames<T ()); static int SizeOf<T () where T : unmanaged = System.Runtime.CompilerServices.Unsafe.SizeOf<T (); Console.WriteLine(Names<DayOfWeek ()); Console.WriteLine($"{SizeOf<int ()} {SizeOf<double ()} {SizeOf<(byte, long) ()}"); - where T : Enum allows only enums; where T : Delegate only delegate types. - where T : unmanaged allows only types with no references inside (numbers, enums, and structs of them), which can be copied as raw bytes. - where T : allows ref struct (C 13) lets a generic method accept Span<T -like types. Check yourself quiz ? Why is IEnumerable<Cat usable as IEnumerable<Animal but List<Cat is not usable as List<Animal ? - IEnumerable<T copies the cats into a new sequence of animals - List<Cat works too, with an explicit cast + IEnumerable<out T only gives items out; List<T also takes items in, so it must stay invariant If a List<Cat were a List<Animal , you could add a dog to it. A sequence you can only read from has no such risk, so it is covariant; no copy is made. ? How many copies of a static field in Box<T exist after using Box<int and Box<string ? - One, shared by every Box<T - None: generic classes cannot have static fields + Two: each closed generic type has its own static fields Box<int and Box<string are different types at run time, and each has its own copy of the static field. ? Which assignment compiles? - List<object l = new List<string (); + IEnumerable<object e = new List<string (); - IEnumerable<object e = new List<int (); - Action<string a = (Action<object )null!; Action<object b = a; IEnumerable is covariant for reference types. List is invariant, and variance does not apply to int.
