title: 1.01  What a DLL Is and Why Programs Use Them
match: 1.01 What a DLL Is and Why Programs Use Them
body: A dynamic-link library is compiled code that is not part of your .exe but is joined to it when the program starts or while it runs. This lesson explains what a DLL contains, how it differs from a static library, and the real reasons programs are split into them, along with the costs. Code that lives in another file Every Windows program you have built so far ends up as one .exe . The compiler turns each .cpp file into an object file, and the linker copies the code from every object file, and from every static library you use, into that one executable. A DLL (dynamic-link library) is the other choice. It is a file with the same format as an .exe (both are PE files, "Portable Executable") that holds compiled functions and data but has no main . It cannot run by itself. Instead, a running program asks Windows to map the DLL into its memory , and from then on it can call the DLL's functions as if they were its own. Look at almost any program on your computer and you find DLLs next to it, and many more in C:\Windows\System32 : kernel32.dll , user32.dll , d3d11.dll . Your own Hello, world already uses several. std::cout ends up calling WriteFile in kernel32.dll , and unless you link the C runtime statically, the C and C++ runtime themselves live in DLLs ( vcruntime140.dll , msvcp140.dll , ucrtbase.dll ). Static library or DLL Static library ( .lib ) DLL ( .dll plus its import .lib ) --- --- --- When the code joins your program At link time, copied into the .exe At load time or run time, mapped from the DLL file Files you ship Just the .exe The .exe and every DLL it needs Update a bug fix in the library Rebuild and reship every program that uses it Replace the DLL; programs pick it up next time they start Two programs using it Each has its own copy on disk and in memory One copy on disk; Windows can share its code pages between processes Calling a function A direct call Usually an indirect call through a table (lesson 1.05) Can go missing No Yes: "The code execution cannot proceed because X.dll was not found" Neither is "better". Lesson 4.05 comes back to choosing between them once you know all the costs. Why programs use DLLs 1. Sharing one copy. user32.dll is used by nearly every program. Windows loads its code once and maps the same physical memory pages into every process that uses it. Only pages a process writes to get private copies. With hundreds of processes, that saves a great deal of memory. 2. Updating parts separately. A graphics driver, a font engine or a game's audio library can be replaced without rebuilding the programs that use it, as long as the replacement keeps the same interface (milestone 3 is about keeping that promise). 3. Loading code you did not have at build time. A program can look in a folder, find DLLs it has never seen, load them and call into them. That is how plugin systems, mods and many editors work (lesson 5.01). 4. Reloading code while running. Game developers put gameplay code in a DLL, change it, rebuild it and swap it into the running game without restarting (lesson 5.03). 5. Language boundaries. A DLL with a plain C interface can be called from C , Python, Rust or a scripting language. The C ABI is the common language they all speak. The costs - Distribution. Every DLL is a file that can be missing, the wrong version, or the wrong architecture (a 32-bit DLL cannot load into a 64-bit process). - A boundary. Memory, exceptions and C++ library types do not cross safely between modules built with different settings (lesson 2.05 and 2.06). - Start-up time. Each DLL must be found, mapped and connected when the program starts. - Security. If Windows looks for a DLL in the wrong place, it can load the wrong file. Lesson 4.02 shows how to load only the files you meant. What is inside a DLL Because it is a PE file, a DLL has the same parts as an .exe : my_library.dll ├── headers which machine (x64), where each section goes, the entry point ├── .text machine code of the functions ├── .rdata read-only data, plus the EXPORT table: the names and addresses it offers ├── .data global variables ├── import table the DLLs and functions it needs in turn └── .reloc how to fix addresses if it is loaded somewhere unexpected (lesson 1.02) The export table is what makes a DLL a library: a list of names (and numbers, called ordinals) with the address of each function inside the file. A program that wants AddNumbers from my_library.dll looks that name up in the export table. !note Build along in Visual Studio The lessons in this course describe Visual Studio projects you build on your own Windows machine: a DLL project and a program that uses it. The website's compiler builds single programs, so the practice tasks here check the logic behind each idea rather than building real DLLs. Common mistakes !warning Thinking a DLL makes code faster Calls into a DLL go through an extra jump. Sharing memory helps the whole system, not one program's speed. !warning Shipping a program without its DLLs Run your program on a clean machine, or a fresh virtual machine, before you share it. Missing runtime DLLs are the most common cause of "it works on my machine". Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference between a static library and a DLL? - A static library is loaded when the program starts; a DLL is copied into the .exe when it is linked - A static library holds only declarations; a DLL holds the compiled code for them + A static library's code is copied into the .exe at link time; a DLL's code stays in its own file and is mapped into the process when it is loaded - A static library can be shared between running programs; a DLL is private to one program Static code joins the executable when it is linked. A DLL stays a separate file, so it can be shared between processes and replaced on its own. ? Which of these is a real reason to put code in a DLL? + Several programs can share one copy, and that part can be updated without rebuilding them - Calls into a DLL run faster than calls inside the .exe - A DLL cannot go missing, unlike a static library - Code in a DLL needs no main , so the program itself can drop its main DLLs give sharing, separate updates, plugins, hot reload and a C interface for other languages. They do not make calls faster: a call goes through an extra indirect jump. ? What file format do DLLs and executables share? - COFF object files, the same as .obj + The PE (Portable Executable) format - The static library ( .lib ) archive format Both .dll and .exe files are PE files with the same headers and sections; a DLL simply has no main and is not run on its own. ? What can a DLL not do on its own? - Contain machine code for its functions - Contain global variables and constants + Run: it has no main of its own - Import functions from other DLLs A DLL holds code and data, and can import from other DLLs, but it only runs once a program has loaded it into its process. ? Two programs use the same DLL. What does Windows share between them? - Their global variables, so a change in one program is seen by the other + The DLL's code pages in physical memory, until a process writes to a page - Their stacks Code pages are read-only and shared. A page a process writes to, such as the DLL's global data, becomes that process's own copy. ? Which table lists the functions a DLL offers to other modules? - The import table - The relocation table + The export table Imports are what a module needs from others; exports are what it offers. The relocation table lists addresses to fix if it loads at a different base.

title: What sharing saves
where: 1.01 What a DLL Is and Why Programs Use Them
body: When several processes use the same DLL, Windows keeps one copy of its code in memory and maps it into all of them. Write two functions: - long long sharedSavings(long long codeBytes, int processes) : how many bytes of memory sharing saves compared with every process having its own copy. With one process (or none) nothing is saved. - long long pagesFor(long long bytes) : how many 4096-byte pages are needed to hold bytes bytes. A part page still takes a whole page; 0 bytes take 0 pages. sharedSavings(1'000'000, 4) == 3'000'000 // four copies would cost 4 MB; sharing costs 1 MB pagesFor(4097) == 2

title: What to ship
where: 1.01 What a DLL Is and Why Programs Use Them
body: A program uses several libraries. Some are static (their code is already inside the .exe ) and some are DLLs (files that must be shipped next to it). Write cpp std::vector<std::string shipList(const std::string& exe, const std::vector<std::pair<std::string, std::string & libraries); Each library is a pair of a file name and its kind, "static" or "dll" . Return the files to put in the folder you give to users: - the .exe first; - then every DLL, sorted alphabetically; - each DLL only once, even if it is listed several times. Windows file names ignore case, so Audio.dll and audio.DLL are the same file: keep the spelling that came first; - no static libraries. shipList("game.exe", { {"physics.lib","static"}, {"audio.dll","dll"}, {"Audio.DLL","dll"}, {"fonts.dll","dll"} }) == { "game.exe", "audio.dll", "fonts.dll" }

title: 1.02  How the Loader Maps a DLL into a Process
match: 1.02 How the Loader Maps a DLL into a Process
body: Before main runs, the Windows loader finds every DLL the program needs, maps each one into memory once, loads their own dependencies, fixes up addresses and fills in the program's tables of function addresses. Knowing these steps explains most "DLL not found" and "entry point not found" errors. The loader When you start a program, Windows creates a process and then runs code in ntdll.dll called the loader . Its job is to turn files on disk into a ready-to-run address space. For each module (the .exe and every DLL) it: 1. Finds the file using the DLL search order (lesson 4.01). 2. Maps it into memory : it reserves a range of the process's address space and makes the file's sections appear there, with the right protection (code readable and executable, data readable and writable). 3. Relocates it if it could not be placed at its preferred address. 4. Loads its dependencies : every DLL listed in its import table, recursively. 5. Binds its imports : looks up each imported function in the other DLL's export table and writes the real address into this module's import address table (IAT). 6. Runs its initialisation : for a DLL, its DllMain with DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH (lesson 2.04), which also constructs its global C++ objects. Only when all of that has worked does the program's own start-up code run, construct its globals and call main . Each DLL is loaded once The loader keeps a list of modules already in the process. If game.exe needs audio.dll and physics.dll , and both of those need math.dll , math.dll is still loaded only once . The second request just finds it in the list and increases its reference count . Dependencies are initialised before the modules that need them, so math.dll is ready by the time audio.dll 's initialisation runs. In the graph above one valid order is kernel32.dll , math.dll , audio.dll , physics.dll , then game.exe itself. That is a depth-first, dependencies-first walk, the order you will compute in the practice. Preferred addresses and relocation Every module is built for a preferred base address . Code that refers to a global variable often contains that variable's absolute address, worked out as base + offset . If the module really lands at its preferred base, all those addresses are already right. If something else already occupies that range, the loader puts the module elsewhere and has to relocate it: for every place listed in the .reloc section, it adds the difference between the actual base and the preferred base. Offsets inside a module are called RVAs (relative virtual addresses): address = base + RVA actual address after relocation = actual base + RVA fix-up applied to each stored address = actual base - preferred base With ASLR (address space layout randomisation), Windows deliberately picks a random base for most modules each time, to make attacks harder, so relocation is normal rather than rare. 64-bit code also uses addresses relative to the instruction pointer for most data, which needs no fix-ups at all. Two ways to connect Load-time linking Run-time linking --- --- --- How Link against the DLL's import library (lesson 1.05) Call LoadLibraryW and GetProcAddress yourself (lesson 2.03) When the DLL is loaded Before main Whenever your code asks If the DLL is missing The program will not start at all LoadLibraryW returns NULL and your code decides what to do Typical use Libraries the program always needs Optional features, plugins, hot reload When it goes wrong The loader's failures have recognisable messages: Message Meaning --- --- "The code execution cannot proceed because X.dll was not found." Step 1 failed for X.dll "The procedure entry point Foo could not be located in the dynamic link library X.dll." Step 5: X.dll was found but does not export Foo , usually because it is a different version "The application was unable to start correctly (0xc000007b)." Usually a 32-bit DLL in a 64-bit process, or the reverse A DllMain returned FALSE Step 6: initialisation of that DLL failed, so loading fails Common mistakes !warning Assuming dependencies are loaded in the order you list them The loader walks the dependency graph. Never rely on one DLL's initialisation having run before another's unless one depends on the other. !warning Mixing 32-bit and 64-bit A process is one or the other, and every DLL it loads must match. Check yourself quiz ? Which list gives the loader's steps for one module in the right order? - Map it, run its initialisation, load its dependencies, bind its imports + Find the file, map it, relocate if needed, load its dependencies, bind its imports, run its initialisation - Find the file, bind its imports, map it, run its initialisation, then load its dependencies - Load its dependencies, run its initialisation, then find and map the file A module's imports can only be bound once its dependencies are loaded, and its initialisation (DllMain) runs last, when everything it calls is ready. ? What is an RVA? - The absolute address a module asked to be loaded at + An offset from the module's base address in memory - The number of times a module has been loaded into a process A relative virtual address stays the same wherever the module lands: the real address is the base plus the RVA. The address a module asks for is its preferred base, not an RVA. ? Why are a DLL's dependencies initialised before the DLL itself? - Because the loader always initialises DLLs in the order they appear in the import table - So that the dependencies can call the DLL's DllMain + So that when the DLL's initialisation runs, every DLL it calls into is already ready The loader walks the dependency graph depth-first, dependencies first. It does not follow the order you list imports in. ? Two DLLs in a program both depend on math.dll. How many times is math.dll mapped? - Twice, once for each DLL that needs it + Once; the second request increases its reference count - It depends on the order of the imports The loader keeps a list of modules already in the process and reuses them. ? A module's preferred base is 0x180000000 but it lands at 0x7FF600000000. A stored address was 0x180001234. What is it after relocation? - 0x180001234 - 0x7FF600000000 - 0x7FF780001234 + 0x7FF600001234 The fix-up adds (actual base - preferred base) to every listed address, so the RVA 0x1234 is kept: 0x7FF600000000 + 0x1234. Adding the actual base to the whole old address would count the preferred base twice. ? Which step of loading produces "The procedure entry point could not be located"? - Mapping the DLL's sections into memory + Binding imports against the DLL's export table - Running the DLL's DllMain entry point - Searching the folders for the DLL file The DLL was found and mapped, but it does not export that name. A missing file gives the "was not found" message instead.

title: Relocate an address
where: 1.02 How the Loader Maps a DLL into a Process
body: A module was built for a preferred base , but the loader put it at a different actual base . Write: - unsigned long long rvaOf(unsigned long long address, unsigned long long base) : the address as an offset from the module's base. - unsigned long long relocate(unsigned long long stored, unsigned long long preferredBase, unsigned long long actualBase) : the value a stored absolute address must become after the module moves. The offset from the base stays the same. rvaOf(0x180001234, 0x180000000) == 0x1234 relocate(0x180001234, 0x180000000, 0x7FF600000000) == 0x7FF600001234

title: The loader's order
where: 1.02 How the Loader Maps a DLL into a Process
body: The loader initialises a module only after every module it imports from. Write cpp std::vector<std::string loadOrder(const std::map<std::string, std::vector<std::string & imports, const std::string& root); imports says which DLLs each module imports, in the order they are listed in its import table. A module that is not a key in the map imports nothing. Return the order the modules are initialised, root included, following these rules: - visit a module's imports in the order listed, depth first, and put the module itself after all of them; - every module appears once , the first time it is reached; - a module that has already been started (even if not finished) is not visited again, so a loop between two DLLs does not run forever. imports = { "game.exe": { "audio.dll", "physics.dll" }, "audio.dll": { "math.dll", "kernel32.dll" }, "physics.dll":{ "math.dll" }, "math.dll": { "kernel32.dll" } } loadOrder(imports, "game.exe") == { "kernel32.dll", "math.dll", "audio.dll", "physics.dll", "game.exe" }

title: 1.03  Your First DLL in Visual Studio
match: 1.03 Your First DLL in Visual Studio
body: Build a DLL and a program that uses it, in one Visual Studio solution. You meet the export macro pattern that lets one header serve both the library and the programs using it, and see where the .dll and its import .lib end up. The plan You will make one solution with two projects: Stones.sln ├── StoneMath/ a DLL project │ ├── stone_math.h the public header: what users of the DLL see │ └── stone_math.cpp the implementation └── StoneDemo/ a console program that calls the DLL └── main.cpp 1. The DLL project In Visual Studio: File, New, Project , choose Dynamic-Link Library (DLL) for C++, name it StoneMath . The template adds pch.h , framework.h and a dllmain.cpp . You can leave dllmain.cpp as it is for now (lesson 2.04 explains it), or turn off precompiled headers in Properties, C/C++, Precompiled Headers to keep things small. Note one setting the template made for you, in Properties, C/C++, Preprocessor, Preprocessor Definitions : STONEMATH_EXPORTS . Only the DLL project defines it. That is what the header uses to tell "building the library" from "using the library". 2. The export macro A function must be marked to appear in the DLL's export table. When building the DLL, the marker is __declspec(dllexport) . When a program uses the DLL, the same declaration should say __declspec(dllimport) , which lets the compiler call it through the import table directly. One header serves both by switching on STONEMATH_EXPORTS : cpp-norun // stone_math.h pragma once ifdef STONEMATH_EXPORTS define STONEMATH_API __declspec(dllexport) else define STONEMATH_API __declspec(dllimport) endif STONEMATH_API int stackHeight(int stones, int stonesPerLayer); STONEMATH_API double stackWeight(int stones, double kilosEach); cpp-norun // stone_math.cpp include "stone_math.h" int stackHeight(int stones, int stonesPerLayer) { if (stonesPerLayer <= 0) return 0; return (stones + stonesPerLayer - 1) / stonesPerLayer; // round up: a part layer is still a layer } double stackWeight(int stones, double kilosEach) { return stones kilosEach; } Build the project. In the output folder ( x64\Debug under the solution) you find: File What it is --- --- StoneMath.dll The library itself, needed at run time StoneMath.lib The import library : small, says "these names live in StoneMath.dll". Needed at link time StoneMath.pdb Debug symbols StoneMath.exp Export file the linker made along the way; you can ignore it !note Only marked functions are exported A function without STONEMATH_API is still in the DLL's code, but no other module can find it. That is how a DLL keeps helpers private. 3. The program that uses it Add a project to the same solution: Console App , named StoneDemo . cpp-norun // main.cpp include <iostream include "stone_math.h" int main() { std::cout << "Layers: " << stackHeight(10, 4) << '\n'; // 3 std::cout << "Weight: " << stackWeight(10, 2.5) << " kg\n"; // 25 } Three settings connect them: 1. Find the header. StoneDemo, Properties, C/C++, General, Additional Include Directories : $(SolutionDir)StoneMath . 2. Link the import library. Right-click StoneDemo, Add, Reference , tick StoneMath. Visual Studio then links StoneMath.lib and builds StoneMath first. 3. Run from the right place. Both projects already write to $(SolutionDir)x64\Debug , so StoneMath.dll sits next to StoneDemo.exe , which is the first place Windows looks. Set StoneDemo as the startup project and run it. 4. Break it on purpose - Delete StoneMath.dll from the output folder and run StoneDemo.exe from Explorer: the loader says it cannot find the DLL. The program never reaches main . - Remove STONEMATH_API from stackWeight , rebuild both: now the linker fails with LNK2019: unresolved external symbol , because the import library no longer lists it. Exporting a class You can put the macro on a class to export all its members: cpp-norun class STONEMATH_API Xenon { public: explicit Xenon(int stones); int height() const; private: int m_stones; }; It works, but it ties every program to the exact compiler, settings and class layout the DLL was built with. Milestone 3 shows why most long-lived DLLs export plain C functions instead. Common mistakes !warning Defining STONEMATH_EXPORTS in the program too Then the program's copy of the header says dllexport , and you get confusing link errors. Only the DLL project defines it. !warning Copying the DLL by hand into the wrong folder Debug and Release, and x64 and x86, each have their own output folder. Keep both projects writing to the same one. Check yourself quiz ? What does __declspec(dllexport) do? + It puts the function, class or variable into the DLL's export table so other modules can find it - It makes the compiler call the function through the import address table - It copies the function's code into every program that includes the header - It marks the function as private to the DLL dllexport is the DLL side. Calling through the import table is what dllimport does on the program's side. ? Which two files from a DLL build do you need, and when? - The .pdb at link time and the .dll at run time - The .exp at link time and the .lib at run time + The import .lib at link time and the .dll at run time The import library tells the linker of each calling program which DLL each function is in; the DLL itself is loaded at run time, next to the program. The .pdb is debug symbols and the .exp can be ignored. ? What does the STONEMATH_EXPORTS symbol do? - It tells the linker to build a DLL instead of an .exe + It is defined only in the DLL project, so the shared header picks dllexport there and dllimport everywhere else - It must be defined in every project that uses the DLL, so they can find its exports Only the DLL project defines it. Defining it in the program as well makes the program's header say dllexport and causes confusing link errors. ? Which file does the program's linker need? - StoneMath.dll, the library itself - StoneMath.pdb, the debug symbols + StoneMath.lib, the import library The import library tells the linker which DLL each function lives in. The DLL itself is needed when the program runs. ? Why does the header switch between dllexport and dllimport? - dllexport only works in Release builds, so Debug needs dllimport + One header must export when building the DLL and import elsewhere - dllimport makes the DLL smaller by removing unused exports The same declaration is used by both sides: the project that defines STONEMATH_EXPORTS is the DLL and exports; every other user of the header imports. ? A helper function in stone_math.cpp has no STONEMATH_API. Can StoneDemo call it? - Yes, any function compiled into a DLL can be called by the program - Only in Debug builds + No; it is in the DLL's code but not in its export table Only exported names can be found from outside the module. Calling it from StoneDemo gives LNK2019, an unresolved external symbol.

title: The library's functions
where: 1.03 Your First DLL in Visual Studio
body: Write the two functions the StoneMath DLL in the lesson exports. On the website they are ordinary functions; in Visual Studio the same code goes into the DLL project. - int stackHeight(int stones, int stonesPerLayer) : how many layers a stack of stones makes. A part layer still counts as a layer. If stonesPerLayer is 0 or less, or there are no stones, the answer is 0. - double stackWeight(int stones, double kilosEach) : the total weight. stackHeight(10, 4) == 3 stackWeight(10, 2.5) == 25.0

title: dllexport or dllimport
where: 1.03 Your First DLL in Visual Studio
body: The export macro in a DLL's public header expands to one thing while the DLL itself is being built and another everywhere else. Write cpp std::string apiMacroFor(bool buildingTheDll); that returns the text the macro should expand to: "__declspec(dllexport)" while building the DLL, "__declspec(dllimport)" for any program that uses it. Then write std::string exportsSymbol(const std::string& projectName) : the preprocessor symbol Visual Studio's DLL template defines for a project, which is the project name in upper case followed by _EXPORTS . Only letters and digits are kept; anything else becomes _ . exportsSymbol("StoneMath") == "STONEMATH_EXPORTS" exportsSymbol("my-lib 2") == "MY_LIB_2_EXPORTS"

title: 1.04  Exporting Functions and Data
body: There are two ways to say what a DLL exports, __declspec(dllexport) and a module-definition file ( .def ). This lesson covers both, plus ordinals , exporting variables, and what goes into the export table. The export table, up close Each entry in a DLL's export table has: - a name (optional), such as stackHeight ; - an ordinal , a number unique within the DLL; - an RVA : where the function or variable starts, relative to the DLL's base. Other modules find an export either by name or by ordinal. Names are the normal way. Ordinals are small numbers that are faster to look up and hide the name, but they are fragile: if ordinal 3 means a different function in the next version, every program built against the old one silently calls the wrong code. Way 1: __declspec(dllexport) You met this in lesson 1.03. The compiler writes an instruction for the linker into the object file, and the linker adds the name to the export table. It is easy and keeps the "this is public" information next to the declaration. The catch is the name . For a C++ function the exported name is the compiler's decorated (mangled) name, which also encodes the parameter types: int stackHeight(int, int) is exported as ?stackHeight@@YAHHH@Z Lesson 2.01 explains decoration and how extern "C" gives you the plain name stackHeight instead, which is what you want for anything called from another language or loaded with GetProcAddress . Way 2: a module-definition file A .def file lists exports by hand. Add one to the DLL project ( Add, New Item, Module-Definition File ); Visual Studio sets Linker, Input, Module Definition File to it. LIBRARY StoneMath EXPORTS stackHeight @1 stackWeight @2 internalCounter @3 DATA debugDump @4 NONAME StackHeight = stackHeight Line Meaning --- --- LIBRARY StoneMath The DLL's name stackHeight @1 Export stackHeight with ordinal 1 internalCounter @3 DATA Export a variable , not a function debugDump @4 NONAME Export by ordinal only: no name in the table StackHeight = stackHeight Export the internal function stackHeight under a different public name Lines starting with ; are comments. The names in a .def file must match the symbols the compiler produced, so a .def file works most comfortably with extern "C" functions. Why use a .def file at all? - To give fixed ordinals that never change between versions. - To export a function under a different name than the one in the code. - To export plain names from code you cannot or do not want to change. Exporting variables A DLL can export a global variable: cpp-norun // in the DLL STONEMATH_API int g_stonesCreated = 0; // in the header, for users extern STONEMATH_API int g_stonesCreated; The program then reads and writes the DLL's variable directly. It works, but every program now depends on that variable's type and meaning. A function such as int stonesCreated() can change how it works without breaking anyone, so prefer functions. Lesson 3.01 turns that into a rule. Seeing what you exported Open a Developer Command Prompt and run: dumpbin /exports StoneMath.dll varies ordinal hint RVA name 1 0 00011023 stackHeight = @ILT+30(stackHeight) 2 1 000110A5 stackWeight = @ILT+160(stackWeight) 3 2 0001C000 internalCounter 4 000111D6 NONAME The hint is an index into the name table that lets the loader skip a search when it is right. Lesson 1.06 covers dumpbin and other tools. Common mistakes !warning Reusing an ordinal for a different function Programs that import by ordinal will call the wrong function. Once published, an ordinal belongs to its function forever. !warning Putting a C++ name with no extern "C" in a .def file The linker looks for a symbol called exactly that and does not find the decorated one. Use extern "C" for exported functions listed in a .def file. Check yourself quiz ? What three things does an export table entry hold? - A name, the function's parameter types and its return type + A name (optional), an ordinal, and the RVA of the function or variable - The DLL's file name, a version number and an absolute address Each entry has an optional name, a number unique in the DLL, and where the export starts relative to the DLL's base. ? Which is a good reason to use a .def file? - It is the only way to export a function from a DLL - It makes exported functions run faster than dllexport does + It gives fixed ordinals and lets an export use another name A .def file can export a function under a different name than the code uses, and it also exports plain names without changing the code. __declspec(dllexport) exports functions too, so a .def file is never required. ? Why prefer exporting a function such as int stonesCreated() over exporting a variable? - Variables cannot be exported from a DLL, only functions + A function can change internally; a variable fixes its type for good - Each program gets its own copy of an exported variable A function can change how it works without breaking callers, while an exported variable fixes its type and meaning for every program. Exported variables do work, and both modules see the same memory. ? What does NONAME mean in a .def file? - The function is kept out of the export table entirely + The function is exported by ordinal only, with no name - The function is exported with its decorated C++ name The export table holds no name for it, so other modules can only find it by its number. ? Why are ordinals risky across versions? - Ordinals are slower for the loader to look up than names - Windows no longer supports importing a function by ordinal + A reused ordinal makes old programs silently call the wrong function Names describe what you call; numbers only describe a position, so if an ordinal later refers to a different function nothing warns you. Ordinals are actually faster to look up than names. ? Which .def line exports the function stack_impl under the public name Stack ? - stack_impl = Stack - Stack @stack_impl + Stack = stack_impl The public name comes first, then the internal one.

title: Read a .def file
body: Write a reader for the EXPORTS lines of a module-definition file. cpp struct DefExport { std::string name; // the public name std::string internal; // the function in the code; the same as name when there is no "= ..." int ordinal{ -1 }; // -1 when no @number is given bool noName{ false }; // NONAME bool data{ false }; // DATA }; std::vector<DefExport readDef(const std::string& text); Rules: - Lines are separated by \n . Leading and trailing spaces do not matter. - Skip blank lines, comment lines starting with ; , the LIBRARY line and the EXPORTS line itself. - Every other line is one export: name , optionally = internal , optionally @number , then optionally the words NONAME and DATA in any order. Words are separated by spaces; = and @ may have spaces around them or not. LIBRARY StoneMath EXPORTS stackHeight @1 internalCounter @3 DATA debugDump @4 NONAME StackHeight = stackHeight gives four exports: {stackHeight, stackHeight, 1} , {internalCounter, internalCounter, 3, data} , {debugDump, debugDump, 4, noName} , {StackHeight, stackHeight, -1} .

title: Did the ordinals stay put?
body: A DLL exports by ordinal, so a new version must keep every published ordinal. Write cpp std::vector<std::string ordinalProblems(const std::map<std::string, int & oldVersion, const std::map<std::string, int & newVersion); Each map is export name to ordinal. Report, in this order: 1. for each name in the old version (in alphabetical order, as the map stores them): - missing from the new version: "<name was removed" ; - present with a different ordinal: "<name moved from @<old to @<new " ; 2. then, for each name that is new (alphabetical): if its ordinal was used by a different name in the old version, "@<n now means <newName , was <oldName " . An empty list means old programs keep working. old: { stackHeight: 1, stackWeight: 2, debugDump: 3 } new: { stackHeight: 1, stackWeight: 5, layers: 3 } problems: "debugDump was removed", "stackWeight moved from @2 to @5", "@3 now means layers, was debugDump"

title: 1.05  Import Libraries and Load-Time Linking
body: When a program links against a DLL's import library , the linker writes an import table into the program and calls go through the import address table , which the loader fills in. This lesson follows one call from your source code to the DLL. What an import library contains StoneMath.lib from lesson 1.03 is small. It contains no machine code for stackHeight . It contains, for each export: - the symbol the linker is looking for ( __imp_stackHeight , and a stub called stackHeight ), and - a record saying "this comes from StoneMath.dll , under the name stackHeight ". When StoneDemo's linker sees a call to stackHeight , it finds the symbol in the import library and records the dependency. The result in StoneDemo.exe is an import table : StoneDemo.exe imports StoneMath.dll stackHeight stackWeight KERNEL32.dll WriteFile GetStdHandle ... The import address table Alongside the names, the program has an import address table (IAT): one pointer-sized slot for every imported function. In the file the slots hold placeholders. At load time, the loader looks up each name in the DLL's export table and writes the real address into the slot (lesson 1.02, step 5). Your call compiles into an indirect call through that slot: asm ; with __declspec(dllimport) on the declaration call qword ptr __imp_stackHeight ; jump to whatever address the loader wrote into the slot Without dllimport , the compiler does not know the function is in a DLL. It emits a normal call stackHeight , and the linker makes stackHeight a tiny stub that jumps through the slot. It works, just with one extra jump. That is why the header from lesson 1.03 says dllimport for users. Following one call The cost is one memory read to fetch the address. The benefit is that the program does not need to know where StoneMath.dll will be loaded. When a name cannot be resolved At load time, every import must be found. If StoneDemo.exe was built against a StoneMath.dll that exported stackHeight and stackWeight , but the DLL on disk is an older one with only stackHeight , the loader stops with: varies The procedure entry point stackWeight could not be located in the dynamic link library StoneMath.dll. The program does not start. This is the strongest argument for never removing an export from a published DLL (milestone 3). Linking against a DLL without a project reference The project reference from lesson 1.03 is the easiest way in one solution. For a DLL from somewhere else you set two linker properties yourself: - Linker, General, Additional Library Directories : the folder with StoneMath.lib . - Linker, Input, Additional Dependencies : add StoneMath.lib . Or, in code, a comment that tells the linker: cpp-norun pragma comment(lib, "StoneMath.lib") You still need the DLL next to the program when it runs. Making an import library from a DLL Sometimes you have only a DLL (and its documentation). You can rebuild an import library from a .def file listing its exports: lib /def:StoneMath.def /out:StoneMath.lib /machine:x64 Common mistakes !warning Shipping only the .lib The import library is for building. Users of your program need the .dll . !warning Using an import library from a different version of the DLL The program then imports names the DLL on disk may not have. Keep the .lib and .dll from the same build together. Check yourself quiz ? What is the import address table? - The table in a DLL that lists the names and RVAs it offers to other modules + An array of slots in a module, one per imported function, that the loader fills with the real addresses; calls into DLLs jump through them - A list the linker fills with the final addresses of every DLL function when the program is built The list of what a DLL offers is its export table. The IAT slots hold placeholders in the file, because the real addresses are only known at load time. ? Why does __declspec(dllimport) make calls slightly better? - It copies the function's code into the program, so no DLL call is needed - It makes the loader bind that import before all the others + The compiler calls through the IAT slot directly, with no stub Without dllimport the call still works, through a small stub the linker adds that then jumps through the slot: one extra jump. ? Why should a published DLL never remove an export? - The DLL would no longer build without that export + Programs that import that name will no longer start - The removed function's ordinal would be given to the next export Load-time linking resolves every import before main , and the loader refuses to start a program whose imported name is missing. ? What does an import library contain? + The DLL's export names and which DLL each is in, but no code - A full copy of the DLL's machine code, linked in statically - The debug symbols for every function the DLL exports It lets the linker connect calls to the DLL without including its code. Debug symbols are in the .pdb . ? Who fills in the import address table? - The linker, when the program is built + The loader, when the program starts - The DLL's DllMain The real addresses are not known until the DLL is mapped. ? A program imports stackWeight but the DLL on disk does not export it. What happens? - stackWeight returns 0 - The program starts and crashes when stackWeight is called + The program fails to start with "procedure entry point could not be located" Load-time linking resolves every import before main , so the program never starts.

title: Resolve the imports
body: At load time, every import must be found or the program does not start. Write the check the loader makes: cpp std::string resolveImports(const std::map<std::string, std::set<std::string & exportsByDll, const std::vector<std::pair<std::string, std::string & imports); - exportsByDll maps each DLL that exists to the names it exports. - imports is the program's import table: pairs of (DLL name, function name), in order. - DLL names ignore upper and lower case ( KERNEL32.dll is kernel32.dll ); function names do not. Return the message for the first import that fails, or an empty string if all of them resolve: - DLL not found: The code execution cannot proceed because <dll was not found. - Function not exported: The procedure entry point <function could not be located in the dynamic link library <dll . Use the DLL name as the import table spells it.

title: Fill the import address table
body: The loader writes the real address of each imported function into the import address table. Write cpp std::vector<unsigned long long fillIat(const std::vector<std::string & imports, const std::map<std::string, unsigned long long & exportRvas, unsigned long long dllBase); For each imported name, in order, the slot holds dllBase + rva of that export, or 0 if the DLL does not export it. fillIat({ "stackHeight", "stackWeight" }, { {"stackHeight", 0x1023}, {"stackWeight", 0x10A5} }, 0x7FFA10000000) == { 0x7FFA10001023, 0x7FFA100010A5 }

title: 1.06  Inspecting DLLs with dumpbin and Dependencies
match: 1.06 Inspecting DLLs with dumpbin and Dependencies
body: When a program will not start or calls the wrong thing, you need to see what a module exports, what it imports, and where each DLL really came from. This lesson covers dumpbin , the Dependencies tool, the debugger's Modules window and Process Monitor. dumpbin dumpbin comes with Visual Studio. Run it from a Developer Command Prompt (Start menu: "Developer Command Prompt for VS"). Command Shows --- --- dumpbin /exports X.dll The export table: ordinal, hint, RVA, name dumpbin /imports X.exe Every DLL the module imports from, and every function dumpbin /dependents X.exe Just the list of DLLs it needs directly dumpbin /headers X.dll Machine type (x64 or x86), preferred base, subsystem, characteristics A typical check when a program refuses to start: dumpbin /dependents on the .exe , then make sure every listed DLL exists, then dumpbin /exports on the suspicious one and compare against dumpbin /imports . varies Dump of file StoneDemo.exe Image has the following dependencies: StoneMath.dll MSVCP140D.dll VCRUNTIME140D.dll VCRUNTIME140_1D.dll ucrtbased.dll KERNEL32.dll The D at the end of the runtime names means debug runtime. Those DLLs exist only on machines with Visual Studio installed, which is why a Debug build will not run on a friend's computer (lesson 4.04). dumpbin /headers answers "is this 32-bit or 64-bit?": look for machine (x64) or machine (x86) . Dependencies Dependencies (https://github.com/lucasg/Dependencies) is a free, open-source tool that shows the whole dependency tree of a module, recursively, and marks in red anything it cannot find. It understands Windows' API sets (names like api-ms-win-core-file-l1-1-0.dll , which are redirected to real system DLLs), which confuses older tools. Open StoneDemo.exe in it, expand StoneMath.dll , and you see what StoneMath itself needs. The debugger's Modules window While debugging, Debug, Windows, Modules lists every module actually loaded, with: - Path : exactly which file was loaded. This answers "which copy of the DLL did it pick?" - Address : where it was mapped (lesson 1.02). - Symbol Status : whether its .pdb was found, so you can step into it. - Version : from its version resource (lesson 4.04). A DLL loaded with LoadLibraryW appears in the list the moment the call returns. Process Monitor When Windows looks for a DLL, it tries a sequence of folders (lesson 4.01). Process Monitor (https://learn.microsoft.com/sysinternals/downloads/procmon) from Sysinternals records every file access. Filter on your process name and on paths ending in .dll , start the program, and you see each place the loader tried, with NAME NOT FOUND until it finds the file. That tells you exactly why the wrong copy was loaded, or why none was. Reading a loader failure, step by step 1. Note the exact message (lesson 1.02's table). 2. dumpbin /dependents the .exe : which DLLs does it need? 3. For each one, is it next to the program, or in a folder Windows searches? 4. Is it the right architecture? ( dumpbin /headers ) 5. If the message names a missing entry point , dumpbin /exports the DLL that was loaded (find its path in Process Monitor or the Modules window) and compare with what the program imports. Common mistakes !warning Inspecting the wrong copy There are often several copies of a DLL on a machine. Check the path Windows actually loaded, not the one you expected. !warning Running dumpbin from an ordinary prompt It is only on the PATH in a Developer Command Prompt. Check yourself quiz ? How do you tell whether a DLL is 32-bit or 64-bit? - dumpbin /exports lists the machine type next to each export + dumpbin /headers shows the machine type: x86 or x64 - A 64-bit DLL always has "64" in its file name The headers hold the machine type. Names are no guide: 64-bit Windows keeps its 64-bit DLLs in a folder called System32. ? Where can you see which file a running program actually loaded for a DLL? - In dumpbin /dependents , which lists the full path of each DLL - In the project's Linker, Input settings + In the debugger's Modules window (the Path column), or in Process Monitor dumpbin /dependents only lists DLL names the program needs, not which copy Windows picked at run time. ? What does the Dependencies tool add over dumpbin? + The whole dependency tree, with missing DLLs highlighted - The ability to edit and rewrite a DLL's export table - The source code behind each of the DLL's exports dumpbin shows one module at a time; Dependencies follows every DLL's own dependencies recursively, handles API set names correctly and marks in red what it cannot find. ? Which command answers "which DLLs does this program need directly?" + dumpbin /dependents - dumpbin /exports - dumpbin /headers /imports gives the same list plus every function; /dependents is the short version. ? How can you see every folder Windows tried while looking for a DLL? - Run dumpbin /imports on the program's .exe + Record the start in Process Monitor, filtered on .dll - Read the Output window of the Visual Studio debugger Process Monitor records every path Windows tried, including the ones that failed with NAME NOT FOUND. dumpbin only lists which DLLs are imported, not where they were searched for. ? What does a name ending in D, such as MSVCP140D.dll, tell you? - The DLL file is damaged and must be reinstalled - The DLL is the 32-bit build of the C++ runtime + It is the debug C++ runtime, used by Debug builds The program was built in Debug. Debug runtimes are only installed with Visual Studio, so a Debug build will not run on most other machines.

title: Read dumpbin's export list
where: 1.06 Inspecting DLLs with dumpbin and Dependencies
body: Write a reader for the table dumpbin /exports prints, so a tool can compare two versions of a DLL. cpp std::vector<std::string exportedNames(const std::string& dumpbinOutput); The table starts after the heading line that contains the words ordinal , hint , RVA and name . Each following line that starts (after spaces) with a number is one export: 1 0 00011023 stackHeight = @ILT+30(stackHeight) 2 1 000110A5 stackWeight = @ILT+160(stackWeight) 4 000111D6 NONAME - The columns are the ordinal, the hint (missing for an export without a name), the 8-digit hexadecimal RVA, then the name. - The name is the word right after the RVA. Anything after it ( = @ILT+... ) is ignored. - For NONAME , use followed by the ordinal, such as 4 . - Stop at the first blank line after the table has started, or at a line starting with Summary . Return the names in the order they appear.

title: Debug runtime or API set

Windows redirects those to real DLLs, so a tool should not report them as missing.
