title: A loader report
body: Put the milestone together: simulate what the Windows loader does when a program starts, and explain the result the way a good tool would. A module is described by what it imports and what it exports: cpp struct Module { std::vector<std::pair<std::string, std::string imports; // (dll, function), in import-table order std::set<std::string exports; // names this module offers }; std::vector<std::string loaderReport(const std::map<std::string, Module & onDisk, const std::string& program); onDisk holds every module that exists, keyed by file name. DLL names ignore case when you look them up; function names do not. The report is a list of lines: 1. Work out the load order exactly like lesson 1.02's practice: depth first, a module's dependencies (the DLLs in its imports, each counted once, in the order they first appear) before the module itself, every module once. Only modules that exist are visited. 2. Before printing anything, check every module you would load, in load order, including the program : - for each of its imports, in order: the DLL must exist, and must export the function; - stop at the first problem and return a single line, the loader's message from lesson 1.05's practice. 3. If everything resolves, return one line load <name per module in load order, then a final line start <program . If the program itself is not on disk, the report is the single line <program was not found. onDisk: game.exe imports (audio.dll, play) (KERNEL32.dll, WriteFile) audio.dll imports (kernel32.dll, CreateFileW) exports play, stop kernel32.dll exports WriteFile, CreateFileW loaderReport(onDisk, "game.exe") == { "load kernel32.dll", "load audio.dll", "load game.exe", "start game.exe" } Use the name of each module the way it is spelled as a key in onDisk .

title: 2.01  Name Mangling and extern "C"
body: C++ lets two functions share a name if their parameters differ, so the compiler gives every function a decorated name that encodes its parameter types. Those names are what a DLL exports by default. extern "C" turns decoration off, giving the plain names that GetProcAddress , .def files and other languages need. Why names are decorated In C++ these are three different functions: cpp-norun int area(int side); int area(int width, int height); double area(double radius); The linker, though, only knows symbol names: strings. To keep the three apart, the compiler gives each a decorated name (also called a mangled name) that includes the parameter types, the return type, the namespace and class, and more. With MSVC: Declaration Decorated name --- --- int area(int) ?area@@YAHH@Z int area(int, int) ?area@@YAHHH@Z double area(double) ?area@@YANN@Z int stackHeight(int, int) ?stackHeight@@YAHHH@Z void reset() ?reset@@YAXXZ GCC and Clang use a completely different scheme ( _Z4areai ). That alone is a good reason not to export C++ names from a DLL meant for anyone else. Reading an MSVC name For a plain function outside any class or namespace, the pattern is: ? name @@ YA <return type <parameter types @Z (no parameters: XZ) - ? marks a decorated C++ name. - @@ ends the name and its (empty) scope. - Y means "a function outside a class", A means the default calling convention ( __cdecl ). - The type codes: Type Code Type Code --- --- --- --- void X int H char D unsigned int I bool _N long long _J float M double N - After the parameters comes @Z . A function with no parameters has X (void) as its parameter list and ends XZ with no @ . So ?add@@YAHHH@Z is "a free function add , returning int ( H ), taking int, int ( HH )". You will build exactly this decorator in the practice. To decode a name you do not recognise, Visual Studio ships undname : undname ?stackHeight@@YAHHH@Z varies Undecoration of :- "?stackHeight@@YAHHH@Z" is :- "int __cdecl stackHeight(int,int)" extern "C" Wrapping a declaration in extern "C" tells the compiler to use C linkage : no overloading, no decoration, the plain name. cpp-norun // stone_math.h ifdef __cplusplus extern "C" { endif STONEMATH_API int stackHeight(int stones, int stonesPerLayer); STONEMATH_API double stackWeight(int stones, double kilosEach); ifdef __cplusplus } endif Now dumpbin /exports lists stackHeight and stackWeight . The ifdef __cplusplus lets the same header be used from C, which does not know the words extern "C" . What you give up: - No overloading. Two extern "C" functions cannot share a name. Use distinct names: area_square , area_rect . - No C++ types in the signature that C cannot express , if you want other languages to call it. The compiler allows std::string in an extern "C" function, but no other language can construct one (lesson 2.06). The body of an extern "C" function is still C++. You can use classes, templates and the standard library inside it; only the name and signature are C. Which names to export A good rule for any DLL that outlives one build of one program: Export extern "C" functions with plain C types in their signatures. Keep C++ on the inside. Milestone 3 builds whole interfaces this way, including ones that give users objects and methods. Common mistakes !warning GetProcAddress(dll, "stackHeight") returns NULL The function was exported with its decorated name. Add extern "C" , or ask for the decorated name (fragile). !warning extern "C" in the .cpp file but not the header Callers then look for the decorated name and the linker cannot find it. Put extern "C" on the declaration everyone sees. Check yourself quiz ? What is a decorated (mangled) name? - A shortened name the linker uses to make the export table smaller - The name a function gets when it is exported by ordinal only + The compiler's symbol for a C++ function, encoding its scope and types - A name scrambled on purpose so other programs cannot call the function It encodes the scope, calling convention, return and parameter types so overloads can coexist, because the linker only compares strings. It is not compression or protection: undname turns it back into the declaration. ? What does extern "C" give up? + Overloading, and C++-only types in the signature if other languages are to call the function - The use of classes, templates and the standard library inside the function's body - The ability to export the function from a DLL Only the name and signature follow C rules. The body is still ordinary C++. ? What does ?reset@@YAXXZ decode to? - int __cdecl reset(void) - void __cdecl reset(int) + void __cdecl reset(void) YA is a free __cdecl function, the first X is the void return, and XZ means no parameters. An int would be H . ? Why does C++ decorate function names? + So overloads with the same name get different linker symbols - To make the linker's symbol lookups faster at build time - To hide each function's real name from debuggers and tools The linker only compares names, so the types have to be part of the name. Tools such as undname turn a decorated name straight back into the declaration. ? What is the MSVC decorated name of int twice(int) ? - ?twice@@YAXXZ - ?twice@@YANN@Z + ?twice@@YAHH@Z H for the int return, H for the one int parameter, then @Z . N would be double , and XZ is a void function with no parameters. ? What does extern "C" change about a function? - Its body must be written in plain C, not C++ + Its linkage: a plain, undecorated name and no overloading - It is compiled with the C compiler instead of C++ Only the name and signature follow C rules; the body is ordinary C++ compiled by the C++ compiler.

title: Decorate a name like MSVC
body: Write the decorator from the lesson for free functions with simple types: cpp std::string decorate(const std::string& name, const std::string& returnType, const std::vector<std::string & parameters); The result is ? + name + @@YA + the return type's code + the parameter codes + an ending: - with at least one parameter, the ending is @Z ; - with no parameters, the parameter list is X (void) and the ending is Z , so the name ends in XZ . Type Code Type Code --- --- --- --- void X int H char D unsigned int I bool _N long long _J float M double N If any type is not in the table, return an empty string. decorate("add", "int", { "int", "int" }) == "?add@@YAHHH@Z" decorate("reset", "void", {}) == "?reset@@YAXXZ" decorate("ratio", "double", { "float", "bool" }) == "?ratio@@YANM_N@Z"

title: Mangled or not
body: Write bool isDecorated(const std::string& symbol) that says whether an exported name is an MSVC-decorated C++ name. Those start with ? . Plain extern "C" names, and 32-bit names such as _name@8 , do not.

title: 2.02  Calling Conventions at the Boundary
body: A calling convention is the agreement about where a function's arguments go and who cleans up afterwards. On 64-bit Windows there is essentially one; on 32-bit Windows there are several, and they change the exported name. Getting the convention wrong across a DLL boundary corrupts the stack. The agreement every call relies on When main calls stackHeight(10, 4) , both sides must agree on: - where the arguments go: registers or the stack, and in which order; - where the return value comes back; - which registers the called function may change; - who removes the arguments from the stack afterwards. That agreement is the calling convention . Inside one program the compiler uses the same one everywhere, so you never think about it. Across a DLL boundary, the caller and the DLL were compiled separately, possibly by different compilers or languages, so the convention is part of the interface. 64-bit Windows: one convention On x64 Windows every function uses the Microsoft x64 calling convention : - the first four integer or pointer arguments go in RCX , RDX , R8 , R9 ; the first four floating-point ones in XMM0 to XMM3 ; - further arguments go on the stack; - the caller reserves 32 bytes of "shadow space" on the stack and cleans up; - the return value comes back in RAX (or XMM0 ). Keywords like __stdcall and __cdecl are accepted on x64 but ignored . Names are not decorated for them either: an extern "C" function is exported exactly as stackHeight . 32-bit Windows: several conventions 32-bit code is still around (older plugins, some game engines), and there the keyword matters: Convention Arguments Who cleans the stack extern "C" name --- --- --- --- __cdecl (default for C/C++) stack, right to left the caller _name __stdcall (the Win32 API, WINAPI ) stack, right to left the callee _name@N , N = bytes of arguments __fastcall first two in ECX , EDX , rest on stack the callee @name@N N is the total size of the arguments, each rounded up to 4 bytes: int stackHeight(int, int) as __stdcall is exported as _stackHeight@8 . That decoration is why so many old DLLs use a .def file: to export the plain name stackHeight from a __stdcall function. When the two sides disagree Suppose a DLL defines __stdcall but the program declares the function __cdecl and calls it through a function pointer (lesson 2.03). On 32-bit Windows: 1. The program pushes 8 bytes of arguments. 2. The DLL's function returns and, being __stdcall , removes 8 bytes. 3. The program, believing it is __cdecl , removes 8 more. The stack pointer is now 8 bytes wrong. Local variables and return addresses are read from the wrong places, and the program crashes somewhere unrelated, often much later. In a Debug build MSVC catches it with: varies Run-Time Check Failure 0 - The value of ESP was not properly saved across a function call. A portable habit Pick a convention for your public API and spell it out with a macro, so the header says it once: cpp-norun ifdef _WIN32 define STONEMATH_CALL __cdecl else define STONEMATH_CALL endif STONEMATH_API int STONEMATH_CALL stackHeight(int stones, int stonesPerLayer); typedef int (STONEMATH_CALL StackHeightFn)(int, int); // for GetProcAddress users On x64 the macro does nothing. On x86 it makes both sides agree, including people writing their own declarations from your documentation. Common mistakes !warning Declaring a function pointer without the convention A GetProcAddress result cast to the wrong function pointer type is the most common way to get a convention mismatch. Put the convention in the typedef. !warning Assuming 32-bit rules on x64 On x64 _name@8 decoration never happens. If you see it, you are looking at a 32-bit DLL. Check yourself quiz ? What does a calling convention decide? - Which DLL a function is loaded from and under which name + Where arguments and results go and who cleans up the stack - Whether a function's name is decorated with its parameter types It also fixes which registers a function may change: the low-level agreement every call relies on. On 32-bit Windows it also changes the exported name, but that is a side effect, not its purpose. ? Why does the calling convention matter more across a DLL boundary than inside one program? - Because calls into a DLL always use __stdcall - Because the loader converts every call to the DLL's convention + The two sides were compiled separately and may not agree Inside one program the compiler uses one convention everywhere; across a DLL nothing guarantees agreement unless the interface says so. Nothing converts between conventions at the boundary. ? On 32-bit Windows, what are the exported names of extern "C" int f(int, double) as __cdecl and as __stdcall ? + _f and _f@12 - _f and _f@8 - f and f@12 - _f@12 and _f __cdecl adds a leading underscore; __stdcall also adds @ and the bytes of arguments: 4 for the int plus 8 for the double . ? How many calling conventions does ordinary x64 Windows code use? - Three, like 32-bit Windows + One: the Microsoft x64 convention - Two: one for C and one for C++ __stdcall and __cdecl still compile on x64, but they are ignored. ? What is the 32-bit exported name of extern "C" int __stdcall area(int, int)? - area - @area@8 + _area@8 __stdcall adds a leading underscore and @ plus the bytes of arguments. @area@8 is the __fastcall form. ? On 32-bit Windows, a __stdcall function is called as if it were __cdecl. What goes wrong? - Nothing; on 32-bit Windows the two are the same - The return value is read from the wrong register + The arguments are popped twice, corrupting the stack pointer __stdcall 's callee and __cdecl 's caller both clean up, so the stack pointer is off by the size of the arguments. Both conventions return values the same way.

title: 32-bit export names
body: On 32-bit Windows an extern "C" function's exported name depends on its calling convention. Write cpp std::string exportName32(const std::string& name, const std::string& convention, const std::vector<int & argumentSizes); - argumentSizes holds the size in bytes of each argument. Each one counts as at least 4 bytes and is rounded up to a multiple of 4 (a char takes 4 bytes on the stack, a double 8). Their total is N . - "cdecl" : _name - "stdcall" : _name@N - "fastcall" : @name@N - any other convention: the name unchanged. Then write int stackBytes(const std::vector<int & argumentSizes) returning N on its own. exportName32("area", "stdcall", { 4, 4 }) == "_area@8" exportName32("f", "stdcall", { 4, 8 }) == "_f@12" exportName32("g", "stdcall", { 1, 2 }) == "_g@8"

title: 2.03  Run-Time Loading with LoadLibrary and GetProcAddress
match: 2.03 Run-Time Loading with LoadLibrary and GetProcAddress
body:
Instead of linking against an import library, a program can load a DLL whenever it likes with LoadLibraryW , look up functions by name with GetProcAddress , call them through function pointers, and unload the DLL with FreeLibrary . This is the foundation of plugins and hot reload. Three functions cpp-norun HMODULE LoadLibraryW(LPCWSTR fileName); // map the DLL (and its dependencies); NULL on failure FARPROC GetProcAddress(HMODULE module, LPCSTR name); // address of an export; NULL if not found BOOL FreeLibrary(HMODULE module); // drop one reference; unmap at zero HMODULE is a handle to a loaded module. Its value is in fact the module's base address. Note that GetProcAddress takes an ANSI string (there is no W version), because export names are plain bytes. A complete example StoneMath from lesson 1.03, now with extern "C" exports (lesson 2.01). The program does not link StoneMath.lib and does not include its header: cpp-norun include <windows.h include <iostream using StackHeightFn = int ( )(int, int); // must match the DLL's declaration exactly int main() { HMODULE dll{ LoadLibraryW(L"StoneMath.dll") }; if (!dll) { std::cerr << "Could not load StoneMath.dll, error " << GetLastError() << '
'; return 1; } auto stackHeight{ reinterpret_cast<StackHeightFn (GetProcAddress(dll, "stackHeight")) }; if (!stackHeight) { std::cerr << "StoneMath.dll has no stackHeight
"; FreeLibrary(dll); return 1; } std::cout << stackHeight(10, 4) << '
'; // 3 FreeLibrary(dll); } The reinterpret_cast is needed because GetProcAddress returns a generic FARPROC . The compiler cannot check that the type you cast to is right: if the DLL's function takes (double, int) and you cast to int( )(int, int) , the call compiles and silently passes garbage. Keep function pointer types in a header shared with the DLL. !note Why not just link? Run-time loading lets the program start even when the DLL is missing, choose which DLL to load (say, renderer_d3d11.dll or renderer_vulkan.dll ), load DLLs it has never heard of (plugins), and unload and reload a DLL (hot reload). Errors When LoadLibraryW returns NULL , GetLastError() says why: Code Name Usual cause --- --- --- 126 ERROR_MOD_NOT_FOUND The DLL, or one of its dependencies , was not found 127 ERROR_PROC_NOT_FOUND A dependency is missing an export the DLL imports 193 ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT 32-bit DLL in a 64-bit process, or not a DLL at all 1114 ERROR_DLL_INIT_FAILED The DLL's DllMain returned FALSE Error 126 is confusing: the DLL you named may be right there, but something it needs is not. Lesson 1.06's tools find out which. Reference counting Each successful LoadLibraryW of the same DLL increases its reference count and returns the same HMODULE . Each FreeLibrary decreases it. The DLL is unmapped only when the count reaches zero. cpp-norun HMODULE a{ LoadLibraryW(L"StoneMath.dll") }; // count 1, maps the DLL HMODULE b{ LoadLibraryW(L"StoneMath.dll") }; // count 2, a == b FreeLibrary(a); // count 1, still mapped FreeLibrary(b); // count 0, unmapped After the last FreeLibrary , every function pointer you got from that DLL points at memory that no longer belongs to it. Calling one crashes. So does using any object, string or vtable the DLL created. Lesson 5.03 deals with this carefully. A small RAII wrapper Forgetting FreeLibrary on an error path is easy. Wrap the handle: cpp-norun class Library { public: explicit Library(const wchar_t file) : m_module{ LoadLibraryW(file) } {} ~Library() { if (m_module) FreeLibrary(m_module); } Library(const Library&) = delete; Library& operator=(const Library&) = delete; explicit operator bool() const { return m_module != nullptr; } template <typename Fn Fn get(const char name) const { return reinterpret_cast<Fn (GetProcAddress(m_module, name)); } private: HMODULE m_module; }; Common mistakes !warning Casting to the wrong function type The compiler cannot catch it. Share the typedef with the DLL. !warning Calling a function after FreeLibrary Pointers into an unloaded DLL are dangling. Drop them before you free the library. !warning Passing a relative name and getting the wrong file LoadLibraryW(L"StoneMath.dll") searches several folders. Lesson 4.02 shows how to load exactly the file you mean. Check yourself quiz ? What do LoadLibraryW, GetProcAddress and FreeLibrary each do? - Load a DLL's import library; call an exported function by name; delete the DLL file + Map a DLL and return its handle; look up an exported function's address by name; drop one reference and unmap the DLL when none remain - Map a DLL and call its exports; return a typed function pointer; unmap the DLL immediately GetProcAddress only returns an untyped address, and FreeLibrary unmaps the DLL only when its reference count reaches zero. ? What happens to function pointers from a DLL after its last FreeLibrary? - They keep working, because the code stays in the process until it exits - They become null automatically + They dangle: the code they point to is no longer mapped, so calling them crashes Nothing resets your pointers. Drop them before the last FreeLibrary . ? Which of these does run-time loading make possible that load-time linking does not? + Starting without the DLL and choosing between several DLLs while running - Calling the DLL's functions without any function pointer - Using the DLL's exports without them being in its export table Run-time loading also allows plugins found at run time and unloading and reloading code. GetProcAddress can still only find exported names. ? LoadLibraryW fails with error 126, but StoneMath.dll is next to the program. What is the most likely cause? - The file is too large + One of StoneMath.dll's own dependencies is missing - GetProcAddress was called first - StoneMath.dll is 32-bit and the program is 64-bit 126 means "module not found", and it covers every module the loader needs. A wrong architecture gives 193 instead. ? A DLL is loaded twice and freed once. Is it still mapped? - No; one FreeLibrary always unmaps it - Only in Debug builds + Yes; its reference count is still 1 Each LoadLibrary is matched by one FreeLibrary. ? Why must the function pointer type match the DLL's function exactly? + The address is untyped, so a wrong cast breaks the call silently - Otherwise GetProcAddress returns NULL for that name - The DLL checks the caller's type and refuses the call GetProcAddress looks up a name only; the type exists only in your cast, so a mismatch passes arguments the wrong way with no compiler error.

title: LoadLibrary's reference counts
where: 2.03 Run-Time Loading with LoadLibrary and GetProcAddress
body: Simulate how LoadLibraryW and FreeLibrary count references. Write a class cpp class ModuleTable { public: explicit ModuleTable(std::set<std::string filesOnDisk); int load(const std::string& name); // like LoadLibraryW bool free(int handle); // like FreeLibrary int count(const std::string& name) const; bool isLoaded(const std::string& name) const; }; - load returns 0 if the file is not on disk. Otherwise, if the module is not loaded yet, it is mapped and gets a new handle: 1 for the first module ever mapped, 2 for the next, and so on (never reused). If it is already loaded, its count goes up and the same handle is returned. - free with a handle of a loaded module decreases its count; at 0 the module is unmapped. It returns false for a handle that is not loaded (including one already freed completely). - count is the current reference count, 0 if not loaded. - Names ignore case: StoneMath.dll and stonemath.DLL are the same module. A module that is unmapped and loaded again gets a new handle, just as a real DLL may land at a new address.

title: Look it up or say why
match: Look it up or say why
where: 2.03 Run-Time Loading with LoadLibrary and GetProcAddress
body: A program loads a DLL at run time and looks up several functions with GetProcAddress . If any is missing it should say which. Write cpp std::string missingFunctions(const std::set<std::string & exports, const std::vector<std::string & wanted); Return an empty string if every wanted name is exported. Otherwise return "missing: " followed by the missing names in the order they were wanted, separated by ", " . Names are case-sensitive, as GetProcAddress is. missingFunctions({ "stackHeight", "stackWeight" }, { "stackHeight", "layers", "Stackweight" }) == "missing: layers, Stackweight"

title: 2.04  DllMain and the Loader Lock
body: A DLL can have an entry point, DllMain , that Windows calls when the DLL is loaded and unloaded and when threads start and end. It runs while the loader holds a lock, which makes most interesting work inside it dangerous. This lesson shows what DllMain is for, what it must never do, and what to do instead. The entry point cpp-norun include <windows.h BOOL APIENTRY DllMain(HMODULE module, DWORD reason, LPVOID reserved) { switch (reason) { case DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH: // the DLL was just mapped into a process DisableThreadLibraryCalls(module); // we do not need the two thread notifications break; case DLL_THREAD_ATTACH: // a new thread started in the process break; case DLL_THREAD_DETACH: // a thread is ending cleanly break; case DLL_PROCESS_DETACH: // the DLL is about to be unmapped // reserved != nullptr: the whole process is exiting; reserved == nullptr: FreeLibrary break; } return TRUE; // FALSE from PROCESS_ATTACH makes the load fail (error 1114) } The template in lesson 1.03 created exactly this in dllmain.cpp . You do not have to write a DllMain ; if you do not, the C runtime supplies one. What really runs at load time Before your DllMain is called with DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH , the C runtime's own entry point ( _DllMainCRTStartup ) runs. It initialises the CRT for this DLL and then runs the constructors of the DLL's global C++ objects . At DLL_PROCESS_DETACH , after your DllMain returns, it runs their destructors . So a global like cpp-norun std::vector<std::string g_names{ "basalt", "granite" }; Logger g_log{ "stonemath.log" }; // opens a file in its constructor runs its constructor under the same conditions as DllMain , with the same rules. The loader lock While the loader maps DLLs, runs their entry points and updates its module list, it holds a process-wide lock: the loader lock . DllMain and global constructors run while it is held. Any other thread that wants to load a DLL, unload one, or even look up certain module information, waits for the lock. That makes these things dangerous inside DllMain (and in global constructors and destructors of a DLL): Do not Why --- --- Call LoadLibrary or FreeLibrary Changes the module list while it is being changed; can deadlock or load in the wrong order Create a thread and wait for it The new thread's start needs the loader lock (it sends DLL_THREAD_ATTACH ), which you hold: deadlock Wait on any lock another thread might hold while it needs the loader lock Deadlock Call into other DLLs that may not be initialised yet Only kernel32.dll is guaranteed ready Use COM, sockets, the registry, or user interface functions Each may load DLLs or wait on locks internally Microsoft's guidance is blunt: do as little as possible in DllMain . Setting variables, DisableThreadLibraryCalls , InitializeCriticalSection , TlsAlloc : fine. Anything that loads, waits or talks to other components: not fine. !warning Deadlocks here are intermittent Code that waits inside DllMain often works on your machine and hangs on someone else's, depending on timing and on which DLLs happen to be loaded already. What to do instead: explicit initialisation Give the DLL functions for setting up and tearing down, and have the program call them at a normal time: cpp-norun extern "C" STONEMATH_API int stonemath_init(const char logPath); // after LoadLibrary returns extern "C" STONEMATH_API void stonemath_shutdown(); // before FreeLibrary Inside stonemath_init , the loader lock is not held. You can open files, start worker threads and wait for them, load other DLLs, read settings. That is the pattern every plugin system in milestone 5 uses. Another useful pattern is lazy initialisation: set things up the first time a function needs them, guarded by std::call_once or a function-local static (which C++ makes thread-safe). Thread notifications DLL_THREAD_ATTACH arrives for threads started after the DLL was loaded, not for threads that already existed. DLL_THREAD_DETACH arrives when a thread ends cleanly, but not for every thread if the process is ending. Code that tries to track every thread through these notifications always has gaps; use thread-local storage ( thread_local ) instead, which the CRT manages for you. DisableThreadLibraryCalls turns the two notifications off, which saves work in programs with many threads. Process exit When the whole process exits, Windows ends every other thread first, abruptly, and then sends DLL_PROCESS_DETACH with reserved non-null. At that point other threads may have died holding locks, and memory your DLL depends on may already be gone. In that case the safest thing is to do nothing: the operating system reclaims all memory and handles anyway. Only clean up when reserved is null (an explicit FreeLibrary ). Common mistakes !warning Starting a worker thread in DllMain and joining it The join waits for a thread that is waiting for the loader lock you hold. Start and stop threads from an explicit init and shutdown function. !warning Global objects with heavy constructors in a DLL They run inside the loader lock too. Prefer creating them in an init function or on first use. Check yourself quiz ? What is the loader lock? - A lock each DLL holds while one of its exported functions is running + A process-wide lock held while modules load, unload and run DllMain - A lock that stops a DLL file on disk from being replaced while a program uses it Global constructors run under it too. Any other thread that wants to load or unload a module waits for it, which is why waiting inside DllMain is dangerous. ? Why can creating and waiting for a thread in DllMain deadlock? - Because threads cannot be created until main has started - Because the new thread runs DllMain again with DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH + The new thread needs the loader lock that the waiting DllMain holds A new thread must send DLL_THREAD_ATTACH notifications, which need the loader lock. Creating the thread is allowed; waiting for it is the problem. ? What is the alternative to doing work in DllMain? - Doing the work in DLL_THREAD_ATTACH instead - Doing the work in a global object's constructor + Init and shutdown functions the program calls, or lazy setup The program calls init after loading and shutdown before unloading, or the DLL sets itself up on first use; neither runs under the loader lock. Global constructors run under the loader lock too. ? Which of these is safe inside DllMain? + Calling DisableThreadLibraryCalls - Calling LoadLibraryW - Starting a thread and waiting for it to finish Anything that loads modules or waits for another thread can deadlock on the loader lock. ? When do the constructors of a DLL's global objects run? - When the first exported function is called + At DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH, before your DllMain - When the program's main function starts The CRT's entry point constructs globals as part of attaching the DLL, under the loader lock, then calls your DllMain. ? What should a DLL that needs worker threads do instead of starting them in DllMain? - Start them in DLL_THREAD_ATTACH - Use a global object whose constructor starts them + Offer an init function the program calls after LoadLibrary returns Outside DllMain the loader lock is not held, so waiting and loading are safe.

title: Which notifications arrive?
body: Simulate the calls a DLL's DllMain receives. Write cpp std::vector<std::string dllMainCalls(const std::vector<std::string & events, bool disableThreadCalls); events describes what happens in the process, in order: Event Meaning --- --- "thread start" a thread starts "thread end" a thread ends cleanly "load" the program calls LoadLibraryW on the DLL "free" the program calls FreeLibrary on the DLL "exit" the process exits Return the DllMain calls in order, as strings: "PROCESS_ATTACH" , "THREAD_ATTACH" , "THREAD_DETACH" , "PROCESS_DETACH" and, for process exit, "PROCESS_DETACH (exit)" . The rules: - The DLL starts unloaded. load counts references (lesson 2.03): only the first load sends PROCESS_ATTACH , and only the free that brings the count to zero sends PROCESS_DETACH . A free while unloaded does nothing. - Thread events only reach DllMain while the DLL is loaded, and only if thread calls are not disabled. - disableThreadCalls means DisableThreadLibraryCalls is called in PROCESS_ATTACH : no THREAD_ notifications at all. - exit while loaded sends PROCESS_DETACH (exit) and nothing after it is processed. exit while unloaded sends nothing, and also ends the list. dllMainCalls({ "thread start", "load", "thread start", "thread end", "free" }, false) == { "PROCESS_ATTACH", "THREAD_ATTACH", "THREAD_DETACH", "PROCESS_DETACH" } The first thread started before the DLL was loaded, so it never produces a notification.

title: Safe in DllMain?
body: Write bool safeInDllMain(const std::string& action) for a list of things a programmer might want to do in DllMain . Return true only for these, which are safe: "DisableThreadLibraryCalls" , "InitializeCriticalSection" , "TlsAlloc" , "set a variable" , "OutputDebugString" . Everything else, such as "LoadLibrary" , "CreateThread and wait" , "open a socket" or "CoInitialize" , returns false : when in doubt, do it later in an init function.

title: 2.05  Memory Across the Boundary: Who Allocates, Who Frees
match: 2.05 Memory Across the Boundary: Who Allocates, Who Frees
body: Memory allocated in one module and freed in another can crash, because each module may have its own copy of the C runtime and its own heap . The fix is a simple rule: whoever allocates, frees. This lesson shows why it breaks and the standard patterns that keep it safe. The crash A DLL function returns a string the caller should free: cpp-norun // in StoneMath.dll extern "C" STONEMATH_API char describeStack(int stones) { char text{ new char 64 }; snprintf(text, 64, "%d stones", stones); return text; } // in the program char s{ describeStack(12) }; std::cout << s << '\n'; delete s; // may crash, may corrupt memory, may seem fine Whether it works depends on how both modules were built. Why: one CRT per module, sometimes new , delete , malloc and free belong to the C runtime library (CRT). Each module chooses how it gets its CRT: Setting What the module gets --- --- /MD (Multi-threaded DLL, the default) The shared runtime DLLs ( ucrtbase.dll , vcruntime140.dll ). Modules using the same version share one heap /MT (Multi-threaded, static) Its own private copy of the CRT linked inside, with its own heap /MDd , /MTd The same, but debug versions, with a different heap layout again If the DLL is built with /MT , its new takes memory from the DLL's private heap, and the program's delete gives it back to the program's heap, which has never seen that block. If the DLL is Debug and the program is Release, the heaps disagree about the block's layout. Either way the heap is corrupted, and the crash can come much later. Even when both use /MD today, a future version of the DLL might be built with a different compiler or setting. You cannot rely on it. The rule Memory is freed by the module that allocated it. Three patterns follow from it. 1. The library frees what it allocates cpp-norun extern "C" STONEMATH_API char stonemath_describe(int stones); // caller must call stonemath_free extern "C" STONEMATH_API void stonemath_free(char text); // frees with the DLL's own delete 2. The caller provides the buffer The Win32 API's favourite: the caller owns the memory, the DLL only writes into it. cpp-norun // Returns the number of characters needed, not counting the terminating zero. // Writes at most capacity characters including the zero. extern "C" STONEMATH_API int stonemath_describe_into(int stones, char buffer, int capacity); // Asking twice: once for the size, once for the text int needed{ stonemath_describe_into(12, nullptr, 0) }; std::string text(static_cast<std::size_t (needed), '\0'); stonemath_describe_into(12, text.data(), needed + 1); The practice has you write a function with exactly this contract. 3. Objects with a create/destroy pair For anything bigger than a string, the DLL hands out an opaque handle and offers a function to release it (lesson 3.01 builds a whole API this way): cpp-norun extern "C" STONEMATH_API Xenon xenon_create(int stones); extern "C" STONEMATH_API void xenon_destroy(Xenon xenon); What about std::string and std::vector? Passing a std::string by value or reference across the boundary means one module may grow or free a buffer the other allocated. And the layout of std::string differs between Debug and Release, and has changed between compiler versions. That is lesson 2.06's topic. For now: inside a DLL, use whatever you like; at its C interface, use pointers, sizes and plain structs. Finding leaks across a boundary Because ownership is now explicit, you can track it. Keep a count of live objects in the DLL: increase it in every create function, decrease it in every destroy function, and report anything left over in stonemath_shutdown . The practice builds such a tracker. Common mistakes !warning Freeing a DLL's memory with your own free or delete Use the DLL's free function. Even if it works today, it will break when either side's build settings change. !warning Off-by-one in buffer sizes Document whether a size includes the terminating zero, and test the boundary: a buffer exactly one character too small. Check yourself quiz ? Why can freeing memory across a DLL boundary crash? - Because a DLL's memory is unmapped as soon as the function returns + The modules may use separate C runtime heaps that don't share blocks - Because delete cannot be called on memory from another module's address space So one module frees a block the other's heap never allocated. Both modules live in the same address space; the problem is two heaps (a static CRT, or Debug versus Release). ? Which set follows the rule "whoever allocates, frees"? - The DLL returns new char and the caller calls delete ; or the DLL returns a std::string + The library offers a free function; the caller provides the buffer; or objects come with a create/destroy pair - The caller allocates with new and the DLL frees with delete ; or both use malloc In each pattern the module that allocated a block is the one that frees it. ? Why not pass std::string across a DLL's C interface? - Because std::string cannot be used inside a DLL at all - Because an extern "C" function will not compile with it + Its layout and allocator can differ between the two modules So one side may misread or free the other's buffer. Inside a DLL use any C++ you like; at its C interface use pointers, sizes and plain structs. ? A DLL built with /MT allocates with new. The program frees with delete. What is wrong? + The DLL's static CRT has its own heap, separate from the program's - Nothing; new and delete always share one process heap - delete is slow across a DLL boundary but otherwise works So the program frees memory its heap never allocated. Each statically linked CRT has its own heap. ? Which interface follows the "whoever allocates, frees" rule? - A function returning new char that the caller deletes + A create function paired with a destroy function in the same DLL - A function returning std::string by value The DLL's destroy function frees with the same heap that allocated. ? In the "caller provides the buffer" pattern, why call the function first with a null buffer? - To initialise the DLL - Because the first call always fails + To find out how large a buffer is needed The caller then allocates exactly enough and calls again.

title: Track who owns what
where: 2.05 Memory Across the Boundary: Who Allocates, Who Frees
body: A DLL can catch leaks across its boundary by counting what it hands out. Write a class cpp class OwnershipTracker { public: int create(const std::string& kind); // returns a new id: 1, 2, 3... bool destroy(int id); // false if the id is not live (never made, or destroyed already) int live() const; // how many objects are live std::vector<std::string leakReport() const; // one line per live object, oldest first }; The leak report lines look like "leaked xenon 3" : the kind and the id. OwnershipTracker t; int a = t.create("xenon"); // 1 int b = t.create("text"); // 2 t.destroy(a); t.leakReport() == { "leaked text 2" }

title: 2.06  Exceptions and C++ Types at the Boundary
match: 2.06 Exceptions and C++ Types at the Boundary
body: Besides memory, two other things must not cross a stable DLL boundary - exceptions and C++ library types such as std::string . This lesson shows what goes wrong, the "exception barrier" that turns exceptions into error codes at the edge of a DLL, and the rare case where exporting C++ types is fine. Exceptions escaping a DLL Inside a DLL, use exceptions as you normally would. The problem is an exception that leaves an exported function: - A program written in C, C , Rust or Python has no idea what a C++ exception is. Its stack is unwound by machinery it never set up, and it usually crashes. - Two C++ modules built with different compilers, or different exception settings ( /EHsc versus /EHa ), may not agree on how exceptions are represented. - An exception object such as std::runtime_error contains a std::string allocated by one module's CRT and destroyed by the other's (lesson 2.05). An extern "C" function is promising C behaviour, and C has no exceptions. So the rule is: No exception crosses a DLL's C interface. Catch everything at the edge and turn it into an error code. The exception barrier Every exported function gets the same wrapper. Writing it once as a helper keeps it consistent: cpp-norun enum StonemathResult : int { STONEMATH_OK = 0, STONEMATH_INVALID_ARGUMENT = 1, STONEMATH_OUT_OF_MEMORY = 2, STONEMATH_FAILED = 3, STONEMATH_UNKNOWN_ERROR = 4, }; template <typename Fn int barrier(Fn&& body) noexcept { try { body(); return STONEMATH_OK; } catch (const std::invalid_argument&) { return STONEMATH_INVALID_ARGUMENT; } catch (const std::bad_alloc&) { return STONEMATH_OUT_OF_MEMORY; } catch (const std::exception&) { return STONEMATH_FAILED; } catch (...) { return STONEMATH_UNKNOWN_ERROR; } } extern "C" STONEMATH_API int stonemath_load(const char path, int stonesOut) { return barrier( & { if (!path !stonesOut) throw std::invalid_argument("null argument"); stonesOut = loadStonesFromFile(path); // ordinary C++ inside, may throw }); } The order of the catch clauses matters: the most specific types first, std::exception after them, and catch (...) last for anything else. noexcept on the barrier documents, and enforces, that nothing gets out. Lesson 3.02 adds a way to fetch the error's message as well. C++ types in the interface What about a DLL that exports functions like this? cpp-norun STONEMATH_API std::string describeStack(const std::vector<int & weights); It compiles, and it works as long as the DLL and every program using it are built with: - the same compiler and the same major version of its standard library; - the same configuration: std::string and std::vector have a different layout in Debug ( _ITERATOR_DEBUG_LEVEL=2 ) than in Release; - the same CRT setting ( /MD everywhere), so that one heap is shared. MSVC even helps: if you link modules with different _ITERATOR_DEBUG_LEVEL values, the linker stops with error LNK2038: mismatch detected . But that only catches modules linked together, not a DLL loaded at run time. So there are two kinds of DLL: Internal DLL Public, stable DLL --- --- --- Built Together with the program, same solution, same settings Separately, perhaps years apart, perhaps by others Interface C++: classes, std::string , exceptions are acceptable C: plain types, handles, error codes Example Splitting your own game into engine.dll and game.exe built together A plugin API, a library you sell, anything other languages call Most games' internal DLLs, and the hot-reload DLL in lesson 5.03, are the first kind. Plugin interfaces are always the second. Passing text and lists through a C interface Instead of std::string , pass a pointer and a length (or a zero-terminated string); instead of std::vector<int , a pointer and a count: cpp-norun extern "C" STONEMATH_API int stonemath_total_weight(const int weights, int count, long long totalOut); Inside, wrap them in std::string_view and std::span and you are back in comfortable C++. Common mistakes !warning Forgetting catch (...) Code you call can throw types that do not derive from std::exception . Without the last clause they escape. !warning Mixing Debug and Release modules with C++ types in the interface The layout of standard library types differs. Keep internal C++ interfaces to modules built together. Check yourself quiz ? What does an exception barrier do? - It turns on /EHa so the caller can catch the DLL's exceptions + It wraps an exported function's body in try/catch and returns an error code instead of letting any exception escape - It rethrows the DLL's exceptions as std::runtime_error so every caller sees one type It catches specific exceptions first, then std::exception , then catch (...) , and turns each into an error code. ? Which three things must match for C++ types to cross a DLL boundary safely? - The Windows version, the DLL's file name and its ordinals + Compiler and library version, build configuration and CRT setting - The calling convention, the .def file and the import library std::string and std::vector change layout between compiler versions and between Debug and Release (the iterator debug level), and the CRT setting must give one shared heap. ? How do you pass a list of numbers through a C interface? - As a std::vector<int by const reference - As a zero-terminated string of digits + As a pointer to the first element and a count A pointer and a count are plain C types any language can pass; inside, the DLL can wrap them in a std::span for comfortable C++ again. ? Why must exceptions not leave an extern "C" function? + Other callers can't handle C++ exceptions, and they cross heaps - Exceptions thrown from a DLL are much slower to catch - An extern "C" function is not allowed to contain a try block Callers written in other languages, or built differently, cannot catch C++ exceptions, and the exception object crosses heaps. Catch at the edge and return an error code; try blocks are fine inside an extern "C" function. ? In an exception barrier, why does catch (const std::exception&) come after catch (const std::invalid_argument&)? - It does not matter; the most specific clause is always chosen + Catch clauses are tried in order, so the general one would otherwise catch everything first - Because invalid_argument does not derive from std::exception Specific types first, then the base class, then catch (...). ? When is exporting std::string from a DLL acceptable? - Never; std::string cannot be exported from a DLL - Always; std::string is part of the standard library + When both sides always build together with the same settings That is an internal DLL built with the same compiler and settings as its users; a public one uses C types.

title: An exception barrier
where: 2.06 Exceptions and C++ Types at the Boundary
body: Write the barrier every exported function wraps its body in: cpp enum Result : int { RESULT_OK = 0, RESULT_INVALID_ARGUMENT = 1, RESULT_OUT_OF_MEMORY = 2, RESULT_FAILED = 3, RESULT_UNKNOWN = 4 }; int barrier(const std::function<void() & body) noexcept; It runs body and returns: - RESULT_OK if it returns normally; - RESULT_INVALID_ARGUMENT for std::invalid_argument and std::out_of_range (both mean the caller passed something bad); - RESULT_OUT_OF_MEMORY for std::bad_alloc ; - RESULT_FAILED for any other std::exception ; - RESULT_UNKNOWN for anything else that is thrown, such as an int . Then use it in an exported function: cpp extern "C" int parse_stones(const char text, int out) noexcept; It stores std::stoi(text) in out . A null text or out is an invalid argument (throw std::invalid_argument inside the barrier). std::stoi itself throws std::invalid_argument for text that is not a number and std::out_of_range for a number too large. A negative number of stones is also invalid. out is only written on success.
