title: A C interface for a C++ class
match: A C interface for a C++ class
body: You have a C++ class, StoneBag , that you want to put in a DLL so that programs in any language, built with any compiler, can use it. Write its C interface , following every rule of this milestone: - plain extern "C" functions with C types only; - an opaque handle, created and destroyed by the library (whoever allocates, frees); - no exception escapes: every function returns a result code; - text is returned through a caller-provided buffer; - the library counts live bags so leaks can be reported. The class (keep it as it is, it is the "C++ on the inside"): cpp class StoneBag { public: void add(const std::string& name, int weight); // throws std::invalid_argument for an empty name or weight <= 0 int count() const; int totalWeight() const; std::string heaviest() const; // throws std::logic_error if the bag is empty }; The C interface to write: cpp enum BagResult : int { BAG_OK = 0, BAG_INVALID_ARGUMENT = 1, BAG_EMPTY = 2, BAG_OUT_OF_MEMORY = 3, BAG_FAILED = 4 }; struct BagHandle; // opaque: callers only ever see pointers to it extern "C" int bag_create(BagHandle out); extern "C" int bag_destroy(BagHandle bag); // null is allowed and does nothing (BAG_OK) extern "C" int bag_add(BagHandle bag, const char name, int weight); extern "C" int bag_count(const BagHandle bag, int out); extern "C" int bag_total_weight(const BagHandle bag, int out); extern "C" int bag_heaviest(const BagHandle bag, char buffer, int capacity, int lengthOut); extern "C" int bag_live_count(); // how many bags exist now - Any null handle or null output pointer is BAG_INVALID_ARGUMENT . - bag_add maps std::invalid_argument from the class to BAG_INVALID_ARGUMENT . - bag_heaviest on an empty bag returns BAG_EMPTY . Otherwise it stores the name's length in lengthOut and copies the name into buffer like lesson 2.05's practice (cut off and zero-terminated if too small; nothing written if buffer is null or capacity is 0). lengthOut may not be null. - Output values are only written when the result is BAG_OK .

title: 3.01  Designing a Stable C Interface
body: A library that other programs depend on for years needs an interface that can grow without breaking them. The standard shape is a set of extern "C" functions around opaque handles , with a consistent naming scheme and clear ownership. This lesson designs one from scratch and lists the rules that keep it stable. What "stable" means A DLL interface has two kinds of compatibility: - Source compatibility : code written against version 1's header still compiles with version 2's. - Binary compatibility (the ABI ): a program already built against version 1 still works when you replace the DLL with version 2, without recompiling. Binary compatibility is the one DLLs are about, and it is much stricter. Changing a function's parameter from int to long long is fine for source code (it still compiles) and fatal for binaries (the old program passes 4 bytes; the new DLL reads 8). The opaque handle The core idea: the library's types are never visible to callers. They get a pointer to a type they cannot see inside. cpp-norun // xenon.h, the public header pragma once include <stdint.h ifdef __cplusplus extern "C" { endif typedef struct xenon_world xenon_world; // opaque: declared, never defined here XENON_API int xenon_world_create(xenon_world out); XENON_API void xenon_world_destroy(xenon_world world); XENON_API int xenon_world_add_stone(xenon_world world, int32_t x, int32_t y, int32_t weight); XENON_API int xenon_world_stone_count(const xenon_world world, int32_t out); XENON_API int xenon_world_tallest(const xenon_world world, int32_t x, int32_t y, int32_t height); ifdef __cplusplus } endif Inside the DLL: cpp-norun // xenon.cpp struct xenon_world // the real definition, only here { std::unordered_map<Point, std::vector<int , PointHash stacks; int stoneCount{ 0 }; }; Because callers never see the definition, you can change it in every version: add members, reorder them, swap the unordered_map for a grid. Their compiled code only stores a pointer. Naming Exported names share one flat namespace in the process. Prefix everything with the library's name, and name functions <library _<type _<verb : - xenon_world_create , xenon_world_destroy - xenon_world_add_stone , xenon_world_stone_count Callers can guess names, and nothing collides with another library's create . Fixed-size types int is 32 bits on Windows today, but long is 32 bits on Windows and 64 bits on Linux. For anything that crosses the boundary, use the <stdint.h types whose size is part of their name: int32_t , uint64_t , uint8_t . Use size_t only when you mean "a size in this process". Avoid bool in C interfaces (its size has varied between compilers); use int32_t with 0 and 1. Results and outputs Every function that can fail returns a result code, and returns values through out-parameters . That keeps one shape everywhere: cpp-norun int32_t count{ 0 }; if (xenon_world_stone_count(world, &count) != XENON_OK) { / handle it / } Lesson 3.02 designs the result codes and adds error messages. The stability rules Once version 1 is published: You may You may not --- --- Add new functions Remove or rename a function Add new result codes (callers must treat unknown codes as failure) Change a function's parameters or return type Change anything behind an opaque handle Change the layout of a struct callers can see (lesson 3.03 shows the safe way to grow one) Add a new enum value at the end Change the meaning or number of an existing enum value Fix bugs Change documented behaviour callers rely on If you truly must break one of these, it is a new major version (lesson 3.05), often with a new DLL name ( xenon2.dll ) so both can be installed side by side. Common mistakes !warning Putting a struct definition in the public header "just for convenience" Callers' code now knows its size and layout, so it can never change. Keep it opaque, or version it (lesson 3.03). !warning Using long or bool in the interface Their sizes are not the same everywhere. Use int32_t , int64_t , and int32_t for true/false. Check yourself quiz ? What is an opaque handle? - A small integer index that the library maps to an object in a table - A pointer to a struct whose full definition is in the public header but marked private + A pointer to a type that is declared but not defined in the public header - A void that the caller casts to the library's real struct type Callers can store and pass the pointer but never see the type's size or members, so their code never depends on its contents. ? Why prefix every exported name, as in xenon_world_create ? + All exported names share one namespace, so a prefix avoids clashes - The linker refuses to export a name shorter than a library prefix - The prefix tells the loader which DLL to search for the function - A prefix stops the C++ compiler from decorating the name Another library's create would clash with yours, and <library _<type _<verb also lets callers guess names. Name decoration is turned off by extern "C" , not by a prefix. ? Which list contains only changes that are safe after version 1 is published? - Adding a function, renaming a function, adding an enum value at the end - Adding a result code, changing a parameter from int32_t to int64_t , fixing a bug - Adding a member in the middle of a visible struct, adding a function, fixing a bug + Adding a function, adding a result code, changing what is behind an opaque handle Removing or renaming functions, changing parameter types and changing a visible struct's layout all break programs already built against version 1. ? What is binary compatibility? - Code written against the old header still compiles with the new one + Programs already compiled against the old DLL keep working with the new one, without recompiling - The old and new DLL export exactly the same list of functions That is the promise a DLL interface makes. Still compiling is source compatibility, which is weaker; the new DLL may also export more functions. ? Why can a library change everything behind an opaque handle? - Because the handle is an integer that the library looks up in a table + Because callers only hold a pointer and never see the type's size or members - Because the loader relocates the struct to match each caller's layout The callers' compiled code does not depend on the definition, so members can be added, reordered or replaced. ? Which change breaks binary compatibility? - Adding a new exported function - Adding members to a struct that is only defined inside the DLL + Changing a parameter from int32_t to int64_t - Adding a new result code that callers treat as a failure Old programs still pass 4 bytes where the new DLL reads 8. The other changes leave existing programs' compiled calls valid.

title: An opaque counter library
body: Write a small C interface around a C++ class, with an opaque handle: cpp typedef struct tally tally; // opaque extern "C" int32_t tally_create(const char name, tally out); // name must not be null or empty extern "C" void tally_destroy(tally t); // null is allowed extern "C" int32_t tally_add(tally t, int32_t amount); // amount may be negative extern "C" int32_t tally_value(const tally t, int64_t out); extern "C" int32_t tally_name_length(const tally t, int32_t out); Result codes: 0 success, 1 invalid argument (a null pointer, or an empty name). Inside, keep the running total as a 64-bit number and the name as a std::string : those details are yours to change later because callers never see them. tally_add adds to the total; the total starts at 0.

title: Is this change compatible?
body: Write bool breaksBinaryCompatibility(const std::string& change) for a published C interface. These changes break programs already compiled against it: "remove a function" , "rename a function" , "change a parameter type" , "change a return type" , "reorder struct members" , "renumber an enum value" , "change a visible struct's size" . These do not, and return false : "add a function" , "add a result code" , "change an opaque type's members" , "add an enum value at the end" , "fix a bug" . Anything not in either list: return true (assume it breaks until you have checked).

title: 3.02  Error Reporting Across a C API
match: 3.02 Error Reporting Across a C API
body: A C interface reports failure with result codes , but a code alone rarely tells a developer what went wrong. This lesson designs a result enum that can grow, adds a thread-local last error message like GetLastError , and shows how callers should handle codes they have never seen. Result codes Every function returns an int32_t result. Zero means success, which makes checks cheap and readable: cpp-norun typedef enum xenon_result { XENON_OK = 0, XENON_INVALID_ARGUMENT = 1, XENON_OUT_OF_MEMORY = 2, XENON_NOT_FOUND = 3, XENON_IO_ERROR = 4, XENON_UNSUPPORTED = 5, XENON_INTERNAL_ERROR = 99, } xenon_result; Rules for codes: - Give every value an explicit number and never change it. A program compiled against version 1 has the numbers baked in. - Only add at the end (or in gaps you reserved). - Callers must treat an unknown nonzero code as a failure. Version 3 might return XENON_RATE_LIMITED = 6 , which version 1's program has never heard of. A switch over the codes needs a default: that says "failed". The return type is int32_t , not xenon_result , because the size of a C enum is not guaranteed to be the same everywhere. Messages: a thread-local last error A code says what kind of failure. A message says what exactly : "file 'world.xenon' line 12: weight must be positive". Windows itself solves this with GetLastError ; the same pattern works for any library: cpp-norun // in the DLL namespace { thread_local std::string t_lastError; } static int32_t fail(int32_t code, std::string message) { t_lastError = std::move(message); return code; } extern "C" XENON_API int32_t xenon_world_load(xenon_world world, const char path) { if (!world !path) return fail(XENON_INVALID_ARGUMENT, "world and path must not be null"); ... } // returns the length; copies into buffer with the usual caller-buffer contract (lesson 2.05) extern "C" XENON_API int32_t xenon_last_error(char buffer, int32_t capacity); Why thread-local ? Two threads can call the library at once. With one global string, thread A's message could be overwritten by thread B's before A reads it. thread_local gives each thread its own. Should success clear the message? Windows does not (a successful call may leave the previous error), and callers should only read the message right after a failure. Either way, document it. A message for every code It also helps to have a fixed description for each code, which never changes and needs no buffer: cpp-norun extern "C" XENON_API const char xenon_result_name(int32_t code); // "XENON_OK", "XENON_INVALID_ARGUMENT", ... and "XENON_UNKNOWN_RESULT" for anything else Returning a const char to a string literal is safe across the boundary: it lives in the DLL's read-only data and is never freed. Callers must not keep it after unloading the DLL. Checking results without drowning in ifs In C++ callers, a small helper turns codes back into exceptions on their side of the boundary, where both sides of the throw are in the same module: cpp-norun inline void check(int32_t result) { if (result == XENON_OK) return; std::string message(static_cast<std::size_t (xenon_last_error(nullptr, 0)), '\0'); xenon_last_error(message.data(), static_cast<int32_t (message.size()) + 1); throw std::runtime_error(std::string(xenon_result_name(result)) + ": " + message); } check(xenon_world_load(world, "world.xenon")); Lesson 3.06 builds a full C++ wrapper this way. Common mistakes !warning A switch with no default New versions add codes. Without a default, an unknown failure is silently treated as... whatever the code after the switch does. !warning A global last-error string Threads overwrite each other's messages. Use thread_local . !warning Returning a pointer to a std::string's buffer It dangles as soon as the string changes. Return string literals, or copy into a caller buffer. Check yourself quiz ? Which set of rules keeps result codes stable across versions? - Number them automatically in the enum, add new codes in alphabetical order, and treat unknown codes as success + Give every code an explicit number that never changes, add new codes only at the end, and treat unknown nonzero codes as failure - Renumber the codes in each major version, and make callers handle every code in a switch with no default Programs built against version 1 have the numbers baked in, and later versions will return codes they have never seen. ? How does a library report a detailed error message through a C interface? - It throws a std::runtime_error carrying the message across the boundary - It returns a std::string holding the message instead of a result code + It stores a per-thread message that a function copies into a buffer - It writes the message to a global char array that every thread reads On failure it saves the message for the current thread, and a function copies it into a caller-provided buffer: the GetLastError pattern. Exceptions and std::string must not cross a C boundary, and a single global would be overwritten by other threads. ? When is returning a const char across the boundary safe? - Whenever the pointer comes from a std::string 's c_str() inside the DLL - Only if the caller frees it with free afterwards + When it points to a string literal or other data that lives as long as the DLL and is never freed A string literal sits in the DLL's read-only data. A std::string 's buffer dangles as soon as the string changes or is destroyed. ? Version 3 of a DLL returns code 6, which version 1's program does not know. What should the program do? + Treat it as a failure, because every nonzero code means failure - Treat it as success, because only codes it knows can mean failure - Retry the call until it gets a code it recognises Unknown nonzero codes must count as failures; that is what lets the set of codes grow. ? Why is the last error message stored in a thread_local variable? - To make the DLL use less memory than a global string would - Because a DLL cannot have global variables of class type + So threads calling the library at the same time cannot overwrite each other's message Each thread reads the message of its own last failure. With one global, thread B could replace thread A's message before A reads it. ? Why do the functions return int32_t rather than the xenon_result enum type? - An enum cannot be used as a return type in an extern "C" function - int32_t is faster to compare than an enum + The size of a C enum is not guaranteed to be the same for every compiler A fixed-size integer keeps the ABI exact. Returning an enum is legal C, but its size could differ between the DLL's and the caller's compiler.

title: A last-error message per thread
where: 3.02 Error Reporting Across a C API
body: Write the error-reporting half of a C library: cpp extern "C" const char lib_result_name(int32_t code); extern "C" int32_t lib_last_error(char buffer, int32_t capacity); int32_t lib_fail(int32_t code, const std::string& message); // used inside the library extern "C" int32_t lib_divide(int32_t a, int32_t b, int32_t out); // an example function that uses it - lib_result_name returns "LIB_OK" for 0, "LIB_INVALID_ARGUMENT" for 1, "LIB_DIVIDE_BY_ZERO" for 2, and "LIB_UNKNOWN_RESULT" for anything else. These are string literals, safe to return. - lib_fail stores message as the current thread's last error and returns code . - lib_last_error copies the current thread's last error into a caller buffer with the contract from lesson 2.05: returns the message length, writes a cut-off zero-terminated copy if the buffer is too small, writes nothing for a null buffer or capacity below 1. Before any failure on a thread, the message is empty. - lib_divide stores a / b in out . A null out fails with code 1 and the message "out must not be null" ; b == 0 fails with code 2 and "cannot divide <a by zero" . Success does not clear the last error.

title: 3.03  Versioned Structs and Function Tables
body: Sometimes callers need to see a struct, such as an options block. Windows' trick is to start every such struct with its own size , so the library can tell which version the caller was built with. The same idea, applied to a struct full of function pointers, gives a function table that can grow across versions. The problem with visible structs A creation function with many options is clumsy with a long parameter list. A struct is nicer: cpp-norun typedef struct xenon_world_options { int32_t width; int32_t height; int32_t gravity; } xenon_world_options; XENON_API int32_t xenon_world_create_ex(const xenon_world_options options, xenon_world out); Then version 2 needs a seed . Add it to the struct, and a program compiled against version 1 passes a 12-byte struct where version 2 reads 16. The seed comes from whatever memory follows: garbage. Size first The Win32 API's answer, used by hundreds of its structs ( cbSize in WNDCLASSEXW , dwSize in many others): the first member is the size of the struct, filled in by the caller . cpp-norun typedef struct xenon_world_options { uint32_t size; // the caller sets this to sizeof(xenon_world_options) int32_t width; // version 1 int32_t height; // version 1 int32_t gravity; // version 1 uint32_t seed; // version 2: added at the END } xenon_world_options; The caller always writes: cpp-norun xenon_world_options options{}; options.size = sizeof(options); options.width = 64; A program compiled against version 1 sets size to 16; one compiled against version 2 sets 20. The library reads only the fields that fit: cpp-norun int32_t xenon_world_create_ex(const xenon_world_options options, xenon_world out) { if (!options options- size < offsetof(xenon_world_options, seed)) return fail(XENON_INVALID_ARGUMENT, "options too small"); WorldSettings s; s.width = options- width; s.height = options- height; s.gravity = options- gravity; // a field is present if the struct reaches past its end s.seed = options- size = offsetof(xenon_world_options, seed) + sizeof(options- seed) ? options- seed : 12345u; ... } offsetof(T, member) is the byte position of a member, from <stddef.h . A member is present when size = offsetof(T, member) + sizeof(member) . The rules that make this work: - New members only ever go at the end . - Never remove, reorder or resize a member. - Every new member has a sensible default for callers who did not send it. - A size bigger than the library knows (a newer program with an older DLL) is fine: read what you know, ignore the rest. Or reject it if you cannot honour fields you do not understand; decide and document. Function tables The same trick works for a whole interface. Instead of exporting thirty functions, export one that returns a table of function pointers: cpp-norun typedef struct xenon_api { uint32_t size; // of this table uint32_t version; // e.g. 2 int32_t ( world_create)(xenon_world out); void ( world_destroy)(xenon_world world); int32_t ( world_add_stone)(xenon_world , int32_t, int32_t, int32_t); // version 2: int32_t ( world_save)(const xenon_world , const char path); } xenon_api; XENON_API const xenon_api xenon_get_api(uint32_t wantedVersion); A program asks for the version it was built for. The library returns its table if it is at least that new, or NULL if it is too old. The program checks size before touching later members. This is how Vulkan, OpenXR and many game engines expose their APIs, and it suits plugins (milestone 5): one GetProcAddress gets everything. Common mistakes !warning Forgetting to set size A zero size makes the library reject or misread the struct. Many APIs return an error for that; yours should too. !warning Inserting a new member in the middle Every member after it moves, so old programs' values land in the wrong fields. Always append. Check yourself quiz ? What are the rules for growing a versioned struct? - Add members wherever they fit best, as long as size is updated + Add members only at the end, never remove, reorder or resize one, and give each new member a default - Add members at the start so old members keep their meaning, and bump size - Replace members that are no longer needed with new ones of the same size Old programs know the old offsets, so every existing member must stay where it is, and callers that did not send a new member need a sensible default. ? How does the library decide whether a member is present in the caller's struct? - It checks that the member's value is nonzero - It compares the caller's size with sizeof of the newest struct it knows + It checks that the caller's size is at least the member's offset plus the member's size size = offsetof(T, member) + sizeof(member) . A nonzero value says nothing, and comparing with the whole newest struct would reject every older caller. ? Why are function tables popular for plugin and graphics APIs? + One exported function gives the whole interface, and the table itself can be versioned and grown - Calls through a function pointer are faster than calls through the import table - Function pointers do not need a calling convention One GetProcAddress gets everything, and the table starts with size and version like any versioned struct. ? Why does a versioned struct start with its size? - To make the struct line up on an 8-byte boundary - Because C requires the size to be the first member of a struct + So the library can tell which members the caller's version of the struct contains Old callers send smaller sizes, and the library only reads what is there. ? A member seed sits at offset 16 and is 4 bytes. The caller's size is 16. Is seed present? - Yes, because the size reaches offset 16 + No, it would need a size of at least 20 - Only if seed is nonzero Present means size = offset + sizeof(member), so 16 + 4 = 20 bytes at least. ? What does a function table export instead of many separate functions? - One DLL per function, loaded on demand - A .def file that lists every function's address + One function returning a versioned struct of function pointers The table can grow like any versioned struct, and the caller asks for the version it was built for.

title: Read a versioned options struct
body: A library's options struct has grown over three versions. Members were only ever added at the end: cpp struct WorldOptions { uint32_t size; // set by the caller to sizeof the struct it was compiled with int32_t width; // version 1 int32_t height; // version 1 int32_t gravity; // version 2 uint32_t seed; // version 3 }; Write cpp struct Settings { int32_t width; int32_t height; int32_t gravity; uint32_t seed; }; int32_t readOptions(const WorldOptions options, Settings out); - A member is present when options- size = offsetof(WorldOptions, member) + sizeof(member) . - width and height are required: a null options , a null out , or a size too small for height is an error, code 1 , and out is not written. - Missing later members get defaults: gravity 10, seed 12345. - A size larger than sizeof(WorldOptions) comes from a newer program: read what you know and ignore the rest. - Return 0 on success. Then write uint32_t versionOfSize(uint32_t size) : which version of the struct a size belongs to (1, 2 or 3; 3 for anything at least the version-3 size; 0 if smaller than version 1). Because each member's position is fixed, a version-1 caller's struct is just the first bytes of the full struct. The tests build smaller structs by setting size to what a version-1 or version-2 caller would send.

title: A versioned function table
body: A library exposes its interface as one function that returns a table of function pointers: cpp struct StoneApi { uint32_t size; uint32_t version; int32_t ( add)(int32_t, int32_t); // version 1 int32_t ( multiply)(int32_t, int32_t); // version 1 int32_t ( power)(int32_t, int32_t); // version 2 }; const StoneApi getStoneApi(uint32_t wantedVersion); Write getStoneApi for a library at version 2 : it returns a pointer to one static, fully filled table (with size set to sizeof(StoneApi) and version 2) when wantedVersion is 1 or 2, and nullptr for version 0 or anything above 2. power(b, e) raises b to the whole power e ; for e < 0 it returns 0. Then write the caller's side, which must not touch members its table lacks: cpp int32_t powerOrFallback(const StoneApi api, int32_t base, int32_t exponent); It uses api- power when the table is version 2 or newer and its size reaches past power ; otherwise it multiplies base by itself exponent times using api- multiply , starting from 1. A null api returns 0.

title: 3.04  COM-Style Interfaces with vtables
body: A C interface can still give callers objects with methods , if the object's layout is just a pointer to a table of functions. On Windows, an abstract C++ class with only virtual functions has exactly that layout, which is how COM, DirectX and many plugin systems work. This lesson builds a COM-style interface with reference counting and QueryInterface . An object is a pointer to a table Lesson 3.03's function table is close to an object already. Put the table pointer inside the object, and pass the object to each function: c typedef struct IStone IStone; typedef struct IStoneVtbl { uint32_t ( AddRef)(IStone self); uint32_t ( Release)(IStone self); int32_t ( Weight)(IStone self); } IStoneVtbl; struct IStone { const IStoneVtbl vtbl; }; // a C caller: int32_t w = stone- vtbl- Weight(stone); Now look at how MSVC lays out a C++ class that has only pure virtual functions and no data: cpp-norun struct IStone { virtual uint32_t AddRef() = 0; virtual uint32_t Release() = 0; virtual int32_t Weight() = 0; }; An IStone object is one hidden pointer, the vptr , to a table of three function pointers, in the order the functions are declared. A call stone- Weight() loads the vptr, loads entry 2, and calls it with the object pointer as the hidden first argument ( this ). That is the same layout as the C version. On Windows this layout is fixed by the platform's ABI, which is why a C++ interface like this can safely cross a DLL boundary between different compilers, and even be called from C, C , Rust or Python. What keeps it safe: - Only pure virtual functions , no data members, no constructors, and no virtual destructor : destructors' place in the vtable differs between compilers. The object deletes itself in Release . - Plain C types in every method's signature. - Never change an interface once published. Add a new interface instead ( IStone2 ), which is what QueryInterface is for. - Everything uses the __stdcall convention on 32-bit Windows (COM's STDMETHODCALLTYPE ); on x64 that does nothing. Reference counting Who deletes an object that several parts of a program hold? The object itself, when the last holder lets go. Each holder calls AddRef when it takes a reference and Release when it is done; Release deletes the object when the count reaches zero. cpp-norun class Basalt final : public IStone { public: uint32_t AddRef() override { return ++m_refs; } uint32_t Release() override { const uint32_t left{ --m_refs }; if (left == 0) delete this; // deleted by the module that created it return left; } int32_t Weight() override { return 7; } private: std::atomic<uint32_t m_refs{ 1 }; // the creator holds the first reference }; delete this inside the DLL means memory is freed by the module that allocated it (lesson 2.05) no matter who calls Release . The count is atomic so threads can share objects. QueryInterface: asking for more A later version adds a method. Changing IStone would break every compiled caller, so you define a new interface , and let callers ask an object whether it supports it: cpp-norun struct IStone2 : IStone { virtual int32_t Hardness() = 0; // appended after IStone's methods }; // Every interface identifies itself with a unique id (COM uses 128-bit GUIDs): constexpr uint32_t IID_IStone = 0x5354'0001; constexpr uint32_t IID_IStone2 = 0x5354'0002; // The base interface gains one more method, first in the table in real COM: virtual int32_t QueryInterface(uint32_t iid, void out) = 0; QueryInterface(IID_IStone2, &p) returns success and an AddRef -ed pointer if the object implements it, or "not supported" and nullptr if it does not. A caller built for version 2 asks for IStone2 ; if the DLL is older, it falls back to IStone . Old callers never ask, so nothing changes for them. Real COM's base interface is IUnknown with exactly three methods: QueryInterface , AddRef , Release . DirectX, the Windows shell and many audio APIs are built on it. You can use the pattern without any of COM's registration machinery. Smart pointers Calling AddRef and Release by hand is as error-prone as new and delete . Microsoft's Microsoft::WRL::ComPtr (and winrt::com_ptr ) call them automatically, like a std::shared_ptr whose count lives in the object. Lesson 3.06 writes a small one. Common mistakes !warning A virtual destructor in a cross-compiler interface Its vtable slot (or slots) are compiler-specific. Delete through Release instead. !warning QueryInterface that forgets to AddRef The caller will Release what it was given, which then frees the object too early. !warning Changing a published interface Add a new one. That is the whole point of QueryInterface. Check yourself quiz ? What are the three methods of IUnknown ? - Create builds the object, AddRef adds a reference, Release drops one and deletes the object at zero + QueryInterface asks for another interface the object supports, AddRef adds a reference, Release drops one and deletes the object at zero - QueryInterface asks for another interface, AddRef adds a reference, and a virtual destructor deletes the object Every COM-style interface starts with these three. There is no virtual destructor: the object deletes itself in Release . ? How do COM-style interfaces gain new methods without breaking old callers? - New methods are appended to the published interface, since old callers never call them - The interface is changed and its DLL is renamed for each new method + A published interface never changes; new methods go in a new interface that callers request with QueryInterface Even appending changes the published table that old code was compiled against; a new interface such as IStone2 keeps the old one exactly as it was. ? Why does Release call delete this instead of the caller deleting the object? - Because delete cannot be called on a pointer to an abstract class + So the memory is freed by the module that allocated it, whoever releases the last reference - Because delete this is faster than calling delete from outside - So the object can be deleted even while other holders still use it Freeing in the DLL that called new avoids the mismatched-heap crash from lesson 2.05, and it only happens when the count reaches zero. ? Why can an abstract class with only pure virtual functions cross a DLL boundary between compilers on Windows? + Its layout, a vptr to a table in declaration order, is fixed by the ABI - Because pure virtual functions never get name-mangled - Because the compiler checks each caller's layout at run time The platform ABI fixes it as a single vptr to a table of function pointers in declaration order, the same layout as a C struct holding a pointer to a table of function pointers. ? Who deletes a reference-counted object? - Whoever created it, always, with delete - The last caller that used it, with delete + The object itself, in Release , when the count reaches zero delete this runs inside the module that allocated it, so no caller ever deletes it directly. ? A caller asks QueryInterface for an interface the object does not implement. What should it get? - A pointer to the base interface instead, already AddRef -ed + A "not supported" result and a null pointer - A success result and a null pointer The caller can then fall back to an older interface. Returning a different interface would let it call methods that are not there.

title: A COM-style stone
body: Implement a COM-style object with reference counting and QueryInterface : cpp constexpr uint32_t IID_IStone = 1; constexpr uint32_t IID_IStone2 = 2; constexpr int32_t OK = 0, NOT_SUPPORTED = 1, INVALID_ARGUMENT = 2; struct IStone { virtual int32_t QueryInterface(uint32_t iid, void out) = 0; virtual uint32_t AddRef() = 0; virtual uint32_t Release() = 0; virtual int32_t Weight() = 0; }; struct IStone2 : IStone { virtual int32_t Hardness() = 0; }; int32_t CreateStone(int32_t weight, int32_t hardness, IStone out); int liveStones(); - CreateStone makes a stone that implements both interfaces and hands back an IStone holding one reference. If hardness is 0 or less, make a plainer stone that implements only IStone (asking it for IStone2 must fail). A null out is INVALID_ARGUMENT . - AddRef and Release return the new count. Release deletes the object at 0. - QueryInterface(iid, &p) : for a supported interface, set p to the object as that interface, AddRef it , return OK . Otherwise set p to nullptr and return NOT_SUPPORTED . A null out is INVALID_ARGUMENT . - liveStones() returns how many stone objects exist right now (increase in the constructor, decrease in the destructor), so tests can check nothing leaks.

title: 3.05  Versioning and Compatibility
body: A version number is a promise about compatibility. Semantic versioning turns that promise into rules: major for breaking changes, minor for additions, patch for fixes. This lesson applies it to DLLs, shows how a program checks the version it got at run time, and covers side-by-side installs for breaking changes. Semantic versioning A version is three numbers, MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH , such as 2.4.1 : Part Increase it when Example --- --- --- MAJOR You break compatibility: remove or change a function, change a visible struct 2.4.1 to 3.0.0 MINOR You add something without breaking anything: new functions, new codes, new struct fields at the end 2.4.1 to 2.5.0 PATCH You fix bugs without changing the interface 2.4.1 to 2.4.2 Increasing one part resets the parts after it to 0. A version can carry a pre-release label after a hyphen, 3.0.0-beta.2 , which sorts before 3.0.0 . For a DLL, this tells users exactly what is safe: A program built against version X.Y.Z works with any DLL version X.y.z where y.z ≥ Y.Z : the same major version, and at least as new. A newer minor version only adds things the old program does not use. An older minor version might lack a function the program needs. A different major version may have changed anything. Comparing versions Versions compare part by part, as numbers , not as text. As strings, "2.10.0" < "2.9.0" because '1' < '9' ; as versions, 2.10.0 is newer. The practice has you write this comparison properly. Checking at run time Load-time linking catches a missing function (the program will not start), but not a function whose behaviour changed in a breaking way. So well-behaved libraries let callers check: cpp-norun define XENON_VERSION_MAJOR 2 define XENON_VERSION_MINOR 4 define XENON_VERSION_PATCH 1 // The version of the DLL actually loaded, packed as major << 22 minor << 12 patch XENON_API uint32_t xenon_version(void); The header's macros say which version the program was compiled against; the function says which DLL it is running with: cpp-norun const uint32_t running{ xenon_version() }; const uint32_t major{ running 22 }, minor{ (running 12) & 0x3FF }; if (major != XENON_VERSION_MAJOR minor < XENON_VERSION_MINOR) { std::cerr << "This program needs xenon " << XENON_VERSION_MAJOR << '.' << XENON_VERSION_MINOR << " or newer\n"; return 1; } Packing the three parts into one integer, as Vulkan does, makes the version easy to pass around and compare: with 10 bits for minor and 12 for patch, a larger packed number is always a newer version. When you must break things Sometimes a major version is unavoidable. Then change the DLL's file name along with it: xenon2.dll . Programs built for version 1 keep loading xenon.dll ; programs built for version 2 load xenon2.dll ; both can be installed together. That is how the Visual C++ runtime does it ( msvcp140.dll versus the older msvcp120.dll ) and how Windows' own system DLLs stay compatible for decades. The alternative, replacing xenon.dll with an incompatible one, is what was once called DLL Hell : installing one program broke another that used the same file name with different expectations. The file version resource Windows also stores a version number inside the DLL file as a resource, shown in Explorer's Properties, Details tab. Lesson 4.04 adds one to your build. It is for people and installers; your code should check versions through its own function as above. Common mistakes !warning Comparing version strings as text "2.10" sorts before "2.9". Split them and compare numbers. !warning Shipping a breaking change as a minor version Every program built for the previous minor version may now fail. If you broke something, it is a major version. Check yourself quiz ? What does each part of MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH mean for a DLL? - Major: a new feature; minor: a bug fix; patch: a rebuild with no source change - Major: a new release year; minor: a new feature or a breaking change; patch: a bug fix + Major: a breaking change; minor: additions that keep compatibility; patch: fixes with no interface change Only a major increase may break programs built against earlier versions; adding functions is a minor increase. ? What is the compatibility rule for a program built against version X.Y.Z? + It works with any DLL that has the same major X and a minor.patch of at least Y.Z - It works with any DLL whose version is at least X.Y.Z, whatever the major number - It works only with exactly version X.Y.Z - It works with any DLL that has the same major X, older or newer A newer minor only adds things; an older minor might lack a function the program needs; a different major may have changed anything. ? What was DLL Hell, and how does renaming the DLL for a new major version avoid it? - Programs could not find DLLs outside the system folder; a new name puts the DLL in the search order + Installers replaced a shared DLL with an incompatible one of the same name; a new name lets both versions be installed side by side - DLLs from two compilers clashed in one process; a new name gives each its own CRT Programs built for version 1 keep loading xenon.dll while version 2 programs load xenon2.dll , as the Visual C++ runtime does with msvcp140.dll . ? A DLL adds two new functions and changes nothing else. Its version was 1.6.3. What is the next version? - 2.0.0 - 1.6.4 + 1.7.0 - 1.7.3 Additions without breaks are a minor increase, which resets the patch number to 0. ? A program was built against version 2.3.0. Which DLL version works with it? + 2.5.1 - 2.2.9 - 3.0.0 It needs the same major and at least 2.3.0. 2.2.9 is too old and may lack a function; 3.0.0 may have broken anything. ? How do you ship a breaking version without breaking programs that use the old one? - Overwrite the old DLL and increase the minor number - Keep the file name and only increase the patch number + Give the new major version a different DLL file name so both can be installed Old programs keep loading the old file, so nothing they rely on changes.

title: Semantic versions
body: Write the version tools a library and its callers need: cpp struct Version { int major{ 0 }; int minor{ 0 }; int patch{ 0 }; std::string pre; }; bool parseVersion(const std::string& text, Version& out); int compareVersions(const Version& a, const Version& b); // -1, 0 or 1 bool compatible(const Version& builtAgainst, const Version& running); std::string nextVersion(const Version& current, const std::string& change); - parseVersion accepts MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH with non-negative whole numbers and no leading zeros (except 0 itself), optionally followed by - and a non-empty label: 2.4.1 , 3.0.0-beta.2 . Anything else returns false . - compareVersions compares major, minor, patch as numbers . With those equal, a version with a pre-release label is older than one without; two labels compare as plain strings. - compatible : the running version has the same major as the one the program was built against and is not older than it. - nextVersion(current, change) for change "break" , "add" or "fix" returns the next version as text, with no label: 1.6.3 + "add" is "1.7.0" . compareVersions(2.10.0, 2.9.0) == 1 compatible(2.3.0, 2.5.1) == true compatible(2.3.0, 3.0.0) == false

Write cpp uint32_t packVersion(uint32_t major, uint32_t minor, uint32_t patch); void unpackVersion(uint32_t packed, uint32_t& major, uint32_t& minor, uint32_t& patch); Values that do not fit are cut to their field width: minor & 0x3FF , patch & 0xFFF .

title: 3.06  Wrapping a C API in Modern C++
match: 3.06 Wrapping a C API in Modern C++
body: A stable C interface is pleasant for the DLL and other languages, but tedious to use from C++. The answer is a thin header-only C++ wrapper on the caller's side - RAII classes that create and destroy handles, exceptions instead of result codes, std::string instead of buffers - while the DLL boundary stays pure C. Both worlds You now have a C interface that is safe across compilers and languages. Using it directly from C++ looks like this: cpp-norun xenon_world world{ nullptr }; if (xenon_world_create(&world) != XENON_OK) { / ... / } if (xenon_world_add_stone(world, 3, 4, 7) != XENON_OK) { xenon_world_destroy(world); / ... / } int32_t count{ 0 }; if (xenon_world_stone_count(world, &count) != XENON_OK) { xenon_world_destroy(world); / ... / } xenon_world_destroy(world); Every early return has to remember the destroy call. C++ programmers would rather write: cpp-norun xenon::World world; world.addStone(3, 4, 7); std::cout << world.stoneCount() << '\n'; A header-only wrapper Put a C++ wrapper in a second header, xenon.hpp , that includes xenon.h . Because it is header-only , its code compiles into the caller's module, with the caller's compiler and settings. Nothing C++ crosses the boundary: the wrapper only calls the C functions. cpp-norun // xenon.hpp pragma once include "xenon.h" include <stdexcept include <string include <utility namespace xenon { class Error : public std::runtime_error { public: Error(int32_t code, const std::string& what) : std::runtime_error(what), m_code{ code } {} int32_t code() const noexcept { return m_code; } private: int32_t m_code; }; inline void check(int32_t result) { if (result == XENON_OK) return; std::string message(static_cast<std::size_t (xenon_last_error(nullptr, 0)), '\0'); xenon_last_error(message.data(), static_cast<int32_t (message.size()) + 1); throw Error(result, std::string(xenon_result_name(result)) + ": " + message); } class World { public: World() { check(xenon_world_create(&m_handle)); } ~World() { xenon_world_destroy(m_handle); } World(World&& other) noexcept : m_handle{ std::exchange(other.m_handle, nullptr) } {} World& operator=(World&& other) noexcept { if (this != &other) { xenon_world_destroy(m_handle); m_handle = std::exchange(other.m_handle, nullptr); } return this; } World(const World&) = delete; World& operator=(const World&) = delete; void addStone(int32_t x, int32_t y, int32_t weight) { check(xenon_world_add_stone(m_handle, x, y, weight)); } int32_t stoneCount() const { int32_t n{ 0 }; check(xenon_world_stone_count(m_handle, &n)); return n; } xenon_world get() const noexcept { return m_handle; } // for calling C functions the wrapper lacks private: xenon_world m_handle{ nullptr }; }; } The pieces: - RAII : the constructor creates, the destructor destroys. No path can forget. - Move-only : copying would mean two objects destroying the same handle. A move transfers the handle and leaves the source empty, so its destructor does nothing ( xenon_world_destroy(nullptr) must be allowed, which lesson 2.05's project required). - Exceptions on the caller's side : check turns a result code into an exception thrown and caught entirely in the caller's module, which is perfectly safe. - get() keeps the escape hatch open. A reference-counted handle For COM-style objects (lesson 3.04), the wrapper is a smart pointer that calls AddRef and Release : cpp-norun template <typename T class RefPtr { public: RefPtr() = default; explicit RefPtr(T adopt) noexcept : m_p{ adopt } {} // takes over an existing reference RefPtr(const RefPtr& o) noexcept : m_p{ o.m_p } { if (m_p) m_p- AddRef(); } RefPtr(RefPtr&& o) noexcept : m_p{ std::exchange(o.m_p, nullptr) } {} ~RefPtr() { if (m_p) m_p- Release(); } RefPtr& operator=(RefPtr o) noexcept { std::swap(m_p, o.m_p); return this; } T operator- () const noexcept { return m_p; } T get() const noexcept { return m_p; } private: T m_p{ nullptr }; }; Copying adds a reference, destroying releases one. The practice asks you to write the move-only kind for a C handle. Common mistakes !warning Putting the wrapper's code in the DLL Then C++ types cross the boundary again. Keep the wrapper header-only, compiled by the caller. !warning A copyable wrapper around a handle Two copies, two destroy calls, one crash. Delete the copy operations or count references. Check yourself quiz ? What does a header-only C++ wrapper add on top of a C interface? - A second DLL that exports C++ classes alongside the C functions + RAII handles, exceptions and C++ types, compiled into the caller - A faster calling convention for the C functions it wraps It gives RAII ownership of handles, exceptions instead of result codes, and types such as std::string . Its code is compiled by the caller, so only the C functions cross the boundary. ? What must the C destroy function accept for move-only wrappers to be simple? + A null handle, doing nothing, so a moved-from wrapper can be destroyed safely - The same handle twice, ignoring the second call - A handle together with its size, so it knows how much to free After a move the source holds nullptr , and its destructor still calls xenon_world_destroy . ? How does a reference-counting smart pointer such as RefPtr behave on copy and on destruction? - A copy calls Release on the old pointer; destruction calls delete - A copy duplicates the object; destruction calls Release on each copy + A copy calls AddRef ; destruction calls Release Each holder owns one reference, and the object deletes itself in Release when the count reaches zero. ? Why is the C++ wrapper header-only? - Header files compile faster than .cpp files do - A DLL cannot contain any C++ code, only C + It compiles into the caller, so only C crosses over The wrapper's code is built into the caller's module with the caller's compiler and settings, so only C crosses the DLL boundary and its C++ types never meet another module's. ? Why is the World wrapper move-only? + A copy would destroy the same handle twice - Moving is the only way to return a class from a function - The C handle cannot be stored in a member that is copied Ownership of a handle must belong to exactly one object; a move hands it over and leaves the source empty. ? Is it safe for the wrapper's check function to throw an exception? - No; exceptions must never be used in a program that uses DLLs + Yes; it is thrown and caught in the caller's module, never across the DLL boundary - Only if the DLL was built with the same compiler as the caller The rule is about exceptions leaving the DLL, not about the caller's own code.

title: A move-only handle wrapper

body: Here is a C interface (already written, in the starter) that counts how many handles exist: cpp typedef struct counter counter; extern "C" int32_t counter_create(counter out); extern "C" void counter_destroy(counter c); // null is fine extern "C" int32_t counter_add(counter c, int32_t n); extern "C" int32_t counter_value(const counter c, int32_t out); int liveCounters(); Write a C++ wrapper class Counter on top of it: - The constructor creates a handle; if counter_create fails, it throws std::runtime_error . - The destructor destroys the handle. - It is move-only : copying is deleted; moving transfers the handle and leaves the moved-from object empty ( get() returns nullptr ), so it destroys nothing. - Move assignment destroys the handle it held before taking the new one, and is safe for self-assignment. - void add(int32_t n) and int32_t value() const call the C functions and throw std::runtime_error on a nonzero result (including use of an empty, moved-from object). - counter get() const noexcept . The tests use liveCounters() to check every handle is destroyed exactly once.

title: A library that can grow
body: Design and write version 2.1.0 of a small library, quarry , so that programs built against version 1.x of its interface and programs built against 2.x both work with it. Everything you need is in this milestone. The public interface (already declared in the starter) has: cpp // result codes: never renumbered enum : int32_t { QUARRY_OK = 0, QUARRY_INVALID_ARGUMENT = 1, QUARRY_NOT_FOUND = 2, QUARRY_UNSUPPORTED = 3 }; // a versioned options struct: version 1 had size, capacity; version 2 added depth at the end struct quarry_options { uint32_t size; int32_t capacity; int32_t depth; }; typedef struct quarry quarry; // opaque // a versioned function table struct quarry_api { uint32_t size; uint32_t version; // 1 or 2 int32_t ( create)(const quarry_options options, quarry out); // v1 void ( destroy)(quarry q); // v1 int32_t ( dig)(quarry q, const char stone); // v1 int32_t ( count)(const quarry q, const char stone, int32_t out); // v1 int32_t ( depth)(const quarry q, int32_t out); // v2 }; extern "C" uint32_t quarry_version(); // packed like lesson 3.05 extern "C" const quarry_api quarry_get_api(uint32_t major); // 1 or 2, else null extern "C" int32_t quarry_last_error(char buffer, int32_t capacity); // per thread, caller buffer What the functions do: - create : needs options and out ; options- size must cover capacity , and capacity must be at least 1, else QUARRY_INVALID_ARGUMENT . depth is read only if the caller's struct has it; the default is 3. A depth below 1 is invalid too. - dig(q, stone) records one stone of that kind (a non-empty name). It fails with QUARRY_UNSUPPORTED and the message "quarry is full" when the total number of stones would go above capacity . - count gives how many stones of that kind were dug; a kind never dug is QUARRY_NOT_FOUND . - depth (version 2 only) gives the depth the quarry was created with. - Every failure sets the thread's last-error message; use "<name must not be null" for null pointers (name being the parameter's name), and pick clear messages for the rest. Tests check the messages for null q in dig ( "q must not be null" ) and the full quarry. - quarry_version() is 2.1.0 packed as major << 22 minor << 12 patch . - quarry_get_api(1) must return a table a version-1 program can use safely: version 1 and a size that ends before depth . quarry_get_api(2) returns the full table with version 2.

title: 4.01  The DLL Search Order
body: When a program asks for a DLL by name rather than by full path, Windows tries a fixed list of places. Knowing that list explains why the wrong copy of a DLL sometimes loads, why "it works on my machine", and why putting your DLLs next to your .exe is the reliable choice. A name, not a path Most DLLs are requested by name only: the import table of your .exe says StoneMath.dll , and LoadLibraryW(L"StoneMath.dll") gives no folder either. Windows then has to decide which file that means. Before any folder is searched Two checks come first: 1. Already loaded? If a module with that name is already in the process, it is reused. This is why loading StoneMath.dll from two places never gives you two copies: the second request finds the first. 2. Known DLLs. Windows keeps a list of core system DLLs ( kernel32.dll , user32.dll , ole32.dll and others, listed in the registry under KnownDLLs ). For those it always uses the copy in System32 , whatever folders come later. You cannot override kernel32.dll by putting a file next to your program. (There are also API sets , the api-ms-win-... names from lesson 1.06, which are redirected to real system DLLs without any search.) The standard search order If neither check settles it, a desktop application searches these places in order, and loads the first file with that name it finds: 1. The folder the application's .exe is in. 2. The system folder , C:\Windows\System32 . 3. The 16-bit system folder, C:\Windows\System . 4. The Windows folder , C:\Windows . 5. The current directory (the program's working directory). 6. Every folder on the PATH environment variable, in order. This is the order with safe DLL search mode , which has been on by default for many years. Without it, the current directory was searched second, which is why it was moved down: an attacker who could put a file in your working directory (a downloaded folder, a network share) could get it loaded before the system's copy. Lesson 4.02 goes further. What this means in practice - Put your DLLs next to your .exe . The application folder is searched first, so your copy wins, and the program works no matter what the user's PATH or working directory is. - Never rely on the current directory. It changes with shortcuts, command lines and file dialogs. - Never rely on PATH for your own DLLs. It is the last place searched and differs on every machine. Something earlier on PATH with the same name wins, which is the classic "works on my machine" story. - Avoid generic names. utils.dll or zlib.dll may already be loaded into the process by some other component, and Windows will happily give you that one instead (check 1 above). Seeing the search happen Process Monitor (lesson 1.06) shows every attempt. A program in C:\Games\Xenon asking for missing.dll produces a trail like: varies C:\Games\Xenon\missing.dll NAME NOT FOUND C:\Windows\System32\missing.dll NAME NOT FOUND C:\Windows\System\missing.dll NAME NOT FOUND C:\Windows\missing.dll NAME NOT FOUND C:\Users\you\Desktop\missing.dll NAME NOT FOUND (the current directory) C:\Program Files\Git\cmd\missing.dll NAME NOT FOUND (PATH...) A dependency's dependencies When StoneMath.dll itself imports zlib.dll , the same search runs, still based on the application's folder, not the folder StoneMath.dll came from. So if you load a DLL from a subfolder by full path, its own dependencies are not found in that subfolder unless you say so. Lesson 4.02 shows the flags that fix this, and lesson 5.01 uses them for plugins in their own folders. Common mistakes !warning Testing only on the development machine Your PATH contains Visual Studio, SDKs and tools with DLLs in them. A clean machine has none of that. Test there before shipping. !warning Assuming a DLL from a subfolder finds its friends in that subfolder Its dependencies are searched for from the application's folder. Use full paths and the search flags from lesson 4.02. Check yourself quiz ? What is the standard search order for a desktop application (with safe DLL search mode)? - Current directory, application folder, System32, the Windows folder, then PATH - Application folder, current directory, System32, the 16-bit System folder, the Windows folder, then PATH + Application folder, System32, the 16-bit System folder, the Windows folder, the current directory, then PATH - System32, the Windows folder, application folder, PATH, then the current directory The current directory was moved down to fifth place by safe DLL search mode, and PATH is always searched last. ? Which two checks come before any folder is searched? + Whether a module with that name is already loaded, and whether it is one of the known DLLs - Whether the file is digitally signed, and whether it is in the application folder - Whether the name is on PATH, and whether the DLL's version matches the import library A module already in the process is reused, and known DLLs such as kernel32.dll always come from System32 . ? Why is relying on PATH for your own DLLs a bad idea? - PATH folders are only searched for 32-bit programs - Windows refuses to load a DLL found through PATH unless it is signed + It is searched last and differs per machine, so the wrong DLL can win Something earlier on PATH with the same name wins, or none is found at all: the classic "works on my machine" story. Put your DLLs next to the .exe instead. ? Where does Windows look first for a DLL requested by name, after the already-loaded and known-DLL checks? - The program's current directory + The folder of the application's .exe - The folders listed on PATH - C:\Windows\System32 That is why shipping DLLs next to the .exe is reliable. ? Why was the current directory moved later in the search order? - To make loading faster, because the current directory is often on a slow drive + A file planted in the working directory could otherwise be loaded before the real system DLL - Because the current directory is usually empty That change is safe DLL search mode. The working directory may be a downloaded folder or a network share that someone else controls. ? Can you replace kernel32.dll by putting your own copy next to your program? - Yes, the application folder is searched first - Only for 32-bit programs + No; it is a known DLL and always loaded from System32 Known DLLs bypass the folder search entirely.

title: Which file gets loaded?
body: Simulate the standard DLL search order for a request by name. Write cpp struct Machine { std::string appDir; // e.g. "C:\\Games\\Xenon" std::string currentDir; std::vector<std::string pathDirs; // PATH, in order std::set<std::string files; // every file that exists, as full paths std::set<std::string knownDlls; // names of known DLLs std::set<std::string alreadyLoaded; // full paths of modules already in the process }; std::string findDll(const Machine& m, const std::string& name); Return the full path that would be loaded, or an empty string if none is found. Folders are joined to the name with one backslash: appDir + "\\" + name . The order: 1. Already loaded : if any full path in alreadyLoaded ends with "\\" + name , return that path. 2. Known DLLs : if name is in knownDlls , return "C:\\Windows\\System32\\" + name (whether or not it is in files ). 3. Then the first folder, in this order, where the file exists: appDir , C:\Windows\System32 , C:\Windows\System , C:\Windows , currentDir , then each folder of pathDirs . Upper and lower case do matter in this simulation: compare names exactly.

title: 4.02  Loading Only the Files You Mean
match: 4.02 Loading Only the Files You Mean
body: Loading a DLL by bare name leaves the choice of file to the search order, which an attacker or an accident can influence. This lesson shows how to load exactly the file you intend - full paths, SetDefaultDllDirectories , AddDllDirectory and the LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_ flags - and how to check a plugin folder before loading anything from it. The risk If a program loads renderer.dll by name and that name is not found in the application folder, Windows keeps searching, eventually in the current directory and on PATH. Anyone who can put a file called renderer.dll in one of those places gets their code run inside your program. This is called DLL planting or DLL search-order hijacking , and it has been the cause of many real security problems. Accidents follow the same path: an old copy of a DLL in some folder on PATH gets loaded instead of yours. The defence is the same for both: never let Windows guess . 1. Use full paths for run-time loading Build the path from a folder you trust, normally the application's own: cpp-norun include <windows.h include <filesystem std::filesystem::path appFolder() { wchar_t buffer MAX_PATH {}; const DWORD length{ GetModuleFileNameW(nullptr, buffer, MAX_PATH) }; // full path of our own .exe return std::filesystem::path(std::wstring(buffer, length)).parent_path(); } HMODULE renderer{ LoadLibraryW((appFolder() / L"renderer.dll").c_str()) }; GetModuleFileNameW(nullptr, ...) returns the path of the .exe . With a full path, LoadLibraryW loads exactly that file (or fails). 2. Restrict the search for everything else Even with full paths for your own DLLs, those DLLs import others by name. Call this once, first thing in main : cpp-norun SetDefaultDllDirectories(LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DEFAULT_DIRS); From then on, every name-only load in the process searches only: - the application folder ( LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_APPLICATION_DIR ), - System32 ( LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_SYSTEM32 ), - folders you add yourself with AddDllDirectory ( LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_USER_DIRS ). The current directory and PATH are not searched any more. For a new program there is no reason not to do this. 3. LoadLibraryExW with search flags LoadLibraryExW takes flags that control the search for one call: cpp-norun HMODULE m{ LoadLibraryExW(path, nullptr, LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DLL_LOAD_DIR LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DEFAULT_DIRS) }; Flag Searches --- --- LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_APPLICATION_DIR The .exe 's folder LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_SYSTEM32 System32 LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_USER_DIRS Folders added with AddDllDirectory LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DLL_LOAD_DIR The folder of the DLL being loaded (only with a full path) LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DEFAULT_DIRS The first three together LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DLL_LOAD_DIR solves lesson 4.01's subfolder problem: a plugin loaded from plugins\fog\fog.dll can now find plugins\fog\noise.dll , which it depends on. 4. Check what you are about to load A plugin folder is a place users (and installers) write files to. Before loading, check: - the path is absolute and really inside the folder you meant (no .. escaping out of it); - the file name ends in .dll ; - for software you distribute widely, that the file is signed with your certificate ( WinVerifyTrust ), so a replaced file is refused. Lesson 5.01's plugin loader does the first two; the practice for this lesson writes the path check. Data files that look like DLLs If you only want to read a DLL's resources (icons, strings, version info) without running any of its code, load it as data: cpp-norun HMODULE resources{ LoadLibraryExW(path, nullptr, LOAD_LIBRARY_AS_DATAFILE LOAD_LIBRARY_AS_IMAGE_RESOURCE) }; No DllMain runs and nothing is executable. Common mistakes !warning Calling SetDefaultDllDirectories after DLLs were already loaded by name It only affects loads that happen after it. Call it at the very start. !warning Building a plugin path from user input without checking it "..\\..\\Windows\\something.dll" escapes the plugin folder. Normalise the path and check its parent. Check yourself quiz ? Which three things together make a program load only the DLLs it means? - Putting every DLL in System32 , adding its folder to PATH, and loading it by name + Full paths from trusted folders, SetDefaultDllDirectories , and checked files - Loading every DLL with LOAD_LIBRARY_AS_DATAFILE , then calling GetProcAddress on it Full paths from a trusted folder stop guessing for run-time loads, SetDefaultDllDirectories at start-up restricts the search for name-only imports, and checking files before loading protects folders users can write to. ? How do you get the folder of your own .exe ? - Read the current directory with std::filesystem::current_path() - Take the first folder on the PATH environment variable + Call GetModuleFileNameW with a null module handle, then take the parent folder The current directory changes with shortcuts and file dialogs; GetModuleFileNameW(nullptr, ...) always gives the .exe 's own path. ? How do you read a DLL's resources without running its code? + LoadLibraryExW with LOAD_LIBRARY_AS_DATAFILE - LoadLibraryW , then skip calling any of its functions - LoadLibraryExW with LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DLL_LOAD_DIR Usually together with LOAD_LIBRARY_AS_IMAGE_RESOURCE . Loaded as data, no DllMain runs and nothing is executable; a plain LoadLibraryW still runs its DllMain . ? What does SetDefaultDllDirectories(LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DEFAULT_DIRS) remove from the search? - System32 and the known DLLs + The current directory and the PATH folders - The application's own folder Only the application folder, System32 and folders added with AddDllDirectory remain. ? A plugin loaded by full path from plugins\fog needs noise.dll from the same folder. Which flag helps? - LOAD_LIBRARY_AS_DATAFILE - LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_SYSTEM32 + LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DLL_LOAD_DIR - LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_APPLICATION_DIR It adds the loaded DLL's own folder to the search for its dependencies; the application folder flag would look next to the .exe instead. ? What is DLL planting? - Copying your own DLLs into System32 so every program can find them + Placing a file with a DLL's name where the search order finds it before the real one - Linking a DLL statically into the .exe Full paths and restricted search directories prevent it.

title: Is this plugin path safe?

A .. that would go above the drive (or above the start of a relative path) makes the whole result empty, "" . safePluginPath(folder, candidate) is true only if: - candidate is absolute : it starts with a drive letter, a colon and a backslash or slash ( C:\... ); - after normalising both, the candidate is inside the folder: it starts with the folder followed by \ (comparison ignores upper and lower case, as Windows does); - its file name ends with .dll (any case). normalizePath("C:\\Games//Xenon\\plugins\\.\\fog\\..\\fog.dll") == "C:\\Games\\Xenon\\plugins\\fog.dll" safePluginPath("C:\\Games\\Xenon\\plugins", "C:\\Games\\Xenon\\plugins\\..\\..\\Windows\\evil.dll") == false
