title: 4.03  Delay Loading
body: Delay loading gives you the convenience of linking against an import library with the timing of run-time loading. The DLL is loaded the first time one of its functions is called, not when the program starts. This lesson shows how to turn it on, what happens on the first call, and how to handle a DLL that turns out to be missing. Between the two Load time Delay load Run time --- --- --- --- Write code with Normal calls Normal calls LoadLibraryW and GetProcAddress DLL loaded Before main On the first call into it When you ask Missing DLL Program does not start An exception on the first call NULL , you decide Delay loading is ideal for a DLL that only some users need: an exporter for one file format, a voice-chat library, a crash reporter. The program starts faster and works without it, and your code still calls its functions normally. Turning it on Two linker settings on the program (nothing changes in the DLL): - Linker, Input, Delay Loaded Dlls : StoneMath.dll (this adds /DELAYLOAD:StoneMath.dll ). - Linker, Input, Additional Dependencies : add delayimp.lib , the helper library that does the loading. Keep linking StoneMath.lib as before. Your code does not change at all. What happens on the first call The linker writes each delay-loaded import with a placeholder that points at a small thunk instead of the real function. On the first call: 1. The thunk calls the delay-load helper, __delayLoadHelper2 . 2. The helper loads the DLL with LoadLibrary (if this is the first function from it) and finds the function with GetProcAddress . 3. It writes the real address into the delay-load import table, so the next call goes straight to the function. 4. It jumps to the function. So the first call is slower, every later call is as fast as a normal import. The practice simulates exactly this: a slot that resolves itself once. When the DLL is missing With load-time linking, a missing DLL stops the program before main . With delay loading, the problem appears on the first call, as a structured exception (not a C++ exception) with the code VcppException(ERROR_SEVERITY_ERROR, ERROR_MOD_NOT_FOUND) , or ERROR_PROC_NOT_FOUND for a missing function. Two ways to handle it: Check first. Before calling into the DLL, try to load it yourself: cpp-norun bool stoneMathAvailable() { // Loads the delay-loaded DLL now, or returns a failure instead of an exception. return SUCCEEDED(__HrLoadAllImportsForDll("StoneMath.dll")); } A failure hook. The helper calls a function you provide when loading fails, which can return a fallback: cpp-norun include <delayimp.h FARPROC WINAPI onDelayLoadFailure(unsigned notification, PDelayLoadInfo info) { if (notification == dliFailGetProc && std::strcmp(info- dlp.szProcName, "stackWeight") == 0) return reinterpret_cast<FARPROC (&fallbackStackWeight); // used instead of the missing function return nullptr; // nullptr: raise the exception as usual } ExternC const PfnDliHook __pfnDliFailureHook2 = onDelayLoadFailure; Unloading A delay-loaded DLL can also be unloaded with __FUnloadDelayLoadedDLL2("StoneMath.dll") if you link with /DELAY:UNLOAD . The thunks are reset so the next call loads it again. It is rarely needed; plugin systems and hot reload use LoadLibraryW directly instead. Limits - You cannot delay-load a DLL whose data (exported variables) you use directly; only function calls go through thunks. - kernel32.dll cannot be delay-loaded (the helper itself needs it). - Do not delay-load DLLs called from DllMain or global constructors (lesson 2.04): the first call would load a DLL under the loader lock. Common mistakes !warning Forgetting delayimp.lib The linker reports __delayLoadHelper2 as an unresolved external symbol. !warning Catching the failure with try/catch It is a structured exception, not a C++ exception. Check availability first, or use the failure hook. Check yourself quiz ? Which two linker settings turn on delay loading? - /DELAYLOAD:name.dll on the DLL's project, and removing the import library from the program + /DELAYLOAD:name.dll on the program, and linking delayimp.lib - /DELAY:UNLOAD on the program, and linking kernel32.lib Both go on the program; the DLL does not change, and you keep linking its import library as before. ? How does a program recover if a delay-loaded DLL is missing? - It wraps the first call in try / catch (std::exception&) - It cannot recover; the program stops before main + It checks with __HrLoadAllImportsForDll or sets a failure hook __HrLoadAllImportsForDll tests availability first, and a failure hook ( __pfnDliFailureHook2 ) can return a fallback. The failure is a structured exception, not a C++ exception, so a normal catch does not see it. ? Which two things cannot be delay-loaded? + Exported data used directly, and kernel32.dll - Functions with more than four parameters, and any DLL from System32 - extern "C" functions, and DLLs with a version resource Only function calls go through thunks, and the delay-load helper itself needs kernel32.dll . Calls made under the loader lock should not be delay-loaded either. ? When is a delay-loaded DLL loaded? - Before main , like a normal import + The first time the program calls one of its functions - Only when the program calls LoadLibraryW for it The thunk loads it on demand, so a program that never calls it never loads it. ? What changes in the DLL to make it delay-loadable? - It must export a special initialisation function - It must be rebuilt with /DELAYLOAD + Nothing; delay loading is set up on the program's linker /DELAYLOAD and delayimp.lib go on the program that imports the DLL. ? Why is only the first call into a delay-loaded DLL slower? + The helper writes the real address into the import slot, so later calls skip the helper - Windows keeps the DLL file in its disk cache after the first read - The CPU's branch predictor learns the call after the first time After the first call, the slot holds the function's address and calls are as fast as normal imports.

title: A slot that loads itself
body: Delay loading replaces each import with a thunk that resolves the real function the first time it is called. Build the same mechanism with ordinary C++: cpp using Fn = int ( )(int); using Resolver = std::function<Fn(const std::string& name) ; // like LoadLibrary + GetProcAddress; nullptr if missing class DelaySlot { public: DelaySlot(std::string name, Resolver resolver, Fn fallback = nullptr); int call(int argument); // resolves on first use, then calls int resolveCount() const; // how many times the resolver has been asked bool resolved() const; // has a real function (not the fallback) been found? }; - The first call asks the resolver for the function. If it returns a function, the slot remembers it, and every later call goes straight to it without asking again. - If the resolver returns nullptr and there is a fallback , call the fallback this time. The slot does not remember failure: the next call asks the resolver again (the DLL might have been installed since). - If the resolver returns nullptr and there is no fallback, throw std::runtime_error with the message "cannot resolve <name " .

title: 4.04  Version Resources, Runtimes and Shipping
body: Getting a program with DLLs onto someone else's computer means three things - giving each file a version resource so people and installers can tell versions apart, making sure the Visual C++ runtime is there (or not needed), and laying out the files so the search order finds the right ones. The version resource Right-click any DLL in Explorer, Properties, Details : file version, product version, description, copyright. That comes from a version resource compiled into the file. In Visual Studio, Add, Resource, Version creates one in a .rc file: VS_VERSION_INFO VERSIONINFO FILEVERSION 2,4,1,0 PRODUCTVERSION 2,4,1,0 BEGIN BLOCK "StringFileInfo" BEGIN BLOCK "040904b0" BEGIN VALUE "CompanyName", "Xenon" VALUE "FileDescription", "Stone maths for Xenon games" VALUE "FileVersion", "2.4.1.0" VALUE "OriginalFilename", "StoneMath.dll" VALUE "ProductVersion", "2.4.1" END END BLOCK "VarFileInfo" BEGIN VALUE "Translation", 0x409, 1200 END END The binary FILEVERSION is four 16-bit numbers , stored as two 32-bit values: dwFileVersionMS = major << 16 minor and dwFileVersionLS = build << 16 revision . Installers compare these numbers to decide whether a file on disk is older than the one they carry, so increase them with every release. The practice converts between the text and the two numbers. Reading it at run time takes GetFileVersionInfoSizeW , GetFileVersionInfoW and VerQueryValueW (from version.lib ), which return a VS_FIXEDFILEINFO with those two values. That is for display and diagnostics; your code's compatibility checks belong in the library's own version function (lesson 3.05). The Visual C++ runtime A program built with the default /MD setting needs the runtime DLLs: vcruntime140.dll , vcruntime140_1.dll , msvcp140.dll and the Universal CRT ( ucrtbase.dll , part of Windows 10 and later). On a fresh machine they may be missing. Three ways to deal with it: Approach How Notes --- --- --- Redistributable installer Run vc_redist.x64.exe from your installer The standard way; shared by all programs, updated by Windows Update App-local copy Copy the runtime DLLs next to your .exe Works without an installer; you must update them yourself Static runtime Build everything with /MT No runtime DLLs at all, but each DLL gets its own CRT and heap (lesson 2.05) The redistributable is the usual choice. The runtime DLLs from Visual Studio 2015 to 2022 are binary compatible : a program built with an older toolset works with the newer redistributable (never the other way round). !warning Never ship Debug builds Debug builds need the debug runtimes ( msvcp140d.dll , ucrtbased.dll ), which you are not allowed to redistribute and which only exist where Visual Studio is installed. Laying out the files XenonGame\ ├── XenonGame.exe ├── StoneMath.dll your DLLs: next to the .exe, found first (lesson 4.01) ├── engine.dll ├── vcruntime140.dll only if you ship the runtime app-locally ├── msvcp140.dll └── plugins\ └── fog\ ├── fog.dll loaded by full path (lesson 4.02) └── noise.dll found with LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DLL_LOAD_DIR Before shipping, check the result on a clean machine (a fresh virtual machine is ideal): run dumpbin /dependents on every binary (lesson 1.06), confirm each listed DLL is either part of Windows, installed by the redistributable, or in your folder. Side-by-side assemblies, briefly Older Windows software uses manifests to bind a program to an exact version of a shared DLL in C:\Windows\WinSxS . You still meet them for one purpose: telling Windows to use version 6 of the common controls (modern-looking buttons) in a Win32 program. For your own DLLs, the app-local layout above is simpler and is what nearly every modern program does. Common mistakes !warning Forgetting to increase the file version An installer that compares versions may then refuse to replace an older file with yours. !warning Copying only some runtime DLLs msvcp140.dll without vcruntime140_1.dll fails on machines without the redistributable. Use the installer, or copy the whole set from the Visual Studio redist folder. Check yourself quiz ? How is a four-part file version stored in VS_FIXEDFILEINFO ? - As four 8-bit numbers packed into one 32-bit value + As two 32-bit values (MS and LS) of two 16-bit parts - As the text "2.4.1.0" , compared character by character dwFileVersionMS = major << 16 minor and dwFileVersionLS = build << 16 revision , so installers can compare numbers. ? Which pairing of a way to provide the Visual C++ runtime with its drawback is correct? - Static runtime /MT : the program needs vc_redist.x64.exe on every machine - Redistributable installer: you must update the DLLs yourself + App-local copies next to the .exe : you must update them yourself, because Windows Update does not - App-local copies: each module gets its own CRT and heap The redistributable needs an installer step but is updated by Windows Update; /MT needs no runtime DLLs but gives every module its own CRT and heap. ? Where should your own DLLs go when you ship? - In System32 , so every program on the machine finds them - In a folder you add to the user's PATH at install time + Next to the .exe , with plugins in their own folders The application folder is searched first, so your copies win without depending on PATH or the current directory. Plugins are loaded by full path. ? A file version is 2.4.1.0. What is dwFileVersionMS ? + 2 << 16 4 - 4 << 16 2 - 1 << 16 0 MS holds major (high 16 bits) and minor (low 16 bits); build and revision are in LS. ? Why should a shipped program never be a Debug build? - Debug builds cannot load DLLs at run time + It needs debug runtime DLLs that normal machines don't have - Debug builds are larger but otherwise run fine anywhere The debug runtimes ( msvcp140d.dll , ucrtbased.dll ) are not redistributable and only exist where Visual Studio is installed. ? What is the usual way to make sure the Visual C++ runtime is on a user's machine? - Copy only msvcp140.dll next to the .exe - Ask the user to install Visual Studio + Run the vc_redist installer from your installer The redistributable is shared by all programs and kept up to date; copying only some DLLs fails on clean machines.

title: File version numbers
body: A version resource stores the file version major.minor.build.revision as two 32-bit numbers. Write cpp struct FileVersion { uint32_t ms{ 0 }; uint32_t ls{ 0 }; }; bool parseFileVersion(const std::string& text, FileVersion& out); std::string formatFileVersion(const FileVersion& v); bool isNewer(const FileVersion& candidate, const FileVersion& installed); - parseFileVersion reads 1 to 4 parts separated by dots (missing parts are 0: "2.4" is 2.4.0.0 ). Each part is a whole number from 0 to 65535. Then ms = major << 16 minor and ls = build << 16 revision . Anything else returns false . - formatFileVersion gives back all four parts: "2.4.1.0" . - isNewer is how an installer decides to replace a file: compare ms first, then ls .

title: 4.05  Static Libraries, DLLs or Header-Only
body: You now know what DLLs cost and what they give. This lesson compares the three ways to package reusable C++ code - header-only, static library, DLL - and gives a short set of questions for choosing, with examples from real projects. The three packages Header-only. All the code is in headers, often templates or inline functions. Every program that includes them compiles its own copy. Examples: much of the standard library, {fmt} , nlohmann/json , Dear ImGui's helpers. Static library ( .lib ). Compiled once into object code; the linker copies what each program uses into its .exe . Examples: most libraries you get through a package manager by default. DLL. Compiled once into its own file; programs load it when they start or while they run. Examples: the Windows API, graphics drivers, the C runtime, plugin systems. Side by side Header-only Static library DLL --- --- --- --- Build cost for users Highest: recompiled in every file that includes it Low Low Optimisation across the boundary Full: the compiler sees everything Good (with link-time code generation) None: calls go through the import table Templates in the interface Yes Only already-used types Only through a C or COM-style interface Files to ship None None The DLL Update without rebuilding programs No No Yes Load or unload while running No No Yes Shared between processes No No Yes , code pages Usable from other languages No Only from C/C++ Yes , with a C interface ABI concerns None Same compiler and settings Must be designed for (milestone 3) Questions to choose with Ask them in order; the first "yes" usually decides. 1. Do other languages or other teams' programs need to call it? A DLL with a C interface. 2. Must it be loaded, swapped or unloaded while running (plugins, mods, hot reload)? A DLL. 3. Must it be updated without rebuilding the programs that use it (a driver, a shared component)? A DLL. 4. Is it mostly templates, or small? Header-only. 5. Otherwise: a static library. It is the simplest thing that works: one file to ship, no ABI to design, no search order, no loader lock. How real game projects use them - Engine as DLLs, during development only. Engines such as Unreal build each module ( Core , Renderer , Physics ...) as a DLL in development, so editing one module relinks one small DLL instead of the whole game, and enables hot reload. Shipping builds link the same code statically into one executable for speed and simplicity. Both use the same source; a build setting switches the export macro to nothing. - Gameplay code as a DLL while developing, reloaded on every rebuild (lesson 5.03). - Mods and plugins as DLLs with a stable C or COM-style interface (lessons 5.01 and 5.02). - Third-party SDKs (audio middleware, platform services) usually as DLLs, because they are updated separately from your game. One codebase, both ways The export macro from lesson 1.03 can do double duty: cpp-norun if defined(STONEMATH_STATIC) define STONEMATH_API // linked statically: no import or export elif defined(STONEMATH_EXPORTS) define STONEMATH_API __declspec(dllexport) else define STONEMATH_API __declspec(dllimport) endif Define STONEMATH_STATIC in both the library and the program when you build the library as a static .lib . Common mistakes !warning Making everything a DLL "for modularity" Modularity is about interfaces, not file formats. Every DLL adds a boundary with real rules. Use one when you need what only a DLL gives. !warning A header-only library that is huge Every file that includes it pays to compile it. Split heavy code into a compiled library and keep the header light. Check yourself quiz ? Which list names only things that a DLL can do and a static library cannot? - Be optimised across the boundary, use templates freely in its interface, ship with no extra files + Be updated without rebuilding programs, be loaded and unloaded while running, be called from other languages - Be linked by the linker, be compiled once, avoid ABI concerns A DLL also shares its code pages between processes. Cross-boundary optimisation and free use of templates belong to header-only libraries instead. ? When is a static library the right choice? - When the library must be updated without rebuilding the programs that use it + When nothing needs a DLL: it's simplest, with no extra files or ABI - When the library is called from C or Python code A static library needs no extra files, no ABI design and no loading rules. Updating separately and calling from other languages are exactly the reasons to pick a DLL. ? How can one library be built either as a DLL or statically? - By shipping two different headers, one with __declspec(dllexport) and one without - By building the DLL and then renaming its import library to a static .lib + With an export macro that is empty when a STATIC symbol is defined Otherwise the macro is dllexport when building the DLL and dllimport in programs; define STONEMATH_STATIC in both the library and the program for a static .lib . An import library contains no code, so renaming it does not make a static library. ? A library must be callable from C and Python. What should it be? - A header-only library + A DLL with a C interface - A static library Other languages can load DLLs and call C functions, but they cannot use C++ headers or .lib files. ? Which kind of package lets the compiler optimise across the boundary the most? + Header-only - DLL - They are all the same The compiler sees all of the code in each program. A DLL allows no optimisation across the boundary, since calls go through the import table. ? Why do engines often use DLLs in development but static linking for shipping? - Static linking is not allowed by Visual Studio for Debug builds - DLLs are faster to call than statically linked functions + DLLs allow fast rebuilds and hot reload; static ships one simple file Static linking gives one fast, simple executable to ship. The same source is built both ways with a switch in the export macro.

title: Choose the package
body: Turn the lesson's questions into a function: cpp struct Needs { bool otherLanguages{ false }; // other languages or teams' programs call it bool loadWhileRunning{ false }; // plugins, mods, hot reload bool updateSeparately{ false }; // replaced without rebuilding programs bool mostlyTemplates{ false }; bool small{ false }; }; std::string choosePackage(const Needs& needs); Return "DLL with a C interface" if other languages call it; otherwise "DLL" if it must load while running or update separately; otherwise "header-only" if it is mostly templates or small; otherwise "static library" .

title: Which file gets loaded?
body: Follow the DLL search order to see which copy of a DLL a program would load. looking for helper.dll: C:\Game\ found - loads C:\Game\helper.dll looking for zlib.dll: C:\Game\ no C:\Windows\System32\ no C:\Windows\ no current folder found - loads C:\Users\me\Downloads\zlib.dll (dangerous!)

title: Only the file you meant
body: Check plug-in paths before loading them. plugins\fire.dll - refused: relative path C:\Game\plugins\fire.dll - ok C:\Game\plugins\..\..\Windows\evil.dll - refused: leaves the plugin folder C:\Game\plugins\notes.txt - refused: not a .dll

title: Delay loading, by hand
body: Resolve a function the first time it is called, the way delay loading does. first call to compress(): loading zlib... resolved second call: already resolved zlib missing: compress() falls back to "store without compressing"

title: What to ship
body: Decide which runtime files must ship with a program from its imports. game.exe imports: VCRUNTIME140.dll, MSVCP140.dll, api-ms-win-crt-runtime-l1-1-0.dll, KERNEL32.dll, d3d11.dll ship: the Visual C++ Redistributable (x64) already on Windows: KERNEL32.dll, d3d11.dll API sets (part of Windows 10+): api-ms-win-crt-runtime-l1-1-0.dll debug runtime found: no

title: LoadLibraryExW, simulated
body: Combine this milestone's rules into one simulation of LoadLibraryExW that loads a DLL and all of its dependencies , and reports where each one came from. cpp struct World { std::string appDir; std::string currentDir; std::vector<std::string pathDirs; std::vector<std::string userDirs; // added with AddDllDirectory bool defaultDirsSet{ false }; // SetDefaultDllDirectories(LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DEFAULT_DIRS) was called std::set<std::string knownDlls; std::map<std::string, std::vector<std::string files; // full path - the DLL names it imports }; std::vector<std::string loadLibraryEx(const World& w, const std::string& file, unsigned flags); - file is either a full path (starts with a drive letter and :\ ) or a bare name. - The result lists every module loaded, dependencies first (as in lesson 1.02), each as name - full path , then ends with ok . If any module cannot be found, the result is instead the single line missing <name for the first one that fails, in load order. - Each module is loaded once; a dependency already loaded earlier in this call is reused (rule "already loaded"). Finding a file. A full path loads that exact file if it exists. For a bare name: 1. Already loaded in this call: reuse it. 2. A known DLL: C:\Windows\System32\<name , no search. 3. Otherwise search the folders, in order: - if the call's flags contain any LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_ value, or defaultDirsSet is true: the folders from lesson 4.02's drill (the flags of this call, plus LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DEFAULT_DIRS when defaultDirsSet and the call has none of its own), where the "DLL load dir" is the folder of the top DLL being loaded, and only applies if it was loaded by full path; - otherwise the standard order from lesson 4.01: application folder, C:\Windows\System32 , C:\Windows\System , C:\Windows , current directory, PATH folders. The flag values are those of lesson 4.02's drill. A folder and a name are joined with one backslash.

title: 5.01  A Plugin System
body: A plugin system lets your program load DLLs it was never built with - written later, by you or by players making mods. This lesson designs one for a game - a plugin folder, one required export, an API version check, an interface the host gives to the plugin, and clean loading and unloading - using everything from milestones 2 to 4. The contract A plugin system is a contract between the host (your game) and plugins (DLLs in a folder). Write it down as a header both sides compile against, xenon_plugin.h . It contains: 1. A version number for the contract itself. 2. What the host offers plugins: a table of functions they may call (lesson 3.03). 3. What a plugin offers the host: a table of callbacks the host calls. 4. The one exported function every plugin must have, with a fixed name. cpp-norun // xenon_plugin.h: shared by the game and every plugin pragma once include <stdint.h define XENON_PLUGIN_API_VERSION 1 // What the game offers a plugin. typedef struct xenon_host_api { uint32_t size; void ( log)(const char message); int32_t ( spawn_stone)(int32_t x, int32_t y, int32_t weight); double ( time_seconds)(void); } xenon_host_api; // What a plugin offers the game. typedef struct xenon_plugin { uint32_t size; uint32_t api_version; // the XENON_PLUGIN_API_VERSION it was built with const char name; // string literal, lives as long as the DLL int32_t ( start)(const xenon_host_api host); // after loading void ( update)(double dt); // every frame void ( stop)(void); // before unloading } xenon_plugin; // Every plugin exports this, with exactly this name (extern "C"). typedef const xenon_plugin ( xenon_get_plugin_fn)(void); define XENON_GET_PLUGIN_NAME "xenon_get_plugin" Everything crosses as plain C: no std::string , no exceptions, no shared heap (milestone 2). Each side only calls through tables, so neither needs an import library for the other. A plugin cpp-norun // fog.cpp, built as fog.dll include "xenon_plugin.h" static const xenon_host_api g_host{ nullptr }; static int32_t start(const xenon_host_api host) { g_host = host; g_host- log("fog: hello"); return 0; } static void update(double) {} static void stop() { g_host- log("fog: goodbye"); g_host = nullptr; } static const xenon_plugin g_plugin{ sizeof(xenon_plugin), XENON_PLUGIN_API_VERSION, "Fog", start, update, stop }; extern "C" __declspec(dllexport) const xenon_plugin xenon_get_plugin(void) { return &g_plugin; } Note what it does not do: nothing in DllMain or global constructors (lesson 2.04). Real work starts in start , called by the host after LoadLibrary returns. The host's loader cpp-norun struct LoadedPlugin { HMODULE module; const xenon_plugin plugin; }; std::vector<LoadedPlugin loadPlugins(const std::filesystem::path& folder, const xenon_host_api& host) { std::vector<LoadedPlugin loaded; for (const auto& entry : std::filesystem::directory_iterator(folder)) { const auto& path{ entry.path() }; if (!entry.is_regular_file() path.extension() != L".dll") continue; HMODULE module{ LoadLibraryExW(path.c_str(), nullptr, LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DLL_LOAD_DIR LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DEFAULT_DIRS) }; if (!module) { logf("skipped %ls: could not load (error %lu)", path.c_str(), GetLastError()); continue; } auto get{ reinterpret_cast<xenon_get_plugin_fn (GetProcAddress(module, XENON_GET_PLUGIN_NAME)) }; const xenon_plugin plugin{ get ? get() : nullptr }; if (!plugin plugin- size < sizeof(xenon_plugin) plugin- api_version != XENON_PLUGIN_API_VERSION) { logf("skipped %ls: not a plugin for this version", path.c_str()); FreeLibrary(module); continue; } if (plugin- start(&host) != 0) { logf("skipped %s: start failed", plugin- name); FreeLibrary(module); continue; } loaded.push_back({ module, plugin }); } return loaded; } Every check matters: - Only .dll files , by full path , with the safe search flags (lesson 4.02). Plugins with their own dependencies keep them in their own folder. - The export must exist. A random DLL in the folder is skipped, not crashed on. - Size and version. A plugin built for another version of the contract is refused politely (lesson 3.05). - start can fail , and then the plugin is unloaded again. - A failing plugin never stops the others from loading. Unloading At shutdown, or when the player disables a plugin, the order is: call stop , forget every pointer the plugin gave you (its name , its tables, any objects), then FreeLibrary . Unload in the reverse order of loading, so a plugin that relied on another's services stops before them. Mods and trust A plugin runs inside your process with all of its permissions. For plugins you write yourself, that is fine. For mods made by players, treat the plugin folder as "code the player chose to run", like any program they download, and say so in your game's documentation. Many games that want untrusted mods use a scripting language with limited access (Lua, a WebAssembly runtime) instead of DLLs. Common mistakes !warning Keeping a plugin's name string after unloading it It points into the DLL's read-only data. Copy it into a std::string if you need it later. !warning Letting one bad plugin crash the whole load Check every step and skip what does not fit. Check yourself quiz ? What goes in a plugin contract header? - The host's import library, the plugin's .def file, and the DllMain every plugin must have + The contract's version, the host's function table, the plugin's function table, and the name and type of the one exported function - The C++ classes the host and plugins share, with their std::string members Both sides compile against it, and everything in it is plain C: function tables in both directions and one export with a fixed name. ? Which list gives the checks a host makes before keeping a plugin? - It is in System32 , it is signed, and its DllMain returns TRUE - It loads by name through PATH, its file version is newer, and it has a .def file + Loaded by full path, has the export, a valid table version, and start succeeds It must be a .dll loaded by full path with safe search flags, and its table must be big enough with the right API version. Any failed step skips that plugin, unloads it again and carries on with the others. ? Why should a plugin do nothing in DllMain ? - DllMain is never called for DLLs loaded with LoadLibraryExW + DllMain runs under the loader lock; real work belongs in start - DllMain runs before the plugin's static data is in memory start is called after loading completes. Lesson 2.04's rules apply: under the loader lock, loading other DLLs or waiting on threads can deadlock. ? Why does the plugin contract use tables of function pointers in both directions? + Neither side needs an import library for the other, and the tables can be versioned - Calls through function pointers are faster than calls to exported functions - Plugins are not allowed to export functions One GetProcAddress gets the plugin's table, and the host passes its own table in start . ? A DLL in the plugin folder has no xenon_get_plugin export. What should the host do? - Stop loading plugins and report that the folder is corrupt - Call the DLL's DllMain again to make it register itself + Log it, FreeLibrary it and carry on with the other files Not every DLL in the folder is a plugin, and one bad file must not stop the others. ? What is the correct order for unloading a plugin? - FreeLibrary first, then call the plugin's stop + Call stop , drop its pointers, then FreeLibrary - Only FreeLibrary ; calling stop is optional After FreeLibrary , none of the plugin's code or data exists any more, so stop and every pointer it gave you must be finished with first.

title: Which files are plugins?
body: The host scans its plugin folder. For each file it gathers what it found, and must decide which plugins to keep. Write cpp struct Candidate { std::string file; // file name, e.g. "fog.dll" bool loads{ true }; // LoadLibraryExW succeeded bool hasExport{ true }; // GetProcAddress found xenon_get_plugin uint32_t tableSize{ 0 }; // plugin- size uint32_t apiVersion{ 0 }; // plugin- api_version std::string name; // plugin- name bool startOk{ true }; // plugin- start returned 0 }; struct ScanResult { std::vector<std::string kept; std::vector<std::string log; }; ScanResult scanPlugins(const std::vector<Candidate & files, uint32_t hostApiVersion, uint32_t requiredTableSize); Go through the files sorted by file name (case-insensitive) and apply the checks in this order. The first one that fails adds a line to log and skips the file: 1. The name must end in .dll (any case), otherwise: "<file : not a DLL" . 2. loads , otherwise: "<file : could not load" . 3. hasExport , otherwise: "<file : not a plugin" . 4. tableSize = requiredTableSize and apiVersion == hostApiVersion , otherwise: "<file : built for API version <apiVersion , need <hostApiVersion " . 5. A plugin name that has not been kept already (exact comparison), otherwise: "<file : duplicate plugin <name " . 6. startOk , otherwise: "<file : start failed" . A file that passes everything adds its plugin name to kept and the log line "<file : loaded <name " .

title: 5.02  A Plugin Registry and Capabilities
body: Once several plugins are loaded, the host needs to know what each one provides - new stone types, weather effects, console commands - and route requests to the right one. This lesson builds a registry that plugins register into during start , handles name clashes and dependencies between plugins, and cleans up everything a plugin registered when it unloads. Registering instead of exporting In lesson 5.01 a plugin offered fixed callbacks: start , update , stop . Real plugins add things to the game: three new stone types, a weather effect, two console commands. Rather than one export per thing, the host offers registration functions in its table, and the plugin calls them from start : cpp-norun typedef struct xenon_stone_type { uint32_t size; const char id; // "fog.ghost_stone" int32_t weight; int32_t ( on_place)(int32_t x, int32_t y); } xenon_stone_type; typedef struct xenon_host_api { uint32_t size; void ( log)(const char message); int32_t ( register_stone_type)(const void owner, const xenon_stone_type type); int32_t ( register_command)(const void owner, const char name, void ( run)(const char args)); } xenon_host_api; In the plugin: cpp-norun static const xenon_stone_type g_ghost{ sizeof(xenon_stone_type), "fog.ghost_stone", 2, onPlaceGhost }; static int32_t start(const xenon_host_api host) { if (host- register_stone_type(&g_plugin, &g_ghost) != 0) return 1; host- register_command(&g_plugin, "fog.thickness", setThickness); return 0; } The owner argument (the plugin's own table, a unique address) lets the host remember who registered each thing. The host's registry cpp-norun class Registry { public: int32_t addStoneType(const void owner, const xenon_stone_type& type); const xenon_stone_type stoneType(std::string_view id) const; void removeEverythingFrom(const void owner); // when a plugin unloads private: struct Entry { const void owner; xenon_stone_type type; std::string id; }; std::map<std::string, Entry, std::less< m_stones; }; Design decisions: - Copy what you keep. The registry stores its own copy of the struct and of the id text. Pointers into the plugin ( on_place ) are still pointers into its code, which is why... - Remove everything on unload. Before FreeLibrary , the host calls removeEverythingFrom(plugin) . Otherwise the registry holds function pointers into unmapped memory (lesson 2.03). - Names are namespaced by convention: pluginname.thing . Two plugins can both have a "ghost_stone" without clashing. - A clash is refused, not overwritten. If fog.ghost_stone is already registered by someone else, the second registration fails and the plugin can decide what to do. Silently replacing a registration makes bugs that depend on load order. Plugins that depend on plugins A "seasons" plugin might need the "weather" plugin's commands. Give each plugin a list of the plugins it requires , by name, and load them in dependency order: the same depth-first, dependencies-first walk as the loader itself (lesson 1.02). A plugin whose requirement is missing, or that is part of a cycle, is not started, and the host says why. Capabilities and versions per feature Instead of one version for the whole contract, a host can offer capabilities : named features with their own version, such as "stone_types": 2 , "commands": 1 . A plugin lists what it needs; the host starts it only if every need is met with at least that version. This lets the contract grow one feature at a time without every plugin being rebuilt. Common mistakes !warning Storing the plugin's pointers in the registry without an owner You then cannot find and remove them on unload, and the game crashes the first time it calls one. !warning Last registration wins The result depends on which DLL the directory listing returned first. Refuse duplicates and report them. Check yourself quiz ? What does the host do with a plugin's registrations when the plugin unloads? - Keeps them, so the things the plugin added stay in the game + Removes every registration with that plugin as owner, before calling FreeLibrary - Removes them after FreeLibrary , once the plugin's memory is gone The registrations hold function pointers into the plugin's code, which must be gone from the registry before the DLL is unmapped. ? Why should the registry copy the id string? + The plugin's string is in DLL memory and vanishes when it unloads - Copying the string makes comparisons faster than comparing pointers - The plugin frees the string as soon as its start function returns A const char into an unloaded DLL dangles, and a copy can also be used safely as a map key. The plugin's string literal lasts exactly as long as the DLL. ? What are capabilities in a plugin contract? - The Windows privileges a plugin needs, such as access to the registry + Named, versioned features a plugin can require exactly as it uses them - The list of other plugins a plugin depends on, loaded first For example "stone_types": 2 , "commands": 1 : the host starts a plugin only if each need is met with at least that version, so the contract can grow feature by feature. Dependencies on other plugins are a separate list. ? Why does the plugin pass an owner pointer when it registers something? - To prove to the host that it is a real plugin + So the host can remove everything that plugin registered before unloading it - Because a function pointer can only be called through its owner Removal by owner keeps the registry free of dangling pointers. ? Two plugins register the same id. What should the registry do? - Keep the second registration, replacing the first - Keep both and pick one at random when the id is used + Refuse the second registration and report the clash Refusing makes the result independent of the order in which the directory listing returned the DLLs. ? In what order should plugins with dependencies be started? - Alphabetically by plugin name, so the order is stable - In the order the plugin folder lists their files + Dependencies first, depth first, each started once Like the Windows loader: a plugin's requirements must be running before it starts, and a missing requirement or a cycle means it is not started.

body: Write the host's registry for stone types: cpp class Registry { public: bool add(const std::string& owner, const std::string& id, int weight); // false if the id is taken int weightOf(const std::string& id) const; // -1 if unknown std::string ownerOf(const std::string& id) const; // "" if unknown int removeOwner(const std::string& owner); // removes all of its entries, returns how many std::vector<std::string ids() const; // all ids, sorted }; - An id may only be registered once. A second add with the same id fails and changes nothing, even if it comes from the same owner. - An id must be namespaced : it contains a . with at least one character before and after it, and the part before the first . must equal the owner. Otherwise add fails. - removeOwner is what the host calls before FreeLibrary .

title: Start plugins in dependency order
body: Each plugin lists the plugins it requires. Write cpp std::vector<std::string startOrder(const std::map<std::string, std::vector<std::string & requires_, std::vector<std::string & problems); requires_ maps every available plugin to the names it requires. Return the order to start them in, and fill problems with one line per plugin that cannot start: - Visit plugins in alphabetical order; for each, start its requirements first (in the order listed, depth first), then the plugin itself, each only once. - A plugin whose requirement is not available cannot start: "<plugin needs <missing " . Any plugin that requires a plugin that cannot start also cannot start: "<plugin needs <requirement " . - A plugin that is part of a cycle (it requires itself directly or through others) cannot start: "<plugin is part of a cycle" . Plugins that require a plugin in a cycle cannot start either, with the needs message. - Each plugin gets at most one problem line: the first reason found. Problems are listed in the order they are discovered. requires_: { fog: , seasons: fog, weather , weather: , storms: weather, wind } order: fog, weather, seasons problems: "storms needs wind"

title: 5.03  Hot Reloading Code
body: Hot reloading means changing game code, rebuilding, and having the running game pick up the new code within a second, without restarting or losing your place. The trick is to put gameplay code in a DLL and swap it. This lesson covers the loop - watch, copy, unload, load - and the problems each step solves. The idea Split the game into two parts: - The host ( game.exe ): window, main loop, memory, input, loading assets. It rarely changes and keeps running. - The game code ( gameplay.dll ): the rules, movement, enemy behaviour. You change it all day. The host calls into the DLL through a small table, exactly like a plugin: cpp-norun typedef struct game_api { uint32_t size; void ( update)(game_state state, const game_input input, float dt); void ( render)(const game_state state, render_list out); } game_api; extern "C" __declspec(dllexport) const game_api get_game_api(void); All game state lives in memory the host owns and passes in (lesson 5.04 explains why). The DLL is just functions. The reload loop Every frame, before calling update , the host checks whether the DLL file has changed: cpp-norun FILETIME lastWrite(const wchar_t path); void Host::reloadIfChanged() { const FILETIME now{ lastWrite(L"gameplay.dll") }; if (CompareFileTime(&now, &m_loadedWriteTime) == 0) return; // unchanged // 1. Copy the new DLL to a fresh name and load the copy. const std::wstring copy{ L"gameplay_" + std::to_wstring(++m_generation) + L".dll" }; if (!CopyFileW(L"gameplay.dll", copy.c_str(), FALSE)) return; // the compiler may still be writing it: try next frame HMODULE fresh{ LoadLibraryW(copy.c_str()) }; auto get{ fresh ? reinterpret_cast<const game_api ( )() (GetProcAddress(fresh, "get_game_api")) : nullptr }; if (!get) { if (fresh) FreeLibrary(fresh); return; } // keep running the old code // 2. Swap: drop every pointer into the old DLL, then unload it. m_api = get(); if (m_module) FreeLibrary(m_module); m_module = fresh; m_loadedWriteTime = now; } Why copy before loading? A loaded DLL's file is locked : Windows maps it into memory and will not let anyone overwrite it. If the game loaded gameplay.dll itself, the next build would fail with "cannot open file for writing". Loading a copy leaves the original free for the compiler. Each reload uses a new name ( gameplay_7.dll ) because the previous copy may still be loaded at the moment you copy. Why only after the build has finished? The linker writes the DLL over several hundred milliseconds. If the host notices the new time stamp half-way through, it may copy a half-written file. Two common fixes: - Wait until the time stamp has been stable for a few checks (say 200 ms) before reloading. - Have the build write a small "lock" file first and delete it when done; reload only when the lock file is gone. The practice builds the "stable for several polls" watcher. The PDB problem The debugger also locks the DLL's PDB (debug symbols) while the DLL is loaded, so the next link fails to write gameplay.pdb . Give each build's PDB a unique name in Linker, Debugging, Generate Program Database File , for example $(OutDir)gameplay_$( System.DateTime ::Now.Ticks).pdb . Old PDB files pile up; delete them on start-up. What must not survive a reload After FreeLibrary on the old DLL, everything that pointed into it is invalid: - function pointers (the old game_api table, callbacks stored anywhere); - string literals from the old DLL; - vtables : any C++ object created by the old DLL's code has a vptr into the old DLL; - static and global variables inside the DLL, which are reset to their initial values in the new one. That is why state lives in host memory, and why the state is plain data without virtual functions. Lesson 5.04 handles state whose layout changes between builds. Common mistakes !warning Loading the DLL itself instead of a copy The next build cannot overwrite the locked file. !warning Keeping the old table after unloading Read the new table before freeing the old module, and never keep pointers to the old one. Check yourself quiz ? Which describes the hot-reload loop correctly? - Unload the old DLL, wait for the build, then load gameplay.dll itself and get its table + On a new complete build, load a fresh copy, swap to its table, then free the old copy - Every frame, call FreeLibrary and LoadLibraryW on gameplay.dll so the newest code always runs When the DLL's write time changes and the file is complete, copy it to a fresh name and load the copy. Loading a copy keeps the original writable, and the old copy is only freed after the new table is in place, so the game never runs without code. ? Why does each build's PDB need a unique name? + The debugger locks the PDB of the loaded DLL, so the linker could not overwrite it - Windows refuses to load a DLL whose PDB has the same name as another - The PDB holds the game state, which must not be overwritten The next link would fail to write gameplay.pdb . A unique name per build avoids the clash. ? Which list contains only things that become invalid after unloading the old DLL? - Its function pointers, the host's own globals, and game state in host memory - Its string literals, the window handle, and the input state + Its function pointers, its string literals, and vtables of objects it created Static variables inside the DLL are also reset. Memory the host owns survives, which is why state lives there. ? Why does the host load a copy of the DLL instead of the DLL itself? - Copies load faster than the original build output + The loaded file is locked, so the next build couldn't write it - So the debugger can find the PDB file next to it Windows locks a loaded DLL's file, and the original must stay writable for the compiler's next build. ? The host sees a new time stamp on gameplay.dll . Why might reloading straight away fail? - FreeLibrary must always be called before checking the time stamp + The linker may still be writing the file - Windows only updates time stamps after a reboot Wait until the time stamp has been stable for a few checks, or until a lock file disappears. ? Which of these survives a hot reload? - A static variable inside the DLL - A C++ object with virtual functions created by the old DLL + Game state stored in memory the host owns Everything inside the old DLL's image is gone after FreeLibrary ; the host's memory is untouched.

title: When to reload
body: The host checks the gameplay DLL's last-write time once per frame. It must reload only when the file has changed and the build has finished : the time has stayed the same for a few checks in a row. Write cpp class ReloadWatcher { public: ReloadWatcher(long long loadedTime, int stablePolls); bool poll(long long fileTime); // called once per frame with the file's current write time int generation() const; // how many reloads have happened std::string copyName() const; // the name of the copy to load for the current generation }; - loadedTime is the write time of the DLL that is loaded right now. - poll returns true exactly when the host should reload now : the file time differs from loadedTime , and this same time has now been seen on stablePolls consecutive polls (counting this one). After returning true , loadedTime becomes that time and generation() increases by one. - If the time changes again while waiting, the count starts over for the new time. - If the time goes back to loadedTime while waiting (the build was undone), stop waiting. - copyName() is "gameplay_<generation .dll" , starting at gameplay_0.dll before any reload. ReloadWatcher w{ 100, 3 }; w.poll(100) == false // unchanged w.poll(150) == false // changed, seen once w.poll(150) == false // twice w.poll(150) == true // three times: reload now, generation 1, copy gameplay_1.dll w.poll(150) == false // that is what is loaded now

title: 5.04  Keeping State Across a Reload
body: Hot reload is only useful if the game keeps its state - the player's position, the enemies, the score - while the code changes. This lesson shows the two strategies, host-owned memory and save and restore , and how to handle the hard case: a reload that changes the layout of the state itself. Strategy 1: the host owns the memory The simplest and fastest approach, popularised by Casey Muratori's Handmade Hero : the host allocates one big block of memory at start-up and hands it to the DLL every frame. The DLL keeps all of its state in that block, and none in its own globals: cpp-norun struct game_memory { uint64_t size; void storage; // allocated by the host once, never freed until exit bool initialised; // false the first time }; extern "C" __declspec(dllexport) void game_update(game_memory memory, const game_input input, float dt) { auto state{ static_cast<GameState (memory- storage) }; if (!memory- initialised) { new (state) GameState{}; memory- initialised = true; } state- player.x += input- moveX dt; } When the DLL is swapped, the block is untouched, so the new code finds the state exactly as the old code left it. The rules that make it work: - GameState is plain data : no virtual functions (their vptrs would point into the old DLL), no std::string or std::vector whose memory came from the old DLL's heap if it used its own CRT. Arrays with fixed sizes, plain structs, indices instead of pointers into code. - Memory that the game needs to grow comes from a simple arena inside the block, not from new . - No pointers to functions or string literals of the DLL are stored in the state. Strategy 2: save and restore If the state has to contain richer C++ objects, the DLL can instead write its state to bytes just before it is unloaded and read it back after the new one is loaded: cpp-norun // in the DLL's table uint64_t ( save_state)(void buffer, uint64_t capacity); // returns bytes needed int32_t ( load_state)(const void buffer, uint64_t size); The host calls save_state on the old DLL, unloads it, loads the new one and calls load_state . Slower, but it handles any state, and the same code doubles as your save-game system. When the layout changes Both strategies face the same hard case: you add a member to GameState , or change a type. The new code then reads the old bytes with the new layout, which is lesson 3.03's versioned-struct problem in another form. The same solution works: - Put a version number (and size) at the start of the saved state or the memory block. - When the new code sees an older version , it migrates : reads the old layout, fills new fields with defaults, writes the new layout. - When it sees a version it cannot read, it starts fresh rather than reading garbage, and logs why. cpp-norun struct StateHeader { uint32_t version; uint32_t size; }; // version 1: { int32_t x, y; } version 2: { int32_t x, y; int32_t health; } if (header.version == 1) { / copy x, y; health = 100; / } else if (header.version == 2) { / read as is / } else { / unknown: start a new game / } Many developers simply restart when the state layout changes, and reload freely for everything else. A version number makes that decision automatic instead of a crash. What hot reload is good for, and what not Excellent for: tuning movement and feel, fixing gameplay bugs while reproducing them, iterating on enemy behaviour, UI layout. Poor for: changes to data the host owns, changes to the host itself, and big structural changes, which still need a restart. Common mistakes !warning A static variable inside the gameplay DLL It resets on every reload. Move it into the state. !warning Reading old state with a new layout Values land in the wrong fields. Version the state and migrate or start fresh. Check yourself quiz ? Which describes the host-owned-memory strategy? - The DLL allocates its state with new in its own globals and gives the host a pointer to it + The host allocates one memory block and passes it to the DLL every frame; the DLL keeps all state as plain data in it - The host copies the DLL's global variables into its own memory just before every reload Swapping the DLL leaves the block untouched, so the new code finds the state exactly as the old code left it. ? What makes state safe to keep across a reload? - C++ objects with virtual functions, as long as they were created with new - Any data, as long as it is stored in a static variable inside the DLL + Plain data with no pointers into the DLL, in memory the host owns No vptrs, no pointers to the DLL's functions or string literals, and memory from the host rather than the DLL's heap. Anything that points into the old DLL's image dangles after FreeLibrary , and the DLL's statics reset on every reload. ? How do you handle a change in the state's layout? + Store a version number and migrate older versions to the new layout - Read the old bytes with the new layout; new fields simply start as zero - Increase the DLL's file version so Windows converts the state Migration gives new fields defaults, and versions you cannot read start fresh. Reading old bytes with a new layout puts values in the wrong fields; it is lesson 3.03's versioned-struct problem again. ? Why must game state kept in host memory have no virtual functions? - Virtual functions are too slow to call every frame + Each object's vptr would point into the old, unloaded DLL - The host cannot allocate memory for objects with virtual functions Plain data survives the swap; code pointers, including vtables, do not. ? The state gained a new field and the new DLL finds version 1 data. What should it do? - Read it with the new layout and carry on as usual + Migrate it: read the old layout, default the new field - Crash on purpose, so the developer knows to restart Then write the new layout. A version number turns layout changes into a decision instead of garbage. ? Which strategy also works as a save-game system? - Host-owned memory + Save and restore through save_state and load_state - Neither; save games need a separate format The DLL serialises its state to bytes, which can just as well be written to a file.

title: Migrate saved state
body: The gameplay DLL saves its state to bytes before a reload, and the new DLL reads it back. The state's layout has changed between versions: Version Fields after the header, in order --- --- 1 x (int32), y (int32) 2 x , y , health (int32) 3 x , y , health , stones (int32) Every saved state starts with a header of two uint32_t values: the version , then the size of everything that follows. All numbers are little-endian, 4 bytes each. Write the current (version 3) code's functions: cpp struct State { int32_t x{ 0 }; int32_t y{ 0 }; int32_t health{ 100 }; int32_t stones{ 0 }; }; std::vector<uint8_t saveState(const State& s); // always writes version 3 bool loadState(const std::vector<uint8_t & bytes, State& out); // reads version 1, 2 or 3 - loadState checks the header: at least 8 bytes, a version from 1 to 3, and a size that matches what that version needs (8, 12 or 16) and fits in the bytes after the header. If anything is wrong it returns false and leaves out untouched. - Missing fields get their defaults: health 100, stones 0. - A version above 3 comes from a newer DLL: return false (start fresh rather than guess).

title: 5.05  Capstone: A Moddable Game
body: Bring the whole course together in one Visual Studio solution - a small game whose gameplay hot-reloads while it runs, and which loads plugins that add new content through a versioned C interface. This lesson is the plan, the checklist and the order to build it in. What you build A small top-down game, "Xenon Builder": the player walks around a field and stacks stones into towers. It has three kinds of module: XenonBuilder.sln ├── Host/ XenonBuilder.exe: window, loop, input, memory, plugin loader, hot reload ├── Gameplay/ gameplay.dll: rules and movement, hot-reloaded ├── PluginApi/ xenon_plugin.h, xenon.hpp: shared headers only (no code) └── Plugins/ ├── Fog/ fog.dll: a new stone type and a console command └── Seasons/ seasons.dll: requires Fog; changes stone colours over time Milestone by milestone Part Lessons Done when --- --- --- A window and a loop in the host (Win32 or the console from earlier courses) The player moves with the arrow keys Gameplay in a DLL, loaded at run time 2.03, 3.03 get_game_api returns a versioned table the host checks Host-owned state 5.04 No globals in gameplay.dll ; the state has a version header Hot reload 5.03 Change the walking speed, rebuild: the running game changes speed without moving the player Safe loading 4.02 SetDefaultDllDirectories first thing; every DLL loaded by full path The plugin contract 5.01, 3.03 xenon_plugin.h with version, host table, plugin table The registry 5.02 Fog registers fog.ghost_stone and the fog.thickness command Plugin dependencies 5.02, 1.02 Seasons starts after Fog; without Fog, Seasons is skipped with a message Error handling at every boundary 2.06, 3.02 No exception crosses a DLL edge; failures are logged with messages Clean shutdown 2.04, 5.01 stop on each plugin in reverse order, registries emptied, then FreeLibrary Shipping 4.04 A Release build runs on a clean virtual machine Order to build in 1. Get the host working with the gameplay code statically linked first: the simplest version that runs. 2. Move gameplay into a DLL loaded with LoadLibraryW . Fix everything that breaks: globals, ownership, the interface. 3. Add hot reload. Edit, rebuild, watch it change. This is the part you will enjoy most. 4. Add the plugin loader with one plugin, then the registry, then the second plugin with its dependency. 5. Shut down cleanly and ship. Checklist before you call it finished - dumpbin /exports on each DLL shows only plain, intended names. - dumpbin /dependents on the Release build shows no debug runtime. - Removing fog.dll makes Seasons skip with a clear message, and the game still runs. - A DLL that is not a plugin in the plugin folder is skipped, not loaded into the game. - Ten hot reloads in a row leave no leaked plugin registrations and no growing memory. - Building while the game runs never fails with a locked file (DLL or PDB). - A plugin built against an older contract version is refused with a message, not a crash. Where to go next - The Tool Interfaces with Dear ImGui course adds an in-game editor to this project, which can reload with the gameplay DLL. - The Game Programming with raylib course gives the host a real renderer. - The Windows Programming with the Win32 API course goes deeper into the window and message loop the host is built on. Check yourself quiz ? Which course lessons does hot reload depend on? - Delay loading (4.03), the version resource (4.04) and name mangling (2.01) - The plugin registry (5.02), capabilities (5.02) and COM-style interfaces (3.04) + Run-time loading (2.03), versioned tables (3.03), the reload loop (5.03) and host-owned, versioned state (5.04) Hot reload loads the gameplay DLL with LoadLibraryW , reads its versioned table, swaps it in the reload loop, and keeps state in host memory. ? What makes plugin shutdown safe? + Stop each plugin in reverse order, unregister it, then FreeLibrary - Calling FreeLibrary on every plugin in load order, then emptying the registries - Letting Windows unload every plugin at process exit, without calling stop Each plugin's stop runs in reverse load order and its registrations and pointers are dropped before it is unloaded. Anything left in a registry after FreeLibrary points into unmapped memory, and reverse order stops a plugin before the plugins it relies on. ? Why build the game with the gameplay code statically linked first? - DLLs cannot be used in the first version of a project + To get the simplest version working before the DLL rules - Static linking is required before hot reload can work Then the move to a DLL shows exactly what the boundary changes: globals, ownership and the interface. ? What should happen when a plugin's dependency is missing? - Refuse to start the game until the dependency is installed - Load the plugin anyway and let it fail when it calls the dependency + Skip that plugin with a clear message and keep running One missing mod must not stop the game, and loading it anyway would only move the failure somewhere harder to read. ? The checklist says building while the game runs must never fail with a locked file. What makes that true? - Running the game from a Debug build + Loading a copy of the gameplay DLL and giving each build's PDB a unique name - Calling SetDefaultDllDirectories first thing in main A loaded DLL and the PDB the debugger has open are both locked, so the host loads a copy and each link writes a new PDB (lesson 5.03).

title: A plugin host that reloads
body: Write the bookkeeping of a plugin host: which plugins run, in what order, what each one registered, and what happens when one is reloaded. Each plugin file is described by: cpp struct PluginFile { std::string name; // "fog" uint32_t apiVersion{ 1 }; std::vector<std::string requires_; // names of plugins that must be running first std::vector<std::string provides; // ids it registers when it starts, e.g. "fog.ghost_stone" }; class Host { public: explicit Host(uint32_t apiVersion); void addFile(const PluginFile& file); // a new file, or a new build replacing one with the same name std::vector<std::string startAll(); // start every plugin that is not running; returns log lines std::vector<std::string reload(const std::string& name); std::vector<std::string running() const; // names, in the order they were started std::string providerOf(const std::string& id) const; // "" if nobody provides it }; Starting. startAll visits the plugins that are not running in alphabetical order and starts each one's requirements first (in the order listed, depth first). A plugin starts if every check passes, in this order: 1. its apiVersion equals the host's, else log skip <name : API version <v , need <host ; 2. every requirement exists and is running (or can be started now), else skip <name : needs <requirement for the first one that fails; reaching a plugin that is already being started in this chain is a cycle: skip <name : cycle ; 3. it registers its provides ids in order. Each must start with <name . (else skip <name : <id is not <name . ) and must not be registered already (else skip <name : <id is taken ). If any registration fails, the ids it registered before the failure are removed again. A plugin that starts logs start <name and is added to the end of the running list. Each plugin is logged at most once per startAll (its first result). Reloading. reload(name) stops the plugin and every running plugin that requires it, directly or indirectly, in reverse start order , logging stop <x for each and removing everything each one registered. Then it calls startAll and appends its log. Reloading a plugin that is not running only runs startAll .

title: Cheat Sheet - DLL API
body: Building and exporting cpp-norun // One header for the DLL and its users (the DLL project defines MYLIB_EXPORTS) if defined(MYLIB_STATIC) define MYLIB_API elif defined(MYLIB_EXPORTS) define MYLIB_API __declspec(dllexport) else define MYLIB_API __declspec(dllimport) endif ifdef __cplusplus extern "C" { endif MYLIB_API int32_t mylib_thing_create(mylib_thing out); MYLIB_API void mylib_thing_destroy(mylib_thing thing); ifdef __cplusplus } endif LIBRARY MyLib ; a .def file EXPORTS mylib_thing_create @1 mylib_thing_destroy @2 PublicName = internal_name hidden_entry @9 NONAME Loading at run time Function Use --- --- LoadLibraryW(path) Map a DLL; NULL on failure, see GetLastError() LoadLibraryExW(path, nullptr, flags) The same, with search flags or as a data file GetProcAddress(module, "name") An export's address ( FARPROC ); cast to the exact function type FreeLibrary(module) Drop one reference GetModuleHandleW(L"name.dll") Handle of an already-loaded module, no new reference GetModuleFileNameW(nullptr, buf, n) Full path of your own .exe SetDefaultDllDirectories(LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DEFAULT_DIRS) First line of main : no current directory or PATH in searches AddDllDirectory(folder) Add a folder to LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_USER_DIRS Flag Searches --- --- LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DLL_LOAD_DIR The loaded DLL's own folder (full paths only) LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_APPLICATION_DIR The .exe 's folder LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_USER_DIRS Folders from AddDllDirectory LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_SYSTEM32 System32 LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DEFAULT_DIRS Application, user folders, System32 LOAD_LIBRARY_AS_DATAFILE Map for resources only; no code runs Error codes from LoadLibrary Code Meaning --- --- 126 ERROR_MOD_NOT_FOUND The DLL or one of its dependencies was not found 127 ERROR_PROC_NOT_FOUND A dependency lacks an export that is imported 193 ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT Wrong architecture (32/64-bit) or not a PE file 1114 ERROR_DLL_INIT_FAILED DllMain returned FALSE The standard search order (name-only requests) Already loaded, then known DLLs, then: application folder, System32 , System , Windows , current directory, PATH. DllMain cpp-norun BOOL APIENTRY DllMain(HMODULE module, DWORD reason, LPVOID reserved) { if (reason == DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH) DisableThreadLibraryCalls(module); return TRUE; } Safe: set variables, DisableThreadLibraryCalls , InitializeCriticalSection , TlsAlloc . Not safe: LoadLibrary , FreeLibrary , waiting for threads or locks, COM, sockets, registry, UI. Do real work in an explicit init function. Rules at the boundary - Whoever allocates, frees: free functions, caller buffers, or create/destroy pairs. - No exceptions out of exported functions: catch everything, return codes. - No C++ library types in a public interface; pointer and length instead. - Fixed-size types ( int32_t , uint64_t ), no bool or long in C interfaces. - Result codes never renumbered; callers treat unknown nonzero codes as failure. - Visible structs start with their size and only grow at the end. Tools Command Shows --- --- dumpbin /exports X.dll Export table dumpbin /imports X.exe Imported DLLs and functions dumpbin /dependents X.exe Directly needed DLLs dumpbin /headers X.dll Machine type, base, characteristics undname ?name@@... Decodes a decorated C++ name Debug, Windows, Modules Every loaded module, its path and address Process Monitor Every place Windows looked for a file
