title: Glossary
body: Every term from the course, in alphabetical order. The lesson that introduces each one is in brackets. Term Meaning --- --- ABI Application binary interface: the rules compiled code follows to work together, such as type sizes, struct layout, calling conventions and name decoration. A DLL's interface is a promise about its ABI. (3.01) AddRef / Release The two reference-counting methods of a COM-style interface. AddRef takes a reference; Release drops one and deletes the object at zero. (3.04) API set A name such as api-ms-win-core-file-l1-1-0.dll that Windows redirects to a real system DLL without any search. (1.06) ASLR Address space layout randomisation: Windows loads modules at random addresses to make attacks harder, so relocation is normal. (1.02) Binary compatibility Programs already compiled against one version of a DLL keep working with a newer one without being rebuilt. (3.01) Calling convention The agreement about where arguments go, where the result comes back and who cleans up the stack. x64 Windows has one; 32-bit Windows has several. (2.02) Capability A named feature of a plugin contract with its own version, which a plugin can require. (5.02) CRT The C runtime library: malloc , new , printf and friends. A module gets it shared ( /MD ) or private ( /MT ). (2.05) Decorated (mangled) name The symbol name a C++ compiler gives a function, encoding its scope and types so that overloads differ, such as ?add@@YAHHH@Z . (2.01) .def file A module-definition file that lists a DLL's exports by hand, with optional ordinals, NONAME and DATA . (1.04) Delay loading Linking against a DLL's import library but loading it only when one of its functions is first called. (4.03) DLL Dynamic-link library: compiled code and data in a separate PE file that a process maps and calls into. (1.01) DLL Hell Programs breaking because an installer replaced a shared DLL with an incompatible version of the same name. (3.05) DLL planting Placing a file with a DLL's name where the search order finds it before the real one. Also called search-order hijacking. (4.02) DllMain A DLL's optional entry point, called when the DLL is attached to or detached from a process and when threads start and end. (2.04) dllexport / dllimport __declspec attributes that put a symbol in a DLL's export table, and tell the compiler a symbol comes from a DLL. (1.03) Exception barrier A try/catch around the body of an exported function that turns every exception into an error code. (2.06) Export table The part of a PE file listing the names, ordinals and RVAs of what a module offers to others. (1.01) extern "C" C linkage: no name decoration and no overloading, so the exported name is plain. (2.01) FreeLibrary Drops one reference to a loaded DLL; at zero the DLL is unmapped. (2.03) Function table A versioned struct of function pointers returned by one exported function, used as an interface. (3.03) GetProcAddress Returns the address of a DLL's exported function by name or ordinal. (2.03) Header-only library Reusable code entirely in headers, compiled into every program that includes it. (4.05) Host The program that loads plugins or a hot-reloaded DLL and calls into them. (5.01) Hot reload Replacing a running program's code (a DLL) with a rebuilt version without restarting or losing state. (5.03) Import address table (IAT) A module's array of slots, one per imported function, filled by the loader with real addresses. (1.05) Import library A small .lib that tells the linker which DLL each function comes from, without containing their code. (1.05) Known DLLs Core system DLLs that Windows always loads from System32, whatever the search order says. (4.01) Loader The part of Windows (in ntdll.dll ) that maps modules into a process, resolves imports and runs initialisation. (1.02) Loader lock A process-wide lock held while modules are loaded and unloaded; DllMain and global constructors run under it. (2.04) LoadLibraryW / LoadLibraryExW Map a DLL into the process at run time, the second with flags that control the search. (2.03, 4.02) Opaque handle A pointer to a type that is declared but never defined for callers, so its contents can change between versions. (3.01) Ordinal A DLL export's number. Exports can be found by ordinal instead of name. (1.04) PE file Portable Executable: the file format of Windows executables and DLLs. (1.01) Plugin A DLL the host finds and loads at run time through a fixed contract, which it was not built with. (5.01) QueryInterface The COM-style method that asks an object for another interface it supports. (3.04) Reference count A count of holders. DLLs are counted by LoadLibrary and FreeLibrary; COM-style objects by AddRef and Release. (2.03, 3.04) Relocation Fixing stored absolute addresses when a module is loaded away from its preferred base. (1.02) RVA Relative virtual address: an offset from the start of a loaded module. (1.02) Safe DLL search mode The setting, on by default, that searches the current directory after the system folders. (4.01) Search order The list of places Windows tries when a DLL is requested by name only. (4.01) Semantic versioning MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: major for breaking changes, minor for additions, patch for fixes. (3.05) SetDefaultDllDirectories Restricts every later name-only load in the process to safe folders. (4.02) Static library A .lib whose code the linker copies into the executable. (1.01) Thunk A small piece of code that stands in for a function, such as the delay-load stub that loads the DLL on the first call. (4.03) Version resource Version information compiled into a PE file, shown in Explorer's Details tab. (4.04) Versioned struct A struct whose first member is its own size, so a library can tell which version the caller sent. (3.03) vtable / vptr The table of a class's virtual function pointers, and the hidden pointer to it at the start of each object. (3.04)

title: 1.01  Kinds of Documentation
body: Why reading documentation is a core programming skill, the four kinds of documentation (tutorials, how-to guides, reference and explanation) and what each is for, the other sources you will meet, and how to pick the right one for the question you have. The skill under every other skill Nobody remembers every function. Working programmers spend a large part of each day reading: a reference page to check what a function returns on failure, a guide to set up a library, a specification to see what a file format allows. The difference between a beginner and an experienced programmer is often not what they know, but how quickly and precisely they can find out . Reading documentation well means three things: 1. Knowing which kind of document answers your question. 2. Reading it precisely : every word on a reference page is there for a reason. 3. Turning what it says into code that handles every case it describes. This course trains all three, mostly with C++, then with Windows, Python, JavaScript and specifications. Four kinds of documentation Good documentation sets are usually split into four kinds, because each answers a different need. (This division is often called the Diátaxis framework.) Kind Answers Reads like Example --- --- --- --- Tutorial "I'm new, show me" a lesson: do this, then this "Your first window with raylib" How-to guide "How do I do X?" a recipe with steps "How to read a file asynchronously" Reference "What exactly does this do?" a dry, complete description the page for std::vector::insert Explanation "Why is it like this?" an essay or background article "About processes and threads" They mix badly. A tutorial that stops to list every parameter loses the learner; a reference page that tells a story hides the one fact you need. So when you search, decide first which one you want: - Learning something new: a tutorial , then explanation . - Trying to get a task done: a how-to , then the reference for each function it uses. - Debugging, or checking an edge case: the reference , always. Other sources you will meet Source Good for Watch out for --- --- --- Specifications and standards (the C++ standard, RFCs, file format specs) the final word on what is allowed dense, precise language (milestone 4) Header files and source code what really exists, in the version you have no explanations, easy to misread (lesson 4.03) Doc comments in code ( /// , docstrings) quick help in your editor may be short or out of date Release notes and changelogs what changed between versions easy to skip, costly when you do (lesson 5.03) Examples and samples seeing the pieces used together usually skip error handling (lesson 5.01) Q&A sites, forums, blog posts, AI answers quick pointers to the right function may be old, wrong, or for another version; confirm against the reference Treat the last row as leads, not facts : they tell you where to look, and the reference page tells you whether it is true. Where documentation lives For the languages and platforms in this course: - C++ standard library : cppreference.com (community reference), the standard itself for the final word. - Windows : Microsoft Learn (learn.microsoft.com), the Win32 and C runtime references. - Python : docs.python.org, the library reference and the language reference. - JavaScript : MDN Web Docs for the language and browser APIs, nodejs.org/docs for Node. - Unix-like systems : man pages ( man 2 open ). - Libraries : their own site, README, and headers. Bookmark the reference for each language you use. Searching the web for every question costs time and often lands on an old forum answer instead of the reference. Check yourself quiz ? You need to know whether a function throws when its argument is empty. Which kind of document do you want? - A tutorial, because it shows the function being used + Reference, because it describes every case precisely - An explanation, because it says why the function exists - A how-to guide, because it solves a real task A tutorial shows one happy path and an explanation discusses ideas. Only the reference page promises to cover every input, edge cases included. ? You have never used a library and want to get something working. Where do you start? - The reference, reading every page from A to Z + A tutorial, then the reference for the functions it uses - The library's source code - A forum thread about the library's bugs A tutorial gets you to something working quickly. Then the reference pages tell you exactly what each function you used really does. ? A forum answer says a function returns -1 on error. How should you treat that? - As correct, since someone has tested it - As wrong, since forum answers are never reliable + As a lead to confirm on the reference page - As correct for every version of the library Forum answers can be right, outdated or about a different version. They tell you where to look; the reference page, for the version you are using, decides. ? Why should a reference page not tell a story? - Stories make pages too long to download + Its job is to let readers find exact facts quickly, and narrative hides them - Reference pages are generated by tools that cannot write prose - Readers of reference pages are always experts Readers arrive with a specific question. A predictable layout of precise facts answers it; a story makes them read everything to find one sentence.

title: Implement it from the page
body: Two functions are documented below in the style of a reference page (lesson 1.02). Implement them so they behave exactly as described, edge cases included. slice cpp-norun std::string slice(const std::string& s, std::size_t pos, std::size_t count = std::string::npos); Returns the part of s that starts at pos and is count characters long, or as many as there are if fewer than count remain. - Return value : the characters in the range pos, pos + n) , where n is the smaller of count and s.size() - pos . When pos == s.size() the result is empty. - Exceptions : throws std::out_of_range if pos s.size() . lastChars cpp-norun std::string lastChars(const std::string& s, std::size_t count); Returns the last count characters of s . If count is at least s.size() , returns all of s . Never throws (except std::bad_alloc ).

title: 1.02  Anatomy of a Reference Page
body: The sections nearly every reference page has - synopsis, description, parameters, return value, errors, complexity, notes, requirements, examples and see also - what each one tells you, and the order to read them in when you have a question. The same shape everywhere Reference pages from cppreference, Microsoft, Python, MDN and man pages look different, but they share a structure. Once you know it, you can read any of them quickly. Here is a reference page for an imaginary function, written in the usual style. trim_left (sample page) Declared in header <textutil.h cpp-norun std::string trim_left(std::string_view s, std::string_view chars = " \t\n"); // (1) std::string trim_left(std::string_view s, char c); // (2) Removes leading characters from s . 1. Removes every leading character that appears in chars . 2. Removes every leading character equal to c . Parameters - s : the text to trim - chars : the set of characters to remove; if empty, nothing is removed - c : the character to remove Return value A copy of s without the removed characters. If every character is removed, an empty string. Exceptions May throw std::bad_alloc if allocation fails. Complexity Linear in the size of s times the size of chars . Notes Characters are compared as bytes; multi-byte UTF-8 sequences in chars are treated as separate bytes. Example trim_left(" hello ") returns "hello " . See also trim_right , trim The sections Section Tells you Read it for --- --- --- Name and header / module what to include or import getting it to compile Synopsis / syntax every overload with exact types which version you are calling Description what it does, often per overload the main behaviour Parameters meaning and allowed values of each what you may pass Return value what comes back, in every case handling the result Errors / exceptions how failure is reported handling failure Complexity how cost grows choosing between options Notes / remarks surprises, edge cases, history the bugs you have not had yet Requirements / availability version, platform, library to link will it work where you ship Example the function in use a starting point (not production code) See also related functions finding a better fit Reading order Do not read a reference page top to bottom like a story. Go to the section that answers your question, then check the ones that could change the answer: 1. Synopsis : find the overload you are calling. With default arguments and overloads, trim_left(s, 'x') calls (2), not (1) with a one-character string. 2. Description and Parameters : what it does with your arguments, including the edge values (empty, zero, null, negative, too large). 3. Return value and Errors : every outcome you must handle. 4. Notes : always skim them. This is where pages hide "not thread-safe", "the result is not null-terminated", "deprecated", and "behaviour changed in version 3". 5. Requirements : once, before you rely on it. Words that matter Reference pages are written carefully, so small words carry meaning: - "must" , "shall" : a rule for you ; breaking it is an error, often undefined behaviour (lesson 1.04). - "may" : the function is allowed to do this. "May throw" means you must be ready for it even if you have never seen it happen. - "unspecified" : one of several results, with no promise which. "implementation-defined" : the compiler or library chooses and documents it. - "if ... otherwise" : two cases; check which applies. - "the behaviour is undefined" : anything can happen, including appearing to work. Check yourself quiz ? You call trim_left(s, "x") . Which overload is used? + (1), because a string literal converts to std::string_view , not to char - (2), because "x" is a single character - Neither: the call is ambiguous and does not compile - (2), after the string is converted to its first character "x" is an array of two char s (with the zero), which converts to std::string_view . Only 'x' , in single quotes, is a char and picks (2); a string never converts to a char . ? What does trim_left("xxx", "x") return, according to the page? - "xxx" , because only spaces, tabs and newlines are removed - "xx" , because only one leading character is removed + An empty string, because every character is removed - It throws, because the result would be empty The function removes every leading character that is in chars . When all of them are, nothing is left, and that is a normal result, not an error. ? What does "may throw std::bad_alloc " mean for your code? - It never throws in practice, so it can be ignored - It throws std::bad_alloc every time memory is low and you must retry - It returns nullptr instead of throwing in Release builds + It can throw that exception, so code that must not fail has to be ready for it, even if it rarely happens "May" means it is part of the contract. It will rarely happen, but code that must not fail has to plan for it anyway. ? Which section should you always skim even when you think you have your answer? - See also, for related functions - Examples, for typical calls + Notes, where the surprises live - Complexity, for the cost Notes (or remarks) are where pages hide "not thread-safe", "not null-terminated", "deprecated" and "behaviour changed in version 3".

title: The trim family
body:
Lesson 1.02 shows a reference page for trim_left . Implement it, and its "see also" functions trim_right and trim , exactly as documented: cpp-norun std::string trim_left(std::string_view s, std::string_view chars = " 	
"); // (1) std::string trim_left(std::string_view s, char c); // (2) std::string trim_right(std::string_view s, std::string_view chars = " 	
"); // (3) std::string trim_right(std::string_view s, char c); // (4) std::string trim(std::string_view s, std::string_view chars = " 	
"); // (5) std::string trim(std::string_view s, char c); // (6) 1. Removes every leading character that appears in chars . If chars is empty, nothing is removed. 2. Removes every leading character equal to c . 3. and 4. are the same at the end of s . 5. and 6. remove from both ends. Return value : a copy of s without the removed characters; an empty string if every character is removed. Characters are compared as single bytes.

title: 1.03  Reading Signatures
body: Decoding the declarations at the top of C++ reference pages - parameter and return types, const, references and pointers, default arguments, overload sets, templates and their named requirements, noexcept and nodiscard - so a signature tells you how to call a function before you read a word of prose. A signature is a summary The declaration at the top of a reference page already answers most questions: what you pass, what you get back, what may be changed, and what may fail. Learn to read it first. cpp-norun nodiscard std::size_t count_words(const std::string& text, char separator = ' ') noexcept; Read it piece by piece: Piece Means --- --- nodiscard ignoring the result is almost certainly a bug; the compiler warns std::size_t returns a count, never negative const std::string& text reads your string without copying it and without changing it char separator = ' ' a default argument: you may leave it out noexcept never throws an exception Parameters: who owns what, who changes what Parameter type Meaning for the caller --- --- T (by value) the function gets its own copy; yours is untouched const T& read-only access to yours, no copy T& an output or in-out parameter : your object may be changed T&& the function may take over (move from) your object const T read-only access through a pointer; check the docs whether null is allowed T may be changed through the pointer; check whether null is allowed std::string_view , std::span<const T a read-only view; the function will not keep it after returning (unless it says so) std::unique_ptr<T by value the function takes ownership A non-const reference or pointer is the strongest signal on the page: something of yours changes. Find out what. Overload sets Many functions come as a numbered set of overloads. cppreference shows them as (1) , (2) ..., each with its own description: cpp-norun iterator insert(const_iterator pos, const T& value); // (1) iterator insert(const_iterator pos, size_type count, const T& value); // (3) template<class InputIt iterator insert(const_iterator pos, InputIt first, InputIt last); // (4) iterator insert(const_iterator pos, std::initializer_list<T list); // (5) The compiler picks one from your arguments, and the surprises come from conversions: v.insert(v.begin(), 3, 7) inserts three sevens (3), not 3 and 7. Identify the overload you are calling before reading the description. Templates and named requirements Generic functions are templates, and the names of their parameters are documentation: cpp-norun template<class InputIt, class T InputIt find(InputIt first, InputIt last, const T& value); template<class RandomIt, class Compare void sort(RandomIt first, RandomIt last, Compare comp); InputIt and RandomIt refer to named requirements : an input iterator can only be read once going forward; a random-access iterator can jump anywhere (like a vector's, unlike a list's). So std::sort on a std::list fails to compile, and the signature already told you. Compare must be a strict weak ordering : comp(a, a) must be false, which is why passing <= breaks std::sort in ways that are hard to see. Ranges and concepts (C++20) state requirements directly: cpp-norun template<std::random_access_iterator I, std::sentinel_for<I S, class Comp = std::ranges::less requires std::sortable<I, Comp constexpr I sort(I first, S last, Comp comp = {}); Long, but each line is a rule about what you may pass. Return types - bool : success or a yes/no answer; check which. - An iterator : often "end" means "not found". - std::pair<iterator, bool : std::map::insert tells you where the element is and whether it was inserted. - std::optional<T : may be empty. - void : nothing to check, but failure may still be reported by exception. - auto or a long template type: read the Return value section. Check yourself quiz ? A parameter is std::vector<int & out . What does that tell you? - The function takes a copy of your vector - The function only reads your vector + The function writes to (or changes) your vector: it is an output or in-out parameter - The function takes ownership of your vector and destroys it A non- const reference lets the function change your object. Read-only access would be const std::vector<int & ; a copy would be std::vector<int . ? Why does std::sort not compile on a std::list ? - std::list cannot hold elements that can be compared + It requires random-access iterators, and a list's iterators are only bidirectional - std::sort only works on arrays - Lists are already sorted The template's named requirement, LegacyRandomAccessIterator , is part of the signature. A list cannot jump to its middle, so it has its own list::sort instead. ? What does nodiscard on a function tell you? - The function cannot be called twice in a row - The function's result is cached after the first call - The function never returns to its caller + Ignoring its return value is almost certainly a bug The compiler warns if you drop the result. Functions like empty() and std::async are marked this way because ignoring them is a common mistake. ? std::map::insert returns std::pair<iterator, bool . What does the bool mean? - Whether the map was empty before the call + Whether the element was actually inserted - Whether the map had to allocate memory - Whether the returned iterator is valid If the key already exists, insert does not replace the value: the bool is false and the iterator points at the existing element.

title: An overload set
body: Implement the four overloads of countOf documented below (lesson 1.03). Read each overload's description: they do not all count the same way. cpp-norun std::size_t countOf(std::string_view text, char c); // (1) std::size_t countOf(std::string_view text, std::string_view word); // (2) std::size_t countOf(const std::vector<int & values, int value); // (3) template<class Pred std::size_t countOf(const std::vector<int & values, Pred pred); // (4) 1. The number of characters in text equal to c . 2. The number of non-overlapping occurrences of word in text , searching from the left: after a match, the search continues after the end of that match. If word is empty, the result is text.size() + 1 (an empty word is found before every character and at the end). 3. The number of elements equal to value . 4. The number of elements x for which pred(x) returns true. pred is called exactly once per element, in order. Complexity : (1), (3) and (4) are linear in the size of the input; (2) is at most linear in text.size() times word.size() .

title: 1.04  Preconditions and Undefined Behaviour
body: The contract a reference page describes - preconditions you must meet, what the function guarantees in return, what happens on failure - half-open ranges, the difference between checked and unchecked functions, exception guarantees, and why "the behaviour is undefined" is the most important sentence on a page. A contract Every reference page describes a contract between you and the function: - Preconditions : what must be true when you call it. Your responsibility. - Postconditions : what will be true afterwards, if you met the preconditions. The function's responsibility. - Failure behaviour : what happens when it cannot do its job even though you called it correctly (out of memory, file missing). Preconditions are often written as "must", "shall", "requires", "expects", or as a list of allowed values: " count must not exceed size() ", " first and last must form a valid range", "the pointer must not be null". Undefined behaviour When a page says "the behaviour is undefined if ..." , it means breaking that precondition voids the contract completely. The program may crash, return garbage, corrupt something far away, or work perfectly on your machine and fail on another. The compiler is even allowed to assume it never happens and optimise accordingly. cpp-norun std::vector<int v; int x{ v 0 }; // operator : undefined if the index is not less than size() int y{ v.at(0) }; // at(): checks, and throws std::out_of_range v.front(); // undefined on an empty vector Many libraries offer such pairs: an unchecked fast version whose misuse is undefined, and a checked version that reports misuse. The reference page tells you which one you are calling. (Debug builds of the Microsoft library add checks to many unchecked functions, which helps while testing but is not a guarantee.) So, for every function you call, ask: what are its preconditions, and how do I know they hold? Either they are guaranteed by the code around the call (you just checked !v.empty() ), or you check them first. Half-open ranges Almost every C++ library function that takes a range uses the half-open convention first, last) : first is included, last is not. So: - the number of elements is last - first ; - an empty range has first == last ; - "not found" is usually returned as last . The same idea appears as "position and count" ( substr(pos, count) ) and in Python's slices s start:stop . When a page says "the range pos, pos + count) ", read it exactly that way. What happens on failure Reference pages describe failure in one of a few ways (lesson 2.02 goes deeper): Style You see You do --- --- --- exception "Throws std::out_of_range if ..." catch it where you can handle it, or let it propagate error value "Returns -1 / nullptr / end() / an error code" check the result every time error state "sets errno ", "call GetLastError " read it immediately after the call precondition only "the behaviour is undefined if ..." make sure it never happens Exception guarantees Pages for C++ functions that can throw often say what state things are left in: - No-throw guarantee ( noexcept ): it never throws. - Strong guarantee : if it throws, nothing changed, as if it was never called. std::vector::push_back gives this (for most element types). - Basic guarantee : if it throws, everything is still valid, but may have changed. - No guarantee : the page will say so, or say nothing; assume the worst. Check yourself quiz ? A page says " n must be less than size() ; otherwise the behaviour is undefined". Who is responsible for checking? + You, before calling, because the function does not check - The function, which throws if n is too large - The compiler, which rejects calls with a bad n - Nobody: undefined behaviour just returns an unspecified value A precondition is your side of the contract. Undefined behaviour means anything can happen, including a crash or silent memory corruption, not just a strange value. ? A range is first, last) with first == last . How many elements does it hold? + None, it is empty - One, the element at first - Two, first and last - It is not a valid range A half-open range includes first and excludes last , so equal ends mean nothing in between: the standard way to write an empty range. ? What is the difference between v i and v.at(i) for an index that is too large? - Both throw std::out_of_range - v i returns 0; v.at(i) throws + v i is undefined behaviour; v.at(i) throws std::out_of_range - v.at(i) is undefined behaviour; v i throws operator has a precondition and no check; at checks and reports the error. That difference is written on both reference pages. ? push_back gives the strong guarantee. What does that mean if it throws? - The new element was added, but the old ones may be lost - The vector is valid but its contents are unspecified + The vector is exactly as it was before the call - The program terminates The strong guarantee is commit-or-roll-back. "Valid but unspecified" is the weaker basic guarantee.

title: A string library built from its reference

body:
You are given the reference pages of a small string library, modelled on Python's string methods. Implement every function so that it matches its page exactly . The tests check each edge case the pages describe, and nothing they do not. cpp std::vector<std::string splitWhitespace(std::string_view s, int maxSplit = -1); std::vector<std::string split(std::string_view s, std::string_view sep, int maxSplit = -1); std::string join(const std::vector<std::string & parts, std::string_view sep); std::string replaceAll(std::string_view s, std::string_view from, std::string_view to, int maxCount = -1); bool startsWith(std::string_view s, std::string_view prefix, std::size_t start = 0); std::vector<std::string splitLines(std::string_view s, bool keepEnds = false); Whitespace in this library means the six characters space, 	 , 
 ,  ,   and \v . splitWhitespace splits s into words separated by runs of whitespace. Leading and trailing whitespace is ignored, so an empty or all-whitespace string gives an empty list . If maxSplit is zero or more, at most maxSplit splits are made: after that many words, the rest of the string, with its leading whitespace removed but its trailing whitespace kept, is the last element. A negative maxSplit means no limit. split splits s at every occurrence of sep , from the left. Consecutive separators produce empty strings between them, and a separator at either end produces an empty string there; an empty s gives a list holding one empty string. At most maxSplit splits are made when it is zero or more; the rest of the string is the last element. Throws std::invalid_argument if sep is empty. join returns the parts with sep between each pair; no parts give an empty string. replaceAll returns a copy of s with occurrences of from replaced by to , found from the left without overlapping; if maxCount is zero or more, only the first maxCount are replaced. If from is empty , it matches at the start of s , between every two characters and at the end, so replaceAll("abc", "", "-") is "-a-b-c-" and with maxCount 2 it is "-a-bc" . startsWith returns whether the part of s beginning at index start begins with prefix . If start is greater than s.size() the result is false, even for an empty prefix; if it equals s.size() , only an empty prefix matches. splitLines splits s at line boundaries, which in this library are 
 ,  and the pair 
 (one boundary). A line ending at the very end of s does not create an extra empty line, so "a
" gives one line and the empty string gives none. If keepEnds is true, each line keeps its boundary characters.

title: 2.01  Finding Your Way Around cppreference
body: How cppreference.com is organised - by header and by topic - the layout of a class page with its member tables and version markers, what a function page adds (possible implementation, defect reports, examples), how it relates to the C++ standard, and fast ways to land on the right page. The reference for C++ cppreference.com is the reference most C++ programmers use every day. It is written by volunteers, closely follows the C++ standard, and covers the language and the whole standard library, version by version. The standard itself (the ISO document, with free drafts at eel.is/c++draft) is the final word; cppreference is its readable map. Two ways in - By header : the "Standard library headers" page lists every header ( <vector , <string , <charconv ...) and what it declares. Use it when you know where something lives or want to see what a header offers. - By topic : the main page groups the library: containers, algorithms, strings, numerics, input/output, filesystem, concurrency and so on. Use it when you know what you want to do but not the name. The fastest route in practice is a web search with the site name and the exact name: cppreference std::from_chars , cppreference vector insert . A class page The page for a class such as std::vector is mostly tables: Part What it gives you --- --- declaration template<class T, class Allocator = std::allocator<T class vector; , and the header description what it is, its guarantees (contiguous storage), its requirements on T member types value_type , size_type , iterator ... member functions every member, grouped: element access, iterators, capacity, modifiers non-member functions operator== , std::erase , std::swap ... deduction guides, notes, example, see also as on any page Each row links to a page of its own. Markers such as (C++11) , (C++20) , (deprecated in C++17) , (removed in C++20) tell you which version a member belongs to (lesson 2.04). A member listed as (constexpr since C++20) works in older versions too, just not at compile time. A function page Function pages follow the anatomy of lesson 1.02, with a few extras: - Overloads numbered (1) , (2) ..., each with version markers, and the description refers to them by number. - Template parameter requirements : " InputIt must meet the requirements of LegacyInputIterator ", with a link explaining exactly what that means. - Return value and Exceptions sections that cover every overload. - Complexity stated precisely: "Exactly last - first applications of the predicate". - Possible implementation : a short version of the code. Excellent for understanding; but the real library may differ, so rely on the stated behaviour, not on the sample code. - Defect reports : corrections to the standard after publication ("LWG 2192: behaviour changed for ..."). If your compiler behaves differently from the page, look here. - Example : a complete program with its output. You can usually run it on Compiler Explorer with one click. Reading a page for real Here is how you would answer "does std::stoi accept leading spaces, and what happens with "12abc" ?": 1. Open the page for std::stoi . The signature shows int stoi(const std::string& str, std::size_t pos = nullptr, int base = 10); . 2. The description says it discards leading whitespace and then reads as many characters as form a valid number, like std::strtol . So "12abc" gives 12. 3. The pos parameter: if not null, it receives the number of characters processed. So you can tell that "abc" was left over. 4. Exceptions: std::invalid_argument if no conversion could be performed, std::out_of_range if the value does not fit. And the neighbour in "see also", std::from_chars , works differently: it never skips whitespace, never throws, does not accept a leading + , and reports both where it stopped and an error code. Same job, different contract; the pages tell you which you need. cpp include <charconv include <iostream include <string int main() { std::size_t used{ 0 }; std::cout << std::stoi(" 12abc", &used) << " used " << used << '\n'; const std::string text{ "+12" }; int value{ 0 }; const auto ptr, ec { std::from_chars(text.data(), text.data() + text.size(), value) }; std::cout << "from_chars on +12: " << (ec == std::errc{} ? "ok" : "failed") << '\n'; } Check yourself quiz ? Which is the final word on C++: cppreference or the standard? - cppreference, because the standard committee maintains it + The standard; cppreference is a careful community reference that follows it - Whichever was updated most recently - Your compiler's documentation, which overrides both cppreference is written by volunteers who track the ISO standard closely. When they disagree, the standard decides, and the page usually gets fixed. ? A member function is marked (C++20). Can you call it when compiling as C++17? - Yes, because markers are only advice - Yes, if your compiler is new enough + No, it was added in C++20 - Only with a warning The marker says when the member appeared in the standard. In C++17 mode it is not declared at all, so the call does not compile. ? Why not rely on a page's "possible implementation"? - It is written in an old version of C++ - It is always slower than the real library + Only the documented behaviour is guaranteed - It contains deliberate bugs to test readers It is an illustration, not your library's code, and the real library may be implemented differently. Details it happens to show, such as the order of calls, are not promised unless the description says so. ? What does std::stoi(" 12abc", &used) set used to? - 2, the number of digits + 4, because two spaces and two digits were processed - 6, the length of the whole string - Nothing: it throws because of the letters stoi skips leading whitespace, reads as many digits as it can and stops at the first character that cannot be part of the number. It throws only when no digits at all could be read.

Use their reference pages to implement two functions with very different contracts. cpp-norun std::optional<int parseStrict(std::string_view text); struct Leading { std::optional<int value; std::size_t used; std::string error; }; Leading readLeadingInt(const std::string& text); parseStrict accepts exactly: an optional single + or - , then one or more decimal digits, and nothing else : no spaces anywhere, no other characters, nothing after the digits. The value must fit in an int . Anything else gives an empty optional. (Note that std::from_chars itself does not accept a leading + .) readLeadingInt behaves like std::stoi in base 10, and reports what happened instead of throwing: - Leading whitespace is skipped, then an optional sign and as many digits as follow are read; reading stops at the first other character. - On success: value holds the number, used the count of characters processed (whitespace included), error is empty. - If there is no number at the start: value empty, used 0, error is "no number" . - If the number does not fit in an int : value empty, used 0, error is "out of range" .

title: 2.02  Return Values and Error Reporting
body: The many ways standard library functions report their results - end iterators, npos, pairs with a bool, optional, error codes, exceptions and the paired throwing and non-throwing overloads of std::filesystem - and how to read each from the reference page and handle it correctly. Read the Return value section every time Two functions that look alike can report results in completely different ways. The Return value and Exceptions sections are where you find out. The common patterns in the standard library: Pattern Example "Not found" or failure looks like --- --- --- end iterator std::find , map::find the last / end() you passed or own npos std::string::find std::string::npos , the largest size_t pair with a bool map::insert , set::insert .second == false : already there; .first points to the existing one std::optional your own APIs, many libraries empty optional result struct std::from_chars ec != std::errc{} ; ptr says where it stopped exception vector::at , std::stoi , std::filesystem std::out_of_range , std::invalid_argument , filesystem_error bool std::filesystem::remove false: there was nothing to remove (not an error!) Insert, and what "inserted" means Maps have several ways to add an element, and their pages differ in one crucial detail: what happens when the key already exists . Call Key missing Key present --- --- --- m key = value inserts overwrites m.insert({key, value}) inserts does nothing ; returns {it, false} m.try_emplace(key, args...) inserts does nothing, and does not even build the value m.insert_or_assign(key, value) inserts, returns {it, true} overwrites, returns {it, false} m.at(key) throws std::out_of_range returns a reference A common bug: using insert to update a value. It compiles, runs, and silently keeps the old value; the page said so. Two overloads: throwing and not throwing std::filesystem offers most functions twice: cpp-norun std::uintmax_t file_size(const std::filesystem::path& p); // (1) std::uintmax_t file_size(const std::filesystem::path& p, std::error_code& ec) noexcept; // (2) (1) throws std::filesystem::filesystem_error on failure. (2) never throws: it sets ec and returns a documented value, here static_cast<std::uintmax_t (-1) . Use (2) where failure is expected and normal (a file that may not exist), (1) where failure means something is really wrong. Results that need two answers std::from_chars reports where it stopped and whether it worked : cpp include <charconv include <iostream include <string_view void show(std::string_view text) { int value{ -1 }; const auto result{ std::from_chars(text.data(), text.data() + text.size(), value) }; std::cout << '"' << text << "\": "; if (result.ec == std::errc::invalid_argument) std::cout << "no number"; else if (result.ec == std::errc::result_out_of_range) std::cout << "too big"; else std::cout << value << ", stopped after " << (result.ptr - text.data()) << " chars"; std::cout << '\n'; } int main() { show("42"); show("42px"); show("px"); show("99999999999"); } To accept only a whole string, you must check both: no error, and ptr reached the end. The page tells you this indirectly ("on success, ptr points at the first character not matching the pattern"); turning such sentences into checks is the skill. Errors you can ignore and errors you cannot Some outcomes look like failures but are normal: std::filesystem::remove returning false for a missing file, map::insert finding the key. Others look harmless but are bugs: discarding the result of a nodiscard function, or an std::stoi that read "12abc" as 12 when you expected an error. The page decides which is which, not your intuition. Check yourself quiz ? m.insert({"a", 5}) is called when m "a" is already 1. What is m "a" afterwards? + Still 1, because insert does nothing when the key exists - 5, because insert replaces the value - 6, because the values are added - Both: the map now holds two entries for "a" insert only inserts a new key; its returned bool is false here. To overwrite, use m "a" = 5 or insert_or_assign . A std::map never holds two entries with one key. ? How do you know std::from_chars parsed the whole string? - It returns true - It throws if anything is left over + ec is std::errc{} and ptr equals the end of the input - The parsed value is not 0 from_chars stops at the first character it cannot use and reports success if it read a number at all. Only ptr == end tells you nothing was left over. ? When would you choose the std::error_code& overload of a filesystem function? - Always, because exceptions are slow - Never, because it ignores errors + When failure is an expected, normal outcome you want to handle without exceptions - Only on Windows, where the throwing overload does not exist A missing file you are about to create, for example, is not exceptional. The error_code overload reports it without throwing; the other overload throws filesystem_error . ? What does std::string::find return when the text is not found? - -1 - s.size() - 0 + std::string::npos npos is the largest size_t value. Comparing with -1 happens to work after conversion, but npos is what the page documents, and 0 would mean "found at the start".

title: Choosing the right map call
body: Implement a small inventory on top of std::map<std::string, int . Every member's page states what happens when the item already exists or is missing; the map member functions in lesson 2.02 differ in exactly those cases, so pick each one to match. cpp-norun class Inventory { public: bool addNew(const std::string& item, int count); bool set(const std::string& item, int count); int countOf(const std::string& item) const; bool take(const std::string& item, int n); std::size_t removeEmpty(); std::size_t size() const; std::vector<std::string items() const; }; - addNew : adds the item with count only if it is not there yet. Returns true if it was added. An existing item's count is not changed. - set : sets the item's count, adding the item if it is missing. Returns true if the item was new . - countOf : the item's count, or 0 if it is missing. Never adds an item. - take : if the item exists and has at least n , subtracts n and returns true. Otherwise returns false and changes nothing. An item that reaches 0 stays in the inventory. - removeEmpty : removes every item whose count is 0 and returns how many were removed. - size : the number of items. items : their names in sorted order.

title: 2.03  Complexity and Invalidation
body: Two promises every container page makes - how cost grows (constant, amortised constant, logarithmic, linear) and which iterators, pointers and references stay valid after each operation - how to read the invalidation rules, and the bugs that come from ignoring them. Complexity is a guarantee Every function page on cppreference ends its description with Complexity . It is not a hint, it is a promise the library must keep, and it decides which container and which function you choose: Phrase Means Example --- --- --- constant the same cost whatever the size vector::operator , vector::size amortised constant usually constant, occasionally expensive, constant on average vector::push_back (sometimes reallocates) logarithmic grows slowly, like a binary search map::find , std::lower_bound linear in n proportional to the size std::find , vector::insert in the middle average constant, worst linear hash tables unordered_map::find O(n log n) comparisons sorting std::sort Read the exact wording: "linear in the distance between pos and the end" (inserting near the end of a vector is cheap), "exactly N applications of the predicate" (you can count on side effects happening exactly once each). Invalidation: when your iterators go bad Iterators, pointers and references into a container can become invalid when the container changes. Using an invalid one is undefined behaviour (lesson 1.04): it may read freed memory, read the wrong element, or crash. Each modifying function's page says what it invalidates, and the container pages have a summary table. For the containers you use most: Container Operation Invalidated --- --- --- vector , string push_back , insert , reserve if capacity changes all iterators, pointers, references vector , string insert / push_back without reallocation those at or after the insertion point (and end() ) vector erase those at or after the erased element deque insert at either end all iterators, but not references list , map , set insert nothing list , map , set erase only the erased element unordered_map insert causing a rehash all iterators, but not references The classic bugs cpp-norun // 1. Growing a vector while iterating over it for (int x : v) if (x % 2 == 0) v.push_back(x); // push_back may reallocate: the loop's iterators dangle // 2. Keeping a reference across a push_back int& first{ v 0 }; v.push_back(7); // may reallocate std::cout << first; // may read freed memory // 3. Erasing in a loop the wrong way for (auto it{ v.begin() }; it != v.end(); ++it) if ( it < 0) v.erase(it); // 'it' is invalid after erase; ++it is undefined The fixes come straight from the pages: - erase returns an iterator to the element after the erased one: it = v.erase(it); and only ++it when you did not erase. - Better still, std::erase_if(v, pred) (C++20) removes all matching elements in one linear pass. - For growing while reading, loop over indices up to the original size, or build the new elements in a separate vector and append them afterwards. - reserve before taking pointers, if the page's guarantee is what you need: "no reallocation takes place until the size exceeds the capacity". Microsoft's debug library checks many of these and stops the program with a debug assertion about an invalid or incompatible iterator. The release build does not check: the bug is still there, just silent. Check yourself quiz ? What does "amortised constant" mean for push_back ? - Always exactly the same time, whatever the size - Constant time, but only after reserve has been called + Constant on average, with an occasional costly reallocation - Constant time for the first call, then linear Most calls just write one element. Every so often the vector reallocates and moves everything, but capacity grows geometrically, so the average cost per call over many calls stays constant. ? You hold a reference to an element of a std::map and insert another element. Is the reference still valid? + Yes, because inserting into a map invalidates nothing - No, because the map may rebalance and move its elements - Only if the map did not need to allocate - Only if the new key is larger than the old one Map nodes never move: rebalancing changes links, not where elements live. The map's page says insert invalidates no iterators or references. ? What is wrong with v.erase(it); ++it; ? - Nothing, erase moves it to the next element anyway - erase cannot be called with an iterator + it is invalid after erase , so use the iterator erase returns - ++it skips one element, so it should be it++ After erasing, it must not be used at all, not even incremented. it = v.erase(it); gives a valid iterator to the element after the erased one. ? Does push_back always invalidate every iterator of a vector? - Yes, every time it is called - No, it never invalidates anything + Only when it reallocates; otherwise only end() changes - Only iterators to elements after the middle A reallocation happens when the size would exceed the capacity. Without one the elements stay put, so existing iterators remain valid and only the past-the-end iterator changes.

title: Fixing invalidation bugs
body: Each function below was first written like this, and each version has undefined behaviour that the container's reference page warns about (lesson 2.03). Do not copy them; write correct versions with the documented results. cpp-norun // 1. Grows the vector while a range-for is walking it. void appendSquares(std::vector<int & v) { for (int x : v) v.push_back(x x); } // 2. Inserts through an iterator, then keeps using the old iterator. void duplicateEvens(std::vector<int & v) { for (auto it{ v.begin() }; it != v.end(); ++it) if ( it % 2 == 0) { v.insert(it + 1, it); ++it; } } // 3. Uses an iterator after erasing it. std::size_t removeNegatives(std::vector<int & v) { std::size_t n{ 0 }; for (auto it{ v.begin() }; it != v.end(); ++it) if ( it < 0) { v.erase(it); ++n; } return n; } // 4. The same, on a map. std::size_t removeShortKeys(std::map<std::string, int & m, std::size_t minLength) { std::size_t n{ 0 }; for (auto it{ m.begin() }; it != m.end(); ++it) if (it- first.size() < minLength) { m.erase(it); ++n; } return n; } What each must do: 1. appendSquares appends the square of every element that was in v when it was called, in order: {1, 2, 3} becomes {1, 2, 3, 1, 4, 9} . 2. duplicateEvens inserts a copy of each even element directly after it: {1, 2, 3, 4} becomes {1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4} . 3. removeNegatives removes every negative element, keeping the others in order, and returns how many it removed. 4. removeShortKeys removes every entry whose key is shorter than minLength and returns how many it removed.
