body: Implement IntVector , a growable array of int , from the reference below. It follows std::vector closely, but its pages pin down details the standard leaves open, such as exactly how capacity grows, so the tests can check them. Manage the memory yourself ( std::unique_ptr<int or new / delete ); do not use std::vector inside it. cpp class IntVector { public: static constexpr std::size_t maxSize() { return std::size_t{ 1 } << 28; } IntVector(); explicit IntVector(std::size_t count, int value = 0); IntVector(std::initializer_list<int values); IntVector(const IntVector& other); IntVector(IntVector&& other) noexcept; IntVector& operator=(const IntVector& other); IntVector& operator=(IntVector&& other) noexcept; std::size_t size() const; std::size_t capacity() const; bool empty() const; int data(); int& operator (std::size_t i); int& at(std::size_t i); int& front(); int& back(); void push_back(int value); void pop_back(); std::size_t insert(std::size_t pos, int value); std::size_t insert(std::size_t pos, std::size_t count, int value); std::size_t erase(std::size_t pos); std::size_t erase(std::size_t first, std::size_t last); void resize(std::size_t n, int value = 0); void reserve(std::size_t n); void shrinkToFit(); void clear(); bool operator==(const IntVector& other) const; }; Construction. The default vector is empty with capacity 0. IntVector(count, value) holds count copies of value ; the initializer-list constructor holds the listed values (so IntVector{ 3 } holds one element, 3, while IntVector(3) holds three zeros). In all three, capacity equals size. A copy has the same elements and capacity equal to its size; copies are independent. After a move , the target has the source's elements and capacity, and the source is empty with capacity 0. Access. operator , front , back and pop_back do not check: calling them out of range or on an empty vector is undefined behaviour (never tested). at throws std::out_of_range if i = size() . data returns a pointer to the first element. Growth. A reallocation moves the elements to a new block of a given capacity. Reallocation happens only where stated below; otherwise pointers from data() stay valid. Member Behaviour Capacity --- --- --- push_back appends if full, becomes max(1, 2 × capacity) insert(pos, value) inserts before index pos ; returns pos if full, as push_back insert(pos, count, value) inserts count copies before pos ; returns pos ; count 0 changes nothing if size + count capacity , becomes max(2 × capacity, size + count) erase(pos) removes element pos ; returns pos unchanged erase(first, last) removes first, last) ; returns first unchanged resize(n, value) shrinks to n , or grows filling with value if n capacity , becomes n reserve(n) nothing else if n capacity , becomes n ; never shrinks shrinkToFit nothing else becomes size clear removes all elements unchanged Errors. Both insert s throw std::out_of_range if pos size() . erase(pos) throws std::out_of_range if pos = size() ; erase(first, last) if first last or last size() . reserve throws std::length_error if n maxSize() . In every case the vector is unchanged when they throw. Comparison. Two vectors are equal if they have the same size and the same elements in order; capacity does not matter.

title: 3.01  A Win32 Reference Page
body: Reading a Microsoft Learn page for a Windows API function from top to bottom - the syntax block and its types, parameter directions, the exact wording of the return value, the remarks where the surprises live, and the requirements table with header, library, DLL and minimum Windows version - using GetModuleFileNameW as the example. Where Windows documents itself Every Windows API function has a page on Microsoft Learn (learn.microsoft.com), under "Windows App Development Win32 API" or by searching the function name. The pages share one layout, and once you know it you can use functions you have never seen before. The Win32 course uses these functions; this milestone is about reading their pages precisely. We will read the page for GetModuleFileNameW , which gives the full path of an executable or DLL. What follows describes the page in our own words, section by section. Syntax cpp-norun DWORD GetModuleFileNameW( in, optional HMODULE hModule, out LPWSTR lpFilename, in DWORD nSize ); - Types are Windows typedefs: DWORD is a 32-bit unsigned integer, LPWSTR a pointer to a wide (UTF-16) string, HMODULE a handle to a loaded module. The "Windows Data Types" page lists them all. - Directions in brackets: in you provide, out the function fills, in, out both, and optional means you may pass null. (In headers these appear as SAL annotations; lesson 3.02.) - Names use the old Hungarian prefixes, which are worth decoding: lp long pointer, n or cch a count of characters, cb a count of bytes, h a handle, dw a DWORD , b a BOOL . Parameters The page describes each parameter. For this function: - hModule : the module whose path you want; null means the executable of the current process . - lpFilename : the buffer that receives the path. - nSize : the size of that buffer in characters ( WCHAR s), not bytes. "Characters, not bytes" is the kind of detail that causes buffer overruns when missed: a buffer of MAX_PATH wchar_t s is 520 bytes, and passing sizeof(buffer) would claim twice the real size. Return value This section must be read word by word. Paraphrased, it says: - On success , the return value is the length of the string copied, in characters, not including the terminating null. - If the buffer is too small , the path is truncated to nSize characters including the null, the function returns nSize , and the last error is set to ERROR_INSUFFICIENT_BUFFER . - On failure , the return value is 0 ; call GetLastError for the reason. So a return value equal to nSize is not success; it is a truncated result. Code that only checks for 0 silently uses a cut-off path. The correct pattern, a loop that grows the buffer, is the first practice task. Remarks The remarks hold the surprises: which module handle to use for a DLL, what happens when the module was loaded from a long path, and an old Windows XP note that the result may not be null-terminated when truncated. Older pages often keep notes like this about past versions; check whether they apply to the systems you support. Requirements A table at the bottom: Requirement Value (summarised) --- --- Minimum supported client / server the first Windows version that has the function Header libloaderapi.h (include windows.h ) Library Kernel32.lib , to link against DLL Kernel32.dll , where it lives at run time There is also the line " Unicode and ANSI names : GetModuleFileNameW (Unicode) and GetModuleFileNameA (ANSI)". The plain name GetModuleFileName is a macro that picks one depending on whether UNICODE is defined. Call the W versions explicitly with wide strings: the A versions convert through the current code page and lose characters. Check yourself quiz ? nSize is described as a size in characters. You have wchar_t buffer 260 . What do you pass? + 260, std::size(buffer) , not sizeof(buffer) , which is 520 - 520, sizeof(buffer) , the size of the buffer in bytes - 259, leaving room for the terminating null - 261, counting the terminating null as well Characters are not bytes: each wchar_t is 2 bytes. The page asks for characters and its remarks say the function itself handles the null within that count. ? GetModuleFileNameW returns exactly nSize . What happened? - It succeeded and filled the buffer exactly + The buffer was too small and the path was truncated - It failed because hModule was invalid - The path is nSize characters long, plus a null On success the return value is the length without the null, which is always less than nSize . Returning nSize is the page's signal for truncation. ? What does a null hModule mean for this function? - The call fails with ERROR_INVALID_HANDLE - The path of the DLL that called the function + The executable file of the current process - The path of kernel32.dll The Parameters section says that if hModule is NULL , the function retrieves the path of the current process's executable file. ? What is the difference between the Library and DLL lines in the requirements? - They are two names for the same file - The library is for 32-bit programs and the DLL for 64-bit ones - The DLL is what you link against; the library is loaded at run time + You link against the library; the DLL is loaded at run time Kernel32.lib tells the linker how to import the function; Kernel32.dll holds the code the loader maps into your process.

title: The grow-until-it-fits loop
body: Lesson 3.01 read the return value of GetModuleFileNameW : success returns the length without the null, a truncated result returns exactly the buffer size, and failure returns 0. The starter contains FakeGetModuleFileName , a stand-in with exactly that contract (and the tests change the path it reports). Do not change it. Write the caller: cpp-norun std::optional<std::wstring modulePath(); modulePath returns the full path, or an empty optional if the function fails or the path does not fit even in the largest buffer: 1. Start with a buffer of 260 characters ( MAX_PATH ). 2. Call FakeGetModuleFileName(buffer, size) . 3. A result of 0 is a failure: return an empty optional. 4. A result equal to size means the path was truncated : double the size, but to no more than 32 768 characters, and call again. If the call with 32 768 characters is still truncated, return an empty optional. 5. Any other result is the length of the path: return those characters.

title: 3.02  SAL Annotations and Buffer Sizes
body: The source annotation language in Windows headers - _In_, _Out_, _Inout_, _opt_, _Out_writes_ and friends - what each promises about a parameter, characters versus bytes, and the three patterns Windows uses for buffers whose size you do not know in advance. Annotations in the headers Open a Windows header and the declarations look like this: cpp-norun DWORD GetEnvironmentVariableW( _In_opt_ LPCWSTR lpName, _Out_writes_to_opt_(nSize, return + 1) LPWSTR lpBuffer, _In_ DWORD nSize); The _In_ , _Out_writes_... markers are SAL , the Source Annotation Language. They compile to nothing, but they document the contract precisely, and the compiler's code analysis ( /analyze ) checks calls against them. The documentation's in , out and optional come from the same information. Annotation Means --- --- _In_ read only; must not be null _In_opt_ read only; may be null _Out_ the function writes it; must not be null _Inout_ read and then written _In_reads_(n) reads n elements _In_reads_bytes_(n) reads n bytes _Out_writes_(n) writes up to n elements (the buffer must hold n ) _Out_writes_to_(n, count) buffer holds n , the function writes count _Outptr_ receives a pointer the function allocates or returns _Ret_maybenull_ the return value may be null _Success_(expr) the out parameters are valid only when expr is true _Out_writes_to_opt_(nSize, return + 1) above reads: the buffer may be null; it holds nSize characters; on success the function writes "return value + 1" characters (the string plus its null). Characters or bytes Windows counts in two units, and the names and annotations tell you which: - cch... , nSize "in characters", _Out_writes_(n) on a WCHAR : count wchar_t s . - cb... , "in bytes", _Out_writes_bytes_(n) : count bytes . A wide string of 10 characters plus its null is 22 bytes. Mixing them is one of the most common Windows bugs, either an overrun (bytes passed where characters were expected) or a truncation (the other way round). Three patterns for unknown sizes Often you cannot know how big the result will be. Windows functions use one of three patterns, and the Return value section tells you which: 1. Ask for the size first. Call with a null buffer (or too small a one); the function returns the size needed, then you allocate and call again. GetEnvironmentVariableW : if the buffer is too small, it returns the size required including the null; on success it returns the length excluding the null. Those two different meanings of the return value are how you tell the cases apart. 2. Grow until it fits. Some functions never tell you the size; they truncate. GetModuleFileNameW (lesson 3.01) returns nSize when truncated, so you double the buffer and try again. 3. Size in, size out. A pointer parameter holds the buffer size going in and receives the size needed or used coming out, often with the error ERROR_MORE_DATA (234) when the buffer was too small. The registry function RegQueryValueExW works this way with lpcbData , in bytes. Passing a null data pointer with a valid size pointer asks only for the size. In all three, the value can change between the calls : an environment variable or a registry value may be rewritten by another thread or process. Robust code loops: query, allocate, fetch, and if it is still too small, go round again. Check yourself quiz ? What does _In_opt_ on a parameter tell you? - The function writes to it, and it may be null + The function only reads it, and null is allowed - The function only reads it, and it must not be null - The parameter is optional and can be left out of the call _In_ means read-only input and _opt_ means NULL is accepted. You still have to pass something, as C has no way to leave an argument out. ? A function takes _Out_writes_bytes_(cb) . You have a buffer of 50 wchar_t s. What do you pass as cb ? - 50, the number of characters - 49, leaving room for the null + 100 (50 × sizeof(wchar_t) ), the size in bytes - 25, because each wchar_t holds two characters The _bytes_ form counts bytes; plain _Out_writes_ counts elements. Passing 50 here would tell the function the buffer is half its real size. ? GetEnvironmentVariableW returns 12 for a buffer of 10 characters. What does 12 mean? - It copied 12 characters and overran the buffer + The buffer is too small: 12 characters, including the null, are needed - The variable's value is 12 - Error 12 occurred; call GetLastError for details This is the size-query pattern: a return value bigger than the buffer means "too small, here is what you need". Allocate 12 and call again. ? Why should a size-query-then-fetch sequence be a loop? - Windows only returns the full value on the second call - The first call always fails + The value may change between the calls and need a bigger buffer the second time - Loops are required by the SAL annotations Another thread or process can change the value between your two calls. Loop until the fetch fits.

title: Ask for the size, then fetch
match: Ask for the size, then fetch
body: FakeGetVariable in the starter imitates GetEnvironmentVariableW (lesson 3.02). Its page, in short: cpp-norun DWORD FakeGetVariable(const wchar_t name, wchar_t buffer, DWORD size); - If the variable does not exist: returns 0 , and g_lastError is ERROR_ENVVAR_NOT_FOUND (203). - If buffer is null or size is too small for the value and its terminating null: returns the size needed, including the null . The buffer is not written. - Otherwise: copies the value and a null, returns the length not including the null , and sets g_lastError to 0. An existing variable with an empty value therefore returns 0 here, with g_lastError 0. Other code may change the variable between your calls (the tests do, through g_beforeCall ). Write: cpp-norun std::optional<std::wstring readVariable(const std::wstring& name); It returns the value, an empty string for an existing empty variable, or an empty optional if the variable does not exist. Ask for the size with a null buffer first, then fetch; if the fetch reports that the buffer is too small (the value grew), go round again with the new size. If the variable disappears between the calls, the result is an empty optional.

title: 3.03  GetLastError, HRESULT and NTSTATUS
body: The three error systems you meet in Windows documentation - the per-thread last error, COM's HRESULT with its severity, facility and code bits, and the kernel's NTSTATUS - how a page tells you which one a function uses, how to decode each, and how to turn them into readable messages. Which system does this function use? The Return value section always names it. The common phrases: The page says System --- --- "If the function fails, the return value is zero (or NULL , INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE ). To get extended error information, call GetLastError ." last error "Returns ERROR_SUCCESS if successful, or a system error code." (registry functions) the error code is the return value; GetLastError is not used "If this function succeeds, it returns S_OK . Otherwise, it returns an HRESULT error code." HRESULT "Returns STATUS_SUCCESS or an error status" (native and driver APIs) NTSTATUS Note the second row: some functions return the error code directly, and calling GetLastError after them gives an unrelated value. The last error GetLastError returns a number kept per thread , set by the last function that chose to set it. Rules from the pages: - Read it immediately after the failed call; almost anything else may overwrite it. - Only read it when the page says the function failed. Many functions do not clear it on success, and some set it even on success (the page says so when it matters: CreateMutexW sets ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS while succeeding, which is how you detect an existing mutex). - The values are the system error codes : 2 ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND , 5 ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED , 87 ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER , 122 ERROR_INSUFFICIENT_BUFFER , 234 ERROR_MORE_DATA ... listed on the "System Error Codes" pages. HRESULT COM and many newer APIs return an HRESULT , a 32-bit value with fields: text bit 31 severity: 0 success, 1 failure bits 16-26 facility: which area produced it (7 = Win32, 4 = ITF ...) bits 0-15 code So negative means failure : test with SUCCEEDED(hr) ( hr = 0 ) and FAILED(hr) ( hr < 0 ), never with hr == S_OK alone, because S_FALSE (1) is a success that means "it worked, but the answer is no". Values you will see constantly: Name Value Means --- --- --- S_OK 0x00000000 success S_FALSE 0x00000001 success, negative answer E_FAIL 0x80004005 unspecified failure E_INVALIDARG 0x80070057 an argument was invalid E_OUTOFMEMORY 0x8007000E allocation failed E_ACCESSDENIED 0x80070005 access denied Notice E_INVALIDARG is 0x8007 followed by 0x0057 : facility 7 (Win32) and code 87, ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER . The macro HRESULT_FROM_WIN32(x) builds such values: for a positive error code it ORs in the failure bit and facility 7; zero and values that are already HRESULT s (zero or negative) pass through unchanged. So when you see 0x8007xxxx , the low 16 bits are a plain Win32 error code you can look up. NTSTATUS The kernel and ntdll use NTSTATUS , also 32 bits, but with two severity bits at the top: Top two bits Severity Example --- --- --- 00 success STATUS_SUCCESS = 0 01 informational 0x40000000 and up 10 warning STATUS_BUFFER_OVERFLOW = 0x80000005 11 error STATUS_ACCESS_VIOLATION = 0xC0000005 That last one is familiar: a crashing program's exit code 0xC0000005 (lesson 1.03 of the Processes and Communication course) is an NTSTATUS . Turning codes into messages FormatMessageW with FORMAT_MESSAGE_FROM_SYSTEM turns a system error code (and many HRESULT s) into the text shown on the System Error Codes page. Log the number and the text: the number is searchable, the text is readable. Visual Studio's "Error Lookup" tool and the watch-window format @err,hr do the same while debugging. Check yourself quiz ? A function returns S_FALSE . Did it fail? - Yes, any value other than S_OK is a failure + No, S_FALSE is a success code meaning "no" - Yes, because FAILED(S_FALSE) is true - It depends on what GetLastError returns S_FALSE is 1, with the severity bit clear, so SUCCEEDED is true; it means "no" or "nothing to do". That is why you test with SUCCEEDED / FAILED , not by comparing with S_OK . ? What Win32 error is inside the HRESULT 0x80070002 ? - 7, ERROR_ARENA_TRASHED + 2, ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND (facility 7 means Win32) - 0x8007 , an unknown error - None: HRESULTs never contain Win32 errors 0x8007xxxx is HRESULT_FROM_WIN32 : severity bit set, facility 7 (Win32), and the low 16 bits are the Win32 code, here 2. ? A registry function returns 5. Should you call GetLastError ? - Yes, the return value only says that an error happened - Yes, but only if 5 means failure + No: registry functions return the error code directly, and 5 is ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED - No: 5 means success for registry functions The page's Return value section says which system a function uses. Registry functions return a LSTATUS code and do not set the last error. ? What severity does the NTSTATUS 0xC0000005 have? - Success, because the low bits are 5 - Informational, because the top bit is set - Warning, because the top two bits are 10 + Error, because its top two bits are 11 0xC is 1100 in binary, so the top two bits are 3: error. 0xC0000005 is STATUS_ACCESS_VIOLATION .

title: Decoding Windows error values
body: Implement the decoding that lesson 3.03 describes, for HRESULT and NTSTATUS values. cpp-norun using HRESULT = std::int32_t; bool succeeded(HRESULT hr); bool failed(HRESULT hr); HRESULT hresultFromWin32(std::uint32_t error); struct HrParts { bool failure; unsigned facility; unsigned code; }; HrParts splitHresult(HRESULT hr); std::string describeHresult(HRESULT hr); std::string ntSeverity(std::uint32_t status); - succeeded is true for zero and positive values; failed for negative ones. - hresultFromWin32 : if the error code, read as an HRESULT , is zero or negative, it is returned unchanged; otherwise the result keeps its low 16 bits, with facility 7 and the failure bit set. - splitHresult : failure is bit 31, facility bits 16 to 26, code bits 0 to 15. - describeHresult returns, in this order of preference: the name for S_OK , S_FALSE , E_FAIL , E_INVALIDARG , E_OUTOFMEMORY or E_ACCESSDENIED (values in lesson 3.03); for any other failure with facility 7, Win32 error N with the code in decimal; otherwise HRESULT 0x and 8 upper-case hex digits. - ntSeverity returns success , information , warning or error from the top two bits.

title: 3.04  Structures, Flags and Versions
body: Reading the parts of Windows pages that describe data - structures whose first member gives their size, reserved fields, zero-initialisation, flag parameters that combine with OR versus parameters that take one value, mutually exclusive flags, and version requirements and _WIN32_WINNT. Structures that know their size Many Windows structures start with a member holding their own size: cb , cbSize , dwSize , dwOSVersionInfoSize . The page always says the same thing about it in some form: "The size of the structure, in bytes. You must set this member before calling the function." cpp-norun STARTUPINFOW si{}; // zero every member si.cb = sizeof(si); // then the size PROCESS_INFORMATION pi{}; CreateProcessW(..., &si, &pi); Why? Structures grow in new Windows versions. The size tells the function which version of the structure you compiled against , so it reads and writes only the members you have. A function that receives a size it does not know fails with ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER rather than writing past the end of your memory. Forgetting to set it usually makes the call fail; setting it to the size of the wrong structure can make it write outside your object. Two more habits from the same pages: - Zero-initialise every structure ( {} ): members you do not set must usually be zero or null, and reserved members "must be zero" even though nothing uses them yet. Garbage in a reserved field is a bug waiting for the Windows version that starts using it. - Read each member's description for whether it is in (you fill it), out (the function fills it) or both. The same structure is often used both ways. Flags or a single value Parameters with named constants come in two kinds, and the wording says which: - "This parameter can be one or more of the following values": flags , combined with . Each value is a separate bit: FILE_SHARE_READ FILE_SHARE_WRITE . - "This parameter can be one of the following values": an enumeration . Combining values is wrong, and since they are often consecutive numbers ( CREATE_NEW 1, CREATE_ALWAYS 2, OPEN_EXISTING 3, OPEN_ALWAYS 4, TRUNCATE_EXISTING 5), OR-ing two gives a third, unintended one. CREATE_NEW CREATE_ALWAYS is 3, which is OPEN_EXISTING . Flag lists often come with rules: "cannot be combined with", "requires", "if this flag is specified, the x parameter must be ...". When a page has such rules, the function usually checks them and fails with ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER ; some combinations are just documented as undefined. Versions The Requirements table gives the minimum Windows version. To use a function or structure member from a newer version, the headers must be told your target, through _WIN32_WINNT (or NTDDI_VERSION ), defined before including windows.h : cpp-norun define _WIN32_WINNT 0x0A00 // Windows 10 include <windows.h If you target an older version than a function needs, the declaration is hidden and the code does not compile; if you call a function your users' Windows does not have, the program fails to start, so for optional features look the function up at run time with GetProcAddress (the DLLs course covers this). Some members are documented "Windows 10, version 1703 and later": the structure is the same size, but older systems ignore the member. Check yourself quiz ? Why must you set cbSize before calling a function that takes the structure? + It tells the function which version of the structure you have - It tells the function how much memory to allocate for you - It is a checksum that proves the structure was initialised - It is only needed on 32-bit Windows Newer Windows versions add members to the end. cbSize tells the function how many of them your program knows about, so it reads and writes only those and never touches memory past your structure. ? A page says "can be one of the following values". May you combine two with ? - Yes, flags can always be combined + No, it takes a single value - Yes, but only two at a time - Only if both values are powers of two "One of" means an enumerated value, not a set of bit flags. OR-ing two such values produces some other number, which may be a third value or invalid. ? What should you put in a member documented as "reserved; must be zero"? - Any value, because it is ignored - The size of the structure, like cbSize + Zero, for example by initialising with {} - The Windows version you target Reserved members may get a meaning in a later Windows version. Leaving garbage there could ask for behaviour you never intended; zero-initialising the whole structure with {} takes care of it. ? What does define _WIN32_WINNT 0x0A00 do? - Makes your program refuse to run on versions older than Windows 10 - Turns on Windows 10 features in the operating system + Tells the Windows headers you target Windows 10, making declarations up to that version available - Sets the version number shown in the program's properties It is a compile-time switch for the headers. It does not check the version at run time; your program can still be started on older Windows and fail there.

title: Sized structures and flag rules
body: This time you are on the other side of the page: implement two functions of an imaginary system API so that they behave as their documentation (below) promises, the way lesson 3.04 describes. fillInfo cpp-norun struct InfoV1 { std::uint32_t cbSize; std::uint32_t processors; std::uint32_t pageSize; }; struct InfoV2 { std::uint32_t cbSize; std::uint32_t processors; std::uint32_t pageSize; std::uint32_t flags; std::uint64_t totalMemory; }; bool fillInfo(void info); info points to an InfoV1 or an InfoV2 whose cbSize the caller has set. The function fills in every member of that version except cbSize , using the constants kProcessors , kPageSize , kFlags and kTotalMemory , and returns true with g_lastError set to 0. It never writes beyond cbSize bytes. If info is null, or cbSize is not the size of one of the two structures, it returns false with g_lastError set to ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER and writes nothing. (The memory may not be aligned for the structure: copy bytes rather than casting the pointer.) checkOpenFlags and checkDisposition cpp-norun std::uint32_t checkOpenFlags(std::uint32_t flags); // "one or more of the following values" std::uint32_t checkDisposition(std::uint32_t value); // "one of the following values" flags combines FLAG_READ (0x1), FLAG_WRITE (0x2), FLAG_CREATE (0x4), FLAG_TRUNCATE (0x8), FLAG_APPEND (0x10) and FLAG_EXCLUSIVE (0x20). checkOpenFlags returns ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER if any other bit is set, if neither FLAG_READ nor FLAG_WRITE is set, if FLAG_TRUNCATE or FLAG_APPEND is set without FLAG_WRITE , if FLAG_TRUNCATE and FLAG_APPEND are both set, or if FLAG_EXCLUSIVE is set without FLAG_CREATE ; otherwise ERROR_SUCCESS (0). checkDisposition accepts exactly one of the values 1 to 5 ( CREATE_NEW to TRUNCATE_EXISTING ) and returns ERROR_SUCCESS ; anything else gives ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER .

title: A registry-style API built to its documentation
match: A registry-style API built to its documentation
body: Implement ValueStore , a small store of named values whose functions follow the conventions of the Windows registry API: error codes as return values, sizes in bytes passed through pointers, null meaning "I only want the size", and ERROR_MORE_DATA for buffers that are too small (lessons 3.01 to 3.04). The pages below are the whole contract; the tests check every sentence. cpp using DWORD = std::uint32_t; using LONG = std::int32_t; using BYTE = std::uint8_t; constexpr LONG ERROR_SUCCESS = 0, ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND = 2, ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER = 87, ERROR_MORE_DATA = 234, ERROR_NO_MORE_ITEMS = 259; constexpr DWORD REG_NONE = 0, REG_SZ = 1, REG_BINARY = 3, REG_DWORD = 4, REG_QWORD = 11; class ValueStore { public: LONG setValue(const wchar_t name, DWORD type, const BYTE data, DWORD cbData); LONG queryValue(const wchar_t name, DWORD type, BYTE data, DWORD cbData) const; LONG deleteValue(const wchar_t name); LONG enumValue(DWORD index, wchar_t name, DWORD cchName, DWORD type) const; DWORD count() const; }; Names. A null name and an empty name both mean the default value , whose name is the empty string. Names are compared ignoring the case of the letters A to Z , so Volume and VOLUME are the same value. A value keeps the spelling it was first created with. Names longer than 255 characters are rejected with ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER . setValue creates the value or replaces an existing one's type and data (it keeps its place in the enumeration order; new values go at the end). It returns ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER , changing nothing, if data is null while cbData is not 0; if the type is REG_DWORD and cbData is not 4; if the type is REG_QWORD and cbData is not 8; or if the type is REG_SZ and cbData is odd. For REG_SZ , data that does not end with a null wchar_t (including empty data) is stored with one added. Any other type stores the bytes exactly. Returns ERROR_SUCCESS . queryValue : - If the value does not exist: ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND , nothing written. - If data is not null but cbData is null: ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER , nothing written. - If type is not null, it receives the value's type (also when the result is ERROR_MORE_DATA ). - If data is null: when cbData is not null it receives the size of the data in bytes; returns ERROR_SUCCESS . (Both null just checks that the value exists.) - If cbData is smaller than the data: cbData receives the size needed and the result is ERROR_MORE_DATA ; the buffer is not written. - Otherwise the data is copied, cbData receives its size, and the result is ERROR_SUCCESS . deleteValue removes the value, or returns ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND . Later values move up one place in the enumeration. enumValue gives the name (and, if type is not null, the type) of the value at index , in enumeration order. name and cchName must not be null ( ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER ). An index at or past the end gives ERROR_NO_MORE_ITEMS . cchName is the buffer size in characters, including the null ; if the name and its null do not fit, cchName receives the size needed including the null, and the result is ERROR_MORE_DATA . Otherwise the name and a null are copied, cchName receives the length without the null, and the result is ERROR_SUCCESS . count is the number of values.

title: 4.01  Python's Documentation
body: Finding and reading docs.python.org - the tutorial, library reference and language reference - Python signature notation with defaults, / and , the version notes that say when behaviour changed, how a page describes exceptions, and help(), docstrings and type stubs from inside Python. Three books in one site docs.python.org holds several documents, and knowing which to open saves time: Document For --- --- Tutorial learning the language from the start Library Reference built-in functions, types ( str , list , dict ) and every standard module: the one you will use most Language Reference the exact rules of the syntax and semantics, like the C++ standard HOWTOs how-to guides on single topics: sorting, logging, regular expressions What's New per version, what was added and changed Use the version selector at the top: pages differ between Python 3.9 and 3.13, and search engines often land on an old one. Reading a Python signature Python pages write signatures in Python syntax: python-norun str.split(sep=None, maxsplit=-1) sorted(iterable, /, , key=None, reverse=False) int(x, /, base=10) - name=value : a default ; you may leave the argument out. - A / marks the end of positional-only parameters: sorted(iterable=x) is an error; you must write sorted(x) . - A marks the start of keyword-only parameters: sorted(x, None, True) is an error; you must write sorted(x, reverse=True) . - Older pages use brackets for optional arguments: range(start, stop , step ) . Defaults such as sep=None often stand for a different behaviour , not a value, and the description explains it. For str.split , sep=None means "split on runs of whitespace and drop empty strings", while any given separator means "split exactly at each occurrence, keeping empty strings". The project of milestone 1 implemented exactly this difference. What the description promises Python pages are prose more than tables, so read for these phrases: - "Raises ValueError if ..." , "If ... a TypeError is raised" : the exceptions to handle. - "Return a new list ..." versus "... in place" : sorted() returns a new list, list.sort() changes the list and returns None . Using x = x.sort() is a classic bug the page warns about. - "The result is guaranteed to be stable" , "CPython implementation detail: ..." : the first you may rely on; the second you may not, other Pythons can differ. - Exact edge rules: slicing s i:j:k documents what happens with negative and out-of-range indices and with a negative step (practice 4.01 implements them). Version notes Pages carry boxed notes that matter as much as the text: - Added in version 3.9. You cannot use it on 3.8. - Changed in version 3.7: for example, "dictionary order is guaranteed to be insertion order". Code relying on the new behaviour silently misbehaves on older versions. - Deprecated since version 3.12, will be removed in version 3.14. Plan to move away. From inside Python - help(str.split) prints the docstring, which usually summarises the page. - obj.__doc__ is the same text; your own functions get one when their first statement is a string literal. - Type hints and the typeshed stubs (what editors use for completion) show parameter and return types, which the prose sometimes leaves implicit. python-norun help(str.split) split(self, /, sep=None, maxsplit=-1) Return a list of the substrings in the string, using sep as the separator string. ... Check yourself quiz ? Can you call sorted( 3, 1 , None, True) ? - Yes, the arguments are matched by position - Yes, but True is ignored without a name + No, key and reverse are keyword-only - No, sorted takes exactly one argument In the signature sorted(iterable, /, , key=None, reverse=False) , everything after must be passed by name: sorted( 3, 1 , reverse=True) . ? What does "a,,b".split(",") return, and how is that different from "a b".split() ? + 'a', '', 'b' ; with no separator you get 'a', 'b' - 'a', 'b' both times, because empty strings are dropped - 'a', '', 'b' both times, because runs are never merged - 'a', ',', 'b' ; with no separator, 'a', ' ', 'b' With an explicit separator, every occurrence splits, so two commas give an empty string between them. With no separator, runs of whitespace count as one and empty strings are dropped. ? What does a "CPython implementation detail" note mean for your code? - It is guaranteed by the Python language itself - It applies only to Python 2 and can be ignored + It holds for the reference interpreter only - It describes a bug that will be fixed soon Other implementations, such as PyPy, may behave differently, and CPython itself may change it. Do not rely on it. ? Why is x = x.sort() a bug? - sort() returns a sorted copy and leaves x unsorted + sort() sorts in place and returns None - sort() cannot be called on a list in a statement - sort() returns the list reversed The list is sorted, but then x is set to the None that sort() returns. Use x.sort() alone, or x = sorted(x) for a new list.

title: Python's slice and division rules
body: Python's documentation defines slicing and integer division precisely, and both differ from C++. Implement them from these descriptions (summarised from the library and language references). Slices. s start:stop:step selects indices of a sequence of length len : cpp-norun std::vector<std::size_t sliceIndices(std::size_t length, std::optional<long start, std::optional<long stop, long step); 1. A step of 0 is an error: throw std::invalid_argument . 2. A missing start means the first index in the direction of travel: 0 for a positive step, len - 1 for a negative one. A missing stop means "past the end" in that direction: len for a positive step, and a position before index 0 for a negative step. 3. A given negative start or stop has len added to it. If it is still negative, it becomes 0 for a positive step, or the position before index 0 for a negative step. 4. A given start or stop at or beyond len becomes len for a positive step, or len - 1 for a negative step. 5. The result is start , start + step , start + 2 × step ... continuing while the index is before stop (less than it for a positive step, greater for a negative one). Floor division. Python's // rounds the quotient down (towards minus infinity), and % gives a result with the sign of the divisor , so that (a // b) b + a % b == a always holds. C++'s / and % truncate towards zero instead. cpp-norun long floorDiv(long a, long b); long floorMod(long a, long b); Both throw std::invalid_argument when b is 0 (Python raises ZeroDivisionError ).

title: 4.02  JavaScript, MDN and Node
body: Reading MDN Web Docs - syntax lines with optional parameters, return values and exceptions, the specification links and the browser compatibility tables - the ECMAScript specification behind them, and Node.js documentation with its stability index, callback and promise signatures and error codes. MDN Web Docs For JavaScript in the browser, the reference is MDN Web Docs (developer.mozilla.org), maintained by Mozilla with the other browser makers. Each page for a method follows a fixed layout: Section Contains --- --- Syntax every form of the call, one per line Parameters each parameter; optional ones marked Return value what comes back Exceptions TypeError , RangeError ... and when Description the behaviour in detail, including conversions Examples runnable snippets, often with live output Specifications a link to the exact section of the standard Browser compatibility a table of which browser version supports what The Syntax section lists each form separately instead of using brackets: js-norun parseInt(string) parseInt(string, radix) The traps are in the Description JavaScript converts types freely, and the Description section is where each method says how. Two famous examples, both clearly documented: - parseInt(string, radix) skips leading whitespace, reads an optional sign, and then as many valid digits as it can , ignoring the rest: parseInt("42px") is 42 and parseInt("1e3") is 1. Without a radix, a string starting with 0x is read as hexadecimal; with radix 10 it is not, so parseInt("0x1A", 10) is 0. A radix outside 2 to 36 gives NaN , and so does a string with no digits. Practice 4.02 implements these rules. - Array.prototype.sort() without a compare function converts the elements to strings and sorts them as text, so 10, 9, 1 .sort() gives 1, 10, 9 . The page says so in its first paragraph, and recommends passing (a, b) = a - b for numbers. Compatibility and Baseline The Browser compatibility table shows, per browser, the first version supporting each feature, with notes for partial support. Newer pages also show a Baseline badge: "widely available" means it has worked in all major browsers for a long time; "newly available" means only recent versions. Check it before using a new API in a site people visit with older browsers. The specification Behind MDN is the ECMAScript specification (tc39.es/ecma262) for the language and the WHATWG and W3C specifications for browser APIs. They are written as step-by-step algorithms ("1. Let S be ? ToString( string ). 2. Let R be ..."), which makes them precise and readable once you get used to them. MDN's Specifications section links straight to the right step list when you need the final word. Node.js documentation For JavaScript outside the browser, nodejs.org/docs has one page per module ( fs , http , path ...). Things to read for: - The Stability index next to each API: 0 Deprecated, 1 Experimental (may change or vanish), 2 Stable, 3 Legacy (kept, but there is a better way). Production code should stay on 2. - Signatures with types in a bulleted list: fs.readFile(path , options , callback) , where options can be a string or an object, and callback receives (err, data) . - Many modules come in three styles : callbacks ( fs.readFile ), promises ( fs/promises , await readFile(...) ), and synchronous ( fs.readFileSync , which blocks the whole program while it runs). - Errors carry a code such as ENOENT (no such file) or ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE , documented on the Errors page; check err.code , not the message text, which may change. - "Added in: v18.0.0" and History tables, like Python's version notes. Check yourself quiz ? What does parseInt("12.5kg") return? - NaN , because the string is not a number - 12.5 , reading as far as the number goes + 12 , stopping at the first non-digit - An exception, because of the letters parseInt reads digits until the first character that cannot be part of an integer, here the . , and ignores the rest. parseFloat would give 12.5. ? Why does 10, 9, 1 .sort() give 1, 10, 9 ? - sort() sorts in descending order by default + Without a compare function, elements are compared as strings - sort() only looks at the first digit of each number - Arrays of numbers must be sorted with Math.sort As strings, "1" < "10" < "9" . Pass a compare function, sort((a, b) = a - b) , to sort numbers by value. ? Should production code use an API marked Stability: 1? - Yes, 1 is the most stable level - Yes, as long as it works in your tests + Better not: experimental APIs may change or vanish - No, because it is already removed Node's stability index runs 0 (deprecated), 1 (experimental), 2 (stable) and 3 (legacy). Experimental APIs can change or be removed in any release. ? Why compare err.code instead of err.message in Node? - Messages are only available in debug builds + Codes are documented and stable; messages can change - err.message is always empty for system errors - Comparing strings is slower than comparing numbers Error codes such as ENOENT or ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE are a documented interface. Message texts are for people and may be reworded in any version.

title: JavaScript's parseInt and default sort
body: Implement two JavaScript behaviours in C++, following the descriptions on their MDN pages (lesson 4.02) as summarised here. parseInt(string, radix) , with NaN represented by an empty optional: cpp-norun std::optional<double jsParseInt(std::string_view s, std::optional<int radix = std::nullopt); 1. Skip leading whitespace (here: space, \t , \n , \v , \f , \r ). 2. If the next character is - or + , remember the sign and skip it. 3. If radix is given and not 0: if it is below 2 or above 36 the result is NaN . If it is not 16, do not strip a 0x prefix in step 4. If radix is missing or 0, use 10. 4. Unless step 3 said not to, if the text now starts with 0x or 0X , skip those two characters and use radix 16. 5. Read the longest run of characters that are digits in the radix ( 0 - 9 , then a - z or A - Z for 10 to 35). Stop at the first character that is not; ignore the rest of the string. 6. If no digit was read, the result is NaN . Otherwise it is the sign times the value. Array.prototype.sort() without a compare function: cpp-norun std::vector<int jsDefaultSort(std::vector<int values); The elements are converted to strings ( -1 , 10 ...), compared as strings, character by character, and the sort is stable . The result is the elements in that order (still as numbers).

title: 4.03  Reading Headers and Source Code
body: What to do when the documentation is thin or missing - reading a library's header for its real declarations, defaults and doc comments, Doxygen tags, finding the implementation with Go to Definition, using a project's tests as examples, and reading the source of the standard library itself. When the docs are not enough Many libraries, especially small open-source ones, have a README and little else. Even good documentation has gaps. Then the code is the documentation, and it has one great advantage: it is exactly the version you are using. The usual order to look: 1. The header (or the module's public file): every declaration, with its exact types and defaults. 2. Doc comments in that header. 3. The project's tests : they show how the authors expect the API to be called, including edge cases. 4. The examples folder, if there is one. 5. The implementation , for what is still unclear. 6. The issue tracker : someone may have hit the same question; the answer may be "that is a bug". Reading a header A header is a contract summary. From this one you can learn a lot without seeing any code behind it: cpp-norun namespace tinyini { /// A parsed configuration file. class Config { public: /// Parses text . Returns std::nullopt on a malformed line and, if errorLine /// is not null, stores that line's number (1-based) there. static std::optional<Config parse(std::string_view text, int errorLine = nullptr); /// @return the value, or nullptr if the section or key does not exist. /// @note The pointer is valid until this Config is modified or destroyed. const std::string find(std::string_view section, std::string_view key) const; /// @return the value as an integer; std::nullopt if it is missing /// or is not a complete integer. std::optional<long long findInt(std::string_view section, std::string_view key) const; }; } // namespace tinyini - static + std::optional<Config : you create one by parsing, and parsing can fail. - int errorLine = nullptr : optional out-parameter; pass a pointer to get the line. - const std::string returned from a const function: you read it but do not own it, and the note tells you how long it lives. - findInt 's comment reveals a design decision: "missing" and "not a number" give the same result. If your program must tell them apart, use find first. Practice 4.03 depends on noticing exactly this. Doc comments and Doxygen Most C and C++ libraries write doc comments in the Doxygen style ( /// or / / ), which tools turn into web pages: Tag Means --- --- @brief one-line summary @param name a parameter; @param out name for outputs @return / @returns the return value @throws / @exception exceptions @pre , @post preconditions and postconditions @note , @warning remarks you should not skip @deprecated do not use in new code Editors show these comments when you hover over a call, so the habit of hovering often answers the question without opening a browser. Into the implementation In Visual Studio or VS Code, Go to Definition (F12) jumps from a call to its declaration, and again to the implementation if the source is available. Read with a question in mind ("what happens if the key is empty?") and follow only the code paths that answer it; reading a library front to back is rarely worth it. Two cautions: - Behaviour you find in the implementation but not in the documentation is not a promise . It may change in the next version. If you rely on it, write a test (lesson 5.02) so you notice. - Check you are reading the same version you build with: the main branch on GitHub may be ahead of your release. The standard library's own source Microsoft's C++ standard library is open source (github.com/microsoft/STL), as are libstdc++ (GCC) and libc++ (LLVM). It is dense code, with names like _Myfirst and _Mylast to avoid clashing with your macros, but stepping into std::vector::push_back in the debugger and seeing the growth and the debug checks for yourself is a good way to understand what the reference pages describe. Check yourself quiz ? A function returns const T and has no documentation. What can you assume about ownership? - You own it and must delete it when done - It is always a pointer to a static object + Probably that you do not own it, but check - You own it and must free it with free Nothing is certain without documentation, but a const T usually means borrowed: do not delete it. Look for a comment, tests or the implementation to confirm how long it lives. ? findInt returns an empty optional. What two situations could that mean? - The key exists but its value is 0, or the store is empty + The key is missing, or its value is not a complete integer - The function failed to allocate, or the key is too long - The value is negative, or it is larger than INT_MAX An empty optional only says "no result". Its doc comment says both reasons give the same result; use find first if you must tell them apart. ? Why look at a project's tests when its docs are thin? - Tests are generated from the documentation - Tests show only the cases that fail + They show intended use and edge cases, and they really run - Tests are always better written than the code Tests are examples that the build checks, so they match the code's real behaviour, edge cases included. ? You find in the source that a function happens to sort its output. May you rely on that? - Yes, the source is the final word - Yes, as long as you use the same compiler + Not safely, because it is not documented - No, sorting is never guaranteed by any library Undocumented behaviour may change in the next version. If you must rely on it, pin it with a test of your own so you notice when it changes.

title: Using a library from its header
match: Using a library from its header
body: The starter contains tinyini , a small configuration library like the one in lesson 4.03. It has no web page: everything you need is in its doc comments . Do not change the library; read it, and use it to write loadSettings . cpp-norun struct ServerSettings { std::string host; int port; bool tls; int workers; }; std::optional<ServerSettings loadSettings(std::string_view text, std::string& error); loadSettings reads a configuration text and checks it in this order, stopping at the first problem. On a problem it returns an empty optional and sets error to the message shown; on success it sets error to an empty string. Setting Rule Message --- --- --- the text must parse line N , where N is the malformed line server host optional, default localhost ; if present it must not be empty bad server.host server port required missing server.port a whole number from 1 to 65535 bad server.port server tls optional, default false; if present it must be a boolean the library understands bad server.tls pool size optional, default 4; if present a whole number from 1 to 256 bad pool.size Notice that two messages for the port need you to tell "missing" from "not a number". Read what the library's functions return in each case.

title: 4.04  Man Pages, RFCs and Specifications
body: Reading the most precise documents you will meet - Unix man pages with their sections and ERRORS lists, RFCs with the MUST, SHOULD and MAY keywords of RFC 2119, ABNF grammars, errata, and turning one section of a specification into code and tests. Man pages On Linux and macOS, man shows the manual for commands and C functions. The manual is split into numbered sections, and the same name can exist in several: Section Contains Example --- --- --- 1 commands man 1 ls 2 system calls man 2 open 3 C library functions man 3 printf 5 file formats man 5 passwd 7 overviews and conventions man 7 signal A function's page has standard headings: NAME , SYNOPSIS (the include and prototype), DESCRIPTION , RETURN VALUE , ERRORS , NOTES , BUGS , SEE ALSO . The ERRORS section lists every errno value the call can set and why ( ENOENT : a component of the path does not exist; EACCES : permission denied), which is exactly the list your error handling has to consider. The same pages are online at man7.org, and many describe behaviour that Windows' C runtime copies. RFCs Internet protocols and formats are specified in RFCs (Requests for Comments) at rfc-editor.org: HTTP, TLS, JSON (RFC 8259), Base64 (RFC 4648), URIs (RFC 3986). An RFC never changes once published; corrections are listed as errata , and a newer RFC obsoletes or updates an older one (the header of each says which). Always check you are reading the current one. Requirement keywords Almost every RFC uses the keywords of RFC 2119 , in capitals, with exact meanings: Keyword Means --- --- MUST , REQUIRED , SHALL an absolute requirement MUST NOT , SHALL NOT an absolute prohibition SHOULD , RECOMMENDED do it unless you have a good, understood reason not to SHOULD NOT avoid unless you have a good reason MAY , OPTIONAL truly optional; others must cope either way A "MAY" for the sender becomes a "must handle" for the receiver: if a sender MAY add whitespace, every parser must accept it. Reading a spec well means sorting its sentences into these buckets. ABNF grammars Syntax in RFCs is written in ABNF (RFC 5234): text version = 1 DIGIT "." 1 DIGIT ; one or more digits, a dot, one or more digits DIGIT = %x30-39 ; the characters 0 to 9 hex-pair = 2HEXDIG ; exactly two hex digits header = name ":" WSP value ; WSP: zero or more spaces or tabs flag = "on" / "off" ; / is "or" option = "-" name ; is optional means "any number", 1 "at least one", n "exactly n", optional, / alternatives, "..." a literal (case-insensitive in ABNF), and %x41 a character by code. A grammar like this is a ready-made checklist for a parser and its tests. Turning a section into code The method that works for specifications of any size: 1. Read the section twice : once for the idea, once for the rules. 2. List every MUST and MUST NOT as a test case, including what to do with input that breaks them (reject? ignore?). 3. Collect the spec's own examples and test vectors ; many RFCs have an appendix of them (RFC 4648 section 10 lists Base64 test vectors). 4. Write the code, then run it against both lists. 5. Note every SHOULD and MAY you chose to follow or not, in a comment, so the next reader knows it was a decision. Practice 4.04 does this for Base64, and the milestone project for Semantic Versioning, a short specification with famously precise ordering rules. Check yourself quiz ? man open shows a shell command page. How do you get the system call? - man open(2) - man -s open + man 2 open - man syscall open System calls are in section 2 of the manual. Asking for the section number first picks that page instead of the command in section 1. ? A spec says senders SHOULD NOT send trailing whitespace. Must a receiver handle it? - No, SHOULD NOT means it never happens + Yes, senders may still do it with good reason - No, the receiver should reject the message - Only if the spec also says MAY RFC 2119's SHOULD NOT is a strong recommendation, not a ban: a sender may have a valid reason to do it. A robust receiver therefore copes. ? What does 1 DIGIT mean in ABNF? - Exactly one digit + One or more digits - Zero or more digits - The digit 1 In ABNF, n m means between n and m repetitions; 1 with no upper bound is one or more. DIGIT alone would be zero or more. ? How do you find corrections to a published RFC? - The RFC itself is edited when a mistake is found + In its errata, and in newer RFCs that update it - By reading the mailing list for each RFC - Published RFCs are never corrected RFCs are never changed once published. Corrections are listed as errata, and later RFCs that update or obsolete it are noted in its header.

title: Base64 from its specification
body: Implement Base64 encoding and decoding as RFC 4648 specifies it, following this summary of the relevant sections (lesson 4.04). Where the RFC lets a decoder choose ("MAY"), this summary makes the stricter choice, and your code MUST follow it. cpp-norun std::string base64Encode(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & data, bool url = false); std::optional<std::vector<std::uint8_t base64Decode(std::string_view text, bool url = false); Encoding. Take the input 3 bytes (24 bits) at a time and write 4 characters, each standing for 6 bits, most significant first, using the alphabet A - Z (0 to 25), a - z (26 to 51), 0 - 9 (52 to 61), + (62) and / (63). A final group of 1 byte produces 2 characters, and of 2 bytes 3 characters, the missing low bits filled with zeros; the output is then padded with = to a multiple of 4 characters. The URL-safe variant ( url true) uses - instead of + and _ instead of / , and in this library is written without padding. Decoding MUST reject (return an empty optional) any input that encoding could not have produced: - standard variant: a length that is not a multiple of 4; = anywhere except as the last one or two characters; - URL-safe variant: any = ; a length that leaves 1 character over after the groups of 4 (one character cannot hold a byte); - both: any character outside the variant's alphabet (including spaces and line breaks); - both: a final character whose unused low bits are not zero (RFC 4648 calls such data non-canonical). Empty text decodes to no bytes.

title: split, as Python documents it
body: Reproduce Python's str.split in C++ from its documentation. split(" a b ") - a b (no separator: runs of spaces) split("a,,b", ",") - a b (a separator: empty parts kept) split("a b c", " ", 1) - a b c (maxsplit)

title: Base64 from RFC 4648
body: Implement Base64 by reading the RFC, and check it with the RFC's own test vectors. "" - "" "f" - "Zg==" "fo" - "Zm8=" "foo" - "Zm9v" "foobar" - "Zm9vYmFy" all 7 test vectors pass, decode(encode(x)) == x
