body: Implement part of printf by reading its man page carefully. fmt("%d %5d %-5d %05d", 42, 42, 42, 42) - 42 42 42 00042 fmt("%s and %c", "tea", '!') - tea and ! fmt("%x %X %%", 255, 255) - ff FF % fmt("%q", 1) - error: unknown conversion q

title: Semantic Versioning from the specification
body: Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 (semver.org) is a short specification that almost every package manager relies on, and its rules for what counts as a valid version and which version is newer are exact. Below is a summary of the parts you need, plus a small range syntax defined for this project. Implement it so that every rule holds. cpp struct Version { std::uint64_t major, minor, patch; std::vector<std::string prerelease; std::vector<std::string build; }; std::optional<Version parseVersion(std::string_view text); int compareVersions(const Version& a, const Version& b); std::string toString(const Version& v); bool satisfies(const Version& v, std::string_view range); Valid versions (the specification's rules 2, 9 and 10): - The core is MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH : exactly three non-negative whole numbers separated by dots. They must not have leading zeros ( 0 itself is fine). In this project they must also fit in 64 bits. - A pre-release may follow, after a hyphen: one or more identifiers separated by dots. Identifiers are non-empty and use only 0 - 9 , A - Z , a - z and - . An identifier made only of digits is numeric and must not have leading zeros. - Build metadata may follow, after a plus sign: one or more identifiers separated by dots, with the same characters, never empty, but leading zeros are allowed. - Nothing else is allowed: no spaces, no v prefix. parseVersion returns the parts, or an empty optional for anything invalid. toString writes a version back in the same form. Precedence (rule 11). compareVersions returns -1, 0 or 1 as a is lower than, equal to, or higher than b : 1. Compare major, minor and patch numerically, in that order. 2. If those are equal, a version without a pre-release is higher than one with a pre-release. 3. Otherwise compare the pre-release identifiers left to right: two numeric identifiers compare as numbers; two others compare as ASCII text; a numeric identifier is lower than a non-numeric one. If all compared identifiers are equal, the version with more identifiers is higher. 4. Build metadata is ignored : 1.0.0+a and 1.0.0+b are equal. Ranges (this project's own syntax). A range is one or more comparators separated by spaces, and a version satisfies it when it satisfies every comparator: Comparator Satisfied when the version is --- --- =V , V , =V , <V , <=V equal to, higher than ... V , by precedence ~X.Y.Z = X.Y.Z and < X.(Y+1).0 ^X.Y.Z = X.Y.Z and below the next version that changes the first non-zero part: < (X+1).0.0 if X 0; else < 0.(Y+1).0 if Y 0; else < 0.0.(Z+1) The versions in comparators may have pre-releases. Comparisons use plain precedence, so, for example, 2.0.0-alpha does satisfy ^1.2.3 (it is lower than 2.0.0 ). An empty range, a comparator with no operator, or an invalid version in a comparator throws std::invalid_argument .

title: 5.01  Turning an Example into Your Code
match: 5.01 Turning an Example into Your Code
body: Why documentation examples are not production code - what they leave out on purpose - and a dependable routine for adapting one - run it unchanged, understand every line against the reference, make it a function, add every error path the reference describes, release resources on every path, and test the edges. Examples are written to teach The example on a reference page exists to show one idea as clearly as possible. To stay short it usually leaves out exactly what your program needs: Left out Why it matters --- --- error handling the failure cases are on the page, just not in the example cleanup on error paths a handle or allocation leaks when something fails halfway loops for partial results a single read or send may do only part of the work buffer sizing fixed buffers like char buf 256 that are too small for real data real inputs hard-coded names, paths and values thread safety, encoding, limits outside the example's one idea Copying an example straight into a program is the most common way documentation causes bugs. The fix is a routine. The routine 1. Run it unchanged. In a scratch project, or Compiler Explorer. If it does not work as shown, you have learned something about your setup (version, platform, missing library) before mixing it with your own code. 2. Explain every line. For each call, open its reference page and check: what does each argument mean here? What can it return? This is where you find the cases the example ignores. 3. Make it a function with real parameters instead of hard-coded values, and a return type that can express failure ( std::optional , an error code, an exception, matching the rest of your program). 4. Add every error path the reference pages list. For each call: what happens if it fails, and what must already-acquired resources do then? 5. Release resources on every path. Wrap handles in RAII types (a small class whose destructor closes them, or std::unique_ptr with a custom deleter), so early returns cannot leak. 6. Handle partial results. Anything that reads, writes, sends or receives in pieces needs a loop (the Networking course's sendAll is the classic case). 7. Test the edges the reference describes: empty input, the largest input, the failure of each call (practice 5.01 fakes them). An example, adapted A typical example for a file API looks like this: cpp-norun Handle h = fakeOpen("notes.txt"); char buffer 256 ; long n = fakeRead(h, buffer, sizeof buffer); std::cout << std::string(buffer, n); fakeClose(h); Reading the three reference pages shows five problems: fakeOpen can fail and return INVALID ; fakeRead may return fewer bytes than the file has, so one call does not read the whole file; it returns -1 on an error, which std::string(buffer, n) would turn into a huge length; a file longer than 256 bytes is cut off; and if anything throws between open and close, the handle leaks. The adapted version: cpp-norun class File { public: explicit File(Handle h) : h_{ h } {} ~File() { if (h_ != INVALID) fakeClose(h_); } File(const File&) = delete; File& operator=(const File&) = delete; Handle get() const { return h_; } private: Handle h_; }; std::optional<std::string readWholeFile(const std::string& name) { File file{ fakeOpen(name) }; if (file.get() == INVALID) return std::nullopt; std::string contents; char buffer 4096 ; for (;;) { const long n{ fakeRead(file.get(), buffer, sizeof buffer) }; if (n < 0) return std::nullopt; // error: the destructor still closes if (n == 0) return contents; // end of file contents.append(buffer, static_cast<std::size_t (n)); } } Longer than the example, and every added line traces back to a sentence on a reference page. Check yourself quiz ? Why run an example unchanged before adapting it? - Examples only work when run exactly once + So later problems are known to come from your changes - The documentation licence requires it - Running it unchanged makes it compile faster later Running it first confirms it works in your environment. If it then breaks after your edits, you know where to look. ? An example calls read once. When is that not enough? - When the file is opened in binary mode - When the buffer is on the stack + When a read can return fewer bytes than requested - Never, a single read always reads the whole file Many read functions may return less than you asked for, for example from a pipe or a socket, or near the end. Real code loops until it has everything or reaches the end. ? How do you make sure a handle is closed on every error path? - Close it at the end of the function, after the last line - Let the operating system close it when the program exits + Wrap it in an RAII object whose destructor closes it - Add a close call in a catch (...) block only A destructor runs on every way out of the scope, early returns and exceptions included, so no path can forget the close. ? What is wrong with std::string(buffer, n) when n can be -1? - It creates an empty string, losing the data + -1 becomes a huge size_t , so it reads far past the buffer - It throws std::invalid_argument for negative lengths - It reads the buffer backwards from the end The length parameter is unsigned, so -1 converts to the largest size_t . Check the error value before using it as a length.

title: From example to robust code
where: 5.01 Turning an Example into Your Code
body: The starter contains a stand-in file API whose reference pages say: - Handle fakeOpen(const std::string& name) : opens a file; returns INVALID if it does not exist. - long fakeRead(Handle h, char buffer, std::size_t size) : reads up to size bytes (it may return fewer even before the end); returns the number read, 0 at the end of the file , or -1 on an error . - void fakeClose(Handle h) : closes the handle. Every handle that was opened must be closed exactly once. The documentation's example (lesson 5.01) is: cpp-norun Handle h = fakeOpen(name); char buffer 256 ; long n = fakeRead(h, buffer, sizeof buffer); return std::string(buffer, n); Write the robust version, and one function built on it: cpp-norun std::optional<std::string readWholeFile(const std::string& name); std::optional<std::size_t countLines(const std::string& name); - readWholeFile returns the whole contents, however many reads it takes and however long the file is; an empty optional if the file cannot be opened or any read fails. The handle is always closed. - countLines returns the number of lines: the number of \n characters, plus one if the file is not empty and does not end with \n . An empty file has 0 lines. An empty optional if reading fails.

title: 5.02  Checking Your Understanding with Experiments
body: Confirming what you think a page says with small, focused programs - one question per experiment, predicting the result first, trying the edge cases, using Compiler Explorer, turning experiments into learning tests that keep checking the behaviour - and the limits of experiments when behaviour is undefined or unspecified. Reading is not knowing After reading a reference page you have a belief about how a function behaves. A two-minute experiment turns it into knowledge, or shows you misread. Experienced programmers do this constantly, especially for anything with edge cases: rounding, string splitting, time zones, encodings, regular expressions. How to run an experiment 1. One question. "What does std::round(-2.5) return?" not "how does rounding work?". 2. Predict first. Write down what you expect before running it. A surprise is the whole point; without a prediction you will not notice one. 3. Smallest program. No framework, no project: a main with a few prints, or a test. 4. Cover the edges. Zero, negative, empty, the boundary value, one past it, the largest value. 5. Compare with the page. If the result disagrees with your reading, re-read. If it disagrees with the page itself, see lesson 5.03. cpp include <cmath include <iostream int main() { // Question: how do the rounding functions treat halves? // Prediction: round goes away from zero; nearbyint goes to even. for (double x : { 0.5, 1.5, 2.5, -0.5, -2.5, 2.4999 }) std::cout << x << ": round " << std::round(x) << ", nearbyint " << std::nearbyint(x) << ", trunc " << std::trunc(x) << ", cast " << static_cast<int (x) << '\n'; } The pages explain the results: std::round rounds halves away from zero ; std::nearbyint uses the current rounding mode, which is round-half-to-even by default (so 0.5 and 2.5 both go to the even neighbour); std::trunc and the cast drop the fraction towards zero. Seeing all four side by side fixes it in memory better than reading four pages. Compiler Explorer godbolt.org compiles and runs small programs in the browser with many compilers and versions. It is ideal for experiments: you can check whether the behaviour differs between MSVC, GCC and Clang, or between C++17 and C++20, in seconds, and share a link to the result with a colleague. Learning tests An experiment you run once is forgotten; an experiment written as a test keeps checking: cpp-norun TEST("std::round rounds halves away from zero") { CHECK_EQ(std::round(2.5), 3.0); CHECK_EQ(std::round(-2.5), -3.0); } TEST("our JSON library keeps the order of object keys") { CHECK_EQ(json::parse(R"({"b":1,"a":2})").keys(), (std::vector<std::string { "b", "a" })); } Tests like the second one are called learning tests : they pin down behaviour of a library that your code relies on, especially behaviour the documentation is vague about. When you upgrade the library and one fails, you know immediately which assumption broke, instead of finding out from a bug report. What experiments cannot tell you An experiment shows what this compiler, library and machine did this time. That is the documented behaviour only when the page promises it: - Undefined behaviour can "work" in an experiment and fail elsewhere: reading past the end of an array may print plausible numbers. Never take a successful run as proof that something is allowed. - Unspecified and implementation-defined results (the order of iteration of an unordered_map , the size of long , the text of what() ) may differ between compilers or versions. - Timing and threads : a race condition may hide in a hundred runs and appear in the hundred-and-first. So the rule is: the page says what you may rely on; the experiment confirms you read it correctly. Check yourself quiz ? Why write down a prediction before running an experiment? - The compiler needs it to choose the right test + So you notice when the result surprises you - Predictions make the experiment run faster - It is required to use Compiler Explorer A surprise is when you learn something. Without a prediction written first, it is easy to tell yourself afterwards that you expected whatever happened. ? What does std::nearbyint(2.5) return by default, and why? - 3.0, because halves always round up - 2.5, because nearbyint does not round halves + 2.0, because halves round to the even neighbour - 3.0, because halves round away from zero nearbyint uses the current rounding mode, which by default is round-to-nearest-even. std::round is the one that rounds halves away from zero. ? What is a learning test? - A test that checks what a student has learned - A test that the compiler writes for you + A test that pins down library behaviour you rely on - A test that only runs in debug builds It turns an experiment into a check that keeps running, so when the library is upgraded and that behaviour changes, a test fails instead of your program. ? An experiment reading one element past the end of a vector prints 0. What have you learned? - That the element past the end is always 0 - That vectors zero their spare capacity + Nothing you can rely on: it is undefined behaviour - That operator checks the index Undefined behaviour can print 0 today and crash elsewhere or tomorrow. Experiments only tell you about behaviour the documentation defines.

title: Rounding, pinned down
body: Lesson 5.02 ran an experiment on the standard rounding functions. Use what it found, and their reference pages, to write four functions with exactly these behaviours. Run your own small experiment first if any row surprises you. cpp-norun double roundHalfAway(double x); double roundHalfEven(double x); double towardZero(double x); std::optional<int toIntChecked(double x); Function Rounds to the nearest whole number, and halves go ... Examples --- --- --- roundHalfAway away from zero 2.5 → 3, -2.5 → -3, 0.5 → 1 roundHalfEven to the even neighbour 2.5 → 2, 3.5 → 4, -2.5 → -2, 0.5 → 0 towardZero (no rounding: drops the fraction) 2.9 → 2, -2.9 → -2 toIntChecked drops the fraction like towardZero and returns the result as an int , or an empty optional if x is NaN, infinite, or the result does not fit in an int . (Converting such a value with static_cast<int is undefined behaviour, which is why this function exists.)

title: 5.03  When the Docs Are Wrong or Missing
match: 5.03 When the Docs Are Wrong or Missing
body: What to do when documentation and behaviour disagree - checking the version first, reading changelogs and migration guides, errata and known issues, weighing community answers and AI suggestions, reporting documentation bugs well, and protecting your code against behaviour that is not documented. First suspect: the version Most "the documentation is wrong" moments are really "I am reading the documentation for a different version". Check, in this order: 1. Which version of the library, language or OS are you actually using? ( --version , the package file, _MSC_VER , sys.version .) 2. Which version is the page about? Look for a version selector, "Added in", "(since C++20)", "Changed in version" notes. 3. Is there a changelog or release notes entry between the two? Changelogs and migration guides A changelog lists what changed in each release, usually grouped as Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed and Security. Many projects follow Semantic Versioning (the milestone 4 project), so the version number already warns you: a new major version may break your code, minor and patch versions should not. When you upgrade across several versions, read every entry in between, not only the latest: a key renamed in version 2 and a default changed in version 3 both affect you. Larger projects publish a migration guide ("Upgrading from 2.x to 3.0") that lists breaking changes with before-and-after code. Practice 5.03 is a migration written from a changelog. Things a changelog entry tells you that a reference page often does not: - what the old behaviour was, so you can recognise it in existing code; - whether a change is breaking or only a fix; - the deprecation timeline: a function marked deprecated in 2.3 may be removed in 3.0. When the page really is wrong Documentation is written by people and has mistakes, especially in corners: a wrong default, a missing error case, an example that no longer compiles. Signs you have found one: - your experiment (lesson 5.02) contradicts the page, on the version the page describes; - the implementation (lesson 4.03) clearly does something else; - the issue tracker or errata list mentions it. Then: 1. Trust the behaviour you can test , but write a learning test for it, since a fix might change it. 2. Check errata and issues : RFCs have errata pages; libraries have issue trackers; cppreference pages have discussion pages and are corrected quickly. 3. Report it , briefly and concretely: the page and section, what it says, what actually happens (with a minimal program), and the version. Most documentation is open to contributions: cppreference is a wiki, Microsoft Learn pages have an "Edit" link to GitHub, MDN is on GitHub too. Community answers and AI suggestions Answers from forums, Q&A sites, blog posts and AI assistants are often the fastest way to find which function to use. They are also often out of date, written for another platform or version, or simply wrong in a detail, and an AI suggestion can name a function or parameter that does not exist at all. Treat them as leads : - Look up every function they use on its reference page. - Check the date and version they were written for. - Prefer answers that link to documentation, and be suspicious of ones that only say "this works for me". - Run the experiment yourself. Building on undocumented behaviour Sometimes you must rely on something no page promises: an undocumented message format, the order of results, a timing. If you do: - Isolate it in one function, so there is one place to change. - Write a test that fails loudly if the behaviour changes. - Leave a comment saying it is undocumented and how you found out. - Prefer a documented alternative the moment one exists. Check yourself quiz ? An example from the docs does not compile. What do you check first? - Whether your compiler has a bug + Whether the docs match your installed version - Whether the example uses the right font - Whether to report the page as wrong Most mismatches between docs and behaviour come from reading the documentation for a different version than the one you have. ? You upgrade a library from 1.4 to 3.1. Which changelog entries should you read? - Only the entry for 3.1 - Only the entries for 2.0 and 3.0 + Every release from 1.4 to 3.1, major ones above all - None, the migration happens automatically Changes accumulate across every release in between. The major versions 2.0 and 3.0 are where breaking changes are most likely, but smaller releases can deprecate things too. ? What makes a good documentation bug report? - A clear statement that the documentation is wrong - A link to a forum thread discussing the problem + The page, what it says, a minimal program and the version - A rewritten version of the whole page Maintainers need to see the exact section, what it claims, what really happens with a minimal program they can run, and which version you used. ? How should you treat a function an AI assistant suggests? - As correct, since it was generated from documentation - As wrong, since AI suggestions never work + As a lead to check on its reference page, then test - As correct if it compiles Suggestions can name functions that do not exist or behave differently. Confirm it on its reference page and test it, as you would a forum answer.

title: A migration written from a changelog
match: A migration written from a changelog
where: 5.03 When the Docs Are Wrong or Missing
body: An application stores its settings as key-value pairs, and its file format has changed twice. Here is its changelog (lesson 5.03), newest first: text 3.0.0 Changed - The log_level value "warn" is now spelled "warning". Other values are unchanged. - host and port are replaced by a single key, address, written host:port. A missing host means localhost and a missing port means 80; if both are missing, no address is written. Added - retries, with the default "3" when it is absent. 2.0.0 Changed - timeout (whole seconds) is renamed timeout_ms and is now in milliseconds. Removed - legacy_mode is gone and must be dropped. - verbose ("true" or anything else) is replaced by log_level: "debug" when verbose was "true", otherwise "info". If verbose is absent, no log_level is added. Write the migration: cpp-norun std::map<std::string, std::string migrate(std::map<std::string, std::string config, int fromVersion); It takes settings written by version fromVersion (1, 2 or 3) and returns them as version 3 writes them: apply the 2.0.0 changes if fromVersion is 1, then the 3.0.0 changes if it is 1 or 2. Keys the changelog does not mention are kept unchanged. The result always has version set to "3" . Throw std::invalid_argument if fromVersion is not 1, 2 or 3, or if a timeout being migrated is not a whole number of seconds (digits only).

title: 5.04  Writing Documentation Others Can Use
body: Turning everything this course taught about reading documentation into writing it - doc comments that state the contract, what every function's documentation must answer, examples that are correct, READMEs that get someone started, changelogs, and keeping documentation true as the code changes. Write the page you wished you had Every frustration in this course came from documentation that left something out: the return value when the buffer is too small, the difference between missing and invalid, the version a feature arrived in. When you write code others use (including yourself in six months), write the documentation that would have saved you that time. Doc comments that state the contract For each public function, the comment should answer the questions of lesson 1.02, in a few lines: cpp-norun /// Reads a whole file into memory. /// /// @param path the file to read; may be relative to the current directory. /// @return the file's contents, or std::nullopt if the file cannot be opened /// or a read fails part way. An empty file gives an empty string. /// @throws std::bad_alloc if the file does not fit in memory. /// @note Not safe to call while another thread writes the same file. std::optional<std::string readWholeFile(const std::filesystem::path& path); A checklist for each function: - What it does, in one sentence starting with a verb. - Each parameter : meaning, units (bytes or characters, seconds or milliseconds), allowed values, whether null or empty is allowed. - The result in every case, including the empty, missing and failed ones. - Errors : exceptions, error codes, what state things are left in. - Preconditions the caller must meet, and what happens if they do not. - Ownership and lifetime of anything returned by pointer or reference. - Thread safety and complexity , when they are not obvious. Leave out what the signature already says (" count : the count"), and do not describe the implementation: say what , not how , so you can change the how. Examples that are correct An example in documentation is copied more than anything else you write (lesson 5.01), so: - make it compile and run , ideally by building it as part of your tests; - handle errors in it, or say plainly that it skips them for brevity; - show the most common use first, then the tricky ones. README and the four kinds A project's README is often the only page someone reads. It should say, in order: what the project does and for whom, how to install or build it, a minimal example that works, where the full documentation is, and the licence. Beyond that, keep the four kinds of documentation from lesson 1.01 apart: a tutorial for newcomers, how-to guides for tasks, the reference generated from your doc comments, and explanation for the design decisions. Changelogs Keep a CHANGELOG.md with one section per release and entries under Added , Changed , Deprecated , Removed , Fixed , Security . Write each entry for the person upgrading: what changed and what they must do about it. Mark breaking changes clearly, and match them to your version numbers (a breaking change means a new major version under Semantic Versioning). Keeping it true Documentation that is wrong is worse than none, because people trust it. Habits that keep it true: - Change the doc comment in the same commit as the behaviour. - Let tests check the claims you can test: every documented error case is a test case. - Compile the examples. - When someone asks a question the docs should have answered, fix the docs , not just the person's question. Check yourself quiz ? Why should a doc comment say what a function does rather than how? - Saying how makes the comment too long to read + So the implementation can change without the docs going wrong - Readers are not allowed to know how it works - Doxygen cannot format descriptions of how code works The contract is what readers can rely on. Describing the implementation ties the documentation to details that will change. ? A parameter is a timeout. What must its documentation include? - Only its type, since that says everything - An example value, such as 1000 + Its unit and allowed values, including 0 and negatives - The name of the function that uses it Without a unit, 1000 could be milliseconds or seconds. Readers also need to know what 0 or a negative value means: wait forever, fail at once, or an error. ? What belongs in a changelog entry for a breaking change? - Only the version number and the date - The full diff of the code that changed + What changed and what users must do, marked as breaking - A note to read the source code for details Users need to know what broke and how to adapt their code. Breaking changes belong in a new major version and should be clearly marked. ? How can tests help keep documentation true? - Tests generate the documentation automatically - Tests stop anyone from changing the code + Each documented behaviour becomes a test that fails if it changes - Tests are part of the documentation's appendix Turn each documented behaviour, especially each error case, into a test. A change that makes the documentation wrong then fails the build.

title: Reading doc comments with a program
match: Reading doc comments with a program
body: Documentation tools such as Doxygen read /// comments out of source code (lessons 4.03 and 5.04). Write a small one. cpp-norun struct DocParam { std::string name; std::string text; }; struct DocComment { std::string summary; std::vector<DocParam params; std::string returns; std::vector<std::string throws; }; std::optional<DocComment docFor(std::string_view source, std::string_view functionName); std::vector<std::string missingParams(const DocComment& doc, const std::vector<std::string & parameterNames); Finding the function. Split source into lines (ignore a \r before each \n ). The declaration is the first line that is not itself a comment (after leading spaces it does not start with // ) and contains functionName followed, after optional spaces, by ( , where the character before the name is not a letter, digit or _ . If there is no such line, return an empty optional. The comment is the run of lines directly above the declaration that start (after leading spaces) with /// . Take each line's text after /// and trim the spaces at both ends. Then, in order: - A line starting with @param gives a new parameter: the next word is its name and the rest (trimmed) its text. - @return or @returns sets the return text; @throws adds an entry to throws . - Any other line starting with @ is an unknown tag: ignore it, and the lines after it, until the next known tag. - An empty line is skipped. - Any other line is a continuation : before the first tag it is part of the summary; after a known tag it continues that tag's text. Parts are joined with one space. If the declaration has no comment, the result is a DocComment with everything empty. missingParams returns the names in parameterNames that have no @param entry, in the order given.
