title: Two libraries, one report
where: From Docs to Working Code projects
body: The starter contains two small libraries, each documented only by the comments in its code: minicsv , which reads CSV records, and minitpl , which fills in text templates. Without changing them, use them to build a report generator. Everything you need to know about how they behave, including how they report errors, is in their comments: read them as you would a reference page. cpp-norun std::optional<std::string report(std::string_view csv, std::string_view rowTemplate, std::string& error); report turns each data row of a CSV table into one line of text: 1. The first record of the CSV is the header: the column names. 2. For every following record (data rows numbered 1, 2, 3 ...), make a set of variables: each column name with that row's value, plus row , the row's number, unless a column is already called row . Render rowTemplate with them and add the result and a \n to the report. 3. Return the whole report and set error to an empty string. A table with a header and no data rows gives an empty report. On the first problem, stop, return an empty optional, and set error : Problem error --- --- the CSV has no records at all no header a record has a different number of fields from the header csv line N: expected K fields the CSV reader reports an error csv line N: followed by the reader's error text rendering a row fails row R: followed by the template's error text N is the line on which the problem record starts (the reader can tell you), K the number of header fields and R the data row number.

title: Cheat Sheet
body: Which document (milestone 1) You want to Read --- --- learn something new a tutorial, then explanation get a task done a how-to guide, then the reference for each call know exactly what a call does the reference page know what is allowed, finally the specification or standard know what changed the changelog, release notes, migration guide A reference page, in reading order 1. Synopsis : find the overload you are calling. 2. Description and Parameters : your arguments, including empty, zero, null, negative, too large. 3. Return value and Errors : every outcome. 4. Notes / Remarks : always skim. 5. Requirements : version, header, library, platform. Word Means --- --- must, shall, requires a rule for you may allowed to happen: be ready for it unspecified one of several results, no promise which implementation-defined the compiler or library chooses and documents it the behaviour is undefined breaking this voids everything C++ signatures and contracts You see It means --- --- const T& read, no copy T& your object is changed T&& may be moved from nodiscard do not ignore the result noexcept never throws first, last) half-open: last excluded InputIt , RandomIt named iterator requirements strong guarantee on throw, nothing changed Standard library results (milestone 2) Call "Not found" / failure --- --- std::find , map::find the end iterator string::find std::string::npos map::insert , try_emplace .second == false : key existed, nothing changed map::insert_or_assign .second == false : key existed, value overwritten std::from_chars ec != std::errc{} ; check ptr reached the end; no + , no spaces std::stoi throws invalid_argument / out_of_range ; skips spaces; stops at junk std::filesystem (two overloads) throws filesystem_error , or sets std::error_code& Container Invalidated by insertion --- --- vector , string all, if it reallocates; else at and after the point deque all iterators, not references (at the ends) list , map , set nothing unordered_ all iterators on rehash, not references Erase in a loop: it = c.erase(it); , or std::erase_if(c, pred) . Versions: (since C++20) markers, /std:c++20 , __cpp_lib_ macros from <version , _MSVC_LANG . std::format spec: {:fill align sign 0 width .precision type} ; numbers align right, strings left. Windows pages (milestone 3) Prefix / annotation Means --- --- cch , nSize "in characters" count of wchar_t cb count of bytes _In_ , _In_opt_ read; _opt_ : null allowed _Out_writes_(n) buffer holds n elements _Out_writes_bytes_(n) buffer holds n bytes Unknown size pattern Example --- --- ask for the size (null buffer) GetEnvironmentVariableW : too small returns size with null; success returns length without grow until it fits GetModuleFileNameW : returns nSize when truncated size in, size out RegQueryValueExW : ERROR_MORE_DATA (234) Error system Test --- --- last error GetLastError() immediately after a documented failure return code ERROR_SUCCESS (0) is success HRESULT SUCCEEDED(hr) is hr = 0 ; 0x8007xxxx = Win32 error xxxx NTSTATUS top bits: 00 success, 01 info, 10 warning, 11 error Structures: zero-initialise ( {} ), set cbSize = sizeof(...) , reserved members zero. "One or more of" = flags with ; "one of" = a single value. Other languages and specifications (milestone 4) Source Watch for --- --- Python / positional-only, keyword-only; "Changed in version"; in place vs new object MDN Syntax lines, Exceptions, Browser compatibility, Baseline Node Stability index; callback, promise and sync variants; err.code headers defaults, const , pointers vs references, /// comments man pages section number; RETURN VALUE; ERRORS RFCs MUST / SHOULD / MAY; ABNF; errata; obsoleted by From docs to code (milestone 5) 1. Run the example unchanged. 2. Look up every call. 3. Make it a function. 4. Add every error path. 5. RAII for every resource. 6. Loop for partial results. 7. Test the edges. Experiment: one question, predict first, smallest program, edge cases. Keep it as a learning test. Undefined behaviour proves nothing.

title: Common Problems
body: Problem Usual cause Fix Lesson --- --- --- --- The example from the docs does not compile docs for a different version, or a missing header check the version marker and the Requirements section 2.04, 5.03 The search result shows old behaviour an old page or forum answer open the official reference and pick your version 1.01 A call does something different from what you expected a different overload was chosen match your arguments to the numbered overloads 1.03 A program works in Debug and crashes in Release undefined behaviour the page warned about find the precondition you broke 1.04 A value was not updated in a map insert or try_emplace used to update use insert_or_assign or operator 2.02 "12abc" was accepted as a number std::stoi stops at the first bad character use std::from_chars and check ptr reached the end 2.01 A crash after push_back or erase an iterator or reference was invalidated follow the container's invalidation rules 2.03 A Windows path or string is cut off a truncated result was treated as success check for the documented truncation result and grow the buffer 3.01 A buffer overrun with a wide string bytes passed where characters were expected, or the reverse read whether the size is cch or cb 3.02 GetLastError returns a meaningless value read too late, or after a function that returns its own code read it at once, and only when the page says to 3.03 A COM call "failed" with S_FALSE tested hr == S_OK use SUCCEEDED(hr) and handle S_FALSE as documented 3.03 A Windows call fails with ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER cbSize not set, or flags combined wrongly zero-initialise, set the size, check "one of" vs "one or more of" 3.04 Python x = x.sort() makes x None sort works in place and returns None use x.sort() or x = sorted(x) 4.01 JavaScript sorts numbers wrongly the default sort compares strings pass a compare function 4.02 A function returns nothing useful and has no docs undocumented library read the header, tests and source; write a learning test 4.03 Your parser rejects input another program accepts a MAY or SHOULD in the spec was treated as MUST sort the spec's sentences by RFC 2119 keyword 4.04 Code copied from an example leaks or crashes on errors examples skip error handling follow the adaptation routine 5.01 An upgrade broke something with no error a behaviour change listed in the changelog read every changelog entry between the versions 5.03 An AI or forum answer uses a function that does not exist an invented or outdated answer check every function on its reference page 5.03

title: Glossary
body: ABNF : Augmented Backus-Naur Form, the grammar notation used in RFCs. (4.04) Amortised constant : constant time on average over many calls, though a single call may be slow. (2.03) Basic guarantee : if a function throws, everything is still valid but may have changed. (1.04) Changelog : a list of what changed in each release: added, changed, deprecated, removed, fixed. (5.03) Compiler Explorer : godbolt.org, a website that compiles and runs small programs with many compilers. (5.02) Contract : the preconditions a caller must meet and the results a function promises in return. (1.04) cppreference : the community reference for C++ and its standard library. (2.01) Defect report : a correction to the C++ standard after publication. (2.01) Deprecated : still available but discouraged, and likely to be removed. (2.04) Doc comment : a comment in a special form ( /// , / / , a docstring) that tools turn into documentation. (4.03) Doxygen : the common tool and tag style ( @param , @return ) for C and C++ doc comments. (4.03) Errata : published corrections to a document such as an RFC. (4.04) Explanation : documentation that says why things are the way they are. (1.01) Feature-test macro : a macro such as __cpp_lib_format that says whether a feature is available. (2.04) Half-open range : first, last) , including first and excluding last . (1.04) How-to guide : documentation that walks through a task. (1.01) HRESULT : a 32-bit COM status code with severity, facility and code fields. (3.03) Implementation-defined : chosen by the compiler or library, which must document it. (1.02) Invalidation : an iterator, pointer or reference becoming unusable after a container changes. (2.03) Keyword-only parameter : a Python parameter after that must be passed by name. (4.01) Learning test : a test that pins down a library's behaviour your code relies on. (5.02) Man page : a Unix manual page, in numbered sections. (4.04) MDN : MDN Web Docs, the reference for JavaScript and web APIs. (4.02) Migration guide : instructions for upgrading across a breaking release. (5.03) Named requirement : a set of rules a template argument must meet, such as LegacyInputIterator. (1.03) NTSTATUS : the kernel's 32-bit status code, with two severity bits. (3.03) Overload set : several functions with the same name and different parameters. (1.03) Positional-only parameter : a Python parameter before / that cannot be passed by name. (4.01) Postcondition : what is true after a call that met its preconditions. (1.04) Precondition : what must be true before a call. (1.04) Reference : documentation that describes exactly what each part does. (1.01) RFC : a Request for Comments, the published specification of an internet standard. (4.04) RFC 2119 keywords : MUST, SHOULD, MAY and their negations, with exact meanings. (4.04) SAL : Microsoft's source annotation language, such as _In_ and _Out_writes_ . (3.02) Semantic Versioning : MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH version numbers that signal breaking changes. (4.04) Stability index : Node's label for how settled an API is. (4.02) Strong guarantee : if a function throws, nothing changed. (1.04) System error code : a Windows error number such as 2 ( ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND ). (3.03) Tutorial : documentation that teaches by leading a newcomer step by step. (1.01) Undefined behaviour : what happens when a precondition is broken: anything, with no guarantees. (1.04) Unspecified : one of several allowed results, with no promise which. (1.02)

title: 1.01  Complexity and Big O
body: How to describe an algorithm's speed independently of the computer - counting basic steps, Big O and its relatives Omega and Theta, the common growth classes, analysing sequential, nested and halving loops, best, worst and average cases, amortised cost, and space complexity. Why count instead of time? A stopwatch tells you how long one program took on one computer with one input. It cannot tell you what happens when the input is a thousand times bigger, and it changes with the compiler, the processor and whatever else is running. To compare algorithms we count how the number of basic steps grows with the size of the input, called n . A basic step is anything that takes a fixed amount of time: an arithmetic operation, a comparison, reading or writing one array element, a function call. cpp include <iostream include <vector int steps = 0; bool contains(const std::vector<int & values, int target) { for (int v : values) { ++steps; // one comparison per element if (v == target) return true; } return false; } bool hasDuplicate(const std::vector<int & values) { for (std::size_t i = 0; i < values.size(); ++i) for (std::size_t j = i + 1; j < values.size(); ++j) { ++steps; // one comparison per pair if (values i == values j ) return true; } return false; } int main() { for (int n : { 10, 100, 1000 }) { std::vector<int data(n); for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) data i = i; steps = 0; contains(data, -1); int linear = steps; steps = 0; hasDuplicate(data); std::cout << "n = " << n << ": contains " << linear << " steps, hasDuplicate " << steps << " steps\n"; } } Ten times more data means ten times more work for contains , but about a hundred times more for hasDuplicate . That growth rate is what Big O describes. Big O We say an algorithm is O(f(n)) if, for large enough n , its number of steps is at most some constant times f(n) . Two rules make this easy to use: 1. Drop constant factors. 3n + 5 steps is O(n). The constant depends on the machine; the growth does not. 2. Keep only the fastest-growing term. n²/2 + 100n is O(n²): for big n , the n² part dominates everything else. hasDuplicate does (n−1) + (n−2) + ... + 1 = n(n−1)/2 comparisons in the worst case, so it is O(n²). Big O is an upper bound . Two relatives complete the picture: Notation Meaning Informally --- --- --- O(f) grows no faster than f "at most" Ω(f) (Omega) grows at least as fast as f "at least" Θ(f) (Theta) both: grows exactly like f "exactly" In everyday use people say "O(n)" when they mean Θ(n), the tight bound. This course does the same unless the difference matters. The common growth classes Class Name Example n = 1,000,000 --- --- --- --- O(1) constant v i , push_back (amortised) 1 O(log n) logarithmic binary search 20 O(n) linear scanning a vector 10⁶ O(n log n) linearithmic good sorting 2 × 10⁷ O(n²) quadratic comparing every pair 10¹² O(2ⁿ) exponential trying every subset more than the atoms in the universe A modern computer does very roughly 10⁸ to 10⁹ simple steps per second. So for a million items, O(n log n) finishes in a fraction of a second, while O(n²) takes many minutes. Choosing the right growth class matters far more than tuning code. The three lines are n , n log n and n² . Analysing code Sequential parts add , and the bigger one wins: an O(n) loop followed by an O(n²) loop is O(n²). Nested loops multiply : a loop of n iterations, each doing O(n) work, is O(n²). Watch for hidden loops: std::find , v.erase(v.begin()) , s.substr and copying a vector are all O(n) themselves. Halving gives a logarithm. If each step cuts the remaining work in half, there are about log₂ n steps: cpp include <iostream int main() { for (long long n : { 8LL, 1000LL, 1000000LL, 1000000000000LL }) { int steps = 0; for (long long i = n; i 1; i /= 2) ++steps; std::cout << n << " halves to 1 in " << steps << " steps\n"; } } A trillion takes only 39 halvings. Logarithmic algorithms barely notice the size of their input. Recursion : count the calls and the work per call. A function that calls itself twice on inputs of size n − 1 makes about 2ⁿ calls, which is why the naive Fibonacci in lesson 6.02 is so slow. Best, worst and average case The same algorithm can take different times on different inputs of the same size. contains finds the target in the first slot in the best case (O(1)) and scans everything in the worst case (O(n)). On average, if the target is equally likely to be anywhere, it looks at about half: still O(n). - Worst case is the usual guarantee, and the default meaning of "this algorithm is O(...)". - Average case matters for algorithms like quicksort and hash tables, whose worst case is rare. - Best case is rarely useful on its own. Amortised cost Some operations are usually cheap but occasionally expensive. std::vector::push_back normally writes one element, but when the vector is full it allocates a bigger block and copies everything. Because the capacity doubles , the copies over n pushes add up to less than 2n : the cost is amortised O(1) per push. Lesson 1.03 builds such a vector and counts the copies. Amortised is not the same as average: it is a guarantee about any sequence of operations, with no luck involved. Space complexity Memory is analysed the same way. hasDuplicate uses O(1) extra space. Sorting a copy first and then comparing neighbours makes it O(n log n) in time but O(n) in extra space. Recursion uses stack space: a recursion n levels deep uses O(n) memory even if it allocates nothing. Often you can trade one for the other: a hash set finds duplicates in O(n) time using O(n) space. Summary - Count basic steps as a function of n ; drop constants and lower-order terms. - O is an upper bound, Ω a lower bound, Θ both. - Sequential code adds, nested loops multiply, halving gives log n. - Worst case is the default guarantee; amortised cost averages over a sequence of operations. - Space is analysed the same way, and recursion depth counts. Check yourself quiz ? What is the Big O of a loop for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) containing for (int j = 0; j < 10; ++j) ? - O(n²) + O(n) - O(10n²) - O(log n) The inner loop always runs 10 times, a constant. 10n steps is O(n). ? A function does for (int i = 1; i < n; i = 2) and, inside, for (int j = 0; j < n; ++j) . What is its complexity? - O(n²) + O(n log n) - O(log n) - O(n) The outer loop runs about log₂ n times and the inner one n times per outer iteration. ? Which is true of 5n² + 1000n + 7? - It is O(n) because 1000n is the biggest term for small n + It is O(n²) and also Θ(n²) - It is O(1000n) - It is only O(n³) For large n the n² term dominates. It is also O(n³), since Big O is only an upper bound, but Θ(n²) is the tight answer.

title: From quadratic to fast
body: Each of these has an obvious O(n²) solution. Write them faster; the tests include inputs of 100,000 elements, where O(n²) takes far too long. cpp bool hasDuplicate(std::vector<int values); // O(n log n): sort a copy, compare neighbours bool hasPairWithSum(const std::vector<int & sorted, int target); // O(n): two indexes moving towards each other long long maxSubarraySum(const std::vector<int & values); // O(n): the largest sum of a non-empty run of neighbours std::size_t countBelow(const std::vector<int & sorted, int limit); // O(log n): how many values are < limit - hasPairWithSum gets a vector sorted in ascending order and reports whether two different positions add up to target . Start one index at each end: if the sum is too small, move the left one right; too big, move the right one left. - maxSubarraySum (Kadane's algorithm): walk once, keeping the best sum of a run that ends here : either this value alone, or this value added to the best run ending at the previous one. The answer is the largest of those. For an empty vector it returns 0. - countBelow halves the search range each step (or uses std::lower_bound ).

title: 1.02  Measuring Real Performance
body:
Turning theory into measurements - timing code with std::chrono, avoiding the traps of optimisation and noise, doubling experiments that reveal the growth class, how the memory hierarchy and cache lines make some O(n) loops much faster than others, and when constant factors matter. Timing with std::chrono Big O predicts how running time grows. Measurements check the prediction and reveal what Big O hides: constant factors and the hardware. std::chrono::steady_clock is the clock to use, because it never jumps backwards when the system time changes. cpp include <chrono include <iostream include <vector int main() { std::vector<int data(10'000'000, 1); auto start = std::chrono::steady_clock::now(); long long total = 0; for (int x : data) total += x; auto stop = std::chrono::steady_clock::now(); auto us = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::microseconds (stop - start).count(); std::cout << "sum " << total << " in " << us << " microseconds
"; } Always use the result (here, print total ). An optimising compiler may delete a computation whose result nobody uses, and you end up timing nothing. Making measurements trustworthy - Build with optimisations (Release in Visual Studio, -O2 elsewhere). Debug builds can be ten times slower, and not uniformly so. - Repeat and take the minimum or the median. Other programs, the processor's turbo boost and caches all add noise; the fastest of several runs is closest to the true cost. - Warm up. The first run pays for page faults and cold caches. - Make the input big enough that the run takes at least a few milliseconds; timers are not precise below that. - Time only what you mean to time : build the input before starting the clock. The doubling experiment To find the growth class of a piece of code, time it at n , 2n , 4n ... and look at the ratio between consecutive times: Ratio when n doubles Growth class --- --- about 1 O(1) or O(log n) about 2 O(n) a little more than 2 O(n log n) about 4 O(n²) about 8 O(n³) cpp include <chrono include <iostream include <vector long long countPairsBelow(const std::vector<int & a, int limit) // O(n²) { long long count = 0; for (std::size_t i = 0; i < a.size(); ++i) for (std::size_t j = i + 1; j < a.size(); ++j) if (a i + a j < limit) ++count; return count; } int main() { double previous = 0; for (int n = 1000; n <= 8000; n = 2) { std::vector<int a(n); for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) a i = (i 7919) % 1000; double best = 1e18; long long result = 0; for (int run = 0; run < 3; ++run) { auto t0 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now(); result = countPairsBelow(a, 1000); auto t1 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now(); best = std::min(best, std::chrono::duration<double, std::milli (t1 - t0).count()); } std::cout << "n = " << n << ": " << best << " ms (" << result << " pairs)"; if (previous 0) std::cout << ", ratio " << best / previous; std::cout << '
'; previous = best; } } The ratios should come out near 4, confirming O(n²). Shared online compilers are noisy, so expect some wobble; on your own machine in a Release build the pattern is clearer. The memory hierarchy Big O counts every memory access as one step, but real memory is a hierarchy: Level Typical size Typical latency --- --- --- Registers a few hundred bytes under 1 ns L1 cache 32-64 KB per core about 1 ns L2 cache 0.5-2 MB per core about 4 ns L3 cache 8-64 MB shared about 15 ns Main memory gigabytes about 80-100 ns Memory moves between levels in cache lines of 64 bytes. Reading one int brings its 15 neighbours along for free, and the processor prefetches the next lines when it sees you walking forward. So: - Walking an array in order is very fast: almost every access hits the cache. - Jumping around memory (following pointers in a linked list, or indexing randomly) can be 10 to 100 times slower for the same number of steps. cpp include <chrono include <iostream include <vector int main() { const int n = 2048; std::vector<int grid(n n, 1); auto time = & (bool rowsFirst) { auto t0 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now(); long long sum = 0; for (int a = 0; a < n; ++a) for (int b = 0; b < n; ++b) sum += rowsFirst ? grid a n + b : grid b n + a ; auto t1 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now(); std::cout << (rowsFirst ? "row by row: " : "column by column: ") << std::chrono::duration<double, std::milli (t1 - t0).count() << " ms (sum " << sum << ")
"; }; time(true); time(false); } Both loops are O(n²) and add up the same numbers, yet walking column by column is several times slower: each step jumps 8 KB ahead and lands on a new cache line. When constant factors matter Big O wins for large inputs, but for small ones the constants decide: - Insertion sort (O(n²)) beats merge sort (O(n log n)) below a few dozen elements, which is why real sort functions switch to it for small pieces (lesson 3.01). - A linear scan of a small sorted std::vector often beats a std::map lookup, because the vector is one contiguous block. - A std::vector usually beats a std::list even for inserting in the middle, until the list is very long, because finding the position in a list means chasing pointers (lesson 1.04). The rule of thumb: choose the right growth class first, then measure before optimising constants. Summary - Time with std::chrono::steady_clock , in an optimised build, repeated, using the result. - The doubling experiment reveals the growth class from the ratio of times. - Memory is a hierarchy; contiguous, in-order access is far faster than scattered access. - Big O picks the algorithm; measurement and the memory hierarchy decide between algorithms of the same class. Check yourself quiz ? Doubling n makes a function take about 4 times as long. What is its likely growth class? - O(n) - O(n log n) + O(n²) - O(2ⁿ) 2² = 4, so the time grows with the square of n. ? Why is summing a std::vector usually much faster than summing a std::list of the same length? - The vector's loop is O(1) instead of O(n) + Its elements are contiguous, so the cache serves the reads - A std::list cannot hold integers directly - Summing a list is O(n²) Both are O(n), but the list's nodes are scattered, so many reads wait for main memory, while the vector's neighbours arrive with each cache line and the prefetcher keeps up. ? Why print the result of a computation you are timing? - Printing makes the timer more precise - steady_clock needs output to start + So the optimiser cannot remove the computation as unused - It warms up the cache If the result is never used, the compiler may skip the work entirely.

title: Read the timings
body: Write the helpers of a small benchmarking tool: cpp template <class F double bestOfMs(F work, int runs); // runs work() runs times; returns the fastest run in milliseconds double median(std::vector<double samples); // the middle value (the mean of the two middle ones for an even count) double growthExponent(const std::vector<double & times); // times i is the time for input size n 2^i std::string bigO(double exponent); // "O(1)", "O(n)", "O(n^2)", "O(n^3)" or "worse than O(n^3)" - bestOfMs times each run with std::chrono::steady_clock . runs below 1 throws std::invalid_argument . - median of an empty vector throws std::invalid_argument . - growthExponent estimates k in "time grows like nᵏ" from a doubling experiment. Over m doublings the time grows by times.back() / times.front() , so the average growth per doubling is that ratio to the power 1/m , and k is its base-2 logarithm. It needs at least two times, all greater than 0 (otherwise std::invalid_argument ). - bigO rounds the exponent to the nearest whole number ( std::lround ): 0 or less gives O(1) , 1 O(n) , 2 O(n^2) , 3 O(n^3) , anything bigger worse than O(n^3) .

title: 1.03  Dynamic Arrays
body:
How std::vector works inside - a contiguous block with a size and a capacity, growth by doubling and why it gives amortised O(1) push_back, the cost of inserting and erasing in the middle, building a small vector class with a rule-of-five, and what invalidates iterators. An array that grows A plain array has a fixed size. A dynamic array keeps its elements in one contiguous block like an array, but can grow. It tracks three things: - a pointer to the block, - its size , the number of elements in use, - its capacity , the number of elements the block can hold. Reading or writing v i is O(1): the address is start + i × sizeof(T) . Appending is O(1) while there is spare capacity. When the block is full, the array must: 1. allocate a bigger block, 2. move every element across, 3. free the old block. That step is O(n). The trick is how much bigger to make the new block. Why doubling gives amortised O(1) If the capacity grew by a fixed amount, say 10, every tenth push would copy everything: about n²/20 copies for n pushes, O(n) per push on average. If instead it doubles , the copies happen at sizes 1, 2, 4, 8, ..., and their total is less than 2n. Spread over n pushes, that is fewer than 2 copies each: amortised O(1) . cpp include <iostream include <vector int main() { std::vector<int v; std::size_t lastCapacity = v.capacity(); for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) { v.push_back(i); if (v.capacity() != lastCapacity) { std::cout << "size " << v.size() << ": capacity " << lastCapacity << " - " << v.capacity() << '
'; lastCapacity = v.capacity(); } } } Microsoft's library grows by 1.5×, GCC's and Clang's by 2×. Any constant factor greater than 1 gives amortised O(1); smaller factors waste less memory but copy a little more often. If you know the final size, v.reserve(n) allocates once up front and no reallocation happens at all. Inserting and erasing in the middle To insert at position i , every element from i onward must shift one place right; erasing shifts them left. That is O(n − i): cheap at the end, expensive at the front. Operation Cost --- --- v i , v.back() O(1) push_back , pop_back amortised O(1), O(1) insert(v.begin() + i, x) , erase(v.begin() + i) O(n − i) insert(v.begin(), x) O(n) find a value (unsorted) O(n) If you only need to remove an element and do not care about order, swap it with the last element and pop : O(1). cpp include <iostream include <vector void unorderedErase(std::vector<int & v, std::size_t i) { v i = v.back(); v.pop_back(); } int main() { std::vector<int v{ 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 }; unorderedErase(v, 1); for (int x : v) std::cout << x << ' '; std::cout << '
'; } Building one Here is a minimal dynamic array of int s. It owns raw memory, so it follows the rule of five : a destructor, copy constructor, copy assignment, move constructor and move assignment. cpp include <algorithm include <cstddef include <iostream include <stdexcept include <utility class IntVector { public: IntVector() = default; ~IntVector() { delete data_; } IntVector(const IntVector& other) : data_(new int other.capacity_ ), size_(other.size_), capacity_(other.capacity_) { std::copy(other.data_, other.data_ + size_, data_); } IntVector& operator=(IntVector other) noexcept // copy-and-swap handles both copy and move assignment { swap(other); return this; } IntVector(IntVector&& other) noexcept : data_(std::exchange(other.data_, nullptr)), size_(std::exchange(other.size_, 0)), capacity_(std::exchange(other.capacity_, 0)) {} void push_back(int value) { if (size_ == capacity_) grow(capacity_ == 0 ? 1 : capacity_ 2); data_ size_++ = value; } void pop_back() { if (size_ == 0) throw std::out_of_range("pop_back on empty"); --size_; } int& operator (std::size_t i) { return data_ i ; } int& at(std::size_t i) { if (i = size_) throw std::out_of_range("index"); return data_ i ; } std::size_t size() const { return size_; } std::size_t capacity() const { return capacity_; } void swap(IntVector& other) noexcept { std::swap(data_, other.data_); std::swap(size_, other.size_); std::swap(capacity_, other.capacity_); } private: void grow(std::size_t newCapacity) { int bigger = new int newCapacity ; std::copy(data_, data_ + size_, bigger); delete data_; data_ = bigger; capacity_ = newCapacity; } int data_ = nullptr; std::size_t size_ = 0; std::size_t capacity_ = 0; }; int main() { IntVector v; for (int i = 1; i <= 10; ++i) v.push_back(i i); IntVector copy = v; copy 0 = -1; std::cout << "size " << v.size() << ", capacity " << v.capacity() << ", v 0 " << v 0 << ", copy 0 " << copy 0 << '
'; try { v.at(10); } catch (const std::out_of_range& e) { std::cout << "at(10): " << e.what() << '
'; } } The real std::vector adds a lot on top: it is a template, it constructs elements only when they are pushed (so it works for types without a default constructor), it moves rather than copies elements when it grows (if their move constructor is noexcept ), and it gives iterators. The practice for this lesson builds a template version. Iterator invalidation Because a dynamic array moves its elements when it grows, any pointer, reference or iterator into it may dangle after a push_back , insert or reserve that reallocates. Erasing invalidates everything after the erased position. cpp-norun std::vector<int v{ 1, 2, 3 }; int& first = v 0 ; v.push_back(4); // may reallocate std::cout << first; // undefined behaviour if it did Keep indexes instead of pointers when the vector may grow, or reserve enough first. Summary - A dynamic array is a contiguous block with a size and a capacity. - Growing by a constant factor makes push_back amortised O(1); reserve avoids growing at all. - Inserting and erasing cost O(n − i) because elements shift; swap-and-pop removes in O(1) when order does not matter. - Reallocation invalidates pointers, references and iterators. Check yourself quiz ? A dynamic array grows its capacity by 1.5× when full. What is the amortised cost of push_back? - O(log n) + O(1) - O(n) - O(1.5ⁿ) Any constant growth factor above 1 keeps the total copying proportional to n. ? Why does erasing the first element of a std::vector take O(n)? - The vector has to reallocate + Every other element shifts one place to the left - The vector searches for the element first - It has to update the capacity The elements must stay contiguous, so they all move down by one. ? You hold a reference to v 2 and then call v.push_back(x). Is the reference still safe to use? - Yes, always: v 2 itself did not change - Yes, as long as x is not equal to v 2 + Only if the push did not reallocate - No: push_back always invalidates everything Reallocation moves the elements to a new block, leaving old references dangling. If capacity was reserved first, no reallocation happens.

title: A vector template
body: Build Vec<T , a dynamic array like std::vector , that works even for types without a default constructor : cpp template <class T class Vec { public: Vec(); ~Vec(); Vec(const Vec& other); Vec(Vec&& other) noexcept; Vec& operator=(const Vec& other); Vec& operator=(Vec&& other) noexcept; void push_back(const T& value); void pop_back(); // throws std::out_of_range if empty void reserve(std::size_t capacity); // never shrinks void insert(std::size_t index, const T& value); // index may equal size(); otherwise std::out_of_range void erase(std::size_t index); // std::out_of_range if index = size() T& operator (std::size_t i); const T& operator (std::size_t i) const; std::size_t size() const; std::size_t capacity() const; T begin(); T end(); // so range-for works }; - Growth: capacity 0 becomes 1, then doubles whenever a push or insert finds the array full. - Use raw storage : allocate with static_cast<T (::operator new(n sizeof(T))) , build elements in place with placement new (ptr) T(value) , destroy them with ptr- ~T() , and free with ::operator delete(ptr) . new T n would need a default constructor and would construct n elements you never asked for. - When growing, move the elements into the new block ( std::move ), then destroy the old ones. - Every element constructed must be destroyed exactly once, and nothing may leak (the tests count).

title: 1.04  Linked Lists
body:
Nodes connected by pointers - singly linked lists with push_front, insertion after a node and reversal, owning nodes with std::unique_ptr, doubly linked lists with a sentinel, the costs compared with a vector, std::list and std::forward_list, and the two-pointer techniques for finding the middle and detecting a cycle. Nodes and links A linked list stores each element in its own node , which also holds a pointer to the next node. The list itself only remembers the first node, the head . Because nodes are linked rather than adjacent, inserting or removing a node only rewires a couple of pointers: O(1) once you are at the right place . The price is that there is no list i : reaching the i-th node means following i links, O(i). A singly linked list cpp include <iostream struct Node { int value; Node next; }; int main() { Node head = nullptr; for (int x : { 9, 3, 7 }) head = new Node{ x, head }; // push_front: O(1) for (Node n = head; n != nullptr; n = n- next) std::cout << n- value << ' '; std::cout << '
'; // insert 5 after the node holding 3 for (Node n = head; n != nullptr; n = n- next) if (n- value == 3) { n- next = new Node{ 5, n- next }; break; } // reverse the list in place: O(n), O(1) extra space Node previous = nullptr; while (head != nullptr) { Node next = head- next; head- next = previous; previous = head; head = next; } head = previous; for (Node n = head; n != nullptr; n = n- next) std::cout << n- value << ' '; std::cout << '
'; while (head != nullptr) // free every node { Node next = head- next; delete head; head = next; } } Reversal is the classic linked-list exercise: walk the list once, turning each next pointer around. Draw the three pointers ( previous , head , next ) on paper for a three-node list and the loop becomes obvious. Owning the nodes Raw new and delete make it easy to leak or double-free nodes. In modern C++ each node can own the next one through a std::unique_ptr : destroying the head destroys the whole chain. cpp include <iostream include <memory struct Node { int value; std::unique_ptr<Node next; }; class IntList { public: void push_front(int value) { head_ = std::make_unique<Node (Node{ value, std::move(head_) }); ++size_; } void pop_front() { if (head_) { head_ = std::move(head_- next); --size_; } } std::size_t size() const { return size_; } void print() const { for (const Node n = head_.get(); n; n = n- next.get()) std::cout << n- value << ' '; std::cout << '
'; } ~IntList() { while (head_) head_ = std::move(head_- next); } // iterative, so a long list cannot overflow the stack private: std::unique_ptr<Node head_; std::size_t size_ = 0; }; int main() { IntList list; for (int i = 1; i <= 5; ++i) list.push_front(i); list.pop_front(); list.print(); std::cout << "size " << list.size() << '
'; } The destructor matters: the default one destroys head_ , which destroys its next , which destroys its next ... one nested call per node. A list of a million nodes would overflow the call stack. Unlinking one node at a time in a loop avoids that. Doubly linked lists and sentinels A doubly linked list gives each node a prev pointer too, so you can walk backwards and remove a node knowing only its address. Implementations often add a sentinel : a dummy node that sits before the first and after the last element, making the list circular. Then there are no special cases for an empty list or for the ends: every real node always has a real prev and next . cpp include <iostream struct DNode { int value; DNode prev; DNode next; }; void insertBefore(DNode pos, int value) { DNode n = new DNode{ value, pos- prev, pos }; pos- prev- next = n; pos- prev = n; } void unlink(DNode n) { n- prev- next = n- next; n- next- prev = n- prev; delete n; } int main() { DNode sentinel{ 0, &sentinel, &sentinel }; // empty: points to itself for (int x : { 1, 2, 3, 4 }) insertBefore(&sentinel, x); // push_back insertBefore(sentinel.next, 0); // push_front unlink(sentinel.next- next- next); // remove the third node (2) for (DNode n = sentinel.next; n != &sentinel; n = n- next) std::cout << n- value << ' '; std::cout << " backwards: "; for (DNode n = sentinel.prev; n != &sentinel; n = n- prev) std::cout << n- value << ' '; std::cout << '
'; while (sentinel.next != &sentinel) unlink(sentinel.next); } Notice that insertBefore and unlink contain no if s at all. That is the point of the sentinel. std::list is built this way. Lists or vectors? Operation std::vector linked list --- --- --- index i O(1) O(i) push/pop at the back amortised O(1) O(1) (doubly linked) push/pop at the front O(n) O(1) insert/erase at a known node O(n) O(1) find a value O(n) O(n) memory per element the element the element + 1 or 2 pointers + allocation overhead cache behaviour excellent poor: every step can miss the cache On paper the list wins at inserting in the middle. In practice you must first find the middle, which is O(n) pointer chasing, and a vector's O(n) shifting of contiguous memory is so fast that vectors usually win anyway . Lists win when you already hold pointers to nodes and splice them around: LRU caches (the milestone 2 project), free lists in allocators, and the ready queues of schedulers. The standard library has std::list (doubly linked, with splice to move nodes between lists in O(1)) and std::forward_list (singly linked, the smallest). Two-pointer techniques Several list problems are solved by walking two pointers at different speeds. The middle node : move slow one step and fast two steps; when fast reaches the end, slow is in the middle. Cycle detection (Floyd's "tortoise and hare"): if a list loops back on itself, a fast pointer eventually laps the slow one and they meet. If there is no cycle, the fast pointer reaches nullptr . O(n) time, O(1) space. cpp include <iostream include <vector struct Node { int value; Node next; }; Node middle(Node head) { Node slow = head; Node fast = head; while (fast && fast- next) { slow = slow- next; fast = fast- next- next; } return slow; } bool hasCycle(Node head) { Node slow = head; Node fast = head; while (fast && fast- next) { slow = slow- next; fast = fast- next- next; if (slow == fast) return true; } return false; } int main() { std::vector<Node nodes(7); for (int i = 0; i < 7; ++i) nodes i = { i 10, i + 1 < 7 ? &nodes i + 1 : nullptr }; std::cout << "middle " << middle(&nodes 0 )- value << ", cycle " << hasCycle(&nodes 0 ) << '
'; nodes 6 .next = &nodes 2 ; // make the tail point back into the list std::cout << "after linking the tail back: cycle " << hasCycle(&nodes 0 ) << '
'; } Summary - A linked list stores elements in nodes joined by pointers: O(1) to insert or remove at a known node, O(i) to reach position i. - Own nodes with std::unique_ptr and destroy long lists iteratively. - Doubly linked lists with a sentinel remove every special case. - Vectors usually beat lists in practice because of the cache; lists shine when you keep pointers to nodes and splice them. - Fast and slow pointers find the middle and detect cycles in O(1) space. Check yourself quiz ? What does it cost to reach the 500th node of a singly linked list? - O(1) - O(log n) + O(500): follow 500 links from the head - It is impossible There is no indexing: every node must be visited on the way. ? What does a sentinel node in a doubly linked list buy you? - O(1) access to any index - Half the memory per node + No special cases for the ends or an empty list - The list stays sorted automatically Every real node always has real neighbours, so insertion and removal use the same pointer updates everywhere. ? Why can a destructor that relies on unique_ptr chains crash for a very long list? - unique_ptr objects cannot be nested + The destructors recurse once per node and overflow the stack - The nodes are destroyed twice - unique_ptr leaks the last node Each node's destruction calls the next one's destructor. Unlinking nodes one at a time in a loop keeps the stack depth constant.

title: A singly linked list
body: Build IntList , a singly linked list whose nodes are owned by std::unique_ptr , with a raw pointer to the last node so that push_back is O(1): cpp class IntList { public: void push_front(int value); void push_back(int value); int pop_front(); // returns the value; std::out_of_range if empty std::size_t size() const; bool empty() const; std::vector<int toVector() const; void reverse(); // in place, O(n), no new nodes std::size_t removeAll(int value); // removes every node holding value; returns how many bool hasValue(int value) const; int middle() const; // the middle value (the second of the two middles for an even size); std::out_of_range if empty ~IntList(); // must not recurse once per node }; Keep tail_ correct after every operation, including reverse and removeAll (the tests push to the back afterwards). middle uses the fast and slow pointers from lesson 1.04.

title: 1.05  Stacks, Queues and Deques
body:
The restricted containers - stacks (last in, first out) for undo, matching brackets and evaluating expressions, queues (first in, first out) built as ring buffers, deques open at both ends, the standard adapters std::stack, std::queue and std::deque, and the monotonic-deque trick for sliding-window maximums. Restricting a container on purpose A stack and a queue offer fewer operations than a vector, and that is their strength: the restriction says exactly how the data will be used, and every operation is O(1). Structure Add Remove Order --- --- --- --- Stack push on top pop from the top last in, first out (LIFO) Queue push at the back pop from the front first in, first out (FIFO) Deque at either end from either end both Stacks A stack is a pile of plates: you only touch the top one. A std::vector makes a perfect stack ( push_back , back , pop_back ), and std::stack is an adapter that exposes just those operations. Stacks appear wherever work must be undone or finished in reverse order : the call stack of a program, undo in an editor, the back button in a browser, and depth-first search (lesson 5.02). Matching brackets is the classic example: push each opening bracket; on a closing bracket the top of the stack must be its partner. cpp include <iostream include <stack include <string bool balanced(const std::string& text) { std::stack<char open; for (char c : text) { if (c == '(' c == ' ' c == '{') open.push(c); else if (c == ')' c == ' ' c == '}') { char want = c == ')' ? '(' : c == ' ' ? ' ' : '{'; if (open.empty() open.top() != want) return false; open.pop(); } } return open.empty(); } int main() { for (std::string s : { "f(a i , {b})", "( ", "((x)", "" }) std::cout << '"' << s << "" " << (balanced(s) ? "balanced" : "not balanced") << '
'; } Evaluating expressions How does a calculator know that 2 + 3 4 is 14? Edsger Dijkstra's shunting-yard algorithm uses two stacks, one of numbers and one of operators. When an operator arrives, it first applies every operator on the stack that binds at least as tightly; brackets fence off sub-expressions. cpp include <cctype include <iostream include <stack include <stdexcept include <string int precedence(char op) { return op == '+' op == '-' ? 1 : 2; } void apply(std::stack<long long & values, std::stack<char & ops) { char op = ops.top(); ops.pop(); long long b = values.top(); values.pop(); long long a = values.top(); values.pop(); switch (op) { case '+': values.push(a + b); break; case '-': values.push(a - b); break; case ' ': values.push(a b); break; case '/': if (b == 0) throw std::domain_error("division by zero"); values.push(a / b); break; } } long long evaluate(const std::string& text) { std::stack<long long values; std::stack<char ops; for (std::size_t i = 0; i < text.size(); ++i) { char c = text i ; if (std::isspace(static_cast<unsigned char (c))) continue; if (std::isdigit(static_cast<unsigned char (c))) { long long n = 0; while (i < text.size() && std::isdigit(static_cast<unsigned char (text i ))) n = n 10 + (text i++ - '0'); --i; values.push(n); } else if (c == '(') ops.push(c); else if (c == ')') { while (ops.top() != '(') apply(values, ops); ops.pop(); } else { while (!ops.empty() && ops.top() != '(' && precedence(ops.top()) = precedence(c)) apply(values, ops); ops.push(c); } } while (!ops.empty()) apply(values, ops); return values.top(); } int main() { for (std::string e : { "2 + 3 4", "(2 + 3) 4", "100 / 10 / 5", "7 - 2 - 1", "2 (3 + 4) 5" }) std::cout << e << " = " << evaluate(e) << '
'; } The = makes operators of equal precedence apply left to right, so 7 - 2 - 1 is (7 - 2) - 1 = 4 . This sketch trusts its input; the milestone project makes it robust, with error messages for every kind of mistake. Queues A queue is a line at a shop: people join at the back and leave from the front. Queues hold work in the order it arrived : print jobs, network packets, events in a game, and the frontier of breadth-first search (lesson 5.01). A vector is a poor queue, because removing from the front is O(n). A ring buffer (circular buffer) fixes that: keep the elements in a fixed array with a head index, and let the indexes wrap around with % . The queue above holds B, C, D, E, F in that order: the elements after the end of the array continue at the start. cpp include <iostream include <stdexcept include <vector class RingQueue { public: explicit RingQueue(std::size_t capacity) : slots_(capacity) {} void push(int value) { if (size_ == slots_.size()) throw std::length_error("queue full"); slots_ (head_ + size_) % slots_.size() = value; ++size_; } int pop() { if (size_ == 0) throw std::out_of_range("queue empty"); int value = slots_ head_ ; head_ = (head_ + 1) % slots_.size(); --size_; return value; } std::size_t size() const { return size_; } private: std::vector<int slots_; std::size_t head_ = 0; std::size_t size_ = 0; }; int main() { RingQueue q(4); for (int i = 1; i <= 4; ++i) q.push(i); std::cout << q.pop() << ' ' << q.pop() << ' '; q.push(5); q.push(6); // these wrap around to the start of the array while (q.size() 0) std::cout << q.pop() << ' '; std::cout << '
'; } A fixed-size ring buffer is ideal for audio samples, logs that keep the last N lines, and producer-consumer queues. To grow it, allocate a bigger array and copy the elements across in queue order, exactly like a vector (practice 1.05 does this). Deques and the standard adapters A deque ("deck", double-ended queue) supports push and pop at both ends in O(1), and still allows indexing. std::deque stores its elements in fixed-size blocks with a table of pointers to them, so it can grow at either end without moving existing elements. Type What it is Underlying container --- --- --- std::stack<T push , pop , top std::deque by default; std::stack<T, std::vector<T is common std::queue<T push , pop , front , back std::deque std::deque<T both ends plus i blocks of elements Note that pop() returns nothing in the standard adapters: read top() or front() first. This is so that a copy constructor that throws cannot lose an element. The sliding-window maximum Given a sequence and a window of size k , report the maximum of every window. Recomputing each one costs O(nk). A deque of indexes whose values are kept in decreasing order does it in O(n): each new value pushes out the smaller values behind it (they can never be a maximum again), and the front falls off when it leaves the window. cpp include <deque include <iostream include <vector std::vector<int windowMax(const std::vector<int & a, std::size_t k) { std::deque<std::size_t idx; // indexes into a, values decreasing from front to back std::vector<int result; for (std::size_t i = 0; i < a.size(); ++i) { while (!idx.empty() && a idx.back() <= a i ) idx.pop_back(); idx.push_back(i); if (idx.front() + k <= i) idx.pop_front(); if (i + 1 = k) result.push_back(a idx.front() ); } return result; } int main() { for (int m : windowMax({ 1, 3, -1, -3, 5, 3, 6, 7 }, 3)) std::cout << m << ' '; std::cout << '
'; } Every index enters and leaves the deque at most once, so the whole thing is O(n) even though there is a loop inside the loop. This kind of reasoning, counting the total work over the whole run rather than per iteration, is amortised analysis again. Summary - Stacks are LIFO: undo, brackets, expression evaluation, depth-first search. - Queues are FIFO: work in arrival order, breadth-first search. Build them as ring buffers. - Deques are open at both ends; std::stack and std::queue are adapters over one. - A monotonic deque finds every sliding-window maximum in O(n). Check yourself quiz ? Which structure suits an undo feature? - A queue: the oldest action is undone first - A ring buffer with no size limit - A hash table + A stack: the most recent action is undone first Undo reverses actions newest first, which is LIFO. ? Why is a std::vector a poor queue? - It cannot add at the back + Removing from the front shifts every remaining element, O(n) - It does not keep elements in order - It cannot hold more than 1000 elements A ring buffer or deque removes from the front in O(1). ? A ring buffer of capacity 8 has head = 6 and size = 4. Which slot does the next push write to? - 10 + 2 - 7 - 0 (6 + 4) % 8 = 2: the queue occupies slots 6, 7, 0, 1, so the next free slot is 2.

title: A growable ring deque
body: Build Ring<T , a double-ended queue stored in a ring buffer that grows when full: cpp template <class T class Ring { public: void push_back(T value); void push_front(T value); T pop_back(); // std::out_of_range if empty T pop_front(); // std::out_of_range if empty T& front(); T& back(); // std::out_of_range if empty T& operator (std::size_t i); // i counts from the front std::size_t size() const; std::size_t capacity() const; }; - Keep the elements in a std::vector<T of slots, with the index of the front element ( head_ ) and the number of elements ( size_ ). Element i lives in slot (head_ + i) % capacity . - push_front steps head_ back by one, wrapping from 0 to capacity - 1 . - When a push finds the ring full, grow to capacity 4 (if it was 0) or double it, copying (moving) the elements across in queue order so that the front ends up in slot 0. - Every operation is O(1), amortised for pushes. T may be assumed to be default-constructible and movable.
