title: 2.04  Object Lifetime: When Memory Is Valid
match: 2.04 Object Lifetime: When Memory Is Valid
body:
An object's lifetime runs from the end of its construction to the start of its destruction. Outside that window its memory may still be there, but using it is a bug. This lesson traces lifetimes for locals, temporaries, heap objects and members, and introduces RAII : tying every resource to an object's lifetime so it is released automatically. Memory and objects are not the same thing Memory is bytes at an address. An object is a value of some type that lives in those bytes for a while. The two have separate lives: - The memory can exist before the object is created in it (a stack frame is set up before its locals are constructed). - The memory can exist after the object is gone (a freed heap block is still mapped; a returned function's frame is still part of the stack). An object's lifetime starts when its constructor finishes and ends when its destructor starts. C++ only promises anything about an object during its lifetime. Reading or writing it outside that window is undefined behaviour , even if the bytes are still there. Watching constructors and destructors The clearest way to see lifetimes is a type that announces itself. cpp include <iostream include <string struct Noisy { std::string name; explicit Noisy(std::string n) : name{ std::move(n) } { std::cout << " + " << name << '
'; } ~Noisy() { std::cout << " - " << name << '
'; } }; Noisy g_global{ "global" }; void level() { std::cout << "level starts
"; Noisy a{ "a" }; { Noisy b{ "b" }; std::cout << "inner block ends
"; } Noisy c{ "c" }; std::cout << "level ends
"; } int main() { std::cout << "main starts
"; level(); Noisy boss{ new Noisy{ "boss" } }; delete boss; std::cout << "main ends
"; return 0; } + global main starts level starts + a + b inner block ends - b + c level ends - c - a + boss - boss main ends - global Read it carefully. Every rule of object lifetime is in that output: Kind of object Lifetime starts Lifetime ends --- --- --- Global Before main After main returns Local At its declaration At the end of the enclosing block { } Several locals in one block In declaration order In reverse order: c before a Heap object At new At delete The reverse order matters: c was created after a and might depend on it, so it is destroyed first. Temporaries A temporary is an unnamed object created in the middle of an expression, such as the result of std::string("Lv") + "1" . It lives until the end of the full expression : roughly, until the next semicolon. cpp include <iostream include <string std::string levelName(int n) { return "Level " + std::to_string(n); } int main() { std::cout << levelName(3) << '
'; // fine: used within the same expression const char text{ levelName(4).c_str() }; // the string dies at the semicolon... // ...so text now points into freed memory. Using it here would be a bug. const std::string& kept{ levelName(5) }; // a const reference extends the temporary's life std::cout << kept << '
'; return 0; } Level 3 Level 5 The middle line is a classic: c_str() returns a pointer into the string's buffer, and the string is a temporary destroyed at the end of the line. The pointer survives; the characters do not. Binding the temporary to a const reference, as on the third line, keeps it alive as long as the reference, but only in that direct form. Lifetime bugs in real code These are the shapes lifetime bugs take. Each compiles. Each "works" sometimes. cpp include <string include <string_view include <vector struct Enemy { int health; }; int dangling() { int local{ 5 }; return &local; // 1. address of a local that is about to die } std::string_view nameView() { std::string name{ "Grim" }; return name; // 2. a view of a string that is about to die } void invalidated(std::vector<Enemy & enemies) { Enemy& first{ enemies 0 }; enemies.push_back(Enemy{ 10 }); // 3. may move every element to a new block... first.health = 0; // ...so first may refer to freed memory } The third one deserves attention because it involves no delete at all. When a std::vector runs out of capacity, it allocates a bigger block, moves the elements across and frees the old block. Every pointer, reference and iterator into the old block is now dangling . Lesson 3.07 shows exactly when this happens. RAII: let lifetimes do the cleaning up Destructors run automatically and reliably: at the end of a block, on return , and when an exception passes through. C++ uses this to manage every kind of resource, not just memory. The idea is called RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialisation), and it is simple: 1. Acquire the resource in a constructor. 2. Release it in the destructor. 3. Hold the object by value (as a local or a member), so its lifetime is the resource's lifetime. Resource RAII type --- --- Heap memory std::unique_ptr , std::vector , std::string A file std::ifstream , std::ofstream A lock std::lock_guard , std::scoped_lock A Windows handle A small class of your own that calls CloseHandle (chapter 5) "Undo this change when I'm done" A small class of your own, as in the practice task cpp include <iostream class ScopedTimerName { public: explicit ScopedTimerName(const char name) : m_name{ name } { std::cout << "begin " << m_name << '
'; } ~ScopedTimerName() { std::cout << "end " << m_name << '
'; } private: const char m_name; }; int loadLevel(bool fail) { ScopedTimerName scope{ "loadLevel" }; if (fail) return -1; // the destructor still runs return 1; } int main() { loadLevel(true); loadLevel(false); return 0; } begin loadLevel end loadLevel begin loadLevel end loadLevel Whichever way loadLevel leaves, "end" is printed. Code written in this style cannot forget to clean up, because there is no cleanup code to forget. Common mistakes !warning Keeping c_str() , data() or a string_view of a temporary The pointer outlives the string. Keep the std::string itself if you need the text later. !warning Holding a reference into a vector while adding to it push_back , insert , resize and reserve can move every element. Store indices instead, or re-read the reference after the change. !warning Manual cleanup at the end of a function An early return or an exception skips it. Put the cleanup in a destructor. !warning Capturing locals by reference in a lambda that outlives them A callback stored for later that captured & refers to locals of a function that has long since returned. Check yourself quiz ? When does an object's lifetime begin and end? - It begins when its memory is allocated and ends when the memory is freed + It begins when its constructor finishes and ends when its destructor starts - It begins at the start of main and ends when the program exits Outside that window, using the object is undefined behaviour, even if its memory still exists. ? Why is const char p = makeString().c_str(); a bug? - c_str() returns a copy that must be freed with delete - c_str() cannot be called on a returned value + The returned string is a temporary destroyed at the end of the line - A const char cannot point at a std::string 's characters The temporary only lives until the end of the full expression. Keep the string in a named variable first if you need the pointer later. ? Name three kinds of resource that RAII can manage. - Local int s, double s and bool s - Function calls, loops and branches - Only heap memory; other resources need manual cleanup + Heap memory, open files and Windows handles RAII ties a resource to an object: the constructor acquires it and the destructor releases it, whatever the resource is. Locks, or any "undo this when finished" action, work the same way. ? Three locals a , b , c are declared in that order in one block. In which order are they destroyed? - a , b , c + c , b , a - In no particular order Reverse order of construction, so later objects, which may depend on earlier ones, go first. ? How long does the temporary in std::cout << makeName() << '
'; live? - Until the end of the function + Until the end of the full expression, at the semicolon - Until the next delete Temporaries die at the end of the full expression they were created in. ? Why can Enemy& first = enemies 0 ; enemies.push_back(e); first.health = 0; be a bug? - References to vector elements are never allowed - push_back destroys the first element + push_back may move the elements, leaving first dangling When capacity runs out, the vector reallocates and frees the old block. ? What is RAII? - A way to allocate memory faster + Releasing a resource in the destructor of its owner - A Windows API for opening and closing handles Because destructors run automatically, the resource is released on every path out of the scope.

title: Undo it on the way out
match: Undo it on the way out
where: 2.04 Object Lifetime: When Memory Is Valid
body: A debug tool sometimes changes a setting for a moment, for example making the game run at quarter speed while a single frame is examined, and must always put it back, however the function exits. Write the RAII class ScopedValue . Its constructor receives a reference to an int and a temporary value. It remembers the old value and sets the int to the temporary one. Its destructor puts the old value back. cpp int speed{ 100 }; { ScopedValue slow{ speed, 25 }; // speed is 25 here } // speed is 100 again Copying a ScopedValue would restore the value twice, so delete the copy constructor and copy assignment.

title: 2.05  Alignment and Padding in Detail
body:
Every type has an alignment : the addresses it may start at must be a multiple of it. To keep each member of a struct aligned, the compiler inserts unused padding bytes. This lesson gives the exact rules, shows how to predict a struct's size and members' offsets, and how to arrange members so less memory is wasted. Why alignment exists Memory is a row of bytes, but the processor does not read it one byte at a time. It fetches aligned chunks: 8, 16 or 64 bytes at once. A 4-byte int that starts at an address divisible by 4 always falls inside one chunk. One that starts at address 6 might straddle two chunks and need two fetches, and some instructions refuse misaligned data altogether. So compilers follow a simple rule: a value of a type with alignment N is placed at an address that is a multiple of N. On x64 Windows, a basic type's alignment is the same as its size: Type Size Alignment --- --- --- char , bool , std::uint8_t 1 1 short , std::int16_t 2 2 int , float , std::int32_t 4 4 long long , double , any pointer 8 8 alignof(T) gives a type's alignment, just as sizeof(T) gives its size. The three rules for a struct The compiler lays out a struct's members in the order they are declared and follows three rules: 1. Each member starts at the next offset that is a multiple of its own alignment. Any skipped bytes are padding . 2. The struct's own alignment is the largest alignment of any member. 3. The struct's size is rounded up to a multiple of its alignment, adding tail padding if needed. This keeps every element of an array of the struct aligned. Work through one by hand: cpp struct Pickup { char kind; // offset 0, size 1 // padding: offsets 1..3, so the int can start at a multiple of 4 int amount; // offset 4, size 4 bool active; // offset 8, size 1 // padding: offsets 9..15 double expires; // offset 16, size 8 }; // largest alignment is 8; 24 is already a multiple of 8, so sizeof is 24 Of 24 bytes, 14 hold data and 10 are padding. See it laid out, then try the packed view to compare: demo-memory title: struct Pickup, in declaration order char kind = 'H' int amount = 25 bool active = true double expires = 12.5 Reordering to save space The fix is to declare members from the largest alignment to the smallest. Then each member already lands on a suitable offset and padding only appears at the very end, if at all. cpp include <cstddef include <iostream struct PickupWasteful { char kind; int amount; bool active; double expires; }; struct PickupTidy { double expires; // 0 int amount; // 8 char kind; // 12 bool active; // 13, then 2 bytes of tail padding }; int main() { std::cout << "wasteful: " << sizeof(PickupWasteful) << " bytes
"; std::cout << "tidy: " << sizeof(PickupTidy) << " bytes
"; std::cout << "offsets: expires " << offsetof(PickupTidy, expires) << ", amount " << offsetof(PickupTidy, amount) << ", kind " << offsetof(PickupTidy, kind) << ", active " << offsetof(PickupTidy, active) << '
'; return 0; } wasteful: 24 bytes tidy: 16 bytes offsets: expires 0, amount 8, kind 12, active 13 A third smaller for the same information. For one object it does not matter. For a game holding 100,000 pickups, particles or tiles, it is the difference between 2.4 MB and 1.6 MB, and fewer bytes means fewer trips to memory when the game loops over them every frame. !tip offsetof and the Watch window offsetof(Type, member) from <cstddef gives a member's offset in bytes. In Visual Studio you can also type &obj.member and &obj into the Watch window and subtract. Controlling alignment Sometimes you need a different layout on purpose. More alignment with alignas . Data used with wide maths instructions often has to start on a 16-byte boundary, and data shared between threads is sometimes aligned to 64 bytes so two threads never write the same cache line. cpp include <iostream struct alignas(16) Vec4 { float x, y, z, w; }; struct alignas(64) PerThreadCounter { long long value; }; int main() { std::cout << alignof(Vec4) << ' ' << sizeof(Vec4) << '
'; std::cout << alignof(PerThreadCounter) << ' ' << sizeof(PerThreadCounter) << '
'; return 0; } 16 16 64 64 Less alignment with pragma pack . File formats and network packets have exact byte layouts with no padding. pragma pack(push, 1) tells the compiler to place members one after another with no gaps. cpp include <cstdint include <iostream pragma pack(push, 1) struct SaveHeader { char magic 4 ; // "SAVE" std::uint16_t version; std::uint32_t length; }; pragma pack(pop) int main() { std::cout << sizeof(SaveHeader) << '
'; // 4 + 2 + 4, no padding return 0; } 10 Use packing only for data that has to match an outside format byte for byte. Accessing misaligned members is slower, and taking a pointer to one is dangerous because code using that pointer assumes it is aligned. Chapter 9 uses packed structs to read the headers of .exe files. Padding is not zero Padding bytes are not set to anything in particular. In a Debug build a local struct's padding shows CC ; elsewhere it holds leftovers. Two consequences: - Comparing structs with memcmp can say two equal structs differ, because their padding differs. Compare member by member, or define operator== . - Writing a struct to a file or the network as raw bytes writes the padding too, which may leak leftover memory contents and wastes space. Write members individually, or use a packed struct you fully initialise. Common mistakes !warning Adding up member sizes to get sizeof The struct also contains padding. Use sizeof , or work through the three rules. !warning Packing everything to save memory Reordering members usually saves the same space without misaligned access. Keep pragma pack for outside formats. !warning Forgetting pragma pack(pop) Without it, every struct after it in the file, including ones in headers included later, is packed too. Check yourself quiz ? State the three layout rules for a struct. + Each member starts at a multiple of its alignment; the struct's alignment is its largest member's; its size is a multiple of that - Members are sorted by size; each starts at a multiple of 8; the size is the sum of the members - Each member starts at a multiple of 4; the struct's alignment is 8; padding goes only at the end - Members are packed with no gaps; the size is rounded to 16; the alignment is the first member's Members are never reordered by the compiler. Padding can appear between members and at the end. ? How do you usually reduce a struct's padding? - Add pragma pack(1) to every struct - Declare the members in order of increasing alignment + Declare the members in order of decreasing alignment: 8-byte first, then 4, 2 and 1 - Replace every member with a char array Largest first leaves no gaps between members. pragma pack removes padding too, but makes access slower and is meant for fixed file or network layouts. ? Why should structs with padding not be compared with memcmp ? - memcmp only compares the first member + Padding bytes hold no set value, so equal structs can differ - memcmp cannot read memory that belongs to a struct - memcmp compares the addresses, not the contents Compare the members one by one (or with a defaulted operator== ) instead. ? What is the size of struct A { char c; double d; }; on x64 Windows? - 9 - 12 + 16 d needs an offset that is a multiple of 8, so 7 padding bytes follow c . 1 + 7 + 8 = 16. ? What is the alignment of struct B { char c; int i; short s; }; ? - 1 + 4 - 8 A struct's alignment is the largest alignment of its members, here the int 's 4. ? Why is struct C { int i; char c; }; 8 bytes, not 5? + Tail padding makes the size a multiple of its alignment - char takes 4 bytes inside a struct - The compiler adds a hidden pointer In an array, the second element starts right after the first. Size 8 keeps its int at a multiple of 4. ? When is pragma pack(push, 1) the right tool? - Whenever memory is tight and structs are large + When matching an outside layout, like a file header - To make access faster Packing removes padding at the cost of misaligned access. Reordering members is the usual way to save space.

title: Be the compiler's layout engine
body: Write layout(members) , which works out the layout of a struct the way the compiler does. Each member is described by its size and its alignment, in declaration order. The function returns a Layout holding the offset of every member, the struct's total size and its alignment, following the three rules from the lesson: 1. Each member starts at the next offset that is a multiple of its own alignment. 2. The struct's alignment is the largest member alignment (1 for an empty struct). 3. The size is rounded up to a multiple of the struct's alignment. For an empty list, return no offsets, alignment 1 and size 0. { {1,1}, {4,4}, {1,1}, {8,8} } - offsets 0 4 8 16, size 24, align 8 { {8,8}, {4,4}, {1,1}, {1,1} } - offsets 0 8 12 13, size 16, align 8

title: 2.06  How Structs and Classes Are Laid Out
match: 2.06 How Structs and Classes Are Laid Out
body:
A class in memory is only its data members, laid out by the alignment rules. Member functions, static members and access specifiers take no space in the object. Inheritance puts the base class's members first, and a class with virtual functions gains a hidden pointer at the front. Knowing this lets you read any object's bytes in a debugger. What is, and is not, inside an object Here is a class that looks large: cpp include <iostream include <string class Character { public: static int s_count; // one shared copy, in static storage Character(int hp, float x, float y) : m_health{ hp }, m_x{ x }, m_y{ y } { ++s_count; } void move(float dx, float dy) { m_x += dx; m_y += dy; } int health() const { return m_health; } bool alive() const { return m_health 0; } private: int m_health; float m_x; float m_y; }; int Character::s_count{ 0 }; int main() { Character hero{ 100, 2.0f, 3.5f }; hero.move(1.0f, 0.0f); std::cout << "sizeof(Character) = " << sizeof(Character) << '
'; std::cout << "characters made = " << Character::s_count << '
'; return 0; } sizeof(Character) = 12 characters made = 1 Twelve bytes: just m_health , m_x and m_y . The rest is not stored in objects at all: Part of the class Where it lives --- --- Non-static data members In every object, laid out by the rules of lesson 2.05 Member functions Once, in the program's .text section, like any function static data members Once, in static storage (lesson 2.03) public , private , protected Nowhere. They are checked by the compiler and leave no trace in the program How does move know which object to change, then? It receives the object's address as a hidden first argument called this . hero.move(1.0f, 0.0f) compiles to roughly Character::move(&hero, 1.0f, 0.0f) , and inside, m_x means this- m_x : "the float 4 bytes after the address in this ". On x64 Windows, this arrives in rcx like any first argument. You will see this in chapter 7. struct and class are the same thing The only difference between struct and class is the default access: public for struct , private for class . Their layout rules are identical. This course uses struct for plain bundles of data and class for types that guard their data, but the memory looks the same. Inheritance: the base comes first A derived class contains a complete copy of its base class's members, called the base subobject , at the start, followed by its own members. cpp include <cstdint include <iostream struct Entity { int id; float x, y; }; struct Monster : Entity { int health; std::uint8_t level; }; template <typename T, typename M std::ptrdiff_t offsetIn(const T& object, const M& member) { return reinterpret_cast<const char (&member) - reinterpret_cast<const char (&object); } int main() { Monster m{}; std::cout << "id " << offsetIn(m, m.id) << '
'; std::cout << "x " << offsetIn(m, m.x) << '
'; std::cout << "y " << offsetIn(m, m.y) << '
'; std::cout << "health " << offsetIn(m, m.health) << '
'; std::cout << "level " << offsetIn(m, m.level) << '
'; std::cout << "size " << sizeof(Monster) << '
'; Entity asEntity{ &m }; // a Monster converts to an Entity with no adjustment std::cout << "same address: " << (static_cast<void (asEntity) == static_cast<void (&m)) << '
'; return 0; } id 0 x 4 y 8 health 12 level 16 size 20 same address: 1 Because the Entity part sits at offset 0, a Monster and the Entity made from it hold the same address. Code that only knows about Entity can work with a Monster without knowing anything else about it. That is what makes inheritance-based designs work at the machine level. With multiple inheritance , each base gets its own region, one after the other. Converting to the second base then changes the address: the compiler adds that base's offset. It is one reason game code tends to avoid deep or multiple inheritance. Virtual functions add a hidden pointer As soon as a class has a virtual function, every object of it carries one extra hidden member: a pointer, called the vptr , at offset 0. It points to a table of function addresses for that object's actual type, the vtable . Lesson 3.05 is about exactly this; for now, watch the size change: cpp include <iostream struct Plain { int health; void hurt(int n) { health -= n; } }; struct WithVirtual { int health; virtual void hurt(int n) { health -= n; } virtual ~WithVirtual() = default; }; int main() { std::cout << sizeof(Plain) << ' ' << sizeof(WithVirtual) << '
'; return 0; } 4 16 Eight bytes for the vptr, then the int , then 4 bytes of tail padding to keep the size a multiple of 8. If you look at an object of a class with virtual functions in the Memory window, its first 8 bytes always look like an address inside the program's image: that is the vptr. Empty classes A class with no data members still has sizeof 1, because every object must have a distinct address. But when an empty class is used as a base , the compiler may give it no space at all (the empty base optimisation ). Since C++20, the attribute no_unique_address (spelled msvc::no_unique_address for MSVC) lets an empty member take no space either. Reading an object in the debugger Put it together and you can decode objects by hand. Suppose a Monster from above shows this in the Memory window: 07 00 00 00 00 00 20 41 00 00 a0 c0 3c 00 00 00 05 cc cc cc Bytes Member Value --- --- --- 07 00 00 00 id 7 00 00 20 41 x 10.0 (the bit pattern of a float ; lesson 2.11) 00 00 a0 c0 y −5.0 3c 00 00 00 health 60 05 level 5 cc cc cc tail padding (Debug fill) This is the core skill behind using memory views, and later behind chapter 9's work of reconstructing the layout of a type from compiled code. Common mistakes !warning Thinking member functions make objects bigger They do not. Only data members (and a vptr, if there are virtual functions) take space. !warning Assuming private members are protected at run time Access control is a compile-time rule. In memory, private members are bytes like any others. !warning Writing an object with virtual functions to a file Its first 8 bytes are a pointer that will be wrong the next time the program runs. Save the data members, not the raw object. Check yourself quiz ? Which parts of a class take up space in each object? - Data members, member functions and static members + Non-static data members, padding, and a vptr if it has virtuals - Only public data members - Data members and one pointer to each member function Member functions are code, stored once; static members live in static storage; access specifiers cost nothing. ? Why can a Monster be used as an Entity without changing the address? + With single inheritance the Entity subobject is at offset 0 of the Monster - The compiler copies the Monster into a new Entity object - Every pointer to a class points at its vtable, which is shared - Pointers to classes do not hold addresses, only type names The base comes first in the derived object's layout, so both pointers hold the same address. ? What is this ? - A global pointer to the object created most recently - The vtable pointer stored at the start of every object - A copy of the object passed to each member function + A hidden argument holding the address of the object called on On x64 Windows it arrives in the first argument register, rcx . It is a pointer, not a copy. ? A class has three int members, ten member functions and a static int . What is its sizeof ? - 16 - 56 + 12 Only the non-static data members are stored in each object. ? Where does a derived class's base subobject go? + At the start of the derived object, at offset 0 - At the end of the derived object - In a separate heap block The base's members come first, so a pointer to the derived object is also a valid pointer to its base. ? Why is sizeof(WithVirtual) 16 when its only data member is an int ? - virtual doubles the size of every member + A hidden 8-byte vptr is added, and the size is padded to 16 - Virtual functions are stored inside the object The vptr points to the class's table of virtual functions. The functions themselves are in the code section. ? How does a member function know which object it is working on? - Each object stores a copy of its functions + The object's address is passed as a hidden argument, this - It looks the object up in a global list obj.f(x) is compiled much like f(&obj, x) .

title: Save a player as bytes
where: 2.06 How Structs and Classes Are Laid Out
body: Writing a struct to a file as raw memory would include its padding (leftover bytes) and depend on the compiler's layout. Save files are written member by member instead, in a fixed format. Write savePlayer(p) , which returns the bytes of a Player in this exact format, with no padding, all numbers little-endian: Bytes Field --- --- 0 to 3 id , a std::uint32_t 4 to 5 health , a std::int16_t 6 level , a std::uint8_t 7 to 10 gold , a std::uint32_t So every saved player is exactly 11 bytes, even though sizeof(Player) is 12. Then write loadPlayer(bytes) , which reads the same format back.

title: 2.07  Arrays and Multi-Dimensional Data in Memory
match: 2.07 Arrays and Multi-Dimensional Data in Memory
body:
An array is the simplest data structure there is: elements side by side, with no gaps and no bookkeeping. Element i is at the start address plus i times the element size. Two-dimensional data such as a tile map is stored the same way, one row after another. This lesson shows the arithmetic, why the order you loop in matters for speed, and how games store grids. Side by side, nothing else cpp include <iostream int main() { int scores 5 { 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 }; std::cout << "sizeof(scores) = " << sizeof(scores) << '
'; for (int i{ 0 }; i < 5; ++i) std::cout << "scores " << i << " is " << (reinterpret_cast<char (&scores i ) - reinterpret_cast<char (&scores 0 )) << " bytes from the start
"; return 0; } sizeof(scores) = 20 scores 0 is 0 bytes from the start scores 1 is 4 bytes from the start scores 2 is 8 bytes from the start scores 3 is 12 bytes from the start scores 4 is 16 bytes from the start Twenty bytes for five 4-byte int s: an array holds nothing but its elements. It does not store its own length, and nothing at run time stops you reading scores 5 or scores -1 . The compiler turns scores i into exactly the arithmetic from lesson 1.03: address of scores i = address of scores 0 + i × sizeof(int) That is a multiplication and an addition, which is why indexing an array is as fast as memory access gets. Arrays of structs The same rule holds for any element type. An array of Pickup from lesson 2.05 places each struct right after the previous one, padding included, which is exactly why a struct's size is rounded up: so that pickups 1 starts properly aligned. pickups 0 pickups 1 pickups 2 ┌──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┬────────── │ 24 bytes │ 24 bytes │ ... └──────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────┴────────── +0 +24 +48 std::array<T, N is a plain array wrapped in a struct: same bytes, but it knows its size, can be copied and returned, and checks bounds in Debug builds with .at() . std::vector<T keeps its elements in exactly the same side-by-side form, in a heap block (lesson 3.07). Everything in this lesson applies to all three. Two dimensions: rows one after another Memory is one-dimensional. A grid has to be flattened. C++ stores a two-dimensional array row by row (called row-major order ): all of row 0, then all of row 1, and so on. cpp include <iostream int main() { char map 3 4 { { ' ', ' ', ' ', ' ' }, { ' ', '.', '.', ' ' }, { ' ', ' ', ' ', ' ' }, }; const char flat{ &map 0 0 }; for (int i{ 0 }; i < 12; ++i) std::cout << flat i ; std::cout << '
'; std::cout << "map 1 2 is element " << (&map 1 2 - flat) << " of the flat run
"; return 0; } .. map 1 2 is element 6 of the flat run The formula, with width the number of columns: index of (row, column) = row × width + column Games almost always store maps this way on purpose, as one flat std::vector of size width × height , with a small function for the index. The size can then be chosen at run time, the whole map is one allocation, and saving it is one write. cpp include <iostream include <vector struct TileMap { int width{ 0 }; int height{ 0 }; std::vector<char tiles; TileMap(int w, int h, char fill) : width{ w }, height{ h }, tiles(static_cast<std::size_t (w h), fill) {} char& at(int x, int y) { return tiles static_cast<std::size_t (y width + x) ; } bool inside(int x, int y) const { return x = 0 && y = 0 && x < width && y < height; } }; int main() { TileMap map{ 6, 3, '.' }; map.at(0, 0) = '@'; map.at(5, 2) = ' '; for (int y{ 0 }; y < map.height; ++y) { for (int x{ 0 }; x < map.width; ++x) std::cout << map.at(x, y); std::cout << '
'; } return 0; } @..... ...... ..... Notice (x, y) in the interface and y width + x inside: x is the column, y the row. Mixing these up is the most common grid bug there is. Loop order and the cache The processor does not fetch single bytes from main memory. It fetches 64-byte blocks, called cache lines , and keeps recently used ones in small, very fast memories called caches . Reading the next byte along is almost free, because it arrived with the line. Jumping far away means waiting for a new line, which can take a hundred times longer than a cache hit. So the order in which you visit a grid matters: cpp // Fast: walks memory in order, using every byte of each cache line. for (int y{ 0 }; y < height; ++y) for (int x{ 0 }; x < width; ++x) total += map.at(x, y); // Slow for big maps: jumps a whole row ahead every step. for (int x{ 0 }; x < width; ++x) for (int y{ 0 }; y < height; ++y) total += map.at(x, y); Both visit every tile once and give the same answer. On a 4000 × 4000 map, the first is typically several times faster. The rule: make the innermost loop walk along the last index , so it moves through memory in order. Chapter 17 measures effects like this properly. Arrays decay to pointers Passing a plain array to a function passes only the address of its first element. The size is lost: cpp void printAll(int scores ) // really: int scores { // sizeof(scores) here is 8, the size of a pointer, not of the array. } That is the root of many overruns: the function has no idea where the array ends. Pass a std::span<int (C++20), which carries the pointer and the length together, or pass a std::vector or std::array by reference. Common mistakes !warning Swapping x and y With y width + x , x must be less than width and y less than height . Writing x width + y works only for square maps and scrambles everything else. !warning Off-by-one at the edges A map width wide has columns 0 to width - 1 . Looking at a neighbour at x + 1 from the last column reads into the next row, not off the map. Check with an inside function first. !warning Looping column by column over big grids Put the row loop outside and the column loop inside. !warning Expecting a function to know an array's size A plain array passed to a function becomes a pointer. Use std::span , std::array or std::vector . Check yourself quiz ? How is the address of a i worked out? + The address of a 0 plus i times the size of one element - The address of a 0 plus i bytes - The address of a 0 plus i times 8, the size of an address - The address of a i-1 looked up in a table Array elements sit side by side with nothing between them, so the arithmetic is all it takes. ? What does row-major order mean? - Each column is stored one after another, so (row, column) is at column × height + row + Each complete row is stored after the previous one, so (row, column) is at row × width + column - The rows are stored in separate blocks reached through pointers - The largest rows are stored first Built-in two-dimensional arrays in C++ are row-major. Column × height + row would be column-major, the other order. ? Why does loop order affect speed over a big grid? - Inner loops over columns are compiled into fewer instructions - Walking down a column skips padding bytes + Rows use each 64-byte cache line fully; columns fetch a new line each step - The CPU can only prefetch memory in a backwards direction Same number of elements, very different number of cache-line fetches. Make the inner loop walk along rows for a row-major grid. ? An array of double starts at address 0x1000 . Where is element 3? - 0x1003 - 0x100C + 0x1018 3 × 8 bytes = 24 = 0x18 , so element 3 is at 0x1000 + 0x18 . ? A tile map is 10 wide and stored row-major. Which index holds the tile at x = 3, y = 2? - 32 + 23 - 5 2 × 10 + 3 = 23. ? Which loop order is faster for a large row-major grid? - Columns in the outer loop, rows in the inner loop - Both are always the same speed + Rows in the outer loop, columns in the inner loop The inner loop should walk through memory in order, so each cache line fetched is fully used. ? Inside void f(int a ) , what is sizeof(a) on x64? - The size of the whole array + 8, the size of a pointer - 4, the size of one int An array parameter is really a pointer. The length is not passed.

title: Count the neighbours
where: 2.07 Arrays and Multi-Dimensional Data in Memory
body: A tile map is stored as one flat string, row after row, width tiles per row. Write countAround(tiles, width, x, y, wanted) . It returns how many of the eight tiles around (x, y) equal wanted . Tiles outside the map do not count, and the tile at (x, y) itself does not count. tiles = " . " "..." " . " (stored as " . ... . ", width 3) countAround(tiles, 3, 1, 1, ' ') = 4 countAround(tiles, 3, 0, 0, '.') = 3 The number of rows is tiles.size() / width .

title: 2.08  Strings in Memory: C Strings, std::string and Encodings
match: 2.08 Strings in Memory: C Strings, std::string and Encodings
body:
Text in memory is a run of numbers, one or more per character. A C string is a char array ending in a zero byte. std::string keeps its own length and stores short text inside the object itself. And which numbers stand for which characters depends on the encoding : ASCII, UTF-8, or the UTF-16 that Windows uses internally. Characters are numbers A char is a one-byte number. When text is printed, each number is looked up in a table to find the character to draw. The original table is ASCII , which covers English letters, digits and punctuation in the values 0 to 127: Character Decimal Hex --- --- --- '0' to '9' 48 to 57 0x30 to 0x39 'A' to 'Z' 65 to 90 0x41 to 0x5A 'a' to 'z' 97 to 122 0x61 to 0x7A space 32 0x20 newline '
' 10 0x0A the terminator '\0' 0 0x00 A few patterns are worth knowing because they turn up in code all the time: '7' - '0' is 7, which converts a digit character to its value; and upper and lower case letters differ by exactly 32 ( 0x20 ), a single bit. cpp include <iostream int main() { const char digit{ '7' }; std::cout << digit - '0' << '
'; // 55 - 48 std::cout << static_cast<char ('g' - 32) << '
'; // lower to upper case std::cout << static_cast<int ('A') << ' ' << static_cast<int ('a') << '
'; return 0; } 7 G 65 97 C strings: up to the zero C, and the Windows API, represent text as a C string : a pointer to the first character of a char array, with the end marked by a byte holding 0. Nothing records the length; functions like strlen find it by walking along until they reach the zero. cpp include <cstring include <iostream int main() { const char name { "Rook" }; // 5 bytes: R o o k \0 std::cout << sizeof(name) << ' ' << std::strlen(name) << '
'; for (unsigned char c : name) std::cout << std::hex << static_cast<int (c) << ' '; std::cout << '
'; return 0; } 5 4 52 6f 6f 6b 0 sizeof counts the array, terminator included. strlen counts the characters before it. The difference of one is behind countless bugs: - Copying a 10-character name into a char 10 leaves no room for the terminator. The next function to read it walks off the end until it happens to find a zero. - Forgetting the terminator at all, for example after copying bytes with memcpy , has the same effect. - strcpy and strcat write until they hit the source's terminator, however small the destination. They are a classic source of buffer overruns, which is why MSVC warns about them and offers strcpy_s and friends, which take the destination size. std::string: length, capacity and a small buffer std::string fixes these problems by storing the length itself and managing its memory. On 64-bit MSVC a std::string object is 32 bytes in a Release build: std::string (Release x64, 32 bytes) ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐ │ 16 bytes: either the characters │ short text lives right here │ themselves (up to 15), or │ │ a pointer to a heap block │ long text lives on the heap ├──────────────────────────────────────┤ │ 8 bytes: size (characters in use) │ ├──────────────────────────────────────┤ │ 8 bytes: capacity (room available) │ └──────────────────────────────────────┘ (Debug builds add 8 more bytes for iterator checking, so sizeof differs between configurations.) The interesting part is the small string optimisation (SSO) . Strings of up to 15 characters are stored directly inside the object, with no heap allocation at all. Longer strings get a heap block, and the first 8 of those 16 bytes hold a pointer to it. cpp include <iostream include <string int main() { std::string shortName{ "Rook" }; std::string longName{ "Rook the Unbreakable of the Northern Wastes" }; std::cout << shortName.size() << " chars, capacity " << shortName.capacity() << '
'; std::cout << longName.size() << " chars, capacity " << longName.capacity() << '
'; const auto object{ reinterpret_cast<const char (&shortName) }; const char text{ shortName.data() }; std::cout << "short text is inside the object: " << (text = object && text < object + sizeof(shortName)) << '
'; return 0; } 4 chars, capacity 15 43 chars, capacity 47 short text is inside the object: 1 For games this matters: short names, tags and keys cost no allocation, and long text does. A std::string still keeps a zero after its characters, so c_str() can hand it straight to C-style functions. std::string_view is a pointer and a length, 16 bytes, with no ownership. It is ideal for passing text to a function that only reads it, provided the text outlives the view (lesson 2.04). Encodings: beyond ASCII ASCII has no room for é , ß , Ж , 日 or emoji. Modern text uses Unicode , which gives every character a number called a code point ( é is U+00E9, 日 is U+65E5). An encoding decides how those numbers become bytes. Encoding Unit ASCII text Used by --- --- --- --- UTF-8 1 to 4 bytes per character Identical to ASCII Files, the web, most libraries, Linux UTF-16 2 or 4 bytes per character Every character takes 2 bytes Windows internally, wchar_t on Windows cpp include <iostream include <string int main() { std::string utf8{ "caf\xC3\xA9" }; // "café" in UTF-8: é is two bytes std::wstring utf16{ L"café" }; // the same text in UTF-16 std::cout << "UTF-8 bytes: " << utf8.size() << '
'; std::cout << "UTF-16 units: " << utf16.size() << " (" << utf16.size() sizeof(wchar_t) << " bytes)
"; std::cout << "sizeof(wchar_t) = " << sizeof(wchar_t) << '
'; return 0; } UTF-8 bytes: 5 UTF-16 units: 4 (8 bytes) sizeof(wchar_t) = 2 Two consequences for low-level work: - size() is not the number of characters once text is not plain ASCII. "café" is 4 characters but 5 UTF-8 bytes. - In memory, UTF-16 text looks spaced out. L"Rook" is 52 00 6F 00 6F 00 6B 00 00 00 : every ASCII letter followed by a zero byte. When you search memory for text, search for both forms. Visual Studio's Memory window can show bytes as ANSI or Unicode text; right-click to switch. Chapter 5 deals with the Windows side: most Windows API functions come in an A version taking narrow strings and a W version taking UTF-16, and the course uses the W versions with conversions at the edges. Common mistakes !warning Forgetting room for the terminator A C string of n characters needs n + 1 bytes. !warning Using strcpy into a fixed buffer Use std::string , or strcpy_s / strncpy_s with the destination size, and make sure the result is terminated. !warning Treating size() as a character count It counts bytes (or UTF-16 units). For player-facing text, use a Unicode-aware library when the count matters. !warning Keeping c_str() after changing the string Appending can move the characters to a new heap block, or out of the small buffer. Get the pointer again after any change. Check yourself quiz ? How does strlen find the length of a C string? - It reads the length stored in the byte before the first character - It asks the heap how large the block is + It walks along from the first character, counting, until it finds the zero byte A C string stores no length; that is why strlen costs time proportional to the string and why a missing zero byte runs off the end. ? What is the small string optimisation? - Compressing short strings so they take fewer bytes - Sharing one copy of identical short strings between all std::string s - Storing short strings in .rdata instead of on the heap + Storing short strings directly inside the std::string object, so they need no heap allocation On MSVC, strings of up to 15 characters fit in the object's own buffer. ? What is the difference between UTF-8 and UTF-16? - UTF-8 covers only English characters; UTF-16 covers all of Unicode + Both cover Unicode; UTF-8 uses 1-4 bytes, UTF-16 uses 2 or 4 - UTF-8 is always 8 bytes per character; UTF-16 is always 16 - UTF-16 is the encoding of char ; UTF-8 is the encoding of wchar_t Both cover all of Unicode. On Windows, wchar_t strings are UTF-16. UTF-8 matches ASCII for English text; Windows uses UTF-16 internally. ? How many bytes does char word { "Lava" }; occupy? - 4 + 5 - 8 Four characters plus the terminating zero byte. ? On 64-bit MSVC, which of these strings is stored inside the std::string object with no heap allocation? - "The Goblin King of the Eastern Mountains" - Neither: std::string always uses the heap + "Goblin" Up to 15 characters fit in the small buffer. ? In memory you see 48 00 50 00 00 00 . What is most likely there? - Two large numbers + The UTF-16 string "HP" - The UTF-8 string "HP" 0x48 is H , 0x50 is P ; the zero byte after each is the high half of a 2-byte UTF-16 unit, and 00 00 ends it. ? What does '5' - '0' evaluate to? - 53 + 5 - '5' Digits are consecutive in ASCII, so subtracting '0' gives the digit's value.

title: A safe name copy
where: 2.08 Strings in Memory: C Strings, std::string and Encodings
body: An old part of a game keeps player names in fixed char buffers. Write copyName(dest, destSize, src) , a safe version of strcpy : - It copies the C string src into the buffer dest , which has room for destSize bytes. - If src is too long, it copies as many characters as fit and still ends dest with a zero byte . - It never writes more than destSize bytes. - It returns the number of characters copied, not counting the terminator. - If destSize is 0 it writes nothing and returns 0. char buf 5 ; copyName(buf, 5, "Rook") - 4, buf holds "Rook" copyName(buf, 5, "Grimbold") - 4, buf holds "Grim" Write the loop yourself: library string functions are not allowed here.

title: 2.09  Memory Bugs: Overruns, Dangling Pointers and Leaks
match: 2.09 Memory Bugs: Overruns, Dangling Pointers and Leaks
body: Memory bugs are the hardest bugs in C++ because the symptom often appears far from the cause, or only sometimes. This lesson names the main kinds ( buffer overruns , use after free , double free , uninitialised reads and leaks ), shows what each one looks like when it strikes, and gives the habits that prevent them. Why these bugs are different Most bugs are wrong logic: the code does what it says, and what it says is wrong. Memory bugs are worse. The code breaks one of the language's rules, the behaviour becomes undefined , and anything can happen: - it works perfectly, every time you test it; - it works in Debug and crashes in Release; - it crashes, but somewhere else entirely, minutes later; - it quietly changes a different variable, and the game misbehaves in a way that seems impossible. That last one is the nastiest. A write past the end of one array changes whatever happens to sit next to it in memory, which might be a player's health, a pointer, or the allocator's own bookkeeping. You will see these effects in this course's tools, so it is worth knowing their shapes. 1. Buffer overrun Writing (or reading) past the end of an array or buffer. cpp struct Player { char name 8 ; int gold; }; void rename(Player& p, const char newName) { int i{ 0 }; while (newName i != '\0') { p.name i = newName i ; ++i; } // no limit! p.name i = '\0'; } // rename(p, "Maximilian") writes 11 bytes into an 8-byte array. // The extra bytes land in gold, which suddenly holds 28,257 if it was 0: the bytes 61 6E 00 are "an" and its terminator. The program does not crash. The player's gold changes to a nonsense number, and nobody looking at the gold code will ever find out why. Off-by-one loops ( <= instead of < ) are the most common cause; unchecked copies like this one are the most dangerous, because the length comes from outside. Prevention: use containers that know their size ( std::string , std::vector , std::array , std::span ), use .at() or Debug iterator checks while developing, and never copy data whose length you have not checked against the destination. 2. Use after free Using memory through a pointer after it has been freed. cpp Enemy target{ findNearestEnemy() }; removeDeadEnemies(); // deletes target's Enemy, among others target- health -= 10; // writes into freed memory If the freed block has been handed out again, the write corrupts whatever now lives there. If not, it may seem to work. In a Debug build the freed block is filled with DD , so reading it gives obviously wrong values like -572662307 ( 0xDDDDDDDD ). Prevention: be clear about who owns each object. Use std::unique_ptr for ownership; refer to objects that can disappear by id or handle and look them up each time, instead of keeping raw pointers to them. Lesson 3.10 builds exactly such a system for game entities. 3. Dangling pointers and references The general form of use after free: a pointer or reference that outlives what it refers to. Lesson 2.04 showed the common shapes: a pointer to a local that has returned, a view of a temporary string, a reference into a vector that has since grown. Prevention: return values, not pointers to locals; do not store views or pointers into containers that might change; prefer indices into a vector over pointers to its elements. 4. Double free Freeing the same block twice. cpp Texture t{ new Texture{} }; cache.add(t); // the cache will delete it when cleared... delete t; // ...and so does this code The allocator's bookkeeping is corrupted. The Debug runtime usually stops the program on the second delete ; a Release build may crash much later, inside an unrelated allocation. Prevention: one owner per object. Smart pointers make ownership visible in the type: a std::unique_ptr cannot be copied, so two owners cannot both think they should free it. 5. Uninitialised reads Reading a variable before giving it a value. cpp int damage; // no initialiser if (critical) damage = 50; health -= damage; // garbage when critical is false In Debug, the garbage is 0xCCCCCCCC (-858993460), which at least looks wrong. In Release it is whatever was on the stack, which is often a plausible-looking number, so the bug hides. Prevention: always initialise, with braces: int damage{ 0 }; . Turn on warning level 4: MSVC warns about many uninitialised uses (C4700, C4701). 6. Leaks Memory that is allocated and never freed. Leaks do not corrupt anything; they just make the process grow until it runs out of memory or slows the machine down. cpp void spawnWave() { for (int i{ 0 }; i < 20; ++i) { Monster m{ new Monster{} }; if (!placeOnMap(m)) continue; // leaked: nobody will ever delete m world.add(m); } } Prevention: never write new without immediately handing the result to an owner ( std::make_unique , a container). Then early return s, continue s and exceptions cannot leak. The Debug runtime can list leaks when the program exits: call _CrtSetDbgFlag(_CRTDBG_ALLOC_MEM_DF _CRTDBG_LEAK_CHECK_DF) at the start of main , and Visual Studio's Output window shows every block still allocated at the end, with its size and contents. A summary table Bug Typical symptom Debug-build clue --- --- --- Buffer overrun Neighbouring data changes; heap corruption message on delete FD guard bytes changed Use after free Strange values, or corruption elsewhere Values like 0xDDDDDDDD Double free Crash in delete or a later allocation Debug assertion in the heap Uninitialised read Random behaviour, different in Release Values like 0xCCCCCCCC or 0xCDCDCDCD Leak Memory use grows over time Leak report at exit Debugging a memory bug When something changes that should not: 1. Make it repeatable. Find inputs that trigger it every time. 2. Find what changed. Use a data breakpoint (lesson 4.09) on the variable that goes wrong: the debugger stops on the exact instruction that writes it, and the Call Stack shows who did it. 3. Run a sanitizer. AddressSanitizer, in the next lesson, catches overruns and use after free at the moment they happen, with the line numbers of the allocation, the free and the bad access. Common mistakes !warning "It works on my machine" Undefined behaviour may happen to work in one build and not another. Code that only works by luck is not working. !warning Fixing the symptom Adding a check where the corrupted value is used hides the problem. Find the write that caused it. !warning Raw new in game code Every raw new is a potential leak, double free or dangling pointer. Prefer containers and smart pointers. Check yourself quiz ? Why are memory bugs harder to find than logic bugs? + The symptom often appears far from the cause, and only sometimes - They only happen in Release builds - The compiler hides them by optimising the code away - They always crash at once, so there is no state left to inspect The bad write lands on some unrelated value, which only misbehaves when it is used later. That is why watching the corrupted variable with a data breakpoint helps. ? What is the difference between a dangling pointer and a leak? + A dangling pointer refers to memory that was freed or whose object ended; a leak is memory still allocated that nothing will free - A dangling pointer is a null pointer; a leak is a pointer that was never initialised - They are the same bug seen from two sides - A leak crashes at once; a dangling pointer never causes harm They are opposites: one keeps a reference without memory, the other keeps memory without a reference. ? How do ids or handles help avoid use-after-free bugs? - They lock the object so it cannot be destroyed - They make the object's memory read-only after it is freed + Code looks the object up by id, and a lookup of a gone object fails - They are smart pointers that free the object automatically Instead of holding a pointer that can dangle, code asks "is object 42 still there?" each time and gets a clear answer. ? A player's gold changes to a huge random number right after they rename their character. What kind of bug is most likely? - A memory leak in the renaming code - A double free of the old name + A buffer overrun from the name into the gold The name copy wrote past the end of its array into the next member. ? In a Debug build a variable reads -572662307 ( 0xDDDDDDDD ). What does that point to? - An uninitialised local + Use of heap memory after it was freed - An integer overflow The Debug heap fills freed blocks with DD . ? Which habit prevents leaks from early returns and exceptions? - Calling delete at the end of every function + Giving every allocation an owner such as std::unique_ptr - Using malloc instead of new Owners free memory in their destructors, which run on every path out of the scope. ? What is the best tool for finding which instruction changes a variable unexpectedly? - More std::cout lines + A data breakpoint on that variable's address - Rebuilding in Release A data breakpoint stops the program on the exact write, with the call stack showing who made it.

title: Plug the leak
where: 2.09 Memory Bugs: Overruns, Dangling Pointers and Leaks
body: spawnWave(count, blocked) creates count monsters and returns the ones that could be placed. A monster is placed unless its index appears in blocked . Monsters that cannot be placed are thrown away. It gives the right answers, but every monster that cannot be placed is leaked. The tests check for leaks. Fix it so that nothing leaks, and keep it returning a std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Monster .

title: 2.10  Catching Memory Bugs with AddressSanitizer
body: AddressSanitizer (ASan) is a compiler feature that adds a check to every memory access. It stops the program at the exact moment of a buffer overrun or use after free, and prints where the memory was allocated, where it was freed and where it was misused. Visual Studio supports it with one switch. This lesson shows how it works and how to read its reports. The idea The previous lesson's bugs are hard because nothing happens at the moment of the mistake. A Debug build's patterns help after the fact; AddressSanitizer catches the mistake as it happens . When you compile with ASan, the compiler adds a small check before every load and store. The check asks: "is the address about to be touched part of a live object?" If not, the program stops immediately with a report. To answer that question quickly, ASan keeps shadow memory : for every 8 bytes of the program's memory, one byte of shadow says how many of those 8 are valid to use. Around every heap block, stack array and global it places red zones , bytes marked as forbidden. Freed heap blocks are marked forbidden too, and held back for a while before being reused, so a late use of one is still caught. heap block of 10 bytes, as ASan sees it ┌────────┬──────────┬──┬──────────────────┐ │ red │ 10 bytes │ │ red zone │ │ zone │ usable │6 │ (forbidden) │ └────────┴──────────┴──┴──────────────────┘ ▲ bytes 10..15: forbidden, though in the same 8-byte group The checks make a program about twice as slow and use more memory. That is fine for testing, and ASan builds are not meant for shipping. Turning it on in Visual Studio 1. Install the C++ AddressSanitizer component (lesson 1.07 ticked it). 2. Project Properties → C/C++ → General → Enable Address Sanitizer: Yes ( /fsanitize=address ). 3. In the same properties, under C/C++ → General , set Debug Information Format to Program Database (/Zi) if it is not already, and turn Edit and Continue off; ASan is not compatible with it. 4. Build and run under the debugger (F5). When ASan finds an error, the debugger stops on the bad line and the Output window shows the report. Reading a report: heap buffer overflow cpp-norun include <iostream int main() { int scores{ new int 4 { 10, 20, 30, 40 } }; int total{ 0 }; for (int i{ 0 }; i <= 4; ++i) // <= is one too many total += scores i ; std::cout << total << '\n'; delete scores; return 0; } Without ASan this usually prints a wrong total and carries on. With ASan it stops on the fifth read: ==14260==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow on address 0x11b5c0420040 READ of size 4 at 0x11b5c0420040 thread T0 0 0x7ff6d4e81103 in main C:\code\scores\main.cpp:8 1 0x7ff6d4e8b4e8 in invoke_main exe_common.inl:78 ... 0x11b5c0420040 is located 0 bytes to the right of 16-byte region 0x11b5c0420030,0x11b5c0420040) allocated by thread T0 here: 0 0x7ffe4c0d8d5b in operator new ... 1 0x7ff6d4e81069 in main C:\code\scores\main.cpp:5 Read it from the top: Line What it tells you --- --- heap-buffer-overflow The kind of bug: past the end of a heap block READ of size 4 An int was read (a write would say WRITE) 0 ... main.cpp:8 The exact line that did it: total += scores i ; 0 bytes to the right of 16-byte region It touched the byte just after a 16-byte block, which is 4 int s allocated by ... main.cpp:5 Where that block came from: the new int 4 That is the whole investigation done for you: what went wrong, where, and with which block. Reading a report: use after free cpp-norun include <iostream include <vector int main() { std::vector<int health{ 100, 80 }; int& first{ health 0 }; health.push_back(60); // reallocates: first now refers to freed memory first -= 10; std::cout << health 0 << '\n'; return 0; } ASan reports heap-use-after-free , with three stacks: where the bad access happened ( first -= 10 ), where the memory was freed (inside push_back , called from your line), and where it was originally allocated (the vector's constructor). That third-party "freed inside push_back " line is exactly the clue that points at iterator and reference invalidation from lesson 2.04. What ASan catches, and what it does not Catches Does not catch --- --- Heap buffer overflow and underflow Reading uninitialised memory Stack buffer overflow Leaks, on Windows (use the CRT leak report) Global buffer overflow Overruns that stay inside the same object, such as from one struct member into the next Use after free Logic errors Use after return or scope (with extra options) Data races between threads Double free, mismatched new / delete The "same object" row deserves attention: the Player::name overrun in lesson 2.09 writes into gold , which is part of the same struct. Both are inside one live object, so ASan sees nothing wrong. Prevention there is still std::string and bounds checks. Using it well - Run your tests and a play session under ASan regularly , not only when something breaks. Bugs that have not caused a crash yet are the cheapest to fix. - Fix the first report first. One overrun can cause later, confusing reports. - Keep a separate configuration. In Configuration Manager, copy Debug to a new configuration called ASan with the option on, so normal debugging stays fast. - Third-party code may need to be rebuilt with ASan, or its errors may show up inside your program's reports. Common mistakes !warning Shipping an ASan build It is slower and depends on the ASan runtime DLL. ASan is for testing only. !warning Mixing ASan and Edit and Continue Visual Studio refuses to build with both. Switch Edit and Continue off for the ASan configuration. !warning Assuming no report means no memory bugs ASan only checks code paths that actually ran, and it misses overruns within one object. It finds a lot; it does not prove correctness. Check yourself quiz ? How does AddressSanitizer know an access is invalid? - It compares each pointer with the list of variables in the .pdb - It runs the program twice and compares the results - It asks the operating system to protect every page after each allocation + It checks shadow memory, which marks red zones and freed memory, on every access The compiler inserts the shadow check before each memory access, which is why ASan needs a rebuild and slows the program down. ? What three locations can an ASan use-after-free report give you? - The file name, the line number and the column of the bad access + Where the bad access happened, where the memory was freed, and where it was originally allocated - The address of the stack, the heap and the program image - The function that leaked, the function that freed and main Each comes with a call stack, so you can see the whole story of the block. ? Why keep a separate ASan build configuration? - ASan only works with Release builds - ASan changes the program's behaviour so tests cannot be trusted + ASan is slow and clashes with some options, such as Edit and Continue - Visual Studio only allows ASan in a configuration named "ASan" Normal debugging stays fast, and the ASan build is run regularly to catch memory bugs. ? When does AddressSanitizer report a buffer overrun? + At the moment the bad read or write happens - When the program exits - When the corrupted value is next used Every access is checked as it happens, which is what makes ASan so much more useful than finding the damage later. ? A report says "0 bytes to the right of 16-byte region". What happened? - The code read a 16-byte value + The code touched the byte just after a 16-byte block - 16 bytes leaked "To the right" means past the end; "0 bytes" means immediately after it. ? Which of these does ASan not catch? - Use after free of a heap block - Heap buffer overflow past a block + An overrun between members of one struct Both members belong to one live object, so the access is to valid memory as far as ASan can tell. ? What is shadow memory? - A copy of the program kept for debugging + Where ASan records which bytes are valid to use - Memory used by the GPU One shadow byte describes eight bytes of real memory.

title: 2.11  Reading the Memory Window in Visual Studio
match: 2.11 Reading the Memory Window in Visual Studio
body: The Memory window shows raw bytes, and this chapter has given you everything you need to read them. This lesson puts it together: setting the window's display, recognising pointers, Debug patterns, text and floating-point numbers at a glance, and decoding a whole object by hand. Setting the window up Open it while paused: Debug → Windows → Memory → Memory 1 (Visual Studio has four, so you can keep several places open). The useful controls: Control What it does --- --- Address box Type any expression that gives an address: &hero , ptr , names.data() , 0x00000052A3CFF7A8 , rsp . Press Enter. Reevaluate automatically (the circular arrows) Keeps following the expression as you step: useful for a pointer that changes. Columns How many units per row. Set it to 16 bytes, or to 8 when looking at pointers. Right-click → 1-, 2-, 4- or 8-byte integer Groups bytes into numbers, already put back into the right order for little-endian. Right-click → 32-bit or 64-bit floating point Shows each group as a float or double . Right-click → Signed / Unsigned / Hexadecimal display How the numbers are written. Right-click → ANSI / Unicode text (the column on the right) Shows the bytes as one-byte or UTF-16 characters. You can also drag a variable from the code editor or Locals window into the Memory window to jump to its address. Recognising what you are looking at With practice you can tell what a group of bytes is from its shape alone. Here is the catalogue for a 64-bit Windows program: You see (bytes, as shown) It is probably --- --- xx xx xx xx f6 7f 00 00 A pointer into the program's own image (code or globals): high bytes 00 00 7f f6 or nearby xx xx xx xx fe 7f 00 00 A pointer into a system DLL xx xx xx xx 0X 0X 00 00 with small X A heap pointer: two high bytes zero, then smallish xx xx xx xx xx 00 00 00 , 8-byte aligned, near rsp A stack address cc cc cc cc Uninitialised stack memory (Debug) cd cd cd cd Allocated, never written heap memory (Debug) dd dd dd dd Freed heap memory (Debug) fd fd fd fd Heap guard bytes (Debug) 00 00 80 3f The float 1.0 00 00 00 00 00 00 f0 3f The double 1.0 xx 00 xx 00 xx 00 , letters in the right-hand column with dots between UTF-16 text Small numbers followed by 00 00 00 Small int s: counts, ids, health Pointers stand out most: eight bytes ending in 00 00 , with the high bytes repeating the same few values. Since x64 programs only use the lower 47 bits of an address, the top two bytes of a user-mode pointer are always zero. Reading floating-point numbers float and double are not stored like integers. A 32-bit float has three parts: bit 31 30 ......... 23 22 ...................... 0 ┌──────┬─────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┐ │ sign │ exponent (8) │ fraction (23) │ └──────┴─────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┘ value = (-1)^sign × 1.fraction × 2^(exponent − 127) You will rarely decode one by hand, because the Memory window can do it for you. But a few values are worth recognising, because they appear constantly in game data such as positions, speeds and scales: Value float bits Bytes in memory --- --- --- 0.0 0x00000000 00 00 00 00 0.5 0x3F000000 00 00 00 3f 1.0 0x3F800000 00 00 80 3f 2.0 0x40000000 00 00 00 40 10.0 0x41200000 00 00 20 41 100.0 0x42C80000 00 00 c8 42 −1.0 0xBF800000 00 00 80 bf A rule of thumb: a 4-byte group whose last byte is 3f , 40 , 41 , 42 , bf , c0 , c1 or c2 and whose first bytes are often 00 is very likely a float of modest size. You can see a value's bits from C++ by copying its bytes into an integer. std::bit_cast (C++20) does it in one step: cpp include <bit include <cstdint include <format include <iostream int main() { for (float f : { 1.0f, -1.0f, 0.5f, 100.0f, 0.1f }) std::cout << std::format("{: 6} - 0x{:08X}\n", f, std::bit_cast<std::uint32_t (f)); return 0; } 1 - 0x3F800000 -1 - 0xBF800000 0.5 - 0x3F000000 100 - 0x42C80000 0.1 - 0x3DCCCCCD 0.1 has no exact binary form, which is why its bits look busy. It is also why comparing floats with == after arithmetic often fails. Decoding a whole object Here is the routine for any object, using everything from this chapter. 1. Find its type's layout. Work through the members and the alignment rules (lesson 2.05), or let the Watch window tell you with &obj.member . 2. Point the window at the object. Type &obj in the Address box. Set 8 or 16 columns. 3. Split the bytes by offset. Mark where each member starts. 4. Read each member with the right rule: little-endian integers, float bits, a pointer (follow it by typing it into a second Memory window), padding to skip. 5. Check against the Locals window. Once your reading matches, you understand the layout. Try it on this object: cpp struct Item { const char name; // 0 float weight; // 8 std::int32_t count; // 12 bool stackable; // 16, then 7 bytes of tail padding }; 0x0000004F8C8FF8A0 e8 4c 2b a1 f6 7f 00 00 00 00 00 3f 0c 00 00 00 0x0000004F8C8FF8B0 01 cc cc cc cc cc cc cc - Bytes 0 to 7: e8 4c 2b a1 f6 7f 00 00 is the pointer 0x00007FF6A12B4CE8 : in the program's image, so name points at a string literal in .rdata . - Bytes 8 to 11: 00 00 00 3f is the float 0.5. - Bytes 12 to 15: 0c 00 00 00 is 12. - Byte 16: 01 is true . - Bytes 17 to 23: cc , tail padding in a Debug build. Common mistakes !warning Reading pointers byte by byte Switch the window to 8-byte integers in hexadecimal and the pointers read naturally, already reversed into the right order. !warning Forgetting the window keeps the old address When you step into a different function, the window still shows the same address, which may now belong to a different frame. Use Reevaluate automatically , or type the expression again. !warning Treating every 4-byte group as an int Positions and speeds are usually floats. If an "int" is a huge number like 1,065,353,216, try reading it as a float: that one is 1.0. Check yourself quiz ? How can you tell a pointer from other data in the Memory window? + 8 aligned bytes ending in 00 00 , such as f6 7f 00 00 - It always starts with the bytes cc cc - It is 4 bytes long and ends in ff ff - It is shown in a different colour from other data User-mode addresses on x64 Windows are far below the top of the 64-bit range, and little-endian order puts their zero high bytes last. ? What are the three parts of a 32-bit float? - A sign bit, a 16-bit whole part and a 15-bit fractional part + One sign bit, an 8-bit exponent stored with a bias of 127, and a 23-bit fraction - One sign bit, a 23-bit exponent and an 8-bit fraction - A 24-bit number and an 8-bit count of decimal places 1 + 8 + 23 = 32 bits. The exponent's bias of 127 is why 1.0f is stored as 00 00 80 3f . ? What steps decode an unknown object in memory? - Copy the bytes into the Watch window and let it guess the type - Read the bytes from left to right as one large integer + Work out member offsets, split the bytes, read each member by its kind - Look up each byte in an ASCII table Each member needs the right reading rule: integer, float, pointer or padding. Checking against the Locals window confirms you got the offsets right. Then check the result against the Locals window. ? You see the eight bytes 30 12 4a 9c f6 7f 00 00 . What is it most likely to be? - A double-precision number + A pointer into the program's own code or data - UTF-16 text Eight bytes ending in f6 7f 00 00 is the typical shape of an address in the program's image. ? What float is stored as the bytes 00 00 80 3f ? - 128.0 + 1.0 - 0.0 Read little-endian, the bits are 0x3F800000 : sign 0, exponent 127, fraction 0, which is 1.0. ? An int that should be small reads 1,065,353,216 in the Watch window. What is a likely explanation? + The memory holds the float 1.0, read as an int - The int overflowed when it was added to - The memory was freed and then reused 1,065,353,216 is 0x3F800000 , the bit pattern of 1.0f. ? Why do user-mode pointers on x64 Windows always end in 00 00 in memory? - Pointers are always multiples of 65,536 + Their top two bytes are zero, and little-endian stores them last - The Memory window adds them The highest bytes of the value come last in memory, and for user-mode addresses they are zero.

If the value would run past the end of bytes , the reader returns std::nullopt instead. bytes: 0c 00 00 00 00 00 80 3f 9c ff readU32(bytes, 0) = 12 readF32(bytes, 4) = 1.0 readI16(bytes, 8) = -100 readU32(bytes, 8) = nullopt (only 2 bytes left) For the float, build the 32-bit pattern first, then turn the pattern into a float with std::bit_cast (from <bit ) or std::memcpy .
