title: 3.01  Pointers to Pointers
body:
A pointer is a variable, so it has an address too, and a pointer can hold that address. A pointer to a pointer lets a function change which object another pointer points at, and it is how arrays of pointers, command-line arguments and many Windows API "out" parameters work. A pointer is just another variable Lesson 1.03 showed that a pointer is a variable holding an address. Like every variable, the pointer itself lives somewhere in memory and has an address of its own. Nothing stops you storing that address in another variable: cpp include <iostream int main() { int gold{ 250 }; int p{ &gold }; // p holds the address of gold int pp{ &p }; // pp holds the address of p std::cout << "gold = " << gold << '
'; std::cout << " p = " << p << '
'; std::cout << " pp = " << pp << '
'; pp = 300; // follow pp to p, follow p to gold, write there std::cout << "gold = " << gold << '
'; return 0; } gold = 250 p = 250 pp = 250 gold = 300 Read the types from the right: int is a pointer to (a pointer to an int). Each in an expression follows one arrow. Expression Type Means --- --- --- pp int The address of p pp int The value of p : the address of gold pp int The value of gold In memory, all three are just numbers in boxes: pp 's 8 bytes hold p 's address, p 's 8 bytes hold gold 's address, and gold 's 4 bytes hold 250. Why you would want one: changing someone else's pointer A function receives copies of its arguments. Pass it a pointer and it can change the thing pointed at, but not the caller's pointer itself. To change the caller's pointer, the function needs that pointer's address. cpp include <iostream struct Enemy { const char name; int health; }; // Makes target point at the weakest living enemy, or nullptr if none are alive. void pickWeakest(Enemy enemies, int count, Enemy target) { target = nullptr; for (int i{ 0 }; i < count; ++i) { Enemy e{ &enemies i }; if (e- health 0 && ( target == nullptr e- health < ( target)- health)) target = e; } } int main() { Enemy pack { { "wolf", 30 }, { "bat", 0 }, { "rat", 12 } }; Enemy aim{ nullptr }; pickWeakest(pack, 3, &aim); std::cout << "aiming at the " << aim- name << '
'; return 0; } aiming at the rat pickWeakest writes into target , which is the caller's aim . This "out parameter" style is everywhere in C and in the Windows API, where functions return an error code and hand back the object they created through a pointer to your pointer. Chapter 5 is full of calls like this: cpp // The function writes the new object's address into iface. IUnknown iface{ nullptr }; HRESULT hr{ CreateSomething(IID_PPV_ARGS(&iface)) }; In modern C++ code you would more often return the pointer, or pass Enemy & (a reference to a pointer, lesson 3.03). But you need to read the form fluently. Arrays of pointers The other common use is an array whose elements are pointers. main can receive the program's command-line arguments that way: cpp include <iostream int main(int argc, char argv) { // argv points at an array of argc pointers, each pointing at one argument's characters. std::cout << "argc = " << argc << '
'; for (int i{ 1 }; i < argc; ++i) std::cout << "argument " << i << ": " << argv i << '
'; return 0; } Run with game.exe --level 3 , argv 0 is the program's path, argv 1 points at "--level" and argv 2 at "3" . argv 1 2 is 'l' : index into the array of pointers, then into the characters. argv ──▶ ┌─────────┐ │ argv 0 │──▶ "C:\games\game.exe" ├─────────┤ │ argv 1 │──▶ "--level" ├─────────┤ │ argv 2 │──▶ "3" ├─────────┤ │ nullptr │ └─────────┘ Arrays of pointers also let you sort or reorder large objects cheaply: shuffle 8-byte pointers instead of copying the objects. Pointer arithmetic still works one level down argv + 1 moves along the array of pointers by one pointer (8 bytes). (argv + 1) + 2 moves along the characters of the second argument by two characters. Each level has its own element size, and pointer arithmetic always uses the size of the thing pointed at. Common mistakes !warning Passing the pointer when the function needs its address pickWeakest(pack, 3, aim) does not compile, which is good. With void parameters it might, and then the function writes over the wrong thing. Match the number of s. !warning Forgetting the parentheses in ( target)- health target- health means (target- health) , which is something else entirely. !warning Following a null pointer at either level Check pp before pp , and pp before pp . Check yourself quiz ? What does a pointer to a pointer hold? - The value of the object at the end of the chain + The address of another pointer variable - Two addresses, one for each level - The address of the first element of an array An int holds the address of an int . Dereference it once to get that pointer, twice to get the int . ? Give two common reasons to use a pointer to a pointer. - To make code run faster, and to save memory - To point at a function, and to point at a member + To let a function re-aim the caller's pointer, and for arrays of pointers - To avoid null checks, and to make a pointer constant A function given an Enemy can only change the enemy; given an Enemy it can change which enemy the caller's pointer refers to. ? How many bytes does argv + 1 move on x64? + Eight, the size of one pointer - One, because argv holds characters - Four, the size of an int - It depends on how long the first argument is Pointer arithmetic moves by the size of the thing pointed at, and argv points at char pointers, which are 8 bytes on x64. ? int x{ 5 }; int p{ &x }; int pp{ &p }; What is the type of pp ? - int + int - int One removes one level: pp is p , an int . ? Why does a function need an Enemy parameter to change which enemy the caller's Enemy points at? - Pointers cannot be passed to functions + It needs the caller's pointer's address to write into it - Enemy parameters are read-only Arguments are copies. To change the caller's variable, a function needs its address, and here the variable is itself a pointer. ? In int main(int argc, char argv) , what is argv 2 0 ? - The third character of the first argument - The number of arguments + The first character of the third command-line argument argv 2 is the third pointer in the array; 0 takes the first character it points at.

title: Aim at the largest
body: Write aimAtLargest(values, count, target) . It makes the caller's pointer, whose address is target , point at the largest of the count ints starting at values . If several are equally large, aim at the first of them. If count is 0, set the caller's pointer to nullptr . The function returns nothing: its only result is the change to the caller's pointer. cpp int scores { 4, 9, 2, 9 }; int best{ nullptr }; aimAtLargest(scores, 4, &best); // best now points at scores 1

title: 3.02  Following Pointers Through Objects
body: Real programs are webs of objects joined by pointers: a world holds a player, a player holds an inventory, an inventory holds items. Getting from one object to another means following a chain of pointers, each step a read of an address and an offset. This lesson shows what that looks like in memory, how to follow it safely, and what it costs. A small web of objects cpp include <iostream include <string include <vector struct Item { std::string name; float weight; }; struct Inventory { std::vector<Item slots; // pointers to items stored elsewhere float maxWeight{ 30.0f }; }; struct Player { int health{ 100 }; Inventory inventory{ nullptr }; }; struct World { Player player{ nullptr }; }; int main() { Item sword{ "sword", 6.5f }; Item rope{ "rope", 2.0f }; Inventory bag{ { &sword, &rope } }; Player hero{ 100, &bag }; World world{ &hero }; // world - player - inventory - slots 0 - name std::cout << world.player- inventory- slots 0 - name << '\n'; return 0; } sword That one line follows four arrows. Each - means "read the pointer stored here, go to that address, then move to a member at a fixed offset". In memory it looks like this: (The offsets here are those of a Release build, where std::vector is 24 bytes and std::string 32.) What the CPU actually does Following one link is two simple steps: load 8 bytes from (object address + member offset), and use the result as the next address. Written as the arithmetic a debugger or a memory tool would do: player = read8(address of world + 0) inventory = read8(player + 8) slotArray = read8(inventory + 0) the vector's data pointer item = read8(slotArray + 0 8) name = item + 0 This is exactly what the debugger's Watch window does when you expand world.player- inventory , and it is the skill chapter 9 uses to rebuild an unknown program's data structures: find an object, see that offset 8 holds a pointer, follow it, and work out what kind of object is there. Every arrow can be null Each link in the chain can be missing: the player might not have an inventory yet, a slot might be empty. Following a null pointer is undefined behaviour, and on Windows it crashes with an access violation reading location 0x0000000000000008 or similar. The small number in that message is a clue: it is the offset of the member being read from a null object. So code that walks a chain checks each step, or guarantees in its design that the link cannot be null: cpp float carriedWeight(const World& world) { if (!world.player !world.player- inventory) return 0.0f; float total{ 0.0f }; for (const Item item : world.player- inventory- slots) if (item) total += item- weight; return total; } Two habits help: - Prefer references or values where a link is always present. If every player always has an inventory, make it a member Inventory inventory; rather than a pointer. Then there is nothing to check and one fewer arrow to follow. - Use a pointer when the link is genuinely optional, and check it. std::optional and nullptr checks say so in the code. The cost of chasing pointers Each arrow is a memory read whose address depends on the previous read. The processor cannot start fetching the item until it knows the item's address, which it only learns after fetching the inventory, and so on. If the objects are scattered around the heap, each step is likely to miss the cache and wait for main memory. This chain of dependent loads is called pointer chasing , and it is one of the main reasons data-heavy code is slow. Game engines therefore prefer: - objects stored by value inside the objects that own them, so they sit in the same cache lines; - arrays of objects rather than arrays of pointers to objects, so a loop walks memory in order (lesson 2.07); - indices or handles into such arrays instead of raw pointers (lesson 3.10). std::vector<Item above is the slow shape; std::vector<Item is the fast one, when the items do not need to be shared. Common mistakes !warning Long unchecked chains a- b- c- d- value crashes if any link is null, and the crash message only tells you the final offset. Check optional links, or restructure so they are not optional. !warning Storing pointers to elements of a vector The vector may move its elements (lesson 2.04). Store indices instead. !warning Assuming the debugger's offsets match your release build Debug builds of standard containers are bigger. Offsets you work out in one configuration can differ in the other. Check yourself quiz ? What two steps does following p- member take? + Read the address held in p , then access the bytes at that address plus the member's offset - Look up member by name in a table, then read its value - Copy the whole object p points at, then read the member from the copy The member's offset is fixed at compile time, so p- member is just one address calculation and one memory access. ? How can you tell from a crash address that a null pointer was followed? - The crash address is always exactly zero - The crash address is very large, near the top of memory + The address is small, equal to the offset of the member being read from address zero - The crash message names the null variable Reading p- member with p null reads address 0 + offset, so a crash at 0x10 suggests reading the member at offset 16 of a null object. ? Name two ways games reduce pointer chasing. - Making every member a pointer, and allocating each object separately - Using more virtual functions, and deeper class hierarchies - Replacing arrays with linked lists, and caching each pointer twice + Storing objects by value inside their owners, and keeping objects in arrays referred to by index or handle Objects next to each other in memory share cache lines; every pointer hop to a scattered heap object can be a cache miss. ? A crash says "access violation reading location 0x0000000000000010". What is the most likely cause? + Reading the member at offset 16 through a null pointer - The program ran out of memory - A function returned 16 Null plus a member offset gives a tiny address like 0x10. Look for an unchecked pointer whose member at offset 16 was being read. ? Why is following a long chain of pointers through scattered heap objects slow? - Pointers are slower to read than integers + Each read waits for the last, and each may miss the cache - The compiler cannot optimise - Dependent loads cannot overlap, so every cache miss along the chain is paid in full. ? When should a member be a pointer rather than a value? - Always, because pointers are smaller - Never: values are always faster + When the link is optional, or the object is owned elsewhere If an object always has exactly one of something, a value member is simpler, safer and faster.

title: Weigh the backpack safely
body: Write carriedWeight(world) . It follows the chain world.player , then inventory , then every item pointer in slots , and returns the total weight of the items. Any link may be missing: a null player, a null inventory or a null slot. A missing player or inventory means the weight is 0; a null slot is simply skipped. The function must never follow a null pointer.

title: 3.03  References Under the Hood
body:
A reference looks like a second name for an object, and in the language that is exactly what it is. In the machine, a reference that has to be stored or passed is an address, the same as a pointer. This lesson shows both views, the rules that make references safer than pointers, and the ways they can still dangle. Two views of the same thing In C++, a reference is an alias: another name for an existing object. cpp include <iostream void heal(int& health, int amount) { health += amount; // changes the caller's variable } int main() { int hp{ 40 }; int& alias{ hp }; // alias is another name for hp alias -= 10; heal(hp, 25); std::cout << hp << '
'; std::cout << (&alias == &hp) << '
'; // same object, same address return 0; } 55 1 Now look at what the compiler generates. These two functions compile to identical machine code: cpp void healRef(int& health, int amount) { health += amount; } void healPtr(int health, int amount) { health += amount; } asm healRef PROC ; healPtr is exactly the same add DWORD PTR rcx , edx ; add amount (edx) to the int at the address in rcx ret 0 healRef ENDP The caller passes the address of hp in rcx in both cases. At the machine level, a reference parameter is a pointer . The difference is entirely in the rules the compiler enforces at the source level. The rules that make references safer Pointer Reference --- --- --- Can be null Yes No: must be bound to an object when created Can be changed to refer to something else Yes No: bound once, for life Needs or - to reach the object Yes No: used like the object itself Can do arithmetic Yes No Can be stored in containers Yes No (use std::reference_wrapper ) Each rule removes a way to go wrong. A function taking Player& never needs to check for null, and its body reads like normal code. That is why modern C++ uses references for "must be there" parameters and pointers only where "might be absent" or "can be re-aimed" is part of the meaning. cpp void applyDamage(Player& target, int amount); // there is always a target Enemy findNearest(const Vec2& from); // there might be none: nullptr const references: reading without copying Passing a large object by value copies it. Passing it by const reference passes 8 bytes (an address) and promises not to change it: cpp include <iostream include <string include <vector struct Level { std::string name; std::vector<int tiles; }; int countWalls(const Level& level) // no copy of a possibly huge vector { int walls{ 0 }; for (int t : level.tiles) if (t == 1) ++walls; return walls; } int main() { Level cave{ "cave", { 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0 } }; std::cout << countWalls(cave) << '
'; return 0; } 3 The rule of thumb: pass small, cheap-to-copy types ( int , float , a small Vec2 ) by value, and everything else by const& , unless the function needs its own copy. A const& can also bind to a temporary, which it then keeps alive (lesson 2.04). That is why countWalls(Level{ "tmp", { 1 } }) works. When a reference takes no space at all When a reference is a local alias inside one function, the compiler usually does not store it anywhere. int& alias{ hp }; just tells the compiler that alias means hp , and it generates code using hp 's location directly. Only references that must cross a boundary (parameters, return values, members) become stored addresses. A reference member makes the object hold an 8-byte address: cpp include <iostream struct Camera { const float& targetX; // follows something else's x position float offset; }; int main() { float playerX{ 10.0f }; Camera cam{ playerX, -2.0f }; playerX = 15.0f; std::cout << cam.targetX + cam.offset << '
'; std::cout << sizeof(Camera) << '
'; return 0; } 13 16 Sixteen bytes: an 8-byte address, a 4-byte float, 4 bytes of padding. Reference members also make the class impossible to assign (a reference cannot be re-bound), which is usually more trouble than it is worth. Prefer a pointer member for "refers to something owned elsewhere". References can dangle too A reference is an address with no null check needed, but it is still an address, and the object can die before the reference does: cpp const std::string& badName() { std::string name{ "Ghost" }; return name; // the local dies; the caller gets a dangling reference } MSVC warns about this one (C4172). It cannot warn about the subtler cases: a reference into a std::vector that later grows, or a reference member to an object destroyed first. The rules from lesson 2.04 apply to references exactly as they do to pointers. Common mistakes !warning Returning a reference to a local Return by value. Copies of return values are usually optimised away completely. !warning Thinking references are free in every case Passing an int by const int& passes an address and makes the function read through it. For small types, pass by value. !warning Reference members in classes that need to be copied or assigned Use a pointer, or std::reference_wrapper , instead. Check yourself quiz ? How is a reference parameter passed at the machine level? - As a full copy of the object - As the name of the variable, looked up at run time + As an address, exactly like a pointer The machine code for void f(int& x) and void f(int x) is usually identical: the address arrives in a register. ? Why are references safer than pointers? - They are checked by the operating system on every use + They cannot be null, cannot be re-aimed, and need no or - - They keep the object alive for as long as the reference exists - They can never dangle These rules remove several common mistakes, but a reference can still dangle if the object it refers to is destroyed. ? When should you still use a pointer instead of a reference? - Whenever the object is larger than 8 bytes - Whenever the function only reads the object - Never: references can do everything a pointer can + When it may be null, must be re-aimed, or must be stored A reference must refer to something and cannot be re-aimed, which also makes it awkward as a class member or container element. Storing a reference in a container or an assignable class is awkward because it cannot be re-aimed. ? What does void f(int& x) receive in its first register when called? + The address of the caller's int - A copy of the int 's value - Nothing: references are compile-time only A reference parameter is passed exactly like a pointer. ? Which of these can a pointer do that a reference cannot? - Refer to an object on the heap + Be re-aimed at a different object later - Be passed to a function A reference is bound once, when it is created, and always refers to that object. ? Which is the best parameter type for a function that reads a large Level without changing it? - Level - Level + const Level& No copy, no null check, and the const documents that the function only reads it.

title: Clamp and swap in place
body: Write two small functions that change their caller's variables through references. - clampInPlace(value, low, high) changes value so it is no less than low and no more than high . Assume low <= high . - orderPair(a, b) swaps a and b if needed so that afterwards a <= b . Neither returns anything. Do not use pointers.

title: 3.04  Function Pointers and Callbacks
body:
Functions live in memory too, so they have addresses, and a variable can hold one. A function pointer lets code decide at run time which function to call: the basis of callbacks, command tables, state machines and plugin systems. This lesson covers raw function pointers, std::function and lambdas, and what each costs. A function has an address Lesson 1.04 showed that a function is a run of machine-code bytes in the .text section. Calling it means jumping to its first byte. That address can be stored in a variable, passed around and called later. cpp include <iostream int doubleIt(int x) { return x 2; } int squareIt(int x) { return x x; } int main() { int ( op)(int){ &doubleIt }; // op is a pointer to a function taking int and returning int std::cout << op(7) << '
'; op = &squareIt; // aim it at a different function std::cout << op(7) << '
'; std::cout << "doubleIt lives at " << reinterpret_cast<void (&doubleIt) << '
'; return 0; } varies 14 49 doubleIt lives at 00007FF6E1A21082 The declaration syntax is awkward. Read int ( op)(int) as " op is a pointer to a function that takes an int and returns an int ". A type alias makes it readable: cpp using UnaryOp = int ( )(int); UnaryOp op{ &doubleIt }; In assembly, a normal call is call doubleIt , with the address fixed when the program is linked. A call through a pointer is call rax (or call qword ptr ... ): the address is read from a register or memory at run time. That small difference is what makes everything in this lesson possible. Callbacks: letting the caller decide A callback is a function you pass to other code for it to call. The standard library's algorithms are built on them, and so are event systems. cpp include <iostream include <vector struct Enemy { const char name; int health; bool flying; }; // Calls visit for every enemy that matches. void forEachEnemy(const std::vector<Enemy & enemies, bool ( matches)(const Enemy&), void ( visit)(const Enemy&)) { for (const Enemy& e : enemies) if (matches(e)) visit(e); } bool isFlying(const Enemy& e) { return e.flying; } void printName(const Enemy& e) { std::cout << e.name << '
'; } int main() { std::vector<Enemy enemies{ { "bat", 8, true }, { "rat", 5, false }, { "wasp", 3, true } }; forEachEnemy(enemies, &isFlying, &printName); return 0; } bat wasp forEachEnemy knows nothing about flying or printing. The caller supplies both decisions. Command tables A table of function pointers maps names or numbers to actions. Debug consoles, input bindings, network message handlers and bytecode interpreters all work this way. cpp include <iostream include <map include <string include <utility include <vector struct Game { int gold{ 0 }; int health{ 100 }; }; void giveGold(Game& g, int n) { g.gold += n; } void heal(Game& g, int n) { g.health += n; } void hurt(Game& g, int n) { g.health -= n; } int main() { using Command = void ( )(Game&, int); const std::map<std::string, Command commands{ { "gold", &giveGold }, { "heal", &heal }, { "hurt", &hurt } }; Game game; const std::vector<std::pair<std::string, int typed{ { "gold", 50 }, { "hurt", 30 }, { "heal", 5 } }; for (const auto& name, amount : typed) { const auto found{ commands.find(name) }; if (found != commands.end()) found- second(game, amount); } std::cout << "gold " << game.gold << ", health " << game.health << '
'; return 0; } gold 50, health 75 Adding a command means adding one line to the table. Chapter 11 builds the game's debug console exactly like this, and chapter 13 uses the same idea for plugins: a plugin is, at heart, a table of function pointers the game calls. Lambdas and std::function Raw function pointers can only point at plain functions. They cannot carry extra data, such as "only enemies within 10 metres of this position". C++ has two tools for that. A lambda is an unnamed function written in place. A lambda that captures nothing converts to a plain function pointer. One that captures variables is an object holding copies of (or references to) them, with an operator() . std::function<Signature holds any callable: a function pointer, a lambda with captures, or an object with operator() . cpp include <functional include <iostream include <vector int main() { std::vector<std::function<void() onLevelEnd; int score{ 0 }; onLevelEnd.push_back( { std::cout << "save the game
"; }); onLevelEnd.push_back( &score { score += 100; std::cout << "bonus, score now " << score << '
'; }); for (const auto& callback : onLevelEnd) callback(); return 0; } save the game bonus, score now 100 Tool Can carry data Cost of a call Typical use --- --- --- --- Function pointer No One indirect call C APIs, Windows callbacks, plugin tables Template parameter taking a lambda Yes Often none: the compiler can inline it std::sort , algorithms std::function Yes An indirect call, and possibly a heap allocation when created Stored callbacks, event lists The Windows API uses plain function pointers for its callbacks, because it is a C interface. A window's message handler (chapter 5) is a function pointer you give to Windows, and Windows calls it for every message. Common mistakes !warning Capturing by reference in a callback that outlives the scope &score stores a reference to score . If the callback runs after the function holding score has returned, it writes into a dead frame (lesson 2.04). Capture by value, or make sure the data outlives the callback. !warning Calling a null function pointer It jumps to address 0 and crashes. Check optional callbacks before calling them. !warning Using std::function in the hottest loops Each call is indirect and cannot be inlined. For per-element work in a tight loop, pass the lambda as a template parameter instead. Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference in machine code between a direct call and a call through a function pointer? + A direct call's target is fixed at link time; a pointer call reads it at run time - A pointer call copies the function's code into the caller first - A direct call uses the stack and a pointer call does not - There is no difference; the linker turns both into the same instruction An indirect call such as call rax reads its target from a register or memory, so the same instruction can reach different functions. ? What is a callback? + A function passed to other code so that code can call it when needed - A function that calls itself - A function that runs when the program exits - The return address a function jumps back to The caller decides part of the behaviour, for example what to do with each item a search finds. ? When would you choose std::function over a plain function pointer? - When the function returns void - When speed matters more than flexibility - When passing the callback to a Windows API function + When it must store a callable with data, like a capturing lambda A plain function pointer can only hold a function (or a capture-less lambda). Windows APIs need plain function pointers, and std::function costs a little more. ? What does int ( f)(float) declare? + A pointer to a function that takes a float and returns an int - A function that returns a pointer to an int - An array of floats Read from the name outwards: f is a pointer ( f ) to a function taking (float) returning int . ? Which kind of lambda can be converted to a plain function pointer? - One that captures by value + One that captures nothing - Any lambda A captureless lambda has no data to carry, so it is just a function. Capturing lambdas are objects. ? Why do Windows API callbacks use plain function pointers instead of std::function ? - std::function is slower to call + The Windows API is a C interface, and C has no std::function - Function pointers can carry captured data C++ types like std::function cannot cross a C boundary.

title: A debug console's command table
body: Build the core of a debug console. A Console holds a table that maps command names to functions. Each command function receives the Game and one whole-number argument. - addCommand(name, fn) registers a command. Registering a name again replaces the old function. - run(line) takes a line such as "gold 50" : a name, one space, and a number. It calls the matching command and returns true . If there is no such command, or the line is not a name followed by a number, it changes nothing and returns false . Commands are plain function pointers of type void ( )(Game&, int) . cpp Console console; console.addCommand("gold", &giveGold); console.run("gold 50"); // true, gold is now 50 console.run("fly 1"); // false, nothing happens

title: 3.05  Virtual Functions and Vtables in Memory
match: 3.05 Virtual Functions and Vtables in Memory
body:
A virtual call picks the function to run from the object's real type, at run time. Compilers do it with a vtable : a table of function pointers, one per class, and a hidden vptr in every object pointing at its class's table. This lesson shows the layout, walks through a virtual call step by step, and explains what it costs. The problem virtual functions solve cpp include <iostream include <memory include <vector struct Entity { virtual ~Entity() = default; virtual void update() { std::cout << "entity idles
"; } virtual int damage() const { return 0; } }; struct Goblin : Entity { void update() override { std::cout << "goblin sneaks
"; } int damage() const override { return 4; } }; struct Dragon : Entity { void update() override { std::cout << "dragon breathes fire
"; } int damage() const override { return 40; } }; int main() { std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Entity world; world.push_back(std::make_unique<Goblin ()); world.push_back(std::make_unique<Dragon ()); world.push_back(std::make_unique<Entity ()); int total{ 0 }; for (const auto& e : world) { e- update(); // which update? decided by the object, at run time total += e- damage(); } std::cout << "total damage " << total << '
'; return 0; } goblin sneaks dragon breathes fire entity idles total damage 44 The loop only knows it has an Entity . The compiler cannot know, when it compiles e- update() , which function to call: that depends on the object at run time. So it cannot emit call Goblin::update . It needs a way to look the function up. One table per class, one pointer per object For every class with virtual functions, the compiler builds a vtable : an array of function pointers, one slot per virtual function, stored in the read-only .rdata section. Every object of that class gets a hidden first member, the vptr , holding the address of its class's vtable. The constructor sets it. Every Goblin shares the one Goblin vtable. Slots are in the order the virtual functions were first declared in the base class, so update is in the same slot in every class's table. That is the key: the caller knows the slot number at compile time, even though it does not know the class. A virtual call, step by step e- update() compiles to roughly this (MSVC x64, with e in rcx ): asm mov rax, QWORD PTR rcx ; 1. read the vptr from offset 0 of the object call QWORD PTR rax+8 ; 2. read slot 1 of the vtable, and call that address 1. Load the vptr from the object. 2. Load the function pointer from the vtable at slot × 8 . Here slot 1, offset 8, because slot 0 holds the destructor. 3. Call it, with the object's address still in rcx as this . Two memory reads and an indirect call. That is all "dynamic dispatch" is. Seeing the vptr The vptr is ordinary memory. Implementation details like this should never be relied on in real code, but looking at them once makes the idea concrete: cpp include <cstdint include <cstring include <iostream struct Entity { virtual ~Entity() = default; virtual int damage() const { return 0; } }; struct Goblin : Entity { int damage() const override { return 4; } }; struct Dragon : Entity { int damage() const override { return 40; } }; std::uintptr_t vptrOf(const void object) { std::uintptr_t vptr{}; std::memcpy(&vptr, object, sizeof vptr); // the first 8 bytes of the object return vptr; } int main() { Goblin a, b; Dragon c; std::cout << "two goblins share a vtable: " << (vptrOf(&a) == vptrOf(&b)) << '
'; std::cout << "a dragon has a different one: " << (vptrOf(&a) != vptrOf(&c)) << '
'; std::cout << "sizeof(Goblin) = " << sizeof(Goblin) << '
'; return 0; } two goblins share a vtable: 1 a dragon has a different one: 1 sizeof(Goblin) = 8 Goblin has no data members, yet it is 8 bytes: just the vptr. In the Visual Studio debugger, expanding an object shows the vptr as __vfptr , and expanding that lists the vtable's entries with their function names. This is also why the first 8 bytes of many objects in a memory view look like an address inside the program's image: they are vptrs into .rdata . Chapter 9 uses vtables to discover the classes in a compiled program, because each vtable is a list of a class's virtual functions. Construction and destruction The vptr changes while an object is being built. During the Entity part of constructing a Goblin , the vptr points at Entity 's vtable; only when the Goblin constructor body runs does it point at Goblin 's. So a virtual call inside a constructor or destructor calls the version for the class currently being built , not the most derived one. This surprises people once, and then they remember it. It is also why a base class used through pointers needs a virtual destructor . delete e on an Entity calls the destructor through the vtable; without virtual , only ~Entity runs and the Dragon part is never destroyed. The cost Cost Size --- --- Memory 8 bytes per object for the vptr, one small table per class Each call Two dependent loads and an indirect call Optimisation The compiler usually cannot inline a virtual call For a few hundred calls per frame, none of this matters. For millions (every particle, every tile), it can. Engines often avoid virtual calls in the hottest loops by keeping objects of one type together in arrays and processing each array with ordinary calls. Chapter 10's entity-component designs are partly a response to this. Common mistakes !warning Forgetting the virtual destructor Deleting a derived object through a base pointer without one is undefined behaviour and usually leaks the derived part. !warning Calling virtual functions from constructors They do not dispatch to the derived class yet. Move such work to a separate init step if needed. !warning Misspelling an override Without override , a typo in the name or a missing const silently creates a new function instead of overriding. Always write override . !warning Copying objects with vptrs as raw bytes Saving them to a file or memcpy -ing into unrelated memory copies an address that means nothing elsewhere. Check yourself quiz ? What is a vtable? - A table of every object of a class and its address - A copy of an object's data members used by virtual functions + A per-class array of function pointers, one slot per virtual function - A list of the classes a class inherits from Objects use their class's vtable, reached through the hidden vptr, to find the right function at run time. ? Why does every class put a given virtual function in the same slot? - So the linker can merge all vtables into one + So a base pointer can call it by slot without knowing the real class - Because the slots are sorted alphabetically by function name - So the debugger can show the function's name The caller compiles call vtable + slot 8 ; whichever class the object really is, its table has the right function in that slot. ? What does a virtual call cost compared with a normal call? - Nothing: the compiler turns every virtual call into a direct call - A search through the class's functions by name + Two extra dependent memory reads (vptr and table entry), an indirect call, and usually no inlining - A system call into the kernel to find the function The cost is small for one call but adds up in tight loops over many objects, mostly because the call cannot be inlined. ? Where is the vptr stored? + In each object, normally at offset 0 - In each class's vtable - In a global list of objects Every object of a class with virtual functions carries its own vptr, set by its constructor. ? Two Goblin objects exist. How many Goblin vtables are there? - Two, one per object + One, shared by both - None until a virtual function is called The vtable belongs to the class and lives in .rdata . Objects only hold pointers to it. ? What does call QWORD PTR rax+8 do in a virtual call? - Calls the function at address 8 + Calls the function in vtable slot 1, read via rax - Jumps forward 8 bytes rax holds the vptr; rax+8 is the second 8-byte entry of the table. ? A virtual function is called from inside the base class's constructor while a Dragon is being built. Which version runs? + The base class's version - Dragon 's version - Neither: it is a compile error During the base constructor the vptr still points at the base class's vtable.

title: Build your own vtable
where: 3.05 Virtual Functions and Vtables in Memory
body: C has no virtual functions, so C programs (and the Windows COM system) build vtables by hand. Do the same, to see there is no magic. A Shape holds a pointer to a ShapeVTable (its "vptr") and two numbers. The table holds two function pointers: area and name . Write: - circleArea , rectArea : compute the area from the shape's numbers. A circle uses a as its radius (use 3.14159265358979 for pi); a rectangle uses a and b as width and height. - circleName , rectName : return "circle" and "rectangle" . - the two tables kCircleTable and kRectTable , filled with the right functions; - makeCircle(r) and makeRect(w, h) , which return a Shape aimed at the right table; - totalArea(shapes) , which adds up the areas by calling through each shape's table .

title: 3.06  Linked Lists from Scratch
body: A linked list stores each element in its own node, and each node points to the next. Inserting and removing anywhere is cheap, but finding anything means following pointers one at a time. Building one by hand is the best practice there is for pointers, and it explains why games use them rarely and carefully. Nodes and links An array keeps its elements side by side. A linked list scatters them: each element sits in a separately allocated node , together with a pointer to the next node. The list itself only remembers the first node, the head . cpp struct Node { int value; Node next; // nullptr in the last node }; Walking the list means following next until it is null: cpp include <iostream struct Node { int value; Node next; }; int main() { Node c{ 9, nullptr }; Node b{ 3, &c }; Node a{ 7, &b }; Node head{ &a }; for (Node n{ head }; n != nullptr; n = n- next) std::cout << n- value << ' '; std::cout << '\n'; return 0; } 7 3 9 Inserting Adding at the front takes a constant amount of work, however long the list is: make a node, point it at the old head, make it the new head. cpp void pushFront(Node & head, int value) { head = new Node{ value, head }; } Inserting after a node you already have is just as cheap: two pointer writes, no elements moved. Compare an array, where inserting at the front means shifting every element along by one. Removing, and the pointer-to-pointer trick Removing a node means making whatever pointed at it point at its successor instead. The first node is pointed at by head ; every other node is pointed at by the previous node's next . Treating those two cases separately is clumsy: cpp // Clumsy: a special case for the head. void removeFirstClumsy(Node & head, int value) { if (head && head- value == value) { Node dead{ head }; head = head- next; delete dead; return; } for (Node n{ head }; n && n- next; n = n- next) if (n- next- value == value) { Node dead{ n- next }; n- next = dead- next; delete dead; return; } } The neat way is to walk with a pointer to the link itself, a Node (lesson 3.01). It starts at &head and moves to &node- next . Whichever link it holds, removing the node it points at is the same one line: cpp void removeFirst(Node & head, int value) { for (Node link{ &head }; link != nullptr; link = &( link)- next) { if (( link)- value == value) { Node dead{ link }; link = dead- next; // whoever pointed at dead now skips it delete dead; return; } } } This is one of the few places where makes code shorter and clearer, and it is a classic interview question. The practice task asks you to write it. The cost: walking is slow Operation Array / std::vector Linked list --- --- --- Get element number i One calculation Follow i pointers Insert or remove at the front Move every element Two pointer writes Insert or remove in the middle, given its position Move the elements after it Two pointer writes Loop over everything Walks memory in order Jumps around the heap: one cache miss per node, likely Extra memory None One pointer (8 bytes) per element, plus allocator overhead That last-but-one row usually decides it. Looping over a std::vector<int of a million elements reads contiguous memory the processor can stream in. Looping over a list of a million nodes follows a million dependent pointers into scattered heap blocks (lesson 3.02's pointer chasing). In practice the vector is often ten times faster or more, even for workloads with many inserts, because shifting contiguous memory is so cheap. So the standard advice is: default to std::vector . Use a list only when you have measured a reason. Where lists do appear in games - Intrusive lists : the next pointer lives inside an object that already exists for another reason, such as all the enemies in one grid cell of a spatial partition. No extra allocations, and an object can unlink itself in constant time. - Free lists in pools (lesson 3.10): unused slots point to the next unused slot, so allocating is "take the head". - Engines' own systems , such as lists of timers or render commands, often allocated from an arena so the nodes are close together anyway. The standard library has std::list (doubly linked) and std::forward_list (singly linked) if you need one. Common mistakes !warning Using a node after deleting it In n = n- next after delete n , the read is from freed memory. Save next first. !warning Losing the rest of the list Overwriting head before saving the old head leaks every node. Draw the arrows before writing the code. !warning Forgetting to free the nodes A list built with new needs a loop that deletes every node, or nodes owned by std::unique_ptr . Check yourself quiz ? What does each node of a singly linked list hold? + An element's value and a pointer to the next node, or nullptr in the last node - Only a pointer to the next node - An element's value and pointers to both the next and the previous node Pointers in both directions make a doubly linked list. A singly linked list only links forward. ? Why is inserting at the front of a list cheap? - Because the list keeps spare nodes ready + Because it creates one node and changes two pointers, whatever the list's length - Because the new node is placed next to the old first node in memory - Because nodes are never freed Nothing has to move, unlike inserting at the front of a vector, which shifts every element. ? Give two situations where games use linked structures sensibly. - Storing all game objects for a fast loop, and storing tile maps + Intrusive lists inside existing objects, and pool free lists - Replacing every std::vector , and holding strings - Sorting large arrays, and looking up items by name Lists are slow to walk, so they appear where links are cheap to keep and walking is rare or short. An intrusive list keeps the link inside objects that already exist, such as the objects in one grid cell. ? What is the cost of reading the 1000th element of a linked list? - One memory read + Following 999 next pointers from the head - Sorting the list first There is no index arithmetic: the only way to a node is through the ones before it. ? In removeFirst , why does link have type Node ? - Because nodes are stored in a two-dimensional array - To make the function faster + It points at the link ( head or a next ) that may change Changing a pointer requires its address. link = dead- next updates whichever pointer pointed at the dead node. ? Why is a std::vector usually faster to loop over than a linked list with the same elements? + Its elements are contiguous and cache-friendly; list nodes are scattered - Vectors use less memory per element because they compress values - Linked lists must be sorted Contiguous memory is streamed efficiently; pointer chasing waits on memory at every step.

title: A singly linked list
body: Complete the functions for a singly linked list of int s. A list is represented by its head pointer, which is nullptr for an empty list. - pushFront(head, value) adds a node at the front. - size(head) counts the nodes. - removeAll(head, value) removes and deletes every node holding value , and returns how many it removed. - clear(head) deletes every node and sets head to nullptr . Use the pointer-to-pointer technique from the lesson for removeAll , so the head needs no special case. The tests check that nothing leaks.

title: 3.07  How std::vector Really Works
body:
std::vector is three pointers and a heap block. Its size is how many elements are in use, its capacity how many fit before it must grow. When it grows, it allocates a bigger block, moves everything across and frees the old one, which is why pointers into a vector can suddenly dangle. Knowing this lets you use the most important container in C++ efficiently. Three pointers A std::vector<T object is 24 bytes in a Release build, three pointers: std::vector<int (Release x64) heap block ┌───────────────┐ ┌────┬────┬────┬────┬────┬────┐ │ first ────────┼──────────────────────▶│ 10 │ 20 │ 30 │ 40 │ ?? │ ?? │ │ last ────────┼───────┐ └────┴────┴────┴────┴────┴────┘ │ end ────────┼───┐ │ ▲ ▲ └───────────────┘ │ └───────────────────────────────────┘ │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ size() = last − first = 4 (last points just past the 40) capacity() = end − first = 6 (end points just past the block) - first points at element 0 ( data() returns it), - last points just past the last element in use, - end points just past the end of the block. size() and capacity() are subtractions. The elements in use are exactly an array, which is why everything from lesson 2.07 applies: indexing is one calculation, and looping walks memory in order. Growing When push_back finds size() == capacity() , there is no room. The vector then: 1. allocates a new, bigger block; 2. moves (or copies) every element into it; 3. destroys the old elements and frees the old block; 4. adds the new element. That is expensive, so the new block is not just one bigger. Microsoft's implementation grows by half again each time (a factor of 1.5); others use 2. Because the growth is a fixed factor, the total work averages out to a constant amount per push_back , but individual pushes are occasionally very slow. cpp include <iostream include <vector int main() { std::vector<int v; std::size_t lastCapacity{ v.capacity() }; std::cout << "capacity " << lastCapacity; for (int i{ 0 }; i < 100; ++i) { v.push_back(i); if (v.capacity() != lastCapacity) { lastCapacity = v.capacity(); std::cout << ' ' << lastCapacity; } } std::cout << '
'; return 0; } capacity 0 1 2 3 4 6 9 13 19 28 42 63 94 141 Thirteen reallocations to reach 100 elements, each copying everything so far. If you know roughly how many elements are coming, say so up front: cpp std::vector<Bullet bullets; bullets.reserve(512); // one allocation; no regrowth until 512 reserve changes capacity, not size: the vector is still empty, but the room is there. resize(n) changes size, creating or destroying elements. Growth invalidates pointers Step 3 above frees the old block. Every pointer, reference and iterator to an element pointed into that block, and now dangles: cpp-norun include <iostream include <vector int main() { std::vector<int v{ 1, 2, 3 }; int first{ &v 0 }; v.push_back(4); // capacity was 3: reallocates std::cout << first << '
'; // reads freed memory return 0; } The rules, briefly: Operation What it invalidates --- --- push_back , emplace_back , insert Everything, if it reallocates; otherwise elements at or after the insertion point reserve (to a bigger capacity) Everything erase Elements at or after the erased position pop_back Only the removed element Reading, writing existing elements Nothing The robust habit in game code is to refer to vector elements by index , not by pointer. An index stays meaningful when the block moves. Lesson 3.10 builds on this. Inserting and erasing in the middle The elements are contiguous, so inserting or erasing anywhere except the end has to shift every later element by one place. Erasing the first of a million elements moves 999,999 of them. When order does not matter, which in games it often does not, use swap and pop : move the last element into the hole and shrink by one. cpp include <iostream include <vector void removeAtUnordered(std::vector<int & v, std::size_t i) { v i = std::move(v.back()); // the last element fills the hole v.pop_back(); // and the end shrinks by one } int main() { std::vector<int enemies{ 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 }; removeAtUnordered(enemies, 1); for (int e : enemies) std::cout << e << ' '; std::cout << '
'; return 0; } 10 50 30 40 Constant time, however big the vector. And to remove every element that matches a condition, std::erase_if(v, predicate) (C++20) does it in one pass, moving each kept element at most once. emplace_back versus push_back push_back(obj) copies or moves an existing object into the vector. emplace_back(args...) constructs the element directly in the vector's memory from constructor arguments, skipping the temporary. For simple types the difference is nothing; for objects that are expensive to move, emplace_back can save work. A vector of objects or of pointers? std::vector<Enemy std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Enemy --- --- Enemies stored side by side: fast to loop over Pointers side by side; enemies scattered on the heap Growing moves the enemies themselves Growing moves only the pointers; the enemies stay put Pointers to enemies dangle after growth Pointers to enemies stay valid All elements must be the same type Can hold derived classes (polymorphism) Games favour the left column for anything numerous and processed every frame, and use indices to refer to elements. Common mistakes !warning Keeping &v i or an iterator across a push_back Store the index instead, or re-take the pointer after the change. !warning Erasing inside a range-based for loop The loop's hidden iterators are invalidated. Use std::erase_if , or an index loop that does not advance when it erases. !warning Calling reserve inside a loop v.reserve(v.size() + 1) before each push defeats the growth factor and reallocates every time. Reserve once, before the loop. !warning Confusing reserve with resize After reserve(10) , v 0 is still out of range: the size is 0. Check yourself quiz ? What three pointers make up a std::vector , and how are size and capacity worked out? - First element, last element, middle element; size is last minus first - Start of the block, end of the block and a pointer to the allocator; size is stored separately + Start of the block, end of the elements in use, end of the block; size is used end minus start, capacity is block end minus start - One pointer per element; size and capacity are counted on demand Size and capacity are not stored as numbers; they are worked out from the three pointers. ? Why can a pointer to a vector element become invalid after push_back ? + If the vector is full, push_back moves every element to a new block and frees the old one - push_back always sorts the elements, so they change places - push_back clears the vector before adding the new element - Pointers to vector elements are only valid until the next statement If there is spare capacity the elements stay put, but you cannot rely on that unless you have reserved enough. ? When is swap-and-pop the right way to remove an element? - When the vector must stay sorted - When removing the first element of a queue + When the order of the elements does not matter - Whenever the vector holds pointers Moving the last element into the gap removes in constant time, but it changes the order. ? A vector has size 6 and capacity 6. What happens on push_back ? - The block is extended in place by one element + It moves the 6 elements to a bigger block, then adds the new one - The program throws an exception A heap block cannot grow in place, so the vector moves to a new, larger one. ? Why does a vector grow by a factor (such as 1.5×) instead of by one element at a time? - To waste less memory + So the cost of many push_back s averages to a constant each - Because the heap only allocates in powers of two Growing by one would copy everything on every push: the cost would grow with the square of the size. ? What does v.reserve(100) do to an empty vector's size? + Nothing: the size stays 0, only the capacity changes - Sets it to 100 - Sets it to 100 default-constructed elements reserve makes room; resize changes the number of elements. ? What is the cost of swap-and-pop removal? - Proportional to the number of elements after the removed one + Constant, whatever the size of the vector - Proportional to the size of the vector One move and one pop_back . The order of the elements changes, which is the price.

title: 3.08  Hash Tables
body:
A hash table finds a value by its key in about the same time however many entries it holds. A hash function turns the key into a number that picks a bucket , and the table only has to look in that one place. This lesson explains hashing, collisions and load factor, compares std::unordered_map with std::map , and shows where games use them. The problem A game has 5,000 item definitions and looks them up by name: "iron_sword", "health_potion". Searching a vector of them means comparing names one by one, up to 5,000 comparisons per lookup. A sorted vector with binary search needs about 13. A hash table usually needs one or two. The idea: compute where it goes A hash function turns a key into a number, its hash . The table keeps an array of buckets and stores each entry in bucket number hash % bucketCount . To find a key, compute its hash, go straight to that bucket, and look only there. A good hash function has two properties: - Deterministic : the same key always gives the same hash. - Well spread : similar keys give very different hashes, so entries scatter evenly over the buckets. Here is a simple, widely used string hash, FNV-1a . It mixes each byte in with an XOR, then multiplies by a carefully chosen prime to spread the bits: cpp include <cstdint include <format include <iostream include <string_view std::uint32_t fnv1a(std::string_view text) { std::uint32_t hash{ 2166136261u }; // the FNV "offset basis" for (unsigned char c : text) { hash ^= c; hash = 16777619u; // the FNV prime } return hash; } int main() { for (const char key : { "iron_sword", "iron_swore", "health_potion", "" }) std::cout << std::format("{: 14} - 0x{:08X} bucket {}
", key, fnv1a(key), fnv1a(key) % 8); return 0; } iron_sword - 0xAB515E15 bucket 5 iron_swore - 0xAA515C82 bucket 2 health_potion - 0xA92D125F bucket 7 - 0x811C9DC5 bucket 5 A change in the last letter moves the key to a different bucket. Notice, though, that iron_sword and iron_swore share some hex digits: FNV-1a is simple and fast, and the last byte it sees is only mixed in lightly. Hash tables that need better spreading run a short final "mixing" step over the result, like the hash function in this lesson's practice task. Games often hash asset names once, at build time, and refer to assets by the 32-bit hash at run time: comparing two numbers is much cheaper than comparing two strings. Collisions Different keys can land in the same bucket: there are endlessly many possible keys and only so many buckets. This is a collision , and every hash table has a strategy for it. Strategy How it works Used by --- --- --- Separate chaining Each bucket holds a small linked list of the entries that landed there std::unordered_map Open addressing Entries live directly in the bucket array; on a collision, try the next bucket (or another probe sequence) until a free one is found Many fast game-engine and third-party hash maps A lookup computes the hash, goes to the bucket, then compares keys until it finds a match. With a good hash and enough buckets, that is one or two comparisons. Load factor and rehashing The load factor is entries divided by buckets. As it rises, collisions become common and lookups slow down. So when the load factor passes a limit (1.0 for std::unordered_map by default), the table rehashes : it allocates more buckets and reinserts every entry, because hash % bucketCount changes when bucketCount does. Like vector growth, this is expensive once and cheap on average, and reserve(n) avoids it if you know the size in advance. std::unordered_map and std::map cpp include <iostream include <map include <string include <unordered_map int main() { std::unordered_map<std::string, int prices{ { "rope", 5 }, { "lantern", 12 }, { "sword", 40 } }; prices "shield" = 30; // insert if (auto it{ prices.find("lantern") }; it != prices.end()) std::cout << "lantern costs " << it- second << '
'; std::cout << "contains torch: " << prices.contains("torch") << '
'; std::map<std::string, int sorted{ prices.begin(), prices.end() }; for (const auto& name, price : sorted) std::cout << name << ' '; // always in key order std::cout << '
'; return 0; } lantern costs 12 contains torch: 0 lantern rope shield sword std::unordered_map std::map --- --- --- Structure Hash table Balanced binary tree (lesson 3.09) Lookup About constant time on average Grows with the logarithm of the size Iteration order Unspecified, changes as it grows Sorted by key Key needs A hash and == < Pick unordered_map for fast lookup, map when you need the keys in order. Both allocate a node per entry, so neither is especially cache friendly; performance-sensitive engines often use open-addressing tables instead. Where games use hashing - Asset and string lookup by name or by precomputed hash. - Spatial hashing : hash a grid cell's (x, y) to find the objects near a point without a grid for the whole world. - Caches : remember the result of an expensive calculation keyed by its inputs. - Detecting change : hash a save file or a block of data and compare hashes. (Hashes for this need to be strong; FNV-1a is fine for spotting accidents, not for detecting deliberate tampering.) Common mistakes !warning Relying on unordered_map iteration order It can differ between runs, compilers and sizes. Sort the keys, or use std::map , when order matters, such as when writing a save file. !warning Using operator to check whether a key exists m key inserts a default value if the key is missing. Use find or contains . !warning Keeping pointers or iterators across a rehash Rehashing invalidates iterators (though unordered_map keeps pointers to elements valid, since each lives in its own node). Check yourself quiz ? What two properties should a hash function have? - It should be reversible, and it should produce a number smaller than the key + It must give the same hash for the same key, and it should spread keys evenly - It should be random each time, and it should never collide - It should sort the keys, and it should be cryptographically secure Same key, same hash, or lookups would fail. Collisions cannot be avoided entirely; a good spread just keeps them rare. ? What is the load factor, and why does it matter? - The time a lookup takes; tables slow down as it rises - The number of collisions so far; it decides when to sort the table - The number of buckets divided by the number of entries; it measures wasted space + The number of entries divided by the number of buckets; a high one means more collisions, so tables rehash past a limit Growing and rehashing keeps buckets short so lookups stay fast. ? When would you choose std::map over std::unordered_map ? - When you need the fastest possible lookup + When you need the keys in sorted order, or a key's neighbours - When the keys are strings - When the map will hold more than a million entries std::map is a sorted tree; std::unordered_map is usually faster for plain lookup but has no order. ? What does a hash table do with a key's hash? - Stores the hash instead of the key - Sorts the entries by hash + Uses it to pick the one bucket a lookup must search hash % bucketCount picks the bucket; only the entries there are compared. ? Two different keys land in the same bucket. What is that called? - A rehash + A collision - Undefined behaviour Collisions are normal; the table's strategy (chaining or probing) handles them. ? Why does a hash table rehash when its load factor gets high? - To sort its entries by their hash values + To keep buckets short so lookups stay fast - To free the memory of removed entries Keeping entries per bucket low keeps lookups near constant time. ? You need to print all items in alphabetical order. Which container fits best? - std::unordered_map<std::string, Item + std::map<std::string, Item - Either; they iterate the same way std::map keeps its keys sorted; unordered_map has no meaningful order.

title: A hash table with open addressing
match: A hash table with open addressing
body: Build IdTable , a hash table mapping std::uint32_t ids to int values, using open addressing with linear probing . The table has a fixed number of slots, given to the constructor. Each slot is either empty or holds one key and its value. - The home slot of a key is hash(key) % slotCount , where hash is the function given below. - insert(key, value) : start at the home slot and move one slot at a time (wrapping round to 0 after the last slot) until you find either the same key, whose value you then replace, or an empty slot, where you put the new entry. Return true . If every slot is full of other keys, return false . - find(key) : probe the same way. Return the value if you meet the key; return std::nullopt when you reach an empty slot or have looked at every slot. - size() : how many keys are stored. There is no removing in this task (removal in open addressing needs special "deleted" markers).

title: 3.09  Trees and Graphs
body: When data has branches rather than a single line, pointers or indices join it into trees and graphs . Games are full of them: the scene graph of objects attached to other objects, the binary search tree inside std::map , the graph of rooms in a dungeon, and the grid a monster searches to find the player. This lesson covers the shapes, the two ways to walk them, and a shortest-path search. Trees A tree is a set of nodes where each node has one parent (except the single root ) and any number of children . There are no loops. The most visible tree in a game is the scene graph : a sword is attached to a hand, the hand to an arm, the arm to a knight, the knight to a horse. Move the horse and everything attached moves with it. cpp include <iostream include <memory include <string include <vector struct SceneNode { std::string name; float x{ 0 }; // position relative to the parent std::vector<std::unique_ptr<SceneNode children; SceneNode add(std::string childName, float childX) { children.push_back(std::make_unique<SceneNode (SceneNode{ std::move(childName), childX, {} })); return children.back().get(); } }; // Depth-first: handle a node, then each child's whole subtree in turn. void printWorld(const SceneNode& node, float parentX, int depth) { const float worldX{ parentX + node.x }; std::cout << std::string(depth 2, ' ') << node.name << " at " << worldX << '\n'; for (const auto& child : node.children) printWorld( child, worldX, depth + 1); } int main() { SceneNode world{ "world", 0, {} }; SceneNode horse{ world.add("horse", 10) }; SceneNode knight{ horse- add("knight", 0.5f) }; knight- add("sword", 0.75f); world.add("tree", 3); printWorld(world, 0, 0); return 0; } world at 0 horse at 10 knight at 10.5 sword at 11.25 tree at 3 Each node owns its children through std::unique_ptr , so destroying a node destroys its whole subtree. Each position is relative to the parent, and the walk adds them up on the way down: that is how attaching works. Binary search trees A binary search tree gives each node at most two children with a rule: everything in the left subtree is smaller than the node, everything in the right is larger. Finding a key means comparing at each node and going left or right, so a balanced tree of a million entries needs about 20 comparisons. std::map and std::set are balanced binary search trees (red-black trees in the common implementations). That is why they keep keys in order and why lookups cost "about log n" comparisons, not constant time like a hash table (lesson 3.08). Graphs A graph drops the tree's rules: any node can connect to any other, and connections can form loops. The nodes are often called vertices and the connections edges . Game graph Vertices Edges --- --- --- Dungeon layout Rooms Doors Navigation mesh Walkable regions Shared borders Tile map Walkable tiles Steps to neighbouring tiles Dialogue Lines of dialogue Player choices Quest dependencies Quests "Must finish first" Graphs are usually stored as an adjacency list : for each vertex, a list of the vertices it connects to. A tile map is a graph that needs no stored edges at all, because a tile's neighbours can be calculated from its position. Two ways to walk Every tree and graph algorithm builds on one of two orders of visiting: Depth-first search (DFS) Breadth-first search (BFS) --- --- --- Order Go as deep as possible down one branch, then back up Visit everything 1 step away, then everything 2 steps away, ... Natural tool A stack (or recursion) A queue Good for Visiting everything, scene graphs, flood fills Shortest paths where every step costs the same On a graph with loops, both must remember which vertices they have already visited, or they go round forever. The flood fill in lesson 2.01 was a depth-first search on a tile map. Shortest path on a grid with BFS To find how many steps a monster needs to reach the player, run a breadth-first search from the monster. Because BFS visits tiles in order of distance, the first time it reaches a tile, it has found the shortest way there. cpp include <iostream include <queue include <string include <vector // Steps from (sx, sy) to (tx, ty) moving up, down, left or right through '.' tiles; -1 if unreachable. int shortestSteps(const std::vector<std::string & map, int sx, int sy, int tx, int ty) { const int h{ static_cast<int (map.size()) }, w{ static_cast<int (map 0 .size()) }; std::vector<int dist(static_cast<std::size_t (w h), -1); // -1 means not reached yet std::queue<std::pair<int, int frontier; dist static_cast<std::size_t (sy w + sx) = 0; frontier.push({ sx, sy }); const int dx { 1, -1, 0, 0 }, dy { 0, 0, 1, -1 }; while (!frontier.empty()) { const auto x, y = frontier.front(); frontier.pop(); if (x == tx && y == ty) return dist static_cast<std::size_t (y w + x) ; for (int d{ 0 }; d < 4; ++d) { const int nx{ x + dx d }, ny{ y + dy d }; if (nx < 0 ny < 0 nx = w ny = h map ny nx == ' ') continue; int& seen{ dist static_cast<std::size_t (ny w + nx) }; if (seen != -1) continue; seen = dist static_cast<std::size_t (y w + x) + 1; frontier.push({ nx, ny }); } } return -1; } int main() { const std::vector<std::string map{ " ", " M.. ... ", " . . . . ", " . ... P ", " ", }; std::cout << shortestSteps(map, 1, 1, 7, 3) << '\n'; return 0; } 12 The queue is the whole trick: tiles are taken out in the order they were discovered, so all tiles at distance 3 come out before any at distance 4. Storing which tile each one was reached from (a "came from" array) lets you walk back from the target to recover the actual path. When steps have different costs (mud is slower than road), BFS becomes Dijkstra's algorithm , and with a distance estimate to guide it, A\ , which most game pathfinding uses. Chapter 11's monsters use this. Common mistakes !warning Forgetting the visited set on a graph A search on a graph with loops never ends. Mark vertices when you first discover them. !warning Recursion on deep trees A very deep or degenerate tree (one long chain) can overflow the stack, as in lesson 2.01. Use an explicit stack for data that might be deep. !warning Marking visited when popping instead of when pushing In BFS, mark a tile when you add it to the queue. Otherwise the same tile can be queued many times. Check yourself quiz ? What is a scene graph, and why do positions in it add up on the way down? + A tree of attached objects, each placed relative to its parent - A list of every object sorted by distance from the camera - A graph of which objects can see each other, with distances on the edges - A table of positions that the renderer adds together each frame A sword attached to a hand moves with the hand because its position is stored relative to the hand. ? What is the difference between depth-first and breadth-first search? - Depth-first uses a queue; breadth-first uses a stack + Depth-first follows one branch first (a stack); breadth-first goes by distance (a queue) - Depth-first only works on trees; breadth-first only works on grids - They visit the same places in the same order Visiting by distance is why breadth-first search finds the shortest path when every step costs the same. ? How do you recover the actual path, not just its length, from a BFS? + Record where each place was reached from, then follow it back - Run the search again backwards from the target - Keep a copy of the whole queue at every step One "came from" entry per place is all it takes; following them from the target to the start gives the path in reverse. ? What makes a tree different from a general graph? + Every node except the root has exactly one parent, and there are no loops - Trees cannot be stored with pointers - Trees always have exactly two children per node A binary tree has at most two children; a tree in general may have any number. ? Why does breadth-first search find the shortest path when every step costs the same? - It tries every possible path and keeps the shortest + It visits places by distance, so it reaches the target by a shortest route - It always moves towards the target first The queue ensures all places at distance n are handled before any at distance n + 1. ? What data structure drives a breadth-first search? - A stack + A queue - A hash table First in, first out: places are explored in the order they were discovered. ? What kind of structure is std::map built on? - A hash table + A balanced binary search tree - A sorted vector That is why it keeps keys in order and looks them up in logarithmic time.

title: 3.10  Containers of Game Objects: Entity Lists and Pools
match: 3.10 Containers of Game Objects: Entity Lists and Pools
body: A game creates and destroys objects constantly: bullets, particles, enemies, pickups. This lesson puts the chapter together into the structures engines use for them: dense arrays with swap-and-pop, object pools with free lists, and generational handles that let code refer to an object safely even after it has been destroyed and its slot reused. What games need A shooter might fire 50 bullets a second, each living for a second or two. A particle effect might spawn thousands of sparks. The container holding them must: 1. Loop fast , every frame, over everything alive. 2. Add and remove cheaply , many times per frame. 3. Let other code refer to an object (the missile's target, the player's selected unit) without that reference turning into a dangling pointer when the object dies. No single standard container does all three. These are the patterns engines combine. Pattern 1: a dense vector with swap-and-pop Keep live objects side by side in a std::vector , and remove with swap-and-pop (lesson 3.07): cpp include <iostream include <vector struct Bullet { float x; float speed; float life; }; void update(std::vector<Bullet & bullets, float dt) { for (std::size_t i{ 0 }; i < bullets.size(); ) { Bullet& b{ bullets i }; b.x += b.speed dt; b.life -= dt; if (b.life <= 0) { bullets i = bullets.back(); // swap-and-pop: the last bullet takes this slot bullets.pop_back(); // don't advance i: the moved bullet needs updating too } else ++i; } } int main() { std::vector<Bullet bullets{ { 0, 10, 0.05f }, { 0, 20, 1 }, { 0, 30, 0.05f }, { 0, 40, 1 } }; update(bullets, 0.1f); for (const Bullet& b : bullets) std::cout << b.speed << ' '; std::cout << '\n'; return 0; } 40 20 Fast to loop over, cheap to remove from. But it fails requirement 3: an object's position in the vector changes whenever another object is removed, so neither a pointer nor an index to it stays valid. Pattern 2: a pool with a free list A pool allocates a fixed array of slots once and never moves them. Each slot is either in use or free. The free slots form a linked list threaded through the slots themselves (an intrusive list, lesson 3.06), so finding a free slot is "take the head of the free list" and freeing one is "push it back on". slots: 0: bullet 1: free → 3 2: bullet 3: free → 4 4: free → end freeHead = 1 No heap allocations after start-up, objects never move, so a slot index stays valid while its object lives. Looping over the live objects means skipping free slots, which is slower than a dense vector when the pool is mostly empty. The remaining problem: stale references Suppose a missile stores "my target is slot 7". The target dies and slot 7 is freed. A moment later a new enemy is spawned into slot 7. The missile now chases the wrong enemy, and nothing tells it so. Index 7 is a dangling reference, just as a pointer would have been. Pattern 3: generational handles The fix is to give every slot a generation counter, incremented each time the slot is freed. A handle to an object is the pair (slot index, generation at the time). To use a handle, check that the slot's current generation still matches: The missile's handle says generation 3, the slot now says 4, so the lookup returns null: "your target no longer exists". The new bat in slot 7 gets handles with generation 4, which work normally. cpp struct Handle { std::uint32_t index; std::uint32_t generation; }; Eight bytes, trivially copyable, safe to store anywhere, safe to save to a file, and impossible to dangle. This is the approach used by most modern engines for entities, resources and anything else whose lifetime other systems cannot predict. The practice task is to build one. Choosing Need Use --- --- Many short-lived objects nobody else refers to (particles, bullets) Dense std::vector with swap-and-pop Objects referred to from elsewhere (enemies, units, items in the world) A pool with generational handles Both fast loops and stable handles A pool for identity plus a dense array of the data, with an index map between them (a "slot map" or "sparse set": the same idea, one step further) Few objects, created rarely Whatever is simplest: std::vector<std::unique_ptr<T is fine Chapter 10 uses these in its entity-component system. Common mistakes !warning Advancing the index after swap-and-pop The element moved into slot i has not been processed yet. Only advance when nothing was removed. !warning Storing raw pointers to pooled objects for later They stay valid in memory, but may point at a different object after reuse. Store handles. !warning Letting the generation counter wrap round quickly With a 32-bit counter it would take billions of reuses of one slot, which is fine. An 8-bit counter wraps after 256 and can, rarely, let a stale handle match again. Check yourself quiz ? What three things does a container of game objects usually need to do well? - Sort the objects, save them to disk and print them - Keep objects in creation order, never move them, and free them automatically + Loop quickly over live objects, add and remove them cheaply, and let other code refer to an object safely The patterns in the lesson each trade these three off differently. ? How does a generational handle detect that its object is gone? - It holds a pointer and checks whether it is null + The slot's generation changes on free, so the handle's no longer matches - The pool keeps a list of every handle ever made and deletes them - It asks the operating system whether the memory is still allocated The handle remembers the generation from when it was made, so a reused slot is recognised as a different object. ? Why are handles safer to store than pointers? - Handles are smaller than pointers - Handles keep the object alive - Handles cannot be copied + A stale handle is caught on lookup; a stale pointer is not The lookup turns a silent memory bug into a clear "the object is gone" result. ? Why does a dense vector with swap-and-pop not give objects stable references? - Vectors cannot be indexed + Removing one moves another into its slot - Swap-and-pop allocates memory The last element is moved to fill the gap, so its index changes. ? What does a pool's free list link together? - The live objects, in creation order - Every slot, used or not + The unused slots, through an index stored in each Allocating takes the head of the free list; freeing pushes the slot back on. ? A handle says (slot 12, generation 5). The pool's slot 12 has generation 6. What does a lookup return? - The object in slot 12 + Nothing: the object the handle referred to has been destroyed - The object, after updating the handle A different generation means the slot has been freed since the handle was made.

title: A pool with generational handles
where: 3.10 Containers of Game Objects: Entity Lists and Pools
body: Build EnemyPool , a pool of Enemy objects with a fixed number of slots, handed out through generational handles. - The constructor receives the number of slots. All start free, with generation 0. - create(enemy) puts enemy in a free slot and returns a Handle holding that slot's index and current generation. If no slot is free, it returns std::nullopt . - get(handle) returns a pointer to the enemy if the handle is still valid (the index is in range, the slot is in use, and its generation matches), otherwise nullptr . - destroy(handle) frees the slot if the handle is valid, incrementing the slot's generation so old handles stop working, and returns true ; otherwise it returns false and changes nothing. - alive() returns how many slots are in use. When creating, any free slot may be used; a free list is the efficient way, but a simple search is accepted.
