title: 4.01  Solutions, Projects and Build Configurations
where: Visual Studio and the Build Pipeline
body: A real game is not one .cpp file. It is a solution holding several projects , such as the game, an engine library, a tools DLL and a test runner, each built in several configurations and for one or more platforms . This lesson shows how Visual Studio organises that, where the settings live, and how to set up a multi-project solution you will reuse for the rest of the course. Solutions and projects Lesson 1.07 created one console project. From now on the course builds several things that belong together: a game, a library it uses, a DLL it loads, tests that check them. Visual Studio's structure for this is: Thing File What it is --- --- --- Solution .sln A list of projects, plus which of them to build in which configuration Project .vcxproj One output (an .exe , .dll or .lib ), its source files, and all its compiler and linker settings Filters .vcxproj.filters Only the folders shown in Solution Explorer. They do not have to match folders on disk User settings .vcxproj.user Your personal debugging settings, such as command arguments. Not shared A .vcxproj file is XML that you can open in a text editor. Everything in the Properties dialog ends up in it, which is useful when comparing two projects' settings or reviewing a change in version control. A solution for the course Here is the layout the rest of the course assumes. Create it now so later lessons can add to it. course\ course.sln engine\ Static library (.lib): shared code, such as maths, the tile map, memory helpers game\ Console app (.exe): the game itself, uses engine plugin\ Dynamic library (.dll): built in lesson 4.05 tests\ Console app (.exe): unit tests for engine 1. File → New → Project → Blank Solution , name it course . 2. Right-click the solution → Add → New Project → Static Library , name it engine . 3. Add a Console App named game , and another named tests . 4. Right-click game → Add → Reference → tick engine . Do the same for tests . 5. Right-click game → Set as Startup Project : F5 now runs the game. The reference does two things: it makes engine build before game , and it links engine.lib into game.exe automatically. You still have to tell the compiler where engine 's headers are: in game 's properties, C/C++ → General → Additional Include Directories , add $(SolutionDir)engine . Configurations and platforms Every project is built in a configuration for a platform . Visual Studio starts you with two of each: x64 Win32 (x86) --- --- --- Debug Debug, 64-bit Debug, 32-bit Release Release, 64-bit Release, 32-bit Each of the four combinations has its own complete set of settings. That is powerful (Debug can have checks Release does not), and it is the cause of the most common project mistake: changing a setting in one combination and wondering why another behaves differently. When a setting should apply everywhere, select All Configurations and All Platforms at the top of the Properties dialog before changing it. You can add your own configurations in Build → Configuration Manager . Common additions: - ASan : Debug plus AddressSanitizer (lesson 2.10). - Profile : Release with debug information and profiling hooks, for measuring (chapter 8). Macros in settings Paths in project settings use macros so they work on any machine. The ones you will use most: Macro Expands to --- --- $(SolutionDir) The folder holding the .sln , with a trailing backslash $(ProjectDir) The folder holding the .vcxproj $(Configuration) Debug or Release (or your own) $(Platform) x64 or Win32 $(OutDir) Where the project's output goes $(TargetPath) The full path of the .exe or .dll being built A tidy convention is to send every project's output to one folder per configuration, so the game, its DLLs and its tests end up side by side: set General → Output Directory to $(SolutionDir)bin\$(Platform)\$(Configuration)\ for all projects and all configurations. Property sheets When five projects need the same settings (C++20, warning level 4, the same output folder), setting them five times invites mistakes. A property sheet ( .props file) holds settings that several projects share. Open View → Other Windows → Property Manager , right-click a project → Add New Project Property Sheet , set things there, then add the same sheet to the other projects. Change it once and every project follows. Building from the command line Everything Visual Studio does can be done from the Developer PowerShell, which is how build servers do it: powershell msbuild course.sln /p:Configuration=Release /p:Platform=x64 /m /m builds projects in parallel. Being able to build without the IDE is useful for scripts, and for checking that a build does not secretly depend on something only your IDE session had set up. Common mistakes !warning Settings changed in one configuration only If Debug works and Release does not, compare the two configurations' settings. Use All Configurations for project-wide options. !warning Including another project's headers by relative path include "../engine/tilemap.h" breaks when files move. Add the folder to Additional Include Directories and write include "tilemap.h" . !warning Committing .vs , bin , obj and x64 folders They are build output and caches. A .gitignore for Visual Studio projects excludes them. Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference between a solution and a project? - A solution builds one exe; a project groups several solutions - A project is a folder of source files; a solution is the program they build + A project builds one output (exe, dll or lib) from its sources and settings; a solution groups related projects - They are the same; Visual Studio uses both words for one file The solution also records which projects to build in which configuration. ? Why might a setting work in Debug but not in Release? + Each configuration has its own settings, so a Debug-only change misses Release - Release builds ignore all project settings - Release builds reset the settings to defaults every time - Settings only take effect after the solution is closed and reopened Check the Configuration and Platform boxes at the top of the Property Pages before changing a setting, or choose All Configurations. ? What is a property sheet for? + Holding settings shared by several projects, so they are set once and stay consistent - Listing the files a project contains - Storing the breakpoints of a debugging session - Recording which version of Visual Studio created the solution Each project that imports the sheet picks up its settings, so changing them in one place changes them everywhere. ? What does adding a project reference from game to engine do? + Builds engine first and links its output into game - Copies engine 's source files into game - Adds engine 's headers to the include path It sets the build order and the linking. Include directories are a separate setting. ? Where are a project's compiler and linker settings stored? - In the .sln file + In the .vcxproj file and its property sheets - In the Windows registry The solution only lists projects; each project file holds its own settings. ? What does $(Configuration) expand to? - The full path of the output file - The project's folder + The configuration being built, such as Debug Macros let one setting work for every configuration and machine.

title: 4.02  Preprocessor, Compiler, Linker: Who Does What
match: 4.02 Preprocessor, Compiler, Linker: Who Does What
where: Visual Studio and the Build Pipeline
body: Lesson 1.04 introduced the four build stages. This lesson goes deeper into the rules that decide which file needs what: declarations versus definitions , headers and include guards, the one definition rule , inline and static , and how the linker matches symbols between object files. These rules explain almost every "already defined" and "unresolved" error you will meet. Declarations and definitions C++ separates saying something exists from saying what it is. Declaration: "this exists" Definition: "here it is" --- --- --- Function int addBonus(int score); int addBonus(int score) { return score + 50; } Global variable extern int g_highScore; int g_highScore{ 0 }; Class class Player; (a forward declaration) class Player { int health; }; A declaration is enough to use a function: the compiler only needs to know its name, parameters and return type to generate a call. The call's target address is left for the linker. A definition is what produces machine code or storage. Headers carry declarations Each .cpp file is compiled alone (it becomes one translation unit ). For main.cpp to call a function defined in score.cpp , main.cpp needs its declaration. A header file is simply a convenient way to paste the same declarations into every file that needs them: cpp // score.h pragma once int addBonus(int score); // declaration // score.cpp include "score.h" int addBonus(int score) { return score + 50; } // the one definition // main.cpp include "score.h" int main() { return addBonus(10); } // a call, resolved by the linker pragma once stops a header from being pasted twice into the same translation unit, which would otherwise repeat its class definitions and fail. The older, portable form is an include guard : cpp ifndef SCORE_H define SCORE_H int addBonus(int score); endif The one definition rule The one definition rule (ODR) says, roughly: - every function and global variable that is used must be defined exactly once in the whole program; - a class, an inline function or a template may be defined in every translation unit that uses it, but all those definitions must be identical. That second point is why class definitions and templates live in headers, and why ordinary function bodies do not. Break the first point and the linker complains: Situation Linker error --- --- A function is declared and called, but defined nowhere LNK2019: unresolved external symbol A function body written in a header included by two .cpp files LNK2005: already defined in main.obj A global int g_score{ 0 }; in a header LNK2005 as well Ways to make a definition safe in a header Keyword Effect Use for --- --- --- inline "Identical definitions may appear in many files; keep one" Small functions in headers; inline variables (C++17) for header constants static (at namespace scope) "Private to this translation unit": each file gets its own separate copy Helpers used only in one .cpp Unnamed namespace { ... } Same as static , for everything inside Several file-private helpers constexpr variable Implicitly inline (since C++17) for static data members; namespace-scope constexpr variables are internal to each file Compile-time constants Templates and functions defined inside a class body are implicitly inline , which is why they can live in headers. Symbols: what the linker actually matches Each object file contains a symbol table : names it defines and names it needs. C++ names are mangled into strings that encode the namespace, parameter types and more, so that overloads get different symbols: int addBonus(int) ?addBonus@@YAHH@Z int addBonus(float) ?addBonus@@YAHM@Z void Player::heal(int) ?heal@Player@@QEAAXH@Z The linker matches these strings exactly. So a declaration that differs from its definition in any detail (a const , a parameter type, a namespace) produces a different symbol, and the result is LNK2019 even though "the function is right there". The error message shows the mangled name and a readable version; compare it carefully with your definition. extern "C" turns mangling off, giving the plain name addBonus . That is how C++ code exposes functions to C, and how DLLs usually export functions so other languages and GetProcAddress (lesson 4.05) can find them by a simple name. You can see an object file's symbols with: powershell dumpbin /symbols score.obj dumpbin /exports plugin.dll undname "?addBonus@@YAHH@Z" Order of the stages, once more Changing a.cpp recompiles only a.obj , then re-links. Changing a header recompiles every .cpp that includes it, directly or indirectly. That is why large projects keep headers small, use forward declarations where they can, and avoid including heavy headers in other headers. Common mistakes !warning A declaration that does not quite match its definition void heal(int) declared, void heal(long) defined: two different symbols, and an unresolved external. Copy declarations from definitions exactly. !warning Globals defined in headers Declare extern int g_score; in the header and define it in one .cpp , or use inline int g_score{ 0 }; . !warning Including a header to get a type you only point to If a header only uses Player or Player& , a forward declaration class Player; is enough, and saves recompiling when player.h changes. Check yourself quiz ? What does the one definition rule require? - Every function may be declared only once in the program - Each .cpp file may define only one function + Each used function and variable is defined exactly once in the program - Every header may be included only once in the whole program Declarations may be repeated freely. It is definitions of ordinary functions and variables that must be unique. Classes, templates and inline functions may be defined in several files, but only if every definition is identical. ? Why do class definitions go in headers but function bodies usually do not? - Function bodies are too long for headers - Headers can only contain types, not code - The compiler reads headers before .cpp files, so bodies there would run first + Classes may be defined (identically) in every translation unit; ordinary functions must be defined only once A function body in a header included by two .cpp files is defined twice, which breaks the one definition rule unless it is marked inline . ? What is name mangling? - Shortening long names to save space in the .exe + Encoding a function's namespace, class and parameter types into its symbol - Hiding names so the program cannot be reverse engineered - Renaming variables that clash with keywords That is how overloads such as heal(int) and heal(unsigned) get distinct symbols, and why they do not link to each other. ? Which is a definition, not just a declaration? - int addBonus(int score); - extern int g_lives; + int g_lives{ 3 }; It creates the variable's storage. The others only announce that something exists elsewhere. ? Two .cpp files include a header containing int square(int x) { return x x; } . What happens? - It compiles and links fine + The linker reports that square is already defined - The compiler reports a syntax error Each file gets a definition, breaking the one definition rule. Marking it inline fixes it. ? Why does a declaration void heal(int) not link to a definition void heal(unsigned) ? - The linker ignores parameters - unsigned cannot be used in definitions + Parameter types are part of the mangled symbol name C++ symbols encode the parameter types so that overloads can coexist. ? What does extern "C" change? + It turns off name mangling, so the symbol is the plain name - It makes the function run faster - It makes the function private to one file Plain names are what C code, other languages and GetProcAddress expect.

title: Be the linker
where: 4.02 Preprocessor, Compiler, Linker: Who Does What
body: Write linkErrors(objects) , a tiny linker that only checks symbols. Each ObjectFile has a name, the symbols it defines and the symbols it needs . The function returns the list of errors, in this order: 1. For every symbol defined in more than one object file: "duplicate X" , once per symbol, with symbols in alphabetical order. 2. For every symbol needed by some object file but defined in none: "unresolved X" , once per symbol, with symbols in alphabetical order. A symbol that an object file both needs and defines itself is fine. No errors means an empty list. main.obj defines main needs addBonus, printf score.obj defines addBonus needs (nothing) crt.lib defines printf - no errors without score.obj - { "unresolved addBonus" }

title: 4.03  Reading Compiler and Linker Errors
where: Visual Studio and the Build Pipeline
body: Build errors look intimidating because one mistake can produce a screen of messages. This lesson gives a method (find the first error, read its code, go to its line, ignore the cascade), and a field guide to the MSVC errors and warnings you will meet most often, with what each usually means. The method 1. Use the Output window, not just the Error List. The Error List sorts and groups messages; the Output window ( View → Output , "Show output from: Build") shows them in the order they happened, with the full text and the "see declaration of..." notes that follow each one. 2. Fix the first error first. One missing ; or } makes the compiler misread everything after it, producing dozens of follow-on errors that vanish once the first is fixed. Rebuild after each fix. 3. Read the code. C codes come from the compiler, LNK codes from the linker. Warnings are C4xxx . Searching for the code (for example "C2664") finds Microsoft's page explaining it. 4. Go to the line, then look just before it. The compiler reports where it noticed the problem, which is often the line after the real mistake. 5. Read the types in the message slowly. Most of a long message is the names of the types involved. The interesting part is usually "cannot convert from X to Y". A worked example cpp-norun include <string include <vector struct Item { std::string name; int weight; }; int totalWeight(const std::vector<Item & items) { int total{ 0 } for (const Item& item : items) total += item.weight; return total; } MSVC reports: main.cpp(8,19): error C2143: syntax error: missing ';' before 'for' main.cpp(10,9): error C2065: 'item': undeclared identifier main.cpp(10,9): error C2228: left of '.weight' must have class/struct/union Three errors, one mistake. The first one names the real problem: int total{ 0 } on line 7 is missing its ; , which the compiler only noticed on reaching for on line 8. Because it then misread the for , it never declared item , so lines 10's errors are just a cascade. Add the semicolon and all three disappear. Compiler errors you will see most Code Message (shortened) Usually means --- --- --- C2143 syntax error: missing ';' before ... A missing ; , ) or } just before the reported spot C2065 undeclared identifier A typo, a missing include , or a name used before its declaration C3861 identifier not found Same, for a function call C2039 is not a member of Typo in a member name, or the wrong type C2664 cannot convert argument N from X to Y The argument has the wrong type; read X and Y carefully (const? pointer vs reference?) C2440 cannot convert from X to Y An assignment or initialisation with the wrong type C2662 cannot convert 'this' pointer from const X to X& Calling a non- const member function on a const object: make the function const C2280 attempting to reference a deleted function Copying something that cannot be copied, such as a std::unique_ptr ; use std::move or a reference C2027 use of undefined type Only a forward declaration is visible where the full class is needed: include its header C2011 type redefinition A header included twice without pragma once C1083 cannot open include file Wrong file name, or the folder is missing from Additional Include Directories Linker errors Code Usually means --- --- LNK2019 Unresolved external symbol : declared and used, never defined in anything linked. Missing .cpp in the project, missing library in Linker → Input, or a declaration that does not match its definition exactly (lesson 4.02). LNK2001 Also unresolved, usually for a variable or a virtual function's vtable: a class with a virtual function declared but never defined LNK1120 "N unresolved externals": a summary; fix the LNK2019s above it LNK2005 Already defined : a function or global defined in a header included by several .cpp files LNK1104 Cannot open file: often the .exe is still running and locked, or a library path is wrong LNK1168 Cannot open X.exe for writing: the program is still running. Close it. A linker error message contains the symbol, mangled and readable. The readable form tells you exactly which function and which overload is missing. Warnings worth treating as errors Warnings point at code that compiles but is probably wrong. At warning level 4 these are the most valuable: Warning Meaning --- --- C4700 Uninitialised local variable used C4701 Potentially uninitialised local variable used C4172 Returning the address of a local variable C4244 Conversion that may lose data, such as double to int C4267 size_t to int conversion, possible loss of data C4018 / C4389 Signed and unsigned comparison C4715 Not all control paths return a value C4996 Using a function marked unsafe or deprecated, such as strcpy Turning on Treat Warnings As Errors ( /WX ) keeps the list at zero, which is the only way warnings stay useful: once there are fifty of them, nobody reads the fifty-first. Template errors Errors inside templates (including the standard library) can run to dozens of lines, because the compiler reports the whole chain of instantiations. Read them from the bottom of the "see reference to..." chain, where the template was first used from your code: that is the line to look at. The usual causes are passing a type that lacks something the template needs (no < for std::sort , not copyable for std::vector::push_back ). Common mistakes !warning Fixing errors from the bottom of the list Later errors are often caused by earlier ones. Fix the first and rebuild. !warning Trusting the reported line exactly Look at the line before, especially for missing semicolons and braces. !warning Ignoring warnings C4700, C4172 and C4715 are bugs the compiler has already found for you. Check yourself quiz ? Why fix the first error first? - Because the compiler only reports the first error correctly - Because errors are listed from easiest to hardest + Because later errors are often caused by the compiler misreading code after the first mistake - Because fixing errors in any other order breaks the build One missing semicolon or bracket can produce dozens of errors; fixing it often clears the rest. ? How can you tell a compiler error from a linker error? - Compiler errors are red; linker errors are yellow - Linker errors always name a line number; compiler errors do not - Compiler errors only appear in Release builds + Compiler errors have codes starting with C ; linker errors start with LNK Linker errors only appear once every file has compiled, and they name symbols rather than source lines. ? What does C2664 usually tell you, and what should you read in it? + An argument has the wrong type; compare the "from X to Y" types - A function is missing its definition; read the symbol name - A header could not be found; read the include path - A variable is used before it is declared; read the line number The two types often differ only by a const , a or a & , so compare them character by character. Look closely at const-ness, pointers and references: the two types often differ only there. ? A build shows 40 errors. What should you do first? - Fix the error that appears most often + Fix the first error in the Output window and rebuild - Start from the last error Most of the rest are probably a cascade from the first. ? error C2280: attempting to reference a deleted function appears when pushing a std::unique_ptr into a vector. What is the fix? - Make the pointer const - Use new instead + Move it in: v.push_back(std::move(ptr)); unique_ptr cannot be copied; its copy constructor is deleted. It can be moved. ? LNK1168: cannot open game.exe for writing . What is the most likely cause? - A missing library + The program is still running from the last build - A syntax error in main Windows will not let the linker overwrite an executable that is running. ? Which warning tells you a function can end without returning a value? - C4244 + C4715 - C4996 Falling off the end of a non-void function is undefined behaviour.

title: 4.04  Static Libraries
where: Visual Studio and the Build Pipeline
body: A static library ( .lib ) is a bundle of object files. Linking it into a program copies in the parts the program uses, so the result is one self-contained .exe . This lesson builds the course's engine library, shows how the linker pulls code out of it, and covers the settings that must match between a library and the program that uses it. A bundle of object files When a project's Configuration Type is Static library (.lib) , its build stops after compiling: instead of linking the object files into an executable, the librarian ( lib.exe ) packs them into one .lib file with an index of the symbols each defines. When a program links against engine.lib , the linker looks up each unresolved symbol in the index and copies in only the object files that define what is needed . If the game never calls anything in random.obj , none of it ends up in the .exe . Building the engine library In the course solution from lesson 4.01, engine is already a static library project. Give it some real code: cpp // engine/vec2.h pragma once struct Vec2 { float x{ 0 }; float y{ 0 }; }; Vec2 operator+(Vec2 a, Vec2 b); Vec2 operator (Vec2 v, float s); float length(Vec2 v); cpp // engine/vec2.cpp include "vec2.h" include <cmath Vec2 operator+(Vec2 a, Vec2 b) { return { a.x + b.x, a.y + b.y }; } Vec2 operator (Vec2 v, float s) { return { v.x s, v.y s }; } float length(Vec2 v) { return std::sqrt(v.x v.x + v.y v.y); } cpp // game/main.cpp include <iostream include "vec2.h" int main() { Vec2 position{ 1, 2 }; Vec2 velocity{ 3, 4 }; position = position + velocity 0.5f; std::cout << position.x << ", " << position.y << " speed " << length(velocity) << '\n'; return 0; } With the project reference and include directory from lesson 4.01 in place, building the solution builds engine.lib first, then compiles main.cpp and links it with engine.lib . The output prints 2.5, 4 speed 5 . Without a project reference (for example, a library someone else built), you tell the linker yourself: - Linker → General → Additional Library Directories : the folder containing the .lib ; - Linker → Input → Additional Dependencies : the file name, engine.lib ; - or, in code, pragma comment(lib, "engine.lib") . Settings that must match Object files compiled with different settings may not work together, and the linker catches some (not all) of these mismatches: Setting Must match because Mismatch error --- --- --- Platform (x64 / x86) 64-bit and 32-bit code cannot be mixed LNK1112: module machine type conflicts Runtime library ( /MD , /MDd , /MT , /MTd ) Each object file asks for a particular C runtime; they must agree LNK2038: mismatch detected for 'RuntimeLibrary' Debug / Release ( _ITERATOR_DEBUG_LEVEL ) Standard containers have different layouts in Debug and Release LNK2038: mismatch detected for '_ITERATOR_DEBUG_LEVEL' C++ standard, struct packing, other defines that change layout A class laid out differently in two files is a silent ODR violation Usually none: just strange crashes The LNK2038 checks exist because these mismatches used to cause baffling crashes: a std::vector passed from a Release library to Debug code has a different layout on each side. So build every library in the same configuration as the program . A project reference does this automatically; a pre-built library usually ships in both Debug and Release forms for this reason. The runtime library choice deserves a note. /MD links the C and C++ runtime as DLLs (the user needs the Visual C++ Redistributable installed); /MT copies the runtime into your executable. Either is fine for this course; just be consistent across every project in the solution. Static libraries versus DLLs Static library DLL (next lesson) --- --- --- When code is joined At link time, copied into the .exe At run time, loaded from a separate file Files to ship Just the .exe The .exe and every .dll Updating the library Rebuild and relink the program Replace the .dll Loading code chosen at run time (plugins) Not possible Possible Sharing between programs Each program has its own copy One file can be shared The course uses a static library for the engine, which the game always needs, and a DLL for plugins, which the game chooses to load. Common mistakes !warning Linking a Debug library into a Release program LNK2038 warns you. Use project references, or link the matching build of the library. !warning Expecting a static library to work without its headers The .lib holds code; your program still needs the declarations from its headers to call it. !warning Global objects in a static library that nothing references The linker only pulls in object files that define something needed. A self-registering global in an otherwise unreferenced .obj is silently left out. Check yourself quiz ? How does the linker decide which parts of a static library go into the program? - It copies the whole library into every program + It takes each object file that defines a symbol still needed - It copies only the functions named in the project settings - It copies nothing; the library is loaded at run time Unused object files are left out, which is why a program using one function from a large library stays small. It repeats until nothing more is needed, so unused object files are left out. ? Why must a library be built with the same runtime library and configuration as the program? + Mismatches disagree about the runtime and standard type layouts - Otherwise the linker cannot find the .lib file - Because the library's functions would run in a different process - Because Visual Studio only allows one configuration per solution LNK2038 "mismatch detected" errors are the linker catching exactly this. ? When would you choose a DLL over a static library? - When you want the program to start faster - When the library is small and only used by one program - When you want every function inlined into the program + When code must be loaded or replaced at run time, as with plugins A static library is copied into each program at link time; a DLL stays a separate file loaded when needed. ? What does a static library contain? - A finished program - Only header files + Object files and an index of their symbols It is an archive of compiled code, ready to be linked. ? The game uses only length from engine.lib . What gets copied into game.exe ? + The object file that defines length , and what it needs - The whole library - Nothing; it is loaded at run time The linker pulls in object files on demand, by symbol. ? LNK2038: mismatch detected for '_ITERATOR_DEBUG_LEVEL' . What does it mean? - The library was built as 32-bit code + Debug-built and Release-built code are mixed - A function in the library is missing Debug and Release standard containers have different layouts; mixing them is unsafe.

title: 4.05  Dynamic Libraries: Building and Loading Your Own DLL
match: 4.05 Dynamic Libraries: Building and Loading Your Own DLL
where: Visual Studio and the Build Pipeline
body:
A DLL is a library that stays a separate file and is joined to a program when it runs. This lesson builds a DLL, exports functions from it, uses it in the two ways Windows offers ( load-time linking through an import library, and run-time loading with LoadLibrary and GetProcAddress ), and covers the rules about DllMain , memory and C++ types across the boundary. What a DLL is A dynamic-link library is built much like an .exe : compiled and linked into a PE file (chapter 9) with code, data and imports. The difference is that it has no main ; instead it exports functions and variables for programs to use. kernel32.dll , user32.dll and the C++ runtime are all DLLs, and every Windows program uses dozens of them. The Windows loader maps a DLL into the process's address space and fills in the addresses of its exports wherever the program needs them. One DLL file on disk can be loaded into many processes at once. Building one Add a project to the course solution: Dynamic-Link Library (DLL) , named plugin . Replace its code with: cpp // plugin/plugin.h: shared with the programs that use the DLL pragma once ifdef PLUGIN_EXPORTS define PLUGIN_API extern "C" __declspec(dllexport) else define PLUGIN_API extern "C" __declspec(dllimport) endif PLUGIN_API int pluginVersion(); PLUGIN_API int scaleDamage(int damage, int level); cpp // plugin/plugin.cpp include "plugin.h" int pluginVersion() { return 3; } int scaleDamage(int damage, int level) { return damage + damage level / 10; } In the plugin project's properties, add PLUGIN_EXPORTS to C/C++ → Preprocessor → Preprocessor Definitions (the DLL template usually adds a similar name already). The same header then means "export" inside the DLL and "import" everywhere else. - __declspec(dllexport) puts the function in the DLL's export table . - extern "C" gives it a plain, unmangled name (lesson 4.02), so it can be found as scaleDamage rather than ?scaleDamage@@YAHHH@Z . Building produces two files: plugin.dll , the code, and plugin.lib , a small import library that only says "these symbols live in plugin.dll". powershell dumpbin /exports plugin.dll ordinal hint RVA name 1 0 00011023 pluginVersion 2 1 00011028 scaleDamage Using it, way 1: load-time linking Add a project reference from game to plugin (or link plugin.lib ), include plugin.h , and call the functions normally: cpp include <iostream include "plugin.h" int main() { std::cout << "plugin version " << pluginVersion() << '
'; std::cout << "level 5 damage: " << scaleDamage(40, 5) << '
'; return 0; } The linker uses the import library to record, in game.exe 's import table , that it needs scaleDamage from plugin.dll . When the game starts, the loader finds plugin.dll (in the .exe 's folder first, then the system folders and PATH ), maps it, and fills in the addresses. If the DLL is missing, the game does not start at all: Windows shows "The code execution cannot proceed because plugin.dll was not found." Using it, way 2: run-time loading The program can instead load the DLL itself, when and if it chooses, and look functions up by name. No import library and no reference are needed, which is exactly what a plugin system wants: the game does not know at build time which plugins exist. cpp include <windows.h include <iostream using ScaleDamageFn = int ( )(int, int); int main() { HMODULE module{ LoadLibraryW(L"plugin.dll") }; if (!module) { std::cout << "no plugin found, error " << GetLastError() << '
'; return 1; } auto scale{ reinterpret_cast<ScaleDamageFn (GetProcAddress(module, "scaleDamage")) }; if (scale) std::cout << "level 5 damage: " << scale(40, 5) << '
'; FreeLibrary(module); return 0; } - LoadLibraryW maps the DLL and returns an HMODULE , which is the address the DLL was loaded at. - GetProcAddress looks a name up in its export table and returns the function's address, or null. - The result is cast to the right function pointer type (lesson 3.04). The cast is a promise you make: if the signature is wrong, the call corrupts the stack or registers. - FreeLibrary unloads it. Any pointer into the DLL is invalid after that. Chapter 13 builds a full plugin system on this. DllMain: keep it tiny A DLL may define DllMain , which Windows calls when the DLL is loaded into a process, unloaded, and when threads start and stop: cpp include <windows.h BOOL APIENTRY DllMain(HMODULE module, DWORD reason, LPVOID) { if (reason == DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH) DisableThreadLibraryCalls(module); return TRUE; } DllMain runs while Windows holds the loader lock , a lock that serialises all DLL loading in the process. Doing almost anything interesting there (loading another DLL, waiting for a thread, calling into COM, even some C++ static initialisation that does those things) can deadlock the process. The rule: in DllMain , do nothing that could wait or load. Put real initialisation in an exported init function that the program calls after loading. Rules for the boundary A DLL and the program that loads it are built separately, possibly by different compilers or settings. So the interface between them should be simple: - Plain C types across the boundary : integers, floats, pointers to plain structs, function pointers. Passing std::string or std::vector across works only if both sides were built with the same compiler version and settings, and is a common source of crashes. - Free memory on the side that allocated it. If the DLL allocates with its own runtime, it should provide a function to free it too. Mixing heaps between modules is a classic crash. - Version your interface. An exported pluginVersion (like the one above) lets the program refuse a plugin built for an incompatible interface. Common mistakes !warning The DLL is not next to the .exe Set every project's output directory to the same folder (lesson 4.01), or the loader cannot find it. !warning Forgetting extern "C" GetProcAddress(module, "scaleDamage") returns null because the exported name is mangled. !warning Calling functions after FreeLibrary The code is gone from memory; the call jumps into nothing and crashes. !warning Real work inside DllMain Deadlocks under the loader lock are hard to diagnose. Export an init function instead. Check yourself quiz ? What are the two ways a program can use a DLL? - Copying its code into the program, or running it as a separate process - Including its header, or compiling its source into the program + Load-time linking through an import library, or run-time loading with LoadLibrary and GetProcAddress With load-time linking the loader resolves the DLL when the program starts; with run-time loading the program loads it and looks functions up itself. ? Why should only simple C types cross a DLL boundary? - Because DLLs cannot contain classes - Because simple types are faster to copy + Each side may lay out standard library types differently - Because the Windows loader rejects DLLs that export C++ types An int or a plain struct of fixed types means the same on both sides; a std::string may not. The DLL and the program may use different compilers, settings or heaps. ? What does GetProcAddress return, and what must you do with it? + An exported function's address; cast it to the exact signature - A handle to the DLL; pass it to LoadLibrary to start the function - The function's name as a string; look it up in the import library - A copy of the function's code; run it with CreateThread Calling through a pointer with the wrong signature compiles fine and then corrupts the call, so the signature must match exactly. ? What is the import library ( plugin.lib ) produced alongside plugin.dll for? - It contains a copy of the DLL's code - It is needed by LoadLibrary + It tells the linker which symbols are in the DLL The import library holds no code. It lets the linker record the DLL dependency in the program's import table. ? Why is extern "C" usually used for DLL exports meant for GetProcAddress ? + It exports the plain function name instead of a mangled C++ name - It makes the function faster - GetProcAddress only works with C code GetProcAddress looks names up exactly as they appear in the export table. ? A program links to plugin.dll at load time, and the DLL is missing. What happens? - The program starts and calls to the DLL return 0 + The program fails to start, with a message naming the missing DLL - The program starts and crashes on the first call Load-time dependencies are resolved before main runs. Run-time loading lets a program cope with a missing DLL. ? Why should DllMain do as little as possible? - It runs before memory is available - It is called only once per computer + It runs under the loader lock, where waiting can deadlock Do real setup in a separate exported function the program calls after loading.

title: 4.06  Managing Dependencies with vcpkg
where: Visual Studio and the Build Pipeline
body: Real projects use other people's libraries: a window and input library, an image loader, a user interface toolkit. vcpkg is Microsoft's package manager for C and C++: you list the libraries a project needs in a vcpkg.json file, and it downloads, builds and links them with settings that match your project. This lesson sets it up for the course's later chapters. The problem vcpkg solves Using a third-party C++ library by hand means: find its source, build it with the right compiler, platform, runtime library and configuration (lesson 4.04's matching rules), copy its headers somewhere, add include and library paths to your project, and repeat for every library it depends on, and again for every machine that builds your project. vcpkg automates all of that. It knows how to build thousands of libraries, builds each one to match your project's triplet (for example x64-windows : 64-bit, DLL runtime), and plugs the results into MSBuild so your project finds headers and libraries automatically. Getting vcpkg Visual Studio 2022 includes a copy of vcpkg, available in the Developer PowerShell as vcpkg . To check: powershell vcpkg --version If the command is not found, install the vcpkg package manager component from the Visual Studio Installer (Individual components tab), or clone it yourself: powershell git clone https://github.com/microsoft/vcpkg C:\dev\vcpkg C:\dev\vcpkg\bootstrap-vcpkg.bat C:\dev\vcpkg\vcpkg integrate install integrate install connects vcpkg to every MSBuild project for your user account. Manifest mode: dependencies in a file The modern way to use vcpkg is manifest mode : a vcpkg.json file next to your solution lists what the project needs, so anyone who builds it gets the same libraries. powershell cd course vcpkg new --application vcpkg add port fmt vcpkg add port sdl2 That creates and fills vcpkg.json : json { "dependencies": "fmt", "sdl2" } Then, in each project that should use vcpkg: Properties → vcpkg → Use Vcpkg Manifest: Yes . The next build reads the manifest, builds the listed libraries (the first time takes a while; later builds reuse the results) and adds their include folders, libraries and DLLs to the project. DLLs are copied next to your .exe automatically. cpp-norun include <fmt/core.h int main() { fmt::print("{} has {} health\n", "Rook", 87); return 0; } No include paths, no library paths, no copying: the manifest is the only thing you wrote. Triplets: matching the build A triplet names the platform and the linkage vcpkg should build for. Triplet Platform Libraries built as C runtime --- --- --- --- x64-windows 64-bit DLLs DLL ( /MD ) x64-windows-static 64-bit Static .lib Static ( /MT ) x64-windows-static-md 64-bit Static .lib DLL ( /MD ) vcpkg picks x64-windows for an x64 project by default and builds Debug and Release versions of every library, linking the right one for each configuration. If your projects use /MT (as the course's static builds might), set Properties → vcpkg → Use Static Libraries: Yes so the libraries match. Pinning versions By default, vcpkg uses whichever versions its own copy currently has. For a project you want to build the same way next year, add a baseline , which pins every library to the versions vcpkg had at a particular commit: powershell vcpkg x-update-baseline --add-initial-baseline The manifest gains a "builtin-baseline" line. Commit vcpkg.json to version control; do not commit the vcpkg_installed folder it creates, which is build output. Libraries this course uses later Library vcpkg port Used in --- --- --- SDL2: windows, input, simple 2D drawing sdl2 Chapter 11 (the small game) Dear ImGui: immediate-mode user interfaces imgui sdl2-binding,sdl2-renderer-binding Chapter 14 (tool interfaces) Catch2 or GoogleTest: unit testing catch2 , gtest Chapter 17 fmt: formatting (most of it is now std::format ) fmt Optional Common mistakes !warning Mixing manifest mode and manually copied libraries Two copies of a library's headers on the include path, from different versions, cause confusing errors. Let vcpkg own each library. !warning A triplet that does not match the runtime library A static-runtime project with DLL-runtime libraries gives LNK2038 . Match them with the vcpkg project settings. !warning Committing vcpkg_installed It is large and machine-specific build output. Add it to .gitignore . Check yourself quiz ? What three jobs does vcpkg do for each dependency? + Downloads the source, builds it to match the project's triplet, and connects headers, libraries and DLLs to the project - Writes the library's code, tests it and publishes it - Downloads a prebuilt .exe , installs it in Program Files and adds it to PATH - Checks the licence, compresses the library and emails it to the team The triplet describes platform and runtime, so the library is built to match the project's settings. ? What does manifest mode mean? - vcpkg installs every library it knows about once for the whole machine + The project's dependencies are listed in vcpkg.json , and vcpkg installs them automatically on build - Dependencies are listed in the project's .vcxproj file by hand - vcpkg reads the include lines and guesses what to install The manifest lives with the project, so anyone who builds it gets the same dependencies. ? Which files from vcpkg belong in version control? - The whole vcpkg_installed folder, so others need not rebuild - None: vcpkg files are personal settings - Only the built .lib and .dll files + vcpkg.json (and vcpkg-configuration.json if present), not the vcpkg_installed output The manifest is enough to recreate the build output, which is large and machine-specific. ? What does vcpkg.json describe? + The libraries a project depends on - How to build vcpkg itself - The project's compiler settings Anyone building the project gets the same dependencies from the manifest. ? What is a vcpkg triplet? - Three versions of the same library + The target platform and linking, e.g. x64-windows-static - A group of three packages It ensures the libraries are built to match the project. ? Why add a baseline to the manifest? - To make the build faster - To enable static linking + To pin library versions for later builds Without it, versions follow whatever vcpkg copy is installed.

title: 4.07  The Debugger: Breakpoints, Stepping and the Call Stack
match: 4.07 The Debugger: Breakpoints, Stepping and the Call Stack
where: Visual Studio and the Build Pipeline
body: Lesson 1.08 was a first session. This lesson covers the debugger as a daily tool: every way of controlling execution (run to cursor, step into a specific call, set the next statement), moving around the Call Stack, breaking when an exception is thrown, Just My Code, and attaching to a program that is already running. How a debugger stops a program It helps to know what a breakpoint is. When you set one on a line, the debugger finds the first machine instruction for that line and overwrites its first byte with 0xCC , the int 3 instruction. When the CPU reaches it, the processor raises a breakpoint exception ; Windows sees that a debugger is attached to the process and hands it the event. The debugger then puts the original byte back, shows you the line, and waits. Stepping works similarly: the debugger sets temporary breakpoints, or turns on the processor's trap flag , which raises an exception after every single instruction. Chapter 12 uses these same Windows debugging events to build a tiny debugger of your own. Controlling execution Command Key What it does --- --- --- Start Debugging / Continue F5 Run until a breakpoint, an exception, or the end Step Over F10 Run the current line, including calls, stop at the next line Step Into F11 Go into the function the line calls Step Out Shift+F11 Run until the current function returns Run To Cursor Ctrl+F10 Run until the line the cursor is on, as if it had a one-time breakpoint Run to Click The green arrow that appears when hovering at the left of a line Same, with the mouse Step Into Specific Right-click → Step Into Specific Choose which call to step into when a line makes several, such as update(getPlayer(), clamp(x)) Set Next Statement Ctrl+Shift+F10, or drag the yellow arrow Make a different line run next, skipping or repeating code Break All Ctrl+Alt+Break Pause the program wherever it is, for example when it seems stuck Stop Debugging Shift+F5 End the program Restart Ctrl+Shift+F5 End and start again Set Next Statement is powerful and dangerous: it changes where the CPU goes next without running the code in between. It is excellent for re-running a function after changing a variable, and can crash the program if you skip something important such as a constructor. Use it within one function. Break All is the answer to "my game froze": pause, open the Call Stack, and see what every thread is doing (chapter 8 covers threads). The Call Stack window, as a tool Debug → Windows → Call Stack (Ctrl+Alt+C) lists the frames from the current function down to the start of the thread (lesson 1.05). Using it well: - Double-click a frame to make it current: the editor shows that function's line, and Locals and Watch show that frame's variables. This is how you find out why a function was called with a bad argument: go up one frame and look at the caller's variables. - Right-click → Show External Code reveals frames from the standard library and Windows, hidden by default. - Right-click → Show Parameter Values / Parameter Types puts the arguments on each line. - Run To Cursor in an earlier frame (select it, then Ctrl+F10 on a line) runs until control comes back up to that point. Just My Code By default, Visual Studio's Just My Code setting hides and skips code that is not yours: the standard library, Windows, third-party libraries without debug information. Step Into then does not wander into std::vector 's internals. When you need to see inside them (for example, to watch a std::vector reallocate), turn it off in Tools → Options → Debugging → General → Enable Just My Code . Breaking on exceptions By default, the debugger stops only on exceptions nobody catches. That is often too late: by then the stack has unwound past the code that threw. Open Debug → Windows → Exception Settings (Ctrl+Alt+E) and tick the categories you want to stop on when thrown : - C++ Exceptions : stop at any throw , even if it will be caught. Good for "something throws and gets swallowed somewhere". - Win32 Exceptions → Access violation (0xC0000005) : usually already on. Stops at the exact instruction that read or wrote bad memory, with the full stack intact. When the debugger stops on an access violation, the message says "reading location 0x..." or "writing location 0x...". As lesson 3.02 explained, a small address there means a null pointer plus an offset. Attaching to a running program You do not have to start a program from Visual Studio to debug it. Debug → Attach to Process (Ctrl+Alt+P) lists running processes; pick yours and press Attach. Breakpoints, Break All and the windows all work, provided the debugger can find the program's .pdb symbols (lesson 8.02). This is how you debug a game that only misbehaves after an hour of play, a program started by another program, or a tool you want to inspect without restarting it. You can attach only to your own processes unless Visual Studio runs as administrator, and Windows refuses debugging of protected system processes entirely. Debug → Detach All lets the program carry on without the debugger. Common mistakes !warning A breakpoint that never hits A hollow red circle means the debugger could not place it: the code is not loaded yet, the build is out of date, or the line has no code (in Release, the compiler may have removed or merged it). Rebuild in Debug. !warning Set Next Statement across function boundaries Moving the yellow arrow into a different function leaves the stack in a state the code does not expect. Stay within one function. !warning Stopping too late on exceptions Turn on "break when thrown" for C++ exceptions to see where an exception starts, not just where it ends. Check yourself quiz ? How does Windows involve the debugger when a breakpoint is hit? - The debugger checks the program counter thousands of times a second - The compiler builds a pause into every line of a Debug build + The int 3 instruction raises a breakpoint exception, and Windows delivers it to the attached debugger - The program sends the debugger a message through a pipe The debugger writes int 3 over the instruction at the breakpoint; because a debugger is attached, Windows hands it the event instead of the program. ? How do you find out why a function was called with a bad argument? + In the Call Stack window, double-click the caller's frame and look at its variables in Locals and Watch - Set the argument to a better value in the Watch window and continue - Restart the program with Step Into until you reach the function - Read the Output window for the argument's history The caller's frame shows where the bad value came from, which is usually where the real bug is. ? Why attach to a process instead of starting it in the debugger? - Attaching makes the program run faster than starting it under the debugger - Only attached processes can use breakpoints - Attaching is the only way to debug a Release build + When the bug appears only after a while, or another program starts it Debug, Attach to Process lets you join a program already running, in whatever state it has reached. ? What does the debugger write into your program's code to make a breakpoint? + The byte 0xCC ( int 3 ) over the instruction's first byte - A call to a special debugging function - Nothing; the CPU checks a list of breakpoints itself The CPU raises an exception when it executes int 3 , and Windows passes it to the debugger. ? A line calls three functions. How do you step into only the second? - Press F11 twice + Right-click → Step Into Specific, and choose it - Set a breakpoint and press F10 Step Into Specific lists every call on the line. ? Your game freezes. What do you do in the debugger first? - Restart it - Add more breakpoints + Break All, then read each thread's stack Break All pauses the program wherever it is, which shows what it is stuck doing. ? Where do you go to stop as soon as any C++ exception is thrown, even if it is caught later? + Exception Settings, ticking C++ Exceptions - The Call Stack window - The Breakpoints window By default the debugger only stops on unhandled exceptions.

title: 4.08  Watch, Locals, Memory and Registers Windows
match: 4.08 Watch, Locals, Memory and Registers Windows
where: Visual Studio and the Build Pipeline
body: The debugger's windows show a paused program's state at every level, from C++ expressions down to CPU registers and machine instructions. This lesson covers the tricks that make them far more useful: format specifiers , pseudo-variables , viewing arrays through pointers, the Registers and Disassembly windows, and how they connect to everything in chapters 1 to 3. Locals, Autos and Watch Window Shows --- --- Locals Every local variable in the current frame Autos Variables used on the current and previous line, plus the return value of a function you just stepped over Watch 1-4 Any expressions you type, kept up to date as you step QuickWatch (Shift+F9) One expression, in a dialog, for a quick look DataTips Hover over a variable in the editor; pin it to keep it on screen The Watch window evaluates nearly any C++ expression: player.health 2 , enemies.size() , &grid 3 4 , target , levels current .name , even function calls (careful: a call runs real code and can change state). Format specifiers Add a comma and a specifier after an expression to change how it is shown: Expression Shows --- --- health,x In hexadecimal flags,b In binary ptr,10 or ptr, 10 The 10 elements starting at ptr , as an array name,s A char as a string; ,su for a UTF-16 wchar_t ; ,s8 for UTF-8 value,d In decimal obj,! The raw structure, ignoring any custom visualiser ptr,na A pointer without the "address and then the value" decoration hr,hr An HRESULT decoded into its name err,wm A Windows error code as its message, such as "The system cannot find the file specified." ,10 is the one you will use most: a raw int scores shows only the first element, and scores,10 shows ten. For a std::vector , the debugger already shows all elements, using a visualiser that understands the type. Pseudo-variables The Watch window understands some names that are not in your code: Name Value --- --- $err The thread's current GetLastError() value. Use $err,hr to see its meaning (chapter 5) $ReturnValue The value the function you just stepped out of returned $tid , $pid Current thread and process id @rsp , @rip , @rax , ... (or $rsp ) A CPU register's value (int )(@rsp + 0x28) reads an int at an offset from the stack pointer: useful when reading an optimised function whose locals have no names. The Memory window, revisited Lesson 2.11 covered reading bytes. Two more tricks: - Drag a variable from the editor or from Locals into the Memory window to jump to its address. - Edit in place : click a byte and type new hex digits. The program continues with the change. This is a quick way to test how code reacts to an unusual value without changing the source. The Registers window Debug → Windows → Registers (Ctrl+Alt+G) shows the CPU's registers for the current thread at the current instruction: RAX = 0000000000000041 RBX = 0000000000000000 RCX = 000000F3A1AFF6C8 RDX = 0000000000000032 RSI = 0000000000000000 RDI = 0000000000000000 R8 = 0000000000000000 R9 = 0000000000000000 R10 = 0000000000000000 RIP = 00007FF6E1A2185E RSP = 000000F3A1AFF6A0 RBP = 0000000000000000 EFL = 00000246 - RIP is the instruction pointer: the address of the next instruction (the program counter from lesson 1.01). - RSP is the stack pointer (lesson 1.05). - RCX, RDX, R8, R9 hold the first four arguments at the start of a function, and RAX holds a function's return value just after it returns (lesson 2.01). - EFL is the flags register; right-click to show individual flags such as ZF (zero) and CF (carry), which chapter 7 explains. Values that changed in the last step are shown in red, just as in Locals. The Disassembly window Debug → Windows → Disassembly (Ctrl+Alt+D), or right-click → Go To Disassembly , shows the machine instructions the compiler produced, interleaved with your source lines: player.health -= amount; 00007FF6E1A21859 mov rax,qword ptr player 00007FF6E1A2185E mov ecx,dword ptr rax 00007FF6E1A21860 sub ecx,dword ptr amount 00007FF6E1A21863 mov rax,qword ptr player 00007FF6E1A21868 mov dword ptr rax ,ecx In this window, F10 and F11 step one instruction at a time instead of one line, and the Registers window changes with every step. This is the bridge between C++ and the machine: one line of source became five instructions, each of them a simple step like the tiny computer's. Right-click options let you show code bytes (the actual numbers, as in lesson 1.04), hide source lines, and show symbol names. Chapter 7 teaches how to read all of this. For now, step through a simple function in the Disassembly window with the Registers window open and watch RIP move along by each instruction's size. Common mistakes !warning Watch expressions that call functions They run real code every time the window updates. A function with side effects changes your program while you look at it. !warning Reading a raw pointer to an array scores shows one element. Use scores,10 . !warning Trusting $err much later GetLastError is overwritten by later API calls. Check it straight after the call that failed. Check yourself quiz ? What are format specifiers for? - Changing a variable's type in the program + Changing how Watch shows a value: hex, arrays, strings - Formatting the source code in the editor - Choosing the format of the .pdb file For example data,20 shows 20 elements of data , and x,h shows x in hex. The program itself is not changed. ? Which registers hold the first four integer arguments on x64 Windows, and which the return value? - RAX, RBX, RCX and RDX for the arguments; RSP for the return value - RDI, RSI, RDX and RCX for the arguments; RAX for the return value + RCX, RDX, R8 and R9 for the arguments; RAX for the return value - R8 to R11 for the arguments; RCX for the return value RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX is the Linux convention; Windows uses RCX, RDX, R8, R9. ? What does the Disassembly window show? - The source code with comments removed - The bytes of the .exe file on disk - The assembler's error messages + The generated instructions, interleaved with source lines You can also show each instruction's bytes, and step one instruction at a time with F10 while it has focus. ? How do you see 20 elements of an int data in the Watch window? - Type data 20 + Type data,20 - Type data 20 The ,N format specifier shows N elements starting at the pointer. ? Which register holds the address of the next instruction to run? - RSP + RIP - RAX RIP is the instruction pointer; RSP is the stack pointer. ? You just stepped out of a function. Where can you see what it returned? + In $ReturnValue , or the Autos window - In RIP - Only by adding a print statement The debugger records the return value as you step out or over a call. ? What does F10 do while the Disassembly window has focus? - Steps one source line + Steps one machine instruction - Continues to the next breakpoint In the Disassembly window, stepping is per instruction.

title: 4.09  Conditional and Data Breakpoints
where: Visual Studio and the Build Pipeline
body: A plain breakpoint stops every time. In a game loop that runs 60 times a second, that is useless. Conditions , hit counts and filters make a breakpoint stop only when it matters; tracepoints log without stopping; and data breakpoints stop on the exact instruction that changes a piece of memory, which is the fastest way to find who corrupted a value. Making breakpoints selective Right-click a breakpoint's red dot → Conditions (or hover and press the gear icon) to add any of these: Setting Stops when Example --- --- --- Conditional expression, Is true The expression is true enemy.health < 0 Conditional expression, When changed The expression's value differs from last time player.state Hit count It has been reached a given number of times = 500 , = 100 , is a multiple of 60 Filter On a particular thread or process ThreadId = 12345 Conditions are evaluated by the debugger each time the line is reached, which makes the program slower while the breakpoint is set; that is usually fine. A typical use: an enemy occasionally gets negative health and you do not know which one or when. Put a breakpoint on the line that subtracts damage, with the condition health - amount < 0 && id == 17 . The game runs normally until exactly that moment. Tracepoints: printing without stopping Tick Actions in the same settings panel and the breakpoint becomes a tracepoint : instead of (or as well as) stopping, it writes a message to the Output window. Put expressions in braces: frame {frameCount}: {name} takes {amount} damage, health now {health} Leave Continue code execution ticked and the program does not pause at all. It is std::cout debugging without editing, rebuilding or remembering to remove the lines afterwards. Special keywords like $FUNCTION , $CALLER and $TID add context. Data breakpoints: who changed this? Lesson 2.09's hardest bug was "something overwrote this value, and I don't know what". A data breakpoint stops the program on the instruction that writes to a given address, whoever does it, wherever the code is. 1. Run to a point where the variable exists, for example a breakpoint just after hero is constructed. 2. In Locals or Watch, right-click the variable → Break When Value Changes . Or Debug → New Breakpoint → Data Breakpoint , and enter an address expression such as &hero.gold and a size of 4 bytes. 3. Continue (F5). When any instruction changes those bytes, the debugger stops just after it, showing the line and the Call Stack. If the culprit is an overrun from the neighbouring name array (lesson 2.09), the stack points straight at the copy loop. How it works, and its limits Data breakpoints use the processor's debug registers . x64 CPUs have four of them, DR0 to DR3 , each holding an address to watch for writes (or reads). The CPU itself checks every memory access against them, so the program runs at full speed. The hardware imposes limits: Limit Why --- --- At most 4 data breakpoints at a time 4 debug registers Each watches 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes The hardware's sizes The address must be aligned to that size Hardware requirement An address, not a variable A local's address is only valid while its frame exists; the breakpoint stays on the address after the frame is gone That last row matters. Set a data breakpoint on a local, return from the function, and the breakpoint now watches whatever reuses that stack memory. Visual Studio removes data breakpoints when the process ends, but not when a frame ends; delete them yourself when they are no longer meaningful. A worked hunt The Debug heap reported "HEAP CORRUPTION DETECTED after normal block 312". Steps: 1. Turn on _CrtSetDbgFlag leak checking and rerun to confirm block 312 is the same each run (allocation numbers are stable if the program does the same things). 2. Call _CrtSetBreakAlloc(312) at the start of main : the debugger stops when block 312 is allocated, and the Call Stack shows what it is. 3. Note its address and size. Set a data breakpoint on the 8 bytes just after its end, where the guard bytes are. 4. Continue. The program stops on the instruction that writes past the end. That is the whole bug, found in four steps without reading a single line of unrelated code. Common mistakes !warning Slow conditions on very hot lines A condition evaluated millions of times per second makes the game crawl. Put the breakpoint on a less frequent line, or add a cheap check in code temporarily. !warning Data breakpoints left on reused memory After the variable's lifetime ends, the address belongs to something else. Delete the breakpoint. !warning Watching more than 8 bytes Hardware only watches up to 8 bytes per breakpoint. For a larger region, watch the specific field that goes wrong, or the guard bytes at its edge. Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference between a breakpoint and a data breakpoint? - A data breakpoint stops only on lines that declare variables + A data breakpoint stops when an address is written, by any code - A data breakpoint prints a value instead of stopping - They are the same, but data breakpoints work only in Release A data breakpoint answers "who changed this?", which an ordinary breakpoint cannot. A tracepoint is the one that prints without stopping. ? What are the hardware limits on data breakpoints? + Four at a time, each covering 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes at an address aligned to that size - Sixteen at a time, each covering up to 64 bytes - One at a time, covering any range of memory - No limits; the debugger can watch any amount of memory The CPU has four debug address registers, which is where the limit comes from. ? How would you find the code that writes past the end of a heap block? - Add a breakpoint on every line that uses the block - Watch the block's pointer in the Watch window until it changes - Run the program in Release so the bug shows up sooner + Set a data breakpoint on the bytes just after the block's end The debugger then stops on the exact instruction that writes there. ? How do you make a breakpoint stop only on the 500th time it is reached? - Press F5 499 times - Use a data breakpoint + Give it a hit count condition of = 500 Hit counts let the debugger count for you. ? What does a tracepoint do? + Prints a message, with values, without stopping - Stops the program on every line - Records the program so it can be replayed It is logging added from the debugger, without changing the code. ? Why can there be at most four data breakpoints at once? - Visual Studio limits them to save memory + They use the CPU's four debug address registers - Windows only allows four per process The processor checks memory accesses against DR0 to DR3 in hardware. ? A data breakpoint is set on a local variable, and its function returns. What does the breakpoint watch now? - Nothing; it is removed automatically - The variable's new location + The same address, now reused by other stack data Data breakpoints watch addresses, not variables.

title: Which write hits the watch?
body: A data breakpoint watches size bytes starting at address watch . The program performs a series of memory writes; each Write has a starting address and a length in bytes. Write firstHit(writes, watch, size) , which returns the index of the first write that touches any byte of the watched range, or -1 if none does. A write of length bytes at address touches the bytes address to address + length - 1 . The watched range is watch to watch + size - 1 . Two ranges touch if they overlap by at least one byte. watch 0x1008, size 4 (bytes 0x1008..0x100B) writes: { 0x1000, 8 } bytes 0x1000..0x1007: just misses { 0x100C, 4 } bytes 0x100C..0x100F: just misses { 0x1004, 8 } bytes 0x1004..0x100B: hits - answer 2

title: 4.10  Debug and Release Builds: What Optimisation Changes
match: 4.10 Debug and Release Builds: What Optimisation Changes
where: Visual Studio and the Build Pipeline
body: A Release build runs the same source code many times faster, because the optimiser rewrites it: it keeps values in registers, inlines functions, removes work whose result is unused, and assumes your code has no undefined behaviour. This lesson shows each transformation, explains why some bugs only appear in Release, and sets up a build that is both optimised and debuggable. The same code, two programs Compile this function in each configuration: cpp int sumTo(int n) { int total{ 0 }; for (int i{ 1 }; i <= n; ++i) total += i; return total; } Debug ( /Od , no optimisation) does exactly what the source says, keeping every variable in memory so the debugger can show it: asm sumTo PROC mov DWORD PTR rsp+8 , ecx ; store n to its stack slot sub rsp, 24 mov DWORD PTR total$ rsp , 0 mov DWORD PTR i$ rsp , 1 jmp SHORT $check $next: mov eax, DWORD PTR i$ rsp inc eax mov DWORD PTR i$ rsp , eax $check: mov eax, DWORD PTR n$ rsp cmp DWORD PTR i$ rsp , eax jg SHORT $done mov eax, DWORD PTR i$ rsp mov ecx, DWORD PTR total$ rsp add ecx, eax mov DWORD PTR total$ rsp , ecx jmp SHORT $next $done: mov eax, DWORD PTR total$ rsp add rsp, 24 ret 0 sumTo ENDP Release ( /O2 ) keeps everything in registers, and may restructure the loop, unroll it, or even recognise the pattern and compute the answer with arithmetic. Every loop iteration in the Debug version reads and writes memory several times; the Release version barely touches memory at all. For code like this, Release is commonly 5 to 50 times faster. What the optimiser does Transformation What it means What you see in the debugger --- --- --- Register allocation Variables live in registers instead of on the stack "Variable is optimised away and not available" Inlining A small function's body is pasted into its caller; there is no call The function never appears in the Call Stack; breakpoints in it may not hit Constant folding Expressions with known values are computed at compile time int x = 60 60; becomes 3600 ; no multiplication in the code Dead code elimination Work whose result is never used is removed Breakpoints on those lines have nowhere to go Loop transformations Unrolling, moving invariant work out of loops, vectorising with SIMD instructions Stepping jumps around unpredictably Reordering Instructions are moved to keep the processor busy The yellow arrow seems to go backwards None of this changes what a correct program does. The C++ standard lets the compiler make any change whose effect on the program's visible behaviour cannot be detected, the as-if rule . Why some bugs only appear in Release The as-if rule only applies to programs without undefined behaviour. The optimiser is allowed to assume there is none, and it uses that assumption aggressively: - Uninitialised variables hold 0xCC filler in Debug, which is at least consistent. In Release they hold whatever was in that register or stack slot, which changes with unrelated code. - Signed overflow : the compiler may assume i + 1 i is always true for an int , and remove a check that relied on wrap-around. - Out-of-bounds reads : in Debug, the read gets the neighbouring variable; in Release, the neighbour may be in a register and the read gets something else. - Timing and threads : a variable shared between threads without synchronisation may be kept in a register in Release, so one thread never sees the other's change (chapter 6). And Debug builds hide bugs with their extra help: 0xCC fill, guard bytes, iterator checks and assert all vanish in Release, because NDEBUG is defined there. So when something "only breaks in Release", the answer is almost never "the optimiser has a bug". It is almost always undefined behaviour in your code that Debug happened to tolerate. AddressSanitizer (lesson 2.10) and warnings at level 4 find most of these. Debugging an optimised build You can debug Release builds, and you sometimes must, because the bug only happens there. Make it easier: 1. Generate debug information in Release : C/C++ → General → Debug Information Format: Program Database (/Zi) and Linker → Debugging → Generate Debug Info: Yes . This costs nothing at run time; the .pdb is a separate file. 2. Keep optimisation on, but optionally add /Zo (enhanced optimised debugging, on by default in recent versions), which records where variables live in registers so more of them can be shown. 3. To debug one function without optimisation inside an optimised build, wrap it: cpp pragma optimize("", off) void suspiciousFunction() { // compiled without optimisation, so every variable is visible } pragma optimize("", on) Many studios use a third configuration for day-to-day work: optimised enough to run at a playable speed, with full debug information and asserts still enabled. In Visual Studio you can create it by copying Release in Configuration Manager and removing NDEBUG from its preprocessor definitions. The settings that differ Setting Debug Release --- --- --- Optimisation /Od (off) /O2 (speed) Runtime library /MDd (debug runtime) /MD _DEBUG / NDEBUG _DEBUG defined NDEBUG defined: assert does nothing Basic runtime checks /RTC1 : stack frame checks, uninitialised use Off Iterator debugging On ( _ITERATOR_DEBUG_LEVEL=2 ) Off Whole-program optimisation Off /GL and /LTCG : the linker can inline across files Incremental linking On (fast rebuilds) Off Common mistakes !warning Measuring performance in Debug Debug can be ten times slower, unevenly. Always measure speed in Release (chapter 17). !warning Putting real work inside assert assert(loadLevel(name)); loads the level in Debug and does nothing at all in Release. Do the work first, then assert on the result. !warning Blaming the optimiser Look for undefined behaviour first: uninitialised values, overruns, signed overflow, data races. Check yourself quiz ? What is the as-if rule? + The compiler may transform the program any way that does not change its observable behaviour, provided it has no undefined behaviour - The compiler must translate every line exactly as written, as if there were no optimiser - The program must behave as if it were running in a debugger - Code may only be optimised if it is marked inline If the program has undefined behaviour, the optimiser's transformations can change what you see, which is why some bugs only show in Release. ? Name four things the optimiser does. - Adds bounds checks, fills memory with 0xCC , keeps every variable in memory, disables inlining - Removes comments, renames variables, sorts functions alphabetically, compresses the .exe + Keeps variables in registers, inlines functions, folds constants, removes dead code (also loop transforms and reordering) - Turns signed overflow into errors, adds asserts, zeroes locals, logs every call The first group describes what a Debug build adds, the opposite of optimisation. ? How do you make a Release build debuggable without slowing it down? - Turn optimisation off for the whole project - Build Debug and rename it Release + Generate debug information with /Zi , which changes no code - Add assert calls, which stay in Release builds Debug information goes in a separate .pdb and does not change the generated code. assert is removed in Release. Use pragma optimize("", off) around one function that needs closer inspection. ? Why does the debugger say "variable is optimised away" in Release? + It lives only in a register, or was removed - Release builds have no variables - The .pdb file is missing With /Zi the debugger can sometimes still find it in a register, but not always. ? A program works in Debug and crashes in Release. What is the most likely cause? - A bug in the compiler's optimiser + Undefined behaviour that Debug happened to tolerate - Release builds use less memory Uninitialised values, overruns and data races behave differently once code is optimised. ? What happens to assert(x 0); in a Release build? - It still checks, but does not stop the program - It becomes a compile error + It is removed entirely, because NDEBUG is defined Asserts are a Debug-only safety net. ? What does inlining do? + Replaces a call with a copy of the called function's body - Moves a function to a DLL - Makes a function inline in the header No call happens, which is faster and lets the optimiser work across the two.
