title: 5.01  Handles and Kernel Objects
body:
Files, threads, processes, events and many other resources are kernel objects : they live inside the Windows kernel, and your program refers to them only through handles . This lesson explains what a handle is, the rules for getting and closing one, the two different "invalid" values, and how to wrap handles in an RAII class so they can never leak. Objects you cannot touch When a program opens a file, Windows creates a file object inside the kernel: a structure recording which file, the current position, the access rights granted, and more. That structure lives in kernel memory, which user-mode code cannot read (lesson 1.06). So instead of a pointer, the program gets a handle , a small number that identifies the object within this process. Every process has its own handle table . A handle value means nothing outside its process, just like a virtual address. When you pass the handle back to Windows, for example to ReadFile , the kernel looks it up in your table, checks the rights recorded there, and acts on the object. Many kinds of object work this way: Object Created by Used for --- --- --- File CreateFileW Reading and writing files, pipes, devices Thread CreateThread Running code in parallel (chapter 6) Process CreateProcessW , OpenProcess Starting programs, waiting for them (chapter 6) Event, mutex, semaphore CreateEventW , CreateMutexW , ... Synchronising threads (chapter 6) File mapping CreateFileMappingW Shared memory between processes (chapter 12) Windows also has window handles ( HWND ), GDI handles ( HBRUSH , HDC ) and module handles ( HMODULE ). They look similar but are managed by different parts of Windows and closed with different functions. This lesson is about kernel object handles, closed with CloseHandle . Getting and closing a handle cpp include <windows.h include <iostream int main() { HANDLE ready{ CreateEventW(nullptr, TRUE, FALSE, nullptr) }; // a manual-reset event, not yet signalled if (ready == nullptr) { std::cout << "CreateEventW failed: " << GetLastError() << '
'; return 1; } SetEvent(ready); // signal it const DWORD result{ WaitForSingleObject(ready, 0) }; // is it signalled? (don't wait) std::cout << (result == WAIT_OBJECT_0 ? "the event is signalled" : "not signalled") << '
'; CloseHandle(ready); // give the handle back return 0; } the event is signalled The rules: 1. Every handle you open, you must close , exactly once, with the matching function. Kernel objects are reference-counted: the object is destroyed when its last handle is closed. 2. After closing, the value is meaningless. Windows reuses handle values, so a stale handle can end up referring to a different object, just like a dangling pointer (lesson 2.09). 3. When the process ends, Windows closes everything it left open. That is a safety net, not a plan: a game that leaks a handle per frame runs out within hours. Task Manager can show leaks: on the Details tab, right-click the column headers → Select columns → Handles . A number that keeps growing while the game runs is a handle leak. Two kinds of "invalid" A historical wart: failing functions do not all return the same value. Function Returns on failure --- --- CreateFileW INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE (which is -1 ) CreateEventW , CreateThread , OpenProcess , most others nullptr (0) The documentation for each function says which. Checking for the wrong one is a classic bug: if (h == nullptr) after CreateFileW never catches a failure. An RAII wrapper Lesson 2.04's RAII idea is a perfect fit. A small class owns the handle and closes it in its destructor: cpp include <windows.h include <iostream include <utility class UniqueHandle { public: UniqueHandle() = default; explicit UniqueHandle(HANDLE h) : m_handle{ h } {} ~UniqueHandle() { reset(); } UniqueHandle(const UniqueHandle&) = delete; // one owner only UniqueHandle& operator=(const UniqueHandle&) = delete; UniqueHandle(UniqueHandle&& other) noexcept : m_handle{ std::exchange(other.m_handle, nullptr) } {} UniqueHandle& operator=(UniqueHandle&& other) noexcept { if (this != &other) { reset(); m_handle = std::exchange(other.m_handle, nullptr); } return this; } HANDLE get() const { return m_handle; } explicit operator bool() const { return m_handle != nullptr && m_handle != INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE; } void reset() { if ( this) CloseHandle(m_handle); m_handle = nullptr; } private: HANDLE m_handle{ nullptr }; }; int main() { UniqueHandle event{ CreateEventW(nullptr, TRUE, TRUE, nullptr) }; if (!event) return 1; std::cout << (WaitForSingleObject(event.get(), 0) == WAIT_OBJECT_0) << '
'; return 0; } // closed here, on every path out of main 1 Treating both nullptr and INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE as "no handle" makes the class safe whichever function produced the value. The Windows Implementation Libraries (WIL, available through vcpkg as wil ) provide polished versions of this for every handle type: wil::unique_handle , wil::unique_hfile , wil::unique_event . Common mistakes !warning Checking CreateFileW 's result against nullptr It returns INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE on failure. Read each function's documentation. !warning Closing a handle twice The second CloseHandle may close an unrelated object that reused the value. Under a debugger, Windows raises an "invalid handle" exception for it. !warning Closing a window, module or GDI handle with CloseHandle They have their own functions: DestroyWindow , FreeLibrary , DeleteObject , ReleaseDC . !warning Copying a raw handle into two owners Only one should close it. If two parts of the program genuinely need their own handle, use DuplicateHandle . Check yourself quiz ? Why does Windows give programs handles instead of pointers to kernel objects? - Handles are smaller than pointers and save memory + Kernel memory is off-limits; a handle lets the kernel check each use - Pointers would change every time the program restarted - Handles can be shared with other computers over a network A pointer into kernel memory would be useless to user-mode code, and it would skip the kernel's permission check. ? What happens to a process's open handles when it exits? + Windows closes them all, and any object whose last handle that was is destroyed - They stay open until the computer restarts - They are passed on to the parent process - They become invalid but the objects leak until someone closes them Leaked handles are still a bug while the program runs, but they do not outlive the process. ? Why does the UniqueHandle class treat both nullptr and INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE as empty? - Because they are the same value on 64-bit Windows - Because CloseHandle crashes on any other value - Because nullptr means "not opened yet" and the other means "already closed" + Because different Windows functions use different values to mean failure CreateFileW fails with INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE , many others with null, so checking both makes the class safe whatever produced the handle. ? What is a handle? + A per-process number naming a kernel object it opened - A pointer to the kernel object's memory - A global id shared by every process The object lives in kernel memory; the handle is how your process names it. ? What does CreateFileW return when it fails? - nullptr + INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE - 0 or -1, at random Most other creation functions return nullptr ; CreateFileW is one of the exceptions. ? A kernel object has two open handles. One is closed. What happens to the object? - It is destroyed immediately - The other handle becomes invalid + Nothing yet: it goes when its last handle closes Kernel objects are reference-counted. ? Why wrap handles in an RAII class? + So they are closed exactly once, automatically, on every path out of the scope - Because raw handles cannot be passed to Windows functions - To make them faster The destructor guarantees CloseHandle runs, even on early returns and exceptions.

title: An owner for any kind of handle
match: An owner for any kind of handle
body: Windows has many handle types, each closed by a different function. Write ScopedResource , an RAII owner that works for all of them: it holds a raw value of type void and a pointer to the function that closes it. - The constructor takes the value and the close function. The value nullptr and the value kInvalid (which stands in for INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE ) both mean "nothing owned". - The destructor calls the close function on the value, if something is owned. - release() gives up ownership without closing, returning the value. - reset() closes whatever is owned now and becomes empty. - get() returns the value; owns() says whether something is owned. - It can be moved (ownership passes to the new object, the old one becomes empty) but not copied. The tests use a pretend close function that counts calls, so this runs anywhere.

title: 5.02  Errors, GetLastError and Reading the Documentation
match: 5.02 Errors, GetLastError and Reading the Documentation
body:
The Windows API reports failure in several ways: a BOOL that is FALSE , a null or invalid handle, an HRESULT , or a status code. The details usually come from GetLastError . This lesson shows each pattern, how to turn an error number into a readable message, how HRESULT s are built, and how to read a Microsoft documentation page so you know which pattern a function uses. Three patterns 1. BOOL plus GetLastError. Many functions return BOOL (an int ): non-zero for success, FALSE (0) for failure. On failure, the reason is a number kept per thread, fetched with GetLastError() . cpp include <windows.h include <iostream int main() { if (!DeleteFileW(L"C:\this\file\does\not\exist.txt")) { const DWORD error{ GetLastError() }; // read it straight away std::cout << "DeleteFileW failed with error " << error << '
'; } return 0; } DeleteFileW failed with error 3 Error 3 is ERROR_PATH_NOT_FOUND . GetLastError must be called immediately : almost any later API call, including some done inside std::cout , may overwrite it. 2. Handles plus GetLastError. Creation functions return nullptr or INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE (lesson 5.01), and again GetLastError says why. 3. HRESULT. COM-based APIs (DirectX, the Windows shell, audio) return an HRESULT directly: a 32-bit code where negative means failure. Test them with the SUCCEEDED(hr) and FAILED(hr) macros, never with == 0 or != 0 , since some success codes are not zero. Turning a number into a message FormatMessageW looks up the text Windows has for an error code, in the user's language: cpp include <windows.h include <iostream include <string std::wstring describeError(DWORD error) { wchar_t buffer{ nullptr }; const DWORD length{ FormatMessageW( FORMAT_MESSAGE_ALLOCATE_BUFFER FORMAT_MESSAGE_FROM_SYSTEM FORMAT_MESSAGE_IGNORE_INSERTS, nullptr, error, 0, reinterpret_cast<wchar_t (&buffer), 0, nullptr) }; std::wstring text{ length ? std::wstring(buffer, length) : L"unknown error" }; LocalFree(buffer); // FormatMessage allocated it while (!text.empty() && (text.back() == L'
' text.back() == L'')) text.pop_back(); return text; } int main() { HANDLE file{ CreateFileW(L"no_such_save.dat", GENERIC_READ, 0, nullptr, OPEN_EXISTING, FILE_ATTRIBUTE_NORMAL, nullptr) }; if (file == INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE) { const DWORD error{ GetLastError() }; std::wcout << L"error " << error << L": " << describeError(error) << L'
'; } else CloseHandle(file); return 0; } error 2: The system cannot find the file specified. The ones you will meet most: Code Name Meaning --- --- --- 2 ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND No such file 3 ERROR_PATH_NOT_FOUND A folder in the path does not exist 5 ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED You do not have the rights (lesson 6.08) 6 ERROR_INVALID_HANDLE A closed or wrong handle 32 ERROR_SHARING_VIOLATION Another program has the file open without sharing 87 ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER An argument is wrong 122 ERROR_INSUFFICIENT_BUFFER The buffer you passed is too small: call again with a bigger one 126 ERROR_MOD_NOT_FOUND LoadLibrary could not find the DLL or one it depends on In the debugger, $err,hr in the Watch window shows the current value with its name (lesson 4.08), and Tools → Error Lookup decodes any number. Inside an HRESULT An HRESULT packs three fields into 32 bits: 31 30..27 26..16 15..0 ┌───┬───────┬───────────────┬────────────────┐ │ S │ flags │ facility (11) │ code (16) │ └───┴───────┴───────────────┴────────────────┘ S = 1: failure (so failures are negative as signed ints) - Severity (bit 31): 1 is failure. - Facility : which subsystem the code comes from, such as FACILITY_WIN32 (7) or FACILITY_DXGI . - Code : the error number within that facility. A Win32 error code can be wrapped as an HRESULT with HRESULT_FROM_WIN32(error) : error 2 becomes 0x80070002 . You will recognise that shape everywhere: 0x8007xxxx is "a Win32 error, number xxxx". Reading a documentation page Every function's page on Microsoft's site (search "CreateFileW function") has the same sections, and each answers a question you must ask: Section Answers --- --- Syntax The exact declaration, parameter types and annotations such as in , out , in, optional Parameters What each one means, what values are allowed, and whether null is accepted Return value What success and failure look like, and whether to call GetLastError Remarks The important details: threading rules, ownership of buffers, what to free and with what, common traps Requirements Which header to include, which .lib to link, which DLL implements it, and the oldest Windows version The Return value and Remarks sections are where most bugs are prevented. For example, CreateFileW 's Return value section says it returns INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE on failure; ReadFile 's Remarks explain when it can succeed but read fewer bytes than asked. Many functions also follow a two-call pattern for variable-sized results: call once with a null or small buffer to learn the size needed (often failing with ERROR_INSUFFICIENT_BUFFER ), allocate, then call again. Common mistakes !warning Calling GetLastError too late Store it in a variable on the very next line after the failing call. !warning Calling GetLastError after success Its value is only meaningful when the function reported failure. Some functions leave an old value there on success. !warning Testing an HRESULT with if (hr) S_FALSE is 1 and means success. Use SUCCEEDED and FAILED . Check yourself quiz ? Name the three main ways Windows API functions report failure. + A BOOL returning FALSE , a null or invalid handle, or an HRESULT with its severity bit set - Throwing a C++ exception, returning -1, or printing to the console - Setting errno , returning nullptr , or ending the process - Returning 0, returning 1, or returning INFINITE For the first two, GetLastError gives the reason. Windows API functions do not throw C++ exceptions. ? What are the three fields of an HRESULT? - Error number, line number and file name + Severity, facility (which subsystem) and code - Process id, thread id and error code - Major version, minor version and build number In 0x80070005 the top bit says failure, facility 7 is Win32, and code 5 is access denied. ? What is the two-call pattern? - Calling a function twice in case the first call fails - Calling the A version, then the W version, and comparing the results + Calling once to learn how big a buffer the result needs, then allocating it and calling again - Calling a function, then calling GetLastError to confirm it succeeded Many functions report the required size when given a buffer that is too small or null. ? A function returns FALSE . How do you find out why? - Check errno + Call GetLastError() immediately afterwards - Look at the return value's bits Many Windows functions record the reason per thread, for GetLastError to read. ? What does 0x80070005 mean? - Success with a warning - Memory address 0x80070005 + A failure HRESULT for Win32 error 5, access denied Severity bit set, facility 7 (Win32), code 5. ? Which section of a documentation page says whether to call GetLastError ? - Syntax + Return value - Requirements It describes what success and failure look like for that particular function. ? Why use FAILED(hr) instead of hr != 0 ? - HRESULT values are always negative + Some success codes, such as S_FALSE , are not zero - The comparison does not compile Only the severity bit separates success from failure.

title: Take an HRESULT apart
where: 5.02 Errors, GetLastError and Reading the Documentation
body: Write decode(hr) , which splits a 32-bit HRESULT value into its parts and returns them in an HrParts : - failed : true if bit 31 is set; - facility : bits 16 to 26 (11 bits); - code : bits 0 to 15. Then write fromWin32(error) , which builds the HRESULT that wraps a Win32 error code the way HRESULT_FROM_WIN32 does: 0 stays 0 (success); anything else becomes failure, facility 7, and the low 16 bits of the error as the code. decode(0x80070005) - failed, facility 7, code 5 decode(0x00000001) - not failed, facility 0, code 1 fromWin32(2) - 0x80070002 Work with the bits yourself: the Windows macros are not available here.

title: 5.03  Strings on Windows: ANSI, UTF-16 and UTF-8
match: 5.03 Strings on Windows: ANSI, UTF-16 and UTF-8
body: Most Windows API functions that take text exist twice: an A version for 8-bit "ANSI" strings and a W version for UTF-16 "wide" strings. Windows works in UTF-16 internally; the rest of the world, and most libraries, use UTF-8. This lesson explains the A/W split, why the course always calls the W functions, and how to convert between UTF-8 and UTF-16 at the edges of your program. Two versions of everything Look up CreateFile in the documentation and you find CreateFileA and CreateFileW . The same goes for MessageBox , LoadLibrary , GetModuleFileName and hundreds of others. Version Strings are C++ type Literal --- --- --- --- A ("ANSI") 8-bit, in the system's current code page char , std::string "text" W ("wide") UTF-16 wchar_t , std::wstring L"text" The plain name CreateFile is a macro that becomes CreateFileW when the project defines UNICODE (Visual Studio's default, "Use Unicode Character Set") and CreateFileA otherwise. The TCHAR type and TEXT("...") macro follow the same switch. They exist for code that once had to build both ways; new code does not need them. The W versions are the real ones. Windows has stored and processed text as UTF-16 since Windows NT. An A function converts your string to UTF-16 using the current code page (a table, such as Windows-1252 for Western Europe), calls the W function, and converts any results back. Characters that do not exist in that code page are lost, typically turned into ? . A player named Zoë or Сергей , or a save folder under a user name with such letters, breaks A-function code on many machines. So the rule for this course: call the W functions explicitly ( CreateFileW , MessageBoxW ), with std::wstring or L"..." strings. But the rest of the program uses UTF-8 Files, network protocols, JSON, most cross-platform libraries and your own source code use UTF-8 (lesson 2.08). So programs keep text as UTF-8 internally and convert to UTF-16 only when calling Windows. The conversion functions are MultiByteToWideChar and WideCharToMultiByte , using the two-call pattern from lesson 5.02: cpp include <windows.h include <iostream include <string std::wstring widen(const std::string& utf8) { if (utf8.empty()) return {}; const int needed{ MultiByteToWideChar(CP_UTF8, MB_ERR_INVALID_CHARS, utf8.data(), static_cast<int (utf8.size()), nullptr, 0) }; std::wstring out(static_cast<std::size_t (needed), L'\0'); MultiByteToWideChar(CP_UTF8, MB_ERR_INVALID_CHARS, utf8.data(), static_cast<int (utf8.size()), out.data(), needed); return out; } std::string narrow(const std::wstring& utf16) { if (utf16.empty()) return {}; const int needed{ WideCharToMultiByte(CP_UTF8, 0, utf16.data(), static_cast<int (utf16.size()), nullptr, 0, nullptr, nullptr) }; std::string out(static_cast<std::size_t (needed), '\0'); WideCharToMultiByte(CP_UTF8, 0, utf16.data(), static_cast<int (utf16.size()), out.data(), needed, nullptr, nullptr); return out; } int main() { const std::string name{ "Zo\xC3\xAB" }; // "Zoë" in UTF-8: 4 bytes const std::wstring wide{ widen(name) }; // 3 UTF-16 units std::cout << name.size() << " UTF-8 bytes, " << wide.size() << " UTF-16 units\n"; std::cout << "round trip ok: " << (narrow(wide) == name) << '\n'; return 0; } 4 UTF-8 bytes, 3 UTF-16 units round trip ok: 1 These two small functions are worth keeping in your engine library. With them, the pattern is: UTF-8 everywhere in your code, widen() right before a W call, narrow() on anything Windows gives back. How UTF-8 and UTF-16 encode a character Knowing the encodings lets you recognise text in memory and write conversions yourself, which is this lesson's practice task. UTF-8 uses 1 to 4 bytes per code point. The first byte's high bits say how many bytes follow: Code points Bytes Pattern --- --- --- U+0000 to U+007F 1 0xxxxxxx U+0080 to U+07FF 2 110xxxxx 10xxxxxx U+0800 to U+FFFF 3 1110xxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx U+10000 to U+10FFFF 4 11110xxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx ë is U+00EB, binary 000 1110 1011 . In the 2-byte pattern that is 110 00011 10 101011 = C3 AB , the two bytes in the example. UTF-16 uses one 16-bit unit for code points up to U+FFFF. Anything above (most emoji, some rare scripts) is split into two units called a surrogate pair : subtract 0x10000, put the top 10 bits in a unit 0xD800 + top , and the bottom 10 bits in 0xDC00 + bottom . So even in UTF-16, one character can take two units. Telling Windows to use UTF-8 Since Windows 10 version 1903, an application can declare in its manifest that its A functions should use UTF-8 as the code page ( <activeCodePage UTF-8</activeCodePage ). That makes A functions safe for any text. It is a reasonable option for new programs, but calling W functions works on every version and makes the intent obvious, so the course sticks with W. The console is a separate matter: to print UTF-8 correctly in a console window, call SetConsoleOutputCP(CP_UTF8) at start-up (lesson 5.09). Common mistakes !warning Calling A functions with UTF-8 Without the UTF-8 manifest, A functions interpret bytes in the current code page, garbling everything that is not ASCII. !warning Casting between char and wchar_t (LPCWSTR)"file.txt" compiles, and passes bytes that Windows reads as nonsense UTF-16. Convert with widen , or use L"..." literals. !warning Counting characters with size() UTF-8 bytes and UTF-16 units are not characters. std::wstring{ L"😀" }.size() is 2. !warning Mixing std::cout and std::wcout Using both on the same stream in one program leads to missing output. Pick one, or convert and use std::cout throughout. Check yourself quiz ? Which of the A and W versions does Windows implement natively, and why does it matter? - The A versions; the W versions are slower wrappers around them + The W versions; A converts via the code page and can lose characters - Both equally; the choice only changes the parameter types - The A versions; W is only for East Asian Windows A file name with characters outside the code page cannot be opened reliably through an A function. ? What is the usual strategy for text in a Windows program? - Use char and the A functions everywhere so no conversion is needed - Use UTF-16 for all text, including files and network data + Keep text as UTF-8 internally, convert to UTF-16 just before calling W functions, and convert results back - Store text as ASCII and replace other characters with ? UTF-8 matches the rest of the world's files and libraries; the conversion happens only at the Windows boundary. ? What is a surrogate pair? - Two bytes that make up one UTF-8 character - A pair of A and W functions that do the same thing - An escape character followed by a command letter + Two UTF-16 units that together encode one code point above U+FFFF That is why std::wstring{ L"😀" }.size() can be 2: one character, two UTF-16 units. ? What does CreateFileA do with its file name? - Uses it directly; Windows works in 8-bit text - Converts it to UTF-8 + Converts it from the code page to UTF-16 and calls CreateFileW Windows works in UTF-16 internally; the A functions are converting wrappers. ? How many bytes does UTF-8 use for the character é (U+00E9)? - 1 + 2 - 4 U+0080 to U+07FF take two bytes in UTF-8. ? A program keeps all its text as UTF-8. What should it do to open a file whose name the user typed? - Call CreateFileA with the UTF-8 bytes + Convert it to UTF-16 and call CreateFileW - Cast the char to wchar_t Convert at the boundary, then call the W function. ? Why can std::wstring{ L"😀" }.size() be 2? - Wide strings always store two units per character - Because of the terminating zero + The emoji is above U+FFFF, so UTF-16 needs a surrogate pair of two units Only code points up to U+FFFF fit in one UTF-16 unit.

title: UTF-8 to UTF-16 by hand
where: 5.03 Strings on Windows: ANSI, UTF-16 and UTF-8
body: Write toUtf16(utf8) , which converts UTF-8 text into UTF-16 units, the job MultiByteToWideChar does. Use std::u16string so the code works on any platform. Decode each character from its UTF-8 bytes (1 to 4 of them, using the table in the lesson) into a code point, then encode the code point as UTF-16: - code points up to U+FFFF become one unit; - code points from U+10000 to U+10FFFF become a surrogate pair: subtract 0x10000, then the high unit is 0xD800 + (value 10) and the low unit 0xDC00 + (value & 0x3FF) . If the input is not valid UTF-8 (a byte that cannot start a character, a sequence cut short, or a continuation byte that does not start with the bits 10 ), return std::nullopt .

title: 5.04  Files and Directories
body:
Games read assets and configuration and write save files and logs. This lesson uses the Windows file API directly ( CreateFileW , ReadFile , WriteFile ), shows where a game should keep its files, how to list a directory, how to save without ever leaving a half-written file, and when the portable std::filesystem and std::fstream are the better choice. Opening a file Every file operation starts with CreateFileW , which both creates new files and opens existing ones despite its name: cpp HANDLE file{ CreateFileW( L"settings.ini", // path GENERIC_READ, // what you want to do: GENERIC_READ, GENERIC_WRITE or both FILE_SHARE_READ, // what others may do while you have it open nullptr, // security attributes: default OPEN_EXISTING, // what to do if it exists or not (see below) FILE_ATTRIBUTE_NORMAL, // flags nullptr) }; // template file: unused The creation disposition decides what happens depending on whether the file exists: Value If it exists If it does not --- --- --- OPEN_EXISTING Open it Fail (error 2) CREATE_NEW Fail (error 80) Create it CREATE_ALWAYS Truncate it to empty Create it OPEN_ALWAYS Open it Create it TRUNCATE_EXISTING Truncate it Fail The share mode is often overlooked. It says what other handles may do to the file while yours is open. With 0 , no one else can even read it, and they get ERROR_SHARING_VIOLATION (32). That is why a game that holds its log file open with share mode 0 stops you viewing the log while it runs. Reading and writing cpp include <windows.h include <iostream include <string include <vector int main() { wchar_t tempDir MAX_PATH {}; GetTempPathW(MAX_PATH, tempDir); const std::wstring path{ std::wstring{ tempDir } + L"xenon_demo_save.txt" }; // Write HANDLE out{ CreateFileW(path.c_str(), GENERIC_WRITE, 0, nullptr, CREATE_ALWAYS, FILE_ATTRIBUTE_NORMAL, nullptr) }; if (out == INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE) { std::cout << "create failed " << GetLastError() << '
'; return 1; } const std::string text{ "level=4
gold=1250
" }; DWORD written{ 0 }; WriteFile(out, text.data(), static_cast<DWORD (text.size()), &written, nullptr); CloseHandle(out); // Read it back HANDLE in{ CreateFileW(path.c_str(), GENERIC_READ, FILE_SHARE_READ, nullptr, OPEN_EXISTING, FILE_ATTRIBUTE_NORMAL, nullptr) }; if (in == INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE) { std::cout << "open failed " << GetLastError() << '
'; return 1; } LARGE_INTEGER size{}; GetFileSizeEx(in, &size); std::vector<char buffer(static_cast<std::size_t (size.QuadPart)); DWORD read{ 0 }; ReadFile(in, buffer.data(), static_cast<DWORD (buffer.size()), &read, nullptr); CloseHandle(in); DeleteFileW(path.c_str()); std::cout << "wrote " << written << " bytes, read " << read << ":
" << std::string(buffer.data(), read); return 0; } wrote 18 bytes, read 18: level=4 gold=1250 Note the DWORD out parameters: WriteFile and ReadFile report how many bytes they actually moved. A ReadFile that returns success with read == 0 means end of file. A read can also return fewer bytes than asked (for pipes and network files especially), so code that needs an exact amount loops until it has it. Where a game should put its files The folder the .exe is in ( C:\Program Files\... ) is read-only for normal users. Writing saves there fails with ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED , or worse, gets silently redirected by compatibility shims. Windows provides per-user folders, found with SHGetKnownFolderPath : Folder Known folder id Typical path For --- --- --- --- Saved Games FOLDERID_SavedGames C:\Users
ame\Saved Games Save files Local AppData FOLDERID_LocalAppData C:\Users
ame\AppData\Local Settings, caches, logs Roaming AppData FOLDERID_RoamingAppData ...\AppData\Roaming Settings that follow the user between PCs on a domain Documents FOLDERID_Documents C:\Users
ame\Documents Things the user made and wants to find, such as screenshots cpp include <shlobj.h pragma comment(lib, "shell32.lib") std::wstring savedGamesFolder() { PWSTR path{ nullptr }; std::wstring result; if (SUCCEEDED(SHGetKnownFolderPath(FOLDERID_SavedGames, 0, nullptr, &path))) result = path; CoTaskMemFree(path); // the documentation says to free it this way return result + L"\MyGame"; } Saving safely If the game crashes, or the power goes, halfway through writing a save file, the player loses their save. The standard technique: write to a temporary file, then replace the real one in a single step . 1. Write the whole save to slot1.sav.tmp . 2. Call FlushFileBuffers and close it, so the data is on disk. 3. MoveFileExW(L"slot1.sav.tmp", L"slot1.sav", MOVEFILE_REPLACE_EXISTING MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH) , or ReplaceFileW . At every moment, either the old complete save or the new complete save is on disk, never a broken mixture. Listing a directory cpp include <windows.h include <iostream int main() { WIN32_FIND_DATAW entry{}; HANDLE find{ FindFirstFileW(L"C:\Windows\ .exe", &entry) }; if (find == INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE) return 1; int count{ 0 }; do { if (!(entry.dwFileAttributes & FILE_ATTRIBUTE_DIRECTORY)) ++count; } while (FindNextFileW(find, &entry)); FindClose(find); // not CloseHandle: find handles have their own close function std::cout << "found " << (count 0 ? "some" : "no") << " programs
"; return 0; } found some programs The portable alternative For ordinary game files, the C++ standard library is simpler and works on every platform: cpp include <filesystem include <fstream namespace fs = std::filesystem; for (const auto& entry : fs::directory_iterator{ "levels" }) if (entry.path().extension() == ".lvl") loadLevel(entry.path()); std::ofstream log{ fs::path{ "logs" } / "game.log", std::ios::app }; On Windows, std::filesystem::path stores UTF-16 internally and calls the W functions, so it handles any characters correctly. Use the Windows API directly when you need what the standard library does not expose: share modes, overlapped (asynchronous) I/O, memory-mapped files (chapter 12), file change notifications, or exact error codes. Common mistakes !warning Writing next to the .exe It works on your machine because you are an administrator or the game is in your own folder. On players' machines it fails. Use Saved Games or AppData. !warning Overwriting a save in place A crash mid-write destroys it. Write a temporary file and replace atomically. !warning Share mode 0 on files others need to read Logs and config files should usually allow FILE_SHARE_READ . !warning Assuming one ReadFile reads everything Check the bytes-read count, and loop when you need an exact amount. Check yourself quiz ? What does the share mode in CreateFileW control? + What other handles may do with the file while this one is open - How many bytes are read at a time - Whether the file is shared over the network - Whether other users of the computer can see the file A share mode of 0 locks others out completely, which is why another program can fail with error 32 (sharing violation). ? Where should a Windows game keep save files and settings? + Saves in Saved Games; settings and logs under AppData - Next to the .exe in the installation folder - In C:\Windows\Temp , which every program can write to - In the registry, as one large binary value The installation folder is usually not writable by normal users, and different users need their own saves. Both folders are found with SHGetKnownFolderPath . ? When would you use the Windows file API instead of std::fstream and std::filesystem ? - Always, because the standard library cannot write files on Windows - Only for files smaller than 4 GB - Never; the standard library exposes everything Windows offers + When you need share modes, async I/O, mapped files or exact error codes The standard library is portable and fine for most work; the Windows API exposes features it does not. ? Which creation disposition opens a file if it exists and creates it if not? - CREATE_ALWAYS + OPEN_ALWAYS - OPEN_EXISTING CREATE_ALWAYS also creates when missing, but truncates an existing file to empty. ? Another program cannot open your game's log while the game runs, getting error 32. Why? - The log file is too large + The game's share mode does not allow others to read - Windows locks all files a game opens Error 32 is a sharing violation: the existing handle's share mode forbids it. ? Why should save files not be written to the game's installation folder? - Windows deletes files there on restart - It is slower + Under Program Files it is read-only for normal users Use the per-user Saved Games or AppData folders. ? How do you update a save file so a crash can never leave it half-written? + Write a temporary file fully, then swap it in one step - Write the new save in small pieces - Delete the old file first, then write the new one The move or replace is atomic: the file is always either the old version or the new one.

title: Split a Windows path
body: Write splitPath(path) , which splits a Windows file path into its folder, its file name without the extension, and its extension, the way a game might when deciding where to put a backup or which loader to use. - The folder is everything before the last \ or / (either separator may appear), without that separator. If there is no separator, the folder is empty. - The extension is everything from the last . in the file-name part onwards, including the dot. A dot at the very start of the file name (as in .gitignore ) does not start an extension. No dot means no extension. - The stem is the file-name part without the extension. C:\Games\Save\slot1.sav - "C:\Games\Save", "slot1", ".sav" levels/forest.v2.lvl - "levels", "forest.v2", ".lvl" README - "", "README", "" C:\Users\.config - "C:\Users", ".config", ""

title: 5.05  Windows and the Message Loop
body: A Windows program with a window does not ask "has a key been pressed?". Windows tells it, by putting messages in a queue that the program reads in a message loop and hands to a window procedure . This lesson explains window classes, messages, the loop, and the variant games use so they can keep rendering when no messages arrive. Event-driven programs A console program runs top to bottom and asks for input when it wants it. A windowed program is the other way round: it sits waiting, and the operating system sends it events : a key was pressed, the mouse moved, the window was resized, the window needs repainting, the user clicked Close. Windows delivers these as messages . Each message is a small structure: cpp struct MSG { HWND hwnd; // which window it is for UINT message; // what happened: WM_KEYDOWN, WM_MOUSEMOVE, WM_PAINT, ... WPARAM wParam; // extra information, meaning depends on the message LPARAM lParam; // more extra information DWORD time; POINT pt; }; Every thread that creates a window gets a message queue . Windows appends messages to it; the program takes them out one at a time. Window classes and the window procedure Before creating a window you register a window class : a template naming, among other things, the window procedure , the function Windows calls for every message to windows of that class. It is a callback (lesson 3.04): you give Windows a function pointer, and Windows calls it. cpp LRESULT CALLBACK WindowProc(HWND hwnd, UINT message, WPARAM wParam, LPARAM lParam) { switch (message) { case WM_KEYDOWN: if (wParam == VK_ESCAPE) DestroyWindow(hwnd); // Esc closes the window return 0; case WM_DESTROY: PostQuitMessage(0); // ask the message loop to end return 0; } return DefWindowProcW(hwnd, message, wParam, lParam); // default handling for everything else } The switch handles the messages the program cares about. Everything else must go to DefWindowProcW , which implements the standard behaviour: moving the window when its title bar is dragged, resizing, the system menu, closing on Alt+F4. A window procedure that returns 0 for everything produces a window that cannot be moved or closed. The message loop cpp MSG msg{}; while (GetMessageW(&msg, nullptr, 0, 0) 0) { TranslateMessage(&msg); // turns key presses into WM_CHAR messages for typed text DispatchMessageW(&msg); // calls the window procedure of msg.hwnd } - GetMessageW takes the next message from the queue, waiting if it is empty. It returns 0 when it finds WM_QUIT , which PostQuitMessage puts in the queue, and -1 on error. - DispatchMessageW looks up the window's class and calls its window procedure. That is the whole skeleton of every classic Windows program: register a class, create a window, loop until WM_QUIT . The next lesson writes a complete one. Some messages skip the queue entirely: Windows calls the window procedure directly for them (they are "sent" rather than "posted"), for example WM_CREATE during CreateWindowExW and WM_SIZE during resizing. So a window procedure can be called from inside other API calls, not only from DispatchMessageW . Messages you will handle most Message Sent when Useful data --- --- --- WM_CREATE The window is being created WM_DESTROY The window is being destroyed Post WM_QUIT here WM_CLOSE The user asked to close (X button, Alt+F4) Ask "save first?" here, or call DestroyWindow WM_PAINT Part of the window needs redrawing Use BeginPaint / EndPaint WM_SIZE The client area changed size New width and height in lParam WM_KEYDOWN , WM_KEYUP A key went down or up Virtual-key code in wParam (lesson 5.07) WM_CHAR Text was typed (after TranslateMessage ) The UTF-16 character in wParam WM_MOUSEMOVE , WM_LBUTTONDOWN , ... Mouse movement and buttons Coordinates in lParam (lesson 5.07) WM_TIMER A timer set with SetTimer fired Timer id in wParam WM_ACTIVATE The window gained or lost focus Pause the game when it loses focus The game loop variant GetMessageW waits when there are no messages. A game cannot wait: it must update and draw 60 or more times a second whether or not the player touches anything. Games use PeekMessageW , which returns immediately, and run a frame whenever the queue is empty: cpp bool running{ true }; while (running) { MSG msg{}; while (PeekMessageW(&msg, nullptr, 0, 0, PM_REMOVE)) // handle everything waiting... { if (msg.message == WM_QUIT) running = false; TranslateMessage(&msg); DispatchMessageW(&msg); } if (!running) break; updateGame(); // ...then run one frame renderGame(); } Draining all waiting messages each frame, not just one, keeps input responsive and the window behaving normally. Chapter 10 builds the full game loop with proper timing around this. Common mistakes !warning Not calling DefWindowProcW for unhandled messages The window cannot be moved, resized or closed normally. !warning Forgetting PostQuitMessage in WM_DESTROY The window disappears but the message loop keeps waiting, and the process keeps running invisibly. Check Task Manager. !warning Long work inside the window procedure While it runs, no other messages are handled, and after a few seconds Windows marks the window "Not Responding". Do slow work elsewhere, or in steps. !warning Using GetMessageW in a game The game only updates when a message arrives, such as when the mouse moves. Use PeekMessageW . Check yourself quiz ? What is a window procedure? - The function that creates a window - The loop that reads messages from the queue + The callback Windows calls with each message for the class - A list of the messages a window can receive DispatchMessageW delivers each message to it. ? How does a message loop end? - When the window is closed, GetMessageW returns -1 + PostQuitMessage queues WM_QUIT ; GetMessageW then returns 0 - DestroyWindow ends the loop directly - The loop ends when the queue is empty A window closing does not end the loop by itself, which is why a process can keep running after its window has gone. ? How does a game's loop differ from a classic message loop? - It does not handle messages at all - It uses GetMessageW and draws inside WM_PAINT only - It runs messages on a second thread + It drains messages with PeekMessageW , then runs one frame GetMessageW waits until a message arrives, which would freeze the game whenever nothing happens. ? What does DispatchMessageW do? - Puts a message in the queue + Calls the window procedure of the window the message is for - Translates key presses into characters It finds the window's class and calls the function registered for it. ? A program's window closes but the process keeps running. What is the most likely cause? - DefWindowProcW was called - The window class was not registered + WM_DESTROY never calls PostQuitMessage The loop keeps waiting for messages for a window that no longer exists. ? Why do games use PeekMessageW instead of GetMessageW ? + It returns at once when the queue is empty, so frames keep running - PeekMessageW is faster at reading messages - GetMessageW does not work with games A game must update continuously, not only when messages arrive. ? What should a window procedure do with a message it does not handle? - Return 0 to say it was handled + Pass it to DefWindowProcW and return that - Ignore it and return 1 The default procedure implements the standard window behaviour.

title: 5.06  A First Win32 Application
body: Put the last lesson together into a complete windowed program: wWinMain , registering a class, creating a window, a game-style loop, and drawing a moving square with GDI using a back buffer so it does not flicker. About 120 lines of plain Windows API, and every one explained. The project In Visual Studio, create a new Windows Desktop Application project (not Console App), or change an existing project's Linker → System → SubSystem to Windows (/SUBSYSTEM:WINDOWS) . A Windows-subsystem program has no console, and starts at wWinMain instead of main . This program cannot run on the course website, which runs console programs only. Build it in Visual Studio. The whole program cpp include <windows.h // ---------- the game state ---------- struct Game { float x{ 100.0f }, y{ 100.0f }; // square position, in pixels float vx{ 180.0f }, vy{ 120.0f }; // velocity, in pixels per second int width{ 640 }, height{ 360 }; // client area size }; static Game g_game; // ---------- drawing ---------- static void render(HWND hwnd) { HDC screen{ GetDC(hwnd) }; // Draw into an off-screen bitmap first, then copy it to the window in one go: no flicker. HDC back{ CreateCompatibleDC(screen) }; HBITMAP bitmap{ CreateCompatibleBitmap(screen, g_game.width, g_game.height) }; HGDIOBJ oldBitmap{ SelectObject(back, bitmap) }; RECT all{ 0, 0, g_game.width, g_game.height }; HBRUSH background{ CreateSolidBrush(RGB(18, 20, 26)) }; FillRect(back, &all, background); DeleteObject(background); RECT square{ static_cast<LONG (g_game.x), static_cast<LONG (g_game.y), static_cast<LONG (g_game.x) + 40, static_cast<LONG (g_game.y) + 40 }; HBRUSH teal{ CreateSolidBrush(RGB(95, 211, 196)) }; FillRect(back, &square, teal); DeleteObject(teal); BitBlt(screen, 0, 0, g_game.width, g_game.height, back, 0, 0, SRCCOPY); SelectObject(back, oldBitmap); // put the original back before deleting DeleteObject(bitmap); DeleteDC(back); ReleaseDC(hwnd, screen); } // ---------- updating ---------- static void update(float dt) { g_game.x += g_game.vx dt; g_game.y += g_game.vy dt; if (g_game.x < 0 g_game.x + 40 g_game.width) g_game.vx = -g_game.vx; // bounce if (g_game.y < 0 g_game.y + 40 g_game.height) g_game.vy = -g_game.vy; } // ---------- messages ---------- static LRESULT CALLBACK WindowProc(HWND hwnd, UINT message, WPARAM wParam, LPARAM lParam) { switch (message) { case WM_SIZE: g_game.width = LOWORD(lParam); g_game.height = HIWORD(lParam); return 0; case WM_KEYDOWN: if (wParam == VK_ESCAPE) DestroyWindow(hwnd); return 0; case WM_ERASEBKGND: return 1; // we paint everything ourselves: skip the default erase (less flicker) case WM_DESTROY: PostQuitMessage(0); return 0; } return DefWindowProcW(hwnd, message, wParam, lParam); } // ---------- start-up and the loop ---------- int WINAPI wWinMain(HINSTANCE instance, HINSTANCE, PWSTR, int showCommand) { WNDCLASSEXW wc{}; wc.cbSize = sizeof(wc); wc.lpfnWndProc = WindowProc; // the callback wc.hInstance = instance; // this program's module wc.hCursor = LoadCursorW(nullptr, IDC_ARROW); wc.lpszClassName = L"XenonWindow"; if (!RegisterClassExW(&wc)) return 1; RECT size{ 0, 0, 640, 360 }; // the client area we want... AdjustWindowRect(&size, WS_OVERLAPPEDWINDOW, FALSE); // ...grown to include borders and title bar HWND hwnd{ CreateWindowExW(0, wc.lpszClassName, L"Bouncing square", WS_OVERLAPPEDWINDOW, CW_USEDEFAULT, CW_USEDEFAULT, size.right - size.left, size.bottom - size.top, nullptr, nullptr, instance, nullptr) }; if (!hwnd) return 1; ShowWindow(hwnd, showCommand); LARGE_INTEGER frequency{}, previous{}, now{}; QueryPerformanceFrequency(&frequency); // ticks per second of the high-resolution clock QueryPerformanceCounter(&previous); bool running{ true }; while (running) { MSG msg{}; while (PeekMessageW(&msg, nullptr, 0, 0, PM_REMOVE)) { if (msg.message == WM_QUIT) running = false; TranslateMessage(&msg); DispatchMessageW(&msg); } if (!running) break; QueryPerformanceCounter(&now); const float dt{ static_cast<float (now.QuadPart - previous.QuadPart) / static_cast<float (frequency.QuadPart) }; previous = now; update(dt); render(hwnd); Sleep(1); // be polite to the CPU; chapter 10 does timing properly } return 0; } Walking through it Start-up. wWinMain receives the program's HINSTANCE (the address its .exe was loaded at, lesson 4.05's HMODULE ) and how the window should first appear. It fills in a WNDCLASSEXW , registers it, and creates one window of that class. AdjustWindowRect matters: the size passed to CreateWindowExW includes the title bar and borders, so without it the drawable client area would be smaller than 640 by 360. Time. QueryPerformanceCounter reads a high-resolution clock, typically ticking 10 million times a second. The difference between two readings, divided by the frequency, is the elapsed time in seconds. Moving by velocity × dt makes the square move at the same speed on a fast PC and a slow one, a theme chapter 10 develops. Drawing. GDI (the Graphics Device Interface) is Windows' original 2D drawing API. It is slow by modern standards but simple and always available. Every GDI object you create ( CreateSolidBrush , CreateCompatibleBitmap , CreateCompatibleDC ) must be deleted, and an object selected into a device context must be deselected before it is deleted: that is the oldBitmap dance. Handle leaks here show up in Task Manager's GDI objects column and eventually stop the program drawing at all. Double buffering. Drawing the background and then the square directly onto the window would briefly show the empty background each frame: flicker. Drawing both into an off-screen bitmap and copying it to the window with one BitBlt means the window only ever shows complete frames. What a real game does differently This program is the skeleton every Windows game has underneath. Real games replace the GDI drawing with a GPU API (Direct3D, Vulkan or OpenGL) and usually use a library such as SDL to create the window and read input, which chapter 11 does. But the window class, the message loop and the timing are the same ideas, and when something goes wrong at that level (a window that will not close, input that stops, a frame-rate collapse when the window is dragged) this is the code you will be debugging. Common mistakes !warning Building as a console application The linker complains that main is missing. Set SubSystem to Windows, or create the project from the Windows Desktop Application template. !warning Creating GDI objects every frame without deleting them The program runs out of GDI handles (10,000 per process by default) and stops drawing. Delete each one, or create them once at start-up. !warning Sizing the window instead of the client area Use AdjustWindowRect so the drawable area is the size you intended. Check yourself quiz ? What are the main steps of a Win32 program's start-up? - Create a window, register its class, run the message loop, then show it + Register a window class with a window procedure, create a window of that class, show it, then run the message loop - Call main , open a console, then create a window inside it - Run the message loop, then register the window class when the first message arrives A window can only be created from a class that has already been registered. ? What is the client area of a window? - The whole window, including borders and title bar - The part of the screen not covered by any window + The part inside the borders and title bar, where the program draws That is why AdjustWindowRect is used: to make the client area the size you want, the whole window must be a little larger. ? What must you do with every GDI object you create? + Delete it when finished, after deselecting it from any device context it was selected into - Nothing; GDI objects are freed when the window is repainted - Call free on it like heap memory - Close it with CloseHandle GDI objects are a limited resource; leaking them every frame eventually stops drawing working. ? Why does the program call AdjustWindowRect before CreateWindowExW ? - To centre the window on the primary screen - To make the window resizable by the player + The size includes borders, so it must grow to fit the client area The client area is the drawable part inside the frame. ? What does drawing into an off-screen bitmap and copying it with BitBlt prevent? + Flicker: no half-drawn frame is ever shown - Memory leaks - The window becoming unresponsive This technique is called double buffering. ? Why does the square move by velocity dt ? - Because GDI requires positions in seconds + So its speed is the same at any frame rate - To make it bounce off the window's edges A fixed step per frame would make it faster on faster computers.

title: 5.07  Keyboard, Mouse and Timers
body: Input arrives as messages whose details are packed into wParam and lParam . This lesson unpacks them: virtual-key codes, the bits of a key message, typed characters, mouse coordinates and buttons, and when to read the keyboard's current state instead. It ends with timers and the high-resolution clock that games use for timing. Keys: messages and virtual-key codes When a key goes down, the window with keyboard focus receives WM_KEYDOWN ; when it comes up, WM_KEYUP . (Alt combinations and F10 arrive as WM_SYSKEYDOWN and WM_SYSKEYUP instead.) wParam holds a virtual-key code : a number for the key, independent of keyboard layout. Key Code --- --- Letters 'A' to 'Z' (0x41 to 0x5A): the upper-case letter, whatever the shift state Digits (top row) '0' to '9' (0x30 to 0x39) Arrows VK_LEFT , VK_UP , VK_RIGHT , VK_DOWN Space, Enter, Escape, Tab VK_SPACE , VK_RETURN , VK_ESCAPE , VK_TAB Shift, Ctrl, Alt VK_SHIFT , VK_CONTROL , VK_MENU (or VK_LSHIFT , VK_RCONTROL ... for one side) F1 to F12 VK_F1 to VK_F12 The bits in lParam A key message's lParam packs several facts into 32 bits: 31 30 29 28..25 24 23..16 15..0 ┌────┬────┬────┬───────┬────┬───────────────┬────────────────┐ │ up │was │alt │ │ext │ scan code (8) │ repeat count │ │ │down│ │ │ │ │ (16) │ └────┴────┴────┴───────┴────┴───────────────┴────────────────┘ Bits Meaning --- --- 0 to 15 Repeat count : how many auto-repeats this message stands for 16 to 23 Scan code : the physical key's position, independent of layout 24 Extended key (right-hand Ctrl and Alt, the arrow block) 30 Previous state : 1 if the key was already down before this message 31 Transition: 0 for key down, 1 for key up Bit 30 is the useful one for games. Holding a key generates a stream of WM_KEYDOWN messages (auto-repeat). If "jump" should happen once per press, ignore messages where bit 30 is set: cpp case WM_KEYDOWN: { const bool repeat{ (lParam & (1 << 30)) != 0 }; if (wParam == VK_SPACE && !repeat) jump(); return 0; } Reading bit fields like this, with shifts and masks, is exactly lesson 1.02's material applied, and you will do it constantly in low-level code. The practice task is a set of these decoders. Typed text: WM_CHAR For text entry (a player name, a chat box, a debug console) do not use WM_KEYDOWN : it knows nothing about Shift, Caps Lock, dead keys or the user's keyboard layout. TranslateMessage in the message loop turns key presses into WM_CHAR messages whose wParam is the actual UTF-16 character typed, 'a' , 'A' , 'é' or 'Ж' as appropriate. Use Message --- --- Game controls (move, jump, fire) WM_KEYDOWN / WM_KEYUP , or the current state Typing text WM_CHAR Polling the current state Sometimes you want to ask "is W held down right now?" rather than track every message. GetAsyncKeyState(vk) answers: its top bit ( 0x8000 ) is set when the key is currently down. cpp if (GetAsyncKeyState('W') & 0x8000) player.y -= speed dt; Games often combine both: messages for discrete events (a press that toggles a menu), and either polling or a key-state array kept up to date from the messages for continuous movement. GetAsyncKeyState reports keys even when your window is not focused, so check focus ( WM_ACTIVATE ) before acting on it. The mouse Mouse messages put the cursor position, in client-area coordinates , in lParam : x in the low 16 bits, y in the high 16 bits, both signed (they can be negative when the mouse is captured and dragged outside the window). cpp include <windowsx.h // GET_X_LPARAM, GET_Y_LPARAM case WM_MOUSEMOVE: { const int x{ GET_X_LPARAM(lParam) }; const int y{ GET_Y_LPARAM(lParam) }; const bool leftHeld{ (wParam & MK_LBUTTON) != 0 }; aimAt(x, y, leftHeld); return 0; } Do not use LOWORD and HIWORD for coordinates: they are unsigned, so -1 becomes 65535. GET_X_LPARAM casts to short first. Message Meaning --- --- WM_MOUSEMOVE The cursor moved WM_LBUTTONDOWN / UP , WM_RBUTTON... , WM_MBUTTON... Buttons WM_MOUSEWHEEL Wheel turned: amount in the high word of wParam , in multiples of WHEEL_DELTA (120) wParam flags MK_LBUTTON , MK_RBUTTON , MK_SHIFT , MK_CONTROL : what is held during the message For first-person camera controls, cursor positions are the wrong tool: the cursor stops at the screen edge. Games use raw input ( RegisterRawInputDevices and WM_INPUT ), which reports the mouse's actual movement without acceleration or edge limits. Timers and clocks SetTimer(hwnd, id, milliseconds, nullptr) posts WM_TIMER every so often. It is fine for "autosave every five minutes" or blinking a cursor. It is not precise: messages only arrive when the queue is checked, and the default resolution is about 15.6 ms. For anything to do with frame timing, use the high-resolution performance counter , as lesson 5.06 did: cpp include <windows.h include <iostream int main() { LARGE_INTEGER frequency{}, start{}, end{}; QueryPerformanceFrequency(&frequency); QueryPerformanceCounter(&start); volatile double sink{ 0 }; for (int i{ 0 }; i < 1'000'000; ++i) sink = sink + i 0.5; // something to time QueryPerformanceCounter(&end); const double ms{ 1000.0 static_cast<double (end.QuadPart - start.QuadPart) / static_cast<double (frequency.QuadPart) }; std::cout << "frequency is " << (frequency.QuadPart 0 ? "positive" : "zero") << ", took " << (ms = 0 ? "a measurable" : "a negative") << " time\n"; return 0; } frequency is positive, took a measurable time (The example prints words instead of numbers because the actual times differ on every machine.) std::chrono::steady_clock uses the same counter on Windows and is the portable choice. Common mistakes !warning Using WM_KEYDOWN for text input It ignores Shift, layout and accents. Use WM_CHAR . !warning Acting on every auto-repeat Check bit 30 of lParam for one-shot actions. !warning LOWORD(lParam) for mouse coordinates Negative coordinates become huge positive numbers. Use GET_X_LPARAM and GET_Y_LPARAM . !warning Timing frames with SetTimer or GetTickCount Both are too coarse. Use QueryPerformanceCounter or std::chrono::steady_clock . Check yourself quiz ? What is a virtual-key code? + A layout-independent number for a key, given in wParam - The character a key types, in UTF-16 - The hardware scan code of the key - A code that changes with the keyboard language For typed text, use WM_CHAR , which carries the character; the virtual-key code names the key itself. Letter keys use their upper-case ASCII code. ? Where are a mouse message's coordinates, and in what coordinate system? + In lParam as two signed 16-bit halves, relative to the client area - In wParam , as screen coordinates - In two global variables, relative to the top-left of the screen - In lParam , unsigned, relative to the window's title bar They are signed because a captured mouse can be left of or above the client area; GET_X_LPARAM reads them as signed. ? When should a game read input from messages and when from the current key state? - Always messages: the current state is out of date by a frame - Always the current state: messages arrive too late for games + Messages for presses and typing; the current state for held keys - Messages in Debug builds, the current state in Release A single press must not be missed, which messages guarantee; holding a key is about what is true right now. ? A key held down produces many WM_KEYDOWN messages. How do you tell the first one from the repeats? - The repeat count is always 0 for the first - wParam changes for repeats + Bit 30 of lParam is 0 for the first and 1 for repeats Bit 30 records whether the key was already down. ? The player types é . Which message carries that character? - WM_KEYDOWN + WM_CHAR - WM_MOUSEMOVE TranslateMessage turns key presses into characters according to the keyboard layout. ? Why use GET_X_LPARAM instead of LOWORD for a mouse x coordinate? - It is faster than LOWORD + It reads the 16 bits as signed, so negatives work - LOWORD gives the y coordinate Coordinates can be negative while the mouse is captured outside the window. ? Which is the right clock for measuring frame times? - SetTimer - GetTickCount + QueryPerformanceCounter It has sub-microsecond resolution; the others are about 15 ms coarse. std::chrono::steady_clock is a portable equivalent.

title: Unpack the input messages
body: Window messages pack several values into wParam and lParam . Write the decoders a window procedure needs. Treat lParam as the 64-bit value it is on x64, but only its low 32 bits matter here. - mouseX(lParam) and mouseY(lParam) : the low 16 bits and the next 16 bits, each read as a signed 16-bit number. - repeatCount(lParam) : bits 0 to 15 of a key message. - scanCode(lParam) : bits 16 to 23. - isRepeat(lParam) : true if bit 30 is set. - isKeyUp(lParam) : true if bit 31 is set. - wheelSteps(wParam) : the high 16 bits of the low 32 bits of wParam as a signed number, divided by 120 (one notch of the wheel). mouseX(0x00C80064) = 100, mouseY(0x00C80064) = 200 mouseX(0x0000FFFF) = -1 repeatCount(0x40150001) = 1, scanCode(...) = 0x15, isRepeat(...) = true wheelSteps(0xFF880000) = -1

title: 5.08  Loading Libraries at Run Time
body:
Lesson 4.05 loaded a DLL of your own. This lesson looks at the loader's side: the search order Windows uses to find a DLL, why that order is a security risk and how to restrict it, finding modules that are already loaded, getting a module's file path, using functions that only exist on newer versions of Windows, and delay loading . Where Windows looks for a DLL When a program calls LoadLibraryW(L"plugin.dll") with a bare file name, or when its import table lists plugin.dll , the loader searches a sequence of places. For a normal desktop application the standard search order, simplified, is: 1. DLLs already loaded in the process with that name, and a list of known DLLs (core system DLLs that always come from the system folder). 2. The folder the application's .exe is in. 3. The system folder, C:\Windows\System32 . 4. The Windows folder. 5. The current working directory . 6. Each folder on the PATH environment variable. The first match wins. This is why putting your DLLs next to your .exe (lesson 4.01's shared output folder) works. The risk: loading the wrong DLL A search order is also an attack surface. If an attacker can put a file with the right name in a folder that is searched before the real one, your program loads their code with your program's rights. This is called DLL search-order hijacking (or "DLL planting"), and it has affected many real applications. The current directory (step 5) and PATH (step 6) are the classic weak points: a double-clicked document can make its own folder the current directory. Defend your programs: Defence How --- --- Remove the current directory and other unsafe locations from the search for the whole process Call SetDefaultDllDirectories(LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DEFAULT_DIRS) at the very start of main Search only the system folder for system DLLs LoadLibraryExW(L"bcrypt.dll", nullptr, LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_SYSTEM32) Load your own DLLs by full path Build the path from the .exe 's folder (below) and pass it to LoadLibraryExW Do not load DLLs from folders ordinary users can write to Especially for anything that runs with administrator rights This matters for the plugin system in chapter 13: a game that loads every .dll in a mods folder is, by design, running code from that folder, so the folder's location and permissions are part of the design. Finding the program's own folder cpp include <windows.h include <iostream include <string std::wstring exeFolder() { std::wstring path(MAX_PATH, L'\0'); for (;;) { const DWORD length{ GetModuleFileNameW(nullptr, path.data(), static_cast<DWORD (path.size())) }; if (length == 0) return {}; if (length < path.size()) { path.resize(length); break; } path.resize(path.size() 2); // truncated: try a bigger buffer } return path.substr(0, path.find_last_of(L"\/")); } int main() { const std::wstring folder{ exeFolder() }; std::cout << "found the program's folder: " << (folder.empty() ? "no" : "yes") << '
'; return 0; } found the program's folder: yes GetModuleFileNameW(nullptr, ...) gives the path of the .exe ; passing a DLL's HMODULE instead gives that DLL's path. It does not report how much space it needed; it truncates silently and returns the buffer size, hence the loop. Modules that are already loaded GetModuleHandleW(L"kernel32.dll") returns the HMODULE of a DLL that is already loaded, without loading it or changing its reference count. GetModuleHandleW(nullptr) returns the .exe 's own module, the same value as wWinMain 's HINSTANCE . An HMODULE is simply the address where the module's image starts in memory, which is why chapter 9 can read a loaded module's headers directly from it. cpp include <windows.h include <iostream int main() { HMODULE kernel{ GetModuleHandleW(L"kernel32.dll") }; HMODULE self{ GetModuleHandleW(nullptr) }; std::cout << "kernel32 is loaded: " << (kernel != nullptr) << '
'; std::cout << "the exe's first two bytes: " << static_cast<const char (static_cast<const void (self)) 0 << static_cast<const char (static_cast<const void (self)) 1 << '
'; return 0; } kernel32 is loaded: 1 the exe's first two bytes: MZ Every executable and DLL starts with the letters MZ , the signature of its header. Chapter 9 starts there. Using newer functions when they exist A game may want a function that only exists on newer versions of Windows, while still running on older ones. Linking to it normally would stop the game starting at all on an older system (the loader fails on the missing import). Look it up at run time instead: cpp using SetThreadDescriptionFn = HRESULT (WINAPI )(HANDLE, PCWSTR); void nameThisThread(const wchar_t name) { auto fn{ reinterpret_cast<SetThreadDescriptionFn ( GetProcAddress(GetModuleHandleW(L"kernel32.dll"), "SetThreadDescription")) }; if (fn) fn(GetCurrentThread(), name); // shown in the debugger's Threads window (chapter 8) } Delay loading Delay loading is a linker feature that gives you run-time loading with normal-looking calls. Add a DLL to Linker → Input → Delay Loaded Dlls and link its import library as usual. The linker replaces each import with a small stub; the first call to any function in that DLL loads it then. If the DLL never gets used (an optional feature the player never turns on), it is never loaded, and the program still starts when it is missing. Common mistakes !warning Loading DLLs by bare name from a program with high privileges Use full paths and SetDefaultDllDirectories . Search-order hijacking is a real attack. !warning Calling FreeLibrary on a handle from GetModuleHandleW GetModuleHandleW does not increase the reference count, so freeing it can unload a DLL that something else still uses. !warning Assuming GetModuleFileNameW fits in MAX_PATH Long paths are possible. Check the returned length and grow the buffer. Check yourself quiz ? What is DLL search-order hijacking, and how do you prevent it? - A DLL taking over another DLL's exports; prevented by extern "C" + Planting a DLL in a folder searched first; prevented by restricting the search - Two programs loading the same DLL at once; prevented by a mutex - Windows loading DLLs in alphabetical order; prevented by renaming them The program loads whichever DLL with that name it finds first, so the defence is controlling where it looks. Use SetDefaultDllDirectories , full paths, and folders untrusted users cannot write to. ? What is an HMODULE ? - A handle to a kernel object that must be closed with CloseHandle - The file name of a DLL as a wide string - A pointer to the DLL's DllMain + The address at which a module (an exe or DLL) is loaded in the process; its headers start there That is why GetModuleHandleW(nullptr) gives the base address of the program's own image. ? How can a program use a function that might not exist on the user's version of Windows? - Call it inside a try block and catch the error + Look it up with GetProcAddress and call it only if found - Link it statically from the newer Windows SDK - Check the Windows version number and assume the function is there A direct call to a missing function makes the program fail to start; a run-time lookup lets it carry on without it. ? Why is the current working directory in the DLL search order a security risk? + Whoever controls that folder can plant a DLL there - It makes loading slower - The current directory is always read-only This is DLL search-order hijacking. ? What does GetModuleHandleW(nullptr) return? - A handle to the current thread + The load address of the program's own .exe - Null, because no module name was given It is the same value as the HINSTANCE given to wWinMain . ? A game wants to use a function that only exists on Windows 11 but still start on Windows 10. What should it do? - Link to it normally - Copy the function's code into the game + Find it with GetProcAddress and use it only if found A normal import of a missing function stops the program from starting at all. ? What does delay loading do? + Loads a DLL the first time one of its functions is called, instead of at start-up - Loads DLLs in the background - Delays the program's start until all DLLs are found Unused DLLs are never loaded, and a missing optional DLL does not stop the program starting.

title: 5.09  The Console API
body:
The console window is more than a place for std::cout . With the console API and virtual terminal sequences you can move the cursor, use colours, hide the cursor, read individual key presses and redraw a whole screen without flicker: enough for a text-mode game or a live tool display. This lesson covers both the classic API and the modern escape sequences. Handles to the console A console program has three standard handles, fetched with GetStdHandle : Handle For --- --- STD_INPUT_HANDLE Keyboard and mouse input STD_OUTPUT_HANDLE Text output STD_ERROR_HANDLE Error output They are like file handles (lesson 5.01): WriteFile works on the output handle. But the console also has its own functions that understand it as a grid of character cells with colours and a cursor. !note Run these in a real console The examples in this lesson need a real console window. The course website captures program output instead of showing a console, so build and run them in Visual Studio. Colours and positions, the classic way cpp-norun include <windows.h include <iostream int main() { HANDLE out{ GetStdHandle(STD_OUTPUT_HANDLE) }; SetConsoleTextAttribute(out, FOREGROUND_GREEN FOREGROUND_INTENSITY); std::cout << "HP 87/100
"; SetConsoleTextAttribute(out, FOREGROUND_RED FOREGROUND_INTENSITY); std::cout << "Poisoned
"; SetConsoleTextAttribute(out, FOREGROUND_RED FOREGROUND_GREEN FOREGROUND_BLUE); // back to grey SetConsoleCursorPosition(out, COORD{ 20, 0 }); // column 20, row 0 std::cout << "Gold 1250"; SetConsoleCursorPosition(out, COORD{ 0, 3 }); return 0; } Colours are 4 bits each for text and background (16 colours); positions are a COORD of column and row, counted from 0. Virtual terminal sequences Modern Windows consoles (and Windows Terminal) also understand the same escape sequences used by Linux and macOS terminals: special strings starting with the ESC character ( \x1b ) that the terminal interprets instead of printing. They are often simpler than the API, work across platforms, and support 24-bit colour. Turn them on once: cpp HANDLE out{ GetStdHandle(STD_OUTPUT_HANDLE) }; DWORD mode{ 0 }; GetConsoleMode(out, &mode); SetConsoleMode(out, mode ENABLE_VIRTUAL_TERMINAL_PROCESSING); SetConsoleOutputCP(CP_UTF8); // and print UTF-8 correctly (lesson 5.03) Sequence Effect --- --- \x1b H Cursor to the top-left \x1b row;colH Cursor to a position, counted from 1 \x1b 2J Clear the screen \x1b 31m ... \x1b 37m Text colour: red, green, yellow, blue, magenta, cyan, white (30 is black) \x1b 1m Bold / bright \x1b 38;2;r;g;bm Any 24-bit text colour \x1b 0m Reset all colours and styles \x1b ?25l / \x1b ?25h Hide / show the cursor cpp-norun std::cout << "\x1b 2J\x1b ?25l"; // clear, hide cursor std::cout << "\x1b 1;1H\x1b 32mHP 87/100\x1b 0m"; // green, top-left std::cout << "\x1b 1;21H\x1b 38;2;255;200;60mGold 1250\x1b 0m"; // gold-coloured, column 21 Drawing a whole screen without flicker Clearing and reprinting the screen every frame flickers, for the same reason as lesson 5.06: the user sees the empty screen in between. The text-mode version of double buffering is to build the entire frame as one string and write it in a single call, starting with "cursor home" rather than "clear": cpp-norun std::string frame{ "\x1b H" }; // home, not clear: overwrite in place for (int y{ 0 }; y < height; ++y) { for (int x{ 0 }; x < width; ++x) frame += (x == px && y == py) ? '@' : map y x ; frame += '
'; } WriteConsoleA(out, frame.data(), static_cast<DWORD (frame.size()), nullptr, nullptr); One write per frame means the console updates all at once. Reading keys without Enter std::cin waits for a whole line. A game needs individual key presses as they happen. ReadConsoleInputW returns input records , one per event, and GetNumberOfConsoleInputEvents says whether any are waiting, so a loop never blocks: cpp-norun HANDLE in{ GetStdHandle(STD_INPUT_HANDLE) }; DWORD waiting{ 0 }; GetNumberOfConsoleInputEvents(in, &waiting); while (waiting-- 0) { INPUT_RECORD record{}; DWORD read{ 0 }; ReadConsoleInputW(in, &record, 1, &read); if (record.EventType == KEY_EVENT && record.Event.KeyEvent.bKeyDown) handleKey(record.Event.KeyEvent.wVirtualKeyCode); // the same virtual-key codes as lesson 5.07 } Put the three pieces together (an input loop, game state, a whole-frame string) and you have a complete text-mode game engine in under a hundred lines. Many classic roguelike games are exactly this. A console for a windowed game A game built for the Windows subsystem (lesson 5.06) has no console, which makes std::cout logging disappear. During development you can give it one: cpp AllocConsole(); // create a console window for this process FILE stream{ nullptr }; freopen_s(&stream, "CONOUT$", "w", stdout); // point stdout at it Chapter 11's debug console uses a different approach, drawing text inside the game itself, but AllocConsole is the quickest way to get logging into a windowed program. Common mistakes !warning Escape sequences printing as garbage Enable ENABLE_VIRTUAL_TERMINAL_PROCESSING first. Older consoles may not support it at all. !warning Counting rows and columns from 0 in escape sequences \x1b 1;1H is the top-left. The COORD API counts from 0; escape sequences count from 1. !warning Clearing the screen every frame Home the cursor and overwrite instead, writing the whole frame in one call. !warning Using std::cin for game input It waits for Enter. Read input records instead. Check yourself quiz ? What are virtual terminal sequences? - Keyboard shortcuts that control a terminal window - Commands sent to a remote computer over a network terminal + Escape-character strings the console treats as commands - Special Unicode characters that draw boxes and lines \x1b 5;10H , for example, moves the cursor to row 5, column 10 instead of printing anything. ? How does a console game read single key presses without blocking? + It reads waiting events with ReadConsoleInputW , only if any wait - It reads std::cin with a timeout - It calls getchar in a loop - It waits for WM_KEYDOWN messages in a message loop std::cin waits for Enter; reading the console's input events gives each key press as it happens. GetNumberOfConsoleInputEvents says whether any are waiting. ? How can a windowed game show std::cout output during development? + Call AllocConsole to create a console and reopen stdout on CONOUT$ - Change the project's subsystem to Console in Release builds - Use MessageBoxW for each line - std::cout already appears in the game window automatically A windowed program has no console by default; AllocConsole creates one and reopening stdout sends output there. ? What does the sequence \x1b 5;10H do? - Prints the numbers 5 and 10 + Moves the cursor to row 5, column 10 - Sets the colour to 5;10 H positions the cursor; escape-sequence rows and columns start at 1. ? How do you avoid flicker when redrawing a text-mode game screen? - Clear the screen before each frame - Print one character at a time + Build the whole frame as one string and write it once The console then shows complete frames only. ? Why use ReadConsoleInputW instead of std::cin for a text-mode game? + It gives single key events without waiting for Enter - std::cin cannot read letters - It is the only way to read numbers Games need each key press as it happens.
