title: 7.01  Registers and the Shape of an Instruction
match: 7.01 Registers and the Shape of an Instruction
body: x64 assembly is the text form of the machine code your C++ becomes. This chapter teaches you to read it, and occasionally to write it. It starts with the registers , the processor's handful of built-in variables, their 64, 32, 16 and 8-bit names, and the shape every instruction follows: an operation and its operands. Why learn to read assembly You will rarely write assembly. You will read it often: - in the debugger's Disassembly window, when a crash happens in code without source, or in optimised code where the source view no longer matches what runs (lesson 4.10); - in compiler output , to see what your C++ really costs (lesson 7.11); - in reverse engineering , where it is all there is (chapter 9). The tiny computer of lesson 1.01 had one register and seven instructions. An x64 processor has the same ideas on a larger scale. The general-purpose registers x64 has sixteen 64-bit general-purpose registers. Each is a variable built into the processor: reading and writing them takes no memory access at all. Register Traditional role In the Windows calling convention (lesson 7.06) --- --- --- rax Accumulator Return value rbx Base Must be preserved by functions rcx Counter 1st integer argument rdx Data 2nd integer argument rsi Source index Must be preserved rdi Destination index Must be preserved rbp Base pointer Must be preserved; sometimes the frame pointer rsp Stack pointer The top of the stack (lesson 1.05) r8 , r9 3rd and 4th integer arguments r10 , r11 Scratch r12 to r15 Must be preserved There are also special registers: rip (the instruction pointer, the program counter of lesson 1.01), rflags (the flags, lesson 7.04), and sixteen 128-bit xmm registers for floating point (lesson 7.09). Smaller names for parts of a register Each register can be used at several widths, through different names for its lower parts: 63 31 15 7 0 ┌────────────────────────────────┬───────────────┬────────┬──────┐ │ rax │ │ │ eax │ │ │ │ ax │ │ │ │ ah │ al │ └────────────────────────────────┴───────────────┴────────┴──────┘ 64-bit 32-bit 16-bit 8-bit --- --- --- --- rax eax ax al rbx ebx bx bl rcx ecx cx cl rdx edx dx dl rsi , rdi , rbp , rsp esi , edi , ebp , esp si , di , bp , sp sil , dil , bpl , spl r8 ... r15 r8d ... r15d r8w ... r15w r8b ... r15b So an int (4 bytes) usually lives in an e register, a char or bool in an 8-bit one, a pointer or long long in a full r register. One rule surprises everyone once: writing a 32-bit register clears the upper 32 bits of the 64-bit register. Writing 8 or 16 bits leaves the rest unchanged. Compilers rely on this constantly: mov eax, 1 is a shorter instruction than mov rax, 1 and has the same effect. The shape of an instruction Each line of assembly is one instruction: an operation (the mnemonic ) and up to two or three operands . In the syntax Microsoft's tools use (Intel syntax), the destination comes first : asm mov eax, 5 ; eax = 5 add eax, ecx ; eax = eax + ecx mov rsp+8 , eax ; the 4 bytes at address rsp+8 = eax An operand is one of three kinds: Kind Example Means --- --- --- Register ecx The value in a register Immediate 5 , 0FFh , -1 A constant stored inside the instruction itself (lesson 1.04 saw 0x32 inside an lea ) Memory rsp+8 , dword ptr rcx The value at an address, worked out from registers and constants Most instructions allow at most one memory operand: there is no "add memory to memory". Values are brought into registers, worked on, and written back, just like the tiny computer's LOAD, ADD, STORE. Watching registers change Step through this. Watch which register changes on each line, and especially what mov eax does to the upper half of rax : demo-asm title: Register widths init: rax=-1 mov al, 7 mov ax, 300 mov eax, 5 mov rcx, rax add rcx, 10 ret - After mov al, 7 and mov ax, 300 , only the low bits change: rax was all ones (-1), and its upper bytes stay ones. - mov eax, 5 clears the whole upper half: rax becomes exactly 5. - ret ends the function, and whoever called it finds its answer in rax . !note Two syntaxes Microsoft's tools and most Windows debuggers use Intel syntax (destination first, mov eax, 5 ). Linux tools default to AT&T syntax ( movl $5, %eax : source first, % before registers, $ before constants). They are the same instructions written differently. This course uses Intel syntax throughout. Common mistakes !warning Reading operands in the wrong order In Intel syntax, mov a, b copies b into a. The destination is first. !warning Forgetting that writing a 32-bit register zeroes the top half mov eax, -1 leaves rax as 0x00000000FFFFFFFF , not -1. !warning Expecting two memory operands add a , b does not exist. One side must be a register or a constant. Check yourself quiz ? What is a register? - A numbered byte of RAM that the CPU reads fastest + A small, fixed storage slot inside the processor itself - A table the operating system keeps of every running program - A line of the program's machine code x64 has sixteen general-purpose 64-bit registers. Reading one needs no memory access at all, which is why arithmetic happens in them. ? What are eax , ax and al ? - Three separate registers that have nothing to do with rax - The high 32, 16 and 8 bits of rax + The low 32, 16 and 8 bits of rax , usable as registers in their own right - Older names for rax that mean exactly the same 64 bits Writing to eax also zeroes the top half of rax , which is why mov eax, 2 leaves rax holding 2. ? What three kinds of operand can an instruction have? - A variable, a function and a type - A register, a file and a handle - A byte, a word and a dword + A register, an immediate constant, or a memory location byte , word and dword describe operand sizes, not kinds of operand. ? Which register holds a function's return value on x64 Windows? + rax - rcx - rsp rcx , rdx , r8 and r9 bring arguments in; rax carries the result out. ? rax holds -1 (all bits set). After mov eax, 2 , what is in rax ? - 0xFFFFFFFF00000002 + 2 - -2 Writing a 32-bit register clears the upper 32 bits. ? In sub ecx, 10 , which operand receives the result? - 10 - Neither; the result goes to rax + ecx , the first operand Intel syntax puts the destination first. ? Which of these is a memory operand? - r9d - 0x40 + qword ptr rdx+16 Square brackets mean "the value at this address".

title: A register with many names
where: 7.01 Registers and the Shape of an Instruction
body: Model one x64 general-purpose register and the rules for writing its smaller parts. Write the class Register : - get64() , get32() , get16() , get8() return the low 64, 32, 16 or 8 bits (as unsigned values). - set64(v) replaces all 64 bits. - set32(v) writes the low 32 bits and clears the upper 32 , as the processor does. - set16(v) writes the low 16 bits and leaves the other 48 unchanged. - set8(v) writes the low 8 bits and leaves the other 56 unchanged. Values passed to the smaller setters may have extra high bits: only the bits that fit are used. Register r; r.set64(0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF); r.set8(7); // get64() = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFF07 r.set16(300); // get64() = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFF012C r.set32(5); // get64() = 5

title: 7.02  Moving Data: mov, lea and Addressing Modes
match: 7.02 Moving Data: mov, lea and Addressing Modes
body: Most instructions in real code just move data: between registers, from memory into a register, from a register back to memory. This lesson covers mov and its widening relatives movzx and movsx , the addressing modes that let one instruction compute an address like base + index × scale + offset , and lea , which does that arithmetic without touching memory at all. mov mov destination, source copies a value. It never changes the source and never sets the flags. asm mov eax, 10 ; constant into a register mov ecx, eax ; register to register mov eax, dword ptr rcx ; 4 bytes from memory at the address in rcx, into eax mov qword ptr rsp+20h , rax ; 8 bytes from rax into memory at rsp+0x20 mov byte ptr rdx , 1 ; the constant 1 into one byte of memory The size comes from the register ( eax is 4 bytes, rax 8). When there is no register to tell it (a constant stored to memory), the size is written out: byte ptr , word ptr (2), dword ptr (4), qword ptr (8). Disassemblers show the ptr sizes on every memory operand, which is a gift when reading code: dword ptr rcx+8 tells you there is a 4-byte value 8 bytes into whatever rcx points at. Widening: movzx and movsx Loading a 1-byte char or 2-byte short into a 32-bit register needs to fill the extra bits, and how depends on whether the type is signed: Instruction Fills the new upper bits with For --- --- --- movzx eax, byte ptr rcx Zeros ( zero extension ) unsigned char , bool , std::uint16_t movsx eax, byte ptr rcx Copies of the sign bit ( sign extension ) signed char , short movsxd rax, ecx Sign extension from 32 to 64 bits int to long long or to an index The byte 0xFF becomes 255 with movzx and -1 with movsx . This is two's complement from lesson 1.02, done by hardware. Addressing modes A memory operand can compute its address from up to four parts: base + index × scale + displacement reg reg 1,2,4,8 constant Form Typical C++ --- --- rcx p rcx+8 p- member at offset 8 (lesson 2.06) rcx+rdx 4 array i for 4-byte elements: base address rcx , index rdx rcx+rdx 8+10h p- items i where items is an array of 8-byte values at offset 0x10 rip+1234h A global variable, relative to the instruction (lesson 6.09) The scale can only be 1, 2, 4 or 8: exactly the sizes of char , short , int / float and pointers/ double . Indexing arrays of those types costs no extra instructions at all. Step through a loop that sums an array. rdi holds the array's address; rdi+rcx 4 is values i : demo-asm title: Summing int values 4 through rdi+rcx 4 init: rdi=0x2000, mem@0x2000=10 20 30 40 xor eax, eax xor ecx, ecx next: add eax, dword ptr rdi+rcx 4 inc ecx cmp ecx, 4 jl next ret lea: the address calculator lea ("load effective address") computes the address of a memory operand and puts the address itself into the destination, without reading memory: asm lea rax, rcx+rdx 4 ; rax = rcx + rdx 4 (&array i ) lea rax, rcx+10h ; rax = rcx + 16 (&p- member) lea rcx, rip+1F2Ah ; rcx = the address of a global or string literal Because the address hardware can add two registers, scale one of them and add a constant in a single step, compilers also use lea for plain arithmetic that has nothing to do with addresses: C++ Compiled --- --- x + 50 (into a different register) lea eax, rcx+32h (lesson 1.04's example) a + b lea eax, rcx+rdx x 5 lea eax, rcx+rcx 4 x 9 + 3 lea eax, rcx+rcx 8+3 When you see lea in compiler output, ask whether it is computing a pointer or just doing quick arithmetic. Both are common. Common mistakes !warning Confusing mov rax, rcx with lea rax, rcx mov reads the 8 bytes at the address; lea puts the address itself in rax . One is p , the other is p . !warning Reading rcx+rdx 4 as "rcx plus rdx plus 4" The 4 scales the index: it is element rdx of an array of 4-byte values. !warning Assuming mov sets flags It does not. A comparison needs cmp or test . Check yourself quiz ? What four parts can a memory operand's address have? + A base register, an index register multiplied by 1, 2, 4 or 8, and a constant displacement - A segment, a page number, an offset and a size - Two registers added together, a multiplier of any value, and a variable name - A base register, a displacement, a protection flag and a length rcx+rdx 8+10h uses all of them: base rcx , index rdx scaled by 8, displacement 10h . ? What is the difference between movzx and movsx ? + Both widen; movzx fills with zeros, movsx with the sign bit - movzx moves to memory, movsx moves to a register - movzx clears the destination, movsx swaps the two operands - movzx is for 32-bit values and movsx for 64-bit values So the byte 0xFE becomes 254 with movzx and -2 with movsx . ? What does lea do? - It loads the value stored at an address into a register - It locks a memory location for one thread + It computes a memory operand's address without reading memory - It loads the address of the next instruction Because it only computes, compilers also use it for fast arithmetic such as lea eax, rcx+rcx 2 for x 3 . ? What does mov eax, dword ptr rcx+8 do? - Sets eax to rcx+8 + Copies the 4 bytes at address rcx+8 into eax - Adds 8 to the value at rcx The brackets read memory; lea would compute the address instead. ? The byte at rdx is 0xFE . What does movsx eax, byte ptr rdx put in eax? - 254 - 0xFE000000 + -2 Sign extension copies the top bit, so 0xFE as a signed byte, -2, stays -2. ? Which C++ expression is rcx+rdx 8 most likely to come from? + p i where p points at 8-byte values - p + i + 8 on a char pointer - p- member at offset 8 of a struct Base, index and a scale equal to the element size: array indexing. ? Why might a compiler emit lea eax, rcx+rcx 2 ? - To read memory at x 3 + To compute x 3 in one instruction - To compare x with 3 lea does arithmetic with the address hardware and never touches memory.

title: Work out the address
where: 7.02 Moving Data: mov, lea and Addressing Modes
body: Write effectiveAddress(base, index, scale, displacement) , which computes the address a memory operand base + index scale + displacement refers to, exactly as the processor does: in 64-bit arithmetic that wraps round. displacement may be negative. Also write widen(byte, isSigned) , which returns the 32-bit value movsx (when isSigned is true) or movzx (when false) would produce from one byte, as an unsigned 32-bit number. If scale is not 1, 2, 4 or 8, the instruction cannot be encoded: effectiveAddress returns std::nullopt . effectiveAddress(0x2000, 3, 4, 0) = 0x200C effectiveAddress(0x1000, 0, 1, -8) = 0xFF8 widen(0xFE, true) = 0xFFFFFFFE widen(0xFE, false) = 0xFE

title: 7.03  Arithmetic and Bit Operations
body: The arithmetic instructions ( add , sub , imul , inc , dec , neg , div ) and the bit instructions ( and , or , xor , not , shl , shr , sar ) are the processor's whole calculator. This lesson covers each, the flags they set as a side effect, and the tricks compilers use, such as replacing division by a constant with multiplication. The two-operand pattern x64 arithmetic usually has two operands, and the result replaces the first: Instruction Effect C++ --- --- --- add a, b a = a + b a += b sub a, b a = a - b a -= b imul a, b a = a × b (signed, keeps the low bits) a = b imul a, b, 7 a = b × 7 (three-operand form) a = b 7 inc a / dec a a = a ± 1 ++a / --a neg a a = -a a = -a There is no separate instruction for unsigned multiplication of the kind C++ needs: since the low bits of a product are the same either way (two's complement again), imul serves both. The flags Most arithmetic and logic instructions also set bits in the flags register describing their result. Four matter most: Flag Set when the result... --- --- ZF (zero) is zero SF (sign) has its top bit set: negative, read as signed CF (carry) did not fit as an unsigned number (a carry out of, or borrow into, the top bit) OF (overflow) did not fit as a signed number Watch them change. The first add overflows as signed (127 + 1 in a byte), the second as unsigned: demo-asm title: Flags after arithmetic on bytes mov al, 127 add al, 1 mov al, 255 add al, 1 mov al, 5 sub al, 5 ret - 127 + 1 in a byte is 0x80 : SF set (negative as signed), OF set (signed overflow), CF clear (128 fits unsigned). - 255 + 1 is 0 with a carry out: ZF and CF set (unsigned overflow), OF clear. - 5 - 5 is 0: ZF set. The processor does not know whether your bytes are signed or unsigned. It computes the bits once and reports both kinds of overflow; the next instruction decides which flags it cares about. Lesson 7.04 uses this for comparisons. Division div (unsigned) and idiv (signed) are the odd ones out. They divide the double-width value in rdx:rax (or edx:eax ) by the operand, putting the quotient in rax and the remainder in rdx : asm mov eax, ecx ; the number to divide cdq ; sign-extend eax into edx:eax idiv r8d ; eax = quotient, edx = remainder Division is slow: tens of cycles, against one for an add. Dividing by zero, or INT_MIN / -1 , raises an exception (integer divide by zero, code 0xC0000094 ). So compilers avoid div whenever they can: C++ What the compiler emits --- --- x / 8 (unsigned) shr eax, 3 x % 8 (unsigned) and eax, 7 x / 10 (unsigned) A multiplication by a "magic" constant ( 0xCCCCCCCD ) and a shift x / 8 (signed) A shift plus a small correction so negative numbers round towards zero When you see a strange large constant multiplied and then shifted in compiler output, it is almost always division by a constant. Bit operations Instruction Effect Typical use --- --- --- and a, b Keep bits set in both Masking: x & 0xFF , testing flags or a, b Set bits set in either Combining flags xor a, b Flip bits set in b Toggling; xor eax, eax sets eax to zero not a Flip every bit ~x shl a, n Shift left by n: multiply by 2ⁿ x << n shr a, n Shift right, filling with zeros: unsigned divide by 2ⁿ x n for unsigned sar a, n Shift right, copying the sign bit x n for signed xor eax, eax deserves a mention because it is everywhere: XOR of anything with itself is zero, and the instruction is shorter than mov eax, 0 . Whenever you see it, read "eax = 0". Bit tricks are everywhere in game and systems code: packing flags into one integer, extracting fields (lesson 5.07's lParam ), hashing (lesson 3.08), rounding up to alignment (lesson 2.02's arena). Common mistakes !warning Reading CF as "the result was negative" CF is unsigned overflow. "Negative" is SF. !warning Assuming shr and sar are interchangeable For negative numbers they differ: sar keeps the sign, shr makes the number large and positive. !warning Forgetting that div uses rdx Code that divides must set up rdx first ( cdq , cqo , or xor edx, edx ), and the remainder overwrites it. Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference between the carry flag and the overflow flag? - CF is set by addition, OF by multiplication + CF: the result does not fit unsigned; OF: it does not fit signed - CF means the result was zero; OF means it was negative - They are the same flag under two names The CPU does not know whether the bits are signed, so it reports both and the code picks the one it needs. ? Why do compilers avoid div ? - div cannot divide negative numbers - div only works on 8-bit values - div gives the wrong answer for powers of two + Division is very slow, so it is replaced by faster operations The replacement gives the same result, only faster. Division by a constant becomes shifts, masks or a multiply by a precomputed constant. ? How is x % 8 computed for unsigned x ? - With shr x, 3 + With and x, 7 - With div by 8 and keeping the quotient - With sub x, 8 in a loop Keeping the low three bits gives the remainder after dividing by 8. shr x, 3 would give the quotient, x / 8 . ? After mov al, 200 then add al, 100 , which flag tells you the unsigned result did not fit? - OF - ZF + CF 300 does not fit in a byte; the carry out of the top bit sets CF. ? What does xor ecx, ecx do? + Sets ecx to zero - Flips every bit of ecx - Leaves ecx unchanged Any value XOR itself is 0. It is the usual way to zero a register. ? A compiler turned n / 16 into shr eax, 4 . What does that tell you about n ? - It is a float + It is unsigned - It is always zero A logical right shift divides an unsigned number by a power of two. A signed value would need a correction for negative numbers. ? Which instruction shifts right while keeping the sign of a negative number? - shr + sar - shl Arithmetic shift right copies the sign bit into the new top bits.

title: The flags after an add
body: Write add8(a, b) , which simulates the instruction add al, bl on two bytes and returns the 8-bit result together with the four flags it sets: - zf : the result is zero; - sf : bit 7 of the result is set; - cf : the true unsigned sum did not fit in 8 bits; - of : the true signed sum (treating a and b as std::int8_t ) did not fit in 8 bits. Then write sub8(a, b) for sub al, bl . For subtraction, cf is set when b is larger than a as unsigned numbers (a borrow), and of when the true signed difference does not fit. add8(127, 1) - result 0x80, sf, of add8(255, 1) - result 0, zf, cf sub8(3, 5) - result 0xFE, sf, cf

title: 7.04  Flags, Comparisons and Jumps
body: Every if , loop and switch in C++ becomes a comparison that sets the flags and a conditional jump that reads them. This lesson covers cmp and test , the family of j cc jumps and which ones mean signed or unsigned, and the branch-free alternatives setcc and cmov . cmp and test Lesson 7.03 showed that arithmetic sets the flags. Two instructions exist only to set them: Instruction Computes Keeps Used for --- --- --- --- cmp a, b a − b Only the flags; a is unchanged Comparing two values test a, b a AND b Only the flags Checking for zero ( test eax, eax ) or particular bits test eax, eax is the idiom for "is eax zero?": ANDing a value with itself gives the value, so ZF is set exactly when it is zero, and SF when it is negative. Conditional jumps A conditional jump goes to a label if a condition on the flags holds, and otherwise falls through to the next instruction. The condition names come in signed and unsigned versions, because "less than" means different things for signed and unsigned numbers (lesson 1.02): After cmp a, b , jump if... Signed Unsigned Flags tested --- --- --- --- a == b je / jz je / jz ZF = 1 a != b jne / jnz jne / jnz ZF = 0 a < b jl jb ("below") SF ≠ OF / CF = 1 a <= b jle jbe ZF = 1 or SF ≠ OF / CF = 1 or ZF = 1 a b jg ja ("above") ZF = 0 and SF = OF / CF = 0 and ZF = 0 a = b jge jae SF = OF / CF = 0 always jmp jmp none So the jump tells you the type : jl / jg after a cmp means the compiler treated the values as signed; jb / ja means unsigned (or pointers, or sizes). When reverse engineering, that is often your first clue to a variable's type. An if, compiled cpp int clampHealth(int h) { if (h 100) h = 100; return h; } asm clampHealth PROC cmp ecx, 100 ; compare h with 100 jle keep ; if h <= 100, skip the assignment mov ecx, 100 keep: mov eax, ecx ; return h ret clampHealth ENDP Notice the inverted condition : C++ says "if h 100, do this", and the compiler writes "if h <= 100, jump over this". That inversion is so common that reading compiled code, you learn to flip conditions automatically. demo-asm title: clampHealth with h = 140 init: ecx=140 cmp ecx, 100 jle keep mov ecx, 100 keep: mov eax, ecx ret With a value of 100 or less in ecx , the jle would be taken instead and mov ecx, 100 skipped. Branch-free versions: setcc and cmov A jump that the processor cannot predict is expensive: modern CPUs guess which way each branch goes and start working ahead, and a wrong guess throws that work away (10 to 20 cycles). For simple choices, compilers often avoid the jump entirely: Instruction Effect --- --- setl al (and sete , setg , setb ...) al = 1 if the condition holds, else 0: a bool result cmovg eax, edx (and every other condition) eax = edx if the condition holds; otherwise eax is unchanged asm ; return a b; ; return a b ? a : b; (std::max) cmp ecx, edx mov eax, edx setg al cmp ecx, edx ret cmovg eax, ecx ret demo-asm title: std::max(8, 3) without a jump init: ecx=8, edx=3 mov eax, edx cmp ecx, edx cmovg eax, ecx ret Common mistakes !warning Reading the jump as the C++ condition Compilers usually jump around the body, so the jump's condition is the opposite of the if . !warning Mixing up jl and jb jl is signed less-than, jb unsigned. For -1 against 1, jl jumps (−1 < 1) and jb does not (0xFFFFFFFF is above 1). !warning Forgetting what set the flags A conditional jump uses whatever instruction last set the flags, which is not always the line right above it. Check yourself quiz ? What do cmp and test compute, and what do they keep? + cmp subtracts and test ANDs their operands; both keep only the flags and throw the result away - cmp compares and stores 1 or 0; test checks whether a register is valid - Both subtract, and both store the result in the first operand - cmp ANDs and test subtracts; both keep the result That is why a conditional jump comes after them: it reads the flags they set. ? How can you tell from compiled code whether a comparison was signed or unsigned? - From the cmp instruction, which has a signed and an unsigned form - From the size of the registers used + From the jump or set instruction that reads the flags: l / g are signed, b / a are unsigned - You cannot; the information is lost when compiling cmp is the same either way; the choice of jl or jb (and so on) shows how the bits were meant. ? What do setcc and cmovcc do? - They set and clear the carry flag - They save the flags to the stack and restore them - They jump only if a condition holds + setcc writes 1 or 0 by a condition; cmovcc copies only if it holds Both avoid a branch, which can be faster when the condition is hard to predict. ? What does test eax, eax followed by jz done do? + Jumps to done if eax is zero - Jumps if eax is not zero - Compares eax with zero and stores the result AND of a value with itself is zero only when the value is zero, setting ZF. ? After cmp ecx, edx , the compiler uses ja . What does that suggest about ecx and edx? - They are being compared as signed values + They are being compared as unsigned values - They are floats ja / jb are the unsigned conditions; jg / jl the signed ones. ? The C++ says if (x == 0) { ... } . Which jump is the compiler most likely to emit before the body? - je , to enter the body - jmp , always + jne , to skip the body The jump goes around the body, so its condition is inverted. ? Why do compilers sometimes use cmov instead of a jump? + To avoid a branch that might be mispredicted - Because cmov is shorter than mov - Because jumps cannot be conditional A mispredicted branch costs many cycles; a conditional move never mispredicts.

title: Will it jump?
body: Write taken(condition, flags) , which says whether a conditional jump with that condition is taken, given the four flags. condition is the part after the j : "e" , "z" , "ne" , "nz" , "l" , "le" , "g" , "ge" , "b" , "be" , "a" , "ae" , "s" , "ns" . Use the flag rules from the lesson's table. For an unknown condition, return std::nullopt . flags after cmp 3, 5: ZF 0, SF 1, CF 1, OF 0 taken("l", ...) = true (3 < 5 as signed) taken("b", ...) = true (3 < 5 as unsigned) taken("g", ...) = false

title: 7.05  The Stack, push, pop, call and ret
match: 7.05 The Stack, push, pop, call and ret
body: Four instructions manage the stack from lesson 1.05 at the machine level. push and pop add and remove 8-byte values; call pushes a return address and jumps; ret pops it and jumps back. This lesson steps through them, shows a function's prologue and epilogue , and explains what a corrupted stack does to ret . push and pop The stack grows downwards, and rsp always points at the value on top (lesson 1.05). Instruction Does Equivalent to --- --- --- push rbx rsp −= 8, then store rbx at rsp sub rsp, 8 / mov rsp , rbx pop rbx load rsp into rbx, then rsp += 8 mov rbx, rsp / add rsp, 8 On x64, push and pop always move 8 bytes. Their main use in compiled code is saving and restoring the non-volatile registers ( rbx , rbp , rdi , rsi , r12 to r15 ) that a function must give back unchanged (lesson 2.01). call and ret Instruction Does --- --- call target push the address of the next instruction (the return address ), then jump to target ret pop the return address into rip : continue there ret 0 the same (the number is how many extra bytes to pop; always 0 on x64) Step through a function that saves rbx , uses it, and returns. Watch the stack panel: call pushes the return address, push rbx saves the caller's rbx below it, and they come off again in reverse order. demo-asm title: call, push, pop and ret init: ecx=6, rbx=77 call square add eax, 1 ret square: push rbx mov ebx, ecx imul ebx, ecx mov eax, ebx pop rbx ret At the end, rax is 37 and rbx is back to 77: square used rbx but restored it, as the calling convention requires. Prologue and epilogue Most compiled functions start and end with a fixed pattern that builds and dismantles their stack frame: asm update PROC push rbx ; prologue: save non-volatile registers used below push rdi sub rsp, 40 ; reserve the frame: locals + 32 bytes of shadow space, aligned ... ; the body add rsp, 40 ; epilogue: release the frame pop rdi ; restore in reverse order pop rbx ret update ENDP The numbers follow the alignment rule from lesson 2.01: on entry rsp is 8 off a multiple of 16 (the return address), two pushes make it 8 off again (24 bytes), and sub rsp, 40 brings the total to 64, a multiple of 16, ready for this function's own calls. Older code, and code compiled for easier debugging, also sets up rbp as a frame pointer : asm push rbp mov rbp, rsp ; rbp marks the frame; locals are at rbp-8, rbp-16 ... sub rsp, 48 ... mov rsp, rbp pop rbp ret x64 Windows code usually omits it. The debugger and Windows find frames through unwind information that the compiler stores in the .pdata and .xdata sections, describing each function's prologue so the stack can be walked without a frame pointer (lesson 8.02). When the stack is corrupted ret trusts whatever 8 bytes are at rsp . If a buffer overrun on the stack (lesson 2.09) has overwritten the return address, ret jumps to that garbage, and the crash happens at a nonsense address with a nonsense call stack. This is also the classic way attackers hijack programs, which is why compilers add defences: - Stack cookies ( /GS , on by default): the prologue puts a secret value between the locals and the return address, and the epilogue checks it before ret . An overrun that reaches the return address changes the cookie first, and the program is stopped with a security check failure instead of jumping. - Control-flow guard and shadow stacks (on recent CPUs and Windows) check calls and returns against what is allowed. When you see a crash at a strange address with a broken call stack, suspect a stack overrun and turn on AddressSanitizer (lesson 2.10). Common mistakes !warning Unbalanced push and pop Every push in a function must be matched by a pop (or an add rsp ) before ret , or ret pops the wrong value. !warning Popping in the wrong order Registers must be restored in the reverse order they were saved. !warning Reading ret 0 as "return 0" The 0 is a byte count for the stack, not the return value. The return value is in rax . Check yourself quiz ? What do push and pop do to rsp ? - push adds 8, pop subtracts 8 + push subtracts 8 then stores; pop loads then adds 8 - push stores at rsp without changing it; pop clears it - push and pop change rbp , not rsp The stack grows towards lower addresses, so pushing moves rsp down. ? What are a function's prologue and epilogue? + The code that saves registers and sets up the frame, and that undoes it - Its first and last lines of C++ source - The comments the compiler writes before and after it - The call that enters it and the ret that leaves it The epilogue undoes the prologue in reverse order. ? Why can a stack buffer overrun make a program jump to a random address? - Because the overrun changes the value of rip directly - Because the CPU jumps to the address of any data it reads past the end + The overrun can overwrite the return address above the locals, and ret then jumps to whatever is there - Because the operating system moves the stack after an overrun ret trusts whatever value is at the top of the stack. Stack cookies exist to detect this before ret runs. ? What does call square push onto the stack? - The address of square + The address of the instruction after the call - The value of rax ret later pops it to continue after the call. ? A function's prologue is push rbx then push rsi . In what order must its epilogue restore them? - pop rbx , then pop rsi - Either order + pop rsi , then pop rbx The stack is last in, first out. ? What does a stack cookie protect? + The return address, from stack overruns - The heap, from double frees - The code section, from writes The epilogue checks the cookie and stops the program if it changed. ? In square above, why does the function push and pop rbx ? - rbx holds the return address + rbx is non-volatile, so it must be preserved - imul requires it Functions may use non-volatile registers only if they restore them.

title: 7.06  The Microsoft x64 Calling Convention
body: A calling convention is the agreement between a caller and the function it calls: where arguments go, where the result comes back, which registers survive the call and who cleans up the stack. On 64-bit Windows there is one convention for everything. Knowing it lets you read any function's arguments in the debugger, follow calls in disassembly, and write assembly that C++ can call. Why a convention is needed The compiler that builds a caller and the compiler that built the function might be different programs, years apart: your game calling CreateFileW in kernel32.dll , a plugin calling the engine, C++ calling assembly. They only work together if both follow the same rules. On x64 Windows those rules are the Microsoft x64 calling convention , and every compiler targeting Windows follows it. Arguments The first four arguments go in registers, the rest on the stack: Argument Integer or pointer Floating point --- --- --- 1st rcx xmm0 2nd rdx xmm1 3rd r8 xmm2 4th r9 xmm3 5th and later On the stack, at rsp+28h , rsp+30h , ... at the moment of the call The position decides the register, not the type: in f(int a, float b, int c) , a is in rcx , b in xmm1 (second position), and c in r8 . - A member function's hidden this is the first argument: it is in rcx , and the visible arguments shift along by one. - Structs of 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes are passed in a register as if they were an integer. Any other size is copied by the caller to memory, and a pointer to the copy is passed. Return values - Integers, pointers, and structs of 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes come back in rax . - float and double come back in xmm0 . - Larger structs: the caller passes a hidden pointer (in rcx , moving the other arguments along) to space it has reserved, the function fills it in, and returns that pointer in rax . Shadow space The caller always reserves 32 bytes of shadow space (home space) on the stack just above the return address, even if the function takes fewer than four arguments (lesson 2.01). The function may store its register arguments there. Debug builds do exactly that, which is why the debugger can show a function's arguments even after the registers have been reused. at the moment the function starts: rsp+28h 5th argument (if any) rsp+20h shadow space for r9 rsp+18h shadow space for r8 rsp+10h shadow space for rdx rsp+8 shadow space for rcx rsp return address Volatile and non-volatile registers Volatile: the function may destroy them Non-volatile: the function must preserve them --- --- rax , rcx , rdx , r8 , r9 , r10 , r11 rbx , rbp , rdi , rsi , r12 , r13 , r14 , r15 , rsp xmm0 to xmm5 xmm6 to xmm15 A caller that needs a volatile register's value after a call must save it somewhere first. A function that wants to use a non-volatile register must save and restore it (lesson 7.05's push rbx / pop rbx ). Reading a call in disassembly cpp float applyDamage(Player& p, int amount, float armour, bool critical); ... applyDamage(hero, 40, 0.25f, true); asm mov r9b, 1 ; 4th: critical = true (in r9) movss xmm2, dword ptr __real@3e800000 ; 3rd: armour = 0.25f (3rd position: xmm2) mov edx, 40 ; 2nd: amount (rdx) lea rcx, hero ; 1st: &hero (a reference is a pointer, in rcx) call applyDamage movss dword ptr result , xmm0 ; the float result comes back in xmm0 Arguments are often loaded in an order unrelated to the C++ order; what matters is which register each ends up in. 0x3e800000 is the bit pattern of 0.25 (lesson 2.11). Variadic functions For printf and other functions with ... , floating-point values among the first four arguments are passed in both the integer register and the xmm register for their position, because the callee cannot know which one to look at. Common mistakes !warning Mapping the 2nd argument to xmm0 because it is the first float Registers follow the argument's position. The 2nd argument, float or not, uses the 2nd slot: rdx or xmm1 . !warning Forgetting this In a member function, rcx is this and the first visible argument is in rdx . !warning Calling a function with less than 32 bytes reserved Hand-written assembly must reserve shadow space before every call, even to functions with no arguments. Check yourself quiz ? Which registers carry the first four arguments? - rax , rbx , rcx , rdx for every kind of argument - rdi , rsi , rdx , rcx for integers; xmm0 to xmm3 for floats - All arguments go on the stack + rcx , rdx , r8 , r9 for integers and pointers; xmm0 to xmm3 for floating point, by position "By position" means a double as the second argument goes in xmm1 , and rdx is then left unused. rdi , rsi first is the Linux convention. ? What is shadow space? + 32 bytes the caller reserves on the stack above the return address, where the callee may store its four register arguments - Memory the operating system keeps for saving registers during a context switch - A copy of the stack used by the debugger - Padding added after each local variable The caller always reserves it, even if the called function takes fewer than four arguments. ? What is the difference between volatile and non-volatile registers? - Volatile registers lose their value when the power fails - Non-volatile registers can only be read, not written + A callee may overwrite volatile ones but must preserve non-volatile ones - Volatile registers are shared between threads; non-volatile are not So a caller that needs a value across a call keeps it in a non-volatile register such as rbx , or saves it itself. ? Where is the third argument of void f(int a, int b, int c, int d, int e) ? - rdx - On the stack + r8 rcx, rdx, r8, r9 for the first four; the fifth goes on the stack. ? Where is y in void g(int x, double y) ? + xmm1 , because it is the second argument - xmm0 , because it is the first floating-point argument - rdx The position decides the register. ? In player.heal(25) , which register holds 25? - rcx , the first argument + rdx , as this is in rcx - r8 , the third argument The hidden this is the first argument. ? A function changes rbx and r10 . Which must it restore before returning? - Only r10 - Both + Only rbx rbx is non-volatile; r10 is volatile and may be destroyed.

title: Where does each argument go?
body: Write argumentLocations(types, isMember) . types lists a function's parameter types in order, each 'i' (integer or pointer) or 'f' (float or double). If isMember is true, there is also a hidden this pointer before them, which takes the first slot but is not included in the result. Return where each listed parameter is passed under the Microsoft x64 calling convention: - slots 1 to 4: "rcx" , "rdx" , "r8" , "r9" for integers, "xmm0" to "xmm3" for floats, chosen by the slot number ; - slot 5 and later: " rsp+28h " , " rsp+30h " , " rsp+38h " and so on (8 bytes apart, as seen at the start of the function), whatever the type. argumentLocations("ifi", false) = { "rcx", "xmm1", "r8" } argumentLocations("ii", true) = { "rdx", "r8" } (this is in rcx) argumentLocations("iiiiif", false) = { "rcx", "rdx", "r8", "r9", " rsp+28h ", " rsp+30h " }

title: 7.07  Reading Compiler Output: if, Loops and switch
match: 7.07 Reading Compiler Output: if, Loops and switch
body: Control flow in C++ compiles into a small set of recognisable shapes built from comparisons and jumps. This lesson teaches you to recognise them: if and if / else , while and for loops (and how compilers rotate them), short-circuit && and , and the jump table a switch becomes. Recognising shapes is how you read disassembly quickly. The method When reading compiled code, do not try to understand each instruction in isolation. Look for the shape : 1. Find the jumps. Each conditional jump is a decision; each backward jump (to a lower address) is a loop. 2. Group the instructions between jumps into basic blocks : straight runs with one way in and one way out. 3. Draw the blocks and the arrows between them. The picture is the control flow, and it maps back to if , while and switch . Disassemblers such as Ghidra and IDA draw this graph for you (chapter 9). With practice you see it directly in the listing. if and if/else cpp int grade(int score) { if (score = 50) return 1; return 0; } asm cmp ecx, 50 jl fail ; inverted: skip the "then" part when score < 50 mov eax, 1 ret fail: xor eax, eax ret With an else , the "then" block ends with an unconditional jmp over the "else" block to the code after both: (Optimisers often replace small if/else assignments with cmov , lesson 7.04, so there may be no jump at all.) Loops A while loop literally compiled would test at the top and jump back to the test at the bottom: two jumps per iteration. Compilers rotate loops instead: test once before entering, then test again at the bottom with a single backward jump. cpp int sum(const int values, int count) { int total{ 0 }; for (int i{ 0 }; i < count; ++i) total += values i ; return total; } asm xor eax, eax ; total = 0 test edx, edx ; count <= 0? then skip the loop entirely jle done xor r8d, r8d ; i = 0 top: add eax, rcx+r8 4 ; total += values i inc r8d ; ++i cmp r8d, edx ; i < count? jl top ; backward jump: the loop done: ret The backward jump to top is the signature of a loop. The block before it is the guard that skips the loop when it would run zero times. Step through it with three values: demo-asm title: The rotated loop, count = 3 init: rcx=0x2000, edx=3, mem@0x2000=5 7 9 xor eax, eax test edx, edx jle done xor r8d, r8d top: add eax, dword ptr rcx+r8 4 inc r8d cmp r8d, edx jl top done: ret In optimised builds, loops may also be unrolled (the body repeated several times per jump) or vectorised (processing four or eight elements per instruction, lesson 7.11), which changes the shape but not the backward jump. && and C++ guarantees short-circuit evaluation: in a && b , b is not evaluated if a is false. That becomes a chain of jumps, each able to skip straight to the outcome: cpp if (enemy != nullptr && enemy- health 0) attack(enemy); asm test rcx, rcx ; enemy == nullptr? je skip ; then the whole condition is false cmp dword ptr rcx+8 , 0 ; enemy- health 0? jle skip call attack skip: Two conditional jumps to the same label is the shape of && . For , the first test jumps to the "true" block instead. switch and jump tables A switch over a few cases compiles to a chain of comparisons. Over many dense cases (values close together), the compiler builds a jump table : an array of addresses, one per case, and jumps through it with a single indexed jump. cpp const char stateName(int state) { switch (state) { case 0: return "idle"; case 1: return "walking"; case 2: return "running"; case 3: return "jumping"; case 4: return "falling"; default: return "?"; } } asm cmp ecx, 4 ja default_case ; unsigned compare: also catches negative values! movsxd rax, ecx lea rdx, __ImageBase mov eax, rdx+rax 4+table_rva ; read the case's offset from the table add rax, rdx jmp rax ; jump to that case Three things to recognise: - One unsigned comparison ( ja ) checks the range: a negative value, seen as unsigned, is huge, so it also goes to default . One check covers both ends. - An indexed load from a table, scaled by 4 or 8. - An indirect jump ( jmp rax ). Sparse cases (1, 100, 5000) get a chain of comparisons or a binary search instead. Common mistakes !warning Reading every jump as an if Backward jumps are loops; a jmp at the end of a block is usually the "skip the else" jump. !warning Expecting the loop test at the top Rotated loops test at the bottom, with a guard before the loop. !warning Missing the range check before a jump table The cmp and ja before it tell you the number of cases. Check yourself quiz ? What is a basic block? - One line of C++ source and its instructions + Straight-line code with one entry at the top and one exit - The code between a function's prologue and epilogue - A block of 64 bytes of machine code Nothing jumps into the middle or out of the middle of a basic block, which makes blocks the boxes of a control-flow graph. ? How does a compiler implement a && b ? + With jumps: if a is false, skip straight past b and the body - By computing both, ANDing the results, then testing once - With a single and instruction - By calling a helper function that evaluates both sides && must not evaluate b when a is false, so the code jumps over it. ? What three parts make up a jump table's code? - A loop over all cases, a compare for each, and a call - A signed compare, a cmov and a ret - A hash of the value, a search, and a direct jump + A range check, a load from a table, and an indirect jump The range check is one unsigned compare and jump to the default case, which also catches negative values. ? What is the signature of a loop in disassembly? + A conditional jump backwards - Any cmp instruction - A call Looping means going back to code that already ran. ? Why does a rotated loop have a test before the loop as well as at the bottom? - Because the CPU requires two tests + To skip the loop entirely when it should run zero times - To count the iterations The bottom test decides whether to go round again; the guard handles the zero-iteration case. ? Two conditional jumps lead to the same label just before a call . What C++ is this likely to be? - if (a b) call(); - A switch + if (a && b) call(); Either condition failing skips the call. ? Why does a jump table's range check use ja instead of jg ? + Unsigned, it also sends negatives to default - jg does not exist - The cases are always unsigned Negative numbers read as unsigned are larger than any case.

title: 7.08  Structs, Arrays and Pointers in Assembly
match: 7.08 Structs, Arrays and Pointers in Assembly
body: In assembly there are no types, only addresses and sizes. A struct member is a fixed offset from a pointer; an array element is base plus index times size; a pointer chain is a series of loads. This lesson shows how each C++ data access compiles, and how to work backwards from the offsets and sizes in disassembly to the data structures behind them. Members are offsets cpp struct Monster { int id; // +0 float x, y; // +4, +8 int health; // +12 Monster target; // +16 }; void hurt(Monster m, int amount) { m- health -= amount; if (m- health <= 0) m- target = nullptr; } asm hurt PROC sub dword ptr rcx+0Ch , edx ; m- health -= amount (offset 12, 4 bytes) jg alive mov qword ptr rcx+10h , 0 ; m- target = nullptr (offset 16, 8 bytes) alive: ret hurt ENDP Every member access is pointer + offset with a size. Reading this cold, with no source, you could still say: the first argument points at a structure; at offset 0xC there is a 4-byte integer that is compared with zero; at offset 0x10 an 8-byte value that is set to zero, probably a pointer. That is how chapter 9 rebuilds unknown structs. sub also set the flags, so the compiler used them directly for the <= 0 test with jg : no separate cmp . Optimisers do this whenever they can. Arrays of structs An element of an array of structs is base + index × sizeof(struct) + member offset . When the size is 1, 2, 4 or 8 the scale does it; otherwise the index is multiplied first: cpp struct Particle { float x, y, vx, vy, life; }; // 20 bytes float lifeOf(const Particle particles, int i) { return particles i .life; } asm movsxd rax, edx ; i, widened to 64 bits lea rax, rax+rax 4 ; i 5 movss xmm0, dword ptr rcx+rax 4+10h ; particles + i 20 + 16: the life member ret i 5 4 = i 20 (the struct size) plus 0x10 (the offset of life ). When you see an index multiplied by an odd constant, divide to get the element size. Pointer chains world- player- inventory- gold (lesson 3.02) is one load per arrow: asm mov rax, qword ptr rcx+18h ; world- player (player is at offset 0x18 in World) mov rax, qword ptr rax+40h ; - inventory (inventory at 0x40 in Player) mov eax, dword ptr rax+8 ; - gold (gold at 8 in Inventory) Each qword load produces the address for the next. A run of dependent 8-byte loads like this is a pointer chain, and its offsets are the layouts of each struct in turn. Objects with virtual functions A virtual call (lesson 3.05) has its own fingerprint: asm mov rax, qword ptr rcx ; load the vptr from offset 0 call qword ptr rax+18h ; call slot 3 of the vtable (0x18 / 8) A load from offset 0 of an object followed by an indirect call through that value plus an offset: a virtual call. The offset divided by 8 is the slot number. Working backwards: a reading table You see Probably --- --- dword ptr rcx+N A 4-byte member ( int , float , enum) at offset N of the struct rcx points to qword ptr rcx+N then used as an address A pointer member at offset N movss / movsd with a memory operand A float / double member movzx eax, byte ptr rcx+N , then test al, al A bool member rcx+rdx 4 , rcx+rdx 8 An array of 4- or 8-byte elements imul rdx, rdx, 38h then rcx+rdx An array of 56-byte structs mov rax, rcx then call rax+N A virtual call, slot N/8 lea rcx, rdi+20h then call Passing the address of a member (or base subobject) at offset 0x20 Common mistakes !warning Assuming the same register means the same object Registers are reused constantly. Track what each one holds at each point. !warning Forgetting padding when guessing a layout A 4-byte member at offset 0 followed by an 8-byte one at offset 8 means padding at 4 to 7, not a hidden member (lesson 2.05). !warning Reading lea as a load lea rcx, rdi+20h takes an address; it does not read the member. Check yourself quiz ? How does a member access appear in assembly? - As a call to a getter function generated by the compiler - As the member's name in the instruction + As pointer + offset with a size such as dword ptr The size tells you the member's type width, and the offset tells you where in the struct it is. ? How do you find the element size of an array of structs from compiled code? + From how the index is scaled before it is added - Read the size from the .exe header - Count the instructions in the loop - It is always 8, the size of a pointer lea rax, rax+rax 2 then rcx+rax 8 scales the index by 3 × 8, so each element is 24 bytes. The multiply or lea combination, times the addressing-mode scale, gives the struct size. ? What does a chain of dependent 8-byte loads represent? - Copying a large struct 8 bytes at a time - Reading an array of double s + Following pointers: each load gives the next address - Saving registers in the prologue Each load needs the previous one's result, which is why pointer chasing is slow. ? mov eax, dword ptr rcx+0Ch with rcx holding a struct pointer. What is being read? - The 12th element of an array + A 4-byte member at offset 12 - A pointer at offset 12 dword ptr is 4 bytes; +0Ch is the member's offset. ? Code computes lea rax, rax+rax 2 and then reads rcx+rax 8 . What is the element size? - 8 bytes - 3 bytes + 24 bytes The index is multiplied by 3, then scaled by 8. ? What does mov rax, rcx followed by call qword ptr rax+10h indicate? + A virtual call to slot 2 of the object's vtable - A call to a function at address rcx + 16 - Reading an array The first load fetches the vptr; 0x10 / 8 = slot 2.

title: Rebuild a struct from its accesses
match: Rebuild a struct from its accesses
where: 7.08 Structs, Arrays and Pointers in Assembly
body: A reverse engineer has collected every memory access a function makes through one struct pointer: each one an offset and a size in bytes (1, 2, 4 or 8). Write guessLayout(accesses) , which turns them into a list of fields, the way a disassembler's "create structure" feature does: - Each distinct offset becomes one field. If an offset was accessed with different sizes, use the largest. - Fields are listed in order of offset. - Each field's type name comes from its size: 1 "uint8_t" , 2 "uint16_t" , 4 "uint32_t" , 8 "uint64_t" . - Gaps between fields (bytes not covered by any field) become padding fields named "pad" of type "uint8_t N " , where N is the gap size, so the offsets add up. There is no padding after the last field. accesses: {0x0,4} {0x10,8} {0xC,4} {0x0,4} fields: 0x0 uint32_t 0x4 uint8_t 8 (pad) 0xC uint32_t 0x10 uint64_t

title: 7.09  Floating Point with SSE
body: x64 code does floating-point maths in the 16 xmm registers with SSE instructions. Scalar instructions like addss work on one float ; packed ones like addps work on four at once, the start of SIMD . This lesson reads typical game maths in assembly: loading constants, arithmetic, comparisons, conversions between ints and floats, and a first look at vectorised code. The xmm registers Each xmm0 to xmm15 register is 128 bits wide: room for four float s or two double s. (Newer processors extend them to 256-bit ymm and 512-bit zmm registers with AVX; the ideas are the same.) For ordinary scalar maths the compiler uses only the lowest lane: xmm0: float 3 float 2 float 1 float 0 <- scalar code uses lane 0 only 127 31 0 Instruction names end in a suffix saying what they work on: Suffix Means Example --- --- --- ss S calar S ingle: one float addss xmm0, xmm1 sd S calar D ouble: one double mulsd xmm0, xmm2 ps P acked S ingle: four float s addps xmm0, xmm1 pd P acked D ouble: two double s subpd xmm3, xmm4 Everyday float code cpp float speedAfterFriction(float speed, float friction, float dt) { return speed (1.0f - friction dt); } asm speedAfterFriction PROC mulss xmm1, xmm2 ; friction dt movss xmm3, dword ptr __real@3f800000 ; load the constant 1.0f subss xmm3, xmm1 ; 1.0f - friction dt mulss xmm0, xmm3 ; speed (...) ret ; result in xmm0 speedAfterFriction ENDP - Arguments arrive in xmm0 , xmm1 , xmm2 by position (lesson 7.06); the result leaves in xmm0 . - There are no float immediates: constants live in read-only data and are loaded from memory. MSVC names them after their bits, so __real@3f800000 is 1.0f (lesson 2.11's table). Reading those names tells you the constants directly. - movss loads and stores one float; movaps / movups move all 128 bits (aligned or unaligned). Conversions and comparisons Instruction Does C++ --- --- --- cvtsi2ss xmm0, eax int to float static_cast<float (i) cvttss2si eax, xmm0 float to int, truncating towards zero static_cast<int (f) cvtss2sd xmm0, xmm0 float to double passing a float to printf comiss xmm0, xmm1 / ucomiss compare, setting ZF, CF (and PF) a < b sqrtss , minss , maxss square root, minimum, maximum std::sqrt , std::min xorps xmm0, xmm0 zero the register 0.0f Float comparisons set the flags like an unsigned integer compare, so they are followed by ja , jb , jae , jbe , not jg / jl . Comparisons involving NaN ("not a number") are "unordered" and set the parity flag, which is why you sometimes see an extra jp after them. SIMD: four at once The packed instructions do the same operation on every lane in one go. Adding two arrays of floats four elements per instruction is up to four times the work per instruction: asm top: movups xmm0, rcx+rax ; load 4 floats from a movups xmm1, rdx+rax ; load 4 floats from b addps xmm0, xmm1 ; 4 additions in one instruction movups r8+rax , xmm0 ; store 4 results add rax, 16 ; advance by 4 floats cmp rax, r9 jb top Optimising compilers produce loops like this automatically from plain C++ ( auto-vectorisation ) when the loop is simple enough: no dependencies between iterations, no function calls in the body, data laid out contiguously. That last condition is a big part of why engines store data as structures of arrays (all x values together, all y values together) rather than arrays of structures for the hottest loops. You can also write SIMD by hand with intrinsics ( _mm_add_ps and friends from <immintrin.h ), which map one-to-one onto these instructions. Precision and determinism float has about 7 significant decimal digits; double about 16. Results can differ with optimisation settings (the compiler may reorder a + b + c only under /fp:fast , which is not the default) and between processors for some library functions. For lockstep multiplayer games and replays, which need bit-identical results everywhere, programs keep the default /fp:precise , avoid /fp:fast , and sometimes use fixed-point integers for game logic instead. Common mistakes !warning Expecting float arguments in rcx/rdx Floating-point arguments use the xmm register of their position. !warning Reading a float comparison's ja as unsigned integers After comiss , ja / jb are simply "greater"/"less" for floats. !warning Converting with truncation when rounding was meant static_cast<int (2.9f) is 2. Use std::lround to round. Check yourself quiz ? What do the suffixes ss , sd , ps and pd mean? - Signed short, signed double, positive single, positive double + Scalar single, scalar double, packed single (four floats), packed double (two doubles) - Single step, single double, page single, page double - Short store, short double, packed store, packed double addss adds one float; addps adds four floats at once. ? Where do a function's float arguments and float result go on x64 Windows? - On the stack, with the result in rax - In rcx , rdx , r8 , r9 , with the result in xmm0 - In the x87 floating-point stack + The first four arguments in xmm0 to xmm3 by position; the result in xmm0 Integer results come back in rax ; float and double results come back in xmm0 . ? What does a loop need for the compiler to vectorise it? - A pragma on every line of the body + Independent iterations, a simple body and contiguous data - A loop counter of type float - At least a million iterations Then several elements can be processed per instruction, four floats at a time with SSE. ? What does mulss xmm0, xmm1 do? - Multiplies four floats in each register + Multiplies the lowest float of xmm0 by xmm1's - Multiplies two doubles ss means scalar single precision. ? Why does compiled float code load constants from memory? - Constants are faster from memory - The compiler cannot compute them + x64 instructions cannot hold floating-point immediates They are stored in read-only data, often named after their bit pattern. ? What is the advantage of addps over addss ? + It adds four pairs of floats in one instruction - It is more precise - It works with integers Packed instructions operate on every lane at once: SIMD. ? After comiss xmm0, xmm1 , which jump means "xmm0 is greater"? - jg + ja - jl Float compares set the flags like an unsigned comparison.

title: 7.10  Writing Assembly Functions with MASM
body: Microsoft's assembler, MASM ( ml64.exe ), ships with Visual Studio. This lesson writes a few functions in assembly, adds them to a C++ project, and calls them from C++, following the calling convention by hand. Writing even a little assembly makes reading it much easier, and shows exactly what the compiler does for you. When to write assembly Almost never in game code. Compilers produce excellent code, and intrinsics (lesson 7.09) cover most hand-tuned SIMD. Hand-written assembly survives in a few places: the start-up code of operating systems and runtimes, a handful of instructions compilers cannot express, and teaching. 64-bit MSVC does not even support inline __asm blocks; assembly goes in separate .asm files. We write it here to learn: every rule in this chapter must be followed by hand, and the assembler will not save you. Setting up a project 1. In your course solution, right-click the project → Build Dependencies → Build Customizations → tick masm . 2. Add a new file named maths.asm (choose a C++ file and rename it). In its properties, Item Type should now be Microsoft Macro Assembler . 3. Build: ml64.exe assembles maths.asm into maths.obj , and the linker joins it with your C++ objects like any other (lesson 4.02). A first function masm ; maths.asm: int addThree(int a, int b, int c) .code addThree PROC lea eax, rcx+rdx ; a + b (a in ecx, b in edx) add eax, r8d ; + c (c in r8d) ret ; result in eax addThree ENDP END cpp-norun // main.cpp include <iostream extern "C" int addThree(int a, int b, int c); // declared in C++, defined in assembly int main() { std::cout << addThree(1, 2, 39) << '\n'; } extern "C" matters: the assembly defines the plain name addThree , and without extern "C" the C++ side would look for the mangled ?addThree@@YAHHHH@Z and fail with LNK2019 (lesson 4.02). A loop and a non-volatile register masm ; long long sumArray(const int values, long long count) .code sumArray PROC push rbx ; we use rbx below, and it is non-volatile: save it xor eax, eax ; total = 0 (64-bit: writing eax clears the top of rax) xor ebx, ebx ; i = 0 test rdx, rdx jle done ; count <= 0: nothing to add next: movsxd r9, dword ptr rcx+rbx 4 ; values i , sign-extended to 64 bits add rax, r9 inc rbx cmp rbx, rdx jl next done: pop rbx ; restore it before returning ret sumArray ENDP END Nothing here needed rbx : r10 (volatile) would have done without the push and pop. Using it shows the rule: touch a non-volatile register, and you must save and restore it. Calling C++ from assembly Calling out is where the convention bites. Before a call , rsp must be 16-byte aligned and 32 bytes of shadow space reserved: masm ; void logTwice(int value) calls the C++ function extern "C" void logValue(int) EXTERN logValue:PROC .code logTwice PROC push rbx ; entry: rsp was 8 off a multiple of 16; after this push it is aligned sub rsp, 32 ; shadow space for the calls: still aligned (8 + 8 + 32 = 48 bytes in all) mov ebx, ecx ; keep value in a non-volatile register across the calls call logValue ; ecx still holds value mov ecx, ebx ; ecx is volatile: logValue may have changed it call logValue add rsp, 32 pop rbx ret logTwice ENDP END The arithmetic: on entry rsp is a multiple of 16 minus 8 (the return address). push rbx subtracts 8 (now a multiple of 16), sub rsp, 32 keeps it a multiple of 16, and leaves the 32 bytes of shadow space the callee may use. Getting this wrong works most of the time and then crashes inside some library function that uses aligned SSE stores: one of the hardest bugs to trace back. !note Unwind information Functions that change rsp or save registers should, strictly, also describe their prologue to Windows with MASM's .PUSHREG , .ALLOCSTACK and .ENDPROLOG directives (using PROC FRAME ), so exceptions and the debugger can walk the stack through them. For learning exercises that never throw, it can be left out; production assembly must include it. Common mistakes !warning Forgetting extern "C" The linker cannot match the assembly's plain name with a mangled C++ declaration. !warning Misaligned stack at a call Count every push and sub rsp from entry: at the call , rsp must be a multiple of 16, with 32 bytes of shadow space reserved. !warning Keeping values in volatile registers across a call rcx , rdx , r8 to r11 and rax may all change. Keep anything you need afterwards in a non-volatile register or on the stack. Check yourself quiz ? How do you add an assembly file to a Visual Studio C++ project? + Enable the masm build customisation, then add a .asm file - Rename a .cpp file to .asm ; it is assembled automatically - Paste the assembly into a .cpp file inside an __asm block - Install a separate assembler and add its output by hand to the linker MSVC does not support inline __asm blocks for x64, which is why separate .asm files are used. Check that the file's item type is Microsoft Macro Assembler. ? What does an assembly function have to do with non-volatile registers? - Nothing; the C++ caller saves all registers before the call - Clear them to zero before returning - Avoid them completely + Save any it uses (for example with push ) and restore them before returning The caller relies on non-volatile registers such as rbx keeping their values across the call. ? How do you check the stack is aligned at a call? - Make sure rsp is a multiple of 8 at the call - Assume it is aligned; the assembler fixes it automatically + Add up pushes and sub rsp from entry; rsp must end a multiple of 16 - Check that the number of pushes equals the number of pops The return address pushed by your own caller is what makes rsp 8 off at entry. At entry rsp is 8 off a multiple of 16, and 32 bytes of shadow space must be reserved too. ? Why must the C++ declaration of an assembly function be extern "C" ? - Because assembly is written in C - To make the call faster + So C++ looks for the plain, unmangled name Otherwise the linker searches for a mangled symbol that does not exist. ? Inside logTwice , why is the value kept in ebx between the two calls? + rbx is non-volatile, so calls leave it alone - ebx is faster than ecx - call requires it Anything needed after a call must be in a non-volatile register or memory. ? What two conditions must hold at every call instruction in your assembly? - rax is zero and rbx holds the return address + rsp is a multiple of 16, with 32 bytes of shadow space reserved - The flags are cleared Both come from the Microsoft x64 calling convention.

title: 7.11  What Optimised Code Looks Like
body: Release builds rarely look like their source. Functions disappear into their callers, loops are unrolled and vectorised, variables never touch memory, and branches become arithmetic. This lesson is a field guide to the transformations you will meet in optimised disassembly, so that you can map it back to the C++ (or, when reverse engineering, to something like it). The same function, three ways cpp int countAlive(const int health, int n) { int alive{ 0 }; for (int i{ 0 }; i < n; ++i) if (health i 0) ++alive; return alive; } Debug ( /Od ): every variable in memory, every line separate, one element per iteration, a real branch for the if . Easy to follow, slow. Optimised ( /O2 ), roughly: asm xor eax, eax ; alive = 0 test edx, edx jle done ; ... (a vectorised loop handles 8 elements at a time here, see below) scalar: cmp dword ptr rcx , 0 setg r8b ; r8b = health i 0 ? 1 : 0 (no branch) add eax, r8d ; alive += that add rcx, 4 ; walk a pointer instead of indexing dec edx jnz scalar done: ret Notice what changed: - alive and i live only in registers. - The if became setg plus add : branchless code, because whether a monster is alive is unpredictable and a mispredicted branch is costly (lesson 7.04). - health i became a pointer that moves along ( add rcx, 4 ), and the loop counts down to zero, so dec sets ZF for the jump without a cmp . The vectorised part, for large n , compares 4 or 8 values at once with pcmpgtd (packed compare greater-than), uses the all-ones result lanes as -1, and subtracts them from a counter vector: eight comparisons and additions per instruction pair, then adds the lanes together at the end. Field guide You see It was probably --- --- A call is missing; the callee's body appears inline Inlining : small functions are copied into their callers A loop body repeated 4 or 8 times per jump Unrolling : fewer jumps, more work per iteration xmm / ymm packed instructions in integer or float loops Vectorisation (lesson 7.09) setcc , cmov , sbb , and with -1 masks instead of jumps Branch removal A constant where you expected arithmetic Constant folding A multiply by a large odd constant then a shift Division by a constant (lesson 7.03) lea doing sums and small multiplies Strength reduction (lesson 7.02) A loop that counts down, or a pointer that advances Induction variable rewriting jmp to another function at the end instead of call + ret Tail call : the callee returns straight to our caller Code you wrote is gone entirely Dead code elimination : its result was never used A function's code shared by several functions with identical bodies Identical COMDAT folding ( /OPT:ICF ) Inlining and the missing functions Inlining matters most for reading. A small getter like int health() const { return m_health; } usually vanishes: the caller simply reads rcx+0Ch . Calls to it no longer exist in the program, so a breakpoint in it may never hit, and a reverse engineer sees one large function where the source had ten small ones. With link-time code generation ( /GL + /LTCG ), functions from different .cpp files can be inlined into each other too. Tail calls cpp int damageFor(const Weapon& w, int level) { return scaleDamage(w.baseDamage, level); } asm damageFor PROC mov ecx, dword ptr rcx+8 jmp scaleDamage ; not call: scaleDamage's ret returns to our caller damageFor ENDP damageFor has nothing to do after the call, so it jumps instead of calling, and damageFor never appears in the call stack while scaleDamage runs. Debugger call stacks in optimised code can skip frames for this reason. Reading optimised code well 1. Find the structure first : loops (backward jumps), calls, returns. Ignore the clever arithmetic until you know what the function's shape is. 2. Track values, not variables : one C++ variable may live in different registers at different points, and one register may hold different variables. 3. Expect the vectorised and scalar versions of a loop side by side : a SIMD loop for most of the elements and a plain "remainder" loop for the last few. 4. Use the symbols : with a .pdb , the Disassembly window interleaves source lines; even when they are out of order, they tell you which C++ each instruction came from. Common mistakes !warning Concluding a function is never called It may be called everywhere, inlined into each caller. !warning Reading a vectorised loop instruction by instruction First find the scalar remainder loop, which does the same thing one element at a time and is much easier to read. !warning Assuming the source order of operations The optimiser reorders anything whose order does not change the result. Check yourself quiz ? Name five transformations an optimiser applies. - Adding bounds checks, filling memory, zeroing locals, logging calls, keeping frame pointers - Renaming functions, sorting variables, removing comments, compressing code, encrypting strings + Inlining, unrolling, vectorisation, branch removal with setcc/cmov, constant folding (also strength reduction, tail calls, dead code removal) - Turning loops into recursion, adding virtual calls, splitting functions, padding structs, reordering members The first group is what a Debug build does; optimisation removes overhead rather than adding it. ? Why can a breakpoint in a function fail to hit in a Release build? + The function may have been inlined into its callers or removed, so there is no separate code there to stop in - Release builds ignore all breakpoints - Breakpoints only work in functions with a .pdb entry, and Release has no .pdb - The function runs too fast for the debugger to stop it Release builds can have a .pdb ; the problem is that the code you set the breakpoint on was folded into other code. ? What is the best first step when reading an unfamiliar optimised function? + Find its loops, calls and returns before the arithmetic tricks - Decode every instruction in order from the top - Look up each arithmetic trick before reading on - Rebuild it in Debug and read that instead The shape tells you what the function does; the tricks only make it faster. ? A small getter function has no call to it anywhere in an optimised build. Why? - It is never used - Getters cannot be called in Release + It was inlined: its body was copied into each caller Inlining removes the call entirely. ? Why might an if inside a loop compile to setg and add instead of a jump? + To avoid mispredicted branches - Because jumps are not allowed in loops - Because if is not supported in Release Branchless code costs the same every iteration. ? A function ends with jmp otherFunction instead of call and ret . What is this? - An infinite loop + A tail call into otherFunction - A crash The current function has no more work after the call, so it jumps instead. ? What usually accompanies a vectorised loop? - A second vectorised loop doing the same work again - A call to a library function + A scalar loop handling the leftover elements The number of elements is rarely a multiple of the vector width.
