title: 8.01  Thinking Like a Debugger
body: Debugging is a method, not a talent. This lesson sets out the method experienced engineers use: make the bug happen reliably, form a hypothesis, test it with the smallest possible experiment, and narrow the search by halving it. It covers minimal reproductions , bisecting code and history, and the habits that make the tools in the rest of this chapter effective. The loop Every effective debugging session runs the same loop: The common failure is skipping steps: changing code at random ("maybe it's this"), or fixing the first suspicious thing without confirming it caused the symptom. A fix you cannot explain is a guess, and guesses usually move a bug rather than remove it. Step 1: reproduce A bug you can trigger on demand is half solved. A bug that happens "sometimes" is the hardest kind, so the first job is to make it reliable: - Write down the exact steps, inputs, save file, settings and build. - Remove randomness: fix the random seed, fix the time step, record the input. - For "sometimes" bugs, run it in a loop (a script that starts the game a hundred times) and look for what the failing runs have in common. - Check the obvious variables: Debug or Release? Your machine or another? Fresh install or old settings? Step 2: observe precisely "It crashes" is not an observation. "It crashes with an access violation reading 0x10 , in Inventory::weight , called from Hud::draw , only after picking up an item while the inventory screen is open" is. The debugger's job (chapter 4) is to turn vague symptoms into precise ones: the exact instruction, the exact values, the exact call stack. Read error messages and crash details completely, as lesson 4.03 said for compiler errors. The address, the exception code (lesson 8.04) and the module are each clues. Step 3: one hypothesis at a time A good hypothesis is specific and testable: "the item pointer is stale because the inventory vector grew" can be tested with a data breakpoint or a log line. "Something's wrong with memory" cannot. Test it with the cheapest experiment that could prove it wrong : a conditional breakpoint, a log line, an assert, changing one input. If the experiment shows the hypothesis is wrong, that is progress too: one possibility is gone. Narrowing the search: halve it When you do not know where a bug is, do not read code hoping to spot it. Bisect : split the search space in half, find out which half contains the bug, repeat. Each step halves the remaining space, so even a huge search is short: about 10 steps for a thousand possibilities, 20 for a million. What to bisect How --- --- History : which change introduced the bug? git bisect : mark a known good and a known bad commit; Git checks out the midpoint, you test and answer "good" or "bad", repeat Input : which part of a level or save file triggers it? Delete half the content; does the bug remain? Code path : where does a value go wrong? Check the value at the midpoint of the computation with a breakpoint or log Time : when does state become corrupt? Log or assert the invariant every frame; find the first frame it fails The practice task implements the search at the heart of this. Minimal reproductions Once a bug is reliable, shrink it: remove everything that is not needed for it to happen. A 30-line program that shows the bug is far easier to reason about than a whole game, and very often the act of shrinking it reveals the cause. It is also what you need to report a bug in someone else's library or compiler. Habits that pay off - Check your assumptions out loud. Explaining the code line by line to someone else, or to a rubber duck, forces you to notice the step you were skipping. - Change one thing at a time , and keep notes of what you tried. - Suspect your newest code first , and your oldest assumptions second. - When the impossible happens, an assumption is wrong. "This pointer can't be null here" is a hypothesis to test, not a fact. - After fixing, write a test that would have caught it (chapter 17), so it stays fixed. Common mistakes !warning Changing several things at once If the bug disappears, you do not know which change fixed it, or whether one of them just hid it. !warning Debugging a different build than the one that fails If it only fails in Release, debug the Release build (lesson 8.06). !warning Stopping at the first suspicious code Confirm it causes the symptom: does the bug go away when it is fixed, and come back when it is restored? Check yourself quiz ? What are the steps of the debugging loop? - Read the code, guess the cause, change it, ship it - Add logging everywhere, run, then fix whatever looks odd + Reproduce, observe, form one testable hypothesis, test it, repeat - Fix the most likely cause first, then try to reproduce the bug The fix is checked against the original reproduction, which is why reproducing comes first. Then fix it and check the fix against the original reproduction. ? What is bisecting, and why is it so effective? + Halving the search space each step, so steps grow only logarithmically - Testing every commit one by one from the newest; it never misses anything - Splitting the program into two threads to see which one fails - Running the Debug and Release builds side by side to compare them 512 commits need at most 9 tests, because each test halves what is left. ? Why make a minimal reproduction? - Because the debugger cannot load large programs - Because small programs run faster in Release builds + It is easier to reason about, and shrinking it often shows the cause Every piece you remove without losing the bug rules something out. ? Why is reproducing a bug reliably the first step? + Without it, you cannot tell whether an experiment or fix made any difference - Because the debugger only works on reproducible bugs - It is not important; finding the code matters more Every later step depends on being able to trigger the bug on demand. ? A bug appeared somewhere in the last 512 commits. How many tests does bisecting need, at most? - 256 + About 9 - 512 Each test halves the range: 2⁹ = 512. ? What makes a good hypothesis? - It explains every bug in the program - It is the first idea that comes to mind + A specific cause that a quick experiment could disprove Specific and testable is what makes progress possible.

title: Find the first bad build
body: A bug appeared somewhere in a list of builds numbered 0 to count - 1 . Build 0 is known to be good and the last build is known to be bad; once a build is bad, every later build is bad too. Write firstBad(count, isBad) , which returns the number of the first bad build. isBad(n) tests build n , and testing is slow, so the function must use as few tests as possible: a binary search, like git bisect . The tests count your calls. You may assume count = 2 , isBad(0) is false and isBad(count - 1) is true; do not test those two. count 10, builds 0..5 good, 6..9 bad - 6

title: 8.02  Call Stacks and Symbols
body: A call stack turns a crash address into a story: which function, called from where, with what. Making that work needs symbols : the .pdb files that map machine code back to names and source lines. This lesson covers what is in a PDB, how debuggers find the right one, Microsoft's symbol server for Windows' own DLLs, how stacks are walked without frame pointers, and how to capture a stack trace from inside your own program. What symbols are The compiler and linker throw names away: in the .exe , a function is just bytes at an RVA. The program database ( .pdb ) file written alongside it keeps everything a debugger needs to get the names back: In the PDB Lets the debugger --- --- Function names and their RVA ranges Name the function containing any address Line number tables Map each instruction to a source file and line Types and struct layouts Show player.health instead of raw bytes Local variables and where they live Fill the Locals window Frame data Help walk the stack A PDB matches exactly one build . The exe records a unique signature (a GUID and an age) and the PDB's file name in its debug directory; the debugger only loads a PDB whose signature matches. Rebuild even without changing anything, and the old PDB no longer fits. That is why you keep the PDB of every build you ship : without it, a crash report from that build can only show raw addresses. How the debugger finds symbols For each loaded module, the debugger searches, in order: 1. The path recorded in the exe (where the PDB was written at build time). 2. The folder the module was loaded from. 3. The symbol path : folders and symbol servers you configure ( Tools → Options → Debugging → Symbols ). Visual Studio's Modules window shows, for every DLL and exe, whether symbols loaded and from where. "Cannot find or open the PDB file" there explains a call stack full of game.exe!00007ff6a1235f10() instead of names. The Microsoft symbol server Windows' own DLLs have public symbols too: Microsoft publishes them on a symbol server , a web service that hands out the PDB matching each DLL's signature. Turn it on in Visual Studio (tick Microsoft Symbol Servers ) or set the environment variable used by WinDbg and other tools: _NT_SYMBOL_PATH=srv C:\Symbols https://msdl.microsoft.com/download/symbols srv means "use a symbol server", C:\Symbols is a local cache, and the URL is Microsoft's server. With it, call stacks through Windows code show names like ntdll.dll!RtlUserThreadStart and kernel32.dll!BaseThreadInitThunk instead of raw addresses, which is often exactly where the interesting part of a crash is. Studios run their own symbol servers for their builds, so any crash from any shipped version can be symbolised. Walking the stack without frame pointers Lesson 7.05 said x64 Windows code usually does not keep a frame pointer in rbp . So how does a debugger find each caller? Every function's prologue is described in unwind information in the exe's .pdata and .xdata sections: "this function pushed rbx and rdi, then subtracted 40 from rsp". Given the current rip and rsp , the debugger finds the function containing rip , applies its unwind description in reverse to recover the caller's rsp and the return address, and repeats. Windows uses the same data to unwind the stack when an exception is thrown. This is also why corrupt stacks look so strange: if the return address on the stack has been overwritten (lesson 7.05), the unwinder follows garbage, and the call stack ends abruptly or shows nonsense. Capturing a stack in your own program A crash reporter or an assert (next lesson) wants the call stack as text. C++23's std::stacktrace does it portably: cpp include <iostream include <stacktrace void deepInside() { const auto trace{ std::stacktrace::current() }; std::cout << "captured " << (trace.size() = 2 ? "a stack with several frames" : "almost nothing") << '\n'; // std::cout << trace; // prints each frame: function, file and line, when symbols are available } void middle() { deepInside(); } int main() { middle(); return 0; } captured a stack with several frames Printing the whole trace (the commented line) gives function names and source lines when the PDB is next to the exe. On Windows the lower-level tools are CaptureStackBackTrace (just the return addresses) and the DbgHelp library ( SymFromAddr , SymGetLineFromAddr64 ) to turn them into names. Without symbols, store the addresses as module + RVA (lesson 6.09) and symbolise them later on a machine that has the PDB. Reading a call stack game.exe!Inventory::totalWeight() Line 42 game.exe!Hud::drawWeight(const Player & player) Line 118 game.exe!Hud::draw(const World & world) Line 87 game.exe!Game::render() Line 210 game.exe!wWinMain(...) Line 35 kernel32.dll!BaseThreadInitThunk() ntdll.dll!RtlUserThreadStart() Read from the top: the crash is in totalWeight at line 42; it was called by drawWeight , which was called by draw , and so on down to the thread's start in Windows. Double-click any frame to see its variables (lesson 4.07). The bug is often not in the top frame, but in a caller that passed it something bad. Common mistakes !warning Not keeping the PDBs of shipped builds A crash report from players is then just numbers. Archive every released build's PDB, or run a symbol server. !warning A PDB from a different build It will not load, even if the code looks the same. Rebuild and keep exe and PDB together. !warning Shipping PDBs to players Private PDBs contain your full source structure. Ship none, or stripped public ones ( /PDBSTRIPPED ), and keep the full ones yourself. Check yourself quiz ? What does a PDB contain? + Function names, line tables, types and locals for the build - The program's source code, compressed - A copy of the .exe with debugging turned on - The program's settings and its saved breakpoints The source itself is not in the PDB; the debugger finds the source files separately using the paths and line tables it holds. ? Why must you keep the PDB of every build you release? - Because the program will not start without it + Only its own PDB can turn a build's crash reports into names - Because Windows needs it to install updates - Because PDBs are needed to rebuild the program later A PDB from a later build of the same source does not match, because addresses and the build signature differ. ? What is a symbol server? - A server that compiles code and returns a PDB - A program that renames functions in an .exe to make it smaller - A database of known crash codes + A service that hands out the PDB matching a module's signature A studio can run its own for its builds, so crash dumps from players resolve automatically. ? Why does a call stack show game.exe!00007ff6a1235f10() instead of a function name? + The debugger could not load a matching PDB for game.exe - The function has no name - The program was built in Release Without symbols, only addresses are known. Check the Modules window. ? How does the debugger know a PDB belongs to a particular exe? - By the file name alone + By a signature (GUID and age) both must share - By the date the files were made Each build gets a new signature, so only that build's PDB fits. ? How can a debugger walk an x64 stack when functions do not use a frame pointer? - It guesses from the stack contents - It cannot + From the unwind information in .pdata and .xdata The same data drives exception unwinding. ? What does srv C:\Symbols https://msdl.microsoft.com/download/symbols in a symbol path do? + Fetches Microsoft's symbols and caches them in C:\Symbols - Uploads your symbols to Microsoft - Disables symbols Public symbols turn Windows frames into names.

title: Read a stack frame
body: Tools print stack frames in the form module!function+0xOFFSET , for example game.exe!Player::update+0x2a . When symbols are missing, the function part is absent: game.exe+0x35f10 . Write parseFrame(text) , returning the module, the function (empty if absent) and the offset as a number. The offset is hexadecimal, written with 0x , in either case. If the text does not fit the form (no +0x , nothing before it, no hex digits after it), return std::nullopt . "game.exe!Player::update+0x2a" - module "game.exe", function "Player::update", offset 0x2A "ntdll.dll+0x1F00" - module "ntdll.dll", function "", offset 0x1F00 "no offset here" - nullopt Function names can contain :: , < , and spaces, but never ! or + .

title: 8.03  Asserts and Logging That Help
body:
The best bugs to fix are the ones the program reports itself, at the moment things go wrong. Asserts check assumptions and stop immediately when one is false; logs record what happened so you can reconstruct it later. This lesson shows how to write both well: static_assert and assert , a better assert macro, log levels, and a ring buffer that keeps the last moments before a crash. Asserts: check your assumptions Every piece of code assumes things: this index is in range, this pointer is not null, this list is sorted. An assert turns an assumption into a check that stops the program, in a debugger-friendly way, the moment it is violated: cpp include <cassert int& Grid::at(int x, int y) { assert(x = 0 && x < width && "x out of range"); assert(y = 0 && y < height && "y out of range"); return cells static_cast<std::size_t (y width + x) ; } When an assert fails in a Debug build, the program stops with the condition, file and line; under the debugger it breaks right there, with the call stack showing who passed the bad coordinates. The string after && is a trick: a string literal is always true, so it does not change the condition, but it appears in the failure message. Two properties to remember: - assert does nothing in Release builds ( NDEBUG is defined, lesson 4.10). Never put work that must happen inside it. - Asserts are for programming errors ("this can never happen if the code is right"), not for things that can legitimately happen at run time, such as a missing file or bad player input. Those need real error handling. static_assert: checks at compile time Some assumptions can be checked by the compiler, costing nothing at run time: cpp include <cstdint struct SaveHeader { char magic 4 ; std::uint32_t version; std::uint32_t length; }; static_assert(sizeof(SaveHeader) == 12, "SaveHeader must match the file format"); static_assert(sizeof(void ) == 8, "This code assumes a 64-bit build"); static_assert(alignof(SaveHeader) == 4); int main() { return 0; } If someone adds a member to SaveHeader , the build fails with that message instead of saves silently breaking. Use static_assert for layouts, sizes, and template requirements. A better assert The standard assert is minimal. Most engines write their own, adding a formatted message, a log line, a break into the debugger, and the option to keep checks on in some release builds: cpp include <cstdio include <cstdlib include <intrin.h ifndef GAME_ASSERTS ifdef NDEBUG define GAME_ASSERTS 0 else define GAME_ASSERTS 1 endif endif if GAME_ASSERTS define GAME_ASSERT(condition, message) \ do { \ if (!(condition)) { \ std::fprintf(stderr, "Assertion failed: %s
 %s
 at %s:%d
", condition, message, \ __FILE__, __LINE__); \ std::fflush(stderr); \ __debugbreak(); / stops here under a debugger; crashes cleanly without one / \ std::abort(); \ } \ } while (false) else define GAME_ASSERT(condition, message) do { (void)sizeof(condition); } while (false) endif - condition turns the condition's source text into a string for the message. - __debugbreak() is the int 3 instruction from lesson 4.07: under a debugger it stops exactly at the failing line. - do { ... } while (false) makes the macro behave like one statement, so it is safe after an if without braces. - The disabled version uses sizeof(condition) so the condition is still compiled (and type-checked) but never evaluated. Logging Logs record what the program did, so you can understand a bug after the fact, on a player's machine, or in a situation you cannot reproduce. Useful logs have: Property Why --- --- Levels : trace, debug, info, warning, error So you can turn detail up or down without changing code A time stamp and frame number So you can line events up A category : "audio", "net", "save" So you can filter Facts, not feelings "loaded level 3 (forest) in 412 ms, 1,204 entities", not "level loaded!!" Cheap when disabled Messages below the current level should cost almost nothing What to log: start-up and configuration, level loads and saves, network connections, every error and warning with the values involved, and occasional performance summaries. What not to log: anything every frame at normal levels (the file becomes useless), passwords, tokens or personal data. The last moments before a crash Writing every debug message to a file is too slow, but the most useful messages are the ones just before a crash. A ring buffer solves this: keep the last N messages in memory, overwriting the oldest, and dump them in the crash handler (next lesson). The practice task builds one. Common mistakes !warning Side effects inside asserts assert(file.open(path)) opens the file only in Debug. Do the work, then assert on its result. !warning Asserting on things that can really happen A missing file, bad input or a lost connection must be handled in Release too. !warning Logging every frame Nobody can read it, and it slows the game. Log events and summaries. !warning Logging secrets or personal data Logs get attached to bug reports and shared. Keep them clean. Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference between an assert and error handling? + An assert catches bugs; error handling copes with expected failures - An assert is for Release builds and error handling is for Debug builds - They are the same; an assert is just shorter to write - Error handling stops the program; an assert logs a warning and continues A missing file is not a bug in your code, so it needs real handling that stays in Release, not an assert. A missing file can legitimately happen; it needs real handling that stays in Release. ? Why wrap a macro's body in do { ... } while (false) ? - So the body runs at least once and then repeats until false - So the compiler can remove it in Release builds + So the macro acts as one statement, even after a braceless if - So the macro's local variables are freed afterwards Without it, a multi-statement macro after an unbraced if would only have its first statement controlled by the if . ? What makes a log line useful? - As much text as possible, so nothing is missed - A unique message for every line of code - Colour, so it stands out in the console + A level, a time or frame, a category, and the values involved "Loading failed" says little; "level 3: failed to open textures/rock.png, error 2" tells you what to check. ? What happens to assert(x 0) in a Release build? - It still checks but only logs + Nothing is checked: the line compiles to nothing - It becomes a static_assert NDEBUG disables it. ? Which kind of check is right for "this struct must be exactly 16 bytes"? - assert(sizeof(T) == 16) - A log line + static_assert(sizeof(T) == 16) Sizes are known at compile time, so the compiler can check them. ? Why use __debugbreak() in a custom assert? + It stops the debugger right at the failing line - It makes the program faster - It writes a crash dump It is the int 3 breakpoint instruction. ? What is a ring buffer of log messages good for? - Sorting messages + Keeping recent messages to write out on a crash - Sending logs over the network The oldest messages are overwritten, so memory use stays fixed.

title: The last N log lines
body: Build RecentLog , which keeps only the most recent log lines in a fixed amount of memory, overwriting the oldest when full. - The constructor receives the capacity (at least 1). - add(line) stores a line. When the log is full, the oldest line is dropped. - lines() returns the stored lines, oldest first . - size() returns how many lines are stored; dropped() how many have been overwritten so far. Store the lines in a std::vector<std::string of exactly capacity slots, used as a ring: keep the index where the next line goes and wrap it round to 0 at the end. Do not erase from the front of a vector. RecentLog log{ 3 }; add "a", "b", "c", "d" - lines() = { "b", "c", "d" }, dropped() = 1

title: 8.04  Crash Dumps
body: When a game crashes on a player's machine, you cannot attach a debugger. A crash dump captures the crashed process's state (threads, stacks, registers, some or all memory) into a file you can open later in Visual Studio or WinDbg as if you had been there. This lesson explains exception codes, writing a minidump from your own crash handler, collecting dumps with Windows Error Reporting, and opening them. What happens when a program crashes A "crash" on Windows is an unhandled exception : the processor or the program raised an exception (an access violation, a divide by zero, a C++ throw nobody caught), and nothing handled it. Windows then calls the process's unhandled exception filter , which by default hands the crash to Windows Error Reporting and ends the process. Each exception has a code. The ones you will see most: Code Name Usual cause --- --- --- 0xC0000005 Access violation Null or dangling pointer, out-of-bounds access, writing to read-only memory 0xC00000FD Stack overflow Runaway recursion, huge locals (lesson 1.05) 0xC0000094 Integer divide by zero x / 0 or x % 0 with integers 0xC000001D Illegal instruction Jumping into data, or an instruction the CPU does not support 0xC0000409 Stack buffer overrun / fail fast A /GS cookie check failed (lesson 7.05), or abort() -style fast fail 0x80000003 Breakpoint An int 3 / __debugbreak() with no debugger attached 0xE06D7363 C++ exception A throw that was never caught (the hex spells "msc" in ASCII) For an access violation, the exception record also says whether it was a read, write or execute, and the address: the clues from lessons 3.02 and 6.02. Minidumps A minidump ( .dmp ) is a snapshot of a process: the list of modules with their versions and signatures, every thread's registers and stack, the exception record, and optionally some or all of the heap. Opened with the matching PDBs (lesson 8.02), it shows the call stack and variables at the moment of the crash. Dump type Contains Size --- --- --- Small ( MiniDumpNormal ) Modules, threads, stacks, exception Tens to hundreds of KB With data segments and indirectly referenced memory Also globals and memory pointed to from the stacks A few MB Full memory ( MiniDumpWithFullMemory ) Everything in the address space As big as the process's memory Small dumps are usually enough for a call stack and the locals on the stack. Full dumps let you inspect any object, at a cost. Writing one yourself A game installs its own filter at start-up, so it can write a dump (and its recent log lines, lesson 8.03) before exiting: cpp include <windows.h include <dbghelp.h pragma comment(lib, "dbghelp.lib") static LONG WINAPI writeCrashDump(EXCEPTION_POINTERS info) { HANDLE file{ CreateFileW(L"crash.dmp", GENERIC_WRITE, 0, nullptr, CREATE_ALWAYS, FILE_ATTRIBUTE_NORMAL, nullptr) }; if (file != INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE) { MINIDUMP_EXCEPTION_INFORMATION exception{}; exception.ThreadId = GetCurrentThreadId(); exception.ExceptionPointers = info; exception.ClientPointers = FALSE; MiniDumpWriteDump(GetCurrentProcess(), GetCurrentProcessId(), file, static_cast<MINIDUMP_TYPE (MiniDumpWithDataSegs MiniDumpWithIndirectlyReferencedMemory), &exception, nullptr, nullptr); CloseHandle(file); } return EXCEPTION_EXECUTE_HANDLER; // let the process end } int wmain() { SetUnhandledExceptionFilter(&writeCrashDump); // ... the game ... } Notes from experience: - Write dumps to a folder the user can write (lesson 5.04), with a time stamp in the name. - The crashed process may be badly damaged (a corrupt heap, an exhausted stack). The most robust crash reporters do as little as possible in the crashed process and let a separate small watchdog process write the dump, using MiniDumpWriteDump on the crashed process from outside. - Some failures ( 0xC0000409 fast fail, stack overflow on a thread with no stack left) bypass or break the filter; the system's own reporting is the fallback. Letting Windows collect dumps Windows Error Reporting can save a dump for every crash of a given program, with no code at all, using a registry key (for developers' and testers' machines): HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\Windows Error Reporting\LocalDumps\game.exe DumpFolder (REG_EXPAND_SZ) %LOCALAPPDATA%\CrashDumps DumpType (REG_DWORD) 1 = mini, 2 = full DumpCount (REG_DWORD) 10 You can also write a dump of any running process from Task Manager → Details → right-click → Create dump file , which is handy for a game that is hung rather than crashed. Opening a dump In Visual Studio, File → Open → File and choose the .dmp . The summary page shows the exception code, the faulting module and the module list; press Debug with Native Only . With matching symbols (and the source, if you have it), you land on the crashing line with the Call Stack, Locals and Threads windows working, though you cannot step: the process is a snapshot, not running. WinDbg (next lesson) opens the same files and has !analyze -v , which reads the exception, finds the faulting frame and summarises the likely cause. Common mistakes !warning Dumps without matching PDBs A dump is only as useful as the symbols you can load for it. Archive the PDBs of every build you give to anyone. !warning Doing heavy work inside the crash handler Allocating, loading DLLs or taking locks in a crashed process can hang. Keep the handler minimal. !warning Only collecting full dumps They can be gigabytes. Small dumps with a little extra memory are usually enough and far easier to collect from players. Check yourself quiz ? What is a crash dump? - A log of every function the program called before crashing + A file of a process's threads, stacks and memory, for later debugging - A copy of the .exe saved at the moment of the crash - The error message Windows shows when a program stops Opening the dump is like being paused at the crash, though the program can no longer run on. ? How does a program write its own minidump when it crashes? - It catches the crash with try / catch and copies its memory to a file - It calls abort , which writes a dump automatically + It installs an unhandled exception filter with SetUnhandledExceptionFilter , and calls MiniDumpWriteDump in it - It asks the debugger to attach and save the state An access violation is a structured exception, not a C++ exception, so try / catch does not see it. ? What do you need to turn a dump from a player into a readable call stack? - The player's whole Windows installation - A Debug build of the game - The source code of every DLL in the process + The exact PDB files of the build the player was running Windows' own PDBs come from Microsoft's symbol server; your game's must be the ones you kept for that build. ? A crash report shows exception code 0xC0000005 . What kind of error is it? - A stack overflow - An uncaught C++ exception + An access violation on memory Look at the access type and address in the exception record next. ? What does a small minidump contain? + Modules, each thread's registers and stack - The program's source code - Only the address of the crash Enough for call stacks and stack locals when symbols are available. ? Why might a crash reporter write the dump from a separate process? - MiniDumpWriteDump only works between processes + The crashed process may be too damaged to run much code safely - To make the file smaller A healthy watchdog process can capture the crashed one from outside. ? What does 0xE06D7363 mean? - Divide by zero - A breakpoint + An uncaught C++ exception The low bytes spell "msc", for Microsoft C++.

title: Describe a crash
body: A crash reporter receives an exception code and, for access violations, two more facts: the kind of access (0 read, 1 write, 8 execute) and the address. Write describe(code, access, address) , which returns a one-line summary: Code Summary --- --- 0xC0000005 "access violation reading 0x..." , "writing 0x..." or "executing 0x..." with the address in upper-case hex, followed by " (null pointer)" if the address is below 0x10000 0xC00000FD "stack overflow" 0xC0000094 "integer divide by zero" 0xC0000409 "stack buffer overrun" 0xE06D7363 "unhandled C++ exception" anything else "exception 0x..." with the code as 8 upper-case hex digits access and address are only used for access violations. describe(0xC0000005, 0, 0x10) = "access violation reading 0x10 (null pointer)" describe(0xC0000005, 1, 0x7FF6A1230000) = "access violation writing 0x7FF6A1230000" describe(0x80000003, 0, 0) = "exception 0x80000003"

title: 8.05  A First Look at WinDbg
body: WinDbg is Microsoft's command-line-driven debugger. It does everything Visual Studio's debugger does and much more, opens any crash dump, and is the only debugger for the Windows kernel (chapter 16). This lesson installs it and teaches the two dozen commands that cover nearly all everyday work, mapped to the Visual Studio windows you already know. Why another debugger Visual Studio's debugger is the most comfortable way to debug your own code. WinDbg is worth knowing because: - it opens crash dumps from anywhere, quickly, with !analyze summarising them; - it can debug programs and machines where Visual Studio is not installed; - it has powerful commands for heaps, handles, locks and Windows internals; - it is the kernel debugger: chapters 15 and 16 depend on it. Install WinDbg from the Microsoft Store (search "WinDbg"; older guides call the new version "WinDbg Preview"). It has a modern window with source, locals and call stack panes, but its heart is the command window . Getting started - File → Launch executable to start a program under the debugger, Attach to process for a running one, or Open dump file for a .dmp . - First, set up symbols (lesson 8.02): .symfix C:\Symbols ; use Microsoft's symbol server, caching in C:\Symbols .sympath+ C:\code\game\x64\Debug ; add your own PDB folder .reload ; load symbols with the new path The everyday commands Task WinDbg Visual Studio equivalent --- --- --- Continue g F5 Step over / into p / t F10 / F11 Step out gu Shift+F11 Breakpoint on a function bp game!Player::update F9 Breakpoint on a source line bp main.cpp:42 (with backticks) F9 List / clear breakpoints bl / bc Breakpoints window Data breakpoint: break on write to 4 bytes ba w4 0x0000004f8c8ff8a0 Lesson 4.09 Call stack k ( kp with parameters, kn numbered) Call Stack Switch to frame n .frame n Double-click a frame Locals dv ( dv /t with types) Locals Show a typed object dt game!Player 0x... or dt player Watch Registers r ( r rax for one) Registers Memory as bytes / dwords / qwords db addr / dd addr / dq addr Memory window Memory as text da addr (ASCII), du addr (UTF-16) Memory window, text column Disassemble u addr ( uf function for the whole function) Disassembly Loaded modules lm ( lmvm game for details) Modules Threads ~ ( ~2s switches to thread 2; ~ k stacks of all threads) Threads Evaluate an expression ? rsp + 0x20 Watch Help .hh command Commands that start with . are debugger meta-commands; those starting with ! are extensions , larger commands supplied by DLLs loaded into the debugger. Analysing a crash dump Open a dump from lesson 8.04 and run: !analyze -v It reads the exception record, finds the faulting thread and frame, applies heuristics, and prints a summary: EXCEPTION_CODE: (NTSTATUS) 0xc0000005 - The instruction at 0x7ff6a1235f10 referenced memory at 0x10. The memory could not be read. FAULTING_SOURCE_LINE: C:\code\game\inventory.cpp FAULTING_SOURCE_LINE_NUMBER: 42 STACK_TEXT: game!Inventory::totalWeight+0x20 game!Hud::drawWeight+0x45 game!Hud::draw+0x9a ... Then dig in with k , .frame , dv and dt as in a live session. .ecxr switches the debugger's context to the moment of the exception (the registers when it happened), which matters for dumps where the current context is the crash handler. Useful extensions Command Shows --- --- !heap -s Summary of the process heaps !handle Open handles and their types (spotting handle leaks, lesson 5.01) !locks Critical sections that are held, and by which thread (deadlocks, lesson 8.07) !peb The process environment block: command line, environment, loaded modules !address addr What kind of memory an address is in (lesson 6.04's VirtualQuery , done for you) Common mistakes !warning Forgetting symbols Without .symfix and your PDB path, everything is addresses. Fix symbols before anything else. !warning Reading a dump's stack without .ecxr You may be looking at the crash handler's stack instead of the crash. !warning Typing g by habit in a dump A dump is not running: it cannot continue. Use the inspection commands. Check yourself quiz ? Why learn WinDbg when Visual Studio has a debugger? + It is quick with dumps, needs no Visual Studio, and debugs the kernel - Because Visual Studio cannot open crash dumps - Because WinDbg is the only debugger that supports breakpoints in Release builds - Because WinDbg can recompile code while debugging Visual Studio can open dumps too, but WinDbg is lighter and goes deeper into Windows itself. ? What is the difference between commands starting with . and with ! ? + . commands control the debugger itself; ! commands are extensions provided by debugger DLLs - . commands read memory; ! commands write memory - . commands work on dumps; ! commands only on live processes - They are the same; the prefix is optional .symfix sets up the symbol path (debugger control); !analyze comes from an extension DLL. ? Which commands show locals, a typed structure and raw memory? - lm for locals, k for structures, g for memory - dq for locals, dv for structures, dt for memory + dv for locals, dt for a typed structure, and db / dd / dq for memory - bp for locals, bl for structures, u for memory db , dd and dq show memory as bytes, dwords or qwords; k is the call stack and lm lists modules. ? Which WinDbg command shows the call stack? + k - g - lm kp adds parameters, kn frame numbers. ? What does !analyze -v do? - Lists all the loaded modules + Summarises the likely cause of a crash - Steps one instruction forward It is the usual first command on a crash dump. ? How do you look at the 4-byte values at an address? - db address - du address + dd address db shows bytes, dd double words (4 bytes), dq quad words, du UTF-16 text. ? What does .symfix do? + Points the symbol path at Microsoft's server - Fixes corrupted PDB files - Removes all symbols Follow it with .reload .

title: 8.06  Debugging Optimised Code
body: Some bugs only appear in Release builds, and crash dumps from players are always from optimised code. Debugging it is harder (variables vanish, lines run out of order, functions disappear into their callers) but entirely possible. This lesson gives a practical toolkit: make Release builds debuggable, read values from registers and the disassembly, switch optimisation off selectively, and use logging where stepping fails. What goes wrong in the debugger Lesson 4.10 explained what the optimiser does; here is what that looks like when you debug: Symptom Cause --- --- "Variable is optimised away and not available" It lives only in a register, which has since been reused, or it was removed The yellow arrow jumps backwards and forwards Instructions from different lines were interleaved A breakpoint in a function never hits The function was inlined into its callers A function is missing from the call stack Inlined, or left by a tail call (lesson 7.11) Locals show wrong values The debugger reads a stack slot the optimised code no longer uses None of this means the debugger is broken. It means the source is only an approximation of what runs, and you sometimes have to look at what really runs. Make Release builds debuggable These settings cost nothing at run time and should be on for every Release build: Setting Effect --- --- C/C++ → General → Debug Information Format: /Zi Writes a full PDB for Release Linker → Debugging → Generate Debug Info: /DEBUG Links the PDB C/C++ → Command Line: /Zo (default in recent versions) Records which register each variable is in at each point, so more locals are visible Linker → Optimization → /OPT:REF, /OPT:ICF (keep them) Unaffected; note that ICF can merge identical functions, so a call stack may show a different name with the same body Reading values the debugger cannot show When a variable is "optimised away", the value usually still exists somewhere: 1. Open the Disassembly window (Ctrl+Alt+D) at the current instruction. 2. Find the instruction that last loaded or computed the value. mov ebx, dword ptr rcx+0Ch tells you ebx holds the member at offset 12 of whatever rcx pointed to. 3. Read the register in the Registers window, or in Watch as @ebx . 4. For objects, cast a register in Watch: (Player )@rdi . Function arguments are in rcx , rdx , r8 , r9 only at the very start of a function (lesson 7.06); optimised code moves them into non-volatile registers or overwrites them soon after. Set the breakpoint on the function's first instruction (right-click → Go To Disassembly, F9 on the first line) to catch them in place. Turn optimisation off where you are looking When you need to step through one area of a Release build comfortably: cpp pragma optimize("", off) void Inventory::recalculate() { // compiled without optimisation in an otherwise optimised build } pragma optimize("", on) Or disable it for a whole .cpp file: right-click the file → Properties → C/C++ → Optimization: Disabled (/Od) . Remember to remove these: they are debugging aids, not fixes. If the bug disappears when optimisation is turned off in one place, that is itself a strong clue: undefined behaviour (uninitialised values, overruns, data races, lesson 4.10) in or near that code. Logging and asserts in Release Stepping is often impractical in timing-sensitive or rare bugs. Use the tools from lesson 8.03, kept enabled in a test configuration: - a ring-buffer log dumped on crash; - asserts enabled in an "optimised with checks" configuration; - tracepoints (lesson 4.09), which work in optimised code at instruction level. Bugs that only appear in Release A checklist, roughly in order of how often each is the cause: 1. Uninitialised variables : Debug's 0xCC fill was consistent; Release's garbage is not. Turn on warning level 4 (C4700, C4701). 2. Out-of-bounds access : Debug's padding and guard bytes absorbed it. Run AddressSanitizer (lesson 2.10). 3. Data races : Release keeps values in registers and reorders memory accesses (lesson 6.06). 4. Code inside assert that no longer runs. 5. Timing : Release runs faster, changing the order of events between threads or frames. 6. Signed overflow or other undefined behaviour the optimiser exploited. 7. A compiler bug : possible, but almost always the last explanation, after everything above. Common mistakes !warning Giving up when a variable is optimised away Look at the disassembly: the value is usually in a register. !warning Fixing a Release-only bug by turning optimisation off That hides it. Find the undefined behaviour. !warning Trusting the source view's line in optimised code Check the Disassembly window to see which instruction actually faulted. Check yourself quiz ? Which settings make a Release build debuggable without slowing it down? - Turning optimisation off with /Od + A full PDB ( /Zi , linker /DEBUG ) plus /Zo - Defining _DEBUG in the Release configuration - Linking the Debug runtime library Debug information does not change the generated code, so the build stays as fast as before. ? How do you see a value the debugger reports as optimised away? - Rebuild in Debug, since the value cannot be recovered in Release - Add the variable to the Watch window with a format specifier + Find its register or stack slot in the disassembly and read that - Restart the program with Just My Code turned off The value still exists somewhere while it is in use; the PDB just cannot say where. ? Name three common causes of bugs that only appear in Release builds. - Missing PDBs, wrong breakpoints and the Output window being closed - Too many comments, long function names and deep folders - Using std::vector , using const and using references + Uninitialised variables, out-of-bounds accesses and data races Debug builds fill memory, run slower and keep asserts, which can hide all of these. Side effects in asserts, timing differences and other undefined behaviour are common too. ? The debugger says a local is "optimised away". What should you try? - Rebuild in Debug and hope it reproduces + Find the register that holds it in the disassembly - Assume the value is zero Optimised code keeps most values in registers. ? A bug disappears when one file is compiled with /Od . What does that suggest? - The optimiser has a bug in that file - The file should always be built with /Od + Undefined behaviour near that code, exposed by the optimiser UB behaves differently under optimisation; find and fix it. ? Where are a function's first four arguments most reliably found in optimised code? + In rcx , rdx , r8 , r9 on entry - In the shadow space, always - On the heap Optimised code soon moves or overwrites them.

title: 8.07  Debugging Threads
body: Multithreaded bugs are timing-dependent, so they hide when you look for them. This lesson covers the tools that make them visible: naming threads, the Threads and Parallel Stacks windows, freezing threads to force an ordering, diagnosing deadlocks from call stacks, and finding races with careful logging and data breakpoints. Name your threads The first step costs one line per thread. Give each thread a name, and every tool shows it instead of a bare id: cpp include <windows.h include <thread void startAudioThread() { std::jthread audio{ { SetThreadDescription(GetCurrentThread(), L"Audio mixer"); // ... } }; } SetThreadDescription (Windows 10 1607 and later; lesson 5.08 showed how to call it safely on older systems) names the thread for Visual Studio, WinDbg, crash dumps and profilers. The Threads window Debug → Windows → Threads lists every thread when the program is paused: its id, name, location (the function it is in) and priority. Double-click a thread to switch to it: the Call Stack, Locals and editor then show that thread's view. A yellow arrow marks the current thread. Right-click → Freeze suspends a thread so it will not run when you continue; Thaw releases it. Freezing is a powerful way to force an interleaving : freeze the main thread at a chosen line, let a worker run past a critical point, then thaw the main thread. A race that appears once in a thousand runs can be reproduced every time this way. Parallel Stacks Debug → Windows → Parallel Stacks draws every thread's call stack at once, merging the frames they share into a graph. With twenty worker threads, you see at a glance that eighteen are idle in the job queue's wait, one is in physics, and one is stuck somewhere unexpected. Diagnosing a deadlock The game freezes and the CPU usage is near zero: the signature of a deadlock (lesson 6.06), as opposed to an infinite loop, which shows 100% of a core. 1. Break All (Ctrl+Alt+Break). 2. Open Parallel Stacks or go through the threads in the Threads window. Look for threads waiting inside lock functions: std::mutex::lock , EnterCriticalSection , WaitForSingleObject , RtlpWaitOnCriticalSection . 3. For each, find which lock it waits for (the argument to the lock call, visible in its frame) and which locks it holds (locks taken in earlier frames of its own stack). 4. Draw the arrows: "thread A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2; thread B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1". A cycle is a deadlock. In WinDbg, !locks lists Windows critical sections that are held, with the owning thread, and ~ k prints every thread's stack, which does steps 2 and 3 quickly. The practice task automates step 4: finding a cycle in "who waits for whom". Finding races Data races are harder: there is no hang and no crash at the moment of the race, only a wrong value later. Approaches, cheapest first: - Think about ownership. For each piece of shared data, which threads touch it and which lock protects it? Data touched by two threads with no lock in common is the suspect. - Data breakpoints (lesson 4.09) on the corrupted value: the debugger stops on whichever thread writes it, and the Threads window shows what the others were doing. - Logging with thread ids and sequence numbers , written to a lock-free per-thread ring buffer (formatting and locks inside logging change the timing enough to hide the bug). - Stress : run the suspected code in a tight loop with many threads to make the race frequent. - Tools : Clang's ThreadSanitizer (on Linux builds, or Clang on Windows with limits) detects races automatically; on MSVC, the Concurrency Visualizer extension shows which threads ran when. Common mistakes !warning Stepping a single thread and expecting others to wait When you step, all threads run (unless frozen). Breakpoints in shared code can hit on any thread. !warning Adding a log line and the bug disappears Logging changes timing. That does not mean the bug is fixed; it confirms it is timing-dependent. !warning Fixing a deadlock by adding a timeout The cycle is still there. Fix the lock order. Check yourself quiz ? How do you find the threads involved in a deadlock? + Break All and match what each thread waits for with what it holds - Look for the thread using the most CPU time - Remove locks one at a time until the freeze stops - Run the program in Release, where deadlocks show an error message A deadlock uses almost no CPU: the threads are all waiting, so their stacks show exactly where. ? What is the Parallel Stacks window good for? - Running several threads one step at a time together - Showing each thread's stack memory as raw bytes - Listing the threads in the order they were created + Seeing all threads' stacks at once to spot the odd one out Twenty identical worker stacks collapse into one, and the odd one out stands out. ? Why do races often disappear when you add logging? - Because logging takes a lock that fixes the race permanently + Logging changes the timing, so the accesses may no longer overlap - Because the compiler stops optimising code that logs - Because logging runs on its own thread The race is still there; it has only become less likely to show, which is why races need tools and reasoning, not just prints. ? The game freezes with almost no CPU use. What is most likely? - An infinite loop + A deadlock: threads waiting on each other - A memory leak An infinite loop would keep a core busy. ? What does freezing a thread in the Threads window let you do? - Make it run faster - Kill it permanently + Hold it while others run, to force an order Forced interleavings make rare races reproducible. ? Why is SetThreadDescription worth calling? + Tools then show each thread's name - It makes threads safer - It sets the thread's priority Named threads make every multithreaded investigation faster.

title: Find the deadlock
body: From a paused program you have collected, for each thread, the locks it holds and the single lock it is waiting for (or none). Write findDeadlock(threads) , which returns the ids of the threads in a deadlock cycle, or an empty vector if there is none. Thread A "waits for" thread B when A is waiting for a lock that B holds. A deadlock is a cycle in that relation: A waits for B, B waits for C, ..., which waits for A. Return the cycle's thread ids starting from the smallest id in the cycle and following the waits-for direction. If several cycles exist, return the one containing the smallest thread id of any cycle. thread 1: holds {A}, waits for B thread 2: holds {B}, waits for A thread 3: holds {}, waits for A - { 1, 2 } (3 is blocked behind the deadlock but not part of the cycle)

title: 8.08  Profiling: Finding Where the Time Goes
match: 8.08 Profiling: Finding Where the Time Goes
body: When a game is slow, the cause is almost never where you would guess. A profiler measures where the time actually goes. This lesson covers the two kinds of profiler ( sampling and instrumenting ), Visual Studio's CPU Usage tool, frame-based instrumentation with scoped timers, and how to read the results to find the few places worth optimising. Measure, don't guess Programmers are famously bad at predicting which code is slow. A function that looks expensive runs once per level; an innocent-looking std::string built every frame runs a million times. So the rule is: measure first , in a Release build (lesson 4.10), on realistic content, and optimise only what the measurement points at. Typically a small fraction of the code accounts for most of the time; finding that fraction is the whole job. Two kinds of profiler Sampling profiler Instrumenting profiler --- --- --- How Interrupts the program thousands of times a second and records the call stack each time Code you add (or the compiler adds) records the start and end time of each marked section Shows Statistically, which functions are on the stack most often Exact times for each marked section, frame by frame Overhead Low; no code changes Small per marker; you choose what to mark Good for "Where does the time go overall?" "Why was this frame slow?", spikes, timelines across threads Examples Visual Studio CPU Usage, Windows Performance Analyzer, Superluminal, VTune Tracy, Optick, PIX markers, your own scoped timers Games use both: sampling to find hot spots, instrumentation to understand frame-to-frame behaviour. Visual Studio's CPU Usage tool 1. Switch to Release (with /Zi and /DEBUG for symbols, lesson 8.06). 2. Debug → Performance Profiler (Alt+F2), tick CPU Usage , press Start . 3. Play the slow part of the game, then stop. The report lists functions by: - Self CPU : time spent in the function's own code; - Total CPU : time in the function and everything it calls . Start from the hot path (the report highlights it): the chain of calls with the highest total time from main down. A function with high total but low self time is not itself slow; something it calls is. A function with high self time is where the actual work happens. Double-click to see the source with per-line costs. Instrumenting frames yourself A scoped timer measures the time from its construction to its destruction (RAII again, lesson 2.04): cpp include <chrono include <cstdio class ScopedTimer { public: explicit ScopedTimer(const char name) : m_name{ name }, m_start{ std::chrono::steady_clock::now() } {} ~ScopedTimer() { const auto us{ std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::microseconds (std::chrono::steady_clock::now() - m_start).count() }; std::printf("%-12s %6lld us\n", m_name, static_cast<long long (us)); } private: const char m_name; std::chrono::steady_clock::time_point m_start; }; void updateFrame() { ScopedTimer frame{ "frame" }; { ScopedTimer t{ "physics" }; / ... / } { ScopedTimer t{ "ai" }; / ... / } { ScopedTimer t{ "render" }; / ... / } } Printing every frame is too noisy and too slow; real systems record the samples into a buffer and either show a live overlay (average and worst over the last second) or send them to a viewer such as Tracy, which draws a timeline of every frame across all threads. The practice task builds the aggregation step: totals, counts and worst cases per name. Reading frame times A game at 60 frames per second has 16.7 ms per frame for everything. A useful habit is to think in milliseconds per frame rather than frames per second, because milliseconds add up: physics 3 ms + AI 2 ms + rendering 9 ms = 14 ms, room to spare. Frames per second do not add. Look at the worst frames as well as the average. A game that averages 8 ms but has a 40 ms frame every few seconds stutters , and players notice stutter more than a lower steady frame rate. Spikes usually come from occasional work: an allocation-heavy event, loading, garbage collection in a script language, a file write on the main thread. What usually turns out to be slow Common culprit Usual fix --- --- Allocations every frame (strings, vectors, new ) Reuse, reserve, pools, arenas (lessons 2.02, 3.10) Pointer chasing over scattered objects Contiguous arrays, data-oriented layouts (lessons 2.07, 3.02) Searching linearly in large containers every frame Hash maps, spatial grids (lesson 3.08) Work done every frame that could be done once Cache the result, recompute only on change Waiting: locks, file I/O, synchronous GPU reads on the main thread Move it to another thread or make it asynchronous Chapter 17 returns to performance with careful benchmarking. Common mistakes !warning Profiling a Debug build Debug distorts everything: some functions are ten times slower, others hardly change. Profile Release. !warning Optimising what you guess is slow Measure first; you will usually be surprised. !warning Reading total time as self time A function at the top of the call tree always has a large total. Look for where the self time is. !warning Only watching the average frame time Spikes cause stutter. Track the worst frames too. Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference between sampling and instrumenting profilers? - Sampling measures memory; instrumenting measures CPU time - Sampling only works in Debug; instrumenting only in Release + Sampling records stacks statistically; instrumenting times marked sections - They are the same thing, with different names in different tools Sampling needs no code changes; instrumenting gives exact per-frame timelines of the sections you mark. ? What is the difference between self and total time? + Self time is spent in the function's own instructions; total time includes everything it calls - Self time is measured by the program; total time by the profiler - Self time is per call; total time is for the whole run - Self time includes waiting; total time does not 90% total and 1% self means the function itself is cheap, and the time is in something it calls. ? How long is a frame at 60 frames per second? - About 6 milliseconds - About 60 milliseconds + About 16.7 milliseconds - About 33.3 milliseconds 1000 ms divided by 60 is about 16.7 ms. 33.3 ms is a frame at 30 fps. ? What does a sampling profiler do? - Records the exact start and end time of every function + Records the call stack at intervals to show where time goes - Measures memory use It needs no code changes and has low overhead. ? A function shows 90% total CPU but 1% self CPU. What does that mean? - It is the slowest function in the program - The profiler is wrong + It is not slow itself; functions it calls account for the time Follow the hot path into its callees. ? Why think in milliseconds per frame rather than frames per second? + Milliseconds of each system add up; frame rates do not - Milliseconds are more precise - Frames per second cannot be measured 60 fps means a budget of 16.7 ms shared by everything. ? A game averages 60 fps but stutters. What should you look at? - Only the average frame time + The worst frame times, and what happened then - The size of the executable Occasional spikes cause stutter.

title: Summarise the timings
where: 8.08 Profiling: Finding Where the Time Goes
body: A frame profiler records samples: each one a section name and how many microseconds it took. Write summarise(samples) , which returns one Row per name with: - name ; - count : how many samples it had; - total : the sum of its times; - worst : its largest single time; - average : total / count , as a double . Rows are sorted by total , largest first; names with equal totals are sorted alphabetically. { "render", 9000 } { "physics", 3000 } { "render", 11000 } { "ai", 2000 } - render count 2 total 20000 worst 11000 average 10000 physics count 1 total 3000 worst 3000 average 3000 ai count 1 total 2000 worst 2000 average 2000

title: Asserts with values
