title: 9.01  What Reverse Engineering Is, and Its Ground Rules
match: 9.01 What Reverse Engineering Is, and Its Ground Rules
body: Reverse engineering means working out how a program works from the program itself, without its source. It is how security researchers find vulnerabilities, how malware is analysed, how old software is kept running and how file formats are documented for interoperability. This lesson sets out what it involves, the tools, and the legal and ethical ground rules this course follows. Running the pipeline backwards Lesson 1.04's pipeline turned source into machine code. Reverse engineering goes the other way, recovering understanding, never the original source, from the compiled program: The earlier chapters were the preparation: the PE format of chapter 6's modules, the assembly of chapter 7, the debuggers of chapters 4 and 8, and the layouts of chapters 2 and 3. Who does it, and why Field What they reverse engineer --- --- Security research Software, to find and responsibly report vulnerabilities before attackers do Malware analysis Malicious programs, to understand them, detect them and remove them Interoperability File formats and protocols, so that other programs can read and write them (many open-source tools exist because of this) Preservation and compatibility Old software and games whose source is lost, to keep them running on new systems Debugging and support Third-party libraries and drivers without source, when they misbehave inside your program Learning How compilers, operating systems and well-written programs work Static and dynamic analysis - Static analysis examines the program without running it: reading the file's headers and the disassembly, following cross-references (lessons 9.02 to 9.06, 9.08). Tools: Ghidra, IDA, Binary Ninja, dumpbin . - Dynamic analysis runs it and watches: breakpoints, memory, calls into the operating system (lesson 9.07). Tools: x64dbg, WinDbg, Visual Studio, Process Monitor. Each answers what the other cannot. Static analysis sees every path, including ones that rarely run; dynamic analysis sees real values and resolves indirect calls. Real work alternates between them. The ground rules for this course Reverse engineering is a legitimate, widely practised skill. Like any capability, how it is used matters, and the law varies by country. The rules this course follows: 1. Practise on programs you have the right to analyse : programs you compiled yourself (lesson 9.10 builds a series of practice targets), open-source programs (where you can check your conclusions against the source), and challenges published specifically as practice ("crackmes" and capture-the-flag tasks). 2. Read the licence. Many licences restrict reverse engineering. Some laws allow limited reverse engineering for specific purposes such as interoperability (for example, Article 6 of the EU Software Directive) or good-faith security research, with conditions. When it matters, ask someone qualified rather than assuming. 3. Do not use it to cheat other people. Altering online games to gain an advantage over other players, or bypassing anti-cheat systems, harms those players, breaks the terms you agreed to and can break the law. This course does not teach that, and it does not teach defeating copy protection or licence checks. 4. Report vulnerabilities responsibly. If you find a security flaw, tell the vendor privately, through their security contact or bug bounty programme, and give them time to fix it before discussing it publicly. 5. Handle malware with care. Real malicious samples belong in an isolated virtual machine with no access to your files or network, which lesson 15.08 sets up. The practice targets in this course are harmless programs you build yourself. What you can expect to recover Survives compilation Lost --- --- The machine code and its control flow Comments, formatting, local variable names String literals and constants Most type information (structs become offsets, lesson 7.08) Imported and exported function names Templates and inline functions as separate entities Class names (through RTTI, lesson 9.06), if not disabled Macros, constexpr values folded into code Everything, if a PDB is available The original structure of the source files Recovering a program's logic is slow, careful work, done function by function. Recovering its exact source is impossible. Good reverse engineers are patient, take notes, and name things as they understand them. Common mistakes !warning Starting with a large, unfamiliar program Practise on small programs you wrote, where you can check every conclusion against the source. !warning Trusting the decompiler blindly Decompiler output is a guess at C code. Check important conclusions against the assembly. !warning Assuming that being able to do it means being allowed to Check the licence and the law, and stay within the ground rules. Check yourself quiz ? Name four legitimate uses of reverse engineering. - Copying a game's code into your own, removing licence checks, unlocking paid content, cheating online + Security research, malware analysis, interoperability with file formats and protocols, and preserving old software - Changing a program's author name, redistributing it, selling it, renaming it - Speeding up the compiler, shrinking source files, writing comments, formatting code Debugging third-party code and learning are also legitimate. The ground rules of the course rule out piracy and cheating in online games. ? What do reverse engineers recover, and what can they not recover? + Logic, strings and imports, but not comments, local names or source - They recover the original source code exactly, but not the strings - They recover comments and local names, but not the control flow - They recover nothing useful without a PDB Compiling throws away comments and local names for good; the behaviour remains in the machine code. ? What should you do if you find a security vulnerability? - Publish the details at once so users can protect themselves - Keep it secret and say nothing - Sell it to whoever offers the most + Report it privately to the vendor and give them time to fix it before discussing it publicly This is responsible disclosure: users get a fix before attackers learn the details. ? What is the difference between static and dynamic analysis? + Static examines the program unrun; dynamic runs and observes it - Static analysis is for small programs, dynamic for large ones - They are the same thing Each reveals things the other cannot; real work uses both. ? Which of these is lost when a program is compiled without a PDB? - String literals - Imported function names + Local variable names Locals become registers and stack offsets. ? Which practice targets does this course use? - Commercial online games you own - Anti-cheat software and its drivers + Programs you build yourself, and open source These are targets you clearly have the right to analyse.

title: 9.02  The PE File Format
body:
Every .exe and .dll on Windows is a Portable Executable (PE) file: a set of headers describing the program, followed by its sections of code and data. This lesson walks through the headers in order (the DOS header and MZ , the PE signature, the file header, the optional header and its data directories, and the section table) and reads them from C++. The overall shape ┌──────────────────────────┐ offset 0 │ DOS header ("MZ") │ 64 bytes; e_lfanew at offset 0x3C says where the PE header is ├──────────────────────────┤ │ DOS stub │ a tiny DOS program: "This program cannot be run in DOS mode." ├──────────────────────────┤ offset e_lfanew │ "PE\0\0" signature │ 4 bytes │ File header (COFF) │ 20 bytes: machine, number of sections, ... │ Optional header │ 240 bytes for 64-bit: entry point, image base, data directories ├──────────────────────────┤ │ Section table │ 40 bytes per section: name, RVA, size, file offset, flags ├──────────────────────────┤ │ .text │ code │ .rdata │ constants, import and export tables, RTTI │ .data │ writable globals │ .pdata │ unwind information (lesson 8.02) │ .rsrc │ resources: icons, version information │ .reloc │ relocations (lesson 6.09) └──────────────────────────┘ The same layout appears in memory once the loader maps the file: GetModuleHandleW(nullptr) points at the MZ (lesson 5.08), and every RVA in the headers is an offset from there. The DOS header For backward compatibility with 1980s DOS, every PE file starts with a DOS header. Only two fields matter now: Offset Field Value --- --- --- 0x00 e_magic 0x5A4D : the bytes 4D 5A , "MZ" 0x3C e_lfanew The file offset of the PE signature (often 0x80 to 0x100) The NT headers At e_lfanew come the NT headers : the signature, the file header and the optional header. Field Where Meaning --- --- --- Signature +0 0x00004550 : the bytes 50 45 00 00 , "PE\0\0" FileHeader.Machine +4 0x8664 for x64, 0x14C for 32-bit x86, 0xAA64 for ARM64 FileHeader.NumberOfSections +6 How many entries the section table has FileHeader.TimeDateStamp +8 When it was linked (or a hash, for reproducible builds) FileHeader.SizeOfOptionalHeader +20 Where the section table starts, relative to the optional header FileHeader.Characteristics +22 Flags: executable, DLL, large-address-aware ... OptionalHeader.Magic +24 0x20B for 64-bit (PE32+), 0x10B for 32-bit OptionalHeader.AddressOfEntryPoint +24+16 RVA where execution starts (the C runtime's start-up code, which calls main ) OptionalHeader.ImageBase +24+24 Preferred load address: 0x140000000 for exes (lesson 6.09) OptionalHeader.SizeOfImage Size of the whole image in memory OptionalHeader.DllCharacteristics Security flags: ASLR (dynamic base), DEP (NX compatible), CFG ... OptionalHeader.DataDirectory 16 the last 128 bytes RVA and size of the import table, export table, resources, relocations, debug data ... The data directories are the index of the file: each entry points (by RVA and size) at one important table. The ones you will use most: Index Directory --- --- 0 Export table (lesson 9.03) 1 Import table (lesson 9.03) 2 Resources 3 Exception (unwind) data, .pdata 5 Base relocations 6 Debug directory: the PDB's name and signature (lesson 8.02) 12 Import address table (IAT) The section table After the optional header, one 40-byte entry per section: Field Meaning --- --- Name 8 bytes, such as .text\0\0\0 VirtualSize Size in memory VirtualAddress RVA where the section starts in memory SizeOfRawData Size in the file (rounded up to the file alignment, often 512) PointerToRawData Offset where the section starts in the file Characteristics Flags: code, initialised data, readable, writable, executable Sections start on 4 KB page boundaries in memory, but only 512-byte boundaries in the file, so an RVA and a file offset differ: converting between them needs the section table (lesson 9.03's practice task). Reading the headers from C++ <windows.h defines all these structures ( IMAGE_DOS_HEADER , IMAGE_NT_HEADERS64 , IMAGE_SECTION_HEADER ), so a loaded module's headers can be read directly: cpp include <windows.h include <iostream include <string int main() { const auto base{ reinterpret_cast<const unsigned char (GetModuleHandleW(nullptr)) }; const auto dos{ reinterpret_cast<const IMAGE_DOS_HEADER (base) }; const auto nt{ reinterpret_cast<const IMAGE_NT_HEADERS64 (base + dos- e_lfanew) }; std::cout << "MZ found: " << (dos- e_magic == IMAGE_DOS_SIGNATURE) << '
'; std::cout << "PE found: " << (nt- Signature == IMAGE_NT_SIGNATURE) << '
'; std::cout << "x64: " << (nt- FileHeader.Machine == IMAGE_FILE_MACHINE_AMD64) << '
'; std::cout << "64-bit header: " << (nt- OptionalHeader.Magic == IMAGE_NT_OPTIONAL_HDR64_MAGIC) << '
'; std::cout << "ASLR enabled: " << ((nt- OptionalHeader.DllCharacteristics & IMAGE_DLLCHARACTERISTICS_DYNAMIC_BASE) != 0) << '
'; const IMAGE_SECTION_HEADER section{ IMAGE_FIRST_SECTION(nt) }; bool hasText{ false }; for (int i{ 0 }; i < nt- FileHeader.NumberOfSections; ++i) if (std::string(reinterpret_cast<const char (section i .Name), 5) == ".text") hasText = true; std::cout << "has .text: " << hasText << '
'; return 0; } MZ found: 1 PE found: 1 x64: 1 64-bit header: 1 ASLR enabled: 1 has .text: 1 dumpbin /headers game.exe prints all of this from the file on disk, and tools like PE-bear and CFF Explorer show it graphically. For an untrusted file, never cast raw file bytes to these structures without checking every offset against the file's size first: malformed files are a classic attack on parsers. The practice task parses from a byte buffer with those checks. Common mistakes !warning Mixing RVAs and file offsets Header fields are RVAs (memory offsets). In a file on disk, convert through the section table before reading. !warning Assuming a fixed offset for the PE header Always read e_lfanew . !warning Trusting the sizes in a file Check every offset and count against the actual file size before using it. Check yourself quiz ? In what order do the parts of a PE file come? + DOS header, PE signature, file header, optional header, sections - PE signature, section table, DOS header, sections - Sections, then the section table, then the headers - File header, DOS header, sections, section table e_lfanew in the DOS header gives the offset of the PE signature, where the NT headers start. The optional header ends with the data directories, and the section table comes just before the sections. ? What does the section table tell you for each section? - Only its name and the functions it contains - The source files the section was compiled from + Its name, memory and file positions and sizes, and its flags - The DLLs the section imports The memory and file positions differ, which is why converting an RVA to a file offset needs the section table. ? Why should a PE parser check offsets against the file size? - Because Windows rejects PE files larger than 4 GB - Because offsets in a PE file are always relative to the end - Because the file size is needed to find the entry point + Because malformed or malicious files can contain offsets and counts pointing outside the file Using them unchecked reads out of bounds, which can crash the parser or worse. ? Which two bytes start every PE file? + 4D 5A ("MZ") - 50 45 ("PE") - 7F 45 ("\x7FE") "MZ" is the DOS header's signature; the PE signature comes later, at e_lfanew. ? What does e_lfanew hold? - The entry point + The file offset of the PE signature - The number of sections It is at offset 0x3C of the DOS header. ? What is the value of FileHeader.Machine for a 64-bit x86 program? - 0x14C - 0x20B + 0x8664 0x20B is the optional header's magic for PE32+. ? What are the data directories? + RVAs and sizes of key tables such as imports and exports - The folders the program was built in - The list of sections They are the index of the file's important tables.

title: Parse a PE header safely
body: Write parseHeaders(file) , which reads the main facts from the bytes of a PE file, checking every offset before reading. Return std::nullopt if anything is missing or wrong. Read these, all little-endian (lesson 1.02): 1. At offset 0: the two bytes 'M' 'Z' . 2. At offset 0x3C : a 4-byte e_lfanew . 3. At e_lfanew : the four bytes 'P' 'E' 0 0 . 4. At e_lfanew + 4 : Machine (2 bytes). At e_lfanew + 6 : NumberOfSections (2 bytes). At e_lfanew + 20 : SizeOfOptionalHeader (2 bytes). 5. At e_lfanew + 24 , the optional header: Magic (2 bytes) must be 0x20B (64-bit); AddressOfEntryPoint at optional + 16 (4 bytes); ImageBase at optional + 24 (8 bytes). 6. The section table starts at e_lfanew + 24 + SizeOfOptionalHeader . Each entry is 40 bytes: the name is the first 8 bytes (stop at the first zero byte), VirtualAddress at entry + 12 (4 bytes). Return the machine, the entry point, the image base, and the sections' names and virtual addresses.

title: 9.03  Imports, Exports and the Loader
body: A program's import table lists every function it uses from DLLs; a DLL's export table lists every function it offers. Together they are a map of what a program can do and how its modules connect. This lesson reads both, explains the import address table that the loader fills in at start-up, and shows how to convert RVAs to file offsets so tables can be read from a file on disk. Why imports matter so much For a reverse engineer, the import table is often the most informative part of a program. A program that imports CreateFileW , ReadFile and CryptDecrypt reads and decrypts files; one importing WSAStartup and send uses the network; one importing CreateWindowExW has a window. Before reading a single instruction, the imports outline what the program does. Tools list them first for this reason: powershell dumpbin /imports game.exe dumpbin /exports plugin.dll The import table Data directory 1 (lesson 9.02) points at an array of import descriptors , one per DLL, ending with an all-zero entry: Field Meaning --- --- Name RVA of the DLL's name, such as "KERNEL32.dll" OriginalFirstThunk RVA of the import lookup table : what to import FirstThunk RVA of the import address table (IAT): where the addresses go Each lookup table entry is 8 bytes. If the top bit is set, the function is imported by ordinal (a number); otherwise the entry is the RVA of a hint/name entry: a 2-byte hint followed by the function's name, "CreateFileW\0" . What the loader does When the program starts (lesson 1.06), the loader, for each import descriptor: 1. loads the DLL (finding it by the search order, lesson 5.08) if it is not already loaded; 2. for each function in the lookup table, finds its address in the DLL's export table; 3. writes that address into the corresponding slot of the IAT . The program's code never contains the address of CreateFileW itself. Every call to an imported function goes through the IAT: asm call qword ptr __imp_CreateFileW ; read the address from the IAT slot, then call it So in disassembly, calls to imported functions are indirect calls through a fixed set of memory slots, and disassemblers label them with the function names, which makes them easy landmarks. After loading, the IAT is made read-only, so it cannot be changed by accident. The export table A DLL's data directory 0 points at its export directory , which holds three parallel arrays: Array Holds --- --- AddressOfFunctions RVAs of the exported functions, indexed by ordinal minus the base AddressOfNames RVAs of the exported names, sorted alphabetically so they can be binary-searched AddressOfNameOrdinals For each name, the index into the functions array GetProcAddress(module, "scaleDamage") (lesson 4.05) binary-searches the names, takes the matching ordinal index, and returns module + AddressOfFunctions index . An export can also be forwarded : its "address" points at a string such as "NTDLL.RtlAllocateHeap" , meaning "this function really lives in another DLL". Many kernel32.dll exports are forwarders. RVA to file offset All these tables use RVAs, which are offsets in memory . To read them from the file on disk, convert each RVA through the section table (lesson 9.02): find the section whose range contains the RVA, then file offset = RVA − section.VirtualAddress + section.PointerToRawData because a section's bytes are at VirtualAddress in memory and at PointerToRawData in the file. An RVA that falls in no section's file data (for example in zero-filled .bss space) has no file offset. The practice task writes this function; every PE tool has it at its core. Reading your own imports at run time A loaded module's tables are already in memory at module + RVA , with no conversion needed: cpp include <windows.h include <iostream include <string int main() { auto base{ reinterpret_cast<unsigned char (GetModuleHandleW(nullptr)) }; const auto nt{ reinterpret_cast<IMAGE_NT_HEADERS64 (base + reinterpret_cast<IMAGE_DOS_HEADER (base)- e_lfanew) }; const IMAGE_DATA_DIRECTORY dir{ nt- OptionalHeader.DataDirectory IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_IMPORT }; bool importsKernel32{ false }; int dlls{ 0 }; for (auto d{ reinterpret_cast<IMAGE_IMPORT_DESCRIPTOR (base + dir.VirtualAddress) }; d- Name != 0; ++d) { ++dlls; std::string name{ reinterpret_cast<const char (base + d- Name) }; if (_stricmp(name.c_str(), "KERNEL32.dll") == 0) importsKernel32 = true; } std::cout << "imports from several DLLs: " << (dlls = 1 ? "yes" : "no") << ", including KERNEL32.dll: " << (importsKernel32 ? "yes" : "no") << '\n'; return 0; } imports from several DLLs: yes, including KERNEL32.dll: yes Delay-load and dynamic imports Not every DLL a program uses appears in its import table. Delay-loaded DLLs (lesson 5.08) have their own table (data directory 13), and anything loaded with LoadLibraryW and GetProcAddress at run time appears only as strings in the program, which is why reverse engineers search for DLL and function names among a program's strings (lesson 9.06) as well as reading the import table. Common mistakes !warning Reading table RVAs as file offsets Convert through the section table first, or the tables will appear to contain garbage. !warning Assuming every import is by name Entries with the top bit set are imported by ordinal; there is no name to read. !warning Concluding a program never uses a function because it is not imported It may be loaded at run time with GetProcAddress . Check yourself quiz ? What three things does an import descriptor point to? - The DLL's code, its data and its resources + The DLL's name, its lookup table, and its import address table - The DLL's path on disk, its version and its size - The functions' source files, their line numbers and their PDB Functions are named by name or ordinal in the lookup table; calls in the program go through the address table. The lookup table says which functions; the address table is where the loader writes their addresses. ? How does GetProcAddress find a function by name? - It searches the DLL's code for a function with that name - It reads the name from the PDB file + It binary-searches the sorted export names and returns base + RVA - It asks the kernel, which keeps a list of all functions in memory Export names are stored sorted precisely so this search is fast. ? How do you convert an RVA to a file offset? - Subtract the module's base address from the RVA - The RVA and the file offset are always the same number - Add the size of the headers to the RVA + RVA − the section's VirtualAddress + its PointerToRawData Sections are laid out differently in memory and in the file, so the offset depends on which section holds the RVA. ? What does the loader write into the import address table? - The names of the functions + The real addresses of the imported functions - The program's own functions Calls to imports go through these slots. ? How does a call to an imported function look in disassembly? - A direct call to the DLL's address - A jump to the import descriptor + An indirect call through a slot, call __imp_X The code reads the address from the IAT at run time. ? A section has VirtualAddress 0x5000 and PointerToRawData 0x3400. What is the file offset of RVA 0x5120? + 0x3520 - 0x5120 - 0x8520 0x5120 − 0x5000 + 0x3400. ? What is a forwarded export? - A function exported twice + An export that redirects to another DLL's function - A function that has been removed Many kernel32 exports forward to ntdll.

title: RVA to file offset
body: Write rvaToOffset(sections, rva) , which converts a relative virtual address into a file offset using a PE file's section table. An RVA belongs to a section when it is at least the section's virtualAddress and less than virtualAddress + max(virtualSize, rawSize) . The file offset is rva - virtualAddress + pointerToRawData . But a section's file data only covers rawSize bytes: if the RVA is inside the section but at or beyond virtualAddress + rawSize , it is zero-filled memory with no file data, so return std::nullopt . Also return std::nullopt for an RVA in no section. The sections may be given in any order. .text VA 0x1000 vsize 0x3A10 raw 0x3C00 at 0x400 .data VA 0x5000 vsize 0x2000 raw 0x200 at 0x4000 rvaToOffset(0x1234) = 0x634 rvaToOffset(0x5100) = 0x4100 rvaToOffset(0x5300) = nullopt (beyond .data's file data)

title: 9.04  Static Analysis with a Disassembler
body:
A disassembler turns a program's machine code back into assembly and organises it into functions, cross-references and control-flow graphs; a decompiler goes one step further, to C-like pseudocode. This lesson sets up Ghidra , the free, open-source reverse engineering suite, and walks through analysing a small program you built yourself: finding main , reading the listing and the decompiler side by side, and annotating as you learn. The tools Tool Cost Notes --- --- --- Ghidra Free, open source (from the US National Security Agency) Disassembler and decompiler for many processors; the course uses it IDA Free / IDA Pro Free version is limited; Pro is expensive The long-time industry standard Binary Ninja Paid, affordable personal licence Modern interface and scripting dumpbin /disasm Comes with Visual Studio A raw listing with no analysis: useful for quick checks Ghidra needs a Java runtime (JDK 17 or later). Download it from its official GitHub releases page, unzip it, and start ghidraRun.bat . A target to analyse Build this in Visual Studio in Release , x64, and keep the source closed while you analyse it. (You will check your conclusions at the end.) cpp include <cstdio include <cstring struct Hero { char name 16 ; int level; int xp; }; int xpForLevel(int level) { return level level 100; } void gainXp(Hero& hero, int amount) { hero.xp += amount; while (hero.xp = xpForLevel(hero.level + 1)) { ++hero.level; std::printf("%s reached level %d!
", hero.name, hero.level); } } int main() { Hero hero{}; std::strcpy(hero.name, "Rook"); hero.level = 1; for (int quest{ 0 }; quest < 5; ++quest) gainXp(hero, 250); std::printf("Final: level %d, %d xp
", hero.level, hero.xp); return 0; } To make it a fair exercise, do not give Ghidra the PDB at first: move x64\Release\ .pdb somewhere else. Importing and analysing 1. File → New Project , non-shared, in a folder of your choice. 2. File → Import File , pick the .exe . Ghidra recognises it as "Portable Executable (PE)", x86:LE:64. Accept. 3. Double-click it to open the CodeBrowser , and say Yes to analyse it with the default analysers. Ghidra now disassembles everything reachable from the entry point and exports, finds functions, follows cross-references, identifies standard library code it recognises ( function signatures for the C runtime), and builds a decompilation for each function. The main windows Window Shows --- --- Program Trees The PE sections (lesson 9.02) Symbol Tree Imports, exports, functions, labels Listing The disassembly, with addresses, bytes, labels and cross-references Decompile C-like pseudocode for the function under the cursor Function Graph (Window menu) Basic blocks and arrows (lesson 7.07) Defined Strings (Window menu) Every string Ghidra found Finding main The entry point is the C runtime's start-up code, not main . Two quick ways to find main : - In Defined Strings , find "Final: level %d, %d xp
" , double-click it, and look at its cross-reference (the XREF annotation): the function that uses it is main . Strings are the fastest way into unfamiliar code (lesson 9.08). - Or follow the entry point's code until a call with three arguments set up from argc , argv , envp -like values just before the program exits: that is the start-up code calling main . Reading the decompiler with the listing Ghidra's decompiler for gainXp might show something like: c void FUN_140001070(longlong param_1, int param_2) { int iVar1; (int )(param_1 + 0x14) = (int )(param_1 + 0x14) + param_2; while (iVar1 = (int )(param_1 + 0x10), (iVar1 + 1) (iVar1 + 1) 100 <= (int )(param_1 + 0x14)) { (int )(param_1 + 0x10) = iVar1 + 1; printf("%s reached level %d!
", param_1, iVar1 + 1); } return; } Everything from earlier chapters is visible: param_1 is a pointer (it is used with offsets); offset 0x10 and 0x14 are 4-byte members (lesson 7.08); xpForLevel has been inlined (lesson 7.11), so its formula appears directly; and the printf format string tells us param_1 points at a name and offset 0x10 is a level. Now annotate , which is most of the work: - Rename the function ( L key): gainXp . - Rename the parameters: hero , amount . - Create a structure (Data Type Manager → New → Structure) Hero with a char 16 name, an int level at 0x10 and an int xp at 0x14, and retype param_1 as Hero ( Ctrl+L ). The decompiler now prints hero- level and hero- xp . - Add comments ( ; key) for anything you work out. Annotations propagate: every other function that uses a Hero now reads better too. That snowball effect is why careful naming early pays off. Checking your work Open the source and compare. Then give Ghidra the PDB ( File → Load PDB File ) and look at the same function: names, types and line numbers appear, and you can see exactly what the PDB contributes (lesson 8.02) and what you had to reconstruct. Common mistakes !warning Believing every detail of the decompiler output It is reconstructed C, sometimes with wrong types or awkward casts. For anything important, check the listing. !warning Reading top to bottom from the entry point Start from something meaningful: a string, an import, an exported function. !warning Not saving your annotations Ghidra saves them in the project; save often, and keep the project with your notes. Check yourself quiz ? What does Ghidra's automatic analysis do? - It runs the program and records what it does + It disassembles, finds functions, follows xrefs and decompiles - It downloads the program's source code from the symbol server - It removes the program's protection so it can be edited All of this is static: the program is never run. ? Why does main not start at the entry point? + The entry point is C runtime start-up code that later calls main - Because main is inlined into the entry point in Release - Because Windows calls main from a separate thread - Because the linker places main at the end of the file Finding main means following the start-up code to the call that passes argc and argv . ? What does annotating a program in a disassembler involve? + Renaming things, applying struct types, and adding comments - Changing the program's bytes so it behaves differently - Recompiling the program with debug information - Printing the listing and highlighting it by hand Each name you add makes every other function that uses it easier to read. ? What does a decompiler produce? - The original source code - The program's PDB file + C-like pseudocode from the machine code It is a readable approximation, not the original source. ? What is the quickest way to find the function that prints a particular message? + Find the string, then follow its cross-reference - Read every function from the entry point - Search the import table Strings and their cross-references are the usual way in. ? Why does creating a struct type and applying it to a parameter help so much? - It makes the program run faster + The decompiler shows member names instead of offsets - It recovers the original variable names automatically Annotations propagate across the program.

title: 9.05  Recognising Functions, Loops and Branches
body: Disassemblers find most functions automatically, but understanding a function means recognising its parts: where it starts and ends, what its arguments and result are, and how its control flow maps to if , loops and switch . This lesson turns chapter 7's patterns into a reading routine for unknown functions, and covers the cases where automatic analysis gets function boundaries wrong. Where functions start and end A disassembler finds functions by following calls from known starting points (the entry point, exports, the .pdata unwind table from lesson 8.02, which lists most functions' start and end RVAs on x64). Signs of a function start: - it is the target of call instructions; - it begins with a typical prologue : saving non-volatile registers ( push rbx , mov rsp+8 , rbx ), sub rsp, N ; - it is listed in .pdata ; - it follows padding bytes ( CC or 90 ) after the previous function's ret . Signs of an end: ret after an epilogue, or a jmp to another function (a tail call, lesson 7.11). Automatic analysis goes wrong when code is only reached through pointers (a vtable, a callback table, a jump table it did not decode), or when data sits in a code section. Ghidra then shows bytes that are not disassembled; pressing D (disassemble) and F (create function) at a likely start fixes it. A reading routine For each unknown function: 1. Signature first. Which of rcx , rdx , r8 , r9 , xmm0 to xmm3 are read before being written? Those are the arguments (lesson 7.06). Is rax / eax / xmm0 set just before every ret ? That is a result. eax set but only al used by callers suggests a bool . 2. Calls next. Which functions does it call, and are any of them imports (named for you) or functions you already named? Calls often explain more than everything else together. 3. Constants and strings. Format strings, error messages, magic numbers ( 0x5A4D is "MZ"; 0x3F800000 is 1.0f). 4. Control flow. Draw or view the graph: loops are back edges, decisions are diamonds, switch is a jump table (lesson 7.07). 5. Memory accesses. Offsets from argument registers are struct members (lesson 7.08). 6. Name it , even provisionally ("probably_load_config"), and move on. Refine later. Loops in the graph A loop shows up in a function graph as an arrow going back up to a block that dominates it (one that every path into the loop passes through). Its parts: Recognising the induction variable (the register incremented each time round and compared against a limit) tells you what the loop iterates over; the memory accesses that use it tell you the array and its element size. The practice task finds loops from a list of jumps, the first step automatic tools perform. Branches that are not ifs Not every conditional jump is an if in the source: Pattern Source --- --- A compare and jump straight after a call, to an error path if (!ok) return error; or an exception-free error check test rax, rax / je after a call returning a pointer A null check A jump to a block that calls a function with a string like "Assertion failed" An assert cmp against a value, then a call to a function that never returns ( abort , a throw helper) A bounds check or failed precondition Several jumps to one block that sets the same return value Early returns merged by the compiler When there are no symbols for library code Functions from the C and C++ runtime are compiled into your program. Without a PDB, they look like any other unknown function. Ghidra's Function ID analyser recognises many by their bytes, and recognising the common ones by behaviour saves a lot of time: memcpy / memset (byte loops or rep movsb / rep stosb ), strlen (a loop looking for a zero byte), operator new (calls malloc , throws on failure), std::string constructors (lesson 2.08's small buffer: compares a length with 15). Common mistakes !warning Assuming the disassembler found every function Code reached only through pointers may be missing. Look for undisassembled bytes in code sections. !warning Reading every register as an argument Only registers read before being written in the function's first block are arguments. !warning Spending hours inside runtime library code Recognise it, name it, and move on to the program's own logic. Check yourself quiz ? What are signs that an address is the start of a function? - It is a multiple of 4,096 - It holds the bytes 00 00 00 00 + Calls target it, it has a prologue, or .pdata lists it - It is the first address of the .data section Several of these signs together make it almost certain. ? What is an induction variable? - A variable that holds a function's return value + The variable that changes by a fixed step each time round a loop and is compared with the limit - A variable the compiler created that has no name in the source - A pointer used to call a virtual function It shows what the loop iterates over, such as an index into an array. ? What is the most useful first step when reading an unknown function? - Read every instruction in order from the top - Rename every register - Look for the longest loop + Work out its arguments, its return value and its calls Arguments and calls frame everything else in the function. ? How can you tell which registers are a function's arguments? - They are the registers used most in the function - They are always all four + Argument registers that are read before being written Unused argument registers are simply never read. ? What marks a loop in a function graph? + A back edge to an earlier block - Any conditional jump at all - A call instruction in a block The target of the back edge is the loop's head. ? test rax, rax / je error straight after a call. What is it probably? - A loop over the result + A null check of the result - A switch on the result Functions returning pointers use null to signal failure.

title: Find the loops
body: A disassembler has listed every jump in a function: each one has the address it is at and the address it jumps to. A jump whose target is at or before its own address is a back edge , and its target is the head of a loop. Write loopHeads(jumps) , which returns the distinct loop-head addresses, sorted ascending, together with, for each head, how many back edges lead to it (a loop with continue statements can have several). jumps: 0x1010 - 0x1040 (forward: an if) 0x1030 - 0x1018 (back edge) 0x1050 - 0x1018 (back edge to the same head) 0x1060 - 0x1060 (a jump to itself: an infinite loop of one instruction) result: { 0x1018, 2 }, { 0x1060, 1 }

title: 9.06  Recognising Classes, Vtables and Strings
body: C++ programs leave distinctive traces even without symbols: vtables in read-only data list each polymorphic class's virtual functions, RTTI records often hold class names outright, constructors write vptrs, and strings reveal messages, file names and formats. This lesson shows how to find and use each, and how a strings -style scan works. Vtables Lesson 3.05 showed that each class with virtual functions has a vtable, an array of function pointers, in .rdata , and each object stores a pointer to it at offset 0. In a stripped program, vtables are among the most useful structures you can find: - Each vtable is a list of one class's virtual functions , in declaration order. - Classes related by inheritance have vtables with the same layout : slot 3 is the same virtual function (overridden or not) in every one. - A vtable entry pointing at the same function as the base class's entry means that function was not overridden . How to find them: in Ghidra, look in .rdata for runs of 8-byte values that are all addresses of functions in .text . Ghidra's analysis usually labels them vftable when RTTI is present. Constructors and destructors A constructor can be recognised by what it does with the vptr: asm Goblin_ctor: mov rsp+8 , rcx sub rsp, 28h call Entity_ctor ; base class constructor first lea rax, Goblin_vftable ; then store this class's vtable... mov rcx, rsp+30h mov rcx , rax ; ...into offset 0 of the object mov dword ptr rcx+18h , 10 ; initialise members ... The pattern "call another constructor, then store a vtable address into this , then initialise members" identifies a constructor, its base class's constructor, and its vtable all at once. Destructors do the reverse: store their own vtable, destroy members, then call the base destructor. Every place a vtable's address is written is a constructor or destructor of that class. RTTI: class names for free Unless a program is compiled with /GR- , MSVC stores run-time type information for each polymorphic class, used by dynamic_cast and typeid . Just before each vtable sits a pointer to a "complete object locator", which leads to a type descriptor containing the class's decorated name as a string: .?AVGoblin@@ .?AVEntity@@ .?AV?$vector@HV?$allocator@H@std@@@std@@ .?AV means "a class", and the rest is the class name in MSVC's name-mangling format (lesson 4.02); undname or Ghidra demangles them. A class hierarchy descriptor also lists each class's base classes , so RTTI can recover the whole inheritance tree. Searching a stripped program's strings for .?AV often lists every polymorphic class it has. Strings Programs are full of text: messages, log lines, file names, registry keys, format strings, URLs, error descriptions, command names. They survive compilation unchanged (lesson 2.03's .rdata ), and each one is a label for the code that uses it: String found Suggests --- --- "Failed to open save file %s" The function using it loads saves; the %s argument is the path "config.ini" , "Settings" Configuration loading "Assertion failed: %s, file %s, line %d" The program's assert handler (lesson 8.03) "kernel32.dll" , "VirtualAlloc" A function loaded at run time with GetProcAddress (lesson 9.03) "%d/%d" , "HP" Interface drawing Remember both encodings (lesson 2.08): Windows programs often store UTF-16 strings, which look like H.P. with zero bytes between the letters in a byte view. Tools search for both. The classic tool is strings (in Microsoft's Sysinternals suite): it scans any file for runs of printable characters of at least some minimum length. The practice task writes one. Common mistakes !warning Assuming RTTI is always there Programs built with /GR- have none; vtables still exist but are unnamed. !warning Treating every run of addresses in .rdata as a vtable Jump tables and other pointer arrays look similar. A vtable is referenced by constructors that store it into objects. !warning Searching only for ASCII strings Windows programs use UTF-16 heavily. Search both forms. Check yourself quiz ? What can vtables tell you about an unknown program? - The program's source file names - The values of every object's data members + Which classes exist, their virtual functions, and overrides - Which DLLs the program imports Vtables sit in read-only data and are written into objects by constructors, so they are a map of the class design. Through the constructors that reference them, vtables also show which code creates each class. ? What does RTTI provide to a reverse engineer? + Class names and inheritance, linked from each vtable - The full source code of each class - The names of local variables - The offsets of every data member A string such as .?AVGoblin@@ names the class Goblin . Building with /GR- removes RTTI and makes analysis harder. ? How does a strings -style tool work? - It reads the program's string table from the PDB - It runs the program and records what it prints - It decompiles the code and lists every string literal + It scans bytes for runs of printable characters, ASCII and UTF-16 Searching UTF-16 too matters on Windows, where much text is stored that way. ? Where is a class's vtable stored? - In each object - On the heap + In read-only data, once per class Objects hold only a pointer to it. ? How can you recognise a constructor without symbols? + It writes a vtable address into offset 0 of the object - It is the first function in the program - It always has the most arguments Every write of a vtable address into an object marks a constructor or destructor. ? What is .?AVGoblin@@ ? - An error message in the binary + The RTTI decorated name of Goblin - A file name stored by the linker .?AV introduces a class's decorated name. ? Why search for UTF-16 strings as well as ASCII? - UTF-16 strings are always longer - ASCII strings are not stored in programs + Windows programs often store text as UTF-16 Wide strings appear with a zero byte between ASCII letters.

title: Your own strings tool
body: Write findStrings(bytes, minLength) , which scans a block of bytes for text the way the strings tool does, in both encodings: - ASCII : a run of at least minLength printable bytes (0x20 to 0x7E inclusive). - UTF-16 : a run of at least minLength two-byte units, each a printable ASCII byte followed by a zero byte, starting at an even offset. Return every string found, as an offset and the text (UTF-16 strings converted to their ASCII letters), sorted by offset. A UTF-16 string's bytes are not also reported as ASCII (its letters are separated by zeros, so they are never minLength long as ASCII anyway, for minLength = 2 ). bytes: 00 'H' 'P' ':' ' ' '9' '9' 01 'S' 00 'a' 00 'v' 00 'e' 00 00 00 minLength 4 - { 1, "HP: 99" } { 8, "Save" }

title: 9.07  Dynamic Analysis with a Debugger
body: Static analysis shows every path a program could take; dynamic analysis shows what it actually does, with real values. This lesson uses a debugger on a program without its source ( x64dbg as well as the debuggers you know): breaking on API calls, watching arguments and return values, following indirect calls, and tracing the path through code to confirm what static analysis suggested. Why run it Some questions are slow to answer from the listing alone: - Which of five possible callbacks does this indirect call rax actually reach? - What does this decryption routine produce? - Which branch is taken with real input? - What values does this function receive? A debugger answers them in seconds. The usual rhythm is: form a hypothesis in the disassembler, confirm it in the debugger, write the conclusion back as a name or comment in the disassembler. x64dbg x64dbg is a free, open-source debugger designed for working without source. Its main window shows the disassembly, registers, the stack and a memory dump all at once, much like the Visual Studio windows of lesson 4.08 side by side. Download it from its official site, and use x64dbg.exe (not x32dbg ) for 64-bit programs. Visual Studio and WinDbg can do everything below too; x64dbg is simply convenient when there is no source or PDB. As always in this chapter, practise on the targets from lesson 9.10 or other programs you have the right to analyse. Breaking on API calls Imports are the landmarks (lesson 9.03). Breaking on them shows you exactly when the program does something significant, and with what: Want to know Break on --- --- Which files it opens CreateFileW What it writes WriteFile Which DLLs it loads at run time LoadLibraryW , LoadLibraryExW , GetProcAddress Which registry keys it reads RegOpenKeyExW , RegQueryValueExW When it allocates large blocks VirtualAlloc In x64dbg type bp CreateFileW in the command bar; in WinDbg bp kernelbase!CreateFileW . When it stops, the arguments are in rcx , rdx , r8 , r9 (lesson 7.06): for CreateFileW , rcx points at the file name, so follow it in the dump as a UTF-16 string. Then run to return (Ctrl+F9 in x64dbg) to see the result in rax , and step out to land in the code that called it: that is the program's own function that opens the file, now found. Following indirect calls Virtual calls, callbacks and function tables (lessons 3.04, 3.05) appear as call rax or call qword ptr rax+18h , which static analysis cannot always resolve. Put a breakpoint on the indirect call, run, and step into it: you are now in the actual target, and can name it in your static notes ("slot 3 of this vtable is Goblin::update "). Tracing a path When you need to know which way a series of branches went for a given input: - Step over the region (F8), watching the jumps: x64dbg shows whether each conditional jump will be taken before you step it. - Use conditional breakpoints and logging breakpoints (lesson 4.09) to record values each time a location is hit without stopping. - Use trace features (x64dbg's "Trace over" with a condition, or WinDbg's wt ) to record every instruction executed until a condition holds, then inspect the record. Watching memory change Data breakpoints (hardware breakpoints, lesson 4.09) work the same without source: right-click an address in the dump → Breakpoint → Hardware, on write. Run, and the debugger stops on whatever instruction changes it, telling you which function owns that data. Combined with lesson 9.08's cross-references, this is how unknown data is tied to the code that uses it. Patching for experiments Debuggers can change instructions in memory. During analysis this is useful for experiments: force a branch the other way to see what the alternative path does, or skip a call. Changes are made only to the running copy in memory, are gone on restart, and are for understanding your practice targets. (Changing software to bypass licence checks or protections is outside this course's ground rules, lesson 9.01.) Common mistakes !warning Breaking on a high-traffic function without a condition CreateFileW or VirtualAlloc may be called thousands of times at start-up. Add a condition or enable the breakpoint only when you reach the interesting part. !warning Reading arguments after the function has started The argument registers are reliable only at the function's first instruction. !warning Forgetting that the program may behave differently under a debugger Timing changes, and some programs check for debuggers. If behaviour differs, note it as a finding. Check yourself quiz ? What does dynamic analysis add to static analysis? - The original variable names + Real values, real call targets, and which branches run - The source code of the program - A list of every function in the program A call qword ptr rax+18h has no fixed target in the listing; running it shows where it really goes. ? Why are API calls good breakpoints in an unknown program? + They mark key actions, and their arguments show what is happening - Because API functions are the only ones with names - Because the program cannot run while an API breakpoint is set - Because API calls are always at the start of main Breaking on CreateFileW shows the file name in rcx ; stepping out lands in the code that opened it. ? Where can you see whether a conditional jump will be taken, before stepping it? - In the PDB file - In the Memory window at the jump's address - Nowhere; you can only find out by stepping + From the flags, or the debugger's mark on the jump x64dbg marks the jump as taken or not taken based on the current flags. ? You break on CreateFileW . Where is the file name? + Pointed to by rcx , as a UTF-16 string - In rax - At the top of the stack It is the first argument. ? How do you find the program's own function that opens a particular file? - Search the import table for the file name + Break on CreateFileW , check the name, step out - Look at the entry point Stepping out lands in the code that made the call. ? What is the advantage of dynamic analysis for call qword ptr rax+18h ? - It removes the indirect call - It lists every possible target + Stepping into it shows the actual target at run time Static analysis may not know which object rax points to.

title: 9.08  Cross-References: Finding Where Data Is Used
match: 9.08 Cross-References: Finding Where Data Is Used
body: A cross-reference (xref) records that one place in a program refers to another: a call to a function, a read of a global, a use of a string. Following xrefs, backwards to "who uses this?" and forwards to "what does this use?", is how you navigate an unknown program. This lesson covers the kinds of xref, how disassemblers find them, and how to decode a call instruction's target yourself. What a cross-reference is When an instruction mentions an address (calls it, jumps to it, reads or writes it, or takes it with lea ), the disassembler records a reference from that instruction to that address. Seen from the target, those are its xrefs : every place that refers to it. Kind Example Meaning --- --- --- Call call 140001070 Code that calls this function Jump jmp 140001200 / jne ... Code that branches here Read mov eax, 140005010 Code that reads this data Write mov 140005010 , eax Code that writes this data Offset (address taken) lea rcx, 140004120 Code that takes this address: passing a string, a callback, a table Data an 8-byte pointer in a vtable or table Data that points here In Ghidra, the XREF n : annotation at each label lists them, and References → Show References to (Ctrl+Shift+F) opens the full list. Navigating with xrefs Most reverse engineering is moving along xrefs from something you understand to something you do not: Typical starting points: - Strings (lesson 9.06): follow the string's xref to the code that prints or uses it. - Imports : xrefs to CreateFileW list every place the program opens files. - A global you found in the debugger (lesson 9.07): its read and write xrefs list every function that uses it. - A vtable : its xrefs are constructors and destructors (lesson 9.06). How call targets are found Disassemblers find most code xrefs by decoding instructions. The most common, the near call , is easy to decode by hand: the byte E8 followed by a 4-byte signed displacement relative to the address of the next instruction: address 140001000: E8 6B 00 00 00 call 140001070 └┘ └──────────┘ op rel32 = 0x0000006B target = address of next instruction + rel32 = (140001000 + 5) + 0x6B = 140001070 The displacement is relative (lesson 6.09's RIP-relative idea), so the same bytes work wherever the module is loaded. Negative displacements call backwards. Scanning code for E8 bytes and computing targets finds call xrefs, with one caveat: E8 can also appear inside other instructions' operands, so real disassemblers decode instruction by instruction rather than scanning blindly. The practice task does the simple scan on a buffer known to contain only calls and padding. RIP-relative data references ( mov eax, rip+disp32 , lea rcx, rip+disp32 ) work the same way: target = next instruction's address + displacement. Xrefs the analysis misses Some references are invisible to static analysis: - Addresses computed at run time ( base + index 8 into a table it did not decode). - Functions found with GetProcAddress from a string. - Pointers stored in data structures built at run time. Dynamic analysis fills these gaps: a breakpoint or hardware watchpoint shows the real reference, and you add it manually (Ghidra lets you add references by hand). Common mistakes !warning Forgetting reads versus writes "Who writes this global?" usually narrows things far more than "who uses it?". Filter xrefs by kind. !warning Computing a relative target from the instruction's own address Relative displacements count from the address of the next instruction. !warning Trusting a lack of xrefs No xrefs found does not mean unused: the reference may be computed at run time. Check yourself quiz ? What is a cross-reference? + A recorded reference from one place to another, such as a call - A comment linking two functions with the same name - A pointer stored in the PDB - A link between a DLL and the program that imports it Listing the xrefs to a string or function shows every place that uses it. ? How is the target of an E8 call computed? - The four bytes after E8 are the absolute target address + The next instruction's address plus the signed displacement - Add the displacement to the start of the .text section - Add the displacement to the call's own address The displacement is relative to the next instruction, not to the call itself. F0 FF FF FF is -16. ? Why might static analysis miss a reference? - Because the disassembler only reads the first megabyte of a file - Because references to functions are encrypted by the linker + The address may only be computed or looked up at run time - Because references only exist in Debug builds These are exactly the cases where running the program fills the gaps. ? A call at 0x140002000 is encoded E8 F0 FF FF FF . Where does it call? + 0x140001FF5 - 0x140002005 - 0x1400020F0 rel32 = 0xFFFFFFF0 = -16; next instruction at 0x140002005; 0x140002005 - 16 = 0x140001FF5. ? What do the xrefs to a vtable usually point to? - Every virtual call + The constructors and destructors - The class's data members Virtual calls read the vptr from the object, not the vtable's address directly. ? How can you find every place a program opens a file? - Search for .txt in the strings - Read the entry point + List the cross-references to the imported CreateFileW Every call to an import goes through its IAT slot, and each is an xref.

title: Who calls this function?
where: 9.08 Cross-References: Finding Where Data Is Used
body: You are given a block of machine code that contains only near calls ( E8 followed by a 4-byte little-endian signed displacement) and single-byte padding ( CC or 90 ), and the address the block is loaded at. Write two functions. - callTargets(code, base) returns every call in the block as a pair: the call's own address and the address it calls, in order. - callersOf(code, base, target) returns the addresses of the calls whose target is target . A call's target is the address of the next instruction ( call address + 5 ) plus the displacement. A call cut off by the end of the block is ignored. base 0x140001000, code: E8 6B 00 00 00 CC E8 F0 FF FF FF callTargets - { 0x140001000, 0x140001070 }, { 0x140001006, 0x140000FFB }

title: 9.09  Reconstructing Structs from Compiled Code
body: Types disappear in compilation, but every struct leaves a trail of offsets and sizes in the code that uses it. This lesson is a step-by-step method for rebuilding a struct definition from those accesses, combining static evidence (offsets, sizes, instructions used) with dynamic evidence (values seen in the debugger), and recording the result as a type the disassembler can apply everywhere. The evidence an access gives Each instruction that touches a struct member tells you three things (lesson 7.08): Evidence Example Tells you --- --- --- Offset rcx+14h A member starts at 0x14 Size dword ptr , byte ptr , qword ptr It is 4, 1 or 8 bytes Instruction movss vs mov ; movsx vs movzx ; jl vs jb afterwards float or integer; signed or unsigned Use Passed to printf with %s ; followed as a pointer; compared with 0 and branched A string pointer or buffer; a pointer; a flag or count A method 1. Pick one struct pointer and find every function that receives it (from xrefs and from the calls in its creator). 2. Collect accesses : every reg+offset with that pointer, noting offset, size and instruction. The disassembler's structure editor helps: Ghidra's Auto Create Structure on a parameter does a first pass. 3. Lay them out by offset (this is lesson 7.08's practice task). Gaps are either padding (lesson 2.05) or members this code never touches. 4. Type the members using instructions and uses: movss means float; a value compared with jl / jg is signed; an 8-byte member that is dereferenced is a pointer, and what it points to is another struct to rebuild. 5. Name them from strings and context: a member printed with "HP: %d" is health. 6. Check alignment : a 4-byte member at an offset that is not a multiple of 4 suggests the struct is packed, or you mis-read an access. 7. Confirm dynamically : break where the struct is used and look at it in the debugger's memory view (lesson 2.11); the values should make sense with your types (floats look like floats, pointers like pointers, counts are small). 8. Apply the type to the parameter and globals, and iterate: the decompiler output improves, revealing more. A worked example A function in a stripped target contains: asm movss xmm0, dword ptr rcx+8 ; float at 8 addss xmm0, dword ptr rcx+10h ; float at 0x10 movss dword ptr rcx+8 , xmm0 mov eax, dword ptr rcx+18h ; 4-byte integer at 0x18 test eax, eax jle dead ; signed compare with 0: health-like movzx edx, byte ptr rcx+1Ch ; 1-byte unsigned at 0x1C, then tested: a bool test dl, dl ... mov rax, qword ptr rcx+20h ; 8 bytes at 0x20, then used as an address: a pointer mov rcx, qword ptr rax ; reading through it: its first member Elsewhere, a constructor stores a vtable address at rcx , and a function prints rcx+0Ch as a float alongside rcx+8 with "pos %.1f,%.1f" . Reconstruction: cpp struct Entity // reconstructed { void vftable; // 0x00 written by the constructor (lesson 9.06) float x; // 0x08 printed with "pos %.1f,%.1f" float y; // 0x0C float vx; // 0x10 added to x each update: a velocity float vy; // 0x14 (by symmetry with x/vx; confirm in the debugger) int health; // 0x18 signed, compared with 0 bool alive; // 0x1C // 0x1D..0x1F padding before the pointer Entity target; // 0x20 dereferenced, and its first member looks like a vtable }; // size 0x28 if nothing follows (check the allocation size in the creator) The size can usually be confirmed where objects are created: operator new(0x28) or a HeapAlloc with that size right before the constructor call. Recording it In Ghidra, create the structure in the Data Type Manager , fill in the members, and Retype the parameter ( Ctrl+L ) in every function that receives it. Keep a notes file alongside: which evidence supports each member, and which are guesses. When new evidence contradicts a guess, you will know which to revisit. Common mistakes !warning Assuming you have seen every member Code you have not looked at may use offsets you have not seen. Mark uncertain regions as unknown rather than as padding. !warning Ignoring the creator The allocation size and the constructor's initial values are some of the best evidence for a struct's size and members. !warning Over-trusting names A member you called "health" is a hypothesis until behaviour confirms it. Check yourself quiz ? What three pieces of evidence does each member access give? - The member's name, its type and its comment - The member's address, its owner and its default value + The member's offset, its size, and clues to its type - The struct's name, its total size and its alignment A movss read suggests a float ; an 8-byte value used as an address is a pointer. ? Why look at the code that creates the struct? + The allocation gives the size; the constructor shows members - Because creation code always contains the member names - Because only creation code accesses every member - Because the struct's layout changes after it is created A new of 0x40 bytes says the struct is 64 bytes, and stores in the constructor reveal members you have not seen used yet. ? What should you do with members you are unsure about? - Leave them out of the struct definition - Guess a type and move on without noting it - Assume they are padding + Mark them as guesses, with evidence, until confirmed Wrong guesses written down as facts spread through every function that uses the struct. ? A member is read with movss at offset 0x8. What type is it most likely? + float - int - A pointer movss moves a single-precision float. ? How can you find a struct's total size? - Add up the member offsets + From the size passed to its allocation - It cannot be found Creators reveal sizes directly. ? An 8-byte member is loaded and then used as an address. What is it? - A double - A pair of ints + A pointer to another object Following it leads to the next struct.

title: 9.10  Practice Targets You Compile Yourself
body: The best way to learn reverse engineering is on programs whose source you can check afterwards. This lesson gives a graded series of practice targets to write, build without symbols, and analyse with the chapter's tools, from a single function to a small game with classes and a file format, along with how to set up the builds and how to check your answers. The routine For each target: 1. Write it, or have a friend write it so you do not know the answers. 2. Build it Release, x64 , and move the .pdb out of the folder. 3. Analyse it statically in Ghidra and dynamically in x64dbg or Visual Studio, writing down your conclusions: names, types, what each function does, the format of any file. 4. Check against the source. For each mistake, find which evidence misled you. 5. Load the PDB into Ghidra and compare the two views. Repeat a target with /Od (unoptimised) for an easier version, and with /O2 /GL (whole-program optimisation, more inlining) for a harder one. Level 1: single functions Write a program with half a dozen small functions and call them from main with values read from std::cin , so the optimiser cannot fold everything into constants: - int clamp(int v, int lo, int hi) - unsigned popcount(unsigned x) (count set bits with a loop) - int sumSquares(const int a, int n) - bool isPalindrome(const char s) - float lerp(float a, float b, float t) Goal : name each function and give its signature from the assembly alone. Watch for cmov in clamp , the loop in popcount (or the popcnt instruction, if the compiler uses it), vectorisation in sumSquares , and xmm registers in lerp . Level 2: control flow - A switch on a command letter with eight cases (find the jump table, lesson 7.07). - A state machine with an enum and a loop. - A function with early returns and && / conditions. Goal : reconstruct the control flow as C++ that behaves identically, and test it against the original with the same inputs. Level 3: data structures - A struct with mixed members ( int , float , bool , pointer, char 16 ) passed to several functions. - A singly linked list built from user input and walked. - A std::vector<Item with push_back and a loop. Goal : rebuild the structs (lesson 9.09), including size and padding, and recognise the standard library's inlined code (vector growth, lesson 3.07). Level 4: classes - A small hierarchy with virtual functions: Shape with area() and name() , three derived classes, a vector of std::unique_ptr<Shape . Goal : find every vtable and its RTTI name (lesson 9.06), match each slot to a function, identify constructors and destructors, and draw the hierarchy. Then rebuild with /GR- and do it again without the names. Level 5: a file format Write a program that saves and loads a simple binary file: a header with a magic number and version, a count, then records of mixed fields, little-endian (lesson 2.06's practice). Analyse the program and a file it wrote. Goal : write a specification of the format (offsets, sizes, meanings) good enough that someone could write a compatible reader, and then write that reader yourself. This is exactly what interoperability work looks like. Level 6: a small game Take the game you will build in chapter 11 (or any small game of your own), build it without symbols, and pick a feature: how damage is calculated, how a level file is loaded, how the save format works. Goal : document the feature completely from the binary, as if you had never seen the source. Other sources of practice - Open-source programs : build one in Release without symbols and analyse it; the source is there to check you. - Capture-the-flag competitions often include reverse engineering challenges, made and published for exactly this purpose. - Crackme collections : small programs published by their authors as reverse engineering exercises. Use ones explicitly offered for practice, run unfamiliar binaries only inside a virtual machine (lesson 15.08), and treat downloaded executables as untrusted. Common mistakes !warning Starting with something too big Each level should take an evening or two. If a target takes weeks, step back a level. !warning Not checking your answers The value of self-made targets is the answer key. Use it, and learn from each mistake. !warning Running downloaded practice binaries on your main machine Use a virtual machine for anything you did not build yourself. Check yourself quiz ? What is the routine for a practice target? + Build it optimised without symbols, analyse it, then check the source - Write it, build it in Debug with symbols, read the source - Download a game, analyse it, then write a cheat for it - Build it, decompile it, and compile the decompiled output again Checking against your own source is what makes self-built targets so valuable: you find out exactly where you were wrong. Write down conclusions before checking, then compare again with the PDB loaded. ? How can you make a practice target easier or harder? - Easier by adding more code; harder by removing code - Easier by building in Release; harder by building in Debug + Easier unoptimised; harder with more inlining and no RTTI - Easier by stripping strings; harder by adding comments Unoptimised code follows the source closely; inlining and missing RTTI hide structure. ? Why do level 5 targets include a file the program wrote? - Because the program cannot run without it - So the file can be patched to change the program + Documenting a file format is core interoperability work - So the PDB can be found from it Interoperability is one of the main legitimate reasons for reverse engineering. ? Why read values from std::cin in a practice target? + So the optimiser cannot precompute the results - Because std::cin is easier to reverse engineer - To make the program interactive With constant inputs, an optimising compiler may fold everything into a few printed constants. ? What does building with /GR- change for a reverse engineer? - Optimisation is turned off + RTTI, and so class names, are removed - Symbols are added Vtables remain, but nameless. ? What is the most valuable part of a self-built target? - Its small size - That it is fast to compile + The source, which lets you check every conclusion Checking answers is how you calibrate your judgement.
