title: 10.01  The Game Loop
body: Every real-time game is built around one loop that runs as long as the game does: read input , update the world, render a frame, repeat, dozens of times a second. This lesson builds that loop step by step, explains what belongs in each phase, and shows how an engine is organised around it. The heart of every game A word processor waits for the user to do something. A game does not wait: monsters move, timers tick and the screen redraws whether or not the player touches anything. So at the centre of every game engine is a loop: Each trip round the loop produces one frame . At 60 frames per second the whole loop has 16.7 ms (lesson 8.08). cpp include <chrono include <iostream struct World { float x{ 0 }; float speed{ 2.0f }; int frames{ 0 }; bool running{ true }; }; void processInput(World&) { / read keys; set flags such as world.running = false on Escape / } void update(World& w, float dt) { w.x += w.speed dt; // move 2 units per second, however long the frame was ++w.frames; if (w.x = 1.0f) w.running = false; } void render(const World& w) { std::cout << "frame " << w.frames << ": x = " << w.x << '\n'; } int main() { World world; const float dt{ 0.1f }; // pretend each frame takes 0.1 s, so the output is the same every run while (world.running) { processInput(world); update(world, dt); render(world); } return 0; } frame 1: x = 0.2 frame 2: x = 0.4 frame 3: x = 0.6 frame 4: x = 0.8 frame 5: x = 1 A real game measures dt with a clock (lesson 5.07) instead of pretending; the next lesson covers how to use it well. What goes in each phase Phase Does Must not --- --- --- Input Drain the window messages (lesson 5.05's PeekMessage loop), read devices, turn them into actions (lesson 10.05) Change the world directly Update Advance the simulation by dt : movement, physics, AI, timers, animation, game rules, spawning and removing entities Draw anything, or wait for anything Render Draw the world as it is now : sprites, models, effects, interface Change the world Keeping these separate is what lets engines run update at a fixed rate while rendering as fast as possible (lesson 10.02), run rendering on another thread, record and replay input, or run a server with no rendering at all. The engine around the loop An engine is mostly the systems that the loop calls each frame: A small game calls these in a fixed order on one thread. A large engine spreads their work across worker threads with a job system (lesson 6.05) while keeping the same overall order, because order matters: physics must run after movement is decided and before rendering, or the frame shows stale positions. Starting and stopping Around the loop sit initialisation (create the window, load the first level, start subsystems in dependency order) and shutdown (stop them in the reverse order, as RAII does for objects, lesson 2.04). Many engine bugs are ordering bugs here: audio shut down before the entities that still play sounds, a resource released before the renderer stops using it. Common mistakes !warning Updating in the render phase Rendering must only read the state, or the result depends on how often frames are drawn. !warning Waiting inside the loop Blocking on a file, the network or a lock stalls every frame. Move slow work to other threads (lesson 6.05) and check its result each frame. !warning Moving by a fixed amount per frame x += 2 moves twice as fast at 120 fps as at 60. Multiply by dt . Check yourself quiz ? What is a frame? + One pass of the loop: input, one update, one image - One sixtieth of a second, whatever the game is doing - One image stored in the GPU's memory - One call to the operating system's message loop Frames are not tied to a fixed length of time; how long one takes depends on the work in it. ? Why keep input, update and render separate? + So each can run at its own rate, and rendering never changes the world - Because the compiler requires them to be in separate functions - Because rendering must happen before input each frame - So that each phase can use a different programming language If rendering changed game state, the game would behave differently depending on the frame rate. Separating them also lets input be recorded and replayed. ? Why does the order of systems in the update matter? - Because systems that run later get more time - Because the order decides which systems are drawn on top + Later systems use earlier ones' results, or see stale data - It does not; systems are independent by design Running collision before movement, for example, checks positions from the previous frame. ? What are the three phases of the game loop? + Input, update, render - Load, play, then save - Compile, link, then run They repeat every frame for as long as the game runs. ? Why should rendering never change the game state? - Rendering is too slow + The state would depend on how many frames get drawn - The GPU cannot write to memory Updates belong in the update phase, driven by time. ? Why multiply speeds by dt ? - To make the game run faster - Because the compiler requires it + So movement per second is the same at any frame rate A fixed step per frame makes speed depend on frame rate.

title: 10.02  Time Steps and Frame Rates
body: How much time does each update simulate? Using the real frame time (a variable time step ) is simple but makes physics behave differently on fast and slow machines. Most games run the simulation at a fixed time step , consuming real time from an accumulator , and smooth the picture with interpolation . This lesson builds that loop and covers frame limiting and vsync. Variable time step The simplest loop measures how long the last frame took and updates by that much: cpp while (running) { const double now{ clock() }; const double dt{ now - previous }; previous = now; update(dt); render(); } It works, and many small games use it. Its problems show up at the edges: - Physics depends on dt . Integrating motion in bigger steps gives different results: a jump reaches a different height at 30 fps than at 144 fps, collisions can be missed when a fast object moves past a wall in one big step ("tunnelling"). - One slow frame (a disk read, a hitch) produces a huge dt that throws objects across the level. - Nothing is reproducible : the same input gives different results on different machines, which breaks replays and networked games that must agree exactly. Fixed time step The standard solution: the simulation always advances in the same small step (for example 1/60 s), and the loop runs as many of those steps as real time requires. cpp include <iostream int main() { const double step{ 1.0 / 60.0 }; // the simulation always moves in 1/60 s steps double accumulator{ 0.0 }; int updates{ 0 }; // Real frame times, in seconds: a fast frame, normal frames, and one slow hitch. const double frames { 0.008, 0.016, 0.017, 0.050, 0.016 }; for (double frameTime : frames) { accumulator += frameTime; // real time owed to the simulation int thisFrame{ 0 }; while (accumulator = step) { // update(step); // always the same step accumulator -= step; ++thisFrame; } updates += thisFrame; const double alpha{ accumulator / step }; // how far we are into the next step, 0 to 1 std::cout << "frame of " << frameTime 1000 << " ms: " << thisFrame << " update(s), alpha " << static_cast<int (alpha 100) << "%\n"; } std::cout << "total updates " << updates << '\n'; return 0; } frame of 8 ms: 0 update(s), alpha 48% frame of 16 ms: 1 update(s), alpha 44% frame of 17 ms: 1 update(s), alpha 46% frame of 50 ms: 3 update(s), alpha 46% frame of 16 ms: 1 update(s), alpha 42% total updates 6 Real time flows into the accumulator ; the simulation takes it out in fixed bites. A fast frame may run no update at all; a slow frame runs several to catch up. The simulation always sees the same step , so it behaves identically on every machine, and with the same inputs, it produces the same results every time. The spiral of death If one update takes longer than step to compute, each frame owes more updates than the last, and the game grinds to a halt trying to catch up. Guard against it by capping how much time one frame may add: cpp accumulator += std::min(frameTime, 0.25); // never try to catch up more than a quarter of a second The game then runs in slow motion under extreme load instead of freezing. Interpolation: smooth pictures between steps With a 60 Hz simulation on a 144 Hz monitor, several frames are rendered between two updates. Drawing the latest state each time would make movement stutter. Instead, keep the previous and current state of each object and draw a blend, using alpha from the loop above: drawn position = previous + (current − previous) × alpha What is drawn lags the simulation by up to one step (about 16 ms), which players do not notice, in exchange for perfectly smooth motion. The practice task computes these numbers. Frame rate, vsync and limiting Technique Effect --- --- Vsync on The GPU waits for the monitor's refresh before showing a frame: no tearing, frame rate capped at the refresh rate, slightly more input latency Vsync off Frames shown as soon as ready: lowest latency, possible tearing (top and bottom of the screen from different frames) Variable refresh (G-Sync, FreeSync) The monitor refreshes when a frame is ready: no tearing, low latency A frame limiter The game waits until a target frame time has passed: saves power and heat; must wait precisely ( Sleep is coarse, lesson 6.05), typically sleeping most of the remaining time and spinning briefly at the end Common mistakes !warning Feeding a variable dt straight into physics Use a fixed step for anything that must be stable or reproducible. !warning No cap on the accumulator One long stall leads to a spiral of catch-up updates. !warning Interpolating game logic Interpolation is only for drawing. Game rules always use the simulated state. Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference between a variable and a fixed time step? - A variable step changes the frame rate; a fixed step locks it at 60 - A fixed step only works with vsync turned on + Variable steps by the last frame's time; fixed always steps the same amount - A variable step is used for rendering and a fixed step for input The fixed step makes the simulation repeatable, which is what replays and networking need. ? How does the accumulator work? - It counts frames and runs an update every 60th one + It gains real time each frame and runs one update per whole step held - It stores the total time since the game started and divides it by the step - It adds up the time each system took and slows the game if it is too high A 50 ms frame with 1/60 s steps runs three updates and carries the leftover into the next frame. Each update subtracts one step; whatever is left carries over to the next frame. ? Why interpolate when rendering? - To make the simulation run faster - To hide loading screens - To reduce the number of draw calls + To draw smooth motion between fixed steps alpha is how far the leftover time is into the next step, so positions are blended between the last two steps. ? With a fixed step of 1/60 s, how many updates does a 50 ms frame run (starting with an empty accumulator)? + 3 - 1 - 50 50 ms holds three 16.7 ms steps, with a small remainder carried to the next frame. ? Why does a fixed time step make replays possible? - It records every frame + The same inputs always give the same updates - It makes the game run faster A variable step makes results depend on frame timings. ? What does alpha in the fixed-step loop represent? - The frame rate - The number of updates this frame + How far time has got into the next step It is the leftover accumulator divided by the step. It is used to blend the previous and current states when drawing. ? What problem does capping the accumulator solve? + The spiral of death - Screen tearing - Input lag Under extreme load the game slows down instead of freezing.

title: A fixed-step clock
body: Write the class FixedStepClock , the timing part of a fixed-time-step game loop. - The constructor receives the step length in seconds and the maximum frame time that will be counted (the cap against the spiral of death). - advance(frameTime) adds the frame's real time (capped at the maximum) to the accumulator, then removes whole steps while at least one step is held. It returns how many updates should run this frame. - alpha() returns the leftover fraction of a step, accumulator / step , from 0 up to (but not including) 1. Also write interpolate(previous, current, alpha) , which blends two positions for drawing. FixedStepClock clock{ 0.01, 0.25 }; clock.advance(0.025) - 2, alpha 0.5 clock.advance(0.005) - 1, alpha 0.0 (0.005 + 0.005 left over = one step) clock.advance(5.0) - 25 (capped at 0.25 s) To avoid floating-point surprises, the tests use steps and frame times that are exact in binary or compare with a small tolerance.

title: 10.03  Entities, Components and Systems
body: How should a game represent its thousands of objects? Deep inheritance trees ( Monster : Character : Entity ) become rigid and slow. Many engines use entity-component-system (ECS) design instead: an entity is just an id, components are plain data attached to it, and systems are loops over every entity with a given set of components. This lesson explains why, and builds a small ECS on the sparse set structure. The trouble with deep hierarchies The object-oriented first attempt at a game world looks like this: Then the designers ask for a barrel that can fly, a monster that can be picked up like a prop, and a player who can turn into a barrel. Each request fits awkwardly into the tree, and features drift up into the base class until Entity has a hundred members, most unused by most objects. Performance suffers too: each object is a separate heap allocation with a vptr, updating them means a virtual call each, and their data is scattered (lessons 3.02, 3.05). Composition: entities, components, systems ECS splits things differently: Part Is Example --- --- --- Entity An id. Nothing else. Entity{ 42 } Component A small, plain struct of data, attached to an entity Position{ x, y } , Velocity{ vx, vy } , Health{ hp } , Sprite{ textureId } System A function that loops over every entity having certain components Movement: every entity with Position and Velocity A flying barrel is just an entity with Position , Velocity , Sprite and Breakable . A monster you can pick up has Carryable added. No class hierarchy has to change: behaviour comes from which components an entity has, and which systems act on them. cpp void movementSystem(World& world, float dt) { for (Entity e : world.with<Position, Velocity ()) { Position& p{ world.get<Position (e) }; const Velocity& v{ world.get<Velocity (e) }; p.x += v.vx dt; p.y += v.vy dt; } } Why it is fast Each component type is stored in its own dense array : all Position s side by side, all Velocity s side by side. A system walks those arrays in order, which is exactly what caches and vectorisation want (lessons 2.07, 7.09): no pointer chasing, no virtual calls, every byte loaded is used. This layout is called data-oriented design , and it is the main reason large engines adopted ECS. The sparse set How do you store components so that you can (a) loop over all of them densely, (b) find an entity's component instantly, and (c) add and remove them cheaply? The usual answer is a sparse set per component type: sparse: indexed by entity id → position in the dense arrays (or "none") 0 : none 1 : 0 2 : none 3 : 2 4 : 1 dense: entity ids in order 1 4 3 components, same order {P1} {P4} {P3} Operation How Cost --- --- --- Does entity e have it? sparse e != none Constant Get e's component components sparse e Constant Add to e Append to the dense arrays; sparse e = new index Constant (amortised) Remove from e Swap-and-pop (lesson 3.07): move the last element into e's slot, fix the moved entity's sparse entry Constant Loop over all Walk the dense arrays Fast, contiguous It combines lesson 3.07's swap-and-pop with lesson 3.10's stable ids. The practice task builds one. Systems that need several components world.with<Position, Velocity () must find entities that have both . With sparse sets, loop over the smaller of the two sets and check the other with a constant-time lookup. Larger engines group entities by their exact set of components into archetypes , each stored as its own table, so every system's loop is a straight walk with no checks; that is how Unity's DOTS and the flecs library work. EnTT , a popular open-source C++ ECS, is built on sparse sets. When not to use ECS ECS shines with many similar objects and simple, repeated behaviour. For a game with a few dozen unique objects, or for one-off logic (a boss's scripted sequence, the user interface), plain classes are simpler and fine. Many shipped games mix both: an ECS for the crowd, ordinary objects for the rest. Common mistakes !warning Putting logic in components Components are data. Behaviour lives in systems. !warning Keeping pointers to components Removing another entity's component can move this one (swap-and-pop). Store the entity id and look the component up. !warning Adding or removing components while a system loops over them The arrays change under the loop. Queue structural changes and apply them after the system finishes. Check yourself quiz ? What are entities, components and systems? - Entities are classes, components are their virtual functions, systems are their base classes + Entities are ids; components are plain data attached to entities; systems are functions processing every entity with a given set of components - Entities are files, components are folders, systems are the build tools - Entities are threads, components are locks, systems are queues An entity has no behaviour of its own: what it is comes from which components it has. ? What problem with deep inheritance does ECS solve? - That inheritance cannot be used with templates - That virtual functions cannot be called from other threads - That classes cannot have more than one constructor + Rigid hierarchies, and scattered virtual-heavy memory Composition lets any entity have any mix of components, and systems loop over tightly packed arrays. ? What does a sparse set store, and why? + An id-to-index array plus dense arrays, for O(1) changes and fast loops - A hash table from entity names to components, for fast lookup by name - A linked list of components, so removal never moves anything - One array per entity listing its components, so systems can find them Removal swaps the last dense element into the gap and fixes the sparse entry, which keeps it constant time. ? In ECS, what is an entity? - A class with virtual functions + Just an id that components are attached to - A system All its data lives in components; all behaviour in systems. ? Why are ECS systems often faster than looping over objects with virtual update functions? - Systems run on the GPU - Components are smaller than objects + They walk contiguous plain data with no virtual calls Data-oriented layout suits caches and vectorisation. ? In a sparse set, how is a component removed in constant time? + Swap-and-pop, then fix the moved entity's entry - All later components are shifted down - The slot is marked empty and skipped The dense arrays stay dense.

title: 10.04  A Tour of the Rendering Pipeline
match: 10.04 A Tour of the Rendering Pipeline
body: Rendering turns the game's state into pixels, mostly on the GPU . This lesson follows a frame from the CPU's side (what to draw, culling, sorting, draw calls ) through the GPU's pipeline ( vertex shaders , rasterisation , pixel shaders , depth testing) to the screen, with the coordinate transforms in between. It is a map for the graphics work in chapter 11 and beyond. The CPU and the GPU The GPU is a separate processor with thousands of simple cores, built to run the same small program on huge numbers of vertices and pixels in parallel. The CPU does not draw pixels; it prepares work for the GPU and submits it through a graphics API: Direct3D 11/12 on Windows, Vulkan , OpenGL , or Metal on Apple systems. Libraries like SDL and raylib (chapter 11) sit on top of these. The CPU's part Each frame the renderer: 1. Collects what might be visible: sprites, models, particles, interface. 2. Culls : skips everything outside the camera's view (a rectangle in 2D, a pyramid-shaped frustum in 3D). Cheap bounding-box tests remove most objects before any GPU work. The practice task does this for 2D. 3. Sorts : transparent objects back to front (so blending is correct); opaque objects by material or texture, to minimise state changes. 4. Submits draw calls : each tells the GPU "draw these triangles with this shader, these textures and these settings". Draw calls have a CPU cost of their own. Drawing ten thousand sprites as ten thousand separate calls is slow; batching them (many sprites sharing a texture atlas in one call) or instancing (one model drawn many times in one call) is how games draw large scenes. Coordinates and transforms Positions pass through several coordinate systems on the way to the screen: Space Meaning --- --- Model (local) space Relative to the object itself: a character model's feet at (0, 0, 0) World space Where it is in the level (the scene graph of lesson 3.09 combines these) View (camera) space Relative to the camera Clip space / NDC After projection: what lies inside the view becomes the range −1 to 1 Screen space Pixels on the render target Each step is a matrix multiplication, combined into one matrix per object and applied to every vertex by the vertex shader. In 2D the idea is the same with simpler maths: subtract the camera's position, multiply by the zoom, and add half the screen size to put the camera's centre in the middle. The GPU's part - Vertex shader : a small program run once per vertex, transforming its position into clip space and passing along data such as texture coordinates and colours. - Rasterisation : fixed hardware works out which pixels each triangle covers and interpolates the vertex data across them. - Pixel (fragment) shader : run once per covered pixel, computing its colour: sampling textures, applying lighting. - Output merging : the depth test discards pixels behind something already drawn (using the depth buffer); blending combines transparent pixels with what is behind them. Shaders are written in their own languages (HLSL for Direct3D, GLSL for OpenGL and Vulkan) and compiled for the GPU. Buffers and presenting The GPU draws into a back buffer while the monitor shows the front buffer ; at the end of the frame they are swapped ( present ), the same idea as lesson 5.06's double buffering. With vsync, the swap waits for the monitor's refresh (lesson 10.02). Where the time goes Bottleneck Symptom Typical fix --- --- --- CPU: too many draw calls GPU often idle; CPU busy in the renderer Batching, instancing, fewer state changes GPU: too many pixels (fill rate) Slower at higher resolutions; heavy effects Cheaper pixel shaders, lower resolution effects, less overdraw GPU: too many vertices Slower with detailed models regardless of resolution Level of detail (simpler models far away) Transfers Stalls when uploading textures mid-game Upload during loading, or asynchronously GPU profilers (PIX for Direct3D, RenderDoc for most APIs, vendor tools) show where a frame's GPU time goes, like lesson 8.08's CPU profiling. Common mistakes !warning One draw call per sprite Batch sprites that share a texture, or use an atlas. !warning Reading back from the GPU every frame The CPU waits for the GPU to finish. Avoid it, or read results a frame or two later. !warning Drawing everything without culling Off-screen objects still cost CPU and GPU time. Check yourself quiz ? What are the main stages a triangle goes through on the GPU? + Vertex shader, rasterisation, pixel shader, then output merging - Rasterisation, vertex shader, culling, then presenting - The pixel shader runs first, then the vertex shader positions the result - The CPU colours the pixels and the GPU only copies them to the screen The depth test in output merging decides which surface is in front at each pixel. ? What coordinate spaces does a vertex pass through? - Screen space, then world space, then model space - World space only, which the GPU draws directly + Model, world, view, clip and screen space - Texture space, model space and screen space Each step is a transform: placing the model in the world, seeing it from the camera, projecting it, then mapping to pixels. ? What is the difference between being CPU-bound and GPU-bound in rendering? - CPU-bound means the game uses too much memory; GPU-bound means it uses too little - They mean the same thing in different engines + CPU-bound: submitting work is too slow; GPU-bound: drawing it is - CPU-bound happens only on laptops; GPU-bound only on desktops Too many draw calls is a typical cause of being CPU-bound, which is why batching helps. ? What does a vertex shader do? - Runs once per pixel to compute its colour + Transforms each vertex's position for rasterisation - Sorts the objects in the scene Pixel shaders compute colours; vertex shaders place vertices. ? Why batch many sprites into one draw call? - The GPU can only draw one call per frame - Batching makes the sprites sharper + Each draw call costs CPU time, so fewer is faster Submission overhead adds up with thousands of calls. ? What does the depth test do? + Discards pixels that are behind something already drawn at that position - Measures how far the camera is from the scene - Sorts transparent objects It uses the depth buffer, one depth value per pixel. ? What is culling? - Removing objects from the game + Skipping objects that cannot be seen - Compressing textures Cheap tests save expensive drawing.

title: A 2D camera with culling
where: 10.04 A Tour of the Rendering Pipeline
body: Write the core of a 2D renderer's camera. - toScreen(camera, worldX, worldY) converts a world position to screen pixels: subtract the camera's position (the world point at the centre of the screen), multiply by the zoom, then add half the screen's width and height. Screen y grows downwards and so does world y here, so no flip is needed. - visible(camera, box) says whether an axis-aligned world rectangle ( x , y of its top-left corner, w , h ) overlaps the area the camera shows. A box exactly touching the edge, with no overlap, is not visible. - cull(camera, boxes) returns the indices of the visible boxes, in order. camera at (100, 50), zoom 2, screen 800 x 600 toScreen(100, 50) = (400, 300) the camera's centre is the screen's centre toScreen(110, 50) = (420, 300) the camera shows world x 100 ± 200 and y 50 ± 150

title: 10.05  Input Handling
body: Raw input (keys, mouse buttons, gamepad sticks) is not what game code should depend on. Engines turn it into actions ("jump", "move left"), track for each one whether it was pressed , held or released this frame, and let players rebind the keys. This lesson builds that layer, and covers gamepads, dead zones and input buffering. From devices to actions Game code should never ask "is the space bar down?". It should ask "does the player want to jump?". The difference matters as soon as you support rebinding, a gamepad, or a second keyboard layout: Pressed, held and released Lesson 5.07 showed two ways to read keys: messages, and the current state. For game controls the cleanest model is: once per frame, take a snapshot of every action's state (down or up), and keep the previous frame's snapshot. Then for each action: Query Previous Now Use for --- --- --- --- held (any) down Continuous actions: walking, aiming, charging pressed up down One-shot actions: jump, fire one shot, open a menu released down up Releasing a charged attack, ending a drag Because the snapshot is taken once at the start of the frame (lesson 10.01's input phase), every system in that frame sees the same answer. Checking the live key state in the middle of an update lets two systems disagree about whether a key was pressed. There is one trap: a tap shorter than a frame can be missed by pure polling, because the key is already up again when the snapshot is taken. Recording "went down at least once this frame" from the key-down messages, as well as the current state, fixes it. Bindings and rebinding A binding maps a physical input to an action. Keep them in data, not code: cpp enum class Action { MoveLeft, MoveRight, Jump, Attack, Count }; struct Binding { int key; Action action; }; std::vector<Binding bindings{ { 'A', Action::MoveLeft }, { VK_LEFT, Action::MoveLeft }, { 'D', Action::MoveRight }, { VK_RIGHT, Action::MoveRight }, { VK_SPACE, Action::Jump }, { 'J', Action::Attack }, }; Several keys may map to one action (an action is down if any of its keys is down). Rebinding is then just editing the table and saving it with the settings (lesson 10.07). Use virtual-key codes or, for layout-independent positions such as WASD, scan codes (lesson 5.07). Gamepads and dead zones On Windows, Xbox-compatible controllers are read with XInput ( XInputGetState ) or the newer GameInput API; libraries like SDL (chapter 11) cover many controllers. Analogue sticks report numbers (for XInput, −32768 to 32767 per axis), and a stick at rest never reads exactly zero: it drifts by a few percent. A dead zone ignores small values: cpp float applyDeadZone(float value, float deadZone) // value from -1 to 1 { const float magnitude{ std::abs(value) }; if (magnitude < deadZone) return 0.0f; // Rescale so movement starts smoothly from 0 just outside the dead zone. return std::copysign((magnitude - deadZone) / (1.0f - deadZone), value); } For a 2D stick, apply the dead zone to the length of the (x, y) vector, not each axis separately, or diagonal movement feels wrong. Input buffering Players press buttons slightly early. If the jump button was pressed three frames before the character landed, a strict game ignores it and the player feels the game "ate" their input. Buffering remembers recent presses for a short window (often 100 to 150 ms) and acts on them as soon as the action becomes possible. Its cousin, coyote time , still allows a jump for a few frames after walking off a ledge. Small touches like these are a large part of why some games "feel" responsive. Common mistakes !warning Hard-coding keys in game logic Map keys to actions in one place, so rebinding and gamepads work everywhere. !warning Reading live key state during the update Snapshot once per frame so every system agrees. !warning No dead zone on analogue sticks Characters drift on their own. Apply a dead zone to the stick vector. !warning Acting on input while the window is unfocused GetAsyncKeyState sees keys typed in other programs. Ignore input when the game is not in front. Check yourself quiz ? Why should game code use actions rather than keys? + So controls can be rebound and gamepads work unchanged - Because reading keys directly is slower - Because Windows does not report which key was pressed - So that input can only be read once per frame Game code asks "is Jump pressed?", and the binding table decides which keys or buttons mean Jump. ? How are pressed and released worked out? - From how long the key has been held + By comparing this frame's state with last frame's - From the number of key-down messages received this frame - By asking the operating system for the key's repeat count Keeping last frame's snapshot is all it takes; "held" is simply down in this frame. ? Why apply a 2D stick's dead zone to its length rather than to each axis? + Because per-axis dead zones distort diagonal directions and make movement snap to the axes - Because the length is cheaper to compute than two axes - Because each axis already has a dead zone built into the hardware - Because gamepads report only one axis at a time A radial dead zone ignores small movements in every direction equally. ? An action was up last frame and is down now. Which queries are true? - Only released - Only held + pressed and held Pressed is the transition; held is the current state. ? Why take one input snapshot per frame? + So every system in that frame sees the same input state - To save memory - Because keys can only be read once Mixing live reads makes systems disagree. ? What is a dead zone for? - Disabling input during loading screens + Ignoring a resting stick's small readings - Making buttons harder to press Without it, characters creep around on their own. ? What does input buffering do? - Stores all input for replays - Delays input to make the game harder + Remembers a press until the action is possible It forgives presses that come slightly early.

title: Actions from keys
body: Build the class InputMap , which turns key states into action states each frame. - bind(key, action) adds a binding. Several keys may share an action, and one key may drive several actions. - update(keysDown) takes the set of keys that are down this frame and computes each action's state. An action is down if any of its bound keys is down. The previous frame's state is kept. - held(action) , pressed(action) , released(action) as in the lesson. Before the first update , everything is up. Actions and keys are plain int s here. bind(32, JUMP); bind(87, JUMP) // Space and W both jump update({32}) pressed(JUMP), held(JUMP) update({32, 87}) held(JUMP) only (still down: no new press) update({}) released(JUMP)

title: 10.06  Loading and Managing Resources
body: Textures, sounds, models, levels and fonts are resources : large, loaded from disk, shared between many users, and expensive to load twice. A resource manager loads each one once, hands out handles to it, counts who is still using it, unloads it when nobody is, and ideally loads in the background. This lesson designs one, and covers asset pipelines and hot reloading. What a resource manager does Without one, every part of the game that needs goblin.png loads it itself: the same texture ends up in memory five times, loaded five times, and nobody knows when it is safe to free. A resource manager fixes that: Job How --- --- Load each resource once Keep a table from name (or a hash of the name, lesson 3.08) to the loaded resource Share it Hand out handles (or reference-counted pointers) instead of copies Know when it is unused Count references; or unload a whole level's resources together Keep the game responsive Load in the background, show a placeholder until ready Handles, not raw pointers As with entities (lesson 3.10), handing out raw pointers to resources is fragile: if the resource is unloaded or reloaded, the pointer dangles. Engines hand out handles (an index and generation), and the renderer looks the resource up each time it uses it. That also makes hot reloading possible: replace the texture behind the handle, and everything using it shows the new one next frame. Reference counting The simplest lifetime rule: each resource counts how many users hold it. acquire increments the count (loading the resource the first time); release decrements it, and at zero the resource can be unloaded. std::shared_ptr does exactly this automatically, which makes it a reasonable first design: cpp include <iostream include <map include <memory include <string struct Texture { std::string name; int width{ 0 }, height{ 0 }; }; class TextureCache { public: std::shared_ptr<Texture get(const std::string& name) { if (auto existing{ m_loaded name .lock() }) return existing; // still alive: share it auto fresh{ std::make_shared<Texture (Texture{ name, 64, 64 }) }; // "load" it ++m_loads; m_loaded name = fresh; // remember it without owning it return fresh; } int loads() const { return m_loads; } private: std::map<std::string, std::weak_ptr<Texture m_loaded; int m_loads{ 0 }; }; int main() { TextureCache cache; auto a{ cache.get("goblin.png") }; auto b{ cache.get("goblin.png") }; // the same texture, not loaded again std::cout << "shared: " << (a == b) << ", loads: " << cache.loads() << '\n'; a.reset(); b.reset(); // nobody uses it now: it is freed auto c{ cache.get("goblin.png") }; // so it is loaded again std::cout << "loads after release: " << cache.loads() << '\n'; return 0; } shared: 1, loads: 1 loads after release: 2 The cache holds weak_ptr s, which observe without keeping the resource alive. In practice, unloading the moment the count reaches zero causes churn (a texture unloaded and reloaded as an enemy dies and another spawns), so engines often keep unused resources for a while, or unload per level. The practice task builds an explicit reference-counted cache. Loading without freezing Loading a large file on the main thread stalls the game for its duration. Better: 1. The main thread requests the resource and immediately gets a handle whose state is "loading". 2. A worker thread (lesson 6.05) reads the file and decodes it. 3. GPU resources must be created through the graphics API, often on the main or render thread, so the worker passes the decoded data back through a queue (lesson 6.06's job queue). 4. Until the resource is ready, the game uses a placeholder (a grey texture, a silent sound), or the level waits behind a loading screen. Asset pipelines Source assets ( .psd , .blend , .wav ) are rarely what the game loads. An asset pipeline converts them at build time into formats that load fast: textures compressed into GPU formats with mipmaps, models flattened into vertex buffers, many small files packed into one archive with a table of contents. The game then reads exactly what it needs with almost no processing, and a level loads in a few large reads instead of thousands of small ones. Hot reloading During development, reloading a resource the moment its file changes (watching the folder with ReadDirectoryChangesW , then replacing the data behind the handle) lets artists and designers see changes without restarting the game. It is one of the biggest productivity features an engine can have, and handles make it straightforward. Common mistakes !warning Loading the same file in several places Go through the manager, so it is loaded once and shared. !warning Keeping raw pointers to resources They dangle on unload or reload. Use handles or reference-counted pointers. !warning Loading synchronously in the middle of gameplay The game freezes for the load. Preload, or load in the background with a placeholder. Check yourself quiz ? Why hand out handles instead of raw pointers to resources? - Because handles are smaller than pointers - Because textures cannot be referred to by pointer + Handles stay safe when resources unload or reload - Because handles make loading faster A pointer to an unloaded texture dangles; a handle can be checked or pointed at the reloaded version. ? How does reference counting decide when to unload? - It unloads the least recently used resource every minute - It unloads a resource when the level changes, whatever is using it - It never unloads; resources stay until the game exits + Acquire adds one, release subtracts; at zero it may unload This is what std::shared_ptr does internally, and why the cache in the lesson holds weak_ptr s that do not count. ? How can a game load resources without freezing? - Load everything before the main menu + Load on worker threads and show placeholders until ready - Load one byte per frame on the main thread - Turn off rendering while loading The main thread keeps running frames while workers do the slow reading and decoding. ? What problem does a resource manager solve first? + Loading each resource only once - Compressing files - Drawing textures Loading the same texture several times wastes time and memory. ? Why does the cache in the example hold weak_ptr s? - Because shared_ptr cannot be stored in a map + To find resources still in use without keeping them alive itself - To make lookups faster When the last user lets go, the texture is freed even though the cache remembers its name. ? What is an asset pipeline? - The order resources are drawn in - A thread that loads files + Build tools converting assets into fast formats Games load preprocessed data, not artists' source files.

title: A reference-counted resource cache
body: Build ResourceCache , which loads resources by name, shares them, and unloads them when unused. - The constructor receives a loader function, int(const std::string&) , which "loads" a resource and returns its id (in a real engine, a texture). The cache must call it only when needed. - acquire(name) returns the resource's id, calling the loader only if the resource is not currently loaded, and increments its reference count. - release(name) decrements the count. When it reaches zero, the resource is unloaded (forgotten). Releasing a name that is not loaded does nothing. - refCount(name) returns the current count (0 if not loaded); loadedCount() how many resources are loaded.

title: 10.07  Game State and Save Files
body: Saving a game means deciding what state matters, writing it in a format that will still load after the game is updated, and never leaving a corrupted file behind. This lesson covers what to save and what to rebuild, binary and text formats, versioning and migrating old saves, checksums that detect damage, and writing files safely. What to save A running game holds far more state than needs saving. Divide it: Save Rebuild on load Do not save --- --- --- The player's position, stats, inventory, quest flags Anything derived: collision grids, pathfinding data, cached totals Pointers and handles (lesson 6.09): they mean nothing next time What has changed in the world: opened chests, killed bosses Static level content: it comes from the level file Rendering state, GPU resources Settings the player chose Temporary effects that do not matter A useful principle: save the minimum from which everything else can be rebuilt . Small saves are fast to write, and less saved state means fewer ways for a save to be inconsistent. References between saved objects (a quest that refers to an NPC) are saved as ids , and resolved back to objects after loading, never as pointers. Binary or text Binary Text (JSON, INI, your own) --- --- --- Size and speed Small and fast Larger and slower to parse Readable by people No Yes: easy to inspect and debug Robust to change Needs explicit versioning Easier to add fields (unknown keys can be ignored) Editable by players Hard Easy, which may or may not be wanted Many games use text during development and binary when shipping, or text for settings and binary for saves. Whichever you choose, write fields individually in a defined byte order (lesson 2.06), never by dumping structs from memory: padding, pointers and compiler differences would all leak into the file. A header with a version Every save file should start with a small fixed header: cpp // Written field by field, little-endian, 16 bytes: // magic 4 bytes 'S','A','V','E' what kind of file this is // version 4 bytes format version how to read the rest // length 4 bytes bytes after the header // checksum 4 bytes CRC-32 of those bytes - The magic number rejects files that are not saves at all. - The version lets the game read old formats after updates. - The checksum detects corruption: truncated writes, disk errors, a file damaged in transfer. Versioning and migration Games change after release, and players expect their saves to keep working. The usual approach: each format version gets a loader, and old versions are migrated step by step to the current one: Each migration is small and tested once, and a save from any old version passes through all of them. Never reuse a version number for a different layout, and keep test saves from every released version so you can check old saves still load. Checksums A checksum is a number computed from all the bytes, stored alongside them. On loading, recompute it; if it differs, the data is damaged. CRC-32 is the standard choice: it catches accidental corruption (bit flips, truncation, garbage) with very high probability, and it is cheap. The practice task implements it. A CRC detects accidents , not deliberate tampering: anyone who edits a save can recompute it. Preventing cheating in a single-player game is rarely worth it; in multiplayer, anything that matters must live on the server, not in a file on the player's machine. Writing safely Lesson 5.04's technique applies fully: write the whole save to a temporary file, flush it, then atomically replace the old save. Keeping the previous save as a backup ( slot1.sav.bak ) as well means even a save that was written correctly but contains a game bug can be recovered. Common mistakes !warning Dumping structs to disk with fwrite(&state, sizeof state, ...) Padding, pointers and layout differences make the file fragile and unportable. Write fields one by one. !warning No version number The first update that changes the format breaks every existing save. !warning Overwriting the save in place A crash mid-write destroys it. Write a temporary file and replace. !warning Trusting the file A save may be damaged or edited. Check the magic, the version, the checksum and every length before using the data. Check yourself quiz ? What should a save contain, and what should be rebuilt? - Everything in memory, so loading is a single copy + Only state that cannot be derived; the rest is rebuilt on load - Only the level number; everything else is reset - The game's code and its data, so the save works on any version Saving derived data wastes space and risks it disagreeing with what it was derived from. ? What goes in a save file's header? - The player's name and the date only - The compiled code needed to read the file + A magic number, a version, a length and a checksum - The pointers of every saved object The magic number and version say how to read the rest; the length and checksum detect truncated or damaged files. ? How do old saves keep working after the format changes? - The game refuses old saves and asks the player to start again - Old saves are read with the newest loader, ignoring any differences - The game stores every save in every format at once + Each version is migrated step by step up to the current one Each migration step only needs to know about two neighbouring versions. ? Why are references between saved objects stored as ids rather than pointers? + Addresses differ the next time the game runs - Ids are smaller - Pointers cannot be written to files ASLR and new allocations change every address between runs. ? What is a save file's version number for? - Showing the player which save is newest + Telling the loader which format the file uses - Detecting corruption Each format change gets a new version and a migration from the old one. ? What does a CRC-32 checksum detect? - Deliberate editing by the player - Which version of the game wrote the file + Accidental damage to the data, such as truncation or flipped bits Anyone can recompute it after editing, so it is not tamper protection.

title: CRC-32
body: Implement crc32(data) , the standard CRC-32 used by ZIP, PNG and countless save formats, the bit-by-bit way: 1. Start with crc = 0xFFFFFFFF . 2. For each byte: crc ^= byte ; then 8 times: if the lowest bit of crc is 1, crc = (crc 1) ^ 0xEDB88320 , otherwise crc = 1 . 3. The result is crc ^ 0xFFFFFFFF . Then write verify(data, expected) , which says whether data 's CRC-32 equals expected . crc32("") = 0x00000000 crc32("123456789") = 0xCBF43926 (the standard check value)

title: 10.08  Scripting and Data-Driven Design
body: Engines get faster to work with when behaviour and content move out of C++ and into data : monster stats in a file, levels from an editor, dialogue in a table, and, for logic, scripts in an embedded language such as Lua. Designers can then change the game without recompiling it. This lesson covers data files, a small configuration parser, embedding a scripting language, and the trade-offs. Hard-coded versus data-driven cpp // Hard-coded: changing a goblin needs a programmer and a rebuild. Monster makeGoblin() { return Monster{ "Goblin", 30, 4, 1.2f }; } ini ; monsters.ini: a designer edits this, the game reloads it goblin health = 30 damage = 4 speed = 1.2 troll health = 120 damage = 15 speed = 0.6 When monster stats, weapon tables, level layouts, loot tables and dialogue live in data files: - Designers iterate without programmers : change a number, reload (lesson 10.06's hot reloading), play. - Modders can change the game too (chapter 13). - The code gets smaller and more general : one Monster loader instead of a function per monster. Formats Format Good for --- --- INI / key-value Settings, simple tables. Trivial to parse (the practice task) JSON Nested data: items with lists of effects. Many C++ libraries (nlohmann/json, simdjson, RapidJSON) CSV / spreadsheets Large tables edited by designers in a spreadsheet: balance numbers, localisation Custom binary Shipping builds, produced by the asset pipeline from the formats above (lesson 10.06) Whatever the format, validate on load : a misspelt key or a negative health should produce a clear message naming the file and line, not a crash three levels later. Scripting languages Data files describe what ; some things need logic : a boss's attack pattern, a quest's conditions, a cutscene's sequence. Writing all of that in C++ means a rebuild for every tweak. Many engines embed a scripting language : Language Notes --- --- Lua Tiny, fast, easy to embed in C++; used in a great many games Python Common in tools and editors, heavier to embed in a shipping game C Unity's language; managed runtime GDScript Godot's own Visual scripting Node graphs for non-programmers (Unreal's Blueprints) Your own small command language Enough for debug consoles and simple sequences (lesson 3.04's command table) Embedding Lua looks like this: the C++ side registers functions scripts may call, then runs script files: cpp-norun include <lua.hpp static int luaSpawn(lua_State L) // callable from Lua as spawn("goblin", x, y) { const char kind{ luaL_checkstring(L, 1) }; const double x{ luaL_checknumber(L, 2) }; const double y{ luaL_checknumber(L, 3) }; world.spawn(kind, static_cast<float (x), static_cast<float (y)); return 0; // no return values } int main() { lua_State L{ luaL_newstate() }; luaL_openlibs(L); lua_register(L, "spawn", &luaSpawn); if (luaL_dofile(L, "scripts/wave1.lua") != LUA_OK) std::fprintf(stderr, "script error: %s\n", lua_tostring(L, -1)); lua_close(L); } lua -- scripts/wave1.lua for i = 1, 5 do spawn("goblin", 100 + i 32, 200) end spawn("troll", 300, 240) The script can only do what the registered functions allow, which keeps it safe and the engine in charge. Trade-offs Benefit Cost --- --- Fast iteration, no recompiling Scripts run slower than C++; keep heavy loops in C++ Designers and modders can work independently Two languages to debug; errors appear at run time instead of compile time Behaviour can change after shipping (patches as data) The boundary between C++ and script needs careful design The rule most engines follow: systems in C++, content and one-off logic in data and scripts . Common mistakes !warning No validation of data files Report problems with the file name, line and key at load time. !warning Moving hot loops into scripts Scripts are for decisions, not for processing ten thousand particles per frame. !warning Exposing everything to scripts Register a deliberate, small set of functions; scripts and mods should not reach arbitrary engine internals. Check yourself quiz ? What belongs in C++ and what in data or scripts? + Engine and hot code in C++; content and balance in data - Everything in C++, because scripts are too slow for games - Everything in scripts, so nothing needs compiling - Rendering in scripts; content in C++ Designers can then change content and balance without rebuilding the engine. ? Why validate data files when loading? + So mistakes are reported at once, naming the file and line - To make loading faster - Because the compiler cannot check data files - So the data can be encrypted A misspelled key found at load time costs seconds; found as a strange bug in play it can cost hours. ? What does registering a function with Lua do? - It compiles the Lua script into C++ - It copies the function's code into the Lua virtual machine - It lets Lua replace the C++ function at run time + It makes a C++ function callable from scripts by name Scripts can only do what the engine has chosen to expose this way. ? What is the main advantage of data-driven design? + Content can change without recompiling - The game runs faster - No validation is needed Designers iterate on data files directly. ? When is an embedded scripting language more appropriate than a data file? - For a table of monster stats + When content needs logic, like a boss's attacks - For the physics engine Data describes what; scripts describe how and when. ? How does a Lua script call into the engine? - By reading the engine's memory directly - It cannot + Through C++ functions the engine registered with the Lua state The registered set defines what scripts are allowed to do.

title: Read an INI file
body: Write parseIni(text) , which reads INI-style data into a map from "section.key" to value, and reports errors with line numbers. Rules, line by line (lines are separated by \n ; ignore a \r at the end of a line): - Blank lines and lines whose first non-space character is ; or are ignored. - name starts a section. Keys before any section belong to the section "" , stored as ".key" . - key = value stores a value. Spaces around the key and the value are trimmed. The value may contain = . - Anything else is an error: record "line N: ..." (N counted from 1, the message after the colon is up to you) and carry on. - A key repeated in the same section keeps the last value. ; enemies goblin health = 30 name = Goblin = small - "goblin.health" = "30", "goblin.name" = "Goblin = small"

title: 10.09  Reading the Source of an Open-Source Game
match: 10.09 Reading the Source of an Open-Source Game
body: One of the best ways to learn engine architecture is to read a real one. Many shipped games and engines have released their source. This lesson is a method for approaching a large, unfamiliar codebase: building it, finding the main loop, tracing one feature end to end, and recognising the patterns from this chapter in someone else's code. Why read real code Everything in this chapter (the loop, time steps, entities, rendering, input, resources, saves, scripting) exists in every shipped game, solved under real constraints. Reading how experienced teams did it shows trade-offs no tutorial covers: what they simplified, what they optimised, which corners they cut to ship. Where to find source Project Notes --- --- id Software's games (Doom, Quake, Quake III Arena) Released under the GPL; small, clear C codebases, widely studied OpenTTD , Wesnoth , SuperTuxKart , Cataclysm: DDA Large open-source games in C++, actively developed Godot A complete open-source engine in C++ raylib A small, very readable C library for games (used in the planned raylib course) Dear ImGui The interface library of chapter 14, a famously readable single codebase Respect each project's licence: reading and learning is always fine; reusing code in your own project means following the licence's terms. A method 1. Build and run it Clone the repository, follow its build instructions, and get it running under your debugger. A codebase you can run and step through is ten times easier to understand than one you can only read. Note what you had to install: the dependencies are a first map of the architecture. 2. Map the top level Look at the folder structure and the largest directories. Typical names: engine , game , render / gfx , audio / snd , net , ui , script , tools , platform / sys . Write a one-line guess for each and correct it later. 3. Find the main loop Search for the entry point ( main , WinMain , wWinMain , or the platform layer's equivalent), then step into it with the debugger until you reach the loop that runs every frame. Note what it calls each frame and in which order: that is lesson 10.01's diagram for this engine. Quake III, for example, has Com_Frame doing exactly input, events, server frame, client frame and rendering. 4. Trace one feature end to end Pick something small and visible: what happens when the player presses fire, picks up an item or opens a door. Follow it from input to effect: Use the tools you have: search for the string on screen or in the console, set breakpoints, use the IDE's "find all references" (Shift+F12 in Visual Studio) and "go to definition" (F12), and the call stack at each breakpoint. 5. Look for the patterns As you go, match what you see with this chapter: Look for Lesson --- --- Fixed or variable time step, and how dt is computed 10.02 How game objects are stored: inheritance tree, components, arrays of structs 10.03 Handles versus pointers between objects 3.10 Where the renderer culls and batches 10.04 Binding tables and action layers 10.05 The resource cache and file formats 10.06 Save code, and how it handles versions 10.07 Data files and any scripting 10.08 6. Write it down Keep notes as you go: a diagram of the main systems, the frame's order of calls, the path of your traced feature. Explaining the architecture in a page of your own words is the test of whether you understood it. Common mistakes !warning Reading files top to bottom Large codebases are read by following execution, not alphabetically. !warning Trying to understand everything Pick one feature and follow it; the rest will become familiar along the way. !warning Not running it Reading without a debugger leaves you guessing which code actually runs. Check yourself quiz ? What steps does the method follow? - Read every file in alphabetical order, then build it + Build it, map folders, find the loop, trace one feature, write it down - Search for the biggest file and start reading there - Rewrite the game in your own style, then compare Running it first means you can always check your reading against what really happens. ? How do you find the main loop? - Look for the file called loop.cpp - It is always the first function in main.cpp + Step from the entry point until the once-per-frame loop - Read the documentation, which always names it The debugger follows the real path, which is more reliable than guessing from file names. ? What should you check before reusing code from an open-source game? - That it compiles with your version of Visual Studio - That it has comments - That it was written recently + Its licence, and that your use follows the licence's terms Open source does not mean free of conditions: many licences require attribution or that your code uses the same licence. ? What is the best first step with an unfamiliar game codebase? + Build it and run it under a debugger - Read every file in alphabetical order - Rewrite it in another language Being able to step through it makes everything else faster. ? How do you find the code behind a visible feature? - Guess the file name + Search for the strings it shows - Read the main loop only Follow execution from something you can see. ? Why trace one feature end to end? - Because features are independent - To find bugs + It crosses most major systems on one real path Input, logic, entities, rendering and audio all appear along the way.

title: An event queue
