title: A tiny engine core
body: Put together a fixed-step loop, entities with components, and input actions into one small engine core. frame 1: input "right" - player velocity (1, 0) step x2 (fixed 1/60) - player at (0.033, 0) render alpha 0.4 - drawn at (0.023, 0) 120 frames run, 120 steps, no frame skipped

title: 11.01  Project Setup and a Window
body: This chapter builds a complete small game, a top-down dungeon crawler called Delve , using the ideas from chapters 1 to 10. It starts here: a Visual Studio project with SDL2 from vcpkg, a window and renderer, and the fixed-time-step game loop from lesson 10.02. By the end of the chapter you will have a game with a map, a player, monsters, items, levels, saves and a debug console. What we are building Delve is a top-down, tile-based dungeon crawler: - a map made of tiles (walls, floor, doors, stairs) loaded from text files; - a player moved with the keyboard, one tile at a time; - monsters that hunt the player with breadth-first search (lesson 3.09); - health, items and an inventory; - several levels, saving and loading; - an in-game debug console; - and a packaged Release build you can give to a friend. It is small enough to finish and large enough to need everything from chapters 1 to 10. Later chapters use it as their test subject: chapter 12 builds tools that inspect it, chapter 13 adds mods to it, and chapter 14 gives those tools an interface. Why SDL2 SDL2 (Simple DirectMedia Layer) is a widely used, open-source C library that handles the platform-specific parts of a game: creating a window, a hardware-accelerated 2D renderer, keyboard, mouse and gamepad input, audio, and timing. It runs on Windows, Linux, macOS and consoles. Underneath, on Windows, it does exactly what chapter 5 did by hand (a window class, a message loop, Direct3D for drawing), so we can concentrate on the game. Setting up the project 1. Create an empty solution delve and a Console App project delve inside it (lesson 4.01). A console app is convenient while developing: std::cout output appears in the console window next to the game. 2. In the project's properties, for All Configurations: C++ standard C++20 , warning level 4 , platform x64 (lesson 1.07). 3. In a terminal in the solution folder, set up vcpkg in manifest mode (lesson 4.06): powershell vcpkg new --application vcpkg add port sdl2 4. In the project properties, vcpkg → Use Vcpkg Manifest: Yes . 5. Create the folder layout: delve\ vcpkg.json delve.sln delve\ main.cpp the loop game.h/.cpp the game state and rules tilemap.h/.cpp the map (lesson 11.02) render.h/.cpp drawing input.h/.cpp actions and bindings (lesson 10.05) data\ levels\ level files (lesson 11.02) A window and a loop cpp-norun // main.cpp define SDL_MAIN_HANDLED // we write our own main; SDL must not replace it include <SDL.h include <algorithm include <cstdio int main() { if (SDL_Init(SDL_INIT_VIDEO SDL_INIT_EVENTS) != 0) { std::fprintf(stderr, "SDL_Init failed: %s\n", SDL_GetError()); return 1; } SDL_Window window{ SDL_CreateWindow("Delve", SDL_WINDOWPOS_CENTERED, SDL_WINDOWPOS_CENTERED, 960, 640, SDL_WINDOW_RESIZABLE) }; SDL_Renderer renderer{ SDL_CreateRenderer(window, -1, SDL_RENDERER_ACCELERATED SDL_RENDERER_PRESENTVSYNC) }; if (!window !renderer) { std::fprintf(stderr, "could not create the window: %s\n", SDL_GetError()); return 1; } const double step{ 1.0 / 60.0 }; // fixed simulation step (lesson 10.02) double accumulator{ 0.0 }; Uint64 previous{ SDL_GetPerformanceCounter() }; const double frequency{ static_cast<double (SDL_GetPerformanceFrequency()) }; float boxX{ 100.0f }; bool running{ true }; while (running) { // 1. Input: drain every waiting event (lesson 5.05's PeekMessage loop, done by SDL). SDL_Event event; while (SDL_PollEvent(&event)) { if (event.type == SDL_QUIT) running = false; if (event.type == SDL_KEYDOWN && event.key.keysym.sym == SDLK_ESCAPE) running = false; } // 2. Update in fixed steps. const Uint64 now{ SDL_GetPerformanceCounter() }; accumulator += std::min((now - previous) / frequency, 0.25); previous = now; while (accumulator = step) { boxX += 120.0f static_cast<float (step); // 120 pixels per second if (boxX 900.0f) boxX = 0.0f; accumulator -= step; } // 3. Render. SDL_SetRenderDrawColor(renderer, 18, 20, 26, 255); SDL_RenderClear(renderer); SDL_Rect box{ static_cast<int (boxX), 300, 40, 40 }; SDL_SetRenderDrawColor(renderer, 95, 211, 196, 255); SDL_RenderFillRect(renderer, &box); SDL_RenderPresent(renderer); // swap buffers (lesson 10.04); waits for vsync } SDL_DestroyRenderer(renderer); // shut down in reverse order of creation SDL_DestroyWindow(window); SDL_Quit(); return 0; } Build and run: a dark window with a teal box sliding across it. Every concept is from earlier lessons: the event loop is lesson 5.05's, the fixed step and accumulator lesson 10.02's, the clear-draw-present cycle lesson 10.04's double buffering. Structuring for growth Before adding features, split the game state from the platform code. main.cpp will only own the window, the loop and timing; a Game class owns everything else: cpp-norun // game.h pragma once include "input.h" struct SDL_Renderer; class Game { public: bool load(const char firstLevel); void update(const InputState& input, double dt); // fixed step: game rules only void render(SDL_Renderer renderer) const; // drawing only: never changes state bool wantsToQuit() const { return m_quit; } private: bool m_quit{ false }; // map, entities, inventory ... added in the next lessons }; The division follows lesson 10.01: update changes state, render only reads it. Keeping SDL out of Game::update also means the game's rules can be unit-tested without a window (chapter 17), which is how this chapter's practice tasks work: they test the game's logic pieces on their own. Common mistakes !warning Forgetting SDL_MAIN_HANDLED Without it, SDL renames main and expects its SDL2main library to provide the real entry point, and the link fails. !warning The DLL is missing at run time vcpkg copies SDL2.dll next to the exe. If you move the exe, move the DLL with it (lesson 11.08 packages both). !warning Drawing in the update loop Keep update and render separate, as lesson 10.01 explained. Check yourself quiz ? What three things happen each time round Delve's main loop? - The level is loaded, the player is saved, and the window is created + Waiting events are processed, the game is updated in fixed steps for the elapsed time, and the frame is rendered and presented - Input is read, the frame is rendered, and the program sleeps for 16 ms - The game is updated once, then events are processed, then the frame is drawn twice Fixed steps keep the rules independent of the frame rate, and every waiting event is handled before updating. ? What does SDL_RenderPresent do? - It clears the screen to black - It draws one sprite at the given position + It shows the frame drawn in the back buffer - It creates the window and its renderer Drawing happens off-screen first, so the player never sees a half-drawn frame. ? Why does main.cpp own only the window, loop and timing? - Because SDL requires all game code to be in one file - Because main must be shorter than 100 lines - Because the game state cannot be created before the window + So the rules live in Game , apart from platform code and testable Game::update never touches SDL, so it can be tested without a window. ? Why use SDL2 instead of the raw Windows API from chapter 5? + It handles windows, input and drawing portably - The Windows API cannot create windows - SDL2 is faster than Direct3D Underneath, it does on Windows what chapter 5 did by hand. ? What does SDL_PollEvent correspond to in chapter 5? - A single GetMessage call + The PeekMessage loop - The CreateWindowEx call It returns immediately when no events are waiting. ? Why keep SDL out of Game::update ? - Because SDL is slow - Because SDL cannot be used in classes + So the game rules can run and be tested without a window Logic separated from the platform is testable and portable.

title: 11.02  Drawing a Tile Map
body: Delve's world is a grid of tiles stored in a flat array (lesson 2.07) and loaded from a plain text file (lesson 10.08), where each character is a tile and special characters mark where the player and monsters start. This lesson writes the level format, the loader with validation, and the renderer that draws the visible part of the map around a camera. The level format Levels are text files that anyone can edit in Notepad: data/levels/01.txt: the first floor @... ..g .... ... ..k.+... .... .. Character Meaning --- --- Wall . Floor + Door (closed; opens when walked into) Stairs down to the next level @ Player start (floor underneath) g , k , t A goblin, kobold or troll start (floor underneath) Lines starting with followed by a space are comments. Every map row must be the same width. The tile map cpp-norun // tilemap.h pragma once include <string include <vector enum class Tile : unsigned char { Floor, Wall, Door, Stairs }; struct Spawn { char kind; int x; int y; }; class TileMap { public: int width() const { return m_width; } int height() const { return m_height; } bool inside(int x, int y) const { return x = 0 && y = 0 && x < m_width && y < m_height; } Tile at(int x, int y) const { return inside(x, y) ? m_tiles static_cast<size_t (y m_width + x) : Tile::Wall; } void set(int x, int y, Tile t) { if (inside(x, y)) m_tiles static_cast<size_t (y m_width + x) = t; } bool walkable(int x, int y) const { const Tile t{ at(x, y) }; return t == Tile::Floor t == Tile::Stairs; } int m_width{ 0 }, m_height{ 0 }; std::vector<Tile m_tiles; // row-major: index = y width + x }; Note at returns Wall outside the map: anything that asks about a tile beyond the edge gets a sensible answer instead of an out-of-bounds read, which removes a whole class of bugs (lesson 2.09) from the movement and AI code. Loading with validation Loading follows lesson 10.08's rules: read line by line, skip comments, and report problems with a line number. The practice task writes parseLevel , which turns the text into a TileMap , the player's start and a list of monster spawns, and rejects levels that are ragged, have no player or several players, or contain unknown characters. Drawing it Each tile is drawn as a 32-pixel square. Lesson 10.04's camera keeps the player in the middle of the screen, and culling skips tiles that are off screen: cpp-norun // render.cpp include <SDL.h include "tilemap.h" constexpr int kTile{ 32 }; void drawMap(SDL_Renderer r, const TileMap& map, float cameraX, float cameraY, int screenW, int screenH) { // Which tiles can be on screen? Only loop over those (culling, lesson 10.04). const int firstX{ std::max(0, static_cast<int ((cameraX - screenW / 2.0f) / kTile)) }; const int firstY{ std::max(0, static_cast<int ((cameraY - screenH / 2.0f) / kTile)) }; const int lastX{ std::min(map.width() - 1, static_cast<int ((cameraX + screenW / 2.0f) / kTile)) }; const int lastY{ std::min(map.height() - 1, static_cast<int ((cameraY + screenH / 2.0f) / kTile)) }; for (int y{ firstY }; y <= lastY; ++y) // rows outside, columns inside (lesson 2.07) { for (int x{ firstX }; x <= lastX; ++x) { switch (map.at(x, y)) { case Tile::Wall: SDL_SetRenderDrawColor(r, 58, 63, 72, 255); break; case Tile::Floor: SDL_SetRenderDrawColor(r, 26, 29, 35, 255); break; case Tile::Door: SDL_SetRenderDrawColor(r, 140, 98, 57, 255); break; case Tile::Stairs: SDL_SetRenderDrawColor(r, 240, 198, 116, 255); break; } const SDL_Rect cell{ static_cast<int (x kTile - cameraX + screenW / 2.0f), static_cast<int (y kTile - cameraY + screenH / 2.0f), kTile - 1, kTile - 1 }; SDL_RenderFillRect(r, &cell); } } } Coloured squares are enough to play with. To use artwork, load one tile sheet image with SDL_image ( vcpkg add port sdl2-image ) into an SDL_Texture , and draw each tile with SDL_RenderCopy from the right part of the sheet: one texture shared by every tile, which is lesson 10.04's batching in practice. Common mistakes !warning Indexing with x height + y Row-major storage is y width + x (lesson 2.07). !warning Trusting level files Validate shape and characters on load, with line numbers in the messages. !warning Drawing every tile of a huge map Loop only over the tiles that can be on screen. Check yourself quiz ? How is the map stored in memory? - As a vector of rows, each a separate vector of tiles + As one flat vector of tiles in row-major order, with (x, y) at index y × width + x - As a hash map from (x, y) pairs to tiles - As one flat vector in column-major order, with (x, y) at x × height + y One flat block keeps the tiles together in memory and makes the index calculation trivial. ? What does the level loader need to check? + Equal row widths, known characters, exactly one player start - Only that the file exists - That the file is smaller than one megabyte - That the level was saved by the same version of the game A clear message naming the line beats a strange crash in play. It should report each problem with its line number. ? How does a tile sheet make drawing more efficient? + All tiles share one texture, so they can be batched - It compresses the tiles so they load faster - It lets the GPU skip tiles that are the same as the one before - It stores each tile as text, which is faster to draw Switching textures between draws prevents batching, which is costly. ? Why does TileMap::at return Wall for positions outside the map? + So movement and AI code never read out of bounds and treat the edge as solid - Because the map is surrounded by walls in memory - To make drawing faster A safe default removes a class of out-of-bounds bugs. ? A level is 40 tiles wide. Which index holds the tile at x = 5, y = 3? - 83 + 125 - 205 3 × 40 + 5. ? How does the renderer avoid drawing off-screen tiles? - It draws everything and the GPU discards the rest - It never scrolls + It loops only over the tiles the camera can see Culling by range is cheap and exact for a grid.

title: Load a level
body: Write parseLevel(text) for Delve's level format. The text has lines separated by \n (ignore a trailing \r ). Lines that start with " " (hash and space) are comments, and blank lines are ignored; every other line is a map row. Tiles: wall, . floor, + door, stairs. @ is the player start and g , k , t are monster starts; all four have floor underneath. Return a Level with the width, height, the tiles as a row-major string using only , . , + and , the player's start, and the monster spawns in reading order (top to bottom, left to right). If the level is invalid, return std::nullopt : - no map rows at all, - rows of different lengths, - an unknown character, - not exactly one @ . / @.g / - width 5, height 3, tiles " ... ", player (1,1), spawns { g at (3,1) }

title: 11.03  A Player That Moves
body: Delve is turn-based on a grid: each key press moves the player one tile, and the world (monsters, doors) responds. This lesson connects lesson 10.05's input actions to movement, handles walls, doors and stairs, adds key repeat for held keys, and makes moves look smooth by sliding between tiles in the renderer only. Turns on a grid Many roguelike games, Delve included, are turn-based : nothing in the world happens until the player acts, then every monster takes its turn. The game loop still runs at 60 frames per second (input, animation and drawing need it), but the game rules advance one turn per player action. Actions and moves Using lesson 10.05's input map, the movement actions become a direction: cpp-norun struct Dir { int dx; int dy; }; std::optional<Dir movementFrom(const InputMap& in) { if (in.pressed(Action::Up)) return Dir{ 0, -1 }; if (in.pressed(Action::Down)) return Dir{ 0, 1 }; if (in.pressed(Action::Left)) return Dir{ -1, 0 }; if (in.pressed(Action::Right)) return Dir{ 1, 0 }; return std::nullopt; } Bindings put both the arrow keys and WASD on these actions, and a gamepad's d-pad later just adds more bindings. Moving into a tile What happens depends on what is in the target tile. Keeping the decision in one function makes the rules easy to read and test: Target Result Takes a turn? --- --- --- Floor Move there Yes Stairs Move there; the level is complete (lesson 11.06) Yes Closed door The door opens and becomes floor; the player stays Yes Wall, or outside the map Nothing: a bump No A monster Attack it instead of moving (lesson 11.05) Yes A bump not costing a turn matters for feel: walking into a wall by mistake should not let monsters catch up. The practice task implements this table as tryMove . Holding a key Pressing an arrow for every step is tiring in long corridors. Holding the key should repeat the move, after a short delay, at a steady rate: cpp-norun // A held movement key repeats: the first move on press, then after 0.25 s, then every 0.08 s. if (auto dir{ movementFrom(input) }) { tryMove( dir); m_repeatTimer = 0.25; m_heldDir = dir; } else if (heldDirection(input) == m_heldDir) { m_repeatTimer -= dt; if (m_repeatTimer <= 0) { tryMove(m_heldDir); m_repeatTimer += 0.08; } } The update runs at a fixed step, so the repeat rate is the same on every machine (lesson 10.02). Smooth movement, without changing the rules The player's logical position is a whole tile: the rules (collision, monster AI, saving) only ever see whole tiles. To avoid the character teleporting a tile at a time on screen, the renderer draws it sliding from the previous tile to the current one over a short time: cpp-norun // In the player's state: int x, y; int fromX, fromY; float slide; (slide goes 0 → 1 after each move) const float t{ std::min(player.slide, 1.0f) }; const float drawX{ (player.fromX + (player.x - player.fromX) t) kTile }; const float drawY{ (player.fromY + (player.y - player.fromY) t) kTile }; This is lesson 10.02's interpolation applied to a turn-based game: the simulation is exact and simple, and only the picture is smooth. The camera follows the drawn position, not the logical one, so it glides too. Common mistakes !warning Letting a bump cost a turn Players feel cheated when walking into a wall lets monsters move. Only real actions take turns. !warning Mixing drawn and logical positions Collision and AI must use the whole-tile position; only rendering uses the sliding one. !warning Moving on held without a repeat timer The player rushes across the map at 60 tiles per second. Check yourself quiz ? What does "turn-based on a real-time loop" mean for Delve? - The game pauses its loop until a key is pressed - Monsters act every frame and the player acts once per second + The loop runs every frame, but rules advance only when the player acts - Two loops run on separate threads, one for turns and one for drawing The window stays responsive and animated even while the world waits for the player. ? Which moves cost a turn? - Every key press, including bumping into a wall - Only attacking + Moving, opening a door and attacking; not bumping a wall - Only moving onto a new tile A wasted bump that let monsters act would feel unfair. ? How does the renderer make tile-by-tile movement look smooth? - It moves the player one pixel per turn - It changes the player's tile position gradually over several turns - It runs the game rules at 60 turns per second + It slides the player's picture from the old tile to the new The sliding position is only used for drawing; the rules still see the player on whole tiles. ? The player walks into a wall. What should happen? + Nothing, and no turn passes - The player moves into the wall - A turn passes but the player stays still Bumps should be free, so mistakes do not let monsters act. ? What does walking into a closed door do in Delve? - Moves the player through it + Opens it, using the turn - Nothing at all happens Opening and passing are separate actions. ? Why is the sliding position used only for drawing? - Because floats cannot be compared - To save memory + The rules stay exact on whole tiles It is interpolation for presentation only.

title: The rules of a step
body: Write tryMove(map, width, x, y, dx, dy, monsterAt) for Delve. map is the level's row-major tile string ( wall, . floor, + door, stairs, as in the previous practice task) and width its width; (x, y) is the player; (dx, dy) the direction. monsterAt(tx, ty) returns true if a monster stands on that tile. Return a MoveResult : what happened, whether a turn was used, and the player's new position. Apply the lesson's table, in this order: 1. The target is outside the map, or a wall: Bump , no turn, position unchanged. 2. A monster is on the target: Attack , a turn, position unchanged. 3. A door: OpenDoor , a turn, position unchanged, and the door becomes floor in map . 4. Stairs: Descend , a turn, the player moves there. 5. Floor: Move , a turn, the player moves there.

title: 11.04  Monsters and Simple AI
body: Delve's monsters need to notice the player, chase them around walls, and attack when adjacent. This lesson gives each monster a small state machine , and replaces per-monster pathfinding with one distance map (a breadth-first search from the player, lesson 3.09) that every monster follows downhill. It is simple, fast, and the basis of AI in many roguelikes. A state machine per monster Each monster is in one of a few states, and simple rules move it between them: State Each turn --- --- Idle Wander randomly, or stand still; check whether the player is within sight range Chasing Step one tile towards the player Attacking Hit the player (lesson 11.05) States are just an enum in a component (lesson 10.03) and a switch in the AI system: small, readable and easy to debug, which matters more than sophistication for most game AI. Chasing: one search for all monsters Each chasing monster needs the next step towards the player around the walls. Running a separate BFS from every monster to the player works, but it repeats almost the same work for each one. Instead, run one BFS starting from the player , recording every reachable tile's distance (in steps) to the player: ....... 8765456 . ... → 9 345 . @.... A @1234 map distance map (A is 10; walls have none) Now every monster, wherever it is, finds its next step by looking at its four neighbours and moving to the one with the smallest distance : it walks "downhill" to the player. One search per turn serves any number of monsters, and each monster's decision is just four lookups. This structure is called a distance map (or "Dijkstra map", or flow field). The practice task builds it. Useful variations come almost for free: - Fleeing : a monster with low health moves to a neighbour with a larger distance, away from the player. - Several goals : start the search from every item and the monster heads to the nearest one. - Terrain costs : treat mud as costing 2 steps (Dijkstra's algorithm instead of BFS) and monsters route around it. Taking turns fairly After the player acts, every monster acts once, in a fixed order (for example by entity id). A few details make it robust: - Recompute the distance map once after the player moves, before any monster acts. - Two monsters may want the same tile. Process them in order and let the second one choose again (or wait) if the tile is now taken. - Monsters that are far away and idle can skip the expensive parts entirely. Seeing the player "Sees the player" can start simple: within 8 tiles by distance-map steps (which already accounts for walls, so monsters do not notice the player through a wall). A proper line-of-sight check traces a line across the grid (Bresenham's line algorithm) and stops at the first wall; it is a good extension once the basics work. Common mistakes !warning Running a pathfinding search per monster per turn One distance map from the player serves them all. !warning Letting monsters move onto each other Check occupancy as each monster moves, not only before the turn starts. !warning AI that is too clever Players enjoy monsters that are readable and predictable. Simple rules, clearly communicated, beat complex ones. Check yourself quiz ? What are a Delve monster's states, and what moves it between them? + Idle, Chasing and Attacking, moved by seeing and reaching the player - Alive and Dead: a monster switches when its health reaches zero - Moving and Waiting: monsters alternate every turn - Hunting, Fleeing and Sleeping, chosen at random each turn A state machine keeps each monster's behaviour simple and easy to follow. Noticing the player starts a chase, being adjacent starts attacking, and losing the player for a while returns to idle. ? What is a distance map? + Steps from every tile to a goal, from one breadth-first search - A list of every monster sorted by distance from the player - The straight-line distance from each tile to the player - A map of which tiles the player has already seen Each monster steps to a neighbouring tile with a smaller number, so one search serves all monsters. ? How do monsters avoid moving onto the same tile? - The distance map gives each monster a different tile - They move all at once and any that collide go back - Two monsters are allowed on one tile + They move one at a time, checking the tile is free Acting in turn means each monster sees the moves of those before it. ? How does a monster use the distance map to chase the player? + It steps to whichever neighbouring tile has the smallest distance value - It runs its own search each turn - It moves in a straight line towards the player Walking downhill on the distance map follows a shortest path around walls. ? Why build the distance map from the player rather than from each monster? - Monsters cannot be searched from + One search serves every monster - It gives longer paths The work is shared instead of repeated. ? How can a frightened monster flee using the same map? - Delete the map and wander - Move in a random direction + Step to a larger distance value Uphill on the map leads away from the player.

title: 11.05  Health, Items and Inventory
body: Combat and loot turn Delve into a game. This lesson adds health and attack components, a damage formula with a little randomness, death and drops, item definitions loaded from data, pickups, and an inventory where identical items stack . Every number lives in a data file, so balancing never needs a rebuild. Components for combat Following lesson 10.03, combat is a few components and one system: cpp-norun struct Health { int current; int maximum; }; struct Attack { int power; int accuracy; }; // accuracy: chance to hit, in percent struct Defence { int armour; }; struct Drops { std::string itemId; int chance; }; // percent The player and every monster have Health , Attack and Defence ; values come from monsters.ini (lesson 10.08), so a troll is just a different set of numbers. The damage formula When an attacker hits a defender: 1. Roll to hit : a random number from 1 to 100; it hits if the roll is at most the attacker's accuracy. 2. Damage : power − armour / 2 , plus a small random spread (−1 to +1), but at least 1 so every hit matters. 3. Subtract from the defender's health; at 0 or below, the defender dies. cpp-norun int rollDamage(const Attack& a, const Defence& d, Random& rng) { if (rng.range(1, 100) a.accuracy) return 0; // a miss const int base{ a.power - d.armour / 2 }; return std::max(1, base + rng.range(-1, 1)); } Two habits make combat code easy to balance and test: - One random number generator object , passed in, never rand() scattered around. Seed it from the time in normal play and from a fixed number for tests and replays (lesson 10.02's determinism). - Log every combat event to the message log (lesson 8.03's ring buffer, shown on screen): "The goblin hits you for 3. (HP 17/20)". Players need the feedback, and you need it to see whether the numbers feel right. Death and drops When a monster dies, the combat system removes its entity (lesson 3.10's handles mean nothing else is left pointing at it) and, according to its Drops component, may place an item on its tile. The player dying ends the run with a "you died" screen showing the last few log lines, so the player knows why. Items from data ini ; items.ini potion name = Healing potion heal = 10 stack = 5 dagger name = Rusty dagger power = 2 stack = 1 gold name = Gold coins stack = 999 An item definition (the data) is shared; an item in the world or inventory is just a definition id and a count. That keeps inventories small and makes "how many potions do I have?" a lookup. The inventory The inventory is a fixed number of slots (say 10). Each slot holds an item id and a count, up to that item's stack limit. Picking up items: 1. First top up existing slots of the same item, up to the stack limit. 2. Then put the rest into empty slots. 3. Whatever does not fit stays on the floor. picking up 7 potions (stack 5) with slots: potion 4 dagger 1 empty empty → potion 5 dagger 1 potion 5 potion 1 nothing left over Using an item removes one from its slot, and an empty slot becomes free. The practice task implements adding and removing with exactly these rules, which is the part most likely to hide off-by-one bugs. Common mistakes !warning Damage that can be zero or negative High armour should reduce damage, not heal the target. Clamp to at least 1 on a hit. !warning Calling rand() everywhere Use one seeded generator object so tests and replays are repeatable. !warning Copying item definitions into every slot Store an id and a count; look the definition up when needed. Check yourself quiz ? What are the steps of the damage formula? - Damage is always the attacker's power; armour is ignored - Subtract armour from health, then roll to see if the attack missed + Roll to hit, then power minus half armour plus spread, at least 1 - Multiply power by armour, divide by the defender's health Clamping to at least 1 means a hit always does something, however strong the armour. ? What is the difference between an item definition and an item in the inventory? + A definition is shared data; a slot holds just its id and count - The definition is in the inventory; the item is on the floor - They are the same struct, copied into each slot - The definition is C++ code; the item is a script Sharing one definition means changing a potion in the data file changes every potion. ? In what order does picking up fill the inventory? - Empty slots first, then existing stacks - Only empty slots; stacks are never topped up + Top up matching stacks, then use empty slots - The item replaces whatever is in the first slot Topping up stacks first keeps empty slots free for as long as possible; whatever does not fit stays on the floor. ? Why clamp damage to at least 1 on a hit? + So every hit matters, and never heals - To make the game easier - Because health cannot be negative Without it, high armour makes damage zero or negative. ? Why pass a random generator object around instead of calling rand() ? - rand() does not exist in C++ + It can be seeded, so tests and replays repeat - It is always faster Determinism needs control over the random numbers. ? An inventory has potion 4 and one empty slot; potions stack to 5. Seven potions are picked up. What happens? - All seven fit in the first slot - The pickup fails + Slots become 5 and 5; 1 stays on the floor Top up existing stacks first, then fill empty slots, and leave the rest.

title: A stacking inventory
body: Build Delve's Inventory : a fixed number of slots, each empty or holding an item id and a count. - The constructor receives the number of slots and a map from item id to its stack limit . - add(id, count) puts items in following the lesson's rules: first top up existing slots holding the same id (in slot order) to the stack limit, then fill empty slots (in slot order). It returns how many items did not fit. Unknown ids do not fit at all. - remove(id, count) takes items out, from the last slot holding that id backwards, emptying slots that reach 0. If there are fewer than count in total, it removes nothing and returns false . - count(id) returns the total held; slot(i) returns slot i as a pair of id and count (an empty slot is {"", 0} ).

title: 11.06  Levels and Saving
body: Delve gets several floors connected by stairs, and the ability to save and continue. This lesson handles level transitions (what persists between floors and what is rebuilt), designs Delve's save format using lesson 10.07's header, version and checksum, and writes it safely, so a crash or power cut never costs the player their run. Moving between floors When the player steps onto the stairs (lesson 11.03's Descend ), the game: 1. Keeps what belongs to the player : health, inventory, experience. 2. Discards everything belonging to the old floor : its map, monsters, items on the ground, its distance map. 3. Loads the next level file (lesson 11.02) and spawns its monsters. 4. Places the player at the new level's start and shows "Floor 2" in the message log. Making that split explicit (a PlayerState that survives levels, a FloorState that does not) keeps the transition simple and is exactly the line the save format follows. cpp-norun struct PlayerState { int health{ 20 }, maxHealth{ 20 }; int power{ 3 }, armour{ 1 }; Inventory inventory{ 10, itemStackLimits() }; }; struct FloorState { int floor{ 1 }; TileMap map; std::vector<MonsterInstance monsters; // kind, position, health, AI state std::vector<ItemOnFloor items; std::vector<bool openedDoors; }; What a Delve save contains Lesson 10.07's principle: save the minimum from which everything else can be rebuilt. Saved Rebuilt on load --- --- The floor number The map: reload data/levels/NN.txt Changes to the map: doors opened Distance maps, rendering state Each surviving monster: kind, position, health, state Monster stats: from monsters.ini by kind Items on the floor: id, count, position Item names and effects: from items.ini by id The player's position, health and inventory The random generator's state Saving the random generator's state means a reloaded game continues exactly as it would have, which makes bugs that happen after loading reproducible. The format A text body inside lesson 10.07's binary header is a practical choice: easy to read while developing, protected by the checksum. SAVE version 1 length 214 crc 0x9A3C11F0 (16-byte binary header) floor 2 player 7 4 hp 14 20 power 4 armour 1 inv potion 3 inv dagger 1 door 12 5 monster g 9 4 hp 6 chasing monster g 15 2 hp 9 idle item gold 40 3 7 rng 2463534242 Each line starts with a keyword, so loading is a loop over lines with a switch on the first word, and an old save missing a newer keyword still loads with defaults. The version in the header decides which keywords exist (lesson 10.07's migrations). Saving safely Following lesson 5.04: 1. Build the whole save in memory as a string. 2. Compute the CRC-32 (lesson 10.07) and write the header and body to slot1.sav.tmp in the Saved Games folder. 3. Flush and close it, then replace slot1.sav with it atomically, keeping the previous file as slot1.sav.bak . On loading, check the magic, the version and the checksum before reading a single line; if anything fails, offer the backup. Delve saves automatically on each new floor and when quitting, so a run can always be continued, and the practice task writes the save and load of the player's part. Common mistakes !warning Saving the level map wholesale The map comes from the level file; save only what changed (opened doors). !warning Forgetting the random generator's state A reloaded game then diverges from the original, and bugs after loading cannot be reproduced. !warning Saving during a monster's turn Save only between turns, when the state is consistent. Check yourself quiz ? How does Delve divide its state for level transitions and saving? - Into what is on screen and what is off screen + Player state, which persists, and floor state, which is rebuilt - Into one block for each monster and one for the player - Into Debug state and Release state Saving only the changes keeps saves small and lets the level file supply the rest. Floor state is rebuilt from the level file plus a record of changes. ? What does a Delve save contain? - The whole level file and a screenshot - Only the player's position and health - Every tile, sprite and sound loaded in memory + The floor's changes, the player, and the random generator's state Saving the generator's state makes a loaded game continue exactly as it would have. That means opened doors, surviving monsters, floor items, and the player's position, stats and inventory. ? How is the save written so a crash cannot destroy it? + Written to a temporary file, flushed, then swapped in atomically - It is written directly over the old save as quickly as possible - It is written in small pieces over several frames - It is written twice to the same file At every moment either the old or the new save is complete on disk. ? What survives a transition to the next floor? + The player's state: health, inventory, stats - The old floor's monsters - The old floor's map Everything belonging to the floor is discarded and rebuilt from the next level file. ? Why save the random generator's state? - To make saves smaller + So play continues exactly as before - To prevent cheating Without it, the reloaded game takes different random outcomes. ? Why start each line of the save body with a keyword? - To make the file larger - Because the checksum needs it + Loading is a simple loop; missing keys get defaults Keyword lines are easy to extend across versions.

title: Save and load the player
body:
Write the player part of Delve's save format. savePlayer(p) returns the text, one line per fact, each ending in 
 : player X Y hp HEALTH MAXHEALTH power POWER armour ARMOUR inv ID COUNT (one line per inventory entry, in order) loadPlayer(text) reads it back. It must accept the lines in any order, ignore blank lines and lines whose keyword it does not know (a newer version may have added some), and return std::nullopt if the player line is missing or malformed (wrong number of fields, wrong labels, or non-numbers), or an inv line is malformed or has a count below 1. savePlayer({ 7, 4, 14, 20, 4, 1, { { "potion", 3 }, { "dagger", 1 } } }) == "player 7 4 hp 14 20 power 4 armour 1
inv potion 3
inv dagger 1
"

title: 11.07  A Debug Console
body: Every serious game has a hidden console for its developers: press a key, type god , give potion 5 or goto 3 , and test anything without playing up to it. This lesson builds Delve's console from lesson 3.04's command table: text input, a command registry with help text, argument parsing, history, output, and a rule that keeps it out of the shipped game. Why a console Testing the troll on floor 5 by playing through floors 1 to 4 every time wastes hours. A debug console lets developers and testers change the game's state directly: Command Effect --- --- help List every command with a one-line description god Toggle invulnerability give potion 5 Add items to the inventory heal Restore full health goto 3 Jump to floor 3 spawn troll Spawn a monster next to the player reveal Show the whole map seed 1234 Re-seed the random generator, to reproduce a bug save / load Save and load immediately Chapter 13 extends the same idea into an in-game debug menu, and chapter 14 gives tools a full interface; the console is the simplest and most flexible form. The registry Lesson 3.04's command table becomes a registry where each command has a name, a short help text and a function that receives the arguments: cpp-norun using Args = std::vector<std::string ; using Handler = std::function<std::string(Game&, const Args&) ; // returns a line to print struct Command { std::string help; Handler run; }; class Console { public: void add(std::string name, std::string help, Handler run) { m_commands std::move(name) = { std::move(help), std::move(run) }; } std::string execute(Game& game, const std::string& line) { const Args words{ splitCommandLine(line) }; // lesson 6.01's practice task: quotes allowed if (words.empty()) return ""; const auto found{ m_commands.find(words 0 ) }; if (found == m_commands.end()) return "unknown command: " + words 0 + " (try help)"; return found- second.run(game, Args(words.begin() + 1, words.end())); } private: std::map<std::string, Command m_commands; // sorted, so help lists them alphabetically }; Registering a command is one line wherever the feature lives: cpp-norun console.add("give", "give ITEM COUNT : add items to the inventory", (Game& g, const Args& a) { if (a.empty()) return std::string{ "usage: give ITEM COUNT " }; const int count{ a.size() 1 ? std::atoi(a 1 .c_str()) : 1 }; const int left{ g.player.inventory.add(a 0 , count) }; return "gave " + std::to_string(count - left) + " " + a 0 ; }); Each command validates its own arguments and returns a message, so mistakes produce a helpful line instead of a crash. Text input with SDL The console opens with the backquote key ( , below Escape). While it is open: - SDL's SDL_StartTextInput delivers typed characters as SDL_TEXTINPUT events, already in UTF-8 and respecting the keyboard layout (lesson 5.07's WM_CHAR , through SDL). - Backspace, Enter, Escape and the arrow keys come through as normal key events. - Game controls are ignored, so typing w does not move the player. The console draws a dark band over the top third of the screen with the last lines of output (from lesson 8.03's ring buffer) and the input line. History Pressing Up recalls the previous command, as in a terminal. The history is a list of past commands and a cursor; the practice task implements its exact behaviour, including the detail that typing a new line and pressing Up then Down restores what you were typing. Keeping it out of the shipped game The console is a cheat menu. In a single-player game that may be fine to leave reachable, but at least the game-changing commands should be compiled only into development builds: cpp-norun ifndef DELVE_SHIPPING registerDebugCommands(console); // god, give, goto, spawn ... endif with DELVE_SHIPPING defined in a separate Shipping configuration (lesson 4.01). In multiplayer games, anything that changes shared state must also be refused by the server: a client-side console can only ever be trusted for the client's own view. Common mistakes !warning Commands that crash on bad arguments Every handler checks its arguments and returns a usage message. !warning Typing in the console also moves the player While the console is open, route keys to it only. !warning Shipping cheat commands by accident Compile them out of shipping builds. Check yourself quiz ? What does the console's registry store for each command? - Only the command's name - The command's source code, so it can be compiled at run time + Its name, a help line, and a handler function - The key that runs the command The help text lets a help command list everything automatically. ? What should the game do with key presses while the console is open? - Send them to both the console and the game + Send them only to the console (text, editing keys, history), not to the game's controls - Ignore them until the console closes - Send them to the game, and type into the console only with the mouse Typing "go" should not make the player walk. ? How does command history recall work? + Up goes back, Down goes forward, past the newest is the current line - Up runs the last command again immediately - History is shown as a list that must be clicked - Down deletes the most recent command from the history Returning to the line being typed means nothing half-written is lost. ? Why does each command carry a help text? + So help can list every command - Because the compiler needs it - To make commands faster A console nobody remembers how to use is not much use. ? Why use SDL's text input events rather than key-down events for typing? - Key-down events do not exist in SDL + They give the actual characters typed - They are faster Like WM_CHAR in lesson 5.07. ? How do you keep cheat commands out of the released game? - Hide the console key - Ask players not to use them + Register them only in development builds Code that is not compiled cannot be used.

title: Console history
body: Build History , the command history behind Delve's console, with the behaviour of a typical terminal. - submit(line) records a submitted command (empty lines and a line identical to the most recent entry are not recorded), and resets browsing. - up(current) is called when Up is pressed, with the text currently in the input line. The first press saves current as the draft and returns the most recent command; each further press returns an older one, stopping at the oldest (pressing Up there returns the oldest again). With no history, it returns current unchanged. - down() moves to a newer entry. Moving past the newest returns the saved draft, and browsing ends. If not browsing, it returns the draft (initially empty). - The history keeps at most capacity entries (given to the constructor), dropping the oldest. submit "give potion 5", submit "heal" up("go") - "heal" up("...") - "give potion 5" up("...") - "give potion 5" (the oldest; stays) down() - "heal" down() - "go" (the draft is back)

title: 11.08  Polish and Packaging
body: The difference between a working prototype and a game people enjoy is polish : feedback for every action, a little motion, sound, and no rough edges. The difference between a game on your machine and one on a friend's is packaging : a Release build with everything it needs, version information, and a test on a clean system. This lesson finishes Delve. Feedback for every action Players should never wonder whether something happened. Each action gets a visible, and ideally audible, response: Event Feedback --- --- Hitting a monster A brief flash on the monster, a number floating up, a short sound Being hit A red flash at the screen's edges, a small screen shake Missing "miss" floating up, a different sound Picking up an item The item slides to the inventory bar; the slot pulses Low health The health bar pulses; a heartbeat sound Bumping a wall A tiny nudge of the player sprite towards the wall and back All of these are presentation only : they live in the renderer and never change game state (lesson 10.01), so they cannot introduce gameplay bugs. Screen shake, for example, is a random offset added to the camera that decays over a fraction of a second: cpp-norun // Called when the player is hit: strength in pixels. void addShake(float strength) { m_shake = std::min(m_shake + strength, 12.0f); } // Each frame, in the renderer: const float ox{ m_shake rng.unit() 2 - m_shake }; const float oy{ m_shake rng.unit() 2 - m_shake }; drawWorld(cameraX + ox, cameraY + oy); m_shake = std::max(0.0f, m_shake - 40.0f frameTime); // fades in about a quarter of a second Use a separate random generator for presentation, so effects do not consume numbers from the gameplay generator and change the game's outcomes (lesson 11.05). Sound SDL_mixer ( vcpkg add port sdl2-mixer ) plays sound effects and music in a few lines. Keep sounds short and quiet by default, give every sound a slight random pitch or choose between two or three variants so repetition does not grate, and give players volume settings for effects and music separately. Settings and accessibility A settings screen (saved like lesson 10.07's files, in AppData) should cover at least: key bindings (lesson 10.05), volume, window or full screen, screen shake on/off, and text size. Turning off screen shake and flashes matters to players sensitive to motion, and costs one boolean. The Release build Lesson 4.10's checklist, applied: 1. Build Release x64 with /Zi and linker /DEBUG , and archive the PDB with the version number (lesson 8.02): crash dumps from players are useless without it. 2. Define DELVE_SHIPPING to remove debug commands (lesson 11.07). 3. Install the crash handler that writes a minidump and the recent log (lesson 8.04). 4. Add version information : a VERSIONINFO resource (Add → Resource → Version) with the product name and version, shown in the file's Properties dialog and recorded in crash dumps. 5. Turn on all the security options that are on by default (ASLR, DEP, /GS , control-flow guard) and leave them on. Packaging A Delve release is a folder: Delve-1.0.0\ Delve.exe SDL2.dll from vcpkg_installed\x64-windows\bin SDL2_mixer.dll data\ levels\ .txt items.ini monsters.ini sounds\ .wav README.txt how to play, controls, where saves are kept LICENSES.txt SDL's licence (zlib) and any others you used Zip it, or build an installer (Inno Setup and WiX are free; MSIX for the Microsoft Store). Two details people forget: - Third-party licences. SDL's zlib licence is permissive, but you must keep its notice; check every library you ship. - The Visual C++ runtime. If you build with /MD (the default), players need the Visual C++ Redistributable. Either ship its installer, or build with /MT so the runtime is inside your exe (lesson 4.04). Test on a clean machine The game works on your PC because everything it needs is already installed there. Test the zip on a clean Windows installation, ideally a virtual machine (lesson 15.08 sets one up) restored to a fresh snapshot each time: missing DLLs, a missing runtime, paths that assume your folders, and writing next to the exe (lesson 5.04) all show up immediately. Common mistakes !warning Not keeping the PDB of the build you released Every crash report from that version becomes unreadable. !warning Testing only on the development machine Use a clean virtual machine. !warning Polish that changes the game Effects belong in the renderer, with their own random numbers. Check yourself quiz ? What makes an action feel good to perform? - A long animation that the player must wait for - Changing the rules so the action is more powerful + Immediate feedback in effects and sound, not in the rules - A message box confirming what happened Feedback belongs to presentation, so it never changes how the game plays. ? What goes into a Delve release folder? - The whole Visual Studio solution and its build output - Only the exe - The exe, the PDB and the source code + The exe, its DLLs, the data, a readme and licences PDBs are kept by you, not shipped; the libraries' licences usually require including their notices. ? What are the two ways to handle the Visual C++ runtime? - Ask players to install Visual Studio, or ship the source code + Ship the Redistributable, or link it in with /MT - Copy the Debug runtime DLLs next to the exe, or build with /MDd - Nothing is needed; every Windows computer has every version Debug runtime DLLs may not be redistributed, and /MDd is the Debug DLL runtime. ? Why should screen shake use a different random generator from the gameplay? + So effects cannot change gameplay outcomes - Because shake needs better random numbers - To make it faster Presentation must never affect game state. ? Why test the packaged game on a clean virtual machine? - Games run faster in virtual machines + It reveals missing DLLs and runtimes - To check the graphics card Your development PC hides missing dependencies. ? What must you keep for every build you release? - Its obj files - Its vcpkg cache + Its PDB files Symbols match exactly one build.

title: 12.01  Looking at Another Process with Documented APIs
match: 12.01 Looking at Another Process with Documented APIs
body:
Development tools often need to see inside a running game from a separate program: a stats panel, a level editor that previews live, a profiler. Each process has its own private memory (lesson 6.02), so tools need a deliberate channel. This lesson surveys the documented ways (the game publishing data through shared memory , pipes or sockets; the debugging API for a process you start; dumps) and builds a shared-memory channel, the method the rest of this chapter uses. The problem The game and the tool are separate processes. A pointer in one means nothing in the other, and Windows' access checks (lesson 6.08) decide who may look at whom. So how does a tool show the game's frame time, the player's health or the number of live monsters? There are several documented ways, and they differ in who cooperates : Method The game cooperates? Good for --- --- --- Shared memory (file mapping) Yes: the game writes a block of data that the tool maps too Fast, continuous data: stats, graphs, live values Named pipes or sockets Yes: they exchange messages Commands and events: "spawn a troll", "level loaded" Log files and ETW events Yes Records over time, profiling (lesson 8.08) The debugging API on a process the tool starts No code in the game, but the tool must be its debugger Debuggers and crash catchers (lesson 12.03) Crash dumps No Inspecting state after the fact (lesson 8.04) The first rows are how professional engines connect their editors and tools: the game publishes what tools may see, through an interface designed for it. That is reliable (no guessing at memory layouts), fast, survives game updates when versioned properly (lesson 12.06), and needs no special rights. This chapter builds that kind of tooling for Delve, plus a small debugger for a program the tool launches itself. !note Ground rules The tools here inspect programs you build yourself, or programs started by your own tool. Reading or changing the memory of other people's software, particularly online games and anything protected by anti-cheat, is outside this course (lesson 9.01's ground rules): it harms other players, breaks the terms you agreed to, and is often illegal. Shared memory with a file mapping Windows can map the same block of physical memory into two processes' address spaces. Each sees it at its own virtual address, but writes by one are visible to the other. The block is a file mapping object, created by name: cpp include <windows.h include <iostream struct Telemetry // the agreed layout: plain data only, no pointers (lesson 6.09) { unsigned version; unsigned frame; float frameMs; int playerHp; }; int main() { // The game creates a named, page-file-backed mapping big enough for the struct... HANDLE game{ CreateFileMappingW(INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE, nullptr, PAGE_READWRITE, 0, sizeof(Telemetry), L"Local\XenonDemoTelemetry") }; auto written{ static_cast<Telemetry (MapViewOfFile(game, FILE_MAP_WRITE, 0, 0, sizeof(Telemetry))) }; // ...and a tool opens the same name. (Here in one process, to keep the example runnable.) HANDLE tool{ OpenFileMappingW(FILE_MAP_READ, FALSE, L"Local\XenonDemoTelemetry") }; const auto read{ static_cast<const Telemetry (MapViewOfFile(tool, FILE_MAP_READ, 0, 0, sizeof(Telemetry))) }; written = Telemetry{ 1, 1234, 16.4f, 17 }; std::cout << "two different addresses: " << (static_cast<const void (written) != static_cast<const void (read)) << '
'; std::cout << "the tool sees frame " << read- frame << ", hp " << read- playerHp << '
'; UnmapViewOfFile(read); CloseHandle(tool); UnmapViewOfFile(written); CloseHandle(game); return 0; } two different addresses: 1 the tool sees frame 1234, hp 17 Two different virtual addresses, one block of physical memory. Points to note: - INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE as the file means "backed by the page file": pure shared memory, no file on disk. - The name Local\... is visible to processes in the same login session. Choose names unique to your game. - The tool opens the mapping read-only ( FILE_MAP_READ ): least privilege (lesson 6.08). A stats panel has no business writing into the game. - The layout contains only plain values, never pointers: an address in the game is meaningless in the tool. - Reading while the game writes can produce a torn snapshot (half old, half new). Lesson 12.04 fixes this with a sequence counter. Pipes for commands Shared memory is ideal for "the current state". For messages ("load level 3", "screenshot taken") a named pipe ( CreateNamedPipeW in the game, CreateFileW on \.\pipe
ame in the tool) carries a stream of bytes both ways, like a local network connection. Many engines run a small command server this way so editors can control the game; it is the debug console of lesson 11.07, reachable from outside. Common mistakes !warning Putting pointers or std::string in shared memory Their contents are addresses in one process. Use fixed-size plain data. !warning Opening the mapping writable in the tool Read-only is all a viewer needs, and protects the game from tool bugs. !warning Treating the shared block as always consistent Without a protocol (lesson 12.04), the tool may read a half-updated state. Check yourself quiz ? Name three documented ways for a tool to get data from a game. - Guessing addresses, scanning memory, and patching the game's code + Shared memory, named pipes or sockets, and log files - Reading the game's .exe on disk, its PDB, and its installer - Screenshots, keyboard hooks and the clipboard These work because the game takes part, or because Windows documents them for exactly this purpose. ETW events, the debugging API and crash dumps are documented routes too. ? Why is it best for the game to publish data deliberately? + An agreed, versioned layout keeps working as the game changes - Because Windows forbids reading another process's memory - Because it makes the game run faster - Because published data is encrypted Guessed memory layouts break with every new build; an agreed layout does not. ? What may and may not go into a shared-memory block? - Anything, as long as the block is large enough - Only strings, never numbers - std::string and std::vector , but not raw pointers + Fixed-size plain data; never pointers or heap-owning types A pointer means nothing in another process's address space, and std::string holds one internally. ? Why can a tool not simply follow a pointer it got from the game? + It is an address in the game's own space - Pointers are encrypted by Windows - Tools have no memory of their own Each process has its own private address space (lesson 6.02). ? What makes shared memory work between two processes? - Windows copies the data between them every frame + Both map the same named file-mapping object - They use the same virtual addresses Each sees it at its own address, but it is the same memory. ? Which channel suits sending a command such as "load level 3" from an editor to the game? - A crash dump - A file mapping holding the current frame number + A named pipe (or socket) carrying messages Pipes carry streams of messages; shared memory holds current state.

title: 12.02  A Memory Viewer
body: A hex viewer that shows raw memory with addresses, bytes and text is one of the most useful debugging tools there is, and the Memory window of lesson 2.11 is one. This lesson builds one for your own process and for a process your tool launched: reading with ReadProcessMemory , coping with pages that cannot be read, and formatting the classic three-column view. The classic layout Address 00 01 02 03 04 05 06 07 08 09 0A 0B 0C 0D 0E 0F Text 0000020E6C8F5E30 52 6F 6F 6B 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 Rook............ 0000020E6C8F5E40 0E 00 00 00 14 00 00 00 00 00 80 3F ?? ?? ?? ?? ...........?.... Three columns: the address of the row, sixteen bytes in hex, and the same bytes as text (printable characters as themselves, everything else as a dot). Bytes that could not be read are shown as ?? , which a good viewer must handle because memory can be freed, never committed, or protected (lesson 6.03). Reading your own process safely In your own process you can read memory directly through a pointer, but only if it is committed and readable; touching anything else crashes the viewer. Ask first with VirtualQuery (lesson 6.04): cpp bool readable(const void address, size_t size) { MEMORY_BASIC_INFORMATION info{}; if (!VirtualQuery(address, &info, sizeof(info))) return false; if (info.State != MEM_COMMIT) return false; if (info.Protect & (PAGE_NOACCESS PAGE_GUARD)) return false; const auto end{ static_cast<const char (info.BaseAddress) + info.RegionSize }; return static_cast<const char (address) + size <= end; // a longer read may cross into the next region } Even this has a gap: another thread could free the memory between the check and the read. In a viewer for your own process that is acceptable; in a tool that must never crash, read through ReadProcessMemory on the current process, which returns failure instead of faulting. Reading another process you started For a process the tool launched itself (and so has full rights to, lesson 6.08), ReadProcessMemory copies bytes from its address space: cpp SIZE_T got{ 0 }; std::vector<unsigned char buffer(256); const BOOL ok{ ReadProcessMemory(child, reinterpret_cast<LPCVOID (address), buffer.data(), buffer.size(), &got) }; - The handle needs PROCESS_VM_READ (and PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION for VirtualQueryEx ). A process you created with CreateProcessW comes with a full-access handle. - If any page in the range is unreadable, the call fails and got reports how much was copied, which may be less than asked. A robust viewer reads page by page (4,096 bytes, lesson 6.02), so one bad page only blanks its own part. - VirtualQueryEx(child, ...) is VirtualQuery for another process, and tells you in advance which pages are readable. Formatting The practice task writes the formatter: given a starting address, the bytes, and which of them were readable, produce the three-column lines. Separating reading (the platform part) from formatting (pure logic) means the formatter can be tested without any process at all, as every practice task in this course has done. Making it useful Features that turn a hex dump into a tool: - Follow a pointer : click 8 bytes that look like an address (lesson 2.11) and jump there. - Interpretations : show the selected bytes as int , float , double , and as a pointer, side by side. - Highlight changes : re-read every 100 ms and colour bytes that changed (Visual Studio's Memory window does this when stepping). - Bookmarks and type overlays : apply a struct layout (lesson 9.09) so offsets show member names. Chapter 14 gives the viewer a proper interface with Dear ImGui; chapter 18's first capstone completes it. Common mistakes !warning Reading a whole range in one call One unreadable page fails the whole read. Read page by page. !warning Showing stale data as current Mark the time of the last successful read, and show unreadable bytes as ?? , never as zeros. !warning Asking for more access than reading needs A viewer needs PROCESS_VM_READ and query rights only. Check yourself quiz ? What are the three columns of a hex view? + The address, the bytes in hex, and the same bytes as text - The variable name, its type and its value - The byte's offset, its decimal value and its binary value - The module name, the function name and the line number This classic layout is the same in Visual Studio's Memory window and most hex editors. ? What rights does a tool need to read another process's memory? - Administrator rights, always - PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS , because reading needs every right + PROCESS_VM_READ , plus query rights to list regions - None; any process can read any other Ask for only what you need. A process the tool created itself already comes with a full-access handle. ? How does ReadProcessMemory report a partial read? - It throws a C++ exception - It returns success and fills the rest with zeros - It crashes the target process + It fails and reports how many bytes it did copy Reading page by page avoids losing a whole range because one page in it is not readable. ? What does a viewer show for bytes it could not read? + A marker such as ?? , never a made-up value like 0 - Zeros - Nothing: the row is skipped Showing zeros would mislead whoever reads the dump. ? Why read another process's memory one page at a time? - Pages are the only size ReadProcessMemory accepts + An unreadable page then blanks only its own bytes - It is faster Protection and commitment are per page. ? Why keep the formatting separate from the reading? - Formatting must run on another thread - Windows requires it + Formatting is pure logic, testable without a process Testable logic, thin platform layer.

title: Format a hex view
body:
Write hexView(address, bytes, readable) . bytes and readable have the same length; readable i says whether bytes i was actually read. Produce one line per 16 bytes, starting at address (which you may assume is a multiple of 16): - the row's address as 16 upper-case hex digits, then two spaces; - 16 byte columns, each two upper-case hex digits (or ?? if unreadable) followed by one space, with one extra space after the eighth; for a short last row, pad the missing bytes with three spaces each (and the extra space if the gap includes the middle); - then two more spaces (in addition to the last column's trailing space) and the text: each readable byte from 0x20 to 0x7E as itself, anything else (including unreadable bytes) as . . Missing bytes on a short last row add nothing to the text. Lines end with

" "0000000000001010 ?? .

title: 12.03  A Minimal Debugger of Your Own
match: 12.03 A Minimal Debugger of Your Own
body:
Visual Studio, WinDbg and x64dbg are all built on the same Windows debugging API . This lesson uses it directly to write a tiny debugger: it launches a program of yours as its debuggee, receives debug events (process and thread creation, DLL loads, exceptions, debug output, exit), reports them, and continues. It demystifies every debugger you have used, and is the core of crash-catching tools. How debugging works on Windows A debugger is an ordinary program that has a special relationship with its debuggee : Windows suspends the debuggee whenever something interesting happens and sends the debugger a debug event describing it. The debuggee stays frozen until the debugger says to continue. Every debugger you have used is this loop with a large interface around it. The debug event loop cpp-norun include <windows.h include <cstdio include <string int wmain(int argc, wchar_t argv) { if (argc < 2) { std::wprintf(L"usage: tinydbg program.exe
"); return 1; } std::wstring command{ L""" + std::wstring(argv 1 ) + L""" }; STARTUPINFOW si{ sizeof(si) }; PROCESS_INFORMATION pi{}; if (!CreateProcessW(nullptr, command.data(), nullptr, nullptr, FALSE, DEBUG_ONLY_THIS_PROCESS, nullptr, nullptr, &si, &pi)) { std::wprintf(L"could not start it: %lu
", GetLastError()); return 1; } bool running{ true }; while (running) { DEBUG_EVENT ev{}; if (!WaitForDebugEvent(&ev, INFINITE)) break; DWORD status{ DBG_CONTINUE }; switch (ev.dwDebugEventCode) { case CREATE_PROCESS_DEBUG_EVENT: std::wprintf(L"process started, image at %p
", ev.u.CreateProcessInfo.lpBaseOfImage); CloseHandle(ev.u.CreateProcessInfo.hFile); // the event hands us a file handle: close it break; case LOAD_DLL_DEBUG_EVENT: std::wprintf(L"DLL loaded at %p
", ev.u.LoadDll.lpBaseOfDll); CloseHandle(ev.u.LoadDll.hFile); break; case OUTPUT_DEBUG_STRING_EVENT: std::wprintf(L"debuggee says something (OutputDebugString)
"); break; case EXCEPTION_DEBUG_EVENT: { const EXCEPTION_RECORD& er{ ev.u.Exception.ExceptionRecord }; const bool firstChance{ ev.u.Exception.dwFirstChance != 0 }; std::wprintf(L"exception 0x%08lX at %p (%s chance)
", er.ExceptionCode, er.ExceptionAddress, firstChance ? L"first" : L"second"); if (er.ExceptionCode == EXCEPTION_BREAKPOINT) status = DBG_CONTINUE; // the initial breakpoint, or ours else status = DBG_EXCEPTION_NOT_HANDLED; // let the program's own handlers see it break; } case EXIT_PROCESS_DEBUG_EVENT: std::wprintf(L"process exited with code %lu
", ev.u.ExitProcess.dwExitCode); running = false; break; } ContinueDebugEvent(ev.dwProcessId, ev.dwThreadId, status); } CloseHandle(pi.hThread); CloseHandle(pi.hProcess); return 0; } Run it on any small program of your own ( tinydbg.exe delve.exe ) and you will see the process start, every DLL load in order ( ntdll , kernel32 , KernelBase , the C++ runtime, SDL...), an initial breakpoint exception ( 0x80000003 , lesson 8.04) that Windows raises in every debugged process just before its own code runs, and finally the exit. First and second chance When the debuggee raises an exception, the debugger gets it twice if needed: 1. First chance : before the program's own exception handlers run. A debugger normally continues with DBG_EXCEPTION_NOT_HANDLED , letting the program handle it (a C++ throw that is caught arrives here and is harmless). 2. Second chance : only if nothing in the program handled it. The program is about to crash. This is the moment to write a crash dump (lesson 8.04) with the process frozen exactly at the fault, which is how out-of-process crash reporters work: they are tiny debuggers. Breakpoints, by hand A software breakpoint (lesson 4.07) is now easy to understand in code: 1. Read and remember the byte at the address ( ReadProcessMemory ). 2. Write 0xCC there ( WriteProcessMemory , then FlushInstructionCache ). 3. When the EXCEPTION_BREAKPOINT arrives with that address, the instruction pointer has moved one byte past the CC . Restore the original byte, move rip back by one with GetThreadContext / SetThreadContext , and continue (setting the trap flag to single-step once, so the breakpoint can be re-armed after the instruction runs). Reading registers is GetThreadContext on the thread from the event (with CONTEXT_FULL ), and the call stack is StackWalk64 from the DbgHelp library with symbols loaded (lesson 8.02). Everything Visual Studio's debugger shows is built from these calls. Rights and limits A debugger needs full access to its debuggee. Launching the debuggee yourself grants that. Attaching to a running process ( DebugActiveProcess ) requires the same rights as Visual Studio's Attach (lesson 4.07): your own processes at your integrity level; protected processes refuse (lesson 6.08). Only one debugger can be attached to a process at a time. Common mistakes !warning Forgetting to close the file handles in events CREATE_PROCESS_DEBUG_EVENT and LOAD_DLL_DEBUG_EVENT hand you file handles; not closing them leaks one per DLL. !warning Continuing every exception as handled DBG_CONTINUE on a real exception re-executes the faulting instruction forever. Pass the program's own exceptions on with DBG_EXCEPTION_NOT_HANDLED . !warning Exiting the debugger while the debuggee runs By default the debuggee is killed with it. Call DebugActiveProcessStop (or DebugSetProcessKillOnExit(FALSE) ) to detach first. Check yourself quiz ? What is the shape of a debugger's main loop? - Read the target's memory every millisecond and look for changes + Wait for a debug event, handle it, continue, until exit - Set a breakpoint on every instruction and step through them - Start the debuggee, sleep until it exits, then read its exit code While the debugger handles an event, every thread of the debuggee is stopped. ? Name five kinds of debug event. - Key press, mouse click, window resize, paint and timer - Function call, function return, loop start, loop end and variable change + Process and thread start and exit, DLL loads, exceptions, debug output - File open, file read, file write, file close and file delete Process exit is another. Windows sends these to the debugger, not to the program. ? Why are out-of-process crash reporters built as debuggers? - Because only debuggers can read files - Because a crashed program cannot be restarted otherwise - Because Windows sends crash reports only to Visual Studio + As debugger they get the crash with it frozen, and dump from outside Writing a dump from inside a crashing process is risky; a separate healthy process is reliable. ? What happens to the debuggee while the debugger handles an event? + It is suspended until ContinueDebugEvent - It keeps running normally - It is restarted Every thread waits while the debugger inspects it. ? What is a second-chance exception? - A breakpoint hit twice + One the program did not handle, so it will crash - An exception in the debugger The debugger saw it first-chance, passed it on, and nothing handled it. ? How does a software breakpoint work? - The processor watches a list of addresses - Windows pauses the program every few instructions + 0xCC over an instruction raises an exception for the debugger Hardware breakpoints use debug registers instead (lesson 4.09).

title: Follow the debug events
where: 12.03 A Minimal Debugger of Your Own
body: A debugger keeps a picture of its debuggee from the stream of debug events. Write Tracker , which processes simplified events and answers questions. Each Event has a kind and, depending on the kind, a base address, a name , a code and a firstChance flag: kind Meaning --- --- "load" A module name loaded at base "unload" The module at base unloaded "exception" An exception code at address base , first or second chance "exit" The process exited with code handle(event) returns what the debugger should tell Windows, as the lesson describes: "continue" for everything except exceptions that are not breakpoints ( 0x80000003 ), for which it returns "not-handled" . The tracker also answers: - modules() : the names of the currently loaded modules, ordered by base address; - crashed() : whether a second-chance exception was seen; - exitCode() : the exit code, or std::nullopt if the process has not exited.

title: 12.04  A Telemetry Channel: Letting the Game Publish Its State
match: 12.04 A Telemetry Channel: Letting the Game Publish Its State
body: Delve will publish its live state (frame time, floor, the player's health and position, monster count) in shared memory for tools to read. The hard part is consistency: the game writes while the tool reads, so the tool must never see half an update. This lesson designs the shared block with a header and version, and protects it with a sequence lock , a lock-free scheme where the writer never waits. What the game publishes cpp-norun // telemetry.h: shared by Delve and its tools. Plain data, fixed sizes, no pointers. pragma once include <atomic include <cstdint struct TelemetryV1 { std::uint32_t magic; // 'DLVT' std::uint32_t version; // 1 std::uint32_t size; // sizeof(TelemetryV1): lets old tools read newer games (lesson 12.06) std::atomic<std::uint32_t sequence; // the sequence lock, below std::uint64_t frame; float frameMs; std::int32_t floor; std::int32_t playerX, playerY; std::int32_t playerHp, playerMaxHp; std::int32_t monstersAlive; std::uint32_t turn; }; Every field is a fixed-size number at a fixed offset (lesson 2.05), the same in both programs because both include the same header. The header fields ( magic , version , size ) let a tool check, before trusting anything, that it is looking at the right kind of block and knows how to read it (lesson 10.07's save header, applied to memory). The consistency problem The game updates all these fields once per frame. A tool reading them at the same moment might copy playerX from the new frame and playerY from the old one, a position the player was never at. With a dozen fields, torn reads happen often enough to matter (lesson 6.06's data races, between processes). A mutex shared between processes would work (a named mutex), but then the game could be made to wait by a slow or stuck tool, which is unacceptable: a tool must never be able to make the game stutter. The sequence lock A sequence lock (seqlock) lets one writer update freely while readers detect and retry torn reads: Writer (the game, once per frame): 1. Increment sequence (it becomes odd : "update in progress"). 2. Write all the fields. 3. Increment sequence again (it becomes even : "consistent"). Reader (the tool): 1. Read sequence . If it is odd, the writer is mid-update: try again shortly. 2. Copy all the fields into a local struct. 3. Read sequence again. If it changed, the writer updated during the copy: discard and retry. If it is the same (and even), the copy is consistent. cpp-norun // Game side, each frame: t- sequence.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_acq_rel); // odd: writing t- frame = frame; t- frameMs = ms; t- playerX = x; / ... / t- sequence.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_release); // even: done // Tool side: bool readSnapshot(const TelemetryV1 t, TelemetryV1& out) { for (int attempt{ 0 }; attempt < 100; ++attempt) { const std::uint32_t before{ t- sequence.load(std::memory_order_acquire) }; if (before & 1) continue; // being written: try again copyFields(out, t); // plain copy of the data fields std::atomic_thread_fence(std::memory_order_acquire); if (t- sequence.load(std::memory_order_relaxed) == before) return true; // nothing changed meanwhile } return false; // the game is writing constantly: report "busy" } The writer never waits for anyone: tools can be slow, stuck or crashed and the game does not notice. Readers occasionally retry, which costs nothing noticeable because the write takes well under a microsecond. Seqlocks are used in operating system kernels for exactly this pattern: frequently updated data with one writer and readers that can retry. The memory-order arguments make sure the processor and compiler do not reorder the field writes across the sequence updates (lesson 6.06's atomics); the practice task models the protocol's logic. Creating the channel in Delve At start-up, Delve creates the mapping Local\Delve.Telemetry.<process id (including the id lets several copies of the game run side by side), fills in magic , version and size , and publishes each frame. If creating it fails, the game simply runs without telemetry: tools are optional, the game is not. In shipping builds the channel can be left on (it is harmless) or compiled out like the console (lesson 11.07). Common mistakes !warning Locking between the game and a tool A stuck tool must never be able to stall the game. The writer must not wait. !warning Trusting the block without checking its header Check the magic, version and size before reading fields. !warning Forgetting that a reader can loop forever Bound the retries and report "busy" instead of hanging the tool. Check yourself quiz ? What is a sequence lock's writer protocol? + Increment the sequence, write the data, increment it again - Lock a mutex, write the data, unlock the mutex - Write the data, then set the sequence number to zero - Write the data twice and compare the copies An odd number means a write is in progress; the writer never waits for readers. ? How does a reader know its copy is consistent? - The data's checksum matches + The sequence number was even before copying and unchanged after - The sequence number is odd after copying - The writer sends a message when it has finished If the number was odd or changed, the reader copies again. ? Why does the telemetry block start with magic, version and size? - To make the block a multiple of 16 bytes - Because Windows requires every file mapping to have a header + So a tool can check what it is reading before trusting any field - To store the date the game was built Wrong data, or the right data in a newer layout, would otherwise be read as garbage. ? What does an odd sequence number mean? + A write is in progress; do not trust the copy - The data is consistent - The game has crashed The writer increments once before and once after writing. ? A reader copies the fields and then finds the sequence number has changed. What should it do? - Use the copy anyway + Discard its copy and try again - Wait for the writer with a mutex The writer updated during the copy, so it may be torn. ? Why is a seqlock better than a shared mutex here? - It uses less memory - It works without shared memory + The game never waits for a slow tool Only readers retry; the writer always proceeds.

title: The sequence-lock protocol
where: 12.04 A Telemetry Channel: Letting the Game Publish Its State
body: Model a sequence lock without threads, so its logic can be tested step by step. A SharedBlock holds a sequence number and two values that must always be read together.
