The writer is split into steps so tests can interleave it with readers: - beginWrite() increments the sequence; - writeA(v) and writeB(v) set the values; - endWrite() increments the sequence again. The reader is also split: - beginRead() returns the sequence number it saw (the reader's "ticket"), or std::nullopt if it is odd (a write is in progress); - copy() returns the two values as they are right now; - validate(ticket) returns true if the sequence still equals the ticket. Finally, readConsistent(block) is a complete reader using those steps: try up to 3 times; return the pair if a copy is validated, otherwise std::nullopt .

title: 12.05  A Live Stats Panel for Your Game
match: 12.05 A Live Stats Panel for Your Game
body: With Delve publishing its telemetry, a separate tool can show it live: frame times with a graph, the floor, the player's health and position, how many monsters are alive. This lesson builds that tool as a console program (chapter 14 gives it a graphical interface): finding running copies of the game, reading snapshots on a timer, keeping a history for graphs, and coping when the game starts, stops or restarts. What the panel shows Delve telemetry · pid 18324 · v1 connected ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── frame 48211 frame time 7.9 ms (min 6.8 · avg 8.2 · max 21.4) ▁▁▂▁▁▁▂▁▁▁▁▂▁▁▇▁▁▁▂▁▁▁▁▁▂▁▁▁▁▁▁▂▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▂▁▁▁▁▁▁▂▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▂▁▁▁▁ last 60 samples floor 3 turn 412 player (17, 9) hp 14 / 20 ███████░░░ monsters alive 6 Every value comes from one consistent snapshot (lesson 12.04). The graph shows the last 60 frame times, scaled so the slowest is the tallest bar, and the spike in it is exactly the kind of stutter lesson 8.08 warned about, now visible while playing. Finding the game The telemetry block's name includes the game's process id (lesson 12.04), so the tool: 1. Lists processes named delve.exe (lesson 6.07's snapshot). 2. For each, tries OpenFileMappingW(FILE_MAP_READ, FALSE, L"Local\\Delve.Telemetry.<pid ") . 3. Maps the first that opens and checks magic , version and size before reading anything else (lesson 12.06 covers what to do with versions it does not know). If several copies are running, it can show a list to choose from. The read loop cpp-norun while (running) { TelemetryV1 snap{}; if (!connected) tryConnect(); else if (!readSnapshot(block, snap)) showStatus("busy"); // retries exhausted (lesson 12.04) else if (snap.frame == lastFrame) staleFor += interval; // the game is paused, or frozen else { staleFor = 0; lastFrame = snap.frame; history.push(snap.frameMs); draw(snap, history); } if (connected && !processStillRunning(pid)) disconnect(); // the game exited: start looking again Sleep(100); // 10 updates a second is plenty for people } Three states matter and should be shown clearly: State Detect Show --- --- --- Connected and live The frame number advances The values Connected but stale The frame number has not changed for a second "paused or not responding", values greyed out Not connected No mapping found, or the process exited "waiting for Delve...", and keep looking Checking whether the process is still running uses a process handle opened with SYNCHRONIZE and WaitForSingleObject(handle, 0) (lesson 6.01: a process handle is signalled when it exits). The mapping itself stays valid while the tool has it open, even after the game exits, so the frame counter alone cannot tell "exited" from "frozen". Drawing in the console Lesson 5.09's techniques do the drawing: enable virtual terminal sequences, build the whole screen into one string starting with "cursor home", and write it in one call so it never flickers. The bars use the Unicode block characters ▁▂▃▄▅▆▇█ , written in UTF-8 after SetConsoleOutputCP(CP_UTF8) . The practice task computes the statistics and the bar characters from the history. Common mistakes !warning Treating an unchanged frame number as "the game exited" It also means paused or frozen. Check the process handle separately. !warning Reading as fast as possible People cannot read 1,000 updates a second, and it wastes a core. 10 to 30 per second is plenty. !warning Crashing when the game restarts Unmap, close and go back to searching; the new copy has a new process id and a new block. Check yourself quiz ? What three connection states should a monitoring tool show? + Live, stale (paused or frozen), and not connected - Starting, running and closed - Fast, slow and very slow - Debug, Release and unknown Stale and not connected look similar in the numbers but mean very different things to the person watching. ? How does the tool find the game's telemetry? - It searches the whole of memory for the magic number - It reads a file the game writes to the desktop + It opens the mapping named with each delve.exe 's process id - It attaches as a debugger and reads the game's variables Naming the mapping with the process id keeps two running copies of the game apart. It opens it read-only and checks the header before trusting it. ? How does the panel draw without flickering? - It clears the console before each line - It redraws only once per second - It uses a second console window + It writes the whole screen as one string, once Clearing and redrawing line by line is what causes flicker. ? How does the tool tell "the game is paused" from "the game has exited"? + By whether its process handle is signalled - Both are shown by the frame number - The tool cannot tell The mapping outlives the game while the tool holds it open. ? Why does the tool include the process id when opening the mapping? - Mapping names must be numbers + Each running copy uses a name with its id - To make the name secret It lets several copies run side by side. ? How often should a stats panel read snapshots? - As fast as possible - Once a minute + About 10 to 30 times a second Faster than people can read wastes CPU for nothing.

title: Frame-time history and a sparkline
where: 12.05 A Live Stats Panel for Your Game
body: Build FrameHistory , which keeps the last capacity frame times (milliseconds) for the stats panel. - push(ms) adds a sample, dropping the oldest when full. - min() , max() , average() over the stored samples (0 when empty). - sparkline() returns one character per sample, oldest first, chosen from the eight levels " ▁▂▃▄▅▆▇█" without the space, that is the characters ▁▂▃▄▅▆▇█ (as UTF-8 strings). The tallest bar ( █ ) is the maximum; a sample v gets level round(7 v / max) , from 0 ( ▁ ) to 7 ( █ ). If the maximum is 0, every sample is ▁ . Return the characters joined into one UTF-8 std::string . push 8, 8, 16, 8 - min 8, max 16, average 10 sparkline = "▅▅█▅" (7 8 / 16 = 3.5, rounds to 4: ▅)

title: 12.06  Versioning the Interface Between a Game and Its Tools
match: 12.06 Versioning the Interface Between a Game and Its Tools
body: The game will change: new fields in the telemetry, new commands on the pipe. Tools built for last month's game should keep working, and new tools should cope with old games. This lesson designs for that: append-only layouts with a size field, version and capability checks, feature flags, and the rules that let both sides evolve without breaking each other. Why interfaces need versions A tool and a game are built separately, often by different people, and updated at different times. Every shared structure and message format is an interface , and like lesson 4.05's DLL interfaces, changing it carelessly breaks whoever is on the other side: - Insert a field in the middle of the telemetry struct, and every older tool reads the wrong offsets: health shows the floor number. - Rename a pipe command, and old tools send commands the game no longer understands. The goal is compatibility in both directions : Situation Should --- --- New tool, old game Read what the old game provides; hide features it lacks Old tool, new game Keep working with the fields it knows; ignore new ones Truly incompatible change Be detected and reported clearly, never misread Rule 1: append, never insert or reorder Add new fields only at the end of a structure. Then every field keeps its offset forever, and an older tool reading the beginning of a newer block reads exactly what it expects. cpp-norun struct TelemetryV2 // version 2 = version 1 + new fields at the end { // ---- version 1: never change these ---- std::uint32_t magic, version, size; std::atomic<std::uint32_t sequence; std::uint64_t frame; float frameMs; std::int32_t floor, playerX, playerY, playerHp, playerMaxHp, monstersAlive; std::uint32_t turn; // ---- added in version 2 ---- std::uint32_t features; // capability flags, below float cpuMs; // time spent in update std::int32_t itemsOnFloor; }; Removing a field becomes "stop updating it" (leave it in place, write 0), never actually deleting it. Rule 2: the size field tells the reader what exists The header's size is the size of the struct the writer used. A reader then knows exactly which fields are present: - A field whose end offset is within size exists and is valid. - A field beyond size does not exist in this game: show "not available". cpp-norun bool has(const TelemetryHeader& h, std::size_t fieldOffset, std::size_t fieldSize) { return fieldOffset + fieldSize <= h.size; } // has(header, offsetof(TelemetryV2, cpuMs), sizeof(float)) - is CPU time published? The reader copies min(h.size, sizeof(its own struct)) bytes and zero-fills the rest, so an old tool reading a new game copies only what it knows, and a new tool reading an old game gets zeros it knows not to trust. Rule 3: major and minor versions Some changes cannot be made compatible (a field's meaning changes, units change from pixels to tiles). Split the version into major and minor : Change Version --- --- Fields added at the end Minor + 1: compatible, nothing breaks Meaning or layout of existing data changed Major + 1: incompatible; tools for the old major must refuse A tool accepts any minor version of the majors it supports, and clearly reports "this game uses telemetry format 3.x; this tool supports 2.x" otherwise. The practice task implements this decision. Rule 4: feature flags for optional things Not everything is "present or not" by version. A features bit field (lesson 1.02's bits) says which optional parts the game actually provides right now: 0x1 "AI debug data", 0x2 "physics counters". Tools show panels only for set flags. It also lets a shipping build publish less than a development build of the same version. Messages on pipes The same rules apply to messages (lesson 12.01's pipes): - Every message starts with a type and a length , so a reader can skip types it does not know. - New message types get new numbers; old numbers are never reused for different meanings. - On connecting, each side sends a hello with its version and features, and both use the common subset. Common mistakes !warning Inserting a field in the middle "where it belongs" Every later field moves, and every older tool misreads them. Append. !warning Reading fields beyond the writer's size They contain whatever is in memory there, or nothing. Check against size . !warning Silently accepting an unknown major version Refuse with a clear message; misread data is worse than none. Check yourself quiz ? What does "append-only" mean for a shared layout? + New fields go only at the end; old ones never move or change - The writer may only add data and never overwrite it - The file grows by one snapshot each frame - Readers may only read the newest field Old readers then keep finding every field they know at the same offset. ? How does a reader use the size field? + A field exists only if it lies within the writer's size - It refuses to read anything if the sizes differ - It always reads its own size, whatever the writer says - It uses the size to find the end of the string data A newer tool reading an older game sees the new fields as missing instead of reading garbage. The reader copies the smaller of the two sizes and treats the rest as unavailable. ? What are feature flags for? - Turning debug features on in Release builds - Recording which version of the tool is running + Saying which optional parts the writer provides now - Marking which fields have changed since the last frame A field can exist in the layout but be unused right now; the flag says whether to trust it. ? Where must new fields go in a shared structure? + At the end, so old offsets stay - Wherever they fit best - At the start Inserting moves later fields and breaks older readers. ? A tool's struct is 64 bytes; the game's header says size 48. What does that mean? - The game is newer than the tool + The game is older; fields past 48 are missing - The data is corrupt and unusable The size field tells the reader what the writer provided. ? When must the major version change? - Whenever a field is added - Every release + When existing data changes meaning or layout Additions at the end only need a minor version.

title: Can this tool read that game?
match: Can this tool read that game?
where: 12.06 Versioning the Interface Between a Game and Its Tools
body: A tool supports telemetry major version toolMajor and knows minor versions up to toolMinor . A game publishes a header with its major , minor and size (bytes). Write check(toolMajor, toolMinor, gameMajor, gameMinor) : - different major versions: Incompatible ; - same major, game minor higher than the tool's: NewerGame (works; the tool ignores fields it does not know); - same major, game minor lower than the tool's: OlderGame (works; some fields will be missing); - otherwise Exact . Then fieldAvailable(gameSize, offset, size) : true if a field at offset of size bytes lies entirely within the game's struct size. Guard against overflow in offset + size .

title: 12.07  Testing and Hardening a Tool
body: A tool that crashes, hangs or shows wrong numbers is worse than none: people stop trusting it. This lesson hardens the chapter's tools: treating everything read from another process as untrusted input, validating snapshots, timeouts and reconnection, running with least privilege, and testing the logic separately from the platform code, including deliberately feeding it garbage. Everything from outside is untrusted The telemetry block, pipe messages and memory read from another process all come from a different program, which may be an older or newer version, half-initialised, crashed in the middle of writing, or simply buggy. Treat it exactly like a file from the internet: Check Why --- --- Header: magic, version, size (lesson 12.06) Is this even the right kind of data? Sizes and counts against limits A count of 2 billion monsters means corruption, not a busy floor Ranges Health between 0 and its maximum; positions inside the map; frame time positive and below, say, 10 seconds Consistency Frame number never goes backwards (except after a restart, which the process id change reveals) Strings Fixed-size character arrays must contain a terminator within their size (lesson 2.08) A value that fails a check is shown as invalid, not used to index arrays or size allocations. The practice task writes a validator returning a list of problems. Never hang Every wait in a tool needs a limit: - Sequence-lock reads retry a bounded number of times (lesson 12.04). - Pipe reads use overlapped I/O or a timeout, so a game that stops responding does not freeze the tool. - Opening the game's mapping happens on a timer, not in a tight loop. If the game is frozen, the tool should say so (lesson 12.05's "stale" state) and stay responsive. Least privilege The chapter's tools need very little: - Read-only views of the shared memory ( FILE_MAP_READ ). - PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION SYNCHRONIZE on the game's process, to watch whether it runs. - No administrator rights, ever: if a tool seems to need elevation, something in its design is wrong (lesson 6.08). Asking for little keeps the tool working for ordinary users and limits the harm any bug in it can do. Testing the logic Every practice task in this course has followed one structure: the logic (formatting, validation, version checks, statistics, protocols) is plain C++ with no Windows calls, tested in isolation; a thin platform layer does the Windows calls. That pays off most in tools: - Unit tests feed the logic known inputs, including recorded real snapshots, and check the outputs. - Garbage tests feed it random bytes, truncated blocks, wrong versions, extreme values. The tool must report problems, never crash. Chapter 17 automates this as fuzzing . - End-to-end tests run the real game with a scripted input and check the tool shows what was expected. Failure modes to rehearse Before calling a tool done, try each of these on purpose: 1. Start the tool with no game running. 2. Start the game, then the tool; close the game; start it again. 3. Pause the game in the debugger while the tool watches. 4. Run two copies of the game. 5. Run an older and a newer build of the game against the same tool. 6. Corrupt the shared block from a test program (write random bytes into it). A tool that handles all six calmly can be trusted. Common mistakes !warning Using an untrusted count to size an allocation A corrupt count of billions turns into a crash or an out-of-memory. Validate against a sensible limit first. !warning Waiting without a timeout A frozen game must not freeze its tools. !warning Testing only the happy path Rehearse the failure modes; they are what users will hit. Check yourself quiz ? Why treat data from another process as untrusted? - Because other processes may be run by hackers - Because Windows changes the data when copying it between processes + It may be another version, half written or corrupt - Because shared memory is slower than normal memory A count of 3 billion monsters is more likely a bug or a layout mismatch than a real number. ? Which waits in a tool need limits? + All of them, including retries and pipe reads - Only connection attempts - Only pipe reads - None, if the game is well written A tool that hangs because the game froze is no help in finding why the game froze. ? What does "garbage testing" mean for a tool? - Running the tool on an old, slow computer - Deleting the tool's temporary files after each test - Testing the tool with no game running + Feeding its logic random and broken data to check it copes Keeping the logic free of Windows calls is what makes it easy to feed it such data in tests. ? A telemetry snapshot says 3 billion monsters are alive. What should the tool do? + Reject the snapshot as invalid and report it - Display 3 billion - Allocate an array of 3 billion entries Implausible values mean corruption or a version mismatch. ? Why keep a tool's logic free of Windows calls? - Windows calls are slow + So it can be unit-tested without a game - The compiler requires it A thin platform layer around pure logic is easy to test. ? What rights does a read-only stats tool need on the game's process? - Full access - Administrator rights + Limited query information and synchronize Least privilege: nothing more than its job needs.

title: Validate a snapshot
body: Write problems(snapshot, previousFrame) , which checks a telemetry snapshot from Delve and returns a list of problem names, in this order, for each check that fails: Check Problem name --- --- magic is 0x54564C44 "magic" version is 1 "version" size is at least 48 "size" frame is not less than previousFrame "frame went backwards" frameMs is greater than 0 and less than 10000 "frame time" floor is between 1 and 99 "floor" playerMaxHp is between 1 and 10000, and playerHp between 0 and playerMaxHp "health" monstersAlive is between 0 and 10000 "monsters" If the magic number is wrong, return only { "magic" } : nothing else in the block can be trusted. An empty list means the snapshot is valid. Remember that frameMs could be NaN (not a number): it must fail the check.

title: A watch list
body: Show named values from your game and highlight the ones that changed. frame 100: hp 20, x 5.0, enemies 3 frame 101: hp 17 , x 5.5 , enemies 3 ( changed since the last frame)

title: A telemetry message
body: Define the message your game sends to its own tools, with a version so both can change. TelemetryV2: magic "XNTL", version 2, frame 5521, player (12.5, 4.0), hp 17, enemies 3 tool built for v1 reads v2: ok (ignores the new field) tool built for v3 reads v2: missing field - default

title: Sample, don't flood
body: Send telemetry at a steady rate instead of every frame. game runs at 144 fps, tool wants 10 updates a second frames 0..143: 10 samples sent (every 14.4 frames on average) a value that changed a lot between samples: max kept, not just the last

title: Paging through bytes
body: Show a large block of your own program's memory one page at a time, like a memory viewer. page 1 of 16 (256 bytes per page) 00000000 48 65 6c 6c 6f 00 00 00 ... Hello... next page, previous page, jump to offset 0x400

title: A stats panel
body: Turn telemetry samples from your game into the numbers and text a stats panel shows. FPS 143 (min 120) frame 6.9 ms Player (12.5, 4.0) hp 17/20 Enemies 3 Bullets 41 memory 212 MB (+4 in the last 10 s)

title: 13.01  How Games Support Mods
body: Many of the most loved games owe much of their life to mods : changes and additions made by players. Games that support modding on purpose provide layers for it: replaceable data and assets, scripting, plugin APIs and official editors. This lesson surveys those layers, how mods are found and loaded in order, how conflicts arise, and the responsibilities that come with letting other people's code run inside your game. Layers of modding Layer What modders change Example Risk to the game --- --- --- --- Data Numbers and definitions: items, monsters, levels A monsters.ini with tougher trolls Low: data is validated on load Assets Textures, models, sounds, text A new tile set or translation Low Scripts Behaviour, through an embedded language (lesson 10.08) A new boss fight in Lua Medium: limited by the API the game exposes Plugins Native code (DLLs) through a plugin API A new rendering effect or game system High: native code can do anything the game can Official tools Whole levels and campaigns, in the developers' editor Map editors, mod kits Low to medium Delve will support the first four in this chapter: data and asset overrides (lesson 13.02), and a plugin API for DLLs (13.03, 13.04), with scripting as an extension of lesson 10.08. Mods as a folder with a manifest Each mod is a folder with a small description, its manifest : mods\ tougher-trolls\ mod.ini name, version, author, which game versions it supports data\monsters.ini overrides the base game's file lantern-light\ mod.ini plugin.dll native code (lesson 13.04) textures\light.png ini ; mod.ini name = Lantern light version = 1.2.0 author = Ada game = 1.0, 1.1 requires = tougher-trolls The game reads every manifest at start-up, shows a list where players enable mods and choose their order, and refuses mods for incompatible game versions with a clear message, rather than loading them and crashing. Load order and conflicts When two mods change the same thing, one has to win. Games resolve this with a load order : mods later in the list override earlier ones, and the base game is first. Whole-file replacement means the last mod's file wins completely and the earlier mod's changes vanish: a conflict . Smarter games merge at the level of individual entries, so tougher-trolls can change troll health and easy-mode change goblin damage without fighting (lesson 13.02's practice task). Dependencies ( requires ) add ordering constraints: a mod must load after the mods it builds on (lesson 13.04's practice task sorts them). Responsibilities Supporting mods means letting other people's work run inside your game, for your players. That brings duties: - Stability : a broken mod should fail clearly ("mod X failed to load: ..."), not crash the game or corrupt saves. Lesson 13.07 covers isolation. - Safety : native plugins can do anything, so players should only install them from sources they trust, and the game should make it obvious when native code is involved. Data and script mods are much safer, which is why many games restrict mods to them. - Saves : record which mods (and versions) a save was made with, and warn when loading it without them. - Online play : anything affecting other players must be controlled by the server, and mods that change gameplay usually belong only in single-player or in servers that opt in. Modding games you did not make is governed by their licence and community rules. Common mistakes !warning Loading every mod without checking versions Read the manifest and refuse incompatible mods with a clear message. !warning Silent conflicts Show which mods change the same files or entries, so players can fix their load order. !warning Letting mods corrupt saves Record the mod list in each save, and warn before loading it with different mods. Check yourself quiz ? Name the layers through which a game can support mods. - Debug builds, Release builds and test builds - Patching the exe, injecting DLLs and editing memory + Data overrides, assets, scripting, native plugins and official tools - Save files, screenshots and settings Each layer gives modders more power and the game more risk; data overrides are the safest. ? What is a mod conflict? + Two mods changing the same entry, so only the later one counts - A mod that crashes the game when loaded - A mod made for a different version of the game - Two mods with the same name Load order decides which change wins, which is why games let players order their mods. ? What responsibilities come with supporting mods? - Testing every mod anyone publishes - Fixing bugs in other people's mods - Making sure every mod works with every other mod + Failing safely, flagging native code, and keeping online play fair The game cannot make mods correct, but it can make their failures safe and visible. Recording the mods in each save also helps when diagnosing problems later. ? What decides which mod wins when two change the same entry? + The load order: later mods win - Whichever mod file is newest - Whichever mod is largest The base game is first; each mod in the list overrides what came before. ? Why are data and script mods safer than plugin DLLs? - They are smaller to download + They can only do what the game exposes - They load faster at start-up Many games limit mods to data and scripts for this reason. ? What does a mod's manifest typically contain? - Its source code and build files - A copy of the game's own data + Name, version, author, and requirements The game uses it to list, order and check mods.

title: 13.02  Data Mods and Scripting
body: The simplest and safest mods change data. This lesson gives Delve a layered file system that looks for each file in the enabled mods (last first) before the base game, then improves on whole-file replacement by merging data entries so several mods can change different things in the same file. It ends by opening the game's scripting to mods, with limits. A layered file system The game never opens data\monsters.ini directly. It asks the virtual file system for monsters.ini , which searches the layers from the top: layer 3: mods\easy-mode\data\ (last in the load order: searched first) layer 2: mods\tougher-trolls\data\ layer 1: data\ (the base game: searched last) cpp-norun class VirtualFileSystem { public: void addLayer(std::filesystem::path root) { m_layers.push_back(std::move(root)); } // base first, mods after // The path of the file that wins, or nothing if no layer has it. std::optional<std::filesystem::path find(const std::string& relative) const { for (auto it{ m_layers.rbegin() }; it != m_layers.rend(); ++it) // top layer first if (auto candidate{ it / relative }; std::filesystem::exists(candidate)) return candidate; return std::nullopt; } // Every layer's version, base first: for merging. std::vector<std::filesystem::path findAll(const std::string& relative) const; private: std::vector<std::filesystem::path m_layers; }; Every asset the game loads, textures, sounds, levels, goes through find . Replacing a texture is then just putting a file with the same name in a mod folder. This is the same idea games use for their own patches: a patch is a layer above the original data. Validate paths. A mod asks for files by relative name; reject names containing .. or absolute paths, so a mod cannot reach files outside its own and the game's folders (lesson 17.04). Merging instead of replacing Whole-file replacement makes mods fight: two mods both shipping monsters.ini means only the last one's file is used. Merging works entry by entry: 1. Load the base game's monsters.ini into a map of section.key → value (lesson 10.08's INI parser). 2. For each enabled mod in load order, load its monsters.ini (if any) and overwrite only the keys it contains . 3. The result is the base game plus every mod's changes, with later mods winning only where they touch the same key. base: troll.health = 120 goblin.damage = 4 tougher-trolls: troll.health = 200 easy-mode: goblin.damage = 2 merged: troll.health = 200 goblin.damage = 2 both mods apply The practice task implements the merge and reports which keys were changed by more than one mod, the true conflicts a mod manager should show. Mod scripts If the game embeds a scripting language (lesson 10.08), mods can add behaviour too: each mod's scripts\ folder is run at start-up, and scripts register for events the game publishes ("monster died", "level loaded"; lesson 13.05 builds the event system): lua -- mods/lantern-light/scripts/main.lua on("level_loaded", function(floor) if floor = 3 then message("It is getting dark. Your lantern flickers.") end end) The game decides exactly which functions scripts may call ( on , message , spawn ...), and each mod's scripts should run in their own environment so they cannot overwrite another mod's functions. A script error is caught, reported with the mod's name, and the mod is disabled for the session, without taking the game down (lesson 13.07). Common mistakes !warning Opening files directly in game code Go through the virtual file system so mods (and patches) can override them. !warning Accepting .. in paths from mods A mod could then read or overwrite files anywhere. Reject them. !warning Whole-file replacement for shared data Merge entries so independent mods can coexist. Check yourself quiz ? What is a virtual file system for mods? - A copy of the game's files on a separate drive - A zip file holding every mod + A layer that looks in enabled mods' folders before the base game - A database of mod names and authors The game asks for monsters.ini and gets the highest-priority mod's copy, or the base game's if no mod has one. ? How does merging data from several mods work? - The last mod's file replaces all the others - Each mod's file is used in turn, one per play session - Entries are averaged across all mods + Apply each mod's keys over the base entries, in load order Two mods changing different keys of the same file then both take effect. ? What should happen when a mod's script has an error? - The game exits with an error message + Report it with the mod's name, disable that mod, and carry on - The game ignores the error and runs the rest of the script - The game deletes the mod Naming the mod tells the player what to remove or update. ? In which order does the layered file system search? + Last mod first, down to the base game - From the base game up to the last mod - Alphabetically The topmost layer that has the file wins. ? Two mods change different keys of monsters.ini . With merging, what happens? - Only the last mod's file is used + Both changes apply - The game refuses to start Merging overwrites only the keys each mod contains. ? Why reject .. in file names requested by mods? - Windows does not allow it - It is slower + It could reach files outside the allowed folders Mods must stay within their own layer.

title: Merge mod data
body: Write mergeData(base, mods) . base maps "section.key" to a value. mods is the list of enabled mods in load order; each has a name and its own map of entries. Return: - values : the merged data, starting from base and applying each mod's entries in order, later mods overwriting earlier ones; - source : for each key in values , the name of the mod that set it last, or "base" ; - conflicts : the keys set by two or more mods (whatever the base had), in alphabetical order. base: troll.health 120, goblin.damage 4 tougher-trolls: troll.health 200 easy-mode: goblin.damage 2, troll.health 90 - troll.health 90 (from easy-mode), goblin.damage 2 (from easy-mode) conflicts: { "troll.health" }

title: 13.03  Designing a Plugin Interface
body: A plugin is native code built separately from the game, possibly with a different compiler version, that the game loads at run time. The interface between them must therefore be a stable C interface : plain types, function pointers, explicit versions and sizes. This lesson designs Delve's plugin API in both directions (the host API the game offers plugins, and the plugin API plugins offer the game) using lessons 4.05, 3.04 and 12.06. Two directions - The host API is what the game lets plugins do. It defines the plugin's powers, so it is designed carefully and kept small. - The plugin API is what every plugin must provide, so the game can initialise it, call it each frame, and shut it down. Rule 1: a C interface, not C++ classes The game and a plugin may be built with different compilers, settings or standard library versions. Lesson 4.05 explained why std::string , std::vector and C++ classes with virtual functions must not cross that boundary. The interface uses only: - integers, floats, and fixed-size plain structs; - const char strings in UTF-8, valid only for the duration of the call (copy them if you need them later); - function pointers; - opaque handles ( typedef struct DelveEntity DelveEntityHandle; , or plain integer ids, lesson 3.10). Rule 2: tables of function pointers, with a version and a size Both directions are structs of function pointers , the hand-made vtables of lesson 3.05's practice task, each starting with lesson 12.06's version and size: cpp-norun // delve_plugin.h: the only header plugins include. C-compatible. pragma once include <stdint.h define DELVE_API_VERSION_MAJOR 1 define DELVE_API_VERSION_MINOR 0 typedef struct DelveHostApi { uint32_t size; // sizeof(DelveHostApi) as the game was built: fields past it do not exist uint16_t versionMajor, versionMinor; void ( log)(const char message); int ( spawnMonster)(const char kind, int x, int y); // returns an entity id, or -1 int ( giveItem)(const char itemId, int count); // returns how many did not fit int ( playerHealth)(void); void ( subscribe)(const char eventName, void ( handler)(const char eventName, int64_t value, void user), void user); // version 1.1 and later add fields here, at the end only } DelveHostApi; typedef struct DelvePluginApi { uint32_t size; uint16_t versionMajor, versionMinor; const char name; int ( init)(const DelveHostApi host); // return 0 for success void ( update)(double dt); // may be null if the plugin needs no per-frame work void ( shutdown)(void); } DelvePluginApi; // The one function every plugin DLL exports: // extern "C" __declspec(dllexport) int delvePluginEntry(DelvePluginApi out); // The game passes a zeroed struct whose size it sets; the plugin fills it in. Why this shape: - One exported function ( delvePluginEntry ) instead of many keeps GetProcAddress lookups to one and the export table simple (lesson 4.05). - Function pointers in a struct let the game add functions later (at the end, lesson 12.06) without breaking old plugins. - size and the version let each side check what the other supports: a plugin built for API 1.0 runs on a 1.3 game; a plugin needing 1.3 refuses politely on a 1.0 game. - void user in callbacks lets a plugin get back its own state when the game calls it, since C function pointers carry no data (lesson 3.04). Rule 3: ownership is explicit Every pointer crossing the boundary has a documented owner and lifetime: - Strings passed into a plugin call are valid only during the call. - The host API table stays valid until shutdown returns. - Memory a plugin allocates, the plugin frees; memory the game allocates, the game frees (lesson 4.05: different heaps). Write these rules in comments in the header: it is the plugin authors' only documentation. Rule 4: the host API decides what plugins can do Every function in DelveHostApi is a capability given to code you did not write. Expose gameplay-level operations (spawn, give, read health, subscribe to events), validated like console commands (lesson 11.07), not raw pointers into the game's internals. A plugin that can only call spawnMonster("goblin", x, y) cannot corrupt the entity storage; one handed a pointer to it can. Native code can still do anything in principle (it runs in your process), but a good API means well-behaved plugins never need to. Common mistakes !warning C++ types in the interface std::string , std::vector , exceptions and classes do not cross a DLL boundary safely. Use C types. !warning No version or size The first change to the API breaks every existing plugin silently. !warning Exposing internal pointers Give plugins operations, not access to your data structures. !warning Throwing exceptions across the boundary C++ exceptions must not escape a plugin into the game (or the reverse). Catch them at the boundary and return error codes. Check yourself quiz ? What are the host API and the plugin API? + What the game offers plugins, and what each plugin offers the game - The host API runs on the server; the plugin API runs on the client - They are the same table, used in both directions - The host API is for Debug builds; the plugin API is for Release builds Two tables, two directions: the game calls into plugins, and plugins call back into the game. The plugin API lets the game initialise, update and shut each plugin down. ? What may cross the plugin boundary? + Numbers, plain structs, C strings, function pointers and handles - std::string , std::vector and any C++ class - Only integers - Anything, provided both sides use the same header Standard library types can differ in layout and heap between builds, so only simple C types are safe. ? How should errors cross the boundary? - As C++ exceptions, caught by the other side - By calling exit with an error code + As return codes; exceptions never cross - They should not; plugins must never report errors An exception thrown through a C interface into code built differently is undefined behaviour. ? Why is the plugin interface written in C rather than C++ classes? + Only plain C types are compatible across builds - C is faster than C++ at run time - DLLs cannot contain any C++ code Lesson 4.05's rules for DLL boundaries. ? Why does every API table start with a size and version? - To make the struct correctly aligned + So each side knows which functions the other has - Windows requires it for every DLL Lesson 12.06's versioning, applied to function tables. ? What is the void user parameter in the event callback for? - It holds the event's value - It is reserved for the game + The plugin's own state, handed back to it C function pointers carry no data; this pointer does.

title: Check a plugin's table
body: Before the game calls a plugin, it checks the PluginTable the plugin filled in. Write validatePlugin(table, hostMajor, hostMinor) , which returns a list of problems (empty if the plugin can be used), checking in this order: 1. size must be at least kMinimumSize (the size of version 1.0 of the table): otherwise "table too small" , and stop. 2. versionMajor must equal hostMajor : otherwise "wrong major version" , and stop. 3. versionMinor must not be greater than hostMinor : otherwise "needs a newer game" . 4. name must not be null or empty: otherwise "no name" . 5. init and shutdown must not be null: otherwise "missing init" / "missing shutdown" . ( update is optional.) Then write callUpdate(table, dt) , which calls update only if it is not null and the table's size covers it, and returns whether it was called.

title: 13.04  Plugins as DLLs
body: With the interface designed, Delve can load plugins: find each enabled mod's DLL, load it safely, call its entry point, validate what it returns, order plugins by their dependencies, call them each frame, and unload them cleanly. This lesson writes the plugin manager, and adds hot reloading of your own plugins during development. Loading one plugin cpp-norun using EntryFn = int ( )(DelvePluginApi ); std::optional<LoadedPlugin loadPlugin(const std::filesystem::path& dll, const DelveHostApi& host) { // Load by full path, searching only the plugin's own folder and the system for its dependencies (lesson 5.08). HMODULE module{ LoadLibraryExW(dll.c_str(), nullptr, LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DLL_LOAD_DIR LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DEFAULT_DIRS) }; if (!module) { logError("could not load ", dll, ": error ", GetLastError()); return std::nullopt; } auto entry{ reinterpret_cast<EntryFn (GetProcAddress(module, "delvePluginEntry")) }; DelvePluginApi api{}; api.size = sizeof(api); // tell the plugin how big our table is if (!entry entry(&api) != 0 !validatePlugin(api, DELVE_API_VERSION_MAJOR, DELVE_API_VERSION_MINOR).empty()) { logError(dll, " is not a valid Delve plugin"); FreeLibrary(module); return std::nullopt; } if (api.init(&host) != 0) { logError(api.name, " failed to initialise"); FreeLibrary(module); return std::nullopt; } return LoadedPlugin{ module, api }; } Each step can fail, and each failure is logged with the plugin's path or name and leaves the game running without it. validatePlugin is lesson 13.03's practice task. Load order with dependencies Mods declare what they require (lesson 13.01's manifest). A plugin must be initialised after everything it requires, and shut down before them. Finding such an order is a topological sort : repeatedly take a mod whose requirements are all already placed. If at some point no mod can be placed, the requirements form a cycle (A requires B, B requires A), and those mods cannot be loaded. The practice task implements it, preferring the player's chosen order where the dependencies allow. Calling plugins cpp-norun void PluginManager::update(double dt) { for (LoadedPlugin& p : m_plugins) // in load order if (p.api.update) p.api.update(dt); } void PluginManager::shutdown() { for (auto it{ m_plugins.rbegin() }; it != m_plugins.rend(); ++it) // reverse order { it- api.shutdown(); FreeLibrary(it- module); // after this, no pointer into the DLL may be used } m_plugins.clear(); } Shutting down in reverse order mirrors lesson 2.04's destructor order: a plugin may depend on those loaded before it. Before FreeLibrary , the game must forget every callback the plugin registered (event handlers, console commands), or a later event would call into unloaded code (lesson 4.05). Hot reloading your own plugins During development, rebuilding a plugin and reloading it without restarting the game makes iteration fast: 1. Watch the plugin's DLL file for changes (lesson 10.06's ReadDirectoryChangesW ). 2. Copy the new DLL to a temporary name and load the copy, because Windows locks a loaded DLL file and the compiler could not overwrite it otherwise. (The PDB has the same problem; give each build a unique PDB name.) 3. Call the old plugin's shutdown , remove its callbacks, FreeLibrary it, then init the new one. 4. State that must survive the reload (a debug tool's settings) is saved by shutdown and restored by init , or kept on the game's side. Hot reloading is for your own development builds; players restart the game to update mods. Common mistakes !warning Loading plugins by bare name Use full paths and restricted search flags, so a plugin's dependencies cannot be hijacked (lesson 5.08). !warning Keeping callbacks after unloading Unregister everything a plugin registered before FreeLibrary . !warning Shutting down in load order Shut down in reverse, so dependents go before what they depend on. Check yourself quiz ? What are the steps of loading a plugin? - Copy its source into the game and recompile + Load by full path, find and call its entry point, validate, then init - Call LoadLibrary with the bare file name and start calling its functions - Run the DLL as a separate exe and connect to it with a pipe Every step can fail, and each failure must leave the game running without that plugin. ? In what order are plugins initialised and shut down? - Alphabetically, both times - In the order the files were created + By dependencies, and shut down in reverse - All at once on separate threads A plugin's dependencies are ready before it starts and still there while it shuts down. ? How does hot reloading work? - Overwrite the loaded DLL file while the game runs - Restart the game automatically when the DLL changes - Load the new DLL alongside the old and call both + Load a copy of the new build, unload the old one cleanly, init the new Loading a copy keeps the original file free for the compiler to overwrite next time. Remove the old plugin's callbacks before unloading it. ? What does a topological sort of mods produce? + An order with each mod after its requirements - The mods sorted by their names - The mods sorted by their sizes A cycle in the requirements makes such an order impossible. ? Why copy a plugin DLL before loading it for hot reloading? - Copied DLLs load faster + A loaded DLL's file is locked against writes - To make the file read-only Loading the copy leaves the original free for the compiler. ? Why must a plugin's callbacks be removed before FreeLibrary ? - To save memory in the game - Windows requires it for every DLL + Calling them later would jump into unloaded code A dangling function pointer is as dangerous as a dangling data pointer.

title: 13.05  Instrumenting Functions in Your Own Program
match: 13.05 Instrumenting Functions in Your Own Program
body: Instrumentation means adding observation points to a program: measuring how long functions take, counting calls, recording events, letting plugins react to what happens. The cleanest way is to design the points in from the start: scoped timers, an event bus that plugins and tools subscribe to, and indirection through function pointers where behaviour should be replaceable. This lesson builds those, and looks at compiler-assisted instrumentation for your own builds. Observation points you design in Code becomes observable and extensible when it announces what it does at well-chosen places. Three patterns cover nearly everything: Pattern Use Example --- --- --- Scoped timers How long did this take? PROFILE_SCOPE("ai") at the top of the AI system Events Something happened; whoever cares can react "monster died", "level loaded", "item picked up" Replaceable functions Let a plugin or test change one behaviour A damage formula stored in a function pointer the plugin can replace Scoped timers Lesson 8.08's ScopedTimer , wrapped in a macro so it can be compiled out: cpp-norun ifdef DELVE_PROFILE define PROFILE_SCOPE(name) ProfileScope profileScope_ __LINE__{ name } else define PROFILE_SCOPE(name) ((void)0) endif void updateMonsters(World& w) { PROFILE_SCOPE("monsters"); // ... } Each ProfileScope records a start and end time into a per-thread buffer; once a frame the samples are summarised (lesson 8.08's practice task) and published through the telemetry channel (lesson 12.04), where the stats panel graphs them. That is a complete profiling pipeline built from this course's pieces. An event bus Hard-wiring "when a monster dies, update the quest, play a sound, drop loot, notify plugins" into the combat code makes it grow without end. An event bus decouples them: the combat code publishes "monster died", and any number of systems, plugins and tools subscribe to it. Design details that matter: - Subscriptions return a handle used to unsubscribe, which is essential for plugins being unloaded (lesson 13.04). - Priorities decide the order handlers run in, when it matters (the quest system before the "you win" check). - Unsubscribing during dispatch (a handler that removes itself) must be safe: mark the handler removed and clean up after the dispatch finishes, rather than erasing from the list being iterated (lesson 3.07). - A handler that throws must not stop the others, and must be reported (lesson 13.07). The practice task builds this bus. Replaceable functions Where you want behaviour to be swappable, put a function pointer at the decision point, with a default: cpp-norun using DamageFn = int ( )(const Attack&, const Defence&, Random&); DamageFn g_damageFormula{ &defaultDamage }; // plugins may set this through the host API int resolveHit(const Attack& a, const Defence& d, Random& rng) { return g_damageFormula(a, d, rng); } Tests use the same indirection to substitute a fixed formula. It costs one indirect call (lesson 3.04), which is nothing outside the hottest loops. Compiler-assisted instrumentation For deeper investigation of your own builds, MSVC can insert a call at the start and end of every function: compile with /Gh (calls a function named _penter on entry) and /GH ( _pexit on exit), which you write yourself, for example to record a call trace or count calls per function. It slows the program considerably, so it belongs in a special build configuration, but it instruments every function without touching the source. For instrumenting functions of your own program at run time in test builds, Microsoft's open-source Detours library intercepts calls to chosen functions (including Windows API functions your program calls) and redirects them to your own code, which can record the call and pass it on. It is useful for testing how your program behaves when, say, file writes fail. As with the rest of this chapter, it is for your own programs and your own test builds. Common mistakes !warning Hard-coding every reaction at the source of an event Publish events and let systems subscribe; the source stays small. !warning Erasing handlers while dispatching Mark them and remove them after the dispatch. !warning Leaving profiling in shipping builds by accident Compile it out with a macro. Check yourself quiz ? Name three designed-in instrumentation patterns. - Breakpoints, data breakpoints and tracepoints + Scoped timers, an event bus, and replaceable functions - Code injection, function hooking and memory patching - Asserts, static asserts and logging These are observation points the program offers on purpose, so tools and plugins need no tricks. ? How should a handler that unsubscribes itself during dispatch be handled? + It is marked as removed and actually removed after the dispatch loop finishes - It is removed immediately, and the loop restarts from the beginning - Unsubscribing during dispatch is forbidden and throws an exception - It is ignored until the next frame, when it is called once more Changing a list while iterating it can skip handlers or read freed memory. ? When is compiler-inserted entry and exit instrumentation appropriate? - In every build, because it costs nothing - In Release builds shipped to players - Never; it does not work with MSVC + In special tracing builds of your own program /Gh and /GH call a hook on every function entry and exit, which is far too slow for normal builds. ? What problem does an event bus solve? + The sender need not know who reacts - It makes events happen faster - It replaces function calls entirely Publishers and subscribers are decoupled. ? Why must subscribing return something that can unsubscribe? - To count subscribers + Handlers that go away must be removed - Because events are expensive Lesson 13.04's unloading depends on it. ? What do MSVC's /Gh and /GH options do? - Turn on optimisation - Generate debug symbols + Call hooks on every function entry and exit You supply those functions, for example to trace calls.

title: An event bus
where: 13.05 Instrumenting Functions in Your Own Program
body: Build EventBus for Delve. - subscribe(event, priority, handler) registers a std::function<void(long long value) for an event name and returns a subscription id (any number unique to this bus). - publish(event, value) calls every handler for that event, highest priority first ; handlers with equal priority run in the order they subscribed. It returns how many handlers ran. - unsubscribe(id) removes a subscription and returns whether it existed. It must be safe to call from inside a handler during publish , including for the handler itself or for one that has not run yet in this dispatch (which then must not run). - Handlers subscribed during a publish do not run in that same dispatch.

title: 13.06  A Debug Menu Inside the Game
match: 13.06 A Debug Menu Inside the Game
body: A console is fast for people who remember commands; a debug menu drawn over the game is faster for everyone else: checkboxes for god mode and map reveal, sliders for monster speed, buttons to spawn things, live graphs. This lesson registers tweakable variables in one place, draws them with Dear ImGui (previewing chapter 14), and lets plugins add their own sections. Tweakables Game feel comes from dozens of numbers: player move time, monster sight range, screen shake strength, drop chances. Changing them by editing code and rebuilding is slow. A tweakable is a variable registered once with a name, a range and a description, which the debug menu (and console, and save of settings) can then show and change while the game runs: cpp-norun float g_moveSlideSeconds{ 0.12f }; int g_sightRange{ 8 }; bool g_godMode{ false }; void registerTweakables(Tweakables& t) { t.addFloat("player.slide", &g_moveSlideSeconds, 0.0f, 0.5f, "Seconds to slide between tiles"); t.addInt ("monster.sight", &g_sightRange, 1, 30, "Tiles at which monsters notice the player"); t.addBool ("cheat.god", &g_godMode, "Player takes no damage"); } The registry stores, for each name, a pointer to the variable, its type and its limits. Everything else is built on that table: - the debug menu draws a slider or checkbox per entry, grouped by the part of the name before the dot; - the console gets set monster.sight 12 and get player.slide for free (lesson 11.07); - values can be saved to tweaks.ini and loaded at start-up (lesson 10.08), so a good setting found while playing survives. Setting from text must parse, range-check and clamp, which is exactly the part worth testing: the practice task builds the registry's core. Drawing it with Dear ImGui Dear ImGui draws interfaces in immediate mode : every frame, the code that draws the menu simply calls one function per widget, and the function returns whether the user changed it. There is no separate interface state to keep in sync. Chapter 14 covers it fully; here is enough for a menu: cpp-norun void drawDebugMenu(Tweakables& t, Game& game) { ImGui::Begin("Debug"); if (ImGui::CollapsingHeader("Cheats")) { ImGui::Checkbox("God mode", &g_godMode); if (ImGui::Button("Reveal map")) game.revealMap(); if (ImGui::Button("Full health")) game.player.health = game.player.maxHealth; } if (ImGui::CollapsingHeader("Tweakables")) for (Tweakable& tw : t.all()) tw.drawWidget(); // SliderFloat / SliderInt / Checkbox by type if (ImGui::CollapsingHeader("Performance")) ImGui::PlotLines("Frame ms", frameHistory.data(), frameHistory.size()); ImGui::End(); } ImGui is added with vcpkg ( imgui sdl2-binding,sdl2-renderer-binding , lesson 4.06), initialised once with the SDL window and renderer, and drawn last each frame, on top of the game. The menu opens with F1; while it has the mouse or keyboard focus, the game ignores that input ( ImGui::GetIO().WantCaptureMouse and WantCaptureKeyboard ). Plugin sections Plugins (lesson 13.04) can add their own sections: the host API gains addDebugSection(name, drawFunction, user) , the game calls each registered draw function inside the menu, and unregisters it when the plugin unloads. A plugin author then gets a place for their own debugging tools without touching the game. Keep it out of release builds Like the console's cheat commands (lesson 11.07), the menu and every tweakable that changes gameplay are compiled only into development builds. Tweakables that are really player settings (volume, shake) move to the real settings screen instead. Common mistakes !warning Tweaking values that are cached elsewhere If a system copied g_sightRange at start-up, changing it does nothing. Read tweakables where they are used. !warning No limits on tweakables A slider from 0 to a billion is useless and a typed value out of range can break the game. Give every tweakable a sensible range, and clamp. !warning The game reacting to clicks meant for the menu Check ImGui's capture flags before passing input to the game. Check yourself quiz ? What does the tweakable registry store for each entry? - Only the variable's current value - The source line where the variable is declared + Name, variable pointer, type, limits and description - A copy of the variable for each frame With the pointer and type, the menu can show and change the real variable directly. ? Why must setting a tweakable from text clamp the value? + So typed or loaded values cannot go outside the range the game is designed for - Because text cannot hold negative numbers - So the value always has the same number of digits - Because ImGui cannot show values outside the range A gravity of -9000 typed by mistake should not break the game. ? How do plugins add to the debug menu? - By drawing over the game window with their own ImGui context - By editing the game's menu source code - By registering tweakables only; sections are fixed + By registering a named section with a draw callback Removing the section on unload prevents the menu calling into an unloaded DLL. ? What does registering a tweakable give you? + One table that the menu and console are built from - A faster variable - A constant that cannot change Register once, use everywhere. ? What does "immediate mode" mean for Dear ImGui? - The interface appears instantly + The interface is described again every frame - The interface has no memory No separate widget objects to keep in sync with the data. ? Why check WantCaptureMouse before handling game input? - To find out where the mouse is - To enable the menu + So menu clicks do not also act in the game The menu and the game must not both react to the same input.

title: A tweakable registry
where: 13.06 A Debug Menu Inside the Game
body: Build Tweakables , the registry behind the debug menu. It holds integer, floating-point and boolean variables by name. - addInt(name, int value, min, max) , addFloat(name, float value, min, max) , addBool(name, bool value) register a variable. Registering a name again replaces the old entry. - set(name, text) parses text for that variable's type and stores it, clamped into its range: integers with std::stoi -like rules (the whole text must be a number), floats likewise, booleans from "true" / "false" / "1" / "0" / "on" / "off" . It returns a message: "name = value" on success (integers as digits, floats with std::to_string -like default formatting is not required: use std::format("{}", v) , booleans as true / false ), "unknown: name" for an unknown name, or "bad value: text" if the text cannot be parsed. On failure the variable is unchanged. - get(name) returns the current value as text in the same format, or std::nullopt for an unknown name. - names() returns all names, sorted. int sight = 8; addInt("monster.sight", &sight, 1, 30) set("monster.sight", "50") - "monster.sight = 30" (clamped) set("monster.sight", "lots") - "bad value: lots" (sight still 30)

title: 13.07  Architecture: Keeping Mods Modular and Stable
match: 13.07 Architecture: Keeping Mods Modular and Stable
body: A game with mods is a platform other people build on. This lesson covers the architecture that keeps it stable: isolating failures so one broken mod cannot take the game down, budgets for mod work, keeping saves safe, versioning everything mods touch, diagnosing problems from players' reports, and the honest limits of isolating native code. Failures must stay local With twenty mods installed, something will go wrong eventually. The architecture decides whether that means "mod X stopped working, the game told you why" or "the game crashes on start-up and nobody knows why". Kind of mod How to contain a failure --- --- Data Validate on load; report the mod, file, line and key; skip the bad entry (lessons 10.08, 13.02) Scripts Catch script errors at each call into the script; report the mod and line; disable that mod's scripts for the session Plugins Catch C++ exceptions at the boundary; validate tables (lesson 13.03); count failures and disable a plugin that keeps failing The practice task builds the plugin guard: every call into a plugin goes through it, exceptions are caught and recorded against the plugin, and after a few failures the plugin is switched off for the rest of the session with a message to the player. The limits of isolating native code A plugin DLL runs inside the game's process with the same memory and rights (lesson 13.04). Catching exceptions handles the polite failures. An impolite one (a plugin writing through a dangling pointer, corrupting the heap) cannot be contained in-process: it can corrupt anything, and the crash may appear somewhere else entirely (lesson 2.09). The honest options: - Accept it and diagnose well : crash dumps (lesson 8.04) that record which plugins were loaded and which module the crash was in, so players and authors can find the culprit. - Offer safer layers : data and scripts (sandboxed, with only the functions the game exposes) cover most mods; native plugins are for the few that need them. - Out-of-process plugins : run plugins in a separate process talking through pipes or shared memory (chapter 12's channels). A crash there kills only the helper process. It costs speed and complexity, so it is used where stability matters most, such as editors and browsers. Budgets A mod that spends 20 ms per frame turns a smooth game into a slideshow, and players blame the game. Measure each plugin's and script's time per frame with lesson 13.05's scoped timers, show it in the debug menu and a mod list, and warn when one exceeds its budget. Scripting languages can also limit instruction counts per call, stopping infinite loops. Saves and mods Lesson 11.06's save format records the enabled mods and their versions. On loading: - Missing mod: warn, and either refuse or load with its content removed (items from a missing mod become "unknown item" placeholders rather than crashing the loader). - Different version: warn; the mod may provide a migration (lesson 10.07) for its own saved data. - Mods store their own data in namespaced sections ( mod.lantern-light.fuel ) so they cannot collide with each other or with the game. Diagnosing players' problems Most mod problems arrive as "the game crashes, I have 40 mods". Make diagnosis possible: 1. The log (lesson 8.03) starts with the game version and the full, ordered mod list with versions. 2. Every warning and error names the mod responsible. 3. Crash dumps include the module list; the crash report says which module the crash happened in (lesson 8.02). 4. A safe mode start option disables all mods, so players can confirm whether mods are involved, and a "disable half" option lets them bisect (lesson 8.01) to the culprit. Common mistakes !warning One bad mod stops the game from starting Validate, report and skip; never let a single mod's failure become the game's failure. !warning Claiming plugins are "sandboxed" Native code in your process is not. Be honest with players and offer safer layers. !warning Logs that do not say which mod Every message about a problem should name its source. Check yourself quiz ? How is each kind of mod failure contained? - Every failure ends the game, so the player notices - Failures are ignored and logged at the end of the session + Each layer catches its own failures and disables that mod - All mods are disabled whenever any one fails Each layer stops the failure where it happens, so one broken mod does not take the others down. Bad data entries are skipped, script errors disable the mod's scripts, and plugin exceptions are caught at the boundary. ? What are the options for native plugins that might corrupt memory? - Catch the corruption with try / catch + Diagnose well, prefer data and scripts, or use a separate process - Copy the game's memory before each plugin call and restore it afterwards - Run plugins only in Debug builds A plugin in the same process can write anywhere, so it cannot be fully contained there. ? What should a log contain to make mod problems diagnosable? - Every frame's timing and memory use - A copy of each mod's files - The player's hardware details only + The game version, the mod list, and the mod in each error With that, a player's log alone usually shows which mod is at fault. ? A plugin's update throws a C++ exception every frame. What should the game do? + Catch it at the boundary, and disable the plugin - Let it crash the game so the author notices - Ignore it forever Failures stay local, and are reported. ? Why can a native plugin's memory corruption not be fully contained inside the game process? - Because exceptions are disabled + It shares the game's memory, so it can damage anything - Because DLLs are read-only Isolation from memory corruption needs a separate process. ? What is safe mode for? - Running the game faster - Protecting saves from players + Starting with every mod disabled Then bisect the mod list to find the culprit.

title: A plugin guard
where: 13.07 Architecture: Keeping Mods Modular and Stable
body: Build PluginGuard , through which the game calls every plugin. - call(plugin, fn) calls fn (a std::function<void() ) for the named plugin, unless that plugin is disabled. If fn throws any exception, the guard catches it, records one failure for the plugin together with the exception's message ( what() for std::exception , "unknown error" otherwise), and returns false . A successful call returns true ; a call to a disabled plugin returns false without running fn . - After maxFailures failures (given to the constructor) a plugin is disabled for the rest of the session. - disabled(plugin) says whether it is disabled; failures(plugin) how many failures it has; lastError(plugin) the last recorded message (empty if none). - report() lists, alphabetically, a line for every plugin with at least one failure: "name: N failure(s), last: MESSAGE" , followed by " (disabled)" if it is disabled.

title: 13.08  Working with a Game's Official Modding Tools
match: 13.08 Working with a Game's Official Modding Tools
body: Many games ship official modding support: editors, mod kits, scripting APIs and workshop integration. Working with them is the most productive and least fragile way to mod other people's games. This lesson covers what official tools usually provide, how to learn an unfamiliar one, the licensing of mod content, and how the design ideas of this chapter look from the modder's side. What official support usually provides Provided What it means for you --- --- An editor or mod kit The developers' own tools (or a version of them) for building levels, items and quests Documented data formats Files you can change with confidence, often with a schema A scripting API The functions the game exposes to mods, with documentation (lesson 13.02) A plugin SDK Headers and libraries for native plugins (lesson 13.03), versioned with the game Distribution A workshop or mod portal: upload, update, dependencies, ratings Rules A licence or end-user agreement for mods: what you may do and distribute Games known for strong official support include those built on engines that ship their editors (Unreal Engine's mod kits for particular games, the Source SDK, Bethesda's Creation Kit) and games with scripting layers designed for mods (Factorio's Lua API, Minecraft's data packs and resource packs, many strategy games). Godot and Unity games sometimes expose their own systems in similar ways. Learning an unfamiliar mod kit The approach is the same as lesson 10.09's for reading source: 1. Read the official documentation and examples first. Mod kits encode the developers' intentions; working against them leads to fragile mods. 2. Start from an example mod that does something close to what you want, change one thing, and get it loading. 3. Learn the data model : what objects exist (items, actors, quests), how they reference each other (by id, lesson 10.07), and how load order and overrides work (lesson 13.02). 4. Use the official debugging aids : in-game consoles, log files, validation tools. The log is where most "why does my mod not load" questions are answered. 5. Join the community : modding communities keep wikis of undocumented behaviour, which save days. Making mods that last The game will be patched. Mods that survive updates: - use only documented interfaces, not internal details; - change entries , not whole files, where the game supports merging (lesson 13.02), so they coexist with other mods; - declare their dependencies and supported game versions in their manifest (lesson 13.01); - namespace their own ids ( yourname_lantern , not lantern ) so they cannot collide with other mods; - keep their own saved data separate and versioned (lesson 13.07). These are the same rules this chapter followed from the game's side, now applied as a mod author. Licensing and permissions - A game's mod licence or end-user agreement says what you may do: commonly, mods may be shared free of charge but not sold, and may not include the game's own assets beyond what the tools produce. - Content you include must be yours or properly licensed: music, textures and models from other sources carry their own licences. - Other modders' work belongs to them: ask before building on or redistributing it, and credit it. - Online games deserve particular care: mods that change shared gameplay are usually allowed only where the game explicitly supports them (official servers with mod support, or private servers), never as a way to gain an advantage over other players. Common mistakes !warning Ignoring the official tools and working around them Unsupported approaches break with every patch. !warning Shipping assets you do not own Use your own work or properly licensed material, and credit it. !warning Generic ids Namespace everything your mod adds. Check yourself quiz ? What do official modding tools usually provide? + Mod kits, documented formats and an SDK - The game's full source code - A debugger that can attach to the game - A way to cheat in online matches Official support defines what modders may change and how. ? What makes a mod survive game updates? + Documented interfaces, entry-level changes and namespaced ids - Replacing whole files so nothing from the base game remains - Patching the game's exe at fixed addresses - Never updating the mod after release Replacing whole files throws away every change the update made to them. ? Which licences matter when releasing a mod? - Only the licence of the compiler used - None; mods are always free to release + The game's mod licence, and those of all content used - Only the licence you choose for your own mod Your mod's licence only covers your own work; everything you use from others has its own terms. ? What is usually the first step with an unfamiliar mod kit? + Read the official documentation and start from an example mod - Reverse engineer the game's executable - Rewrite the game's data files from scratch Mod kits encode how the developers intend mods to work. ? Why namespace the ids your mod adds? - To make them shorter + So they cannot collide with the game's ids or other mods' ids - Because the game requires capital letters Two mods adding a lantern item would otherwise conflict. ? What do mod licences commonly allow and forbid? - Anything at all, with no conditions - Nothing at all, in every case + Free sharing yes; selling or game assets no Always read the specific game's terms.
