title: 14.01  Immediate-Mode Interfaces
body: Most application toolkits are retained mode : you create widget objects once and keep them in sync with your data. Immediate mode turns that around: every frame, code describes the whole interface with function calls, and each call both draws its widget and reports what the user did. This lesson explains the model, why it suits tools and games so well, and how it works underneath, with ids , hot and active widgets. Two ways to build an interface Retained mode (Windows controls, Qt, web pages): you create a button object, give it a callback, and it lives until you destroy it. When your data changes, you must update every widget that shows it; when a widget changes, a callback updates your data. Keeping the two in sync is a large part of interface code. Immediate mode (Dear ImGui, Nuklear, many in-house game tools): there are no widget objects in your code. Every frame you call functions that describe the interface as it should look now , reading directly from your data: cpp-norun // Every frame: ImGui::Begin("Player"); ImGui::Text("Health: %d / %d", player.hp, player.maxHp); // always shows the current value ImGui::SliderInt("Speed", &player.speed, 1, 10); // writes straight into your variable if (ImGui::Button("Heal")) player.hp = player.maxHp; // true on the frame it was clicked ImGui::End(); There is nothing to keep in sync: the interface is a function of your data, recomputed each frame, like rendering the game itself (lesson 10.01). Retained Immediate --- --- --- Widget objects in your code Yes, created and destroyed No Keeping data and interface in sync Your job Automatic: redrawn from data each frame Showing or hiding parts Create, destroy, show, hide An if around the calls Lists of changing length Add and remove widgets A for loop Cost Only changes are redrawn The whole interface is re-described every frame (cheap for tools) Best for Polished applications, accessibility, text-heavy forms Tools, debug interfaces, editors inside games How a button knows it was clicked If no button object exists between frames, how does Button("Heal") know the mouse went down on it last frame and up on it now? The library keeps a little state itself, keyed by an id for each widget, computed from its label (and the window and any pushed ids): - The hot widget is the one the mouse is over this frame. - The active widget is the one the mouse button went down on, and it stays active until the button is released. - A button reports a click when the mouse is released over it while it is active : press on it, release on it. So the only state that survives between frames is "which id is active" (plus a few things like scroll positions and window placement), not a tree of objects. The practice task implements exactly this logic. Ids and why labels must be unique Because ids come from labels, two buttons both labelled "Delete" in one window would share an id and behave as one. ImGui's answers: - "Delete 3" : text after is part of the id but not shown; - ImGui::PushID(i) / PopID() around each item in a loop, so every row's widgets get distinct ids. Forgetting this is the most common immediate-mode bug: clicking one row's button activates another. Why tools and games use it Game engines are already redrawing everything every frame, already have the data in memory, and need interfaces that change constantly with the game (debug views, editors, profilers). Immediate mode fits that loop exactly, and a tool window is a few dozen lines, so engineers actually write them. That is why Dear ImGui is in so many engines and tools, and why the next lessons use it for the chapter 12 tools. Common mistakes !warning Duplicate labels in one window Widgets share an id and behave strangely. Use suffix or PushID . !warning Keeping your own copies of values just for the interface The point is to read and write your real data directly. !warning Doing expensive work while describing the interface The description runs every frame; cache anything slow. Check yourself quiz ? What state does an immediate-mode library keep between frames? - A full tree of widget objects, updated when the data changes - Nothing at all; every frame starts completely fresh + Small amounts keyed by widget id: which widget is active, plus things like window positions and scroll offsets - A copy of the application's data, compared each frame to find changes The widgets themselves are described again every frame; only small bits of interaction state persist. ? What are the hot and active widgets? + Hot is under the mouse; active is the one the button went down on - The hot widget was clicked last frame; the active one is being drawn now - The hot widget has keyboard focus; the active one is visible - They are the same widget seen at two moments A button reports a click when the mouse is released while it is both hot and active. ? Why does immediate mode suit game tools? - Because it is the only kind of interface that works on Windows - Because it uses less memory than any other approach - Because it needs no graphics API + Games redraw from data every frame anyway, so no syncing is needed Retained-mode interfaces need code to keep widget objects in step with the data; immediate mode just reads the data. ? What is the main difference between immediate and retained mode? + Immediate re-describes the interface each frame; retained keeps widgets - Immediate mode is drawn by the GPU, retained mode by the CPU - Retained mode cannot show buttons No widget objects means nothing to keep in sync. Retained-mode widget objects must be kept in step with the data. ? When does an immediate-mode button report a click? - As soon as the mouse is pressed over it + When the mouse is released over it after being pressed on it - Whenever the mouse is over it Press and release on the same widget. ? Two "Delete" buttons in one window both react when either is clicked. Why? - ImGui cannot draw two buttons - The window is too small + They have the same label, so the same id Use Delete 1 , or PushID per row.

title: An immediate-mode button
body: Implement the heart of an immediate-mode interface: the hot and active logic for buttons. A Ui object is used once per frame: - beginFrame(mouseX, mouseY, mouseDown) starts a frame with the current mouse state. - button(id, x, y, w, h) is called for each button this frame. It returns true when the button was clicked : the mouse button was released this frame, over this button, and this button was the active one. - endFrame() finishes the frame. Rules, as in the lesson: - A button is hot if the mouse is inside its rectangle ( x <= mouseX < x + w , likewise for y). - If the mouse button goes down this frame (it was up last frame) while a button is hot, that button becomes active (if several overlap, the last one drawn wins). - The active button stays active while the mouse is held, even if the mouse moves off it. - When the mouse button is released, the active id is cleared at the end of the frame (whether or not a click happened). - active() returns the active id, or 0 for none; hot() the hot id of the last frame (0 for none; the last one drawn wins).

title: 14.02  Setting Up Dear ImGui
body: Dear ImGui is a small, widely used C++ library for immediate-mode interfaces. It does not draw anything itself: back ends connect it to a platform (for windows and input) and a renderer (for drawing). This lesson sets it up with vcpkg and the SDL2 back ends used by Delve, explains the per-frame calls, fonts and DPI scaling, and builds a standalone tool application for chapter 12's tools. How ImGui is put together The core turns widget calls into draw lists (triangles, textures, clip rectangles); a renderer back end submits them with whatever graphics API the program uses (lesson 10.04). Back ends exist for SDL, Win32, GLFW, DirectX 9 to 12, OpenGL, Vulkan, Metal and more, so ImGui fits into almost any engine. Installing In the project's vcpkg.json (lesson 4.06): powershell vcpkg add port imgui sdl2-binding,sdl2-renderer-binding The features in brackets build the SDL2 platform back end and the SDL renderer back end along with the core. The setup and the frame cpp-norun define SDL_MAIN_HANDLED include <SDL.h include <imgui.h include <imgui_impl_sdl2.h include <imgui_impl_sdlrenderer2.h int main() { SDL_Init(SDL_INIT_VIDEO); SDL_Window window{ SDL_CreateWindow("Delve Tools", SDL_WINDOWPOS_CENTERED, SDL_WINDOWPOS_CENTERED, 1280, 800, SDL_WINDOW_RESIZABLE SDL_WINDOW_ALLOW_HIGHDPI) }; SDL_Renderer renderer{ SDL_CreateRenderer(window, -1, SDL_RENDERER_ACCELERATED SDL_RENDERER_PRESENTVSYNC) }; IMGUI_CHECKVERSION(); ImGui::CreateContext(); ImGuiIO& io{ ImGui::GetIO() }; io.ConfigFlags = ImGuiConfigFlags_NavEnableKeyboard; // keyboard navigation ImGui::StyleColorsDark(); ImGui_ImplSDL2_InitForSDLRenderer(window, renderer); ImGui_ImplSDLRenderer2_Init(renderer); bool running{ true }; while (running) { SDL_Event e; while (SDL_PollEvent(&e)) { ImGui_ImplSDL2_ProcessEvent(&e); // ImGui sees every event first if (e.type == SDL_QUIT) running = false; } ImGui_ImplSDLRenderer2_NewFrame(); // 1. start the frame ImGui_ImplSDL2_NewFrame(); ImGui::NewFrame(); ImGui::ShowDemoWindow(); // 2. describe the interface ImGui::Begin("Hello"); ImGui::Text("Frame time %.2f ms", 1000.0f / io.Framerate); ImGui::End(); ImGui::Render(); // 3. build the draw lists SDL_SetRenderDrawColor(renderer, 18, 20, 26, 255); SDL_RenderClear(renderer); ImGui_ImplSDLRenderer2_RenderDrawData(ImGui::GetDrawData(), renderer); // 4. draw them SDL_RenderPresent(renderer); } ImGui_ImplSDLRenderer2_Shutdown(); // shut down in reverse order ImGui_ImplSDL2_Shutdown(); ImGui::DestroyContext(); SDL_DestroyRenderer(renderer); SDL_DestroyWindow(window); SDL_Quit(); } Every ImGui program has these four steps per frame: new frame, describe, render, draw. In a game (lesson 13.06) the same steps run after the game has drawn its own frame, so the interface sits on top. The demo window ImGui::ShowDemoWindow() shows every widget ImGui has, each with a short explanation. Its source, imgui_demo.cpp , is the best reference there is: when you want a widget, find it in the demo window, then find the code that drew it. Keep the demo one menu click away in every tool you write. Fonts and DPI ImGui's built-in font is small and sharp at 100% display scaling. On high-DPI screens (laptops at 150%, 4K monitors) load a proper font at a size scaled for the display: cpp-norun const float scale{ dpiScaleForWindow(window) }; // e.g. from SDL_GetDisplayDPI / 96 io.Fonts- AddFontFromFileTTF("fonts/Inter-Regular.ttf", 16.0f scale); ImGui::GetStyle().ScaleAllSizes(scale); Include the font file with the tool, under its own licence (Inter, for example, uses the SIL Open Font License). Input sharing ImGui_ImplSDL2_ProcessEvent gives ImGui every event. In a game, check io.WantCaptureMouse and io.WantCaptureKeyboard before the game uses an event (lesson 13.06); in a standalone tool, ImGui is the whole interface and there is nothing to share. Common mistakes !warning Forgetting one of the four frame steps Missing NewFrame or Render produces assertion failures or nothing on screen. !warning Calling ImGui functions outside a frame Widget calls are only valid between NewFrame and Render . !warning Blurry or tiny text on high-DPI screens Load a real font at a scaled size and scale the style. Check yourself quiz ? Why does ImGui need separate platform and renderer back ends? - Because the core is written in a different language + The core knows no platform or graphics API; back ends supply both - Because Windows and the GPU cannot be used from the same file - So that ImGui can run on a separate thread The same core works with SDL or Win32 for input and DirectX, OpenGL or Vulkan for drawing. ? How does ImGui fit into a game frame? + After the game draws, ImGui is described and drawn on top - ImGui draws first, and the game draws over it - ImGui runs on its own thread and draws whenever it likes - ImGui replaces the game's rendering while it is open Drawing the interface last puts it on top of the game. ? What should a game check before handling input when ImGui is active? - Whether ImGui's demo window is open - Whether the mouse is inside the game window + io.WantCaptureMouse and io.WantCaptureKeyboard - Whether the frame rate is above 60 Clicking a slider should not also fire the player's weapon. ? What do ImGui's back ends do? + Connect the core to input, windows and a graphics API - Store your data - Compile the interface ahead of time The core only produces draw lists. ? What are the four steps of every ImGui frame? - Load, parse, layout, save + New frame, describe the interface, render, draw the lists - Create widgets, show them, hide them, destroy them Describe happens between NewFrame and Render . ? Where is the best reference for how to use a particular widget? - The draw lists - The back end's source + The demo window and imgui_demo.cpp Every widget is shown there with the code that draws it.

title: 14.03  Windows, Widgets and Layout
body: This lesson covers the ImGui toolkit you will use in every tool: windows and child regions, the common widgets (text, buttons, checkboxes, sliders, inputs, combos), how ImGui lays widgets out (top to bottom by default, SameLine to go across, groups, columns of fixed width), ids in loops, and disabling widgets. Windows cpp-norun ImGui::SetNextWindowSize({ 420, 300 }, ImGuiCond_FirstUseEver); // only the first time ever; afterwards the user's size is kept if (ImGui::Begin("Monsters", &m_showMonsters)) // the bool adds a close button { // ... widgets ... } ImGui::End(); // always call End, even if Begin returned false Begin returns false when the window is collapsed or hidden, so you can skip describing its contents, but End must still be called. Child windows ( BeginChild / EndChild ) create scrolling regions inside a window: a log view, a list that scrolls while buttons stay put. The everyday widgets Widget Call Changes --- --- --- Text Text("HP %d", hp) , TextColored , TextWrapped , TextDisabled Nothing Button if (Button("Heal")) ... Returns true on click Checkbox Checkbox("God mode", &god) Toggles a bool Slider SliderInt("Sight", &sight, 1, 30) , SliderFloat Drag to set a value in a range Drag DragFloat("Speed", &speed, 0.05f) Drag to change without fixed limits Input InputInt("Gold", &gold) , InputText("Name", buf, sizeof buf) Typed values Combo Combo("Kind", &index, kinds, count) Picks one from a list Colour ColorEdit3("Tint", rgb) Edits a colour Separator, spacing Separator() , Spacing() , SeparatorText("Combat") Visual grouping Every widget that edits a value returns true on the frame the value changed, which is when to apply side effects (save a setting, send a command to the game): cpp-norun if (ImGui::SliderInt("Sight range", &m_sight, 1, 30)) sendToGame("set monster.sight " + std::to_string(m_sight)); // only when it actually changed Layout ImGui places widgets top to bottom , each on its own line, at the window's full width minus padding. To change that: Need Call --- --- Next widget on the same line SameLine() A fixed width for the next widget SetNextItemWidth(120) , or PushItemWidth / PopItemWidth for several Fill the remaining width SetNextItemWidth(-FLT_MIN) Treat several widgets as one block BeginGroup() / EndGroup() Indent Indent() / Unindent() Align text with framed widgets on the same line AlignTextToFramePadding() Columns A table (lesson 14.04) with no borders cpp-norun ImGui::AlignTextToFramePadding(); ImGui::Text("Floor"); ImGui::SameLine(80); // continue at x = 80, so rows line up ImGui::SetNextItemWidth(120); ImGui::InputInt(" floor", &m_floor); // hides the label but keeps an id ImGui::SameLine(); if (ImGui::Button("Go")) sendToGame("goto " + std::to_string(m_floor)); This layout model is simple: a cursor moves down (or right, after SameLine ), and each widget advances it by its size plus spacing. The practice task implements a version of it. Ids in loops As lesson 14.01 warned, widgets in a loop need distinct ids: cpp-norun for (const MonsterInfo& m : snapshot.monsters) { ImGui::PushID(m.id); // every widget inside gets an id including m.id ImGui::Text("%s (%d, %d) hp %d", m.kind, m.x, m.y, m.hp); ImGui::SameLine(); if (ImGui::SmallButton("kill")) sendToGame("kill " + std::to_string(m.id)); ImGui::PopID(); } Disabling BeginDisabled(condition) / EndDisabled() greys out and blocks the widgets between them: for example, the commands that need a connection to the game, while the tool is not connected (lesson 12.05). Common mistakes !warning Skipping End when Begin returns false Begin and End must always be paired. !warning Applying side effects every frame Act on the frame a widget returns true, not every frame. !warning Labels used as both text and id in loops PushID per item, or suffixes. Check yourself quiz ? How does ImGui lay widgets out by default, and how do you change it? + One per line, top to bottom; SameLine keeps the next on the same line - In a grid of equal cells, changed with SetGrid - Left to right, wrapping at the window edge, changed with NewLine - Wherever each widget's position is given in pixels Most layout is just the order of calls plus a few SameLine s. ? When should side effects of a widget be applied? - Every frame, whether or not the widget changed - Only when the window is closed + On the frame its function returns true - When the mouse leaves the widget Applying effects every frame would, for example, re-send a command to the game sixty times a second. ? What do BeginDisabled and EndDisabled do? - Hide the widgets between them - Remove the widgets between them from the layout - Stop the window from being moved + Grey out and block the widgets between them The widgets are still drawn, so the layout does not jump when the condition changes. ? What does a slider's return value mean? + The value was changed by the user this frame - The slider is visible - The value is within range Use it to apply side effects only when needed. ? How do you put a button to the right of a text label? - Put them in the same function call + Call SameLine() between them - Use two windows Widgets go top to bottom unless told otherwise. ? What does " floor" do as a label? - Shows " floor" - Disables the widget + Shows no text, with the id "floor" Text after is part of the id only.

title: A layout cursor
body: Implement the layout model behind ImGui-style windows. A Layout places widgets inside a content area that starts at (left, top) and is width wide. - Each item(w, h) places a widget of that size and returns its top-left position. - Normally an item goes at the start of a new line: x at left , y below the previous line. A line's height is the tallest item on it; the next line starts spacingY below that. - sameLine() makes the next item continue on the current line, spacingX to the right of the previous item. - sameLineAt(x) makes the next item continue on the current line at left + x . - indent(d) moves left (for new lines) by d ; negative values unindent. - An item with w of -1 fills the remaining width of the line: from its x to left + width (where left is the content area's original left edge plus any indent). Return its size too. Return Placed{ x, y, w, h } for each item. Layout l{ 10, 20, 300, 8, 4 }; // left, top, width, spacingX, spacingY item(100, 20) - (10, 20) item(50, 30) - (10, 44) // new line: 20 + 20 + 4 sameLine(); item(60, 10) - (68, 44) item(-1, 16) - (10, 78, 300, 16) // new line below the 30-high line; fills the width

title: 14.04  Tables, Trees and Plots
body: Tools mostly show data: lists of entities, hierarchies of objects, numbers over time. ImGui's tables give sortable, resizable, scrollable columns; trees show hierarchies such as a scene graph; plots show values over time. This lesson uses each for Delve's tools, including clipping long lists so a table of ten thousand rows stays fast. Tables cpp-norun const ImGuiTableFlags flags{ ImGuiTableFlags_Borders ImGuiTableFlags_RowBg ImGuiTableFlags_Resizable ImGuiTableFlags_Sortable ImGuiTableFlags_ScrollY }; if (ImGui::BeginTable("monsters", 4, flags, { 0, 300 })) { ImGui::TableSetupScrollFreeze(0, 1); // keep the header row visible when scrolling ImGui::TableSetupColumn("Id", ImGuiTableColumnFlags_DefaultSort); ImGui::TableSetupColumn("Kind"); ImGui::TableSetupColumn("Position"); ImGui::TableSetupColumn("HP"); ImGui::TableHeadersRow(); if (ImGuiTableSortSpecs sort{ ImGui::TableGetSortSpecs() }; sort && sort- SpecsDirty) { sortRows(m_rows, sort- Specs 0 .ColumnIndex, sort- Specs 0 .SortDirection == ImGuiSortDirection_Ascending); sort- SpecsDirty = false; // sort only when the user changed the order } for (const Row& r : m_rows) { ImGui::TableNextRow(); ImGui::TableNextColumn(); ImGui::Text("%d", r.id); ImGui::TableNextColumn(); ImGui::TextUnformatted(r.kind.c_str()); ImGui::TableNextColumn(); ImGui::Text("%d, %d", r.x, r.y); ImGui::TableNextColumn(); ImGui::Text("%d", r.hp); } ImGui::EndTable(); } ImGui handles the header clicks, resizing and scrolling; your code sorts the data when SpecsDirty says the order changed. A filter box above the table ( InputText with a hint) completes it. The practice task writes the sorting and filtering logic, with stable sorting so rows with equal values keep their relative order. Long lists: clipping Describing ten thousand rows every frame is wasteful when only thirty are visible. ImGuiListClipper tells you which rows are on screen: cpp-norun ImGuiListClipper clipper; clipper.Begin(static_cast<int (m_rows.size())); while (clipper.Step()) for (int i{ clipper.DisplayStart }; i < clipper.DisplayEnd; ++i) drawRow(m_rows static_cast<size_t (i) ); It is lesson 10.04's culling, for interfaces: the cost depends on what is visible, not on the size of the data. Trees Hierarchies (a scene graph, lesson 3.09; folders; a struct's members, lesson 9.09) use tree nodes: cpp-norun void drawNode(const SceneNode& n) { const ImGuiTreeNodeFlags flags{ n.children.empty() ? ImGuiTreeNodeFlags_Leaf : ImGuiTreeNodeFlags_None }; if (ImGui::TreeNodeEx(&n, flags, "%s (%.1f, %.1f)", n.name.c_str(), n.x, n.y)) // the pointer is the id { for (const auto& child : n.children) drawNode( child); ImGui::TreePop(); } } TreeNodeEx returns true when the node is open, and you then draw its children and call TreePop . Selection, drag and drop and context menus ( BeginPopupContextItem ) build an editor's hierarchy panel from the same pieces. Plots ImGui::PlotLines and PlotHistogram draw simple graphs from an array, enough for lesson 12.05's frame times: cpp-norun ImGui::PlotLines(" frame", m_frameMs.data(), static_cast<int (m_frameMs.size()), 0, "frame ms", 0.0f, 33.0f, ImVec2(-FLT_MIN, 80)); For real charting (several series, axes, zoom, markers) the separate ImPlot library (also in vcpkg) extends ImGui with full plotting. A frame-time plot with a line at 16.7 ms (lesson 8.08's budget) makes stutter obvious. Common mistakes !warning Sorting every frame Sort only when SpecsDirty is set, or when the data changes. !warning Describing every row of a huge list Use ImGuiListClipper . !warning Unstable sorting Rows with equal values jump around each time the list is re-sorted. Use a stable sort with a tie-breaker. Check yourself quiz ? What do you need to do when the user clicks a sortable column header? - Nothing; ImGui sorts the rows itself + When the sort specs are dirty, sort your data and clear the flag - Rebuild the table with the columns in a new order - Call ImGui::SortTable with the column number ImGui only records what the user asked for; your code owns and sorts the data. ? Why use a list clipper? + So only visible rows are described each frame - To cut long text in a row down to fit the column - To copy rows to the clipboard - To stop the list scrolling past its end Describing ten thousand rows every frame is wasted work when only thirty are on screen. ? What is ImPlot for? - Drawing the game's world map - Saving ImGui layouts to a file - Plotting the path of the mouse for testing + Full charts with series, axes and zooming ImGui's own PlotLines is enough for a sparkline; ImPlot is for real charts. ? Who sorts a sortable ImGui table's data? + Your code, when ImGui reports the sort order changed - ImGui sorts its own copy of the rows - The renderer ImGui only tracks which column and direction the user chose. ? What does ImGuiListClipper do? - Removes rows from the data + Tells you which rows are visible - Clips text that is too long Cost then depends on what is on screen. ? How does a tree node know whether to draw its children? - It always draws them - A separate call checks + TreeNodeEx returns true when the node is open Then draw the children and call TreePop .

title: Filter and sort table rows
body: Write visibleRows(rows, filter, column, ascending) for a monster table. Each Row has an id , a kind , an x , a y and hp . 1. Filter : keep rows whose kind contains filter as a substring, ignoring upper and lower case. An empty filter keeps everything. 2. Sort by column : 0 id, 1 kind, 2 position (by y , then x ), 3 hp; ascending or descending. 3. Rows that compare equal on the chosen column are ordered by id , ascending, whatever the direction, so the order never jumps around. Return the resulting rows.

title: 14.05  Settings That Persist
body: A tool that forgets its window positions, open panels and last connection every time it starts is tiring to use. ImGui saves window layout itself to an .ini file; your tool saves its own settings alongside. This lesson covers both, where to store them, versioning them, and the classic bug of windows restored onto a monitor that is no longer connected. What ImGui saves for you ImGui remembers each window's position, size, collapsed state and (with docking) its docked layout, keyed by window title, and writes them to imgui.ini in the current directory every few seconds and on exit. Two adjustments make that robust: cpp-norun static std::string g_iniPath; // must outlive the ImGui context: ImGui keeps the pointer g_iniPath = (settingsFolder() / "layout.ini").string(); io.IniFilename = g_iniPath.c_str(); - Store it in the user's settings folder (Local AppData, lesson 5.04), not the current directory, which may be read-only or change with how the tool was started. - Window titles are ids: renaming a window loses its saved layout. "Monsters monsters" shows "Monsters" but uses the stable id monsters , so the visible title can change (with a count, say) without forgetting the layout. Your own settings Everything else the tool needs to remember is yours to save: Setting Example --- --- Which panels are open show.monsters = true Preferences refresh.ms = 100 , theme = dark , font.size = 16 Recent things Last connected process name, recent files Table state Sorted column (ImGui can also save table column widths and order itself, with ImGuiTableFlags_Reorderable , _Hideable ) Lesson 10.08's INI format is ideal: readable, easy to edit by hand when something goes wrong, tolerant of new and missing keys. Save on exit and whenever a setting changes (debounced, for example at most once per second), so a crash does not lose them, using lesson 5.04's write-to-temporary-then-replace. Versioning settings As with saves (lesson 10.07), include a version, and handle: - Missing keys (an older settings file): use the default. - Unknown keys (a newer one): ignore them, and preserve them when writing back if you can, so switching between tool versions does not destroy settings. - Invalid values (hand-edited): validate and fall back to the default, with a log message, never crash on bad settings. Restoring windows safely The classic bug: a tool remembers that its main window was at x = 2600 on the second monitor. The user unplugs that monitor, starts the tool, and the window opens off-screen where it cannot be seen or dragged back. Before restoring a saved window rectangle: 1. Get the work areas of the monitors currently connected (on Windows, EnumDisplayMonitors / GetMonitorInfoW ; with SDL, SDL_GetDisplayUsableBounds ). 2. If the saved rectangle does not overlap any of them enough to grab its title bar, move it onto the primary monitor. 3. If it is larger than the monitor, shrink it to fit. The practice task implements this clamping, which applies equally to the main window of a game. Common mistakes !warning imgui.ini in the current directory Point io.IniFilename at the user's settings folder, with a string that outlives the context. !warning Renaming windows and losing their layout Use id for a stable id with a changing title. !warning Restoring a window off-screen Check the saved position against the monitors that exist now. Check yourself quiz ? Where should a tool keep its layout and settings files? - In the current working directory - In the installation folder, next to the exe + In the user's settings folder, such as Local AppData - In the registry, under HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE The current directory changes with how the tool is started, and the installation folder is often not writable. ? How should a settings loader treat missing, unknown and invalid keys? - Refuse to load the file if anything is wrong - Reset every setting to its default if any key is missing + Defaults for missing or invalid keys; keep unknown ones - Keep invalid values, since the user chose them A settings file from an older or newer version should still mostly work. Log each invalid value that was replaced. ? How do you make sure a restored window is visible? + Check it against the monitors' work areas and move it on if needed - Always open windows in the centre of the primary monitor - Trust the saved position; Windows corrects it automatically - Save positions as percentages of the screen size A window saved on a monitor that is no longer connected would otherwise open where nobody can see it. ? What does ImGui save automatically? + Window positions, sizes and docking - All your tool's settings - The data shown in windows Everything else is up to your code. ? What does the title "Monsters (12) monsters" achieve? - It creates three windows + It shows a count but keeps the id "monsters" - It hides the window Text before is shown; the id comes from after it. ? A saved window position is on a monitor that is no longer connected. What should the tool do? - Restore it exactly where it was - Delete the settings file + Move it onto a monitor that exists Otherwise the window opens where the user cannot see it.

title: Keep a restored window on screen
match: Keep a restored window on screen
body: Write restoreWindow(saved, monitors) . saved is the window rectangle from the settings file; monitors lists the work areas of the monitors connected now, the first being the primary one. Rectangles are { x, y, w, h } . Rules: 1. A window is reachable on a monitor if its title bar strip, the top 32 pixels of the window ( y to y + 32 , full width), overlaps that monitor by at least 64 pixels horizontally and some amount vertically. 2. If the window is reachable on some monitor, keep its position, but shrink its width and height so it is no larger than that monitor (use the first monitor on which it is reachable). 3. Otherwise, place it on the primary monitor: shrink it to fit, then centre it there. 4. If there are no monitors at all, return the saved rectangle unchanged. primary {0, 0, 1920, 1040}, second {1920, 0, 1920, 1040} saved {2600, 100, 800, 600}, both monitors - unchanged saved {2600, 100, 800, 600}, only the primary - {560, 220, 800, 600} (centred)

title: 14.06  A Complete Tool Window
body: This lesson assembles the chapter into one application: Delve Inspector , a tool with a docked layout that connects to a running copy of Delve and shows its live stats, monsters, a memory view of the telemetry block and a command panel, with a command palette, settings that persist, and the hardening from chapter 12. It is the template for the tools in chapter 18's capstones. The layout ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ File View Game Help ● connected · delve 18324 │ ├───────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ Overview │ Frame time ▁▁▂▁▁▇▁▁▂▁▁▁▁▂ avg 8.2 ms · worst 21.4 ms │ │ floor 3 ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ turn 412 │ Monsters filter: gob │ │ hp 14 / 20 │ Id │ Kind │ Position │ HP │ │ monsters 6 │ 3 │ goblin │ 17, 9 │ 6 │ │ │ 7 │ goblin │ 20, 4 │ 9 │ │ Heal God ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ │ Telemetry block (hex) │ │ │ 0000 44 4C 56 54 01 00 00 00 40 00 00 00 ... DLVT....@ │ └───────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ With ImGui's docking (enable ImGuiConfigFlags_DockingEnable ; the vcpkg port's docking-experimental feature on versions where docking lives on its own branch), each panel is an ordinary Begin / End window that the user can dock, undock, tab and rearrange, and the arrangement is saved with the layout (lesson 14.05). The structure Three layers, as chapter 12 recommended: a thin platform layer that talks to the game, a model of pure, tested logic, and views that only draw the model and send user actions back. Each view is a function a few dozen lines long. The frame cpp-norun void Inspector::frame() { m_connection.poll(); // reconnect if needed; read a snapshot at most every 100 ms if (auto snap{ m_connection.latest() }) m_model.update( snap); ImGui::DockSpaceOverViewport(); drawMenuBar(); drawOverview(); // reads m_model only drawFrameTimes(); drawMonsters(); drawHexView(); drawCommandPalette(); // Ctrl+P if (m_showDemo) ImGui::ShowDemoWindow(&m_showDemo); } Commands ("heal", "god", "goto 3") go to the game through its command pipe (lesson 12.01) as console lines (lesson 11.07), never by writing into the game's memory: the game stays in charge of its own state, and the tool works with any build that understands the commands. The command palette Tools grow many commands. A command palette (Ctrl+P, as in many editors) lists them all, filtered as you type by fuzzy matching : typing gt3 finds "Goto floor 3". Matching characters in order, with bonuses for matches at the start of words, ranks useful results first. The practice task implements the scoring. Finishing touches - Status bar : connection state, game version, telemetry version (lesson 12.06), last error. - Keyboard shortcuts for common actions, shown in menus. - Logging of the tool's own actions and errors to a file (lesson 8.03). - Hardening : the six failure modes of lesson 12.07, rehearsed. - Packaging : like lesson 11.08, a Release build with its DLLs, licences (ImGui's MIT licence, SDL's zlib) and a readme. Common mistakes !warning Views that compute Keep logic in the model, where it can be tested; views only draw and forward actions. !warning Tools that write into the game's memory Send commands through the game's interface and let it change its own state. !warning A tool with no status Always show whether it is connected, to what, and whether the data is current. Check yourself quiz ? What does ImGui docking add to a tool? + Users can rearrange and tab panels, saved with the layout - A second ImGui context per window - A way to run the tool inside the game's process - Automatic resizing of fonts for high-DPI screens Each user can arrange the panels the way they work, and it is restored next time. ? Why should views only draw and forward actions? - Because ImGui cannot call functions from inside a window + So all logic is in the model, where it can be tested - Because views run on a different thread - So the tool uses less memory Logic inside drawing code can only be tested by clicking through the interface. ? What should a tool's status bar show? - The current time and date - The frame rate of the tool itself only - A list of all keyboard shortcuts + The connection, the versions, and the last error When something looks wrong, the status bar is the first place to see why. ? What are the three layers of the inspector? + A platform layer, a pure model, and views - Input, update and render - Debug, Release and Shipping Separating them keeps the logic testable and the views simple. ? How does the inspector change things in the game? - By writing into the game's memory + Through commands on the game's pipe - By editing the save file The game stays in charge of its own state. ? What does fuzzy matching in a command palette do? - Matches only exact names - Sorts commands alphabetically + Finds names containing the typed letters in order gt3 finds "Goto floor 3".

title: Fuzzy matching for a command palette
match: Fuzzy matching for a command palette
body: Write fuzzyScore(query, candidate) , which decides whether a command palette entry matches what was typed, and how well. - Matching ignores case. Every character of query must appear in candidate in order (not necessarily next to each other). If not, return std::nullopt . An empty query matches everything with score 0. - Score: start at 0. For each matched query character, add 1. Add 5 more if that candidate character is at the start of a word (the first character, or after a space, - , _ or . ). Add 3 more if it directly follows the previously matched character. - Match greedily: each query character matches the earliest possible candidate character after the previous match. Then write rank(query, candidates) , which returns the matching candidates sorted by score (highest first), ties in their original order. fuzzyScore("gt3", "Goto floor 3") - 1+5 (G, word start) + 1 (t) + 1+5 (3, word start) = 13 fuzzyScore("xyz", "Goto floor 3") - nullopt
