title: 15.01  User Mode and Kernel Mode
body: Lesson 1.06 introduced the kernel as the part of Windows with full control of the hardware. This chapter looks inside. It starts with the boundary itself: the processor's privilege levels , what runs in kernel mode (the kernel, the HAL, drivers), how kernel memory is shared by all processes, and why code running there must be held to a far higher standard than anything in user mode. Two privilege levels x64 processors have hardware privilege levels , called rings . Windows uses two: Ring Mode What runs there What it can do --- --- --- --- 0 Kernel mode The Windows kernel, the hardware abstraction layer, device drivers Everything: any memory, any instruction, the hardware 3 User mode Every application, including games and most services Only its own address space; privileged instructions fault; hardware only through the kernel The processor itself enforces the difference. In ring 3, instructions that control the hardware (disabling interrupts, loading page tables, talking to devices directly) cause an exception, and pages marked "supervisor only" in the page tables (lesson 6.02) cannot be touched. The only way up is a controlled gate: the system call (lesson 15.02). What lives in kernel mode - ntoskrnl.exe holds the executive (the managers this chapter covers: objects, memory, I/O, processes, security) and the kernel proper (scheduling, interrupts, low-level synchronisation). - hal.dll , the hardware abstraction layer, hides differences between motherboards and interrupt controllers. - Drivers ( .sys files) are kernel modules: PE files like DLLs (lesson 9.02), loaded into kernel space, extending the kernel with support for devices and file systems. - win32k.sys is the kernel side of windows and graphics (lesson 5.05's messages are partly managed here). One kernel address space, shared by everything Lesson 6.02 showed each process's private lower half of the address space. The upper half is kernel space, and it is the same in every process: the kernel, every driver, and the kernel's data (the pools, lesson 15.04) are mapped at the same kernel addresses whichever process is running. Pages there are marked supervisor-only, so user code cannot touch them, but all kernel-mode code can touch all of it. That sharing is the key to the rest of this chapter: - A driver's global variable is one variable for the whole machine, not per process. - A driver writing through a bad pointer can corrupt the kernel, other drivers, or any process's data, because there is no boundary between kernel components. - There is no "this driver crashed, the rest carries on". An unhandled fault in kernel mode means the system cannot know what else is damaged, so Windows stops the machine with a bug check (the blue screen, lesson 15.07). The standard kernel code is held to In user mode, a crash ends one process and the operating system cleans up (lesson 1.06). In kernel mode: User mode Kernel mode --- --- A crash ends the process A crash stops the whole machine A leak is freed when the process exits A leak lasts until reboot Bad pointers fault in your own space Bad pointers can silently corrupt anything Many runtime libraries and C++ features available A restricted environment: no standard library, careful exceptions, limited stack (lesson 16.02) Debug with Visual Studio on the same machine Debug from a second machine or a VM's host (lesson 15.08) That is why the rest of this course treats kernel work as something done only in a virtual machine , only with drivers you write for learning, with testing tools turned on, and why production drivers go through extensive testing and Microsoft's signing requirements (lesson 16.09). Common mistakes !warning Thinking a driver is "like a DLL that runs as administrator" It runs in ring 0 with the whole kernel's memory reachable. The rules, and the consequences of mistakes, are different. !warning Assuming kernel globals are per process Kernel space is shared; a driver's globals are machine-wide. !warning Experimenting with kernel code on your main PC Use a virtual machine you can restore (lesson 15.08). Check yourself quiz ? What runs in kernel mode on Windows? - Every program started by an administrator - Services, such as the print spooler and Windows Update + ntoskrnl, the HAL, device and file-system drivers, and win32k - ntdll.dll and kernel32.dll, which every program loads Services and system DLLs run in user mode; ntdll only contains the stubs that make system calls. ? How does kernel address space differ from user address space? + The user half is per process; the kernel half is shared by all - The kernel has a separate physical computer's worth of memory - Each process has its own copy of the kernel - Kernel addresses are 32-bit and user addresses are 64-bit One kernel serves every process, so its half of the address space is the same wherever you look. Only kernel-mode code can touch the kernel half. ? Name three ways kernel-mode mistakes are worse than user-mode ones. - They are harder to type, slower to compile, and need more comments - They show a dialog box, write a log, and close the program - They only appear in Release builds, on laptops and with antivirus installed + Crashes stop the whole machine, leaks last until reboot, and bad pointers can silently corrupt any part of the system A user-mode crash ends one process; a kernel-mode crash ends everything. ? What enforces the separation between user mode and kernel mode? + The processor itself, by faulting privileged use - Windows checks every instruction in software - Nothing; programs promise to behave Hardware privilege levels are the foundation. ? Why is the kernel half of the address space the same in every process? - Each process gets a copy of the kernel + One kernel serves the whole system, mapped alike - Kernel memory is not virtual Supervisor-only pages keep user code out. ? Why does an unhandled fault in a driver stop the whole machine? - Drivers are always critical - Windows cannot restart drivers + Nothing in the kernel is walled off from it Continuing could corrupt data, so Windows bug-checks.

title: 15.02  System Calls: Crossing the Boundary
body: Every time a program opens a file, allocates memory or waits on an event, it crosses from user mode into the kernel and back. This lesson follows one call, CreateFileW , through kernelbase.dll and ntdll.dll to the syscall instruction and into the kernel's system service dispatcher, and explains the rule that makes the boundary safe: the kernel never trusts anything that comes from user mode. Following CreateFileW down - The documented Windows API (lesson 5.x) lives in kernel32.dll and kernelbase.dll . It translates friendly parameters into the kernel's. - The native API is in ntdll.dll : functions named Nt... (and Zw... ). Each is a few instructions: put the system call number in eax , and execute syscall . - The syscall instruction switches the processor to ring 0 and jumps to the kernel's single entry point, which uses the number to find the right kernel function in its system service table . - The kernel's function does the work and returns an NTSTATUS code; sysret returns to user mode; kernelbase converts the status into a Win32 error for GetLastError (lesson 5.02). You can see a stub in the debugger: in any program, open the Disassembly window at ntdll!NtCreateFile (lesson 4.08): asm ntdll!NtCreateFile: mov r10, rcx ; the syscall instruction overwrites rcx, so the first argument moves to r10 mov eax, 55h ; the system call number (it differs between Windows versions) test byte ptr 7FFE0308h , 1 jne use_int2e ; an alternative path on some systems syscall ; into the kernel ret The numbers change between Windows builds, which is one reason programs use the documented API rather than calling syscall themselves. NTSTATUS Kernel functions return NTSTATUS values, 32-bit codes like HRESULT s (lesson 5.02): negative for errors. Common ones: STATUS_SUCCESS (0), STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED ( 0xC0000022 ), STATUS_OBJECT_NAME_NOT_FOUND ( 0xC0000034 ), STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER ( 0xC000000D ). Lesson 8.04's exception codes are NTSTATUS values too: 0xC0000005 is STATUS_ACCESS_VIOLATION . Chapter 16's drivers return these from every function. The kernel never trusts user mode A system call hands the kernel values from user mode: numbers, and pointers into user memory . Any of them may be wrong by accident or by malice: a pointer into kernel space, a length that overflows, a buffer another thread changes while the kernel reads it. The kernel defends itself with three rules, and every driver that accepts requests from user mode must follow them too (lesson 16.07): 1. Probe : check that a user pointer and length describe memory entirely within the user part of the address space ( ProbeForRead , ProbeForWrite ), so a caller cannot trick the kernel into reading or writing kernel memory on its behalf. Watch for overflow: address + length must not wrap around. 2. Capture : copy the user's data into kernel memory once , and then use only the copy. Otherwise another user thread can change the data between the kernel checking it and using it: a time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) bug. 3. Guard the access : user memory can be freed or protected at any moment by another thread, so kernel code touches it only inside a structured exception handler ( __try / __except ) that turns a fault into an error status instead of a bug check. The practice task implements the probing arithmetic. Previous mode The kernel records whether a call came from user mode or from kernel code (the previous mode ). Calls from kernel mode (drivers calling ZwCreateFile ) skip some checks because kernel callers are trusted. This is why drivers must be careful never to pass user-supplied pointers on to kernel functions as if they were their own: the checks that protected the kernel would be skipped. Common mistakes !warning Calling Nt functions or syscall directly in applications Undocumented, changing between versions, and unnecessary. Use the Windows API. !warning Checking a user buffer, then reading it again later Capture it once into kernel memory; the user can change it between the two reads. !warning Forgetting overflow in range checks address + length can wrap past the end of the address space and appear valid. Check yourself quiz ? What layers does a call to CreateFileW pass through? - CreateFileW writes to the disk directly through the hardware ports + kernelbase, ntdll's stub, syscall , the kernel, then the I/O manager - CreateFileW sends a window message to the file-system driver - CreateFileW calls the disk driver's DLL loaded into the program Only kernel code can reach drivers and hardware; the syscall instruction is the crossing. Inside the kernel the system service dispatcher calls the kernel's NtCreateFile , which reaches the drivers through the I/O manager. ? What are the three rules for handling user-mode data in the kernel? - Trust it, copy it, and free it - Encrypt it, compress it, and log it + Probe the range, capture the data once, and use exception handlers - Check it with assert , read it twice, and return an error if it changed Capturing once stops another user thread changing the data between the check and the use. ? What is an NTSTATUS? - A Win32 error code returned by GetLastError - A flag saying whether a thread is running - A text message describing an error + A 32-bit status code, negative for errors Win32 functions translate NTSTATUS values into the error codes GetLastError reports. ? What does a function in ntdll like NtCreateFile do? + Loads the call number and runs syscall - Opens the file itself in user mode - Calls kernelbase It is a tiny stub; the work happens in the kernel. ? Why must the kernel copy user data before checking and using it? - Copying makes it faster + Another thread could change it between check and use - User memory cannot be read from the kernel This is the time-of-check to time-of-use problem. ? What does probing a user buffer check? - That the buffer contains valid data - That the buffer is aligned to a page + That the whole range lies in user address space Otherwise a caller could make the kernel touch kernel memory for it.

title: Probe a user buffer
body: A kernel component receives a pointer and a length from user mode. Write probe(address, length, alignment) , which applies the kernel's rules: - A zero length is always accepted (nothing will be touched). - alignment (1, 2, 4 or 8) must divide address : otherwise "misaligned" . - The whole range address to address + length - 1 must lie in user space, that is below kUserLimit ( 0x00007FFFFFFF0000 ), and the addition must not wrap round: otherwise "out of range" . - Otherwise "ok" . Check alignment before the range. probe(0x1000, 16, 8) - "ok" probe(0x1004, 16, 8) - "misaligned" probe(0x00007FFFFFFEFFF0, 32, 1) - "out of range" (runs past the user limit) probe(0xFFFFF80000000000, 8, 8) - "out of range" (kernel address)

title: 15.03  Kernel Objects and the Object Manager
match: 15.03 Kernel Objects and the Object Manager
body: Lesson 5.01 showed handles from the user's side. Inside the kernel, the object manager creates every kernel object (files, processes, threads, events, devices, registry keys), gives each a header with its type, reference counts and security, keeps a namespace of named objects, and maintains each process's handle table. This lesson looks at all of that, and at the object names drivers use. Every object has a header Each kernel object is a block of kernel memory: an object header managed by the object manager, followed by the object's own body (an event's signalled state, a file's position): In the header Meaning --- --- Type Which kind of object: Process, Thread, File, Event, Device, Key, Section ... Each type has its own procedures (open, close, delete) and its own access rights Handle count How many handles, in all processes, refer to it Pointer (reference) count How many references in total, including the kernel's own pointers Security descriptor Who may do what (lesson 6.08) Name For named objects, its place in the namespace An object is deleted only when both counts reach zero. Kernel code that keeps a pointer to an object takes a reference ( ObReferenceObject ) and later releases it ( ObDereferenceObject ), the kernel's equivalent of lesson 10.06's reference counting. Forgetting to release keeps the object alive until reboot; releasing twice frees it while still in use, usually ending in a bug check. Handles, from the inside A handle (lesson 5.01) is an index into the process's handle table , maintained by the object manager. Each entry holds a pointer to the object and the access mask granted when it was opened. When a user calls, say, SetEvent(h) , the kernel: 1. looks up h in the calling process's table ( ObReferenceObjectByHandle ); 2. checks the object's type is right (an Event), and the granted access includes what the operation needs; 3. takes a reference while it works, and drops it afterwards. The access check against the security descriptor happened only once, when the handle was created (lesson 6.08). The object namespace Named objects live in a tree, like a file system for the kernel: \ ├── Device\ │ ├── HarddiskVolume3 the C: volume │ ├── Null │ └── XenonEcho a device created by chapter 16's driver ├── Driver\ loaded drivers ├── GLOBAL??\ "DOS device" names: symbolic links │ ├── C: → \Device\HarddiskVolume3 │ └── XenonEcho → \Device\XenonEcho ├── BaseNamedObjects\ named events, mutexes, sections from user mode │ └── (Local\ and Global\ names, lesson 12.01) └── Sessions\ ... per-session namespaces Symbolic links connect friendly names to devices. The user-mode path C:\save.dat becomes \??\C:\save.dat in the kernel; \?? looks in the caller's own and then the global DOS device directory, where C: is a symbolic link to \Device\HarddiskVolume3 ; the object manager follows it, and the rest of the path ( \save.dat ) is handed to the file system driver on that device. The practice task resolves paths through links like this, including stopping a link that points back at itself. Chapter 16's driver creates a device object ( \Device\XenonEcho ) and a symbolic link to it ( \??\XenonEcho ), so a user program can open it with CreateFileW(L"\\\\.\\XenonEcho", ...) : the \\.\ prefix is user mode's way of saying \??\ . Seeing it Sysinternals WinObj shows the whole namespace: devices, drivers, symbolic links and named objects. Sysinternals Handle and Process Explorer's lower pane list every handle a process holds, with types and names, which is how you find which program has a file locked (lesson 5.04's sharing violations). Common mistakes !warning Holding an object pointer without a reference The object can be deleted underneath you. Reference it for as long as you keep the pointer. !warning Unbalanced reference counts A missing dereference leaks the object until reboot; an extra one frees it while still in use. !warning Confusing user-mode and kernel-mode names \\.\Name from user mode corresponds to \??\Name (a link) in the kernel, which points at \Device\Name . Check yourself quiz ? What does an object header contain? + Its type, counts, security descriptor and name - The object's data, such as a file's contents - The process ids of every process using the object - The source file of the driver that created it The object is deleted when both counts reach zero. ? How does the kernel use a handle passed in a system call? - It treats the handle as an address and reads the object there + Looks it up in the caller's table, checks access, holds a reference - It searches every process for an object with that number - It asks the program which object it meant The extra reference keeps the object alive even if another thread closes the handle mid-call. ? How does a user-mode program open a device created by a driver? - It loads the driver's .sys file with LoadLibrary - It sends the driver a window message - It calls the driver's functions through a function pointer + It opens the driver's symbolic link, \.\LinkName , with CreateFileW After that, the program talks to the driver with ReadFile , WriteFile and DeviceIoControl on the handle. ? When is a kernel object deleted? + When its handle and reference counts reach zero - When its creator exits - When its first handle is closed Kernel code's own references keep it alive too. ? What does a handle table entry store? - The object's whole contents + The object pointer and the granted rights - The object's name only Rights are checked once, at open time. ? What does \??\C: refer to? - The C: folder on the disk - A key in the registry + A symbolic link to a volume device The object manager follows the link to the device.

title: Resolve a path through symbolic links
match: Resolve a path through symbolic links
where: 15.03 Kernel Objects and the Object Manager
body: Model how the object manager resolves names. links maps symbolic-link names to their targets, for example "\??\C:" to "\Device\HarddiskVolume3" . Write resolve(path, links) : - Repeatedly find the longest link name that is a prefix of the current path at a component boundary (the link name is the whole path, or is followed by \ ). Replace that prefix with the link's target. - Stop when no link matches, and return the final path. - If more than 16 replacements happen, the links form a loop: return std::nullopt . links: \??\C: - \Device\HarddiskVolume3 \??\Echo - \Device\XenonEcho resolve("\??\C:\Games\save.dat") = "\Device\HarddiskVolume3\Games\save.dat" resolve("\??\Echo") = "\Device\XenonEcho" resolve("\??\Cx\file") = "\??\Cx\file" (\??\C: is not a whole component of \??\Cx)

title: 15.04  The Memory Manager
body: The kernel's memory manager provides every process's virtual address space (chapter 6) and also manages kernel memory. This lesson covers the kernel side: paged and non-paged pool , why the difference matters so much in drivers, pool tags for tracking allocations, memory descriptor lists (MDLs) for describing buffers, and how the memory manager handles page faults. What the memory manager does Job Seen before --- --- Building and switching each process's page tables Lesson 6.02 Reserving, committing and protecting user memory ( VirtualAlloc ends here) Lesson 6.03 Handling page faults: demand-zero pages, paging in from disk Lesson 6.02 Working sets: deciding which pages stay in RAM Lesson 6.02 File mappings and shared memory Lesson 12.01 Kernel memory: the pools This lesson Paged and non-paged pool Kernel code allocates memory from pools , the kernel's heaps, shared by all drivers: Pool Can be paged out to disk? Usable at --- --- --- Paged pool Yes Only when page faults are allowed: IRQL below DISPATCH_LEVEL (lesson 15.06) Non-paged pool No: always in RAM Any IRQL, including interrupt handlers Why both? Non-paged memory is precious: it permanently consumes RAM. But some kernel code runs at times when a page fault cannot be handled (while holding a spin lock, in an interrupt or DPC, lesson 15.06), and touching paged memory then, if it has been paged out, crashes the machine with IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL or PAGE_FAULT_IN_NONPAGED_AREA . So drivers put in non-paged pool exactly the data that code at high IRQL touches, and everything else in paged pool. The same rule applies to code : a driver function that may run at DISPATCH_LEVEL must be in non-paged memory. Drivers mark functions that only run at PASSIVE_LEVEL as pageable with pragma alloc_text(PAGE, ...) and assert their IRQL with the PAGED_CODE() macro. Allocating with tags cpp-norun // A 4-character tag identifies who allocated it: here 'Echo', written backwards in memory as a little-endian integer. constexpr ULONG kTag{ 'ohcE' }; auto buffer{ static_cast<char (ExAllocatePool2(POOL_FLAG_NON_PAGED, size, kTag)) }; if (!buffer) return STATUS_INSUFFICIENT_RESOURCES; // allocation can fail: always check // ... use it ... ExFreePoolWithTag(buffer, kTag); - ExAllocatePool2 (Windows 10 2004 and later) zero-initialises memory, unlike its predecessor ExAllocatePoolWithTag , which avoided a whole class of information-leak bugs. - Every allocation carries a pool tag , a four-character code chosen by the driver. Tools such as !poolused in WinDbg and Sysinternals PoolMon show how much memory each tag holds, which is how kernel memory leaks are found: a tag whose usage keeps growing points at the guilty driver. The practice task builds this kind of tracking. - Leaked pool memory is never reclaimed until reboot, because there is no process to clean up after (lesson 15.01). Memory descriptor lists When a driver needs to work with a buffer that belongs to a user process, for example to read data directly into it, it cannot simply keep the user's virtual address: that address is only valid in that process, and the pages could be paged out or freed. An MDL (memory descriptor list) describes the buffer by its physical pages : 1. Build an MDL for the user range ( IoAllocateMdl ). 2. Lock the pages in RAM ( MmProbeAndLockPages , inside __try , with the probing rules of lesson 15.02). 3. Map them into kernel space if needed ( MmGetSystemAddressForMdlSafe ), giving an address valid in any process context and at raised IRQL. 4. Unlock and free when done. Chapter 16's "direct I/O" (lesson 16.07) has the I/O manager do these steps for the driver. Page faults, from the kernel's side When a thread touches a page that is not present (lesson 6.02), the processor raises a page fault and the memory manager runs: - Is the address valid for this process (committed or a mapping)? If not: an access violation exception in user mode, a bug check in kernel mode if nothing handles it. - If valid: find a free physical page, fill it (zeros, or read from the page file or a mapped file, which means waiting for disk I/O), update the page table, and resume the thread. Waiting for disk is why a page fault can only be handled at low IRQL: at DISPATCH_LEVEL and above, the thread cannot wait. Common mistakes !warning Paged memory touched at DISPATCH_LEVEL or higher Works until the page happens to be paged out, then crashes the machine. Use non-paged pool for anything touched at raised IRQL. !warning Not checking pool allocations Pool allocation can fail; return STATUS_INSUFFICIENT_RESOURCES . !warning Keeping a user virtual address in a driver It is meaningless in another process context. Use an MDL or copy the data. Check yourself quiz ? Why does Windows have both paged and non-paged pool? + Code that cannot fault needs RAM-resident memory, which is scarce - Paged pool is for drivers and non-paged pool is for applications - Non-paged pool is faster, so it is used for everything important - Paged pool is on disk and non-paged pool is in the CPU cache Code running at DISPATCH_LEVEL or above cannot handle a page fault, so its data must always be in RAM. ? What happens to leaked pool memory? - It is freed when the driver's process exits - It is freed by the garbage collector after a few minutes + It stays allocated until the machine reboots; pool tags help find which driver leaked it - It is returned automatically when the driver unloads The kernel has no per-process cleanup for pool, so the four-character tag is the main clue to the culprit. ? What are the steps for a driver to use a user buffer safely through an MDL? + Allocate an MDL, probe and lock the pages, map them, then unlock - Copy the user address into a global and read it whenever needed - Call ReadProcessMemory on the caller's process - Allocate non-paged pool and ask the user program to write into it Locking keeps the pages in RAM, and the system-space mapping stays valid whatever process is current. ? What is the difference between paged and non-paged pool? + Paged can go to disk; non-paged stays in RAM - Paged pool is faster - Non-paged pool is for user mode High-IRQL code must only touch non-paged memory. ? What is a pool tag for? - Encrypting allocations + Showing which driver owns each block - Aligning memory Tools like PoolMon show usage per tag. ? Why does a driver use an MDL rather than a user virtual address? - MDLs are faster to type - User addresses are always invalid + Its locked pages work from any process context The user address only means something in the original process.

title: Track pool usage by tag
body: Kernel memory leaks are found by tracking allocations per pool tag. Build PoolTracker , a model of what PoolMon shows. - allocate(tag, bytes) records an allocation and returns an id for it (unique, starting at 1). - free(id, tag) records that allocation's release. If the id is unknown or was already freed, or the tag does not match the one it was allocated with, return a description of the error ( "double free or bad id" , "tag mismatch" ) and change nothing; otherwise return "" . - usage() returns, for every tag that still holds memory, the tag, the number of live allocations and their total bytes, sorted by bytes, largest first (ties alphabetical by tag). - tagText(tag) turns a tag as stored in memory (four characters, little-endian in a 32-bit number, so 'ohcE' in code reads Echo ) into a 4-character string.

title: 15.05  The I/O Manager and the Driver Model
match: 15.05 The I/O Manager and the Driver Model
body: Every read, write and device request in Windows becomes an I/O request packet (IRP) handed to a stack of drivers by the I/O manager . This lesson explains IRPs, driver and device objects, how a request travels down a device stack and its completion travels back up, the kinds of drivers (filter, function, bus), and the frameworks (WDM and KMDF) drivers are written with. Requests as packets When a program calls ReadFile on a file or a device, the I/O manager in the kernel builds an IRP , a structure describing the request: Part of an IRP Meaning --- --- Major function What kind of request: IRP_MJ_CREATE (open), IRP_MJ_READ , IRP_MJ_WRITE , IRP_MJ_DEVICE_CONTROL (custom commands, lesson 16.05), IRP_MJ_CLOSE ... Parameters Length, offset, the control code ... in the current stack location Buffers Where the data is, described in one of three ways (lesson 16.07) I/O status When finished: an NTSTATUS and how many bytes were transferred The I/O manager then hands the IRP to the driver responsible for the target device. Drivers never call each other's functions directly; everything goes through IRPs. Driver objects and device objects Object One per Holds --- --- --- Driver object Loaded driver The table of dispatch routines : one function per major function the driver handles Device object Device the driver manages (a disk, a port, or a purely software device like chapter 16's) The device's state, and which driver handles it When DriverEntry (lesson 16.02) runs, the driver fills its driver object's dispatch table: driver- MajorFunction IRP_MJ_READ = EchoRead; . When an IRP for one of its devices arrives, the I/O manager calls the matching routine. Device stacks Most hardware is handled by several drivers layered on top of each other, each adding something: Each driver, given an IRP, does one of three things: 1. Complete it itself ( IoCompleteRequest ) with a status, if it can satisfy the request. 2. Pass it down to the next driver in the stack ( IoCallDriver ), possibly after changing it, optionally asking to be told when it completes (a completion routine). 3. Queue it (mark it pending) to finish later, for example when hardware responds. The practice task simulates a request going down a stack until one driver completes it, and the completion coming back up through the drivers that asked to see it. Kind of driver Role --- --- Bus driver Discovers devices on a bus (PCI, USB) and creates their lowest device objects Function driver The main driver for a device: knows how to operate it Filter driver Sits above or below and adds or changes behaviour: encryption, compression, monitoring Software-only driver No hardware; provides a service to user mode through a device object (chapter 16's driver is one) Asynchronous by design Device I/O takes time. Rather than making the caller's thread wait inside the driver, an IRP can be pending : the driver returns STATUS_PENDING at once, and completes the IRP later from an interrupt or a worker. User mode sees this as overlapped (asynchronous) I/O, or simply as ReadFile returning when the I/O manager finally completes the request. This design is why Windows I/O can keep thousands of requests in flight. WDM and KMDF Framework Notes --- --- WDM (Windows Driver Model) The original model: drivers handle IRPs directly, including all the plug-and-play and power management requests. Powerful and error-prone KMDF (Kernel-Mode Driver Framework) A library over WDM that handles the standard plug-and-play, power and queueing logic, and gives drivers objects with reference counting and cleanup. Microsoft's recommended choice for new drivers UMDF Drivers for some device classes that run in user mode , so a bug crashes only a host process, not the machine. Preferred whenever the device type allows it Chapter 16 starts with a minimal WDM-style driver to see the raw mechanism, and the same ideas carry over to KMDF. Common mistakes !warning Completing an IRP and then touching it After IoCompleteRequest , the IRP belongs to the I/O manager and may already be freed. !warning Both completing and passing down the same IRP Each IRP must be completed exactly once, by one driver. !warning Writing a kernel driver when a user-mode one would do UMDF, or an ordinary service, keeps bugs out of the kernel. Check yourself quiz ? What three things can a driver do with an IRP? - Read it, write it, or delete it - Copy it, encrypt it, or log it + Complete it, pass it down to the next driver in the stack, or mark it pending and complete it later - Send it to user mode, return it to the I/O manager, or ignore it Ignoring an IRP leaves the caller waiting forever; every IRP must eventually be completed. ? What is the difference between a driver object and a device object? - They are the same object under two names + The driver object holds the dispatch routines; IRPs go to device objects - A driver object is in user mode; a device object is in kernel mode - A device object is the .sys file; a driver object is its process One driver can manage many devices, each with its own device object. ? Name the kinds of drivers in a device stack. - Kernel drivers, user drivers and service drivers - Primary drivers, secondary drivers and backup drivers - Input drivers, output drivers and storage drivers + Bus drivers, function drivers and filter drivers An IRP travels down the stack, and each driver can handle it or pass it on. ? What is an IRP? + A structure describing one I/O request - A kind of interrupt - A driver's configuration file Major function, parameters, buffers and status. ? A filter driver receives an IRP it does not need to change. What does it do? - Completes it with success + Passes it down with IoCallDriver - Deletes it Filters add behaviour only where they need to. ? Why is KMDF recommended over writing WDM drivers directly? - KMDF drivers run in user mode - WDM no longer works + It gets the standard driver logic right for you UMDF is the user-mode framework.

title: Send a request down a device stack
match: Send a request down a device stack
where: 15.05 The I/O Manager and the Driver Model
body: Simulate an IRP travelling through a device stack. The stack is a list of drivers from the top down. Each Driver has a name, a function decide(major) returning what it does with a request of that major function ( "complete" or "pass" ), the status it completes with, and whether it wants a completion callback . Write send(stack, major) , returning a Trace : - path : the names of the drivers the request visited going down, in order; - completedBy : the driver that completed it; - status : its status; - callbacks : the names of drivers above the completing one that asked for a completion callback, in the order the completion travels back up (nearest the completing driver first). If every driver passes the request, the bottom of the stack has no one left to pass to: the request completes with "STATUS_INVALID_DEVICE_REQUEST" , completedBy is "(none)" , and every driver that asked for a callback gets one.

title: 15.06  Interrupts, IRQLs and Scheduling
body: Hardware demands attention at any moment through interrupts , and the kernel must decide what can interrupt what. Windows does this with interrupt request levels (IRQLs). The IRQL a piece of code runs at decides what it may do: whether it can wait, touch paged memory, or be preempted. This lesson explains the levels, DPCs , spin locks , and the rules that cause the most famous blue screen of all. Interrupts When a device needs the processor (a network packet arrived, a disk read finished, a key was pressed) it raises an interrupt . The processor stops what it is doing, saves enough state to resume, and runs the driver's interrupt service routine (ISR). A clock also interrupts regularly, which is how the scheduler gets control to switch threads (lesson 6.05). But an interrupt can arrive while the kernel is in the middle of something delicate, even while handling another interrupt. Windows needs rules for what may interrupt what. IRQLs Each processor has a current IRQL (interrupt request level). Code at a given IRQL can only be interrupted by something at a higher level. The levels that matter for drivers: IRQL Runs May wait? May touch paged memory? Scheduler can switch thread? --- --- --- --- --- PASSIVE_LEVEL (0) Normal threads: all user code, most driver code, DriverEntry , most dispatch routines Yes Yes Yes APC_LEVEL (1) Asynchronous procedure calls, some file system code Limited Yes Yes DISPATCH_LEVEL (2) The scheduler itself, DPCs , code holding a spin lock No No No: the thread keeps the processor DIRQL (3 and up) Device interrupt service routines No No No The two crucial rules for DISPATCH_LEVEL and above: 1. No waiting. The scheduler runs at DISPATCH_LEVEL, so code at that level or above cannot be switched out. Waiting on an event or a mutex there would wait forever, so it is forbidden. 2. No paged memory. A page fault may need to wait for the disk (lesson 15.04), which is impossible at DISPATCH_LEVEL. Touching paged memory there crashes the machine with bug check IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL ( 0xA ) or DRIVER_IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL ( 0xD1 ), the most famous blue screens, usually caused by a driver. The practice task encodes these rules as a checker. DPCs: doing the work later An ISR runs at a high IRQL, blocking everything below, so it must be very short: acknowledge the device and note what happened. The rest of the work goes into a deferred procedure call (DPC), queued by the ISR and run soon after at DISPATCH_LEVEL, where other device interrupts can still get through. Work that needs to wait or touch paged memory goes one step further down, into a work item that runs in a system thread at PASSIVE_LEVEL. Spin locks Lesson 6.06's mutexes make a waiting thread sleep, which is impossible at DISPATCH_LEVEL. For data shared with DPCs or ISRs, drivers use spin locks : - Acquiring a spin lock raises the IRQL to DISPATCH_LEVEL (so the holder cannot be preempted on its processor), then spins (busy-waits) until the lock is free, in case another processor holds it. - Code holding a spin lock therefore follows every DISPATCH_LEVEL rule: no waiting, no paged memory, and should hold it for only a few microseconds, because other processors may be spinning. cpp-norun KIRQL old; KeAcquireSpinLock(&m_lock, &old); // IRQL is now DISPATCH_LEVEL m_queue.push(item); // short, non-paged work only KeReleaseSpinLock(&m_lock, old); // back to the previous IRQL For data used only at PASSIVE_LEVEL, drivers use waiting locks such as fast mutexes or executive resources instead. Finding out the current IRQL KeGetCurrentIrql() returns it. Well-written drivers assert their assumptions: PAGED_CODE() at the top of pageable functions checks the IRQL is below DISPATCH_LEVEL, and Driver Verifier (lesson 15.07) adds checks that catch IRQL mistakes immediately rather than in rare situations. Common mistakes !warning Waiting at DISPATCH_LEVEL Including while holding a spin lock. It hangs or bug-checks the machine. !warning Touching paged memory or calling pageable code at DISPATCH_LEVEL Works until the page is paged out; then IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL . !warning Long work in an ISR or under a spin lock Everything else on that processor, and processors spinning for the lock, waits. Defer to a DPC or a work item. Check yourself quiz ? What two things are forbidden at DISPATCH_LEVEL and above? - Allocating memory and returning values + Waiting, and touching paged memory or calling pageable code - Reading registers and calling functions - Using integers and using pointers The scheduler and the page-fault handler cannot run there, so a wait or page fault cannot be serviced. ? How is work split between an ISR, a DPC and a work item? - The ISR does everything; DPCs and work items are for logging + ISR does the minimum, the DPC the main work, a work item what must wait - The work item runs first, then the DPC, then the ISR - All three run at the same IRQL in different threads Each step down lowers the IRQL, allowing more but giving up urgency. The ISR runs at device IRQL, the DPC at DISPATCH_LEVEL, and the work item at PASSIVE_LEVEL. ? What is the difference between a spin lock and a mutex? - A spin lock is for user mode, a mutex for kernel mode - They are identical, except spin locks have shorter names - A mutex raises the IRQL; a spin lock lowers it + A spin lock busy-waits at DISPATCH_LEVEL; a mutex sleeps Sleeping is impossible at DISPATCH_LEVEL, which is why code there must spin instead. Spin locks are only for very short work but can be used with DPCs and ISRs; a mutex only works at low IRQL. ? At which IRQL do normal threads, including DriverEntry , run? + PASSIVE_LEVEL - DISPATCH_LEVEL - DIRQL Everything that may wait and use paged memory runs at PASSIVE_LEVEL. ? Why can code at DISPATCH_LEVEL not wait on an event? - Events do not exist in the kernel + The scheduler cannot switch it out to let it wait - It would use too much memory Waiting there would hang that processor. ? What does acquiring a spin lock do to the IRQL? - Lowers it to PASSIVE_LEVEL - Nothing; IRQL is unchanged + Raises it to DISPATCH_LEVEL So all DISPATCH_LEVEL rules apply while holding it. ? What is a DPC for? + An interrupt's follow-up work, so the ISR is short - Waiting for a user-mode thread - Loading a driver Work that must wait goes further down, to a work item at PASSIVE_LEVEL.

title: An IRQL rule checker
body: Driver Verifier and static analysis tools catch IRQL mistakes. Write a simple checker for a sequence of operations a driver performs on one code path. The code path starts at a given IRQL (0 PASSIVE, 1 APC, 2 DISPATCH, 3 and up device levels). Each operation is a string: Operation Effect / rule --- --- "acquire_spinlock" Raises the IRQL to 2 (remember the old level). Not allowed above 2 "release_spinlock" Restores the IRQL from before the matching acquire. Not allowed without a matching acquire "wait" Only allowed below 2 "touch_paged" Only allowed below 2 "touch_nonpaged" Always allowed "call_pageable" Only allowed below 2 Write checkPath(startIrql, ops) , returning a list of problems, each "step N: OPERATION at IRQL L" (N from 1). When an operation is not allowed, report it and carry on as if it had happened (a release without an acquire leaves the IRQL unchanged). At the end, if spin locks are still held, add "end: N spin lock(s) still held" .

title: 15.07  Why Kernel Bugs Take the Whole Machine Down
match: 15.07 Why Kernel Bugs Take the Whole Machine Down
body: When kernel-mode code fails, Windows stops the machine with a bug check (the blue screen) rather than risk corrupting data. This lesson explains why, what the stop code and parameters mean, the most common driver bug checks, how kernel crash dumps are collected and read with !analyze , and how Driver Verifier turns rare driver bugs into immediate, diagnosable ones. Why stop everything? In user mode, an access violation ends one process; Windows still has an intact kernel to clean up after it (lesson 1.06). In kernel mode there is no such referee. If a driver writes through a bad pointer, the damage could be anywhere in the shared kernel address space (lesson 15.01): the file system's caches, another driver's data, the memory manager's tables. Continuing might write corrupted data to disk. So when the kernel detects a condition it cannot safely recover from, it calls KeBugCheckEx , which: 1. stops all processors, 2. writes a crash dump to the page file (copied to C:\Windows\MEMORY.DMP or C:\Windows\Minidump\ on the next boot), 3. shows the stop screen with a stop code , and restarts. Stopping is the safe choice. A blue screen loses unsaved work; silent corruption could lose everything. Reading a stop code A bug check has a code and four parameters whose meaning depends on the code. The ones caused most often by drivers: Code Name Usual meaning --- --- --- 0x0A IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL Paged or invalid memory touched at DISPATCH_LEVEL or above (lesson 15.06) 0xD1 DRIVER_IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL The same, in a driver; parameter 4 is the faulting address in the driver 0x50 PAGE_FAULT_IN_NONPAGED_AREA Referenced invalid memory: a bad or freed pointer 0x3B SYSTEM_SERVICE_EXCEPTION An exception during a system call, often in a driver handling a user request 0x7E SYSTEM_THREAD_EXCEPTION_NOT_HANDLED An exception in a system thread that nothing handled 0xC4 DRIVER_VERIFIER_DETECTED_VIOLATION Driver Verifier caught a rule violation (below) 0x19 BAD_POOL_HEADER Pool corruption: an overrun into the next allocation 0xC2 BAD_POOL_CALLER Bad pool request: double free, wrong IRQL for the pool type 0xCE DRIVER_UNLOADED_WITHOUT_CANCELLING_PENDING_OPERATIONS A driver unloaded while timers, DPCs or IRPs still referred to its code 0xEF CRITICAL_PROCESS_DIED A process Windows cannot run without ended Microsoft's Bug Check Code Reference documents every code and its parameters. The practice task decodes the common ones. Reading a kernel dump Open MEMORY.DMP or a minidump in WinDbg (lesson 8.05), fix the symbols ( .symfix , .reload ) and run: !analyze -v It reports the bug check and its parameters, the faulting module (very often the culprit driver's name, such as XenonEcho.sys ), the call stack at the crash, and the source line if the driver's PDB is available. lm lists loaded drivers; !irql shows the IRQL at the time of the crash; !pool and !poolused investigate pool problems (lesson 15.04). Kernel dumps are configured in System Properties → Advanced → Startup and Recovery : a small memory dump is enough for most driver bugs; a kernel memory dump contains all kernel memory for harder ones. Driver Verifier Many driver bugs only crash in rare situations: when memory happens to be paged out, when an allocation fails, when two processors race. Driver Verifier ( verifier.exe , built into Windows) makes them happen every time , by adding checks to chosen drivers: Option Catches --- --- Special pool Overruns and use-after-free in pool memory, at the faulting instruction (like page heap, lesson 6.03) Force IRQL checking Paged memory touched at DISPATCH_LEVEL even when it is currently in RAM (by paging it out) Pool tracking Leaks: unfreed pool when the driver unloads I/O verification IRPs completed twice, completed with bad status, leaked Deadlock detection Lock order violations Low resources simulation Code that does not handle allocation failure DDI compliance checking Calls made against the documented rules Turn it on for your own driver , in the virtual machine (lesson 15.08), from an administrator prompt ( verifier /standard /driver XenonEcho.sys , then reboot), and leave it on throughout development. A bug Verifier catches gives bug check 0xC4 with parameters describing exactly which rule was broken, instead of a mysterious crash weeks later. Microsoft requires drivers to pass Verifier testing before signing them for release. Common mistakes !warning Ignoring the faulting module !analyze names it; that is where to look first. !warning Developing a driver without Driver Verifier Its checks find in minutes what otherwise takes months of rare crashes. !warning Testing kernel code on your everyday PC A bug check there costs your work and possibly your data. Use a VM with snapshots. Check yourself quiz ? What does KeBugCheckEx do? + Stops every processor, writes a dump, and restarts - Checks the driver for bugs and fixes them - Ends the process that caused the fault - Logs an error and carries on Continuing after a kernel fault could corrupt data, so Windows stops everything instead. ? Which WinDbg command is the first step with a kernel dump? + !analyze -v , after fixing the symbol path - k , before setting any symbols - lm , to list loaded modules - g , to let the machine continue It reports the bug check, its parameters, the faulting module and the stack. A dump cannot continue running. ? Why leave Driver Verifier on throughout driver development? - It makes drivers run faster - It is required to load unsigned drivers - It fixes common driver bugs automatically + It makes rare driver bugs fail at once, with the rule named A bug found the moment it happens, with the rule named, is far cheaper than one found months later. ? Why does Windows stop the whole machine on a kernel-mode fault? - To force the user to restart + The damage could be anywhere, so going on risks data - Because kernel code cannot handle exceptions at all Stopping with a dump is the safe choice. ? What usually causes bug check 0xD1 ? - Running out of disk space - A user program crashing + Touching paged memory at DISPATCH_LEVEL Parameter 4 is the faulting address in the driver. ? What does Driver Verifier do? + Makes rare driver bugs fail clearly - Speeds up the drivers it checks - Signs drivers for release It turns occasional crashes into reproducible ones.

title: Decode a stop code
where: 15.07 Why Kernel Bugs Take the Whole Machine Down
body: Write describeBugCheck(code, parameters) , which turns a bug check into a short summary for a crash report. parameters holds the four bug check parameters. Code Return --- --- 0x0A "IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL: address 0x{p1} at IRQL {p2}" 0xD1 "DRIVER_IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL: address 0x{p1} at IRQL {p2}, code at 0x{p4}" 0x50 "PAGE_FAULT_IN_NONPAGED_AREA: {read or write} 0x{p1}" , where parameter 2 is 0 for a read and anything else for a write 0xC4 "DRIVER_VERIFIER_DETECTED_VIOLATION: rule 0x{p1}" 0x19 "BAD_POOL_HEADER" anything else "BUGCHECK 0x{code}" Addresses and codes are written in upper-case hex without leading zeros; the IRQL in decimal. ( 0x0A and 0x19 as codes are written exactly as in the table's names, not formatted.) describeBugCheck(0xD1, { 0x10, 2, 0, 0xFFFFF80612345678 }) == "DRIVER_IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL: address 0x10 at IRQL 2, code at 0xFFFFF80612345678"

title: 15.08  Building a Virtual Machine Lab
body: Kernel experiments belong in a virtual machine : a whole Windows installation running as a program on your PC, which can crash, be debugged from outside, and be restored to a clean state in seconds. This lesson sets up the lab used by chapter 16: a Windows VM with snapshots , test signing enabled inside it, kernel debugging from the host with WinDbg over the network, and the habits that keep your real machine safe. Why a VM Without a VM With a VM --- --- A driver bug crashes your PC and loses your work It crashes the VM; your PC carries on A kernel debugger needs a second physical computer The host debugs the guest A broken system takes hours to repair Restore a snapshot in seconds Test-signing mode weakens your everyday system Only the lab VM is in test mode Every kernel lesson from here on assumes this lab. Never load a driver you are developing on your everyday machine. Choosing a hypervisor Hypervisor Notes --- --- Hyper-V Built into Windows 10/11 Pro, Enterprise and Education (enable "Hyper-V" in Windows Features). Good kernel debugging support VMware Workstation Pro Free for personal use; mature, good snapshots VirtualBox Free and open source Any works. Give the VM 2 or more processors, 4 GB or more of RAM, and 64 GB of disk. Install Windows 10 or 11 from Microsoft's official ISO; an unactivated installation is fine for a lab. Setting up the guest Inside the VM, from an administrator command prompt: cmd :: 1. Allow test-signed drivers (lesson 16.09). Only in the lab VM. bcdedit /set testsigning on :: 2. Turn on kernel debugging over the network to the host. :: Replace the IP with the host's address on the VM network; the command prints a key for the host. kdnet.exe 192.168.50.1 50000 :: 3. Write a kernel memory dump on bug checks. :: (Or System Properties Advanced Startup and Recovery.) kdnet.exe comes with the Windows Driver Kit's debugging tools (lesson 16.01); copy it and VerifiedNICList.xml from the host's C:\Program Files (x86)\Windows Kits\10\Debuggers\x64\ into the VM. Restart the VM; the desktop shows "Test Mode" in a corner, which is how you know it worked. Also: - Turn Secure Boot off in the VM's settings if test signing will not enable (Secure Boot prevents changing boot configuration this way). - Disable automatic restart on system failure so you can read stop codes. - Create a shared folder, or copy files over the network, to move built drivers from host to guest. Snapshots Take a snapshot as soon as the guest is set up and working: "clean, test mode, debugging on" . Before each experiment, take another or know which to return to. When a driver leaves the VM unbootable, revert in seconds instead of repairing it. Snapshots are the most valuable feature of the lab. Connecting the kernel debugger On the host, start WinDbg (lesson 8.05) → Attach to kernel → Net , enter the port (50000) and the key printed by kdnet in the guest, and start the session. Restart the guest; WinDbg connects as it boots. Now WinDbg controls the guest's whole kernel : Command Effect --- --- Break (Ctrl+Break) Freezes the entire VM, every processor, at once g Lets it run again lm Loaded kernel modules (drivers) bp XenonEcho!DriverEntry Breakpoint in your driver, even before it loads ( bu , "unresolved breakpoint", for drivers not yet loaded) !process 0 0 Every process in the guest !analyze -v After a bug check, analyse it live ed nt!Kd_DEFAULT_Mask 0xF Show DbgPrint / KdPrint output from drivers in the debugger Kernel debugging stops the entire guest operating system while you inspect it, which is exactly what is needed: nothing changes underneath you. Habits that keep you safe - Build on the host; copy to the guest; load only in the guest. - Keep the guest off your main network shares and without your personal accounts. - Revert to a clean snapshot after anything unusual. - Keep test signing only in the lab VM, never on your main machine (lesson 16.09 explains why). Common mistakes !warning Loading a development driver on your main PC One mistake costs a blue screen and possibly your work. Always the VM. !warning No snapshot before an experiment Take one; restoring takes seconds, repairing takes hours. !warning Enabling test signing on your everyday system It weakens its protection against unsigned drivers. Lab VM only. Check yourself quiz ? What does the lab VM need before chapter 16? - Visual Studio installed and the driver source code on its desktop + Test signing, kernel debugging, dumps, and a clean snapshot - Antivirus turned off and administrator rights for every user - Nothing beyond a fresh Windows install The clean snapshot is what lets you undo any mistake in seconds. ? How does WinDbg on the host debug the guest's kernel? - By attaching to the VM's process on the host - By reading the guest's memory through a shared folder + Through a network kernel-debugging connection set up with kdnet in the guest, using the port and key it prints - By installing WinDbg inside the guest and debugging the kernel from there When you break in, the whole guest stops, which is only possible because the debugger is outside it. ? What is the rule about where development drivers are loaded? + Only ever in the lab VM, never on your everyday machine - On any machine, as long as Driver Verifier is on - On your everyday machine first, then the VM - Wherever is fastest to test A driver bug can crash or corrupt the whole system it runs on. ? Why develop drivers in a virtual machine? - Drivers run faster in VMs + Crashes stay in the VM, and snapshots undo them - Drivers cannot run on real hardware And it keeps test signing off your everyday system. ? What does bcdedit /set testsigning on do? - Turns off all driver checks - Enables Driver Verifier + Lets test-signed drivers load Lab VM only. ? What happens to the guest when you break into it with the kernel debugger? + The whole guest freezes until you continue - Only your driver pauses - Nothing; it keeps running So nothing changes while you inspect it.

title: A system call table
body: Model how a system call number selects a kernel function. syscall 0 (read) - handled syscall 2 (open, "save.dat") - handle 4 syscall 99 - STATUS_INVALID_SYSTEM_SERVICE

title: A handle table

title: Four-level page tables
body: Translate a 48-bit virtual address through four levels of page tables. VA 0x00007FF6A1C34123 PML4 index 255, PDPT 474, PD 270, PT 52, offset 0x123 walk: present, present, present, present - physical 0x1A2B3123 VA 0x0000000000001000 - PT entry not present - page fault

title: A scheduler
body: Simulate a priority scheduler with time slices. threads: A (priority 8), B (8), C (4) slices: A B A B A B ... (C waits while A and B are ready) A blocks on I/O - B B B C runs only when A and B are both waiting

title: A tiny kernel model
body: Put processes, handle tables and system calls together in one small model of a kernel. create process "game" (pid 4) game: open("save.dat", read) - handle 4 game: write(handle 4) - access denied game: exit - handles closed, object freed kernel log: 4 calls, 1 refused

title: 16.01  Installing the Windows Driver Kit
body: Drivers are built with the Windows Driver Kit (WDK), an extension to Visual Studio that adds kernel headers and libraries, driver project templates, signing, deployment and analysis tools. This lesson installs matching versions of Visual Studio, the SDK and the WDK on the host, creates the chapter's driver project, and explains what is different about building kernel code. What the WDK adds Part What it is for --- --- Kernel headers ( ntddk.h , wdm.h , wdf.h ) Declarations of kernel functions and structures Kernel libraries ntoskrnl.lib , hal.lib , the KMDF libraries Project templates Empty WDM driver, KMDF driver, UMDF driver, and more Build settings The kernel environment: no C runtime, /kernel mode, special linker options Signing Test-signs the driver automatically on build (lesson 16.09) Tools Debugging tools (WinDbg, kdnet ), Driver Verifier helpers, static analysis (Code Analysis for drivers), InfVerif for installation files Installing The WDK must match your Visual Studio and Windows SDK versions exactly. Microsoft's "Download the Windows Driver Kit" page lists the current combination; follow its steps in order: 1. Visual Studio 2022 with the Desktop development with C++ workload (lesson 1.07). In Individual components , add the MSVC Spectre-mitigated libraries for x64 (driver projects require them) and the Windows SDK version the WDK page names. 2. The Windows SDK of the matching version, if not installed by step 1. 3. The WDK installer of the same version. At its end, let it install the Windows Driver Kit Visual Studio extension . Everything is installed on the host . The VM (lesson 15.08) only runs the result. The chapter's project In Visual Studio: File → New → Project , search for Kernel Mode Driver, Empty (KMDF) or Empty WDM Driver , and name it XenonEcho . This chapter uses a minimal WDM-style software driver first (lessons 16.02 to 16.07), because seeing the IRPs directly makes the I/O model of lesson 15.05 concrete; lesson 16.10 notes what KMDF would take care of for you. Project settings to check (Configuration All , Platform x64 ): Setting Value Why --- --- --- Driver Settings → Target OS Version Windows 10 or later The oldest Windows the driver supports C/C++ → Warning level Level 4, warnings as errors Kernel code deserves every warning Driver Signing → Sign Mode Test Sign Signs the .sys with a test certificate on build (lesson 16.09) Inf2Cat / Stampinf Off for a software-only driver loaded with sc No installation package needed for this chapter's driver Add a second project to the solution, an ordinary Console App called EchoClient , for the user-mode program that talks to the driver (lesson 16.06). What is different about kernel builds - No C runtime and no C++ standard library. There is no printf , std::vector or new by default. Kernel code uses kernel functions: ExAllocatePool2 for memory (lesson 15.04), RtlCopyMemory , RtlStringCbPrintfA , KdPrint for debug output. - C++ is allowed, carefully. Classes, templates, RAII and constexpr work. Exceptions and RTTI are off; global objects with constructors are not supported without extra work; anything that allocates must use the pools. - Stack is small : 12 KB to 24 KB on x64 kernel threads, versus 1 MB in user mode (lesson 2.01). Large locals and deep recursion are not acceptable. - Every function's IRQL matters (lesson 15.06): document and assert it. - Static analysis is part of the build: run Analyze → Run Code Analysis with the driver rules; it understands IRQL annotations and catches real bugs. The output of a build is XenonEcho.sys (a PE file like a DLL, lesson 9.02), its .pdb , and with test signing a test certificate ( .cer ). Common mistakes !warning Mismatched Visual Studio, SDK and WDK versions Install the exact combination Microsoft's download page lists. !warning Missing Spectre-mitigated libraries Driver builds fail with an error naming them; add them in the Visual Studio installer. !warning Reaching for the standard library It is not available in the kernel. Use the kernel's functions. Check yourself quiz ? What does the WDK add to Visual Studio? - A second C++ compiler that only builds drivers - A virtual machine for testing drivers + Kernel headers and libraries, driver templates and driver tools - The source code of the Windows kernel Visual Studio, the SDK and the WDK must be versions that match, so they work together. ? Name three ways building kernel code differs from user code. + No C runtime or standard library, no exceptions, and a tiny stack - It must be written in C, compiled in Debug, and linked statically - It needs more memory, a faster CPU and a second monitor - It runs only in 32-bit mode, without optimisation, from one source file That is why a driver cannot call printf or use std::vector . Drivers can be written in C++ and are built optimised. Every function also has IRQL rules about where it may be called. ? What files does a driver build produce? - An .exe and a .dll - A .lib and a .obj for each source file - A .sys file only + The .sys file, its .pdb , and a test certificate The .pdb is what lets the kernel debugger show your driver's source and names. ? Where are the Visual Studio, SDK and WDK installed? + On the host; the VM only runs the driver - In the virtual machine - On both, with different versions Build on the host, test in the VM. ? Why can a driver not call printf or use std::vector ? - They are too slow + The C and C++ libraries are not in the kernel - Drivers cannot output text KdPrint and the pool allocation functions take their place. ? Roughly how big is a kernel thread's stack on x64? - 1 MB - Unlimited + 12 KB to 24 KB So large locals and deep recursion are out.

title: 16.02  A Driver That Says Hello
body: The smallest useful driver has two functions: DriverEntry , called when it loads, and an unload routine, called when it is removed. This lesson writes them, prints to the kernel debugger, loads the driver in the lab VM as a service, watches its messages in WinDbg, and unloads it, the complete cycle every later lesson builds on. The code cpp-norun // driver.cpp include <ntddk.h extern "C" DRIVER_INITIALIZE DriverEntry; // declarations with the WDK's annotation types DRIVER_UNLOAD EchoUnload; void EchoUnload(PDRIVER_OBJECT driver) { UNREFERENCED_PARAMETER(driver); KdPrint(("XenonEcho: unloading\n")); } extern "C" NTSTATUS DriverEntry(PDRIVER_OBJECT driver, PUNICODE_STRING registryPath) { UNREFERENCED_PARAMETER(registryPath); driver- DriverUnload = EchoUnload; // without this, the driver can never be unloaded KdPrint(("XenonEcho: hello from the kernel, IRQL %u\n", KeGetCurrentIrql())); return STATUS_SUCCESS; } Line by line: - DriverEntry is the driver's main . The I/O manager calls it once, at PASSIVE_LEVEL (lesson 15.06), with the driver object (lesson 15.05) and the path of the driver's registry key. It must be extern "C" so its name is not mangled (lesson 4.02). - It returns an NTSTATUS (lesson 15.02). Returning a failure code makes the I/O manager unload the driver at once, without calling its unload routine, so a failing DriverEntry must clean up anything it already did (lesson 16.03). - DriverUnload must be set for the driver to be stoppable. It undoes everything DriverEntry set up. - KdPrint sends text to an attached kernel debugger. It compiles to nothing in Release builds. ( DbgPrintEx is the always-present version with component ids and levels.) - UNREFERENCED_PARAMETER silences warning C4100 for unused parameters, which matters because warnings are errors. Loading it in the VM Copy XenonEcho.sys (and its test certificate, lesson 16.09) to the lab VM, for example to C:\Drivers\ . A software-only driver like this one can be loaded as a kernel service with the built-in sc tool, from an administrator prompt in the VM: cmd sc create XenonEcho type= kernel binPath= C:\Drivers\XenonEcho.sys sc start XenonEcho sc stop XenonEcho sc delete XenonEcho (The space after each = is required by sc .) sc create writes the service's registry key under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\XenonEcho ; sc start asks the kernel to load the driver and call DriverEntry ; sc stop calls the unload routine and unloads it. Hardware drivers are installed differently, through an INF file that plug and play uses to match them with devices; software drivers like this one do not need one. Seeing the output With WinDbg connected to the VM's kernel (lesson 15.08), enable debug output once per session and start the driver: kd ed nt!Kd_DEFAULT_Mask 0xF kd g XenonEcho: hello from the kernel, IRQL 0 XenonEcho: unloading Without a debugger attached, Sysinternals DebugView run as administrator in the VM (with "Capture Kernel" enabled) shows the same messages. To stop in your code, set a breakpoint before starting the driver: kd bu XenonEcho!DriverEntry kd g bu sets an unresolved breakpoint that is placed when the module loads. When sc start runs, the whole VM freezes at DriverEntry , and you can step through it with p and inspect driver with dt nt!_DRIVER_OBJECT poi(driver) (lesson 8.05). When it goes wrong - sc start fails with error 577 ( ERROR_INVALID_IMAGE_HASH ): the driver is not signed in a way the VM accepts. Check test signing is on and the driver is test-signed (lesson 16.09). - Error 2: the path in binPath is wrong. - A bug check: the VM stops, WinDbg breaks in with the bug check, and !analyze -v names your driver (lesson 15.07). Revert to your snapshot if the VM cannot boot. Common mistakes !warning Forgetting to set DriverUnload The driver can then never be stopped without a reboot. !warning Missing extern "C" on DriverEntry The linker cannot find the entry point. !warning Loading on the host Only in the lab VM. Check yourself quiz ? What are the two functions every unloadable driver needs? - main and exit + DriverEntry and an unload routine - DllMain and DriverUnload - DriverEntry and IRP_MJ_CLOSE Without an unload routine the driver can be loaded but never unloaded until reboot. ? How is a software-only driver loaded for testing? + With sc create ... type= kernel and sc start , in the VM - By double-clicking the .sys file - By calling LoadLibrary from a test program - By copying it into C:\Windows\System32\drivers on the host Loading happens only in the lab VM, where a crash costs nothing but a snapshot restore. ? How do you break into a driver as soon as it loads? - Put __debugbreak() at the end of DriverEntry - Start the driver, then press Break in WinDbg quickly - Set bp Driver!DriverEntry after the driver has loaded + Set bu Driver!DriverEntry before starting it bu is resolved when the module loads; bp needs the module to be loaded already. ? When is DriverEntry called, and at which IRQL? + Once, when the driver is loaded, at PASSIVE_LEVEL - Every time a program opens the driver - At DISPATCH_LEVEL It is the driver's equivalent of main . ? What happens if DriverEntry returns a failure status? - Windows bug-checks + It is unloaded without its unload routine - The driver keeps running Lesson 16.03 handles partial set-up. ? Where does KdPrint output go? - To a console window - To a log file automatically + To an attached kernel debugger It compiles away in Release builds.

title: Read an NTSTATUS
body: Every driver function returns an NTSTATUS . Its top two bits are the severity : 0 success, 1 informational, 2 warning, 3 error. The NT_SUCCESS macro treats success and informational codes (severity 0 or 1) as success. Write: - ntSuccess(status) : what NT_SUCCESS returns (true when the value, read as a signed 32-bit number, is not negative); - severity(status) : "success" , "informational" , "warning" or "error" ; - name(status) : the name for these well-known codes, or "" : Code Name --- --- 0x00000000 STATUS_SUCCESS 0x00000103 STATUS_PENDING 0x80000005 STATUS_BUFFER_OVERFLOW 0xC0000001 STATUS_UNSUCCESSFUL 0xC000000D STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER 0xC0000010 STATUS_INVALID_DEVICE_REQUEST 0xC0000022 STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED 0xC0000023 STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL 0xC000009A STATUS_INSUFFICIENT_RESOURCES

title: 16.03  The Driver Lifecycle
body: A driver sets things up in DriverEntry (devices, links, memory, timers) and must tear every one of them down in its unload routine, in reverse order, leaving nothing behind. If set-up fails halfway, it must undo exactly the steps that succeeded. This lesson builds that discipline: the load and unload sequence, the service registry key, cleanup on partial failure, and why anything left behind after unload crashes the machine. Load to unload The service's registry key ( HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\XenonEcho ) records the type (kernel driver), the file, and the start type : on demand ( sc start ), at boot, or at system start. The lab always uses on-demand, so a broken driver never loads automatically. The unload rule After DriverUnload returns, the driver's code and global data are unmapped . Anything that still refers to them becomes a pointer into nothing: Left behind What happens later --- --- A timer or DPC still queued It fires and jumps into unmapped code: bug check 0xCE (DRIVER_UNLOADED_WITHOUT_CANCELLING_PENDING_OPERATIONS) A device object Requests can still be routed to a driver that is gone A symbolic link Programs can open a name pointing at a deleted device Pool memory Leaked until reboot (lesson 15.04); Driver Verifier reports it A registered callback The kernel calls it later: bug check An IRP still pending Completing it later touches freed state So unload undoes everything , in reverse order of creation, waiting where necessary (for example, KeCancelTimer and flushing queued DPCs with KeFlushQueuedDpcs ) until nothing can call into the driver any more. It is lesson 2.04's RAII and destructor-order rule, enforced by the hardware. Partial failure in DriverEntry DriverEntry does several steps that can each fail. If step 3 fails, steps 1 and 2 must be undone before returning the failure, because the unload routine will not be called. The clear way to write it is to record what succeeded and undo it in reverse: cpp-norun extern "C" NTSTATUS DriverEntry(PDRIVER_OBJECT driver, PUNICODE_STRING) { NTSTATUS status{ STATUS_SUCCESS }; PDEVICE_OBJECT device{ nullptr }; bool linkCreated{ false }; do { status = IoCreateDevice(driver, sizeof(EchoState), &kDeviceName, FILE_DEVICE_UNKNOWN, FILE_DEVICE_SECURE_OPEN, FALSE, &device); if (!NT_SUCCESS(status)) break; status = IoCreateSymbolicLink(&kLinkName, &kDeviceName); if (!NT_SUCCESS(status)) break; linkCreated = true; // ... more steps, each followed by a check and a "created" flag ... } while (false); if (!NT_SUCCESS(status)) // undo, in reverse, only what succeeded { if (linkCreated) IoDeleteSymbolicLink(&kLinkName); if (device) IoDeleteDevice(device); return status; } driver- DriverUnload = EchoUnload; return STATUS_SUCCESS; } The practice task simulates this: given which steps succeed, produce the cleanup calls in the right order. Reference counting and in-flight work Unload can arrive while requests are still being processed on other processors. The I/O manager will not unload a driver while it still has device objects with open handles (the device's reference count, lesson 15.03), so a program holding the device open keeps the driver loaded, and sc stop fails until it closes. Work the driver started itself (timers, work items, threads) is the driver's responsibility to stop and wait for in unload. Common mistakes !warning Unload that forgets one thing Every resource created in DriverEntry needs a matching release in unload. Write them as pairs. !warning Cleanup in the wrong order Reverse order of creation: links before devices, timers stopped before freeing what they use. !warning Partial failure that leaks Undo exactly the steps that succeeded before returning a failure from DriverEntry . Check yourself quiz ? Why must a driver's unload routine leave nothing behind? - Because unloading frees the driver's process - Because Windows will refuse to unload the driver otherwise + Its code is unmapped, so leftovers would later reach freed code - Because leftovers are saved and reused the next time the driver loads A forgotten timer firing later jumps into unmapped code, which is a bug check. ? How should DriverEntry handle a failure partway through? + Undo, in reverse order, exactly the steps that succeeded, then return the failure status - Return success anyway so the driver stays loaded - Call the unload routine, which frees everything whether or not it was created - Retry the failed step until it works The unload routine is not called when DriverEntry fails, so it must clean up itself. ? Why can sc stop fail while a program has the device open? - Because sc cannot stop kernel services - Because the driver is busy handling a timer - Because test mode prevents unloading + A driver with open device handles is not unloaded Close the client program's handle first, then stop the driver. ? What happens to a timer the driver forgot to cancel when it unloads? + It fires into unloaded code: a bug check - Windows cancels it automatically - Nothing; timers do not outlive drivers Bug check 0xCE is exactly this. ? In which order does unload release resources? - The same order as creation + The reverse of creation - Any order at all Later resources may depend on earlier ones. ? DriverEntry created a device, then failed to create the link. What must it do? - Return the failure; unload will clean up - Ignore it and return success + Delete the device and return the failure status The unload routine is not called when DriverEntry fails.

title: Set up and roll back
body: Model a driver's set-up sequence. Each Step has a name, the name of the call that undoes it, and whether it succeeds. Write initialise(steps) , which runs the steps in order and returns a Result : - If every step succeeds: ok is true, calls lists the step names in order. - If a step fails: stop there. calls lists the names of the steps attempted (including the failing one), followed by the undo calls of the steps that succeeded , in reverse order. ok is false. Then write unload(steps) , the unload routine for a fully initialised driver: the undo calls of all steps in reverse order. steps: create device / delete device, create link / delete link (fails), allocate state / free state initialise - ok false, calls { "create device", "create link", "delete device" }

title: 16.04  Device Objects and Symbolic Links
body: For a user program to talk to a driver, the driver needs a device object to receive requests and a symbolic link that gives it a name user mode can open. This lesson creates both in DriverEntry , removes them in unload, controls who may open the device with a security descriptor , and adds the create and close dispatch routines that make opening and closing work. The device object cpp-norun UNICODE_STRING kDeviceName = RTL_CONSTANT_STRING(L"\\Device\\XenonEcho"); UNICODE_STRING kLinkName = RTL_CONSTANT_STRING(L"\\??\\XenonEcho"); PDEVICE_OBJECT device{ nullptr }; NTSTATUS status{ IoCreateDevice( driver, // the owning driver sizeof(EchoState), // extra bytes for the driver's per-device state (the device extension) &kDeviceName, // its name in the object namespace FILE_DEVICE_UNKNOWN, // device type: also used in the IOCTL codes (lesson 16.05) FILE_DEVICE_SECURE_OPEN, // apply the device's security to every open, including of sub-paths FALSE, // not exclusive: several handles may be open at once &device) }; - The device appears as \Device\XenonEcho in the object namespace (lesson 15.03), visible in WinObj. - The device extension is a block of non-paged memory attached to the device, sized by the second argument, where the driver keeps its state ( static_cast<EchoState (device- DeviceExtension) ). Keeping state there instead of in globals keeps the driver ready for more than one device. - UNICODE_STRING is the kernel's string type: a length in bytes , a maximum length, and a pointer to UTF-16 characters that are not necessarily zero-terminated . Always use the length. The symbolic link Device names under \Device are not reachable from the Win32 API directly. A symbolic link in the \?? directory (lesson 15.03) gives the device a DOS device name: cpp-norun status = IoCreateSymbolicLink(&kLinkName, &kDeviceName); From user mode, the device is then opened as \\.\XenonEcho (lesson 16.06). In unload, the link is deleted ( IoDeleteSymbolicLink ) before the device ( IoDeleteDevice ), the reverse of creation (lesson 16.03). Create and close Opening the device sends an IRP_MJ_CREATE to the driver, and closing the last handle sends IRP_MJ_CLOSE (after IRP_MJ_CLEANUP ). A driver that does not handle them gets the default, which fails the request, so even a minimal driver handles them: cpp-norun NTSTATUS EchoCreateClose(PDEVICE_OBJECT, PIRP irp) { irp- IoStatus.Status = STATUS_SUCCESS; irp- IoStatus.Information = 0; IoCompleteRequest(irp, IO_NO_INCREMENT); return STATUS_SUCCESS; } // in DriverEntry: driver- MajorFunction IRP_MJ_CREATE = EchoCreateClose; driver- MajorFunction IRP_MJ_CLOSE = EchoCreateClose; Every dispatch routine follows this shape: fill in IoStatus (the status, and in Information how many bytes were transferred), complete the IRP exactly once (lesson 15.05), and return the same status. Who may open it By default a device created with IoCreateDevice gets the security of its device type, which for many types lets any user open it. That is rarely what a driver wants: every request a user can send is code the kernel will run on their behalf. Choose deliberately: - IoCreateDeviceSecure (from wdmsec.h ) takes an SDDL string describing the security descriptor. For example SDDL_DEVOBJ_SYS_ALL_ADM_ALL allows only SYSTEM and administrators; a custom string can add specific users or groups. - Each IOCTL can also require read or write access to the handle (lesson 16.05), so a user with read access cannot perform write operations. For the lab's echo driver, administrators only is the right default. Common mistakes !warning Treating UNICODE_STRING as zero-terminated Always use its Length (in bytes). !warning Deleting the device before the link Delete in reverse order of creation. !warning Leaving the device open to every user Use IoCreateDeviceSecure with an SDDL string that allows only who needs access. !warning Not handling create and close Opening the device then fails with "invalid device request". Check yourself quiz ? What do IoCreateDevice and IoCreateSymbolicLink each create? - A user-mode window and a file + A device object, and a name user mode can open - A kernel thread and a timer - A registry key and a service User mode cannot open names in \Device directly, which is why the link is needed. ? Why handle IRP_MJ_CREATE and IRP_MJ_CLOSE ? - Because they are needed to unload the driver - Because Windows sends them every second to check the driver is alive + Opening and closing send them; unhandled, they fail - Because they create and delete the device object The handlers can be tiny, just completing the request successfully. ? How do you restrict who may open a device? - Give the symbolic link a secret name - Check the caller's user name in DriverEntry - Only load the driver when the right user is logged on + Use IoCreateDeviceSecure with an SDDL string A secret name is not security: anyone can list the object namespace. Each IOCTL should also require specific access rights. ? How does a user-mode program open the device \Device\XenonEcho ? + As \.\XenonEcho , through its link - Directly by \Device\XenonEcho - Through the registry The link gives the device a name in the DOS device directory. ? What is the device extension? - A file name extension + Per-device state memory - An extra driver Its size is passed to IoCreateDevice . ?
