What must a dispatch routine always do with an IRP it handles itself? - Pass it down the stack - Free it with ExFreePool + Complete it exactly once Lesson 15.05's rules.

title: Names for a device
body: Write deviceNames(base) , which builds the three names a driver and its client use for a device called base : - the kernel device name \Device\<base ; - the symbolic link name \??\<base ; - the user-mode path \\.\<base . base must be 1 to 32 characters, each a letter, a digit or an underscore; otherwise return std::nullopt . (Driver authors keep names simple: no spaces, no backslashes that would create sub-paths.) Also write byteLength(text) : the Length a UNICODE_STRING holding text would have: the number of UTF-16 units times 2, without a terminator. text here is plain ASCII.

title: 16.05  IOCTLs: Talking to a Driver
body: Reads and writes move bytes; most driver interfaces need commands : "echo this", "give me your statistics", "reset". Those are I/O control codes (IOCTLs), sent with DeviceIoControl and received as IRP_MJ_DEVICE_CONTROL . This lesson explains how a control code packs device type, function, buffering method and required access into 32 bits, and writes the driver's dispatch routine for the echo driver's commands. Control codes An IOCTL is a 32-bit number built by the CTL_CODE macro from four fields: 31 16 15 14 13 2 1 0 ┌────────────┬──────┬────────────────────┬──────┐ │ DeviceType │Access│ Function │Method│ │ (16 bits) │ (2) │ (12 bits) │ (2) │ └────────────┴──────┴────────────────────┴──────┘ Field Meaning --- --- DeviceType The device's type, as passed to IoCreateDevice . Values below 0x8000 are reserved for Microsoft; your own drivers use 0x8000 and up Function Which command. Values 0x800 and up are for vendors Method How buffers are passed: METHOD_BUFFERED (0), METHOD_IN_DIRECT (1), METHOD_OUT_DIRECT (2), METHOD_NEITHER (3); lesson 16.07 Access The access the caller's handle must have: FILE_ANY_ACCESS (0), FILE_READ_ACCESS (1), FILE_WRITE_ACCESS (2), or both (3) cpp-norun // echo_ioctl.h: shared by the driver and the client, like lesson 13.03's plugin header. define ECHO_DEVICE_TYPE 0x8001 define IOCTL_ECHO_PING CTL_CODE(ECHO_DEVICE_TYPE, 0x800, METHOD_BUFFERED, FILE_ANY_ACCESS) define IOCTL_ECHO_ECHO CTL_CODE(ECHO_DEVICE_TYPE, 0x801, METHOD_BUFFERED, FILE_READ_ACCESS FILE_WRITE_ACCESS) define IOCTL_ECHO_STATS CTL_CODE(ECHO_DEVICE_TYPE, 0x802, METHOD_BUFFERED, FILE_READ_ACCESS) struct EchoStats { unsigned long long requests; unsigned long long bytesEchoed; }; The access bits are enforced by the I/O manager before the driver ever sees the request: a handle opened without write access cannot send IOCTL_ECHO_ECHO . Choosing them carefully is part of the driver's security (lesson 16.04). The practice task encodes and decodes these codes. The dispatch routine cpp-norun NTSTATUS EchoDeviceControl(PDEVICE_OBJECT device, PIRP irp) { auto state{ static_cast<EchoState (device- DeviceExtension) }; const PIO_STACK_LOCATION stack{ IoGetCurrentIrpStackLocation(irp) }; const auto& p{ stack- Parameters.DeviceIoControl }; NTSTATUS status{ STATUS_INVALID_DEVICE_REQUEST }; ULONG_PTR information{ 0 }; switch (p.IoControlCode) { case IOCTL_ECHO_PING: status = STATUS_SUCCESS; break; case IOCTL_ECHO_STATS: if (p.OutputBufferLength < sizeof(EchoStats)) { status = STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL; break; } // METHOD_BUFFERED: the I/O manager gave us one system buffer for input and output (lesson 16.07). static_cast<EchoStats (irp- AssociatedIrp.SystemBuffer) = state- stats; information = sizeof(EchoStats); status = STATUS_SUCCESS; break; case IOCTL_ECHO_ECHO: status = EchoEcho(state, irp, p, information); // lesson 16.07 writes this, carefully break; } irp- IoStatus.Status = status; irp- IoStatus.Information = information; // how many bytes to copy back to the caller IoCompleteRequest(irp, IO_NO_INCREMENT); return status; } // in DriverEntry: driver- MajorFunction IRP_MJ_DEVICE_CONTROL = EchoDeviceControl; - Unknown codes fall through to STATUS_INVALID_DEVICE_REQUEST . Never assume a code is one you know. - Every length is checked before any buffer is touched (lesson 16.07 is entirely about this). - Information tells the I/O manager how many bytes of the output to copy back for METHOD_BUFFERED ; it must never exceed the output length. - Updating state- stats from several processors at once needs synchronisation: interlocked operations ( InterlockedIncrement64 ) or a lock (lesson 15.06). Common mistakes !warning Function numbers below 0x800 or device types below 0x8000 Those ranges are reserved for Microsoft. !warning FILE_ANY_ACCESS for commands that change state Require the access the operation needs, so read-only handles cannot perform it. !warning Trusting the control code Handle only codes you define; everything else returns STATUS_INVALID_DEVICE_REQUEST . Check yourself quiz ? Which ranges should your own device types and function numbers use? - Device types below 0x100 , function numbers below 0x10 + Device types 0x8000 and above; function numbers 0x800 and above - Any values, as long as they are even - The same values as an existing Microsoft driver The lower ranges are reserved for Microsoft. ? What does the dispatch routine do with an unknown control code? + Completes it with STATUS_INVALID_DEVICE_REQUEST - Ignores it and returns without completing it - Completes it with STATUS_SUCCESS and no data - Passes it to the unload routine Every IRP must be completed; an unknown request gets a clear error. ? Why should the IOCTL definitions live in a shared header? - Because the kernel can only read headers, not source files - So the driver compiles faster - Because DeviceIoControl reads the header at run time + So the driver and its user-mode client use exactly the same codes and structures Two hand-copied definitions drift apart and produce baffling mismatches. ? What four fields make up an IOCTL code? + Device type, required access, function number and buffering method - Driver name, version, size and checksum - Process id, thread id, address and length Packed by the CTL_CODE macro into 32 bits. ? Who enforces an IOCTL's access bits? - The driver, if it remembers to + The I/O manager, before the driver sees it - Nobody A handle without the required access cannot send the code. ? What does IoStatus.Information hold when completing a buffered IOCTL? - The control code of the request - The status of the request + The output byte count to copy back It must never exceed the output buffer's length.

title: Build and read control codes
body: Implement ctlCode(deviceType, function, method, access) , which packs the four fields exactly as the CTL_CODE macro does: (deviceType << 16) (access << 14) (function << 2) method and decode(code) , which splits a control code back into its fields. Also write isVendorCode(code) : true when the device type is at least 0x8000 and the function is at least 0x800 , the ranges set aside for drivers other than Microsoft's. ctlCode(0x8001, 0x801, 0, 3) = 0x8001E004 decode(0x8001E004) = device 0x8001, function 0x801, method 0, access 3

title: 16.06  A User-Mode Client
body:
The other half of the driver is an ordinary program: it opens the device by its symbolic link with CreateFileW , sends commands with DeviceIoControl , and reports errors clearly. This lesson writes the echo driver's client using chapter 5's handles and errors, wraps the protocol in a small class, and covers the details that trip people up: buffer sizes, ERROR_MORE_DATA , and the driver not being loaded. Opening the device cpp-norun include <windows.h include <cstdio include "echo_ioctl.h" // shared with the driver (lesson 16.05) UniqueHandle openEcho() // lesson 5.01's RAII handle { HANDLE h{ CreateFileW(L"\\.\XenonEcho", // the symbolic link, as \.\XenonEcho GENERIC_READ GENERIC_WRITE, // the access our IOCTLs require (lesson 16.05) 0, nullptr, OPEN_EXISTING, 0, nullptr) }; return UniqueHandle{ h }; // treats INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE as empty } If the driver is not loaded, CreateFileW fails with error 2 ( ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND : there is no such name); if the device's security does not allow this user, error 5 ( ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED , lesson 16.04). A good client reports these in plain words: "The XenonEcho driver is not loaded: run sc start XenonEcho in the lab VM." Sending a command cpp-norun bool ping(HANDLE device) { DWORD returned{ 0 }; return DeviceIoControl(device, IOCTL_ECHO_PING, nullptr, 0, nullptr, 0, &returned, nullptr) != FALSE; } std::optional<EchoStats stats(HANDLE device) { EchoStats s{}; DWORD returned{ 0 }; if (!DeviceIoControl(device, IOCTL_ECHO_STATS, nullptr, 0, &s, sizeof(s), &returned, nullptr)) return std::nullopt; if (returned != sizeof(s)) return std::nullopt; // never trust the length blindly, even from our own driver return s; } DeviceIoControl takes the control code, an input buffer and its size, an output buffer and its size, and returns how many bytes the driver put in the output (the IRP's Information , lesson 16.05). The driver's NTSTATUS becomes a Win32 error for GetLastError (lesson 5.02): STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL arrives as ERROR_INSUFFICIENT_BUFFER , STATUS_INVALID_DEVICE_REQUEST as ERROR_INVALID_FUNCTION . Echo, with a variable size cpp-norun std::optional<std::string echo(HANDLE device, const std::string& text) { std::string reply(text.size(), '\0'); DWORD returned{ 0 }; if (!DeviceIoControl(device, IOCTL_ECHO_ECHO, const_cast<char (text.data()), static_cast<DWORD (text.size()), reply.data(), static_cast<DWORD (reply.size()), &returned, nullptr)) return std::nullopt; reply.resize(returned); return reply; } The protocol is the client and driver's shared contract, exactly like lesson 13.03's plugin API: a shared header, explicit sizes, versions if it will change (lesson 12.06), and validation on both sides. The practice task builds a versioned message format for requests and replies with careful parsing. A small client program cpp-norun int wmain() { UniqueHandle device{ openEcho() }; if (!device) { const DWORD error{ GetLastError() }; if (error == ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND) std::wprintf(L"XenonEcho is not loaded (sc start XenonEcho, in the lab VM)
"); else std::wprintf(L"could not open XenonEcho: error %lu
", error); return 1; } std::wprintf(L"ping: %s
", ping(device.get()) ? L"ok" : L"failed"); if (auto reply{ echo(device.get(), "hello, kernel") }) std::printf("echo: %s
", reply- c_str()); if (auto s{ stats(device.get()) }) std::printf("requests %llu, bytes echoed %llu
", s- requests, s- bytesEchoed); return 0; } Run it in the VM with the driver loaded, under the kernel debugger with a breakpoint in EchoDeviceControl , and you can follow one request from DeviceIoControl in user mode, through the system call (lesson 15.02), to your dispatch routine and back. Common mistakes !warning Opening the device with less access than the IOCTL requires The request fails with access denied before reaching the driver. !warning Ignoring the returned byte count Use it to size the result, and check it is what you expected. !warning Cryptic errors Translate the common cases (not loaded, access denied) into instructions the user can follow. Check yourself quiz ? How does a client open a driver's device? + CreateFileW on the link's name, \.\Name - With LoadLibrary on the driver's .sys file - With OpenProcess on the System process - With CreateFileW on \Device\Name In C++ source the backslashes are doubled: L"\\.\XenonEcho" . ? What arguments does DeviceIoControl take? - The driver's file name, a function name and its arguments - The device handle and a single buffer used both ways + A handle, a code, input and output buffers and sizes, and more - The control code and a callback that receives the result The bytes-returned value comes from the Information field the driver set when completing the request. The rest is a place for the bytes returned and an optional OVERLAPPED structure. ? Why treat the client–driver protocol like a plugin API? - Because the driver is loaded as a plugin DLL into the client - Because both must be written in C - Because Windows requires IOCTLs to use the plugin format + Both are built separately and need a shared, versioned contract The same lessons as chapter 13 apply: an interface between separately built pieces needs a contract. ? The client's CreateFileW(L"\\.\XenonEcho", ...) fails with error 2. What is the likely cause? + The driver is not loaded, so no link exists - The user is not an administrator - The IOCTL code is wrong Error 5 would suggest access denied. ? How does a driver's NTSTATUS reach the client? - As the return value of DeviceIoControl + DeviceIoControl fails; GetLastError maps it - Through the output buffer For example STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL becomes ERROR_INSUFFICIENT_BUFFER . ? What does the returned argument of DeviceIoControl receive? - The NTSTATUS - The size of the input buffer + The Information byte count the driver set Size results by it, and check it.

title: A versioned request format
body: The echo protocol's next version sends structured requests. Each message is bytes laid out as: Offset Size Field --- --- --- 0 2 version , little-endian, currently 1 2 2 flags 4 4 length of the payload that follows, little-endian 8 length the payload Write encode(flags, payload) , which builds a version 1 message, and decode(bytes) , which parses one and returns the version, flags and payload, or std::nullopt if: - the message is shorter than the 8-byte header; - the version is not 1; - length is larger than the bytes actually present after the header, or larger than kMaxPayload (4096); - there are extra bytes after the payload. Use only explicit byte arithmetic, no memcpy of structs (lesson 2.06).

title: 16.07  Validating Buffers and Staying Safe
body: A driver that accepts requests from user mode is a doorway into the kernel, and many serious Windows vulnerabilities have been driver bugs in exactly this code. This lesson covers the three ways buffers reach a driver ( buffered , direct and neither I/O), and the rules that keep a driver safe: check every length, never return more than was written, never leak kernel memory, and handle every failure. Why this matters Lesson 15.02 explained that the kernel never trusts user mode. A driver's dispatch routines are kernel code run with user-supplied inputs: lengths, control codes and buffer contents chosen by whoever opened the device. A bug that lets a caller read or write memory it should not becomes a way to take over the machine. Vulnerable drivers are a well-known attack route, which is why Windows maintains a blocklist of known-vulnerable signed drivers and why Microsoft's signing process includes testing (lesson 16.09). Writing this code carefully is not optional. Three ways to pass buffers The method in the control code (lesson 16.05) decides how the I/O manager presents the caller's buffers: Method What the driver gets Safety --- --- --- METHOD_BUFFERED One system buffer in non-paged pool, max(input, output) bytes. The I/O manager copies the input in before the call and copies Information bytes out after Safest: the driver never touches user memory. Best for small requests METHOD_IN_DIRECT / METHOD_OUT_DIRECT Input in a system buffer; the output (or second) buffer described by an MDL whose pages the I/O manager has probed and locked (lesson 15.04) Safe, avoids copying large data METHOD_NEITHER The raw user pointers The driver must probe, capture and guard every access itself (lesson 15.02's three rules). Avoid unless there is a strong reason The echo driver uses METHOD_BUFFERED throughout, and so should yours unless measurements show copying is too slow. The rules for every request 1. Check every length before touching any buffer. Input at least as large as the structure you will read; output at least as large as what you will write. Return STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL (or STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER ) otherwise. 2. Treat every field read from the input as hostile. Counts, sizes, offsets and indices inside the request get the same checks as the lengths, including overflow in arithmetic ( count sizeof(T) can wrap, lesson 15.02). 3. Set Information to exactly the number of bytes written, never more than the output length. With buffered I/O, the I/O manager copies Information bytes from the system buffer back to the caller; a larger number copies out whatever else is in that pool memory: an information leak . 4. Never leak kernel memory. Zero output structures before filling them (padding bytes too, lesson 2.05). ExAllocatePool2 zero-initialises, which is one reason it replaced the older function (lesson 15.04). 5. Handle every failure. Allocations can fail; return STATUS_INSUFFICIENT_RESOURCES . Never assume. 6. Keep the state consistent across processors. Requests can arrive on several processors at once (lesson 15.06): protect shared state. The echo handler, carefully cpp-norun NTSTATUS EchoEcho(EchoState state, PIRP irp, const auto& p, ULONG_PTR& information) { const ULONG in{ p.InputBufferLength }; const ULONG out{ p.OutputBufferLength }; if (in == 0) return STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER; if (in kMaxEchoBytes) return STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER; // a limit protects the pool if (out < in) return STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL; // we will write exactly in bytes // Buffered I/O: input and output share the system buffer, and the input is already there. // Echoing means leaving it in place and reporting that many bytes as output. information = in; // never more than out InterlockedIncrement64(&state- stats.requests); InterlockedAdd64(&state- stats.bytesEchoed, in); return STATUS_SUCCESS; } Every number that comes from the caller ( in , out ) is checked before it is used; the output count is exactly what is valid; the shared statistics use interlocked operations. The practice task writes the general validator that checks a request against these rules. Tools that help - Driver Verifier (lesson 15.07) with I/O verification catches IRPs completed wrongly and leaks. - Code Analysis for drivers (lesson 16.01) and its annotations ( _In_reads_bytes_ , _IRQL_requires_max_ ) find length and IRQL mistakes at build time. - Fuzzing the IOCTL interface from user mode with random codes, lengths and contents (lesson 17.03) finds what review misses. Run it in the lab VM, with Verifier on. Common mistakes !warning Reading the input before checking its length Even one field read from a too-short buffer reads past it. !warning Information larger than what was written Leaks pool contents to user mode. !warning METHOD_NEITHER without probing, capturing and guarding A classic source of exploitable driver bugs. Prefer buffered I/O. !warning Trusting sizes inside the request A count field in the request is as untrusted as the buffer length. Check yourself quiz ? What are the three buffering methods, and which is safest? - Fast, normal and slow; normal is safest + Buffered, direct and neither; buffered is safest - Stack, heap and pool; pool is safest - Input, output and both; input is safest With buffered I/O the driver never touches user memory directly; with neither, it must probe and capture everything itself. Buffered uses a system buffer, direct uses MDLs of locked pages, and neither passes raw user pointers. ? What are the main rules for handling a request? - Trust the client if it runs as administrator - Check lengths only in Debug builds + Check lengths, distrust fields, report exact sizes, leak nothing - Copy the whole buffer, whatever its size, then check it Each rule closes a way for a hostile caller to read or corrupt kernel memory. Also handle every failure and synchronise shared state. ? Why are vulnerable drivers such a concern? - Because they make games run slowly + A validation bug can hand a caller the kernel - Because they cannot be uninstalled - Because they show advertisements Attackers even load old, signed but vulnerable drivers on purpose to get into the kernel. ? With METHOD_BUFFERED , what does the driver work with? + A system buffer the I/O manager copies - The caller's user-mode pointers - An MDL The driver never touches user memory directly. ? Why must Information never exceed the bytes actually written? - It would crash the client + Extra bytes copied back leak kernel memory - It makes the request slower An information leak can reveal kernel addresses and data. ? A request contains a count of items. How should the driver treat it? - Trust it, since the length was already checked - Ignore it + As hostile: check it and its arithmetic first Fields inside requests are as hostile as the lengths.

title: Validate an IOCTL request
body: A driver's "read records" command takes a request header from the input buffer and writes records to the output buffer. Write validate(input, inputLength, outputLength) , the checks the dispatch routine performs before touching anything, returning a Decision : a status name and the exact number of bytes the driver will write. The input begins with a header, if the input is long enough: Offset Size Field --- --- --- 0 4 first : index of the first record wanted 4 4 count : how many records Each record is 24 bytes; the driver holds 100 records (indices 0 to 99). Check, in this order: 1. inputLength is at least 8 (the header): otherwise "STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL" . 2. count is at least 1: otherwise "STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER" . 3. first + count does not exceed 100, computed without overflow : otherwise "STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER" . 4. outputLength is at least count 24 : otherwise "STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL" . If all pass: "STATUS_SUCCESS" with bytes equal to count 24 . On any failure, bytes is 0. input holds inputLength bytes; read the fields little-endian from it only after check 1.

title: 16.08  Kernel Debugging with WinDbg
body: With WinDbg attached to the lab VM (lesson 15.08), you can break into your driver's code, step through it, and inspect every kernel structure involved in a request. This lesson is a working session: breakpoints on driver load and on dispatch routines, debug output with levels, examining driver and device objects and IRPs with !drvobj , !devobj and !irp , and analysing a bug check your driver caused. Before you start - WinDbg on the host is connected to the VM's kernel (lesson 15.08) and the VM is running. - Symbols: .symfix for Microsoft's, plus your build folder for the driver's PDB: .sympath+ C:\code\XenonEcho\x64\Debug , then .reload . - Debug output enabled: ed nt!Kd_DEFAULT_Mask 0xF (or for DbgPrintEx with your own component and level, ed nt!Kd_IHVDRIVER_Mask 0xF ). Breaking into your driver Goal Command --- --- Stop at DriverEntry before the driver is loaded bu XenonEcho!DriverEntry (an unresolved breakpoint, placed when the module loads) Stop in a dispatch routine bp XenonEcho!EchoDeviceControl Stop only for one control code Set the breakpoint on a line inside that case (F9 in the source window), rather than on the function Step over / into / out p / t / gu Show locals and parameters dv /t Show the call stack k ( kP with parameters) Continue g Break in at any time Ctrl+Break Start the driver in the VM ( sc start XenonEcho ); WinDbg stops at DriverEntry , and the entire VM freezes while you step through it. Then run the client (lesson 16.06) and stop in EchoDeviceControl for each request. With the PDB loaded, WinDbg's source window follows along; the Locals and Call Stack panes behave like Visual Studio's (lesson 4.07). Looking at kernel structures The ! extensions understand the I/O manager's objects (lesson 15.05): kd !drvobj XenonEcho 7 Driver object (ffffa50c1a2b3e30) is for: \Driver\XenonEcho Device Object list: ffffa50c19f0c8a0 ... Dispatch routines: 00 IRP_MJ_CREATE fffff8063f5e1010 XenonEcho!EchoCreateClose 02 IRP_MJ_CLOSE fffff8063f5e1010 XenonEcho!EchoCreateClose 0e IRP_MJ_DEVICE_CONTROL fffff8063f5e1080 XenonEcho!EchoDeviceControl ... kd !devobj ffffa50c19f0c8a0 Device object (ffffa50c19f0c8a0) is for: XenonEcho \Driver\XenonEcho DriverObject ffffa50c1a2b3e30 Current Irp 00000000 RefCount 1 Type 00008001 Flags 00000040 DevExt ffffa50c19f0c9f0 ... - !drvobj shows the driver's devices and, with flag 7, its dispatch table: a quick check that DriverEntry filled it in correctly. - !devobj shows a device's reference count (open handles, lesson 16.03), type (your 0x8001 ) and extension. - Inside a dispatch routine, !irp @rdx (the IRP is the second argument, so it is in rdx at the routine's first instruction, lesson 7.06) shows the request: major function, control code, buffer lengths, and the system buffer's address, which db can then dump. - dt XenonEcho!EchoState <address shows your device extension with field names, from the PDB. A bug check, end to end Introduce a bug on purpose in the lab driver, for example reading the input header before checking its length in a copy of lesson 16.07's handler, and send it a 1-byte request. With Driver Verifier's special pool on (lesson 15.07), the read past the system buffer faults at once. WinDbg breaks in with the bug check; then: kd !analyze -v ... PAGE_FAULT_IN_NONPAGED_AREA (50) Invalid system memory was referenced. ... FAULTING_SOURCE_LINE: C:\code\XenonEcho\dispatch.cpp FAULTING_SOURCE_LINE_NUMBER: 48 ... STACK_TEXT: XenonEcho!EchoReadRecords+0x1a XenonEcho!EchoDeviceControl+0x6c nt!IofCallDriver+0x55 nt!IopSynchronousServiceTail+0x1a8 nt!IopXxxControlFile+0x5e5 nt!NtDeviceIoControlFile+0x56 nt!KiSystemServiceCopyEnd+0x25 ntdll!NtDeviceIoControlFile+0x14 KERNELBASE!DeviceIoControl+0x6b EchoClient!wmain+0x84 That one stack is the whole of chapters 15 and 16: the client's DeviceIoControl , the system call (lesson 15.02), the I/O manager building and dispatching the IRP (lesson 15.05), and your dispatch routine at the line that read too far. Fix the check, rebuild, revert the VM to the snapshot if needed, and test again. Common mistakes !warning Breakpoints that never hit Check symbols with lm v m XenonEcho and that the loaded driver is the build whose PDB you gave WinDbg. !warning Forgetting the debug output mask KdPrint output is filtered until the mask is set. !warning Leaving the VM frozen While stopped in the debugger the whole guest is frozen: continue with g when done. Check yourself quiz ? How do you see a driver's dispatch table in WinDbg? + !drvobj <name 7 - lm m XenonEcho - k while inside DriverEntry - dt _DRIVER_OBJECT with no address It lists the driver's device objects and the routine for each IRP major function. ? Where is the IRP when a dispatch routine starts, and how do you look at it? - In rcx ; dt _IRP @rcx - On the top of the stack; dq @rsp - In a global variable named Irp + In rdx ; look with !irp @rdx A dispatch routine's arguments are the device object ( rcx ) and the IRP ( rdx ). ? What does a bug check's stack show for a request from user mode? + The path from the client, through the kernel, to the driver - Only the driver's own functions - The client program's source code - The order in which drivers were loaded Frames such as nt!NtDeviceIoControlFile mark where the request entered the kernel. ? Why use bu rather than bp for DriverEntry ? + It resolves when the driver loads - bp does not work in the kernel - bu is faster Unresolved breakpoints wait for the module. ? What does !drvobj XenonEcho 7 show? - The driver's source code + Its devices and dispatch routines - All IRPs in the system A quick check that DriverEntry set things up correctly. ? In the bug check stack, what does nt!NtDeviceIoControlFile represent? - A function in the driver - The client program + The kernel side of the system call Lesson 15.02's path, seen in a real stack.

title: 16.09  Test Signing
body: 64-bit Windows loads only kernel drivers with a trusted digital signature: driver signature enforcement . During development, drivers are signed with a test certificate and loaded on machines in test mode , which is why the lab VM has it on. This lesson explains how signing works, sets up test signing, explains how real drivers are signed for release, and why test mode belongs only in a lab. Why Windows requires signatures A kernel driver can do anything (lesson 15.01). If any program could load any driver, malware would simply load its own and take full control of the machine. So 64-bit Windows enforces driver signature enforcement (DSE): a driver is loaded only if it carries a valid signature chaining to a certificate Windows trusts for kernel code, and for current Windows releases that means a signature from Microsoft itself, obtained through Microsoft's signing service after the driver's author has been verified. A signature does two things: it proves who published the driver (accountability), and that the file has not been changed since it was signed (integrity). Microsoft can also revoke signatures and block known-vulnerable drivers (lesson 16.07), and features such as Hypervisor-protected Code Integrity (memory integrity) enforce these rules even against kernel-level tampering. How a signature works, briefly 1. A hash of the driver file is computed. 2. The hash is signed with the publisher's private key ; the signature and the publisher's certificate are embedded in the file (or in a catalog .cat file for installed driver packages). 3. When loading, Windows recomputes the hash, checks the signature with the certificate's public key, and checks the certificate chains to a root it trusts for kernel drivers, and that it has not been revoked. Change one byte of a signed driver and the hash no longer matches: it will not load. Test signing for development Getting every development build signed by Microsoft would be impossible, so Windows has a test mode for development machines: - On the test machine (the lab VM): bcdedit /set testsigning on , then restart (lesson 15.08). The desktop shows "Test Mode". - The driver is signed with a test certificate that the developer creates. Visual Studio's driver projects do this automatically: with Driver Signing → Sign Mode: Test Sign , the build creates a test certificate ( XenonEcho.cer ) and signs XenonEcho.sys with it. - In test mode, Windows accepts drivers signed with test certificates, provided the certificate is trusted on that machine. For drivers loaded as services with sc , test mode with a test-signed driver is usually enough; installing the test certificate into the VM's Trusted Root and Trusted Publishers stores (with certmgr or the Certificates console) covers the remaining cases. You can check a signature with signtool verify /v /kp XenonEcho.sys (kernel-mode policy), or in the file's Properties → Digital Signatures tab. Why test mode stays in the lab Test mode weakens a fundamental protection: it lets the machine load drivers signed by anyone who can make a test certificate, which is anyone at all. That is fine in a disposable VM that holds nothing of value, and unacceptable on a computer you use for anything else. Never turn on test signing (or disable signature enforcement in any other way) on your everyday machine, and be suspicious of any software that asks you to. Signing for release Drivers distributed to other people go through Microsoft's Partner Center (Hardware Dev Center): Step Purpose --- --- An extended validation (EV) code-signing certificate for the company Proves the publisher's identity to Microsoft Attestation signing (for testing and limited release), or full Windows Hardware Compatibility Program certification with the HLK test suite Microsoft checks and tests the driver Microsoft signs the driver Windows then trusts it on every machine That process is deliberate: it is why Windows users can trust that a driver came from an accountable publisher, and it is far outside an individual learner's needs. For this course, test signing in the lab VM is all you need. Common mistakes !warning Disabling signature checks on your main PC "to make it work" Use the lab VM. Test mode on an everyday machine weakens its security for everything. !warning Changing the .sys after signing Any change breaks the signature. Sign as the last build step (Visual Studio does). !warning Assuming a signed driver is safe A signature proves who published it and that it is unchanged, not that it has no bugs; vulnerable signed drivers exist, which is why Windows blocks known ones. Check yourself quiz ? Why does 64-bit Windows require signed drivers? - Because unsigned drivers run more slowly - So Microsoft can charge for every driver + Drivers control everything, so they must be accountable - Because signatures make drivers smaller A signature also proves the file has not been changed since it was signed. ? How is a driver test-signed in Visual Studio? - By running it once in Debug - By copying a certificate from another driver - By turning off signature checks in the project settings + Set Sign Mode to Test Sign; the build signs it Test signatures are only accepted when the machine has test signing turned on. The test machine must also be running in test mode. ? Why must test mode never be used on an everyday computer? - Because it slows the computer down - Because it disables Windows Update + It lets anyone's test-signed drivers load - Because it deletes signed drivers Anyone can make a test certificate, so test mode trusts anyone. ? What does driver signature enforcement do? + Loads only validly signed drivers - Scans drivers for viruses - Makes drivers run faster Without it, any program could load code into the kernel. ? What does test mode ( bcdedit /set testsigning on ) allow? - Loading any unsigned file + Loading drivers signed with test certificates, for development - Running user programs as administrator Only ever in a lab machine. ? What does a valid signature prove? - That the driver has no bugs - That the driver is fast + Who published it, and that it is unchanged Signed drivers can still be vulnerable.

title: 16.10  Project: An Echo Driver in a Virtual Machine
match: 16.10 Project: An Echo Driver in a Virtual Machine
body: This project assembles chapter 16 into a complete, working pair: the XenonEcho driver with ping, echo and statistics commands, and its client. It gives the full driver source with every rule from the chapter applied, a build-load-test-unload checklist for the lab VM with Driver Verifier on, a test plan including hostile inputs, and a note on what KMDF would do for you. The driver cpp-norun // XenonEcho: an educational software driver. Build in Debug, test-signed; load only in the lab VM. include <ntddk.h include "echo_ioctl.h" namespace { UNICODE_STRING kDeviceName = RTL_CONSTANT_STRING(L"\\Device\\XenonEcho"); UNICODE_STRING kLinkName = RTL_CONSTANT_STRING(L"\\??\\XenonEcho"); constexpr ULONG kMaxEchoBytes{ 4096 }; struct EchoState { EchoStats stats; // updated with interlocked operations }; } extern "C" DRIVER_INITIALIZE DriverEntry; DRIVER_UNLOAD EchoUnload; _Dispatch_type_(IRP_MJ_CREATE) _Dispatch_type_(IRP_MJ_CLOSE) DRIVER_DISPATCH EchoCreateClose; _Dispatch_type_(IRP_MJ_DEVICE_CONTROL) DRIVER_DISPATCH EchoDeviceControl; static NTSTATUS Complete(PIRP irp, NTSTATUS status, ULONG_PTR information) { irp- IoStatus.Status = status; irp- IoStatus.Information = information; IoCompleteRequest(irp, IO_NO_INCREMENT); // exactly once; do not touch irp afterwards return status; } NTSTATUS EchoCreateClose(PDEVICE_OBJECT, PIRP irp) { return Complete(irp, STATUS_SUCCESS, 0); } NTSTATUS EchoDeviceControl(PDEVICE_OBJECT device, PIRP irp) { auto state{ static_cast<EchoState (device- DeviceExtension) }; const auto& p{ IoGetCurrentIrpStackLocation(irp)- Parameters.DeviceIoControl }; void buffer{ irp- AssociatedIrp.SystemBuffer }; // METHOD_BUFFERED for every code below switch (p.IoControlCode) { case IOCTL_ECHO_PING: return Complete(irp, STATUS_SUCCESS, 0); case IOCTL_ECHO_ECHO: { const ULONG in{ p.InputBufferLength }; if (in == 0 in kMaxEchoBytes) return Complete(irp, STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER, 0); if (p.OutputBufferLength < in) return Complete(irp, STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL, 0); InterlockedIncrement64(reinterpret_cast<volatile LONG64 (&state- stats.requests)); InterlockedAdd64(reinterpret_cast<volatile LONG64 (&state- stats.bytesEchoed), in); return Complete(irp, STATUS_SUCCESS, in); // the input is already in the system buffer } case IOCTL_ECHO_STATS: { if (p.OutputBufferLength < sizeof(EchoStats)) return Complete(irp, STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL, 0); EchoStats copy{}; // zeroed: no stray bytes leave the kernel copy.requests = static_cast<unsigned long long (InterlockedCompareExchange64(reinterpret_cast<volatile LONG64 (&state- stats.requests), 0, 0)); copy.bytesEchoed = static_cast<unsigned long long (InterlockedCompareExchange64(reinterpret_cast<volatile LONG64 (&state- stats.bytesEchoed), 0, 0)); RtlCopyMemory(buffer, &copy, sizeof(copy)); return Complete(irp, STATUS_SUCCESS, sizeof(copy)); } default: return Complete(irp, STATUS_INVALID_DEVICE_REQUEST, 0); } } void EchoUnload(PDRIVER_OBJECT driver) { IoDeleteSymbolicLink(&kLinkName); // reverse order of creation if (driver- DeviceObject) IoDeleteDevice(driver- DeviceObject); KdPrint(("XenonEcho: unloaded\n")); } extern "C" NTSTATUS DriverEntry(PDRIVER_OBJECT driver, PUNICODE_STRING) { PDEVICE_OBJECT device{ nullptr }; NTSTATUS status{ IoCreateDevice(driver, sizeof(EchoState), &kDeviceName, ECHO_DEVICE_TYPE, FILE_DEVICE_SECURE_OPEN, FALSE, &device) }; if (!NT_SUCCESS(status)) return status; RtlZeroMemory(device- DeviceExtension, sizeof(EchoState)); status = IoCreateSymbolicLink(&kLinkName, &kDeviceName); if (!NT_SUCCESS(status)) { IoDeleteDevice(device); // undo what succeeded (lesson 16.03) return status; } driver- MajorFunction IRP_MJ_CREATE = EchoCreateClose; driver- MajorFunction IRP_MJ_CLOSE = EchoCreateClose; driver- MajorFunction IRP_MJ_DEVICE_CONTROL = EchoDeviceControl; driver- DriverUnload = EchoUnload; KdPrint(("XenonEcho: loaded\n")); return STATUS_SUCCESS; } For production you would create the device with IoCreateDeviceSecure and an SDDL string limiting access (lesson 16.04); in the lab, testing from an administrator prompt, the plain call keeps the listing short. The client is lesson 16.06's program. Checklist 1. Build both projects (x64, Debug). The driver build test-signs XenonEcho.sys (lesson 16.09). Run Code Analysis and fix every warning. 2. Revert the VM to the clean snapshot (lesson 15.08). Connect WinDbg; set ed nt!Kd_DEFAULT_Mask 0xF . 3. Copy XenonEcho.sys and EchoClient.exe into the VM. 4. Enable Driver Verifier for the driver (administrator prompt in the VM), and restart: verifier /standard /driver XenonEcho.sys 5. Load : sc create XenonEcho type= kernel binPath= C:\Drivers\XenonEcho.sys then sc start XenonEcho . WinDbg shows "XenonEcho: loaded". 6. Test with the client, then the hostile tests below. 7. Unload : sc stop XenonEcho , check "unloaded" appears and !poolused shows nothing left for your tag. sc delete XenonEcho . 8. Revert the VM. Test plan Test Expect --- --- Ping Success Echo "hello, kernel" The same text back, returned = 13 Echo 0 bytes ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER Echo 4097 bytes ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER Echo 100 bytes into a 50-byte output ERROR_INSUFFICIENT_BUFFER Stats into a 4-byte output ERROR_INSUFFICIENT_BUFFER Stats after 3 echoes requests 3, bytes the sum An undefined code (function 0x900 ) ERROR_INVALID_FUNCTION Echo from 8 threads at once, 10,000 times each Correct totals (interlocked statistics) sc stop while the client holds the device open Fails until the client closes it Random codes and lengths for a minute (lesson 17.03's fuzzing) No bug check, no Verifier violation All of this with Driver Verifier on. A pass means the driver behaves correctly on every path you can reach from user mode. What KMDF would do for you The same driver in KMDF (lesson 15.05) would replace the dispatch table with I/O queues ( WdfIoQueueCreate ), get request buffers with checked helpers ( WdfRequestRetrieveInputBuffer(request, minimumSize, ...) fails if the buffer is too small), tie the device's lifetime and cleanup to framework objects so unload ordering is automatic, and handle plug and play and power for hardware drivers. For any real driver, start with KMDF; you now know what it is doing underneath. Common mistakes !warning Testing without Driver Verifier Bugs that only appear under memory pressure or particular timing will otherwise reach users. !warning Skipping the hostile tests Correct requests passing proves little; the incorrect ones are where drivers fail. !warning Running any of this outside the lab VM Everything in this chapter is for the VM. Check yourself quiz ? What does the XenonEcho driver do on load, and undo on unload? + Creates its device and link; unload deletes them in reverse - It starts a thread that echoes data; unload ends the thread - It allocates a large pool buffer; unload frees it - It registers a window class; unload unregisters it Unload undoes the steps in reverse order: link first, then device. ? Which rules from lesson 16.07 does the echo handler apply? + Length checks, exact byte counts, zeroed output and atomic statistics - None; the echo handler trusts its buffers because it uses METHOD_BUFFERED - Only the length check on the input buffer - It copies the whole system buffer back, whatever was written Even buffered I/O needs length checks, and zeroing prevents leaking uninitialised kernel memory. ? What does a complete test of a driver include besides correct requests? - Testing on as many real computers as possible - Running it in Release only - Measuring how fast it loads + Hostile inputs, concurrency, fuzzing, all under Verifier Correct requests only prove the easy path works; drivers fail on the hostile ones. ? Why are the statistics updated with interlocked operations? + Several processors may handle requests at once - Interlocked operations are required for all kernel code - To make the numbers larger Lesson 6.06's data races, in the kernel. ? What does the driver do with an undefined control code? - Ignores it silently + Fails it as invalid - Bug-checks the system Only defined codes are handled. ? What must be true after sc stop for the driver to have unloaded cleanly? - The VM must restart - The client must still be running + Nothing remains: no device, link, work or pool Lesson 16.03's rule: leave nothing behind.

title: IOCTL codes
body: Build and decode the control codes a driver and its client agree on. IOCTL_ECHO = CTL_CODE(0x8000, 0x800, METHOD_BUFFERED, FILE_ANY_ACCESS) = 0x80002000 decode 0x80002000 - device 0x8000, function 0x800, buffered, any access

title: Routing requests
body: Send each request to the right handler and complete it exactly once. IRP_MJ_CREATE - ok IRP_MJ_DEVICE_CONTROL IOCTL_ECHO - echoed 5 bytes IRP_MJ_DEVICE_CONTROL unknown code - STATUS_INVALID_DEVICE_REQUEST IRP_MJ_READ (not supported) - STATUS_INVALID_DEVICE_REQUEST

title: The echo buffer
body: Model the driver side of an echo request with buffered I/O. input "hello" (5 bytes), output buffer 16 - output "hello", Information 5 input 20 bytes, output 8 - STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL, Information 0 input 0 bytes - STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER

title: The client side
body: Write the user-mode side: build requests, check results and report errors clearly. open \\.\XenonEcho - ok (simulated) echo "hello" - "hello" (5 bytes) echo 5000 bytes - refused before sending: more than the 4096 limit driver not loaded - "could not open the device: is the driver started?"

title: Echo, end to end
body: Model the whole path of an echo request, from the client through a simulated I/O manager to the driver and back. client: echo "ping" (out 16) I/O manager: allocates 16-byte system buffer, copies 4 bytes in driver: echoes 4 bytes, Information 4, STATUS_SUCCESS I/O manager: copies 4 bytes back client: got "ping" bad request (out 2): driver says BUFFER_TOO_SMALL, client reports it

title: 17.01  Unit Tests for Low-Level Code
body: Every practice task in this course has been checked by unit tests. This lesson turns that around: writing tests for your own low-level code with a framework such as Catch2 or GoogleTest, structuring code so it can be tested (pure logic, injected clocks, random numbers and platform calls), and deciding what is worth testing in games, tools and drivers. What a unit test is A unit test calls one piece of code with chosen inputs and checks its outputs, automatically, in milliseconds. A suite of them runs on every build: cpp-norun include <catch2/catch_test_macros.hpp include "inventory.h" TEST_CASE("potions stack up to their limit") { Inventory inv{ 4, { { "potion", 5 } } }; REQUIRE(inv.add("potion", 7) == 0); CHECK(inv.slot(0) == std::pair<std::string, int { "potion", 5 }); CHECK(inv.slot(1) == std::pair<std::string, int { "potion", 2 }); } The course's practice harness works the same way ( TEST , CHECK , CHECK_EQ ). Real projects use a framework: Framework Notes --- --- Catch2 Header-friendly, readable, TEST_CASE and sections; vcpkg port catch2 GoogleTest Widely used, fixtures and mocking (GoogleMock); vcpkg port gtest ; Visual Studio's Test Explorer runs it Microsoft Native Unit Test Framework Built into Visual Studio's C++ test project template doctest Very fast to compile, Catch2-like Put tests in a separate project (lesson 4.01's tests ), linked against the engine library, and run it after every build, locally and in continuous integration (lesson 17.08). Designing code to be testable Code is easy to test when its logic does not reach directly for things the test cannot control: Hard to test Make it testable by --- --- Calls QueryPerformanceCounter or std::chrono directly Passing a clock (an interface or function) in; tests use a fake clock they advance by hand Calls rand() Passing a seeded random generator in Opens files, windows, devices Separating the platform layer from pure logic (lesson 12.07): parse text, not files Uses global state Passing state in, or resetting it per test Big functions doing everything Small functions with inputs and outputs This is why the practice tasks always asked for a function taking data and returning data: parseLevel(text) rather than loadLevel(path) , tryMove(map, ...) rather than code buried in the game loop. The practice task for this lesson injects a clock into a cooldown timer. What to test Test Example --- --- Normal cases A potion heals 10 Edges Health exactly 0; an inventory exactly full; the first and last tile of a map Invalid input A ragged level file, a negative count, an unknown command Regression tests For every bug fixed, a test that would have caught it (lesson 8.01) Round trips Save then load gives the same state (lesson 11.06) Properties For any random input, sorting gives an ordered result of the same length Not everything needs a unit test: rendering and "does it feel right" are checked by people, and drivers' kernel code is tested in the VM (lesson 16.10). But every piece of pure logic, the majority of most programs, can and should be. Testing low-level code specifically - Bit and byte code (lessons 1.02, 2.06, 9.02): test against known byte sequences, written out in the test, including the edges (0, maximum values, negative numbers). - Parsers of untrusted data (save files, network messages, PE headers): test valid, truncated, oversized and nonsense inputs; then fuzz them (lesson 17.03). - Concurrency (lesson 6.06): tests that run many threads are useful but cannot prove absence of races; combine with careful design and tools. - Memory : run the test suite under AddressSanitizer (lesson 2.10) in a separate configuration, so tests also catch overruns and use-after-free. Common mistakes !warning Tests that depend on time or randomness They pass and fail at random. Inject the clock and the generator. !warning Testing only the happy path Bugs live at edges and in invalid input. !warning Tests that are slow or need setup Unit tests should run in seconds with no outside dependencies, or nobody runs them. Check yourself quiz ? What makes code easy to unit test? - Large functions that do everything in one place - Code that reads the clock and random numbers inside itself + Small functions that take clocks and data as parameters - Code that prints its results to the console A function that reads the system clock itself cannot be tested at a chosen time; one given a clock can. Platform calls are kept in a separate layer, so the logic runs without them. ? What kinds of cases should tests cover? + Normal cases, edges, bad input, regressions and round trips - Only the normal case, since edge cases are rare - Only the cases that have already failed in play - Whatever the code's author thought of while writing it Edges and invalid input are where low-level code most often breaks. ? Why run the test suite under AddressSanitizer? - Because tests only compile with ASan turned on - So the tests run faster - Because ASan writes the tests automatically + So the tests also catch overruns and use-after-free A test can pass while silently overrunning a buffer; ASan turns that into a clear failure. ? Why pass a clock into a cooldown timer instead of reading the system time inside it? + So a test can control time exactly - Reading the system time is slow - Timers cannot read the time A fake clock makes timing logic testable. ? What is a regression test? - A test that runs slowly + A test that keeps a fixed bug from returning - A test of old features only Every fixed bug deserves one. ? Which code benefits most from tests with truncated and nonsense inputs? - Rendering code for sprites - Constant definitions in headers + Parsers of untrusted data, such as saves Then fuzz them too.

title: A cooldown you can test
body: Write Cooldown , an ability cooldown that reads time through an injected clock, so tests can control time. - The constructor takes a clock ( std::function<double() , returning seconds) and a duration in seconds. - ready() : true if the ability may be used now: it has never been used, or at least duration seconds have passed since the last use. - use() : if ready, records the current time as the last use and returns true ; otherwise returns false and changes nothing. - remaining() : seconds until ready (0 if ready now). Then write the test-side helper FakeClock : now() returns the current fake time (starting at 0), advance(seconds) moves it forward.

title: 17.02  Sanitizers and Static Analysis
body: Tools find bugs that tests and reviews miss. Sanitizers add checks while the program runs (AddressSanitizer for memory, UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer for undefined behaviour); static analysis examines the code without running it (compiler warnings, MSVC's /analyze , clang-tidy, annotations). This lesson sets up each for a Visual Studio project and shows the classes of bug each one catches. Two kinds of tool Sanitizers (dynamic) Static analysis --- --- --- How Instrument the program; check while it runs Analyse the source without running it Finds Bugs on the paths actually executed Possible bugs on any path, including rare ones False alarms Almost none: it saw the bug happen Some: it may flag code that cannot actually go wrong Cost A slower test build Longer build time They complement each other, and both complement tests. Sanitizers Sanitizer Catches On Windows --- --- --- AddressSanitizer (ASan) Overruns, use-after-free, double free (lesson 2.10) MSVC /fsanitize=address ; clang-cl too UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer (UBSan) Signed overflow, invalid shifts, misaligned pointers, out-of-range enum values, null dereferences clang-cl ( -fsanitize=undefined ) ThreadSanitizer (TSan) Data races (lesson 6.06) Not on Windows; run tests on Linux builds with clang or gcc if your code is portable MemorySanitizer Reads of uninitialised memory Linux only A practical setup: an ASan configuration in Visual Studio for the test suite and play sessions (lesson 2.10), and, if the code builds with clang, a clang-cl configuration with ASan and UBSan together. Visual Studio installs clang-cl with the "C++ Clang tools for Windows" component. UBSan catches problems ASan cannot, such as int overflow (lesson 1.02), which can silently break checks like if (a + b < a) because the optimiser assumes signed overflow never happens. Compiler warnings The cheapest static analysis is already in your compiler: - Warning level 4 ( /W4 ) and warnings as errors ( /WX ): lesson 4.03's table of valuable warnings. - /permissive- for standard conformance (Visual Studio's default for new projects). - Selected extra warnings with /w14xxx (enable warning xxxx at level 1), for example /w14062 (an enumerator not handled in a switch ) and /w14265 (a class with virtual functions but no virtual destructor). MSVC Code Analysis Analyze → Run Code Analysis (or /analyze on every build) runs a deeper analysis: null dereferences on some paths, buffer overruns it can prove, uninitialised memory, resource leaks, misuse of Windows APIs, and the C++ Core Guidelines checks ( /analyze with the Core Check rule sets). It understands SAL annotations (source annotation language) that describe what functions expect: cpp-norun // "dest points to destSize bytes the function writes; src is a zero-terminated string it reads." size_t copyName(_Out_writes_z_(destSize) char dest, size_t destSize, _In_z_ const char src); With the annotation, the analyzer checks every caller passes a buffer at least destSize long, and checks the function itself never writes past it. The Windows headers are fully annotated, which is how /analyze catches misuse of Windows API calls. Driver projects use the same annotations for IRQL rules (lesson 16.01). clang-tidy clang-tidy (included with Visual Studio's clang tools; enable it in Properties → Code Analysis → Clang-Tidy ) checks style and bug patterns with hundreds of configurable checks: bugprone- (suspicious patterns such as sizeof mistakes, swapped arguments), performance- (unnecessary copies), modernize- (C++ idioms), cppcoreguidelines- . A .clang-tidy file in the solution folder chooses the checks for everyone. Making it routine Tools only help when they run all the time: 1. Warnings at level 4, as errors, from day one. 2. Code Analysis on every build in at least one configuration. 3. The test suite run under ASan regularly, and in continuous integration (lesson 17.08). 4. New warnings are fixed, not suppressed; when a suppression is genuinely right, it is narrow (one line, pragma warning(suppress: ...) ) with a comment saying why. The practice task writes the overflow-checked arithmetic that UBSan and the analyzers push you towards. Common mistakes !warning Turning tools on late in a project Hundreds of warnings at once get suppressed wholesale. Start clean and keep it clean. !warning Blanket suppressions pragma warning(disable: ...) for a whole file hides future bugs too. !warning Assuming a clean run means no bugs Sanitizers only see the paths that ran; analysers cannot see everything. Use all of them, plus tests. Check yourself quiz ? Which sanitizers can you use with Visual Studio on Windows? - All of them: Address, Thread, Memory and UndefinedBehavior, with MSVC + ASan with MSVC or clang-cl, and UBSan with clang-cl - Only ThreadSanitizer, with MSVC - None; sanitizers are a Linux-only feature MSVC itself supports ASan; clang-cl adds UBSan. ThreadSanitizer and MemorySanitizer need Linux builds. ? What does /analyze add beyond compiler warnings? - It runs the program and watches for crashes - It formats the code to a standard style + Path-sensitive checks for nulls, overruns and leaks, using SAL - It speeds up the build by skipping unchanged files It reasons about the paths through a function without running it, which plain warnings do not. ? How should a genuine false alarm be suppressed? - By turning the warning off for the whole project - By deleting the code the tool complains about - By ignoring it in the build output + Narrowly, on the one line, with a comment why it is safe A project-wide switch hides the real bugs the warning would find elsewhere. ? What is the main difference between a sanitizer and static analysis? + Sanitizers check running code; static analysis reads the source - Sanitizers are only for Linux - Static analysis requires running the program They complement each other. ? Which tool catches signed integer overflow as it happens? - AddressSanitizer + UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer - Compiler warning C4244 ASan is about memory accesses. ? What does a SAL annotation like _Out_writes_z_(destSize) give the analyzer? - A runtime check of the buffer - Faster code for the function + The size of the buffer it writes The Windows headers use these throughout.

title: Arithmetic that cannot overflow silently
body: Signed overflow is undefined behaviour, and unsigned overflow wraps silently. Code that computes sizes from untrusted numbers must detect both. Write, without using any type wider than the inputs: - checkedAdd(a, b) for std::int32_t : the sum, or std::nullopt if it would overflow; - checkedMul(a, b) for std::uint64_t : the product, or std::nullopt if it would exceed the maximum; - allocationSize(count, elementSize, header) : header + count elementSize as std::uint64_t , or std::nullopt if any step overflows. Do not compute the overflowing result and then test it (that is already undefined for signed values). Check before the operation.

title: 17.03  Fuzzing
body: Fuzzing feeds a program huge numbers of automatically generated, mostly broken inputs and watches for crashes, hangs and sanitizer reports. Coverage-guided fuzzers such as libFuzzer learn which inputs reach new code and mutate those further, finding bugs no human would think to test. This lesson writes fuzz targets for Delve's parsers, runs them with MSVC's fuzzer support and AddressSanitizer, and minimises the crashing inputs. The idea Tests check the cases you thought of. Bugs live in the cases you did not: a level file with a 2-billion-character line, a save whose length field says 0xFFFFFFFF, a message cut off mid-header. A fuzzer generates such inputs automatically, millions per hour: Coverage guidance is what makes modern fuzzers effective: the compiler instruments the program to record which code each input reaches, and inputs that reach something new are kept and mutated further. The fuzzer gradually learns the format's structure (the magic number, the version field, valid section headers) without being told. Writing a fuzz target A fuzz target is one function that takes a block of bytes and passes them to the code under test: cpp-norun // fuzz_level.cpp: fuzz Delve's level parser (lesson 11.02's practice task) include <cstddef include <cstdint include <string include "level.h" extern "C" int LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput(const uint8_t data, size_t size) { const std::string text(reinterpret_cast<const char (data), size); const auto level{ parseLevel(text) }; // must never crash, hang or trip a sanitizer if (level) { // Check invariants the parser promises: the result is self-consistent. if (level- tiles.size() != static_cast<size_t (level- width level- height)) __debugbreak(); } return 0; } Good fuzz targets: - target one parser or decoder of untrusted data: level files, saves (lessons 10.07, 11.06), INI settings (10.08), telemetry snapshots (12.04), IOCTL request structures (16.05), PE headers (9.02); - are deterministic and fast (thousands of runs per second); - check invariants as well as crashes: a successful parse should produce a consistent result; - do not touch the file system, network or global state. Running it with MSVC Visual Studio 2022 supports libFuzzer directly: 1. A new console project fuzz_level containing the target and the parser's source. 2. C/C++ → Command Line : /fsanitize=fuzzer /fsanitize=address (ASan makes memory bugs crash immediately instead of silently). 3. A corpus folder with a few valid level files as starting points. 4. Run: fuzz_level.exe corpus -max_total_time=600 The fuzzer prints progress ( cov: grows as it discovers code). On a crash it stops, prints the sanitizer report, and writes the input to a file such as crash-3f2a... . Running fuzz_level.exe crash-3f2a... reproduces it under the debugger. Minimising Fuzzer-found inputs are often large and noisy. Minimisation shrinks one to the smallest input that still fails, which usually makes the bug obvious. libFuzzer does it with -minimize_crash=1 ; the underlying idea is simple enough to write yourself, and the practice task does: repeatedly try removing parts of the input, keeping any removal after which it still fails. Fuzzing a driver's interface Lesson 16.10's test plan included fuzzing the driver from user mode: a program in the lab VM that opens the device and sends random control codes, lengths and buffer contents in a loop, with Driver Verifier on. Any bug check is a finding; the last request is logged before sending, so it can be reproduced. That is exactly how many real driver vulnerabilities are found, which is why driver authors should do it first. Common mistakes !warning Fuzzing without sanitizers Most memory bugs do not crash on their own. Combine fuzzing with ASan. !warning Slow targets A target doing file I/O or logging runs a hundred times slower and finds far less. !warning Fixing the crash but not adding the input to the tests Every fuzzer finding becomes a regression test (lesson 17.01). Check yourself quiz ? What makes a good fuzz target? + It feeds the bytes to one parser, fast, deterministic, side-effect free - It runs the whole game with the bytes as keyboard input - It writes each input to a file so a person can check it - It uses random numbers so each run tests something different Randomness or side effects make crashes impossible to reproduce from the saved input. It should also check invariants, not only wait for crashes. ? How do you run libFuzzer with MSVC? + Build with /fsanitize=fuzzer,address , run it on a corpus folder - Install a separate fuzzing program and point it at the .exe - Add include <fuzzer and call fuzz() from main - Build in Debug and run it under the Visual Studio debugger libFuzzer supplies main itself and calls your LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput with each input. ? What should happen to every input a fuzzer finds? - It should be deleted once the crash is understood - It should be shared publicly at once - It should be ignored if the crash is rare + Minimise it, fix the bug, and keep it as a regression test The regression test makes sure the same bug cannot quietly come back. ? What makes a coverage-guided fuzzer better than random inputs? + It keeps and mutates inputs that reach new code - It uses a list of known bugs - It runs faster New coverage guides the search. ? Why run a fuzz target with AddressSanitizer? - To make it faster + So silent memory errors are caught at once - Fuzzers require it to compile Silent overruns become clear failures. ? What does minimising a crashing input achieve? - A faster fuzzer for later runs - An automatic fix for the bug + The smallest input that still fails Then add it as a regression test.

title: Minimise a failing input
body: A fuzzer found an input that makes a parser fail. Write minimise(input, fails) , which shrinks it to a smaller input that still fails, by greedy single-character removal: 1. Try removing the character at position 0, then 1, then 2, and so on, of the current input. 2. As soon as removing one gives an input for which fails still returns true, keep that shorter input and start again from position 0 . 3. When no single removal still fails, return the current input. fails(input) is guaranteed to be true for the original input. Also return how many times fails was called, so the cost can be compared with smarter methods. fails = "contains both 'x' and 'y'" minimise("abxcdye") - "xy"

title: 17.04  Secure Coding: Buffers, Integers and Trust
match: 17.04 Secure Coding: Buffers, Integers and Trust
body: Security bugs are ordinary bugs in code that handles input an attacker can control. This lesson collects the course's lessons into secure coding practice for C++: trust boundaries , the classic bug classes (buffer overruns, integer errors, use after free, path traversal, format strings, time-of-check to time-of-use), and the habits and safe building blocks that prevent them. Trust boundaries A trust boundary is any place where data crosses from something you do not control into something you do. Everything this course built has them: Boundary Untrusted side --- --- Files loaded by the game Level files, saves, settings, mods (lessons 10.07, 13.02) Network messages Other players, servers, anything on the internet Plugins and scripts Mod authors' code and data (lesson 13.07) Shared memory and pipes The other process (lesson 12.07) Command-line arguments and environment Whoever started the program A driver's IOCTLs Any user who can open the device (lesson 16.07) The rule is the same at every one: validate at the boundary , before the data is used for anything (sizes, indices, paths, allocations, decisions). Inside, code can rely on data being valid because it was checked once, at the edge. The classic bug classes Bug How it happens Prevention --- --- --- Buffer overrun Copying or indexing past a buffer's end with a length from input (lessons 2.08, 2.09) std::string , std::vector , std::span ; check lengths against the destination; .at() in debug paths Integer overflow and truncation count size wraps; a 64-bit length truncated to 32 bits; signed/unsigned mix-ups (lessons 1.02, 17.02) Checked arithmetic; consistent unsigned sizes; compiler warnings C4244, C4267, C4018 Use after free / dangling Keeping pointers to objects that can disappear (lessons 2.04, 3.10) Ownership through smart pointers; ids and handles instead of raw pointers Uninitialised memory Reading or sending memory never written, leaking its old contents (lesson 16.07) Always initialise; zero output structures Path traversal A file name like ..\..\Windows\system.ini from input reaches files outside the intended folder (lesson 13.02) Reject .. , absolute paths and drive letters; resolve and check the result stays under the base; the practice task Format string printf(userText) interprets % sequences in input Always printf("%s", text) ; prefer std::format with a constant format Time of check to time of use Data checked, then read again after it may have changed (lessons 15.02, 12.04) Copy once, then check and use the copy Injection Building commands, SQL or scripts by concatenating input Pass input as data (arguments, parameters), never as code Nearly every security advisory for C and C++ software falls in this table. Safe building blocks Modern C++ removes whole classes of these bugs if you let it: - std::span<T carries a pointer and a length together, so functions can never lose track of a buffer's size (lesson 2.07). - std::string_view for read-only text, with the lifetime caveat of lesson 2.04. - Containers instead of raw arrays and new . - std::optional and status returns instead of sentinel values that can be mistaken for data. - std::format instead of printf -family formatting. - RAII for every resource, so error paths cannot leak (lesson 2.04). Defence in depth No single measure is perfect, so layers are combined: 1. Correct code : validation at boundaries, safe building blocks. 2. Tools : warnings, analysis, sanitizers, fuzzing (lessons 17.02, 17.03). 3. Platform mitigations left on: ASLR (lesson 6.09), DEP and non-executable data (6.03), stack cookies (7.05), control-flow guard. They turn many exploitable bugs into crashes. 4. Least privilege : programs and tools that run with only the rights they need (lesson 6.08) limit what any remaining bug can do. Common mistakes !warning Validating deep inside the code instead of at the boundary Some path will skip the check. Validate where the data enters. !warning Trusting your own file formats Users and attackers can edit any file on their machine. !warning Turning mitigations off for convenience They cost almost nothing and defeat whole classes of attack. Check yourself quiz ? What is a trust boundary? - The edge of the screen, beyond which the player cannot click - A line in the code past which exceptions are not caught + Where data you do not control enters, and must be validated - The limit on how much memory a program may use Files, mods, network messages and other processes all cross trust boundaries. ? Name five classic bug classes. - Typos, slow code, missing comments, long functions, bad names + Overruns, integer overflow, use after free, uninitialised reads, path traversal - Compiler errors, linker errors, warnings, asserts and logs - Stack, heap, static, thread-local and register bugs Each of these has caused real security vulnerabilities in games and drivers. Format strings, time-of-check to time-of-use, and injection are classic too. ? What does "defence in depth" mean here? - Writing every check twice in the same function - Running the program inside two virtual machines - Using the deepest possible class hierarchy + Several layers, so a bug past one is stopped by another No single layer is perfect, so several independent layers are used together. The layers are correct code, testing and analysis tools, platform mitigations and least privilege. ? Where should untrusted input be validated? + At the boundary where it enters - Wherever it is finally used - Only in Debug builds Then the inside of the program can rely on it. ? A mod asks the game to load ..\..\saves\other.sav . What bug class is this? - Format string + Path traversal - Integer overflow Reject parent-directory components and check the resolved path stays inside the mod's folder. ? Why use std::span for buffer parameters? - It is faster than a pointer - It allocates memory + It keeps the pointer and length together Lost lengths are the root of many overruns.

title: Join paths safely
where: 17.04 Secure Coding: Buffers, Integers and Trust
body: A mod asks for files by relative path. Write safeJoin(base, relative) , which returns base joined with relative , or std::nullopt if the request could reach outside base . Paths use \ or / as separators; the result uses \ . Reject (return std::nullopt ) if relative : - is empty; - is absolute: starts with \ or / , or has a drive letter ( C: ), or contains : anywhere (which on Windows also names alternate data streams); - contains any component that is .. ; - contains an empty component (two separators in a row such as a//b , or a trailing separator), or a component that ends with a space or a dot (Windows silently strips those, so secret.txt. would open secret.txt ), except the component . itself, which is simply skipped. Otherwise return base , a single \ , and the components joined with \ (skipping . components). If only . components remain, return base unchanged. safeJoin("C:\Game\mods\lantern", "textures/light.png") - "C:\Game\mods\lantern\textures\light.png" safeJoin("C:\Game\mods\lantern", "../../saves/a.sav") - nullopt

title: 17.05  Threat Modelling
body: A threat model is a structured answer to "what could go wrong, and what are we doing about it?" written before the code, not after the breach. This lesson walks through the four questions of threat modelling, draws a data-flow diagram with trust boundaries, applies STRIDE to find threats systematically, and ranks them so effort goes where it matters. The worked example is Delve with mods, saves and an online leaderboard. The four questions Threat modelling sounds formal, but it comes down to four questions: 1. What are we building? A diagram of the parts and the data flowing between them. 2. What can go wrong? Threats, found systematically rather than by guessing. 3. What are we going to do about it? A mitigation, an acceptance, or a design change for each one. 4. Did we do a good job? Review it as the design changes, and check mitigations were really built. It takes an hour for a small project and saves weeks of fixes later, because design changes are cheap before the code exists. Step 1: a data-flow diagram Draw the processes, data stores, external parties and flows, and mark where trust changes: Trust boundaries in this diagram: between the mod folder and the game (anyone can write files there), between the player's machine and the server (the server cannot trust anything the client sends), and between the server and other players viewing scores (their browsers will render whatever names are stored). Step 2: STRIDE STRIDE is a checklist of six threat types. Walk every element and flow in the diagram and ask each question: Letter Threat Question Property it violates --- --- --- --- S Spoofing Can someone pretend to be another user or component? Authentication T Tampering Can someone change data or code they should not? Integrity R Repudiation Can someone deny doing something, with no way to prove otherwise? Accountability I Information disclosure Can someone read what they should not? Confidentiality D Denial of service Can someone stop it working for others? Availability E Elevation of privilege Can someone gain rights they should not have? Authorisation Step 3: threats and responses for Delve Element STRIDE Threat Response --- --- --- --- Mod folder → game T, E A malicious mod's data overflows a parser and runs code Validate at the boundary (17.04), fuzz the parsers (17.03), data-only mods by default, native plugins opt-in with a warning (13.07) Mod folder → game I A mod path like ..\..\ reads files outside its folder safeJoin (17.04's practice) Save files T A player edits their save Accept for single player: it is their game Game → leaderboard T, S A client submits an impossible score, or one in someone else's name Server-side validation and replay checks (17.06), accounts with tokens Leaderboard D One client floods submissions Rate limiting per account and address Leaderboard → other players T, E A player name containing a script runs in viewers' browsers Escape output; limit name characters Score database I Leaked email addresses Store only what is needed; access control on the database Game → leaderboard R A player disputes a ban Keep submitted replays and the server's decision log Note the save-file row: accepting a threat is a legitimate answer, when the impact falls only on the person causing it. Step 4: ranking Not every threat deserves the same effort. A simple ranking multiplies likelihood (1 to 5) by impact (1 to 5) and handles the highest scores first, with ties broken by whichever is cheapest to fix. Many teams use richer schemes, but any explicit ranking beats fixing whatever someone noticed last. The practice task implements one. Keeping it alive A threat model is a document in the repository next to the design notes. Update it when a feature adds a new data flow or trust boundary (an online feature, a plugin API, a new file format), and check the "response" column against the code during reviews. Common mistakes !warning Starting from attacks you have heard of STRIDE over a diagram finds the threats specific to your design, not just famous ones. !warning Treating every threat as "must fix" Some are accepted, some are cheap to fix, some need a design change. Rank and decide. !warning Writing it once A threat model of last year's design protects last year's design. Check yourself quiz ? What are the four questions of threat modelling? + What are we building, what can go wrong, what are we going to do about it, and did we do a good job - Who is the attacker, where do they live, what do they want, and how much will it cost - What language is it in, what compiler, what platform, and what licence - How fast, how big, how many users, and how many servers They work for any system, from a save file to an online game. ? What does STRIDE stand for? - Speed, Throughput, Reliability, Integrity, Durability, Efficiency - Security, Testing, Review, Inspection, Design, Encryption + Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service and Elevation of privilege - Signing, Tracing, Recovery, Isolation, Debugging, Encryption Each letter is a kind of threat against one security property, such as tampering against integrity. ? What are the possible responses to a threat? - Fix it immediately, whatever the cost - Ignore it unless it has already happened - Move it to the next project + Mitigate it, design it out, or accept it, and record why Players editing their own single-player saves only affect themselves, which is why accepting that threat is reasonable. Accepting fits when the risk is low or falls only on the person causing it. ? What does the T in STRIDE stand for, and which property does it violate? + Tampering, which violates integrity - Theft, which violates confidentiality - Timing, which violates availability Changing data or code without permission. ? Why is "accept" a valid response for players editing their own single-player saves? - Saves cannot be edited + The impact falls only on the person making the change - Accepting is always the best response Effort goes to threats that harm others. ? Where do trust boundaries appear on a data-flow diagram? - Around every function - Only around the database + Wherever data crosses between trust levels Those are where validation is needed.

title: Rank the threats
body: Write rankThreats(threats) , which returns the threats' names in the order they should be handled: - by score ( likelihood impact ), highest first; - ties broken by lower cost first (cheaper fixes earlier); - remaining ties by name alphabetically. Threats marked accepted are left out. Likelihood and impact are 1 to 5; any threat with a value outside that range is a mistake in the threat model and is also left out.

title: 17.06  Software Integrity, Anti-Tamper and Fair Play
match: 17.06 Software Integrity, Anti-Tamper and Fair Play
body: This course taught how programs look from the inside, which is also how cheats and tampering work. This lesson takes the defender's side: why a game can never fully trust the client, why server authority is the foundation of fair online play, how to verify the integrity of your own files and updates with hashes and code signing, what client-side anti-tamper can and cannot do, and the legal, ethical and privacy limits that apply to both sides. The client is in the player's hands Every technique in chapters 5 to 16 works on a program running on your own machine: reading its memory, changing its code, injecting a DLL, inspecting its traffic. A player can do all of that to a game on their machine. That leads to the most important rule of game security: !important Never trust the client Anything that runs on the player's computer can be read and changed by the player. Decisions that affect other players must be made, or at least checked, somewhere the player does not control. Client-side protection can make tampering slower and more obvious; it cannot make it impossible. Fair play in online games rests on design first and detection second. Server authority In an authoritative server design, clients send inputs ("move forward", "fire at this direction") and the server runs the simulation and decides the results. A modified client can still send inputs, but it cannot directly set its health, teleport, or award itself a score. What the server validates: Check Example --- --- Physics limits A move longer than maximum speed times elapsed time is clamped or rejected (the practice task) Rates and cooldowns No more shots than the weapon's fire rate allows Visibility The server sends a player only what that player could legitimately see, so there is nothing hidden in memory to reveal Game rules Items can only be used if owned; doors only opened if unlocked Plausibility over time Statistics that are consistently beyond human limits are flagged for review, never banned automatically For single-score games like Delve's leaderboard, the equivalent is submitting a replay (the seed and the inputs) instead of a score; the server re-simulates it deterministically and computes the score itself (the leaderboard threat in lesson 17.05).
