Integrity of your own files Separately from cheating, you need to know the code and data you ship are the code and data that run, and that updates come from you: - Hash manifests : a list of every shipped file with its SHA-256 hash. The launcher or updater checks files against it, which catches corruption and incomplete updates (lesson 3.08's checksums, made cryptographic). - Code signing : an Authenticode signature on your executables and DLLs (and the manifest) proves who published them and that they were not changed. Windows shows the publisher and SmartScreen builds reputation from it; drivers must be signed to load at all (lesson 16.01). - Signed updates : an updater verifies the signature of a downloaded update before installing it, so a compromised download server cannot push malicious code. - Safe loading : load DLLs only from your own folder with full paths (lesson 13.04), so a planted DLL is not picked up instead. What client-side anti-tamper does Commercial games add protection on the client. Understanding its purpose, at a high level, helps you design around it and judge its trade-offs: Measure Purpose Limit --- --- --- Integrity checks of the game's own code and data Detect modified files or patched code Runs on the same machine it is protecting Obfuscation Make analysis (chapter 9) slower Slows, never prevents Detecting debuggers and injected modules Notice the tools of chapters 8 and 13 False positives on legitimate software Kernel-mode components Observe from a more privileged level Very high trust demanded from players; a driver bug crashes their machine (chapter 16) The cost side matters: kernel-level anti-cheat asks players to trust your code with full control of their computer, and some players reasonably refuse. Collect only what is needed, document what is collected, and remove the component when the game is uninstalled. The rules for both sides - Terms of service and the law apply. Modifying or analysing a game you do not own can break its licence, and creating or selling cheats for online games has led to lawsuits. Cheating in online games harms other players, and this course does not teach it. - Fair-play enforcement must be fair : decisions reviewed by humans, an appeal process, and evidence kept (the repudiation row in 17.05). - Privacy : anti-cheat that scans the player's machine is handling personal data and falls under laws such as the GDPR. - Single-player modding is a different matter: it harms no one, and many developers support it with official tools (chapter 13). Common mistakes !warning Trusting client-reported results "The client says it hit for 9999 damage" must never be believed. !warning Sending hidden information to clients If the client receives every enemy position, a modified client can show them. Send only what can be seen. !warning Relying on obfuscation instead of design Obfuscation buys time. Server authority removes whole classes of cheats. Check yourself quiz ? What is the most important rule of game security? + Never trust the client; decide on the server - Encrypt every file the game uses - Hide the game's code with obfuscation - Run the game with administrator rights Encryption and obfuscation only slow tampering down; server authority makes it irrelevant for what matters. Anything on the player's machine can be changed, so decisions that affect others must be made or checked on the server. ? How do you verify the integrity of your own shipped files and updates? + Hash manifests, Authenticode signing, and signed updates - Checking each file's size when the game starts - Asking the player to reinstall when something looks wrong - Storing all files inside the exe Signing proves who made a file and that it has not changed since. Also load DLLs only by full path from your own folder. ? What are the costs of kernel-mode anti-cheat? - None; it runs invisibly with no effect on players - It makes games run faster, which some players dislike - It only works on older versions of Windows + Players must trust it fully, and its bugs can crash the system It sits at the highest privilege level, with all the risks of any kernel driver. It also handles personal data, with the privacy obligations that brings. ? Why can client-side protection never fully stop tampering? + It runs on the player's own machine, which they control completely - Because clients are always slower than servers - It can, if it is obfuscated enough Protection there can only raise the cost. ? In an authoritative-server design, what do clients send? - Their positions and health, which the server trusts + Their inputs, which the server validates and simulates to decide the results - Nothing; the server guesses The server owns the game state. ? What does code signing an update prove? - That it has no bugs - That it runs faster + Who published it, and that it is unchanged The updater checks the signature before installing.

title: Validate movement on the server
where: 17.06 Software Integrity, Anti-Tamper and Fair Play
body: An authoritative server receives each client's reported position every tick and must not trust it. Write validateMove(previous, reported, dt, maxSpeed, walls) : - The allowed distance is maxSpeed dt plus a tolerance of 1% of it (network timing is never perfect). - If the reported move is within the allowed distance, the move is accepted at the reported position. - If it is further, the move is clamped : the position becomes previous moved towards reported by exactly maxSpeed dt (no tolerance). - Either way, if the resulting position is inside any wall rectangle ( x = left && x < right && y = top && y < bottom ), the move is rejected and the position stays previous . - A dt that is not positive, or a reported position that is not finite (NaN or infinity), is rejected . Return the outcome and the position the server will use.

title: 17.07  Performance Without Guessing
body: Programmers are famously bad at guessing where time goes. This lesson replaces guessing with measurement: frame budgets, profilers (Visual Studio's CPU Usage tool and sampling in general), microbenchmarks done properly, and the statistics that make timings trustworthy (medians and percentiles instead of averages). It ends with the common real causes of slow C++: cache misses, allocations, and work repeated every frame. Budgets first "Fast enough" needs a number. A game at 60 frames per second has 16.7 ms per frame for everything: input, simulation, rendering, audio, and the tools of chapter 12 if they are running. At 144 Hz it is 6.9 ms. A budget turns "it feels slow" into "the overlay takes 3.1 ms of our 16.7". For tools the budget is different (a memory scan should finish in under a second, an overlay should cost under 0.5 ms a frame), but it is still a number. Measure, then change one thing, then measure again Always measure Release builds (lesson 4.10: Debug builds can be ten times slower, and differently slow), on the same machine, with the same input, several times. Profilers A sampling profiler interrupts the program thousands of times a second and records which function was running. Functions that appear in many samples are where the time goes. In Visual Studio: Debug → Performance Profiler → CPU Usage , run the scenario, stop, and read the Hot Path and the list of functions sorted by Total CPU (including callees) and Self CPU (excluding them). Other useful tools: Tool Shows --- --- Visual Studio CPU Usage Where CPU time goes, by function and line Visual Studio Memory Usage Allocations and their call stacks Windows Performance Recorder and Analyzer Whole-system timelines: threads, waits, disk, GPU PIX GPU and frame timing for Direct3D games An in-game frame timer Per-system timings every frame, for regressions Microbenchmarks done properly Sometimes you want to compare two versions of one function. Timing it naively lies in several ways: cpp include <algorithm include <chrono include <iostream include <numeric include <vector volatile long long sink; // stops the optimiser removing the work long long sumVector(const std::vector<int & v) { return std::accumulate(v.begin(), v.end(), 0LL); } int main() { std::vector<int data(1'000'000); std::iota(data.begin(), data.end(), 0); std::vector<double samples; for (int run{ 0 }; run < 25; ++run) { const auto start{ std::chrono::steady_clock::now() }; sink = sumVector(data); const auto end{ std::chrono::steady_clock::now() }; samples.push_back(std::chrono::duration<double, std::micro (end - start).count()); } std::sort(samples.begin(), samples.end()); std::cout << "min " << samples.front() << " us, median " << samples samples.size() / 2 << " us\n"; } varies min 212.4 us, median 231.9 us The rules it follows: - Repeat many times and look at the distribution; one run means nothing. - Use the result (here through a volatile variable) so the optimiser cannot delete the work. - Use steady_clock , which never jumps, not the wall clock. - Report the median and a high percentile (p95, p99), not just the mean: a single slow run caused by the operating system can pull the mean far away, while players feel the slow frames that the percentiles show. The practice task computes these. - Keep input sizes realistic: data that fits in the cache behaves completely differently from data that does not. The usual real causes When you do measure, the culprit in C++ is usually one of a short list: Cause Sign Typical fix --- --- --- Cache misses Time in simple loops over large data; pointer-heavy structures (lesson 2.06) Contiguous arrays, structure of arrays, smaller structs Allocations in the frame loop operator new and malloc high in the profile Reserve once, reuse buffers, pools (lesson 3.10) Repeated work The same computation or lookup every frame Cache the result; recompute only on change Algorithmic cost Time grows much faster than input size A better algorithm: hashing instead of searching, sorting once Waiting Low CPU but slow; threads blocked Profile waits (WPA); avoid blocking calls on the main thread Debug-only overhead Fast in Release Nothing to fix; measure Release Note what is not on the list: rewriting clear code into clever code with no measurement. That rarely helps and often hurts. Common mistakes !warning Profiling Debug builds You will optimise the wrong things. !warning Trusting one timing Run many times; report the median and a percentile. !warning Benchmarks the optimiser deletes If the result is unused, the compiler may remove the code and report it as free. Check yourself quiz ? What is the measurement loop? - Change everything that might be slow, then measure once + Measure, change one thing, measure again, keep it only if better - Read the code, guess what is slow, and rewrite it in assembly - Measure in Debug, optimise, then ship Changing one thing at a time is the only way to know which change helped. ? How does a sampling profiler work? - It adds timing code to every function at compile time - It runs each function on its own and times it + It records what code is running, many times a second - It counts how many lines each function has Instrumenting every function is a different technique and slows the program much more. ? What are the usual real causes of slow C++ code? - Using const , references and small functions - Too many comments and long variable names + Cache misses, hot-loop allocations and poor algorithms - Using std::vector instead of raw arrays const , references and comments cost nothing at run time. Repeated work, blocking waits, and measuring a Debug build are other usual culprits. ? What is the frame budget at 60 frames per second? + About 16.7 milliseconds - 60 milliseconds - 1 millisecond 1000 ms divided by 60. ? Why report the median and p95 rather than only the mean? - The mean is harder to compute + A few slow runs skew the mean - Percentiles are always smaller Distributions, not single numbers. ? Why store a benchmark's result in a volatile variable? - To make it run faster - To avoid cache misses + So the optimiser cannot remove the work Unused results invite dead-code elimination.

title: Benchmark statistics
body: Write summarise(samples) for a list of timings in milliseconds. It returns: - min and max ; - median : the middle value after sorting, or the mean of the two middle values for an even count; - p95 : the nearest-rank 95th percentile: sort, then take the value at 1-based rank ceil(0.95 n) ; - trimmedMean : the mean after dropping the lowest 10% and highest 10% of the sorted values, where 10% is n / 10 rounded down (so with fewer than 10 samples nothing is dropped). An empty list returns all zeros. The input must not be modified.

title: 17.08  Shipping and Maintaining What You Build
match: 17.08 Shipping and Maintaining What You Build
body: A program is not finished when it works on your machine. This lesson covers what it takes to put a tool or game in other people's hands and keep it working: reproducible Release builds, versioning with semantic versions , crash reports with symbols kept for every release, installers and updates, documentation, licences, and the habits of maintenance (changelogs, issue tracking, and deciding what not to build). A reproducible Release build Anyone on the team, or a build server, should produce the same release from the same commit: - The build is one command or one button: Build → Batch Build or msbuild Delve.sln /p:Configuration=Release /p:Platform=x64 . - Dependencies are pinned: the SDL2 version from lesson 11.01 is checked in or fetched at a fixed version (vcpkg with a manifest and baseline does this). - Release settings are deliberate: optimisation on, warnings as errors, /guard:cf and other mitigations on (lesson 17.04), and /Zi with PDBs even for Release. - A continuous integration service (GitHub Actions, Azure Pipelines) builds and runs the tests (17.01) on every push, so a broken build is noticed in minutes. Semantic versions A semantic version MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH tells users what an update means: Part Increase when Example --- --- --- MAJOR You make a change that breaks compatibility: an old save format no longer loads, a plugin API function changes 1.4.2 → 2.0.0 MINOR You add features compatibly 1.4.2 → 1.5.0 PATCH You fix bugs compatibly 1.4.2 → 1.4.3 Pre-releases add a suffix ( 2.0.0-beta.1 ) and sort before the final version. Versioning interfaces between components (lesson 12.06's telemetry protocol, lesson 13.07's plugin API) follows the same rule, which is why those had version fields. The practice task compares and bumps versions. Put the version in the executable's version resource (Add → Resource → Version) so it shows in the file's properties, in the crash report, and in the title or about screen. Crash reports and symbols Users will hit crashes you never saw. Lesson 8.04's minidumps are how you find out: 1. The program installs an unhandled-exception filter that writes a minidump with MiniDumpWriteDump and offers to send it. 2. For every release, you keep the exact PDBs produced by that build, in a symbol store ( symstore add ) or a folder named by version. 3. When a dump arrives, WinDbg or Visual Studio loads it with the matching symbols and shows the call stack and variables at the crash. Without the matching PDB, a dump is a list of addresses. Losing a release's symbols means losing the ability to debug its crashes. Installers and updates Option Suits --- --- A zip file with a portable folder Small tools; nothing to install or uninstall An MSIX package or an MSI (WiX) Applications that need Start menu entries, file associations, clean uninstall A store or launcher (Steam, itch.io, Microsoft Store) Games: it handles distribution, updates and signing Your own updater Only when nothing else fits; it must verify signatures (17.06) Whatever the method: code-sign the files, install per-user without administrator rights when possible (lesson 6.08), and keep settings and saves in the user's folders ( %APPDATA% , Saved Games ), not next to the program. Documentation Three documents cover most needs: - A README : what it is, how to install it, how to use the common features, system requirements. - A changelog : each version, with what was added, changed, fixed and removed, in plain language. - For anything with an interface others build on (a plugin API, a protocol, a driver's IOCTLs), a reference : every function or message, its parameters, errors and version. Licences Every dependency's licence must allow your use: SDL2 uses the zlib licence (very permissive), Dear ImGui is MIT, some libraries are GPL (which places conditions on your own code if you distribute it). List them in a third-party notices file. Choose a licence for your own code too, if you publish it; without one, others have no right to use it. Maintenance After release, most of the work is maintenance: - Track bugs and requests in an issue tracker , each with steps to reproduce, version and logs. - Fix with a regression test first (17.01), then the fix. - Release patches from a known commit, tagged with the version ( git tag v1.4.3 ). - Say no to features that do not fit. Each one is code to maintain forever, a lesson that applies with special force to low-level tools, where every new feature is also new attack surface (17.05). Common mistakes !warning Not keeping Release PDBs Crash reports become useless. !warning Breaking compatibility in a minor version Users and plugin authors trusted the version number. !warning Saving data next to the executable Program Files is not writable by normal users, and updates may replace the folder. Check yourself quiz ? What does each part of a semantic version mean? - MAJOR is the year, MINOR the month, PATCH the day - MAJOR counts releases, MINOR counts builds, PATCH counts commits - All three increase together on every release + MAJOR: incompatible; MINOR: new features; PATCH: fixes A change that breaks old saves is incompatible, so it needs a new MAJOR version. ? What makes a Release build reproducible? + One documented command, pinned dependencies, and CI builds - Building on the same developer's computer every time - Copying the last build and changing the version number - Turning optimisation off so the output is predictable Anyone, on any machine, can then make the same build from the same source. ? What is needed to debug a crash reported by a user? + A minidump from the user's machine and the exact PDB files from the build they were running - The user's whole hard disk image - A Debug build of the game installed on the user's machine - The source code and nothing else Without the matching PDBs, the dump's call stack is just raw addresses. ? A change makes old save files fail to load. Which part of the version increases? + MAJOR - MINOR - PATCH It breaks compatibility. ? Why keep the PDB files of every release? - Windows needs them to run the program + Only they can read that build's dumps - They make the program faster Without them a dump is just addresses. ? Where should a game store its saves? - Next to the executable in Program Files - In the Windows folder + In the user's folders, such as Saved Games or AppData Per-user, writable, and untouched by updates.

title: Compare and bump versions
where: 17.08 Shipping and Maintaining What You Build
body: Write three functions for semantic versions of the form MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH with an optional pre-release suffix after a - (such as 2.0.0-beta.1 ): - parseVersion(text) : the version, or std::nullopt if the text is not three non-negative whole numbers separated by dots (each made only of digits, at least one, no leading zeros except 0 itself), optionally followed by - and a non-empty suffix. - compareVersions(a, b) : negative if a < b , zero if equal, positive if a b . Compare MAJOR, then MINOR, then PATCH numerically. If those are equal, a version with a suffix is lower than one without; two suffixes compare as plain strings. - bump(v, part) : "major" gives MAJOR+1.0.0 , "minor" gives MAJOR.MINOR+1.0 , "patch" gives MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH+1 . The suffix is always removed. Return it formatted as text. compareVersions(1.10.0, 1.9.0) 0 (numeric, not text) compareVersions(2.0.0-beta.1, 2.0.0) < 0 bump(1.4.2, "minor") 1.5.0

title: A tiny test framework
body: Write the smallest useful test framework: register tests, run them, report. ok addition FAIL parse empty: expected 0, got -1 (test.cpp:21) ok parse number 2 of 3 passed

body: Compute buffer sizes from untrusted counts without overflowing. count 1000, size 16 - 16000 count 0x20000000, size 16 - refused (overflows 32 bits) header 12 + count 16 with count 0xFFFFFFFF - refused

title: Never trust a save file
body: Validate a save file completely before using any of it. good file - loaded: level 3, 2 items truncated file - refused: header says 2 items, data for 1 item id 9999 - refused: unknown item negative gold - refused

title: A threat model table

title: 18.01  Capstone: A Memory Inspector with a Full Interface
match: 18.01 Capstone: A Memory Inspector with a Full Interface
body: The first capstone joins chapters 6, 12 and 14 into one polished tool: a read-only memory inspector for programs you built yourself , with a Dear ImGui interface showing the region map, a hex view with typed overlays, snapshots with change highlighting, and the telemetry channel from chapter 12. This lesson gives the specification, an architecture, the milestones in order, the acceptance tests and stretch goals. What you are building Xenon Inspector is a desktop tool for looking inside your own running programs while you develop them: Delve, the practice targets of lesson 9.10, and anything else you compile. It answers questions like "what does this struct look like in memory right now?", "which bytes changed when I picked up that item?" and "how is this program's address space laid out?". The ground rules from chapter 12 are part of the specification, not an afterthought: !important Scope - The inspector only opens processes whose executable lies under a folder you configure as your build output (for example D:\dev\bin ), or processes it starts itself from there. It refuses anything else, with a message explaining why. - It is read-only : it never writes to the target's memory. - It uses documented APIs only ( OpenProcess with PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION PROCESS_VM_READ , VirtualQueryEx , ReadProcessMemory , the Tool Help snapshot functions) and needs no administrator rights. Features Panel Shows Built in --- --- --- Process picker Running processes under the build folder, with a Launch button for executables there 6.07, 12.01 Region map Every region: base, size, state, protection, type, and the module it belongs to; filters and sorting 6.04, 14.04 Hex view Bytes of a selected address range, 16 per row with ASCII; Go to address; follows a pointer on double-click 12.02 Typed overlay A struct definition (from a small text file) laid over the hex view, showing each field's name, type and value 2.06, 9.09 Snapshots Take a snapshot of a range, take another later, and list and highlight the changed ranges the practice task Telemetry If the target publishes chapter 12's telemetry channel, its live values in a table 12.04, 12.05 Settings Build folder, refresh rate, window layout, persisted 14.05 Architecture Keep the layers separate, as lesson 17.01 recommends: the struct parser and the snapshot diff are pure functions with unit tests; the process access layer is the only code that calls Windows; the panels only draw the model and send it commands. Then most of the program can be tested without a target running. Milestones Build it in order; each milestone is usable on its own. 1. Skeleton : the ImGui window from lesson 14.02 with an empty dock space, a settings file and the build-folder setting. 2. Process access : list processes, apply the scope check (resolve the executable path with QueryFullProcessImageNameW , then check it is under the build folder after normalising both), open with the minimum rights. Unit-test the path check with lesson 17.04's lessons about .. and case. 3. Region map : the VirtualQueryEx walk from lesson 6.04 on the target, shown in a sortable table with module names. 4. Hex view : read on demand only the visible rows, handle unreadable pages ( ReadProcessMemory fails or reads partially: show ?? ), and refresh at the configured rate. 5. Snapshots and diff : copy a range, compare later, list changed ranges, highlight them in the hex view. 6. Typed overlay : parse definitions such as struct Player { i32 health; f32 x; f32 y; u8 flags; } with natural alignment (lesson 2.05) and show the values. 7. Telemetry : connect to the target's telemetry channel if it exists, and show its version check from lesson 12.06. 8. Hardening : lesson 12.07's checklist: the target exiting at any moment, huge regions, invalid addresses typed by the user, and a fuzz test of the struct parser (17.03). Acceptance tests The inspector is done when: - it refuses a process outside the build folder, including one reached by a path with .. , a different case, or a short 8.3 name; - it shows Delve's region map and its main module's base matches the one Delve prints (lesson 6.09); - the overlay of Delve's Player struct shows the health dropping when a monster hits; - a snapshot diff around the inventory shows exactly the bytes that change when an item is picked up; - closing Delve while the inspector is reading it gives a clear message, not a crash; - the unit tests pass under AddressSanitizer; - it never opens a handle with write or operation rights (verify with Process Explorer's handle view). Stretch goals - Read the target's PDB with the DIA SDK or dbghelp to show real type names and fields instead of hand-written definitions. - A "watch list" of addresses with a plot of each value over time (lesson 14.04). - Export a snapshot and its overlay as a report for a bug ticket. Common mistakes !warning Reading huge ranges every frame Read only what is visible, and only at the refresh rate. !warning Mixing Windows calls into the UI code It makes the inspector untestable and the UI slow when a read blocks. !warning Loosening the scope check "just for testing" The rule is the feature. Keep test targets in the build folder. Check yourself quiz ? What are the inspector's scope rules? - Any process on the machine, read and write, run as administrator + Only processes from your build folder, read-only, minimum rights - Only processes with a window, with full access so values can be changed - Any game the user owns, using whatever technique works Keeping the tool to your own builds and read-only access keeps it safe and within the course's ground rules. It also uses documented APIs only and never needs administrator rights. ? How is the inspector structured so it can be tested? - All code in the panels, tested by clicking through every window - One large main function, tested by running the tool on a real game + Tested pure logic, one Windows access layer, and drawing-only panels - Each panel calls Windows directly, so each can be tested on its own Pure logic can be tested without any process to read, which is why it is kept away from Windows calls. ? How should the hex view handle a page that cannot be read? - Stop reading and show an error dialog - Show zeros for the unreadable bytes - Retry until the read succeeds + Show ?? for those bytes and keep working Zeros would look like real data; ReadProcessMemory may fail or read only part of a range, so the view must cope. ? Why is the process scope check done on the full executable path after normalising it? + So .. , case or short names cannot evade it - Because process names are always unique - To make it faster The same lessons as safe path joining. ? Why read only the visible rows of the hex view? - ReadProcessMemory can only read 16 bytes + Reading large ranges every frame is slow - The target would crash Read what you show. ? Which access rights does the inspector need? - PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS - PROCESS_VM_WRITE and PROCESS_VM_OPERATION + PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION and PROCESS_VM_READ The least rights for a read-only tool.

title: Diff two snapshots
where: 18.01 Capstone: A Memory Inspector with a Full Interface
body: The inspector's snapshot panel compares two copies of the same memory range. Write diffSnapshots(before, after, base, mergeGap) , which returns the changed ranges as a list of { address, length } : - before and after are the bytes of the range starting at address base . If their sizes differ, only the common length is compared. - A changed byte is one where before i != after i . - Neighbouring changed bytes form one range. Two changed ranges separated by at most mergeGap unchanged bytes are merged into one range (which then includes the unchanged bytes between them), because a field that changed in two places reads better as one block. - Ranges are returned in address order. base 0x1000, before 00 00 00 00 00 00, after 00 11 00 22 00 00, mergeGap 0 - {0x1001,1} {0x1003,1} the same with mergeGap 1 - {0x1001,3}

title: 18.02  Capstone: A Moddable Game with a Plugin System
match: 18.02 Capstone: A Moddable Game with a Plugin System
body: The second capstone turns Delve into a game built to be modded, joining chapters 10, 11 and 13 with the security of chapter 17. Mods add data (levels, items, monsters), scripts and optional native plugins through a versioned API; a mod manager resolves load order and dependencies; the game survives broken mods. This lesson gives the specification, the mod format, the plugin API shape, milestones, acceptance tests and stretch goals. What you are building Delve: Open Depths is Delve with a mod system that strangers could use safely: - Data mods add or override levels, items, monsters and text, with no code at all (lesson 13.02). - Script mods add behaviour through the small scripting layer from lesson 10.08. - Native plugins are DLLs using a versioned C interface (lessons 13.03, 13.04), disabled by default and enabled per mod with a clear warning. - A mod manager screen lists installed mods, shows conflicts and missing dependencies, and lets the player enable, disable and reorder them. - The game never crashes because of a mod : bad data is rejected with a message, and a plugin that fails is disabled for the next start. The mod format Each mod is a folder under Mods\ with a manifest: ini ; Mods\lantern\mod.ini mod id = lantern name = The Lantern version = 1.2.0 api = 1 requires = core-items = 1.0.0 after = brighter-torches content items = data/items.ini levels = data/levels plugin = lantern.dll ; optional, native code Field Rules --- --- id Lower-case letters, digits and - ; unique version A semantic version (lesson 17.08) api The plugin and script API version it was built for; the game refuses mods for a newer major version requires Other mod ids, with optional minimum versions; a missing one disables this mod with a message after Soft ordering: load after these if present, without requiring them content paths Relative to the mod folder, passed through safeJoin (lesson 17.04) Load order Mods that override the same item need a deterministic order. Build a graph where an edge a → b means "a loads before b" (from requires and after ), then a topological sort , with alphabetical order breaking ties so the result never depends on folder listing order. A cycle is reported to the player, naming the mods in it, and those mods are disabled. The practice task implements this. The plugin API The native API follows lesson 13.07: a C interface with a version, a table of functions the game provides, and a table the plugin fills in. cpp-norun // delve_api.h, shipped to plugin authors define DELVE_API_VERSION 1 struct DelveHost // functions the game gives the plugin { uint32_t size; // sizeof(DelveHost), so fields can be added later void ( log)(const char text); int ( registerItem)(const char id, const char name, int value); int ( onEvent)(const char event, void ( handler)(const char payload)); }; struct DelvePlugin // functions the plugin gives the game { uint32_t size; const char id; void ( shutdown)(); }; // The one export every plugin provides: extern "C" __declspec(dllexport) int DelvePluginInit(uint32_t apiVersion, const DelveHost host, DelvePlugin out); Rules for the host side: - Check the apiVersion and each table's size before using it. - Load plugins only from their own mod folder, by full path, with LoadLibraryExW and LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_DLL_LOAD_DIR LOAD_LIBRARY_SEARCH_SYSTEM32 (lesson 13.04). - Never let a C++ exception or a structured exception cross the boundary: wrap every call into a plugin, and on failure disable the plugin and record it in Mods\disabled.ini . - Plugins run with the game's rights: the warning to the player says so plainly (lesson 17.06). Milestones 1. Manifests : find and parse every mod.ini , validate fields, report problems in a log and on screen. 2. Load order : dependency checks, the topological sort, cycle reports. 3. Data mods : item and level overrides applied in load order; later mods win; the debug menu (lesson 13.06) shows which mod defined each item. 4. Mod manager screen : enable, disable, reorder (which edits after hints in a user file, never the mod's own manifest), and show errors. 5. Scripts : event hooks ( onPickup , onLevelStart ) calling the script layer, with a time limit per call. 6. Native plugins : the API above, with the version and size checks and crash containment. 7. A sample mod pack : three small mods (a new item set, a new level, and a plugin that adds an achievement log) that exercise every feature, shipped with a short modding guide. 8. Hardening : fuzz the manifest and item parsers (lesson 17.03), and work through the threat model from lesson 17.05 for the mod folder. Acceptance tests - With the sample pack installed in any folder order, the load order is the same every time. - A mod requiring a missing mod is disabled with a message naming the missing id. - Two mods that require each other are both disabled with a message naming the cycle. - A manifest with a content path of ..\..\saves is refused. - A plugin built for API version 2 is refused by a version 1 game with a clear message. - A plugin that throws during DelvePluginInit is disabled, and the game starts normally the next time. - Removing every mod gives exactly the original game. Stretch goals - Hot reload of data mods while the game runs. - A mod.ini linter as a separate command-line tool for mod authors. - Packaging mods as a single zip file with a hash in the manifest, verified on load. Common mistakes !warning Load order that depends on the file system Folder listing order differs between machines. Sort explicitly. !warning Passing C++ types across the plugin boundary std::string and exceptions differ between compiler versions. Keep the API in C. !warning Letting one bad mod stop the game Report, disable, continue. Check yourself quiz ? What does each mod's manifest contain? - The mod's compiled code and its source + Its id, version, target API, requirements and content paths - Only the mod's name and author - The absolute path of the mod's folder on the author's machine Absolute paths would break on every other machine; the manifest lists paths relative to the mod. ? How is the load order computed? - Mods load in the order their folders were created - Mods load alphabetically and dependencies are ignored + A topological sort of requires and after , ties alphabetical - The player must list every mod in order by hand Alphabetical tie-breaking makes the order the same every time for the same set of mods. Any cycle is reported and the mods in it are disabled. ? How does the game protect itself from native plugins? - It runs every plugin in Debug mode - It cannot; plugins are trusted completely - It scans plugins with antivirus before loading + Version checks, full-path loading, and catching failures None of this makes a native plugin safe, which is why players are warned, but it contains ordinary failures. It also keeps the API in plain C, disables failing plugins, and warns that plugins run with the game's rights. ? Why is alphabetical order used to break ties in the load order? + So the order is the same every time - Because mods are always named alphabetically - To make loading faster The same mods must load the same way everywhere. ? Why does each API table start with its size ? - To align the structure + So each side can tell which fields exist - Windows requires it A common pattern for versioned C interfaces. ? A plugin throws an exception during initialisation. What should the game do? - Crash, so the player notices - Ignore it and keep calling the plugin + Catch it, disable that plugin, and carry on Mods must not be able to break the game.

title: Mod load order
where: 18.02 Capstone: A Moddable Game with a Plugin System
body: Write loadOrder(mods) . Each mod has an id , a list requires_ (mods that must be present and load first) and a list of after (mods that should load first if present ). Return: - order : the ids of the mods that can load, in load order; - disabled : the ids of mods that cannot load, sorted alphabetically. Rules: 1. A mod whose requires_ names a mod that is not in the list, or that is itself disabled, is disabled. Repeat until nothing more is disabled (disabling one mod can disable those that require it). 2. Among the remaining mods, requires_ and after entries naming present mods are edges "that one loads first". after entries naming absent mods are ignored. 3. Produce a topological order ; whenever several mods are ready, take the alphabetically smallest first. 4. Mods that cannot be ordered because they are in a cycle, or depend on a mod in a cycle, are disabled too.

title: 18.03  Capstone: A Driver and Client Pair in a Virtual Machine
match: 18.03 Capstone: A Driver and Client Pair in a Virtual Machine
body: The third capstone grows chapter 16's echo driver into XenonLog , a small, well-engineered driver and client pair that runs only in your lab virtual machine. The driver keeps a bounded in-kernel message log that clients append to and read back through versioned IOCTLs; the client is an ImGui tool with live statistics. The emphasis is engineering quality: validation, locking at the right IRQL, Driver Verifier, a fuzzing client, kernel debugging and a written design. What you are building XenonLog is a teaching driver: it does nothing a user-mode program could not, which is exactly why it is a good capstone. All the difficulty is in doing it correctly in kernel mode . - The driver ( XenonLog.sys ) creates \Device\XenonLog , keeps a ring buffer of up to 256 messages of up to 200 bytes each, and supports four control codes: append a message, read messages from a sequence number, get statistics, and clear. - The client ( XenonLogUI.exe ) is an ImGui window that sends messages, shows the log live, plots messages per second, and displays the driver's statistics and version. - The fuzzer ( XenonLogFuzz.exe ) sends random and malformed requests for hours with Driver Verifier enabled. !important Lab rules (from chapters 15 and 16) - Everything runs in the lab VM from lesson 15.08, with a snapshot taken before every test, test signing on in the VM only, and kernel debugging over the network from the host. - The driver touches only its own buffers . It never reads or writes another process's memory, never registers callbacks on other processes or threads, and never hides anything. Those are out of scope for this course. - It never ships outside the VM and is never installed on your everyday machine. The interface cpp-norun // xenonlog_ioctl.h, shared by the driver and its clients define XENONLOG_VERSION 1 define XENONLOG_MAX_TEXT 200 define XENONLOG_DEVICE_TYPE 0x8001 define IOCTL_XENONLOG_APPEND CTL_CODE(XENONLOG_DEVICE_TYPE, 0x801, METHOD_BUFFERED, FILE_WRITE_DATA) define IOCTL_XENONLOG_READ CTL_CODE(XENONLOG_DEVICE_TYPE, 0x802, METHOD_BUFFERED, FILE_READ_DATA) define IOCTL_XENONLOG_STATS CTL_CODE(XENONLOG_DEVICE_TYPE, 0x803, METHOD_BUFFERED, FILE_READ_DATA) define IOCTL_XENONLOG_CLEAR CTL_CODE(XENONLOG_DEVICE_TYPE, 0x804, METHOD_BUFFERED, FILE_WRITE_DATA) pragma pack(push, 8) struct XenonLogHeader { UINT32 version; UINT32 size; }; // every request starts with this struct XenonLogAppend { XenonLogHeader h; UINT32 length; CHAR text XENONLOG_MAX_TEXT ; }; struct XenonLogReadRequest { XenonLogHeader h; UINT64 fromSequence; UINT32 maxMessages; }; struct XenonLogMessage { UINT64 sequence; LARGE_INTEGER time; UINT32 processId; UINT32 length; CHAR text XENONLOG_MAX_TEXT ; }; struct XenonLogStats { XenonLogHeader h; UINT64 appended; UINT64 dropped; UINT64 rejected; UINT32 stored; }; pragma pack(pop) Every request carries a header with the interface version and the structure's size, as lesson 12.06 taught for user-mode protocols. The driver rejects a request whose header does not match before reading anything else. The practice task writes that validation as plain C++ that can be unit-tested outside the kernel. Engineering requirements Area Requirement From --- --- --- Validation Check input and output lengths for every code; validate the header; check length <= XENONLOG_MAX_TEXT and that length bytes fit in the input; count rejected requests 16.07, 17.04 Output Zero output buffers before filling; set Information to exactly the bytes written 16.07 Locking Protect the ring buffer with a spin lock or a fast mutex, choosing by the IRQL the code runs at; hold it only while copying 15.06 Memory Allocate the ring buffer once in DriverEntry from non-paged pool with a pool tag; free it in unload 15.04 Access The device's security descriptor allows administrators and the client group only; FILE_READ_DATA and FILE_WRITE_DATA in the control codes 16.04, 6.08 Cleanup Unload deletes the symbolic link and device and frees everything; no leaks reported by Driver Verifier's pool tracking 16.03 Analysis Builds with /W4 /WX and passes Code Analysis with the driver rule set 17.02 Milestones 1. Design document : a page describing the interface, the ring buffer's behaviour when full (oldest messages dropped and counted), locking, and the threat model from lesson 17.05 for the device interface. 2. User-mode core : the ring buffer and request validation as plain C++ with unit tests on the host (the practice task covers validation). 3. Driver skeleton : lesson 16.10's echo driver renamed, with the new device name and the four control codes returning STATUS_NOT_IMPLEMENTED . 4. Append and read : the ring buffer in the driver, with locking and validation; a command-line client to test. 5. Statistics and clear . 6. ImGui client : live log, sending, statistics, a plot, and a clear message when the driver is not loaded. 7. Verification : Driver Verifier with standard settings plus pool tracking; a kernel debugging session stepping through an append; the fuzzer running for an hour without a bug check. 8. Write-up : the design document updated with what changed, test results, and one bug you found and how. Acceptance tests - Two clients appending at the same time never corrupt a message (check sequence numbers are unique and continuous). - Appending 1000 messages leaves the 256 newest, with dropped equal to 744. - A request with the wrong version, a wrong size , length of 201, or a too-small output buffer is rejected with STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER or STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL , and rejected increases. - The fuzzer runs for an hour with Driver Verifier on and no bug check. - Load, use, unload and reload ten times without a leak or bug check. - A standard user who is not in the client group cannot open the device. Stretch goals - Rewrite the driver with KMDF and compare the amount of code (lesson 16.10's note). - Add an event that the driver signals when new messages arrive, so the client waits instead of polling. - Write the ring buffer once and compile the same source into the unit tests and the driver. Common mistakes !warning Testing outside the VM One mistake costs a blue screen on the machine you work on. Use the lab. !warning Holding a spin lock while calling anything that can wait At raised IRQL that is an immediate bug check. Copy under the lock, do everything else outside it. !warning Validating the length field but not that the bytes are there length must fit inside the input buffer the I/O manager actually passed. Check yourself quiz ? What does the XenonLog driver do, and what does it never do? + Keeps a bounded log via validated IOCTLs; never touches other processes - It records every key pressed on the machine and sends it to a client - It reads game memory for the client and hides itself from the task manager - It logs every system call made by every process The project is deliberately limited to its own buffer, which is what makes it a safe learning driver. It also never registers callbacks on other processes, hides anything, or runs outside the lab VM. ? Name four engineering requirements for the driver. + Validate lengths, set exact byte counts, lock correctly, free in unload - Use std::vector for the buffer, throw exceptions on errors, log with printf , and skip unload - Run only in Release, disable Driver Verifier, allow any caller, and allocate on every request - Accept any buffer size, return the whole buffer every time, use no locks, and never unload Restricting device access and passing warnings and Code Analysis are also required. ? How is the driver verified? - By loading it once on the host machine and checking it does not crash - By reading the code carefully - By asking a classmate to try it + Unit tests, Driver Verifier, kernel debugging, fuzzing and reload cycles Repeated load and unload cycles catch anything the unload routine forgot to release. ? Why does every XenonLog request start with a version and a size? + So mismatched requests are rejected first - Windows requires it for all IOCTLs - To align the structures Check the header first. ? What happens when the ring buffer is full and a new message arrives? - The driver bug checks + The oldest message is dropped and the dropped count increases - The new message is silently ignored with no record Bounded memory, visible behaviour. ? Where must all XenonLog testing happen? - On your everyday machine with test signing on - Anywhere, since it is only a log + In the lab virtual machine with test signing and a snapshot The rules from chapters 15 and 16 do not change.

title: Validate an append request
where: 18.03 Capstone: A Driver and Client Pair in a Virtual Machine
body: XenonLog's append request must be checked before the driver uses it. Write the check as plain C++ so it can be unit-tested outside the kernel: validateAppend(input, inputLength) , where input points to the bytes the I/O manager passed and inputLength is how many there are. The layout (all little-endian, no padding): Offset Size Field --- --- --- 0 4 version , must be 1 4 4 size , must equal inputLength 8 4 length of the text 12 length the text Return a Status : - TooSmall if inputLength is less than 12 (the header and length field), or input is null; - BadVersion if version is not 1; - BadSize if size is not equal to inputLength ; - TooLong if length is greater than 200; - Truncated if 12 + length is greater than inputLength ; - Ok otherwise, and also set text to the message. Check in exactly that order, and read the fields with std::memcpy (the input may not be aligned).

title: 18.04  Capstone: Analysing and Documenting a Program You Did Not Write
match: 18.04 Capstone: Analysing and Documenting a Program You Did Not Write
body: The last capstone applies chapter 9's reverse engineering, chapter 8's debugging and chapter 7's assembly to a program whose source you have not read, and turns the findings into a clear technical report. Targets are chosen so the analysis is legal and checkable: open-source programs you build yourself with the source set aside, practice programs published for analysis, and programs a classmate writes for you. The lesson covers choosing a target, the method, the report's structure and how to check your conclusions against the truth. Choosing a target The analysis must be legal and checkable . Good targets: Target Why it works --- --- An open-source program you compile yourself, in Release, then analyse without reading the source; the source is the answer key afterwards Legal under its licence; you can check every conclusion A practice program written for analysis (often called a "crackme" or reversing challenge) from a site whose rules allow it Made for this; usually comes with write-ups to compare A program a classmate or friend writes for you with a short brief ("a small file format and a checksum"), who keeps the source until you finish Realistic and fun; both of you learn One of your own old programs whose source you no longer remember Surprisingly instructive Not suitable: commercial software or games whose licence forbids reverse engineering, anything protected by anti-tamper (lesson 17.06), online games, and anything you would analyse to get around a protection or a payment. Lesson 9.01's ground rules apply unchanged. A good size is 50 to 500 KB of code: large enough to need a method, small enough to finish. A command-line tool with a file format (a compressor, an image converter, a small game with save files) is ideal. The method 1. Triage (lessons 9.02, 9.03): architecture, sections, imports (file, network, crypto, UI?), exported functions, strings. Write down hypotheses: "it reads .cfg files", "it uses zlib". 2. Run it in a VM or sandbox folder and watch with Process Monitor: files it opens, registry keys, what it prints. 3. Find the interesting code (lesson 9.08): from a string such as "invalid header" or an import such as CreateFileW , follow cross-references back to the functions that use them. 4. Understand it (lessons 9.04 to 9.06, 9.09, chapter 7): rename functions and variables in the disassembler as you go, reconstruct structs from field offsets, recognise loops, switches, vtables and library code. 5. Confirm dynamically (lesson 9.07): break on the function, check arguments and results match your reading, change an input byte and predict what happens. 6. Document : names, structures and the report below. Keep a lab notebook : every address, hypothesis, test and result, dated. It is what turns hours of clicking into a report. The report Section Contents --- --- Summary What the program does, in one paragraph, for someone who will not read further Target and method Exact file, version, hash, how it was obtained and why analysing it is permitted; tools used Architecture Main modules or components and how they interact, with a diagram Function map A table of the important functions: address, your name, purpose, confidence Data structures Reconstructed structs with offsets, sizes and field meanings File format or protocol A byte-level description, if the program has one, with an example decoded by hand Findings Anything notable: bugs, unsafe patterns (lesson 17.04), surprising design choices Verification How each major conclusion was confirmed, and what is still uncertain Comparison (open-source targets) What you got right, wrong and missed, once you read the source The confidence column matters: "high (confirmed in the debugger)", "medium (consistent with the code)", "low (a guess from the name of a string)". Honest uncertainty is what makes a report trustworthy. Acceptance criteria - The target is one of the permitted kinds, recorded with its hash and licence. - The function map covers the program's main path from main (or WinMain ) to its output, with at least 15 functions named. - At least two structures are reconstructed with every field's offset. - If the program has a file format, a small program of yours reads or writes it correctly (proof of understanding). - Every high-confidence claim has a recorded dynamic confirmation. - For an open-source target, the comparison section is honest about errors. Stretch goals - Write a script for your disassembler (Ghidra's Python or Java API) that applies your function names and struct definitions automatically, and include it. - Analyse two builds of the same program (Debug and Release, or two versions) and document what changed. - Turn the report into a short talk for classmates. Common mistakes !warning Reading everything in order Start from strings, imports and behaviour, and work towards the interesting code. !warning Not writing things down Without a notebook, you will analyse the same function twice. !warning Stating guesses as facts Give every conclusion a confidence and the evidence for it. Check yourself quiz ? Which targets are suitable for this capstone? - Any program you can download, including commercial games + Permitted, checkable programs, such as open source you build - Online games, as long as you do not cheat while playing - Protected software, since protections are the most interesting part Not commercial software that forbids it, protected or online games, or anything analysed to defeat a protection. Practice programs published for analysis, a classmate's program, and your own old programs also qualify. ? What are the six steps of the method? - Decompile, copy, rename, recompile, test, publish - Read the licence, buy the program, install it, play it, uninstall it, write a review - Patch, run, crash, dump, analyse, repeat + Triage, observe, find code via strings, understand, confirm, document Confirming dynamically is what turns a reading of the code into a verified claim. ? What makes the report trustworthy? - Its length and the number of screenshots + Recorded permission, a method, verified claims and confidence levels - Using the same words as the program's documentation - Leaving out anything you were unsure about Saying how confident you are, and why, is more useful to a reader than hiding the uncertain parts. ? Why is an open-source program built yourself a good target? + It is permitted, and the source checks you - Open-source programs have no machine code - It is the only legal target An answer key, with permission. ? What is the best starting point for finding a program's interesting code? - The first byte of the .text section + Strings and imports, then their xrefs - A random function Work from what you can observe. ? Why does the function map have a confidence column? - To sort the table - It is a legal requirement + To show which claims were confirmed Honest uncertainty makes a report trustworthy.

title: Name an address
where: 18.04 Capstone: Analysing and Documenting a Program You Did Not Write
body: While analysing a program, you keep a function map : each function's start address, size and the name you gave it. Write a small symboliser over it: - FunctionMap(entries) stores the entries. Entries may arrive in any order. If two entries overlap , the constructor keeps only the earlier of the two in the list given (the later one is discarded), since it was probably a mistake in the notes. - describe(address) returns: - "name" if the address is a function's first byte; - "name+0x1f" (offset in lower-case hex, no padding) if it is inside a function ( start <= address < start + size ); - "?" if it is in no function. - count() returns how many entries were kept. Make describe faster than checking every entry: sort the kept entries once and use a binary search ( std::upper_bound ).

title: Glossary
body: Terms from the lessons written so far, in alphabetical order. The lesson that introduces each one is given in brackets. Term Meaning --- --- Access violation The error Windows raises when a program reads or writes memory it is not allowed to touch, such as address 0. It stops the program. (1.03) Address The number of a byte in memory. A variable's address is the number of its first byte. Written in hexadecimal. (1.03) Address space layout randomisation A Windows security feature that loads programs at a different place in memory on each run. (1.03) Alignment The rule that a value should start at an address that is a multiple of its size, because the processor reads it fastest there. (1.03) Base plus offset Describing a location as "where something starts this time" plus a fixed distance, because absolute addresses change between runs. (1.03) Binary Base 2. Numbers written with only the digits 0 and 1. (1.02) Bit One binary digit: a switch that is on or off. (1.02) Byte Eight bits. The unit that memory is measured and numbered in. (1.02) Compiler The program that translates C++ into the processor's own instructions. (1.01) CPU The processor: the part that carries out instructions. (1.01) Decode The step of the cycle in which the CPU works out what a fetched instruction means. (1.01) Dereference To go to the address a pointer holds and use the value there. Written p . (1.03) Execute The step of the cycle in which the CPU carries out an instruction. (1.01) Fetch The step of the cycle in which the CPU copies the next instruction out of memory. (1.01) Heap The region of memory a program asks for while it runs. (1.03) Hexadecimal Base 16, with the digits 0 to 9 and A to F. One hex digit is exactly four bits. Written with 0x in front. (1.02) Instruction register The register that holds the instruction the CPU is currently working on. (1.01) Little-endian A byte order in which the lowest-value byte of a number is stored at the lowest address. PCs use it. (1.02) Memory (RAM) Where a running program and the values it is using are held. Emptied when the power goes off. (1.01) Null pointer A pointer holding address 0, meaning it is not aimed at anything. Written nullptr . (1.03) Overflow Going past the largest value a type can hold. Unsigned values wrap round to zero. (1.02) Padding Unused bytes the compiler leaves between values to keep them aligned. (1.03) Pointer A variable whose value is an address. (1.03) Pointer arithmetic Adding to or subtracting from a pointer. It moves by whole elements, not single bytes. (1.03) Process A program that has been loaded into memory and is running. (1.01) Program counter The register that holds the address of the next instruction to fetch. (1.01) Register A small, very fast storage slot inside the CPU. (1.01) Stack The region of memory that holds the local variables of functions that are currently running. (1.03) Storage Disks and SSDs: where files are kept for the long term. (1.01) Two's complement The way negative whole numbers are stored: the top bit is worth minus its usual amount. (1.02) Undefined behaviour Something the C++ language makes no promise about. The program may crash, misbehave, or appear to work. (1.02, 1.03)
