title: 1.01  Immediate Mode versus Retained Mode
body: Most user-interface toolkits keep a tree of widget objects that you create once and update. Dear ImGui does the opposite - you describe the whole interface again every frame, as ordinary code, and it draws it. This lesson explains the idea, why it suits tools and debug views so well, and where its limits are. Two ways to build an interface Retained mode is what Windows Forms, Qt, HTML and Unity's UI Toolkit do. You create objects once - a window, a slider, a label - and the toolkit keeps them. To change what the user sees, you change the objects; to react to the user, you register callbacks: cpp-norun // retained mode (pseudo-code) auto slider = new Slider(window, "Speed", 0.0f, 10.0f); slider- setValue(player.speed); slider- onChanged( & (float v) { player.speed = v; }); // keep the copy and the real value in sync There are now two copies of the speed: player.speed and the slider's value. Keeping them in sync is your job, and most UI bugs live in that gap. Immediate mode is what Dear ImGui does. There are no widget objects for you to keep. Every frame, you call functions that describe the interface as it should be right now , and each call returns what the user did: cpp-norun // immediate mode: this runs every frame ImGui::Begin("Player"); ImGui::SliderFloat("Speed", &player.speed, 0.0f, 10.0f); // shows player.speed, writes to it if dragged if (ImGui::Button("Reset")) player.speed = 4.0f; // true on the frame it was clicked ImGui::End(); The slider reads player.speed directly and writes to it directly. There is no second copy, no callback, no "update the UI when the data changes". If the game changes the speed, the slider shows it next frame because it is drawn from the data again. Why tools love it - Interfaces are just code. Loops and if s produce lists and optional parts: for (auto& enemy : enemies) ImGui::Text(...) . When an enemy dies, it disappears from the list with no extra work. - Fast to write. A debug window for a new system is often ten lines, written in the system's own file. - Always in sync with the data, because it is drawn from it. - Drops into any engine. ImGui only produces triangles and textures to draw; a small back end feeds them to DirectX, OpenGL, Vulkan or Metal, and passes mouse and keyboard input in. That is why game studios use it for editors, debug overlays, profilers and in-house tools: those are exactly the interfaces where speed of writing matters more than polish. But ImGui does keep some state "Immediate mode" describes the API , not the library's insides. ImGui remembers what it must between frames: window positions and sizes, which tree nodes are open, which widget is being dragged, scroll positions, text being edited. It finds that state by each widget's ID , which it computes from the label you pass (lesson 1.05). That is the one rule you have to learn early. It also means the cost is real: building the UI runs your code every frame. For tools, that is a few hundred microseconds; for a game's main menu shown to players, a retained toolkit or a hand-made UI is often a better fit (lesson 6.03). Where immediate mode is not the best choice - Player-facing game UI with animation, art direction and controller navigation everywhere. - Large text documents or anything needing rich text layout. - Accessibility : screen readers and similar tools rely on a widget tree that ImGui does not expose. For the tools this course builds - inspectors, editors, profilers, consoles - it is excellent. Common mistakes !warning Copying values into the UI and back Pass pointers to the real data. SliderFloat("Speed", &player.speed, ...) needs no copy. !warning Trying to store widget objects There are none to store. If something should appear, call its function this frame; if not, don't. Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference between retained and immediate mode? - Retained mode redraws every frame; immediate mode only redraws when a value changes - Retained mode is for 3D scenes; immediate mode is for 2D interfaces + Retained mode keeps widget objects you update; immediate mode describes the UI each frame - Retained mode uses callbacks for input; immediate mode cannot react to input at all In immediate mode there are no widget objects for you to keep: each frame's calls read and write your data directly and return what the user did. ? Does Dear ImGui keep any state between frames? - No, nothing at all; that is what "immediate mode" means + Yes: interface state such as window positions and open tree nodes, found by ID - Only the values of your variables, which it copies into its own widgets "Immediate mode" describes the API, not the insides. ImGui keeps interface state (window positions and sizes, open nodes, the active widget, scroll and text editing) looked up by ID, but never a copy of your data. ? Why does immediate mode avoid synchronisation bugs? - Because ImGui locks your data while the frame is drawn - Because every widget registers a callback that runs when the data changes + Because widgets read and write the program's real data directly every frame, so there is no second copy With SliderFloat("Speed", &player.speed, ...) the slider shows and changes player.speed itself; there is no widget value to keep in step. ? What does ImGui::Button return? - A pointer to the button object + true on the frame the button was clicked - The button's ID, so you can look it up later Immediate-mode functions return what the user did this frame; there is no button object to keep. ? A value changes in the game. What must you do so an ImGui slider shows the new value? - Call an update function on the slider - Register a callback that copies the value into the slider + Nothing; the slider is drawn from the value again next frame The slider reads the real variable every frame, so there is no copy to keep in sync. ? Which of these is a poor fit for Dear ImGui? - A debug window listing every enemy - A property editor in a level editor + A heavily styled main menu shown to players with a controller - An in-game profiler showing frame times Tools are its strength; polished, animated, player-facing UI is usually better served by a retained toolkit or a hand-made UI.

title: Drawn from the data
body: In immediate mode the interface is rebuilt from the data every frame, so it can never be out of date. Write the text lines a debug window would show for a list of enemies: cpp struct Enemy { std::string name; int hp; }; std::vector<std::string enemyWindow(const std::vector<Enemy & enemies); - The first line is "Enemies alive: N" , counting enemies with hp 0 . - Then one line per living enemy, in order: "<name (<hp hp)" . - If none are alive, the second line is "(none)" . Call it twice with different data and you get two different "frames": nothing has to be updated or removed.

title: 1.02  Setting Up ImGui with Win32 and DirectX 11
match: 1.02 Setting Up ImGui with Win32 and DirectX 11
body: Dear ImGui is a handful of source files you add to your project, plus a platform back end (input and windows) and a renderer back end (drawing). This lesson builds the standard Win32 + DirectX 11 program step by step, the same set-up as ImGui's own example. What you download Get Dear ImGui from its GitHub repository ( ocornut/imgui ). Use a release tag; for docking and multiple viewports (lesson 4.04), use the docking branch, which most tools do. You need: Files What they are --- --- imgui.cpp , imgui_draw.cpp , imgui_tables.cpp , imgui_widgets.cpp , imgui_demo.cpp The library itself imgui.h , imconfig.h , imgui_internal.h , imstb_ .h Its headers backends/imgui_impl_win32.cpp/.h Platform back end: Win32 window messages to ImGui input backends/imgui_impl_dx11.cpp/.h Renderer back end: ImGui's triangles to Direct3D 11 ImGui has no build system of its own on purpose: add these .cpp files to your Visual Studio project like your own. Then link d3d11.lib and d3dcompiler.lib (and dxgi.lib ). The shape of the program cpp-norun include "imgui.h" include "imgui_impl_win32.h" include "imgui_impl_dx11.h" include <d3d11.h // Forward-declared in imgui_impl_win32.h behind an if: declare it yourself. extern IMGUI_IMPL_API LRESULT ImGui_ImplWin32_WndProcHandler(HWND hWnd, UINT msg, WPARAM wParam, LPARAM lParam); LRESULT CALLBACK WndProc(HWND hwnd, UINT msg, WPARAM wParam, LPARAM lParam) { if (ImGui_ImplWin32_WndProcHandler(hwnd, msg, wParam, lParam)) return true; // ImGui sees input first switch (msg) { case WM_SIZE: / resize the swap chain buffers (see ImGui's example) / return 0; case WM_DESTROY: PostQuitMessage(0); return 0; } return DefWindowProcW(hwnd, msg, wParam, lParam); } int WINAPI wWinMain(HINSTANCE instance, HINSTANCE, PWSTR, int) { // 1. A window and a Direct3D 11 device and swap chain (ordinary Win32 and D3D11 code). HWND hwnd = createWindow(instance, WndProc); createDeviceAndSwapChain(hwnd); // fills g_device, g_context, g_swapChain, g_renderTarget // 2. ImGui itself. IMGUI_CHECKVERSION(); ImGui::CreateContext(); ImGuiIO& io = ImGui::GetIO(); io.ConfigFlags = ImGuiConfigFlags_NavEnableKeyboard; // arrow keys and Tab move between widgets ImGui::StyleColorsDark(); // 3. The two back ends. ImGui_ImplWin32_Init(hwnd); ImGui_ImplDX11_Init(g_device, g_context); // 4. The loop (lesson 1.03). bool running = true; while (running) { MSG msg; while (PeekMessageW(&msg, nullptr, 0, 0, PM_REMOVE)) { TranslateMessage(&msg); DispatchMessageW(&msg); if (msg.message == WM_QUIT) running = false; } if (!running) break; ImGui_ImplDX11_NewFrame(); ImGui_ImplWin32_NewFrame(); ImGui::NewFrame(); ImGui::ShowDemoWindow(); // every widget ImGui has, to explore (lesson 1.06) ImGui::Render(); const float clear 4 = { 0.1f, 0.1f, 0.12f, 1.0f }; g_context- OMSetRenderTargets(1, &g_renderTarget, nullptr); g_context- ClearRenderTargetView(g_renderTarget, clear); ImGui_ImplDX11_RenderDrawData(ImGui::GetDrawData()); g_swapChain- Present(1, 0); // 1 = wait for vertical sync } // 5. Shut down in reverse order. ImGui_ImplDX11_Shutdown(); ImGui_ImplWin32_Shutdown(); ImGui::DestroyContext(); destroyDeviceAndWindow(); return 0; } The parts that are not ImGui (creating the window, the device, the swap chain, resizing) are copied almost word for word from examples/example_win32_directx11/main.cpp in the ImGui repository. Start from that file; it is the reference everyone uses. What each piece does - ImGui_ImplWin32_WndProcHandler turns Windows messages (mouse moves, clicks, keys, characters, focus) into ImGui input. It must run first in your window procedure. - ImGui::CreateContext makes the one object that holds all of ImGui's state. Most programs have exactly one. - ImGui_ImplWin32_Init and ImGui_ImplDX11_Init connect the context to the window and to the device. The DirectX back end creates its own shaders, a font texture and buffers. - In the loop, the two back ends' NewFrame calls feed ImGui the window size, time and input, then ImGui::NewFrame starts recording widgets. - ImGui::Render finishes the frame and produces draw data : lists of triangles, textures and clipping rectangles. The renderer back end draws them over your scene. In a game that already has a renderer In a real game, step 1 already exists. You add steps 2 and 3 after your device is created, call the three NewFrame functions at the start of your frame, and call ImGui::Render plus ImGui_ImplDX11_RenderDrawData after your scene is drawn, so ImGui appears on top. Lesson 2.05 deals with sharing the mouse and keyboard between ImGui and the game. Common mistakes !warning Not forwarding window messages Without ImGui_ImplWin32_WndProcHandler first in the window procedure, windows draw but nothing reacts to the mouse. !warning Forgetting the extern declaration imgui_impl_win32.h hides ImGui_ImplWin32_WndProcHandler behind an if 0 . Declare it yourself, as above. !warning Mismatched versions of imgui.h and the back ends Back ends must come from the same version of ImGui. IMGUI_CHECKVERSION() catches a header and a .cpp from different versions. Check yourself quiz ? Which files make up a typical Win32 + DirectX 11 ImGui set-up? + The ImGui core .cpp and .h files plus imgui_impl_win32 and imgui_impl_dx11 from the backends folder - Only imgui.h, because the rest is in a prebuilt ImGui DLL that Windows provides - The ImGui core files plus imgui_demo.cpp, which contains the Win32 and DirectX 11 code - imgui_impl_win32 and imgui_impl_dx11 only, as the back ends include the core You compile the core files into your program and add one platform back end (Win32) and one renderer back end (DX11) from backends/. ? List the calls at the start and end of every frame. - ImGui::NewFrame, then the back ends' NewFrame; at the end ImGui::EndFrame only - ImGui::NewFrame only; ImGui::Render, which also draws everything to the screen + Both back ends' NewFrame, then ImGui::NewFrame; ImGui::Render, then the DX11 RenderDrawData Start with ImGui_ImplDX11_NewFrame, ImGui_ImplWin32_NewFrame and ImGui::NewFrame; end with ImGui::Render and ImGui_ImplDX11_RenderDrawData(ImGui::GetDrawData()). Render only builds the draw data; the renderer back end draws it. ? In what order do you shut ImGui down? - DestroyContext first, then the platform back end, then the renderer back end - The platform back end, the renderer back end, then DestroyContext + The renderer back end, the platform back end, then DestroyContext: the reverse of setting up Shut down in the reverse order of setting up, so nothing uses the context after it is gone. ? What does the renderer back end do? - Reads the mouse and keyboard and passes them to ImGui + Draws ImGui's triangles and textures with your graphics API - Decides where each widget goes inside its window The platform back end handles input and the window; the renderer back end draws. ? Where must ImGui_ImplWin32_WndProcHandler be called? - Once, right after creating the window with CreateWindowExW - Every frame, after ImGui::Render has built the draw data + At the start of your window procedure, so ImGui sees input first It turns every window message into ImGui input, so it must see each message as it arrives. ? When should a game draw ImGui? - Before clearing the screen, so the game draws over it + After its own scene, so the interface appears on top - In a separate window only, never over the game ImGui's draw data is rendered over the finished frame, just before Present.

title: Are the files all there?
where: 1.02 Setting Up ImGui with Win32 and DirectX 11
body: A Win32 + DirectX 11 project needs these Dear ImGui source files: imgui.cpp , imgui_draw.cpp , imgui_tables.cpp , imgui_widgets.cpp , imgui_impl_win32.cpp , imgui_impl_dx11.cpp . Write cpp std::vector<std::string missingImGuiFiles(const std::vector<std::string & projectFiles); Project files may include folders ( third_party/imgui/imgui.cpp , backends\imgui_impl_dx11.cpp ): only the name after the last / or \ counts, compared without regard to case. Return the missing required names, in the order listed above.

title: 1.03  The Frame and the Draw Data
match: 1.03 The Frame and the Draw Data
body: Every ImGui frame follows the same steps - input in, widgets described, draw data out. This lesson looks inside them, explains what draw data is, and covers the timing questions every tool runs into - frame rate, delta time, and only drawing when something changed. Inside a frame - Input in. The platform back end sets io.DisplaySize , io.DeltaTime , and queues input events (mouse position, buttons, keys, characters). - NewFrame. ImGui processes the events, decides which window is under the mouse, which widget is hovered , and clears last frame's draw lists. - Your code. Each widget function does three things at once: it lays itself out (takes space from the window's cursor), handles input (was it clicked?), and adds shapes to the window's draw list. It returns the result immediately. - Render. ImGui sorts windows by depth and collects every window's draw list into one ImDrawData . - Draw. The back end uploads vertices and indices to the GPU and issues one draw call per command. You can call widget functions anywhere between NewFrame and Render : in your game's update, in each system's own debug function, in a loop over entities. They all add to the same frame. Draw data cpp-norun ImDrawData data = ImGui::GetDrawData(); for (int n = 0; n < data- CmdListsCount; ++n) { const ImDrawList list = data- CmdLists n ; // one per window, roughly // list- VtxBuffer: vertices (position, texture coordinate, colour) // list- IdxBuffer: triangle indices for (const ImDrawCmd& cmd : list- CmdBuffer) { // cmd.ClipRect: scissor rectangle; cmd.TextureId: which texture; cmd.ElemCount: how many indices } } Everything ImGui draws, including text, is textured triangles. Text uses a font atlas : one texture containing every glyph, built at start-up (lesson 4.05). That is why ImGui is so portable: a back end only needs to draw coloured, textured triangles with scissor rectangles. You rarely touch draw data yourself, but it helps to know that ImGui::GetWindowDrawList() gives you the current window's draw list, so you can add your own lines, circles and text (useful for graphs and minimaps): cpp-norun ImDrawList draw = ImGui::GetWindowDrawList(); ImVec2 p = ImGui::GetCursorScreenPos(); draw- AddCircleFilled(ImVec2(p.x + 20, p.y + 20), 12.0f, IM_COL32(240, 180, 70, 255)); ImGui::Dummy(ImVec2(40, 40)); // reserve the space so the next widget goes below Delta time and frame rate ImGui needs to know how much time passed since the last frame ( io.DeltaTime ) for double-click detection, key repeat, blinking cursors and animations. The Win32 back end measures it with QueryPerformanceCounter . Your own code can read it too: cpp-norun ImGuiIO& io = ImGui::GetIO(); ImGui::Text("%.1f FPS (%.2f ms)", io.Framerate, 1000.0f / io.Framerate); io.Framerate is an average over the last 60 frames or so, so the number does not jump around. Tools that sleep A game redraws every frame anyway. A standalone tool (a level editor, an asset browser) does not need to burn a CPU core redrawing an unchanged screen at 144 Hz. Common approaches: - V-sync: Present(1, 0) waits for the display, capping the frame rate at its refresh rate. - Wait for input when idle: if nothing is animating, block in MsgWaitForMultipleObjects or WaitMessage until a message arrives, then draw a few frames (ImGui sometimes needs one or two extra frames to settle a layout). - Minimised: when IsIconic(hwnd) is true, sleep instead of drawing. The practice for this lesson has you write the "how many frames should I still draw?" logic a sleeping tool uses. Common mistakes !warning Calling widget functions before NewFrame or after Render ImGui asserts. Every widget call belongs between the two. !warning Assuming one frame is enough after input Some layouts settle over two frames (a window measuring its content). Draw a couple more frames after the last input. Check yourself quiz ? What is ImDrawData? - The list of widgets your code created this frame, kept until the next frame + Per-window lists of vertices, indices and draw commands for this frame - A bitmap of the finished interface that the back end copies to the screen It is everything ImGui wants drawn: each draw command also names its texture and clipping rectangle. ImGui::Render collects every window's draw list into one ImDrawData, and the renderer back end turns it into GPU draw calls. ? What is a font atlas? - A list of the fonts installed on the computer that ImGui can choose from - A file format ImGui uses to save fonts between runs + One texture holding every glyph of the loaded fonts, so text can be drawn as textured triangles It is built at start-up; text then needs nothing special from the back end. ? What is io.DeltaTime used for? + The time since the last frame, used for double clicks, key repeat, cursor blinking and animations - The time the GPU took to draw the last frame, used to lower quality when it is slow - The average frame rate over the last 60 frames The platform back end measures it each frame. The averaged frame rate is a different field, io.Framerate . ? What does a widget function do in one call? - Only adds itself to a list that ImGui processes at Render + Lays itself out, handles input, adds shapes, and returns the result - Draws itself on screen directly with Direct3D, right away Layout, input and adding shapes to the draw list happen together, immediately; the actual drawing happens later from the draw data. ? Why can ImGui run on almost any graphics API? - It contains a back end for every API inside imgui.cpp - It uses the operating system's drawing functions + It only needs textured, coloured triangles with scissor rectangles drawn A back end is a small piece of code that draws ImDrawData with one API. ? How should a standalone tool avoid using a full CPU core while idle? - Call ImGui::Render less often but NewFrame every time + Wait for input when nothing changes, and use v-sync - Skip ImGui::NewFrame on frames where the mouse did not move A tool only needs to redraw when something happens; skipping parts of a frame breaks ImGui's frame rules.

title: Only draw when something happens
where: 1.03 The Frame and the Draw Data
body: A standalone tool should not redraw an unchanged screen hundreds of times a second. Write the logic that decides, each time round the loop, whether to draw a frame or to sleep until the next input: cpp class IdleTracker { public: explicit IdleTracker(int settleFrames); // extra frames to draw after the last input void onInput(); // some input arrived void setAnimating(bool animating); // something on screen moves (a spinner, a live graph) bool shouldDraw(); // called once per loop iteration }; - shouldDraw returns true while animating, every time. - Otherwise, after onInput , it returns true for the next settleFrames calls (ImGui sometimes needs a frame or two to settle a layout), then false until the next input. - At the very start (before any input) it returns true for settleFrames calls too, so the first screen is drawn. - Input while frames are still pending starts the count again from settleFrames .

title: A steady frame rate
where: 1.03 The Frame and the Draw Data
body: io.Framerate is not the rate of the last frame, which jumps around: it averages the last frames. Write the same thing: cpp class FrameRate { public: explicit FrameRate(int window); // how many recent frames to average void add(double deltaSeconds); // one frame's duration double fps() const; // frames per second over the recent frames, 0 if none yet double averageMs() const; // average frame time in milliseconds, 0 if none yet }; fps() is the number of frames in the window divided by their total duration. Keep only the last window durations: when a new one arrives and the window is full, the oldest is dropped. Keep a running total rather than adding all durations up on every call.

title: 1.04  Windows, Text and Buttons
body: The first real interface - windows with Begin and End , every way of showing text, and buttons. Along the way you learn ImGui's rules for Begin / End pairs, what the boolean returned by Begin means, and how to open and close a window from code. A window cpp-norun ImGui::Begin("Stones"); // a window titled "Stones"; created the first time, remembered afterwards ImGui::Text("Hello from Xenon"); ImGui::End(); // ALWAYS called, whatever Begin returned The first time, ImGui creates the window with a default size and position; you can move and resize it, and it remembers (lesson 4.06 saves that to disk). Two Begin("Stones") calls in the same frame append to the same window , which is handy: different systems can add to one "Debug" window. Begin returns false when the window is collapsed (folded by its title-bar arrow) or entirely clipped. You may skip its contents then, to save time, but End must still be called: cpp-norun if (ImGui::Begin("Stones")) { expensiveStoneList(); // skipped while the window is collapsed } ImGui::End(); Begin / End is a different rule from most pairs in ImGui. For nearly everything else that starts with Begin ( BeginMenu , BeginTable , BeginPopup , BeginCombo ...), you call the matching End only if Begin returned true . Lesson 4.01 comes back to this; it is the most common beginner bug. A closable window Pass a pointer to a bool and the window gets a close button that sets it to false : cpp-norun static bool showStones = true; if (showStones) { if (ImGui::Begin("Stones", &showStones)) ImGui::Text("Close me with the x"); ImGui::End(); } From code, set showStones = true again (from a menu item, a key) to reopen it. Size and position cpp-norun ImGui::SetNextWindowPos(ImVec2(20, 20), ImGuiCond_FirstUseEver); ImGui::SetNextWindowSize(ImVec2(320, 240), ImGuiCond_FirstUseEver); ImGui::Begin("Stones"); SetNextWindow... applies to the next Begin . The condition says when: ImGuiCond_FirstUseEver only if the window has never been seen (not even in imgui.ini ), ImGuiCond_Once once per run, ImGuiCond_Always every frame (the user can then no longer move it). Use FirstUseEver for defaults. Window flags change behaviour: ImGuiWindowFlags_NoResize , NoMove , NoCollapse , AlwaysAutoResize (fits its content), NoTitleBar , MenuBar (lesson 4.01), and more, combined with . Text Function Shows --- --- ImGui::Text("Score %d", score) printf-style formatted text ImGui::TextUnformatted(text) Text as is, fastest, no % processing; takes a begin and optional end pointer ImGui::TextColored(ImVec4(1, 0.6f, 0.2f, 1), "Warning") Coloured text ImGui::TextDisabled("(none)") Greyed-out text ImGui::TextWrapped("long text...") Wraps at the window's edge ImGui::BulletText("item") A bullet point ImGui::LabelText("Label", "%d", value) Value with a label on the right, aligned like other widgets ImGui::SeparatorText("Section") A separator line with a title Text uses printf formatting: never pass user-provided text as the format string ( Text(name) ), because a % in it reads garbage. Use TextUnformatted(name) or Text("%s", name) . Buttons cpp-norun if (ImGui::Button("Add stone")) // true on the frame it was clicked (mouse released over it) stones.push_back(Stone{}); if (ImGui::Button("Clear", ImVec2(120, 0))) // width 120, default height stones.clear(); ImGui::SmallButton("x"); // no frame padding, for inline buttons ImGui::ArrowButton(" left", ImGuiDir_Left); // an arrow, no visible label A button counts as clicked when the mouse is pressed and released over it . Pressing, dragging away and releasing elsewhere does not click it. Lesson 1.05's practice and the next lessons look at how that works. Common mistakes !warning Calling End only when Begin returned true For windows, End is always called. For most other Begin functions, it is only called if Begin returned true. Learn the two rules. !warning Text(userString) A % in the string crashes or prints garbage. Use TextUnformatted. Check yourself quiz ? What does Begin's return value mean, and what must you always do afterwards? - Whether the window was created this frame; call End only if it returned true + Whether the window's contents are visible (not collapsed or clipped); End must always be called - Whether the user closed the window; call End only if it returned false For windows, End is always paired with Begin. Calling End only when Begin returned true is the rule for most other Begin functions, not for windows. ? How do you give a window a default size the user can change? - SetNextWindowSize with ImGuiCond_Always before Begin - SetWindowSize after End, once the window exists + SetNextWindowSize with ImGuiCond_FirstUseEver before Begin FirstUseEver applies only if the window has never existed. Always would reset the size every frame, so the user could not change it. ? When does ImGui::Button return true? - As soon as the mouse button is pressed over it + On the frame the mouse button is released over it after being pressed over it - On every frame the mouse button is held down over it Pressing, dragging away and releasing elsewhere does not click it. ? Begin returns false because the window is collapsed. What must you still do? + Call End - Nothing; the window is already closed - Call Begin again with the same name For windows, End is always paired with Begin, whatever Begin returned. ? What does ImGuiCond_FirstUseEver mean for SetNextWindowSize? - Use the size every frame, overriding the user + Use it only if the window has no saved settings yet - Use the size once each time the program runs It applies only if the window has never existed, not even in imgui.ini, so it sets a default without overriding what the user chose. Once per run is ImGuiCond_Once. ? Why is ImGui::Text(name) with a player's name dangerous? - Text copies the name into a fixed buffer that is too short for long names - Text only accepts string literals, so a variable does not compile + The name is used as a printf format string, so a % in it reads garbage Use TextUnformatted(name) or Text("%s", name).

title: When is a button clicked?
body: A button is clicked when the mouse is pressed over it and released over it . Pressing, dragging off and releasing elsewhere does not click it; pressing elsewhere and releasing over it does not either. Write the logic ImGui's buttons use, over a sequence of frames: cpp struct Rect { float x, y, w, h; }; struct MouseFrame { float x, y; bool down; }; std::vector<int clickFrames(const Rect& button, const std::vector<MouseFrame & frames); For each frame i , the button: - is hovered if the mouse is inside the rectangle ( x <= mx < x + w and y <= my < y + h ); - becomes active on a frame where the mouse button goes down (it was up on the previous frame, or this is frame 0) while hovered; - stays active while the mouse button is held, wherever the mouse moves; - on the frame the mouse button goes up while it is active, it is clicked if the mouse is hovering it then; either way it stops being active. Return the indexes of the frames on which it was clicked.

title: 1.05  How ImGui Identifies Widgets
body: ImGui remembers a widget between frames by its ID , a number computed from the widget's label and the ID stack . Two widgets with the same ID in the same place behave as one, which is the classic "my second button does not work" bug. This lesson explains IDs, the and label rules, and PushID . The problem cpp-norun for (Stone& stone : stones) { ImGui::Text("%s", stone.name.c_str()); ImGui::SameLine(); if (ImGui::Button("Delete")) remove(stone); // only the first one works! } Every button has the label "Delete". ImGui computes each widget's ID from its label, so all the buttons get the same ID. When you press the third one, ImGui thinks the widget with that ID is active, but the first button with that ID claims it. The result: only the first button works, or the wrong one reacts. How an ID is made An ID is a 32-bit hash. ImGui keeps an ID stack : a stack of seed values. Each widget's ID is the hash of its label, seeded with the value on top of the stack. Every window pushes its own seed (from its name), so a "Delete" button in window A and one in window B already differ. ID = hash(label, seed = top of the ID stack) To make widgets in a loop differ, push something unique onto the stack around each iteration: cpp-norun for (int i = 0; i < (int)stones.size(); ++i) { ImGui::PushID(i); // changes the seed for everything inside ImGui::Text("%s", stones i .name.c_str()); ImGui::SameLine(); if (ImGui::Button("Delete")) toDelete = i; // now each has a different ID ImGui::PopID(); } PushID accepts an integer, a string, or a pointer ( PushID(&stone) is a good choice: the stone's address is unique and stable). Every PushID needs a PopID . Label tricks: and Labels do two jobs: the text shown and the source of the ID. Two markers separate them: - : everything after it is part of the ID but not shown . "Delete 3" shows "Delete" and hashes the whole string. " speed" shows nothing (a slider with no label). - : only the part from onward is used for the ID. "Score: 120 score" shows "Score: 120" and hashes just " score" , so the ID stays the same when the score changes. Useful for window titles that show changing text: Begin("Level 3 - 12 enemies LevelWindow") keeps its position and size even though the title changes. Label Shown Hashed for the ID --- --- --- "Delete" Delete Delete "Delete 3" Delete Delete 3 " speed" (nothing) speed "HP: 87 hp" HP: 87 hp The practice has you implement exactly this table, plus the stack, with a simple hash. When IDs matter IDs are how ImGui finds a widget's remembered state: whether it is hot (hovered) or active (being clicked or dragged), whether a tree node is open, a text box's cursor, a window's position. If two widgets share an ID, they share that state. If a widget's ID changes every frame (say its label contains a timer), it loses its state every frame: a tree node never stays open, a drag stops immediately. Debugging IDs - Tools, ID Stack Tool in the demo window, or ImGui::ShowIDStackToolWindow() , shows the ID stack under the mouse. - Recent versions of ImGui detect duplicate IDs in the same window and draw a warning over them ( io.ConfigDebugHighlightIdConflicts , on by default in debug builds). Common mistakes !warning Buttons with the same label in a loop Wrap each iteration in PushID / PopID, or add and a unique suffix. !warning A label that changes every frame The widget gets a new ID each frame and forgets its state. Use with a fixed part. !warning Forgetting PopID Every widget after it gets a different ID than intended. ImGui asserts at the end of the window. Check yourself quiz ? How does ImGui compute a widget's ID? - It numbers widgets in the order they are drawn: the first is 1, the second 2, and so on + It hashes the widget's label (or the part from on), seeded with the value on top of the ID stack, which windows and PushID change - It uses the address of the widget object ImGui creates for each call Because the ID comes from the label and the stack, the same label in the same place gives the same ID every frame. ? What do and do in a label? - makes the text after it bold; turns the whole label into a heading - starts a comment that is ignored entirely; hides the whole label + hides the rest from view but keeps it in the ID; uses only the rest as the ID "Delete 3" shows "Delete" and hashes the whole string; "HP: 87 hp" shows "HP: 87" and hashes only " hp". ? What goes wrong if a widget's ID changes every frame? + It loses its remembered state, so drags stop and tree nodes close - Nothing, as long as the label text on screen looks the same - ImGui creates a new window for it every frame instead State such as open, active or the text cursor is found by ID; a new ID means starting from nothing every frame, so text editing resets too. Use with a fixed part. ? Two buttons labelled "Delete" are drawn in the same window without PushID. What happens? - ImGui renames the second one automatically + They share one ID, so clicking one can trigger the other or only the first works - Both work normally, because they are at different positions IDs come from labels, not positions; the same label gives the same ID. ? What is shown and what is hashed for the label "Gold: 50 gold"? - Shown "Gold: 50 gold"; hashed "Gold: 50" - Shown "gold"; hashed "Gold: 50" + Shown "Gold: 50"; hashed " gold" keeps the ID stable while the visible text changes. ? Why does PushID(&stone) work well in a loop? - Pointers are faster to hash than integers - It shows the stone's address next to each widget + The address is unique for each stone and stays the same between frames A good ID source is unique and stable. (If stones move in memory, for example when a vector grows, the IDs change too.)

title: Labels, IDs and the ID stack
match: Labels, IDs and the ID stack
body: Implement ImGui's label rules with a simpler hash. ImGui really uses a CRC32-based hash; here use FNV-1a , which is short to write: hash = seed XOR 2166136261 (both 32-bit unsigned) for each byte b of the text: hash = (hash XOR b) 16777619 (wrapping 32-bit arithmetic) Write cpp std::string displayText(const std::string& label); // what the widget shows std::string idText(const std::string& label); // the part of the label that is hashed uint32_t hashText(const std::string& text, uint32_t seed); class IdStack { public: explicit IdStack(uint32_t windowSeed); void push(const std::string& text); // like PushID(text): the new seed is hashText(text, current seed) void push(int n); // like PushID(int): the same as push(std::to_string(n)) void pop(); // never pops the window's seed uint32_t idOf(const std::string& label) const; // hashText(idText(label), current seed) }; The label rules: Label displayText idText --- --- --- "Delete" Delete Delete "Delete 3" Delete Delete 3 " speed" (empty) speed "HP: 87 hp" HP: 87 hp displayText is everything before the first (which also covers ). idText is the whole label, unless it contains : then it is the part from the first to the end.

title: 1.06  The Demo Window and the Debug Tools
match: 1.06 The Demo Window and the Debug Tools
body: Dear ImGui ships its best documentation as a program - ShowDemoWindow shows every widget with the code beside it. It also ships tools for finding your own bugs - the Metrics window, the ID Stack tool, the Item Picker and debug logs. This lesson shows how to use them all. ShowDemoWindow cpp-norun ImGui::ShowDemoWindow(); One call opens a window that demonstrates almost every feature of ImGui: widgets, layout, tables, popups, drag and drop, styling, fonts. It is the real documentation : when you want to know how to do something, find it in the demo window, then open imgui_demo.cpp and search for the label you saw. The code you need is right there. The demo's "Tools" menu (top of the window) opens the other tools below. Keep imgui_demo.cpp in every project during development; it costs nothing until called. Leave the call out of shipping builds (lesson 6.03). The style editor cpp-norun ImGui::ShowStyleEditor(); Every size, rounding and colour of the current style, editable live. Tune a style here, then click "Export" to copy the C++ code that sets it (lesson 4.05). The Metrics/Debugger window cpp-norun ImGui::ShowMetricsWindow(); It shows ImGui's own state: every window with its position, size and draw list (how many vertices, how many draw commands), the active and hovered widget IDs, the ID stack, the font atlas, tables' internal state, and more. Hover a draw command and it highlights what it draws. Use it when: - the interface is slow (which window has thousands of vertices?); - something is drawn but you cannot see why (where is its clip rectangle?); - a window behaves oddly (what are its flags and size constraints?). The ID Stack tool cpp-norun ImGui::ShowIDStackToolWindow(); Hover any widget: it shows the ID stack for it, level by level - the window's seed, every PushID , the label - and the final ID. The fastest way to understand why two widgets clash (lesson 1.05). The Item Picker In the Metrics window, Tools, Item Picker : click any widget in your program, and ImGui stops in the debugger inside the code that drew it . When you have a complex tool and cannot find which of fifty functions draws a misbehaving checkbox, this finds it in one click. Debug log The Metrics window has a Debug Log section that records what ImGui does in categories you choose: focus changes, popups, navigation, I/O events, docking. Turn on "I/O" and you see every mouse and keyboard event the back end feeds in, which answers "is ImGui even receiving my input?". Assertions are your friends ImGui uses IM_ASSERT heavily: unmatched Begin / End , PushID / PopID , calls outside a frame, bad parameters. In a Debug build the debugger stops on the exact line, with a comment in the source explaining the rule you broke. Read the comment above the assert; it nearly always says what to do. You can route assertions to your own handler by defining IM_ASSERT in imconfig.h . Common mistakes !warning Guessing instead of looking When a widget misbehaves, the ID Stack tool, the Metrics window and the Item Picker usually find the cause in seconds. !warning Disabling assertions to make a crash go away The assert is reporting a real mistake that will cause worse problems later. Fix the pairing or the call order instead. Check yourself quiz ? Which list names debugging tools built into ImGui? - ShowDemoWindow, the Visual Studio profiler, PIX and RenderDoc + ShowDemoWindow, the style editor, the Metrics/Debugger window (with its debug log and Item Picker), and the ID Stack tool - The Metrics window, the ID Stack tool, the Win32 back end log and imgui.ini viewer All four ship with ImGui itself and open from the demo window's Tools menu. Profilers and graphics debuggers are separate programs. ? What should you do when an IM_ASSERT fires? - Define IM_ASSERT as nothing in imconfig.h so the program keeps running - Restart the program; asserts usually come from a race between frames + Read the comment above it in the source, which explains the rule, and fix the code that broke it The assert reports a real mistake (an unmatched Begin/End or PushID/PopID, a call outside a frame). Silencing it only moves the crash elsewhere. ? Why keep imgui_demo.cpp in the project during development? - ImGui will not compile or link without its definitions + It shows every feature, and costs nothing unless ShowDemoWindow is called - It sets up the default style, which every other window needs Find a feature in the demo window, then search imgui_demo.cpp for its label to see the code. Leave the call out of shipping builds. ? What is the quickest way to find example code for a widget you saw in ShowDemoWindow? + Search imgui_demo.cpp for the label shown in the demo - Read imgui.cpp from the top - Open the Metrics window and look for the widget's code there The demo is the documentation, with its source beside it. ? Which tool tells you why two widgets share an ID? - The style editor + The ID Stack tool - The font atlas viewer in the Metrics window It shows each level of the ID stack for the hovered widget: the window's seed, every PushID and the label. ? You cannot find which function draws a misbehaving widget. What helps? - The Debug Log with the I/O category turned on, to trace clicks - The style editor's Export button, to dump each widget's source + The Item Picker, which breaks into the code that drew the widget you click It is in the Metrics window's Tools and breaks into the debugger at the drawing code. The I/O debug log shows input events, not where a widget is drawn.

title: Check the pairs, like ImGui's asserts

body: ImGui asserts when Begin / End and PushID / PopID calls do not pair up. Write a checker that reports the first mistake in one frame's calls: cpp struct Call { std::string name; bool result{ true }; }; // result: what a Begin... function returned std::string checkFrame(const std::vector<Call & calls); The calls are Begin , End , BeginChild , EndChild , BeginTable , EndTable , BeginMenu , EndMenu , PushID and PopID . The rules: - Begin and BeginChild : the matching End / EndChild is always required, whatever they returned. - BeginTable and BeginMenu : the matching end is required only if it returned true , and must not be called if it returned false . - PushID needs a PopID before the scope it was pushed in ends. - Ends must match the most recent open thing: EndTable when the innermost open item is a Begin window is wrong. Return the first problem as one of these messages (with the call's position i , counting from 0): - "<End... at <i has no matching <Begin... " : an end with nothing matching open, or that does not match the innermost open item; - "<End... at <i was called although <Begin... returned false" : ending a BeginTable / BeginMenu that returned false (when its end would be the next end of that type); - "missing <End... for <Begin... at <i " : the frame ended while something was still open (report the innermost one, with the position of its begin). Return "" when everything pairs up.

title: A tiny immediate-mode UI of your own
match: A tiny immediate-mode UI of your own
body: The best way to understand Dear ImGui is to write a very small version of it. Build a UI context that, like ImGui, lays widgets out, handles the mouse, remembers state by ID, and produces a list of things to draw. No graphics: the "draw list" is a list of strings a test can read. cpp struct Input { float mouseX{ -1 }, mouseY{ -1 }; bool mouseDown{ false }; }; class Ui { public: void beginFrame(const Input& input); void endFrame(); void label(const std::string& text); bool button(const std::string& label); bool checkbox(const std::string& label, bool value); void pushId(const std::string& id); void popId(); const std::vector<std::string & drawList() const; // what the last frame drew }; Layout. Widgets stack vertically. The first widget's top is at y = 0 ; every widget is 20 high and 100 wide at x = 0 , and the next widget starts 4 below the previous one (so tops at 0, 24, 48...). beginFrame resets the cursor to the top and clears the draw list. Drawing. Each widget adds one line to the draw list: - label : "text <shown text " - button : "button <shown text " , followed by hot if the mouse is over it and active if it is the active widget (both can appear, in that order) - checkbox : "checkbox <shown text x " or "... " (after any change this frame), then the same hot / active marks. The shown text follows lesson 1.05's rule. IDs. A widget's ID is its label's ID text (lesson 1.05, including ) combined with the current ID stack, which starts empty each frame. You may represent an ID simply as a string, the stack's entries and the ID text joined with / . Behaviour (lesson 1.04's practice): - A widget is hot if the mouse is inside its rectangle this frame. - If the mouse button goes down this frame over a widget, that widget becomes the active ID (only one widget can be active). - When the mouse button goes up , the active widget is clicked if the mouse is over it, and the active ID is cleared. button returns true on that frame; checkbox flips value and returns true . - The active ID lives between frames in the Ui object (it is ImGui's remembered state); everything else is rebuilt every frame. - If the active widget is not drawn in a frame at all, the active ID is cleared at endFrame (like ImGui, which forgets widgets that disappear).

title: 2.01  Sliders, Drags and Checkboxes
body: Most tool interfaces are numbers and switches. This lesson covers checkboxes, radio buttons, sliders and drags for floats, integers and vectors, how a slider maps the mouse to a value, logarithmic sliders, format strings, and how to know when a value changed or finished changing. Checkboxes and radio buttons cpp-norun ImGui::Checkbox("God mode", &settings.godMode); // bool static int difficulty = 1; ImGui::RadioButton("Easy", &difficulty, 0); ImGui::SameLine(); ImGui::RadioButton("Normal", &difficulty, 1); ImGui::SameLine(); ImGui::RadioButton("Hard", &difficulty, 2); // sets difficulty to 2 when chosen ImGui::CheckboxFlags("Collides", &body.flags, FLAG_COLLIDES); // one bit of an integer All of them return true on the frame the value changed. Sliders cpp-norun ImGui::SliderFloat("Speed", &player.speed, 0.0f, 20.0f); // drag the grab across the width ImGui::SliderFloat("Gravity", &world.gravity, 0.0f, 30.0f, "%.2f m/s^2"); // a format for the shown value ImGui::SliderInt("Lives", &player.lives, 0, 9); ImGui::SliderFloat3("Position", &player.pos.x, -100.0f, 100.0f); // three sliders for x, y, z ImGui::SliderAngle("Heading", &player.headingRadians); // stored in radians, shown in degrees A slider maps the mouse's position across its width to a value between min and max . With the grab's width taken out of the track, the mapping is simply linear: t = (mouseX - trackStart) / trackWidth clamped to 0..1 value = min + t (max - min) and back again to place the grab: t = (value - min) / (max - min) . For integer sliders the value is rounded to the nearest whole number. The practice writes both directions. Ctrl+click (or double-click) on a slider turns it into a text field so you can type an exact value. By default a typed value can go outside the range; pass ImGuiSliderFlags_AlwaysClamp to prevent that. Logarithmic sliders For values that span orders of magnitude (a light's intensity from 0.01 to 1000), a linear slider puts nearly all its width on the large numbers. ImGuiSliderFlags_Logarithmic maps the position to the logarithm of the value instead, so 0.01 to 0.1 gets as much room as 100 to 1000: cpp-norun ImGui::SliderFloat("Intensity", &light.intensity, 0.01f, 1000.0f, "%.3f", ImGuiSliderFlags_Logarithmic); Drags A drag changes the value by dragging horizontally, with no fixed track, so it suits values without natural limits: cpp-norun ImGui::DragFloat("Mass", &body.mass, 0.1f); // 0.1 per pixel dragged ImGui::DragFloat("Radius", &body.radius, 0.05f, 0.0f, 50.0f); // with optional limits ImGui::DragInt("Count", &spawner.count, 1.0f, 0, 1000); ImGui::DragFloat3("Scale", &obj.scale.x, 0.01f); ImGui::DragFloatRange2("Spawn delay", &spawner.minDelay, &spawner.maxDelay, 0.05f, 0.0f, 10.0f); Holding Shift while dragging moves faster, Alt slower. Drags are the most common number widget in professional tools because they take little space and work for any range. Knowing when a value changed Every widget returns true when it changed the value this frame. Tools often need more: cpp-norun if (ImGui::DragFloat("Height", &terrain.height, 0.1f)) terrain.rebuildPreview(); // every frame during the drag if (ImGui::IsItemDeactivatedAfterEdit()) // the drag ended and the value had changed undo.record("Change height"); // record ONE undo step for the whole drag (lesson 5.04) if (ImGui::IsItemActive()) { / being dragged right now / } The IsItem... functions ask about the widget just drawn: IsItemHovered , IsItemActive , IsItemActivated (started this frame), IsItemEdited , IsItemDeactivatedAfterEdit . Format strings The format argument is printf-style and controls only what is shown : "%.0f" rounds the display, "%d px" adds a unit, "%.1f%%" shows a percent sign ( %% ). The stored value keeps its full precision. Common mistakes !warning A slider with min greater than or equal to max It cannot map anything. ImGui asserts in debug builds. !warning Recording an undo step on every frame of a drag One drag would create sixty undo steps a second. Use IsItemDeactivatedAfterEdit. Check yourself quiz ? How does a linear slider map the mouse position to a value? + t = (mouse x minus track start) / track width, clamped to 0..1; value = min + t (max - min) - value = mouse x minus track start, clamped to min..max - t = track width / (mouse x minus track start); value = min + t max The position becomes a fraction of the track, and the fraction picks a point between min and max. Placing the grab goes back with t = (value - min) / (max - min). ? What does ImGuiSliderFlags_Logarithmic change? - The shown value is printed as a logarithm, while the slider stays linear + The position maps to the logarithm of the value, giving equal room to each order of magnitude - The slider moves faster the further you drag, like holding Shift With it, 0.01 to 0.1 gets as much width as 100 to 1000. The format string is unchanged. ? Which IsItem function and meaning go together? - IsItemActive: the widget just finished an edit that changed the value - IsItemHovered: the widget is being dragged right now + IsItemDeactivatedAfterEdit: the edit just finished and it changed the value - IsItemActivated: the value changed this frame IsItemHovered means the mouse is over it, IsItemActive that it is being used now, IsItemActivated that use started this frame, and IsItemDeactivatedAfterEdit that the edit just ended with a change. ? A slider from 0 to 20 is 200 pixels wide. The mouse is 50 pixels from its start. What value does it set? - 50 - 2.5 + 5 - 10 t = 50 / 200 = 0.25, and 0 + 0.25 20 = 5. ? When should you use a drag instead of a slider? - Only for integers, since drags cannot hold fractions + For values with no natural limits, or where space is short - When the value must stay inside a fixed range Drags change by a speed per pixel and need no track. A slider suits a value with a fixed min and max. ? How do you record one undo step for a whole drag? - Record a step whenever the widget returns true - Record a step while IsItemActive() is true + Check ImGui::IsItemDeactivatedAfterEdit() after the widget It is true once, when the edit ends and the value changed. The return value is true on every frame of the drag, which would record many steps.

title: Slider maths
body: Write the mapping a slider uses between the mouse and the value: cpp float valueFromMouse(float mouseX, float trackStart, float trackWidth, float minValue, float maxValue); float positionOf(float value, float trackStart, float trackWidth, float minValue, float maxValue); int intValueFromMouse(float mouseX, float trackStart, float trackWidth, int minValue, int maxValue); float logValueFromMouse(float mouseX, float trackStart, float trackWidth, float minValue, float maxValue); - valueFromMouse : t = (mouseX - trackStart) / trackWidth , clamped to 0..1; the value is min + t (max - min) . - positionOf : the reverse, the x position of the grab for a value; values outside the range are clamped to its ends. - intValueFromMouse : like valueFromMouse with the integer range, rounded to the nearest whole number. - logValueFromMouse : for a logarithmic slider (both limits above 0), t maps to the logarithm: value = min pow(max / min, t) . A track of width 0 or less always gives min (and positionOf gives trackStart ). valueFromMouse(150, 100, 200, 0, 20) == 5 logValueFromMouse(200, 100, 200, 0.01, 100) == 1 // halfway on a log scale from 0.01 to 100

title: 2.02  Text Input and Validation
body: Text fields in ImGui write into a buffer you own. This lesson covers InputText with character arrays and std::string , number fields, multi-line text, flags that restrict what can be typed, callbacks for custom filtering and completion, and validating a value before you accept it. InputText with a buffer cpp-norun static char name 64 = "Granite"; ImGui::InputText("Name", name, IM_ARRAYSIZE(name)); // edits the array in place ImGui edits your buffer directly and never writes more than its size (including the terminating zero). IM_ARRAYSIZE gives the number of elements of an array. InputText with std::string The file misc/cpp/imgui_stdlib.cpp (add it to your project) gives overloads that resize a std::string as you type: cpp-norun include "misc/cpp/imgui_stdlib.h" ImGui::InputText("Name", &stone.name); // std::string ImGui::InputTextMultiline("Notes", &level.notes, ImVec2(-FLT_MIN, 120)); // full width, 120 high ImGui::InputTextWithHint(" search", "Search stones...", &search); // grey hint when empty -FLT_MIN as a width means "all the space up to the right edge"; it is ImGui's idiom for "fill". Number fields cpp-norun ImGui::InputInt("Count", &count); // with - and + buttons ImGui::InputInt("Count", &count, 0); // step 0: no buttons ImGui::InputFloat("Weight", &weight, 0.1f, 1.0f, "%.2f"); ImGui::InputScalar("Seed", ImGuiDataType_U64, &seed); // any numeric type Restricting what can be typed Flags filter characters as they are typed: Flag Allows --- --- ImGuiInputTextFlags_CharsDecimal 0123456789.+- / ImGuiInputTextFlags_CharsHexadecimal 0123456789ABCDEFabcdef ImGuiInputTextFlags_CharsUppercase Turns letters to upper case ImGuiInputTextFlags_CharsNoBlank No spaces or tabs ImGuiInputTextFlags_CharsScientific Decimal plus e / E Others change behaviour: EnterReturnsTrue (return true only when Enter is pressed, ideal for a console), ReadOnly , Password (shows ), AutoSelectAll , EscapeClearsAll . Callbacks: custom filters, history, completion For anything the flags cannot do, pass a callback: cpp-norun int onlyIdentifierChars(ImGuiInputTextCallbackData data) { const ImWchar c = data- EventChar; const bool ok = (c = 'a' && c <= 'z') (c = 'A' && c <= 'Z') (c = '0' && c <= '9') c == '_'; return ok ? 0 : 1; // return 1 to reject the character } ImGui::InputText("Id", id, sizeof(id), ImGuiInputTextFlags_CallbackCharFilter, onlyIdentifierChars); ImGuiInputTextFlags_CallbackCompletion calls you when Tab is pressed (for auto-completing a console command), and CallbackHistory when Up or Down is pressed (for recalling previous commands). The console example in the demo window shows both. Validating a value Filtering stops characters ; validation checks the whole value . A common, friendly pattern: edit a copy, show what is wrong, and only apply it when it is valid and the edit is finished. cpp-norun static std::string editing = level.name; ImGui::InputText("Level name", &editing); const std::string problem = validateLevelName(editing); // "" if fine if (!problem.empty()) ImGui::TextColored(ImVec4(1, 0.4f, 0.4f, 1), "%s", problem.c_str()); if (ImGui::IsItemDeactivatedAfterEdit() && problem.empty()) level.name = editing; The practice writes validateLevelName and a character filter. Keyboard focus ImGui::SetKeyboardFocusHere() before a text field gives it the keyboard focus on that frame: useful when a search window or console opens. ImGui::IsItemFocused() tells whether the field has focus. Common mistakes !warning Passing sizeof of a pointer as the buffer size InputText("x", ptr, sizeof(ptr)) passes 8. Use the real buffer size, IM_ARRAYSIZE for arrays, or the std::string overload. !warning Applying invalid text immediately Edit a copy and apply when it validates, so half-typed values never reach your data. Check yourself quiz ? How do you edit a std::string with InputText? - Pass name.data() and name.size(); ImGui grows the string when it gets full - Pass name.c_str() and IM_ARRAYSIZE(name) + Include misc/cpp/imgui_stdlib and pass a pointer to the string; it resizes as you type The imgui_stdlib overloads take a std::string and resize it. c_str() is read-only, and the core InputText never resizes a buffer. ? Which of these flags change what InputText accepts or how it behaves? + CharsDecimal, CharsUppercase, EnterReturnsTrue and Password - CharsDecimal, AlwaysClamp, Logarithmic and ReadOnly - NoResize, NoMove, EnterReturnsTrue and Password AlwaysClamp and Logarithmic are slider flags, and NoResize and NoMove are window flags. Other text flags include CharsHexadecimal, CharsNoBlank and ReadOnly. ? What is the pattern for validated editing? - Validate inside a CallbackCharFilter and reject the whole value there - Write straight into the real data, and undo the change if it turns out invalid + Edit a copy, show the validation message as you type, and copy it back only when the edit finishes and the value is valid Half-typed values never reach your data. A character filter sees one character at a time, not the whole value. ? Which flag makes InputText return true only when Enter is pressed? - ImGuiInputTextFlags_ReadOnly + ImGuiInputTextFlags_EnterReturnsTrue - ImGuiInputTextFlags_CallbackCompletion Ideal for console commands and search boxes. CallbackCompletion is called when Tab is pressed. ? What does a CallbackCharFilter return to reject a character? - 0 - The character itself + 1 Returning nonzero discards the typed character; returning 0 keeps it. ? What is the difference between filtering and validating? - They are the same thing under two names - Validating happens in the back end, filtering in your code + Filtering stops individual characters as they are typed; validating checks the whole value A name can contain only allowed characters and still be invalid as a whole, for example when it is empty or already taken.

title: Validate a level name
body: Write the two checks a level-name field uses: cpp bool allowedChar(char32_t c); // the character filter: is this character allowed at all? std::string validateLevelName(const std::string& name, const std::vector<std::string & existing); allowedChar allows lower-case letters a - z , digits, _ and - . Everything else is filtered out as it is typed. validateLevelName checks the whole value and returns the first problem, or an empty string: 1. empty: "Give the level a name." 2. longer than 32 characters: "Keep the name to 32 characters." 3. a character allowedChar refuses (for text pasted in): "Use a-z, 0-9, _ and - only." 4. starts with - or _ : "Start the name with a letter or digit." 5. already in existing (exact match): "A level called <name already exists."

title: 2.03  Combo Boxes and List Boxes
body: Choosing one item from many is everywhere in tools - a material, a level, an enemy type. This lesson covers BeginCombo with Selectable , the simple Combo overloads, list boxes, filtering a long list as you type, and showing enums by name. BeginCombo and Selectable The flexible way to make a drop-down: cpp-norun static const char materials = { "Granite", "Basalt", "Slate", "Marble", "Limestone" }; static int current = 0; if (ImGui::BeginCombo("Material", materials current )) // the text shown when closed { for (int i = 0; i < IM_ARRAYSIZE(materials); ++i) { const bool selected = (i == current); if (ImGui::Selectable(materials i , selected)) current = i; if (selected) ImGui::SetItemDefaultFocus(); // keyboard navigation starts here } ImGui::EndCombo(); // only if BeginCombo returned true! } BeginCombo returns true while the drop-down is open; then you draw its contents and call EndCombo . If it returns false , you do not call EndCombo (lesson 1.04's second rule). Selectable is a full-width clickable row that can be shown as selected. You will use it in lists, tables and trees too. The simple overloads For a plain list of strings there is a one-line version: cpp-norun ImGui::Combo("Material", &current, materials, IM_ARRAYSIZE(materials)); ImGui::Combo("Quality", &quality, "Low\0Medium\0High\0\0"); // items separated by \0, ending with \0\0 Use BeginCombo when the items are not a simple array: a std::vector of objects, items with icons, items you want to filter. Enums by name A table of names next to the enum keeps a combo honest: cpp-norun enum class Weather { Clear, Rain, Snow, Fog, Count }; constexpr const char weatherNames = { "Clear", "Rain", "Snow", "Fog" }; static_assert(IM_ARRAYSIZE(weatherNames) == static_cast<int (Weather::Count)); int w = static_cast<int (level.weather); if (ImGui::Combo("Weather", &w, weatherNames, IM_ARRAYSIZE(weatherNames))) level.weather = static_cast<Weather (w); The static_assert fails the build if someone adds an enum value without a name. List boxes A list box is the same idea, always open, with a fixed height: cpp-norun if (ImGui::BeginListBox(" levels", ImVec2(-FLT_MIN, 8 ImGui::GetTextLineHeightWithSpacing()))) { for (int i = 0; i < (int)levels.size(); ++i) if (ImGui::Selectable(levels i .name.c_str(), i == selectedLevel)) selectedLevel = i; ImGui::EndListBox(); } Size the height in lines ( GetTextLineHeightWithSpacing ) so it adapts to the font. Filtering long lists A list of 400 assets needs a search box. Keep a filter string, and only draw matching items: cpp-norun static std::string filter; ImGui::InputTextWithHint(" filter", "Filter...", &filter); for (const Asset& a : assets) if (matches(a.name, filter)) if (ImGui::Selectable(a.name.c_str(), &a == selected)) selected = &a; A good matches ignores case and lets the words of the filter appear anywhere, in any order: "rock big" matches "big_mossy_rock". The practice writes it. ImGui also ships ImGuiTextFilter for include/exclude filters, which lesson 5.02 uses. Common mistakes !warning Calling EndCombo when BeginCombo returned false ImGui asserts. EndCombo belongs inside the if. !warning Selectables with the same text They share an ID (lesson 1.05). PushID per item, or add and the index. Check yourself quiz ? What does Selectable do and where is it used? - It draws a checkbox that can be ticked; it is used only inside combos + Draws a full-width clickable row that can show as selected; used in many list widgets - It opens a drop-down list of choices; it is used instead of BeginCombo Selectable is the building block of combos, list boxes, tables and trees; you decide which row counts as selected. ? When would you use BeginCombo instead of the one-line Combo? - Whenever the list has more than ten items to choose from - Only when the combo must be shown inside a table cell + When items are not a simple string array, such as a vector of objects The one-line Combo takes an array of strings or a "\0"-separated string; BeginCombo lets you draw anything inside, such as objects, items with extra drawing or a filtered list. ? What makes a good filter for a long list? + Case-insensitive matching where every word of the filter appears somewhere in the item, in any order - Matching items that start with exactly the text typed, case included - Matching items that contain the whole filter text as one piece, case included Then "rock big" finds "big_mossy_rock", which a prefix or exact-substring match would miss. ? When is EndCombo called? - Always, like End for windows + Only when BeginCombo returned true - Never; it is called automatically when the drop-down closes BeginCombo returns true while the drop-down is open; calling EndCombo otherwise makes ImGui assert. ? Why add a static_assert next to an enum's name table? - So the combo can look up names faster at run time - Because Combo will not compile without a size check + So the build fails if an enum value is added without a matching name The table and the enum must stay the same length, and the check costs nothing at run time. ? How do you size a list box to show eight items? - Pass ImVec2(0, 8) as its size - You cannot; a list box always shows eight items + Use 8 ImGui::GetTextLineHeightWithSpacing() as its height The size is in pixels, and measuring in lines adapts to the font size.

title: Filter a long list
body: Write the matching a filter box above a long list uses, and the list it produces: cpp bool matches(const std::string& item, const std::string& filter); std::vector<int visibleItems(const std::vector<std::string & items, const std::string& filter); int keepSelection(const std::vector<int & visible, int selected); - matches : split the filter into words at spaces. The item matches if every word appears somewhere in it, in any order, ignoring upper and lower case. An empty filter (or one with only spaces) matches everything. - visibleItems : the indexes of the matching items, in order. - keepSelection : after the filter changes, keep the selected item if it is still visible; otherwise select the first visible item; if nothing is visible, return -1 . matches("big_mossy_rock", "rock BIG") == true matches("big_mossy_rock", "rock small") == false

title: 2.04  Colours and Colour Pickers
body: ImGui works with colours in two forms - four floats from 0 to 1 ( ImVec4 ) and one packed 32-bit integer ( ImU32 , built with IM_COL32 ). This lesson covers the colour widgets, converting between the forms and to HSV, and why packed colours store their bytes in the order they do. Colour widgets cpp-norun ImGui::ColorEdit3("Fog colour", &fog.color.x); // float 3 : r, g, b from 0 to 1 ImGui::ColorEdit4("Tint", &sprite.tint.x); // float 4 : with alpha ImGui::ColorPicker4("Sky", &sky.x); // the big picker with a hue wheel or square ImGui::ColorButton(" swatch", ImVec4(0.9f, 0.6f, 0.2f, 1.0f)); // a clickable swatch ColorEdit shows the colour as numbers with a swatch; click the swatch for a picker popup. Flags choose the details: ImGuiColorEditFlags_NoAlpha , DisplayHex , DisplayHSV , PickerHueWheel , Float (0..1 numbers instead of 0..255), HDR (values above 1). Two forms of colour ImVec4 : four floats, red, green, blue, alpha, each from 0 to 1. Widgets and styles use this form. ImU32 : four bytes packed into one 32-bit unsigned integer. Draw lists use this form, because millions of vertices each carry a colour and four bytes are much smaller than four floats. The macro builds one: cpp-norun ImU32 gold = IM_COL32(240, 180, 70, 255); // r, g, b, a from 0 to 255 draw- AddRectFilled(min, max, gold); With ImGui's default settings, IM_COL32(r, g, b, a) is (a << 24) (b << 16) (g << 8) r Red is in the lowest byte. Written in memory on a little-endian PC (lesson 1.02 of the gamedev course), the bytes are in the order R, G, B, A , which is exactly the vertex format the GPU reads. That is why it looks "backwards" as a hexadecimal number: opaque red is 0xFF0000FF . Converting between them: cpp-norun ImVec4 v = ImGui::ColorConvertU32ToFloat4(gold); ImU32 u = ImGui::ColorConvertFloat4ToU32(ImVec4(1, 0.5f, 0, 1)); // rounds to the nearest of 0..255 ImU32 w = ImGui::GetColorU32(ImGuiCol_Text); // a style colour, with the current alpha HSV Hue, saturation, value is a friendlier space for adjusting colours: change the hue to cycle through the rainbow while keeping brightness; lower the saturation to grey something out. cpp-norun float h, s, v; ImGui::ColorConvertRGBtoHSV(c.x, c.y, c.z, h, s, v); // all in 0..1, hue too h = std::fmod(h + 0.1f, 1.0f); // shift the hue ImGui::ColorConvertHSVtoRGB(h, s, v, c.x, c.y, c.z); A classic tool trick is to give each item a distinct colour from its index: hue = i 0.618034f modulo 1 (the golden ratio spreads them evenly), saturation 0.6, value 0.9. The practice writes the conversions. Hexadecimal colour codes Artists often paste colours as F0B446 or F0B446CC . Parsing them into an ImVec4 is a small, useful function, which the practice also has you write. Common mistakes !warning Building an ImU32 by hand in the wrong byte order 0xF0B446FF is not gold with full alpha in ImGui's layout. Use IM_COL32 or ColorConvertFloat4ToU32. !warning Passing 0-255 values to ColorEdit ColorEdit edits floats from 0 to 1. Convert when your data stores bytes. Check yourself quiz ? What are ImGui's two forms of colour, and where is each used? - ImVec4, four bytes 0..255, used by draw lists; ImU32, four floats 0..1, used by widgets + ImVec4, four floats 0..1, used by widgets and styles; ImU32, four packed bytes, used by draw lists - ImVec4 for colours with alpha and ImU32 for colours without alpha, both used everywhere Widgets and styles edit ImVec4 floats; draw lists store a compact ImU32 per vertex. Both carry alpha. ? Why does IM_COL32 put red in the lowest byte? - So that opaque red reads as 0xFF000000, the easiest form to type by hand - Because the Windows API stores colours that way, and ImGui copies it + So that in memory on a little-endian machine the bytes are R, G, B, A, the vertex colour format the GPU reads The lowest byte comes first in memory on a little-endian PC. That is why the hexadecimal number looks backwards: opaque red is 0xFF0000FF. ? How do you give each of many items a distinct colour? + Spread hues by the golden ratio (i 0.618 mod 1) at fixed saturation and value - Add 10 to the red channel for each item, wrapping at 255 - Pick a random RGB colour for each item, a new one every frame Golden-ratio hues spread evenly however many items there are; convert each HSV colour to RGB. Random colours change every frame and can land close together. ? What does IM_COL32(255, 0, 0, 255) equal with ImGui's default byte order? - 0xFFFF0000 + 0xFF0000FF - 0x00FF00FF - 0xFF00FF00 Alpha in the top byte, then blue, green, and red in the lowest byte. ? Why do draw lists use ImU32 instead of ImVec4? - ImVec4 cannot hold an alpha value, only red, green and blue + Four bytes per vertex colour is far smaller than four floats - The GPU cannot read floating-point colours from a vertex Every vertex carries a colour, so the saving adds up over millions of vertices. ? Which colour space makes "rotate through the rainbow at the same brightness" easy? - RGB - Packed ImU32 + HSV In HSV you change only the hue and keep saturation and value.

title: Colour conversions
body: Write ImGui's colour conversions yourself: cpp struct Vec4 { float r, g, b, a; }; uint32_t col32(int r, int g, int b, int a); // like IM_COL32: (a << 24) (b << 16) (g << 8) r uint32_t toU32(const Vec4& c); // floats 0..1 to bytes, rounded to nearest, clamped Vec4 toVec4(uint32_t packed); // bytes to floats: byte / 255 void rgbToHsv(float r, float g, float b, float& h, float& s, float& v); // all in 0..1, hue too bool parseHex(const std::string& text, Vec4& out); // " RRGGBB" or " RRGGBBAA" - toU32 : each float is clamped to 0..1, multiplied by 255 and rounded to the nearest whole number ( + 0.5 then truncate). - rgbToHsv : v is the largest of r, g, b; s is (max - min) / max (0 when max is 0); hue is in sixths of a turn: if max is r, h = (g - b) / (max - min) ; if max is g, h = 2 + (b - r) / (max - min) ; if max is b, h = 4 + (r - g) / (max - min) ; then divide by 6 and add 1 if negative. For a grey (max equal to min) the hue is 0. - parseHex : a then exactly 6 or 8 hexadecimal digits (either case). Without alpha digits, alpha is 1. Anything else returns false .

title: 2.05  Sharing Input with Your Game
body: When ImGui runs on top of a game, the same click could mean "press this button" or "shoot". ImGui tells you which with io.WantCaptureMouse and io.WantCaptureKeyboard . This lesson shows how to route input correctly, read keys and the mouse through ImGui yourself, and add keyboard shortcuts to your tools. Who gets the click? Your game reads the mouse and keyboard too. Without care, typing a level name into a text field also walks the player around, and clicking a button also fires the gun. ImGui sets three flags every frame: Flag True when --- --- io.WantCaptureMouse The mouse is over an ImGui window, or ImGui is using it (dragging a slider that left the window) io.WantCaptureKeyboard An ImGui widget has keyboard focus (a text field, or keyboard navigation is active) io.WantTextInput A text field wants characters (on consoles and phones: show the on-screen keyboard) The rule is simple: ImGui first; the game only if ImGui does not want it. cpp-norun ImGuiIO& io = ImGui::GetIO(); if (!io.WantCaptureMouse) { if (mouse.leftPressed) player.shoot(mouse.worldPosition); camera.zoom(mouse.wheel); } if (!io.WantCaptureKeyboard) { player.move(keys.wasd()); } Read the flags after ImGui::NewFrame() and use them for this frame's game input. They are computed from last frame's layout, which is fine: windows do not move faster than a frame. Reading input through ImGui Your tool code can ask ImGui directly about keys and the mouse, using the same input the back end fed in: cpp-norun if (ImGui::IsKeyPressed(ImGuiKey_F5)) reloadLevel(); // pressed this frame (with key repeat by default) if (ImGui::IsKeyDown(ImGuiKey_LeftShift)) speed = 4.0f; // held if (ImGui::IsMouseClicked(ImGuiMouseButton_Right)) openMenuAt(ImGui::GetMousePos()); if (ImGui::IsMouseDragging(ImGuiMouseButton_Middle)) pan(ImGui::GetIO().MouseDelta); if (ImGui::IsMouseDoubleClicked(ImGuiMouseButton_Left)) focusSelection(); ImGuiKey_ values name every key independent of the platform: ImGuiKey_A , ImGuiKey_Escape , ImGuiKey_Delete , ImGuiKey_LeftCtrl , ImGuiMod_Ctrl (either Ctrl key). Keyboard shortcuts Recent versions of ImGui have a proper shortcut system that respects focus (a shortcut in one window does not fire while you type in another): cpp-norun if (ImGui::Shortcut(ImGuiMod_Ctrl ImGuiKey_S)) saveLevel(); if (ImGui::Shortcut(ImGuiMod_Ctrl ImGuiKey_Z)) undo(); if (ImGui::Shortcut(ImGuiMod_Ctrl ImGuiMod_Shift ImGuiKey_Z)) redo(); For a global shortcut that should work whichever window has focus, pass ImGuiInputFlags_RouteGlobal . Menu items show their shortcut text but do not trigger it by themselves (lesson 4.01). Tools often store shortcuts as text in a settings file: "Ctrl+Shift+S" . Parsing that text into modifiers and a key is a good small exercise, which the practice has you write. Gamepads With io.ConfigFlags = ImGuiConfigFlags_NavEnableGamepad and a back end that reports the gamepad (the Win32 back end supports XInput), the D-pad moves between widgets and A activates them. Useful for debug menus on a game being tested with a controller. Common mistakes !warning The game reading input before ImGui Typing in a text field moves the player. Check WantCaptureKeyboard before the game handles keys. !warning Checking the flags before NewFrame They are only updated in NewFrame. Check them after it. Check yourself quiz ? What is the rule for sharing input between ImGui and a game? - Give the game the input first; ImGui only gets what the game did not use + Give ImGui the input first; the game uses only what ImGui does not want - Give both all the input, but turn ImGui off while the game has focus The game handles the mouse only when WantCaptureMouse is false and the keyboard only when WantCaptureKeyboard is false. Otherwise typing in a text field also walks the player around. ? Which of these are input queries ImGui offers your code? - GetAsyncKeyState, GetCursorPos and WM_MOUSEWHEEL - IsItemHovered, IsItemActive and IsItemEdited + IsKeyPressed, IsKeyDown, IsMouseClicked, IsMouseDragging and GetMousePos They read the same input the back end fed ImGui. GetAsyncKeyState and GetCursorPos are Win32 functions, and the IsItem functions ask about the last widget, not the keys. ? Why prefer ImGui::Shortcut over checking keys yourself in a tool? - It is the only way to read a key that is being held down + It respects focus, so shortcuts do not fire while you type elsewhere - It makes the menu item show the shortcut text automatically It also routes keys and handles modifiers consistently. IsKeyDown reads held keys too, but ignores focus; menu items show shortcut text, yet do not trigger it. ? The player is typing a level name in an ImGui text field. Which flag tells the game to ignore the keyboard? - io.WantCaptureMouse + io.WantCaptureKeyboard - io.WantTextInput only It is true while an ImGui widget has keyboard focus. WantTextInput is for showing an on-screen keyboard. ? The mouse is over an ImGui window and the player clicks. Should the game fire? - Yes; games always get the mouse - Only on a double click + No; io.WantCaptureMouse is true ImGui gets first claim on the input. ? Which call checks the shortcut Ctrl+S with ImGui's focus rules? - ImGui::IsKeyDown(ImGuiKey_S) - ImGui::MenuItem("Save", "Ctrl+S") + ImGui::Shortcut(ImGuiMod_Ctrl ImGuiKey_S) MenuItem only shows the text, and IsKeyDown ignores Ctrl and focus; Shortcut detects the keys.

title: Who gets the input?
body: Each frame, decide which input the game may act on. Write cpp struct Frame { bool wantCaptureMouse; bool wantCaptureKeyboard; bool mouseClicked; std::vector<char keys; // keys pressed this frame }; struct GameInput { bool shoot{ false }; std::string moves; }; GameInput gameInput(const Frame& f); - The game shoots only if the mouse was clicked and ImGui does not want the mouse. - The game moves for each of w , a , s , d in keys , in order (other keys are ignored), only if ImGui does not want the keyboard. moves is those letters as a string.

title: Parse a shortcut
body: Tools store shortcuts as text, such as "Ctrl+Shift+S" . Write cpp struct Chord { bool ctrl{ false }, shift{ false }, alt{ false }; std::string key; }; bool parseShortcut(const std::string& text, Chord& out); std::string formatShortcut(const Chord& c); parseShortcut : - parts are separated by + ; spaces around them are ignored; names ignore case; - the modifiers are Ctrl (also Control ), Shift and Alt , each at most once; - exactly one part is the key, and it comes last : a single letter or digit (stored in upper case, "S" ), F1 to F12 , or one of Enter , Escape , Space , Tab , Delete (stored with that spelling); - anything else returns false . formatShortcut writes the modifiers in the order Ctrl, Shift, Alt, then the key, joined with + : "Ctrl+Shift+S" .

title: Slider maths
body: Map between a slider's value and its position in pixels. range 0..100, width 200 px: value 25 - x 50 x 150 - value 75 x -10 - value 0 (clamped) log range 1..1000: x 100 of 200 - value 31.6
