Use a fixed per-user settings folder. ? What does a settings handler let you do? - Change ImGui's colours from the ini file - Save the draw data of the last frame + Store your tool's own settings as sections of the same ini file Your data then loads and saves together with the window layout. ? How do you implement named layouts? - Copy imgui.ini to another name by hand and restart the program + Keep strings from SaveIniSettingsToMemory and apply one with LoadIniSettingsFromMemory - Call the DockBuilder functions every frame with the chosen layout A layout is just the ini text, so a map from name to string holds them all.

title: Read and write imgui.ini
body: Write a reader and writer for the ini format ImGui uses, that keeps sections it does not understand untouched: cpp struct Section { std::string type; // "Window" std::string name; // "Stones" std::vector<std::string lines; // the lines inside, as written (without the newline) }; std::vector<Section readIni(const std::string& text); std::string writeIni(const std::vector<Section & sections); std::string getValue(const Section& s, const std::string& key); // "" if missing void setValue(Section& s, const std::string& key, const std::string& value); - readIni : a section starts with a line Type Name . The type and name are between the brackets; the name may itself contain (for example Table 0x8A4C2B11,4 ), so the name ends at the last of the line. Every following line, up to the next header, belongs to the section, except empty lines, which are dropped. Lines before the first header are ignored. Lines may end with \r\n . - writeIni : each section as Type Name , then its lines, then one empty line, all separated by \n . - getValue(s, "Size") : the text after = on the first line that starts with Size= . - setValue : replace the first Key= line's value, or append Key=value if there is none.

title: A command palette
where: Menus, Popups, Docking and Style projects
body: Code editors open a command palette with Ctrl+Shift+P: type a few letters of any command and it appears at the top. Write the search behind one, for the command table from lesson 4.01's practice. cpp class Palette { public: void add(const std::string& name); // "File/Save Level" void ran(const std::string& name); // the user ran this command (it becomes the most recent) int score(const std::string& query, const std::string& name) const; // -1 when it does not match std::vector<std::string search(const std::string& query, std::size_t limit) const; }; Matching and scoring ( score ), ignoring upper and lower case: - Every character of the query must appear in the name in order (not necessarily next to each other): "svl" matches "File/Save Level" . Spaces in the query are ignored. - Match each query character at the earliest position after the previous match (left to right, no backtracking). If some character cannot be found, the score is -1 . - Each matched character scores 1 , plus 5 if it comes right after the previous matched character, plus 8 if it is at the start of a word : the first character of the name, a character after a space, / , _ or - , or an upper-case letter right after a lower-case one (in the original spelling: "saveLevel" , the L ). - An empty query (or only spaces) scores 0 for every name. Searching ( search ): the names with a score of 0 or more, best first; ties go to the more recently run command (commands never run come after those that were); then alphabetical. Return at most limit names. add "File/Save Level", "File/Save As", "View/Show Stats", "Edit/Select All" score("sl", "File/Save Level") = (1 + 8) + (1 + 8) = 18 (S and L both start words) score("sl", "Edit/Select All") = (1 + 8) + 1 = 10 (the l of Select follows an unmatched e: no bonus)

title: 5.01  Plots and Live Graphs
body: A number that changes every frame is hard to read; a graph of its last few seconds is easy. This lesson covers ImGui's built-in PlotLines and PlotHistogram , the ring buffer that feeds them, scaling and statistics, drawing your own graph with the draw list, and when to reach for the ImPlot library. Built-in plots cpp-norun static float frameTimes 120 = {}; static int offset = 0; frameTimes offset = ImGui::GetIO().DeltaTime 1000.0f; // this frame, in ms offset = (offset + 1) % IM_ARRAYSIZE(frameTimes); ImGui::PlotLines("Frame ms", frameTimes, IM_ARRAYSIZE(frameTimes), offset, nullptr, 0.0f, 33.3f, ImVec2(0, 80)); ImGui::PlotHistogram("Enemies per room", roomCounts, roomCount, 0, nullptr, 0.0f, FLT_MAX, ImVec2(0, 60)); Arguments: label, values, count, values_offset , overlay text, scale min, scale max, size. Pass FLT_MAX for the scale and ImGui fits it to the data each frame. The values_offset is the key to live graphs: the array is a ring buffer where the newest value overwrites the oldest, and the offset tells PlotLines where the oldest value now is, so the graph scrolls from left to right without shifting the whole array every frame. A ring buffer class Wrap that pattern so every graph in your tools can use it: cpp-norun template <std::size_t N class History { public: void push(float v) { m_data m_next = v; m_next = (m_next + 1) % N; if (m_count < N) ++m_count; } int offset() const { return m_count < N ? 0 : static_cast<int (m_next); } // where the oldest sample is int count() const { return static_cast<int (m_count); } const float data() const { return m_data.data(); } // plus min(), max(), average() for the overlay text private: std::array<float, N m_data{}; std::size_t m_next{ 0 }, m_count{ 0 }; }; Before the buffer is full, the samples are in 0 .. count-1 and the offset is 0. After it fills, the oldest sample is wherever the next write will go. The practice writes this class with its statistics, which go well in the overlay: "avg 16.7 ms max 21.3" . Smoothing Raw values jitter. Two cheap smoothers: - Moving average over the last N samples (the ring buffer has them). - Exponential smoothing : smoothed += (value - smoothed) k with k around 0.1, which reacts quickly but filters noise, and needs no buffer. Show the raw graph and the smoothed number together. Your own graph with the draw list For anything the built-ins do not do (several lines in one graph, thresholds, labels), draw it yourself: cpp-norun ImDrawList dl = ImGui::GetWindowDrawList(); const ImVec2 p0 = ImGui::GetCursorScreenPos(); const ImVec2 size(ImGui::GetContentRegionAvail().x, 100); dl- AddRectFilled(p0, ImVec2(p0.x + size.x, p0.y + size.y), IM_COL32(20, 22, 28, 255)); // the 16.6 ms (60 fps) budget line const float budgetY = p0.y + size.y (1.0f - 16.6f / 33.3f); dl- AddLine(ImVec2(p0.x, budgetY), ImVec2(p0.x + size.x, budgetY), IM_COL32(240, 180, 70, 160)); // the data as a polyline: map sample i to x and value to y std::vector<ImVec2 pts; for (int i = 0; i < history.count(); ++i) { / x = p0.x + i size.x / (N - 1); y = p0.y + size.y (1 - value / maxValue) / } dl- AddPolyline(pts.data(), (int)pts.size(), IM_COL32(120, 200, 255, 255), ImDrawFlags_None, 1.5f); ImGui::Dummy(size); // reserve the space in the layout Mapping a value to a pixel row is the same linear mapping as a slider (lesson 2.01), upside down: larger values are higher on screen, which means smaller y . ImPlot For serious charts (axes with ticks, zoom and pan, legends, many series, scatter plots, heat maps), use ImPlot ( epezent/implot ), a companion library built on ImGui: cpp-norun if (ImPlot::BeginPlot("Frame time")) { ImPlot::SetupAxes("frame", "ms"); ImPlot::PlotLine("cpu", cpuMs, count, 1.0, 0.0, 0, offset); ImPlot::PlotLine("gpu", gpuMs, count, 1.0, 0.0, 0, offset); ImPlot::EndPlot(); } It needs its own context ( ImPlot::CreateContext() after ImGui's). Common mistakes !warning Shifting the whole array every frame Use a ring buffer and pass the offset; nothing needs to move. !warning Auto-scaling a graph that should be compared over time FLT_MAX rescales every frame, so a spike shrinks everything else. Fix the scale for budgets like frame time. Check yourself quiz ? How does a ring buffer feed a scrolling graph? - Each new sample is appended and every older sample is shifted one place left + New samples overwrite the oldest; the offset says where the oldest sample is - The array grows by one sample each frame and the graph draws only the last part Nothing moves in the fixed array: the write position goes round it, and values_offset tells PlotLines to start drawing at the oldest sample. ? Name two ways to smooth a noisy value. - Rounding each sample to a whole number, and drawing the graph thicker - Auto-scaling with FLT_MAX, and sampling only every other frame + A moving average over the last N samples, and exponential smoothing: smoothed += (value - smoothed) k The moving average uses the samples already in the ring buffer; exponential smoothing needs no buffer at all. ? How do you map a value to a y position in a custom graph? - y = top + height (value - min) / (max - min) + y = top + height (1 - (value - min) / (max - min)) - y = top + (value - min) (max - min) / height Screen y grows downwards, so the fraction is flipped with 1 - : larger values get smaller y and appear higher. ? What is the values_offset argument of PlotLines for? - It moves the graph to the right on screen by that many pixels - It skips that many values at the start of the array + It says where the oldest sample of a ring buffer is, so the graph scrolls without moving data Pass the ring buffer's write position once it is full. ? A ring buffer of 120 samples is full and its next write position is 37. Where is the oldest sample? - At index 0 - At index 36 + At index 37 - At index 119 The next write overwrites the oldest sample, so the oldest is where the next write will go. Index 36 is the newest. ? When should you use ImPlot instead of PlotLines? + When you need axes, zooming, legends or several series - Whenever the graph has more than 120 samples - Only for histograms; PlotLines handles every line graph PlotLines is a quick single-series graph; ImPlot is a companion library with its own context for full charts.

title: A history for live graphs
body: Write the ring buffer that feeds PlotLines , with the statistics for its overlay: cpp class History { public: explicit History(int capacity); void push(float value); int count() const; // samples stored, up to capacity int offset() const; // index of the oldest sample (0 until the buffer is full) float at(int i) const; // the i-th oldest sample, 0 = oldest float average() const; // 0 when empty float maximum() const; // 0 when empty std::string overlay() const; // "avg 16.7 max 21.3", one decimal each }; float smooth(float previous, float value, float k); // exponential smoothing: previous + (value - previous) k at(i) must give samples in order from oldest to newest, whether or not the buffer has wrapped round.

title: 5.02  A Log Window with Filters
body: Every engine prints far more log lines than anyone can read. A good log window lets you filter by severity and by text, follows new lines without fighting the user, colours errors, and copes with a million lines. This lesson builds one with ImGuiTextFilter , a level filter and the list clipper. The data Keep log entries as data, not one big string, so they can be filtered: cpp-norun enum class Level { Trace, Info, Warning, Error }; struct LogEntry { double time; Level level; std::string category; std::string text; }; class Log { public: void add(Level level, std::string category, std::string text); const std::vector<LogEntry & entries() const; void clear(); private: std::vector<LogEntry m_entries; // or a ring buffer with a maximum size std::mutex m_mutex; // other threads log too }; Log calls come from many threads (loading, audio, networking). Protect the container with a mutex, or have each thread push into a lock-free queue that the UI thread drains once per frame. ImGuiTextFilter ImGui ships a small text filter with a useful syntax: cpp-norun static ImGuiTextFilter filter; filter.Draw("Filter (\"inc,-exc\")", 240.0f); for (const LogEntry& e : log.entries()) if (filter.PassFilter(e.text.c_str())) ImGui::TextUnformatted(e.text.c_str()); The filter text is a comma-separated list of words: - texture shows lines containing "texture"; - texture,shader shows lines containing either ; - -vsync hides lines containing "vsync"; - -missing,texture shows texture lines except those containing "missing". The terms are checked in order , and the first one that matches the line decides: an exclusion that matches hides the line, an inclusion that matches shows it. So order matters: with texture,-missing , a line "texture missing" matches texture first and is shown. Put exclusions first. Spaces around terms are ignored and matching ignores case. If no term matches, the line passes only if the filter has no inclusions at all. The practice reimplements these exact rules. Severity and category Add check boxes for levels and a combo for categories, and combine them with the text filter: cpp-norun static bool showLevel 4 = { false, true, true, true }; // hide Trace by default ImGui::Checkbox("Info", &showLevel 1 ); ImGui::SameLine(); ImGui::Checkbox("Warnings", &showLevel 2 ); ImGui::SameLine(); ImGui::Checkbox("Errors", &showLevel 3 ); Each line then passes if its level is shown, its category matches, and the text filter passes. Drawing a million lines Filtering every line every frame is fine for thousands, not for millions. Keep a list of the indexes of matching entries, rebuild it only when the filter changes, and append to it as new entries arrive (checking only the new ones). Then draw it with the clipper (lesson 3.02): cpp-norun ImGuiListClipper clipper; clipper.Begin((int)visible.size()); while (clipper.Step()) for (int row = clipper.DisplayStart; row < clipper.DisplayEnd; ++row) { const LogEntry& e = entries visible row ; ImGui::PushStyleColor(ImGuiCol_Text, colourFor(e.level)); ImGui::TextUnformatted(e.text.c_str()); ImGui::PopStyleColor(); } Follow new lines only when the user was at the bottom (lesson 3.02), and offer "Copy" ( ImGui::SetClipboardText ) and "Clear" buttons. Common mistakes !warning Logging from other threads into a vector without a lock Two threads pushing at once corrupt it. Lock, or queue and drain on the UI thread. !warning Filtering the whole log every frame Rebuild the visible index list only when the filter changes; append for new lines. Check yourself quiz ? Describe ImGuiTextFilter's syntax. - Space-separated words that must all appear in the line, matched with case - A regular expression matched against the whole line, ignoring case + Comma-separated terms, ignoring case; a - term excludes, others include Terms are checked in order and the first one found in the line decides; if none is found, the line passes only when there are no inclusions. ? How do you make logging thread-safe? + Protect the entries with a mutex, or have threads push into a queue the UI thread drains each frame - Call add only from inside the ImGui window's Begin/End block - Make the vector of entries static Two threads pushing into a vector at once corrupt it; static changes its lifetime, not its safety. ? How do you keep filtering cheap? - Filter the whole log every frame, but only while the window is visible - Keep only the last 100 entries + Recompute the list of matching indexes only when the filter changes, and check only new entries as they arrive Then the per-frame cost depends on the new lines and the clipper's visible rows, not the size of the log. ? Which lines does the filter -missing,texture show? - Lines containing "texture" or "missing" + Lines containing "texture" but not "missing" - Only lines containing both words Terms are checked in order: the exclusion comes first and hides "missing" lines, then the inclusion shows "texture" lines. ? With the filter texture,-missing , is the line "texture missing" shown? - No: an exclusion always wins over an inclusion - Only if the filter text is empty + Yes: "texture" matches first and decides The first matching term decides, so put exclusions first. ? A filter contains only -vsync . What passes? - Nothing, because there is no inclusion to match - Only lines containing "vsync" + Every line that does not contain "vsync" With no inclusions, every line that is not excluded passes. ? How does a log window stay fast with a million entries? + Keep an index of matching entries, update it as lines arrive, draw it with the clipper - Draw every line each frame inside a scrolling child window, filtering as you go - Refilter all entries each frame and draw them with the clipper The clipper submits only the visible rows, and the index list avoids refiltering everything.

title: ImGuiTextFilter's rules
body: Reimplement ImGui's text filter exactly: cpp class TextFilter { public: explicit TextFilter(const std::string& text); bool pass(const std::string& line) const; }; - The filter text is split at commas into terms ; spaces at the start and end of each term are removed; empty terms are ignored. - A term starting with - is an exclusion (the rest of it is the text to look for); any other term is an inclusion . A lone - is ignored. - pass(line) : if there are no terms, every line passes. Otherwise check the terms in order , looking for each one's text inside the line without regard to case : the first term found decides: an exclusion returns false , an inclusion returns true . - If no term is found in the line: the line passes only if there are no inclusions at all. "-missing,texture" "texture loaded" - true; "texture missing" - false; "shader" - false "texture,-missing" "texture missing" - true (texture is found first) "-vsync" "frame done" - true; "vsync on" - false

title: Keep the visible lines up to date
match: Keep the visible lines up to date
body: Filtering a huge log every frame is too slow. Keep a list of the indexes of lines that pass, update it only for new lines, and rebuild it only when the filter changes: cpp class FilteredLog { public: void add(const std::string& line); void setFilter(const std::string& filter); // rebuilds the visible list const std::vector<int & visible() const; // indexes of passing lines, in order int checks() const; // how many times a line was tested against the filter }; Use lesson 5.02's filter rules (write them again, or reuse your TextFilter ). checks counts every test of one line against the filter, so the tests can see that adding a line costs one check and that changing the filter costs one check per line, not more.

title: 5.03  A Property Inspector
body: An inspector shows and edits the properties of whatever is selected. Writing one widget call per field for every type gets tedious; describing each type's fields once, as data, lets one function draw an inspector for anything. This lesson builds that property table , handles editing several selected objects at once, and shows "mixed" values. By hand first cpp-norun void inspect(Light& l) { ImGui::DragFloat3("Position", &l.pos.x, 0.1f); ImGui::ColorEdit3("Colour", &l.color.x); ImGui::SliderFloat("Intensity", &l.intensity, 0.0f, 100.0f, "%.1f", ImGuiSliderFlags_Logarithmic); ImGui::Checkbox("Casts shadows", &l.shadows); } Perfectly fine for three types. With forty component types, and the same fields needing undo, saving and copy-paste, a description of the fields pays off. Describing fields as data cpp-norun enum class Kind { Float, Int, Bool, Color3, Vec3, String }; struct Field { const char name; Kind kind; std::size_t offset; // where the field is inside the object (offsetof) float min = 0, max = 0; // for sliders; 0, 0 means "a drag with no limits" }; static const Field lightFields = { { "Position", Kind::Vec3, offsetof(Light, pos) }, { "Colour", Kind::Color3, offsetof(Light, color) }, { "Intensity", Kind::Float, offsetof(Light, intensity), 0.0f, 100.0f }, { "Casts shadows", Kind::Bool, offsetof(Light, shadows) }, }; One function then draws any object described this way: cpp-norun bool inspect(void object, std::span<const Field fields) { bool changed = false; for (const Field& f : fields) { void p = static_cast<char (object) + f.offset; switch (f.kind) { case Kind::Float: changed = f.max f.min ? ImGui::SliderFloat(f.name, (float )p, f.min, f.max) : ImGui::DragFloat(f.name, (float )p, 0.1f); break; case Kind::Int: changed = ImGui::DragInt(f.name, (int )p); break; case Kind::Bool: changed = ImGui::Checkbox(f.name, (bool )p); break; case Kind::Color3: changed = ImGui::ColorEdit3(f.name, (float )p); break; case Kind::Vec3: changed = ImGui::DragFloat3(f.name, (float )p, 0.1f); break; case Kind::String: changed = ImGui::InputText(f.name, (std::string )p); break; } } return changed; } The same table drives saving (write each field by name), loading, copy and paste, and undo (record which field changed and its old value). That is a small reflection system; big engines generate these tables from their source code. offsetof is only guaranteed for standard-layout types (plain structs without virtual functions or mixed access); keep component data like that. Editing several objects at once When the user selects five lights and changes the intensity, all five should change. Show each field once: - if all selected objects have the same value, show it normally; - if they differ , show it as mixed (ImGui's ImGuiItemFlags_MixedValue draws a dash in a checkbox, and you can display "--" in a number field); - when the user edits it, write the new value to every selected object. For drags, the most useful behaviour is often relative: dragging position by +2 moves every object by +2, keeping their arrangement. The practice computes the shown values for a multi-selection. Common mistakes !warning Editing only the first selected object Users expect the change to apply to everything selected. !warning Using offsetof on a class with virtual functions It is not guaranteed to work. Keep inspectable data in plain structs. Check yourself quiz ? How does a field table let one function inspect any type? - It stores a pointer to every field of every object, so the function can edit them directly + Each entry gives a field's name, kind and offset, so the function can find the field inside any object and pick the right widget - It lists the widget functions to call, one per type, and the inspector calls the matching one The offset locates the field inside whatever object is passed, and the kind chooses Checkbox, DragFloat, ColorEdit3 and so on. ? How should an inspector show a field for several selected objects? - It shows the first selected object's value, and an edit changes only that object - It shows the average of the values, and an edit writes the new value to all of them + Normally if all values are equal, as mixed if they differ, and an edit writes the new value to every selected object Users expect an edit to apply to everything selected, and a made-up average would hide that the values differ. ? What must be true of a type for offsetof to be reliable? - It must have a default constructor and no const members - It must be declared final so no class can derive from it + It must be standard-layout, such as a plain struct with no virtual functions offsetof is only guaranteed for standard-layout types (no virtual functions, no mixed access specifiers), so keep inspectable component data in plain structs. ? Why describe a type's fields in a table? + One table drives the inspector, saving, loading, copy and paste and undo for every type - Field tables make ImGui draw the widgets faster - ImGui requires a field table before it can draw an inspector It is a small reflection system that you write once; ImGui itself knows nothing about it. ? Three selected lights have intensities 5, 5 and 8. What should the intensity field show? - 5, the value most of them have - 6, the average of the three + A mixed value, such as "--" Values that differ are shown as mixed until the user edits them. ? What does offsetof(Light, intensity) give? - The size of intensity in bytes + The byte position of intensity inside a Light - The value of intensity in a default Light Add it to an object's address (as a char ) to reach the field.

title: Mixed values in an inspector
body: With several objects selected, each field shows one value or "mixed". Write cpp struct Object { int id; std::map<std::string, double fields; }; std::string shownValue(const std::vector<Object & selected, const std::string& field); void setAll(std::vector<Object & selected, const std::string& field, double value); void addAll(std::vector<Object & selected, const std::string& field, double delta); - shownValue : "--" if the values differ between the selected objects; otherwise the common value written with std::to_string and trailing zeros after the decimal point removed (and the point too if nothing is left after it): 5 , 2.5 , -0.125 . An object without the field does not count; if no selected object has it (or nothing is selected), return "" . - setAll writes the value into every selected object that has the field. - addAll adds delta to the field of every selected object that has it (a relative drag: their differences stay the same).

title: 5.04  Undo and Redo for Tools
body: No one trusts an editor without undo. This lesson builds the classic command pattern undo stack, explains why redo history is cleared by a new edit, shows how to merge the sixty small changes of one drag into one step using ImGui's item queries, and how to mark a document as saved. Commands Every change to the document is an object that knows how to do and undo itself: cpp-norun struct Change { virtual ~Change() = default; virtual void apply(Level& level) = 0; virtual void revert(Level& level) = 0; virtual std::string label() const = 0; // shown in Edit Undo "Move rock" }; struct SetIntensity final : Change { int lightId; float before, after; void apply(Level& l) override { l.light(lightId).intensity = after; } void revert(Level& l) override { l.light(lightId).intensity = before; } std::string label() const override { return "Change intensity"; } }; Two stacks undo stack: create rock move rock change colour <- top: the most recent change redo stack: - Do a change: apply it, push it on the undo stack, and clear the redo stack . - Undo : pop from the undo stack, revert it, push it on the redo stack. - Redo : pop from the redo stack, apply it, push it back on the undo stack. Why clear redo on a new change? After undoing "change colour", the redo stack holds it. If the user now moves a tree, the colour change belonged to a history that no longer exists: redoing it on top of the new state could make no sense. Every editor you know behaves this way. One drag, one undo step A slider drag changes the value every frame. Recording each frame would make one drag sixty undo steps. Use ImGui's item queries (lesson 2.01): cpp-norun static float before; if (ImGui::IsItemActivated()) before = light.intensity; // the drag started: remember the old value ImGui::SliderFloat("Intensity", &light.intensity, 0, 100); // edits live, for immediate feedback if (ImGui::IsItemDeactivatedAfterEdit()) // the drag ended with a change undo.record(std::make_unique<SetIntensity (light.id, before, light.intensity)); // record, do not re-apply Note record , not apply : the value is already set. Another approach is merging : when a new change has the same target as the top of the stack and arrives within a short time, combine them into one (keeping the oldest before and the newest after ). Text editors use merging for typing. Saved and dirty The document is dirty (has unsaved changes) when the undo stack differs from what it was at the last save. Remember a saved marker : the size of the undo stack at save time (or a pointer to the top change). - After saving, the marker equals the current position: not dirty. - Undoing back to the saved point makes it clean again, which a simple dirty = true flag cannot do. - If a new change clears redo history that included the saved point, the saved state can never be reached again: always dirty until saved. The practice builds the whole stack with labels, the saved marker and a limit on how many steps are kept. Groups "Delete 40 selected objects" is 40 changes but one action for the user. Put several changes into a group that applies them in order and reverts them in reverse order, and push the group as one step. Common mistakes !warning Forgetting to clear redo after a new change Redo then applies a change from an abandoned history. !warning A change that stores pointers to objects Deleting and undoing recreates the object at a new address. Store ids. !warning Reverting a group in the same order it was applied Later changes may depend on earlier ones. Revert in reverse. Check yourself quiz ? Describe the do, undo and redo operations on two stacks. - Do: apply, push on redo. Undo: pop redo, revert, push on undo. Redo: pop undo, apply, push on redo + Do: apply, push on undo, clear redo. Undo: pop undo, revert, push on redo. Redo: pop redo, apply, push on undo - Do: apply, push on undo. Undo: pop undo, revert, discard it. Redo: apply the last discarded change again Each change moves between the two stacks, and a new change clears redo because that history no longer exists. ? Why should changes store ids rather than pointers? - Ids take less memory than pointers + Objects can be deleted and recreated by undo at a different address; ids stay valid - Pointers cannot be stored inside a class with virtual functions Undoing a delete makes a new object, so a pointer to the old one would dangle. ? How does a group of changes undo correctly? - It reverts its changes in the same order they were applied - It reverts only its last change, which contains the others + It reverts its changes in the reverse order they were applied Later changes may depend on earlier ones, so they must be undone first. ? The user undoes twice, then makes a new change. What happens to the redo stack? - It keeps both undone changes, so they can be redone after the new change + It is cleared - The new change is pushed onto it Those undone changes belong to a history that no longer exists; redoing them on top of the new state could make no sense. ? How do you record one undo step for a whole slider drag? - Record a change in every frame where the slider returns true - Record the change on the frame IsItemHovered becomes false + Save the value on IsItemActivated ; record on IsItemDeactivatedAfterEdit That gives one step from the value before the drag to the value after it. Record it without applying it again, since the value is already set. ? Why does a saved marker work better than a dirty flag? + Undoing back to the saved state makes the document clean again - It uses less memory than a bool kept on the document - It saves the document automatically when you undo Compare the current undo position with the position at the last save; a plain flag cannot tell that you got back there.

title: An undo stack
body: Write the undo stack a tool uses, with labels, a saved marker, groups and a size limit: cpp struct Change { std::string label; std::function<void() apply; std::function<void() revert; }; class UndoStack { public: explicit UndoStack(int limit); // keep at most this many undo steps void push(Change c); // the change has ALREADY been applied: just record it void pushGroup(const std::string& label, std::vector<Change changes); // already applied, one step bool undo(); // false if nothing to undo bool redo(); // false if nothing to redo std::string undoLabel() const; // "Undo <label ", or "" if nothing to undo std::string redoLabel() const; // "Redo <label ", or "" void markSaved(); bool dirty() const; }; - push and pushGroup clear the redo history. - A group undoes by reverting its changes in reverse order, and redoes by applying them in order. - When the undo history would exceed limit , the oldest step is dropped. - dirty() is false right after markSaved() , and becomes false again if the user undoes or redoes back to exactly that point. If the saved point is lost for good (it was in redo history that a new change cleared, or it was dropped by the limit), the document stays dirty until the next save. A new stack is not dirty.

title: An undoable inspector
body: Combine lessons 5.03 and 5.04 into the model behind a real inspector: several objects selected, fields shown as one value or mixed, drags that edit live but create one undo step, undo and redo, and a dirty flag for the title bar. cpp class Inspector { public: void addObject(int id, std::map<std::string, double fields); void select(std::vector<int ids); // ids that do not exist are ignored std::string shown(const std::string& field) const; // lesson 5.03's rules over the selection void beginEdit(const std::string& field); // like IsItemActivated: a drag starts void editValue(const std::string& field, double value); // every frame of the drag: write live void endEdit(); // like IsItemDeactivatedAfterEdit bool undo(); bool redo(); std::string undoLabel() const; // "Undo Change range" or "" (see below) double value(int id, const std::string& field) const; // NaN if the object or field does not exist void markSaved(); bool dirty() const; }; Editing. - beginEdit(field) remembers the current value of field for every selected object that has it. - editValue(field, v) writes v to that field on every selected object that has it, immediately, so the view updates during the drag. - endEdit() records one undo step that takes every affected object from its remembered value to its current value. If nothing changed (every value is what it was), it records nothing. - editValue called without a beginEdit for that field (a checkbox click, a value typed in) applies and records its own one-step change at once. - The step's label is Change <field for one object, or Change <field (<n objects) for several. - The selection at the time of the edit is part of the step: undoing after the selection changed still restores the right objects. Undo, redo and dirty follow lesson 5.04's practice (a new step clears redo; dirty compares the current position with the saved one; there is no limit here).

title: 6.01  Project: A Level Editor
body: Build a tile-based level editor with Dear ImGui - a docked layout with a viewport, a tile palette, an inspector and a log; painting, erasing, rectangle and flood-fill tools; panning and zooming; undo and redo; and saving to a text file. This lesson is the plan, the key pieces of code, and the order to build them in. What you build Xenon Level Editor ┌ File Edit View Tools ───────────────────────────────────────┐ │ ┌ Palette ┐ ┌ Viewport ─────────────────────────┐ ┌ Inspector ┐ │ │ │ grass │ │ the tile map, drawn with the │ │ tile 12,7 │ │ │ │ stone │ │ draw list; pan with the middle │ │ kind:stone│ │ │ │ water │ │ button, zoom with the wheel │ │ ... │ │ │ │ ... │ │ │ │ │ │ │ └─────────┘ └───────────────────────────────────┘ └───────────┘ │ │ ┌ Log ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐│ │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘│ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ Everything in it comes from earlier lessons; this project is about putting them together well. The pieces and where they come from Piece Lessons --- --- Win32 + DX11 host, docking, default layout 1.02, 4.04 Main menu with File, Edit, View and a command table 4.01 Palette as a list of selectables with colour swatches 2.03, 2.04 Viewport drawn with the draw list 1.03, 5.01 Tools: paint, erase, rectangle, flood fill this lesson's practice Undo and redo, one step per stroke 5.04 Inspector for the tile under the mouse 5.03 Unsaved-changes guard on New, Open, Quit 4.02 Log window 5.02 Settings and layout saved in the ini 4.06 The viewport: from screen to tiles and back The viewport needs a camera : a pan offset (where the map's origin is on screen) and a zoom (pixels per tile). cpp-norun struct Camera { ImVec2 pan{ 0, 0 }; float zoom{ 32.0f }; }; // zoom = pixels per tile ImVec2 tileToScreen(const Camera& c, ImVec2 origin, float tx, float ty) { return ImVec2(origin.x + c.pan.x + tx c.zoom, origin.y + c.pan.y + ty c.zoom); } // and the reverse, screenToTile, for the mouse Zooming around the mouse feels right only if the tile under the mouse stays under the mouse: remember which tile it is before changing the zoom, then adjust the pan so it is back under the cursor. The practice writes these functions; they are the same maths any 2D editor or map view uses. Drawing only what is visible matters for big maps: compute the visible range of tiles from the viewport rectangle (lesson 3.02's clipper idea in 2D) and loop over just those. cpp-norun ImGui::Begin("Viewport"); const ImVec2 origin = ImGui::GetCursorScreenPos(); const ImVec2 size = ImGui::GetContentRegionAvail(); ImGui::InvisibleButton("canvas", size, ImGuiButtonFlags_MouseButtonLeft ImGuiButtonFlags_MouseButtonMiddle); const bool hovered = ImGui::IsItemHovered(); ImDrawList dl = ImGui::GetWindowDrawList(); dl- PushClipRect(origin, ImVec2(origin.x + size.x, origin.y + size.y), true); // draw visible tiles, the grid, the hovered tile's outline, the rectangle tool's preview dl- PopClipRect(); if (hovered && ImGui::IsMouseDragging(ImGuiMouseButton_Middle)) camera.pan += ImGui::GetIO().MouseDelta; if (hovered && ImGui::GetIO().MouseWheel != 0) zoomAround(camera, ImGui::GetMousePos(), ImGui::GetIO().MouseWheel); ImGui::End(); InvisibleButton covering the canvas gives you hover, active and clicks for the whole area, and stops the window from being dragged when you paint. Tools and undo Each tool turns mouse input into changes to tiles : - Paint and Erase : while the left button is held, set the tile under the mouse. Collect every tile changed during the stroke, with its old value, and record one undo step when the button is released (lesson 5.04's "one drag, one step"). - Rectangle : show a preview while dragging; on release, fill the rectangle as one step. - Flood fill : replace the connected region of the clicked tile's kind with the new kind, as one step. Use an explicit stack or queue, not recursion: a large region would overflow the call stack. The file format A readable text format makes levels easy to diff in version control: xenon-level 1 size 40 24 palette . grass, stone, ~ water tiles ........................................ ... .........~~~~~................... One character per tile, rows top to bottom, with a version number on the first line so a future editor can read old files. The project at the end of this milestone has you write the editor's core: map, tools, undo and file format. Order to build in 1. Host, docking, menu, empty windows: it runs. 2. Map data, the viewport drawing it, pan and zoom. 3. Paint and erase with the palette, then undo for them. 4. Save and load, the dirty flag in the title, the unsaved-changes guard. 5. Rectangle and flood fill. 6. Inspector, log, settings. Check yourself quiz ? Why does zooming need to adjust the pan? - Because the zoom value is only allowed to change while the pan is zero + To keep the point under the mouse in place; otherwise the view jumps towards the origin with every zoom step - To keep the whole map visible inside the viewport after every zoom step Remember which tile is under the mouse before zooming, then move the pan so it is under the cursor again. ? Why use an InvisibleButton over the canvas? - Because the draw list can only draw inside a button's rectangle - Because without it the tiles cannot be clipped to the viewport + It gives hover, active and click state, and stops drags from moving the window The draw list only draws; the invisible button is the item covering the whole canvas that ImGui's item queries and clicks refer to. ? Why should flood fill not be recursive? + A large region needs one call per tile, which can overflow the call stack; an explicit stack or queue cannot - Recursion visits the tiles in the wrong order, so the fill looks different - A recursive function cannot change the map it was given The explicit stack or queue lives on the heap and grows as needed, so even a huge region is fine. ? How many undo steps should one paint stroke (press, drag across 30 tiles, release) record? - 30, one for each tile that changed during the drag - Two, one recorded on press and one on release + One, holding every changed tile's old value, recorded on release Collect the changed tiles while the button is held and record them as a single step, as in lesson 5.04's "one drag, one step".

title: The editor's camera
body: Write the camera maths for a 2D editor viewport: cpp struct Vec2 { float x, y; }; struct Camera { Vec2 pan{ 0, 0 }; float zoom{ 32 }; }; // zoom: pixels per tile Vec2 tileToScreen(const Camera& c, Vec2 origin, Vec2 tile); Vec2 screenToTile(const Camera& c, Vec2 origin, Vec2 screen); void zoomAround(Camera& c, Vec2 origin, Vec2 mouse, float factor, float minZoom, float maxZoom); void visibleTiles(const Camera& c, Vec2 origin, Vec2 size, int mapW, int mapH, int& x0, int& y0, int& x1, int& y1); - tileToScreen : origin + pan + tile zoom (for each of x and y). - screenToTile : the reverse: (screen - origin - pan) / zoom . - zoomAround : multiply the zoom by factor , clamped to minZoom..maxZoom , and change pan so that the point under mouse (in tile coordinates, before the zoom) is still under mouse afterwards. - visibleTiles : the range of whole tiles that touch the viewport rectangle ( origin to origin + size ): x0 = floor of the left edge in tiles, x1 = ceil of the right edge (exclusive end), likewise for y, each clamped to 0..mapW or 0..mapH .

title: 6.02  Project: An In-Game Profiler
body: Build a profiler that runs inside your game - scoped timers you sprinkle through the code, a per-frame tree of where the time went with total and self times, a frame-time graph with the budget line, and a flame view drawn with the draw list. This lesson covers measuring, collecting, aggregating and showing the data. Measuring with scopes A zone is a named span of time. Mark zones with a small RAII object that records a begin event when constructed and an end event when destroyed: cpp-norun class Zone { public: explicit Zone(const char name) : m_name{ name } { Profiler::get().begin(m_name, now()); } ~Zone() { Profiler::get().end(m_name, now()); } private: const char m_name; }; // Two steps, so __LINE__ is replaced by the number before the names are joined. define PROFILE_JOIN2(a, b) a b define PROFILE_JOIN(a, b) PROFILE_JOIN2(a, b) define PROFILE_ZONE(name) Zone PROFILE_JOIN(profileZone, __LINE__){ name } void updateEnemies() { PROFILE_ZONE("updateEnemies"); for (auto& e : enemies) { PROFILE_ZONE("think"); e.think(); } } now() should be a high-resolution clock: QueryPerformanceCounter on Windows, or std::chrono::steady_clock . The string is a literal, so storing the pointer is fine and cheap. Zones nest naturally: "think" begins and ends inside "updateEnemies". Recording only begin and end events, in order, captures the whole tree. From events to a tree At the end of a frame, the events of that frame form a list like: begin frame 0 begin update 10 begin physics 12 end physics 40 begin think 41 end think 52 begin think 52 end think 60 end update 61 begin render 61 end render 150 end frame 152 Walk them with a stack : a begin pushes a new node as a child of the top of the stack; an end pops it and stores its duration. Each node's total time is its own duration; its self time is the total minus its children's totals: the time spent in that zone's own code. Zones with the same name under the same parent (the two "think" zones) are usually merged into one row with a call count. The practice builds exactly this. frame 152.0 ms self 12.0 update 51.0 self 4.0 physics 28.0 think 19.0 (2 calls) render 89.0 Showing it - A table tree (lessons 3.03 and 3.04): name, total, self, calls, with tree nodes in the first column and sorting by total or self. - A frame graph (lesson 5.01): the last few hundred frame times with the 16.6 ms line; clicking a bar pauses on that frame to inspect its tree. - A flame view : each zone as a bar whose x position and width are its start and duration in the frame, and whose row is its nesting depth. Draw it with AddRectFilled and AddText , coloured by name (the golden-ratio hue trick from lesson 2.04 keeps colours stable per name). Hover a bar for a tooltip with the exact numbers. Threads Zones on other threads (loading, audio, job workers) need their own event lists: give each thread its own buffer ( thread_local ) and merge them at the end of the frame, showing one lane per thread in the flame view. Keep the profiler cheap - Two clock reads and two small writes per zone: keep zones out of loops that run millions of times, or profile a sample of them. - No memory allocation per event: pre-allocate the event buffer. - Compile zones out of shipping builds: define PROFILE_ZONE(name) to nothing (lesson 6.03). Professional tools such as Tracy and Optick follow this design and add network streaming, GPU timing and much more; after this project you will know how to read them. Check yourself quiz ? How do begin and end events become a tree? - Sort the events by name, then group each begin with the next end of the same name - Each begin event becomes a child of the previous begin event in the list + Walk them in order with a stack: a begin pushes a child of the current top; an end pops the top and records its duration The stack's top is always the zone that is currently open, so every begin knows its parent. ? What is the difference between total and self time? + Total time is the whole span of a zone; self time is the total minus the time spent in its child zones - Total time adds up every call of the zone in the frame; self time is the time of one call - Total time includes the profiler's own cost; self time does not Self time is the time spent in that zone's own code, not in the zones nested inside it. ? Why should zone names be string literals? - Because define macros only accept string literals - Because a std::string cannot be compared with another + Their pointers stay valid forever, so recording a zone costs no allocation or copying A literal lives for the whole program, so storing just the const char is safe and cheap. ? A zone "update" lasts 51 ms and has child zones of 28 ms and 19 ms. What is its self time? - 51 ms + 4 ms - 47 ms - 19 ms Self time is total minus the children's totals: 51 - (28 + 19) = 4 ms. 47 ms is the children's sum, not the remainder.

title: Where did the frame go?
body: Turn one frame's profiler events into the rows of a profiler table: cpp struct Event { bool begin; std::string name; double time; }; // time in milliseconds std::vector<std::string profileRows(const std::vector<Event & events); - Walk the events with a stack. A begin starts a zone inside the zone on top of the stack; an end finishes the zone on top (its name will match). - Zones with the same name under the same parent are merged into one row: their totals add up and their call count increases. Merging also merges their children, by name. - A row's total is the sum of its zones' durations; its self time is its total minus the totals of its children. - Rows are listed depth first: a zone, then its children in the order they first appeared, then its next sibling. Each row is two spaces of indentation per level of depth, then: <name total <t self <s with one decimal place each, followed by (<n calls) when merged from more than one zone. frame 0..152: update 10..61 (physics 12..40, think 41..52, think 52..60), render 61..150 frame total 152.0 self 12.0 update total 51.0 self 4.0 physics total 28.0 self 28.0 think total 19.0 self 19.0 (2 calls) render total 89.0 self 89.0 An end event with an empty stack, or events left open at the end, make the result the single line unbalanced events .

title: 6.03  ImGui in a Game You Ship
match: 6.03 ImGui in a Game You Ship
body: Dear ImGui is a development tool first. Before a game ships, decide what happens to the debug interface - compile it out, hide it behind a key, or keep a few tools for players - and check what it costs. This lesson covers build switches, performance, security and licensing. Three choices Choice When How --- --- --- Compile it out Most shipped games A build switch removes every debug window and the ImGui calls Hidden behind a key or a flag Games tested by others, early access Present but not drawn until a debug key or a command-line flag Keep some tools for players Modding tools, level editors shipped with the game Treated as real product UI: styled, tested, translated A build switch Give your project a configuration flag, say XENON_DEV_TOOLS , defined in Debug and in an internal "Development" configuration, and not in Shipping: cpp-norun if XENON_DEV_TOOLS drawDebugWindows(); ImGui::ShowMetricsWindow(&showMetrics); endif Keep tool code in its own files ( debug_ui/ .cpp ) so the shipping build can leave whole files out. If the game uses ImGui for nothing else, the shipping build need not link ImGui at all, which also removes the font atlas and its texture memory. What it costs Measure before guessing: - CPU : building the UI runs your code every frame. Debug windows that loop over every entity are the usual culprits; use the clipper and only build windows that are open (lesson 1.04's Begin return value). - GPU : usually tiny, a few draw calls. Watch for thousands of custom draw-list primitives. - Memory : the font atlas (a few megabytes with large fonts and icon fonts), plus vertex buffers. - Input : if a debug window has keyboard focus, the game must not react to keys (lesson 2.05). In a shipping build with hidden tools, make sure nothing can grab focus while hidden. The Metrics window (lesson 1.06) shows vertex counts per window. Security and cheating Debug tools that edit memory, spawn items or teleport are cheats in a multiplayer game. In anything online: - compile them out of client builds, rather than hiding them; - never trust the client: the server decides what is allowed, whatever the client's interface can do. Licensing Dear ImGui is under the MIT licence : free to use in commercial games, provided the licence text is included with the software (usually in an "open source licences" screen or file). The same goes for ImPlot and most companion libraries; check each one's licence. Fonts have their own licences (Font Awesome Free and most Google Fonts allow embedding with attribution). Checklist - Shipping configuration builds without XENON_DEV_TOOLS and runs. - No debug window can be opened in a shipping build by any key combination. - Debug-only assets (tool fonts, icon fonts) are not in the shipping package. - Licence texts for every library and font are included. - For a game with shipped tools: those windows are styled, scale with the display, work with a controller if the game does, and are translated. Check yourself quiz ? Name the three choices for ImGui in a shipped game. - Compile it out, replace it with Win32 controls, or move it to a separate process + Compile it out, keep it hidden behind a key or flag, or keep some tools as real player-facing features - Ship it unchanged, ship it with a different style, or ship it only in the Debug build Most shipped games compile it out; hidden tools suit test builds, and shipped tools must be treated as real product UI. ? Where does ImGui's cost usually come from? - GPU time drawing ImGui's vertices, which takes most of a typical frame - Memory for the copy of every widget's state ImGui keeps between frames + CPU time building debug windows each frame, mostly ones that loop over many objects The GPU work is usually a few draw calls, and most memory goes to the font atlas. Use the clipper and only build windows that are open. ? What must you check about input when tools are hidden? - That the hidden windows still receive the keyboard, so they are ready when shown + That nothing can take keyboard or mouse focus while hidden, so the game always receives its input - That io.WantCaptureKeyboard is set to true every frame If a hidden window kept focus, the game would stop reacting to keys while showing no reason why. ? What should happen to cheat-like debug tools in an online game's client? - Hide them behind a secret key combination only developers know - Leave them in, since players are unlikely to ever find them + Compile them out, and make sure the server does not trust the client anyway Hidden tools can still be found and enabled; compiled-out code cannot. Even then, the server decides what is allowed. ? What does the MIT licence require when you ship Dear ImGui? - Paying a fee per copy sold + Including the licence text with the software - Publishing your game's source code It is a permissive licence: free for commercial use as long as the licence text is included, usually in an "open source licences" screen or file. ? Why put debug UI code in its own files? - Because ImGui calls only work in separate translation units - To make the debug windows load faster + So the shipping build can leave whole files out A build switch is cleaner at the file level, and without the tools the shipping build may not need to link ImGui at all.

title: The level editor's core
body: Write the core of lesson 6.01's level editor: the map, the four tools, undo and redo, and the file format. The ImGui part on top of it (palette, viewport, menus) is then a thin layer that calls these functions. cpp class Level { public: Level(int width, int height, char fill); int width() const; int height() const; char at(int x, int y) const; // ' ' outside the map void strokeBegin(); // mouse pressed with the paint or erase tool void strokePaint(int x, int y, char tile); // every frame while held: set one tile (outside the map: ignored) void strokeEnd(); // mouse released: one undo step for the whole stroke void rectangle(int x0, int y0, int x1, int y1, char tile); // corners in any order, both included, one step void floodFill(int x, int y, char tile); // the connected region (4 directions) of that tile's kind, one step bool undo(); bool redo(); bool dirty() const; void markSaved(); std::string save() const; static bool load(const std::string& text, Level& out); }; Steps. Each stroke, rectangle or fill is one undo step holding, for every tile it changed, the old and the new character. A step that changes nothing is not recorded. A new step clears redo; dirty works like lesson 5.04's practice (a new level is not dirty). Rectangles and fills clip to the map. A flood fill on a tile that already has the new kind does nothing. Use an explicit stack or queue for the fill, not recursion. The file format ( save ): lines separated by \n : xenon-level 1 size <width <height tiles <height lines of exactly width characters load accepts exactly this (lines may end with \r\n ), with version 1 only, a width and height from 1 to 1000, and the right number of rows of the right length; otherwise it returns false and leaves out unchanged. A loaded level has empty undo history and is not dirty.
