title: Common Errors
body: Message or symptom Usual cause Fix Lesson --- --- --- --- Assertion "Missing End()" or "Mismatched Begin/End calls" End was skipped when Begin returned false, or an early return left a scope open Always call End after Begin ; pair every Push and Pop 1.04 Assertion about the ID stack ("PushID/PopID mismatch") A PushID without a PopID on some path Pop on every path; keep pushes and pops in one function 1.05 Clicking one button triggers another, or only the first of several works Several widgets with the same label in the same scope share an ID suffix or PushID(i) around each row 1.05 A text box loses its contents or focus every frame Its label changes each frame, so its ID changes Put the changing part before 1.05 Nothing appears, but there is no error Render or the backend draw call is missing, or the window is off screen Check the frame order; delete imgui.ini 1.03 An assertion about WithinFrameScope A widget called outside NewFrame ... Render Submit UI only during a frame 1.03 The game moves when you drag a slider or type in a box Game input ignores WantCaptureMouse and WantCaptureKeyboard Check them before handling input 2.05 TreePop assertion, or children drawn at the wrong indent TreePop called when TreeNode returned false, or not at all Call TreePop only inside if (TreeNode(...)) 3.04 A long list makes the frame slow Every row is submitted even when not visible ImGuiListClipper 3.02 A popup never opens OpenPopup and BeginPopup used different IDs, often in different ID scopes Call both in the same scope with the same string 4.02 A modal opens and closes at once, or cannot be closed OpenPopup is called every frame Call it once, on the event 4.02 Drag and drop does nothing The payload type strings differ, or the payload is the wrong size One shared constant for the type; check DataSize 4.03 Docking does not work ImGuiConfigFlags_DockingEnable not set, or the master branch is used instead of the docking branch Use the docking branch; set the flag 4.04 Text is blurry or shows "?" boxes Font loaded at the wrong size, or glyph ranges missing for the characters Load at the display size; add the ranges you need 4.05 A font change has no effect The font was added after the atlas was built Add fonts before the first frame, or rebuild the atlas 4.05 Windows reset their layout every start IniFilename is nullptr , or the program runs from another folder Give the ini file a full path 4.06 A drag creates hundreds of undo steps One step is recorded per frame of the drag Record on IsItemDeactivatedAfterEdit 5.04 Stack overflow in a flood fill Recursive fill on a large region Explicit stack or queue 6.01

title: Glossary
body: Every term from the course, in alphabetical order. The lesson that introduces each one is in brackets. Term Meaning --- --- Backend The code that connects ImGui to a platform (input, window, clock: imgui_impl_win32 ) and a renderer (drawing: imgui_impl_dx11 ). ImGui itself does neither. (1.02) Begin / End The pair that opens and closes a window. End must always be called, even when Begin returns false. (1.04) BeginChild A scrolling region inside a window with its own size, border and scroll position. (3.02) Clipper ImGuiListClipper : tells you which rows of a long list are visible so you submit only those. (3.02) Collapsing header A full-width header that shows or hides the widgets after it, without indenting them. (3.05) Command list A list of draw commands (vertices, indices, texture, clip rectangle) that the renderer backend turns into GPU draw calls. (1.03) Context ImGuiContext : all of ImGui's state. Created with CreateContext , destroyed with DestroyContext . (1.02) Dear ImGui A C++ immediate-mode GUI library for tools and debug UI, by Omar Cornut. (1.01) Docking The docking-branch feature that lets windows be docked into each other as tabs and splits, arranged by a dock space. (4.04) Dock space An area that windows can be docked into; DockSpaceOverViewport makes the whole main window one. (4.04) DockBuilder The internal API for building a default dock layout in code on first run. (4.04) Drag and drop source / target A widget that starts a drag with a typed payload, and a widget that accepts payloads of a matching type. (4.03) Draw data ImDrawData : everything ImGui wants drawn this frame, produced by Render . (1.03) Draw list ImDrawList : the list of shapes a window draws, which you can add lines, rectangles, circles and text to yourself. (1.03, 5.01) Font atlas One texture holding every glyph of every loaded font at its size. (4.05) Frame One pass of NewFrame , your UI code, Render and drawing the draw data. ImGui rebuilds the UI every frame. (1.03) Hot, active, focused The widget under the mouse, the widget being pressed or dragged, and the widget receiving keyboard input. (1.01) ID The number ImGui uses to tell widgets apart, hashed from the label and the ID stack. (1.05) ID stack PushID / PopID : scopes that make the same label unique in different places, such as rows of a list. (1.05) Immediate mode A GUI style where the program describes the UI from its own data every frame, and the library keeps almost no widget objects. (1.01) ini file imgui.ini : where ImGui saves window positions, sizes, docking and table settings, and where your own settings handlers can save more. (4.06) and In a label, hides what follows but keeps it in the ID; makes only what follows the ID, so the visible text can change. (1.05) Item The last widget submitted; IsItemHovered , IsItemActive , IsItemDeactivatedAfterEdit and friends ask about it. (1.04) Metrics window ShowMetricsWindow : ImGui's own debug view of windows, draw lists and IDs. (1.06) Modal A popup that blocks the rest of the UI until it is closed, such as a confirmation dialog. (4.02) Multiple viewports The feature that lets ImGui windows leave the main window and become real OS windows. (4.04) Payload The typed data carried by a drag and drop. (4.03) Popup A window opened with OpenPopup and shown with BeginPopup , closing when you click elsewhere. (4.02) Retained mode A GUI style where the library keeps a tree of widget objects that the program creates, changes and destroys. (1.01) Selectable A widget that can be highlighted as selected, used for lists and menus. (2.03) Self time In a profiler, a zone's total time minus the time spent in its child zones. (6.02) Settings handler ImGuiSettingsHandler : your own section in the ini file, read and written by callbacks. (4.06) Style ImGuiStyle : sizes, roundings and colours for every widget. (4.05) Table BeginTable : columns with headers, resizing, reordering, sorting and scrolling. (3.03) Text filter ImGuiTextFilter : a box where the user types comma-separated terms, with - for exclusions, to filter lines. (5.02) Tree node A widget that expands to show indented children; TreePop closes its scope. (3.04) Undo step One user action recorded as the change needed to undo and redo it; a whole drag is one step. (5.04) WantCaptureMouse / WantCaptureKeyboard Flags ImGui sets when it is using the mouse or keyboard, so the game should ignore them. (2.05) Zone In a profiler, a named span of time marked by a begin and an end event. (6.02)

title: 1.01  What a Process Is
body: A process is a running program's container - a private address space, a table of handles, a security token, one or more threads and an exit code. Process IDs and handles, why processes cannot see each other's memory, and why that isolation is the reason inter-process communication needs special tools. A container for a running program When you start a program, Windows creates a process : not the code itself, but everything the running code needs and owns. Part What it is --- --- Address space a private range of virtual addresses (Pointers and Memory course, lesson 6.04) holding the program, its DLLs, heaps and stacks Threads the things that actually execute; a process has at least one Handle table the kernel objects it has opened: files, pipes, events, other processes Access token who it runs as, and what it is allowed to do Environment and command line text handed over at start-up Exit code a number left behind when it ends Every process has a process ID (PID), a number unique among running processes. PIDs are reused after a process is gone, so a PID alone is not a safe long-term reference to "that process". Isolation Each process has its own address space. The address 0x2C409610 in one process and the same number in another refer to entirely different memory, or to nothing. A bug in one program cannot overwrite another program's variables, and a crash ends only the process that crashed. That isolation is the whole reason this course exists. Two threads in one process share memory and can talk by just writing variables (with care). Two processes cannot: everything they exchange has to go through something the operating system provides and both can reach: - a pipe carrying bytes from one to the other; - a file mapping that the kernel maps into both address spaces; - a socket , even when both ends are on the same machine; - named kernel objects (events, mutexes, semaphores) for signalling; - window messages , for programs with windows; - plain files , and higher layers built on the above (COM, RPC). Handles to processes To do anything with another process, you need a handle to it, with the access you ask for: cpp-norun HANDLE process{ OpenProcess(SYNCHRONIZE PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION, FALSE, pid) }; if (process) { WaitForSingleObject(process, INFINITE); // wait until it ends DWORD code{}; GetExitCodeProcess(process, &code); CloseHandle(process); } A process handle is better than a PID for keeping track of a process: while you hold the handle, the process object stays valid (even after the process ends, so you can read its exit code), and its PID cannot be reused for another process. When you start a child yourself, CreateProcessW gives you its handle directly. Threads, processes and jobs - A thread runs code inside a process. Several threads share the process's memory and handles. - A process owns resources and isolates them from other processes. - A job object groups processes so they can be managed together: limits on memory or CPU, and ending them all at once (lesson 1.03). When should work be split across processes instead of threads? When isolation is worth the cost of communication: a crash in a plugin should not take down the editor; an untrusted file parser should run with fewer rights; a long build should continue even if the window closes. Browsers run each site in its own process for exactly these reasons. Lifetime A process ends when its last thread ends, when it calls ExitProcess , or when another process ends it with TerminateProcess . Windows then closes every handle it had open, which matters for IPC: a pipe whose other end belonged to a process that died is closed, and a mutex it owned is released as abandoned (lesson 4.03). Good IPC code always plans for the other side disappearing without warning. Check yourself quiz ? Why can two processes not share data by writing to the same address? - Windows locks each address so only one process can write to it at a time + Each has its own private address space; the same address refers to different memory in each - The address is only valid while both processes run on the same thread - Writes to another process's memory are queued until it calls ReadProcessMemory Every process has its own virtual address space, so 0x2C409610 in one process and in another are unrelated memory (or nothing). That isolation is why IPC needs kernel-provided channels. ? Why is holding a process handle better than remembering its PID? - A handle is shorter and faster to compare than a PID - A PID cannot be passed to WaitForSingleObject , but it stays unique for ever - A handle lets you read the other process's memory directly + A PID can be reused once the process ends; a held handle cannot be PIDs are recycled after a process is gone. While you hold a handle, the process object stays valid (you can still read its exit code) and its PID cannot be given to another process. ? Which of these is a list of ways processes on one machine can exchange data or signals? + Pipes, file mappings, sockets and named events - Pipes, global variables, sockets and named events - File mappings, thread-local storage, window messages and files - Sockets, shared static variables, mutexes and pipes Anything that crosses processes must be provided by the OS: pipes, file mappings, sockets, named kernel objects, window messages and files. Global, static and thread-local variables live inside one address space. ? What happens to a pipe when the process at its other end crashes? - The pipe stays open and buffers data until a new process takes over that end - Windows suspends the surviving process until the pipe is reconnected + Windows closes its handles, so the pipe breaks and I/O on it fails - Nothing until the surviving process calls CloseHandle on its own end When a process ends, Windows closes every handle it held. The pipe's other end is then gone, so reads and writes on the surviving end fail; good IPC code plans for that.

title: Handles outlive PIDs
body: PIDs are reused, handles are not (lesson 1.01). Model that difference: a tracker that hands out tickets , like handles, each referring to one particular run of a process even after its PID has been given to another. cpp class Tracker { public: void started(std::uint32_t pid, const std::string& name); void exited(std::uint32_t pid, std::uint32_t code); int open(std::uint32_t pid); bool isRunning(int ticket) const; std::optional<std::string nameOf(int ticket) const; std::optional<std::uint32_t exitCodeOf(int ticket) const; }; - started records that a process with this PID and name is now running. (The PID is never in use twice at the same time.) - exited records that the currently running process with that PID ended with code . An unknown PID is ignored. - open returns a new ticket (0, 1, 2, ...) for the process currently running with that PID, or -1 if none is. - A ticket keeps referring to the same process: nameOf and exitCodeOf answer for it even after it exits and its PID is reused. exitCodeOf is std::nullopt while it runs; any unknown ticket gives std::nullopt and isRunning false.

title: 1.02  Starting Processes Well
body: Everything that goes into a new process besides its command line - the environment block and how to build one, the working directory, which handles it inherits and how to limit them to exactly the ones you mean, and the creation flags that matter. More than a command line The Win32 API course (lesson 5.03) covered CreateProcessW , quoting arguments and waiting for the result. A child process inherits much more than its arguments from the call that creates it, and getting the rest right is what makes launching helpers reliable: cpp-norun BOOL CreateProcessW( LPCWSTR application, // nullptr: take it from the command line LPWSTR commandLine, // writable buffer LPSECURITY_ATTRIBUTES, LPSECURITY_ATTRIBUTES, BOOL inheritHandles, // may the child inherit handles at all? DWORD flags, // CREATE_NO_WINDOW, CREATE_UNICODE_ENVIRONMENT, ... LPVOID environment, // nullptr: a copy of ours LPCWSTR currentDirectory, // nullptr: ours LPSTARTUPINFOW startup, // standard handles, window settings, attributes LPPROCESS_INFORMATION info); // the handles and IDs of the new process and its thread The environment block Every process has a set of environment variables ( PATH , TEMP , your own settings). By default a child gets a copy of the parent's. To give it a different set, pass an environment block : one buffer of NAME=value strings, each ending with a zero, the whole block ending with an extra zero. text A=1\0Path=C:\Tools;C:\Windows\System32\0TEMP=C:\Temp\0\0 Rules that matter: - With CREATE_UNICODE_ENVIRONMENT the block is UTF-16 ( wchar_t ); use it always. - Windows expects the variables sorted by name, ignoring case . Names are case-insensitive: Path and PATH are the same variable, and a block must not contain both. - A block replaces the whole environment. Start from the parent's ( GetEnvironmentStringsW ), change what you need, and keep SystemRoot , Path and TEMP , which many programs need to work at all. Passing settings to a helper through environment variables is common and simple; but they are visible to anything that can inspect the process, so never put secrets in them. The working directory Relative paths in the child, and the order it searches for some files, depend on its current directory . By default it inherits yours, which is often not what you want (your own current directory can be anything the user chose). Pass the directory explicitly, usually the folder of the tool or of the project it works on. Handle inheritance A kernel object handle can be marked inheritable . If inheritHandles is TRUE , the child receives a copy of every inheritable handle the parent has, at the same values. That is how a child gets the ends of pipes for its standard streams (lesson 1.04). The danger is "every". In a multi-threaded program, another thread may create an inheritable handle at the same moment, and it leaks into your child; the child then keeps a pipe or file open that you expected to close, and the other end never sees end-of-file. The fix is to name the exact handles to inherit with an attribute list : cpp-norun SIZE_T size{}; InitializeProcThreadAttributeList(nullptr, 1, 0, &size); std::vector<std::byte storage(size); auto list{ reinterpret_cast<LPPROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_LIST (storage.data()) }; InitializeProcThreadAttributeList(list, 1, 0, &size); HANDLE inherit { childStdin, childStdout }; UpdateProcThreadAttribute(list, 0, PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_HANDLE_LIST, inherit, sizeof(inherit), nullptr, nullptr); STARTUPINFOEXW si{ { sizeof(si) } }; si.lpAttributeList = list; CreateProcessW(nullptr, cmd.data(), nullptr, nullptr, TRUE, EXTENDED_STARTUPINFO_PRESENT CREATE_UNICODE_ENVIRONMENT, env.data(), directory.c_str(), &si.StartupInfo, &pi); DeleteProcThreadAttributeList(list); Now only those two handles are passed, whatever else is inheritable. Creation flags Flag Effect --- --- CREATE_NO_WINDOW a console program runs without opening a console window CREATE_NEW_CONSOLE give it its own console window CREATE_SUSPENDED create it with its main thread paused, for example to add it to a job before it runs (lesson 1.03) CREATE_UNICODE_ENVIRONMENT the environment block is UTF-16 EXTENDED_STARTUPINFO_PRESENT startup is a STARTUPINFOEXW with an attribute list BELOW_NORMAL_PRIORITY_CLASS run it at lower priority, good for background work Check yourself quiz ? How does an environment block end? - With a single zero after the last NAME=value string, which is also that string's terminator + Each NAME=value string ends with a zero, and the whole block ends with one more zero - With a count of variables written at the start of the block - With the text END= followed by a zero Each string is zero-terminated and an extra zero marks the end of the block, so the block finishes with two zeros in a row. ? In what order must variables appear in an environment block? - In the order the parent's environment listed them - Sorted by name, with uppercase names before lowercase ones - Any order, as long as Path comes first + Sorted by name, ignoring case Windows expects the block sorted by name, case-insensitively. Names themselves are case-insensitive, so Path and PATH are the same variable and must not both appear. ? What goes wrong when inheritHandles is TRUE without a handle list in a multi-threaded program? - The child inherits no handles at all, because the list is required + Every inheritable handle leaks in, even ones other threads just made - The child gets only its standard handles, so its other pipes stay closed - CreateProcessW fails with an invalid-parameter error With inheritance on, every inheritable handle is copied into the child. A handle another thread creates at that moment leaks in too, so a pipe may never see end-of-file. PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_HANDLE_LIST limits it to the handles you name. ? Why start a child with CREATE_SUSPENDED ? - So that it starts at a lower priority than its parent - So that it does not open a console window - So that it waits for input on its standard input before starting + To do something before it runs any code, such as adding it to a job object The main thread is created paused; you can assign the process to a job (or anything else) and then call ResumeThread . Lower priority and no window are other flags ( BELOW_NORMAL_PRIORITY_CLASS , CREATE_NO_WINDOW ).

title: Environment blocks
body: Build and edit the environment block a child process receives (lesson 1.02). Here it is a std::string of NAME=value entries, each followed by a zero byte, with one more zero at the end (the real block is UTF-16, with exactly the same layout). cpp using Variables = std::vector<std::pair<std::string, std::string ; std::string buildBlock(const Variables& vars); Variables parseBlock(const std::string& block); std::string withVariable(const std::string& block, const std::string& name, const std::string& value); std::string withoutVariable(const std::string& block, const std::string& name); - buildBlock sorts the variables by name ignoring case (compare the names with every letter in upper case), and if two names are the same ignoring case, keeps only the last one given. An empty list gives a block of two zeros. - parseBlock reads the entries back in order, splitting each at its first = after the first character (Windows keeps hidden entries like =C:=C:\Work , whose names start with = ). - withVariable returns a new block with the variable set (replacing any existing one with the same name ignoring case, and keeping the spelling of the new name); withoutVariable removes it.

title: 1.03  Waiting, Exit Codes and Jobs
body: Knowing how a child process ended - waiting with timeouts, exit code conventions and the NTSTATUS codes a crash leaves behind - and job objects that group processes, end them all at once and limit what they can use. Waiting A process handle becomes signalled when the process ends, so every wait function works on it: cpp-norun switch (WaitForSingleObject(process, 30'000)) // up to 30 seconds { case WAIT_OBJECT_0: / it ended / break; case WAIT_TIMEOUT: / still running: decide whether to keep waiting or end it / break; case WAIT_FAILED: / bad handle: GetLastError() / break; } Always choose a timeout. A child that hangs (waiting for input it will never get, stuck on a dialog box, deadlocked) would otherwise freeze the parent for ever. WaitForMultipleObjects waits for any of several processes (up to 64 handles) at once. Exit codes GetExitCodeProcess gives the code a process ended with. While it is still running it returns STILL_ACTIVE (259), which is one reason not to use 259 as a real exit code, and why you should check the process has really ended before trusting the value. Conventions: Code Usually means --- --- 0 success 1, 2, ... small numbers the program's own errors (documented by each tool: robocopy uses 0 to 7 for success!) 0xC0000005 access violation: it crashed 0xC0000409 stack buffer overrun or fail-fast: the /GS check or abort style termination 0xC00000FD stack overflow 0xC0000374 heap corruption 0xC000013A ended with Ctrl+C 0x40010004 ended by a debugger 0xE06D7363 an unhandled C++ exception ( msc in its last three bytes) Codes starting with 0xC are NTSTATUS error values: the process did not choose to exit, Windows ended it after an unhandled exception. A supervisor that restarts helpers (milestone 6) needs to tell "the job failed" (a small code) from "the program crashed" (an NTSTATUS), and log them differently. Ending a process TerminateProcess(process, code) ends a process immediately: no destructors, no flushing of files, no clean-up of any kind. It is a last resort. Prefer asking the process to stop through your own channel (a "quit" message on a pipe, an event it watches), waiting a few seconds, and only then terminating. Job objects A job object groups processes. Its most useful features: Kill on close. End every process in the job when the last handle to the job closes, including when your process crashes: cpp-norun HANDLE job{ CreateJobObjectW(nullptr, nullptr) }; JOBOBJECT_EXTENDED_LIMIT_INFORMATION info{}; info.BasicLimitInformation.LimitFlags = JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE; SetInformationJobObject(job, JobObjectExtendedLimitInformation, &info, sizeof(info)); // start each helper with CREATE_SUSPENDED, then: AssignProcessToJobObject(job, pi.hProcess); ResumeThread(pi.hThread); Without this, helper processes outlive a crashed parent and pile up in Task Manager. Children that the helpers start themselves join the job automatically. Limits. A job can cap memory per process or for the whole job, CPU time, CPU rate, and the number of active processes. A build tool can use them to stop one runaway compiler from taking the whole machine. Accounting. QueryInformationJobObject reports the total CPU time, I/O and peak memory of everything in the job, which is a simple way to measure what a group of processes really cost. Check yourself quiz ? Why should a wait for a child process always have a timeout? + A hung child would otherwise freeze the parent indefinitely - Without a timeout, WaitForSingleObject returns immediately - The child's exit code is only kept for the length of the timeout - INFINITE waits are not allowed on process handles A child stuck on a dialog, on input it never gets, or in a deadlock never ends, so an INFINITE wait would block the parent for ever. A timeout lets the parent decide to keep waiting or end it. ? A helper's exit code is 0xC0000005 . What happened? - It returned 5 from main to report its own error - It was ended with Ctrl+C + It crashed with an access violation, an NTSTATUS error - It is still running, and this is the value meaning "still active" 0xC... codes are NTSTATUS errors: the process did not choose to exit. 0xC0000005 is an access violation; Ctrl+C is 0xC000013A , and "still running" is STILL_ACTIVE (259). ? Why is TerminateProcess a last resort? - It only works on processes in a job object - It waits for the process's destructors, which can take a long time - It cannot set the process's exit code + It ends the process at once, with no clean-up of any kind TerminateProcess stops the process at once, so nothing gets a chance to clean up. Ask it to stop through your own channel first, wait a little, and terminate only if it does not. ? What does JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE give you? - Each process in the job is ended as soon as it uses too much memory + Every process in the job is ended when the last job handle closes, even if the parent crashes - The job object is deleted when its last process exits - A child ends automatically when its own parent exits normally, but not when it crashes When the last handle to the job closes (including because the owning process crashed and Windows closed its handles), every process in the job is ended, so helpers do not outlive their parent.

title: Reading exit codes
body: Turn a child process's exit code into something a person or a supervisor can act on (lesson 1.03): cpp bool crashed(std::uint32_t code); std::string describeExit(std::uint32_t code); - crashed is true for NTSTATUS error codes: those whose top two bits are both set ( 0xC0000000 to 0xFFFFFFFF ). - describeExit returns: Code Text --- --- 0 success 259 still running 0xC0000005 crashed: access violation 0xC00000FD crashed: stack overflow 0xC0000409 crashed: stack buffer overrun or fail-fast 0xC0000374 crashed: heap corruption 0xC000013A stopped with Ctrl+C any other crash code crashed: 0xC0001234 (8 uppercase hex digits) 0xE06D7363 unhandled C++ exception anything else failed with code N (in decimal)

title: 1.04  Talking Through Standard Streams
body:
The simplest channel between a parent and a child - its standard input, output and error redirected to pipes - and the deadlocks waiting for anyone who reads them carelessly, plus line-based protocols over stdio as used by language servers and many tools. Three streams for free Every process has three standard handles: input , output and error . A console program reads from the first and writes to the others. When you start a program, you can connect any of them to a pipe you hold the other end of, and you have a two-way channel with no extra setup on the child's side: it just uses std::cin and std::cout . That is why so many tools talk this way: compilers report errors on stderr, git writes results on stdout, and language servers (the processes behind code completion in editors) exchange JSON messages over stdin and stdout. Wiring it up cpp-norun SECURITY_ATTRIBUTES inheritable{ sizeof(inheritable), nullptr, TRUE }; HANDLE inRead, inWrite, outRead, outWrite; CreatePipe(&inRead, &inWrite, &inheritable, 0); // parent writes inWrite - child reads inRead CreatePipe(&outRead, &outWrite, &inheritable, 0); // child writes outWrite - parent reads outRead SetHandleInformation(inWrite, HANDLE_FLAG_INHERIT, 0); // the parent's ends must NOT be inherited SetHandleInformation(outRead, HANDLE_FLAG_INHERIT, 0); STARTUPINFOW si{ sizeof(si) }; si.dwFlags = STARTF_USESTDHANDLES; si.hStdInput = inRead; si.hStdOutput = outWrite; si.hStdError = outWrite; // or a third pipe, to keep errors apart CreateProcessW(/ ... / TRUE / inherit /, CREATE_NO_WINDOW, / ... / &si, &pi); CloseHandle(inRead); // the child has its own copies now CloseHandle(outWrite); // essential: otherwise reading outRead never ends Closing the parent's copies of the child's ends is the step people forget. A pipe reports end-of-file to the reader only when every write handle is closed; if the parent still holds outWrite , reading outRead waits for ever after the child exits. Likewise, when the parent has nothing more to send, it closes inWrite , and the child's next read sees end-of-file. Many tools read until end of input before they start working. The deadlock Pipes have a fixed buffer, typically a few kilobytes. A writer whose pipe is full blocks until the reader takes something out. That creates a classic deadlock: 1. The parent writes a large input to the child's stdin, all of it, before reading anything. 2. The child reads a little, then writes a lot of output, filling its stdout pipe. 3. The child blocks writing; the parent blocks writing; neither ever reads. The same happens with stdout and stderr on two pipes: the parent reads stdout to the end while the child blocks writing to a full stderr. The rule: read every output pipe continuously while also writing . In practice, read each output pipe on its own thread (or use overlapped I/O, lesson 2.05), collecting what arrives, and write input on another. Lines and encodings Output arrives in arbitrary chunks, not lines: one read can return half a line, or three and a half. To process line by line, keep a buffer per stream, append each chunk, and take out complete lines (ending in 
 , with a  before it on Windows) as they appear; whatever is left waits for the next chunk. The final partial line is complete only when the stream reaches end-of-file. Console programs write in the console's code page or in UTF-8; when you capture them you receive raw bytes and must decode them yourself. Many tools let you choose ( git -c core.quotepath=off , Python's PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8 ); for your own helpers, always write UTF-8. Protocols over stdio Stdio becomes a real protocol once both sides agree on message boundaries. Two common choices: - One message per line (JSON Lines, for example): simple, as long as messages never contain a raw newline. - Headers then a body of known length , as the Language Server Protocol does: text Content-Length: 52
 
 {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize",...} The reader parses headers up to the blank line, then reads exactly Content-Length bytes. Milestone 2 builds framing like this properly. !warning A child that writes anything else to stdout (a debug printf , a library's warning) corrupts a stdout protocol. Send logs to stderr, or to a file. Check yourself quiz ? Why must the parent close its copy of the child's stdout write handle after starting it? - The child cannot write to stdout while the parent holds a copy + Otherwise a write handle stays open and the read never sees EOF - Pipes allow only one open handle per end at a time - It frees the pipe's buffer so the child can write more A pipe's reader sees end-of-file only when all write handles are closed. If the parent still holds outWrite , reading outRead waits for ever after the child exits. ? What is the stdout and stderr deadlock? - The parent and child both write to stderr at once, and their lines mix together - The child exits before the parent has read stderr, so that output is lost - Both pipes share one buffer, so a full stdout also blocks stderr + The parent waits on stdout while the child blocks on a full stderr Each pipe has a fixed buffer. If the parent reads only stdout until end-of-file, a child that fills stderr blocks and never closes stdout. Read every output pipe continuously, for example one thread per pipe. ? Why can a single read return half a line? + Pipes carry bytes in arbitrary chunks; line boundaries are not preserved - The pipe's buffer is always exactly half a line long - ReadFile stops at the first  and leaves the 
 for the next read - The child's std::cout flushes in the middle of each line A pipe is a byte stream: one read can return half a line or several. Keep a buffer per stream and take out complete lines as they arrive. ? How does the Language Server Protocol mark where a message ends? - Each message ends with a blank line - Each JSON message is on its own line, ending in 
 + A Content-Length header gives the size of the body after it - The reader parses the JSON until its closing brace LSP sends headers, a blank line, then a body of the length the Content-Length header gave. The reader parses headers up to the blank line, then reads exactly that many bytes.

title: Lines from a stream
body:
Output from a child arrives in arbitrary chunks (lesson 1.04). Collect it into lines, one collector per stream: cpp class LineCollector { public: void add(std::string_view chunk); void finish(); std::vector<std::string take(); std::size_t pending() const; }; - add appends a chunk. Every 
 ends a line; a  directly before it is dropped (Windows line endings), and so is a lone  at the very end of a line. Lines do not include their 
 . - finish is called at end-of-file: whatever is left becomes a last line, unless nothing is left. - take returns the complete lines collected so far, in order, and forgets them. - pending is the number of bytes waiting for the end of their line. A 
 split across two chunks (  at the end of one, 
 at the start of the next) must still give one line ending, not a stray  .

title: 1.05  Choosing an IPC Method
body: A map of the ways processes communicate on Windows - pipes, shared memory, sockets, kernel objects, window messages, files, COM and RPC - compared on speed, simplicity, who can connect and what happens when one side dies, with a guide to choosing. Many tools, different jobs Every IPC method moves data or signals between address spaces through the kernel, but they differ a great deal in what they are good at. The rest of the course covers each in depth; this lesson is the map. Method Moves Strengths Weaknesses --- --- --- --- Anonymous pipe a byte stream, one way trivial for parent and child; stdio only between related processes Named pipe a byte or message stream, two way any two processes on the machine (or network); per-client connections; access control Windows-specific API Shared memory (file mapping) nothing: both see the same bytes fastest by far, no copying you build every structure and all synchronisation yourself Socket (loopback TCP, AF_UNIX) a byte stream same code works across a network; every language has it some overhead; open ports need care Events, mutexes, semaphores signals, not data waiting without spinning; combine with shared memory carry no data Window messages ( WM_COPYDATA ) small messages easy between GUI programs needs windows and a message loop; blocked between privilege levels Files anything simple, survives restarts slow; coordinating readers and writers is hard COM, RPC method calls rich, typed interfaces heavy machinery to learn and debug Questions that decide Are the processes related? A parent and the child it starts can share anonymous pipes or inherited handles. Unrelated programs need a name both know: a named pipe, a named mapping, a port number. How much data, how often? A few messages a second: any method. Megabytes per frame (a video stream, a game's state for an external tool): shared memory , with a small signal to say "new data". Copying through a pipe costs time per byte; shared memory costs nothing per byte once mapped. Request and response, or a stream? Pipes and sockets fit conversations naturally. Shared memory suits "latest state" and ring buffers of records. What if one side dies? Pipes and sockets tell you : the other end is closed and reads fail. Shared memory does not: a dead writer leaves the last data in place and a mutex abandoned (lesson 4.03). Anything built on shared memory needs its own liveness checks, such as watching the other process's handle. Across machines later? If there is any chance, use sockets from the start; the protocol is then the same locally and remotely. Who may connect? Named pipes and kernel objects carry Windows security descriptors (lesson 5.05); TCP ports on localhost are open to every local process, so the protocol must check who is talking. Common combinations - Editor and language server : stdio pipes with length-framed JSON messages. - Game and external debug tool : shared memory holding the game's state, plus an event or a seqlock so the tool reads consistent snapshots; a named pipe for commands back to the game. - Single-instance app : a named mutex to detect the running copy, a named pipe or WM_COPYDATA to hand it the new command line. - Browser : one process per site, communicating with the main process over named pipes with a custom message system, shared memory for rendered frames. - Background service and its settings app : a named pipe with an access control list allowing only the user's session. The shape of every IPC design Whatever the method, a robust design has the same parts, which the following milestones build one by one: 1. Discovery : how the two sides find each other (a name, an inherited handle, a port). 2. Framing : where each message begins and ends. 3. Format : how values are encoded so both sides agree. 4. Flow : who speaks when; requests, responses, events. 5. Failure : timeouts, the other side vanishing, bad input. 6. Security : who is allowed to connect, and never trusting what arrives. Check yourself quiz ? Which method has no per-byte cost once set up, and what does it lack? - A named pipe; it lacks access control - A socket; it lacks a way to detect the other side dying + Shared memory; it lacks framing and synchronisation - Window messages; they lack a size limit Once a file mapping is mapped into both processes, nothing is copied per byte. But you build every structure and all synchronisation yourself, usually with events or a seqlock beside it. ? Which methods tell you automatically when the other side has died? - Shared memory and named events - Window messages and files - Mutexes and semaphores only + Pipes and sockets Pipes and sockets close when the other process ends, so the next read or write fails. Shared memory just keeps the last data, so it needs its own liveness checks. ? Two unrelated programs need to talk. What do they need that a parent and child do not? + A name both know: a pipe name, a mapping name or a port number - The same process ID - A handle inherited from a common parent - To be started by the same user with CREATE_NEW_CONSOLE A parent and its child can share anonymous pipes or inherited handles. Unrelated processes have no such handle to share, so they find each other through a name such as a named pipe, a named mapping or a port. ? Why might you choose sockets even when both processes are on one machine? - Loopback sockets are the fastest method, faster than shared memory - Sockets are the only method that carries Windows security descriptors + The same code then works across a network, in any language - Sockets need no framing, because each send arrives as one recv Sockets cost a little more than pipes or shared memory locally, but the same code works remotely and every language has them. They are byte streams, so they still need framing.

title: Running a compiler from an editor
match: Running a compiler from an editor
body: An editor runs the compiler as a child process and shows its errors in a list, the way Visual Studio, VS Code and the Xenon desktop app do. Build the part that turns the child's captured output and exit code into a result the editor can display. cpp enum class Stream { Out, Err }; struct Chunk { Stream stream; std::string bytes; }; struct Diagnostic { std::string file; int line; int column; // 0 when the message has none std::string severity; // "error", "warning" or "note" std::string code; // "C2065", or "" when the message has none std::string message; }; struct BuildResult { std::vector<std::string outLines, errLines; std::vector<Diagnostic diagnostics; int errors, warnings; bool succeeded; std::string status; }; std::optional<Diagnostic parseDiagnostic(const std::string& line); BuildResult collect(const std::vector<Chunk & chunks, std::uint32_t exitCode); parseDiagnostic understands the MSVC and Clang styles: text C:\src\game.cpp(12,5): error C2065: 'hp': undeclared identifier C:\src\game.cpp(40): warning C4244: 'argument': conversion from 'double' to 'int' src/main.cpp:7:3: error: expected ';' after expression src/main.cpp:9:1: note: to match this '{' The file ends where ( or : starts the line number (but a drive letter's colon, as in C:\ , is part of the file). The severity is error , warning or note ; an MSVC code (a letter followed by digits) may follow it; the message is what remains after : . Anything else is std::nullopt . collect splits each stream's chunks into lines separately (the rules of practice 1.04, with a final partial line at the end), parses every line of both streams in stream order (all of Out first, then Err ) as diagnostics, counts errors and warnings, and sets the result: - succeeded is true when the exit code is 0 and there are no errors; - status is succeeded , failed: N errors (always the plural), or for a crash code (top two bits set) compiler crashed: 0xC0000005 (8 uppercase hex digits). A failure with no error lines is failed: exit code N .

title: 2.01  Anonymous Pipes
body: The one-way byte channel behind standard streams - creating a pipe, its buffer and what happens when it fills, end-of-file and broken pipes, peeking without blocking, and passing pipe ends to a child. Two ends, one direction CreatePipe makes an anonymous pipe : a buffer in the kernel with a read end and a write end , each a handle. cpp-norun HANDLE readEnd{}, writeEnd{}; if (!CreatePipe(&readEnd, &writeEnd, nullptr, 64 1024)) // ask for a 64 KB buffer throw std::runtime_error("CreatePipe failed"); const char message { "hello" }; DWORD n{}; WriteFile(writeEnd, message, 5, &n, nullptr); // into the pipe char buffer 16 ; ReadFile(readEnd, buffer, sizeof(buffer), &n, nullptr); // n == 5 Bytes come out in the order they went in, with no boundaries: two writes of 5 bytes may be read as one read of 10, or as reads of 3 and 7. For two-way communication, use two pipes. "Anonymous" means it has no name: the only way for another process to use it is to be given a handle to one end, by inheritance when it starts (lesson 1.04) or by DuplicateHandle . That makes anonymous pipes ideal between a parent and its children, and useless between unrelated programs (lesson 2.02). When the buffer fills The buffer size passed to CreatePipe is a suggestion (0 means a default of a few kilobytes). When it is full, WriteFile blocks until the reader takes data out. When it is empty, ReadFile blocks until data arrives. Blocking is what makes simple pipe code correct, and also what causes the deadlocks of lesson 1.04 when both sides wait on each other. To find out without blocking whether data is waiting, use PeekNamedPipe (it works on anonymous pipes too): cpp-norun DWORD available{}; if (PeekNamedPipe(readEnd, nullptr, 0, nullptr, &available, nullptr) && available 0) / a ReadFile of up to available bytes returns at once /; End-of-file and broken pipes How each side learns that the other has finished: Situation What the other side sees --- --- every write handle is closed, buffer empty ReadFile fails with ERROR_BROKEN_PIPE (109): this is end-of-file for a pipe the read handle is closed WriteFile fails with ERROR_NO_DATA (232) ("the pipe is being closed") Note " every write handle": any copy of the write end left open anywhere, in the parent or inherited by another child, keeps the reader waiting. Close your copies of ends you do not use, immediately. Treat ERROR_BROKEN_PIPE on a read as a normal, expected end of the conversation, not as an error to report. Sizes and speed Each ReadFile and WriteFile is a call into the kernel and a copy of the data. Many tiny writes are slow; batch output into larger writes (a few kilobytes) where you can. Anonymous pipes on Windows are actually implemented as named pipes with generated names, so everything about performance in the next lessons applies to them too. Inside one process Pipes also work between threads of one process, which is occasionally handy for code that already speaks in handles. But between threads, a std::queue with a mutex and condition variable is simpler and faster: pipes earn their keep crossing process boundaries. Check yourself quiz ? Two writes of 4 bytes each go into a pipe. What might a single read of 16 bytes return? - Exactly the first 4 bytes, because each read returns one write - Always all 8 bytes, because the read buffer is big enough + Anything from a few bytes up to all 8 - Nothing until 16 bytes are available An anonymous pipe is a byte stream: the read returns whatever is there, up to the buffer size, with no record of how it was written. It does not wait to fill the buffer. ? How does a reader of an anonymous pipe recognise end-of-file? + ReadFile fails with ERROR_BROKEN_PIPE - ReadFile succeeds and returns a single zero byte - ReadFile fails with ERROR_NO_DATA as soon as the writer stops writing - PeekNamedPipe reports -1 bytes available For a pipe, end-of-file is ReadFile failing with ERROR_BROKEN_PIPE (109) after every write handle is closed. ERROR_NO_DATA is what a writer sees when the read end has been closed. ? Why can't an unrelated program connect to an anonymous pipe? - Anonymous pipes only work between threads of one process - Its buffer is private to the process that created it + It has no name; you can only be handed a handle to it - Only processes in the same job object may open it With no name there is nothing to open. Another process can use an end only if it is handed a handle, by inheritance at start-up or by DuplicateHandle . ? How do you check whether data is waiting without blocking? - Call ReadFile with a buffer size of 0 and check the result - Call WaitForSingleObject on the read end with a zero timeout - Check whether GetFileSize on the read end is non-zero + PeekNamedPipe reports the number of bytes available PeekNamedPipe works on anonymous pipes too and fills in the number of bytes waiting; a ReadFile of up to that many bytes then returns at once.

title: A pipe that behaves like the real one
match: A pipe that behaves like the real one
body: Model an anonymous pipe's rules (lesson 2.01) so they can be tested: a bounded buffer, end-of-file only when every writer is closed, and broken pipes. cpp enum class Status { Ok, WouldBlock, EndOfFile, BrokenPipe }; struct ReadResult { Status status; std::string data; }; class Pipe { public: explicit Pipe(std::size_t capacity); int openWriter(); void closeWriter(int writer); void closeReader(); Status write(int writer, std::string_view data, std::size_t& accepted); ReadResult read(std::size_t maxBytes); std::size_t available() const; }; - The pipe starts with one writer, number 0, and one reader. openWriter adds another writer handle (as duplicating or inheriting one does) and returns its number (1, 2, ...). - write with a closed or unknown writer returns BrokenPipe . If the reader is closed, it also returns BrokenPipe and accepts nothing. Otherwise it accepts as many bytes as fit in the free space, sets accepted , and returns Ok if it accepted everything, or WouldBlock if some did not fit (a real pipe would block until there was room). - read returns up to maxBytes bytes in order with Ok . With nothing buffered, it returns EndOfFile if every writer is closed, otherwise WouldBlock . - available is the number of buffered bytes, like PeekNamedPipe .

title: 2.02  Named Pipes
body: Pipes any program can find by name - creating a server instance, waiting for a client to connect, connecting as a client and handling a busy server, byte and message modes, disconnecting, and the rules for pipe names. A pipe with a name A named pipe is created by a server under a name such as \\.\pipe\xenon-indexer . Any program on the machine that knows the name can connect as a client . Each connection is a private, two-way channel between the server and that one client. The server cpp-norun HANDLE pipe{ CreateNamedPipeW( LR"(\\.\pipe\xenon-indexer)", PIPE_ACCESS_DUPLEX, // read and write PIPE_TYPE_MESSAGE PIPE_READMODE_MESSAGE PIPE_WAIT // message mode (below) PIPE_REJECT_REMOTE_CLIENTS, // this machine only PIPE_UNLIMITED_INSTANCES, // how many clients at once 64 1024, 64 1024, // out and in buffer sizes 0, // default client wait timeout nullptr) }; // security: lesson 5.05 if (pipe == INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE) / GetLastError() /; if (!ConnectNamedPipe(pipe, nullptr) && GetLastError() != ERROR_PIPE_CONNECTED) / failed /; // a client is connected: ReadFile / WriteFile on pipe CreateNamedPipeW creates one instance : a single connection slot. ConnectNamedPipe waits until a client connects to it. ( ERROR_PIPE_CONNECTED means a client connected between the create and the connect call, which is success.) To serve another client at the same time you create another instance (lesson 2.04). When the conversation ends, DisconnectNamedPipe drops the client and the same instance can ConnectNamedPipe again; or close it. The client cpp-norun HANDLE pipe{}; for (;;) { pipe = CreateFileW(LR"(\\.\pipe\xenon-indexer)", GENERIC_READ GENERIC_WRITE, 0, nullptr, OPEN_EXISTING, 0, nullptr); if (pipe != INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE) break; if (GetLastError() != ERROR_PIPE_BUSY) / no server: ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND (2) / return; if (!WaitNamedPipeW(LR"(\\.\pipe\xenon-indexer)", 2000)) return; // every instance busy: wait up to 2 s } DWORD mode{ PIPE_READMODE_MESSAGE }; SetNamedPipeHandleState(pipe, &mode, nullptr, nullptr); // read whole messages too The client opens the pipe like a file. Two errors matter: ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND means no server is running (start it, or report that), and ERROR_PIPE_BUSY means the server exists but every instance is in use, so wait with WaitNamedPipeW and try again. Another client can win the race after the wait, which is why it is a loop. Byte mode and message mode - Byte mode ( PIPE_TYPE_BYTE ): a stream like an anonymous pipe. Boundaries are lost. - Message mode ( PIPE_TYPE_MESSAGE with PIPE_READMODE_MESSAGE on the reading side): each WriteFile is one message, and each ReadFile returns at most one message. If your buffer is too small, the read returns what fits and fails with ERROR_MORE_DATA ; keep reading to get the rest of the same message. Message mode is convenient, but it is Windows-only and ties your protocol to pipes. Many programs use byte mode with their own framing (lesson 2.03), which then works unchanged over sockets too. Names - Local pipes are \\.\pipe\ followed by the name. Remote ones are \\server\pipe\name (blocked by PIPE_REJECT_REMOTE_CLIENTS , which you should set unless you need them). - The name part may contain any character except \ . The whole string can be up to 256 characters. Names are not case-sensitive . - Names are global to the machine: two programs, or two users, choosing \\.\pipe\server collide. Make names specific: product, purpose, and usually the user or session ( \\.\pipe\xenon-indexer-S-1-5-21-... or a per-user random suffix stored where the client can find it). - A name that another program created first can be squatted : your client might connect to an impostor. Lesson 5.05 covers how to guard against it. Check yourself quiz ? What does one call to CreateNamedPipeW create? - A pipe that any number of clients can share at once + One instance: a slot for one client at a time - A pipe and its first client connection - A read end and a write end, like CreatePipe Each call creates one instance, which serves one client at a time. To serve several clients at once, the server creates more instances of the same name. ? A client gets ERROR_PIPE_BUSY . What does it mean and what should it do? - No server is running; it should start one and try again - The pipe name is wrong; it should report an error - The server crashed; it should wait for the pipe to be recreated with Sleep + Every instance is in use; wait with WaitNamedPipeW and retry ERROR_PIPE_BUSY means every instance is taken. Wait with WaitNamedPipeW and loop, since another client can win the race. No server at all gives ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND . ? In message mode, what does ERROR_MORE_DATA on a read mean? - The pipe has several messages waiting; this read returned the first + The message did not fit; the rest of it comes with the next read - The read failed and the message was lost - The other side wrote more data than the pipe's buffer can hold In message mode each read returns at most one message. If it does not fit, you get what fits and ERROR_MORE_DATA ; read again to get the rest of that same message. ? Are pipe names case-sensitive? - Yes, \\.\pipe\Indexer and \\.\pipe\indexer are different pipes - Only the part after \\.\pipe\ is case-sensitive + No, names differing only in case refer to the same pipe - Yes, unless the pipe was created with PIPE_TYPE_MESSAGE Pipe names are not case-sensitive, and they are global to the machine, which is why names should be specific to the product, purpose and user.

title: Pipe names
body: Apply the naming rules of lesson 2.02: cpp bool validPipeName(const std::string& name); bool samePipe(const std::string& a, const std::string& b); std::string pipeNameFor(const std::string& product, const std::string& purpose, const std::string& user); - validPipeName : the name starts with \\.\pipe\ or \\SERVER\pipe\ (a server name of letters, digits, - , _ or . , not empty), the part after pipe\ is not empty and contains no \ , and the whole string is at most 256 characters. The word pipe may be in any case. - samePipe : two names refer to the same pipe if they are equal ignoring case. - pipeNameFor builds \\.\pipe\product-purpose-user in lower case, replacing every character that is not a letter or digit in each part with _ .

title: 2.03  Message Framing
body: Turning a byte stream into messages - length prefixes and why they beat delimiters for binary data, choosing the size and byte order of the length, refusing absurd lengths, reading exactly N bytes, and recovering when the other side sends nonsense. Streams have no boundaries A pipe in byte mode, a TCP socket and stdio all deliver a stream : bytes in order, with no record of how they were written. If one side writes "hello" and then "world", the other may read "hellow" and "orld". A program that exchanges messages must therefore mark where each one ends. That is framing . Three ways to frame Method How Good for Problem --- --- --- --- delimiter end each message with \n (or \0 ) text, line-based protocols the delimiter cannot appear inside a message without escaping fixed size every message is N bytes very simple records wastes space; inflexible length prefix each message starts with its length binary data, anything the reader must trust the length Length prefixes are the usual choice for program-to-program protocols. A message is sent as: text length: 4 bytes, little-endian payload: length bytes 05 00 00 00 68 65 6C 6C 6F - "hello" Choosing the length field - Size : 2 bytes allows 64 KB messages, 4 bytes up to 4 GB. 4 bytes is the common default. - Byte order : say which, and stick to it. Little-endian matches x86 and ARM; network protocols traditionally use big-endian. It matters only that both sides agree. - What it counts : the payload only, or the whole frame including the length? Document it; the bug where one side counts the header and the other does not is a classic. Reading a frame On a stream, a single read may return part of a header, a header and part of a payload, or several frames at once. The robust pattern keeps a buffer (lesson 6.03 of the Reverse Engineering course used it for a protocol): 1. Append whatever arrives to the buffer. 2. While the buffer holds at least a header: read the length; if the whole frame is there, take it out and handle it; otherwise wait for more. When you know how much you need and are happy to block, a "read exactly N bytes" helper is simpler: cpp-norun bool readExactly(HANDLE pipe, void buffer, DWORD size) { auto at{ static_cast<char (buffer) }; while (size 0) { DWORD got{}; if (!ReadFile(pipe, at, size, &got, nullptr) got == 0) return false; // closed or failed at += got; size -= got; } return true; } std::uint32_t length{}; if (!readExactly(pipe, &length, 4) length MAX_MESSAGE) return false; std::vector<char payload(length); if (!readExactly(pipe, payload.data(), length)) return false; Never trust a length The length comes from the other process, which may be buggy, old, or hostile. A length of 0xFFFFFFFF must not make you allocate 4 GB. Always: - enforce a maximum message size that suits your protocol (a few megabytes at most for most uses) and treat anything larger as a protocol error; - decide what a length of 0 means (an empty message, or an error); - on any framing error, close the connection . After a bad length you no longer know where the next frame starts, so there is nothing safe to continue with. Message mode instead Named pipes in message mode (lesson 2.02) do the framing for you: one write is one message. The reading side still has to handle messages larger than its buffer, by reading again after ERROR_MORE_DATA and joining the pieces. It also still needs a maximum size. And everything breaks the day the protocol moves to a socket, which is why many designs frame by hand even on pipes. Check yourself quiz ? Why is a newline delimiter a poor choice for binary messages? - Newlines take more bytes than a length prefix - Pipes drop newline bytes in byte mode + The newline byte can occur inside binary data and split a message - A reader cannot search for a byte value, only read fixed sizes Binary data can contain any byte, including \n , so a delimiter would end the message early. A length prefix says how many bytes follow, whatever they are. ? A frame header says the payload is 3 000 000 000 bytes. What should the reader do? - Allocate the buffer and read it, since a 4-byte length allows up to 4 GB - Read the first megabyte and skip the rest + Treat it as a protocol error, refuse to allocate, and close the connection - Ask the sender to resend the message in smaller pieces The length comes from another process and must not be trusted. Enforce a maximum suited to the protocol; anything above it is a protocol error that ends the connection. ? Why close the connection after a framing error rather than skip the bad message? + The reader no longer knows where the next frame starts - Skipping a message would make the sender's next write block - The bad message may still be in the pipe's buffer, which cannot be cleared - Closing is faster than reading the bad bytes The only way to find the next frame is the length of this one. Once that is wrong, every later header would be read from the wrong place, so there is nothing safe to continue with. ? What must a message-mode reader do when a read fails with ERROR_MORE_DATA ? - Discard the partial message and wait for the next one - Close the connection, because the message is malformed - Make the buffer bigger and ask the writer to send it again + Read again and join the pieces of the same message ERROR_MORE_DATA is not a failure of the message: the rest of it is still waiting. Read again and append until a read succeeds, still enforcing a maximum size.

title: Length-prefixed frames
body: Frame messages on a byte stream with a 4-byte little-endian length prefix (lesson 2.03): cpp std::vector<std::uint8_t frame(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & payload); class Deframer { public: explicit Deframer(std::uint32_t maxMessage); void feed(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & bytes); std::optional<std::vector<std::uint8_t next(); bool failed() const; }; struct MessageRead { std::vector<std::uint8_t bytes; bool moreData; }; std::vector<MessageRead readInMessageMode(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & message, std::size_t bufferSize); - frame returns the 4-byte length of the payload followed by the payload. - Deframer : feed appends received bytes; next returns the next complete payload, or std::nullopt if more bytes are needed. A length above maxMessage is a protocol error: the deframer becomes failed , discards everything, and from then on next always returns std::nullopt and feed ignores input. A length of 0 is an empty message. - readInMessageMode shows how a message-mode pipe read loop (lesson 2.02) sees one message: successive reads of at most bufferSize bytes, each marked moreData (the ERROR_MORE_DATA case) except the last. An empty message is one read of 0 bytes.

title: 2.04  Serving Many Clients
body: A pipe server that handles several clients at once - one instance per client, the accept loop with a thread per connection, keeping an instance always listening, identifying who connected, limits, and shutting the server down cleanly. One instance per client A named pipe instance is one connection. To serve several clients at the same time, the server creates several instances of the same name. The standard shape is an accept loop : cpp-norun for (;;) { HANDLE instance{ CreateNamedPipeW(name, PIPE_ACCESS_DUPLEX, PIPE_TYPE_BYTE PIPE_WAIT PIPE_REJECT_REMOTE_CLIENTS, PIPE_UNLIMITED_INSTANCES, 65536, 65536, 0, &security) }; if (instance == INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE) break; const BOOL connected{ ConnectNamedPipe(instance, nullptr) GetLastError() == ERROR_PIPE_CONNECTED }; if (!connected) { CloseHandle(instance); continue; } std::thread{ serveClient, instance }.detach(); // serveClient reads, replies, and closes the handle } Each loop iteration creates a fresh instance and waits on it, so as soon as one client is handed to its thread, the next client can connect. Between ConnectNamedPipe returning and the next CreateNamedPipeW , there is a moment with no free instance; a client arriving then gets ERROR_PIPE_BUSY , waits with WaitNamedPipeW (lesson 2.02) and gets in. Some servers keep two or more instances listening to make that window smaller. Thread per client A thread per client is the simplest correct design: each thread runs straightforward blocking code (read a request, handle it, write a reply) and closes its instance when the client disconnects ( ReadFile fails with ERROR_BROKEN_PIPE ). It is the right choice for tens of clients. For hundreds or thousands, the threads' stacks and scheduling cost too much, and overlapped I/O with a completion port (lesson 2.05) serves them all with a few threads. Shared state that client threads touch (a list of connected clients, a cache) needs a mutex, like any multi-threaded code. Limits nMaxInstances (the fourth argument) caps how many instances may exist. With a cap of 4, a fifth client keeps getting ERROR_PIPE_BUSY until one of the four disconnects. Set a cap that matches what your server can handle, and give clients a sensible wait and retry policy. Who connected? A server can ask about the process at the other end: cpp-norun ULONG clientPid{}; GetNamedPipeClientProcessId(instance, &clientPid); // the client's PID and, with care, run code in the client's security context with ImpersonateNamedPipeClient (lesson 5.05). The PID is useful for logging and for watching the client process; it is not proof of who the client is, since PIDs can be reused and any program may connect. Access control on the pipe itself is the real gate. Shutting down The accept loop above blocks in ConnectNamedPipe , so how does it ever stop? Common answers: - Set a "stopping" flag, then connect to your own pipe as a client: the blocked ConnectNamedPipe returns, the loop sees the flag and exits. - Use overlapped ConnectNamedPipe (lesson 2.05) and wait on both the connection event and a "stop" event. - CancelIoEx(instance, nullptr) from another thread cancels the pending connect. Then tell each client thread to finish: close their handles (their reads fail) or set a flag they check between messages, and wait for them to end before the program exits. Check yourself quiz ? How does a pipe server handle three clients at the same time? - It creates one instance and lets all three clients share it - It creates three pipes, each with a different name + It creates three instances of the same pipe name, one per client - It calls ConnectNamedPipe three times on the same instance Each instance carries one connection. The accept loop creates a fresh instance, waits for a client on it, hands it to a thread, and creates the next one. ? Why might a client get ERROR_PIPE_BUSY even though the server serves unlimited clients? - PIPE_UNLIMITED_INSTANCES actually allows only 4 instances + Briefly, between accepting one client and the next instance, none is free - The server's thread for the previous client is still starting - Unlimited servers reject clients from other user accounts with that error For a moment after ConnectNamedPipe returns, no instance is listening. A client arriving then waits with WaitNamedPipeW and gets in; some servers keep two instances listening to narrow the gap. ? When is a thread per client a poor choice? - With only two or three clients, where threads are overkill - When the clients send requests and expect replies - When the pipe is in byte mode rather than message mode + With hundreds or thousands of clients A thread per client is simple and right for tens of clients. For hundreds or thousands, their stacks and scheduling cost too much, and overlapped I/O with a completion port serves them all with a few threads. ? Why is the client's PID not proof of its identity? + PIDs are reused and any process may connect to the pipe - GetNamedPipeClientProcessId returns the server's own PID - The PID is only available after the client disconnects - PIDs are random numbers assigned by each client itself The PID is useful for logging and watching the client, but any program may connect and PIDs get reused. Security descriptors on the pipe are the real gate.

title: Instances and clients
body: Model a named pipe server's instances (lesson 2.04): how many are listening, which are connected, and what a client trying to connect experiences. cpp enum class Connect { Connected, Busy, NoServer }; class PipeServer { public: explicit PipeServer(int maxInstances); bool createInstance(); Connect clientConnects(std::uint32_t pid, int& instance); void clientDisconnects(int instance); void closeInstance(int instance); int listening() const; std::vector<std::uint32_t clients() const; }; - Instances are numbered 0, 1, 2, ... in the order created. createInstance adds a listening instance; it returns false (and creates nothing) if maxInstances instances already exist. - clientConnects : if no instance exists at all, NoServer (like ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND ). If none is listening, Busy (like ERROR_PIPE_BUSY ). Otherwise the lowest-numbered listening instance becomes connected to that client, instance is set to its number, and the result is Connected . - clientDisconnects makes a connected instance listen again (like DisconnectNamedPipe and a new ConnectNamedPipe ). - closeInstance removes an instance, whatever its state; its number is not reused. - clients lists the PIDs of connected clients in instance order.

title: 2.05  Overlapped I/O and Completion Ports
body: Doing pipe I/O without blocking a thread per operation - FILE_FLAG_OVERLAPPED, OVERLAPPED structures and events, ERROR_IO_PENDING, GetOverlappedResult, and I/O completion ports that let a few threads serve thousands of connections as state machines. Asking now, finding out later Blocking I/O ties up a thread while it waits. Overlapped I/O starts an operation and returns at once; the result arrives later. To use it, open or create the handle with FILE_FLAG_OVERLAPPED (for a pipe server, PIPE_ACCESS_DUPLEX FILE_FLAG_OVERLAPPED ), and pass an OVERLAPPED structure to each call: cpp-norun OVERLAPPED ov{}; ov.hEvent = CreateEventW(nullptr, TRUE, FALSE, nullptr); // signalled when the operation completes char buffer 4096 ; if (!ReadFile(pipe, buffer, sizeof(buffer), nullptr, &ov)) { if (GetLastError() != ERROR_IO_PENDING) / a real failure /; // ... the read is in progress; do other work, or wait ... } DWORD got{}; if (GetOverlappedResult(pipe, &ov, &got, TRUE / wait /)) { / got bytes are in buffer / } Rules that bite: - The OVERLAPPED and the buffer must stay alive and untouched until the operation completes . Putting them on the stack of a function that returns while the read is pending is a classic memory corruption. - One OVERLAPPED per outstanding operation. - An operation may complete immediately (the call returns TRUE ); handle that path too. - CancelIoEx(handle, &ov) cancels a pending operation; you must still wait for its completion (with ERROR_OPERATION_ABORTED ) before freeing the buffer. With an event per operation, one thread can wait for many with WaitForMultipleObjects , up to 64 handles. Beyond that, use a completion port. I/O completion ports An I/O completion port (IOCP) is a queue that collects the completions of many handles. Associate each handle with the port and a key of your choosing (usually a pointer to the connection's state): cpp-norun HANDLE port{ CreateIoCompletionPort(INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE, nullptr, 0, 0) }; CreateIoCompletionPort(pipe, port, reinterpret_cast<ULONG_PTR (connection), 0); // associate Then start overlapped operations as usual (no event needed), and have a few worker threads pull completions: cpp-norun for (;;) { DWORD bytes{}; ULONG_PTR key{}; OVERLAPPED ov{}; const BOOL ok{ GetQueuedCompletionStatus(port, &bytes, &key, &ov, INFINITE) }; auto connection{ reinterpret_cast<Connection (key) }; if (!ok bytes == 0 && connection- expectingData()) { connection- close(); continue; } connection- onCompleted(ov, bytes); // advance its state machine, start the next operation } PostQueuedCompletionStatus adds your own items to the queue, which is how you wake the workers to shut down. Connections as state machines With completions arriving one at a time, each connection is no longer a thread running top to bottom; it is a state machine that reacts to each completion and starts the next operation: text read 4 header bytes complete READING_HEADER --------------------------- READING_BODY (start a read of length bytes) ^ write complete body complete: handle the request +------------- WRITING <-----------------+ (start writing the reply) Each state knows which operation it is waiting for and how many bytes it still needs (a read may return fewer bytes than asked; then it simply reads again for the rest). This is more code than a thread per client, but a handful of worker threads can serve thousands of connections, and the same design works for sockets: it is how high-performance Windows servers are written. For smaller servers the Windows thread pool API ( CreateThreadpoolIo ) wraps completion ports for you, and C++ libraries such as Asio provide the same model portably. Check yourself quiz ? What must stay alive until an overlapped operation completes? - Only the event in ov.hEvent + The OVERLAPPED structure and the buffer passed to the call - The thread that started the operation - Nothing: the kernel copies the buffer when the call is made The kernel writes into your buffer and OVERLAPPED when the operation finishes. If they were on the stack of a function that has returned, it corrupts memory. ? What does ERROR_IO_PENDING from ReadFile on an overlapped handle mean? - The pipe is busy and the read must be retried - The read failed because no data was waiting + The read has started and will finish later - The read completed immediately with zero bytes With overlapped I/O, ReadFile returns FALSE with ERROR_IO_PENDING to say the operation is in progress. The result comes later through GetOverlappedResult , the event or a completion port. ? What does the key passed to CreateIoCompletionPort give a worker thread? - The number of bytes transferred by the operation - The handle of the thread that started the operation - A priority that decides which completion is delivered first + Your own value, usually a pointer to the connection's state You choose the key when you associate a handle with the port; GetQueuedCompletionStatus returns it with each completion, so the worker knows which connection the completion belongs to. ? Why do servers using completion ports structure connections as state machines? - Completion ports deliver completions in the order operations started - Each connection must have its own worker thread + Completions arrive one at a time, so each connection tracks its state - State machines avoid the need for OVERLAPPED structures No thread runs one connection from top to bottom any more. A connection records its state (reading the header, the body, writing) and, on each completion, advances and starts the next operation.

title: A connection as a state machine
match: A connection as a state machine
body: Write the state machine of lesson 2.05: one connection served with overlapped I/O, reacting to completions one at a time. Requests are framed with a 4-byte little-endian length; the reply to each request is the request's bytes reversed, framed the same way. cpp enum class Op { Read, Write, Close }; struct Request { Op op; std::size_t size; std::vector<std::uint8_t data; }; class Connection { public: explicit Connection(std::uint32_t maxMessage); Request start(); Request onRead(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & bytes); Request onWritten(std::size_t bytes); int served() const; }; Each call returns the next operation to start : - Read with size : read up to size bytes; the result comes back through onRead (it may be fewer bytes). - Write with data : write these bytes; onWritten reports how many were written (it may be fewer; then write the rest). - Close : the connection is finished. The flow: start asks to read the 4-byte header. While the header is incomplete, keep asking for the missing bytes. A length above maxMessage means Close . Then read the body (asking for exactly the bytes still missing). With the whole body, write the framed reply; when all of it is written, count one served request and ask for the next header. An onRead with 0 bytes means the client disconnected: Close .

body: Build and check named pipe names. pipeName("xenon-build") - \\.\pipe\xenon-build pipeName("xenon-build", session) - \\.\pipe\xenon-build-S1 "bad\name" - refused: backslash not allowed a 300-character name - refused: longer than 256
