body: Simulate a pipe with a small buffer to see why a writer blocks. buffer 8 bytes writer: wrote 8, blocked with 4 left reader: read 5 writer: wrote 4 reader: read 7

title: Typed messages on a pipe
body: Frame messages with a type and length so the reader always knows where one ends. send Hello{"ada"} - 01 00 00 00 03 61 64 61 send Ping - 02 00 00 00 00 reader got: Hello ada, Ping unknown type 7: skipped 3 bytes and carried on

title: A completion queue
body: Model I/O completion ports: start operations, and let worker loops handle them as they finish. start read 1 (takes 30 ms), read 2 (10 ms), write 3 (20 ms) t=10 completed 2 read 512 bytes - handler started a write 4 (5 ms) t=15 completed 4 write t=20 completed 3 write t=30 completed 1 read 4096 bytes

title: A log collector
body: Several helper processes send log records to one collector over a named pipe, one connection each, in byte mode with their own framing. Build the collector's core: per-client reassembly, validation, disconnects in the middle of a record, and draining records by level. Each record on the wire is: text length: 2 bytes, little-endian level: 1 byte text: length - 1 bytes so length counts the level byte and the text. cpp struct Record { int client; std::uint32_t pid; std::uint8_t level; std::string text; }; class LogCollector { public: int connect(std::uint32_t pid); void received(int client, const std::vector<std::uint8_t & bytes); void disconnected(int client); std::vector<Record drain(std::uint8_t minLevel); bool isConnected(int client) const; int partialDropped() const; int protocolErrors() const; }; - connect registers a new client connection from process pid and returns its id (0, 1, 2, ...). - received appends bytes from that client and extracts every complete record, in order. Records from different clients are kept in the order they completed . Bytes for an unknown or disconnected client are ignored. - A record whose length is 0 or greater than 1025, or whose level is above 5, is a protocol error : count it, drop the client's buffered bytes and disconnect the client (as the server would close a misbehaving connection). Records completed before the error are kept. - disconnected : the client is gone; if it had an incomplete record buffered, count one partial drop . - drain returns every collected record with level = minLevel , in order, and forgets all collected records (lower levels are discarded).

title: 3.01  File Mappings
body:
Shared memory on Windows - a named file mapping backed by the page file, views mapped into each process at different addresses, sizes and page rounding, Local and Global names, who creates and who opens, and when the memory goes away. The fastest channel there is Every method so far copies data: from the sender into the kernel, and from the kernel into the receiver. Shared memory copies nothing. The kernel maps the same physical pages into two (or more) processes' address spaces; a byte written by one is immediately visible to the other. On Windows, shared memory is a file mapping object. It can be backed by a real file (lesson 3.04) or, for pure IPC, by the page file: cpp-norun constexpr DWORD SIZE{ 64 1024 }; // The creator (often the server, or whichever process starts first) HANDLE mapping{ CreateFileMappingW(INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE, // page-file backed: no real file &security, // who may open it (lesson 5.05) PAGE_READWRITE, 0, SIZE, // size: high and low 32 bits LR"(Local\xenon-telemetry)") }; const bool existed{ GetLastError() == ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS }; // someone created it first void view{ MapViewOfFile(mapping, FILE_MAP_READ FILE_MAP_WRITE, 0, 0, SIZE) }; // ... use view as SIZE bytes of memory ... UnmapViewOfFile(view); CloseHandle(mapping); cpp-norun // Another process HANDLE mapping{ OpenFileMappingW(FILE_MAP_READ, FALSE, LR"(Local\xenon-telemetry)") }; const void view{ MapViewOfFile(mapping, FILE_MAP_READ, 0, 0, 0) }; // 0: map all of it CreateFileMappingW with a name opens the existing object if it already exists (and sets ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS ), so it serves both sides when either might start first. OpenFileMappingW only opens, failing with ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND if nobody created it. Different addresses The view appears at some address in each process, chosen independently: 0x1F0000 in one, 0x2A0000 in the other. The bytes are the same; the addresses are not. That one fact shapes everything you put into shared memory (lesson 3.02): a pointer stored in shared memory is meaningless to the other process . Sizes and pages Memory is mapped in whole pages (4 KB), so a mapping's real size is rounded up to a page. A view's starting offset must be a multiple of the allocation granularity , 64 KB on Windows ( GetSystemInfo reports it). Pages are committed lazily: a 1 GB page-file mapping costs nothing until its pages are touched, then each touched page costs RAM or page file. The size is given as two 32-bit halves because mappings can be larger than 4 GB: high word size 32 , low word size & 0xFFFFFFFF . Names: Local and Global Kernel object names (mappings, and the events and mutexes of milestone 4) live in a namespace per session : - Local
ame (or just name ): visible only within the current login session. The usual choice for programs on a user's desktop. - Global
ame : visible across sessions, so a service in session 0 and a desktop program can share it. Creating global objects needs the SeCreateGlobalPrivilege right, which services and administrators have. After the prefix the name may not contain another backslash. As with pipe names, choose names that will not collide: product, purpose, and a user or session identifier. Lifetime A mapping exists as long as any process holds a handle to it or has a view mapped. When the last one is gone, a page-file mapping and its contents vanish. So: - If the creator exits while another process still has it open, the data stays. - If every process closes it, the next process to create it gets fresh, zeroed memory. A page-file mapping always starts zeroed, which is useful: an all-zero header can mean "not yet initialised" (lesson 3.02). What it does not give you Shared memory moves no messages and sends no signals. It does not tell a reader that new data has arrived, it does not stop two writers from colliding, and it does not tell you when the other process has died. Every one of those must be built on top: atomics and ring buffers (lesson 3.03), events (milestone 4), seqlocks (lesson 3.05), and watching the other process's handle. Check yourself quiz ? Why is shared memory faster than a pipe for large amounts of data? - The kernel compresses the data before mapping it + Nothing is copied: both processes see the same physical pages - It bypasses the CPU cache, so writes are quicker - It sends data in 64 KB blocks instead of byte by byte A pipe copies bytes from the sender into the kernel and again into the receiver. A file mapping puts the same physical pages in both address spaces, so a byte written by one is simply there for the other. ? Why is a pointer stored in shared memory useless to the other process? - Pointers are encrypted by the kernel when written to a mapping - The other process cannot dereference pointers to page-file memory + The view is mapped at different addresses in each process - Pointers are 8 bytes but mappings store values in 4-byte units Each process's view appears at an address chosen independently, so the same bytes live at different addresses. Store offsets from the start of the block instead. ? What is the difference between Local
ame and Global
ame ? - Local objects are page-file backed; Global ones are backed by a real file - Local is visible only to the creating process; Global to every process in the session - Global names are case-sensitive; Local names are not + Local is per session; Global spans sessions and needs a privilege Kernel object names live in a namespace per login session. Global\ objects are shared across sessions (for example with a service in session 0), and creating them needs SeCreateGlobalPrivilege . ? When does a page-file backed mapping's content disappear? - When the process that created it exits + When every handle and view in every process is gone - After a timeout once no process has touched it - Only when the machine restarts The mapping lives while any process holds a handle or a view. If the creator exits but another process still has it open, the data stays; once all are gone, the next creator gets fresh zeroed memory.

title: Mapping arithmetic
body: The numbers behind CreateFileMappingW and MapViewOfFile (lessons 3.01 and 3.04): cpp struct ViewPlan { std::uint64_t viewOffset; std::uint64_t delta; std::uint64_t viewLength; }; std::uint64_t pagesFor(std::uint64_t bytes); std::pair<std::uint32_t, std::uint32_t splitSize(std::uint64_t size); ViewPlan planView(std::uint64_t fileOffset, std::uint64_t length); bool validObjectName(const std::string& name); - pagesFor : how many 4096-byte pages hold bytes (0 bytes need 0 pages). - splitSize gives the high and low 32-bit halves a mapping size is passed as. - planView : to read length bytes at fileOffset , the view must start at a multiple of 65 536: viewOffset is the offset rounded down, delta how far into the view the data starts, viewLength is delta + length . - validObjectName : a name for a mapping, event or mutex is either a plain name, or Local\ or Global\ followed by a name; the name part must not be empty and must not contain \ . The whole string is at most 260 characters.

title: 3.02  Laying Out Shared Data
body: What may live in shared memory and what may not - offsets instead of pointers, fixed-size types instead of std::string and std::vector, a header with a magic number, version and size, safe initialisation when either side may start first, and lock-free atomics. The rules A block of shared memory is seen by several processes, at different addresses, possibly built by different versions of your program, possibly by different compilers. So everything in it must mean the same thing to all of them: 1. No pointers. Store offsets from the start of the block instead, and turn them into pointers locally: base + offset . 2. No types that own heap memory. A std::string or std::vector placed in shared memory holds a pointer to its own process's heap. Use fixed-size arrays ( char name 64 ) or offsets to data inside the block. 3. Fixed-size types. std::uint32_t , std::int64_t , float : never long (4 bytes on Windows, 8 on Linux) or size_t (different in 32- and 64-bit processes). 4. Explicit layout. Put members in a stable order, use static_assert on sizes and offsets, and remember padding (Pointers and Memory course, lesson 3.01). 5. No virtual functions , which would put a vtable pointer in the block. cpp-norun struct TelemetryHeader { std::uint32_t magic; // 'XTEL': this really is our block std::uint32_t version; // the layout version std::uint32_t size; // total bytes the creator made std::uint32_t ready; // 0 until the creator has finished initialising std::uint64_t firstSample; // offset of the sample table std::uint32_t sampleCount; std::uint32_t reserved; }; static_assert(sizeof(TelemetryHeader) == 32); A header first Begin every shared block with a header like that: - A magic number confirms the block is what you think: a stale mapping from an old version, or an unrelated program using the same name, is caught at once. - A version lets a newer reader refuse, or adapt to, an older layout. - A size stops a reader from trusting offsets that point past the end. Check every offset against it before use: the other process may be buggy, or hostile. Offsets instead of pointers A linked structure in shared memory stores offsets. A node at offset 0 is impossible (the header is there), so 0 can mean "none": cpp-norun struct Node { std::uint64_t next; std::int32_t value; std::uint32_t pad; }; template <typename T T at(std::byte base, std::uint64_t offset) { return offset ? reinterpret_cast<T (base + offset) : nullptr; } for (Node n{ at<Node (base, header- first) }; n; n = at<Node (base, n- next)) { / ... / } Because offsets are relative to the block, the structure is correct in every process however its view is placed. (The same idea is how memory-mapped file formats and pointer-free serialisation libraries such as FlatBuffers work.) Initialising safely Both processes may start at nearly the same moment. The creator (the one that did not get ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS ) fills in the header and the data, and sets ready last . Every other process waits until ready is set before trusting anything. Because a page-file mapping starts zeroed, ready == 0 reliably means "not yet". For this to be safe, ready must be written and read as an atomic with release and acquire ordering, so the data written before it is visible once it is seen: cpp-norun auto ready{ reinterpret_cast<std::atomic<std::uint32_t (&header- ready) }; ready- store(1, std::memory_order_release); // creator, after filling everything in while (ready- load(std::memory_order_acquire) == 0) Sleep(1); // others (with a timeout in real code) Atomics in shared memory std::atomic<T works across processes only if it is lock-free : a lock-based fallback uses a lock inside each process's own runtime, which the other process cannot see. For 32- and 64-bit integers on x64 they always are; check with static_assert(std::atomic<std::uint64_t ::is_always_lock_free) . Construct them in place in the block (with placement new, or by relying on the zeroed memory for types whose zero state is valid), and never put std::mutex in shared memory; use the named kernel objects of milestone 4 instead. Check yourself quiz ? Why store offsets instead of pointers in shared memory? - Offsets take less space than pointers - Pointers into shared memory are blocked by the kernel + Views sit at different addresses; an offset means the same in each - Offsets let the block be larger than 4 GB A pointer is only valid at the address where this process's view sits. Each process turns an offset into a pointer locally with base + offset . ? Why is std::string unsuitable as a member of a shared struct? + It points into its own process's heap, which others cannot reach - It is too large to fit in a 4 KB page - Its characters are stored as UTF-16 in shared memory - It cannot be copied with memcpy , so the mapping cannot load it A std::string (like std::vector ) holds a pointer to memory in its own process's heap. Use fixed-size arrays such as char name 64 , or offsets to data inside the block. ? What are a shared header's magic number, version and size for? - To make the block's size a power of two - To encrypt the block so other programs cannot read it - To record which process wrote the block last + To recognise the block, check its layout and bound its offsets The magic number catches an unrelated or stale block, the version tells a reader whether it understands the layout, and the size lets it reject offsets that point past the end. ? Why must std::atomic be lock-free to work in shared memory? - Lock-free atomics are the only ones that can be zero-initialised - A lock-based atomic would be too slow across processes + A lock-based one uses a lock private to each process's runtime - Only lock-free atomics have a fixed size A non-lock-free atomic falls back on a lock kept inside the process's runtime, so two processes would use two different locks. Check is_always_lock_free , and use named kernel objects instead of std::mutex .

title: A list that works at any address
match: A list that works at any address
body: Build a linked list inside a block of bytes using offsets instead of pointers (lesson 3.02), so that a copy of the block placed anywhere else, as another process's view would be, still works. cpp class SharedList { public: static constexpr std::uint32_t MAGIC{ 0x5453494C }; // "LIST" explicit SharedList(std::vector<std::byte & block); void create(); bool valid() const; bool push(std::int32_t value); std::vector<std::int32_t values() const; std::uint32_t count() const; }; The block starts with a 24-byte header, followed by nodes of 16 bytes each: Header offset Field --- --- 0 std::uint32_t magic 4 std::uint32_t count 8 std::uint64_t offset of the first node (0 = none) 16 std::uint64_t offset where the next node will be placed Node offset Field --- --- 0 std::uint64_t offset of the next node (0 = none) 8 std::int32_t value 12 4 bytes of padding - create writes a fresh header: magic, count 0, no first node, next free offset 24. - valid checks the block is big enough for a header and holds the magic. - push adds a node holding value at the end of the list, placing it at the next free offset; if the block has no room for another node it returns false and changes nothing. - values walks the list from the first node. It must never read outside the block: a next offset that is not inside the block (or not a whole node from the end) stops the walk. - Read and write the fields with std::memcpy at byte offsets. The tests copy the whole block into a different vector and read it there.

title: 3.03  Ring Buffers
body: A queue in shared memory without locks - a single-producer single-consumer ring buffer with a write counter and a read counter, power-of-two capacities, detecting full and empty, acquire and release ordering, and what to do when the buffer is full. A queue made of a circle To stream messages through shared memory (a game sending events to an external debug tool, an audio engine passing samples), you need a queue that two processes can use at once without a lock. The standard answer is a ring buffer : an array of slots used in a circle, with two counters. text tail (next to read) head (next to write) slots: . A B C D . . . - The producer writes a slot at head , then advances head . - The consumer reads the slot at tail , then advances tail . - Each counter is written by only one side. That is what makes it work without locks: there is never a moment where both sides write the same variable. This is a single-producer, single-consumer (SPSC) ring. With several producers or consumers you need more machinery (compare-and-swap loops, or a lock); keep one writer and one reader per ring, and use several rings if needed. Counters that only grow Store head and tail as ever-increasing counters, not as slot indexes. Then: - the number of items is head - tail ; - empty is head == tail ; - full is head - tail == capacity ; - the slot for counter n is n % capacity , or n & (capacity - 1) when the capacity is a power of two , which is why ring sizes almost always are. With unsigned 32- or 64-bit counters, head - tail stays correct even when the counters wrap past their maximum, as long as the capacity is less than the wrap-around range. The code cpp-norun struct RingHeader { std::atomic<std::uint32_t head; // written only by the producer std::atomic<std::uint32_t tail; // written only by the consumer std::uint32_t capacity; // a power of two }; bool push(RingHeader h, std::uint32_t slots, std::uint32_t value) { const std::uint32_t head{ h- head.load(std::memory_order_relaxed) }; // our own counter const std::uint32_t tail{ h- tail.load(std::memory_order_acquire) }; // the consumer's if (head - tail == h- capacity) return false; // full slots head & (h- capacity - 1) = value; // write the slot first, h- head.store(head + 1, std::memory_order_release); // then publish it return true; } std::optional<std::uint32_t pop(RingHeader h, std::uint32_t slots) { const std::uint32_t tail{ h- tail.load(std::memory_order_relaxed) }; const std::uint32_t head{ h- head.load(std::memory_order_acquire) }; // see the slots written before it if (head == tail) return std::nullopt; // empty const std::uint32_t value{ slots tail & (h- capacity - 1) }; h- tail.store(tail + 1, std::memory_order_release); // hand the slot back return value; } The ordering is the important part. The producer writes the slot before publishing the new head with release ; the consumer reads head with acquire before reading the slot. That pair guarantees the consumer never sees an advanced head without the slot's data. The same pairing in the other direction guarantees the producer never overwrites a slot the consumer is still reading. When the ring is full The producer has to choose a policy: - Fail and let the caller decide (the code above). Good for commands, which must not be lost. - Drop the new item and count the loss : good for telemetry and logs, where a live process must never wait for a slow observer. Keep a "dropped" counter in the header so the consumer can report the gap. - Wait : spin briefly, then wait on an event the consumer signals (milestone 4). Only when the producer can afford to block. Avoiding false sharing head and tail sit next to each other but are written by different processes on different cores. Each write invalidates the other core's copy of the 64-byte cache line containing both, which slows everything down. Put them on separate cache lines with alignas(64) padding. The counters are tiny; the padding is cheap. Check yourself quiz ? Why does an SPSC ring buffer need no lock? - The kernel serialises access to every shared page - The producer and consumer always run on the same core - Each slot is protected by its own atomic flag + Each counter has one writer: the producer or the consumer No variable is ever written by both sides, so there is nothing to lock; acquire and release ordering on the counters is enough. With several producers or consumers this no longer holds. ? With ever-increasing counters, how do you test for full? - head == tail + head - tail == capacity - head % capacity == tail % capacity - head + 1 == tail The number of items is head - tail , so the ring is full when it equals the capacity. head == tail means empty, and comparing the slot indexes cannot tell full from empty. ? Why must the producer store the new head with release ordering after writing the slot? - So that the consumer's tail is updated at the same time - So that the slot is written to disk before the consumer reads it + So a consumer that sees the new head also sees the slot's data - So that two producers cannot advance head together Release on the store and acquire on the load pair up: every write before the release (the slot) is visible to a thread that sees the stored value. Without it the consumer could read a stale slot. ? Why are ring capacities usually powers of two? + The slot index becomes a cheap mask, counter & (capacity - 1) - Shared memory can only be allocated in power-of-two sizes - It makes head - tail impossible to overflow - Atomics require arrays whose length is a power of two With a power of two, n % capacity is a cheap mask, and since the counter's range is a multiple of the capacity, slots stay in order when the counter wraps past its maximum.

title: A lock-free ring buffer
body: Build the single-producer, single-consumer ring buffer of lesson 3.03 over a block of memory. The producer and the consumer each make their own Ring object over the same block, as two processes would over one mapping. cpp struct alignas(64) RingHeader { std::atomic<std::uint32_t head; char pad1 60 ; std::atomic<std::uint32_t tail; char pad2 60 ; std::uint32_t capacity; std::atomic<std::uint32_t dropped; }; class Ring { public: Ring(void memory, std::uint32_t capacity, bool create); bool push(std::uint32_t value); void pushOrDrop(std::uint32_t value); std::optional<std::uint32_t pop(); std::uint32_t size() const; std::uint32_t dropped() const; }; The memory holds a RingHeader followed by capacity slots of std::uint32_t (the tests provide a block large enough and aligned to 64). - With create true, the constructor sets up the header (placement new or plain stores): head 0, tail 0, the capacity, dropped 0. Otherwise it uses the header that is there. The capacity is a power of two. - push adds a value, or returns false if the ring is full. pushOrDrop adds it, or counts it in dropped if full. - pop removes the oldest value, or gives std::nullopt if empty. - size is head - tail . - Use acquire and release ordering exactly as in the lesson. The tests include a real producer thread and consumer thread.

title: 3.04  Memory-Mapped Files
body: Mapping a real file into memory - reading huge files as if they were arrays, views of part of a file and the 64 KB granularity rule, writing through a mapping and flushing it, growing a mapped file, sharing a mapped file between processes, and the errors that arrive as exceptions. A file as memory A file mapping can be backed by a real file instead of the page file. Then the file's contents appear in memory, and reading memory reads the file: cpp-norun HANDLE file{ CreateFileW(path, GENERIC_READ, FILE_SHARE_READ, nullptr, OPEN_EXISTING, FILE_ATTRIBUTE_NORMAL, nullptr) }; LARGE_INTEGER size{}; GetFileSizeEx(file, &size); HANDLE mapping{ CreateFileMappingW(file, nullptr, PAGE_READONLY, 0, 0, nullptr) }; // 0, 0: the file's size const auto data{ static_cast<const std::uint8_t (MapViewOfFile(mapping, FILE_MAP_READ, 0, 0, 0)) }; std::span<const std::uint8_t bytes{ data, static_cast<std::size_t (size.QuadPart) }; // parse bytes directly: no ReadFile, no buffer, no copy Pages are read from disk only when first touched, so mapping a 2 GB file is instant, and reading only its index touches only the index's pages. Parsers for big binary formats (game assets, databases, the PE files of the Reverse Engineering course) often work this way: the file is the data structure, navigated by offsets. Views of part of a file A 64-bit process can map even very large files whole. When you need only a window (a 32-bit process, or a file larger than you want mapped), map a view of part of it. The view's starting offset must be a multiple of the allocation granularity (64 KB): text want bytes 100 000 to 100 499 aligned start = 100 000 rounded down to 65 536 = 65 536 delta = 100 000 - 65 536 = 34 464 map from 65 536 for 34 464 + 500 bytes; the data starts delta bytes into the view Writing Open the file and mapping for writing ( GENERIC_READ GENERIC_WRITE , PAGE_READWRITE , FILE_MAP_WRITE ) and writes to memory become writes to the file. The operating system writes changed pages back to disk in its own time; FlushViewOfFile(view, 0) starts it now, and FlushFileBuffers(file) waits until it is on the disk, which matters for anything that must survive a power cut. A mapping cannot make a file bigger than the size it was created with. To append, close the views and mapping, extend the file ( SetFilePointerEx and SetEndOfFile , or create the mapping with a larger size, which extends the file), and map again. Programs that grow mapped files usually extend in large steps (doubling) to avoid remapping constantly. Sharing a mapped file Two processes mapping the same file see each other's writes immediately, through the same pages, exactly like a page-file mapping, and the data also persists in the file afterwards. This is how some databases share their data between processes. Coordinating writers still needs the synchronisation of milestone 4. Errors become exceptions With ReadFile , a disk error is a return value. With a mapped file, the error happens when you touch a page, inside an ordinary memory access, so it arrives as a structured exception, EXCEPTION_IN_PAGE_ERROR : a file on a network share that disappears, a USB drive pulled out, a file truncated by another process. Code that maps files it does not fully control wraps access in __try / __except , or prefers ReadFile for such files. Mapped files also hold the file open: it cannot be deleted while mapped, which surprises users of tools that leave mappings around. Check yourself quiz ? Why is mapping a 2 GB file and reading a few bytes from its end fast? - Windows loads the whole file in the background on another core - The mapping reads the file in one large sequential ReadFile + Pages are read only when touched, so only the pages actually read are loaded - Memory-mapped files are cached in the page file after the first run Mapping just sets up the address range; each page is read from disk the first time it is accessed. Reading a few bytes touches one or two pages. ? You want a view starting at file offset 200 000. Where must the view actually start? - At 200 000, since views may start at any byte - At 196 608 + 4 096 = 200 704, the next 4 KB page boundary - At 262 144, the next 64 KB boundary above it + At 196 608, the 64 KB boundary below; the data is 3 392 bytes in A view's offset must be a multiple of the 64 KB allocation granularity, so round down to 196 608 and skip 200 000 - 196 608 = 3 392 bytes into the view. Rounding up would miss the data. ? How do you make sure written data has reached the disk? + FlushViewOfFile , then FlushFileBuffers on the file - UnmapViewOfFile , which waits until every page is on the disk - CloseHandle on the mapping, which flushes synchronously - Nothing: writes through a mapping go straight to disk The OS writes changed pages back in its own time. FlushViewOfFile starts writing them; FlushFileBuffers waits until they are really on the disk. ? How does a disk error show up when reading through a mapped file? - MapViewOfFile returns nullptr when the mapping is created - The read returns zeros and GetLastError is set + As an EXCEPTION_IN_PAGE_ERROR structured exception at the memory access - The next call to ReadFile on the file fails The error happens when a page is touched, inside an ordinary memory access, so it arrives as a structured exception. Code mapping files it does not control wraps access in __try / __except .

title: Indexing a mapped file
body: A mapped file is just a span of bytes (lesson 3.04). Navigate one without copying it. The file holds records, each a 4-byte little-endian length followed by that many bytes: cpp struct Index { std::vector<std::size_t offsets; bool truncated; }; Index buildIndex(std::span<const std::uint8_t file); std::span<const std::uint8_t recordAt(std::span<const std::uint8_t file, const Index& index, std::size_t i); std::optional<std::size_t findRecord(std::span<const std::uint8_t file, const Index& index, std::string_view text); - buildIndex walks the file from the start and records the offset of each record's data (just after its length). If a length runs past the end of the file, it stops there and sets truncated (a file cut short by a crash, or corrupt). Trailing bytes too short for a length also count as truncated. - recordAt returns a view of record i 's data inside the file (no copy), or an empty span for an index out of range. - findRecord returns the number of the first record whose bytes equal text .

title: 3.05  Seqlocks and Snapshots
body: Publishing a state that changes constantly, such as a game's player positions for an external tool - why readers can see torn data, double buffering, and the seqlock - a sequence counter that lets readers detect a write in progress and retry without ever blocking the writer. The problem: torn reads A game updates a block of shared state every frame: player position, health, the current level. An external tool (an overlay, a stats panel, a test harness) reads it whenever it likes. If the tool reads while the game is halfway through writing, it can see the new x with the old y: a torn read , a state that never existed. A lock would fix it, but a lock lets a slow reader stall the game, which is exactly what must not happen. We want: the writer never waits; readers always get a consistent snapshot, retrying if needed. Double buffering Keep two copies of the state and an index saying which one is current. The writer fills the other copy, then flips the index (atomically, with release ordering). Readers read the index (acquire), then copy that buffer. It is simple, but not quite safe on its own: a reader that is slow enough could still be copying buffer A when the writer, two frames later, starts filling A again. It works when readers are known to be fast compared with the update rate; otherwise add a check, which leads to the seqlock. The seqlock A seqlock pairs the data with a sequence counter : - The writer increments the counter (it becomes odd : "writing"), writes the data, then increments it again ( even : "stable"). - A reader reads the counter; if it is odd, a write is in progress, try again. Otherwise it copies the data, then reads the counter again. If the counter changed, a write happened during the copy, so the copy may be torn: try again. cpp-norun // writer: never waits seq.store(s + 1, std::memory_order_relaxed); // odd: writing std::atomic_thread_fence(std::memory_order_release); copyIn(data, state); seq.store(s + 2, std::memory_order_release); // even: stable // reader: retries instead of blocking anyone for (;;) { const std::uint32_t before{ seq.load(std::memory_order_acquire) }; if (before & 1) continue; // writer is busy State copy{ copyOut(data) }; std::atomic_thread_fence(std::memory_order_acquire); if (seq.load(std::memory_order_relaxed) == before) return copy; // nothing changed meanwhile } The writer never blocks, readers never block the writer, and a reader only retries in the rare case that it overlapped a write. Linux uses seqlocks for the system clock for exactly these reasons. Doing it correctly in C++ The data is read while it may be being written, which is a data race and undefined behaviour if the data is ordinary memory, however carefully the counter is checked afterwards. The clean way is to store the payload in atomic words and copy it word by word with relaxed atomic loads and stores; the fences then order those against the counter. That is what the practice does: the state is any trivially copyable struct, copied into and out of an array of std::atomic<std::uint64_t . Requirements and limits: - One writer at a time. Several writers need a lock among themselves (they can still let readers use the seqlock). - The state must be trivially copyable: plain numbers and arrays, no pointers into a process's heap. - Readers must cope with retrying; under constant updates of a huge state they could retry several times, so keep the published state small. Check yourself quiz ? What is a torn read? - A read that fails because the mapping was closed - A read of a slot the producer has not written yet + A mix of old and new state that never existed as a whole - A read that returns fewer bytes than requested If a reader copies while the writer is halfway through, it may get the new x with the old y. A seqlock detects that and retries. ? What does an odd sequence counter tell a seqlock reader? + A write is in progress, so it must try again - The data is stable and can be copied - The writer has exited and the data is stale - Another reader is copying the data at the moment The writer makes the counter odd before writing and even again after. An odd value means the data is being changed right now. ? Why does the reader read the counter a second time after copying? - To tell the writer it has finished copying - To make the counter even again for the next reader + If it changed, a write overlapped the copy, which may be torn - To check that the copy is not larger than the shared block The reader never writes the counter. Comparing it before and after the copy shows whether a write overlapped the copy; if so, the reader retries. ? Why is a seqlock better than a mutex for a game publishing state to a tool? - It lets several writers update the state at once - It uses less shared memory than a mutex - It guarantees readers never need to retry + The writer never waits, so a slow tool cannot slow the game With a lock, a reader holding it would make the game wait. A seqlock's writer never blocks; readers retry only when they overlapped a write. It still allows only one writer.

title: A seqlock
body: Build the seqlock of lesson 3.05 for any trivially copyable state, storing the payload in atomic words so that reading during a write is not undefined behaviour: cpp template <typename T class SeqLock { public: static_assert(std::is_trivially_copyable_v<T ); void write(const T& value); std::optional<T tryRead() const; T read() const; std::uint32_t sequence() const; }; - write (one writer only): increment the sequence (now odd), copy the value into the words with relaxed atomic stores, increment the sequence again (now even). Use the fences from the lesson. - tryRead makes one attempt: if the sequence is odd, or changes during the copy, return std::nullopt ; otherwise the copied value. - read retries tryRead until it succeeds. - sequence returns the current counter (twice the number of completed writes when nothing is writing). - Before the first write, reads return a value-initialised T .

title: A message ring in shared memory
match: A message ring in shared memory
body: Lesson 3.03's ring carries fixed-size numbers. Real messages vary in size. Build a single-producer, single-consumer ring of variable-size messages inside one block of memory, as a game would use to stream events to an external tool through a file mapping. cpp class MessageRing { public: static constexpr std::uint32_t MAGIC{ 0x474E4952 }; // "RING" static std::size_t bytesNeeded(std::uint32_t capacity); MessageRing(void memory, std::uint32_t capacity, bool create); bool valid() const; bool send(std::span<const std::uint8_t payload); std::optional<std::vector<std::uint8_t receive(); std::uint64_t pending() const; }; Layout. The block starts with a header, then capacity bytes of data area. capacity is a power of two and at least 64. The header holds the magic, the capacity, and two std::atomic<std::uint64_t counters on separate cache lines: head (total bytes ever written to the data area) and tail (total bytes ever consumed). bytesNeeded returns the header's size plus capacity . With create false, the object reads the capacity from the header; valid checks the magic. Records. A message is written at data position head % capacity as a 4-byte length followed by the payload, the whole record padded to a multiple of 8 bytes. Because every record starts at a multiple of 8, there are always at least 8 bytes before the end of the data area. Wrapping. If a record does not fit in the space before the end of the data area, the producer writes a wrap marker (length 0xFFFFFFFF ) at the current position, counts the rest of the data area as used, and writes the record at the start. A record never straddles the end. send returns false, changing nothing, if the payload is longer than capacity / 2 - 4 bytes, or if there is not enough free space ( capacity - (head - tail) ) for the record plus any wrap padding. It writes the record then publishes the new head with release ordering. receive returns std::nullopt when empty. It skips a wrap marker (moving tail to the start of the next lap), reads the record, and publishes the new tail with release ordering. pending is head - tail .

title: 4.01  Named Kernel Objects
body: Events, mutexes and semaphores that several processes can open by name - creating versus opening, ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS, the session namespaces, signalled and non-signalled states, and why a kernel object outlives the handle that made it until the last handle closes. Synchronisation that crosses processes std::mutex and std::condition_variable work between threads of one process. Between processes you use kernel objects : objects that live in the Windows kernel, reached through handles, and that can be given a name so another process can open the same one. Object Create Open Used for --- --- --- --- event CreateEventW OpenEventW "something happened": new data, stop now mutex CreateMutexW OpenMutexW exclusive access to a shared resource semaphore CreateSemaphoreW OpenSemaphoreW allow up to N at once waitable timer CreateWaitableTimerW OpenWaitableTimerW signal at a time or interval Processes, threads, file mappings and pipes are kernel objects too, which is why the same wait functions work on all of them. Create or open The usual pattern is for both sides to call Create... with the same name: cpp-norun HANDLE ready{ CreateEventW(&security, FALSE, FALSE, LR"(Local\xenon-telemetry-ready)") }; if (!ready) / failed: GetLastError() /; const bool someoneElseCreatedIt{ GetLastError() == ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS }; If the object exists, Create... opens it instead (and the creation parameters, such as the initial state, are ignored), so it does not matter which process starts first. Open... fails with ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND if the object does not exist, which is what you want when only one side should create it (a client must not create the server's objects). ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS is how a single-instance application detects a copy already running (lesson 6.01). Note that GetLastError() must be read immediately after the call, and that the call succeeds in that case. Names and namespaces Kernel object names follow the rules from lesson 3.01: Local\ (the default) within the session, Global\ across sessions. Names share one namespace across object types: an event and a mutex cannot both be called xenon-lock (the second create fails with ERROR_INVALID_HANDLE ). Choose specific names, and prefix them with your product and purpose. Signalled or not Every waitable kernel object is either signalled or non-signalled , and the wait functions block until an object is signalled: Object Signalled when --- --- event it has been set (lesson 4.02) mutex nobody owns it semaphore its count is above zero process, thread it has ended waitable timer its time has come Some objects change state when a wait succeeds on them (a mutex becomes owned, a semaphore's count drops, an auto-reset event resets); others stay signalled (a process stays ended). Lifetime A kernel object exists as long as any process holds a handle to it. When the last handle closes, the object, and its name, are gone. Practical consequences: - If the creator exits but another process still has the object open, the object stays and keeps its state. - A process that crashes has all its handles closed by Windows, so it cannot leave objects behind for ever. - To keep an object available between runs you need some process to hold it open, typically a long-running service. Security Every named object can carry a security descriptor saying who may open it and with which rights. The default allows the creating user and administrators, which is usually right for Local\ objects. Objects shared with a service or another user need an explicit descriptor (lesson 5.05). And because anyone allowed can create an object with your name first , a client should check it really talks to your server, not an impostor. Check yourself quiz ? Two programs both call CreateEventW with the same name. What happens to the second call? - It fails with ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS and returns nullptr - It creates a second, separate event with the same name + It opens the existing event and succeeds, with ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS - It replaces the first event, resetting it to the new initial state Create... opens an existing object of that name and still succeeds, so either side may start first. Read GetLastError() straight away to learn whether you created it. ? When should a program use OpenEventW instead of CreateEventW ? + When it must fail if nobody created the object yet - When it needs to wait on the event rather than set it - When the event is in the Global\ namespace - When the event is manual-reset Open... fails with ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND if nobody created the object, which is exactly what a client wants: it must not create the server's objects and then wait on them for ever. ? When is a mutex signalled? - When a thread has just acquired it - When it has been released twice in a row + When no thread owns it - When its owning process has ended, and only then A mutex is signalled while unowned; a successful wait makes the waiter the owner and the mutex non-signalled. An owner dying also releases it, but as abandoned. ? When does a named kernel object disappear? - When the process that created it exits - When its name is no longer used for a few seconds - When the session ends, whoever holds it + When the last handle to it, in any process, is closed A kernel object lives as long as any process holds a handle. If the creator exits while another process has it open, it stays and keeps its state.

title: A namespace of kernel objects
body: Model how named kernel objects are created, opened and destroyed (lesson 4.01): cpp enum class Kind { Event, Mutex, Semaphore }; enum class Result { Created, Opened, NotFound, WrongType }; class ObjectNamespace { public: Result create(Kind kind, const std::string& name, int& handle); Result open(Kind kind, const std::string& name, int& handle); void close(int handle); bool exists(const std::string& name) const; int handleCount(const std::string& name) const; }; - Handles are numbered 1, 2, 3, ... and never reused. Each successful create or open returns a new handle to the object. - create : if no object has that name, it makes one and returns Created . If an object of the same kind exists, it opens it and returns Opened (the ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS case). If an object of a different kind has the name, WrongType and no handle. - open : like create, but returns NotFound instead of creating. - Names are compared ignoring case . - close releases a handle; when an object's last handle closes, the object and its name are gone. Closing an unknown or already closed handle does nothing. - handleCount is the number of open handles to the named object (0 if none).

title: 4.02  Events and Waiting
body: Signalling between processes with events - auto-reset versus manual-reset, SetEvent and ResetEvent, the lost-wakeup trap and how to avoid it, WaitForMultipleObjects for waiting on several things at once, and the return values every wait must check. An event is a flag the kernel can wait on An event is a kernel object with two states, set (signalled) and reset (non-signalled). A process waits on it with WaitForSingleObject ; another process sets it with SetEvent . The waiting thread uses no CPU while it waits. cpp-norun // producer, after putting a message in the shared ring buffer ring.send(message); SetEvent(dataReady); // consumer for (;;) { if (WaitForSingleObject(dataReady, 1000) == WAIT_TIMEOUT) { / check the producer is alive / continue; } while (auto m{ ring.receive() }) handle( m); } Shared memory carries the data; the event carries the "look now". Together they give a fast channel that neither spins nor polls. Auto-reset and manual-reset The second argument of CreateEventW chooses the kind: Kind When set When a wait succeeds --- --- --- auto-reset ( FALSE ) wakes one waiting thread the event resets itself manual-reset ( TRUE ) wakes all waiting threads stays set until someone calls ResetEvent - Use auto-reset for "there is work": each set lets one waiter through. - Use manual-reset for a state that everyone should see: "shutting down", "initialisation complete". Once set, every current and future wait returns at once. Events do not count Setting an auto-reset event that is already set does nothing: two SetEvent calls before the consumer wakes up still wake it only once. An event is a flag, not a counter. That is fine as long as the consumer, once woken, processes everything that is waiting (the while loop above), not just one item. If you need to count, use a semaphore (lesson 4.03). The lost wakeup The classic bug is checking for work and then waiting, with a gap between: cpp-norun if (ring.empty()) // 1. consumer sees nothing { // 2. producer sends and calls SetEvent ResetEvent(dataReady); // 3. consumer clears the signal it never saw WaitForSingleObject(dataReady, INFINITE); // 4. waits for ever, with a message waiting } The safe pattern never resets a manual event while data may be waiting, and always re-checks the data after waking : with an auto-reset event, wait first, then drain everything; with timeouts on every wait, a missed signal costs at most one timeout instead of a hang. Waiting for several things A consumer usually needs to wake for more than one reason: new data, or "stop", or "the producer process died". WaitForMultipleObjects waits on up to 64 handles at once: cpp-norun HANDLE handles { stopEvent, producerProcess, dataReady }; switch (const DWORD r{ WaitForMultipleObjects(3, handles, FALSE, 5000) }) { case WAIT_OBJECT_0 + 0: return; // stop requested case WAIT_OBJECT_0 + 1: reportProducerDied(); return; // its process handle became signalled case WAIT_OBJECT_0 + 2: drain(); break; // data ready case WAIT_TIMEOUT: break; // nothing in 5 s default: / WAIT_FAILED or WAIT_ABANDONED_0 + i (lesson 4.03) / break; } With bWaitAll FALSE , it returns when any is signalled and tells you which (the lowest index if several are). Put the most important handle first: if stop and data arrive together, stop wins. Waiting on the other process's handle alongside your event is how a shared-memory channel learns that its peer has gone, which shared memory alone never tells you. Check every wait Return Meaning --- --- WAIT_OBJECT_0 + i object i is signalled WAIT_TIMEOUT the time ran out WAIT_ABANDONED_0 + i object i is a mutex whose owner died (lesson 4.03) WAIT_FAILED an error, such as an invalid handle: GetLastError() Code that treats every non-timeout return as success sooner or later acts on an abandoned mutex or a closed handle as if all were well. Check yourself quiz ? When should an event be manual-reset rather than auto-reset? - When only one waiter should wake for each SetEvent + When it marks a state, like "stopping", for all waiters - When the producer sets it many times a second - When it is shared between processes rather than threads A manual-reset event wakes every waiter and stays set until ResetEvent , so it suits a state like "stopping". Auto-reset lets one waiter through per set, which suits "there is work". ? SetEvent is called three times on an auto-reset event before the consumer wakes. How many times does the consumer's wait succeed? - Three times, one per SetEvent - Twice, because the first set is consumed when the event is created + Once: an event is a flag, not a counter - None, because setting a set event resets it Setting an event that is already set does nothing. Once woken, the consumer must process everything waiting. To count signals, use a semaphore. ? How can a consumer of shared memory find out that the producer process has died? - Shared memory is zeroed when the producer dies, so it checks for zeros - SetEvent fails in the consumer when the producer is gone - The event becomes abandoned, and the wait returns WAIT_ABANDONED_0 + Also wait on the producer's process handle, signalled when it ends Shared memory never tells you its peer has gone, and an event a dead process will never set just stays unset. A process handle is signalled when the process ends. Only mutexes are abandoned. ? With bWaitAll FALSE , which index is returned if two handles are signalled at once? - The highest one, so the most important handle should come last + The lowest one, so the most important handle should come first - Whichever was signalled first in time - A random one, so the caller must check every handle afterwards WaitForMultipleObjects reports the lowest signalled index. Put "stop" first so it wins when it arrives together with data.

title: Auto-reset, manual-reset and waiting for several
match: Auto-reset, manual-reset and waiting for several
body: Model events and WaitForMultipleObjects (lesson 4.02): cpp class Event { public: explicit Event(bool manualReset, bool initiallySet = false); void set(); void reset(); bool isSet() const; bool tryWait(); }; struct Waitable { Event event; bool processEnded; }; std::optional<std::size_t waitAny(std::vector<Waitable & objects); - tryWait is a wait with a zero timeout: if the event is set it succeeds, and an auto-reset event resets itself; a manual-reset event stays set. If not set, it returns false. - set and reset change the state; setting an event that is already set does nothing more (events do not count). - waitAny is WaitForMultipleObjects with "any" and a zero timeout: each entry is either an event ( event not null) or a process handle ( event null; signalled when processEnded ). It returns the lowest index that is signalled, consuming an auto-reset event at that index only, or std::nullopt if none is.

title: 4.03  Mutexes, Semaphores and Abandonment
body: Exclusive access across processes with a named mutex - ownership, recursion, releasing, and WAIT_ABANDONED when the owner died holding it - and semaphores for limiting how many can do something at once. A mutex across processes A named mutex gives exclusive access to something several processes share: a block of shared memory with a structure too large for atomics, a log file, a device. cpp-norun HANDLE lock{ CreateMutexW(&security, FALSE, LR"(Local\xenon-settings-lock)") }; switch (WaitForSingleObject(lock, 2000)) { case WAIT_OBJECT_0: editSharedSettings(); ReleaseMutex(lock); break; case WAIT_ABANDONED: // We own it now, but the previous owner died while holding it: the data may be half-written. repairOrResetSharedSettings(); ReleaseMutex(lock); break; case WAIT_TIMEOUT: / someone has held it for 2 s: report, retry later / break; } A successful wait makes the calling thread the owner; only that thread may ReleaseMutex . A Win32 mutex is recursive : the owner can wait on it again without blocking, and must release it once per successful wait. Releasing a mutex you do not own fails with ERROR_NOT_OWNER . A kernel mutex costs a system call per wait and release, far more than a std::mutex within a process. Use it for coarse operations (edit the settings block, append a record), not in a tight loop. Abandonment What if a process crashes while holding the mutex? A std::mutex in shared memory would stay locked for ever. A kernel mutex is better: when its owning thread ends, Windows releases it and marks it abandoned , and the next successful wait returns WAIT_ABANDONED instead of WAIT_OBJECT_0 . That return means: you now own the mutex, but whatever it protected may be inconsistent , because the dead owner may have stopped halfway through an update. Do not treat it as plain success. Validate the shared data (checksums and version numbers in the shared header pay for themselves here), repair or reinitialise it, and carry on. The abandoned state is cleared once reported, so only the first waiter gets the warning. Semaphores A semaphore holds a count between 0 and a maximum. A successful wait takes one from the count (blocking while it is 0); ReleaseSemaphore(handle, n, &previous) adds n . cpp-norun // At most 4 builds may run at once, across every process that opens this name HANDLE slots{ CreateSemaphoreW(nullptr, 4, 4, LR"(Local\xenon-build-slots)") }; if (WaitForSingleObject(slots, INFINITE) == WAIT_OBJECT_0) { runBuild(); ReleaseSemaphore(slots, 1, nullptr); } Unlike a mutex, a semaphore has no owner : any thread or process may release it. That makes it suitable for producer and consumer counting (the producer releases one per item, the consumer waits once per item), and means there is no abandonment : if a process dies holding a "slot", the count is lost for good. A watchdog that tracks which processes took slots, or a design where slots are tied to process handles, guards against that. Choosing Need Use --- --- exclusive access, must survive a crashed owner mutex (and handle WAIT_ABANDONED ) at most N at once semaphore count items between a producer and a consumer semaphore "something happened" or "a state is now true" event fast exclusive access inside one process std::mutex Check yourself quiz ? What does WAIT_ABANDONED mean on a mutex wait? - The wait failed and the caller does not own the mutex - The mutex was closed by its creator and no longer exists + You own it, but its last owner died holding it; check the data - The timeout ran out while the mutex was owned by a dead thread Windows releases a mutex whose owner died and marks it abandoned. The next waiter owns it but must validate or repair the data, then still call ReleaseMutex . ? Why is a Win32 mutex called recursive? - Releasing it once releases every wait on it + Its owner can wait on it again, releasing once per wait - Any thread may release it, not only the owner - It can be locked by several processes at once The owner can re-acquire without deadlocking itself, but it must release once per successful wait. Only the owning thread may release; others get ERROR_NOT_OWNER . ? Why is there no abandonment for semaphores? + A semaphore has no owner, so nobody is known to hold a slot - Windows restores the count automatically when a process dies - Semaphores cannot be shared between processes - A semaphore's count is reset to its maximum when any handle closes Taking a slot records nobody as its holder. If a process dies holding one, the count is simply lost, which is why long-running systems track slots themselves. ? A semaphore created with initial count 4 and maximum 4 has five waiters. How many get through at once? - One, like a mutex - Five, because the maximum is only checked on release - Three, because one slot is kept for the creator + Four; the fifth waits until one releases Each successful wait takes one from the count, blocking at 0. Four waits succeed, and the fifth proceeds after a ReleaseSemaphore .

title: Mutex ownership and abandonment
body: Model a Win32 mutex and semaphore (lesson 4.03) with a zero-timeout wait: cpp enum class Wait { Acquired, Abandoned, Timeout }; class Mutex { public: Wait tryWait(int thread); bool release(int thread); void threadEnded(int thread); std::optional<int owner() const; }; class Semaphore { public: Semaphore(int initial, int maximum); bool tryWait(); bool release(int count); int count() const; }; Mutex - If unowned, a wait makes thread the owner with a recursion count of 1 and returns Acquired , or Abandoned if the mutex was abandoned (the abandoned mark is then cleared). - If thread already owns it, the count goes up and the result is Acquired . - If another thread owns it, Timeout . - release by the owner lowers the count, freeing the mutex at 0; it returns false (and changes nothing) for a thread that does not own it. - threadEnded : if that thread owns the mutex, it becomes unowned and abandoned . Semaphore - tryWait takes one from the count if it is above 0. - release adds count unless that would exceed the maximum: then it returns false and changes nothing.

title: 4.04  Window Messages Between Programs
body: Programs with windows can talk through messages - finding another program's window, WM_COPYDATA for sending a block of data, registered message numbers, message-only windows, SendMessage versus PostMessage, and the privilege boundary UIPI puts in the way. Messages are already IPC Every window receives messages through its message loop (Win32 API course, lesson 1.03), and a program can send messages to another program's windows. For two desktop programs that both have windows, this is the simplest IPC there is: no pipes, no shared memory, and the message arrives in the receiver's normal message loop on its UI thread. Finding the window The sender needs the receiver's window handle ( HWND ): cpp-norun HWND target{ FindWindowW(L"XenonMainWindowClass", nullptr) }; // by window class name Give your windows a distinctive class name so they can be found reliably; titles change with documents and languages. Background programs without a visible window create a message-only window ( CreateWindowExW with parent HWND_MESSAGE ): it has no screen presence, cannot be enumerated by accident, but can be found with FindWindowExW(HWND_MESSAGE, nullptr, className, nullptr) and receives messages. WM_COPYDATA Ordinary messages carry only two numbers ( wParam and lParam ), and a pointer in them would be meaningless in the other process. WM_COPYDATA is the exception: Windows copies a block of data into the receiver for the duration of the message. cpp-norun // sender const std::wstring path{ LR"(C:\Projects\demo.xproj)" }; COPYDATASTRUCT cds{}; cds.dwData = 1; // your own "message type" cds.cbData = static_cast<DWORD ((path.size() + 1) sizeof(wchar_t)); cds.lpData = const_cast<wchar_t (path.c_str()); DWORD_PTR result{}; SendMessageTimeoutW(target, WM_COPYDATA, reinterpret_cast<WPARAM (myWindow), reinterpret_cast<LPARAM (&cds), SMTO_ABORTIFHUNG, 2000, &result); // receiver, in the window procedure case WM_COPYDATA: { const auto cds{ reinterpret_cast<const COPYDATASTRUCT (lParam) }; if (cds- dwData == 1 && cds- cbData = sizeof(wchar_t) && cds- cbData % sizeof(wchar_t) == 0) openProject(std::wstring(static_cast<const wchar_t (cds- lpData), cds- cbData / sizeof(wchar_t) - 1)); return TRUE; } Rules: - The data is valid only while the receiver handles the message . Copy what you need before returning. - WM_COPYDATA must be sent , not posted, because the copy only lives during the call. Use SendMessageTimeoutW with a timeout so a hung receiver cannot hang the sender. - Validate everything: dwData , the size, and the content. Any program on the desktop can send you WM_COPYDATA . Registered messages For simple notifications without data ("reload your settings"), define your own message number. Numbers from WM_APP up are private to one program; to agree on a number between programs, register a name: cpp-norun const UINT reloadMessage{ RegisterWindowMessageW(L"Xenon.ReloadSettings") }; // same number in every process PostMessageW(HWND_BROADCAST, reloadMessage, 0, 0); // tell every top-level window SendMessage and PostMessage - PostMessageW puts the message in the receiver's queue and returns immediately. Fire and forget; works only with plain numbers. - SendMessageW waits until the receiver has processed the message and returns its result. If the receiver is hung, so is the sender, which is why cross-process sends should always be SendMessageTimeoutW . UIPI: the privilege boundary User Interface Privilege Isolation stops a process from sending most messages to a window of a process running at a higher integrity level . A normal program cannot send WM_COPYDATA to a program running as administrator: the message is silently dropped. The elevated program can allow specific messages with ChangeWindowMessageFilterEx(hwnd, WM_COPYDATA, MSGFLT_ALLOW, nullptr) , after which it must treat every such message as coming from a less trusted sender. When not to use messages Window messages need a window and a message loop on both sides, run on the UI thread (so heavy work blocks the interface), and are limited to one desktop. For services, background workers, large data or high rates, use pipes or shared memory. For "hand a file to the running instance of my editor", they are perfect. Check yourself quiz ? Why can a normal message not carry a pointer to data for another process? - Message parameters are only 16 bits wide + The pointer is only valid in the sender's address space - Windows clears lParam when a message crosses processes - Pointers can only be sent with PostMessageW Each process has its own address space, so a pointer from the sender means nothing to the receiver. WM_COPYDATA is the exception because Windows copies the data across. ? How long is the data of a WM_COPYDATA message valid in the receiver? - Until the receiver calls LocalFree on it - Until the sender's process exits + Only while the receiver is handling the message - Until the next WM_COPYDATA message arrives Windows copies the block in for the duration of the call only. That is also why WM_COPYDATA must be sent, not posted. ? Why use SendMessageTimeoutW rather than SendMessageW to another program? - SendMessageW cannot cross process boundaries - SendMessageTimeoutW posts the message, so it never waits - SendMessageW drops the message if the receiver is busy + A hung receiver would otherwise hang the sender indefinitely SendMessageW waits until the receiver has processed the message. With a timeout (and SMTO_ABORTIFHUNG ), a hung receiver costs at most the timeout. ? Why might WM_COPYDATA from a normal program never reach a program running as administrator? - Elevated programs ignore all messages from other processes - FindWindowW cannot find windows of elevated programs + UIPI drops it unless the elevated program allows that message - Administrator programs run on a separate desktop User Interface Privilege Isolation silently drops most messages to higher-integrity windows. The elevated program can allow one with ChangeWindowMessageFilterEx , and must then distrust its senders.

title: Packing WM_COPYDATA
body: Build and check the data of a WM_COPYDATA message (lesson 4.04) that asks a running editor to open a file. On Windows the path is UTF-16, wchar_t ; here it is std::u16string , which has the same 2-byte characters on every compiler. cpp struct CopyData { std::uint64_t type; std::vector<std::uint8_t bytes; }; constexpr std::uint64_t OPEN_FILE{ 1 }; CopyData openFileMessage(const std::u16string& path); std::optional<std::u16string readOpenFile(const CopyData& message); - openFileMessage puts the path's characters into bytes , each as 2 little-endian bytes, followed by a terminating zero character (2 zero bytes), with type OPEN_FILE . - readOpenFile accepts only messages that any program could have sent, so it checks everything: type must be OPEN_FILE ; the size must be even and at least 4 bytes (one character and the terminator); the last character must be the terminating zero; no other character may be zero; the path may be at most 32 767 characters. It returns the path without the terminator, or std::nullopt .

title: 4.05  Deadlocks and Timeouts
body: How cooperating processes get stuck waiting for each other - lock-order deadlocks, request-reply deadlocks over pipes, waiting for a peer that died - and the disciplines that prevent them - a global lock order, timeouts on every wait, never holding a lock across IPC, and watchdogs. Stuck for ever A deadlock is a set of threads or processes each waiting for something only another of them can provide. Nothing crashes, nothing logs an error; the programs simply stop responding. Across processes they are harder to find than within one, because no single debugger sees both sides. Lock-order deadlocks Two processes and two named mutexes: text Process A: lock "settings", then lock "cache" Process B: lock "cache", then lock "settings" If A takes "settings" and B takes "cache" at the same moment, each then waits for the other's mutex, for ever. Drawn as a wait-for graph (an arrow from each waiter to the holder of what it wants), a deadlock is a cycle : A waits for B, B waits for A. The fix is a global lock order : give every lock a rank and always take them in increasing order, in every process. Then a cycle cannot form, because every arrow points "up" the ranking. Writing the order down (in the code next to the names) is the cheapest deadlock prevention there is. Request-reply deadlocks Locks are not the only thing you wait for. Over pipes: - Both sides send a large message at the same time, before reading. Both pipes fill, both writes block, neither side ever reads (the stdio version was in lesson 1.04). - A server, while handling client A's request, calls into client A (a callback), while client A is blocked waiting for the reply to its request. - Process A sends a WM_COPYDATA to B while B is blocked in SendMessageW to A. The disciplines that prevent these: - Never hold a lock while doing IPC. Copy what you need, release, then send or wait. A lock held across a pipe write turns a slow peer into a frozen one. - Read continuously. A side that may need to receive while it is sending must read on another thread or with overlapped I/O. - Avoid synchronous calls back into the caller. Make callbacks asynchronous (post a message, queue an event) or design the protocol so only one side initiates requests. Waiting for the dead A process that died while you wait for its reply, its event or its mutex is the most common "deadlock" of all. Kernel objects help (pipes break, mutexes are abandoned), but an event that a dead process will never set just stays unset. - Time out every wait. INFINITE belongs only where something else (a stop event, a process handle in the same WaitForMultipleObjects ) guarantees an end. After a timeout, check whether the peer is alive (wait on its process handle with 0 timeout) before deciding to wait again or give up. - Include the peer's process handle in multi-object waits (lesson 4.02). - Use a watchdog for long-running systems: each worker updates a heartbeat (a counter in shared memory, or a periodic message); a supervisor that sees no heartbeat for a few seconds treats the worker as hung, ends it and starts another (lesson 6.02). Finding a deadlock When it happens anyway: 1. Attach a debugger to each stuck process and look at every thread's call stack: you will see each waiting in WaitForSingleObject , ReadFile or SendMessage . 2. Find out what each is waiting for: which handle, which object name. Process Explorer's handle view (and the "wait chain" view in Resource Monitor's Analyze Wait Chain) shows which objects each process has and who holds what. 3. Draw the wait-for graph. The cycle is the bug; the fix is usually an ordering rule or a lock released before an IPC call. Check yourself quiz ? What shape does a deadlock have in a wait-for graph? - A long chain that ends at a process that has exited + A cycle: each waits for the next, the last for the first - A tree with one process waiting for all the others - Two arrows pointing at the same lock Arrows go from each waiter to the holder of what it wants. A deadlock is a cycle; many waiters on one healthy holder is only contention. ? How does a global lock order prevent lock-order deadlocks? - Each lock may only be taken by one process - Locks are released in the order they were taken + Everyone takes locks in increasing rank, so no cycle can form - The process with the highest rank always wins a wait If locks are always taken lowest rank first, every wait-for arrow points "up" the ranking, so arrows can never loop back into a cycle. ? Why should a lock never be held during a pipe write or SendMessage ? - Pipe writes fail with an error while any mutex is held - Holding a lock makes the message arrive out of order - Windows releases every lock the thread holds when it writes to a pipe + A slow or hung peer then blocks everyone waiting for the lock The write or send can block on the peer, so the lock stays held for as long as the peer takes. Copy what you need, release the lock, then do the IPC. ? An event the other process should set never arrives. Why should the wait have a timeout? + The other process may have died; a timeout lets you check - Events reset themselves after a few seconds, so a long wait misses them - WaitForSingleObject with INFINITE uses a full CPU core - A timeout makes the kernel set the event for you An event a dead process will never set just stays unset. After a timeout, wait on the peer's process handle with a 0 timeout to see if it is alive, then decide.

title: Finding deadlocks
body: Given who holds which lock and who is waiting for which, find a deadlock (lesson 4.05), and check an acquisition sequence against a lock order: cpp using Holders = std::map<std::string, std::string ; // lock - process holding it using Waits = std::map<std::string, std::string ; // process - lock it is waiting for std::optional<std::vector<std::string findDeadlock(const Holders& holders, const Waits& waits); std::optional<std::string orderViolation(const std::vector<std::string & locksTaken, const std::map<std::string, int & rank); - findDeadlock builds the wait-for graph: a process waiting for a lock waits for that lock's holder. If there is a cycle, it returns the processes in the cycle in waiting order (each waits for the next, the last for the first), starting with the alphabetically smallest process in the cycle. Otherwise std::nullopt . A process waiting for a free lock, or for a lock held by a process that is not waiting, is not deadlocked. - orderViolation takes the locks one process acquires, in order (it holds them all), and returns the first lock taken while a lock of equal or higher rank is already held, or std::nullopt if the order is respected. Locks missing from rank are not checked.
