title: A lock manager
body: Build a lock service for a group of cooperating processes: named recursive locks with a declared order, fair queues of waiters, refusal of requests that would deadlock, and correct handling of a process that dies holding locks. It brings milestone 4 together in one model. cpp enum class Outcome { Acquired, AcquiredAbandoned, Waiting, Deadlock, OrderViolation }; using Grant = std::pair<int, Outcome ; // (process, how it got the lock) class LockManager { public: void setRank(const std::string& lock, int rank); Outcome acquire(int process, const std::string& lock); std::vector<Grant release(int process, const std::string& lock); std::vector<Grant processDied(int process); std::optional<int owner(const std::string& lock) const; std::vector<std::string held(int process) const; std::vector<int waiters(const std::string& lock) const; }; acquire checks, in this order: 1. If process already owns lock : its recursion count goes up; Acquired . 2. Order : if the lock has a rank and the process holds any other ranked lock of equal or higher rank: OrderViolation (nothing changes). 3. If the lock is free: the process owns it with count 1; Acquired , or AcquiredAbandoned if its last owner died holding it (that mark is then cleared). 4. Deadlock : if waiting would close a cycle (the owner, directly or through a chain of waiting processes, is waiting for a lock process holds): Deadlock (it does not wait). 5. Otherwise the process joins the end of the lock's queue: Waiting . A process waits for at most one lock at a time. release lowers the owner's count (doing nothing for a non-owner); at zero the lock passes to the first waiter in its queue, who gets it with count 1. It returns the grants made (empty or one), as Acquired . processDied removes the process from every queue, and releases every lock it owned completely (whatever the count). Each such lock passes to its first waiter with AcquiredAbandoned , or, if nobody waits, stays free but marked abandoned for the next acquirer. It returns the grants in order of lock name. held lists a process's locks sorted by name; waiters a lock's queue in order.

title: 5.01  Sockets on One Machine
body: Using sockets for local IPC - Winsock start-up, a TCP server bound to 127.0.0.1 and never to every interface, letting the system choose a port and publishing it in a file, Unix domain sockets on Windows, and how sockets compare with named pipes. Why sockets locally Named pipes are Windows-specific. Sockets are everywhere: every language, every operating system, the same API whether the other end is in the next process or on another continent. Many tools use a local socket for IPC: debuggers' remote protocols, language tooling, local web dashboards, game editors talking to a running game. The Networking course covers sockets in depth; this lesson covers what is special about using them on one machine . A loopback server cpp-norun WSADATA wsa{}; WSAStartup(MAKEWORD(2, 2), &wsa); // once per process SOCKET listener{ socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, IPPROTO_TCP) }; sockaddr_in addr{}; addr.sin_family = AF_INET; addr.sin_addr.s_addr = htonl(INADDR_LOOPBACK); // 127.0.0.1 only addr.sin_port = htons(0); // 0: let the system pick a free port bind(listener, reinterpret_cast<sockaddr (&addr), sizeof(addr)); listen(listener, SOMAXCONN); int length{ sizeof(addr) }; getsockname(listener, reinterpret_cast<sockaddr (&addr), &length); const unsigned short port{ ntohs(addr.sin_port) }; // the port it actually got SOCKET client{ accept(listener, nullptr, nullptr) }; // wait for a connection // recv / send on client , with the framing of lesson 2.03 Three choices matter for local IPC: 1. Bind to 127.0.0.1 (loopback), never to 0.0.0.0 (all interfaces). Bound to everything, your private IPC endpoint is reachable from the network, and Windows Firewall asks the user whether to allow it. Bound to loopback, only local processes can connect and no prompt appears. 2. Let the system choose the port (port 0). Fixed port numbers collide with other programs and with a second copy of your own. 3. Publish the port where the client can find it: a small file in the user's profile ( %LOCALAPPDATA%\Xenon\agent.port ) holding the port, the server's PID, and a random token the client must present (lesson 5.05). The client reads the file, connects to 127.0.0.1:port , and proves it read the file by sending the token. Unix domain sockets on Windows Windows 10 (version 1803) and later support AF_UNIX stream sockets: socket endpoints that are paths in the file system instead of ports. cpp-norun include <afunix.h SOCKET s{ socket(AF_UNIX, SOCK_STREAM, 0) }; sockaddr_un addr{}; addr.sun_family = AF_UNIX; strcpy_s(addr.sun_path, R"(C:\Users\sam\AppData\Local\Xenon\agent.sock)"); bind(s, reinterpret_cast<sockaddr (&addr), sizeof(addr)); Advantages: no ports at all, and access is controlled by the file's permissions : put it in a folder only the user can read and other users cannot connect. Code written for Linux and macOS (which have had Unix sockets for decades) ports with little change. Delete the socket file before binding again ( bind fails if it exists) and when shutting down. Sockets versus named pipes Named pipe Loopback TCP AF_UNIX --- --- --- --- Portable Windows only everywhere Windows 10+, Linux, macOS Who can connect controlled by a security descriptor any local process controlled by file permissions Discovery a name you choose a port, published somewhere a path Message mode yes no (frame yourself) no Client identity GetNamedPipeClientProcessId , impersonation nothing built in limited Across machines yes (SMB) yes no For a Windows-only program that wants strong access control, named pipes remain a good choice. For anything that might be portable, or that a tool in another language must talk to, prefer sockets, and design the security in from the start. Check yourself quiz ? Why bind a local IPC server to 127.0.0.1 rather than 0.0.0.0 ? - 0.0.0.0 only accepts IPv6 connections - 127.0.0.1 is faster because it skips the TCP handshake + 0.0.0.0 is reachable from the network; 127.0.0.1 only locally - 127.0.0.1 lets only the same user connect, while 0.0.0.0 allows every user Bound to all interfaces, a private endpoint is reachable from the network. Loopback limits it to this machine, but still to every local process, so the protocol must check who is talking. ? Why bind to port 0? + The system picks a free port, so nothing collides - Port 0 is reserved for loopback-only servers - Port 0 makes the socket invisible to other processes - Port 0 lets several servers share one port Port 0 asks the system for any free port; getsockname then tells you which one you got. A fixed number can collide with another program or a second copy of yours. ? How does a client find a server that bound to port 0? - It tries every port from 1024 upward until one answers - It asks Windows for the port with getsockname on its own socket - It always connects to port 0 on 127.0.0.1 , which is forwarded to the server + The server writes the port, its PID and a token to a known file The port changes every run, so the server publishes it, for example in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Xenon\agent.port , along with a token the client must present. getsockname only works on the server's own socket. ? What controls who may connect to an AF_UNIX socket? - The port number chosen when binding + The permissions of its path in the file system - A security descriptor passed to listen - Nothing: any local process can connect An AF_UNIX endpoint is a file system path, so the folder's and file's permissions decide who can reach it. Loopback TCP is the one with no access control.

title: Loopback endpoints and port files
body: Lesson 5.01's server binds to loopback on a system-chosen port and publishes it in a file. Write both sides of that file, and the checks a client makes: cpp struct Endpoint { std::string host; std::uint16_t port; }; struct PortFile { std::uint16_t port; std::uint32_t pid; std::string token; }; bool isLoopback(const std::string& host); std::optional<Endpoint parseEndpoint(const std::string& text); std::string writePortFile(const PortFile& f); std::optional<PortFile readPortFile(const std::string& text); - isLoopback : localhost (any case), ::1 , or an IPv4 address 127.a.b.c with each part 0 to 255. - parseEndpoint reads host:port or ::1 :port (IPv6 in brackets). The port is 1 to 65535, digits only. The host must be loopback; anything else gives std::nullopt . - writePortFile writes three lines: port=50123 , pid=4120 , token=... , each ending in \n . - readPortFile reads them back in any order, ignoring blank lines and \r ; all three keys must appear exactly once, the port must be valid, the pid a number, and the token 32 lowercase hex characters.

title: 5.02  Designing a Message Protocol
body: The decisions behind a protocol two programs will speak for years - a handshake with a magic number and version, an envelope with type, id, flags and length, kinds of messages, version negotiation, error replies, and writing it all down. A protocol is a contract Two programs talking over a pipe or a socket depend on a set of agreements: what bytes come first, what each message means, what happens when one side is newer than the other. That contract is the protocol , and it outlives the code: once two released versions of your programs speak it, changing it means staying compatible. A little design up front saves years of trouble. The handshake The first exchange on a new connection should establish that both sides speak the same protocol: text client - server HELLO magic "XIPC", version 2.3, client name "xenon-editor" server - client WELCOME version 2.1, server name "xenon-agent", capabilities - A magic number catches connections from something that is not your client at all (a port scanner, an old program on a reused port, a browser) before you try to parse its bytes as messages. - A version lets both sides agree on the dialect. A common scheme: the major version changes when old and new cannot talk at all; the minor version changes when features are added compatibly. Both sides use the same major and the lower of the two minors, and simply avoid features newer than that. - Capabilities (a list of feature names or flag bits) are an alternative or complement to minor versions: "I support compression and batch requests". If the handshake fails, say why (a message with an error code, if possible) and close the connection. The envelope Every message after the handshake shares one outer structure, the envelope , so that any message can be framed, routed and logged without understanding its payload: Field Size Purpose --- --- --- length 4 frame length (lesson 2.03) type 1 or 2 what kind of message flags 1 bits such as "this is a reply", "this is an error" id 4 matches replies to requests (lesson 5.04) payload rest type-specific content (lesson 5.03) Kinds of messages Almost every protocol needs the same three kinds: - Requests : "do this and tell me the result". Carry an id. - Responses : the result of one request, carrying its id; either a success with data or an error with a code and a message. - Events (notifications): sent without being asked, such as "file changed" or "build finished". No reply expected. Keep error replies structured: a numeric code that programs can act on ("not found", "bad argument", "busy", "not supported in this version") plus a human-readable message for logs. Rules that keep a protocol healthy - Unknown message types : reply "not supported" (for requests) or ignore (for events). Never crash, never close the connection. - Unknown fields : skip them, if the encoding allows (lesson 5.03). This is what lets a newer sender add fields that an older receiver ignores. - Limits : maximum message size, maximum outstanding requests, maximum string lengths. Write them in the specification and enforce them. - Text or binary? Text (JSON) is easy to debug and to speak from any language; binary is compact and fast. JSON lines or JSON with a length header (like the Language Server Protocol) are fine for most tools; reach for binary when messages are frequent or large. - Write it down. A short specification (one page with the envelope, the message types and their payloads, versions and limits) is worth more than any amount of "the code is the documentation", especially when the other side is written by someone else or in another language. Check yourself quiz ? What is the magic number in a handshake for? - To encrypt the rest of the conversation - To tell the server which version the client speaks + To spot at once a peer that does not speak this protocol - To give each connection a unique identifier A port scanner, a browser or an old program can connect to your endpoint. A fixed magic number at the start catches that at once; the version field, not the magic, says which dialect. ? A client speaks 2.3 and the server 2.1. Which version do they use? - 2.3: the higher minor version, since the client is newer + 2.1: the same major version and the lower minor version - None: different minor versions cannot talk - 3.0: the next major version both can support Minor versions add features compatibly, so both sides agree on the lower minor and avoid newer features. Only a different major version means they cannot talk at all. ? Why do all messages share one envelope? - So that every message has the same total size - So that the payload can be encrypted separately - So that messages can be sent without a length field + So generic code can frame, route and log any message The envelope's length, type, flags and id are the same for every message, so generic code can frame, dispatch, match replies and log, leaving the payload to type-specific code. ? What should a receiver do with a request type it does not know? - Close the connection, because the sender is broken - Ignore it silently and send nothing back + Reply "not supported" and carry on with the connection - Treat it as a ping and reply with its own version A newer sender may use types an older receiver lacks. A request still deserves a reply, so the client is not left waiting; unknown events can simply be ignored.

title: Handshake and envelope
body: Implement the opening of lesson 5.02's protocol: the handshake, version negotiation, and the envelope every later message uses. cpp struct Version { std::uint16_t major, minor; }; struct Envelope { std::uint8_t type; std::uint8_t flags; std::uint32_t id; std::vector<std::uint8_t payload; }; std::vector<std::uint8_t encodeHello(Version v); std::optional<Version decodeHello(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & bytes); std::optional<Version negotiate(Version client, const std::vector<Version & serverSupports); std::vector<std::uint8_t encodeEnvelope(const Envelope& e); std::optional<Envelope decodeEnvelope(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & bytes); - A hello is 8 bytes: X I P C , then the major and minor versions as 2-byte little-endian numbers. decodeHello checks the length and the magic. - negotiate : the server supports one or more major versions, each with its highest minor. If it supports the client's major, the result is that major with the lower of the two minors; otherwise std::nullopt . - An envelope is type (1 byte), flags (1 byte), id (4 bytes little-endian), then the payload. decodeEnvelope needs at least those 6 bytes.

title: 5.03  Serialising Data
body: Turning values into bytes both sides read the same way - fixed-width little-endian numbers, length-prefixed UTF-8 strings, variable-length integers and zigzag encoding, tag-length-value records that let new fields be added without breaking old readers, and when to use JSON or a library instead. Never send a struct's memory The tempting shortcut is send(socket, &settings, sizeof(settings)) . It breaks as soon as anything differs between the two sides: padding between members, the size of long , a std::string member (a pointer into the sender's heap), a newer version with an added field. Serialise instead: write each value in a defined byte format, and read it back the same way. Building blocks Fixed-width integers , in a stated byte order. Little-endian is the usual choice for new protocols between PCs: cpp-norun void putU32(std::vector<std::uint8_t & out, std::uint32_t v) { for (int i{ 0 }; i < 4; ++i) out.push_back(static_cast<std::uint8_t (v (8 i))); } Strings as a length followed by the bytes, in UTF-8 (convert from Windows' UTF-16 at the edge). Never rely on a terminating zero in the data. Booleans as one byte, 0 or 1; reject other values on reading. Floating point as the IEEE bit pattern ( std::bit_cast<std::uint32_t (f) ), which every modern machine shares. Variable-length integers Most numbers in messages are small (ids, counts, lengths), so spending 8 bytes on each is wasteful. A varint (LEB128) uses 7 bits per byte, with the top bit saying "more bytes follow": text 1 - 01 127 - 7F 128 - 80 01 (low 7 bits 0000000 with "more", then 1) 300 - AC 02 (300 = 0b10_0101100: 0101100 more = 0xAC, then 10 = 0x02) Small numbers take one byte, large ones up to ten. Negative numbers would always take ten bytes, so signed values are first zigzag-encoded , mapping 0, −1, 1, −2, 2, ... to 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, ...: (n << 1) ^ (n 63) . Protocol Buffers uses exactly these two tricks. Readers must reject varints that are too long (more than 10 bytes) or that overflow, since the bytes come from another process. Tag, length, value For messages that will grow over time, write each field as a tag (which field), a length (how many bytes), and the value . A reader that meets a tag it does not know skips length bytes and carries on: text field 1 (name): 01 05 41 64 61 4D 73 tag 1, 5 bytes, "AdaMs" field 2 (volume): 02 01 4B tag 2, 1 byte, varint 75 field 9 (new!): 09 02 xx xx an old reader skips these 2 bytes This is what makes schema evolution possible: a newer sender adds fields; an older receiver ignores them; a newer receiver handles their absence from an older sender with defaults. The rules: never reuse a tag number for a different meaning, never change a field's type, and treat every field as optional. Or use JSON, or a library - JSON is self-describing text: easy to read in logs, available in every language, naturally tolerant of extra fields. It is slower and bigger, and numbers lose precision beyond 2^53. Excellent for tools and control messages. - Protocol Buffers , FlatBuffers , MessagePack and Cap'n Proto give compact binary formats, code generation from a schema, and the evolution rules above, already tested. For a large or long-lived protocol, a library beats a home-made format. Writing the building blocks yourself once, as this lesson's practice does, is still the best way to understand what those libraries do and to debug their output in a hex dump. Check yourself quiz ? Why not send a struct's raw bytes? - send cannot take a pointer to a struct - Structs are always larger than their serialised form + Padding, type sizes and heap pointers can differ between the sides - The receiver must allocate the struct before the bytes arrive Raw memory depends on the compiler, the platform and the version: padding, long 's size, a std::string 's heap pointer, added fields. Serialise each value in a defined format instead. ? Encode 300 as a varint. - 2C 01 - 01 2C + AC 02 - 82 2C 300 is 0b10_0101100 . The low 7 bits 0101100 (0x2C) with the "more" bit become 0xAC ; the remaining bits 10 are 0x02 . 2C 01 is 300 as a plain little-endian 16-bit number. ? Why zigzag-encode signed numbers before writing them as varints? - So that the varint fits in exactly 4 bytes + Negatives would take ten bytes; zigzag keeps small ones short - So that the reader can tell signed fields from unsigned ones - Varints cannot store the sign bit at all In two's complement a small negative number has all its high bits set, so as a varint it takes ten bytes. Zigzag maps 0, -1, 1, -2, ... to 0, 1, 2, 3, ..., keeping small values short. ? How does tag-length-value let old readers handle new fields? - New fields are always put at the end, so old readers stop before them - Old readers ask the sender to resend without the new fields - The tag tells the reader the field's type, so it can decode any field + They skip any tag they do not know by its length and continue with the next field Every field carries its own length, so an unknown tag can be skipped exactly. That is what lets a newer sender add fields without breaking older receivers.

title: Varints and tagged fields
body: Write the serialisation building blocks of lesson 5.03 and use them for a message that can grow new fields: cpp void putVarint(std::vector<std::uint8_t & out, std::uint64_t value); std::optional<std::uint64_t getVarint(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & in, std::size_t& at); std::uint64_t zigzag(std::int64_t n); std::int64_t unzigzag(std::uint64_t z); struct Settings { std::optional<std::string name; std::optional<std::int64_t volume; std::optional<bool fullscreen; }; std::vector<std::uint8_t encodeSettings(const Settings& s); std::optional<Settings decodeSettings(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & bytes); - putVarint writes LEB128: 7 bits at a time, lowest first, top bit set on every byte except the last. getVarint reads one at at and moves at past it; it fails (returning std::nullopt ) if the bytes run out or the value would need more than 10 bytes. - zigzag maps 0, -1, 1, -2, 2 ... to 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 ...; unzigzag undoes it. - encodeSettings writes each field that is present, in tag order, as: tag (varint), length (varint), value. Tag 1 name : the UTF-8 bytes. Tag 2 volume : a varint of its zigzag. Tag 3 fullscreen : one byte, 0 or 1. - decodeSettings reads fields in any order. Unknown tags are skipped using their length. It fails on a truncated field, a field whose value does not fill its length exactly, a boolean other than 0 or 1, or a field that appears twice.

title: 5.04  Requests, Responses and Events
body: The flow of a conversation - request ids that match responses to requests, many requests in flight at once, timeouts and cancellation, events the server sends unasked, what ordering a stream does and does not guarantee, and safe retries. One at a time is too slow The simplest client sends a request and waits for the response before sending the next. That works, but a slow request (indexing a large project) blocks every quick one behind it, and every request pays the full round trip. Real protocols let several requests be in flight at once, which needs a way to tell responses apart. Correlation ids Each request carries an id chosen by the sender, unique among its outstanding requests (a counter is fine). The response carries the same id. The client keeps a table of pending requests: text id 41 findSymbol("Player") sent at 10.000 s id 42 formatFile("a.cpp") sent at 10.002 s id 43 ping sent at 10.003 s <- response id 43 "pong" (answered first: it was quick) <- response id 41 3 results <- response id 42 error "file locked" When a response arrives, the client looks up its id, removes the entry and delivers the result to whoever is waiting: a callback, a promise, or a coroutine. A response with an unknown id (late, after a timeout; or a bug) is logged and dropped. JSON-RPC 2.0, used by the Language Server Protocol, is exactly this: {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":41,"method":"findSymbol","params":{...}} and a response {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":41,"result":...} , with notifications having no id . Timeouts and cancellation Every pending request needs a deadline . A periodic check (or a timer) finds requests past their deadline, removes them from the table and reports a timeout to the caller. If the server answers later, the response no longer matches anything and is dropped. A timeout on the client does not stop the work on the server. For expensive requests, add a cancel message ( cancel id 41 ) that the server uses to abandon the work. It may still send a response (a result or a "cancelled" error), and the client must cope with either. Events The server often needs to speak first: a file changed on disk, a build finished, a log line. These are events (notifications): a message type with no id and no response. Clients subscribe to the events they want, so a server does not flood clients with messages they will ignore. Events and responses share one connection, so the client's reading loop dispatches each incoming message by kind: response (match the id) or event (call the subscriber). Ordering A single stream (one pipe or TCP connection) delivers messages in the order they were sent . That gives useful guarantees: two events sent in order arrive in order, and a response sent after an event arrives after it. It does not mean responses come back in the order requests were sent, if the server handles requests concurrently. Design so that clients never depend on response order, only on ids. Across several connections there is no ordering at all. Retries and idempotency After a timeout or a dropped connection, the client may not know whether the server performed a request. Retrying is safe only if the request is idempotent : doing it twice has the same effect as once ( setVolume(70) , getStatus ). For requests that are not ( appendLog , createFile ), either let the server recognise a repeated request by a request key chosen by the client and return the original result, or report the uncertainty to the user instead of retrying blindly. Check yourself quiz ? How does a client match a response to its request? - By the order responses arrive in + By the id it sent, echoed back - By the time the response arrives - By the message type of the response Each request carries an id unique among the client's outstanding requests; the response returns it, so the client finds the pending entry whatever order responses come in. ? What should a client do with a response whose id matches no pending request? - Deliver it to the oldest pending request - Close the connection as a protocol error + Log it and drop it: it is probably a late answer - Resend the request with that id After a timeout the client removes the request from its table, so a late answer matches nothing. It is expected occasionally, not a reason to drop the connection. ? Does one connection guarantee responses arrive in the order requests were sent? - Yes: a stream delivers everything in order, so responses do too - Yes, as long as the server uses a thread per request + No: a concurrent server may answer requests in any order - No: a stream can reorder any messages, even in one direction The stream keeps the order the server sends in, but the server may answer a quick request before a slow one. Clients should rely on ids, never on response order. ? Which of these is safe to retry blindly: setVolume(70) or appendLog("x") ? - appendLog("x") : the log ignores duplicate lines - Both, because the server will see each request only once - Neither: no request is ever safe to retry + setVolume(70) , because it is idempotent Doing setVolume(70) twice leaves the same result as once. A non-idempotent request needs a request key the server recognises, or the uncertainty reported to the user.

title: Pending requests
body: Keep the client's table of requests in flight (lesson 5.04): ids, deadlines, matching responses, and timeouts. cpp struct Done { std::uint32_t id; std::string method; std::string outcome; }; class PendingRequests { public: explicit PendingRequests(std::uint32_t maxInFlight); std::optional<std::uint32_t send(const std::string& method, std::uint64_t now, std::uint64_t timeout); std::optional<Done response(std::uint32_t id, const std::string& result); std::vector<Done expire(std::uint64_t now); std::vector<Done connectionLost(); std::size_t inFlight() const; }; - send gives the request the next id (1, 2, 3, ... never reused) and a deadline of now + timeout , and returns its id; if maxInFlight requests are already pending it returns std::nullopt and uses no id. - response completes the pending request with that id, returning it with outcome set to result ; an unknown id (late or bogus) returns std::nullopt . - expire completes every request whose deadline is at or before now , with outcome timeout , in id order. - connectionLost completes every pending request with outcome connection lost , in id order.

title: 5.05  Securing Local Communication
body: Local IPC is an attack surface - other users, other programs and even web pages can reach it. Access control on pipes and objects, preventing pipe squatting, checking which program you are talking to, tokens for localhost sockets, the Host header against DNS rebinding, validating every message, and the dangers of impersonation. "Local" is not "safe" It is tempting to assume that anything talking to your local pipe or port is your own program. It is not: - Other users on the same machine (a shared PC, a terminal server) can reach Global\ objects, pipes with default permissions, and every localhost port. - Any program the user runs, including malware with no special rights, can connect to the user's own pipes and ports. - Web pages in a browser can make requests to http://127.0.0.1:port and, with tricks such as DNS rebinding, read the answers. A local IPC endpoint that performs actions (run a build, write a file, read settings) is a privilege boundary. Design it like one. Access control on pipes and objects Named pipes, mappings, events and mutexes accept a security descriptor that lists who may open them. Written in SDDL (Security Descriptor Definition Language): cpp-norun // Only the current user (the owner) and SYSTEM may connect; nothing inherited from defaults. PSECURITY_DESCRIPTOR sd{}; ConvertStringSecurityDescriptorToSecurityDescriptorW(L"D:P(A;;GA;;;OW)(A;;GA;;;SY)", SDDL_REVISION_1, &sd, nullptr); SECURITY_ATTRIBUTES sa{ sizeof(sa), sd, FALSE }; HANDLE pipe{ CreateNamedPipeW(name, PIPE_ACCESS_DUPLEX FILE_FLAG_FIRST_PIPE_INSTANCE, / ... /, &sa) }; LocalFree(sd); D:P is a protected list of permissions; (A;;GA;;;OW) allows ( A ) all access ( GA ) to the object's owner ( OW ); SY is the system account. For a service that desktop programs must reach, allow the specific group or user that should connect, not "Everyone". Pipe squatting A malicious program can create your pipe name before your server starts, and your client then connects to the impostor and sends it whatever it sends the real server. Defences: - The server creates its first instance with FILE_FLAG_FIRST_PIPE_INSTANCE : if the name already exists, creation fails and the server knows something is wrong instead of silently sharing the name. - The client verifies the server: GetNamedPipeServerProcessId gives the server's PID; check that process's image path (and, for high-value cases, its code signature) is your server's. - Use names that include something an attacker cannot predict, such as a random value from a file only the user can read. Tokens for sockets Localhost TCP ports have no access control at all. The usual defence is a secret token : the server generates a random token at start-up ( BCryptGenRandom , at least 128 bits), writes it with the port into a file in the user's profile (readable only by that user), and requires every client to send it first. Compare tokens in constant time (examine every byte, whatever the first mismatch), so the comparison's timing cannot leak how many leading bytes were right. Browsers and DNS rebinding If your local server speaks HTTP, any web page can try to talk to it. Browsers' same-origin rules stop a page reading responses from 127.0.0.1 directly, but DNS rebinding gets around that: an attacker's domain first resolves to their server and then to 127.0.0.1 , so the browser thinks the page and your local server share an origin. Defences: - Check the Host header : accept only localhost:PORT or 127.0.0.1:PORT . A rebinding attack arrives with the attacker's domain in Host . - Check the Origin header on requests that change anything, and refuse unknown origins. - Require the token as well; a web page cannot read the user's token file. Validate everything, assume nothing Every byte from the other side is untrusted input: lengths (lesson 2.03), message types, string contents, paths. A path from a client must be checked before use (no .. escaping an allowed folder, no device names); a request to run something must never become a command line built from client text. Treat a local client with the same suspicion as a network client. Impersonation, carefully A pipe server can call ImpersonateNamedPipeClient to act with the client's rights, which is how a service safely opens a file on behalf of a user: Windows checks the user's permissions, not the service's. The danger runs the other way: a client that connects to a malicious server lets that server impersonate the client. Clients of pipes they do not fully trust should open them with SECURITY_SQOS_PRESENT SECURITY_IDENTIFICATION in CreateFileW 's flags, which lets the server identify the client but not act as it. Check yourself quiz ? What does FILE_FLAG_FIRST_PIPE_INSTANCE protect against? + Pipe squatting: an impostor creating the pipe's name first - Remote clients connecting over the network - A client connecting before the server is ready - Two clients using the same instance at once Without the flag, a server whose name was taken first would just create another instance of the impostor's pipe. With it, creation fails and the server knows something is wrong. Remote clients are blocked by PIPE_REJECT_REMOTE_CLIENTS . ? Why do localhost TCP servers need a token? - Loopback connections are not encrypted, and the token encrypts them + Any local process, and web pages, can reach a localhost port - The token tells the server which port the client used - Windows refuses loopback connections without a token Localhost ports have no access control. A random token stored in a file only the user can read is something other users, malware without access and web pages cannot present. ? How does checking the Host header defend against DNS rebinding? - It makes the browser resolve the name again - It proves the request came from the same user's process - It blocks every request that does not use HTTPS + A rebinding request carries the attacker's domain in Host The browser connects to 127.0.0.1 but still sends the attacker's domain in Host . A server that accepts only localhost:PORT or 127.0.0.1:PORT turns it away. ? Why should a client open an untrusted pipe with SECURITY_IDENTIFICATION ? - So the server must prove its own identity before the connection opens - So the client can impersonate the server + So the server can identify the client but not impersonate it - So the pipe is encrypted between the two processes A malicious server could call ImpersonateNamedPipeClient and act as the client. The identification level lets it see who the client is, but not act with the client's rights.

title: Guarding a localhost endpoint
body: A local tool exposes a small HTTP API on 127.0.0.1:PORT . Write the checks from lesson 5.05 that every request must pass before it is handled: cpp struct Request { std::string method; // "GET", "POST", ... std::map<std::string, std::string headers; // header names in lower case }; bool constantTimeEquals(const std::string& a, const std::string& b); std::string checkRequest(const Request& r, std::uint16_t port, const std::string& token); - constantTimeEquals : false if the lengths differ; otherwise it compares every byte, combining the differences, and only decides at the end (no early return on the first mismatch). - checkRequest returns "ok" or the reason for refusing, checking in this order: 1. host must be exactly localhost:PORT or 127.0.0.1:PORT : else "bad host" (the DNS rebinding defence). 2. For any method other than GET , an origin header, if present, must be http://localhost:PORT or http://127.0.0.1:PORT : else "bad origin" . 3. authorization must be Bearer followed by the token, compared in constant time: else "bad token" .

title: Agreeing on a version
body: Let a client and server agree on a protocol version when they connect. client supports 1-3, server supports 2-4 - use 3 client supports 1-1, server supports 2-4 - no common version

title: Matching replies to requests
body: Send requests with ids and match replies that come back in any order. send 1 getUser, 2 getScore, 3 getUser reply 2 - getScore done (score 77) reply 1 - getUser done (ada) reply 9 - unknown id, ignored 3 timed out after 500 ms

title: A TLV encoder
body: Serialise values as type-length-value records that old readers can skip. encode {name: "ada", level: 7, admin: true} - 01 03 'ada' 02 04 07 00 00 00 03 01 01 decode - name ada, level 7, admin true unknown tag 09 skipped

title: Only my programs may connect
body: Make a local server check that a client knows a secret before serving it, without sending the secret. server sends challenge 8f3a... client answers HMAC(secret, challenge) server: answer correct - connected another client with a wrong secret - refused replaying an old answer - refused (new challenge each time)

title: A small RPC layer
body: Put milestone 5 together: a remote procedure call layer that lets one process call named methods in another, with ids, errors, timeouts and events. The transport (a pipe or socket with framing) is left out: messages are passed as byte vectors, one per frame. Wire format. Every message is: a type byte ( 1 request, 2 response, 3 error, 4 event), a 4-byte little-endian id, then fields. A string is a 2-byte little-endian length and that many bytes. A list is a 1-byte count followed by that many strings. Type Fields after the id --- --- request method name (string), arguments (list) response result (string) error message (string) event event name (string), arguments (list); its id is 0 cpp using Message = std::vector<std::uint8_t ; using Method = std::function<std::string(const std::vector<std::string &) ; class RpcServer { public: void method(const std::string& name, Method fn); Message handle(const Message& incoming); Message event(const std::string& name, const std::vector<std::string & args); }; class RpcClient { public: Message call(const std::string& method, const std::vector<std::string & args, std::uint64_t now, std::uint64_t timeout, std::uint32_t& id); void handle(const Message& incoming); std::optional<std::string result(std::uint32_t id); std::optional<std::string error(std::uint32_t id); std::vector<std::uint32_t expire(std::uint64_t now); std::vector<std::pair<std::string, std::vector<std::string takeEvents(); }; Server. method registers a handler. handle decodes a request and returns the reply: a response with the handler's result; an error unknown method NAME ; an error with the exception's message if the handler throws std::invalid_argument ; or, if the bytes are not a well-formed request (wrong type, truncated, leftover bytes), an error with id 0 and message malformed message . event encodes an event. Client. call gives the request the next id (from 1), remembers it with a deadline of now + timeout , sets id and returns the encoded request. handle decodes a message from the server: a response or error for a pending id completes that request (anything for an unknown id is ignored); an event is queued. Malformed messages are ignored. result and error return a completed request's outcome once , then forget it. expire removes and returns, in id order, pending requests whose deadline is at or before now . takeEvents returns the queued events in order and clears them.

title: 6.01  A Single-Instance Application
body: Making a second launch hand its work to the copy already running - a named mutex to detect the first instance, forwarding the command line through a pipe or WM_COPYDATA, resolving relative paths with the sender's folder, bringing the window to the front, and the races when two copies start at once. One copy, many launches Double-click a document while your editor is open, and the user expects the document to open in the running editor , not in a second copy. The pattern is common enough to have a name: a single-instance application . It combines three pieces from this course: a named kernel object to detect the first instance, an IPC channel to hand over the command line, and window activation. Detecting the first instance cpp-norun const std::wstring name{ LR"(Local\Xenon.Editor.)" + currentUserSid() }; // per user HANDLE instance{ CreateMutexW(nullptr, FALSE, name.c_str()) }; const bool primary{ GetLastError() != ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS }; // keep instance open for the whole life of the primary: its existence is the signal The first process creates the mutex and becomes the primary ; every later one sees ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS and becomes a secondary . The mutex is never locked; only its existence matters, and because Windows closes it when the primary exits (even by crashing), a stale "running" signal cannot survive. Choose the scope with the name: Local\ plus the user's identity gives one instance per user per session, which is usually right. A global name would make two users on one machine fight over one instance. Forwarding the command line The secondary must hand its arguments to the primary and exit. Either channel works: - WM_COPYDATA to the primary's window (lesson 4.04): simple, if the primary has a window and runs at the same integrity level. - A named pipe the primary listens on (milestone 2): works for background processes too, and lets the primary reply ("opened", or an error). What to send is not just the arguments. Relative paths ( notes.md , ..\docs\a.md ) mean something only relative to the secondary's current folder, which the primary does not share. Send the secondary's current directory along with the arguments, and let the primary resolve paths against it (or resolve them before sending). Bringing the window forward Windows restricts which process may steal the foreground, so that background programs cannot pop up over what the user is doing. The secondary was just launched by the user, so it may set the foreground, and it can pass that right on: cpp-norun AllowSetForegroundWindow(primaryPid); // in the secondary, before forwarding // the primary, on receiving the request: if (IsIconic(window)) ShowWindow(window, SW_RESTORE); SetForegroundWindow(window); Without that, the primary's window just flashes in the taskbar. The races - Two launches at once. Both call CreateMutexW at nearly the same moment; the kernel guarantees exactly one creates it. But the secondary may try to forward before the primary has created its pipe or window. The secondary must retry for a short while (a second or two) before giving up. - The primary is shutting down. The secondary forwards to a primary that is about to exit, and the request is lost. Have the primary close the mutex first when shutting down, so new launches become primaries themselves, and accept that a request arriving during shutdown may need a retry. - The primary is hung. Forwarding with a timeout ( SendMessageTimeoutW , or a pipe with a timeout) lets the secondary tell the user, or start anyway as a second instance, rather than hanging too. Check yourself quiz ? How does a launched copy know another instance is already running? - CreateMutexW on the shared name fails and returns nullptr - WaitForSingleObject on the mutex returns WAIT_TIMEOUT , because the primary holds it + CreateMutexW on the shared name succeeds with ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS - FindWindowW returns the window of the program that launched it Creating an existing named object opens it and succeeds, with GetLastError() set to ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS . The mutex is never locked; only its existence matters. ? Why must the secondary send its current directory with the arguments? + Its relative paths mean nothing in the primary's folder - The primary needs it to find the secondary's executable - Windows requires a directory in every WM_COPYDATA message - So the primary can change its own current directory to match notes.md or ..\docs\a.md only mean something relative to where the secondary was started. Send the directory so the primary can resolve them, or resolve them before sending. ? Why call AllowSetForegroundWindow in the secondary? - It brings the secondary's own window to the front before it exits - It lets the secondary send WM_COPYDATA across integrity levels + It hands the primary the right to take the foreground - It restores the primary's window if it is minimised Background processes may not steal the foreground. The secondary, just launched by the user, may, and passes that right on; otherwise the primary's window only flashes in the taskbar. ? Why should the secondary retry forwarding for a short time? - The primary only reads its pipe once a second - WM_COPYDATA messages are dropped the first time they are sent - The mutex takes a moment to become signalled + The primary may not have created its pipe or window yet The kernel guarantees only one process creates the mutex, but the primary still needs time to create its pipe or window. A short retry covers that gap.

title: Forwarding a command line
body: A second launch of a single-instance editor forwards its arguments and its current folder to the running copy (lesson 6.01). Write the encoding of that request and the primary's resolution of the files to open: cpp struct Forwarded { std::string cwd; std::vector<std::string args; }; std::string encodeForward(const Forwarded& f); std::optional<Forwarded decodeForward(const std::string& text); std::string resolvePath(const std::string& cwd, const std::string& path); std::vector<std::string filesToOpen(const Forwarded& f); - encodeForward writes cwd , then each argument, each followed by a zero byte ( '\0' ); decodeForward reads them back. Text that is empty or does not end with a zero is malformed. - resolvePath uses Windows rules with \ : a path starting with a drive ( C:\ ) or \\ (a network path) is already absolute; otherwise it is joined to cwd . Then . parts are removed and .. removes the previous part (never going above the drive or the \\server\share ). The result never ends with \ unless it is just a drive root ( C:\ ). - filesToOpen takes the arguments that are not options (options start with - or / ) and resolves each against cwd , keeping their order and skipping exact duplicates of a path already listed (compare ignoring case).

title: 6.02  Worker Processes
body: Doing work in separate processes on purpose - isolating crashes, using several cores, running with fewer rights - and the supervisor that starts workers, watches their heartbeats, restarts them with exponential backoff, and stops trying when they keep crashing. Why split work into processes Threads are cheaper, so why would a program start extra worker processes ? Because a process gives things a thread cannot: - Crash isolation. A worker parsing an untrusted file, running a third-party plugin, or compiling user code can crash without taking the main program with it. The main program reports the failure and starts a new worker. - Memory isolation. A worker that leaks or fragments its heap can simply be restarted from time to time. - Fewer rights. A worker can run with a restricted token or inside an AppContainer, so even a compromised worker can do little. Browsers render every site in such a sandboxed process. - Parallelism without shared state. Workers that share nothing need no locks between them. The cost is communication: everything a worker needs must be sent to it, and results sent back, through the channels of this course. The supervisor A process that starts and watches workers is a supervisor . Its jobs: 1. Start each worker, inside a job object so they all end if the supervisor dies (lesson 1.03), with a channel to talk to it. 2. Watch it: wait on its process handle to learn the moment it exits, and on a heartbeat (a regular "still alive" message, or a counter it increments in shared memory) to detect a worker that is alive but hung. 3. Stop it gracefully when asked: send "stop", wait a few seconds, then TerminateProcess if needed. 4. Restart it when it fails, according to a policy. A restart policy Restarting immediately and for ever is a bad policy: a worker that crashes at start-up (a missing file, a bad configuration) would restart hundreds of times a second, filling logs and burning CPU. Good supervisors use: - Exponential backoff : wait 1 s before the first restart, then 2 s, 4 s, 8 s... up to a maximum (say 60 s). Transient problems get quick retries; persistent ones stop hammering the system. - A reset after success : if the worker ran for a good while (say 5 minutes) before failing, the next restart starts again from 1 s; it was a one-off failure, not a crash loop. - Giving up : if it has crashed, say, 5 times within 10 minutes, stop restarting, mark the feature unavailable and tell the user (or an administrator). A human needs to look. - Clean exits are not failures : a worker that exits with code 0 because it finished its job is not restarted. Windows services have this built in (the "Recovery" tab of a service's properties sets first, second and later failure actions with delays); your own supervisor implements the same idea. Heartbeats and hangs A hung worker is worse than a crashed one: its process handle never signals. A heartbeat closes the gap. The worker sends one every second, for example; the supervisor treats three seconds without one as a hang, terminates the worker (it is not going to stop gracefully) and handles it like a crash, with a distinct reason in the log. The heartbeat must come from the worker's real work loop , not from a separate timer thread that keeps ticking while the work is stuck. Logging Every start, exit (with its exit code described as in lesson 1.03), restart delay and give-up should be logged with the worker's name and PID. Crash loops are diagnosed from these logs, often long after the fact. Check yourself quiz ? Which pair are both reasons to run work in a separate process instead of a thread? - Faster communication and shared memory by default + Crash isolation and running with fewer rights - Cheaper start-up and a smaller memory footprint - Shared heaps and no need for serialisation Processes give crash isolation, memory isolation, fewer rights and parallel work without shared state. They cost more to start and to talk to than threads. ? Why use exponential backoff for restarts? - It makes each restart faster than the last - Windows refuses to restart a process more than once a second + So a worker that crashes at start-up does not restart in a tight loop - It spreads the workers' memory use over time Restarting at once for ever turns a crash at start-up into hundreds of restarts a second. Delays of 1, 2, 4, 8 s up to a cap retry quickly for transient faults and stop hammering for persistent ones. ? When should a supervisor stop restarting a worker? - After its first crash, so the user is told at once - When it exits with code 0 + After too many failures in a short time, such as 5 in 10 minutes - Never: a supervisor should always restart its workers A burst of failures means something is persistently wrong. Mark the feature unavailable and tell someone. A clean exit with code 0 is not a failure and is not restarted. ? Why must the heartbeat come from the worker's main work loop? - Timer threads are not allowed to write to pipes + A timer thread could tick on while the real work is hung - The main loop is the only thread that can access shared memory - Heartbeats from other threads arrive out of order The heartbeat should prove the work is progressing. A timer thread keeps ticking even when the work loop is stuck, so the supervisor would never notice the hang.

title: A restart policy
body: Decide what a supervisor does when a worker exits (lesson 6.02). Times are in seconds. cpp struct Decision { bool restart; std::uint64_t at; std::string reason; }; class RestartPolicy { public: void started(std::uint64_t now); Decision exited(std::uint32_t exitCode, std::uint64_t now); bool gaveUp() const; }; - started records that the worker (re)started at now . - exited decides: - exit code 0: no restart, reason finished . - Otherwise it is a failure. Remember the time of the failure. If there have been 5 failures within the last 600 seconds (counting this one, times now - 600 to now inclusive), give up: no restart, reason crash loop , and gaveUp stays true; any later exit is also answered with crash loop . - If the worker had run for 300 seconds or more since its last start, the delay resets to 1 second. - Otherwise the delay is 1 second for the first failure and doubles with each failure in a row, up to 60 seconds. - Restart at now + delay , reason restart in Ns .

title: 6.03  Plugins in Separate Processes
body: Running extensions out of process, as editors and browsers do - the host and plugin protocol, manifests and API version compatibility, subscribing plugins to events, timeouts for slow plugins, disabling misbehaving ones, and what isolation does and does not protect. In-process and out-of-process plugins The DLLs course built plugins as DLLs loaded into the host: fast, direct function calls, but a plugin that crashes or corrupts memory takes the host down with it, and a plugin cannot be stopped without stopping the host. Out-of-process plugins run in their own processes and talk to the host through IPC. VS Code runs every extension in a separate extension host process; browsers run extensions and every site in separate processes; audio workstations can run plugins "sandboxed". The host survives any plugin failure, can stop a plugin at any moment, and can give plugins fewer rights than itself. The price is that every interaction is a message: calls are slower, data must be serialised, and the plugin API must be designed as a protocol (milestone 5) rather than as C++ interfaces. The manifest Each plugin ships a manifest the host reads before starting anything: json { "name": "word-count", "version": "1.4.0", "api": "2.3", "entry": "word-count.exe", "events": "documentSaved", "selectionChanged" , "commands": "wordCount.show" } From it the host decides whether the plugin is compatible (API major version equal, minor version not newer than the host's: the rules of lesson 5.02), which events to send it, and which commands it provides, all without running its code. A host that starts plugins only when one of their events or commands is first needed (lazy activation) starts fast even with many plugins installed. The conversation A typical host and plugin protocol: 1. The host starts the plugin process (with a pipe on its stdio, or a named pipe whose name it passes as an argument) in a job object. 2. Handshake : versions and capabilities. 3. The host sends events the plugin subscribed to; the plugin sends requests to the host API (read the document, show a message) and gets responses. 4. The host sends commands the user invoked; the plugin replies. 5. On shutdown, a "deactivate" message, a short wait, then termination. Slow and broken plugins Plugins will misbehave, and the host must stay responsive whatever they do: - Every request to a plugin has a timeout. A command that takes too long is reported to the user as failed; the host does not wait for ever. - Count failures per plugin. After several timeouts or crashes in a short period, disable the plugin and tell the user which one it was, so they know what to update or remove. - Do not let one plugin block another. Each plugin has its own connection and queue; a busy plugin delays only its own messages. (VS Code puts all extensions in one host process, which is a compromise: one heavy extension slows the others, but the editor itself stays responsive.) What isolation protects, and what it does not A separate process protects the host from a plugin's crashes, hangs and memory corruption . It does not stop a plugin from doing harm with the rights it has: a plugin process running as the user can read the user's files, whatever API the host offers it. Real protection from untrusted plugins needs a restricted process (a low-integrity token, an AppContainer, a job object with UI restrictions) that cannot reach files or the network directly, so everything must go through the host's API, which can check each request. Browsers do exactly that for web content. Check yourself quiz ? What does running a plugin out of process protect the host from? - A plugin reading the user's files - A plugin sending data over the network + Its crashes, hangs and memory corruption - Every security problem, since the plugin cannot see the host's memory A separate process contains crashes and corruption, and the host can stop it. It does not stop the plugin from using the user's rights; that needs a restricted token or sandbox. ? Why read a manifest before starting a plugin? - To load the plugin's DLL into the host faster + To check it is compatible without running its code - To find out how much memory the plugin will use - To sign the plugin so Windows will run it The manifest tells the host whether the API version is compatible, which events to send and which commands it offers, so the host can start plugins only when first needed. ? A plugin times out on three commands in a minute. What should the host do? - Raise its timeout so the commands can finish - Restart the host so the plugin starts cleanly - Keep sending commands; timeouts are expected for plugins + Disable it and tell the user which plugin was at fault Count failures per plugin and disable one that keeps failing, naming it so the user knows what to update or remove. The host must stay responsive whatever plugins do. ? Why is a separate process alone not a security boundary against a malicious plugin? - The host can read the plugin's memory, so secrets leak - Plugins share the host's handle table + It still has the user's rights and can read the user's files - Windows lets any process debug its children Isolation protects against faults, not intent. A plugin running as the user can do whatever the user can; a low-integrity token or AppContainer forces everything through the host's checked API.

title: A plugin host's bookkeeping
body: Decide which plugins a host may load, which ones receive each event, and when to disable a misbehaving one (lesson 6.03): cpp struct Manifest { std::string name; int apiMajor; int apiMinor; std::vector<std::string events; }; class PluginHost { public: PluginHost(int apiMajor, int apiMinor); bool load(const Manifest& m); std::vector<std::string route(const std::string& event) const; bool reportTimeout(const std::string& plugin, std::uint64_t now); std::vector<std::string enabled() const; }; - load accepts a plugin only if its API major equals the host's and its API minor is not newer than the host's, and no plugin of the same name (ignoring case) is loaded. It returns whether it was loaded. - route lists the enabled plugins subscribed to event , in the order they were loaded. The event name in a manifest subscribes to everything. - reportTimeout records a timeout for a plugin; if it has had 3 timeouts within 60 seconds (times now - 60 to now ), it is disabled. It returns true if this report disabled it. Disabled plugins are never routed to, and reports about them or unknown plugins return false. - enabled lists enabled plugin names in load order.

title: 6.04  Testing and Debugging IPC
body: Making communicating programs testable - keeping the protocol logic separate from the transport, in-memory transports and fault injection, golden transcripts, logging both sides with ids and times, and the tools for seeing handles, pipes and traffic, including debugging two processes at once. Separate logic from transport IPC code is hard to test when the protocol logic is tangled with ReadFile , WriteFile and real processes. Structure it in layers, as every practice in this course has: - a transport that moves bytes (a pipe, a socket, shared memory); - framing that turns bytes into messages; - protocol logic that turns messages into actions and replies. Then the framing and the logic can be unit-tested with byte vectors and no processes at all, running in milliseconds. A thin integration test checks that the real transport is wired up correctly. Fault injection The bugs that matter in IPC appear only under conditions that rarely happen on a developer's machine. Make them happen on purpose with a fault-injecting transport used in tests: - deliver messages split into small chunks, and several joined into one read (the deframer must not care); - delay messages, and deliver responses out of order ; - drop the connection halfway through a message; - kill the peer process in the middle of an exchange; - send garbage : random bytes, absurd lengths, unknown types. Deterministic patterns (split every frame into 3-byte pieces) are easier to debug than random ones; a seeded random generator gives variety while keeping failures reproducible. Golden transcripts Record the messages of a known-good session as text, one per line ("client to server: REQUEST id=1 method=open path=a.md"), and keep it as a golden transcript . A test replays the client side and compares the server's replies with the transcript. To keep it stable, normalise fields that legitimately change (timestamps, generated ids) before comparing. When a change alters the protocol on purpose, regenerate the golden file and review the diff; when it does so by accident, the test catches it. Logging both sides When something goes wrong between two processes, you need both sides' view. Log every message sent and received with: - a timestamp (milliseconds, from a monotonic clock), - the direction and the peer (client id, PID), - the message id and type. With ids in both logs, lining up the two sides is mechanical: find request 41 in the client log and in the server log, and the gap between them is the time it spent in the pipe and the queue. Tools - Process Explorer : the lower pane's handle view shows every pipe, event, mutex and mapping a process has open, by name. "Find Handle or DLL" finds which process holds an object. - Sysinternals PipeList ( pipelist.exe ): every named pipe on the machine with instance counts. (In PowerShell: Get-ChildItem \\.\pipe\ .) - Process Monitor : pipe operations appear as file operations on \Device\NamedPipe\... . - Wireshark with the Npcap loopback adapter captures localhost TCP traffic. - Resource Monitor , CPU tab, "Analyze Wait Chain": shows what a hung process is waiting for, including another process. Debugging two processes Visual Studio can debug several processes in one session: start the server under the debugger, then Debug Attach to Process for the client (or set both as startup projects in the solution's properties). Breakpoints in both work, and the Processes window switches between them. For child processes started by your program, Microsoft's Child Process Debugging Power Tool extension attaches automatically. Remember that stopping one side at a breakpoint makes the other side's timeouts fire; raise timeouts in debug builds, or expect them. Check yourself quiz ? Why separate framing and protocol logic from the transport? + So they can be tested quickly with byte vectors, without real pipes - Because pipes and sockets cannot be used from the same program - So the transport can be written in another language - Because framing must run in the kernel Layers let the deframer and the protocol logic be unit-tested in milliseconds with byte vectors; a thin integration test then checks that the real transport is wired up. ? Which of these is a set of faults a fault-injecting transport should simulate? - Slow disks, low memory and a full page file + Split and joined messages, dropped connections and garbage input - Compiler warnings, missing DLLs and wrong file paths - Mouse clicks, key presses and window resizes The IPC faults worth simulating are split and joined messages, delays and reordering, dropped connections, a killed peer and garbage such as absurd lengths and unknown types. ? Why normalise a transcript before comparing it with the golden one? - To make the transcript smaller to store - To sort the messages so their order does not matter + Timestamps and generated ids change on every run - To remove error messages that are expected Fields that legitimately change each run would make every comparison fail. Normalised, the test catches real protocol changes, including accidental ones. ? Which tool shows the named pipes, events and mutexes a process has open? - Task Manager's Details tab - Wireshark with the loopback adapter - Visual Studio's Processes window + Process Explorer's handle view Process Explorer's lower pane lists every handle a process holds, by name, and "Find Handle or DLL" finds who holds an object. Wireshark shows traffic, not handles.

title: Golden transcripts
body: Compare a recorded session against a golden transcript (lesson 6.04), after normalising the fields that change from run to run: cpp std::string normalise(const std::string& line, std::map<std::string, std::string & ids); std::optional<std::string firstDifference(const std::vector<std::string & golden, const std::vector<std::string & actual); A transcript line looks like +12ms c s REQUEST id=41 method=open path=a.md . - normalise : - drops a leading timestamp token (one that starts with + and ends with ms ); - replaces the value of every id= field with a stable name: the first distinct id seen becomes 1 , the next 2 , and so on, using the ids map so the same id gets the same name on every line; - leaves everything else as it is, with single spaces between tokens. - firstDifference normalises both transcripts (each with its own id map) and compares line by line. It returns std::nullopt if they match, or a description: line N: expected "...", got "..." (normalised lines, N counting from 1), or for different lengths line N: expected "...", got end of transcript / line N: expected end of transcript, got "..." .

title: 6.05  Case Studies
body: How real systems combine the techniques of this course - a multi-process browser, an editor and its language servers, a game and its live editor link, a Windows service with a tray application - and the questions to ask when designing your own. A browser A modern browser such as Chrome or Edge runs as many processes: one browser process (the window, tabs, network, storage), a renderer process per site (running its HTML, CSS and JavaScript), a GPU process , and utility processes for audio, network and storage. - Isolation : a crash or exploit in one site's renderer is contained; renderers run in a strict sandbox with almost no rights. - Communication : named pipes carrying a custom message system (Mojo) with typed interfaces generated from definition files. - Shared memory : rendered frames and large data move through shared memory, with only small messages over the pipes. - Supervision : a crashed renderer shows the "Aw, Snap!" page; the browser process carries on. Every idea from this course is there: processes for isolation, pipes for messages, shared memory for bulk data, protocol design with versioned interfaces, and security at every boundary. An editor and its language servers VS Code and many other editors get code intelligence from language servers : separate processes, one per language, speaking the Language Server Protocol. - Transport : usually the server's stdin and stdout (lesson 1.04), with Content-Length framing. - Protocol : JSON-RPC 2.0, with requests and ids (completion, go to definition), notifications (document changed), and capabilities negotiated in an initialize handshake (lesson 5.02). - Independence : the server can be written in any language, by anyone, and work with any editor that speaks the protocol. That is the strongest argument for a documented, language-neutral protocol. A game and its live editor Game engines often connect a running game to an editor or debug tool: change a value in the editor and see it in the game at once. - Discovery : the game listens on a loopback port (or named pipe) and announces itself through a port file, or the editor launches the game with the endpoint on the command line. - Commands : a request and response protocol over a socket or pipe: set this property, spawn this object, reload this asset. - Telemetry : frame times, memory and object counts streamed back, or published in shared memory with a seqlock so the tool never slows the game (lesson 3.05). - Robustness : either side can restart; the connection is re-established automatically, and the game never blocks waiting for the tool. A service and its tray application A Windows service runs in session 0 under its own account; the user's tray icon runs in the user's session. They cannot share windows or Local\ objects, so: - the service creates a named pipe with a security descriptor that allows the interactive users (lesson 5.05); - the tray application connects as a client, sends commands (pause, settings), and receives events (status changes); - the service impersonates the client when it must act with the user's rights, and validates every request, because any program the user runs can connect. Designing your own Faced with a new system, walk through the questions this course has raised: 1. Which processes, and why? Isolation, rights, crash containment, or just separate products? 2. Who finds whom? Inherited handles, names, port files, command-line arguments. 3. Which channel? Pipes or sockets for messages, shared memory for bulk or latest-state data, events and mutexes for signalling. 4. What is the protocol? Handshake, envelope, versioning, requests, responses and events, limits. 5. What fails, and how do you notice? Timeouts, process handles, heartbeats, abandoned mutexes. 6. Who could abuse it? Access control, tokens, validation, impersonation. 7. How will you test and debug it? Layers, fault injection, transcripts, logs with ids. The project that ends this course answers all seven for one complete system. Check yourself quiz ? Why does a browser move rendered frames through shared memory rather than pipes? - Pipes cannot carry binary data - Shared memory tells the browser when a renderer crashes + Frames are large, and shared memory avoids copying them - Renderers are not allowed to open pipes in the sandbox Frames are big, and a pipe copies every byte twice. Shared memory moves them with no copying, and the pipes carry the small messages saying a frame is ready. ? What makes the Language Server Protocol usable from any editor and any language? - It is a C++ library every editor links against - It uses Windows named pipes, which every language supports - Each editor ships its own language servers + It is a documented protocol, not a library for one language Because it is a protocol over stdio with JSON messages, a server written in any language works with any editor that speaks it. ? Why can a service and a tray application not use a Local\ event to talk? + They run in different sessions, and Local\ names are per session - Services cannot create events - Events only work between a parent and its child - Local\ objects are visible only to the process that created them A service runs in session 0 and the tray app in the user's session; Local\ names are separate in each. They use a named pipe with a suitable security descriptor (or Global\ objects) instead. ? Which of the seven design questions covers heartbeats and abandoned mutexes? - How will you test and debug it? - Which channel? + What fails, and how do you notice? - Who could abuse it? Heartbeats, timeouts, process handles and abandoned mutexes are all ways of noticing failure. Abuse is about access control, tokens and validation.

title: One copy only
body: Make a second launch of an app pass its file to the first one and exit. launch 1 "a.txt": first instance, opens a.txt launch 2 "b.txt": already running - sent "b.txt" to instance 1, exiting instance 1 now has: a.txt b.txt

title: A client and server
body: The final project: the server of a small multi-user workspace chat, as it would run behind a named pipe or loopback socket, with every concern of the course in it: a handshake with a version, validation of everything a client sends, rate limiting, events to other clients, clean handling of clients that quit or vanish. The transport is left out: the server receives one text line at a time from a client and returns the lines to send, and to whom. cpp struct Out { int client; std::string line; }; class ChatServer { public: int connect(); std::vector<Out receive(int client, const std::string& line, std::uint64_t nowMs); std::vector<Out disconnect(int client); std::vector<std::string users() const; }; connect registers a new connection and returns its id (1, 2, 3, ...). A client starts not joined . receive handles one line. First, for any line from an open connection: - more than 512 characters: reply ERROR line too long ; - rate limit : if this client has already sent 5 lines in the last 1000 ms (lines at times greater than now - 1000 ), reply ERROR slow down and do nothing else. Every line received counts, including refused ones. Then the command is the text up to the first space; the rest (after that one space) is its argument: Line Before joining After joining --- --- --- HELLO 1 name join (below) ERROR already joined SAY text ERROR say hello first others get FROM name text ; empty text: ERROR empty message ; text over 200 characters: ERROR message too long TELL name text ERROR say hello first that user gets PRIVATE sender text ; unknown user: ERROR no such user name ; missing text: ERROR usage: TELL name text WHO ERROR say hello first USERS a,b,c (all joined names) QUIT BYE , connection closed BYE , others get LEFT name , connection closed anything else ERROR unknown command X ERROR unknown command X Joining with HELLO version name : a version other than 1 gets ERROR unsupported version and the connection is closed . A name must be 1 to 16 characters of letters, digits, _ and - ( ERROR bad name ) and not already used, ignoring case ( ERROR name taken ). On success the client gets WELCOME name and every other joined client gets JOINED name . Replies to the sender come first, then messages to others in client id order. "Others" means joined clients other than the sender. Names in USERS and users are sorted ignoring case. A closed or unknown connection: receive and disconnect return nothing. disconnect is a connection that vanished: if the client had joined, the others get LEFT name .
