title: 3.01  Classes and Objects
body: Defining your own classes with fields, constructors and instance methods, creating objects with new, the this reference, references and null, toString, object identity versus equality, and how to design a class around the data it owns. A class A class is a blueprint: it describes the data an object holds ( fields ) and what it can do ( methods ). Each object made from it with new is an instance with its own copy of the fields. java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Counter clicks = new Counter("clicks"); Counter errors = new Counter("errors"); clicks.increment(); clicks.increment(); errors.increment(); System.out.println(clicks.describe()); System.out.println(errors.describe()); clicks.reset(); System.out.println(clicks); // uses toString } } class Counter { private final String name; // fields: every Counter has its own private int count; // starts at 0 Counter(String name) { // the constructor: runs when new Counter(...) is called this.name = name; } void increment() { count++; } void reset() { count = 0; } int getCount() { return count; } String describe() { return name + ": " + count; } @Override public String toString() { return "Counter " + name + "=" + count + " "; } } - new Counter("clicks") allocates an object and runs the constructor , which has the class's name and no return type. - Methods without static are instance methods : they run on one object and use its fields. - this is the object the method or constructor is running on. this.name = name copies the parameter into the field with the same name. - Overriding toString decides how the object prints. @Override asks the compiler to check that you really are overriding a method. Several classes can live in one file, but only one can be public , and it gives the file its name. In larger programs each class gets its own file. Objects are references A variable of a class type holds a reference to an object. Assigning it copies the reference: java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Point a = new Point(1, 2); Point b = a; // the same object Point c = new Point(1, 2); // a different object with the same values b.x = 10; System.out.println(a.x); // 10 System.out.println(a == b); // true: same object System.out.println(a == c); // false: different objects System.out.println(a.equals(c)); // false too: Object.equals compares identity unless overridden Point nothing = null; try { System.out.println(nothing.x); } catch (NullPointerException e) { System.out.println("NullPointerException: there is no object"); } } } class Point { int x, y; Point(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; } } To make equals compare contents , a class must override equals (and hashCode ; lesson 4.02). Records (lesson 3.05) do that automatically. Methods that work with other objects Methods can take and return objects, including objects of their own class: java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Fraction half = new Fraction(1, 2); Fraction third = new Fraction(1, 3); Fraction sum = half.plus(third); System.out.println(half + " + " + third + " = " + sum); System.out.println(new Fraction(6, 8)); } } class Fraction { private final int num, den; Fraction(int num, int den) { if (den == 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("denominator is zero"); int g = gcd(Math.abs(num), Math.abs(den)); int sign = den < 0 ? -1 : 1; this.num = sign num / g; this.den = sign den / g; } Fraction plus(Fraction other) { return new Fraction(num other.den + other.num den, den other.den); } private static int gcd(int a, int b) { return b == 0 ? Math.max(a, 1) : gcd(b, a % b); } @Override public String toString() { return num + "/" + den; } } Fraction keeps its fields final : once made, a fraction never changes, and plus returns a new fraction. Immutable objects like this (and String ) are simple to reason about and safe to share. Designing a class Ask: what data belongs together, and what operations keep that data correct? A BankAccount owns a balance and offers deposit and withdraw , which refuse to make it invalid. A class with good methods means the rest of the program never has to repeat those rules. Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference between a class and an object? - A class holds the data; an object holds only the methods - They are the same thing: "object" is just another word for a class + A class is the blueprint; an object is one instance made from it with new , with its own field values - An object is a class that has a main method The class describes the fields and methods. Each new creates a separate instance, and every instance has its own copy of the fields. ? What does this.name = name; do in a constructor? + Copies the parameter name into the object's field called name - Copies the object's field name into the parameter - Declares a new local variable called this.name - Nothing: a parameter and a field cannot share a name this is the object being constructed, so this.name is its field, while plain name is the parameter that hides it. ? Point a = new Point(1, 2); Point b = new Point(1, 2); Without an equals override, what is a.equals(b) ? - true - It does not compile + false - It throws NullPointerException Object.equals compares references unless the class overrides it, and a and b are two different objects.

title: A shopping cart class
body: Write a class ShoppingCart that keeps prices in whole cents: java ShoppingCart cart = new ShoppingCart(); cart.add("Tea", 250, 2); // name, unit price in cents, quantity cart.add("Cake", 425, 1); cart.add("tea", 250, 1); // the same item (names ignore case): quantity becomes 3, the first name is kept cart.itemCount(); // 4: total quantity cart.totalCents(); // 1175 cart.remove("TEA"); // true; false if not in the cart cart.receipt(); // see below - add throws IllegalArgumentException for a blank name, a negative price or a quantity below 1. Adding an existing item with a different price also throws. - receipt() lists the items in the order they were first added, one per line, as <name x<qty <line total with euros and 2 decimals ( Tea x3 7.50 ), then Total: <total . Lines end with \n . An empty cart gives just Total: 0.00\n . Keep the items in a private list; you may write a small helper class for an item below ShoppingCart in the same file (only one class per file can be public ). The class lives in ShoppingCart.java : in Java, a top-level class goes in a file with its own name.

title: 3.02  Encapsulation, Constructors and static
body: Access modifiers and why fields should be private, getters and setters with validation, constructor overloading and this(...), immutable classes with final fields, static fields and methods, static factory methods, constants, and when a class should be a utility class. Encapsulation Encapsulation means an object guards its own data: fields are private , and the only way to change them is through methods that keep them valid. java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { BankAccount acc = new BankAccount("Ada", 100); acc.deposit(50); System.out.println(acc.withdraw(500)); // false: refused System.out.println(acc.getBalance()); try { acc.deposit(-10); } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println("refused: " + e.getMessage()); } // acc.balance = -1000; // error: balance has private access } } class BankAccount { private final String owner; private long balance; // in cents would be safer for money; whole euros keep the example short BankAccount(String owner, long opening) { this.owner = owner; deposit(opening); } BankAccount(String owner) { this(owner, 0); // calls the other constructor } void deposit(long amount) { if (amount < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative deposit"); balance += amount; } boolean withdraw(long amount) { if (amount < 0 amount balance) return false; balance -= amount; return true; } long getBalance() { return balance; } String getOwner() { return owner; } } Modifier Visible to --- --- private Only this class (none) Classes in the same package protected The same package and subclasses public Everyone Make fields private , offer methods for what callers need, and only add a setter when changing a field is really part of the class's job; then validate in the setter. Constructors A class can have several constructors (overloading). One can call another with this(...) as its first statement, so the setup logic lives in one place. If you write no constructor, Java provides an empty one; as soon as you write any constructor, that free one disappears. Immutable classes A class whose fields are all final and set only in the constructor is immutable . Immutable objects cannot be changed by accident, are safe to share between parts of a program and between threads, and make good map keys. String , Integer and LocalDate are immutable; records (lesson 3.05) are the short way to write your own. static A static field belongs to the class, not to any object: there is exactly one, shared by all instances. A static method has no this and can use only static fields and its parameters. java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Ticket a = new Ticket(); Ticket b = new Ticket(); System.out.println(a.getNumber() + " " + b.getNumber() + " issued: " + Ticket.issued()); Temperature t = Temperature.fromFahrenheit(212); System.out.println(t.celsius() + " " + Temperature.ABSOLUTE_ZERO); System.out.println(MathUtil.clamp(15, 0, 10)); } } class Ticket { private static int next = 1; // shared by all tickets private final int number; Ticket() { number = next++; } int getNumber() { return number; } static int issued() { return next - 1; } } class Temperature { static final double ABSOLUTE_ZERO = -273.15; // a constant: static final, UPPER_CASE private final double celsius; private Temperature(double celsius) { this.celsius = celsius; } // private: use the factory methods static Temperature fromCelsius(double c) { return new Temperature(c); } static Temperature fromFahrenheit(double f) { return new Temperature((f - 32) 5 / 9); } double celsius() { return celsius; } } final class MathUtil { private MathUtil() { } // a utility class: no instances static int clamp(int v, int lo, int hi) { return Math.max(lo, Math.min(hi, v)); } } - Static factory methods like Temperature.fromFahrenheit have descriptive names, unlike constructors, and can validate or reuse objects. List.of , Integer.valueOf and LocalDate.of are examples. - static final fields are constants . - A utility class ( Math , Arrays , Collections ) has only static methods and a private constructor. - Avoid mutable static fields outside of small cases like counters: shared state makes programs hard to test and reason about. Check yourself quiz ? Why make fields private instead of public ? - Private fields use less memory - Only private fields can be final + So only the class's own methods can change them and keep the object valid - So that subclasses can still change them directly Callers then have to go through methods like deposit , which can refuse nonsense values. Subclasses cannot see private fields either. ? Can a static method use this ? - Yes, this is then the class itself + No: a static method runs without any object - Only when it is called from a constructor - Only if the class has exactly one instance A static method belongs to the class, so it has no this ; it can use only static fields, other static methods and its parameters. ? A class has private static int count = 0; and its constructor does count++ . After creating 3 objects, what is count ? - 1 in each object - 0 - It depends on the object + 3, shared by all objects A static field is a single variable shared by the whole class, so every constructor call adds to the same one.

title: An immutable time class
body: Write an immutable final class Time for times of day, with static factories and constants: java static final Time MIDNIGHT, NOON static Time of(int hour, int minute) // IllegalArgumentException outside 0-23 / 0-59 static Time parse(String text) // "9:05" or "09:05"; anything else: IllegalArgumentException Time plusMinutes(int minutes) // a NEW time, wrapping around midnight; minutes may be negative int minutesUntil(Time later) // minutes going forward: 23:00 to 01:00 is 120 boolean isBefore(Time other) String toString() // "09:05" boolean equals(Object o), int hashCode() // equal when hour and minute are equal - The constructor is private; the fields are private final . - parse trims spaces; the hour has one or two digits and the minute exactly two.

title: 3.03  Inheritance and Polymorphism
body: Extending a class with extends, calling the superclass constructor with super, overriding methods and @Override, protected members, dynamic dispatch and polymorphism, the Object class with toString, equals and hashCode, casting with instanceof patterns, final, and when to prefer composition. extends A class can extend one other class, its superclass , inheriting its fields and methods and adding or changing some: java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Employee staff = { new Employee("Ada", 4000), new Manager("Grace", 5000, 3), new Intern("Linus", 1200, 6), }; double total = 0; for (Employee e : staff) { System.out.println(e.describe()); // each object answers in its own way total += e.monthlyCost(); } System.out.println("Total: " + total); } } class Employee { private final String name; protected final double salary; // visible to subclasses Employee(String name, double salary) { this.name = name; this.salary = salary; } String getName() { return name; } double monthlyCost() { return salary; } String describe() { return name + " costs " + monthlyCost(); } } class Manager extends Employee { private final int reports; Manager(String name, double salary, int reports) { super(name, salary); // must be the first statement this.reports = reports; } @Override double monthlyCost() { return super.monthlyCost() + 200 reports; } @Override String describe() { return super.describe() + " (manages " + reports + ")"; } } class Intern extends Employee { private final int months; Intern(String name, double stipend, int months) { super(name, stipend); this.months = months; } @Override String describe() { return getName() + " is an intern for " + months + " months"; } } - super(...) runs the superclass constructor; it must come first. If you leave it out, Java calls super() with no arguments. - Overriding : a subclass method with the same signature replaces the inherited one. @Override makes the compiler check that it really overrides something (a typo would otherwise create a new method silently). - super.method() calls the superclass's version. Polymorphism A variable of type Employee can refer to a Manager . When a method is called, Java uses the version of the actual object's class, decided at run time ( dynamic dispatch ). So describe() in Employee calls monthlyCost() , and for a manager that is the manager's version. Code written for Employee works for every subclass, including ones written later. The Object class Every class extends Object , directly or indirectly, and inherits toString , equals and hashCode . Override them to give your class sensible behaviour: java import java.util.HashSet; import java.util.Objects; import java.util.Set; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Book a = new Book("Dune", 1965); Book b = new Book("Dune", 1965); System.out.println(a + " " + a.equals(b)); Set<Book shelf = new HashSet< (); shelf.add(a); shelf.add(b); System.out.println(shelf.size()); // 1: equal books count once } } class Book { private final String title; private final int year; Book(String title, int year) { this.title = title; this.year = year; } @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { if (this == o) return true; if (!(o instanceof Book other)) return false; return year == other.year && title.equals(other.title); } @Override public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(title, year); } @Override public String toString() { return title + " (" + year + ")"; } } The rule: objects that are equal must have equal hash codes. Override both together, or HashSet and HashMap will misbehave (lesson 4.02). instanceof and casting instanceof checks an object's type; the pattern form also gives you a variable of that type: java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Object things = {"text", 42, 3.5, new int {1, 2}}; for (Object o : things) { if (o instanceof String s) System.out.println("a string of length " + s.length()); else if (o instanceof Integer i && i 40) System.out.println("a big int " + i); else System.out.println("something else: " + o.getClass().getSimpleName()); } } } The old form, ((String) o).length() , casts explicitly and throws ClassCastException if the object is not that type. Many instanceof checks in a row usually mean a method should be overridden instead. final A final class cannot be extended ( String is final); a final method cannot be overridden. Use final for classes not designed for inheritance. Composition over inheritance Inheritance means "is a": a Manager is an Employee . When the relationship is "has a" (a Car has an Engine ), hold the other object in a field instead: composition . It is more flexible, since you can swap the part, and avoids deep hierarchies that are hard to change. Java allows only one superclass, but any number of interfaces (next lesson). Check yourself quiz ? Employee e = new Manager(...); e.monthlyCost(); Which version of the overridden method runs? - Employee 's, because that is the variable's type + Manager 's, because the actual object's class decides at run time - Both, the superclass version first - Whichever class was compiled last Dynamic dispatch picks the method of the object's real class when the program runs. The variable's type only decides which methods you may call. ? Why must equals and hashCode be overridden together? - The compiler refuses a class that overrides only one of them - hashCode is what equals calls to compare the fields - toString uses both to build its text + Hash-based collections look up by hash code before calling equals The rule is that equal objects must have equal hash codes, because a HashSet or HashMap only calls equals on objects in the same hash bucket. Override only equals , and a HashSet can hold two "equal" books. The compiler does not check this. ? A subclass constructor does not call super(...) . What happens? - The superclass fields stay uninitialised - It never compiles: super(...) is required + Java calls the superclass's no-argument constructor for it - The superclass constructor is skipped entirely super() is called implicitly. If the superclass has no no-argument constructor, that is a compile error.

title: Bank accounts with inheritance
body: Build a small hierarchy, one class per file ( Account.java , SavingsAccount.java , CheckingAccount.java ). Money is in whole cents ( long ). java class Account // Account(String owner, long balance) String getOwner(), long getBalance() void deposit(long amount) // IllegalArgumentException if amount <= 0 boolean withdraw(long amount) // false (and no change) if amount <= 0 or not allowed long available() // how much can be withdrawn now: the balance void monthEnd() // nothing for a plain account String toString() // "<Kind <owner : <balance in euros, 2 decimals ", Kind is the class's simple name class SavingsAccount extends Account // SavingsAccount(String owner, long balance, double yearlyRate) monthEnd(): adds interest of balance yearlyRate / 12, rounded to the nearest cent class CheckingAccount extends Account // CheckingAccount(String owner, long balance, long overdraftLimit) available(): balance + overdraftLimit withdraw(...): allowed up to available(); every successful withdrawal also costs a fee of 25 cents monthEnd(): if the balance is negative, charges 2% of the overdrawn amount, rounded to the nearest cent withdraw in Account should use available() , so that CheckingAccount only needs to override available() and add its fee. The fee may take the balance further below zero.

title: 3.04  Interfaces and Abstract Classes
body: Abstract classes and abstract methods, interfaces as contracts, implementing several interfaces, default and static interface methods, programming to an interface, the built-in Comparable and Iterable, functional interfaces as a preview of lambdas, and choosing between an interface and an abstract class. Abstract classes An abstract class cannot be instantiated. It holds shared code and declares abstract methods , without bodies, that every concrete subclass must implement: java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Shape shapes = {new Circle(1), new Rectangle(2, 3), new Circle(0.5)}; double total = 0; for (Shape s : shapes) { System.out.println(s.describe()); total += s.area(); } System.out.printf("Total area: %.2f%n", total); // new Shape("x"); // error: Shape is abstract; cannot be instantiated } } abstract class Shape { private final String name; protected Shape(String name) { this.name = name; } abstract double area(); // no body: subclasses must provide it String describe() { return String.format("%s with area %.2f", name, area()); } // shared code } class Circle extends Shape { private final double r; Circle(double r) { super("circle"); this.r = r; } @Override double area() { return Math.PI r r; } } class Rectangle extends Shape { private final double w, h; Rectangle(double w, double h) { super("rectangle"); this.w = w; this.h = h; } @Override double area() { return w h; } } Interfaces An interface is a contract: a list of methods a class promises to provide. A class implements any number of interfaces: java import java.util.List; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { List<Notifier channels = List.of(new EmailNotifier("ada@example.com"), new SmsNotifier("+3161234")); for (Notifier n : channels) { if (n.isAvailable()) n.send("Your order has shipped"); } Notifier quiet = new EmailNotifier("not-an-address"); quiet.sendAll(List.of("a", "b")); // a default method } } interface Notifier { boolean isAvailable(); void send(String message); default void sendAll(List<String messages) { // a default method: implementers get it for free if (!isAvailable()) { System.out.println("not available"); return; } for (String m : messages) send(m); } } class EmailNotifier implements Notifier { private final String address; EmailNotifier(String address) { this.address = address; } public boolean isAvailable() { return address.contains("@"); } public void send(String message) { System.out.println("email to " + address + ": " + message); } } class SmsNotifier implements Notifier { private final String number; SmsNotifier(String number) { this.number = number; } public boolean isAvailable() { return number.startsWith("+"); } public void send(String message) { System.out.println("sms to " + number + ": " + message); } } Interface methods are public automatically, so implementing methods must be public too. Interfaces can also have static methods and constants, but no instance fields. Program to an interface Declare variables and parameters with interface types ( List , Notifier ), and create concrete classes ( ArrayList , SmsNotifier ) in one place. Code that depends only on the interface works with any implementation, including test fakes, and the implementation can change without touching it. Built-in interfaces Comparable<T gives a class a natural order , used by Collections.sort , Arrays.sort , TreeSet and TreeMap : java import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Collections; import java.util.List; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { List<Version versions = new ArrayList< (List.of(new Version(1, 10), new Version(1, 2), new Version(0, 9))); Collections.sort(versions); System.out.println(versions); } } class Version implements Comparable<Version { private final int major, minor; Version(int major, int minor) { this.major = major; this.minor = minor; } @Override public int compareTo(Version other) { // negative, zero or positive if (major != other.major) return Integer.compare(major, other.major); return Integer.compare(minor, other.minor); } @Override public String toString() { return major + "." + minor; } } Other everyday interfaces: Iterable<T (usable in an enhanced for), Comparator<T (an external ordering, lesson 4.03), Runnable (a task for a thread, lesson 6.04), and AutoCloseable (try-with-resources, lesson 4.05). An interface with exactly one abstract method is a functional interface ; a lambda can implement it in one line (lesson 6.01): Comparator<String byLength = (a, b) - a.length() - b.length(); Interface or abstract class? Interface Abstract class --- --- A capability that unrelated classes share ( Comparable , Notifier ) A family of closely related classes sharing code and state ( Shape ) A class can implement many A class can extend only one No instance fields Fields and constructors Prefer interfaces; reach for an abstract class when subclasses really share state and code. Often both: an interface for the contract and an abstract class with a partial implementation. Check yourself quiz ? Can you create an object of an abstract class with new ? - Yes, as long as it has a constructor - Yes, but its abstract methods then do nothing + No; only of concrete subclasses that implement every abstract method - No, and abstract classes cannot have constructors either new Shape(...) does not compile when Shape is abstract. An abstract class can still have constructors, which its subclasses call with super(...) . ? Why must a method that implements an interface method be public ? + Interface methods are implicitly public, and an implementation may not reduce visibility - Only public methods can be called on objects in another file - The interface's default methods require it - It does not have to be: package access is enough Leaving out public gives the method package access, which is narrower than the interface's public method, so the compiler refuses it. ? A class wants to be sortable with Collections.sort . What should it implement? - Iterable<T - Runnable + Comparable<T - Cloneable Comparable defines the natural order through compareTo , which Collections.sort uses. Iterable only makes it usable in an enhanced for.

title: Text filters behind an interface
body: Write an interface and several implementations that clean up text, plus a pipeline that combines them. The project has three files: java // TextFilter.java interface TextFilter { String apply(String text); default String name() { return getClass().getSimpleName(); } } // Filters.java: the simple filters, as static nested classes class Filters { static class Trim implements TextFilter // removes spaces at both ends and collapses runs of spaces to one static class LowerCase implements TextFilter static class ReplaceWords implements TextFilter // ReplaceWords(Map<String, String replacements): whole words, case-sensitive static class MaxLength implements TextFilter // MaxLength(int max): cuts to max characters, ending with "..." when cut } // Pipeline.java class Pipeline implements TextFilter, Iterable<TextFilter Pipeline add(TextFilter filter) // returns this, so calls can be chained String apply(String text) // applies every filter in order String name() // "Pipeline Trim, LowerCase " - new Filters.ReplaceWords(Map.of("teh", "the")) turns "teh cat ate teh fish" into "the cat ate the fish" , but leaves "tehran" alone. Words are separated by single spaces. - MaxLength throws IllegalArgumentException for a max below 3. - A Pipeline is itself a TextFilter , so pipelines can contain pipelines.

title: 3.05  Records, Enums and Sealed Types
body: Modern Java data modelling - records with compact constructors and value equality, enums with fields, methods and switch, EnumMap, sealed interfaces that list their implementations, and pattern matching in switch with record patterns for exhaustive handling of every case. Records A record is a class for plain data. One line gives you private final fields, a constructor, accessors, and equals , hashCode and toString based on the values: java import java.util.HashSet; import java.util.Set; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Point a = new Point(1, 2); Point b = new Point(1, 2); System.out.println(a + " " + a.equals(b) + " " + a.x()); // accessors are x() and y() Set<Point set = new HashSet< (Set.of(a)); System.out.println(set.contains(b)); // true: value equality System.out.println(a.plus(new Point(10, 10))); System.out.println(new Range(3, 7).length()); try { new Range(5, 1); } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println(e.getMessage()); } } } record Point(int x, int y) { Point plus(Point other) { return new Point(x + other.x, y + other.y); } // records can have methods } record Range(int start, int end) { Range { // a compact constructor: validation if (start end) throw new IllegalArgumentException("start after end: " + start + " " + end); } int length() { return end - start; } } Records are immutable : to "change" one, create a new one. Use them for values that are compared, stored in sets and maps, returned from methods, and passed between parts of a program. Enums An enum is a type with a fixed set of named values. Enums can have fields, constructors and methods: java import java.util.EnumMap; import java.util.Map; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Planet home = Planet.EARTH; System.out.printf("%s: %.2f m/s2%n", home, home.surfaceGravity()); for (Planet p : Planet.values()) System.out.print(p.name().toLowerCase() + " "); System.out.println(); System.out.println(Planet.valueOf("MARS").ordinal()); Map<Planet, Integer visits = new EnumMap< (Planet.class); visits.merge(Planet.MARS, 1, Integer::sum); visits.merge(Planet.MARS, 1, Integer::sum); System.out.println(visits); Level level = Level.WARN; String colour = switch (level) { case DEBUG, INFO - "grey"; case WARN - "orange"; case ERROR - "red"; }; // no default needed: every constant is covered System.out.println(colour + " " + level.isAtLeast(Level.INFO)); } } enum Planet { MERCURY(3.303e23, 2.4397e6), EARTH(5.976e24, 6.37814e6), MARS(6.421e23, 3.3972e6); private final double mass, radius; Planet(double mass, double radius) { this.mass = mass; this.radius = radius; } double surfaceGravity() { return 6.67300e-11 mass / (radius radius); } } enum Level { DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR; boolean isAtLeast(Level other) { return compareTo(other) = 0; } } Use enums instead of int or String codes for fixed sets: directions, card suits, order states, log levels. The compiler then rejects invalid values, and a switch can be checked for completeness. Sealed types A sealed interface or class lists exactly which classes may implement or extend it. Together with records, that models data that is "one of these kinds": java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Shape shapes = {new Circle(1), new Square(2), new Rect(2, 3)}; for (Shape s : shapes) System.out.printf("%s - %.2f%n", s, area(s)); System.out.println(describe(new Rect(4, 4)) + ", " + describe(new Rect(2, 5))); } static double area(Shape s) { return switch (s) { // pattern matching for switch case Circle c - Math.PI c.r() c.r(); case Square sq - sq.side() sq.side(); case Rect(double w, double h) - w h; // a record pattern takes the record apart }; // exhaustive: every permitted type is covered } static String describe(Shape s) { return switch (s) { case Rect(double w, double h) when w == h - "a square-shaped rectangle"; // a guard case Rect r - "a rectangle"; default - "another shape"; }; } } sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square, Rect { } record Circle(double r) implements Shape { } record Square(double side) implements Shape { } record Rect(double w, double h) implements Shape { } Because the compiler knows every possible Shape , the switch in area needs no default . If someone adds Triangle to the permits list, every switch that does not handle it stops compiling, showing exactly what to update. This style, data as records and behaviour as functions that switch over them, complements classic object-oriented polymorphism. Check yourself quiz ? What does record Point(int x, int y) { } give you? - Public fields x and y that can be changed, plus a constructor + Private final fields, a constructor, accessors x() and y() , and value-based equals , hashCode and toString - A constructor and accessors getX() and getY() ; equals still compares references - Only a constructor; every method must be written by hand A record generates all of that from its components. The accessors are named after the components ( x() , not getX() ), and the fields are final, so a record is immutable. ? Why can a switch over a sealed interface leave out default ? - Every switch expression may leave out default - A sealed interface has exactly one implementation + The compiler knows every permitted subtype, so it can check that all are handled - default is not allowed together with record patterns The permits list names every possible subtype, so the compiler can prove the switch is exhaustive, and it stops compiling when a new subtype is added but not handled. ? Which is the best type for the four card suits? + An enum Suit { HEARTS, DIAMONDS, CLUBS, SPADES } - int constants 0 to 3 - String values "hearts", "spades"... - A record Suit(String name) An enum gives a fixed, type-checked set of values, and a switch over it can be checked for completeness. Ints, strings and records all allow invalid values.

title: Expressions with sealed records
body: Model arithmetic expressions as a sealed interface whose cases are records nested inside it, and write three operations with pattern matching, all in Expr.java : java sealed interface Expr { record Num(double value) implements Expr { } record Var(String name) implements Expr { } record Add(Expr left, Expr right) implements Expr { } record Mul(Expr left, Expr right) implements Expr { } record Neg(Expr inner) implements Expr { } static double eval(Expr e, Map<String, Double vars) // IllegalArgumentException("unknown variable x") when missing static String show(Expr e) // fully parenthesised, see below static Expr simplify(Expr e) } Records nested in a sealed interface are its permitted subtypes automatically; from outside they are written Expr.Num , Expr.Add ... show : numbers without a trailing .0 when whole ( 2 , 2.5 ), variables by name, (a + b) , (a b) , and -a for negation. For example show(new Add(new Num(2), new Mul(new Var("x"), new Num(3)))) is "(2 + (x 3))" . simplify works bottom-up (simplify the parts first), then applies these rules: - Add : both numbers → their sum; 0 + e or e + 0 → e - Mul : both numbers → their product; 0 e or e 0 → Num(0) ; 1 e or e 1 → e - Neg : of a number → the negated number; Neg(Neg(e)) → e Use switch with patterns, with no default , so the compiler checks every case is handled.

title: Cards and poker hands
body: Model a deck of playing cards with enums and records, and rank five-card poker hands. Each type goes in its own file, named after it, as in any Java project: Suit.java , Rank.java , Card.java , Deck.java , Category.java , HandValue.java and Poker.java . java enum Suit { CLUBS, DIAMONDS, HEARTS, SPADES } // symbols C, D, H, S enum Rank { TWO, THREE, ..., TEN, JACK, QUEEN, KING, ACE } // symbols 2-9, T, J, Q, K, A record Card(Rank rank, Suit suit) // toString: "AS", "TH", "2C"; static Card parse(String) class Deck // a full 52-card deck enum Category { HIGH_CARD, PAIR, TWO_PAIR, THREE_OF_A_KIND, STRAIGHT, FLUSH, FULL_HOUSE, FOUR_OF_A_KIND, STRAIGHT_FLUSH } record HandValue(Category category, List<Rank tiebreak) implements Comparable<HandValue class Poker static List<Card parseHand(String text) // "AS KD 7H 7C 2S" static HandValue evaluate(List<Card five) static int compare(String hand1, String hand2) // positive if hand1 wins, negative if hand2 wins, 0 for a tie Cards and deck - Card.parse("QH") gives the queen of hearts; anything else (wrong length, unknown symbol) throws IllegalArgumentException . Symbols are upper case. - new Deck() has 52 different cards in order: suits in enum order, and within each suit ranks from two to ace. size() , deal() (removes and returns the top card, the first one; IllegalStateException when empty) and shuffle(Random random) (use Collections.shuffle(list, random) ). Evaluating a hand (exactly 5 different cards, else IllegalArgumentException ): - Categories from lowest to highest as in the enum. A straight is five consecutive ranks; the ace can also be low in A 2 3 4 5 (a five-high straight). A flush is five cards of one suit. - tiebreak lists the ranks that decide between two hands of the same category, most important first: ranks ordered by how many times they occur (more first), then by rank (higher first). So 7H 7C AS KD 2S (a pair) gives SEVEN, ACE, KING, TWO , and KS KH 4D 4C KC (full house) gives KING, FOUR . For straights and straight flushes it is just the highest card, with FIVE for the ace-low straight. - HandValue.compareTo compares the category first, then the tiebreak lists rank by rank.

title: 4.01  Generics
body: Type parameters on classes, interfaces and methods, why generics replaced Object and casts, bounded types with extends, wildcards with ? extends and ? super (PECS), type erasure and its limits, and writing your own generic container. Why generics Before generics (Java 5), a list held Object s. Every read needed a cast, and putting the wrong type in was only discovered when the program crashed: java-norun List names = new ArrayList(); // a "raw" list names.add("Ada"); names.add(42); // nothing stops this String first = (String) names.get(0); String second = (String) names.get(1); // ClassCastException at run time With a type parameter , List<String holds only strings, the compiler checks every add , and no casts are needed. Mistakes become compile errors. A generic class java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Box<String name = new Box< ("Ada"); Box<Integer age = new Box< (36); String n = name.get(); // no cast int a = age.get() + 1; System.out.println(n + " " + a + " " + name.map(String::length).get()); Pair<String, Integer entry = new Pair< ("apples", 4); System.out.println(entry + " " + entry.swap()); } } class Box<T { private final T value; Box(T value) { this.value = value; } T get() { return value; } <R Box<R map(java.util.function.Function<T, R f) { return new Box< (f.apply(value)); } // a generic method } record Pair<A, B (A first, B second) { Pair<B, A swap() { return new Pair< (second, first); } } By convention, type parameters are single capital letters: T (type), E (element), K / V (key/value), R (result). Type arguments must be reference types: Box<int is not allowed, use Box<Integer . Generic methods A method can have its own type parameters, written before the return type. The compiler infers them from the arguments: java import java.util.List; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { System.out.println(last(List.of("a", "b", "c"))); System.out.println(last(List.of(1, 2, 3))); System.out.println(max(List.of(4, 9, 2)) + " " + max(List.of("pear", "apple"))); } static <T T last(List<T items) { return items.get(items.size() - 1); } static <T extends Comparable<T T max(List<T items) { // a bounded type parameter T best = items.get(0); for (T item : items) if (item.compareTo(best) 0) best = item; return best; } } T extends Comparable<T means "any T that can be compared with itself", which is what lets the body call compareTo . Wildcards A List<Integer is not a List<Number , even though Integer is a Number . (If it were, you could add a Double to a list of integers through the List<Number variable.) Wildcards express "a list of some type": java import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { List<Integer ints = List.of(1, 2, 3); List<Double doubles = List.of(1.5, 2.5); System.out.println(sum(ints) + " " + sum(doubles)); List<Number numbers = new ArrayList< (); List<Object objects = new ArrayList< (); addOnes(numbers, 2); addOnes(objects, 1); System.out.println(numbers + " " + objects); } static double sum(List<? extends Number values) { // read Numbers from it double total = 0; for (Number n : values) total += n.doubleValue(); return total; } static void addOnes(List<? super Integer target, int count) { // write Integers into it for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) target.add(1); } } The rule of thumb is PECS : Producer Extends, Consumer Super . A parameter you only read from takes ? extends T ; one you only write to takes ? super T . Collections.copy(List<? super T dest, List<? extends T src) uses both. Type erasure Generics exist only at compile time: the compiler checks the types and then erases them, so at run time a List<String is just a List . Consequences: - new T() and new T 10 are not allowed (the type is unknown at run time). - For an Object x , x instanceof List<String is not allowed (the check cannot be made at run time); x instanceof List<? is. - You cannot overload f(List<String ) and f(List<Integer ) : after erasure they are the same. Check yourself quiz ? Why can't you pass a List<Integer where a List<Number is expected? - Integer is not a subclass of Number + The method could add a Double through the List<Number type, breaking the list of integers - Generic types are erased, so the compiler cannot tell the two lists apart - A List<Number can only hold double values Integer is a Number , but a list of integers is not a list of numbers: a List<Number accepts any number. Use List<? extends Number for a parameter you only read from. ? Which parameter type lets a method add Integer s to a list of Integer s, Number s or Object s? - List<? extends Integer - List<Integer - List<? + List<? super Integer PECS: a consumer that you write into takes ? super T . ? extends Integer only lets you read, and List<Integer accepts only lists of exactly Integer . ? What does <T extends Comparable<T allow inside the method? - Creating new T objects - Using T as an int + Calling compareTo on values of type T - Nothing extra The bound guarantees every T has compareTo . new T() is still impossible because of type erasure.

title: Generic methods and types
body: Write a generic record and generic static methods: java // Pair.java record Pair<A, B (A first, B second) { static <A, B Pair<A, B of(A first, B second) Pair<B, A swap() } // Generics.java class Generics { static <T extends Comparable<? super T T max(Collection<T items) // NoSuchElementException when empty static double sum(Collection<? extends Number numbers) static void fill(List<? super Integer target, int from, int to) // adds from, from+1, ..., to-1 static <K, V Map<V, List<K invert(Map<K, V map) // keys grouped by value static <T List<Pair<T, T pairs(List<T items) // a, b, c, d gives (a, b), (c, d) ; an odd last item is dropped } The bound on max must also accept LocalDate , which implements Comparable<ChronoLocalDate rather than Comparable<LocalDate . invert returns a LinkedHashMap and keeps both the values and each list of keys in the order the map gives them, so with a LinkedHashMap or TreeMap input the result is predictable.

title: 4.02  The Collections Framework
body: The interfaces and implementations of java.util - List, Set, Map, Queue and Deque with ArrayList, LinkedList, HashSet, LinkedHashSet, TreeSet, HashMap, LinkedHashMap, TreeMap, ArrayDeque and PriorityQueue - choosing between them, iterating, counting and grouping with maps, the equals and hashCode contract, and immutable collections. The big picture Program to the interface ( List , Set , Map ) and pick the implementation for its performance and ordering. Need Use --- --- A sequence, access by index ArrayList Unique items, fast contains HashSet (no order), LinkedHashSet (insertion order), TreeSet (sorted) Look up by key HashMap (no order), LinkedHashMap (insertion order), TreeMap (sorted keys) A stack or a queue ArrayDeque Always take the smallest (or largest) next PriorityQueue LinkedList is rarely the right choice: ArrayList and ArrayDeque are faster for almost everything. Sets java import java.util. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { List<String words = List.of("pear", "apple", "pear", "fig", "apple"); System.out.println(new HashSet< (words)); // some order System.out.println(new LinkedHashSet< (words)); // first-seen order System.out.println(new TreeSet< (words)); // sorted Set<Integer a = new TreeSet< (Set.of(1, 2, 3, 4)); Set<Integer b = Set.of(3, 4, 5); Set<Integer both = new TreeSet< (a); both.retainAll(b); // intersection Set<Integer either = new TreeSet< (a); either.addAll(b); // union a.removeAll(b); // difference System.out.println(both + " " + either + " " + a); System.out.println(new HashSet< (words).add("fig")); // false: already there } } Maps java import java.util. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Map<String, Integer ages = new HashMap< (); ages.put("Ada", 36); ages.put("Grace", 85); ages.put("Ada", 37); // replaces System.out.println(ages.get("Ada") + " " + ages.get("Bob") + " " + ages.getOrDefault("Bob", -1)); System.out.println(ages.containsKey("Grace") + " " + ages.size()); String text = "the cat and the hat and the bat"; Map<String, Integer counts = new TreeMap< (); for (String w : text.split(" ")) counts.merge(w, 1, Integer::sum); // counting System.out.println(counts); Map<Character, List<String byLetter = new TreeMap< (); for (String w : List.of("apple", "avocado", "banana", "cherry")) { byLetter.computeIfAbsent(w.charAt(0), k - new ArrayList< ()).add(w); // grouping } System.out.println(byLetter); for (Map.Entry<String, Integer e : counts.entrySet()) { if (e.getValue() 1) System.out.print(e.getKey() + "=" + e.getValue() + " "); } System.out.println(); } } map.get(missing) returns null , and unboxing that null into an int throws NullPointerException . Use getOrDefault , containsKey , or merge / computeIfAbsent . Queues and stacks java import java.util. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Deque<String stack = new ArrayDeque< (); stack.push("a"); stack.push("b"); stack.push("c"); System.out.println(stack.pop() + " " + stack.peek()); // c b: last in, first out Queue<String queue = new ArrayDeque< (); queue.offer("first"); queue.offer("second"); System.out.println(queue.poll() + " " + queue.size()); // first 1: first in, first out PriorityQueue<Integer pq = new PriorityQueue< (List.of(5, 1, 4, 2)); StringBuilder out = new StringBuilder(); while (!pq.isEmpty()) out.append(pq.poll()).append(' '); // always the smallest next System.out.println(out); } } equals and hashCode HashSet and HashMap find objects by hashCode() first, then confirm with equals() . For your own classes used as keys or set members: - override both equals and hashCode , using the same fields; - objects that are equals must have the same hashCode ; - do not change those fields while the object is in a hash set or map key (it would be filed under the old hash). Records do all of this for you, which makes them ideal keys. TreeSet and TreeMap use compareTo (or a Comparator ) instead, and treat items that compare as 0 as duplicates. Iterating and removing All collections work with the enhanced for . To remove while iterating, use removeIf(...) or an explicit Iterator and its remove() ; removing through the collection itself during a for loop throws ConcurrentModificationException . Immutable collections List.of , Set.of and Map.of create unmodifiable collections; List.copyOf(list) makes an unmodifiable copy. Returning unmodifiable views ( Collections.unmodifiableList(items) ) from a class protects its internal lists from outside changes. Check yourself quiz ? Which set keeps its items sorted? - HashSet - LinkedHashSet + TreeSet - Set.of(...) TreeSet keeps its items in sorted order. HashSet has no useful order, and LinkedHashSet keeps the order the items were first added. ? What does map.merge(word, 1, Integer::sum) do? + Puts 1 if word is not yet a key, otherwise adds 1 to its current value - Always sets the value for word to 1 - Adds 1 to the value for word , and throws if it is not yet a key - Sums all the values in the map and stores the total under word merge stores the given value for a new key; for an existing key it combines the old value and the given one with the function, here Integer::sum . That makes it the one-line way to count. ? A class overrides equals but not hashCode , and two equal objects are added to a HashSet . How many items does the set hold? - Always 1 - 0 - It throws an exception + Probably 2, because their hash codes differ HashSet looks in the bucket for the hash code first; with different hash codes, equals is never even asked.

title: Choosing collections
body: Write these methods in Text.java , each with the collection that fits: java class Text { static List<String topWords(String text, int n) // the n most frequent words, ties alphabetical static Character firstUnique(String s) // the first character that appears exactly once, or null static SortedMap<Integer, List<String byLength(List<String words) // lengths sorted; words in input order, no repeats static boolean isBalanced(String s) // brackets ( ) { } properly nested; other characters ignored } - Words in topWords are runs of letters, compared in lower case. - byLength( "fig", "pear", "kiwi", "fig", "plum" ) is {3= fig , 4= pear, kiwi, plum } .

title: 4.03  Comparable, Comparator and Sorting
body: Natural ordering with Comparable, external orderings with Comparator, building comparators with comparing, thenComparing, reversed and nullsFirst, sorting lists and arrays, stability, sorted collections with custom orderings, the compareTo contract, and common mistakes like subtracting to compare. Natural order: Comparable A class that implements Comparable<T has a natural order : compareTo returns a negative number when this comes first, zero when equal, positive when this comes after. Strings, numbers and dates already have one. java import java.util. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { List<Student students = new ArrayList< (List.of( new Student("Grace", 88), new Student("Ada", 95), new Student("Linus", 88))); Collections.sort(students); // uses compareTo System.out.println(students); } } record Student(String name, int score) implements Comparable<Student { @Override public int compareTo(Student other) { return name.compareTo(other.name); // natural order: by name } } Other orders: Comparator A Comparator is an ordering kept outside the class, so one class can be sorted many ways. The Comparator helper methods build them from the fields to compare: java import java.util. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { List<Student students = new ArrayList< (List.of( new Student("Grace", 88, 2), new Student("Ada", 95, 1), new Student("Linus", 88, 1), new Student("Barbara", 72, 3))); students.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(Student::score).reversed() .thenComparing(Student::name)); // by score, highest first; ties by name System.out.println(students); students.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(Student::year).thenComparing(Student::score, Comparator.reverseOrder())); System.out.println(students); Comparator<String byLength = Comparator.comparingInt(String::length); List<String words = new ArrayList< (List.of("kiwi", "fig", "banana", "pear")); words.sort(byLength.thenComparing(Comparator.naturalOrder())); System.out.println(words); } } record Student(String name, int score, int year) { } Builder Meaning --- --- Comparator.comparing(f) , comparingInt(f) , comparingDouble(f) Compare by a key .thenComparing(g) Break ties with a second key .reversed() The opposite order Comparator.naturalOrder() , reverseOrder() Natural order and its reverse Comparator.nullsFirst(c) , nullsLast(c) Allow nulls Student::score is a method reference : shorthand for the lambda s - s.score() (lesson 6.01). Sorting java import java.util. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { int nums = {5, 3, 9, 1}; Arrays.sort(nums); // primitives: natural order only Integer boxed = {5, 3, 9, 1}; Arrays.sort(boxed, Comparator.reverseOrder()); // objects: any comparator System.out.println(Arrays.toString(nums) + " " + Arrays.toString(boxed)); List<String names = new ArrayList< (List.of("bob", "Alice", "carol")); names.sort(String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER); System.out.println(names); TreeSet<String byLength = new TreeSet< (Comparator.comparingInt(String::length).thenComparing(s - s)); byLength.addAll(List.of("pear", "fig", "banana", "kiwi")); System.out.println(byLength + " first=" + byLength.first()); } } Sorting objects in Java ( List.sort , Collections.sort , Arrays.sort on objects) is stable : equal items keep their relative order. That is what makes sorting by one key and then another work as expected. The compareTo contract A correct comparison must be consistent: if a < b then b a ; if a < b and b < c then a < c ; and ideally compareTo returns 0 exactly when equals is true (a TreeSet treats compare-0 items as duplicates). A classic bug is comparing by subtraction: java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { int a = Integer.MIN_VALUE, b = 1; System.out.println(a - b 0); // true: the subtraction overflows, so the order is wrong System.out.println(Integer.compare(a, b)); // -1: correct } } Always use Integer.compare , Double.compare , or the Comparator builders. Check yourself quiz ? When do you use a Comparator instead of Comparable ? - Whenever the class is a record - Only for sorting arrays of primitives + When you need an order other than the class's natural order, or the class has none you can add - Never: Comparator is the old way and Comparable replaced it Comparable gives one natural order, written inside the class. A Comparator is kept outside, so a class can be sorted many ways, including classes you cannot change. ? Why is return a.score - b.score; a risky compareTo ? - It returns an int instead of a boolean + The subtraction can overflow for large values and give the wrong sign - It sorts in descending order instead of ascending - compareTo must only ever return -1, 0 or 1 Any negative, zero or positive result is allowed, but Integer.MIN_VALUE - 1 overflows to a large positive number. Integer.compare cannot overflow. ? A list of people is sorted by name, then sorted again by age (a stable sort). How are people of the same age ordered? - Randomly - By age only, in no particular order - In reverse name order + By name A stable sort keeps the earlier (name) order among items that compare equal on age.

title: Sorting with comparators
body: Employees are records: java // Employee.java record Employee(String name, String dept, int salary, int age) { } Write the queries in Staff.java using Comparator builders ( comparing , thenComparing , reversed ): java class Staff { static List<Employee bySalary(List<Employee staff) // highest salary first, ties by name static List<Employee byDeptThenAge(List<Employee staff) // department A-Z, then youngest first, then name static Map<String, Employee oldestPerDept(List<Employee staff) // TreeMap by department; ties: the earlier name static List<String topEarners(List<Employee staff, int n) // names of the n best paid, ties by name } None of the methods may change the list they are given.

title: 4.04  Exceptions
body: Throwing and catching exceptions, the exception hierarchy, checked versus unchecked exceptions and the throws clause, multi-catch, finally, try-with-resources, custom exception classes with causes, stack traces, and good practice for validating arguments and handling errors. throw and catch When a method cannot do its job it throws an exception. The exception travels up the call stack until a catch block handles it; if none does, the program stops and prints a stack trace . java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { String inputs = {"42", "abc", "-5"}; for (String input : inputs) { try { int age = parseAge(input); System.out.println("age " + age); } catch (NumberFormatException e) { System.out.println("'" + input + "' is not a number"); } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println(e.getMessage()); } } } static int parseAge(String text) { int age = Integer.parseInt(text); // may throw NumberFormatException if (age < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("age cannot be negative: " + age); return age; } } Catch blocks are tried in order, so put specific types first: NumberFormatException is a subclass of IllegalArgumentException , so the other order would not compile (the second catch could never run). The hierarchy - Unchecked exceptions ( RuntimeException and its subclasses) usually mean a bug or bad argument. The compiler does not force you to handle them. - Checked exceptions (other Exception subclasses, like IOException ) are problems a correct program can still meet: a missing file, a lost connection. A method that may throw one must declare it with throws , and callers must catch it or declare it too. - Error s are serious problems of the JVM itself; do not catch them. java import java.io.IOException; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { try { System.out.println(loadSetting("theme")); System.out.println(loadSetting("missing")); } catch (IOException e) { System.out.println("could not load: " + e.getMessage()); } } static String loadSetting(String key) throws IOException { // callers must deal with IOException if (key.equals("missing")) throw new IOException("no setting " + key); return "dark"; } } finally and try-with-resources finally runs whether or not an exception happened, for clean-up. For anything that must be closed (files, connections), try-with-resources closes it automatically, even if an exception is thrown: java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { try (Resource a = new Resource("first"); Resource b = new Resource("second")) { System.out.println("using both"); throw new IllegalStateException("something failed"); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("caught: " + e.getMessage()); } finally { System.out.println("finally runs too"); } } } class Resource implements AutoCloseable { private final String name; Resource(String name) { this.name = name; System.out.println("open " + name); } @Override public void close() { System.out.println("close " + name); } // closed in reverse order } Any class implementing AutoCloseable works in a try-with-resources statement. Your own exceptions Create an exception class when callers need to recognise your specific problem. Pass the original exception as the cause when you wrap one: java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { try { Config.port("80x"); } catch (ConfigException e) { System.out.println(e.getMessage() + " <- caused by " + e.getCause().getClass().getSimpleName()); } } } class ConfigException extends Exception { // checked ConfigException(String message, Throwable cause) { super(message, cause); } } class Config { static int port(String text) throws ConfigException { try { return Integer.parseInt(text); } catch (NumberFormatException e) { throw new ConfigException("bad port '" + text + "'", e); } } } Extend RuntimeException instead for exceptions that signal programming errors, so callers are not forced to catch them. Good practice - Validate arguments early with clear messages: Objects.requireNonNull(name, "name") , if (qty < 1) throw new IllegalArgumentException("qty must be at least 1: " + qty) . - Catch only what you can handle , where you can do something useful. Never swallow an exception with an empty catch ; at least log it. - Do not use exceptions for normal control flow : check with hasNextInt() , containsKey() or Optional (lesson 6.03) when a missing value is normal. - Read stack traces from the top : the first line names the exception and message; the first at line in your own code is usually where to look. Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference between checked and unchecked exceptions? + Checked exceptions must be caught or declared with throws ; unchecked ones ( RuntimeException subclasses) need not be - Checked exceptions are found by the compiler; unchecked ones are found only at run time - Unchecked exceptions cannot be caught with catch - Checked exceptions are Error s of the JVM; unchecked ones come from your own code Both kinds are thrown at run time and both can be caught. The difference is that the compiler forces you to handle or declare checked ones like IOException . ? What does try-with-resources guarantee? - Exceptions thrown inside it are caught and ignored - The block is retried until it finishes without an exception + Its resources are closed when the block ends, even by an exception - Resources are closed only if no exception is thrown It works with any AutoCloseable and closes the resources in reverse order of opening, whether the block ends normally or not; exceptions still travel on to a catch or the caller. ? A method calls Files.readString(path) , which throws IOException , and does not catch it. What must its signature include? - Nothing - catch IOException + throws IOException - extends IOException IOException is checked: it must be caught or declared with throws in the method signature.

title: A config parser with exceptions
body: Parse simple configuration text such as server settings port = 8080 host = example.org debug = true into a map, reporting problems with your own checked exception: java // ConfigException.java class ConfigException extends Exception { ConfigException(int line, String message) // getMessage(): "line <n : <message " ConfigException(int line, String message, Throwable cause) int line() } // Config.java class Config { static Map<String, String parse(List<String lines) throws ConfigException static int getInt(Map<String, String config, String key, int min, int max) throws ConfigException } parse : - skips blank lines and lines starting with (after trimming); - every other line must be key = value (one = ; spaces around key and value are trimmed); else ConfigException(n, "expected key = value") ; - keys are non-empty and made of letters, digits, . and _ ; else "bad key" ; - a key defined twice: "duplicate key <key " ; - line numbers count from 1; the result keeps the order of the file. - A null list throws NullPointerException (a bug in the caller, not a config problem). getInt reports problems with line 0: a missing key gives "missing <key " , a value that is not a whole number gives "<key is not a number" with the NumberFormatException as the cause, and a number outside min..max gives "<key must be between <min and <max " .

title: 4.05  Files and I/O
body:
Reading and writing text files with java.nio.file - Path and Files, readString, readAllLines, lines and write, BufferedReader and BufferedWriter for large files, character encodings, directories and walking them, handling IOException, parsing CSV records, and the older java.io classes you will still meet. Path and Files Modern Java uses java.nio.file : a Path names a file, and the Files class does the work: java import java.io.IOException; import java.nio.file. ; import java.util.List; public class Main { public static void main(String args) throws IOException { Path file = Path.of("notes.txt"); Files.writeString(file, "first line
second line
"); Files.writeString(file, "appended
", StandardOpenOption.APPEND); String all = Files.readString(file); List<String lines = Files.readAllLines(file); System.out.println(all.length() + " characters, " + lines.size() + " lines, last: " + lines.get(lines.size() - 1)); Files.write(Path.of("numbers.txt"), List.of("1", "2", "3")); long sum = 0; try (var stream = Files.lines(Path.of("numbers.txt"))) { // lazy: one line at a time sum = stream.mapToLong(Long::parseLong).sum(); } System.out.println(sum + " " + Files.exists(file) + " " + Files.size(file)); } } main declares throws IOException here to keep the example short; real programs catch it where they can report the problem. Paths and directories java import java.io.IOException; import java.nio.file. ; import java.util.stream.Stream; public class Main { public static void main(String args) throws IOException { Path dir = Path.of("data", "2026"); Files.createDirectories(dir); // all missing levels; fine if it exists Path report = dir.resolve("report.csv"); // data/2026/report.csv Files.writeString(report, "id,total
1,9.50
"); System.out.println(report.getFileName() + " in " + report.getParent()); try (Stream<Path all = Files.walk(Path.of("data"))) { all.filter(Files::isRegularFile).forEach(p - System.out.println("found " + p.toString().replace('\', '/'))); } Files.copy(report, dir.resolve("backup.csv"), StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING); Files.delete(dir.resolve("backup.csv")); } } Build paths with Path.of(a, b, c) and resolve , never by gluing strings with / or \ : the separator differs between systems. Large files: buffered readers and writers readAllLines loads the whole file into memory. For big files, read line by line with a BufferedReader , and write with a BufferedWriter , both in try-with-resources: java import java.io. ; import java.nio.file. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) throws IOException { Path log = Path.of("log.txt"); try (BufferedWriter out = Files.newBufferedWriter(log)) { for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) { out.write("entry " + i); out.newLine(); } } // closing flushes the buffer to disk int count = 0; try (BufferedReader in = Files.newBufferedReader(log)) { String line; while ((line = in.readLine()) != null) { if (line.endsWith("3") line.endsWith("5")) count++; } } System.out.println(count); } } Text is stored as bytes using an encoding . Files methods use UTF-8 by default, which handles every language; pass StandardCharsets.UTF_8 explicitly when using older APIs. Errors File operations fail for reasons outside your program. The specific exceptions tell you why: java import java.io.IOException; import java.nio.file. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { try { String text = Files.readString(Path.of("settings.ini")); System.out.println(text); } catch (NoSuchFileException e) { System.out.println("no settings file: using defaults"); } catch (AccessDeniedException e) { System.out.println("not allowed to read " + e.getFile()); } catch (IOException e) { System.out.println("could not read settings: " + e.getMessage()); } } } Reading records A common task is reading structured lines into objects. Keep parsing in its own method, and decide what to do with bad lines: java import java.util. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { List<String lines = List.of("name,score", "Ada,95", "Grace,abc", "Linus,72", ""); List<Result results = new ArrayList< (); List<String problems = new ArrayList< (); for (int i = 1; i < lines.size(); i++) { String line = lines.get(i); if (line.isBlank()) continue; String f = line.split(","); try { results.add(new Result(f 0 .trim(), Integer.parseInt(f 1 .trim()))); } catch (NumberFormatException ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException e) { problems.add("line " + (i + 1) + ": " + line); } } System.out.println(results); System.out.println(problems); } } record Result(String name, int score) { } catch (A B e) is a multi-catch : one handler for several exception types. Real CSV can contain quoted commas; use a library such as Apache Commons CSV for files you do not control. The older java.io You will meet older code using java.io.File , FileReader , FileWriter and Scanner(new File(...)) . They still work; Path and Files are the modern replacements with better error messages. file.toPath() and path.toFile() convert between them. Check yourself quiz ? Why read a large file with Files.lines or a BufferedReader instead of readAllLines ? - readAllLines cannot read files with more than 1000 lines - readAllLines does not use UTF-8 - They skip empty lines automatically + They read one line at a time instead of loading the whole file into memory readAllLines returns a List holding every line at once, which can use a lot of memory for a big file. Close Files.lines and readers with try-with-resources. ? Why must a BufferedWriter be closed? - Otherwise the file is deleted when the program ends + Writing is buffered; closing flushes the remaining data to the file and releases it - Closing is what creates the file on disk - It must not be: Java closes every writer as soon as write returns Text goes into a buffer first and only reaches the file when the buffer is flushed. Without close (or try-with-resources), the last part can be lost. ? Which builds the path to data/2026/report.csv portably? - "data" + "/" + "2026" + "/" + "report.csv" + Path.of("data", "2026", "report.csv") - "data\2026\report.csv" - new String("data/2026/report.csv") Path.of joins the parts with the right separator for the system; gluing strings hard-codes one separator.
