title: An inventory with files
body: Build a shop's stock system that loads and saves CSV files, with collections for fast lookups, comparators for reports and a checked exception for bad data. One type per file: java // Item.java record Item(String sku, String name, int quantity, long priceCents) // compact constructor validates // InventoryException.java class InventoryException extends Exception // InventoryException(int line, String message) int line() // getMessage(): "line <n : <message " // Inventory.java class Inventory { void add(Item item) // IllegalArgumentException("duplicate sku <sku ") if the sku exists Item find(String sku) // null when unknown; skus ignore case void restock(String sku, int amount) // amount = 1; NoSuchElementException("no item <sku ") when unknown void sell(String sku, int amount) // amount = 1; IllegalStateException("only <n left") when short long totalValueCents() List<Item lowStock(int threshold) // quantity below threshold; lowest quantity first, then sku List<Item search(String term) // name contains term, ignoring case; sorted by name, then sku List<Item all() // sorted by sku void save(Path file) throws IOException static Inventory load(Path file) throws IOException, InventoryException } Items : sku is 3 to 12 letters, digits or - , stored in upper case; name is not blank and is trimmed; quantity is 0 or more; priceCents is 0 or more. A record's compact constructor checks this and throws IllegalArgumentException (it may also normalise the values it is given). Files are CSV with a header line sku,name,quantity,price . Prices are written in euros with 2 decimals ( 2.50 ). Names never contain commas. Example: sku,name,quantity,price TEA-01,Green tea,40,2.50 MUG-01,Large mug,3,8.00 - save writes the header and then all() in sku order, creating missing parent folders. - load reads such a file. A missing file lets the IOException through. It throws InventoryException for: a wrong header ( line 1: bad header ), a line without exactly 4 fields ( wrong number of fields ), a quantity or price that is not a number ( bad number , with the NumberFormatException as the cause), an item the record rejects (its message, with the IllegalArgumentException as the cause), and a duplicate sku ( duplicate sku <SKU ). Blank lines are skipped. Line numbers count from 1 (the header).

title: 5.01  Algorithm Analysis and Big O
body: How to compare algorithms independently of computers - counting basic steps, Big O notation and the common growth classes from O(1) to O(2^n), analysing loops, nested loops and halving, best, worst and average cases, the costs of Java's collection operations, measuring with System.nanoTime, and space complexity. Counting steps How fast is an algorithm? Timing it depends on the computer, the JVM warming up and what else is running. Instead we count how the number of basic steps grows with the size of the input, n . java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { int data = new int 1000 ; for (int i = 0; i < data.length; i++) data i = i; System.out.println(contains(data, 999) + " " + hasDuplicate(data) + " " + binarySearch(data, 999)); } static boolean contains(int a, int target) { // up to n comparisons: O(n) for (int x : a) if (x == target) return true; return false; } static boolean hasDuplicate(int a) { // about n n/2 comparisons: O(n²) for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) for (int j = i + 1; j < a.length; j++) if (a i == a j ) return true; return false; } static int binarySearch(int a, int target) { // halves the range each step: O(log n) int lo = 0, hi = a.length - 1; while (lo <= hi) { int mid = (lo + hi) 1; if (a mid == target) return mid; if (a mid < target) lo = mid + 1; else hi = mid - 1; } return -1; } } Big O Big O describes the growth rate, ignoring constant factors and smaller terms: 3n² + 5n + 20 steps is O(n²) , because for large n the n² term dominates everything else. Class Name Example n = 1 000 n = 1 000 000 --- --- --- --- --- O(1) constant array index, HashMap.get 1 1 O(log n) logarithmic binary search 10 20 O(n) linear one loop over the data 1 000 1 000 000 O(n log n) linearithmic merge sort, Arrays.sort 10 000 20 000 000 O(n²) quadratic nested loops over the data 1 000 000 10¹² (hours) O(2ⁿ) exponential trying every subset, naive Fibonacci 10³⁰¹ forever The difference between O(n log n) and O(n²) is the difference between a program that sorts a million items in a fraction of a second and one that takes days. Analysing code - Simple statements are O(1). - A loop that runs n times around O(1) work is O(n). - Nested loops multiply: an O(n) loop inside an O(n) loop is O(n²). - Sequential parts add, and the biggest wins: O(n) followed by O(n²) is O(n²). - A loop that halves (or doubles) its range each step is O(log n). - A method call costs whatever that method costs: calling an O(n) method inside an O(n) loop is O(n²). That last rule hides many slow programs: java-norun for (String word : words) { // n times if (!unique.contains(word)) { // ArrayList.contains is O(n): the whole loop is O(n²) unique.add(word); } } // With a HashSet, contains is O(1) on average, and the loop is O(n). Best, worst and average Linear search finds the target immediately in the best case (it is first), checks everything in the worst case (it is last or missing), and about half in the average case. Big O usually describes the worst case, because that is the guarantee. Quicksort is O(n log n) on average but O(n²) in its worst case; merge sort is O(n log n) always. Costs of Java's collections Operation ArrayList LinkedList HashMap / HashSet TreeMap / TreeSet --- --- --- --- --- get by index O(1) O(n) - - add at the end O(1) amortised O(1) - - insert / remove at the front O(n) O(1) - - contains / find by key O(n) O(n) O(1) average O(log n) add / remove by key - - O(1) average O(log n) iterate in sorted order - - no order O(n) "Amortised O(1)" means that occasionally an add costs O(n), when the array is full and must be copied into a bigger one, but spread over many adds the average is constant (lesson 5.04 builds such a list). Measuring Analysis predicts; measurement confirms. System.nanoTime() measures elapsed time: java import java.util. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { for (int n : new int {2_000, 4_000, 8_000}) { List<Integer list = new ArrayList< (); Set<Integer set = new HashSet< (); for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { list.add(i); set.add(i); } long t0 = System.nanoTime(); int found = 0; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) if (list.contains(n - 1 - i)) found++; // O(n²) in total long t1 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) if (set.contains(n - 1 - i)) found++; // O(n) in total long t2 = System.nanoTime(); System.out.printf("n=%d list=%d ms set=%d ms (%d)%n", n, (t1 - t0) / 1_000_000, (t2 - t1) / 1_000_000, found); } } } Doubling n roughly quadruples the list time (quadratic) and roughly doubles the set time (linear). Small timings are noisy: the JVM compiles hot code while running, so measure repeatedly with large inputs, or use a benchmarking tool such as JMH. Space Algorithms also use memory . Making a copy of the input is O(n) extra space; a few variables are O(1); recursion uses stack space proportional to its depth (O(log n) for binary search written recursively, O(n) for a recursive sum). Check yourself quiz ? What is the Big O of 5n² + 100n + 7 ? - O(5n² + 100n) - O(n² + n) + O(n²) - O(n³) The fastest-growing term dominates and constant factors are dropped, so only n² is left. ? Why is a loop over n words that calls contains on an ArrayList inside it usually O(n²)? + contains scans the list, O(n), and it runs once per iteration of an O(n) loop - ArrayList copies its whole array every time contains is called - Any loop with an if inside it is O(n²) - contains sorts the list before it searches it A method call costs what the method costs: an O(n) scan inside an O(n) loop multiplies to O(n²). A HashSet makes each contains O(1) on average. ? A loop does for (int i = 1; i < n; i = 2) . How many times does it run? - n - n / 2 - n² + about log₂ n i doubles each time, so it reaches n after about log₂ n steps. ? Quicksort is O(n log n) on average. What is its worst case? - O(n log n) + O(n²) - O(log n) - O(2ⁿ) Quicksort can degrade to O(n²) when its pivots split the data badly; merge sort is the one that is O(n log n) always.

title: Make it fast
body: The starter's methods give the right answers but are O(n²). Rewrite each one to be O(n) (or O(n log n)), so that the tests with 200 000 numbers finish in time: java class Fast { static boolean hasDuplicate(int a) // any value twice? static int twoSum(int sorted, int target) // indexes {i, j}, i < j, with sorted i + sorted j == target, or null static int longestRun(int a) // length of the longest run of consecutive equal values static int countDistinct(int a) } For twoSum the array is sorted ascending; return the pair with the smallest i (and for that i , the smallest j ).

title: 5.02  Searching and Sorting
body: Linear and binary search with their invariants and the overflow-safe midpoint, the simple sorts (selection and insertion) and why they are O(n²), divide and conquer with merge sort and quicksort, stability, choosing a pivot, and what Java's own sorts use. Searching Linear search checks every item: O(n), but it works on any list. Binary search needs a sorted array and halves the range each step: O(log n). java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { int sorted = {2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 56, 72, 91}; for (int target : new int {23, 2, 91, 7}) System.out.print(binarySearch(sorted, target) + " "); System.out.println(); } static int binarySearch(int a, int target) { int lo = 0, hi = a.length - 1; // the target, if present, is always in a lo..hi while (lo <= hi) { int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2; // not (lo + hi) / 2: that can overflow for huge arrays if (a mid == target) return mid; if (a mid < target) lo = mid + 1; // the target is to the right else hi = mid - 1; // the target is to the left } return -1; } } The comment on the first line is the loop's invariant : a statement that is true before every round. Binary search is famously easy to get subtly wrong (infinite loops, off-by-one bounds); keeping the invariant in mind is how to get it right. Arrays.binarySearch and Collections.binarySearch do it for you. Simple sorts Selection sort repeatedly finds the smallest remaining item and swaps it into place. Insertion sort takes each item and slides it left into the sorted part, like sorting playing cards in your hand: java import java.util.Arrays; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { int a = {29, 10, 14, 37, 13}; selectionSort(a); System.out.println(Arrays.toString(a)); int b = {5, 2, 4, 6, 1, 3}; insertionSort(b); System.out.println(Arrays.toString(b)); } static void selectionSort(int a) { for (int i = 0; i < a.length - 1; i++) { int min = i; for (int j = i + 1; j < a.length; j++) if (a j < a min ) min = j; int tmp = a i ; a i = a min ; a min = tmp; } } static void insertionSort(int a) { for (int i = 1; i < a.length; i++) { int key = a i ; int j = i - 1; while (j = 0 && a j key) { a j + 1 = a j ; // shift bigger items right j--; } a j + 1 = key; } } } Both are O(n²) in the worst case. Insertion sort is O(n) on data that is already nearly sorted, which is why fast library sorts use it for small pieces. Merge sort Divide and conquer : split the array in half, sort each half recursively, then merge the two sorted halves in one pass. There are log n levels of splitting and each level does O(n) merging work, so merge sort is O(n log n) in every case. It needs O(n) extra space and is stable (equal items keep their order). java import java.util.Arrays; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { int a = {38, 27, 43, 3, 9, 82, 10}; mergeSort(a, 0, a.length); System.out.println(Arrays.toString(a)); } static void mergeSort(int a, int from, int to) { // sorts a from..to) if (to - from < 2) return; int mid = (from + to) 1; mergeSort(a, from, mid); mergeSort(a, mid, to); int merged = new int to - from ; int i = from, j = mid, k = 0; while (i < mid && j < to) merged k++ = a i <= a j ? a i++ : a j++ ; // <= keeps it stable while (i < mid) merged k++ = a i++ ; while (j < to) merged k++ = a j++ ; System.arraycopy(merged, 0, a, from, merged.length); } } Quicksort Quicksort picks a pivot , partitions the array so smaller items come before it and larger after, and recursively sorts both sides. It sorts in place and is very fast in practice: O(n log n) on average, but O(n²) when the pivots are consistently bad (for example, always the first item of already sorted data). Choosing the middle item or a random one avoids the common bad cases. java import java.util.Arrays; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { int a = {10, 80, 30, 90, 40, 50, 70}; quickSort(a, 0, a.length - 1); System.out.println(Arrays.toString(a)); } static void quickSort(int a, int lo, int hi) { if (lo = hi) return; int pivot = a (lo + hi) 1 ; int i = lo, j = hi; while (i <= j) { // Hoare-style partition while (a i < pivot) i++; while (a j pivot) j--; if (i <= j) { int t = a i ; a i = a j ; a j = t; i++; j--; } } quickSort(a, lo, j); quickSort(a, i, hi); } } Java's own sorts Call Algorithm Stable --- --- --- Arrays.sort(int ) and other primitives Dual-pivot quicksort Not needed (equal numbers are identical) Arrays.sort(Object ) , List.sort , Collections.sort TimSort (merge sort + insertion sort, fast on partly sorted data) Yes Use the library sorts in real programs. Writing the algorithms yourself is how you learn the ideas they rely on: divide and conquer, invariants, and analysing recursive work. Check yourself quiz ? Why is binary search O(log n)? - It skips every second item of the array + Each comparison halves the range that can still contain the target - It only looks at the first log n items - It sorts the array first, which takes log n steps Halving the range each step means a range of n items is down to one after about log₂ n comparisons. ? Merge sort is stable. What does that mean, and what in the merge makes it so? - It never uses extra memory; copying back with System.arraycopy does that - It is always O(n log n); splitting at mid does that - Equal items keep their original order; the while (i < mid) loop does that + Equal items keep their original order; taking from the left half when a i <= a j does that On a tie the merge takes the item from the left half, which came first in the original. With < instead of <= equal items could swap places. ? Which sort is O(n log n) even in the worst case? - Quicksort - Insertion sort - Selection sort + Merge sort Merge sort always splits evenly; quicksort can degrade to O(n²) with bad pivots.

title: Sorting algorithms
body: Implement sorting yourself (no Arrays.sort , Collections.sort or List.sort ): java class Sorts { static void insertionSort(int a) // in place static int mergeSort(int a) // returns a new sorted array; a is unchanged static long countInversions(int a) // pairs i < j with a i a j , in O(n log n) static <T void stableSort(List<T list, Comparator<? super T cmp) // a stable merge sort of the list, in place } countInversions measures how far an array is from sorted: {2, 4, 1, 3, 5} has 3 (2 1, 4 1, 4 3). Count them while merge sorting: when an item from the right half is taken before the remaining items of the left half, it forms an inversion with each of them. The tests use 100 000 numbers, too many for an O(n²) count.

title: 5.03  Linked Lists
body: Building a singly linked list from nodes - adding at the front and back with a tail reference, getting by index, removing, reversing in place, iterating with Iterator, the edge cases of empty and one-element lists, doubly linked lists and sentinel nodes, and comparing linked lists with array lists. Nodes and links A linked list stores each item in a node that also holds a reference to the next node. The list keeps a reference to the first node, the head ; the last node's next is null . Adding at the front is O(1): make a new node point at the old head. There is no indexing in O(1): reaching item i means following i links. A singly linked list java import java.util.Iterator; import java.util.NoSuchElementException; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { MyList<String list = new MyList< (); list.addLast("b"); list.addFirst("a"); list.addLast("c"); list.addLast("d"); System.out.println(list + " size " + list.size() + " get(2)=" + list.get(2)); list.remove("c"); list.reverse(); System.out.println(list); for (String s : list) System.out.print(s.toUpperCase()); System.out.println(); } } class MyList<T implements Iterable<T { private static class Node<T { T value; Node<T next; Node(T value, Node<T next) { this.value = value; this.next = next; } } private Node<T head, tail; private int size; void addFirst(T value) { head = new Node< (value, head); if (tail == null) tail = head; // the list was empty size++; } void addLast(T value) { Node<T node = new Node< (value, null); if (tail == null) head = tail = node; // the list was empty else { tail.next = node; tail = node; } size++; } T get(int index) { if (index < 0 index = size) throw new IndexOutOfBoundsException("index " + index); Node<T n = head; for (int i = 0; i < index; i++) n = n.next; return n.value; } boolean remove(T value) { Node<T prev = null; for (Node<T n = head; n != null; prev = n, n = n.next) { if (n.value.equals(value)) { if (prev == null) head = n.next; else prev.next = n.next; // unlink if (n == tail) tail = prev; size--; return true; } } return false; } void reverse() { Node<T prev = null, cur = head; tail = head; while (cur != null) { Node<T next = cur.next; cur.next = prev; // turn the arrow around prev = cur; cur = next; } head = prev; } int size() { return size; } public Iterator<T iterator() { return new Iterator< () { private Node<T next = head; public boolean hasNext() { return next != null; } public T next() { if (next == null) throw new NoSuchElementException(); T v = next.value; next = next.next; return v; } }; } @Override public String toString() { StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(" "); for (Node<T n = head; n != null; n = n.next) sb.append(n.value).append(n.next != null ? ", " : ""); return sb.append(" ").toString(); } } Points to notice: - Node is a private static nested class : it is part of the list's implementation, invisible outside. - Keeping a tail reference makes addLast O(1) instead of walking the whole list. - Every method that changes the list must handle the edge cases : the empty list, a one-node list, and changes at the head or the tail. Most linked-list bugs live there; draw the boxes and arrows on paper for each case. - Implementing Iterable lets the list work with the enhanced for . Reversing in place reverse walks the list once with three references ( prev , cur , next ) and turns each link around: O(n) time and O(1) extra space. It is a classic interview question because it tests exactly the pointer handling above. Doubly linked lists A doubly linked node also points to the previous node. Removing a node you already hold becomes O(1) (no need to find its predecessor), and the list can be walked backwards. java.util.LinkedList is doubly linked. Many implementations use a sentinel (dummy) node at both ends, so that the first and last real nodes are not special cases. Linked list or array list? ArrayList Linked list --- --- --- get(i) O(1) O(n) add/remove at the front O(n) O(1) add at the end O(1) amortised O(1) with a tail memory compact array one object per item, with extra references cache friendliness excellent poor In practice ArrayList (and ArrayDeque for queues) win almost every benchmark, because modern processors are very fast at reading consecutive memory. Linked structures matter as building blocks : queues, hash table buckets, adjacency lists in graphs, and trees, which are linked lists with more than one next . Check yourself quiz ? Why is get(i) O(n) for a linked list? - Every node has to be copied into an array first - It has to check every node for the value + There is no index: it must follow i links from the head - It walks backwards from the tail Nodes are not stored next to each other, so the only way to item i is to follow next links one at a time. ? Besides a node in the middle, which cases must remove handle? - Only the empty list; every other case works the same way - Only removing the head, since it has no predecessor - Only removing the tail, so that tail is updated + The head, the tail, a one-node list, and a value that is not there Most linked-list bugs live at the edges: the head has no predecessor, the tail reference must move back, and a missing value must leave the list untouched. ? In the reverse method, what would happen without Node<T next = cur.next; at the start of the loop? - Nothing: the variable is only there to make it faster - The list would be reversed twice and end up unchanged + The rest of the list would be lost after cur.next = prev - It would not compile, because next is not declared The original next link must be saved before it is overwritten; otherwise there is no way to reach the following node.

title: A linked list of ints
body: Write a singly linked list from scratch, with a private nested Node class and head and tail references (no java.util collections inside): java class IntLinkedList { void addFirst(int value) void addLast(int value) int removeFirst() // NoSuchElementException when empty int get(int index) // IndexOutOfBoundsException outside 0..size-1 int indexOf(int value) // first index, or -1 int removeAll(int value) // removes every node holding value; returns how many void reverse() // in place, O(n), no new nodes int middle() // the middle value, the second of the two middles for an even size; one pass int size() String toString() // " 1, 2, 3 " } middle must walk the list once, using two references that move at different speeds; removeAll must also keep tail correct, so that addLast still works afterwards.

title: 5.04  Stacks, Queues and Hash Tables
body: Implementing a growable array list with amortised O(1) appends, a stack and its uses (undo, bracket matching, expression evaluation), a circular-buffer queue, and a hash table with chaining - hash functions, buckets, load factor and resizing - and why equals and hashCode matter. A growable array ArrayList is an array with spare room. When the array is full, it allocates a bigger one (typically 1.5 or 2 times bigger) and copies everything: java import java.util.Arrays; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { IntList list = new IntList(); for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) list.add(i i); System.out.println(list.size() + " " + list.get(19) + " capacity " + list.capacity()); } } class IntList { private int data = new int 4 ; private int size; void add(int value) { if (size == data.length) data = Arrays.copyOf(data, data.length 2); // grow: O(n), but rarely data size++ = value; } int get(int i) { if (i < 0 i = size) throw new IndexOutOfBoundsException(i); return data i ; } int size() { return size; } int capacity() { return data.length; } } Because the capacity doubles, adding n items copies at most 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + n < 2n items in total: amortised O(1) per add. Stacks A stack is last in, first out: push on top, pop from the top, peek at the top, all O(1). Stacks undo actions, track nested structure, and evaluate expressions: java import java.util.ArrayDeque; import java.util.Deque; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { System.out.println(evalPostfix("3 4 + 2 ")); // (3 + 4) 2 System.out.println(evalPostfix("5 1 2 + 4 + 3 -")); // 5 + (1 + 2) 4 - 3 } static int evalPostfix(String expr) { Deque<Integer stack = new ArrayDeque< (); for (String tok : expr.split(" ")) { switch (tok) { case "+", "-", " ", "/" - { int b = stack.pop(), a = stack.pop(); // note the order stack.push(switch (tok) { case "+" - a + b; case "-" - a - b; case " " - a b; default - a / b; }); } default - stack.push(Integer.parseInt(tok)); } } return stack.pop(); } } The method-call stack itself (lesson 2.04) is the same idea: each call is pushed, and returning pops it. Queues A queue is first in, first out: offer at the back, poll from the front. A circular buffer implements it in an array without shifting: front and back indexes move forward and wrap around. java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { RingQueue q = new RingQueue(3); q.offer(1); q.offer(2); q.offer(3); System.out.println(q.poll() + " " + q.poll()); q.offer(4); q.offer(5); // wraps around the end of the array StringBuilder out = new StringBuilder(); while (!q.isEmpty()) out.append(q.poll()).append(' '); System.out.println(out); } } class RingQueue { private final int data; private int front, size; RingQueue(int capacity) { data = new int capacity ; } boolean offer(int x) { if (size == data.length) return false; // full data (front + size) % data.length = x; size++; return true; } int poll() { if (size == 0) throw new IllegalStateException("empty"); int x = data front ; front = (front + 1) % data.length; size--; return x; } boolean isEmpty() { return size == 0; } } Queues schedule work fairly (print jobs, requests, breadth-first search in graphs). Hash tables A hash table finds a key in O(1) on average. A hash function turns the key into a number; that number modulo the array length chooses a bucket . Different keys can land in the same bucket (a collision ); with chaining , each bucket holds a small list of entries. java import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.LinkedList; import java.util.List; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { HashTable<String, Integer ages = new HashTable< (); ages.put("Ada", 36); ages.put("Grace", 85); ages.put("Ada", 37); for (int i = 0; i < 50; i++) ages.put("user" + i, i); System.out.println(ages.get("Ada") + " " + ages.get("Bob") + " size " + ages.size() + " buckets " + ages.buckets()); } } class HashTable<K, V { private record Entry<K, V (K key, V value) { } private List<LinkedList<Entry<K, V table = newTable(8); private int size; private static <K, V List<LinkedList<Entry<K, V newTable(int n) { List<LinkedList<Entry<K, V t = new ArrayList< (n); for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) t.add(new LinkedList< ()); return t; } private int indexFor(K key, int buckets) { return Math.floorMod(key.hashCode(), buckets); // hashCode may be negative } V get(K key) { for (Entry<K, V e : table.get(indexFor(key, table.size()))) { if (e.key().equals(key)) return e.value(); } return null; } void put(K key, V value) { LinkedList<Entry<K, V bucket = table.get(indexFor(key, table.size())); for (var it = bucket.listIterator(); it.hasNext(); ) { if (it.next().key().equals(key)) { it.set(new Entry< (key, value)); return; } // replace } bucket.add(new Entry< (key, value)); size++; if (size table.size() 3 / 4) resize(); // load factor 0.75 } private void resize() { List<LinkedList<Entry<K, V bigger = newTable(table.size() 2); for (LinkedList<Entry<K, V bucket : table) for (Entry<K, V e : bucket) bigger.get(indexFor(e.key(), bigger.size())).add(e); table = bigger; } int size() { return size; } int buckets() { return table.size(); } } - The load factor is entries ÷ buckets. Keeping it below about 0.75 (by doubling and re-inserting everything) keeps buckets short, so get and put stay O(1) on average. - A poor hash function that sends many keys to the same bucket turns the table into a linked list: O(n). Java's HashMap even turns long buckets into small trees to limit the damage. - This is why keys must have consistent equals and hashCode (lesson 4.02): hashCode picks the bucket, equals finds the entry inside it. Check yourself quiz ? Why does doubling the capacity make ArrayList.add amortised O(1)? - Copying an array is O(1) in Java - The list never has to copy anything after the first resize + Copies happen at sizes 1, 2, 4, ..., n, which add up to less than 2n copies for n adds - Each add copies only the half of the array that is full A single resize is O(n), but they are so rare that the total copying stays below 2n, a constant amount per add on average. ? What happens to a hash table's speed if every key has the same hashCode ? - Nothing: equals still finds each key in O(1) + All entries share one bucket, so lookups scan a list: O(n) - The table resizes until every key has its own bucket - put throws an exception for the duplicate hash codes hashCode picks the bucket; if they are all equal, one bucket holds everything and resizing does not help, because the keys still all land together. ? Evaluating the postfix expression 6 2 / with the stack method above gives: - 0 - 1/3 + 3 - an error b = 2 is popped first, then a = 6 , and a / b = 3 ; the order matters for - and / .

title: A min-stack and a hash set
match: A min-stack and a hash set
body: Write two data structures from scratch. java // MinStack.java: a stack of ints that also reports its minimum, every operation O(1) class MinStack { void push(int x) int pop() // NoSuchElementException when empty int peek() int min() // the smallest value currently in the stack boolean isEmpty() } // IntHashSet.java: a set of ints using an array of buckets with chaining class IntHashSet { boolean add(int x) // false if already present boolean contains(int x) boolean remove(int x) // false if absent int size() int capacity() // the number of buckets: starts at 8, doubles when size would exceed 0.75 x capacity } Use arrays and your own node classes; java.util collections are not allowed inside these classes (exceptions are fine). Negative numbers must work in the hash set.

title: 5.05  Trees and Binary Search Trees
body: Trees and their vocabulary, binary trees, the binary search tree property, recursive insert, search and delete including the two-child case, in-order, pre-order, post-order and level-order traversal, height and balance, why balanced trees like Java's TreeMap guarantee O(log n), and heaps for priority queues. Trees A tree is made of nodes connected by edges, with one root at the top. Each node has zero or more children ; nodes without children are leaves . The height of a tree is the number of edges on the longest path from the root to a leaf. File systems, HTML pages, organisation charts and parsed expressions (practice 3.05) are trees. In a binary tree every node has at most two children, left and right . Binary search trees A binary search tree (BST) keeps this property at every node: everything in the left subtree is smaller, and everything in the right subtree is larger. Searching follows one path down, discarding half the tree at each step when the tree is balanced: java import java.util. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Bst tree = new Bst(); for (int x : new int {50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80, 30}) tree.insert(x); System.out.println(tree.inOrder() + " size " + tree.size() + " height " + tree.height()); System.out.println(tree.contains(60) + " " + tree.contains(65) + " min " + tree.min()); tree.delete(30); // a node with two children tree.delete(80); // a leaf System.out.println(tree.inOrder() + " " + tree.preOrder() + " " + tree.levelOrder()); } } class Bst { private static class Node { int key; Node left, right; Node(int key) { this.key = key; } } private Node root; private int size; void insert(int key) { root = insert(root, key); } private Node insert(Node n, int key) { if (n == null) { size++; return new Node(key); } if (key < n.key) n.left = insert(n.left, key); else if (key n.key) n.right = insert(n.right, key); return n; // duplicates are ignored } boolean contains(int key) { Node n = root; while (n != null) { if (key == n.key) return true; n = key < n.key ? n.left : n.right; } return false; } int min() { if (root == null) throw new NoSuchElementException(); Node n = root; while (n.left != null) n = n.left; return n.key; } void delete(int key) { root = delete(root, key); } private Node delete(Node n, int key) { if (n == null) return null; if (key < n.key) n.left = delete(n.left, key); else if (key n.key) n.right = delete(n.right, key); else { if (n.left == null) { size--; return n.right; } // zero or one child: replace by the child if (n.right == null) { size--; return n.left; } Node successor = n.right; // two children: take the smallest key on the right while (successor.left != null) successor = successor.left; n.key = successor.key; n.right = delete(n.right, successor.key); } return n; } int size() { return size; } int height() { return height(root); } private int height(Node n) { return n == null ? -1 : 1 + Math.max(height(n.left), height(n.right)); } List<Integer inOrder() { List<Integer out = new ArrayList< (); inOrder(root, out); return out; } private void inOrder(Node n, List<Integer out) { if (n == null) return; inOrder(n.left, out); out.add(n.key); inOrder(n.right, out); // left, node, right: sorted } List<Integer preOrder() { List<Integer out = new ArrayList< (); preOrder(root, out); return out; } private void preOrder(Node n, List<Integer out) { if (n == null) return; out.add(n.key); preOrder(n.left, out); preOrder(n.right, out); // node first: copies the shape } List<Integer levelOrder() { // breadth first, with a queue List<Integer out = new ArrayList< (); Deque<Node queue = new ArrayDeque< (); if (root != null) queue.add(root); while (!queue.isEmpty()) { Node n = queue.poll(); out.add(n.key); if (n.left != null) queue.add(n.left); if (n.right != null) queue.add(n.right); } return out; } } Recursive methods that return the (possibly new) subtree, like insert and delete , avoid special cases for the root: root = insert(root, key) . Deleting Deleting has three cases: 1. a leaf : just remove it; 2. a node with one child : replace it by that child; 3. a node with two children : copy in its in-order successor (the smallest key in its right subtree), then delete the successor from the right subtree, which has at most one child. Traversals Order Visits Typical use --- --- --- In-order left, node, right A BST's keys in sorted order Pre-order node, left, right Copying or printing the tree's structure Post-order left, right, node Deleting a tree, evaluating an expression tree Level-order level by level, with a queue Shortest paths in unweighted trees, printing by depth Balance A BST's operations take time proportional to its height . Random insertions give a height of O(log n) on average (about 3 log₂ n), but inserting keys in sorted order makes every node a right child: the "tree" becomes a linked list and everything is O(n). Self-balancing trees fix this by restructuring (rotating) nodes during insertions and deletions so the height stays O(log n). Java's TreeMap and TreeSet are red-black trees : their get , put and remove are O(log n) guaranteed, and they iterate in sorted order. Heaps A binary heap is a different tree property: every parent is smaller than (or equal to) its children, so the minimum is always at the root. It is stored compactly in an array (the children of index i are 2i + 1 and 2i + 2 ), and both adding and removing the minimum are O(log n). Java's PriorityQueue is a binary heap; heap sort and Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm are built on one. Check yourself quiz ? What does an in-order traversal of a BST produce? + The keys in sorted order - The keys in the order they were inserted - The keys level by level, starting at the root - The root first, then the left and right subtrees In-order visits left, node, right; with smaller keys on the left that is ascending order. Root first is pre-order, level by level is level-order. ? Why can inserting 1, 2, 3, ..., n into a plain BST be slow? - Every insert has to rebalance the whole tree - Duplicate keys pile up in the left subtree - Recursion is slower than a loop for every insert + Each key becomes the right child of the last, so the tree is a chain The chain has height about n, so operations become O(n): a plain BST does not rebalance, and sorted input turns it into a linked list. Self-balancing trees like TreeMap keep the height O(log n). ? Deleting a node with two children replaces its key with: - its left child's key - the root's key - the largest key in the whole tree + the smallest key in its right subtree The in-order successor keeps the BST property; the largest key in the left subtree would also work.

title: An LRU cache
body: A least-recently-used (LRU) cache keeps a limited number of entries; when it is full, adding a new one evicts the entry that was used longest ago. Web browsers, databases and operating systems all use one. Every operation must be O(1) , which needs two structures working together: - a HashMap from key to node, for finding an entry in O(1); - a doubly linked list of nodes in order of use, most recent at the front, for moving and evicting in O(1). Write the list yourself (no LinkedHashMap , LinkedList or ArrayDeque ): java // LruCache.java class LruCache<K, V { LruCache(int capacity) // capacity = 1, else IllegalArgumentException V get(K key) // null when absent; a hit makes the entry the most recent void put(K key, V value) // adds or replaces (and makes it the most recent); evicts when full boolean remove(K key) int size() List<K keys() // most recent first void onEvict(BiConsumer<K, V listener) // called with each evicted entry (not for remove or replace) Stats stats() } // Stats.java record Stats(long hits, long misses, long evictions) { double hitRate() // hits / (hits + misses), or 0 when there were no gets }

title: 6.01  Lambdas and Functional Interfaces
body: Passing behaviour as a value - functional interfaces, lambda syntax, method references, the java.util.function interfaces (Function, Predicate, Consumer, Supplier, BiFunction, UnaryOperator), composing functions, effectively final captured variables, and lambdas with the collections API (forEach, removeIf, replaceAll, sort, computeIfAbsent). Behaviour as a value A functional interface is an interface with exactly one abstract method. A lambda is a short way to write an object that implements it: java import java.util. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Comparator<String byLength = (a, b) - Integer.compare(a.length(), b.length()); // a lambda Runnable hello = () - System.out.println("hello"); hello.run(); List<String words = new ArrayList< (List.of("banana", "fig", "cherry", "kiwi")); words.sort(byLength); System.out.println(words); Calculator add = (x, y) - x + y; // our own functional interface Calculator power = (x, y) - { // a block body needs return int result = 1; for (int i = 0; i < y; i++) result = x; return result; }; System.out.println(add.apply(2, 3) + " " + power.apply(2, 10)); } } @FunctionalInterface interface Calculator { int apply(int x, int y); } Lambda syntax: (parameters) - expression , or (parameters) - { statements; } . Parameter types are inferred; a single parameter needs no parentheses: s - s.length() . @FunctionalInterface asks the compiler to check that the interface has exactly one abstract method. The standard functional interfaces java.util.function provides interfaces for the common shapes, so you rarely define your own: Interface Method Shape Example --- --- --- --- Function<T, R R apply(T t) T to R String::length BiFunction<T, U, R R apply(T t, U u) two inputs to R (a, b) - a + b Predicate<T boolean test(T t) a yes/no question s - s.isEmpty() Consumer<T void accept(T t) uses a value System.out::println Supplier<T T get() makes a value ArrayList::new UnaryOperator<T T apply(T t) T to T s - s.trim() BinaryOperator<T T apply(T a, T b) two Ts to T Integer::sum Primitive versions ( IntPredicate , ToIntFunction , IntBinaryOperator ...) avoid boxing in performance-sensitive code. Method references When a lambda only calls an existing method, a method reference says the same more briefly: java import java.util. ; import java.util.function. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Function<String, Integer length = String::length; // an instance method of the argument Function<String, Integer parse = Integer::parseInt; // a static method Consumer<Object print = System.out::println; // an instance method of a specific object Supplier<List<String newList = ArrayList::new; // a constructor BinaryOperator<Integer sum = Integer::sum; print.accept(length.apply("hello") + parse.apply("41") + sum.apply(1, 0)); List<String list = newList.get(); list.add("made by a supplier"); print.accept(list); } } Composing functions The functional interfaces have default methods for combining them: java import java.util.function. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Function<Integer, Integer doubleIt = x - x 2; Function<Integer, Integer addTen = x - x + 10; System.out.println(doubleIt.andThen(addTen).apply(5)); // (5 2) + 10 = 20 System.out.println(doubleIt.compose(addTen).apply(5)); // (5 + 10) 2 = 30 Predicate<String notEmpty = s - !s.isEmpty(); Predicate<String shortWord = s - s.length() < 5; Predicate<String keep = notEmpty.and(shortWord.negate()); System.out.println(keep.test("banana") + " " + keep.test("fig") + " " + keep.test("")); } } Capturing variables A lambda can use local variables from the surrounding code only if they are effectively final (never reassigned after initialisation): java import java.util. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { int threshold = 3; // effectively final: fine to capture List<String words = List.of("a", "abcd", "ab", "abcdef"); words.stream().filter(w - w.length() threshold).forEach(System.out::println); // int count = 0; // words.forEach(w - count++); // error: count is not effectively final int count = {0}; // a common workaround; a stream's count() is better words.forEach(w - count 0 ++); System.out.println(count 0 ); } } Lambdas with collections Many collection methods take functions: java import java.util. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { List<String names = new ArrayList< (List.of("ada", "", "grace", "linus", "")); names.removeIf(String::isEmpty); names.replaceAll(s - Character.toUpperCase(s.charAt(0)) + s.substring(1)); names.sort(Comparator.comparing(String::length).thenComparing(Comparator.reverseOrder())); names.forEach(n - System.out.print(n + " ")); System.out.println(); Map<Integer, List<String byLength = new TreeMap< (); for (String n : names) byLength.computeIfAbsent(n.length(), k - new ArrayList< ()).add(n); byLength.forEach((len, group) - System.out.println(len + ": " + group)); Map<String, Integer stock = new HashMap< (Map.of("tea", 3)); stock.merge("tea", 2, Integer::sum); stock.computeIfPresent("tea", (k, v) - v 4 ? v - 4 : v); System.out.println(stock); } } Check yourself quiz ? What makes an interface usable with a lambda? - It is marked @FunctionalInterface + It has exactly one abstract method - All of its methods are default methods - It is in the java.util.function package Any interface with exactly one abstract method is a functional interface. @FunctionalInterface only asks the compiler to check that; it is not required. ? Which functional interface fits "takes a String , returns true or false"? - Function<String, String - Supplier<Boolean - Consumer<String + Predicate<String Predicate<T has boolean test(T t) . A Consumer returns nothing and a Supplier takes no input. ? What is f.andThen(g).apply(x) the same as? - f.apply(g.apply(x)) + g.apply(f.apply(x)) - f.apply(x) + g.apply(x) - g.apply(x) andThen runs f first, then g on its result; compose is the other order.

title: Functions as values
body: Write helpers that take and return functions, in Funcs.java : java class Funcs { static <T UnaryOperator<T pipeline(List<UnaryOperator<T steps) // applies the steps left to right static <T Predicate<T allOf(List<Predicate<T tests) // true when every test passes (true for none) static <T, R Function<T, R memoize(Function<T, R f) // calls f once per distinct argument static Supplier<Integer counter(int start, int step) // each get() returns the next value: start, start+step, ... static <T Map<Boolean, List<T split(List<T items, Predicate<T test) // {true= matching , false= others }, order kept } Each call to counter or memoize returns an independent function with its own state.

title: 6.02  The Stream API
body: Processing data declaratively with streams - creating streams, intermediate operations (filter, map, flatMap, sorted, distinct, limit), terminal operations (collect, toList, count, reduce, anyMatch, min, max), primitive streams and summary statistics, Collectors for grouping, partitioning, joining and mapping, laziness, and when a loop is clearer. A pipeline A stream is a sequence of values flowing through a pipeline of operations. It describes what to compute, not how to loop: java import java.util. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { List<String words = List.of("stream", "lambda", "java", "list", "map", "filter", "java"); List<String result = words.stream() .filter(w - w.length() 3) // keep some .map(String::toUpperCase) // transform each .distinct() // drop repeats .sorted() // order .toList(); // collect (Java 16+) System.out.println(result); System.out.println(words.stream().filter(w - w.startsWith("l")).count()); } } A pipeline has a source ( list.stream() , Arrays.stream(array) , Stream.of(...) , IntStream.range(0, 10) , Files.lines(path) ), any number of intermediate operations that return a new stream, and one terminal operation that produces a result. Intermediate Does --- --- filter(pred) Keeps matching items map(f) , mapToInt(f) Transforms each item flatMap(f) Replaces each item by a stream of items, flattened distinct() , sorted() , sorted(cmp) Removes repeats, sorts limit(n) , skip(n) , takeWhile(p) , dropWhile(p) Cuts the stream peek(f) Looks at items as they pass (for debugging) Terminal Gives --- --- toList() , collect(...) A collection forEach(f) Runs f on each item count() , sum() , average() , min() , max() Numbers (some as Optional ) anyMatch , allMatch , noneMatch Booleans findFirst() , findAny() An Optional item reduce(identity, op) Combines all items into one Numbers IntStream , LongStream and DoubleStream have arithmetic built in: java import java.util. ; import java.util.stream. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { System.out.println(IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 100).sum()); System.out.println(IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 10).filter(n - n % 2 == 0).map(n - n n).boxed().toList()); int scores = {72, 95, 88, 61, 79}; IntSummaryStatistics stats = Arrays.stream(scores).summaryStatistics(); System.out.println(stats.getMin() + " " + stats.getMax() + " " + stats.getAverage()); System.out.println(Stream.of("a", "bb", "ccc").mapToInt(String::length).sum()); System.out.println(Stream.iterate(1, x - x 2).limit(10).reduce(0, Integer::sum)); } } Collectors collect with the Collectors helpers builds maps, groups and strings: java import java.util. ; import java.util.stream. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { List<Person people = List.of( new Person("Ada", "London", 36), new Person("Grace", "New York", 85), new Person("Linus", "Helsinki", 55), new Person("Alan", "London", 41)); Map<String, List<String byCity = people.stream() .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Person::city, TreeMap::new, Collectors.mapping(Person::name, Collectors.toList()))); System.out.println(byCity); Map<String, Long countByCity = people.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Person::city, Collectors.counting())); System.out.println(new TreeMap< (countByCity)); Map<Boolean, List<String over50 = people.stream() .collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(p - p.age() 50, Collectors.mapping(Person::name, Collectors.toList()))); System.out.println(over50); String names = people.stream().map(Person::name).sorted().collect(Collectors.joining(", ", " ", " ")); double avgAge = people.stream().collect(Collectors.averagingInt(Person::age)); Map<String, Integer ageByName = people.stream().collect(Collectors.toMap(Person::name, Person::age)); Optional<Person oldest = people.stream().max(Comparator.comparingInt(Person::age)); System.out.println(names + " " + avgAge + " " + ageByName.get("Linus") + " " + oldest.map(Person::name).orElse("-")); } } record Person(String name, String city, int age) { } toMap throws if two items have the same key; pass a merge function as a third argument to combine them. flatMap java import java.util. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { List<String lines = List.of("the quick brown fox", "jumps over", "the lazy dog"); List<String words = lines.stream() .flatMap(line - Arrays.stream(line.split(" "))) // each line becomes many words .distinct() .toList(); System.out.println(words.size() + " " + words); } } Laziness Intermediate operations do nothing until a terminal operation runs, and then items flow through one at a time. That allows infinite sources with limit , and lets findFirst stop early. A stream can be used once ; calling a second terminal operation on it throws IllegalStateException . Stream lambdas should not change shared state (no adding to an outside list in map ); use collectors instead. parallelStream() splits work across cores, but only helps for large, CPU-heavy, side-effect-free pipelines. Streams or loops? Streams shine for transform-filter-collect pipelines and grouping. A plain loop is often clearer when you need indexes, early exits with complex conditions, checked exceptions, or several results at once. Use whichever reads better. Check yourself quiz ? What happens if a stream pipeline has no terminal operation? - It runs, but the result is thrown away - It does not compile + Nothing runs: intermediate operations are lazy - It throws IllegalStateException Intermediate operations only describe the work; it happens when a terminal operation such as toList() or count() asks for results. ? What does Collectors.groupingBy(Person::city, Collectors.counting()) produce? + A Map from each city to the number of people in it - A Map from each city to the list of people in it - The number of different cities - A List of cities sorted by how many people live there The second collector decides what each group becomes: counting() turns each city's people into a Long count. Without it, each group would be a List<Person . ? What is Stream.of(1, 2, 3, 4).filter(n - n % 2 == 0).map(n - n 10).toList() ? - 10, 30 - 10, 20, 30, 40 - 60 + 20, 40 The even numbers 2 and 4 remain and are multiplied by 10.

title: Stream queries
body: Books are records: java // Book.java record Book(String title, String author, int year, int pages, List<String genres) { } Answer each question in Shelf.java with one stream pipeline (no loops): java class Shelf { static List<String titlesBy(List<Book books, String author) // sorted by year, then title static Map<String, Double averagePagesByGenre(List<Book books) // TreeMap: genre - average pages static Map<Integer, Long countByDecade(List<Book books) // TreeMap: 1960 - 3, ... static List<String genresByPopularity(List<Book books) // most books first, ties alphabetical static Optional<Book longestBefore(List<Book books, int year) // most pages among books before year static String authorsLine(List<Book books) // distinct authors, sorted, "A; B; C" }

title: 6.03  Optional and Modern Java
body: Representing maybe-missing values with Optional and its methods (map, filter, orElse, orElseGet, orElseThrow, ifPresent), when not to use it, and a tour of modern Java features - var, text blocks, switch expressions and pattern matching, records and sealed types together, the java.time date API, and immutable collections. Optional null as "no value" causes NullPointerException s far from where the null came from. Optional<T makes "maybe missing" part of a method's type, so callers must decide what to do: java import java.util. ; public class Main { static final Map<String, String EMAILS = Map.of("ada", "ada@example.com", "bob", ""); public static void main(String args) { System.out.println(findEmail("ada").orElse("no email")); System.out.println(findEmail("zed").orElse("no email")); String domain = findEmail("ada") .map(e - e.substring(e.indexOf('@') + 1)) // transform if present .orElse("unknown"); System.out.println(domain); findEmail("bob").ifPresentOrElse(e - System.out.println("send to " + e), () - System.out.println("bob has none")); try { String e = findEmail("zed").orElseThrow(() - new NoSuchElementException("no email for zed")); } catch (NoSuchElementException ex) { System.out.println(ex.getMessage()); } } static Optional<String findEmail(String user) { return Optional.ofNullable(EMAILS.get(user)).filter(e - !e.isBlank()); } } Method Does --- --- Optional.of(x) , ofNullable(x) , empty() Create (of throws for null) isPresent() , isEmpty() Test map(f) , flatMap(f) , filter(p) Transform, keeping "missing" missing orElse(v) , orElseGet(supplier) A default ( orElseGet computes it only when needed) orElseThrow() , orElseThrow(supplier) The value, or an exception ifPresent(f) , ifPresentOrElse(f, g) Act on it Streams return Optional from findFirst , min and max . Use Optional as a return type for "maybe nothing". Do not use it for fields or parameters, do not call get() without checking (use orElseThrow() to make the intent clear), and never return null from a method declared to return an Optional . Modern Java in one place Java has changed a lot since Java 8. Code written today looks like this: java import java.time. ; import java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter; import java.time.temporal.ChronoUnit; import java.util. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { var orders = List.of( // var: inferred local types new Order("A-1", new Paid(LocalDate.of(2026, 3, 1), 4999)), new Order("A-2", new Pending()), new Order("A-3", new Refunded("damaged", 1250))); for (var order : orders) System.out.println(order.id() + ": " + describe(order.status())); String report = """ Orders: %d Generated: %s """.formatted(orders.size(), LocalDate.of(2026, 3, 14).format(DateTimeFormatter.ISO_DATE)); // a text block System.out.print(report); LocalDate due = LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 31).plusMonths(1); // java.time: immutable dates System.out.println(due + " " + due.getDayOfWeek() + " " + ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 1), due)); Duration d = Duration.ofMinutes(135); System.out.println(d.toHours() + "h " + d.toMinutesPart() + "m"); } static String describe(Status s) { return switch (s) { // pattern matching over a sealed type case Paid(LocalDate on, long cents) when cents 10_000 - "large payment on " + on; case Paid(LocalDate on, long cents) - "paid %d.%02d on %s".formatted(cents / 100, cents % 100, on); case Pending p - "waiting for payment"; case Refunded(String reason, long cents) - "refunded (" + reason + ")"; }; } } sealed interface Status permits Paid, Pending, Refunded { } record Paid(LocalDate on, long cents) implements Status { } record Pending() implements Status { } record Refunded(String reason, long cents) implements Status { } record Order(String id, Status status) { } Feature Since Lesson --- --- --- Lambdas, streams, Optional , java.time 8 6.01, 6.02, here var for local variables 10 here List.of , Map.of , Set.of 9 2.03 Switch expressions with - 14 1.05 Text blocks """ 15 1.04 Records, instanceof patterns 16 3.05, 3.03 Sealed types 17 3.05 Pattern matching for switch, record patterns 21 3.05 Virtual threads 21 6.04 Unnamed variables _ , compact source files 22, 25 java.time Use java.time for dates and times (never the old Date and Calendar ): Class Holds --- --- LocalDate , LocalTime , LocalDateTime A date / time / both, without a time zone ZonedDateTime , Instant A moment in time, with a zone / in UTC Duration , Period An amount of time / of days, months, years DateTimeFormatter Formatting and parsing All are immutable: date.plusDays(1) returns a new date. Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference between orElse and orElseGet ? + orElse always evaluates its default; orElseGet only calls its supplier when the Optional is empty - orElse returns null when empty; orElseGet throws an exception - orElseGet always calls its supplier; orElse only evaluates its default when empty - There is none: they are two names for the same method The argument of orElse is computed before the call even when a value is present; orElseGet takes a Supplier and runs it only if needed. ? Where should Optional be used? - As the type of fields that may be unset - As the type of every parameter that may be null + As the return type of methods that may have no result - In place of every null check in a program Optional is meant for return types that may be "nothing"; for fields and parameters it only adds clutter. ? What does Optional.of(" ").map(String::trim).filter(s - !s.isEmpty()).orElse("blank") return? - " " - "" - it throws + "blank" trim gives "" , the filter removes it, and orElse supplies the default.

title: Optional and java.time
body: A staff directory keeps people by id. Write it with Optional for everything that may be missing, and dates with java.time : java // Person.java record Person(String id, String name, String managerId, String city, LocalDate born) { } // managerId and city may be null // Directory.java class Directory { Directory(List<Person people) Optional<Person find(String id) Optional<String managerName(String id) // the name of the person's manager, if both exist String cityOf(String id) // the city, or "unknown" when the person or the city is missing Optional<Person oldest() static int age(LocalDate born, LocalDate today) // whole years static long daysUntilBirthday(LocalDate born, LocalDate today) // 0 on the birthday; Feb 29 birthdays count on Feb 28 in other years } Use map , flatMap , filter and orElse rather than isPresent() and get() .

title: 6.04  Threads and Concurrency
body: Running work at the same time - threads and Runnable, joining, race conditions and why count++ is unsafe, synchronized and locks, atomic variables and concurrent collections, ExecutorService and Future, CompletableFuture, virtual threads, deadlock, and the rule of sharing as little mutable state as possible. Threads The practice sandbox runs every program on a single thread, so the examples in this lesson are for reading and for running with your own JDK ( java Main.java ). The practice task shows how concurrent code is designed so that its logic can be tested without real threads. A thread is an independent path of execution. A program starts with one ( main ); more threads let it use several processor cores, or keep working while one task waits: java-norun public class Main { public static void main(String args) throws InterruptedException { Thread worker = new Thread(() - { for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) System.out.println("worker " + i); }); worker.start(); // runs at the same time as main System.out.println("main continues"); worker.join(); // wait for it to finish System.out.println("worker finished"); } } start() begins the new thread; calling run() directly would just run the code on the current thread. The order of output from different threads is not guaranteed. Race conditions When threads share mutable data, their steps interleave unpredictably. count++ is really read, add one, write back; two threads can read the same old value, and one increment is lost: java-norun import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; public class Main { static int unsafeCount = 0; static int syncCount = 0; static final AtomicInteger atomicCount = new AtomicInteger(); static synchronized void incrementSync() { syncCount++; } public static void main(String args) throws InterruptedException { Runnable work = () - { for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) { unsafeCount++; // a race incrementSync(); // one thread at a time atomicCount.incrementAndGet(); // an atomic hardware operation } }; Thread a = new Thread(work), b = new Thread(work); a.start(); b.start(); a.join(); b.join(); System.out.println((unsafeCount <= 200_000) + " " + syncCount + " " + atomicCount.get()); } } synchronized lets only one thread at a time run the method (or a synchronized (lock) { ... } block) for the same lock object, and makes changes visible to the next thread that takes the lock. AtomicInteger , AtomicLong and LongAdder do single-variable updates without locks. Thread-safe collections ArrayList and HashMap are not safe for concurrent changes. Use the java.util.concurrent collections: Instead of Use --- --- HashMap ConcurrentHashMap (with merge , compute for atomic updates) ArrayList with rare writes CopyOnWriteArrayList a queue between threads ArrayBlockingQueue , LinkedBlockingQueue Executors Creating threads by hand is low level. An ExecutorService keeps a pool of threads and runs tasks you submit; Callable tasks return a result through a Future : java-norun import java.util. ; import java.util.concurrent. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4)) { List<Future<Long results = new ArrayList< (); for (int part = 0; part < 4; part++) { long from = part 250_000L, to = from + 250_000; results.add(pool.submit(() - sumOfSquares(from, to))); // a Callable<Long } long total = 0; for (Future<Long f : results) total += f.get(); // waits for each result System.out.println(total == sumOfSquares(0, 1_000_000)); } // closing waits for the tasks and shuts the pool down } static long sumOfSquares(long from, long to) { long s = 0; for (long i = from; i < to; i++) s += i i % 1000; return s; } } Splitting work so that each task computes its own result, and combining the results at the end, avoids shared mutable state entirely. That is the safest kind of concurrency. CompletableFuture and virtual threads CompletableFuture chains asynchronous steps: java-norun import java.util.concurrent. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { CompletableFuture<String user = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() - slow("Ada", 100)); CompletableFuture<Integer score = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() - slow(42, 100)); String summary = user.thenCombine(score, (u, s) - u + " scored " + s) .exceptionally(e - "failed: " + e.getMessage()) .join(); System.out.println(summary); try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { // Java 21: virtual threads for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) { int n = i; executor.submit(() - slow(n, 10)); // ten thousand cheap threads } } System.out.println("10 000 waiting tasks done"); } static <T T slow(T value, long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } return value; } } Virtual threads (Java 21) are very cheap threads managed by the JVM. They make it practical to give each waiting task (a web request, a database call) its own thread, written as simple blocking code. Deadlock and other dangers - Deadlock : thread A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2, while B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1. Both wait forever. Always take locks in the same order, and hold them briefly. - Visibility : without synchronisation, a change made by one thread may never be seen by another. Use volatile for simple flags, or locks and atomics. - InterruptedException : it means someone asked the thread to stop. Do not swallow it; finish up, or restore the flag with Thread.currentThread().interrupt() . The best concurrency advice is to avoid sharing mutable state: use immutable objects (records), give each task its own data, and communicate through concurrent queues or futures. Testable concurrent code Code that creates its own threads is hard to test: the results depend on timing. Instead, let the caller pass in an Executor (the interface behind every thread pool). Production code passes a real pool; a test passes Runnable::run , which runs each task immediately on the calling thread, so the result is the same every time: java-norun static long sumInChunks(int data, int chunks, Executor executor) { List<CompletableFuture<Long parts = new ArrayList< (); for (int c = 0; c < chunks; c++) { int from = c data.length / chunks, to = (c + 1) data.length / chunks; parts.add(CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() - sum(data, from, to), executor)); } return parts.stream().mapToLong(CompletableFuture::join).sum(); } sumInChunks(data, 8, Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8)); // in the program sumInChunks(data, 8, Runnable::run); // in a test: deterministic Check yourself quiz ? Why can two threads incrementing the same int with count++ lose updates? - Java only lets one thread at a time change an int - The second thread always overwrites the first thread's whole loop + count++ is a read, an add and a write, and the threads' steps can interleave - int is too small to hold the total, so it overflows Two threads can both read the old value, both add one, and both write it back: one increment is lost. synchronized or AtomicInteger prevents that. ? What does future.get() do? - Returns the result at once, or null if the task is still running + Waits until the task has finished and returns its result, or throws if the task failed - Starts the task on a new thread - Cancels the task and returns what it has computed so far get() blocks the calling thread until the result is ready; submitting the task to the executor is what starts it. ? Thread A locks X then Y; thread B locks Y then X. What can happen? - Nothing: Java prevents it - A race condition on X - An InterruptedException + A deadlock, with both threads waiting forever Each holds the lock the other needs; taking locks in a fixed order prevents it.

title: Concurrent code you can test
body: Concurrent code is easiest to test when it does not create threads itself but receives an Executor . The program passes a thread pool; a test passes Runnable::run , which runs every task at once on the calling thread. Write: java // Parallel.java class Parallel { static <T List<T runAll(List<Callable<T tasks, Executor executor) throws Exception static long sumInChunks(int data, int chunks, Executor executor) } // SafeCounter.java: a counter that many threads may update at the same time class SafeCounter { void increment() void add(long n) long get() long getAndReset() // returns the current value and sets it to 0, as one atomic step } - runAll submits every task to the executor (one execute call per task, in order) and returns their results in task order. If tasks fail, it throws the exception of the first failing task in the list (the original exception, not a wrapper). - sumInChunks splits data into chunks consecutive parts of nearly equal size ( chunks from 1 up; never more chunks than items, except that an empty array gives 0), sums each part as its own task on the executor, and adds the part sums. chunks below 1 throws IllegalArgumentException . - SafeCounter must be correct when used from many threads: use AtomicLong (or LongAdder , or synchronized ).

title: 6.05  Project: A Complete Program
body: How a real Java program is organised - packages and the folder layout, access across packages, Maven and Gradle with a pom.xml or build.gradle, dependencies, unit tests with JUnit 5, building a runnable JAR, and the plan for the final project, a command-driven event planner. Packages Real programs put classes into packages , named like reversed domain names, matching the folder structure: text planner/ pom.xml (or build.gradle) src/main/java/ com/example/planner/ App.java package com.example.planner; model/Event.java package com.example.planner.model; model/Schedule.java io/CommandParser.java package com.example.planner.io; src/test/java/ com/example/planner/model/ScheduleTest.java java-norun package com.example.planner.model; // first line of the file import java.time.LocalDateTime; // imports come after the package line import java.util.List; public record Event(String title, LocalDateTime start, int minutes) { } - A class in another package is used with an import (or its full name, com.example.planner.model.Event ). - public members are visible everywhere; members without a modifier are visible only inside their own package. This lets a package hide its helper classes. - Each public class lives in a file with its name, in the folder of its package. Build tools Maven and Gradle compile the code, download libraries, run the tests and package the program. With Maven, a pom.xml describes the project: xml <project <modelVersion 4.0.0</modelVersion <groupId com.example</groupId <artifactId planner</artifactId <version 1.0.0</version <properties <maven.compiler.release 25</maven.compiler.release </properties <dependencies <dependency <groupId org.junit.jupiter</groupId <artifactId junit-jupiter</artifactId <version 5.11.4</version <scope test</scope </dependency </dependencies </project bash mvn compile compile src/main/java mvn test run the tests in src/test/java mvn package build target/planner-1.0.0.jar java -cp target/planner-1.0.0.jar com.example.planner.App Gradle does the same with a build.gradle (or build.gradle.kts ) script: gradle build , gradle test , gradle run . IDEs import either kind of project directly. Unit tests with JUnit JUnit 5 is the standard Java test framework. Test classes mirror the main classes' packages: java-norun package com.example.planner.model; import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test; import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions. ; class ScheduleTest { @Test void overlappingEventsAreRejected() { Schedule s = new Schedule(); s.add(new Event("Lunch", at(12, 0), 60)); assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class, () - s.add(new Event("Call", at(12, 30), 15))); } @Test void eventsAreListedInTimeOrder() { Schedule s = new Schedule(); s.add(new Event("Late", at(18, 0), 30)); s.add(new Event("Early", at(9, 0), 30)); assertEquals(List.of("Early", "Late"), s.titles()); } } assertEquals(expected, actual) , assertTrue , assertThrows and @ParameterizedTest work like the checkEq and checkThrows you have used throughout this course. The final project The project for this milestone is an event planner that reads commands, keeps a schedule, refuses overlapping events, and answers questions about free time. It brings the course together: Part Uses --- --- Event record with validation records, java.time (3.05, 6.03) Schedule with sorted events collections, comparators, exceptions (4.02 to 4.04) Free-slot search and the daily summary algorithms over sorted data, streams (5.02, 6.02) Command loop with error messages parsing, exceptions, switch (1.05, 4.04) Build it in layers, testing each before the next: the record, then the schedule's add and list, then overlaps, then free slots, then the commands. Keep the rules in Schedule and the input handling in Main , so the rules can be tested without typing commands. Where to go next - Web services with Spring Boot or Quarkus, which build on everything here: classes, interfaces, collections, exceptions and streams. - Android apps (with Kotlin or Java). - Data structures and algorithms in more depth: graphs, dynamic programming and balanced trees, in this site's DSA course. - Concurrency in depth with "Java Concurrency in Practice", and modern Java features as each release adds them. Check yourself quiz ? In a Maven or Gradle project, which file holds the class com.example.planner.model.Event ? - src/main/java/Event.java + src/main/java/com/example/planner/model/Event.java - src/com.example.planner.model/Event.java - src/test/java/com/example/planner/model/Event.java Each part of the package name is a folder under src/main/java ; src/test/java is for the tests. ? Which members of a class can a class in another package use? - All of them, as long as it imports the class - Only static ones + Only public ones (and protected ones from subclasses) - Public ones and those without a modifier Members without a modifier are package-private: visible only inside their own package. That is how a package hides its helpers. ? What does mvn test do? - Compiles the main code only, without running anything - Runs the program's main method to see if it works - Downloads Java and the libraries listed in pom.xml + Compiles the code and runs the unit tests under src/test/java Maven's test phase runs after compile and runs the JUnit tests.

title: Parsing planner commands
body: The final project reads commands like add 2026-03-14 09:00 90 Team meeting . Parse a line into a sealed command type, so the rest of the program can switch over it: java // Command.java sealed interface Command { record Add(LocalDateTime start, int minutes, String title) implements Command { } record Remove(String title) implements Command { } record Day(LocalDate date) implements Command { } record Free(LocalDate date, int minutes) implements Command { } record Summary() implements Command { } record Quit() implements Command { } record Invalid(String message) implements Command { } static Command parse(String line) } Input Result --- --- add <yyyy-MM-dd <HH:mm <minutes <title... Add ; the title is the rest of the line, words joined by single spaces remove <title... Remove day <yyyy-MM-dd Day free <yyyy-MM-dd <minutes Free summary , quit Summary , Quit The command word ignores case and extra spaces. Problems give Invalid with one of these messages: - Usage: add <date <time <minutes <title (and likewise Usage: remove <title , Usage: day <date , Usage: free <date <minutes ) for missing or extra arguments; summary and quit ignore extra words; - Bad date or time when a date or time does not parse (strict yyyy-MM-dd and HH:mm , so 2026-02-30 is bad); - Minutes must be between 5 and 720 for a number outside that range, and Bad number for text that is not a whole number; - Unknown command: <word for anything else, and Empty line for a blank line.
