title: An event planner
body: Build a command-driven event planner. It reads one command per line until quit or the end of the input, keeps a schedule, refuses overlapping events, and finds free time. Commands are parsed by Command.parse from practice 6.05, which is already in the project ( Command.java ). The program is four files: Main.java (the command loop), Event.java , Schedule.java and Command.java . add 2026-03-14 09:00 90 Team meeting add 2026-03-14 12:00 60 Lunch add 2026-03-14 10:00 30 Call day 2026-03-14 free 2026-03-14 60 summary quit prints Added: 2026-03-14 09:00-10:30 Team meeting Added: 2026-03-14 12:00-13:00 Lunch Overlaps with Team meeting (09:00-10:30) Saturday 2026-03-14 09:00-10:30 Team meeting 12:00-13:00 Lunch Free: 08:00-09:00 2 events, 2h 30m planned Busiest day: 2026-03-14 (2 events) Bye. Event is a record Event(String title, LocalDateTime start, int minutes) with end() and a method telling whether it overlaps another event (they overlap when each starts before the other ends; one ending exactly when the next starts is fine). Commands (no prompts): Command Output --- --- add Added: <date <HH:mm -<HH:mm <title , or Overlaps with <title (<HH:mm -<HH:mm ) naming the earliest-starting event it overlaps remove <title Removes the earliest event with that title (ignoring case): Removed: <title as stored , or No event called <title day <date The day name and date ( Saturday 2026-03-14 ), then each event starting that day in time order as <HH:mm -<HH:mm <title , or Nothing planned. free <date <minutes The earliest gap of at least that many minutes between 08:00 and 18:00 that day, as Free: <HH:mm -<HH:mm (the whole gap), or No free slot of <minutes minutes on <date . Any event overlapping the window counts, including its parts outside the window. summary <n events, <h h <m m planned ( 1 event for one) and Busiest day: <date (<n events) (the earliest on a tie), or just No events. invalid input The Invalid message from Command.parse quit Ends the loop The program always ends by printing Bye.

title: 7.01  Nested, Inner and Anonymous Classes
body: Classes inside classes - static nested classes for helpers that belong to one class, inner classes that reach their outer object, local classes inside methods, anonymous classes, how lambdas replaced most of them, and the builder pattern. A class can live inside another When a class only makes sense together with another (a list's node, a map's entry, a builder), it can be declared inside it. Java has four kinds: Kind Declared Has an outer object? --- --- --- static nested class in a class, with static no inner class in a class, without static yes local class inside a method yes (if the method is not static) anonymous class in an expression, with no name yes (if created in an instance method) Static nested classes A static nested class is an ordinary class that happens to be named through its outer class. It is the right choice most of the time: java import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; public class Main { static class Route { private final List<Stop stops = new ArrayList< (); static class Stop { // Route.Stop final String name; final int minutes; Stop(String name, int minutes) { this.name = name; this.minutes = minutes; } } Route add(String name, int minutes) { stops.add(new Stop(name, minutes)); return this; } int totalMinutes() { return stops.stream().mapToInt(s - s.minutes).sum(); } } public static void main(String args) { Route r = new Route().add("Depot", 0).add("Market", 12).add("Station", 7); Route.Stop first = r.stops.get(0); // nested classes can see each other's private parts System.out.println(first.name + ", total " + r.totalMinutes() + " min"); } } Inner classes Without static , a nested class is inner : every object of it is tied to an object of the outer class and can use that object's fields directly. Iterators are the classic example: the iterator needs the collection it walks. java import java.util.Iterator; import java.util.NoSuchElementException; public class Main { static class Countdown implements Iterable<Integer { private final int start; Countdown(int start) { this.start = start; } public Iterator<Integer iterator() { return new Steps(); } private class Steps implements Iterator<Integer { // inner: sees start private int next = start; public boolean hasNext() { return next 0; } public Integer next() { if (!hasNext()) throw new NoSuchElementException(); return next--; } } } public static void main(String args) { for (int n : new Countdown(3)) System.out.print(n + " "); System.out.println("lift-off"); } } Because an inner object keeps a hidden reference to its outer object, it keeps that object alive. Prefer static nested classes unless you really need the outer object. Anonymous classes An anonymous class declares and creates a one-off class in one expression. Before Java 8 it was the only way to pass behaviour around: java import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Comparator; import java.util.List; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { List<String words = new ArrayList< (List.of("kiwi", "fig", "banana")); words.sort(new Comparator<String () { // an anonymous class @Override public int compare(String a, String b) { return Integer.compare(a.length(), b.length()); } }); System.out.println(words); words.sort(Comparator.comparing(String::length).reversed()); // the same idea today System.out.println(words); } } For an interface with one abstract method (a functional interface , lesson 6.01) a lambda is shorter and clearer. Anonymous classes are still useful when you need several methods, or state of their own. Local classes and capture A class (or lambda) declared inside a method can use the method's local variables, but only if they are effectively final (never changed after being set): java public class Main { interface Greeter { String greet(String name); } static Greeter politeGreeter(String title) { class Polite implements Greeter { // a local class public String greet(String name) { return "Good day, " + title + " " + name; } } return new Polite(); } public static void main(String args) { System.out.println(politeGreeter("Dr.").greet("Hopper")); } } The builder pattern A static nested Builder gives objects with many optional settings a readable way to be made, and keeps the finished object immutable: java public class Main { static final class Email { private final String to, subject, body; private final boolean urgent; private Email(Builder b) { to = b.to; subject = b.subject; body = b.body; urgent = b.urgent; } static Builder to(String to) { return new Builder(to); } static final class Builder { private final String to; private String subject = "(no subject)", body = ""; private boolean urgent; private Builder(String to) { this.to = to; } Builder subject(String s) { subject = s; return this; } Builder body(String b) { body = b; return this; } Builder urgent() { urgent = true; return this; } Email build() { return new Email(this); } } @Override public String toString() { return (urgent ? " ! " : "") + to + ": " + subject; } } public static void main(String args) { Email e = Email.to("ada@example.com").subject("Notes").urgent().build(); System.out.println(e); } } Check yourself quiz ? When should a nested class be static ? - Only when all of its methods are static + Whenever it does not need an object of the outer class - Only when it is private - Never: inner classes are the normal choice That is most of the time. A static nested class has no hidden reference to an outer object, so it is simpler and does not keep the outer object alive. Its methods can still be ordinary instance methods. ? What does "effectively final" mean for a local variable? - It is declared with the final keyword - It is a static final constant - It cannot be read inside a lambda + It is never assigned again after it is first set The final keyword is not needed: any local variable that is never reassigned counts, and only those can be captured by a lambda or local class. ? What does an inner (non-static) class object always hold? - a copy of every outer field - its own main method + a reference to an object of the outer class - nothing extra That hidden reference is how inner classes reach the outer object's fields, and why they keep it alive.

A negative step counts down (to just above end ). A step of 0 throws IllegalArgumentException . - iterator() returns an object of a private inner class that walks the range; next() past the end throws NoSuchElementException . - size() returns how many numbers the range contains (0 if it is empty). - toList() returns the numbers as a List<Integer . java for (int n : Range.of(10, 0, -3)) System.out.print(n + " "); // 10 7 4 1

title: 7.02  equals, hashCode and the Object Contract
match: 7.02 equals, hashCode and the Object Contract
body: What every class inherits from Object and the rules that come with it - equals and its five properties, why hashCode must agree with equals, compareTo consistent with equals, toString, what records write for you, and the bugs that appear in HashSet and HashMap when the rules are broken. What every object has Every class extends Object and so has equals , hashCode , toString , getClass and a few more. The first three are meant to be overridden, but they come with a contract : rules that collections and libraries rely on. Break them and HashMap , HashSet and contains silently misbehave. equals == on objects compares references : are these the same object? equals should compare values : do these two objects mean the same thing? The default equals is just == . The contract says equals must be: 1. reflexive : x.equals(x) is true; 2. symmetric : x.equals(y) exactly when y.equals(x) ; 3. transitive : if x.equals(y) and y.equals(z) , then x.equals(z) ; 4. consistent : the answer does not change unless the objects change; 5. x.equals(null) is false. java import java.util.Objects; public class Main { static final class Point { private final int x, y; Point(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; } @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { if (this == o) return true; if (!(o instanceof Point other)) return false; // also false for null return x == other.x && y == other.y; } @Override public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(x, y); } @Override public String toString() { return "(" + x + ", " + y + ")"; } } public static void main(String args) { Point a = new Point(1, 2), b = new Point(1, 2); System.out.println((a == b) + " " + a.equals(b)); // false true } } Make such classes final (or compare with getClass() ), otherwise a subclass that adds fields cannot keep equals symmetric. hashCode must agree A HashMap or HashSet first uses hashCode to pick a bucket, then equals inside it. So the rule is: equal objects must have equal hash codes . (Unequal objects may share one; that only costs speed.) Override equals without hashCode and this happens: java import java.util.HashSet; import java.util.Set; public class Main { static final class Tag { final String name; Tag(String name) { this.name = name; } @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { return o instanceof Tag t && t.name.equals(name); } // no hashCode: each object keeps the default, based on its identity } public static void main(String args) { Set<Tag tags = new HashSet< (); tags.add(new Tag("java")); System.out.println(tags.contains(new Tag("java"))); // almost certainly false } } Objects.hash(field1, field2, ...) is the easy, correct way to write hashCode . Use the same fields as equals . Do not change keys If a field used by hashCode changes while the object is in a HashSet or is a HashMap key, the object is now in the wrong bucket and cannot be found or removed. Make key classes immutable. compareTo consistent with equals Comparable.compareTo (lesson 4.03) defines natural order. It should return 0 exactly when equals is true; TreeSet and TreeMap use compareTo instead of equals , so if two different objects compare as 0, a TreeSet keeps only one of them. java import java.util.Comparator; import java.util.List; import java.util.TreeSet; public class Main { record Person(String name, int age) {} public static void main(String args) { var byAge = new TreeSet<Person (Comparator.comparingInt(Person::age)); byAge.addAll(List.of(new Person("Ada", 36), new Person("Alan", 36))); System.out.println(byAge.size()); // 1: same age counts as "equal" var full = new TreeSet<Person (Comparator.comparingInt(Person::age).thenComparing(Person::name)); full.addAll(List.of(new Person("Ada", 36), new Person("Alan", 36))); System.out.println(full.size()); // 2 } } Records do it for you A record (lesson 3.05) writes equals , hashCode and toString from its components automatically and correctly. For a plain data class, a record is the simplest way to get the contract right. (Arrays inside a record are compared by reference, so prefer List components.) toString toString is used by string concatenation, println , debuggers and logs. Return something short that identifies the object; the default ClassName@1b6d3586 helps nobody. Check yourself quiz ? Why must equal objects have equal hash codes? - So that equals can run faster - So that toString prints the same text for both + Hash collections look in the bucket that hashCode picks - Because == compares hash codes HashSet and HashMap pick a bucket by hashCode and only then ask equals , so an equal object with another hash code is looked for in the wrong bucket and never found. Unequal objects may share a hash code; equal ones must. ? Two different people compare as 0 in a TreeSet 's comparator. What happens? - The set keeps both, because their equals says they differ + The set treats them as the same element and keeps only one - add throws an exception for the second one - The set keeps both, ordered by name TreeSet uses the comparator instead of equals : comparing as 0 means "already there". Adding thenComparing(Person::name) keeps both. ? A class overrides equals but not hashCode . Which collection is most likely to misbehave? - ArrayList - LinkedList + HashSet - an array HashSet uses hashCode to find elements; ArrayList.contains uses equals alone.

title: 7.03  Annotations and Reflection
body: Code that describes and inspects code - the built-in annotations, writing your own with @interface, retention and targets, reading annotations and members at run time with reflection, calling methods and creating objects by name, and the costs that come with it. Annotations An annotation is a label on code, written with @ . It changes nothing by itself; a tool that reads it decides what it means. You have used several: Annotation Read by Meaning --- --- --- @Override the compiler error if the method does not override anything @Deprecated the compiler warning wherever it is used @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") the compiler silence one kind of warning @FunctionalInterface the compiler error unless the interface has one abstract method @Test JUnit (lesson 6.05) this method is a test Frameworks such as Spring, JPA and Jackson are driven mostly by annotations. Writing your own An annotation type is declared with @interface . Its "methods" are its settings, optionally with defaults. Two meta-annotations say where it may go and how long it is kept: java-norun import java.lang.annotation. ; @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME) // keep it in the class file and visible to reflection @Target(ElementType.METHOD) // only on methods public @interface Command { String value(); // the command's name String help() default ""; } RetentionPolicy.SOURCE annotations disappear after compiling (for compiler checks), CLASS ones are in the class file but invisible at run time, and RUNTIME ones can be read by reflection. Reflection Reflection lets a program look at classes while it runs: their fields, methods, constructors and annotations. It starts from a Class object: java import java.lang.reflect. ; import java.util.Arrays; public class Main { public static class Account { private final String owner; private long cents; public Account(String owner) { this.owner = owner; } public void deposit(long amount) { cents += amount; } public long balance() { return cents; } } public static void main(String args) throws Exception { Class<? type = Account.class; // or object.getClass(), or Class.forName("...") System.out.println(type.getSimpleName()); for (Field f : type.getDeclaredFields()) System.out.println("field " + f.getName() + ": " + f.getType().getSimpleName()); Object acc = type.getConstructor(String.class).newInstance("Ada"); Method deposit = type.getMethod("deposit", long.class); deposit.invoke(acc, 250L); System.out.println(type.getMethod("balance").invoke(acc)); // 250 Field cents = type.getDeclaredField("cents"); cents.setAccessible(true); // reach a private field System.out.println(cents.getLong(acc)); System.out.println(Arrays.toString(type.getConstructors())); } } getMethods() returns public methods including inherited ones; getDeclaredMethods() returns every method declared in that class, private ones too. Annotations plus reflection Together they let a small framework find and call your code: java import java.lang.annotation. ; import java.lang.reflect.Method; import java.util.Arrays; import java.util.Comparator; public class Main { @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME) @Target(ElementType.METHOD) @interface Check { String value(); } public static class Checks { @Check("addition works") public boolean add() { return 1 + 1 == 2; } @Check("strings compare") public boolean strings() { return "a".compareTo("b") < 0; } public boolean notACheck() { return false; } } public static void main(String args) throws Exception { Object target = new Checks(); Method methods = Checks.class.getDeclaredMethods(); Arrays.sort(methods, Comparator.comparing(Method::getName)); // the order is not guaranteed otherwise for (Method m : methods) { Check c = m.getAnnotation(Check.class); if (c == null) continue; boolean ok = (boolean) m.invoke(target); System.out.println((ok ? "pass " : "FAIL ") + c.value()); } } } That is a test runner in twenty lines: JUnit works on the same idea. The costs - Speed : reflective calls are slower than direct ones (much less so in modern JVMs, but still). - Safety : names are strings, so a typo is found only when the code runs, and refactoring tools may miss them. - Encapsulation : setAccessible(true) breaks private , and the module system (Java 9+) blocks it for classes in other modules unless they open themselves. - Exceptions : invoke wraps whatever the method throws in an InvocationTargetException ; the real one is getCause() . Use reflection in frameworks and tools, not in everyday application logic. Check yourself quiz ? Why must an annotation read by reflection have @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME) ? + Other retention policies drop the annotation before the program runs, so reflection never sees it - Without it the annotation may only be placed on classes - RUNTIME makes the compiler check the annotation's settings - Reflection can only read annotations that have default values SOURCE annotations vanish after compiling and CLASS ones are in the class file but invisible at run time; only RUNTIME ones reach getAnnotation . ? A method called through Method.invoke throws IllegalStateException . What does the caller receive? - The IllegalStateException itself - Nothing: invoke swallows the exception and returns null + An InvocationTargetException whose getCause() is the IllegalStateException - An IllegalAccessException invoke wraps whatever the method throws; unwrap it with getCause() to get the real exception. ? Which returns a class's private methods too? - getMethods() - getConstructors() - getSimpleName() + getDeclaredMethods() getDeclaredMethods lists every method declared in the class itself, whatever its access; getMethods lists only public ones, inherited ones included.

title: List the getters
body: Write class Inspect with static List<String getters(Class<? type) returning the names of the type's public methods that are getters, sorted alphabetically. A getter: - takes no parameters, - does not return void , - is named getX... (with at least one character after get ) or, if it returns boolean , isX... , - is not getClass (which every object inherits).

title: A tiny test runner
body: Write an annotation and a runner: - @Retention(RUNTIME) @Target(METHOD) public @interface Check { String value(); } in Check.java . - class Runner with static List<String run(Object target) that finds the target's declared methods annotated with @Check , sorts them by method name, calls each (they take no arguments) and returns one line per check: - "pass <description " when the method returns normally (whatever it returns); - "FAIL <description : <message " when it throws, where the message is the real exception's getMessage() (unwrap the InvocationTargetException ); - private methods are run too ( setAccessible(true) ). - A method annotated with @Check that takes parameters gives "SKIP <description : needs arguments" .

title: 7.04  Dates and Times with java.time
body: Getting time right - Instant for moments, LocalDate and LocalDateTime for calendar values, ZonedDateTime and time zones, Duration and Period, adding and comparing, ChronoUnit.between, formatting and parsing with DateTimeFormatter, and a Clock for testable code. Which type? Lesson 6.03 gave a first look at java.time . The key to using it well is picking the type that means what you mean: Type Means Example --- --- --- Instant a moment on the global timeline when an order was placed LocalDate a calendar date, no time or zone a birthday LocalTime a time of day, no date or zone "the shop opens at 09:00" LocalDateTime date and time, no zone a meeting written on a wall calendar ZonedDateTime date, time and time zone "10:00 in Tokyo on 20 November" Duration an amount of time in seconds and nanoseconds 90 minutes Period an amount in years, months and days 3 months All of them are immutable : plusDays returns a new object. Local values java import java.time. ; import java.time.temporal.ChronoUnit; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { LocalDate start = LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 31); System.out.println(start.plusMonths(1)); // 2026-02-28: clamped to the month's end System.out.println(start.getDayOfWeek()); // SATURDAY System.out.println(start.isLeapYear()); // false LocalDate due = LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 20); System.out.println(ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(start, due)); // 293 Period p = Period.between(start, due); System.out.println(p.getMonths() + " months " + p.getDays() + " days"); LocalTime opens = LocalTime.of(9, 0); System.out.println(opens.plusMinutes(90).isBefore(LocalTime.NOON)); // true } } Moments and zones An Instant is what a server should store: it is the same everywhere. Turn it into local date and time only to show it to a person, with their zone: java import java.time. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Instant placed = Instant.parse("2026-11-20T23:30:00Z"); ZonedDateTime tokyo = placed.atZone(ZoneId.of("Asia/Tokyo")); ZonedDateTime london = placed.atZone(ZoneId.of("Europe/London")); System.out.println(tokyo.toLocalDate() + " in Tokyo, " + london.toLocalDate() + " in London"); ZonedDateTime meeting = ZonedDateTime.of(2026, 3, 29, 0, 30, 0, 0, ZoneId.of("Europe/London")); System.out.println(meeting.plusHours(2)); // daylight saving starts that night: 03:30+01:00 } } Adding hours to a ZonedDateTime follows the real clock across daylight-saving changes; a LocalDateTime knows nothing about them. Duration and Period Duration measures exact time ( Duration.ofMinutes(90) , Duration.between(instantA, instantB) ); Period measures calendar steps ( Period.ofMonths(1) ), whose length in days depends on where you start. "One day" as a Period across a daylight-saving change is 23 or 25 hours; as a Duration it is always 24. java import java.time. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Duration call = Duration.ofSeconds(4000); System.out.println(call.toHours() + "h " + call.toMinutesPart() + "m " + call.toSecondsPart() + "s"); System.out.println(call.compareTo(Duration.ofHours(1)) 0); } } Formatting and parsing DateTimeFormatter turns values into text and back. Use the predefined ISO formats for data, and a pattern (with a locale) for people: java import java.time. ; import java.time.format. ; import java.util.Locale; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { LocalDateTime t = LocalDateTime.of(2026, 11, 20, 14, 5); System.out.println(t.format(DateTimeFormatter.ISO_LOCAL_DATE_TIME)); // 2026-11-20T14:05:00 var human = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("EEEE d MMMM yyyy, HH:mm", Locale.UK); System.out.println(t.format(human)); // Friday 20 November 2026, 14:05 LocalDate parsed = LocalDate.parse("20/11/2026", DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("dd/MM/yyyy")); System.out.println(parsed); try { LocalDate.parse("31/02/2026", DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("dd/MM/uuuu").withResolverStyle(ResolverStyle.STRICT)); } catch (DateTimeParseException e) { System.out.println("not a real date"); } } } Pattern letters are case-sensitive: MM is month, mm is minute; HH is 0–23, hh is 1–12. With ResolverStyle.STRICT , use uuuu for the year. Testable time: Clock Code that calls LocalDate.now() gives a different answer every day, which makes it hard to test. Pass a Clock in instead; tests use a fixed one: java import java.time. ; public class Main { static boolean isOverdue(LocalDate due, Clock clock) { return LocalDate.now(clock).isAfter(due); } public static void main(String args) { Clock fixed = Clock.fixed(Instant.parse("2026-11-20T12:00:00Z"), ZoneOffset.UTC); System.out.println(isOverdue(LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 19), fixed)); // true, today and every day } } Check yourself quiz ? Which type should a server store for "when did this happen"? - A LocalDateTime in the server's own zone + An Instant , a moment that is the same everywhere - A LocalDate , since the time rarely matters - A String formatted with DateTimeFormatter An Instant means the same moment for everyone; a zone is applied only when showing it to a person. A LocalDateTime has no zone, so it does not pin down a moment. ? Why does LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 31).plusMonths(1) give 28 February? - It adds 28 days, the length of February - It throws, then falls back to the last day of the month - It adds 30 days and then rounds down + February has no 31st, so the result is clamped to the last valid day of the month plusMonths moves the month and keeps the day if it can; when the day does not exist, it uses the month's last day. ? What is the difference between Duration.ofDays(1) and Period.ofDays(1) ? - There is none: both are always exactly 24 hours - Period is more precise, down to nanoseconds + Duration is always 24 hours; Period is a calendar day, which can be 23 or 25 - Duration only works with LocalDate , Period with Instant Duration measures exact time; Period counts calendar units, so across a daylight-saving change one day can be 23 or 25 hours.

title: Age and next birthday
body: Write class Birthdays with two methods that take today's date as a parameter (so they are testable): - static int age(LocalDate born, LocalDate today) : whole years. - static long daysUntilNextBirthday(LocalDate born, LocalDate today) : 0 if today is the birthday. Someone born on 29 February celebrates on 28 February in years that are not leap years.

title: Opening hours across time zones
body: A shop in one time zone is open at set hours on some days. Write record OpeningHours(ZoneId zone, Set<DayOfWeek days, LocalTime opens, LocalTime closes) with: - boolean isOpen(Instant moment) : true when, in the shop's zone, the day is one of days and the time is at or after opens and before closes . - Instant nextOpening(Instant moment) : the next moment (at or after moment ) when the shop opens. If it is open right now, return moment itself. Search at most 7 days ahead; days empty throws IllegalStateException . - String describe(Instant moment, ZoneId viewer) : if open, "open until HH:mm" ; otherwise "opens EEE HH:mm" (for example "opens Mon 09:00" ), both shown in the viewer's zone, with an English locale. opens is always before closes (no overnight hours).

title: 7.05  Byte Streams and Binary Data
body: Reading and writing bytes - InputStream and OutputStream, byte arrays and ByteArrayOutputStream, buffering, DataOutputStream and DataInputStream for numbers in a fixed format, ByteBuffer and byte order, designing a small binary file format, checksums, and decorating streams. Text is bytes too Lesson 4.05 read and wrote text with Files and readers and writers, which turn characters into bytes using an encoding (UTF-8). Underneath, every file, network connection and compressed archive is a sequence of bytes . Java reads and writes them with two abstract classes: - InputStream : read() returns the next byte (0–255) or -1 at the end; read(byte ) fills an array and returns how many bytes it got. - OutputStream : write(int) writes one byte; write(byte ) writes many. Always close them, which try with resources does for you. Bytes in memory ByteArrayOutputStream collects written bytes in memory and ByteArrayInputStream reads from an array: perfect for building data and for tests. java import java.io. ; import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets; import java.util.Arrays; public class Main { public static void main(String args) throws IOException { var out = new ByteArrayOutputStream(); out.write(72); out.write("ello".getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)); byte bytes = out.toByteArray(); System.out.println(Arrays.toString(bytes)); // 72, 101, 108, 108, 111 System.out.println(new String(bytes, StandardCharsets.UTF_8)); try (var in = new ByteArrayInputStream(bytes)) { int b; while ((b = in.read()) != -1) System.out.print(Integer.toHexString(b) + " "); } System.out.println(); } } A Java byte is signed (−128 to 127). b & 0xFF gives its unsigned value (0 to 255). Streams wrap streams Streams are designed to be stacked : each wrapper adds one ability to the stream inside it. java-norun try (var out = new DataOutputStream( // numbers in a fixed binary format new BufferedOutputStream( // fewer, larger writes to the disk new FileOutputStream("scores.bin")))) { out.writeInt(3); } BufferedInputStream and BufferedOutputStream make many small reads and writes fast. GZIPOutputStream compresses, CipherOutputStream encrypts, and CheckedOutputStream keeps a checksum, all by wrapping another stream. Numbers as bytes DataOutputStream writes int , long , double and so on in a fixed big-endian format, and DataInputStream reads them back in the same order: java import java.io. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) throws IOException { var buffer = new ByteArrayOutputStream(); try (var out = new DataOutputStream(buffer)) { out.writeInt(2); // how many records follow out.writeUTF("Ada"); // a length-prefixed string out.writeDouble(98.5); out.writeUTF("Linus"); out.writeDouble(87.25); } System.out.println(buffer.size() + " bytes"); try (var in = new DataInputStream(new ByteArrayInputStream(buffer.toByteArray()))) { int count = in.readInt(); for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) System.out.println(in.readUTF() + " " + in.readDouble()); } } } Reading must follow exactly the order of writing; there are no labels in the data. Reading past the end throws EOFException . ByteBuffer and byte order Many file formats are little-endian (the low byte first), which DataOutputStream cannot do. ByteBuffer can, and also reads and writes at any position: java import java.nio.ByteBuffer; import java.nio.ByteOrder; import java.util.HexFormat; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { ByteBuffer big = ByteBuffer.allocate(4).putInt(0x12345678); ByteBuffer little = ByteBuffer.allocate(4).order(ByteOrder.LITTLE_ENDIAN).putInt(0x12345678); System.out.println(HexFormat.of().formatHex(big.array())); // 12345678 System.out.println(HexFormat.of().formatHex(little.array())); // 78563412 ByteBuffer read = ByteBuffer.wrap(little.array()).order(ByteOrder.LITTLE_ENDIAN); System.out.println(Integer.toHexString(read.getInt())); // 12345678 } } Designing a small format A robust binary file usually has: 1. a magic number at the start (a few fixed bytes) so you can tell the file is yours; 2. a version so newer programs can still read older files; 3. lengths before variable-sized data (strings, lists); 4. a checksum at the end to detect damage. java import java.util.zip.CRC32; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { CRC32 crc = new CRC32(); crc.update("hello".getBytes()); System.out.println(Long.toHexString(crc.getValue())); // 3610a686 } } Check yourself quiz ? What does in.read() return at the end of a stream? - 0 + -1 - null - It throws an EOFException Real bytes come back as 0 to 255, so -1 cannot be confused with data. 0 is a perfectly valid byte. ( DataInputStream 's readInt and friends are the ones that throw EOFException .) ? Why wrap a FileOutputStream in a BufferedOutputStream ? - To compress the data before it is written - So the bytes are written in big-endian order - So the stream is closed automatically + So many small writes reach the disk as a few large blocks The buffer gathers small writes in memory, which is much faster. Each wrapper adds one ability: buffering adds speed. Compression is GZIPOutputStream , and closing is the job of try with resources. ? How is the int 0x0A0B0C0D laid out in little-endian order? - 0A 0B 0C 0D - 0B 0A 0D 0C + 0D 0C 0B 0A - it depends on the file Little-endian puts the lowest byte first.

title: Hex dump
body: Write class Hex with static String dump(byte data) that formats bytes the way hex viewers do, 8 per line: 00000000 48 65 6c 6c 6f 2c 20 4a Hello, J 00000008 61 76 61 21 0a ava!. - Each line starts with the offset as 8 hex digits, then two spaces. - Then each byte as two lower-case hex digits followed by a space, padded with spaces so the text column always starts at the same place (a full line of 8 bytes takes 24 characters). - Then one more space and the bytes as characters: printable ASCII (32–126) as itself, anything else as . . - Lines are joined with "\n" ; no data gives "" .

title: A save-game format
body: Write a binary format for a game's save file with record Save(String player, int level, List<Integer scores) and a class SaveFormat : - static byte write(Save save) : the bytes, in this order (all numbers big-endian, as DataOutputStream writes them): 1. the magic bytes 'X' 'S' 'A' 'V' ; 2. the version, an int 1; 3. the player name with writeUTF ; 4. the level, an int ; 5. the number of scores, an int , then each score as an int ; 6. a CRC-32 ( java.util.zip.CRC32 ) of everything before it , as a long . - static Save read(byte data) : the reverse. It throws IOException with a clear message when the magic bytes are wrong ( "not a save file" ), the version is not 1 ( "unsupported version 2" ), the checksum does not match ( "damaged file" ), or the data ends too early.

title: A room booking system
body: Build the core of a small hotel's booking system, using what this milestone covered: a builder, value objects with a correct equals and hashCode , java.time , an inner iterator, and a binary save file. java var hotel = new Hotel(); hotel.addRoom(new Room("101", 2)); hotel.addRoom(new Room("102", 4)); Booking b = Booking.forGuest("Ada") .room(new Room("101", 2)) .from(LocalDate.of(2026, 12, 1)) .nights(3) .build(); hotel.book(b); hotel.available(LocalDate.of(2026, 12, 2), LocalDate.of(2026, 12, 4), 2); // 102 Write these classes: record Room(String number, int beds) : a record, so equals and hashCode come for free. final class Booking with a static nested Builder started by Booking.forGuest(String guest) , with room(Room) , from(LocalDate) and nights(int) . build() throws IllegalStateException if the room or start date is missing, or nights is below 1. A booking has guest() , room() , checkIn() , checkOut() (check-in plus nights) and overlaps(LocalDate from, LocalDate to) : true when the stay shares at least one night with the range from, to) (check-out day is free again). class Hotel implements Iterable<Booking : - addRoom(Room) ; adding a room whose number is already there throws IllegalArgumentException . - book(Booking) : the room must be one of the hotel's rooms ( IllegalArgumentException ) and must not have an overlapping booking ( IllegalStateException ). - available(LocalDate from, LocalDate to, int guests) : the numbers of rooms with at least guests beds and no booking overlapping from, to) , sorted by number. - iterator() : the bookings sorted by check-in date, then guest name, from a private inner class or a sorted copy. - byte save() and static Hotel load(byte data) with DataOutputStream and DataInputStream : the rooms (count, then number and beds) and the bookings (count, then guest, room number, check-in as toEpochDay() and nights). load(save()) gives a hotel with the same rooms and bookings.

title: 8.01  Regular Expressions
body: Finding and taking apart text with java.util.regex - Pattern and Matcher, matches versus find, groups and named groups, looping over every match, replacing with a function, splitting, flags such as CASE_INSENSITIVE, the escaping rules in Java strings, and when a regular expression is the wrong tool. Patterns in Java A regular expression describes a shape of text: "one or more digits", "a word followed by @". Java's support lives in java.util.regex : a Pattern is the compiled expression and a Matcher applies it to one piece of text. java import java.util.regex. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Pattern date = Pattern.compile("(\\d{4})-(\\d{2})-(\\d{2})"); Matcher m = date.matcher("due 2026-11-20, paid 2026-12-01"); while (m.find()) { System.out.println(m.group() + " - year " + m.group(1) + ", month " + m.group(2)); } } } Backslashes must be doubled inside Java strings: the regex \d is written "\\d" . Text blocks and Pattern.quote help, but the doubling is the most common stumbling block. The pattern language in brief piece matches --- --- . any character except a new line \d , \w , \s a digit, a word character (letter, digit, _ ), a space abc , a-z , ^0-9 one of, a range, anything except , + , ? , {2,5} 0 or more, 1 or more, 0 or 1, 2 to 5 times ? , +? the same, but as few as possible (lazy) ^ , $ the start and end of the text (or line, with MULTILINE ) \b a word boundary (...) , (?<name ...) , (?:...) a group, a named group, a group that is not captured a b either matches, find and lookingAt java import java.util.regex. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Pattern number = Pattern.compile("\\d+"); System.out.println(number.matcher("123").matches()); // true: the whole text System.out.println(number.matcher("abc 123").matches()); // false System.out.println(number.matcher("abc 123").find()); // true: somewhere inside System.out.println(number.matcher("123abc").lookingAt()); // true: at the start System.out.println("2026".matches("\\d{4}")); // String.matches = whole text } } Use matches for validation ("is this a postcode?") and find for searching. Named groups Names make complex patterns readable and survive changes in the number of groups: java import java.util.regex. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Pattern line = Pattern.compile("(?<time \\d{2}:\\d{2}) (?<level INFO WARN ERROR) (?<msg . )"); Matcher m = line.matcher("14:03 ERROR disk full"); if (m.matches()) { System.out.println(m.group("level") + " at " + m.group("time") + ": " + m.group("msg")); } } } Every match as a stream Matcher.results() gives a Stream<MatchResult , which fits the stream style of lesson 6.02: java import java.util.regex. ; import java.util.stream. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { String text = "Contact ada@example.com or bob@mail.example.org today."; var emails = Pattern.compile(" \\w. +@ \\w- +(?:\\. \\w- +)+") .matcher(text) .results() .map(MatchResult::group) .collect(Collectors.toList()); System.out.println(emails); } } Replacing replaceAll with a replacement string can refer to groups with $1 or ${name} . With a function, each match can be replaced by anything you compute: java import java.util.regex. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { String date = "2026-11-20"; System.out.println(date.replaceAll("(\\d{4})-(\\d{2})-(\\d{2})", "$3/$2/$1")); Matcher m = Pattern.compile("\\$(\\d+(?:\\.\\d+)?)").matcher("tea $2.50, cake $4"); String doubled = m.replaceAll(r - "\\$" + String.format("%.2f", Double.parseDouble(r.group(1)) 2)); System.out.println(doubled); System.out.println("a.b.c".replace(".", "/")); // replace (not replaceAll) takes plain text } } In a replacement string, $ and \ are special; Matcher.quoteReplacement(text) makes any text safe to use there. Splitting java import java.util. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { System.out.println(Arrays.toString("a, b,, c".split("\\s ,\\s "))); System.out.println(Arrays.toString("one two\tthree".split("\\s+"))); System.out.println(Arrays.toString("1.2.3".split("\\."))); // . must be escaped System.out.println(Arrays.toString("a,b,,".split(","))); // trailing empty parts dropped System.out.println(Arrays.toString("a,b,,".split(",", -1))); // kept with a negative limit } } Flags java import java.util.regex. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Pattern hello = Pattern.compile("^hello$", Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE Pattern.MULTILINE); System.out.println(hello.matcher("Hi\nHELLO\nbye").find()); System.out.println("HeLLo".matches("(?i)hello")); // a flag inside the pattern } } COMMENTS ( (?x) ) allows spaces and comments in a pattern, which helps with long ones. Compile once String.matches , split and replaceAll compile the pattern on every call. In a loop, keep a private static final Pattern and reuse it. When not to use a regex Regular expressions are great for tokens, simple formats and searching. They are the wrong tool for nested structures (HTML, JSON, arithmetic with brackets): use a parser. And a pattern like (a+)+$ on a long string of a s can take exponential time; keep patterns simple, and limit input length when the pattern comes from users. Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference between matches() and find() ? + matches() must match the whole text; find() looks for the next place the pattern occurs anywhere - matches() returns the matched text; find() returns its position - find() must match the whole text; matches() searches anywhere - matches() ignores case; find() does not Use matches() to validate a whole string and find() to search inside one. lookingAt() is the one that matches only at the start. ? Why is "1.2.3".split(".") an empty array? - split cannot split on punctuation - The dots are removed before splitting + . means "any character", so every character is a separator - split needs a limit argument to return anything The argument of split is a regex; escape the dot as "\\." to split on a literal dot. Trailing empty parts are dropped, which leaves nothing. ? How is the regex \d+ written in a Java string literal? - "\d+" - "/\d+/" - "\\\\d+" + "\\d+" Java strings use backslash for their own escapes, so each regex backslash is doubled.

title: Hashtags and hidden emails
body: Write final class Extract with two static methods built on java.util.regex : - List<String hashtags(String text) returns the hashtags in order of first appearance, lower-cased, without the and without duplicates. A hashtag is followed by one or more letters, digits or _ , and the must not follow a letter or digit (so C and a b are not hashtags). - String maskEmails(String text) replaces the part before the @ of every email address with its first character and : ada.lovelace@example.com becomes a @example.com .

title: A tiny template engine
body: Write final class Template with static String render(String template, Map<String, Object values) : - ${name} is replaced by String.valueOf(values.get(name)) ; - ${name:FORMAT} formats the value with String.format(Locale.ROOT, FORMAT, value) , for example ${price:%.2f} ; - names are letters, digits, _ and . ; a name that is not in the map leaves the placeholder exactly as it was; - $${ produces a literal ${ (an escape), and a $ or \ inside a value never causes trouble. java Template.render("Hello ${name}, you owe ${amount:%.2f}.", Map.of("name", "Ada", "amount", 12.5)) // "Hello Ada, you owe 12.50."

title: 8.02  CompletableFuture and Virtual Threads
body: Modern concurrency in Java - CompletableFuture for chaining work that finishes later (supplyAsync, thenApply, thenCompose, thenCombine, allOf), handling failures with exceptionally and handle, timeouts with orTimeout, and virtual threads that make one cheap thread per task practical again. Beyond Future Lesson 6.04 used ExecutorService and Future : you submit work and later call get() , which blocks until it is done. To do something with the result, you have to wait for it first. CompletableFuture lets you say what happens next without blocking. A pipeline of steps The examples in this lesson start real threads, which the runner in your browser does not allow, so run them on your computer with java Main.java . The practice tasks are written so they need no threads of their own. java-norun import java.util.concurrent. ; public class Main { static String fetchUser(int id) { sleep(50); return "user" + id; } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } public static void main(String args) { CompletableFuture<String greeting = CompletableFuture .supplyAsync(() - fetchUser(7)) // runs on another thread .thenApply(String::toUpperCase) // then transform the result .thenApply(name - "Hello, " + name); System.out.println("started, not waiting yet"); System.out.println(greeting.join()); // wait only at the very end } } - supplyAsync(supplier) starts work that returns a value ( runAsync for work with no value). - thenApply(fn) transforms the result when it arrives, like map on a stream. - join() waits and returns the result (like get() , without checked exceptions). Steps that are themselves asynchronous When the next step also returns a CompletableFuture , use thenCompose (like flatMap ), so you do not end up with a future of a future: java-norun import java.util.concurrent. ; public class Main { static CompletableFuture<Integer findUserId(String name) { return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() - name.length() 10); } static CompletableFuture<String loadOrders(int userId) { return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() - "orders of " + userId); } public static void main(String args) { String result = findUserId("ada") .thenCompose(Main::loadOrders) .join(); System.out.println(result); } } Waiting for several thenCombine joins two independent results; allOf waits for any number: java-norun import java.util. ; import java.util.concurrent. ; import java.util.stream. ; public class Main { static CompletableFuture<Integer price(String item, int ms, int value) { return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() - { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { throw new RuntimeException(e); } return value; }); } public static void main(String args) { long start = System.nanoTime(); var total = price("tea", 100, 3).thenCombine(price("cake", 100, 4), Integer::sum); System.out.println("tea + cake = " + total.join()); List<CompletableFuture<Integer all = List.of(price("a", 80, 1), price("b", 120, 2), price("c", 60, 3)); CompletableFuture.allOf(all.toArray(new CompletableFuture 0 )).join(); int sum = all.stream().mapToInt(CompletableFuture::join).sum(); long ms = (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000; System.out.println("sum " + sum + ", about " + (ms < 400 ? "as long as the slowest" : "the sum of all")); } } anyOf completes with the first one to finish. Failures An exception inside a stage completes the future exceptionally, and the following thenApply steps are skipped. Recover with exceptionally (only on failure) or handle (always, with the result or the error): java-norun import java.util.concurrent. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { CompletableFuture<Integer parsed = CompletableFuture .supplyAsync(() - Integer.parseInt("forty-two")) .thenApply(n - n 2) // skipped .exceptionally(e - { System.out.println("failed: " + e.getCause().getClass().getSimpleName()); return 0; }); System.out.println(parsed.join()); String status = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() - 10 / 2) .handle((value, error) - error == null ? "ok " + value : "error " + error.getMessage()) .join(); System.out.println(status); } } The error passed to these callbacks is usually a CompletionException wrapping the real one; getCause() gives the original. Timeouts java-norun import java.util.concurrent. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { String r = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() - { try { Thread.sleep(2000); } catch (InterruptedException e) { } return "slow answer"; }) .completeOnTimeout("default answer", 100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) .join(); System.out.println(r); } } orTimeout(ms, unit) fails with a TimeoutException instead of giving a default. Which threads? supplyAsync without an executor uses the shared ForkJoinPool.commonPool() , sized for the number of processor cores: right for calculations, wrong for work that mostly waits (network, files). Pass your own executor for waiting work: supplyAsync(task, executor) . Virtual threads Classic Java threads are operating system threads: each costs memory, and a few thousand is a lot. Since Java 21, virtual threads are managed by the JVM and are cheap enough to create one per task, even a million. When a virtual thread waits (sleep, I/O, a lock), it gives up its carrier thread for others. java-norun import java.util.concurrent. ; import java.util.stream. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) throws Exception { long start = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { var futures = IntStream.range(0, 10_000) .mapToObj(i - executor.submit(() - { Thread.sleep(100); // 10,000 tasks that each wait 100 ms return i; })) .toList(); long sum = 0; for (var f : futures) sum += f.get(); System.out.println("sum " + sum); } long ms = (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000; System.out.println(ms < 5000 ? "finished in well under a second per thousand" : "slow"); Thread t = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() - System.out.println("virtual: " + Thread.currentThread().isVirtual())); t.join(); } } With virtual threads you can write plain, blocking, easy-to-read code ( var page = fetch(url); ) and still handle many tasks at once. They help with waiting, not with calculating: CPU-heavy work still needs about one thread per core. Check yourself quiz ? When do you use thenCompose rather than thenApply ? - When the next step should run on a different thread - When you want to combine two independent futures + When the next step itself returns a CompletableFuture - When the next step may throw an exception thenCompose flattens the result, like flatMap ; thenApply would give a future of a future. Combining two independent futures is thenCombine . ? Why are virtual threads good for a server handling many requests? + Each request can block in its own thread, and waiting ones cost almost nothing - They run calculations faster than operating system threads - They never need to wait for network or files - They use one processor core per request A waiting virtual thread gives up its carrier thread, so many thousands can wait at once. They help with waiting, not with CPU-heavy work. ? A stage throws an exception. What happens to the thenApply steps after it? - they run anyway, with null as their input - the program stops at once with the exception + they are skipped until an exceptionally or handle step - the exception is ignored and the chain goes on The future completes exceptionally; later transformation steps are skipped, and recovery steps see the error.

If any part fails, the result fails too. It must not block: it returns straight away, even while parts are unfinished. - static <T T valueNow(CompletableFuture<T future, T fallback) : without waiting, returns the value if the future has already completed normally, and fallback if it is not finished yet or failed. title: 8.03  Collectors in Depth
body: Getting the most out of collect - groupingBy with downstream collectors (counting, summing, mapping, averaging, maxBy), choosing the map type, partitioningBy, toMap with merge functions, joining, summarizing statistics, teeing two collectors at once, and writing your own Collector with Collector.of. Collect is a toolbox Lesson 6.02 ended streams with toList() , count() and a simple groupingBy . The Collectors class has much more: most "report" questions are one collect call. The examples use this record: java-norun record Sale(String region, String product, int qty, double price) { double value() { return qty price; } } Grouping with a second step groupingBy(key) alone gives lists. Its second argument, a downstream collector , decides what to do with each group: java import java.util. ; import java.util.stream. ; public class Main { record Sale(String region, String product, int qty, double price) { double value() { return qty price; } } public static void main(String args) { List<Sale sales = List.of( new Sale("North", "tea", 3, 2.5), new Sale("South", "tea", 1, 2.5), new Sale("North", "cake", 2, 4.0), new Sale("North", "tea", 4, 2.5), new Sale("South", "coffee", 5, 3.0)); Map<String, Long count = sales.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Sale::region, Collectors.counting())); Map<String, Integer qty = sales.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Sale::product, Collectors.summingInt(Sale::qty))); Map<String, Double avg = sales.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Sale::region, Collectors.averagingDouble(Sale::value))); Map<String, Set<String products = sales.stream().collect( Collectors.groupingBy(Sale::region, TreeMap::new, Collectors.mapping(Sale::product, Collectors.toCollection(TreeSet::new)))); Map<String, Optional<Sale biggest = sales.stream().collect( Collectors.groupingBy(Sale::region, Collectors.maxBy(Comparator.comparingDouble(Sale::value)))); System.out.println(new TreeMap< (count)); System.out.println(new TreeMap< (qty)); System.out.println(new TreeMap< (avg)); System.out.println(products); System.out.println(biggest.get("North").map(Sale::value).orElse(0.0)); } } - The middle argument ( TreeMap::new ) picks the map type; a TreeMap gives sorted keys. - mapping(fn, downstream) transforms each item before collecting it. - Downstream collectors nest: groupingBy(region, groupingBy(product, counting())) gives a two-level map. Two groups: partitioningBy java import java.util. ; import java.util.stream. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { Map<Boolean, List<Integer evenOdd = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 10).boxed() .collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(n - n % 2 == 0)); System.out.println(evenOdd.get(true) + " " + evenOdd.get(false)); Map<Boolean, Long passed = Stream.of(91, 48, 77, 50, 12).collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(s - s = 50, Collectors.counting())); System.out.println(passed); } } The map always has both true and false keys, even when one group is empty. toMap and duplicate keys toMap(keyFn, valueFn) throws IllegalStateException if two items have the same key. A third argument, the merge function , says how to combine them: java import java.util. ; import java.util.stream. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { List<String words = List.of("apple", "avocado", "banana", "blueberry", "cherry"); Map<Character, String longestByLetter = words.stream().collect(Collectors.toMap( w - w.charAt(0), w - w, (a, b) - a.length() = b.length() ? a : b, TreeMap::new)); System.out.println(longestByLetter); Map<String, Integer lengths = words.stream().collect(Collectors.toMap(w - w, String::length)); System.out.println(lengths.get("cherry")); } } Joining and statistics java import java.util. ; import java.util.stream. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { System.out.println(Stream.of("tea", "cake", "milk").collect(Collectors.joining(", ", " ", " "))); IntSummaryStatistics s = Stream.of(4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42).collect(Collectors.summarizingInt(n - n)); System.out.println(s.getMin() + " " + s.getMax() + " " + s.getAverage() + " " + s.getSum() + " " + s.getCount()); } } Two results in one pass: teeing teeing(c1, c2, combine) sends every item to two collectors and combines their results: java import java.util. ; import java.util.stream. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { String range = Stream.of(4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42).collect(Collectors.teeing( Collectors.minBy(Integer::compare), Collectors.maxBy(Integer::compare), (min, max) - min.get() + ".." + max.get())); System.out.println(range); } } Your own collector Collector.of(supplier, accumulator, combiner, finisher) builds one from four functions: make an empty container, add one item, merge two containers (for parallel streams), and turn the container into the result. java import java.util. ; import java.util.stream. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { // collects into the top 3 values, largest first Collector<Integer, PriorityQueue<Integer , List<Integer top3 = Collector.of( PriorityQueue::new, (q, x) - { q.add(x); if (q.size() 3) q.poll(); }, (a, b) - { b.forEach(x - { a.add(x); if (a.size() 3) a.poll(); }); return a; }, q - q.stream().sorted(Comparator.reverseOrder()).toList()); System.out.println(Stream.of(5, 1, 9, 3, 7, 8).collect(top3)); } } Check yourself quiz ? What does groupingBy(Sale::region, counting()) give? - A list of the regions, one per sale - The number of different regions - A map from each region to the list of its sales + A map from each region to the number of sales in it The downstream counting() turns each group into a Long . Without a downstream collector, each group would be a List<Sale . ? When does toMap throw, and how do you prevent it? - When a value is null ; filter the nulls out first + When two items produce the same key; pass a merge function as the third argument - When the map grows too large; pass TreeMap::new as the fourth argument - When the stream is empty; check with isEmpty() first toMap(keyFn, valueFn) throws IllegalStateException on a duplicate key; the merge function decides which value to keep, or how to combine them. ? Which collector always gives a map with exactly the keys true and false ? - groupingBy(x - x 0) - toMap(x - x 0, x - x) - teeing(...) + partitioningBy(x - x 0) partitioningBy always has both keys; groupingBy only has keys that occur.

title: 8.04  BigInteger, BigDecimal and Exact Arithmetic
body: When int, long and double are not enough - silent overflow and the Math.addExact family that refuses it, BigInteger for whole numbers of any size, why 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3 in double, BigDecimal for exact decimal money with scale and RoundingMode, comparing with compareTo, and choosing the right type. Overflow is silent int holds values up to 2,147,483,647. One more wraps around to the most negative number, with no error: java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { int big = Integer.MAX_VALUE; System.out.println(big + 1); // -2147483648 long ms = 30L 24 60 60 1000; // 30 days in milliseconds: needs long int wrong = 30 24 60 60 1000; // computed in int: wrapped System.out.println(ms + " " + wrong); } } The L on the first number makes the whole expression long . Without it, the multiplication happens in int and wraps before being stored. Arithmetic that refuses to overflow Math.addExact , subtractExact , multiplyExact , incrementExact , negateExact and toIntExact throw ArithmeticException instead of wrapping: java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { System.out.println(Math.multiplyExact(1_000_000, 1_000)); try { Math.multiplyExact(1_000_000, 1_000_000); } catch (ArithmeticException e) { System.out.println("refused: " + e.getMessage()); } System.out.println(Math.toIntExact(42L)); } } Use them wherever an overflow would be a bug: sizes, money in cents, counters that must not wrap. BigInteger: whole numbers of any size java import java.math.BigInteger; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { BigInteger f = BigInteger.ONE; for (int i = 2; i <= 30; i++) f = f.multiply(BigInteger.valueOf(i)); System.out.println("30! = " + f); System.out.println(f.bitLength() + " bits, " + f.toString().length() + " digits"); BigInteger a = new BigInteger("123456789012345678901234567890"); System.out.println(a.add(BigInteger.TEN).mod(BigInteger.valueOf(97))); System.out.println(BigInteger.TWO.pow(100)); System.out.println(BigInteger.valueOf(97).isProbablePrime(20)); } } BigInteger objects never change: every operation returns a new one, so always use the result ( f = f.multiply(...) ). They are slower than long , so use them only when values can really be that large (cryptography, exact combinatorics, IDs from other systems). The trouble with double double stores numbers in binary, and most decimal fractions have no exact binary form, just as 1/3 has no exact decimal form: java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { System.out.println(0.1 + 0.2); // 0.30000000000000004 System.out.println(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3); // false double total = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) total += 0.1; System.out.println(total); // 0.9999999999999999 System.out.println(Math.abs(total - 1.0) < 1e-9); // compare with a tolerance instead } } For measurements and science, double is right and the tiny errors do not matter. For money , they do: a bank cannot lose a penny in a sum. BigDecimal: exact decimals java import java.math. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { BigDecimal a = new BigDecimal("0.1"); BigDecimal b = new BigDecimal("0.2"); System.out.println(a.add(b)); // 0.3 exactly System.out.println(new BigDecimal(0.1)); // the double's real value: not what you want System.out.println(BigDecimal.valueOf(0.1)); // goes through the double's text: 0.1 BigDecimal price = new BigDecimal("19.99"); BigDecimal qty = BigDecimal.valueOf(3); BigDecimal vat = new BigDecimal("0.20"); BigDecimal net = price.multiply(qty); BigDecimal gross = net.add(net.multiply(vat)).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP); System.out.println(net + " + VAT = " + gross); } } Always create BigDecimal from a string (or valueOf ), never with new BigDecimal(double) , which copies the double's binary error. Scale and rounding A BigDecimal is a whole number and a scale (how many digits after the point): 19.99 is 1999 with scale 2. Division can produce endless digits, so you must say how to round: java import java.math. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { BigDecimal ten = new BigDecimal("10.00"); try { ten.divide(BigDecimal.valueOf(3)); } catch (ArithmeticException e) { System.out.println("needs rounding: " + e.getMessage()); } System.out.println(ten.divide(BigDecimal.valueOf(3), 2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP)); System.out.println(new BigDecimal("2.5").setScale(0, RoundingMode.HALF_UP) + " " + new BigDecimal("2.5").setScale(0, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN)); } } HALF_UP is school rounding; HALF_EVEN (banker's rounding) rounds halves to the even neighbour, which avoids a bias when adding many rounded values. Comparing BigDecimal equals compares the scale too, so 2.0 and 2.00 are not equal. Compare values with compareTo : java import java.math.BigDecimal; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { BigDecimal a = new BigDecimal("2.0"), b = new BigDecimal("2.00"); System.out.println(a.equals(b) + " " + (a.compareTo(b) == 0)); System.out.println(a.stripTrailingZeros().equals(b.stripTrailingZeros())); } } This also means BigDecimal values make poor HashMap keys unless you normalise them first. Choosing need type --- --- counts, indexes, ids int , long (with Math. Exact where overflow is a bug) measurements, physics, graphics double money, prices, tax BigDecimal , or long cents whole numbers beyond long BigInteger Check yourself quiz ? Why is new BigDecimal(0.1) a mistake? - It does not compile: the constructor only takes strings + The double 0.1 is already slightly wrong in binary, and this constructor copies that exact wrong value - It rounds 0.1 to 0 - It throws an ArithmeticException because 0.1 has no exact binary form The result has dozens of digits of binary error. Use new BigDecimal("0.1") or BigDecimal.valueOf(0.1) . ? What does Math.addExact do that + does not? - It adds the numbers as long so they never overflow - It rounds the result to the nearest int - It returns Integer.MAX_VALUE when the result is too big + It throws an ArithmeticException when the result does not fit + on int wraps past 2,147,483,647 to a negative number with no error; addExact refuses. ? new BigDecimal("2.0").equals(new BigDecimal("2.00")) is... - true - a compile error + false , because the scales differ - an ArithmeticException equals compares value and scale; compareTo compares only the value.

title: 8.05  Formatting, Locales and Text
body: Turning values into text people can read - format specifiers in String.format and formatted, padding and alignment, NumberFormat and DecimalFormat, Locale and why numbers and dates look different around the world, text blocks, Unicode code points and characters outside the basic plane, and comparing text for people with Collator. Format strings String.format (and the method form "...".formatted(...) ) build text from a pattern of format specifiers : java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { System.out.println(String.format("%s scored %d (%.1f%%)", "Ada", 91, 91.25)); System.out.println(" %8s %-8s %08.3f ".formatted("right", "left", 3.14159)); System.out.println("%,d bytes".formatted(1234567)); System.out.println("%x %X %o %e".formatted(255, 255, 8, 12345.678)); System.out.println("%b %c %n".formatted(true, 'Z').trim()); } } specifier meaning --- --- %s , %d , %f , %c , %b text, whole number, decimal, character, boolean %x , %e hexadecimal, scientific notation %8s , %-8s width 8, right- or left-aligned %.2f , %08.3f 2 decimals; width 8 with leading zeros %,d thousands separators %% , %n a literal % , the system's new line Locale People in different countries write numbers and dates differently. A Locale names a language and region, and formatting uses it: java import java.text.NumberFormat; import java.util.Locale; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { double amount = 1234567.891; for (Locale l : new Locale { Locale.UK, Locale.GERMANY, Locale.FRANCE, Locale.of("en", "IN") }) { System.out.println(l + ": " + String.format(l, "%,.2f", amount) + " " + NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance(l).format(amount) + " " + NumberFormat.getPercentInstance(l).format(0.256)); } } } String.format without a locale uses the computer's default locale, which may differ between your machine and a server. For text meant for people, pass their locale. For text meant for programs (files, logs, network messages), use Locale.ROOT , so the format never changes: java import java.util.Locale; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { String forAFile = String.format(Locale.ROOT, "%.2f", 3.5); System.out.println(forAFile + " " + Double.parseDouble(forAFile)); } } DecimalFormat: patterns for numbers java import java.math.RoundingMode; import java.text. ; import java.util.Locale; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { DecimalFormat money = new DecimalFormat(" , 0.00", DecimalFormatSymbols.getInstance(Locale.UK)); System.out.println(money.format(1234.5) + " " + money.format(0.5)); DecimalFormat compact = new DecimalFormat("0. "); compact.setRoundingMode(RoundingMode.HALF_UP); System.out.println(compact.format(2.0) + " " + compact.format(2.345)); System.out.println(NumberFormat.getCompactNumberInstance(Locale.US, NumberFormat.Style.SHORT).format(1_250_000)); } } 0 is a digit that is always shown, a digit shown only if needed, , a grouping separator. Text blocks Multi-line text (JSON, SQL, HTML) is easiest with a text block. Indentation common to all lines is removed, and quotes need no escaping: java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { String json = """ { "name": "%s", "level": %d } """.formatted("Ada", 3); System.out.print(json); String oneLine = """ a long sentence that \ continues here"""; System.out.println(oneLine); } } A \ at the end of a line joins it with the next. Characters and code points A Java char is a 16-bit UTF-16 unit. Most characters fit in one, but emoji and some rare scripts need two (a surrogate pair ), so length() counts units, not characters: java public class Main { public static void main(String args) { String s = "café 😀"; System.out.println(s.length() + " units, " + s.codePointCount(0, s.length()) + " characters"); s.codePoints().forEach(cp - System.out.print(Character.charCount(cp) + " ")); // 1 1 1 1 1 2: the emoji takes two units System.out.println(); String reversed = new StringBuilder(s).reverse().toString(); System.out.println(reversed.codePointCount(0, reversed.length())); // StringBuilder keeps pairs together System.out.println(Character.isLetter('é') + " " + Character.isDigit('٣') + " " + Character.toUpperCase('ß')); } } Loop with codePoints() instead of charAt when text may contain any character. Comparing for people compareTo compares character codes, so "Zoe" comes before "anna" and "Émile" after everything. A Collator sorts the way a dictionary in a given language does: java import java.text.Collator; import java.util. ; public class Main { public static void main(String args) { List<String names = new ArrayList< (List.of("Zoe", "anna", "Émile", "Eve", "bob")); Collections.sort(names); System.out.println(names); names.sort(Collator.getInstance(Locale.FRANCE)); System.out.println(names); System.out.println("STRASSE".equalsIgnoreCase("straße")); // false: simple case rules only } } Use plain comparison for identifiers and keys, and a Collator for lists people read. Check yourself quiz ? Why format numbers for a file with Locale.ROOT ? - It makes the numbers shorter + So every computer writes the same decimal point and no grouping - It formats them for the reader's own country - String.format only accepts Locale.ROOT for decimals Then the file can be read back anywhere. Without a locale, String.format uses the computer's default, so a German machine would write 3,50 , which Double.parseDouble cannot read back. ? Why might "😀".length() be 2? - length() counts bytes, and the emoji takes two in UTF-8 - Java stores every character in two char s - The emoji is followed by a hidden space + length() counts UTF-16 code units, and the emoji needs two of them (a surrogate pair) Most characters fit in one char , but emoji and some rare scripts need two; codePointCount counts real characters. (In UTF-8 the emoji is four bytes.) ? Which format prints 3.14 padded with zeros to width 8? - "%8.2f" - "%.8f" + "%08.2f" - "%-08.2f" The 0 flag pads with zeros, 8 is the width, and .2 gives two decimals: 00003.14 . "%8.2f" pads with spaces instead.
