title: Common Errors
body: Compiler errors Message Usual cause Fix Lesson --- --- --- --- ';' expected A missing semicolon, often at the end of the line before Add it 1.01 cannot find symbol A typo, wrong case ( system.out ), a missing import, or a variable used outside its block Check spelling and case; add the import ; declare it in the right scope 1.01 class X is public, should be declared in a file named X.java The public class and file name differ Rename the file or the class 1.01 incompatible types: String cannot be converted to int Assigning a value of the wrong type Convert with Integer.parseInt , or fix the type 1.02 incompatible types: possible lossy conversion from double to int A narrowing conversion without a cast Cast (int) x , or use Math.round 1.02 integer number too large A big literal without L 8_100_000_000L 1.02 variable x might not have been initialized Reading a local variable before every path assigns it Initialise it when declared 1.02 missing return statement A path through a non-void method ends without return Return (or throw) on every path 2.01 bad operand types for binary operator '&&' / incompatible types: int cannot be converted to boolean Using a number as a condition Compare: if (n != 0) 1.03 non-static method m() cannot be referenced from a static context Calling an instance method from main without an object Create an object, or make the method static 3.02 X is abstract; cannot be instantiated new on an abstract class or interface Create a concrete subclass 3.04 X is not abstract and does not override abstract method m() A class misses an interface or abstract method Implement it (public, same signature) 3.04 unreported exception IOException; must be caught or declared to be thrown Calling a method that throws a checked exception try / catch it, or add throws IOException 4.04 local variables referenced from a lambda expression must be final or effectively final A lambda uses a variable that is reassigned Don't reassign it, or use a stream result or an AtomicInteger 6.01 the switch expression does not cover all possible input values A switch over a sealed type or enum misses a case Add the case (or a default ) 3.05 generic array creation / cannot select from a type variable Trying new T or T.class Use a List<T , or pass a Class<T 4.01 Exceptions at run time Exception Usual cause Fix Lesson --- --- --- --- NullPointerException Using a member of null : an unset field, a missing map key, unboxing a null Initialise fields; check map results; use getOrDefault or Optional 3.01 ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException / IndexOutOfBoundsException An index equal to length / size() or negative Indexes run from 0 to length - 1 2.02 NumberFormatException Integer.parseInt on text that is not a whole number Catch it, or check the input first 1.04 InputMismatchException Scanner.nextInt() met text Read lines and parse them 1.04 ArithmeticException: / by zero Integer division by 0 Check the divisor 1.03 ConcurrentModificationException Changing a collection inside an enhanced for over it removeIf , an Iterator 's remove , or loop backwards with indexes 2.03 UnsupportedOperationException Changing a List.of(...) or other unmodifiable collection Copy it: new ArrayList< (List.of(...)) 2.03 ClassCastException A cast to a type the object does not have Use instanceof patterns 3.03 StackOverflowError Recursion without a reachable base case Fix the base case, or use a loop 2.04 NoSuchElementException next() past the end, Optional.get() on empty, Scanner out of input Check hasNext , use orElse , check hasNextLine 6.03 IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon Using a stream twice Create a new stream each time 6.02 NoSuchFileException A wrong path or missing file Check the path; Files.exists ; handle the IOException 4.05 IllegalArgumentException (your own) A method received a bad argument Read the message; fix the caller 4.04 Wrong results without an error Symptom Usual cause Fix Lesson --- --- --- --- 7 / 2 is 3 Integer division Use 7 / 2.0 or a cast 1.03 "Total: " + 1 + 2 prints Total: 12 + joins strings left to right Parenthesise the sum 1.03 Two equal strings are not == == compares references equals 1.04 nextLine() returns "" after nextInt() The line break was left in the input Read whole lines and parse 1.04 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3 Binary floating point Compare with a tolerance; use long cents or BigDecimal for money 1.02 A large int became negative Overflow Use long , or Math.addExact 1.02 An array prints as I@1b6d3586 Arrays have no readable toString Arrays.toString(a) 2.02 list.remove(1) removed the wrong item On a List<Integer it removes index 1 list.remove(Integer.valueOf(1)) 2.03 Two Integer s with the same value are not == == compares wrapper objects equals 2.03 A HashSet holds "duplicates" of your objects equals overridden without hashCode (or neither) Override both, or use a record 4.02 A sort comparator gives a wrong order for big numbers Comparing by subtraction overflows Integer.compare or Comparator.comparingInt 4.03 A classic switch runs several cases Missing break (fall-through) Use the arrow form case X - 1.05 A counter updated from threads is too low A race condition AtomicInteger , synchronized , or no shared state 6.04 A written file is empty or cut off The writer was not closed or flushed try-with-resources 4.05

title: Glossary
body: Every term from the course, in alphabetical order. The lesson that introduces each one is in brackets. Term Meaning --- --- Abstract class A class that cannot be instantiated; it shares code and declares abstract methods subclasses must implement. (3.04) Access modifier public , protected , private or none (package-private): who may use a member. (3.02) Amortised O(1) Usually constant time, with rare expensive steps that average out, like ArrayList.add . (5.04) Annotation A label on code written with @ , read by the compiler, frameworks or reflection. (7.03) Anonymous class A class declared and created in one expression, with no name. (7.01) Array A fixed-size, indexed sequence of values of one type. (2.02) ArrayList A list backed by an array that grows as needed. (2.03) Autoboxing Automatic conversion between a primitive and its wrapper, such as int and Integer . (2.03) Base case The input a recursive method answers directly, without calling itself. (2.04) Big O Notation for how an algorithm's work grows with input size, ignoring constants. (5.01) BigDecimal An exact decimal number with a scale, used for money (8.04) BigInteger A whole number of any size (8.04) Binary search Finding a value in a sorted array by halving the range each step: O(log n). (5.02) Binary search tree A binary tree where left subtrees hold smaller keys and right subtrees larger ones. (5.05) Builder pattern A helper object that collects settings step by step and then creates an immutable object. (7.01) ByteBuffer A buffer of bytes with a chosen byte order and methods to read and write numbers. (7.05) Bytecode The instructions javac produces for the Java Virtual Machine. (1.01) Cast An explicit conversion, such as (int) 3.9 . (1.02) Checked exception An exception that must be caught or declared with throws , such as IOException . (4.04) Class A blueprint for objects: fields, constructors and methods. (3.01) Clock A source of the current time that can be fixed in tests. (7.04) Code point The number of one Unicode character; some need two Java chars (8.05) Collator A comparator that sorts text the way a given language does (8.05) Collection The interface of groups of objects: lists, sets and queues. (4.02) Comparable The interface giving a class its natural order through compareTo . (3.04) Comparator An ordering kept outside the compared class. (4.03) CompletableFuture A result that arrives later, with steps such as thenApply and thenCompose that run when it does (8.02) Consistent with equals A compareTo that returns 0 exactly when equals is true. (7.02) Constructor Code that initialises a new object; it has the class's name and no return type. (3.01) CRC-32 A checksum used to detect accidental damage to data. (7.05) DataOutputStream Writes numbers and strings in a fixed big-endian binary format. (7.05) DateTimeFormatter Formats and parses dates and times with a pattern or a standard format. (7.04) Deadlock Threads waiting forever for locks the others hold. (6.04) Downstream collector The collector a groupingBy applies to each group, such as counting() or mapping(...) (8.03) Dynamic dispatch Choosing which overridden method to run from the object's actual class at run time. (3.03) Effectively final A local variable never reassigned, which lambdas may capture. (6.01) Encapsulation Keeping an object's data private and changing it only through its methods. (3.02) Endianness The order of a number's bytes: big-endian puts the high byte first, little-endian the low byte. (7.05) Enhanced for for (T x : collection) : a loop over every item. (1.05) Enum A type with a fixed set of named constants, which can have fields and methods. (3.05) equals / hashCode Value equality and its matching hash; overridden together. (3.03) equals contract The rules equals must follow: reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent, false for null. (7.02) Exception An object thrown to signal an error, caught with try / catch . (4.04) ExecutorService A pool of threads that runs submitted tasks. (6.04) Field A variable that belongs to an object (or to the class, if static). (3.01) final Cannot be reassigned (variables), overridden (methods) or extended (classes). (1.02) Functional interface An interface with exactly one abstract method, implementable by a lambda. (6.01) Garbage collector The JVM part that frees objects no longer referenced. (1.01) Generics Type parameters such as List<String , checked at compile time. (4.01) Hash table An array of buckets indexed by hash code, giving O(1) average lookup. (5.04) hashCode contract Equal objects must return equal hash codes. (7.02) Immutable Cannot change after creation, like String , records and LocalDate . (3.02) Inheritance A class extending another and reusing its members. (3.03) Inner class A non-static nested class; each object holds a reference to an object of the outer class. (7.01) InputStream The abstract class for reading bytes; read() returns -1 at the end. (7.05) Instant A moment on the global timeline, the same everywhere. (7.04) Interface A contract of methods that implementing classes provide. (3.04) Invariant A condition that stays true, such as at the start of every loop round. (5.02) InvocationTargetException What Method.invoke throws when the called method throws; getCause() is the real exception. (7.03) Iterator An object that walks through a collection with hasNext and next . (5.03) JDK / JVM The Java Development Kit (compiler, tools, library) / the Java Virtual Machine that runs bytecode. (1.01) Lambda A short anonymous function: x - x 2 . (6.01) Linked list Nodes that each hold a value and a reference to the next node. (5.03) Load factor Entries divided by buckets in a hash table; kept low by resizing. (5.04) Locale A language and region, which decides how numbers, dates and text are formatted (8.05) Magic number Fixed bytes at the start of a file that identify its format. (7.05) Map Key-to-value lookup: HashMap , TreeMap , LinkedHashMap . (4.02) Matcher Applies a Pattern to one text: matches, find, group and replaceAll (8.01) Memoization Storing results of earlier calls to avoid recomputing them. (2.04) Merge sort Divide-and-conquer sort: split, sort halves, merge; O(n log n), stable. (5.02) Method A named block of code with parameters and a return type. (2.01) Method reference Shorthand for a lambda calling one method: String::length . (6.01) Named group A part of a regular expression written (?<name ...) and read back with group("name") (8.01) NullPointerException Thrown when a member of null is used. (3.01) Object An instance of a class; also the root class of all classes. (3.01) Optional A container for a value that may be absent, used as a return type. (6.03) OutputStream The abstract class for writing bytes. (7.05) Overflow A whole-number result too big for its type, which silently wraps around in Java (8.04) Overloading Several methods with the same name and different parameters. (2.01) Overriding A subclass replacing an inherited method. (3.03) Package A named group of classes matching a folder, such as com.example.app . (6.05) partitioningBy A collector that splits items into two groups under the keys true and false (8.03) Pass by value Java copies argument values; for objects, it copies the reference. (2.01) Pattern A compiled regular expression in java.util.regex (8.01) Pattern matching Testing and taking apart values with instanceof and switch patterns. (3.05) Period An amount of calendar time in years, months and days. (7.04) Polymorphism Code written for a supertype working with any subtype's behaviour. (3.03) Primitive type One of the eight value types: int , long , double , boolean , char , byte , short , float . (1.02) Queue First in, first out: offer at the back, poll from the front. (4.02) Race condition A bug where the result depends on how threads' steps interleave. (6.04) Record A concise immutable data class with generated equals, hashCode and toString. (3.05) Recursion A method calling itself on a smaller problem. (2.04) Reference type A type whose variables hold references to objects. (1.02) Reflection Inspecting and using classes, fields, methods and constructors while the program runs. (7.03) Retention How long an annotation is kept: SOURCE, CLASS or RUNTIME (visible to reflection). (7.03) RoundingMode How BigDecimal rounds: HALF_UP, HALF_EVEN and others (8.04) Scanner The class that reads text input, such as from System.in . (1.04) Sealed type An interface or class that lists the only classes allowed to implement or extend it. (3.05) Set A collection without duplicates: HashSet , TreeSet , LinkedHashSet . (4.02) Stable sort A sort that keeps equal items in their original order. (4.03) Stack Last in, first out: push , pop , peek . (5.04) static Belonging to the class rather than to an instance. (3.02) Static nested class A class declared inside another with static ; it needs no object of the outer class. (7.01) Stream A pipeline of operations over a sequence of values. (6.02) StringBuilder A mutable buffer for building strings efficiently. (2.05) switch expression switch with - arms that produces a value. (1.05) synchronized Lets only one thread at a time run a block for the same lock. (6.04) teeing A collector that sends every item to two collectors and combines their results (8.03) Text block A multi-line string between """ delimiters. (1.04) thenCompose Chains a step that itself returns a CompletableFuture, without nesting futures (8.02) Thread An independent path of execution. (6.04) try-with-resources try (Resource r = ...) , which closes the resource automatically. (4.04) Type erasure Generic types being removed after compile-time checking. (4.01) Unchecked exception A RuntimeException , which need not be declared or caught. (4.04) var Declares a local variable whose type the compiler infers. (6.03) Virtual thread A cheap thread managed by the JVM, so one thread per waiting task is practical (8.02) Wildcard ? in a generic type: List<? extends Number . (4.01) Wrapper class The object version of a primitive: Integer , Double , Boolean ... (2.03) ZonedDateTime A date and time in a particular time zone. (7.04)

title: 1.01  What JavaScript Is and Running It
match: 1.01 What JavaScript Is and Running It
body: JavaScript is the language every web browser runs, and with Node.js it runs on servers and in tools too. This lesson explains where it runs, how it is executed, the console, and how TypeScript relates to it. The language of the web Every web browser contains a JavaScript engine. HTML describes a page, CSS styles it, and JavaScript makes it do things: respond to clicks, check forms, fetch data, draw, play games. Because every browser runs it, it is the most widely deployed programming language there is. JavaScript also runs outside the browser: Where Engine / runtime Used for --- --- --- Browsers V8 (Chrome, Edge), SpiderMonkey (Firefox), JavaScriptCore (Safari) Web pages and apps Node.js , Deno, Bun V8 or JavaScriptCore Servers, command-line tools, build tools Desktop apps Electron (VS Code, Discord, this site's desktop app) Apps built with web technology How it runs Like Python, JavaScript is not compiled ahead of time by you. The engine parses your code and runs it, compiling hot parts to machine code on the fly ( just-in-time compilation ), which makes modern JavaScript fast. A first program javascript console.log("Hello, Xenon!"); console.log("2 + 3 =", 2 + 3); console.log( 1, 2, 3 , { name: "Ada", age: 36 }); console.log prints its arguments separated by spaces; arrays and objects are shown in a readable form. Press Run to try it. Statements end with a semicolon. JavaScript inserts missing semicolons automatically in most places, but the rules have surprising corners, so this course always writes them. Running it yourself - In a browser : open the developer tools (F12), choose the Console tab, and type JavaScript; it runs on the current page. - With Node.js : install it from nodejs.org, save code in hello.js , and run node hello.js . Running node alone opens an interactive prompt. An editor such as VS Code understands JavaScript out of the box and shows errors as you type. Comments javascript // a comment to the end of the line / a comment over several lines / const answer = 42; // the meaning of everything JavaScript and TypeScript TypeScript is JavaScript with types added: you write let count: number = 0 , and a checker tells you before running that count = "ten" is a mistake. TypeScript compiles to plain JavaScript by removing the types, so it runs everywhere JavaScript does. Most large JavaScript projects today are written in TypeScript. This course teaches JavaScript first (milestones 1-4), then TypeScript on top (milestone 5); everything you learn about JavaScript applies to TypeScript unchanged. Check yourself quiz ? Besides web browsers, where does JavaScript run? - Nowhere: outside the browser the code must be rewritten in another language - Only on servers, and only after you compile it ahead of time to machine code + On servers and in tools via Node.js, Deno or Bun, and in Electron desktop apps - Only inside code editors such as VS Code, which ship their own engine Node.js (and Deno or Bun) run JavaScript on servers and in tools, and Electron apps are built from it. Nobody compiles it ahead of time: the engine compiles hot code on the fly. ? What does TypeScript add to JavaScript? - A faster engine that browsers use instead of V8 + Types that a checker verifies before the program runs - A new language that browsers run instead of JavaScript - Automatic semicolons, so you never have to write them TypeScript adds static types checked before running. It compiles to plain JavaScript by removing the types, so it runs wherever JavaScript runs. ? What does console.log("1 + 1 =", 1 + 1) print? - 1 + 1 = 1 + 1 - "1 + 1 =" 2 + 1 + 1 = 2 - 1 + 1 =2 The text is printed as it is (without quotes), then a space, then the value of the expression.

title: 1.02  Values, Variables and Types
body: JavaScript's types - number, string, boolean, undefined, null, bigint, symbol and objects - declaring variables with const and let (and why not var), typeof, and how values are copied or shared. Declaring variables javascript const name = "Ada"; // cannot be reassigned let score = 10; // can be reassigned score = score + 5; console.log(name, score); Use const by default and let only when the variable really must change. The old var has confusing rules (function scope, hoisting): never use it in new code. const means the name cannot be pointed at another value. If the value is an object or array, its contents can still change: javascript const list = 1, 2 ; list.push(3); // fine: the same array, changed console.log(list); // list = ; // TypeError: Assignment to constant variable The types Type Examples Notes --- --- --- number 42 , 3.14 , -0 , NaN , Infinity One type for whole and fractional numbers (64-bit floats) bigint 9007199254740993n Arbitrarily large whole numbers string "hi" , 'hi' , hi Text boolean true , false undefined undefined A variable with no value yet, a missing property null null "Deliberately nothing" symbol Symbol("id") Unique keys (advanced) object { a: 1 } , 1, 2 , functions, dates Everything else javascript console.log(typeof 42, typeof "x", typeof true, typeof undefined, typeof 10n); console.log(typeof {}, typeof , typeof null, typeof function () {}); Two famous oddities: typeof null is "object" (a historical bug that cannot be fixed), and arrays are objects too; use Array.isArray(x) to check for an array. Numbers All numbers are 64-bit floating point, so whole numbers are exact only up to Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (about 9 × 10¹⁵), and decimal fractions are approximate ( 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004 , exactly as in Python's lesson 1.04). Invalid arithmetic gives NaN ("not a number"), which is not even equal to itself: test it with Number.isNaN(x) . undefined and null javascript let pending; console.log(pending); // undefined: declared but not assigned const user = { name: "Ada" }; console.log(user.email); // undefined: no such property const selected = null; // "no selection", on purpose Treat undefined as "not set" and null as "set to nothing". Both are falsy, and x == null is true for both (one of the few good uses of == , lesson 1.03). Copying and sharing Primitive values (numbers, strings, booleans...) are copied; objects and arrays are shared by reference: javascript let a = 5; let b = a; b += 1; // a is still 5 const p = { x: 1 }; const q = p; q.x = 99; // p.x is also 99: one object, two names const r = { ...p }; // a (shallow) copy r.x = 0; console.log(a, p.x, r.x); Naming Variables and functions use camelCase ; classes use PascalCase ; constants that are true configuration values are often UPPER_CASE . Names are case-sensitive. Check yourself quiz ? When should you use let instead of const ? - Whenever the value is an array or object you plan to change + Only when the variable itself must be reassigned later - For every variable declared inside a loop or a function - Whenever the value is a number rather than a string Use const by default and let only for a name that must point at a new value. A const array or object can still have its contents changed. ? What does typeof null give? - "null" - "undefined" + "object" - "boolean" It gives "object", a historical quirk that cannot be fixed. To check for null, compare with === null . ? After const a = 1 ; const b = a; b.push(2); , what is a ? - 1 - 2 - an error, because a is const + 1, 2 b names the same array; const only stops a from being reassigned, not the array from changing.

title: What type is it?
body: Write two functions: javascript function describeType(value) { } // "null", "array", or what typeof says function copyWith(obj, key, value) { } // a NEW object: obj's properties plus key set to value; obj unchanged describeType(null) is "null" and describeType( 1 ) is "array" (fixing typeof 's two oddities); everything else is typeof value .

title: 1.03  Operators, Comparisons and Conversions
body: Arithmetic and assignment operators, strict versus loose equality, truthiness, the logical operators and the nullish operators ?? and ?., and converting between strings and numbers without surprises. Arithmetic Operator Meaning Example --- --- --- + - / Add, subtract, multiply, divide 7 / 2 is 3.5 % Remainder (keeps the sign of the left side) -7 % 3 is -1 Power 2 10 is 1024 ++ , -- Add or subtract 1 count++ += , -= , = , ... Update total += price Whole-number division is Math.trunc(a / b) (towards zero) or Math.floor(a / b) (down). Note % differs from Python for negative numbers. Strict equality Always compare with === and !== : equal value and type. javascript console.log(1 === 1, 1 === "1", "a" === "a"); // true false true console.log(1 == "1", 0 == "", null == undefined); // true true true: loose equality converts types Loose == converts its operands with complicated rules ( == false is true). The one common use is x == null , which is true for both null and undefined . Objects (including arrays) are equal only if they are the same object: 1 === 1 is false . Truthiness In conditions, these values are falsy : false , 0 , -0 , 0n , "" , null , undefined , NaN . Everything else is truthy, including "0" , "false" , and {} . Logical operators && and return one of their operands , not necessarily true or false : javascript console.log("" "default"); // "default": the first truthy value console.log("Ada" && "admin"); // "admin": the first falsy value, or the last console.log(!0, !!"text"); // true true: !! converts to a boolean a b is often used for defaults, but it replaces every falsy value, including 0 and "" . The nullish operators only react to null and undefined : javascript const volume = 0; console.log(volume 50); // 50: wrong, 0 was a real value console.log(volume ?? 50); // 0: ?? only replaces null and undefined const user = { profile: null }; console.log(user.profile?.email); // undefined instead of a TypeError console.log(user.settings?.theme ?? "light"); ?. (optional chaining) stops and gives undefined if the left side is null or undefined . Converting Want Use Watch out --- --- --- Number from text Number("42") Number("") is 0 ; Number("4x") is NaN Whole number from text parseInt("42px", 10) Reads until the first non-digit: 42 ; always pass the base 10 Decimal from text parseFloat("3.5kg") 3.5 Text from a number String(42) , ${42} , (3.14159).toFixed(2) toFixed returns a string Boolean Boolean(x) or !!x Truthiness rules above + with a string concatenates : "5" + 3 is "53" , while "5" - 3 is 2 . Convert explicitly before doing arithmetic on text from forms or files. Check yourself quiz ? Why should you prefer === to == ? - === also compares the contents of arrays, while == does not - == only works on numbers, so text needs === + === compares without converting types, so its result is predictable - == assigns a value, while === compares two values === needs equal value and equal type, so 1 === "1" is false. == converts its operands with complicated rules, and neither compares the contents of arrays. ? What is the difference between a b and a ?? b ? - replaces only null / undefined ; ?? any falsy a (even 0 , "" ) + replaces any falsy a (even 0 , "" ); ?? only null / undefined - They are the same, except that ?? also works on objects - ?? always returns a boolean, while returns one of its operands gives b for every falsy a, so 0 50 is 50. ?? gives b only for null and undefined, so 0 ?? 50 stays 0. ? What is "10" + 5 - 5 ? - 10 - "105" - NaN + 100 "10" + 5 is the string "105"; subtracting converts it to the number 105, giving 100.

title: 1.04  Strings and Template Literals
body: Working with text - template literals with ${} expressions, indexing and length, the most useful string methods, splitting and joining, padding and formatting numbers, and Unicode characters. Three kinds of quotes javascript const single = 'It\'s'; const double = "She said \"hi\""; const name = "Ada"; const template = Hello, ${name}! 2 + 3 = ${2 + 3} ; console.log(single, double, template); Template literals (backticks) insert any expression with ${...} and can span several lines. Use them whenever text and values are mixed. Reading strings javascript const word = "JavaScript"; console.log(word.length, word 0 , word.at(-1), word.slice(4), word.slice(0, 4), word.slice(-6)); at(-1) counts from the end; slice(start, end) takes a part (end not included; negative values count from the end). Strings are immutable : methods return new strings. Useful methods Method Example Gives --- --- --- toUpperCase , toLowerCase "Ada".toUpperCase() "ADA" trim , trimStart , trimEnd " hi ".trim() "hi" includes , startsWith , endsWith "photo.png".endsWith(".png") true indexOf "banana".indexOf("na") 2 ( -1 if absent) split "a,b,c".split(",") "a", "b", "c" replace , replaceAll "a-b-c".replaceAll("-", "+") "a+b+c" repeat "ab".repeat(3) "ababab" padStart , padEnd "7".padStart(3, "0") "007" replace with a string replaces only the first match; use replaceAll (or a regular expression with the g flag, lesson 7.01) for all. Joining a list: "a", "b" .join(", ") is "a, b" . Formatting numbers javascript const price = 1234.5; console.log(price.toFixed(2)); // "1234.50" console.log(price.toLocaleString("en-US")); // "1,234.5" console.log(price.toLocaleString("en-US", { style: "currency", currency: "USD" })); console.log(String(5).padStart(3, " "), (0.256 100).toFixed(1) + "%"); Intl.NumberFormat and toLocaleString format numbers, currencies and dates for a language and region. Comparing strings < and compare strings by character codes: "Zebra" < "apple" is true because capitals come first. For human sorting, use a.localeCompare(b) (lesson 2.02 uses it with sort ). Unicode JavaScript strings are UTF-16 (the Win32 course's lesson 1.02 explains the encoding). "é".length is 1, but an emoji such as "😀".length is 2 , because it is stored as two code units. To count or walk characters properly, use ...text or for (const ch of text) , which handle such pairs: javascript const text = "hi 😀"; console.log(text.length, ...text .length); // 5 4 Check yourself quiz ? How do you put the value of total into a string? - With double quotes: "Total: ${total}" - With a template literal: Total: {total} + With a template literal: Total: ${total} - With single quotes: 'Total: ${total}' Only backtick strings (template literals) insert ${...} expressions; in ordinary quotes ${total} is just text, and without the $ nothing is inserted. ? Why is "😀".length 2? + The emoji is stored as two UTF-16 code units (a surrogate pair) - length counts bytes, and the emoji takes two bytes - length always counts one extra for the hidden end-of-text marker - Emoji count as two characters so that they display wider JavaScript strings are UTF-16 and length counts code units; characters outside the basic range need a pair. ...text .length counts real characters. ? What does "a-b-c".replace("-", "+") give? - "a+b+c" + "a+b-c" - "a-b-c" - "a", "b", "c" replace with a string argument changes only the first occurrence; replaceAll changes them all.

title: 1.05  Control Flow
body: Making decisions and repeating work - if and else, the conditional operator, switch, for loops in their three forms, while and do-while, break and continue, and labelled loops. if and else javascript const temperature = 18; if (temperature < 0) { console.log("Freezing"); } else if (temperature < 15) { console.log("Cold"); } else { console.log("Mild or warm"); } Conditions go in parentheses, blocks in braces. Braces are optional for a single statement, but always writing them avoids a classic bug when a second line is added later. The conditional operator chooses between two values: javascript const age = 20; const label = age = 18 ? "adult" : "minor"; console.log(label); switch switch compares one value against several cases with === : javascript function dayType(day) { switch (day) { case "Sat": case "Sun": return "weekend"; case "Mon": return "start of the week"; default: return "weekday"; } } console.log(dayType("Sun"), dayType("Wed")); Without return or break , execution falls through into the next case. That is useful for grouping cases ( "Sat" and "Sun" above) and a bug when forgotten. for loops javascript for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) { // counting console.log("round", i); } const fruits = "apple", "pear", "plum" ; for (const fruit of fruits) { // the VALUES of an array (or string, Map, Set...) console.log(fruit); } const scores = { ada: 95, grace: 88 }; for (const key in scores) { // the KEYS of an object console.log(key, scores key ); } Use for...of for arrays and strings; for...in is for object keys only (on arrays it gives the indexes as strings, which is rarely what you want). To get indexes with for...of : for (const i, fruit of fruits.entries()) . while and do...while javascript let n = 27; let steps = 0; while (n !== 1) { n = n % 2 === 0 ? n / 2 : 3 n + 1; steps++; } console.log(steps); let attempt = 0; do { attempt++; } while (attempt < 3); // the body runs at least once console.log(attempt); break and continue break leaves the loop; continue skips to the next round. In nested loops, a label says which loop to leave: javascript outer: for (let row = 0; row < 3; row++) { for (let col = 0; col < 3; col++) { if (row col === 2) { console.log("found at", row, col); break outer; } } } Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference between for...of and for...in ? - for...of gives the keys of an object; for...in gives the values of an array + for...of gives the values of an array (any iterable); for...in gives object keys - for...of counts with an index; for...in walks the values of any array - There is none: both give the values of an array in order Use for...of for arrays and strings; for...in is for object keys (on an array it gives the indexes as strings). ? What happens when a switch case has no break or return ? - The switch ends after that case anyway - JavaScript reports a syntax error - The default case runs next + Execution falls through into the next case Without break or return, execution carries on into the following case's code. That is handy for grouping cases and a bug when forgotten. ? How many times does the body of do { } while (false); run? + 1 - 0 - forever - it is a syntax error A do...while loop checks its condition after the body, so the body always runs at least once.

title: A receipt printer
body: Write formatReceipt(items, tipPercent) , which turns a list of items into the text of a receipt: javascript formatReceipt( { name: "Green tea", price: 2.5, qty: 2 }, { name: "Chocolate cake", price: 4.25, qty: 1 }, , 10) Green tea x2 5.00 Chocolate cake 4.25 --------------------------- Subtotal 9.25 Tip 10% 0.93 Total 10.18 Rules: - Each item line is the name, followed by x<qty when the quantity is more than 1, padded on the right to 19 characters, then the line total (price × qty) with 2 decimals right-aligned in 8 characters. Names longer than 19 characters (with the quantity) are cut to 18 characters plus … . - Then a line of 27 dashes, then Subtotal , Tip <percent % and Total lines in the same layout. The tip is the subtotal × percent / 100, rounded to cents ; the total is subtotal + tip. - With a tip of 0, the tip line is left out. - To avoid floating-point errors, work in whole cents: Math.round(price 100) . - Items with a quantity of 0 or less are skipped. If no items are left, the receipt is just No items . - Lines are joined with \n (no newline at the end).

title: 2.01  Functions
body: Function declarations, function expressions and arrow functions, parameters with defaults, rest parameters and spread, returning values, functions as values, and callbacks. Three ways to write a function javascript function area(width, height) { // declaration: usable anywhere in its scope return width height; } const perimeter = function (w, h) { // expression assigned to a variable return 2 (w + h); }; const square = x = x x; // arrow function: short form for one expression const describe = (w, h) = { const a = area(w, h); return ${w}x${h} has area ${a} ; }; console.log(area(3, 4), perimeter(3, 4), square(5), describe(2, 3)); Arrow functions with one expression return it automatically; with braces they need return . To return an object literal from a one-line arrow, wrap it in parentheses: () = ({ ok: true }) . A function without return returns undefined . Parameters Missing arguments are undefined ; extra ones are ignored. Default values apply when an argument is undefined : javascript function greet(name, greeting = "Hello") { return ${greeting}, ${name}! ; } console.log(greet("Ada"), greet("Ada", "Hi")); A rest parameter collects any number of arguments into an array; spread does the reverse: javascript function total(...numbers) { return numbers.reduce((sum, n) = sum + n, 0); } const prices = 3, 4, 5 ; console.log(total(1, 2), total(...prices), Math.max(...prices)); For functions with many options, pass one object and destructure it (lesson 2.03): function connect({ host, port = 443, timeout = 10 }) . Calls then name every option. Functions are values Functions can be stored, passed and returned like any value. A function passed to another function is a callback : javascript function repeat(times, action) { for (let i = 0; i < times; i++) action(i); } repeat(3, i = console.log("round", i)); const operations = { double: x = x 2, negate: x = -x }; console.log(operations.double(21), operations "negate" (5)); The array methods of lesson 2.02 ( map , filter , sort ) and all asynchronous code (milestone 4) are built on callbacks. Pure functions A pure function's result depends only on its arguments, and it changes nothing outside itself. Pure functions are the easiest to test and reuse; keep reading files, printing and changing shared data at the edges of a program, and the logic in pure functions in between. Hoisting Function declarations are hoisted: they can be called before the line that defines them. Functions assigned to const cannot, because the variable does not exist yet ("temporal dead zone"). Define helpers before use, or rely on declarations deliberately. Check yourself quiz ? What does an arrow function with braces return if its body has no return statement? + undefined - The value of its last expression - null - The arguments it was called with With braces the body needs an explicit return ; without one the function returns undefined . Only the one-expression form without braces returns its value automatically. ? What is the difference between a rest parameter and spread? - Rest expands an array into separate arguments; spread collects arguments into an array - They are two names for the same thing and can be swapped freely + Rest collects arguments into an array in a definition; spread expands an array in a call - Rest copies an array deeply; spread only copies the top level function total(...numbers) gathers the arguments into an array; total(...prices) spreads an array out into separate arguments. ? What does (() = { value: 1 })() return? - { value: 1 } - 1 - an error + undefined The braces are a function body with a label "value", not an object; wrap an object in parentheses to return it.

title: Functions that take functions
body: Write three functions: javascript function average(...numbers) { } // the average of any number of arguments; 0 when there are none function applyTimes(f, times, start) { } // f applied times times: applyTimes(x = x 2, 3, 1) is 8 function compose(...fns) { } // a function that applies fns right to left: compose(f, g)(x) is f(g(x)) compose() with no functions returns a function that gives back its argument unchanged.

title: 2.02  Arrays and Array Methods
body: Creating and changing arrays, and the methods that make array code short and clear - map, filter, reduce, find, some and every, includes, sort with a compare function, slice versus splice, flat and flatMap, and which methods change the array. Basics javascript const fruits = "apple", "pear" ; fruits.push("plum"); // add at the end fruits.unshift("fig"); // add at the start const last = fruits.pop(); // remove from the end console.log(fruits, last, fruits.length, fruits.includes("pear"), fruits.indexOf("pear")); Transforming without loops Method Returns --- --- map(f) A new array of f(item) for each item filter(f) A new array of the items where f(item) is truthy reduce(f, start) One value built up from all items find(f) / findIndex(f) The first matching item / its index ( undefined / -1 if none) some(f) / every(f) Whether any / all items match forEach(f) Nothing: just runs f on each item javascript const orders = { item: "tea", qty: 2, price: 2.5 }, { item: "cake", qty: 1, price: 4 }, { item: "mug", qty: 3, price: 8 }, ; const totals = orders.map(o = o.qty o.price); const big = orders.filter(o = o.qty o.price 5).map(o = o.item); const sum = totals.reduce((acc, t) = acc + t, 0); console.log(totals, big, sum, orders.find(o = o.item === "cake"), orders.some(o = o.qty 2)); Chaining filter then map then reduce reads like a description of the result. The callbacks also receive the index as a second argument: map((item, i) = ...) . Sorting sort() changes the array and, without arguments, compares items as strings : 10, 9, 1 .sort() gives 1, 10, 9 . Always give numbers a compare function, which returns a negative number when a comes first: javascript const nums = 10, 9, 1, 100 ; console.log( ...nums .sort((a, b) = a - b)); // ascending const people = { name: "bob", age: 30 }, { name: "Ada", age: 36 }, { name: "carol", age: 30 } ; people.sort((a, b) = a.age - b.age a.name.localeCompare(b.name)); console.log(people.map(p = p.name)); // by age, then name a.localeCompare(b) compares text the way people expect. chains criteria: if the first difference is 0, the second decides. toSorted() returns a sorted copy instead of changing the array. Changing versus copying Changes the array Returns a new array --- --- push , pop , shift , unshift map , filter , concat splice(start, deleteCount, ...items) slice(start, end) sort , reverse , fill toSorted , toReversed , with(i, value) Copy an array with ...arr or arr.slice() . Code that does not change its inputs is easier to reason about: prefer the right-hand column. Nested arrays javascript console.log( 1, 2 , 3 , .flat()); // 1, 2, 3 console.log( "a b", "c" .flatMap(s = s.split(" "))); // "a", "b", "c" const grid = Array.from({ length: 2 }, () = Array(3).fill(0)); // 2 separate rows of 3 zeros Array.from({ length: n }, (_, i) = ...) builds an array of n computed items. Check yourself quiz ? What does 10, 9, 1 .sort() give? - 1, 9, 10 , because numbers are sorted from smallest to largest - 10, 9, 1 , because the array is already in order + 1, 10, 9 , because without a compare function items are compared as strings - 9, 10, 1 , because sort only swaps neighbouring items once As strings, "10" comes before "9" (the first character "1" is smaller than "9"). Pass (a, b) = a - b to sort numbers. ? Which of map , splice , slice and sort change the array they are called on? - map and sort - slice and splice - Only splice + splice and sort splice and sort change the array in place; map and slice return new arrays. Use toSorted() or ...arr .sort() for a sorted copy. ? What is 1, 2, 3, 4 .filter(n = n % 2).map(n = n 10) ? - 20, 40 + 10, 30 - 10, 20, 30, 40 - 40 n % 2 is truthy for odd numbers, so 1 and 3 remain, then each is multiplied by 10.

title: 2.03  Objects and Destructuring
body: Objects as collections of named values - creating and reading them, dot and bracket access, adding and deleting properties, shorthand and computed names, Object.keys, values and entries, spread and copying, and destructuring objects and arrays. Object literals javascript const book = { title: "Dune", author: "Frank Herbert", year: 1965, "page count": 412, // names with spaces need quotes }; console.log(book.title, book "page count" ); book.rating = 5; // add delete book.year; // remove console.log(book, "year" in book, book.missing); // undefined for missing properties Use dot access for fixed names and brackets when the name is in a variable: book field . Shorthand and computed names javascript const title = "Dune"; const year = 1965; const field = "genre"; const entry = { title, year, field : "sci-fi", describe() { return ${this.title} (${this.year}) ; } }; console.log(entry, entry.describe()); { title } is short for { title: title } ; field uses the variable's value as the name; describe() {...} is a method. Looping over an object javascript const scores = { ada: 95, grace: 88, linus: 72 }; console.log(Object.keys(scores), Object.values(scores)); for (const name, score of Object.entries(scores)) { console.log( ${name}: ${score} ); } const curved = Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(scores).map(( n, s ) = n, s + 5 )); console.log(curved); Object.entries and Object.fromEntries turn an object into key, value pairs and back, so array methods can transform objects. Copying and merging Spread copies properties into a new object; later properties win: javascript const defaults = { theme: "light", size: 12 }; const user = { size: 14 }; const settings = { ...defaults, ...user, wrap: true }; console.log(settings); Spread makes a shallow copy: nested objects are still shared. structuredClone(obj) makes a deep copy. Destructuring Destructuring takes values out of objects and arrays into variables: javascript const person = { name: "Ada", age: 36, address: { city: "London" } }; const { name, age: years, email = "none", address: { city } } = person; console.log(name, years, email, city); const first, second = 0, ...others = 10, 20, 30, 40 ; console.log(first, second, others); let a = 1, b = 2; a, b = b, a ; // swap console.log(a, b); age: years renames; = "none" gives a default when the property is undefined ; nested patterns reach inside. It is especially useful in parameters: javascript function formatUser({ name, age, city = "unknown" }) { return ${name}, ${age}, ${city} ; } console.log(formatUser({ name: "Grace", age: 85 })); Check yourself quiz ? When must you use brackets instead of a dot to read a property? - Whenever the property holds an array or a nested object + When the name is in a variable or is not an identifier, like "page count" - Only when the property might be missing, to avoid a TypeError - When the object was created with spread rather than as a literal book field uses the value of field as the name, and book "page count" reaches a name with a space; for fixed, simple names a dot works. ? Is { ...obj } a deep copy? - Yes: every nested object is copied as well - No: it is the same object under a second name - Yes, but only for objects whose values are all arrays + No, a shallow copy: nested objects are still shared Spread makes a new object with the same top-level properties, so nested objects are shared between the copy and the original; structuredClone(obj) makes a deep copy. ? What is x after const { a: x = 5 } = { a: null }; ? - 5 + null - undefined - an error Defaults apply only when the value is undefined; null is a real value.

title: Objects and destructuring
body: Write three functions: javascript function mergeSettings(defaults, user) { } // a new object: defaults overridden by user; neither input changes function invert(obj) { } // swap keys and values: { a: "x" } becomes { x: "a" } function summary({ name, age, city = "unknown", ...rest }) { } summary returns a string like "Ada (36) from London, 2 more fields" . When age is missing, leave out (36) ; the count is the number of other fields, with field for 1 and fields otherwise; when there are none, leave out the comma part. mergeSettings also merges one level deeper: if both have a plain object (not an array) under the same key, such as colors , the result has both sets of inner properties.

title: 2.04  Scope and Closures
body: Where variables live - block scope with let and const, function scope, the scope chain, closures that remember variables, private state with closures, and the classic closure-in-a-loop bug that let fixes. Block scope let and const are visible only inside the block (the braces) where they are declared: javascript const x = "outer"; { const x = "inner"; // a different variable, hiding the outer one inside this block console.log(x); } console.log(x); for (let i = 0; i < 2; i++) { } // console.log(i); // ReferenceError: i only exists inside the loop When a name is used, JavaScript looks in the current block, then the enclosing ones, then the function, then the module and global scope: the scope chain . Closures A function remembers the variables of the scope where it was created , even after that scope has finished. A function together with those variables is a closure : javascript function makeCounter() { let count = 0; return () = ++count; } const a = makeCounter(); const b = makeCounter(); console.log(a(), a(), a(), b()); // 1 2 3 1: separate counts count cannot be reached from outside except through the returned function: closures give private state . Modules of functions Closures can bundle several functions around shared private data: javascript function createStack() { const items = ; return { push(x) { items.push(x); }, pop() { return items.pop(); }, get size() { return items.length; }, }; } const s = createStack(); s.push(1); s.push(2); console.log(s.pop(), s.size); // 2 1: items itself is unreachable Classes (lesson 3.01) with private fields do the same job; both styles are common. The loop bug With var , there is one variable for the whole loop, so every callback sees its final value. let creates a new binding for each iteration: javascript const fns = ; for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) fns.push(() = i); console.log(fns.map(f = f())); // 0, 1, 2 ; with var it would be 3, 3, 3 Functions that make functions Closures let you configure a function once and use it many times: javascript const multiplier = n = x = x n; const double = multiplier(2); const triple = multiplier(3); console.log(double(5), triple(5)); function once(fn) { let done = false, result; return (...args) = { if (!done) { done = true; result = fn(...args); } return result; }; } const init = once(() = { console.log("initialising"); return 42; }); console.log(init(), init()); // prints "initialising" only once Check yourself quiz ? What is a closure? - A function that has finished running and whose variables were thrown away - A function that can only be called once + A function together with the variables of the scope it was created in - A block of braces that hides the variables declared inside it A closure keeps using the variables of the scope where it was created, even after that scope has finished, which is how makeCounter keeps a private count. ? Why does let fix the closure-in-a-loop problem that var has? + let creates a new binding for each iteration, so each callback keeps its own value - let copies the value into the callback when the callback is created - let makes the loop wait until each callback has run - let variables cannot change, so the callbacks all see the first value With var there is one variable for the whole loop, so every callback sees its final value; let gives each round its own i . ? After let n = 1; const show = () = n; n = 2; , what does show() return? - 1 + 2 - undefined - an error A closure remembers the variable, not its value at the time it was created.

title: Closures

Each wrapped function has its own count.

title: 2.05  Maps, Sets and JSON
body: Map for key-value data with any key type and reliable ordering, Set for unique values, when to use them instead of plain objects and arrays, grouping with Map and Object.groupBy, and converting data to and from JSON text. Map A Map stores key-value pairs. Unlike a plain object, its keys can be any value (numbers, objects), it remembers insertion order, and it has a size: javascript const stock = new Map(); stock.set("apples", 4).set("pears", 0); stock.set("apples", stock.get("apples") + 1); console.log(stock.get("apples"), stock.has("plums"), stock.size); for (const fruit, count of stock) console.log(fruit, count); stock.delete("pears"); console.log( ...stock.keys() , Object.fromEntries(stock)); Counting with a Map: javascript const words = "the cat and the hat".split(" "); const counts = new Map(); for (const w of words) counts.set(w, (counts.get(w) ?? 0) + 1); console.log(counts); Use a Map when keys are data (user names, ids) and change at run time; use a plain object for a fixed set of named fields (a record). Set A Set holds unique values with fast has : javascript const tags = new Set( "js", "web", "js" ); tags.add("ts"); console.log(tags.size, tags.has("web"), ...tags ); const unique = ...new Set( 3, 1, 3, 2, 1 ) ; console.log(unique); const a = new Set( 1, 2, 3 ), b = new Set( 2, 3, 4 ); console.log( ...a .filter(x = b.has(x))); // intersection Recent engines also have a.union(b) , a.intersection(b) and a.difference(b) . Objects in Maps and Sets are compared by identity : new Set( {}, {} ).size is 2. Grouping Object.groupBy (and Map.groupBy ) group items by a key function: javascript const people = { name: "Ada", team: "red" }, { name: "Bob", team: "blue" }, { name: "Cy", team: "red" } ; const byTeam = Object.groupBy(people, p = p.team); console.log(Object.keys(byTeam), byTeam.red.map(p = p.name)); In older environments, the same is a few lines with reduce or a loop and a Map. JSON JSON is the text format of web APIs, written exactly like JavaScript literals (with double-quoted keys): javascript const order = { id: 7, items: "tea", "cake" , paid: true, note: null }; const text = JSON.stringify(order); console.log(text); console.log(JSON.stringify(order, null, 2)); // pretty-printed const back = JSON.parse(text); console.log(back.items 1 , back.paid); JSON has strings, numbers, booleans, null , arrays and objects. undefined and functions are left out, Date objects become strings, and Maps and Sets become {} : convert them first ( Object.fromEntries(map) , ...set ). JSON.parse throws a SyntaxError on invalid text (lesson 3.03 shows how to handle it). Check yourself quiz ? When is a Map a better choice than a plain object? - When the data is a record with a fixed set of named fields + When the keys are data that change at run time or are not strings - When you want to turn the data straight into JSON with JSON.stringify - When every value has the same type Map keys can be any value, it keeps insertion order and has size . A record with fixed fields is a plain object, and a Map does not survive JSON.stringify. ? What does JSON.stringify do with a Map? - It writes the entries as an object of keys and values - It writes the entries as an array of key, value pairs - It throws a TypeError, because Maps cannot be converted + It writes {} , so the entries are lost Maps (and Sets) become {} . Convert first with Object.fromEntries(map) (or ...set for a Set). ? What is new Set("hello").size ? - 5 - 1 + 4 - an error A string is iterable, giving h, e, l, l, o; the set keeps the 4 distinct letters.

title: A gradebook
body: Write gradebook(records) , which turns a list of raw score records into a report object. Each record is { student, subject, score } : javascript gradebook( { student: "Ada", subject: "maths", score: 92 }, { student: "Bob", subject: "maths", score: 61 }, { student: "Ada", subject: "art", score: 78 }, { student: "Bob", subject: "art", score: 85 }, { student: "Cy", subject: "maths", score: 47 }, ) returns javascript { students: { name: "Ada", average: 85, grade: "B", subjects: { maths: 92, art: 78 } }, { name: "Bob", average: 73, grade: "C", subjects: { maths: 61, art: 85 } }, { name: "Cy", average: 47, grade: "F", subjects: { maths: 47 } }, , subjects: { maths: { average: 66.67, best: "Ada" }, art: { average: 81.5, best: "Bob" } }, top: "Ada", } Rules: - Clean the data first : skip records whose score is not a number between 0 and 100 (inclusive), or whose student or subject is not a non-empty string. Trim names and subjects; subjects are compared in lower case ( "Maths" and "maths" are the same subject, reported as "maths" ). - If the same student has several records for one subject, the last one counts. - A student's average is the mean of their subject scores, rounded to 2 decimals ( Math.round(x 100) / 100 ). Grades from the unrounded average: 90 and above A , 80 B , 70 C , 60 D , below 60 F . - students is sorted by average, highest first; ties by name alphabetically. subjects inside each student keeps first-seen order. - In the report's subjects , keys appear in first-seen order; average is the mean of that subject's scores rounded to 2 decimals, and best is the student with the highest score (on a tie, the one whose name comes first alphabetically). - top is the first student in students , or null when there are none. - The function must not change records .

title: 3.01  Classes
body: Defining classes with constructors, fields and methods, private fields with , getters and setters, static members, inheritance with extends and super, overriding methods, instanceof, and when a plain object or function is simpler. A class A class describes a kind of object: the data each one holds and what it can do. javascript class Account { owner; // a public field balance = 0; // a private field: only code inside the class can use it constructor(owner, opening = 0) { this.owner = owner; this.deposit(opening); } deposit(amount) { if (amount < 0) throw new RangeError("deposit must not be negative"); this. balance += amount; return this; // returning this allows chaining } get balance() { // read like a property: acc.balance return this. balance; } toString() { return ${this.owner}: ${this. balance.toFixed(2)} ; } } const acc = new Account("Ada", 10); acc.deposit(5).deposit(2.5); console.log(acc.balance, String(acc)); // acc. balance // SyntaxError outside the class new Account(...) creates an object and runs constructor with this set to it. Inside methods, this is the object the method was called on. Getters, setters and static members javascript class Temperature { celsius; constructor(celsius) { this. celsius = celsius; } get fahrenheit() { return this. celsius 9 / 5 + 32; } set fahrenheit(f) { this. celsius = (f - 32) 5 / 9; } static fromFahrenheit(f) { const t = new Temperature(0); t.fahrenheit = f; return t; } static count = 0; } const t = Temperature.fromFahrenheit(212); console.log(t.fahrenheit); t.fahrenheit = 32; console.log(t.fahrenheit); A setter runs code when a property is assigned, which is the place to validate. Static members belong to the class itself, not to each object: Temperature.fromFahrenheit , Math.max , Number.isInteger . Static factory methods like fromFahrenheit give alternative ways to build an object. Inheritance extends makes a class that starts with everything of another. The child's constructor must call super(...) before using this : javascript class Shape { constructor(name) { this.name = name; } area() { return 0; } describe() { return ${this.name} with area ${this.area().toFixed(1)} ; } } class Circle extends Shape { constructor(r) { super("circle"); this.r = r; } area() { return Math.PI this.r 2; } // overrides Shape's area } class Square extends Shape { constructor(side) { super("square"); this.side = side; } area() { return this.side 2; } describe() { return super.describe() + " (a square)"; } // extends the parent's version } const shapes = new Circle(1), new Square(2) ; for (const s of shapes) console.log(s.describe()); console.log(shapes 0 instanceof Circle, shapes 0 instanceof Shape, shapes 0 instanceof Square); describe in Shape calls this.area() , which runs the child's version: each object answers in its own way ( polymorphism ). When to use a class Use a class when many objects share behaviour and keep state that must stay consistent (a bank account, a game entity, a connection). For plain data, an object literal is enough; for a single operation, a function is enough. Prefer shallow hierarchies: one level of extends is common, three is usually a sign that composition (an object holding other objects) fits better. Check yourself quiz ? What does a in front of a field name, as in balance , mean? - The field is static: it belongs to the class, not to each object - The field is a number that cannot be changed after the constructor + The field is private: only code inside the class body can use it - The field is left out when the object is printed with console.log fields can be read and written only by code inside the class; acc. balance outside it is a SyntaxError. Static members are marked with static . ? Why must a subclass constructor call super() before it uses this ? + The parent's constructor sets up the object; this does not exist until it has run - super() copies the parent's methods onto the new object, one by one - It does not have to: super() may be called anywhere in the constructor - Calling super() later would run the parent's constructor twice In a class with extends , the object is created by the parent's constructor, so using this before super(...) throws a ReferenceError. ? A class Thing has static create() {} . How is it called? - new Thing().create() - Thing.prototype.create() + Thing.create() - create(Thing) Static members belong to the class itself, not to its instances.

title: A class with private state
body: Write a class Inventory that keeps item counts: javascript const inv = new Inventory(); inv.add("apple", 3).add("pear").add("apple", 2); // add(name, count = 1) returns this inv.remove("apple", 4); // returns true; false (and no change) if there are not enough inv.count("apple"); // 1; 0 for unknown items inv.total; // a getter: the sum of all counts (2 here) inv.names(); // names with a count above 0, sorted Inventory.from({ tea: 2, cake: 1 }); // a static factory building an Inventory from an object - The counts are stored in a private field, so inv.items and similar do not exist. - add and remove throw a RangeError when count is not a positive whole number. - An item whose count reaches 0 is removed completely. Then write class LimitedInventory extends Inventory , built with new LimitedInventory(max) , whose add throws a RangeError with the message full when the total would go above max ; otherwise it adds as usual.

title: 3.02  Prototypes and this
body: How JavaScript objects really share behaviour - the prototype chain under classes, Object.create, own versus inherited properties, the four rules for this, losing this when passing methods, and fixing it with arrow functions and bind. The prototype chain Every object has a hidden link to another object, its prototype . When a property is not found on an object, JavaScript looks on its prototype, then that object's prototype, and so on: the prototype chain . javascript const animal = { speak() { return ${this.name} makes a sound ; } }; const dog = Object.create(animal); // dog's prototype is animal dog.name = "Rex"; console.log(dog.speak()); // found on animal, run with this = dog console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(dog) === animal); console.log(Object.hasOwn(dog, "name"), Object.hasOwn(dog, "speak")); Classes are built on this: methods live once on ClassName.prototype , and every instance links to it. javascript class Point { constructor(x, y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; } length() { return Math.hypot(this.x, this.y); } } const p = new Point(3, 4); console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(p) === Point.prototype, Object.keys(p), p.length()); Object.keys shows only an object's own properties ( x , y ); length is inherited. Arrays get map from Array.prototype , and everything ends at Object.prototype , whose prototype is null . Never add methods to built-in prototypes ( Array.prototype.sum = ... ): it can clash with future versions of the language and with other code. What this is this is decided when a function is called , not where it is written: Call this --- --- obj.method() obj new Fn() the new object fn.call(x, ...) / fn.apply(x, ... ) / a bind(x) copy x fn() on its own undefined (in modules and classes) Arrow functions do not have their own this ; they use the this of the code around them. Losing this Taking a method out of its object and calling it later loses this . This happens whenever a method is passed as a callback: javascript class Timer { constructor() { this.ticks = 0; } tick() { this.ticks++; } } const timer = new Timer(); const f = timer.tick; try { f(); } catch (e) { console.log(e.constructor.name, e.message); } 1, 2, 3 .forEach(() = timer.tick()); // fix 1: an arrow function calling the method 1, 2 .forEach(timer.tick.bind(timer)); // fix 2: bind makes a copy with this fixed console.log(timer.ticks); A third fix is a class field holding an arrow function: tick = () = { this.ticks++; }; . Each instance then gets its own copy with this fixed, which is convenient for event handlers (milestone 6). call, apply and bind javascript function introduce(greeting, punctuation) { return ${greeting}, I am ${this.name}${punctuation} ; } const ada = { name: "Ada" }; console.log(introduce.call(ada, "Hi", "!")); console.log(introduce.apply(ada, "Hello", "." )); const adaIntro = introduce.bind(ada, "Hey"); console.log(adaIntro("?")); bind can also fix leading arguments, as "Hey" here. Check yourself quiz ? Where does a class's method live? - A copy is made on each instance when the constructor runs + Once on ClassName.prototype ; instances find it through the prototype chain - In a private field of each object, so Object.keys cannot see it - On the class itself, like a static method Methods are stored once on the prototype and every instance links to it, which is why Object.keys(p) shows only the instance's own fields. ? Why does setTimeout(obj.method, 100) often break? - setTimeout cannot call methods, only plain functions - The method runs before obj has finished being created - setTimeout makes a copy of obj, so changes are lost + The method is called later on its own, so this is not obj Passing obj.method hands over the function alone; called later without obj. in front, this is undefined. Pass () = obj.method() or obj.method.bind(obj) . ? Inside an arrow function defined in a class method, what is this ? - undefined + the same this as in the method - the arrow function - the global object Arrow functions have no this of their own; they use the surrounding one.

title: Prototypes and this
body: Write three functions: javascript function ownAndInherited(obj) { } // { own: ... , inherited: ... }: property names, each list sorted function bindMethods(obj) { } // binds every function-valued own property of obj to obj, in place; returns obj function later(obj, methodName) { } // a function that calls obj methodName with its arguments and the right this - ownAndInherited lists the enumerable own property names ( Object.keys ) and, separately, the enumerable names found on its prototype chain but not on the object itself (a for...in loop sees both). Each name appears once. - After bindMethods(obj) , const f = obj.method; f() works with this as obj . - later(obj, "greet") looks up the method when it is called , so replacing obj.greet afterwards changes what runs.

title: 3.03  Errors and Exceptions
body: Throwing and catching errors, the built-in error types, finally for clean-up, writing your own error classes, rethrowing what you cannot handle, error causes, validating input at the edges, and returning results instead of throwing. throw and try/catch When code cannot do its job, it throws an error. The error travels up through the calling functions until a try / catch handles it; if none does, the program stops with the message. javascript function parseAge(text) { const age = Number(text); if (!Number.isInteger(age)) throw new TypeError( "${text}" is not a whole number ); if (age < 0 age 150) throw new RangeError( age ${age} is out of range ); return age; } for (const input of "42", "abc", "-5" ) { try { console.log("age:", parseAge(input)); } catch (err) { console.log( ${err.name}: ${err.message} ); } } Always throw Error objects (or subclasses), never strings: they carry a name , a message and a stack showing where they came from. Built-in error types Type Thrown when --- --- TypeError A value has the wrong type: calling something that is not a function, reading a property of undefined RangeError A number is outside the allowed range SyntaxError Code or JSON.parse input is not valid ReferenceError A variable does not exist finally A finally block runs whether or not an error happened, even after return . It is the place for clean-up: javascript function withLog(task) { console.log("start"); try { return task(); } finally { console.log("end"); // runs before the value is returned, or while the error travels on } } console.log(withLog(() = 7)); try { withLog(() = { throw new Error("boom"); }); } catch (e) { console.log("caught", e.message); } Your own error classes Subclass Error so callers can tell your errors apart with instanceof : javascript class ValidationError extends Error { constructor(field, message) { super(message); this.name = "ValidationError"; this.field = field; } } function checkUser(user) { if (!user.email?.includes("@")) throw new ValidationError("email", "email needs an @"); return user; } try { checkUser({ email: "nope" }); } catch (err) { if (err instanceof ValidationError) console.log( bad ${err.field}: ${err.message} ); else throw err; // not ours: rethrow } Catch only what you can handle. A catch that swallows every error also hides bugs, like a typo that throws ReferenceError . Check the type and rethrow the rest. When wrapping a low-level error in a clearer one, keep the original as its cause : javascript function loadConfig(text) { try { return JSON.parse(text); } catch (err) { throw new Error("config file is not valid JSON", { cause: err }); } } try { loadConfig("{oops"); } catch (e) { console.log(e.message, "<-", e.cause.name); } Throwing or returning Throw for situations the caller usually cannot continue from. When failure is an ordinary outcome (a search that finds nothing, a user typing a bad value), returning null or a result object such as { ok: false, error: "..." } is often clearer than making every caller write try . Validate input once, at the edge where it enters the program, so inner functions can trust their arguments. Check yourself quiz ? Why throw new Error("...") instead of throw "..." ? - Throwing a string is a SyntaxError in JavaScript - Only Error objects can be caught by try/catch + Error objects carry a name, a message and a stack, and work with instanceof - A thrown string stops the program even inside a try block Any value can be thrown and caught, but an Error tells you what went wrong and where (its stack), and callers can check its type with instanceof . ? What should a catch block do with an error it does not know how to handle? - Log it and carry on, so the program keeps running + Rethrow it, so it is not silently hidden - Return null , so the caller knows something failed - Ignore it: an unknown error is usually harmless Catch only what you can handle: check the type, deal with your own errors and throw err for the rest, or bugs such as a ReferenceError from a typo are hidden. ? What does f() return, where function f() { try { return "try"; } finally { console.log("cleanup"); } } ? - "cleanup" - undefined - "try", without printing anything + "try", after printing cleanup finally runs before the return completes, but does not change the value unless it returns itself.

title: Validating with errors
body: Write an error class and two functions: javascript class ValidationError extends Error { } // new ValidationError(field, message): has .name "ValidationError" and .field function parseSignup(json) { } // the validated user object, or throws function trySignup(json) { } // { ok: true, user } or { ok: false, field, message }; never throws for bad input parseSignup(json) first throws a plain TypeError with the message "json must be a string" when json is not a string: that is a bug in the calling code, not bad user input. Then it parses the JSON text and checks, in this order: 1. Invalid JSON: throw ValidationError with field "json" and message "not valid JSON" , with the SyntaxError as its cause . 2. The result must be a plain object (not null , not an array): field "json" , message "expected an object" . 3. name : a string with at least 2 characters after trimming, else field "name" , message "name is too short" . 4. age : a whole number from 13 to 120, else field "age" , message "age must be 13 to 120" . 5. email : a string with one @ that has text on both sides, else field "email" , message "email is not valid" . It returns { name, age, email } with the name trimmed and the email in lower case (other properties are dropped). trySignup turns a ValidationError into the result object, but any other error is rethrown.

title: 3.04  Iterators and Generators
body: What for...of and spread really use - the iteration protocol, making your own objects iterable with Symbol.iterator, generator functions with yield, lazy and infinite sequences, and helpers that combine generators. The iteration protocol for...of , spread ...x , destructuring and Array.from work on any iterable : an object with a Symbol.iterator () method that returns an iterator . An iterator has next() , which returns { value, done } . javascript const letters = "a", "b" ; const it = letters Symbol.iterator (); console.log(it.next(), it.next(), it.next()); Arrays, strings, Maps and Sets are iterable; plain objects are not (use Object.entries ). Making a class iterable javascript class Range { constructor(start, end, step = 1) { Object.assign(this, { start, end, step }); } Symbol.iterator () { let current = this.start; const { end, step } = this; return { next() { if (current = end) return { value: undefined, done: true }; const value = current; current += step; return { value, done: false }; }, }; } } console.log( ...new Range(0, 10, 3) ); for (const n of new Range(1, 3)) console.log(n); Generators Writing next() by hand is tedious. A generator function ( function ) does it for you: each yield hands out one value and pauses until the next one is asked for. javascript function range(start, end, step = 1) { for (let n = start; n < end; n += step) yield n; } console.log( ...range(0, 10, 3) ); class Bag { items = ; add(x) { this. items.push(x); return this; } Symbol.iterator () { yield this. items; } // yield hands out everything from another iterable } console.log( ...new Bag().add("x").add("y") ); Lazy and infinite sequences A generator does no work until a value is requested, so it can describe a sequence that never ends, as long as the consumer stops: javascript function naturals() { let n = 1; while (true) yield n++; } function take(iterable, count) { if (count <= 0) return; for (const x of iterable) { yield x; if (--count === 0) return; } } function mapIter(iterable, f) { for (const x of iterable) yield f(x); } function filterIter(iterable, keep) { for (const x of iterable) if (keep(x)) yield x; } const firstSquaresOfOdds = take(mapIter(filterIter(naturals(), n = n % 2), n = n n), 5); console.log( ...firstSquaresOfOdds ); Only the first nine natural numbers are ever produced: each stage asks the one before it for exactly as many values as it needs. This is useful for reading large data piece by piece, paging through API results, or game loops that produce states on demand. Iterators are single-use: once a generator is finished, iterating it again gives nothing. Call the generator function again for a fresh one. Check yourself quiz ? What makes an object usable in for...of ? - A length property and items stored under the keys 0, 1, 2 and so on - A next() method directly on the object that returns the items as an array + A Symbol.iterator () method returning an iterator whose next() gives { value, done } - Being created with class , since class instances are always iterable That is the iteration protocol used by for...of , spread and destructuring. Plain objects and class instances do not have it unless you add it; use Object.entries for objects. ? Why can a generator describe an infinite sequence such as naturals() ? - It runs the loop in the background and keeps the values in a buffer - JavaScript stops any while (true) loop inside a generator after a few thousand rounds - It stores only the last value, so memory never runs out + It is lazy: it computes the next value only when asked, so a consumer can stop Each yield pauses the generator until the next value is requested. A consumer such as take that stops early means the loop never runs forever. ? What is ...take(naturals(), 3) after ...take(naturals(), 3) was already spread once? - - 4, 5, 6 + 1, 2, 3 - an error Each call to take(naturals(), 3) creates new generators, so it starts again from 1.

title: Generators
