title: 3.05  Modules
body: Splitting a program into files with ES modules - named and default exports, import forms, renaming and namespace imports, module scope and strict mode, live bindings, side effects, CommonJS require in older Node code, and how to organise modules. Why modules A module is one file with its own scope: nothing inside it is visible to other files unless it is exported , and nothing from other files is visible unless it is imported . That keeps names from clashing and makes the dependencies of each file explicit. javascript-norun // money.js export const CURRENCY = "EUR"; export function format(cents) { return ${(cents / 100).toFixed(2)} ${CURRENCY} ; } function round(x) { return Math.round(x); } // not exported: private to this file export { round as roundCents }; // export under another name javascript-norun // main.js import { format, CURRENCY } from "./money.js"; import { roundCents as round } from "./money.js"; import as money from "./money.js"; // namespace: money.format, money.CURRENCY console.log(format(1250), CURRENCY, money.format(round(99.6))); Relative imports start with ./ or ../ . In browsers and Node, the file extension is required. Default exports A module may have one default export, imported without braces under any name: javascript-norun // cart.js export default class Cart { / ... / } export const MAX_ITEMS = 50; // main.js import Cart, { MAX_ITEMS } from "./cart.js"; Many teams prefer named exports only: names stay the same everywhere, editors can auto-import them, and renaming finds every use. How modules behave - Modules always run in strict mode and top-level this is undefined . - Each module runs once , the first time it is imported; later imports share the same instance. A module-level let count is shared by every importer. - Imports are live, read-only bindings : if the exporting module changes an exported let , importers see the new value, but they cannot assign to it themselves. - import statements are hoisted and resolved before any code runs. To load a module only when needed, use dynamic import : const { chart } = await import("./chart.js"); - In modules, top-level await is allowed. Code that runs at the top level of a module (connecting, printing, changing globals) is a side effect of importing it. Keep modules mostly to declarations so that importing them is safe. CommonJS Older Node code uses CommonJS , which you will meet in many packages: javascript-norun // math.cjs function add(a, b) { return a + b; } module.exports = { add }; // main.cjs const { add } = require("./math.cjs"); Node treats .mjs files, and .js files in a package whose package.json says "type": "module" , as ES modules; .cjs files and other .js files as CommonJS. New code should use ES modules. Organising modules - One module per idea: money.js , cart.js , storage.js , not utils.js with everything. - Keep pure logic in modules without side effects, and wire them together in one entry file ( main.js ). - Avoid circular imports (a imports b, b imports a): move the shared part into a third module. In this course's practice tasks, files of a project can import each other with ./name.js , just like in Node. Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference between import { x } from "./m.js" and import x from "./m.js" ? + { x } takes the named export x ; x alone takes the default export under any name - { x } imports a copy of x ; x alone imports a live binding to it - { x } takes the default export; x alone takes the named export x - There is none: the braces are optional With braces you name a named export exactly (or rename it with as ); without braces you get the module's one default export and choose the name yourself. ? If two files import the same module, does the module run twice? - Yes: each import runs the module's code again - Yes, unless the module has a default export + No: it runs once, and both files share the same instance and its state - No: only the first file can import it, the second gets an error Each module runs the first time it is imported; later imports get the same instance, so a module-level let is shared by every importer. ? A module has export let count = 0; export function inc() { count++; } . Another file runs inc() then reads count . What does it see? - 0 - undefined - an error + 1 Imports are live bindings to the exporting module's variables.

title: 4.01  The Event Loop and Callbacks
body: Why JavaScript code never blocks - one thread, the call stack, the task queue and the event loop, setTimeout and what a delay of 0 means, microtasks, callback-style APIs with error-first callbacks, and why deeply nested callbacks led to promises. One thread JavaScript runs your code on one thread : one thing at a time, from start to finish. Yet a web page can wait for a click, a timer and a download all at once. It does this by never waiting: slow operations are handed to the environment (the browser or Node), and your code is called back when they finish. javascript console.log("1: start"); setTimeout(() = console.log("3: timer fired"), 0); console.log("2: end of script"); Even with a delay of 0, the timer's callback runs after the current code has finished. The event loop - The call stack holds the functions running now. - When a timer fires or a download finishes, its callback is put in the task queue . - The event loop takes the next task only when the stack is empty. - Microtasks (promise callbacks, queueMicrotask ) run as soon as the current code finishes, before the next task. javascript setTimeout(() = console.log("task"), 0); Promise.resolve().then(() = console.log("microtask")); queueMicrotask(() = console.log("microtask 2")); console.log("sync"); Prints sync , microtask , microtask 2 , task . Do not block the loop While your code runs, nothing else can: no clicks, no redraws, no timers. A loop that takes 3 seconds freezes a page for 3 seconds: javascript-norun const end = Date.now() + 3000; while (Date.now() < end) { } // the whole page is frozen Long work belongs in small pieces between which the loop can breathe, or in a Web Worker. Callbacks Before promises, asynchronous APIs took a callback. Node's convention is error-first : the callback's first argument is an error or null : javascript function loadUser(id, callback) { setTimeout(() = { if (id <= 0) callback(new Error( no user ${id} )); else callback(null, { id, name: user${id} }); }, 10); } loadUser(1, (err, user) = { if (err) return console.log("failed:", err.message); console.log("loaded", user.name); }); loadUser(0, (err) = console.log("failed:", err.message)); Callback hell Doing things in sequence means nesting callbacks inside callbacks, and every level repeats the error check: javascript-norun loadUser(1, (err, user) = { if (err) return done(err); loadOrders(user, (err, orders) = { if (err) return done(err); loadInvoice(orders 0 , (err, invoice) = { if (err) return done(err); done(null, invoice); }); }); }); Promises (lesson 4.02) and async / await (lesson 4.03) turn this into straight-line code. You will still meet callbacks in event handlers, setTimeout , array methods and older libraries. Check yourself quiz ? Why does setTimeout(f, 0) not run f immediately? - A delay of 0 is rounded up to one second + It puts f in the task queue, which runs only after the current code and the microtasks - f runs immediately, but its output is printed later - The timer starts only after the next click or other event The event loop takes the next task only when the stack is empty and all waiting microtasks have run, so f always runs after the current code. ? What happens to a web page while a long synchronous loop runs? - The loop is paused automatically so the page can redraw - Clicks are handled in parallel on a second thread + It freezes: no events, timers or redraws can run until the loop ends - The browser runs the loop in a Web Worker by itself JavaScript runs one thing at a time on one thread, so while your code runs nothing else can. Long work belongs in small pieces or in a Web Worker you create. ? In what order are these printed: setTimeout(() = log("A")) , Promise.resolve().then(() = log("B")) , log("C") ? - A B C - C A B - B C A + C B A Synchronous code first, then microtasks (promises), then tasks (timers).

title: Callback helpers
body: Write three helpers for callback-style code. A task is a function that takes one error-first callback, like cb = setTimeout(() = cb(null, 42), 10) . javascript function afterCalls(count, done) { } // returns a function; once it has been called count times, done() runs (once) function series(tasks, done) { } // runs tasks one after another function parallel(tasks, done) { } // starts all tasks at once - afterCalls(0, done) runs done straight away. Calls after the count is reached do nothing. - series starts each task only after the one before it has called back. When all are finished it calls done(null, results) with the results in order. At the first error it calls done(err) and starts no more tasks. - parallel calls done(null, results) with the results in task order (not in finishing order) when all are finished. At the first error it calls done(err) ; later errors or results are ignored, so done runs only once. - Both call done(null, ) for an empty list.

title: 4.02  Promises
body: A promise as a value that arrives later - its three states, creating one with new Promise, chaining then and catch, returning promises from then, finally, wrapping callback APIs, and combining promises with Promise.all, allSettled, race and any. A value that arrives later A promise stands for the result of an operation that has not finished. It is in one of three states: - pending : still working; - fulfilled : finished with a value; - rejected : failed with an error (a reason). Once fulfilled or rejected, it is settled and never changes again. javascript const wait = ms = new Promise(resolve = setTimeout(resolve, ms)); function delayedSquare(n) { return new Promise((resolve, reject) = { if (typeof n !== "number") { reject(new TypeError("not a number")); return; } setTimeout(() = resolve(n n), 10); }); } delayedSquare(4).then(v = console.log("value", v)); delayedSquare("x").catch(err = console.log("error", err.message)); wait(20).then(() = console.log("20 ms later")); The function given to new Promise (the executor ) runs immediately and calls resolve(value) or reject(error) when done. Chaining then(f) returns a new promise for whatever f returns. If f returns a promise, the chain waits for it. That makes sequences flat: javascript const step = (label, ms) = new Promise(r = setTimeout(() = { console.log(label); r(label.length); }, ms)); step("load user", 10) .then(n = step("load orders", 10).then(() = n)) .then(n = { console.log("first label had", n, "letters"); return n 2; }) .then(doubled = console.log("doubled", doubled)) .catch(err = console.log("something failed:", err.message)) .finally(() = console.log("done either way")); A catch at the end handles a rejection from any step above it, like a try around the whole chain. A throw inside a then callback rejects the chain too. finally runs whatever happened, without changing the result. Always end a chain with catch (or await it inside try ): an unhandled rejection prints a warning in the browser and stops a Node program. Wrapping callback APIs javascript function loadUser(id, cb) { setTimeout(() = (id 0 ? cb(null, { id }) : cb(new Error("bad id"))), 5); } const loadUserAsync = id = new Promise((resolve, reject) = { loadUser(id, (err, user) = (err ? reject(err) : resolve(user))); }); loadUserAsync(3).then(u = console.log("user", u.id)); Node's util.promisify does this for any error-first function. Many promises at once Combinator Fulfils when Rejects when --- --- --- Promise.all(list) all fulfil: with an array of values in list order any rejects (the first error) Promise.allSettled(list) all settle: with { status, value } or { status, reason } for each never Promise.race(list) the first one settles, with its value the first one to settle rejects Promise.any(list) the first one fulfils all reject ( AggregateError ) javascript const after = (ms, v, fail = false) = new Promise((res, rej) = setTimeout(() = (fail ? rej(new Error(v)) : res(v)), ms)); Promise.all( after(30, "a"), after(10, "b") ).then(v = console.log("all", v)); Promise.allSettled( after(5, "ok"), after(5, "bad", true) ).then(r = console.log(r.map(x = x.status))); Promise.race( after(20, "slow"), after(5, "fast") ).then(v = console.log("race", v)); Promise.all runs the operations at the same time : three 100 ms requests take about 100 ms, not 300. Promise.resolve(v) and Promise.reject(e) make already-settled promises, useful in tests and for returning a promise from a function that sometimes has the answer ready. Check yourself quiz ? What does promise.then(f) return? - The value that f returns, once the promise has fulfilled - The same promise it was called on, so calls can be chained + A new promise for what f returns, waiting for it if that is a promise - undefined , because the result is passed on to f instead then returns a new promise straight away; it fulfils with f's return value, or follows it if f returns a promise, which is what keeps chains flat. ? What is the difference between Promise.all and Promise.allSettled ? + all rejects as soon as one rejects; allSettled waits for all and reports each outcome - all runs the promises one after another; allSettled runs them at the same time - all gives the first value to arrive; allSettled gives all the values - allSettled rejects with an AggregateError when every promise rejects allSettled never rejects: it fulfils with { status, value } or { status, reason } for each promise. Both start everything at once; Promise.any is the one with AggregateError. ? Promise.resolve(1).then(x = { throw new Error("no"); }).then(x = 2).catch(e = 3) fulfils with: - 1 - 2 - it rejects + 3 The throw rejects the chain, the second then is skipped, and catch returns 3.

title: Making and combining promises
body: Write three functions: javascript function delay(ms, value) { } // a promise that fulfils with value after ms milliseconds function promisify(fn) { } // turns an error-first callback function into one that returns a promise function settle(promises) { } // like Promise.allSettled, written yourself - promisify(fn) returns a function that passes its arguments to fn plus a callback, and rejects with the error or fulfils with the value. - settle(promises) fulfils, once every input has settled, with an array in input order of { status: "fulfilled", value } or { status: "rejected", reason } . It never rejects. Inputs that are plain values (not promises) count as fulfilled. An empty list gives .

title: 4.03  async and await
body: Writing asynchronous code that reads like ordinary code - async functions always return promises, await pauses only the function, try/catch/finally for errors, running steps in sequence versus in parallel, awaiting in loops, and top-level await. async functions An async function always returns a promise. Inside it, await pauses the function until a promise settles, then gives its value (or throws its error): javascript const wait = ms = new Promise(r = setTimeout(r, ms)); const fetchUser = async id = { await wait(10); return { id, name: user${id} }; }; const fetchOrders = async user = { await wait(10); return ${user.name}-order1 , ${user.name}-order2 ; }; async function firstOrder(id) { const user = await fetchUser(id); const orders = await fetchOrders(user); return orders 0 ; } firstOrder(7).then(o = console.log(o)); console.log("this prints first: await only paused firstOrder"); This is the callback-hell example from lesson 4.01, written as straight lines. Errors A rejected promise makes await throw , so ordinary try / catch / finally works: javascript async function risky(n) { await new Promise(r = setTimeout(r, 5)); if (n 2) throw new RangeError( ${n} is too big ); return n; } async function main() { try { console.log(await risky(1)); console.log(await risky(5)); console.log("not reached"); } catch (err) { console.log("caught", err.name, err.message); } finally { console.log("clean up"); } } main(); A throw inside an async function rejects the promise it returns. Sequence or parallel Each await waits before the next line starts. When steps do not depend on each other, start them all first and await them together: javascript const wait = (ms, v) = new Promise(r = setTimeout(() = r(v), ms)); async function sequential() { const t = Date.now(); const a = await wait(50, "a"); const b = await wait(50, "b"); return ${a}${b} in about ${Math.round((Date.now() - t) / 50) 50} ms ; } async function parallel() { const t = Date.now(); const a, b = await Promise.all( wait(50, "a"), wait(50, "b") ); return ${a}${b} in about ${Math.round((Date.now() - t) / 50) 50} ms ; } sequential().then(console.log); parallel().then(console.log); Loops await inside for...of processes items one at a time, in order. forEach with an async callback does not wait: it starts everything and returns at once, and errors go unhandled. javascript-norun for (const id of ids) { const user = await fetchUser(id); // one after another console.log(user.name); } const users = await Promise.all(ids.map(id = fetchUser(id))); // all at once, results in order ids.forEach(async id = { await fetchUser(id); }); // BUG: nothing waits for these To process many items with a limit (say 3 at a time), see lesson 4.05. Top-level await In modules (and in this course's sandbox), await works at the top level of a file, outside any function. In older scripts, wrap the code in async function main() { ... } and call main().catch(console.error) . Check yourself quiz ? What does an async function return if its body says return 5 ? - The number 5 + A promise that fulfils with 5 - A promise that fulfils with undefined - 5 when awaited, otherwise undefined An async function always returns a promise; its return value becomes the fulfilled value, and a throw rejects it. ? Why is ids.forEach(async id = { ... }) a bug when you need to wait for the work? - forEach runs the callbacks one after another, which is too slow - An async function cannot be passed as a callback - forEach waits for each promise, but throws away the results + forEach ignores the promises the callback returns, so nothing waits and errors go unhandled forEach starts every callback and returns at once. Use for...of with await for one at a time, or await Promise.all(ids.map(...)) for all at once. ? const a, b = await Promise.all( slowA(), slowB() ) , where each takes 1 second, takes about: - 2 seconds + 1 second - 0 seconds - it depends on which finishes first Both operations are started before the await, so they run at the same time.

title: async and await
body: Each function takes a list of ids and fetchOne(id) , which returns a promise: javascript async function loadInOrder(ids, fetchOne) { } // one at a time, in order; returns the values async function loadAll(ids, fetchOne) { } // all at the same time; returns the values in id order async function loadSafely(ids, fetchOne) { } // all at the same time; never rejects loadInOrder and loadAll reject with the first error. loadSafely returns { loaded, failed } : the values of the successful ids in id order, and the ids that failed, in id order.

title: 4.04  Fetching Data
body: Loading data over HTTP with fetch - responses and status codes, reading JSON and text, why fetch does not reject on 404, sending JSON with POST, headers, query strings with URLSearchParams, timeouts and cancelling with AbortController, and a small API client. fetch fetch(url) starts an HTTP request and returns a promise for a Response . Reading the body is a second step, also asynchronous: javascript-norun const response = await fetch("https://api.example.com/users/1"); console.log(response.status, response.ok, response.headers.get("content-type")); const user = await response.json(); // or response.text() In this course's sandbox, programs cannot reach the internet, but fetch("name.json") reads a file of the project, with the same API. Practice tasks use that. Check the status fetch rejects only when the request cannot be made at all (no network, a bad URL, a blocked request). A 404 or 500 still fulfils , with response.ok false. Check it yourself: javascript-norun async function getJSON(url) { const response = await fetch(url); if (!response.ok) throw new Error( ${url}: HTTP ${response.status} ); return response.json(); } Status Meaning --- --- 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content It worked 400 Bad Request, 422 Your request was wrong; do not retry unchanged 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden Not signed in / not allowed 404 Not Found No such resource 429 Too Many Requests Slow down; retry later 500, 502, 503 The server failed; retrying may help Sending data javascript-norun const response = await fetch("https://api.example.com/todos", { method: "POST", headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json", Authorization: Bearer ${token} }, body: JSON.stringify({ title: "Learn fetch", done: false }), }); Build query strings with URLSearchParams , which escapes values correctly: javascript const params = new URLSearchParams({ q: "tea & cake", page: 2 }); console.log( /search?${params} ); const url = new URL("https://example.com/search"); url.searchParams.set("q", "café"); console.log(url.href); Timeouts and cancelling A request can hang for a long time. An AbortController cancels it; AbortSignal.timeout(ms) makes a signal that cancels by itself: javascript-norun try { const response = await fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5000) }); ... } catch (err) { if (err.name === "TimeoutError" err.name === "AbortError") console.log("gave up waiting"); else throw err; } const controller = new AbortController(); searchButton.onclick = () = controller.abort(); // cancel on demand await fetch(url, { signal: controller.signal }); A small API client Put the details in one place, so the rest of the program just calls functions: javascript-norun const BASE = "https://api.example.com"; async function request(path, { method = "GET", body } = {}) { const response = await fetch(BASE + path, { method, headers: body ? { "Content-Type": "application/json" } : {}, body: body ? JSON.stringify(body) : undefined, }); if (!response.ok) throw new Error( ${method} ${path} failed: ${response.status} ); return response.status === 204 ? null : response.json(); } export const getTodos = () = request("/todos"); export const addTodo = title = request("/todos", { method: "POST", body: { title } }); Browsers and CORS In a web page, the browser only lets you read responses from another domain if that server allows it with CORS headers. A "CORS error" is the server's setting, not a bug in your fetch call; it is fixed on the server or by calling through your own backend. Never put secret API keys in browser code: anyone can read them. Check yourself quiz ? Does fetch reject when the server answers 404? - Yes: any status of 400 or above rejects the promise - Yes, but only when the body cannot be read as JSON + No: it fulfils with response.ok false, so you check ok or status - No: it fulfils with null instead of a Response fetch rejects only when the request cannot be made at all (no network, a bad URL, a blocked request). A 404 or 500 is still a response. ? How do you send a JavaScript object as a JSON body with fetch ? - Pass the object as body and fetch converts it to JSON itself - Put the object in the URL with URLSearchParams and use method: "GET" - Call JSON.parse(object) and pass the result as body + Use method: "POST" , a JSON Content-Type header and body: JSON.stringify(object) The body must be text, so JSON.stringify turns the object into JSON; the header tells the server what the text is. JSON.parse goes the other way, from text to a value. ? What is String(new URLSearchParams({ a: "x y", b: 1 })) ? - a=x y&b=1 - {"a":"x y","b":1} + a=x+y&b=1 - ?a=x%20y&b=1 URLSearchParams escapes values, writing spaces as +, and has no leading ?.

title: Fetching JSON
body: The project has a file users.json (open it in the file list; the tests expect its original contents), which fetch("users.json") reads like a web API. Write: javascript async function getJSON(url) { } // the parsed JSON; throws Error( ${url}: HTTP ${status} ) when the response is not ok async function activeByTeam(url) { } // { team: names of active users, sorted }, teams in first-seen order function searchUrl(base, params) { } // base + "?" + the encoded params, leaving out null, undefined and "" values searchUrl("/search", { q: "tea & cake", page: 2, sort: null }) is "/search?q=tea+%26+cake&page=2" ; with no params left, it is just the base.

title: 4.05  Timers, Debouncing and Concurrency
body: setTimeout, setInterval and clearing them, a sleep helper, debounce and throttle for noisy events, timeouts for promises, retrying with backoff, and running async work with a concurrency limit. Timers javascript const id = setTimeout(() = console.log("never runs"), 100); clearTimeout(id); let ticks = 0; const timer = setInterval(() = { ticks++; console.log("tick", ticks); if (ticks === 3) clearInterval(timer); }, 20); Delays are minimums, not exact: a timer runs when its time has passed and the event loop is free. Browsers slow timers down in background tabs. A promise-based sleep is a one-liner: javascript const sleep = ms = new Promise(resolve = setTimeout(resolve, ms)); (async () = { console.log("waiting"); await sleep(30); console.log("done"); })(); Debounce Some events fire many times a second: typing, scrolling, resizing. Debouncing waits until the events stop for a while, then runs once. A search box that queries a server should debounce, or it sends a request per key press. javascript function debounce(f, ms) { let timer; return (...args) = { clearTimeout(timer); timer = setTimeout(() = f(...args), ms); }; } const search = debounce(q = console.log("searching for", q), 30); search("c"); search("ca"); search("cat"); // only "cat" is searched Throttle Throttling runs at most once per period, ignoring calls in between. It suits continuous updates, such as saving the position while dragging: javascript function throttle(f, ms) { let last = -Infinity; return (...args) = { const now = Date.now(); if (now - last = ms) { last = now; f(...args); } }; } const log = throttle(x = console.log("ran with", x), 1000); log(1); log(2); log(3); // only 1 runs Timeouts for promises Promise.race with a timer gives any operation a time limit: javascript function withTimeout(promise, ms) { let timer; const timeout = new Promise((_, reject) = { timer = setTimeout(() = reject(new Error( timed out after ${ms} ms )), ms); }); return Promise.race( promise, timeout ).finally(() = clearTimeout(timer)); } const slow = new Promise(r = setTimeout(() = r("slow result"), 100)); withTimeout(slow, 20).then(console.log, err = console.log(err.message)); The finally clears the timer so it does not keep the program alive after the work is done. Retrying Network calls fail now and then. Retry a few times with a growing wait ( exponential backoff ), and only for errors where retrying can help: javascript-norun async function retry(task, { attempts = 3, delay = 100 } = {}) { for (let i = 1; ; i++) { try { return await task(); } catch (err) { if (i = attempts) throw err; await sleep(delay 2 (i - 1)); // 100, 200, 400 ms... } } } A concurrency limit Promise.all(items.map(work)) starts everything at once. With 1000 items, that is 1000 requests at the same moment, which servers may refuse. A pool keeps at most limit running: javascript async function mapLimit(items, limit, work) { const results = new Array(items.length); let next = 0; async function worker() { while (next < items.length) { const i = next++; // safe: only one piece of code runs at a time results i = await work(items i , i); } } await Promise.all(Array.from({ length: Math.min(limit, items.length) }, worker)); return results; } let running = 0, peak = 0; const job = async n = { running++; peak = Math.max(peak, running); await new Promise(r = setTimeout(r, 10)); running--; return n 2; }; mapLimit( 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 , 3, job).then(r = console.log(r, "peak", peak)); Results stay in input order, because each is stored at its own index. Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference between debounce and throttle? + Debounce runs once after the calls stop for a while; throttle runs at most once per period - Debounce runs at most once per period; throttle runs once after the calls stop - Debounce runs on the first call only; throttle runs on the last call only - Both delay every call by the same time; throttle also queues the calls A debounced search waits until typing pauses, then runs once; a throttled drag handler keeps running, but never more than once per period. ? In mapLimit , why is next++ safe without locks, even with several workers? - Each worker has its own copy of next - Promise.all runs the workers one after another, never at the same time + JavaScript runs one piece of code at a time; a worker can only pause at an await - ++ on a let variable is always done by the engine as one locked step All workers share the one next through a closure, but code runs on one thread and a worker is only interrupted at an await , never in the middle of const i = next++ . ? A debounced function with 100 ms is called at 0, 50 and 120 ms. When does it run? - At 100 ms only - At 100 and 220 ms - At 0, 50 and 120 ms + At 220 ms only Each call restarts the wait; the last call at 120 ms runs 100 ms later because no call follows it.

title: Timing helpers
body: Write three helpers: javascript function debounce(f, ms) { } // returns a debounced function with a cancel() method async function retry(task, attempts, delayMs) { } async function mapLimit(items, limit, work) { } - The debounced function runs f with the last arguments once ms have passed without another call. cancel() drops a pending call. - retry calls task() (which returns a promise) and returns its value. If it rejects, it waits and tries again, up to attempts calls in total, waiting delayMs , then 2 delayMs , then 4 delayMs ... between them. After the last failure it rejects with the last error. - mapLimit calls work(item, index) for each item with at most limit running at a time and returns the results in input order. If a call rejects, mapLimit rejects with that error and starts no further items.

title: A resilient data loader
body: Real apps wrap fetch in a layer that caches, retries and limits how many requests run at once. Build one: javascript const loader = createLoader({ fetcher: fetch, retries: 2, limit: 3, timeoutMs: 1000 }); const user = await loader.get("/users/1.json"); const many = await loader.getMany( "/users/1.json", "/users/2.json", "/nope.json" ); // { url, ok: true, data }, { url, ok: true, data }, { url: "/nope.json", ok: false, error: "/nope.json: HTTP 404" } loader.stats(); // { requests, cacheHits, failures } LoadError extends Error : name is "LoadError" , and status is the HTTP status, or null when there was no usable response. createLoader(options) takes fetcher (a function like fetch , default fetch ), retries (extra attempts, default 2), limit (default 3) and timeoutMs (default 1000), and returns an object with: get(url) returns a promise for the parsed JSON: - Each call to fetcher(url) is one attempt . A response that is not ok fails with LoadError message <url : HTTP <status . - An attempt that takes longer than timeoutMs fails with message <url : timed out (status null ). - When fetcher itself rejects (a network error), the attempt fails with message <url : <the error's message (status null ). - When the body is not valid JSON, it fails with message <url : bad JSON and the response's status. - Failures with status null , 429 or 500 and above are retried , up to retries more attempts, waiting 10 ms, then 20 ms, then 40 ms... before each retry. Other failures (like 404 or bad JSON) are not retried. The last failure is the error get rejects with. - A successful result is cached : a later get of the same url returns it without calling fetcher . Failures are not cached. - While a load of a url is running, another get of the same url shares it instead of starting a second one. getMany(urls) gets every url with at most limit gets running at a time, and returns { url, ok: true, data } or { url, ok: false, error: <message } for each, in input order. It never rejects. stats() returns a copy of { requests, cacheHits, failures } : requests counts attempts (calls to fetcher ), cacheHits counts get calls answered from the cache or by sharing a running load, and failures counts loads that ended in an error.

title: 5.01  Why TypeScript and Basic Types
body: What TypeScript adds to JavaScript and what it does not change, compiling and type-checking, annotating variables, parameters and return values, type inference, arrays and tuples, any versus unknown, null and undefined under strict mode, and reading type errors. JavaScript with types TypeScript is JavaScript plus type annotations . A compiler ( tsc ) checks that values are used consistently, then removes the types and produces plain JavaScript. Types exist only while you write and check the code: at run time it is the same JavaScript as before. typescript-norun function area(width: number, height: number): number { return width height; } area(3, 4); // fine area("3", 4); // error TS2345: Argument of type 'string' is not assignable to parameter of type 'number'. area(3); // error TS2554: Expected 2 arguments, but got 1. Errors like these appear as you type , before the code runs. Whole classes of bugs (a typo in a property name, a forgotten argument, a possibly-undefined value) are caught at once, and the editor can complete names because it knows each value's shape. In this course, files ending in .ts are type-checked in the editor: problems are underlined and listed in the Problems panel. Running and checking a task executes the JavaScript that remains, so a task's tests check what the code does, and its requirements check that you wrote the types. Annotations and inference typescript let title: string = "Dune"; let pages = 412; // inferred: number const done = false; // inferred: the literal type false const ratings: number = 5, 4 ; const pair: string, number = "age", 36 ; // a tuple: fixed length, a type per position function describe(name: string, age?: number): string { // ? = optional return age === undefined ? name : ${name} (${age}) ; } console.log(describe(title), describe("Ada", 36), ratings, pair); TypeScript infers types from values, so annotate where it helps: function parameters (always), return types of exported functions, and variables that start empty ( const names: string = ). Do not annotate what is obvious: const count: number = 0 adds nothing. The basic types Type Values --- --- string , number , boolean , bigint As in JavaScript null , undefined Only those values T or Array<T Arrays of T A, B Tuples void A function returns nothing useful never Never happens: a function that always throws unknown Anything, but you must check before using it any Anything, with checking switched off any and unknown any turns the type checker off for that value: everything is allowed, so mistakes slip through. unknown also accepts anything, but you must narrow it (lesson 5.03) before use: typescript function lengthOf(value: unknown): number { if (typeof value === "string" Array.isArray(value)) return value.length; return 0; } console.log(lengthOf("hello"), lengthOf( 1, 2 ), lengthOf(42)); Use unknown for data from outside: JSON.parse results, fetch responses, user input. Avoid any . strict mode and null With "strict": true in tsconfig.json (always use it), null and undefined are separate types. A value that may be missing must say so, and you must check before using it: typescript-norun function firstWord(text: string undefined): string { return text.split(" ") 0 ; // error TS18048: 'text' is possibly 'undefined'. } typescript function firstWord(text: string undefined): string { if (text === undefined) return ""; return text.split(" ") 0 ; } console.log(firstWord("hello world"), JSON.stringify(firstWord(undefined))); The ! operator ( text!.split(...) ) tells the compiler "trust me, it is not null". Use it rarely: it is exactly the kind of claim the checker exists to verify. Reading type errors Type errors read from the general to the specific: the last line usually names the actual mismatch. Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number' means a string was given where a number is required. Fix the code, not the type, unless the type is what is wrong. Check yourself quiz ? Does TypeScript check types while the program runs? - Yes: annotated values are checked again each time they are used - Only in strict mode, where tsc adds run-time checks + No: they are checked before running, then removed - Only for values typed as unknown Types exist only while you write and check the code; tsc strips them and the running code is plain JavaScript. Strict mode makes the compile-time checks stricter, it adds nothing at run time. ? Why prefer unknown over any for data from JSON.parse ? + unknown must be checked before use; any switches checking off - unknown is checked at run time, so bad data throws at once - any can only hold primitives, not objects or arrays - unknown converts the parsed data to the right type for you Both accept every value, and neither does anything at run time; the difference is that unknown must be narrowed before use, so mistakes are caught. ? What type does TypeScript infer for const names = under strict mode, before anything is pushed? - string , because names usually hold strings - unknown , so you must check each element - never , so nothing can ever be pushed + An evolving any that takes the types you push An empty array literal gets an evolving type; writing const names: string = states the intent up front.

title: Annotating functions
body: Write three typed functions in TypeScript: typescript function parseScores(text: string): number // "3, 5,x, 8" gives 3, 5, 8 : skip parts that are not numbers function stats(values: number ): number, number, number null // min, max, mean , or null for an empty list function describe(value: unknown): string // see below parseScores splits on commas, trims each part, and keeps the parts that are non-empty and convert to a finite number. describe returns: - "text of length N" for a string, - "number N" for a number ( "number 3.5" ), - "list of N items" for an array, - "nothing" for null or undefined , - "something else" for anything else. Write the types shown: the editor underlines type errors, and the requirements check that the parameters are typed and that any is not used.

title: 5.02  Interfaces and Type Aliases
body: Describing the shape of objects with interfaces and type aliases, optional and readonly properties, function types, index signatures and Record, extending and intersecting types, structural typing, and excess property checks. Describing objects An interface names the shape of an object: typescript interface Book { title: string; author: string; year: number; tags?: string ; // optional readonly isbn: string; // cannot be reassigned } function cite(book: Book): string { return ${book.author}, ${book.title} (${book.year}) ; } const dune: Book = { title: "Dune", author: "Frank Herbert", year: 1965, isbn: "978-0441013593" }; console.log(cite(dune)); A type alias gives a name to any type, including object shapes: typescript type Point = { x: number; y: number }; type Id = string number; type Pair<T = T, T ; const origin: Point = { x: 0, y: 0 }; const ids: Id = 1, "a7" ; const range: Pair<number = 1, 10 ; console.log(origin, ids, range); For object shapes both work; a common rule is: interface for objects and classes, type for unions, tuples and everything else. Structural typing TypeScript compares types by their shape , not their name. Any object with the right properties fits, whatever it was declared as: typescript interface Named { name: string } const user = { name: "Ada", age: 36 }; function hello(x: Named) { return hello ${x.name} ; } console.log(hello(user)); // fine: user has a name, the extra age does not matter One exception: an object literal written directly where a type is expected may not have unknown properties ( hello({ name: "Ada", agee: 36 }) is an error), because that is usually a typo. Functions and indexes typescript type Compare<T = (a: T, b: T) = number; const byLength: Compare<string = (a, b) = a.length - b.length; interface Scores { player: string : number; // an index signature: any string key, number values } const scores: Scores = { ada: 3, bob: 5 }; const lives: Record<string, number = { ada: 2 }; // the same idea with the Record utility type console.log( "ccc", "a", "bb" .sort(byLength), scores.bob, lives.ada); With an index signature, reading a key that is not there gives undefined at run time even though the type says number . The compiler option noUncheckedIndexedAccess makes such reads number undefined . Combining types An interface can extend others; a type alias can intersect them with & : typescript interface Entity { id: number; createdAt: string } interface User extends Entity { name: string; email: string } type Timestamped = { updatedAt: string }; type SavedUser = User & Timestamped; const u: SavedUser = { id: 1, createdAt: "2026-01-01", name: "Ada", email: "ada@example.com", updatedAt: "2026-02-01" }; console.log(Object.keys(u).length); readonly readonly stops reassignment through that type: book.isbn = "x" is an error. readonly string (or ReadonlyArray<string ) has no push , sort or other changing methods, which documents that a function will not change your array: typescript-norun function total(prices: readonly number ): number { prices.push(0); // error TS2339: Property 'push' does not exist on type 'readonly number '. return prices.reduce((a, b) = a + b, 0); } Like all types, readonly is checked only at compile time. Check yourself quiz ? An object has more properties than an interface asks for. Can it be passed where the interface is expected? - No: the extra properties are always a type error + Yes, from a variable; only a fresh object literal is rejected - Yes, but the extra properties are removed when it is passed - Only if the interface has an index signature Types are compared by shape, so extra properties do not matter. Only an object literal written in place is checked for unknown properties, because that is usually a typo; nothing is removed at run time. ? What is the difference between extends on an interface and & on types? - extends copies the members at run time; & exists only for the compiler - & makes a union: a value needs the members of either type - extends works only with classes, & only with interfaces + Both combine members: extends builds a new interface, & an intersection type Both give a type with all the members of the parts. & is an intersection (a union is written ), and neither exists at run time. ? Which declares an object whose keys are any strings and values are booleans? - type Flags = boolean + type Flags = Record<string, boolean - type Flags = { string: boolean } - type Flags = string, boolean Record<K, V (or an index signature key: string : boolean) describes a dictionary. { string: boolean } is an object with one property named "string".

title: Interfaces for a library
body: Declare the types and write three functions: typescript interface Book { isbn: string; title: string; author: string; year: number; tags?: string } interface Loan { isbn: string; member: string; due: string } // due is "YYYY-MM-DD" function addBook(books: readonly Book , book: Book): Book function byAuthor(books: readonly Book ): Record<string, string function overdue(loans: readonly Loan , books: readonly Book , today: string): string - addBook returns a new array with the book added, or throws an Error duplicate isbn <isbn when a book with that isbn is already there. The input array is not changed. - byAuthor maps each author to their titles sorted by year (then by title). - overdue returns lines "<member : <title (due <due )" for loans whose due is before today , sorted by due date and then member. Dates in YYYY-MM-DD form compare correctly as strings. A loan whose isbn matches no book uses unknown book as the title.

title: 5.03  Unions and Narrowing
body: Union types for values that can be one of several things, literal types, narrowing with typeof, instanceof, in and equality checks, discriminated unions with a kind field, exhaustive switches with never, and type guard functions for validating unknown data. Unions A union type A B means "an A or a B": typescript function pad(value: string number): string { if (typeof value === "number") return value.toFixed(2).padStart(8); // here value is number return value.padStart(8); // here value is string } console.log( ${pad(3.5)} ${pad("abc")} ); Inside the if , TypeScript knows value is a number ; after it, a string . This is narrowing : checks you would write anyway in JavaScript teach the compiler which type you have. Literal types limit a value to exact options: typescript type Direction = "up" "down" "left" "right"; type Dice = 1 2 3 4 5 6; function move(d: Direction, steps: Dice) { return ${d} ${steps} ; } console.log(move("up", 3)); // move("north", 7) // two errors: neither value is allowed Ways to narrow Check Narrows --- --- typeof x === "string" primitives: string, number, boolean, bigint, symbol, undefined, function x instanceof Date class instances "radius" in shape objects that have that property x === null , x !== undefined , if (x) removes null / undefined (careful: if (x) also removes 0 and "") Array.isArray(x) arrays Discriminated unions The most useful pattern in TypeScript: each variant has a common tag property with a literal type. typescript type Shape = { kind: "circle"; radius: number } { kind: "rect"; width: number; height: number } { kind: "triangle"; base: number; height: number }; function area(s: Shape): number { switch (s.kind) { case "circle": return Math.PI s.radius 2; // s is the circle variant here case "rect": return s.width s.height; case "triangle": return (s.base s.height) / 2; default: { const unreachable: never = s; // error if a variant is not handled throw new Error( unknown shape ${JSON.stringify(unreachable)} ); } } } const shapes: Shape = { kind: "circle", radius: 1 }, { kind: "rect", width: 2, height: 3 } ; console.log(shapes.map(area).map(a = a.toFixed(2))); The never line makes the switch exhaustive : if someone adds { kind: "hexagon" } to Shape and forgets area , the assignment fails to compile, pointing at the exact place to update. Results are often modelled the same way: typescript type Result<T = { ok: true; value: T } { ok: false; error: string }; function parsePort(text: string): Result<number { const n = Number(text); return Number.isInteger(n) && n 0 && n < 65536 ? { ok: true, value: n } : { ok: false, error: bad port "${text}" }; } const r = parsePort("80"); if (r.ok) console.log("port", r.value); else console.log(r.error); Type guards A function returning x is T is a type guard : when it returns true, the caller's value is narrowed to T . Use them to validate unknown data: typescript interface User { name: string; age: number } function isUser(x: unknown): x is User { return typeof x === "object" && x !== null && typeof (x as User).name === "string" && typeof (x as User).age === "number"; } const data: unknown = JSON.parse('{"name": "Ada", "age": 36}'); if (isUser(data)) console.log(data.name.toUpperCase(), data.age + 1); x as User is a type assertion : it tells the compiler to treat the value as a User without any check. Inside a guard that verifies each property it is fine; elsewhere, an assertion is a claim the compiler cannot verify, so prefer narrowing. Check yourself quiz ? What makes a union discriminated? - Every variant is an interface with a different name - The union has a never member for the default case + Each variant has a shared tag property with its own literal type - Each variant is a class, so instanceof can tell them apart Checking the shared tag property narrows the value to one variant. Interface names do not exist at run time, so they cannot be checked. ? What does assigning the value to a variable of type never in the default case achieve? + Compiling fails if any variant is left unhandled - It lets the switch accept values of any type - It removes unhandled variants from the union - It makes the switch skip variants it does not know If a variant has no case, the value in default is still that variant, not never , so the assignment is a compile error that points at the switch to update. ? Given x: string number , which check narrows x to string ? - if (x.length) - if (x instanceof String) - if ("length" in x) + if (typeof x === "string") Both types have length; typeof distinguishes the primitive string. instanceof String checks for String objects, not string values.

title: A robot with a discriminated union
match: A robot with a discriminated union
body: A robot starts at (0, 0) facing north and follows commands: typescript type Command = { kind: "move"; steps: number } { kind: "turn"; direction: "left" "right" } { kind: "say"; text: string }; function run(commands: Command ): { x: number; y: number; facing: string; log: string } function isCommand(x: unknown): x is Command function parseProgram(json: string): Command - move goes steps squares in the facing direction: north is y + 1 , east x + 1 , south y - 1 , west x - 1 . - turn turns 90 degrees; the facings are "north" , "east" , "south" , "west" . - say adds "(<x , <y ): <text " to the log. - isCommand checks an unknown value really is one of the three variants with the right property types ( steps a number, direction exactly "left" or "right" , text a string). - parseProgram parses JSON text that must be an array, and returns only the elements that pass isCommand . Use a switch on kind with an exhaustive never check in run .

title: 5.04  Generics
body: Writing functions, interfaces and classes that work for any type while keeping type information - type parameters, inference of type arguments, constraints with extends, keyof and indexed access types, default type parameters, and generic containers. Type parameters A function that works for any type, and still knows what it returns, takes a type parameter : typescript function first<T (items: T ): T undefined { return items 0 ; } const n = first( 3, 1, 2 ); // T is number, so n is number undefined const s = first( "a", "b" ); // T is string console.log(n, s); Without generics you would choose between first(items: any ): any (losing the type) and one function per type. TypeScript infers T from the arguments; you can also write it: first<string ( ) . Several parameters typescript function mapValues<K extends string, A, B (obj: Record<K, A , f: (value: A) = B): Record<K, B { const out = {} as Record<K, B ; for (const key of Object.keys(obj) as K ) out key = f(obj key ); return out; } const prices = { tea: 2.5, cake: 4 }; const labels = mapValues(prices, p = ${p.toFixed(2)} EUR ); // Record<"tea" "cake", string console.log(labels); function groupBy<T, K extends string (items: T , key: (item: T) = K): Record<K, T { const out = {} as Record<K, T ; for (const item of items) (out key(item) ??= ).push(item); return out; } console.log(groupBy( "apple", "avocado", "banana" , w = w 0 )); Constraints T extends Something limits T to types that have certain members, so the body can use them: typescript function longest<T extends { length: number } (a: T, b: T): T { return b.length a.length ? b : a; } console.log(longest("tea", "coffee"), longest( 1, 2 , 1 )); // longest(10, 20) // error: number has no length keyof and indexed access keyof T is the union of T 's property names, and T K is the type of property K . Together they type functions that take a property name: typescript function pluck<T, K extends keyof T (items: T , key: K): T K { return items.map(item = item key ); } const users = { name: "Ada", age: 36 }, { name: "Linus", age: 55 } ; const names = pluck(users, "name"); // string const ages = pluck(users, "age"); // number // pluck(users, "email") // error: "email" is not a key of the user type console.log(names, ages); Generic interfaces and classes typescript interface ApiResponse<T { status: number; data: T } class Stack<T { items: T = ; push(item: T): void { this. items.push(item); } pop(): T undefined { return this. items.pop(); } peek(): T undefined { return this. items.at(-1); } get size(): number { return this. items.length; } } const s = new Stack<number (); s.push(1); s.push(2); // s.push("3") // error: string is not number const res: ApiResponse<string = { status: 200, data: "a" }; console.log(s.pop(), s.size, res.data); Type parameters can have defaults: interface Page<T = unknown { items: T ; next?: string } . When to use generics Use a type parameter when it connects types: the input type determines the output type, or two arguments must match. If T appears only once in a signature, it is not doing anything: function log<T (x: T): void is just function log(x: unknown): void . Check yourself quiz ? In function f<T, K extends keyof T (obj: T, key: K) , what does K extends keyof T mean? - K must be a class that extends T + K must be one of the property names of T - K must be an object with the same keys as T - K can be any string; it is checked when the function runs keyof T is the union of T's property names, and extends limits K to that union, so a wrong name is a compile error. ? Why is first<T (items: T ): T undefined better than first(items: any ): any ? - It runs faster because the element type is known in advance - It accepts more kinds of arrays than the any version - It refuses empty arrays at compile time + The result keeps the element type, so it is still checked The type parameter connects input and output: first( 3, 1 ) gives number undefined , while any switches checking off for the result. Both accept every array. ? For pluck<T, K extends keyof T (items: T , key: K): T K called with users and "age", the result type is: - T + number - K - (string number) T K is the type of the age property, number, so the result is number .

title: Generic helpers
body: Write generic functions and a generic class: typescript function uniqueBy<T, K (items: readonly T , key: (item: T) = K): T function pluck<T, K extends keyof T (items: readonly T , key: K): T K function indexBy<T, K extends keyof T (items: readonly T , key: K): Map<T K , T class Cache<K, V { constructor(capacity: number) get(key: K): V undefined set(key: K, value: V): void get size(): number } - uniqueBy keeps the first item for each key, in order. - indexBy maps each item's key value to the item; later items replace earlier ones with the same value. - Cache holds at most capacity entries. When a new key is set while it is full, the least recently used entry is dropped. Both get (of a key that is there) and set count as using a key.

title: 5.05  Classes, Enums and Utility Types
body: Typed classes with access modifiers, parameter properties, implements and abstract classes, enums and why unions of literals are often better, as const, and the built-in utility types Partial, Required, Pick, Omit, Readonly, Record, ReturnType and Awaited. Typed classes typescript interface Account { readonly id: string; balance(): number; deposit(amount: number): void; } class SavingsAccount implements Account { cents = 0; constructor(public readonly id: string, private rate: number) {} // parameter properties balance(): number { return this. cents / 100; } deposit(amount: number): void { if (amount <= 0) throw new RangeError("amount must be positive"); this. cents += Math.round(amount 100); } addInterest(): void { this. cents += Math.round(this. cents this.rate); } } const acc = new SavingsAccount("S-1", 0.02); acc.deposit(100); acc.addInterest(); console.log(acc.id, acc.balance()); - public readonly id: string in the constructor's parameters declares and assigns the property: a parameter property . - private and protected are checked only by the compiler; private fields are private at run time too. Prefer for real privacy. - implements Account makes the compiler check that the class has everything the interface promises. Abstract classes An abstract class cannot be created with new ; it provides shared code and declares methods that subclasses must write: typescript abstract class Report { abstract rows(): string ; render(): string { return this.rows().map(r = r.join(" ")).join("\n"); } } class SalesReport extends Report { rows() { return "tea", "12" , "cake", "7" ; } } console.log(new SalesReport().render()); Enums, or unions of literals An enum names a set of constants and, unlike most TypeScript, produces real JavaScript: typescript enum Level { Debug, Info, Warn, Error } console.log(Level.Warn, Level Level.Warn ); // 2 Warn enum Color { Red = "red", Green = "green" } console.log(Color.Red); Many codebases prefer a union of string literals , which is plain JavaScript values, needs no import, and reads clearly in JSON and logs: typescript const LEVELS = "debug", "info", "warn", "error" as const; type LevelName = typeof LEVELS number ; // "debug" "info" "warn" "error" function atLeast(level: LevelName, min: LevelName): boolean { return LEVELS.indexOf(level) = LEVELS.indexOf(min); } console.log(atLeast("error", "warn"), atLeast("debug", "info")); as const makes the array readonly with literal element types, so the list of values and the type come from one place. Utility types TypeScript includes generic types that transform other types: Utility Result --- --- Partial

title: A typed todo store

Each property in the filter must match; an empty filter lists everything.

title: A typed calculator
body: Write a calculator for expressions like 2 (x + 1) ^ 2 - max(a, 3) in TypeScript, in three stages: text to tokens, tokens to a syntax tree , and the tree to a number. Errors are returned as values, not thrown. typescript type Result<T = { ok: true; value: T } { ok: false; error: string }; type Expr = { kind: "num"; value: number } { kind: "var"; name: string } { kind: "unary"; op: "-"; arg: Expr } { kind: "binary"; op: "+" "-" " " "/" "^"; left: Expr; right: Expr } { kind: "call"; name: string; args: Expr }; function parse(source: string): Result<Expr function evaluate(source: string, vars?: Record<string, number ): Result<number Tokens : numbers ( 12 , 1.5 , .5 , 3. ), names (a letter or _ , then letters, digits or _ ), and the symbols + - / ^ ( ) , . Spaces are skipped. Any other character is the error unexpected "<char " at <index (the index counts from 0). Grammar , from loosest to tightest: - + and - between terms, left to right: 8 - 3 - 2 is 3. - and / , left to right. - unary minus: --3 is 3. - ^ , which groups to the right ( 2 ^ 3 ^ 2 is 512) and binds tighter than unary minus ( -2 ^ 2 is -4); its right side may itself start with a minus ( 2 ^ -1 is 0.5). - a number, a name, a call name(arg, arg, ...) (possibly with no arguments), or ( expression ) . A token in the wrong place is the error unexpected "<token " at <index , and running out of tokens is unexpected end . Text left over after a complete expression is an unexpected token too: 1 2 gives unexpected "2" at 2 . Evaluating : - unknown variable <name when a name is not an own property of vars . - division by zero when dividing by 0. - Functions: abs and sqrt take exactly 1 argument (else <name takes 1 argument ), min and max take 1 or more (else <name needs at least 1 argument ). Any other name is unknown function <name . sqrt of a negative number is sqrt of a negative number . parse does not look at names, so parse("-f(2)") succeeds.

Changing the DOM changes the page immediately. html

title: 6.02  Events and Forms
body: Reacting to the user - addEventListener, the event object, bubbling and event delegation, preventDefault, keyboard events, forms with submit, FormData and built-in validation, custom validation messages, and keeping handlers small. Listening javascript-norun const button = document.querySelector(" save"); button.addEventListener("click", event = { console.log("clicked", event.target); }); The event object describes what happened: event.target (the element the event started on), event.key for keyboard events, event.clientX for the mouse. Common events: click , input (each change of a field), change (a field is committed), submit , keydown , focus , blur , DOMContentLoaded . removeEventListener(type, sameFunction) stops listening; pass { once: true } to listen for one event only. Bubbling and delegation An event first runs listeners on its target, then bubbles up through each parent to document . So one listener on a list can handle clicks on every item, including items added later. This is event delegation : javascript-norun list.addEventListener("click", event = { const button = event.target.closest("button data-action "); if (!button !list.contains(button)) return; const index = Number(button.closest("li").dataset.index); if (button.dataset.action === "delete") state.items.splice(index, 1); if (button.dataset.action === "toggle") state.items index .done = !state.items index .done; render(); }); closest(selector) walks up from the clicked element to the nearest match, so a click on an icon inside the button still finds the button. event.stopPropagation() stops bubbling; it is rarely needed and easy to misuse. Default actions Some events have a built-in action: a link navigates, a form submits and reloads the page, a key types a letter. event.preventDefault() cancels it: javascript-norun form.addEventListener("submit", event = { event.preventDefault(); // handle the form in JavaScript instead of reloading ... }); input.addEventListener("keydown", event = { if (event.key === "Enter" && !event.shiftKey) { event.preventDefault(); send(); } if (event.key === "Escape") input.value = ""; }); Forms html

body: Write the pure functions behind a signup form and a keyboard handler: javascript function validateSignup(values) { } // values from Object.fromEntries(new FormData(form)): all strings function keyCommand(event) { } // a command name for a keydown event, or null validateSignup returns { ok, data, errors } : - name : trimmed, at least 2 characters, else error "Enter at least 2 characters." - email : trimmed and lower-cased; one @ with text before it and a . somewhere after it, else "Enter a valid email." - age : optional. Empty means null ; otherwise a whole number from 13 to 120, else "Enter an age from 13 to 120." - password : at least 8 characters with a letter and a digit, else "Use 8 or more characters with a letter and a digit." - confirm must equal password , else "The passwords do not match." (only checked when the password itself is valid). errors has one message per bad field (an empty object when all is well), ok is true when there are none, and data holds the cleaned { name, email, age } (no passwords) when ok , else null . keyCommand gets { key, ctrlKey, metaKey, shiftKey } , where Ctrl on Windows and Linux and Cmd (meta) on a Mac count the same, and returns: - Ctrl/Cmd + s : "save" ; Ctrl/Cmd + z : "undo" ; Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + z or Ctrl/Cmd + y : "redo" - Escape (with no modifier): "close" ; / with no modifier: "search" - anything else: null . Letters may arrive as upper case when Shift is held.

title: 6.03  Storing Data in the Browser
body: Keeping data between visits - localStorage and sessionStorage, storing objects as JSON, handling missing, corrupt and old data with versions, storage limits and errors, cookies in brief, IndexedDB for larger data, and what never to store in the browser. localStorage localStorage keeps strings per site, across reloads and restarts: javascript-norun localStorage.setItem("theme", "dark"); localStorage.getItem("theme"); // "dark"; null if missing localStorage.removeItem("theme"); localStorage.clear(); // everything for this site sessionStorage has the same API but forgets when the tab closes. Both are synchronous and limited to a few megabytes per site. Storing objects Storage holds strings only. Objects go through JSON (lesson 2.05): javascript-norun localStorage.setItem("todos", JSON.stringify(todos)); const todos = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem("todos") ?? " "); Treat stored data as untrusted input : the user may have cleared it, another version of your app may have written it, an extension may have changed it, or it may be cut off. Reading must never crash the app: javascript function load(storage, key, fallback) { try { const text = storage.getItem(key); if (text === null) return fallback; return JSON.parse(text); } catch { return fallback; // corrupt JSON or storage not available (private mode, blocked) } } function save(storage, key, value) { try { storage.setItem(key, JSON.stringify(value)); return true; } catch { return false; // full (QuotaExceededError) or blocked } } const fake = new Map(); const storage = { getItem: k = fake.get(k) ?? null, setItem: (k, v) = fake.set(k, String(v)) }; save(storage, "todos", { title: "tea" } ); fake.set("broken", "{oops"); console.log(load(storage, "todos", ), load(storage, "broken", ), load(storage, "missing", )); Passing the storage in as a parameter, instead of using localStorage directly, lets tests use a fake. The practice tasks use exactly this. Versions Apps change. Store a version with the data and upgrade old shapes when loading: javascript function migrate(saved) { let data = saved; if (data.version === 1) data = { version: 2, items: data.todos.map(t = ({ ...t, tags: })) }; if (data.version !== 2) return { version: 2, items: }; return data; } console.log(migrate({ version: 1, todos: { title: "a" } })); Other storage Storage For --- --- localStorage / sessionStorage Small settings and app state (a few MB, strings) Cookies Small values the server must see on each request, such as a session id; set by the server with HttpOnly and Secure IndexedDB Large or structured data, files, offline apps; asynchronous (libraries such as idb make it pleasant) Cache API Responses for offline use, with service workers What not to store Anything in localStorage can be read by every script on the page, including injected ones (lesson 6.01's XSS). Never store passwords there, and be careful with access tokens; a server-set HttpOnly cookie cannot be read by JavaScript at all. Storage is per browser and per device: for data the user must not lose, save it on a server too. Check yourself quiz ? What does localStorage.getItem return for a key that was never set? - undefined - "" - It throws an Error + null getItem gives null for a missing key, which is why the lesson writes ?? " " before JSON.parse. ? Why wrap JSON.parse of stored data in try/catch? + Stored data may be corrupt or unavailable; reading must not crash - JSON.parse always throws for text that comes from localStorage - try/catch makes JSON.parse turn the strings back into numbers - Without it, the object JSON.parse returns would be read-only Data may have been cut off, changed by an extension or written by another version, and storage may be blocked; catching the error lets you fall back to defaults. ? You store localStorage.setItem("count", 5) . What does localStorage.getItem("count") return? - 5 + "5" - null - an error Storage keeps strings only; the number is converted to "5".

title: A versioned settings store
body: Write createSettings(storage) , which keeps an app's settings in a localStorage -like object ( getItem , setItem , removeItem ) under the key "settings" : javascript const settings = createSettings(localStorage); settings.get("theme"); // "light" by default settings.set("theme", "dark"); // saves at once; returns true, or false if saving failed settings.all(); // a copy of every setting settings.reset(); // back to the defaults, and the key is removed from storage - Defaults: { theme: "light", fontSize: 14, sounds: true } . - Stored format: {"version": 2, "values": {...}} . Only keys that exist in the defaults are kept. - Version 1 stored {"version": 1, "dark": true, "size": "16"} : it becomes theme "dark" (or "light" when dark is false), and fontSize the number 16. Missing parts use the defaults. - Missing, corrupt JSON, an unknown version, or a getItem that throws: use the defaults. - Values of the wrong type are replaced by the default for that key (so a stored fontSize: "big" reads as 14). - set with an unknown key throws an Error unknown setting <key , and with a value of the wrong type a TypeError <key must be a <type . - If setItem throws (the storage is full), set still keeps the value in memory and returns false .

title: 6.04  Tooling
body: The tools around a JavaScript project - Node and npm, package.json and scripts, installing packages and semantic version ranges, the lock file, a dev server and bundler with Vite, TypeScript's tsconfig, ESLint and Prettier, testing with Vitest, and building for production. Node and npm Node.js runs JavaScript outside the browser: build tools, servers, scripts. It comes with npm , the package manager. A project is a folder with a package.json : bash npm init -y create package.json npm install date-fns a dependency your code imports npm install -D vitest typescript a devDependency: only needed while developing npm run test run a script from package.json npx tsc --version run a tool installed in the project json { "name": "shopping-list", "version": "1.0.0", "type": "module", "scripts": { "dev": "vite", "build": "tsc && vite build", "test": "vitest run", "lint": "eslint ." }, "dependencies": { "date-fns": "^4.1.0" }, "devDependencies": { "typescript": "~5.6.0", "vite": "^6.0.0", "vitest": "^2.1.0" } } "type": "module" makes .js files ES modules (lesson 3.05). Versions Packages use semantic versioning : MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH . A patch fixes bugs, a minor version adds features, a major version may break existing code. Range Allows --- --- 4.1.0 exactly 4.1.0 ^4.1.0 4.1.0 up to, not including, 5.0.0 (the npm default) ~4.1.0 4.1.0 up to, not including, 4.2.0 =4.1.0 anything from 4.1.0 Below 1.0.0, a caret is stricter: ^0.3.2 allows up to, not including, 0.4.0, because every 0.x minor may break things. npm install writes package-lock.json with the exact version of every package. Commit it, so everyone (and the build server) installs the same versions; use npm ci to install exactly what it says. Never commit node_modules ; add it to .gitignore . Vite A bundler with a dev server makes browser development fast: it serves your files, reloads the page as you save, handles TypeScript and npm imports, and produces optimised files for production. bash npm create vite@latest my-app -- --template vanilla-ts cd my-app npm install npm run dev http://localhost:5173, reloads on save npm run build optimised files in dist/, ready for any static host TypeScript configuration tsconfig.json controls the compiler. A good starting point: json { "compilerOptions": { "target": "ES2022", "module": "ESNext", "moduleResolution": "Bundler", "strict": true, "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true, "noEmit": true, "lib": "ES2022", "DOM" }, "include": "src" } With Vite, the bundler removes the types and tsc --noEmit (in the build script) only checks them. Linting, formatting and tests - ESLint finds likely bugs: unused variables, missing await , comparisons that are always false. npx eslint . - Prettier formats code the same way for everyone, ending arguments about style. Run it on save in your editor. - Vitest (or Jest) runs tests written like this course's: test("adds", () = { expect(add(2, 3)).toBe(5); }) . Pure functions, which this course has encouraged throughout, are the easiest to test. Security of dependencies Every package can run code on your machine when installed and in your users' browsers when bundled. Prefer few, well-known packages; read what a small package does before adding it; run npm audit for known vulnerabilities; and update regularly. Check yourself quiz ? Which versions does ^2.3.1 allow? - Exactly 2.3.1 - From 2.3.1 up to, but not including, 2.4.0 + From 2.3.1 up to, but not including, 3.0.0 - Any version from 2.3.1 upward, including 3.x The caret allows new minor and patch versions but not a new major one; the tilde ( ~2.3.1 ) is the one that stops below 2.4.0. ? Why commit package-lock.json? - npm cannot install any package without a lock file - It holds the project's scripts, name and dependency ranges - It makes the node_modules folder smaller and faster + It pins exact versions, so every install gets the same code It records the exact version of every package, and npm ci installs exactly that; scripts and the name live in package.json. ? Which belongs in devDependencies? + The test runner - A date library the app imports at run time - A UI component library used by the page - The app's own source code devDependencies are tools needed only while developing and building, like test runners and compilers.

title: Semantic versions
body: npm decides which package versions to install from ranges like ^4.1.0 . Write the core of that logic: javascript function parseVersion(text) { } // "4.1.0" gives 4, 1, 0 ; throws an Error "bad version <text " otherwise function compareVersions(a, b) { } // negative, 0 or positive, like a sort compare function function satisfies(version, range) { } // whether the version is inside the range function maxSatisfying(versions, range) { } // the highest version in the list that satisfies the range, or null A version is exactly three whole numbers without leading zeros ( 0 itself is fine) separated by dots. Ranges: Range Allows --- --- 1.2.3 exactly 1.2.3 =1.2.3 1.2.3 or higher ~1.2.3 at least 1.2.3, below 1.3.0 ^1.2.3 at least 1.2.3, below 2.0.0 ^0.2.3 at least 0.2.3, below 0.3.0 ^0.0.3 exactly 0.0.3 any version Compare numerically: 1.10.0 is higher than 1.9.0. Any other range throws an Error bad range <range .

title: 6.05  Project: A Web App
body: Putting the course together in a complete browser app - a single state object, actions and a pure update function, rendering from state with escaped HTML, event delegation, saving to localStorage with versions, and how the parts are split into modules and tested. The plan A small but complete app, a habit tracker : add habits, tick them off per day, see streaks, and keep everything after a reload. The structure works for most small apps: - State : one plain object that describes everything on screen. - Actions : plain objects such as { type: "add", name: "Read" } describing what the user did. - update : a pure function (state, action) = newState . No DOM, no storage: easy to test. - render : draws the page from the state. - storage : saves the state after each change and loads it at start. Modules text index.html src/ state.ts types, the initial state, update() - pure view.ts render(state) - HTML string, escapeHtml - pure storage.ts load() and save() with versions main.ts wiring: events - update - render + save Only main.ts touches the DOM and localStorage ; the other three can be tested without a browser. The project for this milestone is exactly those pure parts. State and actions typescript-norun export interface Habit { id: number; name: string; days: string } // days: "YYYY-MM-DD" ticked export interface State { version: 1; habits: Habit ; nextId: number } export type Action = { type: "add"; name: string } { type: "toggle"; id: number; day: string } { type: "remove"; id: number }; export function update(state: State, action: Action): State { switch (action.type) { case "add": return { ...state, habits: ...state.habits, { id: state.nextId, name: action.name.trim(), days: } , nextId: state.nextId + 1 }; case "toggle": return { ...state, habits: state.habits.map(h = h.id !== action.id ? h : { ...h, days: h.days.includes(action.day) ? h.days.filter(d = d !== action.day) : ...h.days, action.day .sort(), }) }; case "remove": return { ...state, habits: state.habits.filter(h = h.id !== action.id) }; } } update never changes the old state; it returns a new one. That makes undo trivial (keep old states) and bugs easier to find (nothing changes behind your back). Rendering typescript-norun export function render(state: State, today: string): string { if (state.habits.length === 0) return

title: Undo and redo
body: With a pure update(state, action) function (lesson 6.05), undo is just keeping old states. Write a wrapper that adds history to any update function: javascript function withHistory(update, limit = 50) { } It returns a new update function that works on { past, present, future } : javascript const counter = (n, action) = (action.type === "add" ? n + action.by : n); const update = withHistory(counter); let h = { past: , present: 0, future: }; h = update(h, { type: "add", by: 5 }); // { past: 0 , present: 5, future: } h = update(h, { type: "undo" }); // { past: , present: 0, future: 5 } h = update(h, { type: "redo" }); // { past: 0 , present: 5, future: } - Any action other than undo and redo goes to the inner update . If it returns the same present ( === ), nothing changes and the same history object is returned. Otherwise the old present joins past , and future is cleared. - undo with nothing in past , and redo with nothing in future , return the same history object. - past keeps at most limit states: the oldest are dropped. - The function never changes the history object it is given.
