title: A habit tracker
body: Build the tested core of the habit tracker from lesson 6.05, in TypeScript. With it, the app's main.ts only has to wire events to dispatch . Dates are "YYYY-MM-DD" strings. typescript interface Habit { id: number; name: string; days: string } // days ticked, sorted, no repeats interface State { version: 2; habits: Habit ; nextId: number } type Action = { type: "add"; name: string } { type: "rename"; id: number; name: string } { type: "toggle"; id: number; day: string } { type: "remove"; id: number }; const initialState: State // { version: 2, habits: , nextId: 1 } function update(state: State, action: Action): State function streak(days: readonly string , today: string): number function render(state: State, today: string): string function load(storage: StorageLike): State function save(storage: StorageLike, state: State): boolean where StorageLike is { getItem(key: string): string null; setItem(key: string, value: string): void } . update never changes the state it is given. When an action changes nothing, it returns the same state object. - add : trims the name. An empty name, or one that matches an existing habit's name ignoring case, changes nothing. Otherwise adds { id: nextId, name, days: } and increases nextId . - rename : the same name rules (the habit's own current name does not count as a clash); an unknown id changes nothing. - toggle : adds the day if it is not ticked, removes it if it is; days stays sorted. An unknown id changes nothing. - remove : an unknown id changes nothing. streak counts consecutive ticked days ending today ; if today is not ticked yet, ending yesterday (so a streak is not lost before the day is over). Otherwise 0. Work with UTC dates: Date.UTC or new Date(day + "T00:00:00Z") . render returns HTML on one line, with every name escaped ( & < " ' ): - no habits:

title: 7.01  Regular Expressions
body: Patterns that find and take apart text - writing a RegExp, character classes and quantifiers, anchors, groups and named groups, flags (g, i, m, s, u, y), test, match, matchAll, replace with a function, split, and keeping patterns readable. A pattern language for text A regular expression describes a set of strings: "a word", "a date like 2026-11-20", "anything between quotes". JavaScript writes them between slashes: javascript const datePattern = /\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}/; console.log(datePattern.test("due 2026-11-20")); // true console.log(datePattern.test("due tomorrow")); // false new RegExp("\\d+", "g") builds one from a string, which you need when the pattern is only known at run time (note the doubled backslash inside a string). The building blocks Pattern Matches --- --- abc exactly those characters . any character except a new line \d \w \s a digit, a word character (letter, digit, _ ), whitespace \D \W \S anything but those aeiou a-z0-9 ^, one character from a set, a range, or not in a set x x+ x? zero or more, one or more, zero or one x{3} x{2,5} x{2,} exactly 3, 2 to 5, at least 2 ^ $ start and end of the text (of each line with the m flag) \b a word boundary a\ b either \. \( \\ a special character taken literally Quantifiers are greedy : ".+" on "a" and "b" takes everything from the first quote to the last. Add ? to make them lazy: ".+?" stops at the first closing quote. Groups Parentheses group part of a pattern and capture what it matched. match (without the g flag) returns the whole match and every group: javascript const m = "Order 4512 shipped".match(/ (\d+)\s+(\w+)/); console.log(m 0 , " ", m 1 , " ", m 2 ); // 4512 shipped 4512 shipped Named groups make the result readable: javascript const { groups } = "2026-11-20".match(/(?<year \d{4})-(?<month \d{2})-(?<day \d{2})/); console.log(groups.year, groups.month, groups.day); (?:...) groups without capturing, when you only need the grouping for or a quantifier. Flags Flag Meaning --- --- g global: find every match, not just the first i ignore case m ^ and $ match at each line s . matches new lines too u Unicode: \u{1F600} and \p{L} (any letter) work y sticky: match only at lastIndex (for tokenizers) Finding every match With g , match returns just the matched strings. matchAll gives each match with its groups and position, which is usually what you want: javascript const text = "x=1, y=22, z=333"; console.log(text.match(/\d+/g)); // '1', '22', '333' for (const m of text.matchAll(/(\w)=(\d+)/g)) { console.log(m 1 , Number(m 2 ), "at", m.index); } Replacing and splitting replace with g (or replaceAll ) changes every match. The replacement can use $1 or $<name , or be a function that receives the match and its groups: javascript console.log("2026-11-20".replace(/(\d+)-(\d+)-(\d+)/, "$3/$2/$1")); // 20/11/2026 const shouted = "make it loud".replace(/\b\w/g, letter = letter.toUpperCase()); console.log(shouted); // Make It Loud console.log("a, b;c ,d".split(/\s ,; \s /)); // 'a', 'b', 'c', 'd' A word of caution A regular expression is great for finding and checking shapes of text. It is a poor tool for nested structures such as HTML or JSON: use a real parser ( JSON.parse , the DOM) for those. And a long pattern is hard to read, so build it from named pieces: javascript const number = String.raw \d+(?:\.\d+)? ; const unit = String.raw (?:kg g lb) ; const weight = new RegExp( ^(${number})\\s (${unit})$ , "i"); console.log("2.5 KG".match(weight).slice(1)); String.raw keeps backslashes as written, so you do not have to double them. Check yourself quiz ? On the text "a" and "b" , what is the difference between ".+" and ".+?" ? - The first stops at the first closing quote; the second runs to the last + The first runs to the last quote; the second stops at the first - ? makes the group optional, so the second may match nothing - There is none: both match "a" Quantifiers are greedy and take as much as they can; adding ? makes them lazy, so they stop as soon as the rest can match. ? When do you need new RegExp(...) instead of /.../ ? - When the pattern uses flags such as g or i - When the pattern contains named groups + When the pattern is only known at run time - Whenever it is used with matchAll A literal is fixed when you write the code. Flags, named groups and matchAll all work with literals too. ? What does "a1b22".match(/\d+/g) return? - '1', '2', '2' - '1' + '1', '22' - 'a1b22' With g, match returns every match; \d+ takes as many digits as it can each time.

title: Check a username
body: Write isValidUsername(name) using one regular expression. A valid username: - is 3 to 16 characters long, - uses only letters a – z (either case), digits and _ , - starts with a letter. javascript isValidUsername("ada_99"); // true isValidUsername("9lives"); // false: starts with a digit isValidUsername("al"); // false: too short

title: Parse a log line
body: Write parseLog(text) that reads lines like these and returns an array of objects, one per valid line: 2026-11-20 14:03:12 WARN disk: 91% used 2026-11-20 14:03:15 ERROR net: timeout after 30s garbage line 2026-11-20 14:04:00 info auth: user ada logged in javascript { date: "2026-11-20", time: "14:03:12", level: "WARN", source: "disk", message: "91% used" }, { date: "2026-11-20", time: "14:03:15", level: "ERROR", source: "net", message: "timeout after 30s" }, { date: "2026-11-20", time: "14:04:00", level: "INFO", source: "auth", message: "user ada logged in" }, - The level is any letters in square brackets, returned in upper case. - The source is word characters before the colon; the message is the rest of the line, trimmed. - Lines that do not have this shape are skipped. Lines may end with \n or \r\n . Then write countByLevel(entries) returning an object like { WARN: 1, ERROR: 1, INFO: 1 } .

title: 7.02  Getters, Setters and Symbols
body: Controlling properties - get and set on objects and classes, property descriptors with Object.defineProperty, freezing and sealing, Symbols as hidden keys, and the well-known symbols (Symbol.iterator, Symbol.toPrimitive, Symbol.toStringTag) that hook into the language. Getters and setters A getter is a function that runs when a property is read; a setter runs when it is assigned. From outside they look like plain properties: javascript class Temperature { celsius = 0; get celsius() { return this. celsius; } set celsius(value) { if (value < -273.15) throw new RangeError("below absolute zero"); this. celsius = value; } get fahrenheit() { return this. celsius 9 / 5 + 32; } // read-only: no setter } const t = new Temperature(); t.celsius = 25; console.log(t.fahrenheit); // 77 They work in object literals too: { get total() { return this.a + this.b; } } . Assigning to a getter-only property is silently ignored outside strict mode and an error inside it (and modules and classes are always strict). Property descriptors Every property has hidden settings. Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor shows them and Object.defineProperty sets them: javascript const config = {}; Object.defineProperty(config, "version", { value: "1.0", writable: false, // cannot be changed enumerable: false, // hidden from Object.keys and for...in configurable: false, // cannot be deleted or redefined }); console.log(config.version, Object.keys(config)); // 1.0 console.log(Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(config, "version")); Properties made the ordinary way are writable, enumerable and configurable. Freezing and sealing Call New properties Delete Change values --- --- --- --- Object.preventExtensions(o) no yes yes Object.seal(o) no no yes Object.freeze(o) no no no javascript "use strict"; const settings = Object.freeze({ theme: "dark", sizes: 1, 2 }); try { settings.theme = "light"; } catch (e) { console.log(e.constructor.name); // TypeError } settings.sizes.push(3); // freezing is shallow: nested objects can still change console.log(settings.sizes); Symbols A Symbol is a unique value that can be used as a property key. Two symbols with the same description are still different, so a symbol key never clashes with anyone else's property: javascript const id = Symbol("id"); const user = { name: "Ada", id : 42 }; console.log(user id , Object.keys(user), JSON.stringify(user)); // 42 'name' {"name":"Ada"} console.log(Symbol("id") === id); // false Symbol keys are skipped by Object.keys , for...in and JSON.stringify , which makes them good for attaching data to objects you do not own. Symbol.for("name") returns the same symbol everywhere for that name, when you do want sharing. Well-known symbols The language looks up some symbols on your objects to decide how to treat them. You met Symbol.iterator in lesson 3.04. Two more: javascript class Money { constructor(cents) { this.cents = cents; } // How the object turns into a primitive: hint is "number", "string" or "default". Symbol.toPrimitive (hint) { return hint === "number" ? this.cents / 100 : $${(this.cents / 100).toFixed(2)} ; } get Symbol.toStringTag () { return "Money"; } } const price = new Money(1250); console.log( ${price} , +price 2, Object.prototype.toString.call(price)); // $12.50 25 object Money Check yourself quiz ? Why does Object.freeze(settings) not stop settings.sizes.push(3) ? - push is allowed on frozen arrays; only assignment is blocked - Freezing only takes effect in strict mode + Freezing is shallow: the array inside is not frozen - The sizes property was added after the freeze The property sizes cannot be replaced, but the array it points to is a separate object that was never frozen. ? Why use a Symbol as a property key instead of a string? - Symbol keys are faster to look up than string keys - Symbol keys are included when JSON.stringify writes the object - Only symbol keys can be made non-enumerable with defineProperty + A symbol is unique, so it cannot clash with any other property Two symbols are different even with the same description, and symbol keys stay out of Object.keys, for...in and JSON. Any key can be made non-enumerable with defineProperty. ? An object has a getter area and no setter. In a module, what does shape.area = 5 do? - sets area to 5 - nothing at all - deletes the getter + throws a TypeError Modules are strict mode, where assigning to a property with only a getter is an error. Outside strict mode it would be silently ignored.

title: A checked rectangle
body: Write a class Rect with width and height accessors and a read-only area : - new Rect(width, height) sets both through the setters. - Setting width or height to anything that is not a positive finite number throws a RangeError . - area is computed from the current sizes and has no setter.

title: Money that behaves
body: Write a class Money that stores an amount in whole cents and a currency code: - new Money(cents, currency = "USD") ; cents must be an integer ( Number.isInteger ), otherwise TypeError . - add(other) returns a new Money ; adding a different currency throws Error with a message containing both codes. - Symbol.toPrimitive (hint) : for "number" the amount in units (1250 → 12.5); for "string" and "default" the text "12.50 USD" . - get Symbol.toStringTag () returns "Money" . - Objects are frozen after construction ( Object.isFrozen is true), so nobody can change an amount afterwards. - Money.sum(list) adds up an array of Money , returning new Money(0, currency) of the first item's currency, or new Money(0) for an empty array.

title: 7.03  Proxy, Reflect and Weak References
body: Intercepting what code does to an object - Proxy with get, set, has and deleteProperty traps, Reflect for doing the default, validation and change tracking with proxies, and WeakMap, WeakSet and WeakRef for data that must not keep objects alive. A stand-in for an object A Proxy wraps an object (the target ) and lets a handler step in whenever code reads, writes, deletes or checks a property. Each kind of operation has a trap : javascript const target = { name: "Ada" }; const logged = new Proxy(target, { get(obj, key, receiver) { console.log( read ${String(key)} ); return Reflect.get(obj, key, receiver); }, set(obj, key, value, receiver) { console.log( write ${String(key)} = ${value} ); return Reflect.set(obj, key, value, receiver); }, }); logged.age = 36; console.log(logged.name, target.age); Code using logged cannot tell it is not the real object. The set trap must return true when the write succeeded. Reflect: do the normal thing Reflect has one function per trap that performs the default behaviour: Reflect.get , Reflect.set , Reflect.has , Reflect.deleteProperty , Reflect.ownKeys . A trap that only wants to add something (logging, checking) does its extra work and then calls the matching Reflect function, as above. Common traps Trap Runs for --- --- get(target, key, receiver) p.x , p key set(target, key, value, receiver) p.x = v has(target, key) key in p deleteProperty(target, key) delete p.x ownKeys(target) Object.keys(p) , for...in apply(target, thisArg, args) calling p(...) when the target is a function Validation javascript function typed(shape) { return new Proxy({}, { set(obj, key, value) { if (!(key in shape)) throw new TypeError( unknown field ${String(key)} ); if (typeof value !== shape key ) throw new TypeError( ${String(key)} must be a ${shape key } ); obj key = value; return true; }, }); } const user = typed({ name: "string", age: "number" }); user.name = "Ada"; try { user.age = "old"; } catch (e) { console.log(e.message); } // age must be a number Default values javascript const counts = new Proxy({}, { get: (obj, key) = (key in obj ? obj key : 0), }); for (const word of "the cat the hat".split(" ")) counts word += 1; console.log(counts.the, counts.cat, counts.dog); // 2 1 0 Vue's reactivity, MobX and many test mocks are built on exactly these traps. Proxies are slower than plain objects, so keep them for the places where interception is the point. WeakMap and WeakSet A normal Map keeps its keys alive: as long as the map exists, the objects in it are never garbage-collected. A WeakMap holds its keys weakly : when nothing else refers to a key object, the entry disappears. Keys must be objects, and a WeakMap cannot be iterated (its contents depend on when the garbage collector runs). Use it to attach extra data to objects you do not own, without leaking memory: javascript const clickCount = new WeakMap(); function recordClick(element) { clickCount.set(element, (clickCount.get(element) ?? 0) + 1); } const button = { id: "save" }; // stands in for a DOM element recordClick(button); recordClick(button); console.log(clickCount.get(button)); // 2 // when the button is removed and forgotten, its count goes with it A WeakSet is the same idea for "have I seen this object?", for example to avoid visiting an object twice while walking a structure with cycles. WeakRef A WeakRef points at an object without keeping it alive; deref() returns the object, or undefined once it has been collected. It suits caches of large objects that may be rebuilt. When collection happens is up to the engine, so never write logic that depends on it. Check yourself quiz ? Why call Reflect.set(...) inside a set trap instead of obj key = value ? - obj key = value would run the set trap again, forever + It does the default assignment and returns whether it worked - Reflect.set also records the change for you - Assigning to the target is not allowed while a Proxy exists Reflect.set handles setters and the receiver like a normal assignment and returns true or false, which the trap must return. Writing to the target does not run the trap; only writes to the proxy do. ? Why can a WeakMap not be iterated? - Its keys are symbols, which loops skip - It only stores one entry at a time - Its entries are in random order, so a loop would be meaningless + Its entries vanish when the garbage collector removes their keys Its contents depend on when the garbage collector runs, so they are not something code could rely on. ? Which suits "remember extra data about objects owned by someone else, without keeping them alive"? - Map + WeakMap - an array - a Proxy A WeakMap entry goes away when nothing else refers to its key object; a Map would keep the object alive.

title: Read-only view
body: Write readOnly(obj) that returns a Proxy over obj which allows reading but refuses every change: - Reading properties works as normal. - Setting a property throws a TypeError whose message contains the property name. - Deleting a property throws a TypeError too. - The original object can still be changed directly, and the proxy shows those changes.

title: Watch for changes
body: Write observe(obj, onChange) returning a Proxy that reports every change, including changes inside nested objects and arrays : - Setting a property calls onChange(path, oldValue, newValue) , where path is the property path as an array, such as "settings", "theme" or "items", "2" . - Setting a property to the value it already has ( Object.is ) calls nothing. - Deleting a property calls onChange(path, oldValue, undefined) . - Reading a property whose value is an object or array returns an observed version of it, so nested changes are reported with the full path. - Reading the same nested object twice returns the same proxy (keep them in a WeakMap ). javascript const state = observe({ settings: { theme: "dark" }, items: }, (path, from, to) = console.log(path.join("."), from, "- ", to)); state.settings.theme = "light"; // settings.theme dark - light state.items.push("a"); // items.0 undefined - a

title: 7.04  Numbers, Dates and Intl
body: Getting numbers and times right - floating-point limits and Number.EPSILON, safe integers and BigInt, rounding money, the Date object and its pitfalls, ISO strings and time zones, and formatting numbers, dates, lists and plurals for any language with Intl. Every number is a double Ordinary JavaScript numbers are 64-bit floating point, the same as double in C. They hold integers exactly only up to 2^53 − 1, and most decimal fractions only approximately: javascript console.log(0.1 + 0.2, 0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3); // 0.30000000000000004 false console.log(Math.abs(0.1 + 0.2 - 0.3) < Number.EPSILON); // true: compare with a tolerance console.log(Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, 2 53 === 2 53 + 1); // 9007199254740991 true For money, count whole cents (integers) and format at the end, as the Money class in practice 7.02 does. Rounding javascript const x = 2.345; console.log(Math.round(x 100) / 100); // 2.35 (usually; x 100 may land just below) console.log(x.toFixed(2)); // "2.35": a string, for display console.log(Math.trunc(-2.7), Math.floor(-2.7), Math.ceil(-2.2)); // -2 -3 -2 BigInt When integers must be exact beyond 2^53 (ids, cryptography, factorials), use BigInt : write an n after the number or call BigInt(...) . javascript const big = 2n 64n; console.log(big, typeof big); // 18446744073709551616n bigint let factorial = 1n; for (let i = 1n; i <= 25n; i++) factorial = i; console.log(factorial.toString()); console.log(7n / 2n); // 3n: BigInt division truncates BigInts and numbers cannot be mixed in arithmetic ( 1n + 1 is a TypeError ); convert one side with Number(...) or BigInt(...) . JSON.stringify refuses BigInts, so send them as strings. Dates A Date is a moment in time, stored as milliseconds since 1 January 1970 UTC. It displays in the computer's local time zone unless you ask for UTC: javascript const d = new Date(Date.UTC(2026, 10, 20, 14, 30)); // months count from 0: 10 is November console.log(d.toISOString()); // 2026-11-20T14:30:00.000Z console.log(d.getUTCDay()); // 5: Friday (0 is Sunday) const later = new Date(d.getTime() + 90 60 1000); // add 90 minutes console.log(later.toISOString()); Pitfalls worth remembering: - months are 0 to 11, days of the month 1 to 31; - new Date("2026-11-20") is midnight UTC , but new Date("2026-11-20T00:00") is midnight local time; - a Date is mutable: setDate changes the object in place; - store and send dates as ISO strings ( toISOString() ), and convert to local time only when displaying. For calendar arithmetic across time zones, the coming Temporal API (and libraries like date-fns or Luxon today) are much safer than Date . Intl: formatting for people Intl formats values the way each language and country expects: javascript const n = 1234567.891; console.log(new Intl.NumberFormat("en-US").format(n)); // 1,234,567.891 console.log(new Intl.NumberFormat("de-DE").format(n)); // 1.234.567,891 console.log(new Intl.NumberFormat("en-US", { style: "currency", currency: "EUR" }).format(12.5)); console.log(new Intl.NumberFormat("en", { notation: "compact" }).format(n)); // 1.2M const when = new Date(Date.UTC(2026, 10, 20, 14, 30)); console.log(new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-GB", { dateStyle: "long", timeZone: "UTC" }).format(when)); // 20 November 2026 console.log(new Intl.ListFormat("en", { type: "conjunction" }).format( "tea", "cake", "jam" )); // tea, cake, and jam const plural = new Intl.PluralRules("en"); for (const count of 0, 1, 2 ) console.log(count, plural.select(count)); // other one other Intl.RelativeTimeFormat writes "3 days ago", and Intl.Collator sorts text the way a language expects ( "ä", "z", "a" .sort(new Intl.Collator("de").compare) ). Check yourself quiz ? Why should money be stored in whole cents? - Doubles lose precision for any amount larger than 100 + Decimal fractions are not exact as doubles, but whole numbers are - Intl.NumberFormat can only format whole numbers of cents - Whole cents take less memory than amounts with decimals 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004, so sums of fractions drift; whole cents add exactly and are formatted at the end. ? What is new Date(2026, 0, 31) ? - 31 January 2026, midnight UTC - An Invalid Date, because there is no month 0 + 31 January 2026, in local time - 28 February 2026, because months count from 1 Months count from 0, so 0 is January, and these number arguments are read in local time; Date.UTC(...) gives UTC. ? What does 10n + 5 do? + throws a TypeError: the two cannot be mixed - gives 15n, turning 5 into a BigInt - gives 15, turning 10n into a number - gives "105", joining them as text BigInt and number cannot be mixed in arithmetic; convert one of them first with BigInt(...) or Number(...).

title: Big factorials and digit sums
body: Write two functions with BigInt: - factorial(n) returns n! as a BigInt for a whole number n from 0 up ( factorial(0) is 1n ). A negative or fractional n throws RangeError . - digitSum(big) returns the sum of the decimal digits of a non-negative BigInt, as an ordinary number. javascript factorial(25); // 15511210043330985984000000n digitSum(factorial(100)); // 648

title: A friendly receipt
body: Write receipt(items, locale, currency) that formats a shopping list with Intl . items is an array of { name, cents, qty } . - Each line is "<qty × <name : <line total " , the total formatted with Intl.NumberFormat(locale, { style: "currency", currency }) from qty cents / 100 . - Then a line "Total: <sum " . - Then a line listing the item names with Intl.ListFormat(locale, { type: "conjunction" }) , followed by " — " and the item count with the right plural: "1 item" or "<n items" (use Intl.PluralRules("en") to choose). - Lines are joined with "\n" . For locale = "en-US" and currency = "USD" : 2 × Tea: $5.00 1 × Cake: $3.75 Total: $8.75 Tea and Cake — 3 items An empty list gives "Total: <zero " and nothing else.

title: 7.05  Advanced TypeScript Types
body: Types that compute other types - keyof, typeof and indexed access, mapped types, conditional types and infer, template literal types, satisfies, user-defined type guards and assertion functions, and declaration files for JavaScript code. Types from values and from other types Lessons 5.01 to 5.05 wrote types by hand. TypeScript can also derive types, so they stay in step with the code automatically. typescript const defaults = { theme: "dark", fontSize: 14, showTips: true }; type Settings = typeof defaults; // { theme: string; fontSize: number; showTips: boolean } type SettingName = keyof Settings; // "theme" "fontSize" "showTips" type FontSize = Settings "fontSize" ; // number (an indexed access type) function get<K extends SettingName (name: K): Settings K { return defaults name ; } const size = get("fontSize"); // number, known from the argument console.log(size + 1); typeof (in a type position) turns a value into its type; keyof gives the union of a type's keys; T K looks up the type of a property. Mapped types A mapped type builds a new object type by going over the keys of another: typescript type Settings = { theme: string; fontSize: number }; type Flags<T = { K in keyof T : boolean }; // same keys, every value boolean type Getters<T = { K in keyof T as get${Capitalize<string & K } : () = T K }; type Mutable<T = { -readonly K in keyof T : T K }; // removes readonly const changed: Flags<Settings = { theme: true, fontSize: false }; const api: Getters<Settings = { getTheme: () = "dark", getFontSize: () = 14 }; console.log(changed.theme, api.getFontSize()); The utility types you already use ( Partial , Readonly , Pick , Record ) are mapped types in the standard library. Conditional types and infer A conditional type chooses between two types: T extends U ? X : Y . With infer , it can pull a type out of another: typescript type IsString<T = T extends string ? "yes" : "no"; type A = IsString<"hi" ; // "yes" type ElementOf<T = T extends readonly (infer E) ? E : never; type B = ElementOf<number ; // number type Awaited2<T = T extends Promise<infer V ? V : T; type C = Awaited2<Promise<string ; // string const check: A, B, C = "yes", 42, "done" ; console.log(check); Given a union, a conditional type is applied to each member separately, which is how Exclude<T, U removes members: type Exclude<T, U = T extends U ? never : T; . Template literal types Strings can be built at the type level too: typescript type Side = "top" "bottom"; type Edge = "left" "right"; type Corner = ${Side}-${Edge} ; // "top-left" "top-right" "bottom-left" "bottom-right" type EventName<T extends string = on${Capitalize<T } ; const corner: Corner = "bottom-left"; const handler: EventName<"click" = "onClick"; console.log(corner, handler); satisfies satisfies checks a value against a type without widening the value's own type: typescript type Colour = "red" "green" "blue"; const palette = { red: 255, 0, 0 , green: " 00ff00", } satisfies Partial<Record<Colour, string number ; console.log(palette.green.toUpperCase()); // still known to be a string console.log(palette.red.length); // still known to be an array With : Partial<Record<... instead, both properties would have the wide type string number undefined . Type guards and assertion functions A function returning value is Type teaches TypeScript to narrow (lesson 5.03) with your own check: typescript type Cat = { kind: "cat"; meow(): string }; type Dog = { kind: "dog"; bark(): string }; function isCat(pet: Cat Dog): pet is Cat { return pet.kind === "cat"; } function assertDefined<T (value: T undefined, name: string): asserts value is T { if (value === undefined) throw new Error( ${name} is missing ); } function speak(pet: Cat Dog): string { return isCat(pet) ? pet.meow() : pet.bark(); // pet is Cat, then Dog } console.log(speak({ kind: "dog", bark: () = "woof" })); const port: number undefined = 8080; assertDefined(port, "port"); console.log(port + 1); // number from here on Declaration files A plain JavaScript library has no types. A declaration file ( .d.ts ) describes it without any code: typescript-norun // greet.d.ts export function greet(name: string, options?: { shout?: boolean }): string; export const version: string; Most popular libraries ship their own, and the rest have community ones installed with npm install --save-dev @types/<library . Check yourself quiz ? What is keyof { a: number; b: string } ? - number string + "a" "b" - "a", "b" - string keyof gives the union of the property names; T keyof T would give the union of the value types. ? What does satisfies give you that a type annotation does not? - It converts the value to that type when the code runs - It switches off the excess property check for literals + The value is checked but keeps its own, more precise type - It makes every property of the value readonly With an annotation the variable takes the wide annotated type; with satisfies, palette.green is still known to be a string. ? What is ElementOf<string with type ElementOf<T = T extends readonly (infer E) ? E : never? - string - never + string - unknown infer E captures the element type of the array.

title: A typed event emitter
body: Write a class Emitter<Events where Events maps each event name to the type of its payload: typescript type AppEvents = { login: { user: string }; logout: undefined; error: Error }; const bus = new Emitter<AppEvents (); const off = bus.on("login", e = console.log(e.user)); // e is { user: string } bus.emit("login", { user: "ada" }); off(); // stops listening - on<K extends keyof Events (name: K, listener: (payload: Events K ) = void): () = void adds a listener and returns a function that removes it. - emit<K extends keyof Events (name: K, payload: Events K ): number calls every listener of that event in the order they were added and returns how many were called.

title: Validate a config by its schema
match: Validate a config by its schema
body: Write parseConfig(schema, input) where schema describes the expected fields and the return type is computed from the schema : typescript const schema = { port: "number", host: "string", debug: "boolean" } as const; const config = parseConfig(schema, { port: 8080, host: "localhost", debug: false }); config.port.toFixed(0); // config: { port: number; host: string; debug: boolean } - Define type FieldType = "string" "number" "boolean" . - Define type TypeOf<F extends FieldType , a conditional type giving string , number or boolean . - Define type Parsed<S extends Record<string, FieldType = { K in keyof S : TypeOf<S K } , a mapped type. - parseConfig<S extends Record<string, FieldType (schema: S, input: unknown): Parsed<S checks that input is a non-null object, that every field in the schema is present with a value of the right typeof , and returns an object with only the schema's fields. Anything wrong throws a TypeError whose message names the field (or says the input is not an object).

title: 7.06  Node.js
body: JavaScript outside the browser - what Node.js adds, ES modules and CommonJS, reading and writing files with node:fs/promises, paths, command-line arguments and environment variables, exit codes, streams for big files, and package.json scripts. One language, two places The browser gives JavaScript the DOM, fetch and localStorage . Node.js runs the same language on a computer or server and gives it the operating system instead: files, processes, network sockets. Tools you already use (npm, Vite, the TypeScript compiler, ESLint) are Node programs. javascript-norun // hello.mjs, run with: node hello.mjs Ada const name = process.argv 2 ?? "world"; console.log( hello, ${name} ); Xenon's practice sandbox imitates a small part of Node ( console , process.argv , require("fs") for the project's own files). The examples marked as not runnable here are for your own machine. Modules: two systems ES modules CommonJS --- --- --- Syntax import x from "./x.js" , export const x = require("./x") , module.exports Files .mjs , or .js with "type": "module" in package.json .cjs , or .js by default Loading can await at the top level synchronous New code uses ES modules (lesson 3.05). You still meet CommonJS in older packages, and import can load it. Files node:fs/promises has promise-based versions of every file function: javascript-norun import { readFile, writeFile, readdir, mkdir } from "node:fs/promises"; import path from "node:path"; const text = await readFile("notes.txt", "utf8"); const words = text.split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean).length; await mkdir("out", { recursive: true }); await writeFile(path.join("out", "count.txt"), ${words} words\n ); for (const entry of await readdir(".", { withFileTypes: true })) { console.log(entry.isDirectory() ? "dir " : "file", entry.name); } A missing file rejects with an error whose code is "ENOENT" ; check err.code to tell "not there" from other problems. node:path builds paths correctly on every system: path.join , path.basename , path.extname , path.resolve . Arguments, environment and exit codes javascript-norun // node tool.mjs --limit 5 input.csv const args = process.argv.slice(2); // '--limit', '5', 'input.csv' const debug = process.env.DEBUG === "1"; // set with: DEBUG=1 node tool.mjs (PowerShell: $env:DEBUG=1) if (args.length === 0) { console.error("usage: tool --limit N FILE"); process.exit(2); // non-zero means failure to whoever started the program } node:util has parseArgs for real argument parsing; for anything bigger, packages such as commander do the work. Write errors to console.error (standard error) so they do not mix with the program's real output. Streams for big files readFile loads a whole file into memory. For a file of several gigabytes, read it as a stream , piece by piece: javascript-norun import { createReadStream } from "node:fs"; import { createInterface } from "node:readline"; let lines = 0; for await (const line of createInterface({ input: createReadStream("huge.log") })) { if (line.includes("ERROR")) lines++; } console.log(lines, "error lines"); for await (lesson 4.03) reads one line at a time, so memory use stays flat whatever the file size. package.json and npm scripts npm init -y creates a package.json describing the project: its name, dependencies, and scripts : json { "name": "word-tool", "type": "module", "scripts": { "start": "node src/main.js", "test": "node --test" }, "dependencies": { "chalk": "^5.3.0" } } npm install chalk adds a dependency, npm run start runs a script, and npm test runs the test script. node --test is Node's built-in test runner: files that call test(...) from node:test with assert from node:assert/strict . A pure core, a thin shell Keep the logic (parsing, counting, deciding) in plain functions that take values and return values, and keep the file and process handling in a thin outer layer. The core can then be tested anywhere, including Xenon's sandbox, and the shell is small enough to check by running it. Check yourself quiz ? Why read a huge file as a stream instead of with readFile ? - readFile cannot read files that have more than one line - Streams make the disk itself read the file faster + A stream handles one piece at a time, so memory use stays flat - readFile can only be used in ES modules, not in scripts readFile loads the whole file into memory; a stream read with for await keeps only the current piece. ? What does process.exit(2) tell the program that started yours? + That it failed: any non-zero exit code means failure - That it finished successfully with two results - That it should start the program again - Nothing: exit codes are only shown to the user 0 means success; any other number means failure, and the number can say which kind. ? Which is the ES module way to bring in path? - const path = require("node:path"); - include <path - using path; + import path from "node:path"; import is ES modules; require is the older CommonJS system.

title: 8.01  Binary Data with Typed Arrays
body: Working with raw bytes in JavaScript - ArrayBuffer as a block of memory, typed arrays such as Uint8Array and Float32Array as views of it, DataView for reading numbers in a chosen byte order, TextEncoder and TextDecoder for UTF-8, and parsing a binary file format. Why bytes? Images, sound, network packets, game save files and WebAssembly all deal in raw bytes. Ordinary arrays hold any JavaScript value and are a poor fit: each element might be a number, a string or an object. JavaScript has separate types for binary data. ArrayBuffer and typed arrays An ArrayBuffer is a fixed block of bytes, all zero at first. You cannot read it directly; you look at it through a view : javascript const buffer = new ArrayBuffer(8); const bytes = new Uint8Array(buffer); bytes 0 = 255; bytes 1 = 256; // wraps to 0: a Uint8 holds 0 to 255 bytes 2 = -1; // wraps to 255 console.log(bytes, buffer.byteLength); Each typed array has a fixed element type: type size range --- --- --- Int8Array / Uint8Array 1 byte -128..127 / 0..255 Uint8ClampedArray 1 byte 0..255, clamping instead of wrapping (for pixels) Int16Array / Uint16Array 2 bytes Int32Array / Uint32Array 4 bytes Float32Array / Float64Array 4 / 8 bytes floating point BigInt64Array / BigUint64Array 8 bytes BigInt values Typed arrays have most array methods ( map , filter , reduce , slice , indexOf , fill ), but a fixed length: there is no push . javascript const scores = Float32Array.from( 1.5, 2.25, 3 ); console.log(scores.map(x = x 2), scores.reduce((a, b) = a + b, 0)); const clamped = new Uint8ClampedArray( 300, -20, 128.6 ); console.log(clamped); // Uint8ClampedArray(3) 255, 0, 129 Several views of the same bytes Two views over one buffer share the memory: javascript const buffer = new ArrayBuffer(4); const asInt = new Uint32Array(buffer); const asBytes = new Uint8Array(buffer); asInt 0 = 0x11223344; console.log( ...asBytes .map(b = b.toString(16))); // '44', '33', '22', '11' on a little-endian machine The order of those bytes depends on the computer. That is fine inside one program, but not for files or networks, which need a fixed order. DataView: numbers in a chosen byte order DataView reads and writes numbers of any size at any byte offset, with the byte order you choose ( true means little-endian): javascript const view = new DataView(new ArrayBuffer(12)); view.setUint16(0, 7, true); view.setUint32(2, 1_000_000, true); view.setFloat32(6, 1.5, true); view.setUint16(10, 0x1234, false); // big-endian const hex = ...new Uint8Array(view.buffer) .map(b = b.toString(16).padStart(2, "0")).join(" "); console.log(hex); console.log(view.getUint16(0, true), view.getUint32(2, true), view.getFloat32(6, true), view.getUint16(10, false).toString(16)); Reading past the end throws a RangeError , so a broken file cannot make you read random memory. Text and bytes TextEncoder turns a string into UTF-8 bytes, and TextDecoder turns bytes back into a string: javascript const bytes = new TextEncoder().encode("café"); console.log(bytes, bytes.length); console.log(new TextDecoder().decode(bytes)); console.log(new TextDecoder("utf-8", { fatal: false }).decode(new Uint8Array( 0xff, 0x41 ))); "café".length is 4 but its UTF-8 form has 5 bytes, because é takes two. Parsing a small format A record format: a 4-byte magic "XNSV" , a 2-byte count, then for each record a 1-byte name length, the name, and a 4-byte score, all little-endian. javascript function parse(buffer) { const view = new DataView(buffer); const magic = new TextDecoder().decode(new Uint8Array(buffer, 0, 4)); if (magic !== "XNSV") throw new Error("not a save file"); const count = view.getUint16(4, true); const records = ; let pos = 6; for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) { const len = view.getUint8(pos); const name = new TextDecoder().decode(new Uint8Array(buffer, pos + 1, len)); const score = view.getUint32(pos + 1 + len, true); records.push({ name, score }); pos += 1 + len + 4; } return records; } // build a file to test with const enc = new TextEncoder(); const parts = enc.encode("XNSV"), new Uint8Array( 2, 0 ) ; for (const name, score of "ada", 1500 , "bob", 80 ) { const n = enc.encode(name); const s = new Uint8Array(4); new DataView(s.buffer).setUint32(0, score, true); parts.push(new Uint8Array( n.length ), n, s); } const total = parts.reduce((a, p) = a + p.length, 0); const file = new Uint8Array(total); let at = 0; for (const p of parts) { file.set(p, at); at += p.length; } console.log(parse(file.buffer)); new Uint8Array(buffer, offset, length) is a view of part of the buffer without copying, and set copies one typed array into another at a position. Where these appear - fetch(url).then(r = r.arrayBuffer()) and File.arrayBuffer() give an ArrayBuffer . - A canvas's getImageData().data is a Uint8ClampedArray of RGBA pixels. - In Node.js, Buffer is a subclass of Uint8Array with extra methods. Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference between a Uint8Array and a DataView over the same buffer? - A DataView copies the bytes, while a Uint8Array shares them + A DataView reads any number type at any offset and byte order - A Uint8Array can only be read; a DataView can also write - There is none: DataView is an older name for Uint8Array A Uint8Array sees the buffer as single bytes (one element type). Both are views of the same memory, and both can read and write. ? Why is "café".length different from its UTF-8 byte count? - UTF-8 always stores every character in two bytes - TextEncoder adds an end marker byte to every string it encodes + length counts UTF-16 units; UTF-8 needs two bytes for é - length skips accented letters when it counts "café".length is 4, but its UTF-8 form has 5 bytes: one each for c, a and f, two for é. ? A Uint8Array element is set to 300. What does it hold? + 44, because it wraps around modulo 256 - 300, because the array widens the element - 255, the largest value a byte can hold - Nothing: it throws a RangeError Uint8Array wraps modulo 256 (300 - 256 = 44). Uint8ClampedArray would hold 255.

title: Bytes to hex and back
body: Write two helpers: - toHex(bytes) takes a Uint8Array and returns its bytes as two-digit lower-case hex separated by spaces: toHex(new Uint8Array( 0, 255, 16 )) is "00 ff 10" . An empty array gives "" . - fromHex(text) does the reverse and returns a Uint8Array . Spaces anywhere are ignored, upper case is fine, and anything that is not an even number of hex digits throws a SyntaxError .

title: Reading a bitmap header
body: BMP image files start with a header. Write readBmpHeader(buffer) that takes an ArrayBuffer and returns { fileSize, dataOffset, width, height, topDown, bitsPerPixel } , using a DataView (every value is little-endian): offset type meaning --- --- --- 0 2 bytes the letters BM 2 uint32 file size 10 uint32 where the pixel data starts 14 uint32 header size, at least 40 18 int32 width 22 int32 height: negative means the rows are stored top-down 26 uint16 planes, must be 1 28 uint16 bits per pixel: 1, 4, 8, 16, 24 or 32 Return height as a positive number and topDown as a boolean. Throw an Error when the buffer is shorter than 54 bytes, the letters are wrong, the header size is under 40, the planes are not 1, the bits are not allowed, or the width is 0 or less.

title: 8.02  Async Generators and Iteration
body: Data that arrives a piece at a time - async iterables and for await...of, async generator functions with async function , paging through an API lazily, transforming async streams with small helper generators, stopping early with break and return, and the Symbol.asyncIterator protocol. A loop that waits Lesson 3.04 showed generators: functions that yield values one by one to a for...of loop. Lesson 4.03 showed await . Put them together and you get a loop whose values arrive over time : pages from an API, lines from a file, messages from a socket. javascript const sleep = ms = new Promise(r = setTimeout(r, ms)); async function countdown(from) { for (let i = from; i 0; i--) { await sleep(10); yield i; } } (async () = { for await (const n of countdown(3)) console.log(n); console.log("lift off"); })(); async function declares an async generator . It can await inside, and each yield hands one value to the loop. for await...of waits for each value before running the body. Paging through an API, lazily Many APIs return results a page at a time with a "next" cursor. An async generator hides the pages, so the caller sees one stream of items: javascript const pages = { start: { items: 1, 2, 3 , next: "p2" }, p2: { items: 4, 5 , next: "p3" }, p3: { items: 6 , next: null } }; let requests = 0; async function fetchPage(cursor) { requests++; await new Promise(r = setTimeout(r, 5)); return pages cursor ; } async function allItems() { let cursor = "start"; while (cursor) { const page = await fetchPage(cursor); yield page.items; // yield each item of the page cursor = page.next; } } (async () = { for await (const item of allItems()) { console.log("item", item); if (item === 4) break; // stop early } console.log("requests made:", requests); })(); Because the generator is lazy, stopping at 4 means page 3 is never requested. break (or return , or an exception) in a for await loop also tells the generator to finish, running any finally block inside it, so it can close connections. Helpers for streams Small async generators that take a stream and give back a changed one can be chained like array methods: javascript async function map(source, fn) { for await (const x of source) yield fn(x); } async function filter(source, test) { for await (const x of source) if (test(x)) yield x; } async function take(source, n) { if (n <= 0) return; for await (const x of source) { yield x; if (--n === 0) return; } } async function toArray(source) { const out = ; for await (const x of source) out.push(x); return out; } async function numbers() { for (let i = 1; ; i++) yield i; // endless } (async () = { const result = await toArray(take(filter(map(numbers(), x = x x), x = x % 2 === 1), 4)); console.log(result); // 1, 9, 25, 49 })(); Working on an endless source is only possible because each step pulls one value at a time. for await over ordinary promises for await also accepts a normal array of promises, waiting for each in order: javascript const later = (v, ms) = new Promise(r = setTimeout(() = r(v), ms)); (async () = { for await (const v of later("a", 30), later("b", 10) ) console.log(v); // a, then b })(); To handle results as they finish rather than in order, use Promise.race in a loop, or a library helper; for await keeps the order you gave. The protocol An object is async-iterable when it has a Symbol.asyncIterator () method returning an object with an async next() that resolves to { value, done } . Async generators build this for you, but you can write it by hand: javascript const ticker = { Symbol.asyncIterator () { let n = 0; return { async next() { await new Promise(r = setTimeout(r, 5)); return n < 3 ? { value: n++, done: false } : { value: undefined, done: true }; }, }; }, }; (async () = { for await (const t of ticker) console.log("tick", t); })(); Node.js streams, fs.promises file handles ( file.readLines() ), and the browser's ReadableStream are all async-iterable. Errors An error thrown inside an async generator comes out of the for await loop, where an ordinary try / catch handles it: javascript async function risky() { yield 1; throw new Error("connection lost"); } (async () = { try { for await (const x of risky()) console.log(x); } catch (e) { console.log("caught:", e.message); } })(); Check yourself quiz ? Why does breaking out of the paging loop save requests? - break cancels the requests that are already in flight + The generator fetches a page only when the loop asks for more - break throws inside fetchPage, which stops it - for await caches the pages, so they are never fetched twice The generator is lazy: after break nothing asks for the next item, so page 3 is never requested. ? What runs when a for await loop ends early with break ? - Nothing: the generator just stays paused forever - The generator keeps running to its end, with nobody listening + The generator's return() is called, so its finally runs - An AbortError is thrown into the generator at its yield break, return or an exception tells the generator to finish, which runs any finally inside it so it can close connections. ? Which declares an async generator? - async function gen() { yield 1; } + async function gen() { yield 1; } - function async gen() { yield 1; } - await function gen() { yield 1; } The star after function makes it a generator; async in front lets it await.

title: 8.03  Cancelling Work with AbortController
body: Stopping work that is no longer wanted - AbortController and AbortSignal, cancelling fetch, timeouts with AbortSignal.timeout, combining signals with AbortSignal.any, making your own async functions cancellable, cleaning up listeners, and the AbortError convention. Work nobody is waiting for A user types in a search box: each key starts a search, and only the last result matters. A user leaves a page while it is still loading. A request takes too long. In each case the program should stop the work, not just ignore its result: stopping saves the network, the battery and the server. JavaScript's standard way to ask for that is a pair of objects: - an AbortController , held by the code that may want to cancel; - its AbortSignal ( controller.signal ), passed to the work that should stop. javascript const controller = new AbortController(); const signal = controller.signal; signal.addEventListener("abort", () = console.log("abort event, reason:", signal.reason)); console.log(signal.aborted); // false controller.abort("user left"); console.log(signal.aborted); // true abort() can only happen once; calling it again does nothing. Cancelling fetch fetch accepts a signal . When it is aborted, the request stops and the promise rejects with an error whose name is "AbortError" : javascript-norun const controller = new AbortController(); const promise = fetch("/api/search?q=tea", { signal: controller.signal }); controller.abort(); try { await promise; } catch (e) { if (e.name === "AbortError") console.log("cancelled, as asked"); else throw e; } Treat AbortError differently from real failures: it is not a problem to report to the user. Timeouts AbortSignal.timeout(ms) gives a signal that aborts itself after a time (with a "TimeoutError" ), and AbortSignal.any( ... ) gives a signal that aborts when any of several does: javascript-norun const userCancel = new AbortController(); const signal = AbortSignal.any( userCancel.signal, AbortSignal.timeout(5000) ); const response = await fetch("/api/report", { signal }); Making your own functions cancellable Any async function can take a signal. The two rules: 1. Check signal.aborted (or call signal.throwIfAborted() ) before starting and between steps. 2. While waiting, listen for the abort event and stop waiting at once. javascript function sleep(ms, signal) { return new Promise((resolve, reject) = { if (signal?.aborted) return reject(signal.reason); const timer = setTimeout(() = { signal?.removeEventListener("abort", onAbort); resolve(); }, ms); function onAbort() { clearTimeout(timer); reject(signal.reason); } signal?.addEventListener("abort", onAbort, { once: true }); }); } async function slowCount(n, signal) { for (let i = 1; i <= n; i++) { signal?.throwIfAborted(); await sleep(20, signal); console.log("step", i); } return "finished"; } const controller = new AbortController(); setTimeout(() = controller.abort(new Error("stopped by the user")), 50); slowCount(10, controller.signal).then(console.log, e = console.log("ended:", e.message)); The listener is removed when the timer finishes normally. Forgetting to remove listeners from a long-lived signal is a memory leak. The newest search wins Cancelling the previous request each time a new one starts: javascript let current = null; const log = ; function fakeSearch(text, signal) { return sleepValue(text.length 15, results for ${text} , signal); } function sleepValue(ms, value, signal) { return new Promise((resolve, reject) = { const t = setTimeout(() = resolve(value), ms); signal.addEventListener("abort", () = { clearTimeout(t); reject(signal.reason); }, { once: true }); }); } async function search(text) { current?.abort(); current = new AbortController(); try { log.push(await fakeSearch(text, current.signal)); } catch (e) { if (e.name !== "AbortError") throw e; log.push( cancelled ${text} ); } } Promise.all( search("t"), search("te"), search("tea") ).then(() = console.log(log)); controller.abort() with no argument gives a DOMException named "AbortError" as the reason, which is why the check works. Not only for async work Event listeners accept a signal too: aborting removes every listener that was added with it, which is a tidy way to clean up a component. javascript-norun const controller = new AbortController(); window.addEventListener("resize", onResize, { signal: controller.signal }); document.addEventListener("keydown", onKey, { signal: controller.signal }); // later, when the component goes away: controller.abort(); // both listeners removed Check yourself quiz ? Who holds the AbortController and who gets the signal? + The code that may cancel keeps the controller; the work gets only the signal - The work keeps the controller, and the caller listens to the signal - Both share the controller, so either side can cancel - fetch creates the controller and returns its signal The work can listen for abort but cannot cancel anything; only whoever holds the controller can call abort(). ? Why should a cancellable wait remove its abort listener when it finishes normally? - A listener left on the signal aborts the next wait at once - Removing the listener is what resolves the promise + The signal can outlive the wait, so leftover listeners leak memory - A signal allows only one listener at a time Listeners left on a long-lived signal keep their closures alive and would run later for no reason. ? What does fetch do when its signal is aborted? - returns a response with status 499 (client closed) - ignores it until the response has fully arrived + stops the request and rejects with an AbortError - resolves with undefined instead of a response The promise rejects, with an error whose name is "AbortError".

title: A sleep you can cancel
body: Write sleep(ms, signal) that returns a promise resolving after ms milliseconds, unless the optional AbortSignal aborts first: - if the signal is already aborted, reject at once with signal.reason ; - if it aborts while waiting, clear the timer and reject with signal.reason ; - when the time passes normally, remove the abort listener and resolve.

title: A timeout for any task
body: Write withTimeout(task, ms, outerSignal) : - task is a function that takes an AbortSignal and returns a promise; - call it with a new signal that aborts when ms milliseconds pass or when outerSignal (optional) aborts, whichever comes first; - resolve or reject as the task does; when the time runs out, reject with an Error whose name is "TimeoutError" ; when the outer signal aborts, reject with its reason; - clear the timer and remove listeners from outerSignal when it settles. Do not use AbortSignal.timeout or AbortSignal.any : build it from an AbortController .

title: 8.04  Testing JavaScript
body: Automated tests for JavaScript and TypeScript - what a test runner does, node:test and node:assert, deepStrictEqual versus strictEqual, testing errors and async code, fakes and spies made from plain functions, fake timers, and the shape of tests in Vitest and Jest. Why write tests? Every practice task on this site is checked by tests. Writing your own gives the same safety for your projects: change code, run the tests, and know within seconds whether something broke. A test runner does three jobs: finds the tests, runs each one even if others fail, and reports which failed and why. Node.js has one built in ( node:test ), and most front-end projects use Vitest or Jest, which look almost the same. node:test and node:assert javascript-norun // math.test.js, run with: node --test import { test } from "node:test"; import assert from "node:assert/strict"; import { average } from "./math.js"; test("average of two numbers", () = { assert.equal(average( 2, 4 ), 3); }); test("empty input throws", () = { assert.throws(() = average( ), RangeError); }); node --test finds files named like .test.js and runs them. The strict assert module gives: assertion passes when --- --- assert.equal(a, b) a === b assert.deepEqual(a, b) the two have the same structure and values assert.ok(x) x is truthy assert.throws(fn, Kind) calling fn throws an error of that kind await assert.rejects(promise, Kind) the promise rejects assert.match(text, /re/) the text matches Equal and deep equal javascript-norun import("node:assert/strict").then(({ default: assert }) = { assert.deepEqual({ a: 1, 2 }, { a: 1, 2 }); // passes: same contents try { assert.equal({ a: 1 }, { a: 1 }); // fails: two different objects } catch (e) { console.log(e.name); } console.log("done"); }); === compares objects by identity, so two objects with the same contents are not equal. Use the deep version for arrays and objects. Testing async code A test function can be async ; the runner waits for it. An assertion that fails inside it, or a rejection that is not caught, fails the test: javascript-norun test("loads the user", async () = { const user = await loadUser(1, fakeApi); assert.equal(user.name, "Ada"); }); test("a missing user rejects", async () = { await assert.rejects(loadUser(99, fakeApi), /not found/); }); Forgetting await before assert.rejects is a classic mistake: the test finishes before the check happens. Fakes and spies Code that talks to the network, the clock or the disk is hard to test. The cure is the same as in every language: pass those things in, and give the test a fake. javascript function makeSpy(result) { const spy = (...args) = { spy.calls.push(args); return typeof result === "function" ? result(...args) : result; }; spy.calls = ; return spy; } async function notifyOverdue(books, today, send) { let sent = 0; for (const b of books) { if (b.due < today) { await send(b.borrower, "${b.title}" is overdue ); sent++; } } return sent; } const send = makeSpy(Promise.resolve()); notifyOverdue( { title: "Dune", borrower: "ada", due: "2026-11-01" }, { title: "Emma", borrower: "bob", due: "2026-12-01" } , "2026-11-20", send) .then(n = console.log(n, send.calls)); A spy records how it was called; a stub returns what the test wants. Test frameworks provide them ( mock.fn() in node:test, vi.fn() in Vitest, jest.fn() ), but they are only functions that remember. Fake timers Waiting for real timers makes tests slow. Frameworks can replace setTimeout with a fake clock that you move by hand: javascript-norun import { test, mock } from "node:test"; test("debounce waits 300 ms", () = { mock.timers.enable({ apis: "setTimeout" }); const calls = ; const save = debounce(() = calls.push("saved"), 300); save(); save(); mock.timers.tick(299); assert.deepEqual(calls, ); mock.timers.tick(1); assert.deepEqual(calls, "saved" ); mock.timers.reset(); }); Vitest has the same with vi.useFakeTimers() and vi.advanceTimersByTime(ms) . Vitest and Jest javascript-norun import { describe, it, expect, vi } from "vitest"; describe("cart", () = { it("totals the lines", () = { expect(total( { price: 2, qty: 3 } )).toBe(6); }); it("calls the logger once", () = { const log = vi.fn(); checkout( , log); expect(log).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1); }); }); describe groups tests, it is one test, and expect(x).toBe(y) , .toEqual(y) (deep), .toThrow() and .toHaveBeenCalledWith(...) are the assertions. Jest's API is the same. What makes a good test - It checks one behaviour and its name says which. - It sets up everything it needs and does not depend on other tests. - It fails for one reason only, and the message shows what was expected and what came instead. - It runs fast, without the network or real waiting. Check yourself quiz ? Why does assert.equal({ a: 1 }, { a: 1 }) fail with node:assert/strict? - The strict module refuses to compare objects + It compares with ===, and these are two different objects - Object literals get their properties in a random order - equal only works on numbers and strings === compares objects by identity, so two objects with the same contents are not equal; deepEqual compares contents. ? How can a test check that a function sent an email without sending one? - Turn the network off so the email cannot leave - Catch the error that the mail server sends back - Read the mail server's log after the test has run + Pass the send function in and give the test a spy The code under test receives send as a parameter; the spy records its arguments, which the test then checks. ? An async test calls assert.rejects(p) without await. What happens? + the test can finish and pass before the check runs - it works the same as with await, only less clearly - it throws a SyntaxError when the test file loads - the runner notices and adds the await for you Without await the test function returns before the promise settles, so a failure is not reported for that test.

title: A spy
body: Write spy(impl) that returns a function which: - calls impl with the same arguments (if impl is given) and returns its result; - records every call: fn.calls is an array of argument arrays, and fn.results an array of what each call returned; - has fn.calledWith(...args) that is true when some call had exactly those arguments (compared with === one by one); - has fn.reset() that clears both arrays.

title: A tiny test runner
body: Write runTests(tests) where tests is an array of { name, fn } . It runs every test, one after another, and returns a promise of a report: javascript { passed: 2, failed: 1, results: { name: "adds", ok: true }, { name: "divides", ok: false, error: "expected 2, got 3" }, ... } - fn may be synchronous or async ; a test fails when it throws or its promise rejects, and the error's message (or the value itself turned into a string, if it is not an Error ) goes in error ; - a test that takes longer than 200 ms fails with the error "timed out" , and the runner moves on; - one failing test never stops the others; results keep the order of the tests.

title: 8.05  Immutable Data and Functional Patterns
body: Code that does not change data behind your back - why shared mutable objects cause bugs, updating with spread instead of mutating, the non-mutating array methods toSorted, toReversed, toSpliced and with, deep copies with structuredClone, deep freezing, pure functions, composing functions with pipe, and currying. The bug that shared objects cause javascript const defaults = { theme: "light", sizes: 12, 14 }; function withLargeText(settings) { settings.sizes.push(18); // changes the caller's array! return settings; } const mine = withLargeText(defaults); console.log(defaults.sizes); // 12, 14, 18 : the defaults changed too Objects and arrays are passed by reference, so a function that changes its argument changes it for everyone who holds it. In a small script that is manageable; in an app with state shared by many parts (lesson 6.05), it causes bugs that are hard to trace. The cure is to not change data: make a new version instead. Updating with spread javascript const state = { user: { name: "Ada", level: 3 }, items: "map" }; const next = { ...state, user: { ...state.user, level: state.user.level + 1 }, items: ...state.items, "sword" , }; console.log(state.user.level, state.items); // 3 'map' (unchanged) console.log(next.user.level, next.items); // 4 'map', 'sword' console.log(next.user === state.user); // false: changed, so copied Spread copies one level. Every level on the path to the change is copied; everything else is shared, which is cheap and safe as long as nobody mutates it. Array methods that do not mutate sort , reverse and splice change the array in place. Their newer twins return a changed copy: javascript const scores = 30, 10, 20 ; console.log(scores.toSorted((a, b) = a - b)); // 10, 20, 30 console.log(scores.toReversed()); // 20, 10, 30 console.log(scores.toSpliced(1, 1)); // 30, 20 console.log(scores.with(0, 99)); // 99, 10, 20 console.log(scores); // 30, 10, 20 : unchanged map , filter , slice , concat and reduce never mutated, which is why lesson 2.02's array style already works well with immutable data. Deep copies structuredClone copies a value all the way down, including nested objects, arrays, Map , Set and Date : javascript const original = { when: new Date(0), tags: new Set( "a" ), deep: { list: 1, 2 } }; const copy = structuredClone(original); copy.deep.list.push(3); console.log(original.deep.list, copy.deep.list, copy.when instanceof Date, copy.tags.has("a")); It cannot copy functions or class instances' methods (a class instance comes back as a plain object). JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)) also copies, but loses dates, undefined , Map and Set . Freezing Object.freeze stops changes to an object, but only one level deep. A small recursive function freezes everything: javascript function deepFreeze(value) { if (value && typeof value === "object" && !Object.isFrozen(value)) { Object.freeze(value); for (const key of Reflect.ownKeys(value)) deepFreeze(value key ); } return value; } const config = deepFreeze({ server: { port: 8080 }, flags: "a" }); config.server.port = 1; // ignored here; in strict mode it throws a TypeError console.log(config.server.port, Object.isFrozen(config.flags)); // 8080 true In strict mode (every module, lesson 3.05) writing to a frozen object throws; outside it, the write is silently ignored. Freezing in development builds catches accidental mutation early. Pure functions A pure function's result depends only on its arguments, and it changes nothing outside itself. Pure functions are easy to test (no set-up), easy to reuse, and safe to call twice. javascript // impure: reads and changes outside state let total = 0; function addToTotal(price) { total += price; return total; } // pure: everything comes in, the answer goes out const addPrice = (total, price) = total + price; console.log( 3, 4, 5 .reduce(addPrice, 0)); Programs still need side effects (saving, drawing, sending). The pattern is to keep them at the edges and the logic in the middle pure, as the update function in lesson 6.05 did. Building functions from functions pipe runs functions one after another, each getting the result of the last: javascript const pipe = (...fns) = input = fns.reduce((value, fn) = fn(value), input); const slug = pipe( s = s.trim(), s = s.toLowerCase(), s = s.replace(/ ^a-z0-9 +/g, "-"), s = s.replace(/^- -$/g, ""), ); console.log(slug(" Hello, World! 2026 ")); // hello-world-2026 Currying turns a function of several arguments into functions of one, so you can fix some arguments now and give the rest later: javascript const multiply = a = b = a b; const double = multiply(2); console.log( 1, 2, 3 .map(double)); // 2, 4, 6 const hasTag = tag = item = item.tags.includes(tag); console.log( { tags: "red" }, { tags: "blue" } .filter(hasTag("red")).length); When to mutate anyway Immutability costs copies. Inside one function, building a local array with push is fine: nobody else can see it until you return it. Mutate freely what you just created; do not mutate what you were given. Check yourself quiz ? After const next = { ...state, items: ...state.items, x } , which parts of next are shared with state ? - Nothing: spread copies everything deeply + Every property except items - Only items , because it was spread - Only primitive values; nested objects are copied Spread copies one level: next.items is a new array, while every other property points at the same values as in state . ? What is the difference between sort and toSorted ? - sort returns a new array; toSorted sorts in place - toSorted sorts numbers correctly without a compare function + sort reorders the array in place; toSorted returns a sorted copy - toSorted can only sort strings Both compare the same way (as strings unless you pass a compare function); toSorted leaves the original alone. ? Which copies nested objects, Maps and Dates? - { ...obj } - Object.assign({}, obj) - Object.freeze(obj) + structuredClone(obj) Spread and Object.assign copy one level, and freeze copies nothing; structuredClone copies all the way down.

title: Update a nested value
body: Write updateIn(obj, path, fn) that returns a new object where the value at path (an array of keys) is replaced by fn(oldValue) . Nothing in obj is changed, objects on the path are copied, and everything else is shared: javascript const state = { user: { name: "Ada", stats: { level: 3 } }, items: }; const next = updateIn(state, "user", "stats", "level" , n = n + 1); next.user.stats.level // 4 state.user.stats.level // 3 next.items === state.items // true Arrays on the path are copied as arrays (numeric keys). A missing object on the path is created as {} . An empty path returns fn(obj) .

title: A to-do reducer
body: Write a pure function reduce(state, action) for a to-do list that never changes state and returns a new state. The state is { todos: { id, text, done } , nextId } . Actions: - { type: "add", text } adds { id: nextId, text, done: false } at the end and increases nextId ; text is trimmed, and empty text changes nothing (return the same state object); - { type: "toggle", id } flips done of that to-do; - { type: "rename", id, text } changes its text (trimmed; empty text changes nothing); - { type: "clearDone" } removes finished to-dos; - { type: "move", id, to } moves a to-do to index to (clamped to the list); - an unknown action or id returns the same state object unchanged. Then write replay(actions, initial) that applies a list of actions with reduce .
