title: Cheat Sheet - JavaScript
body: Basics javascript-norun const name = "Ada"; // cannot be reassigned let count = 0; // can be reassigned console.log( ${name} has ${count + 1} items ); const n = Number("42"), s = String(42), b = Boolean(""); // conversions Operators --- --- === !== Equal / not equal without conversion (never use == ) && \ \ ! Logic, short-circuit; \ \ falls back on any falsy value ?? Falls back only on null / undefined : volume ?? 50 a?.b , a?. k , f?.() Stop with undefined when a (or f ) is nullish , % Power, remainder cond ? a : b Conditional expression Falsy values: false , 0 , "" , null , undefined , NaN . Everything else, including and {} , is truthy. Strings Code Gives --- --- s.length , s 0 , s.at(-1) , s.slice(1, 4) Length, first, last, part s.toUpperCase() , s.trim() , s.padStart(5, "0") Case, trimmed, padded s.split(",") , parts.join(", ") Split, join s.includes(x) , s.startsWith(x) , s.indexOf(x) Tests, position (-1 if absent) s.replaceAll(a, b) , s.repeat(3) Replace every match, repeat n.toFixed(2) , parseInt("12px") , Number.isInteger(n) Format, parse, test numbers Functions javascript-norun function area(w, h = 1) { return w h; } // declaration, default parameter const square = x = x x; // arrow function const sum = (...nums) = nums.reduce((a, b) = a + b, 0); // rest parameter Math.max(...values); // spread const makeCounter = () = { let c = 0; return () = ++c; }; // closure Arrays Code Gives --- --- a.push(x) , a.pop() , a.unshift(x) , a.shift() Add / remove at the end and start (changes a ) a.map(f) , a.filter(f) , a.reduce(f, start) New array / new array / one value a.find(f) , a.findIndex(f) , a.some(f) , a.every(f) First match, its index, any, all a.includes(x) , a.indexOf(x) Membership, position a.slice(i, j) , a.splice(i, n, ...items) Copy part / remove and insert (changes a ) ...a .sort((x, y) = x - y) , a.toSorted(f) Sorted copy; sort alone changes a and compares as strings a.flat() , a.flatMap(f) Flatten one level Array.from({ length: n }, (_, i) = i) 0, 1, ..., n-1 Objects, Maps and Sets javascript-norun const user = { name, age: 36, key : value, greet() { return this.name; } }; const { name, age: years = 0, ...rest } = user; // destructuring const copy = { ...defaults, ...overrides }; // shallow merge Object.keys(o); Object.values(o); Object.entries(o); Object.fromEntries(pairs); const counts = new Map(); counts.set(k, (counts.get(k) ?? 0) + 1); const unique = ...new Set(items) ; JSON.stringify(value, null, 2); JSON.parse(text); Classes and errors javascript-norun class Account { balance = 0; // private field constructor(owner) { this.owner = owner; } get balance() { return this. balance; } // getter static from(data) { return new Account(data.owner); } } class Savings extends Account { constructor(o) { super(o); } } class ValidationError extends Error { constructor(message) { super(message); this.name = "ValidationError"; } } try { risky(); } catch (err) { if (!(err instanceof ValidationError)) throw err; } finally { cleanUp(); } Iterators and modules javascript-norun function range(a, b) { for (let i = a; i < b; i++) yield i; } for (const x of range(0, 3)) console.log(x); export function format(x) { } // named export export default class Cart { } // default export import Cart, { format } from "./cart.js"; const { chart } = await import("./chart.js"); // dynamic import Asynchronous code javascript-norun const sleep = ms = new Promise(resolve = setTimeout(resolve, ms)); async function load(url) { const response = await fetch(url); if (!response.ok) throw new Error( HTTP ${response.status} ); return response.json(); } try { const data = await load("/api/items"); } catch (err) { console.error(err); } const a, b = await Promise.all( load("/a"), load("/b") ); // in parallel for (const id of ids) await process(id); // one at a time Combinator Result --- --- Promise.all All values in order; rejects at the first error Promise.allSettled { status, value \ reason } for each; never rejects Promise.race The first to settle Promise.any The first to fulfil TypeScript typescript-norun let title: string = "Dune"; function f(x: number, label?: string): string { return ${label ?? ""}${x} ; } interface User { readonly id: number; name: string; email?: string } type Id = string number; type Shape = { kind: "circle"; r: number } { kind: "rect"; w: number; h: number }; function first

title: Common Errors
body: Messages Message or symptom Usual cause Fix Lesson --- --- --- --- ReferenceError: x is not defined A typo in a name, or a variable used outside its block Check the spelling; declare it where it is used 2.04 ReferenceError: Cannot access 'x' before initialization A let / const (or a const function) used above its declaration Move the declaration up, or use a function declaration 2.01 TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'name') Reading a property of something that is undefined : a missing argument, a wrong key, a find with no match Check where the value comes from; use ?. when it may really be missing 1.03 TypeError: Cannot read properties of null document.querySelector matched nothing Check the selector and that the element exists when the script runs 6.01 TypeError: x is not a function Calling a value that is not a function: a typo in a method name, a missing () elsewhere, a wrong import Log typeof x ; check imports and names 2.01 TypeError: Assignment to constant variable. Reassigning a const Use let if it really must change 1.02 TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined inside a method used as a callback this was lost: setTimeout(obj.method) , arr.map(obj.method) () = obj.method() or obj.method.bind(obj) 3.02 SyntaxError: Unexpected token '<' in JSON.parse The text is HTML (often a 404 page), not JSON Check response.ok and the URL before parsing 4.04 SyntaxError: Unexpected end of JSON input Parsing an empty string Check the text is non-empty; handle missing data 2.05 SyntaxError: await is only valid in async functions await in a normal function Mark the function async , or use a module's top level 4.03 SyntaxError: Cannot use import statement outside a module Node treats the file as CommonJS "type": "module" in package.json , or a .mjs file 3.05 RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded Recursion without a base case, or a getter or setter that calls itself Add the base case; store the value in a different ( private ) field 3.01 Uncaught (in promise) / unhandled rejection A rejected promise nobody handled await it inside try , or add .catch 4.02 Failed to fetch / CORS error The server does not allow your page's origin, or the network is down Fix the server's CORS headers, or call through your own backend 4.04 Wrong results without an error Symptom Usual cause Fix Lesson --- --- --- --- "2" + 3 gives "23" + joins when either side is a string; form and prompt values are strings Convert first: Number(text) 1.03 0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3 Floating-point rounding Compare with a tolerance, or work in whole cents 1.02 10, 9, 1 .sort() gives 1, 10, 9 sort compares as strings by default sort((a, b) = a - b) 2.02 A setting of 0 or "" is replaced by the default value \ \ fallback treats them as missing value ?? fallback 1.03 A copied object changes when the original does Spread and Object.assign copy one level only Copy nested objects too, or structuredClone 2.03 The caller's array was changed sort , reverse , splice change the array in place Work on a copy: ...arr .sort() , toSorted() 2.02 An async function returns Promise {<pending } Its result was not awaited await f() or f().then(...) 4.03 forEach(async ...) finishes before the work does forEach ignores the returned promises for...of with await , or Promise.all(arr.map(...)) 4.03 A 404 response is treated as success fetch only rejects on network failure Check response.ok 4.04 Every callback from a loop sees the last value var shares one variable across the loop Use let 2.04 typeof null === "object" A historical quirk Check x === null first 1.02 NaN === NaN is false NaN is never equal to anything Number.isNaN(x) 1.03 A spread of a Map into JSON gives {} JSON.stringify ignores Map and Set contents Object.fromEntries(map) , ...set 2.05 User text shows up as HTML or runs a script innerHTML with unescaped text textContent , or escape the text 6.01 A form reloads the page The submit's default action was not cancelled event.preventDefault() 6.02 A number from FormData or localStorage compares wrongly Both give strings Number(value) 6.03 TypeScript Message Usual cause Fix Lesson --- --- --- --- TS2345: Argument of type 'string' is not assignable to parameter of type 'number' The wrong type passed Convert the value, or fix the parameter type if it is wrong 5.01 TS18048: 'x' is possibly 'undefined' A value that may be missing is used directly Check it first ( if (x === undefined) ... ), or give a default with ?? 5.01 TS2339: Property 'radius' does not exist on type 'Shape' Using a variant's property without narrowing Check shape.kind first 5.03 TS2322: Type '"north"' is not assignable to type 'Direction' A value outside a literal union Use one of the allowed values, or extend the type 5.03 TS7006: Parameter 'x' implicitly has an 'any' type A parameter without a type in strict mode Annotate it 5.01 TS2353: Object literal may only specify known properties A typo or extra property in an object literal Fix the name, or add the property to the type 5.02 TS2322: Type 'X' is not assignable to type 'never' A switch over a union is missing a case Handle the new variant 5.03 TS2540: Cannot assign to 'id' because it is a read-only property Changing a readonly property Create a new object instead 5.02

title: Glossary
body: Every term from the course, in alphabetical order. The lesson that introduces each one is in brackets. Term Meaning --- --- AbortController An object whose signal cancels a fetch or other operation when abort() is called. (4.04) AbortError The name of the error a cancelled fetch or operation rejects with (8.03) AbortSignal The object passed to cancellable work, with aborted, reason and an abort event (8.03) Abstract class A TypeScript class that cannot be created with new ; it shares code and declares methods subclasses must write. (5.05) Action A plain object describing what happened, such as { type: "add", name: "Read" } , handled by an update function. (6.05) any The TypeScript type that switches checking off for a value. Avoid it. (5.01) ArrayBuffer A fixed block of raw bytes, read and written through typed arrays or a DataView (8.01) Arrow function A short function form: x = x 2 . It has no this of its own. (2.01) async function A function that always returns a promise and may use await inside. (4.03) Async generator A function declared async function that can await and yields values over time (8.02) await Pauses an async function until a promise settles, then gives its value or throws its error. (4.03) BigInt An integer of any size, written with an n suffix: 2n 64n . (7.04) Bubbling An event running listeners on its target, then on each parent up to the document. (6.02) Bundler A tool, such as Vite, that serves files during development and combines and optimises them for production. (6.04) Call stack The functions running right now, each waiting for the one above it. (4.01) Callback A function passed to another function, to be called later. (2.01) Capture group Part of a regular expression in parentheses whose match is kept; (?<name ...) names it. (7.01) Class A description of a kind of object: its fields, constructor and methods. (3.01) Closure A function together with the variables of the scope it was created in, which it keeps using. (2.04) CommonJS Node's older module system, with require and module.exports . (3.05) Concurrency limit Running at most N asynchronous tasks at the same time, for example with a worker pool. (4.05) Conditional type A type that chooses between two: T extends U ? X : Y . (7.05) const Declares a variable that cannot be reassigned (its object can still change). (1.02) CORS The browser rule that a page may read responses from another site only if that site allows it. (4.04) Currying Turning a function of several arguments into a chain of functions of one argument each (8.05) DataView A view that reads and writes numbers of any size at any byte offset, in a chosen byte order (8.01) Debounce Running a function once the calls to it have stopped for a while. (4.05) Declaration file A .d.ts file that describes the types of JavaScript code. (7.05) Default export The one unnamed export of a module, imported without braces. (3.05) Destructuring Taking values out of objects and arrays into variables: const { name } = user . (2.03) devDependency A package needed only while developing or building, such as a test runner. (6.04) Discriminated union A union whose variants share a tag property with different literal types, such as kind . (5.03) DOM The tree of objects a browser builds from HTML, which JavaScript reads and changes. (6.01) Enum A TypeScript set of named constants that also exists at run time. (5.05) Error-first callback Node's callback style: (err, value) = ... , with err null on success. (4.01) ES module A file with its own scope that shares values with export and import . (3.05) Event delegation Handling events of many child elements with one listener on a parent. (6.02) Event loop The mechanism that runs queued tasks and microtasks one at a time when the call stack is empty. (4.01) Exhaustive check Assigning to never in a switch's default, so that unhandled variants fail to compile. (5.03) Exit code The number a program ends with; 0 means success, anything else failure. (7.06) Fake timers A test tool that replaces setTimeout with a clock moved by hand (8.04) fetch The function that makes HTTP requests and returns a promise for a Response. (4.04) for await...of A loop over an async iterable that waits for each value (8.02) FormData An object collecting a form's named fields; all values are strings. (6.02) Generator A function that produces values one at a time with yield , pausing between them. (3.04) Generic A function, interface or class with a type parameter, such as first<T (items: T ): T . (5.04) Getter A function that runs when a property is read, written get name() {} . (7.02) Getter / setter Methods that run when a property is read ( get ) or assigned ( set ). (3.01) Greedy A quantifier that matches as much as it can; adding ? makes it lazy. (7.01) Hoisting Function declarations being usable before the line that defines them. (2.01) Immutability Not changing existing values; building new ones instead, as update does. (6.05) Immutable update Making a changed copy instead of changing the original, for example with spread (8.05) infer Captures part of a type inside a conditional type, such as the element of an array. (7.05) Inference TypeScript working out a type from a value, so it need not be written. (5.01) Interface A named description of an object's shape. (5.02) Intl The built-in API that formats numbers, dates, lists and plurals for a language and region. (7.04) ISO string A date written like 2026-11-20T14:30:00.000Z , the safe way to store and send dates. (7.04) Iterable An object with a Symbol.iterator () method, usable in for...of and spread. (3.04) JSON The text format for data, written like JavaScript literals with double-quoted keys. (2.05) keyof The union of a type's property names. (5.04) let Declares a block-scoped variable that can be reassigned. (1.02) Literal type A type allowing one exact value, such as "up" or 3 . (5.03) localStorage Per-site string storage in the browser that survives reloads. (6.03) Lock file package-lock.json : the exact version of every installed package. (6.04) Map A collection of key-value pairs with keys of any type, in insertion order. (2.05) Mapped type A type built by going over the keys of another: { K in keyof T : ... } . (7.05) Microtask A callback, such as a promise reaction, that runs as soon as the current code finishes, before the next task. (4.01) Migration Converting stored data from an older version's shape to the current one. (6.03) Narrowing TypeScript working out a more exact type after a check such as typeof x === "string" . (5.03) never The type with no values: code that cannot be reached. (5.03) Node.js The runtime that runs JavaScript outside the browser, with access to files and processes. (7.06) npm Node's package manager, which installs packages and runs scripts from package.json . (6.04) Nullish null or undefined , the values that ?? and ?. look for. (1.03) Number.EPSILON The gap between 1 and the next double; a tolerance for comparing floats. (7.04) Object.freeze Makes an object's own properties unchangeable; it is shallow. (7.02) Optional chaining a?.b : stops and gives undefined when a is null or undefined. (1.03) package.json The file describing a Node project: its name, dependencies and scripts. (7.06) Parameter property A TypeScript constructor parameter with public , private or readonly that also declares the property. (5.05) Polymorphism Different classes answering the same method call in their own way. (3.01) Private field A class field whose name starts with , reachable only inside the class. (3.01) Promise An object standing for a result that arrives later: pending, then fulfilled or rejected. (4.02) Property descriptor The settings of a property: value or get/set, writable, enumerable, configurable. (7.02) Prototype The object another object falls back to for properties it does not have itself. (3.02) Proxy An object that stands in for another and lets traps intercept reads, writes and more. (7.03) Pure function A function whose result depends only on its arguments and that changes nothing outside itself. (2.01) Reflect Functions that perform each object operation the default way, for use inside traps. (7.03) Regular expression A pattern that describes text, written /.../flags or built with new RegExp . (7.01) Rest parameter ...args in a function definition: collects the remaining arguments into an array. (2.01) satisfies Checks a value against a type without widening the value's own type. (7.05) Scope The region of code where a variable can be used. (2.04) Semantic versioning MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH version numbers, where a major change may break code. (6.04) Set A collection of unique values. (2.05) Setter A function that runs when a property is assigned, written set name(value) {} . (7.02) Spread ...x in a call, array or object literal: expands its items or properties. (2.01) Spy A test function that records how it was called (8.04) State The data that describes everything an app shows; the page is rendered from it. (6.01) Stream Data read or written piece by piece instead of all at once. (7.06) Strict equality === : equal without type conversion. (1.03) Structural typing TypeScript comparing types by their shape rather than their name. (5.02) structuredClone A built-in function that copies a value deeply, including Map, Set and Date (8.05) Symbol A unique value usable as a property key that never clashes with others. (7.02) Template literal A string in backticks that can contain ${expressions} and line breaks. (1.04) Template literal type A string type built from others: on${Capitalize<T } . (7.05) TextEncoder Turns a string into UTF-8 bytes; TextDecoder turns bytes back into a string (8.01) this The object a function was called on, decided at call time. (3.02) Throttle Running a function at most once per period. (4.05) Trap A handler function of a Proxy, such as get or set . (7.03) Truthy / falsy How a value counts in a condition; the falsy values are false , 0 , "" , null , undefined and NaN . (1.02) Tuple A TypeScript array type with a fixed length and a type per position: string, number . (5.01) Type alias A name for any type: type Id = string \ number . (5.02) Type assertion value as Type : telling the compiler to treat a value as a type without checking. (5.03) Type guard A function returning x is T , which narrows its argument when it returns true. (5.03) Typed array A view of an ArrayBuffer as numbers of one type, such as Uint8Array or Float32Array (8.01) typeof The operator giving a value's type as a string, such as "number" . (1.02) TypeScript JavaScript with type annotations, checked by a compiler and then removed. (5.01) Union type A \ B : a value that is one of several types. (5.03) unknown The TypeScript type for any value that must be checked before use. (5.01) Utility type A built-in generic that transforms a type: Partial , Pick , Omit , Record . (5.05) WeakMap A Map whose object keys do not stay alive because of it; it cannot be iterated. (7.03) WeakRef A reference that does not keep its object alive; deref() gives it or undefined . (7.03) Well-known symbol A symbol such as Symbol.iterator or Symbol.toPrimitive that the language looks for on objects. (7.02) XSS Cross-site scripting: injected HTML or script running in a page, often through innerHTML . (6.01)

title: 1.01  User Mode, Kernel Mode and Why Drivers Are Different
match: 1.01 User Mode, Kernel Mode and Why Drivers Are Different
body: What the kernel is, why the processor separates user mode from kernel mode, what drivers are for, and why a bug in a driver takes the whole machine down. This lesson also sets the rules for the course - everything happens in a virtual machine. Two privilege levels The processor runs code at different privilege levels . Windows uses two: User mode Kernel mode --- --- --- Who runs there Applications, services, most of Windows' own programs The kernel, the executive, the HAL and drivers Memory Its own process's address space only All of memory, every process, the hardware A crash Ends that one process Stops the whole machine: a bug check (blue screen) Errors Exceptions, error codes Must be handled perfectly; there is no one to clean up User-mode code cannot touch the hardware or another process's memory; when it needs something the system provides (reading a file, creating a window), it makes a system call , and the processor switches to kernel mode to run trusted code on its behalf, then switches back. What lives in the kernel Drivers are modules that run in kernel mode, loaded by the system, to extend it: a driver for a graphics card or a USB device, a file system, a network filter, an antivirus filter. They follow the same rules as the rest of the kernel and have the same power. Why drivers are different Everything in the Win32 API course still applies in spirit, but a kernel driver adds rules that user-mode code never sees: - No safety net : dereferencing a bad pointer, leaking memory, or holding a lock too long affects the whole machine, and a crash stops everything with a bug check. - No C++ runtime as you know it : no exceptions, no new without care, no standard library containers, no printf . Drivers are written in C or a careful subset of C++. - Interrupt levels (IRQLs, lesson 3.02) decide what code may do at any moment: some code may not wait, may not touch pageable memory, may not even call most functions. - Everything coming from user mode is hostile until checked : a driver is a door into the kernel, and an unchecked buffer is a security hole for the whole system (lesson 2.05). Most of the time, the right answer is not to write a driver : user-mode services, ETW, Windows' built-in APIs and user-mode driver frameworks cover far more than people expect (lesson 5.04). This course is about understanding the kernel and building drivers correctly when they are needed. The rules of this course 1. Everything runs in a virtual machine (lesson 1.02). Never load a test driver on the computer you work on. 2. The drivers in this course echo, count and log : they talk to their own user-mode client and observe documented events. They never read or write other processes' memory, never hide anything, and never try to get around any of Windows' protections. 3. Test drivers are loaded with test signing , Microsoft's documented mechanism for driver development, enabled only inside the virtual machine. How the practice works Compiler Explorer runs ordinary programs, not drivers. So the practice checks the logic that goes inside drivers in plain C++: the I/O control codes, the kernel's string type, buffer validation, linked lists, ring buffers, IRQL rules. Each practice declares the few kernel types it needs, exactly as the WDK headers do. Check yourself quiz ? What happens when kernel-mode code crashes? - Windows closes the driver and carries on, as it does for a crashed program - The driver is restarted automatically + The whole machine stops with a bug check (blue screen), because there is nothing above the kernel to recover - Only the program that called the driver is closed A crashing user-mode program is cleaned up by the kernel. A crash in the kernel has nothing above it to clean up, so Windows stops everything to avoid further damage. ? How does user-mode code get something done that only the kernel can do? - It calls the kernel's functions directly, like any DLL + It makes a system call, which switches the processor to kernel mode to run trusted code on its behalf - It loads a driver into its own process - It asks for administrator rights, which lets it run in kernel mode User-mode code cannot jump into kernel code. A system call is the controlled door: the processor changes privilege level and runs only the kernel's own handler. Being an administrator does not change the processor mode. ? Why must all driver testing happen in a virtual machine? - Drivers can only be built inside a virtual machine - Windows refuses to load drivers on a physical machine + A driver bug can crash or corrupt the whole system - Virtual machines run drivers faster than real hardware The machine you test on will crash, possibly with corrupted files. In a virtual machine with snapshots that costs a snapshot restore, not your work.

title: Reading NTSTATUS values
where: 1.01 User Mode, Kernel Mode and Why Drivers Are Different
body: Kernel functions return an NTSTATUS : the top two bits are the severity (0 success, 1 informational, 2 warning, 3 error), bits 16-27 the facility and the low 16 bits the code. Write the helpers a driver and its user-mode client use: cpp using NTSTATUS = std::int32_t; bool ntSuccess(NTSTATUS s); // NT_SUCCESS: s = 0 std::string severity(NTSTATUS s); // "success", "informational", "warning" or "error" std::string statusName(NTSTATUS s); // a few well-known names, else "0x%08X" std::uint32_t toWin32Error(NTSTATUS s); // what GetLastError shows in user mode Known names: 0x00000000 STATUS_SUCCESS, 0x00000103 STATUS_PENDING, 0x80000005 STATUS_BUFFER_OVERFLOW, 0xC0000002 STATUS_NOT_IMPLEMENTED, 0xC000000D STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER, 0xC0000010 STATUS_INVALID_DEVICE_REQUEST, 0xC0000022 STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED, 0xC0000023 STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL, 0xC000009A STATUS_INSUFFICIENT_RESOURCES. Unknown ones are printed as 0x and 8 upper-case hex digits. toWin32Error maps: SUCCESS → 0, PENDING → 997, BUFFER_OVERFLOW → 234, NOT_IMPLEMENTED → 1, INVALID_PARAMETER → 87, INVALID_DEVICE_REQUEST → 1, ACCESS_DENIED → 5, BUFFER_TOO_SMALL → 122, INSUFFICIENT_RESOURCES → 1450; anything else → 317.

title: 1.02  Building a Safe Lab
body: Setting up the virtual machine where every driver in this course runs - Hyper-V or VMware, snapshots, test signing inside the VM only, kernel debugging over the network with KDNET, and a routine that makes crashes cheap. Two machines Driver development uses two machines: Machine Role --- --- Host (your computer) Visual Studio, the WDK, WinDbg. Builds the driver and debugs the target. Never loads test drivers. Target (a virtual machine) Runs Windows with test signing and a kernel debugger attached. Loads the driver. Crashes are expected. Hyper-V (built into Windows 10/11 Pro and later) or VMware Workstation both work. Give the VM 2 processors (synchronisation bugs only show up with more than one), 4 GB of memory and a fresh Windows installation of the same version you target. Snapshots Take a snapshot (Hyper-V calls it a checkpoint) once the VM is set up: Windows installed, updated, debugging configured. Before each test session, you can go back to it in seconds. A driver that corrupts the system, or a VM that no longer boots, costs nothing. Test signing, in the VM only Windows only loads drivers signed by Microsoft (lesson 5.04). For development, Microsoft provides test signing : the WDK signs your driver with a test certificate, and a machine in test-signing mode accepts it. Inside the VM , from an administrator command prompt: cpp-norun bcdedit /set testsigning on and restart. Test signing requires Secure Boot to be off for that VM (in Hyper-V: the VM's Settings Security uncheck Enable Secure Boot). The desktop then shows "Test Mode" in a corner as a reminder. Never do this on your own computer: it is a development setting for a machine that exists to be crashed. Kernel debugging with KDNET A kernel debugger stops the whole target machine, lets you inspect it, and catches crashes before the blue screen. KDNET runs it over the network: 1. On the host, find its IP address ( ipconfig ) and choose a port from 50000 to 50039. 2. Copy kdnet.exe and VerifiedNICList.xml from the WDK ( C:\Program Files (x86)\Windows Kits\10\Debuggers\x64 ) to the VM. 3. In the VM, as administrator: kdnet.exe <host-ip <port . It enables debugging and prints a key like 1.2.3.4 . Restart the VM. 4. On the host: WinDbg File Attach to kernel Net, enter the port and the key. When the VM boots, WinDbg connects. Break (Ctrl+Break) freezes the whole VM at once, and g lets it run again. Lesson 1.05 uses this connection. The routine 1. Build the driver on the host (lesson 1.03). 2. Copy the .sys file (and its .inf or .cat , if any) to the VM through a shared folder. 3. Load it (lesson 1.04), with WinDbg attached and showing DbgPrint output. 4. If it crashes, WinDbg stops at the bug check: run !analyze -v , read the call stack, fix the code. 5. Restore the snapshot if the VM is in a bad state. Why bother Kernel bugs are expensive in the real world: a crashing driver can take down thousands of machines at once. The lab makes every one of your mistakes cheap and visible, and the debugger makes them understandable. Professionals work exactly this way. Check yourself quiz ? Why does the VM need more than one virtual processor? - The kernel debugger needs a processor of its own - Windows will not boot with only one processor + Many race bugs appear only on several processors at once - Drivers can only be loaded on processor 1 With one processor, two pieces of code never really run at the same time, so synchronisation bugs between them may never show up in testing. ? Where is test signing turned on, and why only there? - On the development machine, so you can build drivers - On both machines, so they can talk over KDNET + Only in the target VM, a machine meant to be crashed - Nowhere: the course uses drivers signed by Microsoft Test signing is a development setting that lets test-signed drivers load. Loosening that protection is fine on a throwaway VM; your everyday machine keeps the normal driver signing rules. ? What does the kernel debugger do when the target crashes? - Nothing; it only works while the target is running normally - It restarts the target and replays the crash - It saves a crash dump and closes the connection + It stops at the bug check, before the blue screen With a kernel debugger attached, the bug check breaks into the debugger first, with the machine frozen exactly at the crash, so you can analyse it with commands such as !analyze -v .

title: Checking the debugger settings
body: Before restarting the VM for kernel debugging, a helper script checks the KDNET settings from lesson 1.02 and prints the command for the host. Write it: cpp struct Kdnet { std::string host; int port{ 0 }; std::string key; }; bool parseSettings(const std::string& text, Kdnet& out, std::string& error); std::string hostCommand(const Kdnet& k); // "windbg -k net:port=50005,key=1.2.3.4" The text is name=value pairs separated by spaces, in any order: host= , port= and key= , each exactly once. Rules, checked in this order with these errors: 1. a pair without = , or an unknown or repeated name: "bad setting: <the pair " 2. any of the three missing: "missing host" , "missing port" or "missing key" (checked in that order) 3. host must be an IPv4 address: four numbers 0-255 without leading zeros ( 0 itself is fine): "bad host" 4. port must be a number from 50000 to 50039: "port must be 50000-50039" 5. key must be four parts separated by dots, each 1 to 13 characters from 0-9 and a-z (lower case): "bad key"

title: 1.03  The Windows Driver Kit
body: Installing Visual Studio with the Windows Driver Kit, creating a driver project, what is different about building a driver, the kernel's types and calling conventions, and the kernel's string type UNICODE_STRING. Installing On the host : 1. Visual Studio 2022 with the Desktop development with C++ workload, plus the individual components MSVC (latest) Spectre-mitigated libraries for x64. 2. The Windows SDK and the Windows Driver Kit (WDK) of the same version, from Microsoft's "Download the WDK" page, including the Visual Studio extension. After installation, Visual Studio has project templates such as Kernel Mode Driver, Empty (KMDF) and Empty WDM Driver . KMDF and WDM Model What it is --- --- WDM (Windows Driver Model) The underlying model: you handle IRPs, device objects and power yourself KMDF (Kernel-Mode Driver Framework) A framework on top of WDM that handles the boilerplate, power management and Plug and Play correctly UMDF The same framework for drivers that run in user mode Microsoft recommends KMDF (or UMDF) for new hardware drivers. This course uses small WDM drivers that are not tied to hardware ("software drivers"), because they show plainly how the kernel's I/O model works; everything you learn carries over to KMDF, which wraps the same objects. What is different about the build - The output is a .sys file: a PE image like a DLL, loaded into kernel space. - No C runtime: the driver links against ntoskrnl.exe (and a few other kernel modules) instead. include <ntddk.h replaces <windows.h . - Warnings are errors, and code analysis runs on every build (lesson 5.02). - The build signs the driver with a test certificate automatically (Driver Signing Test Sign). - C++ is allowed, but without exceptions or RTTI, and with new only if you define it yourself on top of the pool allocator (lesson 3.01). Kernel types The kernel has its own type names, close to Win32's: Type Meaning --- --- NTSTATUS The result of almost every kernel function: STATUS_SUCCESS (0), or an error such as STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER ; check with NT_SUCCESS(status) ULONG , USHORT , UCHAR , ULONG_PTR 32, 16, 8-bit unsigned, pointer-sized unsigned PVOID , PCHAR Pointers PDRIVER_OBJECT , PDEVICE_OBJECT , PIRP The kernel's objects (milestone 2) UNICODE_STRING The kernel's string (below) NTSTATUS values have a severity in the top two bits: 0 success, 1 informational, 2 warning, 3 error. So every error is negative as a 32-bit signed number, and NT_SUCCESS is just status = 0 . UNICODE_STRING The kernel does not use null-terminated strings. It uses a counted UTF-16 string: cpp-norun typedef struct _UNICODE_STRING { USHORT Length; // bytes in use, NOT characters, NOT including any null USHORT MaximumLength; // bytes in the buffer PWSTR Buffer; // may not be null-terminated! } UNICODE_STRING; UNICODE_STRING name = RTL_CONSTANT_STRING(L"\\Device\\XenonEcho"); UNICODE_STRING copy; RtlInitUnicodeString(&copy, L"literal"); // only for null-terminated literals if (RtlEqualUnicodeString(&a, &b, TRUE)) { ... } // TRUE: ignore case Three facts cause most bugs: 1. Lengths are in bytes. A string of 5 characters has Length = 10 . 2. The buffer is not necessarily null-terminated. Passing Buffer to anything that expects a C string reads past the end. Always use Length . 3. The maximum length is a USHORT , so a string is at most 32 767 characters. Printing one uses the %wZ format, which reads the counted structure: DbgPrint("name: %wZ\n", &name); . The practice implements the copy, append, compare and prefix functions on this structure. Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference between WDM and KMDF? - WDM is for 64-bit drivers and KMDF for 32-bit drivers + KMDF is a framework built on top of the WDM model - KMDF drivers run in user mode and WDM drivers in kernel mode - They are two names for the same driver model Every driver ends up as WDM underneath. KMDF wraps the hard, error-prone parts, such as power management and IRP handling, and gets the boilerplate right. User-mode drivers are UMDF, a different framework. ? In what unit is UNICODE_STRING 's Length measured? - In characters, not counting the terminating null - In characters, including the terminating null + In bytes, not characters, and without any terminating null - In bytes, including the terminating null Length is a byte count of the text, so L"abc" has a Length of 6. The buffer is not required to be null-terminated at all. ? How do you test whether an NTSTATUS means success? - status == 0 , since only STATUS_SUCCESS is a success - status != 0 , since non-zero values mean success + NT_SUCCESS(status) , which is true for status = 0 - status 0 , since errors are 0 or negative Several statuses besides STATUS_SUCCESS (0) are successes, such as STATUS_PENDING . Errors have the top bit set, which makes them negative as a signed number.

title: UNICODE_STRING
body: Write the kernel's counted string functions from lesson 1.03 (simplified versions of the Rtl functions): cpp using NTSTATUS = std::int32_t; constexpr NTSTATUS STATUS_SUCCESS = 0; constexpr NTSTATUS STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL = static_cast<NTSTATUS (0xC0000023u); struct UNICODE_STRING { std::uint16_t Length; std::uint16_t MaximumLength; char16_t Buffer; }; void initString(UNICODE_STRING& s, const char16_t nullTerminated); // RtlInitUnicodeString void copyString(UNICODE_STRING& dest, const UNICODE_STRING& src); // RtlCopyUnicodeString NTSTATUS appendString(UNICODE_STRING& dest, const UNICODE_STRING& src); // RtlAppendUnicodeStringToString bool equalStrings(const UNICODE_STRING& a, const UNICODE_STRING& b, bool ignoreCase); bool isPrefix(const UNICODE_STRING& prefix, const UNICODE_STRING& s, bool ignoreCase); std::u16string toStd(const UNICODE_STRING& s); // only the first Length bytes - Lengths are in bytes. initString points Buffer at the given text, sets Length to its length in bytes without the null, and MaximumLength to that plus 2. A null pointer gives an empty string (all zero). - copyString copies as many whole characters as fit into dest 's buffer ( MaximumLength ), and sets dest.Length ; if there is room for another character, it also writes a null after the copy (not counted in Length ). - appendString adds src after dest 's text if the result fits in dest.MaximumLength , else changes nothing and returns STATUS_BUFFER_TOO_SMALL . - Case-insensitive comparison only needs to fold a - z to upper case here.

title: 1.04  A First Driver
body: The smallest driver - DriverEntry and an Unload routine that frees everything - printing with DbgPrintEx, loading and unloading it as a service with sc.exe, and what happens to each step inside the kernel. DriverEntry Every driver has an entry point, DriverEntry , called once when the driver is loaded. It receives the driver object the I/O manager created for it, and the path of its registry key: cpp-norun include <ntddk.h void XenonUnload(PDRIVER_OBJECT driverObject) { UNREFERENCED_PARAMETER(driverObject); DbgPrintEx(DPFLTR_IHVDRIVER_ID, DPFLTR_INFO_LEVEL, "XenonHello: unloaded\n"); } extern "C" NTSTATUS DriverEntry(PDRIVER_OBJECT driverObject, PUNICODE_STRING registryPath) { UNREFERENCED_PARAMETER(registryPath); driverObject- DriverUnload = XenonUnload; DbgPrintEx(DPFLTR_IHVDRIVER_ID, DPFLTR_INFO_LEVEL, "XenonHello: loaded\n"); return STATUS_SUCCESS; } - extern "C" because the kernel looks the function up by its plain name. - Setting DriverUnload makes the driver unloadable ; without it, it stays until the machine restarts. - Returning a failure status from DriverEntry means the driver is not loaded at all, and the kernel will not call Unload , so DriverEntry must clean up everything it did before failing. The golden rule of Unload Everything the driver creates (device objects, symbolic links, memory, registered callbacks, timers, threads) must be undone in Unload , in reverse order. A driver that leaves a callback registered and is then unloaded leaves the kernel pointing at code that no longer exists: the next call crashes the machine. Milestone 2 onwards builds drivers whose Unload mirrors DriverEntry step by step. Seeing DbgPrint output DbgPrintEx messages go to the kernel debugger (WinDbg on the host, lesson 1.02). By default the INFO level is filtered out; enable it once in the VM's registry or from WinDbg: cpp-norun ed nt!Kd_IHVDRIVER_Mask 0xF Without a debugger attached, the Sysinternals tool DebugView (run as administrator, Capture Kernel enabled) shows the same messages inside the VM. Loading as a service A software driver is installed as a kernel service . In the VM, as administrator: cpp-norun sc create XenonHello type= kernel binPath= C:\Drivers\XenonHello.sys sc start XenonHello :: DriverEntry runs: "XenonHello: loaded" sc stop XenonHello :: Unload runs: "XenonHello: unloaded" sc delete XenonHello (The space after each = is required by sc .) The service lives under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\XenonHello , which is the registryPath passed to DriverEntry : drivers keep their configuration there. If sc start fails with error 577, the driver's signature was not accepted: check that test signing is on in the VM and the driver was test-signed by the build. What happens inside 1. sc start asks the Service Control Manager , which asks the kernel to load the driver. 2. The I/O manager maps the .sys file into kernel memory, checks its signature, resolves its imports against ntoskrnl.exe , creates a DRIVER_OBJECT , and calls DriverEntry . 3. sc stop makes the I/O manager call DriverUnload , then unmap the image. In WinDbg, lm m XenonHello shows the loaded module, and bp XenonHello!DriverEntry (set before sc start ) stops in your code so you can step through it. Check yourself quiz ? What happens if a driver does not set DriverUnload ? - Windows calls a default unload routine that frees everything + It cannot be unloaded; it stays until the machine restarts - The driver fails to load - The machine crashes when the driver is stopped Without an Unload routine, the kernel has no safe way to remove the driver, so sc stop fails and the driver stays loaded. ? What must DriverEntry do before returning a failure status? - Call its own Unload routine, which the kernel will not call - Nothing; the kernel frees everything the driver allocated + Undo everything it already did, because Unload will not run - Print the error with DbgPrintEx , so the kernel can clean up A driver that fails to load is removed without calling Unload. Anything it created or registered before failing would be leaked or left pointing at freed code. ? Why is a callback left registered after unload so dangerous? - It makes the driver impossible to load again - The callback runs with too little privilege + The kernel later calls code that is no longer there - It slows the system down with extra calls Unloading frees the driver's image, but the kernel still holds the callback's address. The next event jumps into freed memory and crashes the machine.

title: Setting up and tearing down
body: Lesson 1.04's golden rule: Unload undoes everything DriverEntry did, in reverse order, and a DriverEntry that fails undoes what it already did. Write a small helper that enforces this, and that driver code can be written against: cpp class Setup { public: void done(const std::string& step, std::function<void() undo); // a step succeeded; remember how to undo it void rollback(); // undo every remembered step, newest first, once std::size_t count() const; }; std::vector<std::string runDriverEntry(const std::vector<std::string & steps, int failAt, std::vector<std::string & log); - Setup::rollback calls the undo functions in reverse order and forgets them, so a second call does nothing. count is how many steps are remembered. - runDriverEntry simulates a DriverEntry : for each step in order, if its index equals failAt , it logs "fail <step " , rolls back, and returns an empty list; otherwise it logs "do <step " and remembers an undo that logs "undo <step " . If all steps succeed, it returns the steps that Unload must undo, in the order Unload must undo them (newest first), without undoing anything yet.

title: 1.05  Kernel Debugging with WinDbg
body: Using WinDbg on the VM - breaking in, symbols, breakpoints in your driver, inspecting structures, reading a bug check with !analyze, and the handful of commands you will use every day. Symbols first A debugger without symbols shows addresses; with them it shows function names, types and source lines. Set the symbol path once (in WinDbg's settings or with a command) to Microsoft's symbol server plus your build folder: cpp-norun .sympath srv C:\Symbols https://msdl.microsoft.com/download/symbols;C:\Projects\XenonHello\x64\Debug .reload Your driver's .pdb (built next to the .sys ) gives your function names and source lines. Everyday commands Command Does --- --- g Go: let the target run Ctrl+Break Break in: freeze the whole target lm / lm m Xenon List loaded modules bp XenonHello!XenonDispatch Breakpoint on a function bu XenonHello!DriverEntry Breakpoint that waits for the module to load bl , bc List / clear breakpoints p , t , gu Step over, step into, step out k / kb Call stack dv Local variables dt nt!_UNICODE_STRING addr Show a structure at an address dx Explore objects with the data model ( dx @$curprocess ) !analyze -v Explain a bug check Reading a crash When the driver crashes, the target stops with a bug check and WinDbg shows something like: cpp-norun Fatal System Error: 0x000000d1 (0xFFFFA00012345678, 0x0000000000000002, 0x0000000000000000, 0xFFFFF80123456789) !analyze -v explains it: - The bug check code : 0xD1 DRIVER_IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL (touched pageable or invalid memory at a high IRQL, lesson 3.02), 0x50 PAGE_FAULT_IN_NONPAGED_AREA (a bad pointer), 0x3B SYSTEM_SERVICE_EXCEPTION , 0xC4 DRIVER_VERIFIER_DETECTED_VIOLATION (lesson 5.01), 0xCE DRIVER_UNLOADED_WITHOUT_CANCELLING_PENDING_OPERATIONS . - The parameters : for 0xD1 , the address that was touched, the IRQL, whether it was a read or a write, and the instruction's address. - The faulting module and stack : which driver, which function, which line. Most crashes in your own driver are found in a minute this way: the stack ends in your function, the source line shows the bad pointer. Crash dumps Without a live debugger, Windows writes a dump on a bug check ( C:\Windows\MEMORY.DMP or minidumps in C:\Windows\Minidump ). Open it in WinDbg (File Open dump file) and run the same !analyze -v . Configure "Kernel memory dump" in the VM's System Properties Startup and Recovery. Debugging habits - Put a DbgPrintEx at the start and end of every dispatch routine while developing; remove or quieten them later (lesson 4.02). - Set bu breakpoints before loading the driver, so DriverEntry can be stepped through. - When something "randomly" crashes, turn on Driver Verifier for your driver (lesson 5.01): it turns hidden bugs into immediate, explained crashes. Check yourself quiz ? Why does WinDbg need the driver's .pdb file? - It holds the driver's code, which WinDbg loads into the target + It holds the symbols: function names, types and source lines for the driver's code - It holds the driver's signature, which WinDbg checks - It holds the KDNET connection key Without symbols the debugger shows bare addresses. The PDB lets it show your function names, structures and the source line you are on. ? What does bug check 0xD1 usually mean? - The driver ran out of stack - The driver called a function that does not exist - The driver freed the same memory twice + Code at a raised IRQL touched pageable or invalid memory 0xD1 is DRIVER_IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL : at DISPATCH_LEVEL or above, page faults cannot be handled, so touching paged-out or invalid memory stops the machine. ? What is the difference between bp and bu ? + bu resolves its name when the module loads, so it can be set early - bp breaks on data access; bu breaks on execution - bu breaks only once, then removes itself - bp works only in user mode; bu works in the kernel bp needs the address now, so it fails for a driver that is not loaded yet. bu keeps the symbolic name and sets the breakpoint when the module appears.

title: Reading a bug check
body: Parse the line WinDbg prints when the VM stops on a bug check (lesson 1.05), and explain the common ones: cpp struct BugCheck { std::uint32_t code; std::uint64_t p 4 ; }; bool parseBugCheck(const std::string& line, BugCheck& out); std::string bugCheckName(std::uint32_t code); std::string explain(const BugCheck& b); The line looks like Fatal System Error: 0x000000d1 (0xFFFFA00012345678,0x0000000000000002,0x0000000000000000,0xFFFFF80123456789) , possibly with spaces after the commas; the code and parameters are hexadecimal with 0x , in either case. Anything that does not have exactly this shape (with four parameters) fails. Names: 0x0A IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL, 0x3B SYSTEM_SERVICE_EXCEPTION, 0x50 PAGE_FAULT_IN_NONPAGED_AREA, 0x7E SYSTEM_THREAD_EXCEPTION_NOT_HANDLED, 0xC4 DRIVER_VERIFIER_DETECTED_VIOLATION, 0xCE DRIVER_UNLOADED_WITHOUT_CANCELLING_PENDING_OPERATIONS, 0xD1 DRIVER_IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL; others UNKNOWN_BUG_CHECK . explain : - 0xD1 and 0x0A : "<read write execute of 0x<p0 at IRQL <p1 " where p2 is 0 read, 1 write, 8 execute (anything else access ), and p0 is printed as 16 upper-case hex digits; - 0x50 : "<read write of invalid address 0x<p0 " with p1 0 for read, anything else write; - others: the name.

title: Is the lab safe?
body: Check a driver lab's setup before loading anything. virtual machine: yes snapshot taken: yes test signing on (VM): yes host test signing: no (good: never on your main machine) kernel debugger: attached - ready to load the test driver

title: What a bug check says
body: Decode the codes from a blue screen. 0x0000000A IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL p1 0x0000000000000000 address referenced p2 0x0000000000000002 IRQL at the time (DISPATCH_LEVEL) 0x00000050 PAGE_FAULT_IN_NONPAGED_AREA 0x000000C4 DRIVER_VERIFIER_DETECTED_VIOLATION

title: Counted strings
