title: 2.01  Loops
body: The numeric for loop with its start, stop and step, while and repeat-until, break, skipping to the next round with goto continue, and the loop variable belonging to the loop. The numeric for lua for i = 1, 5 do io.write(i, " ") end print() for i = 10, 1, -3 do io.write(i, " ") end print() for x = 0, 1, 0.25 do io.write(x, " ") end print() 1 2 3 4 5 10 7 4 1 0 0.25 0.5 0.75 1 (The third loop counts in floats, because its step is a float. io.write writes a float like 0.0 as plain 0 ; print and tostring would show 0.0 .) for i = start, stop, step do ... end . The step is 1 when left out, and may be negative. Both ends are included : for i = 1, 5 runs five times. The start, stop and step are worked out once, before the first round, so changing them inside the loop has no effect. A loop that cannot start does not run at all: for i = 5, 1 do runs zero times (the step is +1, and 5 is already past 1). The loop variable is local to the loop . After end it is gone, and assigning to it inside the loop does not change the number of rounds. lua local total = 0 for n = 1, 100 do total = total + n end print(total) 5050 while while repeats as long as its condition is true, checking it before each round: lua local n, steps = 27, 0 while n ~= 1 do if n % 2 == 0 then n = n // 2 else n = 3 n + 1 end steps = steps + 1 end print(steps) 111 repeat ... until repeat checks its condition after each round, so the body always runs at least once. It stops when the condition becomes true: lua local value = 1 repeat value = value 3 until value 100 print(value) 243 A local declared inside the body is still visible in the until condition, which makes repeat natural for "ask until the answer is valid": lua-norun local age repeat io.write("Age? ") age = tonumber(io.read()) until age and age = 0 break break leaves the innermost loop at once: lua for i = 2, 100 do if i i 50 then print("first square over 50: " .. i i) break end end first square over 50: 64 Skipping a round Lua has no continue . Use goto with a label at the end of the body: lua for i = 1, 10 do if i % 3 ~= 0 then goto continue end io.write(i, " ") ::continue:: end print() 3 6 9 ::continue:: is a label ; goto continue jumps to it. The name is your choice, but continue is what everyone writes. Often an if around the rest of the body reads just as well. Loops inside loops lua for row = 1, 3 do local line = "" for col = 1, 4 do line = line .. row col .. "\t" end print(line) end 1 2 3 4 2 4 6 8 3 6 9 12 break leaves only the inner loop. To leave both, put the loops in a function and return , or use a flag. Reading until input ends io.read() returns nil when there is no more input, which ends a while loop neatly: lua-norun local count = 0 local line = io.read() while line do count = count + 1 line = io.read() end print(count .. " lines") Lesson 6.02 shows the shorter for line in io.lines() do . Check yourself quiz ? How many times does for i = 1, 10, 2 run? - Four + Five - Six - Ten i takes 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9. The next value, 11, is past 10, so the loop stops. ? What is the difference between while and repeat? - They are the same loop with different keywords - repeat tests before each round and may run zero times; while runs at least once + while tests before each round; repeat tests after, runs at least once, and stops when its condition becomes true repeat ... until cond checks after the body and ends when cond is true. while cond do checks first and runs while cond is true. ? What is printed? for i = 3, 1 do print(i) end - 3 2 1 - 3 + nothing - an error The step is +1 and 3 is already past 1, so the loop runs zero times. Write 3, 1, -1 to count down. ? What does Lua use instead of continue? - The next keyword - The skip keyword + goto continue , with a ::continue:: label - break 2 , to leave one level Lua has goto and labels; a ::continue:: label at the end of the loop body is the usual idiom.

title: 2.02  Tables as Lists
body: The table as Lua's only data structure, lists that start at index 1, the length operator, adding and removing with table.insert and table.remove, ipairs, and why holes in a list break . One structure for everything Lua has exactly one way to group values: the table . A table maps keys to values. Used with the keys 1, 2, 3 and so on, it is a list (an array); with other keys it is a dictionary, a record or an object. This lesson is about lists. lua local fruits = { "apple", "banana", "cherry" } print(fruits 1 , fruits 3 , fruits) print(fruits 4 ) apple cherry 3 nil !important Lists start at 1 The first item is fruits 1 , the last is fruits fruits . fruits 0 is nil. Every library function counts from 1 too. t is the list's length. Reading past the end is not an error, it is nil . Changing a list lua local t = { 10, 20, 30 } t 2 = 25 -- replace t t + 1 = 40 -- add at the end table.insert(t, 50) -- add at the end table.insert(t, 1, 5) -- insert at position 1, the rest move up print(table.concat(t, ", ")) local last = table.remove(t) -- remove the last, and return it local first = table.remove(t, 1) -- remove position 1, the rest move down print(first, last, table.concat(t, ", ")) 5, 10, 25, 30, 40, 50 5 50 10, 25, 30, 40 table.concat(t, sep) joins a list of strings or numbers into one string. It is the quickest way to print a list; print(t) only shows something like table: 0x55d0c8a3e2a0 . Looping over a list lua local scores = { 72, 95, 64 } for i = 1, scores do print(i, scores i ) end for i, score in ipairs(scores) do print("score " .. i .. " is " .. score) end 1 72 2 95 3 64 score 1 is 72 score 2 is 95 score 3 is 64 ipairs(t) gives each position and its value, in order, from 1 until the first nil . Use _ for a value you do not need: for _, score in ipairs(scores) . Do not insert into or remove from a list while looping over it forwards; positions move under you. Loop backwards ( for i = t, 1, -1 ) when removing. Building a list lua local squares = {} for n = 1, 6 do squares squares + 1 = n n end print(table.concat(squares, " ")) local evens = {} for _, n in ipairs(squares) do if n % 2 == 0 then table.insert(evens, n) end end print( evens, table.concat(evens, " ")) 1 4 9 16 25 36 3 4 16 36 Holes A list must not have holes : nil in the middle. Setting an item to nil does not remove it from a list; it makes a hole, and then may give either end of the hole, and ipairs stops at it: lua local t = { "a", "b", "c", "d" } t 2 = nil for i, v in ipairs(t) do print(i, v) end 1 a To remove an item, use table.remove . To mark one as missing, store false or a special value, not nil . Tables are values you share A variable holds a reference to a table, not a copy. Two variables can name the same table: lua local a = { 1, 2, 3 } local b = a b 1 = 99 print(a 1 , a == b) print({ 1, 2 } == { 1, 2 }) 99 true false == on tables asks "the same table?", not "the same contents?". Lesson 2.05 shows how to copy and compare by content. Check yourself quiz ? How do you read the last item of a list t? - t -1 - t t - 1 + t t - t 0 Lua lists start at 1, so the last item is at index t . Negative indexes do not count from the end: t -1 is just the key -1, usually nil. ? Why is t 2 = nil a bad way to remove the second item? - It removes every item after the second one too + It leaves a hole, so and ipairs become unreliable - It is an error to assign nil to a list item Setting an item to nil does not shift the others down, so and ipairs no longer see the items after it reliably. table.remove(t, 2) closes the gap. ? What does this print? local t = {5, 6, 7} print(t 0 , t 3 ) - 5 7 + nil 7 - an error - 5 nil Lists start at 1, so t 0 is nil and t 3 is the last item. ? What does table.remove(t) return? - nothing - the new length + the item it removed (the last one) - the table table.remove returns the value it took out.

None of them may change the list they are given. lua-norun sum(list) -- the total; 0 for an empty list largest(list) -- the biggest value, or nil for an empty list reversed(list) -- a NEW list with the items in the opposite order without(list, value) -- a NEW list with every item equal to value left out lua-norun sum({ 3, 4, 5 }) -- 12 largest({ 3, 9, 2 }) -- 9 reversed({ 1, 2, 3 }) -- { 3, 2, 1 } without({ 1, 2, 1, 3 }, 1) -- { 2, 3 }

title: 2.03  Tables as Dictionaries
body: Tables with any keys, the dot shorthand for string keys, records, adding and removing with nil, pairs and its order, counting and grouping, and using a table as a set. Any value can be a key A table's keys do not have to be 1, 2, 3. Any value except nil can be a key, most often a string: lua local ages = { "Ada" = 36, "Grace" = 85 } ages "Linus" = 21 -- add ages "Ada" = 37 -- replace ages "Grace" = nil -- remove print(ages "Ada" , ages "Grace" , ages "Nobody" ) 37 nil nil Setting a key to nil removes it: a table never stores nil values. Reading a key that is not there gives nil , so if ages name then tests whether a key exists. The dot shorthand When a key is a string that is a valid name, t.name means exactly t "name" , and in a constructor name = value means "name" = value : lua local book = { title = "Programming in Lua", year = 2016, pages = 388 } print(book.title, book "year" ) book.edition = 4 local field = "pages" print(book field , book.field) Programming in Lua 2016 388 nil The last line shows the classic mistake: book.field is the key "field" , not the value of the variable field . Use brackets when the key is in a variable. A table used like this is a record : one thing with named parts. Lists of records are the bread and butter of Lua programs: lua local people = { { name = "Ada", born = 1815 }, { name = "Alan", born = 1912 }, } for _, p in ipairs(people) do print(p.name .. " was born in " .. p.born) end Ada was born in 1815 Alan was born in 1912 A constructor can mix both kinds: { "a", "b", sep = ", " } has 1 , 2 and sep . pairs pairs(t) visits every key and value in a table: lua local stock = { apples = 4, pears = 0, plums = 12 } local total = 0 for fruit, count in pairs(stock) do total = total + count end print(total) 16 !warning pairs has no order The order of pairs is not the order you wrote the keys in, and may differ from run to run. When order matters, collect the keys in a list and sort it (next lesson), or keep a list beside the table. ipairs is for the list part (1, 2, 3... in order); pairs is for everything. t counts only the list part: stock above is 0. Counting and grouping Two patterns that come up all the time: lua local words = { "the", "cat", "and", "the", "hat" } local counts = {} for _, w in ipairs(words) do counts w = (counts w or 0) + 1 end print(counts.the, counts.cat, counts.dog) local by_letter = {} for _, w in ipairs(words) do local first = w:sub(1, 1) by_letter first = by_letter first or {} table.insert(by_letter first , w) end print(table.concat(by_letter.t, " "), by_letter.c) 2 1 nil the the 1 (counts w or 0) + 1 uses the or default from lesson 1.05: a missing count starts at 0. Sets A table whose values are all true is a set : it answers "is this in it?" instantly, however big it is. lua local vowels = { a = true, e = true, i = true, o = true, u = true } local text, n = "programming in lua", 0 for i = 1, text do if vowels text:sub(i, i) then n = n + 1 end end print(n .. " vowels") local seen = {} for _, w in ipairs({ "b", "a", "b", "c", "a" }) do seen w = true end local unique = 0 for _ in pairs(seen) do unique = unique + 1 end print(unique .. " different") 6 vowels 3 different To count the entries of a non-list table you have to loop with pairs ; does not count them. Check yourself quiz ? How do you remove a key from a table? + Assign nil to it: t.key = nil - Call table.remove(t, "key") - Assign an empty string to it: t.key = "" - Call t:delete("key") A key whose value is nil does not exist. table.remove works on list positions, not on named keys. ? What is the difference between t.name and t name ? - None: both use the key "name" + t.name is the key "name"; t name uses the value of the variable name as the key - t.name reads a field; t name reads a list position t.name is short for t "name" . In t name , name is a variable, so the key is whatever it holds. ? local t = { x = 1, y = 2 } What is t ? - 2 + 0 - 1 - nil measures the list part (keys 1, 2, 3...). This table has no list part. ? Which loop visits keys in a guaranteed order? - pairs - both - neither + ipairs over a list ipairs goes 1, 2, 3... in order. pairs has no defined order.

The words arrive already split, as a list of strings. lua-norun count_words(words) -- a table: word - how many times it appears most_common(counts) -- the word with the highest count and that count (two results); -- ties go to the word that comes first alphabetically; nil for an empty table unique_sorted(words) -- a list of the different words, sorted alphabetically lua-norun local counts = count_words({ "b", "a", "b" }) -- { b = 2, a = 1 } most_common(counts) -- "b", 2 unique_sorted({ "b", "a", "b" }) -- { "a", "b" }

title: 2.04  The Table Library
body: table.sort with and without a comparison function, sorting records and sorting by several keys, sorting a dictionary's keys for ordered output, table.concat, table.unpack and table.pack, and table.move. table.sort table.sort(t) sorts a list in place (it changes t and returns nothing), smallest first: lua local nums = { 5, 2, 9, 1, 7 } table.sort(nums) print(table.concat(nums, " ")) local names = { "lua", "C", "Rust", "ada" } table.sort(names) print(table.concat(names, " ")) 1 2 5 7 9 C Rust ada lua Strings sort by byte value, so capitals come first. For any other order, pass a comparison function : it gets two items and returns true when the first must come before the second. lua local nums = { 5, 2, 9, 1, 7 } table.sort(nums, function(a, b) return a b end) print(table.concat(nums, " ")) local names = { "lua", "C", "Rust", "ada" } table.sort(names, function(a, b) return a:lower() < b:lower() end) print(table.concat(names, " ")) 9 7 5 2 1 ada C lua Rust function(a, b) ... end written right inside the call is a function without a name; lesson 3.03 explains it. For now, read it as "the rule for the order". !warning The rule must be strict Return a < b , never a <= b . With <= two equal items each claim to come first, and table.sort can fail with "invalid order function for sorting". table.sort is also not stable: equal items may swap places. Sorting records lua local people = { { name = "Grace", age = 85 }, { name = "Ada", age = 36 }, { name = "Linus", age = 36 }, } table.sort(people, function(a, b) if a.age ~= b.age then return a.age < b.age end -- first by age return a.name < b.name -- then by name end) for _, p in ipairs(people) do print(p.age, p.name) end 36 Ada 36 Linus 85 Grace Comparing the first key and only falling back to the second when they are equal sorts by several keys at once, and also makes the order of equal ages predictable. Ordered output from a dictionary pairs has no order, so to print a dictionary sorted, collect its keys, sort them, then look each one up: lua local stock = { plums = 12, apples = 4, pears = 7 } local keys = {} for k in pairs(stock) do keys keys + 1 = k end table.sort(keys) for _, k in ipairs(keys) do print(k, stock k ) end apples 4 pears 7 plums 12 concat, unpack, pack, move lua local parts = { "2026", "11", "16" } print(table.concat(parts, "-")) print(table.concat(parts, "", 2, 3)) -- only items 2 to 3 print(table.unpack({ 10, 20, 30 })) local a, b = table.unpack({ 10, 20, 30 }) print(a + b) print(math.max(table.unpack({ 4, 9, 2 }))) local packed = table.pack("x", nil, "z") print(packed.n, packed 1 , packed 3 ) local src, dst = { 1, 2, 3 }, { "a", "b", "c", "d" } table.move(src, 1, 3, 2, dst) -- copy src 1..3 into dst from position 2 print(table.concat(dst, " ")) 2026-11-16 1116 10 20 30 30 9 3 x z a 1 2 3 - table.unpack(t) turns a list into separate values: what you need to pass a list to a function that takes separate arguments, like math.max . - table.pack(...) does the opposite and records the count in n , which matters when some values are nil . - table.move(a, from, to, at, b) copies a range, into another table or within the same one. table.concat only joins strings and numbers. A list containing true or a table is an error: convert with tostring first. Check yourself quiz ? What does table.sort return? - A new sorted table, leaving the original as it was - The number of items it sorted + Nothing: it sorts the table you gave it, in place table.sort(t) changes t itself and returns nothing, so t = table.sort(t) would set t to nil. ? How do you sort a list of numbers from largest to smallest? - table.sort(t, " ") - table.sort(t) and then read it from the end - table.sort(t, function(a, b) return a < b end) + table.sort(t, function(a, b) return a b end) The comparison function returns true when a should come before b. a < b is the default ascending order. ? What does table.concat({1, 2, 3}) give? - "1 2 3" + "123" - "1, 2, 3" - 6 The separator defaults to an empty string. ? Why must a sort comparison use < rather than <=? - <= is much slower than < for strings + With <= , equal items both claim to come first - <= only works when comparing numbers - There is no difference for table.sort The function must say "a strictly before b". <= gives an inconsistent order, which can make table.sort fail with "invalid order function".

title: 2.05  Nested Tables and Copies
body: Tables inside tables for grids and data, references and what really gets copied, shallow and deep copies, comparing tables by content, and printing a nested table so you can see it. Tables inside tables A table's values can be tables, which gives you any shape of data you need: lua local grid = { { 1, 2, 3 }, { 4, 5, 6 }, } print(grid 2 3 , grid, grid 1 ) local game = { player = { name = "Ada", hp = 30, items = { "sword", "lamp" } }, level = 3, } print(game.player.name, game.player.items 2 , game.player.items) game.player.hp = game.player.hp - 5 print(game.player.hp) 6 2 3 Ada lamp 2 25 Building a grid takes a loop for the rows and one for the columns. Every row must be its own table: lua local rows, cols = 3, 4 local board = {} for r = 1, rows do board r = {} for c = 1, cols do board r c = "." end end board 2 3 = " " for r = 1, rows do print(table.concat(board r )) end .... .. . .... What gets copied Assigning a table, passing it to a function or storing it inside another table never copies it . Every one of those is the same table: lua local row = { 0, 0, 0 } local bad = { row, row, row } -- the same row three times bad 1 1 = 9 print(bad 1 1 , bad 2 1 , bad 3 1 ) 9 9 9 Numbers, strings and booleans behave like separate copies (they cannot be changed in place anyway); tables and functions are shared. Copying A shallow copy makes a new table with the same keys and values. Nested tables inside are still shared: lua local function shallow_copy(t) local copy = {} for k, v in pairs(t) do copy k = v end return copy end local a = { 1, 2, inner = { 3 } } local b = shallow_copy(a) b 1 = 100 b.inner 1 = 300 print(a 1 , a.inner 1 ) 1 300 A deep copy copies the nested tables too. It calls itself for every table it meets (a function calling itself is recursion , lesson 3.04): lua local function deep_copy(t) if type(t) ~= "table" then return t end local copy = {} for k, v in pairs(t) do copy k = deep_copy(v) end return copy end local a = { 1, inner = { 2, deeper = { 3 } } } local b = deep_copy(a) b.inner.deeper 1 = 99 print(a.inner.deeper 1 , b.inner.deeper 1 ) 3 99 This simple version is fine for data. It does not handle a table that contains itself, and it does not copy metatables (milestone 5). Comparing by content == asks whether two tables are the same table. To ask whether they hold the same things, compare key by key, in both directions: lua local function same(a, b) if type(a) ~= "table" or type(b) ~= "table" then return a == b end for k, v in pairs(a) do if not same(v, b k ) then return false end end for k in pairs(b) do if a k == nil then return false end end return true end print(same({ 1, { 2, 3 } }, { 1, { 2, 3 } }), same({ 1, 2 }, { 1, 2, 3 })) true false The test kit's check_eq compares tables exactly this way, which is why your practice tests can say check_eq(result, { 1, 2, 3 }) . Seeing a nested table print(t) shows only an address. While you work, a small function that writes a table out helps a lot: lua local function show(v) if type(v) ~= "table" then return type(v) == "string" and string.format("%q", v) or tostring(v) end local parts = {} for _, item in ipairs(v) do parts parts + 1 = show(item) end local keys = {} for k in pairs(v) do if not (math.type(k) == "integer" and k = 1 and k <= v) then keys keys + 1 = k end end table.sort(keys, function(x, y) return tostring(x) < tostring(y) end) for _, k in ipairs(keys) do parts parts + 1 = tostring(k) .. " = " .. show(v k ) end return "{" .. table.concat(parts, ", ") .. "}" end print(show({ 1, "two", { 3 }, name = "Ada", ok = true })) {1, "two", {3}, name = "Ada", ok = true} Keep a function like this in your toolbox; you will reuse it in later practice. Check yourself quiz ? After local b = a , where a is a table, does changing b 1 change a? - No: b is a copy of a + Yes: b and a are the same table - Only if a 1 was a number Assigning a table copies the reference, not the contents, so both names reach one table; nothing was copied. ? What does a shallow copy not copy? - The numbers and strings stored in it + The tables nested inside it - The keys that are not numbers A shallow copy makes a new outer table with the same values. A value that is a table is the same inner table in both, so changing it shows in both. ? local t = {}; t.self = t What is t.self.self == t ? - false - an error + true - nil t.self is t itself, so any number of .self steps still leads to t.

Grace 88 B Average: 90.3 A: 1 B: 2 C: 0 D: 0 F: 0 - Grades: A for 90 and over, B 80-89, C 70-79, D 60-69, F below 60. - Each report line is string.format("%2d. %-10s %3d %s", position, name, score, grade) . - The average has one decimal. - A score that is not a whole number from 0 to 100 prints Invalid score, try again. and asks for that score again ( Score? ). - With 0 students, print Report , No students. and nothing else.

title: 3.01  Functions
body: Defining functions with function ... end, local functions, parameters and return, returning several values and where the extra values go, and functions that return nothing. Defining and calling lua local function greet(name) return "Hello, " .. name .. "!" end print(greet("Ada")) print(greet("Lua")) Hello, Ada! Hello, Lua! local function name(parameters) ... end defines a function. return hands a value back to the caller and leaves the function at once. A function is defined when Lua runs the definition, so define it above the code that calls it. Like variables, functions should be local unless something else needs to find them by name. In the practice tasks, the functions the task names are global ( function greet(name) ) so the tests can call them. Parameters A parameter is a local variable that starts with the value the caller passed. Lua does not check how many arguments you pass: missing ones are nil , extra ones are dropped. lua local function describe(name, age) return name .. " is " .. tostring(age) end print(describe("Ada", 36)) print(describe("Ada")) print(describe("Ada", 36, "ignored")) Ada is 36 Ada is nil Ada is 36 The next lesson uses this to give parameters default values. Returning several values A function can return several values, and the caller can take as many as it wants: lua local function min_max(list) local lo, hi = list 1 , list 1 for _, v in ipairs(list) do if v < lo then lo = v end if v hi then hi = v end end return lo, hi end local lo, hi = min_max({ 4, 9, 2, 7 }) print(lo, hi) local just_lo = min_max({ 4, 9, 2, 7 }) print(just_lo) 2 9 2 Lua's own functions do this too: string.find returns a start and an end, pcall returns a success flag and a result. Where the extra values go Every value of a call is kept only when the call is the last item in a list (of arguments, of a table constructor, of a return ). Anywhere else, the call is cut down to its first value: lua local function two() return 1, 2 end print(two()) -- 1 2 print(two(), "x") -- 1 x : not last, so only the first value print("x", two()) -- x 1 2 print((two())) -- 1 : brackets cut it to one value local t = { two(), two() } print( t) -- 3 : {1, 1, 2} 1 2 1 x x 1 2 1 3 Functions that return nothing A function without return , or with a plain return , returns no values. Using its result gives nil : lua local function log(message) print(" log " .. message) end local result = log("started") print(result) log started nil !warning Printing is not returning A function that prints its answer cannot be used in a calculation. When a task says "returns", use return ; the tests read the returned value, not the printed text. return must be the last statement in its block. To leave a function early from the middle, put it inside an if , which is the usual way anyway: lua local function sign(n) if n 0 then return 1 end if n < 0 then return -1 end return 0 end print(sign(-5), sign(0), sign(8)) -1 0 1 Check yourself quiz ? What happens when you call a two-parameter function with one argument? - Lua raises an error about the missing argument + The second parameter is nil - The second parameter gets the value of the first - The second parameter is 0 Lua never checks the number of arguments: missing ones are nil and extra ones are dropped. ? How do you keep only the first result of a call that returns several? - Call it with select(1, f()) + Put the call in brackets, (f()) - Assign it to a table and read 0 Brackets around a call cut it to one value. A call that is not the last item in a list is also cut to one. select(1, ...) returns everything from the first value on. ? local function f() return 1, 2, 3 end What is { f(), f() } ? - 6 + 4 - 2 - 3 The first call is not last, so it gives one value; the last call gives all three: {1, 1, 2, 3}. ? What does a function without return give back? - The number 0 - The value false + No values: nil if you use the result - An error when the call is used Using the result of a call that returned nothing gives nil.

title: Several results

title: 3.02  Optional and Variable Arguments
body: Default values with or, when or is wrong for booleans, functions that take any number of arguments with ..., select and table.pack, and named arguments passed in a table. Defaults A missing argument is nil , and x or default replaces nil : lua local function repeat_text(text, times, sep) times = times or 2 sep = sep or " " local parts = {} for i = 1, times do parts i = text end return table.concat(parts, sep) end print(repeat_text("ha")) print(repeat_text("ha", 3)) print(repeat_text("ha", 3, "-")) ha ha ha ha ha ha-ha-ha !warning or swallows false verbose = verbose or true makes verbose true even when the caller passed false . For a boolean (or any parameter where false is meaningful), test for nil: if verbose == nil then verbose = true end . Any number of arguments Three dots as the last parameter collect every extra argument. Inside the function, ... stands for all of them: lua local function sum(...) local total = 0 for _, n in ipairs({ ... }) do total = total + n end return total end print(sum(), sum(5), sum(1, 2, 3, 4)) 0 5 10 { ... } packs them into a list. Named parameters can come first: local function printf(format, ...) . lua local function printf(format, ...) io.write(string.format(format, ...)) end printf("%s has %d items, %.1f%% full\n", "bag", 3, 37.5) bag has 3 items, 37.5% full Passing ... on to another function forwards every value unchanged. ( %% in a format is a literal % .) nil among the arguments { ... } and ipairs stop at the first nil , so they lose arguments after one. When nil can be an argument, use select or table.pack : lua local function count(...) return select(" ", ...) end print(count(1, nil, 3), count()) local function show_all(...) local args = table.pack(...) for i = 1, args.n do io.write(i, "=", tostring(args i ), " ") end print() end show_all("a", nil, "c") print(select(2, "a", "b", "c")) 3 0 1=a 2=nil 3=c b c - select(" ", ...) is the number of arguments, nils included. - select(n, ...) gives argument n and everything after it . - table.pack(...) gives a table with the count in its field n . Named arguments When a function has many optional settings, take a single table and read fields from it. The call reads almost like a sentence, and you can leave out anything: lua local function make_window(options) local title = options.title or "Untitled" local width = options.width or 640 local height = options.height or 480 return title .. " (" .. width .. "x" .. height .. ")" end print(make_window({ title = "Editor", width = 1024 })) print(make_window{ height = 200 }) Editor (1024x480) Untitled (640x200) When a function's only argument is a table constructor or a string literal, the brackets can be left out: make_window{ ... } , print "hi" . You will see this in configuration files and in libraries. Use it sparingly in your own code. Check yourself quiz ? Why is flag = flag or true a bug? - or cannot be used with booleans + If the caller passes false, false or true is true, so false can never get through - It sets flag to true even when the caller passes true or replaces any false value, not only nil. Test if flag == nil then flag = true end to replace only a missing argument. ? How many arguments did a function receive, counting nils? - {...} - ... + select(" ", ...) select(" ", ...) counts every argument, including nils. {...} can be wrong when there are nils, because they make holes in the table. ? What does select(2, "a", "b", "c") return? - "b" + "b", "c" - "a", "b" - 2 select(n, ...) returns argument n and all the ones after it. ? local function f(...) return {...} end What can go wrong with f(1, nil, 3)? - Nothing: it always returns 3 + The nil makes a hole, so the length is unreliable - It raises an error because of the nil - It always returns 1 A table with a nil in the middle has a hole, and may report either end of it. Use select(" ", ...) .

title: 3.03  Functions as Values and Closures
body: Functions are values you can store, pass and return, anonymous functions, writing map, filter and reduce, closures that remember the variables around them, counters and factories, and the loop variable being fresh each round. Functions are values local function add(a, b) ... end is a shorter way of writing local add = function(a, b) ... end . A function is a value of type function , like a number or a table, so it can be stored in variables and tables, passed to other functions and returned from them: lua local function double(x) return x 2 end local twice = double print(twice(21), type(double)) local ops = { add = function(a, b) return a + b end, mul = function(a, b) return a b end, } print(ops.add(2, 3), ops "mul" (2, 3)) 42 function 5 6 A function written without a name ( function(a, b) ... end ) is an anonymous function . You met one already as the comparison passed to table.sort . Functions that take functions A function that takes or returns another function is a higher-order function. The three classic ones work on lists: lua local function map(list, f) local out = {} for i, v in ipairs(list) do out i = f(v) end return out end local function filter(list, keep) local out = {} for _, v in ipairs(list) do if keep(v) then out out + 1 = v end end return out end local function reduce(list, f, start) local acc = start for _, v in ipairs(list) do acc = f(acc, v) end return acc end local nums = { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 } print(table.concat(map(nums, function(x) return x x end), " ")) print(table.concat(filter(nums, function(x) return x % 2 == 0 end), " ")) print(reduce(nums, function(a, b) return a + b end, 0)) 1 4 9 16 25 36 2 4 6 21 Lua has none of these built in; programs write them (or take them from a library) when they want them. Closures A function can use the local variables of the function it was written inside, even after that outer function has returned. The inner function together with the variables it remembers is a closure : lua local function make_counter() local count = 0 return function() count = count + 1 return count end end local a = make_counter() local b = make_counter() print(a(), a(), a()) print(b()) 1 2 3 1 Each call of make_counter creates a new count , and the returned function keeps it alive. a and b have separate counters. The remembered variables are called upvalues . Closures are how Lua code keeps private state without objects: lua local function make_multiplier(factor) return function(x) return x factor end end local triple = make_multiplier(3) local half = make_multiplier(0.5) print(triple(7), half(7)) 21 3.5 Shared, not copied A closure shares the variable itself, not a copy of its value. Two closures made in the same call share the same variable: lua local function make_account(balance) local function deposit(n) balance = balance + n end local function get() return balance end return deposit, get end local deposit, get = make_account(100) deposit(25) deposit(5) print(get()) 130 The loop variable of a for is a new local in every round, so closures made in a loop each remember their own value: lua local buttons = {} for i = 1, 3 do buttons i = function() return "button " .. i end end print(buttons 1 (), buttons 3 ()) button 1 button 3 (In some languages every one of those would say "button 3". In Lua each round has its own i .) Check yourself quiz ? What is a closure? - A function that has finished running - A function with no name, written inline + A function plus the outer local variables it uses A closure keeps the outer locals it uses alive, even after the function that created them has returned. An anonymous function is only a closure when it captures something. ? Two counters from make_counter: do they share a count? + No: each call of make_counter creates a new count variable - Yes: count belongs to make_counter, so all counters share it - Yes, until one of them is reset Every call runs local count = 0 again, so each returned function captures its own variable. ? What does this print? local x = 1; local f = function() return x end; x = 2; print(f()) - 1 + 2 - nil - an error The function shares the variable x itself, and x is 2 when f is called.

title: Functions that take and make functions

body: Write five higher-order functions: lua-norun map(list, f) -- a new list of f(item) for every item filter(list, keep) -- a new list of the items for which keep(item) is true reduce(list, f, start) -- f(f(f(start, a), b), c)... for the items a, b, c; start when the list is empty compose(f, g) -- a function that returns f(g(x)) make_counter(start, step) -- a function that returns start the first time it is called, -- then start + step, start + 2 step...; step defaults to 1 lua-norun local inc_then_double = compose(function(x) return x 2 end, function(x) return x + 1 end) inc_then_double(4) -- 10 local c = make_counter(10, 5) c(), c(), c() -- 10, 15, 20

title: 3.04  Recursion
body: Functions that call themselves, the base case, why a local recursive function needs local function, walking nested tables, speeding up repeated work with memoisation, and Lua's proper tail calls. A function that calls itself A recursive function solves a problem by solving a smaller copy of the same problem. It needs a base case that stops, and every other call must move towards it: lua local function factorial(n) if n <= 1 then return 1 end -- base case return n factorial(n - 1) -- a smaller problem end print(factorial(5), factorial(20)) 120 2432902008176640000 local function factorial matters here. It declares the local name first, then the function, so the body can see factorial . Written as local factorial = function(n) ... factorial(n - 1) ... end , the name inside refers to a global factorial that does not exist yet, and the call fails. Without a base case (or with one the calls never reach) the program fails with "stack overflow" after about 200,000 nested calls. Walking nested data Recursion fits data that contains smaller versions of itself, like tables in tables: lua local function sum_all(t) local total = 0 for _, v in pairs(t) do if type(v) == "table" then total = total + sum_all(v) else total = total + v end end return total end print(sum_all({ 1, 2, { 3, 4, { 5 } }, { 6 } })) local function depth(t) if type(t) ~= "table" then return 0 end local deepest = 0 for _, v in pairs(t) do deepest = math.max(deepest, depth(v)) end return deepest + 1 end print(depth({ 1, { 2, { 3 } } }), depth({}), depth(5)) 21 3 1 0 A tree of files and folders, a menu with sub-menus, a parsed expression: the shape is always "a value, or a table of more of the same". Remembering answers The direct recursive Fibonacci recomputes the same values over and over, so it gets slow very fast: lua local calls = 0 local function slow_fib(n) calls = calls + 1 if n < 2 then return n end return slow_fib(n - 1) + slow_fib(n - 2) end print(slow_fib(25), calls) 75025 242785 Memoisation stores each answer in a table the first time and looks it up afterwards: lua local memo = {} local function fib(n) if n < 2 then return n end if memo n then return memo n end local result = fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2) memo n = result return result end print(fib(25), fib(90)) 75025 2880067194370816120 From hundreds of thousands of calls down to about a hundred. Tail calls When a function's very last action is return f(args) , Lua does not keep the current call around while f runs: it replaces it. Such a tail call uses no extra stack, so a tail-recursive function can run any number of times: lua local function count_down(n) if n == 0 then return "done" end return count_down(n - 1) -- a tail call end print(count_down(1000000)) done return n f(n - 1) is not a tail call (the multiplication still has to happen afterwards), and neither is return (f(x)) or f(x); return . Only return f(args) exactly. Check yourself quiz ? Why does a recursive local function need local function name ? - Recursion is only allowed for local functions - So the function runs faster when it calls itself + So the name exists before the body is compiled local f = function() ... f() ... end compiles the body before f exists, so the inner f refers to a global, usually nil. local function f declares the name first. ? Is return 1 + f(n - 1) a tail call? - Yes: the call is in a return statement + No: the addition still runs after f returns - Yes, because Lua reorders the addition A tail call is return f(...) with nothing left to do afterwards. Here 1 + still has to run, so the current call must be kept. ? What does memoisation store? - The call stack of each recursive call + Results already computed, looked up by input - Every argument the function was ever passed - The source code of the function A memo table maps inputs to results that were already worked out, so they are looked up instead of recomputed.

title: Recursive functions
body: Write four functions, each one calling itself: lua-norun sum_digits(n) -- the sum of the decimal digits of a whole number n = 0: sum_digits(4096) is 19 to_binary(n) -- the binary digits of a whole number n = 0 as a string: to_binary(10) is "1010", to_binary(0) is "0" flatten(list) -- a new flat list of every value in list and in the lists inside it, in order paths(rows, cols) -- the number of ways from the top-left to the bottom-right corner of a rows x cols grid, -- moving only right or down paths(r, c) is paths(r - 1, c) + paths(r, c - 1) , and 1 when r or c is 1. The tests ask for paths(17, 17) , which takes far too long unless the function remembers answers it has already worked out.

title: 3.05  Scope, Globals and Blocks
body: Where a local is visible, blocks and do ... end, shadowing, how globals live in the table _G, why a typo creates a global, the const and close attributes of Lua 5.4, and keeping a file's names private. A local lives in its block A local variable is visible from the line after its declaration to the end of the block it is in. Every then ... end , loop body, function body and do ... end is a block: lua local x = "outer" do local x = "inner" -- a new x, hiding the outer one local y = 1 print(x, y) end print(x, y) inner 1 outer nil do ... end makes a block on its own, which is useful to keep helper variables from leaking. The inner x shadows the outer one: same name, different variable. Shadowing is legal but confusing; prefer new names. Globals are a table A name that is not a local is a global , and globals are simply fields of a table called _G : lua score = 10 -- no local: a global print(_G.score, _G "score" ) _G.level = 3 print(level) print(type(_G.print), _G.math.pi 3) 10 10 3 function true print , math , string , table and the rest of the standard library are globals too: entries in _G . That has a consequence: lua local function total(list) sum = 0 -- forgot local for _, v in ipairs(list) do sum = sum + v end return sum end print(total({ 1, 2, 3 }), sum) 6 6 sum leaked out of the function into the whole program. A second function using its own sum would silently trample this one. Misspell a variable ( totl = totl + 1 ) and you get a global, plus an "arithmetic on a nil value" error much later. !tip Finding accidental globals Run luac -l -p file.lua (shipped with Lua) and look for SETTABUP lines: each one writes a global. Editors with a Lua language server underline undefined globals as you type. Lesson 5.02 shows how to make reading a missing global an error. Locals are also faster than globals: a local lives in a register, a global is a table lookup every time. That is why Lua code often starts with local insert = table.insert . const and close Lua 5.4 adds two attributes for locals: lua local LIMIT <const = 100 print(LIMIT 2) -- LIMIT = 5 would not compile: attempt to assign to const variable 'LIMIT' 200 <const makes assigning to the variable a compile-time error. <close is for resources: when the block ends, Lua calls the value's __close metamethod, so a file or lock is released even if an error happens. Lesson 6.04 uses it with files. Private names in a file A file is a block too. A local at the top of a file is visible to the rest of that file and to nothing else. A module (lesson 5.05) keeps its helpers local and hands out only what it returns: lua-norun -- shapes.lua local function square(x) return x x end -- private helper local M = {} function M.circle_area(r) return math.pi square(r) end return M Upvalues and blocks together A block can create private state for a function, with no global and no outer variable involved: lua local next_id do local last = 0 next_id = function() last = last + 1 return "id" .. last end end print(next_id(), next_id(), last) id1 id2 nil last is invisible outside the do block, but the closure keeps it alive. Check yourself quiz ? Where do global variables live? - In the stack of the main chunk + In the table _G: x = 5 is the same as _G.x = 5 - In a separate memory area that Lua cannot list Globals are fields of the table _G , so you can read, set and loop over them like any table. ? What does <const do? + Makes it a compile-time error to assign to that local after its declaration - Makes the value itself unchangeable, including the tables inside it - Turns the local into a global that cannot be changed local x <const = 5 stops assignments to x. If x holds a table, the table's contents can still change. ? A function says count = count + 1 without ever declaring count. What is count? - A local variable of that function + A global, nil until set, so the first call fails - A compile-time error - A number that starts at zero Undeclared names are globals. Reading the unset global gives nil, and nil + 1 is an "arithmetic on a nil value" error.

title: A function toolkit
body: Build a small library of tools that wrap other functions, the kind every larger Lua program ends up with. Write them as fields of a module table and return it: lua-norun local fn = {} -- ... return fn Function Returns --- --- fn.memoize(f) a function like f (one argument) that calls f only once per different argument, and gives the remembered result after that, even when the result is nil or false fn.once(f) a function that calls f the first time (with its arguments, returning all its results) and afterwards returns those same results without calling f fn.partial(f, ...) a function that calls f with the given arguments first, followed by its own arguments fn.pipe(...) a function that passes its argument through every given function from left to right; with no functions it returns its argument unchanged fn.count_calls(f) two results: a function that calls f and passes back all its results, and a function that returns how many times it has been called lua-norun local add = function(a, b, c) return a + b + (c or 0) end fn.partial(add, 1)(2) -- 3 fn.partial(add, 1, 2)(3) -- 6 fn.pipe(math.abs, math.sqrt)(-16) -- 4.0

title: 4.01  The String Library
body: Method syntax s:upper(), sub with positive and negative positions, upper, lower, rep, reverse, byte and char, find with plain text, and walking through a string character by character. Method syntax Every string function lives in the table string , and every string knows it. So string.upper(s) can be written s:upper() : the colon passes the string as the first argument. lua local s = "Hello, Lua" print(string.upper(s), s:upper(), s:lower()) print(("abc"):rep(3), ("abc"):rep(3, "-"), s:reverse()) print(s:len(), s) HELLO, LUA HELLO, LUA hello, lua abcabcabc abc-abc-abc auL ,olleH 10 10 A string literal needs brackets around it before the colon: ("abc"):rep(3) . sub: pieces of a string s:sub(i, j) returns the characters from position i to j , both included , counting from 1. Negative positions count from the end: -1 is the last character. lua local s = "programming" print(s:sub(1, 3), s:sub(4), s:sub(-4), s:sub(-4, -2)) print(s:sub(5, 5), s:sub(20), s:sub(3, 1) == "") pro gramming ming min r true sub never fails: positions past the end are clamped, and an empty range gives "" . To get one character, use s:sub(i, i) . Characters and their codes s:byte(i) gives the numeric code of the byte at position i ; string.char turns codes back into text: lua print(("A"):byte(), ("abc"):byte(1, 3)) print(string.char(72, 105, 33)) local shifted = {} for i = 1, "HAL" do shifted i = string.char(("HAL"):byte(i) + 1) end print(table.concat(shifted)) 65 97 98 99 Hi! IBM Walking through a string lua local word = "banana" local count = 0 for i = 1, word do if word:sub(i, i) == "a" then count = count + 1 end end print(count) local reversed = {} for i = word, 1, -1 do reversed reversed + 1 = word:sub(i, i) end print(table.concat(reversed)) 3 ananab Building a new string by .. -ing one character at a time works but copies the whole string each time. For anything long, collect the pieces in a table and table.concat once at the end. find s:find(text, start, true) looks for text and returns where it starts and ends, or nil : lua local s = "one, two, three" print(s:find("two", 1, true)) print(s:find("four", 1, true)) print(s:find(",", 6, true)) print(s:find(".", 1, true), s:find(".")) 6 8 nil 9 9 nil 1 1 The fourth argument true means plain search. Without it, the text is a pattern (next lesson), where . means "any character", which is why the last find(".") matched at 1. Always pass 1, true when you are searching for literal text that might contain . % - + ? ( ) ^ $ . Using find to split at a separator: lua local function split_once(s, sep) local at = s:find(sep, 1, true) if not at then return s, nil end return s:sub(1, at - 1), s:sub(at + sep) end print(split_once("key=value", "=")) print(split_once("no separator", "=")) key value no separator nil Comparing and testing lua local a, b = "Lua", "lua" print(a == b, a:lower() == b:lower()) print(("hello"):sub(1, 2) == "he", ("file.txt"):sub(-4) == ".txt") false true true true Check yourself quiz ? What does ("hello"):sub(-3) give? - "hel" + "llo" - "lo" - "he" A negative index counts from the end, so -3 is the third character from the end, and sub runs to the end by default. ? Why pass true as the fourth argument of find? - To make the search ignore case - To search from the end of the string + To search for plain text instead of a pattern Without it, the search text is a pattern and characters like . or - have special meanings. The third argument is the start position, so pass it too: s:find(".", 1, true) . ? What is ("abcdef"):sub(2, 4) ? - "bc" + "bcd" - "cde" - "bcde" Positions 2 to 4, both included. ? What does ("a.b"):find(".") return? - 2 2 + 1 1 - nil - an error Without plain = true, "." is a pattern meaning any character, so it matches the first one.

title: 4.02  Patterns
body: Lua patterns as a small alternative to regular expressions, the character classes %d %a %s %w and friends, sets in square brackets, the repeat signs + - ?, anchors, captures, and string.match. A small language for text Lua does not have regular expressions. It has patterns , which do most of the same work with a much smaller set of rules. string.match(s, pattern) returns the first part of s that matches, or nil : lua print(("order 66 shipped"):match("%d+")) print(("hello"):match("%d+")) print(("Version 5.4.7"):match("%d+%.%d+")) 66 nil 5.4 Character classes Class Matches Upper case = the opposite --- --- --- . any character %a letters %A not a letter %d digits 0-9 %D %l / %u lower / upper case letters %s whitespace (space, tab, newline) %S %w letters and digits %W %p punctuation %P %x hex digits % also escapes the special characters: %. is a real dot, %% a real percent sign, %- a real minus. (Lua uses % where other languages use \ .) A set in square brackets matches one character from it: aeiou a vowel, %w_ a letter, digit or underscore, 0-9a-f a range. ^... matches any character not in the set: ^, anything but a comma. Repeats Sign Means --- --- + one or more, as many as possible zero or more, as many as possible - zero or more, as few as possible ? optional: zero or one lua local s = "<b bold</b and <i it</i " print(s:match("<. ")) -- greedy: as much as possible print(s:match("<.- ")) -- lazy: as little as possible print(("-42"):match("^-?%d+$"), ("4-2"):match("^-?%d+$")) <b bold</b and <i it</i <b -42 nil Repeat signs apply to one character class only. Lua patterns cannot repeat a group: there is no (ab)+ . When you need that, use a loop or a real parser. Anchors ^ at the start of a pattern means "only at the start of the text", $ at the end means "only at the end". With both, the whole text must match, which is how you validate input: lua local function is_whole_number(s) return s:match("^%d+$") ~= nil end local function is_name(s) return s:match("^ %a_ %w_ $") ~= nil end print(is_whole_number("123"), is_whole_number("12a"), is_whole_number("")) print(is_name("player_1"), is_name("1player")) true false false true false Captures Brackets mark captures : the parts you want back. match then returns each capture instead of the whole match: lua local date = "2026-11-16" local y, m, d = date:match("(%d+)-(%d+)-(%d+)") print(y, m, d, tonumber(m) + 1) local key, value = (" volume = 11 "):match("^%s (%w+)%s =%s (.-)%s $") print(" " .. key .. " ", " " .. value .. " ") print(("John Smith"):match("(%a+) (%a+)")) 2026 11 16 12 volume 11 John Smith Captures are always strings: convert numbers with tonumber . %s (.-)%s $ is the standard way to capture something with the spaces around it trimmed. Trimming on its own is so common it is worth writing once: lua local function trim(s) return (s:match("^%s (.-)%s $")) end print(" " .. trim(" padded text ") .. " ") padded text find works with patterns too and returns the position followed by the captures: lua print(("x = 10"):find("(%d+)")) 5 6 10 Check yourself quiz ? How do you match a literal dot? - \. + %. - . In Lua patterns % escapes a special character; a bare . matches any character. . also works, but %. is the usual way, and the backslash of other regex languages does nothing here. ? What is the difference between . and .- ? - . matches any character and .- matches a dash + . takes as much as possible, .- as little as possible - .- takes as much as possible, . as little as possible Both repeat any character zero or more times. . is greedy, .- is lazy. ? Which pattern checks that the WHOLE string is digits? - "%d+" - "^%d" + "^%d+$" - " %d " ^ and $ anchor the match to the start and end, so nothing else can be around the digits. ? What does ("a1b22c333"):match("%a(%d+)") give? - "a1" - "333" - 1 + "1" The first place the pattern matches is "a1", and the capture is the digits: the string "1".

title: Validating and parsing
body: Write four functions with string.match and patterns: lua-norun trim(s) -- s without spaces, tabs and newlines at either end is_identifier(s) -- true when s is a valid Lua name: a letter or _, then letters, digits or _ parse_time(s) -- "HH:MM" (hour with 1 or 2 digits, minutes with exactly 2) - two numbers, hour and minute; -- nil when the text is not in that form or the hour is over 23 or the minutes over 59 parse_setting(line) -- "key = value" - key, value, both trimmed; the key is an identifier, the value anything -- (it may be empty); nil when the line has no = or the key is not an identifier lua-norun parse_time("9:05") -- 9, 5 parse_time("24:00") -- nil parse_setting(" volume = 11 ") -- "volume", "11" parse_setting("title=My Game") -- "title", "My Game" Do not check whether is_identifier names a reserved word.

title: 4.03  gmatch and gsub
body:
Looping over every match with gmatch, splitting text into words, lines and fields, replacing with gsub using a string, %1 captures, a table or a function, counting replacements, and %f for whole words. gmatch: every match s:gmatch(pattern) gives every match in turn, for use in a for loop: lua local text = "The quick brown fox, the lazy dog." local words = {} for word in text:gmatch("%a+") do words words + 1 = word:lower() end print( words, table.concat(words, " ")) for key, value in ("a=1, b=22, c=333"):gmatch("(%w+)=(%w+)") do io.write(key, "- ", value, " ") end print() 7 the quick brown fox the lazy dog a- 1 b- 22 c- 333 With captures in the pattern, each round gets the captures. Splitting Lua has no split function; gmatch with a "not the separator" set does it: lua local function split(s, sep) local out = {} for field in (s .. sep):gmatch("(.-)" .. sep:gsub("%p", "%%%0")) do out out + 1 = field end return out end local parts = split("red,green,,blue", ",") print( parts, table.concat(parts, " ")) for line in ("first
second
third"):gmatch(" ^
 +") do io.write("<", line, " ") end print() local nums = {} for n in ("4 8 15 16"):gmatch("%S+") do nums nums + 1 = tonumber(n) end print( nums, nums 3 + nums 4 ) 4 red green blue <first <second <third 4 31 The split function keeps empty fields ( ,, gives "" ): adding one separator at the end makes every field end with a separator, and (.-) then takes each field up to it. sep:gsub("%p", "%%%0") escapes punctuation in the separator so that "." means a real dot. When you only need the non-empty pieces, ^, + and %S+ are simpler. gsub: replacing s:gsub(pattern, replacement) returns a new string with every match replaced, and the number of replacements: lua print(("hello world"):gsub("o", "0")) print(("hello world"):gsub("o", "0", 1)) local cleaned = ("too many spaces"):gsub("%s+", " ") print(cleaned) hell0 w0rld 2 hell0 world 1 too many spaces The optional fourth argument limits the number of replacements. Because gsub returns two values, print(s:gsub(...)) shows the count too; assign to one variable, or wrap it in brackets, to keep only the string. Using the captures In the replacement string, %1 is the first capture, %2 the second, %0 the whole match: lua print(("2026-11-16"):gsub("(%d+)-(%d+)-(%d+)", "%3/%2/%1")) print(("John Smith"):gsub("(%a+) (%a+)", "%2, %1")) print(("cat dog"):gsub("%a+", "<%0 ")) 16/11/2026 1 Smith, John 1 <cat <dog 2 A table or a function as the replacement With a table , each match is looked up in it; a match with no entry is left alone. With a function , it is called with the captures and its result is used (returning nil or false keeps the original): lua local vars = { name = "Ada", lang = "Lua" } print((("Hi $name, welcome to $lang. $missing stays."):gsub("%$(%w+)", vars))) local function title_case(s) return (s:gsub("(%a)(%a )", function(first, rest) return first:upper() .. rest:lower() end)) end print(title_case("the LORD of the rings")) print((("1 2 3 4"):gsub("%d+", function(n) return tostring(tonumber(n) 10) end))) Hi Ada, welcome to Lua. $missing stays. The Lord Of The Rings 10 20 30 40 Templates, escaping, renaming: almost every text tool in Lua is a gsub with a function. Counting The second result of gsub makes counting easy. Replace each match with itself ( "%0" ) or with anything, and keep only the count: lua local text = "she sells sea shells" local _, s_count = text:gsub("s", "s") local _, words = text:gsub("%S+", "") print(s_count, words) 6 4 Whole words %f set is a frontier : it matches the empty position where the previous character is not in the set and the next one is. %f %w word%f %W finds word only as a whole word: lua local s = "cat concat cat's catalogue" print((s:gsub("%f %w cat%f %W ", "DOG"))) DOG concat DOG's catalogue Check yourself quiz ? What two values does gsub return? + The new string and the number of replacements - The new string and the position of the first match - The original string and the new string s:gsub(...) returns the changed string and how many replacements it made. Wrap it in brackets to keep only the string. ? In a gsub replacement string, what is %1? - The first character of the original string - The text of the whole match + The first capture of the match - The number of the replacement %1 is whatever the first pair of brackets in the pattern captured. %0 is the whole match. ? What is (("a-b-c"):gsub("-", "+")) ? - "a-b-c" - "a+b-c" + "a+b+c" - an error - is a special character only after something it can repeat; here it is the only thing in the pattern and matches a minus. (Writing %- is clearer.) ? What does gsub do when the replacement function returns nil? - removes the match + keeps the original match - stops replacing - raises an error nil or false from the function means "leave this match as it is".

title: 4.04  string.format and Building Text
body: The format directives %d %s %f %x %q, width, padding, alignment and precision, lining up a table of text, building long strings with a buffer table, and turning values into text with tostring and %q. string.format string.format(template, ...) fills the template's directives with the values, in order: lua print(string.format("%s is %d years old", "Ada", 36)) print(string.format("Pi is about %.3f", math.pi)) print(string.format("%d%% done", 75)) print(("%s = %s"):format("x", 10)) Ada is 36 years old Pi is about 3.142 75% done x = 10 Directive Shows Example Result --- --- --- --- %d a whole number ("%d"):format(42) 42 %f a float, 6 decimals by default ("%.2f"):format(2/3) 0.67 %g a number, short form ("%g"):format(0.5) 0.5 %e scientific notation ("%.1e"):format(12345) 1.2e+04 %x / %X hexadecimal ("%x"):format(255) ff %o octal ("%o"):format(8) 10 %c the character with that code ("%c"):format(65) A %s any value as text (calls tostring) ("%s"):format(true) true %q a value as Lua source (quoted string) ("%q"):format('a"b') "a\"b" %% a literal % Width, padding and alignment A number between % and the letter sets a minimum width . The value is padded on the left with spaces; - pads on the right instead; 0 pads numbers with zeros: lua print(string.format(" %5d %-5d %05d ", 42, 42, 42)) print(string.format(" %8.2f %-8s %3s ", 3.14159, "left", "toolong")) print(string.format("%02d:%02d:%02d", 7, 5, 9)) 42 42 00042 3.14 left toolong 07:05:09 The width is a minimum: longer values are never cut. %.3s does cut a string to 3 characters. Lining up columns Widths make text tables line up: lua local items = { { "Tea", 3, 2.5 }, { "Sandwich", 1, 6.25 }, { "Cake", 2, 3.0 }, } local total = 0 print(string.format("%-10s %3s %8s", "Item", "Qty", "Total")) for _, item in ipairs(items) do local name, qty, price = item 1 , item 2 , item 3 total = total + qty price print(string.format("%-10s %3d %8.2f", name, qty, qty price)) end print(string.rep("-", 23)) print(string.format("%-14s %8.2f", "Sum", total)) Item Qty Total Tea 3 7.50 Sandwich 1 6.25 Cake 2 6.00 ----------------------- Sum 19.75 Building long text Joining strings with .. in a loop copies the growing string every time: fine for ten pieces, slow for ten thousand. The Lua way is a buffer : collect the pieces in a table and join them once. lua local buffer = {} for i = 1, 5 do buffer buffer + 1 = string.format("line %d", i) end local text = table.concat(buffer, "\n") print(text) print( text) line 1 line 2 line 3 line 4 line 5 34 Values as text tostring turns any value into text. %q turns a string into Lua source that reads back as the same string, escapes and all, which is how you save data that Lua can load again: lua print(tostring(12), tostring(1.5), tostring(nil), tostring(false)) local tricky = 'She said "hi"\nthen left' print(string.format("%q", tricky)) print(string.format("%q", 1/3)) 12 1.5 nil false "She said \"hi\"\ then left" 0x1.5555555555555p-2 %q writes a newline as a backslash followed by a real newline, and floats in hexadecimal so that the exact value survives. Check yourself quiz ? How do you show 3.14159 as 3.14? - string.format("%2f", 3.14159) + string.format("%.2f", 3.14159) - string.format("%d.2", 3.14159) .2 after % sets the number of digits after the point. A number without a dot, as in %2f , sets the minimum width instead. ? Which flag aligns a value to the left of its width? - + , as in %+10s - 0 , as in %010s + - , as in %-10s - pads on the right so the value starts at the left. + shows a sign on numbers and 0 pads numbers with zeros. ? What is string.format("%03d", 7) ? - "7 " - " 7" + "007" - "7.000" Width 3, padded with zeros. ? Why collect pieces in a table and use table.concat? - table.concat adds a newline after each piece + Each .. in a loop copies the whole growing string - .. cannot join numbers to strings - Strings have a maximum length Strings never change, so every .. builds a new one. One table.concat at the end builds the result once.

title: 4.05  UTF-8 and Bytes
body: Lua strings as bytes, why counts bytes not letters, UTF-8 in brief, the utf8 library with len, char, codepoint and codes, taking characters safely, and the \u escape. Strings are bytes A Lua string is a sequence of bytes , any bytes at all. Lua does not know about letters, accents or alphabets. For English text one byte is one letter, so you never notice. For anything else you do: lua local word = "café" print( word, word:upper(), word:sub(1, 4)) 5 CAFé caf� é takes two bytes, so the length is 5; upper changes only the ASCII letters; and sub(1, 4) cut the é in half, leaving a broken byte that shows as � . UTF-8 in one paragraph Almost all text today is UTF-8 . Every character (every Unicode code point ) is stored as 1 to 4 bytes: plain ASCII as one byte with the same value as always, é as two, € and most Asian scripts as three, emoji as four. A program that treats the text as bytes still works for copying, joining, searching for ASCII, and comparing. It goes wrong when it counts, cuts or reverses. The utf8 library Lua 5.3 and later include utf8 for exactly those cases: lua local word = "café" print(utf8.len(word)) print(utf8.char(72, 233, 8364, 128512)) print(utf8.codepoint("é"), utf8.codepoint("A€", 1, -1)) for pos, code in utf8.codes("añ€") do print(pos, code, utf8.char(code)) end 4 Hé€😀 233 65 8364 1 97 a 2 241 ñ 4 8364 € Function Does --- --- utf8.len(s) number of characters, or nil plus a position if s is not valid UTF-8 utf8.char(...) the characters with these code points utf8.codepoint(s, i, j) the code points of the characters starting between byte i and j utf8.codes(s) loop over the characters: byte position and code point utf8.offset(s, n) the byte position where character n starts utf8.charpattern a pattern matching one UTF-8 character Working character by character utf8.charpattern with gmatch gives the characters as strings, which makes counting, reversing and cutting safe: lua local function chars(s) local out = {} for ch in s:gmatch(utf8.charpattern) do out out + 1 = ch end return out end local list = chars("¡Olé!") print( list, table.concat(list, " ")) local reversed = {} for i = list, 1, -1 do reversed reversed + 1 = list i end print(table.concat(reversed)) local function first_chars(s, n) local stop = utf8.offset(s, n + 1) return stop and s:sub(1, stop - 1) or s end print(first_chars("café crème", 4), first_chars("hi", 10)) 5 ¡ O l é ! !élO¡ café hi utf8.offset(s, n + 1) is the byte where character n + 1 starts, so everything before it is the first n characters. Escapes \u{XXXX} puts a code point into a string literal as UTF-8; \xXX puts in one byte; \ddd one byte in decimal: lua print("\u{48}\u{E9}\u{20AC}", "\x41\x42", "\65\66") print( "\u{20AC}") Hé€ AB AB 3 Bytes are useful too Because a string can hold any bytes, Lua strings also carry binary data: file contents, network packets, images. string.pack and string.unpack write and read numbers as raw bytes in a given layout: lua local packed = string.pack("<i4 i2", 1000, -2) print( packed, packed:byte(1, -1)) print(string.unpack("<i4 i2", packed)) 6 232 3 0 0 254 255 1000 -2 7 < means little-endian, i4 a 4-byte integer, i2 a 2-byte one. unpack returns the values and then the position after them. (The Computer Fundamentals and C courses explain endianness and two's complement, which is why -2 is 254 255.) Check yourself quiz ? Why is "é" 2? + counts bytes, and é takes two bytes in UTF-8 - counts the accent as a separate character - adds one for the end of the string Lua strings are bytes. Letters outside ASCII take two to four bytes in UTF-8, and counts those bytes. ? How do you count the characters of a UTF-8 string? - s - s:len() + utf8.len(s) s and s:len() both count bytes. utf8.len counts code points, and returns nil when the string is not valid UTF-8. ? Which operations are safe on UTF-8 text treated as bytes? - taking the first 3 characters with sub(1, 3) + joining strings and searching for ASCII text - reversing with string.reverse - counting letters with Joining and ASCII searches never split a character. Cutting, reversing and counting by byte can.
