title: Close resources in order
where: 7.02 Weak Tables and the Garbage Collector
body: Write a small resource tracker with to-be-closed variables: - Resource(name, log) returns a table with a name and a metatable whose __close appends "close <name " to log (a list) and sets the table's closed field to true . Creating it appends "open <name " . - use_all(names, log, fail_at) opens a resource for each name, each in its own <close local inside nested calls or a recursive helper , so they are closed in reverse order when the function ends. After opening all of them it appends "work" . If fail_at is a number, opening the resource at that position (1-based) raises an error instead, after the earlier ones were opened. use_all itself catches nothing: the caller uses pcall . lua local log = {} use_all({ "db", "file", "socket" }, log) -- log: open db, open file, open socket, work, close socket, close file, close db

title: 7.03  Integers, Bitwise Operators and Binary Data
match: 7.03 Integers, Bitwise Operators and Binary Data
body: Lua's 64-bit integers in depth - integer and float subtypes, floor division and wrap-around, the bitwise operators &, , ~, <<, and ~x, flags and masks, unsigned comparison with math.ult, and reading and writing binary formats with string.pack and string.unpack. Two kinds of number Since Lua 5.3 a number is either an integer (64-bit, exact) or a float (a double). They print and compare naturally, but they are different subtypes (lesson 1.03): lua print(math.type(3), math.type(3.0), math.type("3")) -- integer float nil print(3 == 3.0, 7 // 2, 7.0 // 2, 7 / 2) -- true 3 3.0 3.5 print(math.maxinteger + 1 == math.mininteger) -- true: integers wrap around print(math.tointeger(5.0), math.tointeger(5.5)) -- 5 nil // is floor division (it rounds down, also for negative numbers: -7 // 2 is -4 ) and % follows it so that a == (a // b) b + a % b . / always gives a float. The bitwise operators They work on integers (floats with an exact integer value are converted; others are an error): Operator Meaning Example --- --- --- a & b AND 0xF0 & 0x3C is 0x30 a \ b OR 0xF0 \ 0x0F is 0xFF a ~ b exclusive OR 0xFF ~ 0x0F is 0xF0 ~a NOT (flip every bit) ~0 is -1 a << n shift left 1 << 4 is 16 a n logical shift right (fills with zeros) -1 60 is 15 lua local READ, WRITE, EXEC = 1 << 0, 1 << 1, 1 << 2 local perms = READ EXEC print(perms & WRITE ~= 0, perms & EXEC ~= 0) -- false true perms = perms WRITE -- grant perms = perms & ~EXEC -- revoke perms = perms ~ READ -- toggle print(perms) -- 2: only WRITE is left string.format has no binary format, so print bits yourself: lua local function bits(n, width) local out = {} for i = width - 1, 0, -1 do out out + 1 = (n i) & 1 end return table.concat(out) end print(bits(5, 8), bits(0xA5, 8)) -- 00000101 10100101 print(string.format("%x %X %08x", 255, 255, 0xBEEF)) Note that ~ means two different things: between two values it is XOR, in front of one value it is NOT. And ~= is still "not equal". Unsigned numbers Lua's integers are signed, but bit patterns are often unsigned (hashes, IDs, colours). Addition, multiplication and the bitwise operators give the same bits either way; only comparison and division differ. math.ult(a, b) compares as unsigned, and string.format("%u") is not available, but %x shows the bits: lua local big = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF -- all 64 bits set print(big, math.ult(1, big), 1 < big) -- -1 true false A 32-bit hash with masks Many algorithms are defined for 32-bit unsigned arithmetic. Masking with & 0xFFFFFFFF after each step gives exactly that in Lua's 64-bit integers: lua local function fnv1a(text) local hash = 0x811C9DC5 for i = 1, text do hash = hash ~ text:byte(i) hash = (hash 0x01000193) & 0xFFFFFFFF end return hash end print(string.format("%08x", fnv1a("hello"))) -- 4f9f2cab Binary data with string.pack string.pack(format, ...) turns values into a string of bytes in an exact layout, and string.unpack(format, s, pos) reads them back, returning the values and the position after them (lesson 4.05 introduced them): Code Meaning --- --- < little-endian, big-endian b B signed, unsigned 1-byte integer h H 2-byte integer i4 I4 4-byte integer (any size from 1 to 16) d f double, float s1 s2 s4 a string preceded by its length in 1, 2 or 4 bytes z a zero-terminated string lua local record = string.pack("<I2 s1 d", 512, "Ada", 98.5) print( record, string.format(("%02x "):rep( record), record:byte(1, -1))) local id, name, score, next_pos = string.unpack("<I2 s1 d", record) print(id, name, score, next_pos) -- 512 Ada 98.5 15 Spaces in the format are ignored and help readability. string.packsize(fmt) gives the size of a format with no variable-length parts. Check yourself quiz ? What is -7 // 2 in Lua? - -3 + -4 - -3.5 Floor division rounds down, towards negative infinity, so -3.5 becomes -4. Rounding towards zero (-3) is what C does. ? What is the difference between a ~ b and ~a ? - a ~ b tests "not equal"; ~a is "not a" + a ~ b is bitwise XOR; ~a is bitwise NOT - They are the same operation written two ways With two operands ~ is exclusive OR; with one it flips every bit. "Not equal" is ~= . ? What does string.unpack("<I2", "\x01\x02") return first? - 258 - 12 + 513 - "\x01\x02" Little-endian puts the low byte first: 0x01 + 0x02 256 = 513.

title: A modding sandbox
body: Games such as Roblox, World of Warcraft and Factorio let players write Lua mods that run inside the game safely. Build the core of such a system: mods run in sandboxes, talk to the game only through an API you choose, are stopped if they run too long, and their event handlers are held weakly so unloaded mods do not leak. lua local game = Game.new() game:load_mod("greeter", on("player_joined", function(name) say("welcome, " .. name) end) ) game:emit("player_joined", "Ada") print(game.messages 1 ) -- greeter: welcome, Ada Write Game.new() returning a game object with: - messages : a list of every line said by mods, as "<mod : <text " . - game:load_mod(name, code, max_steps) (default 100000 steps): runs the code in a fresh sandbox environment containing on(event, fn) , say(text) , get(key) and set(key, value) (a key-value store private to that mod ), plus pairs , ipairs , tostring , tonumber , type , and copies of string.format , string.upper , string.rep , math.floor , math.max , math.min . Returns true , or false, message if the code fails to load or run (the mod is then not loaded). - game:emit(event, ...) calls every handler registered for that event, in the order mods were loaded, each with the same step limit; a handler that errors is reported as a message "<mod : error: <message " and the others still run. Returns how many handlers ran without error. - game:unload_mod(name) removes the mod; its handlers must stop running. - game:mod_data(name) returns a copy of the mod's private store.

title: 8.01  Data Structures in Lua
body: Building the classic data structures from Lua's one table type - stacks, queues that do not shift (two indexes), double-ended queues, sets with union and intersection, linked lists, and a binary heap for priority queues, with the costs of each operation. Everything is a table Lua has one data structure, the table, and every other structure is built from it. The trick is choosing how to use the table so the common operations are fast. A stack A list with t t + 1 = v to push and t t = nil to pop. Both are O(1): lua local Stack = {} Stack.__index = Stack function Stack.new() return setmetatable({ n = 0 }, Stack) end function Stack:push(v) self.n = self.n + 1; self self.n = v end function Stack:pop() if self.n == 0 then return nil end local v = self self.n self self.n = nil self.n = self.n - 1 return v end function Stack:peek() return self self.n end local s = Stack.new() s:push("a"); s:push("b"); s:push("c") print(s:pop(), s:pop(), s:peek(), s.n) -- c b a 1 Keeping the count in a field ( n ) is faster than self and is not confused by nil values. A queue that does not shift table.remove(t, 1) moves every other element down: O(n). A queue that keeps a first and a last index never moves anything: lua local Queue = {} Queue.__index = Queue function Queue.new() return setmetatable({ first = 1, last = 0 }, Queue) end function Queue:push(v) self.last = self.last + 1; self self.last = v end function Queue:pop() if self.first self.last then return nil end local v = self self.first self self.first = nil -- let the value be collected self.first = self.first + 1 return v end function Queue:size() return self.last - self.first + 1 end local q = Queue.new() for _, name in ipairs({ "ada", "bob", "cy" }) do q:push(name) end print(q:pop(), q:size()) -- ada 2 q:push("dee") while q:size() 0 do io.write(q:pop(), " ") end print() The indexes only grow, but that is fine: Lua integers go far past any queue you will ever fill. Adding pushfront (decrementing first ) and poplast makes it a double-ended queue. Sets A set is a table whose keys are the members and whose values are true : lua local function Set(list) local s = {} for _, v in ipairs(list) do s v = true end return s end local function union(a, b) local r = {} for k in pairs(a) do r k = true end for k in pairs(b) do r k = true end return r end local function intersection(a, b) local r = {} for k in pairs(a) do if b k then r k = true end end return r end local function sorted(s) local out = {} for k in pairs(s) do out out + 1 = k end table.sort(out) return table.concat(out, ",") end local red = Set({ "apple", "cherry", "strawberry" }) local small = Set({ "cherry", "blueberry", "grape" }) print(sorted(union(red, small))) print(sorted(intersection(red, small))) print(red.apple, red.grape) -- true nil Membership ( set x ) is O(1), which is why "is it in the list?" questions should use a set instead of a loop. A linked list Each node is a table with a value and a next field. Inserting at the front is O(1), and removing from the middle needs no shifting: lua local list = nil for _, v in ipairs({ 3, 2, 1 }) do list = { value = v, next = list } -- push at the front end local function each(node) return function() if node then local v = node.value node = node.next return v end end end for v in each(list) do io.write(v, " ") end print() In Lua, plain lists (arrays) are usually faster than linked lists because of how tables are stored; linked lists are worth it mainly when you insert and remove in the middle a lot. A binary heap: a priority queue A heap keeps the smallest item at index 1 and needs only O(log n) work to add an item or take the smallest. Children of position i are at 2i and 2i + 1 : lua local Heap = {} Heap.__index = Heap function Heap.new(less) return setmetatable({ n = 0, less = less or function(a, b) return a < b end }, Heap) end function Heap:push(v) self.n = self.n + 1 local i = self.n self i = v while i 1 do local parent = i // 2 if not self.less(self i , self parent ) then break end self i , self parent = self parent , self i i = parent end end function Heap:pop() if self.n == 0 then return nil end local top = self 1 self 1 = self self.n self self.n = nil self.n = self.n - 1 local i = 1 while true do local l, r, best = 2 i, 2 i + 1, i if l <= self.n and self.less(self l , self best ) then best = l end if r <= self.n and self.less(self r , self best ) then best = r end if best == i then break end self i , self best = self best , self i i = best end return top end local tasks = Heap.new(function(a, b) return a.priority < b.priority end) tasks:push({ priority = 3, name = "write report" }) tasks:push({ priority = 1, name = "fix crash" }) tasks:push({ priority = 2, name = "reply to email" }) while tasks.n 0 do print(tasks:pop().name) end The comparison function makes the same heap work for any items: a game's event queue, path finding, or scheduling. Costs at a glance structure add remove find --- --- --- --- stack (list) O(1) at the end O(1) at the end O(n) queue (two indexes) O(1) at the back O(1) at the front O(n) set (keys) O(1) O(1) O(1) heap O(log n) O(log n) for the smallest smallest in O(1) Check yourself quiz ? Why is table.remove(t, 1) slow for a big queue? - It has to search for the first element + It moves every remaining element down one place - It copies the whole table into a new one Removing at position 1 shifts all other items. A queue with first and last indexes moves nothing. ? In a heap stored in a list, where are the children of position 5? - At positions 6 and 7 - At positions 9 and 10 + At positions 10 and 11 In a list starting at 1, the children of position i are at 2i and 2i + 1. Positions 9 and 10 would be the rule for a heap starting at 0. ? How is membership tested quickly in Lua? - by looping over a list with ipairs + by storing the members as keys and checking set x - with string.find - with table.concat Keys are looked up directly, in constant time.

title: A queue that never shifts
body: Write a Queue class that keeps a first and a last index, so adding and removing never move other elements: - Queue.new() , q:push(v) , q:pop() (the oldest value, or nil when empty), q:peek() , q:size() and q:isEmpty() ; - pop sets the old slot to nil , so the value can be collected; - pushing false works (it is a real value, not "empty").

title: A binary heap
body: Write a Heap (a priority queue) stored in a list, where the children of position i are 2i and 2i + 1 : - Heap.new(less) : less(a, b) says whether a comes first (default a < b , so the smallest comes first); - h:push(v) , h:pop() (the first item, or nil ), h:peek() and h:size() , with push and pop in O(log n); - heapsort(list, less) returns a new sorted list using a heap, leaving list unchanged.

title: 8.02  Functional Lua
body: Writing Lua with functions as building blocks - a small library of map, filter, reduce, find and zip, composing functions and building pipelines, partial application and currying, memoising any function, lazy sequences built from closures, and when a plain loop is clearer. Functions as building blocks Lesson 3.03 showed functions as values and closures. A handful of small general functions, combined, replace many hand-written loops. Lua has no such library built in, so you write one (or reuse one), once. map, filter, reduce lua local F = {} function F.map(t, fn) local out = {} for i, v in ipairs(t) do out i = fn(v, i) end return out end function F.filter(t, keep) local out = {} for _, v in ipairs(t) do if keep(v) then out out + 1 = v end end return out end function F.reduce(t, fn, acc) for _, v in ipairs(t) do acc = fn(acc, v) end return acc end function F.find(t, test) for i, v in ipairs(t) do if test(v) then return v, i end end end local prices = { 4.5, 12, 3.25, 20 } local withTax = F.map(prices, function(p) return p 1.2 end) local cheap = F.filter(prices, function(p) return p < 10 end) local total = F.reduce(prices, function(a, b) return a + b end, 0) print(table.concat(withTax, " "), table.concat(cheap, " "), total, F.find(prices, function(p) return p 10 end)) Each function does one thing, and the function you pass says what should happen to each element. zip and range lua local function zip(a, b) local out = {} for i = 1, math.min( a, b) do out i = { a i , b i } end return out end local function range(from, to, step) local out = {} for i = from, to, step or 1 do out out + 1 = i end return out end for _, pair in ipairs(zip({ "ada", "bob" }, { 91, 48 })) do print(pair 1 , pair 2 ) end print(table.concat(range(10, 1, -3), ",")) Composing functions compose(f, g) makes a function that runs g and then f . A pipe runs any number of functions left to right: lua local function pipe(...) local fns = { ... } return function(x) for _, fn in ipairs(fns) do x = fn(x) end return x end end local slug = pipe( function(s) return s:lower() end, function(s) return s:gsub(" ^%w +", "-") end, function(s) return (s:gsub("^%-+", ""):gsub("%-+$", "")) end ) print(slug(" Hello, World! 2026 ")) Note the brackets around s:gsub(...) : gsub returns two values (the string and a count), and passing both on would surprise the next function. Partial application and currying Fixing some arguments now and giving the rest later: lua local function partial(fn, ...) local fixed = table.pack(...) return function(...) local args = { table.unpack(fixed, 1, fixed.n) } local more = table.pack(...) for i = 1, more.n do args fixed.n + i = more i end return fn(table.unpack(args, 1, fixed.n + more.n)) end end local function greet(greeting, name, mark) return greeting .. ", " .. name .. (mark or ".") end local hello = partial(greet, "Hello") print(hello("Ada"), hello("Bob", "!")) local function curry2(fn) return function(a) return function(b) return fn(a, b) end end end local add = curry2(function(a, b) return a + b end) print(add(2)(3)) table.pack keeps count of the values ( n ) even when some are nil , which a plain {...} cannot do. Memoising any function A memo table remembers results by argument. With several arguments, join them into one key: lua local function memoize(fn) local cache = {} return function(...) local key = table.concat({ ... }, "\0") local hit = cache key if hit == nil then hit = table.pack(fn(...)) cache key = hit end return table.unpack(hit, 1, hit.n) end end local calls = 0 local slowAdd = memoize(function(a, b) calls = calls + 1; return a + b end) print(slowAdd(2, 3), slowAdd(2, 3), slowAdd(3, 2), calls) The "\0" separator keeps (1, 23) and (12, 3) from both becoming "123" . This version only suits arguments that turn into text (numbers and strings). Lazy sequences A generator function that returns the next value each time it is called can describe an endless sequence. Helpers that take and return such functions work lazily, doing only the work asked for: lua local function naturals() local n = 0 return function() n = n + 1; return n end end local function lazyFilter(gen, keep) return function() while true do local v = gen() if v == nil or keep(v) then return v end end end end local function take(gen, count) local out = {} for i = 1, count do local v = gen() if v == nil then break end out i = v end return out end local odd = lazyFilter(naturals(), function(n) return n % 2 == 1 end) local squaresOfOdd = function() local v = odd(); return v and v v end print(table.concat(take(squaresOfOdd, 5), " ")) Coroutines (lesson 6.03) are the other way to write lazy sequences in Lua. When a loop is clearer Functional style shines for simple transformations. A loop is clearer when the steps depend on each other, when you need to stop early on complicated conditions, or when performance matters in a hot path (each map builds a new table). Use whichever reads better. Check yourself quiz ? Why write (s:gsub(...)) with brackets inside a pipeline? + gsub returns two values, and the brackets keep only the first - The brackets make gsub change s in place - Without brackets the pattern is read as plain text gsub returns the new string and the number of replacements. Without the brackets the next function would receive the count as an extra argument. ? Why use table.pack(...) instead of {...} in partial ? - {...} cannot hold more than a few values + It records the number of values in n , so nil arguments are kept in place - table.pack copies the values, but {...} shares them With {...} , a nil argument makes a hole and can be wrong. table.pack stores the real count in field n . ? F.reduce({1, 2, 3}, function(a, b) return a b end, 1) gives... - 1 - 3 + 6 - 7 It multiplies 1 by each element in turn: 1 1 2 3.

title: pipe and partial
body: Write two helpers that build functions from functions: - pipe(...) returns a function that passes its argument through each given function in turn, left to right; with no functions it returns its argument unchanged. Only the first result of each function is passed on. - partial(fn, ...) returns a function that calls fn with the fixed arguments followed by the new ones. nil arguments (fixed or new) must stay in their places. lua local f = pipe(function(x) return x + 1 end, function(x) return x 10 end) f(2) -- 30 local hi = partial(string.format, "%s, %s!") hi("Hello", "Ada") -- Hello, Ada!

title: Lazy sequences
body: A generator here is a function that returns the next value each time it is called, and nil when it has no more. Write helpers that take and return generators, doing no work until values are asked for: - range(from, to, step) : numbers from from to to ( to may be nil for endless; step defaults to 1 and may be negative); - from_list(t) : the values of a list in order; - lmap(gen, fn) and lfilter(gen, keep) ; - take(gen, n) returns a list of at most n values, and must not call gen more often than it needs to; - collect(gen) returns a list of all values (only for generators that end).

title: 8.03  Serialisation
body:
Saving Lua tables as text and reading them back - writing values as Lua source with %q, sorting keys so the output is stable, nesting and indentation, refusing cycles and functions, loading saved data safely in an empty environment, and a small JSON encoder and the parts of JSON that do not map to Lua. Saving a table A game's save file, a tool's settings, a cache: programs need to turn tables into text and back. Lua's own syntax is a natural format, because load can read it back: lua local function serialize(v, indent) indent = indent or "" local t = type(v) if t == "number" or t == "boolean" or t == "nil" then return tostring(v) elseif t == "string" then return string.format("%q", v) elseif t == "table" then local keys = {} for k in pairs(v) do keys keys + 1 = k end table.sort(keys, function(a, b) return tostring(a) < tostring(b) end) local inner = indent .. " " local parts = {} for _, k in ipairs(keys) do local key = type(k) == "string" and k:match("^ %a_ %w_ $") and k or " " .. serialize(k) .. " " parts parts + 1 = inner .. key .. " = " .. serialize(v k , inner) end if parts == 0 then return "{}" end return "{
" .. table.concat(parts, ",
") .. "
" .. indent .. "}" else error("cannot save a " .. t) end end print(serialize({ name = "Ada", level = 3, items = { "map", "sword" }, "two words" = true })) - %q quotes a string so that Lua reads back exactly the same string, escapes included. - Keys are sorted , so saving the same data twice gives the same text, which makes files easy to compare and keep in version control. - Keys that are valid names are written plainly; anything else as key . Functions, userdata and threads cannot be saved, so the function refuses them with an error. Cycles A table that contains itself (directly or through others) would make this recurse forever. Track the tables currently being written: lua local function serialize(v, seen) seen = seen or {} if type(v) ~= "table" then return type(v) == "string" and string.format("%q", v) or tostring(v) end if seen v then error("cannot save a table that contains itself") end seen v = true local parts = {} for i, item in ipairs(v) do parts i = serialize(item, seen) end seen v = nil return "{" .. table.concat(parts, ", ") .. "}" end print(serialize({ 1, { 2, 3 }, "x" })) local loop = { 1 } loop 2 = loop print(pcall(serialize, loop)) Removing the table from seen after writing it lets the same table appear twice in different places (which is not a cycle). Loading it back safely load turns text into a function. Running untrusted text could do anything, so give it an empty environment (lesson 7.01) and check that the result is a table: lua local function deserialize(text) local chunk, err = load("return " .. text, "saved data", "t", {}) if not chunk then return nil, "not valid: " .. err end local ok, value = pcall(chunk) if not ok then return nil, "failed: " .. value end if type(value) ~= "table" then return nil, "not a table" end return value end local data = deserialize('{ name = "Ada", items = { "map", "sword" }, level = 3 }') print(data.name, data.items 2 , data.level) print(deserialize('{ x = os.exit() }')) print(deserialize('{ unclosed = ')) The "t" mode refuses precompiled binary chunks, and with an empty environment the data cannot reach os or io . It can still contain a loop that never ends; lesson 7.01's instruction limit covers that. JSON To talk to other programs and web services, JSON is the usual format. Lua tables map onto it, with two wrinkles: - JSON has separate arrays and objects ; a Lua table can be either, so the encoder must decide (here: a table whose keys are exactly 1 to n is an array). - JSON has null , but a Lua table cannot store nil ; libraries use a special marker value for it. lua local function encode(v) local t = type(v) if t == "nil" then return "null" elseif t == "boolean" then return tostring(v) elseif t == "number" then if v ~= v or v == math.huge or v == -math.huge then error("JSON has no NaN or infinity") end return math.type(v) == "integer" and tostring(v) or string.format("%.14g", v) elseif t == "string" then local escapes = { '"' = '\"', "\" = "\\", "
" = "\n", "" = "\r", "	" = "\t" } return '"' .. v:gsub(' %c"\ ', function(c) return escapes c or string.format("\u%04x", c:byte()) end) .. '"' elseif t == "table" then local n = v local count = 0 for _ in pairs(v) do count = count + 1 end if count == n then local parts = {} for i = 1, n do parts i = encode(v i ) end return " " .. table.concat(parts, ",") .. " " end local keys = {} for k in pairs(v) do if type(k) ~= "string" then error("JSON object keys must be strings") end keys keys + 1 = k end table.sort(keys) local parts = {} for i, k in ipairs(keys) do parts i = encode(k) .. ":" .. encode(v k ) end return "{" .. table.concat(parts, ",") .. "}" end error("cannot encode a " .. t) end print(encode({ name = "Ada "the first"", langs = { "Lua", "C" }, age = 36, pi = 3.14159, active = true })) print(encode({})) Note {} comes out as : an empty table is ambiguous, one of the classic JSON surprises in Lua. Real libraries (dkjson, lua-cjson) let you mark tables as arrays or objects. Check yourself quiz ? Why sort the keys when saving? + So the same data always gives the same text - Lua cannot load a table whose keys are out of order - Sorted keys make the saved file smaller pairs visits keys in no fixed order. Without sorting, saving the same data twice can give different files, which makes changes hard to compare. ? What stops loaded data from calling os.exit ? - Saving the data in binary instead of text + Loading it with an empty environment table - Calling the loaded chunk through pcall With an empty _ENV , names like os and io do not exist inside the chunk. pcall only catches errors; it would not stop os.exit . ? What does string.format("%q", 'a "b"
') produce? - The text a "b" unchanged + Lua source that reads back as the same string - An error, because of the quotes - The text 'a "b"' in single quotes %q writes a string as a quoted Lua literal, with the quotes and the new line escaped, so loading it gives the same string.

title: Save and load a table
body: Write serialize(v) and deserialize(text) : - numbers, booleans and nil are written with tostring ; strings with string.format("%q", s) ; - a table whose keys are exactly 1 to n is written as a list: {1,2,"x"} ; - any other table is written as {key=value,...} with the keys sorted by tostring(key) , a key that is a valid name written plainly and any other key as key , for example {a=1, "two words" =true} ; there are no spaces; - functions (and other types) and tables that contain themselves raise an error; - deserialize(text) loads "return " .. text with an empty environment and returns the value, or nil and a message if the text is not valid or does not give a table.

title: A JSON encoder
body: Write json(v) that turns Lua values into JSON text with no spaces: - nil is null , booleans true / false ; - integers with tostring ; floats with string.format("%.14g", x) ; NaN and infinities raise an error; - strings in double quotes, with " \ and the control characters escaped: \n , \r , \t by name, others as \u00XX (lower-case hex); - a non-empty table whose keys are exactly 1 to n is an array ... ; any other non-empty table is an object {...} with its keys sorted, and every key must be a string (otherwise an error); the empty table is ; - json(v, true) instead writes the empty table as {} .

title: 8.04  Object Patterns Beyond Classes
body: Other ways to build objects in Lua - closures as objects with truly private state, constructors called like functions with __call, mixins that copy behaviour into a class, composition instead of inheritance, an event emitter, and validated objects with a proxy; with the trade-offs of each against the class pattern. More than one way Lesson 5.03's class pattern (a metatable whose __index is the class) is the most common way to write objects in Lua. It is not the only one, and some problems fit other patterns better. Closures as objects An object can be a table of functions that share local variables. The variables are completely private: no code outside can reach them. lua local function newAccount(owner, balance) balance = balance or 0 local history = {} local self = {} function self.deposit(amount) if amount <= 0 then error("amount must be positive", 2) end balance = balance + amount history history + 1 = "+" .. amount end function self.withdraw(amount) if amount balance then return false, "insufficient funds" end balance = balance - amount history history + 1 = "-" .. amount return true end function self.balance() return balance end function self.statement() return owner .. ": " .. table.concat(history, " ") end return self end local a = newAccount("Ada", 100) a.deposit(50) print(a.withdraw(500)) a.withdraw(30) print(a.balance(), a.statement(), a.history) -- 120 Ada: +50 -30 nil Methods are called with a dot ( a.deposit ), not a colon, because they do not need self : they reach the data through the closure. The cost is memory: each object has its own copy of every function, where class objects share one. For a few hundred objects that does not matter; for a million particles it does. Constructors with __call A metatable's __call lets a table be called like a function, which makes Point(1, 2) work instead of Point.new(1, 2) : lua local Point = {} Point.__index = Point setmetatable(Point, { __call = function(cls, x, y) return setmetatable({ x = x, y = y }, cls) end }) function Point:length() return math.sqrt(self.x ^ 2 + self.y ^ 2) end Point.__tostring = function(p) return "(" .. p.x .. ", " .. p.y .. ")" end local p = Point(3, 4) print(tostring(p), p:length()) Mixins A mixin is a table of methods copied into a class, so unrelated classes can share behaviour without inheriting from each other: lua local Comparable = { __lt = function(a, b) return a:compareKey() < b:compareKey() end, __le = function(a, b) return a:compareKey() <= b:compareKey() end, max = function(self, other) if self < other then return other end return self end, } local Serialisable = { toText = function(self) local keys = {} for k in pairs(self) do keys keys + 1 = k end table.sort(keys) local parts = {} for _, k in ipairs(keys) do parts parts + 1 = k .. "=" .. tostring(self k ) end return "{" .. table.concat(parts, ", ") .. "}" end, } local function include(class, mixin) for k, v in pairs(mixin) do class k = v end return class end local Card = { __index = nil } Card.__index = Card include(Card, Comparable) include(Card, Serialisable) function Card.new(rank, suit) return setmetatable({ rank = rank, suit = suit }, Card) end function Card:compareKey() return self.rank end local a, b = Card.new(10, "hearts"), Card.new(3, "spades") print(b < a, a:max(b):toText()) Copying works for metamethods like __lt too, because they are just fields of the metatable. Composition Instead of a Player that inherits from Movable , which inherits from Drawable , give the player parts : lua local function newPosition(x, y) return { x = x, y = y, move = function(self, dx, dy) self.x, self.y = self.x + dx, self.y + dy end } end local function newHealth(max) return { hp = max, max = max, hurt = function(self, n) self.hp = math.max(0, self.hp - n) end } end local player = { name = "Ada", pos = newPosition(0, 0), health = newHealth(20) } player.pos:move(3, 1) player.health:hurt(5) print(player.name, player.pos.x, player.pos.y, player.health.hp) Parts can be mixed freely (a chest has a position but no health), which is exactly why many game engines use components (the game development course's entity systems). An event emitter Objects that tell others when something happens: lua local function newEmitter() local listeners = {} local e = {} function e.on(name, fn) listeners name = listeners name or {} table.insert(listeners name , fn) return function() -- call this to unsubscribe for i, f in ipairs(listeners name ) do if f == fn then table.remove(listeners name , i) return end end end end function e.emit(name, ...) for _, fn in ipairs({ table.unpack(listeners name or {}) }) do fn(...) end end return e end local door = newEmitter() local off = door.on("open", function(who) print(who .. " opened the door") end) door.on("open", function() print("a bell rings") end) door.emit("open", "Ada") off() door.emit("open", "Bob") emit loops over a copy of the list, so a listener that unsubscribes while being called does not upset the loop. Validated objects with a proxy A proxy (lesson 5.02) can check every assignment: lua local function validated(rules) local data = {} return setmetatable({}, { __index = data, __newindex = function(_, k, v) local rule = rules k if not rule then error("unknown field " .. tostring(k), 2) end local ok, msg = rule(v) if not ok then error(k .. ": " .. msg, 2) end data k = v end, }) end local settings = validated({ volume = function(v) return type(v) == "number" and v = 0 and v <= 1, "must be from 0 to 1" end, name = function(v) return type(v) == "string" and v 0, "must be a non-empty string" end, }) settings.volume = 0.5 print(settings.volume, pcall(function() settings.volume = 3 end)) print(pcall(function() settings.colour = "red" end)) Choosing pattern good for --- --- class with metatable many objects of one kind; shared methods; inheritance closures truly private state; few objects mixins sharing behaviour between unrelated classes composition objects made of optional parts, like game entities proxy checking or watching every change Check yourself quiz ? Why are closure-object methods called with a dot instead of a colon? - Closures cannot be called with a colon + They take no self; their data is in captured variables - The dot makes the call faster than a colon Each method already reaches its object's data through captured locals, so it needs no self argument. ? What does __call on a class's metatable allow? - Calling the class's methods without a colon - Counting how many times the class is used + Calling the class like a function: Point(1, 2) When a table with a __call metamethod is called, Lua runs that function with the table and the arguments, which makes a neat constructor. ? Which pattern keeps fields private so no outside code can read them? - a class with __index - a mixin + closures that capture local variables - a proxy with __newindex Local variables captured by closures cannot be reached from outside at all.

title: A counter with private state, and a callable class
match: A counter with private state, and a callable class
body: Write two kinds of object: - newCounter(start) returns a table of functions inc(n) , dec(n) (each by 1 if n is missing), get() and reset() (back to start , default 0). The count lives in a local variable, so the returned table has no field holding it. - A class Vec that is called like a function: Vec(1, 2) makes a vector with fields x and y . Give it __add , __eq and __tostring ( (1, 2) ), and a method v:length() .

title: An event emitter
body: Write newEmitter() returning an object with: - on(name, fn) : adds a listener and returns a function that removes exactly that listener; - once(name, fn) : a listener that removes itself after its first call; - off(name) : removes every listener for name ; - emit(name, ...) : calls the listeners for name in the order they were added, with the extra arguments, and returns how many were called. A listener that adds or removes listeners while emit is running must not upset that emit : it calls exactly the listeners that were there when it started (minus any once listener that already ran).

title: 8.05  Performance in Lua
body: Making Lua code fast where it matters - measuring with os.clock before changing anything, locals versus globals, caching functions in locals, building strings with table.concat instead of .., reusing tables instead of creating them in loops, array-style tables, avoiding closures in hot loops, and the garbage collector's cost. Measure first Most code is fast enough. The slow part of a program is rarely where you guess, so measure before changing anything. os.clock() gives the processor time used so far: lua local function time(label, fn, ...) local start = os.clock() fn(...) print(string.format("%-12s %.3f s", label, os.clock() - start)) end time("empty loop", function() for i = 1, 1e6 do end end) Repeat a measurement a few times and only trust differences that are clearly larger than the noise. Locals are faster than globals A global is a lookup in the table _ENV (lesson 7.01) every time; a local lives in a register. Inside hot loops, copying a library function into a local helps: lua local N = 1e6 local function globalsVersion() local s = 0 for i = 1, N do s = s + math.sin(i) end return s end local function localsVersion() local sin = math.sin -- looked up once local s = 0 for i = 1, N do s = s + sin(i) end return s end local t0 = os.clock(); globalsVersion(); local a = os.clock() - t0 t0 = os.clock(); localsVersion(); local b = os.clock() - t0 print(b <= a 1.2 and "locals were at least as fast" or "no clear difference here") The difference is small for one call and noticeable in millions. It is also one more reason to declare everything local . Building strings Strings never change, so s = s .. piece in a loop copies the whole string every time: O(n²) for n pieces. Collect pieces in a table and join once: lua local N = 20000 local t0 = os.clock() local s = "" for i = 1, N do s = s .. i .. "," end local slow = os.clock() - t0 t0 = os.clock() local parts = {} for i = 1, N do parts parts + 1 = i end local fast = table.concat(parts, ",") .. "," local quick = os.clock() - t0 print( s == fast, quick < slow) table.concat builds the result in one pass. For a few pieces .. is fine; this matters for loops. Do not create tables in hot loops Every {} allocates memory the garbage collector must later free. In a loop that runs every frame, reuse tables: lua local function distanceNew(points) local total = 0 for i = 2, points do local d = { x = points i .x - points i - 1 .x, y = points i .y - points i - 1 .y } -- a new table each time total = total + math.sqrt(d.x d.x + d.y d.y) end return total end local function distanceReuse(points) local total = 0 local sqrt = math.sqrt for i = 2, points do local dx = points i .x - points i - 1 .x -- plain locals instead of a table local dy = points i .y - points i - 1 .y total = total + sqrt(dx dx + dy dy) end return total end local pts = {} for i = 1, 1000 do pts i = { x = i, y = i % 7 } end print(math.abs(distanceNew(pts) - distanceReuse(pts)) < 1e-9) The same applies to closures: function() ... end inside a loop creates a new function object each time. Define it once outside. Arrays are faster than hashes Lua stores the keys 1..n of a table in a compact array part, and other keys in a hash part. Lists built with consecutive integer keys starting at 1 are fast and small; keys like t 1000000 = true on an otherwise empty table go into the hash part. When you know the size, a numeric for filling 1..n keeps everything in the array part. ipairs and numeric for loops over arrays are faster than pairs over the same data. The garbage collector Lua frees memory automatically, but the work happens while your program runs. Fewer temporary tables and strings means less collection work. You can watch memory use: lua collectgarbage() local before = collectgarbage("count") -- kilobytes in use local junk = {} for i = 1, 10000 do junk i = { i } end local after = collectgarbage("count") junk = nil collectgarbage() print(after before, collectgarbage("count") < after) For games, many people run a small step each frame ( collectgarbage("step", n) ) to avoid long pauses. Small wins that add up - Prefer x x to x ^ 2 in hot code ( ^ always works in floating point). - t + 1 is fine for appending; table.insert(t, v) is a function call doing the same. - String patterns are compiled each call; when matching the same pattern in a loop, simpler patterns are faster. - LuaJIT (lesson 6.05) runs many Lua programs several times faster with no changes, when it is available. Check yourself quiz ? Why is s = s .. piece in a long loop slow? - The .. operator converts both sides to numbers first + Each step copies the whole string built so far - Strings longer than 255 characters are stored on disk Strings never change, so each .. builds a new string and the work grows with the square of the pieces. Collect them in a table and join once with table.concat . ? What should you do before optimising a piece of code? - Rewrite it in C straight away + Measure it, to see whether and where it is slow - Replace all of its tables with strings Guesses about speed are often wrong. Measuring shows whether the code matters and which part to work on. ? Which is usually fastest for joining 10,000 numbers with commas? - Repeating s = s .. n .. "," + table.concat(t, ",") on a table of them - Calling string.format in a loop - Calling string.rep once table.concat builds the result once instead of copying a growing string again and again.
