title: A key-value server
body: Build the core of a small networked key-value store, in the style of Redis's text protocol, running on lesson 2.04's event loop: per-connection buffers, partial writes, limits, and a shared store all clients see. Protocol. Each request is one line (ending \n , optional \r before it), words separated by single spaces: Request Reply --- --- SET key value +OK (the value is everything after key , and may contain spaces) GET key $value , or -ERR no such key DEL key :1 if it existed, :0 otherwise INCR key :N after adding 1 (a missing key counts as 0); -ERR not a number if the value is not an integer KEYS a,b,c (all keys, sorted), or when empty QUIT +BYE , then the connection closes once that reply is written anything else -ERR unknown command Every reply ends with \n . Keys are 1 to 64 characters with no spaces; a request with a missing or bad key, or a missing value for SET , gets -ERR bad request . A line longer than 1024 bytes (or 1024 bytes of input without a line end) closes the connection at once. cpp class KvServer { public: explicit KvServer(std::size_t maxQueued); int accept(); void readable(int id, const std::string& bytes); std::string writable(int id, std::size_t capacity); bool isOpen(int id) const; std::size_t keyCount() const; }; The event loop calls readable with bytes received and writable with how many bytes the socket can take (returning what was sent), exactly as in practice 2.04, including closing a client whose unsent replies would exceed maxQueued bytes.

title: 3.01  How HTTP Works
body:
The protocol of the web as plain text over TCP - a request line, headers and an optional body; a status line, headers and a body in reply - methods, status codes, the headers that matter, persistent connections, and where HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 differ. Text over a connection HTTP/1.1 is a text protocol on top of TCP. A client opens a connection (to port 80, or 443 for HTTPS) and sends a request : text GET /courses/networking HTTP/1.1
 Host: xenon.justloofy.dev
 User-Agent: my-client/1.0
 Accept: text/html
 
 - The request line : a method , the target (path and query), and the version. - Headers : Name: value lines. - A blank line ( 
 alone) ends the headers. - Then an optional body , for methods that send data. The server answers with a response in the same shape: text HTTP/1.1 200 OK
 Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
 Content-Length: 1532
 
 <!doctype html ... (exactly 1532 bytes) You can speak it by hand: curl -v https://example.com shows both sides, and over plain HTTP even telnet example.com 80 and typing the request works. Methods Method Means Body Safe to repeat? --- --- --- --- GET fetch a resource no yes HEAD like GET, headers only no yes POST submit data, create something, run an action yes no PUT replace a resource with this body yes yes (idempotent) PATCH change part of a resource yes not necessarily DELETE remove a resource usually no yes (idempotent) OPTIONS ask what is allowed (used by browsers' CORS checks) no yes "Safe to repeat" is the idempotency of the IPC course's lesson 5.04: browsers and proxies retry GETs freely, but never a POST without asking. Status codes The first digit says the class: Class Meaning Common codes --- --- --- 1xx information 101 Switching Protocols (WebSockets) 2xx success 200 OK , 201 Created , 204 No Content 3xx go elsewhere 301 Moved Permanently , 302 Found , 304 Not Modified 4xx the client's fault 400 Bad Request , 401 Unauthorized , 403 Forbidden , 404 Not Found , 429 Too Many Requests 5xx the server's fault 500 Internal Server Error , 502 Bad Gateway , 503 Service Unavailable Clients should handle a code by its class when they do not know it specifically: an unknown 4xx is treated like 400. Headers that matter Header Purpose --- --- Host which website on this server (required in HTTP/1.1: one IP serves many sites) Content-Length the body's size in bytes Transfer-Encoding: chunked the body comes in pieces of announced size (lesson 3.02) Content-Type what the body is: text/html , application/json , image/png Connection: close close the connection after this response Location where a 3xx redirect points; where a 201 created something Cache-Control , ETag , If-None-Match caching and conditional requests (304) Authorization credentials, such as Bearer <token Cookie / Set-Cookie state the browser keeps for a site Header names are case-insensitive ( content-length is the same header); values are not. Connections HTTP/1.1 connections are persistent by default: after a response, the same connection carries the next request, saving a TCP (and TLS) handshake each time. That only works if each side knows exactly where every message ends, which is why every response needs a Content-Length or chunked encoding, or must close the connection to mark its end. On one HTTP/1.1 connection requests are answered in order , one at a time, so browsers open several connections per site to load pages in parallel. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 HTTP/2 keeps the same methods, status codes and headers but sends them as binary frames , compresses headers, and multiplexes many requests over one connection at once. HTTP/3 does the same over QUIC (UDP), so a lost packet delays only its own request (lesson 1.04). Programs usually get both from a library; the meaning of requests and responses is the HTTP/1.1 you see here. Check yourself quiz ? What ends the headers of an HTTP/1.1 message? - The Content-Length header - The TCP segment that carried them + An empty line: 
 on its own - A \0 byte after the last header The headers end at the first blank line; the body, if any, follows it. Content-Length says how long the body is, not where the headers stop. ? Why is the Host header required in HTTP/1.1? + One server address can host many websites, and Host says which one the request is for - It tells the server which IP address to send the response to - It replaces the DNS lookup the client would otherwise need - It is needed to open the TCP connection to the server The connection already reaches the right machine; Host picks the site on it, because one IP often serves many sites. ? A client receives status 418 and does not know it. How should it treat it? - As a server error, like 500 - As success, since the server answered + As a generic 4xx client error, like 400 - As a redirect, and look for a Location header The first digit gives the class; an unknown 4xx is treated like 400. ? Why must every response on a persistent connection have a Content-Length or a chunked body? - So the server can check the body was not corrupted - So the client can allocate memory before the headers arrive - Because HTTP/1.1 forbids bodies without a declared type + Otherwise the client cannot tell where the response ends and the next one begins The same connection carries several messages, so each must say where it ends; a response without either can only end by closing the connection.

title: Status lines
body: Build and read HTTP status lines (lesson 3.01): cpp struct Status { std::string version; int code; std::string reason; }; std::string reasonFor(int code); std::string statusLine(int code); std::optional<Status parseStatusLine(const std::string& line); std::string classOf(int code); - reasonFor : OK for 200, Created 201, No Content 204, Moved Permanently 301, Found 302, Not Modified 304, Bad Request 400, Unauthorized 401, Forbidden 403, Not Found 404, Method Not Allowed 405, Too Many Requests 429, Internal Server Error 500, Service Unavailable 503; anything else Unknown . - statusLine is HTTP/1.1 CODE REASON\r\n . - parseStatusLine reads VERSION CODE REASON (the reason may contain spaces, or be empty after the second space), where the version starts with HTTP/ , and the code is exactly three digits from 100 to 599. A trailing \r\n or \r is ignored. - classOf : informational (1xx), success , redirect , client error , server error , or invalid outside 100 to 599.

title: 3.02  Parsing HTTP Messages
body:
Reading HTTP from a byte stream - finding the end of the headers, splitting the start line and headers, case-insensitive names, finding the body's length from Content-Length or chunked transfer encoding, and the limits and strictness that keep a parser safe. In two stages An HTTP message arrives on a TCP stream in arbitrary chunks (lesson 2.02), so a parser works in two stages: 1. The head : collect bytes until the first 

 . Everything before it is the start line and headers. 2. The body : decide from the headers how many bytes the body has, and collect exactly that many. Anything after the end of the body belongs to the next message on the connection. The start line and headers Split the head into lines at 
 . The first line is the request line ( METHOD TARGET VERSION , separated by single spaces) or, in a response, the status line ( VERSION CODE REASON ). Each following line is a header: text Content-Type: text/plain - name "Content-Type", value "text/plain" - The name is everything before the first : . It must not be empty or contain spaces. - The value is everything after it, with spaces and tabs trimmed from both ends. - Names are case-insensitive : store them in lower case and look them up that way. - A header can appear more than once ( Set-Cookie often does). For most headers repeats are combined with commas; keep them all and let each use decide. How long is the body? The rules, in order: 1. Responses to HEAD , and 1xx , 204 and 304 responses never have a body. 2. If Transfer-Encoding: chunked is present, the body is chunked (below). 3. Otherwise, if Content-Length is present, the body is exactly that many bytes. 4. Otherwise a request has no body, and a response body runs until the server closes the connection. A message with both Transfer-Encoding and Content-Length , or with two different Content-Length values, is ambiguous and must be rejected : front-end proxies and back-end servers that resolve such ambiguity differently are the cause of request smuggling attacks. Chunked transfer encoding When a server does not know the length in advance (a page generated as it goes), it sends the body in chunks , each preceded by its size in hexadecimal , ending with a zero-size chunk: text 4
 Wiki
 6
 pedia 
 D
 in

chunks.
 0
 
 That body is Wikipedia in

chunks. : 4 + 6 + 13 bytes. Each size line may carry extensions after a ; , which you ignore. After the zero chunk come optional trailer headers and a final empty line. Limits and strictness An HTTP parser takes input from anyone on the internet, so it must be strict and bounded: - Limit the head (8 KB is common) and the number of headers; reply 431 or close beyond that. - Limit the body you will accept; reply 413 Payload Too Large . - Reject malformed lines, a Content-Length that is not a plain decimal number, negative or absurd sizes, and the ambiguous combinations above, with 400 Bad Request . - Do not "fix" bad input; a lenient parser behind a strict one (or the other way round) is exactly how smuggling works. For real servers, use a well-tested parser library (llhttp, the one inside Node.js, or your framework's); writing one, as the practice does, teaches what they check and why. Check yourself quiz ? How does a parser know it has received all the headers? - It has received as many bytes as Content-Length - recv returned the end of the request + It has found the first 

 in the stream - It has seen a Host header The head ends at the empty line. Data arrives in arbitrary chunks, so one recv says nothing about message boundaries. ? A response has Content-Length: 120 and Transfer-Encoding: chunked . What should a strict parser do? - Use Content-Length , because it is more precise - Use chunked encoding, because it takes priority + Reject it as ambiguous - Read 120 bytes, then read chunks after them Parsers that resolve this ambiguity differently are what makes request smuggling possible, so a strict parser refuses the message. ? What sizes do the chunk size lines 4 , 6 and E announce? - 4, 6 and 5 bytes + 4, 6 and 14 bytes - 4, 6 and 15 bytes - 4, 6 and 0 bytes, because E is not a number Chunk sizes are hexadecimal, and E is 14. ? A GET request has no Content-Length and no Transfer-Encoding . How long is its body? - It runs until the client closes the connection - It is as long as the next recv returns - It runs until the next empty line + It has no body Without either header a request has no body. Only a response body may run until the connection closes.

title: Headers and the body's length
body: Parse the head of an HTTP request and decide how its body is delimited (lesson 3.02): cpp struct Head { std::string method, target, version; std::vector<std::pair<std::string, std::string headers; // names in lower case, in order }; enum class BodyKind { None, Length, Chunked, Invalid }; struct Body { BodyKind kind; std::size_t length; }; std::optional<Head parseHead(const std::string& head); std::vector<std::string headerValues(const Head& h, const std::string& name); Body requestBody(const Head& h); - parseHead takes everything before the blank line. Lines are separated by \r\n . The request line is exactly three parts separated by single spaces, with a version starting HTTP/ . Each header line has a name (non-empty, no spaces or tabs) before its first : , and a value with spaces and tabs trimmed from both ends; names are stored in lower case. Any malformed line makes the whole head invalid. - headerValues returns every value of a header (compare names ignoring case), in order. - requestBody : - Transfer-Encoding and Content-Length both present, or several Content-Length values that are not all identical: Invalid . - Transfer-Encoding present: Chunked if its value is exactly chunked (ignoring case), otherwise Invalid . - Content-Length present: it must be 1 to 15 digits only, else Invalid ; then Length with that value (0 is allowed). - Neither: None .

title: 3.03  URLs and Encoding
body: The parts of a URL - scheme, host, port, path, query and fragment - percent-encoding and which characters need it, query strings and form encoding, and resolving a relative link against a base URL. The parts of a URL text https://xenon.justloofy.dev:8443/courses/net%20working?tab=lessons&sort=new part-2 \___/ \_________________/ \__/\____________________/ \__________________/ \____/ scheme host port path query fragment Part Notes --- --- scheme http , https , ws , ftp ... case-insensitive host a name or address; IPv6 addresses go in brackets: http:// ::1 :8080/ port optional; defaults to 80 for http, 443 for https path starts with / ; / if absent query after ? ; usually name=value pairs joined with & fragment after ; never sent to the server , used by the browser to jump within a page A URL can also contain user:password@ before the host. Never use it: the credentials end up in logs and histories. For an HTTP request, the client sends the path and query as the request target ( GET /courses/net%20working?tab=lessons HTTP/1.1 ) and the host and port in the Host header. Percent-encoding URLs may only contain a limited set of characters. Anything else is percent-encoded : each byte of its UTF-8 encoding written as % and two hex digits. text space - %20 é (C3 A9) - %C3%A9 / - %2F (when it is part of a name, not a separator) The characters that never need encoding are the unreserved ones: letters, digits, - , . , _ and ~ . Others are reserved because they have meaning in URLs ( / ? & = : @ and more); they must be encoded when used as data. When building a URL from user input, encode every part that comes from outside; when parsing one, decode each part after splitting it at its separators, so an encoded %2F stays part of a name instead of becoming a path separator. Decoding must reject broken sequences: a % not followed by two hex digits. Accepting them sloppily has been the cause of many security bugs (a check passes on the encoded form, then the decoded form means something else). Query strings and forms A query string is a list of name=value pairs separated by & . HTML forms submit their fields the same way (as the body of a POST with Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded ), with one quirk: in form encoding a space is written + , so + itself must be sent as %2B . When parsing form data or queries, turn + into a space before percent-decoding. text q=networking+basics&level=2&tag=c%2B%2B - q = "networking basics", level = "2", tag = "c++" The same name can appear several times ( tag=a&tag=b ); keep all of them in order. Relative URLs Links in a page are often relative to the page's own URL (the base ). Resolving href against https://site/a/b/page.html : href Result --- --- other.html https://site/a/b/other.html (same folder) ../up.html https://site/a/up.html /root.html https://site/root.html (from the host) //cdn.site/x.js https://cdn.site/x.js (same scheme) https://other/x itself: already absolute ?page=2 https://site/a/b/page.html?page=2 The path rules are the same . and .. folding as file paths (the IPC course's lesson 6.01), with / instead of \ . Check yourself quiz ? Which part of a URL is never sent to the server? - The query, after ? - The port, after : + The fragment, after - The path, after the host The browser keeps the fragment to jump within a page. The path and query go in the request line, the host and port in the Host header. ? How is the character é percent-encoded? - %E9 , its code point + %C3%A9 , its UTF-8 bytes - %00E9 , as one 16-bit value - é , as an entity Each byte of the character's UTF-8 encoding is written as % and two hex digits; é is the two bytes C3 A9. ? Why decode each part of a URL only after splitting it at its separators? - Decoding first is slower, because the whole URL must be scanned twice - Splitting needs the % signs to find the separators - Decoded text cannot contain / or ? + An encoded separator such as %2F is data; decoding first would turn it into a real separator %2F inside a name must stay part of that name; decoding before splitting would create a new path segment. ? In form encoding, how are a space and a plus sign written? + A space as + , and a plus sign as %2B - A space as %20 , and a plus sign as + - A space as + , and a plus sign as ++ - A space as _ , and a plus sign as %2B Form encoding writes a space as + , so a real + must be encoded. When parsing, turn + into a space before percent-decoding.

title: URLs, percent-encoding and query strings
body: Take URLs apart and handle their encoding (lesson 3.03): cpp struct Url { std::string scheme, host; int port; std::string path, query, fragment; }; std::optional<Url parseUrl(const std::string& text); std::string percentEncode(const std::string& text); std::optional<std::string percentDecode(const std::string& text); std::vector<std::pair<std::string, std::string parseQuery(const std::string& query); - parseUrl handles scheme://host :port /path ?query fragment . The scheme (letters, digits, + , - , . , starting with a letter) is returned in lower case; the host in lower case, with an IPv6 host written in brackets returned without them. The port defaults to 80 for http and 443 for https (0 for any other scheme when absent); a port must be digits from 1 to 65535. The path is / when absent. Query and fragment exclude their ? and . The parts stay percent-encoded. A missing :// , an empty host, or a bad port gives std::nullopt . - percentEncode leaves letters, digits, - , . , _ and ~ as they are and writes every other byte as % and two uppercase hex digits. - percentDecode turns %XY (either case) back into the byte; a % not followed by two hex digits gives std::nullopt . - parseQuery splits at & into name=value pairs (a pair without = has an empty value; empty pieces are skipped), turns + into a space, then percent-decodes both sides; a pair that fails to decode is skipped.

title: 3.04  A Tiny Web Server
body:
Putting the milestone together - routing requests by method and path with parameters, serving static files with the right Content-Type, building correct responses, and the path traversal attack that a naive file server falls for and how to stop it. The loop A web server is the event loop of lesson 2.04 with HTTP as its protocol: 1. Accept connections; read bytes into each connection's buffer. 2. When a whole request has arrived (lesson 3.02), route it to a handler. 3. The handler produces a response: status, headers, body. 4. Serialise the response into the connection's output queue. 5. Keep the connection for the next request, unless either side asked to close. Routing A router maps a method and a path pattern to a handler. Patterns often contain parameters : text GET / - home page GET /courses/{id} - one course; id from the path GET /courses/{id}/lessons/{lesson} POST /api/progress - save progress Matching splits the path at / , compares segment by segment, and collects {name} segments as parameters (percent-decoded, lesson 3.03). Useful rules: - If a path matches a route but not with this method, reply 405 Method Not Allowed with an Allow header listing the methods that would work, rather than 404. - Prefer exact segments over parameters when both match ( /courses/new before /courses/{id} ), or order routes so the specific one is tried first. - Unknown paths get 404 . Responses A correct response always includes a status line, a Content-Length (or chunked encoding), and a Content-Type when there is a body: cpp-norun std::string response{ "HTTP/1.1 " + std::to_string(status) + " " + reason(status) + "
" }; response += "Content-Type: " + type + "
"; response += "Content-Length: " + std::to_string(body.size()) + "
"; response += "
"; response += body; Content-Type for files comes from the extension: .html is text/html; charset=utf-8 , .css text/css , .js text/javascript , .json application/json , .png image/png , .svg image/svg+xml , and unknown types application/octet-stream . Also send X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff so browsers trust that type instead of guessing. Path traversal A naive static file server maps a URL path straight onto a folder: GET /images/logo.png serves C:\site\public\images\logo.png . Now someone requests: text GET /../../Windows/win.ini GET /images/..%2F..%2F..%2Fsecret.txt GET /images/..\..\config.json If the server joins those to its folder without care, it serves files outside the public folder: configuration, source code, keys. This is path traversal , one of the oldest web vulnerabilities. Defend in layers: 1. Percent-decode the path once , then reject anything containing \ , a NUL byte, or a : (drive letters and Windows alternate data streams). 2. Split at / and resolve . and .. yourself; reject any request whose .. would climb above the root, rather than silently clamping it. 3. Reject segments Windows treats specially: names ending in . or a space, and device names such as CON , NUL or COM1 . 4. As a last check, compute the final absolute path and verify it is still inside the public folder (with std::filesystem::weakly_canonical on the real path). 5. Never serve hidden or dot files ( .env , .git ) unless intended. The practice builds exactly this check. What a tiny server is for A small server like this is useful for local tools (a dashboard for your game's stats, a documentation viewer) and for learning. For anything facing the internet, use a mature server or framework, and put TLS in front (next lesson): they have already handled the thousands of edge cases this milestone only touches. Check yourself quiz ? A path matches a route but the method does not. What status should the server send? - 404 Not Found, since the route did not match - 400 Bad Request, since the method is wrong + 405 Method Not Allowed - 403 Forbidden, since the method is refused The resource exists, so 404 would mislead; 405 with Allow tells the client which methods would work. ? Why should a server send X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff ? - It makes browsers cache the file for longer + So browsers use the declared Content-Type instead of guessing - It stops browsers from downloading the file twice - It tells proxies not to compress the body A browser guessing the type could treat uploaded data as script or HTML; nosniff makes it trust the server's type. ? Why reject a .. that climbs above the root instead of clamping it? + It is never a legitimate request, and rejecting avoids subtle mistakes in clamping - Clamping is impossible once the path has been decoded - Windows refuses to open paths that were clamped - Rejecting it makes the server respond faster A real link never climbs above the root, so such a request is an attack; refusing it is simpler and safer than trying to repair it. ? Which of these must a Windows file server reject in a request path? - Segments that contain digits - Paths with more than one / - File names with an extension + A : (drive letters and alternate data streams) Backslashes, colons, device names such as CON or NUL , and names ending in a dot or space all mean something special to Windows.

title: A router and a safe file path
match: A router and a safe file path
body: Build the two decisions at the heart of lesson 3.04's tiny web server: cpp struct Match { int status; std::string handler; std::map<std::string, std::string params; std::string allow; }; class Router { public: void add(const std::string& method, const std::string& pattern, const std::string& handler); Match route(const std::string& method, const std::string& path) const; }; std::optional<std::string safeRelativePath(const std::string& urlPath); Router - A pattern is a path split at / ; a segment {name} matches any non-empty segment and captures it (percent-decoded; a segment that fails to decode does not match). - route compares the path, segment by segment, with every route. Routes with exact segments are preferred over parameters: among the routes that match, choose the one with the most exact segments, and on a tie the one added first. - Result: status 200 with the handler and parameters; if routes match the path but none for this method, status 405 and allow listing their methods, in the order added, joined by , ; otherwise 404. safeRelativePath turns a URL path into a path relative to the public folder, or refuses it: - The path must start with / . Percent-decode it once (refuse on failure). - Refuse any \ , : or byte 0 in the decoded path. - Split at / , ignore empty and . segments, let .. remove the previous segment, and refuse if a .. has nothing to remove. - Refuse segments that start with . (hidden files), end with . or a space, or whose name before the first . is a Windows device name: con , prn , aux , nul , com1 to com9 , lpt1 to lpt9 (any case). - Return the remaining segments joined with / ; an empty result becomes index.html .

title: 3.05  HTTPS and TLS
body: What TLS adds to a connection - encryption, integrity and server authentication - certificates and the chain of trust, how hostnames are matched including wildcards, the handshake in outline, SNI, and why you always use a library for it. Three promises Plain HTTP travels as readable text: anyone on the path (the café's Wi-Fi, an internet provider, a compromised router) can read it and change it. TLS (Transport Layer Security, the successor of SSL) wraps a TCP connection and adds three guarantees: - Confidentiality : the data is encrypted; observers see only sizes and timing. - Integrity : any change in transit is detected and the connection fails. - Authentication : the client knows it is talking to the real server for that name, not an impostor. HTTPS is simply HTTP inside TLS, on port 443. Everything in this milestone applies unchanged inside the encrypted channel. Certificates Authentication rests on certificates . A server's certificate contains its public key and the names it is valid for, signed by a certificate authority (CA). The client checks: 1. The signature chain: the server's certificate is signed by an intermediate CA, which is signed by a root CA that the operating system or browser trusts. 2. The certificate is within its validity dates and not revoked. 3. The name : the host the client meant to reach is listed in the certificate's subject alternative names. Then, during the handshake, the server proves it holds the private key matching the certificate's public key. An attacker can copy a certificate (it is public) but not the private key. Free, automated certificates from Let's Encrypt made HTTPS the norm; there is no reason to serve anything public over plain HTTP. Matching names Name checking is where many home-made implementations fail. The rules (RFC 6125) for each name in the certificate: - Compare case-insensitively . - An exact name matches only itself: xenon.justloofy.dev matches xenon.justloofy.dev . - A wildcard .justloofy.dev matches exactly one label in its place: xenon.justloofy.dev yes; justloofy.dev no (no label); a.b.justloofy.dev no (two labels). - The wildcard must be the entire leftmost label : .dev style names that cover a whole public suffix are refused by clients, and partial wildcards like x .example.com should be refused too. - IP addresses are matched against IP entries, never against wildcards. The handshake in outline TLS 1.3, the current version, needs one round trip: 1. ClientHello : supported versions and ciphers, a key share, and the server name it wants ( SNI , below). 2. ServerHello with the server's key share; from both shares each side computes the same secret keys. Then, already encrypted, the certificate, a signature proving key ownership, and "finished". 3. The client checks the certificate and signature, sends its own "finished", and application data flows. Resumed connections can even send data in the first flight (0-RTT), with care about replays. SNI One IP address often hosts many HTTPS sites, but the certificate must be chosen before any HTTP is exchanged. So the ClientHello carries the hostname in the Server Name Indication extension. It is sent in clear text (Encrypted Client Hello is being deployed to fix that), which is why packet captures, and network filters, can see which site a TLS connection is for even though they cannot see the pages. Milestone 4's practice extracts it. Use a library TLS involves careful cryptography, certificate parsing, chain building, revocation, and dozens of past attacks that implementations must avoid. Never write your own. On Windows: - WinHTTP or WinINet : HTTPS requests with one API, using the system's certificate store. - SChannel : the system TLS implementation for your own sockets. - OpenSSL , BoringSSL or mbedTLS : cross-platform libraries. - Higher-level HTTP libraries (libcurl, cpp-httplib with OpenSSL) handle it for you. And never "fix" a certificate error by turning verification off. That removes the authentication guarantee entirely and leaves the encryption protecting your traffic for an attacker. Check yourself quiz ? What three guarantees does TLS add to a connection? - Reliability, ordering and flow control - Compression, caching and authentication + Confidentiality, integrity and authentication of the server - Confidentiality, anonymity and faster delivery Reliability and ordering already come from TCP; TLS encrypts, detects tampering and proves who the server is. ? Does .justloofy.dev match a.b.justloofy.dev ? - Yes: the wildcard matches anything before .justloofy.dev + No: a wildcard matches exactly one label - Yes, but only if the certificate also lists b.justloofy.dev - No: wildcards only match names with a single letter The wildcard stands for exactly one whole label, so it matches xenon.justloofy.dev but neither a.b.justloofy.dev nor justloofy.dev . ? Why does the ClientHello carry the hostname (SNI)? - So the server can look up the client's address in DNS - So the encryption keys can be derived from the hostname - So routers can deliver the packet to the right server + One address hosts many sites; the certificate is chosen before HTTP The Host header is only sent inside the encrypted channel, too late to choose the certificate, so the name goes in the ClientHello. ? Why is turning off certificate verification never an acceptable fix? - It makes the connection fall back to plain HTTP - It disables the encryption of the data + Anyone can then pretend to be the server and read your data - It makes the handshake take two extra round trips Encryption still happens, but with whoever answered; without authentication an attacker in the middle can read and change everything.

title: Certificate name matching
body: Write the hostname check every TLS client performs (lesson 3.05): cpp bool nameMatches(const std::string& certificateName, const std::string& host); bool certificateMatches(const std::vector<std::string & names, const std::string& host); - nameMatches compares ignoring case. A trailing dot on either side is ignored ( example.com. ). - A name without matches only the same host. - A wildcard is allowed only as the whole leftmost label ( .example.com ). It matches exactly one non-empty label in that position: a.example.com yes; example.com and a.b.example.com no. - Wildcards are refused (never match) if the rest of the name has fewer than two labels ( .com , ), and anywhere else ( x .example.com , a. .example.com ) never matches. - A host that is an IPv4 address (four dot-separated numbers) never matches a wildcard. - certificateMatches is true if any of the certificate's names matches.

title: A streaming HTTP parser
body:
Build the request side of an HTTP/1.1 server: a parser that takes bytes as they arrive from a connection and produces complete requests, with chunked bodies, pipelining, keep-alive and the limits of lesson 3.02, plus a correct response builder. cpp using Headers = std::vector<std::pair<std::string, std::string ; struct Request { std::string method, target, version; Headers headers; std::string body; bool keepAlive; }; class RequestParser { public: RequestParser(std::size_t maxHead, std::size_t maxBody); void feed(const std::string& bytes); std::optional<Request next(); bool failed() const; int errorStatus() const; std::size_t pending() const; }; std::string buildResponse(int status, const Headers& headers, const std::string& body); The head. It ends at the first 

 . If no terminator has arrived and more than maxHead bytes are buffered, or the head is longer than maxHead , the parser fails with 431 . The head is parsed as in practice 3.02 (names in lower case, values trimmed), except that the version must be exactly HTTP/1.0 or HTTP/1.1 . Any malformed head fails with 400 . The body. Decided as in practice 3.02: an invalid combination fails with 400 ; Content-Length larger than maxBody fails with 413 . A chunked body is a series of chunks: a size line of 1 to 8 hex digits (optionally followed by ; and an extension, which is ignored) ending 
 , that many bytes, and 
 ; a size of 0 ends the chunks, and is followed by optional trailer lines and an empty line ( 
 ). Malformed chunks fail with 400 ; a decoded body larger than maxBody fails with 413 . Keep-alive. For HTTP/1.1 it is true unless a Connection header contains the token close ; for HTTP/1.0 it is false unless a Connection header contains keep-alive (tokens are separated by commas, compared ignoring case and surrounding spaces). The parser. feed appends bytes; next returns the next complete request (several can be waiting, pipelined) or std::nullopt if more bytes are needed. Once failed, the parser ignores further input and next always gives std::nullopt ; errorStatus says why (0 while not failed). pending is the number of buffered bytes not yet consumed. buildResponse writes HTTP/1.1 CODE REASON
 (reasons as in practice 3.01), each header as Name: value
 in order, then Content-Length: N
 unless the status is 1xx, 204 or 304 (which have no body: the body is then left out), then 
 and the body.

title: 4.01  Packet Capture
body: Seeing the actual packets - capturing with Wireshark and Npcap, capture filters versus display filters, the pcap file format with its global and per-packet headers, and the rules about what you may capture. Seeing what is really sent Everything in this course so far has been described from the program's point of view. A packet capture shows what actually crossed the wire: every header, every retransmission, every byte. When a networked program misbehaves, a capture is usually the fastest way to find out whether the bug is in the client, the server, or the network. Tools - Wireshark : the standard graphical capture and analysis tool. It decodes thousands of protocols, shows each packet's layers as a tree, and can follow whole conversations. - Npcap : the capture driver Wireshark installs on Windows. Enable its "loopback" support to capture traffic to 127.0.0.1 , which never touches a real network card. - tshark and dumpcap : Wireshark's command-line tools, for capturing on servers and scripting. - pktmon : built into Windows 10 and later ( pktmon start --capture ), writing captures that Wireshark can open after conversion ( pktmon etl2pcap ). Two kinds of filter Capture filters decide what is recorded at all, in the BPF syntax of libpcap. They keep files small on busy networks: text host 192.168.1.50 tcp port 7777 udp and port 53 not port 3389 Display filters decide what Wireshark shows from a capture, using its own field names, and can be changed freely afterwards: text ip.addr == 192.168.1.50 tcp.port == 7777 && tcp.flags.syn == 1 dns.qry.name contains "justloofy" http.request.method == "POST" tcp.analysis.retransmission tls.handshake.extensions_server_name Capture broadly, filter the display narrowly: you cannot recover packets a capture filter dropped. The pcap file format Captures are saved as pcap files (or the newer pcapng , which Wireshark uses by default and can convert). The classic pcap format is simple, which is why every tool supports it: A 24-byte global header: Offset Size Field --- --- --- 0 4 magic number: 0xA1B2C3D4 (microsecond timestamps) or 0xA1B23C4D (nanoseconds) 4 2 + 2 version, 2.4 8 4 time zone correction (always 0) 12 4 timestamp accuracy (always 0) 16 4 snapshot length : the most bytes stored per packet 20 4 link type : 1 means Ethernet frames The magic number also tells you the byte order of the file: read as little-endian it is 0xA1B2C3D4 on files written by little-endian machines; if it reads as 0xD4C3B2A1 , every field in the file is big-endian. Then, for each packet, a 16-byte record header and the packet bytes: Offset Size Field --- --- --- 0 4 timestamp, seconds 4 4 timestamp, microseconds (or nanoseconds) 8 4 captured length : bytes stored in the file 12 4 original length : bytes the packet really had When a packet was longer than the snapshot length, only the first bytes are stored and the captured length is smaller than the original. Decoders must cope with truncated packets. What you may capture Capturing traffic is reading other people's communication when it is not yours. Capture only on networks and machines you own or are explicitly authorised to examine, only the traffic you need, and treat captures as sensitive data: they can contain passwords sent without encryption, cookies, and private messages. Deleting a capture you no longer need is good practice. Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference between a capture filter and a display filter? - A capture filter hides packets from view; a display filter decides what is recorded - They use the same syntax, but a display filter is applied by the network card + A capture filter decides what is recorded; a display filter only hides packets and can be changed afterwards - A capture filter works only on TCP; a display filter works on every protocol Packets a capture filter drops are gone for good, so capture broadly and narrow the view with display filters. ? A pcap file's magic number reads as 0xD4C3B2A1 . What does that mean? - The file is corrupt and cannot be read + The file was written in the other byte order, so every field must be read big-endian - The timestamps are in nanoseconds instead of microseconds - The file is in pcapng format rather than pcap The magic number doubles as a byte-order mark. The nanosecond variant is 0xA1B23C4D , a different value. ? Why can a packet's captured length be smaller than its original length? - The network card dropped the packet's headers - The packet was fragmented and only one fragment was saved - Ethernet padding is removed before the packet is stored + The capture stored at most the snapshot length of each packet A packet longer than the snapshot length is truncated in the file; decoders must cope with that. ? What must you enable to capture traffic to 127.0.0.1 on Windows? - Promiscuous mode on the network card - A capture filter of host 127.0.0.1 + Npcap's loopback capture support - Wireshark's "Validate TCP checksum" option Loopback traffic never touches a real network card, so it needs Npcap's loopback adapter.

title: Reading a pcap file
body: Read a classic pcap capture file (lesson 4.01): its global header and its packet records, in either byte order. cpp struct PcapInfo { bool bigEndian; bool nanoseconds; std::uint32_t snapLength; std::uint32_t linkType; }; struct PcapPacket { std::uint32_t seconds; std::uint32_t fraction; std::uint32_t originalLength; std::vector<std::uint8_t data; }; std::optional<PcapInfo readHeader(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & file); std::optional<std::vector<PcapPacket readPackets(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & file); - readHeader needs at least 24 bytes. Read the first 4 bytes as a little-endian number: 0xA1B2C3D4 is a little-endian file with microsecond timestamps, 0xA1B23C4D little-endian with nanoseconds, 0xD4C3B2A1 big-endian with microseconds and 0x4D3CB2A1 big-endian with nanoseconds. Any other magic fails. The major version (bytes 4-5, in the file's byte order) must be 2. Then fill in the snapshot length (bytes 16-19) and the link type (bytes 20-23). - readPackets reads the header, then every record up to the end of the file: a 16-byte record header (seconds, fraction of a second, captured length, original length, all in the file's byte order) and captured length bytes of data. fraction is the microseconds or nanoseconds field as stored. It fails if the header is bad, a record header or its data runs past the end of the file, or the captured length is greater than the snapshot length or the original length. A file with no records gives an empty list.

title: 4.02  Ethernet and IP Headers
body: Decoding the first layers of a captured packet - the Ethernet frame with MAC addresses and EtherType, the IPv4 header field by field with its options and checksum, fragments, and the fixed 40-byte IPv6 header. Ethernet A captured Ethernet frame starts with a 14-byte header: Offset Size Field --- --- --- 0 6 destination MAC address 6 6 source MAC address 12 2 EtherType : what follows MAC addresses are written as six hex bytes separated by colons: 3c:22:fb:12:9a:01 . The EtherType values you will meet: EtherType Protocol --- --- 0x0800 IPv4 0x86DD IPv6 0x0806 ARP (finding the MAC address for an IP on the local network) 0x8100 a VLAN tag: 4 more bytes, then the real EtherType (The frame check sequence at the end of the frame is usually not included in captures.) IPv4 The IPv4 header follows at offset 14: Offset Size Field --- --- --- 0 4 bits version: 4 0 4 bits IHL : header length in 32-bit words (5 = 20 bytes, more if options) 1 1 DSCP and ECN (priority and congestion marking) 2 2 total length : header plus data, in bytes 4 2 identification (shared by the fragments of one packet) 6 3 bits + 13 bits flags (bit 1: don't fragment, bit 2: more fragments) and fragment offset in 8-byte units 8 1 TTL 9 1 protocol : 1 ICMP, 6 TCP, 17 UDP 10 2 header checksum 12 4 source address 16 4 destination address 20 ... options, if IHL 5 All big-endian. Decoding rules: - The transport header starts at IHL × 4 bytes, not always 20. - Use the total length to know where the IP data ends: Ethernet pads small frames to 60 bytes, and those padding bytes are not part of the packet. - The checksum covers the header only (lesson 2.03's algorithm over IHL × 4 bytes): a correct header sums to zero. - A packet with the "more fragments" flag or a non-zero fragment offset is a fragment : only the first fragment carries the TCP or UDP header; the others carry continuation data. A decoder that treats every fragment as starting with a TCP header reads garbage. IPv6 IPv6 has a fixed 40-byte header, simpler to parse: Offset Size Field --- --- --- 0 4 bits version: 6 0 8 bits + 20 bits traffic class and flow label 4 2 payload length (everything after the 40-byte header) 6 1 next header : 6 TCP, 17 UDP, 58 ICMPv6, or an extension header 7 1 hop limit (IPv6's TTL) 8 16 source address 24 16 destination address There is no header checksum (the layers above have their own), and optional information comes as a chain of extension headers , each naming the next, which a full decoder must walk before it reaches TCP or UDP. Check yourself quiz ? An Ethernet frame's bytes 12-13 are 86 DD . What comes next? + An IPv6 header - An IPv4 header - An ARP message - A VLAN tag EtherType 0x86DD is IPv6; IPv4 is 0x0800 , ARP 0x0806 and a VLAN tag 0x8100 . ? The first byte of an IPv4 header is 0x47 . Where does the TCP header start? - 20 bytes into the IP header, as always - 7 bytes into the IP header + 28 bytes into the IP header - 47 bytes into the IP header The low nibble is IHL, the header length in 32-bit words: 7 x 4 = 28 bytes, so 8 bytes of options follow the fixed 20. ? Why use the IPv4 total length instead of the frame's length to find the end of the data? - The frame length includes the IP header twice - The frame length is not stored in captures + Short frames are padded, and the padding is not IP data - The total length also counts the bytes of the TCP options Ethernet pads small frames to 60 bytes; only the total length says where the IP packet really ends. ? Which IPv4 fragments carry the TCP header? - Every fragment carries a copy of it - Only the last one, with "more fragments" clear - None: fragments carry only data + Only the first one, with fragment offset 0 The later fragments carry continuation data; a decoder that reads a TCP header from them reads garbage.

title: Ethernet and IPv4 headers
body: Decode the first two layers of a captured frame (lesson 4.02). cpp struct Ipv4 { std::uint8_t headerLength; // in bytes std::uint16_t totalLength; std::uint16_t id; bool dontFragment; bool moreFragments; std::uint16_t fragmentOffset; // in bytes std::uint8_t ttl; std::uint8_t protocol; std::uint32_t source; std::uint32_t destination; bool checksumOk; }; std::string macToString(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & frame, std::size_t offset); std::string ipToString(std::uint32_t ip); std::optional<std::uint16_t etherType(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & frame, std::size_t& payloadOffset); std::optional<Ipv4 parseIpv4(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & packet); - macToString writes the six bytes starting at offset as lower-case hex pairs separated by colons ( 3c:22:fb:12:9a:01 ), or returns an empty string if they do not fit. - ipToString writes dotted decimal: 0xC0A80001 is 192.168.0.1 . - etherType returns the EtherType at bytes 12-13 and sets payloadOffset to 14. If it is a VLAN tag ( 0x8100 ), the real EtherType is at bytes 16-17 and the payload starts at 18. It fails if the frame is too short for what it needs. - parseIpv4 decodes an IPv4 header at the start of packet . It fails if the packet is shorter than 20 bytes, the version is not 4, the header length is under 20 or longer than the packet, or the total length is less than the header length or more than the packet's size (a packet may be longer than its total length: that is Ethernet padding). The fragment offset is converted to bytes. checksumOk says whether the Internet checksum over the header comes out as 0; a bad checksum does not make the parse fail.

title: 4.03  TCP and UDP Headers
body: The transport headers byte by byte - UDP's eight bytes, TCP's ports, sequence and acknowledgement numbers, data offset, flags, window and options such as MSS and window scaling - and the pseudo-header both checksums cover. UDP The UDP header is 8 bytes, all big-endian: Offset Size Field --- --- --- 0 2 source port 2 2 destination port 4 2 length : header plus data 6 2 checksum (0 in IPv4 means "not computed") That is everything UDP adds to IP (lesson 1.04). TCP The TCP header is 20 bytes plus options: Offset Size Field --- --- --- 0 2 source port 2 2 destination port 4 4 sequence number : the number of the first data byte (or of the SYN) 8 4 acknowledgement number : the next byte expected, valid when ACK is set 12 4 bits data offset : header length in 32-bit words (5 to 15) 13 8 bits flags 14 2 window : free receive buffer space 16 2 checksum 18 2 urgent pointer (almost never used) 20 ... options, up to data offset × 4 The flags byte, from the most significant bit: Bit Value Flag Means --- --- --- --- 7 0x80 CWR congestion window reduced 6 0x40 ECE congestion seen (ECN) 5 0x20 URG urgent pointer valid 4 0x10 ACK the acknowledgement number is valid 3 0x08 PSH push this data to the application now 2 0x04 RST reset: abort the connection 1 0x02 SYN synchronise: open a connection 0 0x01 FIN finished sending The payload starts at data offset × 4 , and its length is the IP data length minus that. A SYN or FIN with no data still uses up one sequence number, which is why the handshake's acknowledgements are "seq + 1". Options Options are type-length-value records (type 0 ends the list, type 1 is a one-byte padding "no-op"): Kind Name Purpose --- --- --- 2 MSS the largest segment this side will accept (lesson 1.01) 3 window scale multiply the 16-bit window by 2^n, for fast networks 4 SACK permitted selective acknowledgements may be used 5 SACK which ranges beyond a gap have arrived 8 timestamps for measuring round trips and protecting against wrapped sequence numbers Most appear only in the SYN and SYN-ACK, where the two sides negotiate them. The checksum and the pseudo-header TCP and UDP checksums use the Internet checksum (lesson 2.03), computed over: 1. a pseudo-header : source address, destination address, a zero byte, the protocol number, and the TCP or UDP length (for IPv4: 4 + 4 + 1 + 1 + 2 bytes); 2. the TCP or UDP header (with the checksum field as zero when computing it); 3. the data, padded with a zero byte if its length is odd. Including the addresses means a packet delivered to the wrong machine or port fails its checksum. To verify a received segment, run the sum over the pseudo-header and the whole segment including its checksum: a correct one comes out as zero. In captures taken on the sending machine, Wireshark often reports TCP checksums as wrong: modern network cards compute them in hardware ( checksum offloading ) after the capture point, so the captured packet still has a blank or partial checksum. Wireshark's "Validate TCP checksum" option is off by default for this reason. Check yourself quiz ? A TCP flags byte is 0x12 . Which flags are set? - SYN and FIN + SYN and ACK - ACK and PSH - RST and ACK 0x12 = 0x10 (ACK) + 0x02 (SYN): the second packet of the handshake. ? The data offset nibble is 8. Where does the payload start? - 8 bytes into the TCP header - 28 bytes into the TCP header - 20 bytes into the TCP header, after the fixed part + 32 bytes into the TCP header The data offset counts 32-bit words: 8 x 4 = 32 bytes, so 12 bytes of options follow the fixed 20. ? Why does a SYN with no data still use a sequence number? + SYN and FIN each count as one byte of sequence space, so they can be acknowledged - The SYN carries one hidden byte of data for the server - Every TCP segment uses one sequence number, whatever its length - The sequence number is needed to compute the checksum That is why the handshake acknowledges "seq + 1". Data segments use one number per byte, and pure ACKs use none. ? Why do captures on the sending machine often show bad TCP checksums? - The capture driver corrupts outgoing packets - TCP fills in its checksum only after the first retransmission - Wireshark computes checksums without the pseudo-header + The network card fills in the checksum after the capture point With checksum offloading the card computes it in hardware, so the captured copy still has a blank or partial checksum.

title: TCP headers and the transport checksum
match: TCP headers and the transport checksum
body: Decode a TCP header with its options, name its flags, and compute the checksum TCP and UDP use (lesson 4.03). cpp struct Tcp { std::uint16_t sourcePort; std::uint16_t destinationPort; std::uint32_t sequence; std::uint32_t acknowledgement; std::uint8_t headerLength; // in bytes std::uint8_t flags; std::uint16_t window; std::optional<std::uint16_t mss; std::optional<std::uint8_t windowScale; bool sackPermitted; }; std::optional<Tcp parseTcp(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & segment); std::string flagNames(std::uint8_t flags); std::uint16_t transportChecksum(std::uint32_t source, std::uint32_t destination, std::uint8_t protocol, const std::vector<std::uint8_t & segment); - parseTcp fails if the segment is shorter than 20 bytes, or the header length (data offset × 4) is under 20 or longer than the segment. It then walks the options between byte 20 and the end of the header: kind 0 ends the list, kind 1 is a single padding byte, and any other kind has a length byte that counts the kind and length bytes too. A length under 2, or an option that would run past the header, makes the parse fail. Record MSS (kind 2, length 4), window scale (kind 3, length 3) and SACK permitted (kind 4, length 2); skip other kinds. - flagNames lists the set flags from bit 0 upwards, separated by commas: FIN, SYN, RST, PSH, ACK, URG, ECE, CWR . So 0x12 is "SYN,ACK" and no flags is "" . - transportChecksum runs the Internet checksum over the IPv4 pseudo-header (source, destination, a zero byte, the protocol, and the segment's length as 16 bits) followed by the segment, padding an odd last byte with zero. With the segment's checksum field set to zero it gives the value to write there; over a received segment it gives 0 when the checksum is right.

title: 4.04  Following a TCP Conversation
body: Turning a list of captured segments into the conversation they carry - identifying a connection by its addresses and ports, relative sequence numbers, the handshake, data in both directions, retransmissions and duplicates, and how connections end with FIN or RST. One connection among many A capture interleaves packets from every connection on the machine. A single TCP connection is identified by its four-tuple : the two IP addresses and the two ports. Packets in one direction have it as (A, portA, B, portB); replies have it reversed. A tracker uses a canonical key (the lower endpoint first, say) so both directions land in the same conversation. Relative sequence numbers Each side's initial sequence number (ISN) is random, so raw numbers like 3141592653 are hard to read. Wireshark shows relative numbers by default: the sequence number minus that side's ISN. The SYN is relative 0, the first data byte relative 1 (the SYN used up one number), and the relative number of any byte is its position in the stream plus one. Do the same in your own tools. Reading a conversation text direction flags rel seq rel ack len 1 client- server SYN 0 0 2 server- client SYN,ACK 0 1 0 3 client- server ACK 1 1 0 4 client- server PSH,ACK 1 1 75 request 5 server- client ACK 1 76 1448 response, part 1 6 server- client ACK 1449 76 1448 part 2 7 client- server ACK 76 2897 0 8 server- client FIN,ACK 2897 76 0 9 client- server FIN,ACK 76 2898 0 10 server- client ACK 2898 77 0 - Packets 1 to 3 are the handshake. - The client sent 75 bytes (4); the server acknowledged them (ack 76 in packet 5) and sent 2 896 bytes in two segments. - Each FIN takes one sequence number, so the final acknowledgements are one more than the data. Retransmissions and duplicates When a segment is lost, the sender sends the same bytes again later. In a capture this appears as a segment whose sequence range has already been seen . Wireshark flags these as TCP Retransmission ; duplicate acknowledgements (the same ack number repeated, often three times before a fast retransmit) as TCP Dup ACK . To reassemble the byte stream, as "Follow TCP Stream" does, take each direction's segments in sequence order , keep only bytes not already placed, and stop at any gap (a segment never captured). The result is exactly what each program read with recv , which makes reading application protocols (next lesson) possible. How connections end - FIN in both directions, each acknowledged: an orderly close (lesson 2.02). - RST : an abort. A RST in reply to a SYN means connection refused : nothing listens on that port. A RST in the middle of a conversation usually means a program crashed or closed with unread data, or a firewall killed the connection. - Nothing : a connection that simply stops, often because one side vanished; it is eventually timed out by keep-alives or by the application. Counting how each connection in a capture ended is often the quickest diagnosis of "it sometimes disconnects". Check yourself quiz ? How do you put both directions of one connection under the same key? - Use only the server's address and port as the key - Use the sequence numbers of the two SYNs as the key + Order the two endpoints canonically, for example the lower address and port first - Use the source endpoint, since replies keep the same source Replies have the four-tuple reversed; sorting the two endpoints gives both directions the same key. ? A server's SYN-ACK has relative ack 1. What does it acknowledge? + The client's SYN, which used relative sequence number 0 - The first byte of the client's data - The server's own SYN - Nothing yet: ack 1 means no data has arrived The SYN takes up one sequence number, so acknowledging it means "I expect byte 1 next". ? How does a retransmission appear in a capture? - As a segment with the RST flag set - As a segment with a sequence number of 0 - As an acknowledgement repeated three times + As a segment whose bytes were already sent earlier The sender resends the same bytes, so the range repeats. Repeated acknowledgements are duplicate ACKs, which often trigger a retransmission but are not one. ? A SYN is answered immediately by a RST. What happened? - The connection was opened and then closed in order + Connection refused: nothing was listening on that port - The server crashed in the middle of the conversation - A packet was lost and the handshake will be retried A RST in reply to a SYN means no program listens on that port; an orderly close uses FIN in both directions.

title: Following TCP conversations
body: Group captured TCP segments into conversations, rebuild each direction's byte stream the way "Follow TCP Stream" does, count retransmissions, and say how each connection ended (lesson 4.04). cpp constexpr std::uint8_t FIN{ 0x01 }, SYN{ 0x02 }, RST{ 0x04 }, PSH{ 0x08 }, ACK{ 0x10 }; struct Segment { std::uint32_t sourceIp; std::uint16_t sourcePort; std::uint32_t destinationIp; std::uint16_t destinationPort; std::uint32_t sequence; std::uint8_t flags; std::string data; }; class Tracker { public: void add(const Segment& s); std::size_t conversations() const; std::string stream(std::uint32_t fromIp, std::uint16_t fromPort, std::uint32_t toIp, std::uint16_t toPort) const; int retransmissions() const; std::string state(std::uint32_t ipA, std::uint16_t portA, std::uint32_t ipB, std::uint16_t portB) const; }; - A conversation is one pair of endpoints (address and port), whichever direction a segment goes. Each direction is tracked separately, by its sender. - A direction's initial sequence number comes from its first SYN. Data in a segment at sequence n belongs at stream offset n - (ISN + 1) , computed in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic so it works across the wrap from 0xFFFFFFFF to 0 . Data in the SYN itself, data from a direction whose SYN was not seen, and data that would reach past offset 1 << 24 (16 MiB) are ignored. - The first copy of each byte wins. A segment with data in which every byte had already arrived counts as one retransmission . - stream returns the bytes sent from the first endpoint to the second, from offset 0 up to the first gap; an unknown conversation gives "" . - state describes the conversation between the two endpoints, in either order: "none" if there is no such conversation; "refused" if a RST came from a side that never sent a SYN; "reset" for any other RST; "closed" if both sides sent a FIN; otherwise "open" .

title: 4.05  Reading Protocols in Captures
body: Going up the stack in a capture - DNS queries and answers over UDP, plain HTTP in a reassembled TCP stream, and TLS, where only the handshake is readable - the record layer, the ClientHello, and the server name in its SNI extension. DNS DNS messages travel in single UDP datagrams to and from port 53 (lesson 1.03). The 12-byte header: Offset Size Field --- --- --- 0 2 id: matches answers to questions 2 2 flags: the top bit ( QR ) is 0 for a query, 1 for a response; the low 4 bits are the response code (0 OK, 3 no such name) 4 2 number of questions 6 2 number of answers 8 2 number of authority records 10 2 number of additional records The question follows: a name in label format, a 2-byte type and a 2-byte class. Answers repeat the name (usually as a compression pointer back to the question), then type, class, a 4-byte TTL, a 2-byte data length and the data (4 bytes for an A record). In a capture, DNS tells you which names a program looked up and what it was told, often the first clue to what it is doing. HTTP Plain HTTP (port 80, or your own local server) is readable once the TCP stream is reassembled: the request line, headers and body of lesson 3.01, in clear text. That is also why it should not be used for anything private. TLS: only the handshake Almost all web traffic is HTTPS, and a capture shows its content only as encrypted application data . But the start of the handshake is readable, and it says a lot. TLS sends records : Offset Size Field --- --- --- 0 1 content type: 22 handshake, 23 application data, 21 alert 1 2 legacy version ( 03 01 or 03 03 ) 3 2 length of the record's data The first record from the client is a handshake record containing a ClientHello : Field Size --- --- handshake type 1 (1 = ClientHello) length 3 client version 2 random 32 session id 1-byte length, then that many bytes cipher suites 2-byte length, then 2 bytes per suite compression methods 1-byte length, then the methods extensions 2-byte length, then extensions: each a 2-byte type, 2-byte length, and data Extension type 0 is server name indication (lesson 3.05). Its data is a 2-byte list length, then entries of a 1-byte name type (0 = host name), a 2-byte length and the name. So from a capture you can learn, for each TLS connection, which hostname it was for, which versions and cipher suites the client offered, and the certificate the server sent (in TLS 1.2; TLS 1.3 encrypts it). This is how network monitoring tools label encrypted traffic, and why Encrypted Client Hello is being introduced. When it does not decode Real traffic is messier than tables: a ClientHello split across two TCP segments, records that span segments, protocols on unusual ports, QUIC traffic over UDP 443 that Wireshark decodes only partly. A robust decoder checks every length against the bytes actually available and reports "truncated" or "not this protocol" rather than reading past the end. The practice holds you to that. Check yourself quiz ? In a DNS header, how do you tell a query from a response? - By the number of answers: 0 means a query - By the id: responses use an odd id + By the top bit of the flags, QR: 0 for a query, 1 for a response - By the port: queries go to 53, responses come from 5353 A response can have zero answers (for example "no such name"), so only the QR bit is reliable. ? What does a TLS record with content type 23 contain? - A handshake message such as a ClientHello - An alert that closes the connection + Encrypted application data - The server's certificate in clear text Type 22 is handshake, 21 alert and 23 application data, which a capture cannot read. ? Where in a capture can you see which website an HTTPS connection was for? - In the Host header of the first HTTP request - In the destination IP address only - In the encrypted application data records + In the server name indication extension (type 0) of the ClientHello The Host header is encrypted; the SNI in the ClientHello is sent in clear text, unless Encrypted Client Hello is used. ? Why must a decoder check every length field against the bytes available? - Length fields are often given in 32-bit words rather than bytes - Checking lengths makes decoding faster + Captured data can be truncated or malformed, and trusting a length would read past the end - TLS lengths are encrypted and must be guessed Snapshot limits, split segments and hostile input all produce lengths that do not fit; a robust decoder reports "truncated" instead.

title: The server name in a TLS ClientHello
match: The server name in a TLS ClientHello
body: Read the first bytes a TLS client sends and find the version, the cipher suites it offers, and the hostname in its server name indication extension, checking every length on the way (lesson 4.05). cpp struct ClientHello { std::uint16_t version; std::vector<std::uint16_t cipherSuites; std::optional<std::string serverName; }; std::optional<ClientHello parseClientHello(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & stream); stream is the start of the client's reassembled TCP stream. Parse: 1. The record : content type 22 (handshake), a 2-byte version (ignored), a 2-byte length, and that many bytes. The ClientHello must be inside this one record; bytes after the record are ignored. 2. The handshake message : type 1 (ClientHello) and a 3-byte length; the message must fit in the record. 3. The ClientHello : a 2-byte version, 32 random bytes, a session id (1-byte length and bytes), cipher suites (2-byte length, then 2 bytes each: an odd length is an error) and compression methods (1-byte length and bytes). 4. The extensions , if any bytes are left in the message: a 2-byte total length, then extensions of a 2-byte type, a 2-byte length and that many bytes. In extension type 0, the data is a 2-byte list length and then entries of a 1-byte name type, a 2-byte length and the name. The first entry of name type 0 is the server name. Every length must fit inside whatever contains it: a field that runs past its record, message, extension list or extension makes the whole parse fail. A ClientHello with no server name succeeds with serverName empty.
