title: A packet dissector
body: Build a small tcpdump : give it a pcap file and it prints one line per packet, decoding Ethernet, IPv4, TCP, UDP and DNS, and saying plainly when a packet is truncated or malformed instead of reading past its end. cpp std::string dissect(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & frame); std::vector<std::string dissectFile(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & pcap); Ethernet. A frame shorter than 14 bytes is truncated . One VLAN tag ( 0x8100 ) is allowed, as in practice 4.02. Then, by EtherType: EtherType Line --- --- 0x0806 ARP 0x86DD IP6 next header N, length L , from the IPv6 header's next header and payload length; truncated if the 40-byte header does not fit 0x0800 the IPv4 rules below anything else ethertype 0x88cc, length 60 : four lower-case hex digits and the frame's size IPv4. If fewer than 20 bytes follow the Ethernet header, the line is truncated . If the version is not 4, the header length is under 20, or the total length is less than the header length, it is malformed . If the header is longer than the bytes available, truncated . Otherwise the IP data is the bytes after the header, up to the total length or the end of the captured frame, whichever comes first (a capture's snapshot length may have cut the packet short, and Ethernet padding is not data). L , the data length, is always total length - header length , whatever was captured. A and B below are the source and destination in dotted decimal, a and b the source and destination ports. Packet Line --- --- fragment offset not 0 IP A B: fragment offset O, length L , O in bytes TCP (6) IP A.a B.b: Flags F , seq S, ack K, win W, length P UDP (17) IP A.a B.b: UDP, length P , or a DNS summary ICMP (1) IP A B: ICMP, length L anything else IP A B: proto N, length L A packet whose IP header checksum is wrong still decodes, and its line ends with bad checksum . TCP. If fewer than 20 bytes of TCP header were captured: IP A B: truncated . If the TCP header length is under 20 or longer than L: IP A B: malformed . If the header (options included) was not all captured: IP A B: truncated . The flags are written as letters in the order S (SYN), F (FIN), R (RST), P (PSH), U (URG), then . for ACK, or none if there are none: so a SYN-ACK is S. . The , ack K part appears only when ACK is set. P is L - TCP header length . Only the headers need to have been captured, not the data. UDP. If fewer than 8 bytes were captured: IP A B: truncated . If the UDP length is under 8 or more than L: IP A.a B.b: malformed . P is UDP length - 8 . If either port is 53, try to read DNS from the UDP data (up to the UDP length or the end of what was captured): at least a 12-byte header, at least one question, and a question name made of plain labels (no compression pointers) followed by 4 bytes of type and class, all inside the data. The root name is written . . Then the line is IP A.a B.b: followed by: - DNS query NAME if the QR bit is 0; - DNS response NAME, no such name if the response code is 3; - otherwise DNS response NAME, 1 answer or DNS response NAME, N answers . If the DNS cannot be read, the line is the ordinary UDP, length P . dissectFile reads a pcap file in either byte order, with microsecond or nanosecond timestamps (practice 4.01). If the header is bad or the link type is not 1 (Ethernet), it returns no lines. For each complete record it adds T and the record's dissect line, where T is the time since the first packet as seconds with six decimals ( 0.750100 ; nanoseconds are cut to microseconds, and a time earlier than the first packet shows as 0.000000 ). An incomplete record at the end is left out.

title: 5.01  Why Games Use UDP
body: Why real-time games build their own protocol on UDP instead of using TCP - head-of-line blocking, the newest state making old data worthless - what a game protocol adds on top, virtual connections with timeouts, and testing under simulated loss and delay. TCP's promise is the problem TCP delivers every byte, in order. For a web page that is exactly right. For a game sending the player positions 30 or 60 times a second, it is a trap: - When one segment is lost, every later byte waits until the lost one is retransmitted, at least one round trip later, often more. Positions that arrived perfectly well sit in the receive buffer, unusable. This is head-of-line blocking , and it turns a single lost packet into a visible freeze. - The data being waited for is already out of date . By the time the position from 100 ms ago is resent, three newer positions exist. Nobody wants the old one. - TCP also slows down on loss (congestion control) and may combine small writes (Nagle's algorithm, disabled with TCP_NODELAY ), both of which add delay a game would rather not have. UDP delivers each datagram independently: some are lost, some are duplicated, some arrive out of order, but nothing waits for anything else. A game takes that and adds only what it needs. What a game protocol adds Over the next lessons you build the usual pieces: Piece Purpose Lesson --- --- --- sequence numbers tell newer from older packets, discard duplicates 5.02 acknowledgements learn which packets arrived, cheaply 5.03 round-trip time know how long to wait before resending 5.04 reliable messages the few things that must arrive (chat, "player joined", a purchase) 5.04 fragmentation send a block bigger than one packet 5.05 The key idea: most data is unreliable and newest-wins (positions, inputs, animation state), and only some messages need to be reliable. A game protocol lets each kind travel the way it needs. A virtual connection UDP has no connections, so the protocol makes its own: - Every packet starts with a protocol id (a fixed number such as a hash of the game name and version). Packets without it are dropped at once: stray traffic, port scanners, an old version of the game. - A connection is just "the address and port I hear from". The server keeps a table keyed by address and port. - Connecting uses a small handshake, often with a random salt from each side, so a forged source address cannot create a connection. Real games add encryption and a token from a login server. - Both sides send something at a steady rate (even an empty packet), and a connection that has heard nothing for a few seconds is timed out. There is no FIN: silence is how a UDP connection ends. Testing on a bad network A protocol that works on 127.0.0.1 with no loss proves nothing. Test with simulated conditions: - Latency : hold each packet for, say, 100 ms before delivering it. - Jitter : vary that delay, which also reorders packets. - Loss : drop a share of packets, 1 % to 10 % (and sometimes bursts). - Duplication : occasionally deliver a packet twice. You can put a simulator inside your own code between "send" and the socket, which makes the tests repeatable, or use tools such as clumsy on Windows or tc netem on Linux to degrade real traffic. Make the simulator deterministic (a fixed pattern or a seeded generator), so a failure can be repeated. Check yourself quiz ? What is head-of-line blocking? - A router holding packets back because its queue is full + One lost segment holding back later data that already arrived - TCP combining small writes into one segment before sending - The sender waiting for the receiver's window to open The later data is in the receive buffer but unusable until the gap is filled. Combining small writes is Nagle's algorithm, a different source of delay. ? Why is resending an old player position pointless? - UDP cannot resend a datagram once it has been lost - The receiver would reject it because of its checksum + Newer positions have been sent since, and only the latest state matters - Positions are too large to fit in a resent packet By the time an old position could be resent, several newer ones exist; that is why such data is sent unreliably, newest-wins. ? How does a UDP "connection" in a game protocol end? - With a FIN from each side, as in TCP - With a RST from the side that leaves - When the server's socket is closed and reopened + By timing out after hearing nothing for a few seconds UDP has no FIN; both sides send at a steady rate, so silence for a few seconds is how a connection is known to be gone. ? Why make the network simulator deterministic? + So a failing test loses the same packets every time and can be debugged - So the simulated loss rate never exceeds 10 % - So it runs faster than a random one - So the tests pass on 127.0.0.1 as well With a fixed pattern or seeded generator, a failure can be repeated exactly; random losses that change every run make bugs vanish when you look for them.

title: A deterministic bad network
body: Build the network simulator the rest of this milestone tests against (lesson 5.01): it delays packets, drops some and reorders others, always in the same way, so a failing test can be repeated. cpp class LinkSimulator { public: LinkSimulator(double latency, std::vector<bool dropPattern, std::vector<double extraDelay); void send(double now, const std::vector<std::uint8_t & packet); std::vector<std::vector<std::uint8_t receive(double now); std::size_t inFlight() const; int dropped() const; }; Number the packets passed to send from 0, counting dropped ones too. Packet k : - is dropped if dropPattern is not empty and dropPattern k % dropPattern.size() is true; - otherwise is delivered at now + latency + extra , where extra is extraDelay k % extraDelay.size() , or 0 if extraDelay is empty. receive(now) removes and returns every packet whose delivery time is at or before now , earliest delivery first; packets due at the same time come out in the order they were sent. inFlight is the number of packets waiting, and dropped the number dropped so far.

title: 5.02  Sequence Numbers That Wrap
body: Numbering packets with a small counter that wraps around - comparing sequence numbers correctly across the wrap with half-range arithmetic, the signed difference between two numbers, and discarding duplicates and stale packets with a sliding window. A number on every packet Every packet carries a sequence number that the sender increments each time. Receivers use it to tell which packet is newer, to drop duplicates, and (next lesson) to say which ones arrived. Bytes on the wire are precious, so the number is usually 16 bits . At 60 packets a second it wraps from 65 535 back to 0 every 18 minutes. Comparing with a plain a b fails at the wrap: packet 2 is newer than packet 65 534, though 2 < 65 534. Half-range comparison Treat the numbers as points on a circle. a is newer than b if going forward from b to a is less than half way round : cpp-norun bool sequenceGreater(std::uint16_t a, std::uint16_t b) { return (a b && a - b < 32768) (a < b && b - a 32768); } An equivalent and shorter form uses the signed difference: subtract in 16-bit unsigned arithmetic and reinterpret as a signed 16-bit number. cpp-norun int sequenceDifference(std::uint16_t a, std::uint16_t b) { return static_cast<std::int16_t (static_cast<std::uint16_t (a - b)); } cpp-norun sequenceDifference(5, 3) // 2: 5 is two packets newer sequenceDifference(2, 65534) // 4: across the wrap sequenceDifference(65534, 2) // -4 Exactly half way round (a difference of 32 768) is ambiguous; it never matters in practice because no protocol keeps that many packets in flight. This is the same "serial number arithmetic" TCP uses for its 32-bit sequence numbers (RFC 1982). Duplicates and stale packets Because UDP may duplicate and reorder, a receiver keeps a little history: - the latest sequence number seen so far; - which of the recent numbers before it have also been seen, usually as a bit per number for the last 32 to 256. When a packet arrives: Difference from latest Meaning Action --- --- --- positive newer than anything seen accept; slide the window forward zero, or already marked duplicate drop negative, inside the window late but new accept, mark it seen negative, beyond the window too old to judge drop For newest-wins data (positions), you can go further and ignore any packet older than the latest , since its state is stale anyway; reliable messages inside it must still be processed, which is why the decision belongs to each kind of data, not to the packet. Check yourself quiz ? Why does a b fail for sequence numbers? - Sequence numbers are signed, so large values become negative - Two packets can carry the same sequence number + After the counter wraps, a newer packet has a smaller number than an older one - Packets always arrive in reverse order over UDP A 16-bit counter wraps from 65 535 to 0, so packet 2 is newer than 65 534; half-range comparison handles that. ? What is sequenceDifference(1, 65535) ? - -65534 - 65534 - -2 + 2 Subtracting in 16-bit unsigned arithmetic gives 2, and as a signed 16-bit value that is still 2: packet 1 is two newer, across the wrap. ? A packet arrives whose number is 500 behind the latest, with a 256-number window. What happens? - It is accepted and marked as seen + It is dropped: it is too old to tell whether it is a duplicate - It becomes the new latest, because it is so far away - It is buffered until the window moves back The receiver only remembers the last 256 numbers, so it cannot tell whether a packet older than that was already seen. ? Why might a game drop a late position update but still read the chat message in the same packet? - Chat messages have their own checksum that is still valid - Late packets lose their position data in transit - Chat messages always arrive before positions + Positions are newest-wins, so old ones are useless, but each chat message must be delivered Whether old data is useful depends on the kind of data, not on the packet, so the decision is made per kind.

title: Wrapping sequence numbers
body: Compare 16-bit sequence numbers across the wrap and filter out duplicates and stale packets (lesson 5.02). cpp int sequenceDifference(std::uint16_t a, std::uint16_t b); bool sequenceGreater(std::uint16_t a, std::uint16_t b); class DuplicateFilter { public: bool accept(std::uint16_t sequence); std::optional<std::uint16_t latest() const; }; - sequenceDifference is a - b computed in 16 bits and read as a signed 16-bit number: from -32768 to 32767. - sequenceGreater is true when a is newer than b : their difference is positive. (Exactly half way round counts as greater in neither direction.) - DuplicateFilter remembers the latest sequence number accepted and which of the 256 numbers ending at it (latest - 255 to latest) have been seen. accept returns true and records the number if it has not been seen: the first number ever, a newer one (which becomes the latest), or an older one inside the window that is not yet marked. It returns false for a number already seen or one 256 or more behind the latest. latest is empty until something is accepted.

title: 5.03  Acknowledgement Bitfields
body: Telling the sender which packets arrived without sending a packet per acknowledgement - the latest received number plus a 32-bit field for the ones before it, why the redundancy survives loss, and how the sender turns acks into "delivered" events. Acknowledging cheaply TCP acknowledges bytes cumulatively and retransmits itself. A game protocol wants something different: the sender should simply learn which packets arrived , so it can decide what, if anything, to resend. And since both sides are sending packets all the time anyway, acknowledgements ride along in the header of every packet ( piggybacking ) instead of getting packets of their own. The usual header: Field Size Meaning --- --- --- sequence 16 bits this packet's number ack 16 bits the most recent sequence number received from the other side ackBits 32 bits bit i set means packet ack - 1 - i was also received So every packet acknowledges 33 packets at once. Redundancy beats loss Suppose the other side receives packets 100 to 140 except 137. Its next packets all say: text ack = 140, ackBits: bit 2 clear (137 missing), every other bit of the 32 set It sends this many times a second. Even if most of its packets are lost, any one that gets through tells you the whole story of the last 33 packets. An acknowledgement is lost for good only if the other side's packets are lost for more than about half a second in a row at 60 packets a second, and by then the connection is in trouble anyway. The receiving side Keep latest and bits . When a packet with sequence s arrives (using d = sequenceDifference(s, latest) from lesson 5.02): - d 0 : the new latest is s . The old latest becomes bit d - 1 , and every old bit moves up by d (bits shifted past 31 are forgotten). If d 32 , the old history is gone completely. - d < 0 : set bit -d - 1 , if it is below 32. - d == 0 : a duplicate; nothing changes. Watch out for shifting a 32-bit value by 32 or more: in C++ that is undefined behaviour, so handle d = 32 separately or shift a 64-bit value. The sending side The sender remembers what it put in each packet it sent (a ring buffer of the last few hundred, indexed by sequence % size ). When an ack and ackBits arrive, it walks the 33 numbers they cover. Each that is marked received and was not acknowledged before becomes a "delivered" event: - reliable messages in that packet are done and need no resending; - the time between sending and the ack is a round-trip sample (next lesson); - a packet still unacknowledged long after newer ones were acked was almost certainly lost . Each packet must produce its "delivered" event once , though it will be acknowledged by dozens of incoming packets. Check yourself quiz ? With ack = 200 and only bit 0 of ackBits set, which packets were received? - Only 200 - 200 and 201 + 200 and 199 - 199 only Bit i stands for packet ack - 1 - i , so bit 0 is 199; ack itself, 200, is always received. ? Why put acknowledgements in every packet instead of sending separate ack packets? - Separate ack packets are not allowed over UDP + Both sides send constantly, so acks ride along for a few bytes - Acks must travel in the same packet as the data they acknowledge - It lets the receiver retransmit lost packets itself Piggybacked acks cost only a few header bytes, and since every packet repeats the last 33, losing some of them does no harm: any one that arrives tells the whole story. ? The latest is 50 and packet 90 arrives. What happens to the bits? - They shift up by 40, so the bit for 50 becomes bit 39 - They stay as they are, because 90 is too far ahead - Only bit 0 is set, for packet 89 + They all become 0, since a jump of 40 is more than 32 bits Every old bit falls off, including the one for 50, which would be bit 39, beyond the 32-bit field. Shifting a 32-bit value by 32 or more is undefined, so this case is handled separately. ? Why must the sender remember which packets were already acknowledged? + Each packet is acked many times but is delivered only once - Acknowledged packets must be sent again to confirm the ack - The receiver needs the sender to repeat its acks back - Otherwise the sequence numbers would wrap too soon Every incoming packet repeats the last 33 acks; without remembering, the same delivery would be counted again and again.

title: Acks with a bitfield
body: Build both halves of piggybacked acknowledgements (lesson 5.03): the receiver's ack and ackBits , and the sender's "which of my packets were delivered". cpp class ReceivedPackets { public: void record(std::uint16_t sequence); std::uint16_t ack() const; std::uint32_t ackBits() const; }; class SentPackets { public: void sent(std::uint16_t sequence); std::vector<std::uint16_t onAck(std::uint16_t ack, std::uint32_t ackBits); }; ReceivedPackets. Before anything is recorded, ack is 0 and ackBits is 0. The first recorded number becomes the ack with no bits. After that, with d the signed difference between the new number and the current ack (practice 5.02): - d 0 : the new number becomes the ack; the old ack becomes bit d - 1 and every old bit moves up by d ; bits that would pass bit 31 are dropped; - d < 0 : set bit -d - 1 if it is below 32, otherwise ignore the number; - d == 0 : nothing changes. SentPackets remembers every sequence number passed to sent that has not yet been acknowledged. onAck looks at ack and at ack - 1 - i for each set bit i ; each of those still waiting is now acknowledged and stops waiting. It returns them oldest first (the one furthest behind ack first, ack last), and a packet is never returned twice. Sending the same number again (after the counter wraps) makes it wait again.

title: 5.04  Round Trips and Resending
body: Measuring how long a round trip takes and smoothing it, the retransmission timeout from RFC 6298 with backoff and Karn's rule, and building reliable ordered messages on top of unreliable packets - message ids, resending until acknowledged, and delivering in order. Measuring the round trip The time from sending a packet to receiving its acknowledgement is a round-trip time (RTT) sample. Single samples are noisy (the other side may wait a few milliseconds before sending its next packet), so protocols keep a smoothed estimate. TCP's method, from RFC 6298, works well for games too: text first sample R: srtt = R rttvar = R / 2 each later R: rttvar = 3/4 · rttvar + 1/4 · srtt - R srtt = 7/8 · srtt + 1/8 · R timeout: rto = srtt + 4 · rttvar (clamped to a minimum and maximum) srtt is the smoothed RTT, the number to show the player as "ping". rttvar measures how much it varies; adding four times it to the timeout means a slow-but-normal round trip is not mistaken for a loss. - Before any sample, use a safe initial timeout (TCP uses 1 second). - When a timeout fires and you resend, double the timeout (exponential backoff ), up to the maximum, so a broken connection is not flooded. The next real sample resets it. - Karn's rule : never take a sample from something that was resent, because you cannot tell whether the ack is for the first copy or the second. With per-packet acks (lesson 5.03) this is easy: each packet is sent once, and only resent messages travel in new packets. Reliable messages Some things must arrive: chat, "you picked up the key", a match result. On top of unreliable packets: 1. Give each reliable message an increasing message id (16 bits, compared as in lesson 5.02). 2. Keep it in a send queue until it is acknowledged. 3. Each time you build a packet, include queued messages that were never sent , or were sent longer ago than the timeout . Remember which message ids went into which packet. 4. When the packet is acknowledged (lesson 5.03), the messages in it are done: remove them from the queue. On the receiving side: - Messages may arrive out of order (a resent message overtakes nothing, but a later one may arrive first) and more than once. - Keep the id of the next message to deliver . A message with that id is delivered at once, followed by any buffered ones that now follow it. A later id is buffered. An earlier id is a duplicate and is dropped. If order does not matter (each message independent), deliver immediately and only drop duplicates: that avoids one lost message holding back the others, the same head-of-line problem as TCP but chosen only where it is needed. Many games run several channels : unreliable, reliable unordered and reliable ordered. Resending is expensive Every resend uses bandwidth that newer data could have used. Keep reliable messages small and rare, send state (positions) unreliably, and if something important is large, send it once reliably and then send changes. The next lesson deals with sizes. Check yourself quiz ? The first RTT sample is 80 ms. What are srtt, rttvar and the timeout? - srtt 80 ms, rttvar 0 ms, timeout 80 ms - srtt 80 ms, rttvar 80 ms, timeout 400 ms + srtt 80 ms, rttvar 40 ms, timeout 240 ms - srtt 10 ms, rttvar 20 ms, timeout 90 ms The first sample sets srtt = R and rttvar = R / 2, so rto = 80 + 4 x 40 = 240 ms before clamping. ? Why add 4 × rttvar to the timeout rather than using srtt alone? - So the timeout is always at least one second - So the timeout doubles after every resend + So a normal but slower-than-average round trip is not treated as a loss - So the ping shown to the player is more accurate Half of all round trips are slower than the average; a margin based on the variation stops them triggering needless resends. ? What does Karn's rule say? - Double the timeout after each resend + Do not take an RTT sample from anything that was retransmitted - Resend a message at most three times - Take an RTT sample from every acknowledgement After a resend you cannot tell whether the ack is for the first copy or the second, so the sample would be wrong. Doubling the timeout is backoff, a separate rule. ? A receiver expecting message 10 receives 12, then 10. What is delivered and when? - 12 at once, then 10 when it arrives - Nothing until 11 arrives, then 10, 11 and 12 together - 10 and 12 together when 10 arrives + Nothing at 12 (it is buffered); at 10, message 10 is delivered, and 12 waits for 11 Ordered delivery hands over the next expected id plus any buffered ones that follow it; 12 does not follow 10, so it waits.

title: Round-trip time and the resend timeout
match: Round-trip time and the resend timeout
body: Estimate the round-trip time and the retransmission timeout the way RFC 6298 does (lesson 5.04). cpp class RttEstimator { public: RttEstimator(double minRto, double maxRto); void sample(double rtt); double srtt() const; double rttvar() const; double rto() const; void backoff(); }; - Before any sample, srtt and rttvar are 0 and rto is 1000 (milliseconds), clamped to minRto, maxRto . - The first sample R sets srtt = R and rttvar = R / 2 . - Each later sample sets rttvar = 0.75 rttvar + 0.25 srtt - R (using the old srtt ), then srtt = 0.875 srtt + 0.125 R . - After every sample, rto = srtt + 4 rttvar , clamped to minRto, maxRto . - backoff doubles rto , up to maxRto . The next sample replaces the backed-off value.

title: 5.05  Fragmentation and Bandwidth
body: Keeping packets under the path MTU, why IP fragmentation is avoided, splitting large blocks into fragments and reassembling them with ids, counts and timeouts, budgeting bandwidth per connection, and choosing what to send when it does not all fit. How big can a packet be? An Ethernet frame carries 1 500 bytes of IP packet (lesson 1.01). Paths through tunnels, VPNs and mobile networks carry less. If a UDP datagram is too big, IP fragments it, and then: - losing any fragment loses the whole datagram, so the loss rate multiplies; - some routers and firewalls drop fragments altogether; - with IPv6, routers do not fragment at all. So games keep every datagram under a safe size, typically 1 200 bytes of payload (the same limit QUIC uses), and split large data themselves. Your own fragments To send a block larger than one packet (a map, a full snapshot, a file), split it into fragments , each sent in its own packet with a small header: Field Size Meaning --- --- --- block id 16 bits which block this belongs to fragment index 8 bits 0 to count - 1 fragment count 8 bits how many fragments the block has The receiver keeps a reassembly buffer per block id: which fragments have arrived and their bytes. When all count are there, the block is complete. Rules that make it robust: - Check everything : index below count, count above zero, the same count in every fragment of a block, a fragment size within limits. A wrong value is a dropped packet, never an out-of-range write. - Ignore duplicates of fragments already present. - Time out incomplete blocks, and limit how many are in progress, so a lost fragment or a malicious sender cannot use up memory. - If the block must arrive, either resend the missing fragments (using acks) or resend the whole block reliably. A neat scheme is to make each fragment a reliable message. A bandwidth budget A connection cannot send as much as it likes: the player's upload may be a few hundred kilobits per second, and a server sends to many players. Decide a budget per connection, for example 256 kbit/s, which at 60 packets a second is about 530 bytes per packet. When everything does not fit: - Give each kind of data a priority . Things that have not been sent for a while gain priority (an accumulator : each tick, add each object's priority to its score; send the highest scores; reset the score of what was sent). Far-away objects get a lower priority, so they update less often but are never starved. - Send reliable messages first, but cap them so they cannot crowd out state entirely. - Watch round-trip time and loss: when they climb, the path is congested. Sending less (fewer packets a second, or smaller ones) is kinder to the network and usually improves the game, too. Check yourself quiz ? Why not let IP fragment large UDP datagrams? - IP fragmentation changes the order of the bytes - Fragmented datagrams cannot carry a checksum + Losing any one fragment loses the whole datagram - IP fragments are always sent over TCP Fragmentation multiplies the loss rate; some networks also drop fragments, and IPv6 routers do not fragment at all. So games keep datagrams under about 1200 bytes and split data themselves. ? A fragment says index 7, count 5. What should the receiver do? - Grow the block's buffer to 8 fragments - Store it and wait for the count to be corrected + Drop it: the index must be below the count - Treat it as the last fragment of the block A value out of range is a dropped packet, never an out-of-range write; indexes run from 0 to count - 1. ? Why do incomplete blocks need a timeout? + A lost fragment, or a malicious sender, would otherwise keep reassembly buffers in memory forever - The block id would otherwise wrap around too soon - Fragments become corrupt if kept too long - The sender needs the timeout to know when to send the next block Without timeouts and a limit on blocks in progress, memory can be used up by blocks that will never complete. ? What does a priority accumulator guarantee that plain priorities do not? - That high-priority objects are sent in every packet - That every object is sent at the same rate - That reliable messages are never delayed + That low-priority objects are still sent eventually Each tick adds an object's priority to its score and sending resets it, so far-away objects update less often but are never starved.

title: Splitting and reassembling blocks
body: Send blocks larger than one packet as fragments, and put them back together safely on the other side (lesson 5.05). cpp struct Fragment { std::uint16_t block; std::uint8_t index; std::uint8_t count; std::vector<std::uint8_t data; }; std::vector<Fragment split(std::uint16_t block, const std::vector<std::uint8_t & data, std::size_t maxFragment); class Reassembler { public: explicit Reassembler(double timeout); std::optional<std::vector<std::uint8_t add(const Fragment& f, double now); void expire(double now); std::size_t pending() const; }; split cuts data into pieces of maxFragment bytes (the last may be shorter), numbered from 0, each knowing the total count. Empty data is one empty fragment. If maxFragment is 0 or more than 255 fragments would be needed, it returns no fragments. Reassembler keeps the blocks in progress, keyed by block id. add first calls expire(now) , then: - drops the fragment (returning nothing and changing nothing) if its count is 0, its index is not below its count, its data is longer than 1200 bytes, or a block with the same id is in progress with a different count; - ignores a fragment whose index has already arrived for that block; - starts a new block if none is in progress with that id, unless 16 blocks are already in progress, in which case the fragment is dropped; a block's timer starts with its first fragment; - when a block has all its fragments, removes it and returns its data in index order. expire(now) removes every block whose first fragment arrived more than timeout before now . pending is the number of blocks in progress.

title: A reliable channel over unreliable packets
match: A reliable channel over unreliable packets
body: Build the reliability layer of a game protocol: one endpoint of a connection that sends a packet every tick, acknowledges the other side's packets with a bitfield, and carries reliable, ordered messages that are resent until they are known to have arrived. The tests connect two endpoints through a link that loses, delays and repeats packets, and check that every message arrives once and in order. cpp class ReliableEndpoint { public: explicit ReliableEndpoint(double resendAfter); bool send(const std::string& message); std::vector<std::uint8_t update(double now); void receive(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & packet); std::vector<std::string take(); std::size_t unacked() const; }; The packet (all numbers big-endian): Bytes Field --- --- 0-1 sequence 2-3 ack 4-7 ack bits 8 message count then, per message message id (2 bytes), length (2 bytes), the bytes Sending. send queues a message, giving it the next message id (0, 1, 2 ..., wrapping at 65 536), and returns true; a message longer than 1 000 bytes is refused with false. unacked is the number of queued messages not yet acknowledged. update(now) builds and returns exactly one packet, every time it is called, even with no messages in it: - its sequence number is the next one (0 for the first packet, then 1, 2, ...); - ack and ack bits describe the packets received from the other side, exactly as in practice 5.03; before any packet has been received they are 65 535 and 0 (the other side's numbers start at 0, so this acknowledges nothing); - it then goes through the queue in id order and includes each message that has never been sent, or was last sent resendAfter or more before now . It stops at the first such message that would make the packet larger than 1 200 bytes, or when the packet already holds 255 messages. Each included message is marked as sent at now ; - it remembers which messages went into this sequence number. Receiving. receive first checks the whole packet: at least 9 bytes, every message fits, and nothing is left over. A malformed packet is ignored completely. Otherwise: 1. Record its sequence number for your own acks (practice 5.03). 2. Read its ack and ack bits . Each of your packets they acknowledge for the first time is delivered: every message in it is acknowledged and leaves the queue (it may be in several packets; the first ack is enough). 3. Deliver its messages in order: keep the id of the next message to deliver (starting at 0). A message whose id is that one or up to 1 023 after it (by the signed difference of practice 5.02) is buffered if it is not already; anything else is a duplicate or nonsense and is dropped. Then, as long as the next id is buffered, move it to the delivered list and advance. take returns the messages delivered since the last call, in order, and clears that list.

title: 6.01  The Authoritative Server
body: How multiplayer games are organised - the server owns the truth and clients send only inputs, why that is the basis of fair play, the fixed tick with an accumulator, tick numbers as the shared clock, and choosing tick and send rates. Who decides what happened? In a multiplayer game, several machines each run a copy of the world, and their copies drift apart: messages take time, packets are lost, clocks differ. Someone has to decide what really happened. Almost every modern action game uses an authoritative server : - The server runs the real simulation. Its state is the truth. - Clients send only their inputs ("move left, jump, fire at this angle"), never results ("I am now here", "I hit him for 100"). - The server applies the inputs, simulates, and sends the resulting state back to every client, which shows it. This is also the foundation of fair play: a modified client can send odd inputs, but it cannot declare that it teleported or that its shot hit. The server validates every input : movement is limited to what the rules allow (a move vector longer than 1 is clamped, not trusted), a player cannot fire faster than the weapon allows, and actions are checked against the server's own state. The alternatives have their places: peer-to-peer lockstep (every machine runs the same deterministic simulation from everyone's inputs, common in strategy games with thousands of units) and client authority for casual cooperative games where cheating does not matter. This milestone builds the server-authoritative model. The tick The server simulates in fixed steps called ticks , for example 60 per second (a step of 16.67 ms) or 20 to 30 for slower games. Fixed steps make physics stable and the simulation reproducible: the same inputs give the same results. Real time does not arrive in neat steps, so a loop accumulates elapsed time and runs as many ticks as fit: cpp-norun accumulator += elapsed; while (accumulator = step) { simulateOneTick(); accumulator -= step; } alpha = accumulator / step; // how far we are towards the next tick, for smooth drawing If the machine falls far behind (a long pause, a debugger stop), running hundreds of ticks to catch up makes things worse: each slow frame causes even more ticks the next frame. Cap the ticks per frame and drop the rest of the backlog. Clients run the same loop, drawing with alpha to blend between the last two simulated states, so motion is smooth on a 144 Hz screen while the simulation runs at 60. Tick numbers are the clock Every snapshot the server sends carries its tick number , and every input a client sends carries a sequence number (and often the tick it was made for). These numbers, not wall-clock times, are how the two sides talk about time: - "This snapshot is the world at tick 4 512." - "The last input of yours I applied was number 917." - "When you fired, you were seeing the world at tick 4 505." (lesson 6.05) Tick rate and send rate The server need not send a snapshot every tick. Typical choices: simulate at 60, send snapshots at 20 to 60, and clients send inputs every tick (often several inputs per packet, for redundancy against loss, as in milestone 5). Higher rates feel more responsive and cost bandwidth and server CPU per player; many games pick 30 or 64 and tune from there. Check yourself quiz ? Why do clients send inputs rather than positions? - Inputs are smaller, and bandwidth is the only concern - The server cannot read floating-point positions + So a client cannot simply claim where it is or what it hit - Positions would arrive out of order, but inputs never do With an authoritative server, clients only say what they want to do; the server's simulation decides what actually happened, which is the basis of fair play. ? A client sends a movement vector of length 3. What should the server do? - Apply it as sent, since the client knows its own input + Clamp it to the allowed maximum (length 1) - Divide it by the tick rate before applying it - Ask the client to send it again Input values are never trusted as they arrive; anything beyond what the rules allow is clamped or rejected. ? Why cap the number of ticks run in one frame? - So the simulation runs at exactly the same rate as the screen - So the accumulator never becomes negative - So that snapshots are sent once per frame + To avoid a spiral where catching up takes so long that the next frame falls even further behind After a long pause, running hundreds of catch-up ticks makes each frame slower still; capping them and dropping the backlog breaks the spiral. ? What does alpha in the accumulator loop represent? + How far the time is between the last tick and the next - The number of ticks run this frame - The time the last tick took to simulate - The share of packets that arrived this frame alpha = accumulator / step is a fraction from 0 to 1, letting a 144 Hz screen draw smoothly between two 60 Hz simulation states.

title: The fixed tick and input checks
match: The fixed tick and input checks
body: Write the two pieces every authoritative server starts with (lesson 6.01): a fixed-timestep accumulator that never spirals, and a check that keeps movement input inside the rules. cpp class FixedStep { public: FixedStep(std::int64_t step, int maxSteps); int advance(std::int64_t elapsed); double alpha() const; std::int64_t ticks() const; std::int64_t dropped() const; }; std::pair<float, float clampMove(float x, float y); Times are whole microseconds, so the arithmetic is exact. - advance adds elapsed (a negative value counts as 0) to the accumulator and returns how many ticks to run now: the number of whole steps in the accumulator, which it removes. If that is more than maxSteps , it returns maxSteps and throws away the extra whole steps too, keeping only the remainder below one step; the time thrown away is added to dropped . - alpha is the accumulator divided by the step, from 0 up to (not including) 1. - ticks is the total number of ticks returned so far. - clampMove returns a move vector a server can trust: if either part is not finite (infinity or NaN) the move is (0, 0) ; if its length is more than 1 it is scaled down to length 1; otherwise it is returned unchanged.

title: 6.02  Snapshots and Delta Compression
body: Sending the world to clients efficiently - what goes in a snapshot, quantising floats into a few bits, sending only what changed against a baseline the client has acknowledged, change masks, and what happens when packets are lost. A snapshot A snapshot is the server's world state at one tick, as one client needs to see it: for each relevant entity, an id and the fields that matter (position, angle, health, animation). Sending it all, every time, is simple and robust: each snapshot stands alone, so a lost one does not matter. It is also big. Thirty players with 20 bytes each is 600 bytes, times 60 snapshots a second, times 30 clients: over 8 Mbit/s of upload for one server. Two techniques shrink it dramatically. Quantisation A float is 4 bytes with far more precision than a game needs. If the map is 0 to 1 000 units wide, storing the position as a 16-bit integer gives steps of 1 000 / 65 535 ≈ 0.015 units, invisible on screen: cpp-norun std::uint16_t quantize(float v, float min, float max) { const float t{ (std::clamp(v, min, max) - min) / (max - min) }; return static_cast<std::uint16_t (std::lround(t 65535.0f)); } float dequantize(std::uint16_t q, float min, float max) { return min + (max - min) (q / 65535.0f); } The same idea everywhere: an angle in 8 or 10 bits, health as a byte, a boolean as a single bit. The error is at most half a step. Crucially, the server simulates with the quantised values too (or rounds its state the same way), so client and server agree exactly on what was sent. Delta compression Most of the world does not change from one snapshot to the next: a player standing still, a door that is closed. So send only the difference against a snapshot the client already has: - The client acknowledges the snapshots it receives (milestone 5's acks). - The server keeps the last few dozen snapshots per client and encodes each new one against the latest one the client acknowledged , the baseline . - For each entity it writes the id and a change mask , one bit per field, followed by only the fields whose bit is set. Unchanged entities are left out entirely; new entities have every bit set; removed ones get a "removed" marker. The client reconstructs the new snapshot by copying the baseline and applying the changes. A typical scene shrinks from hundreds of bytes to tens. When packets are lost Delta compression against an acknowledged baseline stays correct under loss: if snapshots 101 to 103 are lost, the server simply keeps encoding against 100 (the last one acknowledged) until a newer one is acknowledged. Deltas grow a little while packets are being lost, and shrink again once acks get through. What must never happen is encoding against a snapshot the client might not have. Then the client applies changes to the wrong base and its world is silently wrong. If there is no usable baseline (a new client, or a baseline too old to keep), send a full snapshot. Check yourself quiz ? A map is 0 to 4 096 units wide and positions use 16 bits. What is the step size? - About 0.015 units + About 0.06 units - About 0.25 units - Exactly 1 unit 4 096 / 65 535 is roughly 0.0625 units. 0.015 is the step for a 1 000-unit map. ? Why should the server simulate with quantised values? - Quantised values are faster to simulate with - Floats cannot be sent over UDP - It halves the size of the server's memory + So the client's rebuilt state matches the server's exactly If the server kept full precision, the client's dequantised values would differ slightly from the truth, and the two would disagree. ? Why encode against the last acknowledged snapshot rather than the last one sent? - The last one sent is always larger than the acknowledged one - Acknowledged snapshots are stored on the client in compressed form + The last one sent might have been lost, while the acknowledged one is known to be on the client - The client can only decode deltas that are exactly one snapshot apart Applying changes to a baseline the client does not have would leave its world silently wrong; an acknowledged baseline is safe under loss. ? What does an entity look like in a delta if it has not changed? - Its id with every bit of the change mask set - Its id with an empty change mask and all its fields - A "removed" marker + It is not included at all Unchanged entities are left out entirely; new ones have every bit set and removed ones get a marker.

title: Quantised snapshots and deltas
body: Shrink snapshots the way lesson 6.02 describes: quantise floats into 16 bits, and encode a snapshot as the changes from a baseline the client already has. cpp struct Entity { std::uint16_t id; std::uint16_t x; std::uint16_t y; std::uint8_t angle; std::uint8_t health; }; std::uint16_t quantize(float value, float min, float max); float dequantize(std::uint16_t q, float min, float max); std::vector<std::uint8_t encodeDelta(const std::vector<Entity & baseline, const std::vector<Entity & current); std::optional<std::vector<Entity decodeDelta(const std::vector<Entity & baseline, const std::vector<std::uint8_t & delta); Quantising. quantize clamps the value to min, max , maps it to 0..65 535 and rounds to the nearest integer (halves away from zero, as std::lround does); NaN gives 0. dequantize maps back: min + (max - min) q / 65535 . The delta format. Snapshots are lists of entities sorted by id, each id once. A delta is a 2-byte entry count, then the entries in increasing id order, each a 2-byte id, a 1-byte mask , and the fields the mask names, in this order (all numbers big-endian): Mask bit Field --- --- 0x01 x, 2 bytes 0x02 y, 2 bytes 0x04 angle, 1 byte 0x08 health, 1 byte 0x80 removed, alone, with no fields encodeDelta writes one entry for each id that is in current but differs from the baseline (only the changed fields), each id new in current (mask 0x0F ), and each id in the baseline missing from current (mask 0x80 ). Unchanged entities are left out. decodeDelta starts from the baseline and applies the entries, returning the new snapshot sorted by id. It fails if the data is truncated or has bytes left over, the ids are not strictly increasing, a mask is 0 or uses other bits, a removal is combined with other bits or names an id not in the baseline, or an entry for an id not in the baseline is not a full 0x0F .

title: 6.03  Interpolation
body: Making other players move smoothly from snapshots that arrive 20 to 60 times a second with jitter and loss - rendering a little in the past, blending between the two snapshots around the render time, the size of the delay, and limited extrapolation. The problem Snapshots arrive 20 to 60 times a second, unevenly (jitter), and some are lost. If a client simply placed every other player at the position from the latest snapshot, they would jump from point to point, stutter when a snapshot arrived late, and freeze when one was lost. Render in the past The standard answer is entity interpolation : show other entities slightly in the past, at renderTime = now - delay , and blend between the two snapshots on either side of that time. text snapshots: t=100 t=150 t=200 t=250 ^ renderTime = 175 position = snapshot150 + (snapshot200 - snapshot150) · (175 - 150) / (200 - 150) Because the render time is behind the newest snapshot, the client usually already holds the snapshot after it, so it can always blend smoothly. The delay is chosen to cover the gap between snapshots plus some jitter, typically two snapshot intervals : about 100 ms at 20 snapshots a second (Counter-Strike's long-standing default), less at higher rates. If one snapshot is lost, the client blends across the wider gap and nobody notices. The cost is that other players are seen where they were about 100 ms ago, plus half the round trip. That is why the next two lessons exist: prediction for your own player, lag compensation for hitting others. Times and buffers - Use the server's tick numbers (or times derived from them), not the time each snapshot happened to arrive: arrival times include jitter, which is exactly what interpolation is meant to hide. - Keep a short buffer of recent snapshots per entity, sorted by time, and drop ones older than the render time needs. - Ignore a snapshot older than the newest one held: it arrived out of order and adds nothing. - Clients keep their idea of "now in server ticks" by tracking the latest snapshot tick and advancing it with their own clock, nudging it gently when snapshots arrive earlier or later than expected. When snapshots stop If the render time passes the newest snapshot (several are lost in a row), there is nothing to blend towards. Options: - Hold the last position: safe, but the entity freezes. - Extrapolate from the last two snapshots' velocity for a short time (dead reckoning), then hold. A little extrapolation hides a short gap; a lot shows players running into walls and snapping back when the truth arrives. Limit it to about one snapshot interval. Interpolate other values the same way: angles (taking the short way round), animation times. Discrete values (alive or dead, which weapon) simply switch when the render time passes their snapshot. Check yourself quiz ? Why render other players in the past? + So the client already has snapshots on both sides of the render time and can blend smoothly - Because the server sends snapshots in reverse order - So that the shooter's hits are tested against the right positions - Because the client's clock always runs behind the server's Rendering about two snapshot intervals behind means the snapshot after the render time has usually arrived, hiding jitter and the odd lost snapshot. ? With snapshots at 20 per second, what delay is typical? - About 20 ms - About 50 ms, one snapshot interval + About 100 ms, two snapshot intervals - About 1 second Two intervals cover the gap between snapshots plus some jitter, so one lost snapshot is blended across without anyone noticing. ? Why use the server's tick numbers instead of arrival times? - Arrival times are not available to the client - Tick numbers take fewer bytes in each snapshot - The client's clock cannot measure milliseconds + Arrival times include jitter; ticks are the states' real times Interpolation exists to hide jitter; timing snapshots by their arrival would put the jitter straight back. ? Why limit extrapolation? - Extrapolation needs at least three snapshots + Guesses go wrong fast and snap back when real data arrives - Extrapolating uses too much bandwidth - The server forbids clients from extrapolating A short extrapolation hides a small gap; a long one shows players running into walls and snapping back, so it is capped at about one interval.

title: An interpolation buffer
body: Show a remote player smoothly from irregular snapshots by rendering a fixed delay in the past and blending between snapshots (lesson 6.03). cpp struct Snapshot { double time; double x; double y; }; class Interpolator { public: Interpolator(double delay, double maxExtrapolation); void add(const Snapshot& s); std::optional<std::pair<double, double positionAt(double now) const; std::size_t buffered() const; }; - add stores a snapshot unless its time is not newer than the newest one already stored (an out-of-order arrival), keeping at most the 32 newest. - positionAt renders at t = now - delay : - with no snapshots, there is no position; - at or before the oldest snapshot, the oldest position; - between two stored snapshots, the straight-line blend of the two around t ; - after the newest snapshot: with only one snapshot, its position; otherwise continue at the velocity between the two newest snapshots for t - newest time , but for no longer than maxExtrapolation , then hold there. - buffered is the number of snapshots stored.

title: 6.04  Prediction and Reconciliation
body: Hiding latency for your own player - running your inputs immediately with the same simulation code as the server, keeping the inputs not yet confirmed, and when the server's state arrives, resetting to it and replaying the rest; plus smoothing corrections and what cannot be predicted. The delay you feel With a pure authoritative server, pressing a key does nothing until the input reaches the server, is simulated, and the result comes back: a full round trip, 50 to 150 ms. Movement feels like wading through syrup. Client-side prediction The client already knows its own inputs and has the same movement code as the server. So it applies each input immediately to its own player and shows the result, without waiting: 1. Make an input, give it the next sequence number, and send it to the server. 2. Simulate it locally at once, exactly as the server will. 3. Keep it in a list of pending inputs: sent, but not yet confirmed. When nothing unexpected happens, the server computes exactly the same positions a round trip later, and the prediction was perfect. Reconciliation Each snapshot tells the client its player's authoritative state and the sequence number of the last input the server applied . That state is in the past: inputs sent since then are still on their way. So the client: 1. Drops pending inputs with sequence numbers up to the last applied one: they are confirmed. 2. Resets its player to the authoritative state. 3. Replays the remaining pending inputs on top of it, with the same simulation. The result is the present again, now based on the truth. If the prediction was right, nothing visibly changes. If something the client could not know happened (another player pushed it, the server rejected a move, an explosion knocked it back), the replay starts from the corrected state and the player ends up where they really are. text client predicted: inputs 1..10 applied, at x = 100 snapshot arrives: server applied up to 7, x = 70 (no surprises) reconcile: drop 1..7, reset to 70, replay 8, 9, 10 → x = 100 (no change) snapshot arrives: server applied up to 7, x = 40 (hit by something at input 5) reconcile: drop 1..7, reset to 40, replay 8, 9, 10 → x = 70 (correction of -30) Making it work well - Same code, same results. The client must run exactly the server's movement code with the same inputs and tick length, and ideally the same quantisation (lesson 6.02). Any difference shows as constant small corrections. - Smooth the corrections. Instead of snapping the camera, move the displayed position towards the corrected one over a few frames, while the simulated position snaps at once. - Ignore old snapshots. A snapshot that confirms fewer inputs than one already applied arrived out of order: drop it. - Predict only what is yours. Your movement and your weapon's animation are predicted. Other players are interpolated (lesson 6.03), and anything that decides the game, such as hits, damage and pickups, waits for the server. Check yourself quiz ? What does the server need to include for reconciliation to work? - Only the player's authoritative position - The positions of every other player + Its state and the number of the last input it applied - A copy of every pending input the client sent Knowing which inputs are already in the state tells the client which pending inputs to drop and which to replay. ? Why replay pending inputs instead of just jumping to the server's position? - Jumping to the server's position is not allowed by the protocol + The server's state is a round trip old; replaying catches it up - Replaying makes the inputs reach the server faster - The server's position is quantised, so it cannot be used directly Without the replay the player would snap back a round trip in time every snapshot, undoing the inputs still on their way. ? Prediction was perfect. What does reconciliation change on screen? - The player snaps back to the server's position - The player moves forward by one round trip - The pending inputs are applied twice + Nothing: the replay arrives at the same position Resetting to the confirmed state and replaying the pending inputs gives exactly what was predicted, so there is no visible correction. ? Why should the client not predict whether its shot killed someone? + Hits decide the game and depend on other players' true positions, so the server must decide them - The client does not know which weapon it is holding - Predicting hits would use too much CPU on the client - Shots are sent over a reliable channel and arrive too late to predict Only your own movement and animation are predicted; anything that decides the game waits for the server.

title: Prediction and reconciliation
body: Make your own player respond instantly: predict each input locally, keep the unconfirmed ones, and when the server's state arrives, reset to it and replay them (lesson 6.04). cpp struct Input { std::uint32_t sequence; float moveX; float moveY; }; struct PlayerState { float x; float y; }; PlayerState simulate(PlayerState s, const Input& in, float speed, float dt); class PredictedPlayer { public: PredictedPlayer(PlayerState start, float speed, float dt); Input applyInput(float moveX, float moveY); void onServerState(std::uint32_t lastProcessed, PlayerState authoritative); PlayerState state() const; std::size_t pending() const; }; - simulate is the movement code the client and server share. It clamps the move vector to length 1 (as in practice 6.01: a non-finite part makes the move zero), then moves by move speed dt in each axis. - applyInput makes the next input (sequence numbers start at 1), simulates it on the current state at once, keeps it as pending, and returns it so it can be sent. - onServerState reconciles. It ignores a state whose lastProcessed is lower than one already reconciled. Otherwise it drops every pending input with a sequence number up to lastProcessed , sets the state to authoritative , and replays the remaining pending inputs in order.

title: 6.05  Lag Compensation
body: Making hits fair when every player sees others in the past - the server keeping a short history of positions, rewinding targets to the moment the shooter saw, testing the shot there, limiting the rewind, and the trade-offs it creates for the player being shot. Aiming at the past Thanks to interpolation (lesson 6.03), a client sees other players where they were about 100 ms ago, plus the time its own input takes to reach the server. A player who aims perfectly at a running enemy on their screen and fires would miss if the server tested the shot against where the enemy is now : by the time the shot arrives, the enemy has moved on. Players would have to aim ahead by an amount that changes with their ping. Nobody wants that. Rewinding the world Lag compensation makes the server test the shot against what the shooter actually saw: 1. The server keeps a history of every player's position (and hitbox) for each of the last few hundred milliseconds of ticks. 2. The fire input says which tick the shooter was seeing : the render time of its interpolation, as a tick number (it can be fractional, between two snapshots). 3. The server rewinds the other players to that tick, interpolating between the two recorded ticks around it, just as the client did. 4. It tests the shot (a ray, the bullet's path) against those rewound positions, then puts everything back. If the shooter's screen showed a hit, the server agrees. The shooter's own position comes from the present, since that is known exactly. Limits The client says which tick it saw, so the server must not trust it blindly: - Clamp the rewind to a maximum, typically 200 ms to 1 second. A client claiming to see the world 3 seconds ago gets the oldest allowed tick instead, so a laggy or dishonest client cannot rewrite history far back. - Reject ticks in the future (newer than the server's current tick). - Check the claimed tick against what the server knows about that client's latency; a value that jumps around is suspicious. The trade-off Lag compensation favours the shooter . The player being shot sometimes feels it is unfair: they reached cover on their screen, then died anyway, because on the shooter's screen (100 ms behind) they had not yet. This "shot around the corner" effect grows with the shooter's latency, which is the main reason for capping the rewind. Every shooter game tunes this balance; some reduce compensation for players with very high ping. Lag compensation is for instant hits (hitscan weapons). Slow projectiles, such as rockets and arrows, are usually simulated on the server from the moment they are fired, sometimes with a small head start to make up for the shooter's latency. Check yourself quiz ? Why would a perfectly aimed shot miss without lag compensation? - The shot packet is usually lost on the way - The server tests shots only every other tick + The shooter sees the past, and the target has moved since - The client's prediction moves the shooter out of position Interpolation shows others about 100 ms behind, plus the input's travel time; without rewinding, players would have to aim ahead by their ping. ? What does the server need to store to rewind? - Every input each client sent - The snapshots it sent to the shooter - The shooter's own position history only + A short history of each player's position (hitbox) per tick It rewinds the other players to the tick the shooter saw, interpolating between recorded ticks, and tests the shot there. ? A client claims it was seeing tick 1 000 while the server is at tick 5 000 and allows 32 ticks of rewind. Which tick is used? - 1 000, as claimed + 4 968, the oldest allowed - 5 000, the current tick - The shot is ignored The rewind is clamped to the maximum: 5 000 - 32 = 4 968. A client cannot rewrite history further back than that. ? Who gets the advantage of lag compensation, and what does the other side experience? - The target; the shooter has to aim ahead - The player with the lowest ping; others see stuttering + The shooter; the target can be hit after reaching cover on their own screen - Neither; both see exactly the same world Testing against what the shooter saw favours the shooter, causing the "shot around the corner" effect, which is why the rewind is capped.

title: Rewinding for hits
body: Build the server side of lag compensation (lesson 6.05): a history of a player's positions per tick, a limit on how far a shot may rewind, and the hit test. cpp class PositionHistory { public: explicit PositionHistory(std::size_t capacity); void record(std::int64_t tick, double x, double y); std::optional<std::pair<double, double at(double tick) const; }; double rewindTick(double claimed, std::int64_t now, int maxRewind); bool segmentHitsCircle(double ox, double oy, double dx, double dy, double range, double cx, double cy, double radius); - record adds a position for a tick that must be newer than the last recorded one (otherwise it is ignored), keeping only the newest capacity entries. - at gives the position at a tick, which may be fractional. Outside the range from the oldest to the newest recorded tick there is no answer. Inside it, blend in a straight line between the recorded ticks either side (ticks may have gaps); at a recorded tick, its position. - rewindTick limits the tick a client claims it was seeing to between now - maxRewind and now . - segmentHitsCircle tests a shot from (ox, oy) in direction (dx, dy) (any length; a zero direction never hits) for range units against a circle: it hits if the closest point of that segment to the centre is within radius .

title: Smooth between snapshots
body: Draw other players between two snapshots, slightly in the past. snapshot t=100: x=0 snapshot t=150: x=10 render at t=110 - x=2 render at t=140 - x=8 render at t=170 - x=10 (no newer snapshot: hold)

title: Delta snapshots
body: Send only what changed since a snapshot the client already has. baseline: {1: (10, 5, 100hp), 2: (3, 3, 80hp)} current: {1: (11, 5, 100hp), 3: (0, 0, 50hp)} delta: changed 1 (x only), removed 2, added 3 applied to baseline - equals current: true

title: Trust no input
body: Make the server refuse moves that are impossible. input move (1, 0) at speed 5 - accepted, x = 5 input move (10, 0) - direction too long, normalised input from tick 90 at tick 100 - too old, ignored input with dt 0.5 (expected 0.016) - refused

title: Predict and correct
body: Move the local player straight away, then fix the position when the server answers. client predicts inputs 1..5 - x = 5 server confirms input 3 at x = 2.5 (a wall slowed it) client replays inputs 4..5 from 2.5 - x = 4.5

title: A multiplayer movement core
body: Build the heart of a small multiplayer action game: an authoritative server that applies players' inputs each tick, sends snapshots and decides hits with lag compensation, and a client that predicts its own movement, reconciles with the server, and interpolates everyone else. The tests run both through a link with several ticks of delay. cpp struct Input { std::uint32_t sequence; int moveX; int moveY; }; struct PlayerSnapshot { int id; int x; int y; std::uint32_t lastInput; }; struct Snapshot { std::int64_t tick; std::vector<PlayerSnapshot players; }; class GameServer { public: explicit GameServer(int speed); int addPlayer(int x, int y); void receiveInput(int player, const Input& in); void teleport(int player, int x, int y); void tick(); Snapshot snapshot() const; int hitscan(int shooter, double viewTick, double dirX, double dirY, double range, double radius) const; }; class GameClient { public: GameClient(int playerId, int speed, int x, int y); Input makeInput(int moveX, int moveY); void receiveSnapshot(const Snapshot& s); std::pair<int, int position() const; std::size_t pendingInputs() const; std::optional<std::pair<double, double remotePosition(int playerId, double tick) const; }; The world. Positions are whole numbers in an arena from 0 to 1 000 on both axes; every position is clamped into it. Movement , shared by server and client: clamp moveX and moveY to -1..1 each, then add move speed to each axis and clamp to the arena. (Integers make prediction exact, as lesson 6.02 recommends.) The server. - addPlayer gives ids 1, 2, 3 ... and places the player (clamped), with last input 0. - receiveInput queues an input for a known player, unless its sequence number is not above the player's last applied input, the same number is already queued, or 64 inputs are already queued. - teleport moves a known player (clamped). It stands for anything the server does that a client cannot predict. - tick advances the tick number (from 0 to 1, and so on). Then, for each player in id order, it applies every queued input in sequence order, recording the last one applied, and empties the queue. Finally it records every player's position for this tick in a history that keeps the last 64 ticks. - snapshot is the current tick and every player, in id order. - hitscan tests an instant shot (lesson 6.05). The shooter must exist and the direction must not be zero. The view tick is clamped to between tick - 32 and the current tick. Each other player is rewound to that tick from the history, blending between the recorded ticks either side of a fractional tick; a player not recorded at those ticks is skipped. The shot starts at the shooter's current position, goes range units along the direction, and hits a player if the closest point of that segment is within radius of them. Return the id of the hit player nearest the shooter along the shot (the lower id on a tie), or 0. The client. - makeInput makes the next input (sequence numbers from 1) with both parts clamped to -1..1, applies it to the predicted position at once, keeps it as pending and returns it. - receiveSnapshot ignores a snapshot whose tick is not newer than the newest one already received. For the client's own player it reconciles (lesson 6.04): drop pending inputs up to the player's last applied input, take the server's position, and replay the rest. Every other player's position is stored with the snapshot's tick, keeping the 32 newest per player. - remotePosition interpolates another player (lesson 6.03) at a tick, which may be fractional: before their oldest stored tick it is the oldest position, after the newest the newest, and in between a straight blend. A player never seen (including the client's own) has no position.
