title: An image buffer
body: Build the core of a small image library on top of strided views (lesson 2.04). Every operation works through pointers and strides, so it works the same on a whole image or on any rectangle inside one. cpp struct View { std::uint32_t pixels; // top-left pixel int width; int height; int stride; // pixels from one row start to the next }; View viewOf(std::vector<std::uint32_t & storage, int width, int height); View subView(View v, int x, int y, int w, int h); void blit(View destination, int x, int y, View source); void flipVertical(View v); std::vector<std::uint32_t copyOut(View v); - viewOf returns a view of a whole image stored in storage , with stride equal to the width. storage must already hold width height pixels. - subView returns the rectangle clipped to v , sharing memory; { nullptr, 0, 0, v.stride } if nothing overlaps. - blit copies source into destination with the source's top-left at (x, y) , clipped to the destination: pixels that would land outside are skipped (and x or y may be negative). Copy each visible row with one std::memcpy . The two views do not overlap. - flipVertical turns the view upside down in place by swapping rows: the top row with the bottom row, and so on inwards. - copyOut returns the view's pixels packed together, row after row, width height of them, without the stride's padding.

title: 3.01  Structs in Memory
body: A struct's members sit at fixed offsets from its start, in the order they are declared, with padding added so each member is suitably aligned. offsetof gives a member's offset, the arrow operator is "base address plus offset", and reordering members can make a struct smaller. Members at fixed offsets A struct is a block of memory with its members placed one after another in declaration order . Each member sits at a fixed distance from the start of the struct: its offset . That offset is the same for every object of that type, which is what makes p- member cheap: it is the address in p plus a number the compiler already knows. cpp include <cstddef include <cstdio struct Enemy { int id; // offset 0 float x, y; // offsets 4 and 8 int health; // offset 12 }; int main() { std::printf("id %zu, x %zu, y %zu, health %zu, size %zu\n", offsetof(Enemy, id), offsetof(Enemy, x), offsetof(Enemy, y), offsetof(Enemy, health), sizeof(Enemy)); } It prints offsets 0, 4, 8, 12 and a size of 16. offsetof (from <cstddef ) is how you ask the compiler for a member's offset. So enemy- health compiles to "take the address in enemy , add 12, read 4 bytes". If enemy holds 0x2000 , the health is the int at 0x200C . Debuggers, memory viewers and anything that reads a struct out of a file or a packet think exactly like this. Alignment and padding The processor reads a 4-byte value fastest when its address is a multiple of 4, and an 8-byte value when its address is a multiple of 8. Each type has an alignment : the number its address must be a multiple of. For the basic types the alignment equals the size: 1 for char , 4 for int and float , 8 for double , long long and pointers. To keep every member aligned, the compiler inserts unused padding bytes: cpp-norun struct Pickup { char kind; // offset 0, then 7 bytes of padding double expires; // offset 8 (must be a multiple of 8) int amount; // offset 16 bool active; // offset 20, then 3 bytes of padding }; // size 24 demo-memory title: struct Pickup, in declaration order char kind = 'H' double expires = 12.5 int amount = 25 bool active = true Two rules produce every layout: 1. Each member goes at the next offset that is a multiple of its alignment. 2. The struct's size is rounded up to a multiple of its largest member alignment, so that in an array every element's members stay aligned too. That trailing padding is why sizeof(Pickup) is 24 and not 21. Ordering to save space Declaring the largest members first removes most of the padding: cpp-norun struct PickupSorted { double expires; // 0 int amount; // 8 char kind; // 12 bool active; // 13, then 2 bytes of padding }; // size 16 A third smaller with the same data. For one object it does not matter; for a million particles in an array it is 8 MB less memory and fewer cache lines to read. Lots of game code sorts members by size for exactly this reason. !note Padding bytes are real bytes with unspecified contents. Writing a struct straight to a file or a socket writes the padding too, which can leak whatever was in that memory. Compare structs member by member, not with memcmp , for the same reason. Nested structs and arrays in structs A member that is itself a struct is placed whole, aligned to its own largest member. An array member is its elements in a row. Offsets add up: cpp-norun struct Vec3 { float x, y, z; }; // size 12, alignment 4 struct Transform { Vec3 position; // 0..11 Vec3 scale; // 12..23 float yaw; // 24 }; // offsetof(Transform, scale) + offsetof(Vec3, y) == 16: transform.scale.y lives 16 bytes in Through a byte pointer Because a member is just "base plus offset", you can reach one through a byte pointer: cpp-norun Enemy e{ 7, 1.0f, 2.0f, 50 }; unsigned char base{ reinterpret_cast<unsigned char (&e) }; int health; std::memcpy(&health, base + offsetof(Enemy, health), sizeof(health)); // 50 You would not write this for a struct you can name; e.health is clearer. It matters when the layout is only known as numbers: a file format, a packet, a structure documented as "the health is at offset 0x0C". The next lessons follow chains of such offsets. Classes are the same A class with private members is laid out the same way. A class with virtual functions has one extra hidden member at offset 0: a pointer to its table of functions, the vtable pointer (lesson 3.05). So a class with virtual functions and one int is 16 bytes on 64-bit: 8 for the hidden pointer, 4 for the int, 4 of padding. Check yourself quiz ? An Enemy holds 0x5000 and health is at offset 12. What address does enemy- health read? - 0x5012 + 0x500C - 0x5030 , twelve 4-byte steps on - 0x5000 , because the arrow always reads the start of the struct The arrow is "base address plus member offset": 0x5000 + 12 = 0x500C , since 12 is 0xC in hex. The offset is in bytes, not in elements. ? struct S { char a; int b; char c; }; What is sizeof(S) , and why? - 6, one byte for each char and four for the int - 8, because the compiler packs the two chars together after b + 12: a at 0, padding, b at 4, c at 8, then trailing padding to a multiple of 4 - 16, because every struct is rounded up to 16 bytes The int needs a 4-aligned offset, so three bytes of padding follow a , and the size is padded to a multiple of 4 so arrays of S stay aligned. The compiler never reorders members. ? How can that struct be made smaller? - Declare it const , so the padding is not needed + Put the int first: int b; char a; char c; gives offsets 0, 4, 5 and size 8 - Add a char d; after c so it fills the trailing padding - It cannot: the padding is fixed by the hardware Ordering members from largest to smallest leaves less padding. Adding a member into the trailing padding keeps the size at 12; it uses the waste but does not remove it. ? Why should a struct not be compared with memcmp ? - memcmp only works on arrays of char - memcmp compares the addresses of the two structs instead of their bytes + Its padding bytes have unspecified contents, so two structs with equal members can still differ byte for byte - memcmp stops at the first zero byte, like strcmp Padding is not part of any member and nothing promises what it holds. Compare the members one by one, or with a defaulted operator== .

title: Working out a struct's layout
body: Do the compiler's job: given a struct's members in declaration order, each with a size and an alignment, work out where each one goes. cpp struct Member { std::string name; int size; int align; }; std::vector<int offsetsOf(const std::vector<Member & members); int sizeOf(const std::vector<Member & members); int paddingOf(const std::vector<Member & members); std::vector<Member smallestOrder(const std::vector<Member & members); - offsetsOf : each member goes at the next offset that is a multiple of its alignment. - sizeOf : the end of the last member, rounded up to a multiple of the largest alignment. An empty struct has size 1 (C++ gives every object at least one byte). - paddingOf : the size minus the sum of the members' sizes. - smallestOrder returns the members sorted by alignment, largest first; members with the same alignment keep their original order. That order never needs more padding than any other. The tests compare your answers with what the real compiler does, using offsetof and sizeof .

title: 3.02  Pointers to Pointers
body:
A pointer is a variable, so it has an address, and a pointer can point at it. int lets a function change which address the caller's pointer holds. Arrays of pointers, argv, and the pointer-to-pointer trick that removes items from a linked list without special cases. One more level A pointer is an ordinary variable with an address of its own, so another pointer can hold that address: cpp include <iostream int main() { int score{ 42 }; int p{ &score }; // p holds the address of score int pp{ &p }; // pp holds the address of p std::cout << pp << '
'; // follow twice: 42 pp = 50; // writes score std::cout << score << '
'; // 50 } text pp p score 0x2010 ---- 0x2000 ---- 50 at 0x2020 at 0x2010 at 0x2000 pp is p , and pp is score . Each star follows one arrow. There is nothing special about two levels; int is three arrows, though you will rarely want more than two. Changing the caller's pointer Lesson 1.04 passed int so a function could change the caller's int. By the same logic, to change the caller's pointer , pass its address, an int : cpp-norun // Makes target point at the larger of two values. void aimAtLarger(int target, int a, int b) { target = ( a = b) ? a : b; // changes the caller's pointer variable } int chosen{ nullptr }; aimAtLarger(&chosen, &x, &y); // chosen now holds &x or &y The C and Windows APIs use this pattern for functions that hand you a newly created object: HRESULT CreateSomething(..., IThing result) . You pass the address of your pointer, and the function fills it in. In C++ the same effect is often written with a reference to a pointer, int & target , but the form is everywhere in C interfaces, so you need to read it fluently. Arrays of pointers An array whose elements are pointers is common and useful: a list of strings, a list of objects that live elsewhere. cpp-norun const char names { "Ada", "Grace", "Linus" }; // three pointers to text const char cursor{ names }; // pointer to the first pointer std::cout << cursor << '
'; // Ada std::cout << (cursor + 2) << '
'; // Linus std::cout << (cursor + 1) << '
'; // G: first char of Grace main 's second parameter is exactly this: cpp-norun int main(int argc, char argv) // argv 0 is the program's path, argv 1 ... argv argc - 1 are the arguments, argv argc is nullptr The pointer-to-pointer trick Removing an item from a singly linked list usually needs a special case for the first node, because removing it changes head while removing any other node changes the previous node's next : cpp-norun struct Node { int value; Node next; }; // the usual way: two cases void removeValue(Node & head, int value) { if (head && head- value == value) { Node dead{ head }; head = head- next; delete dead; return; } for (Node n{ head }; n && n- next; n = n- next) if (n- next- value == value) { Node dead{ n- next }; n- next = dead- next; delete dead; return; } } But head and every next are all just pointers to Node , and a Node can point at any of them. Walk a pointer to "the link that points at the current node", and there is only one case: cpp-norun void removeValue(Node link, int value) { while ( link && ( link)- value != value) link = &( link)- next; // move to the next link if ( link) { Node dead{ link }; link = dead- next; // bypass the node, whether link is head or a next delete dead; } } removeValue(&head, 7); link starts at &head ; after one step it is &head- next , and so on. When it stops, link is the matching node, and assigning to link updates whichever pointer pointed at it. Linus Torvalds famously called this version "good taste", because the special case disappears instead of being handled. Reading the declarations Declarations with several stars and const read right to left: Declaration Reads as --- --- int pp pp is a pointer to a pointer to int const char names names is a pointer to a pointer to const char char const argv argv is a pointer to a const pointer to char int & r r is a reference to a pointer to int Check yourself quiz ? int x{ 1 }; int p{ &x }; int pp{ &p }; What are pp and pp ? - pp is x , 1; pp is the address of x - pp is the address of pp ; pp is p + pp is p (the address of x ); pp is x , 1 - Both are 1, because both lead to x in the end Each follows one level: from pp to p , then from p to x . ? Why does a function that creates an object for the caller often take Thing out ? + It needs to change the caller's pointer variable, so it needs that variable's address - A Thing parameter cannot point at heap memory - Two stars make the object live longer than the function - The extra level makes the call faster for large objects With Thing out the function gets a copy of the caller's pointer, and changing the copy does nothing for the caller. With Thing it can write out = new Thing{} . ? In the pointer-to-pointer removal from a linked list, why is the first node not a special case? - The first node is never removed, so it needs no special case - The list keeps a dummy node in front, so the head never changes + link points at head or at a next , and link is updated either way - Removing the first node simply leaks it, which the trick accepts The trick walks a pointer to the pointer that leads to the current node. Whether that is head or some node's next , assigning through it unlinks the node the same way. ? What is argv argc ? - The last command-line argument - The program's own name - Undefined: it is one past the end of the array + nullptr : the array of argument pointers ends with a null pointer argv 0 is usually the program name and argv argc - 1 the last argument. The standard guarantees an extra null pointer at argv argc .

title: Changing the caller's pointer
body: Write functions that take a pointer to a pointer so they can change the caller's pointer variable: cpp struct Node { int value; Node next; }; void pushFront(Node head, int value); bool removeFirst(Node head, int value); int removeAll(Node head, int value); void skipUntil(const char cursor, char stop); - pushFront puts a new node (made with new ) at the front of the list. - removeFirst deletes the first node holding value and returns true, or returns false if there is none. Write it with the pointer-to-pointer walk from lesson 3.02: one loop, no special case for the head. - removeAll deletes every node holding value and returns how many it removed. - skipUntil moves the caller's cursor forward to the first stop character, or to the terminating zero if there is none.

title: 3.03  Following Pointer Chains
body: Real programs reach data through several levels of pointers - a game reaches a player's health through the world, the level and the player. A chain can be written as a base address and a list of offsets, followed one read at a time with a null check at every step. Why chains survive restarts when single addresses do not. Data at the end of a path In a real program the value you care about is rarely in a variable you can name. A game's code might reach the local player's health like this: cpp-norun struct Stats { int level; int health; int mana; }; struct Player { char name 16 ; Stats stats; }; struct World { int tick; Player players 8 ; }; struct Game { World world; int localIndex; }; Game game{ / created at start-up / }; int health{ game- world- players game- localIndex - stats- health }; Five arrows. Every object along the way lives on the heap, created at a different moment, so none of them is at a predictable address. What is predictable is the shape of the path: from a Game , the World is at some offset; from the World , the player pointers start at another; from a Player , the Stats is at another; and health is at offset 4 of Stats . A chain as base and offsets Write each step as "read the pointer stored at this offset", and the whole path becomes a base address and a list of numbers: text base: &game (the address of the variable holding the Game ) step 1: read the pointer at base + 0 - the Game step 2: read the pointer at Game + 0x00 - the World step 3: read the pointer at World + 0x08 - players 0 step 4: read the pointer at Player + 0x10 - the Stats final: Stats + 0x04 - the address of health So base → 0x00 → 0x00 → 0x08 → 0x10 → 0x04 . Every intermediate step reads 8 bytes and treats them as the next address; the last offset is added without reading, giving the address of the value itself. The offsets come straight from the struct layouts of lesson 3.01: offsetof(World, players) is 8 because tick and its padding come first. Debuggers and memory tools display chains in exactly this form, often with brackets for each read: base + 0 + 0 + 8 + 0x10 + 4 . Following a chain in code With real pointers, following a chain through byte offsets looks like this: cpp-norun // Follows base - offsets 0 - ... - offsets n-1 . Returns the final address, or nullptr. const void follow(const void base, const std::vector<std::size_t & offsets) { const unsigned char at{ static_cast<const unsigned char (base) }; for (std::size_t i{ 0 }; i + 1 < offsets.size(); ++i) { const void next; std::memcpy(&next, at + offsets i , sizeof(next)); // read the pointer stored there if (!next) return nullptr; // a broken link: stop at = static_cast<const unsigned char (next); } return offsets.empty() ? at : at + offsets.back(); } The memcpy reads 8 bytes as an address (lesson 2.05 explains why not a cast). The null check at every step is not optional: any object along the path may not exist yet (no level loaded, the player not spawned), and following its null pointer crashes. !warning A chain is only valid while every object along it is alive. A level being unloaded frees the World ; a pointer you read from it a moment ago now dangles. Code that caches a resolved address must resolve the chain again whenever the structure may have changed. Why chains survive a restart Run the program twice and every heap address changes, and ASLR moves the program itself. So the address of health is different every time. The offsets never change, because they come from the struct layouts compiled into the program. And the first link can be anchored to something stable: a global variable inside the program's own image, whose address is "where the program was loaded" plus a fixed number. text run 1: module at 0x7FF6_1000_0000, global Game at module + 0x51A8, health at 0x0000_01F3_2C40_9A14 run 2: module at 0x7FF7_A230_0000, global Game at module + 0x51A8, health at 0x0000_0229_0E11_3374 the chain module + 0x51A8 - 0 - 0 - 8 - 0x10 - 4 finds health both times This is how debuggers, profilers, save-game editors and the inspection tools you build for your own programs find the same data run after run: not by remembering an address, but by remembering a path. Where you will use this - Your own debug tools. A debug overlay or an external inspector for your own game (the Game Development course builds one) reaches its data through chains like this. - Reading crash dumps. A dump holds raw memory; you follow pointers from a known global by hand or with the debugger's dx command. - File formats and packets. Many binary formats store offsets to other parts of the file, which you follow exactly the same way, with "offset into the file" in place of "address". Check yourself quiz ? In the chain base - 0x00 - 0x00 - 0x08 - 0x10 - 0x04 , why is the last offset added without a read? - The last offset is always 4, so it can be skipped + The last step gives the address of the value itself; every earlier step reads a pointer to the next object - Reading at the last step would follow the value as if it were a pointer, which is what we want to avoid crashing - The last offset is read first, before the chain is followed Every step but the last lands on a pointer, which is read to reach the next object. The final offset points at the value you want, so you stop with its address. ? Why must a chain be checked for nullptr at every step? - Because offsets in a chain can be negative - Because the final value it reaches may be 0 + Any object on the path may not exist at that moment - It does not need to: only the base can ever be null For example, there may be no level loaded yet. Reading through its null pointer would crash; a null check at each read turns that into a clean "not found". ? Why does the address of health change between runs while the chain stays the same? - The chain is recomputed by the compiler on every run + Objects move, but offsets and the anchoring global are fixed - The game moves health on purpose but forgets to move the chain - The chain uses names rather than numbers, so addresses do not matter ASLR and the heap move the objects every run, but the layout of every struct and the position of the first link's global inside the program are fixed when it is built. ? Where does offset 0x08 in the World step come from? - From the total size of the World struct - From the address of the World object in memory + From the layout: offsetof(World, players) after padding - From pointers being 8 bytes, so every chain step adds 8 The pointer member players needs 8-byte alignment, so after the 4-byte int tick there are 4 bytes of padding and players sits at offset 8.

title: Following a chain of offsets
body: Write the chain follower from lesson 3.03 and use it on real objects: cpp const void followChain(const void base, const std::vector<std::size_t & offsets); const int healthByChain(const Game game); followChain starts at base . For every offset except the last, it reads the pointer stored at "current address + offset" and moves there; if that pointer is nullptr it returns nullptr . Finally it returns "current address + last offset" without reading. With no offsets it returns base itself. Read each stored pointer with std::memcpy from a byte address. healthByChain finds the local player's health using only followChain and offsetof , starting from the Game object itself (not from a pointer to it): cpp struct Stats { int level; int health; int mana; }; struct Player { char name 16 ; Stats stats; }; struct World { int tick; Player players 8 ; }; struct Game { World world; int localIndex; }; The local player is world- players localIndex . If anything along the way is missing it returns nullptr .

title: 3.04  Linked Structures
body: Data structures held together by pointers - singly and doubly linked lists, a sentinel node that removes the special cases, trees - what they cost in memory and speed compared with an array, and the intrusive lists that games and operating systems use. Nodes that point at nodes An array keeps its elements side by side. A linked structure keeps each element in its own block, a node , and links the nodes with pointers: cpp-norun struct Node { int value; Node next; // the following node, or nullptr at the end }; text head v 4 --- 9 --- 2 nullptr The list is reached through one pointer, head . Walking it is a pointer that follows next until it meets nullptr : cpp-norun for (Node n{ head }; n != nullptr; n = n- next) std::cout << n- value << '\n'; What linking buys Inserting or removing in the middle of an array moves every element after it. In a linked list it changes two or three pointers, however long the list is: cpp-norun // insert value after node at Node fresh{ new Node{ value, at- next } }; at- next = fresh; And a node never moves, so a pointer to it stays valid while other nodes come and go. That is the property that matters most in practice: a std::vector invalidates pointers into it when it grows; a list never does. What it costs - Memory. Every node carries a pointer (two in a doubly linked list) and is a separate heap block with the allocator's own bookkeeping. A list of ints can easily use 32 bytes per 4-byte value. - Speed. The nodes are scattered around the heap. Walking a list jumps from address to address, and each jump is likely a cache miss: the processor waits for main memory every step. Walking a std::vector of the same values runs from one cache line to the next and is often ten or more times faster. - No indexing. Reaching the 500th element means following 499 pointers. So the default in C++ is std::vector . Linked structures earn their place when nodes must not move, when items are inserted and removed constantly in the middle of very long sequences, or when the structure itself is naturally a graph of objects. Doubly linked, with a sentinel A node with both next and prev can be removed knowing only its own address, and the list can be walked both ways. The neatest version keeps one extra sentinel node that is not an element at all: the list is a ring through it. text +-------------------------------------------+ v sentinel <- 4 <- 9 <- 2 <-------+ An empty list is the sentinel pointing at itself. Every real node always has a real prev and next (possibly the sentinel), so insert and remove have no nullptr checks and no special cases: cpp-norun void unlink(Node n) { n- prev- next = n- next; n- next- prev = n- prev; } void insertBefore(Node where, Node n) { n- prev = where- prev; n- next = where; where- prev- next = n; where- prev = n; } std::list is built this way. Intrusive lists In a game engine or an operating system kernel, the links are often stored inside the objects themselves, instead of in separate nodes that point at them: cpp-norun struct Enemy { Enemy nextActive; // the list of enemies that need updating this frame Enemy prevActive; float x, y; int health; }; No extra allocation per list entry, and from an object you can unlink it directly. The Windows kernel's LIST_ENTRY is this pattern: a struct with Flink and Blink embedded in hundreds of kernel structures, with a macro ( CONTAINING_RECORD ) that subtracts the member's offset to get back from the links to the object around them. That is lesson 3.01's offsets in reverse. Trees A node with two child pointers instead of one next makes a binary tree; a node with a vector of child pointers makes a general tree. A game's scene graph, a file system, a parsed program and a UI layout are all trees of nodes linked by pointers. The same rules apply: whoever creates the nodes must free them, and a parent's destructor usually frees its children. Check yourself quiz ? Why does inserting into the middle of a linked list not depend on its length? - The list keeps a table of every node's address + Only the pointers of the neighbouring nodes change; nothing has to move - The new node is always added at the end and then sorted Once you hold a pointer to the place, linking a node in rewrites two or so pointers. A vector, by contrast, must move every element after the insertion point. ? Why is walking a linked list usually much slower than walking a vector with the same values? - Each node stores more data than a vector element - Following a pointer is a slow instruction compared with adding to an index - The list must be locked while you walk it + The nodes are scattered in memory, so almost every step is a cache miss, while a vector is read sequentially A vector's elements are next to each other, so the processor fetches them in big runs ahead of time. Each list node can be anywhere, so the next one usually has to come from main memory. ? What does a sentinel node remove from a doubly linked list's code? + The nullptr checks and special cases for the first and last nodes - The need for prev pointers - The need to allocate each node separately - The need to free nodes when they are removed With a sentinel, every real node always has a real prev and next , so insert and remove are the same few lines everywhere in the list. ? In an intrusive list, how do you get from a pointer to the embedded links back to the whole object? - Follow the links' prev pointer, which points at the object - Cast the links pointer straight to the object type; they share an address + Subtract the links member's offset from its address, as CONTAINING_RECORD does - Search every object until one has links at that address The links sit at a fixed offset inside the object, so the object starts that many bytes earlier. A plain cast only works when the links are the first member.

title: A doubly linked list with a sentinel
match: A doubly linked list with a sentinel
body: Build a doubly linked list of ints around a sentinel node, so that insert and remove have no special cases (lesson 3.04): cpp class List { public: struct Node { int value; Node prev; Node next; }; List(); ~List(); List(const List&) = delete; List& operator=(const List&) = delete; Node pushFront(int value); Node pushBack(int value); Node insertBefore(Node where, int value); void remove(Node node); void reverse(); int size() const; std::vector<int values() const; std::vector<int valuesBackwards() const; }; - The sentinel is a member Node ; an empty list is the sentinel linked to itself. - pushFront , pushBack and insertBefore create a node with new , link it in, and return it. The returned pointer stays valid until that node is removed, whatever else happens to the list. - remove unlinks and deletes a node of this list. - reverse reverses the list by swapping every node's prev and next (the sentinel's too), without creating or deleting nodes. - values walks forwards, valuesBackwards walks backwards. - The destructor deletes every remaining node.

title: 3.05  Function Pointers and Callbacks
body: Functions live in memory too, and a function pointer holds the address of one. The declaration syntax and how to tame it with using, tables of functions, C-style callbacks with a void context, how virtual functions are tables of function pointers, and std::function. Functions have addresses A program's machine code is in memory like everything else, so every function has an address. A function pointer holds one, and calling through it runs that function: cpp include <iostream int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; } int multiply(int a, int b) { return a b; } int main() { int ( op)(int, int){ add }; // op points at add std::cout << op(3, 4) << '\n'; // 7 op = multiply; std::cout << op(3, 4) << '\n'; // 12 } A function's name turns into a pointer to it, the way an array's name does, so add and &add are the same here. Taming the syntax int ( op)(int, int) reads "op is a pointer to a function taking two ints and returning an int". The brackets around op are required: without them, int op(int, int) declares a function returning int . Give the type a name and the problem goes away: cpp-norun using BinaryOp = int ( )(int, int); BinaryOp op{ add }; int apply(BinaryOp f, int a, int b) { return f(a, b); } Tables of functions An array of function pointers turns a decision into a lookup. Interpreters, state machines and command handlers are built this way: cpp-norun using Handler = void ( )(Game&); void onMove(Game& g); void onAttack(Game& g); void onQuit(Game& g); constexpr Handler handlers { onMove, onAttack, onQuit }; handlers static_cast<int (command) (game); // no switch needed Each entry is just an 8-byte address. A table like this is what a switch statement often compiles into, too: a jump table of addresses indexed by the case value. Callbacks with a context A callback is a function you hand to other code to call later or for each item. C interfaces take a function pointer plus a void context that they pass back unchanged, because a plain function pointer cannot carry any data of its own: cpp-norun // The library's side void forEachFile(const char folder, bool ( visit)(const char name, void context), void context); // Your side: count files, stop after 100 struct Counter { int seen; int limit; }; bool countOne(const char name, void context) { Counter c{ static_cast<Counter (context) }; // turn the void back into what it really is ++c- seen; return c- seen < c- limit; // false: stop early } Counter counter{ 0, 100 }; forEachFile("C:\\Games", countOne, &counter); void is "an address of anything": any object pointer converts to it, and static_cast converts it back to the type it really was. The library never looks inside. The Windows API does this everywhere: EnumWindows(callback, lParam) , CreateThread(..., startRoutine, parameter, ...) , window procedures with GWLP_USERDATA . Virtual functions are tables A class with virtual functions gets a hidden table of function pointers, the vtable , one per class, and every object carries a pointer to its class's table (lesson 3.01's hidden member at offset 0): text object of Archer vtable for Archer vptr ------------- &Archer::attack health &Archer::move arrows &Archer::~Archer A virtual call unit- attack() compiles to: read the vtable pointer at offset 0 of the object, read the function address at the right slot of the table, call it. Two loads and an indirect call, which is why a virtual call costs a little more than a direct one, and why the decision can happen at run time. The DLLs course builds COM-style interfaces from exactly these tables. std::function and lambdas Modern C++ wraps all of this. A lambda with captures carries its own data, so it needs no void context, and std::function can hold any callable with the right signature: cpp-norun int limit{ 100 }; int seen{ 0 }; std::function<bool(const std::string&) visit{ & (const std::string&) { return ++seen < limit; } }; The cost is that a std::function may allocate and always calls indirectly. Inside your own C++ code prefer it, or a template parameter, for clarity; when calling a C API, you still need a plain function pointer and a context, and a lambda without captures converts to a plain function pointer to fill that role. Check yourself quiz ? What does int ( f)(double) declare? - A function f that takes a double and returns an int + f , a pointer to a function that takes a double and returns an int - A pointer f to an int , initialised with a double - An array of functions returning int The brackets around f make f a pointer first; the rest describes what it points at. Without them, int f(double) declares a function returning int . ? Why do C-style callback APIs take a void context argument? - To pass the address of the callback function itself - Because the library needs to free the caller's memory afterwards + A function pointer carries no data, so the caller's state goes as a void - void makes the callback run faster than a typed pointer The library does not know your type, so it stores an untyped address and hands it back unchanged to your callback, which casts it back to what it really is. ? What happens, step by step, in a virtual call unit- attack() ? - The compiler picks the function at compile time from the pointer's type - The program looks up the function by its name in a table of strings + Read the vtable pointer from the object, read attack 's address from its slot in the table, call that address - The object stores a copy of every function's code and runs its own copy Each object of a class with virtual functions holds a hidden pointer to its class's table of function addresses. Calling picks the address from that table at run time. ? Which lambdas can be passed where a plain function pointer is expected? - Any lambda, because every lambda is a function - Lambdas that capture by reference, but not by value + Lambdas with no captures - Only lambdas declared static A lambda without captures has no state and converts to a plain function pointer. A capturing lambda carries data, which a function pointer has no room for; use std::function or a void context instead.

title: Pointer paths in an address space
match: Pointer paths in an address space
body: Debuggers and inspection tools find data by pointer paths (lesson 3.03). Build the engine of such a tool over a simulated address space, so the results are the same on every computer: memory regions, reading values, resolving paths, and scanning for paths that lead to a given address. cpp struct Path { std::uint64_t base; std::vector<std::int64_t offsets; }; class AddressSpace { public: void map(std::uint64_t start, std::vector<std::uint8_t bytes, bool isStatic); std::optional<std::uint64_t read64(std::uint64_t address) const; std::optional<std::uint32_t read32(std::uint64_t address) const; std::vector<std::uint64_t staticPointerSlots() const; }; std::optional<std::uint64_t resolve(const AddressSpace& memory, const Path& path); std::vector<Path scan(const AddressSpace& memory, std::uint64_t target, std::int64_t maxOffset, int maxDepth); AddressSpace - map adds a region of bytes starting at start . Regions never overlap. A static region stands for the program's own image (globals), whose position is stable; the others stand for heap blocks. - read64 and read32 read little-endian values. A read succeeds only if all its bytes are inside one region; otherwise it gives std::nullopt . - staticPointerSlots lists every address inside a static region that is a multiple of 8 and has 8 readable bytes, in increasing order. resolve follows a path: read the 8-byte pointer at base ; then for every offset except the last, read the pointer at "current + offset". A failed read, or a pointer that is 0, gives std::nullopt . The result is "current + last offset". A path with no offsets resolves to the pointer stored at base . scan finds paths from static slots to target : - Depth 1 : a slot s whose pointer p is non-zero with 0 <= target - p <= maxOffset gives { s, { target - p } } . - Depth 2 (when maxDepth = 2 ): a slot s with non-zero pointer p1 ; for each offset o1 from 0 to maxOffset in steps of 8 where the pointer p2 at p1 + o1 is readable and non-zero, with 0 <= target - p2 <= maxOffset , gives { s, { o1, target - p2 } } . - Results are sorted by base, then by number of offsets, then by the offsets themselves. Every path returned must resolve to target .

title: 4.01  Where Memory Comes From
body: A running program's address space holds its code, its static data, one stack per thread and the heap. Each object gets one of four lifetimes - static, automatic, dynamic or thread - and the lifetime decides where it lives, when it starts and when its address stops being valid. The map of a process When Windows starts your program it gives it a private address space : a huge range of addresses (128 TB on 64-bit Windows) of which only a few small areas are actually backed by memory. The areas you will meet are: text high addresses +-----------------------------+ stack of thread 1 grows down; 1 MB reserved by default stack of thread 2 ... heap blocks new / malloc, anywhere the heap finds room ... DLLs: kernel32, ucrtbase... your .exe image: .text machine code read + execute .rdata constants, text read only .data initialised globals .bss zeroed globals +-----------------------------+ low addresses ASLR shuffles where each area starts, but every program has these pieces. When you look at a pointer's value in a debugger, its rough size already says which area it is in: an address near the .exe's load address is a global, a high address near the stack pointer is a local, anything else is probably heap. Four lifetimes C++ gives every object a storage duration , and that decides where it lives: Duration Example Lives Starts Ends --- --- --- --- --- static globals, static variables, string literals in the image (.data, .bss, .rdata) before main , or at the first call for a static local when the program exits automatic ordinary local variables, parameters on the stack when execution reaches the declaration at the closing brace of its block dynamic new , malloc , the inside of std::vector on the heap when you allocate it when you free it, and only then thread thread_local variables per-thread storage when the thread starts or first uses it when the thread ends A pointer is valid only during its object's lifetime. Almost every memory bug is a pointer that outlived what it pointed at. Static storage cpp-norun int frames{ 0 }; // .data: the whole program sees one frames static int hits{ 0 }; // the same storage; static here limits it to this file const char title{ "Xenon" }; // the pointer is in .data, the text in .rdata int nextTicket() { static int next{ 1 }; // initialised once, the first time the function runs return next++; // keeps its value between calls } Static objects exist for the whole run, so a pointer to one is always safe to return or keep . That includes string literals: returning "January" from a function is fine, because the text lives in the image, not on the stack. Writing to a string literal is not fine: it is in read-only memory, and char s = "abc"; s 0 = 'x'; crashes with an access violation (modern C++ does not even let that first line compile). Automatic storage Locals live in the current function's stack frame , created on entry and discarded on return. That is fast (allocating a frame is subtracting from one register) and automatic, and it is why a pointer to a local is valid only until the function returns. The next lesson looks at frames byte by byte. Dynamic storage The heap is for objects whose lifetime does not match a function call: created in one place, used across many calls, freed later, possibly by someone else. You get it with new (or malloc ), and it stays until you give it back. The heap does not know when you have finished with something; you must say so. Lessons 4.03 to 4.05 are about getting that right, and milestone 5 is about making C++ do it for you. Choosing - Default to automatic. A local std::vector or std::string is itself on the stack and manages its own heap memory for you. - Use static for things that genuinely exist once for the whole program, and keep it rare: global state makes code hard to test and to run on several threads. - Use dynamic when the size is only known at run time, when the object must outlive the function that creates it, or when it is too big for the stack (1 MB in total, by default, for everything on a thread's stack). Check yourself quiz ? Is it safe for a function to return a const char pointing at the literal "error" ? - No, the literal is a local and dies when the function returns + Yes, string literals have static storage and live for the whole program - Only if the function is declared static - Only if the caller copies it before the next function call A string literal is stored with the program's static data, not on the stack, so a pointer to it never dangles. A local char array holding the same text would be a different story. ? When is a static local variable initialised? - When the program starts, before main runs - Every time the function is called, like other locals + The first time execution passes its declaration - When the function returns for the first time A static local has static storage but is set up lazily, on the first pass through its declaration; after that it keeps its value between calls until the program ends. ? A function creates a 4 MB array as a local variable. What is likely to happen? - It works, the stack grows as needed up to the size of RAM - The compiler moves it to the heap automatically + A stack overflow, because the default stack is 1 MB; use a std::vector instead - The array is silently cut down to 1 MB Each thread's stack is small and fixed, 1 MB by default on Windows. A std::vector keeps its elements on the heap, which has room for big buffers. ? Which storage duration do the elements inside a std::vector have? - Automatic, when the vector is a local variable - Static, because the vector's size is fixed at compile time - Thread, because each thread gets its own copy + Dynamic: the vector object can be a local, but its elements are allocated on the heap The small vector object (a few pointers) lives wherever you declare it. The elements it manages are always on the heap.

title: Things that live for the whole program
match: Things that live for the whole program
body: Use static storage so that these functions can safely hand out pointers and references that stay valid: cpp int nextTicket(); const char monthName(int month); std::string& lastError(); int sharedCounter(); - nextTicket returns 1 the first time it is called, then 2, 3 and so on. Keep the count in a static local, not a global. - monthName returns "January" for 1 up to "December" for 12, and "?" for anything else. Returning string literals is safe: they live for the whole program. - lastError returns a reference to one std::string that lives for the whole program, so that lastError() = "disk full"; is seen by every later call. - sharedCounter returns a pointer to one int , the same address on every call, starting at 0.

title: 4.02  The Stack Up Close
body: Each function call pushes a frame holding the return address and the function's locals; returning pops it. The stack pointer moves down as frames are added. Why a pointer to a local dangles after the return, what a stack overflow is, and how writing past a local array can overwrite a return address. A stack of frames Every thread has one stack : a block of memory used last-in, first-out. A processor register, the stack pointer ( rsp on x64), holds the address of its current top. On x86 and ARM the stack grows downwards : adding something moves the stack pointer to a lower address. When a function is called: 1. The call instruction pushes the return address , where execution continues afterwards, and jumps to the function. 2. The function subtracts from the stack pointer to make room for its locals. That block, return address included, is its frame . 3. When it returns, it adds the same amount back and the ret instruction pops the return address and jumps there. demo-stack title: main calls total, which calls tax call main main starts with a frame of its own. local items = 3 call total count=3 each=250 A new frame below main's: total's parameters and locals live here. local sum = 750 call tax cents=750 A third frame, at a lower address still. return 150 tax returns: its frame is gone and the stack pointer moves back up. return 900 total returns 900 to main. set price = 900 return 0 main returns and the program ends. Step through the demo and watch the addresses: each new frame sits below its caller's, and returning just moves the stack pointer back. Nothing is erased. The old bytes stay where they were until the next call overwrites them. Why a pointer to a local dangles That last fact explains the classic bug exactly: cpp-norun int makeScore() { int score{ 42 }; return &score; // the address of a byte range in makeScore's frame } void other() { int junk 16 {}; (void)junk; } int main() { int p{ makeScore() }; // the frame is gone, but 42 is still sitting there std::printf("%d\n", p); // may print 42 other(); // other's frame is put in the same place std::printf("%d\n", p); // now prints 0, or anything } The first print often "works", because nothing has reused that memory yet. The next call reuses it. The compiler warns about this ( C4172: returning address of local variable ); treat that warning as an error. The rule: never let a pointer or reference to a local escape its function . Return the value itself; it is copied out (or moved, or built straight into the caller's variable) before the frame goes away. Stack overflow A thread's stack has a fixed size, 1 MB by default on Windows (set by the linker's /STACK option, or per thread in CreateThread ). Every active call uses some of it. Two things run it out: - Deep recursion : each call adds a frame, and a recursion 100 000 deep with 64-byte frames needs over 6 MB. - Big locals : char buffer 2'000'000 ; in a function is 2 MB of stack in one frame. Below the stack is a guard page ; touching it raises EXCEPTION_STACK_OVERFLOW (0xC00000FD) and the program ends. The fix is never a bigger stack. It is to put big data on the heap ( std::vector ) and to turn very deep recursion into a loop with an explicit std::vector used as a stack. Writing past a local array Locals sit in the frame next to each other and, higher up, next to the saved return address. Writing past the end of a local array walks upwards over whatever is there: text higher addresses return address <- where the function goes when it returns saved registers int count char name 16 <- strcpy(name, longInput) writes upward from here lower addresses Copy 40 bytes into name and you overwrite count , the saved registers and the return address. When the function returns, it jumps to whatever the overwritten bytes say. That is a stack buffer overflow : at best a crash with a nonsense address, and historically the most exploited bug in software. It is why lesson 2.03 warned about strcpy . Modern compilers defend against it. MSVC's /GS option (on by default) places a random security cookie between the locals and the return address and checks it before returning; if it changed, the program is stopped at once with STATUS_STACK_BUFFER_OVERRUN . Debug builds' /RTC checks catch overruns of individual locals. Neither is a licence to overrun; they turn silent corruption into a clear crash. Check yourself quiz ? Does the stack pointer go up or down when a function is called on x64? + Down: the new frame is at lower addresses than the caller's - Up: each new frame is at higher addresses than the caller's - It stays the same; only the frame pointer moves The x64 stack grows towards lower addresses, so pushing a frame subtracts from the stack pointer and returning adds back. ? Why might printing through a pointer to a dead local still show the old value? - Locals are copied to the heap when the function returns - The compiler keeps the frame alive while a pointer to it exists + Returning only moves the stack pointer; the bytes stay until reused - It cannot: the bytes are zeroed when the function returns Nothing clears a frame when it is popped. The old value lingers until the next call writes its own frame over that part of the stack, which is why the bug seems to work at first. ? What is the default stack size of a thread on Windows, and what happens when it runs out? - 8 MB, and the thread is paused until memory is free - 64 KB, and the stack wraps round to the top + 1 MB, and a stack overflow exception ends the program - Unlimited, because the stack grows into the heap Windows reserves 1 MB per thread by default with a guard page at the end. Touching it, by deep recursion or a huge local, raises a stack overflow exception. ? What does the /GS security cookie protect? - The heap: it checks every block's header before delete - The program's code: it stops it being changed at run time - Global variables: it detects writes to read-only data + The return address, with a checked value placed before it A random value sits between the locals and the return address and is checked before returning. An overrun that reaches the return address must first overwrite it, so the check catches it.

title: A stack you can watch
body: Simulate a thread's stack the way the processor uses it, with addresses that grow down : cpp class StackSim { public: StackSim(std::uint64_t top, std::uint64_t size); std::optional<std::uint64_t call(std::uint64_t localBytes); bool ret(); std::uint64_t sp() const; int depth() const; std::uint64_t peak() const; }; int deepestRecursion(std::uint64_t stackSize, std::uint64_t localBytes); - The stack occupies addresses from top - size (the bottom) up to top . It starts empty with the stack pointer at top . - call pushes a frame: 8 bytes for the return address plus localBytes , the total rounded up to a multiple of 16. The stack pointer moves down by that much and the new stack pointer is returned. If the frame would take the stack pointer below the bottom, nothing changes and it returns std::nullopt : a stack overflow. - ret pops the most recent frame (the stack pointer moves back up by that frame's size) and returns true, or returns false if no frame is active. - depth is the number of active frames; peak is the most stack ever in use at once, in bytes. - deepestRecursion works out how many nested calls of a function with localBytes of locals fit in a fresh stack of stackSize bytes.

title: 4.03  The Heap
body: new and delete, new and delete , malloc and free - what each does, why they must be paired exactly, what the allocator keeps next to every block, and the bugs that come from getting a pair wrong - double frees, mismatched frees, and memory that was never initialised. Asking for memory The heap gives out blocks of memory that live until you give them back. C++ asks for them with new : cpp-norun int one{ new int{ 42 } }; // one int, initialised to 42 Enemy boss{ new Enemy{ "Golem", 500 } }; // one object; its constructor runs int many{ new int 1000 {} }; // an array of 1000 ints, all zero delete one; // the destructor runs, then the memory is returned delete boss; delete many; // arrays use delete Each new does two things: get raw memory from the allocator, then construct the object in it. Each delete does the reverse: run the destructor, then return the memory. The pairs must match You allocated with Free with --- --- new T delete p new T n delete p std::malloc , std::calloc , std::realloc std::free(p) a library's CreateX / AllocX that library's DestroyX / FreeX HeapAlloc , VirtualAlloc , LocalAlloc HeapFree , VirtualFree , LocalFree Mixing them is undefined. delete on an array runs only the first element's destructor and may hand the allocator a pointer it does not recognise; free on something from new skips the destructor. Memory from a DLL that uses a different C runtime must go back to that DLL's free function, because its heap is not yours (the DLLs course covers this boundary). malloc is not new std::malloc(bytes) returns raw memory, or nullptr if there is none. It constructs nothing, so it is only for plain data such as int , char and simple structs, and its contents start as garbage. std::calloc zeroes the block; std::realloc resizes it, possibly moving it to a new address (so every old pointer into it dangles). new never returns nullptr on failure; it throws std::bad_alloc . In C++ code you use new (or, far better, a container or a smart pointer). You meet malloc in C code and C APIs. What the allocator keeps The heap is not magic. It is ordinary code (on Windows, the C runtime on top of the Windows heap) managing big regions of memory. For every block it hands out it keeps a little bookkeeping : at least the block's size, usually stored in a header just before the address you receive. text your pointer v header: size, flags your 24 bytes ................ next block's header That is why delete p needs no size: the allocator looks just below p . It is also why heap bugs are so destructive. Writing a few bytes past the end of your block overwrites the next block's header . Nothing happens immediately; the crash comes much later, when the allocator next reads that header, in an unrelated new or delete , with a message such as HEAP CORRUPTION DETECTED or a crash inside ntdll.dll . Each block also costs more than you asked for: alignment (blocks are 16-byte aligned on 64-bit Windows) plus the header. A million new int calls use far more than 4 MB. The classic heap bugs cpp-norun int p{ new int{ 1 } }; delete p; delete p; // double free: the allocator's lists are corrupted int q{ new int 10 }; q 10 = 5; // one past the end: overwrites the next block's header int r{ new int 10 }; delete r; // wrong form: should be delete int s{ static_cast<int (std::malloc(40)) }; int sum{ s 0 }; // reading uninitialised memory: 0xCDCDCDCD in a debug build The debug heap in an MSVC Debug build checks a lot of this for you: it fills new blocks with 0xCD , freed blocks with 0xDD , surrounds every block with 0xFD guard bytes and checks them when the block is freed. That turns many silent corruptions into an assertion at the delete that found them. This milestone's project builds a small debug heap of your own. Setting pointers to nullptr after delete delete p; does not change p ; it still holds the old address. If p lives on (a member variable, say), set it to nullptr straight away. A second delete nullptr is harmless by definition, and a later use crashes cleanly at address 0 instead of quietly reading freed memory. Check yourself quiz ? What two things does new Enemy{...} do? - Run Enemy 's constructor, then copy the result to the heap + Get memory from the allocator, then run Enemy 's constructor in it - Reserve space on the stack, then register it with the allocator - Get zeroed memory from the allocator; the constructor runs at first use new is allocation plus construction, and delete is destruction plus freeing. malloc only does the first half. ? Why does delete need no size? - It frees memory one byte at a time until it finds a zero - The compiler stores the size in the pointer's upper bits + The allocator stores the block's size in a header next to the block - It always frees a fixed-size page The allocator keeps bookkeeping next to every block it hands out, so given the address it knows how much to release. ? Writing one int past the end of a heap array often does nothing visible at first. Why does it crash later? - The extra int is ignored until the array is printed + It overwrites the next block's header, and the damage is noticed only when the allocator next uses that header - The operating system checks heap writes once a second - The array grows by one element, and the crash comes when it is freed twice The overrun lands in the allocator's bookkeeping or a neighbour's data. Nothing checks it at the time of the write, so the crash comes at a later new or delete . ? What is wrong with int a = new int 8 ; delete a; ? - Nothing, delete works for arrays and single objects alike - It frees only the first element and leaks the other seven - It should be free(a) , because arrays come from malloc + An array allocated with new must be freed with delete The pairs must match exactly: new with delete , new with delete , malloc with free . A mismatch is undefined behaviour, not merely a leak.

title: Heap arrays by hand
body: Manage heap arrays yourself with new and delete , the way std::vector does inside: cpp int makeArray(int count, int fill); void freeArray(int & array); int grow(int old, int oldCount, int newCount, int fill); char duplicate(const char text); - makeArray allocates count ints with new , all set to fill . A count of 0 or less returns nullptr . - freeArray frees the array with delete and sets the caller's pointer to nullptr , so a second call is harmless. - grow allocates a new array of newCount ints, copies over the first min(oldCount, newCount) values, sets any extra elements to fill , frees the old array and returns the new one. old may be nullptr (with oldCount 0). - duplicate returns a heap copy of a C string, zero included, made with new char . The caller frees it with delete . The tests count allocations to make sure nothing leaks and nothing is freed twice.

title: 4.04  Ownership
body: Every heap object needs exactly one owner responsible for freeing it; every other pointer to it only borrows. Owning versus borrowing pointers, transferring ownership, who frees what across a function or library boundary, and writing ownership down so the next reader does not have to guess. Somebody has to free it The heap does not know when an object is no longer needed, so the program must decide, and one part of the program must actually call delete . That part is the object's owner . Every other piece of code that holds a pointer to the object is a borrower : it may use the object, but must not free it and must not use it after the owner does. cpp-norun class Level { public: ~Level() { for (Enemy e : enemies) delete e; } // the Level owns its enemies Enemy spawn() { enemies.push_back(new Enemy{}); return enemies.back(); } private: std::vector<Enemy enemies; }; Enemy target{ level.spawn() }; // the caller borrows: it must not delete target Nothing in the type Enemy says whether a given pointer owns or borrows. Both are just addresses. That is the root of most memory bugs: If two places think they own it If nobody thinks they own it --- --- both delete: a double free nobody deletes: a leak one deletes while the other still uses it: use after free The rule Every heap object has exactly one owner at any moment, and the owner frees it exactly once. Borrowers must not outlive what they borrow. In practice that means a borrowed pointer is used inside one call, or stored only by something that is guaranteed to be destroyed first. Transferring ownership Ownership can move. A function that creates an object and returns a raw pointer usually hands ownership to the caller : cpp-norun // Returns a new Texture. The caller owns it and must delete it. Texture loadTexture(const char path); Ownership can also be handed in : cpp-norun // Takes ownership of enemy : the level will delete it. void Level::adopt(Enemy enemy); And a function can take an object out of a container and give it away: cpp-norun // Removes the enemy from the level and returns it. The caller now owns it. Enemy Level::release(Enemy enemy); With raw pointers, the only place these facts are recorded is the comment . Milestone 5's std::unique_ptr puts them in the type, so the compiler enforces them; for now, every function that deals in owning pointers must say which way ownership goes. Across a library boundary C libraries and the Windows API each follow a documented convention, and reading the documentation for it is part of using any function that returns memory: - Caller allocates, callee fills : you pass a buffer and its size ( GetModuleFileNameW(nullptr, buffer, size) ). You own the buffer throughout. - Callee allocates, caller frees with a named function : FormatMessageW with FORMAT_MESSAGE_ALLOCATE_BUFFER gives you text you must free with LocalFree ; CommandLineToArgvW gives an array you free with LocalFree ; SHGetKnownFolderPath gives a path you free with CoTaskMemFree . - Callee keeps ownership : getenv returns a pointer into the environment that you must not free; GetCommandLineW returns a pointer you must not free. Freeing with the wrong function, or freeing something you only borrowed, is undefined. When the documentation says "the caller must free this with X", that is the ownership rule written down. Containers own their elements A std::vector<Enemy owns its Enemy objects outright: destroying the vector destroys them. A std::vector<Enemy owns only the pointers ; destroying it frees nothing they point at. That is why the Level above needed its own destructor, and why the next milestone replaces std::vector<Enemy with std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Enemy . Copies and ownership A class that owns a raw pointer has a trap: the default copy constructor copies the pointer, so two objects now "own" one block, and both destructors delete it. cpp-norun Level a; Level b{ a }; // b.enemies holds the same pointers as a.enemies // end of scope: b deletes every enemy, then a deletes them again Until milestone 5 shows how to copy or move properly, a class that owns raw pointers should forbid copying: Level(const Level&) = delete; Level& operator=(const Level&) = delete; . Check yourself quiz ? Two parts of a program both delete the same object. Which rule was broken? - Every object must be deleted in the same function that created it - Only the code that created an object may read it + The object had two owners, and every heap object must have exactly one - Objects must be deleted in the reverse order they were created One owner frees; everyone else only borrows. Two owners means a double free. ? A function's documentation says "the returned string must be freed with LocalFree ". Who owns the string? - The function, which frees it the next time it is called + The caller, who must free it with LocalFree - The caller, who may free it with delete or free - Nobody: Windows frees it when the program exits Ownership passes to the caller when the function returns, and memory must go back to the allocator it came from, so delete or free would be a mismatched free. ? Destroying a std::vector<Enemy frees what? - The vector's array and every Enemy it points at + Only the vector's own array of pointers, not the enemies they point at - Nothing, because vectors of pointers must be freed by hand - Only the first Enemy , through the vector's data() pointer A container owns its elements, and here the elements are pointers. The enemies themselves need an owner that deletes them. ? Why should a class that owns raw pointers delete its copy constructor? - Copying a pointer is slow, so it is better forbidden - A copied pointer becomes nullptr , which would break the copy + The default copy copies the pointers, giving two owners that would both delete the same objects - Classes with raw pointers cannot be stored in containers otherwise The compiler's copy duplicates addresses, not objects, so both copies' destructors free the same memory. Deleting the copy (or writing a real one) prevents the double free.

title: An inventory that owns its items
match: An inventory that owns its items
body: An Inventory owns the Item s it holds, as raw pointers. Callers can borrow an item, or take ownership of one out of the inventory: cpp struct Item { static inline int alive{ 0 }; std::string name; int weight; Item(std::string n, int w) : name{ std::move(n) }, weight{ w } { ++alive; } ~Item() { --alive; } }; class Inventory { public: Inventory() = default; ~Inventory(); Inventory(const Inventory&) = delete; Inventory& operator=(const Inventory&) = delete; Item add(const std::string& name, int weight); void adopt(Item item); Item find(const std::string& name); Item release(const std::string& name); bool destroy(const std::string& name); int totalWeight() const; int count() const; }; - add creates an item with new and keeps it; it returns a borrowed pointer. - adopt takes ownership of an item the caller made with new . - find returns a borrowed pointer to the first item with that name, or nullptr . - release removes the first item with that name from the inventory and returns it: the caller now owns it and must delete it. nullptr if there is none. - destroy deletes the first item with that name and returns true, or returns false. - The destructor deletes every item still held. Item::alive lets the tests see whether anything leaked or was deleted twice.

title: 4.05  Leaks and How to Find Them
match: 4.05 Leaks and How to Find Them
body: A leak is memory nobody frees. Why leaks matter in programs that run for hours, how the MSVC debug heap reports them at exit with an allocation number you can break on, heap snapshots in Visual Studio, AddressSanitizer for leaks and use-after-free, and counting your own allocations. What a leak is A leak is heap memory whose owner is gone: the last pointer to it went out of scope or was overwritten, so nothing can ever free it. cpp-norun void loadLevel(const char path) { char data{ new char 1'000'000 }; if (!readFile(path, data)) return; // early return: data is never freed parse(data); delete data; } When a program exits, Windows takes back all its memory, so a leak in a tool that runs for a second does no harm. A leak in a game, an editor or a server that runs for hours does: a small leak every frame grows to gigabytes, the program slows as it pages to disk, and eventually allocation fails. Leaks are also the visible symptom of unclear ownership (lesson 4.04), which causes the more dangerous bugs too. The debug heap's leak report In a Debug build, the MSVC C runtime can list every block still allocated when the program ends. Turn it on at the start of main : cpp-norun define _CRTDBG_MAP_ALLOC include <crtdbg.h int main() { _CrtSetDbgFlag(_CRTDBG_ALLOC_MEM_DF _CRTDBG_LEAK_CHECK_DF); // ... } When the program exits, the Output window shows a report: text Detected memory leaks! Dumping objects - C:\src\level.cpp(14) : {157} normal block at 0x000001C4B2E8F0A0, 40 bytes long. Data: < CD CD CD CD CD CD CD CD CD CD CD CD CD CD CD CD {156} normal block at 0x000001C4B2E91230, 8 bytes long. Data: < 2A 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 Object dump complete. Each entry gives the allocation number in braces, the address, the size and the first bytes. The file and line appear only for malloc -family calls when _CRTDBG_MAP_ALLOC is defined; new shows just the number. The number is the key: allocations are counted in order, so if the program runs the same way again, allocation 157 is the same allocation. Add cpp-norun _CrtSetBreakAlloc(157); at the top of main , run again, and the debugger stops at the moment the leaked block is allocated , with the call stack showing exactly who made it. The first bytes help too: CD CD CD means it was never written at all; 2A 00 00 00 is the int 42. Heap snapshots For a program that keeps running, Visual Studio's Diagnostic Tools window (Debug Windows Show Diagnostic Tools, Memory Usage tab) can take heap snapshots. Take one, play the game for a minute, take another, and view the difference: it lists the types and call stacks of everything allocated in between and not freed. Growth that should not be there is your leak. AddressSanitizer AddressSanitizer (ASan) is a compiler feature that adds checks around every memory access. Turn it on in Visual Studio with Project Properties C/C++ General Enable Address Sanitizer ( /fsanitize=address ). It reports, at the instant they happen: - reads or writes past the end of heap, stack and global arrays; - use after free, and use after return; - double frees and mismatched new / delete . Each report names the bad access, the call stack, and where the memory was allocated and freed. A program under ASan runs about twice as slow, so it is for testing, not shipping. On Linux and with Clang, ASan also reports leaks at exit (LeakSanitizer). !tip Run your tests and a play session under ASan regularly. Bugs that "work" in a normal build, such as reading one past the end, show up immediately. Counting your own allocations When tools are not available, count. A class can track how many of its objects are alive with a static counter: cpp-norun struct Tracked { static inline int alive{ 0 }; Tracked() { ++alive; } Tracked(const Tracked&) { ++alive; } ~Tracked() { --alive; } }; If Tracked::alive keeps growing during a level that should be steady, something is creating them without destroying them. Tests can check it: create a level, destroy it, and check the count is back to where it started. Games often keep counters like this per system and show them on a debug overlay. Fixing leaks for good Finding one leak is debugging; not writing the next one is design. The real fix is to make freeing automatic so an early return or an exception cannot skip it. That is RAII, the first lesson of the next milestone: cpp-norun void loadLevel(const char path) { std::vector<char data(1'000'000); // freed automatically on every path out if (!readFile(path, data.data())) return; parse(data.data()); } Check yourself quiz ? Why is a leak in a long-running game more serious than in a short command-line tool? - Windows does not reclaim a game's memory when it exits + A game that leaks a little every frame keeps growing for hours until it slows down or runs out of memory - Games use a different heap that cannot be freed - Leaks are only reported for programs that run longer than a minute Windows reclaims everything when any program exits, so a short tool barely notices. A leak per frame adds up to gigabytes over a long session. ? The leak report shows {157} normal block . How do you find the code that allocated it? - Search the source code for the number 157 - Set a breakpoint on line 157 of the file that leaked + Call _CrtSetBreakAlloc(157) early in main and rerun - Look at address 157 in the debugger's Memory window 157 is the allocation's sequence number, not a line or an address. As long as the program runs the same way, the debugger stops when allocation 157 happens. ? A leaked block's data shows CD CD CD CD . What does that tell you? - The block was freed twice + The block was allocated but never written to - The block was written past its end - The block came from malloc rather than new The debug heap fills new blocks with 0xCD ("clean"). Seeing it in a leaked block means nobody ever stored anything there. ? Which pair of bugs does AddressSanitizer report at the moment they happen? - Memory leaks and slow allocations - Uninitialised variables and integer overflow - Data races and deadlocks + Heap buffer overflow and use after free AddressSanitizer catches overflows (heap, stack and global), use after free, use after return, double free and mismatched new / delete . Races are ThreadSanitizer's job, and uninitialised reads are MemorySanitizer's.

title: Reading a leak report
where: 4.05 Leaks and How to Find Them
body: The MSVC debug heap prints leaks like this when a Debug build exits (lesson 4.05): text Detected memory leaks! Dumping objects - C:\src\level.cpp(14) : {157} normal block at 0x000001C4B2E8F0A0, 40 bytes long. Data: < CD CD CD CD CD CD CD CD CD CD CD CD CD CD CD CD {156} normal block at 0x000001C4B2E91230, 8 bytes long. Data: < 2A 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 Object dump complete. Turn such a report into data a tool can sort and summarise: cpp struct Leak { int allocation; std::uint64_t address; std::size_t size; std::string file; // empty when the report has no file int line; // 0 when there is no file std::vector<std::uint8_t data; }; std::vector<Leak parseLeakReport(const std::string& report); std::size_t totalLeaked(const std::vector<Leak & leaks); std::vector<int neverWritten(const std::vector<Leak & leaks); - parseLeakReport finds every block line: an optional file(line) : part, then {number} normal block at 0xADDRESS, SIZE bytes long. The data line that follows it gives the first bytes as hex pairs after the . Lines that are not block lines or data lines are ignored. Leaks are returned in the order they appear. - totalLeaked adds up the sizes. - neverWritten lists the allocation numbers of leaks whose shown data bytes are all 0xCD (memory that was allocated and never written), in increasing order.
