title: A debug heap of your own
match: A debug heap of your own
where: Lifetime: Stack, Heap and Static projects
body: Build a small version of what the MSVC debug heap does (lesson 4.03): fill new memory with a pattern, surround every block with guard bytes, check them on free, keep freed blocks aside to catch writes after free, catch double frees and frees of unknown pointers, and report leaks. cpp enum class Problem { InvalidFree, DoubleFree, Underrun, Overrun, WriteAfterFree }; struct Report { Problem problem; int allocation; }; class DebugHeap { public: static constexpr std::uint8_t CLEAN{ 0xCD }, DEAD{ 0xDD }, GUARD{ 0xFD }; static constexpr std::size_t GUARD_BYTES{ 4 }; ~DebugHeap(); void allocate(std::size_t size); void release(void p); void checkFreed(); std::vector<int leaks() const; const std::vector<Report & problems() const; std::size_t bytesInUse() const; }; - allocate gets GUARD_BYTES + size + GUARD_BYTES bytes from std::malloc , fills the guards with GUARD and the user area with CLEAN , and returns a pointer to the user area. Allocations are numbered 1, 2, 3, ... in order (0 bytes is allowed and still gets a number). - release : - a pointer this heap never returned: report InvalidFree with allocation 0; - a block already released: report DoubleFree with its number; - otherwise check the guard before the block ( Underrun if any byte changed) and after it ( Overrun ), fill the user area with DEAD , and keep the block in quarantine instead of freeing it. - checkFreed looks at every quarantined block: if any user byte is no longer DEAD , report WriteAfterFree (once per block per check). - leaks lists the numbers of blocks never released, in increasing order; bytesInUse adds up their sizes. - problems returns every report so far, in the order they happened. - The destructor really frees every block, quarantined or not. The tests deliberately write just outside blocks and into freed blocks. That is safe here only because the guard bytes and the quarantine are your own memory.

title: 5.01  RAII
body: Resource Acquisition Is Initialisation - tie every resource to an object whose destructor releases it, and C++ frees it on every path out of a scope, early returns and exceptions included. Writing small owning wrappers, scope guards, and why this one idea removes most leaks. The problem with "remember to free" Every resource that must be given back, heap memory, a file, a lock, a Windows HANDLE , a texture on the graphics card, needs its release code to run on every path out of the code that acquired it: cpp-norun bool saveGame(const char path, const Game& game) { char buffer{ new char game.saveSize() }; std::FILE file{ std::fopen(path, "wb") }; if (!file) { delete buffer; return false; } if (!game.serialise(buffer)) { std::fclose(file); delete buffer; return false; } std::fwrite(buffer, 1, game.saveSize(), file); std::fclose(file); delete buffer; return true; } Three exits, three copies of the clean-up, and if serialise throws an exception, none of them run. Add a fourth exit next month and forget one line, and you have a leak. Let the destructor do it C++ guarantees one thing absolutely: when an object goes out of scope, by reaching the closing brace, by return , by break , or because an exception passes through, its destructor runs . So put the release in a destructor: cpp-norun class File { public: File(const char path, const char mode) : handle{ std::fopen(path, mode) } {} ~File() { if (handle) std::fclose(handle); } File(const File&) = delete; File& operator=(const File&) = delete; std::FILE get() const { return handle; } explicit operator bool() const { return handle != nullptr; } private: std::FILE handle; }; bool saveGame(const char path, const Game& game) { std::vector<char buffer(game.saveSize()); // RAII for memory File file{ path, "wb" }; // RAII for the file if (!file) return false; if (!game.serialise(buffer.data())) return false; std::fwrite(buffer.data(), 1, buffer.size(), file.get()); return true; } // both released here, on every path This is RAII : Resource Acquisition Is Initialisation . The name is clumsy; the idea is simple: acquire in the constructor, release in the destructor , and let scope decide when. RAII is everywhere in the standard library You already use it constantly: Class Owns Releases with --- --- --- std::vector , std::string heap memory delete inside std::unique_ptr one heap object delete (next lesson) std::fstream a file closing it std::lock_guard , std::scoped_lock a mutex lock unlocking std::jthread a thread joining it The rule of thumb for modern C++: ordinary code never calls delete , free , fclose or CloseHandle directly . Those calls belong inside a destructor, written once. Destruction order Objects in a scope are destroyed in the reverse order they were created. That is usually exactly right: things created later may depend on things created earlier. cpp-norun { Device device{}; // created first Texture texture{ device }; // uses device } // texture destroyed first, then device Members of a class are destroyed in reverse order of declaration, after the class's own destructor body runs. Copying an RAII object The File class deletes its copy constructor and copy assignment. If it did not, copying a File would copy the FILE , and both copies would close it (lesson 4.04's double owner). An RAII class must decide what copying means: forbid it (most handles), do a deep copy ( std::vector copies its elements), or share with reference counting ( std::shared_ptr ). Lesson 5.05 shows how to let it be moved instead. Scope guards Sometimes the "resource" is just an action that must happen at the end: restore a setting, pop a state, log an exit. A tiny class that runs a lambda in its destructor covers every such case: cpp-norun template <typename F class ScopeExit { public: explicit ScopeExit(F f) : action{ std::move(f) } {} ~ScopeExit() { if (active) action(); } void dismiss() { active = false; } ScopeExit(const ScopeExit&) = delete; ScopeExit& operator=(const ScopeExit&) = delete; private: F action; bool active{ true }; }; void drawDebug(Renderer& r) { r.pushState(); ScopeExit restore{ & { r.popState(); } }; // runs however we leave // ... draw, possibly returning early ... } dismiss() cancels it, which is how "commit or roll back" code works: set up a guard that undoes a change, do the work, and dismiss the guard only once everything has succeeded. Check yourself quiz ? What does C++ guarantee that makes RAII work? - The garbage collector frees every object that is no longer used - Every new is matched with a delete by the compiler + A destructor runs on every way out of its object's scope - Destructors run when the program exits, in any order C++ has no garbage collector, and it does not pair new with delete for you. What it does promise is that a scoped object's destructor runs on return , break , exceptions and falling off the end. ? Two RAII objects a and b are created in that order in one scope. Which is destroyed first? - a , because it was created first + b , because destruction runs in reverse order of creation - Whichever is smaller in memory - Both at once; the order is unspecified Locals are destroyed in reverse order, so something created later, which may depend on an earlier object, is cleaned up before it. ? Why must an RAII class that wraps a FILE do something about copying? - A FILE cannot be copied at all, so the class would not compile + The default copy would copy the pointer, so two objects would both close the same file - Copying would open the file a second time - Copying would make the file read-only The compiler's copy duplicates the pointer, not the open file. Delete the copy operations, or define what a copy means. ? What is a scope guard's dismiss() for? - Running the clean-up action early, before the scope ends - Running the clean-up action a second time if the first failed - Moving the guard to another scope + Cancelling the clean-up action, for commit-or-roll-back code, once the work has succeeded A guard rolls back if the scope is left early. When everything went well you dismiss it, so the roll-back does not happen.

title: Wrapping a resource
body: A pretend C library hands out numbered resources that must be closed. The library is given; it counts how many are open so the tests can see leaks. cpp namespace lib { inline int openCount{ 0 }; inline int nextId{ 1 }; inline int open() { ++openCount; return nextId++; } inline void close(int id) { if (id 0) --openCount; } } Write two RAII classes: cpp class Resource { public: Resource(); ~Resource(); Resource(const Resource&) = delete; Resource& operator=(const Resource&) = delete; int id() const; }; template <typename F class ScopeExit { public: explicit ScopeExit(F action); ~ScopeExit(); void dismiss(); }; - Resource opens one resource in its constructor and closes it in its destructor. id() returns its number. - ScopeExit runs its action when it is destroyed, unless dismiss() was called. Copying it is not allowed. The tests leave scopes by falling off the end, by return and by exceptions, and check that every resource was closed exactly once.

title: 5.02  unique_ptr
body: std::unique_ptr is a pointer that owns its object and deletes it when it goes away. It cannot be copied, only moved, so ownership is written in the type. make_unique, get, release and reset, unique_ptr in containers and as return values, and custom deleters for FILE , HANDLE and anything else. Ownership in the type std::unique_ptr<T (from <memory ) is RAII for one heap object. It holds a pointer and deletes it in its destructor: cpp-norun include <memory { std::unique_ptr<Enemy boss{ std::make_unique<Enemy ("Golem", 500) }; boss- attack(); // used like a pointer Enemy& e{ boss }; } // boss deleted here, automatically std::make_unique<T (args...) does the new for you and passes the arguments to the constructor. You never write new or delete yourself. A unique_ptr is the same size as a raw pointer and compiles to the same code; using it costs nothing at run time. It can be moved, not copied There is exactly one owner, so a unique_ptr cannot be copied . That is the whole point: the compiler now enforces lesson 4.04's rule. cpp-norun std::unique_ptr<Enemy a{ std::make_unique<Enemy () }; std::unique_ptr<Enemy b{ a }; // error: copying is deleted std::unique_ptr<Enemy c{ std::move(a) }; // fine: ownership moves to c, a is now empty (nullptr) Moving transfers ownership, and the source is left holding nullptr . Ownership transfers that lesson 4.04 could only describe in comments are now visible in the code: cpp-norun std::unique_ptr<Texture loadTexture(const char path); // the caller receives ownership void Level::adopt(std::unique_ptr<Enemy enemy); // the level takes ownership level.adopt(std::move(enemy)); // and the call site shows it Returning a unique_ptr from a function needs no std::move ; returning a local moves it automatically. Getting at the pointer Call Does --- --- p.get() returns the raw pointer, still owned by p (for borrowing) p.reset() deletes the object now and leaves p empty p.reset(q) deletes the old object and takes ownership of raw pointer q p.release() gives up ownership without deleting : returns the raw pointer, and you must free it if (p) true when it holds an object get() is how you pass the object to a function that only borrows it: draw(boss.get()) , or better draw( boss) with a reference parameter. release() is rare; it is for handing ownership to code that only understands raw pointers. !warning Never create two unique_ptr s from the same raw pointer, and never delete what get() returned. Both mean two owners. In containers std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Enemy owns its enemies: removing an element deletes that enemy, and destroying the vector deletes them all. That replaces the hand-written destructor of lesson 4.04's Level : cpp-norun class Level { public: Enemy spawn() { enemies.push_back(std::make_unique<Enemy ()); return enemies.back().get(); // borrowed pointer for the caller } private: std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Enemy enemies; // no destructor needed }; And because a unique_ptr cannot be copied, the class automatically becomes non-copyable but movable, which is exactly right. Arrays std::unique_ptr<int buffer{ std::make_unique<int (1000) }; owns an array and uses delete , with buffer i for indexing. In practice std::vector is almost always better; the array form is for interfacing with code that wants a raw buffer. Custom deleters Not everything is freed with delete . A unique_ptr can call any function instead, given as a second template argument. The neatest way is a small struct: cpp-norun struct CloseFile { void operator()(std::FILE f) const { std::fclose(f); } }; using FilePtr = std::unique_ptr<std::FILE, CloseFile ; FilePtr file{ std::fopen("save.dat", "rb") }; // fclose runs automatically if (!file) return false; std::fread(buffer, 1, size, file.get()); The same pattern wraps any C or Windows resource: cpp-norun struct CloseHandleDeleter { void operator()(HANDLE h) const { if (h && h != INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE) CloseHandle(h); } }; using UniqueHandle = std::unique_ptr<void, CloseHandleDeleter ; // HANDLE is a void struct LocalFreeDeleter { void operator()(void p) const { LocalFree(p); } }; Because the deleter struct is empty, the unique_ptr stays the size of one pointer. Check yourself quiz ? Why can a std::unique_ptr not be copied? - Copying it would be too slow, so moves are used instead + It is the sole owner, and a copy would create two owners that both delete the object - Its pointer is const , so it cannot be read - It can be copied, but only with std::copy Making it move-only puts "exactly one owner" into the type: the compiler refuses any code that would make a second owner. ? After auto b = std::move(a); with a a unique_ptr , what does a hold? - The same pointer as b , so both point at the object - A dangling pointer to the old object + nullptr , because ownership moved to b - A copy of the object Moving transfers ownership: b takes the pointer and a is left empty, so only one of them will ever delete the object. ? What is the difference between p.reset() and p.release() ? - reset gives up ownership without deleting; release deletes the object + reset deletes the object; release gives up ownership and returns the pointer - They are the same, except that release also returns the old pointer - reset sets the object to its default value; release deletes it Both leave p empty. Calling release() and ignoring the result leaks the object, because nobody owns it any more; reset() is the one that frees. ? How do you make a unique_ptr that closes a FILE instead of deleting it? - Call fclose on p.get() before the unique_ptr is destroyed - Use std::unique_ptr<FILE , which closes files - Wrap it in a std::shared_ptr , which knows about files + Give it a custom deleter whose operator() calls fclose The deleter, given as the second template argument, decides what "free" means. With fclose as the deleter, the file is closed on every path out, and there is no second close.

title: Owning with unique_ptr
body: Rewrite lesson 4.04's ownership with std::unique_ptr , so the types say who owns what and no code calls delete : cpp struct Enemy { static inline int alive{ 0 }; std::string name; int health; Enemy(std::string n, int h) : name{ std::move(n) }, health{ h } { ++alive; } ~Enemy() { --alive; } }; std::unique_ptr<Enemy makeEnemy(const std::string& name, int health); class Level { public: Enemy spawn(const std::string& name, int health); void adopt(std::unique_ptr<Enemy enemy); std::unique_ptr<Enemy release(const std::string& name); int removeDead(); int count() const; }; struct CloseHandle { void operator()(int handle) const; }; using UniqueHandle = std::unique_ptr<int, CloseHandle ; inline int handlesOpen{ 0 }; UniqueHandle openHandle(int value); - makeEnemy creates one with std::make_unique . - Level keeps a std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Enemy . spawn creates an enemy and returns a borrowed raw pointer; adopt takes ownership of one; release removes the first enemy with that name and hands its ownership back (empty if there is none); removeDead destroys every enemy whose health is 0 or less and returns how many. - openHandle allocates an int holding value with new , adds 1 to handlesOpen and returns it in a UniqueHandle . The custom deleter CloseHandle subtracts 1 from handlesOpen and deletes the int.

title: 5.03  shared_ptr and weak_ptr
body: std::shared_ptr shares ownership through a reference count kept in a control block, and deletes the object when the last owner goes. What it costs, the cycles that make it leak, std::weak_ptr for observing without owning, and when shared ownership is really the right answer. Several owners Sometimes an object really has no single owner: a texture used by several materials, where whichever material is destroyed last should free it. std::shared_ptr<T handles that case. It keeps a reference count , the number of shared_ptr s currently pointing at the object, and deletes the object when the count reaches zero. cpp-norun std::shared_ptr<Texture stone{ std::make_shared<Texture ("stone.png") }; // count 1 { std::shared_ptr<Texture copy{ stone }; // copying is allowed: count 2 std::cout << stone.use_count() << '\n'; // 2 } // copy destroyed: count 1 stone.reset(); // count 0: the texture is deleted The control block The count has to live somewhere every copy can reach, so a shared_ptr is two pointers: one to the object and one to a control block holding the counts. text shared_ptr a ---+-- control block: strong 2, weak 1 shared_ptr b ---+-- Texture object std::make_shared allocates the control block and the object in one heap block, which is faster and uses less memory than std::shared_ptr<T (new T) . Always use it. What it costs - Every shared_ptr is 16 bytes, twice a raw pointer. - Copying one changes the count with an atomic instruction (it must be safe across threads), which is noticeably slower than copying a pointer. Pass a shared_ptr by const& , or pass the object by reference, when the function does not need to keep a share. - It hides who really controls the object's lifetime. When anyone can keep it alive, nobody knows when it dies. So unique_ptr is the default, and shared_ptr is for when ownership is genuinely shared. Cycles leak Reference counting has one blind spot. If two objects hold shared_ptr s to each other, each keeps the other's count above zero for ever: cpp-norun struct Player; struct Team { std::vector<std::shared_ptr<Player members; }; struct Player { std::shared_ptr<Team team; }; { auto team{ std::make_shared<Team () }; auto ada{ std::make_shared<Player () }; team- members.push_back(ada); // team owns ada ada- team = team; // ada owns team } // the locals are gone, but team's count is 1 (from ada) and ada's is 1 (from team): both leak No leak checker running over the heap sees anything wrong while the program runs; the memory is still "owned". Cycles of shared_ptr are the most common leak in modern C++ code. weak_ptr: observe without owning std::weak_ptr<T points at an object managed by shared_ptr s without adding to its strong count. It cannot be dereferenced directly. To use the object you call lock() , which gives a shared_ptr if the object still exists and an empty one if it has gone: cpp-norun struct Player { std::weak_ptr<Team team; }; // a back-reference that does not own if (std::shared_ptr<Team t{ ada- team.lock() }) // still alive? t- announce("Ada scored"); else / the team was disbanded /; The rule for any parent and child: the parent owns the child ( shared_ptr or, better, unique_ptr ), and the child observes the parent ( weak_ptr , or a raw pointer when the child can never outlive the parent). weak_ptr also solves lesson 1.05's dangling pointer problem for shared objects: a cache, a list of listeners or a target reference can hold weak_ptr s and find out cleanly that the object is gone, rather than following a dangling address. The control block stays alive while any weak_ptr refers to it, so lock() can always answer, even though the object itself was destroyed. When shared ownership is right - Resources used by several independent owners with no natural single parent: textures, sounds, fonts in a cache. - Objects handed to work running on other threads, where the caller may finish first. - Graphs where nodes are added and removed from many places. Even then, ask first whether one central owner (a TextureCache holding unique_ptr s and handing out raw pointers or handles) would be simpler. It usually is. Check yourself quiz ? When does a shared_ptr delete its object? + When the last shared_ptr owning it is destroyed or reset - When the first shared_ptr owning it is destroyed - When the program exits, like a global variable - When no weak_ptr refers to it any more Each owner adds one to the strong count and removes one when it goes; at zero the object is deleted. Weak pointers do not keep it alive. ? Why is std::make_shared better than shared_ptr<T (new T) ? - It makes the object thread-safe - It avoids the control block altogether + It allocates the object and the control block in one heap block instead of two - It lets the object be copied without a reference count Every shared_ptr needs a control block for the counts. With new T that is a second allocation; make_shared puts both in one. ? Two objects hold shared_ptr s to each other. What happens when everything else lets go of them? - Both are deleted, because the counts notice the cycle - The first one created is deleted, which then deletes the other + Neither count reaches zero, so both leak - The program crashes with a double delete Each keeps the other's count at one, forever. Break the cycle with a weak_ptr in one direction. ? How do you use the object a weak_ptr refers to? - Dereference it directly with or - - Call get() , which returns a raw pointer to it - Cast it to a shared_ptr with static_cast + Call lock() and check the shared_ptr it returns A weak_ptr cannot be dereferenced, because the object might already be gone. lock() returns an empty shared_ptr if it is, or a temporary owner if it is alive.

title: A cache that does not keep things alive
match: A cache that does not keep things alive
body: A texture cache should hand out the same texture to everyone who asks for it while anyone is using it, but must not keep textures alive by itself. Build it with std::shared_ptr for the users and std::weak_ptr inside the cache: cpp struct Texture { static inline int loads{ 0 }; static inline int alive{ 0 }; std::string name; explicit Texture(std::string n) : name{ std::move(n) } { ++loads; ++alive; } ~Texture() { --alive; } }; class TextureCache { public: std::shared_ptr<Texture get(const std::string& name); bool isLoaded(const std::string& name) const; int prune(); std::size_t entries() const; }; - get returns the texture if it is still alive somewhere; otherwise it creates a new one with std::make_shared , remembers it as a weak_ptr , and returns it. - isLoaded is true while some shared_ptr still keeps that texture alive. - prune forgets entries whose texture is gone and returns how many it removed. - entries is the number of names the cache currently remembers.

title: 5.04  Views That Do Not Own
body: std::span and std::string_view are a pointer and a length bundled together - a cheap, safe way to borrow a sequence without copying or owning it. Passing them to functions, slicing them, and the one way they go wrong - outliving what they view. A pointer and a length C-style functions take a pointer and a count as two separate parameters, and getting the count wrong is a classic bug (lesson 2.01). C++20's std::span<T bundles the two into one small value: cpp-norun include <span int sum(std::span<const int values) { int total{ 0 }; for (int v : values) total += v; // range-for works: it knows its length return total; } int a { 1, 2, 3 }; std::vector<int v{ 4, 5, 6, 7 }; std::array<int, 2 s{ 8, 9 }; sum(a); // a C array: length taken from the type sum(v); // a vector sum(s); // an array sum({ v.data() + 1, 2 }); // any pointer and count: 5 + 6 One function serves every container whose elements sit consecutively in memory, without templates and without copying. std::span<const int borrows read-only; std::span<int lets the function change the elements. A span is 16 bytes: a pointer and a size. Passing it by value is the right way, as cheap as passing two integers. Slicing for free Taking part of a span makes a new span over the same memory: Call Gives --- --- s.first(n) the first n elements s.last(n) the last n s.subspan(offset, count) count elements starting at offset s.size() , s.empty() , s.data() length, emptiness, the pointer Parsing a packet or a file becomes a matter of slicing: read a header from buffer.first(8) , then carry on with buffer.subspan(8) . cpp-norun std::span<const std::byte rest{ packet }; const auto header{ rest.first(8) }; rest = rest.subspan(8); string_view std::string_view is the same idea for text: a pointer to characters and a length, with no ownership and no zero terminator required . Every function that only reads a string should take one: cpp-norun bool startsWithHash(std::string_view line) { return !line.empty() && line.front() == ' '; } startsWithHash(" comment"); // a literal: no std::string is built startsWithHash(someStdString); // a std::string: no copy startsWithHash(std::string_view{ buf, 12 }); // twelve chars from the middle of a buffer substr on a string_view returns another view, not a new string, so splitting a line into words allocates nothing. !warning A string_view is not necessarily followed by a zero. Never pass view.data() to a C function that expects a C string; build a std::string first. The one way views go wrong A view borrows. It must not outlive what it views, and nothing checks that it does not: cpp-norun std::string_view name() { std::string full{ "Ada Lovelace" }; return full; // the view points into full, which dies here } std::string_view first{ std::string("temporary") }; // dangles at the end of the line std::vector<int v{ 1, 2, 3 }; std::span<int view{ v }; v.push_back(4); // may reallocate: view now points at freed memory These are lesson 1.05's dangling pointers wearing a nicer type. The rules that avoid them: - Use views as function parameters , where the caller's object is guaranteed to outlive the call. This is their main job and is always safe. - Be careful storing views in members or returning them. Only do it when the viewed data clearly lives longer, such as string literals or a buffer owned by the same object. - Do not keep a view into a container that may grow. Choosing parameter types Parameter When --- --- std::span<const T read a sequence of any length std::span<T change elements in place (but not the length) std::string_view read text const std::vector<T & you specifically need vector features std::vector<T by value you keep your own copy (move into it) std::string by value you keep your own copy of the text Check yourself quiz ? What does a std::span hold? - A copy of the elements it was made from + A pointer to the first element and the number of elements - A pointer to the container it was made from - A begin pointer, an end pointer and a capacity A span is just a pointer and a length. It owns nothing and copies nothing. ? Why is a std::span passed by value rather than by reference? - Passing it by reference would copy all the elements + It is just a pointer and a size, so copying it is cheap - A std::span cannot be passed by reference - Passing by value makes the elements read-only A span is about 16 bytes. Copying it copies two small values, not the data, so a reference to it would only add an extra level of indirection. ? Why must you not pass a string_view 's data() to a C function expecting a C string? - data() returns a std::string , not a char - C functions cannot read memory owned by a C++ object + A string_view need not be followed by a zero byte, so the function would read past its end - data() is only valid inside the function that made the view A view can be a slice out of the middle of a longer string, so the byte after its last character can be anything. C functions read until they find a zero. ? A span views a vector, then elements are pushed onto the vector. What can go wrong? - The span grows with the vector and now includes the new elements - Nothing, a span always follows its vector + The vector may move its elements to a new block, leaving the span pointing at freed memory - The span becomes read-only A view does not know when what it views changes. If push_back reallocates, the span's pointer dangles, the same bug as a raw pointer into a vector.

title: Parsing with views
body: Read text and binary data without copying any of it, using std::string_view and std::span : cpp std::vector<std::string_view splitWords(std::string_view text); std::uint32_t checksum(std::span<const std::uint8_t bytes); std::optional<std::span<const std::uint8_t nextField(std::span<const std::uint8_t & rest); - splitWords returns the words of text : runs of characters separated by spaces. The returned views must point into text , not at copies. - checksum adds up all the bytes, then multiplies by 31 and adds the next byte: start at 0, and for each byte sum = sum 31 + byte , wrapping as std::uint32_t does. - nextField reads one length-prefixed field from the front of rest : one byte giving the length n , then n bytes of data. It returns a view of the data (pointing into the original buffer) and moves rest past the field. If rest is empty, or too short for the length it announces, it returns std::nullopt and leaves rest unchanged.

title: 5.05  Copy and Move for Owning Types
match: 5.05 Copy and Move for Owning Types
body: A class that owns memory must decide what copying and moving mean. The rule of five, a deep copy, a move that steals the pointer and leaves the source empty, copy-and-swap for safe assignment, self-assignment, and the rule of zero - letting members that already own do it all. The default copy is a shallow copy Here is a minimal owning buffer: cpp-norun class Buffer { public: explicit Buffer(std::size_t n) : data{ new int n {} }, size{ n } {} ~Buffer() { delete data; } private: int data; std::size_t size; }; The compiler writes a copy constructor for it automatically, copying each member. Copying data copies the address , so two Buffer s end up owning one array, and the second destructor deletes it again. A class that owns a resource must write, or delete, the special member functions itself. The rule of five A class that needs a destructor almost certainly needs all five of these: Function Called when --- --- destructor ~Buffer() the object dies copy constructor Buffer(const Buffer&) a new object is made as a copy copy assignment operator=(const Buffer&) an existing object is overwritten with a copy move constructor Buffer(Buffer&&) noexcept a new object takes over a temporary or std::move d one move assignment operator=(Buffer&&) noexcept an existing object takes over another Deep copy A copy that makes its own array and copies the values: cpp-norun Buffer(const Buffer& other) : data{ new int other.size }, size{ other.size } { std::copy(other.data, other.data + other.size, data); } Now each Buffer owns its own memory, and the destructors never collide. Move: steal the pointer Copying a large buffer just to destroy the original straight away (returning from a function, putting a temporary into a vector) is wasteful. A move takes the other object's pointer and leaves it empty: cpp-norun Buffer(Buffer&& other) noexcept : data{ other.data }, size{ other.size } { other.data = nullptr; // the source must no longer own it other.size = 0; } No allocation, no copying of elements: two pointer assignments. The moved-from object must stay valid but empty , because its destructor still runs (and delete nullptr is harmless). Mark moves noexcept . std::vector only moves its elements when it grows if their move cannot throw; otherwise it copies them to stay safe, and all the benefit is lost. Assignment with copy-and-swap Assignment must release what the object already owns, copy the new contents, and survive a = a . Written by hand it is easy to get wrong. The copy-and-swap idiom does it in two lines: cpp-norun friend void swap(Buffer& a, Buffer& b) noexcept { std::swap(a.data, b.data); std::swap(a.size, b.size); } Buffer& operator=(Buffer other) noexcept // taken BY VALUE: copied or moved in by the caller { swap( this, other); // take its contents; give it ours return this; // other's destructor frees our old memory } Taking the parameter by value means the compiler copies or moves into it as appropriate, so this one function serves as both copy and move assignment. If the copy throws (out of memory), it throws before this is touched, so the object is never left half-assigned. And a = a simply copies and swaps, harmlessly. The rule of zero All of that is how std::vector and std::unique_ptr are written, and that is the point: if every member manages itself, the class needs none of the five . Write Buffer with a vector and the compiler's defaults are all correct: cpp-norun class Buffer { public: explicit Buffer(std::size_t n) : data(n) {} private: std::vector<int data; // copy, move and destroy are all handled }; A class holding a std::unique_ptr member is automatically movable and not copyable; one holding std::shared_ptr copies by sharing. So the practical rule is: - Rule of zero for ordinary classes: no destructor, no copy or move functions; members own. - Rule of five only in the small number of classes whose job is to own one raw resource, so that everything else can follow the rule of zero. Check yourself quiz ? What goes wrong when a class owning a raw new array uses the default copy constructor? + Both objects hold the same pointer, so both destructors delete the same array - The compiler refuses to generate a copy constructor for such a class - The copy gets a new array but the elements are not copied - The copy gets a nullptr and crashes when it is used The default copy is a shallow copy of the members, so the pointer is duplicated, not the array. That is a double delete, and a change through one is seen by the other. ? What must a move constructor do to the object it moved from? - Delete the object's array, so no memory is left behind - Leave it untouched, still pointing at the array + Leave it empty, with its pointer set to nullptr - Make a deep copy of the array for it The moved-from object must stay valid but own nothing, so its destructor frees nothing. If it kept the pointer, both destructors would free it; if the move freed it, the new object would dangle. ? Why should a move constructor be noexcept ? - noexcept makes the move run faster - The compiler refuses to call a move constructor that may throw + std::vector only moves elements when growing if the move cannot throw; otherwise it copies them To keep its strong exception guarantee, a growing vector falls back to copying unless the move is marked noexcept . ? What is the rule of zero? - A class that owns memory should define none of the five special functions - A move constructor must leave zero bytes in the source object + If every member manages its own resource, the class needs no destructor and no copy or move functions of its own - A class should have zero raw pointers, owning or not Let members like std::vector , std::string and std::unique_ptr do the owning, and the compiler-generated functions are already right. A class that owns a raw pointer itself still needs the rule of five.

body: Most strings in a program are short: names, keys, words. Allocating heap memory for each is slow, so real string classes (MSVC's std::string included) keep short strings inside the object and only use the heap for long ones. This is the small string optimisation . Build one: cpp class SmallString { public: static constexpr std::size_t INLINE_CAPACITY{ 15 }; SmallString(); SmallString(const char text); ~SmallString(); SmallString(const SmallString& other); SmallString(SmallString&& other) noexcept; SmallString& operator=(SmallString other) noexcept; friend void swap(SmallString& a, SmallString& b) noexcept; void append(std::string_view more); std::size_t size() const; std::size_t capacity() const; bool isInline() const; const char c_str() const; std::string_view view() const; bool operator==(std::string_view other) const; }; - A string of up to 15 characters is stored in a 16-byte array inside the object (15 characters and the zero). isInline() is true and c_str() points inside the object itself. - A longer string is stored on the heap with new char . capacity() is how many characters fit without allocating again (for an inline string, 15). - append adds characters. When they no longer fit, it moves the text to a new heap block with capacity at least max(2 capacity, new size) , copies the text over and frees any old heap block. - c_str() is always zero-terminated. - Copying makes an independent copy (inline when it fits); moving a heap string steals its block and leaves the source an empty inline string; moving an inline string copies its characters. - Every heap block is freed exactly once.

title: 6.01  How an Allocator Works
body: Inside malloc and new - big regions carved into blocks, headers that record each block's size, free lists, first fit, splitting and joining blocks, alignment, fragmentation, and the size classes that make modern allocators fast. Carving up a region An allocator starts with a large region of memory it got from the operating system, and hands out pieces of it. The simplest possible design keeps the region as a sequence of blocks , each with a small header in front of it: text hdr 32 used 32 bytes hdr 64 free 64 bytes hdr 48 used 48 bytes hdr 880 free ... Each header records the block's size and whether it is in use. Because the next header is right after this block, the headers form an implicit list that walks the whole region: from any header, add its size to find the next. Allocating: find a free block To allocate n bytes: 1. Round n up so the block keeps the alignment the allocator promises (16 bytes on 64-bit Windows). 2. Find a free block that is big enough. First fit takes the first one found; best fit searches for the smallest that fits. 3. If the block is much bigger than needed, split it: the front part becomes the allocation, the rest becomes a new, smaller free block with its own header. 4. Mark it used and return the address just after its header. Freeing: join neighbours To free a pointer, step back to its header (pointer minus header size) and mark the block free. Then coalesce : if the next block, or the previous one, is free too, merge them into one larger free block. Without coalescing, a region that has been fully freed would still be chopped into small pieces, and a large request would fail even though all the memory is free. Fragmentation Even with coalescing, a long-running program can end up with plenty of free memory in total but no single free block large enough: text used 16 free 16 used 16 free 16 used 16 free 16 ... 1 MB free in total, largest block 16 bytes This is fragmentation : free space scattered between blocks still in use. A request for 64 bytes now fails, or forces the allocator to ask the operating system for more. Games that allocate and free many differently sized objects every frame suffer from it, which is one reason they use the arena and pool allocators of the next two lessons for their per-frame and per-object memory. Free lists and size classes Walking every block to find a free one gets slow with millions of blocks. Real allocators keep free lists : linked lists of only the free blocks, with the next pointers stored inside the free blocks themselves (their memory is unused, so it costs nothing). Modern allocators go further and keep separate free lists per size class : one for 16-byte blocks, one for 32, 48, 64, and so on. A request is rounded up to its class and served from that list's head in a few instructions, with no searching at all. Only large requests fall back to the slow general path. The Windows heap's Low Fragmentation Heap , which is switched on automatically for frequently used sizes, works this way, as do jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc. Design Allocate Free Fragmentation --- --- --- --- implicit list, first fit walk until a fit mark and coalesce moderate explicit free list walk free blocks only push on the list moderate size classes pop from the class's list push on the class's list low for small sizes, some wasted space from rounding Alignment Every pointer the allocator returns must be aligned for any type ( alignof(std::max_align_t) , 16 on 64-bit Windows). So block sizes and header sizes are kept multiples of 16, and the arithmetic is "round up to a multiple": cpp-norun std::uintptr_t alignUp(std::uintptr_t value, std::uintptr_t align) // align is a power of two { return (value + align - 1) & ~(align - 1); } Adding align - 1 and then clearing the low bits rounds up. It only works when align is a power of two, which alignments always are; checking that is (align & (align - 1)) == 0 . Where the region comes from Allocators get their big regions from the operating system: on Windows with VirtualAlloc (raw pages, lesson 6.04) or HeapCreate ; malloc in the C runtime sits on the process heap, which sits on VirtualAlloc . Large requests (around 512 KB and up on Windows) are usually served directly from fresh pages instead of the block list. Check yourself quiz ? Why does an allocator split a large free block? - To keep every block in the heap the same size + So a small request does not use up the whole block - To make room for the header of the next block - So that freeing the block later is faster Without splitting, a 16-byte request could swallow a 4 KB free block. Splitting gives the request what it asked for and keeps the rest available as a smaller free block. ? What is fragmentation? - Memory that was allocated and never freed - A block that was freed twice and split into pieces + Free memory scattered in small blocks between used ones - The padding the compiler adds inside structs A large request can then fail although enough memory is free in total. A leak is memory nobody frees; fragmentation is free memory in the wrong shape, and joining neighbouring free blocks fights it. ? Where are the next pointers of a free list stored? - In a separate array the allocator keeps next to the region - On the stack of the thread that freed the block + Inside the free blocks themselves, since their memory is not in use - In the header of the region, one slot per block A free block's bytes are not being used for anything, so the allocator stores its bookkeeping there and needs no extra memory. ? What does (value + 15) & ~15 do? - Rounds value down to the previous multiple of 16 - Adds 15 and keeps only the lowest 4 bits + Rounds value up to the next multiple of 16 - Divides value by 16 Adding 15 pushes any value that is not already a multiple of 16 past the next one, and & ~15 clears the low 4 bits to land on it. A value that is already a multiple stays the same.

title: Allocator arithmetic
body: The small calculations every allocator does: cpp bool isPowerOfTwo(std::uint64_t n); std::uint64_t alignUp(std::uint64_t value, std::uint64_t align); bool isAligned(const void p, std::uint64_t align); std::uint64_t sizeClass(std::uint64_t bytes); std::uint64_t footprint(std::uint64_t bytes, std::uint64_t header, std::uint64_t align); - isPowerOfTwo : 1, 2, 4, 8, ... are; 0 is not. - alignUp rounds value up to a multiple of align (a power of two) using the bit trick from lesson 6.01, no division. - isAligned says whether a pointer's address is a multiple of align . - sizeClass rounds a request up to the size classes 16, 32, 64, 128, ... 4096. Requests of 0 bytes use class 16. Anything over 4096 returns 0, meaning "too big for the classes". - footprint is the space a block really takes: header plus bytes, rounded up to align .

title: 6.02  Arena Allocators
body: An arena hands out memory by moving one pointer forward and frees everything at once by moving it back. Bump allocation, alignment, frame arenas reset every frame, markers for rewinding part of an arena, and the rules for what may live in one. The fastest allocator there is An arena (also called a linear or bump allocator) owns one block of memory and an offset into it. Allocating moves the offset forward; that is all. cpp-norun class Arena { public: explicit Arena(std::size_t size) : memory(size) {} void allocate(std::size_t bytes, std::size_t align = alignof(std::max_align_t)) { const std::size_t start{ alignUp(used, align) }; if (start + bytes memory.size()) return nullptr; // full used = start + bytes; return memory.data() + start; } void reset() { used = 0; } // frees everything at once private: std::vector<std::byte memory; std::size_t used{ 0 }; }; text start used end obj A pad obj B C ................ free .......... An allocation is an addition and a comparison. There are no headers, no free lists, no searching, and no fragmentation: everything allocated sits side by side in the order it was made, which is also the best possible order for the cache. No individual frees The price is that you cannot free one object. Memory comes back all at once, with reset() . That sounds limiting and turns out to fit a lot of real work, because many allocations share one lifetime: - Per frame : everything a game computes during one frame (visible-object lists, temporary strings, draw commands) is garbage at the end of the frame. One frame arena , reset at the start of every frame, replaces thousands of new / delete pairs. - Per level : everything loaded for a level dies when the level is unloaded. - Per request : a server handling one request, or a compiler compiling one function. Alignment Each allocation must start at an address suitable for its type, so the offset is rounded up first. Asking for a double after a char wastes up to 7 bytes of padding, just like struct padding (lesson 3.01). The default alignment of alignof(std::max_align_t) (16) is always safe; passing the real alignof(T) packs objects more tightly. The arena's own memory must be aligned too. std::vector<std::byte gets its block from new , which returns memory aligned to at least 16, so offsets that are multiples of 16 are 16-aligned addresses. For larger alignments (64 for a cache line, 4096 for a page), align the address , not the offset: cpp-norun std::uintptr_t address{ reinterpret_cast<std::uintptr_t (memory.data()) + used }; std::uintptr_t aligned{ alignUp(address, align) }; Markers A marker remembers the current offset so you can roll back to it later, freeing everything allocated since, but keeping what came before. That makes the arena a stack allocator : cpp-norun Marker before{ arena.mark() }; buildPathfindingGraph(arena); // lots of temporary allocations Path path{ findPath(arena) }; // ... arena.rewind(before); // all of that is gone; earlier allocations stay Rewinding must happen in last-in, first-out order: rewinding to an older marker discards everything after it, including allocations made after a newer marker. What may live in an arena reset() does not run destructors. It just forgets the memory. So objects in an arena should be trivially destructible , or you must call their destructors yourself before resetting: - Plain structs of numbers, arrays of them, and views over them: perfect. - A std::string or std::vector object placed in an arena still allocates its contents on the normal heap, and resetting without destroying it leaks that. C++17's std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource is a standard arena, and the std::pmr::vector and std::pmr::string types can be told to allocate their contents from it, so a whole frame's worth of containers lives inside one arena. To construct an object in arena memory you use placement new , which runs a constructor at an address you supply: cpp-norun void place{ arena.allocate(sizeof(Particle), alignof(Particle)) }; Particle p{ new (place) Particle{ x, y } }; // no allocation: construct at that address Check yourself quiz ? What does allocating from an arena cost? - A search through a free list for a block that fits - A system call to the operating system for each allocation + Rounding the offset up for alignment, one comparison against the end, and one addition - Writing a header in front of every block An arena only moves one offset forward, which is why it is the fastest allocator there is. It keeps no headers and no free list. ? Why is an arena a good fit for per-frame memory in a game? - It can free individual objects in any order + Everything from a frame dies together, so one reset frees it - Arenas are the only allocators that are thread-safe - Its memory is automatically zeroed every frame When lifetimes all end together, freeing each object separately is wasted work. Resetting the offset to zero releases the whole frame's memory at once. ? What does rewinding to a marker free? - Everything allocated before the marker was taken - Only the single allocation made just before the marker + Everything allocated after the marker was taken; earlier allocations stay - The whole arena, like reset A marker is a saved offset. Moving the offset back to it releases what came after, so a function can use scratch memory and give it all back on return. ? Why should objects in an arena be trivially destructible? - Arenas cannot store objects that have constructors + reset does not call destructors, so anything that owns other resources would leak them - Destructors would run twice, once at reset and once at exit - Trivially destructible objects are smaller, so more fit An arena just forgets its memory. A std::string or std::vector inside would never free its own heap block.

title: An arena with markers
body: Build the arena from lesson 6.02: cpp class Arena { public: using Marker = std::size_t; explicit Arena(std::size_t capacity); void allocate(std::size_t bytes, std::size_t align = 16); template <typename T, typename... Args T make(Args&&... args); Marker mark() const; void rewind(Marker m); void reset(); std::size_t used() const; std::size_t capacity() const; }; - The arena owns one block of capacity bytes, aligned to 64. - allocate returns the next address that is a multiple of align (a power of two, up to 64) with bytes free after it, and moves past them. If they do not fit, it returns nullptr and changes nothing. - make allocates room for a T with alignof(T) and constructs it there with placement new, returning nullptr if it does not fit. - mark returns the current position; rewind goes back to it; reset goes back to the start. - used is the number of bytes from the start to the current position, padding included.

title: 6.03  Pool Allocators
body: A pool hands out blocks of one fixed size from a single region. Free blocks are linked into a list through their own memory, so allocating and freeing are a couple of pointer moves, with no headers and no fragmentation. Building one, and where games use them. Many objects of one size Games create and destroy huge numbers of identical objects: bullets, particles, sound voices, network messages. Each one is the same size. A pool allocator exploits that: it divides one region into equal blocks, and handing one out is just taking any free block. text block 0 block 1 block 2 block 3 block 4 block 5 ... every block 64 bytes Because every block is the same size, there is no searching for a fit, no splitting, no headers to record sizes, and no fragmentation: any free block is as good as any other. The free list lives in the free blocks The pool needs to know which blocks are free. It keeps them on a linked list, and the clever part is where the next pointers go: inside the free blocks themselves . A free block's memory is unused anyway, so its first 8 bytes can hold the address of the next free block. text free -- next: &block 3 .... -- next: &block 5 .... -- next: nullptr .... block 1 block 3 block 5 cpp-norun class Pool { public: Pool(std::size_t blockSize, std::size_t count) : size{ std::max(blockSize, sizeof(void )) }, memory(size count) { for (std::size_t i{ count }; i-- 0;) // push every block onto the list push(memory.data() + i size); } void allocate() { if (!head) return nullptr; // pool exhausted void block{ head }; std::memcpy(&head, block, sizeof(head)); // head = the next pointer stored in the block return block; } void release(void block) { push(static_cast<std::byte (block)); } private: void push(std::byte block) { std::memcpy(block, &head, sizeof(head)); // the block's first bytes point at the old head head = block; } std::size_t size; std::vector<std::byte memory; void head{ nullptr }; }; Allocating pops the head of the list; freeing pushes the block back on. Both are a handful of instructions, always the same speed however full the pool is. Blocks must be at least as big as a pointer, which the constructor makes sure of. LIFO reuse The most recently freed block is the next one handed out. That is good for the cache: memory just touched is likely still in it. It also means a use-after-free bug in pooled objects shows up quickly and strangely, because the freed object's memory is immediately reused by the next allocation of the same type, and its first 8 bytes are overwritten by the free-list pointer as soon as it is freed. Pools in practice - Particle systems and bullets : thousands created and destroyed per second, all the same size. - Network messages and events : fixed-size records queued and processed. - Nodes of linked structures : a pool of Node s makes a linked list or tree far faster than one new per node, and keeps the nodes close together in memory. - Size-class allocators (lesson 6.01) are just one pool per size. A pool can also hand out indices instead of pointers: block numbers from 0 to count - 1. Indices are 4 bytes instead of 8, stay valid if the pool is moved or saved to disk, and combine naturally with the generation counters of lesson 1.05's handles, which catch use-after-free on the spot. Growing A fixed pool can run out. Either treat that as a design limit ("at most 4096 bullets", and refuse more), or let the pool allocate another region when it is exhausted and add its blocks to the free list. Growing never moves existing blocks, so pointers into the pool stay valid, which a std::vector of objects cannot promise. Check yourself quiz ? Why does a pool allocator have no fragmentation? - It never frees any blocks - It returns freed blocks to the operating system at once + Every block is the same size, so any free block satisfies any request - It joins neighbouring free blocks after every free Fragmentation is a free block of the wrong size. In a pool there is only one size, so every free block always fits. ? Where does the pool keep the list of free blocks? - In a std::vector of free block addresses + In the free blocks themselves, as a linked list - In a bitmap at the start of the region, one bit per block - In a header in front of each block, used or not Each free block's first bytes hold the next pointer. That memory is unused anyway, so the list costs nothing extra. A bitmap would work too, but that is not how this pool is built. ? Why must each block be at least sizeof(void ) bytes? - Smaller blocks cannot be aligned at all - The pool writes the block's size into its first bytes + A free block has to hold the pointer to the next free block - The operating system only hands out memory in 8-byte pieces The free list lives inside the free blocks, so each one must be big enough to hold an 8-byte pointer in a 64-bit program. ? Why do use-after-free bugs on pooled objects show up quickly? - The pool fills freed blocks with 0xDD , like the debug heap - The pool returns freed memory to Windows, so any access faults + The free-list pointer overwrites it, and it is reused next Pools reuse in LIFO order: the block just freed is the next one allocated, and its first bytes are overwritten at once by the free-list pointer. The stale pointer soon sees another object's data.

body: Build the pool allocator from lesson 6.03, keeping the free list inside the free blocks : cpp class Pool { public: Pool(std::size_t blockSize, std::size_t blockCount); void allocate(); void release(void block); std::size_t freeCount() const; std::size_t blockSize() const; bool owns(const void p) const; }; - All blocks come from one region. The block size is rounded up to a multiple of 16 (and is at least 16), so every block is 16-aligned. - At the start, blocks are handed out in address order: the first allocate returns the first block, the next the second, and so on. - release puts a block back; the most recently released block is the next one allocate returns. - allocate returns nullptr when every block is in use. - freeCount counts free blocks (keep a counter; do not walk the list). owns says whether a pointer is the start of one of this pool's blocks. - Store each free block's next pointer in the block's own first bytes, with std::memcpy .

title: 6.04  Virtual Memory and Pages
body: Every address a program uses is virtual. The processor translates it, one 4 KB page at a time, through page tables the operating system maintains. Pages that are reserved, committed or free, page protection, page faults, guard pages, and what an access violation really is. Addresses are not where the bytes are Every address in this course so far has been a virtual address . When your program reads 0x000001C4B2E8F0A0 , there is no memory chip at that number. The processor translates the virtual address into a physical address in RAM, using tables that the operating system maintains for each process. This is why two programs can both use address 0x140001000 without clashing: each process has its own translation, its own address space . And it is why one program cannot read another's memory by accident: there is simply no translation from its addresses to the other's RAM. Pages Translating every byte separately would need impossibly large tables, so memory is managed in pages : blocks of 4096 bytes (4 KB) on x86 and ARM Windows. A virtual address splits into a page number and an offset within the page: text virtual address 0x0000_0001_C4B2_E8F0 ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ ^^^ page number offset (low 12 bits, 0 to 4095) page = address 12 (address / 4096) offset = address & 0xFFF (address % 4096) The page table maps each virtual page number to a physical frame number. The physical address is the frame's start plus the same offset. The bytes within a page stay in the same order; only whole pages are moved around. Translations are cached in the processor's TLB (translation lookaside buffer), so most accesses cost nothing extra. Code that jumps around huge areas of memory pays for TLB misses, another reason scattered linked structures are slow. Reserved, committed, free In Windows each page of an address space is in one of three states: State Meaning --- --- free nothing there; any access faults reserved the address range is set aside so nothing else will use it, but it has no memory behind it; any access faults committed backed by memory (RAM or the page file); accessible according to its protection VirtualAlloc does both steps: cpp-norun // Reserve 1 GB of addresses: costs no memory, just address space. void base{ VirtualAlloc(nullptr, 1ull << 30, MEM_RESERVE, PAGE_NOACCESS) }; // Commit the first 64 KB of it when you actually need it. VirtualAlloc(base, 64 1024, MEM_COMMIT, PAGE_READWRITE); This is how a growable array can be built that never moves : reserve a huge range once, commit pages at the end as it grows. Thread stacks work this way too: 1 MB reserved, a little committed, more committed as the stack grows. Committed memory is also only given real RAM when first touched. Committing guarantees it can be provided; the operating system supplies a zero-filled page at the first access. Protection Each committed page has a protection : PAGE_READONLY , PAGE_READWRITE , PAGE_EXECUTE_READ , PAGE_NOACCESS , and a few more. The program image is mapped with its code read+execute and its constants read-only, which is why writing to a string literal crashes. VirtualProtect changes a page's protection, and VirtualQuery reports the state and protection of any address (the Game Development course explores your own process with it). Page faults and access violations When the processor cannot translate an address, or the access breaks the page's protection, it raises a page fault and hands control to the operating system, which decides what it means: - The page is committed but not in RAM yet (first touch, or it was paged out to disk): the OS loads it and the program continues, never knowing. This is a normal, soft or hard page fault. - The page is free or reserved, or the access breaks the protection: the OS raises an access violation ( 0xC0000005 ) in the program. Unhandled, that ends it. So "access violation reading location 0x0000000000000018" is the processor saying: page 0 is not committed, so this address has no translation. Windows deliberately never maps the first 64 KB of the address space, so every null pointer access, plus a small offset, faults immediately. Guard pages A page committed with PAGE_GUARD faults once on first access, and the OS then removes the guard. The stack uses one to grow: touching the guard page below the committed stack commits another page and moves the guard down. Debugging tools use the same idea to catch overruns: page heap (enabled with the gflags tool) places each allocation at the end of a page followed by an inaccessible page, so the first byte written past the end faults at that exact instruction. Check yourself quiz ? For the address 0x12345 , what are the page number and the offset with 4 KB pages? - Page 0x1 , offset 0x2345 - Page 0x123 , offset 0x45 + Page 0x12 , offset 0x345 - Page 0x12345 , offset 0 A 4 KB page is 0x1000 bytes, so the low 12 bits (3 hex digits) are the offset and the rest is the page number. ? What is the difference between reserving and committing memory? + Reserving sets aside addresses; committing puts memory behind them - Reserving allocates memory on the stack; committing allocates on the heap - They are the same, except that committing also zeroes the pages - Committing sets aside addresses; reserving fills them with memory Reserved pages have nothing behind them, so they fault when touched. Committing backs them with memory, which is what makes them usable. ? Why does every null pointer dereference fault immediately on Windows? - The processor has a special check for address 0 - The compiler inserts a null check before every dereference - The memory at address 0 holds an instruction that crashes the program + The lowest 64 KB of the address space is never mapped, so any address near 0 has no translation There is no special hardware rule. Windows simply never maps those pages, so nullptr and small offsets from it always fault. ? How does page heap catch a buffer overrun at the exact instruction? - It checks guard bytes around each block every time delete runs - It runs the program in an emulator that checks every write + It puts each allocation just before an inaccessible page - It makes the whole heap read-only and unlocks one block at a time Each allocation ends at the end of a page with an inaccessible page after it, so the first byte past the end faults. Guard bytes, by contrast, only show the damage when the block is freed.

title: Translating addresses
body: Simulate what the processor and the operating system do with virtual addresses (lesson 6.04), with 4 KB pages: cpp constexpr std::uint64_t PAGE{ 4096 }; struct Entry { std::uint64_t frame; bool writable; }; enum class Access { Ok, NotMapped, ReadOnly }; std::uint64_t pageOf(std::uint64_t address); std::uint64_t offsetIn(std::uint64_t address); std::uint64_t pagesSpanned(std::uint64_t address, std::uint64_t size); Access check(const std::map<std::uint64_t, Entry & table, std::uint64_t address, std::uint64_t size, bool write); std::optional<std::uint64_t translate(const std::map<std::uint64_t, Entry & table, std::uint64_t address); - pageOf and offsetIn split an address into its page number and its offset within the page. - pagesSpanned is how many pages the bytes address to address + size - 1 touch (0 for a size of 0). - check says whether an access of size bytes at address would succeed: every page it touches must be in the table ( NotMapped otherwise) and, for a write, writable ( ReadOnly otherwise). NotMapped wins if both apply. A size of 0 is always Ok . - translate turns a virtual address into a physical one: the frame number times the page size, plus the offset. std::nullopt if the page is not mapped.

title: 6.05  A Field Guide to Memory Bugs
match: 6.05 A Field Guide to Memory Bugs
body: Everything in this course turned into a way of working - reading a crash's address, recognising the debug fill patterns, the symptom-to-cause table, data breakpoints, AddressSanitizer and page heap, and the habits that stop the bugs being written in the first place. Read the address first When a program crashes with an access violation, the most useful single fact is the address it tried to use. The debugger shows it in the exception message and, for a pointer, in the Locals or Watch window. Many bad addresses identify themselves: Address looks like Usually means --- --- 0x0000000000000000 to a few thousand a null pointer; the small number is the offset of the member being reached 0xCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCC (plus a small offset) a pointer read from uninitialised stack memory (MSVC debug) 0xCDCDCDCDCDCDCDCD a pointer read from heap memory never written after new or malloc 0xDDDDDDDDDDDDDDDD a pointer read from freed heap memory: the object holding it was already deleted 0xFEEEFEEEFEEEFEEE a pointer read from memory freed back to the Windows heap 0xFDFDFDFD in your data you are reading the guard bytes around a heap block: past an end a valid-looking heap address, but the data is garbage a dangling pointer to memory that has been reused The first three patterns only appear in Debug builds, which is a good reason to reproduce crashes in one. Symptoms and causes Symptom Likely causes Lessons --- --- --- Crash at a small address null pointer, often a missing check after a lookup 1.05, 3.03 Value changes "by itself" a write through a dangling or out-of-bounds pointer from somewhere else 1.05, 2.01 Run-Time Check Failure 2 - Stack around the variable was corrupted writing past a local array 2.01, 4.02 HEAP CORRUPTION DETECTED or a crash inside ntdll.dll during new / delete heap overrun, double free, mismatched delete / delete 4.03 Works in Debug, fails in Release uninitialised variables, undefined behaviour the optimiser exploited, strict aliasing 2.02, 2.05 Crash only after a container grows pointers or views into a std::vector that reallocated 1.05, 5.04 Memory use climbs steadily leaks, or shared_ptr cycles 4.05, 5.03 Stack overflow ( 0xC00000FD ) deep recursion, huge local arrays 4.02 Image comes out slanted width used instead of stride 2.04 Data breakpoints When a value changes and you do not know who changed it, set a data breakpoint on it. In Visual Studio, stop somewhere the variable exists, right-click it in the Locals or Watch window and choose Break When Value Changes (or Debug New Breakpoint Data Breakpoint with an address). The processor's debug registers watch that address, and the debugger stops at the exact instruction that writes to it, however indirect the pointer was. There are only four such registers, so only a few bytes at a time can be watched. This is the tool for "something is overwriting my health with garbage": the write that should not happen stops in the debugger with its call stack. Make the bug happen at the bug Memory bugs are hard because the damage shows up later than the mistake. Every tool here moves the failure back to the moment of the mistake: - AddressSanitizer ( /fsanitize=address ) checks every access and reports overruns, use after free and double frees as they happen (lesson 4.05). - Page heap ( gflags /p /enable game.exe /full ) puts every heap block against an inaccessible page, so an overrun faults on the exact instruction (lesson 6.04). It uses a lot of memory; enable it for one program at a time. - The debug heap checks guard bytes when blocks are freed and fills memory with recognisable patterns. _CrtCheckMemory() called at points in your code checks every block immediately, narrowing down when the corruption happened. - Debug fill on free in your own allocators: fill freed memory with a pattern (as your debug heap in milestone 4 did) so a use after free reads obvious garbage instead of plausible old data. A way of working 1. Reproduce it reliably, in a Debug build if possible. 2. Read the crash : the faulting address, the instruction, the call stack. Match the address against the patterns above. 3. Turn on the tools : ASan first; page heap or data breakpoints if needed. 4. Find the owner : for the object involved, who created it, who frees it, and who still held a pointer. Most memory bugs are ownership bugs (lesson 4.04). 5. Fix the design, not just the line : a raw owning pointer that should be a unique_ptr , a cached pointer that should be a handle, a stored view that should be a copy. The habits that prevent them - Initialise every variable, pointers above all. - One owner per object, written in the type: values, containers and unique_ptr ; shared_ptr only for real sharing. - No new / delete in ordinary code; RAII for every resource. - Pass views ( span , string_view , references) down, never store them casually. - Indices or handles instead of long-lived pointers into containers. - Bounds-checked access ( at() , spans with known sizes) wherever speed does not demand otherwise. - Run tests under AddressSanitizer regularly. You now know what every one of those habits protects against, byte by byte. Check yourself quiz ? A crash reports reading address 0xDDDDDDDDDDDDDDE5 . What happened? - A null pointer was followed and a member at offset 0xE5 was read - An uninitialised stack variable was used as a pointer + A pointer was read out of freed heap memory (the DD fill), then a member at offset 8 was accessed - The program read past the end of a 0xDD-byte array 0xDD...DD + 8 = 0xDD...E5 . The pointer itself came from a deleted object, a use after free one level removed. Uninitialised stack memory is filled with 0xCC instead. ? Something overwrites a struct's field and you cannot see where. Which debugger feature finds the culprit? - A breakpoint on the line that declares the field - Stepping through the program one line at a time and watching the field + A data breakpoint on the field's address, which stops at the instruction that writes to it - A conditional breakpoint that fires when the program crashes A data breakpoint watches the memory, not a line of code, so it catches the write wherever it comes from, even through a stray pointer. ? What do AddressSanitizer, page heap and the debug heap's fill patterns have in common? - They all make the program run faster in Release builds - They all prevent memory bugs from being written - They all work only on stack memory + They make a memory bug fail at, or near, the moment of the mistake instead of later Memory bugs are hard because the crash comes far from the cause. These tools shrink that distance so the debugger stops close to the bug. ? A program works in a Debug build but crashes in Release. Which pair of causes is likely? - A missing include and a misspelt variable name + An uninitialised variable and undefined behaviour that the optimiser exploited - A memory leak and a slow loop - A wrong sizeof and a missing semicolon Debug builds fill and keep memory differently and do not optimise, so uninitialised reads, aliasing violations and other undefined behaviour often only bite in Release. The other pairs would fail in both builds, or not crash at all.

body: Write the first step of lesson 6.05's way of working: look at the address in a crash and say what it most likely means. cpp std::string diagnose(std::uint64_t address); Return one of these strings: Return When --- --- "null pointer" the address is below 0x10000 (the 64 KB Windows never maps) "uninitialised stack" the address is a fill pattern of CC bytes "uninitialised heap" a fill pattern of CD bytes "freed heap" a fill pattern of DD bytes "freed (Windows heap)" a fill pattern of FEEEFEEE "guard bytes" a fill pattern of FD bytes "unknown" anything else A fill pattern address is the pattern repeated to 64 bits ( 0xCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCC ) or to 32 bits ( 0xCCCCCCCC , as in a 32-bit program or a 32-bit field), plus a small offset of up to 0xFFF, because the bad pointer is usually followed by a member access: 0xDDDDDDDDDDDDDE05 is freed heap plus 0x28. Only offsets added on top count, from 0 to 0xFFF; an address below the pattern is not a match.

title: A general-purpose allocator
body: Build a real allocator over one fixed region, the design of lesson 6.01: blocks with headers stored inside the region , first fit, splitting, and joining free neighbours. cpp class Heap { public: static constexpr std::size_t HEADER{ 16 }; static constexpr std::size_t ALIGN{ 16 }; explicit Heap(std::size_t capacity); void allocate(std::size_t bytes); void release(void p); std::size_t freeBytes() const; std::size_t largestFree() const; std::size_t blockCount() const; bool validate() const; }; The region is capacity bytes (a multiple of 16, at least 32), 16-aligned. It is always a sequence of blocks with no gaps: a 16-byte header , then the block's payload. The header holds the payload size (a multiple of 16) and whether the block is free. At the start there is one free block whose payload is capacity - 16 . allocate : - Round the request up to a multiple of 16 (a request of 0 counts as 16). - Walk the blocks from the start and take the first free block whose payload is big enough. None: return nullptr . - If the leftover would be at least 32 bytes (a header plus 16 of payload), split : the first part becomes the allocation, the rest a new free block. Otherwise hand out the whole block. - Return the address just after the header (always 16-aligned). release : nullptr does nothing. Otherwise mark the block free, then coalesce : merge it with a free block directly after it and with a free block directly before it, so no two free blocks are ever neighbours. freeBytes adds up free payloads; largestFree is the biggest free payload; blockCount counts all blocks; validate checks the invariants: the blocks exactly cover the region, sizes are multiples of 16, and no two free blocks are adjacent. Read and write the headers with std::memcpy at byte offsets in the region.
