title: Glossary
body: Address : the number of a byte in a program's memory. (1.01) Alignment : the number an object's address must be a multiple of; usually its size for basic types. (3.01) Aliasing : two pointers or references reaching the same object. (1.03) Arena : an allocator that hands out memory by moving one offset forward and frees everything at once. (6.02) ASLR : address space layout randomisation; Windows loads each part of a program at a random address every run. (1.01) Borrower : code holding a pointer to an object it does not own and must not free. (4.04) Coalescing : merging neighbouring free blocks into one. (6.01) Commit : back a reserved range of addresses with real memory. (6.04) Control block : the separate block holding a shared_ptr 's reference counts. (5.03) Dangling pointer : a pointer to an object that no longer exists. (1.05) Decay : an array's name turning into a pointer to its first element. (2.01) Dereference : follow a pointer to the object at its address, with or - . (1.03) Fragmentation : free memory split into pieces too small to use. (6.01) Frame : the part of the stack used by one function call: return address and locals. (4.02) Free list : a linked list of free blocks, stored inside the blocks. (6.01, 6.03) Handle : an index plus a generation number, used instead of a pointer so that stale references are detected. (1.05) Heap : memory allocated at run time with new or malloc , alive until freed. (4.03) Little-endian : storing the least significant byte of a number at the lowest address. (1.01) Offset : the distance in bytes from the start of an object to one of its members. (3.01) Owner : the one piece of code responsible for freeing an object. (4.04) Padding : unused bytes the compiler inserts to keep members aligned. (3.01) Page : the 4 KB unit in which virtual memory is mapped and protected. (6.04) Pointer chain : a base address and a list of offsets, followed one pointer read at a time. (3.03) Pool : an allocator for blocks of one fixed size. (6.03) RAII : tying a resource to an object whose destructor releases it. (5.01) Reserve : set aside a range of addresses without memory behind it. (6.04) Sentinel : a dummy node that removes special cases from a linked structure. (3.04) Span : a non-owning view of a sequence: a pointer and a length. (5.04) Stack : per-thread memory used for function frames, growing downwards. (4.02) Stride : the distance from the start of one row to the start of the next. (2.04) Strict aliasing : the rule that an object may only be read through its own type or a char type. (2.05) Use after free : reading or writing an object after it was deleted. (1.05) Virtual address : an address as the program sees it, translated by the processor to a physical one. (6.04) Vtable : a class's table of virtual function addresses. (3.05) Wild pointer : a pointer that was never initialised. (1.05)

title: 1.01  What Python Is and Running Code
match: 1.01 What Python Is and Running Code
body: Python is a language you can read almost like English and run without a separate compile step. This lesson explains what that means, runs a first program, and shows the two ways to run Python - scripts and the interactive prompt. A language built for people Python was designed to be easy to read . Compare printing the numbers 1 to 3: python for number in range(1, 4): print(number) No semicolons, no braces, no type declarations: the indentation shows the structure, and the words say what happens. That makes Python the language people reach for when they want an idea working quickly : scripts that rename a thousand files, tools that read a spreadsheet and send a report, data analysis, web servers, machine learning, and glue between other programs. The price is speed: Python runs much slower than C++ for heavy computation. In practice that rarely matters, because the slow parts are done by libraries written in C (which is what NumPy and friends are), and most programs spend their time waiting for files and networks anyway. How Python runs your code C++ is compiled to machine code before it runs. Python is run by an interpreter : the python program reads your source, turns it into compact bytecode , and executes it straight away. There is no separate build step: you edit and run. One consequence: many mistakes are found only when the line runs. A typo in a function that is never called goes unnoticed. That is why testing (lesson 5.05) matters even more in Python. Your first program python print("Hello, Xenon!") print("Python is", 3 11, "years old in 2024") print writes its arguments separated by spaces and ends with a new line. Text goes between quotes (single or double, both work); numbers do not. Press Run on any example in these lessons to run it, and edit it to try things out. Running Python yourself On your own computer, install Python from python.org (on Windows, tick "Add python.exe to PATH") or the Microsoft Store. Then there are two ways to run it: Way How Good for --- --- --- Script Save code in hello.py , run python hello.py Programs you keep Interactive prompt (REPL) Run python with no file, type a line, see the result Trying things out, a calculator At the interactive prompt, the result of each expression is shown automatically: 2 10 1024 "ab" 3 'ababab' In a script, nothing is shown unless you print it. Editors such as VS Code (with the Python extension) run scripts with one key and show errors as you type. Comments Everything after on a line is a comment , ignored by Python: python Work out the area of a 3 by 4 rectangle. width = 3 height = 4 print(width height) prints 12 Write comments for the why , not the what: the code already says what it does. Check yourself quiz ? What does the Python interpreter do with a .py file? - It compiles it into a machine-code program that you run afterwards + It turns the source into bytecode and runs it straight away - It checks every line for mistakes first, then runs the file - It translates it into C++ and compiles that There is no separate build step: python turns the source into bytecode and executes it immediately. That is why a mistake in a line that never runs can go unnoticed. ? What is the difference between the interactive prompt and a script? - A script shows the value of every expression; the prompt shows only what you print - The prompt can only do arithmetic; a script can run any Python + The prompt runs a line at a time and shows each result; a script shows only what it prints - There is none: both run a whole file and show every result At the prompt (the REPL) each expression's value is shown automatically; in a script nothing appears unless you print it. ? Which line prints 7 when it is in a script? - print("3 + 4") - 3 + 4 + print(3 + 4) - print(3, 4) Quotes make it text, an expression on its own is not shown in a script, and two arguments print as 3 4 .

title: 1.02  Values, Variables and Types
body: Every value in Python has a type - int, float, str, bool, None - and variables are names that refer to values. This lesson covers assignment, naming, dynamic typing, converting between types and checking a value's type. Values have types Every value in Python has a type that decides what you can do with it: Type Examples Holds --- --- --- int 42 , -7 , 1_000_000 Whole numbers, as big as you like float 3.14 , 2.0 , 1e-3 Numbers with a fractional part (about 15 significant digits) str "hello" , 'Ada' Text bool True , False Truth values NoneType None "No value" python print(type(42), type(3.14), type("hi"), type(True), type(None)) Variables are names A variable is a name that refers to a value. = makes the name refer to the value on the right: python score = 10 score = score + 5 the name now refers to 15 player = "Ada" print(player, "has", score, "points") Unlike C++, a variable has no type of its own: the value has the type, and the same name can later refer to a value of another type. This is dynamic typing . It is flexible, and it means mistakes such as adding text to a number are found only when that line runs: python lives = 3 lives = "three" allowed, but now lives + 1 would fail Several names can be assigned at once, and += , -= , = update a variable: python x, y = 2, 5 x = 2, y = 5 x, y = y, x swap: x = 5, y = 2 x += 1 x = 6 print(x, y) Naming Names use letters, digits and _ , cannot start with a digit, and are case-sensitive ( score and Score are different). Python's style guide ( PEP 8 ) uses lower_case_with_underscores for variables and functions, and UPPER_CASE for constants: python MAX_LIVES = 3 player_name = "Ada" Converting between types Functions named after types convert values: python print(int("42") + 1) 43: text to number print(float("2.5") 2) 5.0 print(str(7) + " days") "7 days": number to text print(int(3.99)) 3: int() cuts off the fraction, it does not round print(round(3.99)) 4 print(bool(0), bool(""), bool("no")) False False True A conversion that makes no sense raises an error: int("hello") stops the program with ValueError . Lesson 4.05 shows how to handle that. Truthiness In conditions (lesson 1.05), every value counts as true or false: 0 , 0.0 , "" , None , and empty collections are falsy ; everything else is truthy . So if name: means "if the name is not empty". Check yourself quiz ? In Python, which has the type: the variable or the value? - The variable: its type is fixed by the first value assigned to it + The value: a variable is just a name and can refer to values of any type - The variable: its type is declared when the variable is created - Both: assigning a value of another type raises an error Python is dynamically typed: the value carries the type, so lives = 3 then lives = "three" is allowed. ? What does int(3.99) give? - 4 - 3.99 - an error, because 3.99 is not a whole number + 3 int() cuts off the fraction, it does not round. Use round(3.99) to get 4. ? What does print(str(2) + str(3)) print? - 5 + 23 - 2 3 - an error str turns each number into text, and + joins texts together.

title: Types and conversions

title: 1.03  Input, Output and f-strings
body: Programs that talk to the user - print with its separators and endings, input that always returns text, converting what was typed, and f-strings for building text with values and formatting numbers. print in detail print takes any number of values, separates them with a space, and ends with a new line. Both can be changed: python print("a", "b", "c") a b c print("a", "b", "c", sep="-") a-b-c print("no new line", end="") print(" ... continued") print() an empty line input input(prompt) shows the prompt, waits for the user to type a line, and returns it as text (without the Enter): python name = input("What is your name? ") print("Hello,", name) Because input always returns a str , numbers must be converted: python age = int(input("How old are you? ")) print("Next year you will be", age + 1) Forgetting the conversion is the most common beginner bug: input() + 1 fails, and input() 2 repeats the text ( "55" from "5" ). f-strings An f-string has an f before the quote, and any expression inside {} is evaluated and inserted: python name = "Ada" score = 1234.5678 print(f"{name} scored {score} points") print(f"In two years: {2026 + 2}") After a colon inside the braces comes a format specification : Spec Example Gives --- --- --- .2f f"{3.14159:.2f}" 3.14 (2 decimals) , f"{1234567:,}" 1,234,567 8 / <8 / ^8 f"{'x': 8}" right / left / centre in 8 characters 08.3f f"{3.5:08.3f}" 0003.500 (zero-padded) % f"{0.256:.1%}" 25.6% = f"{score=}" score=1234.5678 (handy for debugging) python for item, price in ("tea", 2.5), ("cake", 12.0) : print(f"{item:<10}{price: 8.2f}") Reading several values split() breaks a line into words, so several numbers can be typed on one line: python a, b = input("Two numbers: ").split() print(int(a) + int(b)) Check yourself quiz ? The user types 42 . What type does input() return? - int - float + str - whichever type matches what was typed input always returns text ( str ), even when the user types a number. Convert it with int() or float() . ? Which f-string shows the float price with two decimal places? - f"{price:2f}" - f"{price}:.2f" - f"{price:.2}" + f"{price:.2f}" .2f means fixed-point with 2 digits after the point. 2f sets a width of 2, .2 without f means 2 significant digits, and outside the braces the spec is just text. ? The user types 7 . What does print(input() 3) print? - 21 + 777 - 7 7 7 - an error The text "7" repeated three times is "777": convert with int() first to multiply.

title: 1.04  Numbers and Arithmetic
body: Calculating in Python - the arithmetic operators, true division versus floor division, remainders, powers, precedence, the math module, and the surprises of floating-point numbers. Operators Operator Meaning Example Result --- --- --- --- + - Add, subtract, multiply 7 6 42 / Division, always gives a float 7 / 2 3.5 // Floor division: rounds down 7 // 2 3 % Remainder (modulo) 7 % 2 1 Power 2 10 1024 -x Negation -(3 - 5) 2 Unlike C++, / between two ints gives a float ( 6 / 2 is 3.0 ). Use // for whole-number division. Floor division rounds towards minus infinity, and % follows it, so for negative numbers: -7 // 2 is -4 and -7 % 2 is 1 . That is often what you want: minute % 60 is always between 0 and 59. divmod(a, b) gives both at once: python total_seconds = 3725 minutes, seconds = divmod(total_seconds, 60) hours, minutes = divmod(minutes, 60) print(f"{hours}:{minutes:02}:{seconds:02}") 1:02:05 Precedence binds tightest, then unary minus, then / // % , then + - . Use parentheses whenever it helps the reader: python print(2 + 3 4) 14 print((2 + 3) 4) 20 print(-2 2) -4: the power happens first print(2 3 2) 512: groups from the right, 2 9 Integers do not overflow Python's int grows as needed, so there is no overflow: python print(2 100) print(len(str(2 1000)), "digits") Floats are approximations Floats are binary fractions, so most decimal fractions are stored approximately: python print(0.1 + 0.2) 0.30000000000000004 print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3) False import math print(math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3)) True Never compare floats with == after calculations; use math.isclose or a tolerance. For money, count in whole cents with ints, or use the decimal module. round(x, 2) rounds to two decimals, and rounds exact halves to the even neighbour ( round(2.5) is 2 , round(3.5) is 4 ), which avoids a bias when many values are rounded. The math module python import math print(math.sqrt(16), math.pi, math.floor(-2.5), math.ceil(2.1)) print(math.hypot(3, 4)) 5.0: the length of a 3-4 diagonal print(math.gcd(12, 18)) 6 abs(x) , min(...) , max(...) , sum(...) and round(...) are built in, without an import. Check yourself quiz ? What are 7 / 2 , 7 // 2 and 7 % 2 ? - 3, 3 and 1 + 3.5, 3 and 1 - 3.5, 3.5 and 1 - 3.5, 4 and 1 / always gives a float, // rounds down, and % is the remainder. Unlike C++, 7 / 2 is not 3. ? Why should you not compare floats with == after calculations? - == raises an error when both sides are floats - Floats keep only two decimals, so different values look equal - Python compares floats as text, so 2.0 == 2.00 is False + Most decimal fractions are stored approximately, so tiny errors creep in 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is False because both sides are binary approximations. Use math.isclose or a tolerance instead. ? What is -7 // 2 ? - -3 - -3.5 + -4 - 3 Floor division rounds towards minus infinity: -3.5 rounds down to -4.

title: 1.05  Decisions with if
body: Making a program choose - comparisons, if, elif and else, indentation as structure, combining conditions with and, or and not, chained comparisons, the conditional expression, and match for many cases. Comparisons Comparisons give True or False : Operator Meaning --- --- == , != Equal, not equal < , <= , , = Ordering in , not in Membership: "a" in "cat" is , is not Same object: use only for None ( x is None ) Python can chain comparisons, which reads like maths: 0 <= x < 10 . if, elif, else python temperature = int(input("Temperature? ")) if temperature < 0: print("Freezing") elif temperature < 15: print("Cold") elif temperature < 25: print("Pleasant") else: print("Hot") The indentation (4 spaces by convention) is the structure: the indented lines belong to the if above them. A colon ends each condition line. Only the first branch whose condition is true runs; else runs when none did. Combining conditions and , or and not combine truth values: python age = 15 has_ticket = True if age = 12 and has_ticket: print("Welcome") if not has_ticket or age < 12: print("Sorry") They short-circuit : a and b does not evaluate b if a is false, which allows guards such as if items and items 0 0: (no error on an empty list). The conditional expression For choosing between two values in one line: python score = 72 grade = "pass" if score = 50 else "fail" print(grade) match When one value is compared against many cases, match (Python 3.10+) is clearer than a chain of elif : python command = input(" ").strip().lower() match command: case "start" "go": print("Starting") case "stop": print("Stopping") case _: print("Unknown command") means "or", and case _ matches anything. match can also take apart lists and objects (lesson 7.04 shows more). Common mistakes - if x = 5: is a syntax error: comparison is == . - Mixing tabs and spaces in indentation causes IndentationError ; editors insert spaces when you press Tab. - if x == 1 or 2: is always true ( 2 is truthy). Write if x == 1 or x == 2: or if x in (1, 2): . Check yourself quiz ? What decides which lines belong to an if ? + Their indentation below the line that ends with the colon - The curly braces placed around them - Every line up to the next blank line - The lines up to a matching end line Indentation (4 spaces by convention) is the structure: the indented lines under the if ...: line belong to it. ? What does if x == 1 or 2: actually test? - Whether x is 1 or x is 2 + (x == 1) or 2 , which is always true because 2 is truthy - x == (1 or 2) , which is the same as x == 1 - Nothing: it is a syntax error or joins two whole conditions, x == 1 and 2 , and a non-zero number is truthy. Write x in (1, 2) instead. ? What does print(1 < 5 < 3) print? - True - an error + False - 3 Chained comparisons mean 1 < 5 and 5 < 3, and 5 < 3 is false.

title: 2.01  Strings in Depth
body:
Working with text - indexing and slicing, the most useful string methods, splitting and joining, searching, escape sequences and raw strings, multi-line strings, and why strings cannot be changed in place. Indexing and slicing A string is a sequence of characters, numbered from 0. Negative indexes count from the end: python word = "Python" print(word 0 , word 5 , word -1 , word -2 ) P n n o print(len(word)) 6 A slice s start:stop:step takes a part: from start up to but not including stop . Missing values mean "from the beginning", "to the end", "step 1": python word = "Python" print(word 0:2 ) Py print(word 2: ) thon print(word :-1 ) Pytho print(word ::2 ) Pto print(word ::-1 ) nohtyP: reversed Slices never raise errors for out-of-range bounds: word 2:100 is just "thon" . Indexing does: word 10 is an IndexError . Strings are immutable A string cannot be changed in place: word 0 = "J" is an error. Every "change" builds a new string: python word = "Python" word = "J" + word 1: print(word) Jython Useful methods Method Does Example --- --- --- upper() , lower() , title() Change case "ada lovelace".title() → Ada Lovelace strip() , lstrip() , rstrip() Remove whitespace (or given characters) at the ends " hi 
".strip() → hi split(sep) Break into a list (on whitespace by default) "a,b,c".split(",") → 'a', 'b', 'c' sep.join(list) Join a list of strings "-".join( "a", "b" ) → a-b replace(old, new) Replace every occurrence "aaa".replace("a", "b") → bbb find(sub) Index of the first occurrence, or -1 "banana".find("na") → 2 count(sub) Number of occurrences "banana".count("a") → 3 startswith , endswith Test the ends "photo.jpg".endswith(".jpg") → True isdigit() , isalpha() , isspace() Test every character "2024".isdigit() → True center , ljust , rjust , zfill Pad "7".zfill(3) → 007 Methods return new strings; the original is unchanged. in tests for a substring: "ana" in "banana" . Escape sequences and raw strings Inside quotes, 
 is a new line, 	 a tab, \ a backslash, " a quote. A raw string r"..." turns escapes off, which is useful for Windows paths and regular expressions (lesson 6.01): python print("line one
line two	tabbed") print(r"C:
ew	able") Triple quotes allow strings over several lines: python poem = """Roses are red, Violets are blue.""" print(poem.splitlines()) Characters and code points Each character has a Unicode code point : ord("A") is 65, chr(97) is "a" . Python strings are Unicode, so "café" and "日本" work like any other text, and len("日本") is 2. Building strings efficiently Joining many pieces with + in a loop creates a new string each time. Collect the pieces in a list and "".join(pieces) once at the end. Check yourself quiz ? What does "Python" 1:4 give? - "Pyth" - "ytho" + "yth" - "yt" A slice runs from index 1 up to but not including index 4: y, t, h. ? Why does word 0 = "J" fail when word is a string? + Strings are immutable: build a new string instead, such as "J" + word 1: - Strings are numbered from 1, so word 0 does not exist - One character must be assigned in single quotes: word 0 = 'J' - Strings can be sliced but never indexed A string cannot be changed in place, whatever quotes you use. Every "change" makes a new string. ? What does " a,b ,c ".strip().split(",") give? - 'a', 'b', 'c' + 'a', 'b ', 'c' - ' a', 'b ', 'c ' - 'a,b ,c' strip only removes whitespace at the two ends of the whole string, not around each piece.

title: 2.02  Lists
body: Python's general-purpose collection - creating lists, indexing and slicing, adding and removing items, sorting, searching, lists of lists, and the important difference between copying a list and naming it twice. Creating and reading lists A list holds values in order, of any types, and can grow and shrink: python scores = 72, 95, 88 mixed = "Ada", 36, True empty = print(scores 0 , scores -1 , len(scores)) 72 88 3 print(scores 1: ) 95, 88 Indexing and slicing work exactly as for strings (lesson 2.01). Changing lists Unlike strings, lists are mutable : Operation Does --- --- xs i = v Replace one item xs.append(v) Add at the end xs.insert(i, v) Insert before index i xs.extend(other) / xs += other Add every item of another list xs.pop() / xs.pop(i) Remove and return the last item / item i xs.remove(v) Remove the first item equal to v (error if missing) del xs i / del xs a:b Delete by index or slice xs.clear() Remove everything python tasks = "write", "test" tasks.append("ship") tasks.insert(0, "plan") done = tasks.pop(0) print(done, tasks) plan 'write', 'test', 'ship' Searching and counting python xs = 3, 1, 4, 1, 5 print(4 in xs, xs.index(4), xs.count(1)) True 2 2 print(min(xs), max(xs), sum(xs)) 1 5 14 Sorting xs.sort() sorts the list in place; sorted(xs) returns a new sorted list and leaves xs alone. Both take reverse=True and a key (lesson 5.03): python names = "bob", "Carol", "ada" print(sorted(names)) 'Carol', 'ada', 'bob' : capitals sort first print(sorted(names, key=str.lower)) 'ada', 'bob', 'Carol' names.sort(reverse=True) print(names) xs.reverse() reverses in place; xs ::-1 makes a reversed copy. Names, not boxes A variable refers to a list; assigning it to another name does not copy it: python a = 1, 2, 3 b = a b and a are the SAME list b.append(4) print(a) 1, 2, 3, 4 c = a.copy() or a : or list(a): a new list c.append(5) print(a, c) This matters for functions too: a function that changes a list it was given changes the caller's list. Lists of lists A grid is a list of rows: python grid = 0 3 for _ in range(2) two rows of three zeros (lesson 5.01 explains this form) grid 1 2 = 9 print(grid) 0, 0, 0 , 0, 0, 9 Beware 0 3 2 : it repeats the same inner list twice, so changing one row changes both. Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference between xs.sort() and sorted(xs) ? - xs.sort() returns a new sorted list; sorted(xs) sorts xs in place - sorted(xs) works only on numbers; xs.sort() works on any list + xs.sort() sorts in place and returns None; sorted(xs) returns a new list - They do the same thing: both change xs and return it That is why xs = xs.sort() is a bug: it leaves xs as None. ? After b = a (where a is a list), does b.append(4) change a ? - No: b = a makes a copy, so only b grows + Yes: both names refer to the same list - No: append builds a new list and gives it to b Assignment never copies a list. Use a.copy() , a : or list(a) to get a separate one. ? After xs = 1, 2, 3 , then ys = xs , then ys = ys + 4 , what does print(xs) show? - 1, 2, 3, 4 + 1, 2, 3 - 4 - an error ys + 4 builds a new list and makes ys refer to it; xs still refers to the original list.

None of them may change the list they are given. python def second_largest(xs): ... the second largest DISTINCT value, or None if there is none def without(xs, value): ... a new list with the first occurrence of value removed (an unchanged copy if it is not there) def rotate(xs, k): ... a new list rotated k places to the right: rotate( 1, 2, 3, 4 , 1) == 4, 1, 2, 3 rotate works for any k , including negative values (to the left) and values larger than the length; rotating an empty list gives an empty list.

title: 2.03  Loops: for and while
body: Repeating work - for loops over lists, strings and ranges, enumerate and zip, while loops that run until a condition changes, break and continue, the loop else, and common loop patterns such as counting, accumulating and searching. for loops over anything A for loop runs its body once for each item of a sequence: python for name in "Ada", "Grace", "Linus" : print("Hello,", name) for letter in "abc": print(letter.upper()) range produces numbers: range(5) is 0 to 4, range(2, 6) is 2 to 5, range(10, 0, -2) is 10, 8, 6, 4, 2. python total = 0 for n in range(1, 101): total += n print(total) 5050 enumerate and zip To have the position as well as the item, use enumerate instead of counting yourself: python for i, name in enumerate( "Ada", "Grace" , start=1): print(i, name) zip walks several sequences side by side, stopping at the shortest: python names = "Ada", "Grace" scores = 95, 88 for name, score in zip(names, scores): print(f"{name}: {score}") while loops A while loop repeats as long as its condition is true. Use it when you do not know in advance how many times: python n = 27 steps = 0 while n != 1: n = n // 2 if n % 2 == 0 else 3 n + 1 steps += 1 print(steps) 111 Make sure something in the body moves towards the end, or the loop runs forever (stop a runaway program with Ctrl+C). break and continue break leaves the loop at once; continue skips to the next round: python while True: line = input("Command (quit to stop): ") if line == "quit": break if line == "": continue print("You said", line) while True with a break is the standard shape for "repeat until the user says stop". The loop else A loop's else runs when the loop finished without break : perfect for searches. python target = 7 for n in 2, 4, 6 : if n == target: print("found") break else: print("not found") Patterns Pattern Shape --- --- Count count = 0 before, count += 1 when it matches Accumulate total = 0 / result = before, add to it inside Best so far best = None before; replace when better Search break when found; else for not found Do not change a list's length while looping over it; loop over a copy ( for x in xs : ) or build a new list. Check yourself quiz ? What numbers does range(10, 0, -3) produce? - 10, 7, 4 + 10, 7, 4, 1 - 9, 6, 3, 0 - 7, 4, 1 It starts at 10 and steps by -3 while it stays above the stop value 0, which is never included. ? When does a loop's else block run? - After every round of the loop - Right after a break leaves the loop + When the loop finishes without a break - When an if inside the loop was false The else belongs to the loop, not to an if : it runs when the loop ended normally, which is why it suits "not found". ? How many times does print(i, j) run in for i in range(3): with an inner loop for j in range(i): ? - 9 + 3 - 6 - 2 i = 0 runs the inner loop 0 times, i = 1 once and i = 2 twice: 3 in total.

Spaces around what is typed do not matter, and DONE works too. If no numbers were entered, print only no numbers .

title: 2.04  Tuples and Unpacking
body: Tuples are fixed sequences for values that belong together - coordinates, records, several return values. This lesson covers creating them, unpacking with , swapping, and when to choose a tuple over a list. Tuples A tuple is like a list that cannot be changed: written with parentheses (or just commas): python point = (3, 4) person = ("Ada", 1815, "London") single = (42,) the comma makes it a tuple; (42) is just 42 print(point 0 , len(person), person 1: ) Tuples support indexing, slicing, in , len , count and index , but not append or item assignment. When to use a tuple List Tuple --- --- Many items of the same kind that may change: a list of scores A fixed group of values with different meanings: a point, a date, a record Grows and shrinks Fixed size Cannot be a dictionary key Can be a dictionary key (if its items can) A good rule: if the position of an item has a meaning (index 0 is the name, index 1 the year), it is a tuple; if all items mean the same thing, it is a list. Unpacking Assigning a tuple (or any sequence) to several names unpacks it: python name, year, city = ("Ada", 1815, "London") x, y = (3, 4) a, b = b_and_a = (1, 2) print(name, year, x + y) The number of names must match, unless one name has a , which collects the rest into a list: python first, rest = 1, 2, 3, 4 body, last = "hello" head, _, tail = range(10) print(first, rest, body, last, head, tail) _ is the conventional name for a value you do not need. Swapping and multiple return values python a, b = 1, 2 a, b = b, a swap, no temporary variable def min_max(values): return min(values), max(values) returns one tuple low, high = min_max( 3, 9, 1 ) print(low, high) Unpacking in loops is where it is used most: python for name, score in ("Ada", 95), ("Grace", 88) : print(name, score) Named tuples When a tuple has many fields, positions become hard to remember. collections.namedtuple (or dataclasses, lesson 4.04) gives them names: python from collections import namedtuple Point = namedtuple("Point", "x", "y" ) p = Point(3, 4) print(p.x, p.y, p) Check yourself quiz ? How do you write a tuple holding just the number 42? - (42) - tuple(42) + (42,) - 42 The comma makes the tuple: (42) is just 42 in brackets, and tuple(42) fails because 42 is not a sequence. ? What does first, rest = 1, 2, 3 give? + first = 1 and rest = 2, 3 - first = 1 and rest = (2, 3) - first = 1 and rest = 2, 3 - an error: three values for two names The starred name collects everything left over, always into a list. ? Which of these can be a dictionary key? - 1, 2 - {1, 2} - {1: 2} + (1, 2) Keys must be unchangeable; tuples of numbers are, lists, sets and dictionaries are not.

"3,4" or " 3 , -4 " - (3, 4) / (3, -4) as ints def distance(p, q): ... straight-line distance between two points def closest(points, target): ... the point nearest to target (the first one on a tie); None for no points def bounds(points): ... ((min_x, min_y), (max_x, max_y)) of all points

title: 2.05  Dictionaries and Sets
body: Looking things up by key with dictionaries - creating, reading with get, updating, looping over items, counting and grouping - and sets for unique values and fast membership, with union, intersection and difference. Dictionaries A dictionary maps keys to values , and finds a value by its key instantly, however big it is: python ages = {"Ada": 36, "Grace": 85} print(ages "Ada" ) 36 ages "Linus" = 21 add ages "Ada" = 37 replace del ages "Grace" remove print(ages, len(ages), "Ada" in ages) Keys must be immutable (strings, numbers, tuples); values can be anything. Dictionaries keep the order in which keys were added. Reading safely d key raises KeyError for a missing key. When a key may be missing, use get with a default: python stock = {"apples": 4} print(stock.get("pears", 0)) 0 print(stock.get("apples", 0)) 4 Looping python prices = {"tea": 2.5, "cake": 3.0} for item in prices: keys print(item) for item, price in prices.items(): pairs print(f"{item}: {price:.2f}") print(list(prices.values()), sum(prices.values())) Counting and grouping Two patterns come up constantly: python words = "the cat and the hat".split() counts = {} for w in words: counts w = counts.get(w, 0) + 1 print(counts) {'the': 2, 'cat': 1, 'and': 1, 'hat': 1} by_length = {} for w in words: by_length.setdefault(len(w), ).append(w) print(by_length) {3: 'the', 'cat', 'and', 'the', 'hat' } setdefault(key, default) returns the value for the key, inserting the default first if it is missing. collections.Counter and defaultdict (lesson 5.04) make both even shorter. Sets A set holds unique values, in no particular order, with very fast in : python seen = {"Ada", "Grace"} seen.add("Ada") no effect: already there print(len(seen), "Grace" in seen) unique = set( 3, 1, 3, 2, 1 ) remove duplicates print(sorted(unique)) 1, 2, 3 Sets do maths with other sets: Operation Meaning --- --- a \ b Union: in either a & b Intersection: in both a - b Difference: in a but not b a ^ b In exactly one of them a <= b a is a subset of b python monday = {"Ada", "Grace", "Linus"} tuesday = {"Grace", "Barbara"} print(monday & tuesday, monday - tuesday, monday tuesday) {} is an empty dictionary ; an empty set is set() . Choosing a collection Need Use --- --- Ordered items, by position list A fixed record tuple Look up by a key dict Unique values, membership tests set Testing x in some_list checks every item; x in some_set is instant. For large collections that you search often, that difference is huge. Check yourself quiz ? How do you read a key from a dictionary d that may be missing, without an error? - d key, default + d.get(key, default) - d.find(key) - d key or default get returns the default when the key is missing. d key raises KeyError before or is even reached. ? What is {} on its own? + An empty dictionary - An empty set - An empty tuple - A syntax error {} is an empty dict; an empty set has to be written set() . ? What is len({"a": 1, "b": 2, "a": 3}) ? - 3 + 2 - 1 - an error A key can appear only once: the later "a": 3 replaces the earlier value.

title: 3.01  Functions
body: Packaging code under a name - def, parameters and return values, returning several values, functions without a return, docstrings, and why small functions with one job make programs easier to change and test. Defining a function python def area(width, height): """Return the area of a width x height rectangle.""" return width height print(area(3, 4)) 12 print(area(2.5, 2)) 5.0 - def names the function and its parameters . - The indented body runs each time the function is called . - return sends a value back and ends the function at once. - The string right after the def line is the docstring : help(area) shows it, and editors display it. A function must be defined before the line that calls it runs, but it can call functions defined later in the file, as long as they exist by the time the call happens. Return values A function without return (or with a bare return ) returns None : python def greet(name): print(f"Hello, {name}!") result = greet("Ada") print(result) None Mixing up "prints" and "returns" is a classic mistake: a function that prints its answer cannot be used in a calculation. Prefer functions that return values and leave printing to the code that calls them. Return several values as a tuple and unpack them (lesson 2.04): python def stats(values): return min(values), max(values), sum(values) / len(values) low, high, mean = stats( 4, 8, 6 ) print(low, high, mean) Early returns Returning early keeps the main path of a function unindented: python def describe(age): if age < 0: return "invalid" if age < 13: return "child" if age < 18: return "teenager" return "adult" Why functions - Name a piece of logic, so the code reads as a series of steps. - Reuse it instead of copying it. - Test it on its own: every unit test in this course calls functions. - Change it in one place. A good function does one thing, has a name that says what (a verb: load_scores , is_valid ), and is short enough to read at a glance. If you need "and" to describe it, it may be two functions. Functions are values A function is an object like any other: it can be stored in a variable, put in a list, or passed to another function: python def shout(text): return text.upper() + "!" def whisper(text): return text.lower() + "..." for style in shout, whisper : print(style("Hello")) Lesson 5.03 uses this for sorting with key functions. Check yourself quiz ? What does a function return if no return statement runs? - 0 + None - An empty string - The value of its last line A function with no return (or a bare return ) gives back None. The last line's value is not returned automatically. ? Why prefer returning a value over printing it inside the function? - Printing inside a function is not allowed in Python - Returning is faster, because print waits for the screen + A returned value can be used in calculations, tests and other functions - A function that prints cannot be called more than once Printed text only goes to the screen and the caller gets None. Leave printing to the code that calls the function. ? def f(x): holds only if x 0: return "positive" . What does print(f(-5)) print? - positive - negative - an error + None No return statement runs for -5, so the function returns None.

"freezing" (<= 0), "cold" (< 15), "mild" (< 25), "hot" otherwise def forecast_line(day, celsius): ... "Mon: 18.0°C / 64.4°F (mild)": one decimal for both temperatures forecast_line must use the other two functions.

title: 3.02  Parameters and Arguments
body: The flexible ways Python passes values to functions - positional and keyword arguments, default values and the mutable default trap, args and kwargs, keyword-only and positional-only parameters, and unpacking arguments. Positional and keyword arguments Arguments can be passed by position or by name : python def describe(name, age, city): return f"{name}, {age}, from {city}" print(describe("Ada", 36, "London")) print(describe(city="London", name="Ada", age=36)) any order print(describe("Ada", city="London", age=36)) positional first, then keywords Keyword arguments make calls readable when there are several values of the same type: resize(width=800, height=600) cannot be confused. Default values Parameters can have defaults, used when the argument is left out: python def greet(name, greeting="Hello", punctuation="!"): return f"{greeting}, {name}{punctuation}" print(greet("Ada")) print(greet("Ada", "Hi")) print(greet("Ada", punctuation=".")) Parameters with defaults come after those without. The mutable default trap Default values are created once , when the function is defined. A list or dictionary default is shared between all calls: python def add_item(item, basket= ): WRONG: one list for every call basket.append(item) return basket print(add_item("apple")) 'apple' print(add_item("pear")) 'apple', 'pear' surprise! The fix is None as the default and a new list inside: python def add_item(item, basket=None): if basket is None: basket = basket.append(item) return basket Any number of arguments args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple; kwargs collects extra keyword arguments into a dictionary: python def total( numbers): return sum(numbers) def tag(name, attributes): parts = " ".join(f'{k}="{v}"' for k, v in attributes.items()) return f"<{name} {parts} " print(total(1, 2, 3)) print(tag("img", src="cat.png", alt="A cat")) The reverse, unpacking , spreads a list or dictionary into arguments: python values = 1, 2, 3 print(total( values)) options = {"greeting": "Hi", "punctuation": "?"} print(greet("Ada", options)) Keyword-only and positional-only A in the parameter list makes everything after it keyword-only ; a / makes everything before it positional-only : python def connect(host, port, /, , timeout=10, retries=3): return f"{host}:{port} timeout={timeout} retries={retries}" print(connect("example.org", 443, timeout=5)) Keyword-only parameters are good for options ( timeout , reverse ): callers must name them, so calls stay readable and the order can change later. Arguments are references Python passes references to objects. A function can change a mutable argument (a list, a dictionary) and the caller sees it, but assigning a new value to the parameter name does not affect the caller's variable. Documenting whether a function changes its arguments ("sorts the list in place") avoids surprises. Check yourself quiz ? Why is a list as a default value, as in def add_item(item, basket= ) , a bug? - Lists cannot be defaults: defining the function raises an error + The one default list is shared by every call, so items pile up - A fresh list is made on each call, so earlier items are lost - The caller's own list is cleared each time the function runs Defaults are created once, when def runs. Use None as the default and make a new list inside the function. ? What does a bare in a parameter list do? - Collects any extra positional arguments into a tuple - Makes every parameter before it positional-only + Makes every parameter after it keyword-only - Lets the function accept any keyword arguments A bare collects nothing; it only marks the rest as keyword-only. args collects extras, and / marks positional-only. ? Given def f(a, b=2, rest, c=3) , what is f(1, 5, 6, 7) 's rest ? - (5, 6, 7) + (6, 7) - 6, 7 - 7 1 and 5 fill a and b; the remaining positional arguments are collected in the tuple rest; c keeps its default.

title: Flexible parameters
body: Write four functions that use lesson 3.02's parameter features: python def format_price(amount, currency="€", decimals=2, , thousands=False): ... def average( numbers): ... None when called with no numbers def merged(defaults, overrides): ... a NEW dict: defaults updated with the overrides def add_tag(tag, tags=None): ... appends tag to tags (or to a new list) and returns the list - format_price(1234.5) is "1234.50 €" ; format_price(1234.5, "$", 0) is "1234 $" (rounded); with thousands=True the number has commas: "1,234.50 €" . - merged must not change defaults . - add_tag must not share a list between calls that do not pass one.

title: 3.03  Scope and Closures
body: Where names live - local and global scope, the LEGB lookup order, global and nonlocal, functions defined inside functions, closures that remember values, and lambda expressions. Local and global A name assigned inside a function is local : it exists only while the function runs and does not affect a name outside with the same spelling: python count = 10 def reset(): count = 0 a new LOCAL name; the global count is untouched return count reset() print(count) 10 Names are looked up in the order L ocal, E nclosing functions, G lobal (the module), B uilt-in ( print , len ): the LEGB rule. Reading a global inside a function works; assigning to it creates a local, unless you say otherwise. global and nonlocal python total = 0 def add(n): global total total += n add(5) print(total) 5 global is rarely a good idea: functions that change globals are hard to test and reason about. Pass values in and return results instead. nonlocal does the same for a variable of an enclosing function, which is how closures keep state (below). A common error: reading a variable that is assigned later in the same function raises UnboundLocalError , because the assignment makes it local for the whole function. Functions inside functions A function can define another function, which can see the outer function's names: python def make_greeter(greeting): def greet(name): return f"{greeting}, {name}!" return greet hello = make_greeter("Hello") howdy = make_greeter("Howdy") print(hello("Ada"), howdy("Grace")) greet remembers greeting even after make_greeter has returned. A function together with the variables it remembers is a closure . Closures with state With nonlocal , a closure can update what it remembers: python def make_counter(): count = 0 def next_value(): nonlocal count count += 1 return count return next_value counter = make_counter() print(counter(), counter(), counter()) 1 2 3 Each call to make_counter creates a separate count . For anything larger, a class (lesson 4.01) is usually clearer. lambda A lambda is a small anonymous function written as an expression: lambda parameters: expression . It is handy where a short function is passed to another: python square = lambda x: x x print(square(7)) pairs = ("Ada", 36), ("Grace", 85), ("Linus", 21) print(sorted(pairs, key=lambda pair: pair 1 )) Keep lambdas to one simple expression; anything more deserves a def with a name. A closure trap Closures remember variables , not values. Lambdas made in a loop all see the loop variable's final value: python funcs = lambda: i for i in range(3) print( f() for f in funcs ) 2, 2, 2 funcs = lambda i=i: i for i in range(3) a default captures the current value print( f() for f in funcs ) 0, 1, 2 Check yourself quiz ? In what order does Python look up a name used inside a function? - Global, Local, Built-in, Enclosing + Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in - Built-in, Global, Enclosing, Local - Local, Global, Enclosing, Built-in The LEGB rule: the function's own names, then enclosing functions, then the module, then built-ins such as len . ? What is a closure? - A function that has finished running and freed its variables - Any function written with lambda instead of def - A function that uses global to keep state between calls + A function plus the enclosing function's variables it still refers to Like greet remembering greeting after make_greeter has returned. A lambda can be a closure too, but being a lambda is not what makes one. ? Global x = 1 ; f sets x = 2 , defines g that returns x , and returns g() . What does print(f(), x) print? - 1 1 + 2 1 - 2 2 - an error g finds x in its enclosing function f (2); the global x is still 1.

title: Functions that remember
body: Write three closure factories: python def make_counter(start=0, step=1): ... returns a function; each call returns the next value: start, start + step, ... def make_averager(): ... returns a function f(x) that adds x and returns the average of all values so far def memoize(func): ... returns a function that calls func only once per argument, remembering results The function returned by memoize must also have an attribute calls counting how many times func really ran: set it with wrapper.calls = 0 and update it as wrapper.calls += 1 .

title: 3.04  Modules and Packages
body: Splitting a program into files - modules and import, the forms of import, the __name__ == "__main__" idiom, packages, how Python finds modules, the standard library, and installing third-party packages with pip in a virtual environment. Modules Every .py file is a module . Another file can import it to use its functions and variables: python geometry.py import math def circle_area(r): return math.pi r r python main.py import geometry print(geometry.circle_area(2)) The forms of import: Form Use as --- --- import geometry geometry.circle_area(2) import geometry as geo geo.circle_area(2) from geometry import circle_area circle_area(2) from geometry import Everything public; avoid: it hides where names come from A module's code runs once , the first time it is imported; later imports reuse it. The main guard When a file is run directly, its __name__ is "__main__" ; when it is imported, __name__ is the module's name. That lets a file be both a module and a script: python geometry.py def circle_area(r): return 3.14159 r r if __name__ == "__main__": print(circle_area(2)) only when run as a script, not on import Put demonstration and start-up code under this guard so importing the module has no side effects. Packages A package is a folder of modules (traditionally with an __init__.py file): shapes/ __init__.py circles.py polygons.py python from shapes.circles import area from shapes import polygons __init__.py runs when the package is imported and can import the most useful names, so users can write from shapes import area . How imports are found Python searches the folder of the script being run first, then the standard library, then installed packages ( sys.path lists the folders). Naming your own file like a standard module ( random.py , json.py ) shadows the real one: import random then imports your file, with confusing errors. The standard library Python comes "with batteries included": math , random , datetime , pathlib , json , csv , re , collections , itertools , statistics , urllib , sqlite3 and many more. Look there first: milestone 6 uses several of them. python import random, statistics rolls = random.randint(1, 6) for _ in range(1000) print(statistics.mean(rolls)) Third-party packages Thousands more packages live on PyPI (the Python Package Index) and are installed with pip . Use a virtual environment per project, so each project has its own packages and versions: python -m venv .venv .venv\Scripts\activate (Windows; source .venv/bin/activate on Linux and macOS) pip install requests pip freeze requirements.txt (record the versions; pip install -r requirements.txt restores them) Check yourself quiz ? What does if __name__ == "__main__": do? - Runs the code below it only when the file is imported by another module - Marks the function Python must call first, like main in C++ + Runs the code below it only when the file is run directly, not on import - Stops other modules from importing the file A file run directly has __name__ set to "__main__"; when imported it is the module's name, so the guarded code is skipped. ? Why should you not name your own file random.py ? - Python refuses to run files named after standard modules + import random would then import your file instead of the real module - The file would replace the standard module for the whole computer - Module names may not be ordinary English words The script's own folder is searched first, so your file shadows the standard module and causes confusing errors. ? A module prints "loading" at the top. How many times is it printed if two other modules both import it? - twice + once - three times - never A module's code runs only on its first import; later imports reuse the loaded module.

title: The standard library
body: Use modules from the standard library (lesson 3.04) instead of writing everything yourself: python def roll_dice(count, sides, seed): ... a list of count rolls from 1 to sides, using random.Random(seed) def summary(values): ... (mean, median, mode) using the statistics module def days_between(start, end): ... days from start to end, dates written "YYYY-MM-DD", using datetime def is_prime(n): ... True for primes; use math.isqrt for the square root random.Random(seed) makes a generator that always produces the same sequence for the same seed; call its randint(1, sides) once per roll.

title: 3.05  Files and Paths
body:
Reading and writing text files safely with with-blocks, reading line by line, encodings, appending, working with paths using pathlib, listing and finding files, and the difference between text and binary files. Opening files with with python with open("notes.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f: f.write("first line
") f.write("second line
") with open("notes.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f: text = f.read() print(text) The with block closes the file when it ends, even if an error happens inside. Always use it. Mode Meaning --- --- "r" Read (the default); error if missing "w" Write: creates the file, empties it if it exists "a" Append: writes at the end "x" Create: error if it already exists "rb" , "wb" Binary (bytes instead of text) Always pass encoding="utf-8" for text: the default depends on the computer, and a file written on one machine can be unreadable on another. Reading line by line A file object is iterable, one line at a time, which works for files of any size: python with open("notes.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f: f.write("apples 3
pears 5

plums 2
") total = 0 with open("notes.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f: for line in f: line = line.strip() remove the "
" (and spaces) if not line: continue skip blank lines name, count = line.split() total += int(count) print(total) f.read() reads everything as one string; f.readlines() gives a list of lines (with their 
 ); f.read().splitlines() gives lines without them. Writing write takes a string and does not add a new line; print(..., file=f) does: python scores = {"Ada": 95, "Grace": 88} with open("scores.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f: for name, score in scores.items(): print(f"{name},{score}", file=f) Paths with pathlib pathlib.Path represents a path and has methods for everything you do with files: python from pathlib import Path folder = Path("reports") folder.mkdir(exist_ok=True) create if missing report = folder / "2026-11.txt" / joins path parts on every system report.write_text("total: 42
", encoding="utf-8") print(report.exists(), report.name, report.stem, report.suffix, report.parent) print(report.read_text(encoding="utf-8")) for path in sorted(folder.glob(" .txt")): files matching a pattern; rglob searches subfolders print(path.name, path.stat().st_size, "bytes") Path.home() is the user's home folder, Path.cwd() the current folder, and path.resolve() the full absolute path. When files are missing Opening a missing file for reading raises FileNotFoundError . Check first with path.exists() or handle the error (lesson 4.05). Paths in a script are relative to the current working directory , not to the script's folder; Path(__file__).parent is the script's own folder when you need files next to it. Text and binary Text files are decoded into str using an encoding; binary files ( "rb" ) give bytes , for images, zip files and anything that is not text. Path.read_bytes() and write_bytes() are the binary versions. Check yourself quiz ? Why open files with a with block? - It opens the file faster than a plain open call - It is the only way to choose an encoding + The file is closed automatically when the block ends, even after an error - It stops other programs from changing the file meanwhile Leaving the with block always closes the file, however the block ends. ? What happens when you open an existing file with mode "w" ? - The new text is added at the end + It is emptied before anything is written - Python raises an error because the file exists - It opens for reading and writing, keeping the contents "w" empties the file. Use "a" to append, and "x" to get an error if the file already exists. ? Which line joins a folder and a file name correctly on every operating system? - "reports" + name - Path("reports" + name) - "reports\" + name + Path("reports") / name The / operator on Path objects puts in the right separator for the system; plain + adds none, or a Windows-only backslash.

A line like Ada,abc or just text is skipped. Write files as UTF-8.

"Ada Lovelace: 90, 85, 77" - ("Ada Lovelace", 90, 85, 77 ); None if not valid def load(path): ... dict name - list of marks, from every valid line, in file order def average(marks): ... rounded to one decimal; None for no marks def letter(avg): ... "A" = 90, "B" = 80, "C" = 70, "D" = 60, else "F"; "-" for None def report(book): ... the report text (below) def save_report(path, book): ... writes report(book) to path Lines : a name, a colon, then marks separated by commas. Spaces around everything are ignored. Marks are whole numbers from 0 to 100. A line with no colon, an empty name, or any mark that is not a valid number is invalid ( None ); a line with a name and no marks after the colon is valid with an empty list. Blank lines are skipped. The header uses the same widths ( Avg right-aligned in 4). - The class average is the average of the students' averages (students without marks are left out), with one decimal, or - if no student has marks. - Every line ends with a new line.

title: 4.01  Classes and Objects
body: Bundling data and behaviour together - defining a class, __init__ and self, attributes and methods, class attributes, keeping an object valid, properties, and when a class is better than a dictionary or a few functions. A class is a new type A class describes a kind of object: what data it holds ( attributes ) and what it can do ( methods ). Each instance has its own data: python class BankAccount: def __init__(self, owner, balance=0): self.owner = owner self.balance = balance def deposit(self, amount): self.balance += amount def describe(self): return f"{self.owner}: {self.balance:.2f}" a = BankAccount("Ada") b = BankAccount("Grace", 100) a.deposit(25) print(a.describe(), " ", b.describe()) - __init__ runs when an instance is created and sets up its attributes. - self is the instance the method is working on. a.deposit(25) is the same as BankAccount.deposit(a, 25) . - Attributes are created by assigning to self.something . Class names use CapitalisedWords ; methods follow function naming ( lower_case ). Keeping objects valid A class can protect its data so the object never gets into a nonsense state: python class BankAccount: def __init__(self, owner, balance=0): if balance < 0: raise ValueError("balance cannot be negative") self.owner = owner self._balance = balance def withdraw(self, amount): if amount <= 0: raise ValueError("amount must be positive") if amount self._balance: raise ValueError("insufficient funds") self._balance -= amount @property def balance(self): return self._balance acct = BankAccount("Ada", 50) acct.withdraw(20) print(acct.balance) 30: read like an attribute A leading underscore ( _balance ) means "internal: do not touch from outside"; Python does not enforce it, but everyone respects it. A property exposes a value for reading while the class controls how it changes. raise (lesson 4.05) refuses invalid requests. Class attributes Attributes defined in the class body belong to the class , shared by all instances: python class Dice: sides = 6 shared def __init__(self): self.rolls = per instance print(Dice.sides, Dice().sides) Use class attributes for constants and defaults; never for mutable data that each instance should have its own copy of (the same trap as mutable default arguments, lesson 3.02). Methods that do not need an instance python class Temperature: def __init__(self, celsius): self.celsius = celsius @classmethod def from_fahrenheit(cls, f): another way to create an instance return cls((f - 32) 5 / 9) @staticmethod def is_valid(celsius): just a function kept with the class return celsius = -273.15 print(Temperature.from_fahrenheit(212).celsius, Temperature.is_valid(-300)) When to write a class Use a class when data and the operations on it belong together and the data has rules (an account's balance cannot go negative). For a few related values with no behaviour, a dictionary, tuple or dataclass (lesson 4.04) is simpler. For a single operation, a function is enough. Check yourself quiz ? What is self in a method? - The class the method belongs to + The instance the method was called on - A keyword Python adds to every function - A copy of the object, so changes stay local In a.deposit(25) , self is a itself: the call is the same as BankAccount.deposit(a, 25) , so changes to self change a . ? What does a leading underscore, as in self._balance , mean? - Python stops code outside the class from reading it - It is a class attribute shared by all instances + It is internal to the class: other code should not use it directly - It marks the value as a constant that cannot change It is a convention that everyone respects, not something Python enforces. A property can still expose the value for reading. ? Two instances share which of these? - attributes set in __init__ with self.x = ... - local variables in methods + attributes assigned in the class body - nothing Attributes in the class body belong to the class; self.x attributes belong to each instance.

title: A bank account
body: Write a BankAccount class that can never get into an invalid state: python class BankAccount: def __init__(self, owner, balance=0): ... ValueError if balance < 0 balance a read-only property def deposit(self, amount): ... ValueError unless amount 0 def withdraw(self, amount): ... ValueError unless 0 < amount <= balance def transfer(self, other, amount): ... withdraw here, deposit there; nothing changes if it fails def history(self): ... list of ("deposit" "withdraw", amount) in order, a copy The opening balance is not part of the history. A transfer appears as a withdraw in this account's history and a deposit in the other's.

title: 4.02  Special Methods
body: Making your classes behave like built-in types - __repr__ and __str__ for printing, __eq__ and ordering, arithmetic operators, __len__, __getitem__ and __iter__ for containers, __contains__, and __hash__ for use in sets and as keys. Methods Python calls for you Methods with double underscores on both sides ("dunder" methods) are called by Python's own syntax: You write Python calls --- --- repr(x) , the REPL, debugging x.__repr__() str(x) , print(x) , f-strings x.__str__() (falls back to __repr__ ) x == y x.__eq__(y) x < y x.__lt__(y) x + y , x y x.__add__(y) , x.__mul__(y) len(x) x.__len__() x i x.__getitem__(i) for item in x x.__iter__() item in x x.__contains__(item) hash(x) , sets, dict keys x.__hash__() A vector python import math class Vector: def __init__(self, x, y): self.x, self.y = x, y def __repr__(self): return f"Vector({self.x}, {self.y})" def __eq__(self, other): if not isinstance(other, Vector): return NotImplemented return (self.x, self.y) == (other.x, other.y) def __add__(self, other): return Vector(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y) def __mul__(self, k): return Vector(self.x k, self.y k) def __rmul__(self, k): k v, when k is on the left return self k def __abs__(self): return math.hypot(self.x, self.y) v = Vector(3, 4) print(v + Vector(1, 1), 2 v, abs(v), v == Vector(3, 4)) __repr__ should look like the code that would create the object: it is what you see when debugging. Returning NotImplemented (not raising) from __eq__ lets Python try the other side or fall back to "not equal". Containers A class that holds items can support len , indexing, in and loops: python class Playlist: def __init__(self, songs): self._songs = list(songs) def __len__(self): return len(self._songs) def __getitem__(self, index): return self._songs index slices work too, because lists support them def __iter__(self): return iter(self._songs) def __contains__(self, song): return song in self._songs p = Playlist("Intro", "Theme", "Outro") print(len(p), p 1 , p -1 , "Theme" in p, s.upper() for s in p ) Ordering and hashing Defining __eq__ and __lt__ , plus functools.total_ordering , gives all six comparisons, so sorted() works on your objects. An object used in a set or as a dictionary key needs __hash__ consistent with __eq__ (equal objects must have equal hashes); a class that defines __eq__ without __hash__ becomes unhashable, which is correct for mutable objects. Dataclasses (lesson 4.04) write most of this for you. Check yourself quiz ? When are __str__ and __repr__ used? - __repr__ for print and f-strings; __str__ only when you call str() yourself + __str__ for print and f-strings; __repr__ for debugging, and as __str__ 's fallback - __str__ when the object is created; __repr__ when it is shown in a list - Both are used only by the interactive prompt print(x) and f-strings call __str__ , which falls back to __repr__ when the class has none; repr() and the REPL use __repr__ . ? Why does 2 v need __rmul__ when v 2 only needs __mul__ ? - only allows the object on the left - __mul__ only works with whole numbers, __rmul__ with floats + Python first asks int, which knows no vectors, then calls v's __rmul__ - 2 v repeats the vector twice, as 2 1, 2 does With the number on the left, int's own multiplication gives up (NotImplemented), so Python tries the right operand's __rmul__ . ? Which method makes len(obj) work? - __length__ - __size__ - len + __len__ Python's built-in len calls obj.__len__().

title: Money that behaves
body: Write a Money class stored as whole cents, with the special methods of lesson 4.02: python m = Money(1250, "EUR") repr(m) "Money(1250, 'EUR')" str(m) "12.50 EUR" m + Money(5, "EUR") Money(1255, 'EUR'); adding different currencies raises ValueError m 3, 3 m Money(3750, 'EUR') m == Money(1250, "EUR"), m < Money(1300, "EUR") comparing different currencies raises ValueError {m, Money(1250, "EUR")} one element: equal money has equal hashes sum( ... , Money(0, "EUR")) works because + works Negative amounts print with a minus sign: Money(-5, "USD") is "-0.05 USD" . Comparing Money with something that is not Money using == gives False .

title: 4.03  Inheritance and Protocols
body: Sharing behaviour between classes - subclasses, overriding methods, super(), abstract base classes, and Python's duck typing, where any object with the right methods will do. This lesson also says when composition is better than inheritance. Subclasses A subclass inherits everything from its base class and can add or override methods: python class Shape: def __init__(self, name): self.name = name def area(self): return 0.0 def describe(self): return f"{self.name} with area {self.area():.2f}" class Rectangle(Shape): def __init__(self, width, height): super().__init__("rectangle") let the base class set up its part self.width, self.height = width, height def area(self): overrides Shape.area return self.width self.height class Circle(Shape): def __init__(self, radius): super().__init__("circle") self.radius = radius def area(self): return 3.141592653589793 self.radius 2 for shape in Rectangle(3, 4), Circle(1) : print(shape.describe()) describe is written once, in Shape , and calls whichever area the actual object has: this is polymorphism . isinstance(shape, Shape) is true for both. super() super() gives access to the base class's version of a method, most often to extend __init__ or to add to a method rather than replace it: python class LoggedRectangle(Rectangle): def area(self): result = super().area() print(f"area computed: {result}") return result Abstract base classes When a base class only describes what subclasses must provide, make it abstract so it cannot be used by mistake: python from abc import ABC, abstractmethod class Exporter(ABC): @abstractmethod def export(self, rows): """Return the rows as text.""" class CsvExporter(Exporter): def export(self, rows): return "\n".join(",".join(map(str, row)) for row in rows) print(CsvExporter().export( (1, 2), (3, 4) )) Exporter() would raise TypeError: abstract methods are missing Duck typing Python does not require a shared base class. If an object has the methods that are used, it works: "if it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck...". len() works on anything with __len__ ; a function that calls .write(text) works with a file, a StringIO , or your own class with a write method. python import io def save_report(out, lines): for line in lines: out.write(line + "\n") buffer = io.StringIO() save_report(buffer, "a", "b" ) works with any object that has write() print(repr(buffer.getvalue())) typing.Protocol (lesson 5.05) lets you describe such a "duck" for type checkers without inheritance. Composition over inheritance Inheritance means "is a": a circle is a shape. When the relationship is "has a" (a car has an engine), store the other object in an attribute instead: composition . It is more flexible (the engine can be swapped) and avoids deep class hierarchies that are hard to change. A good rule: inherit only when the subclass truly can be used everywhere the base class can. Check yourself quiz ? What does super().__init__(...) do in a subclass's __init__ ? - Creates a second, separate object of the base class + Runs the base class's __init__ so its part of the object is set up - Replaces the subclass's __init__ with the base class's - Calls the subclass's own __init__ again The base class sets up its attributes (like name in Shape) on the same object; the subclass then adds its own. ? What is duck typing? - Checking an object's class with isinstance before using it - Making every class inherit from one shared base class - Converting an object to the type a function expects + Code works with any object that has the methods it uses, whatever its class No shared base class is needed: a function that calls .write() accepts a file, a StringIO or your own class with write . ? Class B(A) overrides greet . Inside B, how do you call A's version? - A.greet() - self.greet() + super().greet() - base.greet() super() refers to the next class up the hierarchy; self.greet() would call B's own version again.

title: A family of shapes
body: Write a small class hierarchy: python class Shape(ABC): abstract: area() and perimeter() are abstract methods def describe(self): ... "<Name : area 12.00, perimeter 14.00", with the class name class Rectangle(Shape): def __init__(self, width, height) class Square(Rectangle): def __init__(self, side) a square IS a rectangle class Circle(Shape): def __init__(self, radius) use math.pi def largest(shapes): ... the shape with the greatest area (the first one on a tie); None for an empty list def total_area(shapes): ... works for any objects that have an area() method, shapes or not Shape() itself must raise TypeError (it is abstract). describe is written only once, in Shape ; type(self).__name__ gives the class name.

title: 4.04  Dataclasses and Enums
body: Less boilerplate for data-holding classes - @dataclass generates __init__, __repr__ and __eq__, with defaults, field(default_factory), ordering, frozen instances and __post_init__ validation - and Enum for a fixed set of named values. Dataclasses Many classes mostly hold data. Writing __init__ , __repr__ and __eq__ by hand for them is tedious; @dataclass generates them from annotated fields: python from dataclasses import dataclass, field @dataclass class Book: title: str author: str year: int tags: list str = field(default_factory=list) a NEW list per instance read: bool = False b = Book("Dune", "Frank Herbert", 1965) b.tags.append("sci-fi") print(b) print(b == Book("Dune", "Frank Herbert", 1965, "sci-fi" )) The type annotations ( str , int ) document the fields; Python does not check them at run time. Fields with defaults come after fields without. Use field(default_factory=list) for mutable defaults: a plain = is refused for exactly the reason of lesson 3.02. Options Option Effect --- --- @dataclass(order=True) Adds < , <= , , = comparing fields in order, so instances sort @dataclass(frozen=True) Instances cannot be changed after creation, and become hashable @dataclass(slots=True) Uses less memory per instance python @dataclass(frozen=True, order=True) class Version: major: int minor: int patch: int = 0 print(sorted( Version(2, 0), Version(1, 9, 3), Version(1, 10) )) releases = {Version(1, 0): "first"} frozen: usable as a key Validation __post_init__ runs after the generated __init__ and can check or compute fields: python @dataclass class Rectangle: width: float height: float def __post_init__(self): if self.width <= 0 or self.height <= 0: raise ValueError("sides must be positive") @property def area(self): return self.width self.height print(Rectangle(2, 3).area) Dataclasses are ordinary classes: they can have methods and properties, and inherit. Enums An enum is a fixed set of named values, much safer than strings like "red" that can be misspelt: python from enum import Enum, auto class Status(Enum): TODO = auto() DOING = auto() DONE = auto() s = Status.DOING print(s, s.name, s.value, s is Status.DOING) print( status.name for status in Status ) print(Status "DONE" , Status(1)) by name, by value Enums are compared with is or == , can be iterated, and work well with match (lesson 1.05). StrEnum and IntEnum make members that also behave as strings or numbers, handy when the values are written to files. Check yourself quiz ? What does @dataclass write for you? - Type checks that reject wrong field types at run time + __init__ , __repr__ and __eq__ , from the annotated fields - A __hash__ , so every instance can be a dictionary key - Properties that make every field read-only The annotations only document the types; Python does not check them. Hashing and read-only fields come with frozen=True . ? Why must a list default be written field(default_factory=list) ? - list is not allowed as a type in a dataclass field - default_factory makes the list faster to append to + A plain list default would be shared by every instance - Without it, the list could not be changed after creation default_factory calls list() for each new instance; a plain = is refused because one list would be shared, the trap of lesson 3.02. ? What does @dataclass(frozen=True) add? - type checking of every field - < and comparisons - faster attribute access + instances that cannot be changed Frozen instances raise an error on assignment, and they also get a __hash__ so they can be set members or dict keys. Ordering comes from order=True , not frozen .

title: Tasks as dataclasses
body: Model tasks with a dataclass and an enum: python class Priority(Enum): HIGH = 1; NORMAL = 2; LOW = 3 @dataclass class Task: title: str priority: Priority = Priority.NORMAL tags: list str = field(default_factory=list) done: bool = False def parse_task(text): ... "Write report !high work urgent" - Task("Write report", Priority.HIGH, "work", "urgent" ) def sort_tasks(tasks): ... a new list: not done first, then by priority (HIGH first), then title def with_tag(tasks, tag): ... the tasks that have the tag (compared ignoring case) In parse_task , words starting with are tags (stored without , in lower case, in order, without duplicates); a word !high , !normal or !low (any case) sets the priority; everything else forms the title, words joined by single spaces. An unknown !word raises ValueError .

title: 4.05  Errors and Exceptions
body: Handling what goes wrong - reading tracebacks, try and except, catching specific exceptions, else and finally, raising your own errors, custom exception classes, and the difference between asking permission and asking forgiveness. Exceptions and tracebacks When something goes wrong, Python raises an exception . If nothing handles it, the program stops with a traceback : Traceback (most recent call last): File "main.py", line 3, in <module print(average( )) File "main.py", line 2, in average return sum(values) / len(values) ZeroDivisionError: division by zero Read it from the bottom : the last line says what happened ( ZeroDivisionError ) and why; the lines above show the chain of calls, ending at the line that failed. Common exceptions: Exception Typical cause --- --- ValueError Right type, wrong value: int("abc") TypeError Wrong type: "a" + 1 KeyError Missing dictionary key IndexError List index out of range AttributeError Misspelt attribute or method, or None where an object was expected FileNotFoundError Opening a missing file ZeroDivisionError Division by zero try and except python text = input("A number: ") try: number = int(text) except ValueError: print("That was not a whole number.") else: print("Twice that is", number 2) runs only if there was no exception finally: print("Done.") always runs Catch specific exceptions. A bare except: (or except Exception: ) also hides bugs such as misspelt names, and makes problems silently disappear. Several kinds can share a handler, and the exception object can be inspected: python for raw in "12", "x", None : try: print(int(raw) 2) except (ValueError, TypeError) as e: print("skipping:", e) Raising exceptions A function that cannot do its job should raise rather than return a strange value: python def withdraw(balance, amount): if amount <= 0: raise ValueError(f"amount must be positive, got {amount}") if amount balance: raise ValueError("insufficient funds") return balance - amount The caller decides what to do: show a message, retry, or let it stop the program. Your own exception classes For errors specific to your program, define a class deriving from Exception , so callers can catch exactly them: python class ConfigError(Exception): """The configuration file is invalid.""" def read_port(settings): if "port" not in settings: raise ConfigError("missing port") return int(settings "port" ) try: read_port({}) except ConfigError as e: print("Config problem:", e) raise NewError(...) from e inside an except keeps the original exception attached as the cause, which makes the traceback tell the whole story. Asking forgiveness Python style often prefers trying and handling the failure ( EAFP : easier to ask forgiveness than permission) over checking first ( LBYL : look before you leap): python counts = {"a": 1} try: value = counts "b" except KeyError: value = 0 Checking first can be wrong anyway: a file that exists when you check can be deleted before you open it. For simple cases, dict.get and str.isdigit are clearer than either. Check yourself quiz ? Which line of a traceback do you read first? - The first one, "Traceback (most recent call last)" + The last one: the exception type and message - The first File ... line, where the program started - The line with the most indentation The last line says what happened and why; the lines above it are the chain of calls, ending at the line that failed. ? Why catch specific exceptions instead of everything? - A bare except: is a syntax error in Python 3 - Catching everything makes the program run slower + Catching everything also hides real bugs, such as misspelt names - Only a specific except gives you the exception object with as e A bare except: would also swallow the NameError from a typo, so a bug silently disappears instead of showing a traceback. ? In try/except/else/finally, when does the else block run? - always - only when an exception was caught + only when the try block raised no exception - before finally, if an exception was raised else is for code that should run only after the try block succeeded; finally runs in every case.

title: Reading records safely
body: Read records like Ada,36,ada@example.org from lines of text, collecting errors instead of crashing: python class InvalidRecord(Exception): ... def parse_record(line): ... - (name, age, email); raises InvalidRecord with a message def load_records(lines): ... - (records, errors); errors are "line N: <message ", N counting from 1 parse_record checks, in order, and raises InvalidRecord with these messages: - not exactly three comma-separated fields: "expected 3 fields, got N" - an empty name (after stripping spaces): "missing name" - an age that is not a whole number: "age is not a number: <text " (use int() and catch its ValueError , re-raising as InvalidRecord with from ) - an age outside 0-150: "age out of range: <age " - an email without exactly one @ with text on both sides: "invalid email: <text " Fields are stripped of surrounding spaces. load_records skips blank lines (they are not errors).
