title: An inventory system
body: Write the stock-keeping core of a small shop: products as dataclasses, an Inventory class that behaves like a container, its own exception types, and order processing that reports problems instead of stopping. python class InventoryError(Exception): ... class UnknownProduct(InventoryError): ... str(e) is "unknown product: <sku " class OutOfStock(InventoryError): ... str(e) is "only <n of <sku left"; e.available is <n @dataclass class Product: sku: str name: str price_cents: int quantity: int = 0 class Inventory: def add_product(self, product): ... ValueError if the sku already exists def restock(self, sku, amount): ... UnknownProduct / ValueError if amount <= 0 def take(self, sku, amount): ... UnknownProduct / ValueError / OutOfStock; returns the product def __len__(self): ... number of products def __contains__(self, sku): ... def __iter__(self): ... products in sku order @property def total_value(self): ... sum of price x quantity, in cents def low_stock(self, threshold): ... skus with quantity < threshold, in sku order def process_orders(inventory, orders): ... orders: list of (sku, amount); returns a list of report lines process_orders handles each order in turn and adds one line: "OK <sku x<amount " when it succeeded, or "FAILED <sku x<amount : <message " with the exception's message for any InventoryError or ValueError . A failed order changes nothing. After the orders, it adds "<k of <n orders filled" . take with amount <= 0 raises ValueError("amount must be positive") ; restock the same.

title: 5.01  Comprehensions
body: Building lists, dictionaries and sets in one readable expression - list comprehensions with conditions, nested comprehensions, dictionary and set comprehensions, conditional expressions inside them, and when a plain loop is clearer. List comprehensions A very common loop builds a new list from an old one: python squares = for n in range(1, 6): squares.append(n n) A list comprehension says the same in one expression: python squares = n n for n in range(1, 6) print(squares) 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 Read it as " n × n for each n in the range". The parts are: the expression to collect, then for name in iterable . Filtering An if at the end keeps only some items: python words = "apple", "Kiwi", "banana", "fig", "Cherry" long_words = w for w in words if len(w) 4 capitalised = w for w in words if w 0 .isupper() print(long_words, capitalised) To transform some items rather than drop them, put a conditional expression (lesson 1.05) at the front: python numbers = 3, -1, 4, -5 print( n if n = 0 else 0 for n in numbers ) 3, 0, 4, 0 if at the end filters; if ... else at the front chooses a value. Nested loops Several for clauses work like nested loops, read left to right: python pairs = (x, y) for x in range(3) for y in range(3) if x != y grid = 0 4 for _ in range(3) 3 separate rows of 4 zeros flat = cell for row in 1, 2 , 3, 4 for cell in row print(pairs :3 , flat) Dictionary and set comprehensions python words = "apple", "fig", "banana" lengths = {w: len(w) for w in words} dict initials = {w 0 for w in words} set inverted = {v: k for k, v in {"a": 1, "b": 2}.items()} print(lengths, initials, inverted) Generator expressions With parentheses instead of brackets, the same syntax makes a generator that produces items one at a time without building a list (lesson 5.02). Passed straight to a function, the extra parentheses can be dropped: python print(sum(n n for n in range(1_000_000))) print(any(w.startswith("b") for w in "apple", "banana" )) print(max(len(w) for w in "apple", "fig", "banana" )) When not to use one Comprehensions are for building a collection. If the loop's job is a side effect (printing, writing files), use a plain for . If the expression needs several steps or nested conditions, a loop with good variable names is clearer than a comprehension that has to be read three times. A good rule: one for , at most one condition, one short expression. Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference between x for x in xs if c and a if c else b for x in xs ? - They do the same thing; only the order of the parts differs - The first chooses a value for each item; the second filters items out + The first filters items out; the second keeps every item but chooses a value for each - The second form is a syntax error inside a comprehension An if at the end drops items that fail the test; if ... else at the front keeps every item and picks which value to collect. ? Why is sum(x x for x in data) better than sum( x x for x in data ) for big data? + It makes the values one at a time instead of building the whole list in memory - The generator expression skips items that are zero, so there is less to add - The list version can give a wrong total once the numbers get very large - sum only accepts generators, so the list version raises a TypeError Both give the same total, but the brackets build the full list first; without them the values are made and added one by one. ? What does c 2 for c in "ab" if c != "a" give? - 'aa', 'bb' - 'b', 'b' - 'bb' + 'bb' Only "b" passes the condition, and "b" 2 is "bb". A list comprehension always builds a list.

title: One-line collections
body: Write each function body as a single return with a comprehension: python def squares_of_evens(numbers): ... 4, 16 for 1, 2, 3, 4 def word_lengths(words): ... {"fig": 3, "apple": 5} def initials(names): ... sorted list of the distinct first letters, upper-case (skip empty names) def transpose(matrix): ... rows become columns: 1, 2 , 3, 4 - 1, 3 , 2, 4 def flatten(lists): ... 1, 2 , , 3 - 1, 2, 3 All rows of a matrix have the same length; an empty matrix transposes to an empty list.

title: 5.02  Iterators and Generators
body: How for loops really work - iterables and iterators, iter and next, writing generator functions with yield, lazy pipelines that process data of any size, infinite sequences, and yield from. The iteration protocol A for loop works with any iterable : lists, strings, dictionaries, files, ranges. Behind the scenes it asks the iterable for an iterator with iter() and calls next() on it until it raises StopIteration : python it = iter( 10, 20, 30 ) print(next(it), next(it), next(it)) next(it) now would raise StopIteration: the loop's signal to stop An iterator is used up once it has been walked through; a list can be iterated again and again because each for gets a fresh iterator. Generator functions A function containing yield is a generator function . Calling it does not run the body; it returns a generator, and each next() runs the body up to the next yield : python def countdown(n): print("starting") while n 0: yield n n -= 1 print("done") for value in countdown(3): print(value) The function's local variables survive between yield s, so generators are an easy way to write iterators without a class. Lazy pipelines Generators produce values on demand . That lets you process data far larger than memory, one item at a time, by chaining small steps: python def read_numbers(lines): for line in lines: line = line.strip() if line: yield int(line) def only_even(numbers): for n in numbers: if n % 2 == 0: yield n lines = "4", "", "7", "10", "3" could be a file with millions of lines print(sum(only_even(read_numbers(lines)))) 14 No intermediate list is ever built: each number flows through the whole pipeline before the next is read. Infinite sequences A generator can go on forever; the consumer decides when to stop: python import itertools def fibonacci(): a, b = 0, 1 while True: yield a a, b = b, a + b print(list(itertools.islice(fibonacci(), 10))) itertools.islice takes the first n items; next(gen) takes one. yield from yield from other yields every item of another iterable, which makes recursive generators short: python def flatten(items): for item in items: if isinstance(item, list): yield from flatten(item) else: yield item print(list(flatten( 1, 2, 3, 4 , 5 ))) Iterators in the standard library Many built-ins give lazy objects rather than lists. enumerate , zip , map , filter , reversed and file objects are iterators, used up after one pass; range and dictionary views are lazy iterables that hand out a fresh iterator each time. Wrap one in list(...) when you really need all the items at once, for example to index them or loop over them twice. Check yourself quiz ? What happens when a generator function is called? - Its body runs to the end at once and the yielded values are collected into a list + It returns a generator without running the body; the body runs as values are requested - Its body runs up to the first yield , and that value is returned to the caller - It raises StopIteration unless the call is written inside a for loop Calling it only creates the generator; each next() runs the body on to the following yield , which is why "starting" in countdown prints only when the loop asks for the first value. ? Why can a generator process a file bigger than memory? - It compresses each line in memory while it is reading the file - It reads the whole file once, then throws its copy away line by line - It runs in a separate process, which has a memory of its own + It yields one item at a time, so only the current item needs to be in memory Each item flows through the pipeline before the next one is read, so no full list of the data is ever built. ? What does this print? g = (x 2 for x in 1, 2, 3 ) print(sum(g), sum(g)) - 12 12 + 12 0 - 6 6 - an error A generator is used up after one pass; the second sum gets no items and returns 0.

title: Generators
body: Write four generator functions (each must use yield ): python def chunks(items, size): ... yields lists of size items; the last one may be shorter def running_total(numbers): ... yields the sum so far after each number def primes(): ... yields 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, ... forever def take(n, iterable): ... yields the first n items (fewer if the iterable ends) chunks must work with any iterable, including another generator, and must not read more items than it needs.

title: 5.03  Sorting, Key Functions and Lambdas
body: Putting things in order - sorted and sort with key functions, sorting by several criteria, stable sorting, reverse order per field, operator.itemgetter and attrgetter, min and max with keys, and structural pattern matching on sequences. Key functions sorted(items, key=f) sorts by f(item) instead of the items themselves. key takes any function of one argument: python words = "banana", "Apple", "cherry", "fig" print(sorted(words)) 'Apple', 'banana', 'cherry', 'fig' : capitals first print(sorted(words, key=str.lower)) case-insensitive print(sorted(words, key=len)) by length: 'fig', 'Apple', 'banana', 'cherry' min and max take a key too: max(words, key=len) is the longest word. Several criteria Return a tuple from the key: tuples compare item by item, so the second item breaks ties of the first: python people = ("Ada", 36), ("Grace", 85), ("Alan", 36), ("Bob", 85) print(sorted(people, key=lambda p: (p 1 , p 0 ))) by age, then name To sort one field descending and another ascending, negate the number: key=lambda p: (-p 1 , p 0 ) is "oldest first, then by name". For text fields that cannot be negated, use stability (below). Stable sorting Python's sort is stable : items with equal keys keep their original order. That allows sorting in several passes, least important key first : python people = ("Ada", 36), ("Grace", 85), ("Alan", 36), ("Bob", 85) by_name = sorted(people, key=lambda p: p 0 , reverse=True) names Z-A result = sorted(by_name, key=lambda p: p 1 ) then ages ascending, names stay Z-A print(result) operator helpers operator.itemgetter and attrgetter build key functions that are clearer and a little faster than lambdas: python from operator import itemgetter, attrgetter from dataclasses import dataclass rows = {"name": "Ada", "score": 95}, {"name": "Bob", "score": 72} print(sorted(rows, key=itemgetter("score"), reverse=True)) @dataclass class Player: name: str level: int team = Player("Ada", 7), Player("Bob", 3) print(sorted(team, key=attrgetter("level"))) Sorting your own objects Objects without a key need __lt__ (lesson 4.02) or @dataclass(order=True) (lesson 4.04) to be sortable. A key function is usually better: it does not fix one "natural" order for a class that can be sorted many ways. match on sequences match (lesson 1.05) can also take sequences apart by shape, which helps when processing commands or records: python def describe(command): match command.split(): case "go", direction : return f"going {direction}" case "take", items if items: return f"taking {', '.join(items)}" case "quit" "exit" : return "bye" case _: return "unknown" for c in "go north", "take key lamp", "exit", "dance" : print(describe(c)) Each case matches the list's length and literal words, binds the other positions to names, and can add a guard with if . Check yourself quiz ? Records have a numeric score and a text name . Which key sorts by score descending, then name ascending? - key=lambda r: (r.score, r.name), reverse=True - key=lambda r: (r.score, -r.name) + key=lambda r: (-r.score, r.name) - key=lambda r: -(r.score, r.name) Negating the number flips only that field; reverse=True would flip the names too, and text or a whole tuple cannot be negated. ? What does stable sorting guarantee? + Items with equal keys keep the order they had before sorting - Sorting the same list twice never changes it the second time - The sort raises an error instead of guessing when keys are equal - Items with equal keys end up in alphabetical order Ties are left in their original order, which is what makes sorting in several passes, least important key first, work. ? What is max( "kiwi", "apple", "fig" , key=len) ? - 'kiwi' - 5 - 'fig' + 'apple' The key compares lengths, but max returns the item itself: "apple" has 5 letters, the most.

title: Sorting it out
body: Write sorting and matching helpers: python def leaderboard(players): ... players: list of {"name": ..., "score": ...}; score descending, then name ascending (case-insensitive) def sort_versions(versions): ... "1.10", "1.2", "1.9.1", "1.2.0" - numeric order; equal versions keep their order def longest_words(text, n): ... the n longest distinct words (lower-cased), longest first, ties alphabetical def describe(command): ... uses match (below) describe returns: "going <dir " for go <dir ; "taking <a , <b " for take followed by one or more items; "bye" for quit or exit ; "unknown" otherwise (including take with no items). Words are separated by spaces.

title: 5.04  The Standard Library Toolbox
body: The modules that make everyday code short - collections (Counter, defaultdict, deque, namedtuple), itertools (chain, groupby, product, combinations, accumulate), functools (lru_cache, partial, reduce) and a few more worth knowing. collections Counter counts things: python from collections import Counter words = "the cat and the hat and the bat".split() counts = Counter(words) print(counts "the" , counts "dog" ) 3 0: missing keys count as 0 print(counts.most_common(2)) ('the', 3), ('and', 2) print(Counter("hello") + Counter("world")) counters add up defaultdict creates missing values automatically, which makes grouping one line: python from collections import defaultdict by_letter = defaultdict(list) for word in "apple", "avocado", "banana", "blueberry", "cherry" : by_letter word 0 .append(word) print(dict(by_letter)) deque is a list with fast adding and removing at both ends, ideal for queues and "the last N items": python from collections import deque recent = deque(maxlen=3) for page in "home", "about", "shop", "cart" : recent.append(page) print(list(recent)) 'about', 'shop', 'cart' queue = deque( "a", "b" ) queue.appendleft("z") print(queue.popleft(), queue) itertools Function Gives --- --- chain(a, b) The items of a, then of b islice(it, n) The first n items groupby(sorted_items, key) Runs of consecutive items with the same key product(a, b) Every pair (nested loops) permutations(xs, r) , combinations(xs, r) Orderings, selections accumulate(xs) Running totals count(start) , cycle(xs) , repeat(x) Infinite sequences pairwise(xs) Overlapping pairs: (a, b), (b, c), ... python from itertools import groupby, combinations, accumulate, pairwise scores = sorted( ("Ada", "A"), ("Bob", "B"), ("Cy", "A") , key=lambda s: s 1 ) for grade, group in groupby(scores, key=lambda s: s 1 ): print(grade, name for name, _ in group ) print(list(combinations("ABC", 2))) print(list(accumulate( 3, 1, 4, 1 ))) 3, 4, 8, 9 print( b - a for a, b in pairwise( 1, 4, 9, 16 ) ) groupby only groups consecutive items: sort by the same key first. functools python from functools import lru_cache, partial, reduce @lru_cache(maxsize=None) remembers results: a ready-made version of practice 3.03's memoize def ways(n): return 1 if n <= 1 else ways(n - 1) + ways(n - 2) print(ways(80)) int_from_binary = partial(int, base=2) a function with some arguments filled in print(int_from_binary("1011")) print(reduce(lambda a, b: a b, 1, 2, 3, 4 )) 24: combine items pairwise A few more Module For --- --- statistics mean , median , mode , stdev random choice , shuffle , sample , seeded generators string Constants such as ascii_letters , digits textwrap Wrapping and indenting text heapq Priority queues: always pop the smallest bisect Searching and inserting in sorted lists Check yourself quiz ? What does a Counter return for a key it has never seen? - It raises KeyError , like a normal dictionary + 0, instead of raising KeyError - None - An empty list Missing keys count as 0, which is why counts "dog" printed 0 in the lesson. It is defaultdict(list) that would make an empty list. ? Why must items be sorted before itertools.groupby ? - groupby raises an error if the items are not sorted - Sorting makes groupby faster but does not change the groups - groupby only works on lists of numbers, which have to be in order + It groups only consecutive items with the same key Unsorted input gives several separate groups for the same key; sorting by the same key first puts equal keys next to each other. ? Which collection keeps only the last 5 items added? - list - Counter - defaultdict + deque(maxlen=5) A deque with maxlen drops items from the other end when it is full.

title: Using the toolbox
body: Use collections , itertools and functools from lesson 5.04: python def top_letters(text, n): ... the n most common letters (a-z, ignoring case) as (letter, count); ties alphabetical def by_extension(filenames): ... dict extension - sorted names; files without a dot go under ""; extensions lower-case def moving_average(values, window): ... list of the averages of each full window of consecutive values def staircases(n): ... ways to climb n steps taking 1 or 2 at a time; fast for n = 200 (use lru_cache) moving_average( 1, 2, 3, 4 , 2) is 1.5, 2.5, 3.5 ; a window larger than the list gives . Use a deque(maxlen=window) . The extension is the part after the last dot.

title: 5.05  Type Hints and Testing
body: Making Python code safer as it grows - type hints for functions, collections and optional values, checking them with mypy or Pyright, Protocols for duck typing - and automated tests with assert, pytest, fixtures and parametrised tests. Type hints Type hints say what types a function expects and returns. Python ignores them when running; editors and type checkers use them to find mistakes before the code runs: python def average(values: list float ) - float: return sum(values) / len(values) def find_user(users: dict str, int , name: str) - int None: return users.get(name) print(average( 1.0, 2.5 ), find_user({"ada": 1}, "bob")) Hint Means --- --- int , str , float , bool That type list int , dict str, float , set str , tuple int, str Collections with their item types tuple int, ... A tuple of any length of ints X \ None An X or None Callable int , str ( from collections.abc import Callable ) A function from int to str Iterable str , Iterator int Anything you can loop over / an iterator With hints, find_user(users, "bob") + 1 is reported by the checker: the result may be None . Running mypy main.py or using Pyright (built into VS Code's Python extension) checks a whole project. Protocols typing.Protocol describes a "duck" (lesson 4.03) for the type checker, without requiring inheritance: python from typing import Protocol class HasArea(Protocol): def area(self) - float: ... def total_area(shapes: list HasArea ) - float: return sum(s.area() for s in shapes) Any class with an area() method returning a float is accepted. Tests with assert The simplest test is a function full of assert s: python def slug(title: str) - str: return "-".join(title.lower().split()) def test_slug(): assert slug("Hello World") == "hello-world" assert slug(" many spaces ") == "many-spaces" assert slug("") == "" test_slug() print("all good") The practice on this site works the same way: @test functions with check_eq , or plain test_... functions with assert . pytest pytest ( pip install pytest ) finds every test_ .py file and every test_ function in it, runs them, and reports failures with the values involved: tests/test_slug.py::test_slug PASSED tests/test_money.py::test_add FAILED assert add(2, 3) == 6 where 5 = add(2, 3) Two features make tests short: python import pytest @pytest.mark.parametrize("title, expected", ("Hello World", "hello-world"), (" A b ", "a-b"), ("", ""), ) def test_slug(title, expected): assert slug(title) == expected def test_bad_age_raises(): with pytest.raises(ValueError): int("forty") Fixtures provide prepared objects to tests by naming them as parameters ( tmp_path gives a fresh temporary folder, for testing file code). What to test Test the behaviour callers rely on: normal cases, edge cases (empty input, zero, the largest value, a single item), and error cases (what is raised). Write a test for every bug you fix, so it cannot come back. Small pure functions, which take arguments and return results without printing or reading files, are the easiest to test: one more reason to write code that way. Check yourself quiz ? Does Python check type hints when the program runs? - Yes; a call with the wrong type raises TypeError straight away - Only for hints written on the return value + No; they are used by editors and type checkers such as mypy and Pyright - Only when the file is started with python -O Python ignores hints when running; average("abc") still runs (and fails some other way). A type checker reports the mistake before the code runs. ? What does pytest.mark.parametrize do? + Runs the same test function once for each set of arguments - Gives a test a fresh temporary folder to work in - Checks that the test raises the named exception - Runs all the test functions in parallel Each tuple in the list becomes its own test run with those values; the temporary folder is the tmp_path fixture, and pytest.raises checks for an exception. ? What does the hint int None on a return value tell a caller? - The function always returns an int - The function raises an error instead of returning None + The result may be None and should be checked before use as an int - Nothing; it is only a comment A type checker will report using the result as an int without first handling None.

title: A log analyser
body: Analyse web-server log lines with a generator pipeline, Counter and key-function sorting: 2026-11-15T10:00:01 GET /home 200 532ms 2026-11-15T10:00:07 GET /search 500 1200ms python @dataclass(frozen=True) class Entry: time: str "2026-11-15T10:00:01" method: str path: str status: int ms: int def parse_lines(lines): ... a generator of Entry; skips blank lines, lines starting with , and malformed lines def summarize(entries): ... a dict (below) def report(summary): ... the report text (below) parse_lines expects exactly five space-separated fields; the status must be a whole number and the duration a whole number followed by ms . Anything else is skipped silently. It must be a generator ( yield ). summarize returns a dictionary with: - "requests" : the number of entries; - "server_errors" : entries with status 500 or more; "client_errors" : 400 to 499; - "by_status" : a list of (status, count) pairs sorted by status; - "slowest" : the three slowest (ms, path) pairs, slowest first, ties by path; - "busiest_minute" : (minute, count) for the minute (the time's first 16 characters) with the most requests, the earliest on a tie, or None for no entries; - "average_ms" : a dict path to average duration, rounded to one decimal. report produces lines ending in \n : Requests: 6 Server errors: 1, client errors: 1 Status codes: 200 x4, 404 x1, 500 x1 Slowest: /search 1200ms, /home 532ms, /home 316ms Busiest minute: 2026-11-15T10:00 (4 requests) Average by path: /about 120.0 ms /home 316.0 ms /missing 15.0 ms /search 1200.0 ms The status-code and slowest lines list nothing after the colon when empty ( Status codes: with nothing after). The busiest line reads Busiest minute: none without entries. In "Average by path", paths are sorted, left-aligned in a column as wide as the longest path plus 3, and the average is right-aligned in 6 characters with one decimal, then ms .

title: 6.01  Text Processing and Regular Expressions
body: Finding and extracting patterns in text with the re module - the pattern language, search, findall and fullmatch, groups and named groups, substitution, flags, and when plain string methods are the better tool. What regular expressions are for String methods (lesson 2.01) find fixed text. A regular expression describes a pattern : "a date like 2026-11-15", "an email address", "a word followed by a number". The re module searches for patterns, extracts parts of them and replaces them. Always write patterns as raw strings ( r"..." ), so backslashes reach re unchanged. The pattern language Pattern Matches --- --- abc The text abc . Any character except a new line \d , \w , \s A digit, a word character (letter, digit, _ ), whitespace \D , \W , \S Anything but those aeiou , a-z0-9 , ^, One character from a set, a range, or not in the set , + , ? Zero or more, one or more, zero or one of what precedes {3} , {2,4} Exactly 3, between 2 and 4 ^ , $ Start, end (of the text, or of each line with re.M ) \b A word boundary a\ b a or b ( ) A group: captures the part it matches (?: ) A group that only groups, capturing nothing ( findall then returns whole matches) \. , \( A literal dot or parenthesis and + are greedy (they take as much as possible); ? and +? take as little as possible. Searching python import re text = "Orders: 1042 on 2026-11-15, 1043 on 2026-11-16." print(re.findall(r" (\d+)", text)) '1042', '1043' : the group's text m = re.search(r"(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})", text) the first match, or None if m: print(m.group(0), m.group(1), m.groups()) print(bool(re.fullmatch(r"\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}", "2026-11-15"))) the WHOLE text must match Function Returns --- --- re.search(p, s) First match anywhere, or None re.match(p, s) Match at the start only re.fullmatch(p, s) Match of the whole string: use it for validation re.findall(p, s) List of matches (or of groups) re.finditer(p, s) Match objects one by one, with positions re.split(p, s) Split at matches re.sub(p, repl, s) Replace matches Named groups Names make complicated patterns readable: python import re line = "2026-11-15 10:42:07 ERROR disk full" pattern = re.compile(r"(?P<date \S+) (?P<time \S+) (?P<level A-Z +) (?P<message . )") m = pattern.match(line) print(m "level" , "-", m "message" , m.groupdict()) re.compile builds the pattern once, which is tidier (and a little faster) when it is used many times. Replacing python import re print(re.sub(r"\s+", " ", "too many spaces")) collapse whitespace print(re.sub(r"(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})", r"\3/\2/\1", "2026-11-15")) 15/11/2026: groups in the replacement print(re.sub(r"\d+", lambda m: str(int(m.group()) 2), "3 apples, 10 pears")) Flags re.I ignores case, re.M makes ^ and $ match at every line, re.S lets . match new lines too, and re.X allows spaces and comments inside the pattern for long expressions. When not to use them Regular expressions are compact but hard to read. For fixed text, in , startswith , split and replace are clearer. For structured formats such as CSV, JSON and HTML, use a real parser (lesson 6.02): patterns for them break on the first unusual input. Test patterns on examples, including ones that should not match. Check yourself quiz ? Why write patterns as raw strings? - Raw strings make the pattern run faster, because it is compiled only once - The functions of the re module only accept raw strings as patterns + So backslashes such as \d reach re instead of being read as Python escapes - A raw string makes the pattern ignore the difference between upper and lower case In a normal string Python handles escapes like \b (a backspace) itself; r"..." passes every backslash through unchanged. ? Which function checks that a whole string has a given form? - re.search - re.match + re.fullmatch - re.findall search finds the pattern anywhere and match only checks the start, so both accept extra text; fullmatch needs the whole string to match. ? What does re.findall(r"\d+", "a1b22c333") return? - '1', '2', '2', '3', '3', '3' - 1, 22, 333 - '122333' + '1', '22', '333' \d+ matches one or more digits, as many as possible; findall returns the matched strings, not numbers.

title: Patterns in text
body: Use the re module for four jobs: python def find_emails(text): ... sorted, distinct, lower-cased addresses found anywhere in the text def to_iso_dates(text): ... every DD/MM/YYYY date rewritten as YYYY-MM-DD; the rest unchanged def is_hex_colour(text): ... " 1a2B3c" or " fff": a and exactly 3 or 6 hex digits, nothing else def parse_log(line): ... dict with date, time, level, message; None if the line does not fit - An email here is: one or more of letters, digits, . , _ , % , + , - ; an @ ; then one or more parts of letters, digits and - separated by dots, ending in a dot and 2 or more letters. - Dates have 1 or 2 digit days and months: 5/1/2026 becomes 2026-01-05 (pad with zeros). - Log lines look like 2026-11-15 10:42:07 ERROR disk full : a date, a time, a level of capital letters, and a message (the rest, at least one character).

title: 6.02  CSV and JSON
body:
The two data formats you meet everywhere - reading and writing CSV with the csv module (quoting, DictReader and DictWriter, converting types), and JSON with the json module (loading, dumping, pretty printing, and what maps to what). CSV CSV (comma-separated values) is how spreadsheets and databases exchange tables: name,city,score Ada,London,95 "Hopper, Grace",New York,88 Splitting lines on commas breaks on the second row: a field that contains a comma is quoted . The csv module handles quoting, embedded quotes and line breaks correctly: python import csv, io data = 'name,city,score
Ada,London,95
"Hopper, Grace",New York,88
' reader = csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(data)) with a real file: open(path, newline="", encoding="utf-8") rows = list(reader) print(rows 1 "name" , rows 1 "score" ) Hopper, Grace 88 total = sum(int(r "score" ) for r in rows) every field is TEXT: convert it print(total) csv.reader gives each row as a list; csv.DictReader uses the header row to give dictionaries, which is clearer. Open CSV files with newline="" so the module can handle line endings itself. Writing: python import csv, io out = io.StringIO() writer = csv.DictWriter(out, fieldnames= "name", "score" ) writer.writeheader() writer.writerow({"name": "Hopper, Grace", "score": 88}) writer.writerows( {"name": "Ada", "score": 95} ) print(out.getvalue()) The writer adds quotes where needed. Spreadsheets in some countries use ; as the separator: pass delimiter=";" . JSON JSON is the format of web APIs and many configuration files. It maps directly to Python values: JSON Python --- --- object {...} dict array ... list string str number int or float true / false True / False null None python import json text = '{"name": "Ada", "languages": "en", "fr" , "active": true, "manager": null}' person = json.loads(text) text - Python print(person "languages" 1 , person "active" , person "manager" ) person "score" = 95 print(json.dumps(person)) Python - text print(json.dumps(person, indent=2, sort_keys=True)) With files, json.load(f) and json.dump(obj, f, indent=2) read and write directly. Pass ensure_ascii=False to write accented characters as they are ( é ) rather than as é escapes. Only these types can be written. Dates, sets, tuples (written as lists) and your own classes need converting first, for example with dataclasses.asdict(obj) or a default= function. Keys of JSON objects are always strings: a dict with int keys comes back with string keys. Errors in data Real files contain surprises: missing columns, empty fields, numbers with spaces, invalid JSON. Validate as you convert (lesson 4.05): json.loads raises json.JSONDecodeError (a ValueError ) with the line and column of the problem; for CSV, check each row and collect errors rather than stopping at the first one. The final project does exactly that. Check yourself quiz ? Why should a CSV line not be split with line.split(",") ? - split cannot handle the header row + Quoted fields can contain commas, and the csv module handles them - split(",") drops empty fields at the end of the line - split turns the numbers into strings, while csv keeps them as numbers A field like "Hopper, Grace" would be cut in two; csv also copes with quotes and line breaks inside fields. It gives every field as text, so it does not keep numbers either. ? What type does every CSV field have when read? - Whatever type the value looks like: int for 95, str for Ada - int for numbers and None for empty fields - bytes , until it is decoded + str : numbers must be converted explicitly CSV has no types, so csv.reader and DictReader give text; int(r "score" ) converts it. ? What does json.loads('{"1": 1, 2 }') give? - {1: 1, 2 } + {'1': 1, 2 } - {'1': (1, 2)} - an error JSON keys are always strings, and arrays become lists.

title: CSV in, JSON out
body: Convert between the formats of lesson 6.02: python def read_people(csv_text): ... - (people, errors): people is a list of {"name": str, "age": int, "city": str} def to_json(people): ... pretty JSON: indent 2, keys sorted, non-ASCII characters kept as they are def write_csv(people): ... CSV text with the header name,age,city and one row per person (lines end with \n) read_people reads CSV with a header row (the columns may be in any order; extra columns are ignored). A row whose age is not a whole number is skipped and reported as "row N: bad age <text " , where N counts the data rows from 1. Missing columns in the header: return ( , "missing column: <name " ) for the first missing of name , age , city . Use the csv module (names and cities may contain commas and quotes).

title: 6.03  Dates and Times
body: Working with dates and times in Python - date, time, datetime and timedelta, parsing and formatting with ISO 8601 and strftime, date arithmetic, time zones with zoneinfo, and measuring durations with time.perf_counter. The types python from datetime import date, time, datetime, timedelta d = date(2026, 11, 15) t = time(14, 30) dt = datetime(2026, 11, 15, 14, 30, 5) print(d, t, dt, d.weekday(), d.isoweekday(), d.strftime("%A")) print(date.today(), datetime.now()) weekday() is 0 for Monday to 6 for Sunday. All these objects are immutable: methods such as replace return new ones. Parsing and formatting ISO 8601 ( 2026-11-15 , 2026-11-15T14:30:05 ) is the unambiguous standard format: use it for files and data. python from datetime import date, datetime d = date.fromisoformat("2026-11-15") dt = datetime.fromisoformat("2026-11-15T14:30:05") print(dt.isoformat(), d.isoformat()) For other formats, strptime parses and strftime formats with codes: Code Meaning Example --- --- --- %Y / %y Year 2026 / 26 %m / %d Month / day, two digits 11 / 15 %B / %b Month name / short November / Nov %A / %a Weekday name / short Sunday / Sun %H / %I / %p Hour (24 h) / hour (12 h) / AM-PM 14 / 02 / PM %M / %S Minutes / seconds 30 / 05 python from datetime import datetime dt = datetime.strptime("15/11/2026 14:30", "%d/%m/%Y %H:%M") print(dt.strftime("%A %d %B %Y, %H:%M")) print(f"{dt:%Y-%m-%d}") format codes work inside f-strings too Month and day names depend on the system language; for fixed output, prefer numbers. Arithmetic Subtracting dates gives a timedelta ; adding a timedelta moves a date: python from datetime import date, timedelta start = date(2026, 11, 15) print(start + timedelta(days=30)) print((date(2026, 12, 25) - start).days, "days to go") week = start + timedelta(days=i) for i in range(7) print( d.strftime("%a") for d in week ) timedelta has days, seconds and microseconds; there is no "add one month" because months differ in length: compute it explicitly (practice 6.03). Time zones A datetime without time zone information is naive : it just says "14:30" without saying where. For events that people in different places see, attach a zone with zoneinfo : python from datetime import datetime from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo meeting = datetime(2026, 11, 15, 14, 30, tzinfo=ZoneInfo("Europe/London")) print(meeting.astimezone(ZoneInfo("America/New_York"))) print(meeting.astimezone(ZoneInfo("UTC")).isoformat()) Store times in UTC, convert to local time only for display (the Win32 course's lesson 2.03 gives the same advice). On Windows, pip install tzdata provides the zone database. Measuring durations For timing code, use time.perf_counter() , a high-resolution clock that never jumps: python import time start = time.perf_counter() total = sum(i i for i in range(200_000)) print(f"took {time.perf_counter() - start:.4f} s") Never time code with datetime.now() : the wall clock can be adjusted while the program runs. Check yourself quiz ? Why is ISO 8601 ( 2026-11-15 ) the best format for storing dates? + It is unambiguous, sorts correctly as text, and is parsed directly by fromisoformat - It is the shortest way to write a date - It keeps the time zone with every date automatically - It is the format print(date.today()) uses in every country's language settings 15/11/2026 could be read the other way round in another country; year-month-day text also sorts in date order. ? What is a naive datetime? - One created with datetime.now() instead of a fixed date - One that has no time part, only a date + One without time zone information - One whose seconds and microseconds are zero It just says "14:30" without saying where; attach a zone with tzinfo=ZoneInfo(...) for times people in different places see. ? What is (date(2026, 3, 1) - date(2026, 2, 1)).days ? - 30 - 29 + 28 - 31 February 2026 has 28 days (2026 is not a leap year).

title: Calendar arithmetic
body: timedelta has no months or years, so write the calendar helpers yourself (with datetime.date ): python def add_months(d, n): ... same day n months later (or earlier); clamp to the month's last day def age_on(birthday, day): ... whole years old on day def workdays_between(start, end): ... Monday-Friday dates d with start <= d < end def next_weekday(d, weekday): ... the first date AFTER d with that weekday (0 = Monday) add_months(date(2026, 1, 31), 1) is date(2026, 2, 28) ; add_months(date(2024, 3, 31), -1) is date(2024, 2, 29) . Someone born on 29 February is a year older on 1 March in non-leap years (they have not had a 29 February yet on 28 February). workdays_between returns 0 when end <= start .

title: 6.04  Automation Scripts
body: Turning Python code into tools you run every day - command-line arguments with argparse, exit codes, reading from standard input, working through folders of files safely, running other programs with subprocess, and logging what a script did. A script's shape A useful script has a main function, reads its arguments, does its work, and exits with a status: python import argparse import sys def main(argv=None): parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Count lines in text files.") parser.add_argument("files", nargs="+", help="files to count") parser.add_argument("--min", type=int, default=0, help="only show files with at least this many lines") parser.add_argument("-q", "--quiet", action="store_true", help="print only the total") args = parser.parse_args(argv) total = 0 for name in args.files: try: with open(name, encoding="utf-8") as f: count = sum(1 for _ in f) except OSError as e: print(f"error: {e}", file=sys.stderr) return 1 total += count if not args.quiet and count = args.min: print(f"{count:6} {name}") print(f"{total:6} total") return 0 if __name__ == "__main__": sys.exit(main()) Running python count.py --help prints a help text generated from the definitions; wrong arguments give a clear error. Passing argv explicitly to main makes the script easy to test: main( "notes.txt", "--quiet" ) . argparse in brief Definition Command line --- --- add_argument("path") A required positional argument add_argument("files", nargs="+") One or more add_argument("--limit", type=int, default=10) An option with a value add_argument("-v", "--verbose", action="store_true") A flag add_argument("--mode", choices= "fast", "safe" ) Only these values Exit codes and streams By convention, exit code 0 means success and anything else failure; other programs and scripts (and CI systems) rely on it. Write results to standard output and messages and errors to standard error ( print(..., file=sys.stderr) ), so results can be redirected to a file ( python count.py .txt counts.txt ) without the errors mixed in. Reading standard input makes a script work in pipelines: for line in sys.stdin: . Working through files safely Automation often changes many files at once, so build in safety: python from pathlib import Path def rename_photos(folder, dry_run=True): for i, path in enumerate(sorted(Path(folder).glob(" .jpg")), start=1): target = path.with_name(f"photo-{i:03}.jpg") if target.exists(): print(f"skip {path.name}: {target.name} exists") continue print(f"{path.name} - {target.name}") if not dry_run: path.rename(target) - A dry run that only prints what would happen, as the default. - Never overwrite without checking. - Work on a copy first; keep backups. - Log every change (below), so it can be undone. Running other programs subprocess.run starts another program and waits for it. Pass the command as a list (no shell, no quoting problems: the Win32 course's lesson 5.03 explains why quoting is hard): python import subprocess, sys result = subprocess.run( sys.executable, "--version" , capture_output=True, text=True) print(result.returncode, result.stdout.strip() or result.stderr.strip()) check=True raises an exception if the program fails. Avoid shell=True with any text that comes from users or files. Logging For scripts that run unattended, the logging module records what happened with times and levels, to the screen and a file: python import logging logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(message)s") log = logging.getLogger("backup") log.info("copied %d files", 42) log.warning("skipped %s: locked", "notes.docx") Scheduling To run a script every day, use the system's scheduler: Task Scheduler on Windows (action: python.exe , argument: the script's full path), cron on Linux and macOS. Use full paths everywhere, because scheduled tasks do not start in your usual folder. Check yourself quiz ? What does exit code 0 mean? - The script ran but printed nothing - The script stopped with an error before it started its work + Success; any other value means the program failed - The script needs to be run again with --help Other programs, scripts and CI systems rely on this convention: 0 for success, anything else for failure. ? Why should a script that renames files have a dry-run mode? + To show exactly what would change before anything is changed - To make the renaming run faster on large folders - So the script can rename files that are open in another program - Because Path.rename refuses to run without one A dry run (the safe default) only prints the planned changes, so mistakes are caught before any file is touched. ? Which call runs a program safely with arguments that may contain spaces? - subprocess.run("convert " + name + " out.png", shell=True) - os.system("convert " + name) + subprocess.run( "convert", name, "out.png" ) - subprocess.run("convert", name) A list passes each argument separately, with no shell and no quoting problems.

title: A command-line tool
body: Write the main function of a small wordstat tool with argparse , so it can be run as a script and tested by calling main( ... ) : usage: wordstat -h --top N --ignore-case files files ... - For each file, in the order given, print <file : <lines lines, <words words . - With --top N (default 0: off), then print top words: and the N most common words over all files, one per line as <word <count , most common first, ties alphabetical. With --ignore-case , words are lower-cased before counting. Words are what str.split() gives. - If a file cannot be read, print wordstat: cannot read <file to standard error , skip it, and at the end return exit code 1; otherwise return 0. - main(argv) takes the arguments as a list (without the program name) and returns the exit code; it does not call sys.exit .

title: 6.05  Project: A Data Report Tool
body: Bring the whole course together in a command-line tool that reads sales data from CSV, validates it, groups and summarises it by month and product, and writes a text report and a JSON file. This lesson is the design, the structure and the order to build it in. What it does python sales_report.py sales.csv --from 2026-01-01 --to 2026-06-30 --json summary.json Sales report 2026-01-01 to 2026-06-30 Rows: 1 204 read, 1 198 used, 6 rejected (see errors below) Month Orders Revenue 2026-01 201 12 450.50 2026-02 188 11 980.00 ... Top products 1. Green tea 3 120.00 2. Mug 2 400.00 ... Errors line 17: quantity is not a number: "two" ... The input is a CSV file with a header date,product,quantity,unit_price . The pieces and where they come from Piece Lessons --- --- Reading CSV with DictReader, converting fields 6.02 Validating rows, collecting errors with line numbers 4.05, practice 4.05 A dataclass for a sale 4.04 Filtering by date range 6.03 Grouping by month and product 2.05, 5.04 ( defaultdict , Counter ) Sorting the top products 5.03 Aligned text output 1.03 (format specifications) JSON output 6.02 Command-line arguments, exit codes, stderr 6.04 Tests for every function 5.05 Structure Keep the tool in small, testable functions, with input and output only at the edges: python def read_rows(lines) - tuple list Sale , list str : ... parse and validate def in_range(sales, start, end) - list Sale : ... def by_month(sales) - dict str, tuple int, float : ... month - (orders, revenue) def top_products(sales, n) - list tuple str, float : ... def format_report(...) - str: ... def main(argv=None) - int: ... the only function that touches files read_rows takes lines rather than a path, so tests can pass a list of strings; main opens the file and passes open(path) to it. The final project of this milestone is exactly these functions, checked by tests. Money Revenue is a sum of quantity × unit_price . Floats can show tiny errors over thousands of rows (lesson 1.04). Either round only when displaying, or work in whole cents ( round(float(price) 100) ), or use decimal.Decimal for exact decimal arithmetic. The project uses cents. Order to build in 1. read_rows with tests for good rows, each kind of bad row, and blank lines. 2. by_month and top_products , tested on a few hand-made sales. 3. format_report , compared against an expected text in a test. 4. main with argparse; try it on a real CSV exported from a spreadsheet. 5. Date filtering and JSON output. 6. Run it on messy data: an extra column, a missing header, a different delimiter, an empty file; make each fail clearly. Where to go next With what you have learned so far you can write scripts and tools for almost any everyday task. The next milestones go deeper into the language itself (decorators, context managers, concurrency, testing, typing and databases). Beyond this course: - Data analysis : pandas for tables, matplotlib for charts, Jupyter notebooks for exploring. - Web : requests to call APIs, Flask or FastAPI to build them. - Automation of the desktop and browser : openpyxl for Excel files, playwright for web pages. - Speed : profile first ( cProfile ), then reach for better algorithms (the DSA course) before anything else. Check yourself quiz ? Why does read_rows take lines rather than a file path? - Reading from a path would load too much of the file into memory at once - csv.DictReader cannot open a file from its path by itself + So tests can pass a list of strings instead of creating files - So the function can skip the header line before it starts parsing Keeping input and output at the edges makes the parsing a plain function of its arguments, which is easy to test. ? Why compute revenue in whole cents? + Whole numbers add up exactly, so long totals have no float errors - Whole numbers of cents take far less memory than floats do - The csv module can only read whole numbers from a file - JSON cannot store numbers that have a decimal point in them Floats are approximations (lesson 1.04), and tiny errors add up over thousands of rows; whole numbers of cents add up exactly. ? Which job belongs in main rather than in the other functions of the tool? - Grouping the sales by month and adding up their revenue - Sorting the products by revenue to find the top ones - Building the aligned text of the report from the totals + Reading the command-line arguments and opening the CSV file main is the only function that touches arguments and files; everything else takes values and returns results, so it can be tested directly.

title: The sales report tool
body: Write the functions of lesson 6.05's report tool. The input is CSV with a header date,product,quantity,unit_price : python @dataclass(frozen=True) class Sale: day: date product: str quantity: int cents: int unit price in cents def read_sales(lines): ... - (sales, errors) def in_range(sales, start, end): ... sales with start <= day <= end (either bound may be None) def by_month(sales): ... {"2026-01": (orders, revenue_cents), ...} in month order def top_products(sales, n): ... (product, revenue_cents), ... highest first, ties by name def money(cents): ... 1234567 - "12 345.67" (thin groups of three with spaces) def format_report(sales, errors, n): ... the report text (below) read_sales takes an iterable of lines (a list of strings or an open file) and uses the csv module. For each data row (numbered from 1), the first problem found is reported as "row N: <message " and the row skipped: bad date <text (not ISO YYYY-MM-DD ), missing product , bad quantity <text (not a whole number greater than 0), bad price <text (not a number with at most two decimals and at least 0). A price like 4.5 is 450 cents. Spaces around fields are ignored. A row with the wrong number of fields is wrong number of fields . If the header is not exactly date,product,quantity,unit_price (ignoring spaces and case), return ( , "bad header" ) . Revenue is quantity × cents . format_report produces: Sales: 4 rows, 2 rejected Month Orders Revenue 2026-01 2 34.00 2026-02 2 1 210.50 Top products 1. Mug 1 200.00 2. Green tea 34.00 Errors row 3: bad quantity two row 5: missing product - The month table's rows are built as f"{month:<7}{orders: 10}{money(rev): 14}" , under the header f"{'Month':<7}{'Orders': 10}{'Revenue': 14}" . - Top products: the first n , as f" {i}. {product:<12}{money(rev): 12}" . - The Errors section only appears if there are errors. Every line ends with \n .

title: 7.01  Decorators
body: Functions that wrap other functions - why the @ syntax exists, writing a decorator step by step, keeping the wrapped function's name with functools.wraps, decorators that take arguments, stacking them, and the decorators the standard library gives you. Functions are values A decorator rests on two things you already know (lesson 3.03): a function can be passed to another function, and a function can build and return a new function that remembers its surroundings (a closure). python def shout(text): return text.upper() + "!" def twice(func): def run(text): return func(func(text)) return run louder = twice(shout) print(louder("hi")) HI!! twice takes a function and returns a new one that does something extra around it. That is all a decorator is. The @ syntax Wrapping a function and keeping the same name is so common that Python has a shorthand. These two are exactly the same: python def log_calls(func): def wrapper( args, kwargs): print(f"calling {func.__name__}{args}") result = func( args, kwargs) print(f"{func.__name__} returned {result}") return result return wrapper @log_calls def add(a, b): return a + b the line above is short for: add = log_calls(add) add(2, 3) args, kwargs (lesson 3.02) lets the wrapper accept whatever the original accepts and pass it all on, so one decorator works for any function. Keep the name: functools.wraps After decorating, add is wrapper , so its name and docstring are wrong, which confuses error messages, help text and tests. functools.wraps copies them across: python import functools def log_calls(func): @functools.wraps(func) def wrapper( args, kwargs): return func( args, kwargs) return wrapper @log_calls def add(a, b): """Adds two numbers.""" return a + b print(add.__name__, "-", add.__doc__) add - Adds two numbers. Put @functools.wraps(func) on every wrapper you write. It costs nothing. A useful decorator: timing python import functools import time def timed(func): @functools.wraps(func) def wrapper( args, kwargs): start = time.perf_counter() try: return func( args, kwargs) finally: elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start print(f"{func.__name__} took {elapsed 1000:.1f} ms") return wrapper @timed def slow_sum(n): return sum(range(n)) slow_sum(1_000_000) The finally makes the time print even when the function raises. Decorators that take arguments @retry(times=3) needs one more layer: retry(times=3) is called first and must return the actual decorator. python import functools def repeat(times): def decorator(func): @functools.wraps(func) def wrapper( args, kwargs): result = None for _ in range(times): result = func( args, kwargs) return result return wrapper return decorator @repeat(times=3) def greet(name): print("hello", name) greet("Ada") Read it from the outside in: repeat(3) returns decorator ; decorator(greet) returns wrapper ; calling greet runs wrapper . Stacking Several decorators apply from the bottom up: the one nearest the def wraps first. python-norun @timed @log_calls def mul(a, b): return a b mul = timed(log_calls(mul)) Decorators you already have Decorator What it does --- --- @property a method read like an attribute (lesson 4.01) @staticmethod , @classmethod methods without an instance, or with the class (lesson 4.01) @dataclass writes __init__ , __repr__ and __eq__ for you (lesson 4.04) @functools.lru_cache remembers results for arguments it has seen (lesson 5.04) @functools.cache the same with no size limit A decorator can also be applied to a class: @dataclass is one. It receives the class and returns it (changed) or a replacement. When to write one Write a decorator when the same "before and after" code would otherwise be copied into many functions: logging, timing, checking arguments, retrying, caching, counting calls. If only one function needs it, plain code inside that function is clearer. Check yourself quiz ? What does @log_calls above a def do? - It calls log_calls on every call, then calls the function itself + It replaces the function with whatever log_calls(function) returns - It copies the code of log_calls into the start of the function's body - It marks the function so that log_calls can find it later by its name @log_calls is short for add = log_calls(add) , run once when the def runs; from then on calling add calls whatever log_calls returned. ? Why does a decorator with arguments, such as @repeat(times=3) , need three nested functions? - One handles the arguments, one the return value, and one any exceptions raised - Because functools.wraps only works when it sits two levels deep inside - Python requires every decorator to be written with exactly three levels + The outer one takes the arguments, the middle one the function, and the wrapper runs on each call repeat(times=3) is called first and must return a decorator, which then wraps the function like any one-level decorator. ? Without functools.wraps , what is add.__name__ after decorating it with log_calls ? - add - log_calls + wrapper - an error The name refers to the wrapper function now, so its name is wrapper ; functools.wraps copies the original name across.

title: Count the calls
body: Write a decorator count_calls that counts how many times the decorated function has been called. The count is kept on the wrapper as an attribute named calls , starting at 0. The function's result, name and docstring must be unchanged. python @count_calls def square(x): """Squares x.""" return x x square(3) square(4) print(square.calls) 2 print(square.__name__) square

title: Retry on failure
body: Write a decorator with arguments, retry(times, exceptions=(Exception,)) . The decorated function is called; if it raises one of exceptions , it is called again, up to times calls in total. If the last call still fails, that exception is raised. Exceptions not in exceptions are raised straight away, without retrying. A successful call returns its result at once. python attempts = @retry(times=3, exceptions=(ConnectionError,)) def fetch(): attempts.append(1) if len(attempts) < 3: raise ConnectionError("try again") return "data" print(fetch(), len(attempts)) data 3 times below 1 is a mistake: retry(0) raises ValueError when it is applied.

title: 7.02  Context Managers
body: What a with-block really does - the __enter__ and __exit__ methods, cleaning up even when an error happens, writing context managers as classes and with contextlib.contextmanager, suppress, redirecting output, and ExitStack for a varying number of resources. Setup and cleanup that cannot be forgotten You have used with open(...) as f: since lesson 3.05: the file is closed when the block ends, even if the block raises. That guarantee works for any object that follows the context manager protocol : python-norun with EXPRESSION as name: body 1. Python evaluates EXPRESSION and calls its __enter__() . Whatever that returns is bound to name . 2. The body runs. 3. However the body ends (normally, return , break or an exception), Python calls __exit__(exc_type, exc_value, traceback) . It is the same idea as RAII in C++: the cleanup is attached to the block, so it always happens. A context manager as a class python import time class Timer: def __enter__(self): self.start = time.perf_counter() return self this is what "as t" receives def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_value, traceback): self.elapsed = time.perf_counter() - self.start print(f"took {self.elapsed 1000:.2f} ms") return False do not swallow exceptions with Timer() as t: total = sum(range(100_000)) print(total, t.elapsed 0) __exit__ receives the exception (or three None s if there was none). Returning True tells Python the exception is handled and should not continue; returning False (or nothing) lets it carry on. Swallow exceptions only when that is the whole point of the manager. Cleanup when things go wrong python class Transaction: def __init__(self, account): self.account = account def __enter__(self): self.saved = dict(self.account) remember the state return self.account def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_value, traceback): if exc_type is not None: something failed: undo self.account.clear() self.account.update(self.saved) return False account = {"balance": 100} try: with Transaction(account) as acc: acc "balance" -= 30 raise ValueError("card declined") except ValueError: pass print(account) {'balance': 100}: the change was rolled back The quick way: contextlib.contextmanager Most context managers are "do something, run the body, undo it". A generator (lesson 5.02) with one yield says exactly that: python from contextlib import contextmanager @contextmanager def indented(level): print(f"{' ' level}begin") try: yield level + 1 the body runs here; this value goes to "as" finally: print(f"{' ' level}end") with indented(0) as inner: print(f"{' ' inner}working") Everything before yield is __enter__ ; everything after it is __exit__ . Put the after-part in finally so it runs when the body raises. Ready-made context managers python import contextlib import io Ignore one kind of error with contextlib.suppress(FileNotFoundError): open("does-not-exist.txt") print("carried on") Capture what print writes buffer = io.StringIO() with contextlib.redirect_stdout(buffer): print("hidden") print(repr(buffer.getvalue())) 'hidden\n' Others you will meet: threading.Lock (lesson 7.05), tempfile.TemporaryDirectory , decimal.localcontext , and the unittest.mock.patch used in tests. Several at once, and a varying number One with can open several managers; they are closed in reverse order: python-norun with open("in.txt") as src, open("out.txt", "w") as dst: dst.write(src.read()) When the number is only known at run time, ExitStack collects them: python from contextlib import ExitStack, contextmanager @contextmanager def resource(name): print("open", name) yield name print("close", name) with ExitStack() as stack: names = stack.enter_context(resource(n)) for n in "a", "b", "c" print("using", names) Check yourself quiz ? When does __exit__ run? - Only when the body finishes without an exception - Only when the body raises an exception + Whenever the body ends: normally, by return or break , or with an exception - When the object is garbage-collected, some time after the block That guarantee is the whole point of with : the cleanup is attached to the block, however it ends. ? In a @contextmanager function, why put the cleanup after yield in finally ? + The body's exception is raised at the yield , so code after it would be skipped - Without finally , the generator would yield a second time after the body - finally is what sends the value after yield to the as name - @contextmanager raises TypeError for a generator with no try / finally The body's exception appears at the yield line, so only a finally (or an except ) there guarantees the cleanup runs. ? What does __exit__ returning True do? - Runs the body of the with-block a second time - Re-raises the exception after the cleanup has run - Nothing; Python ignores what __exit__ returns + Stops the exception that ended the block from going any further True means "handled": the exception is swallowed and the program carries on after the with-block.

title: A temporary setting
body: Write a context manager temporarily(settings, key, value) with contextlib.contextmanager . Inside the block, settings key is value . Afterwards, the setting is put back as it was, even if the block raised. If the key did not exist before, it does not exist afterwards. python settings = {"volume": 5} with temporarily(settings, "volume", 0): print(settings "volume" ) 0 print(settings "volume" ) 5

title: A change log as a class
match: A change log as a class
body: Write a class Recorder that is a context manager. Use it like this: python log = with Recorder(log, "import") as r: r.note("read 10 rows") r.note("skipped 2 rows") print(log) 'import: start', 'import: read 10 rows', 'import: skipped 2 rows', 'import: done' - __enter__ appends "<name : start" and returns the recorder. - note(text) appends "<name : <text " . - When the block ends normally, "<name : done" is appended. - When it ends with an exception, "<name : failed (<ExceptionType : <message )" is appended and the exception continues. - If the exception is a KeyboardInterrupt , nothing special: it continues too, with the same "failed" line. - note after the block has ended raises RuntimeError .

title: 7.03  Advanced Classes
body: What happens behind attribute access - properties with setters, descriptors that reuse one rule across many attributes, __slots__ for small memory-light objects, abstract base classes that refuse to be half-finished, __init_subclass__ for registering subclasses, generic classes, and what a metaclass is. Properties with a setter Lesson 4.01 used @property to make a read-only value. A property can also control writing , so a class can check every assignment while users still write plain obj.x = value : python class Temperature: def __init__(self, celsius): self.celsius = celsius goes through the setter below @property def celsius(self): return self._celsius @celsius.setter def celsius(self, value): if value < -273.15: raise ValueError("below absolute zero") self._celsius = value @property def fahrenheit(self): computed, read-only return self._celsius 9 / 5 + 32 t = Temperature(20) t.celsius = 25 print(t.fahrenheit) 77.0 Descriptors: one rule for many attributes If ten attributes all need "must be positive", ten properties repeat themselves. A descriptor is a class whose objects, placed in another class, control access to an attribute. @property is itself built from one. python class Positive: def __set_name__(self, owner, name): self.name = "_" + name where the value is really stored def __get__(self, obj, objtype=None): if obj is None: return self accessed on the class itself return getattr(obj, self.name) def __set__(self, obj, value): if value <= 0: raise ValueError(f"{self.name 1: } must be positive, got {value}") setattr(obj, self.name, value) class Box: width = Positive() height = Positive() def __init__(self, width, height): self.width = width self.height = height b = Box(3, 4) try: b.height = -1 except ValueError as e: print(e) height must be positive, got -1 __set_name__ tells the descriptor which attribute it was assigned to. You will rarely write descriptors, but knowing that @property , methods and @classmethod all work this way explains a lot of Python. __slots__ Each object normally keeps its attributes in a dictionary, which is flexible but costs memory. Listing the attributes in __slots__ replaces that dictionary with fixed storage: objects get smaller and faster, and assigning an attribute that is not listed is an error. python class Point: __slots__ = ("x", "y") def __init__(self, x, y): self.x = x self.y = y p = Point(1, 2) try: p.z = 3 except AttributeError as e: print("no:", e) Use it for classes with millions of instances. @dataclass(slots=True) does the same for a dataclass. Abstract base classes Lesson 4.03 introduced abc next to duck typing. A closer look: an abstract base class cannot be used until the subclass fills in the gaps , and its ordinary methods can already rely on the abstract ones: python from abc import ABC, abstractmethod class Shape(ABC): @abstractmethod def area(self): ... def describe(self): shared code can use the abstract method return f"{type(self).__name__} with area {self.area():.2f}" class Square(Shape): def __init__(self, side): self.side = side def area(self): return self.side 2 print(Square(3).describe()) try: Shape() except TypeError as e: print(e) A subclass that forgets area cannot be created either, so the mistake shows up at once, not later in a half-working object. __init_subclass__: subclasses that register themselves A base class can run code each time someone subclasses it. Plugins use this to collect every subclass by name: python class Command: registry = {} def __init_subclass__(cls, name, kwargs): super().__init_subclass__( kwargs) Command.registry name = cls class Hello(Command, name="hello"): def run(self): return "hi!" class Bye(Command, name="bye"): def run(self): return "see you" print(Command.registry "bye" ().run()) Generic classes A container class can say what it holds with a type parameter (Python 3.12+). Python does not check it while running; editors and type checkers do (lesson 5.05): python class Stack T : def __init__(self) - None: self._items: list T = def push(self, item: T) - None: self._items.append(item) def pop(self) - T: return self._items.pop() s: Stack int = Stack() s.push(1) print(s.pop()) What a metaclass is Classes are objects too, and the class of a class is its metaclass , normally type . type(name, bases, namespace) builds a class from parts, which is what the class statement does for you: python Dog = type("Dog", (), {"sound": "woof", "speak": lambda self: self.sound}) print(Dog().speak()) A custom metaclass can change how classes are built. ORMs and frameworks use them; in your own code, __init_subclass__ , decorators and descriptors almost always do the job more simply. Check yourself quiz ? Why use a descriptor instead of properties? - Descriptors are faster to read than properties, which run a method each time - Properties cannot check the values assigned; only a descriptor can do that + One descriptor holds a rule that many attributes can share; properties repeat it each time - Descriptors also work in classes with __slots__ , and properties do not A property can check values too (the celsius setter does), but each property is written for one attribute; a descriptor such as Positive() is reused for width , height and more. ? What does ABC with @abstractmethod prevent? + Creating an object of a class that still has methods left to fill in - Overriding the abstract method in a subclass - Calling the class's ordinary methods, such as describe - Subclassing the class more than once Shape() raises TypeError , and so does a subclass that forgets area ; a subclass that fills in every abstract method can be created normally. ? What happens when you assign p.z = 3 to an object whose class has __slots__ = ("x", "y") ? - z is added to the object's dictionary - z is ignored silently + AttributeError - z replaces y Slots give the object fixed storage for the listed names only, so any other name is an error.

title: Plugins that register themselves
body: Build a tiny plugin system with an abstract base class. - Exporter is an ABC with an abstract method export(rows) that returns a string. rows is a list of dictionaries with the same keys. - Each subclass gives a format name when it is declared: class CsvExporter(Exporter, fmt="csv") . __init_subclass__ stores the class in Exporter.formats under that name. Declaring a second class with a name already used raises ValueError . - CsvExporter produces a header line of the keys (in the order of the first row) and one line per row, values joined by commas, each line ending in \n . No rows gives an empty string. - MarkdownExporter ( fmt="md" ) produces a table: a b , then --- --- , then a line per row, each ending in \n . No rows gives an empty string. - export_as(fmt, rows) creates the right exporter and calls it; an unknown format raises KeyError . python rows = {"name": "Ada", "age": 36}, {"name": "Alan", "age": 41} print(export_as("csv", rows), end="") name,age Ada,36 Alan,41

title: 7.04  Pattern Matching in Depth
body: Everything match can take apart - literal, capture and wildcard patterns, sequences with rest, dictionaries with rest, objects by class and attribute, __match_args__, nested patterns, alternatives, guards, and when match is clearer than if. More than a switch Lessons 1.05 and 5.03 used match to choose between strings and to split commands by length. A case is a pattern : a description of a shape. If the value has that shape, the names in the pattern are bound to its parts and the block runs. The first matching case wins. The basic patterns Pattern Matches --- --- 42 , "stop" , None , True that exact value name anything, and binds it to name _ anything, binds nothing a \ b either pattern x, y a sequence of exactly two items first, rest a sequence of one or more items {"type": t} a mapping that has at least that key Point(x=0, y=yy) an object of that class whose attributes match A bare name always captures. To compare with a constant, use a dotted name such as Color.RED : dotted names are compared, not bound. Sequences python def describe(items): match items: case : return "empty" case only : return f"one item: {only}" case first, second : return f"a pair: {first} and {second}" case first, rest : return f"{first} and {len(rest)} more" for value in ( , 1 , 1, 2 , 1, 2, 3, 4 ): print(describe(value)) Strings are not treated as sequences here, so "ab" does not match a, b . Dictionaries A mapping pattern checks the keys you name and ignores any others. That is perfect for JSON (lesson 6.02): python def handle(event): match event: case {"type": "click", "x": x, "y": y}: return f"click at {x},{y}" case {"type": "key", "key": "q" "Q"}: return "quit" case {"type": "key", "key": key}: return f"key {key}" case {"type": other, details}: return f"unknown {other} with {sorted(details)}" case _: return "not an event" print(handle({"type": "click", "x": 3, "y": 4, "button": 1})) print(handle({"type": "key", "key": "Q"})) print(handle({"type": "scroll", "dy": -1})) Objects A class pattern checks the type with isinstance and then the attributes: python from dataclasses import dataclass @dataclass class Point: x: float y: float @dataclass class Circle: centre: Point radius: float def where(shape): match shape: case Circle(centre=Point(x=0, y=0), radius=r): return f"circle of radius {r} at the origin" case Circle(centre=Point(x=x, y=y)): return f"circle at {x},{y}" case Point(x=0, y=0): return "the origin" case Point(x=x, y=0): return f"on the x axis at {x}" case _: return "something else" print(where(Circle(Point(0, 0), 2))) print(where(Point(5, 0))) Patterns nest: the circle's centre is matched by a Point pattern inside the Circle pattern. Positional class patterns and __match_args__ Writing Point(x=..., y=...) every time is long. A dataclass sets __match_args__ to its fields in order, so the attributes can be given by position: python from dataclasses import dataclass @dataclass class Move: dx: int dy: int match Move(0, -1): case Move(0, dy) if dy < 0: print("up by", -dy) case Move(dx, 0): print("sideways", dx) For an ordinary class, set __match_args__ = ("dx", "dy") yourself. Guards and binding a whole match if after a pattern adds a condition (a guard ). as binds what an inner pattern matched: python def classify(value): match value: case int(n) if n < 0: return "negative int" case int() float() as number if number == 0: return "zero" case int() float(): return "a number" case str() as text if text.isdigit(): return "digits in a string" case str(): return "text" case _: return type(value).__name__ for v in (-3, 0, 2.5, "42", "hi", 1 ): print(v, "- ", classify(v)) int(n) is the shortcut for built-in types: it matches an int and binds it to n . When to use it match shines when the decision depends on the shape of data: commands, JSON messages, syntax trees, events. For a plain test like if x 10 , keep using if . Check yourself quiz ? Why does case RED: not compare the value with a constant named RED ? - It does compare, but only when RED was defined before the match statement - The constant must be written in quotes, as case "RED": , to be compared + A bare name always captures, so it matches anything; a dotted name like Color.RED compares - Constants can only be compared in a guard such as if x == RED , never in a pattern case RED: binds whatever the value is to a new name RED , so it matches everything; dotted names are compared instead of bound. ? Does the pattern {"type": "key"} match a dictionary with extra keys? - No; the dictionary must have exactly the keys named in the pattern - Only if the pattern ends with rest to take the extra keys - Only if the extra keys come after "type" in the dictionary + Yes; mapping patterns check only the keys they name That is why {"type": "click", "x": x, "y": y} matched the event that also had a "button" key. ? Which case matches the list 1, 2, 3 ? - case a, b : + case a, rest : - case {"a": a}: - case "1, 2, 3": a, rest matches one or more items: a is 1 and rest is 2, 3 .
