title: Evaluate a little expression tree
body: An arithmetic expression is a tree of small dataclasses: python @dataclass class Num: value: float @dataclass class Var: name: str @dataclass class BinOp: op: str "+", "-", " " or "/" left: object right: object Write two functions, each built around match : - evaluate(node, env) returns the value. env is a dict of variable values; an unknown variable raises KeyError , division by zero raises ZeroDivisionError , and an unknown operator or node raises ValueError . - simplify(node) returns a simpler, equal tree using these rules, applied from the leaves up: x + 0 , 0 + x , x - 0 , x 1 , 1 x and x / 1 become x ; x 0 and 0 x become Num(0) ; an operation on two numbers becomes its result as a Num (division by zero is left as it is). python tree = BinOp("+", BinOp(" ", Var("x"), Num(1)), Num(0)) print(simplify(tree)) Var(name='x') print(evaluate(tree, {"x": 5})) 5

title: 7.05  Threads and Processes
body: Doing several things at once - threads with threading and concurrent.futures, why the GIL means threads speed up waiting but not calculating, race conditions and locks, queues for passing work between threads, and processes for calculations that need every core. Why run things at the same time Most slow programs are slow for one of two reasons: - Waiting : for a network reply, a disk, a database. The CPU sits idle. - Calculating : crunching numbers. The CPU is busy. Running work at the same time helps both, but in different ways, and in Python the difference matters because of the GIL (below). Threads A thread is a separate line of execution inside the same program, sharing its memory. threading.Thread runs a function in one: python import threading import time def download(name, seconds): time.sleep(seconds) stands in for waiting on the network print(f"{name} finished") start = time.perf_counter() threads = threading.Thread(target=download, args=(f"file{i}", 0.2)) for i in range(5) for t in threads: t.start() for t in threads: t.join() wait for it to finish print(f"all done in {time.perf_counter() - start:.1f} s") about 0.2 s, not 1.0 Five waits of 0.2 s overlap, so the whole thing takes about 0.2 s. The easier way: a thread pool Starting and joining threads by hand gets tedious. concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor keeps a few threads ready and hands them work. map works like the built-in map and returns results in order : python from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor import time def fetch(n): time.sleep(0.1) return n n with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as pool: results = list(pool.map(fetch, range(8))) print(results) pool.submit(f, arg) returns a future : a placeholder whose .result() waits for the value (and raises the function's exception, if it raised one). The GIL CPython has a global interpreter lock : only one thread runs Python code at any moment. A thread that is waiting (sleeping, reading a socket or a file) releases it, so waiting overlaps beautifully. Pure-Python calculation does not: four threads adding numbers take as long as one. Work Threads help? Use --- --- --- network, files, sleeping yes threads, or asyncio (lesson 7.06) pure Python number-crunching no processes NumPy and other C libraries often they release the GIL inside their C code (Python 3.13 has an experimental build without the GIL. Until it is the default, the table above holds.) Race conditions and locks Threads share variables, and counter += 1 is really three steps (read, add, write). Two threads can read the same old value and one increase is lost: a race condition . A Lock lets one thread at a time into the critical part: python import threading counter = 0 lock = threading.Lock() def add_many(): global counter for _ in range(100_000): with lock: a Lock is a context manager (lesson 7.02) counter += 1 threads = threading.Thread(target=add_many) for _ in range(4) for t in threads: t.start() for t in threads: t.join() print(counter) always 400000 The safest design is to share as little as possible: give each thread its own data and combine the results at the end. Passing work with a queue queue.Queue is made for threads: put and get are already locked, and get waits until something arrives. A classic pattern is producers putting work in and consumers taking it out: python import queue import threading jobs = queue.Queue() results = results_lock = threading.Lock() def worker(): while True: n = jobs.get() if n is None: a sentinel: no more work break with results_lock: results.append(n 10) workers = threading.Thread(target=worker) for _ in range(3) for w in workers: w.start() for n in range(6): jobs.put(n) for _ in workers: jobs.put(None) one sentinel per worker for w in workers: w.join() print(sorted(results)) Processes for calculations A process is a separate Python interpreter with its own memory and its own GIL, so processes really calculate in parallel on several cores. ProcessPoolExecutor has the same interface as the thread pool: python-norun from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor def count_primes(limit): return sum(1 for n in range(2, limit) if all(n % d for d in range(2, int(n 0.5) + 1))) if __name__ == "__main__": required: each process imports this file with ProcessPoolExecutor() as pool: print(list(pool.map(count_primes, 50_000 4))) The price: arguments and results are copied between processes (they must be picklable), and starting a process costs far more than starting a thread. Use processes for big chunks of calculation, not for many tiny jobs. Check yourself quiz ? Why do threads speed up downloading but not adding up numbers in pure Python? - Downloads run in separate processes, while additions stay in the threads - Python spreads network code over all cores but keeps numbers on one core + A waiting thread releases the GIL; a calculating thread holds it, so they take turns - Adding numbers needs a Lock , which makes the threads wait for each other Only one thread runs Python code at a time. While one waits on the network the others can work; pure calculation never waits, so the threads just take turns. ? What does a Lock protect against? - A thread that runs forever and is never joined by the main thread + Two threads changing shared data at once and losing one of the changes - The GIL being released while a thread waits for the network - An exception in one thread stopping all the other threads too counter += 1 is read, add, write; holding the lock around it lets only one thread do those steps at a time, so no increase is lost. ? You must call a slow web API 50 times. Which is the simplest good choice? - A ProcessPoolExecutor - A plain for loop making the calls one after another + A ThreadPoolExecutor - A threading.Lock held around each call The work is waiting, and waiting threads overlap well; processes would add copying and start-up cost for nothing, and a loop or a lock makes each call wait for the previous one.

If fetch raises for a URL, that URL's value is the string "error: <message " instead, and the others still complete. python def fake_fetch(url): if "bad" in url: raise ConnectionError("refused") return len(url) print(fetch_all( "a.com", "bad.org", "xyz.net" , fake_fetch)) {'a.com': 5, 'bad.org': 'error: refused', 'xyz.net': 7}

title: A thread-safe word counter

title: 7.06  asyncio
body: Thousands of waits on one thread - coroutines with async def and await, asyncio.run, running tasks at the same time with gather and TaskGroup, timeouts and cancellation, async with and async for, queues, and how to choose between asyncio, threads and processes. One thread, many waits Threads (lesson 7.05) overlap waiting, but each costs memory and switching between them is up to the operating system. asyncio overlaps waiting on a single thread: each task says where it is willing to pause ( await ), and an event loop runs another task while it waits. Servers and clients that juggle thousands of connections use it. Coroutines async def makes a coroutine function . Calling it does not run it; it returns a coroutine object, which runs when it is awaited or handed to the event loop: python import asyncio async def greet(name, delay): await asyncio.sleep(delay) pause here; other tasks may run print("hello", name) return name.upper() result = asyncio.run(greet("Ada", 0.1)) starts the event loop and runs until done print(result) await can only be used inside an async def . asyncio.run is the bridge from ordinary code: call it once, at the top. Never call time.sleep (or any other blocking function) inside a coroutine: it freezes the whole loop, and every other task waits too. Use await asyncio.sleep . Running several at once: gather Awaiting one coroutine after another runs them one after another. To run them together , use asyncio.gather , which returns their results in the order given: python import asyncio import time async def fetch(n): await asyncio.sleep(0.2) return n 10 async def main(): start = time.perf_counter() results = await asyncio.gather( (fetch(n) for n in range(5))) print(results, f"{time.perf_counter() - start:.1f} s") 0, 10, 20, 30, 40 0.2 s asyncio.run(main()) TaskGroup asyncio.TaskGroup (Python 3.11+) is the safer way to start tasks: when the async with block ends, all of them have finished, and if one fails the others are cancelled and the errors are raised together. python import asyncio async def work(name, seconds): await asyncio.sleep(seconds) return f"{name} done" async def main(): async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as group: a = group.create_task(work("a", 0.1)) b = group.create_task(work("b", 0.2)) print(a.result(), b.result()) asyncio.run(main()) Timeouts and cancellation python import asyncio async def slow(): await asyncio.sleep(10) async def main(): try: async with asyncio.timeout(0.1): await slow() except TimeoutError: print("gave up after 0.1 s") asyncio.run(main()) A timed-out or cancelled task receives asyncio.CancelledError at the await where it was paused, so try/finally inside it still cleans up. async with, async for and queues Some resources need to wait while opening or closing (a network connection); they are used with async with . Some produce values over time; they are looped over with async for . An async generator is an async def with yield : python import asyncio async def ticker(count): for i in range(count): await asyncio.sleep(0.05) yield i async def main(): async for tick in ticker(3): print("tick", tick) asyncio.run(main()) asyncio.Queue works like queue.Queue from lesson 7.05, but put and get are awaited: python import asyncio async def producer(q): for n in range(5): await q.put(n) await q.put(None) async def consumer(q, seen): while (item := await q.get()) is not None: seen.append(item item) async def main(): q = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=2) seen = await asyncio.gather(producer(q), consumer(q, seen)) print(seen) asyncio.run(main()) ( := is the assignment expression: it assigns and gives the value in one step.) asyncio.Semaphore(n) is another async with resource: it lets at most n tasks into the block at a time, and the others wait at the async with until one leaves. It is the usual way to limit how many downloads run at once: python import asyncio async def download(gate, n): async with gate: at most 2 tasks in here at once await asyncio.sleep(0.1) return n async def main(): gate = asyncio.Semaphore(2) print(await asyncio.gather( (download(gate, n) for n in range(6)))) 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 after about 0.3 s asyncio.run(main()) Blocking code inside asyncio If you must call a slow ordinary function, hand it to a thread so the loop keeps running: await asyncio.to_thread(slow_function, arg) . Which one? Situation Choose --- --- a handful of slow calls, ordinary libraries ThreadPoolExecutor thousands of connections, libraries that support asyncio asyncio heavy calculation in Python ProcessPoolExecutor Check yourself quiz ? What happens when you call an async def function without awaiting it? - It runs to the end straight away and returns its value, like a normal function - It runs in a background thread, and the value it returns is thrown away + Nothing runs: you get a coroutine object, and Python warns that it was never awaited - Python raises SyntaxError , because the call has no await in front of it Calling it only creates the coroutine; it runs when it is awaited or handed to the event loop, for example with asyncio.run . ? Why is time.sleep(1) inside a coroutine a bug? + It blocks the only thread, so the event loop cannot run any other task for that second - time.sleep raises a RuntimeError when it is called inside async def - It makes the coroutine sleep for twice as long as it was asked to - It cancels every other task that is waiting on the event loop Only await lets the loop switch tasks; use await asyncio.sleep(1) , or asyncio.to_thread for other blocking functions. ? Three coroutines each await asyncio.sleep(1) . About how long does await asyncio.gather(a(), b(), c()) take? - 3 seconds + 1 second - 0 seconds - It depends on the number of cores gather runs them together on the event loop, on one thread; their waits overlap.

title: Fastest reply wins
body: Write a coroutine first_reply(servers, timeout) . servers is a dict from a name to an async function taking no arguments that returns a reply (they stand in for network calls). Start all of them at once and return (name, reply) for whichever finishes first. If none finishes within timeout seconds, return None . Either way, every call that is still running must be cancelled before you return. python async def quick(): await asyncio.sleep(0.05) return "pong" async def slow(): await asyncio.sleep(1) return "late pong" print(asyncio.run(first_reply({"eu": slow, "us": quick}, 0.5))) ('us', 'pong')

Visit every page reachable from it exactly once. - At most limit calls to get_links may be running at the same moment: use an asyncio.Semaphore(limit) . - Pages at the same distance from start are fetched together (all of one level with asyncio.gather , then the next level). - If get_links raises for a page, that page counts as visited with no links. - Return a dict from every visited URL to its distance from start (0 for start ).

title: An async job runner
body: Put the milestone together: a small job runner that runs async jobs with a limit on how many run at once, times each one with a decorator, records what happened with a context manager, and reports the results with match . python async def resize(name): await asyncio.sleep(0.05) return f"{name}.png resized" async def upload(name): await asyncio.sleep(0.02) raise ConnectionError("server busy") jobs = Job("resize", resize, "cat"), Job("upload", upload, "cat") results = asyncio.run(run_jobs(jobs, limit=2)) print(report(results), end="") resize: ok (cat.png resized) upload: failed (ConnectionError: server busy) 1 ok, 1 failed python @dataclass class Job: name: str func: object an async function taking one argument arg: object @dataclass class Ok: job: str value: object seconds: float @dataclass class Failed: job: str error: str "<ExceptionType : <message " seconds: float def timed(func): ... decorator for async functions (below) async def run_jobs(jobs, limit=3): ... a list of Ok / Failed, in the order of jobs def report(results): ... the report text (below) timed decorates an async function. The wrapper awaits the function and returns (value, seconds) . If the function raises, the exception passes through unchanged. It keeps the function's name ( functools.wraps ). run_jobs runs every job's func(arg) (wrapped with timed ) with at most limit running at once (an asyncio.Semaphore ), all started together with asyncio.gather . A job that succeeds becomes Ok(name, value, seconds) ; one that raises becomes Failed(name, "<Type : <message ", seconds) , where seconds is the time until it failed. One failed job never stops the others. report uses match on each result. Lines: "<job : ok (<value )" for an Ok , "<job : failed (<error )" for a Failed , and a last line "<n ok, <m failed" . Every line ends with \n .

title: 8.01  Logging
body: Telling yourself what a program did - why print is not enough, the logging module's loggers, levels, handlers and formatters, one logger per module with __name__, logging exceptions with tracebacks, lazy formatting, and configuring it once at start-up. Why not print? print is fine while you are writing a script. In a program that runs for hours, or that other people run, you need more: - levels , so you can see only warnings normally and everything when something goes wrong; - where and when : the time, the module and the line of each message; - where it goes : the screen, a file, or both, without changing the code that logs. The logging module in the standard library gives you all three. A first logger python import logging import sys logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s %(name)s: %(message)s", stream=sys.stdout) log = logging.getLogger("shop") log.debug("not shown: below the INFO level") log.info("started with %d items", 3) log.warning("stock low for %s", "tea") log.error("payment failed") INFO shop: started with 3 items WARNING shop: stock low for tea ERROR shop: payment failed The five levels, from least to most serious, are DEBUG , INFO , WARNING , ERROR and CRITICAL . A logger shows a message when its level is at least the configured one. Notice log.info("started with %d items", 3) : the values are passed separately, not with an f-string. The text is only built if the message is actually shown, which saves work when debug messages are switched off. One logger per module The convention is a module-level logger named after the module: python-norun import logging log = logging.getLogger(__name__) "shop.orders" for the file shop/orders.py def place(order): log.info("placing order %s", order.id) Logger names form a tree split by dots: shop.orders is a child of shop . Settings on shop apply to all its children, so you can turn on debug messages for one part of a program only: python import logging import sys logging.basicConfig(level=logging.WARNING, format="%(levelname)s %(name)s: %(message)s", stream=sys.stdout) logging.getLogger("shop.orders").setLevel(logging.DEBUG) logging.getLogger("shop.orders").debug("details about an order") logging.getLogger("shop.stock").debug("not shown: shop.stock is still at WARNING") DEBUG shop.orders: details about an order Handlers and formatters A handler decides where messages go; a formatter decides how they look. One logger can have several handlers, each with its own level: python-norun import logging log = logging.getLogger("app") log.setLevel(logging.DEBUG) screen = logging.StreamHandler() screen.setLevel(logging.WARNING) screen.setFormatter(logging.Formatter("%(levelname)s: %(message)s")) file = logging.FileHandler("app.log", encoding="utf-8") file.setLevel(logging.DEBUG) file.setFormatter(logging.Formatter("%(asctime)s %(name)s %(levelname)s %(message)s")) log.addHandler(screen) log.addHandler(file) Everything goes to the file; only warnings and worse reach the screen. Useful format fields include %(asctime)s , %(name)s , %(levelname)s , %(module)s , %(funcName)s and %(lineno)d . Logging exceptions Inside an except block, log.exception logs at ERROR level and adds the traceback: python import logging import sys logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s: %(message)s", stream=sys.stdout) log = logging.getLogger("demo") try: 1 / 0 except ZeroDivisionError: log.exception("could not work out the average") print("the program carried on") The output shows the message, then the full traceback, then carries on. That traceback is often everything you need to fix a bug reported by someone else. Configure once, at the top Libraries and modules only create loggers and log. The program's entry point configures them, once: python-norun def main(): logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(name)s: %(message)s") ... if __name__ == "__main__": main() basicConfig does nothing if logging was already configured, so call it before anything else logs. For bigger programs, logging.config.dictConfig takes the whole setup as a dictionary (often loaded from a file). Testing what was logged The caplog -style trick without any test framework: attach a handler that keeps records in a list. python import logging class ListHandler(logging.Handler): def __init__(self): super().__init__() self.records = def emit(self, record): self.records.append(record) log = logging.getLogger("test.demo") log.setLevel(logging.DEBUG) log.propagate = False do not also send to the root logger handler = ListHandler() log.addHandler(handler) log.warning("disk at %d%%", 91) print(handler.records 0 .levelname, handler.records 0 .getMessage()) WARNING disk at 91% record.getMessage() gives the finished text; record.args holds the values. Check yourself quiz ? Why write log.info("x is %s", x) instead of log.info(f"x is {x}") ? - The f-string version raises an error when it is used inside a logging call - %s is the only kind of placeholder that the logging module can print + The text is only built if the message is shown, so switched-off messages cost almost nothing - An f-string message is always logged at DEBUG level, whatever the call Both print the same when the message is shown, but an f-string is built every time, even when the message is switched off; tools can also group messages by their unformatted text. ? Where should basicConfig be called? - At the top of every module that logs, before its first message + Once, in the program's entry point; modules only get a logger and log - Just before each call that logs, so the settings are always fresh - Inside each library function, with that function's own level basicConfig does nothing once logging is configured, and libraries should leave the setup to the program that uses them. ? A logger is set to WARNING . Which call produces output? - log.debug("x") - log.info("x") + log.error("x") ERROR is above WARNING , so it is shown; DEBUG and INFO are below it.

title: Counting by level
body: Write a handler class CountingHandler(logging.Handler) that a program can attach to see how it is doing: - counts is a dictionary from level name ( "INFO" , "ERROR" ...) to how many records of that level were handled; - last(n) returns the last n messages (finished text from record.getMessage() , newest last), keeping at most 100 overall; - errors() returns the messages of every ERROR and CRITICAL record still kept, oldest first; - it respects its own level: CountingHandler(level=logging.WARNING) ignores INFO records (the logging module does this for you if you call the parent constructor). python h = CountingHandler() log = logging.getLogger("app"); log.setLevel(logging.DEBUG); log.addHandler(h) log.info("start"); log.error("disk %s", "full") print(h.counts, h.last(1), h.errors()) {'INFO': 1, 'ERROR': 1} 'disk full' 'disk full'

title: 8.02  Testing in Depth
body: Going beyond assert - the unittest module with test cases, setUp and assertions, testing exceptions, running many inputs with subTest, replacing slow or unpredictable parts with unittest.mock, patching, and how pytest's fixtures and parametrize do the same with less code. What a test needs Lesson 5.05 showed tests as functions full of assert . Real projects add three things: 1. A runner that finds the tests, runs each one even if another fails, and reports. 2. Set-up shared between tests, so each starts from a fresh state. 3. Fakes for the parts you cannot run in a test: the network, the clock, random numbers, files. Python ships unittest for the first two and unittest.mock for the third. Most projects use the third-party pytest on top, which you will meet at the end. unittest python import unittest def average(values): if not values: raise ValueError("no values") return sum(values) / len(values) class AverageTests(unittest.TestCase): def test_simple(self): self.assertEqual(average( 2, 4 ), 3) def test_float(self): self.assertAlmostEqual(average( 0.1, 0.2 ), 0.15) def test_empty_raises(self): with self.assertRaises(ValueError): average( ) unittest.main(argv= "x" , exit=False, verbosity=0) Each method whose name starts with test is one test. The assert... methods print both values when they fail, which assert alone does not. The most used are assertEqual , assertTrue , assertIn , assertIsNone , assertAlmostEqual (for floats) and assertRaises . On your own machine, python -m unittest finds files named test .py and runs them. A fresh start for every test setUp runs before each test, tearDown after it, even when the test failed: python import unittest class Cart: def __init__(self): self.items = {} def add(self, name, qty=1): self.items name = self.items.get(name, 0) + qty class CartTests(unittest.TestCase): def setUp(self): self.cart = Cart() self.cart.add("tea", 2) def test_add_more(self): self.cart.add("tea") self.assertEqual(self.cart.items "tea" , 3) def test_starts_with_two(self): self.assertEqual(self.cart.items, {"tea": 2}) not 3: a new cart for each test unittest.main(argv= "x" , exit=False, verbosity=0) Tests must not depend on each other or on their order. A fresh object per test is how you guarantee it. Many inputs, one test subTest reports each failing case separately instead of stopping at the first: python-norun def test_many(self): for text, expected in ("1", 1), ("-2", -2), (" 3 ", 3) : with self.subTest(text=text): self.assertEqual(int(text), expected) Fakes with unittest.mock A Mock is an object that accepts any call and remembers it. You can tell it what to return and later ask how it was used: python from unittest.mock import Mock def notify(user, sender): if user "email" : sender.send(user "email" , "Your order shipped") return True return False sender = Mock() print(notify({"email": "ada@example.com"}, sender)) sender.send.assert_called_once_with("ada@example.com", "Your order shipped") print(sender.send.call_count) True 1 Passing the dependency in (here sender ) makes testing easy: the test gives a mock, the real program gives a real sender. This is the same idea as dependency injection in other languages. return_value and side_effect control what a mock gives back: python from unittest.mock import Mock api = Mock() api.get_price.return_value = 4.5 print(api.get_price("tea")) api.get_stock.side_effect = 3, 0, TimeoutError("slow") one result per call print(api.get_stock(), api.get_stock()) try: api.get_stock() except TimeoutError as e: print("raised", e) 4.5 3 0 raised slow Patching what you cannot pass in When code calls something directly, like time.time() or random.random() , patch swaps it for a mock during the test: python import random from unittest.mock import patch def roll(): return random.randint(1, 6) with patch("random.randint", return_value=6): print(roll(), roll()) print(1 <= roll() <= 6) 6 6 True Patch the name where it is looked up . If a module did from random import randint , you patch "thatmodule.randint" , not "random.randint" . pytest in brief pytest runs plain functions with plain assert , and rewrites the assert so a failure shows the values: python-norun test_cart.py, run with: python -m pytest import pytest @pytest.fixture def cart(): c = Cart() c.add("tea", 2) return c def test_add_more(cart): the fixture is passed in by name cart.add("tea") assert cart.items "tea" == 3 @pytest.mark.parametrize("text, expected", ("1", 1), ("-2", -2) ) def test_parse(text, expected): assert int(text) == expected def test_empty(): with pytest.raises(ValueError): average( ) Fixtures replace setUp , parametrize replaces loops of subTest , and pytest.raises replaces assertRaises . The ideas are the same; pytest only needs less code. Check yourself quiz ? Why does setUp run before every test, not once for the whole class? - Because unittest runs each test in a separate process of its own + So each test starts from the same fresh state, whatever other tests changed - So that a failing test can be run again straight away with new data - Because the objects made in setUp are deleted after the first test In the cart example, test_starts_with_two still sees 2 teas although test_add_more added one: each test got its own new cart. ? Code calls datetime.now() directly. How can a test control the time? - It cannot; tests involving the clock can only check the type of the result - Set the computer's clock to the wanted time before running the tests - Wrap the test in subTest and give it the time wanted as an argument + Patch the name where the code looks it up, or pass the time in as a parameter patch swaps the name for a mock during the test; passing the time in, like passing the sender in, needs no patching at all. ? A mock's side_effect is set to the list 1, 2 . What does the third call do? - Returns 2 again, the last item in the list - Returns None, as a mock does by default - Starts again from the beginning and returns 1 + Raises StopIteration , because the list ran out Each call takes the next item; after the last one there is nothing left and the mock raises StopIteration .

Write a FakeClock and a function that takes a clock as a parameter: - FakeClock(start=0.0) has now() returning the current fake time and advance(seconds) moving it forward (a negative amount raises ValueError ). - is_expired(session, clock) returns True when clock.now() is at least session "started" + session "timeout" . Any object with a now() method works as a clock, so the real program can pass one built on time.time .

title: Retry, tested with mocks
body: Write retry(fn, attempts, sleep, delay=1.0) : - call fn() ; if it returns, give back its result; - if it raises an exception, call sleep(seconds) and try again, doubling the delay each time (1, 2, 4 ... with the default delay); - after attempts failed calls, raise the last exception (do not sleep after the final failure); - attempts below 1 raises ValueError without calling fn . sleep is passed in so tests never wait: the tests give it a Mock and check how it was called.

title: 8.03  Generics and Advanced Typing
body: Type hints that say more - generic functions and classes with type parameters, bounded types, Callable, TypedDict for dictionaries with fixed keys, Literal and Final, overloads, Protocols revisited, and how type checkers use all of it while Python itself ignores it. Hints that follow the data Lesson 5.05 introduced type hints like def total(prices: list float ) - float . Some functions work for any type, but the types of their inputs and outputs are linked. first(items) returns an element of the list, whatever the list holds: python def first T (items: list T ) - T: return items 0 name = first( "ada", "bob" ) a type checker knows: str count = first( 3, 4 ) int print(name.upper(), count + 1) ADA 4 T after the name declares a type parameter (Python 3.12 and later). Older code writes the same thing with T = TypeVar("T") at the top of the file; you will see both. Python does not check any of this when the program runs. Tools such as mypy and Pyright (built into many editors) read the hints and warn about mistakes before you run anything. Generic classes python class Stack T : def __init__(self) - None: self._items: list T = def push(self, item: T) - None: self._items.append(item) def pop(self) - T: return self._items.pop() def __len__(self) - int: return len(self._items) s = Stack int () s.push(1) s.push(2) print(s.pop(), len(s)) 2 1 With Stack int , a checker refuses s.push("x") . Bounds Sometimes "any type" is too wide. A bound says the type must have some ability: python from typing import Protocol class HasLength(Protocol): def __len__(self) - int: ... def longest T: HasLength (items: list T ) - T: return max(items, key=len) print(longest( "fig", "banana", "kiwi" )) print(longest( 1 , 1, 2, 3 )) banana 1, 2, 3 T: HasLength means "any type that has __len__ ", and the result is still the specific type that went in. Functions as values Callable ArgTypes... , ReturnType describes a function: python from collections.abc import Callable def apply_all(values: list int , fn: Callable int , int ) - list int : return fn(v) for v in values print(apply_all( 1, 2, 3 , lambda v: v 10)) 10, 20, 30 Dictionaries with known keys JSON and configuration often arrive as dictionaries with fixed keys. TypedDict describes them without turning them into classes: python from typing import NotRequired, TypedDict class User(TypedDict): name: str age: int email: NotRequired str def greet(user: User) - str: return f"Hello {user 'name' } ({user 'age' })" u: User = {"name": "Ada", "age": 36} print(greet(u), isinstance(u, dict)) Hello Ada (36) True At run time u is an ordinary dict ; only the checker knows its keys. Exact values: Literal and Final python from typing import Final, Literal Mode = Literal "r", "w", "a" MAX_RETRIES: Final = 3 def open_log(mode: Mode) - str: return f"opened in {mode} mode" print(open_log("a")) A checker refuses open_log("x") , and refuses any later assignment to MAX_RETRIES . Overloads When the return type depends on the arguments in a way a single signature cannot say, list the cases with @overload , then write one real implementation: python from typing import Literal, overload @overload def parse(text: str, as_int: Literal True ) - int: ... @overload def parse(text: str, as_int: Literal False ) - str: ... def parse(text, as_int): return int(text) if as_int else text.strip() print(parse("42", True) + 1, parse(" hi ", False)) 43 hi The @overload versions are only for the checker; Python runs the last definition. Using hints well - Hint the edges of your code (function parameters and results, class attributes); local variables are usually inferred. - Prefer abstract types in parameters ( Iterable int , Mapping str, int ) and concrete ones in results ( list int ). - object means "anything, and I will check before using it"; Any means "stop checking", so use it rarely. Check yourself quiz ? What does Python do when a value does not match its hint? - It raises TypeError as soon as the function is called - It converts the value to the hinted type, if it can - It prints a warning on standard error and carries on + Nothing at run time; type checkers and editors report it before running Hints are ignored when the program runs: a TypedDict value is an ordinary dict , and Stack int accepts a string until a checker looks. ? Why write def first T (items: list T ) - T rather than - object ? + The checker then knows first( "a" ) is a str , so string methods are allowed - object is not allowed as a return type hint in Python - The T version makes the function run faster than with object - With T , Python checks at run time that the items share one type T links the result to the list's item type; with - object the checker only knows "anything" and refuses .upper() until you check the type. ? Which describes a function taking a str and returning a bool ? - Callable str, bool - Callable bool, str + Callable str , bool - Function str - bool The argument types go in a list first, then the return type.

Write: python class Product(TypedDict): name: str price: float tags: list str discount: NotRequired float and parse_product(data: object) - Product that returns a new dictionary when data is valid, and raises ValueError with a message naming the problem otherwise: - data must be a dict ; name a non-empty str ; price an int or float (not bool ), at least 0, returned as float ; - tags a list of strings (may be empty); - discount , if present, a number from 0 to 1; if missing it stays missing; - any other key is an error.

title: 8.04  Bytes, Encodings and Binary Data
body: The difference between text and bytes - bytes and bytearray, encoding and decoding with UTF-8, what goes wrong with the wrong encoding, hex and base64, reading and writing binary files, packing numbers with the struct module, and memoryview for working on part of a buffer without copying. Text is not bytes A str holds characters. Files, networks and most other programs deal in bytes : numbers from 0 to 255. Turning text into bytes is encoding ; turning bytes back into text is decoding . python text = "café" data = text.encode("utf-8") print(data, len(text), len(data)) print(data.decode("utf-8")) b'caf\xc3\xa9' 4 5 café é takes two bytes in UTF-8, so the text has 4 characters but 5 bytes. A bytes literal is written b'...' ; bytes that are not printable ASCII show as \x.. . The wrong encoding Decoding with an encoding that does not match gives either an error or quietly wrong text: python data = "café".encode("utf-8") print(data.decode("latin-1")) try: b"\xff\xfe".decode("utf-8") except UnicodeDecodeError as e: print("error:", e.reason) print(b"\xff abc".decode("utf-8", errors="replace")) cafÃ© error: invalid start byte � abc cafÃ© is the classic sign of UTF-8 read as Latin-1. Always say the encoding when opening text files ( open(path, encoding="utf-8") ), and decide on purpose what to do with bad bytes ( errors="replace" or "strict" ). Working with bytes bytes cannot be changed; bytearray can: python b = bytes( 72, 105 ) print(b, b 0 , list(b)) buf = bytearray(b"hello") buf 0 = ord("J") buf += b"!" print(buf, buf.hex(" ")) print(bytes.fromhex("48 69")) b'Hi' 72 72, 105 bytearray(b'Jello!') 4a 65 6c 6c 6f 21 b'Hi' Indexing a bytes gives an int ; slicing gives bytes . Base64 Base64 turns any bytes into plain ASCII text, so binary data can travel through JSON, email or URLs: python import base64 raw = bytes( 0, 255, 128, 64 ) text = base64.b64encode(raw).decode("ascii") print(text, base64.b64decode(text) == raw) AP+AQA== True It is an encoding, not encryption: anyone can decode it. Binary files Open with "rb" or "wb" to read and write bytes with no decoding: python-norun with open("image.png", "rb") as f: header = f.read(8) print(header == b"\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n") Packing numbers with struct Binary formats store numbers as fixed-size groups of bytes. struct.pack turns values into bytes by a format string, and struct.unpack reverses it: python import struct data = struct.pack("<HIf", 7, 1_000_000, 1.5) print(data.hex(" "), len(data)) print(struct.unpack("<HIf", data)) 07 00 40 42 0f 00 00 00 c0 3f 10 (7, 1000000, 1.5) The format starts with the byte order, < for little-endian (most PCs) or for big-endian (network order), then one letter per value: b / B 1 byte, h / H 2, i / I 4, q / Q 8 (lower case signed, upper case unsigned), f and d for floats, 5s for 5 raw bytes. struct.calcsize gives the total size. Reading records one after another: python import struct RECORD = struct.Struct("<I8sB") id, name (8 bytes), score rows = (1, b"Ada", 91), (2, b"Bob", 48) blob = b"".join(RECORD.pack( r) for r in rows) for id_, name, score in RECORD.iter_unpack(blob): print(id_, name.rstrip(b"\0").decode(), score) 1 Ada 91 2 Bob 48 8s pads short names with zero bytes, which is why the reader strips them. Integers to bytes directly python n = 1_000_000 data = n.to_bytes(4, "big") print(data.hex(), int.from_bytes(data, "big")) 000f4240 1000000 memoryview: slices without copying Slicing bytes makes a copy. A memoryview looks at part of a buffer without copying, and can write into a bytearray : python buf = bytearray(8) view = memoryview(buf) view 2:4 = b"\x12\x34" print(buf.hex(" "), view 2:4 .tobytes()) 00 00 12 34 00 00 00 00 b'\x124' For large files or network buffers this avoids copying megabytes just to look at a header. Check yourself quiz ? What does len("é".encode("utf-8")) give, and why? - 1, because é is one character + 2, because UTF-8 stores é (code point 233) in two bytes - 4, because UTF-8 always uses four bytes per character - 233, the character's code point len of a str counts characters, but len of bytes counts bytes; UTF-8 uses one byte for ASCII and more for other characters. ? Why does a struct format string start with < or ? - To say whether the numbers that follow are signed or unsigned - To mark where the format string starts and where it ends - To choose between packing values and unpacking bytes + To fix the byte order, so the bytes mean the same on every machine < is little-endian and big-endian (network order); signed and unsigned are chosen by lower and upper case letters. ? Which turns the bytes b"hi" into the text "hi" ? - str(b"hi") - b"hi".encode() + b"hi".decode("utf-8") - bytes.text(b"hi") decode turns bytes into str . str(b"hi") gives the text "b'hi'", with the b and quotes.

title: Records as bytes
body: Store score records in a fixed binary layout with struct : a little-endian unsigned 32-bit id, a name in 8 bytes (UTF-8, padded with zero bytes) and an unsigned 1-byte score. - pack_record(id, name, score) - bytes (13 bytes); a name longer than 8 bytes once encoded, or a score above 255, raises ValueError . - unpack_record(data) - tuple gives (id, name, score) back, with the zero padding removed. python data = pack_record(1, "Ada", 91) print(data.hex(" ")) 01 00 00 00 41 64 61 00 00 00 00 00 5b print(unpack_record(data)) (1, 'Ada', 91)

title: A WAV header reader
body: Sound files in WAV format start with a 44-byte header. Write read_wav_header(data: bytes) - dict that checks and reads it: offset size meaning --- --- --- 0 4 b"RIFF" 4 4 file size minus 8 (unsigned, little-endian) 8 4 b"WAVE" 12 4 b"fmt " 16 4 16 for plain audio 20 2 format, 1 means PCM 22 2 channels 24 4 sample rate 28 4 bytes per second 32 2 block align 34 2 bits per sample 36 4 b"data" 40 4 size of the sound data Return {"channels", "sample_rate", "bits", "data_size", "seconds"} , where seconds is data_size / bytes per second rounded to 3 places. Raise ValueError for data shorter than 44 bytes, any wrong marker, a format other than 1, or a bytes-per-second value that does not equal sample_rate channels bits // 8 .

title: 8.05  Databases with sqlite3
body: Keeping data in a real database without installing anything - connecting with sqlite3, creating tables, inserting with parameters (never with string formatting), querying and reading rows, transactions with commit and rollback, row factories, indexes, and when a database beats JSON files. Why a database? A JSON file (lesson 6.02) is perfect for settings. It gets awkward when you have thousands of records, need to find a few of them quickly, or two parts of a program write at the same time. A database stores records in tables and answers questions about them in a language called SQL . SQLite is a complete database in one file (or in memory), and Python includes it as sqlite3 . There is nothing to install. Connecting and creating a table python import sqlite3 con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:") a file name like "shop.db" keeps the data con.execute(""" CREATE TABLE products ( id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE, price REAL NOT NULL, stock INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 ) """) print("table created") table created Each column has a type, and rules: PRIMARY KEY gives every row a unique id (filled in for you), NOT NULL refuses missing values, UNIQUE refuses duplicates. Inserting safely Values go into the SQL through ? placeholders, given as a separate tuple: python import sqlite3 con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:") con.execute("CREATE TABLE products (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT UNIQUE, price REAL, stock INTEGER)") con.execute("INSERT INTO products (name, price, stock) VALUES (?, ?, ?)", ("tea", 2.5, 40)) rows = ("coffee", 6.0, 12), ("milk", 1.2, 0) con.executemany("INSERT INTO products (name, price, stock) VALUES (?, ?, ?)", rows) con.commit() print(con.execute("SELECT COUNT( ) FROM products").fetchone() 0 ) 3 Never build SQL with f-strings or + . A name like x'); DROP TABLE products; -- would become part of the command: this is SQL injection , one of the most common security bugs. With ? , the value is always treated as data. Asking questions python import sqlite3 con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:") con.execute("CREATE TABLE products (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, price REAL, stock INTEGER)") con.executemany("INSERT INTO products (name, price, stock) VALUES (?, ?, ?)", ("tea", 2.5, 40), ("coffee", 6.0, 12), ("milk", 1.2, 0), ("cocoa", 3.8, 5) ) for name, price in con.execute("SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE stock 0 ORDER BY price DESC"): print(name, price) row = con.execute("SELECT name FROM products WHERE name = ?", ("milk",)).fetchone() print(row) print(con.execute("SELECT name FROM products WHERE name = ?", ("bread",)).fetchone()) print(con.execute("SELECT ROUND(AVG(price), 2), SUM(stock) FROM products").fetchone()) coffee 6.0 cocoa 3.8 tea 2.5 ('milk',) None (3.38, 57) WHERE filters, ORDER BY sorts ( DESC for largest first), LIMIT n keeps only the first n rows, and functions like COUNT , SUM , AVG , MIN and MAX summarise. Looping over a query gives one tuple per row; fetchone gives the next row or None , fetchall a list. Note the comma in ("milk",) : parameters are always a tuple. Rows with names Tuples are easy to mix up. With a row factory , rows can be read by column name: python import sqlite3 con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:") con.row_factory = sqlite3.Row con.execute("CREATE TABLE people (name TEXT, age INTEGER)") con.execute("INSERT INTO people VALUES (?, ?)", ("Ada", 36)) row = con.execute("SELECT FROM people").fetchone() print(row "name" , row "age" , dict(row)) Ada 36 {'name': 'Ada', 'age': 36} Changing and deleting python-norun con.execute("UPDATE products SET stock = stock - ? WHERE name = ?", (2, "tea")) con.execute("DELETE FROM products WHERE stock = 0") con.commit() con.execute returns a cursor ; after an UPDATE or DELETE , its rowcount says how many rows were touched. Transactions: all or nothing Changes are not saved until commit() . rollback() throws them away. Using the connection as a context manager does it for you: commit if the block succeeds, rollback if it raises. python import sqlite3 con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:") con.execute("CREATE TABLE accounts (name TEXT PRIMARY KEY, balance INTEGER CHECK (balance = 0))") con.executemany("INSERT INTO accounts VALUES (?, ?)", ("ada", 100), ("bob", 20) ) con.commit() def transfer(frm, to, amount): with con: con.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + ? WHERE name = ?", (amount, to)) con.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - ? WHERE name = ?", (amount, frm)) try: transfer("bob", "ada", 50) bob only has 20: the CHECK fails except sqlite3.IntegrityError as e: print("refused:", e) print(con.execute("SELECT FROM accounts ORDER BY name").fetchall()) refused: CHECK constraint failed: balance = 0 ('ada', 100), ('bob', 20) Ada's balance was raised first, but the whole transfer was rolled back, so no money appeared from nowhere. Speed: indexes Finding rows by a column the database must scan is slow for big tables. An index makes it fast, like the index of a book: python-norun con.execute("CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer ON orders (customer_id)") Primary keys and UNIQUE columns get one automatically. Closing Call con.close() when you are done, or use contextlib.closing(sqlite3.connect(...)) in a with . (The connection's own with handles transactions, not closing.) Check yourself quiz ? Why use ? placeholders instead of an f-string to put values into SQL? - Placeholders make the query run faster on tables with many rows + Values stay data, so user text can never change the command (SQL injection) - sqlite3 refuses any SQL text that was built with an f-string - Placeholders convert every value to text before it is stored With an f-string, a name like x'); DROP TABLE products; -- becomes part of the command; with ? it is only ever a value, and quoting is handled for you. ? What happens to changes made inside with con: when the block raises? - They are saved up to the line that raised - They are saved, and the exception is swallowed + They are rolled back; nothing from that block is saved - The connection is closed and the changes wait for the next commit() The connection's with commits when the block succeeds and rolls back when it raises, which is why Ada's balance went back to 100. ? Which query gives the cheapest product's name? - SELECT name FROM products WHERE price = MIN - SELECT MIN(name) FROM products + SELECT name FROM products ORDER BY price LIMIT 1 - SELECT name FROM products ORDER BY price DESC LIMIT 1 Sorting by price ascending and taking one row gives the cheapest; MIN(name) is the alphabetically first name, and DESC gives the dearest.

title: Products in a table

A name with quotes in it, like Jo's tea , must work: that is what the placeholders are for.

Write transfer(con, frm, to, amount) : - amount must be a positive whole number, otherwise ValueError and nothing changes; - both accounts must exist, otherwise KeyError and nothing changes; - frm must have at least amount , otherwise ValueError("insufficient funds") and nothing changes; - otherwise move the money in one transaction , so that either both balances change or neither does. title: 8.06  Packaging, Environments and Tools
body: Turning scripts into a project others can install - virtual environments with venv, installing packages with pip and pinning versions, the src layout and pyproject.toml, entry points for commands, formatters and linters such as Ruff, type checking in CI, and building and sharing a package. The problem with installing everything globally pip install requests without anything else puts the package into the one Python on your computer. Project A needs version 2 of a library and project B needs version 3: one of them breaks. The answer is a virtual environment : a private folder of packages for each project. Virtual environments text python -m venv .venv create one in the project folder .venv\Scripts\activate Windows source .venv/bin/activate macOS and Linux python -m pip install requests installs into .venv only deactivate back to the system Python While it is active, python and pip mean the environment's copies. Do not put .venv in version control; add it to .gitignore and recreate it when needed. Always run pip as python -m pip : it then uses the pip that belongs to the Python you mean. Recording what you depend on text python -m pip freeze requirements.txt exact versions installed now python -m pip install -r requirements.txt recreate them elsewhere A requirements.txt with exact versions ( requests==2.32.3 ) makes a program reproducible. For libraries, version ranges are better, so users can combine them with other libraries. A project layout text weather-tool/ pyproject.toml README.md src/ weather_tool/ __init__.py cli.py forecast.py tests/ test_forecast.py The src folder keeps your package from being imported by accident from the current folder, so tests run against the installed code. Package names use underscores; the project name may use dashes. pyproject.toml One file describes the project for every tool: toml project name = "weather-tool" version = "0.3.0" description = "Forecasts in the terminal" requires-python = " =3.11" dependencies = "requests =2.31" project.scripts weather = "weather_tool.cli:main" build-system requires = "hatchling" build-backend = "hatchling.build" tool.ruff line-length = 100 project.scripts creates a weather command that calls main() in weather_tool/cli.py . During development, python -m pip install -e . installs the project in "editable" mode: changes to the code take effect without reinstalling. A main function for the command python-norun src/weather_tool/cli.py import argparse import sys def main(argv: list str None = None) - int: parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="weather") parser.add_argument("city") args = parser.parse_args(argv) print(f"Forecast for {args.city}: sunny") return 0 if __name__ == "__main__": sys.exit(main()) Taking argv as a parameter lets tests call main( "London" ) directly. Tools that keep code tidy - A formatter rewrites code into one consistent style, so nobody argues about spaces: ruff format or black . - A linter finds likely bugs and bad habits: unused imports, undefined names, a mutable default argument: ruff check . - A type checker reads your hints (lesson 8.03): mypy or pyright . - Tests : python -m pytest . Run them on every change with a CI service (GitHub Actions or similar), so mistakes are caught before they are merged: yaml .github/workflows/check.yml on: push, pull_request jobs: check: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: actions/setup-python@v5 with: { python-version: "3.13" } - run: python -m pip install -e . pytest ruff mypy - run: ruff check . - run: mypy src - run: python -m pytest Building and sharing text python -m pip install build python -m build makes dist/weather_tool-0.3.0-py3-none-any.whl and a .tar.gz The .whl ("wheel") file can be installed with pip install anywhere. Publishing to PyPI (the public package index) uses twine upload dist/ with an account and an API token; try test.pypi.org first. Version numbers Most Python projects follow semantic versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH . Bug fixes raise PATCH, new features that do not break anything raise MINOR, and anything that breaks existing users raises MAJOR. You can read the version of an installed package from code: python from importlib.metadata import version, PackageNotFoundError try: print(version("pip").count(".") = 1) except PackageNotFoundError: print("pip is not installed here") Check yourself quiz ? Why give every project its own virtual environment? - So the project's code runs faster than it would with the system Python - Because pip refuses to install packages outside a virtual environment - So the packages are saved in version control together with the code + So each project gets the versions it needs without affecting the others If project A needs version 2 of a library and project B version 3, one shared install breaks one of them; separate environments keep them apart. ? What does project.scripts in pyproject.toml do? + It creates a command that runs a chosen function once installed - It lists the scripts that the test runner should run on every change - It runs the named function each time the package is imported - It names the other packages the project needs to be installed weather = "weather_tool.cli:main" makes a weather command that calls main() ; dependencies go in dependencies instead. ? Which command recreates the exact packages listed in requirements.txt ? - python -m pip freeze requirements.txt - python -m venv requirements.txt - python -m build -r requirements.txt + python -m pip install -r requirements.txt install -r reads the file and installs every listed package and version; freeze is what wrote the file.

title: Reading a requirement line
body: Lines in a requirements.txt look like requests =2.31,<3 or rich==13.7.1 . Write parse_requirement(line) that returns (name, conditions) : - name is lower-case, with _ and . turned into - (so Typing_Extensions becomes typing-extensions ); - conditions is a list of (operator, version) pairs in order; the operators are == , != , = , <= , , < and ~= ; - spaces anywhere are ignored, a starts a comment, and an empty line (after removing the comment) gives None ; - anything else raises ValueError .

title: Comparing and bumping versions
body: Write the version helpers a release script needs, for versions in the form MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH with an optional pre-release part ( 1.4.0-rc.2 ): - parse_version(text) returns (major, minor, patch, pre) where pre is a tuple of parts (numbers as int , words as str ), or () for none. Anything else raises ValueError . Leading zeros like 01 are not allowed. - compare(a, b) returns -1, 0 or 1. A pre-release is lower than the same version without one ( 1.0.0-rc.1 < 1.0.0 ). Pre-release parts compare one by one: numbers by value, words as text, a number before a word, and fewer parts first when all shared ones are equal. - bump(text, part) with part one of "major" , "minor" or "patch" returns the next version as text, dropping any pre-release: bump("1.4.2", "minor") is "1.5.0" . Bumping the patch of a pre-release gives the release itself: bump("2.0.0-rc.1", "patch") is "2.0.0" .
