title: Glossary
body: Every term from the course, in alphabetical order. The lesson that introduces each one is in brackets. Term Meaning --- --- __init_subclass__ A class method that runs each time the class is subclassed. (7.03) __match_args__ The attribute order a class pattern uses for positional sub-patterns. (7.04) __slots__ A fixed list of attribute names that replaces an object's attribute dictionary. (7.03) Abstract base class A class that only describes methods subclasses must provide; it cannot be instantiated. (4.03) Argument A value passed to a function when it is called. (3.01) Attribute A value stored on an object, reached with a dot: account.owner . (4.01) await Pauses a coroutine until the awaited thing finishes, letting others run meanwhile. (7.06) Bytecode The compact form the interpreter turns source code into before running it. (1.01) Class A description of a kind of object: its data and its methods. (4.01) Closure A function together with variables from an enclosing function that it still uses. (3.03) Comprehension An expression that builds a list, dict or set from an iterable: x x for x in xs . (5.01) Context manager An object with __enter__ and __exit__ , used in a with block so cleanup always happens. (7.02) contextmanager The contextlib decorator that turns a one- yield generator into a context manager. (7.02) Coroutine What calling an async def function returns; it runs when awaited. (7.06) CSV Comma-separated values: a text format for tables. (6.02) Dataclass A class whose __init__ , __repr__ and __eq__ are generated from annotated fields. (4.04) Decorator A @name line above a function or class that wraps or registers it: @property , @dataclass . (4.01) Descriptor An object in a class that controls getting and setting an attribute with __get__ and __set__ . (7.03) Dictionary A mapping from keys to values with fast lookup. (2.05) Docstring The string right after a def or class line, describing it. (3.01) Duck typing Using any object that has the needed methods, whatever its class. (4.03) Dunder method A special method such as __len__ that Python calls for built-in syntax. (4.02) Dynamic typing Values have types, names do not; a name can refer to values of any type. (1.02) Encoding Turning text into bytes (and decoding: back again); UTF-8 is the usual choice (8.04) Enum A fixed set of named values. (4.04) Event loop The asyncio scheduler that runs another task while one is waiting. (7.06) Exception An object raised when something goes wrong; it stops the program unless handled. (4.05) ExitStack A context manager that collects any number of other context managers and closes them all. (7.02) f-string A string with f before it, where {expressions} are inserted and formatted. (1.03) Falsy / truthy Counting as false (0, "", None, empty collections) or true in a condition. (1.02) Fixture Set-up shared by tests; in pytest a function whose result is passed to tests by name (8.02) functools.wraps A decorator for wrappers that copies the wrapped function's name and docstring. (7.01) Future A placeholder for a result that a pool will produce later; .result() waits for it. (7.05) Generator A function with yield that produces values one at a time, on demand. (5.02) GIL The global interpreter lock: only one thread runs Python code at a time in CPython. (7.05) Guard An if condition after a case pattern. (7.04) Handler The part of logging that decides where messages go: the screen, a file, or anything else (8.01) Immutable Cannot be changed after creation: strings, tuples, numbers, frozen dataclasses. (2.01) Inheritance A class taking the attributes and methods of a base class. (4.03) Interpreter The program that reads and runs Python code directly. (1.01) Iterable / iterator Something you can loop over / the object that produces its items one at a time. (5.02) JSON A text format for nested data: objects, arrays, strings, numbers, true, false, null. (6.02) Key function A function passed as key= that decides how items are compared when sorting. (5.03) Keyword argument An argument passed by name: greet(name="Ada") . (3.02) Lambda A small anonymous function written as an expression. (3.03) List An ordered, changeable sequence. (2.02) Literal type A type hint that allows only certain exact values, like Literal 'r', 'w' (8.03) Lock An object that lets one thread at a time into a section of code. (7.05) Log level How serious a log message is: DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR or CRITICAL (8.01) Logger A named object from logging.getLogger that sends messages with a level; names form a tree split by dots (8.01) memoryview A view of part of a bytes-like object without copying it (8.04) Metaclass The class of a class; type by default. (7.03) Method A function defined in a class and called on an instance. (4.01) Mock An object from unittest.mock that accepts any call, returns what you tell it and remembers how it was used (8.02) Module A .py file whose names can be imported. (3.04) Mutable Can be changed in place: lists, dictionaries, sets, most objects. (2.02) Package A folder of modules. (3.04) Parameter A name in a function's definition that receives an argument. (3.01) Patch Temporarily replacing a name with a mock during a test, with unittest.mock.patch (8.02) Pattern The shape after case , which a value must have for that case to run. (7.04) PEP 8 Python's style guide: naming, spacing, layout. (1.02) pip The tool that installs packages from PyPI. (3.04) Process A separate running program with its own memory; processes can calculate in parallel. (7.05) Property A method used like an attribute, for controlled reading (and writing). (4.01) Protocol A description of the methods an object needs, for type checkers. (5.05) pyproject.toml The file that describes a Python project, its dependencies and its tools (8.06) Race condition A bug where threads change shared data at the same time and a change is lost. (7.05) Regular expression A pattern that describes text to search for or extract. (6.01) REPL The interactive prompt that runs one line at a time and shows results. (1.01) Scope Where a name is visible: local, enclosing, global, built-in (LEGB). (3.03) Semaphore A counter that lets at most N tasks or threads through at once. (7.06) Set An unordered collection of unique values with fast membership tests. (2.05) Slice A part of a sequence: xs start:stop:step . (2.01) SQL injection A bug where text from a user becomes part of an SQL command; prevented with ? placeholders (8.05) struct The module that packs numbers into bytes and unpacks them, by a format string such as '<HI' (8.04) TaskGroup An async with block that starts tasks and waits for all of them. (7.06) Test case A class of tests in unittest; each method starting with test is one test (8.02) Thread A separate line of execution in the same program, sharing its memory. (7.05) Traceback The report printed for an unhandled exception, read from the bottom. (4.05) Transaction A group of database changes saved together with commit or undone together with rollback (8.05) Tuple A fixed, unchangeable sequence for values that belong together. (2.04) Type hint An annotation such as - int that tools use to check types. (5.05) Type parameter A placeholder for a type in a generic function or class, written def f T (...) (8.03) TypedDict A type hint for a dictionary with known keys and value types (8.03) Unpacking Assigning the items of a sequence to several names at once. (2.04) Virtual environment A folder with its own Python packages for one project. (3.04) Wheel A built Python package file (.whl) that pip installs (8.06)

title: 1.01  What raylib Is and Setting It Up
match: 1.01 What raylib Is and Setting It Up
body: raylib is a small C library for making games - windows, drawing, input, sound and 3D in a few hundred plain functions. This lesson explains what it does and does not do, installs it with vcpkg, and runs a first window in Visual Studio. A library, not an engine raylib is a C library by Ramon Santamaria for learning and making games. It gives you functions; you write the game: raylib does You do --- --- Open a window, run at a frame rate Decide what happens each frame Draw shapes, textures, text, 3D models Keep the game's data: positions, scores, levels Read keyboard, mouse, gamepad and touch Turn input into movement and actions Load and play sounds and music Decide when to play them Basic collision tests and maths helpers Collision response, physics, AI, menus An engine such as Unity or Godot gives you an editor, a scene tree, physics and a component system, and you fit your game into them. With raylib nothing is hidden: every pixel on screen is there because your code drew it this frame. That is why it is a good way to learn how games actually work, and it is enough for complete, polished 2D and small 3D games. raylib is written in C99, so its API is plain functions and structs: Vector2 , Rectangle , Color , Texture2D . It works fine from C++, and the course uses C++ for everything around it. Installing with vcpkg The simplest way on Windows is vcpkg , Microsoft's C++ package manager: cpp-norun git clone https://github.com/microsoft/vcpkg C:\dev\vcpkg C:\dev\vcpkg\bootstrap-vcpkg.bat C:\dev\vcpkg\vcpkg integrate install C:\dev\vcpkg\vcpkg install raylib:x64-windows integrate install makes every Visual Studio project find vcpkg's headers and libraries automatically. Then create a new Console App (C++) project, set the platform to x64 , and replace the code with: cpp-norun include "raylib.h" int main() { InitWindow(800, 450, "My first raylib window"); SetTargetFPS(60); while (!WindowShouldClose()) // Esc or the close button { BeginDrawing(); ClearBackground(RAYWHITE); DrawText("Hello, raylib!", 280, 200, 32, DARKGRAY); EndDrawing(); } CloseWindow(); } Press F5: a window opens with the text in it, and closes with Esc. If the build cannot find raylib.h , check that the platform is x64 (vcpkg installed the x64 version) and that integrate install was run. !note Other ways work too: the raylib Windows installer comes with its own compiler and editor, and CMake projects can fetch raylib with FetchContent . The code in this course is the same whichever you use. Hiding the console window A console app opens a black console next to the game, which is handy for printf debugging. For a release build, set Linker System SubSystem to Windows and Linker Advanced Entry Point to mainCRTStartup , so main still runs but no console appears. raylib's cheatsheet raylib's website has a one-page cheatsheet listing every function by module: rcore (window, input, timing), rshapes , rtextures , rtext , rmodels , raudio . Keep it open while you work; the function names are descriptive enough that it is often all you need. The examples page has more than a hundred small programs, each a single file, that show one feature each. How the practice works Compiler Explorer, which runs the practice on this site, has no window or GPU. So the practice checks the game logic you would put around raylib's calls: movement, collision, animation timing, cameras, tile maps, pathfinding. Each practice declares the few raylib types it needs, such as struct Vector2 { float x, y; }; , exactly as raylib does, so the code moves into a real raylib project unchanged. Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference between raylib and a game engine? - raylib is an engine too, but with a smaller editor and fewer built-in systems - raylib only draws 2D graphics, while an engine can also draw 3D + raylib is a library of functions you call from your own loop; an engine gives you an editor and systems your game fits into - raylib is a game engine written in C, while a library would be written in C++ raylib has no editor or scene tree: you write the loop and call its functions. It also draws 3D, so the 2D-only answer is wrong. ? What does vcpkg integrate install do? + It makes Visual Studio projects find the headers and libraries vcpkg installed, with no project settings - It downloads and builds raylib for x64 Windows - It adds raylib's source files to the current project so they compile with it - It installs Visual Studio's C++ tools if they are missing Integration is a one-time step that hooks vcpkg into every Visual Studio project. Installing raylib itself is the separate vcpkg install raylib:x64-windows command. ? When does WindowShouldClose() become true? - After CloseWindow() has been called - When the window loses focus to another program - When the frame rate drops below the target set with SetTargetFPS + When the user presses Esc or clicks the window's close button It reports the user's request to quit; your loop then ends and you call CloseWindow() yourself. ? Why does the practice on this site check game logic instead of drawing a window? - Because raylib cannot be called from C++, only from C + Because Compiler Explorer has no window or GPU to draw on - Because drawing code never has bugs worth testing Only the logic around raylib's calls can run there, so the practice declares the raylib types it needs and tests that logic, which moves into a real raylib project unchanged. raylib works fine from C++.

title: The frame budget
where: 1.01 What raylib Is and Setting It Up
body: SetTargetFPS(60) gives each frame a budget of 1000 / 60 = 16.7 milliseconds for input, update and drawing. Write three small helpers a game's debug overlay uses: cpp double frameBudgetMs(int fps); // 1000 / fps; 0 when fps <= 0 (no limit) int framesFor(double seconds, int fps); // how many frames that many seconds takes, rounded to the nearest std::string fpsLabel(double frameTimeSeconds); // "60 FPS (16.7 ms)" fpsLabel shows the frames per second as 1 / frameTime rounded to the nearest whole number, and the frame time in milliseconds with one decimal place. A frame time of 0 or less gives "-- FPS" .

title: 1.02  The Game Loop
body: Every game is a loop that reads input, updates the world and draws it, many times a second. This lesson takes raylib's loop apart - what BeginDrawing and EndDrawing do, why the screen is cleared every frame, and how to keep update and drawing apart. Input, update, draw A film shows 24 still pictures a second; a game makes its pictures as it goes. Each picture is a frame , and each frame the game does three things: 1. Input : which keys are down, where the mouse is. 2. Update : move things, check collisions, change scores and timers. 3. Draw : show the world as it is now. At 60 frames per second that happens every 16.7 ms. The game's state lives in variables that survive from frame to frame; the loop changes them a little each time. cpp-norun include "raylib.h" int main() { InitWindow(800, 450, "Moving square"); SetTargetFPS(60); float x = 100.0f; // state: survives between frames while (!WindowShouldClose()) { // Input and update if (IsKeyDown(KEY_RIGHT)) x += 4.0f; if (IsKeyDown(KEY_LEFT)) x -= 4.0f; // Draw BeginDrawing(); ClearBackground(RAYWHITE); DrawRectangle(static_cast<int (x), 200, 50, 50, MAROON); EndDrawing(); } CloseWindow(); } What the raylib calls do Call Does --- --- InitWindow(w, h, title) Opens the window and creates the OpenGL context: call it before anything that loads or draws SetTargetFPS(60) Makes EndDrawing wait so frames come no faster than 60 a second WindowShouldClose() True once Esc or the close button was pressed BeginDrawing() Starts the frame's drawing ClearBackground(c) Fills the whole frame with one colour EndDrawing() Shows the finished frame (swaps buffers), waits for the target frame rate, and polls input for the next frame CloseWindow() Closes the window and frees the context Note the last point about EndDrawing : raylib reads the keyboard and mouse there, so IsKeyPressed reports what happened since the previous frame. Why clear every frame? The game draws into a back buffer while the screen shows the front buffer; EndDrawing swaps them. The back buffer still holds an old frame, so without ClearBackground the new frame is drawn over old pictures and moving things leave trails. Clear first, then draw everything that should be visible, back to front: later drawing covers earlier drawing. Keep update and draw apart It is tempting to move things inside the drawing code. Keep them apart instead: cpp-norun struct Game { float x{ 100 }; int score{ 0 }; }; void update(Game& g) { if (IsKeyDown(KEY_RIGHT)) g.x += 4.0f; } void draw(const Game& g) { DrawRectangle(static_cast<int (g.x), 200, 50, 50, MAROON); } while (!WindowShouldClose()) { update(game); BeginDrawing(); ClearBackground(RAYWHITE); draw(game); EndDrawing(); } draw takes the game by const& : it can look but not change. This split pays off again and again: you can pause by skipping update , run the update twice as fast for testing, or test update without a window at all, which is exactly what the practice on this site does. Check yourself quiz ? What are the three steps of every frame? - Load assets, draw the world, free assets + Read input, update the world, draw the world - Clear the screen, read input, close the window - Update the world, wait 16.7 ms, read input Each frame reads input, changes the game's state a little, then draws it as it is now. Loading and freeing happen once, outside the loop. ? What happens if you do not call ClearBackground at the start of a frame? - raylib clears the frame automatically, so nothing changes - The window turns black until the next ClearBackground - EndDrawing fails and the window freezes + The new frame is drawn over an old one, so moving objects leave trails The back buffer still holds an older frame. Without clearing, everything drawn earlier stays visible underneath. ? Where does raylib read the keyboard and mouse for the next frame? + In EndDrawing , after showing the frame - In BeginDrawing , before drawing starts - Inside IsKeyDown each time it is called - In WindowShouldClose , at the top of the loop EndDrawing swaps buffers, waits for the target frame rate and polls input, so IsKeyPressed reports what happened since the previous frame. ? Why does the lesson's draw function take the game as const Game& ? - So the game is copied and drawing cannot slow the update down - Because raylib's drawing functions only accept const objects + So drawing can read the game state but cannot change it const& gives read-only access without a copy. Keeping state changes in update lets you pause, speed up or test the update without a window.

title: Update apart from draw
body: Split a tiny game into an update that changes the state and a draw that only describes what to show: cpp struct Input { bool left; bool right; bool pausePressed; }; struct Game { float x{ 100 }; bool paused{ false }; int frames{ 0 }; }; void update(Game& g, const Input& in); std::vector<std::string draw(const Game& g); update - pausePressed toggles paused , always. - While paused, nothing else changes. - Otherwise: right adds 4 to x , left subtracts 4 (both: no movement); x stays within 0..750 ; frames goes up by one. draw returns the draw calls in order, as text: 1. "clear RAYWHITE" 2. "rect <x 200 50 50" with x as a whole number (truncated, like static_cast<int ) 3. "text frames <frames " 4. and only while paused, last: "text PAUSED"

title: 1.03  Coordinates, Shapes and Colours
body: Where things go on the screen and how to draw them - raylib's coordinate system with y pointing down, Vector2 and Rectangle, the shape functions, colours with alpha, and centring things on the screen. Screen coordinates The top-left corner of the window is (0, 0) . x grows to the right and y grows downwards , in pixels. In an 800 × 450 window the bottom-right pixel is (799, 449) . (0,0) ──────────── x ──────────▶ (800,0) │ y (400,225) is the centre │ ▼ (0,450) Y pointing down surprises people used to maths graphs: "up" on screen means subtracting from y, and gravity adds to y. The basic types cpp-norun typedef struct Vector2 { float x; float y; } Vector2; typedef struct Rectangle { float x; float y; float width; float height; } Rectangle; // x, y = top-left corner typedef struct Color { unsigned char r, g, b, a; } Color; C++ can build them with braces: Vector2 p{ 100, 50 } , Rectangle r{ 10, 10, 64, 32 } , Color sky{ 135, 206, 235, 255 } . raylib has named colours ( RED , DARKBLUE , RAYWHITE , BLANK for fully transparent) and helpers such as Fade(RED, 0.5f) for half-transparent red. Shapes Function Draws --- --- DrawPixel(x, y, c) One pixel DrawLine(x1, y1, x2, y2, c) / DrawLineEx(a, b, thick, c) A line DrawRectangle(x, y, w, h, c) / DrawRectangleRec(rect, c) A filled rectangle from its top-left corner DrawRectangleLinesEx(rect, thick, c) A rectangle's outline DrawRectangleRounded(rect, roundness, segments, c) Rounded corners DrawCircle(cx, cy, r, c) / DrawCircleV(centre, r, c) A filled circle from its centre DrawTriangle(a, b, c, colour) A triangle (points counter-clockwise) DrawPoly(centre, sides, radius, rotation, c) A regular polygon Rectangles are placed by their top-left corner, circles by their centre. Mixing the two up is the most common reason a shape is "half a size off". Centring To centre a rectangle of size w × h in the window: cpp-norun const float x = (GetScreenWidth() - w) / 2.0f; const float y = (GetScreenHeight() - h) / 2.0f; Text works the same way with MeasureText(text, fontSize) , which returns the width in pixels: cpp-norun const char title = "GAME OVER"; const int width = MeasureText(title, 48); DrawText(title, (GetScreenWidth() - width) / 2, 180, 48, RED); Colours and alpha a is the alpha (opacity): 255 is solid, 0 is invisible. Drawing a half-transparent black rectangle over the whole screen is the classic "paused" dim. To mix two colours, interpolate each channel: r = a.r + (b.r - a.r) t , which raylib's ColorLerp does (raylib 5.5). Drawing order Shapes drawn later appear on top. A frame is usually drawn in layers: background, world, effects, then the interface on top of everything. Check yourself quiz ? Which way does y grow in raylib's screen coordinates? - Upwards: the bottom of the window is y = 0 + Downwards: the top of the window is y = 0 - Upwards from the centre of the window, which is (0, 0) Screen y points down, so moving "up" subtracts from y and gravity adds to it, unlike a maths graph. ? What does the position of a rectangle and of a circle refer to? - Both are placed by their centre - Both are placed by their top-left corner - A rectangle by its centre, a circle by the top-left of its bounding box + A rectangle by its top-left corner, a circle by its centre Mixing the two up is the most common reason a shape ends up half its size off. ? How do you centre text horizontally? - Start it at screen width / 2 with DrawText + Start it at (screen width - MeasureText width) / 2 - Start it at (screen width - font size) / 2 - Pass a centre alignment flag to DrawText Measure the text with MeasureText and subtract its width. Starting at half the screen width puts the text's left edge in the middle, and the font size is the height, not the width. ? What alpha value makes a colour fully solid? - 0 - 1.0f + 255 - 128 Color stores each channel as an unsigned char from 0 to 255: 255 is solid and 0 is invisible. Fade takes a 0-1 float, but the stored alpha is 0-255.

title: Placing things on screen
body: Write the helpers for putting shapes where you mean them: cpp struct Vector2 { float x, y; }; struct Rectangle { float x, y, width, height; }; struct Color { unsigned char r, g, b, a; }; Rectangle centred(int screenW, int screenH, float w, float h); // a w x h rectangle in the middle of the screen Rectangle circleBounds(Vector2 centre, float radius); // the square around a circle Vector2 rectCentre(Rectangle r); Color colorLerp(Color a, Color b, float t); // each channel a + (b - a) t, rounded; t clamped to 0..1

title: 1.04  Frame Time and Smooth Movement
body: Moving "4 pixels a frame" runs twice as fast on a 120 Hz screen. This lesson moves things in units per second using the frame time, adds velocity and acceleration, normalises diagonal movement, and keeps big frame-time spikes from breaking the game. Pixels per frame is a trap In lesson 1.02 the square moved 4 pixels a frame. With SetTargetFPS(60) that is 240 pixels a second, but on a slow computer at 30 frames a second it is 120, and with the frame rate unlocked on a fast one it could be 1000. The game's speed depends on the computer. The fix is to measure time. GetFrameTime() returns the seconds the last frame took (about 0.0167 at 60 FPS), often called dt (delta time). Movement becomes units per second × dt : cpp-norun const float speed = 240.0f; // pixels per second const float dt = GetFrameTime(); if (IsKeyDown(KEY_RIGHT)) x += speed dt; Now the square moves 240 pixels a second at any frame rate: smaller steps when frames are short, bigger when they are long. Velocity and acceleration Real movement has velocity (how fast, in pixels per second) and acceleration (how fast the velocity changes): cpp-norun struct Body { Vector2 pos; Vector2 vel; }; void step(Body& b, Vector2 accel, float dt) { b.vel.x += accel.x dt; b.vel.y += accel.y dt; b.pos.x += b.vel.x dt; b.pos.y += b.vel.y dt; } This is semi-implicit Euler integration: change the velocity first, then move with the new velocity. It is simple and stable enough for almost every game. A car that speeds up while you hold a key, a ship that drifts, and a falling ball all come from these two lines. Friction or drag slows things down. A simple version multiplies the velocity by a factor each second: vel = pow(0.1f, dt) keeps 10 % of the speed per second regardless of the frame rate. Multiplying by a fixed 0.9f every frame would again depend on the frame rate. Diagonals are too fast Holding right and down adds speed on both axes: the length of (1, 1) is 1.41, so diagonal movement is 41 % faster. Normalise the input direction to length 1 before scaling it: cpp-norun Vector2 dir{ 0, 0 }; if (IsKeyDown(KEY_D)) dir.x += 1; if (IsKeyDown(KEY_A)) dir.x -= 1; if (IsKeyDown(KEY_S)) dir.y += 1; if (IsKeyDown(KEY_W)) dir.y -= 1; const float len = std::sqrt(dir.x dir.x + dir.y dir.y); if (len 0) { dir.x /= len; dir.y /= len; } pos.x += dir.x speed dt; pos.y += dir.y speed dt; raylib's raymath.h has Vector2Normalize , Vector2Scale , Vector2Add and many more for exactly this. Spikes When you drag the window or the program pauses in the debugger, the next frame time can be a whole second. Objects then jump through walls. Clamp dt to a sensible maximum, such as 1/20 s: the game slows down briefly instead of breaking. cpp-norun const float dt = std::min(GetFrameTime(), 0.05f); Milestone 3 goes further with fixed time steps , which make physics behave the same at every frame rate. Timers Many game rules are timers: a power-up lasting 5 seconds, a shot every 0.25 s. Keep a float that counts down by dt: cpp-norun cooldown -= dt; if (IsKeyDown(KEY_SPACE) && cooldown <= 0) { shoot(); cooldown += 0.25f; } if (cooldown < 0) cooldown = 0; Adding the period back ( += 0.25f ) instead of setting it keeps the average rate exact even when frames do not divide the period evenly. Check yourself quiz ? Why multiply speeds by GetFrameTime() ? - To make the game run at exactly 60 frames per second - To make movement smoother by skipping frames that took too long + So movement is measured per second and is the same at every frame rate dt is the length of the last frame, so speed × dt moves the same distance each second whatever the frame rate. Capping the frame rate is what SetTargetFPS does. ? Why is diagonal movement too fast without normalising the direction? + The direction (1, 1) has length about 1.41, so the speed is about 41 % higher - Two keys are read per frame, so the movement is applied twice - Diagonal movement adds the speed twice, so it is 100 % faster - The frame time is longer when two keys are held Each axis gets the full speed, and the combined vector is √2 long. Normalising it to length 1 before scaling fixes that. ? Why clamp dt to a maximum such as 0.05 s? - So the game never runs faster than 20 frames per second - Because GetFrameTime() can return negative values + So one very long frame cannot move objects through walls - So timers count down at the same speed as the frame rate A long frame (a dragged window, a debugger pause) would make one huge step that skips through walls. Clamping makes the game slow down briefly instead of breaking. ? A shot cooldown is reset with cooldown += 0.25f rather than cooldown = 0.25f . Why? - Setting it would make the cooldown negative + Adding it back keeps the average firing rate exact - It makes the first shot fire faster than the later ones - = cannot be used with float variables that dt changed Frames rarely divide the period evenly; with += the time overshot past zero is carried into the next period instead of being lost each shot. ? Why is vel = pow(0.1f, dt) better for friction than vel = 0.9f each frame? - pow is faster to compute than a multiplication - A factor of 0.9f would stop the object at once + It keeps 10 % of the speed per second at any frame rate A fixed factor per frame depends on the frame rate: at 120 FPS a per-frame 0.9 is applied twice as often as at 60 FPS. Raising the factor to the power dt makes it a per-second rule.

title: Moving by the second
body: Write the movement pieces of lesson 1.04: cpp struct Vector2 { float x, y; }; Vector2 inputDirection(bool up, bool down, bool left, bool right); // length 1, or (0, 0) float clampDt(float dt); // at most 0.05, never below 0 void step(Vector2& pos, Vector2& vel, Vector2 accel, float drag, float dt); class Shooter { public: explicit Shooter(float period); int update(bool fireHeld, float dt); // how many shots this frame }; - inputDirection : up is negative y, right is positive x; opposite keys cancel. - step : semi-implicit Euler with drag: first vel += accel dt , then vel = pow(drag, dt) (drag is the fraction of speed kept per second), then pos += vel dt . - Shooter : holding fire shoots once immediately, then once every period seconds. The cooldown counts down by dt every frame; while fire is held and the cooldown is at or below zero, a shot is fired and period is added to the cooldown (several shots in one long frame are possible). When fire is not held, the cooldown stops at zero instead of going negative.

title: 1.05  Keyboard, Mouse and Gamepad Input
body: Reading every kind of input raylib supports - keys held and pressed, typed characters, the mouse and its wheel, and gamepads with their sticks and dead zones - and mapping them to game actions so players can rebind them. Down, pressed, released Function True when --- --- IsKeyDown(KEY_SPACE) The key is held this frame IsKeyPressed(KEY_SPACE) The key went down since the last frame (once per press) IsKeyReleased(KEY_SPACE) The key went up since the last frame IsKeyUp(KEY_SPACE) The key is not held IsKeyPressedRepeat(KEY_LEFT) The key's auto-repeat fired, as in a text box Use Down for continuous actions (moving, accelerating) and Pressed for one-off actions (jumping, shooting once, opening a menu). Using IsKeyDown for a menu choice moves the selection every frame the key is held, which is 60 items a second. Keys are named KEY_A ... KEY_Z , KEY_ZERO ... KEY_NINE , KEY_LEFT , KEY_ENTER , KEY_LEFT_SHIFT and so on, by their position on a US keyboard. For typed text (names, chat) use GetCharPressed() , which returns Unicode characters one by one in a loop, respecting the keyboard layout and Shift: cpp-norun for (int c = GetCharPressed(); c != 0; c = GetCharPressed()) if (c = 32 && c < 127 && name.size() < 12) name += static_cast<char (c); if (IsKeyPressed(KEY_BACKSPACE) && !name.empty()) name.pop_back(); The mouse Function Gives --- --- GetMousePosition() A Vector2 in window pixels GetMouseDelta() How far it moved since the last frame IsMouseButtonPressed(MOUSE_BUTTON_LEFT) Click, once (also Down, Released) GetMouseWheelMove() Wheel movement this frame, positive away from you SetMouseCursor(MOUSE_CURSOR_POINTING_HAND) Changes the cursor shape DisableCursor() / EnableCursor() Hides and locks the cursor, for 3D cameras A button is a rectangle plus a click test: CheckCollisionPointRec(GetMousePosition(), rect) && IsMouseButtonPressed(MOUSE_BUTTON_LEFT) . Gamepads raylib numbers gamepads from 0 and uses positional button names so code works for Xbox and PlayStation pads alike: cpp-norun if (IsGamepadAvailable(0)) { const float lx = GetGamepadAxisMovement(0, GAMEPAD_AXIS_LEFT_X); // -1 .. 1 const float ly = GetGamepadAxisMovement(0, GAMEPAD_AXIS_LEFT_Y); if (IsGamepadButtonPressed(0, GAMEPAD_BUTTON_RIGHT_FACE_DOWN)) jump(); // A on Xbox, Cross on PlayStation } Dead zones A stick at rest rarely reads exactly 0; it drifts by a few hundredths, which would make the character creep. Apply a dead zone : treat small values as zero, and rescale the rest so movement still starts smoothly from zero. cpp-norun float deadZone(float v, float dz) { if (std::fabs(v) < dz) return 0.0f; return (v - std::copysign(dz, v)) / (1.0f - dz); // dz..1 becomes 0..1 } A better version uses the stick's length (a radial dead zone) so diagonal movement is not cut off differently from straight movement; the practice builds both pieces. Actions, not keys Game code should not ask "is W down?" but "is the player moving up?". Map actions to any number of inputs: cpp-norun enum class Action { Left, Right, Jump, Pause }; struct Binding { Action action; int key; int gamepadButton; }; bool actionPressed(Action a, const std::vector<Binding & bindings) { for (const auto& b : bindings) if (b.action == a && (IsKeyPressed(b.key) IsGamepadButtonPressed(0, b.gamepadButton))) return true; return false; } Now a settings screen can change the bindings, and the game code never changes. Check yourself quiz ? When do you use IsKeyDown and when IsKeyPressed ? - IsKeyDown for jumping, IsKeyPressed for moving + IsKeyDown for moving, IsKeyPressed for jumping - They are the same; IsKeyPressed is just the older name - IsKeyPressed for keyboard keys, IsKeyDown for gamepad buttons Down is for actions that continue while held; Pressed is true once per press, for one-off actions such as a jump or a menu choice. Using Down for a menu moves the selection every frame the key is held. ? Why read typed text with GetCharPressed instead of key codes? - Key codes cannot detect letters, only arrows and function keys - GetCharPressed is faster because it reads only one key per frame + It returns real characters for the user's keyboard layout and Shift state Key codes name positions on a US keyboard. GetCharPressed gives the Unicode characters actually typed, one by one in a loop. ? What is a dead zone on a gamepad stick? - The edge of the stick's range, where values are clamped to 1 - A gamepad that is connected but not yet available to the game - The delay between pressing a button and the game seeing it + A small range around the stick's centre that is read as zero A stick at rest reads a few hundredths, not 0, so without a dead zone drift moves the character. The dead zone ignores that and rescales the rest so movement still starts smoothly. ? Why map actions such as Action::Jump to keys instead of testing KEY_SPACE in the game code? + So the bindings can be changed without changing the game code - Because IsKeyPressed only accepts Action values, not keys - So the game reads input faster than with raw key codes The game asks "did the player jump?" and a binding list answers it from any key or gamepad button, which is what a rebinding screen edits.

title: Sticks and bindings
body: Two pieces of an input layer: cpp struct Vector2 { float x, y; }; Vector2 radialDeadZone(Vector2 stick, float dz); enum class Action { Left, Right, Jump, Pause }; class Bindings { public: void bind(Action a, int key); // a key belongs to at most one action void unbind(int key); bool down(Action a, const std::set<int & keysDown) const; std::vector<int keysFor(Action a) const; // in increasing order }; radialDeadZone : take the stick's length. Below dz , the result is (0, 0) . Otherwise keep the direction and rescale the length from dz..1 to 0..1 ; a length above 1 (sticks can report slightly more on diagonals) counts as 1. Bindings : an action can have any number of keys. Binding a key that already belongs to another action moves it to the new one, so one key never does two things. down is true if any of the action's keys is in keysDown .

title: Two-paddle tennis
body: Write the whole game logic of a two-player paddle-and-ball game. The raylib part is then a dozen lines: read the keys, call update , draw two rectangles, a circle and the score. cpp struct Vector2 { float x, y; }; struct Rectangle { float x, y, width, height; }; struct Game { Rectangle left{ 30, 185, 10, 80 }, right{ 760, 185, 10, 80 }; Vector2 ball{ 400, 225 }, vel{ 300, 0 }; float radius{ 8 }; int leftScore{ 0 }, rightScore{ 0 }; int winner{ 0 }; // 0 while playing, 1 left won, 2 right won }; void update(Game& g, float leftDir, float rightDir, float dt); // dirs: -1 up, 0, 1 down float computerDir(const Rectangle& paddle, Vector2 ball); The field is 800 × 450. Each call of update , in this order: 1. If there is a winner, nothing happens. 2. Paddles move at 360 pixels per second in their direction and stay inside the field ( 0 <= y and y + height <= 450 ). 3. The ball moves by vel dt . 4. Walls : if the ball's top goes above 0, put it back at y = radius and make vel.y positive; likewise at the bottom ( y = 450 - radius , vel.y negative). 5. Paddles : the ball hits a paddle when the circle overlaps the paddle's rectangle (closest point test) and it is moving towards that paddle. On a hit: - the new speed is min(speed 1.05, 900) where speed is the length of vel ; - offset = (ball.y - paddle centre y) / (height / 2) , clamped to -1..1 ; - the angle is offset 60 degrees, and vel = (±speed·cos, speed·sin) with x pointing away from the paddle; - the ball is pushed out to touch the paddle's face: x = paddle.x + width + radius for the left one, paddle.x - radius for the right one. 6. Scoring : when the ball is completely past the left edge ( x + radius < 0 ) the right player scores, and past the right edge ( x - radius 800 ) the left player scores. The ball then goes back to (400, 225) with vel = (300, 0) towards the player who lost the point ( -300 if the left player lost). The first to 5 wins. computerDir steers a paddle towards the ball: 1 if the ball is more than 10 pixels below the paddle's centre, -1 if more than 10 above, else 0 .

title: 2.01  Textures and Sprites
body: Loading images onto the GPU as textures, drawing them whole or in part, scaling, rotating and tinting them with DrawTexturePro, the origin point, flipping, and loading and unloading assets at the right time. Images and textures raylib has two kinds of picture: Type Lives in Use --- --- --- Image Main memory (CPU) Loading, editing pixels, generating pictures Texture2D Video memory (GPU) Drawing, every frame Most of the time you load a file straight into a texture: cpp-norun Texture2D player = LoadTexture("assets/player.png"); // after InitWindow // ... game loop: DrawTexture(player, 100, 200, WHITE); UnloadTexture(player); // before CloseWindow LoadTexture needs the OpenGL context, so it must come after InitWindow , and UnloadTexture before CloseWindow . Loading inside the game loop every frame is a classic mistake: it re-reads the file and allocates video memory 60 times a second. Paths are relative to the working directory , which in Visual Studio is the project folder, not the folder of the .exe . Call ChangeDirectory(GetApplicationDirectory()) at start-up and copy the assets next to the program, and the same paths work everywhere. Drawing Function Draws --- --- DrawTexture(tex, x, y, tint) The whole texture at its own size DrawTextureV(tex, pos, tint) The same with a Vector2 DrawTextureEx(tex, pos, rotation, scale, tint) Rotated (degrees) and scaled DrawTextureRec(tex, source, pos, tint) Part of the texture (the source rectangle) DrawTexturePro(tex, source, dest, origin, rotation, tint) Part of it, into any rectangle, rotated around origin The tint multiplies every pixel's colour: WHITE leaves it as it is, RED keeps only the red channel, and Fade(WHITE, 0.5f) makes it half transparent. Flashing a sprite white when it is hit or red when it is low on health is one tint away. DrawTexturePro This one function does everything, so it is worth understanding: cpp-norun const Rectangle source{ 0, 0, 32, 32 }; // which part of the texture, in texture pixels const Rectangle dest{ pos.x, pos.y, 64, 64 }; // where on screen, and how big const Vector2 origin{ 32, 32 }; // pivot, relative to dest's top-left DrawTexturePro(tex, source, dest, origin, angleDegrees, WHITE); - dest.x, dest.y is where the origin ends up on screen. With origin at the centre of dest , pos is the sprite's centre and rotation spins it around its middle. - A negative source width flips the picture horizontally; a negative height flips it vertically. That is how one "facing right" picture serves for both directions. Pixel art Small pixel-art sprites scaled up look blurry with the default bilinear filtering. Set point filtering for crisp pixels: cpp-norun SetTextureFilter(tex, TEXTURE_FILTER_POINT); and scale by whole numbers (2×, 3×, 4×) so every source pixel becomes the same number of screen pixels. Keeping assets together As soon as there are more than a few textures, keep them in one place that loads everything at start-up and unloads it at the end: cpp-norun struct Assets { Texture2D player, tiles, enemy; void load() { player = LoadTexture("assets/player.png"); / ... / } void unload() { UnloadTexture(player); / ... / } }; Lesson 6.02 adds a cache keyed by file name, so the same picture is never loaded twice. Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference between an Image and a Texture2D ? - An Image is for PNG files and a Texture2D is for JPG files + An Image is pixels in main memory for editing; a Texture2D lives in video memory and is what you draw - An Image is drawn every frame; a Texture2D is only used for loading - They are the same type under two names Edit or generate pixels in an Image on the CPU; draw from a Texture2D on the GPU. ? Why must textures be loaded after InitWindow ? - Because InitWindow sets the working directory that file paths are relative to - Because LoadTexture only works inside the game loop + Because creating a texture needs the OpenGL context that InitWindow creates No context, no video memory to put the texture in. For the same reason UnloadTexture must come before CloseWindow . ? How do you draw a sprite facing the other way without a second picture? - Pass a rotation of 180 degrees to DrawTexturePro - Use a negative tint colour - Give dest a negative width + Give the source rectangle a negative width A negative source width flips the picture horizontally. Rotating by 180 would turn it upside down as well. ? Small pixel-art sprites look blurry when scaled up. What fixes it? - Loading the texture inside the game loop each frame + SetTextureFilter(tex, TEXTURE_FILTER_POINT) and scaling by whole numbers - Tinting the sprite with WHITE The default bilinear filtering blends neighbouring pixels. Point filtering keeps them crisp, and whole-number scales make every source pixel the same size. ? What does DrawTexturePro 's origin do? - It picks which part of the texture image to draw + It is the pivot point, measured from dest 's top-left corner - It sets the top-left corner of the window to draw into - It is where the texture is stored in video memory dest.x, dest.y is where the pivot lands on screen, and rotation turns around it. Put the origin at the centre of dest and the sprite spins around its middle. The part of the texture is the source rectangle.

title: Crisp pixels on any screen
body: A pixel-art game is drawn at a small native size, such as 320 × 180, and scaled up by a whole number so every pixel stays square. Write the helpers: cpp struct Vector2 { float x, y; }; struct Rectangle { float x, y, width, height; }; int pixelScale(int screenW, int screenH, int nativeW, int nativeH); // the largest whole scale that fits, at least 1 Rectangle letterbox(int screenW, int screenH, int nativeW, int nativeH); // the scaled picture, centred, whole-pixel position Rectangle spriteSource(Rectangle frame, bool facingLeft); // negative width to flip Rectangle spriteDest(Vector2 centre, float w, float h, float scale); // a dest rectangle for an origin at the centre - letterbox : size is native × scale; x and y centre it, rounded down to whole pixels. - spriteDest : with DrawTexturePro 's origin at (w scale / 2, h scale / 2) , the dest rectangle's x and y are the centre itself, and its size is w scale by h scale .

title: 2.02  Sprite Sheets and Animation
body: Animation is a sequence of frames shown one after another. This lesson cuts frames out of a sprite sheet, plays them at their own speed using a timer, handles looping and one-shot animations, and switches between animations as a character's state changes. Sprite sheets A sprite sheet is one texture holding many frames in a grid. A 4-frame walk cycle of 32 × 32 frames is a 128 × 32 picture. Loading one texture instead of many is faster to draw and easier to manage. The source rectangle of frame i in a sheet with columns frames per row: cpp-norun Rectangle frameRect(int i, int columns, float w, float h) { return { (i % columns) w, (i / columns) h, w, h }; } Playing frames over time An animation shows each frame for a while, then moves to the next. Count time, not game frames, so the animation runs at the same speed at any frame rate (lesson 1.04): cpp-norun struct Animation { int first, count; // frames first .. first + count - 1 in the sheet float fps; // animation frames per second bool loop; }; struct Animator { const Animation anim{ nullptr }; float time{ 0 }; void play(const Animation& a) { if (anim != &a) { anim = &a; time = 0; } } void update(float dt) { time += dt; } int frame() const { int i = static_cast<int (time anim- fps); i = anim- loop ? i % anim- count : std::min(i, anim- count - 1); return anim- first + i; } bool finished() const { return !anim- loop && time anim- fps = anim- count; } }; Notice play only restarts when the animation changes : calling play(walk) every frame while walking must not restart the walk at frame 0 each frame, which would freeze it on the first picture. Looping and one-shot animations - Looping : idle, walk, run. The frame wraps around with % . - One-shot : attack, hurt, death. It stops on the last frame, and finished() tells the game to go back to idle (or to remove the enemy). Some animations need events at a particular frame: the sword's hit should only count on frame 3 of the attack, and a footstep sound should play on frames 1 and 3 of the walk. Check when the frame number changes to a given value, not while it is that value, or the sound plays every game frame. Choosing the animation from the state The character's state picks the animation: cpp-norun if (attacking) animator.play(attackAnim); else if (!onGround) animator.play(jumpAnim); else if (fabs(vel.x) 1) animator.play(walkAnim); else animator.play(idleAnim); animator.update(dt); Rectangle src = frameRect(animator.frame(), 8, 32, 32); if (facingLeft) src.width = -src.width; // lesson 2.01's flip DrawTexturePro(sheet, src, { pos.x, pos.y, 64, 64 }, { 32, 64 }, 0, WHITE); The order of the checks is a priority list: an attack overrides everything, jumping overrides walking. Lesson 4.04 turns this into a proper state machine . Frame timing that varies Hand-made animations often hold some frames longer than others: the wind-up of an attack is slow, the strike is fast. Store a duration per frame instead of one fps , and find the current frame by walking through the durations; the practice does this. Check yourself quiz ? Why should animation time be measured in seconds, not game frames? - Because counting game frames needs an integer, which cannot wrap with % + So the animation plays at the same speed whatever the frame rate - So the animation skips frames when the game is slow Counting game frames would make the walk cycle twice as fast at 120 FPS as at 60, just like moving by pixels per frame. ? Why must play() not restart an animation that is already playing? - Restarting would load the sprite sheet again - Restarting would make it play twice as fast - Restarting would switch it to the next animation in the list + It is called every frame, so restarting each time would keep the animation on its first frame play(walk) runs every frame while walking. Only a change of animation should reset the time to 0. ? What is the difference between a looping and a one-shot animation? + A looping animation wraps back to its first frame; a one-shot stops on its last frame and reports that it has finished - A looping animation uses a sprite sheet; a one-shot uses separate textures - A one-shot animation plays once per game frame; a looping one plays once per second Idle and walk loop with % ; attack, hurt and death stop on their last frame, and finished() tells the game to move on. ? In a sheet with 8 frames per row, which source rectangle holds frame 10 if each frame is 32 × 32? - { 320, 0, 32, 32 } - { 96, 32, 32, 32 } + { 64, 32, 32, 32 } - { 32, 64, 32, 32 } Column 10 % 8 = 2 gives x = 64, row 10 / 8 = 1 gives y = 32. { 320, 0, 32, 32 } forgets the rows, and { 32, 64, ... } swaps column and row. ? A footstep sound should play on frame 1 of the walk. When do you play it? - Every game frame while the current frame is 1 + When the frame number changes to 1 - Once, when the walk animation starts The frame stays at 1 for several game frames; checking while it is 1 would play the sound repeatedly.

title: An animator with timed frames
body: Write an animator where every frame has its own duration, and that reports animation events: cpp struct Animation { std::vector<float durations; bool loop; }; // one duration (seconds) per frame class Animator { public: void play(const Animation a); // restarts only if a is a different animation std::vector<int update(float dt); // the frames entered during this update, in order int frame() const; // current frame index, 0-based bool finished() const; // one-shot animation past its last frame's end }; - After play , the current frame is 0, and frame 0 counts as entered by the next update (so an event on frame 0 fires once). - update(dt) adds dt to the time and returns every frame whose start time was passed during this update (including frame 0 right after play ). A looping animation wraps around, so a long dt can enter the same frames again: report each entry in order. - A one-shot animation stays on its last frame. finished becomes true when the time reaches the total of all durations; no more frames are entered after that. Example: durations { 0.1, 0.2, 0.1 } looping, so the frames start at 0, 0.1 and 0.3, and the loop comes back to frame 0 at 0.4. update(0.05) → {0} ; update(0.1) → {1} (time 0.15); update(0.2) → {2} (time 0.35); update(0.1) → {0} (time 0.45).

title: 2.03  Text, Fonts and a Simple Interface
match: 2.03 Text, Fonts and a Simple Interface
body: Drawing text with raylib's default font and with your own fonts, measuring and aligning it, formatting numbers with TextFormat, and building the interface a small game needs - a score display, health bar, buttons and a menu you can use with keys or the mouse. Drawing text cpp-norun DrawText("Score", 20, 20, 24, DARKGRAY); // default font, size in pixels DrawText(TextFormat("Score: %05d", score), 20, 50, 24, DARKGRAY); // printf-style formatting TextFormat works like printf and returns a const char to a buffer inside raylib. The buffer is reused (raylib keeps a few), so use the result straight away; do not store the pointer. Your own fonts The default font is small pixel art. For anything else, load a TrueType font at the size you will draw it: cpp-norun Font title = LoadFontEx("assets/Kenney Future.ttf", 64, nullptr, 0); // 64 px glyphs, default characters SetTextureFilter(title.texture, TEXTURE_FILTER_BILINEAR); DrawTextEx(title, "XENON QUEST", { 200, 80 }, 64, 2, WHITE); // size and letter spacing // ... UnloadFont(title); A font is a texture of glyphs (an atlas ) plus their positions. Drawing at a very different size from the loaded size looks blurry when bigger and grainy when smaller, so load each size you use a lot. For characters beyond basic Latin (accents, other alphabets), pass the list of code points you need. Measuring and aligning MeasureText(text, size) (default font) and MeasureTextEx(font, text, size, spacing) give the size of a text in pixels. With them you can align anything: Alignment x --- --- Left x Centre x - width / 2 Right x - width Score displays are usually right-aligned, so the digits do not shift left and right when the number gets longer. A health bar cpp-norun void healthBar(Rectangle r, float hp, float maxHp) { const float t = std::clamp(hp / maxHp, 0.0f, 1.0f); DrawRectangleRec(r, DARKGRAY); DrawRectangleRec({ r.x, r.y, r.width t, r.height }, t 0.3f ? LIME : RED); DrawRectangleLinesEx(r, 2, BLACK); } A nice touch is a second, slower bar behind it that catches up with the real value, so the player sees how much damage was just taken. Buttons and menus An interface for a small game needs only buttons: cpp-norun bool button(Rectangle r, const char label) { const bool hover = CheckCollisionPointRec(GetMousePosition(), r); DrawRectangleRec(r, hover ? SKYBLUE : LIGHTGRAY); const int w = MeasureText(label, 20); DrawText(label, static_cast<int (r.x + (r.width - w) / 2), static_cast<int (r.y + (r.height - 20) / 2), 20, BLACK); return hover && IsMouseButtonReleased(MOUSE_BUTTON_LEFT); } This is an immediate-mode button, like the Dear ImGui course's: it is drawn and checked in the same call. For a menu that works with keys and gamepads as well, keep a selected index , move it with up and down (wrapping around), and activate with Enter; hovering the mouse over an item also selects it. raylib also comes with raygui , a single-header immediate-mode GUI library in the same style, with sliders, checkboxes and text boxes, when a game needs more than buttons. Interface coordinates The interface is drawn after the world and outside any camera (lesson 4.01), in screen coordinates, so it stays put while the world scrolls. Anchor it to the screen's edges or centre rather than fixed positions so it still fits when the window is resized. Check yourself quiz ? Why should you not keep the pointer TextFormat returns? - It must be freed with UnloadText after use - It points to the font's texture, which can move + It points to a buffer inside raylib that later calls reuse raylib keeps only a few buffers, so a stored pointer soon holds some other text. Use the result straight away, or copy it into a std::string . ? How do you right-align a score at x = 780? + Measure the text and draw it at 780 - width - Draw it at 780 - width / 2 - Draw it at 780 and pass a negative font size - Draw it at 780 + width x - width / 2 would centre it on 780. Right-aligned digits do not shift when the number gets longer. ? Why is the interface drawn outside the camera? - Because text cannot be drawn inside a camera - So it is drawn before the world and covered by it + So it stays fixed on the screen while the world moves under it The interface is drawn after the world, in screen coordinates; inside the camera it would scroll away with the world. ? Why load a font with LoadFontEx at the size you will draw it? - Because DrawTextEx can only draw at the loaded size + Because the glyphs are stored as pictures at that one size - Because loading at a bigger size uses less video memory A font is an atlas of glyph pictures: drawing much bigger looks blurry and much smaller looks grainy, so load each size you use a lot.

title: Menus and wrapped text
where: 2.03 Text, Fonts and a Simple Interface
body: Two interface pieces: cpp std::vector<std::string wrapText(const std::string& text, int maxWidth, int charWidth); class Menu { public: void add(const std::string& label, bool enabled = true); void move(int delta); // -1 up, +1 down: next enabled item, wrapping around void hover(int index); // the mouse is over an item: select it if enabled int selected() const; // -1 if no item is enabled std::string line(int index) const; // " Label" when selected, " Label" otherwise, " (Label)" when disabled }; wrapText splits on spaces into lines no wider than maxWidth pixels, each character being charWidth wide (a fixed-width font). Words are kept whole and separated by one space; a word wider than a line on its own is put on its own line anyway. Several spaces in a row count as one, and an empty text gives no lines. Menu : the first enabled item added becomes selected. move skips disabled items and wraps from the last to the first and back; if no item is enabled it does nothing.

title: 2.04  Sound and Music
body: Playing sound effects and streaming music with raylib's audio module - the audio device, Sound versus Music, volume and pitch, playing the same sound many times at once, a little random variation, and volume settings in decibels and percentages. The audio device Audio has its own start and end, like the window: cpp-norun InitWindow(800, 450, "Sound"); InitAudioDevice(); // load sounds and music, run the game ... CloseAudioDevice(); CloseWindow(); Sound and Music Type Loaded Use --- --- --- Sound Completely into memory Short effects: jumps, hits, coins. Starts instantly Music Streamed from the file in small pieces Long tracks and ambience. Little memory cpp-norun Sound jump = LoadSound("assets/jump.wav"); Music theme = LoadMusicStream("assets/theme.ogg"); PlayMusicStream(theme); while (!WindowShouldClose()) { UpdateMusicStream(theme); // every frame, or the music stutters and stops if (IsKeyPressed(KEY_SPACE)) PlaySound(jump); // ... } UnloadSound(jump); UnloadMusicStream(theme); UpdateMusicStream refills the stream's buffer. Forget it and the music plays a fraction of a second and stops: the most common audio bug in raylib games. WAV and OGG are the usual formats; OGG is much smaller for music. Volume and pitch SetSoundVolume(s, 0.5f) , SetSoundPitch(s, 1.2f) and SetMusicVolume(m, v) change one sound; SetMasterVolume(v) changes everything. Pitch 2.0 is an octave up and plays twice as fast. Variation : hearing exactly the same footstep fifty times sounds mechanical. Vary the pitch a little each time: cpp-norun SetSoundPitch(step, 0.9f + GetRandomValue(0, 20) / 100.0f); // 0.9 .. 1.1 PlaySound(step); The same sound many times PlaySound on a Sound that is already playing restarts it. For rapid gunfire or many coins collected at once, that cuts each sound off. Make a few aliases that share the same sample data and play them in turn: cpp-norun Sound coin = LoadSound("assets/coin.wav"); Sound coinVoices 4 ; for (Sound& v : coinVoices) v = LoadSoundAlias(coin); int next = 0; // to play: PlaySound(coinVoices next ); next = (next + 1) % 4; // at the end: UnloadSoundAlias for each, then UnloadSound(coin) Volume settings players understand Loudness is heard roughly logarithmically: halving the amplitude ( 0.5 ) sounds only a little quieter, about -6 decibels. A volume slider that maps 0-100 % straight to amplitude feels like it does nothing for most of its range and then drops suddenly at the bottom. A better mapping is through decibels, for example 0 % = silent and 1-100 % spread over -40 dB to 0 dB: cpp-norun float sliderToAmplitude(int percent) { if (percent <= 0) return 0.0f; const float db = -40.0f (1.0f - percent / 100.0f); return std::pow(10.0f, db / 20.0f); } Keep separate music and effects volumes (and multiply each by a master volume) so players can turn the music down without losing the effects. Sound and gameplay Sound is feedback. Each important event deserves one: jumping, landing, hitting, being hit, collecting, a menu choice, a level complete. Playing them from the place in the code where the event happens, not from the drawing code, keeps them in time with the game even when frames are dropped. Check yourself quiz ? When do you use Sound and when Music ? - Sound for WAV files and Music for OGG files, whatever their length - Music for short effects because it starts faster, Sound for long tracks + Sound for short effects loaded fully into memory; Music for long tracks streamed from the file Both types read WAV and OGG; the difference is how they are loaded. A fully loaded Sound starts instantly, while streamed Music uses little memory. ? What happens if you forget to call UpdateMusicStream every frame? - The music plays at the wrong pitch + The stream's buffer is not refilled, so the music stops almost straight away - The music loops forever and cannot be stopped - Nothing; PlayMusicStream keeps it going by itself UpdateMusicStream refills the buffer from the file. Without it you hear a fraction of a second, the most common raylib audio bug. ? Why use sound aliases made with LoadSoundAlias ? - To load the same file faster from a second path - To play a sound at a different pitch without changing the original - To stream a sound from the file instead of keeping it in memory + Because playing a Sound that is already playing restarts it; aliases let several copies play at once Aliases share the sample data, so a few of them played in turn let rapid coins or gunshots overlap instead of cutting each other off. ? Why map a volume slider through decibels instead of straight to amplitude? - Because raylib's volume functions only accept decibels + Because loudness is heard roughly logarithmically - Because amplitudes above 0.5 damage the speakers A straight mapping seems to do nothing for most of its range: halving the amplitude is only about -6 dB. Spreading the slider over -40 to 0 dB makes each step sound like a similar change.

title: Volumes and voices
body: The sound settings and a pool of voices: cpp float sliderToAmplitude(int percent); // 0 - 0; 1..100 - -40 dB .. 0 dB float effectiveVolume(int master, int channel); // both sliders, multiplied as amplitudes class VoicePool { public: explicit VoicePool(int voices); int play(float now, float length); // returns the voice used int playing(float now) const; // how many voices are still sounding at time now }; - sliderToAmplitude : percent is clamped to 0..100 . 0 is silence; otherwise db = -40 (1 - percent / 100) and the amplitude is 10^(db / 20) . - effectiveVolume is sliderToAmplitude(master) sliderToAmplitude(channel) . - VoicePool::play : a voice is free at time now if it never played or its sound ended ( start + length <= now ). Use the lowest-numbered free voice; if none is free, steal the one that started earliest (lowest number on a tie). The voice records now and length .

title: 2.05  Screens and Game States
body: A finished game has a title screen, the game itself, a pause menu, a game-over screen and transitions between them. This lesson organises a game into screens - first with an enum and a switch, then with screen objects on a stack - and fades smoothly from one to the next. One loop, many screens A whole game runs in the same loop, but what the loop does depends on which screen is showing: cpp-norun enum class Screen { Title, Playing, Paused, GameOver }; Screen screen = Screen::Title; while (!WindowShouldClose()) { switch (screen) { case Screen::Title: if (IsKeyPressed(KEY_ENTER)) { resetGame(); screen = Screen::Playing; } break; case Screen::Playing: updateGame(); if (IsKeyPressed(KEY_P)) screen = Screen::Paused; if (lives == 0) screen = Screen::GameOver; break; case Screen::Paused: if (IsKeyPressed(KEY_P)) screen = Screen::Playing; break; case Screen::GameOver: if (IsKeyPressed(KEY_ENTER)) screen = Screen::Title; break; } BeginDrawing(); ClearBackground(BLACK); switch (screen) { / draw each screen / } EndDrawing(); } This is a state machine : a set of states, one current state, and transitions triggered by events. For a small game an enum and two switches is perfectly fine. Screens as objects As screens grow, each switch case becomes a hundred lines. Give each screen its own class: cpp-norun class Scene { public: virtual ~Scene() = default; virtual void update(float dt) = 0; virtual void draw() const = 0; virtual bool coversBelow() const { return true; } // a pause menu does not }; A stack of screens The pause menu shows the game behind it, frozen. A stack of scenes handles that naturally: - push : put a scene on top (open the pause menu). - pop : remove the top (close it, back to the game). - replace : swap the top for another (title to game). Only the top scene is updated. Drawing starts from the highest scene that covers what is below it and goes up to the top, so the frozen game is drawn first and the menu over it. cpp-norun void drawStack(const std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Scene & stack) { std::size_t first = stack.size() - 1; while (first 0 && !stack first - coversBelow()) --first; for (std::size_t i = first; i < stack.size(); ++i) stack i - draw(); } Changing the stack while a scene's update is running (the pause scene pops itself) would destroy the object whose function is running. Instead, scenes request changes, and the stack applies them after the update has finished; the practice builds exactly this. Transitions Cutting straight from one screen to the next is abrupt. A fade is simple: draw a black rectangle over everything with an alpha that rises from 0 to 255, switch the screen when it is fully black, and let it fall back to 0: cpp-norun // fade goes 0 - 1 over 0.3 s, then the screen changes, then 1 - 0 over 0.3 s DrawRectangle(0, 0, GetScreenWidth(), GetScreenHeight(), Fade(BLACK, fade)); While a transition runs, ignore input, or a quick player can press Enter twice and skip two screens. Resetting the game "Play again" must reset everything : score, lives, level, timers, positions, enemies, particles. Keep all of a play-through's state in one struct and reset it by assigning a fresh one: game = Game{}; . Leftover state from the previous round is a very common bug. Check yourself quiz ? What makes a game's set of screens a state machine? - Each screen runs its own separate game loop + There is exactly one current screen, and events switch it - Every screen is a class derived from a Scene base - The screens are stored together in a std::vector States, one current state, and transitions triggered by events. An enum and two switches is already a state machine; classes are just one way to write it. ? Why is a stack of scenes useful for a pause menu? + The game stays below the menu, frozen and still drawn, and popping the menu returns to it exactly as it was - The stack updates every scene at once, so the game keeps running behind the menu - The stack deletes the game while paused and reloads it afterwards Only the top scene is updated, so the game is frozen; the pause menu does not cover what is below, so the game is still drawn behind it. ? Why should scenes request stack changes instead of changing the stack directly? - Because std::vector cannot be changed inside a loop - So the changes happen in the order the scenes were created + Because popping the running scene would destroy it mid-update Popping the scene whose update is running destroys it while its code is still executing. The stack applies the requested push, pop or replace after the update, when no scene's code is running. ? How should "Play again" reset the game? - Reset the score and lives, which are the only values that change + Keep a play-through's state in one struct and assign a fresh one: game = Game{}; - Restart the program Leftover timers, enemies or particles from the last round are a common bug; assigning a new struct resets everything at once.

title: A stack of scenes
body: Write the scene stack from lesson 2.05. Scenes are described by a name and whether they cover what is below them; requests made during an update are applied afterwards: cpp struct Scene { std::string name; bool coversBelow; }; class SceneStack { public: void push(Scene s); // requests: queued, applied by apply() void pop(); void replace(Scene s); // pop the top and push s (on an empty stack: just push) void clear(); // remove every scene void apply(); // carry out the queued requests in order, then forget them std::string top() const; // "" if empty std::vector<std::string drawOrder() const; // bottom to top, starting at the highest covering scene std::size_t size() const; }; - pop on an empty stack does nothing. - drawOrder starts at the highest scene with coversBelow == true (or the bottom scene if none covers) and lists up to the top.
