title: Brick breaker
body: Write the logic of a brick-breaking game: a grid of bricks with hit points, a paddle, a ball that starts on the paddle, lives and score. With it, lesson 2.03's interface, lesson 2.04's sounds and lesson 2.05's screens make a complete game. cpp struct Vector2 { float x, y; }; struct Rectangle { float x, y, width, height; }; struct Brick { Rectangle r; int hp; }; struct Game { std::vector<Brick bricks; Rectangle paddle{ 350, 420, 100, 12 }; Vector2 ball{ 400, 414 }, vel{ 0, 0 }; float radius{ 6 }; bool stuck{ true }; // the ball sits on the paddle until launched int lives{ 3 }, score{ 0 }; bool gameOver{ false }; }; Game makeGame(const std::vector<std::string & rows); void launch(Game& g); void update(Game& g, float paddleDir, float dt); // paddleDir: -1 left, 0, 1 right int bricksLeft(const Game& g); makeGame : each character of each row is a brick slot: . is empty, 1 to 9 is a brick with that many hit points. Bricks are 60 × 20 with no gaps; the slot in row r , column c is at x = 40 + 60c , y = 40 + 20r . Only real bricks are stored, in row order then column order. launch : if the ball is stuck, it leaves the paddle with velocity (0, -360) . update , in this order: 1. Nothing happens once the game is over. 2. The paddle moves at 480 px/s and stays inside the 800-pixel-wide field. 3. A stuck ball sits on the paddle, centred: (paddle.x + width/2, paddle.y - radius) . Nothing else happens. 4. The ball moves; it bounces off the left, right and top walls (put it back at radius from the wall and make the velocity point away from it). 5. Paddle : if the ball moves down and overlaps the paddle (circle against rectangle), it is aimed like lesson 1's paddles but upwards: offset = (ball.x - paddle centre x) / (width/2) clamped to -1..1 , angle = offset 60° , vel = (speed·sin, -speed·cos) keeping the speed, and ball.y = paddle.y - radius . 6. Bricks : the first brick (in stored order) with hit points left that overlaps the ball is hit, and only that one. It loses a hit point: destroyed bricks score 10, others 1. The ball bounces off the side of the brick with the smaller overlap: with ox and oy the overlaps of the ball's bounding square and the brick on each axis, if ox < oy it bounces horizontally ( vel.x points away from the brick's centre and the ball moves ox away), otherwise vertically (the same with y and oy ). 7. Lost ball : when ball.y - radius 450 , a life is lost. With lives left, the ball is stuck on the paddle again (placed as in step 3); at zero lives the game is over. bricksLeft counts bricks with hit points left.

title: 3.01  Detecting Collisions
body: The collision tests 2D games are built on - point in rectangle, rectangle against rectangle, circle against circle and circle against rectangle - how each one works, raylib's functions for them, and choosing the right shape for each object. Shapes stand in for sprites Testing every pixel of two sprites against each other is slow and rarely what you want. Games give each object a simple collision shape , usually a little smaller than its picture so near misses feel fair: Shape Good for --- --- Axis-aligned rectangle ( AABB ) Characters, tiles, platforms, pickups Circle Balls, bullets, round enemies, anything that rotates Point The mouse, a bullet's tip "Axis-aligned" means the rectangle is not rotated: its sides are parallel to x and y. That makes every test a few comparisons. Point in rectangle cpp-norun bool pointInRect(Vector2 p, Rectangle r) { return p.x = r.x && p.x < r.x + r.width && p.y = r.y && p.y < r.y + r.height; } raylib: CheckCollisionPointRec(p, r) . There is also CheckCollisionPointCircle and CheckCollisionPointTriangle . Rectangle against rectangle Two rectangles overlap unless one is completely to the left, right, above or below the other: cpp-norun bool rectsOverlap(Rectangle a, Rectangle b) { return a.x < b.x + b.width && b.x < a.x + a.width && a.y < b.y + b.height && b.y < a.y + a.height; } raylib: CheckCollisionRecs(a, b) , and GetCollisionRec(a, b) returns the overlapping rectangle itself, whose width and height lesson 3.02 uses to push objects apart. Use < rather than <= so that rectangles that only touch (one's right edge exactly at the other's left edge) do not count as overlapping. A character standing exactly on top of a floor tile should not be "inside" it. Circle against circle Two circles overlap when the distance between their centres is less than the sum of the radii. Compare squared distances to avoid the square root: cpp-norun bool circlesOverlap(Vector2 a, float ra, Vector2 b, float rb) { const float dx = b.x - a.x, dy = b.y - a.y, r = ra + rb; return dx dx + dy dy < r r; } raylib: CheckCollisionCircles(a, ra, b, rb) . Circle against rectangle Find the point of the rectangle closest to the circle's centre by clamping the centre to the rectangle on each axis; the shapes overlap when that point is inside the circle: cpp-norun bool circleRect(Vector2 c, float r, Rectangle rect) { const float nx = std::clamp(c.x, rect.x, rect.x + rect.width); const float ny = std::clamp(c.y, rect.y, rect.y + rect.height); const float dx = c.x - nx, dy = c.y - ny; return dx dx + dy dy < r r; } If the centre is inside the rectangle, the closest point is the centre itself and the distance is 0. raylib: CheckCollisionCircleRec(c, r, rect) . The two projects so far used this test. Lines and rays CheckCollisionLines(a1, a2, b1, b2, &point) tests two line segments and gives the crossing point: useful for lasers, line of sight, and fast bullets (lesson 3.02). The maths behind it is a pair of cross products, which the practice writes. Who collides with whom Not everything needs to test against everything. Write down the pairs that matter: player with enemies, player with pickups, player's bullets with enemies, enemies' bullets with the player, everything with walls. Many games give each object a layer and a mask (bit flags) and test a pair only if one's mask contains the other's layer. Check yourself quiz ? What is an AABB? - A rectangle that can be rotated to fit its sprite exactly - A box made of the sprite's opaque pixels + An axis-aligned bounding box: a rectangle whose sides are parallel to the x and y axes Because it is never rotated, testing two AABBs takes only a few comparisons. Rotating objects are usually given circles instead. ? Why compare squared distances when testing two circles? + It gives the same answer as comparing distances, without the cost of a square root - Squared distances are more accurate for small circles - Because std::sqrt cannot take negative differences - So circles that only touch count as overlapping Both sides are non-negative, so dx² + dy² < (ra + rb)² holds exactly when the distance is less than the sum of the radii. ? How do you test a circle against a rectangle? - Test the circle's centre with a point-in-rectangle test - Compare the distance between the centres with the circle's radius plus half the rectangle's width - Treat the circle as its bounding square and use a rectangle test + Clamp the circle's centre to the rectangle to find the closest point, and check whether that point is within the radius The bounding-square shortcut wrongly counts hits near the rectangle's corners, and the centre-only test misses a circle that overlaps an edge. ? Why does the rectangle test use < rather than <= ? - Because <= is unreliable when comparing float values + So rectangles that only touch do not count as overlapping - So fast objects cannot pass through each other between frames With <= , a right edge exactly at another's left edge would be an overlap, and a character standing on a floor tile would always be "inside" it.

title: The four collision tests
body: Write the collision tests of lesson 3.01, and the segment test for lasers and fast bullets: cpp struct Vector2 { float x, y; }; struct Rectangle { float x, y, width, height; }; bool pointInRect(Vector2 p, Rectangle r); bool rectsOverlap(Rectangle a, Rectangle b); // touching edges do not count bool circlesOverlap(Vector2 a, float ra, Vector2 b, float rb); // touching does not count bool circleRect(Vector2 c, float r, Rectangle rect); // touching does not count bool segmentsCross(Vector2 a1, Vector2 a2, Vector2 b1, Vector2 b2, Vector2 where); - pointInRect : the left and top edges are inside, the right and bottom edges are not. - segmentsCross : true if the segments a1-a2 and b1-b2 cross at a single point (parallel segments never count); then where is that point (when where is not null). With d = (a2 - a1) × (b2 - b1) (the 2D cross product x1 y2 - y1 x2 ), the crossing is at a1 + t (a2 - a1) where t = ((b1 - a1) × (b2 - b1)) / d and u = ((b1 - a1) × (a2 - a1)) / d , and both t and u must be in 0..1 .

title: 3.02  Resolving Collisions
body: Knowing two things overlap is half the job; the other half is deciding what happens. This lesson pushes objects apart along the shortest way out, moves one axis at a time so characters slide along walls, and stops fast objects from tunnelling through thin walls. Detection and response When the player walks into a wall, the overlap test says "yes". The response decides what happens: stop, slide along it, bounce, take damage. For solid things the response is to separate the objects so they no longer overlap. The shortest way out For two overlapping rectangles, the overlap is itself a rectangle ( GetCollisionRec ). Push the moving object out along the axis where the overlap is smaller : that is the shortest way out, called the minimum translation vector . cpp-norun void pushOut(Rectangle& mover, Rectangle wall) { const Rectangle o = GetCollisionRec(mover, wall); if (o.width == 0 o.height == 0) return; if (o.width < o.height) mover.x += (mover.x < wall.x) ? -o.width : o.width; // out left or right else mover.y += (mover.y < wall.y) ? -o.height : o.height; // out up or down } The brick breaker of milestone 2 used this idea for the ball. It has one weakness: at a corner, when the overlap is nearly square, it can pick the wrong axis, and a character walking along a floor made of tiles can "catch" on the seam between two tiles. One axis at a time The fix used by almost every 2D platformer is to move and resolve each axis separately : cpp-norun // 1. Move horizontally, then resolve horizontally only. player.x += vel.x dt; for (const Rectangle& wall : walls) if (CheckCollisionRecs(player, wall)) { if (vel.x 0) player.x = wall.x - player.width; // hit a wall on the right else if (vel.x < 0) player.x = wall.x + wall.width; vel.x = 0; } // 2. Then vertically. player.y += vel.y dt; onGround = false; for (const Rectangle& wall : walls) if (CheckCollisionRecs(player, wall)) { if (vel.y 0) { player.y = wall.y - player.height; onGround = true; } // landed else if (vel.y < 0) player.y = wall.y + wall.height; // bumped the head vel.y = 0; } Because each step only moved along one axis, the direction of that movement says exactly which side was hit. The player slides along walls naturally: blocked on x, still free on y. And "landed on something" falls out for free as onGround . Tunnelling A bullet moving 1200 pixels a second moves 20 pixels a frame at 60 FPS. A wall 8 pixels thick can be completely between two frames' positions, so the overlap test never sees it: the bullet tunnels through. Fixes, from simplest: 1. Clamp the frame time (lesson 1.04) and keep walls at least as thick as anything moves in a frame. 2. Sub-steps : split a big movement into several small ones, each no longer than the smallest object. 3. Sweep : test the path, not just the end point. For a small bullet, test the segment from the old position to the new one against each wall ( CheckCollisionLines against its edges), and take the nearest hit. For a moving box, the swept AABB test computes the time t between 0 and 1 at which it first touches the other box. Bouncing and sliding With the normal of the surface (the direction it faces, such as (0, -1) for a floor), other responses are one line each: Response Velocity --- --- Stop v = 0 Slide Remove the part along the normal: v -= dot(v, n) n Bounce Reflect: v -= 2 dot(v, n) n , times a bounciness below 1 Check yourself quiz ? Along which axis do you push an overlapping rectangle out? - Always along y, because gravity pulls along y + The one where the overlap is smaller: the shortest way out - The one where the overlap is larger, so it is pushed far enough Pushing out along the smaller overlap moves the object the least distance; this is the minimum translation vector. ? Why move and resolve one axis at a time? - Because CheckCollisionRecs can only test one axis per call - It halves the number of collision tests each frame + Each move's direction then tells you which side was hit - So diagonal moves are blocked whenever a wall is near After a horizontal-only move, a hit must be on the left or right side. Characters then slide along walls, do not catch on tile seams, and get onGround for free when a downward move is blocked. ? What is tunnelling? - An object getting stuck inside a wall after a collision - Two objects pushing each other back and forth every frame - A character catching on the seam between two floor tiles + A fast object skipping past a thin wall between two frames No overlap is ever detected: a bullet moving 20 pixels a frame can skip over an 8-pixel wall. Clamping dt, sub-steps or sweeping the path fixes it. ? With a floor normal n = (0, -1) , which formula makes a ball bounce off the floor? - v -= dot(v, n) n + v -= 2 dot(v, n) n - v += 2 dot(v, n) n Removing the normal part once makes the ball slide; removing it twice reflects it, and adding it pushes the ball faster into the floor. Multiply by a bounciness below 1 so each bounce loses energy.

title: Move and slide
body: Write the axis-separated movement of lesson 3.02, and the bounce and slide responses: cpp struct Vector2 { float x, y; }; struct Rectangle { float x, y, width, height; }; struct Hits { bool left{ false }, right{ false }, ceiling{ false }, ground{ false }; }; Hits moveAndSlide(Rectangle& box, Vector2& vel, float dt, const std::vector<Rectangle & walls); Vector2 slide(Vector2 v, Vector2 normal); // v - dot(v, n) n Vector2 bounce(Vector2 v, Vector2 normal, float bounciness); // (v - 2 dot(v, n) n), then the part along n times bounciness moveAndSlide 1. Move box.x by vel.x dt . For every wall the box now overlaps (touching does not count): moving right, put the box's right side at the wall's left side ( right = true ); moving left, its left side at the wall's right side ( left = true ). Then vel.x = 0 . With several walls, the box ends at the nearest stop. 2. The same for y: moving down sets ground , moving up sets ceiling , then vel.y = 0 . bounce : reflect, then scale only the component along the normal by bounciness , keeping the sliding component as it is. The normal has length 1.

title: 3.03  Gravity, Jumping and Game Feel
body: Jumping that feels good is designed, not simulated. This lesson derives gravity and jump speed from the height and time you want, then adds the tricks platformers rely on - variable jump height, faster falling, coyote time, jump buffering and acceleration on the ground and in the air. Gravity is acceleration Gravity adds to the vertical velocity every frame (y points down, so it is positive): cpp-norun vel.y += gravity dt; vel.y = std::min(vel.y, maxFallSpeed); // terminal velocity: falls stay readable A jump sets the vertical velocity upwards once: vel.y = -jumpSpeed . Design the jump, then compute the numbers Guessing gravity = 1500, jumpSpeed = 600 and tweaking forever is the slow way. Decide what you want instead: how high (in pixels) and how long the rise takes (in seconds). Physics gives the rest: gravity = 2 height / time² jumpSpeed = 2 height / time A jump of 96 pixels (three 32-pixel tiles) rising in 0.4 s needs gravity = 1200 px/s² and jumpSpeed = 480 px/s. Change the height and the jump still takes 0.4 s; change the time and it still reaches 96 pixels. Level designers can then rely on "the player can jump three tiles". Variable jump height Players expect a tap to make a small hop and holding the button to jump high. When the button is released while still rising, cut the upward speed: cpp-norun if (IsKeyReleased(KEY_SPACE) && vel.y < 0) vel.y = 0.5f; Falling faster Real jumps are symmetrical, but they feel floaty. Most platformers use stronger gravity on the way down (1.5 to 2 times), which makes jumps feel snappy and landings decisive: cpp-norun const float g = vel.y 0 ? gravity 1.8f : gravity; Coyote time When a player runs off a ledge and presses jump a moment too late, a strict game says "you are in the air, no jump". It feels unfair, because the player saw themselves on the ledge. Coyote time allows a jump for a short time (about 0.1 s) after leaving the ground: cpp-norun if (onGround) coyote = 0.1f; else coyote -= dt; Jump buffering The opposite case: the player presses jump a moment before landing. Remember the press for a short time and jump as soon as it becomes possible: cpp-norun if (IsKeyPressed(KEY_SPACE)) buffer = 0.1f; else buffer -= dt; if (buffer 0 && coyote 0) { vel.y = -jumpSpeed; buffer = 0; coyote = 0; } Both timers must be cleared when the jump happens, or one press makes two jumps. Running Instant full speed feels stiff; slow acceleration feels like ice. Move the horizontal velocity towards the target speed by a maximum change per second, with different rates for speeding up, slowing down and turning, and less control in the air: cpp-norun float approach(float v, float target, float maxDelta) { if (v < target) return std::min(v + maxDelta, target); return std::max(v - maxDelta, target); } const float target = inputX runSpeed; const float rate = onGround ? (inputX != 0 ? accel : decel) : airAccel; vel.x = approach(vel.x, target, rate dt); Feel is the sum of small things None of these is realistic, and all of them are in nearly every good platformer. Add the small extras too: a puff of dust on landing, a squash of the sprite, a short sound. Lesson 4.03 builds the particles. Check yourself quiz ? How do you get gravity and jump speed from a jump height h and a rise time t? - gravity = h / t², jump speed = h / t + gravity = 2h / t², jump speed = 2h / t - gravity = 2h / t, jump speed = 2h / t² - gravity = h / 2t², jump speed = 2h / t A 96-pixel jump rising in 0.4 s needs gravity 1200 px/s² and jump speed 480 px/s. The factor 2 comes from starting fast and slowing to zero. ? What is coyote time? - The short pause at the top of a jump before falling - Stronger gravity on the way down so jumps feel snappy + A short time after walking off a ledge during which the player can still jump About 0.1 s of grace, because the player saw themselves on the ledge. Remembering a press made just before landing is jump buffering. ? Why clear both the coyote and buffer timers when the jump happens? + Otherwise the same press or the same ledge can trigger a second jump - Otherwise the jump would be twice as high - Because the timers go negative and break the next frame's gravity Either timer still running after the jump could make one press, or one ledge, count again a frame later. ? How is variable jump height usually done? - By measuring how long the button was held before the jump starts - By lowering gravity while the button is held on the ground + By cutting the upward speed (for example halving it) when the button is released while still rising The jump starts at full speed on the press; letting go early cuts it short, so a tap is a small hop.

title: A jump that feels right
body: Write the pieces of lesson 3.03: cpp float gravityFor(float height, float riseTime); // 2h / t² float jumpSpeedFor(float height, float riseTime); // 2h / t float approach(float v, float target, float maxDelta); struct Jumper { float coyote{ 0 }, buffer{ 0 }; }; bool wantsJump(Jumper& j, bool onGround, bool pressed, float dt, float window); float cutJump(float velY, bool released); - approach moves v towards target by at most maxDelta (which is never negative) and never past it. - wantsJump , called once per frame, in this order: 1. coyote becomes window when on the ground, otherwise it goes down by dt ; 2. buffer becomes window when jump was pressed this frame, otherwise it goes down by dt ; 3. if both are above zero, both are set to zero and the function returns true (jump now). - cutJump halves the vertical speed when the button was released while still rising ( velY < 0 ); otherwise returns it unchanged.

title: 3.04  Fixed Time Steps
body: Physics that depends on the frame time behaves slightly differently at every frame rate. A fixed time step runs the simulation in equal steps whatever the frame rate - this lesson builds the accumulator loop, guards against the spiral of death, and interpolates between steps for smooth drawing. Variable steps are not quite the same Multiplying by dt (lesson 1.04) makes speeds right on average, but the results still differ with the frame rate. A jump simulated in steps of 1/30 s reaches a slightly different height from the same jump in steps of 1/144 s, and collision against thin objects depends on how far things move per step. For a puzzle or platformer where a jump must clear exactly three tiles, or for replays and networked games where every computer must compute the same thing, that is not good enough. The accumulator Run the simulation in fixed steps, such as 1/60 s, however long the frame took. Keep the left-over time for the next frame: cpp-norun const float step = 1.0f / 60.0f; float accumulator = 0.0f; while (!WindowShouldClose()) { accumulator += GetFrameTime(); while (accumulator = step) { updatePhysics(step); // always the same dt accumulator -= step; } draw(); } At 144 FPS most frames run zero steps or one; at 30 FPS each frame runs two. The simulation itself always sees exactly 60 steps a second. The spiral of death If one step takes longer to compute than step of real time, each frame adds more time to the accumulator than the steps remove, frames get slower, and the game freezes completely. Limit the number of steps per frame (or clamp the frame time), accepting that the game slows down instead: cpp-norun accumulator += std::min(GetFrameTime(), 0.25f); int steps = 0; while (accumulator = step && steps < 5) { updatePhysics(step); accumulator -= step; ++steps; } Smooth drawing with interpolation With a 60 Hz simulation on a 144 Hz screen, some frames show the same physics state twice and the motion looks slightly jerky. After the loop, accumulator / step is how far (0 to 1) the real time is between the last step and the next one. Keep the previous state and draw between the two: cpp-norun const float alpha = accumulator / step; const Vector2 drawPos = { prev.x + (curr.x - prev.x) alpha, prev.y + (curr.y - prev.y) alpha }; This draws up to one step behind the newest state, which is not noticeable, and every frame shows a slightly different position. Input with fixed steps Read input once per frame, but let the steps use it. One-off presses need care: if a frame runs zero steps, a jump press in that frame must not be lost; if it runs two , it must not jump twice. Store the press in a flag that the first step consumes. Which approach to use Approach Use when --- --- Variable dt , clamped Simple games where small differences do not matter Fixed step Platformers, physics puzzles, anything with replays or networking Fixed step + interpolation The same, on high-refresh screens Check yourself quiz ? What does the accumulator hold after the step loop? - The total real time since the game started - The number of fixed steps run during this frame + Leftover real time not yet simulated, under one step Each frame adds the frame time and every step removes step ; what remains (less than one step) is carried over to the next frame. ? What is the spiral of death, and how do you avoid it? - Interpolated positions drifting further behind each frame; reset alpha to 0 every step + Steps take longer to compute than they simulate, so frames keep slowing; cap the steps - Too small a step makes objects tunnel through walls; use a larger step - A frame that runs zero steps loses input; store presses in a flag Each slow frame owes more steps, which makes the next frame slower still. Limiting the steps per frame (or clamping the frame time) lets the game slow down instead of freezing completely. ? What is alpha in interpolation? - The opacity used to draw the previous state - The fixed step length divided by the frame time - The number of steps left in the accumulator + accumulator / step , how far between the last two steps It runs from 0 to 1. Drawing prev + (curr - prev) alpha gives every frame a slightly different position, so motion is smooth on high-refresh screens. ? A frame runs zero fixed steps, and in it the player pressed jump. What should happen? - The press is ignored, because no step ran + The press is stored in a flag that the next step consumes - The game runs one extra step just for the press Input is read once per frame but used by the steps; a flag consumed by the first step means the press is neither lost in a zero-step frame nor used twice in a two-step frame.

title: The fixed-step loop
body: Write the accumulator of lesson 3.04 as a class, with the spiral-of-death guard and a one-off press that steps consume: cpp struct Vector2 { float x, y; }; class FixedStep { public: FixedStep(float step, int maxSteps); int advance(float frameTime); // how many steps to run this frame float alpha() const; // accumulator / step after advance void press(); // a one-off input this frame bool takePress(); // true once per press, for the first step that asks }; Vector2 lerp(Vector2 a, Vector2 b, float t); - advance clamps the frame time to at most 0.25 s, adds it to the accumulator, and counts steps while the accumulator holds at least one step, subtracting a step each time. When maxSteps is reached, the accumulator is set to 0 (the game slows down rather than freezing). - press sets a flag; takePress returns it and clears it. A press in a frame with no steps is still there for the next frame's first step.

title: 3.05  Spatial Grids for Many Objects
body: Testing every object against every other is n squared - fine for 50 objects, hopeless for 5000. A uniform grid puts each object in the cells it touches and only tests objects that share a cell. This lesson builds one, rebuilds it every frame, and avoids testing pairs twice. Every pair is too many With n objects there are n(n-1)/2 pairs. For 100 objects that is 4950 tests a frame: no problem. For 5000 bullets and enemies it is 12.5 million, many times the frame budget. Most of those pairs are on opposite sides of the screen and could never touch. The idea of broad phase collision is to cheaply find the pairs that might touch, and only run the real test (the narrow phase ) on them. A uniform grid Divide the world into square cells , a bit bigger than a typical object. Each cell keeps a list of the objects that overlap it: cpp-norun struct Grid { float cellSize; int cols, rows; std::vector<std::vector<int cells; // object indices per cell int cellX(float x) const { return std::clamp(static_cast<int (std::floor(x / cellSize)), 0, cols - 1); } int cellY(float y) const { return std::clamp(static_cast<int (std::floor(y / cellSize)), 0, rows - 1); } void insert(int id, Rectangle r) { for (int cy = cellY(r.y); cy <= cellY(r.y + r.height); ++cy) for (int cx = cellX(r.x); cx <= cellX(r.x + r.width); ++cx) cells cy cols + cx .push_back(id); } }; An object overlapping a cell boundary is put in every cell it touches, so neighbours across a boundary still meet in some cell. Using it Each frame: 1. Clear the cells (keep the vectors' memory; just clear() each). 2. Insert every object. 3. For each cell, test each pair of objects in that cell . Two objects that share several cells would be tested several times, once in each. Avoid duplicates by testing a pair only when a < b and recording tested pairs in a set, or, faster, only in the cell that contains the top-left corner of their overlap. For a query ("which enemies are within the explosion?"), look only in the cells the query area covers, and collect each object once. Choosing the cell size - Too small: big objects are in many cells, and inserting costs more than it saves. - Too large: many objects per cell, back towards n squared. - A cell about twice the size of a typical object is a good start. Measure with a profiler and adjust. Other structures Structure Good when --- --- Uniform grid Objects of similar size spread over a bounded world: most 2D games Spatial hash The same, but the world is unbounded: cells are keys in a hash map Quadtree Sizes vary a lot, or objects cluster in a few places Sort and sweep Objects mostly spread along one axis, as in side-scrollers Static and moving things Walls and tiles never move, so do not put them in the per-frame grid: a tile map is already a grid (lesson 4.02), and you can look up the tiles under an object directly from its position. Only moving objects need inserting every frame. Check yourself quiz ? What are the broad phase and the narrow phase? + The broad phase cheaply finds pairs that might collide; the narrow phase runs the exact test on those pairs only - The broad phase tests large objects; the narrow phase tests small ones - The broad phase runs every frame; the narrow phase runs every few frames A grid is a broad phase: it rules out pairs on opposite sides of the world so the real circle or rectangle test runs on few pairs. ? Why is an object inserted into every grid cell it touches? - So it is drawn once in each cell it covers - So it can be looked up by its index faster + So objects across a cell boundary still share a cell If an object were only in the cell of its centre, a neighbour just across the boundary would never meet it and the pair would not be tested. ? How do you avoid testing the same pair twice when two objects share several cells? - Use cells so large that no object is ever in more than one - Insert each object only into the cell of its top-left corner - Test each cell's pairs only on every other frame + Remember tested pairs (a < b), or test each pair in one agreed cell The agreed cell can be the one containing the top-left corner of the pair's overlap. Inserting into one cell only would miss pairs across boundaries. ? Roughly how big should a grid cell be? - Exactly the size of the smallest object + About twice the size of a typical object, then adjusted after measuring - As big as the screen, so every object is in one cell Too small and big objects fill many cells; too large and each cell holds many objects, back towards n squared.

title: A uniform grid
body: Write the broad phase of lesson 3.05: cpp struct Rectangle { float x, y, width, height; }; class SpatialGrid { public: SpatialGrid(float cellSize, int cols, int rows); void clear(); void insert(int id, Rectangle r); std::vector<int query(Rectangle area) const; // ids of objects overlapping area, sorted, each once std::vector<std::pair<int, int overlappingPairs() const; // (a, b) with a < b, sorted, each once int testsMade() const; // narrow-phase tests in the last overlappingPairs }; - An object goes into every cell its rectangle touches. Cell coordinates are floor(x / cellSize) , clamped to the grid; the far edge uses the rectangle's right and bottom ( x + width , y + height ). - query looks only in the cells the area covers, and returns objects whose rectangles really overlap the area (touching does not count). - overlappingPairs tests each pair of objects that share a cell, once only, and keeps those whose rectangles really overlap. testsMade counts how many distinct pairs were tested.

title: Circle meets rectangle
body: Test whether a circle overlaps a rectangle. circle (50, 50) r 10, rect (55, 40, 30, 20) - hit circle (10, 10) r 5, rect (20, 20, 10, 10) - no hit (corner distance 14.14)

title: Jumps that feel good
body: Add coyote time and jump buffering, two small tricks that make jumping feel fair. left the ledge 0.05 s ago, pressed jump - jumps (coyote time 0.1 s) pressed jump 0.08 s before landing - jumps on landing (buffer 0.1 s) held jump: full height; released early: cut speed in half

title: A fixed time step
body: Run physics at exactly 60 steps per second whatever the frame rate, and draw smoothly in between. each from a fresh start: frame dt 0.040 - 2 physics steps, alpha 0.40 frame dt 0.010 - 0 steps, alpha 0.60 frame dt 0.500 - capped at 0.25 - about 15 steps

title: Platformer physics
body: Write the complete movement of a platformer character on a tile map: running with acceleration, a designed jump with variable height, coyote time and buffering, stronger gravity when falling, and axis-separated collision against solid tiles. This is the heart of every platformer; drawing it in raylib is a sprite at box.x, box.y . cpp struct Vector2 { float x, y; }; struct Rectangle { float x, y, width, height; }; struct Level { std::vector<std::string rows; }; // ' ' solid, anything else empty; tiles are 32 x 32 struct Input { float x{ 0 }; bool jumpPressed{ false }, jumpReleased{ false }; }; struct Player { Rectangle box{ 0, 0, 24, 30 }; Vector2 vel{ 0, 0 }; bool onGround{ false }; float coyote{ 0 }, buffer{ 0 }; }; bool solidAt(const Level& level, int tx, int ty); void step(Player& p, const Level& level, const Input& in, float dt); solidAt : inside the map, ' ' is solid. Outside the map, left, right and above are solid (walls the player cannot leave through); below the map is empty, so the player can fall out. step , in this order (the numbers come from lesson 3.03: a 96-pixel jump rising in 0.4 s): 1. Run : move vel.x towards in.x 200 (lesson 3.03's approach ) by rate dt , where rate is 1600 on the ground with input, 2000 on the ground without input, and 900 in the air. 2. Jump : coyote becomes 0.1 on the ground, else goes down by dt ; buffer becomes 0.1 when jump was pressed, else goes down by dt . If both are above zero: vel.y = -480 , both timers become 0, and onGround becomes false. 3. Variable height : if jump was released and vel.y < 0 , halve vel.y . 4. Gravity : add 1200 dt , or 2160 dt while falling ( vel.y 0 ), then limit vel.y to at most 600. 5. Move x and resolve against the solid tiles the box overlaps (touching does not count), stopping at the nearest one as in practice 3.02; vel.x = 0 when blocked. 6. Move y and resolve the same way. onGround is true exactly when this step landed on something. The tiles a box overlaps run from floor(x / 32) to ceil((x + width) / 32) - 1 , and likewise for y.

title: 4.01  Cameras and Scrolling Worlds
body: A world bigger than the screen needs a camera. This lesson uses raylib's Camera2D - target, offset, zoom and rotation - converts between screen and world coordinates, and makes the camera follow the player smoothly with a dead zone, look-ahead, limits at the level's edges and screen shake. World and screen coordinates So far everything was drawn in screen coordinates. A level 5000 pixels wide does not fit, so objects get world coordinates, and a camera decides which part of the world is on screen. cpp-norun Camera2D camera{}; camera.target = player.pos; // the world point the camera looks at camera.offset = { GetScreenWidth() / 2.0f, GetScreenHeight() / 2.0f }; // where that point appears on screen camera.rotation = 0.0f; camera.zoom = 1.0f; BeginDrawing(); ClearBackground(SKYBLUE); BeginMode2D(camera); drawWorld(); // in world coordinates EndMode2D(); drawInterface(); // in screen coordinates, on top EndDrawing(); Everything between BeginMode2D and EndMode2D is transformed: a world point p appears on screen at (p - target) zoom + offset (plus rotation). Putting offset at the screen's centre keeps the target in the middle. Converting The mouse is in screen coordinates; to click on the world, convert: cpp-norun const Vector2 mouseWorld = GetScreenToWorld2D(GetMousePosition(), camera); const Vector2 labelPos = GetWorldToScreen2D(enemy.pos, camera); // e.g. a name above an enemy in the interface Following the player camera.target = player.pos works, but the camera jerks with every small movement. Better cameras: - Smoothing : move the target part of the way towards the player each frame. Like friction in lesson 1.04, make it independent of the frame rate: target += (player - target) (1 - pow(0.001f, dt)) . - Dead zone : the camera does not move while the player stays inside a box around the screen's centre; it moves only enough to keep the player in the box. Small movements no longer shake the view. - Look-ahead : aim a little ahead of the player in the direction they are moving or facing, so they see more of what is coming. - Platformer vertical rule : many platformers only move the camera vertically when the player lands, so jumps do not bounce the view. Staying inside the level The camera should not show the void beyond the level's edges. After moving it, clamp the target so the visible area stays inside the level: cpp-norun const float halfW = GetScreenWidth() / 2.0f / camera.zoom; const float halfH = GetScreenHeight() / 2.0f / camera.zoom; camera.target.x = std::clamp(camera.target.x, halfW, levelWidth - halfW); camera.target.y = std::clamp(camera.target.y, halfH, levelHeight - halfH); If the level is smaller than the screen, centre it instead (the clamp range would be empty). Zoom Zooming around the mouse, as in the ImGui course's level editor, keeps the point under the mouse fixed: convert the mouse to world coordinates, change the zoom, and set offset to the mouse and target to that world point. Screen shake A short shake on a hit or explosion makes it feel powerful. Keep a trauma value between 0 and 1 that events add to and that decays over time; offset the camera by a random amount proportional to trauma² : cpp-norun trauma = std::max(0.0f, trauma - dt 1.5f); const float shake = trauma trauma; camera.offset = { centre.x + shake 12 randomMinus1To1(), centre.y + shake 12 randomMinus1To1() }; Squaring makes small trauma barely visible and large trauma strong. Always provide an option to turn shake off: some players get motion sickness. Parallax Background layers that move slower than the world make a cheap illusion of depth: draw a far layer with a camera whose target is target 0.2 , a nearer one with 0.5 , then the world at 1 . Check yourself quiz ? What do a Camera2D's target and offset mean? - target is where the camera sits on screen; offset is how far it has scrolled in the world - target is the object the camera follows; offset is the distance it lags behind it + target is the world point the camera looks at; offset is where on the screen that point is drawn - target and offset are both world points, and the camera shows the area between them The target is in world coordinates and the offset in screen coordinates: a world point p appears at (p - target) zoom + offset , so an offset at the screen's centre keeps the target in the middle. ? How do you find which world point the mouse is over? + GetScreenToWorld2D(GetMousePosition(), camera) - GetWorldToScreen2D(GetMousePosition(), camera) - Use GetMousePosition() directly, since BeginMode2D also transforms the mouse - Add camera.target to GetMousePosition() The mouse is in screen coordinates, so convert screen to world. GetWorldToScreen2D goes the other way, and simply adding the target ignores the offset and zoom. ? What is a camera dead zone? - An area at the level's edges the camera is not allowed to show - A short delay before the camera starts following the player - The part of the screen covered by the interface, where nothing from the world is drawn + A box around the screen's centre within which the player can move without the camera moving While the player stays inside the box the camera stays still; it moves only enough to keep the player in the box, so small movements do not shake the view.

title: A camera that follows well
body: Write the camera helpers of lesson 4.01 (no rotation): cpp struct Vector2 { float x, y; }; struct Camera2D { Vector2 offset, target; float rotation, zoom; }; Vector2 worldToScreen(Vector2 p, const Camera2D& c); // (p - target) zoom + offset Vector2 screenToWorld(Vector2 p, const Camera2D& c); Vector2 deadZone(Vector2 target, Vector2 player, float halfW, float halfH); Vector2 smoothTowards(Vector2 from, Vector2 to, float keepPerSecond, float dt); Vector2 clampToLevel(Vector2 target, float screenW, float screenH, float zoom, float levelW, float levelH); - deadZone : the player may be up to halfW and halfH away from the target on each axis; if further, the target moves just enough to bring the player back to the edge of that box. - smoothTowards : the remaining distance shrinks to keepPerSecond of itself each second: from + (to - from) (1 - keepPerSecond^dt) . - clampToLevel : the visible area is screenW / zoom by screenH / zoom around the target. Keep it inside 0..levelW and 0..levelH . On an axis where the level is smaller than the visible area, centre on the level instead.

title: 4.02  Tile Maps and Levels
body: Most 2D levels are grids of tiles. This lesson stores a tile map, draws only the visible part from a tile sheet, loads levels from text files, places objects such as the player's start and enemies from the same file, and picks wall tiles automatically from their neighbours. A grid of numbers A tile map is a 2D grid where each cell holds a tile number: 0 for empty, 1 for grass, 2 for stone and so on. A 200 × 30 level is only 6000 small numbers, and collision is a direct lookup (the platformer of milestone 3 used exactly this). cpp-norun struct TileMap { int width, height, tileSize; std::vector<int tiles; // row by row int at(int x, int y) const { return (x < 0 y < 0 x = width y = height) ? 0 : tiles y width + x ; } }; A flat std::vector indexed with y width + x is faster and simpler than a vector of vectors. Drawing from a tile sheet Tile pictures come from one texture, a tile sheet , like a sprite sheet. Tile n is the n -th cell (lesson 2.02's frameRect ). Draw only the tiles the camera can see, as the ImGui level editor did: cpp-norun const Vector2 tl = GetScreenToWorld2D({ 0, 0 }, camera); const Vector2 br = GetScreenToWorld2D({ (float)GetScreenWidth(), (float)GetScreenHeight() }, camera); const int x0 = std::max(0, (int)std::floor(tl.x / map.tileSize)), x1 = std::min(map.width - 1, (int)std::floor(br.x / map.tileSize)); const int y0 = std::max(0, (int)std::floor(tl.y / map.tileSize)), y1 = std::min(map.height - 1, (int)std::floor(br.y / map.tileSize)); for (int y = y0; y <= y1; ++y) for (int x = x0; x <= x1; ++x) if (const int t = map.at(x, y); t != 0) DrawTextureRec(sheet, frameRect(t, sheetColumns, 16, 16), { (float)x 16, (float)y 16 }, WHITE); At high zoom, thin lines can appear between tiles because of rounding. Draw at whole-pixel positions, use point filtering, and give the tile sheet a 1-pixel border around each tile ( extrusion ) if it still happens. Levels from text files A text file is the easiest level format to make and to change: level 1 size 40 12 legend stone, = grass, ~ water, P player, E enemy, C coin ....................................... ..............C.C.C.................... ...P...........====.........E.......... ==========.......................====== ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ Load it line by line: header lines first, then the grid. Letters for objects (P, E, C) are not tiles: when loading, record their positions in lists (player start, enemy spawns, coins) and put an empty tile in the map. One file then describes both the terrain and what is in it. For bigger projects, the free Tiled editor saves maps as JSON or XML with layers and object lists; the loader is longer but the idea is the same. Several layers Real levels have layers: a background layer drawn behind the player, the solid layer for collision, a decoration layer in front. Each is its own grid of the same size. Only the solid layer is used for collision. Auto-tiling Choosing the right edge and corner pieces for every wall by hand is tedious. Auto-tiling chooses them: for each solid cell, look at its four neighbours and build a 4-bit number, one bit per side: bit 0: solid above bit 1: solid right bit 2: solid below bit 3: solid left The number (0 to 15) picks one of 16 tile pictures: 0 is a lone block, 15 is a solid interior, 5 (above and below) is a vertical column piece, and so on. Paint just "solid" in the level file and the loader draws proper edges. Using all eight neighbours (for inner corners) gives 47 or 256 variations with the same idea. Check yourself quiz ? Why store a tile map as one flat vector? - A vector of vectors cannot hold a grid whose rows have the same length + It is a single block of memory indexed with y width + x , which is fast and simple - A flat vector uses less memory per tile because it stores no positions - It lets the map grow one tile at a time with push_back while the game runs One contiguous block with one index formula is faster and simpler than a vector of vectors, where each row is a separate allocation. ? What happens to object letters such as P or E when loading a level? - They are stored in the tile map as special tile numbers and drawn from the tile sheet - They are skipped, and the objects are placed later from a separate file + Their positions are recorded in object lists, and the map gets an empty tile there - They become solid tiles, so the player and enemies stand on them Objects are not tiles: the loader records the player start, enemy spawns and coins in lists and leaves an empty tile in the grid. ? How does 4-neighbour auto-tiling choose a tile? - It picks the tile whose picture best matches the colours of the neighbouring tiles - It counts how many of the four neighbours are solid and uses that count (0 to 4) as the tile - It looks the cell's position up in a table drawn by hand for each level + It builds a 4-bit number from which neighbours are solid and uses it to pick one of 16 pictures One bit per side (above, right, below, left) gives 0 to 15. A plain count would mix up different shapes, such as a column (above and below) and a corner (above and right).

title: Loading a level file
body: Load lesson 4.02's text level format and auto-tile it: cpp struct Point { int x, y; }; struct LevelData { int width{ 0 }, height{ 0 }; std::vector<std::string grid; // only ' ', '=' and '.' are left in it Point player{ -1, -1 }; std::vector<Point enemies, coins; }; bool loadLevel(const std::string& text, LevelData& out, std::string& error); int wallMask(const LevelData& level, int x, int y); // 4-bit auto-tile number, -1 for a non-wall The format , one item per line ( \r\n endings allowed): - Lines starting with followed by a space, and empty lines, are comments, but only before the grid. - size W H (both 1 to 500) must come before the grid. Other header lines (such as legend ... ) are ignored. - Then exactly H lines of exactly W characters. and = are walls, . is empty, P is the player start (exactly one), E an enemy and C a coin; those letters become . in the grid. Any other character is an error. Errors return false with one of these messages: "missing size" , "bad size" , "wrong row count" , "row N has the wrong length" (N counting from 1), "unknown tile 'X' in row N" , "no player start" , "more than one player start" . wallMask : for a wall cell, bit 0 is set if the cell above is a wall, bit 1 right, bit 2 below, bit 3 left. Cells outside the map are not walls.

title: 4.03  Particles and Effects
body: Dust, sparks, smoke and explosions are particles - many small, short-lived objects. This lesson builds a particle system with a fixed pool, emitters with randomised properties, values that change over a particle's life, and additive blending, plus the small effects that make a game feel alive. What a particle is A particle is a tiny object with a position, a velocity, a lifetime and a look. Hundreds of them, each living a second or less, make dust when landing, sparks when hitting, smoke from a chimney or an explosion. cpp-norun struct Particle { Vector2 pos, vel; float life, maxLife; // seconds left, and at birth float size; Color color; }; Each frame, every living particle moves (often with gravity or drag), its life goes down by dt , and it is drawn. When life reaches 0 it is dead. A pool, not new and delete Creating and destroying hundreds of objects per second with new , or push_back and erase on a vector, wastes time. Use a fixed pool : - A std::vector<Particle with a fixed capacity, such as 2000. - An integer count of living particles, all at the front. - Spawning writes into slot count and increments it (if the pool is full, either skip or overwrite the oldest). - Killing particle i copies the last living particle into slot i and decrements count ("swap and pop"); order does not matter for particles. No memory is allocated after start-up, and updating walks one tight array. Emitters An emitter creates particles with randomised properties: cpp-norun void burst(Pool& pool, Vector2 at, int n) { for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) { const float angle = GetRandomValue(0, 359) DEG2RAD; const float speed = GetRandomValue(60, 180); pool.spawn({ at, { std::cos(angle) speed, std::sin(angle) speed }, 0.6f, 0.6f, 4.0f, ORANGE }); } } A burst emits many at once (explosion, landing dust). A continuous emitter emits a rate per second, carrying the fraction over to the next frame like the shooter in lesson 1.04, so 30 particles per second is exactly 30 at any frame rate. Changing over a lifetime Particles look much better when their properties change as they age. With t = 1 - life / maxLife going from 0 at birth to 1 at death: Property Typical change --- --- Size Grows (smoke) or shrinks (sparks): lerp(startSize, endSize, t) Colour Yellow to red to grey: interpolate between colour stops Alpha Fades out near the end: alpha = 1 - t , or 1 - t² to stay solid longer Speed Slows with drag Blending Draw fire, sparks, magic and lights with additive blending: colours add up, so overlapping particles glow brighter instead of covering each other: cpp-norun BeginBlendMode(BLEND_ADDITIVE); for (const Particle& p : pool.alive()) DrawCircleV(p.pos, p.size, p.color); EndBlendMode(); Smoke and dust use normal (alpha) blending, which darkens and covers. Small effects with a big impact - Hit flash : draw the sprite white for 0.05 s when hit (tint, lesson 2.01). - Hit stop : freeze the game for 2 or 3 frames on a heavy hit. - Squash and stretch : scale the sprite a little on jumping and landing. - Screen shake (lesson 4.01). - Floating numbers : damage values that rise and fade, which are particles with text. These are often called juice : none of them change the rules, all of them change how the game feels. Check yourself quiz ? Why use a fixed pool for particles? - So that particles can be drawn in a single draw call + It avoids allocating and freeing memory for hundreds of short-lived objects every second - So that particles are always updated in the order they were created - Because raylib can only draw a fixed number of circles per frame With a fixed capacity and a living count, nothing is allocated after start-up and the update walks one tight array, instead of new / delete or push_back / erase hundreds of times a second. ? How does "swap and pop" remove particle i ? - Erase element i with erase , which moves every later particle down one slot - Set particle i 's life to 0 and leave it in place until the pool is full - Swap particle i with the first particle and increase the living count + Copy the last living particle into slot i and reduce the living count by one The living particles stay packed at the front without shifting the rest. It changes their order, which does not matter for particles. ? When do you use additive blending? - For smoke and dust, so they darken and cover what is behind them - For every particle, because it is faster than normal blending + For things that emit light, such as fire, sparks and magic, so overlaps glow brighter - For particles that should be drawn behind the world Additive blending adds colours, so overlapping sparks get brighter. Smoke and dust use normal alpha blending, which covers and darkens instead.

title: A particle pool
body: Write lesson 4.03's particle pool and a continuous emitter: cpp struct Vector2 { float x, y; }; struct Particle { Vector2 pos, vel; float life, maxLife; }; class ParticlePool { public: explicit ParticlePool(int capacity); bool spawn(const Particle& p); // false when full void update(float dt, Vector2 gravity); // move, age, remove the dead int count() const; const Particle& at(int i) const; // 0 .. count() - 1 }; float fadeAlpha(const Particle& p); // 1 at birth, 0 at death: 1 - t² with t = 1 - life / maxLife class Emitter { public: explicit Emitter(float perSecond); int emit(float dt); // how many to spawn this frame }; - update , for each living particle: vel += gravity dt , pos += vel dt , life -= dt ; particles whose life is now <= 0 are removed with swap and pop (the last living particle moves into the removed one's slot, so check that slot again). - fadeAlpha is clamped to 0..1 . - Emitter::emit adds perSecond dt to a running total and returns the whole part of it, keeping the fraction for later frames.

title: 4.04  Enemies and State Machines
body: Enemies that patrol, notice the player, chase, attack and give up feel smart, but are a handful of states and the rules for moving between them. This lesson builds enemy behaviour as a finite state machine with enter and exit actions, timers, line of sight, and a little randomness. States Describe an enemy's behaviour as states , each with its own simple behaviour: State Does Leaves when --- --- --- Patrol Walks between two points Sees the player → Chase Chase Runs towards the player Close enough → Attack; lost sight for 3 s → Return Attack Plays the attack, damages on one frame Animation finished → Chase Return Walks back to the patrol route Arrived → Patrol; sees the player → Chase Hurt Knocked back, briefly helpless 0.3 s passed → Chase Each state is easy to write and test on its own, and the diagram is something a designer can read and change. In code cpp-norun enum class State { Patrol, Chase, Attack, Return, Hurt }; struct Enemy { State state{ State::Patrol }; float timer{ 0 }; Vector2 pos; / ... / }; void enter(Enemy& e, State s) { e.state = s; e.timer = 0; // time spent in the new state if (s == State::Attack) e.anim.play(attackAnim); // enter actions } void update(Enemy& e, const World& w, float dt) { e.timer += dt; switch (e.state) { case State::Patrol: walkTowards(e, e.patrolPoints e.nextPoint , dt); if (canSee(e, w.player)) enter(e, State::Chase); break; case State::Chase: walkTowards(e, w.player.pos, dt); if (distance(e.pos, w.player.pos) < 24) enter(e, State::Attack); else if (canSee(e, w.player)) e.lastSeen = e.timer; else if (e.timer - e.lastSeen 3) enter(e, State::Return); break; // ... } } Going through enter for every change is what makes this robust: there is exactly one place where a state starts, so its timer is always reset and its animation always started. Changes from outside (the player hits the enemy) also go through enter(e, State::Hurt) . Seeing the player "Sees the player" is usually three tests, cheapest first: 1. Distance : within the sight range? 2. Angle : within the field of view in front of the enemy? With the facing direction f and the direction to the player d (both normalised), dot(f, d) cos(halfAngle) . 3. Line of sight : no wall in between? Walk along the line through the tile map, or test the segment against walls (practice 3.01). Making it feel alive - Reaction time : wait 0.3 s after spotting the player before chasing, and show a "!" above the enemy. It is fairer and more readable. - Telegraphing : an attack has a wind-up the player can see and react to. - Variety : give each enemy slightly different speeds and timers, randomised at spawn, so a group does not move in lockstep. Beyond state machines When state machines grow to dozens of states, games move to hierarchical state machines (states inside states), behaviour trees or utility AI (score every possible action and pick the best). For most small games, a state machine like this one is all you need. Check yourself quiz ? Why should every state change go through one enter function? + So the timer is always reset and the state's start actions always run, from wherever the change comes - Because a switch statement cannot assign to the state variable directly - So the enemy can be in two states at once while the change happens - So the state changes at most once per second, which keeps enemies from flickering between states One place where a state starts means its timer is always reset and its enter actions (such as starting the attack animation) always run, even for changes from outside like being hit. ? How do you test whether the player is in an enemy's field of view? - Check that the distance to the player is less than the view angle - Check that the player's x is greater than the enemy's x when it faces right + Compare the dot product of the facing direction and the direction to the player with the cosine of half the view angle - Compare the dot product of the facing direction and the direction to the player with half the view angle in degrees With both directions normalised, dot(f, d) is the cosine of the angle between them, so the player is in view when dot(f, d) cos(halfAngle) . Comparing it with the angle itself mixes a cosine with an angle. ? What is telegraphing? - Sending the enemy's state to other enemies so they join the chase - Drawing the enemy's state name above it while debugging - Waiting a moment after spotting the player before chasing + Showing an attack is coming, such as a wind-up animation, so the player has time to react A visible wind-up makes attacks fair and readable. The pause after spotting the player is the reaction time, a related but different idea.

title: An enemy brain
body: Write the state machine of lesson 4.04 and the field-of-view test: cpp struct Vector2 { float x, y; }; bool inView(Vector2 pos, Vector2 facing, Vector2 target, float range, float halfAngleDegrees); enum class State { Patrol, Alert, Chase, Attack, Return, Hurt }; struct Senses { bool seesPlayer; float distance; bool attackFinished; bool atPatrolRoute; bool wasHit; }; struct Brain { State state{ State::Patrol }; float timer{ 0 }; float unseen{ 0 }; }; void think(Brain& b, const Senses& s, float dt); std::string name(State s); // "Patrol", "Alert", ... inView : the target is within range (inclusive) and within halfAngleDegrees of the facing direction ( facing has length 1). A target exactly at pos is in view. think : first timer += dt . A hit ( wasHit ) always enters Hurt , from any state, even Hurt itself. Otherwise, by state: State Changes to --- --- Patrol Alert if it sees the player Alert Chase once timer = 0.3 (the reaction time) Chase Attack if distance < 24 ; otherwise counts unseen up by dt while not seeing the player (back to 0 when seeing them) and goes to Return when unseen = 3 Attack Chase when attackFinished Return Chase if it sees the player; Patrol when atPatrolRoute Hurt Chase once timer = 0.3 Entering a state sets timer and unseen to 0. At most one change happens per call.

title: 4.05  Pathfinding on a Grid
body: Walking straight at the player gets enemies stuck on walls. This lesson finds paths around obstacles on a tile map - breadth-first search for equal costs, A with a heuristic for speed, costs for different terrain, and flow fields when many enemies chase one target. The problem An enemy in a maze cannot just walk towards the player: the straight line goes through walls. It needs a path : a list of tiles from where it is to where it wants to be, around the obstacles. A tile map is already a graph : each walkable tile is a node, connected to its walkable neighbours (4 directions, or 8 with diagonals). Breadth-first search BFS explores tiles in order of distance from the start, like a ripple spreading in water: cpp-norun std::vector<int came(map.width map.height, -1); // where each tile was reached from std::queue<int frontier; frontier.push(start); came start = start; while (!frontier.empty()) { const int cur = frontier.front(); frontier.pop(); if (cur == goal) break; for (int next : neighbours(cur)) if (came next == -1 && walkable(next)) { came next = cur; frontier.push(next); } } // walk back from goal to start through came , then reverse When every step costs the same, the first time BFS reaches the goal it has found a shortest path. The came array records how each tile was reached; following it backwards from the goal gives the path. A BFS explores in all directions, even away from the goal. A\ explores the most promising tiles first. For each tile it knows: - g : the cost of the best path found so far from the start; - h : a heuristic , an estimate of the cost from the tile to the goal; - f = g + h : the estimated cost of a path through this tile. A always expands the tile with the smallest f next, using a priority queue ( std::priority_queue with a comparison on f ). With 4-direction movement, the Manhattan distance dx + dy is the standard heuristic. As long as the heuristic never overestimates the real cost, A still finds a shortest path, usually after exploring far fewer tiles than BFS. Terrain costs Swamp could cost 3 to cross and road 1. Then the cheapest path is not always the shortest, and BFS no longer works: use Dijkstra's algorithm (A with h = 0 ) or A with the costs added to g . The heuristic must use the cheapest possible cost per step so it still never overestimates. Following a path - Recompute the path only every half second or when the target moves to another tile, not every frame. - Move towards the next tile's centre; when close enough, move on to the one after. - Smooth it: skip waypoints when there is a clear line of sight to a later one, so enemies walk diagonally across open rooms instead of zig-zagging along grid lines. Many enemies, one target Fifty enemies chasing the player would run fifty searches. A flow field runs one: a BFS (or Dijkstra) from the player outwards over the whole map, storing each tile's distance. Each enemy then simply steps to its neighbour with the smallest distance. The cost no longer depends on the number of enemies, which is how tower defence and swarm games handle hundreds of units. Check yourself quiz ? Why does BFS find a shortest path when all steps cost the same? - It always moves towards the goal first, so it never takes a detour + It reaches tiles in order of their distance from the start - It tries every possible path and keeps the shortest one - It uses the Manhattan distance to skip tiles that are too far away BFS spreads like a ripple: all tiles at distance 1, then 2, and so on, so the first time it reaches the goal is by a shortest path. It does not aim at the goal at all; that is what A adds. ? What are g, h and f in A ? - g is the goal tile, h is the heuristic, and f is the frontier queue - g is the estimated remaining cost, h is the cost so far, and f = g + h - g is the cost so far, h is the estimated remaining cost, and A expands the smallest h first + g is the cost so far, h is the estimated remaining cost, and f = g + h; A expands the smallest f first A picks the tile with the smallest estimated total f = g + h from a priority queue. Expanding by h alone ignores the cost already paid and can miss the shortest path. ? When is a flow field better than many path searches? + When many units head for the same target: one search from the target serves all of them - When each unit heads for a different target on a small map - When the map has terrain costs, which A cannot handle - When only one enemy needs a path, because it is faster than A One BFS or Dijkstra from the target stores every tile's distance, and each unit steps to its neighbour with the smallest one, so the cost no longer grows with the number of units. A handles terrain costs fine by adding them to g .

title: Paths and flow fields
body: Write lesson 4.05's breadth-first search and a flow field on a map of strings, where is a wall and anything else is walkable: cpp struct Cell { int x, y; }; std::vector<Cell findPath(const std::vector<std::string & map, Cell start, Cell goal); std::vector<std::vector<int flowField(const std::vector<std::string & map, Cell target); Cell nextStep(const std::vector<std::vector<int & field, Cell from); - Movement is in 4 directions, and neighbours are always tried in the order up, right, down, left . Cells outside the map are walls. - findPath returns the cells from start to goal , both included, of a shortest path; with the neighbour order above, BFS gives one particular path, and that is the one expected. It returns an empty vector if there is no path or either end is a wall; start == goal gives just that cell. - flowField gives every cell's number of steps to target (BFS from the target), -1 for walls and unreachable cells. - nextStep returns the neighbour (in the same order) with the smallest non-negative distance that is smaller than the distance at from ; if there is none, from itself.
