title: A dungeon crawler
body: Write the rules of a small turn-based dungeon game: the player walks a tile map, collects coins and reaches the exit, while enemies chase them using a flow field (lesson 4.05) and fight when adjacent. Click-to-travel uses a weighted path through swamp. Drawing it in raylib is a tile map (lesson 4.02) and a few sprites. cpp struct Cell { int x, y; }; struct Enemy { Cell pos; int hp; }; class Dungeon { public: explicit Dungeon(const std::vector<std::string & rows); bool move(int dx, int dy); // the player's turn; false if no turn was taken bool wait(); // pass a turn; false once the game is over std::vector<Cell travelPath(Cell to) const; Cell player() const; int hp() const; int coins() const; int coinsLeft() const; const std::vector<Enemy & enemies() const; bool won() const; bool lost() const; }; The map : wall, . floor, ~ swamp (walkable), P the player's start, E an enemy (2 hit points), C a coin, X the exit; the letters stand on floor. The player has 3 hit points. A player turn ( move ): nothing happens and false is returned if the game is over or the target is a wall. If an enemy is on the target cell, the player attacks it (it loses 1 hit point and disappears at 0) and stays put; otherwise the player moves there and picks up a coin if there is one. If the player is now on the exit with no coins left, the game is won and the enemies do not act. wait is a turn that does nothing on the player's side. The enemies' turn , after every player turn, one enemy at a time in their original order: 1. If it is next to the player (4 directions), it attacks: the player loses 1 hit point. At 0 the game is lost and the remaining enemies do not act. 2. Otherwise, if its walking distance to the player (BFS through everything but walls) is at most 8, it steps to the neighbour with the smallest distance that is smaller than its own, trying up, right, down, left in that order and skipping cells with another enemy. Otherwise it stays. Compute the distances once per enemies' turn, from the player's cell, before any enemy moves. travelPath returns the cheapest path from the player to to , both included, where entering a floor cell costs 1 and entering swamp costs 3 (Dijkstra or A ). Enemies are ignored. A wall or unreachable target gives an empty path. Any cheapest path is accepted.

title: 5.01  A First 3D Scene
body: raylib draws 3D as easily as 2D. This lesson sets up a Camera3D, explains 3D coordinates and perspective, draws cubes, spheres, planes and a grid, loads and draws models, and introduces the vectors and matrices that move things in 3D. Three axes 3D adds a third axis. raylib uses a right-handed, y-up system: Axis Points --- --- x Right y Up (not down, as on the 2D screen) z Towards the viewer Positions are Vector3 { x, y, z } , in whatever unit you choose; most games use 1 unit = 1 metre , which makes gravity 9.81 and a person about 1.8 tall. The camera A 3D camera is defined by where it is, what it looks at and which way is up: cpp-norun Camera3D camera{}; camera.position = { 6.0f, 4.0f, 6.0f }; // where the eye is camera.target = { 0.0f, 0.5f, 0.0f }; // the point it looks at camera.up = { 0.0f, 1.0f, 0.0f }; // which way is up camera.fovy = 45.0f; // vertical field of view, in degrees camera.projection = CAMERA_PERSPECTIVE; // or CAMERA_ORTHOGRAPHIC Perspective makes far things smaller, like a real eye; the field of view is how wide the view is (45-70° is typical). Orthographic keeps sizes constant regardless of distance, which suits strategy and isometric games; then fovy is the height of the view in world units. Drawing cpp-norun BeginDrawing(); ClearBackground(RAYWHITE); BeginMode3D(camera); DrawPlane({ 0, 0, 0 }, { 20, 20 }, LIGHTGRAY); // a floor DrawCube({ 0, 0.5f, 0 }, 1, 1, 1, RED); // centre and size DrawCubeWires({ 0, 0.5f, 0 }, 1, 1, 1, MAROON); DrawSphere({ 2, 1, 0 }, 0.5f, BLUE); DrawCylinder({ -2, 0, 0 }, 0.3f, 0.3f, 1.5f, 16, GREEN); DrawGrid(20, 1.0f); // a helpful reference grid EndMode3D(); DrawFPS(10, 10); // 2D on top, as usual EndDrawing(); Note that 3D shapes are placed by their centre : a 1 × 1 × 1 cube standing on the floor has its centre at y = 0.5. Models Real objects come from 3D files. raylib loads glTF ( .glb / .gltf , the best choice), OBJ, IQM, VOX and M3D: cpp-norun Model tree = LoadModel("assets/tree.glb"); // meshes, materials and textures DrawModel(tree, { 3, 0, -2 }, 1.0f, WHITE); // position, uniform scale, tint DrawModelEx(tree, pos, { 0, 1, 0 }, angleDegrees, { 1, 1, 1 }, WHITE); // rotated around an axis UnloadModel(tree); glTF files can also contain animations : LoadModelAnimations and UpdateModelAnimation play them. Free models in this format are available from sites such as Kenney and Quaternius. Vectors in 3D raymath.h has everything for Vector3 : Vector3Add , Vector3Subtract , Vector3Scale , Vector3Length , Vector3Normalize , Vector3DotProduct and Vector3CrossProduct . - The dot product a · b = a b cos θ measures how much two directions agree: 1 for the same direction (when normalised), 0 for perpendicular, -1 for opposite. It answers "is the enemy in front of me?". - The cross product a × b is a vector perpendicular to both. From a "forward" direction and "up", forward × up gives "right", which is how cameras find their sideways direction. Matrices Objects are placed with a transform : scale, then rotate, then translate. raylib represents it as a 4 × 4 Matrix ( MatrixScale , MatrixRotateY , MatrixTranslate , combined with MatrixMultiply ). DrawModelEx builds it for you; you need matrices yourself for things like a sword attached to a hand, where the child's transform is multiplied by the parent's. Lighting The shapes above are drawn with flat colours, without light. Lighting needs a shader (lesson 5.04); raylib's examples include a basic lighting shader ( shaders_basic_lighting ) that most projects start from. Check yourself quiz ? Which way does y point in raylib's 3D space? - Down, as on the 2D screen + Up - Towards the viewer - Away from the viewer, into the screen raylib's 3D space is right-handed and y-up: x right, y up, z towards the viewer. Only 2D screen coordinates have y pointing down. ? What is the difference between perspective and orthographic projection? - Perspective is for 2D games and orthographic for 3D games - Orthographic makes distant things smaller; perspective keeps sizes the same at every distance + Perspective makes distant things smaller; orthographic keeps sizes the same at every distance - Perspective uses fovy in degrees; orthographic ignores fovy completely Perspective works like a real eye. Orthographic keeps sizes constant, which suits strategy and isometric games, and then fovy is the height of the view in world units rather than being ignored. ? What does the dot product of two normalised directions tell you? - The direction perpendicular to both of them - The distance between the two directions' end points - The angle between them, measured in degrees + The cosine of the angle between them a · b = a b cos θ , so for unit vectors it is cos θ : 1 for the same direction, 0 for perpendicular, -1 for opposite. The perpendicular vector is what the cross product gives.

title: Vectors in three dimensions
body: Write the 3D vector helpers raymath gives you, to see how they work: cpp struct Vector3 { float x, y, z; }; float dot(Vector3 a, Vector3 b); Vector3 cross(Vector3 a, Vector3 b); float length(Vector3 v); Vector3 normalize(Vector3 v); // (0, 0, 0) stays (0, 0, 0) float angleBetween(Vector3 a, Vector3 b); // in degrees, 0 if either is zero Vector3 rotateY(Vector3 v, float degrees); // x' = x cos + z sin, z' = -x sin + z cos Vector3 transformPoint(Vector3 p, float scale, float yawDegrees, Vector3 translate); // scale, then rotate, then move cross(a, b) = (a.y b.z - a.z b.y, a.z b.x - a.x b.z, a.x b.y - a.y b.x) . Clamp the cosine to -1..1 before acos , because rounding can push it slightly outside.

title: 5.02  Moving in 3D
body: Walking around a 3D world - raylib's built-in camera modes, then a first-person controller of your own with yaw and pitch from the mouse, movement relative to where you look, gravity and jumping, and a third-person camera that orbits the player. The built-in camera modes raylib can move a camera for you: cpp-norun DisableCursor(); // hide and lock the mouse while (!WindowShouldClose()) { UpdateCamera(&camera, CAMERA_FIRST_PERSON); // WASD + mouse // ... draw } Modes are CAMERA_FREE , CAMERA_ORBITAL , CAMERA_FIRST_PERSON and CAMERA_THIRD_PERSON . They are fine for trying things out, but a game needs its own controller: collision, gravity, rebindable keys and its own feel. UpdateCameraPro takes movement and rotation you computed yourself. Yaw and pitch A first-person view is described by two angles: - Yaw : turning left and right, around the y axis. The mouse's x movement changes it. - Pitch : looking up and down. The mouse's y movement changes it, clamped to about ±89° so the view never flips over the top. From the angles, the direction you look in: cpp-norun const Vector3 forward{ std::cos(pitch) std::sin(yaw), std::sin(pitch), std::cos(pitch) std::cos(yaw), }; camera.position = eye; camera.target = Vector3Add(eye, forward); Mouse look: yaw -= GetMouseDelta().x sensitivity; pitch -= GetMouseDelta().y sensitivity; . Sensitivity is a setting players expect, along with "invert Y". Moving where you look Walking uses the flat forward direction: the yaw only, so looking at the floor does not make you walk slower or dig into the ground: cpp-norun const Vector3 flatForward{ std::sin(yaw), 0, std::cos(yaw) }; const Vector3 right{ -std::cos(yaw), 0, std::sin(yaw) }; // forward x up, for this yaw Vector3 wish{ 0, 0, 0 }; if (IsKeyDown(KEY_W)) wish = Vector3Add(wish, flatForward); if (IsKeyDown(KEY_S)) wish = Vector3Subtract(wish, flatForward); if (IsKeyDown(KEY_D)) wish = Vector3Add(wish, right); if (IsKeyDown(KEY_A)) wish = Vector3Subtract(wish, right); if (Vector3Length(wish) 0) wish = Vector3Normalize(wish); // lesson 1.04's diagonal fix, in 3D Then the 2D ideas carry over unchanged: acceleration towards wish speed , gravity on y, jumping with coyote time and a buffer, and the eye at about 1.7 units above the feet. Collision with the world The simplest world is boxes (walls, crates, platforms) and the player is a box or a vertical capsule . Resolving one axis at a time (lesson 3.02) works in 3D exactly as in 2D, with three axes instead of two: move on x and push out, then z, then y (landing sets "on ground"). raylib's CheckCollisionBoxes(a, b) tests two BoundingBox es ( min and max corners). A third-person camera A third-person camera orbits the player at a distance, using the same yaw and pitch: cpp-norun const Vector3 offset{ distance std::cos(pitch) std::sin(yaw), distance std::sin(pitch), distance std::cos(pitch) std::cos(yaw), }; camera.target = Vector3Add(player.pos, { 0, 1.5f, 0 }); // look at the shoulders, not the feet camera.position = Vector3Subtract(camera.target, offset); // behind, along the view direction If a wall comes between the camera and the player, cast a ray from the target towards the camera (lesson 5.03) and move the camera in front of the wall, or the player sees the inside of the wall. Smooth the camera's movement (lesson 4.01's smoothTowards works per axis in 3D). Check yourself quiz ? Why is the pitch clamped to about ±89°? - So the mouse cannot move faster than the camera can turn + So the camera never looks straight up or down past the vertical, where the view would flip - Because std::sin only accepts angles between -90° and 90° - So the player cannot turn all the way around to look behind them Past the vertical, the view flips over the top. Turning around is yaw, which is not clamped, and std::sin works for any angle. ? Why walk with the flat forward direction instead of the full look direction? - Because the full look direction is not normalised - So the player walks faster when looking at the ground - Because raylib's Vector3Add only adds the x and z parts + So looking up or down does not change walking speed The flat forward direction uses the yaw only, with y = 0. With the full look direction, looking down would point part of the movement into the ground and make you walk slower. ? How does a third-person camera find its position? - It copies the player's position and adds a fixed offset such as {0, 2, -5} + It starts from a point on the player and moves back along the view direction by the camera distance - It uses the player's position as the camera's target and the camera's position as the player's - It moves forward from the player along the view direction by the camera distance The camera orbits the player: target is a point on the player (about the shoulders) and position = target - offset , where the offset is the view direction from yaw and pitch scaled by the distance. A fixed offset would not turn with the view.

title: Looking and walking in 3D
body: Write the maths of lesson 5.02's controller. Angles are in degrees: cpp struct Vector3 { float x, y, z; }; Vector3 lookDirection(float yaw, float pitch); // (cos p sin y, sin p, cos p cos y) float clampPitch(float pitch); // -89 .. 89 float wrapYaw(float yaw); // into 0 <= yaw < 360 Vector3 wishDirection(float yaw, bool forward, bool back, bool left, bool right); Vector3 orbitPosition(Vector3 target, float yaw, float pitch, float distance); - wishDirection uses the flat forward (sin y, 0, cos y) and right (-cos y, 0, sin y) ; forward and back add and subtract the forward direction, right and left the right direction; the sum is normalised (or (0, 0, 0) ). - orbitPosition is target - lookDirection(yaw, pitch) distance : behind the target along the view.

title: 5.03  Picking and 3D Collision
body: Clicking on things in 3D, shooting, line of sight and camera collision all ask one question - what does this ray hit first? This lesson turns the mouse into a ray, tests rays against planes, spheres and boxes, and adds sphere and box collision for moving objects. Rays A ray is a start point and a direction: Ray { Vector3 position; Vector3 direction; } . Points along it are position + direction t for t = 0 . Every "what is in this direction?" question is a ray test: Question Ray from Direction --- --- --- What did the player click? The camera Through the mouse position What does the gun hit? The muzzle or the eye The aim Can the enemy see the player? The enemy's eyes Towards the player (with the distance as a limit) Is the floor below me? The feet Straight down The mouse as a ray cpp-norun const Ray ray = GetScreenToWorldRay(GetMousePosition(), camera); // raylib 5 (older: GetMouseRay) const RayCollision hit = GetRayCollisionBox(ray, crateBox); if (hit.hit) { / hit.point, hit.normal, hit.distance / } raylib has GetRayCollisionSphere , GetRayCollisionBox , GetRayCollisionMesh (exact, per triangle, slower), GetRayCollisionTriangle and GetRayCollisionQuad . To pick among many objects, test them all and keep the hit with the smallest distance . Ray against a plane The ground plane y = h is hit where position.y + direction.y t = h : cpp-norun if (direction.y != 0) { t = (h - position.y) / direction.y; if (t = 0) hit = position + direction t; } That is how strategy games turn a click into a point on the ground to move units to. Ray against a sphere Substitute the ray into the sphere equation p - centre ² = r² and solve the quadratic in t . With m = position - centre and a normalised direction d : b = m · d , c = m · m - r² ; if c 0 and b 0 the ray starts outside and points away (no hit); otherwise, with disc = b² - c , there is no hit when disc < 0 , and the first hit is at t = -b - sqrt(disc) (or 0 if that is negative, meaning the ray starts inside). Ray against a box: the slab method An axis-aligned box is the overlap of three slabs (between two x planes, two y planes, two z planes). For each axis, compute where the ray enters and leaves that slab; the ray is inside the box between the latest entry and the earliest exit: cpp-norun float tmin = 0, tmax = INFINITY; for each axis a: if (d a == 0) { if (p a < min a p a max a ) no hit; } else { float t1 = (min a - p a ) / d a , t2 = (max a - p a ) / d a ; if (t1 t2) swap(t1, t2); tmin = max(tmin, t1); tmax = min(tmax, t2); if (tmin tmax) no hit; } hit at tmin The axis that produced the final tmin is the face that was hit, which gives the normal for bullet holes or ricochets. The practice writes this test. Moving objects - Sphere against sphere : centres closer than the sum of the radii, exactly as circles in 2D. - Box against box : overlap on all three axes ( CheckCollisionBoxes ). - Sphere against box : clamp the centre into the box for the closest point, as in 2D ( CheckCollisionBoxSphere ). For level geometry that is not boxes, raylib's GetRayCollisionMesh and a few rays (down for the floor, forward for walls) are often enough for a small game; larger games use a physics library such as Jolt or Bullet. Check yourself quiz ? How do you find what the mouse is pointing at in 3D? - Convert the mouse with GetScreenToWorld2D and look up the object at that point + Turn the mouse position into a ray from the camera with GetScreenToWorldRay , test it against the objects and keep the nearest hit - Test a ray from the camera's position towards the camera's target against every object - Turn the mouse into a ray and stop at the first object in the list that it hits The ray goes from the camera through the mouse position. The camera's target is only the centre of the view, and the first object in the list is not necessarily the nearest. ? In the slab method, when does the ray miss the box? - When the ray's start point is outside the box - When the ray's direction is 0 on any axis + When the latest entry into a slab comes after the earliest exit from another ( tmin tmax ) - When the earliest entry into a slab comes before the latest exit from another ( tmin < tmax ) The ray is inside the box only between the latest entry and the earliest exit; if those cross, there is no common stretch. A zero direction on an axis is a miss only when the start lies outside that slab. ? Why keep the hit with the smallest distance? - Because raylib's ray tests only report hits closer than 1 unit - Because the smallest distance is the most accurate result - So the slowest test is skipped for distant objects + A ray can pass through several objects; the nearest one is the one actually seen or hit Testing every object can give several hits along the same ray. The first one along it is what the player sees or the bullet hits.

title: What does the ray hit?
body: Write lesson 5.03's ray tests. Ray directions have length 1: cpp struct Vector3 { float x, y, z; }; struct Ray { Vector3 position, direction; }; struct BoundingBox { Vector3 min, max; }; struct Hit { bool hit{ false }; float distance{ 0 }; Vector3 point{ 0, 0, 0 }, normal{ 0, 0, 0 }; }; Hit rayPlaneY(Ray r, float height); // the horizontal plane y = height, from either side Hit raySphere(Ray r, Vector3 centre, float radius); Hit rayBox(Ray r, BoundingBox b); int pickNearest(Ray r, const std::vector<BoundingBox & boxes); // index of the nearest box hit, -1 for none - Hits only count at distance = 0 . A ray starting inside a sphere or a box hits at distance 0. - rayPlaneY 's normal is (0, 1, 0) when the ray comes from above and (0, -1, 0) from below; a ray parallel to the plane misses. - raySphere 's normal is from the centre to the hit point, normalised (for a ray starting inside, leave it (0, 0, 0) ). - rayBox uses the slab method. The normal points out of the face that was entered: the axis whose entry distance was the final tmin , with the sign opposite to the ray's direction on that axis. Starting inside, the normal is (0, 0, 0) .

title: 5.04  Shaders
body: Shaders are small programs that run on the GPU for every vertex and every pixel. This lesson explains vertex and fragment shaders, writes GLSL fragment shaders for raylib, passes values in with uniforms, and builds a flash effect, a dissolve and a simple light. Programs on the GPU Everything raylib draws goes through two small programs on the graphics card: raylib's default shaders just position vertices with the camera and multiply the texture colour by the tint. Writing your own fragment shader (also called a pixel shader) lets you change how every pixel looks: flashes, outlines, dissolves, lighting, water, colour grading. They are written in GLSL , a C-like language. A first fragment shader raylib on desktop uses OpenGL 3.3, so shaders start with version 330 : cpp-norun // flash.fs version 330 in vec2 fragTexCoord; // from raylib's default vertex shader in vec4 fragColor; // the tint uniform sampler2D texture0; // the texture being drawn uniform float flash; // our own value: 0 = normal, 1 = white out vec4 finalColor; void main() { vec4 texel = texture(texture0, fragTexCoord) fragColor; finalColor = vec4(mix(texel.rgb, vec3(1.0), flash), texel.a); } mix(a, b, t) is linear interpolation, vec3 / vec4 are vectors, and .rgb / .a pick components. The shader runs for every pixel of the sprite, in parallel. Using it from raylib cpp-norun Shader shader = LoadShader(nullptr, "assets/flash.fs"); // nullptr: keep the default vertex shader const int flashLoc = GetShaderLocation(shader, "flash"); // each frame: const float amount = hitTimer 0 ? 1.0f : 0.0f; SetShaderValue(shader, flashLoc, &amount, SHADER_UNIFORM_FLOAT); BeginShaderMode(shader); DrawTexturePro(sprite, src, dest, origin, 0, WHITE); EndShaderMode(); UnloadShader(shader); A uniform is a value that is the same for every pixel of one draw call: a time, a colour, a position. Look its location up once with GetShaderLocation , then set it every frame with SetShaderValue . Other types are SHADER_UNIFORM_VEC2 , VEC3 , VEC4 and INT , and SetShaderValueTexture passes extra textures. A dissolve A dissolve makes an object burn away. Read a noise texture, and throw away pixels whose noise value is below a threshold that rises from 0 to 1: cpp-norun uniform sampler2D noise; uniform float threshold; void main() { vec4 texel = texture(texture0, fragTexCoord) fragColor; float n = texture(noise, fragTexCoord).r; if (n < threshold) discard; // this pixel is not drawn float edge = smoothstep(threshold, threshold + 0.05, n); // 0 at the edge, 1 inside finalColor = vec4(mix(vec3(1.0, 0.5, 0.1), texel.rgb, edge), texel.a); // glowing orange edge } A point light Simple lighting in 2D: brighten pixels near a light and darken the rest: cpp-norun uniform vec2 lightPos; // in screen pixels uniform float radius; void main() { vec4 texel = texture(texture0, fragTexCoord) fragColor; float d = distance(gl_FragCoord.xy, lightPos); float light = clamp(1.0 - d / radius, 0.15, 1.0); finalColor = vec4(texel.rgb light, texel.a); } gl_FragCoord is the pixel's position in the window, but with y measured from the bottom , so pass screenHeight - y for the light's y. Forgetting that flips the light upside down. Debugging shaders A shader that fails to compile is reported in raylib's log (the console window) with a line number, and raylib falls back to the default shader. When a result is wrong, output intermediate values as colours: finalColor = vec4(vec3(n), 1.0); shows the noise as grey levels. Shaders are calculations on numbers, so the maths behind them (interpolation, distances, smoothstep) can be tested on the CPU first, which is what this lesson's practice does. Check yourself quiz ? What do the vertex shader and the fragment shader do? - The vertex shader chooses each pixel's colour; the fragment shader positions each vertex + The vertex shader positions each vertex; the fragment shader chooses the colour of each pixel a triangle covers - The vertex shader loads the textures; the fragment shader draws them to the screen - Both run once per draw call: the vertex shader first, then the fragment shader The vertex shader runs once per vertex and places it on screen; after the rasteriser works out which pixels a triangle covers, the fragment shader runs once per pixel to choose its colour. ? What is a uniform? - A value that is different for every pixel, such as its texture coordinate - A variable the shader writes so the program can read it back - The vertex shader's output, passed on to the fragment shader + A value set from the program that is the same for every vertex and pixel of a draw call Uniforms are set from C++ with SetShaderValue after looking up their location once with GetShaderLocation . Per-pixel values such as fragTexCoord are inputs ( in ), not uniforms. ? Why does a light shader need screenHeight - y for the light position? + gl_FragCoord measures y from the bottom of the window, while raylib's screen coordinates measure it from the top - gl_FragCoord is in the range 0 to 1, so the light must be converted to that range - Shaders cannot take negative numbers, so y must be turned into a positive distance - Render textures are upside down, so every shader must flip y The two coordinate systems count y from opposite edges, so the light's y is flipped. Forgetting it puts the light upside down.

title: Shader maths on the CPU
body: A fragment shader is a function from a pixel's inputs to its colour. Write lesson 5.04's shaders as C++ functions, with GLSL's built-ins: cpp struct Vec3 { float r, g, b; }; float mixf(float a, float b, float t); // a + (b - a) t Vec3 mix3(Vec3 a, Vec3 b, float t); float clampf(float x, float lo, float hi); float smoothstep(float e0, float e1, float x); // t = clamp((x - e0) / (e1 - e0), 0, 1); t² (3 - 2t) Vec3 flash(Vec3 texel, float amount); // towards white bool dissolve(Vec3 texel, float noise, float threshold, Vec3& out); float pointLight(float fragX, float fragY, float lightX, float lightY, float screenH, float radius); - dissolve : returns false (the pixel is discarded) when noise < threshold . Otherwise edge = smoothstep(threshold, threshold + 0.05, noise) and out = mix3({1, 0.5, 0.1}, texel, edge) . - pointLight : the fragment is in OpenGL coordinates (y from the bottom); the light is in raylib coordinates (y from the top). Convert the light's y, then return clamp(1 - distance / radius, 0.15, 1) . - smoothstep also works with e0 e1 (falling instead of rising), which the vignette in lesson 5.05 uses.

title: 5.05  Render Textures and Post-Processing
body: Drawing into a texture instead of the screen opens up a lot - pixel-perfect scaling, minimaps, split screens, and post-processing effects applied to the whole frame such as vignettes, colour grading, blur and scanlines. Drawing into a texture A render texture is a texture you can draw into, like an off-screen window: cpp-norun RenderTexture2D target = LoadRenderTexture(320, 180); // each frame: BeginTextureMode(target); ClearBackground(BLACK); drawWorld(); // everything goes into the texture EndTextureMode(); BeginDrawing(); ClearBackground(BLACK); // draw the texture to the screen; the source height is NEGATIVE because OpenGL textures are upside down DrawTexturePro(target.texture, { 0, 0, 320, -180 }, letterboxRect, { 0, 0 }, 0, WHITE); EndDrawing(); UnloadRenderTexture(target); The negative source height is the one thing everyone forgets: without it, the whole picture is upside down. Pixel-perfect scaling This is the clean way to make a pixel-art game: draw everything at the native resolution (320 × 180) into a render texture with point filtering, then draw that texture scaled up by a whole number, centred, with black bars (the letterbox from practice 2.01). Every pixel is the same size whatever the window size, and the mouse is mapped back with the inverse of the same scale and offset. Other uses Use How --- --- Minimap Draw the level from above with a second camera into a small texture, show it in a corner Split screen One render texture per player, each with its own camera, side by side Mirrors, security cameras Draw the scene from another camera into a texture used on an object Caching Draw something expensive once (a big static background) and reuse the texture Post-processing Post-processing is a shader applied to the whole finished frame: draw the world into a render texture, then draw that texture to the screen inside BeginShaderMode . The fragment shader sees every pixel of the frame: cpp-norun // vignette.fs: darken towards the edges version 330 in vec2 fragTexCoord; uniform sampler2D texture0; out vec4 finalColor; void main() { vec3 c = texture(texture0, fragTexCoord).rgb; float d = distance(fragTexCoord, vec2(0.5)); // 0 in the centre, about 0.7 in the corners c = smoothstep(0.8, 0.3, d); // fade from 1 to 0 between 0.3 and 0.8 finalColor = vec4(c, 1.0); } Common effects: - Vignette (above): focuses the eye on the centre. - Colour grading : adjust brightness, contrast and saturation, or tint the whole frame for mood (blue at night, red when low on health). - Grey scale : dot(c, vec3(0.299, 0.587, 0.114)) gives the perceived brightness, used for a "game over" or flashback look. - Blur : average neighbouring pixels; done in two passes (horizontal, then vertical) for speed, often to put a menu over a blurred game. - Scanlines and curvature : an old CRT look. - Bloom : blur only the bright parts and add them back, so lights glow. raylib's examples include a dozen post-processing shaders ( shaders_postprocessing ) to start from. Keep it optional Post-processing costs a full-screen pass per effect, and some effects (blur, shake, flashing) bother some players. Give each strong effect a setting, and keep the interface outside the effect by drawing it after the post-processed frame. Check yourself quiz ? Why is the source height negative when drawing a render texture? - A negative height tells raylib to scale the texture up to fill the window - It makes raylib use point filtering instead of bilinear filtering + OpenGL stores textures upside down relative to raylib's screen coordinates, so the picture must be flipped vertically - It draws the texture from its bottom edge so it lines up with the letterbox Without the negative height, the whole frame appears upside down. Filtering and scaling are set separately (texture filter and the destination rectangle). ? How do you apply a shader to the whole frame? - Call BeginShaderMode before BeginDrawing and EndShaderMode after EndDrawing + Draw the frame into a render texture, then draw that texture to the screen between BeginShaderMode and EndShaderMode - Draw each object of the world inside its own BeginShaderMode block - Set the shader on the camera before BeginMode2D Post-processing needs the finished frame as a texture, so the fragment shader sees every pixel of it at once. Shading each object separately gives per-object effects, not a whole-frame vignette or blur. ? How do you compute a pixel's perceived brightness for grey scale? - (r + g + b) / 3 - max(r, g, b) + dot(colour, (0.299, 0.587, 0.114)) - dot(colour, (0.114, 0.587, 0.299)) The eye is most sensitive to green and least to blue, so the weights are 0.299 for red, 0.587 for green and 0.114 for blue. A plain average makes blues look too bright. ? Why draw the interface after the post-processed frame? - So the interface is drawn at the render texture's low resolution + So effects such as blur, vignette or shake do not distort the text and buttons - Because a render texture cannot contain text - So the interface appears behind the world Drawing the interface on top after the effect keeps it sharp and readable. Text can be drawn into a render texture; it would just be affected by the shader.

title: Post-processing a frame
body: Write lesson 5.05's effects on a small grey-scale picture, and the mouse mapping for a letterboxed render texture: cpp struct Vector2 { float x, y; }; struct Rectangle { float x, y, width, height; }; float luminance(float r, float g, float b); // 0.299 r + 0.587 g + 0.114 b float vignette(float u, float v); // smoothstep(0.8, 0.3, distance from (0.5, 0.5)) std::vector<float blur3(const std::vector<float & image, int w, int h); bool screenToNative(Vector2 mouse, Rectangle shown, int nativeW, int nativeH, int& px, int& py); - blur3 is a 3-tap box blur in two passes: first horizontal (each pixel becomes the average of itself and its left and right neighbours), then vertical on the result. At the edges, a missing neighbour is replaced by the nearest pixel ( clamp to edge ). The image is stored row by row. - screenToNative : shown is where the native-resolution picture is drawn on screen. Return the native pixel under the mouse ( floor of the scaled position) and true , or false if the mouse is outside shown (its right and bottom edges are outside). - vignette : use the same smoothstep as practice 5.04.

title: A first-person arena
body: Write the core of a small first-person target-shooting game: mouse look, walking relative to the view, gravity and jumping, collision against box-shaped walls in three dimensions, and shooting with a ray that walls block. In raylib it is drawn with DrawCube for the walls and targets and a Camera3D at the player's eye. cpp struct Vector3 { float x, y, z; }; struct Box { Vector3 min, max; }; struct Target { Box box; int hp; }; struct Keys { bool forward{ false }, back{ false }, left{ false }, right{ false }, jump{ false }; }; struct Player { Vector3 feet{ 0, 0, 0 }; Vector3 vel{ 0, 0, 0 }; float yaw{ 0 }, pitch{ 0 }; // degrees bool onGround{ false }; }; void look(Player& p, float mouseDx, float mouseDy, float sensitivity); Vector3 eye(const Player& p); Vector3 viewDirection(const Player& p); void walk(Player& p, const std::vector<Box & walls, const Keys& k, float dt); int shoot(const Player& p, const std::vector<Box & walls, std::vector<Target & targets); look : yaw -= mouseDx sensitivity , wrapped into 0 <= yaw < 360 ; pitch -= mouseDy sensitivity , clamped to -89..89 . eye is the feet plus 1.6 up. viewDirection is practice 5.02's lookDirection(yaw, pitch) . walk , in this order: 1. The wish direction from the keys, using the flat forward and right directions of practice 5.02, normalised; vel.x and vel.z become the wish direction times 5 (metres per second). 2. If jump is held and the player is on the ground, vel.y = 7 . 3. Gravity: vel.y -= 20 dt . 4. Move along x, then z, then y, each followed by collision with the walls. The player's box is feet.x ± 0.3 , feet.z ± 0.3 , and feet.y to feet.y + 1.8 ; touching does not count as overlapping. Blocked on x or z, the player stops at the wall's face (0.3 from it) and that velocity becomes 0. On y, moving down onto a box lands on its top ( onGround ), moving up stops the head at its bottom; vel.y becomes 0. Several walls: the nearest stop, as in practice 3.02. 5. onGround is true exactly when this step landed. shoot casts a ray from the eye along the view direction against all walls and all targets with hit points left (practice 5.03's slab test). If the nearest hit is a target, it loses a hit point and its index is returned; otherwise (a wall or nothing) -1 .

title: 6.01  Saving Progress and Settings
body: Players expect a game to remember their settings, their progress and their best scores. This lesson chooses what to save and where, writes simple versioned text formats, saves safely so a crash never destroys a save, and keeps a high-score table. What to save Kind Examples When --- --- --- Settings Volumes, key bindings, window mode, screen shake on or off When changed Progress Levels unlocked, items collected, the current level and checkpoint At checkpoints, level ends and on quit Records High scores, best times, statistics When a record changes Save data , not objects: the level number and the player's health, not the Player object with its texture handles and pointers. Loading then rebuilds the objects from the data. Where Never write next to the .exe : on Windows, a game installed in Program Files is not allowed to. Each user has a folder for this, %APPDATA% (for example C:\Users\Sam\AppData\Roaming\YourGame\ ): cpp-norun include <cstdlib include <filesystem std::filesystem::path saveFolder() { const char appData = std::getenv("APPDATA"); // Windows std::filesystem::path dir = appData ? appData : "."; dir /= "XenonQuest"; std::filesystem::create_directories(dir); return dir; } On Linux the convention is ~/.local/share/<game , on macOS ~/Library/Application Support/<game . A simple format A text file of key=value lines is readable, easy to debug and easy to extend: version=2 music=70 effects=85 fullscreen=0 key.jump=32 Rules that keep it robust: - Defaults first : start from default settings and overwrite only the keys that are present and valid. A missing or damaged line then simply keeps its default, and new settings added in an update work with old files. - Validate and clamp every value: a volume of 900 or a key code of -5 must not reach the game. - Ignore unknown keys , so an older game can read a newer file. - Version the file, so a later version can convert old data (a migration ). Saving safely If the game crashes or the power fails halfway through writing, the save file is cut off and the player loses everything. Write to a temporary file first, then replace the old one in a single step: cpp-norun void saveSafely(const std::filesystem::path& file, const std::string& text) { const auto temp = file.string() + ".tmp"; { std::ofstream out{ temp, std::ios::binary }; out << text; } // closed (flushed) at the brace std::filesystem::rename(temp, file); // replaces the old file } A rename within one folder is atomic on Windows and Linux: afterwards there is either the complete old file or the complete new one. Keeping the previous save as save.bak adds another layer of protection. Detecting damage A checksum stored with the data detects files that were cut off or damaged: compute a number from the content (such as FNV-1a, a few lines of code), write it on the last line, and when loading, recompute it and compare. On a mismatch, fall back to the backup or to defaults, and tell the player rather than crashing. A checksum is not protection against cheating: anyone can recompute it. For a single-player game that is fine; let players edit their saves if they want to. High scores A high-score table is a sorted list with a maximum length: cpp-norun struct Score { std::string name; int points; }; void addScore(std::vector<Score & table, Score s) { auto pos = std::find_if(table.begin(), table.end(), & (const Score& t) { return s.points t.points; }); table.insert(pos, s); // after equal scores: earlier players keep their place if (table.size() 10) table.pop_back(); } Ask for the name (lesson 1.05's typed text) only when the score actually makes it into the table. Check yourself quiz ? Why start from defaults when loading settings? - So the file can be smaller, holding only the keys the player changed - Because std::ifstream cannot read a file that has every key in it + Missing, damaged or new keys then keep sensible values instead of breaking the game - So the game can tell which settings the player has never opened Overwriting defaults only with keys that are present and valid means a cut-off line or a setting added in an update simply keeps its default. ? How do you save without risking a half-written file? - Write directly over the old file and call flush after every line - Delete the old file first, then write the new one + Write to a temporary file and rename it over the old one, which replaces it in one step - Write the file twice, so one of the copies is always complete A rename in the same folder is atomic, so afterwards there is either the complete old save or the complete new one. Deleting first leaves nothing at all if the game crashes during the write. ? What does a checksum protect against, and what not? - It stops players from editing their saves, but cannot detect a file that was cut off + It detects damaged or cut-off files; it does not stop someone from editing the file on purpose - It repairs damaged files automatically, but cannot detect missing lines - It encrypts the save so only the game can read it The checksum is recomputed on load and compared. Anyone can recompute it after editing, so it is no protection against cheating, which is fine for a single-player game. ? Where should a Windows game write its settings and saves? - Next to the .exe , so they move with the game + In the user's %APPDATA% folder, in a folder named after the game - In the current working directory - In C:\Program Files , next to the other installed programs A game installed in Program Files is not allowed to write there or next to its .exe , and the working directory can be anything. %APPDATA% is the per-user folder meant for this.

title: A settings file
body: Read and write lesson 6.01's settings file: cpp struct Settings { int music{ 70 }, effects{ 85 }; // 0 .. 100 bool fullscreen{ false }; bool shake{ true }; int jumpKey{ 32 }; // 1 .. 512 }; Settings parseSettings(const std::string& text); std::string writeSettings(const Settings& s); parseSettings starts from the defaults and reads key=value lines ( \r\n allowed): - music and effects : whole numbers, clamped to 0..100 ; - fullscreen and shake : 0 or 1 (anything else is ignored); - key.jump : a whole number from 1 to 512 (out of range is ignored); - version must be 1 or 2 if present; a file with any other version is ignored completely (defaults). Version 1 files stored the volumes as 0..10 , so for them music and effects are multiplied by 10; - spaces around keys and values are trimmed; unknown keys, lines without = , and values that are not whole numbers (such as 7x ) are ignored. writeSettings writes version 2, in this order, each line ending in \n : version=2 music=70 effects=85 fullscreen=0 shake=1 key.jump=32

title: 6.02  Packaging a Finished Game
body: Turning a project that runs on your computer into a game anyone can download - release builds, loading assets reliably, an asset cache, the window and icon, testing on a clean machine, a web build with Emscripten, and publishing on itch.io. A release build Switch Visual Studio to Release . Debug builds are often ten times slower and need debug runtime DLLs that players do not have. Then: - Static runtime : set C/C++ Code Generation Runtime Library to /MT , so the game does not need the Visual C++ Redistributable installed. With vcpkg, use the x64-windows-static triplet so raylib is linked in too, and the game is a single .exe plus its assets. - No console : SubSystem Windows with entry point mainCRTStartup (lesson 1.01). - Icon : add a resource file ( .rc ) with an .ico for the file's icon in Explorer, and call SetWindowIcon(LoadImage("icon.png")) for the title bar. Assets that always load The classic bug of a first release: it works in Visual Studio, but double-clicking the .exe shows a black window, because the assets are loaded relative to the working directory , which is now different. Fix it once at start-up: cpp-norun ChangeDirectory(GetApplicationDirectory()); // relative paths now start next to the .exe and make the build copy the assets folder next to the .exe (a post-build step, or CMake's file(COPY ...) ). Check every load: a missing texture has an id of 0 ( IsTextureValid in raylib 5.5). Show a clear message ("assets/player.png is missing") instead of an invisible player. An asset cache When several objects use the same texture, load it once and share it: cpp-norun class TextureCache { public: Texture2D get(const std::string& path) { auto it = m_textures.find(path); if (it != m_textures.end()) return it- second; Texture2D t = LoadTexture(path.c_str()); m_textures.emplace(path, t); return t; } ~TextureCache() { for (auto& path, t : m_textures) UnloadTexture(t); } // before CloseWindow private: std::unordered_map<std::string, Texture2D m_textures; }; Normalise the paths used as keys ( assets/./player.png and assets/player.png are the same file), and destroy the cache before CloseWindow , since unloading needs the graphics context. Reference counting lets the cache free textures a level no longer uses; the practice builds it. Test on a clean machine Your computer has Visual Studio, vcpkg and every DLL; players' computers do not. Before publishing, run the game from a zip on a computer (or a fresh Windows virtual machine, or Windows Sandbox) that has never seen your development tools. Check the window size on a small laptop screen and a big monitor, a gamepad, and that settings and saves end up in %APPDATA% . A web build raylib compiles to WebAssembly with Emscripten , so the game runs in a browser with nothing to install. The main loop must give control back to the browser every frame, so it becomes a function: cpp-norun if defined(PLATFORM_WEB) include <emscripten/emscripten.h endif void frame() { update(); draw(); } int main() { InitWindow(800, 450, "Game"); if defined(PLATFORM_WEB) emscripten_set_main_loop(frame, 0, 1); // the browser calls frame() else SetTargetFPS(60); while (!WindowShouldClose()) frame(); endif CloseWindow(); } Build raylib for the web ( make PLATFORM=PLATFORM_WEB ), compile with emcc ... -s USE_GLFW=3 --preload-file assets , and you get an .html , a .js , a .wasm and a .data file with the assets. Browsers only start audio after the player clicks, so show a "click to start" screen first. Publishing itch.io is the usual home for small games: upload the Windows zip and the web build (as a zip with index.html , set to "playable in the browser"), add screenshots, a short description and the controls. A short GIF of gameplay does more than any description. Use version numbers in the zip names and keep a changelog. Check yourself quiz ? Why does a game often show a black window when started outside Visual Studio? - Release builds disable drawing until SetTargetFPS is called - The graphics driver is not loaded until the game runs inside Visual Studio + The working directory differs, so relative asset paths break - The assets folder is compiled into the .exe only in Debug builds Relative paths start from the working directory, which Visual Studio sets to the project folder. Calling ChangeDirectory(GetApplicationDirectory()) at start-up makes them start next to the .exe . ? Why link the runtime statically for a release? + So players do not need the Visual C++ Redistributable or other DLLs installed - Because a statically linked game runs ten times faster than a dynamically linked one - So the game can be built for the web with Emscripten - So the console window is hidden /MT (and vcpkg's x64-windows-static triplet) puts the runtime and raylib into the .exe . The large speed difference is between Debug and Release, and the console is hidden by the subsystem setting. ? What changes in the main loop for a web build? - The loop stays the same, but SetTargetFPS must be set to the browser's frame rate - The loop runs on a second thread so the browser stays responsive + The browser must call one frame function repeatedly, so the loop becomes emscripten_set_main_loop(frame, 0, 1) - WindowShouldClose is replaced by checking whether the browser tab is open The game has to give control back to the browser every frame, so the body of the loop moves into frame() and the browser calls it.

title: A reference-counted asset cache
body: Write lesson 6.02's asset cache, with the loading and unloading done by functions you pass in (in a real game they call LoadTexture and UnloadTexture ): cpp std::string normalizePath(const std::string& path); class AssetCache { public: AssetCache(std::function<int(const std::string&) load, std::function<void(int) unload); ~AssetCache(); // unloads everything still loaded int acquire(const std::string& path); // the asset's handle; loads it on first use void release(const std::string& path); // one fewer user; unloads at zero int users(const std::string& path) const; // 0 if not loaded std::size_t loaded() const; }; normalizePath : backslashes become / ; empty parts and . parts are removed; .. removes the part before it (a .. with nothing before it is kept); letters become lower case (Windows file names ignore case). So Assets\\.\\sprites//../Player.PNG is assets/player.png . AssetCache : every function normalises the path first, so different spellings of the same file share one asset. acquire calls load only the first time (or again after the asset was fully released) and counts users. release on an asset that is not loaded does nothing. A load result of 0 means it failed: it is not cached, and acquire returns 0.

title: 6.03  Project: A Complete Small Game
body: Put the whole course together into one finished game - choosing a scope you can finish, the order to build it in, data-driven waves and levels, the polish that makes it feel complete, and a checklist for release. The example is a top-down arena survival game. Finishing is the skill Most first games are never finished: the idea grows faster than the code. The goal of this project is a small game that is complete : a title screen, a game that starts, gets harder and ends, a game-over screen with a score, settings that are remembered, sound, and a build someone else can play. The example here is an arena survival game: the player moves around a single arena with the keyboard or a gamepad and shoots in the direction they aim; enemies arrive in waves; each wave is harder; the score is the number of waves survived and enemies defeated. It uses almost every lesson, and is small enough to finish in a few weekends. Choose your own idea if you prefer, but keep it to one mechanic, one screen-sized world and one goal . The pieces and where they come from Piece Lessons --- --- Loop, frame time, input with bindings 1.02 - 1.05 Sprites and animations for the player and enemies 2.01, 2.02 Interface: score, health bar, wave number, menus 2.03 Sounds with variation, music, volume settings 2.04 Title, game, pause and game-over screens with fades 2.05 Circle collisions, a grid for many bullets and enemies 3.01, 3.05 Fixed time step 3.04 Camera with shake 4.01 Particles for hits and deaths 4.03 Enemy state machine: approach, wind-up, charge 4.04 Flow field so enemies go around obstacles 4.05 Post-processing: a vignette, a red flash when hurt 5.04, 5.05 Settings and high scores saved safely 6.01 Release and web builds 6.02 Waves as data Hard-coding "wave 3 has five chargers" makes balancing slow. Describe waves as data in a text file that the game reads: time kind count interval wave 1 0 walker 4 1.0 6 walker 4 0.5 wave 2 0 walker 6 0.6 3 charger 2 2.0 Each line is a spawn group : starting at time seconds into the wave, spawn count enemies of kind , one every interval seconds. The game asks "which enemies spawn between the last frame and this one?" and the answer comes straight from the data. You can rebalance without recompiling, and even reload the file while the game runs. The practice builds this spawner. Difficulty should rise in steps with pauses between them: tension, then relief. After the hand-made waves, generate more by scaling counts and shortening intervals. Order to build in 1. The toy : a player that moves and shoots in an empty arena. Make it feel good before anything else: speed, acceleration, the bullet's speed, a sound and a particle burst for every shot. 2. Something to shoot : one enemy type, collision, health, dying. 3. A game : waves from the data file, a score, losing. 4. Screens : title, pause, game over with the score, play again (reset everything, lesson 2.05). 5. Variety : a second and a third enemy type with different behaviour. 6. Polish : shake, hit flash, hit stop, death particles, music, a vignette. 7. Remembering : settings and the high-score table. 8. Release : icon, release build, clean-machine test, web build, itch.io page. At every step the game runs, and you can stop and still have something to show. The release checklist - It starts with a title screen and can be quit from the menu. - Every input has a keyboard and a gamepad binding, and the controls are shown somewhere. - Pause works and stops everything, including timers and spawns. - Play again resets everything. - Music and effects volumes are separate, saved, and applied at start-up. - Screen shake and flashes can be turned off. - The window can be resized or made fullscreen, and the game still fits. - Settings and scores are in %APPDATA% , saved safely. - It runs from a zip on a clean machine. - Someone who has never seen it played it without your help. The last one matters most: watch a friend play without saying anything. Every place they hesitate is something to make clearer. Check yourself quiz ? Why describe waves as data rather than code? - Reading a file is faster than running code + They can be changed and rebalanced without recompiling, even while the game runs - So players cannot see how many enemies each wave has - Because raylib can only spawn enemies listed in a file Each line is a spawn group (time, kind, count, interval) that the spawner reads, so balancing becomes editing a text file. ? Why build the game in an order where it always runs? - Because the compiler cannot build a game with unfinished parts - So the final release build is smaller - So each step can be thrown away and rewritten later + You can test the feel at every step, and you always have a working game to show if you stop Starting with "the toy" and adding one layer at a time keeps the game playable, so problems with the feel show up early. ? What should be in the game before you call it complete? - Every idea you had at the start, however long it takes + A goal, an end screen with a score, sound, and a build others can run - A 3D world, custom shaders and online high-score tables - At least three levels plus a built-in level editor Also a start screen, play again and saved settings. Complete means finished, not big: one mechanic, one screen-sized world and one goal, with the screens, sound, settings and release build around it.

title: Waves from data
body: Write lesson 6.03's data-driven wave spawner: cpp struct Spawn { double time; std::string kind; }; class Waves { public: bool load(const std::string& text, std::string& error); int count() const; // number of waves std::vector<Spawn schedule(int wave) const; // every spawn of a wave (1-based), sorted by time std::vector<std::string spawnsBetween(int wave, double from, double to) const; // spawns with from < time <= to double length(int wave) const; // time of the wave's last spawn, 0 if none }; The format : lines starting with and empty lines are ignored. wave N starts wave N, and waves must be numbered 1, 2, 3... in order. Every other line inside a wave is a group: time kind count interval (time and interval are decimal numbers, count a whole number of at least 1, interval at least 0). A group spawns count enemies of kind at time , time + interval , time + 2 × interval , ... Errors ( load returns false and leaves the previous waves in place): "line N: expected wave 2" (the wrong number), "line N: group outside a wave" , "line N: bad group" (N counting all lines from 1). schedule sorts by time; spawns at the same time keep the order of their groups in the file, then their order in the group. An unknown wave number gives no spawns.
