title: Saves that survive
body:
Write the save system a finished game needs: a readable, versioned save file with a checksum, migration from the previous version, a fallback to the backup when the main save is damaged, and the high-score table. cpp struct Score { int points; std::string name; }; struct SaveData { int level{ 1 }; int coins{ 0 }; std::vector<std::string unlocked; // area names, in the order they were unlocked std::vector<Score scores; // best first, at most 5 }; enum class LoadResult { Ok, Missing, Damaged, TooNew }; std::uint32_t fnv1a(const std::string& text); std::string writeSave(const SaveData& s); LoadResult loadSave(const std::string& text, SaveData& out); int chooseSave(const std::string& primary, const std::string& backup, SaveData& out); int addScore(std::vector<Score & table, const std::string& name, int points); fnv1a is the 32-bit FNV-1a hash: start at 2166136261 ; for each byte, XOR it in, then multiply by 16777619 (arithmetic wraps around at 2³²). The file (version 2), lines ending in 
 : xenon-save 2 level 3 coins 120 unlocked forest,caves score 1200 Sam score 900 Alex Smith checksum 1a2b3c4d unlocked lists the areas separated by commas (the line is written even when empty: unlocked , with nothing after the space). Each score line is the points then the name (which may contain spaces). The last line is checksum followed by the FNV-1a hash of everything before it (all the earlier lines with their 
 ), as 8 lower-case hex digits. loadSave : - An empty text is Missing . - The first line must be xenon-save N . N greater than 2 is TooNew ; N must be 1 or 2. - The checksum line must be last and must match; otherwise, or for any line that cannot be read, the result is Damaged . Lines may end with 
 (the checksum is computed over the text as stored, so a file with 
 endings hashes them too). - Version 1 files had gold instead of coins and no unlocked line: load them into the version 2 data. - Unknown lines are ignored, so later versions can add lines. level must be at least 1 and coins at least 0, or it is Damaged . - Only on Ok is out changed. chooseSave loads the primary text into out and returns 1; if that is not Ok , it tries the backup and returns 2; if neither loads, out becomes a default SaveData and it returns 0. addScore inserts a score into the table, best first, after existing equal scores, keeps at most 5, and returns the new score's rank (1 to 5), or 0 if it did not make the table.

title: Cheat Sheet - raylib
body: The skeleton cpp-norun include "raylib.h" int main() { InitWindow(800, 450, "Game"); InitAudioDevice(); SetTargetFPS(60); ChangeDirectory(GetApplicationDirectory()); // load assets here while (!WindowShouldClose()) { const float dt = GetFrameTime(); // update BeginDrawing(); ClearBackground(RAYWHITE); // draw EndDrawing(); } // unload assets here CloseAudioDevice(); CloseWindow(); } Window and time Function Does --- --- SetConfigFlags(FLAG_WINDOW_RESIZABLE \ FLAG_VSYNC_HINT \ FLAG_MSAA_4X_HINT) Before InitWindow GetScreenWidth() , GetScreenHeight() Window size ToggleFullscreen() , ToggleBorderlessWindowed() Fullscreen modes GetFrameTime() , GetTime() , GetFPS() Seconds per frame, seconds since start, frames per second GetRandomValue(min, max) Random whole number, both included Input Function True or gives --- --- IsKeyDown(KEY_A) / IsKeyPressed / IsKeyReleased Held / went down / went up GetCharPressed() Next typed character, 0 when none left GetMousePosition() , GetMouseDelta() , GetMouseWheelMove() Mouse IsMouseButtonPressed(MOUSE_BUTTON_LEFT) Click IsGamepadAvailable(0) , GetGamepadAxisMovement(0, GAMEPAD_AXIS_LEFT_X) Gamepad stick, -1..1 IsGamepadButtonPressed(0, GAMEPAD_BUTTON_RIGHT_FACE_DOWN) A / Cross DisableCursor() , EnableCursor() Lock the mouse for 3D Shapes and text Function Draws --- --- DrawRectangleRec(rect, c) , DrawRectangleLinesEx(rect, thick, c) Rectangle from its top-left corner DrawCircleV(centre, r, c) Circle from its centre DrawLineEx(a, b, thick, c) , DrawTriangle(a, b, c, colour) Line, triangle DrawText(text, x, y, size, c) , MeasureText(text, size) Default font DrawTextEx(font, text, pos, size, spacing, c) , MeasureTextEx(...) Your font TextFormat("Score: %d", score) printf-style text (do not keep the pointer) Fade(c, 0.5f) , ColorLerp(a, b, t) Transparency, mixing Textures Function Does --- --- LoadTexture(path) , UnloadTexture(t) After InitWindow / before CloseWindow SetTextureFilter(t, TEXTURE_FILTER_POINT) Crisp pixel art DrawTexturePro(t, src, dest, origin, rotation, tint) Part of a texture, scaled, rotated; negative src.width flips LoadRenderTexture(w, h) , BeginTextureMode(rt) ... EndTextureMode() Draw into a texture; draw it with a negative source height Sound Function Does --- --- LoadSound(path) , PlaySound(s) , LoadSoundAlias(s) Short effects; aliases play over each other SetSoundVolume(s, v) , SetSoundPitch(s, p) , SetMasterVolume(v) Volume 0..1, pitch 1 = normal LoadMusicStream(path) , PlayMusicStream(m) , UpdateMusicStream(m) Streamed music; update every frame Collision Function Tests --- --- CheckCollisionRecs(a, b) , GetCollisionRec(a, b) Rectangles, and their overlap CheckCollisionCircles(c1, r1, c2, r2) , CheckCollisionCircleRec(c, r, rect) Circles CheckCollisionPointRec(p, rect) Point CheckCollisionLines(a1, a2, b1, b2, &point) Segments CheckCollisionBoxes(a, b) , GetRayCollisionBox(ray, box) 3D boxes and rays Cameras cpp-norun Camera2D cam{ / offset / { 400, 225 }, / target / player, / rotation / 0, / zoom / 1 }; BeginMode2D(cam); / world / EndMode2D(); // then the interface Vector2 world = GetScreenToWorld2D(GetMousePosition(), cam); Camera3D cam3{ { 6, 4, 6 }, { 0, 0.5f, 0 }, { 0, 1, 0 }, 45, CAMERA_PERSPECTIVE }; BeginMode3D(cam3); DrawCube({ 0, 0.5f, 0 }, 1, 1, 1, RED); DrawGrid(20, 1); EndMode3D(); Ray ray = GetScreenToWorldRay(GetMousePosition(), cam3); Shaders cpp-norun Shader sh = LoadShader(nullptr, "effect.fs"); // default vertex shader int loc = GetShaderLocation(sh, "amount"); SetShaderValue(sh, loc, &amount, SHADER_UNIFORM_FLOAT); BeginShaderMode(sh); / draw / EndShaderMode(); BeginBlendMode(BLEND_ADDITIVE); / glowing things / EndBlendMode(); Game maths Formula Use --- --- pos += vel dt; vel += accel dt (velocity first) Movement vel = pow(keepPerSecond, dt) Frame-rate independent drag gravity = 2h / t² , jumpSpeed = 2h / t A jump of height h rising in t seconds v - 2 dot(v, n) n Bounce off a surface with normal n (p - target) zoom + offset World to screen (2D camera, no rotation)

title: Common Errors
body: Message or symptom Usual cause Fix Lesson --- --- --- --- cannot open source file "raylib.h" vcpkg installed for another platform, or not integrated Set the platform to x64; run vcpkg integrate install 1.01 LNK2019 for InitWindow or other raylib functions raylib's library is not linked Use vcpkg's integration, or add raylib.lib plus winmm.lib 1.01 A crash or black texture when loading at start-up LoadTexture called before InitWindow Load assets after InitWindow 2.01 Textures are white or missing when started outside Visual Studio Relative paths and a different working directory ChangeDirectory(GetApplicationDirectory()) and copy the assets next to the .exe 2.01, 6.02 Moving objects leave trails The frame is not cleared ClearBackground at the start of every frame 1.02 The game runs faster on a fast screen Movement per frame instead of per second Multiply by GetFrameTime() 1.04 Diagonal movement is too fast The direction is not normalised Normalise the input direction 1.04 A menu choice jumps several items per key press IsKeyDown used for a one-off action IsKeyPressed 1.05 The character creeps with the gamepad untouched Stick drift A dead zone 1.05 An animation is stuck on its first frame play restarts the animation every frame Restart only when the animation changes 2.02 The music plays for a moment and stops UpdateMusicStream is not called every frame Call it every frame 2.04 A rapidly repeated sound cuts itself off PlaySound restarts a Sound that is playing Sound aliases 2.04 "Play again" starts with old enemies or score State not reset Reset the whole game state: game = Game{}; 2.05 Characters catch on the seams between floor tiles Collision resolved on both axes at once Move and resolve one axis at a time 3.02 Bullets pass through thin walls Tunnelling Clamp dt, sub-steps or a swept test 3.02 Jumps reach different heights on different computers Variable time step A fixed time step 3.04 The game freezes after a slow frame The spiral of death Limit steps per frame or clamp the frame time 3.04 The interface scrolls with the world Drawn inside BeginMode2D Draw it after EndMode2D 2.03, 4.01 Clicks select the wrong object in a scrolled world Mouse position used without the camera GetScreenToWorld2D 4.01 Thin lines between tiles when zoomed Rounding and filtering at tile edges Whole-pixel positions, point filtering, extruded tile sheets 4.02 The view flips when looking straight up Pitch not clamped Clamp pitch to ±89° 5.02 A render texture is drawn upside down OpenGL textures are flipped Negative source height 5.05 A light shader's light is mirrored vertically gl_FragCoord measures y from the bottom Pass screenHeight - y 5.04 Shader changes have no effect The shader failed to compile and raylib fell back to the default Read the compile error in the log 5.04 Settings or saves are not written in Program Files Windows does not allow writing there Save in %APPDATA% 6.01 No sound in the web build Browsers start audio only after a user action A "click to start" screen 6.02

title: Glossary
body: Every term from the course, in alphabetical order. The lesson that introduces each one is in brackets. Term Meaning --- --- A\ A path search that expands the most promising cell first, using the cost so far plus an estimate of the cost remaining. (4.05) AABB Axis-aligned bounding box: a rectangle (or box in 3D) whose sides are parallel to the axes. (3.01) Accumulator In a fixed-step loop, the real time that has passed but has not been simulated yet. (3.04) Additive blending Drawing where colours add up, so overlaps glow brighter; used for fire, sparks and light. (4.03) Alpha A colour's opacity, 0 (invisible) to 255 (solid). In interpolation, how far between two steps the current time is. (1.03, 3.04) Atlas One texture holding many smaller pictures, such as the glyphs of a font or the tiles of a level. (2.03) Auto-tiling Choosing a wall's picture automatically from which of its neighbours are walls. (4.02) BFS Breadth-first search: explores cells in order of distance, finding shortest paths when every step costs the same. (4.05) Broad phase The cheap first step of collision detection that finds which pairs might touch. (3.05) Camera2D / Camera3D raylib's descriptions of which part of the world is shown and how. (4.01, 5.01) Checksum A number computed from a file's contents and stored with it, to detect damage. (6.01) Coyote time A short time after leaving a ledge during which a jump is still allowed. (3.03) Dead zone A range of input treated as zero (stick drift), or a box the player can move in without the camera following. (1.05, 4.01) Delta time (dt) The time the last frame took, used to make movement per second instead of per frame. (1.04) Dot product a · b : how much two directions agree; for normalised vectors, the cosine of the angle between them. (5.01) Emitter Something that creates particles, in bursts or at a steady rate. (4.03) Emscripten The compiler that turns C and C++ into WebAssembly so a game runs in a browser. (6.02) Fixed time step Simulating in equal steps regardless of the frame rate. (3.04) Flow field A grid of distances to one target, which any number of units can follow downhill. (4.05) Fragment shader A GPU program that runs once per pixel and chooses its colour. (5.04) Frame One pass of input, update and draw. (1.02) Game loop The loop every game runs: read input, update the world, draw it. (1.02) Jump buffering Remembering a jump press for a short time so it happens as soon as the player lands. (3.03) Juice Small effects that change how a game feels but not its rules: shake, flashes, particles, sounds. (4.03) Letterbox Scaling a picture to fit the screen and filling the rest with bars. (2.01, 5.05) Migration Converting data saved by an older version of the game into the current format. (6.01) Minimum translation vector The shortest move that separates two overlapping shapes. (3.02) Narrow phase The exact collision test, run only on the pairs the broad phase found. (3.05) Normal A direction perpendicular to a surface, pointing out of it. (3.02, 5.03) Parallax Background layers moving slower than the world to suggest depth. (4.01) Particle A small, short-lived object with a position, velocity and lifetime. (4.03) Pitch / yaw Looking up and down / turning left and right. (5.02) Pool A fixed block of pre-allocated objects reused instead of creating and destroying them. (4.03) Post-processing A shader applied to the whole finished frame. (5.05) Ray A start point and a direction; ray tests answer "what is in this direction?". (5.03) Render texture A texture you can draw into instead of the screen. (5.05) Semi-implicit Euler Updating velocity from acceleration first, then position from the new velocity. (1.04) Shader A small program that runs on the GPU for every vertex or pixel. (5.04) Slab method Testing a ray against a box as the overlap of three pairs of parallel planes. (5.03) Sound alias A second Sound that shares another's sample data, so both can play at once. (2.04) Spatial grid Cells that list the objects inside them, so only nearby objects are tested against each other. (3.05) Spiral of death Simulation steps taking longer than real time, making each frame slower than the last. (3.04) Sprite sheet One texture holding the frames of animations in a grid. (2.02) State machine A set of states, exactly one of them current, and the events that move between them. (2.05, 4.04) Swap and pop Removing an element by moving the last one into its place, when order does not matter. (4.03) Telegraphing Showing that an attack is coming so the player can react. (4.04) Texture2D A picture in video memory, ready to draw. (2.01) Tile map A grid of tile numbers describing a level. (4.02) Tint A colour multiplied into every pixel of a drawn texture. (2.01) Trauma A 0 to 1 value that events add to, driving screen shake. (4.01) Tunnelling A fast object passing completely through a thin one between two frames. (3.02) Uniform A value passed to a shader that is the same for every pixel of a draw call. (5.04) Working directory The folder relative paths start from; often not the folder of the .exe. (2.01, 6.02)

title: 1.01  What Reverse Engineering Is
where: Ground Rules, Tools and the PE Format
body: Reverse engineering is working out how a program works from the program itself, without its source. Why people do it - debugging, security, compatibility, preservation, learning - the ground rules about what you may examine, and how this course keeps every target your own. Working backwards A compiler turns source code into machine code and throws most of the meaning away: names of local variables, comments, the structure of classes, often whole functions that it inlined. Reverse engineering is working backwards from what is left, the machine code, the data, the program's behaviour, to an understanding of how it works. You already do a little of it every time you debug a Release build and the debugger shows assembly instead of your source, or when you read a crash dump. This course turns that into a skill. Why people do it - Debugging without source. A crash inside a library you only have as a DLL, a driver, or an old build of your own program whose source has changed since. - Security. Finding vulnerabilities so they can be fixed; analysing malware to understand what it does and how to detect and remove it; checking that a program does what its makers say. - Compatibility and interoperability. Reading a file format or protocol so your program can open the files or talk to the device. Wine, LibreOffice's support for old document formats and many game mods began this way. - Preservation. Keeping old software running after its company is gone: emulators, source ports of classic games, recovered file formats. - Learning. Seeing what the compiler really made of your code is the best way to understand optimisation, calling conventions and C++ objects. The ground rules Reverse engineering is a tool, and like any tool the question is what you point it at. Before you examine any program, ask: 1. Is it mine? Programs you wrote and compiled are always fine to take apart. Most of this course works on exactly those. 2. Do I have permission? Practice targets made to be reversed (crackmes, CTF challenges, this course's targets), bug bounty programs with published rules, and work your employer or client authorised in writing. 3. What does the licence say, and the law where I live? Many end-user licences forbid reverse engineering. Some countries give limited rights to do it anyway for interoperability or security research; the details differ by country and change over time. When it matters, the answer comes from a lawyer, not a forum post. 4. Does it affect other people? Anything that touches an online service, another player, or another person's computer or data is off limits without explicit permission, whatever the technique. This course never goes near defeating copy protection, cheating in online games, bypassing anti-cheat or anti-debugging systems, or getting into systems you do not own. Those are not only against the rules of the services involved; they hurt the people on the other side. !note Every target in this course is either a program you build yourself in Visual Studio or a practice target the course provides: byte arrays, simulated memory, file formats and a tiny virtual machine designed to be taken apart. What you need to know already You should be comfortable with C++ and have seen some x64 assembly: registers, mov , add , cmp , jumps, call and ret . The Assembly course or milestone 7 of the Game Development course covers that. Milestone 2 here starts with a refresher aimed at reading rather than writing. The Pointers and Memory course is useful background too: reverse engineering is mostly memory, offsets and pointers. How the course works Each lesson describes how the work is done with real tools on real programs, and the practice turns the core of each technique into code you write and test: parsing a PE file, finding functions, rebuilding a call stack, scanning memory, encoding jumps, disassembling instructions. By the end you will have written small versions of most of the tools you use. Check yourself quiz ? Which of these is a list of three legitimate reasons to reverse engineer a program? - Removing a game's licence check, debugging without source, and learning what the compiler produced + Debugging without source, analysing malware, and making a program work with a file format or protocol - Cheating in an online game, preserving old software, and finding vulnerabilities - Copying a competitor's product, analysing malware, and interoperability Debugging, security work, malware analysis, interoperability, preservation and learning are all legitimate. Each wrong list hides one reason that is not: defeating protection, cheating against other people, or copying someone's product. ? Which targets are always fine to reverse engineer? - Any program you have bought a licence for - Any program that can be downloaded for free + Programs you wrote and compiled yourself, and practice targets made to be reversed - Any program, as long as you do not share what you find A licence or a free download does not by itself permit reverse engineering; many licences forbid it. Your own programs and practice targets are the only targets that are always fine. ? Where does the final answer on whether a licence or law allows a particular piece of reverse engineering come from? - From the course, which lists what is allowed everywhere - From the program's README file or its website + From a lawyer who knows the law where you are - From whether the program has anti-debugging protection The rules differ between countries and between licences, so no general rule settles a particular case. That is why this course keeps every target your own.

title: 1.02  The Tools of the Trade
where: Ground Rules, Tools and the PE Format
body: Disassemblers and decompilers for static analysis, debuggers for dynamic analysis, hex editors, PE viewers and system monitors - what each kind of tool does, the free ones worth installing, and a first look at your own program in each. Two ways of looking Reverse engineering has two halves that you switch between all the time: - Static analysis : reading the program without running it. Its file, its machine code, its strings and data. - Dynamic analysis : running it and watching. Stepping through code, inspecting memory, recording what it touches. Static analysis sees everything but has to guess what values things have. Dynamic analysis sees real values but only the paths the program actually takes. Each answers the other's questions. Disassemblers and decompilers A disassembler turns machine code back into assembly text. A decompiler goes a step further and produces C-like pseudocode. Both build a database of the program: functions, cross-references, names and comments that you add as you understand things. Tool Notes --- --- Ghidra free and open source (from the NSA), disassembler and decompiler, scripting in Java and Python IDA Free the long-time industry standard; the free version decompiles x64 using a cloud service Binary Ninja modern, scriptable; a free cloud version Compiler Explorer (godbolt.org) not for binaries, but the best way to learn what source compiles into Decompiler output is a guess. It is usually close, sometimes wrong, and never has your original names. Treat it as a map, and check important details in the disassembly. Debuggers A debugger runs a program under control: breakpoints, single-stepping, viewing and changing registers and memory. Tool Notes --- --- Visual Studio debugger best with source and symbols; shows disassembly too (Debug Windows Disassembly) x64dbg free, open source, made for working without source; the usual choice for reversing on Windows WinDbg Microsoft's debugger; powerful command language, crash dumps, kernel debugging Looking at files and bytes - A hex editor (HxD, or ImHex, which also understands file structures) shows a file's raw bytes. - A PE viewer (PE-bear, CFF Explorer, or dumpbin /headers /imports from Visual Studio's Developer Command Prompt) shows the structure of .exe and .dll files: headers, sections, imports. - Strings tools (Sysinternals strings , or the strings window in Ghidra and x64dbg) list readable text in a file. Error messages and file names in a program tell you a lot before you read a single instruction. Watching behaviour The Sysinternals tools from Microsoft are essential: - Process Monitor records every file, registry and network operation a process makes. - Process Explorer shows each process's DLLs, handles, threads and memory. - API Monitor (third party) logs calls to Windows API functions with their arguments. A first look at your own program Build a small program in Visual Studio in Release configuration, so the optimiser has done its work: cpp-norun include <cstdio int score(int hits, int misses) { return hits 10 - misses 3; } int main(int argc, char ) { std::printf("score: %d\n", score(argc 4, argc)); } Then: 1. Open the .exe in a PE viewer and find its sections and its imports. You will see printf is not imported directly; the C runtime DLL ( ucrtbase.dll or vcruntime140.dll plus api-ms-win-crt- ) is. 2. Run strings on it: score: %d is there, among many strings from the runtime. 3. Open it in Ghidra or x64dbg and find main . You may find score has disappeared entirely: the optimiser inlined it and folded the arithmetic. That is the first lesson of reverse engineering: the binary is what the compiler made, not what you wrote. Keep the PDB (the symbol file Visual Studio writes beside the .exe ) out of the way when you practise. With it, every tool shows your function names; without it, you see what a reverse engineer normally sees. Check yourself quiz ? What can dynamic analysis tell you that static analysis cannot, and the other way round? - Dynamic shows all the code; static shows only the code that ran + Dynamic shows real values and paths taken; static sees all the code - Dynamic works only with source code; static works on binaries - Nothing: they are two names for running a disassembler Running the program (dynamic) gives you the actual values, but only on the paths that happened. Reading the binary (static) covers everything, including paths that did not run, but values have to be worked out. ? Why should decompiler output be checked against the disassembly for important details? - The disassembly is easier to read than the decompiled C - The decompiler only shows the first function of each file - The decompiler's C can be compiled back into the original program, so it must match exactly + The decompiler's C is a reconstruction and can be wrong; the disassembly is what the processor really runs A decompiler guesses types, loops and variables from the machine code. When a detail matters, the instructions are the ground truth. ? Which tool records every file and registry operation a process makes? - x64dbg + Process Monitor from Sysinternals - Ghidra - A hex editor Process Monitor watches the whole system's file, registry, process and network activity. x64dbg is a debugger, Ghidra a disassembler and decompiler. ? Why might a small function you wrote not appear at all in a Release build? - Release builds remove every function that is not exported - Release builds strip all function names, so it is hidden under another name + The optimiser inlined it into its caller and folded its code away - The linker moves small functions into a separate DLL Inlining copies a small function's body into the caller, and after optimising there may be nothing left to recognise as a separate function. A missing name alone would not remove the code.

title: Comparing two builds
body: A hex editor's compare view is one of the most used tools in reversing: build your program twice with one small change and compare the files to see exactly which bytes the change touched. Write its core: cpp struct Change { std::size_t offset; std::size_t length; }; std::vector<Change diffBytes(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & before, const std::vector<std::uint8_t & after); std::string describe(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & before, const std::vector<std::uint8_t & after, Change c); - diffBytes returns the runs of consecutive differing bytes, in order. If one file is longer, everything past the end of the shorter one counts as different (joined to a run that reaches the end of the shorter one). - describe formats one change as 0xOFFSET: BEFORE - AFTER : the offset in uppercase hex without padding, then the bytes of each side as two uppercase hex digits separated by spaces. A byte position that a side does not have is shown as -- . text 0x1A: 74 05 - EB 05 0x40: -- -- - 90 C3

title: 1.03  Inside a PE File
where: Ground Rules, Tools and the PE Format
body: Every .exe and .dll on Windows is a Portable Executable - a DOS header pointing at the PE headers, a file header, an optional header with the entry point, image base and data directories, and a table of sections. RVAs versus file offsets, and how to convert between them. One format for every program Windows programs and libraries, .exe , .dll , .sys , all use the Portable Executable (PE) format. It tells the Windows loader how to map the file into memory, where execution starts, which DLLs and functions it needs, and where everything is. Reading it is the first thing every reverse engineering tool does. text file offset 0 +---------------------------+ DOS header ("MZ") e_lfanew at 0x3C - PE headers DOS stub "This program cannot be run in DOS mode." e_lfanew +---------------------------+ "PE\0\0" signature File header (20 bytes) machine, number of sections Optional header (240) entry point, image base, data directories Section table 40 bytes per section +---------------------------+ .text (code) .rdata (constants, imports) .data (globals) .pdata, .rsrc, .reloc ... +---------------------------+ All numbers are little-endian. Every structure here is in winnt.h under names like IMAGE_DOS_HEADER and IMAGE_NT_HEADERS64 . The DOS header The file starts with the two bytes 4D 5A , "MZ", a leftover from MS-DOS that every PE still carries. Of the DOS header's fields only one still matters: the 4-byte e_lfanew at offset 0x3C , the file offset of the real PE headers. The NT headers At e_lfanew are the bytes 50 45 00 00 , "PE" and two zeros. Then: The file header ( IMAGE_FILE_HEADER , 20 bytes): Offset Size Field --- --- --- +0 2 Machine : 0x8664 for x64, 0x14C for 32-bit x86, 0xAA64 for ARM64 +2 2 NumberOfSections +4 4 TimeDateStamp : when it was linked (or a hash, in reproducible builds) +16 2 SizeOfOptionalHeader : 0xF0 for 64-bit images +18 2 Characteristics : flags such as "is a DLL" (0x2000) The optional header ( IMAGE_OPTIONAL_HEADER64 , despite the name always present) starts right after it. The fields you will use most: Offset Size Field --- --- --- +0 2 Magic : 0x20B means 64-bit (PE32+), 0x10B 32-bit +16 4 AddressOfEntryPoint : where execution starts, as an RVA +24 8 ImageBase : the preferred load address, typically 0x140000000 for an .exe +32 4 SectionAlignment : sections start on multiples of this in memory (0x1000) +36 4 FileAlignment : and on multiples of this in the file (0x200) +56 4 SizeOfImage : total size once loaded +70 2 DllCharacteristics : flags such as ASLR-compatible (0x40) +112 16 × 8 the data directories Each data directory is an RVA and a size pointing at a table the loader needs. The important ones by index: 0 exports, 1 imports, 2 resources, 3 exceptions ( .pdata ), 5 base relocations, 6 debug information, 12 the import address table. Sections The section table follows the optional header: NumberOfSections entries of 40 bytes ( IMAGE_SECTION_HEADER ): Offset Size Field --- --- --- +0 8 Name , padded with zeros: .text , .rdata , .data ... +8 4 VirtualSize : size in memory +12 4 VirtualAddress : where it starts in memory, as an RVA +16 4 SizeOfRawData : size in the file +20 4 PointerToRawData : where it starts in the file +36 4 Characteristics : code (0x20), read (0x40000000), write (0x80000000), execute (0x20000000) The usual sections: .text for code (read + execute), .rdata for constants, strings and import tables (read only), .data for globals (read + write), .pdata for exception unwinding information, .rsrc for resources such as icons, .reloc for relocations. A section can be bigger in memory than in the file: .data holds zero-initialised globals that take no space on disk, so its VirtualSize exceeds its SizeOfRawData and the loader fills the rest with zeros. RVAs and file offsets Almost every address inside a PE is a relative virtual address (RVA): an offset from wherever the image is loaded in memory. Loaded at ImageBase , the real address is ImageBase + RVA ; with ASLR, the actual base differs each run, but RVAs stay the same. Reading the file instead of memory, you need to turn an RVA into a file offset. Find the section that contains it, then: file offset = RVA − section.VirtualAddress + section.PointerToRawData text .rdata: VirtualAddress 0x3000, PointerToRawData 0x1E00 RVA 0x3450 - 0x3450 - 0x3000 + 0x1E00 = 0x2250 in the file If the RVA falls in the part of a section beyond SizeOfRawData (the zero-filled tail), it has no bytes in the file at all. RVAs below the first section point into the headers, which are mapped at the same offsets in the file. Check yourself quiz ? Where in a PE file do you find the offset of the PE headers? - In the first 4 bytes of the file, after MZ + In the 4-byte e_lfanew field at offset 0x3C of the DOS header - At the fixed offset 0x200 , where the first section starts - In the optional header's AddressOfEntryPoint The DOS header starts with MZ and, at 0x3C , holds e_lfanew : the file offset of the PE\0\0 signature and the headers after it. ? What does an optional header Magic of 0x20B mean? - The image is a DLL rather than an .exe - The image is 32-bit (PE32) + The image is 64-bit (PE32+) - The image has been packed 0x10B is PE32 (32-bit) and 0x20B is PE32+ (64-bit). Whether it is a DLL is a flag in the file header's characteristics. ? A section has VirtualAddress 0x2000 and PointerToRawData 0x600 . What file offset holds RVA 0x2480 ? - 0x2A80 - 0x480 + 0xA80 - 0x1E80 Subtract the section's RVA and add its file offset: 0x2480 - 0x2000 + 0x600 = 0xA80 . ? Why can a section's VirtualSize be larger than its SizeOfRawData ? + It holds zero-initialised data that takes no space in the file - The section is compressed in the file and expanded when loaded - The extra size is reserved for the debugger's breakpoints - VirtualSize is counted in bits and SizeOfRawData in bytes Data that starts as zero, such as uninitialised globals, need not be stored in the file. The loader maps the raw bytes and fills the rest of the section's memory with zeros.

title: Reading the PE headers
body: Read the headers of a 64-bit PE file from its bytes (lesson 1.03), and convert RVAs to file offsets: cpp struct Section { std::string name; std::uint32_t virtualAddress, virtualSize, rawPointer, rawSize, characteristics; }; struct Headers { std::uint16_t machine; std::uint32_t entryPoint; std::uint64_t imageBase; std::vector<Section sections; }; std::optional<Headers readHeaders(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & file); std::optional<std::uint32_t rvaToOffset(const Headers& h, std::uint32_t rva); readHeaders returns std::nullopt unless the file starts with MZ , has the PE\0\0 signature at e_lfanew (offset 0x3C), and an optional header magic of 0x20B , with every header inside the file. The section table starts right after the optional header, whose size is in the file header. Section names are up to 8 characters, without the zero padding. rvaToOffset finds the section with virtualAddress <= rva < virtualAddress + virtualSize and returns rva - virtualAddress + rawPointer , or std::nullopt if no section contains it or the RVA is past the section's rawSize (in its zero-filled tail).

title: 1.04  Imports, Exports and Relocations
where: Ground Rules, Tools and the PE Format
body: How a PE says which DLL functions it needs - import descriptors, the import name table and the import address table the loader fills in - how a DLL publishes its own functions in the export directory, and the base relocations that let an image load at any address. Imports tell a story A program reaches Windows and other libraries through imported functions. The import table lists every DLL and every function the program asked the linker for. Before reading any code, the imports alone tell you a great deal: - CreateFileW , ReadFile , WriteFile : it works with files. - RegOpenKeyExW , RegSetValueExW : it reads or writes the registry. - WSAStartup , connect , send , recv (from ws2_32.dll ): it talks over the network. - CreateProcessW , OpenProcess , ReadProcessMemory : it starts or inspects other processes. - Very few imports, just LoadLibraryA and GetProcAddress : it looks up what it needs at run time, which hides its intentions from this kind of reading. The import directory Data directory 1 points at an array of import descriptors ( IMAGE_IMPORT_DESCRIPTOR , 20 bytes each), one per DLL, ending with one that is all zeros: Offset Field --- --- +0 OriginalFirstThunk : RVA of the import name table (INT) +12 Name : RVA of the DLL's name, a zero-terminated string such as KERNEL32.dll +16 FirstThunk : RVA of the import address table (IAT) The INT is an array of 8-byte entries (in 64-bit images), ending with a zero entry. Each entry says which function is wanted: - If the top bit is set ( 0x8000000000000000 ), the low 16 bits are an ordinal : the function's number in the DLL's export table. - Otherwise it is the RVA of an IMAGE_IMPORT_BY_NAME : a 2-byte hint (a guess at the function's position in the DLL's name list) followed by the function's name as a zero-terminated string. In the file, the IAT holds the same entries as the INT. When the program loads, the loader looks up each function in its DLL and overwrites each IAT entry with the function's real address . Calls to imported functions in the code are indirect calls through the IAT: nasm-norun call qword ptr rip+0x1A2B ; the IAT slot for CreateFileW That is why a disassembler can label such calls by name: it knows which IAT slot holds which import. Exports A DLL publishes its own functions in the export directory (data directory 0, IMAGE_EXPORT_DIRECTORY ): Offset Field --- --- +12 Name : RVA of the DLL's own name +16 Base : the ordinal of the first function, usually 1 +20 NumberOfFunctions +24 NumberOfNames +28 AddressOfFunctions : RVA of an array of function RVAs +32 AddressOfNames : RVA of an array of name RVAs, sorted alphabetically +36 AddressOfNameOrdinals : RVA of an array of 2-byte indexes into the functions array Finding a function by name, as GetProcAddress does: search the sorted names; at the same position in the name-ordinals array is an index; at that index in the functions array is the function's RVA. A function can also be exported by ordinal only, with no name. If a function's RVA points inside the export directory itself, it is a forwarder : the "address" is really a string such as NTDLL.RtlAllocateHeap , telling the loader to look in another DLL. Many kernel32.dll exports are forwarded this way. Base relocations Code contains some absolute addresses, for example a pointer to a global stored in a table. They are computed assuming the image loads at ImageBase . With ASLR it usually loads elsewhere, so each such address must be adjusted by the difference. The base relocation table (data directory 5, usually the .reloc section) lists every place that needs it, grouped by 4 KB page: a block header with the page's RVA and the block size, then 2-byte entries whose top 4 bits are a type (10, IMAGE_REL_BASED_DIR64 , for a 64-bit address) and low 12 bits an offset within the page. The loader adds actualBase - ImageBase to the 8 bytes at each location. x64 code itself mostly uses RIP-relative addressing ( rip+0x1234 ), which needs no relocation at all; relocations are mostly for pointers stored in data. That is one reason x64 programs relocate cheaply. For a reverse engineer this matters when comparing a running program with its file: bytes at relocated locations differ between the two by exactly the load difference, and tools (and the byte patterns of milestone 4) must allow for it. Check yourself quiz ? What does the loader write into the import address table? - The names of the DLLs the program needs + The real addresses of the imported functions, replacing the name or ordinal entries - The program's own exported functions - The file offsets of the imported functions inside each DLL Before loading, each IAT slot looks like the import name table entry. The loader resolves each import and overwrites the slot with the function's address, which the code then calls through. ? An INT entry is 0x8000000000000014 . What does it import? - The function whose name is at RVA 0x14 - Function number 0x8000000000000014 in the export table + The function with ordinal 0x14 (20), because the top bit marks an import by ordinal - Nothing; the top bit marks the end of the table With the top bit clear, the entry is the RVA of a hint and name. With it set, the low bits are an ordinal. The table ends with an entry of 0. ? How does GetProcAddress find a function by name in the export directory? - It reads every function's code until it finds the name in a string - It looks the name up in the DLL's own import name table - It hashes the name and uses the hash as an index into the functions array + It searches the sorted names, then maps the match through the ordinals array The names array is sorted so it can be searched quickly. The name ordinals array, in the same order, gives the index into the functions array, which holds the RVA. ? Why do x64 programs need relatively few base relocations? - 64-bit programs always load at their preferred image base - The loader patches every instruction at load time instead + Most code is RIP-relative; only absolute pointers in data need fixing - x64 programs have no absolute addresses at all An address relative to the current instruction stays right wherever the image loads. Absolute pointers stored in data, like vtables and pointer tables, still need relocating.

title: Looking up exports
body: Do what GetProcAddress does, on a DLL image already loaded in memory (so every RVA is simply an index into image ): cpp struct Export { std::uint32_t rva; std::string forwarder; }; std::string dllName(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & image, std::uint32_t dirRva); std::optional<Export findByName(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & image, std::uint32_t dirRva, std::uint32_t dirSize, std::string_view name); std::optional<Export findByOrdinal(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & image, std::uint32_t dirRva, std::uint32_t dirSize, std::uint32_t ordinal); The export directory at dirRva is laid out as in lesson 1.04 ( Name at +12, Base at +16, NumberOfFunctions at +20, NumberOfNames at +24, then the three array RVAs at +28, +32 and +36). - dllName reads the zero-terminated name. - findByName finds the name in the sorted names array with a binary search (compare as std::strcmp would), takes the 2-byte index at the same position of the name-ordinals array, and returns the function RVA at that index. - findByOrdinal uses ordinal - Base as the index into the functions array. - In both, a missing name, an index outside the functions array or a function RVA of 0 gives std::nullopt . If the function RVA lies inside the export directory ( dirRva <= rva < dirRva + dirSize ), it is a forwarder : set forwarder to the string at that RVA.

title: 1.05  Triage - First Impressions of a Binary
match: 1.05 Triage - First Impressions of a Binary
where: Ground Rules, Tools and the PE Format
body: The first half hour with an unknown program - strings in ASCII and UTF-16, imports and exports, the compiler and runtime it was built with, the PDB path in its debug directory, resources, section entropy and the signs of packing - before reading any code. Look before you read Opening an unknown program straight in a disassembler and starting at the entry point is the slow way. A short triage first tells you what kind of program it is, what it is likely to do, and where to start reading. Everything here is static and quick. Strings Text in a program is often its most informative content: error messages, file names, registry keys, URLs, format strings, debug messages left in by the developers. Windows programs store text in two encodings, and you need both: - ASCII / UTF-8 : one byte per character, 48 65 6C 6C 6F for "Hello". - UTF-16LE : two bytes per character, the Windows "wide" strings used by every W function: 48 00 65 00 6C 00 6C 00 6F 00 . A strings tool scans the file for runs of printable characters (usually at least 4 or 5 long) in both forms. In a disassembler, each string becomes a landmark: find "Invalid licence file" and look at the code that refers to it, and you are in the licence check; find %s\\saves\\slot%d.dat and you have found the save code. Imports and exports The import table (lesson 1.04) is a summary of capabilities. Sort the imports by DLL and read the list: DLL Suggests --- --- ws2_32.dll , winhttp.dll , wininet.dll network advapi32.dll (Reg , Crypt ) registry, services, older cryptography bcrypt.dll , ncrypt.dll cryptography d3d11.dll , dxgi.dll , opengl32.dll graphics user32.dll (CreateWindowEx, GetMessage) a window and a message loop dbghelp.dll symbol handling, crash dumps A DLL's exports are its whole public interface, often with descriptive names. Compiler and runtime How a program was built changes what its code looks like, so identify it early: - Rich header : MSVC-linked files have an undocumented block between the DOS stub and the PE header (the word Rich marks its end) listing the tool versions used. - Imports of the runtime : vcruntime140.dll and api-ms-win-crt- mean Visual C++ 2015 or later; msvcrt.dll with MinGW-style names means GCC; libstdc++ names mean GCC or Clang with the GNU library. - Characteristic code : MSVC's __security_check_cookie calls at function ends (the /GS check from the Pointers and Memory course), its exception tables in .pdata . - Programs written in .NET are a different world: a tiny native stub and a large block of .NET metadata and bytecode, best opened with a .NET decompiler (ILSpy, dnSpy) instead. The debug directory Data directory 6 points at debug information. For MSVC builds it usually contains a CodeView record with the path of the PDB file as it was on the build machine: text C:\Users\dev\source\repos\Inventory\x64\Release\Inventory.pdb That gives you the project's name and sometimes the developer's folder layout. If the matching PDB is available (Microsoft publishes them for Windows' own DLLs on its symbol server), every tool can show real function names: always look before working without them. Resources The .rsrc section holds icons, dialogs, menus, string tables, version information (product name, company, version number), and sometimes whole embedded files. Resource Hacker or PE viewers list them. Entropy and packing Entropy measures how random a block of bytes looks, from 0 bits per byte (all the same byte) to 8 (perfectly random). Ordinary machine code sits around 5 to 6.5; text lower; compressed or encrypted data close to 8. A section with entropy near 8, together with very few imports and an entry point outside .text , usually means the program is packed : compressed or encrypted, with a small stub that unpacks the real code at run time. Packers are used to make programs smaller and, often, to make them harder to analyse; malware uses them heavily. Static analysis of a packed file mostly sees the stub; the real code appears only in memory, after it unpacks. Shannon entropy over a block of bytes: H = − Σ p(b) × log₂ p(b), over the byte values b that occur, where p(b) is how often b occurs divided by the block size. A triage checklist 1. File type, 32 or 64 bit, .exe or .dll, native or .NET. 2. Compiler and runtime. 3. Sections: names, sizes, permissions, entropy. Anything writable and executable is unusual. 4. Imports, grouped by DLL. Exports, if a DLL. 5. Strings, both encodings, skimmed for landmarks. 6. Debug directory and PDB path; are symbols available? 7. Resources and version information. Write down what you find. The next step, reading code, starts from these landmarks. Check yourself quiz ? How is the word "Hi" stored as a UTF-16LE string? - 48 69 - 00 48 00 69 + 48 00 69 00 - 48 69 00 00 UTF-16 uses two bytes per character here, and little-endian puts the low byte first, so each ASCII letter is followed by a zero byte. 00 48 00 69 would be big-endian. ? A section has entropy 7.95, the program imports only LoadLibraryA and GetProcAddress , and its entry point is in a section called .upx1 . What do you suspect? - It is a debug build with full symbols - It is a .NET program, which always looks like this + It is packed: the real code is compressed or encrypted and unpacked at run time - It is a DLL with no exports Entropy near 8 means compressed or encrypted bytes, two imports are enough to load everything else by hand, and .upx is the UPX packer's section name. ? Where can you find the PDB path a program was built with? - In the DOS stub's message + In the CodeView record of the debug directory (data directory 6) - In the import directory, next to the DLL names - In the resources, under the version information The debug directory points at a CodeView ( RSDS ) record that holds the PDB's GUID, age and the full path it was written to on the build machine. ? Why look at strings before reading code? - Strings are the only part of a program that is not compiled - Reading the strings decrypts the rest of the program - The strings list shows every function name in the program + They are landmarks: the code that uses them is the related logic Error messages, file names and format strings point the way. Finding where a string like "save file is corrupt" is used leads straight to the code that checks the save file.

title: Strings and entropy
where: 1.05 Triage - First Impressions of a Binary
body: Two triage tools from lesson 1.05: cpp struct FoundString { std::size_t offset; std::string text; bool wide; }; std::vector<FoundString findStrings(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & bytes, std::size_t minLength); double entropy(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & bytes, std::size_t begin, std::size_t size); findStrings finds text of at least minLength characters, where a character is a printable byte from 0x20 to 0x7E: - ASCII strings: runs of printable bytes. - Wide (UTF-16LE) strings: runs of pairs "printable byte, then 0x00", starting at any offset. text holds just the characters ( "Wide" , not the zeros), and wide is true. - Results are sorted by offset; at the same offset an ASCII string comes first. Report each whole run once, not the shorter runs inside it. entropy is the Shannon entropy in bits per byte of size bytes starting at begin : -sum(p log2(p)) over the byte values present, where p is that value's count divided by size . An empty range has entropy 0.

title: A strings finder
where: Ground Rules, Tools and the PE Format projects
