title: A PE inspector
where: Ground Rules, Tools and the PE Format projects
body: Build the core of a PE viewer like PE-bear or dumpbin : load a 64-bit PE file from its bytes, list its sections, find which section an RVA belongs to, and list every import. cpp struct Section { std::string name; std::uint32_t virtualAddress, virtualSize, rawPointer, rawSize, characteristics; }; struct Import { std::string dll; std::string function; std::uint16_t ordinal; }; class PeFile { public: bool load(std::vector<std::uint8_t bytes); std::uint32_t entryPoint() const; std::uint64_t imageBase() const; const std::vector<Section & sections() const; std::optional<std::uint32_t rvaToOffset(std::uint32_t rva) const; std::string sectionOf(std::uint32_t rva) const; std::string permissions(const Section& s) const; std::vector<Import imports() const; }; - load keeps the bytes and reads the headers as in lesson 1.03; it returns false (and the object holds nothing) for anything that is not a valid 64-bit PE. - rvaToOffset as in the practice; sectionOf names the section containing an RVA, or returns "" . - permissions gives three characters for a section: r or - , w or - , x or - (read 0x40000000, write 0x80000000, execute 0x20000000). - imports reads the import directory (data directory 1, whose RVA is at offset 120 of the optional header): one descriptor of 20 bytes per DLL, until an all-zero one. For each, read the DLL name, then the 8-byte thunks of its import name table ( OriginalFirstThunk , or FirstThunk when that is 0) until a zero thunk. A thunk with the top bit set is an import by ordinal ( function empty, ordinal the low 16 bits); otherwise it is the RVA of a 2-byte hint and the name ( ordinal 0). Imports are listed in file order. Any RVA that cannot be turned into a file offset stops the reading cleanly, returning what was read so far.

title: 2.01  x64 for Readers
body: The x64 you need to read compiled code rather than write it - registers and their smaller parts, the handful of instructions that make up most programs, flags and conditional jumps, and the Microsoft x64 calling convention that tells you where every argument and return value is. Reading, not writing Writing assembly means choosing instructions. Reading it means recognising patterns quickly, and compiled code uses a surprisingly small set of them. This lesson is a refresher aimed at reading the output of MSVC, in the Intel syntax that Visual Studio, x64dbg, WinDbg and Ghidra all show: destination first. nasm-norun mov rax, qword ptr rcx+10h ; rax = the 8 bytes at rcx + 0x10 (Disassemblers write hex either as 10h or 0x10 . They mean the same.) Registers Sixteen 64-bit general registers. Each has smaller views of its low part: 64 32 16 8 Usual role in compiled code --- --- --- --- --- rax eax ax al return value, scratch rcx ecx cx cl 1st argument, this rdx edx dx dl 2nd argument rbx ebx bx bl kept across calls rsp esp sp spl stack pointer rbp ebp bp bpl kept across calls, sometimes frame pointer rsi , rdi esi , edi kept across calls; string copies r8 , r9 r8d , r9d r8w r8b 3rd and 4th arguments r10 , r11 scratch r12 to r15 kept across calls Plus rip , the instruction pointer, and sixteen 128-bit xmm0 to xmm15 registers for floating point and SIMD. One rule catches everyone: writing a 32-bit register clears the top 32 bits of the 64-bit one. mov eax, 1 sets all of rax to 1, and xor eax, eax is the compiler's favourite way to zero rax (it is shorter than xor rax, rax ). Writing 8 or 16-bit parts leaves the rest alone. The instructions you will see most Instruction Does --- --- mov a, b copy movzx , movsx , movsxd copy a small value into a bigger register, zero- or sign-extending lea a, expr compute the address expression, without reading memory; also used for arithmetic: lea eax, rcx+rcx 4 is eax = ecx 5 add , sub , imul , neg , inc , dec arithmetic and , or , xor , not , shl , shr , sar bits; sar is a signed shift, often division by a power of two cmp a, b compute a - b , set the flags, keep nothing else test a, b compute a & b , set the flags; test eax, eax asks "is eax zero (or negative)?" jcc target jump if a condition holds (table below) jmp target jump always call target , ret function call and return push , pop save and restore registers on the stack cmovcc , setcc conditional move or set a byte from the flags, without jumping Flags and conditional jumps cmp and test set flags; the conditional jump that follows reads them. The jump names say whether the comparison was signed or unsigned , which tells you the type of the variables: Signed Unsigned After cmp a, b , jumps if --- --- --- jl jb a < b jle jbe a <= b jg ja a b jge jae a = b je / jz a == b jne / jnz a != b jl / jg mean the source compared int s; jb / ja mean unsigned , sizes or pointers. A bounds check written as one unsigned comparison, cmp ecx, 10; jae out_of_range , catches negative indexes too, because they look huge when unsigned. The Microsoft x64 calling convention Every function call on 64-bit Windows follows one convention, so you always know where the arguments are: - The first four arguments go in rcx , rdx , r8 , r9 , or in xmm0 to xmm3 if they are float or double . The position counts, not the type: in f(int a, double b, int c) , a is in rcx , b in xmm1 , c in r8 . - Further arguments go on the stack. The caller always reserves 32 bytes of shadow space just above the return address for the callee to save the four register arguments in, so the 5th argument is at rsp+28h on entry to the function (8 for the return address, 0x20 of shadow space), the 6th at rsp+30h , and so on. - The return value comes back in rax , or xmm0 for floating point. - rax , rcx , rdx , r8 to r11 and xmm0 to xmm5 are volatile : a call may destroy them. rbx , rbp , rdi , rsi , r12 to r15 and xmm6 to xmm15 are non-volatile : a function that uses them must save and restore them, which is exactly what its prologue's pushes are. - For a member function, this is the hidden first argument, in rcx . So when you see a call, look just before it for writes to rcx , rdx , r8 and r9 : those are its arguments. Just after it, a read of eax or rax is using its result. nasm-norun mov r8d, 3 ; third argument: 3 lea rdx, rsp+40h ; second argument: the address of a local mov rcx, rbx ; first argument: whatever rbx holds call ReadConfig test eax, eax ; did it return 0? je failed Check yourself quiz ? After mov eax, 0FFFFFFFFh , what is rax ? - 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF , because the value is sign-extended - Whatever the upper 32 bits held before, with the low 32 bits set to FFFFFFFF + 0x00000000FFFFFFFF , because writing a 32-bit register clears the upper 32 bits - 0x00000000000000FF , because eax holds one byte On x64, a write to a 32-bit register zero-extends into the full 64-bit register. Writes to 8- and 16-bit parts like al and ax are the ones that leave the rest alone. ? In f(double x, int y, int z) , which registers hold y and z ? - rcx and rdx , the first two integer registers + rdx and r8 , positions 2 and 3, whatever the type of the first argument - xmm1 and xmm2 , following the double - ecx and edx , because they are 32-bit The Microsoft x64 convention assigns registers by position: position 1 is rcx or xmm0 , position 2 rdx or xmm1 , position 3 r8 or xmm2 . A double in position 1 uses up rcx 's slot too. ? Where is the 5th argument of a function on entry to it? - In r10 , the next integer register after r9 - At rsp+8 , just above the return address + At rsp+28h , above the return address and shadow space - At rsp+20h , just after the shadow space Only four arguments go in registers. The caller leaves 0x20 bytes of shadow space above the 8-byte return address, so the 5th argument starts at 8 + 0x20 = 0x28. ? A comparison is followed by jb . What does that suggest about the variables? + They are unsigned (or pointers or sizes), because jb is the unsigned "below" - They are signed integers, because jb means "jump if bigger" - They are floating-point values - Nothing: jb and jl are the same jump jb / ja test the carry flag, for unsigned comparisons. Signed comparisons use jl / jg . That choice is one of the best clues to a variable's type.

title: Where are the arguments?
body: Apply the Microsoft x64 calling convention (lesson 2.01): cpp enum class Kind { Integer, Floating }; std::vector<std::string argumentLocations(const std::vector<Kind & args); std::string returnLocation(Kind result); bool isVolatile(const std::string& reg); - argumentLocations gives where each argument is on entry to the function. Position decides the register: the first four go in rcx , rdx , r8 , r9 if they are integers or pointers, or xmm0 to xmm3 if floating point. Later arguments are on the stack: the 5th at rsp+0x28 , the 6th at rsp+0x30 , and so on in steps of 8, whatever their kind. - returnLocation is rax for integers and xmm0 for floating point. - isVolatile is true for registers a call may destroy: rax , rcx , rdx , r8 to r11 , and xmm0 to xmm5 . Everything else ( rbx , rbp , rdi , rsi , rsp , r12 to r15 , xmm6 to xmm15 ) is non-volatile.

title: 2.02  Recognising Functions
body: Where functions start and end in a binary without symbols - prologues that save registers and reserve stack, epilogues, leaf functions, int3 padding, the .pdata table that lists every function, thunks and tail calls, and following the C runtime's start-up code to main. No labels in machine code A .exe does not record where one function ends and the next begins. The bytes run on; only the call instructions and a few tables tell you where functions are. Disassemblers find functions with a mix of the evidence below, and when they get it wrong (and they sometimes do) you need to recognise the signs yourself. Prologues A function that calls others or uses non-volatile registers starts by setting itself up: nasm-norun mov qword ptr rsp+8 , rbx ; save rbx in the shadow space the caller reserved push rdi ; save rdi sub rsp, 30h ; reserve stack: 0x20 shadow space for calls it makes, plus locals The common forms in MSVC output: Bytes Instruction --- --- 48 89 5C 24 08 mov rsp+8 , rbx (save to shadow space) 40 53 push rbx with a do-nothing REX prefix, used so the instruction is 2 bytes for hot-patching 55 , 56 , 57 push rbp , push rsi , push rdi 41 54 ... 41 57 push r12 ... push r15 48 83 EC 28 sub rsp, 28h (small frame) 48 81 EC 50 01 00 00 sub rsp, 150h (large frame) The stack must be 16-byte aligned at every call . On entry the return address has just been pushed, so rsp is 8 more than a multiple of 16; that is why frames are odd multiples of 8 when nothing else is pushed: sub rsp, 28h , 38h , 48h . Functions with large local arrays first call __chkstk (it touches each new page of stack in order, for the guard page of the Pointers and Memory course). Functions with buffers start with the /GS cookie: mov rax, __security_cookie ; xor rax, rsp; mov rsp+... , rax , and end with the matching check. Epilogues The end undoes the start, in reverse: nasm-norun mov rbx, qword ptr rsp+40h ; restore rbx (8 + 30h + 8 further up now) add rsp, 30h pop rdi ret There can be several epilogues in one function, one per return , or one shared epilogue that every path jumps to. Leaf functions A function that calls nothing and needs no non-volatile registers needs no frame at all: nasm-norun lea eax, rcx+rdx 2 ; return a + b 2 ret Small leaf functions are common, and they often have no recognisable prologue. In Release builds many of them disappear entirely, inlined into their callers. int3 padding MSVC starts functions on 16-byte boundaries and fills the gaps between them with CC bytes, the int3 breakpoint instruction. A run of CC s after a ret or a jmp is a reliable sign that a new function follows. ( CC can also appear inside an instruction, as part of an immediate or displacement, so it is evidence, not proof.) .pdata: the list of functions On x64 Windows there is a better source. The exception directory (data directory 3, the .pdata section) holds a RUNTIME_FUNCTION entry for every function that has a frame: three RVAs, the function's start, its end, and its unwind information. Windows needs these to unwind the stack for exceptions and to walk call stacks in a debugger, so they are always present and always right. Disassemblers use them first; leaf functions without frames are the only ones missing. The unwind information also records exactly what the prologue does (which registers were pushed, how big the frame is), which is how a debugger rebuilds a call stack without frame pointers. Thunks and tail calls - A thunk is a tiny function that only jumps somewhere else: jmp qword ptr __imp_CreateFileW for an import, or a stub that adjusts this and jumps to the real member function. - A tail call is a function ending with jmp OtherFunction instead of call and ret : the optimiser reuses the frame. Do not mistake that jmp for a jump inside the same function. Finding main The entry point in the PE header is not your main . In an MSVC program it is mainCRTStartup , which sets up the C runtime, runs global constructors and then calls main . A reliable route: from the entry point, follow the jump to __scrt_common_main_seh ; near its end it calls _get_initial_narrow_environment , __p___argv and __p___argc and then a function with those results in r8 , rdx and ecx : that call is main(argc, argv, envp) . For a GUI program it is WinMain , called with the instance handle in rcx . With practice, finding main takes a minute. Check yourself quiz ? Why does a frame of sub rsp, 28h make sense when nothing was pushed? - 28h is exactly the size of the function's locals + It realigns rsp to 16 and includes the 0x20 shadow space - Every function must reserve exactly 40 bytes on Windows - It reserves space for the function's return value On entry rsp is 8 past a multiple of 16, because the call pushed a return address. 0x20 of shadow space for the calls it makes plus 8 for alignment is 0x28. ? What does a run of CC bytes after a ret usually mean? - The function's data, stored after its code - A breakpoint set by a debugger that is attached + int3 padding, so a function likely starts after it - The stack cookie checked by /GS The linker pads functions to aligned starting addresses with int3 (0xCC), so the next non- CC byte is likely a function start. In a file on disk these are filler, not live breakpoints. ? Why is the .pdata table reliable for finding functions? - The compiler writes it only in debug builds, with full names - It is the import table for the program's own functions + Windows needs it to unwind the stack for exceptions - It is a copy of the PDB that is always embedded in the file .pdata lists each function's start, end and unwind information. If it were wrong, exceptions would crash, so every function with a frame has a correct entry even in Release builds without symbols. ? A function ends with jmp SomeFunction instead of ret . What is it? - A loop back to the start of the same function - An infinite loop that never returns to anyone - A function that crashes on purpose when it ends + A tail call: SomeFunction returns to the original caller When a function's last act is to call another and return its result, the compiler can jump instead and reuse the frame. The callee's ret then returns to whoever called the first function.

title: Finding functions in raw code
body: Find likely function starts in a block of MSVC x64 machine code with no symbols, using the two kinds of evidence from lesson 2.02: cpp bool looksLikePrologue(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & code, std::size_t at); std::vector<std::size_t findFunctions(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & code); looksLikePrologue is true when the bytes at at begin with one of these ( ?? is any byte), with every byte of the pattern inside the buffer: Pattern Instruction --- --- 55 , 53 , 56 , 57 push rbp , push rbx , push rsi , push rdi 40 53 , 40 55 , 40 56 , 40 57 the same pushes with a REX prefix 41 54 , 41 55 , 41 56 , 41 57 push r12 to push r15 48 83 EC ?? sub rsp, imm8 48 81 EC ?? ?? ?? ?? sub rsp, imm32 48 89 ?? 24 ?? or 4C 89 ?? 24 ?? where the third byte's bits match 01 ??? 100 saving a register at rsp+imm8 findFunctions returns, in increasing order, every offset that is a candidate and looks like a prologue. Offset 0 is always a candidate; so is any offset whose byte is not CC but the byte before it is CC (the end of int3 padding).

title: 2.03  Branches, Loops and Switches
body: What if, else, && and , for and while loops and switch statements compile into, how to read a function as a graph of basic blocks, and the jump tables that big switch statements become. Basic blocks Inside a function, code runs straight down until a jump. A basic block is a run of instructions with one way in (its first instruction) and one way out (its last). Every disassembler shows a function as a graph of blocks joined by arrows, the control flow graph , and reading that graph is most of reading a function. A new block starts: - at the function's first instruction; - at every jump target; - right after every jump or ret (the fall-through of a conditional jump, or simply code that something else jumps to). A call does not end a block: the call returns and execution carries on. if and else The compiler usually inverts the condition and jumps over the "then" part: cpp-norun if (health <= 0) die(); else heal(5); nasm-norun test ecx, ecx ; health in ecx jg else_part ; NOT (health <= 0): skip the then part call die jmp done else_part: mov ecx, 5 call heal done: When you read test / cmp followed by a jump, the jump is usually the opposite of the condition in the source. && and Short-circuit operators become a chain of jumps. if (a 0 && b 0) f(); jumps past f as soon as either test fails: nasm-norun test ecx, ecx jle skip test edx, edx jle skip call f skip: jumps into the body as soon as one test succeeds. Two jumps to the same place mean && ; a jump into the body followed by a test of the next condition means . Loops A for or while loop has a backwards jump: a jump to an address earlier in the function. That is the quickest way to spot a loop in a listing. cpp-norun for (int i = 0; i < count; ++i) total += values i ; Optimised compilers usually test once before the loop and then use a do-while shape with the test at the bottom, which saves a jump per iteration: nasm-norun xor eax, eax ; total test edx, edx ; count <= 0? skip the loop entirely jle done xor r8d, r8d ; i top: add eax, dword ptr rcx+r8 4 inc r8 cmp r8, rdx jl top ; backwards: the loop done: ret Recognise the parts: initialisation before, the body, the increment, the compare and the backward jump. Optimised loops are often unrolled (the body repeated several times per jump) or vectorised (SIMD instructions handling four or eight elements at once), with a small extra loop for the leftovers. Switch statements A switch with a few cases becomes a chain of comparisons. A switch with many cases over a dense range of values becomes a jump table : an array of addresses indexed by the value. nasm-norun sub ecx, 1 ; cases 1..5: make the index start at 0 cmp ecx, 4 ja default_case ; unsigned: also catches values below 1 lea rdx, __ImageBase ; the module's base address movsxd rcx, ecx mov eax, dword ptr rdx+rcx 4+3A40h ; table of 32-bit RVAs at RVA 0x3A40 add rax, rdx ; RVA + base = address of the case jmp rax MSVC stores the table as RVAs (4 bytes each) and adds the image base, so the table needs no relocations. Reading the table gives you the address of every case. The ja before it handles every value outside the table, including negative ones, with one unsigned comparison. Conditional moves Small if s are often compiled without jumps at all: nasm-norun cmp ecx, edx mov eax, edx cmovl eax, ecx ; eax = (ecx < edx) ? ecx : edx - std::min cmovcc and setcc ( setl al : set al to 1 if less) are branch-free, so they leave the control flow graph simpler than the source was. Check yourself quiz ? What three things start a new basic block? - Every call , every mov to memory, and every ret + The first instruction, jump targets, and the instruction after a jump or ret - Every instruction that changes the flags register - The start of each line of the original source code A basic block runs straight through with no way in except its top and no way out except its bottom. So jumps and their targets mark the edges. ? How do you spot a loop quickly in a listing? - Look for a call to the same function - Look for a cmp instruction + Look for a jump to an earlier address: a backwards jump - Look for a ret in the middle of the function Forward jumps skip code (if and else); a jump back to code already passed repeats it. A call to itself would be recursion, not a loop. ? A switch is compiled to cmp ecx, 4 / ja default followed by an indirect jmp . What is the ja for? - It jumps straight to the code for case 4 - It checks that the jump table has been loaded + It sends values outside the table, negatives too, to default - It handles the cases that share the same code Values 0 to 4 index the table. As an unsigned comparison, a negative value looks huge and is also "above" 4, so one check guards both ends. ? Why does MSVC store switch tables as 32-bit RVAs? - The processor cannot jump to a 64-bit address + They are half the size and need no relocations - So that the switch can have at most 32 cases - So that the table can be stored in the PE headers An RVA stays right wherever the image loads, so no base relocation is needed for each entry; the code adds the image base at run time. And each entry is 4 bytes instead of 8.

title: Basic blocks
body: Split a function's instructions into basic blocks and connect them, as a disassembler does before drawing a graph (lesson 2.03). Instructions are given already decoded: cpp enum class Op { Plain, Call, Jump, Branch, Return }; struct Insn { std::uint32_t address; std::uint32_t length; Op op; std::uint32_t target; }; struct Block { std::uint32_t start; std::uint32_t end; std::vector<std::uint32_t successors; }; std::vector<Block basicBlocks(const std::vector<Insn & code); code is in address order with no gaps. Jump is an unconditional jmp , Branch a conditional jump, Call a call (its target is another function), Return a ret . target only matters for Jump and Branch . - A block starts at the first instruction, at every Jump / Branch target that is one of the instructions, and at the instruction after any Jump , Branch or Return . - A block's end is the address just past its last instruction. - Successors : a block ending in Jump goes to its target; one ending in Branch goes to its target and falls through to the next instruction; one ending in Return has none; any other block falls through to the next block. A target outside the function (a tail call) is not a successor. Successors are sorted with no duplicates, and fall-through past the last instruction does not count. - Blocks are returned sorted by start.

title: 2.04  Data in Machine Code
body: Recognising locals, globals, struct members, arrays and strings in disassembly - what the addressing modes reveal, how sizes and signedness show the types, floating point in xmm registers, and rebuilding a struct by collecting every offset the code uses. Addresses tell you what the data is Every memory operand in x64 has the form base + index scale + displacement , and the shape of it is a strong hint about the data being reached: Operand Usually means --- --- rsp+40h , rbp-10h a local variable or spilled value in the current frame rip+1A2Bh (shown as a name like dword_140005000 ) a global or a constant in the image rcx+18h a member at offset 0x18 of the struct rcx points at rax+rdx 4 element rdx of an array of 4-byte things starting at rax rax+rdx 8+10h element rdx of an array of 8-byte things that starts at offset 0x10 of a struct rcx+rdx byte rdx of a buffer, or an array of 1-byte things The scale (1, 2, 4 or 8) is the element size. A stride that is not a power of two shows up as a multiplication first: imul rdx, rdx, 1Ch then rax+rdx is an array of 28-byte structs. Sizes and signedness The size of a memory access gives the size of the field: Access Size --- --- byte ptr , al , movzx eax, byte ptr 1 word ptr , ax 2 dword ptr , eax 4 qword ptr , rax 8 Signedness shows in how a small value is widened and compared: - movsx / movsxd (sign-extend) and jl / jg mean signed: char , short , int . - movzx (zero-extend) and jb / ja mean unsigned: unsigned char , bool , uint16_t , sizes. An 8-byte value that is later used as rax+... is a pointer. One that is passed to printf with %llu is a number. Floating point float and double live in xmm registers and use their own instructions: Instruction Means --- --- movss xmm0, dword ptr rcx+10h load a float movsd xmm0, qword ptr rcx+10h load a double addss , mulss , subsd , divsd ... arithmetic; ss = single (float), sd = double comiss , ucomisd compare, then ja / jb (floating point compares use the unsigned conditions) cvtsi2ss , cvttss2si int to float, float to int (truncating) So a 4-byte field read with movss is a float , not an int . Strings and constants Code that uses a string literal loads its address with a RIP-relative lea : nasm-norun lea rcx, rip+2F1Ah ; disassemblers show: lea rcx, aSaveFailedS "Save failed: %s" call printf That is how the strings you found in triage (lesson 1.05) lead you to code: ask the disassembler for cross-references to the string, and it lists every instruction that loads its address. Floating-point constants also live in .rdata : mulss xmm0, dword ptr __real@3f000000 is "multiply by 0.5" (0x3F000000 is the bits of 0.5f, readable with lesson 2.05's bit tricks from the Pointers and Memory course). Rebuilding a struct Without source, you reconstruct a struct by collecting every access through the same pointer. Suppose in a function where rcx is a Player you see: nasm-norun mov eax, dword ptr rcx+0Ch ; 4 bytes at 0x0C movss xmm0, dword ptr rcx+10h ; a float at 0x10 movss xmm1, dword ptr rcx+14h ; a float at 0x14 movzx edx, byte ptr rcx+18h ; an unsigned byte at 0x18 mov r8, qword ptr rcx+20h ; 8 bytes at 0x20, used later as r8+... : a pointer Written down as a struct, with gaps kept as padding: cpp-norun struct Player { std::uint8_t unknown_00 0x0C ; std::int32_t field_0C; float field_10; float field_14; // two floats in a row: probably x, y std::uint8_t field_18; // compared with 0 and 1 elsewhere: a bool std::uint8_t pad_19 7 ; Thing field_20; }; Then you rename fields as you learn what they are: field_10 and field_14 are written by the movement code, so they become x and y . Every disassembler lets you define such structs and apply them, so the listing shows rcx+Player.x instead of rcx+10h . The reconstruction grows as you read more functions that use the same struct, and its size usually comes from the new or malloc call that creates it: mov ecx, 30h; call operator new means the object is 0x30 bytes. Check yourself quiz ? What does rax+rdx 8 most likely access? - The 8th byte of the struct at rax - A member at offset rdx of a struct whose size is 8 + Element rdx of an array of 8-byte values (often pointers) that starts at rax - A local variable 8 bytes below the stack pointer Base plus index times scale is the array addressing mode: rax is the array, rdx the index, and the scale 8 the element size. ? A 4-byte field is loaded with movss . What type is it? - int + float - double - char movss moves a scalar single-precision float into an xmm register. A double would use movsd , and integers and pointers use general registers. ? A byte field is read with movzx and compared with jb . Signed or unsigned? - Signed, because movzx keeps the sign + Unsigned - It cannot be told from the code movzx zero-extends, which is how unsigned values are widened ( movsx sign-extends), and jb is an unsigned comparison. Both clues agree. ? How do you find the size of a heap-allocated struct you are reconstructing? - Add up the sizes of the members you have seen accessed - Read it from the PE header's data directories + Look at the size passed to the allocation that creates it - Divide the heap's total size by the number of objects For example mov ecx, 30h before a call to operator new . Members you have seen accessed only give a lower bound; some may never be touched in the code you read.

title: Rebuilding a struct from accesses
body: Turn a list of memory accesses seen through one pointer into a C++ struct definition, as lesson 2.04 does by hand: cpp struct Access { std::uint32_t offset; std::uint32_t size; bool isFloat; bool isSigned; }; std::string recoverStruct(const std::string& name, std::vector<Access accesses, std::uint32_t totalSize); - Sort accesses by offset. Accesses at the same offset merge into one field: the largest size wins, and it is floating point if any of them was, signed if any was. - An access that starts inside the previous field is ignored. - Field types: size 1 std::int8_t / std::uint8_t , 2 std::int16_t / std::uint16_t , 4 std::int32_t / std::uint32_t or float , 8 std::int64_t / std::uint64_t or double . Signed types when isSigned ; float / double when isFloat . - Fields are named field_ and the offset as at least two uppercase hex digits: field_0C , field_1A0 . - A gap before a field, or between the last field and totalSize , becomes std::uint8_t pad_XX n ; with XX the gap's offset written the same way. The output is exactly: text struct Player { std::uint8_t pad_00 12 ; std::int32_t field_0C; float field_10; }; with four spaces before each member and a newline after every line, including the last.

title: 2.05  C++ in Machine Code
body: How C++ features look once compiled by MSVC - this in rcx, constructors that install the vtable pointer, virtual calls through vtable slots, RTTI and the type names it leaves in the binary, name mangling, and the layouts of std::string and std::vector. Methods are functions with this A member function is an ordinary function with a hidden first argument, this , so in MSVC x64 it arrives in rcx . Code that reads rcx+... at the top of a function and never sets rcx first is usually a method reading its own members: nasm-norun Player::takeDamage: sub dword ptr rcx+0Ch , edx ; this- health -= amount ret Ordinary arguments shift up one place: the first visible argument is in rdx , the second in r8 . Constructors install the vtable A class with virtual functions has a hidden pointer at offset 0 to its class's vtable (lesson 3.05 of the Pointers and Memory course). The constructor writes it before anything else: nasm-norun Archer::Archer: lea rax, Archer:: vftable' ; the address of Archer's table in .rdata mov qword ptr rcx , rax ; this- vptr = &table mov dword ptr rcx+8 , 64h ; this- health = 100 mov rax, rcx ; constructors return this ret A derived class's constructor calls the base constructor first (which writes the base vtable) and then overwrites offset 0 with its own. Finding every place that stores a particular vtable address finds every constructor of that class. The vtable itself, in .rdata , is an array of function addresses: listing it gives you every virtual function of the class, in declaration order. Virtual calls A call through a vtable is unmistakable: nasm-norun mov rax, qword ptr rcx ; the object's vtable pointer call qword ptr rax+18h ; slot 3 (0x18 / 8) of the table The displacement divided by 8 is the slot number . To find which function runs, find the object's actual class (its constructor, or the vtable pointer seen in memory in a debugger) and read that slot of its table. The same call can reach different functions for different objects; that is the point of virtual functions, and it is why static analysis alone sometimes cannot say where a call goes. RTTI If run-time type information is on (the default in MSVC; /GR ), every polymorphic class leaves its name in the binary. Just before each vtable (at vftable - 8 ) is a pointer to a Complete Object Locator , which leads to a type descriptor containing the mangled class name: text .?AVArcher@@ class Archer .?AVUnit@Game@@ class Game::Unit .?AUVec3@@ struct Vec3 These strings survive even in Release builds with no PDB, so searching a binary for .?AV lists its polymorphic classes, and the locator next to each vtable tells you which class the table belongs to. Ghidra and IDA read RTTI automatically and name vtables and classes for you. Name mangling C++ allows overloading, so the linker needs a unique name for each function. MSVC encodes the scope, name and signature into a decorated name: Decorated Means --- --- ?update@Player@@QEAAXM@Z public: void Player::update(float) ?attack@Enemy@Game@@QEAAHH@Z public: int Game::Enemy::attack(int) ??0Player@@QEAA@XZ Player::Player(void) : the constructor ??1Player@@UEAA@XZ virtual Player::~Player(void) : the destructor The pieces after ? up to @@ are the name and then its enclosing scopes, innermost first. ??0 and ??1 mark constructors and destructors. The undname tool from Visual Studio decodes any of them fully. You meet decorated names in exports, in imports from C++ DLLs, and in RTTI. Standard library layouts Recognising standard containers in memory saves a lot of time. In MSVC's Release builds: std::string is 32 bytes: Offset Holds --- --- 0x00 either the text itself (up to 15 characters, the small string buffer) or a pointer to it on the heap 0x10 the size 0x18 the capacity: 15 while the text is inline So code that does cmp qword ptr rcx+18h , 0Fh and then picks between rcx and rcx is reading a std::string 's text: "if the capacity is above 15, follow the pointer". std::vector<T is three pointers, 24 bytes: first element, one past the last element, end of the allocated capacity. Its size is (end - begin) / sizeof(T) , which compiles to a subtraction and a shift or division: sub rax, rcx; sar rax, 3 is the size of a vector of 8-byte elements. std::unique_ptr<T is just the pointer; std::shared_ptr<T is two pointers, object then control block. Debug builds add checking members and change these layouts; always reverse the build configuration that you actually have. Check yourself quiz ? A method's first visible argument is in which register? - rcx , as for any function + rdx , because rcx holds this - r8 , because rcx and rdx hold the object and its vtable - On the stack, because methods do not use registers for arguments A member function is a function with a hidden first parameter, this , which takes rcx . The first argument you wrote moves along to rdx . ? What does call qword ptr rax+20h after mov rax, rcx call? - The function at offset 0x20 inside the object - The 32nd virtual function of the class + Slot 4 (0x20 / 8) of the object's vtable: a virtual function - A function whose address is stored in a global at 0x20 mov rax, rcx loads the vtable pointer from the start of the object, and each slot is 8 bytes, so offset 0x20 is slot 4, counting from 0. ? Why can you often learn class names from a Release build with no PDB? - Release builds keep every function name for crash reports - Class names are stored in the program's import table + RTTI keeps polymorphic classes' mangled names in the binary - The constructor of each class prints its name Run-time type information for dynamic_cast and typeid stores names such as .?AVArcher@@ in the image, so a strings search finds them even without symbols. ? In MSVC's std::string , where is the size and what does a capacity of 15 mean? - The size is at offset 0; a capacity of 15 means the string is full + The size is at offset 0x10; a capacity of 15 means the text is stored inline in the first 16 bytes - The size is at offset 0x18; a capacity of 15 means 15 heap blocks - The size is stored before the text on the heap; a capacity of 15 means an empty string MSVC's string has a 16-byte buffer (or heap pointer) first, then the size at 0x10 and the capacity at 0x18. Capacity 15 is the small-string buffer.

title: Virtual calls and decorated names
body: Two everyday jobs when reading C++ binaries (lesson 2.05). Memory is simulated as a map from 8-aligned addresses to 8-byte values: cpp using Memory = std::map<std::uint64_t, std::uint64_t ; int slotOf(std::uint32_t displacement); std::optional<std::uint64_t virtualTarget(const Memory& m, std::uint64_t object, std::uint32_t displacement); std::optional<std::string classOf(const Memory& m, const std::map<std::uint64_t, std::string & locators, std::uint64_t object); std::string undecorate(const std::string& name); - slotOf turns the displacement in call qword ptr rax+disp into a slot number ( 0x18 is slot 3). - virtualTarget does what a virtual call does: read the vtable pointer at object , then the function address at vtable + displacement . Any missing value, or a vtable pointer of 0, gives std::nullopt . - classOf reads the vtable pointer at object , then the locator pointer stored just before the table (at vtable - 8 ), and looks that locator up in locators to get the class name. - undecorate turns an MSVC decorated name into its qualified name: - ?name@Scope1@Scope2@@... becomes Scope2::Scope1::name (the parts after ? up to @@ are the name, then scopes innermost first; everything after @@ is ignored). - ??0Class@...@@... is a constructor: ...::Class::Class . ??1Class@...@@... is a destructor: ...::Class::~Class . - A name not starting with ? is returned unchanged.

title: Where functions start
body: Find likely function starts in x64 code from common prologues. 0x0000 48 89 5C 24 08 mov rsp+8 , rbx (prologue) 0x0010 40 53 push rbx (prologue) 0x0020 48 83 EC 28 sub rsp, 0x28 (prologue) 3 candidates; 0xCC padding between them

title: Arguments by register
body: Say where each argument of a function lives under the Windows x64 calling convention. int f(int a, double b, char c, int d, int e) a - ecx, b - xmm1, c - r8, d - r9d, e - rsp+0x28 return - eax

title: A virtual call explained
body: Show how a virtual call finds its function through the vtable. class Shape { virtual ~Shape(); virtual double area(); virtual void draw(); } call rax+0x10 on a Shape - slot 2 - draw Circle's vtable: ~Circle, Circle::area, Shape::draw (not overridden)

title: A jump table
body: Rebuild the cases of a switch from a compiler's jump table. cmp ecx, 4 / ja default / jump through table at 0x3000 table: 0x1040 0x1060 0x1040 0x1080 0x10A0 case 0, 2 - 0x1040 case 1 - 0x1060 case 3 - 0x1080 case 4 - 0x10A0 default - 0x10C0

title: A control flow graph with loops
match: A control flow graph with loops
body: Build the analysis behind a disassembler's graph view: basic blocks, which blocks can be reached at all, which jumps go backwards, and the natural loops they form. cpp enum class Op { Plain, Call, Jump, Branch, Return }; struct Insn { std::uint32_t address; std::uint32_t length; Op op; std::uint32_t target; }; struct Block { std::uint32_t start; std::uint32_t end; std::vector<std::uint32_t successors; }; struct Loop { std::uint32_t header; std::vector<std::uint32_t body; }; class Graph { public: explicit Graph(const std::vector<Insn & code); const std::vector<Block & blocks() const; std::optional<std::uint32_t blockOf(std::uint32_t address) const; std::vector<std::uint32_t predecessors(std::uint32_t block) const; std::vector<std::uint32_t unreachable() const; std::vector<std::pair<std::uint32_t, std::uint32_t backEdges() const; std::vector<Loop loops() const; }; - Blocks follow exactly the rules of the practice in lesson 2.03. Blocks are identified by their start address. - blockOf gives the start of the block containing an address ( start <= address < end ), or std::nullopt . - predecessors lists, sorted, the blocks that have the given block as a successor. - unreachable lists, sorted, blocks that cannot be reached by following successors from the first block. (Code after a ret that nothing jumps to is often a sign of a misidentified function or a jump table you have not resolved.) - backEdges lists every edge from - to whose target block starts at or before the source block's start, sorted by from then to . In compiled code these are the loops' jumps back to the top. - loops : for each block that is the target of at least one back edge (the loop header ), the body is the header plus every block from which some back-edge source can be reached by walking predecessors without passing through the header. Bodies are sorted; loops are sorted by header.

title: 3.01  How Debuggers Work
body: A debugger is an ordinary program using the Windows debugging API - debug events, software breakpoints made from a single int3 byte, single-stepping with the trap flag, the four hardware breakpoint registers, and first- and second-chance exceptions. A program that controls another A debugger is not magic built into Windows; it is a program that uses a documented API. It either starts the target with CreateProcessW(..., DEBUG_ONLY_THIS_PROCESS, ...) or attaches to a running one with DebugActiveProcess(pid) . From then on, whenever something interesting happens in the target, Windows freezes every thread of the target and reports a debug event to the debugger: cpp-norun DEBUG_EVENT event{}; while (WaitForDebugEvent(&event, INFINITE)) { switch (event.dwDebugEventCode) { case CREATE_PROCESS_DEBUG_EVENT: / the process started: its image base, entry point / break; case LOAD_DLL_DEBUG_EVENT: / a DLL loaded: its base address / break; case EXCEPTION_DEBUG_EVENT: / a breakpoint, a single step, or a real crash / break; case EXIT_PROCESS_DEBUG_EVENT: return; } ContinueDebugEvent(event.dwProcessId, event.dwThreadId, DBG_CONTINUE); // let it run again } While the target is frozen, the debugger reads and writes its memory ( ReadProcessMemory , WriteProcessMemory ) and its registers ( GetThreadContext , SetThreadContext ). Everything a debugger shows you comes from those four calls. Software breakpoints: one byte To stop at an address, the debugger overwrites the first byte of the instruction there with 0xCC , the one-byte int3 instruction, after saving the original byte. text before: 48 89 5C 24 08 mov rsp+8 , rbx armed: CC 89 5C 24 08 int3 (and garbage after it) When the target executes int3 , the processor raises a breakpoint exception, Windows freezes the process, and the debugger gets an EXCEPTION_DEBUG_EVENT with code EXCEPTION_BREAKPOINT (0x80000003). Then it must clean up carefully: 1. int3 has already executed, so rip points one byte past the breakpoint. Set rip back by one. 2. Write the original byte back, so the real instruction can run. 3. To keep the breakpoint for next time, it cannot simply write CC back now: the instruction has not run yet. So it sets the trap flag and continues; after exactly one instruction the processor stops again with a single-step exception; the debugger re-writes CC and continues normally. When the debugger shows you memory, it shows the saved original bytes , not the CC s, so you never see them. But the program can: code that reads its own bytes (a checksum of its code, for example) sees a CC where a breakpoint is set. That is one reason the next kind exists. Single-stepping Bit 8 of the EFLAGS register is the trap flag (TF). When it is set, the processor raises a single-step exception ( EXCEPTION_SINGLE_STEP , 0x80000004) after executing one instruction. "Step into" is: set TF, continue, wait for the event. "Step over" a call is: put a temporary breakpoint on the instruction after the call and run. Hardware breakpoints The processor has four debug registers , DR0 to DR3 , each holding an address, and a control register DR7 that says for each one: - whether it is enabled; - what triggers it: execute , write , or read or write ; - how many bytes it covers: 1, 2, 4 or 8. When the condition is met, the processor raises a single-step exception and DR6 says which one fired. Because nothing in memory changes, hardware breakpoints are invisible to code that checksums itself, and they can do something software breakpoints cannot: stop when data is written or read. A data breakpoint ("break when this address is written") is the tool of lesson 3.03. There are only four, and they are per thread: the debugger sets them in every thread's context. Exceptions: first and second chance Breakpoints are exceptions, but so are real errors. When any exception happens in a debugged process, the debugger hears about it first (a first-chance exception) and can choose: - DBG_CONTINUE : "I handled it" (used for its own breakpoints); - DBG_EXCEPTION_NOT_HANDLED : "pass it to the program's own handlers". If the program's own handlers (C++ catch , __try / __except ) do not handle it either, the debugger is told a second time, second chance , just before the process would die. Many programs throw and catch exceptions in normal operation, which is why debuggers let you choose which first-chance exceptions stop and which only get logged. Check yourself quiz ? What does a debugger write into the target to set a software breakpoint? - A jmp to the debugger's own code, over the first five bytes of the instruction + The byte 0xCC ( int3 ) over the first byte of the instruction, after saving the original byte - A nop over the whole instruction - Nothing; it sets the address in a debug register A software breakpoint is one byte: int3 . Writing nothing and using a debug register is a hardware breakpoint, which is a different mechanism. ? After a software breakpoint fires, why must rip be moved back by one? - The processor always stops one instruction early + The int3 already ran, so rip is one byte past it - The debugger wrote two bytes, and only one is removed - rip counts in 2-byte words, not in bytes int3 is a one-byte instruction that has executed when the exception arrives. To run the real instruction, the debugger restores the byte and sets rip back to its start. ? How does a debugger keep a software breakpoint armed after the instruction under it runs? - It leaves 0xCC in place and emulates the original instruction itself - It sets a second breakpoint on the next line of source + It restores the original byte, single-steps one instruction with the trap flag, then writes 0xCC again - It cannot; software breakpoints fire only once The original byte must be back for the instruction to run correctly. After one step with the trap flag, the debugger regains control and re-arms the breakpoint. ? What can a hardware breakpoint do that a software one cannot? - Stop at any number of addresses at once - Survive the program being restarted from scratch - Stop inside the Windows kernel from a user-mode debugger + Stop on reads or writes of data, without changing memory The four debug registers watch addresses, including data accesses, with no change to the code. There are only four, so software breakpoints are the ones you can have many of.

title: Software breakpoints
body: Manage software breakpoints over a block of code the way a debugger does (lesson 3.01). The code is a byte buffer; address base + i is byte i . cpp class Breakpoints { public: Breakpoints(std::vector<std::uint8_t & code, std::uint64_t base); bool set(std::uint64_t address); bool remove(std::uint64_t address); bool isSet(std::uint64_t address) const; std::vector<std::uint8_t view() const; std::optional<std::uint64_t onBreakpoint(std::uint64_t& rip); void onSingleStep(); }; - set saves the original byte and writes 0xCC . Setting one that is already set, or an address outside the code, returns false. - remove writes the original byte back. False if there is no breakpoint there. - view returns the code as the user should see it: with the original bytes in place of every CC you wrote. - onBreakpoint is called when the target stops on an int3 with rip already past it. If rip - 1 is one of your breakpoints: move rip back by one, put the original byte back so the instruction can run, remember that this breakpoint must be re-armed , and return its address. Otherwise (an int3 that was in the program itself) return std::nullopt and change nothing. - onSingleStep is called after the target has executed that one instruction: write 0xCC again for the breakpoint waiting to be re-armed, if it is still set.

title: 3.02  Tracing Execution
body: Following what a program actually does - stepping into, over and out, rebuilding the call stack from return addresses, naming addresses as module plus symbol plus offset, conditional and logging breakpoints, and recording traces. Getting to the interesting code Static analysis gives you a map; dynamic analysis tells you which roads are travelled. The usual way in is a breakpoint on something you can name: - an imported function the behaviour must use: CreateFileW for "it opens a file", send for "it sends a message"; - the code that references a string you found in triage; - an exported function of a DLL. When it stops, the call stack tells you how the program got there, and the caller is usually the code you want. Step into, over and out Command Usual key Does --- --- --- Step into F7 (x64dbg), F11 (VS) run one instruction; follow calls into the function Step over F8 (x64dbg), F10 (VS) run one instruction; run a whole call as one step Run to return Ctrl+F9 (x64dbg), Shift+F11 (VS) run until the current function returns Run to cursor F4 run until a chosen instruction Stepping over a call to a library function you do not care about, and out of functions you have seen enough of, keeps you in the code that matters. The call stack Every call pushes a return address, so at any moment the stack holds a chain of addresses back through every active function. Turning that into a list of frames is unwinding : - With frame pointers : some code keeps rbp pointing at the saved rbp of the caller, with the return address just above it. Then the stack is a linked list: rbp is the caller's rbp , rbp+8 the return address. Follow it until rbp is 0. - Without frame pointers , which is the usual case for optimised x64 Windows code, the debugger uses the unwind information in .pdata (lesson 2.02): for each function it knows how far rsp moved and where registers were saved, so it can compute the caller's rsp and find the return address. This is why x64 call stacks on Windows are reliable even in Release builds. text frame return address as shown 0 00007FF6 1A2B1074 game!Player::takeDamage+0x14 1 00007FF6 1A2B3410 game!Combat::resolve+0x80 2 00007FF6 1A2B5E2C game!World::update+0x21C 3 00007FF6 1A2B0F90 game!main+0x50 Naming addresses Raw addresses change every run (ASLR), so debuggers show them as module!symbol+offset : the module the address is in, the nearest symbol at or below it, and the distance. Without symbols, module+offset : game.exe+0x1074 , which is the same every run, because it is an RVA (lesson 1.03). Always record addresses this way in your notes; an absolute address from yesterday's session means nothing today. Conditional and logging breakpoints A breakpoint on CreateFileW in a program that opens hundreds of files is useless unless it stops only on the one you care about. Debuggers let you attach a condition : - x64dbg: streq(utf16(rcx), "C:\\Saves\\slot1.dat") , or a simpler test on a register such as rdx == 0xC0000000 . - Visual Studio: a condition in C++ syntax on variables when you have symbols. - WinDbg: bp kernel32!CreateFileW ".if (...) {} .else {gc}" . A logging breakpoint (a tracepoint in Visual Studio) prints a message and continues without stopping: "CreateFileW {utf16@rcx}" logs every file the program opens with its name, which is often all you need. Traces A trace records every instruction executed (or every call, or every block) between two points. x64dbg's trace recording and WinDbg's Time Travel Debugging go further: TTD records a whole run so you can step backwards through it, put a data breakpoint on a value and run backwards to see who last wrote it. For a hard question ("where did this wrong value come from?"), a recorded trace turns hours of re-running into minutes. Traces are large: millions of instructions per second of execution. Trace small windows, between two breakpoints around the behaviour you care about. Check yourself quiz ? You found the string "Save complete" in a program. How do you get to the code that saves? - Change the string in a hex editor and see what breaks + Break on the string's cross-references, save, and read the call stack - Search the program for the word "save" in function names - Set a breakpoint on the string's address and run until it executes Code refers to the string, so its cross-references (or CreateFileW / WriteFile ) lead to the saving logic, and the call stack there shows who started it. A string is data; it is never executed. ? With frame pointers, where are the caller's rbp and the return address? - At rbp-8 and rbp + At rbp and rbp+8 - At rsp and rsp+8 , whatever rbp holds - At rbp+8 and rbp+10h The prologue push rbp / mov rbp, rsp leaves the saved rbp at rbp , with the return address pushed by the call just above it at rbp+8 . ? Why record addresses as module+offset rather than absolute addresses? - Absolute addresses are too long to write down + ASLR moves modules, but offsets from their base stay put - Debuggers can only show addresses as offsets - Module+offset addresses are faster to look up A note saying game.exe+0x1A2B0 is still right next run, while an absolute address is not. ? What does a logging breakpoint do? - Stops the program and writes a crash dump - Records every instruction until the program ends + Prints a message, often with register or memory values, and continues without stopping - Logs the breakpoint to the Windows event log and disables it A logging breakpoint (a tracepoint) lets you watch a function being called many times without stopping the program each time.

title: Rebuilding a call stack
body: Walk a call stack through frame pointers and name every address as module!symbol+offset (lesson 3.02). Memory is simulated as a map from address to 8-byte value. cpp using Memory = std::map<std::uint64_t, std::uint64_t ; struct Symbol { std::uint32_t rva; std::string name; }; struct Module { std::string name; std::uint64_t base; std::uint32_t size; std::vector<Symbol symbols; }; std::vector<std::uint64_t walkStack(const Memory& m, std::uint64_t rip, std::uint64_t rbp, int maxFrames); std::string describe(const std::vector<Module & modules, std::uint64_t address); walkStack returns rip followed by the return address of each frame: while rbp is not 0 and fewer than maxFrames addresses have been collected, read the return address at rbp + 8 and the caller's rbp at rbp . Stop if either read is missing, if the return address is 0, or if the next rbp is not higher than the current one (a stack only grows down, so a frame pointer going down means a corrupt chain). describe names an address: - in a module, with a symbol at or below its RVA: module!symbol+0x1a (offset in lowercase hex), or module!symbol when the offset is 0. Use the nearest symbol below (symbols may be listed in any order); - in a module with no symbol below it: module+0x1a2 (the RVA); - in no module: 0x7ff61a2b1074 , the address itself.

title: 3.03  Finding Where Data Lives
body: Locating a value in a running program you built - value scanning by narrowing a set of candidate addresses, the types and alignments to search for, then a data breakpoint to find the code that writes it, and working back from that code to the structure and the pointer path that reach it. The problem You can see a number on the screen of your own game: the player has 87 health. Where in memory is it, and which code changes it? You have no symbols, or the value is deep inside objects created at run time. Three steps answer it: scan for the value, watch the address to find the code, then walk back from the code to the structures around it. Value scanning A value scanner (the tool you build in this milestone's project) reads all of the process's readable, writable memory and keeps a list of candidate addresses: 1. First scan : every address where the 4 bytes equal 87. In a real program that is thousands of hits. 2. Change the value in the program (take some damage: 87 becomes 72). 3. Next scan : of the previous candidates, keep only those that now hold 72. 4. Repeat until one or a few addresses remain. When you do not know the exact value (a health bar with no number), scan for unknown first (every address is a candidate), then narrow with changed , unchanged , increased and decreased scans: lose health, scan "decreased"; do nothing, scan "unchanged"; heal, scan "increased". To scan efficiently you have to guess the type and alignment right: Value Likely stored as Alignment --- --- --- health, ammo, score int32_t (sometimes int16_t or a float ) 4 position, speed, a fraction float (or double ) 4 (8) money in a big game int64_t or double 8 a flag bool or a byte 1 Compilers align members (Pointers and Memory course, lesson 3.01), so scanning only at multiples of the size is both faster and avoids false hits from overlapping bytes. Floats are compared with a tolerance, because the shown value is rounded: 87 on screen may be 86.99997 in memory. !note Do this on your own programs: the debug build of a game you are writing, or the sample programs of the Game Development course. Online games, and games that forbid it, are off limits. Data breakpoints: who writes this? Once you have the address, set a hardware write breakpoint on it (lesson 3.01): in x64dbg, right-click the address in the dump, Breakpoint Hardware, Write, Dword; in Visual Studio, Debug New Breakpoint Data Breakpoint. Then take damage again. The debugger stops on the instruction just after the write: nasm-norun game.exe+0x2A1F: sub dword ptr rbx+1Ch , eax ; the write game.exe+0x2A22: mov ecx, dword ptr rbx+1Ch ; <- execution stops here Now you know the code ( game.exe+0x2A1F ), and the operand tells you more: rbx points at the object that contains the health, and health is at offset 0x1C in it. So: object address = health address − 0x1C That one fact turns a lone address into a structure. Other accesses through rbx in the same function are other members of the same object, and reverse engineering the struct begins (lesson 2.04). Walking back to a stable path The health address changes every time you start the game, because the player object is created on the heap. To find it again next time you need a pointer path from something stable (Pointers and Memory course, lesson 3.03): 1. You know the object's address (health − 0x1C). Scan memory for pointers with that value: 8-byte values equal to the object address. Those are the places that point at the player. 2. For each one, find what contains it: perhaps a World object's player array at offset 0x28. 3. Repeat from that object until you reach a static address inside the module's image: game.exe+0x51A8 . The result is a path such as game.exe+0x51A8 → 0x28 → 0x1C that finds the health in every run. Tools automate this as a pointer scan : from the target, search backwards for chains of pointers within some offset limit (the Pointers and Memory course's milestone 3 project built exactly that engine). With your own program you can also just read the source, but doing it by hand once makes it clear what every debugger and memory tool is doing. Check yourself quiz ? A first scan for 87 finds 4 000 addresses. What do you do next? - Look at each of the 4 000 addresses by hand - Scan again for 87 without changing anything + Change the value in the program and scan for the new value - Set data breakpoints on all 4 000 addresses Each change and next scan keeps only the addresses that followed the value; repeat until few remain. A rescan without changing anything removes very little. ? How do you scan for a value that is not shown as a number? + Unknown-value scan, then narrow by changed or unchanged - Guess the number and scan for it as a float - Scan for the text the game shows next to it - It cannot be found by scanning at all When you cannot see the number, you can still see whether it went up or down. Increased, decreased, changed and unchanged scans as you change it in the program narrow the candidates step by step. ? A data breakpoint stops after sub dword ptr rbx+1Ch , eax . What does that tell you about the object? - The value is at address 0x1C - eax points at the object, and rbx is the amount subtracted + rbx points at the object holding the value, and the value is at offset 0x1C in it - The object is 0x1C bytes long The instruction writes 4 bytes at rbx + 0x1C , so rbx is the base of the structure and 0x1C the field's offset. eax is the amount subtracted. ? Why is a pointer path more useful than an address for a value on the heap? - A pointer path is shorter to write down - A heap address can only be read by a debugger - Pointer paths also work in other programs + Heap addresses change every run, but the path does not The heap block's address is different every run; a path from a static address through fixed structure offsets finds the value each time.

title: Who writes this address?
body: A trace has recorded every memory write a program made, with the instruction that made it. Answer the questions of lesson 3.03: cpp struct Write { std::uint64_t rip; std::uint64_t address; std::uint32_t size; std::string operand; }; std::vector<std::uint64_t whatWrites(const std::vector<Write & trace, std::uint64_t address, std::uint32_t size); std::optional<std::int64_t displacementOf(const std::string& operand); std::vector<std::uint64_t objectCandidates(const std::vector<Write & trace, std::uint64_t address); - whatWrites lists the instructions ( rip ) whose write overlaps the bytes address to address + size - 1 , each once, in the order they first appear in the trace. - displacementOf reads the displacement from a memory operand in disassembler style: rbx+0x1C gives 0x1C, rax-0x8 gives -8, rbx gives 0, rax+rcx 4+0x10 gives 0x10. Numbers are 0x hex. If there is no ... it returns std::nullopt . - objectCandidates takes every write that covers exactly address (starts at it) and works out the object's start as address - displacement ; it returns the distinct results in increasing order. Operands with an index register (a ) are skipped, because their displacement is not a member offset.

title: 3.04  Watching Behaviour from Outside
body: Learning what a program does without a debugger - Process Monitor's file and registry log and its filters, API Monitor, network captures with Wireshark, Event Tracing for Windows, and Sysmon - and reading their logs systematically. Behaviour first Before reading a program's code you can learn a lot by just watching it from outside: which files it opens, which registry keys it reads, which servers it talks to, which processes it starts. Behavioural analysis needs no understanding of the code, is hard for a program to notice, and often answers the question outright: "where does it keep its settings?" is answered by one Process Monitor capture. Process Monitor Process Monitor (Sysinternals, procmon.exe ) records every file system, registry, process and thread event on the system, with the process, the path, the result and details. A capture is enormous, so the skill is filtering (Filter Filter...): - Process Name is Inventory.exe then Include: only your target. - Operation is WriteFile : only writes. - Path contains \Saves\ : only one folder. - Result is NAME NOT FOUND : things the program looked for and did not find, which reveals optional configuration files, missing DLLs and plugins it would load if they existed. Useful columns and tools: Path , Result , Detail (offsets and lengths of reads and writes); Tools File Summary and Registry Summary to count accesses per path; double-click an event to see its call stack (with symbols for system DLLs), which shows the code in the program that caused it. Logs can be saved as CSV (File Save, Comma-Separated Values), which is the format of this lesson's practice: text "Time of Day","Process Name","PID","Operation","Path","Result","Detail" "10:14:02.1234567","Inventory.exe","4120","CreateFile","C:\Users\sam\AppData\Roaming\Inventory\config.ini","SUCCESS","Desired Access: Generic Read" API Monitor API Monitor (rohitab.com) logs calls to Windows API functions with their arguments and return values : every RegQueryValueExW with the key and value name, every connect with the address. It shows what Process Monitor cannot see, such as calls that do not touch files or the registry (cryptography, window messages, time). Network captures Wireshark captures network traffic and decodes hundreds of protocols. Filters such as ip.addr == 192.168.1.20 && tcp.port == 7777 narrow it to one conversation; Follow TCP Stream shows the whole exchange as text or hex. For a program's own custom protocol you see only bytes, which is where lesson 6.03 picks up. Encrypted traffic (HTTPS, TLS) shows only the handshake and sizes, unless the program is yours and you can log its keys. Event Tracing for Windows ETW is the logging system built into Windows itself: the kernel and many components publish events (process starts, image loads, network, disk, the .NET runtime...). Tools such as Windows Performance Recorder, PerfView and logman capture them with very little overhead. Sysmon (Sysinternals) is a service that logs selected ETW-based events to the Windows event log permanently: process creation with full command lines and hashes, network connections, file creation. Security teams use it constantly, and it is a good way to watch a program over hours. Reading logs systematically Behaviour logs are only useful if you summarise them. A good habit for each capture: 1. Filter to the target process (and its children: the PID of processes it started). 2. List the distinct files written, files read, registry keys read and written, and network endpoints. 3. Note the failures ( NAME NOT FOUND , ACCESS DENIED ): they show what the program expected to exist. 4. Record the sequence of the important operations: what it reads at start-up, what it writes when you press Save. The practice builds exactly that summary from a Process Monitor CSV. Check yourself quiz ? Which Process Monitor result reveals files and registry keys a program looked for but did not find? - ACCESS DENIED + NAME NOT FOUND - BUFFER OVERFLOW - SUCCESS NAME NOT FOUND shows the paths a program tried and did not find, such as optional config files or registry settings it would read if they existed. ? What can API Monitor show that Process Monitor cannot? - Which files a program opened and closed - Which registry keys a program read + API calls of any kind, with their arguments and results - Which network packets a program sent, with their full contents Process Monitor shows file, registry, process and network activity. API Monitor hooks the API calls themselves, such as CryptHashData or MessageBoxW , which touch neither files nor the registry. ? Why might a network capture of a program's traffic show only sizes and no content? - Wireshark only records packet sizes by default + The traffic is encrypted, for example with TLS - The program sends empty packets to keep the connection open - The capture was taken on the wrong network card With encryption, the capture shows who talked to whom, when and how much, but not what was said. ? Which Sysinternals tool logs process creation and network connections permanently to the event log? - Process Monitor - Process Explorer - Autoruns + Sysmon Process Monitor records only while it is running and keeps the log in memory. Sysmon is a service that writes events to the Windows event log all the time.

title: Summarising a Process Monitor log
body: Turn a Process Monitor capture saved as CSV (lesson 3.04) into the summary you would write by hand: cpp struct Event { std::string time, process, pid, operation, path, result, detail; }; struct Summary { std::vector<std::string filesRead, filesWritten, keysRead, keysWritten, notFound; }; std::vector<std::string splitCsvLine(const std::string& line); std::vector<Event parseLog(const std::string& csv); Summary summarise(const std::vector<Event & events, const std::string& process); - splitCsvLine splits one CSV line into fields. Fields may be wrapped in double quotes; inside quotes, commas are part of the field and "" stands for one " . - parseLog skips the header line and blank lines and turns each other line of 7 fields into an Event (lines with a different number of fields are skipped). - summarise looks only at events of process and fills each list with distinct paths, sorted: - filesRead : operation ReadFile with result SUCCESS ; - filesWritten : operation WriteFile with result SUCCESS ; - keysRead : RegQueryValue with result SUCCESS ; - keysWritten : RegSetValue with result SUCCESS ; - notFound : any operation with result NAME NOT FOUND .

title: 3.05  Comparing Runs
body: Differential analysis - snapshot memory before and after an action and diff it, compare which code ran with and without a feature (code coverage diffing), compare files a program wrote, and use time travel debugging to answer questions backwards. Change one thing, compare the rest Many reverse engineering questions have the form "what part of the program handles X?". The most efficient way to answer them is not to read more code, but to run the program twice , once doing X and once not, and compare. Whatever differs is about X. This is differential analysis , and it works on memory, on code coverage and on files. Memory snapshots Take a snapshot of a region of memory (an object, a heap, a whole module's data section), do one thing in the program, and take another. The diff shows exactly which bytes the action changed: text before jump: ... 00 00 C8 42 00 00 00 00 01 00 00 00 ... after jump: ... 00 00 F0 42 00 00 A0 41 00 00 00 00 ... ^ y position ^ vertical ^ on ground: 100.0 - speed 1 - 0 120.0 0 - 20.0 Read changed 4-byte groups both as integers and as floats: 00 00 C8 42 is the float 100.0, which is far more meaningful than the integer 1 120 403 456. Changes by small, sensible amounts are interesting; values that change on every snapshot whatever you do (timers, frame counters, random state) are noise that you learn to filter out by taking a third snapshot without doing anything. Code coverage diffing The same idea applies to code. Record which basic blocks execute (a coverage tool, a trace, or the Lighthouse plugin for Ghidra and IDA with coverage files from DynamoRIO's drcov ) during two runs: 1. Run A: start the program, open the menu, close it. 2. Run B: start the program, open the menu, press the button you are curious about , close it. Blocks executed in B but not in A are the code for that button. A function with a thousand blocks often has only a dozen in the difference, and that is where to start reading. File diffing When a program writes files, compare them across small changes. Save a game, move one step, save again, and diff the two save files (lesson 1.02's practice): the bytes that changed hold the position. Change the player's name and save again: the bytes that changed are the name, and the bytes before them are often its length. Lesson 6.02 builds a whole file format this way. Time travel debugging WinDbg's Time Travel Debugging (TTD) records an entire run of a program into a trace file. Afterwards you can replay it in the debugger and move both forwards and backwards : - g- runs backwards to the previous breakpoint. - A data breakpoint plus g- finds the last write to a value before the current moment: "who set this to the wrong value?" is answered in one command. - Queries such as dx @$cursession.TTD.Calls("kernel32!CreateFileW") list every call to a function anywhere in the recording, with arguments. Recording slows the program down a great deal and produces large files, so record the shortest run that shows the behaviour. For your own programs' hardest bugs, TTD is often the fastest tool there is. Check yourself quiz ? Why take a third memory snapshot without doing anything? - To check that the snapshot tool works properly - To have a backup in case the first one was damaged + To find values that change on their own, and ignore them Many values, such as timers and counters, change constantly. A snapshot pair with no action shows them, and removing them leaves the changes your action really caused. ? The bytes 00 00 C8 42 changed. Why read them as a float as well as an integer? - Every 4-byte value in a game is stored as a float + As a float they are 100.0; as an integer, nonsense - Reading them as a float corrects the byte order - Integers are never stored in 4 bytes Little-endian 00 00 C8 42 is 0x42C80000 : 1 120 403 456 as an integer, but exactly 100.0 as a float. The type that gives a sensible value is the likely one. ? How does code coverage diffing find the code behind one button? - It records the button's pixels and searches the code for them - It compares the program's file before and after the button is pressed + Blocks that ran only in the run with the press are its code - It counts how often each function was called and picks the busiest Record coverage of a run that presses the button and one that does not. Everything both runs share (start-up, drawing, input) cancels out. ? What does a data breakpoint with g- do in a TTD recording? - Runs forwards to the next write of that data - Deletes the breakpoint and goes to the start of the recording - Restarts the program and replays it to the breakpoint + Runs backwards to the last write of that data before the current position Time travel debugging can run in reverse, so g- with a write breakpoint finds who last changed a value, the question you usually have after spotting a wrong one.

title: Diffing memory snapshots
body: Compare two snapshots of the same block of memory, taken before and after an action (lesson 3.05), and report the 4-byte values that changed, read both as integers and as floats: cpp struct Changed { std::uint64_t address; std::int32_t beforeInt, afterInt; float beforeFloat, afterFloat; }; std::vector<Changed changedDwords(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & before, const std::vector<std::uint8_t & after, std::uint64_t base); std::vector<Changed withoutNoise(const std::vector<Changed & changes, const std::vector<Changed & noise); bool looksLikeFloat(float value); - changedDwords compares the two snapshots (the same size) 4 bytes at a time, at offsets 0, 4, 8, ...; every group where any byte differs is reported with its address ( base + offset ) and its values before and after, read little-endian as std::int32_t and as float . A trailing group of fewer than 4 bytes is ignored. - withoutNoise removes every change whose address also appears in noise (changes seen in a snapshot pair taken while doing nothing), keeping the order. - looksLikeFloat is a plausibility check: true for 0 and for finite values whose absolute value is between 0.0001 and 1 000 000. Tiny or enormous values usually mean the bytes are not really a float.

title: A breakpoint by hand
body: Model how a software breakpoint works: put 0xCC in the code, and put the byte back after it hits. code: 48 83 EC 28 E8 ... set breakpoint at 0x4 - saved E8, wrote CC hit at 0x4: restore E8, rewind rip to 0x4, single-step, write CC again remove - E8 back, nothing left changed

title: Where two runs differ
body: Compare two execution traces of your own program to find where they first go different ways. run A (input "abc"): 1240 steps run B (input "abd"): 1238 steps first difference at step 912: A 0x1450 jne taken, B 0x1450 jne not taken
