title: A value scanner
body: Build the engine of a memory value scanner (lesson 3.03). It works on snapshots : a list of memory regions copied out of a process (in a real tool, with VirtualQueryEx and ReadProcessMemory on your own program; here they are given). cpp struct Region { std::uint64_t base; std::vector<std::uint8_t bytes; }; using Snapshot = std::vector<Region ; enum class Type { Int32, Float, Double }; enum class Compare { Exact, Changed, Unchanged, Increased, Decreased, IncreasedBy, DecreasedBy }; class Scanner { public: explicit Scanner(Type type); void firstScan(const Snapshot& memory, double value); void firstScanUnknown(const Snapshot& memory); void nextScan(const Snapshot& memory, Compare how, double value = 0); std::vector<std::uint64_t results() const; std::optional<double read(const Snapshot& memory, std::uint64_t address) const; }; - The size and alignment of a value are 4 for Int32 and Float , 8 for Double . Only addresses that are multiples of the alignment, with all the value's bytes inside one region, are ever results. - read reads the value at an address as the scanner's type (little-endian), or std::nullopt if it is not readable. - firstScan finds every such address whose value equals value . Integers must match exactly; floats and doubles match when they differ from value by at most 0.001. It replaces any earlier results. - firstScanUnknown makes every readable aligned address a result. - nextScan keeps only the results for which the comparison holds between the value now (in memory ) and the value at the previous scan ; results that can no longer be read are dropped: - Exact : now equals value (with the same tolerance as firstScan ); - Changed / Unchanged : now differs from / equals the previous value (exactly, for every type); - Increased / Decreased : now is greater / less than the previous value; - IncreasedBy / DecreasedBy : now minus previous (or previous minus now) equals value , with the tolerance for floats. - Every scan remembers the current values for the next comparison. - results returns the addresses in increasing order.

title: 4.01  Patching Instructions
body: Changing a compiled program's behaviour by changing its bytes - turning a conditional jump into an unconditional one, inverting a condition, filling instructions with nops - in the file or in memory, on programs you built yourself, and what breaks when you do. Why patch your own programs Patching means changing a program's machine code directly instead of recompiling it. On your own software it has real uses: - Testing a hypothesis while reversing: "if I skip this check, does the crash go away?" answers a question in seconds. - Working around a bug in a build you cannot rebuild right now: an old release, a build machine that no longer exists, a tool whose source was lost. - Learning : seeing exactly which bytes encode which instructions makes disassembly far less mysterious. The practice targets here are programs you compile yourself. Build a small test program with a check you can find, for example: cpp-norun include <cstdio include <cstring bool debugMenuAllowed(const char build) { return std::strcmp(build, "internal") == 0; } int main() { if (debugMenuAllowed("release")) std::puts("debug menu on"); else std::puts("debug menu off"); } Compile it in Release, find the comparison in x64dbg (search for the string "debug menu off" and follow the cross-reference), and change the outcome without touching the source. The simplest patches The decision is almost always a conditional jump right after a test or cmp : nasm-norun call debugMenuAllowed test al, al je short off_branch ; 74 0C lea rcx, aDebugMenuOn Three standard edits: Goal Change Bytes --- --- --- always take the jump je becomes jmp 74 0C becomes EB 0C never take the jump replace it with nops 74 0C becomes 90 90 take it in the opposite case je becomes jne 74 0C becomes 75 0C The short conditional jumps are 70 to 7F , and each condition and its opposite differ only in the lowest bit : 74 je / 75 jne, 7C jl / 7D jge, 72 jb / 73 jae. So flipping bit 0 inverts any of them. The 6-byte near forms are 0F 80 to 0F 8F , with the same rule on the second byte. 90 is nop , the one-byte "do nothing". Longer nops exist ( 66 90 , 0F 1F 00 , up to 15 bytes), and compilers use them to pad loops, but a run of 90 s works fine for patching. Patch whole instructions A patch must leave the processor reading valid instructions. Replacing a 2-byte jump with a 5-byte one overwrites the next 3 bytes, which belong to another instruction, and the processor will then decode garbage. Rules: - Keep the patch the same length as what it replaces, padding with nop s. - If you need more room, use a code cave (lesson 4.03). - Always check the original bytes before patching: if they are not what you expect, you are looking at a different build, and patching blindly will break it. In the file or in memory In memory (in the debugger, or with WriteProcessMemory ): instant, undone when the program restarts. Code pages are read+execute, so a program patching memory needs VirtualProtect to make the page writable first, and FlushInstructionCache afterwards. Debuggers do this for you. In the file : permanent. Convert the instruction's address to a file offset (the RVA conversion of lesson 1.03: address − image base − section RVA + section file offset), and change the bytes there. x64dbg can write all your memory patches back to a copy of the file (File Patch file). What breaks - Code signing : a signed .exe or .dll no longer matches its signature after any change. Windows and antivirus software treat it as unsigned. Drivers simply refuse to load. - Integrity checks inside the program (checksums of its own code) will notice. - Updates replace the file and your patch is gone; and the next build of a program has different addresses, which is what lesson 4.05 is about. Keep the original file, record every patch (address, original bytes, new bytes, why), and patch copies. Check yourself quiz ? How do you make a short je ( 74 xx ) always jump? - Change it to 90 90 , two nop s + Change it to EB xx , a short jmp - Change it to 75 xx , a jne - Change the displacement to 00 EB is the unconditional short jump with the same displacement format, so the displacement stays. 75 would invert the condition, nop s would make it never jump, and a displacement of 0 jumps to the next instruction either way. ? What does flipping the lowest bit of 0x7C do? - Turns jl into jg + Turns jl ( 7C ) into jge ( 7D ): the opposite condition - Turns the short jump into a near jump - Turns jl into jle Short conditional jumps come in pairs whose opcodes differ only in the lowest bit, and the pair are exact opposites. The opposite of "less" is "greater or equal", not "greater". ? Why check the original bytes before applying a patch? - Windows refuses to write bytes that have not been read first - Reading them makes the code page writable + If they differ, it is the wrong build or the wrong place - So that the patch can safely be applied twice A patch is made for one exact build. Writing it anywhere else would corrupt the code, so checking the expected bytes first guards against patching the wrong spot. ? Why must a patch replace whole instructions? - The processor reads instructions 4 bytes at a time - Partial instructions are rejected by the loader + Leftover bytes of a cut instruction decode as garbage - Partial instructions break the PE checksum x64 instructions have different lengths. If a patch ends in the middle of one, the bytes after it become the start of whatever instruction they happen to look like; fill the rest with nop s.

title: Safe patches
body: Write the patch operations of lesson 4.01, each checking what it is about to overwrite: cpp struct Patch { std::size_t offset; std::vector<std::uint8_t original; std::vector<std::uint8_t replacement; }; bool apply(std::vector<std::uint8_t & code, const Patch& p); bool revert(std::vector<std::uint8_t & code, const Patch& p); std::optional<Patch forceJump(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & code, std::size_t offset); std::optional<Patch invertJump(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & code, std::size_t offset); Patch nopOut(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & code, std::size_t offset, std::size_t length); - apply writes replacement only if original and replacement have the same length, the bytes fit, and the bytes at offset are exactly original ; it returns whether it did. revert does the reverse (checks for replacement , writes original ). - forceJump makes the conditional jump at offset always taken: - short 7x dd becomes EB dd ; - near 0F 8x dd dd dd dd becomes 90 E9 dd dd dd dd (a nop, then a jump with the same displacement, which still reaches the same target because the jmp ends where the jcc did). - Anything else gives std::nullopt . - invertJump flips the condition: the lowest bit of the 7x byte, or of the 8x byte after 0F . - nopOut makes a patch replacing length bytes with 90 s. The patches returned carry the current bytes as original , so they can be applied and reverted.

title: 4.02  Encoding Jumps and Calls
body: How x64 encodes jumps and calls - short and near relative jumps, conditional jumps, relative calls, why the displacement counts from the end of the instruction, the 2 GB limit, and the absolute jumps used when a target is further away. Relative, from the end Almost every jump and call on x64 is relative : the instruction holds a signed distance, the displacement , and the target is target = address of the next instruction + displacement The distance is counted from the end of the jump, not its start, because by the time the processor uses it, rip already points past the instruction. Instruction Bytes Length Displacement --- --- --- --- jmp short EB dd 2 8-bit, −128 to +127 jmp near E9 dd dd dd dd 5 32-bit jcc short 70+cc dd 2 8-bit jcc near 0F 80+cc dd dd dd dd 6 32-bit call E8 dd dd dd dd 5 32-bit Example: a jmp at 0x1400010A0 to 0x140001200 : text next instruction = 0x1400010A0 + 5 = 0x1400010A5 displacement = 0x140001200 - 0x1400010A5 = 0x15B bytes = E9 5B 01 00 00 Backwards jumps have negative displacements in two's complement: EB FE is a jump to itself (−2), an infinite loop; E9 00 00 00 00 jumps to the next instruction, which does nothing. Because displacements are relative, a block of code containing only relative jumps between its own instructions can be moved anywhere and still works; a relative jump or call to outside the block points somewhere else once it is moved. That fact drives lessons 4.03 and 4.04. The 2 GB limit A 32-bit displacement reaches about ±2 GB. Inside one module that is plenty. But code you allocate at run time with VirtualAlloc may land anywhere in the 128 TB address space, too far for E9 . Then you need an absolute jump: nasm-norun ; 14 bytes: jump to the 8-byte address stored right after the instruction FF 25 00 00 00 00 jmp qword ptr rip+0 xx xx xx xx xx xx xx xx ; the absolute target address nasm-norun ; 12 bytes, but it destroys rax 48 B8 xx xx xx xx xx xx xx xx mov rax, imm64 FF E0 jmp rax The first form changes no registers, which is why hooking libraries use it. Alternatively, allocate your new code within 2 GB of the module ( VirtualAlloc with an address hint near it), so a 5-byte E9 reaches it. Calls through memory Calls to imported functions are not relative calls to the function; they are indirect calls through the import address table: nasm-norun FF 15 xx xx xx xx call qword ptr rip+disp32 ; the IAT slot The displacement here gives the address of the slot , also counted from the end of the instruction (6 bytes long); the slot holds the function's address. Virtual calls are FF 50 xx / FF 90 xx xx xx xx ( call qword ptr rax+disp ) and friends. Encoding in code Choosing the shortest encoding that reaches: cpp-norun std::vector<std::uint8_t encodeJump(std::uint64_t from, std::uint64_t to) { const std::int64_t shortDisp{ static_cast<std::int64_t (to - (from + 2)) }; if (shortDisp = -128 && shortDisp <= 127) return { 0xEB, static_cast<std::uint8_t (shortDisp) }; const std::int64_t nearDisp{ static_cast<std::int64_t (to - (from + 5)) }; if (nearDisp = INT32_MIN && nearDisp <= INT32_MAX) { / E9 + 4 bytes of nearDisp, little-endian / } / otherwise FF 25 00 00 00 00 + 8 bytes of to / } Note that the two candidate displacements are computed from different ends: from + 2 for the short form, from + 5 for the near one. Check yourself quiz ? A call at 0x401000 is encoded E8 FB 0F 00 00 . Where does it go? - 0x401FFB , adding the displacement to the call's own address + 0x402000 , because 0x401000 + 5 + 0xFFB - 0xFB0F0000 , reading the bytes as an absolute address - 0x400FFB , because the displacement is negative The displacement counts from the end of the 5-byte instruction, and FB 0F 00 00 little-endian is 0x00000FFB , a positive number. ? What do the bytes EB FE do? - Nothing; FE is an invalid displacement - Jump two bytes forward, skipping the next instruction + Jump to themselves: an infinite loop - Jump back to the start of the function FE is -2, and the jump counts from its own end, two bytes after its start, so it lands back on itself. ? Why can't an E9 jump reach code allocated anywhere with VirtualAlloc ? - E9 can only jump forwards, never backwards - VirtualAlloc memory can never be executed - E9 only jumps within the same 4 KB page + Its 32-bit displacement reaches only about ±2 GB A 64-bit address space is far bigger than ±2 GB, and the allocation may be further away. To reach memory anywhere you need an absolute jump, or an allocation near the module. ? Which absolute jump changes no registers, and how long is it? - mov rax, target / jmp rax , 12 bytes + FF 25 00 00 00 00 followed by the 8-byte target, jmp rip+0 , 14 bytes - E9 followed by an 8-byte target, 9 bytes - FF 15 00 00 00 00 followed by the 8-byte target, 14 bytes jmp rip+0 reads its target from the 8 bytes right after it, so no register is used. mov rax / jmp rax is shorter but destroys rax , FF 15 is a call, not a jump, and E9 only takes a 32-bit displacement.

title: Encoding and decoding jumps
body: Encode jumps and calls between two addresses, and decode where a branch goes (lesson 4.02): cpp std::vector<std::uint8_t encodeJump(std::uint64_t from, std::uint64_t to); std::optional<std::vector<std::uint8_t encodeCall(std::uint64_t from, std::uint64_t to); std::optional<std::uint64_t branchTarget(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & code, std::size_t at, std::uint64_t address); - encodeJump returns the shortest jump at address from that reaches to : EB + 8-bit displacement if it fits, else E9 + 32-bit displacement if it fits, else the 14-byte absolute form FF 25 00 00 00 00 followed by to as 8 little-endian bytes. Remember each relative form counts from its own end. - encodeCall returns E8 + 32-bit displacement, or std::nullopt if the target is out of range. - branchTarget decodes the branch at code at , which is at address address , and returns its target: EB , E9 , E8 , 70 - 7F and 0F 80 - 0F 8F . Displacements are signed. Anything else, or bytes running past the end of code , gives std::nullopt .

title: 4.03  Code Caves
body: When a patch needs more room than the instructions it replaces - finding unused space in a binary, jumping out to it with a detour, running the overwritten instructions there, and jumping back - plus adding a section or allocating memory instead. When a patch does not fit Turning a je into a jmp fits in the same two bytes. Adding behaviour does not: logging a value, adding a check, calling a function. You need somewhere to put new code. A code cave is unused space in the program where new code can live, reached by a jump from the original code. Where caves are - Padding between functions : MSVC aligns functions to 16 bytes and fills the gaps with CC (lesson 2.02). Each gap is small (up to 15 bytes) but there are many. - The end of a section : sections are padded in the file to a multiple of FileAlignment (0x200) with zeros, and in memory to SectionAlignment (0x1000). The space between a section's VirtualSize and its padded size is mapped with the section's permissions, so in .text it is executable. In the file, it is the bytes between VirtualSize and SizeOfRawData . - A new section : a PE editor (CFF Explorer, or a few lines of code) can add a section with read+execute permissions and as much room as you like, updating NumberOfSections and SizeOfImage . - At run time : VirtualAlloc a page of executable memory, preferably within 2 GB of the module so 5-byte jumps reach it (lesson 4.02). To find caves in a section, look for runs of 00 or CC at least as long as the code you need, preferably not directly after real code (a run of zeros can be a legitimate array of zeros that something reads). The detour Say you want to log every value passed to a function in your own program, at an instruction in the middle of it: nasm-norun 140001A30: 8B 47 1C mov eax, dword ptr rdi+1Ch 140001A33: 2B C3 sub eax, ebx 140001A35: 89 47 1C mov dword ptr rdi+1Ch , eax 140001A38: ... A 5-byte jmp to the cave must overwrite whole instructions, so it takes the first two (3 + 2 = 5 bytes, exactly; with other lengths, the leftover bytes become nop s). Those overwritten instructions are called the stolen bytes , and the cave must run them, or the program loses them: nasm-norun ; at 140001A30, the patch: E9 xx xx xx xx jmp cave ; in the cave: cave: ; ... your new code: save registers, call a logger, restore registers ... 8B 47 1C mov eax, dword ptr rdi+1Ch ; the stolen instructions, 2B C3 sub eax, ebx ; exactly as they were E9 xx xx xx xx jmp 140001A35 ; back to the next original instruction Rules that keep a detour correct: 1. Steal whole instructions : at least 5 bytes' worth, rounded up to the next instruction boundary. 2. Do not steal a jump target : if any other code jumps into the middle of the stolen range, that jump now lands inside your jmp . Check the cross-references for each stolen address. 3. Relocate relative instructions : a stolen call , jmp or jcc , or any instruction with a RIP-relative operand ( mov eax, rip+... ), means something else once it runs at the cave's address. Its displacement must be recalculated for the new location, or the instruction replaced. 4. Preserve state : your new code must save and restore every register and the flags it changes ( pushfq / popfq ), and keep the stack 16-byte aligned before any call . Planning the stolen bytes Given the lengths of the instructions at the patch point, the number of bytes to steal is the smallest sum of whole instructions that reaches 5: text lengths 3, 2, 3, ... - steal 5 (two instructions) lengths 2, 2, 4, ... - steal 8 (three instructions; 3 nops after the jmp) lengths 7, ... - steal 7 (one instruction; 2 nops) Your disassembler (or the one you build in milestone 5) gives the lengths. Check yourself quiz ? Where is a natural code cave at the end of the .text section in the file? + Between its VirtualSize and its SizeOfRawData - Before the section's VirtualAddress - In the PE headers, after the section table - In the .data section, which is always writable The raw data is rounded up to the file alignment, so the last part of the section in the file is padding, usually zeros, that is still mapped and executable with the code. ? What are stolen bytes, and why must the cave execute them? - Bytes copied from another program, which the cave needs to run + The instructions the jump overwrote, which must still run - The bytes of the cave itself, which must run before returning - Padding bytes that the cave must skip over The jump to the cave overwrites real instructions. The cave runs them, then jumps back, so the original code still does everything it did before. ? Instructions at the patch point are 2, 2 and 4 bytes long. How many bytes must be stolen for a 5-byte jump? - 5, exactly the length of the jump - 4, the first two instructions + 8, whole instructions only: 2 + 2 + 4 - 6, rounding up to an even number Two instructions give only 4 bytes, too few for the jump. You cannot split the third, so all 8 bytes are stolen and the leftover 3 are filled with nop s. ? Why is a stolen call E8 xx xx xx xx a problem? - Calls cannot be executed outside the .text section - A call always crashes when it runs in a code cave + Its displacement is relative, so in the cave it calls elsewhere - It pushes a return address that points into the cave A relative call's target depends on where the instruction is. Moved to the cave, the same bytes reach somewhere else, so the displacement must be worked out again for the new address.

title: Planning a detour
body: Plan a code cave detour (lesson 4.03): find caves, decide how many bytes to steal, and build the cave's code. cpp struct Cave { std::size_t offset; std::size_t length; }; std::vector<Cave findCaves(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & code, std::size_t minLength); std::optional<std::size_t bytesToSteal(const std::vector<std::size_t & instructionLengths, std::size_t needed); std::optional<std::vector<std::uint8_t buildCave(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & stolen, const std::vector<std::uint8_t & newCode, std::uint64_t caveAddress, std::uint64_t returnAddress); - findCaves lists runs of the same filler byte, 0x00 or 0xCC , at least minLength long, in order. A run is one byte value only (a run of CC s next to a run of 00 s is two caves). - bytesToSteal takes the lengths of the instructions at the patch point, in order, and returns the total length of the fewest whole instructions that add up to at least needed bytes, or std::nullopt if they never do. - buildCave returns the bytes placed at caveAddress : newCode , then the stolen instructions unchanged, then an E9 jump back to returnAddress . If the stolen bytes start a relative branch or call ( E8 , E9 , EB , 70 - 7F or 0F 8x as the first byte of the stolen bytes) it returns std::nullopt , because copying them unchanged would break them; so does a jump back that does not fit in 32 bits.

title: 4.04  Hooking Functions in Your Own Programs
match: 4.04 Hooking Functions in Your Own Programs
body: Redirecting calls to a function so your code runs first - import address table hooks, inline hooks with a trampoline that still calls the original, libraries that do it safely, and using hooks for instrumentation, logging and testing in software you build. What a hook is A hook makes calls to a function go to your code instead, usually so your code can do something and then call the original. Inside your own software, hooks are a practical tool: - Instrumentation : count and time every call to an allocator or a file function without changing the call sites. - Logging : record the arguments of every call to a third-party library you only have as a DLL. - Testing : make a system function fail on purpose ( CreateFileW returns "access denied") to test error handling. - Fixing : replace a buggy function in a library you cannot rebuild. Profilers, debuggers, crash reporters and the Windows compatibility layer all hook functions. Everything here is about functions in your own process or programs you build. IAT hooks Calls to imported functions go through the import address table (lesson 1.04): call qword ptr IAT slot . Change the slot , and every call from that module goes to your function instead: cpp-norun using CreateFileWFn = HANDLE (WINAPI )(LPCWSTR, DWORD, DWORD, LPSECURITY_ATTRIBUTES, DWORD, DWORD, HANDLE); static CreateFileWFn realCreateFileW{ nullptr }; HANDLE WINAPI loggingCreateFileW(LPCWSTR name, DWORD access, DWORD share, LPSECURITY_ATTRIBUTES sa, DWORD disposition, DWORD flags, HANDLE templ) { std::wprintf(L"opening %s\n", name); return realCreateFileW(name, access, share, sa, disposition, flags, templ); // the original } // Find the slot for CreateFileW in this module's import table, then: DWORD old; VirtualProtect(slot, sizeof(void ), PAGE_READWRITE, &old); realCreateFileW = reinterpret_cast<CreateFileWFn ( slot); slot = reinterpret_cast<void (&loggingCreateFileW); VirtualProtect(slot, sizeof(void ), old, &old); IAT hooks are simple and safe: one pointer changes, no code is rewritten. Their limit is scope: they catch calls from the module whose table you changed , not calls from other DLLs, and not calls made through GetProcAddress . Inline hooks and trampolines An inline hook patches the first bytes of the target function itself, so every caller is caught. It is the detour of lesson 4.03 at a function's start: text target function, before: after: 48 89 5C 24 08 mov rsp+8 ,rbx E9 xx xx xx xx jmp yourFunction 57 push rdi 57 push rdi 48 83 EC 20 sub rsp,20h 48 83 EC 20 sub rsp,20h To still call the original, you build a trampoline : a small block of executable memory holding the stolen instructions followed by a jump back to the rest of the original: text trampoline: 48 89 5C 24 08 mov rsp+8 , rbx ; stolen bytes E9 xx xx xx xx jmp target+5 ; continue the original Your function calls the trampoline whenever it wants the original behaviour. Everything from lesson 4.03 applies: steal whole instructions, relocate RIP-relative ones, and do not overwrite a jump target. Two more problems are specific to hooking a live process: - Other threads may be executing the bytes you are overwriting. Suspend the other threads while you write, and check none of them is stopped inside the stolen range. - Distance : the trampoline must be within 2 GB for 5-byte jumps, or you need the 14-byte absolute form at the function start, which steals more bytes. Use a library Writing a robust inline hook engine means a full instruction-length decoder, relocation of every RIP-relative instruction form, thread handling and more. In practice use one of: - Microsoft Detours (MIT licence): the reference implementation, used by Microsoft's own tools. - MinHook (BSD licence): small, simple API ( MH_CreateHook , MH_EnableHook ). Understanding what they do, as in this lesson, is what lets you debug them when a hook misbehaves. Check yourself quiz ? What exactly does an IAT hook change? - The first bytes of the hooked function - The DLL file on disk + One pointer: the function's slot in one module's IAT - Every call instruction that calls the function Calls to an imported function go through its import address table slot, so changing that one pointer redirects all of that module's calls to it. ? What does an IAT hook not catch? - Calls from the module whose IAT was changed + Calls from other modules or via GetProcAddress - Calls made from a different thread - Calls that pass more than four arguments Each module has its own IAT, and a pointer from GetProcAddress never looks at an IAT. Threads and argument counts make no difference. ? What is in a trampoline? - A jump straight from the hook back to the caller - A copy of the whole original function - The hook function's code, followed by a ret + The stolen first instructions, then a jump back past them The inline hook overwrites the function's first bytes. Calling the trampoline runs those bytes and continues at the first original instruction after them, so the hook can still call the real thing. ? Why suspend other threads while installing an inline hook? + A thread could run a half-written instruction - Windows only allows one thread to write to code pages - Suspending threads makes the code page writable - Other threads would install the hook a second time Writing several bytes is not atomic. A thread whose rip is inside them, or that reaches them mid-write, would execute a mix of old and new bytes.

title: Hooks on paper
where: 4.04 Hooking Functions in Your Own Programs
body: Work out the bytes a hooking library writes (lesson 4.04), for a function at a known address: cpp struct InlineHook { std::vector<std::uint8_t patch; // written over the start of the target function std::vector<std::uint8_t trampoline; // placed at the trampoline address }; std::optional<InlineHook planHook(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & functionStart, const std::vector<std::size_t & lengths, std::uint64_t target, std::uint64_t hook, std::uint64_t trampolineAt); std::uint64_t hookIat(std::vector<std::uint64_t & iat, std::size_t slot, std::uint64_t replacement); planHook : the target function starts at address target ; functionStart holds its first bytes and lengths the lengths of its first instructions. - Steal the fewest whole instructions covering at least 5 bytes. If they are not all available in functionStart , return std::nullopt . - patch is an E9 jump from target to hook , followed by 90 s to fill the rest of the stolen bytes. - trampoline is the stolen bytes unchanged, then an E9 jump from the end of those bytes (at trampolineAt + stolen ) back to target + stolen . - If a stolen instruction starts with a relative branch or call ( E8 , E9 , EB , 70 - 7F , 0F 80 - 0F 8F ), or any jump does not fit in 32 bits, return std::nullopt . hookIat replaces the address in an import address table slot and returns the old one, so the hook can call the original.

title: 4.05  Byte Patterns That Survive Rebuilds
body: Every new build moves code around, so fixed addresses break. Byte patterns with wildcards find the same code in any build - which bytes to keep and which to wildcard, keeping a pattern unique, scanning efficiently, and resolving the RIP-relative address inside a match. Addresses do not survive a rebuild A patch or a pointer path recorded as game.exe+0x2A1F is correct for exactly one build. Change one line of source, rebuild, and functions shift by a few bytes; everything after them moves. Debug tooling for your own game, patch scripts for an old build, and analysis notes all need a way to find "the same code" in a different build. The instructions themselves change much less than their addresses. A byte pattern (also called a signature, or an AOB, "array of bytes") describes the code by its bytes, with wildcards for the bytes that vary between builds. Which bytes vary Take the instruction that subtracts damage from health: nasm-norun 2B C3 sub eax, ebx 89 47 1C mov dword ptr rdi+1Ch , eax 48 8B 0D 6A 2F 01 00 mov rcx, qword ptr rip+12F6Ah ; a global E8 F5 03 00 00 call UpdateHud - Opcodes and registers ( 2B C3 , 89 47 , 48 8B 0D , E8 ): change only if the compiler chooses differently, which is rare for unchanged source. - Struct offsets ( 1C ): change only if the struct changes. - RIP-relative displacements ( 6A 2F 01 00 ) and call/jump displacements ( F5 03 00 00 ): change with almost every build, because they are distances to other code and data that moved. - Absolute addresses in data: change with every build and every relocation. So the pattern is: text 2B C3 89 47 1C 48 8B 0D ?? ?? ?? ?? E8 ?? ?? ?? ?? Making it unique A pattern is only useful if it matches exactly once in the module. Short patterns of common instruction sequences match hundreds of places. Tools that generate signatures (plugins for x64dbg, IDA and Ghidra) start at the instruction you want and keep adding the following instructions, wildcarding the displacements, until the pattern is unique. Good habits: - Prefer patterns built from distinctive instructions: uncommon struct offsets, unusual immediates. - Keep them short enough to survive small code changes nearby; 15 to 30 bytes is typical. - Record the offset of the instruction you care about within the pattern ("the patch goes 2 bytes into the match"). - Check uniqueness again after every rebuild; the build that breaks a pattern is the one that tells you to make a better one. Scanning The simplest scanner compares the pattern at every position, skipping wildcard positions: cpp-norun for (std::size_t i{ 0 }; i + pattern.size() <= bytes.size(); ++i) { bool match{ true }; for (std::size_t k{ 0 }; k < pattern.size() && match; ++k) match = !pattern k .has_value() bytes i + k == pattern k ; if (match) hits.push_back(i); } That is fast enough for one module of a few megabytes. Scan only executable sections ( .text ) for code patterns; it is quicker and avoids accidental matches in data. Faster scanners first look for the pattern's rarest fixed byte with memchr , or use SIMD to compare 16 or 32 bytes at once. Resolving what a match points at Often the pattern finds an instruction that refers to what you want: a global variable, a function. The wildcards hide the displacement, but once you have a match you can read it and compute the target, exactly as the processor does: text match at game.exe+0x2A1F: 48 8B 0D 6A 2F 01 00 mov rcx, rip+0x12F6A instruction starts at match + 5, is 7 bytes long, displacement at its byte 3 target = (address of the instruction + 7) + 0x12F6A The same for a call ( E8 , 5 bytes, displacement at byte 1). This is how a pattern finds a global or function in every build: the pattern survives, and the displacement inside it tells you where the thing is this time. Check yourself quiz ? Why wildcard the bytes of a call's displacement in a pattern? - They are encrypted in Release builds - They always contain CC padding bytes + They change whenever the code between them moves - Wildcards make the scan run faster The displacement is the distance to the called function. The opcode E8 stays the same, but those four bytes change with every rebuild that moves code, so a pattern that includes them breaks. ? A pattern matches 40 places in the module. What do you do? - Use the first match, which is usually the right one - Wildcard more bytes so it matches more reliably + Lengthen it with following instructions until it is unique - Scan the .data section instead of .text A pattern is only useful if it matches exactly once. Wildcarding more makes it match even more places; adding bytes narrows it down. ? A match contains 48 8B 05 followed by a 4-byte displacement d , with the instruction at address A . What address does it read? - A + d - A + 3 + d + A + 7 + d - d , as an absolute address RIP-relative displacements count from the end of the instruction, and this one is 7 bytes long: 3 bytes of opcode and ModRM, then 4 of displacement. ? Why scan only the .text section for code patterns? - Other sections cannot be read - Code patterns are encrypted in other sections - Only .text has a size that is known + It is faster and avoids false matches in data Code lives in .text . Scanning data and resources too costs time and can find look-alike bytes that are not code at all.

title: A pattern scanner
body: Build the byte pattern tools of lesson 4.05: cpp using Pattern = std::vector<std::optional<std::uint8_t ; std::optional<Pattern parsePattern(const std::string& text); std::vector<std::size_t findAll(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & bytes, const Pattern& pattern); std::optional<std::uint64_t ripTarget(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & bytes, std::size_t instruction, std::size_t length, std::size_t displacementAt, std::uint64_t base); - parsePattern reads tokens separated by spaces: two hex digits (either case) for a byte, ?? or ? for a wildcard. Anything else, or no tokens at all, gives std::nullopt . - findAll returns every offset where the pattern matches, in order (matches may overlap). - ripTarget : the instruction at offset instruction of bytes (loaded at address base ) is length bytes long and holds a signed 32-bit displacement at byte displacementAt of the instruction. Return the address it refers to: the address just past the instruction plus the displacement. If the bytes run out, return std::nullopt .

title: Encoding jumps

title: A patch engine
body: Bring lessons 4.01 and 4.05 together into a small patching tool for builds of your own programs: patches written in a text file, located by offset or by a byte pattern so they survive rebuilds, checked before anything is written, and applied all together or not at all. The patch file looks like this: text patches for Inventory.exe skip-intro offset: 0x1A40 original: 74 0C replacement: EB 0C no-cooldown pattern: 2B C3 89 47 ?? 48 8B 0D at: 2 original: 89 47 1C replacement: 90 90 90 cpp struct PatchSpec { std::string name; std::optional<std::size_t offset; std::string pattern; std::size_t at{ 0 }; std::vector<std::uint8_t original, replacement; }; class PatchSet { public: bool parse(const std::string& text, std::string& error); const std::vector<PatchSpec & patches() const; std::optional<std::size_t locate(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & code, const PatchSpec& p) const; std::vector<std::string check(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & code) const; bool applyAll(std::vector<std::uint8_t & code) const; bool revertAll(std::vector<std::uint8_t & code) const; }; parse reads the file line by line (blank lines and lines starting with are ignored; spaces around keys and values are trimmed). name starts a patch. Keys: offset (hex with 0x , or decimal), pattern (lesson 4.05's syntax), at (decimal, default 0), original and replacement (hex bytes). On a problem it returns false with error set: - line N: unknown key for a key it does not know, and line N: key outside a patch for a key before the first name ; - line N: bad bytes for an original or replacement that is not all two-digit hex bytes; - patch NAME: needs offset or pattern when a patch has neither, or both; - patch NAME: original and replacement differ when they are empty or not the same length. locate returns the patch's offset: its offset , or for a pattern, the position of its only match plus at . No match or more than one match gives std::nullopt . check returns the problems that would stop applyAll , in this order, each patch in file order: NAME: not found (cannot locate), NAME: original bytes differ (the bytes there are not original , or would run past the end), then for each pair of located patches whose byte ranges overlap, A and B overlap (A before B in the file). applyAll writes every replacement if check finds nothing, and returns whether it did. revertAll puts back every original , but only if every patch currently holds its replacement ; otherwise it changes nothing and returns false.

title: 5.01  How x64 Instructions Are Encoded
body: The layout of an x64 instruction - legacy prefixes, the REX prefix, one to three opcode bytes, the ModRM and SIB bytes that describe operands, displacements and immediates - and how to work out an instruction's length, the first job of any disassembler. Variable length x64 instructions are between 1 and 15 bytes long, and nothing marks where one ends: you only know an instruction's length by decoding it. That is why a disassembler that starts one byte off produces nonsense, and why the first thing any disassembler, hooking library or patch tool needs is a length decoder . Every instruction has the same overall shape, with most parts optional: text legacy prefixes REX opcode ModRM SIB displacement immediate 0-4 bytes 0-1 1-3 0-1 0-1 0, 1, 2 or 4 0, 1, 2, 4 or 8 Prefixes Legacy prefixes modify the instruction: 66 switches the operand size from 32 to 16 bits, F2 and F3 are the rep prefixes (and select different SSE instructions), F0 is lock , and segment overrides ( 64 for fs: , 65 for gs: ) appear in code that reads thread-local data. The REX prefix is a byte from 40 to 4F that must come directly before the opcode . Its low four bits are flags: Bit Name Effect --- --- --- 3 ( 8 ) W 64-bit operand size 2 ( 4 ) R adds 8 to the ModRM reg field: reach r8 to r15 1 ( 2 ) X adds 8 to the SIB index field 0 ( 1 ) B adds 8 to the ModRM rm field, the SIB base field, or a register in the opcode 48 (W only) is by far the most common byte in x64 code: it turns mov eax, ecx into mov rax, rcx . 40 with no flags still matters: it changes the meaning of 8-bit registers ( spl , bpl instead of ah , ch ), and MSVC uses 40 53 for push rbx so the instruction is 2 bytes long. Opcodes Most common instructions have a one-byte opcode . Some encode a register in the opcode itself: 50 +r is push r , 58 +r is pop r , B8 +r is mov r, imm (with REX.B selecting r8 to r15 ). Two-byte opcodes start with the escape byte 0F : 0F 84 is near je , 0F B6 is movzx , 0F 1F is the long nop . Three-byte opcodes start 0F 38 or 0F 3A (mostly SIMD). ModRM Instructions with a register or memory operand have a ModRM byte after the opcode, split into three fields: text 7 6 5 4 3 2 1 0 mod reg rm - reg : a register operand (or, for some opcodes, an extension of the opcode: 83 /5 means "opcode 83 with reg field 5", which is sub ). - mod and rm together describe the other operand: mod rm Operand Extra bytes --- --- --- --- 11 any the register rm none 00 101 rip + disp32 4 00 100 SIB SIB (+4 if the SIB base is 101 ) 00 other rm none 01 100 SIB + disp8 SIB + 1 01 other rm + disp8 1 10 100 SIB + disp32 SIB + 4 10 other rm + disp32 4 Register numbers: 0 rax , 1 rcx , 2 rdx , 3 rbx , 4 rsp , 5 rbp , 6 rsi , 7 rdi , and 8 to 15 for r8 to r15 with a REX bit. SIB When rm is 100 in a memory form, a SIB byte follows, for base + index scale : text scale index base scale: 00=1, 01=2, 10=4, 11=8 An index of 100 (without REX.X) means no index ; that is how rsp+8 is encoded, since rsp cannot be an index. A base of 101 with mod 00 means no base, disp32 instead. A worked example 4C 8B 44 24 28 : text 4C REX: 0100 1100 - W=1, R=1 8B opcode: mov reg, r/m 44 ModRM: 01 000 100 - mod 01 (disp8), reg 000 (+8 from R = r8), rm 100 (SIB follows) 24 SIB: 00 100 100 - scale 1, index 100 (none), base 100 (rsp) 28 disp8: 0x28 = mov r8, qword ptr rsp+0x28 (5 bytes) Immediates Constants embedded in the instruction come last: 1 byte for 83 /x ib and short jumps, 4 bytes for 81 /x id , C7 /0 id and E8 / E9 displacements, and 8 bytes only for mov r64, imm64 ( 48 B8 + 8 bytes). With the 66 prefix, the 4-byte immediates of 81 and C7 become 2 bytes. Putting it together, an instruction's length is: prefixes + REX + opcode bytes + ModRM (if any) + SIB (if any) + displacement + immediate. The practice writes exactly that for a useful subset. Check yourself quiz ? What does the REX byte 0x41 do to push rax ( 50 )? - Makes it a 64-bit push of eax , zero-extended + REX.B adds 8 to the register in the opcode: 41 50 is push r8 - Pushes the value 0x41 before rax - Nothing; REX prefixes are ignored by push REX.B extends the register field of the opcode (or of ModRM's rm or SIB's base), giving access to r8 to r15 . Register 0 plus 8 is r8 . ? In ModRM 0x45 , what are mod, reg and rm? - mod 01, reg 001, rm 101, meaning rbp with reg rcx - mod 00, reg 100, rm 101, meaning rip + disp32 with reg rsp + mod 01, reg 000, rm 101, meaning rbp + disp8 with reg rax / eax - mod 10, reg 001, rm 000, meaning rax + disp32 with reg rcx 0x45 is 01 000 101 in binary: the top two bits are mod, the next three reg, the last three rm. mod 01 with rm 101 is rbp plus an 8-bit displacement. ? How is rsp+8 encoded, given rsp cannot be an index? - With rm = 100 directly, which means rsp without a SIB byte + With a SIB byte whose index is 100 (no index) and base 100 ( rsp ), plus a disp8 - With a REX prefix that turns rbp into rsp - It cannot be encoded; compilers use rbp instead rm = 100 does not mean rsp ; it means "a SIB byte follows". In the SIB, index 100 means none and base 100 is rsp . ? How long is 48 C7 45 F8 0A 00 00 00 , and why? - 4 bytes: REX, opcode, ModRM and an 8-bit immediate - 5 bytes: the 48 prefix is a separate instruction - 12 bytes: REX.W makes the immediate 8 bytes long + 8 bytes: REX, opcode, ModRM, disp8, 4-byte immediate ModRM 45 has mod 01, so a disp8 ( F8 ) follows. C7 /0 takes a 32-bit immediate even with REX.W, which sign-extends it; only mov r64, imm64 ( B8 +r) has an 8-byte immediate.

title: An instruction length decoder
body: Write the length decoder at the heart of every disassembler and hooking library (lesson 5.01), for a common subset of x64: cpp std::size_t instructionLength(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & code, std::size_t at); It returns the length of the instruction starting at code at , or 0 if the bytes are not in the subset or run out before the instruction ends. 1. Prefixes : any number of 66 , F2 , F3 , then optionally one REX byte ( 40 - 4F ). 2. Opcode and what follows it: Opcode Then --- --- 50 - 5F , 90 , C3 , CC nothing 70 - 7F , EB 1-byte displacement E8 , E9 4-byte displacement B8 - BF 4-byte immediate, or 8 with REX.W 01 03 29 2B 31 33 39 3B 63 85 89 8B 8D ModRM 83 ModRM, then 1-byte immediate 81 , C7 ModRM, then 4-byte immediate (2 bytes with a 66 prefix) 0F 80 - 0F 8F 4-byte displacement 0F 1F , 0F B6 , 0F B7 , 0F BE , 0F BF ModRM 3. ModRM (lesson 5.01's table): mod 11 adds nothing; otherwise rm 100 adds a SIB byte (and 4 more bytes if the SIB base is 101 with mod 00); mod 00 with rm 101 adds 4; mod 01 adds 1; mod 10 adds 4.

title: 5.02  Writing a Disassembler
body: From bytes to text - table-driven decoding, naming registers and building memory operands, formatting immediates and branch targets, linear sweep versus recursive descent, telling code from data, and the real libraries (Zydis, Capstone) behind every tool. Decoding and formatting A disassembler does two jobs for each instruction: 1. Decode : read prefixes, opcode, ModRM, SIB, displacement and immediate into a structure: which operation, which registers, which memory expression, which constant. This also gives the length. 2. Format : turn that structure into text in a chosen syntax: mov rax, qword ptr rcx+0x10 (Intel, as MSVC and x64dbg show it) or movq 0x10(%rcx), %rax (AT&T, as GDB and objdump show by default). Keeping them separate pays off: analysis code (a control flow graph, a pattern generator) wants the structure, not the text. Tables x86 has hundreds of opcodes, so real decoders are table-driven : an array indexed by opcode byte saying what follows (ModRM or not, immediate size, operand roles) and the mnemonic. A small decoder for common instructions is a table like this: Opcode Form Mnemonic --- --- --- 01 / 03 r/m, reg / reg, r/m add 29 / 2B r/m, reg / reg, r/m sub 31 / 33 r/m, reg / reg, r/m xor 39 / 3B r/m, reg / reg, r/m cmp 85 r/m, reg test 89 / 8B r/m, reg / reg, r/m mov 8D reg, m lea 83 /0 /4 /5 /7 r/m, imm8 add and sub cmp 81 /0 /4 /5 /7 r/m, imm32 the same with a 32-bit immediate C7 /0 r/m, imm32 mov B8 +r reg, imm32 (imm64 with REX.W) mov 50 +r / 58 +r reg push / pop E8 / E9 / EB rel32 / rel32 / rel8 call / jmp / jmp 70 +cc / 0F 80 +cc rel8 / rel32 jo jno jb jae je jne jbe ja js jns jp jnp jl jge jle jg C3 , CC , 90 none ret , int3 , nop With just these, most of a typical function decodes. Operands Registers depend on the operand size: with REX.W the 64-bit names ( rax , ..., r15 ), otherwise the 32-bit ones ( eax , ..., edi , r8d , ..., r15d ). Registers inside a memory operand are addresses, so they always use the 64-bit names: dword ptr rbp-0x4 , never ebp-0x4 . Memory operands are built from the ModRM and SIB fields: base, then +index scale , then the displacement as +0x10 or -0x8 , all in brackets. A size keyword in front says how many bytes are accessed: qword ptr , dword ptr , word ptr , byte ptr . lea takes no size keyword, because it accesses no memory. Immediates for arithmetic are sign-extended: 83 C0 FF is add eax, -0x1 , not add eax, 0xff . Branch targets are shown as absolute addresses, computed from the instruction's address, its length and its displacement (lesson 4.02), because that is what a reader needs. Linear sweep and recursive descent How do you choose where to decode? - Linear sweep decodes from the start of a section to the end, each instruction right after the previous one. Simple, and it sees everything, but when it meets data inside code (a jump table, padding, a literal pool), it decodes it as nonsense instructions, and may stay out of step for a few instructions afterwards. objdump works this way. - Recursive descent starts at known entry points (the entry point, exports, .pdata functions) and follows the code: decode until a ret or jmp , and queue every branch and call target. It never decodes data by mistake, but misses code that is only reached indirectly (through function pointers, vtables, jump tables), unless it resolves those too. Ghidra, IDA and Binary Ninja combine this with many heuristics. When a byte does not decode as any known instruction, a disassembler shows it as data, db 0x0f , and moves on by one byte. Use a library for real work A complete x86-64 decoder covers thousands of instruction forms, AVX-512, and many corner cases. For your own tools use a library: - Zydis : fast, thorough, C, MIT licence; decodes into a detailed structure and formats Intel or AT&T. - Capstone : many architectures (x86, ARM, MIPS...), C with bindings for Python and other languages, BSD licence. - iced (Rust and .NET): very complete, also encodes. Writing a small one yourself, as this milestone's project does, is how you learn what those libraries give you, and how to read their output when it surprises you. Check yourself quiz ? Why does mov eax, dword ptr rbp-0x4 use rbp inside the brackets but eax outside? - The disassembler shortens register names to save space - rbp is always 64-bit and eax always 32-bit, whatever the instruction + Addresses are always 64-bit; operand size names the data register - The instruction reads 8 bytes, so the brackets need a 64-bit register In 64-bit code a memory operand's registers form an address, so the base is rbp . The 32-bit operand size applies to the data, so the destination is eax and the access is a dword . ? How is 83 C0 FF shown, and why? - add eax, 0xFF , because the immediate is one byte + add eax, -0x1 , because the 8-bit immediate is sign-extended - sub eax, 0x1 , because the disassembler turns adding -1 into a subtraction - add al, 0xFF , because 83 works on bytes Opcode 83 takes an 8-bit immediate and sign-extends it to the operand size, so FF becomes -1 for a 32-bit add . A disassembler shows it as written, it does not rewrite it as sub . ? What goes wrong when a linear sweep meets a jump table inside .text ? - It skips the table, because tables are marked in .pdata - It stops decoding and reports the rest as data + It decodes the table as instructions and may lose step - It follows every entry of the table as a branch Linear sweep decodes one instruction after another and cannot tell data from code, so it produces nonsense and can misalign the real instructions after the table. Following entries as branches is what recursive descent does once the table is resolved. ? What does recursive descent miss? - Code after a conditional jump - Code reached by a direct call + Code reached only indirectly, such as via vtables - Code in the first function of the program Recursive descent follows the branches and calls it can see. A target that only exists at run time, through function pointers, vtables or unresolved jump tables, is never followed unless something else reveals it.

title: Formatting operands
body: Turn a ModRM byte (with its SIB and displacement) into the two operand strings a disassembler prints (lesson 5.02): cpp struct Operands { std::string reg; std::string rm; std::size_t length; }; std::optional<Operands decodeModRm(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & code, std::size_t at, std::uint8_t rex, int bits); std::string registerName(int number, int bits); - registerName gives register number (0 to 15) at a size: 64 bits rax rcx rdx rbx rsp rbp rsi rdi r8 ... r15 ; 32 bits eax ecx edx ebx esp ebp esi edi r8d ... r15d . - decodeModRm reads the ModRM byte at code at . rex is the REX byte (or 0); bits (32 or 64) is the operand size. - reg is register ( reg field + 8 if REX.R) at bits . - If mod is 11, rm is register ( rm field + 8 if REX.B) at bits . - Otherwise rm is a memory operand: dword ptr (or qword ptr for 64 bits), then , the base, +index scale if there is an index, the displacement, . Base and index are always 64-bit names; REX.B extends the base (or rm ), REX.X the index. The displacement is written +0x1c or -0x8 (lowercase hex), and left out when it is 0 and there is a base. - mod 00 with rm 101 is rip+0x10 (always with its displacement, even 0, signed). - A SIB index of 100 (without REX.X) means no index. A SIB base of 101 with mod 00 means no base: then the displacement is printed as 0x10 with no + if it comes first ( 0x10 , rcx 4+0x10 ). - length counts the ModRM byte, SIB and displacement. - Running out of bytes gives std::nullopt .

title: 5.03  Reading a Process's Memory Map
body: Seeing a running process the way debuggers do, with documented Windows APIs - opening a process with the right access rights, walking its address space with VirtualQueryEx, understanding states, protections and types, listing its modules, and reading memory safely. The documented way in Debuggers, profilers, Process Explorer and memory scanners all look at other processes through a handful of documented Windows functions. Using them on your own programs is how you build inspection tools for them, such as an external stats viewer for a game you are developing (the Game Development course builds one). First, open the process with only the access you need: cpp-norun HANDLE process{ OpenProcess(PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION PROCESS_VM_READ, FALSE, pid) }; if (!process) { / GetLastError(): 5 = access denied / } Windows checks the request against the target's security. You can open processes running as your own user; processes of other users, services and protected processes (antivirus, DRM, system processes) refuse. That is the security boundary working as intended. Walking the address space VirtualQueryEx describes the region of pages containing an address. Starting at 0 and jumping from region to region walks the whole address space: cpp-norun MEMORY_BASIC_INFORMATION info{}; for (std::uintptr_t at{ 0 }; VirtualQueryEx(process, reinterpret_cast<void (at), &info, sizeof(info)) == sizeof(info); at = reinterpret_cast<std::uintptr_t (info.BaseAddress) + info.RegionSize) { // info.BaseAddress, info.RegionSize, info.State, info.Protect, info.Type, info.AllocationBase } Each region is a run of pages with identical attributes: Field Values --- --- State MEM_FREE (0x10000), MEM_RESERVE (0x2000), MEM_COMMIT (0x1000) Protect PAGE_NOACCESS 0x01, PAGE_READONLY 0x02, PAGE_READWRITE 0x04, PAGE_WRITECOPY 0x08, PAGE_EXECUTE 0x10, PAGE_EXECUTE_READ 0x20, PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE 0x40, PAGE_EXECUTE_WRITECOPY 0x80, plus the modifier PAGE_GUARD 0x100 Type MEM_IMAGE (a mapped .exe or .dll), MEM_MAPPED (a mapped file or shared memory), MEM_PRIVATE (heap, stacks, VirtualAlloc ) AllocationBase the start of the VirtualAlloc (or mapping) this region belongs to One allocation often shows up as several regions: an image is one allocation with a region per section ( .text as PAGE_EXECUTE_READ , .data as PAGE_READWRITE ...), and a thread stack is one reservation with a committed part, a guard page and a reserved remainder. Grouping regions by AllocationBase reassembles them. PAGE_WRITECOPY is how image pages that are writable start out: shared between processes until one writes, then copied for that process alone. Modules To list loaded modules with their names and base addresses: cpp-norun HANDLE snap{ CreateToolhelp32Snapshot(TH32CS_SNAPMODULE TH32CS_SNAPMODULE32, pid) }; MODULEENTRY32W entry{ sizeof(entry) }; for (BOOL ok{ Module32FirstW(snap, &entry) }; ok; ok = Module32NextW(snap, &entry)) { // entry.szModule, entry.modBaseAddr, entry.modBaseSize, entry.szExePath } CloseHandle(snap); ( EnumProcessModulesEx with GetModuleBaseNameW is the other route.) With the module list you can turn any address into module+offset (lesson 3.02), and the module's base plus an RVA into a real address. Reading memory cpp-norun std::uint32_t health{}; SIZE_T got{}; if (ReadProcessMemory(process, reinterpret_cast<void (address), &health, sizeof(health), &got) && got == sizeof(health)) { // use health } Rules that keep a reader robust: - Check every read. Memory can be freed between your query and your read; ReadProcessMemory then fails (error 299, partial copy). - Only read committed, readable regions. Skip PAGE_NOACCESS and PAGE_GUARD regions; touching a guard page would change the target's behaviour. - Read in large chunks when scanning (a whole region at a time), not one value per call: each call is a trip into the kernel. - The target keeps running. Values can change between reads; a consistent snapshot needs the target paused ( DebugActiveProcess , or suspending its threads). Writing ( WriteProcessMemory , needing PROCESS_VM_WRITE PROCESS_VM_OPERATION ) and creating threads in another process are what debuggers do to your own programs; outside your own software, they are exactly what security software watches for. Check yourself quiz ? Which VirtualQueryEx state means a region has memory behind it? - MEM_RESERVE - MEM_FREE + MEM_COMMIT - MEM_IMAGE Committed pages have memory behind them; reserved pages are only addresses. MEM_IMAGE is a type (mapped from an executable file), not a state. ? How do you find all the regions that belong to one loaded DLL? + Group regions by AllocationBase : the image is one allocation split into one region per section - Look for the regions whose protection is PAGE_EXECUTE_READ - Find the single region whose BaseAddress matches the DLL's name - Read the DLL's import table An image is mapped as one allocation, but its sections have different protections, so VirtualQueryEx reports several regions sharing one AllocationBase . Executable protection alone would miss the data sections. ? Why skip PAGE_GUARD regions when reading another process's memory? - They hold encrypted data that cannot be read - Reading them always crashes your own program + Touching one fires its one-time exception in the target - They belong to the kernel, not the process Guard pages are used, for example, to grow thread stacks. Reading one uses up its guard and can change what the target does next. ? Why read whole regions instead of one value per ReadProcessMemory call when scanning? - ReadProcessMemory can only read whole regions - Small reads return stale data - Large reads skip guard pages automatically + Each call is a round trip into the kernel, so large reads are far faster Reading millions of 4-byte values one by one means millions of system calls. One read per region copies the data at memory speed.

body: Process the region list VirtualQueryEx returns (lesson 5.03) into what a memory viewer shows: cpp struct RegionInfo { std::uint64_t base, size, allocationBase; std::uint32_t state, protect, type; }; struct Allocation { std::uint64_t base, size; std::uint32_t type; int regions; }; struct ModuleInfo { std::string name; std::uint64_t base, size; }; std::string protection(std::uint32_t protect); bool readable(const RegionInfo& r); std::vector<Allocation allocations(const std::vector<RegionInfo & regions); std::string label(const std::vector<ModuleInfo & modules, std::uint64_t address); - protection turns a Protect value into rwx style: 0x01 --- , 0x02 r-- , 0x04 rw- , 0x08 rw- , 0x10 --x , 0x20 r-x , 0x40 rwx , 0x80 rwx ; if the PAGE_GUARD bit 0x100 is also set, add guard . Any other base value gives ? . - readable is true for regions that are committed ( MEM_COMMIT = 0x1000), not guard pages, and whose protection allows reading ( r in the string above). - allocations groups non-free regions ( MEM_FREE = 0x10000 are skipped) by allocationBase , in order of base: each allocation's base is the allocation base, size runs from there to the end of its last region, type is its first region's type, and regions counts them. - label names an address: name+0x1a2 (lowercase hex offset from the module's base) inside a module, otherwise 0x and the address in lowercase hex.

title: 5.04  Symbols and PDB Files
body: What a PDB holds, how a binary names its exact PDB through a GUID and age, symbol servers and the path layout they use, public versus private symbols, and turning addresses into names with DbgHelp - including Microsoft's symbols for Windows itself. Names live in a separate file When MSVC links a program it writes the machine code into the .exe and the names into a separate PDB (program database) file: function names and addresses, global variables, types and struct layouts, local variables, source file and line information. The .exe itself contains almost none of it, which is why stripped binaries are hard to read. With the matching PDB, every tool in this course shows names: call stacks, disassembly, crash dumps. Always check whether one is available before working without it. Which PDB matches? A PDB is only useful for the exact build it came from. The .exe records which one it needs in a CodeView record in its debug directory (lesson 1.05): Offset Size Field --- --- --- 0 4 signature RSDS 4 16 GUID: a unique id generated at link time 20 4 age: incremented by incremental relinks 24 ... PDB file name or path, zero-terminated (UTF-8) The PDB contains the same GUID and age. Tools refuse a PDB whose GUID or age differs, even if the file name matches: a PDB from yesterday's build of the same project describes different addresses. Symbol servers A symbol server is a store of PDBs indexed by that GUID and age, so a debugger can fetch exactly the right one. The path inside the store is: text <pdb name /<GUID <age /<pdb name Inventory.pdb/3F2504E04F8911D39A0C0305E82C33011/Inventory.pdb The GUID is written as 32 uppercase hex digits in a specific order: its first field as a 32-bit number, the next two as 16-bit numbers, then its last 8 bytes in order; the age follows in hex with no leading zeros. Microsoft publishes PDBs for Windows' own DLLs on its public server. Point your tools at it with the _NT_SYMBOL_PATH environment variable: text srv C:\Symbols https://msdl.microsoft.com/download/symbols ( C:\Symbols is a local cache.) Then call stacks through ntdll.dll , kernel32.dll and user32.dll show real function names. For your own builds, keep every released build's PDBs in a store of your own (the symstore tool from the Windows SDK adds them), and every crash report from a user can be read with names, even months later. Public and private symbols - Private symbols , the full PDB your build creates, include types, local variables and line numbers. - Public symbols contain only the names and addresses of functions and globals. Microsoft's server mostly has these. They are created with the linker's /PDBSTRIPPED option, which is what you would ship if you publish symbols for your own product without giving away its structure. DbgHelp Windows' DbgHelp library ( dbghelp.dll ) loads symbols and answers questions about them; it is what WinDbg and many crash reporters use: cpp-norun SymSetOptions(SYMOPT_UNDNAME SYMOPT_DEFERRED_LOADS); SymInitialize(process, nullptr / use _NT_SYMBOL_PATH /, TRUE / load every module /); char buffer sizeof(SYMBOL_INFO) + MAX_SYM_NAME {}; auto symbol{ reinterpret_cast<SYMBOL_INFO (buffer) }; symbol- SizeOfStruct = sizeof(SYMBOL_INFO); symbol- MaxNameLen = MAX_SYM_NAME; DWORD64 displacement{}; if (SymFromAddr(process, address, &displacement, symbol)) std::printf("%s+0x%llx\n", symbol- Name, displacement); // Player::update+0x1a Other useful calls: SymFromName (name to address), SymGetLineFromAddr64 (address to source line), StackWalk64 (unwinding), and MiniDumpWriteDump for writing crash dumps that you later open with these same symbols. Without any PDB, you still have the export names, RTTI class names (lesson 2.05), and whatever names you recover and add in your disassembler's database, which is effectively a PDB you write by hand. Check yourself quiz ? Why will a debugger refuse a PDB with the right name from a different build? - PDBs are encrypted with the date of the build - The PDB is too large for the new build + Its GUID or age does not match the binary's record - Debuggers only accept PDBs from the symbol server Every build gets a new GUID, recorded in both the binary's CodeView record and the PDB. A mismatched PDB would describe different code, naming the wrong functions at the wrong addresses. ? What does a symbol server path look like? - GUID/name.pdb , with the GUID in lowercase and no age - name/AGE/GUID.pdb , with the age as a folder of its own + name.pdb/GUIDAGE/name.pdb , all in uppercase hex - name.pdb?guid=GUID&age=AGE , as a query string The folder name is the GUID as 32 uppercase hex digits followed by the age in hex, so each build's PDB has its own folder under the PDB's name. ? What is the difference between public and private symbols? - Public symbols are free to download; private ones need a licence + Public have names only; private add types, locals and lines - Public symbols are for Release builds; private ones for Debug builds - Public symbols are stored in the binary; private ones in the PDB Public symbols name functions and globals with their addresses. Microsoft publishes them for Windows; your own builds' full PDBs are private symbols. ? How do you get names for functions inside ntdll.dll in a call stack? - Rebuild ntdll.dll with debug information - Read the names from ntdll.dll 's import table - Copy a PDB with the same name from another computer + Point the symbol path at Microsoft's symbol server Set _NT_SYMBOL_PATH or the debugger's symbol path, and it downloads the matching PDB by GUID and age. Imports only name what ntdll uses, not what it contains.

title: Finding the right PDB
body: Read a binary's CodeView record and work out where its PDB lives on a symbol server (lesson 5.04): cpp struct CodeView { std::array<std::uint8_t, 16 guid; std::uint32_t age; std::string path; }; std::optional<CodeView parseCodeView(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & record); std::string pdbName(const std::string& path); std::string guidText(const std::array<std::uint8_t, 16 & guid); std::string symbolServerPath(const CodeView& cv); - parseCodeView reads the record: RSDS , the 16 GUID bytes, a 4-byte little-endian age, then the PDB path up to a zero byte (or the end). Anything shorter than 24 bytes or with another signature gives std::nullopt . - pdbName is the file name part of the path: everything after the last \ or / . - guidText formats a GUID the symbol server's way: the first 4 bytes as one little-endian 32-bit number (8 hex digits), the next 2 as a little-endian 16-bit number (4 digits), the next 2 the same, then the last 8 bytes one by one (2 digits each). Uppercase, no separators: 32 characters. - symbolServerPath is name/GUIDAGE/name , with the age in uppercase hex without leading zeros.

title: 5.05  Scripting Your Analysis
body: Automating the repetitive parts of reverse engineering - scripting Ghidra, IDA and x64dbg, Python with pefile and Capstone for batch work, generating byte signatures automatically, and keeping your findings in a form you can reuse on the next build. Do it once by hand, then script it Reverse engineering has a lot of repetition: renaming every function that calls a logging function after the string it logs, finding every use of a struct, re-finding fifty functions in a new build. Anything you do more than a few times is worth a script, and every serious tool has a scripting interface. Ghidra Ghidra runs scripts written in Java or Python (Jython, or real Python 3 with the Ghidrathon or PyGhidra extensions) from its Script Manager. A script sees the whole program database: python-norun Rename every function that references a string beginning " net " after that string. from ghidra.program.model.symbol import SourceType for s in currentProgram.getListing().getDefinedData(True): text = s.getValue() if not isinstance(text, str) or not text.startswith(" net "): continue for ref in getReferencesTo(s.getAddress()): f = getFunctionContaining(ref.getFromAddress()) if f and f.getName().startswith("FUN_"): f.setName("net_" + text 6: .split() 0 , SourceType.USER_DEFINED) FUN_ is Ghidra's prefix for unnamed functions, so the check keeps names you already chose. Ghidra also has a headless mode ( analyzeHeadless ) that imports, analyses and runs scripts over many binaries without the user interface: the way to process a hundred builds. IDA and x64dbg - IDAPython gives the same kind of access in IDA ( idautils.Functions() , idc.set_name , cross-references), and IDA Free supports it in recent versions. - x64dbg has a simple command script language ( bp , run , log , conditional commands) for automating debugging sessions, and a plugin SDK in C++ for anything bigger, such as a plugin that logs every call to a function with formatted arguments. - WinDbg has JavaScript extensions and its data model ( dx ) for querying a session like a database. Python outside the tools For batch work on files, plain Python with two libraries goes a long way: python-norun import pefile, capstone pe = pefile.PE("Inventory.exe") text = next(s for s in pe.sections if s.Name.startswith(b".text")) code = text.get_data() base = pe.OPTIONAL_HEADER.ImageBase + text.VirtualAddress md = capstone.Cs(capstone.CS_ARCH_X86, capstone.CS_MODE_64) for insn in md.disasm(code :64 , base): print(f"{insn.address:x} {insn.mnemonic} {insn.op_str}") for entry in pe.DIRECTORY_ENTRY_IMPORT: print(entry.dll.decode(), imp.name.decode() for imp in entry.imports if imp.name ) pefile parses everything in milestone 1; Capstone disassembles as in lesson 5.02. Together they answer questions such as "which of these 200 builds import WinHttpOpen ?" in seconds. Generating signatures The byte patterns of lesson 4.05 are tedious to make by hand. A signature generator automates the recipe: 1. Start at the instruction you care about. 2. Add whole instructions one at a time, writing their bytes into the pattern but wildcarding the bytes that change between builds: RIP-relative and branch displacements, absolute addresses. 3. After each instruction, scan the module. When the pattern matches exactly once, stop. 4. If it grows past a length limit before becoming unique, give up and try starting from a nearby instruction instead. The decoder from this milestone supplies the instruction lengths and tells you which bytes are displacements. The practice writes this generator. Keeping findings Your understanding of a program is an asset: names, struct layouts, comments, signatures. Keep it in a form that survives: - Save the disassembler database and export names and types (Ghidra can export to C headers; IDA to .idc or .h ). - Keep a text file of signatures with what each one finds, so a new build can be re-labelled by running them. - For your own programs, the PDB is the real answer: archive it with every build. Check yourself quiz ? What is Ghidra's headless mode for? - Running Ghidra on a server so others can view its window + Analysing and scripting many binaries with no interface - Analysing a program while it is running - Hiding Ghidra from the program being analysed Headless mode imports, analyses and runs your scripts from the command line, so the same work can be done on many files in a batch. ? Which two Python libraries cover PE parsing and disassembly? - struct and ctypes - requests and numpy + pefile and Capstone - Zydis and DbgHelp pefile reads PE headers, sections and tables; Capstone disassembles bytes. Zydis is a C library and DbgHelp a Windows DLL for symbols. ? In a signature generator, which bytes are wildcarded? - Every byte that is 00 - The opcode bytes, because they change between compilers + Displacements and addresses that change between builds - Every second byte, so the pattern is shorter Branch and RIP-relative displacements and absolute addresses depend on where things ended up. Opcodes and ModRM bytes describe what the code does and stay the same. ? When does a signature generator stop adding instructions? - After exactly 16 bytes, whatever they match - When it reaches the end of the function - When it has wildcarded half of the bytes + When the pattern is unique, or too long The goal is the shortest pattern that matches exactly once in the module. Longer patterns break more easily on the next build, and a length limit stops it when no unique pattern can be found.

title: A signature generator
body: Automate lesson 4.05's patterns as described in lesson 5.05: grow a pattern one instruction at a time, wildcarding the bytes that change between builds, until it is unique. cpp struct Insn { std::size_t offset; std::size_t length; std::size_t variableAt; std::size_t variableLength; }; std::string toPattern(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & code, const std::vector<Insn & insns); std::size_t countMatches(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & code, const std::string& pattern); std::optional<std::string makeSignature(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & code, const std::vector<Insn & insns, std::size_t first, std::size_t maxBytes); insns describes consecutive instructions: each one's offset and length, and which of its bytes vary between builds ( variableLength bytes starting variableAt bytes into the instruction; variableLength 0 means none). - toPattern writes the bytes of the given instructions as a pattern: uppercase two-digit hex, ?? for variable bytes, separated by single spaces. - countMatches counts the places in code where a pattern of that form matches (overlapping matches count). - makeSignature starts with instruction number first and adds the following instructions one at a time; as soon as the pattern matches exactly once, it returns it. If adding the next instruction would make the pattern longer than maxBytes bytes, or the instructions run out, it returns std::nullopt .

title: The REX prefix
