title: A small x64 disassembler
body: Combine the length decoder and the operand formatter of this milestone into a working disassembler for the common instructions of lesson 5.02, using a linear sweep: cpp struct Line { std::uint64_t address; std::size_t length; std::string text; }; std::vector<Line disassemble(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & code, std::uint64_t base); Start at offset 0 and decode one instruction after another. Each Line has the instruction's address ( base + offset), its length and its text. A byte that does not start a known instruction (or an instruction cut off by the end of code ) becomes db 0x0f (two lowercase hex digits) with length 1, and decoding continues at the next byte. (Look at the test that does this: the bytes after an unknown instruction can decode as something plausible but wrong, exactly the weakness of linear sweep from lesson 5.02.) The subset. An optional REX prefix ( 40 - 4F ), then: Opcode Text --- --- 50 +r / 58 +r push r64 / pop r64 (REX.B adds 8) C3 , CC , 90 ret , int3 , nop E8 / E9 rel32, EB rel8 call TARGET / jmp TARGET 70 +cc rel8, 0F 80 +cc rel32 jCC TARGET with cc names o no b ae e ne be a s ns p np l ge le g 01 29 31 39 85 89 add sub xor cmp test mov rm , reg 03 2B 33 3B 8B add sub xor cmp mov reg , rm 8D lea reg , memory without the size keyword 83 /0 /4 /5 /7 ib add and sub cmp rm , IMM (8-bit, sign-extended) 81 /0 /4 /5 /7 id the same with a 32-bit signed immediate C7 /0 id mov rm , IMM (32-bit signed) B8 +r mov r32, IMM (32-bit, unsigned); with REX.W mov r64, IMM (64-bit) Formatting follows lesson 5.02 and the practice of 5.02: operand size 64 with REX.W, else 32; register and memory operands exactly as decodeModRm produced them ( qword ptr rbp-0x8 , rip+0x10 ...). Immediates are 0x plus lowercase hex, with - in front of negative ones ( -0x1 ). Branch and call targets are absolute addresses: 0x and lowercase hex of the address after the instruction plus the signed displacement. A ModRM reg field not listed for 83 , 81 or C7 makes the instruction unknown.

title: 6.01  A Method for Unknown Programs
body: How to approach a program you know nothing about without getting lost - start from a question, triage, find landmarks, form a hypothesis, test it dynamically, write it down, and know when to stop reading and switch technique. The trap The beginner's approach to an unknown binary is to open it at the entry point and read. After two hours you have understood the C runtime's start-up code in detail and know nothing about the program. Real programs are millions of instructions; nobody reads them all. Experienced reverse engineers read a tiny fraction, chosen carefully. Start from a question Every session needs a concrete goal, written down before you start: - "Where does it store its settings, and in what format?" - "Why does it crash when the file name contains a space?" - "How does the save file encode the player's inventory?" - "What does this DLL's exported Init function expect as its arguments?" A question tells you what you can ignore, which is almost everything. The loop 1. Triage (lesson 1.05): what is it, how was it built, what does it import, which strings does it contain? Ten minutes. 2. Find landmarks related to the question: strings ("Save failed"), imports ( CreateFileW , RegSetValueExW ), exports, RTTI class names, behaviour seen in Process Monitor. Each landmark leads to code through cross-references. 3. Form a hypothesis : "this function parses the save file; its first argument is the file contents; rcx+8 is the item count". 4. Test it dynamically : put a breakpoint there, trigger the behaviour, check the registers and memory against your guess. Change an input (a different save) and predict the change. 5. Record what you learned : rename the function, define the struct, add a comment, note the evidence. 6. Repeat , each answer raising the next, smaller question. Static reading suggests; dynamic testing confirms. A claim that has not been checked in a debugger, or against a second sample, is still a guess. Mark it as one. Top down and bottom up - Top down : start from a high-level landmark (the save command in the menu) and descend into the functions it calls until you reach the detail you need. - Bottom up : start from a low-level landmark (the call to WriteFile ) and climb the call stack to find who decided what to write. Bottom up is usually faster for questions about data; top down for questions about behaviour. Switch whenever you stall. Recognise library code A large part of any program is library code: the C runtime, the C++ standard library, compression, image loading, JSON parsing. Do not reverse it. Recognise it and name it: - Ghidra's Function ID and IDA's FLIRT signatures name known library functions automatically. - Strings give libraries away: inflate 1.2.13 Copyright , stb_image , error messages of well-known libraries. - Constants give algorithms away: 0x67452301 starts MD5 and SHA-1, 0xEDB88320 is CRC-32's polynomial, 0x9E3779B9 appears in TEA and in hash functions. Once you know a function is memcpy or zlib's inflate , you know its arguments and can step over it. Keep notes Write as you go, in the disassembler's database and in a plain notes file: - the question, and what you have concluded so far; - each finding with its evidence : address (as module+offset ), what you saw, how you confirmed it; - open questions and things you assumed. Notes make the work resumable tomorrow, shareable with someone else, and checkable when a new build arrives. Know when to switch If you have read the same function for an hour, stop and change technique: run it with different inputs and watch, diff two runs (lesson 3.05), look for a library signature, or find a different landmark. Reverse engineering is mostly choosing the right next small question. Check yourself quiz ? Why start from the entry point only rarely? - The entry point is encrypted in most programs + It leads through runtime start-up code, far from your question - Disassemblers cannot show the entry point - The entry point changes every time the program runs From the entry point you first wade through C runtime initialisation. A string, import or value tied to the question gets you to the relevant code directly. ? What turns a hypothesis about a function into a finding? - Reading the function's disassembly a second time - Seeing that the decompiler's output agrees with your guess + Testing it: breakpoints and predictions that come true - Giving the function a descriptive name in the database A guess becomes a finding when it predicts something you can check, dynamically or against another sample: breakpoints, changed inputs, predictions that come true. The decompiler is a reconstruction too, so agreeing with it is not proof. ? You see the constant 0xEDB88320 in a loop. What is the code probably doing? - Computing an MD5 hash - Generating random numbers + Computing a CRC-32 - Decrypting AES 0xEDB88320 is the reversed CRC-32 polynomial. Well-known constants like this identify algorithms at a glance. ? Why recognise and name library functions instead of reversing them? - Library functions cannot be disassembled + They are documented already, so you can skip them - Library functions are always the cause of bugs - Reversing library code is illegal memcpy , printf or a CRT string routine is already known. Naming it saves hours and lets you focus on the program's own code; the calls to it tell you about the code around them.

title: A triage report
body: Turn the facts gathered in triage (lessons 1.05 and 6.01) into the warnings an analyst writes at the top of their notes: cpp struct SectionFacts { std::string name; double entropy; bool write; bool execute; }; struct Facts { std::vector<SectionFacts sections; int importCount; std::string entrySection; bool hasDebugInfo; }; std::vector<std::string triageFlags(const Facts& f); Return the flags that apply, in exactly this order: Flag When --- --- "no imports" importCount is 0 "few imports" importCount is 1 to 9 "high entropy: NAME" a section's entropy is above 7.2 (one flag per such section, in section order) "writable code: NAME" a section is both writable and executable (one per section) "entry outside .text" entrySection is not .text "probably packed" at least one high-entropy section and fewer than 10 imports "symbols may be available" hasDebugInfo is true

title: 6.02  Reversing a File Format
body: Working out an undocumented binary file format from samples - collecting files from controlled changes, magic numbers and versions, lengths and counts, offsets, byte order, strings, checksums and compression - and proving your understanding by writing a parser that reads every sample and a writer the program accepts. Why formats Formats are where reverse engineering pays off most often in practice: opening old save files, converting a tool's project files, reading a device's logs, importing a game's levels into an editor you are writing. And a format can often be worked out from files alone , with the code only consulted to settle doubts. Collect samples with controlled changes The single most useful technique is to make the program write files that differ in one known way : - Save twice with nothing changed: the bytes that differ are timestamps, random ids or counters. - Change the player's name from "Ada" to "Adam": the name's bytes appear, and something nearby probably grows by one (a length). - Add one item to the inventory: a count goes up by one, and a block of bytes is inserted. - Change one number you can see (gold 100 to 101): find 64 becoming 65 , and you know the field's position, size and byte order. Diff each pair (lesson 1.02's tool) and write down every observation. Twenty careful samples beat a thousand random ones. What to look for Magic numbers. Most formats start with a fixed signature: PK (zip), \x89PNG , RIFF , MZ . A custom format often starts with a readable tag like SAVE or GMDT . Versions. A small number near the start that never changes between your samples, but differs in files from an older version of the program. Lengths and counts. A number just before a variable-length thing: a byte or two before a string that equals its length, a count before a list. Changing the thing changes the number. Offsets. A number that equals the position of something else in the file: a table of contents. Check whether values in the header match positions where blocks start. Byte order. 64 00 00 00 is little-endian 100; 00 00 00 64 big-endian. A value you control, such as gold, settles it. Floats. Positions and fractions are often float s: four bytes that read as nonsense integers but sensible floats ( 00 00 C8 42 is 100.0). Strings. Length-prefixed, zero-terminated, fixed-size padded with zeros, ASCII or UTF-16. Checksums. If every change, however small, also changes a few bytes at the end (or the start), that is probably a checksum, and the program rejects files whose checksum does not match. Try the usual suspects over the rest of the file: a plain byte sum, CRC-32, Adler-32. A search for the CRC-32 constant 0xEDB88320 in the code confirms it. Compression and encryption. A block with entropy near 8 (lesson 1.05) is compressed or encrypted. Try decompressing with zlib (zlib streams usually start 78 9C or 78 DA ); otherwise find the code that reads the block. Writing it down Describe the format as a table of fields, then turn it into a parser : Offset Size Field Evidence --- --- --- --- 0 4 magic SAVE same in all samples 4 2 version, little-endian 2 in all current samples, 1 in an old one 6 1 name length 3 for "Ada", 4 for "Adam" ... Tools help: ImHex has a pattern language that overlays your field definitions on the bytes as you write them, highlighting fields so mistakes are obvious; Kaitai Struct describes formats in YAML and generates parsers in many languages. Proving it Your understanding is complete when: 1. Your parser reads every sample without leftovers or errors, and the values make sense. 2. Your writer produces a file from scratch that the program accepts and loads correctly. 3. Changing a field with your writer changes the right thing in the program. The practice is exactly this, for a small save file format. Check yourself quiz ? You save twice without changing anything and four bytes differ. What are they likely to be? - The player's name, re-encoded + A timestamp, a counter or a random id, which change on every save - The file's length - Corrupted bytes from a bug in the program Nothing you control changed, so these bytes change on their own. Knowing that keeps them out of later comparisons. ? Changing one letter of the player's name also changes four bytes at the end of the file. What do you suspect? - The name's length is stored at the end of the file - The whole file is compressed + A checksum, which is probably verified on load - A pointer to where the name is stored A small change that ripples into four unrelated bytes, the same length as before, is the signature of a checksum over the file. A length would not change for a one-letter swap. ? How do you tell whether a 4-byte field is little- or big-endian? + Set it to a known value and see which order matches - Little-endian fields always start with 00 - Look at the file's extension - Big-endian fields are always at even offsets A known value set through the program, such as 300 gold, shows the answer: 2C 01 00 00 is little-endian, 00 00 01 2C big-endian. ? What finally proves that you understand a format? - A diagram of every field in the file - Being able to find the player's name with a hex editor - A parser that reads one sample correctly + Files you write that the program loads correctly A writer whose files the program accepts shows you got everything it checks, checksums included, and a parser that reads every sample shows it is not just fitted to one file.

title: A save file from samples
body: A small game the course provides writes save files in an undocumented format. You made it save four times with controlled changes (lesson 6.02): text A the start of a game: player "Ada", level 3, standing at x 100, y -2.5, carrying 5 of item 7 53 41 56 45 02 00 03 41 64 61 03 00 00 00 C8 42 00 00 20 C0 01 07 00 05 34 04 00 00 B the same, after renaming the player to "Adam" 53 41 56 45 02 00 04 41 64 61 6D 03 00 00 00 C8 42 00 00 20 C0 01 07 00 05 A2 04 00 00 C A, after picking up 1 of item 300 53 41 56 45 02 00 03 41 64 61 03 00 00 00 C8 42 00 00 20 C0 02 07 00 05 2C 01 01 63 04 00 00 D A, after levelling up to 4 and moving to x 101 53 41 56 45 02 00 03 41 64 61 04 00 00 00 CA 42 00 00 20 C0 01 07 00 05 37 04 00 00 Your notes so far: - The file always starts 53 41 56 45 , then 02 00 in every sample. - The name's bytes are preceded by a byte that equals its length. - The last four bytes change whenever anything changes. Adding up every byte before them gives the same number. - Floats are 4 bytes, little-endian ( 00 00 C8 42 is 100.0). Work out the rest from the samples, then write a reader and a writer: cpp struct Item { std::uint16_t id; std::uint8_t quantity; }; struct Save { std::string name; std::uint16_t level; float x, y; std::vector<Item items; }; std::optional<Save parseSave(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & file); std::vector<std::uint8_t writeSave(const Save& save); parseSave returns std::nullopt for a file with the wrong magic, a version other than 2, a wrong checksum, too few bytes for what the header announces, or bytes left over after the checksum. writeSave produces exactly the bytes the game would.

title: 6.03  Reversing a Network Protocol
body: Working out a custom protocol between a client and a server you run yourself - capturing the traffic, finding how messages are framed in a TCP stream, identifying message types, sequence numbers and fields, handling partial messages, and writing a dissector to decode captures automatically. The setting A protocol is a file format that arrives in pieces over time. The techniques of lesson 6.02 apply, plus the problem of splitting a stream into messages. Typical legitimate cases: the protocol of an old multiplayer game whose servers are gone, so a community server can be written; a device on your desk with its own control protocol; a debugging tool's link to your own game, which you wrote years ago and documented poorly. Work with a client and server you run yourself : capture traffic between them on your own machine or network. Other people's services, accounts and traffic are not yours to analyse. Capturing Wireshark captures the traffic (lesson 3.04). For a TCP connection, Follow TCP Stream shows each direction's bytes in order; save each direction as raw bytes for analysis. Do several captures with controlled actions, as with files: connect and disconnect; connect, send one chat message, disconnect; move one step left; move one step right. If the traffic is encrypted (TLS), the capture shows nothing useful. With your own client you can log the plaintext before encryption, or find the send function in the client and put a logging breakpoint there. Framing TCP delivers a stream of bytes , not messages: one send of 20 bytes may arrive as 20 bytes, or as 7 then 13, or glued to the next message. So every protocol over TCP has a framing rule that says where each message ends. The common ones: Framing Looks like --- --- length prefix every message starts with its length (often 2 or 4 bytes, often big-endian) delimiter messages end with \n or \r\n (text protocols: HTTP headers, SMTP, IRC) fixed size every message is N bytes type then known size a type byte, and each type has a fixed length To find a length prefix, look at the first bytes of each message and compare with the message's length: 00 0B followed by 11 bytes, 00 05 followed by 5. Watch whether the length counts itself or not. Inside a message Once messages are separated: - Type : an early byte with few distinct values, which correlates with actions (always 02 when you move, 03 when you chat). - Sequence numbers : a field that increases by one with every message in a direction. Gaps tell you about lost or filtered messages; the server's acknowledgements often echo them. - Fields : decoded as in a file format. Movement messages hold small signed numbers ( FF FF is −1 in 16 bits); chat messages hold a length and text. - Variable-length integers (varints): bytes with the top bit meaning "more follows", common in modern formats such as Protocol Buffers. Replaying a captured message, or sending a hand-made one from a small script, to your server and watching its reaction confirms what a field means. Partial messages A decoder must not assume messages arrive whole. It keeps a buffer, appends whatever arrives, and repeatedly takes a complete message from the front while enough bytes are present, leaving any partial tail for next time: cpp-norun buffer.insert(buffer.end(), received.begin(), received.end()); while (buffer.size() = 2) { const std::size_t length{ static_cast<std::size_t ((buffer 0 << 8) buffer 1 ) }; if (buffer.size() < 2 + length) break; // wait for the rest handle(std::span(buffer).subspan(2, length)); buffer.erase(buffer.begin(), buffer.begin() + 2 + static_cast<std::ptrdiff_t (length)); } This same loop appears in every network program, and it is half of the Networking course's work too. Dissectors When you understand the protocol, teach Wireshark: a dissector written in Lua (a few dozen lines) decodes your protocol's messages in every capture, showing types, sequence numbers and fields by name. It turns future debugging of the protocol from hex reading into reading. Check yourself quiz ? Why can a decoder not assume each TCP read returns exactly one message? - TCP drops messages that are too long - TCP reorders messages unless they are numbered + TCP is a byte stream: messages can arrive split across reads or joined together - The operating system strips the message boundaries only for encrypted traffic TCP keeps bytes in order and delivers them all, but it has no idea where your messages begin and end. The protocol's framing says that. ? How do you spot a length-prefixed framing? - Every message ends with a zero byte + Each message's first bytes equal its length - Every message has the same length - The messages start with the text LEN Compare the first two or four bytes of each message with the length of the rest of it, or of the whole message. When they match for every message, those bytes are the length. ? A field goes 7, 8, 9, 11 across messages in one direction. What happened? - The field is a timestamp in seconds - The field is a checksum over the message + A sequence number, and message 10 is missing - The protocol skips numbers divisible by 10 A value that counts up by one per message is a sequence number; a gap means a message that is missing from the capture or was dropped. ? What does a Wireshark dissector do for a custom protocol? - Encrypts the protocol's messages - Replays the captured messages to the server + Decodes its messages in captures, showing types and fields by name - Blocks the protocol's traffic A dissector turns raw bytes into named fields in Wireshark's view, so every future capture is decoded for you.

title: Decoding a captured protocol
body: Captures between a small game client and server that the course provides showed this structure (lesson 6.03): every message is a 2-byte big-endian length (of everything after it), a 1-byte type , a 4-byte big-endian sequence number , then a payload: Type Name Payload --- --- --- 1 HELLO 1-byte name length, then the name 2 MOVE 2-byte big-endian signed dx, then dy 3 CHAT 2-byte big-endian text length, then the text 4 BYE nothing Write the decoder for a TCP stream, where messages can arrive split or joined: cpp struct Message { std::uint8_t type; std::uint32_t sequence; std::vector<std::uint8_t payload; }; class Decoder { public: void feed(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & bytes); std::vector<Message take(); std::size_t pending() const; }; std::string describe(const Message& m); std::vector<std::uint32_t missing(const std::vector<Message & messages); - feed adds received bytes; take returns every complete message received so far (in order) and removes them, leaving any incomplete tail; pending is how many bytes are waiting. A message whose length is below 5 cannot hold a type and a sequence: skip its whole frame. - describe formats: 7 HELLO Ada , 8 MOVE dx=3 dy=-1 , 9 CHAT gg , 10 BYE , and 11 TYPE 9 (2 bytes) for unknown types or payloads that do not match their type. - missing lists the sequence numbers skipped between consecutive messages (7, 8, 11 is missing 9 and 10), in order.

title: 6.04  Writing It Up
body: Turning an analysis into something others can use - the structure of a good report, evidence and reproducibility, annotated databases and headers, clean-room reimplementation, and handling security findings responsibly through coordinated disclosure. Analysis nobody can use is wasted The output of reverse engineering is understanding, and understanding that lives only in your head disappears. Whether it is for a teammate, your future self, or the maintainers of software you found a bug in, the work ends with writing it up. The shape of a report A useful report answers, in this order: 1. Summary : the question and the answer, in a few sentences. Many readers stop here. 2. Scope : exactly what was analysed: file name, version, hash (SHA-256), date, and which parts. 3. Findings : one section each, with the claim, the evidence (addresses as module+offset , disassembly excerpts, captured bytes, screenshots) and how confident you are. 4. How to reproduce : the steps someone else follows to see the same thing. 5. Open questions : what you did not resolve, and what you assumed. Evidence and reproduction are what separate a finding from an opinion. "The save file has a CRC-32 at offset 0x7C" is a claim; "changing any byte changes offset 0x7C–0x7F; the value matches crc32(bytes 0..0x7C)) in all 23 samples; the loader at game.exe+0x4A1B0 compares it and shows Corrupt save on mismatch" is a finding. Artefacts Alongside the report, keep what lets someone continue the work: - The disassembler database with your names, types and comments. - Headers for recovered structures, exported from the database or written by hand. - Parsers and scripts that encode the knowledge in executable form: a format parser is its own specification, and its tests are your evidence. - Signatures (lesson 4.05) for the important functions, so the work transfers to the next version. Reimplementation A common end goal is a new program that does what the old one did: a file converter, a replacement server, a source port of an old game. When rights matter, teams use a clean-room process: one person reverse engineers and writes a specification describing behaviour and formats; another, who never sees the original code, implements from the specification. That keeps the new code from being a copy of the old. Whether that is needed depends on the situation and the law; when it matters, take advice before starting. Security findings If your analysis turns up a vulnerability, in your own program or in software you were authorised to examine, the responsible path is coordinated disclosure : 1. Report it privately to the maintainers (a security contact, SECURITY.md , a bug bounty programme), with enough detail to reproduce and fix it. 2. Give them reasonable time to release a fix; 90 days is a common default. 3. Publish details only after a fix is available, or by agreement. Never test a vulnerability against systems you do not own or have explicit permission to test. Bug bounty programmes publish their rules precisely so that research within them is welcome. Check yourself quiz ? What belongs in the scope section of a reverse engineering report? - The tools you would like to have used + Exactly what was analysed: file, version, hash, parts - The conclusions, summed up in one sentence - A list of everything the program does Scope tells the reader what the findings apply to: file name, version, hash, date and which parts were covered. A hash pins down the exact file, so nobody applies the results to a different version. ? What turns a claim into a finding? - Writing it in the report's conclusion - Having two people agree with it + Evidence and steps someone else can reproduce - Making it as detailed as possible Someone else must be able to check it. Addresses, sample data, captures and reproducible steps let them. ? What is a clean-room reimplementation? - Rewriting a program from its decompiled source + One person specifies the original; another implements from that - Writing a program in a virtual machine with no network - Reimplementing a program after deleting all its comments The person who writes the code never saw the original code, only a specification of its behaviour. Keeping the two roles apart means nothing is copied from the original. ? What is coordinated disclosure? - Publishing a vulnerability immediately so everyone can protect themselves - Selling a vulnerability to the highest bidder - Telling only other security researchers about a vulnerability + Reporting privately, and publishing once a fix is out The vulnerability goes to the maintainers first, and details are published after a fix is available or by agreement. That gives them time to fix it before attackers learn the details.

title: 6.05  Where to Go Next
body: Places to keep practising legally - crackmes and CTF reversing challenges, open-source programs compiled yourself, the FLARE-On challenge, malware analysis training in safe labs - the books and courses worth your time, and what reverse engineering work looks like as a job. Keep practising on targets made for it Reverse engineering is learned by doing, and there is plenty to do legally: - Your own programs. Build open-source programs (or your own projects) in Release without the PDB, reverse a function, then compare with the source. It is the best feedback loop there is: you can always check your answer. - Crackmes. Small programs written to be reversed, with a password or key to find, sorted by difficulty: crackmes.one has thousands. This milestone's capstone is one. - CTF challenges. Capture the Flag competitions have "reversing" and "pwn" categories; past challenges with write-ups are archived (CTFtime lists events). picoCTF is aimed at beginners. - FLARE-On. An annual reversing challenge from Google's Mandiant FLARE team, with a dozen or so levels of increasing difficulty and published solutions. - Old games and software with official modding or source releases. Many classic games had their source released; comparing their binaries with the source is excellent practice. Malware analysis, safely Analysing malware is one of the main professional uses of these skills, and it must be done in an isolated lab: a virtual machine with no shared folders, a snapshot to restore, and no network (or a simulated one such as INetSim). Training material comes with prepared samples. Do not go looking for live malware to practise on, and never run a sample outside the lab. Books and courses - Practical Malware Analysis (Sikorski and Honig): the classic on static and dynamic analysis of Windows programs. - Practical Reverse Engineering (Dang, Gazet, Bachaalany): x86, x64, ARM and the Windows kernel. - The Ghidra Book (Eagle and Nance): using Ghidra in depth. - Windows Internals (Yosifovich and others): what the operating system does underneath everything in milestones 3 and 5. - OpenSecurityTraining2's free courses on x86-64 architecture, assembly and debuggers. The work itself Reverse engineering skills are used in several kinds of job: - Malware analysis and threat intelligence : understanding what malicious software does, to detect and remove it. - Vulnerability research : finding security bugs in software, for vendors, security firms or bug bounties. - Compatibility and interoperability : emulators, file converters, drivers for hardware with poor documentation. - Game development and modding : engine programmers reading compiler output, tools programmers working with old assets, modding communities working with official tools. - Software maintenance : every company has a program whose source was lost. All of them value the same things: careful method, notes with evidence, and judgement about what is appropriate to examine. What this course gave you You can read a PE file, find your way through x64 code compiled from C and C++, drive a debugger and know what it is doing underneath, find where data lives and what changes it, patch and hook your own programs, and you have written your own versions of a PE inspector, a control flow graph, a value scanner, a patch engine and a disassembler. The capstone puts it all to work on a program you have never seen. Check yourself quiz ? Why is reversing your own Release builds such good practice? - Release builds are the only ones reverse engineering tools can open - Release builds contain full debug symbols + You can check every conclusion against the source code - They are smaller than Debug builds, so they are faster to read Release builds are optimised like real targets, and you hold the answers: every guess about the machine code can be compared with what you wrote. ? What must a malware analysis lab have? - A fast internet connection so samples can reach their servers - Shared folders, to copy results out quickly + Isolation: a virtual machine with snapshots, no shared folders and no real network access - The latest antivirus running inside the virtual machine Malware must not reach your real machine or network. Snapshots let you go back to a clean state after each run. ? Which of these are places to find legal reversing challenges? - Popular online games and their anti-cheat systems + crackmes.one, CTF reversing challenges (CTFtime, picoCTF) and FLARE-On - Commercial software with its licence check removed - Any program on a public file-sharing site These challenges are made to be reversed. Other people's games, services and commercial software are not practice targets.

title: What is in this file?
body: Guess what kind of data a file holds from its bytes. save.dat: 4096 bytes, entropy 7.98 bits/byte - compressed or encrypted level.bin: entropy 3.1, "LVL1" at 0, repeating 12-byte records from 0x10 notes.txt: all printable - text

title: A save format, reversed
body: Work out a simple save format from samples, then write a reader and writer that round-trip. sample A (name "ada", level 3): 58 53 01 03 61 64 61 03 00 D8 sample B (name "bob", level 12): 58 53 01 03 62 6F 62 0C 00 EE fields: magic "XS", version 1, name length, name, level (u16), checksum checksum = sum of the bytes before it, & 0xFF writer output matches both samples exactly

title: Fields in a protocol
body: Guess the fields of a protocol from captured messages of a program you wrote. 12 messages of the same type bytes 0-1: constant 0xAB 0xCD (magic) byte 2: counts up 1, 2, 3 ... (sequence number) byte 3: equals message length - 4 (length) bytes 4+: varies (payload)

title: A crackme on a tiny virtual machine
match: A crackme on a tiny virtual machine
body: The capstone. The course provides a program for a small virtual machine , the kind of thing crackmes and CTF challenges use: a "licence check" that prints OK for a correct key and NO otherwise. You have its bytecode and, from reversing the interpreter, its instruction set. Build the tools, then use them to find every key it accepts. The machine : eight 32-bit unsigned registers r0 - r7 (all 0 at the start), two flags eq and lt (false at the start), a program counter starting at 0, a read-only input string and an output string. Opcode Bytes Instruction Effect --- --- --- --- 00 1 halt stop 01 4 movi rA, imm16 rA = imm ( 01 A lo hi ) 02 3 mov rA, rB rA = rB 03 3 add rA, rB rA += rB 04 3 sub rA, rB rA -= rB 05 3 xor rA, rB rA ^= rB 06 3 mul rA, rB rA = rB 07 4 andi rA, imm16 rA &= imm 08 3 cmp rA, rB eq = rA == rB , lt = rA < rB 09 / 0A / 0B / 0C 3 jmp / je / jne / jl addr16 jump always / if eq / if not eq / if lt 0D 3 in rA, rB rA = input character at index rB , or 0 past the end 0E 2 out rA append the character rA & 0xFF to the output All arithmetic wraps at 32 bits; 16-bit values are little-endian. cpp struct VmLine { std::uint16_t address; std::string text; }; struct VmResult { std::string output; bool halted; bool error; int steps; }; std::vector<VmLine disassembleVm(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & program); VmResult runVm(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & program, const std::string& input, int maxSteps); std::vector<std::string findKeys(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & program); - disassembleVm works through the program from address 0. Texts: halt , movi r0, 0x30 , andi r0, 0xffff (immediates in lowercase hex), add r1, r7 , jl 0x0065 (jump targets as four lowercase hex digits), in r4, r1 , out r6 . An unknown opcode, a register number above 7, or an instruction cut off by the end becomes db 0xNN for that one byte, and disassembly continues at the next. - runVm executes. Every executed instruction, halt included, counts one step. It stops on halt ( halted true), on an error ( error true: an unknown opcode or bad register, an instruction running off the end of the program, or the program counter leaving the program), or after maxSteps steps (neither flag set). - findKeys runs the program on every 4-digit input from 0000 to 9999 (with a limit of 10 000 steps) and returns, in order, those whose output is exactly OK . Use your disassembler to read the program and understand the check before you brute-force it: the key space here is tiny, but the method of reading the bytecode is the point.

title: Glossary
body: Basic block : a run of instructions with one way in and one way out. (2.03) Calling convention : the rules for where arguments and return values go; on 64-bit Windows, rcx rdx r8 r9 and rax . (2.01) Code cave : unused space in a program used to hold new code reached by a jump. (4.03) CodeView record : the debug directory entry naming a binary's PDB by path, GUID and age. (5.04) Control flow graph : a function drawn as basic blocks connected by the jumps between them. (2.03) Cross-reference : a place in the code that refers to an address, such as a call to a function or a load of a string. (2.04) Data breakpoint : a hardware breakpoint that stops when data at an address is written or read. (3.01) Decompiler : a tool that reconstructs C-like source from machine code. (1.02) Detour : a jump from original code to new code, which runs the overwritten instructions and jumps back. (4.03) Disassembler : a tool that turns machine code into assembly text. (1.02) Dynamic analysis : studying a program while it runs. (1.02) Export : a function or variable a DLL makes available by name or ordinal. (1.04) Forwarder : an export that points at a function in another DLL. (1.04) Hook : redirecting calls to a function so other code runs first. (4.04) IAT : import address table, filled by the loader with the addresses of imported functions. (1.04) Leaf function : a function that calls nothing and often has no stack frame. (2.02) Linear sweep : disassembling from the start of a section to the end, one instruction after another. (5.02) Mangling (decoration) : encoding a C++ name's scope and signature into a linker symbol. (2.05) ModRM : the byte describing an instruction's register and memory operands. (5.01) Packed : compressed or encrypted, with a stub that restores the real code at run time. (1.05) PDB : program database: the symbols, types and line information for a build. (5.04) PE : Portable Executable, the format of Windows .exe and .dll files. (1.03) Pointer path : a stable base and a list of offsets that reaches a value on the heap. (3.03) Recursive descent : disassembling by following control flow from known entry points. (5.02) REX prefix : the byte from 0x40 to 0x4F that selects 64-bit operands and registers r8 to r15. (5.01) RTTI : run-time type information, which leaves class names in the binary. (2.05) RVA : relative virtual address: an offset from the module's load address. (1.03) Signature (pattern) : bytes with wildcards that find the same code in different builds. (4.05) Static analysis : studying a program without running it. (1.02) Stolen bytes : the original instructions overwritten by a hook or detour's jump. (4.03) Thunk : a tiny function that only jumps somewhere else. (2.02) Trampoline : the stolen bytes plus a jump back, used to call the original of a hooked function. (4.04) Triage : the first quick survey of an unknown binary. (1.05) Vtable : a class's table of virtual function addresses. (2.05)

title: 1.01  Rust and Cargo: Your First Program
match: 1.01 Rust and Cargo: Your First Program
body: What Rust is for and what makes it different, installing it with rustup, creating and running a project with Cargo, the shape of a program with fn main, printing with println! and format strings, comments, and how to read the compiler's unusually helpful error messages. Rust Rust is a systems language: it compiles to fast machine code with no garbage collector, like C and C++, so it suits operating systems, browsers, game engines, command-line tools, servers and embedded devices. What makes it different is that the compiler proves memory safety : no dangling pointers, no use-after-free, no data races between threads. The rules that guarantee this (ownership and borrowing, milestone 2) are checked when you compile, so they cost nothing when the program runs. The price is a stricter compiler. Rust programmers say they "fight the borrow checker" at first; the compiler's messages are excellent, and the bugs it stops are the ones that are hardest to find in other languages. Installing and Cargo Install Rust with rustup from rust-lang.org. It provides rustc (the compiler) and Cargo , the build tool and package manager you use for everything: bash cargo new hello a new project folder with Cargo.toml and src/main.rs cd hello cargo run compile and run (debug build) cargo build --release an optimised build in target/release cargo check type-check quickly without producing a program Cargo.toml describes the project and its dependencies ( crates , from crates.io). The practice editor here compiles your code on Rust 1.99 (edition 2024) for you. Your first program rust fn main() { println!("Hello, Xenon!"); let name = "Ada"; let year = 1815; println!("{name} was born in {year}."); println!("{} + {} = {}", 2, 3, 2 + 3); } - fn main() is where the program starts. Functions are declared with fn . - println! prints a line. The ! means it is a macro , not a function: macros can take a format string and a variable number of arguments, checked at compile time. - {} in the format string is filled by the next argument; {name} uses a variable of that name directly. - Statements end with ; . Blocks are in braces. Formatting rust fn main() { let pi = 3.14159265; let item = "tea"; println!(" {pi:.2} "); // 2 decimals: 3.14 println!(" {item: 8} {item:<8} {item:^8} "); // right, left, centred in 8 println!(" {:05} {:+} {:x} {:b} ", 42, 7, 255, 5); // zero-padded, sign, hex, binary println!("{:?}", vec! 1, 2, 3 ); // {:?} is the Debug format: for developers eprintln!("this goes to standard error"); let s = format!("{item} costs {:.2}", 2.5); // format! builds a String instead of printing println!("{s}"); } Comments rust // A line comment. / A block comment. / /// A documentation comment for the item below; cargo doc turns these into web pages. fn main() { println!("comments are ignored"); } Compiler errors Rust's error messages show the code, point at the problem and often suggest the fix: text error E0384 : cannot assign twice to immutable variable x -- src/main.rs:3:5 2 let x = 5; - first assignment to x 3 x = 6; ^^^^^ cannot assign twice to immutable variable help: consider making this binding mutable 2 let mut x = 5; +++ Read the first error first, and read the help: lines: they are usually right. rustc --explain E0384 prints a long explanation of any error code. Check yourself quiz ? Why does println! have an exclamation mark? - It marks a function that may stop the program with an error - It makes the line appear immediately, without buffering + It is a macro, so it can take a format string and any number of arguments - It marks a built-in function that needs no use line The ! means a macro call: macros can take a format string and a varying number of arguments, checked at compile time. Ordinary functions always take a fixed list of parameters. ? What does cargo check do? - Runs the project's tests and reports which ones fail + Type-checks the project without producing a program, faster than a build - Builds an optimised program in target/release - Looks on crates.io for newer versions of the dependencies cargo check only checks the code, so it is quicker than cargo build ; the optimised build is cargo build --release . ? What does println!("{x: 5}") print when x is 42? - 42 followed by three spaces: "42 " - The value 42 five times - Nothing: it does not compile + 42 right-aligned in 5 characters: " 42" aligns right within the given width, so the padding goes on the left; < would align left.

title: 1.02  Variables, Mutability and Types
body: let and mut, why variables are immutable by default, shadowing, constants, the scalar types (integers of every size, floats, bool, char), type inference and annotations, integer overflow in debug and release builds, conversions with as and From, and tuples and arrays. let and mut Variables are immutable by default. Add mut to allow changes: rust fn main() { let x = 5; // x = 6; // error: cannot assign twice to immutable variable let mut count = 0; count += 1; count += 1; println!("{x} {count}"); } Immutability by default means that when you read let total = ... , you know total never changes afterwards. Mark a variable mut only when it must change. Shadowing A new let with the same name shadows the old variable. Unlike mut , it can change the type, which is handy for converting a value in steps: rust fn main() { let input = " 42 "; let input = input.trim(); // &str let input: i32 = input.parse().unwrap(); // now an i32 let input = input 2; println!("{input}"); } Constants rust const MAX_PLAYERS: u32 = 4; // a constant: type required, known at compile time const SECONDS_PER_DAY: u64 = 24 60 60; fn main() { println!("{MAX_PLAYERS} {SECONDS_PER_DAY}"); } Scalar types Type Holds --- --- i8 , i16 , i32 , i64 , i128 Signed integers ( i32 is the default) u8 , u16 , u32 , u64 , u128 Unsigned integers (0 and up) isize , usize Pointer-sized integers; usize is used for indexes and lengths f32 , f64 Floating point ( f64 is the default) bool true or false char One Unicode character, 4 bytes: 'a' , 'é' , '🦀' rust fn main() { let a = 42; // inferred i32 let b: u8 = 255; let big = 1_000_000_000_000i64; let ratio = 0.75; // f64 let crab = '🦀'; let ok = a 40 && b == 255; println!("{a} {b} {big} {ratio} {crab} {ok}"); println!("{} {}", i32::MAX, u64::MAX); println!("{}", 7 / 2); // 3: integer division println!("{}", 7.0 / 2.0); // 3.5 println!("{}", -7 % 3); // -1 println!("{}", (-7i32).rem_euclid(3)); // 2 } Overflow If an integer operation overflows, a debug build panics ("attempt to add with overflow"); a release build wraps around. When wrapping or saturating is what you want, say so: rust fn main() { let x: u8 = 250; println!("{:?}", x.checked_add(10)); // None: would overflow println!("{}", x.wrapping_add(10)); // 4 println!("{}", x.saturating_add(10)); // 255 println!("{:?}", x.checked_add(5)); // Some(255) } Converting between types Rust never converts numbers implicitly; let y: i64 = x; with x: i32 is an error. Convert explicitly: rust fn main() { let small: i32 = 300; let wide: i64 = small.into(); // lossless: From / Into let wide2 = i64::from(small); let truncated = small as u8; // as: may lose information (300 becomes 44) let f = small as f64 / 7.0; let back = 3.99_f64 as i32; // 3: truncates toward zero let checked: Result<u8, _ = u8::try_from(small); // Err: does not fit println!("{wide} {wide2} {truncated} {f:.3} {back} {checked:?}"); } Prefer into() / from() for conversions that can never fail, try_from when they might, and as only when you really want truncation. Tuples and arrays rust fn main() { let point: (i32, f64, &str) = (3, 4.5, "label"); let (x, y, name) = point; // destructuring println!("{x} {y} {name} {}", point.0); let days = "Mon", "Tue", "Wed" ; // an array: fixed length, one type let zeros = 0; 5 ; // five zeros println!("{} {:?} {}", days 1 , zeros, days.len()); // days 10 ; // panics at run time: index out of bounds } Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference between shadowing and mut ? - Shadowing changes the old variable in place; mut creates a second variable - mut lets a variable change its type; shadowing must keep the same type + mut lets one variable change; shadowing makes a new variable, possibly of another type - There is none: let x = x + 1; needs mut just like x += 1; A new let with the same name declares a fresh variable, so its type may differ; mut lets the same variable take new values of the same type. ? Why does let y: i64 = x; not compile when x is an i32 ? + Rust never converts numbers implicitly; write x.into() or i64::from(x) - An i64 cannot hold every i32 value, so the copy could lose data - x has to be declared mut before it can be copied into another variable - Integers can only be converted with as , never with into() Every i32 fits in an i64 , but Rust still wants the conversion written out; into() and from() do it losslessly. ? In a debug build, what happens when a u8 holding 255 has 1 added with + ? - It becomes 0 - It becomes 256 + The program panics - It stays 255 Debug builds check for overflow; use wrapping_add, saturating_add or checked_add when overflow is expected.

title: 1.03  Functions and Expressions
body: Declaring functions with typed parameters and return types, statements versus expressions, returning the last expression without a semicolon, blocks as expressions, early return, unit (), and why Rust has no function overloading or default arguments. Functions rust fn main() { println!("{}", area(3.0, 4.0)); greet("Grace"); println!("{}", is_even(10)); let (q, r) = divide(17, 5); println!("{q} remainder {r}"); } fn area(width: f64, height: f64) - f64 { width height // no semicolon: this is the returned value } fn greet(name: &str) { // no return type: returns () ("unit") println!("Hello, {name}!"); } fn is_even(n: i32) - bool { n % 2 == 0 } fn divide(a: i32, b: i32) - (i32, i32) { (a / b, a % b) // a tuple returns two values } Every parameter needs a type; the return type follows - . Functions can be defined in any order. Names use snake_case . Statements and expressions Rust is an expression language : almost everything produces a value. - An expression evaluates to a value: 5 , a + b , if ... {} else {} , a block { ... } , a function call. - A statement does something and has no value: let x = 5; , or any expression followed by ; . The last expression in a block, without a semicolon, is the block's value: rust fn main() { let y = { let x = 3; x x + 1 // the block's value }; let sign = if y 5 { "big" } else { "small" }; // if is an expression too println!("{y} {sign}"); } Adding a ; after the last expression turns it into a statement, and the block's value becomes () . That is the most common error for newcomers: text error E0308 : mismatched types fn square(x: i32) - i32 { --- expected i32 because of return type x x; - help: remove this semicolon to return this value Early return return leaves a function early, typically after checking for a special case: rust fn main() { println!("{} {} {}", grade(95), grade(72), grade(-5)); } fn grade(score: i32) - char { if !(0..=100).contains(&score) { return '?'; } match score { 90..=100 = 'A', 70..=89 = 'C', _ = 'F', } } 0..=100 is an inclusive range ; 0..100 excludes the end. match (lesson 2.05) picks a branch by pattern. No overloading, no defaults Rust has no function overloading and no default parameter values. Give different functions different names ( area_circle , area_rect ), or use an Option parameter, a struct of options, or a trait (milestone 4). This keeps every call unambiguous. Check yourself quiz ? What does a function return if the last line of its body is x x; with a semicolon? - The value of x x : a semicolon on the last line is ignored + () (unit), which is a type error if the function declares - i32 - 0 , the default value of the declared return type - The value of x , because x x; is thrown away The semicolon turns the expression into a statement, so the body's value becomes () ; the compiler then suggests removing the semicolon. ? Can if be used on the right of a let ? - No: if is a statement, so you need a mut variable set in each branch - Yes, and each branch may give a value of a different type + Yes: if is an expression, as long as both branches give the same type let s = if c { a } else { b }; works because if produces a value; the variable needs one type, so both branches must agree. ? What is the value of { let a = 2; a 3 } ? - () + 6 - 2 - It does not compile The block's value is its last expression, a 3 , which has no semicolon.

title: 1.04  Control Flow
body: if and else as expressions, loop with break values, while, for over ranges and collections, labelled breaks, a first look at match with ranges and multiple patterns, and choosing the right loop. if rust fn main() { let temperature = 23; if temperature = 30 { println!("Hot"); } else if temperature = 18 { println!("Pleasant"); } else { println!("Cold"); } let label = if temperature % 2 == 0 { "even" } else { "odd" }; println!("{label}"); } The condition must be a bool : if count { } does not compile. Braces are required; parentheses around the condition are not used. loop, while and for rust fn main() { // loop runs until break; break can return a value let mut n = 27u64; let mut steps = 0; let result = loop { if n == 1 { break steps; } n = if n % 2 == 0 { n / 2 } else { 3 n + 1 }; steps += 1; }; println!("{result} steps"); // while: repeat while a condition holds let mut countdown = 3; while countdown 0 { print!("{countdown} "); countdown -= 1; } println!("lift-off"); // for: over a range or a collection for i in 1..=5 { print!("{} ", i i); } println!(); let names = "Ada", "Grace", "Linus" ; for (index, name) in names.iter().enumerate() { println!("{index}: {name}"); } for i in (0..10).rev().step_by(3) { print!("{i} "); } println!(); } for is the most common loop: it cannot go out of bounds and needs no index variable. enumerate() adds the index when you need it. break and continue rust fn main() { let numbers = 4, 7, -1, 12, 0, 9 ; let mut sum = 0; for x in numbers { if x < 0 { continue; } if x == 0 { break; } sum += x; } println!("{sum}"); 'outer: for i in 0..5 { for j in 0..5 { if i j == 6 { println!("found {i} x {j}"); break 'outer; // leaves both loops } } } } match match compares a value against patterns , in order, and must cover every possible value: rust fn main() { for day in 1, 6, 7, 9 { let kind = match day { 1..=5 = "weekday", 6 7 = "weekend", _ = "not a day", // _ matches anything else }; println!("{day}: {kind}"); } } If you leave out the _ arm, the compiler refuses: "non-exhaustive patterns". This exhaustiveness check catches forgotten cases at compile time. match becomes much more powerful with enums (lesson 2.05). Choosing a loop Situation Loop --- --- Over a collection or a range for Until a condition becomes false while Until something inside decides (retry, read until done) loop with break Check yourself quiz ? How can a loop produce a value? - With return value; inside the loop body + With break value; , which makes the loop expression evaluate to value - The last expression of the loop body becomes its value - It cannot: set a mut variable before breaking out break value; gives the whole loop expression that value, as in let result = loop { ... }; . return would leave the whole function instead. ? Which numbers does the range 1..=5 include? - 1, 2, 3 and 4 - 2, 3, 4 and 5 - 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 + 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 ..= includes the end; 1..5 would stop at 4. ? A match on an i32 lists arms for 0 and 1 only. What happens? + It does not compile: the patterns are not exhaustive - Other values do nothing - Other values panic at run time - Other values match the last arm match must cover every possible value; add a _ arm for the rest.

title: 1.05  Strings and Input
body: The two string types - owned String and borrowed &str - and when to use each, common string methods, building strings with push_str and format!, reading lines from standard input, parsing numbers with parse and handling failure, and a first taste of Result and unwrap. String and &str Rust has two main string types: - String is an owned , growable string stored on the heap. You can change it. - &str (a "string slice") is a borrowed view of string data that lives somewhere else: in the program itself (string literals), or inside a String . rust fn main() { let literal: &str = "hello"; // a borrowed view of text in the program let mut owned: String = String::from("hello"); // owned, growable owned.push_str(", world"); owned.push('!'); let view: &str = &owned; // borrow a String as &str println!("{literal} {owned} {view} {}", owned.len()); let built = format!("{} has {} characters", literal, literal.len()); let joined = "a", "b", "c" .join("-"); let upper = owned.to_uppercase(); // methods that change text return a new String println!("{built} {joined} {upper}"); } Functions that only read text take &str : they then accept both literals and &String . Functions that keep text (store it in a struct) take String . Milestone 2 explains why. String methods Code Gives --- --- s.len() , s.is_empty() Length in bytes , emptiness s.trim() , s.to_lowercase() , s.to_uppercase() Trimmed slice, new Strings s.contains("x") , s.starts_with("x") , s.find("x") Tests, Option position s.replace("a", "b") A new String s.split(',') , s.split_whitespace() , s.lines() Iterators over pieces s.chars() , s.chars().rev().collect::<String () Characters, reversed s.parse::<i32 () A Result with the number or an error rust fn main() { let line = " Ada Lovelace, 1815 , mathematician "; let parts: Vec<&str = line.split(',').map( p p.trim()).collect(); println!("{:?}", parts); let year: i32 = parts 1 .parse().unwrap(); println!("{}", year + 200); let words: Vec<&str = "the quick brown fox".split_whitespace().collect(); println!("{} words, first {}", words.len(), words 0 ); println!("{}", "racecar".chars().rev().collect::<String ()); } .map( p p.trim()) applies a closure (an inline function, lesson 5.01) to each piece; collect() gathers the results into a Vec . Strings are UTF-8, so you cannot index them by position ( s 0 does not compile): a character may take several bytes. Use chars() (lesson 3.02 explains the details). Reading input rust use std::io; fn main() { let mut name = String::new(); println!("What is your name?"); io::stdin().read_line(&mut name).expect("could not read input"); let name = name.trim(); // read_line keeps the line break let mut age_text = String::new(); io::stdin().read_line(&mut age_text).expect("could not read input"); match age_text.trim().parse::<u32 () { Ok(age) = println!("Hello, {name}! Next year you will be {}.", age + 1), Err(_) = println!("Hello, {name}! That age is not a number."), } } - read_line(&mut name) appends the line (including its \n ) to name and returns a Result : reading can fail. - parse::<u32 () returns Ok(number) or Err(error) . match handles both. - .expect("message") and .unwrap() take the value out of an Ok , and panic (stop the program) on an Err . They are fine in quick programs and for errors that "cannot happen"; real error handling comes in lesson 3.04. To read every line until the input ends: rust use std::io::{self, BufRead}; fn main() { let mut total = 0; for line in io::stdin().lock().lines() { let line = line.unwrap(); if let Ok(n) = line.trim().parse::<i64 () { total += n; } } println!("total {total}"); } if let Ok(n) = ... runs the block only when the pattern matches: a short match with one interesting arm. Check yourself quiz ? Which parameter type should a function that only reads text use? - String - &String + &str - &mut String &str accepts string literals and borrowed String s alike. String would take the caller's string away, and &String would not accept a literal. ? Why must you trim the result of read_line before parsing it? + read_line keeps the line break, and "42\n" does not parse as a number - read_line puts a space in front of the text it reads - parse only works on text without any lower-case letters - trim turns the Result from read_line into a String The line break typed by the user stays at the end of the string; trim() removes it (and any spaces) before parse . ? What does "5x".parse::<i32 () give? - 5 + An Err value - 0 - A panic parse returns a Result ; it only panics if you unwrap the Err .
