title: 2.01  Ownership and Moves
body: The three ownership rules, the stack and the heap, how String owns heap memory and frees it when dropped, moves versus copies, the Copy trait for simple values, clone for explicit deep copies, ownership through function calls and return values, and why this replaces both garbage collection and manual free. Who frees the memory? Every program must give memory back when it is done with it. C and C++ make the programmer call free / delete (forgetting leaks memory; freeing twice or too early corrupts it). Java, C and Python use a garbage collector, which costs run time. Rust takes a third way: the compiler tracks ownership and inserts the clean-up itself, exactly once, at a point it can prove is safe. The rules 1. Every value has exactly one owner : a variable, a struct field, a vector slot... 2. There is only one owner at a time. 3. When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped (its memory is freed). rust fn main() { { let s = String::from("hello"); // s owns a heap buffer holding "hello" println!("{s}"); } // s goes out of scope: the buffer is freed here // println!("{s}"); // error: s does not exist here } Stack and heap Values with a fixed, known size (integers, bool , char , tuples of those) live on the stack and are trivially cheap to copy. A String or Vec is a small struct on the stack (a pointer, a length, a capacity) that points to a buffer on the heap , whose size can change. Copying the small struct is cheap; copying the heap buffer is not, and two owners of one buffer would both try to free it. Moves So, assigning a String (or Vec , or any type that owns heap data) moves ownership. The old variable can no longer be used: rust-norun let s1 = String::from("hello"); let s2 = s1; // the ownership moves to s2; nothing is copied on the heap println!("{s1}"); // error E0382 : borrow of moved value: s1 The compiler message explains exactly this, and points at the line where the move happened. After a move, only s2 will free the buffer, so it is freed once. Copy types Simple stack-only types implement the Copy trait: assignment copies them, and the original stays usable: rust fn main() { let a = 5; let b = a; // i32 is Copy: a is still valid let p = (1.5, true); let q = p; // a tuple of Copy types is Copy println!("{a} {b} {:?} {:?}", p, q); } Integers, floats, bool , char , shared references &T , and tuples and arrays of Copy types are Copy . String , Vec and Box are not. clone To really duplicate heap data, call .clone() . It is explicit on purpose: a deep copy may be expensive, and you can see it in the code. rust fn main() { let s1 = String::from("hello"); let s2 = s1.clone(); // a second, independent buffer println!("{s1} {s2}"); } Ownership and functions Passing a value to a function moves (or copies) it, just like assignment. Returning a value moves it out to the caller: rust fn main() { let name = String::from("Ada"); let n = 42; take(name); // name moves into the function // println!("{name}"); // error: value moved copy_it(n); // n is copied: still usable println!("{n}"); let made = make_greeting("Grace"); // ownership moves out to made let back = give_back(made); // in and out again println!("{back}"); } fn take(s: String) { println!("took {s}"); } // s is dropped here fn copy_it(x: i32) { println!("copied {x}"); } fn make_greeting(name: &str) - String { format!("Hello, {name}!") } fn give_back(s: String) - String { s } Moving values in and out of every function would be tedious. The next lesson's borrowing lets a function use a value without taking it. Check yourself quiz ? When is a String 's heap memory freed? - When the program ends, all at once - When a garbage collector notices it is no longer used + When its owner goes out of scope, unless it was moved elsewhere first - Right after the last line that uses the variable The owner drops the value at the end of its scope; if ownership moved (to another variable or a function), the new owner frees it instead. Rust has no garbage collector. ? Why can you still use a after let b = a; when a is an i32 but not when it is a String ? + i32 is Copy , so it is copied; a String owns heap data, so it is moved - Integers live on the heap, and heap values may have two owners - A String is immutable, so its old name is hidden once it is assigned - let b = a; borrows an i32 but makes a deep copy of a String Copying an i32 is trivial and safe; two owners of one String buffer would both free it, so the String moves and a becomes unusable. A deep copy needs an explicit .clone() . ? After let v = vec! 1, 2 ; let w = v; , which is true? - v and w share one vector + The vector moved to w and v can no longer be used - v is a copy of w - It does not compile Vec owns heap memory, so assignment moves it; the code compiles as long as v is not used afterwards.

title: Ownership in function signatures
body: The starter does not compile: the tests expect report and add_suffix to give the vector back after using it, so that the caller owns it again. Fix the signatures (and bodies) using only ownership: a function that takes a String or a Vec owns it, may change it, and can hand it back by returning it. rust fn report(names: Vec<String ) - (String, Vec<String ) // ("3 names: Ada, Grace, Linus", the same vector); "no names" when empty fn longest(a: String, b: String) - String // the longer text (the first on a tie); the other one is dropped fn shout(text: String) - String // the text upper-cased, with "!" added fn add_suffix(names: Vec<String , suffix: &str) - Vec<String // the vector with suffix appended to every name, in order Read the tests to see how each function is called, and where they use .clone() to keep a value they still need.

title: 2.02  References and Borrowing
body: Using values without taking ownership - shared references &T and mutable references &mut T, the borrowing rules (many readers or one writer), why they prevent data races and invalid pointers, non-lexical lifetimes, dangling references the compiler refuses, and dereferencing with . Borrowing A reference lets code use a value without owning it. Creating one is called borrowing : rust fn main() { let s = String::from("hello world"); let n = length(&s); // lend s; we keep ownership println!("{s} has {n} bytes"); // s is still ours } fn length(text: &String) - usize { // &String: a reference to a String text.len() } // the reference goes away; nothing is dropped &s creates a shared reference ; the function can read through it but not change the value. Mutable references To let a function change a value, lend it a mutable reference , &mut . Both the variable and the borrow must be marked mutable: rust fn main() { let mut s = String::from("hello"); add_world(&mut s); let mut count = 0; bump(&mut count); bump(&mut count); println!("{s} {count}"); } fn add_world(text: &mut String) { text.push_str(", world"); } fn bump(n: &mut i32) { n += 1; // dereferences: change the value the reference points to } The borrowing rules At any moment, a value can have either : - any number of shared references &T , or - exactly one mutable reference &mut T , but not both. And a reference must never outlive the value it points to. rust-norun let mut v = vec! 1, 2, 3 ; let first = &v 0 ; // a shared borrow of v v.push(4); // error E0502 : cannot borrow v as mutable because it is also borrowed as immutable println!("{first}"); This rule prevents a real bug: push may move the vector's buffer to a bigger allocation, leaving first pointing at freed memory. In C++ the equivalent code compiles and corrupts memory at run time; in Rust it does not compile. Across threads, the same rule rules out data races (milestone 6). Borrows end when last used A borrow lasts until its last use , not until the end of the block, so code like this is fine: rust fn main() { let mut scores = vec! 10, 20, 30 ; let total: i32 = scores.iter().sum(); // a shared borrow, used here and finished scores.push(total); // now a mutable borrow is fine let last = scores.last().unwrap(); // shared borrow println!("{last} {}", scores.len()); // more shared borrows: fine together } No dangling references A function cannot return a reference to something it created, because that value is dropped when the function ends: rust-norun fn dangle() - &String { // error E0106 : missing lifetime specifier let s = String::from("hi"); &s // s is dropped here: the reference would point at freed memory } Return the owned value instead: fn no_dangle() - String { String::from("hi") } . Lesson 4.04 explains the lifetimes the compiler uses to check this. &str and &String &String coerces to &str automatically ( deref coercion ), so functions that only read text should take &str and accept both: rust fn shout(text: &str) - String { text.to_uppercase() + "!" } fn main() { let owned = String::from("hey"); println!("{} {}", shout(&owned), shout("you")); } Check yourself quiz ? Why can't you hold &v 0 while calling v.push(4) ? - push needs ownership of v , and the reference has already taken it + push may move the buffer, leaving the reference pointing at freed memory - A vector can only be borrowed once in its whole lifetime - Shared references to a vector can only point at its last element push needs a mutable borrow, which is not allowed while a shared borrow is alive; that rule stops the reference from dangling when the buffer is reallocated. ? How do you add 1 to the i32 behind an &mut i32 parameter n ? - n += 1; - &mut n += 1; + n += 1; - n = n + 1; n is a reference; n dereferences it to reach the i32 it points to. ? Which combination of borrows of one value can exist at the same time? - Two mutable references - One shared and one mutable reference - A mutable reference and the owner changing the value directly + Three shared references Many readers or one writer, never both.

title: Borrowing
body: Write these functions with the right kind of reference: rust fn add_score(scores: &mut Vec<u32 , score: u32) - usize // adds the score, returns the new count fn best<'a (scores: &'a Vec<u32 ) - Option<&'a u32 // a reference to the highest score (the first on a tie) fn normalize(words: &mut Vec<String ) // trims and lower-cases each word in place fn swap_ends(values: &mut Vec<i32 ) // swaps the first and last items (if there are at least two) fn count_starting(words: &Vec<String , prefix: &str) - usize // ignoring case The 'a in best says the returned reference points into scores ; lesson 4.04 explains it. (Lesson 2.03 shows how slices let functions like these accept arrays and parts of vectors too.)

title: 2.03  Slices
body: Borrowing part of a collection with slices - string slices &str and their byte ranges, array and vector slices & T , ranges in indexing, slice methods (len, first, last, split_at, chunks, windows, contains, iter), mutable slices &mut T , and writing functions that take slices to accept arrays, vectors and parts of them. String slices A slice is a reference to a contiguous part of a collection. &s start..end borrows bytes start up to (not including) end : rust fn main() { let s = String::from("hello world"); let hello: &str = &s 0..5 ; let world = &s 6.. ; // to the end let all = &s .. ; // the whole string println!(" {hello} {world} {all} "); println!("{}", first_word("the quick brown fox")); } fn first_word(text: &str) - &str { match text.find(' ') { Some(i) = &text ..i , None = text, } } first_word returns a slice into its argument, without copying. The borrow checker makes sure the original string outlives the slice: you cannot clear the String while a slice of it is in use. String slice ranges are in bytes , and must fall on character boundaries. &"héllo" 0..2 panics, because é takes two bytes and the range cuts it in half. For text from users, prefer chars() and the string methods (lesson 3.02). Array and vector slices & T is a slice of any sequence of T : part of an array, part of a vector, or all of either. rust fn main() { let array = 3, 8, 1, 9, 4 ; let vector = vec! 10, 20, 30 ; println!("{} {} {}", sum(&array), sum(&vector), sum(&array 1..3 )); println!("{:?}", largest(&array)); println!("{:?}", largest(& )); } fn sum(values: & i32 ) - i32 { let mut total = 0; for v in values { total += v; } total } fn largest(values: & i32 ) - Option<i32 { let mut best = values.first()?; // ? returns None early for an empty slice for &v in values { if v best { best = v; } } Some(best) } Write functions that only read a sequence to take & T (and text as &str ): they then work with arrays, vectors and sub-ranges alike, and never need to own the data. Slice methods rust fn main() { let data = 5, 1, 4, 2, 8, 7 ; println!("{} {:?} {:?} {}", data.len(), data.first(), data.last(), data.contains(&4)); let (left, right) = data.split_at(2); println!("{left:?} {right:?}"); for pair in data.windows(2) { print!("{} ", pair 1 - pair 0 ); // differences between neighbours } println!(); for chunk in data.chunks(4) { print!("{chunk:?} "); } println!(); println!("{:?}", data.iter().position( &x x == 2)); let mut sorted = data; // arrays are Copy when their items are sorted.sort(); println!("{sorted:?} {:?}", sorted.binary_search(&7)); } Mutable slices &mut T lets a function change the items in place, without being able to change the length: rust fn main() { let mut v = vec! 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 ; double_all(&mut v 1..4 ); reverse_in_place(&mut v); println!("{v:?}"); } fn double_all(values: &mut i32 ) { for x in values.iter_mut() { x = 2; } } fn reverse_in_place(values: &mut i32 ) { let n = values.len(); for i in 0..n / 2 { values.swap(i, n - 1 - i); } } Check yourself quiz ? Why should a function that sums numbers take & i32 instead of &Vec<i32 ? - A slice is faster to loop over than a vector - &Vec<i32 would move the vector into the function - &Vec<i32 does not allow a for loop over the numbers + A slice also accepts arrays and parts of vectors, not only whole vectors & i32 works for &array , &vector and &vector 1..3 ; &Vec<i32 only for a whole vector. Neither one moves the data. ? What does &s 0..3 contain for s = "hello" ? + "hel" - "hell" - "ell" - "he" The range takes bytes 0, 1 and 2: the end index is not included. ? What does 1, 2, 3, 4 .windows(2).count() return? - 2 + 3 - 4 - 8 windows(2) yields the overlapping pairs 1, 2 , 2, 3 and 3, 4 ; chunks(2) would give 2.

title: Slices
body: Return slices that point into the input instead of building new strings or vectors: rust fn first_word(text: &str) - &str // up to the first space; the whole text if there is none fn last_word(text: &str) - &str // after the last space, ignoring trailing spaces fn trim_zeros(values: & i32 ) - & i32 // without leading and trailing zeros fn max_window_sum(values: & i32 , k: usize) - Option<i32 // the largest sum of k neighbours; None if k is 0 or too big fn split_on(values: & i32 , separator: i32) - Vec<& i32 // like str::split, for numbers split_on(& 1, 0, 2, 3, 0, 0, 4 , 0) gives 1 , 2, 3 , , 4 .

title: 2.04  Structs and Methods
body: Defining structs with named fields, tuple structs and unit structs, creating them with field init shorthand and update syntax, methods in impl blocks with &self, &mut self and self, associated functions like new, deriving Debug, Clone and PartialEq, and privacy with pub. Structs A struct groups named values into one type: rust derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq) struct Book { title: String, author: String, year: u16, pages: u32, } fn main() { let dune = Book { title: String::from("Dune"), author: String::from("Frank Herbert"), year: 1965, pages: 412, }; println!("{} by {} ({})", dune.title, dune.author, dune.year); println!("{dune:?}"); // needs derive(Debug) println!("{dune: ?}"); // pretty-printed let messiah = Book { title: String::from("Dune Messiah"), year: 1969, ..dune.clone() }; // update syntax println!("{} {}", messiah.title, messiah == dune); } derive(...) asks the compiler to generate standard behaviour: Debug for {:?} printing, Clone for .clone() , PartialEq for == (lesson 4.03 covers these traits). A struct owns its fields. A field of type String means each Book owns its text, which is usually what you want; fields holding references need lifetimes (lesson 4.04). Methods Methods are defined in an impl block. The first parameter says how the method uses the value: rust derive(Debug) struct Counter { name: String, count: u32, } impl Counter { fn new(name: &str) - Counter { // an associated function: no self, called as Counter::new Counter { name: name.to_string(), count: 0 } } fn increment(&mut self) { // &mut self: may change the struct self.count += 1; } fn describe(&self) - String { // &self: only reads it format!("{}: {}", self.name, self.count) } fn into_name(self) - String { // self: takes ownership; the counter is used up self.name } } fn main() { let mut clicks = Counter::new("clicks"); clicks.increment(); clicks.increment(); println!("{}", clicks.describe()); let name = clicks.into_name(); println!("{name}"); // clicks.describe(); // error: clicks was moved by into_name } First parameter Meaning Use for --- --- --- &self Borrows the value to read it Getters, calculations &mut self Borrows it to change it Updating fields self Takes ownership Turning it into something else none An associated function Constructors like new The method call clicks.increment() borrows clicks mutably for you; there is no need to write (&mut clicks).increment() . Inside methods, Self is the type being implemented. Tuple structs and unit structs rust derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq) struct Meters(f64); // a tuple struct: a named wrapper derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq) struct Point(i32, i32); struct Marker; // a unit struct: no fields impl Meters { fn to_feet(self) - f64 { self.0 3.28084 } } fn main() { let height = Meters(1.8); let p = Point(3, 4); let _m = Marker; println!("{:.2} {:?} {}", height.to_feet(), p, p.0 + p.1); } Wrapping a number in a tuple struct ( Meters , UserId ) makes the compiler stop you mixing up values that have the same underlying type: the newtype pattern. Privacy Fields and methods are private to their module unless marked pub . Inside one file's module that does not matter; once code is split into modules (lesson 3.05), keep fields private and expose methods, so that a struct's rules (like a non-negative balance) cannot be broken from outside. Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference between &self and &mut self in a method? - &self works on a copy of the struct; &mut self works on the original - &mut self takes ownership of the struct; &self only borrows it + &self borrows the value to read it; &mut self borrows it so fields can change - &self can change fields; &mut self can also replace the whole struct Both are borrows: &self is a shared borrow for reading, &mut self a mutable one for updating fields. Taking ownership is plain self . ? How is an associated function such as new called? + With the type name and :: , as in Counter::new("clicks") - On a value with a dot, as in clicks.new("clicks") - With a new keyword, as in new Counter("clicks") - Through self , as in self.new("clicks") An associated function has no self parameter, so there is no value to call it on; Rust has no new keyword. ? A method takes self (not a reference). What happens to the value it is called on? - It is borrowed for the call and usable again afterwards - It is copied, so the original is never affected - It is borrowed mutably, as with &mut self + It is moved into the method and cannot be used afterwards, unless it is Copy self takes ownership, like passing the value to any function.

title: A struct with methods
body: Write a Rectangle struct with methods: rust derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq) struct Rectangle { x: f64, y: f64, width: f64, height: f64 } // (x, y) is the top-left corner impl Rectangle { fn new(x: f64, y: f64, width: f64, height: f64) - Option<Rectangle // None for a width or height <= 0 fn square(x: f64, y: f64, side: f64) - Option<Rectangle fn area(&self) - f64 fn perimeter(&self) - f64 fn is_square(&self) - bool fn contains_point(&self, px: f64, py: f64) - bool // edges count as inside fn overlaps(&self, other: &Rectangle) - bool // touching edges do not count fn scale(&mut self, factor: f64) // keeps the corner, scales the size fn into_square(self) - Rectangle // a square with the same corner and the smaller side } y grows downwards, as on a screen: the bottom edge is at y + height .

title: 2.05  Enums, Option and match
body: Enums whose variants carry data, methods on enums, matching with destructuring and exhaustiveness, Option instead of null and its everyday methods (unwrap_or, map, and_then, ?), if let and let else, and modelling states so invalid ones cannot be represented. Enums with data An enum lists the possible variants of a type. Unlike enums in many languages, each Rust variant can hold its own data: rust derive(Debug) enum Shape { Circle { radius: f64 }, Rectangle { width: f64, height: f64 }, Triangle(f64, f64, f64), } impl Shape { fn area(&self) - f64 { match self { Shape::Circle { radius } = std::f64::consts::PI radius radius, Shape::Rectangle { width, height } = width height, Shape::Triangle(a, b, c) = { let s = (a + b + c) / 2.0; // Heron's formula (s (s - a) (s - b) (s - c)).sqrt() } } } } fn main() { let shapes = vec! Shape::Circle { radius: 1.0 }, Shape::Rectangle { width: 2.0, height: 3.0 }, Shape::Triangle(3.0, 4.0, 5.0), ; for s in &shapes { println!("{s:?} has area {:.2}", s.area()); } } match destructures each variant, binding its fields to names. The match must be exhaustive : add a variant to Shape and every match that does not handle it stops compiling, showing you exactly where to update the code. Option instead of null Rust has no null . A value that may be missing has type Option<T : rust-norun enum Option<T { Some(T), None, } You must handle None before you can use the value, so "forgot to check for null" bugs cannot happen: rust fn find_index(names: & &str , target: &str) - Option<usize { for (i, name) in names.iter().enumerate() { if name == target { return Some(i); } } None } fn main() { let names = "Ada", "Grace", "Linus" ; match find_index(&names, "Grace") { Some(i) = println!("found at {i}"), None = println!("not found"), } let i = find_index(&names, "Bob").unwrap_or(999); println!("{i}"); let len = find_index(&names, "Linus").map( i names i .len()); // transform if present println!("{len:?}"); } Method Gives --- --- unwrap_or(default) , unwrap_or_default() The value, or a default map(f) Some(f(v)) , or None and_then(f) Chains a step that itself returns an Option filter(p) None unless the value passes ok_or(err) Converts to a Result (lesson 3.04) is_some() , is_none() Tests unwrap() , expect("msg") The value, or a panic : use only when None is impossible Inside a function that returns Option , the ? operator returns None early: let first = values.first()?; . if let and let else When only one variant matters, if let is shorter than a full match , and let ... else handles the "otherwise bail out" case: rust fn parse_pair(text: &str) - Option<(i32, i32) { let Some((a, b)) = text.split_once(',') else { return None; // let-else: must leave the function }; let a = a.trim().parse().ok()?; let b = b.trim().parse().ok()?; Some((a, b)) } fn main() { if let Some((x, y)) = parse_pair("3, 4") { println!("{x} + {y} = {}", x + y); } println!("{:?} {:?}", parse_pair("7,x"), parse_pair("nothing")); } Make invalid states unrepresentable Enums let the type itself rule out impossible combinations. Instead of a struct with a status string and optional fields that only sometimes make sense, model each state: rust derive(Debug) enum Order { Draft { items: Vec<String }, Paid { items: Vec<String , amount_cents: u64 }, Shipped { tracking: String }, } fn describe(order: &Order) - String { match order { Order::Draft { items } if items.is_empty() = "an empty draft".to_string(), Order::Draft { items } = format!("a draft with {} items", items.len()), Order::Paid { amount_cents, .. } = format!("paid {}.{:02}", amount_cents / 100, amount_cents % 100), Order::Shipped { tracking } = format!("shipped, tracking {tracking}"), } } fn main() { let orders = Order::Draft { items: vec! }, Order::Paid { items: vec! "tea".into() , amount_cents: 1250 }, Order::Shipped { tracking: "ZX81".into() }, ; for o in &orders { println!("{}", describe(o)); } } A shipped order has a tracking number and a draft does not, by construction. if after a pattern is a guard ; .. ignores the remaining fields. Check yourself quiz ? Why is Option<T safer than null? - An Option always holds a value, so nothing can be missing - None is replaced by a default value automatically - Using a None is caught by a check that runs in debug builds + The type says the value may be missing, and you must handle None to use it The compiler will not let you use the T inside without dealing with the None case (by match , if let , unwrap_or , ...), so a forgotten check cannot compile. ? What does ? do on an Option inside a function that returns Option ? - It panics if the value is None - It replaces None with a default value and carries on + It unwraps Some(v) to v , or returns None from the function at once - It turns the Option into a Result ? is an early return for the None case; panicking is what unwrap() does. ? What is Some(4).map( x x 2).filter( x x 10).unwrap_or(0) ? + 0 - 8 - 4 - It panics map gives Some(8) , the filter rejects it (8 is not above 10), and unwrap_or supplies 0.

title: 3.01  Vectors
body: Vec<T in depth - creating with vec! and Vec::new, pushing, popping, inserting and removing, indexing versus get, iterating by reference, by mutable reference and by value, sorting and deduplicating, retain, extend and drain, capacity, and the borrow rules that apply to vectors. Creating and growing A Vec<T is a growable array on the heap: Rust's most used collection. rust fn main() { let mut v: Vec<i32 = Vec::new(); v.push(3); v.push(1); v.push(4); let mut w = vec! 1, 5, 9, 2, 6 ; // the vec! macro let zeros = vec! 0; 4 ; println!("{v:?} {w:?} {zeros:?} len={} cap ={}", v.len(), v.capacity()); let last = w.pop(); // Some(6) w.insert(0, 100); // shifts everything right: O(n) let removed = w.remove(1); // returns the removed item w.extend( 7, 7, 8 ); println!("{last:?} {removed} {w:?}"); } Reading items Indexing with v i panics when i is out of range; v.get(i) returns an Option instead: rust fn main() { let v = vec! 10, 20, 30 ; println!("{}", v 1 ); match v.get(10) { Some(x) = println!("found {x}"), None = println!("no item 10"), } println!("{:?} {:?} {}", v.first(), v.last(), v.contains(&20)); if let first, .., last = v.as_slice() { // a slice pattern println!("{first}..{last}"); } } Use indexing when an out-of-range index would be a bug, and get when it is a normal possibility (user input, searching). Iterating rust fn main() { let mut scores = vec! 72, 95, 88 ; for s in &scores { // borrow each item: s is &i32 print!("{s} "); } println!(); for s in &mut scores { // borrow each item mutably: s is &mut i32 s += 5; } let total: i32 = scores.iter().sum(); let doubled: Vec<i32 = scores.iter().map( s s 2).collect(); println!("{scores:?} {total} {doubled:?}"); for s in scores { // by value: the vector is moved and consumed print!("{s} "); } println!(); // println!("{scores:?}"); // error: scores was moved by the loop } Loop Item type The vector afterwards --- --- --- for x in &v / v.iter() &T Unchanged, still usable for x in &mut v / v.iter_mut() &mut T Changed in place for x in v / v.into_iter() T Moved, gone Changing in bulk rust fn main() { let mut v = vec! 5, 3, 8, 3, 1, 8, 8, 2 ; v.sort(); // in place v.dedup(); // removes consecutive repeats println!("{v:?}"); v.retain( &x x % 2 == 1 x 4); // keep the matching items println!("{v:?}"); let mut words = vec! "pear", "Fig", "apple" ; words.sort_by_key( w w.to_lowercase()); println!("{words:?}"); let mut nums = vec! 3.2, 1.5, 2.7 ; nums.sort_by( a, b a.partial_cmp(b).unwrap()); // f64 has no total order: sort_by let drained: Vec<f64 = nums.drain(..2).collect(); println!("{drained:?} {nums:?}"); v.clear(); println!("{} {}", v.is_empty(), v.capacity() 0); } f64 cannot use sort() because NaN makes the order partial; sort_by with partial_cmp (or f64::total_cmp ) says how to compare. Vectors and the borrow rules While you hold a reference into a vector, you cannot push to it (lesson 2.02): pushing may move the whole buffer. Collect what you need first, or work with indexes: rust fn main() { let mut v = vec! 1, 2, 3 ; let first = v 0 ; // copy the value out (i32 is Copy), no borrow kept v.push(first 10); let len = v.len(); v.push(len as i32); println!("{v:?}"); } Capacity A vector keeps spare room and doubles its capacity when it runs out, so push is amortised O(1). If you know the final size, Vec::with_capacity(n) avoids repeated growth. Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference between v 5 and v.get(5) when v has 3 items? - Both give None - v 5 gives 0; v.get(5) gives None + v 5 panics; v.get(5) gives None - v 5 does not compile; v.get(5) panics Indexing panics when the index is out of range (the compiler cannot know the length); get returns an Option instead. ? What happens to a vector v after for x in v { } ? + It is moved into the loop and consumed; loop over &v to keep it - Nothing: the loop only reads the items, so v stays usable - It is emptied, but can still be pushed to afterwards - Each item is copied out, so v is unchanged Looping over v by value moves it, even when the items are Copy ; for x in &v borrows instead. ? What is v after let mut v = vec! 1, 1, 2, 1 ; v.dedup(); ? - 1, 2 - 2 - 1, 1, 2, 1 + 1, 2, 1 dedup only removes consecutive duplicates; sort first to remove all repeats.

title: 3.02  Strings in Depth
body:
How Rust strings really work - UTF-8 bytes, chars and why there is no indexing by position, char_indices and safe slicing, building strings with push, push_str, + and format!, splitting, trimming and searching, case conversion, parsing, and converting between String, &str, char and bytes. UTF-8 A String is a vector of bytes that is always valid UTF-8 . ASCII characters take one byte, but others take two, three or four: rust fn main() { for s in "hello", "héllo", "日本", "🦀" { println!("{s}: {} bytes, {} chars", s.len(), s.chars().count()); } let word = "naïve"; for (byte_index, c) in word.char_indices() { print!("{byte_index}:{c} "); } println!(); println!("{:?}", word.as_bytes()); } That is why s 0 does not compile: a byte position is not a character position, and returning half a character would be wrong. Use: - s.chars() to go through characters (Unicode scalar values); - s.char_indices() to get each character with its byte position, for slicing safely; - s.bytes() when you really work with raw bytes (protocols, ASCII-only formats). s.chars().nth(i) finds the i-th character, but it walks from the start: O(i). If you need random access, collect into a Vec<char first. User-perceived characters can be several char s (an e plus a combining accent, or an emoji with a skin tone). For full text segmentation, the unicode-segmentation crate splits grapheme clusters . Building strings rust fn main() { let mut s = String::with_capacity(32); s.push_str("Hello"); s.push(','); s += " world"; // += takes a &str let greeting = s.clone() + "!"; // + takes ownership of the left side let parts = vec! "a", "b", "c" ; let joined = parts.join("/"); let repeated = "ab".repeat(3); let built = format!("{greeting} {joined} {repeated} {}", 42); println!("{built}"); let from_chars: String = 'R', 'u', 's', 't' .iter().collect(); let reversed: String = "stressed".chars().rev().collect(); println!("{from_chars} {reversed}"); } Searching, splitting and trimming rust fn main() { let text = " name=Ada; lang=Rust;year=2026 "; let t = text.trim(); println!("{:?} {:?}", t.find("lang"), t.find('z')); for pair in t.split(';').map(str::trim).filter( p !p.is_empty()) { if let Some((key, value)) = pair.split_once('=') { println!("{key} - {value}"); } } println!("{:?}", "a,b,,c".split(',').collect::<Vec<_ ()); println!("{:?}", "one two	three
".split_whitespace().collect::<Vec<_ ()); println!("{:?}", "line1
line2
line3".lines().collect::<Vec<_ ()); println!("{}", "Hello".to_lowercase() == "hello"); println!("{}", "Straße".eq_ignore_ascii_case("STRASSE")); // false: ASCII-only comparison println!("{:?}", "x=1".strip_prefix("x=")); println!("{}", "cat".replace('c', "b")); } Converting From To Code --- --- --- &str String s.to_string() , String::from(s) , s.to_owned() String &str &s , s.as_str() number String n.to_string() , format!("{n}") &str number s.parse::<i32 () (a Result ) char String c.to_string() char digit c.to_digit(10) (an Option<u32 ) digit char char::from_digit(7, 10) Vec<u8 String String::from_utf8(bytes) (a Result : bytes may be invalid UTF-8) Slicing safely String slices use byte ranges and panic if a range cuts a character in half. To take "the first n characters" safely, find the byte position with char_indices : rust fn first_chars(s: &str, n: usize) - &str { match s.char_indices().nth(n) { Some((byte_index, _)) = &s ..byte_index , None = s, } } fn main() { println!("{}", first_chars("héllo wörld", 4)); println!("{}", first_chars("hi", 10)); } Check yourself quiz ? Why does "é".len() return 2? - len counts the characters plus an end marker + len counts bytes, and é takes two bytes in UTF-8 - len counts UTF-16 units, as in Java and JavaScript - Every character of a String takes two bytes A String is UTF-8: ASCII takes one byte, é two, and others up to four. s.chars().count() counts characters. ? How do you get each character together with the byte position where it starts? - s.chars().enumerate() + s.char_indices() - s.bytes().enumerate() - s.as_bytes() char_indices() gives (byte position, char) pairs. chars().enumerate() counts characters, so its numbers are wrong for slicing once a multi-byte character appears. ? Which is a valid way to get the first character of a String s ? + s.chars().next() - s 0 - s.get(0) - s.char(0) Strings are not indexable by position; chars() goes through the characters, and next() gives the first (an Option<char ).

They must work for any language, not just ASCII: rust fn capitalize_words(text: &str) - String // "élan VITAL" gives "Élan Vital"; words separated by single spaces in the result fn is_palindrome(text: &str) - bool // ignoring case and anything that is not alphanumeric fn truncate(text: &str, max_chars: usize) - String // at most max_chars characters; if cut, the last one is "…" fn run_lengths(text: &str) - String // "aaabcc" gives "a3bc2"; works on characters, not bytes fn reverse_words(text: &str) - String // "one two three" gives "three two one" truncate("Grüße aus Köln", 6) is "Grüße…" ; if the text fits, it is returned unchanged; max_chars 0 gives "" .

title: 3.03  HashMap and HashSet
body: Key-value lookups with HashMap - insert, get, contains_key, remove, iterating, and the entry API for counting and grouping - unique values with HashSet and its set operations, ordered alternatives BTreeMap and BTreeSet, ownership of keys and values, and which key types are allowed. HashMap HashMap<K, V maps keys to values with O(1) average lookup. It lives in std::collections : rust use std::collections::HashMap; fn main() { let mut ages: HashMap<String, u32 = HashMap::new(); ages.insert("Ada".to_string(), 36); ages.insert("Grace".to_string(), 85); ages.insert("Ada".to_string(), 37); // replaces; insert returns Some(36) println!("{:?}", ages.get("Ada")); // Some(37): look up with &str println!("{}", ages.get("Bob").copied().unwrap_or(0)); println!("{}", ages.contains_key("Grace")); if let Some(age) = ages.get_mut("Grace") { age += 1; } ages.remove("Ada"); for (name, age) in &ages { // order is unspecified println!("{name}: {age}"); } println!("{}", ages.len()); } A HashMap<String, ... can be looked up with a &str , so you do not need to allocate a String just to search. Inserting moves the key and value into the map: the map owns them. Values that are Copy (numbers) are copied in. The entry API Counting and grouping need "insert if missing, then update". The entry API does it in one lookup: rust use std::collections::HashMap; fn main() { let text = "the cat and the hat and the bat"; let mut counts: HashMap<&str, usize = HashMap::new(); for word in text.split_whitespace() { counts.entry(word).or_insert(0) += 1; } let mut sorted: Vec<(&str, usize) = counts.into_iter().collect(); sorted.sort_by( a, b b.1.cmp(&a.1).then(a.0.cmp(b.0))); // by count, then word println!("{sorted:?}"); let words = "apple", "avocado", "banana", "blueberry", "cherry" ; let mut by_letter: HashMap<char, Vec<&str = HashMap::new(); for w in words { by_letter.entry(w.chars().next().unwrap()).or_default().push(w); } let mut letters: Vec<_ = by_letter.keys().collect(); letters.sort(); for l in letters { println!("{l}: {:?}", by_letter l ); } } Entry method Does --- --- entry(k).or_insert(v) Inserts v if missing; returns &mut V entry(k).or_insert_with(f) Same, computing the value only when needed entry(k).or_default() Inserts V::default() (0, empty vec...) if missing entry(k).and_modify(f).or_insert(v) Updates an existing value, or inserts map &key panics when the key is missing; use it only when the key must exist. HashSet HashSet<T holds unique values with fast membership tests: rust use std::collections::HashSet; fn main() { let mut seen = HashSet::new(); for tag in "rust", "cli", "rust", "web" { if !seen.insert(tag) { // insert returns false for duplicates println!("duplicate: {tag}"); } } let a: HashSet<i32 = 1, 2, 3, 4 .into_iter().collect(); let b: HashSet<i32 = 3, 4, 5 .into_iter().collect(); let mut both: Vec<_ = a.intersection(&b).copied().collect(); let mut either: Vec<_ = a.union(&b).copied().collect(); let mut only_a: Vec<_ = a.difference(&b).copied().collect(); both.sort(); either.sort(); only_a.sort(); println!("{both:?} {either:?} {only_a:?} {}", a.contains(&2)); } Ordered maps and sets HashMap and HashSet iterate in an unpredictable order. When order matters (printing, ranges, smallest or largest key), use BTreeMap and BTreeSet , which keep keys sorted (O(log n) operations): rust use std::collections::BTreeMap; fn main() { let mut scores = BTreeMap::new(); for (name, score) in ("linus", 72), ("ada", 95), ("grace", 88) { scores.insert(name, score); } println!("{scores:?}"); // sorted by key println!("{:?} {:?}", scores.first_key_value(), scores.last_key_value()); for (name, s) in scores.range("b".."h") { // keys from "b" up to "h" println!("{name} {s}"); } } Keys A key type must implement Eq and Hash (for HashMap ) or Ord (for BTreeMap ). Strings, integers, char , bool , tuples of those, and your own types with derive(PartialEq, Eq, Hash) all work. f64 does not (NaN breaks equality); use an integer representation instead. Check yourself quiz ? What does counts.entry(word).or_insert(0) += 1 do? - Sets the word's count to 1 every time the word appears + Inserts 0 for a new word, then adds 1 to the stored count either way - Adds 1 only when the word is already in the map - Inserts the word with 0, and panics if it is already there or_insert(0) returns a &mut to the stored count (inserting 0 first if the word is new), and ... += 1 increments it. ? When should you choose BTreeMap over HashMap ? - When you need the fastest possible lookups by key - When the keys are f64 values, which cannot be hashed - When every value stored in the map must be unique + When you need the keys kept in sorted order BTreeMap keeps keys sorted (O(log n) operations), which also gives key ranges and the smallest or largest key; HashMap is faster on average but iterates in no particular order. Neither accepts f64 keys. ? What does HashSet::insert return when the value is already in the set? - true - It panics + false - The old value insert returns whether the value was newly added.

title: 3.04  Error Handling with Result
body: Recoverable errors with Result<T, E and unrecoverable ones with panic!, handling results with match, unwrap_or, map_err and and_then, propagating errors with the ? operator, writing your own error enums with Display and std::error::Error, converting errors with From so ? works across types, Box<dyn Error for quick programs, and when to panic. Two kinds of errors - Recoverable errors are expected possibilities: a file is missing, input is not a number. Functions return Result<T, E : Ok(value) or Err(error) . - Unrecoverable errors are bugs: an index past the end, a broken invariant. The program calls panic! , which stops the thread with a message. rust-norun enum Result<T, E { Ok(T), Err(E), } Handling a Result rust fn parse_age(text: &str) - Result<u32, String { let age: u32 = text.trim().parse().map_err( _ format!("'{text}' is not a number"))?; if age 150 { return Err(format!("{age} is not a realistic age")); } Ok(age) } fn main() { for input in "42", "abc", "200" { match parse_age(input) { Ok(age) = println!("age {age}"), Err(message) = println!("error: {message}"), } } let age = parse_age("x").unwrap_or(0); let doubled = parse_age("21").map( a a 2); println!("{age} {doubled:?}"); } Method Gives --- --- match / if let Ok(v) Full control unwrap_or(v) , unwrap_or_default() , unwrap_or_else(f) A fallback value map(f) , map_err(f) Transform the value / the error and_then(f) Chain a step that may also fail ok() Convert to an Option , dropping the error unwrap() , expect("why") The value, or a panic The ? operator ? after a Result means: if it is Err , return that error from the current function now; otherwise unwrap the Ok value. It turns error plumbing into one character: rust use std::num::ParseIntError; fn sum_line(line: &str) - Result<i64, ParseIntError { let mut total = 0; for part in line.split(',') { total += part.trim().parse::<i64 ()?; // stops at the first bad number } Ok(total) } fn main() { println!("{:?}", sum_line("1, 2, 3")); println!("{:?}", sum_line("1, two, 3")); } ? works in functions returning Result (or Option ), including main if it returns Result<(), E . Your own error type For a library or a larger program, define an error enum that lists what can go wrong, implement Display for messages, and From so ? converts other errors into yours: rust use std::fmt; use std::num::ParseIntError; derive(Debug) enum ConfigError { Missing(String), BadNumber { key: String, source: ParseIntError }, OutOfRange { key: String, value: i64 }, } impl fmt::Display for ConfigError { fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) - fmt::Result { match self { ConfigError::Missing(key) = write!(f, "missing setting '{key}'"), ConfigError::BadNumber { key, source } = write!(f, "'{key}' is not a number ({source})"), ConfigError::OutOfRange { key, value } = write!(f, "'{key}' = {value} is out of range"), } } } impl std::error::Error for ConfigError {} fn get_port(settings: & (&str, &str) ) - Result<u16, ConfigError { let (_, text) = settings.iter().find( (k, _) k == "port") .ok_or_else( ConfigError::Missing("port".into()))?; let value: i64 = text.parse().map_err( e ConfigError::BadNumber { key: "port".into(), source: e })?; u16::try_from(value).map_err( _ ConfigError::OutOfRange { key: "port".into(), value }) } fn main() { for settings in vec! ("port", "8080") , vec! , vec! ("port", "eighty") , vec! ("port", "70000") { match get_port(&settings) { Ok(p) = println!("port {p}"), Err(e) = println!("error: {e}"), } } } With impl From<ParseIntError for ConfigError , a plain text.parse()? would convert automatically. The thiserror crate generates all of this from attributes, and anyhow offers a catch-all error type for applications. Box<dyn Error for quick programs When you just want ? to work with any error type, return Result<T, Box<dyn std::error::Error : rust use std::error::Error; fn run() - Result<i32, Box<dyn Error { let n: i32 = "41".parse()?; // ParseIntError converts automatically if n < 0 { return Err("negative".into()); // a &str converts too } Ok(n + 1) } fn main() { match run() { Ok(v) = println!("{v}"), Err(e) = println!("error: {e}"), } } When to panic Panic for bugs : a condition that should be impossible if the code is correct, a violated precondition in a function documented to panic, or in tests and quick experiments. Return a Result for anything the caller or the user can cause and handle. unwrap() in production code is a promise that it can never fail; expect("reason") documents why. Check yourself quiz ? What does the ? operator do with an Err value? - It panics, printing the error's message to standard error + It returns the error from the current function at once (via From if needed) - It replaces the error with the type's default value and goes on - It ignores the error and goes on with the next line ? is early-return plumbing: Ok(v) becomes v , and Err(e) is returned to the caller. Panicking is what unwrap() does. ? When is panicking the right choice instead of returning a Result ? + For bugs and broken invariants that the caller cannot sensibly handle - Whenever the user types input that does not parse - Whenever a file the program needs is missing - Never: every error should be returned as a Result Bad input and missing files are expected failures the caller can handle, so they deserve a Result ; a panic is for "this should be impossible". ? What is "7".parse::<i32 ().map( n n 2).unwrap_or(0) ? - 7 - Ok(14) + 14 - 0 parse gives Ok(7) , map doubles it, and unwrap_or takes the value out of the Ok .

title: Parsing durations with Result
body: Parse durations such as 1h30m , 45s or 2h5m10s into seconds, with your own error type: rust derive(Debug, PartialEq) enum DurationError { Empty, // "duration is empty" MissingNumber(char), // "unit 'm' has no number" MissingUnit(String), // "number 12 has no unit" UnknownUnit(char), // "unknown unit 'x'" Overflow, // "duration is too long" } impl std::fmt::Display for DurationError { ... } // the messages above fn parse_duration(text: &str) - Result<u64, DurationError fn total(texts: & &str ) - Result<u64, DurationError // sum of several durations; the first error wins fn format_duration(seconds: u64) - String // 5410 gives "1h30m10s"; 0 gives "0s" - Units are d (days), h , m and s , each after a whole number; parts may come in any order and repeat ( 1m1m is 120). Spaces around the text are ignored. - Use checked_mul and checked_add so huge numbers give Overflow instead of wrapping; a number too big for u64 is also Overflow . - total must use ? .

title: 3.05  Modules, Crates and Tests
body: Organising code with mod, pub and use, privacy rules for items and struct fields, splitting modules into files, packages, library and binary crates, adding dependencies from crates.io with Cargo.toml, and writing unit tests with test , assert macros and cargo test, plus integration tests and documentation tests. Modules A module groups related items and controls what is visible outside it. Everything is private by default; pub makes it visible to the parent module and beyond: rust mod geometry { pub struct Point { pub x: f64, pub y: f64, } pub fn distance(a: &Point, b: &Point) - f64 { (square(a.x - b.x) + square(a.y - b.y)).sqrt() } fn square(v: f64) - f64 { v v } // private: only usable inside geometry pub mod shapes { use super::Point; // super: the parent module pub struct Circle { pub center: Point, pub radius: f64 } impl Circle { pub fn area(&self) - f64 { std::f64::consts::PI self.radius self.radius } } } } use geometry::shapes::Circle; use geometry::{distance, Point}; fn main() { let a = Point { x: 0.0, y: 0.0 }; let b = Point { x: 3.0, y: 4.0 }; println!("{}", distance(&a, &b)); let c = Circle { center: b, radius: 1.0 }; println!("{:.3} at ({}, {})", c.area(), c.center.x, c.center.y); // geometry::square(2.0); // error: function square is private } - Paths use :: . crate:: starts at the crate's root, super:: at the parent, self:: at the current module. - use brings a path into scope so you can write the short name. - A pub struct can still have private fields: then code outside the module cannot build it directly and must use its constructor, which keeps its rules intact. Files In a real project each module usually has its own file: text src/ main.rs mod geometry; (tells Cargo to load src/geometry.rs) geometry.rs pub mod shapes; geometry/ shapes.rs mod geometry; with a semicolon means "the module's code is in geometry.rs (or geometry/mod.rs )". Packages and crates - A crate is a unit of compilation: a binary crate (with main , from src/main.rs ) or a library crate (from src/lib.rs ). - A package is a folder with Cargo.toml ; it can contain a library and any number of binaries. Dependencies come from crates.io: toml package name = "wordcount" version = "0.1.0" edition = "2024" dependencies clap = { version = "4", features = "derive" } serde = { version = "1", features = "derive" } cargo add clap --features derive edits the file for you. Cargo.lock records exact versions; commit it for applications. Unit tests Tests live next to the code, in a module that is only compiled for cargo test : rust-norun pub fn add(a: i32, b: i32) - i32 { a + b } pub fn divide(a: i32, b: i32) - i32 { if b == 0 { panic!("division by zero"); } a / b } cfg(test) mod tests { use super:: ; test fn adds_small_numbers() { assert_eq!(add(2, 3), 5); } test fn negative_numbers() { assert!(add(-2, -3) < 0, "expected a negative sum"); assert_ne!(add(-1, 1), 1); } test should_panic(expected = "division by zero") fn dividing_by_zero_panics() { divide(1, 0); } test fn returns_result() - Result<(), String { let n: i32 = "42".parse().map_err( e format!("{e}"))?; assert_eq!(n, 42); Ok(()) } } bash cargo test build and run every test cargo test negative only tests whose name contains "negative" cargo test -- --nocapture show println! output from passing tests Because the tests module is a child of the module it tests, it can test private functions too. Integration tests go in a tests/ folder next to src/ and use the crate only through its public API, like a user would. Documentation tests are code examples inside /// comments, which cargo test compiles and runs, so examples in the documentation never go stale. The practice tasks in this course use the same idea with a small kit: test("name", { check_eq(actual, expected); }) . Check yourself quiz ? Can code outside a module call a function in it that is not marked pub ? - Yes, as long as it writes the full path with :: - Yes, but only after a use brings it into scope + No: items are private to their module and its children unless marked pub - Only from main , which can see every module Privacy applies whatever the path: geometry::square(2.0) is refused because square is not pub . ? Why do unit tests live in a mod tests with cfg(test) ? - So that the tests run each time the program starts + It is compiled only for cargo test , and as a child module it can reach private items - cargo test only finds test functions in a module named tests - It lets the tests run at the same time as the program cfg(test) leaves the module out of normal builds, and use super:: ; gives it the parent's items, private ones included. ? A pub struct Account has a private field balance . What can code in another module do? - Read and write balance directly, like any field - Read balance , but not assign a new value to it - Nothing at all: the whole struct is hidden + Only use it through its public functions and methods Private fields are invisible outside the module, so other code cannot even build an Account with a struct literal: construction must go through a public function such as new .

title: A module with private state
body: Write a module bank whose Account keeps its balance private, so the only way to change it is through methods that keep it valid: rust mod bank { derive(Debug, PartialEq) pub enum BankError { InvalidAmount, InsufficientFunds { needed: u64, available: u64 }, SameAccount } pub struct Account { / private: id, owner, balance in cents / } impl Account { pub fn open(id: u32, owner: &str) - Account pub fn id(&self) - u32 pub fn owner(&self) - &str pub fn balance(&self) - u64 pub fn deposit(&mut self, cents: u64) - Result<(), BankError // 0 is InvalidAmount pub fn withdraw(&mut self, cents: u64) - Result<(), BankError // InsufficientFunds when short } pub fn transfer(from: &mut Account, to: &mut Account, cents: u64) - Result<(), BankError // nothing changes on error pub mod report { pub fn summary(accounts: & super::Account ) - String // "3 accounts, total 12.34" } } - transfer between accounts with the same id fails with SameAccount ; an amount of 0 with InvalidAmount . - summary writes the total in euros with 2 decimals.

title: A gradebook report
body: Write a program that reads exam results as CSV from standard input and prints a report. The first line is the header name,subject,score ; each other line is one result: name,subject,score Ada,maths,92 Bob,maths,61 Ada,art,78 Bob,art,85 Cy,maths,abc Cy,maths,47 prints line 6: bad score 'abc' Students: Ada 85.0 B (2 results) Bob 73.0 C (2 results) Cy 47.0 F (1 result) Subjects: art avg 81.5 best Bob (85) maths avg 66.7 best Ada (92) Errors: 1 Rules: - A wrong header prints error: bad header and stops at once. Blank lines are skipped. - Each line has exactly 3 comma-separated fields, trimmed. Problems are printed as they are read , as line <n : <message (the header is line 1), and the line is skipped: expected 3 fields , empty name , empty subject , bad score '<text ' (not a whole number), score <n out of range (not 0 to 100). - Students are listed by average (highest first), then by name. Each line: two spaces, the name left-aligned in 10 characters, the average right-aligned in 5 with one decimal, a space, the grade (90 A , 80 B , 70 C , 60 D , else F , using the unrounded average), and (<n results) ( 1 result for one). - Subjects are listed by name. Each line: two spaces, the subject left-aligned in 10 characters, avg <average with one decimal , two spaces, and best <name (<score ) for the highest score (on a tie, the name that sorts first). - Last, Errors: <count . With no valid results at all, print No data. instead of the two lists (but still the errors before it and the count after it).

title: 4.01  Generics
body: Writing code once for many types - generic functions with type parameters and trait bounds, where clauses, generic structs and enums like Option and Result, impl blocks for generic types and for specific types, const generics for array sizes, and monomorphization, which makes generics cost nothing at run time. Generic functions A function with a type parameter works for many types. Without a bound , the body can do almost nothing with a T ; bounds say what the type must support: rust fn largest<T: PartialOrd + Copy (items: & T ) - Option<T { let mut best = items.first()?; for &item in items { if item best { best = item; } } Some(best) } fn describe<T: std::fmt::Debug (label: &str, value: T) - String { format!("{label}: {value:?}") } fn main() { println!("{:?} {:?} {:?}", largest(& 3, 9, 2 ), largest(& 1.5, -2.0 ), largest(& 'x', 'b' )); println!("{:?}", largest::<i32 (& )); println!("{}", describe("point", (3, 4))); println!("{}", describe("list", vec! "a", "b" )); } T: PartialOrd + Copy means "any type that can be compared with < and copied". The compiler checks the bounds where the function is defined, so a generic function either works for every allowed type or does not compile at all. where clauses Long bound lists read better in a where clause: rust use std::fmt::Display; fn join_all<T, U (items: & T , extra: U) - String where T: Display, U: Display + Clone, { let mut out: Vec<String = items.iter().map( i i.to_string()).collect(); out.push(extra.to_string()); out.join(", ") } fn main() { println!("{}", join_all(& 1, 2, 3 , "and more")); } Generic structs and enums Vec<T , Option<T , Result<T, E and HashMap<K, V are generic types from the standard library. Your own types can be too: rust derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq) struct Pair<T { first: T, second: T, } impl<T: PartialOrd Pair<T { fn larger(&self) - &T { if self.first = self.second { &self.first } else { &self.second } } } impl<T Pair<T { fn swap(self) - Pair<T { Pair { first: self.second, second: self.first } } } impl Pair<f64 { // only for Pair<f64 fn distance(&self) - f64 { (self.first - self.second).abs() } } derive(Debug) enum Tree<T { Leaf(T), Node(Box<Tree<T , Box<Tree<T ), } fn count_leaves<T (t: &Tree<T ) - usize { match t { Tree::Leaf(_) = 1, Tree::Node(l, r) = count_leaves(l) + count_leaves(r), } } fn main() { let p = Pair { first: 3, second: 8 }; println!("{} {:?}", p.larger(), p.clone().swap()); println!("{}", Pair { first: 1.5, second: 4.0 }.distance()); let t = Tree::Node(Box::new(Tree::Leaf("a")), Box::new(Tree::Node(Box::new(Tree::Leaf("b")), Box::new(Tree::Leaf("c"))))); println!("{}", count_leaves(&t)); } impl<T Pair<T applies to every Pair ; impl<T: PartialOrd Pair<T only when T can be compared; impl Pair<f64 only for one concrete type. Box (lesson 5.04) puts the recursive tree parts on the heap. Const generics Types can also be parameterised by values , most often array lengths: rust fn sum_all<const N: usize (values: i32; N ) - i32 { let mut total = 0; for v in values { total += v; } total } derive(Debug) struct Grid<const W: usize, const H: usize { cells: u8; W ; H , } fn main() { println!("{} {}", sum_all( 1, 2, 3 ), sum_all( 10; 5 )); let g = Grid::<3, 2 { cells: 0; 3 ; 2 }; println!("{:?}", g); } Zero-cost The compiler generates a separate, fully optimised copy of a generic function for each concrete type it is used with ( monomorphization ). largest::<i32 and largest::<f64 are as fast as hand-written versions. The cost is compile time and binary size, not run time. Check yourself quiz ? Why does fn largest<T (items: & T ) - T need a bound such as PartialOrd ? - Every generic function needs at least one bound to compile + Without it the compiler knows nothing about T , so is not allowed - PartialOrd makes the comparisons faster for numbers - The bound only documents the intent; the compiler ignores it The body is checked once for every possible T ; only what the bounds promise (here, comparing with ) may be used. ? What does impl Pair<f64 { ... } mean? - The methods work for every Pair , converting the fields to f64 - From then on, a Pair can only hold f64 values + Those methods exist only for Pair<f64 , not for other Pair types - f64 becomes the type used when T is not given An impl for one concrete type adds methods just to that type; impl<T Pair<T would cover every Pair . ? What does monomorphization mean for generic code? - Generic code is checked again at run time for each new type - Generic functions run slower, because they look the type up as they go - Each generic function can only be used with one type + The compiler makes a specialised copy for each type used, with no run-time cost Each use with a concrete type is compiled as if written by hand for it; the price is compile time and binary size.

title: Generic types and functions
body: Write a generic stack and two generic functions: rust derive(Debug, Default) struct Stack<T { items: Vec<T } impl<T Stack<T { fn new() - Self fn push(&mut self, item: T) fn pop(&mut self) - Option<T fn peek(&self) - Option<&T fn len(&self) - usize fn is_empty(&self) - bool } impl<T: std::fmt::Display Stack<T { fn render(&self) - String // bottom to top, " 1 2 3 "; " " when empty } fn min_max<T: PartialOrd + Copy (items: & T ) - Option<(T, T) fn dedup_sorted<T: PartialEq + Clone (items: & T ) - Vec<T // drops consecutive repeats

title: 4.02  Traits
body: Defining shared behaviour with traits, implementing them for your types and for existing ones, default methods, traits as parameters with impl Trait and generic bounds, returning impl Trait, associated types and constants, supertraits, the orphan rule, and blanket implementations. A trait A trait names a set of methods that types can implement: shared behaviour, like an interface in other languages. rust trait Shape { fn area(&self) - f64; fn name(&self) - String; fn describe(&self) - String { // a default method: implementers may keep it format!("{} with area {:.2}", self.name(), self.area()) } } struct Circle { radius: f64 } struct Rect { w: f64, h: f64 } impl Shape for Circle { fn area(&self) - f64 { std::f64::consts::PI self.radius self.radius } fn name(&self) - String { "circle".to_string() } } impl Shape for Rect { fn area(&self) - f64 { self.w self.h } fn name(&self) - String { "rectangle".to_string() } fn describe(&self) - String { format!("a {}x{} rectangle", self.w, self.h) } // override } fn main() { println!("{}", Circle { radius: 1.0 }.describe()); println!("{}", Rect { w: 2.0, h: 3.0 }.describe()); } Traits as parameters A function can accept any type implementing a trait. Three spellings mean the same thing for one parameter: rust trait Shape { fn area(&self) - f64; } struct Square(f64); impl Shape for Square { fn area(&self) - f64 { self.0 self.0 } } struct Circle(f64); impl Shape for Circle { fn area(&self) - f64 { 3.14159 self.0 self.0 } } fn print_area(s: &impl Shape) { // impl Trait in argument position println!("{:.2}", s.area()); } fn total_area<S: Shape (shapes: & S ) - f64 { // a generic bound: all items the same type shapes.iter().map( s s.area()).sum() } fn bigger<'a (a: &'a impl Shape, b: &'a impl Shape) - f64 { a.area().max(b.area()) } fn main() { print_area(&Square(2.0)); println!("{}", total_area(& Square(1.0), Square(2.0) )); println!("{:.2}", bigger(&Square(1.0), &Circle(1.0))); } A Vec<S with S: Shape holds one concrete shape type. To mix circles and squares in one list you need trait objects (lesson 4.05). Returning impl Trait - impl Trait returns some type that implements the trait without naming it, which is how functions return iterators and closures: rust fn evens(limit: u32) - impl Iterator<Item = u32 { (0..limit).filter( n n % 2 == 0) } fn adder(n: i32) - impl Fn(i32) - i32 { move x x + n } fn main() { println!("{:?}", evens(10).collect::<Vec<_ ()); println!("{}", adder(5)(10)); } Implementing traits for existing types You can implement your own trait for types you did not write, including i32 and String : rust trait Shout { fn shout(&self) - String; } impl Shout for str { fn shout(&self) - String { self.to_uppercase() + "!" } } impl Shout for i32 { fn shout(&self) - String { format!("{}!!!", self) } } fn main() { println!("{} {}", "hello".shout(), 42.shout()); } The orphan rule : you may implement a trait for a type only if the trait or the type is defined in your crate. You cannot implement the standard library's Display for the standard library's Vec , which prevents two crates from giving conflicting implementations. Wrap the type in your own struct (the newtype pattern) when you need to. Associated types and constants A trait can require a type or a constant from its implementers. Iterator uses an associated type for its items: rust trait Unit { const SYMBOL: &'static str; const PER_METER: f64; fn from_meters(m: f64) - f64 { m Self::PER_METER } } struct Feet; impl Unit for Feet { const SYMBOL: &'static str = "ft"; const PER_METER: f64 = 3.28084; } struct Centimeters; impl Unit for Centimeters { const SYMBOL: &'static str = "cm"; const PER_METER: f64 = 100.0; } fn show<U: Unit (meters: f64) - String { format!("{:.1} {}", U::from_meters(meters), U::SYMBOL) } fn main() { println!("{} {}", show::<Feet (1.8), show::<Centimeters (1.8)); } Supertraits and blanket implementations A trait can require another ( trait Named: std::fmt::Display { ... } ). And an implementation can cover every type that meets a bound: the standard library implements ToString for every T: Display , which is why anything printable has .to_string() . Check yourself quiz ? What is a default method in a trait? + A method with a body in the trait, which implementers get for free and may override - A method that every implementer must write, or the code does not compile - A method that runs automatically when a value of the type is created - A method that only works on the type's Default value describe in Shape is a default method: Circle keeps it, while Rect overrides it with its own version. ? Why can't you implement std::fmt::Display for Vec<i32 ? - Vec already has a Display implementation - Display can only be derived, never written by hand + The orphan rule: neither the trait nor the type is defined in your crate - Generic types such as Vec<T cannot implement traits You may implement a trait for a type only if one of them is yours; wrap the Vec in your own struct (a newtype) instead. ? A function takes items: & S with S: Shape . Can it receive a mix of circles and squares? - Yes, as long as both types implement Shape - Yes, if the slice is passed as &mut - Only inside an unsafe block + No: S is one type per call; mixing needs dyn Shape trait objects A generic parameter is filled in with a single type for each call; & Box<dyn Shape can hold different shapes.

title: Traits for scoring words
body: A word game can score words in different ways. Write a trait and three implementations: rust trait Scorer { const NAME: &'static str; fn score(&self, word: &str) - u32; fn total(&self, words: & &str ) - u32 { ... } // default: the sum of the scores } struct LengthScorer; // one point per character struct VowelScorer { bonus: u32 } // bonus points per vowel (a e i o u, either case), 1 per other letter struct LetterScorer; // Scrabble letter values, ignoring case; non-letters score 0 fn best_word<'a, S: Scorer (scorer: &S, words: & &'a str ) - Option<&'a str // highest score, the first on a tie fn describe<S: Scorer (scorer: &S, word: &str) - String // "<NAME : <word scores <n " Scrabble values: 1 for A E I L N O R S T U, 2 for D G, 3 for B C M P, 4 for F H V W Y, 5 for K, 8 for J X, 10 for Q Z.

title: 4.03  The Standard Traits
body: The traits every Rust type should know - Debug and Display for printing, Clone and Copy, PartialEq and Eq, PartialOrd and Ord for comparing and sorting, Hash for map keys, Default, From and Into for conversions, FromStr for parsing, and operator overloading with Add and friends - which to derive and which to write by hand. Deriving Many standard traits can be derived : the compiler writes the obvious implementation field by field. rust derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash, PartialOrd, Ord, Default) struct Version { major: u32, minor: u32, patch: u32, } fn main() { let a = Version { major: 1, minor: 10, patch: 0 }; let b = Version { major: 1, minor: 2, patch: 7 }; let c = a; // Copy: a is still usable println!("{:?} {} {}", a, a == c, a b); // Ord compares fields in order: major, minor, patch let mut list = vec! a, b, Version::default() ; list.sort(); println!("{list:?}"); let mut set = std::collections::HashSet::new(); set.insert(a); // Hash + Eq: usable as a key println!("{}", set.contains(&c)); } Trait Gives Derive when --- --- --- Debug {:?} printing Almost always Clone .clone() The type can be duplicated Copy Implicit copies on assignment Small, stack-only types (all fields Copy ) PartialEq , Eq == Values have meaningful equality ( Eq if it is total: not for floats) PartialOrd , Ord < , sorting There is a natural order (field order decides) Hash Use as HashMap / HashSet key Together with Eq Default Type::default() Every field has a sensible empty value Display Display ( {} ) is for users and is never derived; write it: rust use std::fmt; struct Money { cents: i64 } impl fmt::Display for Money { fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_ ) - fmt::Result { let sign = if self.cents < 0 { "-" } else { "" }; let c = self.cents.abs(); write!(f, "{sign}{}.{:02} EUR", c / 100, c % 100) } } fn main() { let m = Money { cents: -1250 }; println!("{m}"); let s = m.to_string(); // ToString comes free with Display println!(" {s: 14} "); } Conversions: From, Into, TryFrom, FromStr rust use std::str::FromStr; derive(Debug, PartialEq) struct Celsius(f64); derive(Debug, PartialEq) struct Fahrenheit(f64); impl From<Fahrenheit for Celsius { fn from(f: Fahrenheit) - Self { Celsius((f.0 - 32.0) 5.0 / 9.0) } } derive(Debug, PartialEq) struct Rgb(u8, u8, u8); impl FromStr for Rgb { type Err = String; fn from_str(s: &str) - Result<Self, Self::Err { let hex = s.strip_prefix(' ').ok_or("missing ")?; if hex.len() != 6 { return Err(format!("expected 6 hex digits, got {}", hex.len())); } let part = i: usize u8::from_str_radix(&hex i..i + 2 , 16).map_err( e e.to_string()); Ok(Rgb(part(0)?, part(2)?, part(4)?)) } } fn main() { let c: Celsius = Fahrenheit(212.0).into(); // Into comes free with From println!("{c:?}"); println!("{:?} {:?}", " ff8800".parse::<Rgb (), "ff8800".parse::<Rgb ()); } Implement From (never Into directly); x.into() then works too. Implementing From<YourError for AppError is what lets ? convert errors (lesson 3.04). FromStr makes "...".parse::<YourType () work. Operator overloading Operators are traits in std::ops : implementing Add gives your type + : rust use std::ops::{Add, Mul, Neg}; derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq) struct Vec2 { x: f64, y: f64 } impl Add for Vec2 { type Output = Vec2; fn add(self, o: Vec2) - Vec2 { Vec2 { x: self.x + o.x, y: self.y + o.y } } } impl Mul<f64 for Vec2 { type Output = Vec2; fn mul(self, k: f64) - Vec2 { Vec2 { x: self.x k, y: self.y k } } } impl Neg for Vec2 { type Output = Vec2; fn neg(self) - Vec2 { Vec2 { x: -self.x, y: -self.y } } } fn main() { let a = Vec2 { x: 1.0, y: 2.0 }; let b = Vec2 { x: 0.5, y: -1.0 }; println!("{:?}", a + b 2.0 + -a); } Overload operators only where the meaning is obvious (vectors, money, matrices). Check yourself quiz ? Why can't f64 implement Eq and Ord ? - Rounding errors mean == never works on floats + NaN is not equal to itself and has no order, so both are only partial - An f64 is too large to compare in one step - Floats are Copy , and Ord needs a type that is not Eq promises every value equals itself and Ord that any two values are ordered; NaN breaks both, so f64 only has PartialEq and PartialOrd . ? What do you get for free by implementing From<A for B ? + Into<B for A , so a.into() produces a B - From<B for A , the conversion back - Display for B - Clone for B The standard library implements Into for every From , which is why you implement From and never Into directly. Nothing gives you the reverse conversion. ? Two derive(PartialOrd) structs are compared. How is the order decided? - By comparing their memory addresses - By the sum of all the fields + Field by field, in declaration order - By the field with the largest value Derived comparisons are lexicographic: the first field that differs decides, in declaration order, so major decides before minor .
