title: 4.04  Lifetimes
body: How the compiler makes sure references never outlive their data - what a lifetime is, lifetime annotations on functions like longest, the elision rules that let you leave most of them out, structs that hold references, lifetimes in impl blocks and methods, 'static, and practical ways out such as returning owned data. What a lifetime is Every reference is valid for some region of the program: its lifetime . The borrow checker makes sure no reference is used after the value it points to is gone: rust-norun let r; { let x = 5; r = &x; // error E0597 : x does not live long enough } println!("{r}"); // x was dropped at the closing brace above Usually the compiler works lifetimes out by itself. You need to write them when a function returns a reference and the compiler cannot tell which input it comes from. Annotating a function rust-norun fn longest(a: &str, b: &str) - &str { // error E0106 : missing lifetime specifier if a.len() = b.len() { a } else { b } } The result could borrow from a or from b . A lifetime parameter says how they relate: rust fn longest<'a (a: &'a str, b: &'a str) - &'a str { if a.len() = b.len() { a } else { b } } fn main() { let outer = String::from("a fairly long string"); let result; { let inner = String::from("short"); result = longest(&outer, &inner); println!("{result}"); // fine: both strings are alive here } // println!("{result}"); // would not compile: result may borrow from inner } <'a declares a lifetime named a ; &'a str means "a reference valid for at least 'a ". The signature promises: the result lives as long as the shorter of the two inputs. Annotations do not change how long anything lives; they describe the relationship so the compiler can check every caller. Elision: when you can leave them out Most functions need no annotations, thanks to three elision rules : 1. Each reference parameter gets its own lifetime. 2. If there is exactly one input lifetime, the output gets it: fn first_word(s: &str) - &str . 3. In methods, if there is &self or &mut self , the output gets self 's lifetime. So fn trim_end(s: &str) - &str and fn name(&self) - &str just work. Annotations are needed only when there are several input references and the output borrows from one of them. Structs that hold references A struct holding a reference must say that it cannot outlive the data it borrows: rust struct Highlight<'a { text: &'a str, start: usize, } impl<'a Highlight<'a { fn word(&self) - &'a str { // borrows from the original text, not from self let rest = &self.text self.start.. ; rest.split_whitespace().next().unwrap_or("") } } fn find_highlights<'a (text: &'a str, needle: &str) - Vec<Highlight<'a { text.match_indices(needle).map( (start, _) Highlight { text, start }).collect() } fn main() { let book = String::from("call me Ishmael. some years ago, never mind how long"); let hits = find_highlights(&book, "m"); for h in &hits { println!("{} at {}", h.word(), h.start); } } Highlight<'a cannot outlive book ; the compiler checks every use. Such "view" structs are fast (no copying), and lifetimes are what make them safe. 'static 'static means "valid for the whole program". String literals are &'static str , because they are stored in the program itself. You will also see T: 'static bounds on threads (milestone 6): the thread may outlive the current function, so it cannot borrow local variables. Practical advice - Start without annotations; add them only when the compiler asks, and read its suggestion. - If lifetimes get complicated, consider returning owned data ( String , Vec<T ) instead of references. A small copy is often worth the simpler code. - Structs that own their data ( String fields) need no lifetimes at all; reach for borrowed fields only when performance matters. Check yourself quiz ? What does fn longest<'a (a: &'a str, b: &'a str) - &'a str promise? - The result lives as long as the longer-lived of the two inputs + The result is valid while both inputs are, so it may borrow from either - The result is a copy, so it may outlive both inputs - Both inputs must be string literals One lifetime for all three means the result can only be used while both inputs are still alive: the shorter of the two lifetimes. ? Why does fn first_word(s: &str) - &str need no lifetime annotation? - &str references never need lifetime annotations - Functions that return slices are checked at run time instead + With one input reference, elision gives the output that same lifetime - Lifetime annotations are only ever needed on structs The elision rules fill in fn first_word<'a (s: &'a str) - &'a str . With two input references, like longest , you must write them. ? What is the type of the literal "hello" ? + &'static str - String - &String - str Literals are stored in the program binary and live for the whole run.

title: Lifetimes in practice
body: Write functions and a struct that return borrowed data from their inputs, with the lifetime annotations they need: rust fn longest_word(text: &str) - &str // the first longest word; "" for no words fn pick<'a (a: &'a str, b: &'a str, first: bool) - &'a str fn split_pair(line: &str, sep: char) - Option<(&str, &str) // both parts trimmed; None without sep struct Tokenizer<'a { rest: &'a str } impl<'a Tokenizer<'a { fn new(text: &'a str) - Self fn next_token(&mut self) - Option<&'a str // the next word, number or single punctuation character } Tokenizer skips white space; a token is a run of letters, a run of digits, or one other character. For "x1 = 42+y;" the tokens are x , 1 , = , 42 , + , y , ; . The tokens borrow from the original text, so they stay valid after the tokenizer is gone.

title: 4.05  Trait Objects
body: Dynamic dispatch with dyn Trait - storing different types in one collection with Box<dyn Trait and &dyn Trait, how vtables work, static versus dynamic dispatch and when to choose each, dyn-compatibility (object safety) rules, downcasting with Any, and enums as the alternative when the set of types is closed. Different types in one list Generics fill in one concrete type at compile time. To keep circles and squares in the same Vec , use trait objects : values of different types behind a pointer, all used through one trait: rust trait Shape { fn area(&self) - f64; fn name(&self) - String; } struct Circle { r: f64 } struct Square { side: f64 } impl Shape for Circle { fn area(&self) - f64 { std::f64::consts::PI self.r self.r } fn name(&self) - String { format!("circle r={}", self.r) } } impl Shape for Square { fn area(&self) - f64 { self.side self.side } fn name(&self) - String { format!("square {}", self.side) } } fn total_area(shapes: & Box<dyn Shape ) - f64 { shapes.iter().map( s s.area()).sum() } fn print_one(shape: &dyn Shape) { println!("{} - {:.2}", shape.name(), shape.area()); } fn main() { let shapes: Vec<Box<dyn Shape = vec! Box::new(Circle { r: 1.0 }), Box::new(Square { side: 2.0 }), Box::new(Circle { r: 0.5 }), ; for s in &shapes { print_one(s.as_ref()); } println!("total {:.2}", total_area(&shapes)); } dyn Shape is "some type that implements Shape ", whose size is not known at compile time, so it always sits behind a pointer: Box<dyn Shape (owned), &dyn Shape (borrowed), or Rc<dyn Shape . How it works A trait object is a fat pointer : a pointer to the data plus a pointer to a vtable , a table of that type's method implementations. A call s.area() looks up the method in the vtable at run time: dynamic dispatch . Generics ( impl Trait , T: Trait ) Trait objects ( dyn Trait ) --- --- --- Dispatch Static: resolved at compile time, can be inlined Dynamic: a vtable lookup per call Mixed types in one collection No Yes Code size One copy per type One copy Typical use Algorithms, performance-sensitive code Plugins, heterogeneous lists, callbacks The vtable call costs a few nanoseconds; choose by design, not by fear of speed. Plugins and strategies Trait objects suit "pick behaviour at run time": rust trait Discount { fn apply(&self, cents: u64) - u64; fn label(&self) - String; } struct PercentOff(u64); struct FlatOff { cents: u64, minimum: u64 } impl Discount for PercentOff { fn apply(&self, cents: u64) - u64 { cents - cents self.0 / 100 } fn label(&self) - String { format!("{}% off", self.0) } } impl Discount for FlatOff { fn apply(&self, cents: u64) - u64 { if cents = self.minimum { cents.saturating_sub(self.cents) } else { cents } } fn label(&self) - String { format!("{} off over {}", self.cents, self.minimum) } } fn best(cents: u64, offers: & Box<dyn Discount ) - (String, u64) { offers.iter() .map( d (d.label(), d.apply(cents))) .min_by_key( (_, price) price) .unwrap_or(("none".to_string(), cents)) } fn main() { let offers: Vec<Box<dyn Discount = vec! Box::new(PercentOff(10)), Box::new(FlatOff { cents: 800, minimum: 5000 }) ; println!("{:?} {:?}", best(4000, &offers), best(9000, &offers)); } Dyn compatibility Not every trait can be used as dyn Trait . A trait is dyn-compatible (formerly "object safe") when the compiler can build a vtable for it, which rules out, among other things: - methods that return Self (the size of Self is unknown behind the pointer); - generic methods ( fn convert<T (&self) ): there would be one per T , too many for a table. Clone returns Self , so dyn Clone is not allowed. Methods that do not fit can be excluded with where Self: Sized . Closed sets: use an enum If you know every variant up front (the shapes your program supports), an enum with a match (lesson 2.05) is often simpler and faster than trait objects, and the compiler checks you handle every case. Use trait objects when the set is open : other modules, crates or plugins may add types later. Check yourself quiz ? Why must a dyn Trait value sit behind a pointer such as Box or & ? - So that it can be shared between threads - Traits can only be implemented for values on the heap - A dyn value is always mutable, and pointers allow that + Its concrete type, and so its size, is not known at compile time A variable needs a size fixed at compile time; a pointer has one, whatever type it points to. &dyn Shape works too, so the heap is not required. ? When is an enum better than Vec<Box<dyn Trait ? + When the set of types is fixed: match is checked for completeness, with no vtable - When other crates should be able to add new types later - When each type needs a different set of fields - When the number of items in the list is not known in advance A closed set suits an enum; trait objects suit an open set that other code may extend. Both can hold variants with different data. ? Which trait method makes a trait unusable as dyn Trait ? - fn area(&self) - f64 + fn duplicate(&self) - Self - fn name(&self) - String - fn describe(&self) - String with a default body Returning Self needs the concrete type's size, which a trait object hides.

title: A pipeline of trait objects
body: Text filters that can be combined at run time: rust trait Filter { fn apply(&self, text: &str) - String; fn name(&self) - String; } struct Trim; // trims and collapses runs of spaces to one struct Upper; struct Replace { from: String, to: String } // name: "replace(from- to)" struct MaxLen(usize); // cuts to that many characters, ending with "…" when cut; name "maxlen(n)" struct Pipeline { filters: Vec<Box<dyn Filter } impl Pipeline { fn new() - Self fn add(mut self, f: Box<dyn Filter ) - Self // builder style: returns the pipeline fn run(&self, text: &str) - String fn describe(&self) - String // "trim upper maxlen(5)", or "empty" } impl Filter for Pipeline // a pipeline is itself a filter (name: "pipeline ... title: A matrix library
body: Build a small linear-algebra type that feels like a built-in one, using generics-free but trait-heavy Rust: rust derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq) struct Matrix { rows: usize, cols: usize, data: Vec<f64 } // row-major derive(Debug, PartialEq) enum MatrixError { Empty, Ragged, Shape { left: (usize, usize), right: (usize, usize) }, NotSquare, Parse(String) } impl Matrix { fn zeros(rows: usize, cols: usize) - Matrix fn identity(n: usize) - Matrix fn from_rows(rows: Vec<Vec<f64 ) - Result<Matrix, MatrixError // Empty for no rows or empty rows; Ragged for uneven rows fn shape(&self) - (usize, usize) fn transpose(&self) - Matrix fn try_mul(&self, other: &Matrix) - Result<Matrix, MatrixError // Shape error when cols != other.rows fn determinant(&self) - Result<f64, MatrixError // NotSquare for non-square matrices } and these trait implementations: Trait Behaviour --- --- Index<(usize, usize) , IndexMut<(usize, usize) m (r, c) reads and writes an element (panics outside the matrix) Add<&Matrix for &Matrix , Sub<&Matrix for &Matrix Element-wise; panic with a message containing shape when the shapes differ Mul<f64 for &Matrix Multiplies every element Mul<&Matrix for &Matrix Matrix product; panics on a shape mismatch (use try_mul to get an error instead) Display Each row on its own line, elements separated by a space, with 2 decimals: 1.00 2.00\n3.00 4.00 (no newline at the end) FromStr Rows separated by ; , numbers by white space: "1 2; 3 4" ; parse errors become MatrixError::Parse(<the bad text ) , and an uneven shape Ragged The determinant can use cofactor expansion for small matrices or Gaussian elimination; the tests use matrices up to 4 × 4. Results only need to be correct to 1e-9.

title: 5.01  Closures
body: Anonymous functions that capture their environment - closure syntax and type inference, capturing by reference, by mutable reference and by value with move, the Fn, FnMut and FnOnce traits, passing closures to functions with generics or impl Fn, returning closures, storing them in structs and boxing them as dyn Fn. Closure syntax A closure is an anonymous function that can use variables from the scope where it is created: rust fn main() { let add_one = x: i32 x + 1; // types can be written... let double = x x 2; // ...or inferred from the first use let greet = name: &str - String { format!("Hello, {name}!") }; println!("{} {} {}", add_one(5), double(21), greet("Ada")); let threshold = 10; let is_big = n: i32 n threshold; // captures threshold let values = vec! 4, 12, 9, 30 ; let big: Vec<i32 = values.iter().copied().filter( &n is_big(n)).collect(); println!("{big:?}"); } Unlike fn items, closures can capture the variables around them. They are used everywhere iterators, sorting, threads and callbacks take "a bit of code". How closures capture The compiler picks the least powerful way that works: 1. By shared reference if the closure only reads a variable. 2. By mutable reference if it changes it. 3. By value (moving it in) if it consumes it, or if you write move . rust fn main() { let name = String::from("Ada"); let print = println!("{name}"); // borrows name print(); print(); println!("still usable: {name}"); let mut count = 0; let mut tick = count += 1; // borrows count mutably tick(); tick(); println!("count = {count}"); // the mutable borrow ended after the last tick let words = vec! "a".to_string(), "b".to_string() ; let consume = move words.len(); // move: the closure owns words now println!("{}", consume()); // println!("{words:?}"); // error: words was moved into the closure } move is needed when the closure must outlive the current scope, for example when it is returned from a function or sent to another thread. Fn, FnMut and FnOnce Every closure implements one or more of these traits, depending on what it does with its captures: Trait The closure Can be called --- --- --- Fn Only reads its captures Any number of times, even at the same time FnMut Changes its captures Many times, one at a time (needs mut ) FnOnce Moves something out of its captures Once Functions that take closures choose the least demanding bound they can accept: rust fn apply_twice<F: Fn(i32) - i32 (f: F, x: i32) - i32 { f(f(x)) } fn repeat<F: FnMut() (times: usize, mut f: F) { for _ in 0..times { f(); } } fn finish<F: FnOnce() - String (f: F) - String { f() } fn main() { println!("{}", apply_twice( x x 3, 2)); let mut log = Vec::new(); repeat(3, log.push("tick")); println!("{log:?}"); let name = String::from("done"); println!("{}", finish(move name)); // gives away name: FnOnce } Plain functions work too wherever a closure is expected: apply_twice(i32::abs, -4) . Returning and storing closures Each closure has its own unique, unnamed type. Return one with impl Fn , or box it as a trait object when several different closures must share one type: rust fn multiplier(k: i32) - impl Fn(i32) - i32 { move x x k // move: k must live inside the closure } struct Button { label: String, on_click: Box<dyn Fn(&str) - String , } fn main() { let triple = multiplier(3); println!("{}", triple(14)); let buttons = vec! Button { label: "save".into(), on_click: Box::new( l: &str format!("saving via {l}")) }, Button { label: "quit".into(), on_click: Box::new(move l: &str format!("{l} after {}", triple(1))) }, ; for b in &buttons { println!("{}", (b.on_click)(&b.label)); } let mut ops: Vec<(&str, Box<dyn Fn(f64) - f64 ) = Vec::new(); ops.push(("square", Box::new( x: f64 x x))); ops.push(("half", Box::new( x: f64 x / 2.0))); for (name, op) in &ops { println!("{name}(6) = {}", op(6.0)); } } Call a closure stored in a field with parentheses around the field: (b.on_click)(...) . Check yourself quiz ? What does writing move in front of a closure change? - The closure can then be called only once + It captures the variables it uses by value, taking ownership of them - It lets the closure change the variables it captures - It turns the closure into a plain fn item move changes how variables are captured (by value instead of by reference). It does not make a closure FnOnce : a move closure that only reads its captures is still Fn . ? A function calls the closure it receives many times, and the closure may change its captures. Which bound should it use? - Fn - FnOnce + FnMut - Box<dyn Fn FnMut allows changing captures and calling many times (one at a time). Fn would reject closures that change state, and FnOnce allows only one call. ? A closure moves a captured String out (returns it). Which traits does it implement? - Fn, FnMut and FnOnce - Fn only - FnMut only + FnOnce only Giving away a captured value can only happen once, so the closure is only FnOnce .

title: Closures that capture
body: Write functions that take and return closures: rust fn make_counter(start: u32, step: u32) - impl FnMut() - u32 // each call returns the next value fn compose<A, B, C (f: impl Fn(A) - B, g: impl Fn(B) - C) - impl Fn(A) - C // f first, then g fn apply_n(f: impl Fn(i64) - i64, n: usize, x: i64) - i64 // f applied n times fn memoize(f: impl Fn(u64) - u64) - impl FnMut(u64) - u64 // calls f once per distinct argument fn retry<T, E (attempts: usize, mut action: impl FnMut() - Result<T, E ) - Result<T, E // first Ok, or the last Err retry calls action up to attempts times (at least once, even if attempts is 0) and stops at the first Ok .

title: 5.02  Iterators and Adapters
body: The Iterator trait and next, iter, iter_mut and into_iter, laziness, the common adapters (map, filter, filter_map, enumerate, zip, chain, take, skip, rev, flat_map, peekable, windows), consumers (collect, sum, count, fold, any, all, find, position, min_by_key, max_by), collecting into different types including Result, and why iterator chains are as fast as loops. The Iterator trait An iterator produces a sequence of values, one per call to next , until it returns None : rust-norun trait Iterator { type Item; fn next(&mut self) - Option<Self::Item ; // ...and dozens of provided methods built on next } rust fn main() { let v = vec! 10, 20, 30 ; let mut it = v.iter(); println!("{:?} {:?} {:?} {:?}", it.next(), it.next(), it.next(), it.next()); } A for loop calls next for you. Collections give three kinds of iterator: Method Items The collection --- --- --- iter() &T Borrowed iter_mut() &mut T Borrowed mutably into_iter() T Consumed Adapters are lazy Adapters turn one iterator into another. They do nothing until a consumer pulls values through: rust fn main() { let words = "apple", "Banana", "cherry", "date", "Elderberry" ; let result: Vec<String = words.iter() .filter( w w.len() 4) // keep some .map( w w.to_lowercase()) // transform .enumerate() // add indexes .map( (i, w) format!("{i}:{w}")) .collect(); // the consumer: runs the chain println!("{result:?}"); let lazy = (1..).map( n n n).filter( n n % 3 == 1); // an infinite range: fine, nothing runs yet println!("{:?}", lazy.take(5).collect::<Vec<_ ()); } Adapter Does --- --- map(f) , filter(p) , filter_map(f) Transform; keep some; transform and keep the Some s enumerate() , zip(other) , chain(other) Add indexes; pair up; concatenate take(n) , skip(n) , take_while(p) , skip_while(p) , step_by(n) Cut rev() Backwards (for double-ended iterators) flat_map(f) , flatten() One item becomes many peekable() Look at the next item without taking it copied() , cloned() &T to T inspect(f) Look at items as they pass (debugging) Consumers rust fn main() { let scores = 72, 95, 88, 61, 79 ; let total: i32 = scores.iter().sum(); let count = scores.iter().filter( &&s s = 75).count(); let max = scores.iter().max(); let best_index = scores.iter().enumerate().max_by_key( (_, s) s).map( (i, _) i); let all_pass = scores.iter().all( &s s = 60); let any_perfect = scores.iter().any( &s s == 100); let first_low = scores.iter().find( &&s s < 70); let product = scores.iter().take(2).fold(1i64, acc, &s acc s as i64); println!("{total} {count} {max:?} {best_index:?} {all_pass} {any_perfect} {first_low:?} {product}"); let names = "Ada", "Grace", "Linus" ; let ages = 36, 85, 55 ; let pairs: Vec<(&str, i32) = names.iter().copied().zip(ages).collect(); let by_name: std::collections::HashMap<_, _ = pairs.iter().cloned().collect(); println!("{pairs:?} {}", by_name "Linus" ); let joined = names.iter().map( n n.to_uppercase()).collect::<Vec<_ ().join("+"); println!("{joined}"); } Collecting results collect can build any collection that implements FromIterator : Vec , String , HashMap , HashSet , BTreeMap ... Pick the target with a type annotation or the turbofish collect::<Vec<_ () . It can even collect an iterator of Result s into a Result of a collection, stopping at the first error: rust fn main() { let good: Result<Vec<i32 , _ = "1", "2", "3" .iter().map( s s.parse::<i32 ()).collect(); let bad: Result<Vec<i32 , _ = "1", "x", "3" .iter().map( s s.parse::<i32 ()).collect(); println!("{good:?}"); println!("{}", bad.is_err()); let words: String = vec! "a", "b", "c" .into_iter().rev().collect(); println!("{words}"); } Zero-cost Iterator chains compile to the same machine code as hand-written loops (often better, since bounds checks disappear). Prefer them when they read clearly: scores.iter().filter(...).map(...).sum() says what it computes. Use a for loop when the logic has complex early exits or side effects. Check yourself quiz ? Why does (1..).map( n n n).filter( n n % 3 == 1) not run forever? - The range stops by itself once the numbers would overflow + Adapters are lazy: nothing is computed until a consumer asks for values - The compiler turns the infinite range into a finite one - map only computes the first few values in advance Building the chain does no work. Only a consumer such as take(5).collect() pulls values through, and it stops asking after five. ? What does collecting an iterator of Result<T, E into Result<Vec<T , E do? - Gives a Vec holding every Ok and Err in order - Gives Ok with only the successful values, skipping the errors + Gives Ok with all the values, or the first Err , stopping there - Gives the last Err found, after checking every item The errors are not skipped: one Err makes the whole result that Err , and collecting stops at it. ? What is (1..=4).map( x x 10).filter( x x % 20 == 0).sum::<i32 () ? - 100 - 40 - 20 + 60 10, 20, 30, 40 → keep 20 and 40 → 60.

title: Iterator chains
body: Answer each question with one iterator chain (no for or while loops): rust struct Sale { product: String, region: String, cents: u64, qty: u32 } fn revenue_by_region(sales: & Sale ) - BTreeMap<String, u64 // cents qty summed per region fn top_products(sales: & Sale , n: usize) - Vec<String // by total quantity, ties by name fn average_unit_price(sales: & Sale ) - Option<f64 // mean of cents over all sales (not weighted) fn parse_all(texts: & &str ) - Result<Vec<i32 , ParseIntError // every text trimmed and parsed; the first error wins fn running_max(values: & i32 ) - Vec<i32 // 3, 1, 4, 1, 5 gives 3, 3, 4, 4, 5 The tests need use std::collections::{BTreeMap, HashMap}; and use std::num::ParseIntError; at the top of your file.

title: 5.03  Implementing Iterator
body: Writing your own iterators - a struct with state and a next method, getting every adapter for free, infinite iterators, iterators that borrow from a collection, IntoIterator so your type works in for loops, std::iter helpers (from_fn, successors, repeat, once), and extension traits that add your own adapters. A struct with next Implement Iterator by choosing the Item type and writing next . Everything else ( map , filter , sum ...) comes for free: rust struct Countdown { current: u32, } impl Iterator for Countdown { type Item = u32; fn next(&mut self) - Option<u32 { if self.current == 0 { return None; } self.current -= 1; Some(self.current + 1) } } fn main() { let launch: Vec<u32 = Countdown { current: 5 }.collect(); println!("{launch:?}"); let even_sum: u32 = Countdown { current: 10 }.filter( n n % 2 == 0).sum(); println!("{even_sum}"); for n in (Countdown { current: 3 }).map( n n 100) { print!("{n} "); } println!(); } Infinite iterators An iterator may never return None ; the consumer decides when to stop: rust struct Fibonacci { a: u64, b: u64, } impl Iterator for Fibonacci { type Item = u64; fn next(&mut self) - Option<u64 { let value = self.a; let next = self.a.checked_add(self.b)?; // stop instead of overflowing self.a = self.b; self.b = next; Some(value) } } fn fibonacci() - Fibonacci { Fibonacci { a: 0, b: 1 } } fn main() { println!("{:?}", fibonacci().take(10).collect::<Vec<_ ()); println!("{:?}", fibonacci().find( &f f 1000)); println!("{}", fibonacci().count()); // stops when the next value would overflow u64 } Iterators that borrow An iterator over part of your data borrows it, so it needs a lifetime: rust struct Words<'a { rest: &'a str, } impl<'a Iterator for Words<'a { type Item = &'a str; fn next(&mut self) - Option<&'a str { let trimmed = self.rest.trim_start(); if trimmed.is_empty() { return None; } let end = trimmed.find(char::is_whitespace).unwrap_or(trimmed.len()); let (word, rest) = trimmed.split_at(end); self.rest = rest; Some(word) } } fn main() { let text = String::from(" the quick brown fox "); let longest = Words { rest: &text }.max_by_key( w w.len()); println!("{longest:?} {}", Words { rest: &text }.count()); } IntoIterator: making for loops work for x in thing calls IntoIterator::into_iter(thing) . Implement it (usually for &YourType ) so your collection works in for loops: rust struct Playlist { songs: Vec<String , } impl<'a IntoIterator for &'a Playlist { type Item = &'a String; type IntoIter = std::slice::Iter<'a, String ; fn into_iter(self) - Self::IntoIter { self.songs.iter() } } fn main() { let p = Playlist { songs: vec! "Intro".into(), "Theme".into(), "Outro".into() }; for song in &p { print!("{song} "); } println!(); } Small helpers in std::iter Many custom iterators need no struct at all: rust use std::iter; fn main() { let mut n = 0; let squares = iter::from_fn( { n += 1; if n <= 5 { Some(n n) } else { None } }); println!("{:?}", squares.collect::<Vec<_ ()); let powers: Vec<u32 = iter::successors(Some(1u32), &x x.checked_mul(10)).collect(); println!("{powers:?}"); let line: String = iter::repeat('-').take(10).chain(iter::once(' ')).collect(); println!("{line}"); } Your own adapters An extension trait adds methods to every iterator, just like the built-in ones: rust trait EveryOther: Iterator + Sized { fn every_other(self) - std::iter::StepBy<Self { self.step_by(2) } } impl<I: Iterator EveryOther for I {} fn main() { println!("{:?}", (1..=9).every_other().collect::<Vec<_ ()); } Check yourself quiz ? What must you write to implement Iterator for your own type? - The methods next , map , filter and collect - Only next ; the item type is always inferred + The associated type Item and the method next - next , plus an IntoIterator implementation You choose type Item and write next ; every other iterator method ( map , filter , sum ...) is provided for free. ? Why does Words<'a need a lifetime parameter? + Its items borrow from the original text, which must outlive them - Every struct that implements Iterator needs one - The iterator copies its words onto the heap - Without it, next could only be called once Words holds a &str and hands out &'a str slices of it, so the compiler must know how long that text lives. Countdown has no references and needs no lifetime. ? How many items does Countdown { current: 3 } produce? - 4 + 3 - 2 - infinitely many It yields 3, 2 and 1, then returns None.

title: Your own iterators
body: Implement Iterator for three types, and a function returning an iterator: rust struct Collatz { next: Option<u64 } // Collatz::new(6) yields 6, 3, 10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 struct Primes { found: Vec<u64 , candidate: u64 } // Primes::new() yields 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, ... forever struct Chunks<'a, T { data: &'a T , size: usize } // slices of size items; the last one may be shorter fn digits(n: u64) - impl Iterator<Item = u32 // most significant digit first: 905 gives 9, 0, 5 Chunks::new panics for a size of 0. Since Primes is infinite, tests use take ; Primes must test candidates only against the primes found so far, up to their square root.

title: 5.04  Box, Rc and RefCell
body: Smart pointers - Box for heap allocation and recursive types, Deref and Drop, Rc for shared ownership with reference counting, RefCell for interior mutability checked at run time, Rc<RefCell<T for shared mutable data, Weak references to break cycles, and when each is the right tool. Box Box<T stores a value on the heap and owns it. It has the size of a pointer, which makes recursive types possible (a type that contains itself would otherwise be infinitely large): rust derive(Debug) enum List { Cons(i32, Box<List ), Nil, } use List::{Cons, Nil}; fn sum(list: &List) - i32 { match list { Cons(value, rest) = value + sum(rest), Nil = 0, } } fn main() { let list = Cons(1, Box::new(Cons(2, Box::new(Cons(3, Box::new(Nil)))))); println!("{list:?} sum={}", sum(&list)); let big = Box::new( 0u8; 1000 ); // a large value on the heap instead of the stack println!("{}", big.len()); } Box implements Deref , so a Box<T can be used like a &T ( b , method calls, &Box<T coercing to &T ). When the box goes out of scope it is dropped : the Drop trait runs clean-up code, and you can implement it yourself: rust struct Noisy(&'static str); impl Drop for Noisy { fn drop(&mut self) { println!("dropping {}", self.0); } } fn main() { let _a = Noisy("a"); { let _b = Box::new(Noisy("b")); println!("inner scope ends"); } let c = Noisy("c"); drop(c); // drop early println!("main ends"); } Rc: shared ownership Sometimes one value genuinely has several owners: a node shared by two lists, a texture used by many sprites. Rc<T (reference counted) keeps a count of owners and frees the value when the last one goes away: rust use std::rc::Rc; derive(Debug) struct Texture { name: String } struct Sprite { texture: Rc<Texture , x: i32 } fn main() { let grass = Rc::new(Texture { name: "grass.png".into() }); let sprites = vec! Sprite { texture: Rc::clone(&grass), x: 0 }, Sprite { texture: Rc::clone(&grass), x: 16 }, ; println!("owners: {}", Rc::strong_count(&grass)); // 3: grass and two sprites for s in &sprites { println!("{} at {}", s.texture.name, s.x); } drop(sprites); println!("owners: {}", Rc::strong_count(&grass)); // 1 } Rc::clone copies the pointer and increments the count; it does not copy the texture. Rc gives shared, read-only access and works within one thread ( Arc is the thread-safe version, lesson 6.02). RefCell: interior mutability The borrow rules are normally checked at compile time. RefCell<T moves the check to run time : borrow() gives a shared borrow, borrow_mut() a mutable one, and breaking the rules panics instead of failing to compile. This allows changing data through a shared reference when the compiler cannot prove it is safe but you can: rust use std::cell::RefCell; use std::rc::Rc; derive(Debug) struct Account { balance: i64 } fn main() { let shared = Rc::new(RefCell::new(Account { balance: 100 })); let alias = Rc::clone(&shared); alias.borrow_mut().balance -= 30; // change through one owner shared.borrow_mut().balance += 5; // and through the other println!("{}", shared.borrow().balance); let log = RefCell::new(Vec::new()); let record = msg: &str log.borrow_mut().push(msg.to_string()); // a Fn closure that still mutates record("start"); record("stop"); println!("{:?}", log.borrow()); } Rc<RefCell<T is the classic combination for shared, mutable data in single-threaded code (graphs, observers, GUI state). Use it sparingly: it trades compile-time guarantees for run-time checks. Weak: breaking cycles Two Rc s pointing at each other never reach a count of zero: a memory leak. Weak<T is a non-owning reference that does not keep the value alive; upgrade() returns Some(Rc) only if it still exists. Trees use Rc from parent to child and Weak from child to parent: rust use std::cell::RefCell; use std::rc::{Rc, Weak}; struct Node { name: String, parent: RefCell<Weak<Node , children: RefCell<Vec<Rc<Node , } fn main() { let root = Rc::new(Node { name: "root".into(), parent: RefCell::new(Weak::new()), children: RefCell::new(vec! ) }); let leaf = Rc::new(Node { name: "leaf".into(), parent: RefCell::new(Weak::new()), children: RefCell::new(vec! ) }); leaf.parent.borrow_mut() = Rc::downgrade(&root); root.children.borrow_mut().push(Rc::clone(&leaf)); let parent_name = leaf.parent.borrow().upgrade().map( p p.name.clone()); println!("{:?} children={} strong={} weak={}", parent_name, root.children.borrow().len(), Rc::strong_count(&root), Rc::weak_count(&root)); } Choosing Need Use --- --- One owner, value on the heap, recursive type, trait object Box<T Several owners, read-only, one thread Rc<T Several owners, threads Arc<T Change data behind & in one thread RefCell<T (or Cell<T for Copy values) Shared mutable data, one thread Rc<RefCell<T Shared mutable data, threads Arc<Mutex<T A back-reference that must not keep things alive Weak<T Check yourself quiz ? Why does a recursive enum like List need a Box ? - A Box makes the list faster to walk through + Without a pointer the type would contain itself and have infinite size - A Box lets several lists share the same tail - Enums may only hold heap values in their variants A Box has the fixed size of a pointer, so Cons(i32, Box<List ) has a known size. Sharing a tail between owners is what Rc is for. ? What happens if you call borrow_mut() on a RefCell that is already borrowed? - The program fails to compile - It waits until the other borrow ends - It returns a copy of the value instead + It panics at run time RefCell checks the borrowing rules while the program runs, so breaking them is a panic, not a compile error. ? What does Rc::clone(&a) copy? + Only the pointer, incrementing the reference count - The whole value inside the Rc - Nothing: it moves a - The value, then wraps it in a new Rc Rc::clone is cheap: it shares the same allocation.

title: A tree with Rc, Weak and RefCell
match: A tree with Rc, Weak and RefCell
body: Build a tree of named nodes where children are owned with Rc and each node keeps a Weak reference to its parent: rust struct Node { name: String, parent: RefCell<Weak<Node , children: RefCell<Vec<Rc<Node , } fn node(name: &str) - Rc<Node fn add_child(parent: &Rc<Node , child: &Rc<Node ) // also sets the child's parent fn path(node: &Rc<Node ) - String // "root/docs/notes.txt" fn depth(node: &Rc<Node ) - usize // 0 for a node without a parent fn count(node: &Rc<Node ) - usize // the node and everything below it fn find(node: &Rc<Node , name: &str) - Option<Rc<Node // depth-first, children in insertion order fn detach(child: &Rc<Node ) // removes it from its parent's children Because parents are Weak , dropping the root frees the whole tree; a child that is detached gets no parent.

title: 5.05  Pattern Matching in Depth
body: Everywhere patterns appear (let, match, if let, while let, let else, function parameters, for loops), destructuring structs, enums, tuples, references and nested data, slice patterns, ranges, bindings with @, guards, ignoring with _ and .., refutable versus irrefutable patterns, and matches!. Patterns everywhere Patterns are not just for match . They appear wherever a value is bound to names: rust struct Point { x: i32, y: i32 } fn print_coords(&(x, y): &(i32, i32)) { // a pattern in a parameter println!("({x}, {y})"); } fn main() { let (a, b, c) = (1, "two", 3.0); // a tuple pattern in let let Point { x, y: height } = Point { x: 5, y: 9 }; // a struct pattern, renaming y println!("{a} {b} {c} {x} {height}"); print_coords(&(3, 4)); for (i, ch) in "abc".chars().enumerate() { // in a for loop print!("{i}{ch} "); } println!(); let mut stack = vec! 1, 2, 3 ; while let Some(top) = stack.pop() { // while let: loop while the pattern matches print!("{top} "); } println!(); } Destructuring nested data rust derive(Debug) enum Shape { Circle { r: f64 }, Rect { w: f64, h: f64 } } derive(Debug) enum Event { Click { x: i32, y: i32 }, Key(char), Draw(Shape, (u8, u8, u8)), Quit, } fn describe(e: &Event) - String { match e { Event::Click { x: 0, y: 0 } = "click at the origin".into(), Event::Click { x, y } if x == y = format!("click on the diagonal at {x}"), Event::Click { x, .. } = format!("click with x = {x}"), Event::Key(c @ ('a'..='z' 'A'..='Z')) = format!("letter {c}"), Event::Key(c) = format!("other key {c:?}"), Event::Draw(Shape::Circle { r }, (255, _, _)) = format!("a red-ish circle of radius {r}"), Event::Draw(Shape::Rect { w, h }, color) = format!("a {w}x{h} rectangle in {color:?}"), Event::Draw(shape, _) = format!("some other {shape:?}"), Event::Quit = "quit".into(), } } fn main() { let events = Event::Click { x: 0, y: 0 }, Event::Click { x: 4, y: 4 }, Event::Click { x: 7, y: 1 }, Event::Key('q'), Event::Key('7'), Event::Draw(Shape::Circle { r: 2.0 }, (255, 10, 10)), Event::Draw(Shape::Rect { w: 3.0, h: 1.0 }, (0, 0, 255)), Event::Draw(Shape::Circle { r: 1.0 }, (0, 0, 0)), Event::Quit, ; for e in &events { println!("{}", describe(e)); } } Pattern Matches --- --- 0 , 'a' , "text" (on &str ), true A literal x Anything, binding it to x _ Anything, without binding .. The remaining fields or items 1..=9 , 'a'..='z' An inclusive range A \ B Either pattern name @ pattern Matches the pattern and binds the whole value Some(x) , Point { x, .. } , (a, b) Destructuring &x Dereferences a reference pattern if condition A guard (only in match ) Slice patterns rust fn summary(values: & i32 ) - String { match values { = "empty".into(), one = format!("one: {one}"), first, second = format!("two: {first}, {second}"), first, .., last if first == last = format!("starts and ends with {first}"), first, middle @ .., last = format!("{first} .. {} middle .. {last}", middle.len()), } } fn main() { for v in & .. , & 7 .. , & 1, 2 .. , & 5, 0, 0, 5 .. , & 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 .. { println!("{}", summary(v)); } } Refutable and irrefutable A pattern that can fail to match ( Some(x) ) is refutable ; one that always matches ( (a, b) for a pair) is irrefutable . let and function parameters need irrefutable patterns; if let , while let , match arms and let ... else accept refutable ones: rust fn parse_point(s: &str) - Option<(i32, i32) { let Some((a, b)) = s.split_once(',') else { return None }; // refutable: needs else let (Ok(x), Ok(y)) = (a.trim().parse(), b.trim().parse()) else { return None }; Some((x, y)) } fn main() { println!("{:?} {:?} {:?}", parse_point("3, 4"), parse_point("3;4"), parse_point("a,1")); let ok = matches!(parse_point("1,2"), Some((x, _)) if x 0); // matches!: a pattern test as a bool println!("{ok}"); } Check yourself quiz ? What does c @ 'a'..='z' do in a match arm? - Matches only the characters 'a' and 'z' - Binds c to a list of the letters 'a' to 'z' + Matches a char in that range and binds the matched value to c - Binds c to true or false depending on the range test name @ pattern tests the pattern and, if it matches, binds the whole matched value to the name. ? Why can't you write let Some(x) = maybe_value; without else ? + Some(x) is refutable: let needs a pattern that always matches, or an else - It compiles, but panics when the value is None - let cannot destructure enums at all - Some(x) needs a guard before it can appear in a let A refutable pattern can fail to match, so plain let rejects it at compile time. let ... else says what to do when it does not match. ? Which pattern matches a slice with at least two items and binds the first and last? - first, last - (first, .., last) + first, .., last - first, _, last .. in a slice pattern matches any number of items in the middle, including none.

title: 6.01  Threads and Message Passing
body: Fearless concurrency - spawning threads and joining them, move closures that give a thread its data, scoped threads that can borrow, channels with mpsc for sending messages between threads, multiple producers, worker pools fed by a channel, and how Send and Sync let the compiler rule out data races. Spawning threads std::thread::spawn runs a closure on a new operating-system thread. join waits for it and returns its result: rust use std::thread; use std::time::Duration; fn main() { let handle = thread::spawn( { for i in 1..=3 { println!("worker {i}"); thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(5)); } 42 }); println!("main keeps going"); let answer = handle.join().unwrap(); // wait; Err if the thread panicked println!("worker returned {answer}"); } The order of output from different threads is not fixed: run it twice and it may differ. Giving a thread its data A spawned thread may outlive the function that started it, so it cannot borrow local variables. Use a move closure to give it ownership: rust use std::thread; fn main() { let words = vec! "alpha".to_string(), "beta".to_string(), "gamma".to_string() ; let handle = thread::spawn(move { words.iter().map( w w.len()).sum::<usize () // the thread owns words now }); // println!("{words:?}"); // error: words was moved into the thread println!("{}", handle.join().unwrap()); } Without move , the compiler refuses: "closure may outlive the current function, but it borrows words ". This is the first of several ways Rust stops threading bugs at compile time. Scoped threads thread::scope guarantees that every thread started inside it finishes before the scope ends, so those threads may borrow local data: rust use std::thread; fn main() { let data: Vec<u64 = (1..=1_000_000).collect(); let chunk = data.len() / 4; let total: u64 = thread::scope( s { let handles: Vec<_ = data.chunks(chunk) .map( part s.spawn(move part.iter().sum::<u64 ())) // borrows a slice of data .collect(); handles.into_iter().map( h h.join().unwrap()).sum() }); println!("{total} {}", total == 1_000_000 1_000_001 / 2); } This is the simplest way to split work across cores: each thread computes its own part, and the results are combined at the end, with no shared mutable state. Channels A channel sends values from one thread to another. mpsc stands for multiple producer, single consumer : rust use std::sync::mpsc; use std::thread; fn main() { let (tx, rx) = mpsc::channel(); for id in 0..3 { let tx = tx.clone(); // each producer gets its own sender thread::spawn(move { for n in 0..2 { tx.send(format!("worker {id} item {n}")).unwrap(); } }); } drop(tx); // close the original sender let mut received: Vec<String = rx.iter().collect(); // ends when every sender is gone received.sort(); println!("{} messages, first: {}", received.len(), received 0 ); } send moves the value into the channel: once sent, the sending thread cannot use it any more, so two threads can never touch the same data. Receiving with rx.recv() blocks until a value arrives (or returns Err when all senders are dropped); iterating over rx does that in a loop. A worker pool A common shape: one channel of jobs feeding several workers, and another channel collecting results: rust use std::sync::{mpsc, Arc, Mutex}; use std::thread; fn main() { let (job_tx, job_rx) = mpsc::channel::<u64 (); let (result_tx, result_rx) = mpsc::channel::<(u64, bool) (); let job_rx = Arc::new(Mutex::new(job_rx)); // several workers share one receiver (lesson 6.02) let workers: Vec<_ = (0..3).map( _ { let jobs = Arc::clone(&job_rx); let results = result_tx.clone(); thread::spawn(move loop { let job = jobs.lock().unwrap().recv(); match job { Ok(n) = results.send((n, (2..n).take_while( d d d <= n).all( d n % d != 0))).unwrap(), Err(_) = break, // the job channel is closed: stop } }) }).collect(); drop(result_tx); for n in 97, 98, 7919, 7920, 104_729 { job_tx.send(n).unwrap(); } drop(job_tx); // no more jobs let mut results: Vec<_ = result_rx.iter().collect(); results.sort(); for w in workers { w.join().unwrap(); } println!("{results:?}"); } Send and Sync Two marker traits make this safe: - Send : a value can be moved to another thread. Almost everything is Send ; Rc is not (its counter is not thread-safe), so thread::spawn(move rc.clone()) does not compile. - Sync : a value can be shared between threads by reference. RefCell is not Sync . The compiler checks these automatically. Code that could cause a data race (two threads accessing the same memory, at least one writing, without synchronisation) does not compile. That is what Rust calls fearless concurrency . Check yourself quiz ? Why does thread::spawn usually need a move closure? - Without move the thread cannot return a value + The thread may outlive the function, so it must own its data instead of borrowing it - move is what makes the closure run on the new thread - Owned data makes the thread run faster than borrowed data A spawned thread can keep running after the function that started it returns, so borrowing its locals is refused. thread::scope is the way to let threads borrow. ? When does a for loop over an mpsc receiver end? - As soon as the channel is momentarily empty - After one message per spawned thread has arrived - When the main thread calls join on the receiver + When every sender has been dropped and the channel is empty An empty channel only makes the receiver wait. The loop ends once no sender is left, which is why the example drops the original tx . ? Why can't an Rc<T be sent to another thread? - Rc is too large to move between threads - Only primitive types can be sent to threads + Its count is not updated atomically, so it is not Send - It can be sent, once you clone it first Two threads changing the count at once could corrupt it. Arc is the thread-safe version with an atomic count.

title: 6.02  Shared State with Arc and Mutex
match: 6.02 Shared State with Arc and Mutex
body: Sharing data between threads safely - Arc for shared ownership across threads, Mutex for exclusive access with lock guards, RwLock for many readers, atomics for counters and flags, avoiding deadlocks and holding locks briefly, poisoning, and choosing between message passing and shared state. Arc: shared ownership across threads Rc is single-threaded. Arc<T (atomically reference counted) is the thread-safe version: cloning it gives another owner, and the value is freed when the last owner is gone. On its own, Arc gives read-only sharing: rust use std::sync::Arc; use std::thread; fn main() { let config = Arc::new(vec! "fast".to_string(), "safe".to_string() ); let handles: Vec<_ = (0..3).map( i { let config = Arc::clone(&config); thread::spawn(move format!("thread {i} sees {}", config.join("+"))) }).collect(); for h in handles { println!("{}", h.join().unwrap()); } println!("owners now: {}", Arc::strong_count(&config)); } Mutex: one writer at a time To change shared data, wrap it in a Mutex (mutual exclusion). lock() waits until no other thread holds the lock and returns a guard that gives access; the lock is released when the guard is dropped: rust use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex}; use std::thread; fn main() { let counter = Arc::new(Mutex::new(0u64)); let mut handles = Vec::new(); for _ in 0..8 { let counter = Arc::clone(&counter); handles.push(thread::spawn(move { for _ in 0..1000 { counter.lock().unwrap() += 1; // lock, change, guard dropped at the end of the statement } })); } for h in handles { h.join().unwrap(); } println!("{}", counter.lock().unwrap()); // always 8000 } Arc<Mutex<T is the thread-safe counterpart of Rc<RefCell<T . The data lives inside the mutex, so it is impossible to touch it without locking: forgetting the lock, the classic C bug, cannot be written. If a thread panics while holding a lock, the mutex becomes poisoned and later lock() calls return Err . unwrap() then propagates the panic, which is usually right; into_inner() on the error recovers the data if you know it is still valid. RwLock and atomics Tool Use when --- --- Mutex<T Any shared data that changes RwLock<T Data that is read often and written rarely: many read() guards at once, or one write() AtomicUsize , AtomicBool , AtomicU64 ... A single number or flag: no lock at all OnceLock<T / LazyLock<T A value initialised once and then shared read-only rust use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicBool, AtomicUsize, Ordering}; use std::sync::{Arc, RwLock}; use std::thread; fn main() { let hits = Arc::new(AtomicUsize::new(0)); let stop = Arc::new(AtomicBool::new(false)); let settings = Arc::new(RwLock::new(String::from("v1"))); thread::scope( s { for _ in 0..4 { let (hits, settings) = (Arc::clone(&hits), Arc::clone(&settings)); s.spawn(move { for _ in 0..250 { let _version = settings.read().unwrap(); // many readers at once hits.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed); } }); } s.spawn( { settings.write().unwrap() = String::from("v2"); // one writer stop.store(true, Ordering::Release); }); }); println!("{} {} {}", hits.load(Ordering::Relaxed), stop.load(Ordering::Acquire), settings.read().unwrap()); } For simple counters, Ordering::Relaxed is enough; flags that publish other data use Release when storing and Acquire when loading. When unsure, SeqCst is the strongest and simplest. Deadlocks and lock hygiene The compiler prevents data races, but not deadlocks : thread A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2 while thread B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1. Avoid them by: - holding locks briefly: copy what you need out of the guard, drop it, then do the slow work; - always taking several locks in the same order; - never calling unknown code (callbacks) while holding a lock. rust-norun let snapshot = { data.lock().unwrap().clone() }; // the guard is dropped at the end of the block expensive_report(&snapshot); // the lock is free while this runs Message passing or shared state? Both are safe in Rust. Prefer message passing (channels) or splitting the work (scoped threads, each with its own data) when it fits naturally: there is nothing to lock. Use shared state for data many threads read and update, such as a cache or a counter. Libraries like rayon ( data.par_iter().map(...).sum() ) parallelise iterator chains with almost no code. Check yourself quiz ? Why does a Rust Mutex hold the data inside it rather than sit next to it? - So the data is copied for each thread that locks it + So the only way to reach the data is through lock() - So reading the data needs no lock at all - So the data is freed when a thread panics With the data inside, forgetting to lock is impossible to write: the guard from lock() is the only way in. ? What is the thread-safe counterpart of Rc<RefCell<T ? - Rc<Mutex<T - Arc<RefCell<T + Arc<Mutex<T - Box<RefCell<T Arc replaces Rc for shared ownership across threads and Mutex (or RwLock ) replaces RefCell for changing the data. Rc is not Send and RefCell is not Sync . ? When is a Mutex's lock released? + When the guard returned by lock() is dropped - When the thread ends - When unlock() is called - Never: you must call drop on the Mutex The guard releases the lock in its Drop implementation, typically at the end of the statement or block.

title: 6.03  Async Rust
body: An overview of asynchronous Rust - why async exists, futures and async fn, .await, why a runtime such as Tokio is needed, spawning tasks, running futures concurrently with join and select, async I/O, channels and timeouts, Send and 'static bounds on tasks, and choosing between threads and async. Why async Threads are a fine way to do several things at once, but each one costs memory and switching between thousands of them is expensive. A web server waiting on ten thousand slow network connections spends almost all its time waiting . Async code lets one thread juggle many waiting tasks: when a task would block, it yields, and the thread runs another task that is ready. Futures and .await An async fn does not run when called. It returns a future : a value that represents work which can be driven to completion later. .await drives a future, pausing the current async function until the result is ready: rust-norun async fn fetch_price(item: &str) - u32 { // imagine a network request here tokio::time::sleep(std::time::Duration::from_millis(100)).await; if item == "tea" { 250 } else { 400 } } async fn total(items: & &str ) - u32 { let mut sum = 0; for item in items { sum += fetch_price(item).await; // one after another } sum } Futures are lazy : if nobody awaits (or spawns) them, nothing happens. The compiler warns about unused futures. A runtime The standard library defines futures but does not include the machinery that runs them. A runtime does: it polls futures, parks them while they wait for I/O or timers, and wakes them up. Tokio is the most used one: toml dependencies tokio = { version = "1", features = "full" } rust-norun tokio::main async fn main() { let a = fetch_price("tea"); let b = fetch_price("cake"); let (pa, pb) = tokio::join!(a, b); // both at the same time: about 100 ms, not 200 println!("{pa} {pb}"); let handle = tokio::spawn(async { fetch_price("mug").await 2 }); // a separate task println!("{}", handle.await.unwrap()); match tokio::time::timeout(std::time::Duration::from_millis(50), fetch_price("slow")).await { Ok(price) = println!("{price}"), Err(_) = println!("gave up after 50 ms"), } } Tool Does --- --- x.await Wait for one future inside an async function tokio::join!(a, b) Run several futures concurrently, wait for all tokio::select! Wait for whichever finishes first tokio::spawn(fut) Run a future as an independent task (like a lightweight thread) tokio::sync::mpsc , Mutex Async versions of channels and locks tokio::time::sleep , timeout Timers that do not block the thread Rules that trip people up - Never block inside async code. std::thread::sleep , a long CPU loop or a blocking file read stops the whole runtime thread, and every task on it. Use the async versions ( tokio::time::sleep , tokio::fs ), or move blocking work to tokio::task::spawn_blocking . - Spawned tasks may run on other threads and outlive the caller, so their futures must be Send + 'static : own their data ( move ), and use Arc for sharing. Holding a std::sync::MutexGuard across an .await makes the future non- Send ; release it before awaiting, or use tokio::sync::Mutex . - Async functions in traits work directly in modern Rust; returning boxed futures ( Pin<Box<dyn Future ) is still needed in some generic code. Threads or async? Use threads when Use async when --- --- The work is CPU-bound (computing, compressing) The work is mostly waiting (network, many connections) There are a handful of concurrent jobs There are thousands of concurrent tasks You want the simplest code You are writing servers or clients with a runtime anyway Many programs use both: an async web server that hands heavy computations to a thread pool. The practice sandbox has no Tokio, so this lesson's code is for reading and for your own projects. Check yourself quiz ? What does calling an async fn return? - The function's result, once its work is done + A future, which does nothing until it is awaited or spawned - A handle to a thread that is already running the body - A Result that says whether the call succeeded Futures are lazy: calling the function only builds the future, and a runtime drives it when you .await or spawn it. ? Why is calling std::thread::sleep inside an async task a problem? - It does not compile inside an async fn - It pauses only that task, but wastes a little memory + It blocks the runtime's thread, stopping the other tasks on it - The runtime then restarts the task from the beginning It compiles, but it blocks the whole thread, so no other task on that thread can run. Use tokio::time::sleep(...).await instead. ? Two futures each wait 1 second. How long does tokio::join!(a, b) take? - About 2 seconds + About 1 second - 0 seconds - It depends on which is listed first join! runs both concurrently and finishes when both are done.

title: Futures by hand
body: The practice sandbox has no async runtime, which is a chance to see what a runtime does. Write: rust struct YieldNow { remaining: u32 } // a future that returns Pending remaining times, then Ready(()) impl YieldNow { fn new(times: u32) - Self } impl Future for YieldNow { type Output = (); ... } async fn add_slowly(a: u32, b: u32) - u32 // awaits YieldNow::new(2), then returns a + b async fn sum_all(values: Vec<u32 ) - u32 // adds the values one by one with add_slowly fn run<F: Future (future: F) - (F::Output, u32) // drives the future to completion; returns its output and how many times it was polled - YieldNow::poll must call cx.waker().wake_by_ref() before returning Pending , telling the runtime to poll again. - run is a tiny executor: pin the future ( std::pin::pin! ), make a context from std::task::Waker::noop() , and call poll in a loop until it returns Ready , counting the calls. So run(add_slowly(2, 3)) returns (5, 3) : two Pending polls, then Ready(5) .

title: 6.04  Testing, Documentation and Tooling
body: The Rust toolbox - cargo test with unit, integration and documentation tests, test organisation and fixtures, rustfmt and clippy, cargo doc and writing good doc comments, features and profiles, benchmarking, cargo workspaces, and publishing a crate. Tests cargo test builds and runs three kinds of tests: - Unit tests in a cfg(test) mod tests next to the code (lesson 3.05). They can test private functions. - Integration tests in the tests/ folder. Each file is a separate crate that uses your library only through its public API. - Documentation tests : code examples in /// comments are compiled and run, so the docs never go stale. rust-norun /// Splits a duration like "1h30m" into seconds. /// /// Examples /// /// /// use timeparse::parse; /// assert_eq!(parse("1h30m"), Ok(5400)); /// assert!(parse("soon").is_err()); /// /// /// Errors /// /// Returns an error for empty input or unknown units. pub fn parse(text: &str) - Result<u64, ParseError { / ... / } text mycrate/ Cargo.toml src/lib.rs (unit tests inside) tests/ parsing.rs (integration tests) common/mod.rs (shared helpers for integration tests) Helpful patterns: - Name tests after the behaviour: fn rejects_negative_amounts() . - assert_eq!(left, right, "message with {}", context) adds context to failures. - Tests that return Result<(), E can use ? . - ignore marks slow tests; run them with cargo test -- --ignored . - Property-based testing (the proptest crate) generates many random inputs and checks that a property always holds. Formatting and linting bash cargo fmt rustfmt: formats the whole project in the standard style cargo clippy hundreds of lints: bugs, slow code, unidiomatic code cargo clippy -- -D warnings treat every lint as an error (good in CI) Clippy catches things like if x == true , needless clone() s, len() == 0 instead of is_empty() , and loops that should be iterators. Its explanations link to the reasoning, which is a good way to learn idiomatic Rust. Documentation cargo doc --open builds HTML documentation for your crate and all its dependencies . Write doc comments with /// for items and //! for the crate or module itself. The conventional sections are Examples , Errors , Panics and Safety . docs.rs builds the documentation of every crate published on crates.io. Cargo features and profiles toml features default = "json" json = "dep:serde_json" optional dependency enabled by a feature dependencies serde_json = { version = "1", optional = true } profile.release lto = true link-time optimisation: smaller, faster binaries codegen-units = 1 cargo build --release uses the release profile: optimised, without debug checks such as integer-overflow panics. Measure performance with release builds only. For benchmarks, the criterion crate runs code many times and reports statistically meaningful timings. Workspaces A workspace groups several crates that are developed together and share one Cargo.lock and target folder: toml Cargo.toml at the top workspace members = "core", "cli", "server" resolver = "3" Typical layout: a library crate with the logic ( core ), and thin binary crates ( cli , server ) that depend on it, the same separation as the C and Java courses recommend. Publishing cargo publish uploads a library to crates.io after cargo login . Version numbers follow semantic versioning; Cargo treats 0.x minor versions as breaking. Before publishing, fill in description , license and repository in Cargo.toml , and run cargo package to check what will be uploaded. Check yourself quiz ? What are documentation tests? - Checks that every public item has a doc comment + Code examples in /// comments that cargo test compiles and runs - The test files kept in the crate's tests/ folder - Pages that cargo doc generates from the unit tests Because the examples in the docs are compiled and run, they cannot silently go stale. ? Why measure performance only with --release builds? + Debug builds are unoptimised and add checks, so they can be much slower - Release builds print timing information automatically - Debug builds cannot run benchmarks at all - Release builds leave out the code you are not measuring Debug builds skip optimisation and keep checks such as overflow panics, so their timings say little about the real program. ? Where do integration tests live in a Cargo project? - In src/main.rs - In a mod tests inside each file - In Cargo.toml + In the tests/ folder next to src/ Each file in tests/ is compiled as its own crate that uses only the public API.

title: A mini test runner
body: cargo test runs each test function and reports which ones panicked. Write the core of such a runner: rust derive(Debug, PartialEq) enum Outcome { Passed, Failed(String), Ignored } struct TestCase { name: &'static str, ignored: bool, body: fn() } fn run_tests(tests: & TestCase , filter: &str) - Vec<(String, Outcome) fn summary(results: & (String, Outcome) ) - String - run_tests runs every test whose name contains filter (all of them for "" ), in order. A test passes if its body returns normally, fails with the panic message if it panics, and is Ignored without running if ignored is set. - Catch panics with std::panic::catch_unwind . The panic message is the payload as a &str or String (for panic!("x {}", 1) it is a String ); anything else is reported as "panic" . - Silence the default panic output while the tests run ( std::panic::set_hook(Box::new( _ {})) ), and restore the previous hook afterwards with take_hook / set_hook . - summary gives "test result: FAILED. 2 passed; 1 failed; 1 ignored" , or ok instead of FAILED when nothing failed.

title: 6.05  Project: A Command-Line Tool
body: Building a real command-line program in Rust - reading arguments with std::env::args and with clap, reading files or standard input, a library-plus-binary layout, one error type with exit codes, writing output efficiently, and the plan for the final project, a log summariser with filters. The shape of a CLI program A good command-line tool reads arguments , reads input (files or standard input), writes results to standard output and errors to standard error, and exits with code 0 on success and non-zero on failure, so that scripts can tell what happened. rust-norun use std::process::ExitCode; fn main() - ExitCode { match run(std::env::args().skip(1).collect()) { Ok(()) = ExitCode::SUCCESS, Err(e) = { eprintln!("error: {e}"); ExitCode::from(2) } } } fn run(args: Vec<String ) - Result<(), AppError { let options = Options::parse(&args)?; let text = read_input(options.path.as_deref())?; let report = summarise(&text, &options)?; // pure logic, easy to test print!("{report}"); Ok(()) } main stays tiny: everything that can fail returns a Result , and only main decides how to report it. Arguments std::env::args() gives the program name followed by the arguments as String s. Parsing a few flags by hand is fine: rust derive(Debug, PartialEq) struct Options { path: Option<String , level: Option<String , top: usize } fn parse_args(args: & &str ) - Result<Options, String { let mut opts = Options { path: None, level: None, top: 5 }; let mut it = args.iter(); while let Some(&arg) = it.next() { match arg { "--level" = opts.level = Some(it.next().ok_or("--level needs a value")?.to_uppercase()), "--top" = { let n = it.next().ok_or("--top needs a value")?; opts.top = n.parse().map_err( _ format!("--top: '{n}' is not a number"))?; } flag if flag.starts_with("--") = return Err(format!("unknown option {flag}")), path = opts.path = Some(path.to_string()), } } Ok(opts) } fn main() { println!("{:?}", parse_args(& "app.log", "--level", "error", "--top", "3" )); println!("{:?}", parse_args(& "--top", "many" )); println!("{:?}", parse_args(& "--verbose" )); } For anything bigger, the clap crate generates parsing, --help and error messages from a struct: rust-norun use clap::Parser; /// Summarise a log file. derive(Parser) struct Args { /// The log file (reads standard input when left out) path: Option<std::path::PathBuf , /// Only count lines at this level arg(long) level: Option<String , /// How many top sources to show arg(long, default_value_t = 5) top: usize, } let args = Args::parse(); Input from a file or standard input rust-norun use std::io::{self, Read}; fn read_input(path: Option<&str ) - Result<String, AppError { match path { Some(p) = std::fs::read_to_string(p).map_err( e AppError::Io(p.to_string(), e)), None = { let mut text = String::new(); io::stdin().read_to_string(&mut text).map_err( e AppError::Io("stdin".into(), e))?; Ok(text) } } } Reading standard input lets the tool join pipelines: cat app.log logsum --level error . Library plus binary Put the logic in src/lib.rs (a library crate) and keep src/main.rs to argument handling and printing. The library's functions take text and return values, so unit tests need no files or processes, and the same code can later power a web service or a GUI. Writing output println! locks standard output on every call. For large outputs, lock once and use a buffered writer: rust-norun use std::io::{self, BufWriter, Write}; let stdout = io::stdout(); let mut out = BufWriter::new(stdout.lock()); for line in lines { writeln!(out, "{line}")?; } The final project The project for this milestone is a log summariser that reads log lines from standard input and supports command-line style options given on its first line. It combines everything in the course: parsing with Result and your own error type, enums and pattern matching for log levels, HashMap / BTreeMap for counting, iterators for the report, and a small Options struct parsed from arguments. Write the parsing and summarising as functions that take &str and return values; main only reads input and prints. Where to go next - Web services with axum or actix-web on Tokio. - Command-line tools with clap, serde and anyhow: Rust's strongest area, from ripgrep to cargo itself. - Systems and embedded programming: no_std, microcontrollers, operating-system components. - WebAssembly : Rust compiled to run in browsers. - "The Rust Programming Language" book and "Rust for Rustaceans" for depth. Check yourself quiz ? Why should main stay small in a command-line program? - A small main makes the program start faster + The logic then sits in testable functions, and only main reports errors - Rust warns when main grows beyond a few lines - So that main never has to return a value Functions that take text and return a Result are easy to unit test; main alone decides what to print and which exit code to use. ? Why read standard input when no file path is given? - Standard input is faster to read than a file - It means read errors never need handling + The tool can then sit in a pipeline, reading another program's output - Opening files needs the clap crate With standard input, cat app.log logsum --level error works. Reading stdin can still fail, so it still returns a Result . ? What should a command-line tool do when it fails? - Print the error to standard output and exit with code 0 - Panic, always + Print the error to standard error and exit with a non-zero code - Keep running and ignore the error Scripts check the exit code, and errors on stderr do not mix with the real output.

title: Parsing command-line arguments
body: The final project reads options like --level warn --top 3 --source auth . Write the parser: rust derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord) enum Level { Debug, Info, Warn, Error } // in order of severity derive(Debug, PartialEq) struct Options { level: Level, top: usize, sources: Vec<String , help: bool } derive(Debug, PartialEq) enum ArgError { Unknown(String), MissingValue(String), BadValue { option: String, value: String } } impl std::str::FromStr for Level // "debug", "INFO", "Warn"... (any case); Err(()) otherwise impl std::fmt::Display for ArgError fn parse_args(args: & &str ) - Result<Options, ArgError - Defaults: level Debug (everything), top 5, no sources, help false. - --level <level , --top <n (a whole number of 1 or more), --source <name (may be given several times; collected in order), -h / --help . The value can also be written --top=3 . - Errors: an unknown argument gives Unknown(arg) ; an option without a value MissingValue(option) ; a bad level or number BadValue . - Messages: unknown argument '<arg ' , <option needs a value , invalid value '<value ' for <option .

title: A log summariser
body: Build the command-line tool planned in lesson 6.05: a log summariser . It reads its options from the first line of standard input (written the way they would be typed on a command line), then reads log lines until the end of the input and prints a report. The options parser from practice 6.05 is already in the starter. --level warn --top 3 2026-03-14T09:00:01 INFO web GET /index 200 2026-03-14T09:00:05 WARN auth login failed for user 17 2026-03-14T09:01:10 WARN auth login failed for user 4 2026-03-14T09:02:00 ERROR db connection reset after 30s 2026-03-14T09:02:30 warn web slow response 1200ms oops this is not a log line 2026-03-14T09:03:00 ERROR db connection reset after 45s 2026-03-14T09:04:00 DEBUG db pool size 8 2026-03-14T09:05:12 WARN auth login failed for user 17 2026-03-14T25:00:00 ERROR db disk full 2026-03-14T09:06:00 ERROR auth token store unavailable prints Read 9 entries (2 malformed lines skipped) Selected 7 entries From 2026-03-14T09:00:05 to 2026-03-14T09:06:00 By level: ERROR 3 WARN 4 By source: auth 4 db 2 web 1 Top messages: 3x login failed for user 2x connection reset after s 1x slow response ms Malformed: line 6: bad timestamp 'oops' line 10: bad timestamp '2026-03-14T25:00:00' Options (the first line, split on whitespace and given to parse_args ): --level , --top , --source (repeatable) and --help , as in practice 6.05. With -h / --help , print the usage line and Reads log lines after the first line and prints a summary. and stop. If the options are wrong, print error: <message and the usage line, and stop. The usage line is: usage: --level <debug info warn error --top <n --source <name ... -h --help Log lines look like <timestamp <level <source <message , separated by whitespace: - The timestamp is YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS with month 01-12, day 01-31, hour 00-23 and minutes and seconds 00-59. - The level is debug , info , warn or error in any case. - The source is a non-empty name in square brackets; the message is the rest of the line, trimmed, and must not be empty. - Blank lines are ignored. Any other line that does not fit is malformed , for the first reason found, checking in this order: bad timestamp '<word ' , missing level , unknown level '<word ' , missing source , missing message . Log lines are numbered from 1 (the options line does not count; blank lines do). The report : 1. Read <n entries ( 1 entry ), followed by (<m malformed lines skipped) ( 1 malformed line ) when there were any. 2. Selected <n entries : the entries at the chosen level or more severe, and, when any --source was given, from one of those sources (exact names). 3. If none were selected, Nothing to report. Otherwise: - From <earliest to <latest timestamp of the selected entries. - By level: , then one line per level that occurs, most severe first: two spaces, the level in capitals padded to 5 characters, a space, the count. - By source: , then one line per source: most entries first, ties by name; two spaces, the name padded to the longest source name, two spaces, the count. - Top messages: , then the --top most common messages as <count x <message . Messages are grouped after replacing every run of digits with , so user 17 and user 4 both become user . Most common first, ties alphabetically. 4. If there were malformed lines, Malformed: and line <n : <reason for each, in order.

title: 7.01  Macros
body: Code that writes code - what macros can do that functions cannot, macro_rules! with fragment specifiers, repetition with $(...), , several rules in one macro, recursion, hygiene, exporting macros, and a look at derive and procedural macros. Why macros You have used macros since the first lesson: println! , vec! , assert_eq! , format! . The ! marks them. A macro runs at compile time and expands into ordinary code, so it can do things a function cannot: - take any number of arguments ( println!("{} {}", a, b) ); - take code that is not a value, such as a type, a pattern or a block; - check its input at compile time ( println! checks that the {} match the arguments). macro_rules! A declarative macro is a list of rules: a pattern to match the input, and the code to produce. rust macro_rules! square { ($x:expr) = { $x $x }; } fn main() { println!("{}", square!(7)); // 49 println!("{}", square!(2 + 3)); // 25: $x is the whole expression (2 + 3) } $x:expr captures an expression and names it $x . Because an expr fragment is kept as one unit, square!(2 + 3) gives 25, not the 2 + 3 2 + 3 a text substitution would. Fragment specifiers Specifier Matches --- --- expr an expression: a + 1 , f(x) ident a name: count , Point ty a type: Vec<u8 , &str pat a pattern: Some(x) , 1..=5 literal a literal: 42 , "hi" block a block in braces tt any single token tree (the most flexible) Repetition $( ... ), matches the inside any number of times, separated by commas; + instead of means one or more. In the output, $( ... ) repeats once per match: rust use std::collections::HashMap; macro_rules! map { ($($key:expr = $value:expr), $(,)?) = {{ let mut m = HashMap::new(); $( m.insert($key, $value); ) m }}; } fn main() { let ages = map! { "Ada" = 36, "Linus" = 28, }; let mut names: Vec<_ = ages.keys().collect(); names.sort(); println!("{names:?} {}", ages "Ada" ); } $(,)? allows an optional trailing comma. The double braces {{ ... }} make the expansion a block expression, so the macro can be used where a value is expected. Several rules and recursion Rules are tried in order. A macro may call itself, which is how it can process its input piece by piece: rust macro_rules! max_of { ($x:expr) = { $x }; ($x:expr, $($rest:expr),+) = {{ let a = $x; let b = max_of!($($rest),+); if a b { a } else { b } }}; } fn main() { println!("{}", max_of!(3, 9, 4, 7)); // 9 } Generating items Macros can produce whole functions, structs and impl blocks, which removes repetition that generics cannot: rust macro_rules! unit_type { ($name:ident, $suffix:literal) = { derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, PartialOrd) struct $name(f64); impl std::fmt::Display for $name { fn fmt(&self, f: &mut std::fmt::Formatter) - std::fmt::Result { write!(f, "{}{}", self.0, $suffix) } } }; } unit_type!(Metres, " m"); unit_type!(Seconds, " s"); fn main() { println!("{} in {}", Metres(100.0), Seconds(9.58)); } Hygiene Variables created inside a macro do not clash with the caller's: the a and b in max_of! are separate from any a and b where it is used. Names passed in as ident fragments do refer to the caller's names, which is how a macro can declare a variable the caller then uses. Exporting A macro is usable after its definition in the same file. To use it from other modules or crates, mark it macro_export ; it then lives at the crate root ( crate::map! ). Procedural macros derive(Debug) , derive(Serialize) from serde, and attributes like tokio::main are procedural macros : Rust functions, in a crate of their own, that receive the code as tokens and return new tokens. They are more powerful and more work to write (the syn and quote crates help). Reach for macro_rules! first; write a procedural macro when you need a derive . Check yourself quiz ? Why does square!(2 + 3) give 25 rather than 11? - Macros compute their arguments before running, like functions - The macro expands to 2 + 3 2 + 3 , which is 25 + The expr fragment keeps 2 + 3 as one unit, like (2 + 3) (2 + 3) - The compiler evaluates $x $x from right to left A macro expands into code rather than calling anything, but an expr fragment stays one expression; plain text substitution would give 2 + 3 2 + 3 , which is 11. ? What does $( ... ), mean in a macro pattern? + The part in brackets may appear any number of times, separated by commas - The part in brackets must appear exactly once, followed by a comma - The part in brackets may appear one or more times, each ending in a comma - The part in brackets is optional, with at most one comma after it means zero or more repetitions with the separator between them; + would mean one or more, and $(,)? is the optional trailing comma. ? Which fragment specifier would capture the name of a struct to be defined? - expr - literal - block + ident An ident is a name; it can be used to declare a new item.
