title: A struct with builder methods from a macro
match: A struct with builder methods from a macro
body: Write a macro settings! that defines a struct with default values and a "with" method per field: rust settings! { Window { width: u32 = 800, height: u32 = 600, title: String = String::from("untitled"), } } let w = Window::default().with_width(1024).with_title("Game".into()); // w.width == 1024, w.height == 600, w.title == "Game" The macro must produce: - derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq) struct Name { pub field: Type, ... } ; - impl Default for Name using the given default expressions; - for each field, a method with_<field (mut self, value: Type) - Self that sets it and returns self . Method names are made by joining with_ and the field name: since macro_rules! cannot join identifiers on its own, the macro receives the method names too, like this: rust settings! { Window { width: u32 = 800 = with_width, height: u32 = 600 = with_height, title: String = String::from("untitled") = with_title, } }

title: 7.02  Deref, AsRef, Borrow and Cow
body: The traits behind smart pointers and flexible APIs - Deref and deref coercion, implementing Deref for your own wrapper, the newtype pattern, AsRef for functions that accept many kinds of input, Borrow for map lookups, and Cow for data that is borrowed until it has to be changed. Deref and deref coercion Box<T , Rc<T , String and Vec<T all implement Deref : they can be treated as a reference to what is inside. b on a Box<i32 gives the i32 , and method calls look through automatically: rust fn shout(text: &str) - String { text.to_uppercase() } fn main() { let owned = String::from("hello"); let boxed = Box::new(String::from("boxed")); println!("{}", shout(&owned)); // &String becomes &str println!("{}", shout(&boxed)); // &Box<String becomes &String becomes &str println!("{}", boxed.len()); // the method is found through Box } This automatic conversion from &Wrapper to &Inner is deref coercion . It is why functions should take &str instead of &String , and & T instead of &Vec<T : they then accept every kind of string or slice. The newtype pattern A newtype wraps one value in a struct of its own: struct Email(String) . It gives the value a distinct type (so an Email cannot be passed where a Username is expected), lets you implement traits for it, and lets you control which operations exist: rust use std::fmt; derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq) struct Email(String); impl Email { fn parse(text: &str) - Result<Email, String { match text.split_once('@') { Some((user, domain)) if !user.is_empty() && domain.contains('.') = Ok(Email(text.to_lowercase())), _ = Err(format!("not an email address: {text}")), } } fn domain(&self) - &str { self.0.split_once('@').map( (_, d) d).unwrap_or("") } } impl fmt::Display for Email { fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) - fmt::Result { write!(f, "<{} ", self.0) } } fn main() { let e = Email::parse("Ada@Example.com").unwrap(); println!("{e} at {}", e.domain()); println!("{:?}", Email::parse("nobody")); } Once created, an Email is known to be valid everywhere: the check is in one place. Implementing Deref, carefully Implementing Deref for a newtype makes all of the inner type's &self methods available on it. That is right for smart pointers and wrappers that really are the inner thing; it is wrong when the wrapper exists to restrict what can be done (it would let every method through). rust use std::ops::Deref; struct Sorted(Vec<i32 ); // always sorted: only read access is given out impl Sorted { fn new(mut v: Vec<i32 ) - Sorted { v.sort(); Sorted(v) } } impl Deref for Sorted { type Target = i32 ; fn deref(&self) - & i32 { &self.0 } } fn main() { let s = Sorted::new(vec! 5, 1, 4 ); println!("{:?} min {} has 4: {}", &s .. , s 0 , s.binary_search(&4).is_ok()); } Only Deref (not DerefMut ) is implemented, so callers can read the slice but never unsort it. AsRef: accept anything that can give a reference AsRef<T means "can cheaply give a &T ". Taking impl AsRef<Path lets a function accept &str , String , &Path and PathBuf alike; that is how std::fs::read_to_string is declared: rust fn count_words<S: AsRef<str (texts: & S ) - usize { texts.iter().map( t t.as_ref().split_whitespace().count()).sum() } fn main() { let borrowed = "a b", "c" ; let owned = vec! String::from("one two three") ; println!("{} {}", count_words(&borrowed), count_words(&owned)); } Borrow: looking up owned keys with borrowed values A HashMap<String, V can be searched with a &str , without making a String , because String: Borrow<str . The rule behind Borrow is stricter than AsRef : the borrowed form must hash and compare exactly like the owned one. You rarely implement it; you rely on it every time you call map.get("key") . Cow: borrow until you must own Cow<'a, T ("clone on write") holds either a borrowed &'a T or an owned value. A function that usually returns its input unchanged, but sometimes has to build a new value, can avoid allocating in the common case: rust use std::borrow::Cow; fn normalise_spaces(text: &str) - Cow<'_, str { if !text.contains(" ") { return Cow::Borrowed(text); // nothing to do: no allocation } let mut out = String::with_capacity(text.len()); let mut last_space = false; for c in text.chars() { if c == ' ' && last_space { continue; } last_space = c == ' '; out.push(c); } Cow::Owned(out) } fn main() { for t in "already fine", "too many spaces" { let n = normalise_spaces(t); let kind = if matches!(n, Cow::Borrowed(_)) { "borrowed" } else { "owned" }; println!("{n:?} ({kind})"); } } A Cow<str derefs to &str , so callers use it like any string; .into_owned() gives a String when they need one. Check yourself quiz ? Why take &str rather than &String as a parameter? - A &String parameter takes ownership of the caller's string + Deref coercion turns &String into &str , so &str accepts every kind of string - Only a &str parameter lets the function change the text - &str copies the text, so the caller's string stays safe &String , &Box<String and literals all become &str , while a &String parameter accepts only &String . Neither kind owns, copies or changes the text. ? When does Cow save work? - When the function always builds a brand-new value - When the value must be shared between threads + When the function usually returns its input unchanged - When the data is too big to keep on the stack In the common case it hands back the borrowed input ( Cow::Borrowed ) instead of allocating a copy; only the rare changed case pays for a String . ? Which trait lets HashMap<String, i32 ::get accept a &str? - Deref + Borrow - AsRef - Clone String implements Borrow<str , and get takes any borrowed form of the key.

title: Clean up text without needless copies
match: Clean up text without needless copies
body: Write fn tidy(text: &str) - Cow<'_, str that: - trims spaces and tabs from both ends; - replaces each run of several spaces or tabs inside the text with one space; - replaces the "smart" quotes ‘ ’ with ' and “ ” with " . When none of this changes anything, it must return Cow::Borrowed of the input itself (no allocation). When only trimming is needed, it must also borrow: return a slice of the input. Only when characters inside the text have to change does it return Cow::Owned . title: 7.03  Unsafe Rust and FFI
body: What the compiler cannot check - the five things unsafe allows, raw pointers, unsafe functions and their safety contracts, wrapping unsafe code in a safe API, calling C functions through extern "C", making Rust callable from C, and the tools that catch mistakes. What unsafe means The borrow checker proves your references are always valid. Some correct programs cannot be proved that way: talking to C libraries, writing a data structure with raw memory, using hardware. For those, an unsafe block lets you do five extra things: 1. dereference a raw pointer; 2. call an unsafe function (including C functions); 3. access or change a mutable static ; 4. implement an unsafe trait (such as Send or Sync by hand); 5. access the fields of a union . Everything else (the borrow checker, type checks, bounds checks) still applies inside unsafe . The keyword does not turn checking off; it means " I promise these five operations are correct here". Raw pointers const T and mut T are pointers with no lifetime and no guarantee: they may be null, dangling or unaligned. Making one is safe; reading through it is not. rust fn main() { let mut value = 10; let p = &mut value as mut i32; // safe: just an address unsafe { p += 5; // unsafe: we promise p is valid and unaliased right now println!("{}", p); } let numbers = 10, 20, 30 ; let first = numbers.as_ptr(); let third = unsafe { first.add(2) }; // pointer arithmetic, like C println!("{third}"); } Unsafe functions and safety contracts A function is marked unsafe fn when callers must uphold a condition the compiler cannot check. Its documentation states that condition in a Safety section: rust /// Returns the element at index without checking bounds. /// /// Safety /// index must be less than slice.len() . unsafe fn get_fast(slice: & i32 , index: usize) - i32 { unsafe { slice.as_ptr().add(index) } } fn main() { let data = 4, 8, 15 ; // SAFETY: 1 < data.len() let x = unsafe { get_fast(&data, 1) }; println!("{x}"); } A // SAFETY: comment at each unsafe block explains why the promise holds there. Reviewers read those first. Safe abstractions The goal is to keep unsafe small and hidden behind a safe function that cannot be misused. split_at_mut in the standard library is the classic case: two mutable slices of one array cannot be expressed with references alone, but the function checks its input so callers never can do anything wrong: rust fn split_halves(v: &mut i32 ) - (&mut i32 , &mut i32 ) { let mid = v.len() / 2; let len = v.len(); let p = v.as_mut_ptr(); // SAFETY: the two ranges 0, mid) and mid, len) do not overlap and lie inside v. unsafe { (std::slice::from_raw_parts_mut(p, mid), std::slice::from_raw_parts_mut(p.add(mid), len - mid)) } } fn main() { let mut data = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 ; let (left, right) = split_halves(&mut data); left 0 = 100; right 0 = 300; println!("{data:?}"); } (In real code, use the standard v.split_at_mut(mid) , which is exactly this.) Calling C: extern "C" An extern "C" block declares functions that exist in a C library, using C's calling convention. Calling them is unsafe because Rust cannot check what the C code does: rust use std::ffi::CStr; unsafe extern "C" { fn abs(x: i32) - i32; fn strlen(s: const std::ffi::c_char) - usize; } fn main() { let text = c"hello from C"; // a C string literal: zero-terminated unsafe { println!("{} {}", abs(-42), strlen(text.as_ptr())); } let back: &CStr = text; println!("{}", back.to_str().unwrap()); } C strings end with a zero byte, Rust strings do not: CString (owned) and CStr (borrowed) convert between them. Real projects generate these declarations with bindgen and link the library through build.rs . Rust called from C The other direction marks a Rust function so C can call it by name: rust-norun unsafe(no_mangle) pub extern "C" fn add_scores(a: i32, b: i32) - i32 { a + b } Built as a cdylib crate, this becomes a .dll or .so that C, C++, C and Python can load (the DLLs course shows the C++ side). Catching mistakes Undefined behaviour in Rust is as dangerous as in C. Run unsafe code under Miri ( cargo +nightly miri test ), an interpreter that detects invalid pointer use, data races and uninitialised reads, and keep unsafe blocks as small as possible. Check yourself quiz ? Does unsafe turn off the borrow checker? - Yes: inside the block, no checks are made at all - Yes, but only for references created inside the block + No: it allows five extra operations, and all other checks stay on - No, but it does turn off bounds checks inside the block The borrow checker, type checks and bounds checks still apply inside unsafe ; the block only unlocks operations such as dereferencing raw pointers. ? Why is calling a C function always unsafe? + The compiler cannot see inside it to check that it is memory-safe - C functions always take raw pointers as arguments - C functions run on a thread of their own - C functions cannot return Rust types such as i32 Rust cannot check what foreign code does, so the caller must promise that the call is correct, even for something as harmless as abs . ? Which of these needs an unsafe block? - creating a raw pointer from a reference - calling a safe function that uses unsafe inside - using a Box + reading the value a raw pointer points to Making a raw pointer is safe; dereferencing it is one of the five unsafe operations.

title: 7.04  Files, Paths and Processes
body: Working with the operating system - std::fs for reading, writing and listing files, BufReader for large files, Path and PathBuf, io::Error and its kinds, environment variables and arguments, running other programs with std::process::Command, and exit codes. Reading and writing whole files std::fs has one-call helpers for small files. Every one returns a Result with an io::Error , so ? (lesson 3.04) passes failures on: rust-norun use std::fs; use std::io; fn main() - io::Result<() { fs::write("notes.txt", "first line\nsecond line\n")?; let text = fs::read_to_string("notes.txt")?; println!("{} lines", text.lines().count()); let bytes = fs::read("notes.txt")?; // Vec<u8 for binary data println!("{} bytes", bytes.len()); fs::create_dir_all("out/reports")?; fs::copy("notes.txt", "out/reports/notes.txt")?; fs::remove_file("notes.txt")?; Ok(()) } (Examples in this lesson touch your file system, so they run on your own machine rather than in Xenon's sandbox.) Large files, line by line read_to_string loads everything into memory. For a big file, wrap the File in a BufReader and read one line at a time: rust-norun use std::fs::File; use std::io::{self, BufRead, BufReader, BufWriter, Write}; fn main() - io::Result<() { let input = BufReader::new(File::open("server.log")?); let mut output = BufWriter::new(File::create("errors.log")?); for line in input.lines() { let line = line?; if line.contains("ERROR") { writeln!(output, "{line}")?; } } output.flush()?; Ok(()) } BufWriter gathers small writes into large ones. The same BufRead trait works for io::stdin().lock() , so one function can read either a file or standard input. Errors and their kinds An io::Error has a kind() you can match on, to treat "not found" differently from "permission denied": rust use std::fs; use std::io::ErrorKind; fn main() { match fs::read_to_string("does-not-exist.txt") { Ok(text) = println!("{} characters", text.len()), Err(e) if e.kind() == ErrorKind::NotFound = println!("no such file, using defaults"), Err(e) = println!("could not read it: {e}"), } } Paths Path (borrowed) and PathBuf (owned) are to file paths what &str and String are to text. They handle / and \ correctly on every system: rust use std::path::{Path, PathBuf}; fn main() { let p = Path::new("photos/2026/beach.jpg"); println!("{:?} {:?} {:?}", p.file_name(), p.extension(), p.parent()); println!("{:?}", p.file_stem()); let mut out = PathBuf::from("backup"); out.push("2026"); out.push("beach.jpg"); out.set_extension("png"); println!("{}", out.display()); } Paths are not always valid UTF-8, so they print with .display() and convert to &str with to_str() , which returns an Option . Listing a folder rust-norun use std::fs; use std::io; fn main() - io::Result<() { let mut entries: Vec<_ = fs::read_dir(".")?.collect::<Result<_, _ ()?; entries.sort_by_key( e e.file_name()); for entry in entries { let meta = entry.metadata()?; println!("{: 10} {}", if meta.is_dir() { "<dir ".to_string() } else { meta.len().to_string() }, entry.path().display()); } Ok(()) } Arguments, environment and exit codes rust-norun use std::env; use std::process::ExitCode; fn main() - ExitCode { let args: Vec<String = env::args().skip(1).collect(); // skip the program name let verbose = env::var("VERBOSE").is_ok(); if args.is_empty() { eprintln!("usage: tool FILE..."); return ExitCode::from(2); } if verbose { eprintln!("{} files", args.len()); } ExitCode::SUCCESS } eprintln! writes to standard error, so messages do not mix with the real output. For real argument parsing, the clap crate is the standard choice. Running other programs std::process::Command starts a program, passes arguments, and collects its output and exit status: rust-norun use std::process::Command; fn main() - std::io::Result<() { let output = Command::new("git").args( "log", "--oneline", "-3" ).output()?; if output.status.success() { print!("{}", String::from_utf8_lossy(&output.stdout)); } else { eprintln!("git failed: {}", String::from_utf8_lossy(&output.stderr)); } Ok(()) } Arguments are passed as a list, never glued into one string for a shell, so a file name with spaces or quotes cannot break the command. A pure core again As in the command-line project (lesson 6.05), keep parsing and deciding in functions that take &str or impl BufRead and return values, and keep the files, arguments and process handling in a thin main . The core can then be tested without touching the disk. Check yourself quiz ? When should you use a BufReader instead of read_to_string ? - When the file holds binary data rather than text + When the file may be large, so it is read a piece at a time - When the file might not exist - When the file has to be read more than once read_to_string loads the whole file into memory; BufReader with lines() keeps only a little of it at once. Binary data is what fs::read is for. ? Why pass the arguments to Command as a list? - So Command can run the arguments in parallel - So the program's output comes back as a list too - Because Command accepts only one string per call + Each argument stays one argument, whatever characters it contains Nothing is interpreted by a shell, so a file name with spaces or quotes cannot split into several arguments or break the command. ? What does Path::new("a/b/report.txt").extension() return? - "report.txt" + Some("txt") - Some(".txt") - None extension gives the part after the last dot, without the dot, as an Option.

title: 7.05  Type-State and PhantomData
body: Letting the compiler enforce the order of operations - states as types, consuming self to move between them, PhantomData for type parameters that hold no data, typed IDs and units, sealed traits, and when the pattern is worth it. Mistakes the compiler can catch Many APIs have rules about order: a connection must be opened before sending, a builder needs a URL before build , a file must not be written after closing. Usually such rules are checked at run time with a flag and an error. In Rust, they can often be checked at compile time by making each state a different type. States as types rust struct Draft; struct Reviewed; struct Published; struct Post<State { text: String, _state: State, } impl Post<Draft { fn new(text: &str) - Post<Draft { Post { text: text.to_string(), _state: Draft } } fn edit(&mut self, more: &str) { self.text.push_str(more); } fn review(self) - Post<Reviewed { // consumes the draft Post { text: self.text, _state: Reviewed } } } impl Post<Reviewed { fn publish(self) - Post<Published { Post { text: self.text, _state: Published } } } impl Post<Published { fn content(&self) - &str { &self.text } } fn main() { let mut post = Post::new("Hello"); post.edit(", world"); let live = post.review().publish(); println!("{}", live.content()); // post.edit("!"); // error: post was moved by review() // Post::new("x").publish(); // error: no method publish on Post<Draft } Each transition takes self by value, so the old state cannot be used again, and each state's impl block only offers what makes sense in that state. A whole class of bugs cannot compile. PhantomData Draft , Reviewed and Published above are empty structs stored in a field. Often a type parameter is needed only to tell types apart and there is nothing to store. Rust insists every type parameter is used, and std::marker::PhantomData<T is the zero-size field that "uses" it: rust use std::marker::PhantomData; derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash) struct Id<T { value: u32, _for: PhantomData<T , } impl<T Id<T { fn new(value: u32) - Id<T { Id { value, _for: PhantomData } } } struct User; struct Order; fn find_user(id: Id<User ) - String { format!("user {}", id.value) } fn main() { let user: Id<User = Id::new(7); let order: Id<Order = Id::new(7); println!("{}", find_user(user)); // find_user(order); // error: expected Id<User , found Id<Order println!("{}", std::mem::size_of::<Id<Order ()); // 4: PhantomData takes no space let _ = order; } Two IDs with the same number but for different things can no longer be mixed up, and it costs nothing at run time. Units of measure The same trick gives numbers a unit: rust use std::marker::PhantomData; use std::ops::Add; derive(Debug, Clone, Copy) struct Length<U { value: f64, unit: PhantomData<U } derive(Debug, Clone, Copy) struct Metres; derive(Debug, Clone, Copy) struct Feet; impl<U Length<U { fn new(value: f64) - Self { Length { value, unit: PhantomData } } } impl<U Add for Length<U { type Output = Length<U ; fn add(self, other: Self) - Self { Length::new(self.value + other.value) } // only the same unit } impl From<Length<Feet for Length<Metres { fn from(f: Length<Feet ) - Self { Length::new(f.value 0.3048) } } fn main() { let run = Length::<Metres ::new(400.0) + Length::new(100.0); let climb: Length<Metres = Length::<Feet ::new(1000.0).into(); println!("{:.1} m, {:.1} m", run.value, climb.value); } Sealed traits Sometimes the set of states should be closed, so nobody outside your crate can add one. A sealed trait requires a private supertrait that outside code cannot name: rust-norun mod private { pub trait Sealed {} } pub trait State: private::Sealed {} impl private::Sealed for Draft {} impl State for Draft {} // other crates cannot implement State, because they cannot implement private::Sealed When it is worth it Type-state shines when the rules are fixed and getting them wrong is costly: protocols, hardware drivers, builders with required fields, money and IDs. It adds types and generic code, so for rules that change at run time (a user can toggle a setting back and forth) a plain enum field and a check are simpler. Check yourself quiz ? Why do the transition methods such as review take self and not &mut self ? - self is faster than &mut self for small structs - A &mut self method cannot return a value + Taking ownership moves the value, so the old state cannot be used again - So the text is copied into the new state, keeping the old one valid After post.review() , post has been moved and any later post.edit(...) fails to compile. With &mut self , the draft would still be usable. ? What does a PhantomData<T field cost at run time? - As much memory as one value of type T + Nothing: it has size zero - A pointer to information about T - A small check each time the value is used It only tells the compiler that the type uses T ; Id<Order is still just 4 bytes, the size of its u32 . ? fn charge(id: Id<User ) is called with an Id<Order . What happens? - it works, because both hold a u32 - a panic at run time + a compile error: the types differ - the id is converted automatically Id<User and Id<Order are different types, which is the whole point.

Use it to define the length units Metre ( "m" , 1.0), Kilometre ( "km" , 1000.0), Mile ( "mi" , 1609.344) and Foot ( "ft" , 0.3048), and the time units Second ( "s" , 1.0), Minute ( "min" , 60.0) and Hour ( "h" , 3600.0). - Marker traits LengthUnit and TimeUnit , implemented for the right units, so lengths and times cannot be confused. - struct Length<U: LengthUnit { value: f64, unit: PhantomData<U } and struct Duration<U: TimeUnit with the same shape, each with new(value) , value() , to::<V () (converting through the base unit), Add for the same unit, and Display as the value with two decimals , a space and the symbol ( "1.86 mi" ). - fn parse_length(text: &str) - Result<Length<Metre , String : a number, spaces, and one of the length symbols; the result is in metres. Anything else is an Err naming the problem. - fn speed_kmh<L: LengthUnit, T: TimeUnit (distance: Length<L , time: Duration<T ) - f64 : kilometres per hour.

title: 8.01  Error Types in Depth
body: Designing errors for real programs - an error enum per module, implementing Display and std::error::Error, keeping the cause with source(), From conversions so ? converts errors for you, Box<dyn Error for small programs, adding context, and what the thiserror and anyhow crates automate. Beyond String errors Lesson 3.04 used Result<T, String and ? . Strings are fine in small examples, but a caller cannot easily tell one failure from another by looking at text. Real Rust code gives each module an error type : usually an enum with one variant per kind of failure. rust use std::fmt; derive(Debug, PartialEq) enum ConfigError { Missing(String), BadNumber { key: String, value: String }, OutOfRange { key: String, min: i64, max: i64 }, } impl fmt::Display for ConfigError { fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) - fmt::Result { match self { ConfigError::Missing(key) = write!(f, "missing setting {key}"), ConfigError::BadNumber { key, value } = write!(f, "{key} should be a number, not {value:?}"), ConfigError::OutOfRange { key, min, max } = write!(f, "{key} must be from {min} to {max}"), } } } impl std::error::Error for ConfigError {} fn port(settings: & (&str, &str) ) - Result<i64, ConfigError { let (_, text) = settings.iter().find( (k, _) k == "port").ok_or(ConfigError::Missing("port".into()))?; let n: i64 = text.parse().map_err( _ ConfigError::BadNumber { key: "port".into(), value: text.to_string() })?; if !(1..=65535).contains(&n) { return Err(ConfigError::OutOfRange { key: "port".into(), min: 1, max: 65535 }); } Ok(n) } fn main() { println!("{:?}", port(& ("port", "8080") )); for bad in vec! , vec! ("port", "eighty") , vec! ("port", "70000") { match port(&bad) { Ok(p) = println!("port {p}"), Err(e) = println!("error: {e}"), } } } The caller can match on the variant to react differently (ask again for a bad number, give up for a missing file), and Display gives a message for people. Implementing std::error::Error (which needs Debug and Display ) makes the type work with every tool that handles errors generally. Keeping the cause When one error is caused by another (a config error caused by an I/O error), keep the original and return it from source() : rust use std::error::Error; use std::fmt; use std::num::ParseIntError; derive(Debug) enum LoadError { Io(std::io::Error), Parse { line: usize, cause: ParseIntError }, } impl fmt::Display for LoadError { fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) - fmt::Result { match self { LoadError::Io(_) = write!(f, "could not read the scores file"), LoadError::Parse { line, .. } = write!(f, "line {line} is not a number"), } } } impl Error for LoadError { fn source(&self) - Option<&(dyn Error + 'static) { match self { LoadError::Io(e) = Some(e), LoadError::Parse { cause, .. } = Some(cause), } } } fn parse_scores(text: &str) - Result<Vec<i32 , LoadError { text.lines() .enumerate() .map( (i, l) l.trim().parse::<i32 ().map_err( cause LoadError::Parse { line: i + 1, cause })) .collect() } fn main() { let err = parse_scores("10\n20\nthirty").unwrap_err(); println!("{err}"); let mut cause = err.source(); while let Some(c) = cause { println!(" caused by: {c}"); cause = c.source(); } let _ = LoadError::Io(std::io::Error::other("disk")); } Printing the chain of source() s gives messages like "could not read the scores file: caused by: permission denied", which are far more useful than either part alone. collect() into a Result<Vec<_ , _ stops at the first error, as you see above. Letting ? convert errors ? calls From::from on the error before returning it. Implement From for the errors your function meets, and ? converts them automatically: rust use std::fmt; use std::num::ParseIntError; derive(Debug) enum AppError { Parse(ParseIntError), Negative(i64), } impl From<ParseIntError for AppError { fn from(e: ParseIntError) - Self { AppError::Parse(e) } } impl fmt::Display for AppError { fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) - fmt::Result { match self { AppError::Parse(e) = write!(f, "not a number ({e})"), AppError::Negative(n) = write!(f, "{n} is negative"), } } } fn double(text: &str) - Result<i64, AppError { let n: i64 = text.parse()?; // ParseIntError becomes AppError here if n < 0 { return Err(AppError::Negative(n)); } Ok(n 2) } fn main() { for t in "21", "x", "-3" { match double(t) { Ok(v) = println!("{t} - {v}"), Err(e) = println!("{t} - error: {e}"), } } } Box<dyn Error for small programs When you only want to report an error and stop, not handle each kind, Box<dyn Error accepts any error type, and ? converts into it: rust use std::error::Error; fn run() - Result<i32, Box<dyn Error { let a: i32 = "40".parse()?; let b: i32 = "2".parse()?; if a + b != 42 { return Err("the answer is wrong".into()); // a &str becomes a boxed error too } Ok(a + b) } fn main() { match run() { Ok(v) = println!("{v}"), Err(e) = eprintln!("error: {e}"), } } main itself can return Result<(), Box<dyn Error ; an Err then prints its Debug form and exits with code 1. Rule of thumb: libraries define their own error enums so callers can match on them; applications often use Box<dyn Error (or anyhow ) at the top, where errors are only reported. Adding context A bare "No such file or directory" does not say which file. Wrap errors with what you were doing: rust-norun let text = std::fs::read_to_string(&path) .map_err( e format!("reading {}: {e}", path.display()))?; The crates everyone uses - thiserror writes the Display , Error and From implementations from attributes: derive(Error, Debug) enum E { error("missing {0}") Missing(String), error(transparent) Io( from io::Error) } . - anyhow gives one anyhow::Error type for applications, ? from anything, and .context("reading config") to add messages. They save typing, but they generate exactly the code this lesson writes by hand. Check yourself quiz ? What does ? do with an error before returning it? - It prints the error to standard error + It calls From::from to convert it into the function's error type - It wraps the error in a Box<dyn Error - It returns the error exactly as it is, unchanged That conversion is why implementing From<ParseIntError for AppError lets a plain text.parse()? work in a function returning Result<_, AppError . ? When is Box<dyn Error a good choice? - In a library, so callers can match on each kind of failure - Whenever an error has a cause returned by source() - When callers must react differently to each error variant + In applications or small programs that only report errors A boxed error can hold any error type but cannot be matched by variant, so libraries should give callers their own error enum instead. ? What should source() return for an error that wraps an io::Error? + Some(the wrapped io::Error) - None, since the message already says it - the io::Error's message as a String - a new io::Error with the same kind source() gives access to the underlying error, so the cause can be shown or inspected; following source() again and again walks the chain of causes.

title: 8.02  Operators and Conversions
body: Making your types work with Rust's operators and conversions - Add, Sub, Mul and Neg, the assignment forms like AddAssign, Index and IndexMut for , From and Into, fallible conversions with TryFrom and TryInto, parsing with FromStr and str::parse, and AsRef-style flexibility in function arguments. Operators are traits a + b is shorthand for Add::add(a, b) . Every operator has a trait in std::ops , and implementing it lets your type use the operator: rust use std::ops::{Add, Mul, Neg, Sub}; derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq) struct V2 { x: f64, y: f64, } impl Add for V2 { type Output = V2; fn add(self, o: V2) - V2 { V2 { x: self.x + o.x, y: self.y + o.y } } } impl Sub for V2 { type Output = V2; fn sub(self, o: V2) - V2 { V2 { x: self.x - o.x, y: self.y - o.y } } } impl Mul<f64 for V2 { type Output = V2; fn mul(self, k: f64) - V2 { V2 { x: self.x k, y: self.y k } } } impl Neg for V2 { type Output = V2; fn neg(self) - V2 { V2 { x: -self.x, y: -self.y } } } fn main() { let a = V2 { x: 1.0, y: 2.0 }; let b = V2 { x: 3.0, y: 4.0 }; println!("{:?}", a + b); println!("{:?}", (b - a) 2.0); println!("{:?}", -a); } type Output says what the operator produces. Mul<f64 means "times an f64 "; 2.0 v would need a separate impl Mul<V2 for f64 . Because V2 is Copy , using it by value is cheap. For large types, implement the traits for references too ( impl Add for &Matrix ) so &a + &b does not move the operands. Assignment operators a += b uses AddAssign , which changes a in place: rust use std::ops::AddAssign; derive(Debug, Default) struct Totals { count: u32, sum: i64, } impl AddAssign<i64 for Totals { fn add_assign(&mut self, value: i64) { self.count += 1; self.sum += value; } } fn main() { let mut t = Totals::default(); for v in 5, 10, 20 { t += v; } println!("{t:?}"); } Indexing Index and IndexMut give your type : rust use std::ops::{Index, IndexMut}; struct Grid { width: usize, cells: Vec<char , } impl Index<(usize, usize) for Grid { type Output = char; fn index(&self, (x, y): (usize, usize)) - &char { &self.cells y self.width + x } } impl IndexMut<(usize, usize) for Grid { fn index_mut(&mut self, (x, y): (usize, usize)) - &mut char { &mut self.cells y self.width + x } } fn main() { let mut g = Grid { width: 3, cells: vec! '.'; 9 }; g (1, 1) = ' '; let rows: Vec<String = g.cells.chunks(3).map( r r.iter().collect()).collect(); println!("{}", rows.join("\n")); println!("{}", g (1, 1) ); } Indexing should panic on a bad index, like slices do; offer a get method returning Option for callers who want to check. From and Into From describes a conversion that always works. Implementing From<A for B gives you Into<B for A for free: rust derive(Debug) struct Celsius(f64); derive(Debug) struct Fahrenheit(f64); impl From<Celsius for Fahrenheit { fn from(c: Celsius) - Self { Fahrenheit(c.0 9.0 / 5.0 + 32.0) } } fn describe(t: impl Into<Fahrenheit ) - String { let f: Fahrenheit = t.into(); format!("{:.1} °F", f.0) } fn main() { let f = Fahrenheit::from(Celsius(100.0)); println!("{f:?}"); let g: Fahrenheit = Celsius(-40.0).into(); println!("{g:?}"); println!("{}", describe(Celsius(37.0))); let s: String = "text".into(); // the standard library is full of From impls let big: i64 = 5i32.into(); // widening numbers always works println!("{s} {big}"); } Accepting impl Into<T makes functions friendlier: callers can pass anything that converts. Conversions that can fail: TryFrom When a conversion might not work, implement TryFrom and return a Result : rust use std::convert::TryFrom; derive(Debug, PartialEq) struct Percent(u8); impl TryFrom<i32 for Percent { type Error = String; fn try_from(v: i32) - Result<Self, Self::Error { if (0..=100).contains(&v) { Ok(Percent(v as u8)) } else { Err(format!("{v} is not a percentage")) } } } fn main() { println!("{:?}", Percent::try_from(42)); let p: Result<Percent, _ = 150.try_into(); println!("{p:?}"); let small: Result<u8, _ = u8::try_from(300i32); // number narrowing uses it too println!("{small:?}"); } Prefer u8::try_from(x) to x as u8 : as silently truncates (300 becomes 44). Parsing: FromStr "42".parse::<i32 () works because i32 implements FromStr . Implement it for your own types to get parse too: rust use std::str::FromStr; derive(Debug, PartialEq) struct Rgb(u8, u8, u8); impl FromStr for Rgb { type Err = String; fn from_str(s: &str) - Result<Self, Self::Err { let hex = s.strip_prefix(' ').ok_or("must start with ")?; if hex.len() != 6 { return Err("needs 6 hex digits".into()); } let part = i: usize u8::from_str_radix(&hex i..i + 2 , 16).map_err( e e.to_string()); Ok(Rgb(part(0)?, part(2)?, part(4)?)) } } fn main() { let c: Rgb = " ff8800".parse().unwrap(); println!("{c:?}"); println!("{:?}", "ff8800".parse::<Rgb ()); println!("{:?}", " ff88".parse::<Rgb ()); } Check yourself quiz ? Why implement From rather than Into ? - Into can only be implemented for number types - From is checked at compile time, Into only at run time + Implementing From<A for B gives you Into<B for A automatically - Into conversions always copy the value first With one From impl you get both B::from(a) and a.into() , so there is nothing to gain by writing Into by hand. ? What is wrong with x as u8 for an i32 that may be large? - It panics when x is above 255 - It always gives 255 for anything above 255 - It does not compile for i32 values + It silently wraps (300 becomes 44) instead of reporting a problem as keeps only the low 8 bits without any error; u8::try_from(x) returns an Err for values that do not fit. ? Which trait makes "1,2".parse::<Point () possible? - Into<Point for &str + FromStr for Point - TryFrom<String for Point - Display for Point str::parse calls the type's FromStr implementation.

title: 8.03  Collections in Depth
body: The rest of std::collections and the slice methods that save loops - BTreeMap and BTreeSet for sorted keys and ranges, VecDeque for both ends, BinaryHeap with Reverse for priority queues, sorting by keys, dedup, retain, binary_search, windows and chunks, and choosing the right collection. Sorted maps and sets HashMap (lesson 3.03) has no order. BTreeMap keeps its keys sorted, so iteration is in order and you can ask for ranges : rust use std::collections::BTreeMap; fn main() { let mut scores = BTreeMap::new(); for (name, s) in ("cy", 77), ("ada", 91), ("bob", 48), ("dee", 65) { scores.insert(name, s); } println!("{scores:?}"); // sorted by name println!("{:?}", scores.first_key_value()); for (name, s) in scores.range("b".."d") { println!("{name} {s}"); } let mut events = BTreeMap::new(); events.insert(900, "wake"); events.insert(1230, "lunch"); events.insert(1800, "dinner"); let next = events.range(1000..).next(); // the first event at or after 10:00 println!("{next:?}"); } BTreeSet is the sorted set. Use the B-tree types when you need order, ranges, or the smallest and largest; HashMap is usually faster otherwise. VecDeque: a queue with two ends A Vec is fast at the end only. VecDeque is fast at both ends, which makes it the standard queue: rust use std::collections::VecDeque; fn main() { let mut queue: VecDeque<&str = VecDeque::new(); queue.push_back("ada"); queue.push_back("bob"); queue.push_front("vip"); while let Some(next) = queue.pop_front() { println!("serving {next}"); } let mut recent = VecDeque::with_capacity(3); for n in 1..=5 { if recent.len() == 3 { recent.pop_front(); } recent.push_back(n); } println!("{recent:?}"); // the last three: 3, 4, 5 } BinaryHeap: always the largest first BinaryHeap gives back its largest item first. Wrap items in Reverse for the smallest first, which is what a priority queue of tasks or Dijkstra's algorithm needs: rust use std::cmp::Reverse; use std::collections::BinaryHeap; fn main() { let mut heap = BinaryHeap::from(vec! 5, 1, 8, 3 ); heap.push(7); println!("{:?}", heap.pop()); // Some(8) println!("{:?}", heap.peek()); // Some(7) let mut tasks = BinaryHeap::new(); tasks.push(Reverse((3, "write report"))); tasks.push(Reverse((1, "fix crash"))); tasks.push(Reverse((2, "reply to email"))); while let Some(Reverse((priority, task))) = tasks.pop() { println!("{priority}: {task}"); } } Tuples compare field by field, so (priority, task) orders by priority first. Slice methods worth knowing Most of these work on any Vec or slice: rust fn main() { let mut words = vec! "pear", "Fig", "apple", "fig", "kiwi", "apple" ; words.sort_by_key( w w.to_lowercase()); println!("{words:?}"); words.dedup_by_key( w w.to_lowercase()); // removes neighbours that are equal by the key println!("{words:?}"); words.retain( w w.len() 3); // keep only what passes println!("{words:?}"); let sorted = 2, 5, 8, 13, 21 ; println!("{:?} {:?}", sorted.binary_search(&13), sorted.binary_search(&9)); // Ok(3) Err(3): where 9 would go let temps = 12, 14, 13, 17, 19, 18 ; let rises: Vec<i32 = temps.windows(2).map( w w 1 - w 0 ).collect(); println!("{rises:?}"); for chunk in temps.chunks(4) { println!("{chunk:?}"); } let (low, high) = temps.split_at(3); println!("{low:?} {high:?} max {:?}", temps.iter().max()); println!("{:?}", temps.iter().position( &t t 15)); } - sort_by_key and sort_by( a, b ...) sort in place; sort_unstable is faster when equal items may be reordered. - dedup removes neighbouring duplicates, so sort first to remove all duplicates. - binary_search on a sorted slice gives Ok(index) or Err(where it would go) , which is also the place to insert to keep it sorted. - windows(n) gives overlapping groups, chunks(n) separate ones. More of the entry API rust use std::collections::HashMap; fn main() { let text = "the cat and the hat and the bat"; let mut positions: HashMap<&str, Vec<usize = HashMap::new(); for (i, w) in text.split(' ').enumerate() { positions.entry(w).or_default().push(i); } let mut keys: Vec<_ = positions.keys().collect(); keys.sort(); for k in keys { println!("{k}: {:?}", positions k ); } let mut stock = HashMap::from( ("tea", 3) ); stock.entry("tea").and_modify( n n += 5).or_insert(0); stock.entry("milk").and_modify( n n += 5).or_insert(1); let mut s: Vec<_ = stock.into_iter().collect(); s.sort(); println!("{s:?}"); } or_default() inserts the type's default (an empty Vec here); and_modify changes an existing value. Choosing need collection --- --- a list, mostly adding at the end Vec a queue, or adding at both ends VecDeque look up by key, order does not matter HashMap / HashSet keys in order, ranges, first and last BTreeMap / BTreeSet always take the largest (or smallest) next BinaryHeap Check yourself quiz ? Why does dedup on vec! 1, 2, 1 leave all three items? - dedup only works on sorted vectors and does nothing otherwise + It only removes equal items that are next to each other - It always keeps the first and the last copy of each value - It only removes duplicates found at the end of the vector The two 1 s are not neighbours, so nothing is removed. Sort first to remove every duplicate. ? How do you make a BinaryHeap give the smallest item first? - Call pop_min() instead of pop() - Sort the heap before each pop() + Push the values wrapped in std::cmp::Reverse - Read it with peek() instead of pop() A BinaryHeap always gives its largest item; Reverse flips the comparison, so the smallest value counts as the largest. ? 2, 5, 8 .binary_search(&6) gives... - Ok(1) - Err(1) - None + Err(2) 6 is not there, so the result is Err with the place where it would be inserted: index 2, between 5 and 8.

A window of 0 or bigger than the slice gives an empty Vec . rust smallest_k(& 5, 1, 9, 3, 7 , 3) // 1, 3, 5 sliding_max(& 1, 3, -1, -3, 5, 3, 6 , 3) // 3, 3, 5, 5, 6

title: 8.04  Advanced Traits
body: The trait features behind Rust's standard library - associated types and how they differ from generic parameters, default type parameters, supertraits, blanket implementations, const generics for array sizes, implementing Sum and FromIterator so collect and sum work with your types, and extension traits. Associated types Iterator has type Item; rather than a generic parameter. An associated type is chosen once by each implementation: rust trait Container { type Item; fn get(&self, i: usize) - Option<&Self::Item ; fn first(&self) - Option<&Self::Item { self.get(0) } } struct Shelf { books: Vec<String , } impl Container for Shelf { type Item = String; fn get(&self, i: usize) - Option<&String { self.books.get(i) } } fn main() { let s = Shelf { books: vec! "Dune".into(), "Emma".into() }; println!("{:?} {:?}", s.first(), s.get(5)); } With a generic parameter ( trait Container<T ), one type could implement it many times ( Container<String and Container<i32 ), and callers would have to say which. With an associated type, there is exactly one Item per implementing type, so shelf.first() needs no annotation. Use an associated type when each type has one natural answer. Default type parameters Add<Rhs = Self means "add to the same type unless told otherwise", which is why impl Add for V2 (lesson 8.02) needed no parameter. You can give your own traits defaults the same way: rust-norun trait Scale<By = f64 { fn scale(&self, by: By) - Self; } Supertraits A trait can require another: trait Shape: Display means every Shape must also be Display , so Shape methods can use {} : rust use std::fmt; trait Shape: fmt::Display { fn area(&self) - f64; fn describe(&self) - String { format!("{self} with area {:.2}", self.area()) } } struct Square(f64); impl fmt::Display for Square { fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) - fmt::Result { write!(f, "a square of side {}", self.0) } } impl Shape for Square { fn area(&self) - f64 { self.0 self.0 } } fn main() { println!("{}", Square(3.0).describe()); } Blanket implementations An impl can cover every type that meets a bound. The standard library does this a lot: every type that implements Display gets to_string() through impl<T: Display ToString for T . Yours work the same way: rust use std::fmt::Display; trait Shout { fn shout(&self) - String; } impl<T: Display Shout for T { fn shout(&self) - String { format!("{}!", self.to_string().to_uppercase()) } } fn main() { println!("{} {} {}", "hello".shout(), 42.shout(), 'x'.shout()); } This also shows an extension trait : a trait that adds methods to types you did not write. Only code that imports the trait sees the methods. Const generics Types can take values as parameters, most often array sizes: rust derive(Debug) struct Matrix<const R: usize, const C: usize { data: i32; C ; R , } impl<const R: usize, const C: usize Matrix<R, C { fn transpose(&self) - Matrix<C, R { let mut data = 0; R ; C ; for r in 0..R { for c in 0..C { data c r = self.data r c ; } } Matrix { data } } } fn sum<const N: usize (xs: i32; N ) - i32 { xs.iter().sum() } fn main() { let m = Matrix { data: 1, 2, 3 , 4, 5, 6 }; println!("{:?}", m.transpose()); println!("{} {}", sum( 1, 2, 3 ), sum( 10; 5 )); } The sizes are checked at compile time: a 2×3 matrix's transpose is a 3×2 matrix, and mixing them up is a type error. Making sum and collect work with your types iter.sum() needs the item type to implement Sum , and collect() needs the target to implement FromIterator : rust use std::iter::{FromIterator, Sum}; use std::ops::Add; derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, Default, PartialEq) struct Money(i64); impl Add for Money { type Output = Money; fn add(self, o: Money) - Money { Money(self.0 + o.0) } } impl Sum for Money { fn sum<I: Iterator<Item = Money (iter: I) - Money { iter.fold(Money::default(), a, b a + b) } } derive(Debug) struct Basket(Vec<String ); impl FromIterator<String for Basket { fn from_iter<I: IntoIterator<Item = String (iter: I) - Self { let mut items: Vec<String = iter.into_iter().collect(); items.sort(); Basket(items) } } fn main() { let total: Money = Money(250), Money(120), Money(30) .into_iter().sum(); println!("{total:?}"); let b: Basket = "tea", "bread", "milk" .iter().map( s s.to_string()).collect(); println!("{} items: {:?}", b.0.len(), b.0); } Implementing these few traits makes your types fit into iterator chains as smoothly as the built-in ones. Check yourself quiz ? When should a trait use an associated type instead of a generic parameter? - When one type must implement the trait several times, for different types + When each implementing type has exactly one natural choice, like an iterator's item - When the caller should pick the type again at every call - Whenever the trait has default methods With an associated type there is one Item per implementation, so calls need no annotation. Implementing a trait several times for one type is what a generic parameter ( Container<T ) allows. ? What does impl<T: Display Shout for T do? + It implements Shout for every type that implements Display , all at once - It makes every type that implements Shout implement Display too - It implements Shout only for a single type named T - It implements Shout for dyn Display trait objects only That is a blanket implementation, like impl<T: Display ToString for T . Requiring Display for every Shout type would be a supertrait ( trait Shout: Display ). ? What must a type implement for iter.sum::<T () to work? - Add only - FromIterator + Sum - Default Iterator::sum is defined for any S: Sum<Self::Item ; Add alone is not enough.

title: 8.05  Writing Parsers
body: Turning text into data structures by hand - a tokenizer over chars with Peekable, tokens as an enum with positions, a recursive-descent parser that follows a small grammar, operator precedence, good error messages with the column of the problem, and a look at parser libraries such as nom. Why write a parser? Configuration files, commands, small languages, file formats: turning text into structured data is everywhere. split and parse handle simple cases. For anything with nesting or precedence ( 2 + 3 (4 - 1) ), the clean way is two steps: 1. A tokenizer (lexer) turns characters into tokens: numbers, names, symbols. 2. A parser turns tokens into a tree, following a grammar. Tokens rust derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq) enum Tok { Num(f64), Ident(String), Op(char), LParen, RParen, } fn tokenize(src: &str) - Result<Vec<(usize, Tok) , String { let mut out = Vec::new(); let mut chars = src.char_indices().peekable(); while let Some(&(pos, c)) = chars.peek() { if c.is_whitespace() { chars.next(); } else if c.is_ascii_digit() c == '.' { let mut text = String::new(); while let Some(&(_, d)) = chars.peek() { if d.is_ascii_digit() d == '.' { text.push(d); chars.next(); } else { break; } } let n = text.parse().map_err( _ format!("bad number {text:?} at {pos}"))?; out.push((pos, Tok::Num(n))); } else if c.is_alphabetic() { let mut name = String::new(); while let Some(&(_, d)) = chars.peek() { if d.is_alphanumeric() d == '_' { name.push(d); chars.next(); } else { break; } } out.push((pos, Tok::Ident(name))); } else { chars.next(); out.push((pos, match c { '+' '-' ' ' '/' '^' = Tok::Op(c), '(' = Tok::LParen, ')' = Tok::RParen, _ = return Err(format!("unexpected {c:?} at {pos}")), })); } } Ok(out) } fn main() { println!("{:?}", tokenize("2 (x + 1.5)").unwrap()); println!("{:?}", tokenize("3 $ 4")); } peekable() lets the loop look at the next character without taking it, which is how a number knows where it ends. Keeping each token's position pays off later, in error messages. A grammar A grammar describes the shapes the parser accepts. For arithmetic with the usual precedence: text expr = term (("+" "-") term) term = factor ((" " "/") factor) factor = "-" factor atom atom = number name "(" expr ")" Each rule becomes one function, and a rule that uses another calls its function: that is recursive descent . Precedence comes for free from the nesting: term binds tighter than expr , so happens before + . The parser rust derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq) enum Tok { Num(f64), Op(char), LParen, RParen } derive(Debug) enum Expr { Num(f64), Neg(Box<Expr ), Bin(char, Box<Expr , Box<Expr ), } struct Parser { toks: Vec<Tok , pos: usize, } impl Parser { fn peek(&self) - Option<&Tok { self.toks.get(self.pos) } fn next(&mut self) - Option<Tok { let t = self.toks.get(self.pos).cloned(); self.pos += 1; t } fn expr(&mut self) - Result<Expr, String { let mut left = self.term()?; while let Some(Tok::Op(op @ ('+' '-'))) = self.peek().cloned() { self.next(); left = Expr::Bin(op, Box::new(left), Box::new(self.term()?)); } Ok(left) } fn term(&mut self) - Result<Expr, String { let mut left = self.factor()?; while let Some(Tok::Op(op @ (' ' '/'))) = self.peek().cloned() { self.next(); left = Expr::Bin(op, Box::new(left), Box::new(self.factor()?)); } Ok(left) } fn factor(&mut self) - Result<Expr, String { match self.next() { Some(Tok::Op('-')) = Ok(Expr::Neg(Box::new(self.factor()?))), Some(Tok::Num(n)) = Ok(Expr::Num(n)), Some(Tok::LParen) = { let e = self.expr()?; match self.next() { Some(Tok::RParen) = Ok(e), other = Err(format!("expected ')' but found {other:?}")), } } other = Err(format!("expected a number or '(' but found {other:?}")), } } } fn eval(e: &Expr) - f64 { match e { Expr::Num(n) = n, Expr::Neg(x) = -eval(x), Expr::Bin(op, a, b) = { let (a, b) = (eval(a), eval(b)); match op { '+' = a + b, '-' = a - b, ' ' = a b, _ = a / b } } } } fn main() { use Tok:: ; // 2 + 3 (4 - 1) let toks = vec! Num(2.0), Op('+'), Num(3.0), Op(' '), LParen, Num(4.0), Op('-'), Num(1.0), RParen ; let mut p = Parser { toks, pos: 0 }; let tree = p.expr().unwrap(); println!("{tree:?}"); println!("= {}", eval(&tree)); let mut bad = Parser { toks: vec! Num(1.0), Op(' ') , pos: 0 }; println!("{:?}", bad.expr()); } After parsing, check that every token was used ( p.pos == p.toks.len() ); otherwise 1 2 would quietly parse as 1 . The loop in expr builds (1 - 2) - 3 for 1 - 2 - 3 , so operators of equal precedence group from the left, as they should. Good error messages The difference between a toy parser and a useful one is its errors. With positions on tokens, an error can point at the problem: text 2 (3 + ) ^ expected a number or '(' at column 10 Return a struct ParseError { pos: usize, message: String } (lesson 8.01), and print the source line with a ^ under the column. Parser libraries For larger formats, libraries help: - nom builds parsers from small functions ("parser combinators"): tuple((digit1, char(':'), digit1)) . - pest and lalrpop generate a parser from a grammar file like the one above. - serde with serde_json , toml and friends already parses the common data formats into your structs. Hand-written recursive descent remains common in real compilers (including rustc), because it is simple to follow and gives the best error messages. Check yourself quiz ? Why does term handle while expr handles + ? - term is written first in the code, so it runs first + expr calls term for its parts, so multiplications are grouped first - tokens always come before + tokens in the token list - So that 1 - 2 - 3 groups from the right The nesting of the functions is the precedence: each part of a sum is a whole product. Grouping from the left comes from the loop in expr . ? Why keep the position of each token? - So the parser can go back and read the characters again - Because peekable() only works with positions + So error messages can say where the problem is - So the tokens can be put back in order after parsing With positions, an error can point at the column, which helps users more than anything else a parser does. ? In recursive descent, how does a grammar rule become code? - as one big regular expression for the whole grammar - as a lookup table from tokens to results - as a macro_rules! macro for each rule + as a function that calls the functions of the rules it uses Each rule is a function; using another rule means calling its function, so nesting in the grammar becomes recursion.

The grammar: text expr = term (("+" "-") term) term = power ((" " "/") power) power = unary ("^" power)? ^ groups from the right: 2^3^2 = 2^9 unary = "-" unary atom atom = number name "(" expr ")" - names are looked up in vars ; an unknown name is Err("unknown name 'x'") ; - dividing by zero is Err("division by zero") ; - anything left over after a complete expression, a missing ) , or a missing operand is an error (any message).
