title: Common Errors
body: Rust's compiler messages are long because they explain themselves: read the first error, the line it points at, and the help: lines underneath. Each error has a code; rustc --explain E0382 prints a full explanation. Ownership and borrowing Message Usual cause Fix Lesson --- --- --- --- E0382 borrow of moved value / use of moved value Using a variable after its value moved into another variable or a function Pass a reference ( &v ), .clone() it, or use it before the move 2.01 E0499 cannot borrow x as mutable more than once at a time Two &mut borrows alive together Finish with one before making the next; split the work into steps 2.02 E0502 cannot borrow x as mutable because it is also borrowed as immutable Changing a collection while holding a reference into it, such as pushing to a Vec while looping over it Collect what to change first, then change it; or copy the value out of the reference 2.02 E0596 cannot borrow x as mutable, as it is not declared as mutable Changing a variable declared without mut , or calling a &mut self method on it let mut x , or take &mut in the function's parameter 1.02 E0384 cannot assign twice to immutable variable Reassigning a variable without mut Add mut , or shadow it with a new let 1.02 E0507 cannot move out of x which is behind a shared reference Taking ownership of a field or element through & , such as let s = v 0 ; for a Vec<String Borrow it ( &v 0 ), .clone() it, or use std::mem::take with &mut 2.02 E0106 missing lifetime specifier A function returns a reference and the compiler cannot tell which argument it borrows from Name a lifetime: fn f<'a (x: &'a str, y: &str) - &'a str , or return an owned String 4.04 E0597 x does not live long enough / E0515 cannot return reference to local variable A reference outlives what it points to Return the owned value instead, or keep the owner alive longer 4.04 E0373 closure may outlive the current function, but it borrows x thread::spawn (or a returned closure) borrows a local Add move , or use thread::scope so the thread may borrow 6.01 Types and traits Message Usual cause Fix Lesson --- --- --- --- E0308 mismatched types A value of the wrong type, often an i32 where usize or f64 is needed, or &str where String is needed Convert: as usize , as f64 , .to_string() , &s 1.02 E0308 ... expected i32, found () A ; after the last expression of a function, turning the value into a statement Remove the semicolon 1.03 E0277 the trait bound T: Display is not satisfied A generic function uses an operation the bound does not promise Add the bound: T: Display , T: PartialOrd + Copy 4.01 E0277 X doesn't implement Debug / std::fmt::Display Printing a type with {:?} or {} that has no such impl derive(Debug) , or write impl fmt::Display 4.03 E0277 the size for values of type dyn Trait cannot be known A trait object used by value Put it behind a pointer: Box<dyn Trait or &dyn Trait 4.05 E0282 type annotations needed collect() , parse() or Vec::new() with nothing saying what type to make let v: Vec<i32 = ...collect(); or the turbofish .parse::<u32 () 4.01 E0599 no method named x found A typo, a trait not in scope ( use std::io::Write ), or a method on the wrong type, like .len() on an Option Import the trait; unwrap or match first 4.02 E0004 non-exhaustive patterns A match misses a variant or value Add the missing arms, or a _ = arm 2.05 E0277 the ? operator can only be used in a function that returns Result or Option Using ? in main or another function returning () Return Result<(), Box<dyn Error , or handle the error with match 3.04 E0277 ... the trait From<X is not implemented for Y ? cannot convert the error type into the function's error type impl From<X for Y , or .map_err(...) 3.04 E0277 Rc<... cannot be sent between threads safely Moving an Rc or RefCell into another thread Use Arc and Mutex (or atomics) instead 6.02 E0603 x is private Using an item of another module that is not pub Mark it pub (fields too, each one) 3.05 Panics at run time Panic message Usual cause Fix Lesson --- --- --- --- index out of bounds: the len is 3 but the index is 3 Indexing past the end, often an off-by-one in a loop Use 0..v.len() , .get(i) , or iterate directly 3.01 called Option::unwrap() on a None value unwrap on a missing value match , if let , unwrap_or , or ? 2.05 called Result::unwrap() on an Err value: ParseIntError { kind: InvalidDigit } Parsing text that is not a number, often with a trailing newline .trim() the input first, and handle the Err 1.05 byte index 1 is not a char boundary Slicing a string in the middle of a multi-byte character Use .chars() , char_indices() , or find boundaries with find 3.02 attempt to subtract with overflow An unsigned number going below 0 (debug builds check this) checked_sub , saturating_sub , or a signed type 1.02 already borrowed: BorrowMutError Two borrow_mut() calls on one RefCell alive together Keep borrows short; drop the first before the second 5.04 PoisonError on lock().unwrap() Another thread panicked while holding the lock Fix the panic; or recover with into_inner() 6.02 Wrong results without an error Symptom Usual cause Fix Lesson --- --- --- --- An iterator chain does nothing Adapters are lazy: no consumer was called End with collect , sum , count or a for loop 5.02 s.len() is bigger than the number of letters len counts bytes, not characters s.chars().count() 3.02 Integer division gives 0 7 / 2 on integers is 3, and 1 / 2 is 0 Convert first: a as f64 / b as f64 1.02 A loop over a HashMap prints in a different order each run HashMap has no order Use BTreeMap , or sort the keys 3.03 A program with threads never ends A receiver waits forever because a Sender clone was never dropped drop(tx) after cloning it for the threads 6.01 An async function's body never runs A future was created but never .await ed or given to a runtime .await it, or block_on / spawn it 6.03

title: Glossary
body: Every term from the course, in alphabetical order. The lesson that introduces each one is in brackets. Term Meaning --- --- &str A borrowed string slice; string literals are &'static str . (2.03) Adapter An iterator method that wraps another iterator, such as map , filter or zip ; nothing runs until a consumer pulls values. (5.02) Arc Arc<T , an atomically reference-counted pointer that can be shared between threads. (6.02) AsRef A trait for types that can cheaply give a reference to another type. (7.02) Associated function A function in an impl block without self , called as Type::name() , such as String::new . (2.04) Associated type A type a trait leaves to each implementation, such as Iterator::Item . (5.03) async / await async fn returns a future instead of running; .await waits for a future inside another async function. (6.03) Atomic A type such as AtomicU64 whose operations other threads see whole, without a lock. (6.02) Binary crate A crate with a main function that builds into a program. (3.05) BinaryHeap A priority queue that always gives the largest item first; wrap items in Reverse for the smallest (8.03) Blanket implementation An impl for every type that meets a bound, such as impl<T: Display ToString for T (8.04) Borrow Using a value through a reference without taking ownership. (2.02) Borrow checker The part of the compiler that checks every reference is valid and that &mut borrows are exclusive. (2.02) Box Box<T , an owned value on the heap; used for recursive types and trait objects. (5.04) Box<dyn Error A boxed value of any error type, convenient in applications that only report errors (8.01) BTreeMap A map that keeps its keys sorted and supports ranges (8.03) BufReader Wraps a reader to read in large blocks, giving line-by-line reading. (7.04) Cargo Rust's build tool and package manager: cargo new , build , run , test . (1.01) Channel A queue between threads: mpsc::channel() gives a sender and a receiver. (6.01) Clippy Cargo's linter, cargo clippy , which suggests clearer or faster code. (6.04) Clone The trait for making an explicit deep copy with .clone() . (2.01) Closure An anonymous function that can capture variables from where it is written: \ x\ x + 1 . (5.01) Command std::process::Command : starts another program with arguments and collects its output. (7.04) Const generics Generic parameters that are values, such as an array size const N: usize (8.04) Consumer An iterator method that pulls the values out, such as collect , sum , count or for . (5.02) Copy The trait for small types copied bit for bit on assignment instead of moved, such as i32 and bool . (2.01) Cow Clone on write: holds either borrowed or owned data, allocating only when needed. (7.02) Crate A compilation unit: a library or a binary. Crates from crates.io are dependencies. (3.05) CStr A borrowed zero-terminated C string; CString is the owned form. (7.03) Data race Two threads touching the same memory at once with at least one writing; safe Rust rules them out. (6.02) Declarative macro A macro written with macro_rules! : rules that match input and produce code. (7.01) Deref coercion The automatic conversion of &String to &str , &Vec<T to & T and &Box<T to &T . (3.02) Derive derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq) : asking the compiler to write standard trait impls. (4.03) Doc comment A /// comment that becomes documentation; its code examples run as doc tests. (6.04) Drop The trait whose drop runs when a value goes out of scope; it frees what the value owns. (2.01) dyn Trait A trait object: a value of some type implementing the trait, chosen at run time. (4.05) Edition A set of language rules (2018, 2021, 2024) chosen per crate in Cargo.toml . (1.01) Enum A type whose value is one of several variants, each of which may carry data. (2.05) Error type A type (usually an enum) describing the ways a function can fail, implementing Display and std::error::Error (8.01) ErrorKind The category of an io::Error , such as NotFound or PermissionDenied . (7.04) ExitCode The status a program returns from main ; ExitCode::SUCCESS is 0. (7.04) Expression Code that produces a value; blocks, if and match are expressions in Rust. (1.03) extern "C" Declares functions that use the C calling convention. (7.03) FFI Foreign function interface: calling code written in other languages, usually C. (7.03) FnOnce, FnMut, Fn The closure traits: callable once (may consume captures), callable many times with changes, or without changes. (5.01) Fragment specifier The kind of input a macro variable matches, such as expr , ident , ty or tt . (7.01) FromStr The trait behind str::parse (8.02) Future A value that will produce a result later; it does nothing until polled by a runtime. (6.03) Generic Code written once for many types, with type parameters such as T . (4.01) HashMap A key-value map with fast lookup and no order. (3.03) Immutable Unchangeable; every variable is immutable unless declared mut . (1.02) impl Trait "Some type that implements this trait", in argument or return position. (4.02) Interior mutability Changing data behind a shared reference, checked at run time, as RefCell and Mutex do. (5.04) Iterator A trait with one required method, next , which returns Option<Item . (5.03) Lifetime The span of code a reference is valid for, written 'a when it must be named. (4.04) Lifetime elision The rules that let most functions leave lifetimes unwritten. (4.04) Macro Code that writes code, called with ! : println! , vec! , format! . (1.01) Macro hygiene Names created inside a macro do not clash with the caller's names. (7.01) Marker trait A trait with no methods, used to label types for generic code. (7.05) match Comparing a value against patterns; the compiler checks every case is covered. (2.05) Module A namespace inside a crate, declared with mod ; items are private unless pub . (3.05) Monomorphisation Compiling a separate copy of generic code for each concrete type used, so generics cost nothing at run time. (4.01) Move Transferring ownership; the old variable can no longer be used. (2.01) Mutex A lock that lets one thread at a time reach the data inside: lock() returns a guard. (6.02) Newtype A struct wrapping a single value to give it a distinct type and its own rules. (7.02) Operator trait A trait in std::ops, such as Add or Index, that gives a type an operator (8.02) Option Some(value) or None : Rust's replacement for null. (2.05) Orphan rule You may implement a trait for a type only if your crate owns the trait or the type. (4.02) Ownership Every value has one owner; when the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped. (2.01) Panic Stopping the thread because of a bug, such as an out-of-range index or unwrap on None . (3.04) Path A borrowed file system path; PathBuf is the owned form. (7.04) Pattern A shape to match against: literals, ranges, \ , bindings, @ , struct and tuple patterns, guards. (5.05) PhantomData A zero-size field that marks a type parameter as used without storing it. (7.05) Pin Pin<&mut T , a pointer that promises the value will not move; futures are polled through it. (6.03) Prelude The names every Rust file imports automatically, such as Vec , Option and String . (1.05) Procedural macro A Rust function that receives code as tokens and returns new code, used for derive . (7.01) Raw pointer const T or mut T : a pointer with no lifetime or validity guarantee. (7.03) Rc Rc<T , a reference-counted pointer for shared ownership within one thread. (5.04) Recursive descent Parsing with one function per grammar rule, where rules call each other (8.05) RefCell A cell that checks borrowing rules at run time, allowing changes through & . (5.04) Reference &T (shared, read-only) or &mut T (exclusive, may change): a pointer that borrows. (2.02) Result Ok(value) or Err(error) : how Rust functions report recoverable failure. (3.04) Safety contract The conditions a caller must uphold for an unsafe fn , written in its Safety section. (7.03) Scoped thread A thread started with thread::scope that may borrow local data, because it is joined before the scope ends. (6.01) Sealed trait A trait that code outside the crate cannot implement, thanks to a private supertrait. (7.05) Send The marker trait for types that may move to another thread. (6.02) Shadowing Declaring a new variable with an existing name, often to change its type. (1.02) Slice A view into part of a sequence: & T or &str . (2.03) Smart pointer A type that acts like a pointer and owns or manages its target: Box , Rc , Arc . (5.04) source() The Error method that returns the underlying error, forming a chain of causes (8.01) Statement Code that does something but produces no value; a trailing ; turns an expression into one. (1.03) String An owned, growable UTF-8 text buffer. (1.05) Struct A type that groups named fields. (2.04) Sync The marker trait for types that many threads may use through shared references at once. (6.02) The ? operator Returns early with the error from a Result (or None from an Option ), converting the error with From . (3.04) Tokenizer The part of a parser that turns characters into tokens (8.05) Trait A set of methods a type can implement; Rust's interfaces. (4.02) Trait bound A requirement on a type parameter, such as T: Display + Clone . (4.01) Trait object A dyn Trait value behind a pointer, called through a vtable. (4.05) TryFrom The trait for conversions that can fail, returning a Result (8.02) Turbofish ::<T , naming a generic type at the call: "5".parse::<i32 () . (4.01) Type-state Representing each state of an object as a different type, so wrong orders do not compile. (7.05) Unit type () , the type of "no meaningful value". (1.03) unsafe A block or function where five extra operations are allowed and the programmer guarantees safety. (7.03) unwrap Taking the value out of an Option or Result , panicking if there is none. (3.04) UTF-8 The encoding of Rust strings: a character takes 1 to 4 bytes, so strings are not indexed by number. (3.02) Vec Vec<T , a growable array on the heap. (3.01) VecDeque A double-ended queue, fast at both ends (8.03) Workspace Several crates built together with one Cargo.lock . (6.04)

title: 1.01  Handles, Errors and the Documentation
body: The Win32 API is thousands of C functions with their own conventions. This lesson explains handles, the Windows type names, how functions report errors through return values and GetLastError, turning error codes into messages, and how to read the documentation. A C API for everything The Win32 API (or Windows API) is how every Windows program talks to the system: windows, files, processes, threads, the registry, the clipboard. It is a C interface, so it works from C, C++, Rust, C and anything else that can call C functions. It has been extended for thirty years and is still how Windows itself is built. Everything comes from one header: cpp-norun define WIN32_LEAN_AND_MEAN // leave out rarely used parts, compiles faster define NOMINMAX // stop windows.h from defining min and max macros include <windows.h NOMINMAX matters in C++: without it, std::min and std::max collide with macros of the same name and produce baffling errors. The type names Windows has its own names for types, from a time before standard sized integers: Windows Meaning Standard C++ --- --- --- BYTE , WORD , DWORD 8, 16, 32-bit unsigned uint8_t , uint16_t , uint32_t BOOL An int used as true/false (not bool ) int UINT , LONG , ULONGLONG Unsigned int, 32-bit signed, 64-bit unsigned WPARAM , LPARAM , LRESULT Pointer-sized message parameters and results uintptr_t , intptr_t WCHAR , LPCWSTR , LPWSTR UTF-16 character, const and mutable string pointers wchar_t , const wchar_t HANDLE , HWND , HDC , HINSTANCE Handles (below) The LP prefix means "long pointer", a leftover from 16-bit Windows; C means const and W means wide (UTF-16). Handles A handle is an opaque value that refers to an object the system owns: a window ( HWND ), a file ( HANDLE ), a brush ( HBRUSH ), a module ( HMODULE ). You never look inside it; you pass it back to functions. Each kind is closed with its own function: Handle Created by Closed by --- --- --- File, thread, process, event CreateFileW , CreateThread , CreateEventW ... CloseHandle Window CreateWindowExW DestroyWindow GDI objects (pens, brushes, fonts, bitmaps) CreatePen , CreateSolidBrush ... DeleteObject Device context from GetDC GetDC ReleaseDC Loaded DLL LoadLibraryW FreeLibrary Forgetting to close handles is a leak : Task Manager's "Handles" and "GDI objects" columns show it growing. In C++, wrap each handle in a small RAII class (or std::unique_ptr with a custom deleter), so it is closed automatically: cpp-norun struct HandleCloser { void operator()(HANDLE h) const { if (h && h != INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE) CloseHandle(h); } }; using UniqueHandle = std::unique_ptr<void, HandleCloser ; UniqueHandle file{ CreateFileW(L"notes.txt", GENERIC_READ, FILE_SHARE_READ, nullptr, OPEN_EXISTING, 0, nullptr) }; Note the trap in that deleter: some functions return nullptr on failure, but CreateFileW returns INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE (-1). Always check the documentation's "Return value" section. Errors Most functions report failure in their return value ( FALSE , nullptr , INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE ) and store a detailed error code for the calling thread, which GetLastError() returns. Call it immediately : any later API call may overwrite it. cpp-norun HANDLE h = CreateFileW(L"missing.txt", GENERIC_READ, 0, nullptr, OPEN_EXISTING, 0, nullptr); if (h == INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE) { const DWORD error = GetLastError(); // 2 = ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND // ... } Common codes: 2 file not found, 3 path not found, 5 access denied, 32 sharing violation (another program has the file open), 87 invalid parameter, 183 already exists. Error codes to messages FormatMessageW turns a code into the system's text, in the user's language: cpp-norun std::wstring errorText(DWORD code) { wchar_t buffer = nullptr; const DWORD n = FormatMessageW(FORMAT_MESSAGE_ALLOCATE_BUFFER FORMAT_MESSAGE_FROM_SYSTEM FORMAT_MESSAGE_IGNORE_INSERTS, nullptr, code, 0, reinterpret_cast<wchar_t (&buffer), 0, nullptr); std::wstring text = n ? std::wstring(buffer, n) : L"Unknown error"; LocalFree(buffer); while (!text.empty() && (text.back() == L'\r' text.back() == L'\n')) text.pop_back(); // it ends in a line break return text; } COM-based APIs (lesson 3.02 onwards) return an HRESULT instead: negative means failure ( FAILED(hr) ), and HRESULT_FROM_WIN32(code) converts a Win32 error into one. The practice decodes both. Reading the documentation Every function has a page on Microsoft Learn with the same sections: the syntax (with in , out and in, optional on each parameter), return value (what failure looks like and whether GetLastError is set), remarks (the details that matter), and requirements (the header, the library to link, and the minimum Windows version). Read the remarks: they hold most of the surprises. Check yourself quiz ? What is a handle? - A pointer to the object's data that you can read and change directly + An opaque value for a system-owned object, closed by its type's own function - A numeric ID that every kind of object closes with CloseHandle - A copy of the object stored in your program's memory You never look inside a handle; you pass it back to the API. Each kind has its own closing function: CloseHandle for files, DestroyWindow for windows, DeleteObject for GDI objects. ? When must you call GetLastError ? - At the end of the function, after all the API calls are done - Before the call, to clear the previous error + Immediately after the call that failed, before any other API call - Only when the function returned nullptr Any later API call may overwrite the thread's last error code, so read it straight away, whatever form the failure return value takes. ? Why define NOMINMAX before including windows.h ? - It makes windows.h compile faster by leaving out rarely used parts - It turns on the standard std::min and std::max functions - It stops integer overflow checks in the Windows headers + Otherwise windows.h defines min and max macros that break std::min The macros collide with std::min , std::max and numeric_limits<T ::max() and give baffling errors. Leaving out rarely used parts is what WIN32_LEAN_AND_MEAN does.

title: HRESULTs and error codes
body: An HRESULT is a 32-bit value: the top bit is set for failure, bits 16-26 are the facility (7 means "a Win32 error code"), and the low 16 bits are the code . Write the helpers: cpp using DWORD = std::uint32_t; using HRESULT = std::int32_t; bool failed(HRESULT hr); HRESULT hresultFromWin32(DWORD error); int facility(HRESULT hr); // (hr 16) & 0x7FF int code(HRESULT hr); // hr & 0xFFFF std::string describe(HRESULT hr); std::string trimLineBreaks(std::string text); - hresultFromWin32 works like the Windows macro: 0 stays 0 (success); any other code becomes 0x80000000 (7 << 16) (error & 0xFFFF) . - describe gives "S_OK" for 0, "0x80070005 (Win32 error 5)" for a failure with facility 7, "0x80004005" for other failures, and "success 0x00000001" for other successes (hex with 8 lower-case digits). - trimLineBreaks removes every \r and \n from the end of a message, as FormatMessageW leaves them there.

title: 1.02  Strings on Windows
body: Windows uses UTF-16 internally, while files and the web mostly use UTF-8. This lesson explains the W and A versions of functions, wchar_t and L"" literals, surrogate pairs, converting between UTF-8 and UTF-16, and the UTF-8 code page option. W and A Most API functions that take text come in two versions: - CreateFileW , MessageBoxW , SetWindowTextW : W for wide, taking UTF-16 strings ( const wchar_t ). - CreateFileA , MessageBoxA : A for ANSI, taking 8-bit strings in the system's legacy code page. CreateFile without a letter is a macro that picks one depending on whether UNICODE is defined. Modern code calls the W functions explicitly: the A versions convert to UTF-16 internally anyway, and with a legacy code page they lose every character that page cannot represent (try a Japanese file name on an English system). wchar_t and L"..." On Windows, wchar_t is 16 bits and holds one UTF-16 code unit . String literals with an L prefix are wide: L"Grüße" . std::wstring is the matching string class. UTF-16 and surrogate pairs Unicode has more than a million possible code points; 16 bits hold 65 536 values. UTF-16 encodes: - code points up to U+FFFF (all common scripts) as one 16-bit unit; - code points above U+FFFF (emoji, rare scripts) as two units, a surrogate pair : a high surrogate 0xD800-0xDBFF followed by a low surrogate 0xDC00-0xDFFF . U+1F600 (😀): subtract 0x10000 → 0xF600, 20 bits: 0000 1111 0110 0000 0000 high = 0xD800 + (top 10 bits) = 0xD83D low = 0xDC00 + (low 10 bits) = 0xDE00 So wcslen counts code units, not characters: an emoji has length 2. Cursor movement in a text editor must skip both halves of a pair. UTF-8 UTF-8 encodes each code point in 1 to 4 bytes: Code points Bytes --- --- U+0000 - U+007F 0xxxxxxx U+0080 - U+07FF 110xxxxx 10xxxxxx U+0800 - U+FFFF 1110xxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx U+10000 - U+10FFFF 11110xxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx ASCII text is unchanged, which is why UTF-8 is the standard for files, the web and most libraries. Converting MultiByteToWideChar and WideCharToMultiByte convert, called twice: once to get the size, once to convert: cpp-norun std::wstring widen(std::string_view utf8) { if (utf8.empty()) return {}; const int n = MultiByteToWideChar(CP_UTF8, MB_ERR_INVALID_CHARS, utf8.data(), (int)utf8.size(), nullptr, 0); if (n == 0) throw std::runtime_error("invalid UTF-8"); std::wstring out(n, L'\0'); MultiByteToWideChar(CP_UTF8, MB_ERR_INVALID_CHARS, utf8.data(), (int)utf8.size(), out.data(), n); return out; } std::string narrow(std::wstring_view utf16) { if (utf16.empty()) return {}; const int n = WideCharToMultiByte(CP_UTF8, WC_ERR_INVALID_CHARS, utf16.data(), (int)utf16.size(), nullptr, 0, nullptr, nullptr); std::string out(n, '\0'); WideCharToMultiByte(CP_UTF8, WC_ERR_INVALID_CHARS, utf16.data(), (int)utf16.size(), out.data(), n, nullptr, nullptr); return out; } A good rule for a program: keep strings in UTF-8 ( std::string ) inside the program and in files, and convert to UTF-16 at the boundary, right where you call a W function. The practice writes these conversions by hand, to understand exactly what happens to every byte, including invalid input. Invalid input Not every byte sequence is valid UTF-8, and not every wchar_t sequence is valid UTF-16 (a lone surrogate is invalid, and Windows file names can contain them). The usual answer is to replace each invalid part with U+FFFD (�, the replacement character) rather than fail or, worse, silently drop data. The UTF-8 code page Since Windows 10 version 1903, an application manifest (lesson 6.02) can set activeCodePage to UTF-8 . The A functions then take UTF-8, and fopen , std::ifstream and the console understand UTF-8 paths. It is a good option for porting code from Linux; for new Windows code, the W functions remain the clearest choice. Check yourself quiz ? Why call the W functions explicitly? + They take UTF-16 and keep every character; A versions can lose some - They are faster because they skip the UNICODE macro - The A functions only exist on 32-bit Windows - The W functions take UTF-8, which matches the files you read The A versions convert to UTF-16 internally anyway, and characters the legacy code page cannot represent are lost. W functions take UTF-16, not UTF-8. ? What is a surrogate pair? - Two bytes of UTF-8 that encode one character above U+007F - A wchar_t value and its L"" literal form in source code + Two UTF-16 code units that together encode a code point above U+FFFF - A W function and the A function with the same name Code points above U+FFFF, such as emoji, do not fit in one 16-bit unit, so UTF-16 uses a high unit (0xD800-0xDBFF) and a low unit (0xDC00-0xDFFF). That is why wcslen gives 2 for one emoji. ? Where should a program convert between UTF-8 and UTF-16? - Once, when the program starts, converting every string to UTF-16 - Inside every function that handles text - Only when writing files + At the boundary, right where it calls a W function, keeping UTF-8 everywhere else Keep std::string in UTF-8 inside the program and in files, and widen only where a W function needs UTF-16.

title: UTF-8 and UTF-16 by hand
body: Write the two conversions MultiByteToWideChar and WideCharToMultiByte do, replacing invalid input with U+FFFD: cpp std::u16string utf8ToUtf16(const std::string& utf8); std::string utf16ToUtf8(const std::u16string& utf16); std::size_t codePoints(const std::u16string& utf16); // characters, counting a surrogate pair once UTF-8 to UTF-16 : decode each sequence (lesson 1.02's table) and encode the code point as one unit, or as a surrogate pair above U+FFFF. A sequence is invalid if the lead byte is not a valid lead (a continuation byte 10xxxxxx , or 0xF8 and above), a continuation byte is missing, the value is overlong (could have been encoded in fewer bytes), it is a surrogate (U+D800-U+DFFF), or it is above U+10FFFF. For an invalid sequence, output one U+FFFD and continue with the byte after the lead byte . UTF-16 to UTF-8 : a high surrogate followed by a low surrogate is one code point; a surrogate on its own becomes U+FFFD (encoded as EF BF BD ).

title: 1.03  Windows, Classes and the Message Loop
match: 1.03 Windows, Classes and the Message Loop
body: The smallest real Windows program - registering a window class, creating a window, running the message loop, and writing the window procedure that handles messages. This lesson builds it line by line and explains each step. The whole program cpp-norun define WIN32_LEAN_AND_MEAN define NOMINMAX include <windows.h LRESULT CALLBACK WndProc(HWND hwnd, UINT msg, WPARAM wParam, LPARAM lParam) { switch (msg) { case WM_DESTROY: PostQuitMessage(0); // ends the message loop return 0; } return DefWindowProcW(hwnd, msg, wParam, lParam); // default handling for everything else } int WINAPI wWinMain(HINSTANCE instance, HINSTANCE, PWSTR commandLine, int showCommand) { // 1. Describe a kind of window. WNDCLASSEXW wc{ sizeof(wc) }; wc.lpfnWndProc = WndProc; wc.hInstance = instance; wc.hCursor = LoadCursorW(nullptr, IDC_ARROW); wc.hbrBackground = reinterpret_cast<HBRUSH (COLOR_WINDOW + 1); wc.lpszClassName = L"XenonMainWindow"; if (!RegisterClassExW(&wc)) return 1; // 2. Create one. HWND hwnd = CreateWindowExW(0, L"XenonMainWindow", L"Hello, Windows", WS_OVERLAPPEDWINDOW, CW_USEDEFAULT, CW_USEDEFAULT, 800, 500, nullptr, nullptr, instance, nullptr); if (!hwnd) return 1; ShowWindow(hwnd, showCommand); // 3. Run the message loop. MSG msg; while (GetMessageW(&msg, nullptr, 0, 0) 0) { TranslateMessage(&msg); // turns key presses into WM_CHAR messages DispatchMessageW(&msg); // calls the window procedure } return static_cast<int (msg.wParam); } In Visual Studio, create a Windows Desktop Application (or an empty project with SubSystem set to Windows) so wWinMain is the entry point. Step 1: the window class A window class describes a kind of window: which window procedure handles its messages, its cursor, its background brush, its icon. Every window belongs to a class. RegisterClassExW registers it under a name, once per program. Buttons, edit boxes and list boxes are windows of classes Windows registers for you ( L"BUTTON" , L"EDIT" ), which is how controls work (lesson 2.05). COLOR_WINDOW + 1 is an odd convention: a system colour index plus one, cast to a brush, tells Windows to paint the background in the user's window colour. Step 2: creating the window CreateWindowExW takes the extended style, class name, title, style , position, size, parent, menu, instance and a user pointer. WS_OVERLAPPEDWINDOW is the usual top-level window with a title bar, border, and minimise, maximise and close buttons. CW_USEDEFAULT lets Windows choose the position. The size includes the border and title bar. To get a client area (the inside) of exactly 800 × 500, compute the outer size first with AdjustWindowRectEx (or AdjustWindowRectExForDpi , lesson 3.04). Step 3: the message loop Windows does not call your code directly when something happens. It puts a message in your thread's message queue : a key was pressed, the mouse moved, the window must be repainted. The loop takes messages out one by one: - GetMessageW waits until there is a message and returns it. It returns 0 for WM_QUIT (the loop ends) and -1 on error, which is why the loop tests 0 rather than just "true". - TranslateMessage creates character messages from key messages (lesson 2.01). - DispatchMessageW calls the window procedure of the window the message is for. Step 4: the window procedure The window procedure ( WndProc ) is called with each message: the window, the message number ( WM_... ), and two parameters whose meaning depends on the message. It returns a result whose meaning also depends on the message. Anything you do not handle goes to DefWindowProcW , which implements standard behaviour: moving and resizing the window, the system menu, closing on Alt+F4, and so on. Forgetting to call it for unhandled messages gives a window that cannot even be moved. Closing Clicking the close button sends WM_CLOSE ; the default handling calls DestroyWindow , which sends WM_DESTROY . The main window handles WM_DESTROY by calling PostQuitMessage(0) , which posts WM_QUIT , which makes GetMessageW return 0 and the loop end. To ask "save changes?" before closing, handle WM_CLOSE and only call DestroyWindow if the user agrees. Check yourself quiz ? What is a window class? - A C++ class you derive from to make your own window + A registered description of a kind of window, with its window procedure - One window created with CreateWindowExW , and its handle - The style flags, such as WS_OVERLAPPEDWINDOW , a window uses RegisterClassExW registers it once under a name, with its window procedure, cursor and background, and every window belongs to one. It is not a C++ class, and many windows can share it. ? Why does the message loop test GetMessageW(...) 0 ? - GetMessageW returns the number of messages left in the queue - A negative value means a message was skipped and the loop should go on + It returns 0 for WM_QUIT and -1 for an error; both must end the loop - It returns 1 only for messages that need DispatchMessageW Testing just "true" would keep looping on -1, because -1 is non-zero. ? What happens if the window procedure does not call DefWindowProcW for unhandled messages? - Nothing: unhandled messages are simply ignored, which is fine - The program crashes on the first message - Windows calls DefWindowProcW itself after the procedure returns + The window loses standard behaviour such as moving, resizing and closing DefWindowProcW implements the standard behaviour; without it you get a window that cannot even be moved.

title: Window sizes and positions
where: 1.03 Windows, Classes and the Message Loop
body: Lesson 1.03's CreateWindowExW takes the outer size of a window, but programs think in client sizes. Write simplified versions of the sizing helpers: cpp struct RECT { long left, top, right, bottom; }; struct Frame { int border; int caption; int menu; }; // thickness in pixels; 0 for "none" RECT adjustWindowRect(RECT client, Frame f); // like AdjustWindowRectEx RECT centredIn(RECT work, int width, int height); RECT keepOnScreen(RECT window, RECT work); - adjustWindowRect : the border surrounds the window on all four sides; the caption and then the menu bar are above the client area, inside the border. - centredIn : a rectangle of that size centred in work (the monitor's area without the taskbar), rounding the left and top down (towards minus infinity). - keepOnScreen : if the window is larger than the work area on an axis, it shrinks to the work area's size on that axis; then it moves (keeping its size) the least distance needed to be entirely inside. Remember that right and bottom are exclusive: width is right - left .

title: 1.04  Messages in Depth
body: How messages really flow - posted versus sent messages, the order of messages when a window is created and destroyed, how WPARAM and LPARAM pack several values, storing per-window data, and custom messages of your own. Posted and sent There are two ways a message reaches a window procedure: Posted Sent --- --- --- Function PostMessageW SendMessageW Goes Into the queue; the loop dispatches it later Straight to the window procedure (on its thread) Returns Immediately, before it is handled After it is handled, with the procedure's result Typical Input, WM_PAINT , WM_TIMER , WM_QUIT , your own notifications WM_CREATE , WM_SIZE , WM_SETTEXT , asking a control a question SendMessageW is a function call through the window system. If the window belongs to another thread, the calling thread waits while that thread processes the message, which is how two threads can deadlock : each waiting for the other to answer. Use PostMessageW from worker threads (lesson 5.04). Some messages are never really in the queue: WM_PAINT , WM_TIMER and WM_MOUSEMOVE are produced on demand when the queue is otherwise empty, and repeated ones are combined. Ten invalidations before the next paint give one WM_PAINT . A window's life Creating a window sends, in order (among others): WM_NCCREATE , WM_NCCALCSIZE , WM_CREATE , then WM_SIZE and WM_MOVE as it gets its position, and WM_SHOWWINDOW when it is shown. Destroying it sends WM_DESTROY and, last of all, WM_NCDESTROY . "NC" means non-client : the frame and title bar. WM_CREATE is where a window creates its child controls and resources; WM_DESTROY is where it frees them. Packed parameters WPARAM and LPARAM are just numbers; each message defines what they hold. Often two 16-bit values are packed into one parameter: cpp-norun case WM_SIZE: { const int width = LOWORD(lParam); // low 16 bits const int height = HIWORD(lParam); // high 16 bits // wParam: SIZE_MAXIMIZED, SIZE_MINIMIZED, SIZE_RESTORED return 0; } case WM_LBUTTONDOWN: { const int x = GET_X_LPARAM(lParam); // from <windowsx.h ; SIGNED const int y = GET_Y_LPARAM(lParam); return 0; } Use GET_X_LPARAM rather than LOWORD for mouse positions: with several monitors, a position can be negative , and LOWORD would turn -1 into 65535. MAKELPARAM(lo, hi) packs two values for sending. The practice writes these macros as functions. Data for each window The window procedure is a free function, but a window usually belongs to a C++ object. The standard pattern passes this as the last argument of CreateWindowExW , picks it up in WM_NCCREATE , and stores it in the window with SetWindowLongPtrW(hwnd, GWLP_USERDATA, ...) : cpp-norun class MainWindow { public: static LRESULT CALLBACK Proc(HWND hwnd, UINT msg, WPARAM wParam, LPARAM lParam) { MainWindow self = nullptr; if (msg == WM_NCCREATE) { self = static_cast<MainWindow (reinterpret_cast<CREATESTRUCTW (lParam)- lpCreateParams); self- m_hwnd = hwnd; SetWindowLongPtrW(hwnd, GWLP_USERDATA, reinterpret_cast<LONG_PTR (self)); } else self = reinterpret_cast<MainWindow (GetWindowLongPtrW(hwnd, GWLP_USERDATA)); return self ? self- handle(msg, wParam, lParam) : DefWindowProcW(hwnd, msg, wParam, lParam); } private: LRESULT handle(UINT msg, WPARAM wParam, LPARAM lParam); // an ordinary member function HWND m_hwnd{}; }; // CreateWindowExW(..., instance, this); Messages before WM_NCCREATE (there is at least WM_GETMINMAXINFO ) arrive while the pointer is not yet stored, hence the null check. Your own messages For messages of your own, use numbers from WM_APP (0x8000) to 0xBFFF within your application: cpp-norun constexpr UINT WM_APP_SEARCH_DONE = WM_APP + 1; PostMessageW(hwnd, WM_APP_SEARCH_DONE, count, 0); // from a worker thread: "the search finished" WM_USER (0x0400 and up) is reserved for a window class's own private messages; controls use that range, so do not send WM_USER messages to windows you did not write. Between programs, RegisterWindowMessageW(L"name") gives a number unique across the system. Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference between PostMessageW and SendMessageW ? - Post is for other programs, Send is for your own windows + Post queues the message and returns; Send calls the procedure and waits - Send puts the message in the queue; Post calls the window procedure directly - They are the same, except that only Send returns an error code SendMessageW is a function call through the window system. From worker threads prefer Post: a Send to another thread waits for it and can deadlock. ? Why use GET_X_LPARAM instead of LOWORD for mouse positions? - LOWORD gives the y coordinate of the click, not the x - GET_X_LPARAM converts the position to screen coordinates + Positions can be negative on multi-monitor setups, and it keeps the sign - LOWORD only works for size messages such as WM_SIZE LOWORD treats the 16 bits as unsigned, so -1 becomes 65535; GET_X_LPARAM keeps the sign. ? How does a window procedure find the C++ object for a window? - It looks the HWND up in a table that Windows keeps for each program - DispatchMessageW passes this to it in the wParam argument - The window procedure is a normal member function, so this is available + Stored with SetWindowLongPtrW in WM_NCCREATE , read with GetWindowLongPtrW The pointer is passed to CreateWindowExW , arrives in CREATESTRUCTW::lpCreateParams and is stored in GWLP_USERDATA . The window procedure must be a free or static function, so there is no this .

title: Packing message parameters
body: Write lesson 1.04's parameter macros as functions, on 64-bit Windows types: cpp using WPARAM = std::uint64_t; using LPARAM = std::int64_t; using UINT = std::uint32_t; LPARAM makeLParam(int lo, int hi); // the low 16 bits of each, packed into the low 32 bits int loWord(LPARAM v); // unsigned: 0 .. 65535 int hiWord(LPARAM v); int getX(LPARAM v); // signed: -32768 .. 32767, like GET_X_LPARAM int getY(LPARAM v); std::string messageRange(UINT msg); messageRange names the range a message number belongs to: "system" below 0x0400 ( WM_USER ), "class" from 0x0400 to 0x7FFF , "app" from 0x8000 ( WM_APP ) to 0xBFFF , "registered" from 0xC000 to 0xFFFF , and "reserved" above.

title: 1.05  Painting with GDI
body: Windows asks a window to paint itself with WM_PAINT. This lesson handles it with BeginPaint and EndPaint, draws lines, shapes and text with GDI, manages pens, brushes and fonts without leaking them, and invalidates just the part of the window that changed. Windows does not remember your pixels When a window is uncovered, restored or resized, the system does not keep a copy of what was in it. It marks the area as invalid and sends WM_PAINT : the window must draw itself again. So every program keeps its state (the text, the shapes, the score) and paints from it, exactly like a game draws each frame from its data. WM_PAINT cpp-norun case WM_PAINT: { PAINTSTRUCT ps; HDC dc = BeginPaint(hwnd, &ps); // ps.rcPaint: the invalid rectangle RECT client; GetClientRect(hwnd, &client); DrawTextW(dc, L"Hello, GDI", -1, &client, DT_CENTER DT_VCENTER DT_SINGLELINE); EndPaint(hwnd, &ps); // validates the area return 0; } Always pair BeginPaint with EndPaint , even if you draw nothing: EndPaint marks the area valid. Without it, Windows keeps sending WM_PAINT forever and the program uses a whole CPU core. HDC is a device context : a drawing surface with its current pen, brush, font and colours. Outside WM_PAINT you can get one with GetDC / ReleaseDC , but painting belongs in WM_PAINT . Drawing Function Draws --- --- MoveToEx(dc, x, y, nullptr) , LineTo(dc, x, y) Lines with the current pen Rectangle(dc, l, t, r, b) , Ellipse , RoundRect , Polygon Outlined with the pen, filled with the brush FillRect(dc, &rect, brush) A filled rectangle, no outline TextOutW(dc, x, y, text, len) , DrawTextW(...) Text; DrawTextW can wrap and align in a rectangle SetTextColor , SetBkMode(dc, TRANSPARENT) Text colour, and no background box behind text Colours are COLORREF values made with RGB(r, g, b) . Note the byte order: RGB stores red in the lowest byte ( 0x00BBGGRR ), the opposite of the RRGGBB order in HTML. The practice packs and unpacks them. Coordinates are in pixels from the client area's top-left corner. A RECT 's right and bottom are exclusive : {0, 0, 10, 10} covers pixels 0 to 9. Pens, brushes and fonts GDI objects are selected into the device context, and the previous object must be put back before you delete yours: cpp-norun HPEN pen = CreatePen(PS_SOLID, 3, RGB(200, 40, 40)); HBRUSH brush = CreateSolidBrush(RGB(250, 230, 120)); HGDIOBJ oldPen = SelectObject(dc, pen); HGDIOBJ oldBrush = SelectObject(dc, brush); Ellipse(dc, 50, 50, 200, 150); SelectObject(dc, oldBrush); // put the originals back SelectObject(dc, oldPen); DeleteObject(brush); // now safe to delete DeleteObject(pen); Deleting an object while it is still selected fails silently, and the object leaks. A program that leaks a brush per paint eventually reaches the per-process limit of 10 000 GDI objects and stops drawing altogether. GetStockObject(BLACK_PEN) , WHITE_BRUSH and friends are system objects that never need deleting. Creating the pens and brushes you use often once, in WM_CREATE , is both faster and safer. Repainting what changed When the program's state changes, it does not paint directly. It invalidates the affected area and lets the next WM_PAINT do the work: cpp-norun InvalidateRect(hwnd, &changedRect, TRUE); // TRUE: erase the background first InvalidateRect(hwnd, nullptr, TRUE); // the whole client area Several invalidations before the next paint are combined into one region, and the paint's ps.rcPaint is the bounding rectangle of all of them; a careful program draws only what intersects it. UpdateWindow(hwnd) paints immediately instead of waiting for the queue to empty. Background erasing before each paint causes flicker on resizing; lesson 4.01 removes it with double buffering. Check yourself quiz ? Why must WM_PAINT always call EndPaint ? - It copies the drawing from memory to the screen + It validates the area; without it WM_PAINT keeps coming - It deletes the pens and brushes created during painting - It is only needed if the program actually drew something Pair BeginPaint with EndPaint even when you draw nothing; otherwise the area stays invalid and the program uses a whole CPU core. ? Why put the old object back before deleting a pen or brush? - SelectObject makes a copy, and the copy must be returned - Deleting it first changes the colour of everything already drawn + An object still selected into a device context cannot be deleted, so it would leak - Windows deletes the old object if you do not Deleting a selected object fails silently. Leaking one per paint eventually reaches the limit of 10 000 GDI objects. ? How should a program redraw when its state changes? - Call GetDC and draw at once wherever the state changed - Send itself WM_PAINT at once with SendMessageW + Call InvalidateRect on the changed area and paint in WM_PAINT - Wait until the user resizes or uncovers the window Several invalidations are combined into one paint, and all the drawing stays in one place, in WM_PAINT .

title: Colours and invalid rectangles

Anything else (missing , wrong length, a non-hex digit) is rejected.
