title: A model of the message queue
match: A model of the message queue
body: Build a small model of how Windows delivers messages, to understand exactly what the message loop of lesson 1.03 sees: posted and sent messages, WM_QUIT , WM_PAINT that keeps coming until the window is validated, timers whose missed ticks combine, and destroying windows. cpp using HWND = int; using UINT = std::uint32_t; using WPARAM = std::uint64_t; using LPARAM = std::int64_t; using LRESULT = std::int64_t; constexpr UINT WM_DESTROY = 0x0002, WM_PAINT = 0x000F, WM_CLOSE = 0x0010, WM_QUIT = 0x0012, WM_TIMER = 0x0113, WM_APP = 0x8000; struct MSG { HWND hwnd; UINT message; WPARAM wParam; LPARAM lParam; }; class Desktop { public: using Proc = std::function<LRESULT(Desktop&, HWND, UINT, WPARAM, LPARAM) ; HWND createWindow(Proc proc); bool isWindow(HWND hwnd) const; bool destroyWindow(HWND hwnd); LRESULT sendMessage(HWND hwnd, UINT msg, WPARAM w, LPARAM l); bool postMessage(HWND hwnd, UINT msg, WPARAM w, LPARAM l); void postQuitMessage(int code); void invalidate(HWND hwnd); void validate(HWND hwnd); void setTimer(HWND hwnd, UINT id, int periodMs); void killTimer(HWND hwnd, UINT id); void advance(int ms); bool peekMessage(MSG& out); int run(); LRESULT defWindowProc(HWND hwnd, UINT msg, WPARAM w, LPARAM l); }; Windows : createWindow returns handles 1, 2, 3, ... in order. destroyWindow first sends WM_DESTROY to the window, then removes it together with its timers, its invalid state and the messages still posted to it; it returns false for something that is not a window. Sending and posting : sendMessage calls the window procedure straight away and returns its result (0 for a non-window). postMessage queues the message (false for a non-window). postQuitMessage remembers that a quit was requested, with its code. peekMessage removes and returns the next message, in this order (a simplified version of the real order): 1. the oldest posted message; 2. WM_QUIT (hwnd 0, wParam = the code) if a quit was requested; the request is then forgotten; 3. WM_PAINT for the lowest-numbered invalid window. It is not removed by being returned: the window stays invalid, and keeps getting WM_PAINT , until validate is called; 4. WM_TIMER ( wParam = the timer id) for a due timer: one whose next time is at or before the clock. With several due, the one due earliest (then the lower window, then the lower id). Returning it sets the timer's next time to now + period , so ticks missed while the program was busy become a single WM_TIMER . setTimer (re)starts a timer that is first due one period from now; the clock starts at 0 and only advance moves it. run is the message loop: peek a message; on WM_QUIT , return its code; otherwise call the window procedure (if the window still exists). If no message is available, return -1 (a real loop would wait forever). defWindowProc : WM_CLOSE destroys the window, WM_PAINT validates it; it returns 0.

title: 2.01  Keyboard Input
body: Keys arrive as WM_KEYDOWN and WM_KEYUP with virtual-key codes, text arrives as WM_CHAR after TranslateMessage. This lesson explains the difference, the information packed into lParam, auto-repeat, modifier keys, system keys and keyboard focus. Keys and characters Pressing Shift+A produces several messages: Message Means wParam --- --- --- WM_KEYDOWN Shift went down VK_SHIFT WM_KEYDOWN A went down 'A' (the virtual key) WM_CHAR The character "A" was typed L'A' (a UTF-16 unit) WM_KEYUP A went up 'A' WM_KEYUP Shift went up VK_SHIFT Key messages tell you which physical key moved, as a virtual-key code : 'A' to 'Z' , '0' to '9' , VK_LEFT , VK_RETURN , VK_F5 , VK_CONTROL and so on. They are for commands : arrows to move, Delete to delete, F5 to refresh. Character messages tell you which text the user typed, after the keyboard layout, Shift, Caps Lock and dead keys (é from ´ then e) are applied. They are for text input . TranslateMessage in the message loop makes them; leave it out and no WM_CHAR ever arrives. Characters above U+FFFF arrive as two WM_CHAR messages, one per surrogate (lesson 1.02). Never build text from WM_KEYDOWN : it knows nothing about layouts, so a French or German user gets the wrong letters. What lParam holds For key messages, lParam packs details of the keystroke: Bits Meaning --- --- 0 - 15 Repeat count (auto-repeat may combine several) 16 - 23 Scan code (the physical key's hardware code) 24 Extended key (right Ctrl, right Alt, arrow keys of the separate block, Insert/Delete ...) 29 Context code: Alt was down (for WM_SYSKEYDOWN ) 30 Previous key state: 1 if the key was already down (this is an auto-repeat) 31 Transition state: 0 for down, 1 for up Bit 30 is the useful one: holding a key sends WM_KEYDOWN again and again, and bit 30 tells a first press apart from repeats. A game-style "jump once per press" checks it. The practice decodes all the fields. Modifier keys To know whether Ctrl or Shift is held when a key arrives, ask: cpp-norun const bool ctrl = GetKeyState(VK_CONTROL) < 0; // high bit set = down const bool shift = GetKeyState(VK_SHIFT) < 0; GetKeyState gives the state as of the message being processed , which is what you want inside a window procedure. GetAsyncKeyState gives the state right now, which may differ if the program is behind; it is for polling, not for handling messages. Left and right versions exist ( VK_LSHIFT , VK_RSHIFT ) when it matters. System keys Keys pressed with Alt held, and F10, arrive as WM_SYSKEYDOWN / WM_SYSKEYUP / WM_SYSCHAR instead. DefWindowProcW uses them for the menu (Alt opens it, Alt+F opens File) and for Alt+F4. If you handle Alt combinations yourself, still pass the messages you do not use to DefWindowProcW , or Alt+F4 stops working. Focus Keyboard messages go to the window with the keyboard focus : one window in the system at a time. Clicking a control gives it the focus; SetFocus(hwnd) moves it in code. A window learns it gained or lost focus through WM_SETFOCUS and WM_KILLFOCUS : a text editor creates its caret ( CreateCaret , ShowCaret ) on the first and destroys it on the second. When a top-level window is reactivated, it should give the focus back to the control that had it, which dialogs do automatically (lesson 3.01). Check yourself quiz ? When do you use WM_KEYDOWN and when WM_CHAR ? - WM_KEYDOWN for typed text, WM_CHAR for arrow keys and shortcuts + WM_KEYDOWN for commands tied to physical keys; WM_CHAR for typed text, which respects the keyboard layout - WM_CHAR for everything; WM_KEYDOWN is only sent when TranslateMessage is left out - WM_KEYDOWN for letters and digits, WM_CHAR for punctuation Virtual-key codes know nothing about layouts, so text built from WM_KEYDOWN gives a French or German user the wrong letters. WM_CHAR exists only because TranslateMessage makes it. ? How do you tell an auto-repeat from a first press? - Bit 31 of lParam is 1 for repeats - The repeat count in bits 0-15 is 0 for a first press - Auto-repeats arrive as WM_CHAR only, never as WM_KEYDOWN + Bit 30 of lParam is 1 if the key was already down Bit 30 is the previous key state. Bit 31 is the transition state, which tells down (0) from up (1), not first press from repeat. ? Why must WM_SYSKEYDOWN messages you do not use go to DefWindowProcW ? + It implements the menu keys and Alt+F4 - Otherwise the keyboard focus moves to the desktop - TranslateMessage needs them to make WM_CHAR - They hold the Shift and Ctrl state for later key messages Alt combinations and F10 arrive as system keys; swallowing them stops Alt from opening the menu and Alt+F4 from closing the window.

title: Inside a key message
body: Decode and build the lParam of WM_KEYDOWN and WM_KEYUP (lesson 2.01's table), and name virtual keys: cpp using LPARAM = std::int64_t; struct KeyInfo { int repeat; int scanCode; bool extended; bool altDown; bool wasDown; bool released; }; KeyInfo decodeKey(LPARAM lParam); LPARAM encodeKey(const KeyInfo& k); bool isFirstPress(LPARAM lParam); // a key-down that is not an auto-repeat std::string keyName(int vk); keyName : 'A' - 'Z' and '0' - '9' are themselves; 0x70 - 0x87 are F1 - F24 ; 0x08 Backspace, 0x09 Tab, 0x0D Enter, 0x1B Esc, 0x20 Space, 0x21 PageUp, 0x22 PageDown, 0x23 End, 0x24 Home, 0x25 Left, 0x26 Up, 0x27 Right, 0x28 Down, 0x2D Insert, 0x2E Delete; anything else "0x" and two upper-case hex digits (such as 0xBA ).

title: 2.02  Mouse Input and Capture
body: Handling clicks, double-clicks, movement and the wheel, the modifier flags that come with them, capturing the mouse during a drag, knowing when the mouse leaves, setting the cursor, and hit-testing your own shapes. Mouse messages Message When --- --- WM_LBUTTONDOWN / UP , WM_RBUTTON... , WM_MBUTTON... , WM_XBUTTON... A button changes WM_LBUTTONDBLCLK A second click soon after the first (only if the class has CS_DBLCLKS ) WM_MOUSEMOVE The mouse moved over the client area WM_MOUSEWHEEL , WM_MOUSEHWHEEL The wheel turned (vertically, horizontally) WM_MOUSELEAVE The mouse left the window (after you asked for it) The position is in lParam , in client coordinates, read with GET_X_LPARAM / GET_Y_LPARAM (lesson 1.04). wParam holds flags for what else is down: MK_LBUTTON , MK_RBUTTON , MK_SHIFT , MK_CONTROL , MK_MBUTTON . A double-click arrives as down, up, double-click , up: the first click is delivered as an ordinary click first. Design double-click actions so the single click before them does no harm (select on click, open on double-click). The wheel WM_MOUSEWHEEL is different from the others: its position is in screen coordinates (convert with ScreenToClient ), and the amount is in the high word of wParam , signed, in multiples of WHEEL_DELTA (120) per notch: cpp-norun case WM_MOUSEWHEEL: { m_wheelRemainder += GET_WHEEL_DELTA_WPARAM(wParam); const int notches = m_wheelRemainder / WHEEL_DELTA; m_wheelRemainder -= notches WHEEL_DELTA; scrollLines(-notches 3); return 0; } Precision touchpads send small values such as 15 or 30. Accumulating the remainder, as above, keeps slow scrolling working instead of throwing every small movement away. The practice writes this accumulator. Capturing the mouse When the user presses the button inside your window and drags outside it, WM_MOUSEMOVE and the button-up go to whatever window is under the mouse, not yours. A drag (moving a slider, selecting text, drawing a line) needs capture : cpp-norun case WM_LBUTTONDOWN: SetCapture(hwnd); m_dragging = true; m_start = pointFrom(lParam); return 0; case WM_MOUSEMOVE: if (m_dragging) { m_end = pointFrom(lParam); InvalidateRect(hwnd, nullptr, FALSE); } return 0; case WM_LBUTTONUP: if (m_dragging) { ReleaseCapture(); } return 0; case WM_CAPTURECHANGED: m_dragging = false; return 0; // capture lost, for any reason While captured, every mouse message comes to your window, even from outside it, with positions that can be negative or beyond the client size. Handle WM_CAPTURECHANGED to end the drag cleanly: the system can take capture away (an Alt+Tab, a pop-up), and then no button-up will ever arrive. Knowing when the mouse leaves To highlight something on hover, you need to know when the mouse leaves . Ask for one WM_MOUSELEAVE with TrackMouseEvent , and ask again after each one: cpp-norun case WM_MOUSEMOVE: if (!m_tracking) { TRACKMOUSEEVENT t{ sizeof(t), TME_LEAVE, hwnd, 0 }; TrackMouseEvent(&t); m_tracking = true; } updateHover(pointFrom(lParam)); return 0; case WM_MOUSELEAVE: m_tracking = false; clearHover(); return 0; The cursor The class's cursor ( wc.hCursor ) is shown by default. To change it depending on what is under the mouse (a resize arrow over a splitter, a hand over a link), handle WM_SETCURSOR : cpp-norun case WM_SETCURSOR: if (LOWORD(lParam) == HTCLIENT && overSplitter()) { SetCursor(LoadCursorW(nullptr, IDC_SIZEWE)); return TRUE; } break; // let DefWindowProcW set the normal cursor Hit-testing The window only tells you a point; deciding what is under it is your job: test the point against your shapes from the topmost down, and the first hit wins. Rectangles use lesson 1.05's exclusive right and bottom edges; circles compare squared distances. Check yourself quiz ? Why is mouse capture needed for dragging? - Without it WM_MOUSEMOVE is never sent while a button is held - It hides the cursor during the drag so the movement looks smooth + Once the cursor leaves, the button-up can go to another window - It converts the mouse positions to screen coordinates for you Without capture, mouse messages go to whatever window is under the cursor. With SetCapture , every mouse message comes to your window even from outside it, with positions that can be negative or beyond the client size. ? What is special about WM_MOUSEWHEEL 's position and amount? - The position is in client coordinates and the amount is always exactly 120 + Screen coordinates, and a signed amount in WHEEL_DELTA (120) units or finer - The position is in wParam and the amount in lParam - The amount is the number of lines to scroll, set by the user in Settings Convert the position with ScreenToClient . Precision touchpads send small values such as 15, so accumulate the remainder rather than dividing each message by 120. ? Why handle WM_CAPTURECHANGED ? - It is the only message that tells you the drag started - It arrives instead of WM_LBUTTONUP when capture is on - It is needed before the program can call ReleaseCapture + The system can take capture away, and the button-up then never arrives An Alt+Tab or a pop-up can end the capture; ending the drag in WM_CAPTURECHANGED keeps the program from staying stuck in "dragging".

title: Wheels, hits and drags
body: Three pieces of mouse handling from lesson 2.02: cpp struct Shape { int id; bool circle; int x, y, w, h; }; // circle: centre (x, y), radius w class Wheel { public: int add(int delta); // whole notches (WHEEL_DELTA = 120) to act on now, keeping the rest }; int hitTest(const std::vector<Shape & shapes, int x, int y); // topmost = last in the list; -1 for none class Drag { public: explicit Drag(int threshold); void down(int x, int y); void move(int x, int y); bool up(int x, int y); // true if this ended a real drag (not a click) void captureLost(); // the drag is cancelled bool dragging() const; // past the threshold and not ended std::string state() const; // "idle", "pressed" or "dragging" }; - Wheel::add accumulates the signed delta and returns the whole notches in it, rounding towards zero, keeping the remainder (with its sign). - hitTest : rectangles are x .. x + w , y .. y + h with exclusive right and bottom; circles include points at a distance up to the radius. Return the id of the topmost shape containing the point. - Drag : after down it is "pressed". A move farther than threshold pixels from the down point on either axis (strictly more) makes it "dragging", and it stays dragging until up or captureLost . up returns true only if it was dragging, and returns to "idle". Moves while idle do nothing.

title: 2.03  Timers and the Clock
body: Doing things later or repeatedly with SetTimer and WM_TIMER, why timers are not precise, measuring time with QueryPerformanceCounter, the system clock and time zones, and running animation without freezing the interface. SetTimer A timer sends WM_TIMER to a window repeatedly: cpp-norun constexpr UINT_PTR TIMER_BLINK = 1; SetTimer(hwnd, TIMER_BLINK, 500, nullptr); // every 500 ms // ... case WM_TIMER: if (wParam == TIMER_BLINK) { m_caretVisible = !m_caretVisible; invalidateCaret(); } return 0; // ... KillTimer(hwnd, TIMER_BLINK); // e.g. in WM_DESTROY Calling SetTimer again with the same window and id restarts that timer with the new period. A one-shot "do this in two seconds" is a timer that kills itself in its first WM_TIMER . Timers are not precise WM_TIMER is a low-priority message, generated only when the queue has nothing else (like WM_PAINT , lesson 1.04's practice model): - The default resolution is about 15.6 ms : a 10 ms timer fires roughly every 15.6 ms. - If the program is busy, ticks are combined : after a 2-second pause, a 100 ms timer fires once, not twenty times. - So never count ticks to measure time. A countdown that does remaining -= 100 on each tick runs slow; one that checks the real clock is always right. Measuring time For measuring durations, use the high-resolution counter: cpp-norun LARGE_INTEGER frequency, start, now; QueryPerformanceFrequency(&frequency); // counts per second, fixed at boot QueryPerformanceCounter(&start); // ... work ... QueryPerformanceCounter(&now); const double seconds = double(now.QuadPart - start.QuadPart) / double(frequency.QuadPart); It is monotonic (never jumps backwards) and has sub-microsecond resolution. std::chrono::steady_clock is the portable way to the same counter. To convert counts to milliseconds without overflow or loss of precision, split into whole seconds and the remainder; the practice does exactly that. GetTickCount64() gives milliseconds since boot at the 15.6 ms resolution: fine for timeouts, too coarse for measuring. Wall-clock time The time of day is a different thing: it can jump when the user changes the clock, the computer syncs with a time server, or daylight saving changes. - GetSystemTimeAsFileTime gives the current time in UTC as a FILETIME : 100-nanosecond intervals since 1 January 1601 . - FileTimeToSystemTime breaks it into year, month, day, hour ...; SystemTimeToTzSpecificLocalTime converts UTC to local time. - Store and compare times in UTC, and convert to local time only to show them. Converting between FILETIME and Unix time (seconds since 1970) is a fixed offset: 11 644 473 600 seconds between 1601 and 1970. Animation Animating with a timer: on each WM_TIMER , compute the animation's state from the elapsed real time , not from the number of ticks, and invalidate. Then it runs at the right speed whatever the timer actually does: cpp-norun case WM_TIMER: { const double t = secondsSince(m_animStart); m_offset = easeOut(std::min(t / 0.25, 1.0)) m_distance; if (t = 0.25) KillTimer(hwnd, TIMER_ANIM); InvalidateRect(hwnd, nullptr, FALSE); return 0; } For smooth animation at the display's refresh rate, draw with Direct2D (milestone 4) and use DwmFlush or the swap chain's frame timing rather than WM_TIMER . Never block the loop Sleep(2000) in a window procedure freezes the whole window for two seconds: no painting, no input, and after about five seconds Windows marks it "Not responding". Anything that takes time goes to a timer (if it can be split into small steps) or a worker thread (lesson 5.04). Check yourself quiz ? Why should you not measure time by counting WM_TIMER messages? - WM_TIMER is a sent message, so it interrupts painting + Timers are imprecise and missed ticks are combined, so the count drifts from real time - Each timer can fire only 100 times before it must be restarted - Counting ticks is accurate, but slower than reading the clock The default resolution is about 15.6 ms, and after a busy pause a timer fires once instead of many times. Compute elapsed time from a real clock. ? What does QueryPerformanceCounter measure? - The time of day in UTC, in 100-nanosecond units - Milliseconds since boot, at about 15.6 ms resolution + A high-resolution count since boot that never goes backwards - The CPU time your process has used so far It has sub-microsecond resolution; divide by QueryPerformanceFrequency to get seconds. Milliseconds at 15.6 ms resolution is GetTickCount64 ; the UTC time of day is GetSystemTimeAsFileTime . ? Why store times in UTC? - UTC values are smaller and take less space - FILETIME cannot hold local times - Local time cannot be shown to the user without converting it first + Local time jumps with time zones and daylight saving; UTC does not, so it compares correctly Store and compare in UTC, and convert to local time only to show it.

title: Counters and calendars
body: Write the time conversions of lesson 2.03: cpp std::int64_t countsToMicroseconds(std::int64_t counts, std::int64_t frequency); std::int64_t fileTimeToUnixMs(std::uint64_t fileTime); // 100 ns units since 1601-01-01 UTC std::uint64_t unixMsToFileTime(std::int64_t unixMs); std::string formatUtc(std::uint64_t fileTime); // "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS" - countsToMicroseconds must not overflow for large counts (such as a counter of 10 000 000 per second after 30 days of uptime): split the counts into whole seconds and the remainder before multiplying. Round down. - Between 1601 and 1970 there are 11 644 473 600 seconds. fileTimeToUnixMs rounds down to the millisecond (towards minus infinity for times before 1970). - formatUtc converts the file time to a date and time in the Gregorian calendar (leap years: divisible by 4, except centuries, except every 400 years). Times are never before 1601.

title: 2.04  Menus, Accelerators and Resources
body: Adding a menu bar and context menus, handling WM_COMMAND, enabling and checking items as the program's state changes, keyboard shortcuts with accelerator tables, and the resource file that holds menus, icons, strings and version information. Resources A resource file ( .rc ) describes data that is compiled into the .exe : menus, icons, cursors, dialogs, string tables, version information. Visual Studio has editors for them; the text format is simple: cpp-norun // resource.h define IDR_MAINMENU 101 define IDR_ACCEL 102 define IDI_APP 103 define ID_FILE_NEW 40001 define ID_FILE_OPEN 40002 define ID_FILE_SAVE 40003 define ID_FILE_EXIT 40004 define ID_VIEW_STATUS 40010 // app.rc include "resource.h" IDI_APP ICON "app.ico" IDR_MAINMENU MENU BEGIN POPUP "&File" BEGIN MENUITEM "&New\tCtrl+N", ID_FILE_NEW MENUITEM "&Open...\tCtrl+O", ID_FILE_OPEN MENUITEM "&Save\tCtrl+S", ID_FILE_SAVE MENUITEM SEPARATOR MENUITEM "E&xit", ID_FILE_EXIT END POPUP "&View" BEGIN MENUITEM "&Status Bar", ID_VIEW_STATUS, CHECKED END END & marks the letter underlined for Alt navigation (Alt, F, S saves). \t separates the shortcut text shown on the right; it is only text: the shortcut itself comes from the accelerator table below. "..." means the item opens a dialog before doing anything. Load the menu by giving the class wc.lpszMenuName = MAKEINTRESOURCEW(IDR_MAINMENU) , or with LoadMenuW and SetMenu . WM_COMMAND Choosing a menu item sends WM_COMMAND with the item's id in LOWORD(wParam) : cpp-norun case WM_COMMAND: switch (LOWORD(wParam)) { case ID_FILE_NEW: newDocument(); return 0; case ID_FILE_SAVE: save(); return 0; case ID_FILE_EXIT: SendMessageW(hwnd, WM_CLOSE, 0, 0); return 0; // the same path as the close button } break; HIWORD(wParam) tells where the command came from: 0 for a menu, 1 for an accelerator, or a notification code for a control (lesson 2.05). Keeping items up to date "Save" should be greyed out when there is nothing to save, and "Status Bar" should show a check mark when the bar is visible. Update the items just before the menu opens, in WM_INITMENUPOPUP , from the program's state: cpp-norun case WM_INITMENUPOPUP: { HMENU menu = reinterpret_cast<HMENU (wParam); EnableMenuItem(menu, ID_FILE_SAVE, MF_BYCOMMAND (m_doc.dirty ? MF_ENABLED : MF_GRAYED)); CheckMenuItem(menu, ID_VIEW_STATUS, MF_BYCOMMAND (m_statusVisible ? MF_CHECKED : MF_UNCHECKED)); return 0; } Deriving the menu's state from the program's state every time, instead of updating items whenever something changes, means they can never get out of step. Context menus Right-clicking sends WM_CONTEXTMENU (also sent by the Menu key and Shift+F10, with position -1, -1: then show the menu at the selection instead): cpp-norun case WM_CONTEXTMENU: { HMENU menu = CreatePopupMenu(); AppendMenuW(menu, MF_STRING, ID_EDIT_CUT, L"Cu&t"); AppendMenuW(menu, MF_STRING, ID_EDIT_COPY, L"&Copy"); TrackPopupMenu(menu, TPM_RIGHTBUTTON, GET_X_LPARAM(lParam), GET_Y_LPARAM(lParam), 0, hwnd, nullptr); DestroyMenu(menu); return 0; } Accelerators An accelerator table maps key combinations to command ids, so Ctrl+S sends the same WM_COMMAND as the menu item: cpp-norun IDR_ACCEL ACCELERATORS BEGIN "N", ID_FILE_NEW, VIRTKEY, CONTROL "O", ID_FILE_OPEN, VIRTKEY, CONTROL "S", ID_FILE_SAVE, VIRTKEY, CONTROL VK_F5, ID_VIEW_REFRESH, VIRTKEY END The message loop translates them before anything else: cpp-norun HACCEL accel = LoadAcceleratorsW(instance, MAKEINTRESOURCEW(IDR_ACCEL)); while (GetMessageW(&msg, nullptr, 0, 0) 0) { if (!TranslateAcceleratorW(hwnd, accel, &msg)) { TranslateMessage(&msg); DispatchMessageW(&msg); } } Accelerator tables can also be built at run time with CreateAcceleratorTableW , which lets users choose their own shortcuts. Parsing a shortcut such as "Ctrl+Shift+S" into key and modifier flags, and spotting two commands with the same shortcut, is the practice. Strings and versions A string table keeps user-visible text out of the code ( LoadStringW(instance, IDS_TITLE, ...) ), which is how a program is translated. A VERSIONINFO resource gives the file version, product name and copyright shown in the file's Properties dialog. Check yourself quiz ? What makes Ctrl+S work: the \tCtrl+S in the menu text or the accelerator table? - The \tCtrl+S in the menu text: Windows reads it and sets up the shortcut + The accelerator table; the menu text only shows the shortcut - Both are needed: the table maps the key and the text turns it on - Neither: WM_KEYDOWN must check for Ctrl and S by hand The text after \t is only shown on the right of the item. TranslateAcceleratorW in the message loop turns the key into the same WM_COMMAND as the menu item. ? Where should a program enable, disable and check menu items? - In every function that changes the program's state - Once, in WM_CREATE , after loading the menu + In WM_INITMENUPOPUP , just before the menu opens - In WM_COMMAND , after each item is chosen Deriving the items from the program's current state each time the menu opens means they can never get out of step. ? Why should the Exit command send WM_CLOSE instead of destroying the window? - DestroyWindow cannot be called from WM_COMMAND - WM_CLOSE ends the process faster than destroying the window - Destroying the window would leave the menu's resources loaded + So it takes the same path as the close button, "save changes?" included The close button sends WM_CLOSE ; handling the question there once covers both ways of leaving.

title: Shortcuts and mnemonics
body: Parse and print keyboard shortcuts for a run-time accelerator table, find conflicts, and read menu mnemonics: cpp struct Shortcut { int key{ 0 }; bool ctrl{ false }, shift{ false }, alt{ false }; }; bool parseShortcut(const std::string& text, Shortcut& out); std::string formatShortcut(const Shortcut& s); std::vector<std::pair<std::string, std::string conflicts(const std::vector<std::pair<std::string, std::string & commands); char mnemonic(const std::string& menuText); parseShortcut : parts separated by + , case-insensitive, any order of modifiers; the last part is the key. Modifiers are Ctrl (or Control ), Shift and Alt , each at most once. Keys are a letter or digit (stored as its upper-case character code), F1 - F12 ( 0x70 onwards), and Delete (0x2E), Insert (0x2D), Home (0x24), End (0x23), PageUp (0x21), PageDown (0x22), Left (0x25), Up (0x26), Right (0x27), Down (0x28), Enter (0x0D), Esc (0x1B), Space (0x20), Tab (0x09). Spaces around parts are allowed. Anything else fails. formatShortcut writes Ctrl+Shift+Alt+Key in that order with the names above ( F5 , PageUp , S ). conflicts takes (command, shortcut text) pairs and returns each pair of command names whose shortcuts are the same, in the order of the first command, then the second. Shortcuts that do not parse are ignored. mnemonic : the upper-case letter after the first single & in a menu item's text ( && is a literal ampersand), or 0 if there is none.

title: 2.05  Standard Controls
body: Buttons, check boxes, edit boxes, list boxes and combo boxes are child windows of classes Windows provides. This lesson creates them, talks to them with messages, handles their notifications, gives them the right font, and moves the keyboard focus between them with Tab. Controls are windows A control is a child window of a predefined class. Create it in the parent's WM_CREATE with WS_CHILD WS_VISIBLE , and give it an id in the menu parameter: cpp-norun constexpr int IDC_NAME = 1001, IDC_ADD = 1002, IDC_LIST = 1003, IDC_SHOUT = 1004; case WM_CREATE: { const auto instance = reinterpret_cast<CREATESTRUCTW (lParam)- hInstance; CreateWindowExW(WS_EX_CLIENTEDGE, L"EDIT", L"", WS_CHILD WS_VISIBLE WS_TABSTOP ES_AUTOHSCROLL, 10, 10, 200, 24, hwnd, reinterpret_cast<HMENU (IDC_NAME), instance, nullptr); CreateWindowExW(0, L"BUTTON", L"&Add", WS_CHILD WS_VISIBLE WS_TABSTOP BS_DEFPUSHBUTTON, 220, 10, 80, 24, hwnd, reinterpret_cast<HMENU (IDC_ADD), instance, nullptr); CreateWindowExW(0, L"BUTTON", L"&Shout", WS_CHILD WS_VISIBLE WS_TABSTOP BS_AUTOCHECKBOX, 10, 44, 200, 24, hwnd, reinterpret_cast<HMENU (IDC_SHOUT), instance, nullptr); CreateWindowExW(WS_EX_CLIENTEDGE, L"LISTBOX", L"", WS_CHILD WS_VISIBLE WS_TABSTOP WS_VSCROLL LBS_NOTIFY, 10, 78, 290, 200, hwnd, reinterpret_cast<HMENU (IDC_LIST), instance, nullptr); return 0; } Class Control Common styles --- --- --- BUTTON Push button, check box, radio button, group box BS_PUSHBUTTON , BS_DEFPUSHBUTTON , BS_AUTOCHECKBOX , BS_AUTORADIOBUTTON , BS_GROUPBOX EDIT Text box ES_AUTOHSCROLL , ES_MULTILINE , ES_NUMBER , ES_PASSWORD , ES_READONLY STATIC Label, picture, frame SS_LEFT , SS_RIGHT , SS_CENTER LISTBOX List of strings LBS_NOTIFY , LBS_SORT , LBS_EXTENDEDSEL COMBOBOX Drop-down list CBS_DROPDOWNLIST , CBS_DROPDOWN SCROLLBAR A separate scroll bar SBS_HORZ , SBS_VERT Talking to controls Controls are driven by messages . GetDlgItem(parent, id) finds a control's window: cpp-norun HWND list = GetDlgItem(hwnd, IDC_LIST); SendMessageW(list, LB_ADDSTRING, 0, reinterpret_cast<LPARAM (L"Granite")); const int selected = static_cast<int (SendMessageW(list, LB_GETCURSEL, 0, 0)); // LB_ERR (-1) for none const bool shout = SendMessageW(GetDlgItem(hwnd, IDC_SHOUT), BM_GETCHECK, 0, 0) == BST_CHECKED; wchar_t name 256 ; GetDlgItemTextW(hwnd, IDC_NAME, name, 256); // SetDlgItemTextW to change it Each control family has its prefix: BM_ buttons, EM_ edits, LB_ list boxes, CB_ combo boxes. Reading text of unknown length: ask GetWindowTextLengthW first, then size the buffer. Notifications Controls tell their parent about events with WM_COMMAND : LOWORD(wParam) is the control's id, HIWORD(wParam) is the notification code , and lParam is the control's window: cpp-norun case WM_COMMAND: switch (LOWORD(wParam)) { case IDC_ADD: if (HIWORD(wParam) == BN_CLICKED) addName(); return 0; case IDC_NAME: if (HIWORD(wParam) == EN_CHANGE) updateAddButton(); // the text changed return 0; case IDC_LIST: if (HIWORD(wParam) == LBN_DBLCLK) openSelected(); return 0; } break; Newer controls (lesson 3.05) use WM_NOTIFY with a structure instead, because two numbers are not enough to describe their events. Fonts Controls created this way use the old bitmap "System" font, which looks wrong. Give every control the system's message font once they are created: cpp-norun NONCLIENTMETRICSW m{ sizeof(m) }; SystemParametersInfoW(SPI_GETNONCLIENTMETRICS, sizeof(m), &m, 0); m_font = CreateFontIndirectW(&m.lfMessageFont); // delete it in WM_DESTROY EnumChildWindows(hwnd, (HWND child, LPARAM font) { SendMessageW(child, WM_SETFONT, font, TRUE); return TRUE; }, reinterpret_cast<LPARAM (m_font)); With high DPI (lesson 3.04), use SystemParametersInfoForDpi so the font has the right size on each monitor. Tab between controls In an ordinary window, Tab does nothing. IsDialogMessageW adds dialog-style keyboard navigation (Tab and Shift+Tab between WS_TABSTOP controls, arrows within groups, Enter for the default button, Alt+letter for & mnemonics) to any window: cpp-norun while (GetMessageW(&msg, nullptr, 0, 0) 0) { if (!IsDialogMessageW(hwnd, &msg)) { TranslateMessage(&msg); DispatchMessageW(&msg); } } The Tab order is the order the controls were created in, so create them in reading order. Check yourself quiz ? How does a parent window know a button was clicked? - The button calls the parent's window procedure with WM_LBUTTONDOWN - The parent polls the button with BM_GETCHECK on a timer + It receives WM_COMMAND with the button's id and BN_CLICKED - It receives WM_NOTIFY with a structure describing the click The id is in LOWORD(wParam) , BN_CLICKED in HIWORD(wParam) and the control's window in lParam . WM_NOTIFY is how the newer common controls (lesson 3.05) report events. ? Why do controls need WM_SETFONT ? + Otherwise they use the old System font instead of the system's message font - Without a font they draw no text at all - It sets the font for the whole program, including menus - It is what makes the controls scale with high DPI automatically Controls created with CreateWindowExW start with the old bitmap System font; send each one the message font from SystemParametersInfoW . ? What gives an ordinary window Tab navigation between controls? - The WS_TABSTOP style on each control, with nothing else - Handling VK_TAB in WM_CHAR and calling SetFocus on the next id + Calling IsDialogMessageW for each message in the message loop - Registering the window class with CS_DBLCLKS WS_TABSTOP only marks which controls take part; IsDialogMessageW does the moving, in the order the controls were created. Create them in reading order.

title: A list box model
body: Write a model of the LISTBOX control's most used messages, with their real return values: cpp constexpr int LB_ERR = -1; class ListBox { public: explicit ListBox(bool sorted); // LBS_SORT int addString(const std::string& s); // LB_ADDSTRING: the index it went to int insertString(int index, const std::string& s);// LB_INSERTSTRING: -1 appends; never sorts int deleteString(int index); // LB_DELETESTRING: the new count, or LB_ERR int getCount() const; int getCurSel() const; // LB_ERR when nothing is selected int setCurSel(int index); // -1 clears the selection and returns LB_ERR; a bad index returns LB_ERR std::string getText(int index) const; // "" for a bad index int findString(int start, const std::string& prefix) const; // LB_FINDSTRING }; - A sorted list box inserts with addString at its place in case-insensitive order (after equal strings). - Deleting the selected item clears the selection; deleting an item before it moves the selection up by one. Inserting before the selection moves it down. - findString finds the first item that starts with prefix , ignoring case, searching from the item after start to the end and then from the beginning, up to and including start ; start = -1 searches the whole list from the top. It returns LB_ERR if there is no match.

title: Keys held down
body: Track which keys are held from key-down and key-up messages, ignoring auto-repeat. WM_KEYDOWN A (first press) - A down WM_KEYDOWN A (repeat) - ignored (bit 30 set) WM_KEYDOWN SHIFT - held: A, SHIFT WM_KEYUP A - held: SHIFT

title: Dragging with capture
body: Model dragging a box with the mouse, keeping mouse messages even when the cursor leaves the window. down at (50, 50) inside box - capture, dragging move to (90, 70) - box moved by (40, 20) move to (-20, 10) (outside) - still dragging (captured) up - release capture, drop

title: Keyboard shortcuts
body: Match key presses against an accelerator table. Ctrl+S - ID_FILE_SAVE Ctrl+Shift+S - ID_FILE_SAVE_AS F5 - ID_RUN Ctrl+Q - nothing

title: Many timers
body: Model SetTimer : several timers with ids and intervals, each sending WM_TIMER when due. timer 1 every 100 ms, timer 2 every 250 ms t=100 WM_TIMER 1 t=200 WM_TIMER 1 t=250 WM_TIMER 2 t=300 WM_TIMER 1 KillTimer(1) - only timer 2 from now on

title: Commands, shortcuts and recent files
body: Every document program needs the same pieces around its menus: a table of commands with their shortcuts and state, turning key presses into commands (a run-time accelerator table), and a "recent files" list in the File menu. Write them without any windows, so the window procedure just asks them. cpp struct Key { int vk; bool ctrl{ false }, shift{ false }, alt{ false }; }; class CommandTable { public: bool add(int id, const std::string& text, const std::string& shortcut); void setEnabled(int id, bool enabled); void setChecked(int id, bool checked); int translate(const Key& k) const; std::string menuLine(int id) const; }; class RecentFiles { public: explicit RecentFiles(std::size_t max); // at most 9 void add(const std::string& path); void remove(const std::string& path); const std::vector<std::string & items() const; std::vector<std::string menuItems(std::size_t maxChars) const; static std::string shorten(const std::string& path, std::size_t maxChars); std::string save() const; void load(const std::string& text); }; CommandTable - add fails (returns false) if the id is already used, the shortcut does not parse, or another command already has the same shortcut. An empty shortcut means none. Shortcuts use practice 2.04's rules (modifiers Ctrl/Control, Shift, Alt; letters, digits, F1-F12 and the named keys), and commands start enabled and unchecked. - translate returns the id of the enabled command whose shortcut is exactly this key with exactly these modifiers, or 0. - menuLine is the text, then a tab and the shortcut in practice 2.04's canonical form if there is one; with " x " in front when checked, and " (disabled)" at the end when disabled. Unknown ids give "" . RecentFiles - add puts the path at the front; if it is already in the list (compared case-insensitively , as Windows paths are), the old entry is removed first. The list is cut to max . - remove removes a path (case-insensitively), if present. - shorten leaves paths of at most maxChars characters alone. Otherwise, with the path split on \ , it keeps the first part (such as C: ), then \...\ , then as many of the last parts as fit, preferring to keep more; if not even the file name fits that way, it returns ... followed by the last maxChars - 3 characters. - menuItems numbers the entries &1 , &2 , ... followed by the shortened path, with every & in the path doubled ( && ), since a single one would become a mnemonic. - save writes one path per line, each ending in \n ; load replaces the list with the non-empty lines of a text ( \r\n allowed), dropping later duplicates and anything beyond max .

title: 3.01  Dialog Boxes
body: Dialogs are windows built from a template, with keyboard navigation and default buttons for free. This lesson creates modal and modeless dialogs, writes the dialog procedure, moves data in and out of the controls, validates input, and returns a result. What a dialog gives you A dialog box is a window whose controls are described by a template in the resource file, created and laid out by Windows. Compared with creating controls by hand (lesson 2.05) it adds, for free: - Tab and arrow navigation, mnemonics, Enter for the default button and Esc for Cancel; - layout in dialog units , which scale with the dialog's font (so the dialog grows with the user's text size); - IDOK and IDCANCEL handling, and the focus going to the first control. The template cpp-norun IDD_RENAME DIALOGEX 0, 0, 220, 70 STYLE DS_MODALFRAME DS_SHELLFONT WS_POPUP WS_CAPTION WS_SYSMENU CAPTION "Rename" FONT 9, "Segoe UI" BEGIN LTEXT "&New name:", IDC_STATIC, 7, 9, 50, 8 EDITTEXT IDC_NAME, 60, 7, 153, 14, ES_AUTOHSCROLL AUTOCHECKBOX "&Keep the extension", IDC_KEEPEXT, 60, 26, 120, 10 DEFPUSHBUTTON "OK", IDOK, 109, 49, 50, 14 PUSHBUTTON "Cancel", IDCANCEL, 163, 49, 50, 14 END Positions and sizes are in dialog units : horizontally a quarter of the font's average character width, vertically an eighth of its height. Visual Studio's dialog editor writes this for you. The label comes just before its edit box in the template so its mnemonic (Alt+N) moves the focus to the edit box. Modal dialogs A modal dialog disables its owner and runs its own message loop until it is closed; DialogBoxParamW returns only then: cpp-norun struct RenameData { std::wstring name; bool keepExtension{ true }; }; INT_PTR CALLBACK RenameProc(HWND dlg, UINT msg, WPARAM wParam, LPARAM lParam) { auto data = reinterpret_cast<RenameData (GetWindowLongPtrW(dlg, DWLP_USER)); switch (msg) { case WM_INITDIALOG: // data in: fill the controls data = reinterpret_cast<RenameData (lParam); SetWindowLongPtrW(dlg, DWLP_USER, lParam); SetDlgItemTextW(dlg, IDC_NAME, data- name.c_str()); CheckDlgButton(dlg, IDC_KEEPEXT, data- keepExtension ? BST_CHECKED : BST_UNCHECKED); return TRUE; // TRUE: set the focus to the first control case WM_COMMAND: switch (LOWORD(wParam)) { case IDOK: // data out: read and validate { const std::wstring name = getText(dlg, IDC_NAME); if (!validFileName(name)) { MessageBoxW(dlg, L"A name cannot contain \\ / : ? \" < ", L"Rename", MB_ICONWARNING); SetFocus(GetDlgItem(dlg, IDC_NAME)); return TRUE; // stay open } data- name = name; data- keepExtension = IsDlgButtonChecked(dlg, IDC_KEEPEXT) == BST_CHECKED; EndDialog(dlg, IDOK); return TRUE; } case IDCANCEL: EndDialog(dlg, IDCANCEL); return TRUE; // also Esc and the close button } break; } return FALSE; // not handled: the dialog manager does the default } RenameData data{ L"notes.txt" }; if (DialogBoxParamW(instance, MAKEINTRESOURCEW(IDD_RENAME), owner, RenameProc, reinterpret_cast<LPARAM (&data)) == IDOK) rename(data); Note the differences from a window procedure: it returns TRUE or FALSE ("handled or not"), never calls DefWindowProcW , and ends with EndDialog , never DestroyWindow . The last parameter of DialogBoxParamW carries a pointer to the dialog's data, which arrives as lParam in WM_INITDIALOG . The data pattern A dialog is easiest to get right when it works on a plain struct : the caller fills it, WM_INITDIALOG copies it into the controls, IDOK validates and copies it back, and Cancel leaves it untouched. All the rules about valid values can then be written and tested as a normal function on the struct, as in the practice. Good validation tells the user what is wrong and puts the focus on the field, or better, disables OK while the input is invalid (check on EN_CHANGE ) and shows why next to the field. Modeless dialogs A modeless dialog (a Find window, a tool palette) stays open while the user keeps working in the main window. Create it with CreateDialogParamW , show it, and let the main message loop pass its messages through IsDialogMessageW so its keyboard navigation works: cpp-norun if (!(g_findDialog && IsDialogMessageW(g_findDialog, &msg))) { TranslateMessage(&msg); DispatchMessageW(&msg); } Close a modeless dialog with DestroyWindow , not EndDialog , and set g_findDialog back to null in its WM_DESTROY . Message boxes and task dialogs For simple questions, MessageBoxW(owner, text, title, MB_YESNOCANCEL MB_ICONQUESTION) returns IDYES , IDNO or IDCANCEL . TaskDialogIndirect is its modern replacement, with a main instruction, explanatory text, command links, a check box ("Don't ask again") and a progress bar. Always pass the owner window, so the box is modal to it and appears in front of it. Check yourself quiz ? What does a modal dialog do to its owner, and when does DialogBoxParamW return? - It hides the owner; the call returns as soon as the dialog is shown + It disables the owner and runs its own message loop; the call returns when EndDialog is called - It leaves the owner usable; the call returns when the dialog's WM_DESTROY arrives - It disables the owner; the call returns after WM_INITDIALOG has been handled Returning only when closed is what lets the caller test the result ( IDOK ) on the next line. A dialog that leaves the owner usable is modeless. ? How does a dialog procedure differ from a window procedure? - It returns an LRESULT and passes unhandled messages to DefWindowProcW - It handles WM_CREATE and is closed with DestroyWindow + It returns TRUE or FALSE for handled, never calling DefWindowProcW - It receives only WM_COMMAND messages, never WM_INITDIALOG Returning FALSE lets the dialog manager do the default. It initialises in WM_INITDIALOG , not WM_CREATE , and a modal dialog is closed with EndDialog . ? Why should a modeless dialog's messages go through IsDialogMessageW ? - Otherwise the dialog never receives WM_COMMAND + Otherwise its Tab, Enter, Esc and mnemonic keyboard handling does not work - It is what makes the dialog stay in front of the main window - EndDialog only works on dialogs whose messages went through it A modeless dialog uses the main message loop, so that loop must give it the keyboard handling a modal dialog's own loop does. Close it with DestroyWindow , not EndDialog .

title: Validating a rename dialog
body: Write the rules behind lesson 3.01's Rename dialog, as plain functions on its data: cpp std::string fileNameProblem(const std::string& name); // "" if the name is valid, else the message to show std::string applyRename(const std::string& oldName, const std::string& newName, bool keepExtension); fileNameProblem checks in this order and returns the first problem: 1. empty (after nothing is trimmed): "Enter a name." 2. contains any of \ / : ? " < or a character below 32: "A name cannot contain \ / : ? \" < " (with those characters literally) 3. ends with a space or a dot: "A name cannot end with a space or a dot." 4. is a reserved device name, ignoring case and any extension ( CON , PRN , AUX , NUL , COM1 - COM9 , LPT1 - LPT9 ; so con.txt and Lpt3 count, CONSOLE and COM0 do not): "That name is reserved by Windows." 5. longer than 255 characters: "The name is too long." applyRename : the extension is the part from the last dot, if that dot is not the first character ( .gitignore has no extension). With keepExtension , if the new name does not already end with the old extension (ignoring case), the old extension is added.

title: 3.02  Common Dialogs
body: Windows provides the Open, Save, folder, colour and font dialogs every program needs. This lesson uses the modern IFileOpenDialog and IFileSaveDialog through COM, with file type filters, default extensions and folders, and the older colour and font dialogs. COM in five minutes The modern file dialogs are COM objects. COM is Windows' system for objects shared between components: you create an object by its class id, get an interface (a table of virtual functions), call methods that return HRESULT s (lesson 1.01), and Release() the interface when done. cpp-norun include <shobjidl.h // IFileOpenDialog include <wrl/client.h // Microsoft::WRL::ComPtr: a smart pointer that calls Release using Microsoft::WRL::ComPtr; // once per thread that uses COM, at start-up; CoUninitialize at the end CoInitializeEx(nullptr, COINIT_APARTMENTTHREADED COINIT_DISABLE_OLE1DDE); ComPtr is to COM what std::unique_ptr is to new : it releases the object automatically. The UI thread must use the apartment-threaded model (STA) for dialogs. Open cpp-norun std::optional<std::wstring askOpenFile(HWND owner) { ComPtr<IFileOpenDialog dialog; if (FAILED(CoCreateInstance(CLSID_FileOpenDialog, nullptr, CLSCTX_INPROC_SERVER, IID_PPV_ARGS(&dialog)))) return {}; const COMDLG_FILTERSPEC types = { { L"Text documents", L" .txt; .md" }, { L"All files", L" . " }, }; dialog- SetFileTypes(ARRAYSIZE(types), types); dialog- SetFileTypeIndex(1); // 1-based dialog- SetTitle(L"Open a note"); if (FAILED(dialog- Show(owner))) return {}; // also when the user cancels: HRESULT_FROM_WIN32(ERROR_CANCELLED) ComPtr<IShellItem item; if (FAILED(dialog- GetResult(&item))) return {}; PWSTR path = nullptr; if (FAILED(item- GetDisplayName(SIGDN_FILESYSPATH, &path))) return {}; std::wstring result{ path }; CoTaskMemFree(path); // memory allocated by COM is freed with CoTaskMemFree return result; } IID_PPV_ARGS(&dialog) passes both the interface's id and the pointer to fill, so they cannot mismatch. Cancelling is reported as a failed HRESULT with the code ERROR_CANCELLED (1223), which is not an error to show the user. Options set with SetOptions(FOS_...) : FOS_ALLOWMULTISELECT (then use GetResults ), FOS_PICKFOLDERS (a folder picker), FOS_FILEMUSTEXIST . Save IFileSaveDialog works the same way, with a few extras: cpp-norun dialog- SetFileName(L"Untitled.txt"); // suggested name dialog- SetDefaultExtension(L"txt"); // added if the user types a name without one dialog- SetOptions(options FOS_OVERWRITEPROMPT); // "Replace existing file?" (on by default) The default extension follows the selected file type when it changes. The practice computes exactly what file name the user ends up with. The older filter string Older code uses GetOpenFileNameW with an OPENFILENAMEW structure. Its filter is a single string of pairs separated by null characters, ended by two nulls : cpp-norun const wchar_t filter = L"Text documents ( .txt)\0 .txt\0All files ( . )\0 . \0"; // the literal adds the last \0 Building that string from a list, getting the embedded nulls right, is a classic bug source; the practice builds it. Colour and font cpp-norun static COLORREF custom 16 ; // the dialog's 16 custom colours, kept between calls CHOOSECOLORW cc{ sizeof(cc) }; cc.hwndOwner = owner; cc.rgbResult = m_colour; cc.lpCustColors = custom; cc.Flags = CC_FULLOPEN CC_RGBINIT; if (ChooseColorW(&cc)) m_colour = cc.rgbResult; LOGFONTW lf = m_logFont; CHOOSEFONTW cf{ sizeof(cf) }; cf.hwndOwner = owner; cf.lpLogFont = &lf; cf.Flags = CF_SCREENFONTS CF_INITTOLOGFONTSTRUCT; if (ChooseFontW(&cf)) { m_logFont = lf; recreateFont(); } Remembering the folder Users expect the Open dialog to start in the folder they used last. The new dialogs remember it per program automatically; SetFolder sets it explicitly (from an IShellItem made with SHCreateItemFromParsingName ), and SetClientGuid keeps separate memories for different dialogs in one program ("open image" and "open project"). Check yourself quiz ? How does IFileOpenDialog report that the user cancelled? - Show returns S_OK and GetResult gives an empty path - Show returns S_FALSE + Show returns a failed HRESULT equal to HRESULT_FROM_WIN32(ERROR_CANCELLED) - It throws a C++ exception that the caller must catch Cancelling counts as a failure, code ERROR_CANCELLED (1223), which is not an error to show the user. COM methods never throw C++ exceptions. ? What does SetDefaultExtension do? - Picks the file type selected when the dialog opens + Adds that extension when the user types a file name without one - Replaces whatever extension the user typed - Hides files that do not have that extension A name typed with an extension is kept; the default follows the selected file type when it changes. Choosing the starting file type is SetFileTypeIndex . ? How is memory returned by GetDisplayName freed? - With delete - With LocalFree - By Release() on the shell item + With CoTaskMemFree Memory allocated by COM for you is freed with CoTaskMemFree . LocalFree belongs to FormatMessageW 's allocated buffer.

title: File type filters
body: Build and read the double-null filter strings of GetOpenFileNameW (lesson 3.02), and work out the name a Save dialog produces: cpp struct FileType { std::string description; std::string patterns; }; // patterns like " .txt; .md" std::string buildFilter(const std::vector<FileType & types); std::vector<FileType parseFilter(const std::string& filter); std::string defaultExtension(const FileType& type); std::string finalSaveName(const std::string& typed, const FileType& selected); - buildFilter : each type gives its description, a null character, its patterns, a null; the whole string ends with one extra null. No types gives just "\0" (one null). The returned std::string contains the nulls. - parseFilter reads such a string back; it stops at the empty description that marks the end, or at the end of the string, and ignores a description without patterns. - defaultExtension is the extension of the first pattern, without . , when it is a plain .ext (letters and digits only); . or anything else gives "" . - finalSaveName : if the typed name (the part after the last \ ) contains a dot that is not its first character, the name is used as typed; otherwise the selected type's default extension is added (if there is one). Spaces at the ends of the typed name are removed first.

title: 3.03  Layout and Resizing
body: Win32 has no layout engine - when a window is resized, you move its controls. This lesson lays controls out in WM_SIZE with anchors, sets a minimum size with WM_GETMINMAXINFO, moves many controls at once without flicker, and builds a splitter. WM_SIZE When the user resizes a window, it receives WM_SIZE with the new client size. Positioning the controls is up to you: cpp-norun case WM_SIZE: { const int w = LOWORD(lParam), h = HIWORD(lParam); const int pad = 10, buttonW = 80, buttonH = 26; MoveWindow(m_list, pad, pad, w - 2 pad, h - 3 pad - buttonH, TRUE); MoveWindow(m_ok, w - pad - 2 buttonW - pad, h - pad - buttonH, buttonW, buttonH, TRUE); MoveWindow(m_cancel, w - pad - buttonW, h - pad - buttonH, buttonW, buttonH, TRUE); return 0; } Writing that maths for every control gets messy. Most layouts are described better with anchors . Anchors Each control remembers its distances from the edges of the parent at the original size, and which edges it is anchored to: Anchored to When the window grows by dx --- --- Left only Stays where it is Right only Moves right by dx Left and right Stretches by dx Neither Stays centred in the same relative position The same on the vertical axis with top and bottom. A list that fills the window is anchored on all four sides; OK and Cancel at the bottom right are anchored right and bottom; a search box along the top is anchored left, right and top. The practice builds this layout engine. A minimum size Below some size the layout breaks: controls overlap or get negative widths. Tell Windows the minimum window size (frame included) in WM_GETMINMAXINFO : cpp-norun case WM_GETMINMAXINFO: { auto mmi = reinterpret_cast<MINMAXINFO (lParam); mmi- ptMinTrackSize.x = m_minWindowSize.cx; // computed once with AdjustWindowRectExForDpi mmi- ptMinTrackSize.y = m_minWindowSize.cy; return 0; } Moving many controls Moving twenty controls one by one repaints twenty times and flickers. Deferred window positioning moves them all in one step: cpp-norun HDWP batch = BeginDeferWindowPos(static_cast<int (m_controls.size())); for (const auto& c : m_controls) { const RECT r = c.layout(width, height); batch = DeferWindowPos(batch, c.hwnd, nullptr, r.left, r.top, r.right - r.left, r.bottom - r.top, SWP_NOZORDER SWP_NOACTIVATE); } EndDeferWindowPos(batch); Setting WS_CLIPCHILDREN on the parent stops it from painting its background over the children, the other big source of flicker on resizing. Splitters A splitter is the bar between two panes that the user drags to change their sizes. It is not a control: it is a strip of the parent's client area between the two child windows. 1. In WM_SETCURSOR , show IDC_SIZEWE when the mouse is over the strip (lesson 2.02). 2. On WM_LBUTTONDOWN over it, capture the mouse and remember the offset between the mouse and the split position. 3. On WM_MOUSEMOVE while captured, set the split position, clamped so neither pane gets smaller than its minimum, and lay out again. 4. On WM_LBUTTONUP , release the capture, and save the position in the settings (lesson 5.02). Storing the split as a fraction of the width rather than pixels keeps it sensible when the window is resized or moved to a monitor with a different DPI. Keeping the layout in one function Put all layout in one function, layout(width, height) , and call it from WM_SIZE , after the splitter moves, after a font change and after a DPI change (lesson 3.04). When the layout is computed in exactly one place, it cannot disagree with itself. Check yourself quiz ? What does anchoring a control to the left and right edges do? - It keeps the control centred horizontally - It moves the control right by the amount the window grew + It stretches the control horizontally as the window grows or shrinks - It keeps the control at its original position and width Both distances to the edges stay fixed, so the width changes with the window. Right only moves it; left only keeps it in place. ? How do you stop the user from making a window too small? + Set ptMinTrackSize in WM_GETMINMAXINFO - Clamp the width and height in WM_SIZE and call MoveWindow on the window - Leave out WS_OVERLAPPEDWINDOW 's sizing border - Give the window class a minimum size in WNDCLASSEXW The value is the minimum window size including the frame. Fixing the size afterwards in WM_SIZE fights the user's drag and flickers. ? Why use BeginDeferWindowPos to move controls? - It is the only way to move a child window - It animates the controls to their new places - It makes the layout follow the monitor's DPI + It moves them all in one step, with a single repaint Moving twenty controls one by one repaints twenty times and flickers. WS_CLIPCHILDREN on the parent removes the other big source of resize flicker.

title: Anchors and a splitter
body: Write lesson 3.03's anchor layout and the splitter's clamp: cpp struct RECT { long left, top, right, bottom; }; struct Anchors { bool left, top, right, bottom; }; RECT anchorLayout(RECT design, Anchors a, int designW, int designH, int newW, int newH); int clampSplit(int pos, int total, int minLeft, int minRight, int bar); anchorLayout : design is where the control was in a client area of designW × designH . For each axis, with d the change of the client size on that axis: - both edges anchored: the far edge moves by d (the control stretches); - only the near edge (left or top): nothing changes; - only the far edge (right or bottom): both edges move by d ; - neither: the size stays, and the centre is placed at the same fraction of the new size (computed in doubles and rounded to the nearest whole pixel, halves away from zero; the near edge is that centre minus half the size, rounded down). clampSplit : the splitter bar starts at pos and is bar pixels wide inside total . The left pane is 0 .. pos and the right pane pos + bar .. total . Clamp pos so the left pane is at least minLeft and the right pane at least minRight ; if both cannot fit, the left pane wins ( pos = minLeft ).

title: 3.04  High-DPI Screens
body: Laptops and 4K monitors run at 150 % or 200 % scaling, and a program that ignores it is either tiny or blurry. This lesson declares per-monitor DPI awareness, scales sizes and fonts with the DPI, handles moving between monitors with WM_DPICHANGED, and picks the right icon sizes. What DPI scaling is Windows assumes 96 dots per inch at 100 % scaling. A 14-inch 1080p laptop usually runs at 150 % (144 DPI), a 27-inch 4K monitor at 150 % or 200 %. At 150 %, a button that should look 80 pixels wide must be 120 physical pixels wide. A program that does not declare otherwise is DPI-unaware : Windows draws it at 96 DPI and stretches the result, which makes all its text blurry. To look sharp, a program declares that it handles DPI itself, and then scales everything. Declaring awareness Declare per-monitor v2 awareness in the application manifest (lesson 6.02): cpp-norun <application xmlns="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:asm.v3" <windowsSettings <dpiAwareness xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/SMI/2016/WindowsSettings" PerMonitorV2</dpiAwareness </windowsSettings </application or call SetProcessDpiAwarenessContext(DPI_AWARENESS_CONTEXT_PER_MONITOR_AWARE_V2) before creating any window. Per-monitor v2 means: each window has the DPI of the monitor it is on, and the program is told when it changes. It also makes Windows scale the non-client area, dialogs and common controls automatically. Scaling numbers Design at 96 DPI and scale every size by dpi / 96 , rounding to the nearest pixel. MulDiv does exactly that without overflow: cpp-norun const UINT dpi = GetDpiForWindow(hwnd); int scale(int value96) { return MulDiv(value96, dpi, 96); } // rounds half away from zero const int padding = scale(10); // 15 at 144 DPI const int buttonWidth = scale(80); // 120 at 144 DPI Apply it to everything measured in pixels: margins, control sizes, line widths, icon sizes, the minimum window size. Scale from the 96-DPI design value each time, not from the previous scaled value, or rounding errors build up as the window moves between monitors. System metrics have DPI-aware versions: GetSystemMetricsForDpi(SM_CXVSCROLL, dpi) , AdjustWindowRectExForDpi , SystemParametersInfoForDpi . Fonts Font sizes are in points (1/72 inch). The height in pixels is -MulDiv(points, dpi, 72) (the minus sign asks for the character height, not the cell height). Re-create fonts when the DPI changes; for the standard message font, SystemParametersInfoForDpi(SPI_GETNONCLIENTMETRICS, ..., dpi) gives it already scaled. WM_DPICHANGED When a window moves to a monitor with a different DPI (or the user changes the scaling), it receives WM_DPICHANGED with the new DPI and a suggested rectangle : the window's new size and position so it looks the same physical size. Use that rectangle, then re-create fonts and lay out again: cpp-norun case WM_DPICHANGED: { m_dpi = HIWORD(wParam); const RECT suggested = reinterpret_cast<RECT (lParam); SetWindowPos(hwnd, nullptr, suggested- left, suggested- top, suggested- right - suggested- left, suggested- bottom - suggested- top, SWP_NOZORDER SWP_NOACTIVATE); recreateFonts(); layout(); // lesson 3.03's single layout function return 0; } Icons and images An icon at 16 × 16 looks tiny at 200 %. Ship icons in several sizes (16, 20, 24, 32, 40, 48, 64, 256) inside the .ico , and load the right one with LoadIconWithScaleDown or LoadImageW at scale(16) . For toolbars, prefer vector graphics (Direct2D, an icon font such as Segoe Fluent Icons) that scale to any size. When only one bitmap size is available, choose the nearest larger one and scale it down, which looks far better than scaling a small one up. Testing Test at 100 %, 150 % and 200 %, and drag the window between two monitors with different scaling. A second monitor is not required: change the scaling in Settings Display while the program runs, which sends the same WM_DPICHANGED . Check yourself quiz ? What happens to a DPI-unaware program at 150 % scaling? - It is drawn at 96 DPI with no stretching, so it looks tiny + Windows draws it at 96 DPI and stretches it, so it looks blurry - Windows scales all its sizes and fonts properly, so it looks sharp - It refuses to start until it declares DPI awareness Stretching the 96-DPI image makes text blurry. To look sharp, a program declares per-monitor awareness and scales everything itself. ? How do you scale a 10-pixel design value for the window's DPI? - 10 dpi / 72 - Multiply the last scaled value by the new DPI divided by the old one + MulDiv(10, dpi, 96) , always from the 96-DPI design value - 10 96 / dpi 96 DPI is 100 %, so 10 becomes 15 at 144 DPI. Scaling from the previous scaled value builds up rounding errors; 72 is for converting points in font sizes. ? What should a window do on WM_DPICHANGED ? - Nothing: per-monitor v2 rescales its fonts and layout automatically - Keep its current size and only re-create the fonts - Call SetProcessDpiAwarenessContext again for the new monitor + Move to the suggested rectangle, re-create its fonts and lay out its controls again The suggested rectangle keeps the window the same physical size. Windows scales the non-client area and dialogs, but your own fonts and layout are your job.

title: Scaling for DPI
body: Write lesson 3.04's DPI arithmetic: cpp int mulDiv(int number, int numerator, int denominator); // like MulDiv int scaleForDpi(int value96, int dpi); int fontHeight(int points, int dpi); // LOGFONT lfHeight: negative character height int pickIconSize(const std::vector<int & available, int wanted); - mulDiv computes number × numerator / denominator with a 64-bit intermediate and rounds half away from zero ( MulDiv(3, 1, 2) is 2, MulDiv(-3, 1, 2) is -2). A denominator of 0 returns -1, as the real one does. - scaleForDpi is mulDiv(value96, dpi, 96) . - fontHeight is -mulDiv(points, dpi, 72) . - pickIconSize returns the smallest available size that is at least wanted , or the largest available size if none is that big (0 for an empty list). The list is in any order.

title: 3.05  Common Controls
body: The list view, tree view, status bar, progress bar and tab control come from the Common Controls library. This lesson enables visual styles, creates these controls, handles WM_NOTIFY, and uses a virtual list view to show a hundred thousand rows instantly. Enabling them, with visual styles The common controls ( comctl32.dll ) add the controls Explorer uses. Version 6 draws them, and the standard controls, with the modern visual style. Ask for it in the manifest, conveniently with a linker directive, and initialise the library: cpp-norun include <commctrl.h pragma comment(lib, "comctl32.lib") pragma comment(linker, "\"/manifestdependency:type='win32' name='Microsoft.Windows.Common-Controls' \ version='6.0.0.0' processorArchitecture=' ' publicKeyToken='6595b64144ccf1df' language=' '\"") INITCOMMONCONTROLSEX icc{ sizeof(icc), ICC_LISTVIEW_CLASSES ICC_TREEVIEW_CLASSES ICC_BAR_CLASSES ICC_TAB_CLASSES ICC_PROGRESS_CLASS }; InitCommonControlsEx(&icc); Without the manifest entry, buttons and check boxes look like Windows 95. The controls Class Control Typical use --- --- --- WC_LISTVIEW List view: rows with columns, or icons Files, search results WC_TREEVIEW Tree view Folders, outlines, settings categories STATUSCLASSNAME Status bar Line and column, state, progress PROGRESS_CLASS Progress bar Long operations WC_TABCONTROL Tabs Pages of settings TOOLTIPS_CLASS Tooltips Help on hover TRACKBAR_CLASS , UPDOWN_CLASS Slider, spin buttons Numbers A list view with columns cpp-norun HWND lv = CreateWindowExW(0, WC_LISTVIEW, L"", WS_CHILD WS_VISIBLE WS_TABSTOP LVS_REPORT LVS_SHOWSELALWAYS, 0, 0, 0, 0, hwnd, reinterpret_cast<HMENU (IDC_FILES), instance, nullptr); ListView_SetExtendedListViewStyle(lv, LVS_EX_FULLROWSELECT LVS_EX_DOUBLEBUFFER); LVCOLUMNW col{ LVCF_TEXT LVCF_WIDTH }; col.pszText = const_cast<wchar_t (L"Name"); col.cx = scale(240); ListView_InsertColumn(lv, 0, &col); col.pszText = const_cast<wchar_t (L"Size"); col.cx = scale(90); ListView_InsertColumn(lv, 1, &col); ListView_InsertColumn and friends are macros around SendMessageW with LVM_... messages, the same mechanism as lesson 2.05 with nicer names. WM_NOTIFY Common controls report events with WM_NOTIFY . lParam points to an NMHDR (the control's window, id and code ), which is the first member of a bigger, code-specific structure: cpp-norun case WM_NOTIFY: { const auto hdr = reinterpret_cast<NMHDR (lParam); if (hdr- idFrom == IDC_FILES) { switch (hdr- code) { case NM_DBLCLK: openSelected(); return 0; case LVN_COLUMNCLICK: sortBy(reinterpret_cast<NMLISTVIEW (lParam)- iSubItem); return 0; case LVN_GETDISPINFOW: fillDisplayInfo(reinterpret_cast<NMLVDISPINFOW (lParam)); return 0; } } break; } Virtual list views Adding 100 000 items one by one with ListView_InsertItem takes seconds and copies every string into the control. A virtual list view ( LVS_OWNERDATA ) stores nothing: you tell it how many rows there are, and it asks for the text of each row only when it needs to draw it: cpp-norun ListView_SetItemCountEx(lv, static_cast<int (m_results.size()), LVSICF_NOSCROLL); void fillDisplayInfo(NMLVDISPINFOW info) { const auto& row = m_results info- item.iItem ; if (info- item.mask & LVIF_TEXT) { const std::wstring text = info- item.iSubItem == 0 ? row.name : formatSize(row.size); wcsncpy_s(info- item.pszText, info- item.cchTextMax, text.c_str(), _TRUNCATE); } } Showing a million rows is now instant, and sorting means sorting your own vector and calling InvalidateRect . This is the list the file finder of milestone 6 uses. Formatting sizes the way Explorer does ("1.5 KB", "23.4 MB") is part of the practice. The status bar cpp-norun m_status = CreateWindowExW(0, STATUSCLASSNAME, nullptr, WS_CHILD WS_VISIBLE SBARS_SIZEGRIP, 0, 0, 0, 0, hwnd, nullptr, instance, nullptr); const int parts = { scale(200), scale(320), -1 }; // right edges; -1 = to the end SendMessageW(m_status, SB_SETPARTS, 3, reinterpret_cast<LPARAM (parts)); SendMessageW(m_status, SB_SETTEXTW, 0, reinterpret_cast<LPARAM (L"Ln 12, Col 4")); // in WM_SIZE: SendMessageW(m_status, WM_SIZE, 0, 0); it positions itself at the bottom Check yourself quiz ? What does the common controls manifest dependency change? - It adds the list view and tree view, which do not exist without it + It loads version 6 of comctl32, which draws controls with the modern visual style - It makes the program per-monitor DPI-aware - It links comctl32.lib into the program Without it, buttons and check boxes look like Windows 95. Linking is the job of pragma comment(lib, "comctl32.lib") . ? How does a common control describe an event in WM_NOTIFY ? - LOWORD(wParam) is its id and HIWORD(wParam) is the notification code - wParam holds a pointer to the list item that was changed - It sends a separate WM_COMMAND for each item that changed + lParam points to an NMHDR holding its id and a notification code Two numbers in WM_COMMAND are not enough for these events, so the structure starts with NMHDR and you cast to the bigger type for the code. ? What makes a virtual list view fast for huge lists? + It stores no items and asks only for the rows it draws - It inserts the items on a background thread - It keeps the strings compressed inside the control - It draws all rows once into a bitmap and scrolls the bitmap With LVS_OWNERDATA you only set the row count, and the control asks for each visible row's text through LVN_GETDISPINFO . Sorting means sorting your own vector and invalidating.

title: Sizes and natural sorting
body: Two things every file list needs: cpp std::string formatSize(std::uint64_t bytes); bool naturalLess(const std::string& a, const std::string& b); formatSize shows sizes like Explorer: below 1024, "N bytes" ( "1 byte" for one). Otherwise divide by 1024 until the value is below 1024 (at most up to TB), and show three significant digits, rounded down , with the unit KB , MB , GB or TB : 1536 is "1.50 KB" , 10 240 is "10.0 KB" , 123 456 789 is "117 MB" . Use integer arithmetic so there are no rounding surprises: for example, hundredths are bytes 100 / 1024^k . naturalLess compares like Explorer's StrCmpLogicalW : runs of digits are compared as numbers ( file2 before file10 ), everything else character by character ignoring case. When two digit runs have the same value, the shorter run comes first ( a01 after a1 ). If everything compares equal, fall back to a plain case-sensitive comparison so the order is total.
