body:
Write lesson 6.01's detection and conversion, so the editor saves a file exactly the way it found it: cpp enum class Encoding { Utf8, Utf8Bom, Utf16Le, Utf16Be, Legacy }; enum class LineEnding { Crlf, Lf, Cr }; struct Loaded { std::string text; Encoding encoding; LineEnding ending; }; // text: UTF-8 with 
 line endings Loaded decodeFile(const std::string& bytes); std::string encodeFile(const std::string& text, Encoding encoding, LineEnding ending); bool isValidUtf8(const std::string& bytes); decodeFile - Encoding: EF BB BF at the start is Utf8Bom ; FF FE is Utf16Le ; FE FF is Utf16Be (the BOM is not part of the text). Otherwise valid UTF-8 is Utf8 , and anything else is Legacy , decoded as Latin-1 (each byte is the code point of the same value) for this exercise. - UTF-16 is decoded to UTF-8, including surrogate pairs; an odd final byte is ignored. - Line ending: count 
 , lone  and lone 
 in the decoded text; the most common wins, with ties going to Crlf , then Lf . A text without any line ending is Crlf (the Windows default). - The text is returned with every ending converted to 
 . encodeFile converts 
 to the chosen ending, then writes the encoding with its BOM if it has one ( Legacy writes Latin-1, using ? for characters above U+00FF). isValidUtf8 checks strictly: no overlong forms, no surrogates, nothing above U+10FFFF, no truncated sequence.

title: 6.02  Packaging and Installing
body: Getting a Windows program onto other people's computers - the application manifest, version information, icons, static or dynamic runtime, per-user installs without administrator rights, MSIX and installers, code signing and SmartScreen, and updates. The application manifest The manifest is an XML file embedded in the .exe that tells Windows how to treat the program. Several earlier lessons asked for one; here it is in one place: cpp-norun <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8" standalone="yes"? <assembly xmlns="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:asm.v1" manifestVersion="1.0" <assemblyIdentity type="win32" name="Xenon.Notes" version="1.2.0.0"/ <dependency <dependentAssembly <!-- lesson 3.05: visual styles -- <assemblyIdentity type="win32" name="Microsoft.Windows.Common-Controls" version="6.0.0.0" processorArchitecture=" " publicKeyToken="6595b64144ccf1df" language=" "/ </dependentAssembly </dependency <trustInfo xmlns="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:asm.v3" <security <requestedPrivileges <requestedExecutionLevel level="asInvoker" uiAccess="false"/ <!-- no administrator prompt -- </requestedPrivileges </security </trustInfo <application xmlns="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:asm.v3" <windowsSettings <dpiAwareness xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/SMI/2016/WindowsSettings" PerMonitorV2</dpiAwareness <!-- 3.04 -- <longPathAware xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/SMI/2016/WindowsSettings" true</longPathAware <!-- 5.01 -- <activeCodePage xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/SMI/2019/WindowsSettings" UTF-8</activeCodePage <!-- 1.02 -- </windowsSettings </application </assembly Add it in Visual Studio under Manifest Tool Input and Output Additional Manifest Files . asInvoker is right for almost every program: requesting requireAdministrator makes every start show a UAC prompt, which users rightly distrust. Version information and icon A VERSIONINFO resource (lesson 2.04) puts the version, product name, company and copyright in the file's Properties dialog. The version is four 16-bit numbers, major.minor.patch.build , stored as two 32-bit values ( FILEVERSION 1,2,0,0 ). The practice packs, unpacks and compares them, which is also what an update check does. The icon resource with the lowest id becomes the .exe 's icon in Explorer; include all sizes (lesson 3.04). Runtime and dependencies - Link the C runtime statically ( /MT ) to avoid requiring the Visual C++ Redistributable, or install the redistributable with your installer if you link dynamically ( /MD ). - Ship any DLLs you use next to the .exe (the DLL course explains the search order). - Test on a clean Windows virtual machine or Windows Sandbox: the only reliable way to find a missing dependency. Installing per user A program does not need administrator rights to be installed. A per-user install puts it in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\<Name and writes only to HKEY_CURRENT_USER : What Where --- --- Program files %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\XenonNotes\ Start menu shortcut %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\ File associations HKCU\Software\Classes (lesson 5.05) Entry in Settings Apps HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\XenonNotes with DisplayName , DisplayVersion , Publisher , UninstallString Per-machine installs into Program Files need administrator rights once, during installation. Installer options Tool Notes --- --- MSIX Windows' modern package format: clean install and uninstall, automatic updates, required for the Microsoft Store; must be signed WiX Toolset Builds MSI installers from XML; the standard for enterprise deployment Inno Setup , NSIS Script-based .exe installers, simple and popular for small programs A zip For tools that need no installation at all ("portable") Whatever you use, uninstalling must remove everything the installer added, and nothing the user created. Code signing and SmartScreen An unsigned downloaded .exe shows SmartScreen 's "Windows protected your PC" warning. Signing with a code-signing certificate ( signtool sign /fd SHA256 /tr <timestamp server /td SHA256 app.exe ) identifies you as the publisher; the warning disappears as the signature builds reputation. Always add a timestamp so the signature stays valid after the certificate expires. Microsoft's Trusted Signing service and the Microsoft Store are alternatives to buying a certificate. Updates The simplest update check downloads a small file with the latest version number (over HTTPS, with WinHTTP or URLDownloadToFileW ), compares it with the running version, and offers a download page. Never run downloaded code without verifying its signature. MSIX and the Store handle updates themselves. Check yourself quiz ? Why is requestedExecutionLevel level="asInvoker" the right default in a manifest? - It makes the program run as administrator without asking + The program runs with the user's normal rights and never shows a UAC prompt when it starts - It is required for the program to read the registry - It lets the program write to Program Files after installation With asInvoker the program gets the rights of whoever started it. requireAdministrator shows a UAC prompt on every start, which users rightly distrust. ? Where does a per-user install put the program and its entry in Settings Apps? - In Program Files , with the entry under HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall - In %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu , with the entry in a file next to the .exe - In %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs , with the entry under HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall + In %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs , with the entry under HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall A per-user install needs no administrator rights, so it writes only to the user's folders and HKEY_CURRENT_USER . Program Files and HKLM are for per-machine installs. ? Why add a timestamp when code signing a program? - It makes the SmartScreen warning disappear immediately - It records the build date in the file's Properties dialog + So the signature stays valid after the signing certificate expires - It is needed for the signature to use SHA-256 The timestamp proves the file was signed while the certificate was valid, so the signature keeps working after the certificate expires. SmartScreen's warning goes away only as reputation builds.

title: Version numbers
body: Windows stores a file version as four 16-bit numbers in two 32-bit values ( VS_FIXEDFILEINFO 's dwFileVersionMS and dwFileVersionLS ). Write the helpers an about box and an update check need: cpp struct Version { std::uint16_t major{ 0 }, minor{ 0 }, patch{ 0 }, build{ 0 }; }; bool parseVersion(const std::string& text, Version& out); std::string formatVersion(const Version& v, int parts); // 1 to 4 parts, e.g. formatVersion(v, 3) == "1.2.0" void packVersion(const Version& v, std::uint32_t& ms, std::uint32_t& ls); Version unpackVersion(std::uint32_t ms, std::uint32_t ls); int compareVersions(const Version& a, const Version& b); // -1, 0 or 1 bool updateAvailable(const std::string& running, const std::string& latest); - parseVersion accepts 1 to 4 numbers separated by dots, each 0 to 65535, optionally starting with v or V ; missing parts are 0. Anything else (empty parts, letters, a fifth part, spaces) fails. - packVersion : ms = major << 16 minor , ls = patch << 16 build . - updateAvailable is true only if both strings parse and latest is newer.

title: 6.03  Project: A File Finder
body: Build a fast file search tool - a search box with options, a worker thread walking folders, results streaming into a virtual list view, sorting, progress and cancellation, opening results and showing them in Explorer. This lesson ties milestones 3 and 5 together. What you build Xenon Finder ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Look in C:\Users\Sam\Documents Browse... │ │ Names .md; .txt x Subfolders Search │ ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ Name ▲ Folder Size Modified │ │ notes.md C:\...\Projects 2.4 KB 2026-11-02 │ │ plan.txt C:\...\Xenon 812 b 2026-10-18 │ │ ... │ ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ Searching C:\Users\Sam\Documents\Archive... 1 204 found │ └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ The pieces Piece From --- --- Layout that resizes, at any DPI 3.03, 3.04 Folder picker 3.02 ( FOS_PICKFOLDERS ) Wildcards, recursion, skipping links, cancellation project m05 Worker thread and posting results 5.04 Virtual list: sorting, selection, status text 3.05, project m03 Opening a result, "show in folder" 5.03 Copying paths to the clipboard 5.05 Settings: last folder, patterns, column widths 5.02 Threading the search The search runs on a worker; the UI thread only displays. The tricky part is how results travel: - Posting a message per file floods the queue with tens of thousands of messages and the UI stutters. - Collect results in a vector protected by a lock (or a work queue, practice 5.04), and post one "new results" message at most every 100 ms. The UI thread swaps the batch out, appends it to the list's model, and calls ListView_SetItemCountEx once. - The status bar shows the folder currently being searched, also throttled. The practice writes the throttle. cpp-norun case WM_APP_RESULTS: { std::vector<Item batch; { std::lock_guard lock{ m_shared.mutex }; batch.swap(m_shared.pending); m_shared.posted = false; } m_model.append(std::move(batch)); // project m03's ResultList, extended with append ListView_SetItemCountEx(m_list, m_model.count(), LVSICF_NOINVALIDATEALL LVSICF_NOSCROLL); updateStatus(); return 0; } A new search, closing the window, or the Stop button sets the stop flag and joins the old worker before anything else (with std::jthread , assigning a new thread does this). Never let two searches write into the same results. Sorting while results arrive Sorting a list that keeps growing must not make rows jump under the user's mouse. A simple rule: while searching, append in arrival order; when the search finishes (or the user clicks a column), sort once. Selection is kept by id (project m03), so it survives. Actions on results - Enter or double-click: open with the default program ( ShellExecuteExW , lesson 5.03). - Ctrl+Enter or the context menu's "Show in folder": SHOpenFolderAndSelectItems , or explorer.exe /select,"path" (quoted with practice 5.03's rules). - Ctrl+C : copy the selected paths, one per line with CRLF (lesson 5.05). - Delete : move to the Recycle Bin with IFileOperation ( FOFX_RECYCLEONDELETE ), never a permanent delete, and remove the rows. Speed FindFirstFileExW with FindExInfoBasic (no short 8.3 names) and FIND_FIRST_EX_LARGE_FETCH is noticeably faster than plain FindFirstFileW . Skipping folders you cannot open (error 5) silently, rather than reporting each one, keeps the search going through protected system folders. For whole-drive searches, real tools read the NTFS change journal or the Windows Search index; walking folders is fast enough for a few hundred thousand files. Order to build in 1. Window with the controls and layout; the folder picker. 2. A search on the UI thread into a plain list: correct results first. 3. Move it to a worker; post batches; Stop button. 4. Virtual list view with the model from project m03; sorting and status text. 5. Actions: open, show in folder, copy, delete to the Recycle Bin. 6. Settings, high DPI, keyboard navigation everywhere. Check yourself quiz ? Why does the file finder post results in batches instead of one message per file? - PostMessageW can only be called once every 100 ms - One message per file would lose results when the queue is full, but batches cannot + Tens of thousands of messages flood the queue and make the interface stutter; a batch every 100 ms stays smooth - A list view can only add items in groups The UI thread would spend its time handling a message per file. Collecting results under a lock and posting one "new results" message at most every 100 ms keeps it responsive. ? What must happen to the old worker before a new search starts? + It must be told to stop and be joined before the new one starts - Nothing; the new worker simply runs alongside it - It must be detached so the new search can start sooner - The finder window must be destroyed and created again Set the stop flag and join the old thread first (assigning a new std::jthread does both). Otherwise two searches could write into the same results. ? Why should the finder's Delete move files to the Recycle Bin? - A permanent delete needs administrator rights for each file - IFileOperation cannot delete files permanently, only recycle - Moving to the Recycle Bin is faster than deleting the files + Mass mistakes are easy in a results list, and the bin can undo them With many selected results, one key press can remove a lot of files. Moving them to the Recycle Bin ( FOFX_RECYCLEONDELETE ) means a mistake can be undone.

title: Batching results for the UI
body: Write the two pieces between lesson 6.03's worker thread and its window: a throttle that decides when to post, and a batch that collects results in between. Time is given in milliseconds by the caller so the logic can be tested: cpp class Throttle { public: explicit Throttle(int intervalMs); bool ready(long long nowMs); // true at most once per interval; the first call is always ready bool finish(); // true if anything was held back since the last time ready() was true void held(); // something happened that was not reported yet }; template <typename T class Batch { public: bool add(T item); // true if the window must be told (no message is pending) std::vector<T take(); // the UI thread takes everything; the next add() will ask again std::size_t pending() const; }; Throttle : ready(now) returns true if this is the first call, or at least intervalMs have passed since the last time it returned true; then it also forgets anything held. held() marks that something was not reported; finish() returns whether such a thing is still unreported (and clears it), so the final state is always shown when the search ends. Batch (used from two threads, so protect it with a mutex): add appends the item and returns true only if no "new results" message is pending yet, and then marks one as pending; take returns all items, clears the batch and the pending mark. So however many items arrive, at most one message is in the queue.

title: The text editor's document
body:
Write the document model behind lesson 6.01's editor: the text, edits, multi-level undo and redo with typing grouped into words, the unsaved-changes flag, line and column, find, and Replace All as a single undo step. A text view (an EDIT control replacement drawn with DirectWrite, lesson 4.03) then only displays it and turns keys into calls. cpp struct LineCol { int line, col; }; // both 1-based class TextDocument { public: explicit TextDocument(std::string text = ""); const std::string& text() const; void insert(std::size_t pos, const std::string& s); void erase(std::size_t pos, std::size_t count); void replace(std::size_t pos, std::size_t count, const std::string& s); void breakGroup(); bool undo(); bool redo(); bool modified() const; void markSaved(); LineCol lineCol(std::size_t pos) const; std::size_t offsetOf(int line, int col) const; std::optional<std::size_t find(const std::string& what, std::size_t from, bool matchCase, bool wrap) const; int replaceAll(const std::string& what, const std::string& with, bool matchCase); }; Edits and undo : positions beyond the end are clamped to the end (and counts to what is there). Every edit that changes something becomes an undo step and clears the redo list. replace is one step. undo reverts the last step and redo re-applies it; both return false when there is nothing to do. Typing groups : an insert of a single character joins the previous step instead of making a new one when: - the previous step was also made by insert and nothing has broken the group since ( breakGroup , undo , redo , markSaved or any other kind of edit break it), - it continues exactly where the previous step's text ended, - the character is not 
 , and the previous step does not end with a space unless this character is a space too (so a word and the spaces after it form one step). Modified is true when the text differs from the last saved (or initial) state as far as undo can tell: track the position in the undo history. lineCol counts lines from 1, starting after each 
 , and columns from 1 (in bytes). offsetOf clamps the line to the existing lines and the column to 1 .. length of the line + 1 (the line's length excludes its 
 ). find searches forward from from , ignoring case unless matchCase ; with wrap , if nothing is found from from , it searches again from the start. An empty what finds nothing. replaceAll replaces every non-overlapping match from left to right, as one undo step, and returns how many it replaced (0 changes nothing and adds no step).

title: 7.01  Virtual Memory
body: Managing memory a page at a time - reserving address space and committing pages with VirtualAlloc, page size and allocation granularity, protection flags and VirtualProtect, asking about memory with VirtualQuery, decommitting and releasing with VirtualFree, guard pages, and a buffer that grows without moving. Below new and malloc new , malloc and the C++ containers get their memory from a heap , which in turn gets it from the operating system in big pieces. VirtualAlloc is that lower layer: it hands out memory in whole pages , with control over two things the heap hides: - Reserving address space (claiming a range of addresses, with no memory behind it yet) is separate from committing it (backing pages with real memory or the page file). - Each page has a protection : readable, writable, executable, or none. The Pointers and Memory course covers the ideas; this lesson is the Windows API for them. Sizes cpp-norun SYSTEM_INFO info{}; GetSystemInfo(&info); // info.dwPageSize 4096 on x64: the unit of commit and protection // info.dwAllocationGranularity 65536: reservations start at multiples of 64 KB A reservation's base address is always a multiple of the allocation granularity (64 KB), and its size is rounded up to whole pages. Committing, decommitting and protecting work on whole pages : a call covering part of a page affects all of it. Reserve, then commit cpp-norun constexpr SIZE_T reserveSize{ 1ull << 30 }; // 1 GB of addresses, no memory used yet auto base{ static_cast<std::byte (VirtualAlloc(nullptr, reserveSize, MEM_RESERVE, PAGE_NOACCESS)) }; if (!base) return GetLastError(); // Later, when the first 64 KB are needed: if (!VirtualAlloc(base, 64 1024, MEM_COMMIT, PAGE_READWRITE)) return GetLastError(); base 0 = std::byte{ 1 }; // fine: committed and writable // base 64 1024 = ...; // access violation: reserved only MEM_RESERVE MEM_COMMIT does both at once, which is what most callers want for a plain block. Committed pages read as zero until written. Reserving a large range and committing as you go gives a buffer that grows without ever moving : pointers into it stay valid, unlike a std::vector that reallocates. Large arrays, arenas and the stack of every thread work this way. Protection Constant Access --- --- PAGE_NOACCESS none: any access faults PAGE_READONLY read PAGE_READWRITE read and write PAGE_EXECUTE_READ read and run code PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE all three (avoid: it defeats a basic security protection) PAGE_GUARD (combined with one of the above) the first access raises a one-time STATUS_GUARD_PAGE_VIOLATION , then the page behaves normally VirtualProtect(address, size, newProtect, &oldProtect) changes the protection of committed pages and must be given a place for the old value. Making data read-only after setting it up catches stray writes immediately, as an access violation at the bug instead of corruption found later. Asking about memory VirtualQuery(address, &mbi, sizeof mbi) describes the run of pages starting at the page containing address that all share the same state and protection: Field Meaning --- --- BaseAddress , RegionSize where this run starts and how long it is AllocationBase , AllocationProtect the reservation it belongs to, and that reservation's original protection State MEM_COMMIT , MEM_RESERVE or MEM_FREE Protect the protection of committed pages Walking a process's memory with repeated VirtualQuery calls (address = previous base + size) lists every region; debuggers and memory profilers do exactly this, and practice 7.01 simulates it. Giving memory back cpp-norun VirtualFree(base, 64 1024, MEM_DECOMMIT); // the pages go back to reserved VirtualFree(base, 0, MEM_RELEASE); // the whole reservation; size MUST be 0 MEM_RELEASE takes the base address the reservation started at and a size of 0 ; anything else fails with ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER . Check yourself quiz ? What is the difference between reserving and committing memory? - Reserving allocates the memory; committing writes zeros into it - Reserving is for program code and committing is for data + Reserving claims addresses only; committing backs pages with memory - There is none: both do the same with different flags A reserved range has no memory behind it, so touching it is an access violation. Committing backs pages with real memory or the page file; committed pages read as zero until written. ? You reserve 10 000 bytes with VirtualAlloc . Where can the reservation start, and how big is it (4 KB pages)? - Anywhere, and exactly 10 000 bytes - At a multiple of 4 KB, and 65 536 bytes + At a multiple of 64 KB, and 12 288 bytes - At a multiple of 64 KB, and 65 536 bytes Reservations start at multiples of the allocation granularity (64 KB), but their size is rounded up only to whole pages: three 4 KB pages make 12 288 bytes. ? What happens on the first access to a PAGE_GUARD page? - An access violation every time it is touched, until VirtualFree is called + A one-time guard page exception; after that the page behaves with its normal protection - The page is committed automatically and the access succeeds silently - Nothing; PAGE_GUARD only marks the page in VirtualQuery The first access raises STATUS_GUARD_PAGE_VIOLATION once, and the guard flag is cleared. Thread stacks use this to grow a page at a time. ? What size do you pass to VirtualFree with MEM_RELEASE ? - The size you reserved, rounded up to whole pages - The size of the committed part only - The allocation granularity, 65 536 + 0, together with the reservation's base address MEM_RELEASE frees the whole reservation, so it takes the base address and a size of 0. Anything else fails with ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER .

title: A reserved region, page by page
match: A reserved region, page by page
body: Simulate one reservation made with VirtualAlloc(..., MEM_RESERVE, ...) and the page-level operations lesson 7.01 describes, so the rules are clear before you meet them as access violations. cpp enum class Protect { NoAccess, ReadOnly, ReadWrite }; struct RegionInfo { std::size_t start; std::size_t size; bool committed; Protect protect; }; std::size_t alignUp(std::size_t value, std::size_t alignment); class VirtualRegion { public: explicit VirtualRegion(std::size_t requested, std::size_t pageSize = 4096); std::size_t size() const; bool commit(std::size_t offset, std::size_t length, Protect protect); bool decommit(std::size_t offset, std::size_t length); std::optional<Protect protect(std::size_t offset, std::size_t length, Protect protect); bool canRead(std::size_t offset) const; bool canWrite(std::size_t offset) const; RegionInfo query(std::size_t offset) const; }; - alignUp rounds value up to a multiple of alignment (a power of two). - The reservation's size is requested rounded up to whole pages. All pages start reserved (not committed). - An operation on offset, offset + length) affects every page that range touches , even partly. A length of 0, or a range reaching past the end of the reservation, fails ( false , or an empty optional) and changes nothing. - commit commits the pages with the given protection; pages that were already committed keep their protection. - decommit returns the pages to reserved. - protect requires all the pages to be committed (otherwise it fails and changes nothing), sets their protection, and returns the old protection of the first page . - canRead is true for a committed page that is ReadOnly or ReadWrite ; canWrite only for ReadWrite . Reserved pages allow nothing. An offset past the end allows nothing. - query describes, like VirtualQuery , the run of pages that starts at the page containing offset and continues while the pages have the same committed state and protection (reserved pages count as NoAccess ). An offset past the end throws std::out_of_range .

title: 7.02  The Console
body: Writing programs that live in a terminal - console and GUI programs, attaching or creating a console, standard handles, Unicode output with WriteConsoleW and UTF-8 code pages, colour and cursor control with virtual terminal sequences, reading keys as input records, and handling Ctrl+C and closing the window. Console programs and GUI programs Every Windows executable is marked as either a console program or a GUI program (the /SUBSYSTEM:CONSOLE or /SUBSYSTEM:WINDOWS linker option): - A console program started from Explorer gets a new console window; started from a terminal, it shares that terminal. - A GUI program has no console. If it needs one, AttachConsole(ATTACH_PARENT_PROCESS) joins the terminal that started it (for command-line tools with a GUI), and AllocConsole() creates a new one (for a debug window). Standard handles and Unicode GetStdHandle(STD_OUTPUT_HANDLE) (also STD_INPUT_HANDLE , STD_ERROR_HANDLE ) gives the console's handles. Text output has two routes: - WriteConsoleW writes UTF-16 directly to a console: every character appears correctly, whatever the code page. It fails if output is redirected to a file or pipe ( program out.txt ), so check with GetConsoleMode whether the handle is a console and use WriteFile otherwise. - Bytes ( printf , std::cout , WriteFile ) are interpreted in the console's output code page . Call SetConsoleOutputCP(CP_UTF8) at start-up, and write UTF-8, to get the same result. Colour and cursor: virtual terminal sequences Modern Windows consoles understand the same escape sequences as Linux and macOS terminals, once enabled: cpp-norun HANDLE out{ GetStdHandle(STD_OUTPUT_HANDLE) }; DWORD mode{ 0 }; GetConsoleMode(out, &mode); SetConsoleMode(out, mode ENABLE_VIRTUAL_TERMINAL_PROCESSING); std::wprintf(L"\x1b 1;32mOK\x1b 0m done\n"); // bold green "OK", then reset std::wprintf(L"\x1b 2K\r%3d%%", percent); // clear the line, back to its start, rewrite progress Sequence Effect --- --- ESC 0m reset all attributes ESC 1m bold or bright ESC 30m ... ESC 37m foreground colour (black, red, green, yellow, blue, magenta, cyan, white) ESC 40m ... ESC 47m background colour ESC 90m ... ESC 97m bright foreground colours ESC 2K erase the whole line ESC <row ;<col H move the cursor (1-based) ESC ?25l , ESC ?25h hide, show the cursor ESC is the character 27 ( \x1b ). The older SetConsoleTextAttribute API still works, but sequences are portable and work over SSH. Reading keys ReadConsoleW reads a line the console has already edited. To react to individual keys (arrows, function keys, key releases), switch off line input and read input records : cpp-norun INPUT_RECORD records 16 ; DWORD count{ 0 }; ReadConsoleInputW(in, records, 16, &count); for (DWORD i{ 0 }; i < count; ++i) { if (records i .EventType != KEY_EVENT !records i .Event.KeyEvent.bKeyDown) continue; const KEY_EVENT_RECORD& key{ records i .Event.KeyEvent }; // key.wVirtualKeyCode (VK_LEFT, VK_RETURN ...), key.uChar.UnicodeChar, key.dwControlKeyState } Practice 7.02 builds the line editor such a loop feeds. Ctrl+C and closing By default Ctrl+C ends a console program at once. To clean up first (save a file, stop a worker), register a handler: cpp-norun std::atomic<bool g_stop{ false }; BOOL WINAPI onConsoleEvent(DWORD type) { if (type == CTRL_C_EVENT type == CTRL_BREAK_EVENT type == CTRL_CLOSE_EVENT) { g_stop = true; // the main loop notices and exits cleanly return TRUE; // handled } return FALSE; } SetConsoleCtrlHandler(onConsoleEvent, TRUE); The handler runs on a new thread , so it only sets a flag. For CTRL_CLOSE_EVENT (the window's close button) Windows waits only a few seconds before ending the process, so cleanup must be quick. Check yourself quiz ? When does WriteConsoleW fail even in a console program? - When the text contains characters outside ASCII - When the console's output code page is not UTF-8 + When the output is redirected to a file or pipe; use WriteFile then - When it is called from a thread other than the main one WriteConsoleW writes UTF-16 straight to a console, whatever the code page, but a redirected handle is not a console. Check with GetConsoleMode and fall back to WriteFile . ? What must you call before escape sequences work in a Windows console? + SetConsoleMode with ENABLE_VIRTUAL_TERMINAL_PROCESSING - SetConsoleOutputCP(CP_UTF8) before writing any output - AllocConsole() first, even in a console program - SetConsoleTextAttribute with the colour you want to use Virtual terminal processing is a console mode, switched on with SetConsoleMode on the output handle. The output code page only decides how bytes become characters. ? What does writing \x1b 2K\r do? - Clears the whole screen and moves the cursor to the top-left corner - Moves the cursor two lines up, then to the start of the line - Erases from the cursor to the end of the line, then starts a new line + Erases the current line and moves the cursor to its start ESC 2K erases the whole current line and \r returns to its first column, ready to rewrite a progress display in place. ? Why should a console control handler only set a flag? - Handlers may not call any function at all - Returning TRUE from the handler ends the program at once + It runs on a new thread, so cleanup there would race the main code - The flag is the only way to tell Windows the event was handled Windows calls the handler on a new thread, so cleanup there would race the main code. Setting an atomic flag lets the main loop exit cleanly; for CTRL_CLOSE_EVENT it must be quick.

title: Console output and a line editor
match: Console output and a line editor
body: Write the pieces of a console tool from lesson 7.02: coloured text and a progress line using virtual terminal sequences, and a line editor driven by key events like those ReadConsoleInputW returns. cpp std::string colored(std::string_view text, int color, bool bright = false); std::string progressLine(int percent, int width); struct Key { int vk; char ch; }; // a key-down event: virtual-key code and character (0 if none) class LineEditor { public: void press(Key key); const std::string& text() const; std::size_t cursor() const; std::optional<std::string takeLine(); }; colored returns ESC 3Xm (or ESC 9Xm when bright ), the text, then ESC 0m , where X is color from 0 to 7. Any other color throws std::invalid_argument . ( ESC is \x1b .) progressLine returns ESC 2K , \r , then , a bar of width characters, , a space, the percentage right-aligned in 3 characters and % . The bar has percent width / 100 (rounded down) characters followed by . characters. percent is clamped to 0..100. LineEditor keeps the text being typed and the cursor position (0 to the text's length): Key vk Effect --- --- --- a printable character anything, ch from 32 to 126 inserted at the cursor, which moves after it Backspace 0x08 deletes the character before the cursor Delete 0x2E deletes the character at the cursor Left, Right 0x25 , 0x27 moves the cursor by one, staying within the text Home, End 0x24 , 0x23 moves the cursor to the start or the end Escape 0x1B clears the text Enter 0x0D finishes the line: it becomes available to takeLine , is added to the history if not empty, and the text is cleared Up, Down 0x26 , 0x28 recall earlier or later lines from the history, cursor at the end; Down past the newest gives an empty line The editing keys are recognised by vk whatever ch is. takeLine returns the oldest finished line not yet taken, or an empty optional.

title: 7.03  Overlapped I/O
body: Reading and writing without waiting - opening files with FILE_FLAG_OVERLAPPED, the OVERLAPPED structure and its 64-bit offset, ERROR_IO_PENDING and operations that finish at once, waiting with events and GetOverlappedResult, I/O completion ports for many operations, cancellation, and keeping buffers alive. Why not just use a thread? A blocking ReadFile stops its thread until the data arrives. For one file, a worker thread (lesson 5.04) is fine. A program with hundreds of files or sockets in flight cannot have a thread each. Overlapped I/O starts an operation, returns at once, and tells you later when it finished, so a few threads can keep many operations going. It is how high-performance Windows servers, and the pipes of the Processes and Communication course, work. Starting an operation cpp-norun HANDLE file{ CreateFileW(path, GENERIC_READ, FILE_SHARE_READ, nullptr, OPEN_EXISTING, FILE_FLAG_OVERLAPPED, nullptr) }; OVERLAPPED ov{}; // must be zeroed ov.Offset = static_cast<DWORD (position); // low 32 bits of the file position ov.OffsetHigh = static_cast<DWORD (position 32); ov.hEvent = CreateEventW(nullptr, TRUE, FALSE, nullptr); if (!ReadFile(file, buffer, size, nullptr, &ov)) { if (GetLastError() != ERROR_IO_PENDING) { / a real failure / } // otherwise: it is running; buffer and ov must stay alive until it finishes } - With an overlapped handle there is no current file position : every operation states its offset in the OVERLAPPED , split into two 32-bit halves. - ReadFile returning FALSE with ERROR_IO_PENDING means started , not failed. - It may also return TRUE : the operation completed at once (cached data). Your code must handle both paths. - Reading at or past the end of the file fails with ERROR_HANDLE_EOF . Waiting for one: GetOverlappedResult cpp-norun DWORD transferred{ 0 }; if (GetOverlappedResult(file, &ov, &transferred, TRUE)) // TRUE: wait for it process(buffer, transferred); Each operation can have its own event in hEvent , and WaitForMultipleObjects can wait for up to 64 of them. Beyond that, use a completion port. Many at once: I/O completion ports An I/O completion port is a queue the system puts a completion packet on whenever an operation on an associated handle finishes: cpp-norun HANDLE port{ CreateIoCompletionPort(INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE, nullptr, 0, 0) }; // make the port CreateIoCompletionPort(file, port, / key / 1, 0); // associate a handle // start several reads at different offsets ... for (;;) { DWORD bytes{ 0 }; ULONG_PTR key{ 0 }; OVERLAPPED done{ nullptr }; BOOL ok{ GetQueuedCompletionStatus(port, &bytes, &key, &done, INFINITE) }; // 'done' tells you which operation finished (put OVERLAPPED inside your own struct to find its data); // ok == FALSE with done != nullptr: that operation failed (GetLastError says why) } - Completions arrive in the order operations finish , not the order they started. Reads of chunks 3, 1 and 2 may complete as 2, 3, 1: keep track by offset (practice 7.03 does this). - A few worker threads calling GetQueuedCompletionStatus on one port share the work; the port limits how many run at once. - PostQueuedCompletionStatus puts your own packet in the queue, the usual way to tell workers to stop. - An operation that completes at once still queues a packet, unless you opt out with SetFileCompletionNotificationModes(file, FILE_SKIP_COMPLETION_PORT_ON_SUCCESS) and handle the TRUE return yourself. Cancelling and lifetimes CancelIoEx(file, &ov) cancels one operation (or all of the handle's with nullptr ). A cancelled operation still completes , with ERROR_OPERATION_ABORTED . Until its completion arrives, the operation may still write into its buffer and OVERLAPPED : freeing them earlier, for example by letting a stack variable go out of scope, corrupts memory. Track every operation in flight, and free its memory only when its completion has been seen. Check yourself quiz ? Where does an overlapped read get its file position from? - From the handle's current file position, as with a normal read - From SetFilePointerEx , called just before ReadFile + From Offset and OffsetHigh in its OVERLAPPED - From the hEvent member of its OVERLAPPED An overlapped handle has no current position: each operation states its 64-bit offset, split into two 32-bit halves in its OVERLAPPED . ? ReadFile returns FALSE and GetLastError is ERROR_IO_PENDING . Did it fail? - Yes: FALSE always means failure + No: the read was started and will complete later - Yes: the file was opened without FILE_FLAG_OVERLAPPED - No: the read already completed with cached data ERROR_IO_PENDING means started, not failed; keep the buffer and OVERLAPPED alive until it finishes. A read that completes at once returns TRUE instead. ? In what order do completions come out of an I/O completion port? - In the order the operations were started - In order of file offset, lowest first - In order of completion key + In the order the operations finish Reads of chunks 3, 1 and 2 may complete as 2, 3, 1, so the program keeps track of which operation each completion belongs to, for example by its offset. ? When may you free the buffer of a cancelled overlapped operation? - Right after CancelIoEx returns + Only after its completion, with ERROR_OPERATION_ABORTED , has arrived - As soon as the function that started it returns - Never; Windows frees it when the handle is closed A cancelled operation still completes, and until then it may write into its buffer and OVERLAPPED . Freeing them earlier corrupts memory.

title: Offsets and out-of-order completions
body: Overlapped reads give every operation its own 64-bit offset and finish in any order (lesson 7.03). Write the two helpers that make that manageable. cpp struct Overlapped { std::uint32_t Offset; std::uint32_t OffsetHigh; }; void setOffset(Overlapped& ov, std::uint64_t position); std::uint64_t offsetOf(const Overlapped& ov); class ChunkAssembler { public: explicit ChunkAssembler(std::uint64_t start = 0); bool add(std::uint64_t offset, std::string data); std::string takeReady(); std::uint64_t position() const; std::size_t pending() const; }; - setOffset stores the low 32 bits of position in Offset and the high 32 bits in OffsetHigh ; offsetOf puts them back together. - ChunkAssembler receives the data of completed reads in any order and hands it out in file order . position is the offset of the next byte to hand out (it starts at start ). - add stores a chunk. It returns false and stores nothing if the chunk is empty, starts before position , or overlaps a chunk already stored. - takeReady returns all the bytes that are now contiguous from position (joining as many stored chunks as follow each other), removes them, and advances position . If the next chunk has not arrived, it returns an empty string. - pending is the number of chunks stored and not yet handed out.

title: 7.04  Services
body: Programs that run in the background without anyone signed in - what a Windows service is, the service control manager, the service main function and control handler, reporting state with SetServiceStatus, start and stop pending states with checkpoints and wait hints, installing with sc.exe, accounts, and the rules that come with session 0. What a service is A service is a program that the service control manager (SCM) starts, usually at boot, and that runs without a signed-in user and without a window: a backup agent, a database, a web server, an update checker. The Services app ( services.msc ) and sc.exe list them. Writing one is mostly about speaking the SCM's protocol correctly. The shape of a service program cpp-norun SERVICE_STATUS_HANDLE g_statusHandle{}; SERVICE_STATUS g_status{ SERVICE_WIN32_OWN_PROCESS }; HANDLE g_stopEvent{}; void report(DWORD state, DWORD exitCode = NO_ERROR, DWORD waitHint = 0) { static DWORD checkPoint{ 1 }; g_status.dwCurrentState = state; g_status.dwWin32ExitCode = exitCode; g_status.dwWaitHint = waitHint; g_status.dwControlsAccepted = (state == SERVICE_START_PENDING) ? 0 : SERVICE_ACCEPT_STOP SERVICE_ACCEPT_SHUTDOWN; g_status.dwCheckPoint = (state == SERVICE_RUNNING state == SERVICE_STOPPED) ? 0 : checkPoint++; SetServiceStatus(g_statusHandle, &g_status); } DWORD WINAPI handler(DWORD control, DWORD, void , void ) { switch (control) { case SERVICE_CONTROL_STOP: case SERVICE_CONTROL_SHUTDOWN: report(SERVICE_STOP_PENDING, NO_ERROR, 5000); SetEvent(g_stopEvent); return NO_ERROR; case SERVICE_CONTROL_INTERROGATE: return NO_ERROR; default: return ERROR_CALL_NOT_IMPLEMENTED; } } void WINAPI serviceMain(DWORD, LPWSTR ) { g_statusHandle = RegisterServiceCtrlHandlerExW(L"XenonAgent", handler, nullptr); report(SERVICE_START_PENDING, NO_ERROR, 3000); g_stopEvent = CreateEventW(nullptr, TRUE, FALSE, nullptr); // ... start up, calling report(SERVICE_START_PENDING, ...) again if it takes a while ... report(SERVICE_RUNNING); WaitForSingleObject(g_stopEvent, INFINITE); // the real work runs on other threads // ... shut down ... report(SERVICE_STOPPED); } int wmain() { SERVICE_TABLE_ENTRYW table { { const_cast<LPWSTR (L"XenonAgent"), serviceMain }, { nullptr, nullptr } }; if (!StartServiceCtrlDispatcherW(table)) return static_cast<int (GetLastError()); // ERROR_FAILED_SERVICE_CONTROLLER_CONNECT: run from a console } - wmain hands control to the SCM with StartServiceCtrlDispatcherW , which calls serviceMain on a new thread and returns only when the service stops. - serviceMain registers the control handler first, then reports its state. - The handler receives controls (stop, shutdown, pause, interrogate) and must return quickly: it signals the main code and reports a pending state. The state machine State Meaning Checkpoint and wait hint --- --- --- SERVICE_START_PENDING starting checkpoint increases with each report; wait hint = how long until the next SERVICE_RUNNING running 0 SERVICE_STOP_PENDING stopping increasing, with a wait hint SERVICE_STOPPED stopped 0; dwWin32ExitCode says why SERVICE_PAUSE_PENDING , SERVICE_PAUSED , SERVICE_CONTINUE_PENDING pausing, if supported as above In a pending state, the SCM expects either the checkpoint to increase or the state to change before the wait hint runs out; otherwise it decides the service has hung. dwControlsAccepted says which controls the service takes now : none while starting. Practice 7.04 implements these rules. Installing and running text sc create XenonAgent binPath= "C:\Program Files\Xenon\agent.exe" start= auto sc start XenonAgent sc query XenonAgent sc stop XenonAgent sc delete XenonAgent (The space after each = is required by sc .) Installers usually call CreateServiceW instead. A service runs as an account : LocalSystem (all-powerful: avoid), LocalService or NetworkService (limited), or a dedicated account. Choose the least powerful one that works. Life in session 0 Services run in session 0 , separate from users' desktops, so a service cannot show windows or message boxes. Log to the Windows event log or a file, and talk to a user-side program through a named pipe or a socket (the Processes and Communication course), checking who is connecting. During development, give the program a "console mode" switch that runs the same work in a normal console, so you can debug it without installing it. Check yourself quiz ? What does StartServiceCtrlDispatcherW do? + Connects the process to the SCM and runs the service main function - Installs the service so it starts automatically at boot - Starts the service from the command line, like sc start - Registers the control handler and reports SERVICE_RUNNING wmain hands control to the service control manager with it; it runs the service main function on a new thread and returns when the service stops. Installing is sc create or CreateServiceW , and the control handler is registered by the service main function. ? Why must the checkpoint increase during a long start? - So the Services app can show a progress bar - Because SetServiceStatus rejects a report with the same checkpoint + So the SCM knows the service is making progress and has not hung - So the SCM can restart the service from the last checkpoint after a crash In a pending state the SCM expects the checkpoint to increase or the state to change before the wait hint runs out; otherwise it decides the service has hung. ? Which controls should a service accept while it is starting? - Only SERVICE_ACCEPT_STOP - Stop and shutdown, the same as while running + None: dwControlsAccepted is 0 in the start pending state - All of them, so the user can always cancel A service that is still starting cannot handle controls safely, so it accepts none until it reports SERVICE_RUNNING . ? How should a service show information to a user? - With a message box, which appears on the active user's desktop - By creating a window in session 0 and switching the user to it - By writing to the console, which every service has + Not with windows: log it, or send it to a user-side program over a pipe or socket Services run in session 0, separate from users' desktops, so their windows are never seen. They log to the event log or a file and talk to a user-side program.

title: The service status state machine
body: Write the part of a service that talks to the service control manager (lesson 7.04): it keeps SERVICE_STATUS correct for every report, and answers controls. cpp enum class State : std::uint32_t { Stopped = 1, StartPending, StopPending, Running, ContinuePending, PausePending, Paused }; constexpr std::uint32_t ACCEPT_STOP = 1, ACCEPT_PAUSE_CONTINUE = 2, ACCEPT_SHUTDOWN = 4; constexpr std::uint32_t CONTROL_STOP = 1, CONTROL_PAUSE = 2, CONTROL_CONTINUE = 3, CONTROL_INTERROGATE = 4, CONTROL_SHUTDOWN = 5; constexpr std::uint32_t NO_ERROR_CODE = 0, ERROR_CALL_NOT_IMPLEMENTED = 120; struct Status { State state; std::uint32_t controlsAccepted; std::uint32_t checkPoint; std::uint32_t waitHint; std::uint32_t exitCode; }; class ServiceReporter { public: explicit ServiceReporter(bool canPause); Status report(State state, std::uint32_t waitHint = 0, std::uint32_t exitCode = 0); std::uint32_t handle(std::uint32_t control); const Status& current() const; }; report sets the new state and returns the resulting status. The service starts Stopped (all other fields 0). - Allowed moves (anything else throws std::logic_error and changes nothing): Stopped to StartPending; StartPending to StartPending, Running or Stopped; Running to StopPending or PausePending; PausePending to PausePending or Paused; Paused to ContinuePending or StopPending; ContinuePending to ContinuePending or Running; StopPending to StopPending or Stopped. - Pending states (the four ...Pending ) need a wait hint above 0 (otherwise std::invalid_argument , nothing changed). Their checkpoint is the previous checkpoint plus 1. In other states the checkpoint and wait hint are 0. - exitCode is kept only in Stopped ; it is 0 in other states. - controlsAccepted : in Running and Paused , ACCEPT_STOP ACCEPT_SHUTDOWN , plus ACCEPT_PAUSE_CONTINUE if the service can pause; in every other state, 0. handle answers a control and returns NO_ERROR_CODE or ERROR_CALL_NOT_IMPLEMENTED : - CONTROL_INTERROGATE is always answered with NO_ERROR_CODE and changes nothing. - CONTROL_STOP (needs ACCEPT_STOP ) and CONTROL_SHUTDOWN (needs ACCEPT_SHUTDOWN ) report StopPending with a wait hint of 5000. - CONTROL_PAUSE in Running and CONTROL_CONTINUE in Paused (both need ACCEPT_PAUSE_CONTINUE ) report PausePending or ContinuePending with a wait hint of 2000. - Anything else, or a control not accepted now, returns ERROR_CALL_NOT_IMPLEMENTED and changes nothing.

title: 7.05  Access Tokens and Privileges
body: How Windows knows who a program runs as - the access token of your own process, reading the user's SID, groups, elevation and integrity level with GetTokenInformation, SIDs as strings, privileges and why AdjustTokenPrivileges can succeed without granting anything, and asking for elevation through a manifest. Every process has a token When a user signs in, Windows creates an access token describing them: their user SID (security identifier), the groups they belong to, their privileges , and their integrity level . Every process they start gets a copy. Whenever a process opens a file, a registry key or another process, Windows compares its token with the object's security descriptor. This lesson reads the token of your own process , which is what programs need to decide, for example, whether to offer an "install for all users" option. Reading your token cpp-norun HANDLE token{}; if (!OpenProcessToken(GetCurrentProcess(), TOKEN_QUERY, &token)) return GetLastError(); TOKEN_ELEVATION elevation{}; DWORD length{ 0 }; GetTokenInformation(token, TokenElevation, &elevation, sizeof elevation, &length); bool elevated{ elevation.TokenIsElevated != 0 }; Variable-sized information (the user, the groups, the integrity level) uses the "ask for the size first" pattern of the Reading Documentation course: cpp-norun DWORD needed{ 0 }; GetTokenInformation(token, TokenUser, nullptr, 0, &needed); // fails with ERROR_INSUFFICIENT_BUFFER std::vector<std::byte buffer(needed); if (GetTokenInformation(token, TokenUser, buffer.data(), needed, &needed)) { auto user{ reinterpret_cast<TOKEN_USER (buffer.data()) }; LPWSTR text{}; if (ConvertSidToStringSidW(user- User.Sid, &text)) { std::wcout << text << L'\n'; // S-1-5-21-...-1001 LocalFree(text); // the API allocated it } } CloseHandle(token); SIDs A SID identifies a user, group or computer. In binary it is a revision (1), a count of sub-authorities, a 6-byte identifier authority (big-endian), and that many 32-bit sub-authorities (little-endian). Written as text: S-1-5-21-3623811015-3361044348-30300820-1013 , meaning revision 1, authority 5 (NT), then the sub-authorities. Some are well known: S-1-5-18 is LocalSystem, S-1-5-32-544 is the Administrators group, S-1-1-0 is Everyone. Practice 7.05 converts between the two forms. Integrity levels and UAC The token's integrity level is a SID whose last sub-authority gives the level: 0x1000 low (sandboxed processes), 0x2000 medium (normal programs), 0x3000 high (elevated), 0x4000 system. A lower-integrity process cannot write to higher-integrity objects or send certain messages to their windows. With UAC , even an administrator normally runs at medium integrity with a filtered token; elevation ("Run as administrator", a consent prompt) starts a new process with the full token at high integrity. A program that always needs it declares so in its manifest : xml <requestedExecutionLevel level="requireAdministrator" uiAccess="false"/ Most programs should use asInvoker and elevate only a small helper for the few operations that need it ( ShellExecuteExW with the verb runas ), following the principle of least privilege. Privileges Privileges are rights that are not about a specific object: shutting down the system ( SeShutdownPrivilege ), changing the system time, debugging programs, backing up files. A token lists the privileges it has, each enabled or disabled ; most are disabled until a program enables the one it needs, just before using it: cpp-norun TOKEN_PRIVILEGES tp{ 1 }; LookupPrivilegeValueW(nullptr, SE_SHUTDOWN_NAME, &tp.Privileges 0 .Luid); tp.Privileges 0 .Attributes = SE_PRIVILEGE_ENABLED; AdjustTokenPrivileges(token, FALSE, &tp, 0, nullptr, nullptr); // token opened with TOKEN_ADJUST_PRIVILEGES if (GetLastError() == ERROR_NOT_ALL_ASSIGNED) { / the token does not have this privilege at all / } AdjustTokenPrivileges is a famous documentation trap: it returns success even when it could not enable the privilege, because the token never had it. The only way to know is to check GetLastError() for ERROR_NOT_ALL_ASSIGNED (1300) afterwards, even on success. Check yourself quiz ? What does an access token contain? - The user's password hash and the files they may open + The user's SID, the group SIDs, the privileges and the integrity level - The process's handles and its security descriptor - Only whether the process is elevated Every process gets a copy of the token made at sign-in. Windows compares it with each object's security descriptor; passwords are never in it. ? What is S-1-5-32-544 ? - The SID of the LocalSystem account - The SID of the Everyone group + The well-known SID of the Administrators group - The SID of the current user S-1-5-32-544 is Administrators. LocalSystem is S-1-5-18 , Everyone is S-1-1-0 , and user SIDs look like S-1-5-21-... . ? Why can AdjustTokenPrivileges succeed but not enable the privilege? - The privilege was already enabled, so there was nothing to do - The program forgot to call LookupPrivilegeValueW first - Privileges can only be enabled by elevated programs + The token does not hold that privilege at all It returns success even when it could not enable a privilege the token never had. The only way to know is to check GetLastError() for ERROR_NOT_ALL_ASSIGNED (1300), even on success. ? Why prefer an asInvoker program with a small elevated helper over requireAdministrator ? + Least privilege: only the few operations that need elevation run with it - An asInvoker program can elevate itself later without a prompt - requireAdministrator does not work for administrators under UAC - The helper runs at system integrity, which is more powerful than administrator The main program runs at medium integrity, and only the helper started with the runas verb gets the full token, after a prompt. Less code with high rights means less to go wrong.

title: Security identifiers
body: Write the conversions that ConvertSidToStringSidW and ConvertStringSidToSidW perform, and read an integrity level (lesson 7.05). cpp struct Sid { std::uint64_t authority; std::vector<std::uint32_t subAuthorities; }; std::vector<std::uint8_t sidToBytes(const Sid& sid); std::optional<Sid sidFromBytes(const std::vector<std::uint8_t & bytes); std::string sidToString(const Sid& sid); std::optional<Sid sidFromString(std::string_view text); std::string integrityName(const Sid& sid); The binary form : byte 0 is the revision, 1; byte 1 is the number of sub-authorities (at most 15); bytes 2 to 7 are the identifier authority, a 48-bit number, big-endian ; then each sub-authority as 4 bytes, little-endian . sidFromBytes refuses (empty optional) a wrong revision, more than 15 sub-authorities, or a length that is not exactly 8 + 4 × count . sidToBytes may assume a valid Sid (authority below 2⁴⁸, at most 15 sub-authorities). The text form : S-1- , the authority, then - and each sub-authority in decimal. The authority is written in decimal if it is below 2³², otherwise as 0x followed by 12 upper-case hex digits. sidFromString accepts exactly that form (the S may be lower case, hex digits in either case), with each number made of digits only, the authority below 2⁴⁸, each sub-authority below 2³², and at most 15 of them; anything else gives an empty optional. integrityName : for a SID with authority 16 and exactly one sub-authority, the name of the level: untrusted (0), low (0x1000), medium (0x2000), medium plus (0x2100), high (0x3000), system (0x4000), otherwise unknown . Any other SID gives not an integrity level .

title: 7.06  COM Basics
body: The object model behind much of the Windows API - initialising COM and apartments, interfaces and IUnknown with QueryInterface, AddRef and Release, creating objects with CoCreateInstance, HRESULTs, ComPtr to manage reference counts, memory COM hands you, and creating a shortcut with IShellLinkW as a complete example. Why COM Many Windows features are not plain C functions but COM objects : the file dialogs (lesson 3.02), Direct2D, DirectWrite and WIC (milestone 4), shortcuts, the taskbar, the Windows Runtime underneath WinRT. COM (the Component Object Model) is a binary standard for objects: any language that can call through a table of function pointers can use them, which is why the same objects work from C++, C , Python and scripting languages. Initialising Every thread that uses COM initialises it first and uninitialises it at the end: cpp-norun HRESULT hr{ CoInitializeEx(nullptr, COINIT_APARTMENTTHREADED) }; // UI threads: a single-threaded apartment if (FAILED(hr)) return hr; // S_FALSE means "already initialised": still call CoUninitialize // ... use COM ... CoUninitialize(); The apartment says how objects may be called across threads: COINIT_APARTMENTTHREADED (STA) for threads with windows, where calls are delivered through the message loop; COINIT_MULTITHREADED (MTA) for worker threads. A thread cannot switch: a second call with the other model fails with RPC_E_CHANGED_MODE . Interfaces and IUnknown A COM object is used only through interfaces : tables of functions, each identified by a GUID (an IID ). Every interface starts with the three methods of IUnknown : Method Does --- --- QueryInterface(iid, &ptr) asks the object for another interface; E_NOINTERFACE if it has none AddRef() adds one to the object's reference count Release() subtracts one; at zero, the object deletes itself The rules: every interface pointer you receive (from CoCreateInstance , QueryInterface or an out parameter) has already been AddRef ed for you , so you must Release it exactly once. Forgetting leaks the object; releasing twice destroys it while something still uses it. Practice 7.06 implements these rules and the smart pointer that follows them for you. ComPtr Nobody calls AddRef and Release by hand in modern code. Microsoft::WRL::ComPtr (in <wrl/client.h , or winrt::com_ptr and the WIL library's wil::com_ptr ) does it automatically: cpp-norun include <wrl/client.h using Microsoft::WRL::ComPtr; ComPtr<IShellLinkW link; HRESULT hr{ CoCreateInstance(CLSID_ShellLink, nullptr, CLSCTX_INPROC_SERVER, IID_PPV_ARGS(&link)) }; if (FAILED(hr)) return hr; link- SetPath(LR"(C:\Program Files\Xenon\Xenon.exe)"); link- SetDescription(L"Learn to program"); ComPtr<IPersistFile file; hr = link.As(&file); // QueryInterface for IPersistFile if (SUCCEEDED(hr)) hr = file- Save(LR"(C:\Users\Public\Desktop\Xenon.lnk)", TRUE); // both pointers are released automatically here - IID_PPV_ARGS(&p) passes the interface's IID and the address of the pointer together, so they can never mismatch. - ComPtr copies AddRef , destruction and reassignment Release , .As() is a checked QueryInterface , .Get() gives the raw pointer for a call, and &p (or .ReleaseAndGetAddressOf() ) for an out parameter. Errors and memory - COM methods return HRESULT s: test with SUCCEEDED and FAILED (lesson 3.03 of Reading Documentation), and remember S_FALSE is a success. - Strings and buffers that a COM method allocates for you are freed with CoTaskMemFree (for example the path from IShellItem::GetDisplayName ). BSTR strings, used by automation interfaces, are freed with SysFreeString . The method's documentation says which. Check yourself quiz ? What must every thread do before using COM? - Call CoCreateInstance once to load the COM library - Nothing; COM is initialised when the program starts + Call CoInitializeEx (and CoUninitialize when finished) - Call CoInitializeEx once on the main thread, which covers every thread COM is initialised per thread, with an apartment model: STA for threads with windows, MTA for workers. A thread that has not called it cannot use COM. ? You receive an interface pointer from QueryInterface . Who calls Release ? - Nobody; it was not AddRef ed, so you must not release it + You do, exactly once: it was already AddRef ed for you - You call AddRef first, then Release twice - The object you queried releases it when it is destroyed Every pointer you receive from CoCreateInstance , QueryInterface or an out parameter has been AddRef ed for you. Forgetting Release leaks the object; releasing twice destroys it too early. ? What does ComPtr::As do? - It casts the pointer with static_cast , with no checks - It copies the ComPtr and adds a reference - It releases the pointer and returns the raw address + It calls QueryInterface for another interface, into another ComPtr link.As(&file) asks the object for IPersistFile and returns an HRESULT , E_NOINTERFACE if the object has none. A plain cast would skip that check. ? How do you free a string that a COM method allocated for you? - With delete , since the method allocated it with new - With free , since it is a plain null-terminated C string - With LocalFree , like every string the API allocates + With the function its documentation names, usually CoTaskMemFree COM memory comes from the COM allocator, so it is freed with CoTaskMemFree ; automation BSTR strings use SysFreeString . The method's documentation says which.

title: IUnknown and a smart pointer
body: Build COM's rules yourself (lesson 7.06): an object with two interfaces that counts its references, and a ComPtr -like smart pointer that calls AddRef and Release for you. The interfaces are declared in the starter in the same shape as real COM ones. cpp struct Guid { std::uint32_t a; std::uint16_t b, c; std::array<std::uint8_t, 8 d; bool operator==(const Guid&) const = default; }; using HRESULT = std::int32_t; // S_OK = 0, E_NOINTERFACE = 0x80004002, E_POINTER = 0x80004003 struct IUnknownLike { virtual HRESULT QueryInterface(const Guid& iid, void out) = 0; virtual std::uint32_t AddRef() = 0; virtual std::uint32_t Release() = 0; }; struct IShape : IUnknownLike { virtual double area() = 0; }; struct INamed : IUnknownLike { virtual std::string name() = 0; }; HRESULT createSquare(double side, IShape out); template <typename T class Ptr { / ... / }; The object. createSquare makes a square (its area is side side , its name is "square" ) that implements both IShape and INamed , stores an IShape to it in out with a reference count of 1, and returns S_OK ; with a null out it returns E_POINTER . Every live square is counted in the global g_liveObjects . - QueryInterface gives out IShape for IID_IShape and for IID_IUnknown , INamed for IID_INamed , each after AddRef , and returns S_OK . For any other IID it sets out to null and returns E_NOINTERFACE . A null out gives E_POINTER . - AddRef and Release return the new count; when Release brings it to 0, the object deletes itself. Ptr<T holds one T : Member Does --- --- Ptr() , Ptr(nullptr) empty Ptr(T p) holds p and AddRefs it (like ComPtr ) copy AddRefs; copy assignment releases the old pointer first (self-assignment is safe) move takes the pointer; the source becomes empty destructor, reset() Release the held pointer, if any get() , - , explicit operator bool the raw pointer address() releases what it holds and returns T , for functions that fill in a pointer that is already AddRef'ed as<U (Ptr<U & out, const Guid& iid) QueryInterface into out (releasing what out held); returns the HRESULT

title: An overlapped copy engine
body: Write the logic at the heart of a fast file copier built on overlapped I/O and a completion port (lesson 7.03). The engine decides which reads and writes to start; the real program would start them with ReadFile and WriteFile and feed the completions from GetQueuedCompletionStatus back into the engine. The tests play the part of Windows: they carry out the operations and complete them in a scrambled order , with errors and cancellation. cpp enum class OpKind { Read, Write }; struct Op { OpKind kind; std::uint32_t id; std::uint64_t offset; std::uint32_t length; std::string data; }; struct Completion { std::uint32_t id; std::uint32_t error; std::string data; }; constexpr std::uint32_t ERROR_HANDLE_EOF = 38, ERROR_OPERATION_ABORTED = 995; class CopyEngine { public: CopyEngine(std::uint64_t fileSize, std::uint32_t chunkSize, int maxOutstanding); std::vector<Op start(); std::vector<Op onCompletion(const Completion& c); std::vector<std::uint32_t cancel(); bool finished() const; bool failed() const; bool cancelled() const; std::uint32_t error() const; std::uint64_t bytesWritten() const; int outstanding() const; }; Chunks. The file is copied in chunks of chunkSize bytes at offsets 0, chunkSize , 2 × chunkSize ...; the last chunk is shorter if the size is not a multiple. An empty file needs no operations and is finished at once. Operations. Every operation the engine asks for gets the next id, starting at 1. A read asks for length bytes at offset (its data is empty); a write gives the data to write at offset (its length is the data's size). At most maxOutstanding operations, reads and writes together, are ever in flight: started and not yet completed. - start returns the first reads, in offset order, as many as the limit allows. - onCompletion receives the completion of an operation in flight (an unknown id throws std::invalid_argument ), removes it from the in-flight set, and returns the operations to start next: - A successful read ( error 0) must carry exactly the bytes asked for; then the engine returns a write of those bytes at the same offset. If it carries fewer or more (the file changed under us), the copy fails with ERROR_HANDLE_EOF . - A successful write adds its bytes to bytesWritten , and the engine starts the next read , if any chunks are left and the limit allows. - A completion with an error makes the copy fail with that error (the first error is kept), unless the copy was cancelled and the error is ERROR_OPERATION_ABORTED . - Once failed or cancelled, the engine starts nothing new; it only takes in the remaining completions. - cancel stops the copy and returns the ids of every operation in flight, in ascending order, for the program to pass to CancelIoEx . - finished is true when every byte has been written, nothing is in flight, and the copy neither failed nor was cancelled.

title: Cheat Sheet - Win32
body: The skeleton cpp-norun define WIN32_LEAN_AND_MEAN define NOMINMAX include <windows.h LRESULT CALLBACK WndProc(HWND hwnd, UINT msg, WPARAM wParam, LPARAM lParam) { switch (msg) { case WM_CREATE: / create controls / return 0; case WM_SIZE: / layout(LOWORD(lParam), HIWORD(lParam)) / return 0; case WM_PAINT: { PAINTSTRUCT ps; HDC dc = BeginPaint(hwnd, &ps); / draw / EndPaint(hwnd, &ps); return 0; } case WM_CLOSE: / ask to save; then / DestroyWindow(hwnd); return 0; case WM_DESTROY: PostQuitMessage(0); return 0; } return DefWindowProcW(hwnd, msg, wParam, lParam); } int WINAPI wWinMain(HINSTANCE inst, HINSTANCE, PWSTR, int show) { WNDCLASSEXW wc{ sizeof(wc) }; wc.lpfnWndProc = WndProc; wc.hInstance = inst; wc.lpszClassName = L"Main"; wc.hCursor = LoadCursorW(nullptr, IDC_ARROW); wc.hbrBackground = reinterpret_cast<HBRUSH (COLOR_WINDOW + 1); RegisterClassExW(&wc); HWND hwnd = CreateWindowExW(0, L"Main", L"Title", WS_OVERLAPPEDWINDOW, CW_USEDEFAULT, CW_USEDEFAULT, 800, 500, nullptr, nullptr, inst, nullptr); ShowWindow(hwnd, show); MSG m; while (GetMessageW(&m, nullptr, 0, 0) 0) { TranslateMessage(&m); DispatchMessageW(&m); } return static_cast<int (m.wParam); } Messages Message wParam / lParam --- --- WM_SIZE type / LOWORD width, HIWORD height WM_LBUTTONDOWN , WM_MOUSEMOVE MK_ flags / GET_X_LPARAM , GET_Y_LPARAM (signed) WM_MOUSEWHEEL GET_WHEEL_DELTA_WPARAM (120 per notch) / screen position WM_KEYDOWN , WM_KEYUP virtual key / repeat count, scan code, bit 30 = was down WM_CHAR UTF-16 unit / as for keys WM_COMMAND LOWORD id, HIWORD code (0 menu, 1 accelerator, else notification) / control WM_NOTIFY id / NMHDR WM_TIMER timer id / callback WM_DPICHANGED HIWORD new DPI / suggested RECT WM_APP + n your own messages PostMessageW queues and returns; SendMessageW calls and waits.
